# [Complete Works of the Minor Fathers]

[Col. I]

# Preface to the Following Two Volumes

[Col. I] I. Before we discuss Cyprian, at least, just as we previously discussed Tertullian, and before we present—manfully, in proportion to our abilities—contributions drawn more from others than from ourselves, both on his authority and use and on the Cyprianic literary annals, it is fitting to explain briefly what this third and fourth volume contribute to this *New Library of the Ancient Fathers*: which Fathers we have brought forward and with what studies by more recent interpreters or editors we have adorned them.

## Article I. Catalogue of Authors

II. I should like you to recognize, from the very names themselves, that this Library—which we have also chosen to entitle, such as it is, a *Course of Patrology*—has a twofold subject matter. On the one side are the testimonies of the ancients; on the other, the commentaries of modern scholars. Thus the ancient age produced what the hand of the present age stores away; antiquity supplied the words to which the diversity of modern teachers has added explanations. The former, therefore, belong to the *Library*; the latter to the *Course*, if there is any force in that term.

III. Some of the lesser Fathers of the third century appear in this volume. At their head proceed the holy martyrs Felicity and Perpetua, a noble pair of women, both worthy to serve as leaders of their contemporary Fathers. There follows a double triumvirate of authors: namely, three Roman pontiffs—Cornelius, Lucius, and Stephen—and three advocates of the Carthaginian bar, champions of the same Christian cause—Minucius, Octavius, and Caecilius, happily defeated, who is also believed to have won over Cyprian. After them come several authors of unknown name, whose works, humbly concealed in the Christian manner, deserve to be brought to light. Then comes Novatian, the first standard-bearer of the schismatics and an antipope; I should almost wish to count Firmilian, bishop of Caesarea, among them as well, were it not that the letter in which Stephen, a holy pontiff and martyr, is abusively called Antichrist appears to be falsely attributed to him.

Finally, in the other volume, St. Cyprian, the wholly upright bishop of Carthage, appears alone, yet by the bulk of his works scarcely unequal to all the others together.

IV. Once these teachings of the ancient Fathers have been set forth, the companies of modern interpreters follow in close array. Some gather the corrupt readings of manuscripts driven here and there by the storms of time; they untie bundles, scrape parchments, and, so to speak, disembowel palimpsests. Others scrutinize the readings they have received, comparing and elucidating ancient readings by modern ones, doubtful by certain, and like by like. [Col. II]

V. Would you like at least a foretaste of the names of the principal interpreters, those who rank above the rest and sit, as it were, as masters of the various commentators, and who therefore, above all others, are brought into this arena of the whole patristic enterprise?

When the Acts of the holy African Martyrs first present themselves for reading, a twofold kind of commentators and commentary rises to meet them, as is generally the case. One is literal: that of Dom Théodore Ruinart, Lukas Holste, and Father Poussines, who elucidate, correct, and confirm the very text of the Acts word for word. The other is discursive, as in the dispute between Basnage and the most eminent Cardinal Orsi of the Holy Roman Church over the orthodoxy of the holy Martyrs—and certainly not an inconclusive contest. It is regrettable only that the most eminent defender of the holy Martyrs, although he vindicated their faith invincibly, nevertheless conceded that the compiler of these Acts was a Montanist. This opinion, however, is deservedly and vigorously opposed in their prefaces by the already praised Ruinart and the most learned Gallandi. In light of this, I should like you to correct the somewhat harsher statements made in the first volume of this Library by Johann August Nösselt in a dissertation otherwise excellent and indeed very important, which we included among the prolegomena to Tertullian.

VI. Among the most ancient ruins of the third or perhaps even the second century, a certain headless fragment of some value concerning the Canon of Holy Scripture remained hidden for a very long time. At last, in the middle of the last century, the distinguished Muratori was the first to bring it to light. Yet he seemed to hide and bury it once again, amid innumerable monuments of a much later age and of an altogether different character, in that great mass of his *Italian Antiquities of the Middle Ages*.

We gratefully received this little work with both hands, although it is missing its beginning, born of an unknown father, published at an uncertain date, and disfigured by the repulsive grime of corruptions. We have presented Johann Kirchhofer’s cleaner and more recent recension; and we have gladly brought forward all the scholars we found discussing it, namely Dr. Freindaller, Eberhard Stosch, and above all Martin Joseph Routh, the illustrious president of Magdalen College, Oxford, to whom we owe many felicitous restorations and a continuous commentary on the same subject.

[Col. III] VII. In passing on to Minucius Felix’s *Octavius*, however, there is a wider field—or rather, a veritable battle line of extremely fierce combatants. One text preserved in a single manuscript is the sole cause of the contest. It is scarcely credible in what astonishing ways they have dared to distort this single text, how many divergent readings they have drawn from one source, how many discordant meanings they have forced upon the same words, and how thoroughly they have entangled everything, high and low, with empty inventions and foolish conjectures.

We considered it our foremost duty to present this unique text, on the basis of a new and most diligent examination of the sole manuscript, so completely pure and unadulterated that nothing would be added and nothing removed, and not even the scribes’ manifest errors would be omitted; scarcely more than a very few words have been inserted in brackets in order to produce some intelligible sense. We therefore regarded it as a most sacred obligation to provide a true and genuine likeness of the single manuscript, portrayed to the life in its original appearance.

Once the integrity of this sovereign text has been established—not to say that the truth of the first edition has thereby been restored—the *Octavius*, like the other works, is furnished with two kinds of explanation and closely flanked on both sides by two battalions of commentators. Some contend over the letter of the text like grammarians; among them we are pleased to commend Heraldus, Wowerius, Gronovius, Grüner, Elmenhorst, Rigault, Heumann, Cellarius, Mencke, Davies, Ouzel, Wopkens, Lindner, Gallandi, Meursius, Perizonius, and others.

The commentary on this little book would have grown beyond all measure had the more loquacious products of itching interpreters not been diligently rejected, had innumerable notes even by the best commentators not been omitted, and had the extravagance of superabundant annotation not been cut down. Yet those selected remnants still overflow more than enough for you, dear reader, to discover for yourself over what rough terrain the journey must be worn down if a variorum commentary is to proceed in an uninterrupted course all the way to the end—more than enough, I say, for you to recognize in particular how far the unbridled, chattering passion of scholars from beyond the Rhine can flaunt and riot.

VIII. Accordingly, lest our ears ring too loudly from this insane tumult of literal commentators, we have taken care, either in the preliminary materials or at the very end of this little book, to introduce other men of better substance, who apply themselves energetically to constructing a general criticism of the *Octavius*. Thus, at the very threshold, you have Dom Gottfried Lumper’s treatment of the life, eloquence, and writings of Marcus Minucius the apologist, arranging everything previously said on the subject, and arranging it exceedingly well. Likewise, at the outset it was fitting to append François Baudouin’s principal dissertation, in which he was the first to restore the *Octavius* to its true author.

To it we have attached the excellent letter of Johann August Ernesti, appended to Lindner’s first edition—commendable especially in a man belonging to the herd of pseudo-Reformers. Taking his occasion from the exquisite elegance of the *Octavius*, Ernesti discusses at length and with distinction the eloquence both of the ancient Fathers and of more recent writers, and especially that of St. Bernard.

Finally, this rather lengthy preliminary section is closed by Gottlieb Lindner’s introductory inquiry in the form of an analytical compendium, [Col. IV] which presents the entire argument of the Minucian Dialogue comprehended within a single synoptic and dialectical overview.

This is the road laid out to the *Octavius*. Once the entire work has been traversed in an uninterrupted course, despite the tedium of a captious commentary, we have included, by way of refreshment for the mind, Lukas Holste’s charming letter to Cardinal Francesco Barberini concerning the spits of the Ephesian Diana mentioned in the *Octavius*. We did so all the more gladly because this little dissertation is, quite undeservedly, entirely absent from the recent collection of that most learned man’s letters published at Paris by Boissonade.

The procession of commentators on this single little book, which begins with Dom Lumper, is completed by a monk of the same order, Dom Nicolas Le Nourry. With as much applause as we previously received his dissertation on Tertullian’s apologetic writings, so highly must this excellent work of an excellent man now be extolled: this most abundant harvest of ancient and modern learning poured into the *Octavius*; this anthology drawn from the best philosophers, poets, grammarians, and orators of every age and province. He has left nothing untouched, nothing undiscovered, and nothing still to be sought after his passage.

IX. Next comes the Chronicle composed by an anonymous author under Alexander Severus. It is therefore the first of all monuments of this kind, which were so frequent throughout the course of Christianity, and at least the most ancient in the Latin Church. This small ancient work enjoyed the signal distinction of being attributed to one of the greatest among the Fathers, namely St. Hippolytus, bishop of Ostia, and of being outlined and weighed by exact calculation by the most illustrious Francesco Bianchini in the dissertation we have published after Dom Lumper.

X. Thereafter, in chronological order, many letters of the confessors, whether Roman or Carthaginian, are mentioned in selections and their contents briefly indicated; the reader is referred below to the works of St. Cyprian for the letters themselves. For we adopted this principle from the outset: whenever, because of the connection of the subjects and the chronological sequence, certain smaller works had to be detached from a large collection, they should always be mentioned under their proper year and in their proper place, with their subject matter explained. Thus the complete collection from which they are taken—well known by its name, weight, and, so to speak, bearing and countenance—would neither be altered nor broken apart.

XI. Now, however, let the pontifical monuments of the century come forth into the light with the reverence, honor, and care owed to them. Let historical introductions drawn from the best sources go before them; let explicit prolegomena announce whence and amid what circumstances they arose; if some of them have been consumed by the devouring force of time and are missing, let a special notice give advance warning; let the most complete text of whatever has chanced to survive be revised according to the standard of the better edition; let variant readings be collected, compared, and examined with indefatigable labor; let the meaning be weighed by the judgments of all critics, restored or preserved by the conscientiousness of all scholars, and elucidated through the investigations of all interpreters.

Finally, let there be added whatever circulates among Catholics [Col. V] under such great names, lest, carried away excessively by the criticism of modern writers, we rashly cast the sacred gifts of antiquity into destruction, or perhaps trample pearls merely covered for a time with muddy dust.

Thus, for the years of the holy Cornelius, Lucius, and Stephen, pontiffs and martyrs, we have first interwoven a summary chronicle of their deeds and writings, drawn from ancient and modern authors: on the one side from Jerome, Anastasius, the *Synodical Book*, and Syncellus; on the other from Baronius, Binius, Fabricius, Pagi, Labbe, Tillemont, Coustant, Cellerier, Lumper, Gallandi, and the Bollandists. We then give the text of the letters according to the best recensions and, above all, adopt in its entirety the excellent edition of Dom Coustant.

Next, for a complete elucidation of the text, we have made our own the labors of all the interpreters: Pamelius, Labbe, Hardouin, Coustant, Valesius, and Baluze. Nor have we from time to time neglected selected notes from the best of the heterodox scholars, such as Fell, Reading, Routh, Goldhorn, and Schoenemann. With these Rigault is disgracefully coupled, so unworthy of the Catholic name that the English editors and other sectarians themselves rejected him and often branded him with a mark of censure.

As for the variant readings, we present all those found in the English editors, who were most diligent in collecting them, augmented by many others harvested here and there and adapted to our own version. Finally, there are added in appendices letters less certainly attributable to the same pontiffs, decrees of doubtful authenticity, and the very Decretal letters themselves, so long celebrated throughout the learned world that, for that reason alone, it would be wrong not to give them a place in this most complete collection of ours.

Lastly, because councils celebrated under the supreme pontiffs have generally been regarded as their works, written under Peter’s inspiration and preserved and authenticated by their keys—or have been adorned by certain eminent scholars—as was the case with the eight Councils of Carthage and the two Roman Councils held under Sts. Cornelius and Stephen, we therefore considered it a matter of conscience to read through them in passing. We have received and transmitted them only from Mansi’s most recent collection or from Routh’s excellent special recension among his *Sacred Remains*.

XII. Among the greatest questions concerning Christianity debated in this third century, none was more notable and none aroused greater disturbances throughout the whole Church than the most celebrated dispute concerning the baptism of heretics. In order that this controversy might be brought into full light, and that all arguments on either side might be weighed and reconsidered, we have neglected no monument of any value, whether among the writings of the ancients or among the excursuses of modern scholars, produced by that great controversy in which, amid no small disturbance, East and West, the churches of Italy and Africa, pontiffs and martyrs, became inflamed with opposing enthusiasms.

It therefore seemed proper to distribute the records of this dispute into two classes. The first comprises the principal ancient acts and writings dealing with the case. At their head, by right of pontifical preeminence, stand the decretal pronouncements of St. Stephen, which we find scattered through the letters of St. Cyprian [Col. VI] and Firmilian and which, after being reverently received in both East and West, finally brought the controversy to an end.

After these follows the Roman Council celebrated at that time with great authority by St. Stephen himself. It was indeed fitting that Peter’s voice should be heard before the dissensions of the Africans and Easterners were presented. These flow in full stream through the councils, the letters of Cyprian and Firmilian, and certain anonymous books of the ancients.

Since a new recension of the seven Councils of Carthage, adorned with selected notes by Baluze, Fell, Coustant, Valesius, and the editor, has recently been published at Oxford by Joseph Martin Routh, head of Magdalen College, in a collection rare enough to obtain, we have had the whole of it transferred intact to our own use.

We have drawn the letters written on this subject from three widely different sources: first, a fragment of only one letter by “the blessed” (*τοῦ μακαρίου*) Dionysius of Alexandria to Pope Stephen, excerpted from Eusebius; next, four letters of Cyprian—to Magnus, Quintus, Jubaianus, and Pompeianus; and finally one letter, by no means least in celebrity, from Firmilian, bishop of Caesarea, to Cyprian against St. Stephen.

I shall not deny that, in collecting these, it was our intention not only to gather matters treating the same subject into one place, but also to set apart, under a single critical eye, monuments branded with the same charge of spuriousness (*νοθείας*). Whether justly or unjustly, I shall not argue. Yet I think those documents are charged with a sufficiently serious offense, since they are removed from the genuine letters of St. Cyprian and selected for this place as the evidentiary materials of a great lawsuit still pending between theologians and philologists.

However that may be, there are appended to them, in order to confirm the true position proposed at the outset—or at least at the end—two short works without an author’s name but distinguished by excellent teaching that all should accept. With these concludes the series of ancient monuments we have assembled to shed light upon this controversy.

XIII. Many modern scholars have written much on the same dispute; and although they used the same testimonies of the ancients, some arrived at one opinion and others at another. Reviewing only the principal treatments, we have joined to the ancients those that seemed to us above all to be of the greatest value. No one will resent our regarding the most distinguished Louis Thomassin and Dom Coustant as virtually ancient authors.

Nor, unless I am mistaken, will experts deem the final two dissertations worthy of much less praise. They bring this whole array of ancient and modern witnesses to an excellent conclusion.

Yet these preliminary remarks, although prolonged in a style more expansive than I had expected, cannot truly be completed without adding much more concerning the works of St. Cyprian contained in this and the other volume. We have nevertheless thought it better to set these matters out individually in the following articles or to reserve them for the Literary Annals a little further below.

# Article II. On the Authority of St. Cyprian

I. Whatever I previously alleged in the first volume concerning the true authority and proper use of Tertullian, I should venture to ascribe likewise to St. Cyprian, with the necessary changes. Nevertheless, far be it from me in every possible respect to appear to compare a Catholic and holy teacher with a contumacious and obstinate heretic; a lawful and most devout bishop with a proud and unruly presbyter; an outstanding defender of the Church’s unity with a perverse and frenzied Montanist; a martyr with a heresiarch; a shepherd with a wolf.

Although the one is as distant from the other as the whole span of heaven, there are nevertheless certain relationships between them, not only in origin, country, and birth, but also in genius, learning, and apologetic, dogmatic, or exhortatory exposition. Let someone else take care to explain these in detail elsewhere.

Yet it has seemed astonishing to us that, although the moderns ought gladly to have enlisted Tertullian on their side and rejected Cyprian, they have in fact rejected the former the more fiercely in proportion as they have adhered more eagerly to the latter. The name of the heretic Tertullian has always been unfortunate and ill-omened among heretics, but great and commended by the highest authorities among Catholics.

Thus Georg Rosenmüller writes the following about Tertullian:

> “As this man was the foremost author in ecclesiastical Latin, so too in his books are found the first seeds of the African and Latin theology that brought so many evils upon the Church and religion. For although he defected to the Montanists, this nevertheless detracted little from his authority among Catholics. Indeed, he wrote the greatest part of his works while in the communion of Catholics; and the Montanism that he followed disturbed only ecclesiastical discipline and did not violate the faith. Furthermore, Cyprian, who flourished in the ancient Church with a great reputation for learning and orthodoxy, was a constant imitator of Tertullian and admired him so greatly that he habitually called him ‘the Master’ preeminently (*κατ’ ἐξοχήν*).”  
> [Note: [Col. VII] *Histor. Interpret. libror. SS. in Ecclesia christ.*, Hildburghausen, 1798, part II, p. 2.]

If you disregard the errors scattered here and there in these words, you will readily observe that they diminish Tertullian only to the same degree that they exalt Cyprian.

II. Whence came praise unworthy of so great a man? Whence this baleful commendation? From his conflict with the pontiff Stephen. Hence the concentrated interest of modern scholars in him and the great labors they expended; hence that splendid edition of his works published at Oxford; hence the indefatigable efforts of Fell, Pearson, Dodwell, Rigault, Routh, Marshall, Poole, and Matthies, by which all the evidence in the Cyprianic question was weighed, approved or rejected—not without inequitable partiality—and settled by definitive judgment.

This burden therefore falls upon every Catholic editor of St. Cyprian: once the grounds upon which his name is diminished among the moderns have been removed, his true authority should increase among the sons of the Church in the same measure as it seems to be lowered among outsiders. We have accordingly concluded that our whole inquiry into Cyprian’s authority must be concentrated upon explaining his own judgment regarding pontifical preeminence.

III. Everyone accepts that any writer must be judged not from one or another isolated word in his discourse, but from the continuous tenor of his teaching; not from impromptu statements suddenly elicited in correspondence by an abrupt disturbance of affairs, but from a settled opinion treated seriously; not from a position defended piecemeal and subsequently changed, but from a firm, decisive, and defined judgment.

Whoever examines Cyprian’s works with these principles in view will be so far from regarding the holy bishop as an opponent of the Roman See that he will instead discover him among the foremost defenders of Roman privileges and, I would almost say, as the standard-bearer of the Roman theologians.

IV. For these—to show that I am not speaking merely by allusion—are the very doctrines that shine everywhere like luminaries in the writings of the holy Doctor:

1. The Church, outside which no one can live, is one.
2. This one Church is catholic, that is, diffused throughout the whole world.
3. This one and catholic Church is, moreover, Roman: founded upon Peter, neither distinct from the holy Roman See nor different from the supreme pontiff.
4. This one catholic and Roman Church is, in Cyprian’s understanding, the most certain rule of faith, neither stained nor ever to be stained by any blemish of error.

V. I should like you to hear Cyprian himself speak without delay:

### 1. On the Unity of the Church

In the book bearing that title, Cyprian himself testifies that he poured into it, so far as he was able, his entire understanding of the Church:

> “Our modest ability,” he says, “has expressed the unity of the Catholic Church as fully as it could.”

“In that work,” says the deacon Pontius, the most trustworthy witness to his master’s life and mind, “he taught truth to heretics, unity to schismatics, and peace to the sons of God.”

[Note: [Col. VIII] Epistle LI, vol. IV, col. 345: This book was written on the occasion of the Novatian schism and the faction of Felicissimus. Dupin, *Bibliothèque des auteurs*, vol. I, p. 260, Latin ed.: “This book was composed to put an end to the Novatian schism.” Fell, p. 104, Bremen ed. “I am not far,” says Rollin, *Bibliotheca Sanctorum Patrum*, vol. III, p. 192, “from believing that this little book *On the Unity of the Church* is the address Cyprian delivered to the bishops and clergy assembled to end the Novatian schism. The following words from the same treatise give considerable support to this conjecture: ‘This unity we must firmly maintain and vindicate, especially we bishops who preside in the Church, so that we may also prove the episcopate itself to be one and undivided.’” Cf. vol. IV, col. 501.]

From this little book:

1. “In the *Song of Songs*, the Holy Spirit, speaking in the person of the Lord, designates the Church as one and says (Song 6:9): ‘One is my dove, my perfect one; she is the only one of her mother, the chosen one of her who bore her.’”  
   [Note: [Col. VIII] Book *On the Unity of the Church*, vol. IV, col. 500.]

2. “The blessed apostle Paul teaches the same thing and reveals the mystery of unity, saying (Eph. 4:4–6): ‘One body and one spirit, one hope of your calling; one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God.’”  
   [Note: [Col. VIII] Ibid., col. 501.]

3. “This unity we must firmly maintain and vindicate, especially we bishops who preside in the Church, so that we may also prove the episcopate itself to be one [Col. IX] and undivided.”  
   [Note: [Col. IX] Book *On the Unity of the Church*, vol. IV, col. 501.]

4. “Just as the sun has many rays but one light; and a tree many branches but one strength founded upon its tenacious root; and although many streams flow from a single spring . . . unity is nevertheless preserved in the source . . . so too the Church of the Lord. . . .”  
   [Note: [Col. IX] Ibid., col. 502.]

5. “The bride of Christ cannot be adulterated. . . . She knows one house; with chaste modesty she guards the sanctity of one bridal chamber. . . .”  
   [Note: [Col. IX] Book, cols. 502–503.]

6. “She is one, outside whom no one escapes safely, any more than outside Noah’s ark; he can no longer have God as Father who does not have the Church as mother.”  
   [Note: [Col. IX] Ibid., col. 503.]

   And elsewhere:

   > “Nor can any assurance of life or salvation remain for them if they refuse obedience to the bishops and priests. . . . For they cannot live outside, since the house of God is one and no one can have salvation except in the Church.”  
   > [Note: [Col. IX] Epistle LXII, cols. 370–371.]

7. “The Lord says (John 10:30): ‘I and the Father are one.’ And again it is written of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit (1 John 5:7): ‘And these three are one.’ Does anyone believe that this unity . . . can be torn apart in the Church . . .? He who does not maintain this unity does not maintain the law of God; he does not maintain the faith of the Father and the Son; he does not maintain life and salvation.”  
   [Note: [Col. IX] Book *On the Unity of the Church*, vol. IV, col. 504.]

8. “This mystery of unity . . . is revealed when, in the Gospel, the tunic of the Lord Jesus Christ is not divided at all or torn. . . . It reveals the inseparable, joined, and connected concord of our people, we who have put on Christ, clinging together. . . .”  
   [Note: [Col. IX] Book *On the Unity of the Church*, vol. IV, col. 504.]

9. “He himself admonishes and teaches in his Gospel, saying (John 10:16): ‘And there shall be one flock and one shepherd.’”  
   [Note: [Col. IX] Ibid., col. 505.]

10. Let these words of devout prayer serve as the conclusion:

   > “I certainly desire, beloved brethren, and equally counsel and urge, that, if it can be done, none of the brethren should perish, and that the mother may joyfully enclose within her bosom the one body of a people united in agreement. . . . There is one God and one Christ, and his Church is one, and the faith one, and the people one, joined by the cement of concord into the solid [unity] of the body.”  
   > [Note: [Col. IX] Ibid., col. 317.]

VI. ### 2. On the Church as One and Catholic

Cyprian has the following statements in the same book and elsewhere; they have just been cited in excerpts:

> “The Church is one, which by the increase of fruitfulness extends ever more widely into a multitude. . . . Just as the sun has many rays but one light; and a tree many branches but one strength founded upon its tenacious root; and although many streams flow from a single spring, the number may appear widely dispersed by the abundance of the overflowing supply, yet unity is preserved in the source. . . . So too the Church of the Lord, suffused with light, extends her rays throughout the whole world; yet it is one light that is diffused everywhere, and the unity of the body is not divided. By her fruitful abundance she extends her branches over the whole earth and spreads her freely flowing streams ever more widely.”  
> [Note: [Col. IX] Ibid., cols. 501–502.]

And:

> “The universal Church, joined with us throughout the whole [Col. X] world by the bond of unity. . . . Hence you ought to know . . . that those flatter themselves in vain who, having no peace with the priests of God, steal in and secretly believe that they are in communion with certain persons, since the Church, which is catholic and one, has not been torn or divided but is certainly connected and joined together by the cement of bishops who adhere to one another.”  
> [Note: [Col. X] Epistle LXIX, vol. IV, col. 406.]

VII. These and many other statements, clearer than the noonday sun, appear to be clouded by the words that follow and that are more than once attached to the preceding passages:

> “You ought to know that the bishop is in the Church and the Church in the bishop.”  
> [Note: [Col. X] Ibid., loc. cit.]

From this, many have inferred that Cyprian was unfamiliar with the genuine conception of catholic unity. Indeed, they have attributed to him the view—which even now many Protestants would admit in good faith—that the Church’s external unity gradually grew almost imperceptibly: that the individual churches, which at first flourished and were united solely by the inward unity of faith and charity, placed the entire force and bond of catholic communion each in its own bishop; and that, stirred by the influence of this inward power, they were moved to unite other churches to themselves by the same bond.

Thus, they claim, the churches were separate at first and gradually transformed themselves into one; as the centuries passed, they assimilated themselves to one another; they converged from plurality into unity, yet without entirely losing the indefeasible rights of their original freedom and of their individual communities.

The whole crux of this most serious Cyprianic controversy turns upon what Cyprian thought concerning the episcopate; and it is clear that he derived this from the conception of the apostolate that he had formed for himself. Both matters must therefore be investigated briefly. Cyprian had this deeply rooted preconception in his mind: that the Apostles, upon whom the Church rested and was built, were by no means separated from one another, each separately possessing his own rights and authority from the one Christ; rather, all and each were fused into one and the same body, agreeing from the same will, in the same power, toward one end; and that the one Peter was the head, center of unity, and summit of the entire apostolic body. There was therefore not merely one head of the apostolic college, but also one apostolic person. Hence, amid the very turmoil over rebaptism, Cyprian wrote these words to Jubaianus:

> “First to Peter, upon whom he built the Church, and from whom he established and manifested the origin of unity, the Lord gave this power: that what he loosed on earth should be loosed in heaven. And after the resurrection he also speaks to the Apostles, saying: ‘As he sent me,’ etc. [Note: [Col. X] Epistle LXXIII, no. 7, vol. III, col. 1114.] . . . The Lord cries out that whoever thirsts should come . . . to the Church, which is one and was founded by the Lord’s voice upon the one man who also received its keys. [Note: [Col. X] Epistle LXXIII, no. 11, vol. III, col. 1116.] There is one Holy Spirit, and one Church, founded by Christ the Lord upon Peter as the origin and principle of unity. [Note: [Col. X] Epistle LXX, no. 3.]”

Hence, to repeat the passage already quoted:

> “In order to manifest unity, he established one chair, and by his authority arranged that the origin of that same unity should begin from one. Certainly the other Apostles were what Peter was, endowed with an equal partnership in honor and authority; but the beginning proceeds from unity, and primacy is given to Peter, so that the one Church of Christ and the one chair may be shown. And all are shepherds, yet one flock is shown, which is fed by all the Apostles with unanimous agreement, so that the Church of Christ may be shown to be one. [Note: [Col. XI] Book *On the Unity of the Church*, col. 501.]”

And, a few words later:

> “We must firmly maintain and vindicate this unity, especially we bishops who preside in the Church, so that we may also prove that the episcopate itself is one and undivided. . . . The episcopate is one, a share of which is held in its entirety by each individual bishop. [Note: [Col. XI] Ibid., loc. cit.]”

This, then, is Cyprian’s true and genuine doctrine concerning both the Apostles and the bishops: as the apostolate was one in Peter, so too the episcopate is one; as there was one chair among the many Apostles, so among the many shepherds there is one flock, one Church; as in the apostolic college there was one mouth and one head, Peter, so the episcopate is one person, possessed in its entirety by each individual. Hence the bishop is in the Church and the Church in the bishop. Hence the beginning proceeds from unity, rather than gradually coalescing from plurality into one. We ourselves were hewn from the Rock; we did not bring that Rock together into our midst. It is not the final stone brought by the builders, but the stone upon which the whole structure is laid and rises. It is not merely the topmost stone at the final summit, but also the cornerstone and foundation stone. The one Church did not arise from many churches; rather, many churches arose from the one. Thus the order of things and their true principle are turned completely upside down in that successive and adventitious unification of Christianity into one body which, as we said above, has been fabricated from Cyprian.

## VIII. 3rd. This One and Catholic Church Is, Furthermore, Roman, Founded upon Peter, Neither Distinct from the Apostolic See nor Different from the Supreme Pontiff

You may perhaps be troubled by our earlier confident assertion that Cyprian was the standard-bearer of Roman theologians. Indeed, a recent anonymous author among the pseudo-Reformed of Germany, though of a very different mind, judged that St. Cyprian was in fact the first to introduce that dogma: “There is one Church, and outside it there is no salvation.” [Note: [Col. XI] *Neither the Christian Religion nor the Roman . . . Catholic Church Is the Only One That Brings Salvation*. Leipzig and Frankfurt, 1791.] Yet before him no one—not even Irenaeus excepted—commended more splendidly that very “chair of Peter, the principal Church, from which sacerdotal unity arose [Note: [Col. XI] Epistle LV, otherwise XII to Cornelius, vol. III, cols. 818–821.], the root and mother of the Catholic Church. [Note: [Col. XI] Epistle XLV, otherwise IV to Cornelius, vol. II, col. 710.]”

Before him no one—not even Tertullian excepted—extolled with greater praise “the supreme priest, the bishop of bishops”: whether Cornelius, “made bishop by the judgment of God and of his Christ, when the place of Fabian—that is, when the place of Peter and the rank of the sacerdotal chair—was vacant [Note: [Col. XI] Epistle LII, otherwise X to Cornelius, vol. III, cols. 771–772]”; or Stephen himself, “who ought to send the fullest letters to his fellow bishops established in [Col. XII] Gaul, and whom it does not become to allow anyone to mock the bishops and pass judgment on the majesty and dignity of the Church. [Note: [Col. XII] Epistle LXVII, to Stephen, vol. III, col. 993.]”

Neither before nor after him did anyone assail more sharply and vehemently those who departed from the Roman Church, as in the case of Novatian:

> “Maddened by the frenzy of discord, he rends the Church, destroys the faith, disturbs peace, scatters charity, and profanes the sacrament. He bears arms against the Church and fights against God’s ordinance. An enemy of the altar, a rebel against Christ’s sacrifice, faithless under the guise of faith, sacrilegious under the guise of religion, a disobedient servant, an impious son, a hostile brother—despising the bishops and abandoning the priests of God, he dares to establish another altar, to offer another prayer with unlawful words, and to profane the truth of the Lord’s sacrifice through false sacrifices. [Note: [Col. XII] Passim in the book *On Unity*, no. 8 ff.] What an offense it is, which not even the baptism of blood can wash away! What a crime, which martyrdom cannot expiate! [Note: [Col. XII] *On the Lord’s Prayer*, vol. IV.] An inexpiable fault! That stain is not washed away even by blood. [Note: [Col. XII] Book *On the Unity of the Church*.] Though they burn in flames, though handed over to the fires or cast to the beasts, though they lay down their lives, that will not be the crown of faith but the punishment of faithlessness; not a glorious end, but destruction born of despair. Such a man can be killed; he cannot be crowned. [Note: [Col. XII] Ibid., col. 511.]”

## IX

What more need be said? Much indeed remains—namely, the matters we have not yet touched, those propositions we boldly proposed should be established from Cyprian: that in his mind there was no distinction between the one Catholic Church and the Roman Church, between the source of the episcopate and the Apostolic See, between Peter and Christ sitting and teaching upon earth, between Peter and his see and his successors—in a word, between Peter and Peter.

Rather, attend and hear how one who communicates with Cornelius thereby communicates with the Catholic Church:

> “You also wrote,” he says, “that I should transmit a copy of the same letter to our colleague Cornelius, so that, all anxiety laid aside, he might now know that you communicate with him—that is, with the Catholic Church. [Note: [Col. XII] Epistle LII, otherwise X to Cornelius, vol. III, col. 768.]”

Hear and attend how one “opposes and resists the Church”—these are his own words—“who abandons the chair of Peter, upon whom the Church was founded; whoever he may be, let him no longer trust that he is in the Church. [Note: [Col. XII] Book *On the Unity of the Church*, vol. IV, col. 500.]”

Hear that the whole principle and constitution of the Church, as it was founded by Christ, is placed in Peter and his successors. Nor does he say this incidentally or hastily, but frequently, both in his letters and in his special book *On the Unity of the Church*:

> “The Lord speaks to Peter: ‘I say to you,’ he says, ‘that you are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. . . .’ And again, after his resurrection, he says to the same man: ‘Feed my sheep.’ Upon that one man he builds his Church, and to him he entrusts [Col. XIII] his sheep to be fed. And although after his resurrection he grants equal authority to all the Apostles and says, ‘As the Father sent me, so I send you . . .,’ nevertheless, in order to manifest unity, he established one chair, and by his authority arranged that the origin of that same unity should begin from one. The other Apostles were what Peter was, endowed with an equal partnership both in honor and authority; but the beginning proceeds from unity, and primacy is given to Peter, so that the one Church of Christ and the one chair may be shown. [Note: [Col. XIII] Book *On the Unity of the Church*, vol. IV, col. 500.]”

Amid the very turmoil over rebaptism, as we have just said, he writes these words to Jubaianus:

> “First to Peter, upon whom he built the Church, and from whom he established and manifested the origin of unity, the Lord gave this power: that what he loosed on earth should be loosed in heaven. [Note: [Col. XIII] Epistle LXXIII, vol. III, col. 1114.] The Lord cries out that whoever thirsts should come and drink from the rivers of living water that flowed from his belly. To whom is the thirsty man to come? To the heretics . . . or to the Church, which is one and was founded by the Lord’s voice upon the one man who also received its keys? This is the one Church that holds and possesses all the authority of her bridegroom and Lord. [Note: [Col. XIII] Epistle LXXIII, vol. III, col. 1116.]”

He solemnly established these same things in the addresses and decrees of the Carthaginian synods—even at the risk of condemning himself—when he said:

> “There is one Holy Spirit, and one Church, founded by Christ the Lord upon Peter as the origin and principle of unity. [Note: [Col. XIII] Council of Carthage under Cyprian V, *On Baptism* II–III, col. 1043.]”

## X

Those who defected from the Roman faith left no stone unturned in their effort to disperse this mass of testimony. Some, gnawing at the words as though with an envious tooth, loudly boast that certain expressions are missing from certain manuscripts. But what does it matter if one or two words have fallen out of these passages, provided the rest stand? And they do stand—indeed, even more passages stand; they stand unconquered and inescapable.

Others distort the meaning and, treating Peter as a shadowy symbol fit only for derision, find in him nothing but an empty type of any bishop whatever, or an almost vanishing image of the whole episcopate, of which not even a faint shadow passed on to his successors.

Others—especially among our own Gallicans—distinguishing by a certain subtler perception the See from the one seated upon it, lavishly attribute to the See whatever is holy, great, and primary, while granting to the Pontiffs who occupy it weakness, impotence, and error. They maintain that venerable antiquity, and Cyprian above all, fully embraced, cherished, and taught these quibbles of scholastics itching for distinctions.

Yet let the bishop and martyr himself be our witness, for he plainly affirms:

1. that Christ founded the unity of faith and Catholic communion upon Peter;
2. that Cornelius, Lucius, and Stephen succeeded to Peter’s place by a legitimate and most complete right;
3. that one who communicates with them by name—and not merely with their See, vainly apprehended in the abstract—communicates with the Catholic Church;
4. but that one who has departed from those [Col. XIV] Pontiffs, not merely from the shadow of their see, has rent the Church, destroyed the faith, fought against the Church and God’s ordinance, become faithless under the guise of faith, and cannot be expiated even by the confession of that very faith through martyrdom.

Let this suffice to establish, as we intended, our proposition: namely, that in Cyprian’s mind the one Catholic Church was not separated from the Roman See.

## XI. 4th. This One, Catholic, Roman Church, According to Cyprian’s Mind, Is the True and Sole, Most Certain Rule of Faith, Neither Stained nor Capable of Being Stained by Any Taint of Error

Although these propositions may appear to many like prodigies, it is clear that they flow from what has already been said and are necessarily deduced from it. Will not the true and sole rule of faith be found where there is “the one and perfect dove of God”; where there are “one Lord, one faith, one God”; where “the episcopate is one and undivided”; where there is “the spotless bride of Christ, his one house, the sanctity of one bridal chamber”; where there is “one principle of life and salvation”—so much so that “outside her no one can live; no one has God as Father who does not have her as mother; nor does one hold God’s law or the faith of the Father and the Son if one does not hold her as the sole rule of faith”?

Is not that Church the one and true rule of faith, free from error, which, “flooded with the Lord’s light, extends its rays throughout the entire world, and is joined throughout the whole world by the bond of unity”? I mean that one, Catholic, Roman Church “from which sacerdotal unity arose, the root and mother of all churches,” from which no one departs without destroying the faith, rending the Church, disturbing peace, bearing arms against God, becoming a rebel against Christ and faithless under the guise of faith.

I mean that one and infallible rule of faith of the Roman Pontiffs, with whom to communicate is the same as communicating with the Catholic Church; with whom the whole structure of the Church, which the gates of hell shall not prevail against, is established as in the one Peter: namely, one chair, the origin of that same unity, and primacy given to Peter, so that the one Church of Christ and the one chair may be shown.

Indeed, this same infallible authority of the Roman Church is openly proclaimed not merely by way of deduction but in Cyprian’s own words. For behold these exceedingly clear and decisive words, addressed to Pope Cornelius concerning the Novatianists, which stop the mouth of every opponent:

> “After all this, moreover, with a pseudo-bishop established for themselves by heretics, they still dare to set sail and to carry letters from schismatics and profane men to the chair of Peter and to the principal Church, from which sacerdotal unity arose; nor do they consider that these are the Romans whose faith was praised by the Apostle’s proclamation, to whom faithlessness has not yet been able—indeed, can never at any time be able—to gain access. [Note: [Col. XIV] Epistle LV, otherwise XII to Cornelius, vol. III, col. 818.]”

Surely none of the theologians most devoted to the Roman See has spoken more copiously or splendidly concerning Roman infallibility.

## XII

We shall now refrain from adducing further testimonies. Yet we must very briefly meet the commonplace objection on everyone’s lips, arising from Cyprian’s disagreement with Stephen. [Col. XV]

We have no intention, nor is there any necessity, of defending St. Stephen as though he were accused of error or crime. There have been quite enough who vigorously undertook that task, as may be seen in this very work; quite enough who, vindicating the holy Martyr from the unjust abuse of Vossius, Blondel, Basnage, Antonio de Dominis, Launoy, Dupin, and others, firmly established that he not only did not fall into heresy but was the defender both of antiquity and of truth, and deviated neither from the true path of doctrine nor from the straight apostolic course.

## XIII

Cyprian and the other supporters of rebaptism require much more defense. Different writers have paved different paths toward this end. Most have found nothing but a disciplinary blemish in a matter not yet defined, nothing but an offense against a single Pontiff—while preserving the majesty of the supreme See—which could in some fashion be reconciled with Catholic communion and episcopal zeal.

But in defending Cyprian’s cause, acknowledging no advocate more expert or benevolent than Augustine, we judge that only the twofold argument he employed should be used. Either we must candidly confess with him that Cyprian erred and afterward corrected his less-than-sound opinion, and that the Father furthermore cleansed by the pruning-hook of martyrdom whatever in him required correction; or we must plainly affirm that Cyprian neither thought nor wrote the things that audacious interpolators of his letters attributed to him.

Indeed, let us hear the holy Doctor himself in his *Letter to Vincentius*:

> “That Cyprian held a different opinion concerning Baptism from the form and custom maintained by the Church is found not in canonical writings but in his own letters and those of a council; but that he corrected this opinion is not found. Nevertheless, it is not unreasonable to suppose of such a man that he did correct it, and that this fact was perhaps suppressed by those who were excessively delighted with that error and did not wish to be deprived of so great a patronage.
>
> “Although there are those who contend that Cyprian did not hold this opinion at all, but that it was fabricated under his name by presumptuous and mendacious men. For the integrity and knowledge of the letters of any single bishop, however illustrious, could not be preserved in the same manner as canonical Scripture is preserved through the writings of so many languages and through the order and succession of ecclesiastical observance. Yet even against canonical Scripture there have not been lacking those who fabricated many things under the names of the Apostles—vainly indeed, because Scripture is so commended, so celebrated, and so well known. Nevertheless, what the audacity of an impious undertaking can accomplish against writings not founded upon canonical authority is demonstrated by the fact that it did not refrain from raising itself even against those writings established by so great a mass of recognition.
>
> “Cyprian, therefore, either did not hold at all the opinion you recount as his; or he afterward corrected it according to the rule of truth; or he covered this blemish, as it were, upon his most candid breast with the abundance of charity, while he both defended most copiously the unity of the Church growing throughout the whole world and most steadfastly maintained the bond of peace. For it is written: ‘Charity covers a multitude of sins.’ [Col. XVI] To this was also added the fact that, as a most fruitful branch, if anything in him required correction, the Father cleansed it with the pruning-hook of martyrdom. For the Lord says: ‘The branch that bears fruit in me, my Father cleanses, so that it may bear more fruit.’ Why was this? Because, clinging to the far-spreading vine, he did not abandon the root of unity. For even if he delivered his body to be burned, but did not have charity, it would profit him nothing.
>
> [Note: [Col. XVI] Several recent writers have considered Augustine’s doubt concerning the genuineness (*γνησιότης*) of the Cyprianic letters in the controversy over rebaptism to be of no slight importance. Foremost among them are Fathers Missorius and Michael Molkenbuhr, both of the Order of St. Francis, and Father Tournemine of the Society of Jesus. The first and the last arrived at and wrote in support of the same opinion at the same time, without knowledge of one another.
>
> We have printed at the end of this volume M. Molkenbuhr’s principal dissertation. It may perhaps not be inappropriate here briefly to review the principal arguments of Fathers Tournemine and Missorius. The former offers these, much shorter and almost entirely general:
>
> 1. He revives the doubts of St. Augustine that we have just set forth.
> 2. He considers it far removed from the truth that Cyprian should have flared up with such bitter invective against the Supreme Pontiff, since, as we have seen, he so vehemently rebuked schismatics.
> 3. He finds in these Cyprianic writings principles of doctrine very different from those in his other genuine books.
> 4. Indeed, the holy Martyr would openly have taught the harsher dogmas of the Donatists. Hence our critic strongly suspects that the true author of these letters was some Donatist, and he shows that those heretics were not innocent of fraud of this kind.
> 5. He firmly believes that the exact same resemblance found both in these letters attributed to Cyprian, in the one circulated under Firmilian’s name, and in the opinions and letters of the African councils could not have existed unless these similar documents had one and the same author.
> 6. Toward the end of his short dissertation, he observes that the complete silence concerning this controversy in the deacon Pontius’s *Life of Cyprian* is of some value in confirming his opinion. (*Mémoires de Trévoux*, year 1834, vol. IV, December, pp. 2245–2262.)
>
> We shall now touch briefly upon Missorius’s principal arguments. After laying down many preliminary axioms, he constructs his entire thesis from a sevenfold theorem:
>
> 1. From the Donatist system he infers that the Cyprianic letters are mere fabrications of those heretics. For he finds that they were highly skilled in calumny, marked by affected sanctity and certain impiety, false doctrine, and slight learning; and that they contrived an error so densely covered with fallacies that it is evident to very few. From this are explained the arrangement of places, the chronological order, the sequence of events, the disposition of persons, and the origin, progress, and outcome of the doctrine. From this too the foolish obstinacy, cunning, falsehood, and incredible audacity of the Donatists in corrupting ancient documents become very apparent.
> 2. From Augustine’s system, or rather from his defense of Cyprian quoted above, he shows that the Cyprianic letters must likewise be rejected, whether that defense is understood absolutely or hypothetically.
> 3. From the books of St. Optatus—or rather from Optatus’s profound silence—the suspicion of the alleged fabrication is confirmed.
> 4. The same is established from several other considerations: namely, the silence of the deacon Pontius; the opinion of the anonymous author *On the Rebaptism of Heretics*; Eusebius’s disagreement with the Africans; and Rufinus’s disagreement with Eusebius.
> 5. With specific reference to the fabrication of the Seventh Council of Carthage, otherwise called the Third, the following are examined: Augustine’s doubts, the disordered chronology, eight passages in the preface, and the conclusion of the letter to Jubaianus.
> 6. The entire attack upon the Cyprianic letters concerning Baptism is recapitulated, and their absurdities, both common and peculiar, are enumerated. The fictitious decree of Stephen is rejected, and the contradictions of pseudo-Cyprian both with himself and with Cyprian are set forth. [Col. XVII]
> 7. Finally, Missorius endeavors to overthrow the arguments of his opponents.
>
> I have collected these things not in the spirit of a judge or advocate, but solely as a witness or compiler, with unquestionable fidelity. Friar Raymond Missorius, *Critical Disputations on the Two Most Celebrated Letters of Firmilian and Cyprian against the Decree of St. Stephen . . .; The Same Author’s Disputation on the Letter to Pompeius . . ., in Which He Now for the First Time Adjudges That Letter, Together with Five Others and the Third Council of Carthage, Hitherto Regarded as Cyprianic, to the Donatists*; Venice, quarto, 1733. See below, among the literary annals, the works of others concerning the same investigation.
>
> Whatever may be the case with this argument of Missorius, which is supported by the most learned Morcelli in *Sacred Africa*, Friar Molkenbuhr in the dissertations cited, and the distinguished Hebermann in his *Theological Institutes*, *On Baptism*, whoever carefully weighs these matters will surely not consider them foolish cavils, nor indignantly exclaim with Martin Routh:
>
> “A remarkable example of the fallacy called begging the question! But suppose that there are men who have knowingly and deliberately used arguments of this kind in matters of such importance, with the result that the whole history of the faith is destroyed: why should I not pray to God for my soul, that in the age to come it may not be with such unjust and wicked sophists!”
>
> —*Annotations on Firmilian’s Letter to St. Cyprian*, in vol. I of *The Principal Minor Works of Ecclesiastical Writers*, p. 260.
>
> Compare again Molkenbuhr in the theological journal under this title: *The Mastiaux Literary Journal*, issue 7, 1822; issue 4, 1823.—D. Wolfgang Fröhlich, O.S.B., in *A Critical Investigation into the Ecclesiastical History of Eusebius*, Pressburg, 1808. See the literary annals below, col. 24.]”

# ARTICLE III. ON THE USE OF ST. CYPRIAN IN MATTERS OF DISCIPLINE

[Col. XVII]

## I

Everyone recognizes what a most abundant supply of useful material the works of St. Cyprian provide, whether they are consulted on exegetical questions, adduced to establish the dogmas of the Church, examined for the vivid and lifelike portrait they present of the morals of his age, or used to summon forth from the tomb, restored to life before us, the chronology of the times, the succession of years, and the personalities of the most illustrious men.

Nevertheless, passing over matters pertaining to Cyprian’s exegetical, dogmatic, moral, or historical use, lest I exceed the limits of a preface too greatly, it seemed that some benefit might be gained by touching in passing upon a few points concerning his use in matters of discipline, almost all taken from D. Lumper’s *Theologico-Critical History of the Fathers*. [Note: [Col. XVII] Vol. XII, pp. 1–112, passim.]

The holy bishop of Carthage and martyr Cyprian was the first of all the holy Fathers to discuss the discipline of the Church at great length. In his works, and especially in his Letters, there are innumerable highly important instructions and judgments from which the ecclesiastical discipline of those times and the Church’s external condition are known more clearly than in the light of midday. For he treats not only discipline in general but also its particular application to the administration of the sacraments, the correction and reconciliation of sinners, the discipline of the ancient Church concerning penance, the use and abuse of indulgences, and other points of ecclesiastical discipline.

## § I.—On Discipline in General

[Col. XVIII]

## II

“In the Holy Scriptures discipline is frequently and everywhere enjoined,” says St. Cyprian in his treatise *On the Dress of Virgins* [Note: [Col. XVIII] St. Cyprian, *On the Discipline and Dress of Virgins*, shortly after the beginning, vol. IV, col. 441 B.], “and the entire foundation of religion and faith proceeds from observance and fear.”

It is readily discerned that nothing is so necessary, especially in the warfare of persecution, as maintaining the due strictness of divine vigor. Whoever relaxes it, says the Roman Clergy [Note: [Col. XVIII] The same, Epistle XXXI, vol. IV, col. 303 A.] in writing to St. Cyprian, must always wander amid the unstable course of affairs, be driven this way and that by the varied and uncertain storms of events, and, as though the helm of counsel had been wrenched from his hands, dash the ship of ecclesiastical salvation against the rocks. Thus it is evident that the Church’s welfare can be secured in no other way than by repelling, like hostile waves, those who act against it, and by always preserving the rule of discipline itself like a saving helm in the storm.

Furthermore, the discipline of the Church ought, as far as possible, to be uniform in the principal matters, such as penance. St. Cyprian indeed gives this admonition to his clergy in his thirty-fourth letter. [Note: [Col. XVIII] Epistle XXVIII, vol. IV, col. 301 A.] He further directs that this discipline should be prescribed by the counsel of all the bishops, as is gathered from several of his other letters. [Note: [Col. XVIII] See Epistles XI, vol. IV, col. 273; *To the People*, vol. IV, col. 256; XIII, *To His Clergy*, vol. IV, col. 260; XIX, *To Caldonius*; XXVIII, *To the Presbyters and Deacons*, vol. IV, col. 300; XXXI, *The Roman Clergy to Cyprian*, col. 307.]

These are St. Cyprian’s statements concerning discipline in general. Let us now see what is found in his writings concerning discipline in particular.

## § II.—On Discipline with Respect to Baptism

## III. The Blessing of the Water to Be Used for Baptism

The first noteworthy point encountered in this ancient Father with respect to Baptism is that in his age the bishop was already bestowing a blessing upon the water of Baptism.

> “The water,” says St. Cyprian in Epistle LXX, addressed to Januarius and the other Numidian bishops, “must therefore first be cleansed and sanctified by the priest, so that by its baptism it may wash away the sins of the person who is baptized. [Note: [Col. XVIII] Cyprian, Epistle LXX, vol. III, col. 1030 A.]”

He confirms this discipline by the following oracle of Ezekiel:

> “I will pour clean water upon you, and you shall be cleansed from all your defilements, and I will cleanse you from all your idols. [Note: [Col. XVIII] Ezekiel 36:25.]”

## IV. Exorcisms in Baptism

The ceremony of Baptism was preceded by exorcisms, as the most celebrated Fathers of the Council of Carthage teach, of which St. Cyprian was and was regarded as the very soul. Read what [Col. XIX] Caecilius of Bilta relates, vol. III, col. 1054; Crescentius of Cirta, col. 1058 of the Oxford edition; and Lucius of Thebeste, all of whom testify to this practice.

It was likewise customary to perform exorcisms over those who were possessed by demons; when adjured in the name of the true God, the demons were compelled to yield and depart from those bodies.

> “Yet when adjured by us through the true God,” says St. Cyprian in his treatise *On the Vanity of Idols* [Note: [Col. XIX] Cyprian, book *On the Vanity of Idols*, vol. IV, col. 577 A.], “they immediately yield and are compelled to depart from the possessed bodies.”

“You may see them,” the holy Doctor adds,

> “at our voice and by the hidden operation of the divine majesty, beaten with scourges and scorched with fire; stretched out as the increasing punishment spreads; wailing, groaning, and pleading; confessing whence they come and when they depart, even while those who worship them are listening. They either leap out immediately or gradually vanish, according as the faith of the sufferer assists or the grace of the healer breathes upon him.”

There were therefore two kinds of exorcisms: some performed over those preparing for Baptism, and others over the possessed. The former were conducted in the church before the faithful. The latter were not ordinarily conducted there because, as we have seen, pagans themselves were sometimes present. Accordingly, since the work so required, the exorcists went to those who needed their ministry.

## V. The Sign of the Cross upon the Forehead of Those Who Were Washed

The sign of the cross upon the forehead of those who were immersed was another ceremony employed in the administration of Baptism. St. Cyprian bears the clearest testimony to this practice:

1. In his treatise *On the Lapsed*. There, speaking of those who had stood as confessors during persecution, he says that their foreheads had been consecrated by the sign of the cross:

   > “The forehead, pure with the sign of God, could not bear the devil’s crown; it reserved itself for the Lord’s crown. [Note: [Col. XIX] Cyprian, book *On the Lapsed*, col. 466 B.]”

2. In his treatise *On the Unity of the Church*, while discussing Uzziah, whose forehead was stained by the mottling of leprosy, he teaches that this is the part of the body upon which those washed with the water of Baptism are signed:

   > “There [upon the forehead] are signed those who merit the Lord. [Note: [Col. XIX] The same, book *On the Unity of the Church*, vol. IV, col. 514 A.]”

3. In his treatise *Against Demetrianus*, he most plainly asserts with Ezekiel [Note: [Col. XIX] Ezekiel 9:6.] that only those who have been reborn and signed with the sign of Christ will be saved. [Note: [Col. XIX] Cyprian, treatise *Against Demetrianus*, vol. IV, col. 526 B; and *Testimonies*, book II, chapter 22, vol. IV, col. 716 A.]

## VI. The Oxford Editor’s Note on This Matter Is Refuted

In the preceding volumes we have already observed from several Fathers, and especially from Tertullian, that the sign of the cross was in extremely frequent use among the ancient faithful. The Oxford editor of St. Cyprian acknowledges this same fact and states in a note upon one of the holy Doctor’s testimonies quoted above:

> “Christians not only [Note: [Col. XIX] Bremen edition of John Fell, Bishop of Oxford, p. 116.] imprinted the sign of the cross upon their foreheads among the solemn rites of Baptism, but at every advance and movement, at every entrance and departure, when dressing and putting on shoes, at the baths and tables, at thresholds, beds, and seats—whatever activity occupied them—they wore down their foreheads with the sign of the Cross.”

Yet this bishop, who holds no insignificant place among Protestants, adds that religious worship was not yet offered to the Cross: “Meanwhile religious worship was absent.” To prove this falsehood he produces a passage from Minucius Felix in which Octavius observes and asserts that Christians by no means adore the Cross: “We neither worship crosses.” I quoted and explained that passage in its proper place, and I refer the reader there. [Note: [Col. XX] D. Lumper, *Theologico-Critical History*, part VII, section 2, chapter 2, article 7, pp. 183–189.]

Here I shall add only one point: namely, that the use of any object in any religious act is the greatest possible sign of religious worship toward that same object. But the Bishop of Oxford, compelled by Tertullian’s authority, acknowledges that Christians did this in the first centuries of the Church. Catholics, therefore, in the worship they offer to the Cross, today follow the practice of those blessed times.

## VII. Salt in the Mouth of Those Who Were Baptized

One of the ceremonies of Baptism is likewise the placing of salt in the mouth or upon the tongue of the person being baptized; and while the minister does this, he pronounces these words: “Receive the salt of wisdom,” etc.

Now I think, says our distinguished Bernard Marechall [Note: [Col. XX] Marechall, *Harmony of the Holy Fathers*, vol. II, p. 115, Latin edition, Venice, 1767.], that this practice is indicated in the celebrated Council of Carthage of which I spoke above. For there Lucius of Castrogalba, in order to prove that schismatics do not baptize lawfully, says that they cannot impart the salt of spiritual wisdom:

> “Schismatics cannot season others with spiritual wisdom, since by withdrawing from the Church they have themselves become insipid. . . . [Note: [Col. XX] Council of Carthage VII, or III *On Baptism*, vol. III, col. 1058 B.]”

In these words he certainly appears to have had in view both the ceremony under discussion and the words: “Receive the salt of wisdom.”

## VIII. Questions in Baptism

Before neophytes were immersed in the water, they were asked, among other things, whether they believed in eternal life and in the forgiveness of sins through the holy Church.

St. Cyprian himself bears the clearest testimony concerning this matter in Epistle LXIX. He employs the force of the aforesaid question to show that it cannot be asked by those who are separated from the Church’s communion:

> “For when they say”—these are St. Cyprian’s very own words, speaking of heretics and schismatics—“‘Do you believe in the forgiveness of sins and eternal life through the holy Church?’ they lie in their question, since they do not possess the Church. [Note: [Col. XX] Cyprian, Epistle LXIX.]”

Elsewhere he recalls this same custom in these words:

> “The very question asked in Baptism is a witness to this truth—that the Church alone forgives sins. For when we say, ‘Do you believe in eternal life and that the forgiveness of sins is given only in the Church?’—yet among heretics, where the Church does not exist, sins cannot be forgiven. [Note: [Col. XXI] Cyprian, Epistle LXX, vol. III, col. 1040 A.]”

IX. Renunciation of the World and Its Pleasures and Pomps.—Neophytes were likewise required to renounce the devil, the world, and its pleasures and pomps. This is most clearly proved by the authority of St. Cyprian, who, in his treatise *On the Dress of Virgins*, says that the riches of the world are to be despised just as the world itself is despised, “whose pomps and pleasures we renounced at that very time [Note: [Col. XXI] Id., treatise *On the Dress of Virgins*, vol. IV, col. 446 B.].” “We had renounced the world,” he says elsewhere [Note: [Col. XXI] Id., Ep. VII, vol. IV, col. 241 A.], “when we were baptized.” And in his treatise *On the Lapsed*, he expresses amazement that some Christians were found to be so perverse that they dared to renounce Jesus Christ, though they had already renounced the devil and the world. “The servant of God,” says the holy Doctor [Note: [Col. XXI] Id., book *On the Lapsed*, vol. IV, col. 334 A and col. 467 A. “But he who remembers that he has renounced the world recognizes no day belonging to the world.”], “was able to stand there . . . and to renounce Christ, though he had already renounced the devil and the world.”

X. Baptism Conferred by Immersion.—In the first centuries of the Church it was customary for those being baptized to be immersed in water, as may be gathered from St. Cyprian’s Epistle LXIX, addressed to Magnus [Note: [Col. XXI] Id., Ep. LXIX.]. Nowhere in this most ancient Father, however, is mention made of three immersions, although it is absolutely certain that these were in use both before and after his time. On this matter we possess testimony of unquestionable reliability from Clement of Alexandria [Note: [Col. XXI] Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata*, book V, p. 690. See *Critical History of Theology*, part V, p. 155.] and Tertullian [Note: [Col. XXI] Tertullian, *Against Praxeas*, ch. 26. See *Critical History of Theology*, part VI, p. 635.]. The fiftieth Apostolic Canon furthermore commands the deposition of a bishop or presbyter who used a single immersion [Note: [Col. XXI] Apostolic Canons, ch. 26.]. At the present time, however, Baptism is conferred by pouring.

XI. Baptism Conferred by Pouring or Sprinkling.—Formerly, the sick were baptized in this manner and were accordingly called *clinics* (*clinici*), without even the slightest doubt arising about the validity of Baptism conferred in this way. When St. Cyprian was consulted on this point by Magnus, he answered that those baptized in this manner received the grace of God no less than those immersed in water [Note: [Col. XXI] Cyprian, Epistle to Magnus.]. Then, after citing several scriptural pronouncements in which the pouring and sprinkling of water are mentioned, he concludes that the sprinkling of water has the efficacy of the saving bath: “Hence it is apparent that the sprinkling of water likewise has the efficacy of the saving bath.” Shortly thereafter he gives this reason for the fact: namely, that those who had been baptized in this manner were not baptized again; for Baptism would have had to be repeated if any doubt had arisen concerning its validity. He also disapproves of their being called *clinics* [Col. XXII] and commands that they be regarded as true Christians, like all others, and that in no respect should they be judged different from the rest of the faithful. We nevertheless acknowledge that at Rome those who had been baptized by pouring or sprinkling were excluded from the clergy; for this was one of the defects in Novatian’s ordination that Pope Cornelius adduces in his Epistle to Fabius, Bishop of Antioch [Note: [Col. XXII] Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VI, ch. 43. See *Critical History of Theology*, part XI, p. 17. See also the notes 3, 4, 5, and 6 of our most learned Coustant on this Epistle of Cornelius to Fabius, in Mansi, vol. I, *Collection of Councils*, cols. 823–824.]. The Council of Neocaesarea likewise excludes clinics from the presbyterate [Note: [Col. XXII] In Mansi, *Collection of Councils*, vol. II, col. 541, canon 12; and the note of the most illustrious Albaspinaeus on this canon in the cited *Collection of Councils* of Mansi, p. 552.], because, according to the mind of that Council, their faith was not voluntary but had been produced by fear of death. It must moreover be observed that Baptism by pouring was conferred only in a case of necessity.

XII. The Anointings of Baptism.—After immersion, the baptized person was anointed. “It is also necessary,” says the bishop [Note: [Col. XXII] Cyprian, Ep. LXX, vol. III, col. 1040 A.], “that one who has been baptized should be anointed, so that, having received chrism, that is, anointing, he may be one anointed by God and may possess within himself the grace of Christ.” The consecration of this chrism was performed over the altar by acts of thanksgiving: “Moreover, it is the Eucharist from which the baptized are anointed, the oil sanctified upon the altar [Note: [Col. XXII] Id., ibid.].” The opening words of this last text appear somewhat obscure. Some indeed hold that the word *Eucharistia* should be understood in its proper sense, namely, as the Sacrament of the altar; from this they conjecture that in the ancient Church the Eucharist was conferred there together with Baptism [Note: [Col. XXII] See Baluze’s note on this passage; he thinks it should read “with oil sanctified upon the altar.”]; others, however, maintain that the word signifies thanksgiving alone.

XIII. The Kiss Given to the Newly Baptized.—We learn from St. Cyprian’s Epistle to Fidus that the minister of Baptism was accustomed to give a kiss to the newly baptized person. Fidus maintained that, since an infant’s foot in the first days after birth was not clean, everyone ought to recoil from kissing it, and therefore that baptismal grace could not be conferred upon the infant. But the holy bishop replies that none of us ought to recoil from doing what God has deigned to do: “For in kissing an infant, each of us, in keeping with his religious devotion, ought to think of the still-recent hands of God themselves, etc. [Note: [Col. XXII] Cyprian, Epistle to Fidus, vol. III, col. 1017 A.].”

XIV. Confirmation Conferred Immediately after Baptism.—Baptism was generally followed immediately by Confirmation. This is manifestly established from St. Cyprian; for he says that those baptized in the Church were presented to its prelates, received the Holy Spirit, and were perfected through their prayer and the imposition of hands. [Col. XXIII] “This is also done among us now: those who are presented in the Church obtain the Holy Spirit through our prayer and imposition of hands and are brought to completion with the seal of the Lord [Note: [Col. XXIII] Cyprian, Ep. XXIII to Jubaianus, vol. III, col. 1115 A.].”

XV. Infants Baptized at the Beginning of Their Life.—St. Cyprian mentions in two places the custom of baptizing infants at the beginning of their life: namely, in his treatise *On the Lapsed*, where he writes: “And lest anything should be lacking to complete the accumulation of guilt, little children too, either placed in their parents’ arms or drawn along by them, lost what they had obtained at the very beginning of their life.” And in his Epistle to Fidus [Note: [Col. XXIII] Id., Ep. LIX, vol. III, col. 1016.], where he writes as follows: “We all judged that the mercy and grace of God ought to be denied to no human being who has been born. . . . There is for all, whether infants or those older in years, one equal measure of the divine gift. . . . For just as God shows no partiality toward persons, neither does he toward age; but, with impartial equality, he offers himself as Father to all for the attainment of heavenly grace.”

§ III.—Discipline Concerning the Eucharist

XVI. The Faithful Assembled Together with the Bishop to Celebrate the Eucharist.—That the faithful were accustomed to assemble together with the bishop to celebrate the divine mysteries may be gathered from St. Cyprian’s treatise *On the Lord’s Prayer* [Note: [Col. XXIII] Id., treatise *On the Lord’s Prayer*, vol. IV, col. 524 A.]: “And when,” he says, “we assemble together with the brethren and celebrate the divine sacrifices with the priest of God.” The place of this assembly was called the *Dominicum*, as appears to be inferable from St. Cyprian himself, who addresses wealthy women as follows in his treatise *On Works and Almsgiving* [Note: [Col. XXIII] Id., treatise *On Works and Almsgiving*, vol. IV, col. 612 B.]: “You are affluent and wealthy; and do you think that you celebrate the Lord’s rite, when you pay no attention whatever to the treasury; when you come to the Lord’s assembly without a sacrifice; when you take a portion of the sacrifice that the poor person has offered?”

XVII. The Time for Celebrating the Holy Sacrifice.—In St. Cyprian’s time the Eucharist was celebrated both in the morning and in the evening. This is proved by the sixty-third Epistle of this holy Doctor. For in it, arguing against those who were unwilling to pour wine into the chalice at the morning sacrifices, lest the faithful, smelling of wine after Communion, should be recognized by the pagans, he says [Note: [Col. XXIII] Cyprian, Ep. LXIII, vol. IV, col. 386 B.]: “Does anyone flatter himself with the consideration that, although in the morning water alone appears to be offered, nevertheless, when we come to supper, we offer the mixed chalice? . . .” Cyprian’s position is nevertheless that the sacrifice should be celebrated in the morning rather than in the evening. To the objection raised by some—namely, that the Lord offered the mixed chalice not in the morning but after supper—the holy bishop replies that Christ had to offer at about the evening of the day, so that the very hour of the sacrifice might signify [Col. XXIV] the decline and evening of the world: “But we celebrate the Lord’s Resurrection in the morning.”

XVII. It Was Offered Daily, and the Faithful Received the Eucharist.—The holy sacrifice was offered daily. “We who celebrate the sacrifices daily,” says St. Cyprian in his Epistle to Pope Cornelius [Note: [Col. XXIV] Cyprian, Ep. LIV, vol. III, col. 857 A.]. The faithful received the Eucharist daily unless some grave fault intervened [Note: [Col. XXIV] Id., *On the Lord’s Prayer*, col. 533 A. Compare Tertullian, *To His Wife*, book II, vol. I.]: “But we ask that this bread be given to us daily, lest we who . . . receive the Eucharist daily as the food of salvation should, through the intervention of some graver offense . . . be separated from the body of Christ.” Every day they drank the chalice of Christ’s blood, “considering,” in the words of the same holy Doctor [Note: [Col. XXIV] Cyprian, Epistle to the Thibaritans, LVI, vol. IV, col. 350 A.], “that they drink the chalice of Christ’s blood daily for this reason: that they themselves might be able to shed their blood for Christ.”

XVIII. The Eucharist Was Often Given under the Species of Bread Alone.—Although from what has been said and from innumerable other most ancient monuments it may rightly be inferred that the faithful were accustomed to receive Communion under both species, it is nevertheless certain from St. Cyprian that the faithful were sometimes nourished by the Eucharist under the species of bread alone.
