On three occasions St. Cyprian mentions the Eucharist being administered to the faithful under both species. First, in Epistle LIV to Pope Cornelius, where he writes [Note: [Col. XXIV] Cyprian, Ep. LIV, vol. III, col. 856 H.]: “But now peace is necessary not for the weak but for the strong; and Communion must be given by us not to the dying but to the living, so that those whom we stir up and exhort to battle may not be left unarmed and naked, but may be fortified with the protection of Christ’s blood and body; and since the Eucharist is instituted for this purpose, that it may be a safeguard to those who receive it.” Then, in two places in the treatise *On the Lapsed*; indeed, at its very beginning, he says [Note: [Col. XXIV] Id., treatise *On the Lapsed*, col. 466 A.]: “Mouths sanctified by heavenly food, after receiving the body and blood of the Lord, rejected profane contaminations and the remnants of idols.” Later, around the middle of the cited treatise, he writes [Note: [Col. XXIV] Id., book cited, vol. IV, cols. 478, 479 A, B, 484 A.]: “The swollen and proud spirit has not been broken even though it has been conquered. Prostrate, it threatens those who stand unharmed; and the sacrilegious man is angry with the priests because he does not immediately receive the Lord’s body with defiled hands or drink the Lord’s blood with a polluted mouth.” In the same treatise *On the Lapsed*, he adduces several examples from which it is more clearly apparent than the light of midday that Communion, or the Eucharist, was administered under one species—sometimes under the species of wine, sometimes under that of bread. Its administration under the species of wine alone is indeed plain from the account related by St. Cyprian in the book *On the Lapsed*, vol. IV, col. 484 C ff. St. Cyprian relates an example of the Eucharist being administered under the species of bread alone in the same book, vol. IV, col. 486 B: “When a certain woman attempted with her hands to open her chest, in which there was something holy belonging to the Lord, she was deterred from daring to touch it when fire rose from it.” This plainly concerns a woman who wished to receive the Eucharist, in accordance with the practice of the faithful of that age, who carried the Lord’s body to their own homes so that they might eat that sacred bread with their own hands. Yet they could carry only the species of bread with them; therefore, in private Communions they received the species of bread alone. Hence, only with the greatest injustice did some persons in later times reproach the Church, as though it were a crime to be expiated by no penance, for having withdrawn the chalice in the Communion of the faithful. For the very same reasons for which it withdrew the chalice in private Communions during the first centuries, it did the same in succeeding centuries in all Communions generally. If the species of wine had been essential to the reception of the Eucharist, as the Hussites and others among the sectaries believed, the Church would surely never have permitted abstention from the chalice, not even in private Communions themselves.

XIX. The Faithful Received the Body of Christ in Their Hands and Carried It Home.—In former times the faithful received the Eucharist in their hands, as may be gathered from St. Cyprian’s Epistle to the Thibaritans, in which he says that the right hand that has received the Lord’s body should reject deadly sacrifices. “Let us arm,” he says [Note: [Col. XXV] Cyprian, Ep. LVI, vol. IV, col. 357 A.], “the right hand also with the spiritual sword, so that it may resolutely reject the sacrifices . . . that hand which has received the Lord’s body.” “The sacrilegious man is angry,” says the holy Doctor elsewhere [Note: [Col. XXV] Id., book *On the Lapsed*, vol. IV, col. 484 A. And a little above, vol. IV, cols. 478 B, 479 B: “Returning from the altars of the Devil, they approach the Holy One of the Lord with hands filthy and tainted by the smell of sacrifice.”], “because he does not immediately receive the Lord’s body with defiled hands.” In the same place he relates that when a certain defiled person, after the sacrifice had been celebrated by the priest, dared to receive a portion with the others, “he could neither eat nor handle the Holy One of the Lord [Note: [Col. XXV] Id., ibid., col. 486 B.].” Finally, in his treatise *On the Good of Patience*, he says [Note: [Col. XXV] Id., treatise *On the Good of Patience*, vol. IV, col. 631 C.]: “Nor, after tasting the Eucharist, should the hand be stained by sword and blood.” St. Cyprian teaches in addition that the Eucharist must be received in the hands “with fear and honor” [Note: [Col. XXV] Id., *Testimonies*, book III, ch. 94, vol. IV, col. 774 C. Moreover, on the ancient custom of receiving the Eucharist in the hand and carrying it home, see Cardinal Bona, *Liturgical Matters*, book II, ch. 17, no. 3 ff., p. 360 ff., Antwerp ed., 1739; and Henry Valesius’s annotations on Eusebius, book VI, ch. 43, and book VII, ch. 9, where on p. 274 of my edition he writes: “It was the presbyter’s particular office to deliver the Eucharist and the Chalice into the hands of the faithful; and this was properly called ἐπιδοῦναι (*epidounai*, “to hand over”).” And on p. 289 of my edition he says: “The faithful who were to receive Communion approached the altar, and there, standing—not kneeling as today—received the body of Christ from the presbyter’s hand.” The faithful who were to receive the Lord’s body in the hand first approached the altar with their hands carefully washed, as St. Chrysostom teaches in Homily III on Paul’s Epistle to the Ephesians. He writes the same in Homily LII on Matthew. When about to receive the Eucharist, moreover, they extended the right hand slightly cupped, supporting it underneath with the left, lest any part of the sacred food should fall, as St. Cyril of Jerusalem teaches in his final Catechesis.]. From the same holy Doctor we learn that in his time it was customary for participants in the Eucharist, after receiving a portion of the consecrated bread, [Col. XXVI] not only to eat it during the celebration of the sacred rites, but also to reserve some of it, carry it home, and consume it there either before food, in times of danger, or at the commencement of some undertaking—as was afterward done with the *eulogiae*. We gather this from two passages. In the book *On the Public Shows* he writes [Note: [Col. XXVI] Cyprian, book *On the Public Shows*, col. 784 B, vol. IV.]: “One who hastens to a public show while still carrying with him, as is customary, the Eucharist.” And in the book *On the Lapsed*: “When a certain woman attempted with unworthy hands to open her chest, in which there was something holy belonging to the Lord, she was deterred from daring to touch it when fire rose from it.” Tertullian had already shown this in book II of *To His Wife*, ch. 5: “Will your husband not know what you taste secretly before all food? And if he learns that it is bread, he does not believe it to be the bread it is said to be.” And in *On Prayer*, ch. 14: “When the Lord’s body has been received and reserved, both are safeguarded: participation in the sacrifice and the discharge of one’s duty.” This custom appears to have endured until the Council of Caesaraugusta under Damasus.

XX. The Eucharist Was Denied to Those Who Did Penance Only as Death Approached.—We have already seen in the preceding volume [Note: [Col. XXVI] Id., book *On the Lapsed*, vol. IV, col. 486 B.] that St. Cyprian wished those who had lapsed during the persecution and had not yet completed the penance imposed upon them to be reconciled when their lives were in danger. But although the holy bishop exercised such indulgence toward the faithful who, while still in good health, had begun penance for their offenses, he nevertheless treated with great rigor those who gave some signs of conversion only at the time of death, after through their own pride and hardness of heart they had stored up punishments and torments for themselves on the day of judgment. “And therefore,” says St. Cyprian [Note: [Col. XXVI] Id., Ep. LII, vol. III, col. 789 C.], “we have judged that those who do not perform penance, nor attest their sorrow for their offenses with their whole heart and by an open profession of their lamentation, must be entirely excluded from the hope of Communion and peace if they begin to entreat during illness and danger; because it is not repentance for their offense that compels them to ask, but the warning of impending death; nor is he worthy to receive consolation in death who gave no thought to the fact that he would die.”

XXI. The Eucharist Administered to Infants and Martyrs, etc.—The passages of St. Cyprian already cited above establish that in former times the Eucharist was administered to children no less than to adults. St. Cyprian judged that martyrs should be fortified with the protection of the Lord’s body and blood [Note: [Col. XXVI] Id., Ep. LIV, vol. III, col. 856 A.]. From this it is permissible to infer that at that time the reception of the Holy Eucharist, which was also called *Viaticum*, was regarded as necessary for the faithful at the point of death.

XXII. The Preface and Prayers of the Mass.—In St. Cyprian’s time, during the celebration of the holy sacrifice, bishops were accustomed, by first pronouncing a preface, to prepare the minds of the faithful to lift up their hearts to the Lord. “Therefore, before the prayer,” says St. Cyprian in his treatise *On the Lord’s Prayer* [Note: [Col. XXVI] Id., *On the Lord’s Prayer*, vol. IV, col. 541 B in another edition.], “the priest, having first pronounced the preface, prepares [Col. XXVII] the minds of the brethren by saying, ‘Lift up your hearts’; and when the people respond, ‘We have them with the Lord,’ etc.” It is therefore utterly false that in the primitive Church the liturgy comprised only the words of Scripture, since it is established from the quoted words of St. Cyprian that prayers also were poured forth “before the Prayer,” and that the minds of the faithful were customarily prepared for these prayers by a preceding preface. Indeed, that preface was placed beforehand with the same intention with which it is placed beforehand among us today: namely, so that “the faithful may be admonished that they ought to think of nothing other than the Lord.”

XXIII. The Names of the Faithful Were Offered in the Sacrifice of the Mass.—In the sacrifice of the Mass certain faithful were mentioned by name to God through the priests, just as the custom still exists today in the Canon, where, in the words “Remember, Lord, your male and female servants,” certain persons are mentioned by name. This is manifestly established by two Epistles of St. Cyprian. In the first of these, addressed to his clergy [Note: [Col. XXVII] St. Cyprian, Ep. IX, vol. IV, col. 252 A.], he laments that the names of those who had lapsed during the persecution were being offered—offered, I say, before penance had been performed, before *exomologesis* had been made, and before hands had been imposed upon them by the bishop and clergy. “Their name,” says the holy Doctor, “is offered.” In another, addressed to the bishops of Numidia, he writes [Note: [Col. XXVII] Id., Ep. LX, vol. IV, col. 362 [uncertain numeral in source: “3”].]: “I have added the names of each person so that you may remember in your prayers, sacrifices, and petitions our brothers and sisters who contributed to this very necessary work of redemption; I have added the names of each person.” On these words the most learned Rigault makes the following annotation: “Not without purpose, not needlessly; for in the sacrifices of prayers the names were offered of those who had contributed promptly and willingly to this very necessary work.” Exclusion from this privilege was regarded as the gravest punishment, as is established by the Epistle to the people of Furni [Note: [Col. XXVII] Id., Ep. LXVI, vol. IV, col. 398. See vol. XI, *Critical History of Theology*, p. 259.].

XXIV. The Most Holy Sacrifice Was Offered in Prisons; and a Little Water Was Poured into the Chalice.—We learn from an Epistle of St. Cyprian that at that time the most holy sacrifice was performed in prisons. Writing to his clergy while persecution was raging, he says [Note: [Col. XXVII] Id., Ep. IV, col. 231 A, vol. IV.]: “Take counsel, therefore, and make provision that the presbyters who offer there among the confessors should alternate in turn, one presbyter with one deacon”; namely, so that they might not easily be recognized. The very learned Bernard Marechall [Note: [Col. XXVII] Marechall, *Concordance of the Holy Fathers*, vol. II, p. 117, Venice ed.] thinks that in this passage of St. Cyprian there is an example of a private Mass against the more recent sectaries who condemn private Masses; but it seems to me that this most learned man had not formed a sufficiently precise idea of a private Mass. For only that Mass is called private in which the priest alone receives the Eucharist and none of those present [Col. XXVIII] communicates. We have already noted elsewhere that a little water was mixed with the wine in the sacrifice [Note: [Col. XXVIII] See vol. XI, *Critical History of the Theology of the Holy Fathers*, p. 481 ff.; and p. 589, note Z.].

§ IV.—Discipline Concerning Penance

XXV. In the following volume, with the most learned Maran as our guide, we shall demonstrate from the testimonies of St. Cyprian that Penance was numbered among the sacraments; how necessary this holy Doctor judged this sacrament to be for the faithful; and how holily he wished it to be administered. There we have also discussed, first, whether in Africa before this holy bishop Communion after penance had been denied for the gravest crimes; next, whether a new discipline was introduced under this same holy Doctor and the former severity retained only for apostates and deserters; third, whether St. Cyprian denied peace to lapsed persons who died in the course of their penance, with the sole exception of those who had received certificates from the martyrs. Finally, we investigated whether the Council of Carthage imposed penance for the entirety of their lives upon those who had sacrificed.

XXVI. Which Sins Were Subject to Canonical Penance; Whether Even More Secret Sins Were.—Yet other questions concerning the discipline of penance remain to be resolved. First of all, it must be asked which sins were subject to canonical penance in the time of St. Cyprian. St. Cyprian testifies in his Epistles [Note: [Col. XXVIII] Cyprian, Ep. IX, vol. IV, col. 251 B; Ep. XI, col. 257 B.] that, besides idolatry and apostasy from the faith, there were other, less grievous crimes that were subjected to canonical penance. Thus canonical penance was imposed upon heretics and schismatics when they returned to the Church. In St. Cyprian’s time sinners were required to undergo the same penance even for more secret crimes, and their confession was public, provided that no grave misfortune threatening the penitents’ lives would result from it. St. Cyprian discusses this matter at great length in his treatise *On the Lapsed*, where he relates that certain hidden crimes for which the sinners had neither made confession nor performed canonical penance were miraculously punished [Note: [Col. XXVIII] Id., treatise *On the Lapsed*, cols. 484 ff.]. The faithful likewise confessed sins of thought alone and performed penance for them.

XXVII. The Order of Canonical Penance.—The order generally observed in canonical penance was as follows. A certain period of time was established for this penance; it was accompanied by *exomologeses*, or confessions, and examinations; and it was brought to an end through the imposition of the hands of the bishop and clergy [Note: [Col. XXVIII] Id., Ep. IX, vol. IV, col. 251 B, and XI, col. 257 B.]. First, the penitent confessed his own crimes so that he might receive penance from the one who heard that confession. Undoubted traces of this confession are found in the treatise *On the Lapsed*, specifically in the passage [Note: [Col. XXVIII] Id., treatise *On the Lapsed*, vol. IV, col. 488.] in which the holy Doctor reports that the faithful were accustomed [Col. XXIX] to confess even the mere thought of sacrificing to idols and to perform penance for it. These words make it clear that the passage concerns a confession preceding Penance. Once this confession had been completed, the penitent endeavored to make satisfaction to God through laborious works; and this was done throughout the entire period prescribed by the bishop, unless some very grave cause supervened on account of which some portion of the penance was remitted. When the penance, or satisfaction, had been completed, the penitent presented himself again to the bishop, to whom he also confessed his particular crime before the clergy. His dispositions were then subjected to examination. If they appeared to be of such a nature as to merit the grace of reconciliation, the bishop then imposed hands upon him together with the entire clergy and granted him absolution; once this had been bestowed, he became a participant in the sacred mysteries. It must further be noted, concerning the imposition of the bishop’s hands, that this took place both at the beginning of penance and after the penance had been completed: at the beginning, so that sinners might be enrolled among the penitents; and after the completion of penance, so that they might be granted reconciliation. While the faithful were passing through the course of canonical penance, hands were likewise imposed upon them; but this imposition was a kind of exorcism. St. Cyprian mentions these three impositions of hands—or at least the first and second—because he sometimes uses the words “to impose hands” to designate the beginning of penance, but at other times to indicate absolution.

XXVIII. Penance Imposed in Proportion to the Offenses.—Penance, or satisfaction, was imposed in due proportion to the crimes committed and confessed. It was greater for those sins committed directly against God, but less for those that, being committed against one’s neighbor, concerned God only indirectly. Hence idolaters were required to perform a more severe penance than adulterers. Indeed, some distinction was made even between sins of the same nature. A person, for example, who had voluntarily presented himself to sacrifice to idols was punished with a greater and more rigorous penance than one who had sacrificed only after a prolonged struggle. A greater penalty was imposed on one who had defiled himself with the crime of idolatry together with his entire household, but a lesser one on him who had exposed himself to danger in order to free the others [Note: [Col. XXIX] Cyprian, Epistle to Antonianus, LII, vol. III, cols. 779 B–C.]. Some obtained the grace of reconciliation after a very short period of penance, for example after four or five years; others, however, were not granted absolution except at the point of death, apart from a case of most serious illness or the recent outbreak of persecution, as we have said elsewhere [Note: [Col. XXIX] *Critical History of Theology*, vol. XI, p. 450.]. As for those who had not actually sacrificed and were called *libellatici* because they had given pagan magistrates certificates in which they acknowledged that they had sacrificed to idols—even though they had not in fact done so—in order to avoid the infamy of a public sacrifice, [Col. XXX] their penance was less severe [Note: [Col. XXX] Cyprian, Ep. LII, vol. III, col. 781 A.]. And after one year had elapsed, St. Cyprian granted reconciliation to those who had embraced penance immediately after their lapse [Note: [Col. XXX] Id., Ep. XIX, vol. IV, cols. 273 B, C. In Epistle LIII to Fortunatus, vol. IV, col. 347 B, Cyprian writes: “For the lapsed amid tortures, penance begun and continued for three years can suffice.” And in the treatise *On the Lapsed*, book I, col. 489 A, he says: “Pardon can quickly be granted to such a person.”].

XXIX. Bishops and Other Ministers Subject to Canonical Penance.—Canonical penance was imposed upon bishops and the other ministers of the Church just as upon others, whether they had sacrificed to idols or were *libellatici*. They were, however, excluded from the priesthood and from all ecclesiastical offices, and could not be reconciled until after full and completed penance. This is clear from St. Cyprian’s Epistle to Fidus, in which he complains of undue haste in granting reconciliation to Victor, formerly a presbyter, especially before he had performed full penance and when no necessity was pressing. “We have read your letter, dearest brother,” says the holy Doctor [Note: [Col. XXX] Id., Epistle to Fidus, LXIII, vol. III, col. 1014 A.], “in which you reported concerning a certain Victor, a presbyter, that before he had performed full penance . . . our colleague Therapius rashly . . . and with premature haste granted him peace . . . though no illness was pressing and no necessity compelled it.” We shall see in the following centuries that public penance was no longer imposed upon ministers of the Church, but that they were merely deposed and reduced to the Communion of the laity. In St. Cyprian’s time, however, no one could escape this penance, not even bishops, as may be seen in another Epistle of the same holy Doctor to the clergy and people residing in Spain. There he relates that a certain bishop, Basilides, after confessing that he had blasphemed against God, voluntarily resigned the episcopate and turned to performing penance, deeming it sufficient cause for gratitude if it should fall to his lot to communicate even as a layman [Note: [Col. XXX] Id., Ep. LVIII, vol. III, cols. 1029 ff.].

XXX. Certificates of the Martyrs Concerning the Reconciliation of Penitents.—Those who had sacrificed to idols devised a thoroughly deceitful expedient by which the Church’s discipline concerning penance could be notably weakened. They extorted certificates from martyrs and confessors so that they might themselves be granted reconciliation and the period of penance might be shortened [Note: [Col. XXX] Id., Ep. IX, vol. IV, cols. 252 A, B.]. But in order to prevent the abuse that such certificates could create, it was customary for those who had obtained them to present themselves to the bishop, so that he might examine both the requests and the wishes of those who had given the certificates [Note: [Col. XXX] Id., Ep. XXII, vol. IV, col. 284 A.]. This examination was conducted before the people, as may be gathered from Cyprian’s Epistle to the people of Carthage [Note: [Col. XXX] Id., Epistle to the people of Carthage, XI, vol. IV, col. 257 A.]; and the aforesaid certificates benefited only those who had already [Col. XXXI] completed the greater part of their penance: “Those whose penance you perceive to be near satisfaction,” says the holy Doctor in an Epistle to the Martyrs and Confessors [Note: [Col. XXXI] Cyprian, Ep. X, vol. IV, col. 257 A.], in which he warns them not to grant certificates indiscriminately to all who ask, but carefully to consider the penance already performed and to weigh every circumstance.

St. Cyprian was so moderate and prudent concerning these indulgences that he was unwilling to determine anything about them by himself, but only with the counsel of the other bishops. “It befits our sense of restraint,” he says in his Epistle to his clergy concerning those who were hastening toward peace [Note: [Col. XXXI] Id., Epistle to the Clergy of Carthage, XIII, vol. IV, col. 261 A.], “that the prelates, assembling together with the clergy and with the people who have stood firm also present . . . should be able to arrange everything with the conscientiousness of common counsel.” And in another Epistle to the same clergy he says [Note: [Col. XXXI] Id., Ep. XVII to the same clergy, vol. IV, col. 270 A.]: “I have read the letter of all the confessors, which they wished to be made known through me to all my colleagues”; and shortly afterward he continues: “Since this matter awaits the counsel and judgment of all of us, I do not dare to prejudge it or claim for myself alone a matter common to all.” From this it is evident what conception the faithful then had of the discipline concerning penance and how solicitous they were that not even its smallest part should be weakened. “For what,” said the Roman clergy in writing to St. Cyprian [Note: [Col. XXXI] Epistle of the Roman clergy, among the Cyprianic Epistles, XXXI, vol. IV, col. 308 B.], “is more fitting in peace, or more necessary amid the warfare of persecution, than to maintain the due severity of divine rigor? Whoever relaxes it must always wander amid the unstable course of events, be scattered this way and that by the varied and uncertain storms of circumstances, and, as though the rudder of counsel had been wrenched from his hands, drive the ship of ecclesiastical salvation upon the rocks. Thus it is apparent that provision can be made for the Church’s salvation in no other way than by preserving at all times the proper order of discipline itself, like a saving rudder in a storm.”

### XXXI. On Indulgences

Since the certificates of the martyrs (*libelli martyrum*) were a certain kind of indulgence—for they were letters given by the martyrs in which they asked the bishops to pardon certain penitents whom they named, or to shorten the period of their penance [Note: [Col. XXXI] Cyprian throughout his *Letters.]—it is easy to infer from them what St. Cyprian thought about indulgences.

First, the holy Doctor speaks of the martyrs’ certificates in this way both in Letter XXII, addressed to the clergy residing at Rome, concerning the many confessors, the shamelessness of Lucian, and the modesty of the confessor Celerinus (vol. IV, col. 282), and in several other letters written to the same effect: he by no means denies that the fallen can be assisted by their merits. For in Letter XII (vol. IV, col. 259 A) he decrees:

> That those who have received certificates from the martyrs [Col. XXXII] and can be assisted before God by their privilege, if they are overtaken by some affliction and danger of illness, may, without awaiting my presence, make confession (*exomologesis*) of their offense before any presbyter who is present; or, if no presbyter can be found and death begins to press upon them, even before a deacon, etc.

Cyprian therefore believed that they could be assisted in their offenses before the Lord by the privilege of the martyrs, or, as he says in Letter XIII, col. 260 C, “by their aid.” Likewise, in the book *On the Fallen* (vol. IV, cols. 481 A, 483), he admits that something may be granted in accordance with the martyrs’ instructions,

> if what is to be done by God’s priest is just, if lawful, if not contrary to the Lord himself; if the compliance of the one obeying is ready and willing; and if there is religious moderation on the part of the petitioner.

Therefore, he censures not the custom itself, which had long prevailed in the Church, but its abuse and the excessive license of certain confessors, especially Lucian, who issued certificates written in this form (vol. IV, col. 255 C): “Let that man communicate together with his own people.” Nor did they observe what Cyprian had commanded in Letter X (vol. IV, cols. 255 A–B):

> that they should carefully examine the conduct, works, and merits of each individual, as well as the kinds and qualities of the offenses themselves; and that they should designate by name in their certificates those whom they themselves knew and whose penance they perceived to be near satisfaction.

Two further points must be observed:

1. The confessors did not grant peace, but asked that it be granted.
2. They did not even venture to demand that peace be granted to the fallen before Cyprian’s return, but in this matter deferred to their bishop.

Accordingly, it was not by the authority of the confessors that the five presbyters were induced to admit the fallen to communion before the bishop’s return and entirely without consulting him, but by their own wickedness.

### XXXII. That indulgences are founded upon the practice of the Church’s earliest centuries is attested by many of St. Cyprian’s letters

Thus, in Letter XVII, St. Cyprian, seeing that he did not yet have the opportunity to return to Carthage and that summer had already begun—a season beset by persistent and serious illnesses—commands the presbyters, and in case of necessity the deacons, of his Church to exercise a certain “indulgence” toward the fallen whenever they are placed in danger of death:

> Those who have received certificates from the martyrs, says the holy Doctor [Note: [Col. XXXII] St. Cyprian, Ep. XII, vol. IV, col. 250 A.], and can be assisted before God by their privilege, if they are overtaken by some affliction and danger of illness, may, without awaiting our presence, make confession (*exomologesis*) of their offense before any presbyter who is present; or, if no presbyter can be found and death begins to press upon them, even before a deacon, so that, when a hand has been laid upon them for penance, they may come to the Lord with the peace which the martyrs, in letters addressed to us, desired to be granted.

He repeats the same thing in Letter XIII:

> Since, however, you have reported, he says in addressing his clergy [Note: [Col. XXXII] Id., Ep. XIII, vol. IV, col. 260 B.], that some are immoderate [Col. XXXIII] and urgently press to receive communion without delay, and since you have desired that I give you a rule in this matter, I believe that in my recent letter to you I wrote sufficiently fully on this matter: that those who have received a certificate from the martyrs . . . if they begin to be oppressed by some illness and danger, may, after making confession (*exomologesis*) and after a hand has been laid upon them by you for penance, be sent to the Lord with the peace promised to them by the martyrs.

## § V. Discipline Regarding Holy Orders

### XXXIII

Although it would have been necessary to begin with the Supreme Pontiff, who is the head of the ecclesiastical order and of the whole Church, since we have treated very many matters concerning this same subject in the preceding articles, and since many more must be added in the dissertations appended to the end of this volume, no one will be displeased with us if we refer the reader to those places and proceed without delay to present Cyprianic evidence concerning the other orders.

#### The Election of Bishops

As regards the other bishops, their election was conducted by the bishops of the same province in the presence of the clergy and people, who likewise cast their votes for them. A bishop who had been elected in this regular manner could not be deposed so that another might be elected unless he had committed some extremely grave crime.

This point of discipline is admirably demonstrated by the letter mentioned above, in which the divine Cyprian, speaking about Sabinus’s ordination in the place of Basilides, says that it was carried out “by the vote of the entire brotherhood and by the judgment of the bishops who had assembled in person” [Note: [Col. XXXIII] Cyprian, Ep. LXVIII, vol. III, col. 1027 B.].

The holy Doctor maintains that the election of bishops conducted in the manner just described proceeds “from divine Tradition”—that is, with “Tradition” taken in a broader sense—and “from apostolic observance.” The holy bishop says that this election is therefore to take place in the presence of the people, because the laity know most fully the life of each individual and have perceived each man’s conduct from his manner of life.

Moreover, no others are to be chosen except those who are blameless and upright, so that, by offering sacrifices to God in a holy and worthy manner, they may be heard in the prayers they offer for the safety of the Lord’s people. Cyprian presents us with the form of an episcopal election in his Letter to Antonianus [Note: [Col. XXXIII] Id., Ep. LXII, vol. III, col. 768 ff. See vol. XI, *Critical Theological History*, sect. L, on St. Cornelius, Roman Pontiff, art. 1, p. 2, where we quoted the entire passage.].

### XXXIV. There was to be only one bishop in a single Church

Two bishops could not preside over one and the same Church at the same time. We have this expressly in the letter of Pope St. Cornelius to St. Cyprian concerning the confessors who had returned to unity; they declare [Note: [Col. XXXIII] Id., Ep. XVI, vol. III, col. 722 A.] “that there ought to be one bishop in the Catholic Church,” that is, in each individual Church.

The same point is likewise established from St. Cyprian’s Letter to [Col. XXXIV] Antonianus, in which the holy Doctor, declaring that Cornelius’s election was legitimate, adds [Note: [Col. XXXIII] Id., Ep. LII, vol. III, col. 769 ff.]:

> Whoever now wishes to be made bishop at Rome must necessarily be made so outside.

And the man who is appointed after the election of the first “is no longer a second bishop, but no bishop at all.” St. Cyprian further insists upon this unity of the bishop in his Letter to Florentius Puppianus [Note: [Col. XXXIII] Id., Ep. LXIX, vol. IV, col. 400 ff.].

### XXXV. Bishops governed their own Churches with the consent and counsel of their metropolitans, clergy, and people

Bishops communicated the affairs of their Churches not only to their metropolitan, as is gathered from several of St. Cyprian’s letters, especially Letter LIII, but also to the clergy and people. Hence they governed their Churches with the consent of their metropolitans, clergy, and people; and they sought their counsel even for the ordination of inferior ministers.

St. Cyprian, notwithstanding his exceptional merit and the supreme dignity with which he was distinguished in the Church of Carthage, protests and declares in a certain letter to his clergy that from the beginning of his episcopate he had resolved to do nothing privately according to his own judgment and without the counsel and consent of the clergy and laity.

The same holy Doctor informs his clergy and people about the ordination of subdeacons and the other inferior ministers, and asks the counsel of the clergy and people on this matter. St. Cyprian, therefore, was not one who governed his Church with excessive harshness. From his profound humility we learn that what the same holy Doctor writes elsewhere—namely, that the bishop depends upon no one, that freedom has been granted to him, and that he will render an account of his conduct to the Lord alone—is not to be understood too literally and rigorously.

### XXXVI. A council of bishops was celebrated annually to regulate the affairs of the Church

In the African Church the bishops assembled together to regulate the graver affairs of the Church, as St. Cyprian teaches in a certain letter to his clergy, which is Letter XXXII in the Oxford and Pamelius editions [Note: [Col. XXXIV] Id., Ep. XXXII, vol. IV, col. 306 B.].

These meetings or councils were customarily celebrated every year around the Paschal feasts:

> This is the latest and final trial of this persecution, says Cyprian, and it too, with the Lord’s protection, will soon pass, so that I may be restored to you after Easter Day together with my colleagues. In their presence, in accordance also with your judgment and the common counsel of us all, as was once resolved, we shall be able together to arrange and carefully settle the matters that must be dealt with [Note: [Col. XXXIV] Id., Ep. XL, vol. IV, col. 338 B–C.].

And the same holy Doctor says:

> Since you have written [Note: [Col. XXXIV] Id., Ep. LIII, vol. IV, col. 347 C ff.] that I should discuss this very matter most fully with several colleagues, and since so important an affair requires the greater and more earnest counsel produced by the deliberation of many, and since nearly all are now remaining at home with the brethren during the opening solemnities of Easter, when they have fulfilled their duties in celebrating the solemnity among their own people and begin to come to me, I shall discuss the matter more fully with each of them, so that concerning the matter on which you have consulted us, a firm judgment, weighed by the counsel of many bishops, may be established [Col. XXXV] among us and reported to you in writing.

### XXXVII. In matters of greater importance bishops sent their decisions to other bishops, especially to the Bishop of Rome

In matters of greater importance, bishops, even when assembled in council, sent their decisions to other bishops, intending to await from them both their counsel and their consent, partly to manifest and partly to confirm the priestly authority and, likewise, the unity and dignity of the Catholic Church.

The Africans especially sought the counsel and consent of the Bishop of Rome. This is evident from St. Cyprian’s Letter LXXII to St. Stephen, in which the following occurs [Note: [Col. XXXV] Cyprian, Ep. LXXII, vol. III, col. 1046.]:

> For the settlement of certain matters and their careful examination by common counsel, it was necessary for us, dearest brother, when several bishops had assembled in one place, to convene and celebrate a council. In it many matters were indeed presented and transacted; but above all it was necessary to write to you and confer with your gravity and wisdom about that which especially concerns both priestly authority and the unity and dignity of the Catholic Church, proceeding from the ordering of the divine dispensation: namely, that those who have been baptized outside the Church, and stained among heretics and schismatics by the defilement of profane water, must, when they come to us and to the Church, which is one, be baptized; because it is not enough merely to lay a hand upon them so that they may receive the Holy Spirit, unless they also receive the Church’s baptism. . . . We have conveyed these things to your conscience, dearest brother, both for our common honor and out of sincere affection, believing that, in accordance with the truth of your religion and faith, you too approve those things which are alike religious and true.

Some conclude from this that already in Cyprian’s age it was customary for bishops assembled in synods to seek from the Roman Pontiff confirmation of the decrees established in their councils.

### XXXVIII. No bishop could rescind what had been done by another bishop except for the gravest reasons

Not even the metropolitan was permitted, without the gravest reasons, to rescind what had been done by another bishop. For this reason St. Cyprian rebukes Therapios, as is evident from his Letter LIX (vol. III, col. 1014 A).

Elsewhere [Note: [Col. XXXV] Id., Ep. LXVII, vol. III, col. 997 A.] St. Cyprian observes that “there cannot be” among bishops “a diversity of understanding in those in whom there is one Spirit; and therefore it is evident that the man whom we see thinking differently does not hold the truth of the Holy Spirit together with the others.”

And yet afterward Cyprian and Stephen held different views in the controversy concerning the baptism of heretics. These statements are easily reconciled if we say that the cited judgment of St. Cyprian is to be interpreted as referring to matters of faith, as the context teaches, and not to matters of discipline.

### XXXIX. Bishops sent letters to one another

Bishops customarily wrote to one another as a sign [Col. XXXVI] of mutual communion. Therefore, when a new bishop was appointed, the others took care to be informed of his faith and piety.

The first part of this discipline is gathered from Cyprian’s Letter LXVII to Stephen, in which (vol. III, col. 988 A) the following words occur:

> Inform us plainly who has been appointed at Arles in Marcian’s place, so that we may know to whom we ought to direct our brethren and to whom we ought to write.

The second part is gathered from another letter of the same holy Doctor to Pope St. Cornelius, which in this edition is numbered LV (vol. III, col. 809 A).

They sent these letters through clerics, as is evident from Letter XXIV, where (vol. IV, col. 287 B) the following occurs:

> And since it was proper for me to write through clerics, but I know that very many of ours are absent and that the few who are there are scarcely sufficient for the ministry of the daily work, it was necessary to appoint some new men who could be sent.

It is evident also from another letter to Successus, numbered LXXXII, in which he writes the following to Successus (vol. IV, col. 429 B):

> The reason why I did not write to you immediately, dearest brother, was that all the clerics, being placed under the blow of the conflict, were entirely unable to depart from here.

### XL. The clergy governed the Church in the bishop’s absence

In the bishop’s absence, the Church was governed not by some bishop from elsewhere, but by the clergy. This is clear from Cyprian’s Letter XXXIV to the presbyters and deacons of Carthage. In it, indeed, we read that the clergy of Carthage excluded Gaius of Didda from their communion [Note: [Col. XXXVI] Cyprian, Ep. XXVIII, vol. IV, col. 300 B.].

We further know that, after Fabian’s death, the Roman clergy directed that Church while the see was vacant [Note: [Col. XXXVI] “And since it falls to us, who appear to have been placed in authority”—namely, because after the death of the Roman Bishop the care of that Church fell to the clergy of the city—“to guard the flock in the shepherd’s place, etc.” Cyprian, Ep. II, vol. IV, col. 224 A. See also Ep. XXXI, vol. IV, cols. 307 ff.].

Bishops could do nothing in the dioceses of other bishops without the diocesan bishop’s permission. This is most clearly established both by the Letter to Caldonius and Herculanus, whom St. Cyprian, since they were bishops, had sent to Carthage as his vicars, and to whom he had also joined the presbyters Rogatianus and Numidicus, so that they might provide money for the needy and examine those who were to be promoted to ecclesiastical offices [Note: [Col. XXXVI] Cyprian, Ep. XXXVIII, vol. IV, cols. 329 ff.]; and by Letter LV (vol. III, col. 821 A), in which he expressly declares “that a portion of the flock has been assigned to each pastor, which each one is to rule and govern, rendering an account of his conduct to the Lord.”

Hence he also teaches elsewhere that other bishops ought to involve themselves in the government of another diocese only in a case of necessity, when its own bishop causes heresy or schism [Note: [Col. XXXVI] Id., Ep. to Pope Stephen, LXVII, vol. III, col. 995 A.]. In this matter also St. Cyprian acted with the greatest moderation and prudence, as is gathered from some of his letters [Note: [Col. XXXVI] See Ep. LXIV, to Epictetus and the people of Assuras [Col. XXXVII] concerning Fortunatianus, vol. IV, cols. 389 ff.; and LXVIII, to the clergy and people residing in Spain, vol. III, cols. 1021 ff.].

[Col. XXXVII]

### XLI. Honor shown to bishops from elsewhere

Nevertheless, the holy Doctor and bishop permits his clergy to communicate to bishops from elsewhere, should any happen to be present there, the letters he has sent to them.

> But if any, says St. Cyprian [Note: [Col. XXXVII] Cyprian, Ep. XXXII, vol. IV, col. 316 A–B.], of my colleagues among the visiting bishops . . . are present or should arrive, let them hear all these things from you. And if they wish to copy transcripts of the letters and carry them back to their own people, let them be given permission to make copies.

### XLII. Cases reserved to the bishop

Finally, certain cases were reserved to the bishop, as we readily infer from St. Cyprian’s Letter XVIII and from other passages in his works, in which he grants his presbyters the faculty of absolving certain sins in his absence, provided, however, that a case of necessity exists.

Such, at least, is the opinion of the distinguished Bernard Maréchal [Note: [Col. XXXVII] *Concordance of the Holy Fathers*, vol. II, p. 120, no. X.]. But I, thus far, have been unable to discover in the works of the divine Cyprian any trace whatsoever of the reservation of certain cases or sins; nor do I understand how that same point can be gathered from Letter XLII, vol. IV, col. 255.

### XLIII. What bishops ought to be like according to Cyprian

St. Cyprian teaches that a bishop ought to be teachable and gentle; and the teachable man is one who is mild and gentle in the patience required for learning. For a bishop, the holy Doctor continues, ought not only to teach but also to learn, because he teaches better who grows and advances every day by learning better things [Note: [Col. XXXVII] Cyprian, Ep. LXXIV, vol. III, col. 11.].

Nothing ought to hold a bishop back [Note: [Col. XXXVII] Id., Ep. LV, to Cornelius, vol. III, cols. 796 ff.]. Indeed, he ought to be sacrificed in the presence of the brethren like a victim that provides the brotherhood with an example of virtue [Note: [Col. XXXVII] Id., Ep. LVIII, to Pope Lucius, vol. III, col. 976 A.].

### XLIV. Points of discipline concerning presbyters

Certain authors following Blondel [Note: [Col. XXXVII] *Book on Bishops and Presbyters*, ed. 1646, ch. XVI, p. 41 ff.] believed that they could conclude from Cyprian that bishops did not rank above presbyters. But their gross error has been demonstrated both by very many recent scholars, among them the most learned Mamachi [Note: [Col. XXXVII] *Christian Origins and Antiquities*, vol. IV, book IV, p. 443 ff.], and by Cyprian himself in Letters XI, XXXV, LV, etc. [Note: [Col. XXXVII] Below, vol. IV, col. 247, col. 325, etc.].

Only this must be said here: a bishop was permitted to associate presbyters of another Church with his own clergy. This is proved by the example of the presbyter Numidicus, whom the divine Cyprian enrolled in his own Carthaginian clergy, perhaps so that he might succeed him in the episcopate. For at that time the prevailing discipline was that strangers and outsiders were not to be elected to the episcopate, precisely because of [Col. XXXVIII] the danger of a bad election, lest unworthy men should be chosen when their manner of life was not sufficiently known [Note: [Col. XXXVIII] “That the presbyter Numidicus be enrolled in the number of the presbyters of Carthage.” Cyprian, Ep. XXXV, vol. IV, col. 325 A.].

Moreover, from the example just cited we also properly infer the distinction that St. Cyprian made between an ordinary presbyter and a presbyter of the Carthaginian clergy. For the holy Doctor judges that he could not better acknowledge the merits of Numidicus, who was already a presbyter, than by enrolling him among the presbyters of his own Church.

Let us therefore recognize, writes the distinguished Bernard Maréchal [Note: [Col. XXXVIII] *Concordance of the Holy Fathers*, vol. II, p. 120, Venice edition.], in this passage the superior dignity of the presbyters of cathedral Churches, who are called canons. They attended the bishop in all his duties and functions, were his council, celebrated the holy mysteries with him, and governed the Church in his absence. Such indeed are canons today, and such were the presbyters among whom Numidicus was numbered.

### XLV. Origin of the diaconate

According to Cyprian [Note: [Col. XXXVIII] “Deacons ought to remember that the Lord chose the Apostles, that is, the bishops and prelates, whereas after the Lord’s ascension into heaven the Apostles appointed deacons for themselves as ministers of their episcopate and of the Church.” Cyprian, Ep. LXV, vol. IV, col. 396 B.], the institution of deacons belongs to apostolic tradition, and the order of the diaconate was instituted by the Apostles. Hence, according to St. Cyprian, the order of the diaconate is not of divine institution and therefore, strictly speaking, is by no means a sacrament.

### XLVI. Deacons as ministers of bishops and presbyters

Deacons were not only ministers of bishops but also of presbyters, as St. Cyprian confirms in a letter to his clergy with these words [Note: [Col. XXXVIII] Cyprian, Ep. XXVIII, vol. IV, col. 300 B.]:

> You acted uprightly and with discipline, dearest brethren, in judging that . . . communion ought not to be maintained with the presbyter Gaius of Didda and his deacon.

This Gaius was probably equivalent to what is today called a parish priest, who had a deacon with him to minister to him.

### XLVII. The duties of deacons

The duties of deacons were to serve at the altar and distribute the Eucharist to the faithful [Note: [Col. XXXVIII] Id., book *On the Fallen*, vol. IV, col. 485 A.]. They attended the presbyters as assistants in the celebration of the sacrifice of the Mass, as is gathered from Letter IV (vol. IV, col. 231 A), addressed to the clergy of Carthage:

> Take counsel and make provision,

he says to his presbyters and deacons,

> that the presbyters . . . who make the offering there among the confessors

—he is speaking here about prisoners—

> should each take turns with an individual deacon [Note: [Col. XXXVIII] Id., Ep. XLIX, vol. III, col. 726 B.].

They administered the Church’s revenues, participated in ecclesiastical judgments [Note: [Col. XXXVIII] Id., Ep. LV, vol. III, cols. 822 A ff.], and had a place and role in councils both at Rome and in Africa [Note: [Col. XXXVIII] Ep. to Antonianus, LII, vol. III, cols. 761 ff.]. At times they also governed Churches [Note: [Col. XXXVIII] Cyprian, Ep. LXVIII, vol. III, cols. 1021 ff.].

An example of this [Col. XXXIX] is found in Letter LXVIII, which the divine Cyprian addresses to Felix the presbyter and to the people residing at León and Astorga, and likewise to Laelius the deacon and the people of Mérida. For if even one presbyter had existed in this latter Church, he would have addressed his letter to him rather than to the deacon.

Whatever may be said, it is certain from canon 77 of the Council of Elvira that deacons formerly exercised the government of Churches, though only, as is probable, when presbyters were lacking [Note: [Col. XXXIX] “If any deacon governing a congregation without a bishop or presbyter has baptized any persons, the bishop will be obliged to bring them to completion by a blessing.” Vol. I of Labbe’s *Councils*, p. 978; and in Mansi, vol. II, col. 18.].

### XLVIII. Subdeacons and the other inferior ministers

As regards subdeacons, St. Cyprian frequently mentions them in his letters. See, for example, Letter III (vol. IV, col. 229), addressed to the Roman clergy, for in it he speaks of a certain subdeacon called Crementius [Note: [Col. XXXIX] Cyprian, Ep. II, vol. IV, col. 224 A.]; Letter XXIX, in which St. Cyprian speaks of another subdeacon named Optatus [Note: [Col. XXXIX] Id., Ep. XXIV, vol. IV, col. 287 B.]; and the same holy Doctor’s letter to his clergy concerning the presbyter Gaius of Didda, in which two subdeacons, Philumenus and Fortunatus, are mentioned [Note: [Col. XXXIX] Id., Ep. XXVIII, col. 301 B.]. A certain subdeacon is also mentioned in a letter of the Roman clergy to the divine Cyprian [Note: [Col. XXXIX] Id., Ep. XXX, vol. IV, col. 303 B.].

St. Cyprian more than once mentions acolytes [Note: [Col. XXXIX] The acolyte Favorinus is mentioned in Letter XXVIII, vol. IV, col. 301 B.], as well as readers [Note: [Col. XXXIX] Cyprian, Ep. XXIV, vol. IV, col. 287 B; Ep. XXXIII, col. 319; Ep. XXXIV, col. 324 A–B.] and exorcists [Note: [Col. XXXIX] Id., Ep. LXXVI, vol. III, col. 2. See also Firmilian’s Letter, numbered LXXV among Cyprian’s letters.]. He notes that he was accustomed “to examine whether all the qualities that ought to be present in those who were being prepared for the clergy were suitable in them” [Note: [Col. XXXIX] Id., Ep. XXIV, vol. IV, col. 287 B–C.].

Readers read Holy Scripture and were teachers of the “hearers,” or catechumens [Note: [Col. XXXIX] Id., ibid.]; they also read the Gospel from the pulpit [Note: [Col. XXXIX] Id., Ep. XXXIII, vol. IV, col. 319 B.].

## § VI. Discipline Regarding Marriage, Vows, and the Veneration of Relics

### XLIX

The divine Cyprian has very little to say about marriage, since he speaks about it not expressly and systematically, but only in passing. Hence, in the treatise *On the Fallen*, among the evils committed by the faithful before the persecution, he lists the custom of contracting marriages with unbelievers:

> To join, he says [Note: [Col. XXXIX] Id., book *On the Fallen*.], the bond of marriage with unbelievers is to prostitute the members of Christ to pagans.

In the third book of the *Testimonies*, he attempts to show from certain pronouncements of Sacred Scripture that these marriages are unlawful. Hence, he says [Note: [Col. XXXIX] Id., book III of the *Testimonies*, ch. 62, vol. IV, col. 767 B.], we read [Col. XL] in Tobit [Note: [Col. XL] Tobit IV.]:

> Take a wife from the offspring of your parents, and do not take a foreign woman who is not from the tribe of your parents.

Likewise, in Genesis [Note: [Col. XL] Genesis XIV, 3–4.]:

> Abraham sends his servant to take Rebecca from his own stock as a wife for his son Isaac.

Likewise, in Ezra [Note: [Col. XL] 1 Ezra X.]:

> It was not enough for God, when the Jews were being laid waste, unless they abandoned their foreign wives together with the children they had begotten from them.

The holy Doctor further proves his proposition by other pronouncements of Scripture, such as, for example, these words of Paul [Note: [Col. XL] 1 Corinthians VII, 39; 1 Corinthians VI; and 2 Corinthians VI.]:

> Let her marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord.

St. Augustine, however [Note: [Col. XL] Augustine, book I *On Adulterous Marriages*, ch. 25.], says that these words of the Apostle can be understood in two senses and signify nothing more than that this widow ought either to remain in the Christian religion or to be joined to a Christian man. He then adds that the marriages of Christians with unbelievers are not expressly forbidden in the New Testament.

> For I do not recall,

these are the words of the divine Augustine,

> that, in the time of the revealed New Testament, it is declared without ambiguity in the Gospel or the other apostolic writings whether the Lord prohibited the faithful from being joined to unbelievers. Nevertheless, blessed Cyprian has no doubt about it, nor does he rank among minor sins the joining of the bond of marriage with unbelievers; and he says that this is to prostitute the members of Christ to pagans.

### L. The vow of continence was in use in Cyprian’s age

As regards vows, which have not escaped the unjust censures of the innovators, St. Cyprian teaches that they were in use in his own age. In his treatise *On the Dress of Virgins*, the holy Doctor speaks of certain women “who had dedicated themselves to Christ and, withdrawing from carnal concupiscence, had vowed themselves to God in both body and mind” [Note: [Col. XL] Cyprian, book *On the Dress of Virgins*, vol. IV, col. 443 B.].

Nevertheless, we shall soon see that these vows were not absolute and that those who made vows of this kind could enter into marriage in a case of necessity. But the innovators will at least be unable to deny that, in the third century, vows distinct from the vows of Baptism existed in the Church.

Bishop Pomponius had sent a letter to St. Cyprian, asking and desiring that he write back what he thought concerning those virgins who, after they had once resolved to maintain their state continently and steadfastly, were subsequently discovered to have remained together in the same bed with men [Note: [Col. XL] Id., Ep. LXII, vol. IV, col. 364 B ff. See part XI of the *Critical Theological History*, p. 264 ff.].

St. Cyprian replies, among other things, that virgins ought not only not to sleep with men, but not even to live together with them. The holy Doctor then adds:

> But if they have dedicated themselves to Christ in good faith, let them persevere modestly and chastely, without giving occasion for any gossip. If, however, they are unwilling or unable to persevere, it is better that they marry than that they fall into the fire through their offenses.

This indeed admirably confirms the observation we proposed [Col. XLI] a little above: namely, that vows at that time were not so absolute as to bind even in a case of necessity.

Moreover, St. Cyprian teaches that it is impossible for Christ the Lord not “to be angered and indignant when he sees his virgin, dedicated to him and destined for his holiness, lying with another.” Finally, he asserts that those who fall into these crimes must be punished with excommunication and excluded from the Church’s communion until they have performed penance and disclosed their own offense to everyone by public confession.

### LI. On the relics of the saints

The innovators rise up no less bitterly against the veneration of sacred relics; but in this matter they are equally opposed to the whole of antiquity. We have already demonstrated this in the preceding volumes [Note: [Col. XLI] See *Critical Theological History*, part II, pp. 433–434; part VII, p. 349.] from the authority of certain Fathers of the Church. We now confirm the same point from the divine Cyprian.

St. Cyprian’s eighty-first letter furnishes us with very powerful arguments by which the veneration of sacred relics may be established [Note: [Col. XLI] Cyprian, Ep. LXXXI, vol. IV, col. 424 C ff. See part XI of the *Critical Theological History*, p. 268 ff.].

At the beginning of this letter, the holy bishop declares to the confessors to whom it is addressed—declares, I say—the joy with which he would be filled if ever he could embrace those limbs that had been the instruments of their confession; if he could kiss those mouths that had gloriously confessed the name of Jesus Christ; and if he could be seen by those eyes which, having despised the world, had proved worthy to behold God:

> What could be more desirable or joyful for me, he says [Note: [Col. XLI] Id., loc. cit.], than to embrace those hands which . . . preserving the faith of the Lord, rejected sacrilegious acts of homage? What could be more delightful and sublime than to kiss those mouths that confessed the Lord with a glorious voice?

We shall therefore not deserve ridicule if, from this testimony of St. Cyprian, we conclude that the relics of the saints are to be honored. For if their limbs, while they were still alive, were worthy of veneration, they must certainly be judged worthy of greater veneration after they have departed to the greater number, unless we wish to say that their precious relics become worthless through their glorious death. On the contrary, through death they acquire a new degree of glory.

## § VII. Other Points of Discipline from the Works of the Divine Cyprian
LII. On the Revenues of the Church and Their Use.—The Church had its own income and revenues, which it distributed each month among the clergy for their support. These distributions were called *mensurnae*, as though one were to say “monthly distributions.” Clerics who had fallen into some offense or had failed in their proper duty were deprived of them, as is gathered from the twenty-eighth Epistle, in which St. Cyprian speaks as follows [Col. XLII] [Note: [Col. XLII] Cyprian, Ep. XXVIII, vol. IV, col. 301 B. Cf. Ep. XXXIV, cols. 320 ff.]:

> You also requested that I write back concerning what I think should be done about Philumenus and Fortunatus, subdeacons, and Favorinus, an acolyte, who withdrew in the meantime and have now returned. . . . For the present, let them merely abstain from the monthly distribution, not so as to appear deprived of their ecclesiastical ministry, but so that, with all matters left intact, their cases may be deferred until we are present.

Another portion of these revenues was expended on alms for the poor. For in that age the Church both supported the poor, especially those “who, standing firm in the faith and fighting bravely, did not abandon the camp of Christ” [Note: [Col. XLII] The same, Ep. XXXVII, vol. IV, col. 329 A], and assisted destitute artisans by providing them with something so that they could practice their own trades. The Church’s charity toward the poor is indicated quite clearly in St. Cyprian’s Epistle to Euchratius. Speaking there about a certain actor whom he wished to recall from that infamous profession, he says [Note: [Col. XLII] The same, Ep. LXI, vol. IV, col. 363 A–B]:

> But if such a man pleads the want and necessity of poverty, his need too can be assisted among the others who are maintained by the provisions of the Church.

These alms, however, were moderate, and the poor were obliged to be content with more frugal food, as the same holy Doctor states in the same passage:

> Provided, however,

he says, speaking of the same actor,

> that he is content with more frugal but innocent food.

That the Church assisted poor artisans is proved by the authority of the same holy bishop, who in Epistle XLI addresses those to whom the Epistle was written as follows [Note: [Col. XLII] The same, Ep. XXXVIII, vol. IV, col. 330 A]:

> I sent you as my representatives, so that you might meet the needs of our brethren out of the funds, and, if any also wished to practice their trades, might assist their desires by an additional grant sufficient for the purpose.

For this reason a *corba*, that is, a box for receiving alms, was placed in the churches [Note: [Col. XLII] The same, *On Works and Almsgiving*, vol. IV, col. 612 B]. The faithful, even though poor, supplied “material for the sacrifice” [Note: [Col. XLII] The same, ibid.]; they also paid “tithes” [Note: [Col. XLII] The same, *On the Unity of the Church*, vol. IV, col. 518 B].

LIII. On the Care of the Sick.—Among the ministers of the Church were men entrusted with the duty of carrying the Eucharist to the poor and the sick and of baptizing catechumens who were mortally ill. The Roman clergy write [Note: [Col. XLII] Roman Clergy in Cyprian, Ep. II, vol. IV, col. 227 A–B]:

> We have also added the other matters incumbent upon you: that if any who have fallen into this trial begin to be overtaken by illness, repent of what they have done, and desire communion, assistance must certainly be given to them. Whether they are widows, or persons under affliction (*thlibomeni*) who cannot present themselves, or those who are in prison, or those driven from their homes, there must certainly be persons available to minister to them. Catechumens overtaken by illness must likewise not be disappointed, but assistance must be given to them.

LIV. *Sportulae*.—Besides the monthly distributions listed above [Col. XLIII], there were also others called *sportulae*, and the clerics who shared in them were called *sportulantes*. See what St. Cyprian says about these in his Epistle to Clelus of Furni. We must admit, however, that St. Cyprian did not express his meaning clearly concerning these *sportulae*; nor do the authors who discuss them explain themselves clearly enough for us to establish anything certain on the matter.

Rigaltius considers “to be held in the honor of the *sportulantes*,” as St. Cyprian writes, to mean the same thing as receiving a share in a particular distribution distinct from what the same holy Doctor calls the “monthly distribution” (*divisio mensurna*), which was the general distribution. For our part, we most readily add that only the poorer clergy shared in this particular distribution, which consisted of those alms of the faithful that were deposited in chests. Since these chests resembled a kind of basket, they were called *sportulae*; hence those who obtained from these alms part of what they needed to live were called *sportulantes*. I am of the opinion, however, that because of this special distribution the poor clergy were by no means excluded from the general monthly distribution, which consisted both of the Church’s revenues and of what each member of the faithful was obliged to contribute toward the support of the clergy.

LV. The Canonical Hours.—Besides the three hours of the day appointed for public prayer—namely, the third, sixth, and ninth—St. Cyprian likewise mentions morning prayer, saying [Note: [Col. XLIII] Cyprian, *On the Lord’s Prayer*, vol. IV, col. 543 B–C ff.] that one must pray in the morning so that the Lord’s resurrection may be celebrated by morning prayer. He likewise speaks of another prayer made at the end of the day; this corresponds to the prayer that we call Vespers.

Moreover, I do not know whether what the holy Doctor says in the same place about nocturnal prayers may be interpreted as referring to Vigils [Note: [Col. XLIII] “Let there be no loss of prayers during the hours of the night, no idle and slothful neglect of prayer.” Cyprian, loc. cit., col. 545 A. It is quite well known that Christians held assemblies at night. Tertullian calls them “nocturnal gatherings” in Book II *To His Wife*. Pliny calls them “assemblies before dawn” in his *Letter to Trajan*. But in addition, out of private devotion, the faithful tore themselves from bed and rose during the night to pray, as Tertullian says in the passage cited above. Thus in the *Apologeticum*: “They satisfy themselves in such a way as to remember that they must worship God even during the night.”]. On these premises, we have all the canonical hours except Prime and Compline.

Besides these public prayers, there were others performed in private homes, such as prayer before food, which St. Cyprian mentions in his treatise *To Donatus* [Note: [Col. XLIII] Cyprian, Epistle I, *To Donatus*, otherwise the book *To Donatus*, vol. IV, col. 222 B ff.], and which the same holy Doctor presents as a custom already extremely ancient in his own age.

LVI. On the Visions of the Faithful.—From several passages in the works of St. Cyprian it is clearly evident that in his age “many manifest visions occurred” [Note: [Col. XLIII] The same, Ep. LIV, vol. III, col. 855 A], and that “even the innocent age of children sees with its eyes in ecstasy, and hears and speaks those things by which the Lord deigns to admonish and instruct us” [Col. XLIV] [Note: [Col. XLIV] The same, Ep. IX, vol. IV, col. 253 A]. He reproves those, however, to whom these appeared to be “ridiculous dreams and foolish visions” [Note: [Col. XLIV] The same, Ep. LXIX, vol. IX, col. 407 A].

We may likewise observe from St. Cyprian that black garments were formerly used in times of mourning. For he writes in his treatise *On Mortality* [Note: [Col. XLIV] The same, treatise *On Mortality*, vol. IV, col. 596 A]:

> The dead should be missed, not mourned, nor should black garments be assumed here when they have already received white garments in heaven.

ARTICLE IV. LITERARY ANNALS

§ I. Literary Annals of the Lesser Fathers

NINTH CENTURY

Around the Year 850

THE UNIQUE ARNOBIUS–MINUCIUS MANUSCRIPT.—“Only a single manuscript has thus far been discovered. From it Arnobius first issued and was corrected again and again; it is now in the Royal Library at Paris. It would be desirable for some learned man who has access to this royal manuscript to describe it accurately; to prove with sound arguments in what century it appears to have been written; and, above all, to determine whether it was written in characters or scribal abbreviations so unsightly that distinguished scholars—whom we name in the appropriate place—could repeatedly work upon it, never without harvesting a new crop of variant readings.”

Thus writes the distinguished Schoenemann. Although for more than two centuries all who have read Minucius or Arnobius have unanimously requested this, nevertheless, unless I am mistaken, no one has yet been found to undertake the task energetically—not Arnobius’s latest editor, J. C. Orelli, nor the recent Lyon translator of Minucius, although it was fitting for them above all others to assume this responsibility. Since the others have failed, therefore, we shall say a few words, to the best of our ability, in description of this unique manuscript.

That manuscript, formerly in the Vatican and now preserved in the Royal Library at Paris as a gift from Pope Leo X, under no. 1661—formerly 1344 or 3975—is firmly bound in smooth, elegant, and intact parchment; in quarto format; almost two inches taller than it is wide; gilded and polished on the front, but ornamented on the back with three small golden lilies; enclosed between two wooden boards, with the clasps torn from each; covered on both sides with black calfskin sprinkled with various ornaments, among which the emblems of Henry II and the arms of Diana of Poitiers stand out. It bears no title other than the single name *ARNOBIVS*, affixed both to the cover and to the first folio. It consists of twenty-three gatherings of eight folios, in which sixty-two folios contain Arnobius and twenty-eight contain the *Octavius*.

These are the more noteworthy paleographical and grammatical features. The manuscript is written in an uncial or Carolingian minuscule hand, certainly elegant, pure, and thoroughly genuine, unmixed with any Merovingian or Lombard variety. It is divided at the beginnings of the individual chapters by red [Col. XLV] rustic capitals—the first alone excepted—without any pseudomorphic or decorated letters. The two elements of the diphthong *ae* are usually written separately; yet sometimes, in a practice that appears to derive from Lombard script, they are represented by a single letter *e* with a small hook beneath it. The upper strokes of projecting letters appear to swell at the top. In the letters *m*, *n*, and *u*, the initial strokes sometimes bend to the right, but more commonly to the left. The letter *a* is completed by a tighter lower loop, as in uncial script, and is nowhere enclosed from its apex, as in cursive script; *c*, meanwhile, curves around in a rounded form whenever it occurs.

As for the remaining orthographical rather than paleographical signs, we shall add a few observations. The dative and ablative plural endings are represented merely by a point, for example *nostris pedib.*; *esse* and *esset* appear respectively as *ee* and *eet*; *est* is sometimes written *ê*. The letter *m* is very frequently omitted; each omission is ordinarily indicated by a horizontal stroke. Few ligatures occur, almost none except in the syllables *re* and *ra*, in the conjunction *et*, and where the last letters of one word join the first letters of another. Otherwise, the writing abounds in errors; punctuation is placed at random; and the text is divided into inappropriate sections.

Nevertheless, this unique manuscript of two excellent writers is of the greatest value—indeed, beyond all valuation. Its date is not difficult to determine: from the characteristics described above, especially the forms of the letters *m*, *n*, and *u*, and with the support of many authorities of no mean standing, it may safely be assigned to the first part of the ninth century; it appears nearer the middle than the beginning of that century.

SIXTEENTH CENTURY

In the Year 1542

THE ROMAN EDITIO PRINCEPS.—Minucius Felix, together with Arnobius, based on the sole extant manuscript in the Vatican Library, under the supervision of Faustus Sabaeus of Brescia, printed by Ferrari and Priscoanensis, and dedicated to Francis I, King of France—apparently at the command of Pope Leo X—was published at Rome in folio. [Note: [Col. XLV] Much in this and the following entries is taken from the works of Schoenemann, Lumper, and Ceillier. EDITORS.]

1546

FIRST BASEL EDITION, from Froben’s press, according to the recension of Sigismund Gelenius, with Arnobius, in octavo.

1560

SECOND BASEL EDITION, from Froben’s press, in octavo, in the second edition of Gelenius’s Arnobius.

In the Same Year

HEIDELBERG EDITION, the first issued under the author’s proper name. Francis Baudouin was the first to restore the *Octavius*, which until then had been regarded as the eighth book of Arnobius, to Minucius. Yet Hadrianus Junius, a Dutch physician and the most celebrated philologist of his age, had detected the fraud before Baudouin. Indeed, that honor belongs not to Junius but to Antoine Morillon, secretary and librarian to the Most Eminent Cardinal Granvelle, to whom several letters from Junius are extant and to whom Junius himself assigns this credit in his *Critical Observations*, Book III, chapter 1, new edition, Rotterdam, 1709.

Otherwise, this edition of Baudouin [Col. XLVI] presents the bare text. A preface is added, in which both a defense of Minucius Felix as the true author is offered from the testimony of Jerome and Lactantius and from the difference between his style and form of writing and those of Arnobius, and an outline and analysis of the entire book is presented. Baudouin dedicated his Minucius to Frederick, Elector Palatine, as though he were consecrating with these first fruits of the Muses the University of Heidelberg, which that prince had recently established. From the workshop of Ludwig Lucius, printer, Heidelberg, in octavo.

1580

FIRST PARIS EDITION, together with Tertullian and Arnobius, under the supervision of Laurent de La Barre, in folio.

1583

SECOND ROMAN EDITION, printed by Domenico Basa, according to the corrections of Fulvio Orsini with assistance from the papers of Pedro Chacón; preceded by Arnobius but inscribed with the name of Minucius, in quarto. Whether Orsini did not know, or pretended not to know, that the true author had been identified by Baudouin, he claims that Cardinal Sirleto was the first to recognize it.

1589

SECOND PARIS EDITION, in folio, in the Bodleian Library.

1598

Johannes Meursius’s *Minucian Critique*, together with his *Arnobian Critique*. Leiden, in octavo.

SEVENTEENTH CENTURY

In the Year 1603

SECOND BASEL EDITION, from the Froben bookshop, in octavo. *The Octavius of Marcus Minucius Felix and Cyprian’s On the Vanity of Idols*. Johann von Wower edited it. He supplied no preface. He frequently cites readings that for the most part do not agree at all with the Royal manuscript; they have no credibility, since the good man allowed himself to be deceived by someone who falsely claimed that they were found thus in an excellent manuscript. He prepared his notes, learned though not always appropriately placed, in the space of ten days. In the more difficult passages, however, he had the assistance of the most learned Scaliger.

1603

FIRST HANOVER EDITION. Geverhart Elmenhorst, from Wechel’s press, in octavo, with Arnobius, appears to have published nothing but the bare text in this year. Later he added a vast crowd of authors and passages illustrating the same subject, and nothing besides. This nevertheless gave rise to dissensions, quarrels, and insults between two men; on this matter Scaliger’s Epistles CCLX–CCLXIII should be read.

1605

SECOND PARIS EDITION, from Marc Orry, in octavo, with Arnobius, by Desiderius Heraldus—so Schoenemann. Dom Lumper asks, however, whence Fabricius (*Supplement to the Latin Library*, Book IV, chapter 3) and Ceillier (*General History of Ecclesiastical Authors*, vol. II, p. 233) derive this edition of the year 1605. “This much, however,” he says, “I know with certainty: both this edition and the other issued with Arnobius in 1615 are worthless, since Desiderius Heraldus had already published his Arnobius before Minucius, as he testifies in his Preface to Jean Bochard.”

1610

HEIDELBERG EDITION of Baudouin, reprinted at Frankfurt, in octavo. Fabricius, *Argentoratum Delights*, p. 216.

In the Same Year

[Col. XLVII]

THIRD PARIS EDITION, in folio. (*Catalogue of the Barberini Library*, vol. II, folio, p. 76, and *Catalogue of the Bodleian Library*.)

1612

FIRST HAMBURG EDITION, in folio. *The Octavius of Marcus Minucius Felix, according to the recension and with the commentaries of Geverhart Elmenhorst; with Francis Baudouin’s Prolegomena to the Octavius of Marcus Minucius Felix appended*. Rigaltius observed that Elmenhorst’s notes were interspersed with Wower’s commentaries and that Elmenhorst often cited a manuscript where they should merely have been called readings of the Royal manuscript. He was, of course, citing that manuscript on the authority of Wower, as may be learned from what we wrote above concerning Wower’s edition. Otherwise, in his customary manner, he appends entire pages from ancient authors dealing with a similar subject, believing that Minucius is splendidly illuminated by this cloud of witnesses.

1613

FOURTH PARIS EDITION, Paris, in quarto, printed by Pierre Mettayer. *The Octavius of Marcus Minucius Felix. Desiderius Heraldus emended it with the aid of the Royal manuscript and added notes.*—Compare what we have said concerning Tertullian’s *Apologeticum*, edited by the same man in this year. He had already arranged for the text printed here to be published with Arnobius in 1605; now at last he adorned it with notes learned and refined after his fashion.

In sum, he professes to have followed the Roman edition of Fulvio Orsini under this rule: he would not depart from that edition, which he considered the most faithful of all, unless the Royal manuscript led the way. Thus he retained even readings that revealed their corruption at first glance, and did not follow the example of Sigismund Gelenius, who had not hesitated to alter all such readings—meaning the corrupt ones. Nevertheless, and I wish this to be said in praise of the man, he did not abandon several reasonably good readings of Gelenius but preferred them to those of the Roman edition. He had obtained the Royal manuscript through the kindness of de Thou. He dedicated this little book to Jean Bochard, counselor of the Sacred Consistory, etc.—Fabricius mentions another edition of the *Octavius* with Heraldus’s observations, published with Arnobius in 1615, in quarto; nevertheless, neither Fabricius himself in his treatment of Arnobius nor anyone besides him mentions it. (*Latin Library*, Book IV, chapter 3, Venice edition, vol. II, p. 282; and *Argentoratum Delights*, p. 216.)

1617

TRANSLATION, the very first, FIRST FRENCH VERSION, by Thomas Le Révérend, from the press of Jacques Le Bas, in duodecimo, XV–183–5 pp. (Lyon Library.) Dedicated to the nobleman François Le Révérend, sieur de Calix, the author’s maternal uncle and a royal counselor, etc. It is preceded by a notice to the reader in which the translator is said to be only sixteen years old and presents his proper name there as de Baali Le Révérend. Though young and the very first of all the translators, he is not to be despised.

1624

FIFTH PARIS EDITION. Paris, in folio, in the *Library of the Fathers*, vol. IX, col. 1.

1627

[Col. XLVIII]

FIRST OXFORD EDITION. Oxford, in duodecimo. *The Octavius of Minucius*. (*Catalogue of the British Museum*, under FELIX.)

1636–1637

SECOND FRENCH TRANSLATION. *The Octavius of Minucius Felix Rendered into French* by Nicolas Perrot d’Ablancourt; Paris, from Jean Camusat, in duodecimo, XII–96 pp.; the royal privilege was signed on 3 September 1636, and printing was completed on 24 December of the same year. It was dedicated to Philander, under whose name Conrart is concealed, and published in 1637. Again in 1660, in octodecimo; 1662, in duodecimo; 1677, in duodecimo; thereafter reprinted twenty times, sometimes augmented with the Latin text, sometimes with notes, but never more accurate or faithful than the other translations by the same author.

1636

FIRST ENGLISH TRANSLATION. *M. Minucius Felix his Dialogue, called Octavius*, translated into English by Richard James of Corpus Christi College, Oxford, in octavo.

1637
