THIRD FRENCH TRANSLATION. *The Octavius of Minucius Felix Rendered into French*, through the work of Guillaume Du Mas, canon and dean of the cathedral church of Alet. Paris, from the widow of Toussaint du Bray, in quarto, 16–146–135 pp.

1643

SIXTH PARIS EDITION, FIRST RIGALTIUS EDITION. Paris, from the widow of Mathurin Dupuis, in quarto. *The Octavius of Marcus Minucius Felix and Caecilius Cyprian’s Book On the Vanity of Idols; a New Edition Based on the Authority of Ancient Copies, According to the Recension and with the Observations of Nicolas Rigaltius*. The notes are few but learned and appropriate, as Rigaltius’s usually are. It is preceded by a short preface on the various editions of Minucius’s *Octavius*, written with excellent judgment and modesty. Rigaltius once more consulted the Royal manuscript more carefully and not without benefit.

1645

SECOND RIGALTIUS EDITION. Leiden, from the workshop of Justus Livius, in octavo, folio 12. *The Octavius of Marcus Minucius Felix; Caecilius Cyprian’s On the Vanity of Idols, with the Observations of Nicolas Rigaltius; and Julius Firmicus’s On Profane and True Religion, with Notes by Johann Wower, Together with a New Index*.—Julius Firmicus, according to Wower’s recension, has a separate title page and can stand independently. Both books were prepared according to the bookseller’s commercial interests. Besides Rigaltius’s annotations on Minucius and Cyprian, the materials relating to Minucius include a short index of words and Baudouin’s prolegomena, once again printed.

1645

SEVENTH PARIS EDITION, SECOND RIGALTIUS EDITION. Paris, from Mathurin Dupuis, in quarto; a reprint of the Rigaltius edition. Fabricius, *Argentoratum Delights*, p. 216.

1648

FIRST SCHOOL EDITION. Rouen, from Jean le Boullenger, in duodecimo. *The Octavius of Marcus Minucius Felix*. The text was printed for the use of the Jesuit college at Rouen.

1652

FIRST OUZEL EDITION. Leiden, from the workshop of Jean Maire, in quarto. With the complete notes and commentaries of all previous editors and a new recension by Jacques Ouzel, whose own observations are also included; in addition, the book of Julius Firmicus Maternus, *vir clarissimus*, *On the Error of Profane Religions*, is appended. [Col. XLIX]—The flood of notes produced by this most futile commentator far surpasses all the others in sheer volume. To every single word of Minucius he attached, with incredible dullness and indiscretion, everything relevant and irrelevant scraped together from every quarter. Nor did he draw from a store of his own reading, but from heaps amassed by others with an entirely different purpose.

As for the text, he boasts that he accomplished many excellent things in the separation and punctuation of the words; let the judgment concerning them rest with others. Ouzel dedicated his work to Christina of Sweden. Firmicus was edited according to Wower’s recension and with Wower’s observations alone.

1666

EIGHTH PARIS EDITION. Paris, from Jean Dupuis, in folio, with the works of Cyprian, according to Prieur’s edition.

1671–1672

The epistles of Sts. Cornelius, Lucius, Stephen, and others in the *Collection of Councils*, edited at Paris under the supervision of Fathers Labbe and Cossart, one volume in folio.

1672

SECOND OUZEL EDITION. Leiden, from the Hackius press: a reprint of Ouzel’s edition, though not reproduced exactly. In an arrangement ingeniously devised by the printers, the whole mass of notes—which in the first Ouzel edition marched in procession after the text—here presses upon the text itself. Thus, because the observations of the individual authors, distinguished by numbers, are repeated six times or more alongside the same lines, one can scarcely discern the text amid the text.

They newly added, likewise broken into pieces, Meursius’s *Minucian Critique*. Finally, in the most amusing development of all, a separate heading, “Variant Readings,” appears among the observations of the other commentators. You will scarcely guess where these readings were brought from unless you have a thorough knowledge of this bookseller’s diligence in embellishing the edition. They are, in fact, the variant readings that Elmenhorst presented separately at the end of his edition. Just as he had gathered them from the individual annotations of previous editors, so the printers reproduced each in its proper place and then printed them again as a collection.

1678

SECOND OXFORD EDITION, THIRD RIGALTIUS EDITION. Oxford, with the notes of Nicolas Rigaltius. (*Giornale di Roma*, 1679, p. 137; Fabricius, loc. cit.)

1682

SECOND ENGLISH TRANSLATION. *A Dialogue, by Marcus Minucius Felix*, translated into English by P. Lorrain; London, in octavo. Reprinted there in 1695, in duodecimo.

1683

DUTCH EDITION. Amsterdam, in duodecimo, with a new, best, and very rare reprinting of d’Ablancourt’s French translation placed opposite the text.

1685

[Col. L]

Peter Anton Burchard of Schleswig, *Dissertation on Minucius*, which he placed before theses excerpted from Minucius’s books and a *Minucian Chrestomathy*, under this title: *The Octavius of Marcus Minucius Felix—not the Eighth Book of Arnobius—or Minucius’s Most Elegant Dialogue in Defense of the Truth of the Christian Religion, Arranged as Theses*, which he defended under the presidency of the Blessed Dr. Kortholt. Kiel, in quarto. See Moller, *Literary Cimbria*, I, 81.

1689

The Passion of Sts. Felicitas, Perpetua, and the Holy Martyrs, among the *Authentic Acts of the Martyrs*, edited at Paris under the supervision of Dom Thierry Ruinart; in quarto; reprinted at Amsterdam in 1713 and Verona in 1731.

1689

FIRST LEIPZIG EDITION. Leipzig, in duodecimo, with d’Ablancourt’s French translation placed opposite the text. Fabricius, loc. cit., p. 217.

1696

SECOND DUTCH TRANSLATION, from the Elzevir presses, in duodecimo.

1698

L. E. Dupin, on Minucius, in the *New Library of Ecclesiastical Authors*, vol. I, in quarto.

1699

FIRST HALLE EDITION, SECOND SCHOOL EDITION. Halle, at the expense of Johann Friedrich Zeitler and Heinrich Mussel, in octavo. *The Octavius of Minucius and Cyprian; Both Revised and Illustrated by Christoph Cellarius*.—To serve the needs of schools—in keeping with the diligence of this man, who deserved exceedingly well of the young—he arranged for the text of Minucius to be printed in a form improved by the observations of earlier editors and also of Johann Friedrich Gronovius, to whom he deservedly gives first place. He explained it with notes that were neither numerous nor lengthy, but excellent and beneficial to readers at every point, whether they concerned the reading itself, history and mythology, or, finally, Latinity.

He added Cyprian’s little book following Wower’s text, and Baudouin’s dissertation as well. Finally, because they had been supplied only later, after the text had already been printed, certain observations by Jacob Perizonius were added at the end. Lastly—and this is no small merit of the book—he was the first to divide Minucius’s text appropriately into chapters and paragraphs.

EIGHTEENTH CENTURY

1703

THIRD ENGLISH TRANSLATION. *A Dialogue, by Marcus Minucius Felix*, translated into English by M. Combe. London, in octavo.

1707

DAVIES EDITION, THIRD SCHOOL EDITION. Cambridge, printed by the University Press at the expense of John Owen, in octavo.—*The Octavius of Minucius, with the Complete Observations of Nicolas Rigaltius and Selections from Others, Revised and Furnished with His Own Notes by John Davies*.—Francis Baudouin’s dissertation is placed first, and indexes of subject matter and Latinity are appended.

Since Davies considered Rigaltius the leader of the whole company of Minucius’s interpreters, although he conceded that Rigaltius was not safe from every danger of error, he took particular care with his work. Yet he did not neglect the others, nor did he allow observations on Minucius made here and there by learned men while treating other subjects to escape him, whenever any usefulness could be found in them. He adopted Cellarius’s division of the text. Otherwise, this most learned man judges his own work very modestly, although for educating and sharpening young minds it is more useful than the works of many others. [Col. LI]

1708

FOURTH ENGLISH TRANSLATION. *M. Minucius Felix’s Octavius and Tertullian’s Apology for the Primitive Christians*. London, in octavo.

1709

GRONOVIUS EDITION. Leiden, from Cornelis Boutesteyn and Samuel Luchtmans, in octavo.—*The Octavius of Minucius, with the Complete Notes of Wower, Elmenhorst, Heraldus, and Rigaltius, and Others Collected from Various Sources, According to the Recension of Jacob Gronovius, Who Added His Own Corrections and Explanations. Caecilius Cyprian and Julius Firmicus Maternus Are Appended.*—I suppose the booksellers had to be granted this much: that Gronovius should permit the complete notes of the men praised on the title page to be repeated, although he, if anyone, passed a sound judgment upon them.

As a second part of his plan, he carefully sought out and examined scholarly work on Minucius published elsewhere—that is, annotations written on passages of Minucius when occasion arose in commentaries on various authors, whether for illustration or correction. In this connection he especially values Price’s notes on Apuleius.

What study he himself devoted to Minucius will, I think, be best shown by his own words:

> The doctrine implanted in the Dialogue had supplied a cheerful abundance. Moreover, I carried the subject matter of the little book fixed in my memory, and reverence was present for the Latin diction employed so chastely by the writer; thus, having pursued various matters in the course of reading, I was ready for an immense comparison. Although, besides Sabaeus and Orsini and besides Heraldus and Rigaltius, Joseph Scaliger and Salmasius too had worked on collating the manuscript that is at Paris, nevertheless, for a long time I learned of no one journeying there whom I did not exhort and urge to inspect it once again. This very thing also provided the occasion for a sharpened keenness in detecting various possibilities and in restoring the ancient hand or bringing forward the writer’s intended meaning, from which others wandered even while judging themselves especially successful and acute.

At the passage in chapter XXI concerning the Ephesian Diana constructed with spits, he appended an entire dissertation by Lucas Holstenius—certainly a learned and indeed ingenious dissertation, but one whose substance alone might perhaps more suitably have been given [Note: [Col. LI] See above, where we thought that the same dissertation ought to be published. EDITORS.].

Do not, however, be offended that he devotes himself wholly to attacking and ridiculing Ouzel, who scarcely deserved even to be named by him: one must know Jacob Gronovius. That age delighted in placing coins and engraved figures in editions of ancient authors; they contribute nothing to their utility.

1709

The first separate edition of certain works of Novatian, under this title: *An Uncertain Author’s On the Rule of Truth or Faith, Commonly Called Novatian’s Book On the Trinity, Transcribed According to the Text of Pamelius and Illustrated by No Observations*, under the supervision of William Whiston, in *Sermons and Essays upon Several Subjects*.

1709–1716

FIFTH ENGLISH TRANSLATION. *Octavius . . . Translated with Notes . . .* [Col. LII] by William Reeves . . . printed with *The Apologies of the Primitive Fathers*. London, two volumes in octavo.

1711

SECOND DAVIES EDITION. Cambridge, in octavo. According to John Davies’s second recension, with the notes of various scholars and with Commodian added. Cf. *Acta Eruditorum*, vol. IV, supplement, p. 423; *Bibliothèque choisie*, vol. XVIII, p. 341; *Memoirs of Literature*, vol. I, p. 353; *Mémoires de Trévoux*, vol. II, p. 888; *Bibliothèque choisie*, vol. XXIV, p. 120.

1712

THIRD DUTCH TRANSLATION, under the supervision of D. Gargon, Flushing, in octavo.

1715

Dom Nicolas Le Nourry, *Dissertation on the Octavius of Minucius*, vol. II of the *Apparatus*.

In the Same Year

The epistles of Sts. Cornelius, Lucius, Stephen, and others in Jean Hardouin’s largest collection of councils. Paris, in folio, vol. I.

1721

The epistles of the same persons, edited by Dom Pierre Coustant in his excellent and insufficiently praised work entitled: *The Epistles of the Roman Pontiffs and Those Written to Them, from St. Clement I to Innocent III*, etc.

1724

SECOND ENGLISH EDITION OF NOVATIAN. Oxford, from the Sheldonian Theatre, in octavo. *All the Extant Works of Novatian, Published Far More Correctly than Ever Before and Illustrated with Notes by Edward Welchman.*

The little works preserved among those of Tertullian and another [text] appended to Cyprian’s Epistles are presented. Welchman, opposing Whiston, reproduced Gelenius’s text. He says that “with the greatest care he applied a healing hand to all the errors from which it suffered throughout, both in words and in the division of clauses.”

For these claims he endured Jackson’s sharp and not wholly undeserved criticism. Jackson objected that by following Gelenius he had reintroduced errors removed by Pamelius and had, on the whole, left more errors than he eliminated, although he could easily have cleansed away a large proportion of them if he had not neglected the English manuscript transcribed by Pamelius and had not remained entirely ignorant of Fulvio Orsini’s manuscript observations copied by Johann Wower, which he could have obtained.

Jackson adds a second criticism: Welchman had indeed restored dislocated chapters to their proper places, but in this had a predecessor in the author of the *Reply against Dr. Waterland’s Defense of Certain Questions Published by Him concerning the Controversy over the Trinity*, yet did not mention him; and as for the brief notes, he added merely one or two and a very imperfect index of passages of Holy Scripture. This will perhaps appear to many to have been stated by Jackson somewhat unfairly.

1728

THIRD ENGLISH EDITION OF NOVATIAN. London, printed by John Darby and T. Brown, at the expense of John Noon in the street called Cheapside, next to the Mercers’ Chapel.—*All the Surviving Works of Novatian, Presbyter of Rome, Corrected According to Earlier Editions after the Recension of Jacob Pamelius of Bruges and Purged of Many Errors; Also Illustrated with Very Copious Observations* [Col. LIII] *and Notes, in Which the Author’s Entire Argument concerning the Rule of Faith Is Discussed at Length from the Monuments of the Ancient Fathers. Preceded by a Dissertation on the Son of God as Homoousios (ὁμοούσιος), or Co-essential with the One God the Father. By John Jackson, Presbyter of the Church of England and Prebendary of Wherwell in the County of Hampshire.*

Besides the material contained in the preceding edition, this one also includes the second Epistle of the Roman clergy to Cyprian, of which we spoke above. As for the method he followed in reviewing the text, he declares that he never departed from the Pamelian copy unless the author’s meaning and reasoning plainly required correction, or he had other authoritative supporters or the testimony of manuscripts on his side.

In this matter he acknowledges that he owed something to Latino Latini and François du Jon, but that he had received the greatest assistance from the English manuscript and Fulvio Orsini’s manuscript notes. He relates that he expended a great deal of labor in comparing the different translations of Scripture and the citations of the ancient Fathers with the archetypal text, so that he might gather together and present to the reader all noteworthy variant readings deducible from any text cited by Novatian.

> I undertook this labor,

he says,

> not because I wished everyone to think that I had accomplished something, but because I wished, if possible, to move others by my example to follow this method in editing ancient books and to collect all the variant readings of every passage of Scripture cited in each writer; and I trust that this will contribute greatly to advancing the correction and knowledge of Holy Scripture.

Finally, the many careful notes and observations, the learned prolegomena, the very full indexes, and the evident care devoted even to lesser matters show that Jackson performed the editor’s office admirably.

1730–1740.

Various scholars’ notes and commentaries on the *Octavius* of Minucius Felix, among them the critical notes of J. Jortin, as Saxius supposes in the *Onomasticon*, in *Miscell. Observat.*, vol. I, t. I, p. 23; vol. II, t. III, pp. 408–409; vol. III, t. I, pp. 19–22; t. II, pp. 177–181; t. III, pp. 322–324.—Jeremiah Markland’s, in vol. II, t. I, pp. 54–60.—Thomas Wopkens’s, in vol. IX, t. I, pp. 51–73; vol. X, t. I, pp. 11–54.—Heumann’s *Second Course*, in vol. VII, part II, pp. 247–272; *Third Course*, ibid., part III, pp. 421–478; *Fourth Course*, vol. VIII, part I, pp. 115–134; *Fifth and Final Course*, part III, pp. 454–479.—Fr. Otto Mencke’s *Modest Critical Review* (Ἐπίκρισις modesta) of what the celebrated Heumann observed concerning Minucius Felix. Ibid., vol. V, quarto, p. 729.

1730.

Dom Remy Ceillier, O.S.B., *Histoire générale des auteurs ecclésiastiques*, article “Minucius,” t. III, p. 223.

1733.

*On St. Stephen, Pope and Martyr*, among the Bollandist *Acta Sanctorum*, for August 2, t. I, pp. 112–146, by Peter Bosch.

1736.

Christopher August Heumann, an observation by which Minucius Felix is removed from the number of jurisconsults, in his *Parerga, or Additions to Learning of Every Kind*. Göttingen, octavo.

1738.

*An Apologetic Letter of Marcus Minucius Felix on Behalf of Himself and His Standing, Addressed to Franz Otto Mencke*, in which Heumann’s observation is refuted, in *Nova Acta Eruditorum*, year 1738, p. 210.

1743.

**FIRST GRONOVIUS EDITION.** Rotterdam, published by Johann Daniel Beman.—Reprinted from Gronovius’s recension, edition of 1709.

1750.

**SECOND DAVIS EDITION.** Glasgow, at the University Press, printed by Robert and Andrew Foulis, University printers, quarto. *M. Octavius*, according to John Davis’s recension. The text, together with an index, was printed with the customary elegance.

1751.

Johann Werner Meiner, *Several Passages of Minucius Felix Improperly Disturbed, Vindicated from the Suspicion of Corruption*. Langensalza, quarto.

1752.

**FIRST GERMAN VERSION.** The *Octavius* of Minucius Felix, translated by J. F. Hollander, appeared at Frankfurt, octavo.

1754–1755.

Gruner’s critical observations among the *Proceedings of the Latin Society of Jena*, vol. III, p. 33; vol. IV, p. 208; see p. 220.

1756.

**FIRST ITALIAN VERSION.** Venice, published by Simone Occhi, octavo: *The Octavius of M. Minucius Felix, Translated into Italian, with the Latin Text on the Facing Page, and Illustrated with Appropriate Notes by Dom Marco Poleti, Cleric Regular of Somasca.*—The undertaking turned out by no means badly for the editor. (Paitoni, *Biblioteca degli autori antichi Greci e Latini volgarizzati*, II, 250; Gamba, *Serie dei testi di lingua*, no. 2354.)

1760.

**FIRST LINDNER EDITION.** Langensalza, at the expense of Johann Christian Martini, octavo.—The *Octavius* and Cyprian’s *On the Vanity of Idols*;—both revised and illustrated with selected notes of various scholars, as well as his own, by Johann Gottlieb Lindner, then deputy headmaster of the school at Langensalza, with a preface by Johann August Ernesti. The first merit of this edition is the editor’s diligence and care; its second is that it presents, judiciously selected, those contributions which learned men had offered in various places since Gronovius’s time for polishing, elucidating, and even obscuring Minucius; its third is that the editor follows a modest and exact critical method, which, in accordance with the precepts of the great Ernesti, is occupied more with defending and explaining the received reading than with exercising conjecture; and its final merit is that it repeats briefly and summarily—yet without loss of clarity—the sound observations of others and, in general, takes the greatest care over style. Ernesti’s preface instructs that the reading of sacred writers should be joined to that of the earlier Greek and Roman writers. Finally, in addition to Baudouin’s dissertation, there are appended Holstenius’s letter and a threefold index.

1762.

[Col. LV]

J. D. van Hoven, *Historical-Critical Letter on the True Age, Rank, and Native Country of Marcus Minucius Felix*, Kampen, quarto. He argued with great vigor that Minucius flourished before Tertullian, in the time of Marcus Antoninus. This letter was reprinted in the author’s *Critical and Antiquarian Gleanings* and in Lindner’s second supplement to Minucius Felix.

1763.

**SECOND GERMAN VERSION.** The *Octavius*, translated by Magnus Gottfried Lichtwer, octavo.

1766.

**GALLANDI EDITION.** In the new collection of the *Ancient Fathers*, t. II, Venice, folio, following Davis’s twofold recension, with selected notes by various scholars bearing upon the purification of the text.

1767.

The works of St. Cornelius and Novatian in the same collection of Gallandi, t. III, pp. 278–287 and 333–362, Venice, folio.

1778.

**SECOND LINDNER EDITION.** The distinguished Lindner published Minucius at Langensalza after further revision, octavo. In this new edition, following the example of the most learned men Gesner and Heyne, he judged that variant readings, scholars’ conjectures, and matters pertaining solely to textual criticism (κρίσις) should be separated from the rest, lest they weary readers who have little taste for such things. He then brought back beneath the text the annotations which he had formerly relegated to the indexes, and which few or no readers sought there. He examined each point more carefully, and wherever he had erred he did not hesitate candidly to admit it. In place of Baudouin’s dissertation, sufficiently well known and readily available in our lands, he also supplied the letter of the distinguished van Hoven, *On the True Age of Minucius*, and appended to it several brief excursuses which would, however, have exceeded the proper limits of notes.

1781.

**SIXTH ENGLISH VERSION.** *A Dialogue by Marcus Minucius Felix*, Edinburgh, octavo. The anonymous author deserves to have his name disclosed: namely David Dalrymple, who rendered excellent service to Minucius.

1782.

**STAHEL EDITION.** Würzburg, at the Stahel press, octavo, together with t. II of the *Works of Cyprian*, edited by Oberthür.

1786.

An abridged **FRENCH VERSION** of the *Octavius*, by the Abbé de Gourcy, in t. I of the work entitled *Des anciens Apologistes de la Religion*.

1786.

Fr. Ph. Gourdin, well versed in literary and antiquarian matters, wrote to Dom Grappin, O.S.B., in this year that he was on the point of publishing a new French version of Minucius; it has remained undiscovered to the present day.

1791.

G. F. Stephan Stierer, *Several Critical Observations on Certain Passages of P. Virgil and Minucius Felix*. Ausp. [abbreviation unresolved], quarto.

1792.

[Col. LVI]

**FIRST SPANISH VERSION.** The *Octavius* in the work entitled: *Colecion de los apologistas de la Religion cristiana, reunida por el señor Abbate del Gourcy, traduceda al castellano et dedicata al sabio Clero de España por D. Manuel Imeno y Urriera* [*Collection of the Apologists of the Christian Religion, Gathered by the Abbé de Gourcy, Translated into Spanish and Dedicated to the Learned Clergy of Spain by Don Manuel Imeno y Urriera*]. Madrid, t. II, quarto.

## NINETEENTH CENTURY

1823.

**FIRST FRENCH VERSION.** The *Octavius*, by Antoine Péricaud, revised by C. Breghot du Lut, preceded by Tertullian’s *Apologeticus* and treatise *On Prescriptions*.

1824.

**FIFTH FRENCH VERSION.** The same *Octavius*, the work of Dom M. N. S. Guillon, in volume III of his *Select Library of the Fathers of the Latin and Eastern Church*.

1824.

H. Meier, *Dissertation on Minucius Felix*, Zürich, octavo.

1836.

**SIXTH FRENCH VERSION**, by J. D. Buchon, who included it in the collection called *Panthéon*, under this title: *Choix de monuments primitifs de l’Église chrétienne* [*Selection of Primitive Monuments of the Christian Church*], quarto.

1836.

**DE MURALT EDITION** of the *Octavius*, edited by Eduard de Muralt, Zürich, octavo. Appended is a dissertation on the age of Minucius.

1836.

**LÜBKERT EDITION** of the same author, with notes; and the **FOURTH GERMAN VERSION**, edited by Dr. H. B. Lübkert. Leipzig, octavo.

1839.

**SEVENTH FRENCH VERSION.** The *Octavius* among selected works of the Fathers translated into French under the name of Dom Genoude, in t. IV of the collection; Paris, octavo.

1843.

The **FOURTH FRENCH VERSION**, published again by the same Dom Péricaud, with the Latin text according to Lindner’s second edition, enlarged with very many notes, and especially splendidly adorned with dissertations by the most learned Greppo.

1844.

**NEW PARIS EDITION OF MINUCIUS FELIX**, namely the edition which we here present, according to the evidence of the single surviving manuscript, diligently collated, with selected notes by Lindner, Rigault, Heraldus, Wower, Gronovius, Gruner, Elmenhorst, Heumann, Cellarius, Mencke, Davis, Ouzel, Wopkens, Gallandi, Meursius, etc., without neglecting the assistance supplied by more recent editors and translators; preceded by Dom Lumper’s introductory essays, Ernesti’s letter, Baudouin’s dissertation, and Lindner’s synoptic and logical analysis; and carefully supplemented with the letter of Lucas Holstenius and Nicolas Le Nourry’s dissertation on Minucius; edited by the publisher of this Library, J. P. Migne, Paris, quarto.

## § II. Literary Annals of Cyprian

[Col. LVII]

## THIRD CENTURY

### Year 246

**CYPRIAN**, having professed himself a Christian from the year 243 and having devoted two years vigorously to sacred literature, made his beginning as a writer on behalf of his faith in the letter *To Donatus*. (Morcelli; see below, col. 142.)

247–248.

He first wrote the short work *On the Vanity of Idols*. (Pearson, Morcelli.)—Many hold the opinion that, while still a presbyter, he wrote the three books of *Testimonies against the Jews*, and likewise the book *On the Dress of Virgins*. (Morcelli, Maran.)

249.

When the Decian persecution arose at the beginning of his episcopate, Cyprian is believed to have written Epistle LXVI (Maran); Epistle LXII (Morcelli); Epistles LXI and LXV (Pearson).

250.

While the persecution was raging, the Cyprianic Epistles III and IV appear to have been written, as well as thirteen mentioned in Epistle XV, of which seven survive, namely V, IX, X, XII, XIII, and XIV, sent to Rome with XV; then the letters of Cyprian and of the confessors of Carthage and Rome, in approximately the following chronological order: XIX, XX; XVII, XVIII, XXII; XXI; XXIII, XXV; XXIV, XXVII; XXVIII, XXIX; XXXI, XXVI; XXXII, XXX; XXXVII; VIII; XVI, XXXV, XXXIII, XXXIV, VII, VI, XXXVI, XXXVIII, XXXIX; to which perhaps Epistles XVI and XXXV should be added. (Maran, Morcelli.)

251.

To this year are assigned Epistle XI, while Cyprian was still in exile; the book *On the Lapsed*, after his return; the delegates’ Epistles LXI, XLII, XLIII, and XLIV; then the book *On the Unity of the Church*; thereafter Epistles XLV, LXVIII, XLVI, L; XLIX, XLVII, and LI. (Maran, Morcelli.)

252.

At the beginning of the year, Epistle LII (Maran, Pearson); a little later LV (Morcelli); between these, the short work *On the Lord’s Prayer*; around Easter, Epistle LIII; then Epistles LIX and LXIV, followed by LV, LVI, LIV, and LVII (Maran, Morcelli); at the end of the year, LVIII and LXXXI. (Maran, Pearson, Morcelli.)

253.

The book *To Demetrianus* (Morcelli); *On Works and Almsgiving* (Maran, Morcelli); Epistle LX (Maran).

254.

Epistles LXIX, LXVII, and LXVIII. (Maran, Morcelli, Pearson.)

255.

Around autumn, Epistle LXX, then LXXI. (Maran.) The Seventh Council of Carthage, otherwise called the Third, and Firmilian’s Epistle, according to Morcelli’s opinion.

256.

Shortly after Easter, Epistles LXXII, LXXIII, LXXIV, and LXXVI; the aforesaid council, together with Firmilian’s Epistle, according to the opinion of Dom Maran; as winter approached, Epistles LXXV and LXIII. (The same.) The books *On Patience* and *On Jealousy and Envy*. (Maran, Pearson, Morcelli.)

257.

[Col. LVIII]

Epistles LXXVII, LXXVIII, LXXIX, and LXXX; the book *An Exhortation to Martyrdom*. (Maran, Morcelli.)

258.

Epistles LXXXII and LXXIII, shortly before his martyrdom.

## FOURTH CENTURY

### Years 300–328

**LACTANTIUS**, *Divine Institutes*, book V, chapter 1:

> “Cyprian, then, stood forth as the one preeminent and illustrious writer, both because he had won great renown through the profession of rhetoric and because he composed a very large number of works, admirable in their kind. For his talent was fluent, abundant, agreeable, and—what is the greatest virtue of discourse—clear, so that one cannot determine whether he was more ornate in expression, more successful in exposition, or more powerful in persuasion. Yet beyond his words he cannot please those ignorant of the mystery, because the things of which he spoke are mystical and designed to be heard by the faithful alone. Consequently, he is commonly ridiculed by the learned men of this age to whom his writings have happened to become known. I myself heard a certain decidedly eloquent man who, by changing one letter, called him ‘Coprianus’—from the Greek word κόπρος or κοπρία, in Latin *dung*, as though ‘dung-like’—as one who had devoted an elegant intellect, suited to better things, to old women’s tales.”

**EUSEBIUS**, in the *Chronicle*:

> Κυπριανὸς, Καρθαγένης ἐπίσκοπος, τῷ ὑπὲρ Χριστοῦ μαρτυρίῳ τελειοῦται.
>
> “Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, is perfected through martyrdom for Christ.”
>
> “Cyprian, first a rhetorician, then a presbyter, and finally bishop of Carthage, is crowned with martyrdom.”

353–368.

**HILARY**, *Commentaries on Matthew*:

> “Cyprian, a man of holy memory.”

373–390.

**PACIAN**, Epistle 2:

> “Cyprian suffered amid the concord of all, in the peace shared by all, and in the company of confessors; he confessed the faith repeatedly through successive persecutions, was tormented by much laceration, and at the last was given the saving cup to drink.”

328–391.

**ST. GREGORY NAZIANZEN**, Oration XVIII, otherwise XXIV:

> “These are the things which we had to say concerning Cyprian, and I hardly know whether it is necessary to say more; for even if we were to extend our discourse at length, we could nevertheless offer nothing that would in any respect correspond to his virtues and to the esteem in which each person holds him.”

Paris edition, p. 440 and following.

400.

**PRUDENTIUS**, Hymn XIII:

> Cease weeping for so great a righteous man: he possesses heaven’s realms,  
> Yet no less hovers over earth, nor does he withdraw from this world.  
> He expounds, speaks, treats, teaches, instructs, and prophesies.  
> Nor does he govern Libya’s peoples only: from the rising  
> Of the sun even to its setting, he cherishes the Gauls and schools the Britons;  
> He presides over Hesperia and plants Christ among the farthest Iberians.  
> In short, on earth he is a Teacher, and likewise in heaven a martyr;  
> Here he instructs humanity; there, as patron, he bestows holy gifts.

## FIFTH CENTURY

[Col. LIX]

### Years 382–420

**ST. JEROME**, *Catalogue of Illustrious Men*:

> “Cyprian the African at first taught rhetoric with distinction; thereafter, at the persuasion of the presbyter Caecilius—from whom he also acquired his cognomen—he became a Christian and distributed all his property to the poor. Not long afterward, having been chosen as a presbyter, he was also appointed bishop of Carthage. It is superfluous to compile an index of the works of his genius, since his works are clearer than the sun. He suffered under the emperors Valerian and Gallienus, during the eighth persecution, on the same day as Cornelius at Rome, though not in the same year.”

*Letter to Paula*:

> “Blessed Cyprian advances sweetly and calmly, like the purest fountain; and although he is wholly engaged in the exercise of the virtues and beset by the hardships of persecutions, he did not discourse upon the divine Scriptures.”

*Commentary on Jonah*, chapter 3:

> “Let us set before ourselves Blessed Cyprian, who was formerly a defender of idolatry and attained such distinction in eloquence that he even taught oratory at Carthage; who at last heard Jonah’s message and, being converted to repentance, attained such virtue that he publicly preached Christ and bent his neck to the sword for him.”

430.

**ST. AUGUSTINE.**—No one is unaware of the great veneration with which St. Augustine regarded this great bishop of Carthage, how highly he valued his works, and how many excellent lessons and instructions he found even in all that the holy Martyr wrote concerning the repetition of Baptism. It is enough merely to say that St. Augustine loved the eloquence of the divine Cyprian, but at the same time asserted that it was exceedingly difficult to attain the same excellence (book IV, *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter 14). Elsewhere, however, he says:

> “The authority of Cyprian does not alarm me” (book II, *On Baptism*), “because Cyprian’s humility restores me; we certainly know the great merit of Cyprian, bishop and martyr.”

> “No tongue would suffice for the praises of Cyprian, that revered bishop and venerable martyr, not even if he himself were to praise himself” (*Sermon 313 on St. Cyprian*).

> “I could in no way believe that Cyprian—a Catholic bishop, a Catholic martyr, and one who humbled himself before everyone in proportion to his greatness, that he might find grace before God—especially in the holy council of his colleagues, put forward anything other than what he carried in his heart” (book III, *On Baptism*, chapter 3).

> “Following, in accordance with our weakness, the authority of the Catholic Church, of which he is himself an eminent and most illustrious member, let us resolve the question against heretics and schismatics” (book VII, *On Baptism*, chapter 1).

> “Even Pelagius himself, the heresiarch of these men, certainly mentions with due honor the most blessed Cyprian, rendered most glorious also by the crown of martyrdom, who was exceedingly well known not only to the African and Western churches but also to the Eastern churches, as his fame proclaimed him and his writings were disseminated far and wide” (Augustine, book IV, *To Boniface*, chapter 8).

387–465.

[Col. LX]

**ST. MAXIMUS OF TURIN** has two homilies for the feast day of St. Cyprian: one, LXXIX, cols. 255–258; the other, LXXX, cols. 259–260; Rome edition, 1784.

492–496.

**ST. GELASIUS**, Roman pontiff, in his decree *On Ecclesiastical Writings*: “The short works of Cyprian, martyr and bishop of Carthage,” t. IV of Labbe’s *Collection of Councils*, cols. 12, 62; Hardouin, t. II of the *Collection of Councils*, col. 942; and Mansi, t. VIII, col. 161 and following. The works of this Father are indeed listed in the Gelasian Decree among those rejected by the Roman Church as apocryphal: “The apocryphal short works of Thascius Cyprian,” says the author of this Decree. Yet, apart from other considerations which clearly prove that the quoted words were added to Gelasius’s Decree by some outsider, this is most powerfully demonstrated from Gratian; for Gratian lists the works of the divine Cyprian not among the apocryphal books, but among the books approved by the Church. See Tillemont, note 52, *sur S. Cyprien*, t. IV, p. 33.

# MANUSCRIPTS

## FOURTH–SEVENTH CENTURIES

**Paris Manuscript I.** In the Royal Library, under no. 712 of the Latin Supplement; formerly at Saint-Germain under nos. 185–186; previously preserved in the Coislin Library. It was perhaps received from Italy, as the Benedictine monks conjecture. It is in nearly square quarto format, composed of parchment leaves, and elegant ones at that, though wrinkled with age; divided into two columns enclosed between two vertical rules; written in a Roman uncial hand, neat, full, not very large, and somewhat angular, [Col. LXI] with letters not distinctly separated and rounded; with very fine strokes, the lower shafts cut obliquely, but the upper ones straight across; with uncials, in red and sometimes touched with lead, for the first three lines of each book; but for titles and, at the end, in the word *explicit*, alternately red and black. It is distinguished by no punctuation, virtually no abbreviated, conjoined, or corrupted words, and no page marks except on the last folio of the gatherings, where it is also signed in uncials. The letters are of moderate size and written with a finer pen; the lower shafts scarcely descend; in T the transverse stroke, and in G and L the lower strokes, appear to have vanished; at the end of a line only *b.* occurs for *-bus*; elsewhere *ae* is written as *a e*; *Dms*, *Dmi* for *Dominus*, *Domini*; *q.* for *-que*; and ΧΡΙ, in Greek letters, for *Christi*. Although all have attended to these suitable and consistent characteristics, some have assigned the manuscript to the fourth or fifth century, others to the sixth or seventh.

The following words are written on the first folio in Dom Jean Mabillon’s own hand: “A manuscript of approximately the seventh century.” He then records both what it contains and what is missing. Missing above all are all the epistles; the beginning of the book or epistle *To Donatus*; the entire book *On Jealousy and Envy*; the beginning of the book *To Fortunatus*, supplied in the Council by a recent hand; in the Council of Carthage, the opinions of the bishops from 53 to 69; the beginning of the book *In Praise of Martyrdom*; and book III of the *Testimonies against the Jews*.—Mabillon adds:

> “Then follows the Psalter in Greek and Latin, in such a way that the Latin version occupies the facing page, in uncial script, without accents or breathings; it begins at Psalm XVIII, the earlier part of which is missing, and ends in LXXII, the latter part of which is absent.”

But through the destructive misfortune of recent times, and perhaps the fire at the Library of Saint-Germain, this Psalter has perished entirely. Cf. *Nouveau Traité de Diplomatique*, t. III, p. 55, note 1; *Paléographie universelle*, by D. Champollion-Figeac and Aimé Champollion, Paris, published by Firmin Didot, 1840.

**Orléans Manuscript**, in uncial letters, in the Public Library; formerly at Saint-Benoît of Fleury: the books *On Mortality* and *On the Sacrament of the Cup*. (Haenel.)
