**Bruges Manuscript**, works of St. Cyprian and others.

1. Andrea of Aleria had copied from the Paris manuscript the short works of Cyprian which he published in the first Roman edition.

2. Latino Latini had at his disposal, for Paolo Manuzio’s Roman edition, the very ancient Verona Manuscript, which we discussed in its proper place. He did not state explicitly which manuscripts he subsequently used in his second revision.

3. Pamelius used manuscripts of Affligem Abbey, not far from Brussels; an English manuscript belonging to John Clement, who had sent him certain corrections from it; a manuscript of Blandijnberg Abbey near Ghent, called St. Peter’s, which was burned by the sectarians a little later; and a fragment of a manuscript belonging to Louis Carrion, in which several short works of Cyprian were contained.

He also used the printed copy belonging to Johann Canchius of Utrecht, with corrections in the margin drawn from various manuscripts; a manuscript of St. Pantaleon’s at Cologne, which he calls the Cologne manuscript; corrections by Johann Costerius written in the margin of Canchius’s copy; a manuscript of Dunes Abbey in Flanders which survived the sectarians’ fire; a manuscript of the Englishman John Harris, from which he had received corrections by no means to be regretted; a manuscript of Marchiennes Abbey, not far from the University of Douai; and a manuscript of St. Nicholas outside the walls of Tournai.

4. Rigault cites the variant readings of the Royal, Benevento, Corbie, Naples, Reims, Verona, and de Thou manuscripts, Nicolas Le Fèvre’s book, and the Pomposa copy.

5. Finally, the Oxford editors employed the following manuscripts: four Bodleian manuscripts; four belonging to Isaac Vossius; two from New College, Oxford; one from Lincoln College there; one from Pembroke College, Cambridge; one from the Lambeth Library; one from the Arundel Library; one from the York Library; one from the Westminster Library; one from the Salisbury Library; and one from the Cottonian Library. They likewise used collations of a manuscript of Corpus Christi College, Cambridge, and of another London manuscript, made by Thomas Gale; likewise of another Salisbury manuscript by the bishop of St. Asaph. They used collations of the de Thou manuscripts from the monasteries of Mont-Saint-Michel, St. Victor in Paris, St. Maurice at Tossat, and St. Peter at Corbie, prepared at Paris by the Benedictine Fathers; collations of several manuscripts preserved in the Vatican, Verona, and Benevento, as well as of the king of France’s manuscript, through the diligence of Dom Robert Rigby. Account was also taken of the manuscripts used by Jacques Pamelius, Goulart, Nicolas Le Fèvre, Latino Latini, etc.

6. Baluze not only reexamined all the assistance derived from manuscripts in previous editions, but also consulted several new ones, which Maran briefly enumerates in the Prolegomena, p. CXLVII. Baluze had written the variant readings of many of them into his books; but because those books were too quickly dispersed, it was impossible to gather complete information about them.

# EDITIONS OF CYPRIAN

The editions of Cyprian may conveniently be divided into seven classes. The first is to be extended from the year 1471, from the tentative beginnings of the Roman *editio princeps*, to the Rembolt edition; the second from the Rembolt edition to Erasmus’s; the third comprises the edition of Erasmus, so often reprinted; the fourth was established by Pamelius; the fifth by Rigault; the sixth by Fell; and the seventh by Baluze. From that point down to our own edition, based jointly on Baluze and Oxford, there extends a twofold line of editions, some of which must be referred to Baluze and others to Fell.

# FIRST SERIES OF EDITIONS OF ST. CYPRIAN

## The Earliest Editions  
## FIFTEENTH CENTURY

### Year 1471

**FIRST ROMAN EDITION, THE EDITIO PRINCEPS.** Rome, in the house of Pietro and [Col. LXV] Francesco de’ Massimi, by Conrad Sweynheym and Arnold Pannartz, folio: the epistles of St. Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, revised by Giovanni Andrea, and with his letter to Paul II; at the end:

> Whoever you are, illustrious reader, you behold these little books.  
> If you wish to know the craftsmen’s names, read on.  
> You will laugh at their harsh Teutonic surnames; perhaps  
> Their art may soften the men’s words, unfamiliar with the Muses.  
> The masters Conrad Sweynheym and Arnold Pannartz  
> Printed many such works together at Rome.  
> Pietro with his brother Francesco, both de’ Massimi,  
> Contributed to this work the home it desired. 1471.

It is clear from Andrea of Aleria’s letter that this edition of St. Cyprian preceded the edition of the sacred Bible, the printing of which the craftsmen had been forced to interrupt for lack of larger paper. He reports that he had copied these epistles from an ancient Paris manuscript while residing in that city for the sake of his studies. This letter of his—in which he included an explanation of many words used by St. Cyprian which, as he himself says, “on reading through them rapidly, he believed required some interpretation for the sake of certain beginners in literary studies”—together with the index immediately following it, occupies slightly fewer than three folios. Audiffredi sharply corrects Lair, stating that he himself had handled four copies in Roman libraries, whereas Lair had said that, apart from the Crevenna copy, he had seen no other and that one was not easily encountered. It is listed in the catalogue of the Chigi Library.

1471.

**FIRST VENICE EDITION**, commonly called the **SPEYER EDITION**. Venice, by Wendelin of Speyer.

> **Note [Col. LXV].** It may be useful to note briefly an error which had occupied a great many books on this subject in the preceding century and which has since been repeatedly refuted and then revived: namely, that this edition appeared at Speyer, the craftsman’s name occasioning the deception. Yet this error should no more be charged against those who in the preceding age compiled the literary history of these writers than it should be reproached against the editors themselves—that is, those who had the good fortune, scarcely granted to the former scholars, to handle these old editions personally. Among their number is Reinhart of Altdorf, editor of Cyprian’s *Epistles* in 1689, who inspected both editions—the Roman and the Venetian—lent to him from the Nuremberg Library, yet speaks of them no differently than if he had learned of them in a dream, calling the latter the Speyer edition and saying that its craftsman was “a certain Wendelin.” The English editors similarly, and Baluze following them, always call this the Speyer edition. Baluze’s error, moreover, will readily find a reader all the more indignant when, fresh from reading what Maran accurately taught on this subject at the beginning of that edition, he encounters the error. I should also like to know what that “old Venetian edition” may be which Baluze repeatedly cites alongside the Speyer edition. Cf. the notes on the *Testimonies against the Jews*, p. 596. **SCHOENEMANN.**

Folio. The *Epistles of St. Cyprian*. At the end:

> The reader addresses Wendelin, the craftsman from Speyer, who restores the Epistles of Blessed Cyprian to the light.
>
> 1471.

Although I would not prove from the words “restores to the light,” as does the learned editor of the 1776 *Catalogue of the Crevenna Library*, quarto, t. I, p. 59, that this edition is later than the Roman edition, the following may nonetheless serve as a more certain argument on this occasion: whereas the Roman edition identifies the manuscript from which it was printed, the Venetian edition says nothing of any similar aid and, by that very silence, testifies that it reproduces a previously printed old edition. [Col. LXVI] A weightier consideration is the agreement of the text in the two editions, which, according to the same learned scholar, is so great that—apart from certain typographical errors which Wendelin must appear to have removed from the Roman edition—the Venetian reproduces it exactly.

> **Note [Col. LXVI].** Extraordinary are the things that Debure relates concerning this edition in his *Bibliographie instructive*—more accurately, *in need of instruction*: “It earned the distinction of being the edition which M. Baluze chose as the basis for preparing the edition he gave us of this Father of the Church, and he held it in quite exceptional esteem. It has the advantage of containing many original passages which that author was obliged to suppress or alter in his own edition.” **SCHOENEMANN.**

It is thought to surpass the Roman edition in the beauty and elegance of its workmanship. Like nearly all editions of this period, it lacks page or folio numbers, catchwords, and signatures. Before the text stand two folios containing an index.

> **Note [Col. LXVI].** “A special table,” says Debure the Younger. Heaven help us, the man had worn out both editions with his own hands! **SCHOENEMANN.**

Above it is written the title:

> Here begin the Epistles of Caecilius Cyprian to Pope Cornelius, the first being *On Confession*. Auspiciously.

This Venetian edition also contains the books of *Testimonies against the Jews, to Quirinus*, but only two of them, and these marred by many lacunae; doubtless the Roman edition already includes the same books among the letters.

1483.

VENETIAN EDITION II. Venice, printed by Lucas Venetus, folio. *Letters and Short Works*. At the end:

> Lucas Venetus, son of Dominicus, with his customary diligence printed at Venice, in the year of salvation 1483, on the day before the Nones of December, the most carefully revised letters of the divine Caecilius Cyprianus, that most holy and eloquent man.

(Goetze, *Merkwürdigkeiten der Dresdner Bibliothek*.) A copy also existed in the Pinelli Library. Cf. Morelli, *Catalogue*, vol. I, p. 95, no. 578. Audiffredi, in the *Catalogue of the Casanatense Library*, vol. II, p. 524, indicates explicitly that several treatises and sermons were added. Yet certainly the greater part of the material furnished by Rembolt’s edition had already been published here, as we learned from the preface of C. de P. to Jacopo Grasolario, a Venetian citizen who is said to have been especially insistent in demanding this edition; that preface is reprinted in Rembolt’s edition. Its principal advantage is that each letter and treatise is preceded by a brief summary, all of which are displayed in condensed form as a table following the preface.

I think that certain editions produced in this century without indication of the year, or even of the place, should be placed immediately after these.

Uncertain year.

Without year, Brescia, quarto. Caecilius Cyprianus’ sermon *On the Lord’s Prayer*, namely, the *Our Father*, in which he teaches which prayer in particular ought to be used, how one ought to approach it, and what bodily posture and manner of voice befit one who declares himself a Christian.—(*Catalogue de la Bibliothèque du Roi*, p. 366, no. 502, where it is added: “an old edition, about the year 1490.”) I do not remember reading of it elsewhere.

Uncertain year.

UNNAMED EDITION I.—Without place, year, or printer. The first of this kind. *The Letters of Saint Cyprian*, folio. At the beginning appears:

> The table of subjects in the letters of the blessed martyr Cyprian, arranged in alphabetical order [that is, a fairly copious index of noteworthy matters], begins auspiciously.

[Col. LXVII] A short table of contents with brief summaries is appended. There are seventy-three Letters.—Three books *To Quirinus*.—A sermon of Blessed Augustine on Blessed Cyprian.—A prayer of Cyprian the martyr.—Likewise a prayer of the same author, which he uttered on the day of his passion.—The *Passion of Blessed Cyprian*.—Six books *To Quirinus* conclude the series. These occupy eighteen leaves, with signatures A and B VI. Leaf XIX is almost entirely blank, except for a few words from Jerome printed at the bottom of its second page under this title:

> From the book of the blessed Jerome *On Illustrious Men*: on the blessed Cyprian.

The letters begin on fol. XX and extend from signatures a I through R inclusive, with approximately five sheets gathered in each quire. The subscription reads:

> Here end the letters of the glorious martyr Cyprian, bishop of Carthage. With how great an eloquence and how great a learning he shone among the catholic doctors is most excellently attested by his letters, splendid as they are in verbal ornament and richness of thought.

Thereafter, under a new sequence of signatures, follow quires A–D, each of four sheets, with this heading:

> Here begins the prologue to the books of the blessed martyr Cyprian written against the Jews. This prologue is in fact a certain letter written to Quirinus.

At the end of the book:

> Here ends the third book of Caecilius Cyprianus, glorious martyr, archbishop of Carthage, and most excellent orator, addressed to Quirinus. In this book, as also in the two preceding books, the catholic faith is most powerfully defended and confirmed by testimonies from Holy Scripture against the unbelief of the Jews and the errors of the gentiles. Thanks be to God.

Debure the elder, who described this edition with the greatest accuracy in the *Catalogue de la Bibliothèque du duc de La Vallière*, vol. I, p. 131 ff., states that, apart from a few capital letters, the type resembles that seen in the Mainz edition of Cicero’s *Offices* of 1465. The characters stand midway between Gothic and Roman type. I would draw particular attention to the third book of the *Testimonies against the Jews* in this edition, since Erasmus is generally believed to have been the first to publish it from a manuscript codex of the monastery of Gembloux. This edition, therefore, was known neither to Erasmus nor to any of the later editors except Pamelius. That Pamelius knew it may be learned from a comparison with his annotations on this third book. Yet many who professed to have handled a copy of it consistently mention only two books *Against the Jews*, and they have drawn other men of circumspect judgment into the same error.

Plainly, however, something else lies concealed here: there are two unnamed editions. The first, which we have just described, we shall say was employed or known by none of the editors thus far. The other, which we shall discuss immediately, was on everyone’s lips; but because no one described it even in a single word, it gave rise to a serious error. Pamelius, who indeed reported nothing more about it than that it appeared to have been printed immediately after the invention of typography, nevertheless judges it to be much more correct than Erasmus’ text.

UNNAMED EDITION II.—Without place or year, folio. It begins with a table of contents bearing this heading:

> The books and letters of Caecilius Cyprianus, bishop of Carthage and most worthy martyr.—They begin auspiciously. *To Donatus* [Col. LXVIII], *On Vanities and Spectacles* [Note: [Col. LXVIII] Pamelius later included this among the letters as no. 2, and in the Benedictine edition it is no. 1. The Oxford editor, however, entitled it the book *On the Grace of God*, p. 1, where his learned annotations may be consulted. SCHOENEMANN.]—*To Demetrianus*.—*On the Work of Piety and Almsgiving*, XIII.—*To Fortunatus, on Exhortation to Martyrdom*.—*On Jealousy and Envy*.—*On the Benefit of Patience*.—*On Mortality*.—*On the Dress of Virgins*.—*To Caecilius, on the Sacrament of the Lord’s Cup* [Note: [Col. LXVIII] Later included among the letters in the editions of Pamelius and Oxford as LXIII. SCHOENEMANN.]—*Against Novatian the Schismatic, on the Unity of the Church*.—*On the Lapsed*.—*On the Lord’s Prayer*.—*That Idols Are Not Gods*.—*On the Singularity of Clerics* [Note: [Col. LXVIII] Later rejected as non-Cyprianic. SCHOENEMANN.]—*On Mounts Sinai and Zion, against the Jews* [Note: [Col. LXVIII] Later rejected as non-Cyprianic. SCHOENEMANN.]—*To Antonianus, on Cornelius and Novatian* [Note: [Col. LXVIII] Included among the letters in Pamelius’ edition as LV and in the Oxford edition as LII. SCHOENEMANN.]—*An Exhortatory Letter to the Thibaritans* [Note: [Col. LXVIII] Included among the letters by Pamelius as LVIII and in the Oxford edition as LVI. SCHOENEMANN.]—*To Magnus, on Those Who Receive Grace in Bed* [Note: [Col. LXVIII] Letter LXIX in Pamelius, LXXVI in Oxford. SCHOENEMANN.]—*To Quirinus, against the Jews*, two books. The Letters of Caecilius Cyprianus, etc., begin.

At the end:

> Here end the Letters of Caecilius Cyprianus, etc.

Nothing further.

The type is Gothic; the text is printed in divided columns and has signatures for four-sheet gatherings from A IIII to R III.

SIXTEENTH CENTURY

1500.

PARIS EDITION I. Paris, at the press of Jodocus Badius. *Cyprian’s Letters and Short Works; Treatise on the Cardinal Works of Christ*. Concerning this edition, conclusions are possible only by conjecture. Fabricius, in *Delectus Scriptorum pro Veritate Religionis Christianae*, p. 222, mentions a book ascribed to Cyprian, *On the Cardinal Works of Christ*, etc., published at Paris in 1500, but adds no further mention either of the bookseller, the printer, or the edition itself. Erasmus, however, in an annotation on the same book included in his own edition, recalls “the Badian edition, in which this work was contained separately from the rest of the volume.” Now Badius first began to conduct a bookselling business and publish books at Paris in 1500 (Maittaire, vol. II, p. 73). I therefore infer that the Paris edition noted by Fabricius was the Badian edition and that it included not merely that single short work but several works, perhaps even Cyprian’s letters. Nevertheless, I would have it remain excluded from the catalogue of Cyprianic editions until something more certain is discovered.

1501.

VENETIAN EDITION I. Venice, at the press of Aldus, quarto. Cyprian’s poem *On the Wood of the Cross*, among the Christian poets (*Catalogue of the Casanatense Library*, vol. II, p. 525).

CLASS II. From Rembolt’s Edition to the Erasmian Editions

1512.

REMBOLT’S EDITION. PARIS EDITION II. Paris, quarto.

> The works, gathered from various sources, of the most blessed Caecilius Cyprianus, prelate of the Carthaginians, orator, most eloquent herald of the divine Word, and most vehement proclaimer of the triune and one God, collected into one volume and printed through the labors and at the expense of Masters Berthold REMBOLT and Johann WATERLOES, most skilled and trustworthy printers [Col. LXIX]; their arrangement is indicated on the following page.

This appears on the title page, the greater part of which is occupied by Rembolt’s device, with a four-line poem to the readers beneath it. At the end (fol. CLXXX):

> The short works of the blessed Cyprian, newly printed at Paris at the Golden Sun in the Rue Saint-Jacques, at the expense of Masters Berthold Rembolt and Johann Waterloes, dwelling at the sign of Saint George. In the year of the Lord 1512, on the thirteenth day of November.

According to the table printed on the verso of the title page, this edition contains the following: *The Cardinal Works of Christ down to His Ascension, and On the Holy Spirit* (later vindicated for Arnold, abbot of Bonneval).—Four books of Letters. The first book contains twelve letters; the second, twelve; the third, twenty-five; the fourth, ten.—Six treatises by the same author. The first, *Against Demetrianus*. The second, *On the Dress of Virgins*. The third, *On the Simplicity of Prelates*, that is, *On the Unity of the Church*. The fourth, *On the Vanity of Idols*. The fifth, *On Mounts Sinai and Zion, against the Jews*. The sixth, *On the Revelation of the Head of John the Baptist*.—A book of sermons by the same blessed Cyprian, containing six sermons. The first, *On Almsgiving*. The second, *On Jealousy and Envy*. The third, *On the Benefit of Patience*. The fourth, *On Mortality*. The fifth, *On the Lapsed and the Martyrs Already Crowned*. The sixth, *On the Lord’s Prayer*.—The same author’s *Exposition of the Apostles’ Creed*.—A short work by the same author addressed to Fortunatus, *On Exhortation to Martyrdom*.—The same author’s book *On the Singularity of Clerics*.—Two books by the same author *Against the Jews, to Quirinus*; the first divided into twenty-three chapters, the second into twenty-nine.—His *Passion*, written by Pontianus, his deacon.

The items marked with a + sign are to be regarded as newly added; the rest appear to have been taken from the Venetian edition of 1483. Thus indeed says Robert Fortunatus of Saint-Malo in the letter commending the work, prefixed and addressed to Lodovicus Ruvicius (Rusicus or Ruscius) of Blois, dated at Paris, from the house of Plessis, on the Kalends of November:

> For we took care to add to those works you supplied, *The Cardinal Works of Christ down to His Ascension to the Father*, together with the same author’s *Exposition of the Apostles’ Creed* and the account of his passion by Pontianus his deacon; certain works, such as *On Gamblers* and a few others, were omitted for the present because they were insufficiently consistent with his authorship.

[Note: [Col. LXIX] Our library of the former monastery of Saint George, presently at Villingen, possesses this Rembolt edition, in which absolutely nothing is missing at the end, since the complete treatise *On the Cardinal Works of Christ* is present together with that *On the Holy Spirit*. LUMPER.]

And yet that treatise *On the Cardinal Works of Christ*, together with the one *On the Holy Spirit*, which ought to occupy thirty-two leaves [Note: [Col. LXIX] Our copy has not merely thirty-two leaves, but thirty-three. LUMPER.], as the numbers assigned to them indicate, does not appear in our certainly unmutilated copy; rather, the beginning of the Cyprianic text, from Book I of the Letters, is numbered fol. 1 ff.—As for the remainder, Guilielmus Potetus Biscutinus, who took Fortunatus’ place from time to time, is said to have reread it, cleansed it of blemishes, and furnished it with brief annotations and marginal references to passages of the Bible and other authors. Fortunatus’ letter is immediately followed by a poem of this Potetus to the readers, which in turn is followed by another poem by Hieronymus Alexander, professor [Col. LXX] at Paris, in commendation of the printer Rembolt . . . . . in which printers are incidentally reminded of their duty . . . . . Then follow the preface from the Venetian edition and the testimonies of Jerome and Lactantius concerning Cyprian; summaries of the letters and the remaining treatises; and finally a short index of subjects under the title *Repositories of the Letters, Treatises, etc., and Their Subjects*. The type is almost similar to that of books published by Jean Petit, but somewhat more elegant.

1519.

BASEL EDITION I. Basel, folio. Sandius mentions an edition of this year and place; from what source and of what character, I cannot determine.

CLASS III. Erasmian Editions

1520.

BASEL EDITION II, ERASMIAN EDITION I. Basel, from Froben’s press, folio. *The Works of the Most Holy Martyr Caecilius Cyprianus, Bishop of Carthage . . . . . through the study and care of Desiderius Erasmus of Rotterdam.*

“Cyprian appears,” says Erasmus in his distinguished preface to Cardinal Lorenzo Pucci, dated at Louvain in 1519, on the day before the Kalends of August, near its conclusion:

> He appears much more correct, through the removal of errors by our labor; somewhat purer, through the exclusion of works falsely attributed to him; and fuller, through the addition from some very ancient copies of material hitherto lacking. Finally, through Froben’s labor, he appears at once more elegant and more imposing; and he will appear auspiciously, if Your Most Reverend Lordship favors our industry.

The following were added from old manuscripts:

Letters *To Jubaianus, on the Baptism of Heretics* (letter LXXIII in the editions of Pamelius and Oxford); *To Pompeius, against the Letter of Stephen* (LXXIV in the same editions); *To Quintinus, on the Baptism of Heretics and Schismatics: Opinions of the Bishops of the Council of Carthage* (LXXI in the same editions).

He rejected the following as non-Cyprianic, but nevertheless retained them from earlier editions:

*On Mounts Sinai and Zion, against the Jews*.—*On the Revelation of the Head of Saint John the Baptist*.—*An Exposition of the Creed Which They Call the Apostles’*.—*On the Singularity of Clerics*.—*To Pope Cornelius, on the Cardinal Virtues of Christ*.

In addition to these, he appended the following equally spurious works from manuscript copies:

*To Moses, Maximus, and the Others, in Praise of Martyrdom*.—*On Discipline and the Benefit of Chastity*.—*To Novatian the Heretic: That the Hope of Pardon Must Not Be Denied to the Lapsed*.—Two prayers of Blessed Cyprian.—A sermon of Blessed Augustine on Saint Cyprian the martyr.

Erasmus’ very few annotations, together with two indexes of Cyprian’s works—one arranged in the order in which the works follow one another, the other arranged alphabetically—and also an account of Cyprian’s passion by Pontius, which Erasmus nevertheless warns is not Pontius’ actual work but an excerpt made from it by some more recent author, are prefixed to the text; another index, of propositions, is appended to it.

1520.

ERASMIAN EDITION II, COLOGNE EDITION I. At the press of Heinrich Alopecius.

1521.

ERASMIAN EDITION III. In the same place, by the same printer (in November), folio.—*Works cleansed of innumerable errors, with the addition of several short works from very ancient copies that had hitherto been unavailable, and the removal of those that appeared to have been falsely attributed, together with brief annotations. All this was accomplished for us through the immense labor of Erasmus of Rotterdam, a man born to advance the finest studies* [Col. LXXI]. Sandius noted this edition, p. 42; Hamberger cited its full title, vol. II, p. 599; but apart from them it was unknown or neglected by everyone.

1522.

ERASMIAN EDITION IV. In the illustrious city of Cologne. Johann Soter printed it in March, two volumes, octavo. *The Works of the Divine Caecilius Cyprianus, Bishop of Carthage. The first volume revised by Erasmus of Rotterdam; volume II, containing various treatises and sermons, of which the following page will present you with a catalogue*, etc., etc.

1525.

ERASMIAN EDITION V. In the same place, by the same printer (in February), folio.

> Reader, you now have for the third time the *Works of the Most Holy Martyr Caecilius Cyprianus, Bishop of Carthage*, cleansed more thoroughly of errors through comparison of various editions and very ancient manuscripts, with the addition of several works that had not been published and with indications of those reported as either spurious or doubtful, through the study and care of Desiderius Erasmus of Rotterdam.

1527.

Haguenau, Saint Cyprian *On the Eucharist*. (Barberini Library.)

1528.

LYON EDITION I. Lyon, at the press of Sébastien Gryphe, two volumes, octavo. Fabricius, p. 220.

1528.

Without place, duodecimo. Cyprian *On the Lord’s Prayer*. (British Museum.)

1530.

ERASMIAN EDITION VI. Basel, from Froben’s press, folio.—*Works, now for the fourth time cleansed of errors with more exacting vigilance by Desiderius Erasmus of Rotterdam. There has been added an exceedingly pious book by the same author addressed to Fortunatus, On the Twofold Martyrdom, never printed before.* (*Catalogue de la Bibliothèque du Roi*, p. 365.)

Erasmus says that he found this treatise in a very ancient library. But Henricus Gravius declares that Erasmus himself was the actual craftsman of this short work and passed off a product of his own genius under another’s name; Pamelius and Ceillier appear to agree with him. Certainly, to this day no one has learned which library Erasmus took this work from, nor has the codex he says he used come into anyone’s hands. Both subject matter and language savor of Erasmus’ style; and, what increases suspicion still more, as Pamelius observes, several testimonies from Scripture are rendered in this book in precisely the same way as in Erasmus’ other compositions. Lumper, *Historia theologico-critica Patrum*, vol. XII, p. 387.

1535.

LYON EDITION II. Lyon, at the press of Gryphe, octavo, according to Dupin, Ceillier, and Lumper.

1537.

LYON EDITION III. In the same place, by the same printer, octavo, according to the learned Nourry, Maran, Ceillier, and Lumper.

In the same year.

ERASMIAN EDITION VII. Basel, from Froben’s press, two volumes. Fabricius, p. 220.

1538.

GERMAN VERSION I. The treatise *On the Singularity of Clerics*, commonly included among Cyprian’s works, was published in German by the celebrated Cochlaeus, according to Ceillier, who, however, recorded neither the place nor the format of the edition.

[Col. LXXII] 1540.

ERASMIAN EDITION VIII. Basel, at Herwagen’s press, folio (Fabricius, ibid.). Four copies of this edition, collated with manuscripts, were in Baluze’s library.

1541.

PARIS EDITION III. Paris, at the press of Arnoul L’Angelier, folio.—A shamefully interpolated and corrupted edition, although it boasts of purification on its title page. Indeed, its editors carried their impudence so far that beneath Erasmus’ preface dated at Louvain in 1519 they subscribed “Paris, 1541.” Pamelius complains of this in his annotations on the book *On the Lord’s Prayer*, at the words, “You have no excuse,” etc.; this may also be read in Cave, p. 129. Copies of this edition collated with manuscript codices existed in Baluze’s library.

1541.

PARIS EDITION IV. Paris, at the press of Oudin (Audoenus) Petit, doubtless folio. (Barberini Library, catalogue, second edition.)

1541.

PARIS EDITION V, ERASMIAN EDITION IX. In the same place, at the press of François Regnault, folio.—From Erasmus’ edition and with his annotations. (*Catalogue de la Bibliothèque du Roi*, p. 365.)

1541.

PARIS EDITION VI. At the press of Nicolas Guigant, folio (Ceillier, III, p. 218).

1541.

ERASMIAN EDITION X. Antwerp, octavo. *Cyprian*. (*Catalogue of the Library of the British Museum*, London, 1787, folio.)

1541.

ERASMIAN EDITION XI. Basel, from Herwagen’s press, cited by Nourry.

1542.

ERASMIAN EDITION XII. Antwerp, printed by Johann Crinitus. *The Works of the Divine Caecilius Cyprianus, Bishop of Carthage and Martyr, Divided into Two Volumes*. It is the Cologne edition of 1522, but with slighter indexes.

1544.

ERASMIAN EDITION XIII, commonly called GRAVIUS’ EDITION. Cologne, from the printing house of Peter Quentel, in August.

> All the works of the Divine Caecilius Cyprianus that are known to survive, now most recently, following the correction of Desiderius Erasmus of Rotterdam, vindicated from errors with the aid of manuscript copies, far more diligently than ever before. With the addition of a very learned and pious short work ascribed to Cyprian, *On the Twofold Martyrdom, to Fortunatus*. Erasmus’ annotations have also been added—not gathered hastily into a single place, as has been done hitherto, but now for the first time inserted, each in its proper place, in a different typeface: partly so that the reader might be spared the weariness of searching, and partly so that what Cyprian and Erasmus mean might be perceived more conveniently and keenly, as though they were set opposite one another. Also several brief annotations or corrections by Henricus Gravius, a most learned man in both languages; few and brief indeed, but nevertheless timely and learned. And a new index, far fuller and better arranged than the old one, newly added through the labor of Bartholomaeus Laurens. Those who either know the earlier editions of Cyprian well or are willing to take the trouble to compare this one with any of them will easily perceive what value is to be assigned to this edition.

[Col. LXXIII] Several of Erasmus’ annotations, however, because they could not suitably be fitted individually into their proper places, were left separately at the beginning along with Gravius’ corrections. Regarding the book *On the Twofold Martyrdom*, Gravius suspects that its phrasing reflects Erasmus himself, or an author similar to Erasmus, rather than Cyprian. Pamelius later adopted the same opinion and found several others to agree with him. Pamelius is mistaken, however, when he says that both Froben editions contain this book, since, as he himself stated in the proper place, he had carefully examined the editions of 1520 and 1525 [Note: [Col. LXXIII] Neither in the Froben edition of 1521 nor in that of 1525—both of which I carefully examined, since they are present in our library—is the aforementioned treatise *On the Twofold Martyrdom* contained. LUMPER.] . . . . . According to Baluze, Gravius did not himself edit this edition; rather, it was prepared by another man who made use of a printed copy annotated in Gravius’ hand with conjectures and variant readings from manuscript codices. The exceedingly sagacious Baluze seems to me to have inferred this from the arrangement of the edition as a whole, which certainly supports that suspicion.

1544.

ERASMIAN EDITION XIV, GRAVIUS’ EDITION II. The same works of Cyprian were published at Basel in Heinrich Quentel’s printing house, according to our learned Nourry and, after him, Lumper.

1544.

LYON EDITION IV. Lyon, at the press of Gryphe, octavo, two volumes. See the preceding entries.

1546.

VENETIAN EDITION II. Venice, quarto. *Cyprian’s Exorcisms*. (Barberini.)

1547.

VENETIAN EDITION III. Venice, at the sign of Hope, octavo (according to Fabricius). *Works*, with the same author’s poems *On the Cross of the Redeemer* added. (*Catalogue of the Chigi Library*.)

1549.

ERASMIAN EDITION XV, GRAVIUS’ EDITION III. Cologne, folio, I think, from the same recension by Gravius. According to Fabricius.

1549.

ERASMIAN EDITION XVI. Basel, at Froben’s press, according to Dupin, Nourry, Ceillier, and Lumper.

1549.

LYON EDITION V. Octavo, according to the same authorities.

1550.

ERASMIAN EDITION XVII. Basel, at Herwagen’s press, according to Nourry.

1550.

LYON EDITION VI. Octavo, at Gryphe’s press, according to Dupin and Ceillier.

1553.

GERMAN VERSION II, published by Melchior Ambach under this title:

> *The Sermons and Writings of Saint Caecilius Cyprianus, the Ancient Christian Teacher and Bishop, with Summaries and Explanations of Several Obscure Sayings and Words Used by Saint Cyprian, Elucidated from the Writings of Saint Cyprian Himself and of Other Christian Teachers. Testimony, Judgment, and Praise by the Foremost Teachers concerning the Life, Teaching, and Sufferings of Saint Caecilius Cyprianus.*

Nuremberg.—Not all the writings are presented in German.

[Col. LXXIV] 1554.

LYON EDITION VII. Lyon, at Gryphe’s press, octavo, according to Maran.

1556.

LYON EDITION VIII. In the same place, octavo, according to Nourry and Ceillier.

1557.

Saint Cyprian’s book *On the Unity of the Church*, with annotations, together likewise with Augustine’s book on the same subject and preceded by G. Calixtus’ introduction, Helmstedt, octavo.

1558.

ERASMIAN EDITION XVIII. Basel, at Herwagen’s press, folio, from the edition and annotations of Desiderius Erasmus. Dupin, Ceillier, and Maran cite it.

1560.

Paris, format unspecified. Poems *On Genesis* and *On Sodom*. (Barberini.)

1563.

MANUTIUS’ EDITION, ROMAN EDITION II. Rome, at the press of Paulus Manutius, son of Aldus, folio.

> The *Works of the Divine Caecilius Cyprianus, Bishop of Carthage and Most Glorious Martyr*, corrected with the greatest fidelity according to the true text of the most ancient copies, with the addition also of a fifth book of letters, never previously published. Other works ascribed to the same Cyprian. With an index of noteworthy subjects and words compiled with the greatest diligence.

Latino Latini revised it, using a very ancient codex brought from the library at Verona, written in capital letters a thousand years earlier, and other manuscript copies; concerning each of these, however, I would not venture to affirm whether or not it was actually at hand during this first recension. Domenico Macri writes in his *Life* of Latini:

> Through many vigils and labors, he had collected a very great body of material for elucidating certain more obscure passages. He had also prepared several brief annotations in which, after indicating the variant readings of the codices, he stated which reading he himself had especially followed. An authentic book of letters was also added by him; and, finally, many passages had been restored with the greatest fidelity. But because he observed that, contrary to the authority of the written codices, some readings had been retained, others added, and very many altered—partly also through the carelessness of the workmen—he did not permit Manutius to place his name in any way upon the edition, lest he should impair his credibility even in the slightest degree.

He then undertook a second recension in relation to Pamelius’ edition; his work on it is presented in the *Bibliotheca Sacra et Profana*, pp. 174 ff. There he complains sufficiently about Manutius and at the same time resents the praise Pamelius bestowed upon Manutius for this edition. This edition contains everything that had been published in the Erasmian editions and those of Gravius, except Firmilian’s letter to Cyprian against the letter of Pope Stephen, no. 75 in Pamelius and Oxford. Concerning this, Latino Latini writes in the *Bibliotheca*, p. 177, against Pamelius’ annotation:

> I, Latino, omitted it, not Manutius, both because I followed the examples of my predecessors and because I detested the man’s insolence.

Besides the fifth book of letters, consisting of fifteen letters, the following was newly added among the works customarily ascribed to Cyprian but regarded as of doubtful authenticity: the book *On Spectacles* [Note: [Col. LXXIV] Baluze observes that manuscript copies of this work are exceedingly rare [Col. LXXV], and takes no little pride in having obtained two copies, something granted to none of the earlier editors. SCHOENEMANN.]; then the *Life of Cyprian* composed by [Col. LXXV] Pontius, together with the *Act of the Passion* mentioned by Pontius himself, and the *Passion of Cyprian* that appeared in the earlier editions and is here attributed to Paul the Deacon.

As regards the external appearance of this edition, I do not know whether one ought to call it splendid rather than elegant. Certainly the distinction and ἀκρίβεια (*precision*) of the type employed in the dedicatory letter to Cardinal Borromeo are such that one might compare it with even the finest monuments of the art in which Italy glories today; nor, although smaller, is the type of the remaining text much inferior. In the university library there is a copy with collations from the Verona, Vatican, Benevento, and other codices; it formerly belonged to Joseph Smith, British consul at Venice. In Baluze’s library there were two copies collated with manuscripts.

1564.

MORELLI’S EDITION, PARIS EDITION V. Paris, at the press of Guillaume Desbois, folio.—*The Complete Works, Purified by Comparison with Ancient Copies: an Enlarged Edition Illustrated with Observations, through the Diligence and Labor of Guillaume Morel.* Adrien Turnèbe supplied the preface. Firmilian’s letter was restored; letter IV in Pamelius was added. Moreover, the following works ascribed to Cyprian were appended: *On Gamblers*, which Pamelius scarcely doubts to be Cyprian’s; the poems *Genesis*, *Sodom*, *To a Senator*, and *On the Lord’s Passover*.—The preface *To Vigilius Celsus, for the Debate between Jason and Papiscus*.—*Against the Jews Who Persecuted Christ*.—*On the Twelve Abuses of the Age*.—*The Arrangement of the Supper*.—Seven copies of this edition collated with manuscript codices were preserved in Baluze’s library.

1564.

Only the Cyprianic treatises were published after the works of Leo the Great, at Paris, by Claude, according to Nicolas Nourry.

1565.

FRENCH VERSION I. François de Belleforest rendered Saint Cyprian’s sermons into French, according to Ceillier. Paris, octavo.

1566.

An anonymous *Life of Cyprian*, Paris, octavo. It is mentioned by Fabricius, *Bibliotheca Latina*, vol. III, p. 384; Walch, *Bibliotheca Patristica*, ch. 1, § 6, p. 44; Jena, 1834.

1567.

ITALIAN VERSION I. The treatise *On the Twofold Martyrdom*, among the apocryphal works of Saint Cyprian, was translated into Italian by Dom Raphael, a Florentine monk, with the addition of the *Life* and *Passion* of the same holy bishop and martyr. According to Argelati and Paitoni, Florence.

CLASS IV. Editions of Pamelius

1568.

PAMELIUS’ EDITION I. Antwerp, at the press of the widow and heirs of Johann Steelsius, folio.

> The *Works* . . . . . now once again revised with the greatest possible accuracy, by comparison of the editions of Paulus Manutius and Guillaume Morel with several very ancient manuscript copies, and now for the first time divided into three volumes in a definite order that takes chronology into account. [Col. LXXVI] The annotations of Jacques Pamelius . . . . . interspersed throughout the entire work; in these both the reasons for corrections and variant readings are noted incidentally, and everything pertaining to ecclesiastical antiquity is briefly explained. Newly added by the same editor are a *Life of the Divine Cyprian*, compiled from his own writings, and a most copious index of the cited Scriptures, hitherto lacking.

For a fairly long span of years Pamelius had devoted his labor to Cyprian. His application, interrupted first while he was more fully occupied with theological studies and then hindered by a journey to France, was rekindled when two editions of this author, those of Paulus Manutius and Guillaume Morel, appeared at almost the same time. He indeed surpassed the merits of both—though he honored them with distinguished praise, assigning first place, however, to Manutius’ edition—both through repeated attention to the text supported by new resources and through the other scholarly aids with which, as the title promises, he was the first to equip and adorn Cyprian. Foremost among these were the excellent and lucid summaries prefixed to each book and letter, and the industry with which he sought to investigate the chronological sequence of the individual works and letters.

He used very many manuscript codices gathered from almost every part of Belgium. Among the older editions, he examined especially Unnamed Edition I, discussed above, and Rembolt’s edition. Latino Latini, whose second recension we praised above, judges that Pamelius relied too often upon Manutius’ corrections. Pamelius himself affirms that through his labor Cyprian appeared not only with more than seven hundred passages restored in the marginal citation of Scripture alone, but also purified of innumerable errors, adding:

> So that I hope—if it may be said without provoking envy—that no further recension of him will hereafter be necessary.

By this work he anticipated the Englishman John Harris, formerly secretary to Thomas More, by whom in turn he wished to be anticipated in the publication of Tertullian.

Before the *Life of Cyprian* composed by Pamelius were placed the accounts transmitted under the names of Pontius and Paul the Deacon concerning Cyprian’s life and passion, together with Augustine’s oration and a passage of Agobard concerning the translation of the body of the divine Cyprian to Gaul.—Since the complete edition is divided into three volumes, the first contains eighty-three letters, in this sequence: 1. letters written immediately after the baptism of the divine Cyprian; 2. letters written during his entire two-year period of retirement; 3. letters written under the pontificates of Cornelius and Lucius; 4. miscellaneous letters written at various times during the peace of the Church; 5. letters concerning the baptism of heretics, written under the pontificate of Stephen; 6. letters composed during Cyprian’s exile and toward the end of his life. The second volume contains fifteen various books and treatises. The third contains works ascribed to Cyprian.—Pamelius admits that within the text he sometimes omitted or inserted certain things on his own judgment, at times even against the authority of the manuscript codices. By this candid admission and his frank judgment concerning the alterations of Manutius and Morel, he removed from himself any suspicion of dishonest dealing.

1569.

ITALIAN VERSION II.—Annibale Caro translated Saint Cyprian’s treatise *On Almsgiving* into Italian. It was printed by Aldus together with two orations of Saint Gregory Nazianzen likewise translated into Italian, according to Eudoxius Philenius. Venice, quarto.

[Col. LXXVII] 1572.

ITALIAN VERSION III.—Several sermons of Saint Cyprian, translated into Italian by a Florentine monk, together with orations and treatises by other holy Fathers, at the Giunta press, Florence, quarto, according to Ceillier.

1574.

PAMELIUS’ EDITION II. Paris, at the press of Nivelle, folio. A reprint of Pamelius’ edition; a copy in Baluze’s library was collated with manuscript codices by Nicolas Le Fèvre.

1574.

FRENCH VERSION II.—The works of the divine Cyprian were translated into French and published by Jacques Tigeon of Angers, canon of Metz, according to Ceillier.

1574.

FRENCH VERSION III.—Simon Goulart translated the divine Cyprian’s treatise *On the Lapsed* into French, according to Ceillier.

1575.

PAMELIUS’ EDITION III, reprinted at Cologne, folio, according to Baluze.

1577.

ITALIAN VERSION IV.—The book or sermon *On Mortality*, without year, place, or printer’s name, translated into Italian. According to Eudoxius Philenius, it exists in the Zeno library of the learned Dominican Fathers; it is also contained in the *Rhetoric* of Giason Denores and was printed at Padua.

1579.

Prague, quarto. Cyprian’s *Arrangement of the Supper*, with explanations. (*Catalogue of the Barberini Library*.)

1589.

PAMELIUS’ EDITION IV. Antwerp, folio. A reprint of Pamelius’ edition, at Beller’s press.

1593.

GOULART’S EDITION I. Paris, printed by Jean Le Preux, folio. The same edition reprinted, with the same title as above.

> The latest edition, more correct than its predecessors, to which have now been added for the first time new summaries prefixed to each letter and treatise; continuous marginal notes indicating the author’s method; and responses interspersed throughout to the claims advanced by Pamelius from Cyprian and the ancient theologians in confirmation of papal doctrines. Likewise a new index of Cyprian’s chronology and theology, with Simon Goulart’s dedicatory letter to the gathered churches in Holland and Zeeland.

(*Catalogue of the Casanatense Library*, vol. II, p. 523.) Cf. Possevino, *Apparatus Sacer*, vol. I, p. 396, and Sandius. A copy also exists in the Leiden Library and in the British Museum.

Ceillier and Baluze passed the following judgment upon this edition of Goulart: he followed Pamelius’ arrangement and text, but added from his own hand observations that are lengthy and laborious to read, through which he attempted to refute Pamelius and turn Saint Cyprian into a Calvinist.

1593.

GOULART’S EDITION II. Geneva, folio, with the notes of Jacques Pamelius and Simon Goulart’s observations upon them. A copy exists in the Barberini Library (*Catalogue*, vol. I). Rome, 1687, two volumes, folio.

SEVENTEENTH CENTURY

1600.

Thomas James’s *Cyprianus Redivivus*, that is, *An Elenchus* [Col. LXXVIII] *of the Material Added to, Removed from through Typographical Error, or Interpolated in Any Other Way into Cyprian’s Short Work On the Unity of the Church*; London, quarto.—On this subject Andreas Rivet should be read, *Critici Sacri*, book II, ch. 14; *Theological Works*, vol. II, p. 1095.

1603.

PAMELIUS’ EDITION IV. Paris, folio, at the press of Sébastien Nivelle. (Barberini Library, vol. I; Bodleian Library Catalogue, second edition.)

1603.

**THIRD PAMELIAN-GOULART EDITION.** Paris, folio. A reprint of Pamelius’s edition with Goulart’s observations.

1603.

Cyprian, *On the Vanity of Idols*, octavo, without place of publication. (Barberini Library.)

1603.

Theodore Petreius, *The Tertullianic and Cyprianic Confession*, four books, Paris, octavo—“laboring excessively in the interests of faction,” says Walch, *Bibliotheca Patristica*, chap. 9, § 94.

1607.

**FIFTH PAMELIAN EDITION.** Paris, folio, at the press of Sebastian Nivelle. Cf. the edition of 1603.

1616.

**FOURTH PAMELIAN-GOULART EDITION.** Paris, at the press of Sébastien Chappelet, with Goulart’s annotations, and corrected with the aid of the editions of Paulus Manutius and Guillaume Morel, according to Nourry.

1617.

**FIFTH PAMELIAN-GOULART EDITION.** Geneva, folio, with the notes of Goulart and Pamelius, according to Ceillier.

1617.

**SIXTH PAMELIAN EDITION.** Cologne, folio. This edition is mentioned by Maran and Fabricius. (Bodleian Library.)

1620–1664.

Hermann Rotlimann, *Theosophy of the Ancient Fathers Tertullian and Cyprian*, etc., published four times under various titles, Wittenberg, quarto. Cf. the *Annals of Tertullian* in vol. I of this Library, at the years 1620, 1636, 1655, and 1664.

1623.

**SIXTH PAMELIAN EDITION.** Paris, folio. (Vol. III of the Chigi Library.)

1629.

**Third German Version.**—The treatise of St. Cyprian *On Mortality*, translated into German by Ludwig Lavater under this title: *Traktaetlein den heil. Cypriani von der Pestilenz* (*A Little Treatise of St. Cyprian on the Pestilence*). Zurich, octavo. (Zurich Catalogue.)

1632.

**SEVENTH PAMELIAN EDITION.** Cologne, folio. (Barberini Library.)

1632.

**EIGHTH PAMELIAN EDITION.** Paris, folio. (Dupin, Ceillier, Maran.)

1632.

Cyprian, *On the Unity of the Church*, illustrated through comparison with manuscripts and annotations, through the efforts of Jeremiah Stephens. (Catalogues of the Leiden and Zurich Libraries, vol. III.)

1633.

**NINTH PAMELIAN EDITION.** Paris, folio. (Casanatense Library.)

1633.

*On the Good of Patience*, with notes by Jeremiah Stephens, Oxford, octavo.

[Col. LXXIX] 1643.

Cyprian, *On the Vanity of Idols*, with observations by Rigault. (Bodleian and Barberini Libraries.)

1644.

**FOURTH PAMELIAN-GOULART EDITION.** It is commended by Dupin, Nourry, and Ceillier.

1645.

**Fourth French Version.** The treatise *On the Lapsed*, rendered into French by Arnauld, or, in French: *Traité des Chrétiens qui étaient tombés durant la persécution, traduit par M. Arnault* (*Treatise on the Christians Who Had Fallen during the Persecution, translated by M. Arnauld*). (Bünau Library Catalogue, p. 50.)

## CLASS V. The Editions of Rigault

1648.

**FIRST RIGAULT EDITION, TWELFTH PARIS EDITION.** Lutetia Parisiorum [Paris], at the press of the widow of Mathurin Dupuis, rue Saint-Jacques, under the sign of the Crown, folio.—1. The complete works of St. Caecilius Cyprian, revised according to the authority of ancient copies and illustrated with observations by Nicolas Rigault. 2. Nicolas Rigault’s *Observations on the Epistles and Treatises of Caecilius Cyprian*. A discourse by an anonymous ancient author *On the Baptism of Heretics*, now published for the first time from the Library of Remi.

“In the *Epistles* and *Treatises*,” says Rigault, “I have displayed the principal features of the ancient text, faithfully preserved from the author’s own style in the excellent Verona and Benevento copies, collated long ago by Marcello—later Pope Marcellus II—and Antonio Agustín, then bishop of Alife. These readings, copied into a volume of Cyprian in the hand of Cardinal de Montchal, archbishop of Toulouse, with the greatest diligence and fidelity, were constantly available for our use. I do not deny that all of them ought indeed to have been reproduced here within the actual text of Cyprian’s works; nor would I wish it to be thought that I was ever uncertain about this plan. I was exceedingly distressed that, because the printing work was being hurried, I could not be present.”

The *Observations*, therefore, says Schoenemann, are concerned partly with adjudicating among the variant readings of the manuscripts cited, and partly serve in place of scholia. Most of them are brief, but they are exceedingly useful, display sound and elegant judgment, and are remarkable for their admirable παρρησία (*frankness*). In addition there is a supplement of observations on Tertullian, published in earlier years, and the famous treatise *On the Beauty of Christ’s Body*. The order is the same as in the Pamelian edition, although the books are not divided into three volumes. Rigault also omitted the first epistle—or rather the fragment of an epistle—which Pamelius had first published. Four copies of this edition, collated with manuscript codices, were held in the Baluze Library.

Dupin judges Rigault’s edition as follows:

> Following Pamelius’s model, M. Rigault, after bringing Tertullian to light, published Cyprian. Without changing anything in the order observed by Pamelius, he merely corrected this author’s works from two Italian manuscripts whose readings de Montchal, archbishop of Toulouse, had entered in the margins of his own Cyprian. He also composed notes explaining difficult passages and observations illustrating the discipline of those times. Some of these observations do indeed appear bold, but he attempts to excuse them in his preface.

Remi Ceillier adds that Rigault’s unconstrained boldness, by which in his commentaries he endeavored to weaken certain passages of St. Cyprian establishing the prerogatives of the bishops of Rome, raised up not a few opponents against him. Chief among them was Albaspinaeus, who, according to Hugo Grotius (*Letter* [Col. LXXX] *to Salmasius*, p. 323), would have denounced him as a heretic had death not interrupted his efforts. He is also ill spoken of among theologians because he denied that infant baptism was of apostolic tradition.

1649.

**SECOND RIGAULT EDITION.**—Ibid., at the same press, folio, reprinted. A copy collated with a manuscript is recorded in the Catalogue of the Bodleian Library.

1650.

London, octavo: various works of Cyprian—the *Epistles*, *On the Dress and Discipline of Virgins*, *On the Lapsed*, *On the Unity of the Church*, *On the Lord’s Prayer*, etc.—in Francis Rous’s *Honey of the Fathers*, pp. 843–944. (Bünau Library Catalogue.)

1664.

**Fifth French Version.** St. Cyprian’s treatises *On the Lord’s Prayer* and *On Mortality*, rendered into French by Monsieur Laval—that is, by the duke of Luynes, according to Ceillier.

1664.

**Sixth French Version.** According to the same Ceillier, St. Cyprian’s treatise *On Almsgiving* is found at the end of the second volume of the abbé de Saint-Cyran’s *On Christian Almsgiving*, among the works of that abbé.

1666.

**PRIEUR EDITION, FIFTEENTH PARIS EDITION.**—Paris, at the press of Jean Dupuis, folio. From Rigault’s edition, with Rigault’s annotations in full and the commentaries of Jacques Pamelius and others previously published separately. Added are Marcus Minucius Felix’s *Octavius*; the seven books of Arnobius Afer *Against the Nations*; Julius Firmicus Maternus’s book *On the Error of Profane Religions*; and Commodian’s *Instructions against the Gods of the Nations*, with notes by Nicolas Rigault. The edition was enlarged with various scholars’ commentaries and illustrated with notes through the efforts of Philippe Prieur.

1667.

Louis Thomassin, priest of the Congregation of the Oratory, *Dissertation on the Synods Held under Pope Stephen in the Controversy over the Baptism of Heretics—the Roman, Carthaginian, etc.—in the Years of Christ 256, 257, etc.*; among his *Dissertations on Councils, Both General and Particular*. Paris, quarto.

1669.

Sebastian Niemann, *Dissertation on the Libellatici*, Jena.

1681.

Altdorf, printed and published by Heinrich Meyer, quarto: eighty-three [printed “XXCIII,” uncertain] epistles by Cyprian and certain others, written to him or on a similar controversy. They are arranged in the Pamelian order, divided into sections according to the Goulart edition, and furnished in the appropriate places with St. Augustine’s responses to Cyprian’s arguments concerning the baptism of heretics. The various readings and conjectures of Pamelius, Rigault, and others are also supplied, as are marginal references to Gratian’s *Decretum*, Lombard’s *Books of Sentences*, and Thomas Aquinas’s *Summa Theologiae*; finally, several useful indexes were published separately. The whole was prepared through the efforts of Lucas Friedrich Reinhart, professor of theology at the University of Altdorf, etc.

The text, like the order of the epistles, is Pamelian, with marginal variants added from nearly all the manuscripts encountered in Pamelius, Rigault, and Goulart. The editor says that he burned with desire [Col. LXXXI] to obtain several manuscripts from Germany, but that all the patrons whom he approached for this purpose complained of a lack of them. He did, however, receive from the Nuremberg Library for his use the Roman and Venetian editions of 1471, as well as an unnamed edition. He ought at least to have examined these for the benefit of the curious and to have indicated their variant readings more explicitly. In Dupin’s judgment, this edition contains nothing that is not found in others, except that it was revised from a great many manuscripts.

## CLASS VI. The Oxford Editions

1682.

Oxford, at the Sheldonian Theatre, folio: *The Works of St. Cyprian*, revised and illustrated by John Fell, bishop of Oxford. Added are the *Cyprianic Annals; or, A Brief History, Chronologically Arranged, of the Thirteen Years during Which St. Cyprian Lived among the Christians*, by John, bishop of Chester.

The first merit of this edition is that treatises falsely attributed to Cyprian—which previous editors had also demoted, so to speak, and placed separately, yet in such a way that they either passed over the question of their status without examining it or themselves vouched for some of them, as Pamelius did—were entirely removed from the remaining body of writings. Yet, lest readers miss all of them, the editor arranged for them to be printed separately, together with certain other works still unpublished, and in such a format that they could conveniently be bound with the two companion volumes.

As for the genuine writings, he arranged the *Epistles* in a new order, widely differing from that of Pamelius. To the annotations usefully recorded by earlier editors, especially Rigault, which he reproduced in their own words but in a distinctive typeface, he added his own. Of these he speaks almost too modestly, also warning readers that, if he should perhaps seem to anyone excessively devoted to Cyprian’s opinions, they should remember that he had written notes *on* Cyprian, not *against* him. An editor assumes a certain kind of guardianship and cannot acquit himself honorably unless he defends his author.

Among the merits of the arrangement is the considerable convenience afforded readers by placing first the variant readings and then the annotations beneath the text. Moreover, the text itself is divided into short paragraphs, each supplied with marginal summaries. In addition to what the title promises, the Pamelian indexes to the *Life of Cyprian* were prefixed, together with comparative tables of contents for the editions of Erasmus, Manutius, Pamelius, and Oxford. I need say nothing about the typographical elegance and ornament of this edition.

1684.

**Fifth Italian Version.** The treatise against women’s luxury, excerpted from the book *On the Discipline and Dress of Virgins*, rendered into Italian, according to Eudoxius Philenius; Rome, from the press of the Apostolic Camera.

1684.

*Cyprianic Dissertations*, by Henry Dodwell, M.A., of Dublin; Oxford, at the Sheldonian Theatre, duodecimo.

1688.

**Sixth French Version.** Selected epistles of St. Cyprian to confessors and martyrs, translated [Col. LXXXII] into French with historical and moral observations by the celebrated Lenfant, author of the *History of the Councils of Pisa, Constance, and Basel*. (Bünau Library Catalogue; Ceillier.)

1689.

Jean Le Clerc’s *Summary of the Life of St. Cyprian*, which, after being included in his *Bibliothèque universelle*, XII, 212, appeared separately, not only in French, Amsterdam, duodecimo, but also in German in Le Clerc’s *Deutsch übersetzten Lebensbeschreibungen einiger Kirchenväter* (*German Translations of the Lives of Certain Fathers of the Church*), p. 138.

1690.

**SECOND OXFORD EDITION.** Bremen, at the expense of Hermann Brauer, printer to the Gymnasium; an exact reprint of the Oxford edition. Dodwell’s *Cyprianic Dissertations* are appended.

1694.

A commentary by Daniel Frisch *On the Libellatici in the Ancient Church*; Leipzig.

1697.

Rome, folio: St. Cyprian’s work *On the Unity of the Catholic Church*, in Juan Tomás de Rocaberti’s *Bibliotheca Maxima Pontificia Romana*, vol. VI, pp. 903–911.

1699.

**THIRD OXFORD EDITION.** Amsterdam, at the press of Jean-Louis de Lorme, folio. Third edition, to which Henry Dodwell’s *Cyprianic Dissertations* were added. A reprint identical in every respect with the Bremen edition.

## EIGHTEENTH CENTURY

1700.

**FOURTH OXFORD EDITION.** Amsterdam, folio, the same as above. (Catalogue of the Casanatense Library, vol. II.)

1709.

Caecilius Cyprian, *On the Vanity of Idols*, with notes by Nicolas Rigault and Jacob Gronovius; Leiden, together with Minucius Felix’s *Octavius*, pp. 392–401. Catalogues of the Bünau and Zurich Libraries.

1710.

Rome, octavo: the third book of St. Caecilius Cyprian’s *Testimonies to Quirinus*, in *Theological Instruction from the Ancient Fathers*, vol. II, pp. 4–90, from the press of the Sacred Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith, edited by Cardinal Giuseppe Maria Tomasi of the Holy Roman Church.

1716.

**Seventh French Version.** Pre-eminent above all others, with this title: *Les Œuvres de S. Cyprien, évêque de Carthage et martyr, traduites en français par Pierre Lombard, avec des remarques; une nouvelle Vie de S. Cyprien, tirée de ses écrits, et une table des matières* (*The Works of St. Cyprian, Bishop of Carthage and Martyr, Translated into French by Pierre Lombard, with Remarks; a New Life of St. Cyprian Drawn from His Writings; and a Table of Contents*). Rouen, quarto.

1717.

*La Vie de S. Cyprien, docteur de l’Église, évêque de Carthage et martyr, dans laquelle on trouvera l’abrégé des ouvrages de ce Père, des notes critiques et historiques et des dissertations théologiques sur les différentes contestations de son temps* (*The Life of St. Cyprian, Doctor of the Church, Bishop of Carthage and Martyr, Containing a Summary of This Father’s Works, Critical and Historical Notes, and Theological Dissertations on the Various Controversies of His Time*). Paris, quarto. This work was offered for public use without the author’s name; everyone, however, long ago recognized it as the work of Jacques Gervaise.

1717.

**First English Version.** Cyprian, published with the Latin text, an English translation, and notes by Nathaniel Marshall, London, folio.

[Col. LXXXIII] 1719.

**Eighth French Version.** The treatise *On the Singularity of Clerics*, among the doubtful works of St. Cyprian, appeared in French at Paris, at the press of Lottin, according to Ceillier.

1721.

Paris, folio: Cyprian’s epistles to Cornelius and Stephen, supreme pontiffs, and certain other writings, in *The Epistles of the Roman Pontiffs*, by Pierre Coustant of the Congregation of St. Maur, from p. 126.

1724.

*A Dogmatic Dissertation on the Dispute That Arose between St. Stephen and St. Cyprian concerning the Baptism of Heretics*, by an anonymous author. Paris, at the press of the widow of Raymond Mazières and Jean-Baptiste Garnier, rue Saint-Jacques, under the sign of Providence. It was reproduced partly by D. Lumper, vol. XII of the *Theological-Critical History of the Fathers*, but in full both in Soardi’s work *On the Supreme Authority of the Roman Pontiff according to the Present Doctrine of the Gallican Church*, Avignon, 1747, and in this volume of the new *Library of the Fathers*.

## CLASS VII. The Editions of Baluze

1726.

**FIRST BALUZE EDITION.** Paris, from the Royal Press, largest folio: *The Complete Works of St. Caecilius Cyprian, Bishop of Carthage and Martyr, Revised according to Manuscript Codices and Illustrated through the Study and Labor of Étienne Baluze of Tulle*. After Baluze, the work was completed, and the preface and *Life of Cyprian* prepared, by one of the monks of the Congregation of St. Maur, D. Prudentius Maran.

Baluze had planned to append all the spurious writings to Cyprian’s genuine works in the form in which they appear in the Oxford edition, omitting only the *Paschal Computation*, while nevertheless including among the genuine works *On Spectacles*, *On the Praise of Martyrdom*, and the work entitled *An Anonymous Author on Rebaptism*. Accordingly, with the aid of the variant readings accumulated by earlier editions and of nearly thirty new manuscript codices, he had notably corrected the text in many places. He had also furnished it with notes, some explaining the reasons for the corrections, others serving to explain the language or elucidate the subject matter.

Most of the work had already been completed, with the exception of two or three sheets of the treatise *On the Principal Works of Christ*, when sudden death overtook him in the midst of his labor. Since Maran therefore had only to work on what remained and understood that he was merely acting as a substitute—for he admits that, if the preparation of a new edition of Cyprian had fallen to him, he would have relieved himself of no small part of so heavy a burden—he retained, because Baluze had so determined, everything contained in Pamelius’s edition. Of the works with which the English had burdened Cyprian, however, he expunged the compositions of Arnold of Bonneval: *On the Works of the Six Days*, *On the Praises of the Blessed Virgin*, and the *Meditations*.

The English had supplied Cyprian’s *Confession* in a Latin translation that was defective in many places and corrupt in innumerable others. Maran instead presented the Greek text supplied from the library of the comte de Seignelay, accompanied by a new translation. Furthermore, because Baluze had seen that the spurious works of Cyprian—which he had planned to reproduce as they stood in the Oxford edition—had acquired many blemishes through the numerous editions of Cyprian, Maran corrected them from old editions and [Col. LXXXIV] manuscript codices, placing variant readings in the margin. Baluze’s emendations, by contrast, since they are often intermingled with explanations and elucidations, are appended separately after the text.

In place of a preface, Maran also discussed at length Cyprian’s works, editions, doctrine, and deeds, though often departing from the Oxford editors and bringing Cyprian into conformity with the doctrines received by the Catholic Church.

1727.

*Dissertation théologique sur la célèbre dispute entre le pape S. Estienne et S. Cyprien* (*Theological Dissertation on the Famous Dispute between Pope St. Stephen and St. Cyprian*), published without the author’s name and attributed to D. Corgne.

1728.

**SECOND BALUZE EDITION.** Baluze’s edition was reprinted at Venice in folio, according to Eudoxius Philenius in Tricalet’s *Library of the Fathers of the Church*, translated into Latin.

1733.

Paris, folio: St. Cyprian’s poem to Felix *On the Resurrection of the Dead*, in the Zurich Library, vol. III; in vol. IX of Edmond Martène and Ursin Durand, *A Very Extensive Collection of Ancient Writers and Monuments*.

1733.

Francesco Raimondo Missorio, *Critical Disputations on the Two Most Celebrated Epistles of Firmilian and Cyprian against the Decree of St. Stephen*.—The same author’s disputation on the epistle to Pompeius, number LXXIV among the Cyprianic epistles, in which, for the first time, he disallows it—together with five others and the Third Council of Carthage, hitherto regarded as Cyprianic—and attributes them to the Donatists. Venice, quarto.

1734.

Father Tournemine’s conjecture concerning the same epistles. (*Mémoires de Trévoux*, year 1734, p. 2246.) Malleville submitted this most learned Father’s conjecture to critical examination in the work entitled *La Religion naturelle et la révélée établie* (*Natural and Revealed Religion Established*), etc., Dissertation VIII, art. 8, p. 528.

1738.

Georg Gottlob Preu, *Critical-Theological Dissertation Presenting a Defense of the Epistles of Cyprian and Firmilian against the Decree of Pope Stephen I concerning the Baptism of Heretics, in Opposition to Raimondo Missorio*; Jena, quarto.

1741.

Fr. J. Heinrich Sboralea, in a pamphlet against Missorio of the same order, expounded the genuine opinion of St. Cyprian and the Africans, as well as of Firmilian and the Easterners, concerning the baptism of heretics. Bologna, 1741.

1750.

J. F. Cotta, *Historical-Critical Exercise in Which the Conjecture of René-Joseph Tournemine, etc., Is Submitted to Examination*; Tübingen, quarto.

1751.

Bologna: St. Cyprian’s *Exhortation to Repentance*, with notes by J. C. Trombellius, among that author’s *Short Works of the Ancient Latin Fathers*, pp. 3–32, quarto.

1751–1754.

F. J. Reuchlin, three dissertations *On the Doctrine of Cyprian*; Strasbourg, quarto.

1753.

*On SS. Cornelius, Pope and Martyr, and Cyprian, Bishop and Martyr*, among the Bollandist *Acts of the Saints*, at September 14, vol. IV, pp. 143–350, by Constantinus Suyskenus.

1758.

**THIRD BALUZE EDITION.** Venice, from the press of Girolamo [Col. LXXXV] Dorigoni, folio: *The Complete Works of St. Caecilius Cyprian*. It is a reprint of the Baluze-Maran edition, but shamefully marred by typographical errors.

1759.

Florence, at the expense of Antonio Zatta of Venice, folio: St. Cyprian’s epistles to Cornelius, Lucius, and Stephen, supreme pontiffs, and certain other writings, in Mansi’s new and most extensive *Collection of Councils*, vol. I, pp. 793–865, 881–885, and 928.

1760.

Langensalza, octavo, at the expense of Johann Martin: St. Caecilius Cyprian’s book *On the Vanity of Idols*, revised and illustrated with selected notes by various scholars as well as with his own by Johann Gottlieb Lindner, published together with Minucius Felix’s *Octavius*. See the *Acta Eruditorum* of Leipzig, year 1760, p. 275 ff.

1763.

F. E. Boysen, *Proceedings between St. Cyprian and Stephen in the Dispute over the Baptism of Heretics*; Leipzig and Quedlinburg, quarto.

1771.

Christian Gottfried Müller, *Program of Observations on Five Passages of Cyprian*; Gera, quarto.

1771.

Antonio Sandini, *Historical Disputations on the Lives of the Roman Pontiffs*, disputations VII and VIII, octavo, Ferrara.

1773.

Langensalza, octavo: St. Caecilius Cyprian’s book *On the Vanity of Idols*, Lindner’s second edition, much more correct than the first.

1782.

**FIFTH BALUZE EDITION,** octavo, Würzburg, from Stahel’s press, two volumes: *The Works of St. Cyprian*, edited by Oberthür. In the second volume, besides the treatises formerly attributed to Cyprian, augmented from the Oxford and Benedictine editions by the addition of several others, were included Minucius Felix’s *Octavius* and the short works of Novatian.

The distinguished Oberthür himself explains in the following words the plan he followed:

> It reproduces Maran’s edition—not indeed the Paris edition of 1727 (correct this to 1726), nor the Venetian edition of 1728, but the other Venetian edition of 1758, produced by Girolamo Dorigoni—because the earlier editions, which were certainly better than this last, were not at hand. Before committing it to our press for reprinting, however, I corrected the errors with which a rather negligent editor had caused it to abound. This required great labor and frequent recourse to another Paris edition of Cyprian, prepared by Rigault, which was available to me.
>
> I preferred Maran’s recension of St. Cyprian’s works, which I reproduce here, to Rigault’s because it is more recent and more abundant—even to the point of prodigality—and indeed presents a confused chaos of various works: some that cannot be attributed to Cyprian with sufficient certainty; others that sounder criticism requires rather to be denied to Cyprian; others whose author is unknown; and still others that are indeed owed to known authors, but authors far removed from the age of our Cyprian. It caused me no small difficulty to make a selection: what from this medley of pamphlets I should undertake to reprint in this new edition, what I should pass over, and how, after separating them, [Col. LXXXVI] I should arrange the selected works in some prescribed order.

1784.

Ulm, printed by Christian Ulrich Wagner, duodecimo: the short works of St. Caecilius Cyprian, bishop of Carthage and martyr, *On the Lapsed*, *On the Lord’s Prayer*, and *On the Good of Patience*, offered as a gift to the gentlemen associated with the Congregation of the Blessed Virgin Mary in the Imperial Monastery of St. George in the Black Forest.

1790.

**Fourth German Version.** Vienna, octavo, edited by C. C. von Hohenbalken, published under this title: *Die echten Werke des heiligen Caecilius Cyprianus, Bischofs zu Carthago und Märtyrers* (*The Genuine Works of St. Caecilius Cyprian, Bishop of Carthage and Martyr*).

1790.

Fr. Marcellinus Molkenbuhr, O.S.F., of the Strict Observance, two dissertations: the first, *On the Epistle of St. Firmilian, Bishop of Caesarea, to St. Stephen, and on His Other Works*, etc., Münster in Westphalia, quarto; the second, *On the Year of St. Firmilian’s Death*.

1791.

An anonymous dissertation published at Frankfurt and Leipzig under this title: *Weder die christliche Religion, noch die römisch-katholische Kirche ist die alleinseligmachende* (*Neither the Christian Religion nor the Roman Catholic Church Is the Sole Means of Salvation*).

1791.

An anonymous dissertation entitled: *Doctrine de S. Cyprien sur l’unité de l’Église et sur le schisme, appliquée au temps présent* (*St. Cyprian’s Doctrine on the Unity of the Church and on Schism, Applied to the Present Time*). Paris, at the press of Dufraine, in the Palais, duodecimo, 111 pages.

Cyprian and Cornelius concerning the Novatian Heresy and the Discipline for Readmitting Fallen Bishops*, quarto. Münster in Westphalia.

1796.

The Cyprianic epistles among D. Coustant’s *Epistles of the Roman Pontiffs*, from the edition of C. T. Gottlob Schoenemann, Göttingen, octavo.

1815.

1818–1820.

**Fifth German Version,** edited by M. Feyerabend, Munich, four volumes, octavo.

1822–1823.

The authenticity of the Cyprianic epistles concerning the baptism of heretics challenged in *Literatur-Zeitung für katholische Religionslehrer* (*Literary Journal for Catholic Teachers of Religion*), year 1822, issue VII, pp. 79, 102, and year 1823, issue IV, p. 33.

1831.

Franz Wilhelm Rettberg, *Thascius Caecilius Cyprianus, Dargestellt nach seinem Leben und Wirken* (*Thascius Caecilius Cyprian, Portrayed according to His Life and Activity*), Göttingen, octavo.

1832.

St. Caecilius Cyprian’s books *On the Vanity of Idols*, *On Mortality, or the Plague*, *On Works and Almsgiving*, and *On Jealousy and Envy*, as well as Firmilian’s epistle . . . . . . revised, with his own notes and those of others added, by Martin Joseph Routh, S.T.P., president of Magdalen College. Oxford, octavo; a second, enlarged edition at the same place in 1840.

1834.

Friedrich Schem, *Excursus on the Treatise On the Lapsed*, together with a German translation of that book and three others. Münster, octavo.

1838.

**LEIPZIG EDITION.** The genuine works of Thascius Caecilius Cyprian, reproduced according to the authority of the best books and furnished with brief annotation, edited by D. J. H. Goldhorn, two volumes; duodecimo, Leipzig, at the expense and press of Bernhard Tauchnitz the Younger.

1840.

Conrad Stephan Matthies, *Biblical, Historical, and Dogmatic Exposition of Baptism*, octavo, Berlin.

1841.

**Second English Version.** *St. Cyprian’s Treatises*, second edition, Oxford, octavo.

1841.

*On Cyprian’s Anabaptistic Epistles and the Synods Held in the Third Century in Support of Rebaptizers.*

1842.

A *Life of St. Cyprian* written in English by Poole and translated into French under the editorship of Fr. Z. Columbet, Lyon.

1844.

**New Baluze and Oxford Edition.**—Paris, edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of this Library. From the synopsis of this edition prefixed to the opening of vol. IV, everyone will perceive what we have added to the Baluze edition, what we have removed, and what we have altered. The following were added:

1. Throughout the entire Cyprianic text, gleanings of selected variant readings, derived chiefly from the Oxford edition.

2. Here and there, several annotations borrowed from Pamelius, Fell, Routh, and Goldhorn.

3. In the book *On the Vanity of Idols*, a richer harvest of notes adapted for our use from Lindner’s edition.

4. In the doubtful works, the notes of Pamelius retained by the Oxford editor.

5. Three short works: the first omitted by Baluze, namely the *Computation of Easter*, published in the appendix of the Oxford edition; the second first brought to light by J. C. Trombellius, namely St. Cyprian’s *Exhortation to Repentance*; and finally the last, the poem to Felix *On the Resurrection of the Dead*, published by Edmond Martène in the *Very Extensive Collection of Ancient Writers and Monuments*, vol. IV.

6. D. Nicolas Le Nourry’s dissertation on Cyprian’s books *To Demetrianus* and *On the Vanity of Idols*, distinguished by its great abundance of material.

7. Finally, at the very end [Col. LXXXVIII] of the edition, we placed a considerable body of selected Oxford and Routhian notes. In this way, not only the Baluze edition but also, in its best part, the English edition was presented anew in ours.

We decided, however, that the following should either be placed elsewhere or omitted entirely:

1. The *Life of St. Cyprian*, written by Pontius the deacon, and the proconsular Acts are given separately below, under their proper year.

2. The letters of the pontiffs—whether those of Cornelius to Cyprian or those of Cyprian and others to the Roman pontiffs—we were obliged to insert in this third volume, where SS. Cornelius, Lucius, and Stephen are treated. Yet we did not fail repeatedly to notify the reader, and even briefly to indicate what had been omitted, whenever anything had to be referred elsewhere.

3. We set aside the synodical epistles in the same volume, especially among the records concerning the baptism of heretics and the Councils of Carthage.

4. We removed from the Cyprianic corpus two books written by anonymous authors in the same dispute and placed them elsewhere.

5. The preface by a certain Celsus, addressed to Bishop Vigilius, to the disputation of Jason and Papiscus *On Jewish Unbelief*—which was perhaps adopted among Cyprian’s works with excessively hasty judgment because in the Colbert manuscript numbered 1403 its opening reads, “Cyprian to his brother Vigilius, greetings”—we transferred, after correction, to the following volumes, where the complete records of this disputation are to be given.
