6. The *Exposition of the Creed*, deservedly attributed to Rufinus of Aquileia, and the treatise *On the Principal Works of Christ*, plainly composed by Arnold, abbot of Bonneval, are restored to their proper authors and return to their respective places.

7. The poems *Genesis* and *Sodom* are given above in the appendices to Tertullian.

Indeed, to complete this edition, as it seems, there was added—whether in this third or in the fifth volume—a long series of materials, monuments, and dissertations: first, those that now follow concerning the Roman pontiffs contemporary with Cyprian, along with documents of every kind, both ancient and recent, concerning the celebrated controversy over rebaptism; and then those that immediately follow the Cyprianic works, namely three selected dissertations by Henry Dodwell. Through these, unless I am mistaken, our edition readily becomes more complete and more abundant than all those published hitherto.

Enough, then, has been given to Cyprian and to the other Fathers of the same age. As we now prepare, so to speak, to take leave of them and address our readers for the last time, we hold nothing more fitting or more sacred than, as before when we reached the end of Tertullian, to give thanks to God and to the Mother of God, and once again to venture to offer and dedicate this little work, such as it is, to the Church, our most loving mother on earth. We trust especially in that aid and favorable divine power under which we complete this work just as the welcome feast of the holy Apostles Peter and Paul is about to begin. We therefore earnestly beseech them to stand graciously beside us and our affairs, to preserve both us and our readers safe and unharmed under the same protection, and peacefully and happily to assist us forever.

Written at Paris, on the fourth day before the Kalends of July [June 28], in the year of the Lord 1844.

**THE EDITORS.**

## THIRD CENTURY, ABOUT THE YEAR OF CHRIST 203

# ACTS OF THE HOLY MARTYRS PERPETUA AND FELICITY

[Col. 0009]

## PROLEGOMENA

FROM THE *AUTHENTIC ACTS OF THE MARTYRS* OF THE DISTINGUISHED THEODORIC RUINART, P. 77 FF.

## SYNOPSIS

[Col. 0009A] I. On the printed editions and manuscripts of these Acts. II. Were Perpetua and Felicity of Thuburbo? III. They are known to have suffered martyrdom not at Thuburbo but at Carthage. IV. The date of their passion is investigated. V. On the author—or rather compiler—of these Acts. Was it Tertullian? [Col. 0010A] VI. He was not a Montanist: against Valesius. VII. The fiction concerning the author’s Montanism is again refuted. VIII. On the cult and commemoration of these martyrs. IX. Acts of this kind were long ago defended against Samuel Basnage by a most learned man. How highly they should be valued. The proconsular Acts are henceforth to be omitted.

I. The authentic Acts of Saints Perpetua and Felicity, greatly desired and long sought in vain in various libraries, were finally discovered by Lucas Holstenius, that most diligent investigator of sacred antiquity, in a manuscript codex [Col. 0009B] of the holy monastery of Monte Cassino. After they had been brought forth from there and published at Rome, Henri Valois later published the same Acts at Paris with notes by Holstenius.

We, however, present them from two manuscript codices collated with that edition. One belongs to the Church of Salzburg; we received the variant readings of this codex through the kindness of the most wise Antoine Faure, a Parisian theologian and provost of the Church of Reims. The other, which approaches eight hundred years in age, belongs to the library of our monastery of Saint-Corneille at Compiègne. We also found among the papers of our Mabillon excerpts from these same Acts that are not to be disregarded, although there is no indication of the codex from which they were copied.

Moreover, in those passages where the manuscript codices differ from one another or from the printed editions, yet either reading [Col. 0009C] is admissible, we have placed the variation in the notes, lest we appear rashly to have altered anything in so precious a monument of the Church. We have exercised the same caution whenever anything worthy of notice occurs in manuscript codices in which these same Acts survive in a corrupt form.

II. In his preface to these Acts, the learned Valesius investigates three questions: first, where these holy women suffered; second, at what time they consummated their martyrdom; and finally, who was the author—or rather compiler—of these Acts. All these matters must also be treated briefly here.

As for the first, before [Col. 0010A] the authentic Acts of these martyrs had been discovered, scarcely anyone called into doubt that they were the same women whom various authors celebrated under the name of the Holy Women of Thuburbo. This was suggested not only by the authority of certain martyrologies, including ancient ones, but also by the Acts circulated under the names of Perpetua and Felicity, [Col. 0010B] in which it was expressly stated that they had suffered at Thuburbo. Although learned men regarded some things in these Acts as faulty and corrupt, no one had hitherto raised any question concerning the place of their martyrdom.

But when the matter was examined more precisely on the occasion of Holstenius’s edition, the more learned took a different view, especially Henri Valois. After weighing the considerations that could be advanced on both sides, he firmly pronounced that these martyrs had consummated their martyrdom not at Thuburbo but at Carthage. That distinguished scholar proves this opinion both from the Acts themselves and from the authority of ancient writers. [Col. 0010C] From the Acts it is established that these martyrs were condemned by proconsular authority, and consequently, as he says, not at Thuburbo in Mauretania, since proconsuls possessed no jurisdiction in that province. Yet, as was observed in the new edition of Augustine, because there were two places named Thuburbo situated in the proconsular province, because there may perhaps have been an amphitheater in one or the other of those cities, and because one of them was called Thuburbo Maius, this argument of Valesius has little force—unless it be said that nearly all the martyrologies expressly located Thuburbo in Mauretania.

[Col. 0011A] III. More certain is the argument drawn from the authority of the ancients who wrote about Saints Perpetua and Felicitas. For, besides Victor of Vita’s affirmation that they “were buried at Carthage in the greater basilica” [Note: [Col. 0011D] Victor of Vita, *On the Vandal Persecution*, book I, chapter III, p. 5, Paris ed., 1694], Prosper in the Labbean *Chronicle*, Bede in his book *On the Six Ages of the World*, and indeed also in his authentic *Martyrology* (although the work circulated under his name reads otherwise), Regino, Rabanus in his *Martyrology*, and very many other martyrologies, both printed and manuscript—as may be seen in the Bollandists under March 7—expressly assert that these holy martyrs suffered at Carthage.

Nor is it helpful to reply that Augustine, in Sermon XXXII as edited by Sirmond, which is CCCXLV in the new edition, calls these martyrs “the Tuburbitan women.” For in the manuscript codex from which [Col. 0011B] that sermon was taken, one reads not *Tuburbitanarum*, as Sirmond corrected it, but *Suburbitarum*. Someone might perhaps say that they were called *Suburbitanae* because they suffered in a suburb of Carthage. But even if it be granted that this passage was correctly emended by Sirmond, nothing can be inferred from it against Valesius’s opinion. Valesius indeed admits that Augustine is speaking here of the Tuburbitan martyrs, but he flatly denies that they are Perpetua and Felicitas. Elsewhere, when Augustine often discusses Perpetua and Felicitas, he never calls them Tuburbitan, but always calls them by their proper names, Perpetua and Felicitas. The learned man instead maintains that by “the Tuburbitan women” Saint Augustine here meant Maxima, Donatilla, and Secunda, who are said to have suffered at Tuburbium under the emperors Valerian and Gallienus. And indeed [Col. 0011C] this answer of Valesius could be confirmed from the ancient Carthaginian calendar published by Mabillon, in which the feast of the holy Tuburbitan women is commemorated on July 30; on that day Perpetua and Felicitas are nowhere commemorated, whereas Maxima and her companions are reported in all the martyrologies to have died on that date.

IV. We shall not dwell long upon determining the time at which these blessed martyrs completed their passion. The Acts and martyrologies which report that they suffered under Valerian and Gallienus are proved false by the very fact that Tertullian, who mentions Perpetua in his book *On the Soul*, departed this life long before the time of those emperors. Thus the authentic *Martyrology* of Bede and other ancient sources more correctly assign this martyrdom to the reign of the emperor Severus; the genuine Acts [Col. 0011D] agree with them, since there [Note: [Col. 0011D] *Acts of the Passion*, etc., chapter 16] the holy martyrs were exposed to the beasts on the birthday of Geta Caesar. We believe this occurred in the year of Christ 202, or the following year, on the Ides of March. DOM THÉODORE RUINART.

V. Finally, we must inquire who was the author—or rather the compiler—of these Acts, since no one can deny that the greater part of them was written by Perpetua and Saturus. The author of a letter written from Bourges to Henri de Valois attributes that work to Tertullian. To prove this, he compared many passages in the Acts with other works of Tertullian and showed that precisely the same style, the same forms of expression, and very often even the same words are found in both. Whether this entirely proves the matter, however, others will judge.

VI. But I cannot agree with Valesius, who thinks that these Acts were compiled by a follower of Montanus, whoever he may have been. Nevertheless, that most learned man thinks that he can infer this from entirely certain indications. Those indications are that the author professes to accept new prophecies and greatly prefers them to the prophecies of the Old Testament. He proves this from the compiler’s own words, who speaks as follows in the preface: “Therefore we also acknowledge and honor new visions, equally promised beforehand, just as we do prophecies.” And a little earlier he had said: “But let those who judge the one power of the one Holy Spirit according to the ages of the times look to it, since all more recent things, as being the very latest, must be regarded as greater.”

Yet, although at first sight these words may seem to savor of Montanus’s errors, if they are examined somewhat more carefully, you will find that they contain nothing except what is orthodox and entirely consonant with the catholic faith. For this author does not compare the most recent visions with the canonical Scriptures, as Valesius thought, but only with the visions and revelations of the ancient martyrs. He asserts that events occurring in his own time should be held in no less veneration than those which had occurred in ancient times, that is, in the first or second century of the Church. Indeed, he says that in some measure these new revelations should be received with greater attention, since examples are more effective the more recent they are; and, furthermore, because these latest visions, which would one day be ancient, needed to be supported by some authority so that posterity would believe them. This is clear from the same author’s entire preface, in which there is not even a single word about comparing Sacred Scripture with the martyrs’ visions:

“If ancient examples of faith,” he says, “have been set down in writing . . . so that by reading them, as though through a renewed representation of the events, God may be honored and man strengthened, why should new testimonies, equally suited to both purposes, not also be set down? etc.”

Moreover, even if this author believed that these martyrs’ visions were among those which God had promised through Joel, it does not follow that he equated them with Sacred Scripture. Nor did the Church count the faithful’s spoken or written words among these canonical Scriptures, although it did not doubt that they proceeded from Him by whom to some [Col. 0012D] are given various kinds of tongues, to others prophecy, to others the word of wisdom, and to still others other gifts—gifts which, it is certain, had been foretold and promised in the cited testimony of Joel.

VII. But lest the words of the author’s preface, who praises these visions as though divinely inspired, should perhaps disturb anyone, Augustine must be heard on the matter. Although, as they say, he expressly excludes these visions of Perpetua from the canon of Scripture [Note: [Col. 0012D] Augustine, book I, *On the Soul and Its Origin*, to Renatus, chapter 10, no. 12; and book III, to Vincentius, chapter 9, no. 12], he nevertheless calls them “divine revelations” and asserts that the faithful should honor them with religious reverence [Note: [Col. 0012D] The same, Sermon I; new ed., 280, vol. V, p. 1134].

“We heard,” he says, “their exhortations”—those of Perpetua and Felicitas—“in divine revelations, [Col. 0013A] and the triumphs of their passions, when these were read; and we perceived all those things, arranged and illuminated by the lights of words, with our ears, beheld them with our minds, honored them with religious reverence, and praised them with charity.”

Augustine discusses these same visions in several other passages and testifies that they were publicly read in church [Note: [Col. 0013C] The same, Sermon 282]. But finally, to settle the matter in a single word, how could a heretic and follower of Montanus exhort his own people to maintain communion with these women, whom they knew to have died in communion with the Catholics whom they called “Psychics”? Nor could those to whom this author wrote have been ignorant of this, since he addresses those who had been present at the martyrdom: “We proclaim it,” he says, “to you, brothers and little children, so that you also who were present may remember the glory of the Lord, etc.” But enough of this. We must now [Col. 0013B] say a few words about the praises of these martyrs uttered by various authors [Note: [Col. 0013C] Mabillon, vol. I, *Museum Italicum*].

VIII. The memory of Saints Perpetua and Felicitas has always been renowned in the Church, especially in the African Church. Possidius testifies in his *Index* that Saint Augustine delivered three discourses on their anniversary; these are Sermons CCLXXX, CCLXXXI, and CCLXXXII in the new edition. For some time I hesitated over whether to reproduce those sermons here in full. But since Augustine’s works are in almost everyone’s hands, it seemed sufficient, after omitting them, to record in notes upon the text those remarks which relate more particularly to the Acts. The same holy Doctor discusses these martyrs and their companions in many other passages. Tertullian mentions “the most steadfast Perpetua and her fellow martyrs” in *On the Soul*, chapter 55, as we have already said. [Col. 0013C] All the martyrologies assign their feast to March 7, on which day it continues to be celebrated among us.

[Col. 0014A] Their names are also commemorated in the canon of the Roman Mass and in the extremely ancient Gallican Sacramentary published by our Mabillon. They likewise occur in the canon of the Mass in the Gregorian Sacramentary, although the feast of these saints does not appear among the other feasts recorded there, perhaps because it falls during Lent. It is also absent from Mabillon’s very ancient calendar of the African Church. But since it is certain from Augustine that their feast was celebrated in his day, it must be said that, unless they are designated in it by the name “Tuburbitan women,” that calendar is not complete; for it actually lacks twelve days of February and the whole months of March and April.

That their feast was also celebrated at Rome in the earliest times is clear from the missal of Gelasius and from the ancient Bucherian martyrology, where the following appears: “On March 7, Perpetua and Felicitas, in Africa.” The other martyrologies, both ancient and more recent, have the same. They are celebrated with their companions in the Greek *Menologion* of the emperor Basil on February 2.

Their relics are said to have been brought from Africa to Rome during the Vandal persecution. Later, in the ninth century, Rodulfus, archbishop of Bourges, received them from there and deposited them in the monasteries of Dèvres and Beaulieu, which he himself had founded. Certainly even today the Benedictine monks who, after the destruction of Dèvres, migrated to Vierzon, glory in possessing the relics of blessed Perpetua.

But the Acts themselves must now be presented. Anyone who wishes to compare them with the printed editions will readily notice how much more accurately corrected they appear on the basis of our codices. [Col. 0014C] Certainly it is no insignificant achievement that with their aid we have restored the name and martyrdom of Saturninus. Thus far the distinguished RUINART.

[Col. 0013]

# THE PASSION

[Note: [Col. 0013D] [Col. 0014D] The variant readings are taken from Dom Ruinart’s edition [Col. 0015B] among the *Authentic Acts of the Martyrs*, p. 77 ff. The annotations, however, come partly from Ruinart himself, partly from the posthumous notes of Lukas Holste, excerpted from his *Adversaria*, and finally from the shorter supplements made to those notes by Father Pierre Poussines of the Society of Jesus. EDD.

We retain the title *Passion*, which Holste proves to be appropriate to these Acts. In the Salzburg codex the words “in the Turbitan city” are added. But that codex lacks the preface, as does the Compiègne codex.]

## OF THE HOLY MARTYRS PERPETUA AND FELICITAS

(*Authentic Acts of the Martyrs*, Dom Ruinart, p. 77 ff.; *Acta Sanctorum*, Bollandists, March III, 633; Gallandi, *Library of the Ancient Fathers*, vol. II, pp. XXIII–174). (C, G, S)

## PREFACE

[Col. 0013C] [Note: [Col. 0013D]

**The Passion of the Holy Saints.** In the Monte Cassino manuscript no title appears; and for this reason, I think, this most elegant monument of sacred antiquity has until now escaped the inquisitive eyes of researchers. On Augustine’s authority I gave it the title *Passion*, for this is what he himself calls it in the passages cited above, in Psalm XLVII and Sermon 3. Without doubt this title was then read at the head of the many copies of this little work that circulated everywhere, and similar writings were customarily entitled in this way, as we understand from the martyrdom of Saint Cyprian written by Pontius the Deacon and from other works of that kind. If anyone should nevertheless prefer to call it by the Greek name *Martyrdom* (*Martyrium*), he can find in this very narrative grounds with which to support his conjecture. HOLSTE.]

If ancient examples of faith, both testifying to the grace of God [Col. 0014C] and effecting the edification of man, have been set down in writing [Col. 0015A] [Note: [Col. 0015B]

**Have been set down in writing.** I would prefer to read “set down *into* writing.” Thus Pontius at the beginning of his *Book on the Passion* [Col. 0015C] of Saint Cyprian: “To his works and merits this privilege also is due, that his example should be set down in writing”; there the printed reading “directed” is less correct. HOLSTE.

**Are assigned less authority.** Thus Tertullian, *On Repentance*, chapter 3: “It must be assigned to sin, from which God restrains us.” And shortly afterward in the same place: “Things which must be assigned to transgression.” The same author, *On the Veiling of Virgins*: “But I do not wish to assign this custom to truth.” And *Against Hermogenes*, chapter 11: “Things assigned to evil are reckoned according to the condition of evil.” Then, in the same work, chapter 13: “Now not even good things themselves will be assigned to God.” And chapter 25: “Matter, in Hermogenes’s account, is assigned as the origin and cause of evils.” *On Idolatry*, chapter 10: “Necessity is assigned as an excuse.” Finally, book I, *To His Wife*, chapter 4: “Already on earth they are assigned to the angelic household.” HOLSTE.

**All more recent things, as being the very latest.** The Africans allowed themselves this much in such expressions. Thus in Tertullian you will read *extremiora* (“more extreme”) and *extremissimi* (“most extreme”) more than once. Likewise in Apuleius one finds *postremissimus* (“very last”) and “more extreme than the latest.” [Col. 0015D] In Arnobius, *minimissimus* (“very smallest”). HOLSTE.

**Prophecies and likewise new visions.** Irenaeus, in Eusebius, book V, chapter 7, testifies that visions and prophecies were granted to many in the Church in his own time. Dionysius of Alexandria teaches the same about his own time in the same Eusebius. From Eusebius’s notable passage in book V, chapter 3, where he discusses Montanus, it is evident that in the earliest times of the Church prophecy also flourished among Christians, in addition to the other charisms. It appears that the heresiarch Montanus took confidence from this practice to call his doctrine the “New Prophecy.” HOLSTE.

**We assign the powers of the Holy Spirit as an instrument of the Church.** This use of the word *instrumentum* is characteristic of African and Tertullianic usage. Thus Tertullian in *On Flight in Persecution*, chapter [number omitted], says that the devil’s iniquity is an instrument of persecution. The same author in *On Repentance*, chapter [number omitted]: “Fear, the instrument of repentance.” In *On Patience*, chapter [number omitted]: “Patience, the instrument of endurance.” In book II of *On the Dress of Women*, chapter [number omitted]: “Gravity, the instrument of chastity.” In book I, *To His Wife*, chapter [number omitted]: “Continence has been demonstrated to us by the Lord as an [Col. 0016B] instrument of eternity.” In *On Baptism*, discussing the element of water: “How great is its power or grace? How many faculties, how many functions, how great an instrument does it provide for the world?” Finally, chapter 17 of the *Apology*: “God brought forth from nothing this whole mass together with the entire apparatus of elements, bodies, and spirits.” HOLSTE.

**Administering all gifts in everyone, etc.** [Col. 0016C] The passage is taken directly from Paul, 1 Corinthians 12:4, where he discusses the charisms, which our author here renders as “gifts” (*donativa*), in this respect also echoing Tertullian. For in book V *Against Marcion*, chapter [number omitted], Tertullian says: “He gave gifts to the sons of men—that is, *donativa*, which we call charisms.” And in book I, *To His Wife*, chapter [number omitted]: “Let us stretch forward to the things ahead and be followers of the better gifts.” For thus reads the excellent edition of Nicolas Rigault. So too, in *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, he renders Romans 6:23: “The wages of transgression are death, but the gift of God is eternal life.” No one can fail to know that this terminology is derived from imperial largesse and military affairs. HOLSTE.

**Whether of martyrs or in the gracious bestowal of revelations.** The word *dignatio* is extremely frequent in Tertullian and Cyprian and in the other African writers of that age, meaning a grace which God deigns to confer or bestow. Pontius in the *Life of Saint Cyprian*: “Suppose, then, that he had at that time been translated by the gracious bestowal of martyrdom.” In the same work, after the vision shown to Saint Cyprian in exile, he adds: “What could be clearer than this revelation? What more blessed than this gracious favor?” And below: “But that day of tomorrow which divine favor had foretold a year before.” So too Cyprian himself, more than once, in book IV, Letters VII, XXV, and XXXIV. Likewise in the book *On Mortality*, where we read: “Martyrdom is not within your power, but within God’s gracious favor.” And Sermon V, *On the Lapsed*: “The crown descends through God’s gracious favor.” Elsewhere Tertullian likewise says in *On Patience*, chapter 11: “It is fitting that we congratulate ourselves and rejoice in the gracious favor of divine correction.” And in *On the Dress of Women*, chapter 2: “For he promises you also . . . the same gracious privilege of judging.” In *On Baptism*, chapter 18: “If Philip baptized the eunuch so readily, let us consider that a manifest and unmistakable gracious favor of the Lord intervened.” And immediately afterward: “God’s gracious favor sends its privileges before it.” So too in chapter 3 of the same book; chapter 31 of *The Prescription Against Heretics*; chapter 4 of *On Patience*; book *Against the Jews*, chapter 1; etc. HOLSTE.

**For a testimony to unbelievers, for a benefit to believers, etc.** Thus Tertullian, *On the Soul*, chapter 51: “Everywhere God displays signs of his power: for the consolation of his own, for a testimony to outsiders.” HOLSTE.

**CHAPTER I—1. Young catechumens.** I found it written thus in the ancient Monte Cassino parchments, and it is likewise printed throughout Mombritius’s *Sanctuary*. Perhaps words of this kind were pronounced no differently in that age. Thus *Filuminus* is read in Optatus of Milevis. Moreover, aptly for our present subject, Pontius, the Carthaginian deacon, says in the *Life of Saint Cyprian*: “Our predecessors bestowed so much honor, out of reverence for martyrdom itself, upon common believers and catechumens who attained martyrdom, that they recorded many—or, I might almost say, nearly all—details of their passions, so that these might come to the knowledge even of us who had not yet been born.” In that passage “common believers” must be understood as laypersons who had attained no rank in the clergy. For a little below, the same Pontius says: “There are many things which he did while still a layman and many after he became a presbyter.” Pontius seems to allude to these very Acts and others similar to them. At least this is clear: the African Church diligently devoted itself to ensuring that the glorious deeds of the holy martyrs should pass into the memory of posterity.

Moreover, the fact that our martyrs are commemorated as having fought so vigorously when they had scarcely yet been taught the rudiments of the Christian faith and were novices in our religion does not diminish but increases their glory. Thus the church of Lyons, in Eusebius, book V, chapter 1, praises Maturus most highly as νεοφώτιστον μὲν, ἀλλὰ γενναῖον ἀγωνιστήν, “newly enlightened, but a noble combatant.” And in book VI, chapter 4, the same Eusebius commemorates the martyrs Heraclides and Hieron from Origen’s school: ὁ μὲν πρότερος ἔτι κατηχούμενος, ὁ δὲ νεοφώτιστος, “the former still a catechumen, the latter newly baptized.” Rhais, a catechumen, is numbered with them there; Origen said that she had received the baptism of fire.

But the *Apostolic Constitutions*, book V, chapter 5, speak splendidly of the martyrdom of catechumens:

Ὁ δὲ ἀξιωθεὶς μαρτυρίου χαιρέτω τὴν ἐν Κυρίῳ χαράν, κἂν κατηχούμενος ᾖ, ἄλυπος ἀπίτω· τὸ γὰρ πάθος, τὸ ὑπὲρ Χριστοῦ, ἔσται αὐτῷ γνησιώτερον βάπτισμα, ὅτι αὐτὸς μὲν πείρᾳ ἀποθνῄσκει τῷ Κυρίῳ, οἱ δὲ λοιποὶ τύπῳ.

That is: “Let the one who has been deemed worthy of martyrdom rejoice with joy in the Lord; and even if he is a catechumen, let him depart without sorrow. For the suffering endured for Christ will be for him a more genuine baptism, because he himself dies to the Lord in actual experience, whereas the others do so in figure.” HOLSTE.]

so that, by reading them as though through a renewed representation of the events, both God may be honored and man strengthened, why should new testimonies, equally suited to both purposes, not also be set down? Or is it because these too will one day become ancient and necessary to posterity, even if in their own present time they are assigned less authority because of a presumptive veneration for antiquity?

But let those who judge the one power of the one Holy Spirit according to the ages of the times look to it, since all more recent things, as being the very latest, must be regarded as greater, in accordance with the overflowing of grace ordained for the final periods of the age. For “in the last days,” says the Lord, “I shall pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh, and their sons and daughters shall prophesy. And upon my male servants and my female servants I shall pour out of my Spirit; and the young shall see visions, [Col. 0015B] and the old shall dream dreams” (Joel 2:18–19; Acts 2:17–18).

Therefore we also, who acknowledge and honor new visions, equally promised beforehand, just as we do prophecies, and who assign the other powers of the Holy Spirit as an instrument of the Church—to which that same Spirit was sent, administering all gifts in everyone according as the Lord distributes to each—[Col. 0016A] necessarily both set them down and celebrate them by reading them to the glory of God. Thus no weakness or despair of faith may suppose that the grace of divinity operated only among the ancients, whether in the case of martyrs or in the gracious bestowal of revelations, since God always performs what he has promised: as testimony for unbelievers and as benefit for believers.

And therefore what we have heard and touched we proclaim also to you, brothers and little children, so that you who were present may remember the glory of the Lord, and you who now learn of it by hearing may have communion with the holy martyrs, and through them with the Lord Jesus Christ, to whom belong glory and honor for ever and ever. Amen.

# THE PASSION BEGINS

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0016B] **SUMMARY.—**The saints having been arrested, Saint Perpetua overcomes her father, is baptized with the others, and is thrust into a foul prison. Anxious about her infant, she understands from a vision granted to her—in which a ladder is raised toward heaven, and Saint Saturus and she herself ascend it and a morsel of food is offered—that martyrdom will occur very soon.

I. The young catechumens Revocatus [Col. 0017A] [Note: [Col. 0017D]

**Married as a matron.** The circumstance of marriage, especially in a woman, seems to increase the merit and worth of martyrdom because of the particular obstacles which that state presents in such a crisis. Hence Tertullian, book I, *To His Wife*, says that in times of persecution the burdens of marriage are exceedingly inconvenient and dangerous to faith: “For why did the Lord pronounce woe upon pregnant and nursing women, except because the impediments of children, etc.”—indicating that, whether women bear offspring in the womb or in their arms, they are greatly restrained by love of them from the readiness necessary at such a time to offer themselves for death.

Therefore, the fact that these two holy women, Perpetua and Felicitas, had children, one in her womb and the other at her breasts, demonstrates the heroic courage of each all the more. This was perhaps the reason why, although Revocatus, Secundulus, and the others completed their martyrdom on the same occasion, the Church nevertheless honored the memory of Perpetua and Felicitas alone with particular distinction.

But to return to Tertullian: in the same passage, considering the obstacles which marriage presents to women when martyrdom is possible, he proceeds to discourage his wife from marrying again after his death, because, as he says, “Widows are better unencumbered for enduring every affliction and persecution, with no marital burden swelling in the womb or at the breasts.” Therefore, women who broke through so many restraints and ran free and unencumbered toward the trophy of the Cross, trampling upon love for father, husband, and offspring, were regarded as having offered a far more praiseworthy example of heroic courage.

It may be asked here why no mention is made of Perpetua’s husband in these Acts. Was it because he was a Christian, as it seems possible rightly to infer from Perpetua’s own words a little below? Or because, when the woman had been found guilty of a graver crime, the marriage was then considered dissolved, as seems to be implied by law 5, *Digest*, *On the Property of Condemned Persons*? HOLSTE.

**An infant at the breast.** An infant is said to be “at the breast” on the same principle as “a servant at the threshold,” “a boy at hand,” “at one’s feet,” etc. Such children are called *sububeres* in Latin. Isidore’s glosses: “*Sububeres*: infants who are still beneath the breast”; in Greek, ὑποτίτθια, as in the Septuagint at Hosea 14:1; and at Joel 2:16, νήπια θηλάζοντα μαστούς, “little children sucking the breasts.” By others they are called ὑπομάζια or ὑπομάστια and ἐπιμάζια. Thus the Greeks called mares ὑπόπωλοι, αἷς πῶλοι ὕπησαν, “those beneath which there were foals,” as Homer says, *Iliad* XI. HOLSTE.

**II.—While we were still with the persecutors, etc.** How was Saint Perpetua, who wrote this, not “with the persecutors,” when at that very time she was being guarded by them in prison? Shall we say that she intended to indicate the change that occurred in her, which she shortly afterward expresses in these words: “We were taken into prison, and I was terrified because I had never experienced such darkness. O bitter day! There was intense heat because of the crowds, and extortion by the soldiers,” etc.? But after suffering such anguish for some time because of the weakness of nature, and then receiving a richer influx of grace, she says: “Immediately I recovered, and I was relieved of my distress, and the prison suddenly became a palace to me, so that I preferred to be there rather than anywhere else,” etc.

A passage from Tertullian’s book *To the Martyrs* may be relevant here. Comparing life in the world with life in prison, among the many advantages of the latter he includes these: “You are free from scandals and temptations, from evil recollections, and now also from persecution. Prison gives the Christian what the desert gave the prophets. Let us remove the name ‘prison’; let us call it a retreat.” HOLSTE.

**And persisted in casting me down out of his affection, etc.** The word “cast down,” transferred from boxers and the wrestling-ground, is extremely frequent among Christian writers in the sense of tempting and perverting. To omit Tertullian, I shall cite a single example from Cassian, *On the Spirit of Vainglory*, chapter 7: “The one whom it cannot cast down through honor, it trips through humility.” HOLSTE.

**Thus I too cannot call myself anything other than what I am—a Christian.** For it belongs to the upright and truthful, as the Greek iambic line has it, τὰ σῦκα σῦκα, τὴν σκάφην σκάφην λέγειν, “to call figs figs, and a trough a trough.” Tertullian rightly complains in the *Apology* that the pagans tortured Christians for confessing what they were, whereas under the laws people were customarily tortured when they denied what they were. Eusebius, book V, chapter 1, seems to allude to this in the words: ἀλλ’ οἱ μὲν ὁμολογοῦντες ὅπερ ἦσαν [Col. 0019B] συνεκλείοντο, ὡς Χριστιανοί, “But those who confessed what they were were shut up in prison as Christians.” HOLSTE.]

and Felicitas, his fellow slave, Saturninus [Note: [Col. 0017A] Saturninus is absent from the printed edition] and Secundulus, were arrested. Among them was also Vibia [Note: [Col. 0017A] We have restored this passage from our codices. The edition had: “Among these was also Ubia Perpetua, honorable, liberally educated, [Col. 0018A] a matron, though married”] Perpetua, honorably born, liberally educated, married as a matron, having a father and mother and two brothers, one of whom was likewise a catechumen, and an infant son at the breast. She herself was about twenty-two years old. From this point onward she herself will relate the entire course of her martyrdom, just as she left it written in her own hand and according to her own perception.

[Col. 0018A] II. “While we were still,” she says, “with the persecutors [Note: [Col. 0018A] Holste: ‘I was’], and my father, out of his affection, desired to turn me away [Note: [Col. 0018A] Holste: ‘desired to overthrow me’] and persisted in casting me down, I said: ‘Father, do you see, for example, this vessel lying here—a little pitcher or something else?’

“And he said: ‘I see it.’

“And I said to him: ‘Can it be called by any name other than what it is?’

“And he said: ‘No.’

“‘Thus I too cannot call myself anything other than what I am—a Christian.’

“Then my father, provoked by this word, threw—[the supplied source breaks off here] [Col. 0019A] [Note: [Col. 0019B]

**But he only maltreated me.** The verb *vexare* is used here in the milder sense of a violent assault short of severe injury, although elsewhere it generally denotes, as Asconius Pedianus observes on the second *Verrine Oration*, the experience of a tremendous calamity. He confirms this from Virgil, who wrote that Scylla “maltreated the Dulichian ships.” Nevertheless, as is particularly relevant to our passage, the word *vexare*, according to Gellius, book I, chapter 6, is too mild and denotes too slight a hardship to match so dreadful an atrocity as people’s being suddenly seized and torn apart by a monstrously savage beast. He therefore maintains that the poet spoke precisely and pointedly there of the tossing of ships without shipwreck. “For one who is borne and seized,” he says, “and dragged this way and that is properly said to be *vexed*.” Thus I understand that Saint Perpetua was here battered with blows and kicks and dragged about by her enraged father.

Tertullian also includes wounds under “maltreatment,” since in *On Patience*, chapter 3, he says that Malchus was maltreated by Peter, who had of course wounded him with a sword. And in the final chapter of *To Scapula* he said that the Christian name was being maltreated when it was oppressed by a most severe persecution. HOLSTE.

**He was defeated together with the devil’s devices.** Thus Antonius in the *Life of Saint Symeon Stylites*, chapter 6: “When he made the sign of the cross”—before setting foot in the chariot offered him by the demon—“the devil immediately disappeared altogether; he vanished together with his argument,” etc. And Anastasius the Librarian, in *Benedict III*: “He conquered the flesh and the prince of the world, and all his most wicked arguments.” HOLSTE.

**Because I had been deprived of my father, I gave thanks to the Lord, etc.** Pontius in the *Life of Saint Cyprian*: “For us, ‘fatherland’ is a less cherished, ordinary name, since we abhor even our own parents if they counsel anything against the Lord.” HOLSTE.

**His absence refreshed me.** This explains what in Greek would be called ἀνέπαυσεν or δι­ανέπαυσεν—that is, “gave rest, assisted, brought consolation.” This is read in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VIII, chapter 10. HOLSTE.

**And the Spirit instructed me to ask nothing else from the water except endurance of the flesh.** The Holy Spirit, clearly, urges the baptized to ask for the grace of martyrdom. For this reason Tertullian, at the end of *On Flight in Persecution*, calls him “the Paraclete, the exhorter to endurance.”

Moreover, Cyprian speaks splendidly in accordance with the meaning of this passage in his *Letter to the Martyrs Designate*: “Nothing now occupies your hearts and minds except divine precepts and heavenly commandments, by which the Holy Spirit has always encouraged you to endure suffering.” By “from the water,” she means after receiving Baptism, or after the bath of saving water. Thus Tertullian more than once in *On Repentance*: “If we cease sinning from the waters onward.” And in *On Baptism*: “Therefore we too, someone will say, ought rather to fast from the bath onward.” Shortly afterward: “Then the Lord, after the water, withdrew into the desert.” Likewise book I, *To His Wife*: “For how many are there who immediately after the bath seal their flesh?” And in *Exhortation to Chastity*: “A second virginity from the second birth, [Col. 0020A] that is, from the bath.”

Tertullian likewise often calls Baptism simply “water,” as at the beginning of *On Baptism*: “Blessed is the sacrament of our water.” Saint Cyprian, moreover, teaches at length in Letter LXIII that whenever water alone is named in the Holy Scriptures, Baptism is proclaimed.

Furthermore, by this utterly remarkable example of Saint Perpetua the power of Baptism against the new sectarians is confirmed in a marvelous way. By the final words, “except endurance of the flesh,” Saint Perpetua signifies that, instructed by the Spirit whom she received in Baptism, she understood how necessary the endurance not merely of the soul but also of the body would be.

Tertullian speaks excellently on this subject in *On Patience*, chapter 13. After discussing up to that point patience situated solely in the soul, he adds that it also “labors in many ways through the body to win the Lord’s favor, since it was manifested by the Lord himself in the body’s endurance as well. For,” he adds, “the governing soul readily shares with its own dwelling the things brought in by the spirit.” And a little afterward: “What proceeds from the soul’s virtue is perfected in the flesh. Finally, the patience of the flesh does battle in persecutions. If flight presses upon it, the flesh serves amid the hardships of flight. If prison also oppresses it, the flesh is in chains, the flesh in the stocks, the flesh upon the ground, both in that poverty of light and in that deprivation of the world. But when it is brought forth for the trial of blessedness, for the occasion of a second immersion, for the very ascent to the divine seat, nothing is more necessary there than the patience of the body. If the spirit is willing but the flesh is weak for want of patience, where is the salvation of the spirit and of the flesh itself? Yet when the Lord says this of the flesh, pronouncing it weak, he shows what it needs in order to be strengthened: patience, of course, against every preparation for overthrowing or punishing the faith, so that it may endure with the utmost constancy blows, fire, the cross, beasts, and the sword.” For, as he adds below in chapter 15, “patience alone completes martyrdom.”

Cyprian follows his master when, in the same sense but different words, he says: “No consolations are more helpful than those of patience to persons who in the contest of persecution must abandon their estates, undergo prison, bear chains, spend their lives, and endure the sword, beasts, fires, crosses, and, finally, every kind of torture and punishment through the faith and strength of patience.” HOLSTE.

**We were taken into prison.** In the *Proceedings Concerning the Vindication of Caecilian and Felix*, p. 279: “Let him be taken into prison.” Likewise the *Passion of Saints Dativus, Saturninus*, etc., p. 290: “The longed-for prison received Christ’s martyrs.” Ulpian, law 1 of the *Digest*, *On the Custody of Defendants*: “The proconsul is accustomed to determine, regarding the custody of defendants, whether a person should be received into prison, handed over to a soldier, entrusted to sureties, or even committed to his own recognizance. He ordinarily makes this determination either according to the nature of the charge, or because of the person’s distinction or very ample resources, or because of the innocence of the person, or the rank of the accused.” Thus far Ulpian. Raevardus wrote most learnedly on the different kinds of custody in connection with this law, *Various Readings*, book III, chapter 12. HOLSTE.

**And I was terrified, etc.** You see how this most steadfast martyr was terrified by the horror of prison, although a little afterward she received the proconsul’s sentence and death itself not merely with a brave and fearless but even with a joyful spirit. From this it appears that the sufferings of prison were preliminary exercises for her future martyrdom and—to use Eusebius’s word—προκαταικίσματα, “preparatory ordeals,” which through the practice and habitual experience of evils strengthened body and soul for the endurance of torments and death. HOLSTE.]

“[He hurled] himself at me as though to tear out my eyes; but he only tormented me, and departed [Note: [Col. 0019A] “Assuredly” (*profecto*). Holst.] defeated, together with the devil’s arguments. Then, because I had been deprived of my father for a few days, I gave thanks to the Lord, and his absence brought relief [Note: [Col. 0019A] Thus Holstenius. The manuscript codices read: “I was relieved” (*refrigerata sum*). In what follows too Holstenius differs from the manuscripts; we have preferred his reading, since we have observed that this verb is expressed in this way in other African Acts.] to me. [Col. 0020A] During that interval of a few days we were baptized; but the Spirit instructed me that nothing else was to be sought in the water [Note: [Col. 0020A] Holstenius reads “from the water” (*ab aqua*), which one might interpret thus: “from the time when I received baptism.”] except endurance of the flesh. A few days later we were taken into prison, and I was terrified, because [Col. 0021A]

[Note: [Col. 0021A]

**Such darkness.** Tertullian, *To the Martyrs*, chapter 2: “The prison has darkness, but you yourselves are light. It has chains, but you have been set free for God. A foul breath is exhaled there, but you are an aroma of sweetness.” Blessed Cyprian imitated this in Epistle 81: “O blessed prison,” he says, “which your presence has illuminated! O darkness brighter than the sun itself, and more radiant than this light of the world!” Tertullian, *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, chapter 8: “Come now, what do you think of it”—that is, the flesh—“when it is wasted away in prisons, in a most loathsome exile from light, in deprivation of the world, filth, stench, [Col. 0021B] and degrading food; not even free in sleep, since it is chained even to its beds and mangled by the very bedding?”

There is a particularly remarkable passage in Libanius’ recently published *Oration on the Custody of Prisoners*, in which he describes the wickedness and greed of the prison officials, who would scarcely allow even a single lamp except at a high price. His words will more conveniently be quoted shortly below. HOLST.

**Heat.** That heat arises from the confinement of the place and the crowd of people, through which Libanius, in the oration I have just mentioned, complains that many suffocated in prison—and this through the magistrates’ negligence. I shall append his passage from page 68, slightly corrected by me and translated according to the author’s intention:

> ὅταν οὖν οὗτοι πέμπωσιν ἐπὶ τὰ δεσμωτήρια φάλαγγας, ἐῤῥῶσθαι δὲ φράσαντες τοῖς περὶ ἐκεῖνα νόμοις, ἐπ᾽ ἄλλοις διατρίβωσιν, ὡς μὴ φιλάνθρωποι δόξαντες εἶναι, τίς οὐκ ἂν ἀποπνιγείη;

That is: “When, therefore, these magistrates send companies of people into confinement and meanwhile, having told the laws enacted concerning such matters to go hang, occupy themselves with other business so as not to be thought humane, who would not [Col. 0021C] suffocate?” [The accompanying Latin paraphrase instead reads: “so that they may appear popular.”]

Lucian the confessor likewise describes the same hardships of prison in Cyprian, Epistle 22, in these words, also incidentally restored: “By command of the emperor, we were ordered to be killed by hunger and thirst; and we were shut up in two cells so that they might afflict us with hunger and thirst. But the fire too, from the constriction under which we labored, was so unbearable that no one could endure it.” Thus far he. There “fire” seems to mean what St. Perpetua calls “heat.”

From these passages it is understood that the sufferings of prisons were neither the least nor the last of the devil’s devices against the martyrs. The churches of Gaul acknowledge this in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book V, chapter 1, in these words:

> τὰς κατὰ τὴν εἱρκτὴν ἐν τῷ σκότει καὶ τῷ χαλεπωτάτῳ χωρίῳ συγκλείσεις, ὥστε ἀποπνιγῆναι τοὺς πλείστους τῇ εἱρκτῇ.

That is: “Confinements in a dark and most distressing place, so crowded that most were suffocated in the prison.” HOLST.

**Because of the crowds.** That is, “on account of the crowds,” or “the multitude of people.” A pure Graecism, τοῦ [Col. 0021D] ὄχλου χάριν, “for the sake of the crowd.” So shortly afterward, “because of me” (*mei beneficio*), that is, “on my account” or “because of me.” HOLST.

**The soldiers’ rough handling.** This seems to signify the violent shoving of soldiers as they thrust prisoners together, which Procopius calls ὠθισμός (“jostling”) on the last page of the *Secret History*. Note also the soldiers’ barbarous ferocity toward prisoners, attested even by St. Ignatius, who therefore calls them leopards and writes to the Romans that they become more savage when treated well.

Moreover, not only was a fee paid to them for custody, but gifts were also freely offered so that they might deal more mildly and gently with the prisoners; these were effectively payments extorted from them. Thus the *Apostolic Constitutions*, book V, chapter 1, commands alms to be sent to designated martyrs, both for their sustenance and to pay the soldiers’ fee, so that they might lighten their treatment and take care of the prisoners—that is, relax their customary cruelty toward them:

> ἵνα, ὅσον ἐφ᾽ ὑμῖν, μὴ θλίβηται ὁ μακάριος ἀδελφὸς ὑμῶν,

“so that, insofar as it lies with you, your blessed brother may not be violently handled”; that is, to buy relief from harassment and rough handling, for θλῖψις in this passage means rough handling. HOLST.

[Col. 0022A] **Finally, I was tormented by anxiety for my infant.** A most elegant and natural expression of maternal affection, whose example God himself employs in declaring his loving-kindness toward us. HOLST.

**Blessed deacons.** An εὐφημισμός (“honorific expression”) conveying affection or reverence for the person mentioned. It is more familiar today in the common Italian language than in ordinary Latin. It may have passed into African Latin from the Syriac or Hebrew tongue, which the ancient Tyrians and Phoenicians who colonized Carthage used—or one not greatly [Col. 0022B] different from it. For Syrians and Hebrews customarily add the epithet “Blessed” especially when mentioning God, as in Mark 13:61 and often elsewhere in Scripture, but also when addressing good people: “You are blessed by the Lord,” Psalm 123:15, and not infrequently elsewhere.

At the very beginning of his book addressed to those destined for martyrdom, Tertullian says: “Blessed martyrs.” Shortly afterward: “First of all, therefore, blessed ones, do not grieve the Holy Spirit.” And in chapter 2: “You, blessed ones, may perhaps consider yourselves transferred from prison into protective custody.” In the same place: “Thus now, blessed ones, prison is troublesome even to Christians”; and shortly afterward in chapter 3, and in book II of *On the Dress of Women*, he calls Christian women “blessed.” In *Prescription against Heretics*: “During the episcopate of the blessed Eleutherius”; and in *Exhortation to Chastity*: “the blessed patriarchs.”

Thus Lucian the confessor in Cyprian, Epistle 22: “When the blessed martyr Paul was still in the body.” And the Roman clergy in Epistle 2 to Cyprian: “We have learned that the blessed pope Cyprian has withdrawn.” HOLST.

**Who ministered to us.** The Church always took great care [Col. 0022C] of those held in bonds, especially for confessing Christ; in former times deacons were particularly assigned to minister and attend upon them. They supplied them with food and with means to soften the soldiers’ cruelty, as we reported a little above from the *Apostolic Constitutions*. They were present with counsel, encouragement, and consolation. Cyprian, Epistle 11: “It was always the practice under our predecessors that deacons visiting the prison should guide the martyrs’ desires by their counsel and by the precepts of Scripture.”

In short, as good angels stand ready to assist the people entrusted to them, so deacons stood ready for the confessors in labor, duty, and diligence. Hence Ignatius’ statement in the *Epistle to the Trallians*: “What are deacons? Surely imitators of the angelic powers.” See Council of Carthage IV, canon 43. The Council of Orléans V, canon 20, likewise imposes upon the archdeacon or provost of the church the duty of visiting the prison, and upon the bishop that of mercifully relieving the prisoners’ need by assigning them suitable food from the resources of the church. HOLST.

[Col. 0022D] **They arranged it for a payment.** For this purpose both the churches publicly and individual believers contributed from their resources, so that confessors and martyrs in prison might be supplied with food, other supports of life, and necessary relief; or, when need arose, these things might be wrung from the injustice of the guards by bribes, lest, overcome by suffering, they fail before the actual contest. This may be seen from Tertullian’s *To the Martyrs*, St. Cyprian’s Epistles 4 and 5, and other sources.

Eusebius testifies that the Roman Church’s particular solicitude and πατροπαράδοτος (“ancestrally transmitted”) piety in this matter—praised long before by Dionysius of Corinth, a most ancient writer—persisted constantly down to his own time, so that it cared for all martyrs throughout the world and all who suffered for Christ’s name, and provided them with the necessities of life.

Nor is it without reason that the most holy martyr writes that this privilege was “arranged for a payment,” that is, purchased for a price, so that they might be let out of the cramped work-prison for a few hours. For prison officials, to whom punishment was a source of revenue, according to Manilius in book V, customarily relaxed confinement only after being corrupted with payment. Law 8, *Digest*, *On the Custody of Prisoners*, restrains them. Manilius, just cited, plays elegantly upon these guards’ savagery in the passage beginning with the verse:

> Whoever, when Andromeda rises from the sea,  
> Is born, etc.

[Col. 0023A]]

I had never experienced such darkness. O bitter day! There was intense heat [Note: [Col. 0021A] Holstenius reads the singular, “intense” (*validus*).] because of the crowds, and the soldiers’ rough handling. Finally I was tormented by anxiety [Col. 0022A] for my infant. Then Tertius and Pomponius, blessed deacons who ministered to us, arranged, for a payment, that we should be released for a few hours and refresh ourselves in a better [Col. 0023A]

[Note: [Col. 0023C]

Manilius seems to have fashioned this passage from Cicero’s fifth *Verrine Oration*, where we read:

> These fathers whom you see lay at the threshold, and the wretched mothers spent the night at the prison door, shut out from the final embrace of their children. They begged for nothing other than permission to receive their sons’ last breath. The prison doorkeeper was there—Sestius, the praetor’s executioner, the death and terror of allies and citizens—who gained a fixed payment from every groan and every grief: “To approach, you will pay so much; to be allowed to carry food inside, so much.” No one refused, etc.

Christian women especially devoted themselves to this work of mercy. I do not doubt that Libanius had such women in mind in the oration already cited, where, denouncing the utterly greedy cruelty [Col. 0023C] of prison doorkeepers and guards, he relates that the miserable prisoners customarily had to purchase, at a high price, permission to have even a little light. Then, if one of the accused pleaded that he lacked the money, they retorted to the badly abused man:

> διὰ τί οὐ καλεῖς διὰ τῶνδε τῶν ἐξιόντων γυναῖκα δεῦρο τῶν ἐπὶ φιλανθρωπίᾳ φιλοτιμουμένων; εἶτ᾽ αὐτῆς πρὸς τὰ γόνατα προσπεσών, πείθεις προσαιτοῦσαν ἄγειν τί σοι;

“Why do you not send word through some of those leaving here and summon one of the women who devote themselves to works of humanity? Then, falling at her knees, persuade her to collect alms and bring you something.” HOLST.

**That, being released for a few hours, we might refresh ourselves in a better part of the prison.** They had therefore been thrown into the “inner prison,” as it is called in Acts, chapter 16. What is here obtained as a favor from the commander of the guard, appeased by a payment, was later established by Emperor Constantius in Law 1 of the Code, *On the Custody of Prisoners*, where we read:

> Nor indeed ought one who is confined to suffer the darkness of the innermost chamber, but he should be revived and relieved by access to light; and when night has doubled the guard, he should be received in the vestibules of the prisons [Col. 0023D] and in wholesome places. When day returns, he should immediately, at the first rising of the sun, be brought back into public light, lest he be killed by the punishments of prison—a thing recognized as wretched for the innocent and insufficiently severe for the guilty.

This enactment seems to have mitigated a rescript of Antoninus Pius, who wished persons accused of graver crimes to endure the punishment of prison itself before their execution: book III, *Digest*, *On the Custody of Prisoners*. The added phrase “that we might refresh ourselves,” besides what has been said above, seems to render the Greek verb ἀναψύχειν (“to refresh”), although an old lexicon renders “to refresh” by ἀγαλλιᾶσθαι (“to rejoice”). HOLST.

**Already weakened by starvation.** That is, brought almost to death. Tertullian, book II *To the Nations*: “Why is not she a goddess who was more dutiful—the daughter who nourished from her own breasts her father, weakened by hunger in prison?” Seneca and Phaedrus also speak in this fashion. I marvel that a learned man suspected the latter’s passage, since it can be confirmed by innumerable other testimonies of classical authors readily encountered everywhere.

It is consequently apparent how elegantly [Col. 0024A] the common Latin translator rendered the Greek word ἐσχατογήρως in Ecclesiasticus 41:4 as *defecto aetate*, “spent with age.” I add, for good measure, a passage from the *Acts of the Vindication of Caecilianus*: “When I heard this, I became faint in mind.” And Suetonius Tranquillus, in *On Illustrious Grammarians*, concerning [uncertain: *Offio Care* in the supplied text]: “When he was now failing not only in gait but also in sight.” HOLST.

**The prison became a praetorium for me.** That is, not only did the prison’s discomforts no longer disturb me, but I even rejoiced in them as though I were living in splendid and comfortable premises. Properly speaking, the *praetorium* was the public palace in which the proconsul administered justice, as may also be understood from Pontius the deacon; nor is it understood differently in the history of the Lord’s Passion. Since it generally surpassed other private houses in the elegance of its structure and the splendor of its ornamentation, any palaces and magnificently furnished houses—even when privately owned and built in the countryside—were called *praetoria*. Martial:

> At the fourth milestone Torquatus has his praetorium.

The following words of Tertullian nevertheless seem pertinent to the meaning of this passage: “Outside prison the Christian has renounced the world; in prison, even prison itself.” For the mind, strengthened by divine grace, either does not feel the prison’s discomforts and hardships or disregards them and conquers them by constancy. HOLST.

**III.—You are now in great dignity.** Holstenius reads “favor” (*dignatione*) and adds: “For divine favor had already illuminated her with glorious beginnings,” as St. Cyprian says of the confessors held in prison in Epistle 4. The word *dignatio* (“favor”) was discussed above.

Here I add one remarkable and entirely apposite passage from Tertullian. In book I of *To His Wife*, chapter 4, after using the example of sisters who prefer holiness to marriage, he adds:

> For they prefer to marry God. They are beautiful for God; for God they are maidens. With him they live; with him they converse. They occupy themselves with him by day and night. They assign their prayers to the Lord as dowries; and from him they obtain favor, as though bridal gifts, whenever they desire it.

Believing that his sister had advanced into such a state through her endurance of imprisonment, her brother urges her to ask that God reveal to her what is to come, confident that she [Col. 0024D] will be heard. This is the meaning of the words “that I should ask for a vision,” etc. HOLST.

**Whether it is to be martyrdom or release.** Just as many other words from military discipline were transferred to Christ’s holy soldiery, so too was the word *commeatus*. According to Festus, it means “a period customarily granted by the emperor to soldiers, during which it is possible to go and return.” Hence Apuleius, book XI: “He granted a brief furlough from the warfare of love.” In the Code, soldiers are said “to be dismissed upon the grant of furlough” or “by furlough,” and those so dismissed are called *commeatales*, “men on leave.”

Thus Hesychius says that κομίατον means ἐξαίτησιν λαμβάνειν τοῦ ἀφεθῆναι, that is, “to receive permission, obtained by request, to depart freely.” And in the glosses: “*Commeatus*: ἐξουσία”—authority, as it were, or the ability to depart and go wherever one wishes. So Law 3, *Digest*, *On Punishments*: “No one can grant permission to depart and return to an exile except the emperor, for some cause.”

This word has remained in common Italian usage down to the present day, except that it extends beyond military affairs to anyone’s permission to depart from anyone. [Col. 0025B] Among Christians of that period, moreover, this word is found transferred so as to denote deliverance from danger to life, whether that danger threatened from illness or from a judge’s sentence.

Concerning illness, we have a remarkable passage in Palladius’ *Lausiac History*, chapter 86, where Melania obtains from God for the mortally ill Evagrius καιρὸν κομιατοῦ καὶ προθεσμίαν ζωῆς, “a period of reprieve and an extension of life.” In the same sense we read in Cyprian’s sermon *On Mortality*: “to pray for a reprieve for oneself,” that is, deliverance from the danger of plague. Thus Paulinus, in the *Life of St. Ambrose*, writes that Stilicho sent noblemen to the sick Ambrose to persuade him to ask the Lord for leave to go on living.

But in our passage the word *commeatus* signifies escape from danger threatened by a persecutor, as is clear from the fact that it is opposed to *passio*, “martyrdom,” that is, death for Christ. In the same way Cyprian, Epistle 8, opposed reprieve to martyrdom, or the consummation of victory; and in Epistle 52 says that when peace is granted by persecutors, reprieve is granted [Col. 0025C] by God. HOLST.]

part of the prison. Then, coming out of the prison, all attended to their own needs. I nursed my infant, already weakened by starvation. Anxious for him, I spoke to my mother, encouraged my brother, and entrusted my son to them [Note: [Col. 0023A] The Salzburg manuscript reads: “And I encouraged my brother and entrusted my son to him.”]. I was wasting away because I had seen them wasting away on my account. I endured such anxieties for many days, and obtained permission for the infant to remain with me in prison. At once [Col. 0024A] I recovered my strength and was relieved of my distress and anxiety for the infant; and suddenly the prison became, as it were, a praetorium for me, so that I preferred to be there rather than anywhere else [Note: [Col. 0023A] Holstenius reads “somewhere else” (*alicubi*).].

“III. Then my brother said to me: ‘Lady sister, you are now in great dignity [Note: [Col. 0024A] Thus the Compiègne and Salzburg codices; but Holstenius has: “You are in such great favor that I may ask,” etc.], so great that you may ask for a vision and it may be shown to you whether it is to be martyrdom or release.’ And I, knowing that I conversed familiarly with [Col. 0025A]

[Note: [Col. 0025C]

**Knowing that I conversed familiarly with the Lord.** That is, that I held a place of special favor with God, such as those who are intimate with princes and singularly dear to them possess, so that they can address them whenever they wish. Hence those who, as sometimes happens, falsely boast of such intimacy are said by Misitheus, in his letter to Gordian preserved by Capitolinus, to “sell stories about the prince”: “They pose as persons privy to the prince’s secret counsels and arbiters of his intimate conversations, deceive others, and sell smoke.” HOLST.

**And this was shown to me.** So a little above: “and it may be shown to you.” Tertullian and Cyprian likewise speak in this way about visions divinely presented. It is also read more than once in the Apocalypse. Tertullian, moreover, teaches beneficially that visions granted to individuals should be made public, in *On Idolatry*, chapter 15: “Nor is it safe to suppress anything that has been shown to one person.” HOLST.

**Every kind of iron implement.** The glosses explain *ferramenta* as ἐργαλεῖα σιδηρᾶ, “iron tools.” Properly, however, *ferramenta* [Col. 0025D] are weapons suited for harming, or anything possessing an edge or point. Thus Cethegus, questioned in Cicero’s *Catilinarians* about the swords and daggers found in his possession, replied that “he had always been a devotee of good ironware.” And Law 18, *On an Instrumentum Bequeathed*: “Iron implements prepared for cutting flesh are counted among a butcher’s equipment.” HOLST.

**Hooks.** In an old glossary the *hamus*, ἄγκιστρον (“hook”), is listed among bronze implements; but since here it is placed among iron implements and instruments of martyrdom, I would prefer to understand it as the *uncus*, the hook by which, as we read, the saints’ bodies were mangled or suspended and dragged into a river or the sewers. These hooks resemble fishhooks in shape, though they differ in size; hence the same name remained for both.

Alternatively, perhaps we ought to read *amae* here. These are mentioned, after Pliny the Younger in book X of his *Letters* and Juvenal in Satire XIV, by Law 3, [Col. 0026B] *Digest*, *On the Office of the Prefect of the Watch*, in these words: “It should be known that the prefect of the watch ought to keep watch throughout the entire night and make his rounds shod, with hooks and axes.” Those *amae*, as the word itself indicates, were sickles, but larger ones—that is, curved iron implements attached to very long poles. Implements of this sort, prepared for containing or extinguishing fires, are still kept in public places throughout the cities of Germany and Gaul; and the jurisconsult joins them with axes in this passage. Livy establishes that soldiers formerly used them to tear down a rampart or wall.

Law 12, *On an Instrumentum Bequeathed*, joins *amae* and grappling hooks, just as Vegetius, book V, has “sickles and grappling hooks.” Hence Nonius, chapter 18: “Sickles and grappling hooks, kinds of weapons suited to assaulting walls.” And Cicero, *For Milo*: “They fly about at the Temple of Castor with sickles, and throughout the whole Forum with swords.” HOLST.

**Was lying in wait.** Holstenius reads *praestabat*, that is, “was setting, constructing, or devising.” Thus Cyprian says in *On the Dress of Virgins*: “to furnish an enticement to vices.” Expressions of this sort are extremely frequent in Tertullian: [Col. 0026C] in book IV *Against Marcion*, chapter 35, “to grant pardon to a brother even when he does not ask”; in *To Scapula*, chapter 2, “to secure the emperor’s welfare”; in the *Apology*, chapter 46, “to exhibit truth from faith”; in *On Repentance*, chapter 3, “to render justice to God”; and in chapter 11, “to render to the offended Lord chastisement in food and dress”; in *On the Veiling of Virgins*, chapter 13, “to render continence to God alone.”

Passing over other expressions of this sort, there is a remarkable passage in *Against the Jews*, chapter 9, in the explanation of Isaiah’s prophetic oracle in chapter 7: “The contest with men is no small one for you, since God supplies the contest.” There the Septuagint has παρέχειν ἀγῶνα, “to supply a contest,” which Cyprian translates literally as *praestare agonem* in Epistle 8 and book II *Against the Jews*. Minucius Felix likewise says in *Octavius*: “We manifest modesty not in our face but in our mind.” And Pope Gregory, book II of the *Letters*, Epistle 4: “Causing no delay.”

To these I add Rufinus, book V of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 2: “After several days, when they had granted no favor for burial, the martyrs’ bones were burned”; and book VI, chapter 29: “to cause destruction.” [Col. 0026D] In the same way our common Latin text of Acts 24 and 25 translates “to grant a favor” where the Greek reads χάριτας καταθέσθαι. HOLST.

**When we were brought in.** Tertullian, *On Patience*, chapter 3: “When he is handed over, when he is led like a beast to sacrifice,” etc. HOLST.

**Perpetua, I am waiting for you.** In Greek this would be ἐπέχω, ὑπομένω σε, “I wait for you.” Thus the common Latin translator of Scripture, in Tobit 5:9, renders the words ὑπόμεινόν με, καὶ ἐρῶ τῷ πατρί as: “Wait for me, I beg you, until I myself tell my father.” And Matthew 26:38, μείνατε ὧδε, “Wait here.” Acts 20:5, ἔμενον ἡμᾶς ἐν Τρωάδι, “They waited for us at Troas.” Similarly elsewhere.

Tertullian uses it no differently in the *Apology*, chapter 35: “Who has need to inquire anxiously into Caesar’s safety except one from whom something is hoped for and awaited after it?” In *On Repentance*, chapter 6: “to await pardon for sins”; and *Against the Jews*, chapter 6: “If the lawgiver of the new [Col. 0027A] law has already come, he must be served; if he has not yet come, he must be awaited.” And *To the Martyrs*, chapter 2: “The world awaits the judgments not of the proconsul but of God.”

So too in the Roman clergy’s letter to Cyprian, Epistle 31: “Although it is our judgment that the Church’s peace must be awaited”; and toward the end of that epistle: “Meanwhile, while we await a bishop to be given [Col. 0027B] to us by God.” The *Acts of the Passion of St. Cyprian* also say: “When he had stripped off his dalmatic, he stood in his linen garment and began to await the executioner,” etc. Our own text below uses the word in the same way: “For Perpetua too was waiting.” These words allude to the present passage. Ulpian used *sustinere poenam* in the sense of “to defer punishment” in Law 6, *Digest*, *On Punishments*. HOLST.]

the Lord, from whom I had experienced such great benefits [Note: [Col. 0025A] The Salzburg manuscript reads the singular, “benefit.”], confidently promised him in reply [Note: [Col. 0025A] The Salzburg manuscript reads: “I spoke in response to his promises.” Moreover, Cyprian frequently affirms that martyrs were warned beforehand of their approaching martyrdom through visions of this sort; almost all the genuine Acts from Africa attest the same thing.]: ‘Tomorrow I shall report it to you.’

“And I asked, and this was shown to me. I saw a golden ladder [Note: [Col. 0025A] Thus the Compiègne manuscript. The Salzburg manuscript, with the Victorine and Corbie codices, reads [Col. 0026A] “bronze.” In the Cassinese codex used by Holstenius, the material of the ladder is not stated.] of astonishing size, reaching all the way to heaven, and so narrow that people could ascend it only one at a time. On the sides of the ladder every kind of iron implement was fixed. There were swords, lances, hooks, and broad blades, so that if anyone ascended carelessly or without directing his attention upward, he would be mangled and his flesh would cling [Col. 0026A] to the iron implements.

“Beneath the ladder itself lay a dragon of astonishing size, which was lying in wait [Note: [Col. 0026A] Holstenius reads “was setting an ambush” (*praestabat*).] for those ascending and frightening them so that they would not ascend. Saturus [Note: [Col. 0026A] Some codices call him Satyrus, others Saturnus; but it makes no difference.] ascended first. Later he had voluntarily surrendered himself on our account, though he had not been present when we were brought in. He reached the top of the ladder, turned toward me [Note: [Col. 0026A] “Toward me” is absent from Holstenius.], and said: ‘Perpetua, I am waiting for you; but take care that dragon does not bite you.’

“And I said: ‘It will not [Col. 0027A]

[Note: [Col. 0027B]

**It will not harm me.** Thus Tertullian, *Exhortation to Chastity*: “I think we are no more permitted to harm one who is being born than one already born.” And Plautus in *The Braggart Soldier*: “Swear that you will not harm the man.” HOLST.

**From beneath the ladder itself.** Thus in the *Acts of St. Clement, Pope*: “From beneath whose foot,” etc. And in the surveying fragments of Latinus Togatus: “If a boundary marker or natural rock bears the cloven hoof of an animal, it signifies water emerging from beneath the rock,” etc. Innocent also uses a similar expression in *On Letter-Signs*, as Rigault long ago observed in his *Glosses on the Surveyors*.

Among other reputable authors this doubling of prepositions is also found in common use: for example, *de insuper* (“from above”) and *de versus* (“from toward”) in Sallust and Festus, to omit “from behind the bearing sheep” in Psalm 77:71, and *de secus* and *de inter* in the *Acts of the Vindication of Caecilianus* at the Conference of Carthage. Furthermore, one reads *ab ante*, *in ante*, *de intus*, *de trans*, *de super*, and similar forms. HOLST.

**In the garb of a shepherd, milking sheep.** Christ was represented to Perpetua in the form in which he was depicted in the oratories and sacred vessels of that period. Since the Gospels attribute the title and character of shepherd preeminently to Christ, the Christians of the earliest times delighted in placing before their eyes with great frequency this most lovable image of him together with the faithful, who are commonly designated as sheep.

In Bosio’s *Subterranean Rome*, page 59 and following, you have many images copied from the monuments of the cemeteries, in almost all of which Christ is depicted in the form of a shepherd with sheep; and in the first he appears in precisely the form expressed here, that of a shepherd milking sheep. He was also not infrequently depicted carrying on his shoulders the recovered sheep that had been lost, in accordance with the Gospel parable, especially upon chalices. Tertullian indicates this in *On Modesty*, chapter 7, written against the Catholics:

> You may begin [Col. 0027D] with the parables, where the lost sheep is sought by the Lord and carried back on his shoulders. Let the very images upon your chalices come forward, if even in them the interpretation of that sheep will shine forth, etc.

HOLST.

**And standing around him were many thousands clad in white.** The joining of “many thousands” to the word *candidati* (“those clad in white”) without a conjunction has an example not only in the common Latin translator of Apocalypse, chapter 7: “forty thousand sealed,” but also in Trebellius Pollio’s *Life of Emperor Claudius*, where we read: “You will give him as an annual allowance from our private treasury three thousand modii of wheat, six thousand of barley, two thousand pounds of bacon, three thousand five hundred sextarii of old wine,” etc. Similar examples occur in other authors. HOLST.

**Welcome, teknon.** A greeting, as it were, from a parent to a daughter; for the Greek τέκνον (“child”) is applied to both sexes, as everyone knows. HOLST.

**And he called me.** As the Latin language had already begun to become corrupt in everyday use, this construction of the verb *clamare* (“to call”) had passed into popular speech; it was afterward received into vernacular Italian: *mi chiamo*. HOLST.

**And from the cheese he was milking, he gave me, as it were, a morsel.** Augustine, cited above, calls it “a morsel of milk.” Much could be said, from Hesychius on Exodus, page 257, and Tertullian, *On the Crown*, page 121 in Rigault’s edition, about the custom of giving milk and honey symbolically to catechumens. Tertullian says there: “We taste beforehand the concord of milk and honey.” See Albaspinaeus, book II, final Observation. HOLST.

**—And from the cheese he was milking, he gave me, as it were, a morsel; and I received it with joined hands and ate it, and all those standing around said, ‘Amen.’** Concerning these words, the observation I found in Holstenius’ papers about the customary giving of milk to catechumens is insufficient to explain the meaning of the passage. The author would have added other observations if he had been able to put the final hand to this work, as is shown by the blank space he left in his notes after the words of St. Perpetua that we have transcribed, evidently to be filled during his final revision.

It remained to be explained how, upon awakening from this presentation of a morsel administered in the vision, St. Perpetua—and likewise her brother, after she had related the matter to him—understood that it had been divinely signified that those held in prison were by no means to be released, but were to be consummated in martyrdom. For after the words transcribed above, the following are added there:

> And I immediately related it to my brother—who, of course, had asked her to arrange for it to be divinely shown to her whether they were to die or be released safely—and we understood that martyrdom was to occur; and we began now to have no hope in the world.

It is rightly asked how they understood this. I believe it was because the rite of administering the Eucharist had been foreshadowed in the vision for Perpetua. Since, by a very familiar custom of that time, it was ordinarily given to those known to be shortly about to die, Perpetua and her brother rightly interpreted the vision as signifying that the confessors’ death would soon follow.

The rite of receiving the Eucharist is seen foreshadowed in the following details: a morsel, as it were, is offered to Perpetua; she receives it with joined hands; she then eats it; and those standing around acclaim “Amen.” That all these observances were customary in the ancient administration of the Eucharist is better known from the testimony of numerous ancient writers, especially St. Ambrose, than to require extensive demonstration.

It is certainly established, with particular reference to the usage of the African churches, that they customarily administered the Eucharist to confessors standing ready for martyrdom. Indeed, they judged this so necessary that they derived from it an argument for writing to Cornelius, the Roman pontiff—by the hand and pen of Cyprian, but also in the name of thirty-seven other African bishops—asking him to approve an exception to the law previously enacted that those who had once lapsed during persecution should never be admitted to communion with the Church and the Eucharist. For at that time many of these, enrolled among the penitents, were in danger from new persecutors and, as matters stood, seemed likely soon to be killed for confessing Christ. To deny the customary viaticum of Christ’s body to people standing ready for the contest was excessively inhuman.

From this epistle—the second of book I in Cyprian, Epistle 57 in our edition; see below—I shall append some passages appropriate for establishing the point we are considering:
