> But since, they say, we see that the day of another assault has begun once more to approach, and we are admonished by frequent and repeated revelations to be armed and prepared for the contest which the enemy announces against us; since we must also prepare by our exhortations the people entrusted to us [Col. 0029B] through divine favor and gather within the Lord’s camp absolutely all the soldiers of Christ who desire arms and demand battle; under the compulsion of necessity we have judged that peace ought to be granted to those who have not withdrawn from the Lord’s Church, but who, from the first day of their lapse, have not ceased to perform penance, lament, and entreat the Lord, and that they ought to be armed and equipped for the battle that threatens.

And a little afterward:

> But now peace is necessary not for the weak but for the strong, and communion must be granted by us not to the dying but to the living, [Col. 0029C] so that we may not leave unarmed and naked those whom we rouse and exhort to battle, but fortify them with the protection of Christ’s blood and body. Since the Eucharist is given for this purpose, that it may be a safeguard for those receiving it, let us arm with the defense of the Lord’s abundance those whom we wish to be secure against the Adversary. For how do we teach or urge them to shed their own blood in confession of the name if, when they are about to fight, we deny them Christ’s blood? Or how do we make them fit for the cup of martyrdom if we do not, by the right of communion, first admit them in the Church to drink the cup of the Lord?

Indeed, as is added somewhat later:

> He cannot be fit for martyrdom who is not armed by the Church for battle; and the mind that the received Eucharist does not raise and lift up fails.

POSSINUS.]

harm me, in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ.’ From beneath the ladder itself, as though afraid of me, it slowly [Note: [Col. 0027A] Holstenius reads: “It slowly thrust out its head, and as soon as,” etc.] raised its head; and when I stepped upon the first rung, I trod upon its head.

“I ascended and saw an immense expanse of garden. In the middle of the garden sat a white-haired man, [Col. 0028A] tall and dressed as a shepherd, milking sheep; and standing around him were many thousands clad in white. He raised his head, looked at me, and said: ‘Welcome, *teknon* [τέκνον, child].’ He called me and, from the cheese he was milking, gave me what seemed to be a morsel. I received it [Col. 0029A]

[Note: [Col. 0029D]

From these words, “And from the cheese he was milking, he gave me a morsel,” Noesselt wrongly concludes that Perpetua belonged to the Montanist community, since Epiphanius and others say that the Montanists—or at least some of them—used cheese in the sacred supper, from which they derived the name Artotyrites, “bread-and-cheese people.” See Noesselt’s own words above, volume 1 of the latest *Library of the Fathers*, column 174. But it is entirely uncertain whether the Artotyrites belonged to the Montanist sect. Compare what we have said about them in the preface to this volume. EDD.]

And we began to have no hope in this world. Thus Pontius says of Cyprian, when his future passion was already certain: “But he, with his mind raised toward heaven, had already ceased to regard the world.” And Cyprian himself, Epistle VI: “We had renounced the world when we were baptized; but now we have truly renounced the world, when, tested and proved by God, we leave behind all that is ours,” etc. The same author, *On the Dress of Virgins*: “Among the Martyrs there is no thought of the flesh and the world”; doubtless because, as he likewise says in Epistle I, *To Donatus*: “One who is greater than the world can no longer seek or desire anything from the world.” Hence in Epistle XV he exhorts Moyses and the other Confessors condemned to death in these words: “Already hoping for heavenly things alone and contemplating only divine things, through the very delay of your passion you ascend to loftier heights.” For, as the Confessor Celerinus says in Cyprian’s Epistle XXI: “This is what usually happens to God’s servants, [Col. 0030B] especially to those who are established in the confession of Christ; for I know that each now pays no attention to the things of this world, because he hopes for the heavenly crown.” Lucifer of Cagliari, in the book *That One Must Die for the Son of God*: “We know that this discipline has been divinely handed down to us: that, without any terror of wickedness, we should defend the power of so great a name; for the desire of eternal remembrance long ago withdrew us from the desire for this light, and fellowship with Christ set us apart to trample upon all earthly things.”

Furthermore, this contempt for the world, characteristic of Martyrs—τεθνηξομένων, “those about to die immediately”—was sought in imitation by those who, having been seriously converted, undertook the perfect life. Possidius says of St. Augustine after his initiation into the Church’s sacraments by Ambrose: “Soon, converted to God from the innermost depths of his heart, he abandoned every hope that he had in the world.” And because those who embraced the monastic life were said to die to the world, this disposition and affection were likewise characteristic of them; as Augustine himself declares concerning himself in Sermon 49, *On Various Subjects*: “I was seeking where I might establish a monastery, for I had abandoned every hope in the world.” HOLST.

**CHAPTER II.—I. “Lay aside your spirit.”** *Animi* (“spirits” or “high spirits”) seems to be used here for impulses of spirit—that is, more vehement thoughts or emotions. Thus Tertullian, in *On the Shows*: “They proceed to frenzies, passions, and dissensions.” And in *On Patience*, chapter 7: “Anger forbidden, passions restrained, the insolent hand checked.” Unless perhaps Perpetua’s father here called *animi* the loftiness of her spirit and the vigor of a victorious conscience—that is, the martyr’s noble steadfastness—as Cyprian speaks in Epistle LXXVII. HOLST.

**“He called me not daughter, but lady.”** Thus the Vulgate translator at John 13:13: “You call me Teacher and Lord.” In Greek also the nominative stands for the accusative: ὁ διδάσκαλος καὶ ὁ κύριος, “the Teacher and the Lord.” HOLST.

**“Because he alone, out of all my family, would not rejoice in my passion.”** From these words it appears established that Perpetua’s husband, mother, all her brothers, and her relatives were Christians. This will be useful below for understanding that Dinocrates, Perpetua’s brother, who died at the age of seven, had been baptized in a household that was almost entirely Christian. HOLST.

**“What happens on that platform,” etc.** A *catasta* was properly a raised place upon which slaves for sale were displayed, so called ἀπὸ τοῦ καταστῆναι, that is, “from setting forth.” Pamelius so notes on Cyprian’s Epistle XXXIII, adding that Martyrs, when judged or tortured, were likewise customarily displayed to the people upon a raised place. Hence the words of Cyprian in the already cited epistle concerning the Reader who had confessed Christ upon the *catasta* and was afterward promoted to the Church’s pulpit: “to come to the pulpit after the *catasta*”; for as the pulpit was a more elevated place in the church, so was the *catasta* in the forum. The Martyr Romanus in Prudentius:

> Hear, all of you; I cry aloud and proclaim afar;  
> From the lofty platform I send forth my voice.

It is as though he said: “I use the *catasta* as a pulpit.” The word also has another meaning, namely, an instrument of torture. An old glossary: “*Catasta*: the rack, a kind of punishment.” And Prudentius, Hymn I, περὶ στεφάνων (*On the Crowns*), “After the violence of cracking lashes, after the fiery racks.” But this latter meaning is irrelevant here. HOLST.

With my hands joined, I ate it; and all who stood around said, “Amen.” At the sound of their voices I awoke, still chewing something sweet—I know not what. I immediately related this to my brother, and we understood that a passion was to come; and we began now to have no hope in this world.

# CHAPTER II

**SUMMARY.—Perpetua, assailed by her father, strengthens him; led with the others before the tribunal, she confesses herself a Christian, and is condemned with the rest to the beasts; she prays for her dead brother Dinocrates, whom in a vision she understands to be suffering and then delivered from the punishments of purgatory.**

“I. After a few days a report spread that we were to be given a hearing. My father also arrived from the city, worn out with distress, and came up to me in order to cast me down, saying: [Col. 0029B] ‘Have pity, daughter, upon my gray hairs; have pity upon your father, [Col. 0030A] if I am worthy to be called father by you. If with these hands I have brought you to this flower of youth; if I have preferred you to all your brothers, do not deliver me to the disgrace of men. Look upon your brothers; look upon your mother and your maternal aunt; look upon your son, who will not be able to live after you. Lay aside your proud spirit; do not destroy us all [Note: [Col. 0029B] The Compendio and Salisbury manuscripts read: ‘And do not destroy us all.’]. For none of us will be able to speak freely if you suffer anything.’

“My father said these things out of his affection, kissing my hands; and, throwing himself at my feet, with tears he called me not daughter, but lady. And I grieved for my father’s gray hairs, because he alone, out of all my family, would not rejoice in my passion. I strengthened him, saying: ‘Upon that platform there will happen whatever God wills. For know that we have not been placed in our own power, but in God’s.’ And he withdrew from [Col. 0030B] me sorrowful.”

[Col. 0031A] [Note: [Col. 0031B]

**II.—“An immense populace gathered.”** That is, an immense crowd of people assembled. For the word *populus* here signifies a dense and closely packed multitude of people. It is used in this sense also by Apuleius, Book III of the *Metamorphoses*, where he says: “Immediately the entire city, pouring out into a crowd, follows us with astonishing density.” At that passage the acumen of critics who substitute *publicum* (“public place”) or *propatulum* (“open space”) for *populum* is intolerable. HOLST.

**“When questioned, the others confessed.”** They did not confess murders, incestuous unions, injury to the majesty of the Deity or of Caesar, or whatever else a pagan world ignorant of the truth was accustomed to charge against those who professed Christ; they confessed only this: that they were Christians. Justin Martyr, *First Apology*: ἐξεταζόμενοι οὐκ ἀρνούμεθα, διὰ τὸ συνεπίστασθαι ἑαυτοῖς μηδὲν φαῦλον, etc.: “When questioned, we do not deny it, since we are conscious of no evil in ourselves.” This confession sufficed for the formal charge, such as that proclaimed three times by the herald concerning Polycarp, in Eusebius, Book IV, chapter 15: Πολύκαρπος ὡμολόγησεν ἑαυτὸν χριστιανὸν εἶναι, “Polycarp has confessed himself to be a Christian.” So too the inscription upon the placard of Attalus, in the same author, Book V, chapter 1: οὗτός ἐστιν Ἄτταλος ὁ χριστιανός, “This is Attalus the Christian.” HOLST.

**“And he pulled me down from the step.”** She means the higher *catasta*, upon which persons facing a capital charge ascended to plead their case and receive the judge’s sentence—unless we should rather say that upon the *catasta* itself there was a somewhat higher step which the defendants mounted one by one, in order that they might be more conspicuous to judge and people. We have seen this custom observed in Britain. In *Ecclesiastical History*, Book VIII, chapter 9, Eusebius calls τὸ πρὸ τοῦ δικαστοῦ βῆμα “the step or platform erected before the judge.” Translators entirely failed to observe this there, rendering it “the judge’s tribunal.” Eusebius’s words are: ἅμα γοῦν τῇ κατὰ τῶν προτέρων ἀποφάσει, ἐπεπήδων ἄλλοθεν ἄλλοι τῷ πρὸ τοῦ δικαστοῦ βήματι, χριστιανοὺς σφᾶς ὁμολογοῦντες: “As soon as the first had been condemned, others from various quarters leapt upon the raised place erected before the judge, confessing themselves to be Christians.” Likewise in Book V, chapter 1, the governor of Vienne, ἀνῆγεν ἐπὶ τὸ βῆμα θεατρίζων τοὺς μακαρίους μάρτυρας, ἐμπομπεύων τοῖς ὄχλοις: “brought the blessed Martyrs up upon a raised step, presenting them to the multitude as a spectacle, as though in a theater and solemn procession.”

Dionysius of Alexandria, in the same Eusebius, calls it τὸ βάθρον, when speaking of Ammon, Zeno, and the other soldiers who, standing before the tribunal, encouraged Christians who were wavering; and when the cries of the crowd demanded them for execution, φθάσαντες ἐπὶ τὸ βάθρον ἀνέδραμον, “they anticipated them by running voluntarily upon the step,” proclaiming themselves Christians. If, however, anyone prefers to understand this as the tribunal and its steps, I do not stubbornly oppose him. HOLST.

**“Spare your father’s gray hairs.”** Thus the mother of the youthful Origen, when he burned with desire for martyrdom, begged him τῆς περὶ αὐτὸν μητρικῆς διαθέσεως φειδῶ λαβεῖν, that is, in Rufinus’s translation, “to take thought for himself and spare his mother.” HOLST.

**“Offer sacrifice for the welfare of the emperors.”** The Acts of nearly all the Martyrs teach that pagans employed this as the principal means of testing Christians: once the superstition of sacrifice had been rejected, Christians could be convicted of offending both the gods and the emperor. Accordingly, the more insistently the pagans pressed them, the more steadfastly the Christians avoided the guilt of idolatry, as Perpetua steadfastly answers here: “I will not.” “This,” says Tertullian, “is the law peculiar to us Christians, by which we are recognized and tested by the pagans” (*On Idolatry*, final chapter). Hence in *Apology*, chapter 9, he calls “the little hearth and the incense-box” the examiner of Christians. The same author, *Apology*, chapter 10: “You say: ‘You do not worship the gods, and you do not offer sacrifices for the emperors.’ We are therefore arraigned for sacrilege and treason: this is the chief charge—indeed, the entire charge.” He then refutes both heads of this accusation in a long and learned discussion, whose substance he embraces in these few words in the book *To Scapula*: “We sacrifice for the emperor’s welfare, but to our God and his; and in the manner God commands—with pure prayer. Thus we pray all the more for the emperor’s welfare, asking it from the One who can grant it.” HOLST.

**“I will not.”** Thus Polycarp, when they advised him to call Caesar “Lord” and to sacrifice, answered: οὐ μέλλω πράττειν ὃ συμβουλεύετέ μοι, “I will never do what you advise me to do.” Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book IV, chapter 15. HOLST.

**“I am a Christian.”** This is the proper formula of confession. Thus that glorious soldier of God who refused the laurel, in Tertullian, when required to give his reasons, answered: “I am a Christian.” Thus St. Blandina, amid the most savage torments, repeatedly cried: “I am a Christian.” That utterance was an alleviation of pain and a refreshment of spirit. And Sanctus the deacon, Blandina’s companion, answered nothing else to all the torturers’ questions but “I am a Christian”: τοῦτο καὶ ἀντὶ ὀνόματος, καὶ ἀντὶ πόλεως, καὶ ἀντὶ γένους, καὶ ἀντὶ παντὸς ἐπαλλήλως ὡμολόγει, “This served him as name, country, race, and everything.” For Christians regarded this as a πάντιμον καὶ ἔνδοξον καὶ ζωοποιὸν προσηγορίαν, “an all-honored, glorious, and life-giving appellation,” as Eusebius records. HOLST.

**“He condemns us to the beasts.”** Although Christians were frequently condemned to the beasts at Rome and elsewhere, many passages of Tertullian establish that in Africa especially they were savaged with this form of punishment during this very great persecution. HOLST.

**“We went down joyfully.”** For, as Tertullian says, condemned Christians customarily gave thanks, and rejoiced more at being condemned than they would have at being acquitted. HOLST.]

“II. On another day, while we were eating the midday meal, we were suddenly seized and taken to be given a hearing; and we arrived at the forum. The report immediately spread through the areas adjoining the forum, and an immense populace gathered. We ascended the platform [Note: [Col. 0031A] The Salisbury manuscript reads: ‘We ascended the platform’; the Compendio manuscript: ‘onto the platform.’]. When questioned, the others confessed. My turn also came, and at once my father appeared with my son. He pulled me down from the step and said imploringly: ‘Have pity upon the infant’ [Note: [Col. 0031A] Both manuscripts have ‘my gray hairs’ in place of ‘the infant.’].

“And the procurator Hilarianus [Note: [Col. 0032A] The Salisbury manuscript consistently has *Elarianus*; the Compendio manuscript, *Helarianus*.], who at that time had received the power of the sword in place of the deceased proconsul Minucius Timinianus, said: ‘Spare your father’s [Col. 0032A] gray hairs; spare the boy’s infancy. Offer sacrifice for the welfare of the emperors.’

“I answered: ‘I will not.’

“Hilarianus said: ‘Are you a Christian?’

“And I answered: ‘I am a Christian.’

“And while my father stood there trying to cast me down, Hilarianus ordered him to be thrown down, and he was struck with a rod. My father’s misfortune grieved me as though I myself had been struck: so I grieved for his wretched old age. Then Hilarianus pronounced sentence upon us all and condemned us to the beasts; and we went down joyfully to the prison.

“Then, because [Col. 0033A] [Note: [Col. 0033B]

**“But my father refused to give him.”** It is credible that her idolatrous father was moved to refuse his daughter her infant, at a time when the infant ought to have been taking milk, lest some contagion should appear to be transmitted to the child from a mother already condemned for sacrilege. Or perhaps it was because, owing to penal servitude after sentence had already been passed, the mother’s status had changed and, having undergone loss of civil status, she had lost citizenship together with liberty, as stated in Law *In Ser.* in the Digest, *On Penalties*, and the Institutes, *On Loss of Status*; and therefore all bonds and rights of kinship ceased. Thus Calpurnius Flaccus, Declamation IV: “You cannot exercise a father’s right against one condemned; now I have no household, no sacred rites, no father.” So a most learned man recently emended this passage. HOLST.

**III.—“A word escaped me, and I named Dinocrates.”** She seems to say that, while she was praying, an unpremeditated word suddenly escaped her, naming Dinocrates, of whom she had not been thinking for a long time. HOLST.

**“And I knew at once that I was worthy, and that I ought to petition for him.”** That is: by an inward sense of confidence, I understood that I would certainly be heard if I prayed for Dinocrates. [Col. 0033C] Thus in the preceding chapter, § III, Perpetua heard from her brother: “Lady sister, you are now held in great favor,” etc.; signifying, as is clear from what follows, that her favor with God appeared so great that she could obtain anything. HOLST.

**“I see Dinocrates coming out of a dark place, where there were also several dark places,” etc.** This passage seems especially worthy of note because it attests the ancient tradition from which the Scholastic theologians teach with great agreement—as Bellarmine observes in Book II, *On Purgatory*, chapter 6, § “The Eighth”—that there are four distinct places beneath the earth in which the souls of the dead are detained. First is the lowest of all, where the demons and condemned souls are; above it is Purgatory, where souls are purified for a time; next is the Limbo of children, where the souls of those who died in original sin alone are detained; and finally the Limbo of the Fathers, now empty since the death and resurrection of Christ, where the souls of the patriarchs and holy persons who died before Christ were detained, although cleansed of every stain. This is called in the Gospel “Abraham’s bosom,” to which Lazarus was carried by the angels and where the rich glutton saw him from hell.

These appear to have been those several dark places which St. Perpetua testifies in these words that she saw. From one of them—namely, Purgatory—she affirms that she saw Dinocrates come forth: not because he was then being delivered from punishment, for this happened a little later, but because, by God’s permission, he came forth thence with his punishments in order to implore the assistance of his sister’s prayers. Many apparitions of this kind, thoroughly attested, are related in St. Gregory and other authors concerning souls enduring purgatorial punishments. HOLST.

**“Very hot and thirsty.”** These details agree excellently with the Church’s doctrine of Purgatory, where souls are tormented by heat and fire. For Augustine observes that this Dinocrates had been baptized; and it is easy to believe that he afterward fell into some act of impatience or—as St. Augustine suspects—that, when tempted by his impious father, he wavered slightly in the faith. HOLST.

**“My brother according to the flesh.”** Africans commonly spoke in this manner. St. Augustine, Epistle CCXXV: “Nor did they begrudge this to the Church of Thagaste, which is my native country according to the flesh.” This word has persisted in the common Italian tongue, which generally embraces corruptions of the ancient Latin language. HOLST.

**“He died miserably, his face eaten by cancer, so that his death was hateful,” etc.** She signifies that he died a kind of death which inspired horror in those who saw it, because of the deformity of a foul and fetid ulcer projecting from his face. Moreover, in order to know what *cancer* means, we thought that, in addition to all our other diligence, physicians too should be consulted; from their answers, with certain additions, we have assembled the following.

Among the ancient Latins, *cancer* means the same as gangrene. Thus Nonius Marcellus: “Gangrene is cancer”; the old Glossary follows him. Cornelius Celsus, Book VIII, chapter 10, may also be drawn to this sense, where, by saying that “cancers” arise more readily when a wound of the flesh accompanies a fracture of a bone, he seems to signify what experience shows: that in such a case there is greater danger of gangrene. Yet I would not readily assent to the opinion of a learned physician who, after making this observation, denies that the physicians of later times and of our own age agree with the ancients concerning the meaning of this word, because they understand by the name *cancer* what the Greeks call Καρκίνωμα (*karkinōma*, carcinoma)—as though the ancients too had not expressed the Greek name *carcinoma* by the Latin word *cancer*.

Certainly Celsus, Book V, chapter 28, speaks of cancer projecting from the face in these words: “Καρκίνωμα does not entail the same danger unless it has been aggravated through the imprudence of the person treating it. This disease arises chiefly in the upper parts, around the face, nostrils, ears, lips, and women’s breasts.” Thus far Celsus, who also in Book VI, chapter 15, when treating cancer of the mouth, appears to speak of the ulcer which in the other passage he calls *carcinoma*. I would therefore believe that καρκίνωμα is a general name for more severe ulcers. Hence in Hippocrates ulcers are said καρκινωθῆναι τὰ ἕλκεα, “to become cancerous,” when they grow aggravated and incurable. And in the Hippocratic Lexicon καρκινοῦσθαι, “to become cancerous,” is explained by σκληρύνεσθαι, “to harden,” which means “to become aggravated.”

Therefore gangrene properly so called, if it differs from cancer, seems to share with it the common name *carcinoma*, differing from it perhaps because it causes death very rapidly, whereas cancer creeps along in such a way as to consume a person who may remain alive for many years. Nothing, however, prevents the cancer from which Dinocrates died from having been gangrene; for this may be inferred from the representation of his death at so tender an age. It is characteristic of both—of cancer, I say, as well as gangrene—to creep. Hence the words concerning the teaching of heretics at 2 Timothy 2:17: “And their speech creeps like a cancer.” The expression seems transferred from the animal crab, a many-footed creature accustomed to creep forward and backward.

Relevant here is a passage of Lucifer of Cagliari in the book *On Not Associating with Heretics*, addressed to the Arian emperor Constantius: “Thus Sabellius was cut off from the body of the Church, just as that utterly detestable Arius was cut off. His speech has crept like a cancer in you so powerfully that you are now seen to be wholly cancer; nor will you be able to say that you have not been cancered by Arius’s speech, since the stench of your cancerous corruption has reached every place in your kingdom, and all of us have resolved to avoid you, lest we too be cancered by your Arian plague.”

Thus he speaks. From his words we incidentally gather that *facies cancerata* (“a cancered face”), the phrase read here, is not a barbarism born in a later age, as one of the physicians I consulted maintained when he denied that any ancient writer had spoken of a “cancered face.” He argued that it ought to be called *cancrosa*, whereas *cancerosa* and *cancerata* were used only by recent authors speaking barbarously. HOLST.]

the infant was accustomed to take my breasts and remain with me in prison, I immediately sent to Father Pomponius [Note: [Col. 0033A] In the Compendio manuscript, *Pompinianus*.], the deacon, requesting the infant. But my father refused to give him; and, as God willed, the infant no longer desired my breasts, nor did my breasts become inflamed, so that I might not be tormented both by anxiety for the infant and by pain in my breasts.

“III. A few days later, while we were all praying, suddenly in the midst of prayer a word escaped me, and I named Dinocrates. I was astonished that he had never entered my mind until then, and I grieved when I recalled his misfortune. And I knew at once [Col. 0034A] that I was worthy, and that I ought to petition [Note: [Col. 0033A] The Salisbury manuscript has *pati*, ‘to suffer.’] for him. And I began to pray much for him and to groan before the Lord.

“Immediately, that very night, this was shown to me in a vision [*oroma*] [Note: [Col. 0033A] These words are absent from Holstenius’s edition. It appears that *in oramate* should be restored—that is, ‘in a vision’—as below near the beginning of chapter 10.]: I see Dinocrates coming out of a dark place, where there were also several others [Note: [Col. 0034A] Holstenius reads: ‘there were several dark places.’]; he was very hot and thirsty, with a dirty face and pale complexion, and on his face the wound that he had when he died. This Dinocrates had been my brother according to the flesh, seven years old, who died miserably of illness, his face eaten by cancer [Note: [Col. 0034A] The Salisbury manuscript has ‘wasted.’], so that his death was hateful to all people. [Col. 0035A] [Note: [Col. 0035B]

**“For him I had made prayer.”** This too is an African manner of speaking, for the expression “to make a prayer” is also found in Tertullian. As to the substance, however, the Church’s ancient practice and conviction of praying for the dead who pay the penalties of their sins after this life should be noted here. Although there are many other thoroughly trustworthy testimonies to it, this one seems especially important, since it was written by a holy Martyr deemed worthy of divine revelations and already close to her consummation. Nor do the heretics retain any objection concerning the truth and reliability of these Acts after the many splendid testimonies of every kind of author who praises them, which we have appended to this volume. Indeed, they are such that even obstinacy and shamelessness themselves would appear unable to object to them. HOLST.

**“And between me and him there was a great diadem.”** I do not conceal that, if conjecture were permissible, it might appear not without foundation that *diastema* (“interval”) could be restored in place of *diadema*. For one may understand that the Latin writers of that age frequently used the word *diastema* from Julius Frontinus’s book *On the Quality of Lands*, where he writes: “If three equal circles are connected with one another by an equal interval [*diastema*].” And Hyginus, *On the Establishment of Boundaries*: “Furthermore, even in that very region the position of the sun cannot be correctly determined unless the instrument is placed at equal intervals [*diastemata*] from its rising and setting.” Likewise: “The earth is a point of the heavens, and the air sustains it beneath the sun across a vast interval [*diastema*].” HOLST.

—**“And between me and him there was a great diadem, so that neither of us could approach the other.”** Holstenius’s comments here upon his conjecture that *diastema* should be restored for *diadema* appear open to this objection: the passages he cites from the land-surveyors Frontinus and Hyginus certainly do little to persuade us that St. Perpetua used here that word, which was proper to the art of surveying and consequently foreign to common usage, especially that of women in Africa. Accordingly, since—as Holstenius himself acknowledges in the very papers from which we transcribed his note—the manuscript’s consistent and explicit reading gives *diadema*, there is no reason to alter it readily, especially since the word yields a very suitable meaning.

For those dark places which she says above that she saw in their plurality were like certain zones of the sort usefully imagined by cosmographers as embracing heaven and earth—namely, oblong spaces of an appropriate breadth encircling globes. With regard to the lower regions, ancient usage, preserved particularly by Scholastic writers from the old custom of the churches, calls these spaces *limbi*. Now *limbus* is a word of the same meaning as *diadema*. For *diadema*, as is well known, signifies a band longer than it is wide, surrounding the head or bound around it, as the Greek etymology of the name indicates, from the verb διαδέω, “I bind around.”

Therefore Perpetua’s statement that “between Dinocrates and me there was a great diadem” is equivalent to saying that there was a great *limbus*—that is, an oblong space of a certain breadth. In the Gospel it is called a “chasm,” Luke 16:26: “And now between us and you a great chasm has been fixed.” The Greek is χάσμα, which means an opening or gulf, and the added words—“so that those who wish to pass from here to you cannot, nor can they cross from there to us”—agree with what St. Perpetua says here: “So that neither of us could approach the other.” For these spaces were like ditches drawn around fortifications, excluding passage by their very emptiness. This is more readily understood in the case of bodies; but in the case of souls the divine ordinance intervened to keep them apart, as expressed by the verb “to fix”: “A great chasm has been fixed.”

Nor is the foregoing contradicted by the fact that, according to these words, the diadem was not the place in which Dinocrates himself was, but the space lying between him and St. Perpetua; and therefore it does not appear to follow that the name *diadema* or *limbus* is applicable to Purgatory. For since both the subterranean places and the openings or χάσματα by which they were separated possessed the same form and shape, the name *diadema* or *limbus* can equally apply to both.

Although I found nothing concerning the foregoing observations in Holstenius’s adversaria, I nevertheless heard from a trustworthy man that Holstenius was by no means averse to this opinion. Father Jean Besson of our Society reported to me that, when Lucas Holstenius had once shared with him these very Acts of St. Perpetua, which he was preparing for publication, and asked what he thought about this mention of a diadem, Besson replied that the term *limbus* appeared to have been replaced by that word of equivalent meaning. Holstenius indicated that this interpretation pleased him greatly. POSSIN.

**“We were transferred to the camp prison.”** That is, the prison situated within the camp itself. HOLST.

**“For we were to fight in a camp spectacle.”** Since Roman camps outside cities were long-standing and virtually permanent stations for soldiers, the chief amenities of cities were transferred into them so that soldiers would not be deprived of them. Among these were the spectacles, to which the Romans were extraordinarily devoted. Suetonius accordingly mentions “camp games”—that is, games celebrated in the camp to entertain the soldiers—in his *Tiberius*, chapter 72.

But as for the word *munus* (“spectacle”) used here, it signified a combat either of gladiators with one another or of beasts with persons condemned to death, which is properly called θηριομαχία, “combat with wild beasts.” Thus the phrase in Eusebius, Book V, chapter 1, θηριομαχιῶν ἡμέρας, “days of combats with beasts,” is elegantly translated by Rufinus as *munerum dies*, “days of spectacles.” Note here a certain catachresis in the word “fight,” since it is said of persons who, when exposed to beasts, remained entirely passive, as the Martyrs did. Thus Juvenal, after calling the nocturnal assault of drunken men upon unarmed and unresisting passersby a “fight,” adds:

> If it is a fight when you strike and I merely take the beating.

] For him I had made prayer. And between me and him there was a great diadem [Note: [Col. 0035A] The passage is corrupt. The Salisbury manuscript has *dianten*. Holstenius suspects that *diastema* should be written, a Greek word meaning “interval.”], so that neither of us could approach the other.

“Then, in the place where Dinocrates was, there was a pool full of water, having a rim higher than the boy’s stature; and Dinocrates stretched himself upward as though he were going to drink. I grieved that although the pool contained water, nevertheless, because of the rim’s height, he would not be able to drink.

“I awoke and understood that my brother was suffering. But I trusted [Note: [Col. 0036A] The Salisbury manuscript reads: ‘I considered.’ In Holstenius: ‘I trusted that my prayer would benefit his suffering,’ etc.] that my prayer would benefit his suffering, and I prayed for him every day until we were transferred to the camp prison; for we were to fight in a camp spectacle. It was then the anniversary of Geta Caesar: [Col. 0037A] [Note: [Col. 0037C]

Nevertheless usage prevailed so that those who were delivered, bound and defenseless, to the beasts were said in Greek θηριομαχεῖν, “to fight wild beasts,” and in Latin *pugnare ad bestias*, “to fight against the beasts,” although these expressions properly applied to those who were actually ordered to fight beasts in hunts staged in the amphitheater. Such men did so at the utmost risk to life, yet not without some hope of victory, for we read that lions and whatever other beasts were more savage were sometimes killed by them.

There were therefore two kinds of punishment. The former was the supreme penalty and is called capital punishment in Law 8 of the Digest, *On Penalties*; the latter is reckoned among moderate punishments by Paul, *Sentences*, Book V, title 17, and by Ulpian in Law 8 of the Digest, *On the Cornelian Law concerning Forgeries*. For those condemned to the hunting school could be released, whereas those assigned to the beasts had to be consumed without remission. Hence they were either bound to a stake or enclosed in nets and thrown to the wild beasts, so that they had no ability to resist. Then, as we learn from the conclusion of these Acts, whatever life and breath the beasts’ cruelty had left them was finally taken by the sword. HOLST.

—Spectacles or games were called “combats with beasts” because they were given for the entertainment of peoples or soldiers. They were called “camp games” if held in a camp. Augustine delivered a sermon on the day of the spectacles in the Basilica Restituta; it is Sermon 19 in the new edition, volume V. See the notes appended there. RUINART.

**“It was then Geta’s anniversary.”** Antoninus Geta was the son of Severus. After his father’s death he was killed by his brother Caracalla, with whom he had ruled for a time. But here by *birthday* or “anniversary” we must understand the day upon which Geta had been made Caesar. This day was commonly called the emperor’s birthday, just as a bishop’s “birthday” was the day upon which he was consecrated. For otherwise Geta, according to Spartianus, was born on the sixth day before the Kalends of June, that is, May 27. RUINART.

**IV.—“On the day when we remained in the stocks.”** The laws of the Twelve Tables, as quoted by Aulus Gellius, Book XX, chapter 1, mention two kinds of restraints formerly used to bind criminals in prison: the *nervus* or stocks, and fetters. Other authors also frequently join the two kinds. Cato, in Gellius, Book XI, chapter 18: “Thieves convicted of private thefts spend their lives in the stocks and fetters.” And Livy, Book VIII: “No one was to be kept in fetters or in the stocks, unless he had incurred a penalty, until he had paid it.”

Fetters are iron shackles which restrain the feet of prisoners by a shorter or longer chain, more tightly or loosely, in such a manner that they can not only stand upon their feet but also, with some difficulty, advance a step and remain standing. The *nervus*, however, is properly a wooden apparatus pierced by several holes, which encloses prisoners’ feet at nearer or farther intervals so that, sitting upon the ground with their legs spread apart, they are wholly unable to move from the spot. Spreading the legs through several holes, because of the discomfort, served as a torture and punishment before the execution itself.

I know that learned men of our time do not agree concerning the *nervus*; but among the ancients, when both the object and its name were in use, there is no dispute. On occasion of this mention of fetters, we should not omit to observe that, at least in Africa, they appear to have been used only rarely in the custody of Christians imprisoned for religion’s sake. St. Augustine, Discourse II on Psalm 101, near the beginning, volume 10, page 439: “Why are the Martyrs said to be fettered by the feet? Were they not chained rather than fettered? For we know that the holy Martyrs, led after judges traveling through the provinces, were put in chains; but we do not know that they were put in fetters.” HOLST.

**“Then she understood that he had been removed from punishment.”** Behold: St. Perpetua understands by divine revelation that a soul has been delivered from the flames of purgatory.

—**“That he had been removed from punishment.”** An excellent passage for proving that the dead can be delivered, through the prayers of the living, from the punishments they suffer. Some inferred from this passage that even those who had died before baptism could be aided by prayers. Augustine excellently refutes them in *On the Origin of the Soul*, Book I, chapter 10, and Book III, chapter 9, where he says that Dinocrates endured such punishments because of certain sins committed after baptism. For a boy of seven could have lied or, at the persuasion of his pagan father, done something else against God. This opinion of Augustine is confirmed by Perpetua’s earlier statement that her entire family, with the exception of her father, practiced the religion of Christ. RUINART.

**CHAPTER III.—I. “Pudens, a soldier and *optio*, superintendent of the prison.”** The word *optio* is the name of an office or prefecture. In Gruter’s inscriptions the phrase *optio carceris*, “prison *optio*,” occurs, so that the addition made here—“superintendent of the prison”—appears to have been placed by way of explanation. The Greeks call him δεσμοφύλαξ, “prison-keeper.” At Acts 16:27 St. Ambrose, in his commentary on the Epistle to the Ephesians, chapter IV, translates this word as “prison *optio*,” writing: “Nor did Paul and Silas delay the time in which they might baptize the prison *optio*.”

Here the question may arise why this office was entrusted to a soldier. Perhaps it was because, in the camp where the prison then was, as stated above, civic officials could not be employed for duties of this kind, which therefore had to be discharged by soldiers. This may be understood by analogy from Law 4 of the Digest, *On the Office of the Proconsul*, where it is written: “No proconsul may have his own orderlies; rather, soldiers are to perform their service in the provinces in place of them.” Relevant here is an ancient inscription in which a soldier serving as *optio* is mentioned:

> TO AURELIUS CANDIDUS, HIS SWEETEST SON,  
> WHO LIVED FOUR YEARS. AURELIUS CALANDINUS,  
> SOLDIER OF THE EIGHTH PRAETORIAN COHORT,  
> *OPTIO* OF THE CENTURY OF SECUNDUS,  
> ERECTED THIS TO ONE WELL DESERVING.

HOLST.

—*Optio* is the name of a prefecture or some official service. The Bollandists think it means “overseer,” from the Greek verb ὄπτομαι, “I see.” RUINART.]

Who admitted many people to visit us. This was the relaxed custody, as Pontius the Deacon calls it in his *Life of St. Cyprian* [Col. 0039B]; opposed to it is strict custody, concerning which see Cujacius, *Observations*, book XIV, chapter 34, and Heraldus on Tertullian’s *Apology*, p. 97. Yet St. Perpetua does not without reason attribute to the kindness of Pudens this permission to visit her, because people generally approached prisons cautiously and fearfully, and almost always one at a time, lest they betray themselves or arouse hostility among the persecutors if they poured in there in a crowd. St. Cyprian, Epistle IV, vividly sets the circumstances of those times before our eyes:

> I ask also that your vigilance and solicitude not fail in securing peace. And although the brothers, out of their love, are eager to meet with and visit the good confessors, whom divine favor has already illuminated by glorious beginnings, nevertheless I think this must be done cautiously, not in a mass or by a multitude assembled together, lest by that very fact hostility be aroused and access for entering be denied, and, while in our insatiability we desire too much, we lose everything.

HOLST.]

And I prayed for him, groaning and weeping day and night, that he might be granted to me.

“IV. On the day, moreover, on which we remained in the stocks, this was shown to me: I see that place which I had previously seen as dark now become bright, and Dinocrates clean in body, well clothed, and refreshed. And where the wound had been, I see a scar; and that pool which I had previously seen had its rim lowered to the level of the boy’s navel, and he was drawing water from it without ceasing. On the rim there was a bowl [Note: [Col. 0037A] Holstenius adds *golden*], full of water; and Dinocrates approached and began to drink from it, and the bowl did not become empty. When he had drunk his fill, he went away from the water and began joyfully to play in the manner of children. And I awoke. Then I understood that he had been transferred away from punishment.

## CHAPTER III

**SUMMARY.—Perpetua is again assailed by her father; her third vision, in which she is led away to wrestle against an Egyptian, with a prize set before her; she fights, conquers, and receives the prize.**

“I. Then, after a few days, Pudens [Note: [Col. 0037A] *Prudens* in the Salzburg codex], a soldier and *optio*, the officer in charge of the prison, began to hold us in high regard [Note: [Col. 0038A] ‘Who held us in high regard, began to understand that there was great power in us, and admitted many people to visit us,’ Holstenius], understanding that there was great power from God in us; and he admitted many brothers to visit us, so that both we and they might refresh one another. But when [Col. 0039A] [Note: [Col. 0039C]

**II.—I see in a *horoma*.** The matter requires that *horamate* be restored, unless this word in its deformed form was current in the popular speech of the Africans. It is the Greek word ὅραμα (*horama*), meaning a sight or vision. It is used in Acts 12:9. Latin writers used it more rarely; nevertheless Aldhelm, *On Virginity*, chapter 3, where he speaks of St. John the Evangelist, says that he was “caught up on Patmos in an *oroma*.” There Meursius correctly substituted *oramate* in his *Mantissa Critica*—and I find it printed in this form in the *Library of the Holy Fathers*—despite the pointless objection of Swartius, *Analecta*, book III, chapter 9, who tries in vain to persuade us that *chroma* should be restored there. I also find these words in Alcuin, book I of the *Life of St. Willibrord*, chapter 2: “In the repose of the dead of night, his mother saw a heavenly *horama* in her sleep.” HOLST.

**Having numerous *calliculae*.** An old glossary has: “*Galliculae*, τροχάδες.” And in the Greek-Latin Glosses: “Τροχάς, *gallicula*.” There seems no doubt that *gallicula* is the same as *callicula* in this passage; and since it is explained by the word τροχάς, it appears to have been something round and movable. The *calliculae* seem to have been rounded pendants, added for ornament to the pointed ends of military breastplates. They could have been made of fine linen, purple cloth, or similar material; sometimes they were made of metal, as occurs a little below, verse 31: “Having *calliculae* of many forms, made of gold and silver.” Of this kind were the pomegranate-shaped bells placed on the lower hem of the high priest’s garment, as described in Exodus and Leviticus. POSSIN.—Might the *galliculae* be small boots? See Mabillon, *Gallican Liturgy*, p. 473. RUINART.

**An Egyptian hideous in appearance.** Plautus, *The Little Carthaginian*: “And so I will fill him with blackness, so that he becomes far blacker than the Egyptians.” Ausonius:

> Dyed in the color of night,  
> an Egyptian boy, a flute-player  
> with talkative hands, etc.

**I see the Egyptian opposite me rolling in the *apha*.** *Apha* means dust in Greek; it is the Greek noun ἁφή written in Latin letters. Boxers preparing to fight customarily sprinkled their oiled bodies with dust, or rolled in it as it lay on the ground. Ovid, *Metamorphoses* IX, concerning [Col. 0040C] two wrestlers supplying one another with dust for this purpose:

> Scooping dust in hollow palms, he sprinkles me,  
> and in turn grows yellow beneath a shower of tawny sand.

The sand from which the boxers’ bodies thus became yellow is called *Haphe* by Martial, book VI, Epigram 66, in this verse:

> And grows yellow with *Haphe*.

He is speaking of the woman Philaenis, who imitated men in boxing. Since Martial censures this most severely—indeed, detests it—in a woman, it is apparent how fittingly St. Perpetua, even in the vision in which she was matched with the Egyptian boxer who represented the devil, was changed into a male, as she herself says in this very passage: “And I became a male.” POSSIN.

**A man of marvelous height.** Thus, in her first vision, she had seen a tall, gray-haired man in the dress of a shepherd: namely, the one and same Christ, who there, as Shepherd, refreshes his sheep, but here, as Commander and [Col. 0040D] President of the Games, assigns prizes to soldiers and contestants. For in the Christians’ contest, as Clement of Alexandria says, ἀγωνοθέτης ὁ Θεὸς, βραβευτὴς ὁ υἱὸς Θεοῦ, θεαταὶ δὲ οἱ ἄγγελοι: “God is the president of the games, the Son of God is the awarder of the prize, and the angels are the spectators.” HOLST.

**Purple between two stripes.** That is, wearing a purple garment divided by two *clavi*, or bands, and without a belt. The garment of gymnasium superintendents was purple; hence, in Lucian’s dialogue on gymnasia, Anacharsis recognizes the superintendent of the gymnasium by his purple dress. HOLST.

**A staff like a gladiatorial trainer.** Xiphilinus likewise assigns a staff to the trainer in his account of Commodus: ἀντηγωνίζετο δὲ αὐτῷ γυμναστής τις ἢ καὶ μονόμαχος, νάρθηκα ἔχων: “A certain trainer, or perhaps a gladiator, carrying a staff or switch, fought against him.” The addition “like” is correct here. For the person who appeared did not assume the role of a gladiatorial trainer, but that of the superintendent of the gymnasium—that is, the overseer of the wrestlers. Sidonius Apollinaris, book XI, Epistle 2, teaches that such an official also customarily carried a staff, which he calls the master’s staff; and he describes its entirely honorable and disciplinary use in these words [Col. 0041B]: “If the struggles of the young men become indecently entangled, the chaste staff of the gymnasium superintendents immediately separates them.” HOLST.]

the day of the spectacle drew near, my father came in to me, worn out with distress. He began to tear out his beard, to throw himself upon the ground, to prostrate himself on his face, to reproach his years, and to utter such words as would move the whole creation. I grieved for his unhappy old age.

“II. On the day before we were to fight, I see in a vision that Pomponius the deacon had come here to the door of the prison and was knocking forcefully. I went out to him and opened the door for him. He was clothed in a splendid white garment [the Latin reading is grammatically uncertain], having numerous *calliculae* [Note: [Col. 0039B] *Galliculae* in the Salzburg codex]. And he said to me: ‘Perpetua, we are waiting for you; come.’ And he took me by the hand, and we began to go through rough and winding places. At last, with difficulty and out of breath, we reached the amphitheater. He led me into the middle of the arena and said to me [Col. 0039B]: ‘Do not be afraid; I am here with you and I am laboring together with you’ [Col. 0040A]; and he departed.

“And I beheld an immense, astonished crowd. Since I knew that I had been condemned to the beasts, I wondered that no beasts were being sent against me. Then a certain Egyptian came out against me, hideous in appearance, together with his assistants, to fight me. Handsome young men also came to me as my assistants and supporters. I was stripped, and I became a male. My supporters began to rub me down with oil [Note: [Col. 0039B] *Defricare* in the Salzburg codex], as is customary before a contest; and opposite me I saw the Egyptian rolling in the *apha* [Note: [Col. 0039B] *Aqua* in the Compiègne and Salzburg codices, but better *afa*, or *apha*, or *hapha*—that is, the dust with which boxers were sprinkled after being anointed [Col. 0040B]].

“And there came out a man of marvelous height, so that he rose even above the summit of the amphitheater. He wore an ungirded tunic [Note: [Col. 0040B] ‘Ungirded, wearing purple,’ Holstenius] and purple between two stripes down the middle of his chest. He also had *calliculae* [Note: [Col. 0040B] *Galliculae* in the Salzburg codex] of many forms, made of gold and silver; and he carried [Note: [Col. 0040B] ‘holding aloft,’ Holstenius] a staff [Col. 0040B], like a gladiatorial trainer, and a green branch upon which [Col. 0041A] [Note: [Col. 0041B]

**And he called for silence.** This was customarily done through a herald or trumpeter. From Lucian and others we learn that the conventional formula for this in Greece was ἄκουε πᾶς, “Hear, everyone.” This practice was especially employed when prizes were to be publicly distributed. For that reason Apuleius, in the *Florida*, places a herald beside the proconsul on such an occasion. Seneca, Epistle 74, provides testimony concerning the trumpeter: “Let us too overcome all things, whose prizes are neither a crown nor a cloak, nor a trumpeter imposing silence for the proclamation of our name, but virtue and steadfastness of mind.” HOLST.

**If she defeats him, she will receive this branch.** For here he assumed not only the role of superintendent of the gymnasium, as was said above, but also that of the βραβευτής, the awarder of the prize. “The *brabeutae*, or awarders of prizes,” says the *Etymologicum*, “are properly called as though they were *rhabdeustae*—that is, givers of staffs or shoots; for they gave branches of palm or of some similar tree as tokens of victory”: βραβευταὶ κυρίως λέγονται, οἱ τὴν ῥάβδον ἀπὸ φοίνικος ἢ τινος ἄλλου διδόντες σύμβολα τῆς νίκης, ῥαβδευταί τινες ὄντες. Furthermore, it belonged to the same official to announce the contest, which our figure did shortly before, and to present the prize to the victor, which he now promises. Tertullian, *On Flight in Persecution*: “By whom is the contest proclaimed, except by him by whom the crown and prize are offered?” And a little later [Col. 0041D]: “Thus you will recognize that judgment over the contest belongs to the same President of the Games who invites one to the prize.” HOLST.

**I joined my hands, so as to interlock my fingers.** Perpetua means that, after being lifted into the air, she violently pressed the crown of the boxer who was fighting her downward with both palms joined together, the fingers of each hand interlocked, so as to throw him to the ground; as a result, the Egyptian fell upon his face. POSSIN.

**And I approached the gladiatorial trainer.** She calls the person whom we described above rather as superintendent of the gymnasium and awarder of the prize a “gladiatorial trainer,” perhaps not without a certain misuse of the term. HOLST.

**To the Gate of Life.** The passage requires the restoration: “To the *Sanavivarian* Gate,” as below, § XX, verse 24: “They were called back to the *Sanavivarian* Gate.” There perhaps *Sanavivaria* should be restored from the earlier passage. From these places it is clear that there was a gate in the amphitheater which, at least in Africa, was popularly called the *Sanavivaria*. What gate this was must be investigated. Lipsius, *On the Amphitheater*, chapter 21, teaches that, besides various small gates or posterns surrounding the lowest part of the amphitheater and serving various purposes, especially the release of wild beasts, there were two larger gates directly opposite one another. He conjectures that one was called the Libitinarian Gate, and a little later he himself calls it the Gate of the Dead; through it, evidently, the dead bodies of gladiators or the remains of beast-fighters were dragged out of the arena. He gives no name for the other gate, which, as he says, led to the forum. I do not doubt that, if he had seen this passage, he would have affirmed that it was called the *Sanavivarian* Gate. Nor is the etymology obscure: since those who had survived the dangers of the arena safe and alive were through it restored to the forum and the city, it was rightly named *Sanavivaria*, the Gate of the Safe and Living. The two passages here favor this conjecture. In the first, after Perpetua had conquered in the boxing match and overcome her Egyptian adversary in the arena, she began, as she herself says, “to go in glory to the *Sanavivarian* Gate”—evidently in the manner of those victorious in such contests, who after victory went out amid applause through the gate that led to the forum. The other passage, § XX, relates that the crowd, moved by compassion for Saints Perpetua and Felicitas after they had been badly mauled by the beasts, called them back to the *Sanavivarian* Gate. Evidently gladiators or beast-fighters whom the people spared withdrew there, admonished by the crowd’s favorable acclamation, so that they might escape the danger. POSSIN.

**Until the day before the spectacle.** Thus Tertullian, *To Scapula*, chapter 7: “Those who until the day before had sworn by their guardian spirits.” Cicero said, “until the day before the Kalends.” HOLST.

**The account of the spectacle itself.** Below it is called “the order of the spectacle” and “the commencement of the show.” Moreover, whoever was the author of these Acts had in view these words of St. Perpetua when he said that he was discharging the trust committed to his faith. HOLST.

**CHAPTER IV.—I. We began to be carried by four angels, whose hands did not touch us.** This seems to express what is said in Daniel 14:35: “In the force of his spirit.” And of Ezekiel, chapter 8, verse 3 of his prophecy: “He seized me by a lock of my head.” POSSIN.

**And being released.** I would prefer to read *liberati*, “being released,” so that the meaning would be that, after emerging from the darkness and the denser air of the sublunary sphere, they saw an immense light, etc. POSSIN.

**It was like a garden.** The author of a sermon which Holstenius found in the Vatican Library under the name of St. Augustine treats this garden more fully. That sermon is now the last among the doubtful works in the new edition. GALLAND.]

there were golden apples. He called for silence and said: ‘If this Egyptian defeats her, he will kill her with the sword; and if she defeats him, she will receive this branch.’ Then he withdrew.

“And we approached one another and began to exchange blows. He tried to seize my feet [Note: [Col. 0041B] ‘He wished,’ Holstenius], but I struck him in the face with my heels. I was lifted into the air and began to strike him as though I were trampling the earth. But when I saw that the struggle was being prolonged, I joined my hands so as to interlock my fingers. I seized his head, and he fell upon his face; and I trod upon his head. The people began to shout, and my supporters to sing psalms. I approached the gladiatorial trainer and received the branch. He kissed me and said to me: ‘Daughter, peace be with you.’ And I began to go in glory to the *Sanavivarian* Gate.

“And I awoke [Col. 0041B] and understood that I was to fight not against beasts but against the devil; but I knew that victory was imminent for me [Note: [Col. 0041B] ‘would be mine,’ Holstenius]. This is what I recorded up to the day before the spectacle; but as for the account of the spectacle itself, let whoever wishes write it.”

## CHAPTER IV

[Col. 0042A]

**SUMMARY.—St. Saturus, in a vision granted to him, and St. Perpetua are carried by angels into a great light; they see the martyrs; being led to the throne of God, they are received with a kiss; they reconcile Optatus the bishop and Aspasius the presbyter.**

I. Blessed Saturus also made known this vision of his, which he himself wrote down.

“‘We had suffered,’ he says, ‘and had gone out from the flesh; and we began to be carried eastward by four angels, whose hands did not touch us. We did not travel lying on our backs with our faces turned upward, but as though ascending a gentle slope [Note: [Col. 0041B] ‘a clod of earth,’ Compiègne codex]. And being released, we now saw the first immense light [Note: [Col. 0041B] Thus the Salzburg codex. Holstenius: ‘And, freed from the first world, we saw.’ Compiègne: ‘And, being released from the world, we now saw [the immense light] for the first time.’ Formerly: ‘Freed from the first world’]. And I said: “Perpetua”—for she was at my side—“this is what the Lord promised us; we have received the promise” [Col. 0042B].

“‘And while we were being borne by those same four angels, there appeared before us a great open space, which was like a garden, having rose trees [Note: [Col. 0042B] ‘a rose,’ Salzburg] and every kind of flower. [Col. 0043A] [Note: [Col. 0043C]

**Behold, they are here; behold, they are here.** These are the words of those pointing people out with honor, like “This is he,” and similar expressions used when people known by reputation were pointed out by the fingers of those who met them. POSSIN.

**We crossed a stadium along a broad road.** The reading must certainly be “along a broad road,” for in the vision this was adapted to a practice then commonly known. Walkways in gardens and porticoes were customarily measured by stadia. The Glosses of Galen: Σταδιεύς, ὁ σταδίοις ἀναμετρῶν τὸν περίπατον, “a measurer by stadia: one who measures a walkway in stadia.” Hence Vitruvius, book V, chapter 9, speaks of “stadium-porticoes,” where he advises that square or oblong peristyles in wrestling schools be constructed so as to have a circuit of two stadia for walking. HOLST.

**We found Jocundus and Saturninus and Artaxius; a little later, also Quintus.** The restoration of these Acts has only now restored to memory the names of these martyrs. For without them, their names would have remained forever hidden from mortals, known only to God, the βραβευτής καὶ ἀγωνοθέτης, “awarder of the prize and president of the games,” and to the heavenly beings reigning with him. Moreover, it is apparent from this passage that there was then a great and universal persecution of the Christian name. HOLST.—In our Remigian martyrology, the feast of Saturus, Jocundus, and Saturninus is celebrated on March 6. RUINART.

**They were burned alive.** Law 28, *Digest*, *On Punishments*, calls burning alive the supreme punishment. It adds in § 9: “Slaves are generally burned with fire; sometimes also free plebeians and persons of low condition.” Christians were everywhere regarded as such. Hence the people of Smyrna, after demanding a lion for St. Polycarp, subsequently demanded ζῶντα κατακαῦσαι, “that he be burned alive.” Rufinus thus elegantly translated the words of Eusebius. During the Alexandrian persecution under Decius, this burning alive was likewise frequent, as may be seen from the letters of Dionysius in Eusebius, book VI, chapter 34. HOLST.

**Who himself had departed as a martyr in prison.** That is, he had died from the hardships of prison and thus obtained the martyr’s palm without fire or sword. So below, § III, Optatus the bishop and Aspasius the presbyter, still surviving but represented in the vision of Saturus as speaking to Saturus and Perpetua as though they were already dead, say: “Why did you depart and leave us in this condition?” Likewise below, § I: “But God summoned Secundulus from the world while he was still in prison, by an earlier departure.” So too in Eusebius, book V, chapter 1: διῃρεῖτο τὰ μαρτύρια τῆς ἐξόδου αὐτῶν, “They departed through different kinds of martyrdom.” More generally, *to depart* means *to die* in Cyprian, *On Mortality*, in these words: “You fear suffering and are unwilling to depart; what am I to do with you?” HOLST.

**And we had been asking them where they were.** They were certainly not asking this at the moment when they found them; rather, they had asked beforehand and were occupied with that concern when, at the opportune moment, the others appeared, which made the encounter more joyful. POSSIN.

**II.—Like a gray-haired man, having snow-white hair.** From Revelation 1, where it is said of the Lord: “His head and his hair were white as wool or snow.” Hence Cyprian, *On the Dress of Virgins*: “You execrate gray hair and detest whiteness, though it resembles the Lord’s head.” HOLST.

**III.—Aspasius, the presbyter-teacher.** That is, one upon whom the duty of teaching the people rested by virtue of his office. Dionysius of Alexandria in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VII, chapter 24: συγκαλέσας τοὺς πρεσβυτέρους καὶ διδασκάλους τῶν ἐν ταῖς κώμαις ἀδελφῶν, “Having summoned the presbyters and teachers of the brothers who were in the villages.” There is also an excellent passage in Cyprian concerning presbyter-teachers, Epistle XXIV, which Pamelius corrupted by his παραδιόρθωσις, “overcorrection,” on p. 46. Among them he specifically mentions the teacher of the Hearers, or catechumens. For catechumens were called “Hearers” and “Learners.” They had a separate place assigned to them, where they received the elementary teachings of the Christian religion; this was called the κατηχουμενεῖον, the catechumens’ hall. Possidius, in the *Life of St. Augustine*, notes the practice of the African churches, where a presbyter did not have authority to preach and expound the Gospel in church in the presence of the bishop, though this was customary in the Eastern churches. At Alexandria, indeed, there had long been a διδασκαλεῖον τῆς κατηχήσεως, “school of catechetical instruction,” founded by St. Mark, over which the most celebrated ecclesiastical teachers Pantaenus, Clement, and Origen presided. St. Jerome, *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapters 36, 38, and 54. HOLST.]

“‘The height of the trees was like that of cypresses, and their leaves fell [Note: [Col. 0043B] ‘burned,’ Salzburg] without ceasing. There in the garden were four other angels, brighter than the rest. When they [Note: [Col. 0043B] ‘When they saw us there and showed us honor,’ Salzburg codex] saw us, they showed us honor and said to the other angels with wonder: “Behold [Note: [Col. 0043B] “Behold, they are here. In awe and wonder, the four angels who stood there set us down,” Salzburg and [Col. 0043C] Compiègne codices], they are here; behold, they are here.” The four angels who were carrying us were filled with awe and set us down. We crossed a stadium on our own feet along a broad road [Note: [Col. 0043C] “violated,” Holstenius].

“‘There we found Jocundus, Saturninus [Note: [Col. 0043C] Saturninus is absent from the Compiègne and Salzburg codices, but occurs not only in the Monte Cassino codex but also in Mabillon’s excerpts], and Artaxius, who had suffered in the same persecution and were burned alive; and Quintus, who himself had departed as a martyr in prison. We had been asking them [Note: [Col. 0043C] Thus the Salzburg codex. Holstenius and the Compiègne codex: “And we asked concerning them where the others were. The angels said to us”] where the others were. But the angels said to us: “Come first; enter and greet the Lord.”

“II. And we came near a place whose walls seemed to have been constructed from light. Before the entrance to that place stood four angels, who clothed those entering in white robes. We too were clothed and entered, and we saw an immense light and heard [Note: [Col. 0043C] ‘And we entered and heard a voice,’ Holstenius] the united voice of people saying without ceasing: ‘Agios, agios, agios—Holy, holy, holy.’

“And in the middle of that place we saw one seated like a gray-haired man, having snow-white hair [Col. 0044A] and a youthful face; his feet we did not see. On his right and left were twenty-four elders, and behind them stood many others [Note: [Col. 0044B] ‘Four elders, and behind them stood many other elders; and as we entered, we stood in wonder,’ Holstenius]. We entered in great wonder and stood before the throne. Four angels lifted us up, and we kissed him; and with his hand he passed it across our faces [Note: [Col. 0044B] ‘face,’ Holstenius]. The other elders said to us: “Let us stand.” And we stood and exchanged the kiss of peace. The elders said to us: “Go and play.” And I said: “Perpetua, you have what you desire.” She said to me: “Thanks be to God; just as I was joyful in the flesh, so I am even more joyful here now.”

“III. And we went out, and before the doors we saw Optatus the bishop on the right and Aspasius the presbyter-teacher on the left, separated from one another [Col. 0044B] and sorrowful. They threw themselves at our feet and said to us: “Reconcile us, because you departed and left us in this condition” [Note: [Col. 0044C] ‘Left us—to cast yourselves.’ We have restored the text thus, following Holstenius and the Bollandists. Ruinart: ‘You are leaving us—why do you,’ etc. Galland]. We said to them: “Are you not our bishop [Note: [Col. 0044C] ‘Are you not our father?’ Salzburg codex], and are you not a presbyter, that you should cast yourselves at our feet?” And we cast ourselves down [Note: [Col. 0044C] ‘That you should cast yourselves at our feet. And we were moved,’ Holstenius] and embraced them.

“Perpetua began [Note: [Col. 0044C] ‘And Perpetua began to speak with them in Greek,’ Salzburg and Compiègne codices] to speak with them, and we drew them aside into [Note: [Col. 0044C] ‘the garden,’ Holstenius] the garden beneath a rose tree. While we were speaking with them, the angels said [Col. 0045A] [Note: [Col. 0045C]

**And they drove them away.** The expression seems to be used in the sense of “they pushed them away”—that is, removed them to a distance, as though they had advanced beyond what was permissible. For it is added: “And it seemed to us as though they wished to close the gates.” POSSIN.

**Correct your people, etc.** A rebuke of a negligent or erring bishop is not foreign to a vision granted for the benefit of a particular church. Thus certain bishops are rebuked in the Apocalypse. POSSIN.

**As though returning from the circus and contending over their weariness.** So the manuscript; but it should undoubtedly be read, “contending over factions.” This passage signifies that the church of Thuburbo had been divided into parties by the factions and disputes of Optatus the bishop and Aspasius the presbyter. Hence the angels had said to them a little above, § XIII, verse 17: “If you have any disagreements among yourselves, forgive one another.” HOLST.

**CHAPTER V.—I. But God summoned Secundulus from the world while he was still in prison, by an earlier departure.** Cyprian, Epistle VII, concerning one who similarly died beforehand: “Withdrawn by divine favor in the very midst of the torments, he attained glory not through the final completion of his punishment, but through the swiftness of his death.” For, as Seneca says, *Consolation to Marcia*, chapter 20: “Death loosens the chains of captives and leads out of prison those whom powerless authority had forbidden to leave.” HOLST.

**Nevertheless, though not his soul, his flesh certainly knew the sword.** It would seem preferable to read: “Nevertheless, though not his flesh, his soul certainly knew the sword,” etc. By “sword,” evidently, he means the torments and hardships of prison, in accordance with Psalm 104 concerning Joseph: “They humbled his feet in fetters; iron passed through his soul.” And concerning the Blessed Mother of God, Luke 2: “A sword will pass through your own soul.” He means that Secundulus was no less a martyr than the others. For, as Cyprian says in *On Mortality*: “Among the servants of God, in whom confession is contemplated and martyrdom is conceived in the mind, a spirit devoted to the good is crowned by God as judge. It is one thing for the will to be lacking for martyrdom, and another for martyrdom to have been lacking to the will. As the Lord finds you when he calls, so likewise does he judge you. For God seeks not our blood, but our faith.” HOLST.

**II.—Lest she be delayed because of her womb.** Thus Pontius the deacon concerning St. Cyprian: “A man so necessary was delayed from the completion of martyrdom.” HOLST.

**It is not permitted for pregnant women to be presented for punishment.** This was a very ancient Egyptian law: τὴν ἔγκυον, ἂν ἁλῷ θανάτου, μέχρι τέκῃ, φυλάττειν, “If a pregnant woman has been condemned to death, she is to be preserved until she gives birth.” Plutarch reports this in *On the Delays of Divine Vengeance*, where he also records that the Greeks adopted the same law from the Egyptians; Aelian confirms this when, in *Various History*, book V, chapter 18, he relates that it was observed by the Areopagite Council. It must therefore also have been given a place in the collection of Attic laws.

Furthermore, together with other good laws, this law also passed from the Greeks to the Romans. Ulpian, Law 3, *Digest*, *On Punishments*: “The punishment of a pregnant woman condemned to death is deferred until she gives birth. Indeed, I know that it is observed that she is not even subjected to judicial torture so long as she is pregnant.” And Law 18, *Digest*, *On the Status of Persons*, records this rescript of the emperor Hadrian: “A free woman who, while pregnant, has been condemned to the ultimate punishment gives birth to a free child, and it is customary for her to be preserved until she has delivered her offspring.”

Philo, in his book περὶ φιλανθρωπίας, *On Humanity*, testifies that Moses was so far from excluding this most equitable law from his commonwealth that he extended it even to brute animals:

> ἀλλ’ ὅ γε νόμος ἔξω περιῤῥαντηρίων ἐλαύνει καὶ ὅσα τῶν ζώων κυοφορεῖ· μὴ ἐπιτρέπων, ἄχρις ἂν ἀποτέκῃ, σφαγιάζεσθαι, τὰ κατὰ γαστρὸς ἐν ἴσῳ τοῖς ἀποκυηθεῖσι λογιζόμενος.

“The law excludes pregnant animals from the sacred precincts and does not permit them to be slaughtered before they have given birth, regarding the offspring enclosed in the womb in the same way as those already born.”

He then adds:

> συνιέναι δὲ μοι δοκοῦσιν ὁρμηθέντες ἔνιοι τῶν νομοθετῶν καὶ τὸν ἐπὶ κατακρίτοις γυναιξὶν εἰσηγήσασθαι λόγον, ὃς κελεύει τὰς ἐγκυούσας, ἂν ἄξια θανάτου δρῶσι, μὴ θανεῖν, μέχρις ἂν ἀποτέκωσιν· ἵνα μὴ ἀναιρουμένων συναπόληται τὸ κατὰ γαστρός.

“Hence, it seems to me that certain legislators, proceeding from a common understanding, also established the law concerning women condemned to death, which commands that pregnant women, even if they have committed a capital crime, are not to be put to death before they have given birth, lest the offspring in the womb perish together with them when they are executed.”

HOLST. See also Baronius in the notes to the martyrology for March 7. RUINART.]

They said to Optatus: “Correct your people, because they come together before you as though returning from the circus and contending over factions” [Note: [Col. 0045B] ‘over their weariness,’ Holstenius]. And it seemed to us as though they wished to close the gates.
