## CHAPTER V

**SUMMARY.—St. Secundulus dies in prison. St. Felicitas, while pregnant, pours out prayers and gives birth in the eighth month without pain. The unconquered spirit of St. Perpetua and St. Saturus.**

I. These are the more notable visions of the most blessed martyrs Saturus and Perpetua, which they themselves wrote down. But God summoned Secundulus from the world while he was still in prison, by an earlier departure, not without grace, so that he might escape the beasts. Nevertheless, though not his soul, his flesh certainly knew joy [Note: [Col. 0046B] ‘the sword,’ Holstenius].

II. As for Felicitas—for a favor of this kind from the Lord also befell her—she was already eight months pregnant, for she had been pregnant when arrested. As the day of the spectacle drew near, she was in great sorrow [Note: [Col. 0046B] ‘struggle,’ Salzburg], lest she be delayed because of her womb, since it is not permitted for pregnant women to be presented for punishment, and lest later, among certain [Note: [Col. 0046B] ‘other,’ Holstenius] criminals, her holy and innocent blood [Col. 0047A] [Note: [Col. 0047B]

**From the assistants of the *cataractarii*.** *Cataractae* are strong gates suspended by ropes or chains in such a way that they can be lowered and raised as circumstances require. Gates of this kind have remained in widespread use at the entrances of cities and fortresses to repel an enemy incursion, and they are commonly called Saracen gates. Either such gates were once used to guard prisoners—hence καταράκτης is used for “prison” in the Septuagint at Jeremiah 20:2, on which passage see Origen, Homily 18, p. 257—or they were barriers or latticed doors. Because they consisted of wood fitted together in a lattice in the form of a portcullis, they were called *cataractae*, and the doorkeepers of prisons were called *cataractarii*. Their assistants were guards keeping watch at the gate. Libanius, *Oration on the Custody of Prisoners*, calls these men τῆς θύρας κυρίους, “masters of the gate,” and arbiters of access to the prisoners. In Acts 12:6, φύλακες πρὸ τῆς θύρας, “guards stationed before the door,” are mentioned. HOLST.

**Another will be in me who will suffer for me.** Namely, Christ suffering in the martyrs. Thus Christ says to Saul when he was persecuting the Christians: “Why do you persecute me?” Acts 9:4. Thus, when he appeared to Peter as Peter was about to be crucified at Rome, he said: “I am going to be crucified again.” Finally, Eusebius, book V, chapter 1, speaks of the holy deacon whose body, ὅλον τραῦμα καὶ μώλωψ, “one continuous wound and bruise,” had lost its human form, and says: ἐν ᾧ πάσχων Χριστὸς μεγάλας ἐπετέλει δόξας, “in whom the suffering Christ accomplished great and glorious deeds.” I omit similar passages occurring in Cyprian and others. HOLST.

[Col. 0047D] Augustine has an excellent discussion of Felicitas’s premature delivery in Sermon 281 of the new edition, already cited. RUINART.

**III.—We discharge the trust committed to his faith.** As was indicated above, this alludes to those final words of St. Perpetua: “But as for the account of the spectacle itself, let whoever wishes write it.” By these words she delegated to another the responsibility of completing the remainder of the Passion. HOLST.

**When the tribune treated them more severely, etc.** That is, because the tribune only reluctantly allowed food to be brought in, they were fed on daily rations smaller than usual—certainly contrary to custom. For, as Seneca says, Epistle XVIII: “The food of a prison is comparatively unrestricted.” And: “The man who intends to kill those reserved for capital punishment does not feed them so sparingly.” Thus in Tertullian *castigatio victus*, “restriction of diet,” means fasting or more meager food. HOLST.

**On the warnings of utterly foolish men, he feared that they might be removed from prison by incantations, etc.** This is that συκοφαντία μαγείας, “slanderous accusation of magic,” which St. Ignatius, in his *Epistle to the Philippians*, complains was rashly and blasphemously leveled against Christ. Almost all the Acts of the martyrs attest that the persecutors repeatedly leveled the same charge against Christians whenever they accomplished something marvelous beyond human power. HOLST.

**Why, then, do you not permit them to refresh themselves?** That is, to be fed somewhat more generously and abundantly. HOLST.

**Criminals of the Most Noble Caesar.** That is, of Geta, the son of the emperor Severus, on whose birthday, as stated above, they were to fight. The title “Most Noble” was proper to an emperor’s younger sons. See Photius, *Bibliotheca*, p. 187; Leunclavius, *Pandects of Turkish History*, p. 99. Panvinius, in the *Fasti*, pp. 244–245, reports two inscriptions which establish this. The same title appears on a coin of this very Geta in Hulsius, with the figure of *Nobilitas* on the obverse; likewise in Biaeus.

Furthermore, he calls them *noxii*, “criminals,” using the term in the sense of the pagans, who inflicted the extreme penalties appropriate to criminals upon the most innocent class of human beings. Yet we find that, in general, those condemned to death for any cause—even apart from a crime—were called *noxii* when assigned to beast-fights or gladiatorial games. Thus Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 16, calls those hired fighters *noxii* who voluntarily bound themselves over to the gladiatorial trainer for combat with the sword, or freely went to fight the beasts and, as St. Cyprian says, “fought the beasts not from crime but from madness.” Tertullian nevertheless notes that Christians were sometimes distinguished from *noxii* in the persecutors’ own records, truth occasionally escaping from liars.

But to return to the more common usage, the Latin word *noxii* did not always correspond to the Greek κακοῦργοι, “criminals,” but sometimes to ἐπιθανάτιοι, “those destined for death,” indicating persons marked out to die either by gladiatorial weapons or by the teeth of wild beasts. They were called beast-fighters, persons assigned to the games, and slaves of punishment. Hence Tertullian, *On Modesty*, learnedly translates St. Paul’s words in 1 Corinthians 4:9, ἐπιθανατίους ἀπέδειξεν ὡς, as: “He chose us as though we were beast-fighters.” Quintilian, *Declamation* 9, calls them “slaves owed to punishment, who were fed for the games and for certain death.” HOLST.

If we are brought out fatter for the occasion.” Saint Perpetua said this with serene confidence, whereas profane men sometimes acted with reckless confidence, as Apuleius puts it; these are his words in Book IV: “Elsewhere, condemned men, with reckless confidence, furnished banquets for themselves as fattening feed for the beasts,” etc. It was customary for those who had either been sentenced as punishment to gladiatorial combat or beast-fighting, or had voluntarily bound themselves to such contests, first to be fattened by the masters of the training school, so that they might be brought forth fitter and stronger. Saint Cyprian [Col. 0049B], Epistle 2: “The body is filled out into fleshy substance with richer foods, and the robust mass of the limbs grows fat with rolls of grease, so that, fattened for punishment, the man may perish at greater cost.” And Quintilian, *Declamation* 9: “A fattening more grievous than any hunger nourished the devoted body.” HOLST.—In addition to what Holstenius has appropriately noted, this passage may be seen as alluding to the wishes of certain persons who desired to die in the fullness of bodily condition, such as Horace expressed in *Europa*, Ode 27 [Col. 0049C], Book 3:

> Before unsightly wasting seizes  
> My comely cheeks, and the freshness drains  
> From the tender prey, in my beauty I seek  
> To feed the tigers.

pour forth. But her fellow martyrs too were deeply saddened, lest they should leave so good a companion, as it were, alone upon the road of the same hope. Joining, therefore, in a united lament, they poured forth prayer to the Lord three days before the spectacle. Immediately after the prayer, her labor pains seized her. And while she suffered in childbirth because of the natural difficulty of the eighth month, one of the prison guards said to her: “You who suffer so much now—what will you do when you are thrown to the beasts, which you scorned when you refused to sacrifice?” She answered: “Now it is I who suffer what I suffer; but there another will be in me who will suffer for me, because I too am to suffer for him.” Thus she gave birth to a girl, whom one of the sisters took as a daughter and reared.

### III

Since, therefore, the Holy Spirit permitted—and, by permitting, willed—that the order of the spectacle itself should be recorded [Col. 0047B] [Col. 0048A], although we are unworthy to describe anything as a supplement to so great a glory, we nevertheless carry out what was, as it were, the command of the most holy Perpetua—or rather, a trust committed by her faith [Note: [Col. 0047B] For above, at no. X, Saint Perpetua said: “But if anyone wishes to write an account of the spectacle itself, let him do so.”], adding one further testimony to her constancy and nobility of spirit.

When [Note: [Col. 0047B] The Salisbury and Compiègne manuscripts read: “Because the tribune was chastising them and treating them badly, since, owing to warnings...”] they were treated more harshly by the tribune, because, following the warnings of utterly foolish men, he feared that they might be removed from prison by some magical incantations, Perpetua answered him to his face and said: “Why, then, do you not permit us—condemned as we are for the most noble Caesar [Note: [Col. 0048B] The same manuscripts read: “Because we are to fight on his birthday.”], and destined to fight on his birthday—to refresh ourselves? Or is it not to your glory if we are brought out fatter for the occasion?” The tribune was horrified and ashamed; and so he ordered that they be treated more humanely [Note: [Col. 0048B] In the same manuscripts we have restored *optione*; for Holstenius had *manibus hiberi*.], so that her brothers and the others were given the opportunity to enter and refresh themselves with them, by which time even the assistant jailer himself [Note: [Col. 0048B] “Nevertheless,” Holstenius.] had become a believer.

[Col. 0049A] [Note: [Col. 0049C]

### IV.—At the last supper, which they call the “free supper”

Those condemned to the beasts ate an especially sumptuous supper openly on the day before the contest.

“They ate an agape.” We shall not describe what learned men have observed in various places concerning the agapes of the ancient Christians; among others, Albaspinaeus, Book I, Observation 18. The same subject is treated by Chrysostom, Homily 27 on 1 Corinthians 11; Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, chapter 39; Cyprian, *Epistles*, Book III; and the Council of Gangra, canon 11. There were three kinds: birthday, wedding, and funeral agapes; Gregory Nazianzen, *On the Distinctions of Life*. Moreover, this form of expression was also customary for Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, chapter 39: “Thereafter they depart, not into bands of cutthroats, but with the same concern for modesty and chastity, as persons who have partaken not so much of a supper as of discipline.” [Col. 0049D] HOLST.

“Friends today, enemies tomorrow.” Saturus says this to the pagans who were curiously watching the martyrs while they took part in the free supper on the day before the spectacle. He means that those who were then watching peacefully and almost amicably would on the following day demand their death with frenzied shouts. For when the beast-fighters were brought into the arena, the people changed from spectators into adversaries, as Seneca says in Book I of *On Anger*, chapter 2; see him also in *On Tranquillity*, chapter 10. HOLST.

### Chapter VI.—I. “The day of their victory dawned,” etc.

So Pontius the Deacon, who more than once echoes these Acts: “At last another day dawned—that appointed, promised, divine day.” HOLST.

“They came forth from prison.” Thus Pontius concerning Saint Cyprian: “He therefore came forth, now certain that what had long been delayed would be fulfilled: he came forth with a lofty and upright spirit, displaying cheerfulness in his face and courage in his heart.” HOLST.

“Joyful, into the amphitheater as though into heaven.” That is, [Col. 0050B] as Cyprian says on page 166: “Confident of the heavenly reward, the crown of martyrdom, and the kingdom of God.” HOLST.

“Comely in countenance.” Eusebius, Book V, chapter 1, concerning the martyrs of Vienne and Lyons: *οἱ μὲν ἱλαροὶ προσήεσαν, δόξης καὶ χάριτος πολλῆς ταῖς ὄψεσιν αὐτῶν συγκεκραμένης*: “They came forward joyfully, a certain splendor, suffused with abundant grace and beauty, shining in their faces.” Or, as Rufinus translates it: “They were brought forth from their torments rejoicing, displaying something somehow divine in their very countenances.” Conversely, those who had denied Christ were *κατηφεῖς καὶ ταπεινοὶ καὶ δυσειδεῖς, καὶ πάσης ἀσχημοσύνης ἀνάπλεοι*: “Sad, downcast, dreadful even in appearance, and disfigured by every deformity of shame.” HOLST.

“With radiant step.” Thus Xenophon in his *Apology of Socrates*, when Socrates, already condemned to death, was departing from the judges’ presence: *ἀπῄει καὶ ὄμμασι καὶ σχήματι καὶ βαδίσματι φαιδρός*: “He departed radiant in his eyes, bearing, and gait.” HOLST.

“From blood, from the midwife.” Hence Law 2 of the Code, *Concerning Parents Who Sell Their Children*, calls infants “bloodstained.” Juvenal likewise, Satire 7, calls them “still red from their mother.” And Law 1 of the Theodosian Code, *Concerning Exposed Children*: “Still drenched in the blood of the maternal womb, and newly born.” HOLST.

“To be washed in a second baptism.” That is, the baptism of blood and martyrdom. Celerinus the confessor, in Cyprian, Epistle 21: “Unless you have first washed in that holy blood for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.” HOLST.

“They were compelled to put on the costume—the men, indeed, that of the priests of Saturn” [Col. 0050D]. For, as Lactantius says in Book VI, chapter 20, the beast-hunts called *munera*, “spectacles,” were assigned to Saturn. Tertullian, *Scorpiace*, chapter 7, testifies that the Saturn of the Africans was customarily appeased in that age with human victims; he explains this more clearly in the *Apologeticum*, chapter 9, writing thus: “In Africa children were openly sacrificed to Saturn down to the proconsulate of Tiberius.” Condemned persons seem to have been substituted for the children, lest Saturn be deprived of a victim of human blood. Hence the same Tertullian teaches in *On the Testimony of the Soul*, chapter 2, that the priests of the bloodthirsty god wore a scarlet cloak; there, distinguishing the various costumes of pagan priests, he says: “And bound with Ceres’ fillet, and scarleted with Saturn’s cloak, and clad in Isis’ linen,” etc. Then in *On the Pallium*, chapter 4: “The ambition of the broader purple and the superstition of helmeted redness commend Saturn.” HOLST.

“But the women, that of those consecrated to Ceres.” Just as men condemned to the beasts were clothed in the scarlet cloak, which, as has been said, was the distinctive garment of Saturn’s priests [Col. 0051B], so women destined for the same punishment were bound with a fillet. For we have just heard from Tertullian that the priestesses of Ceres were bound with fillets; and he confirms the same in *On the Pallium*, chapter 4: “Why do you not look upon those costumes which falsely claim religion on the basis of their own novelty? For by their entirely white apparel, by the distinguishing fillet, and by the privilege of the cap, they are initiated into the rites of Ceres.” Women thus initiated were called “consecrated to Ceres.” An ancient inscription in Gruter, page CCCIX, nos. 2 and 3, presents Fabia Aconia Paulina as such a woman, consecrated to Ceres and Kore. HOLST.]

### IV

On the preceding day also, when at that last supper which they call the “free supper,” they were, so far as lay in them, eating not a free supper but an agape [Note: [Col. 0049B] “To eat an agape” is a form of expression familiar to Tertullian. Both manuscripts, however, have *adipem*, “fat,” instead of *agapen*.], with the same constancy they hurled these words at the people, threatening them with the Lord’s judgment, bearing witness to the blessedness of their own suffering [Note: [Col. 0049B] “Their sufferings and blessedness,” Salisbury manuscript.], and mocking [Note: [Col. 0049B] “Provoking,” Holstenius.] the curiosity of those who came running together. Saturus said: “Is tomorrow not enough for you, that you gladly gaze upon what you hate? Friends today, enemies tomorrow. But mark our faces carefully [Note: [Col. 0049B] “Your faces,” Salisbury manuscript.], so that you may recognize us on that day of judgment.” Thus they all [Note: [Col. 0049B] “Many,” Salisbury manuscript.] departed from there thunderstruck; and many of them believed.

## CHAPTER VI

**SUMMARY.—**They are led joyfully from prison [Col. 0049B] into the amphitheater, especially Perpetua and Felicitas; they all refuse to put on profane garments; they are scourged; they long [Col. 0050A] for the beasts and are exposed to them; Saturus is twice unharmed; Saints Perpetua and Felicitas are thrown down; they are recalled to the Gate of Life. Saint Saturus, wounded by a leopard, exhorts a soldier; they kiss one another; they are killed by the sword.

### I

The day of their victory dawned, and they came forth from prison into the amphitheater as though into heaven, joyful and comely in countenance—trembling, if at all, with joy, not fear. Perpetua followed with serene [Note: [Col. 0050B] Holstenius, with Rolland: “With serene countenance ... like a matron. With radiant step, like a matron.” And shortly afterward: “Casting down the gaze of all.” Galland.] countenance and measured step, like a matron beloved of Christ God [Note: [Col. 0050B] Holstenius: “With radiant countenance, like a matron of Christ, as God’s cherished one, casting down the gaze of all by the vigor of her eyes.”]: she lowered the vigor of her eyes away from the gaze of all. Likewise Felicitas rejoiced that she had given birth safely, so that she might fight the beasts—passing from blood and the midwife to the net-fighter, to be washed after childbirth in a second baptism.

When they had been brought [Note: [Col. 0050B] “Led,” Holstenius.] [Col. 0050B] to the gate and were compelled to put on costumes—the men, indeed, that of the priests of Saturn, but the women that of those consecrated [Col. 0051A] [Note: [Col. 0051B]

“That noble constancy resisted to the very end.” Tertullian, in *On Idolatry*, chapter 18, teaches, among the other kinds of idolatry, that defiled garments must also be refused by the faithful, since, having been dedicated to idolatry from the beginning, they bear the stain of their profanation. “No one,” [Col. 0051C] he says, “can appear clean in unclean things. If you put on a garment defiled in itself, perhaps it will be possible for it not to be defiled by you; but you cannot be clean through it.” He adds shortly afterward: “If you have renounced the pomp of the devil, know that whatever you touch from it is idolatry.” Likewise: “No garment assigned to an unlawful act is lawful among us.” Cyprian echoed his teacher in the sermon *On the Lapsed*, congratulating confessors on a similar constancy because they had refused similar garments. These are his words: “Your head remained free from the impious and criminal veil with which the captive heads of those sacrificing were veiled there; a forehead pure with the sign of God cannot bear the devil’s crown.” Thus Cyprian. Moreover, the beast-fighters were adorned in these garments to embellish the games with their appearance, being led forth in procession before they were exposed to the beasts. Quintilian, *Declamation* 9: “The bodies of those about to perish, already displayed throughout the arena, had led the procession of their own death.” HOLST.

“We came to this of our own accord.” Thus Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, chapter 49, refutes the pagans who vainly taunted Christians: [Col. 0051D] “As though,” he says, “everything you can do against us were not subject to our own choice. Certainly, if I so choose, I am a Christian. You will therefore condemn me only if I choose to be condemned. Since what you can do to me you cannot do unless I will it, what you can do now belongs to my will, not to your power.” He then explains the manner in which Christians voluntarily offer themselves to torments. “‘Why, then,’ you say, ‘do you complain that we persecute you, if you wish to suffer?’ We certainly wish to suffer, but in the way in which no one willingly suffers war, since trembling and danger are necessarily involved,” etc. HOLST.

“Lest our freedom be obscured.” In an expression customary among Africans, *obducere* means to cloud, obscure, diminish, violate, or injure. Tertullian often uses it thus, as in the *Apologeticum*, chapter 50: “But we are obscured; surely this is when we have prevailed. Therefore we live when we are killed; in short, we escape when we are obscured,” etc. See Rigaltius in the *Glossary of Tertullian*. HOLST.

“We have bound our lives over.” Perhaps one should read *addiximus*, “we have bound over,” rather than *adduximus*, “we have brought”—that is, we have subjected them to capital judgment. [Col. 0052B] Valerius Maximus, Book VII, chapter 6: “Even of those bound over and condemned on a capital charge,” etc. Similar expressions occur everywhere. I have said “perhaps,” because the received reading can be defended with sufficient probability by taking the verb *adducere*, “to bring forward,” in the sense of “to offer,” which the Greeks express by *προσάγειν* (*prosagein*). HOLST.

“The people, enraged.” Seneca, Book I of *On Anger*, chapter 2: “What of gladiators? Why are the people angry with them, and so unjustly that they regard it as an injury when they do not die willingly? They think themselves despised, and by their expression, gestures, and ardor they are transformed from spectators into adversaries.” HOLST.

“That they be tormented with scourges.” By the governor, that is, who could summarily inflict punishment with rods or scourges. Digest, Book IX, §3, *Concerning the Duties of a Proconsul*. HOLST.

“Before the line of beast-fighters.” That is, by the beast-fighters who stood ready equipped with scourges. Hence Tertullian, *To the Martyrs*: [Col. 0052C] “Others have walked between the hunters’ oxhide lashes with shoulders most enduring.” The same, Book I of *To the Nations*: “If a woman has exulted beneath the lashes, she too, after lately traversing the line among the beast-fighters, has measured out this path.” This passage from our Acts, the two passages we have adduced from Tertullian, and this entire *διαμαστίγωσις* (*diamastigōsis*), or scourging in the arena—which has hitherto not been adequately explained—are splendidly illuminated by a truly remarkable passage in Eusebius, Book V, chapter 1: *ὑπέφερον πάλιν τὰς διεξόδους τῶν μαστίγων τὰς ἐκεῖσε εἰθισμένας*: “They again passed through the line of scourges customary there.” Or: “According to custom, they again underwent scourging before the line of beast-fighters.” Here you see that “before the line” means “in front of the line,” or “while passing along the line,” etc. They plainly stood arranged in a long line with scourges; the naked beast-fighters were compelled to walk before them, each man striking the sufferers’ naked limbs with the oxhide lash he held in his hand. I think Damasus had this form of punishment in view in poem 5 on Saint Agatha, when he said: “Thereafter, more joyful and more ardent, she exultantly ran through all the scourges.”

Furthermore, it could easily have happened that, as we have said, the raging people demanded this scourging from the governor, since he presided over the spectacle. For, as Lipsius teaches in *On the Amphitheater*, page 15, the president of the spectacle watched from the podium—that is, from the first or lowest row of seats, where his tribunal or platform stood, as Lipsius likewise observes on page 27, at no great distance from the arena. HOLST.

“They rejoiced that they had obtained some share in the Lord’s sufferings,” etc. Namely, because they remembered that Christ had been scourged, they received the scourges with joy. Thus Dionysius of Alexandria, in Eusebius, Book VI, chapter 34, says that the martyr Nemesius, who was burned with robbers, was honored by a likeness to Christ’s Passion. Many similar passages occur in Tertullian and others. HOLST.

### II.—“So that, namely, he might wear a more glorious crown”

For, as Tertullian says: “Greater contests are followed by greater rewards.” Hence, addressing the pagans shortly afterward, he says: “Your cruelty is our glory.” HOLST.

“They were harried by a bear.” Here you have bears in Africa, something that Pliny long ago, and Lipsius quite recently, denied. But since Pliny himself mentions Numidian bears from the Consular Annals, Virgil recalls a Libystian she-bear, and Martial and Juvenal likewise speak of Libyan bears, Salmasius rightly and deservedly rejects the opinion of both men in his *Plinian Exercises*, page 311. I confess that their opinion cannot be refuted from this passage of ours alone. Bears could have been brought into Africa from elsewhere, just as lions, panthers, and elephants were brought to Rome for use in the theater.

A passage from Seneca, Book III of *On Anger*, chapter 43, may be pertinent here: “We are accustomed to laugh, among the morning spectacles of the arena, at a bull and a bear fastened together in combat; after one has harried the other, its own slayer awaits it.” Likewise this passage from Arnobius, Book VII: “It is customary to throw food to wild beasts, lest they break apart the bars of their cages, so that they may rage madly against it and divert their desire to maul.” In both passages you see the verb “to harry” or “maul” adapted to encounters in the arena. HOLST.]

to Ceres—their noble constancy resisted to the very end. For Perpetua said: “We came to this of our own accord precisely so that our freedom might not be obscured. We bound our lives over [Note: [Col. 0051A] We have restored this from the Salisbury manuscript, as Holstenius had conjectured. Formerly: “We brought our lives.”] precisely so that we might do no such thing. This was our agreement with you.”

Injustice acknowledged justice: the tribune granted that they should be brought in simply as they were. Perpetua sang psalms, already treading upon the Egyptian’s head. Revocatus, Saturninus, and Saturus threatened the watching people concerning this. When they came within Hilarianus’ sight, they began to say to him by gesture and nod: “You judge us,” they said, “but God will judge you.” At this [Col. 0052A] the people, enraged, demanded that they be tormented with scourges before the line [Note: [Col. 0051A] The beast-fighters stood arranged in a line with scourges; the condemned were compelled to pass before them and, as they passed, were beaten by each in turn [Col. 0051B].] of the beast-fighters. And they indeed rejoiced that they had obtained some share in [Note: [Col. 0052A] For the Lord too was beaten with scourges.] the Lord’s sufferings.

### II

But he who had said, “Ask, and you shall receive” (John 16:24), granted those who asked the end that each had desired. For whenever they conversed among themselves about the form they wished their martyrdom to take, Saturninus declared that he wished to be exposed to every beast, so that he might, of course, wear a more glorious crown. Accordingly, during the opening encounter of the spectacle, he and [Note: [Col. 0052A] We have excellently restored this passage from the Compiègne manuscript, which elsewhere is exceedingly corrupt, as anyone making the comparison will see. For nothing was recorded concerning Saturninus’ suffering because of the omission of the words [Col. 0052B] “he and,” while the rest was expressed in the singular.] Revocatus experienced the leopard and were also harried by a bear upon the platform.

Saturus [Col. 0053A] [Note: [Col. 0053C]

“When he had been bound fast for the bear.” And a little above: “He had fastened him to the boar,” etc. These words signify that the beast-fighters were customarily tied up so that they could not flee before the sight of the wild beasts that were to be sent against them. But the beasts themselves were also sometimes tied to one another, as is taught not only by the testimony of Seneca already quoted but also by Claudian in his *Panegyric on Manlius*:

> Let her herself choose daring men who know  
> How artfully to bind the beasts’ necks  
> And drive the hunting spears with unerring force.

Xiphilinus also records that, at the emperor Commodus’ command, gladiators were bound together because the emperor was indignant that they did not rush eagerly and courageously enough into mutual slaughter; he therefore ordered them tied together so that they would kill one another. In a not dissimilar manner of speaking [Col. 0053D], Saint Ignatius the Martyr, when he was being led in chains to Rome by ten soldiers savage with bestial fury, writes that he was “bound to ten leopards.” Gregory of Tours likewise, Book I of *Miracles*, chapter 48, relates that Saint Saturninus the Martyr, “tied to the feet of a raging bull, was hurled down the steps of the Capitol,” etc. HOLST.

“The bear would not come out of the cage,” etc. There were, of course, various cages for keeping wild beasts around the arena, and the beasts were released from them. See Lipsius, *On the Amphitheater*, page 20. Since a bridge was mentioned a little before, this appears to have been done under an arrangement instituted by Commodus, whereby there were bridges in the amphitheater. For Xiphilinus, in his life of Commodus, page 382, relates that this emperor constructed bridges across the arena of the amphitheater so that he might kill beasts from them. HOLST.

### III.—“A most ferocious cow”

Digest, Law 1, § “Beasts,” *Concerning Posthumous Children*: “We must understand ‘beasts’ more from their ferocity than from the species of the animal.” HOLST.

“The devil emulated their sex even in the choice of beast.” Tertullian uses a not dissimilar form of expression in *On Patience*, chapter 16: [Col. 0054B] “So that in this matter too the devil might emulate the Lord.” HOLST.

“Clothed in nets.” Thus Saint Blandina, after various kinds of torture, *εἰς γύργαθον βληθεῖσα ταύρῳ παρεβλήθη*: “Was cast into a net and exposed to a bull.” Rufinus, in his edition, noted the same as a novel and unusual punishment: “Then,” he says, “another kind of cruelty was devised: that, bound in a net, she should be exposed to a fiercely goaded bull. Although she was battered by its innumerable blows and tossed around the entire circuit of the arena, she suffered no harm.” HOLST.

“Mindful more of modesty than of pain.” Tertullian, in *On Modesty*, chapter 1, calls chastity “the foremost discipline of the Christian name,” which, he says, “the world itself bears witness to this extent: whenever it strives to punish chastity in our women, it does so by defilements of the flesh rather than by torments, wishing to take from them what they value above life.” [Col. 0054C] See his *Apologeticum*, chapter 50; Victor of Vita concerning Dionysia; and Saint Hilary, page 289.

Generally speaking, this is a feeling of nature, expressed by Clement of Alexandria, *Paedagogus*, Book II, chapter 10, in these words: *οὐδὲν μέρος ὁτιοῦν ἀπογυμνοῦσθαι γυναικὸς, ευπρεπέστι*: “It is the height of indecency for any part whatever of a woman’s body to be uncovered.” Natural modesty always recoiled from this even among pagan women. Hence Euripides’ words about Polyxena as she was dying, in *Hecuba*, page 51:

> *Ἣ δὲ καί θνήσκουσ᾽ ὅμως*  
> *Πολλὴν πρόνοιαν εἶχεν εὐσχήμως πεσεῖν,*  
> *Κρύπτειν θ᾽ ἃ κρύπτειν ὄμματ᾽ ἀρσένων χρεών.*
>
> Yet even as she died,  
> She took great care to fall with dignity  
> And cover what ought to be concealed from men’s eyes.

Ovid transferred this to Lucretia in *Fasti* II:

> [Col. 0054D] Even then, already dying, she takes care  
> Not to fall indecorously: this concern  
> Remained with her even as she fell.

Thus, according to Pliny, Book IV, Epistle 11, when Cornelia Maximilla, a Vestal condemned for unchastity, “was being lowered into the underground chamber, and her robe caught as she descended, she turned and rearranged it; and when the executioner offered her his hand, she recoiled and drew back, rejecting the foul contact, as though by a final act of holiness, from an utterly chaste and pure body”—observing modesty in every detail: *πολλὴν πρόνοιαν εἶχεν εὐσχήμως πεσεῖν*, “she took great care to fall with dignity.”

As for the manner of speaking in this passage, a parallel occurs in Tertullian, *On Repentance*, chapter 10, concerning those who defer repentance from day to day: “Mindful more of shame than of salvation.” HOLST.

“Then she was recovered.” That is, after she had sustained the charge of the raging cow and had, as it were, already fought out her contest, she was recovered by the beast-fighters and arena attendants—or, as Eusebius says, *ἐκ θηρίων αὖθις ἀναληφθεῖσα*: “taken up again from among the beasts.” HOLST.]

detested nothing more than a bear; but he was already confident that he would be killed by a single bite from a leopard. Accordingly, when a boar was supplied, the beast-fighter who had supplied [Note: [Col. 0053B] “Had fastened him to,” Holstenius.] that boar was instead gored by the same beast and died after the days of the spectacle. Saturus alone was merely dragged about. And when he had been bound fast for the bear upon the bridge, the bear refused to come out of the cage [Note: [Col. 0053B] In both manuscripts: “Pudens the soldier, deliberately asserting that the gates of the enraged beasts were rotten with flesh, instead contrived that it should not be sent out; thus for the second time,” etc.—an uncertain and corrupt reading.]. And so Saturus was recalled unharmed for the second time.

### III

For the young women, however, the devil prepared a most ferocious cow, procured for this very reason contrary to custom [Note: [Col. 0054B] “Prepared,” Holstenius.], emulating their sex even in the choice of beast. And so, stripped and clothed in nets [Note: [Col. 0054B] Both manuscripts read: “Stripped, they were brought forward.”], they were brought out. The people recoiled in horror, seeing that one was a delicate young woman [Col. 0054A], while the other had recently given birth and milk was dripping from her breasts. And so they were recalled [Note: [Col. 0054B] “Recalled and clothed in unbelted garments,” Holstenius.] and their clothing was loosened.

Perpetua was brought in first. She was tossed and fell upon her loins; and when she saw [Note: [Col. 0054B] “When she sat,” Holstenius.] that her tunic had been torn along the side, she drew it over to cover her thighs, mindful more of modesty than of pain. Then, after being recovered, she pinned up her scattered hair; for it was not fitting that a martyr should suffer with disheveled hair, lest she seem to mourn in the hour of her glory.

Thus she rose; and when she saw that Felicitas had been crushed to the ground, she went to her, offered her hand, and raised her up. The two stood together; and once the people’s hardness had been overcome, they were recalled to the Gate of Life. There Perpetua was received by a certain man named Rusticus, then a catechumen, [Col. 0055A] [Note: [Col. 0055B]

“As though awakened from sleep.” Thus Eusebius concerning the martyr Biblias: *ἡ δ᾽ ὥσπερ ἐξανανήψασα*: “But she, as though coming back to herself.” HOLST.

“So deeply had she been in the Spirit and in ecstasy.” As though to say: [Col. 0055C] she had been so completely raised and carried beyond the use of her senses; for this is what is called being “in the Spirit.” Saint John, Revelation, chapter 4: “And immediately I was in the Spirit.” HOLST.

### IV.—“The soldier Pudens”

In Holstenius the name of Pudens is not expressed. I think, however, that this is the man who acted humanely toward the martyrs above. A martyr Pudens is commemorated on 29 April in the ancient Carthaginian Calendar. Is it this man? Or the senator Pudens whom Paul mentions in 2 Timothy 4? Or, finally, the Alexandrian martyr whom the Bollandists discuss on this day? RUINART.

“Washed and saved.” This was an acclamation of the people wantonly mocking Christian rites. For since it was commonly known that Christians believed people were saved through baptism, the people watching from the theater proclaimed the Christian drenched in blood to be “saved” because he had thus been “washed.” POSSIN.

“Leaving him the inheritance of a pledge and a memorial of blood.” Why, then, do our adversaries complain that we devoutly preserve the relics of the saints? Surely that ring stained with a martyr’s blood was not to be thrown away. RUINART.

“To the customary place for execution.” He means the stripping-room, where those whom the arena had released still half-alive were killed. Seneca teaches this in Epistle 94: “Do you suppose anyone to be so foolishly desirous of life that he would rather be killed in the stripping-room than in the arena?” Thus Lampridius writes that after Commodus’ death the acclamation was made: “Let the enemy of the fatherland, the parricide, the gladiator, be torn apart in the stripping-room.” HOLST.—There novice combatants killed the condemned so that they might become accustomed to fighting; hence this young man is said to have stabbed Saint Perpetua. RUINART.

“When the people demanded that they be brought into the center.” Thus Rufinus, Book VIII of the *Ecclesiastical History*, concerning Attalus and Alexander: “But when none of the beasts had touched the bodies of the saints, after torturing them with every punishment of blows and other penalties, he finally ordered them to be killed in the middle of the arena, in the people’s sight.” Moreover, “to demand” is a term proper to the amphitheater. Hence Tertullian’s “demanders of Christians,” *Apologeticum*, chapter 25. HOLST.

“To make their eyes accomplices in the homicide.” Saint Cyprian, Epistle 2: [Col. 0056C] “A gladiatorial spectacle is prepared so that blood may delight the lust of cruel eyes.” And shortly afterward: “At such impious spectacles, so dreadful and deadly, they do not consider themselves parricides with their eyes.” Seneca inveighs against this cruelty in more than one passage, Epistle 7: “In the morning men are thrown to lions and bears; at midday, to their spectators,” etc. Likewise Epistle 87. And Lactantius, *Divine Institutes*, Book VI, chapter 2, most eloquently of all. HOLST.

“Through the solemn rite of peace,” etc. In an ancient glossary, “the solemn rites of peace” are glossed *εὐσέβεια* (“piety”) and *osculum* (“kiss”). Paulinus calls it “the kiss of holy peace.” They were rightly prepared for martyrdom by this symbol of peace. Eusebius, in the passage cited several times: *εἰρήνην ἀγαπήσαντες αὐτοὶ, καὶ εἰρήνην ἡμῖν παρεγγυήσαντες, μετ᾽ εἰρήνης ἐχώρησαν πρὸς Θεόν*: “Having themselves loved peace and enjoined peace upon us, they departed in peace to God.” Rufinus translates it thus: “Above all, they themselves loved peace and commanded us to preserve it; nor did they prepare any road to martyrdom for themselves except through peace.” Hence perhaps Tertullian, *On Patience*, chapter 12, calls love “the supreme sacrament of faith and the treasure of the Christian name.” HOLST.

[Col. 0056D] “Might consummate.” A term proper to completed martyrdom. Thus Tertullian, *On Patience*, chapter 15: “Patience consummates martyrdom.” And Cyprian, Epistle 3, calls martyrdom “consummation.” In Epistle 5 he commands confessors to be humble, modest, and peaceful, “so that, pleasing the Lord in all things, they may through their consummation attain the heavenly crown of praise.” The Latin *consummare* corresponds to the Greek *τελειοῦσθαι* (*teleiousthai*, “to be perfected”), which authors in that language commonly use when recounting martyrdoms. HOLST.

“A novice gladiator.” A man destined to be a victim in the arena laid the foundations of his apprenticeship in the stripping-room so that he might become accustomed to killing. There he cut the throats of beast-fighters whose lives the savagery of the beasts had not taken, so that, trained by dispatching half-dead and unarmed men, he might be brought out for proper contests. Quintilian, *Declamation* 9, calls him “the bloodstained dispatcher”; this was indeed so distinctive a name for that office that the Smyrnaeans, in Eusebius, Book IV, chapter 14, retain it in the account of Saint Polycarp’s martyrdom. HOLST.]

who remained close beside her. As though awakened from sleep—so deeply had she been in the Spirit and in ecstasy—she began to look around and said, to everyone’s astonishment: “When,” she asked, “are we being brought out to that cow? I do not know [Note: [Col. 0055B] The manuscripts read: “To what cow? Where was she,” Augustine asks in the cited Sermon 280, “when she did not perceive herself fighting that most savage cow?” etc.].” When she heard what had already happened, she did not believe it until she recognized certain marks of the mauling on her body and clothing, and saw the catechumen [Note: [Col. 0055B] The words “and saw the catechumen” are absent from the manuscripts.].

Then she summoned her brother and the catechumen and addressed them, saying: “Stand firm in the faith, and all of you love one another; and do not be scandalized by our sufferings.”

### IV

At another gate Saturus was exhorting the soldier [Note: [Col. 0055B] In Holstenius the name of Pudens is not expressed.] Pudens, saying: “Here I am [Note: [Col. 0056B] “At the summit,” Holstenius.], just as I promised and foretold; up to this point I have felt no beast. And now believe with your whole heart. See, I am going out there, and I shall be consummated by a single bite from the leopard.”

Immediately, at [Col. 0055B] the end of the spectacle, he was exposed to the leopard and was so drenched with blood from one bite that, as he was brought back, the people shouted after him in testimony to a second baptism: “Washed and saved! [Col. 0056A] Washed and saved!” Plainly he who had shone forth in this spectacle was indeed saved [Note: [Col. 0056B] “Had just washed,” Holstenius.].

Then he said to the soldier Pudens: “Farewell, and remember my faith. Do not let these things disturb you, but let them strengthen you.” At the same time he asked for the loop [Note: [Col. 0056B] “Ring,” Salisbury manuscript.] from his finger, dipped it into his wound, and returned it to him, leaving him the inheritance of a pledge and a memorial of blood [Note: [Col. 0056B] The Salisbury manuscript has: “He returned it to him as a blessed inheritance, leaving him a pledge and a memorial of such great blood.”].

Then, already unconscious, he was laid down with the others in the customary place for execution. And when the people demanded that they be brought into the center, so that, as the sword penetrated their bodies, they might add their eyes as accomplices in the homicide, they rose of their own accord and moved to the place the people desired. First, however, they kissed one another, so that they might consummate their martyrdom through the solemn rite of peace.

The others received the sword motionless and in silence—Saturus much more so, for, as he had been the first to ascend the ladder [Col. 0056B], he was the first to surrender his spirit; for he was also waiting for Perpetua. But Perpetua, so that she might taste something of pain, was pierced between the ribs [Note: [Col. 0056B] “Her bones pierced,” Holstenius.] and cried aloud; then she herself [apparently directed] the novice gladiator’s wavering right hand toward [Col. 0057A] [Note: [Col. 0057A]

“She herself toward her throat” [lemma fragment]. Gladiators did in fury and rage what Saint Perpetua did devoutly and nobly under divine inspiration. Seneca, Epistle 30: “Thus a gladiator, though exceedingly timid throughout the entire fight, offers his throat to his opponent and adjusts the wandering sword to himself.” [Col. 0057B] See the same author, *On Tranquillity*, chapter 10. Moreover, concerning holy women who either killed themselves or cooperated in their own deaths by divine inspiration, and whose memory the Church celebrates, see Saint Thomas, *Summa Theologiae*, II–II, question 59, article 3, reply to objection 2; question 64, article 5; and question 124, articles 1–2, etc. HOLST.]

Amen. Here, at the end, the subject itself and the just expectation of the learned reader demand that we add something concerning the date of this most celebrated martyrdom. I understand from various notes of the most learned Holstenius that he investigated the matter at great length; nowhere, however, do I find that he definitively determined what conclusion he judged should be followed. After carefully considering everything, it seems to me that one may plausibly affirm that the date of the contest of these Thuburbitan martyrs should be fixed in the year of Christ 203. For these very Acts, which are now appearing for the first time, teach us that they fought in the arena on Geta Caesar’s birthday. This is stated most explicitly [Col. 0057C] in chapters II.3–4 and V.3 of our edition.

Geta was the younger son of the emperor Severus. Herodian, Book III, in agreement with Spartian and Xiphilinus’ excerpts from Dio, relates that Severus, while still alive, declared Geta and his elder brother Antoninus Caracalla joint participants in the imperial power. The most exact Petavius assigns this event to the seventh year of Severus’s reign, while aptly warning that the same honor was not conferred upon both brothers. The prerogative of age was preserved for the elder, who was made entirely equal to his father in the title and dignity of Augustus; whereas the younger brother Geta—then still only ten years old, since he is said to have been born in the consulship of the Silani—received only a share and merely the second rank of supreme dignity, with the appellation Caesar, as Spartian teaches more distinctly.

This distinction between the brothers remained until the twelfth year of Severus’s reign, which was the year of Christ 204, when Petavius observes from Zosimus and Censorinus that the Secular Games were celebrated at Rome. That in this year the name Augustus [Col. 0057D] was also bestowed upon Geta—Severus the father thinking, among the many other measures which Herodian records him as attempting to reconcile the perpetually discordant brothers, that this equalization in supreme power should also be tried—is securely confirmed by Scaliger, *Annotations on Eusebius*, p. 29, both from other distinguished testimonies and from this inscription on an ancient coin:

> IMP. CAES. P. SEPT. GETA. PIUS. AUG. SAECULARIA SACRA. S. C.  
> Emperor Caesar Publius Septimius Geta Pius Augustus. The Secular Rites. By Decree of the Senate.

Since, therefore, the holy martyr wrote in chapter V.3—with a credibility that everyone ought to regard as inviolable—that she had been destined for the arena in celebration of the birthday of Geta, who was still *Most Noble*, still Caesar, and not yet Augustus, we have the limits beyond which conjecture cannot wander in investigating the year of her death: precisely those which reliable history defines for us as the period during which Geta occupied the second rank of supreme authority. This period amounts [Col. 0058A] to exactly four years, namely from AD 199 to 203; for in the following year, 204, the year of the Secular Games, Geta was already Augustus, as we have seen.

But lest we should be free to select any one of the first three [Col. 0058B] years of this period for the martyrdom of the saints, we are restricted by the date assigned by the most exact chronologists to the persecution initiated against the Christians by that emperor: Severus’s tenth year, AD 202. The *Roman Martyrology* and these same Acts demonstrate that the passion of Saints Perpetua and Felicity occurred after this persecution had begun, since in chapter IV.1 they expressly recall that the persecution had already been proclaimed and put into effect—a general persecution, certainly, and one commanded by the Augusti—in which Jocundus, Saturninus, and Artaxius had already earned the palm through being burned alive.

I see that one might oppose to this the authority of most learned men: Pamelius, in his notes on Tertullian’s *To Scapula*; Petavius, in his *Doctrine of Times* and in his *Chronicle* at the year of Christ 201; and finally Philip Labbe, in his work *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under Tertullian. They judge that Tertullian’s book *To Scapula* was written before Severus proclaimed the persecution. From this it follows that the prefecture of Hilarianus, under whom Saints Perpetua and Felicity suffered, must be carried back to a considerably earlier [Col. 0058C] date, namely AD 195 or even earlier. But then those holy martyrs could not have fought in the arena on the birthday of Geta Caesar, as these Acts testify that they did, since, as has been said—and as Petavius himself also holds—Geta was declared Caesar in the seventh year of his father Severus, which was AD 199.

I therefore find it credible that, if those most learned men had been able to see these Acts, which are now being published for the first time, they would never have assigned the composition of Tertullian’s *To Scapula* to AD 199 or 201, before Severus issued his edict against the Christians. For in that book Tertullian indicates that Hilarianus—under whom Saint Perpetua writes in chapter II.2 that she suffered, when the persecution had already been raging—preceded Scapula in the prefecture by an interval of at least several years. These are the holy martyr’s words: “The procurator Hilarianus, who had then received the power of the sword in place of the deceased proconsul Minucius Timinianus,” etc.

What other Hilarianus can we imagine here than the one whom Tertullian mentions when addressing Scapula [Col. 0058D] in these words?

> Just as under the governor Hilarianus, when they had shouted concerning the areas of our burial grounds, “Let there be no areas,” their own threshing floors were no more—for they did not gather in their harvests.

What he immediately adds concerning the rain of the preceding year plainly shows that Hilarianus’s prefecture was earlier than the time of Scapula by more than one or two years. Indeed, it is likely that the African prefects whom Tertullian mentions a little later in the same book—Cincius Severus, Vespronius Candidus, Asper, and Pudens—were, either all or most of them, successors of Hilarianus and predecessors of Scapula.

Anyone who carefully considers these points will be compelled to admit that the book *To Scapula* was by no means written before the beginning of the persecution proclaimed by Severus. Indeed, there are arguments suggesting that the book was written after Severus’s death. This is intimated by the manner in which Severus is spoken of whenever he is mentioned there, which is precisely the manner ordinarily used not of present events, but of matters recalled from an earlier period.

Not content with this, Joseph Scaliger, on p. 110 [Col. 0059A] of his *Annotations on Eusebius*, places Scapula’s prefecture—or at least the composition of the little work by Tertullian with which we are concerned—even after the death of Antoninus, Severus’s son. His conjecture, in my judgment, is by no means contemptible. It is drawn from the words of the same book, where, after naming a certain Christian who was dear to the emperor Severus and retained in the palace until Severus’s death, Tertullian adds:

> Antoninus also knew him very well, having been reared on Christian milk.

Scaliger thinks that no person of sound mind could believe that Tertullian wrote these words while Antoninus Caracalla was still alive.

But why do we struggle with slender subtleties extracted from a single word, when testimony clearer than the noonday sun and irrefragably marked by the heavens is available? In that very same book of Tertullian *To Scapula*, these words are found:

> For that sun also, in the assembly at Utica, was so nearly extinguished in its light and was so great a portent that it could not have suffered this through an ordinary eclipse, being situated [Col. 0059B] in its own *hypsoma* and house. You have astrologers.

These words indicate a great solar eclipse that was witnessed at Utica with public terror some time before Tertullian wrote them. The first—and, so far as I know, the only—man to calculate this eclipse was the most learned Antonius Lalovera of our Society, in an unpublished letter to Joannes Bessonus, likewise of our Society. I shall therefore transcribe his calculations here:

> In the year of Christ 210, on the eleventh day of April, there was an eclipsing new moon at Utica in Africa, at 11 hours, 57 minutes, and 14 seconds after midnight. This was the midpoint of the eclipse:
>
> Beginning: 10 hours, 44 minutes, 44 seconds. Time of immersion: 1 hour, 12 minutes, 30 seconds. End: 1 hour, 12 minutes, 1 second after midday. Time of emergence: 1 hour, 14 minutes, 47 seconds. Duration of the entire eclipse: 2 hours, 27 minutes, 13 seconds. Magnitude: 8 digits, 57 minutes, 30 seconds.

The “house of the sun” mentioned by Tertullian should not here be understood as the sign of Leo, but according to the method of the horoscope, as the portion or cusp [Col. 0059C] of the sign Aries, which the sun then occupied, touching the ecliptic. For, as Jovianus Pontanus observes in Book II of *Celestial Matters*, chapter 4, p. 75, and chapter 5, p. 79, such a place in any *dodecatemorion*—that is, any zodiacal sign—is the sun’s proper house and is often called by the ancients “the place of the sun,” or “of the god.”

At that time the sun was also in its own *hypsoma*, or exaltation, for this is the name that certain astrologers give to the sign Aries. Although—and Lalovera inclines still more strongly to this explanation—it can readily be understood that by the sun’s *hypsoma* Tertullian intended to indicate nothing other than the vertical altitude [Col. 0060A] of the sun as it culminated at midday, when it underwent that eclipse. If Tertullian seems to have denied that this could occur naturally, he erred in accordance with common opinion, with no serious fault, since the art was foreign to his studies and profession. Indeed, he himself appears to intimate as much by immediately referring the reader to astrologers, who concern themselves with such matters. In truth, nothing in the event lay beyond the ordinary course of nature.

Thus far the calculation of this eclipse. From it the point that we have long been striving to establish is manifestly demonstrated: Tertullian’s *To Scapula* was written long after AD 202, Severus’s tenth year, since it recounts a solar eclipse that occurred in AD 210, Severus’s eighteenth and final year, and recounts it in such a manner that it appears to have taken place several years earlier.

This is the place to present a conjecture of the most illustrious Holstenius concerning the date when the book *To Scapula* was written, which I found noted somewhere. After reporting Scaliger’s opinion [Col. 0060B] that it was written under Elagabalus, he says that he himself thinks it was written under Macrinus, since Sulpicius Severus testifies that the clergy were persecuted by Macrinus.

However this matter may stand, from what has thus far been said we seem entitled to draw the following conclusion concerning the subject in hand: we judge with sufficient probability that the martyrdom whose original Acts we now publish occurred in AD 203, when Lucius Septimius Geta Caesar and Lucius Septimius Plautianus were consuls. The fact that Geta Caesar was consul in that year seems to have been the reason why his birthday was honored with gladiatorial games and spectacles in the arena. Our chronology is therefore confirmed by this very indication of Geta’s consulship.

Baronius also agrees with it, relating at length that the holy martyrs Perpetua and Felicity suffered under the same consuls and in the same year of Severus, at no. XXI and following under the year 205. He reckons in this way because of his customary addition of two years, which he subsequently brings into agreement with the common computation by subtracting two years from the reign of the emperor Probus, as all learned chronologists have long observed: [Col. 0060C] Scaliger, Decker, Petavius, Bucherius, Bollandus, Henschenius, Philip Labbe, and others.

Accordingly, by every class of argument—namely, the authorities of weighty writers, reasons drawn from the matter itself, and finally celestial indications—the position we have proposed concerning the date of the triumph of the holy Thuburbitan martyrs Perpetua and Felicity remains confirmed with every degree of certainty: on the Nones of March, AD 203, they attained the palm of immortal glory.

Peter POSSINUS, of the Society of Jesus.]

She presented her own throat [Note: [Col. 0057A] Holstenius translated this.]. Perhaps so great a woman could not otherwise have been killed, because she was feared by the unclean spirit, unless she herself had willed it.

O most valiant and most blessed martyrs! O you who were truly called and chosen for the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ! Whoever magnifies, honors, and adores that glory ought surely to read these examples too, no less than the ancient ones, for the edification of the Church, [Col. 0058A] so that these new deeds of power may also testify that the one and the same Holy Spirit continues to work even to the present day, and may bear witness to almighty God the Father and his Son Jesus Christ our Lord, to whom belong splendor and immeasurable power for ever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0059]

## INDEX OF THE CHAPTERS OF THE PASSION OF THE HOLY MARTYRS PERPETUA AND FELICITY

[Col. 0059D]

**PREFACE.** New events are to be written down, since they will be ancient for posterity. cols. 13–14

**CHAPTER I.** The holy martyrs are arrested; among them is Perpetua, who committed the events to writing. Saint Perpetua prevails over her father and is baptized with the others. She is thrust into prison. Anxious about her infant, she understands from a vision granted to her—of a ladder raised to heaven, of Saint Saturus’s ascent and her own, and of a morsel offered to her—that martyrdom will soon come. col. 16

**CHAPTER II.** She is again assailed by her father and strengthens him. Led with the others before the tribunal, she professes herself a Christian. She is condemned with the rest to the beasts. She prays for her deceased brother Dinocrates, whom she understands from a vision to be suffering the pains of purgatory and to be delivered from them. col. 29

**CHAPTER III.** Perpetua is again assailed by her father. Her third vision: in it she is led away to wrestle against an Egyptian. A prize is set before her; she fights, conquers, and carries off the prize. col. 38

[Col. 0060D]

**CHAPTER IV.** In a vision granted to Saint Saturus and Saint Perpetua, they are carried by angels into the light and see the martyrs. Led to the throne of God, they are received with a kiss. They reconcile the dissenting bishop Optatus and presbyter Aspasius. col. 42

**CHAPTER V.** Saint Secundulus dies in prison. Saint Felicity, while pregnant, pours forth prayers and gives birth in the eighth month without pain. The unconquered spirit of Saint Perpetua and Saint Saturus. col. 45

**CHAPTER VI.** They are led joyfully from prison into the amphitheater, especially Perpetua and Felicity. They all refuse to put on sacrilegious garments; they are scourged; they long for the beasts and are exposed to them. Saint Saturus twice remains unharmed. Saints Perpetua and Felicity are thrown down. They are recalled to the Gate of Life. Saint Saturus is wounded by a leopard and exhorts a soldier. The holy martyrs kiss one another. They are killed by the sword. col. 49

[Col. 0061]

# AN APOLOGETIC DISSERTATION IN DEFENSE OF THE ORTHODOXY OF SAINTS PERPETUA, FELICITY, AND THEIR COMPANIONS

## By Joseph Augustine Orsi, O.P., Cardinal-Priest of the Holy Roman Church

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0061A]

### The orthodoxy of the holy martyrs Perpetua, Felicity, and their companions is vindicated by external arguments drawn from the authority of the Church and the ancient Fathers

I. The testimony of Tertullian, a contemporary writer, concerning Perpetua and her fellow martyrs.  
II. The deacon Pontius praised the Acts of these same martyrs in terms that are not obscure.  
III. The very ancient veneration of Perpetua and Felicity in the Roman Church is demonstrated from Bucherius’s extremely ancient calendar.  
IV. Saint Augustine mentions these martyrs with praise in various places and celebrated them in three treatises. Basnage, on a very slight conjecture, denies that the first of these as published belongs to the holy Doctor, and strives unsuccessfully to diminish and undermine it.  
V. The most celebrated of the churches of Carthage, [Col. 0061B] and the mother church of the others, was adorned with the relics of Perpetua and Felicity and named after them.  
VI. In the daily Canon of the Mass, their names are numbered among the more celebrated martyrs.  
VII. The argument established from these testimonies; Basnage—in vain. [The source heading breaks off here.]

There is absolutely no mark of religious veneration and observance which, from ancient times onward, the piety of the Catholic Church, the unanimous Christian affection for these martyrs throughout the world, and the devotion of the peoples did not immediately bestow upon these holy and most celebrated martyrs. Their names, indeed, appear in the most ancient ecclesiastical registers and are recorded in almost all the martyrologies; their solemnity and feast day were celebrated by great gatherings of the Christian people; their Acts were publicly read in churches; churches and altars were consecrated to God in their [Col. 0061C] honor and over their relics; panegyrical addresses were delivered by the Fathers on their annual festival; and finally, a special commemoration of them during the daily sacrifices has continued down to our own time.

I shall demonstrate all these things by the clearest testimonies. I shall arrange them so that it may be plainly and openly established that, from the time of their [Col. 0062A] death onward, they were regarded as true martyrs by a perpetual and uninterrupted tradition of the Church, and therefore died in the peace and communion of the Catholic Church.

### I

Tertullian, who was Perpetua’s contemporary and an inhabitant of Carthage, where Perpetua and her fellow martyrs were put to death, mentions her in chapter 55 of his book *On the Soul* in these words:

> Perpetua, the most valiant martyr, on the day of her passion, in a revelation of paradise, saw there only her fellow martyrs.

He does not indicate by even a single word that she was attached to the Montanist sect. That exceedingly vain man would certainly never have omitted such a thing, since he was accustomed to proclaim with puffed-up cheeks the glories of that wicked faction.

In chapter 9 of the same book he mentions a certain fanatical woman accustomed, as she believed, to visions of angels and of the Lord himself; nor does he neglect to warn that she belonged to his own communion:

> There is today among us, he says, a sister who has received charisms of revelations,

etc.

Near the end of his book *On the Veiling of Virgins*, he mentions another woman, whom he likewise calls a sister, [Col. 0062B] and declares in explicit words to have been a Montanist:

> For us—that is, the disciples of the Paraclete, who do not despise new prophecies, who honor charisms, and who receive visions and revelations—the Lord has also measured out the dimensions of the veil through revelations. For an angel said in a dream to a certain sister of ours,

etc.

He relates nothing of this kind where he speaks of Perpetua and boasts of nothing of this kind. He calls her only a martyr, and a most valiant one; he does not proclaim her his sister or his martyr, nor does he indicate by even a single word that she had been imbued with the superstitions and delusions of the Montanists.

Is it truly credible that he neglected to claim so singular an ornament of his sect for himself and his followers in explicit words, when he was so anxious to inform us that even insane little women—distinguished by no virtue but devoted solely to dreams—had emerged from the school and instruction [Col. 0062C] of Montanus? I shall refute below the arguments that Basnage brings against this and the case that he fashions out of these words of Tertullian in support of his own opinion.

### II

The deacon Pontius, who flourished approximately fifty years after the death of Perpetua and Felicity, has the following words in his *Life of Saint Cyprian*. In my judgment, they plainly refer to their Acts, as [Col. 0063A] the most illustrious Lucas Holstenius also observed long ago [Note: [Col. 0063D] In the *Notes on the Passion of Saints Perpetua, Felicity, etc.*, § II, verse 1.]:

> Our forebears bestowed so great an honor, out of reverence for martyrdom itself, upon laypeople and catechumens who had attained martyrdom that they committed many things concerning their passions—or, I might almost say, nearly everything—to writing, so that these accounts might come also to the knowledge of us who had not yet been born.

These words of Pontius point, as though with a finger, to the Acts of Perpetua and Felicity and fit them perfectly.

“Laypeople” in this passage, as Holstenius likewise observed, must be understood as laity who had attained no rank in the clergy. For Pontius himself says a little later:

> Many are the things that he did while still a layman, and many those he did when already a presbyter.

That both the women themselves and their companions in the passion were catechumens was carefully noted by the compiler of the Acts at their very beginning:

> [Col. 0063B] The young catechumens were arrested: Revocatus and his fellow slave Felicity, Saturninus and Secundulus, and among them Vibia Perpetua, well born, liberally educated, honorably married, having a father and mother and two brothers, one of them likewise a catechumen,

etc.

This latter appears to be Saturus, whom Perpetua calls her brother in these Acts:

> Then my brother said to me, “Lady sister,”

etc.

And below:

> And I immediately told my brother, and we understood that a passion was to occur.

She is speaking of Saturus, her fellow soldier in the same contest.

Finally, these Acts were written with the sort of care praised by Pontius in the words quoted above. They contain many things—or, I might almost say, nearly everything—pertaining to their passions, down to the smallest circumstances, [Col. 0063C] so that I know of no Acts of any ancient martyrs that were described with greater accuracy and care.

Pontius’s words therefore fit the Acts before us so beautifully that they fit none now extant better. I very much doubt whether, in Pontius’s time, any others existed to which his words could more aptly be referred, since it does not appear to have been so much the custom of the earlier age to commit the deeds of the martyrs to writing with such meticulous care.

Dodwell is therefore mistaken when he concludes from the words quoted [Note: [Col. 0063D] *Cyprianic Dissertation XI, On the Small Number of Martyrs*, §§ 3 and 5.] that:

> The ancients were so diligent in committing the deeds of the martyrs to memory that almost nothing escaped them,

and hence infers the small number of martyrs from the small number of Acts that survive. [Col. 0063D] Pontius does not assert that the ancients exercised equal care in committing the deeds of every individual martyr to memory. For his purpose, the very clear example of these Acts was sufficient, through which the memory of lay and catechumen martyrs had been so diligently transmitted to posterity. From this everyone could readily understand how much more diligently Pontius himself ought to commit to literary monuments the illustrious deeds of a bishop and martyr.

I therefore have no doubt that Pontius had before his eyes the Acts of Perpetua, Felicity, and their companions. They concern both laypeople and catechumens; the period fits readily, since [Col. 0064A] the events occurred before Pontius himself was born; and they were composed with precisely the zeal and care that he describes. Thus, Pontius’s quoted words provide no obscure indication that by the middle of the third century Perpetua and her companions were regarded at Carthage, where they had shed their blood, as true martyrs.

### III

No one will wonder at this who reflects that in the following century—that is, the fourth century of the Church—the festival of Perpetua and Felicity was also celebrated at Rome. This is established by the most ancient calendar of the Roman Church published by Bucherius, which scholars unanimously appear to assign to the time of Liberius. In this monument of venerable antiquity, therefore, the names “Perpetua and Felicity, in Africa” are entered under the Nones of March. [Col. 0064B] This is surely an indisputable proof of exceedingly ancient veneration in the Church.

For when learned men assign the Bucherian calendar to the time of Liberius, they do not mean that the solemnities of the martyrs listed in it were first instituted at Rome at that time. Such a thought would be absurd. This Bucherian or Liberian list was copied from more ancient diptychs and registers. These were not something the churches—especially the Apostolic Church, and above all and preeminently the Roman Church—possessed for the first time at that date. Rather, as we learn from Tertullian [Note: [Col. 0064D] *On Prescription*, chapter 32, and *On the Soldier’s Crown*, chapter 13.] and other authors, they had sacred calendars from the very beginning, arranged with the greatest possible accuracy according to the conditions of those times.

It could therefore very well have happened that the feast day of Perpetua and Felicity had begun to be celebrated in the city several years before Liberius. And is it not extremely probable that their veneration was received and disseminated at Carthage [Col. 0064C] before it was at Rome? Since Liberius, under whom the quoted calendar was compiled, began his pontificate in the middle of the fourth century, it would be the act of an excessively captious critic to deny that the memory of our martyrs was celebrated at Carthage at least at the beginning of the fourth century.

There is another point concerning this Liberian list of martyrs that I should like to have carefully observed, since from it one may readily understand not only the antiquity but also the renown of the veneration of our martyrs. Apart from our martyrs and Cyprian, all the martyrs listed in this calendar are Roman; except for these three, no foreign martyr has a place in it. This certainly demonstrates clearly and openly how renowned [Col. 0064D] those martyrs had been from ancient times.

The Oxford editor of Cyprian’s works aptly observed that, from the earliest centuries of the Christian faith, the holy martyrs were considered to belong not to one particular church but to all. Yet, given the conditions of the periods about which he speaks, there is something in his words that is not expressed with sufficient precision:

> We see, he says [Note: [Col. 0064D] In the notes on Celerinus’s Letter, no. 21 among the Cyprianic letters.], the Acts of martyrs transmitted from one church to others, and the martyrologies of individual churches containing not only the names of their own people but also those of persons living far away.

[Col. 0065A] If he is speaking of later martyrologies—the Hieronymian, for example, and the others derived from it—there is no reason for us to raise any dispute with the learned man. In the most ancient calendars, however, each church presents only its own martyrs, with a few exceptions, or those of neighboring provinces.

Thus, in Bucherius’s Roman calendar, apart from our martyrs and Cyprian, as has been said, all are Romans. In Mabillon’s Carthaginian calendar, nearly all are Carthaginians or Africans, with only a few from certain other provinces with which the Christians of Carthage formerly maintained considerable relations. That more extensive martyrologies were always compiled as time progressed—containing not merely the names belonging to individual churches but also those of people living far away—is clear and evident, [Col. 0065B] as is the fact that the number of festivals greatly increased in later centuries and that solemnities were also adopted in which churches extremely remote and widely separated from one another celebrated one another’s martyrs.

But to return to Perpetua and Felicity: will anyone deny that it must be attributed to their fame and renown that, alone with Cyprian among the African martyrs—and indeed among the martyrs of other provinces as well—they had a place in the Roman calendar during those ancient times, when each church was content with its own martyrs and recorded the solemnities of foreign martyrs only in the rarest cases?

In Cyprian’s case, it is readily understood whence came so distinguished an honor that his name should be recorded with those of the Roman martyrs in the Liberian list. This was granted because of his most illustrious [Col. 0065C] services, which extended far and wide not only throughout the Church of Carthage and all Africa, but throughout the entire Church wherever it reaches, and especially the Roman Church.

But whence did our martyrs obtain the same glorious renown as Cyprian? How was it that, out of all the martyrs who watered the arenas of Africa with their glorious blood, they alone, together with that most holy and celebrated bishop, obtained a special solemnity at Rome at so early a date—that is, not long after the beginning of the fourth century? Surely either from their Acts or from the frequency of miracles at their memorials. Basnage will certainly not say that it came from miracles. It must therefore have come from the Acts, which accordingly were then in everyone’s hands.

Is it not absurd to suppose that within the space of a single century it could have fallen out of human memory that these most celebrated [Col. 0065D] and well-known women, whose Acts Christians read with extraordinary delight, had been tainted by Montanist errors? This is all the harder to believe in proportion to the eminence of their fame. Matters pertaining to obscure persons are readily erased from the memory of posterity through forgetfulness. But so singular a fact—namely, that women admired by all for the glory of their unconquered courage and their heavenly revelations had been devoted to Montanist superstitions—could not, after so short an interval, have been permitted to pass into oblivion and disappear from the memory either of Catholics or of heretics.

It could not have disappeared from the memory of Catholics, for just as they avoided association even with heretics distinguished by the glory of confession, so they took anxious precautions lest false martyrs be received into the sacred diptychs in place of true ones—that is, heretical martyrs in place of Catholic martyrs. Although the names of heretics sometimes slipped into the martyrologies, this happened, as will be demonstrated below, in later centuries, [Col. 0066A] extremely remote from the memory of the events. Yet what we are now discussing would have occurred scarcely a century after their passion, something that certainly lacks any parallel among martyrs of equal renown and reputation. Nor would the Montanists, a far from uncommon heretical faction in Africa, have allowed the Catholics to appropriate their martyrs. But there will be a fuller and more appropriate place to discuss this elsewhere.

### IV

At the beginning of the fifth century Augustine flourished. In his catalogue, Possidius lists three treatises by him *On the Feast Day of Perpetua and Felicity*. [Col. 0066B] In the most recent edition of Augustine’s works, prepared through the efforts of the Benedictine Fathers of the Congregation of Saint-Maur, these appear among the sermons as nos. CCLXXX, CCLXXXI, and CCLXXXII.

Basnage calls the first—that is, Sermon 280, otherwise Sermon 103 *On Various Subjects*—into doubt. Indeed, on the basis of a very slight conjecture, he judges that it is not Augustine’s:

> We do not believe, he says [Note: [Col. 0066D] At the year 203, no. VI.], that the sermon *On the Feast Day of the Holy Martyrs Perpetua and Felicity* is Augustine’s, where these words are read: “As their exhortations in divine revelations and the triumphs of their passions were being read, we heard them.” These words surely do not accord with Augustine’s position, since in explicit terms he excludes Perpetua’s visions from Holy Scripture [Note: [Col. 0066D] Book I of *The Soul and Its Origin*, chapter 10.]: “As for Saint Perpetua’s brother Dinocrates, the writing itself is not canonical.” But what could be more canonical than divine revelations, as the author of the sermon considers them?

[Col. 0066C] Yet not only Augustine, but no Catholic writer whatsoever, would have understood “divine” here to mean “canonical.” For who, apart from the Montanists, regarded private revelations of this kind, committed to writing on private authority, as canonical? Will Basnage therefore say that the author of the sermon was some declaimer from the Montanist sect? I do not think the learned man will say so.

Whoever the author of the sermon may have been, he was certainly learned, Catholic, and thoroughly Augustinian. He called the revelations “divine” because, as he piously believed, they had been sent by God, not because he believed that they had been written under divine authority. For it is one thing for a revelation to be divine, and another for the writing in which such a revelation is presented to us to be divine and canonical.

For us to call a revelation divine, [Col. 0066D] it is sufficient that we judge it probable that the revelation had God as its author. But for us to call the writing in which such a revelation is contained canonical, it must have had a canonical author inspired by the divine Spirit.

Augustine, therefore, as we shall subsequently see, judged it probable that Perpetua’s revelations came from God, and could accordingly have called them divine in this sense and meaning. Yet it did not even enter the author of the sermon’s mind that the Acts of Perpetua in which such revelations are read were canonical Scripture, or that their author had been inspired by the divine Spirit and endowed with divine authority.

There is therefore complete agreement between the author of the sermon, whoever he may have been, and Augustine. On so slight and empty a conjecture the quoted sermon ought not to have been denied to Augustine.

[Col. 0067A] But let it be granted that neither this sermon nor the two following sermons for the feast day of the martyrs Perpetua and Felicity, which now stand among Augustine’s works, is Augustine’s. Will Basnage deny the explicit testimony of Possidius that the holy Doctor delivered three treatises on the feast day of Perpetua and Felicity?
