Will he therefore deny that the holy Doctor regarded them as true and Catholic martyrs and that, at the beginning of the fifth century, their solemnity was celebrated in Africa?

Will he deny that Augustine wrote the exposition of Psalm 47, where he mentions Saint Perpetua and indicates that her Acts were publicly read in the churches?

> As we know, he says, [Col. 0067B] and have read in the Passion of blessed Perpetua.

Moreover, in the books *The Soul and Its Origin* [Note: [Col. 0067D] See Book I, chapter 10; Book III, chapter 11; and Book IV, chapter 18.] he everywhere calls Perpetua holy. Although he excludes the Acts of her passion from the canon of Scripture and refuses to have testimony from them advanced against the mysteries of faith, he nevertheless places them at the same rank and value as the Acts of the other martyrs and gives them the same credit as the others. Nowhere does he regard Perpetua’s visions as the dreams of silly women, reject them as Montanist inventions, or dismiss them as deceptions of the human spirit. He therefore believes, with the degree of confidence that prudent and judicious men customarily grant to monuments of this kind, that they were sent by God and were, in this sense, divine.

### V

But more compelling than all the arguments we have produced thus far is the one drawn from the dignity and antiquity of the basilica [Col. 0067C] that Perpetua and Felicity possessed at Carthage. For what appears to have been the most celebrated and ancient of all the churches of Carthage—and, as it is now called, its mother church—is designated in the ancient records sometimes as the “restored basilica” [Note: [Col. 0067D] In the Acts of the Second Council of Carthage; in Augustine, *Sermon* 19; and in Victor of Vita, book I, *On the Vandal Persecution*], sometimes as the “basilica of the ancestors” [Note: [Col. 0067D] In Augustine, *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, chap. 11, and *Sermon* 294], sometimes as the “greater basilica” [Note: [Col. 0067D] In the same author, *Sermon* 258, and in Victor of Vita, at the place cited above], and sometimes as “at the ancestors” [Note: [Col. 0067D] In Augustine, *Sermon* 34]. Since it was the greater church and was frequented by large gatherings of the people of Carthage, many of Augustine’s sermons delivered at Carthage were preached there. In it the Second Council of Carthage was held under Genethlius in the year 390, as were the subsequent synods of Carthage.

I think that St. Optatus of Milevis should be understood as referring to this same basilica when, speaking of the schismatic ordination of Majorinus, he writes [Note: [Col. 0067D] Book I, *Against Parmenian*]:

> Meanwhile [Col. 0067D] none of those mentioned above came to the basilica where the whole city had assembled in great numbers with Caecilian.

And shortly afterward:

> At that time either he—the accused Caecilian—ought to have been expelled, or communion ought to have been maintained with him as innocent. The church was thronged with people; the episcopal chair was occupied; the altar [Col. 0068A] stood in its proper place, upon which the peaceable bishops of earlier times—Cyprian, Lucian, and the others—had made their offerings. Thus they went outside, and altar was erected against altar, etc.

It is of this basilica, I say—whether called “of the ancestors” or “restored”—that I believe St. Optatus is speaking here, because Victor of Vita recorded [Note: [Col. 0068D] Book I, *On the African Persecution*] that the seat and residence of the bishops of Carthage had always been there. Moreover, the highly authoritative Victor of Vita bears witness that the bodies of Perpetua and Felicity had been laid in this church, which we may most justly establish as at once the most celebrated and the most ancient of all the churches of Carthage [Note: [Col. 0068D] Ibid.]:

> The greater basilica, where the bodies of the holy martyrs Perpetua and Felicity are buried . . . the Vandals, with tyrannical license, subjected to their own religion.

Indeed, it may be inferred with no little clarity from the acts of the Second Council of Carthage that this same [Col. 0068B] basilica had been named after Perpetua, since that council is said to have been held “in the restored basilica Perpetua”—perhaps *Perpetuae*, “of Perpetua.” I regard this as the clearest evidence of a most ancient and celebrated cult and of their orthodoxy.

No one with even a passing acquaintance with ecclesiastical history is unaware that it was a most ancient custom in the Church, almost coeval with the Christian religion itself, for the Catholic people to assemble at the memorials of the martyrs, to frequent those places, and to venerate with religious devotion the sites where their sacred remains had been laid. Concerning the Roman monuments in which the sacred bodies of the Apostles had been deposited, this is explicitly attested by Caius, a contemporary of Zephyrinus and therefore also of Tertullian, Perpetua, [Col. 0068C] and Felicity:

> I can show the memorial-trophies of the Apostles. For whether you choose to go to the Vatican or to the Ostian Way, you will encounter the memorial-trophies of those who founded that church.

[Note: [Col. 0068D] Greek: Ἐγὼ δὲ τὰ τρόπαια τῶν ἀποστόλων ἔχω δεῖξαι· ἐὰν γὰρ θελήσῃς ἀπελθεῖν ἐπὶ τὸν βατικανὸν, ἢ ἐπὶ τὴν ὁδὸν, τὴν Ὠστίαν, εὑρήσεις τὰ τρόπαια τῶν ταύτην ἱδρυσαμένων τὴν ἐκκλησίαν. *Disputation against Proclus*, in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book II, chap. 25.]

It is also established that, when religion subsequently flourished in those same places and the Church obtained respite from persecution, basilicas and sacred buildings dedicated to religious uses were constructed there. Finally, ancient records establish—and reason itself suggests—that the more celebrated and distinguished basilicas were built for the more eminent and illustrious martyrs, or at least that the remains (*λείψανα*) of the more celebrated and distinguished martyrs were transferred to the more celebrated and distinguished basilicas. [Col. 0068D] Above all, bishops took care that the greater churches should be adorned with the relics of the principal martyrs. This was done both for the greater glory of the martyrs themselves, for the splendor of the churches, and, finally, because the Christian people gathered more frequently at the mother churches, so that, attracted by devotion to the principal martyrs, they might assemble there in still greater numbers. Since, therefore, we learn from Victor [Col. 0069A] of Vita that the bodies of Perpetua and Felicity were brought into the greater church of Carthage, we must not doubt that, before being brought there, they had been numbered among the more illustrious martyrs.

But the date of the translation must be ascertained so that the antiquity of their cult may also be established. In the year 390, when the Second Council of Carthage was held, the greater church of Carthage was, as we have seen, designated by Perpetua’s name. We must therefore date the translation of the sacred pledges—their relics—earlier than that year. The Bucherian Calendar was compiled, as we have said, under Liberius. In it, as in all the martyrologies, the feast of Perpetua and Felicity is assigned to the Nones of March, March 7. But the distinguished Pagi proves by the following argument that this was the day not of their martyrdom, but of their translation [Note: [Col. 0069D] Under the year 198, no. V].

The holy martyrs suffered on the day on which the birthday [Col. 0069B] of Geta Caesar was being celebrated:

> We were to fight in the military games. It was then the birthday of Geta Caesar.

And below:

> Why, then, do you not permit the condemned to take refreshment, since they are to fight on the birthday of the Most Noble Caesar?

Yet neither the anniversary of the imperial dignity nor Geta’s actual birthday fell on March 7. For Geta was born, according to Spartianus [Note: [Col. 0069D] *Geta*, chap. 3], on the sixth day before the Kalends of June, May 27; while he was invested with the rank of Caesar in the year 198, no earlier than April 13.

> And the reason is, says Pagi, that, as we shall shortly see, Caracalla obtained the tribunician power and the rank of Augustus from his father after that date; and it is not likely that Geta, the younger son, was styled Augustus by his father before him. Therefore, either both appointments were made at the same time after the month of March, or Caracalla was styled Augustus before Geta [Col. 0069C] was styled Caesar. Consequently, Sts. Perpetua and Felicity are venerated in the martyrologies on a day other than that on which they suffered. We shall observe throughout this work that this happened not infrequently; March 7 is the day on which their relics were subsequently transferred to Carthage, not the day of their death.

Since Liberius began his episcopate around the middle of the fourth century, the translation of their sacred relics had already been performed by that time. We may therefore most justly conclude that this translation was solemnly carried out not long after the beginning of the fourth century, once peace had been restored to the Church by Constantine; and that, when only a century had elapsed since their martyrdom, Perpetua and Felicity were regarded as principal martyrs, while the people of Carthage gathered in very great numbers at their memorials.

[Col. 0069D] We have seen how the celebrity and antiquity of the cult of our martyrs is demonstrated by the translation of their bodies into the greater church of Carthage. It remains to be seen how clearly their orthodoxy is confirmed from the same principle.

As the most illustrious Albaspinaeus notes [Note: [Col. 0069D] In the notes on Optatus, book I, *Against Parmenian*], the bishop’s church, residence, chair, and especially altar were the center of ecclesiastical communion. The Catholic people gathered there in very great numbers; from there the bishop addressed the people; there he received their prayers, offerings, and vows. This was the place of prayer, the place of the sacraments, [Col. 0070A] and, finally, the place of the solemn sacrifice. The other altars, as Albaspinaeus likewise observes, were erected as auxiliaries to the communion whose center, as has been said, was held to be the bishop’s church and altar.

However numerous the Catholics who communicated at this altar, no schismatic or heretic was permitted access to it. Indeed, those who had fallen away from the communion of the Catholic Church were expelled from it even by force, lest, because of the sanctity and grandeur of the place in which the ancients had established the stronghold of Catholic communion, they might be regarded as Catholics. Evidence of this may be found in what Eusebius relates concerning Paul of Samosata: namely, that although this wicked heresiarch had been deprived of authority by the judgment of a synod and deposed from the bishopric of Antioch, he could by no means be driven from the episcopal residence, seat, and church [Col. 0070B] for as long as Zenobia, whose favor and patronage he enjoyed, held power in the East. For he believed that he should be regarded as the legitimate bishop, and that he could retain the Catholic people for himself, for as long as he occupied the residence, chair, basilica, and altar where his predecessors had customarily sat, assembled the congregation, received the people’s offerings and vows, and offered sacrifices to God.

The Catholic bishops, however, strove with every effort and exertion to have this most wicked man expelled and Domnus, who had been appointed in his place, take possession of the episcopal basilica and be installed in the seat and chair of his predecessors. After Zenobia’s defeat, this was accomplished with the aid of Aurelian, who, as Eusebius says [Note: [Col. 0070D] Greek: Βασιλεὺς ἐντευχθεὶς Αὐρηλιανὸς αἰσιώτατα περὶ τοῦ πρακτέου διείληφε· τούτοις νεῖμαι προστάττων τὸν οἶκον, οἷς ἂν οἱ κατὰ τὴν Ἰταλίαν καὶ τὴν Ῥωμαίων πόλιν ἐπίσκοποι τοῦ δόγματος ἐπιστέλλοιεν. “When petitioned, the emperor Aurelian decided most properly what should be done, ordering the building to be assigned to those to whom the bishops in Italy and the city of Rome should write concerning doctrine.” Book VII, *Ecclesiastical History*, chap. 30], when petitioned by the bishops, judged the matter most properly, ordering the residence to be given [Col. 0070C] to those with whom the Christian bishops of Italy and the bishop of Rome corresponded.

Since this is so, everyone, I think, can readily understand from this argument how fixed, constant, and certain was the judgment among the ancients that our martyrs had died in the peace and communion of the Church, since they wished their bodies to be brought to the place where the people of Carthage assembled as though at the center and stronghold of Catholic communion. The bones of the principal martyrs were laid beneath that principal altar of the bishop so that Catholics assembling there might understand that they participated in the communion not only of other believers, but also of the holy martyrs. Conversely, schismatics and heretics, for whom no access to that sanctuary of piety lay open, were to know that they had no communion either with the Catholic Church [Col. 0070D] or with the holy martyrs.

Hence St. Optatus of Milevis denounces the Donatists as schismatics on the ground that they by no means shared communion at the memorials of the holy Apostles in the City of Rome [Note: [Col. 0070D] Book II, *Against Parmenian*]:

> Finally, if Macrobius—the Donatists’ pseudo-bishop in the City—were asked where he sits there, can he possibly say, “In the chair of Peter”? I do not know whether he is even acquainted with it by sight; and he does not approach Peter’s memorial, behaving as a schismatic in opposition to the Apostle, who says [Note: [Col. 0070D] Romans 12:13]: [Col. 0071A] “Sharing communion in the memorials of the saints.” Behold, the memorials of two Apostles are present there. Tell us whether he was able to enter them in such a way as to make an offering there, where it is established that the memorials of the saints are located.

Among the ancients, therefore, it was so well established that Perpetua and Felicity had had nothing in common with heretics while they lived, and that they had consummated their martyrdom in the peace and communion of the Church, that scarcely a century after their martyrdom their sacred relics were brought to the very place from which heretics were most strictly prohibited and where no one communicated unless Catholic.

### VI

Finally, arguments not unlike the preceding ones [Col. 0071B] may be constructed for the antiquity and celebrity of the cult of our martyrs, and for their orthodoxy, from the continually repeated commemoration of them during the daily sacrifices. For in the Gelasian Missal, Gregory’s Sacramentary, and, finally, the most ancient Gallican Sacramentary [Note: [Col. 0071D] In Mabillon, vol. I of the *Museum Italicum*], Perpetua and Felicity are commemorated daily in the canon of the Mass together with a few other martyrs.

Everyone is familiar with the testimonies of the earliest Fathers, particularly Tertullian [Note: [Col. 0071D] *On the Soldier’s Crown*, chap. 3] and Cyprian [Note: [Col. 0071D] Epistle XII, otherwise XXXVII, and Epistle XXXIX, otherwise XXXIV], in which they explicitly testify that the martyrs’ anniversaries were celebrated by a special commemoration of them during the sacrifices. But whether the practice of early times prescribed that, in addition to the annual celebration of the martyrs upon their anniversary, the names either of all of them or of the more eminent ones should be recited from the sacred diptychs during the daily sacrifices is not so well established from ancient testimony.

Nevertheless, St. Cyprian appears to indicate this [Col. 0071C] in Epistle XXXIX to Pam., no. 30. After speaking of Celerinus’s grandmother Celerina, his paternal uncle, and his maternal uncles Laurentinus and Ignatius, who had long since been crowned with martyrdom, he adds:

> We always offer sacrifices for them, as you remember, whenever we celebrate the sufferings and anniversary days of the martyrs with an annual commemoration.

By these words Cyprian plainly indicates that whenever the anniversary solemnity of any martyr recurred, mention of those named above was always renewed during the solemnities of the sacrifices.

It might very well have happened that, when the number of martyrs was not great, just as none of them lacked an annual solemnity—not only the more eminent and those who had undergone more atrocious tortures, but also the more obscure, including those who, having endured no torments, died in prison for confessing the Name, as the same Cyprian prescribed [Note: [Col. 0071D] Epistle XII, otherwise XXXVII]—so at first all of them were commemorated in the daily sacrifices. Later, however, when their number had increased beyond measure, only the principal martyrs, as the ancient calendars teach us, and those whose fame was more illustrious, were retained for the celebration of annual sacrifices and offerings. Likewise, although at first all were commemorated in the daily sacrifices, subsequently, as is established from liturgies that were indeed very ancient, though later than the third century, the names only of the more illustrious were retained in the daily Masses.

But whatever the practice [Col. 0072A] of the more ancient period may have been, no one doubts that those whose memory is renewed daily in the canon of the Mass were, both formerly and now, reckoned among the more illustrious martyrs. Consequently, this proves that Perpetua and Felicity, who received this honor from our ancestors in the most ancient liturgies together with a few others, were numbered not merely among the martyrs, but among the more eminent martyrs.

Nor should it pass without notice here—as was also remarked above—that the liturgies or sacramentaries in which Perpetua and Felicity are commemorated every day belonged not to the Church of Carthage or to other African churches, but to the Roman and Gallican churches. This demonstrates still more forcefully how renowned [Col. 0072B] our martyrs had been from ancient times.

In former times no martyrs were commemorated in the canon of the Roman Mass except Roman martyrs, if we exclude the Apostles and Ignatius, an apostolic man who also suffered at Rome, as well as our martyrs and Cyprian. For Aldhelm writes that Agatha and Lucy, Sicilian martyrs, were added to the canon by Gregory the Great [Note: [Col. 0072D] *On Virginity*, chap. 25]. Cyprian’s distinguished services to the Roman Church, as we say, secured this honor for him. But from what source did our martyrs receive this special prerogative, so that although they were foreigners, strangers, and from a province beyond the sea, their memory was nevertheless celebrated daily at Rome during the sacred mysteries? From what, I ask, did they receive this distinction, unless from that celebrity of fame by which they were always upon people’s lips and were regarded as eminent martyrs? [Col. 0072C] It is certainly inconsistent with such celebrated fame that, within so brief an interval of time, the religion to which they had adhered while alive should have vanished from human memory.

Finally, it must likewise be observed here that this commemoration of the holy martyrs within the sacred synaxis is principally intended to make us understand that we share communion with them in Christ, whose body is offered in sacrifice, as the very words of the canon explicitly attest:

> Sharing communion, and venerating the memory, etc.

Moreover, that commemoration of martyrs from other regions must be understood as intended to make us know that the Catholic Church is everywhere one, and that all churches, however distant in place, possess one communion, since they [Col. 0072D] venerate foreign martyrs no less than their own. As observed above, this clearly and plainly demonstrates that the ancients were so certain of the orthodoxy of our martyrs that they wished their names to serve as a symbol of Catholic communion.

### VII

Basnage thinks he can diminish the authority of all the testimonies we have thus far discussed with this very trifling reply: “The steadfastness of these martyrs, together with the antiquity of the Acts, deceived posterity, so that they came to be held in esteem.” Then, after advancing the conjecture concerning Augustine’s sermon that I refuted above, he adds:

> Let it nevertheless be granted that these are Augustine’s words. The question is one of fact: whether Perpetua [Col. 0073A] was a woman of the Church or of the Montanist sect. Now, in questions of this kind, good men very often go entirely astray, and we have demonstrated in the proper place that heretical martyrs have slipped into the martyrologies.

The Acts and their authority must be discussed below. For the present we must briefly consider whether it is not the height of rashness, on account of the very slight conjectures that I shall hereafter expose, to call into doubt the orthodoxy and sanctity of persons whom, it is established, the universal Church venerated immediately after their passion and thereafter, for fifteen centuries and more, with every mark of religious devotion and reverence—not merely as genuine martyrs, but as among the more celebrated martyrs of Christ. Their memory, indeed, the Church frequented from ancient times; for them it erected altars and basilicas that were centers of Catholic [Col. 0073B] communion; their annual solemnity was celebrated not only by the Church of Carthage but also by the Roman Church in the second century after their passion; their names are recorded among those of the more illustrious martyrs in the most ancient ecclesiastical calendars; their memory, together with that of a few other similarly distinguished martyrs, is renewed daily in the canon of the Mass; and, finally, they are celebrated not merely by one or another private martyrology, but by all of them alike, including those compiled for the use of different churches. In the present chapter I have now sufficiently demonstrated that all these honors together were accorded to our martyrs.

But “the steadfastness of the martyrs and the antiquity of the Acts deceived posterity.” Could they also have deceived writers who were almost contemporary or only slightly later?

But “in such questions of fact good men are often mistaken.” Could the authority of the universal Church also be mistaken? Augustine deferred so greatly to that authority even in questions of this kind that he refused rashly to pass judgment upon women who, in time of persecution, threw themselves into a river that would sweep them away and kill them, in order to escape those who pursued their chastity, and who died in that manner, while the celebrations of their martyrdom are most renowned in the veneration of the Catholic Church:

> Concerning these women, [Col. 0073C] I dare make no rash judgment. For I do not know whether divine authority persuaded the Church through certain trustworthy testimonies that it should honor their memory in this way; and it is possible that this is so. For what if they did this not through human deception or error, but in obedience? Just as we are not permitted to believe anything else concerning Samson.

[Note: [Col. 0073D] Book I, *The City of God*, chap. 26.]

But heretical martyrs have slipped into the martyrologies. Did they also slip into the most ancient calendars? Were sacrifices and Catholic assemblies also celebrated at their monuments? Were altars to God and basilicas consecrated in their memory? Did the ancient Fathers adorn their praises in speeches and public sermons? Finally, have they been commemorated among the more illustrious martyrs in the canon of the Mass for so many years, even to the present day?

Rabanus was the first, in the ninth century, imprudently to introduce Marculus, the Donatists’ pseudo-martyr, into his martyrology [Note: [Col. 0073D] In Mabillon, vol. IV of the *Veteres Analecta*]. From there he slipped into the spurious martyrology of Bede, and from it into several manuscripts and editions of Usuard’s martyrology [Note: [Col. 0074D] In the Bollandist Fathers, vol. VII for the month of June]. But the error was easily detected, and the compilers of the Roman Martyrology substituted Nicomedia for Numidia, Marcellus for Marculus, Constantius for Constans, and Arians for the Macarians.

For, on reading the name of the Nicomedian martyr Marcellus in more ancient martyrologies under approximately the same date, and being ignorant of his acts, they composed for him from the interpolated acts of Marculus this encomium:

> At Nicomedia—instead of “in Numidia”—St. Marcellus—read “Marculus”—a priest who, in the time of Constantius—more correctly, “Constans”—was cast down from a cliff by the Arians—instead of “by the Macarians”—and died as a martyr.

This is the conjecture of the Benedictine Fathers in their notes on Augustine’s book III *Against Cresconius*, chap. 49. On this matter, the distinguished Mabillon should also be consulted in his annotations on the Acts of Marculus, vol. III of the *Veteres Analecta*.

[Col. 0074B] But what does this example—or any other example like it—have in common with our martyrs in any respect? They did not slip into some private martyrology in later centuries through the carelessness of one or another writer. Rather, from the beginning they received a place in the Church’s public and most ancient calendars, in her public prayers through the recitation of their names, and in every form of testimony to religious veneration.

But let us see by what arguments Basnage has attempted to dislodge the holy martyrs from what may be called their perpetual possession of this most sacred reputation and public cult. For the arguments that, after so many centuries since their passion, led him to form this opinion of our martyrs must be exceedingly weighty. [Col. 0074C] Faith in the unanimous testimonies of the ancients and in the Church’s perpetual tradition concerning their orthodoxy and sanctity ought not to have been rejected in a matter of such gravity unless invincible and manifest arguments imposed a different opinion upon an almost unwilling mind. Whether Basnage’s arguments are of that kind we shall discuss in the following chapters.

## CHAPTER II  
## BASNAGE’S EXTERNAL ARGUMENTS AGAINST THE HOLY MARTYRS ARE ANSWERED

I. The compiler of the Acts of Perpetua and Felicity was infected with the heresy of the Montanists. II. Ruinart’s arguments in defense of the compiler of the Acts are refuted, and his Montanism is established by various arguments. [Col. 0074D] III. Dodwell’s argument for the orthodoxy of the same writer. IV. The first foundation of his argument is demolished. V. The second foundation of the same argument is overturned. VI. The Montanists did not regard Catholics as heretics. VII. The Montanists did not consider themselves entirely estranged from the communion of the Catholic churches. VIII. They aspired also to communion with the Catholic martyrs. IX. Tertullian commemorated with praise not only Perpetua, but other Catholic martyrs as well. X. Heretics other than the Montanists published the Acts of Catholic martyrs. XI. From the author of the Acts himself, a Montanist, it is shown that our martyrs were alien to that sect.

### I

[Col. 0075A] Concerning the author—or rather, as he prefers to appear, the compiler—of the Acts of Perpetua and Felicity, scholars do not hold one and the same opinion. Valesius, a man as candid as he was learned, to use Basnage’s words, formerly judged that he belonged to the Montanist party [Note: [Col. 0075D] Preface to the Paris edition of the Acts]. Dodwell, on the contrary, not only removes from him every suspicion of Montanism, but even contends that the man burned with zeal and ardor for the Catholic faith against the Montanists [Note: [Col. 0075D] Fourth Cyprianic Dissertation, *On Visions*, etc., § 8 ff. See the end of this volume]. The distinguished Ruinart can by no means agree with Valesius [Note: [Col. 0075D] In the prefatory notice to the Acts, no. 6]. Basnage, on the other hand, willingly professes his adherence to Valesius’s opinion and derives from it, as we shall see later, his first argument against our martyrs.

The matter plainly demands that we discuss this entire controversy with the greatest possible care, lest, if we embrace Valesius’s opinion, we should be thought to have done so rashly; or, if we reject it, lest that rejection appear to have arisen from the prejudice of some preconceived opinion. Therefore, so that the reader may recognize that I am dealing candidly with him and bring nothing prejudged to this inquiry, I profess that I am strongly inclined toward Valesius’s opinion, although at first sight it is rather inconvenient for my own case.

[Col. 0075C] My evidence is the author’s preface, in which he uses words that, although they might be interpreted in a Catholic sense if they had been written at another time, nevertheless, when the period in which they were written is considered, arouse in us a powerful suspicion of Montanism. He writes as follows:

> But let those see to it who judge the one power of the one Holy Spirit according to the successive ages of time, although all the more recent manifestations, precisely because they are more recent, should be considered the greater, in accordance with the abundance of grace appointed for the final periods of the age [Note: [Col. 0075D] Joel 2:28 and Acts 2:17]. “For in the last days,” says the Lord, “I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh, and their sons and daughters shall prophesy; upon my male and female servants I will pour out of my Spirit; the young shall see visions, and the old shall dream dreams.” Therefore we also, who acknowledge and honor the new visions as having been promised, just as the prophecies were, etc.

Who could believe that a Catholic writer could have let such words escape him [Col. 0075D] at a time when the Montanist heresy was raging most violently in the Church—when the heretics so greatly vaunted and extolled the condition of the last times as reserved for their Paraclete because of the abundance of charisms and the overflowing of the Spirit; when the Church professed that it rejected new visions and prophecies, while those who acknowledged and honored them were regarded as heretics?

> Since all the more recent manifestations, precisely because they are more recent, should be considered the greater, in accordance with the abundance of grace appointed for the final periods of the age.

Could any avowed Montanist ever have spoken more bluntly or shamelessly? Is any egg, as the saying goes, more like another egg than these words of the author are like the following words of Tertullian near the end of his book *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*?

> But against these dispositions of unbelief and perversity, almighty God, pouring forth by his most provident grace in the last days from his Spirit upon all flesh, upon his male and female servants, both revived the struggling faith in the resurrection of the flesh and purified the ancient instruments from every obscurity of ambiguity by manifest illuminations of words and meanings. [Col. 0076A] For because there had to be heresies, so that all those who are approved might be made manifest, and because these heresies could not have ventured forth without some occasions offered by the Scriptures, the ancient instruments therefore seem to have supplied them with certain materials—although materials capable of refuting them by means of the same writings. [Col. 0076B] But because it was no longer fitting for the Holy Spirit to refrain from overflowing also with such utterances as would scatter no seeds for any subtlety of the heretics, but would even uproot their old clods, he has therefore now dispelled all former ambiguities, and what they wish to call parables, through the open and transparent proclamation of the entire sacrament, by means of the new prophecy overflowing from the Paraclete. If you drink from its fountains, you will be able to thirst for no doctrine; no fever of questions will scorch you; by drinking everywhere from it, you will also cool your thirst concerning the resurrection of the flesh.

He sets the latest things before the ancient: that is, the new revelations of Montanus before the ancient instruments, namely the books of both Testaments—not, as Rhenanus and Pamelius interpret him, the books of the New Covenant before the Mosaic and prophetic writings. [Col. 0076C] For the heretics drew material for their doctrines not only from the Law and the Prophets, but especially from certain obscure passages, ambiguities, and parables of the New Testament.

Tertullian teaches that God in his most provident grace had provided against this by pouring forth from his Spirit upon all flesh in the last days, so that the Spirit might overflow with utterances of a kind that would supply no matter or seeds for any subtlety of the heretics, and might dispel all former ambiguities and parables through an open and transparent proclamation of the whole sacrament. He then adds that this was accomplished “through the new prophecy overflowing from the Paraclete.” Accordingly, just as the books of the New Testament surpass the legal and [Col. 0076D] prophetic writings by a more open and transparent revelation of heavenly realities, through which the ancient figures were explained, so the prophecies of Montanus—which dispelled even the ambiguities and parables of the Gospel itself through an open proclamation of the whole sacrament—were to be preferred even to the books of the New Covenant themselves.

The compiler of the Acts certainly insinuated the same doctrine in fewer, but no less explicit, words when he said that “all the more recent manifestations should be considered the greater, precisely because they are more recent, in accordance with the abundance of grace,” etc.; that is, as Tertullian puts it, in accordance with “the new prophecy overflowing from the Paraclete.”

### II

[Col. 0077A] Ruinart replies that, although these words appear at first sight to savor of the errors of Montanus, if they are examined somewhat more carefully, they contain nothing except what is orthodox and entirely consonant with the Catholic faith. For, he says, this author compares the most recent visions not with the canonical Scriptures, as Valesius supposed, but only with the visions and revelations of the ancient martyrs; and he asserts that the events that occurred in his own time should be held in no less veneration than those that had occurred in earlier times, that is, in the first or second century of the Church. Indeed, he says that these new revelations should in some measure be received with greater zeal, since examples are all the more effective the more recent they are; and furthermore, because these latest visions, which were themselves destined one day to be ancient, needed to be supported by some authority so that posterity might believe them.

Ruinart says that this is evident from the same author’s entire preface, in which there is not even one word comparing Sacred Scripture with the martyrs’ visions:

> If ancient examples [Col. 0077B] of the faith were committed to writing so that, by reading them as though by reenacting the events, God might be honored and man strengthened, why should not new testimonies, equally suited to both purposes, also be set down in writing?

But the author did not advance only the reasons cited by Ruinart for wishing the new revelations and prophecies to be esteemed above the ancient. He advanced especially the one reason that no one but a thoroughgoing Montanist would have produced, and that sufficiently shows that he preferred the latest revelations not only to the revelations of the ancient martyrs, but even to the canonical Scriptures themselves: namely, “because of the abundance of grace appointed for the final periods of the age,” in accordance with Joel’s prophecy.

For who in his right mind ever dreamed that the grace of the Holy Spirit abounded more in these latest days—that is, at the beginning of the third century [Col. 0077C]—than in the first or second century? Who, unless carried away by the spirit of Montanus, would ever have used the words of Joel, by which this future overflowing of the Spirit in the last days was foretold, to demonstrate this claim?

Therefore, this author is not to be blamed only for the reason Ruinart supposed: that he regarded the visions of these martyrs as belonging among those that God had promised through Joel. For I do not deny that the cited words of Joel can refer to all the charisms dispensed by God under our Testament. Rather, he betrays himself as a Montanist because he employed the prophet’s words to demonstrate a greater abundance of heavenly charisms in the latest days than in the preceding centuries of the Church.

[Col. 0077D] Moreover, although—as Ruinart likewise adds—the Church has by no means reckoned the spoken or written words of the faithful among the canonical Scriptures, even when it does not doubt that they proceeded from the one by whom varieties of tongues are given to some, prophecies to others, the word of wisdom to others, and different gifts to still others, gifts that were assuredly foretold and promised in the cited testimony of Joel, it nevertheless does not follow that the same judgment should likewise be made concerning the writer of the Acts. For although neither the Church nor Catholic writers ever doubted that the charisms of the New Testament both proceeded from God and were foretold and promised in the cited testimony of Joel, nevertheless neither the Church nor any Catholic ever used Joel’s words to secure greater veneration and authority for the visions and revelations of the latest times than for those of the preceding centuries [Col. 0078A] of the Church.

This is indeed a very serious presumption against the compiler of the Acts, as they call him; yet I do not know whether the argument drawn from the following words is not still weightier. For he continues thus: “Accordingly, we too, who acknowledge and honor new visions as likewise promised, just as we do prophecies.” These words are plainly decisive: the author could not have declared in clearer language what sect he himself professed. They are the watchword of Montanism and a clear and open profession of Montanist doctrine. For at that time the dispute between Catholics and Montanists concerned precisely this question: whether new—that is, extraordinary and unprecedented—visions and prophecies were to be acknowledged and honored, [Col. 0078B] or, on the contrary, repudiated and rejected. Catholics abhorred the new visions and prophecies as a deception of an evil spirit, not because they recognized no visions or prophecies in the Church at that time, or maintained that the fountain of charisms had dried up; rather, by the name “new visions” and “new prophecy” they understood things that were unusual, as I have said, and, in the words of Asterius as quoted by Eusebius, [Note: [Col. 0078D] Παρὰ τὸ κατὰ παράδοσιν καὶ κατὰ διαδοχὴν ἄνωθεν τῆς Ἐκκλησίας ἔθος δῆθεν, “contrary, so it was alleged, to the custom of the Church handed down from above by tradition and continuous succession.” *Hist.* V, ch. 16.] “Contrary to the custom and ordinance of the Church handed down by the forefathers and thereafter propagated through continuous succession.”

The Montanists, by contrast, highly esteemed, embraced, and honored these new revelations and prophecies; and this was the first pretext with which they cloaked their secession from the Church. From it, as is evident from Serapion, [Note: [Col. 0078D] Τῆς ἐπικαλουμένης νέας προφητείας, “of the so-called new prophecy,” etc. *Epistle to Caricus and Ponticus*, in Eusebius, book V, ch. 19.] the wicked faction also received its name and [Col. 0078C] “was called the New Prophecy.” Asterius Urbanus clearly and openly testifies in these words that they themselves gave their sect this name: [Note: [Col. 0078D] Καὶ καταλαβὼν τὴν κατὰ πόντον (read τόπον) Ἐκκλησίαν ὑπὸ τῆς νέας ταύτης, οὐκ ὡς αὐτοί φασι, προφητείας, etc., “And finding the Church of that place troubled by this new—not, as they themselves say—prophecy,” etc. Book I, *Against the Cataphrygians*, in Eusebius, ibid., ch. 16.]: “And I found the Church of that place afflicted by that new—not, as they themselves call it—prophecy, etc.”

After defecting to the Montanists, Tertullian everywhere boasts of and proclaims new prophecies. In the book *On Fasting* [Note: [Col. 0078D] Ch. 1.]: “For this reason the new prophecies are rejected.” And in book III *Against Marcion* [Note: [Col. 0078D] Ch. 24.]: “The word of the New Prophecy, which abides with our faith, bears witness.” And in book IV [Note: [Col. 0078D] Ch. 22.]: “Which we defend in the cause of the New Prophecy.” And in the book *On the Resurrection of the Flesh* [Note: [Col. 0078D] Final chapter.]: “Through the New Prophecy, which pours forth from the Paraclete.” According to Firmilian, [Note: [Col. 0078D] Epistle 75 among those of Cyprian.] the Cataphrygians are those who “endeavor to appropriate new prophecies.” From this we also understand that the Catholics likewise called them “new prophets.” Since this is so, anyone who, amid the disputes then raging between Catholics and Montanists concerning new visions and [Col. 0079A] prophecies, openly and expressly testifies that he acknowledges and honors new visions and prophecies, plainly reveals himself and most openly professes himself to be a Montanist. Certainly no Catholic can be shown to have spoken in this manner. It is the profession of the Montanists, to which Tertullian, after embracing the doctrines of this sect, gave a parallel expression in these words: [Note: [Col. 0079D] *On the Soul*, ch. 19.] “For since we acknowledge spiritual charisms, etc.” So too the editor of the Acts: “We acknowledge and honor new visions and prophecies.” But according to Firmilian, those who endeavor to appropriate new prophecies are called Κατάφρυγες (*Cataphrygians*). The compiler of the Acts can therefore by no reasoning be removed from the catalogue of the Cataphrygians or Montanists.

I derive a third—and likewise extremely weighty—argument from a particular observation made by the author [Col. 0079B] when he relates how Perpetua was not conscious of having fought against the most savage cow: [Note: [Col. 0079D] In the Acts, no. 20.] “There Perpetua . . . awoke as if from sleep (so deeply,” says the author, “had she been in the spirit and in ecstasy), began to look around, and, while everyone stood astonished, said: ‘When are we to be brought out against that cow? I do not know.’” To what purpose can that observation—“so deeply had she been in the spirit and in ecstasy”—have been directed, unless to establish the Montanist doctrine concerning ecstasy?

It is indeed true that the Fathers sometimes used the word *ecstasy* in a favorable sense. Yet in those times when the Montanist heresy was especially rampant, it was generally understood in the worse sense, as signifying alienation of mind, frenzy, and madness. Hence, as Tertullian testifies, when Catholics and Montanists at that time disputed [Col. 0079C] whether ecstasy was compatible with true prophecy, the Montanists defended the affirmative opinion and the Catholics the negative. “In the cause of the New Prophecy,” says Tertullian, [Note: [Col. 0079D] Book IV, *Against Marcion*, ch. 22.] “we maintain that ecstasy—that is, madness—is compatible with grace . . . a matter concerning which there is a dispute between us and the Psychics.” Hence the books Περὶ ἐκστάσεως (*On Ecstasy*) written by that same Tertullian on behalf of the Montanists against the Church, as Jerome records. [Note: [Col. 0079D] *Catalogue*, under Apollonius and Tertullian.] Conversely, Miltiades, as Eusebius records, [Note: [Col. 0079D] Book V, ch. 17, from Asterius Urbanus, book III, *Against the Cataphrygians*.] wrote against the same Montanists under the title Περὶ τοῦ μὴ δεῖν προφήτην ἐν ἐκστάσει λαλεῖν, “That a prophet ought not to speak in ecstasy.”

On this passage of Eusebius, Valesius aptly observes that the Catholics made this their chief objection to the Montanists, who boasted that they were filled with the prophetic spirit: that they prophesied in ecstasy, [Col. 0079D] although neither in the New nor in the Old Testament do we ever read that the prophets prophesied in ecstasy. Who, then, could have so dull a nose that he did not scent Montanism in the foregoing words of our author?

I certainly do not intend to cast the odium of Montanism upon every writer who numbers ecstasies among the charisms of God. I am not unaware that this word was also sometimes understood in a favorable sense by the most ancient Fathers. Besides nocturnal visions, we learn from Cyprian of ecstasies sent by the Holy Spirit to innocent children during the day; and no suspicion of a corrupt opinion on this subject can be transferred to him: [Note: [Col. 0080D] Epistle 16, otherwise 10.] “Besides nocturnal visions, the innocent age of children among us is also filled by day with the Holy Spirit, and in ecstasy sees with its eyes and hears, etc.”

The case of the compiler of the Acts is nevertheless not the same. He committed these celebrated records to writing, not, like Cyprian and the other ancient Fathers afterward, once the disturbances caused by the Montanists had subsided, but while factions and dissensions were growing from day to day. At that time he certainly ought either to have abstained from the word *ecstasy*, or to have used it in such a way as to remove every reproach or suspicion of a corrupt meaning from it.

[Col. 0080B] III. I must now take up Dodwell, whose opinion, as I have already said, is that the compiler of the Acts not only belonged to the Catholic communion and was hostile to the Montanists, but also labored to publish these renowned records in order to convict their new prophecies of falsehood. He gives the following reason for this truly remarkable opinion of his:

“Maximilla had predicted of herself that after her there would be no other prophetess, but the consummation. Her words in Epiphanius are these: [Note: [Col. 0080D] Heresy XLVIII, §2.] Μετ᾽ ἐμὲ προφῆτις οὐκέτι ἔσται, ἀλλὰ συντέλεια, ‘After me there will no longer be a prophetess, but the consummation.’ It is most probable that Maximilla died toward the end of Marcus’s reign. For since Asterius Urbanus [Note: [Col. 0080D] In Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, chs. 16–17.] counts thirteen or fourteen years begun from her death to the year in which he was writing, learned men judge that it cannot more suitably be referred to any period other than the reign of Commodus. Catholics, by contrast, thought that the falsity of their prophetic pretensions could be proved from this very fact: that, even by their own admission, an end would at some point have to be assigned to their prophecy, whereas true prophecy would be perpetual and would in fact endure until the consummation of the world. By this reasoning they were so far from denying the prophecies of their own times that any church in which there were no prophets was not even to be regarded as a Church.”

Asterius Urbanus argued in this fashion: [Note: [Col. 0080D] Εἰ γὰρ μετὰ Καδράτον καὶ τὴν ἐν Φιλαδελφείᾳ Ἀμμίαν, ὥς φασιν, αἱ περὶ Μοντανὸν διεδέξαντο γυναῖκες τὸ προφητικὸν χάρισμα, τοὺς ἀπὸ Μοντανοῦ, καὶ τῶν γυναικῶν τίνες παρ᾽ αὐτοῖς διεδέξαντο, δειξάτωσαν· δεῖν γὰρ εἶναι τὸ προφητικὸν χάρισμα ἐν πάσῃ τῇ Ἐκκλησίᾳ μέχρι τῆς τελείας παρουσίας, ὁ Ἀποστόλος ἀξιοῖ, “For if, after Quadratus and Ammia of Philadelphia, as they say, the women associated with Montanus succeeded to the prophetic gift, let them show who among them succeeded the followers of Montanus and the women; for the Apostle declares that the prophetic gift must exist throughout the whole Church until the final coming.”] “For if, as they proclaim, after Quadratus and Ammia of Philadelphia those women associated with Montanus succeeded to the grace of prophecy, let them show us who among them succeeded Montanus and the women. For the Apostle declares that the gift of prophecy must remain throughout the whole Church until the final [Col. 0080D] coming of the Lord.”

“The ancient author of the Acts of Perpetua and Felicity, whoever he was, a contemporary of the martyrs, argues according to the same pattern. Having proved, by adducing the passage from Joel, that the prophecies of the New Testament were so far from falling short of those of the Old Testament that, on the contrary, even greater prophecies were to be expected under the New Testament, [Col. 0081A] he then adds the following in the sense I have stated: ‘Accordingly, we too, who acknowledge new visions as well as prophecies, etc.’ That whole discussion has precisely this purpose: to prevent the visions that would follow from being discredited because God had deigned to reveal them in the last times of the Church. To prevent this, he undertook to prove that they were chiefly to be expected in the last times, and always until the consummation. These things could perhaps be thought to have been said against the pagans; they could also have been said against the Montanists. I would rather believe that they were said against the Montanists, because he confirmed by the testimony of Scripture what he had said. It is certainly manifest that the points he advanced here were admitted among his own people, something that a Montanist could by no means have written.

[Col. 0081B] “For it should first be noted that these things were written by the author in A.D. 202, that is, about twenty-three years after Maximilla’s death. For we have said that she died in the last year of Marcus, namely A.D. 179. But if she had been a true prophetess, no other prophet was now to be expected. Therefore, one who still expected others, and believed that they were always to be expected, cannot possibly have regarded her as a true prophetess, and consequently could not have been a Montanist. For although that heresy was afterward divided into various sects, all nevertheless agreed that those first women were to be acknowledged as prophetesses.

“Secondly, even if we interpret Maximilla’s words in the most favorable sense and understand them as referring to female prophetesses, not to male prophets, [Col. 0081C] this preface still could not have been written by a Montanist. For he was about to include the visions of the prophetess Perpetua. Yet it is certain that this interpretation cannot be accommodated to Maximilla’s meaning. For when she said that after her there would be the συντέλεια (*consummation*), it necessarily followed that this would utterly exclude every further exercise of prophecy.

“Thirdly, since Asterius Urbanus had used this very argument at least ten years earlier in refuting that sect, who could believe that a patron of the sect would employ the same argument?

“Fourthly, it is also evident from Urbanus himself that they had in fact brought their entire succession of prophets to an end with Maximilla and had admitted no successor whatsoever after her. Epiphanius, employing the same argument, confirms that after her death no one else was acknowledged by the Montanists down to his own time. It is therefore impossible that a Montanist should have enrolled Saturus and Perpetua in the list of the prophets. At the very least, a reader who argues in this way must concede from the reasoning of those others that he ought not on that account to be regarded as a Montanist. Yet the admittedly learned men who think otherwise offer no other evidence.”

Thus Dodwell. Yet although his arguments are learnedly and subtly made, they could by no means wrest from me my assent. For in such matters the records of events possessing unquestionable credibility must prevail over all our subtle and learned observations. From those records, as I shall presently [Col. 0082A] show, it is manifest that Dodwell’s entire discussion contains nothing strong or solid enough to remove the suspicion of Montanism from our author.

IV. The learned man’s entire argument, then, rests upon these two foundations. First, Maximilla died toward the end of Marcus’s reign, about twenty-three years before Perpetua and Felicity and their companions underwent martyrdom. Secondly, the Montanists were persuaded that there would be no prophet after Maximilla’s death, and still less that another prophetess was to be expected after her. Consequently, the writer of the Acts—who regarded Saturus and Perpetua as distinguished by the gifts of prophecy and heavenly revelations, and believed that these same charisms would remain in the Church until the consummation—could not possibly have been imbued with the errors of the Montanists. To me, however, neither of the learned man’s assumptions seems admissible.

As regards the first point, Maximilla’s death, I know indeed that many hold the opinion that it should be assigned to the last year of Marcus. But, as I have shown elsewhere [Note: [Col. 0082D] Dissertation *De capit. crimin. absol.*, §2.] and Valesius observed long ago, [Note: [Col. 0082D] Annotation on Eusebius, book V, ch. 18.] their error arose from their belief that Asterius—who testifies that he wrote his books fourteen years after the death of Montanus and Maximilla—was earlier than Apollonius, by whom it was recorded that Montanus had introduced his prophecy forty years before Apollonius wrote. [Note: [Col. 0082D] In Eusebius, loc. cit.] But that was not how matters stood.

“For,” as Valesius observes, “Apollonius composed his book while Montanus was still alive, together with his frenzied prophetesses [Col. 0082C] Priscilla and Maximilla, as may be gathered from the fragments that Eusebius adduces, and this in more than one place. Thus he said: Ἡ προφῆτις ἡμῖν εἰπάτω τὰ κατὰ Ἀλέξανδρον τὸν λέγοντα ἑαυτὸν μάρτυρα, ᾧ συνεστιᾶται, ᾧ προσκυνοῦσι, καὶ αὐτῷ πολλοί, ‘Let the prophetess tell us about Alexander, who calls himself a martyr, with whom she feasts, and whom many even worship.’ And a little later, speaking about the same Alexander, he says: Ὃν ὁ προφήτης συνόντα πολλοῖς ἔτεσιν ἀνοεῖ, ‘Whom the prophet, though he has associated with him for many years, fails to recognize.’ From these words it is apparent that Alexander, Montanus himself, and Maximilla were still alive when Apollonius wrote these things. Nor does Apollonius say that forty years had elapsed from the death of Montanus to the time at which he was writing; he merely says that Montanus had introduced his false prophecy forty years before Apollonius himself undertook to write.”

Accordingly, since Apollonius composed his books during Severus’s reign, while Maximilla was still alive, [Col. 0082D] I demonstrated in the passage cited above that the fourteen years of undisturbed government and peace for the Church which Asterius mentions as having elapsed since Maximilla’s death must be reckoned from Caracalla’s accession after his father’s death to the earlier years of Alexander, and that Maximilla died around A.D. 212. Once these facts are recognized, Dodwell’s constructions upon his false date for Maximilla’s death readily collapse. For the most probable opinion of learned men, including Dodwell, is that Perpetua [Col. 0083A] and Felicity died as martyrs around A.D. 203, almost at the very beginning of the Severan persecution. Perpetua’s martyrdom therefore preceded Maximilla’s death by at least ten years. Thus a Montanist writer could acknowledge and venerate her prophecies and honor her as a prophetess, even though he knew—indeed, unshakably and firmly believed—that there would be no prophetess after Maximilla.

V. Furthermore, if we suppose that Dodwell’s conclusions concerning Maximilla’s death are true—namely, that she died in the last year of Marcus—it necessarily follows that what he states in the second place regarding Montanist agreement upon the proposition that there would be no prophetess in the Church after Maximilla is altogether false. For it can be demonstrated so clearly and openly that the Montanists acknowledged other prophetesses after Maximilla—if her death is assigned to the last year of Marcus—that it is astonishing that the learned man made this a foundation of his opinion.

Had Tertullian not defected to the Montanists when he wrote the book *On the Soul*? Did he not compose that book nearly thirty years after Maximilla’s death, if she died in the last year of Aurelius? Yet there he professes that he acknowledged other false prophetesses after that frenzied woman: [Note: [Col. 0083D] Ch. 9.] “Today among us there is a sister who has obtained charisms of revelations, which she experiences in the Church amid the Lord’s solemn rites through ecstasy in the spirit. She converses with angels, sometimes even with the Lord, and sees and hears mysteries, discerns the hearts of some, and provides remedies to those who desire them. Moreover, according as the Scriptures are read, or psalms sung, or addresses delivered, or petitions offered, material is thereby supplied for her visions. [Col. 0083C] We happened to have been discussing something about the soul while that sister was in the spirit. After the solemn rites had concluded and the congregation had been dismissed, according to the custom by which she regularly reports to us what she has seen—for the accounts are most carefully arranged so that they may also be tested—she said, among other things, ‘The soul was shown to me corporeally,’ etc.”

Behold an outstanding Montanist prophetess after Maximilla! Moreover, in the same book [Note: [Col. 0083D] Ch. 59.] Tertullian acknowledges and commends Perpetua’s revelations no less than does the author of the Passion, and therefore judged, no less than the compiler of the Acts, that Perpetua should be enrolled in the list of prophets: “Perpetua, the most courageous martyr, in a revelation of the glory of paradise saw there only her fellow martyrs.” Yet Perpetua had scarcely been born when Maximilla died, if she ceased to live toward the end of Marcus’s reign, namely in [Col. 0083D] 179; for in 203, the year in which she died as a martyr, she was, as the Acts state, about twenty-two years old.

Moreover, in the same book Tertullian is so far from believing that the spirit of prophecy failed in the Church after Montanus and Maximilla that he instead indicates that they had opened for him the way to receive new charisms, since those charisms had by no means been spurned in those false prophets. He establishes and confirms this perpetual and unfailing abundance of divine charisms from the testimony both of the Apostle in that passage and of Joel elsewhere, [Note: [Col. 0083D] Book *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, near the end.] just as does the writer of the Acts: [Col. 0084A] “For since we acknowledge spiritual charisms, we too have deserved, even after John, to obtain prophecy. And today there is a sister, etc.” After relating the frenzied prophetess’s vision, he adds: “This is the vision; God is witness, and the Apostle a competent guarantor of the charisms that would exist in the Church.”

Finally, in his book *On Fasting against the Psychics*, does he not reproach them precisely because they set boundaries—or, as he calls them, boundary stakes—to the charisms of divine grace? This charge could readily have been retorted against the Montanists themselves if they had set limits to those same gifts of grace in Maximilla: “But again,” he says, [Note: [Col. 0084D] Ch. 11.] “you fix boundary stakes for God, in discipline as in grace, and in solemn observances as in charisms, as though duties had ceased just as [Col. 0084B] his benefits had.”

While I was reflecting upon these matters, it occurred to me that perhaps the Montanists in Africa were not fully acquainted with all the oracles Maximilla had uttered in Asia. But I was recalled from this thought by Firmilian’s letter to Cyprian, [Note: [Col. 0084D] Epistle LXXV among those of Cyprian.] from which it is evident that even in Asia other prophetesses arose among the Montanists after Maximilla:

“About twenty-two years ago,” he says, “in the period after the emperor Alexander, many conflicts and afflictions occurred there, either commonly to all people or privately to Christians. . . . . . . . While the faithful were situated amid this disturbance . . . . . . a certain woman suddenly appeared there who, being placed in ecstasy, presented herself as a prophet and acted as though filled with the Holy Spirit. But she was borne along by such an impulse of the principal demons that for a long time she agitated and deceived the brotherhood, performing certain marvelous and portentous acts and promising that she would cause the earth to move. . . . . . . . . . . By these falsehoods and boasts she had subdued the mind of each person, so that they obeyed her and followed wherever she commanded and led. That spirit even caused the woman to walk barefoot through harsh snow in the depth of winter, without being distressed or harmed in any respect by that wandering; and she also said that she was hastening to Judaea and Jerusalem, pretending that she had come from there, etc.”

I have copied these words at such length so that everyone may understand what outstanding prophetesses the Montanists had even in Asia after Maximilla. Indeed, if the chronology agreed, one would believe this woman to have been Maximilla herself, so closely [Col. 0084D] does everything correspond to what Eusebius reports of Maximilla from Asterius Urbanus and other writers. For, in addition to what has already been said, the Catholics undertook to expose and refute the spirit of each woman; and just as Maximilla, in Tertullian’s words, [Note: [Col. 0084D] *On Fasting*, ch. 1.] “preached no other God nor,” in the judgment of the same Tertullian, “overthrew any rule of faith or hope,” so this woman, as Firmilian records, baptized “many, employing the customary and legitimate words of interrogation, so that she appeared to differ in no respect from the ecclesiastical rule.” A little earlier he had said of the same woman that “she also frequently dared to sanctify bread by an invocation that was not contemptible, to pretend to celebrate the Eucharist, and to offer sacrifice to the Lord, not without the mystery of the customary formula.” All these things are marks of the Montanist spirit, and ancient writers have recorded that Montanus permitted such things to his prophetesses.

It is therefore evident that no one should be erased from the catalogue of Montanists merely because he acknowledged another prophetess after Maximilla. For although this frenzied prophetess proclaimed concerning herself, Μετ᾽ ἐμὲ προφῆτις οὐκέτι ἔσται, “After me there will no longer be a prophetess,” etc., it could nevertheless happen—and this very frequently befalls sectarians—that they were unwilling to attend to such manifest falsehoods, or that they understood her to mean another kind of prophetess, one who would introduce a new and more perfect doctrine and discipline. In this sense the patriarchs of the Montanists themselves called themselves “new prophets,” because in their own judgment they had inaugurated after the Apostles a new prophecy. However that may be, it is now clear, I think, that Dodwell rests upon a far too feeble prop when he removes the compiler of the Acts from the catalogue of Montanists on the ground that the latter regarded Perpetua as a prophet after Maximilla, since Tertullian too, a professed Montanist, placed her in the same rank and category.

VI. From this point, however, as I said above, Basnage derives his first argument against the holy martyrs:

“From the compiler of the Acts there arises for us a highly probable conjecture that Perpetua and those martyrs who joined themselves to her as companions in death belonged to the flock [Col. 0085C] of the Montanists. Certainly no one of this household would have published the Acts of Catholic martyrs, whom they held in contempt as Psychics. It is also evident that Perpetua, Felicity, and Saturus professed the same faith as the author of the Acts, as is clear from his own words: ‘And so we too announce to you, brethren and little children, what we have heard and touched, so that those of you who were present may remember the glory of the Lord, and that those who now learn of it by hearing may have communion with the holy martyrs.’ But the compiler of the Acts reveals himself by his own testimony to be a Montanist.

“Furthermore, Tertullian, most bitterly hostile to the Catholics and a most ardent defender of Montanus, bestows great praises upon Perpetua and uses her visions to prove that only martyrs are received into heaven before the day of solemn judgment: [Col. 0085D] ‘How,’ he says, ‘did Perpetua, the most courageous martyr, etc.’ This argument is all the weightier because Tertullian, both a contemporary of Perpetua and a resident of Carthage, where Perpetua exchanged life for death, could not have been ignorant of the sect to which either that woman or the compiler of her Passion belonged. It is more certain than certainty itself that Tertullian would not have wished such numerous and great praises to be bestowed upon any of the Psychics, much less to have that person’s words and authority employed to prove the proposition he was maintaining.”

In order that this argument—which, particularly to me, might at first sight appear capable of creating some difficulty—may be thoroughly dispelled and overthrown, I must make certain observations about the Montanists. The entire plausibility of that argument derives from a failure to recognize them.

[Col. 0086A] Let the first observation be that Catholics were not regarded as heretics by those Montanists who had not altogether lost their reason, such as Tertullian. This is established first from his book *On Monogamy*, where at the very beginning he distinguishes the Psychics from heretics: “Heretics abolish marriage; Psychics multiply it.” If one asks how this could be, the explanation is readily available, and the same author adds it a little later: in his judgment, the whole difference between the Montanists and Catholics was a matter not of faith but of discipline. For by this reasoning he endeavors to free his Paraclete from the suspicion of heresy:

“For the adversarial spirit would reveal itself by the diversity of its preaching, first corrupting the rule of faith and then corrupting the order of discipline. For the corruption of that which occupies the prior rank comes first—that is, of faith, which precedes discipline. A person must first be a heretic concerning God and only then concerning an ordinance. But the Paraclete, having many things to teach which the Lord deferred to him, will, in accordance with the prior definition, first attest Christ himself as we believe him, together with the whole order of God the Creator; and he will glorify him and bring him to remembrance. Once recognized in this way by the principal rule, he will reveal those many things that belong to disciplines, the integrity of his preaching concerning them pledging the faith, although they are new because they are only now revealed.”

By the same reasoning, in the book *On Fasting*, [Note: [Col. 0086D] Ch. 11.] he also attempted to repel the charge of heresy raised by Catholics against Montanus and set forth the same rule for judging heresies. For when the Catholics objected against the discipline and institution introduced through Montanus that it was “either false prophecy, if a spiritual voice instituted those solemn observances, or heresy, if human presumption invented them,” he answered as follows: “Without doubt, both heresy and false prophecy will be judged among us by their difference concerning the deity—we who are ministers of the one God, the Creator, and of his Christ.”

He has similar statements near the beginning of his book *On the Veiling of Virgins*. There he explains more clearly the rule of faith mentioned in the preceding passages: one who corrupts that rule is a heretic; one who preserves it, although he corrupts or alters the order of discipline, should not, in Tertullian’s judgment, be regarded as a heretic. He maintains that the things Montanus added to the preaching and institutions of the Apostles were of this kind: they were ordained, while the same rule of faith remained intact, to perfect discipline. Therefore, one should not raise a prescription of antiquity against Montanus; nor should the Montanists be numbered among heretics because of these new [Col. 0086D] institutions; nor, as we shall see below, should they be regarded as excluded from the communion of the apostolic churches:

“The rule of faith is indeed absolutely one, alone immovable and irreformable: namely, belief in one almighty God, Creator of the world, and in his Son Jesus Christ, born of the Virgin Mary, crucified under Pontius Pilate, raised from the dead on the third day, received into heaven, now sitting at the right hand of the Father, and coming to judge the living and the dead, together with the resurrection of the flesh. While this law of faith remains, the other matters of discipline and conduct admit the novelty of correction. . . . [Col. 0087A] What, then, is the administration of the Paraclete, if not this: that discipline is set in order, etc.?”

There follows later a discussion of the communion which the Montanists boasted that they had with the apostolic churches because of their agreement in the same faith and the same sacraments of faith; this we shall examine below.

Meanwhile, I draw the same argument from what Tertullian teaches at the beginning of the book *Against Praxeas*. Although he openly admits that, because of his acknowledgment and defense of the Paraclete, he was separated from the Psychics, he nevertheless sets forth the same rule for judging heresies. From that rule it plainly follows that, in his judgment, this disagreement between Montanists and Psychics did not concern matters that injured the faith or from which heresies could spring:

“But we, both always and now still more, as persons better instructed through the Paraclete, who is indeed the guide into all truth, believe in one God, yet under this dispensation, which we call οἰκονομία (*economy*): that the one God also has a Son, his Word, who proceeded from him, through whom all things were made and without whom nothing was made. He was sent by the Father into the Virgin and was born of her, man and God, Son of Man and Son of God, and surnamed Jesus Christ. He suffered, died, and was buried according to the Scriptures; he was raised by the Father and taken back into heaven; he sits at the right hand of the Father and will come to judge the living and the dead. From there, according to his promise, he sent from the Father the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, the sanctifier of the faith of those who believe in the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit.

“That this rule has run its course from the beginning of the Gospel, [Col. 0087C] even before all the earlier heretics, much more before yesterday’s Praxeas, will be proved as much by the lateness of all the heretics as by the very novelty of yesterday’s Praxeas. Thus from this point onward a prior judgment may be established equally against all heresies: whatever is first is true; whatever is later is corrupted.”

Tertullian certainly was not ignorant—indeed, he openly admitted—that the prophecy of Montanus was new, that his preaching was new, and that his institutions had by no means run their course from the beginning of the Gospel, but had, as the Montanists babbled, been deferred by Christ to these later times. Hence he could remove from his Montanus the blame and infamy of heresy or heretical corruption in no other way than by saying that the traditions introduced by him only yesterday did not corrupt the rule of faith but perfected discipline. Accordingly, the controversies raised between Montanists and Catholics concerned discipline, not faith; and neither the one group nor the other was to be entered upon the register of heretics merely because, while preserving the rule of faith, they disagreed with one another in matters of conduct and discipline.

The same point is also evident—to omit very many other examples—from the entire book *On Prescriptions against Heretics*. Under that title he certainly does not include the Psychics or Catholics, since nothing does he press more strongly against heretics than ancient and apostolic traditions and the authority of the apostolic churches; nothing does he reproach in heretics more strongly than novelty. Indeed, his declared purpose, as we learn from him, was to refute all the sects of heretics on this ground alone: [Col. 0088A] “But another little book,” he says, [Note: [Col. 0088D] Book I, *Against Marcion*, ch. 1.] “will maintain this position against the heretics, who may be refuted even without an examination of their doctrines, because by the prescription of novelty they are shown to be what they are.”

Yet the book just cited, as Basnage himself also teaches, [Note: [Col. 0088D] Under A.D. 200, no. IX. See also Pagi, under A.D. 195, no. IV.] was composed by Tertullian after he had defected to the Montanists. It was written against all heresies, as Tertullian himself expressly testifies elsewhere: [Note: [Col. 0088D] *On the Flesh of Christ*, ch. 2.] “But elsewhere we have already employed such prescriptions more fully against all heresies.” Since, therefore, nothing occurs in that book that could offend Catholics—indeed, nothing that was not stated in accordance with their position—so much so that many have held the opinion [Note: [Col. 0088D] See Pamelius, *Life of Tertullian*, under A.D. 203, vol. I, col. 65; compare Aug. Noesselt, *Dissertations*, vol. I, cols. 171–177.] that Tertullian composed it before embracing the doctrines of Montanus, it follows that the Psychics or Catholics were not [Col. 0088B] numbered by Tertullian among the heretics.

VII. Secondly, it must be noted—something that follows naturally from the foregoing and confirms still more clearly what has already been said—that the Montanists, although they differed in conduct and discipline from the institutions and customs of the apostolic Churches, nevertheless did not consider themselves alienated from their communion in those matters upon which the substance of faith and the Christian religion turns. This is established from the same Tertullian and almost the same passages. For in his book *On the Veiling of Virgins*, after teaching that Catholics and Montanists agreed upon one rule of faith, and that the Paraclete had not corrupted the faith but had applied the finishing touch to discipline, he immediately adds:

> “Throughout Greece and in certain barbarian regions, a number of its Churches [Col. 0088C] conceal their virgins. Under this very sky, too, that institution is observed in some places, lest anyone attribute that custom to Greek paganism or barbarian practice. But I have set before you those Churches which the Apostles themselves, or apostolic men, founded—and, I think, before certain others. Those Churches, therefore, possess the same authority of custom: they can set their antiquity and their predecessors against these later Churches. What shall we observe? What shall we choose? We cannot reject a custom that we cannot condemn, since it is not foreign to us, because it is practiced by no foreigners, but by those with whom we share the right of peace and the name of brotherhood. We and they have one faith, one God, the same Christ, and the same sacraments of the washing. Let me say it once: we are one Church. Thus whatever belongs to our own people belongs to us.”

But nothing clearer can be adduced to prove this [Col. 0088D] than the extremely acute arguments to the same effect in the book *On Prescriptions against Heretics*, which, as I have said, he composed when he was already a Montanist. I have thought it worthwhile to adduce several passages from that book, although they are rather lengthy, because they settle the matter completely and place it in the clearest light.

He therefore says that, in order to convict heretics, this alone must be debated [Note: [Col. 0088D] Chap. 19]:

> “To whom the faith itself belongs; [Col. 0089A] whose the Scriptures are; by whom, through whom, when, and to whom the discipline by which people become Christians was handed down. For wherever the truth of Christian discipline and faith is found to be, there will also be the truth of the Scriptures, their interpretations, and all Christian traditions.”

He then adds that the Apostles, having been instructed by Christ [Note: [Col. 0089D] Chap. 20],

> “and having received the promised power of the Holy Spirit for mighty works and utterance, first bore witness throughout Judaea to faith in Jesus Christ and established Churches; then, setting out into the world, they proclaimed to the nations the same doctrine of the same faith, and accordingly founded a Church in each city. From these Churches, the other Churches thereafter borrowed—and daily continue to borrow—the shoot of faith and the seeds of doctrine, so that they themselves might become Churches. For this reason they too are regarded as apostolic [Col. 0089B], being the offspring of apostolic Churches. Every kind must necessarily be classified according to its origin. Thus the many and great Churches are that one first Church from the Apostles, from which they all derive: in this way all are first and all are apostolic, while all together demonstrate unity—while among them there is the communion of peace, the designation of brotherhood, and the mutual pledge of hospitality. These rights are governed by no principle other than the single tradition of the same sacrament.

> “We therefore lay down this prescription [Note: [Col. 0089D] Chap. 21]: if the Lord Jesus Christ sent the Apostles to preach, no preachers are to be received other than those whom Christ appointed. . . . And as to what they preached—that is, what Christ revealed to them—I prescribe here that this must be proved in no other way than through the very Churches which the Apostles themselves founded, preaching [Col. 0089C] to them personally, both by the living voice, as they say, and later through letters. If these things are so, it follows that every doctrine agreeing with those apostolic Churches, the matrices and origins of the faith, must be accounted true, as undoubtedly preserving what the Churches received from the Apostles, the Apostles from Christ, and Christ from God. Every other doctrine, however, must be prejudged false if it savors of anything contrary to the truth of the Churches, the Apostles, Christ, and God.

> “It therefore remains for us to demonstrate whether this doctrine of ours, whose rule we set forth above, is reckoned as deriving from the tradition of the Apostles, and consequently whether the others proceed from falsehood. We are in communion with the apostolic Churches because our doctrine differs from theirs in no respect: this is the testimony of truth.”
