And below, against the heresies [Col. 0089D] that boasted of their antiquity and represented themselves to the unlearned as apostolic because they had existed under the Apostles, he says that it rested upon them to show either that they had some Apostle, or some apostolic man who had persevered with the Apostles, as the author of their institution, or at least that they possessed the communion of the apostolic Churches [Note: [Col. 0089D] Chap. 32]:

> “But if any of them dare to insert themselves into the apostolic age, so that they may therefore appear to have been handed down by the Apostles because they existed under the Apostles, we can say: let them then produce the origins of their Churches; let them unroll the succession of their bishops, [Col. 0090A] running down from the beginning in such a way that their first bishop had as his founder and predecessor one of the Apostles, or one of the apostolic men who nevertheless persevered with the Apostles. For this is the manner in which the apostolic Churches present their registers: thus the Church of the Smyrnaeans reports that Polycarp was installed by John; thus the Church of the Romans produces Clement, ordained by Peter; and so, of course, the others likewise exhibit those whom they possess as shoots of the apostolic seed, having been appointed to the episcopate by the Apostles.

> “Let the heretics fabricate something of this kind. For what is unlawful to them after blasphemy? Yet even if they fabricate it, they will accomplish nothing. For their very doctrine, when compared with the apostolic doctrine, will declare by its diversity and opposition that it has neither an Apostle nor an apostolic man [Col. 0090B] for its author. For just as the Apostles would not have taught doctrines differing from one another, so apostolic men would not have promulgated doctrines contrary to the Apostles, except for those who deserted the Apostles and preached otherwise.

> “To this standard, therefore, they will be summoned even by those Churches which, being much later—indeed, Churches that are established daily—can produce no Apostle or apostolic man as their founder, yet, because they agree in the same faith, are no less regarded as apostolic by reason of their kinship in doctrine. Thus let all the heresies, when summoned by our Churches to both standards, prove themselves apostolic in whatever way they think possible. But they are not apostolic, nor can they prove what they are not; nor are they received into peace and communion by Churches that are apostolic in any sense, since, because of the diversity of their sacrament, [Col. 0090C] they are in no sense apostolic.”

But nothing is clearer than what, not much further below, he says concerning the principal apostolic Churches, and especially the Roman Church, in these words [Note: [Col. 0090D] Chap. 36]:

> “Come now, you who wish to exercise your curiosity more profitably in the business of your salvation: visit the apostolic Churches, among which the very chairs of the Apostles still preside in their own places, and among which their own authentic letters are recited, sounding forth the voice and representing the face of each one. Achaia is near you: you have Corinth. If you are not far from Macedonia, you have Philippi and Thessalonica. If you can travel into Asia, you have Ephesus; but if you are adjacent to Italy, you have Rome, from which authority is also readily available to us.

> “How fortunate is that Church, upon which the Apostles poured out their whole doctrine together with their blood, [Col. 0090D] where Peter was made equal to the Lord in his manner of suffering; where Paul was crowned with an end like John’s; where the Apostle John, after being plunged into burning oil and suffering no harm, was banished to an island. Let us see what it has said, what it has taught, and what pledge of fellowship it has exchanged even with the African Churches. It knows one God, the Creator of the universe; Christ Jesus, born of the Virgin Mary, the Son of God the Creator; and the resurrection of the flesh. It combines the Law and the Prophets with the evangelical and apostolic writings, and from these it drinks in the faith; that faith it seals with water, clothes with the Holy Spirit, feeds with the Eucharist, and exhorts to martyrdom. And so, against this institution, [Col. 0091A] it receives no one.

> “This is the institution—I no longer say merely that it foretold the heresies that were to come, but that the heresies came forth from it. Yet they did not belong to it from the moment they became opposed to it. Even from the kernel of a mild, rich, and useful olive springs the harsh wild olive; even from the seed of the most pleasing and sweetest fig rises the wind-filled and empty caprifig. So too the heresies bore fruit from our stock, but were not ours: degenerate from the grain of truth, they became wild through falsehood.”

Could Baronius, Bellarmine, or others regarded as most devoted to the Roman Church have proclaimed anything about it more magnificent or more illustrious? Who would believe that these words could have escaped from a heretical man who had been cast out by the Roman Church—words by which absolutely all heresies opposed to the doctrine of that same Church [Col. 0091B] are overthrown? No one at all, unless he has attended to what we have thus far deduced from this author: namely, that it had not entered the minds of the Montanists that, on account of the new prophecy and discipline, they had fallen away from communion with the apostolic Churches in matters of faith and in those upon which the substance of religion turns.

Nevertheless, because not everyone agrees that the book *On Prescriptions* was not composed by Tertullian while he still moved among the Catholics, I shall add from Book IV *Against Marcion*—which, it is agreed, was composed by him after he had begun, as he says, to have disputes with the “Psychics” [Note: [Col. 0091D] See chap. 23]—a similar testimony concerning the apostolic Churches, and especially the Roman Church: namely, that whatever departs from their tradition in matters of faith must be regarded as adulterated and heretical, [Col. 0091C] and whatever does not share with them one and the same faith must be considered foreign [Note: [Col. 0091D] Chap. 5]:

> “In short, if it is established that what is earlier is truer, that what is from the beginning is earlier, and that what is from the Apostles is from the beginning, it will likewise certainly be established that what has been held sacred among the Churches of the Apostles was handed down by the Apostles. Let us see what milk the Corinthians drank from Paul; to what rule the Galatians were corrected; what the Philippians, Thessalonians, and Ephesians read; and what the Romans close at hand also proclaim, to whom both Peter and Paul left the Gospel sealed with their own blood.

> “We also have the Churches fostered by John. For although Marcion rejects his Apocalypse, the succession of bishops, when traced back to its origin, will rest upon John as its author. In the same way the noble descent of the other Churches [Col. 0091D] is recognized. I therefore say that among those Churches—and no longer among the apostolic Churches alone, but among all that are joined to them by fellowship in the sacrament—that Gospel of Luke which we now particularly defend has stood from the beginning of its publication.”

Certainly he would never have dared to write these and similar statements, which occur everywhere in his works, even in those books that were demonstrably published after he had fallen into the dogma of Montanus, unless he believed that he shared the same dogmas of faith as the apostolic Churches. Tertullian certainly was not unaware that the new prophecy was condemned by the Roman Church [Col. 0092A], and that the discipline introduced by Montanus was rejected. Yet everywhere he proclaims the authority of the Roman Church and the other apostolic Churches, and exalts it in a remarkable manner; and he decrees that those who do not agree in one and the same faith with the apostolic Churches are alien to Christianity, the Apostles, and Christ. This is assuredly the most certain proof that the Montanists were not persuaded that they had fallen away from the communion of the Catholic Church in matters of faith.

Finally, to pass over the innumerable statements that might be adduced here to the same effect, Tertullian’s judgment was that the true Church of Christ was not restricted to the Montanist sect alone, but that Catholics also belonged to one and the same body of the Church, [Col. 0092B] whose members, although they did not follow precisely the same institutions of conduct, were nevertheless bound together by the same faith and the same sacraments. This is clearly shown by what he argues against the pagans concerning the breadth of the Christian name and Church [Note: [Col. 0092D] *Apology*, chap. 37]:

> “We are but of yesterday, and yet we have filled everything that belongs to you: cities, islands, fortresses, towns, meeting places, the very camps, tribes, companies, the palace, the senate, and the forum. We leave you only the temples. For what war would we not have been fit and ready, even though unequal in resources—we who so willingly allow ourselves to be slaughtered—if under this discipline it were not more lawful to be killed than to kill?

> “Even unarmed and without rebelling, but merely separating from you, we could have fought against you by the hostile act of separation alone. For if so great a multitude of people had broken away from you [Col. 0092C] into some remote corner of the world, the loss of so many citizens, of whatever sort, would certainly have covered your rule with shame; indeed, it would have punished you by that very abandonment. Without doubt you would have been terrified by your desolation, by the silence of affairs, and by the stupor, as it were, of a dead city; you would have sought people over whom you might rule within it. More enemies than citizens would have remained to you. As things now stand, however, you have fewer enemies because of the multitude of Christians—almost all your citizens, almost all citizens being Christians. But you preferred to call us enemies of the human race rather than enemies of human error.”

These words certainly cannot be understood of the Montanists alone, for that sect never expanded its boundaries so widely. Nor can they be understood of Christians insofar as heretics too are included under that name. For in the same book [Note: [Col. 0092D] Ibid., chap. 46], he plainly excludes heretics from the number of Christians:

> “But someone will say that some of our own people also depart from the rule of discipline: they then cease to be regarded by us as Christians.”

This Church, therefore, whose blameless and most holy conduct he describes and defends throughout the book, and from whose bosom, he says, many—and at that time innumerable—martyrs had come forth, whose blood was the seed of Christians, included neither heretics nor Montanists alone, but especially Catholics. These, as the same Tertullian says [Note: [Col. 0092D] *On Fasts*, chap. 40], boasted of their multitude; and it is established that from among them [Col. 0093A], more than from other sects, innumerable martyrs were crowned. Nevertheless, since in Tertullian’s judgment, at the time when he published the *Apology*—namely, in the midst of intense persecution—the Montanists themselves were still counted among the Catholics, it is clear that, in his view, they and the true Catholics constituted one and the same Church of Christ. Although that Church did not everywhere employ precisely the same institutions of conduct, it was nevertheless to be regarded as one and the same body of religion because it agreed upon the same dogmas of faith and employed the same sacraments of faith.

VIII. Thirdly, it must be noted—something that likewise follows naturally from the foregoing—that Catholic martyrs were regarded by the Montanists as true martyrs, and that the Montanists sought in some manner a path to communion with them. [Col. 0093B] Asterius Urbanus recorded that Catholic martyrs abhorred communion with the Montanists, but not, conversely, that the Montanists rejected communion with Catholic martyrs [Note: [Col. 0093D]

> Ὃθεν τοι καὶ ἐπειδὰν οἱ ἐπὶ τὸ τῆς κατὰ ἀλήθειαν πίστεως μαρτύριον πληθέντες ἀπὸ τῆς Ἐκκλησίας τύχωσι μετά τινων τῶν ἀπὸ τῆς τῶν Φρυγῶν αἱρέσεως λεγομένων μαρτύρων, διαφέρονταί τε πρὸς αὐτοὺς, καὶ μὴ κοινωνήσαντες αὐτοῖς τελειοῦνται, διὰ τὸ μὴ βούλεσθαι συγκαταθέσθαι τῷ διὰ Μοντανοῦ καὶ τῶν γυναικῶν πνεύματι· καὶ ὅτι τοῦτο ἀληθὲς καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν ἡμετέρων χρόνων ἐν Ἀπαμείᾳ τῇ πρὸς Μαιάνδρῳ τυγχάνει γεγενημένον, ἐν τοῖς περὶ Γάϊον καὶ Ἀλέξανδρον ἀπὸ Εὐμενείας μαρτυρήσασι, πρόδηλον.

> “Hence, whenever members of the Church who have been brought to martyrdom for the true faith happen to encounter some of those from the Phrygian heresy who are called martyrs, they differ from them and attain their end without having entered into communion with them, because they are unwilling to assent to the spirit that speaks through Montanus and the women. That this is true is manifest from what occurred in our own times at Apamea on the Maeander in the case of Gaius and Alexander of Eumeneia, who suffered martyrdom.”

In Eusebius, Book V, chap. 16]:

> “Therefore,” he says, “whenever men of the Church called to undergo martyrdom for the true faith have happened by chance to come together with certain persons from the Phrygian heresy who are called martyrs, they always disagree with them; and, carefully avoiding communion with them, they attain the glorious end of martyrdom, since they consider it impious to assent to the spirit of Montanus and the women. That this is true is established by what was done in our own age in the city of Apamea, situated on the Maeander, by the martyrs Gaius and Alexander, natives of Eumeneia.”

Clear proofs of this matter [Col. 0093C] are also available to us from the same Tertullian, first of all from his book *To the Martyrs*. Since this was published while persecution was raging, there is no doubt that it belongs to the class of works he composed while serving in the camp of Montanus.

First, it is certain that this book was dedicated to persons who, even in Tertullian’s judgment, were true martyrs of Christ, since he heaps innumerable praises upon them and repeatedly calls them blessed [Note: [Col. 0093D] Chap. 1]:

> “Among the provisions for the flesh, O blessed martyrs-designate. First, therefore, O blessed ones, etc. [Note: [Col. 0093D] Chap. 2]. Wherefore you, O blessed ones, from prison, etc. [Note: [Col. 0093D] Chap. 3]. So now, O blessed ones. Accordingly, you blessed women, etc. [Note: [Col. 0093D] Chap. 4]. These things, O blessed ones, are not without reason, etc.”

Secondly, it is certain that those upon whom he heaps so many blessings and whom he extols with praises reaching to heaven were not Montanist [Col. 0093D] martyrs, but Catholics, or at least were for the most part drawn from the Catholics. This is established from the first chapter, where he exhorts them to mutual peace in these words [Col. 0094A]:

> “Certain persons who do not possess this peace in the Church have been accustomed to entreat it from the martyrs in prison. And for that very reason you too ought to possess and preserve it among yourselves, so that perhaps you may be able to bestow it upon others also.”

For this was a Catholic custom: those who had been cast out of communion for capital offenses implored the aid of the martyrs. Moreover, Catholics would certainly not have had recourse to Montanists, whom they knew to disapprove of such a custom and practice of the Catholic Church.

Thirdly, it is certain that Tertullian by no means believed the martyrs to whom he addressed a book of this kind to be alien from his own communion. For he asks that, among the provisions for the flesh which the Church supplied to them, they also accept from him this little gift, which would contribute to nourishing the spirit. This is assuredly an indubitable proof [Col. 0094B] of mutual communion.

Finally, it is certain that the Church which, like a devoted mother, sustained the praised martyrs with provisions for the flesh was, even in Tertullian’s judgment, the true Church of Christ:

> “Among the provisions for the flesh, O blessed martyrs-designate, which our lady mother the Church supplies to you in prison from her breasts, and which the individual brethren supply from their own resources, receive something also from us that may contribute to the nourishment of the spirit as well.”

Yet the Catholic Church would not have been concerned for any but Catholic martyrs. Furthermore, among the principal excellences of the Roman Church, on account of which, as we saw above, he commends it so highly, he also lists this: that it exhorted its own people to martyrdom. “It exhorts to martyrdom,” he says. But what praise or glory would there have been in producing for Christ not genuine but adulterous [Col. 0094C] martyrs? Or who can doubt whether Tertullian held the true martyrs of Christ in honor and desired communion with them?

Lastly, Basnage himself, I think, will not deny that the greater part of those martyrs whose faith, constancy, and multitude Tertullian so frequently proclaims both in the *Apology* and in the book *To Scapula*, as well as elsewhere, were Catholics—unless perhaps he wishes to deprive the Catholic, and therefore true, Church of Christ of this exceptional praise: that it was the most fruitful mother of holy martyrs.

IX. Once these points have been observed, I think that no difficulty remains in the arguments proposed by Basnage. For who should wonder—if he has attended to the matters we have discussed thus far—who, I ask, should wonder that a Montanist author wished to publish the acts of Catholic martyrs [Col. 0094D] and exhorted his own people to enter into communion with them? Is this more surprising than the fact that an author who was likewise a Montanist addressed to them a book filled with their praises—surely a token of communion? Or than the fact that he commended so highly the communion of the apostolic Churches, among whose principal members martyrs are numbered?

Who should also wonder that Tertullian lavished great praise upon Perpetua and adorned her with the encomium of a most courageous martyr? Is it not more remarkable that, in a book dedicated to Catholic martyrs, he should heap so many blessings upon them and say that the “director of their contest” (*agonothetes*) was [Note: [Col. 0094D] Chap. 3]:

> “the living God; their master of the training ground (*xystarches*) [Col. 0095A], the Holy Spirit; the prize, the crown of eternity; their citizenship in heaven, that of the angelic substance; their glory, for ever and ever”?

Finally, who should wonder that he wished to use Perpetua’s visions to prove that, before the day of the solemn judgment, martyrs alone are received into heaven? This is assuredly no more remarkable than the fact that, in a book published against the Church, he mentions with great praise the martyr Rutilius and uses his example to prove that one must not flee persecution, because flight is of no avail if God does not will it:

> “Rutilius, a most holy martyr, although he had so often fled persecution from place to place,” he says [Note: [Col. 0095D] *On Flight in Persecution*, chap. 5], “and had even redeemed himself from danger, as he thought, with money, was unexpectedly arrested after all the security he had provided for himself and was brought before the governor. He was torn by tortures [Col. 0095B]—I believe, as chastisement for his flight—and was then given to the flames; and he credited to the mercy of God the suffering he had avoided. What else did the Lord wish to demonstrate to us by this example except that one must not flee, because flight is of no avail if God does not will it?”

Basnage, I think, will not say that this man was a Montanist martyr, since he believed it lawful to provide for his safety by flight and to buy off danger with money—things that were regarded as unlawful under the discipline of Montanus. Nevertheless, Tertullian heaps so many and such great encomia upon him and employs his example, as that of a most holy martyr, to prove the position he was maintaining.

He also mentions with praise Mavilus, the martyr of Hadrumetum, in his book *To Scapula*, and uses his example to prove the position he was maintaining: namely, that no city [Col. 0095C] and no persecutor would shed Christian blood with impunity [Note: [Col. 0095D] Chap. 3]:

> “We also hope that in your case it was only a warning: after you had condemned Mavilus of Hadrumetum to the beasts, this affliction immediately followed; and now, from the same cause, comes this summons concerning blood.”

Will Basnage therefore dare, on so slight a conjecture—namely, that he was praised by Tertullian—to pronounce this man too a martyr of the Montanist sect?

As I have shown, the Montanists did not hold the Psychics in such contempt that they failed to distinguish them from heretics, regarded them as belonging to an alien communion in matters of faith, or treated their martyrs also with ridicule. Nor did Tertullian, although most hostile to the Catholics and a most ardent defender of Montanus, ever advance to such a point of madness that he either denied the crown of martyrdom to those who had died as martyrs in the bosom of the Catholic Church [Col. 0095D], or grudged them the praises and encomia they deserved.

X. So that we may be less surprised at this conduct among the Montanists, there is no lack of similar examples among heretics. For with what great praises do Socrates and Sozomen, although Novatians, adorn not only Catholic martyrs but also Catholic teachers? I do not mean those martyrs or teachers who flourished in the Catholic Church before Novatian created his schism, but those who arose afterward, and concerning whom the authors just praised knew perfectly well that the Novatians numbered them among the heretics.

For with what encomia do they not honor Hosius, Athanasius, Alexander of Constantinople, [Col. 0096A] Basil the Great, Gregory the Theologian, and other Catholic teachers of that kind? What authority do those same writers not grant to the Nicene Fathers? What reverence and honor do they not show to that great council, although it numbered the Cathari, or Novatians, among the heretics?

What, moreover, shall I say of those martyrs who suffered under Julian the Apostate, under the Arian emperor Valens, and in Persia under Sapor? With what praises are they celebrated by Socrates and Sozomen? Do they not number them among the true and genuine martyrs of Christ? Do they not publish their Acts, insofar as the plan followed in writing their histories permitted? Do they not ascribe to them the same authority as to the ancient martyrs, although they were well aware that these men belonged not to the Novatian but to the Catholic communion? [Col. 0096B]

And shall we then wonder if a Montanist author collected the Acts of certain Catholic martyrs and committed them to writing? If Tertullian called them most courageous martyrs and granted some authority and honor to their revelations? Shall we suppose that this constitutes the gravest presumption against their orthodoxy, and that they must consequently be removed from the number of Catholic martyrs and surrendered to the Montanists?

If that is so, then so many most holy teachers—indeed, even the Nicene Fathers themselves—so many most courageous martyrs, and so many most devout monks whose praises neither Socrates nor Sozomen passed over in silence must also be erased from the diptychs of the Catholics. Let them, I say, be erased from the diptychs of the Catholic Churches and assigned to the Novatians, merely because Novatian writers [Col. 0096C] bestowed so many and such great encomia upon them.

XI. But I believe not only that no prejudice against the holy martyrs can be created from the testimony of a Montanist author, but that from it I can fashion a most weighty argument in their favor. For a Montanist writer would not have concealed—or indicated only in ambiguous and obscure words—that the most courageous champions who became martyrs belonged to his sect; that the new prophecy had produced such fruits; and that, through the stricter discipline he had introduced, Montanus had trained even women unsuited to combat for contests of this kind.

On the contrary, he would have openly proclaimed these and other similar matters in plain words, and, whether seasonably or unseasonably, would have impressed them upon his readers on almost every page. Do we not know how heretics boast concerning such matters, how they are accustomed to take empty pride in them, and, when a similar opportunity presents itself, to rage with the greatest shamelessness against Catholics?

An example may be found in the Donatist author who committed to literary record the Acts of the holy martyrs Saturninus, Dativus, and their companions. For although the martyrs just praised did not belong to the Donatist sect—since the schism was not created under the pretext of the surrender of the Scriptures until after the persecution had subsided—nevertheless, because they suffered rather than surrender the divine Scriptures to the persecutors, and seemed by their example to have condemned the *traditores* in advance and cast them out of their communion, it is remarkable how much the writer boasts on that account, and with what shamelessness that most insolent author attacks the Catholics:

> “When the devil had been conquered and overthrown [Col. 0097A],” he says [Note: [Col. 0096D] In the preface], “all the martyrs, bearing the victorious palm in their suffering, sealed with their own blood the sentence against the *traditores* and their associates by which they had cast them out of the communion of the Church. For it was not lawful that martyrs and *traditores* should exist together in the Church.”

Does anything similar occur in the Montanist author? It is remarkable how modestly and respectfully he conducts himself. He does indeed say that he acknowledges and honors new visions and prophecies; but when committing the visions and heavenly revelations of Perpetua and Saturus to writing, he does not on that account insult the Catholics who refused to receive the new prophets. He does indeed exhort his own people to enter into communion with the martyrs; but he does not therefore deter them from communion with the Catholics who rejected the new prophets, as the Donatist author does. [Col. 0097B] Whence did a heretical man derive such modesty, unless because he knew perfectly well that he was committing to writing the deeds not of Montanist but of Catholic martyrs?

# CHAPTER III  
## A GENERAL REPLY IS GIVEN TO BASNAGE’S INTERNAL ARGUMENTS AGAINST OUR MARTYRS

I. Basnage’s internal arguments against the holy martyrs. II. The credibility of the compiler of the Acts should be rejected rather than the orthodoxy of the holy martyrs called into doubt. III. Reasons are adduced by which the genuineness (*γνησιότης*) of the Acts might be called into question. The first reason is drawn from certain foreign expressions that are by no means appropriate to Perpetua, by whom the greater part of the Acts is said to have been written. [Col. 0097C] IV. The second reason is drawn from the similarity of style, which points to one and the same writer, although the Acts are said to have been written by three different persons. V. Neither the authority of Tertullian nor that of a contemporary writer would prevent us from doubting the credibility of the Acts if they truly contained anything unbecoming Catholic martyrs.

I. In the two preceding chapters we have treated what are called the external arguments; in the following chapters we shall examine the internal ones. The learned Basnage discusses them in the following manner:

> “The inherent arguments surpass these”—that is, the external arguments. “For Perpetua conducts herself as though she had the Holy Spirit at her command, [Col. 0097D] enclosed like some jewel in a casket, ready to employ his illuminations at her own discretion whenever she wished. Let her words in chap. I, §3 be heard:

> “‘My brother said to me: “Lady sister, you are now established in great dignity—so great that you may ask for a vision, and it may be shown to you whether what awaits is martyrdom or a reprieve.” And I, knowing that I conversed with the Lord, from whom I had experienced such great benefits, confidently promised him, saying: “Tomorrow I shall report it to you.”’

> “A remarkable confidence indeed, and worthy only of the household of Montanus! Nor are the visions presented to Perpetua joined with sufficient gravity and propriety. A man dressed as a shepherd ‘gave Perpetua, from the cheese he was milking, what looked like a little morsel.’ From this she concludes that death is imminent.

> “More remarkable still is what Perpetua relates in chap. III, §2:

> “‘There came out against me an Egyptian, hideous in appearance, [Col. 0098A] who was to fight me with his assistants. Then handsome young men came to me as my assistants and supporters; and I was stripped, and became a man.’

> “Perpetua therefore goes out to fight the Egyptian with her sex changed, to receive as the prize of victory ‘a green branch upon which there were golden apples.’

> “‘And he called for silence and said: “If this Egyptian defeats her, he will kill her with the sword; and if she defeats him, she will receive this branch.” Then he withdrew. And we approached one another and began to exchange blows. He tried to seize my feet, but I struck his face with my heels.’

> “Are these things worthy of the Holy Spirit? Did he ever present anything similar to the prophets? These, of course, are the visions to which the sacred oracle of Joel is to be applied! Dreams of this kind altogether smell of the workshop of Montanus. They are closely akin to the ecstasy by which Tertullian [Col. 0098B] proves that the soul is ‘of an airy color, and in every respect of human form’ [Note: [Col. 0098D] *On the Soul*, chap. 9].”

II. To all these difficulties I first offer this general reply: if the visions attributed to Perpetua truly contained anything unworthy either of the Holy Spirit or of a martyr, it would be the authenticity of the Acts, rather than the orthodoxy of the martyrs, that ought to be called into question.

Saint Augustine was the first to employ this reply. For when Perpetua’s vision—to be examined below—in which she saw her brother Dinocrates first amid punishments and afterward in a place of refreshment, was objected to him, his first reply was [Note: [Col. 0098D] Book I *On the Soul and Its Origin*, chap. 10] that:

> “the writing itself is not canonical, nor did she write it in that manner—or whoever wrote it, etc.”

By these words he seems to doubt whether Perpetua actually committed her revelations to writing, and therefore [Col. 0098C] not to grant complete credibility to the Acts and their editor. For the editor plainly teaches that Perpetua and Saturus wrote down with their own hands the passages concerning visions and revelations. Near the beginning he says:

> “From this point she herself will relate the entire course of her martyrdom, as she left it written in her own hand and according to her own understanding. ‘While we were still,’ she says, ‘with the persecutors, and my father was trying to turn me away, etc.’”

And below:

> “‘Then my brother said to me, etc.’”

And so both she and Saturus always speak in their own persons. And in chap. III, §2:

> “‘This is what I did up to the day before the spectacle; but as for the events of the spectacle itself, let whoever wishes write them.’”

And immediately afterward, chap. IV, §1:

> “But the blessed Saturus also made known this vision of his, which he himself wrote down.”

And below, chap. V, §1:

> “These are the more notable visions of the most blessed martyrs themselves, which they themselves wrote down.”

And finally, in chap. V, §3, the editor says that he is carrying out Perpetua’s command and committing to the memory of posterity the events that occurred afterward, especially on the very day of the spectacle, just as she had desired:

> “Since, therefore, the Holy Spirit permitted—and by permitting willed—that the course of the spectacle itself should be written down, although we are unworthy to record the supplement to so great a glory, we nevertheless execute what was, as it were, the command of the most holy Perpetua—indeed, a trust committed by her, etc.”

Anyone, therefore, who calls into doubt [Col. 0099A] a matter so often attested and insistently asserted by the author plainly does not place complete confidence in his statements. Yet nowhere does Saint Augustine call into question whether Perpetua was a woman of the Church or of the Montanist sect. Wherever he mentions her—and he mentions her very frequently—he celebrates her as a most holy and most invincible martyr. Hence, in Augustine’s judgment, it would be the credibility of the Acts, rather than the orthodoxy of the martyrs, that ought to be called into question if anything occurred in the Acts that was unworthy either of the Holy Spirit or of true martyrs of Christ.

And indeed, how many accounts or histories—ancient though they may be—of holy martyrs, apostles, or any other distinguished men are, chiefly on this very ground, either called into doubt or rejected outright and dismissed as fables! How many ancient monuments, [Col. 0099B] on this same ground, are denied to the authors whose names they bear! Thus those who number the Epistles of Barnabas, Clement, or Ignatius among spurious productions rely chiefly upon this consideration: that in them the teaching of an apostolic man, and likewise the force and majesty of the apostolic spirit, are lacking. Those who hiss down and reject the visions of Hermas—although they were so highly esteemed by the ancients that they were almost admitted by them into the canon of Scripture—are guided almost by this consideration alone: namely, that in their judgment they contain many things insufficiently worthy of a disciple of the Apostles and altogether foreign to apostolic teaching; and that, to use Basnage’s words, the visions presented to Hermas are not accompanied by sufficient gravity and propriety.

Yet no critic has hitherto advanced to such a degree of audacity [Col. 0099C] that, because of certain blemishes, errors, or even harmful points of doctrine which he seemed to himself to detect in these or similar monuments, he doubted the sound faith and orthodoxy of those to whom even the most ancient Fathers attributed such works. They preferred, that is, to take away from the Fathers in question those things which they judged unworthy of their spirit, rather than to pronounce anything unworthy concerning their piety and religion; and to judge books or visions attributed to them in accordance with their attested virtue, rather than to endanger their reputation and honor because of those books or visions. Nor did they therefore imbibe an adverse opinion of certain holy men because they judged the writings attributed to them to be depraved; rather, they refused to attribute what they judged depraved to men concerning whom [Col. 0099D] it was not lawful to imbibe an adverse opinion. Since, therefore, it would be impious and supremely rash to raise a controversy concerning the religion and right faith of Perpetua and her fellow martyrs—approved throughout all the centuries since their martyrdom by the judgment of the universal Church and the unanimous agreement of the ancient Fathers—if Basnage found anything offensive in their Acts which, in his judgment, did not befit Catholic martyrs, he ought rather to have rejected all of it as spurious than to have pronounced anything unworthy concerning the holy martyrs.

### III

Nor indeed, had Basnage wished to follow the path opened by Augustine, would arguments have been lacking to him—given the intellectual power and critical acumen in which he excelled—by which he could have supported this opinion in some fashion [Col. 0100A] and made it plausible. For, first, no one would readily persuade himself that an African woman was so devoted to Greek literature that, in so short a composition, she could not restrain herself from repeatedly employing Greek expressions. I am well aware that very many Greek words passed even into the common and popular usage of the Latin language. But the words Perpetua employs in describing her visions are not of that kind; indeed, they are almost entirely unusual and scarcely, if ever, occur in Latin authors.

Thus, in Chapter I, §3: “Welcome, *tegnon*.” Here Ruinart observes that τέκνον (*teknon*, “child”), though more rarely, nevertheless sometimes denotes a daughter. But I should like him to have produced a Latin author who wrote τέκνον in the sense of “daughter.”

Chapter II, §3: “This was shown to me in an *oroma*.” And Chapter III, §2: [Col. 0100B] “I see in an *oroma*.” On these passages the distinguished Lucas Holstenius makes the following annotation:

> The matter requires that *horamate* be restored, unless this word was thus corrupted in the popular usage of the Africans. Now ὅραμα (*horama*) is a Greek word meaning a sight or vision. It is used at Acts 12:9. Latin writers employed it more rarely; nevertheless Aldhelm, *On Virginity*, chapter 3, where he speaks of Saint John the Evangelist, says that he was “caught up in an *horoma* on Patmos.” There Meursius rightly substituted *oramate* in his *Mantissa critica*—and so I find it printed in the *Library of the Holy Fathers*—although Suvartius censured him without cause in Book III, chapter 9 of his *Analecta* and vainly tried to persuade readers that *chroma* should be restored there. I also find these words in Alcuin, Book I, chapter 2 of the *Life of Saint Willibrord*: “His mother, in the repose of the dead of night, saw a heavenly [Col. 0100C] *horama* in her dreams.”

What this most learned man says—that Latin writers used this word rather rarely—is manifestly true. But what he seems to suggest, that it was used popularly among the Africans, I should not readily concede. It occurs neither in Tertullian, a writer of the same period, although he was exceedingly fond of exotic expressions of this kind, especially Greek ones, and very frequently discusses visions and revelations; nor in writers nearly contemporary with him, Cyprian and the deacon Pontius, although they too occasionally recount various visions; nor again in Optatus of Milevis, Augustine, Fulgentius, or Victor of Vita, although their style is not so refined and so utterly removed from popular usage.

In the same Chapter III, §2, another word with a Greek meaning occurs: “I see an Egyptian rolling about in the *apha*.” On this passage the aforementioned Holstenius says: [Col. 0100D]

> *Apha* means dust, by Greek signification; for it is the Greek noun ἁφή (*haphē*) written in Latin letters. Wrestlers preparing to compete customarily sprinkled their oiled bodies with dust, or rolled about in it as it lay on the ground. Ovid, *Metamorphoses* 9, speaks of two wrestlers supplying one another with dust for this purpose:
>
> > He scoops up dust in hollow palms and sprinkles me,  
> > And in his turn grows yellow beneath the cast of tawny sand.
>
> Martial, Book VII, Epigram 66, calls the sand from which the wrestlers’ bodies had just grown yellow *Haphe* in this verse:
>
> > And *Haphe* grows yellow. . . .

I do not know, however, whether the word occurs in any Latin [Col. 0101A] author apart from Martial; and perhaps the poet employed it for metrical reasons.

Likewise, in Chapter II, §3, another Greek noun is read shortly afterward: “And between me and him there was a great *diadema*.” Holstenius also has the following on this word in his notes:

> I do not deny that, if conjecture were to be allowed, it might seem possible, not without foundation, to restore *diastema* in place of *diadema*. For it may be understood from L. Frontinus, in his book *On the Qualities of Lands*, that the word *diastema* was frequently used by Latin authors in that century, where he writes as follows: “If three circles are equal and connected with one another at equal intervals (*diastemata*).” And Hyginus, *On the Establishment of Boundaries*: “What of the fact that even in that very region the position of the sun cannot be correctly ascertained unless the surveying instrument is placed at equal intervals from sunrise and sunset?” Likewise: “The earth is a point of heaven, and beneath the sun the atmosphere is suspended across a vast [Col. 0101B] interval (*diastema*).”

Peter Poussines, however, adds the following concerning this most learned man’s observation:

> Holstenius’s remarks here concerning the conjecture by which he suspects that *diastema* should be restored in place of *diadema* seem open to this objection: the passages he cites from the land-surveyors Frontinus and Hyginus do not establish with sufficient certainty that Saint Perpetua used here a word proper to the art of surveying and therefore foreign to common usage, especially that of women in Africa.

Accordingly, on the basis of the consistent and explicit reading of the manuscript codex, he wishes the word *diadema* to be retained and to signify in this passage nearly the same thing as the term *Limbo*. But the learned and subtle arguments he advances in favor of this interpretation do not show that this was at that time a customary and popular meaning of the word, as the term *Limbo* is now among the Scholastics, or consequently that it would suit an African woman better than *diastema*. For although Tertullian, Perpetua’s contemporary and a resident of Carthage, and afterward Saint Augustine, frequently named these hidden receptacles of souls, they never called them *diademata*: although the former, as has been said, was exceedingly fond of exotic and foreign words, and the latter of popular ones. [Col. 0101C]

Who, then, would readily persuade himself that a woman hastening toward martyrdom affected Greek learning, or that amid the shadows and confinement of prison, while committing this brief record to writing, she searched out unusual expressions rather than employing those in familiar use, as they spontaneously and immediately presented themselves to her mind? Saturus too is fond of Greek letters, so much so that in the brief composition in which he explains his vision he could not refrain from Greek expressions: “And we heard the united voice of those saying, *Agios, agios, agios* [ἅγιος, ἅγιος, ἅγιος: ‘Holy, holy, holy’], without ceasing.” [Col. 0101D]

### IV

Second, if we give credence to the editor of the Acts, the Acts do not have a single author but were compiled from the records of three writers: namely Perpetua, Saturus, and the compiler of the Acts themselves, who both added the preface and committed to writing what was done on the very day of the spectacle. But if we bring our eyes closer and read these things neither carelessly nor drowsily, but with an attentive mind and with the concentration they deserve, they immediately seem to present one and the same author. Similar words, [Col. 0102A] similar phrases, and similar turns of expression occur throughout; one and the same style is detected in every part.

The author of an epistle written from Bourges to Henri Valois attributed this work to Tertullian. To prove this, after comparing many passages of the Acts with other works of Tertullian, he showed that precisely the same style, the same formulas of speech, and often even the same words are found in both. But these formulas of speech, these phrases, these words, and finally this style—whatever exactly makes it Tertullianic—are observed not only in those passages which the author admits that he himself added, but also in those which he presents as the words of Perpetua and Saturus.

Basnage, however, denies the aforementioned work to Tertullian on the following grounds: none of the ancients attributes it to Tertullian; furthermore, its style is lower than Tertullian’s [Col. 0102B] and does not flash with equal fire; finally, Tertullian himself praises the Acts of Perpetua while suppressing his own name, although he discloses it when mentioning his own works. There is not much weight in the first and last of these arguments.

To the first one might easily reply, first, that it is an argument from silence and for that reason does not press very strongly. Second, that this work was not numbered among the works of Tertullian because he was regarded as the compiler rather than the author of the Acts. It would likewise be easy to evade the final argument by saying, first, that Tertullian does not cite the Acts but mentions Perpetua’s vision, which he could have received from some source other than the Acts. Next, when he wrote the book *On the Soul*, perhaps he had not yet published the Acts but was keeping them by him to be made public at the proper time. [Col. 0102C]

The second argument therefore has more weight. For it cannot be denied that the Acts employ a lower style of expression and do not stride in Tertullian’s tragic buskin. Yet it is not only Perpetua and Saturus who creep along in a lower style, but also the editor of the Acts himself. Accordingly, just as Saturus and Perpetua have certain phrases and words similar to Tertullian’s words and phrases no less than does the editor of their Passion, so the latter pursues a lower manner of expression no less than Perpetua and Saturus do. And if, because of a certain similarity, the author of the epistle suspected that the editor of the Acts might himself have been Tertullian, there is much greater reason—because virtually one and the same character of discourse appears throughout—to suspect that the Acts may have proceeded from the hand of one and the same author.

I should not like these things to be taken as though I placed great reliance upon conjectures of this kind, [Col. 0102D] or as though I truly intended to cast suspicion upon the authenticity (γνησιότης) of the Acts. My purpose was rather to show by what arguments the opinion could be supported of someone who thought he detected in Perpetua’s visions and revelations something unworthy either of the Holy Spirit or of a martyr in Catholic communion, and who therefore wished to reject all of them as Montanist inventions and fables fabricated by idle and superstitious men. This would certainly be less audacious than expunging the holy martyrs themselves from the diptychs of the Catholics and enrolling them among the Montanists.

### V

Nor, if necessary, would I be deterred from this undertaking and from pursuing this course either by the authority of Tertullian or by the very antiquity [Col. 0103A] of the Acts. Certainly not by Tertullian’s authority. For although he is believed to have had the Acts in his hands and to have praised them as genuine records of unquestionable credibility, this, as I have said, is nevertheless not established, since he could have received the vision of Perpetua which he mentions from another source. Furthermore, not much deference should be paid to this writer’s authority in the present controversy, since he possessed no standard or judgment in matters of this kind: he allowed himself to be most disgracefully deceived by deranged and fanatical little women, and believed that the soul was airy in color and altogether human in shape because a certain false prophetess from the Montanist sect had reported to him that it was furnished with such colors and outlines.

[Col. 0103B] Even if the Acts of the holy martyrs were committed to writing and commended to remote posterity, as is said, by a contemporary author—as he himself testifies in the preface—it would still not follow that everything pertaining to the visions must be received with eager ears and without applying any criterion. How easily, in matters of this kind, may even good men be deceived, and ill-employed men abuse both their leisure and the credulity of others! The author, being, as we have seen, a Montanist, could have fabricated at will everything he reports concerning the visions of Perpetua and Saturus. The events narrated took place in the deepest recesses and hidden chambers of the prison. What passed between God and the martyrs was known only to God himself and to the martyrs, who had already departed. Who, then, could guarantee that the things which to Basnage smell of the Montanists’ workshop [Col. 0103C] must truly be attributed to the martyrs, rather than rejected as the ravings of an idle man devoted to a most deluded sect?

The example of the Donatist author who committed to a written record the Acts of Marculus—a pseudo-martyr of that lost and schismatic faction—would make us all the more inclined to believe this of a Montanist man. For although that writer too was a contemporary, how many things did he fabricate with astonishing license and thrust upon his readers in those Acts with much greater impudence! Who would not reject as the inventions of a supremely audacious mind the revelations he reports concerning this hypocrite, although they would not have been altogether unworthy of a Catholic martyr? With the same liberty, therefore, with which we deny credibility to a Donatist author in what he narrates concerning the visions of Marculus, because they do not befit a heretical man, [Col. 0103D] we could treat a Montanist writer in the same way if any visions of Perpetua and Saturus reported by him did not befit Catholic martyrs.

I certainly would not wish to deny that Saturus and Perpetua were made illustrious by heavenly revelations. But whether they were precisely the revelations which the Montanist writer made public could deservedly be called into controversy, if necessary. Some of those who have wielded the pen against the Ignatian Epistles do not deny that certain letters were written by the holy martyr. Indeed, they even freely admit that these were collected by Polycarp, and that the holy bishop appended a collection (συναγωγή) of them to his own Epistle to the Philippians. But they do not admit that the letters we now possess were either written by Ignatius or [Col. 0104A] published by Polycarp, because in their judgment they contain many things which genuine letters written by Ignatius could not possibly have contained.

By this reply Daillé [Note: [Col. 0104D] In Pearson, *Vindiciae*, Part I, chap. 5.] attempts to weaken the force of Polycarp’s testimony; he even grants that the letters fabricated by an impostor were in some respects similar to the genuine Epistles of Ignatius praised by Polycarp. Basnage, like Daillé, denies to Saint Ignatius the letters now circulated under his name because they contain many things which genuine letters written by Ignatius could not possibly have contained. Why, then, did he not pursue the same course when Perpetua’s revelations were at issue? Would it not have been less rash to admit that Perpetua had indeed been refreshed in prison by heavenly visions, but to deny that they were the same as those published by the Montanist editor, [Col. 0104B] because they contain many things which revelations imparted to Catholic martyrs could not possibly have contained? Would that, I ask, not have been less rash than arraigning Catholic martyrs on a charge of Montanism? He could also readily have granted that the visions of Perpetua and Saturus which he believed had been fabricated by an impostor were in some respects similar to those then in common circulation and attributed to them, yet not altogether identical with them, because to his exceedingly discerning nostrils the extant visions smell of the Montanists’ workshop.

Finally, according to the hypothesis I am pursuing in this chapter—namely, that the Acts of Perpetua and Felicitas truly do smell of Montanism—one could also readily grant that Perpetua and Saturus wrote down their revelations in prison, but that, when by some chance, before they were made public, [Col. 0104C] they came into the hands of a man entangled in Montanus’s superstitions, he interpolated them at will and, wherever it pleased him, polluted them with heretical inventions. Whatever more expert critics thought savored of Montanism would therefore have to be charged against the interpolator, not against the holy martyrs.

# CHAPTER IV

## A Discussion of the Abundance and Profusion of Visions and Other Heavenly Gifts During the Earlier Centuries of the Church. It Is Demonstrated That the Ancient Christians, Including Those Universally Regarded as Genuine Martyrs of Christ, Employed These Divine Charisms of the Holy Spirit with No Less Confidence Than Perpetua Did

[Col. 0104D]

I. Nothing actually occurs in the Acts of our martyrs that smells of Montanus’s workshop.  
II. Saint Justin Martyr compares the prophets of his time with those of old. From this it is concluded that they employed the prophetic spirit with no less confidence than the ancient prophets.  
III. On the beginnings of the Montanists. None of the most ancient writers regarded the Montanists as false prophets on the ground that they employed the revelations of the Holy Spirit as though at will.  
IV. A notable testimony of Saint Irenaeus concerning the variety and abundance of charisms during this period.  
V. How readily the power of the Holy Spirit was available to the ancient Christians for restraining and driving away demons.  
VI. The memorable example of Potamiaena, no less remarkable than that of Perpetua.  
VII. From Cyprian’s Epistles and from the deacon Pontius it is shown how greatly Cyprian’s life abounded in visions and revelations.  
VIII. The Acts of other martyrs are filled with the same gifts of the Holy Spirit.  
IX. In the age of Perpetua and her fellow martyrs the fountain of charisms overflowed more abundantly than in the time of Cyprian. [Col. 0105A]

### I

Since, as I have repeatedly said, I do not wish the matters I presented in the preceding chapter to be understood as though I intended to call the authenticity (γνησιότης) of the Acts into controversy or to bring their editor, although a Montanist, under suspicion of fraud, [Col. 0105B] we must now undertake another course, likewise with Augustine as our guide, and labor to remove every suspicion of Montanism from Perpetua’s visions, even as they are reported in the Acts.

The authority of the Church requires us to deny that the Acts are polluted by any Montanist inventions or that Perpetua’s revelations contain anything that smells of the school and workshop of Montanus; for the Church approved the public reading of these Acts, not yesterday or the day before, but from ancient times, as is evident from Augustine. [Note: [Col. 0105D] *Exposition on Psalm* 47.] The authority of the Fathers likewise requires this, since they detected nothing foreign to the faith, nothing improper, and finally nothing smelling of the Montanists’ workshop in those very revelations of Perpetua upon which suspicion is now most rashly cast. [Col. 0105C]

The Fathers’ noses were not so dull when they discerned matters of faith that they could not immediately distinguish the good fragrance of Christ and the perfume of heavenly charisms from the stench of heretical fables and absurdities. Not only can no heretical martyr be shown whom the Fathers venerated as Catholic, but neither can there be shown any Acts of Catholic martyrs polluted by heretical fables which they wished to be read publicly in the Church for the edification of the faithful. Like good shepherds, they were exceedingly careful to turn their sheep away from harmful and useless plants. Nor do we believe that a fraud unnoticed by anyone throughout so many centuries has at last been scented out by Basnage.

We must therefore strive [Col. 0105D] to wipe away the stains of heretical depravity cast upon these ancient monuments, approved by the judgment of the ancient Fathers, and thereby also to repel the odium of this crime which has been raised against the holy martyrs. I am confident that I shall easily accomplish this by calling each point back to examination and weighing according to the stricter rules of criticism everything that led Basnage into this perverse opinion concerning the holy martyrs.

First, as we have seen, among his arguments against the martyrs which are intrinsic and drawn from the Acts themselves and from Perpetua’s words, he repeats one from what Perpetua narrates at the beginning of Chapter IV in the following words:

> Then my brother said to me: “Lady sister, you are now in great dignity, so great that you may request a vision and it may be shown to you whether it will be martyrdom or release.” And I, who knew that I conversed with the Lord, from whom I had experienced such great benefits, confidently promised him, saying: “Tomorrow I shall report it to you.” [Col. 0106A]

Basnage says that Perpetua conducts herself in such a way as though she had the Holy Spirit at her command, like a kind of necklace enclosed in a casket, to make use of his illuminations at will whenever she wished. After quoting the preceding words, he adds: “A marvelous confidence, and worthy only of the Montanist household!”

I could easily extricate myself from this argument if I were to bring forward innumerable examples of similar, if not even greater, confidence, amassed not only from the histories of more recent saints but also from Theodoret’s *Religious History*, Gregory’s *Dialogues*, John Moschus’s *Spiritual Meadow*, and other such works of the fifth, sixth, and subsequent centuries. [Col. 0106B] But since my dispute is with men of the sort who rashly deny all credibility to records of that kind, I shall leave these aside for the present and turn to other examples and testimonies which only those would dare oppose who either hold the Christian religion in derision or practice no religion at all.

No one, however, should expect me to gather here every example of heavenly visions, prophetic revelations, and other divine charisms by which the Church was so greatly adorned during its first three centuries. For although this would greatly assist us in understanding whence such confidence entered Perpetua’s mind—namely, from the supreme abundance of heavenly gifts in those times and from the almost daily and common exercise of divine charisms, available to any righteous person—nevertheless, because Henry Dodwell, a theologian of no mean standing among Protestants, composed a lengthy and learned dissertation *On Visions* in connection with Cyprian’s Eighth Epistle, [Col. 0106C] in which, beginning with the apostolic Fathers and continuing down to Cyprian, he defended and vindicated against their critics every passage in which the ancient Fathers discuss visions—against those, as he says, “who refer to Montanus and the Montanists whatever they read concerning visions in the authors of that age”—I shall therefore refrain from that labor at present. I shall merely select both testimonies from the writings of the ancient Fathers and examples from the authentic Acts of the martyrs and approved histories which appear to approach my purpose more closely, and from which it may readily be understood that the Montanist household did not possess as its peculiar property that marvelous confidence of Perpetua by which she promised her brother a revelation of the future event. [Col. 0106D]

### II

Certain passages of Justin Martyr’s *Dialogue with Trypho* should be noted first of all. In that work, as Eusebius observes, [Note: [Col. 0106D] Γράφει δὲ καὶ ὡς ὅτι μέχρι καὶ αὐτοῦ χαρίσματα προφητικὰ διέλαμπεν ἐπὶ τῆς ἐκκλησίας: “He also writes that prophetic gifts continued to shine forth in the Church even down to his own time.” Book IV of the *History*, chap. 18.] “he writes that the gifts of prophecy still flourished in the Church in his own age.” But by producing the testimony of the holy martyr, we shall ascertain and establish more clearly how they flourished. Thus [Col. 0107A] he says: [Note: [Col. 0107D] Παρὰ γὰρ ἡμῖν καὶ μέχρι νῦν προφητικά χαρίσματα ἔστιν· ἐξ οὗ καὶ αὐτοὶ συνιέναι ὀφείλετε, ὅτι τὰ πάλαι ἐν τῷ γένει ὑμῶν ὄντα εἰς ἡμᾶς μετετέθη: “For among us prophetic gifts exist even to the present day; from this you yourselves ought to understand that those which formerly existed among your nation have been transferred to us.”]

> For among us prophetic gifts continue to exist even to the present day; from this you too ought to understand that those which formerly existed among your nation have been transferred to us.

And below, just as he teaches that it was evident and before everyone’s eyes that no prophet then remained among the Jewish nation, so it was equally plain and manifest to everyone that among the Christians there were in truth not only men but also women inspired by the spirit of prophecy, in accordance with Joel’s prediction: [Note: [Col. 0107D] Μηκέτι ἐν τῷ γένει ὑμῶν κατὰ τὸ παλαιὸν ἔθος προφήτας γενήσεσθαι, ὅπερ καὶ ὄψει ὑμῖν ἰδεῖν ἔστι· μετ’ ἐκεῖνον γὰρ οὐδεὶς ὅλως προφήτης παρ’ ὑμῖν γεγένηται: “Prophets would no longer arise among your nation according to the ancient custom, as you yourselves can see with your own eyes; for after him no prophet at all has arisen among you.”]

> Thus there would no longer be prophets among your nation according to the ancient custom, as you yourselves can see with your own eyes. For after him no prophet at all has arisen among you.

And a little later: [Note: [Col. 0107D] Καὶ παρ’ ἡμῖν ἔστιν ἰδεῖν καὶ θηλείας καὶ ἄρσενας χαρίσματα ἀπὸ τοῦ Πνεύματος τοῦ Θεοῦ ἔχοντας: “And among us one may see both females and males possessing gifts from the Spirit of God.”]

> Among us one may see both women and men possessing gifts from the Spirit of God.

By this testimony of Justin Martyr, [Col. 0107B] Basnage is first of all convicted of error when he says [Note: [Col. 0107D] Under the year of the Lord 203, no. V.] that in the New Testament it is reported only of the daughters of Philip the Evangelist that, moved by the divine power, they uttered oracles. For Saint Justin states that the gift of prophecy was common and shared by men and women alike. Although it also seems hardly probable that Philip’s daughters, despite having grown old in Asia, as Polycrates writes to Victor, [Note: [Col. 0107D] In Eusebius, Book V of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chap. 14.] survived until that time.

Asterius Urbanus also numbers among the Catholic prophets of the New Testament—whom he says had no connection with the Montanists, μηδὲν αὐτοῖς προσήκοντας (“having nothing to do with them”)—not only Philip’s daughters but also a certain Ammia of Philadelphia. The Montanists boasted that [Note: [Col. 0107D] Μετὰ Κάδρατον καὶ τὴν ἐν Φιλαδελφείᾳ Ἀμμίαν, αἱ περὶ Μοντανὸν διεδέξαντο γυναῖκές τὸ προφητικὸν χάρισμα: “After Quadratus and Ammia in Philadelphia, the women associated with Montanus succeeded to the prophetic gift.” In Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, chap. 17.] “after Quadratus and Ammia of Philadelphia, those women of Montanus succeeded [Col. 0107C] to the grace of prophecy.”

Justin therefore teaches that the prophetic gifts by which the synagogue had formerly been made illustrious were transferred to these prophets—and prophetesses too—of the New Testament, and this with such clarity and evidence that he calls the Jews themselves as witnesses to the fact. This is surely evidence that the spirit of prophecy poured itself upon these new prophets with no less abundance and profusion than upon the ancient prophets.

But did not the prophets of the Old Testament conduct themselves in such a way as though they had the Holy Spirit at their command, like a kind of necklace enclosed within their breast as in a casket, to make use of his illuminations at will? When questioned by the people about future events, did they not promise, with precisely the same confidence as Perpetua, that they would report the answer to them the next day or after a brief interval? [Col. 0107D]

What wonder is it, then, if we say that such confidence was so familiar to the prophets of the New Testament—such as Agabus, Silas, Quadratus, and Polycarp—and to prophetesses such as Philip’s daughters, Ammia [Col. 0108A] of Philadelphia, and later Perpetua, that when questioned by Christians they replied: “Tomorrow we shall report it to you”? Those men and women of old do not appear to have borne the title of prophet or prophetess because they uttered prophetic oracles only once or twice, but because they employed the prophetic spirit familiarly and, I might almost say, at will. Otherwise, when prophetic gifts formerly overflowed in the Church in such abundance, why were only certain persons—and indeed no very great number—called prophets κατ’ ἐξοχήν (“preeminently”), such as those whom Asterius lists in the frequently cited passage of Eusebius? And why was Polycarp called the διδάσκαλος ἀποστολικὸς καὶ προφητικός (“apostolic and prophetic teacher”) of the Church of Smyrna? [Note: [Col. 0108D] The Epistle concerning his martyrdom, in Eusebius, Book IV of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chap. 15.]

### III

The beginnings of the Montanist [Col. 0108B] faction appear to be placed not long after the martyrdom of Justin, if, as Ruinart [Note: [Col. 0108D] Prefatory Notice to the Acts of Saint Justin Martyr, no. 12.] and others maintain, the holy martyr died in the year 167 or even later. For by the year 177, in which the martyrs of Lyons suffered, the foundations of that abominable sect had already been laid, as Eusebius reports.

At first, as is evident from Eusebius himself, their fortunes varied. Some acclaimed them as true prophets; others remained uncertain what judgment to form concerning them, so much so that the Asians asked by letter for the opinion of other churches, and especially of the Gallican Church, concerning this new prophecy. Eusebius states that the reason they were not immediately rejected by everyone was that, since charisms of divine grace still abounded in the Church, it did not seem extraordinary that those too who outwardly pursued an austere manner of life [Col. 0108C] should abound in heavenly charisms:

> When Montanus, says Eusebius, [Note: [Col. 0108D] Τῶν δ’ ἀμφὶ τὸν Μοντανὸν καὶ Ἀλκιβιάδην καὶ Θεόδοτον, περὶ τὴν Φρυγίαν ἄρτι τότε πρῶτον τὴν περὶ τοῦ προφητεύειν ὑπόληψιν παρὰ πολλοῖς ἐκφερομένων· πλεῖσται γὰρ οὖν καὶ ἄλλαι παραδοξοποιΐαι τοῦ θείου χαρίσματος εἰσέτι τότε κατὰ διαφόρους ἐκκλησίας ἐκτελούμεναι, πίστιν παρὰ πολλοῖς τοῦ κἀκείνους προφητεύειν παρεῖχον· καὶ δὴ διαφωνίας ὑπαρχούσης περὶ τῶν δεδηλωμένων, αὖθις οἱ κατὰ τὴν Γαλλίαν ἀδελφοὶ, τὴν ἰδίαν κρίσιν καὶ περὶ τούτων εὐλαβῆ καὶ ὀρθοδοξοτάτην ὑποτάττουσιν· ἐκθέμενοι καὶ τῶν παρ’ αὐτοῖς τελειωθέντων μαρτύρων διαφόρους ἐπιστολάς· ἃς ἐν δεσμοῖς ἔτι ὑπάρχοντες, τοῖς ἐπ’ Ἀσίας καὶ Φρυγίας ἀδελφοῖς διεχάραξαν, οὐ μὴν ἀλλὰ καὶ Ἐλευθέρῳ τῷ τότε Ῥωμαίων ἐπισκόπῳ, τῆς τῶν ἐκκλησιῶν εἰρήνης ἕνεκα πρεσβεύοντες: “When those associated with Montanus, Alcibiades, and Theodotus were then for the first time gaining among many people in Phrygia the reputation of prophesying—for very many other miraculous works of the divine gift were still being performed at that time throughout various churches, thereby persuading many that these men too prophesied—and when disagreement had arisen concerning those who have been named, the brethren in Gaul once again appended their own reverent and thoroughly orthodox judgment concerning these matters, setting forth various letters of the martyrs who had been perfected among them. While still in bonds, those martyrs had written these letters to the brethren in Asia and Phrygia and also to Eleutherus, then bishop of the Romans, acting as ambassadors for the peace of the churches.” Book V, chap. 3.] and Alcibiades and Theodotus had then first begun to be acclaimed in Phrygia, in popular opinion, as prophets—for many miracles of divine grace were still customarily performed in numerous churches, persuading many that they too prophesied—and when dissension arose on account of these men, the brethren in Gaul once again appended to the same letter their own private judgment concerning these matters, a judgment especially reverent and consonant with right faith. They also produced various letters of the martyrs who had been put to death among them, which those martyrs, while still in bonds, had written partly to the brethren living in Asia and Phrygia and partly to Eleutherus, bishop of the city of Rome, acting as ambassadors for the peace of the churches. [Col. 0109A]

Thus Eusebius concerning the beginnings of the Montanists. From his words everyone may readily understand that such was the abundance of divine charisms in the Church during this period that no firm inference could be drawn that certain persons must be struck from the register of prophets merely because they employed the prophetic spirit with great confidence.

In chapters 16 and following of the same book, Eusebius mentions several writers of that age who attacked the Montanists in weighty treatises, including Apollinaris of Hierapolis, Asterius Urbanus, Miltiades, Apollonius, Serapion, Aelius, and Publius Julius, bishop of the colony of Debeltum in Thrace. From some of them he quotes fairly lengthy passages (ῥήσεις), in which one may see by what kind of signs those ancient Fathers detected the spurious spirit of Montanus. Besides [Col. 0109B] their depraved morals and the falsity of their predictions, they especially objected to these new prophets—as we saw above—that, like demoniacs, suddenly struck by a kind of frenzy and displacement of mind, they uttered mad, untimely, and alien things, contrary to the custom and institution of the Church handed down by the ancestors and thereafter propagated in an unbroken succession.

Nowhere, however, do we read that they charged the Montanists with what Basnage charges against Perpetua, for which he consequently represents her as a Montanist: that they awaited heavenly revelations with great confidence. The learned man will certainly be unable to produce any testimony of the ancient Fathers demonstrating that the great confidence which he finds so remarkable in Perpetua was peculiar to the Montanist household. With what confidence, then—not to say [Col. 0109C] rashness and audacity—did he choose to make this evidence of a Montanist spirit in that most holy woman?

## IV

In these same times Irenaeus was especially distinguished for piety and learning. Eusebius adduces a notable passage from the second book of his *Against Heresies*, in which he testifies that “examples of divine and wondrous power,” he says, [Note: [Col. 0109C] “In the second book of the same work, he indicates in the following words that examples of divine and extraordinary power still survived down to his own time in certain churches:

> ‘So far are they from raising the dead, as the Lord raised them and the apostles did through prayer! Indeed, among the brotherhood it frequently happened, when necessity required and the whole church in a particular place petitioned with much fasting and supplication, that the spirit of the deceased returned, and the person was granted in answer to the prayers of the saints.’

And again, after other remarks, he says:

> ‘But if [Col. 0109D] they say that the Lord performed such deeds merely in appearance, we shall refer them to the prophetic writings and demonstrate from them that all these things were both foretold concerning him and certainly came to pass, and that he alone is the Son of God. Therefore, in his name those who are truly his disciples, having received grace from him, perform works for the benefit of the rest of mankind, according as each has received his gift from him. For some assuredly and truly drive out demons, so that those very persons who have been cleansed of evil spirits frequently come to believe and remain in the Church; others have foreknowledge of future things, visions, and prophetic utterances; still others heal the sick through the laying on of hands and restore them to health. Indeed, as we have said, even the dead have been raised and remained with us for many years. And what more? It is impossible to state the number of gifts which the Church throughout the whole world, having received them from God, exercises each day in the name of Jesus Christ, who was crucified under Pontius Pilate, for the benefit [Col. 0110D] of the nations, neither deceiving anyone nor making money from them. For as she has freely received from God, so she also freely ministers.’

And in another place the same author writes:

> ‘We also hear of many brethren in the Church who possess prophetic gifts, who through the Spirit speak in every kind of tongue, bring the hidden things of men into the open for their benefit, and expound the mysteries of God.’

These statements concern the continuance among the worthy, down to the times indicated, of the various gifts.” *Ecclesiastical History*, book V, chapter 7.]

still survived in some churches in his own age, in the following words:

> “So far are they,” he says (*Against Heresies*, II.57), “from raising a dead person through prayer, as the Lord and the apostles did! Indeed, it has very frequently happened among the brethren, when some necessity required it and the whole church in a particular place petitioned with much fasting and prayer, that the soul of the deceased returned to the body, and the person’s life was granted in answer to the prayers of the saints.”

And a little later:

> “But if,” he says, “they are going to claim that the Lord did these things by some simulation and trickery, we shall lead them to the oracles of the prophets and demonstrate from them that all these things were most certainly both foretold concerning him and performed by him, and that he is the Son of God. Hence also, in his name, all who are his true disciples, having received grace from him, [Col. 0110B] perform these things for the salvation and benefit of all others, according as each has received his gift from him. Some drive out demons most certainly and truly, so much so that those who have been delivered from evil spirits of this kind frequently embrace the faith and remain in the Church. Others have been allotted foreknowledge of the future, visions, and prophetic predictions. Others heal the sick through the laying on of hands and restore them to their former health. Moreover, as we said above, the dead have sometimes been raised and afterward remained with us for many years. What more need be said? No reckoning can be made of the gifts which the Church throughout the whole world, having received them from God, exercises daily in the name of Jesus Christ, who was crucified under Pontius Pilate, for the assistance of the nations, neither deceiving anyone [Col. 0110C] nor amassing money. For as she has freely received from God, so she also freely ministers.”

“The same man,” Eusebius says, “writes thus in another place:

> ‘Likewise, we hear of many brethren in the Church who have obtained gifts of prophecy, who through the Spirit speak in every kind of tongue, bring hidden things into the light for the benefit of men, and expound the secret mysteries of God.’

From these statements, therefore, it is apparent that the manifold variety of spiritual gifts remained until those times among those who were worthy.”

Since this was the state of the Church at that time, and there was so great a variety and abundance of divine charisms that their number could not be reckoned; since all who were ἀληθῶς αὐτοῦ μαθηταί, “truly his—that is, Christ’s—disciples,” abounded in prophetic gifts and either raised the dead, cast out demons, foresaw future events, penetrated the secrets of hearts, restored the sick to health through the laying on of hands, or spoke through the Spirit in every kind of tongue: do not those act imprudently who measure the affairs of the Christians of that time by the present state of affairs [Col. 0111A] and express such great astonishment that a holy woman, an ἀληθῶς αὐτοῦ μαθήτρια, “a true disciple of his,” and thus accustomed to these divine charisms—one who “knew that she conversed with the Lord”—released now from every earthly affection and actually setting out upon martyrdom, should have assumed such confidence in the divine favor, “whose benefits she had so greatly experienced,” that she confidently promised to report to her brother whether what was to come would be martyrdom or a reprieve?

In Basnage’s judgment, this is far removed from the customs of those times. But is it not still farther removed from present custom that which Irenaeus testifies happened πολλάκις, “frequently among the brethren”: that, “when some necessity required it and the whole church in a particular place petitioned with much fasting and prayer, the soul of the deceased returned to the body, and the person’s life was granted in answer to the prayers of the saints”? [Col. 0111B]

## V

But so that Basnage may understand with what confidence the ancient Christians administered these divine charisms and powers, let him hear what Tertullian boldly declares concerning their authority over demons [Note: [Col. 0111D] *Apology*, chapter 23]:

> “Let someone be produced here before your tribunals who is clearly possessed by a demon. If commanded by any Christian whatsoever to speak, that spirit will as truly confess itself to be a demon as elsewhere it falsely claims to be a god. Likewise, let someone be brought forward from among those who are thought to be under divine influence, who breathe upon altars and conceive the divinity from the smell of the sacrifice, who labor to belch forth their inspiration and utter their prophecies while gasping. Let that very *Virgo Caelestis* (“Heavenly Virgin”), the promiser of rains, and that very Aesculapius, the revealer of medicines, the supplier of remedies to Socordius, Denatius, and Asclepiodotus, who otherwise would have died—unless they confess themselves to be demons, not daring to lie to a Christian, shed the blood of that most insolent Christian on that very spot. What is more manifest than this deed? What is more trustworthy than this proof? The simplicity of truth stands openly before you. Its own power supports it. No suspicion will be possible. You will say that it is done by magic or some fraud of that kind—if your eyes and ears permit you. But what can be alleged against that which is displayed in naked sincerity?”

Is this not great confidence: to bargain with tyrants over the blood of any Christian whatsoever, if he cannot exercise over the demons whatever power he chooses and at his own discretion? Will Basnage dare to say that this confidence also was proper to the family of Montanus alone, because Tertullian was attached to that sect?

But there is no place here for cavils of that kind. This is not a matter of hidden and private [Col. 0111D] visions or revelations, but of something publicly put to the test under the very tribunals of pagan magistrates. The honor of the Christian religion and the blood of the Christian man are placed in jeopardy unless the proffered sign proceeds as intended. Does not Tertullian conduct himself and speak as though Christians kept the Holy Spirit for restraining demons and subjecting them to themselves, like a certain necklace enclosed in their own casket, ready at their command to employ its power and authority whenever they wished and at their own discretion?
