From what source, moreover, did Christians derive such confidence, if not from daily experience of powers of this kind?

“Fearing Christ,” the cited author continues, [Col. 0112A] “and God in Christ, they are subjected to the servants of God and Christ. Thus, by our touch and by our breath . . . even from bodies they depart at our command, unwillingly and in pain, and blushing in your presence.”

In his book *On the Soldier’s Crown*, moreover, he clearly and openly indicates that not only clerics or more distinguished Christians but Christians of every kind indiscriminately, even laymen, were endowed with this spirit and this power. For he deters Christians—namely, those whom the discipline of the catholic Church permitted to serve—from entering or continuing military service, among other arguments, on the ground that soldiers would have to stand guard at night before the temples of demons over whom the Christian exercised authority by day and whom he put to flight by exorcisms [Note: [Col. 0112D] Chapter 11]:

> “And will he defend by night those whom by day he put to flight with exorcisms, reclining and resting upon the spear with which Christ’s side was pierced?” [The OCR reading *luncho* is uncertain.]

Irenaeus, as we have seen, agrees with him, saying without any distinction that Christ’s true disciples were endowed, among other gifts, with the power to cast out demons βεβαίως καὶ ἀληθῶς, “certainly and truly.”

And Justin, who was earlier than both, calls the pagans themselves as witnesses of these powers, since they were performed openly and before their eyes [Note: [Col. 0112D]

> “Even now you can learn this from what takes place before your eyes. For throughout the world and in your own city, many of our people—Christians, I mean—have exorcised in the name of Jesus Christ, who was crucified under Pontius Pilate, many persons possessed by demons whom all your other exorcists, enchanters, and sorcerers could not cure; and they have cured them and continue to cure them even now, rendering powerless and driving out the demons that possess those persons.”

*Second Apology to the Senate*]:

> “You can understand this very thing from what takes place before your eyes. For throughout the entire world and in this city of yours, very many of our people—Christians, I mean—have, by adjuring them in the name of Jesus Christ, who was crucified under Pontius Pilate, [Col. 0112C] healed many persons seized by the violent disorders of demons whom your other adjurers, enchanters, and sorcerers were unable to cure; and they continue to heal them even now, disarming and expelling from men the demons that had besieged them.”

And in the *Dialogue with Trypho* [Note: [Col. 0112D]

> “For we call him our helper and redeemer; even the demons tremble at the power of his name, and today, when adjured in the name of Jesus Christ, who was crucified under Pontius Pilate, the man who became procurator of Judea, they submit to us.”

And:

> “Even now we who believe in our Lord Jesus, who was crucified under Pontius Pilate, adjure all demons and evil spirits and hold them subject to us.”]:

> “For we call him our helper and redeemer; even the demons tremble and recoil at the power of his name, and today as well, when adjured in the name of Jesus Christ, who was crucified under Pontius Pilate, the man who served as procurator of Judea, they obey us.”

And again:

> “Even now we who believe in our Lord Jesus, who was crucified under Pontius Pilate, adjure all demons and malignant spirits and hold them subjected beneath our power.”

The great Athanasius speaks about this matter with no less confidence than Tertullian, although in the fourth century these charisms of the Holy Spirit did not abound with the same fullness as at the beginning [Col. 0113A] of the third [Note: [Col. 0113D]

> “These things which we say do not consist in words alone, but also possess the testimony of truth from experience itself. Let whoever wishes come forward and behold the mark of virtue in Christ’s virgins and in young men who practice chastity in continence, and the proof of immortality in so great a company of his martyrs. Let whoever wishes to test what has been said come, and amid the very illusions of demons, the deception of oracles, and the wonders of magic, let him use the sign of the cross, which they ridicule, merely naming Christ; and he will see how through him demons flee, oracles cease, and all magic and sorcery are rendered powerless.”

Book *On the Incarnation of the Word of God*, no. 48, new edition]:

> “The things we say do not consist in words alone; experience itself also gives splendid testimony to their truth. Let whoever wishes approach and contemplate the marks of virtue in Christ’s virgins, as well as in young men who profess chastity, and the proof of immortality in so great a company of Christ’s martyrs. Let whoever desires to test what we have said come, and amid the very illusions of demons, the deceptions of oracles, and the wonders of magic, let him employ the sign of the cross—which among them is an object of ridicule—and merely name Christ. He will immediately see how quickly demons are put to flight through him, oracles cease, and every magical art and every sorcery vanish.”

If it is not incredible that the ancient Christians exercised so great a power against demons and possessed the power of the Holy Spirit for restraining malignant spirits, like a sword hanging from the thigh, ready at their command to draw it whenever they wished and at their own discretion, why does it appear incredible that a woman filled with the divine Spirit should have conducted herself as though she possessed that Spirit in her breast, like a certain necklace enclosed in a casket, ready at her command to employ its illuminations whenever she wished and at her own discretion?

I do not see what can be answered to this argument. It rests not upon uncertain or obscure examples, not upon doubtful or perhaps fabricated revelations, not upon vague rumors or traditions of the common people, but upon the reliability of deeds performed openly and before the eyes of all, attested and recorded in the clearest monuments. The ancient Christians employed the power of the Holy Spirit at their discretion to repress [Col. 0113C] demons. “What is more manifest than this deed?” Why, then, could a candidate for martyrdom not obtain the illuminations of the Holy Spirit at her discretion? “What is more trustworthy than this proof? The simplicity of truth stands openly before us; its own power supports it; nothing may be suspected”—neither Montanism nor fanaticism nor anything of that kind.

## VI

In the same persecution of Severus as Perpetua, Saint Potamiaena, the most celebrated among the Alexandrian martyrs of this period, was put to death. In Eusebius there survives not only a notable apparition of hers but also a remarkable example of confidence in God, no less worthy of admiration than Perpetua’s. As usual, I shall append Eusebius’s words [Note: [Col. 0113D]

> “As soon as she had received the sentence pronounced against her, Basilides, one of those enrolled in military service, took charge of her and led her away to death. When the crowd attempted to molest her and insult her with licentious words, he restrained them, driving away those who insulted her and displaying very great pity and humanity toward her. She, accepting the man’s sympathy for her, urged him to take courage, for after her departure she would petition her Lord on his behalf, and before long would repay him for what he had done for her. . . . Such was the contest accomplished by that renowned maiden. Not long afterward Basilides . . . declared himself to be a Christian and openly confessed it. . . . When the brethren in God came to him and inquired about the cause of this sudden and extraordinary impulse, he is said to have replied that Potamiaena had appeared to him at night three days after her martyrdom and placed a crown upon his head. She said that she had entreated the Lord on his behalf, had obtained her request, and would take him to herself before long. Thereupon the brethren imparted to him the seal in the Lord; and on the following day, after distinguishing himself in his testimony to the Lord, he was beheaded.”

Book VI of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 5]:

> “Accordingly, immediately after she had been condemned by the judge’s sentence, [Col. 0114A] Basilides, one of the attendants, led her to execution. When the crowd attempted to harass her and mock her with obscene words, Basilides drove off those who were insulting the virgin and gave many indications of mercy and humanity toward her. She, gladly accepting the man’s kindness toward her, told him to be of good courage: after her death she would obtain his salvation from the Lord and would shortly repay the benefits bestowed upon her. . . . Such was the contest fought by the most noble virgin. Shortly afterward Basilides . . . openly professed himself a Christian. . . . When certain brethren in the Lord came to him and asked the cause of that sudden and unexpected conversion, [Col. 0114B] he is said to have replied that Potamiaena, appearing to him by night on the third day after her martyrdom, had placed a crown upon his head and said that she had prayed to the Lord on his behalf and had obtained what she sought, and that not long afterward he himself would migrate to the realms above. After this, having received the seal of the Lord from the brethren, on the following day he gloriously confessed Christ and was beheaded.”

Did Potamiaena promise Basilides salvation and certain recompense for his benefits with less confidence than Perpetua promised Saturus a prediction of the future event? Does not Potamiaena also conduct herself as though she held the ordinances of divine predestination in ready money, or as though after death she would become the arbiter of the divine counsels, employing at her own discretion the aids of grace that is victorious of itself, by which Christ would grant Basilides “not only to believe in him, [Col. 0114C] but also to suffer for him”?

If Potamiaena hoped that her prayers for Basilides would shortly be heard, why could Perpetua not also have been led to the same hope? If it is counted to Potamiaena’s praise that she gave Basilides a sure hope of future salvation, why is it charged against Perpetua as a fault that she gave Saturus a sure hope of a future revelation? If no one has ever brought Potamiaena’s prophecy under suspicion of Montanism, why shall we drag Perpetua’s similar prophecy into the odium of Montanism? For how do these statements differ: “Be of good courage; after my death I shall obtain salvation for you,” and, “Tomorrow I shall report to you”?

After the persecution of Severus ended, a long peace followed until Decius, interrupted only by the persecution of Maximinus, which was brief and local. During this interval, visions and revelations were not absent from the Church, as is evident from certain examples which Eusebius inserted into his history because they were especially notable and concerned the public condition of the Church and likewise public and particularly celebrated persons. Such were those by which Alexander was chosen bishop of Jerusalem [Note: [Col. 0115D] See Eusebius, book VI, chapter 11], and that by which Saint Fabian was declared pontiff of the Roman Church [Note: [Col. 0115D] See Eusebius, ibid., chapter 29]. But I pass them over because they have scarcely anything in common with our argument, as I also pass over those of Dionysius of Alexandria which the same Eusebius relates [Note: [Col. 0115D] See his letter to Germanus in Eusebius, ibid., chapter 40, and his letter to Philemon in the same author, book VII, chapter 7], since they appear to offer little support to the present case.

## VII

I shall therefore come to Cyprian, for no one conducted himself more as though he possessed the Holy Spirit, like a certain necklace enclosed in his own casket, ready at his command to employ its illuminations whenever he wished and at his own discretion. Two things must be considered in his revelations and visions: their variety and frequency, and the confidence in divine favor and familiarity which that most holy and equally prudent man conceived from them. So that the reader may observe these things more carefully and conveniently, I have thought it proper to set forth here the holy martyr’s visions in the very words in which he himself relates them in his letters.

The eleventh letter—or the eighth according to the numbering of Pamelius’s edition—contains scarcely anything except visions and revelations. It was written from his retreat to the presbyters and deacons and exhorts them to pour forth prayers continually. Hence Augustine, mentioning it in book IV of *On Baptism*, gave it this title: “To the Clergy, on Praying to God.” The Decian persecution was raging with extreme savagery at that time. Cyprian says, moreover, that he was moved especially by divine revelations to write:

> “For you ought to know,” he says, “that what especially persuaded and compelled me to write this letter to you was that—as the Lord deigns to show and reveal—it was said in a vision: ‘Ask, and you shall obtain.’ Then the people who were present were commanded to pray for certain persons specifically designated to them. In their prayer, however, there were discordant voices and conflicting wills; and this greatly displeased him who had said, ‘Ask, and you shall obtain,’ because the disunity of the people was discordant and there was not among the brethren one agreement and a simple and united concord.”

He adds that this lack of unanimity, peace, and concord [Col. 0115D] among the brethren had been the cause of the raging persecution, which he testifies had been shown to him in the following vision long before it was decreed:

> “Indeed, these evils would not have come upon the brethren if the brotherhood had been united in one purpose. For this also was shown: the master of a household was seated, with a young man sitting at his right hand. The young man, anxious and somewhat indignant and sorrowful, sat supporting his cheek with his hand and wearing a mournful countenance. [Col. 0116A] Another, standing on the left, carried a net which he threatened to cast so as to catch the people standing around. When the person who saw this wondered what it meant, he was told that the young man sitting thus on the right was grieved and sorrowful because his commandments were not being observed, but that the one on the left rejoiced because an opportunity was given him to receive from the master of the household the power to rage. This was shown long before the tempest of the present devastation arose. And we have seen the fulfillment of what was shown.”

Just as in time of peace he foresaw the future persecution, so while the persecution raged he likewise understood in a vision that peace would soon come. Of this he writes in the same letter:

> “Finally, he deigned, in his goodness toward us, to give this message to his least servant—one burdened, indeed, with very many offenses and unworthy of his favor: ‘Tell him,’ he said, ‘to be secure, because peace is coming. There is only a short delay in the meantime, because there still remain some who are to be tested.’”

He testifies that he had been admonished by heavenly revelations not only concerning the continual pouring forth of prayers but also concerning other works of piety and duties of religion:

> “We are also admonished by divine favors concerning sparing food and sober drink, etc.”

Indeed, the most holy bishop was so secure about the future fulfillment of his prophecies that, although no ray of the desired tranquillity yet appeared, he nevertheless ordered this letter to be promulgated and also communicated to the people by the clergy to whom it had been written:

> “I ought not to have concealed each of these things and kept them hidden within my conscience alone. . . . [Col. 0116C] You yourselves certainly should not keep this letter hidden among you, but should cause it to be read to the brethren.”

But the minds of the afflicted people were so far removed from every hope of peace that most gave no credence to the letters and revelations of their most venerable pastor. He reproves their unbelief at the beginning of his book *On the Lapsed*, composed after tranquillity had been restored to the Church through the unexpected and sudden death of the Decii:

> “Behold, dearest brethren, peace has been restored to the Church, and our security—which recently appeared difficult to unbelievers and impossible to the faithless—has been reestablished by divine aid and vengeance.”

Letter sixteen in the most recent edition—letter ten according to the numbering of Pamelius—abounds no less in visions. Indeed, it embraces more numerous and varied visions, though in fewer words: [Col. 0116D]

> “Thus the divine judgment does not cease to chastise us either by night or by day. For in addition to nocturnal visions, by day also the innocent age of children among us is filled with the Holy Spirit and in ecstasy sees with its eyes, hears, and speaks those things by which the Lord deigns to admonish and instruct us. And you shall hear everything when the Lord, who commanded me to withdraw, has caused me to return to you. In the meantime, certain rash, incautious, and swollen men among you, who neither take account of man nor fear God, should know that if they persist further in the same conduct, I shall employ that admonition which the Lord commands me to employ, so that for the present they may be prohibited from making offerings.”

Who, on reading this, would not ascribe to our Cyprian that splendid commendation which Polycrates had long before bestowed upon Melito of Sardis [Note: [Col. 0117D] Letter to Pope Victor, in Eusebius, book V, chapter 24]: Τὸν ἐν ἁγίῳ Πνεύματι πάντα πολιτευσάμενον, “one who conducted all things under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit”? Hence Jerome reports from Tertullian, “in the seven books which he wrote against the Church on behalf of Montanus,” that Melito was “regarded by many of our people as a prophet” [Note: [Col. 0117D] *Catalogue*, under Melito].

Yet all these things apply no less to our Cyprian. For what did he do during the persecution that he did not accomplish under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit? So that he might prepare his people for the coming war, he perceived it by divine revelation long before it broke out. When war had been declared, he had God as the author of his decision to seek concealment and avoid the persecution; and, as he himself testifies, and as the deacon Pontius testifies in his *Life*, he did not withdraw without divine revelation.

When the tempest arose, he learned by divine revelation both by what exercises of virtue it was to be overcome and by what duties of piety tranquillity was to be obtained. By divine revelation he likewise foreknew the coming peace no less than the approaching war. He understood what discipline he ought to employ toward the lapsed, both through his own nocturnal visions and through the daytime raptures and ecstasies of innocent children. He likewise received from God, through an open and manifest admonition, the correction with which he ought to punish certain incautious and rash presbyters. Relying upon these continual gifts and favors of the Holy Spirit, he also awaited a heavenly revelation concerning his own return:

> “And you shall hear everything when the Lord, who commanded me to withdraw, has caused me to return to you.”

That this was not withheld from him [Col. 0117C] we shall state afterward.

Meanwhile, before he returned from his retreat to Carthage, he enrolled Aurelius and Celerinus—men distinguished by the glory of their confession—among the clergy. This was not done without the customary visions and divine revelations. For although the practice of those times required clerical ordinations to be celebrated only with the testimony of the people and the vote of the entire clergy, he explains why, while absent, he advanced them to the clergy. Speaking of Aurelius, he gives this reason: one who had been approved by divine testimony did not require human testimony [Note: [Col. 0117D] Letter XXXVIII according to Pamelius, no. 33]:

> “In clerical ordinations, dearest brethren, we are accustomed to consult you beforehand and to weigh the character and merits of each individual by common counsel. But human testimonies are not to be awaited when divine votes precede them. Our brother Aurelius, a distinguished young man, has already been approved by the Lord, etc.”

And in the following letter, speaking of the ordination of Celerinus, he testifies that it too was performed through the spirit of prophecy and not without visions and revelations:

> “For when,” he says, “he hesitated to consent, he was compelled in a vision by night by the admonition and exhortation of the Church herself not to refuse our persuasion; for she who compelled him possessed the greater authority.”

Cyprian himself frequently relates in his letters what disturbances Felicissimus, the author of the schism at Carthage, and the five presbyters who fostered his ruinous faction stirred up against that most holy man. Learned men infer from the following words of the holy martyr that he had received something from God concerning this matter and the persecution that threatened from it, and that a heavenly revelation had not been lacking:

> “This is another persecution and another temptation; and those five presbyters are nothing other than the five leading men who recently had been associated with the magistrates by edict, so that they might overthrow our faith and divert the frail hearts of the brethren, through betrayal of the truth, into deadly snares. The same design and once again the same overthrow are now being introduced, through the five presbyters allied with Felicissimus, for the ruin of salvation.”

Pamelius says that Cyprian appears to allude to some vision in which five leading men seemed to appear with the magistrates and jointly publish an edict against the bishops. Rigaltius does not oppose this interpretation, and Dodwell manifestly embraces it [Note: [Col. 0118D] Fourth *Cyprianic Dissertation on Visions*, etc., §18].

In the same letter—now numbered XLVIII, formerly XL—the last of those which he composed in retirement, he clearly and plainly indicates, as it seems to me, that he had already received the revelation concerning his return which, as we said above, he had been awaiting. For first he complains:

> “That the malice and perfidy of certain presbyters had made it impossible for him to come to his people before Easter.”

He was, of course, taking care lest a greater tumult arise in Carthage from his arrival because of the threats and plots of the faithless, and lest, although a bishop ought in all things to provide for peace and tranquillity, he himself should appear to have furnished material for sedition and inflamed the persecution anew.

Afterward he adds [Col. 0118C] that this is the final persecution and the last temptation, which, he says,

> “will itself also quickly pass, with the Lord’s protection, so that I may be restored to you with my colleagues after Easter Day.”

Do we not have manifest and clear indications of a prophetic revelation? Before Easter he remained in his retreat, fearing lest by his arrival he furnish material for sedition and appear to have inflamed the persecution anew. Yet he confidently promises that he will return after Easter. But could not the same danger threaten after Easter? By no means, for he knew that this last temptation of the persecution would quickly pass. But from what source did he know this, so as to make so certain a promise? Surely from none other than divine revelation.

After the Decii had been removed, Gallus and Volusianus brought upon the Church the second persecution of Cyprian’s time. Saint Cyprian understood that this persecution too would come before it raged—indeed, even before it was decreed—not through one or two, but through many frequent and manifest disclosures and visions. Through the synodical letter of the second Council of Carthage to Cornelius, he made it known not only to his own Church but also to the Roman Church [Note: [Col. 0118D] Letter LVII, formerly LIV]:

> “But since we see that the day of another assault has again begun to approach, and since we are admonished by frequent and continual disclosures to be armed and prepared for the contest which the enemy declares against us, let us also prepare by our exhortations the people entrusted to us by divine favor, etc.”

Afterward:

> “For we must obey just disclosures and admonitions, so that the sheep are not abandoned by their pastors in time of danger, etc.”

Again:

> “It has seemed good to us, at the suggestion of the Holy Spirit and with the Lord admonishing us through many manifest visions—since it is foretold and shown that the enemy threatens us—to gather the soldiers of Christ within the camp, etc.”

The distinguished Dodwell adds the following to these words of Cyprian [Note: [Col. 0119D] *Dissertation on Visions*, etc., §19]:

> “Atheists will perhaps not believe these things. But what reason do they have for refusing to regard them as worthy of belief? Here we have visions that are not merely numerous but also manifest and confirmed by the event. Nor were they recorded upon the obscure testimony of some private person, but by the consenting vote of an entire synod, in writings destined—had they proved false—to remain as everlasting memorials of the matter, writings ‘clearer than the sun,’ as Jerome says. I do not see what more they could desire for the confirmation of a matter of fact, provided they wished to judge impartially and not deprive men of all credibility whatsoever.”

Again, concerning the same persecution he writes thus to the people of Thibaris [Note: [Col. 0119D] Letter LVIII, formerly LVI]:

> “For since, by the favor of the Lord who instructs us, we are repeatedly and still more urgently impelled and admonished, we ought also to bring the solicitude of our admonition to your attention. For you ought to know, believe with certainty, and hold fast that the day of tribulation has begun to hang over our heads. . . . We do not think that the things now coming are such as those which have passed. A struggle more severe and more savage now threatens.”

It is not without reason that one may wonder how the persecution of Gallus was to be more severe and savage than that of Decius, since in fact it was briefer and far milder. I resolved this difficulty as follows in my *Dissertation on Penance, or on Capital Absolution* [Note: [Col. 0119D] Section 3].

Through these visions Cyprian had been shown not only the coming persecution but likewise all the evils that threatened the Church no less than the commonwealth: namely, the incursions of the barbarians and the resulting captivities of Christians and pagans alike, and the most ruinous plague which raged widely throughout the Roman Empire. The severity and innumerable devastations of this calamity are lamented both by Saint Cyprian himself, by the deacon Pontius in his *Life*, and by other authors. These and other calamities, therefore, combined with the persecution, made the reign of Gallus and Volusianus far more grievous for Christians than that of Decius. Since not all the causes of these evils had been clearly and distinctly revealed to the holy martyr, he readily persuaded himself that all the calamities and deaths of Christians which he had foreseen would arise from the persecution alone.

Thus far we have seen how frequent and familiar heavenly revelations were to Cyprian. Let us now see to what confidence the holy martyr was led by their frequency, and whether he too, no differently from Perpetua, conducted himself as though he possessed the Holy Spirit, like a certain necklace enclosed in his own casket, ready at his command to employ its illuminations whenever he wished and at his own discretion.

A sign of such confidence is the assurance he displayed that a heavenly revelation would not fail him which would indicate the proper time for his return—a point we have already noted. I shall now offer another no less evident argument for the same conclusion.

In that most weighty letter in which he reproves Florentius Pupianus, a seditious and turbulent man, with the greatest severity, he at last promises him pardon, if he comes to his senses, upon this condition: that God should permit it and signify his judgment and will in the matter by some perceptible sign [Note: [Col. 0120D] Letter LVI, formerly LXIX]:

> “If, even at this late hour, you begin to repent of your rashness, pride, and insolence . . . we shall be able to take account of your communion, while nevertheless retaining among us respect and fear for the divine judgment, so that I may first consult my Lord whether, by his disclosure and admonition, he permits peace to be given to you and you to be admitted to the communion of his Church. For I remember what has already been shown to me—indeed, what was commanded by dominical and divine authority to an obedient and God-fearing servant. Among the other things which he deigned to show and reveal, he also added this: ‘Thus he who does not believe Christ when he appoints a priest will afterward begin to believe Christ when he vindicates the priest.’”

Dodwell adds the following to these words of the holy martyr [Note: [Col. 0120D] Fourth *Cyprianic Dissertation*, §20]:

> “Divine revelations were so frequent in that age that he did not dare to promise even what he would determine concerning a repentant Pupianus, lest perhaps something else should be commanded by God. Thus he held that God must first be consulted by means of a sign; and at last he awaited God’s punishment of the rebel, precisely such a punishment as learned men acknowledge to have accompanied apostolic censures.”

Again, concerning the presbyters who had communicated with the lapsed without consulting him, he says [Note: [Col. 0120D] Letter XVI, formerly X]:

> “I shall employ that admonition which the Lord commands me to employ, so that for the present they may be prohibited from making offerings, etc.”

Cyprian was not unaware that visions of this kind were held in ridicule and contempt by impious and rash men, such as we now experience in no small number. Nevertheless, he held it so certain that his revelations came from God that he had no doubt about future events. He was not afraid not only to publish the revelations already granted to him but even openly to promise himself new ones. Hence, in the same letter, he immediately adds:

> “Although I know that dreams appear ridiculous and visions foolish to certain persons—namely, to those who prefer to believe against a priest rather than to believe the priest. But this is no wonder, since Joseph’s brothers said of him: ‘Behold, that dreamer comes. Come now, therefore, let us kill him.’ Yet afterward the dreamer obtained what he had dreamed, while his killers and sellers were confounded, so that those who had not previously believed words afterward believed deeds.”

There remains another prophetic vision of Cyprian concerning his martyrdom, but I shall reserve it for the following chapter. Meanwhile, I ask: does he not appear to have possessed the Holy Spirit in his breast as though enclosed in a casket, since even in exercising ecclesiastical discipline he awaited visions and dared determine nothing [Col. 0121A] unless he had first consulted the Lord and had been made certain of his will by some manifest indication? And was Perpetua therefore to be accused of Montanism because she too, being accustomed to divine revelations, conducted herself with the same confidence?

VIII. How frequently heavenly visions and prophetic revelations were granted to martyrs at that time is most fully attested by the authentic and genuine Acts both of James and Marianus, etc., and of the martyrs Montanus, Lucius, and their companions, which are filled with heavenly visions and prophetic predictions. I do not intend to recount them here one by one, for it would be necessary to transcribe almost the entire Acts, which may conveniently be consulted in the learned Ruinart. I shall cite only one example from the Acts of Montanus, which [Col. 0121B] bears more directly on the present argument. It is described in the Acts in these words:

> “But when the executioner was already at hand, and the sword hung poised above his neck, he—that is, Montanus—stretched out his hands toward heaven and prayed in a clear voice, so that its sound reached not only the ears of the people but even the pagans themselves, asking and beseeching that Flavianus, who had been separated from their company through the people’s intercession, might follow on the third day. And to provide confirmation of his prayer, he tore into two pieces the handkerchief with which his eyes had been bound, and ordered one half to be kept so that Flavianus’s eyes might be bound with it the day after the morrow. He also ordered that a plot of ground in the open area between them be reserved, so that they might not be deprived of fellowship even in burial. And before our very eyes there was fulfilled what the Lord promised in the Gospel: that whoever asked with complete [Col. 0121C] faith would obtain whatever he asked. For after two days Flavianus too was brought forth, and perfected his glory through suffering.”

It is no more astonishing that Perpetua foretold that a revelation concerning her impending martyrdom would be given before the following day than that Montanus prophesied that Flavianus’s martyrdom would occur after three days. For by the same prophetic spirit under whose impulse Montanus asked “that Flavianus might follow on the third day,” Perpetua asked that before the next day it should be shown to her whether her future held suffering or release. For, as is established by many examples from Scripture, both belong to the spirit of prophecy: to foresee future events, and to await definite revelations of future events.

IX. Concerning the preceding visions and prophetic predictions both of Cyprian [Col. 0121D] and of the contemporary martyrs, one point must be carefully observed: it is agreed by all that the abundance of charisms was far greater at the beginning of the Church than in later centuries. Thus Origen, who wrote his books *Against Celsus* several years before the persecution of Decius, bears witness that by his time only traces of the signs of the Holy Spirit had survived among a few persons distinguished by purity of character and conforming their conduct to the rule of the Gospel. For after saying that the truth of the Gospel is proved by miracles, he says that these can be demonstrated,

> “from many other things, and also from the fact that certain traces of them still survive among those who live according to the will of the Word.”

[Note: [Col. 0121D] “From many other things, and from the fact that traces—or perhaps *certain traces*—of them [Col. 0122D] still survive among those who live according to the will of the Word” (Ἐκ πολλῶν μὲν ἄλλων, καὶ ἐκ τοῦ ἴχνη δὲ [perhaps τινὰ] αὐτῶν ἔτι σώζεσθαι παρὰ τοῖς κατὰ τὸ βούλημα τοῦ Λόγου βιοῦσι). Book I, p. 5, Cambridge edition.]

[Col. 0122A] And in another book of the same work:

> “The signs of the Holy Spirit were shown in very great number at the beginning of Jesus’ teaching and after his ascension, but afterward in smaller number. Yet even now traces of him remain among a few who have purified their souls by the Word and by conduct consonant with it.”

[Note: [Col. 0122D] “The signs of the Holy Spirit were shown in greater number at the beginning of Jesus’ teaching and after his ascension, but afterward in smaller number; yet even now traces of him remain among a few who have purified their souls by the Word and by practices consonant with it” (Σημεῖα δὲ τοῦ ἁγίου Πνεύματος κατ᾽ ἀρχὰς μὲν τῆς Ἰησοῦ διδασκαλίας, μετὰ δὲ τὴν ἀνάληψιν αὐτοῦ πλείονα ἐδείκνυτο, ὕστερον δὲ ἐλάττονα, πλὴν καὶ νῦν ἔτι ἴχνη ἔστιν αὐτοῦ παρ᾽ ὀλίγοις, τὰς ψυχὰς τῷ Λόγῳ καὶ ταῖς κατ᾽ αὐτὸν πράξεσι κεκαθαρμένοις). Book VII, p. 337.]

He explains more clearly in the following words what those traces were:

> “Even now traces of that Holy Spirit survive among Christians. They cast out demons by incantation, perform many cures, and, according to the will of the Word, see certain things concerning the future.”

[Note: [Col. 0122D] “Even now traces of that Holy Spirit . . . survive among Christians: they cast out demons by incantation, perform many cures, and see certain things concerning the future according to the will of the Word” (Καὶ ἔτι ἴχνη τοῦ ἁγίου ἐκείνου Πνεύματος . . . παρὰ χριστιανοῖς σώζεται· ἐξεπᾴδουσι δαίμονας, καὶ πολλὰς ἰάσεις ἐπιτελοῦσι, καὶ ὁρῶσί τινα κατὰ τὸ βούλημα τοῦ Λόγου περὶ μελλόντων). Book I, p. 31.]

From these words it is evident that the exceedingly abundant fountain of heavenly charisms, which in the time of Irenaeus—as he himself testifies—was poured out upon all who were true disciples of Christ, [Col. 0122B] had not entirely dried up, though it no longer overflowed afterward with the same breadth and abundance. Now Perpetua and Saturus lived very close to the time of Irenaeus; whereas the last years of Cyprian, and the martyrs Montanus and his companions, were far removed from the period when Origen composed his books *Against Celsus*—namely, under Gordian or the Philips, after the Church had enjoyed a long and lasting peace. Consequently, if the holy martyrs were so filled with the Holy Spirit when only certain traces of his signs remained that they seemed able to make use of his illuminations at will, why should we wonder if the Holy Spirit granted Perpetua the same abundance of them, at a time when “no reckoning could be made of the charisms which [Col. 0122C] the Church received from God throughout the whole world”?

# CHAPTER V. NOTHING IS CONTAINED IN PERPETUA’S REVELATIONS THAT IS NOT ENTIRELY FITTING FOR A CATHOLIC MARTYR

I. Christ the Lord is not dishonored by the figure of a shepherd milking sheep.  
II. How Perpetua understood from her first revelation that death was imminent.  
III. Nothing absurd is contained in the revelation in which Perpetua seemed to herself to be transformed into a man and to wrestle with the Devil.  
IV. The inept comparison of Perpetua’s revelations with those of the Montanists.  
V. Perpetua’s vision of Dinocrates situated amid punishments.  
[Col. 0122D] VI. Basnage’s difficulties concerning the aforesaid vision.  
VII. The place in which Perpetua saw Dinocrates was purgatory. Basnage’s cavils are refuted.  
[Col. 0123A] VIII. The Montanists’ opinion concerning the receptacles of souls is not correctly presented by Basnage. Those heretics did not hold a single opinion on this matter.

## I

Basnage constructs another argument against the Martyrs from the very manner and character of the visions presented to Perpetua, which do not seem to him sufficiently compatible with dignity and decorum:

> “A man dressed as a shepherd gave Perpetua what was, as it were, a morsel from the cheese he was milking. From this she concludes that death is imminent for her.”

Basnage thus appears, with censorious authority, to find fault with two things in this vision of Perpetua: first, the humble figure of Christ in the garb of a shepherd milking sheep; second, the fact that Perpetua and Saturus took the morsel offered to her as a sign of her impending death.

But there was no reason for him to take offense at either of these things. [Col. 0123B] Concerning the first, the distinguished Holstenius should be heard in his *Notes*:

> “Christ was represented to Perpetua in the form in which he was depicted in the oratories and sacred vessels of those times. For since the Gospels especially assign to Christ the title and person of shepherd, the Christians of the earliest period delighted in setting before their eyes with great frequency this most lovable appearance of his, together with the faithful, who are everywhere designated by the name of sheep. In Bosio’s *Underground Rome*, p. 59 and following, you have many images reproduced from the monuments of the cemeteries, in almost all of which Christ is depicted as a shepherd with sheep. In the very first of them, reproduced here, he is represented precisely in this form: as a shepherd milking sheep. He was also often depicted carrying upon his shoulders the recovered sheep that had been lost, in accordance with the Gospel parable; [Col. 0123C] and this was done especially upon chalices, as Tertullian indicates in chapter 7 of his book *On Modesty*, written against the Catholics, in these words: ‘You may begin from the parables, where there is the lost sheep, sought by God and carried back upon his shoulders. Let the very pictures on your chalices come forward, if even in them the interpretation of that sheep is made manifest,’ etc.”

To this I add that in the Italian work of the most illustrious and learned senator Filippo Buonarroti, entitled *Observations upon Certain Fragments of Ancient Glass Vessels Ornamented with Figures, Found in the Cemeteries of Rome*, many reproductions may be seen of ancient chalices marked with this figure of Christ in the garb of the Good Shepherd: for example, plate 5, figs. 1 and 2, and plate 6, fig. 2. See also plate 1, fig. 1, and in plate 4 a rather large bronze coin, commonly called a *medallion*, engraved on both sides with the figure of the Good Shepherd; [Col. 0123D] all of which the learned author elucidates with highly erudite observations. But what he discusses concerning figure 2 of plate 6 is especially pertinent to our subject:

> “In this fragment the Good Shepherd is seen between two sheep or rams, wearing the customary shoes with bands crossed in a herringbone pattern. Beside him one must observe that little pail, or vessel for milk, which is also seen in the paintings of the cemeteries, [Note: [Col. 0123D] Arringhi, plate 6, chamber 3, Cemetery of Callistus.] and particularly in plate 3 of the sixth chamber of the Cemetery of Callistus in Arringhi. There it is seen attached to a shepherd’s crook held by a reclining lamb, as a symbol of the Good Shepherd. At the feet of that same [Col. 0124A] shepherd, in plate 1 of the second chamber of the Cemetery of Saint Agnes, one sees the crook with a vessel, though of a different shape and with a handle on the side. These shepherds’ vessels were called *mulctrae*, or *mulctralia* [milk-pails], [Note: [Col. 0124D] Servius on *Eclogue* 3.] and this kind of vessel was called in Greek πέλλα (*pella*). It resembled the *scyphus*, but had a somewhat broader bottom, and so was not very dissimilar to ours; it was used especially for milking. [Note: [Col. 0124D] Athenaeus, LXI, col. 14.] Another milk vessel was called *sino*, [Note: [Col. 0124D] Servius on *Eclogue* 7; Nonius, ch. 15.] which, judging from the force of the name, must have been larger than our little vessel,” etc., etc.

And below:

> “To return to our little milk vessel beside the Good Shepherd, I believe that it was fashioned not only as a continuation of the allegory of pastoral things, but furthermore I regard it as, in a manner, a figure of the most divine sacrament [Col. 0124B] of the altar. This seems to be inferred from the most ancient Acts of Saints Perpetua and Felicity, where it is said that Saint Perpetua received milk in a vision from the divine Shepherd: ‘And from the cheese that he was milking he gave me what was, as it were, a morsel; and I received it with joined hands and ate it, and all who stood around said, Amen.’ These were ceremonies and devotional acts customarily practiced by the ancient Christians when receiving Holy Communion. [Note: [Col. 0124D] Tertullian, *On the Shows*, ch. 25; Cornelius in Eusebius, *History*, book VI, ch. 43; Dionysius in Eusebius, book VII, ch. 9; St. Augustine, *Sermon to the Newly Baptized on the Sacraments*; St. Ambrose, book IV *On the Sacraments*, ch. 5; St. Cyril, *Catechesis* 5; the Council in Trullo, canon 102.] And the words of the Song, [Note: [Col. 0124D] Song of Songs V.1.] ‘I drank my wine with my milk,’ are applied by Saint Ambrose [Note: [Col. 0124D] *On the Sacraments*, book V, ch. 3.] to the sacrament of the Eucharist. Since, moreover, in Arringhi, among the paintings on the vault of the ninth chamber in the Cemetery of Saints Marcellinus and Peter, there appears a lamb with a palm branch, bearing a similar little vessel on its shoulders and surrounded by a nimbus, or diadem, and [Col. 0124C] since the same lamb is there painted no fewer than four times in the corners of the same vault, I have wondered whether perhaps in very ancient times they preserved the Holy Eucharist in a similar vessel placed upon a lamb, just as they later used for the same ministry vessels having the form of a dove. In such matters, however, it is good to observe, but one must suspend judgment until further corroboration is available.”

Thus the most illustrious senator. He also observes that the same shepherd’s tunic is ornamented in its lower part with two disks, or bosses; and that in these Acts of Perpetua and Felicity those ornaments are called *calliculae*, from the Greek word κάλλος (*kallos*, “beauty”). They were for the most part of gold or silver, as is established from the same Acts and from other ancient figures in Lambecius [Note: [Col. 0124D] *Imperial Library*, plate 4, Appendix, p. 301.], Pietro [Col. 0124D] Sante Bartoli [Note: [Col. 0124D] *Ancient Paintings of the Grottoes of Rome*, plate 4.], and the Vatican manuscript of Virgil copied in the time of Constantine the Great. [Note: [Col. 0124D] Before book II of the *Aeneid*.]

[Col. 0125A] But to return πρὸς τὸ πρόβλημα (*pros to problēma*, “to the problem”), to the points noted by these most learned men I further add that images of this kind were not especially pleasing to the Montanists, nor were they in use among them. I infer this most clearly from the same words of Tertullian: “Let,” he says, “the very pictures on your chalices come forward.” He does not say “ours,” but “yours”—that is, those which are in use among you, not among us. And in chapter 10 of the same book:

> “If perchance that shepherd whom you depict upon your chalice shall patronize him, he too is a corrupter of the Christian sacrament, deservedly both an idol of drunkenness and a refuge for the adultery that is to follow the chalice—the chalice from which you drink nothing more willingly than the sheep of a second repentance. But I drink in the Scripture of that Shepherd, which cannot be broken.”

Again, he does not say “whom we depict upon the chalice,” but “whom you depict upon the chalice.” [Col. 0125B] Moreover, he calls this pious picture “an idol of drunkenness and a refuge for adultery.” He would certainly not have assailed it with such insulting words if it had also been in use among the Montanists and if they had adorned with it the sacred vessels intended to receive Christ’s blood. Hence there arises a presumption that Perpetua was accustomed to Catholic rites, since she saw Christ, in the garb of a shepherd, administering to her the Eucharist or a symbol of the Eucharist.

Furthermore, if Christ did not disdain the appearance of a shepherd but so frequently applied it to himself, why would he disdain a shepherd’s duties, among which milking sheep occupies no insignificant place? Does this figure dishonor Christ more than that of a hen gathering her chicks beneath her wings and warming them—a figure that the most gracious Lord, accommodating himself to our capacity, by no means rejected? [Col. 0125C] And certainly no image could be more fitting for prefiguring impending martyrdom than that of a shepherd milking sheep. For with the same eagerness with which a shepherd draws milk from the udders of sheep, Christ the Good Shepherd received blood from the martyrs’ veins.

## II

Concerning the second difficulty, the same distinguished Holstenius has these few remarks:

> “Much could be said about the symbolic use of milk and honey customarily given to catechumens, from Hesychius, *On Exodus*, p. 257, and Tertullian, *On the Crown*, p. 121, Rigault’s edition, where he says, ‘We taste beforehand the concord of milk and honey.’ See Albaspinaeus, book II, final Observation.”

But Pierre Poussines adds much more on this point in his *Supplementary Notes* to the notes of Holstenius, and his observations contribute still more [Col. 0125D] toward resolving the difficulty raised against us by Basnage:

> “‘And from the cheese,’ etc. The observation that I found in Holstenius’s papers on the custom of giving milk to catechumens is insufficient to explain the meaning of this passage. That the author would have added other matters to it if he had been able to put the final hand to this work is shown by the blank space he left in his notebooks, after the words of Saint Perpetua that we have transcribed, obviously to be filled in during his final revision. It still remained to explain how, after awakening, Saint Perpetua understood from this presentation of a morsel administered in a vision—as did her brother after she had related the matter to him—that those held in prison were by no means to be released from it, [Col. 0126A] but were to be consummated in martyrdom. For after the words transcribed above, the following are added there: ‘And I immediately reported it to my brother’—the brother, namely, who had asked her to arrange for it to be shown her by divine means whether they were to die or to be released safely—‘and we understood that suffering was to occur, and we began to have no further hope in this world.’ It is rightly asked how they understood this. I think they did so because the rite of administering the Eucharist to Perpetua had been foreshadowed in the vision. Since by the very well-known practice of that time it was customarily given to those who were certain to die shortly, Perpetua and her brother correctly interpreted this to mean that the vision signified the confessors’ imminent death. That the rite of receiving the Eucharist is foreshadowed there is apparent from the fact that what was, as it were, a morsel is offered to Perpetua; [Col. 0126B] that she herself receives it with joined hands; that she then eats it; and that those standing around acclaim, ‘Amen.’ That all these things were customarily observed in the ancient administration of the Eucharist is too well known from the testimony of many ancient writers, and especially Saint Ambrose, to require further proof. Certainly, as regards the practice of the African churches in particular, it is established that they customarily administered the Eucharist to confessors preparing for martyrdom. Indeed, they regarded this as so necessary that they drew from it an argument for writing to Cornelius, the Roman pontiff—by the hand and pen of Saint Cyprian, but in the name of thirty-seven other African bishops as well—asking him to deem it just that dispensation should be granted from the law previously enacted, under which those who had once lapsed during persecution were never to be admitted to the communion of the Church and of the Eucharist. For at that time many of them, enrolled among the penitents, were endangered by new persecutors and, as matters stood, seemed likely soon to be put to death for confessing Christ. To deny those preparing for the contest the customary viaticum of Christ’s body was excessively inhumane. [Col. 0126C] From this letter, which is the second in book I of Cyprian, I shall append certain passages suitable for establishing the point with which we are dealing:
>
> “‘But since,’ they say, ‘we see that the day of another assault has again begun to draw near, and are warned by frequent and continual revelations to be armed and prepared for the conflict which the enemy declares against us; since we must also prepare by our exhortations the people entrusted to us by divine favor, and gather within the Lord’s camp absolutely all the soldiers of Christ who desire weapons and demand battle—compelled by necessity, we have judged that peace must be granted to those who have not withdrawn from the Lord’s Church, but who have not ceased from the very first day of their lapse to do penance, to lament, and to beseech the Lord; and that they must be armed and equipped for the battle that is imminent.’”
>
> And a little later:
>
> “‘But now peace is necessary not for the weak but for the strong, nor must communion be given by us to the dying but to the living, so that we may not leave unarmed and naked those whom we stir up and exhort to battle, but may fortify them with the protection of Christ’s body and blood. And since the Eucharist is made for this purpose, that it may be a safeguard to those who receive it, let us arm with the fortification of the Lord’s sustenance those whom we wish to be secure against the adversary. [Col. 0126D] For how do we teach or urge them to shed their own blood in confession of the Name if we deny Christ’s blood to those about to fight? Or how do we make them fit for the cup of martyrdom if we do not first admit them, by right of communion, to drink the Lord’s cup in the Church? For’—as is added somewhat later—‘he cannot be fit for martyrdom who is not armed by the Church for battle; and that mind fails which the Eucharist, when received, does not raise up and kindle.’”

[Col. 0127A] I do not deny that these arguments are brilliantly and excellently conceived, and that they can most fully satisfy Basnage’s scruple. Nevertheless, I shall add certain points unnoticed by the learned man which will remove every cause of offense from this passage.

[Col. 0127B] First, then, I observe that something similar occurs in the Acts of Saint Philip, bishop of Heraclea and martyr. In them Hermes, his deacon, who together with him consummated his martyrdom by fire, recounts that he learned through this revelation that death had certainly been prepared for him:

> “I had learned that I was to suffer this through an entirely certain revelation, God and the Lord having already announced it beforehand. For while I lay bound by sweet sleep, a dove appeared to me, shining with snowy whiteness. It entered that room and suddenly settled upon the crown of my head; then, descending from there to my breast, it offered me food of the most delightful kind. I immediately understood that the Lord had deigned to call me and had judged me worthy of suffering.”

[Note: [Col. 0127D] In Ruinart, *Authentic Acts*, § 13.]

Second, I observe that Perpetua does not say that she and her brother understood from the presentation of the morsel alone—as seemed to Poussines [Col. 0127C] and afterward to Basnage—that death would soon follow. Perpetua reported to her brother everything she had seen; but she had seen signs of her future suffering far clearer than this. Why, then, should they not have understood more plainly from these that “suffering was to occur”? She had seen a golden ladder of marvelous size extending all the way to heaven, with every kind of iron implement fixed upon its sides. There were swords, lances, hooks, and large blades. She had seen an enormous dragon lying beneath the ladder itself, which laid snares for those ascending and terrified them to keep them from climbing. She had seen Saturus ascending, reaching the top of the ladder, and from there inviting her also to ascend. She had seen herself, as soon as she stepped upon the first rung of the ladder, also tread upon that dragon’s head. Finally, she had seen Christ [Col. 0127D] in the garb of a shepherd milking sheep, etc. Were not all these the clearest signs of the death that was to follow? Why, then, do we insist that the holy martyrs understood from the presentation of the morsel alone that death was imminent for them?

It is true, as Poussines observes, that after the words “and from the cheese that he was milking,” etc., Perpetua adds: “And I immediately reported it to my brother, and we understood that suffering was to occur.” But just as she did not report to her brother only what she had seen last—namely, that a morsel of milk was offered to her—so they did not understand from this sign alone that “suffering was to occur.”

## III

[Col. 0128A] Basnage seeks to bring another of Perpetua’s visions into disrepute in these words:

> “More remarkable is what Perpetua recounts in chapter III, § 2: ‘A certain Egyptian, hideous in appearance, came out against me, intending to fight with me together with his assistants. And handsome young men also came to me, my assistants and supporters; and I was stripped, and I became a man.’ Perpetua therefore advances to fight the Egyptian with her sex changed, intending to receive as the prize of victory ‘a green branch on which there were golden apples. And he called for silence and said: “If this Egyptian defeats her, he will kill her with the sword; and if she defeats him, she will receive this branch.” And he withdrew. We approached one another and began to exchange blows. He sought to seize my feet, but I struck his face with my heels.’ Are these things worthy of the Holy Spirit? Did he ever present anything similar to the prophets? These, of course, are supposedly the visions to which Joel’s sacred oracle is to be applied. Dreams of this kind smell rather of Montanus’s workshop; and her ecstasy is very like the one by which Tertullian proves that the soul is ‘of an airy color and in every respect of human form.’”

[Col. 0128B] There are, then, three things in this vision of Perpetua that appear especially to offend Basnage:

1. Perpetua’s change of sex;
2. the prize of victory, a green branch with golden apples;
3. Perpetua’s struggle with the Egyptian.

Before responding to each of these points, I shall say in general that very many visions and revelations—not only those recounted in the authentic Acts of the martyrs, in histories of the saints, and in other monuments of unquestioned credibility, but also those found in the sacred books of both Testaments—[Col. 0128C] can easily be exposed to contempt and ridicule if the symbols are considered merely in themselves, without regard to their σχέσις (*schesis*), their relation and connection to divine and incorporeal realities. Indeed, not only in visions and inward revelations, but also in prophetic actions and the ceremonies of the Law, there are many things that vain and arrogant people once received with laughter and still ridicule, because they considered them in themselves and paid no attention to their mystical meanings.

Hence it has happened that what appeared to some unworthy of the Holy Spirit, inept, and ridiculous, others held in honor and admiration and treated with the highest veneration: the former directed their minds no further than what was presented to the senses, while the latter carefully investigated the mysteries also concealed in these figures. We see that this occurred also in the interpretation [Col. 0128D] of Perpetua’s revelation. For what now offends Basnage once delighted Augustine’s devout mind wonderfully:

> “It delights the devout mind,” he says, “to contemplate such a spectacle as blessed Perpetua relates was revealed to her concerning herself: that, having become a man, she fought with the Devil. For in that contest she too was advancing toward the perfect man, toward the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ.”

[Note: [Col. 0128D] Sermon 281, otherwise *On Various Subjects* 104.]

And in another sermon, alluding to the same vision of Perpetua, he repeats similar words:

> “For what is more glorious than these women, whom men more readily admire than imitate? But this is chiefly the praise of him in whom they believed, and in whose name they strove together with faithful zeal: according to the inner person they are found to be neither male nor female, so that even in those who are women in body the virtue of the mind conceals the sex of the flesh, and one is ashamed to consider in their limbs what could not appear in their deeds.”

[Note: [Col. 0128D] Sermon 280, otherwise *On Various Subjects* 103.]

Why Basnage should have been displeased that the prize of victory was represented by a green branch adorned with golden apples [Col. 0129A] I cannot adequately understand. Did not John the Evangelist see palms in the martyrs’ hands? “And palms,” he says, “were in their hands.” If the Holy Spirit represented the martyrs’ victories by palms, why could a green branch not be a figure of the same victory?

Nor was there reason for Basnage to be so offended by Perpetua’s struggle with the Devil, since he had often read of Jacob’s struggle with the angel. For if we do not attend to the mystical meanings of that event, could it not appear more absurd for a man, not in dreams but while awake, to wrestle through the entire night with a good angel, than for a holy woman to wrestle in dreams with the Devil? If it was not unworthy of the Holy Spirit for Jacob’s struggle with the angel to foreshadow something mystical, why does Basnage ask whether the vision presented to Perpetua—in which she seemed to herself to contend against the Devil—was worthy of the Holy Spirit? [Col. 0129B] Why does he also ask whether the same Holy Spirit ever presented anything similar to the prophets? For he did present it, as we have seen. What difference does it make that Jacob and Perpetua wrestled while awake or asleep—the former with an angel, the latter with the Devil?

The green branch offered to Perpetua as the prize of victory also has, as we have seen, something similar in the canonical and [Col. 0129C] genuine revelations of the Holy Spirit: namely, the palms which John saw in the martyrs’ hands. Finally, the change of sex signifies nothing other than what Augustine observes the Apostle to have written: “In Christ Jesus there is neither male nor female”; and that not only males but females also, through the exercise of virtue, become “according to the inner person, a perfect man, unto the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ.” Was it, then, unworthy of the Holy Spirit to signify through a mystical vision what Paul had expressed in mystical words?

Did not the same Holy Spirit, moreover, later signify to the chief of the Apostles, through a linen sheet presented to him in a vision and filled with every kind of unclean [Col. 0129D] animal, what he had foretold through Isaiah concerning the conversion of the nations under the various figures of different animals and in metaphorical words? Has not the same Holy Spirit often foreshadowed through prophetic actions what he had sometimes foretold in words through the prophets—actions which at first sight may appear insufficiently joined with decorum and dignity? Thus Isaiah is commanded to walk naked; Ezekiel to eat bread either covered “with dung that comes out of a man” or prepared over cow dung; and Hosea to take for himself a wife of whoredom and beget children of whoredom.

What would Basnage answer if some atheist asked him: “Are these things worthy of the Holy Spirit? Do these things seem to you sufficiently compatible with dignity and decorum?” Whatever argument he might devise to defend from the ridicule of the impious these prophetic deeds undertaken at the command of the Holy Spirit, we too shall always and easily devise a similar argument to vindicate Perpetua’s vision from Basnage’s own cavils—unless perhaps he requires greater decorum and dignity in the dreams of a sleeping person, however prophetic they may be, than in the likewise prophetic actions of those who are awake. [Col. 0130A]

Yet another point must by no means be omitted: Basnage unreasonably demands that we produce from the sacred books another vision wholly similar to this vision of Perpetua. By this argument he could bring under suspicion almost all the visions of saints reported in ecclesiastical histories, for he will not find many wholly similar to those recounted in the sacred books.

Pontius the deacon relates in his *Life* [Col. 0130B] the revelation granted to Saint Cyprian concerning his future martyrdom, a revelation wholly unlike anything the Holy Spirit ever presented to the prophets. I shall therefore adduce it as an example:

> “On the day when we first remained at the place of exile—for his loving kindness had chosen me as a voluntary exile among his domestic companions, and would that this had been permitted also in his suffering!—there appeared to me,” he says, “when I had not yet sunk into the repose of sleep, a young man of extraordinary size. As he led me, as it were, to the governor’s residence, I seemed to myself to be brought before the tribunal of the proconsul then seated there. As soon as the proconsul looked upon me, he immediately began to write down upon a tablet a sentence unknown to me, for he had asked me nothing according to the customary interrogation.
>
> “But the young man who stood behind him read with great attention everything that had been written down. Since he could not express it from there in words, he showed by an explanatory gesture what was contained in the writing on that tablet. [Col. 0130C] Extending his hand and flattening it like a sword, he imitated the stroke of the customary execution, and expressed what he wished to be understood as clearly as spoken language. I understood that the sentence meant future suffering. I immediately began to ask and entreat that a postponement of even one day be granted me, until I might arrange my affairs in due order.
>
> “When I had repeatedly renewed my entreaties, the judge again began to write something—I do not know what—upon the tablet. From the serenity of his expression, however, I perceived that his mind had been moved, as it were, by my just petition. And that young man who had previously disclosed the indication of suffering by gesture rather than speech now hastened, by another secret sign, to indicate that the postponement requested until the morrow had been granted: he repeatedly twisted his fingers one behind another.” [Col. 0130D]

Basnage will seek in vain for anything wholly similar to this among the prophetic revelations of either the Old or New Testament. Pontius noted passages of Scripture with which this vision of Cyprian seemed to have some similarity; yet they are not so closely related as those which we have noted above in connection with the revelation of Perpetua now under discussion. For he writes as follows:

> “What could be clearer than this revelation? What could be more blessed than this favor? Everything was foretold to him beforehand that later came to pass. Nothing was diminished from God’s words; nothing was mutilated from so holy a promise. Examine each detail, finally, according to the manner in which it was shown.
>
> “He requests a postponement until the morrow while the sentence of suffering was under consideration, asking that he might arrange his affairs [Col. 0131A] on the day he had obtained. That one day signified the year which he was to live in this world after the vision. For, to speak more plainly, he was crowned on that same date, once the year had elapsed, on which this had been shown to him a year before. Although in the divine writings we read of the Lord’s day and not the Lord’s year, we nevertheless understand that period as owed to the promise of future things. Hence it makes no difference if now a single year was shown under the signification of a day, since that which is greater ought to be fuller.
>
> “As for its being explained by gesture rather than speech, the expression in speech was reserved for the time of its realization. For something is customarily uttered in words at the moment when whatever is uttered is fulfilled. And in truth no one understood why this had been shown to him until he was crowned afterward on the same date on which he had seen it. [Col. 0131B] In the intervening time, nevertheless, the impending suffering was known with certainty by everyone; yet the exact day of his suffering was passed over in silence by all of them, as though they did not know it.
>
> “Indeed, I find something similar in the Scriptures as well. For when the priest Zechariah did not believe the angel’s promise that he would have a son, he became mute, so that, when he was to write rather than speak his son’s name, he requested tablets. Rightly, therefore, in this instance too, when God’s messenger expressed the imminent suffering of the bishop by gesture rather than speech, he both admonished his faith and fortified the priest.”

Pontius had precisely these arguments with which to defend the credibility and dignity of Cyprian’s revelation; and I do not think that I have produced arguments less appropriate on behalf of Perpetua’s revelation. Basnage must therefore either reject both alike as wholly unworthy of the Holy Spirit, or certainly accept both [Col. 0131C] and acknowledge that they had the same Spirit as their author. This is especially so because what Pontius carefully demonstrates concerning Cyprian’s revelation, we too shall demonstrate in the following chapter concerning Perpetua’s revelations: namely, that they were confirmed by the realities themselves and by the events that followed.

IV. Basnage further adds that Perpetua’s dreams smell of Montanus’s workshop, and that her ecstasy is very similar to the one by which Tertullian proves that the soul is “of an airy color and in every respect of human form.” But the same claim could equally be applied to every vision in which either the soul, an angel, or God himself is represented under the forms of corporeal things. Did Perpetua actually believe that there is a distinction of sex in the human spirit? Did she believe that her soul had been changed into the male sex [Col. 0131D]? Did she suppose that the form of the Egyptian whom she saw was the demon’s own proper shape? Did she think that Christ truly was a trainer of gladiators, and that the angels were handsome young men? Did she judge that she had actually gone in glory to the Sanavivarian Gate, just as that deranged little woman of Tertullian’s truly believed and affirmed that the soul was “of an airy color and in every respect of human form”? What, then, does Perpetua’s vision have in common with the dreams of this delirious woman, that the former should be called very similar to the latter? For it is just as groundless to suppose that Perpetua believed there really to be a distinction of sex in our soul as it would be to judge that she supposed the other things she then saw to be the things themselves, rather than representations of things and of future events. [Col. 0132A] We should therefore listen to Augustine, a far more reasonable and sympathetic interpreter of this vision than Basnage [Note: [Col. 0132D] Book IV, *On the Origin of the Soul*, chap. 18]:

> Saint Perpetua seemed to herself in a dream to have been changed into a man and to wrestle with a certain Egyptian. But who could doubt that it was her soul, and not her body, that was present in that bodily likeness? Her body, of course, remained in its female sex, lying upon the bed with its senses asleep, while her soul wrestled in that likeness of a male body.

V. I cannot restrain myself here from also briefly refuting what Basnage remarks concerning that celebrated revelation of Perpetua about her brother Dinocrates. For although he does not derive from it an argument for attacking the orthodoxy of the holy martyrs, nevertheless his observations place the martyrs’ unblemished [Col. 0132B] and sincere faith in very great jeopardy. The vision is as follows:

> I see Dinocrates coming out of a dark place, where many others also were. He was very hot and exceedingly thirsty, with a dirty face and pale complexion, and with the wound on his face that he had when he died. . . . I had therefore prayed for him. Between him and me there was a great *diadema* (or *diastema*, “interval”), so that neither of us could approach the other. Then, in the very place where Dinocrates was, there was a pool full of water, whose rim was higher than the child’s stature; and Dinocrates stretched himself out as though about to drink. I was grieved because, although that pool contained water, nevertheless because of the height of its rim he would not be able to drink. I awoke and understood that my brother was suffering. But I trusted that my prayer [Col. 0132C] would benefit him in his suffering, and I prayed for him every day until we were transferred to the military prison. For we were to fight in the military games, which were then being held for the birthday of Geta Caesar. I prayed for him day and night, groaning and weeping, that he might be granted to me. But on the day when we remained in the stocks, this was shown to me. I see that place which I had seen as dark now filled with light, and Dinocrates with a clean body, well clothed, and refreshed, etc. Then I understood that he had been transferred away from punishment.

VI. This passage troubles Protestants, since by it the faith of the Roman Church concerning purgatory and the prayers of the living for the dead is most invincibly established. It is therefore hardly surprising that Basnage attempted to diminish its authority by numerous trifles and cavils [Col. 0132D]:

> Concerning this vision, he says [Note: [Col. 0132D] At the year 205, no. VII], Augustine must be heard [Note: [Col. 0132D] *On the Soul and Its Origin*, chap. 10]: “As for Dinocrates, the brother of Saint Perpetua, the writing itself is not canonical; nor did she—or whoever wrote it—write in such a way as to say that the boy, who had died at the age of seven, had departed without baptism. For him, as she faced martyrdom, she is believed to have been heard, so that he was transferred from punishments to rest. For children of that age can already lie and speak the truth, confess and deny. And therefore, when they are baptized, they already recite the creed and themselves answer the questions on their own behalf. Who knows, then [Col. 0133A], whether that boy, after baptism, had in time of persecution been estranged from Christ by his impious father through idolatry, on account of which he entered into the condemnation of death, and did not leave it unless, as a gift, through the prayers of his sister who was about to die for Christ?”

> That Dinocrates, who died at the age of seven, had not received baptism is evident from the fact that his sister, although already married and twenty-two years old, was nevertheless still among the catechumens, and that their father was alien to the Christian religion. In that case Dinocrates could not have been delivered by Perpetua’s prayers. Next, the fire of purgatory is extinguished by this vision. Perpetua saw Dinocrates dwelling not in flames but in a dark place, subject only to the punishment of loss, not to the punishment of sense. Thus this vision does nothing to help Ruinart prove that the dead can be delivered, by the prayers of the living, from the punishments they suffer [Col. 0133B]. For according to the Latins’ position, only those who have received baptism are delivered from the punishment of sense through the suffrages of the living. But if Dinocrates was defiled by idolatry after baptism, as Augustine suggests, he certainly could not have been exempted by anyone’s prayers from the punishments he deserved. Finally, that dark place in which Dinocrates was confined, entirely different from purgatory, signifies that common prison into which, as very many Fathers and the Montanists believed, all souls except those of the martyrs are cast. Hence Tertullian wrote: “The entire key to paradise is your blood.” And he thought that the patriarchs themselves were held below until they should be delivered by Christ. Dinocrates was thought to have been placed in that prison which more recent writers call Limbo.

VII. I do not think that the learned man would ever have poured forth so many trifles [Col. 0133C] had he not been driven headlong by his passion for attacking Catholic doctrines. First, contrary to Augustine’s opinion, he thinks it evident that Dinocrates, who died at the age of seven, had not received baptism; and he proves this both from his sister’s example and from the fact that their father was alien to the Christian religion. I, however, think it evident that Dinocrates had been washed in the saving waters. For since Perpetua’s whole family, as she herself plainly testifies, practiced the religion of Christ, it is not likely that they failed to take care that, before he died, the endangered boy should be assisted through the sacrament of baptism. Hence the argument he constructs from the sister’s example is utterly worthless. I admit that in former times baptism was postponed for many unless danger to life was imminent. But when a person’s salvation was in immediate peril [Col. 0133D], who could believe there to have been such negligence in a Christian family that they felt no concern for a boy at the point of death, and took no care whatever that, at least with his final breath, he should be washed in the laver of regeneration, even against his father’s wishes?

Next, he says that the fire of purgatory is extinguished by this vision of Perpetua. The distinguished Holstenius did not think so. On Perpetua’s words, “very hot and thirsty,” he added this quite appropriate note:

> These words accord perfectly with the Church’s doctrine concerning purgatory, where souls are tormented by heat and fire.

Furthermore, because Basnage makes these observations not only to extinguish the fire of purgatory but also to overthrow purgatory itself, it will be worthwhile to recall to his mind [Col. 0134A] a doctrine which, I believe, he has often read in the more eminent theologians and the keenest defenders of the Catholic side: it is not a dogma of faith that those who depart this life with something still to be purged in the future life are tormented by corporeal fire rather than by other punishments—darkness, for example, grief, or sorrow. Indeed, at the Council of Florence there was scarcely any controversy between Latins and Greeks concerning purgatory, although the Greeks considered “purgatory to be not fire, but a certain dark place full of sufferings”; and while admitting purgatory they thought it made no difference [Note: [Col. 0134D] Εἴτε πῦρ ἐστιν, εἴτε ζόφος καὶ θύελλα, εἴτε τι ἕτερον, οὐ διαφερόμεθα. “Whether it is fire, darkness and tempest, or something else, we do not dispute.” Session XXV] “whether it was fire, darkness, a tempest, or some other thing of that kind.” The holy synod itself likewise judged this question to be of no great consequence, since in the definition of faith, which the prelates of both Churches signed, only the following was decreed concerning purgatory [Col. 0134B] . . . . [Note: [Col. 0134D] Τὰς ψυχὰς καθαρτικαῖς τιμωρίαις καθαίρεσθαι μετὰ θάνατον· ὥστε δὲ ἀποκουφίζεσθαι αὐτὰς τῶν τοιούτων τιμωριῶν λυσιτελεῖν αὐταῖς τὰς τῶν ζώντων πιστῶν ἐπικουρίας· δηλονότι τὰς ἱερὰς θυσίας, καὶ εὐχὰς, καὶ ἐλεημοσύνας, etc. “Souls are purified after death by purgatorial punishments; and, so that they may be relieved of such punishments, the assistance of the faithful who are alive benefits them—namely, sacred sacrifices, prayers, and alms, etc.”]:

> Souls are purified after death by purgatorial punishments; and, so that they may be relieved from punishments of this kind, the suffrages of the living benefit them—namely, the sacrifices of Masses, prayers, and alms, etc.
