Basnage’s observation would therefore do nothing to diminish the force of this passage, even if Dinocrates had not burned in any corporeal flames. For that dark place in which Perpetua saw him “very hot and thirsty” agrees perfectly with the purgatory admitted by the Greeks at the Council of Florence without contradiction from the Latins. And although the Latins’ opinion concerning the corporeal flames of purgatory is, as Bellarmine says [Note: [Col. 0134D] Book II, *On Purgatory*, chaps. 10 and 11], the most probable, nevertheless, as Bellarmine also teaches [Note: [Col. 0134D] Ibid.], the substance of the faith does not turn upon this point. Moreover, as Holstenius observed [Col. 0134C], Perpetua’s words accord perfectly with the Latins’ opinion.

More astonishing is what Basnage immediately adds: that Perpetua saw Dinocrates subject only to the punishment of loss, not to the punishment of sense. What, then? Do darkness, thirst, heat, a dirty face, a pale complexion, a wound on the face, and so forth seem to him to belong to the punishment of loss rather than to the punishment of sense? The punishment of loss is defined by theologians as deprivation of the divine vision. Was that alone what Dinocrates endured? If so, then when Perpetua later understood that he had been transferred away from punishment, he was refreshed by the divine vision. Basnage certainly will not admit this, since, as he notes, it was the doctrine of the Montanists—to whose impious sect he assigns Perpetua—that before the solemn day of judgment only martyrs are received into heaven.

Still more astonishing is his statement that this vision does nothing [Col. 0134D] to help Ruinart prove “that the dead can be delivered by the prayers of the living from the punishments they suffer.” Since Perpetua affirms in such explicit words that she obtained by her prayers the transfer of Dinocrates from the punishments by which he was tormented, it is truly astonishing how this vision does nothing to help Ruinart prove “that the dead can be delivered from punishments, etc.” Here, surely [Col. 0135A], either the authenticity (*γνησιότης*) of the Acts or the martyr’s trustworthiness is being called into question. Ruinart was touched by no suspicion either concerning the genuineness of the Acts or concerning the martyr’s credibility. But let us see by what arguments Basnage, who raises no question about the Acts, attempts to deprive Perpetua of credibility:

> According to the Latins’ position, only those who have received baptism are delivered from the punishment of sense through the suffrages of the living.

But we, with Augustine, hold it certain that Dinocrates was baptized, and we have demonstrated most clearly that he was subject to the punishment of sense.

> But if, he adds, Dinocrates was defiled by idolatry after baptism, as Augustine suggests, he certainly could not have been exempted by anyone’s prayers from the punishments he deserved.

But if, I say, Dinocrates was defiled by idolatry after baptism, as Augustine suggests, he could not have been subject only [Col. 0135B] to “the punishment of loss, not of sense.” Moreover, we are no longer dealing here with Perpetua, but with Augustine’s opinion. She did not write that he had been estranged from Christ through idolatry by his impious father and brought back to the sacrileges of the pagans, as Augustine suggests. There are many other sins, as Augustine himself observes, on account of which Dinocrates could have been consigned to purgatorial punishments: he could have lied, become angry, played in an unbecoming manner, and so forth. Whatever, according to Augustine’s opinion—which I have no desire to discuss at present—Dinocrates’s sins may have been, or by whatever punishments he was tormented, the holy Doctor does not doubt that “he left that place, as a gift, through the prayers of his sister who was about to die for Christ.” Accordingly, I do not see why this vision does not help Ruinart prove that the dead can be delivered, through the prayers of the living, from the punishments they suffer [Col. 0135C].

VIII. Finally, Basnage says that the dark place in which Dinocrates was confined, being entirely different from purgatory, signifies that common prison into which, as very many Fathers and the Montanists believed, all souls except those of the martyrs are cast. Concerning what are called the receptacles of souls, Tertullian’s opinion was not always one and the same. For in his book *On the Soul* [Note: [Col. 0135D] Chap. 57; see also chaps. 55 and 56], following the doctrine of the Paraclete—that is, of Montanus—he places “all souls in the lower regions,” and there assigns them punishments and refreshments in the meantime:

> For why should you not suppose that the soul is both punished and comforted in the lower regions in the meantime, while awaiting each judgment, in a certain provisional enjoyment and as its candidate [*candida*, reading uncertain]?

Elsewhere, however, he refutes this as Marcion’s opinion by the authority of Scripture [Note: [Col. 0135D] Book IV, *Against Marcion*, chap. 34] [Col. 0135D]:

> But Marcion drives matters in another direction. He determines that both rewards belonging to the Creator—whether torment or refreshment—have been appointed in the lower regions for those who obeyed the Law and the Prophets; but for Christ and his own god he appoints a heavenly bosom and harbor. We shall answer him, with this very Scripture refuting his eyes, since it distinguishes Abraham’s bosom, where the poor man was, from the lower regions. For the lower regions are one thing, as I think, and Abraham’s bosom another. For Scripture says that a great depth lies between those regions and prevents passage in either direction. Nor would the rich man have raised his eyes, and indeed from afar, unless he looked toward higher things and across the immense distance between height [Col. 0136A] and depth. Hence it is apparent to every wise person who has ever heard of the Elysian fields that there is some locally defined region called Abraham’s bosom, intended to receive the souls of his children, including those from the nations. . . . I therefore call that region Abraham’s bosom: though not heavenly, it is nevertheless higher than the lower regions and will meanwhile afford refreshment to the souls of the righteous, until the consummation of all things, through the resurrection of all, discharges the full measure of their reward, when the heavenly promise shall then appear, etc. Without prejudice to that promise, why should Abraham’s bosom not be understood as some temporary receptacle of faithful souls, in which the image of the future is already outlined and a certain preliminary prospect of each judgment is displayed?

According to this second opinion, it cannot be said that the dark place [Col. 0136B] in which Dinocrates was confined was some common prison into which, as very many Fathers and the Montanists believed, all souls except those of the martyrs are cast. For Tertullian teaches that Abraham’s bosom, destined to receive the souls of his children, was a region which, although not heavenly, was nevertheless higher than the lower regions and would meanwhile afford refreshment to the souls of the righteous.

According to the first position, however, just as both punishments and refreshments existed in the lower regions, so purgatory also existed in the lower regions. Accordingly, it cannot be established that the dark place in which Dinocrates was confined was entirely different from purgatory. For by the name “purgatory” we understand the punishments of the next life which, after some time, are to be exchanged for refreshment in the case of the righteous; nor does the question whether it is spatially separate from the lower regions pertain to the dogma of faith concerning [Col. 0136C] purgatory [Note: [Col. 0136D] See Bellarmine, Book II, *On Purgatory*, chap. 6]. Since, therefore, that dark place in which Perpetua saw Dinocrates very hot and thirsty was soon afterward changed into a place of light, in which his most holy sister beheld him “with a clean body, well clothed, and refreshed,” it still cannot in any way be affirmed, even according to the position of certain ancient Fathers and the Montanists, that the dark place in which Dinocrates was first confined was entirely different from purgatory.

If the distinguished Holstenius’s reading were established and certain, the theologians’ common position concerning the receptacles of souls would be splendidly confirmed by this vision of Perpetua, as Possinus observes [Note: [Col. 0136D] *Paralipomena* to Holstenius’s notes]. For his text reads:

> I see Dinocrates coming out of a dark place, where there were also [Col. 0136D] several dark places, etc.

The theologians teach, namely, that beneath the earth there are four distinct places in which the souls of the dead are detained: first, the lowest of all, where demons and condemned souls are held; above this, purgatory, where souls are purified for a time; next, the Limbo of Children, where the souls of those who died in original sin alone are detained; and lastly, the Limbo of the Fathers, now empty since the time of Christ’s death and resurrection, etc. These, Possinus adds, seem to have been the several dark places which Saint Perpetua testifies in the quoted words that she saw. But [Col. 0137A] Ruinart’s text reads: “where there were also many persons.” This is certainly more appropriately referred to the multitude of those confined there than to a diversity of places. Nevertheless, Perpetua does not by these words deny that there are various receptacles of souls beneath the earth. But we shall return to this vision of the holy martyr in the seventh chapter.

# CHAPTER VI

## THE VIRTUES OF OUR MARTYRS AND THE FRUITS OF THEIR VISIONS SHOW THAT THEY WERE INSPIRED BY THE DIVINE SPIRIT AND THAT THEIR REVELATIONS MUST BE ATTRIBUTED TO GOD

I. In distinguishing true prophets from false, account must first be taken of their morals. II. Certain passages of the Acts in which the virtues of our martyrs are vividly described. III. Nothing can be observed in their conduct that [Col. 0137B] smacks of the discipline of Montanus. IV. The example of Ignatius the Martyr demonstrates that Perpetua and her fellow martyrs by no means violated the laws of nature. V. The prayers and vows of other martyrs for the crown of martyrdom. VI. Besides Perpetua, other martyrs either provoked beasts against themselves or voluntarily employed instruments of cruelty to hasten their martyrdom. VII. The examples of ancient Christians who either offered themselves voluntarily or deliberately provoked the savagery of governors against themselves excuse Perpetua’s action. VIII. The memorable deed of Saints Andronicus and Tarachus. IX. The widely differing effects of each demonstrate how different the spirit of Perpetua and her fellow martyrs was from the spirit of the Montanists. [Col. 0137C] X. The honorable and excellent fruit of Perpetua’s and Saturus’s revelations.

I. In the preceding chapters I weakened the arguments that Basnage constructs against the martyrs from their own Acts. In the present and following chapters I shall bring forward arguments which I have gathered from those same Acts in favor of the holy martyrs, and by which, as I believe, their orthodoxy is most invincibly vindicated. Thus, just as our opponent assails the martyrs with arguments both external, as they are called, and internal, so we, after presenting in the first chapter of this dissertation the external arguments drawn from the authority of the Church and the ancient Fathers, shall contend for them in these final two chapters with the internal arguments most abundantly supplied to us by their own Acts.

[Col. 0137D] Let the first argument be that which spontaneously shoots forth and blossoms from the heroic virtues of Perpetua and her fellow martyrs: their patience, piety, moderation, charity, fortitude, and contempt for all human things. The ancients believed that the conduct of prophets carries great weight in distinguishing the true from the false. Hence that ecclesiastical writer Apollonius, according to Eusebius [Note: [Col. 0137D] Τῆς δὲ ΚΑΤΑ ΦΡΥΓΑΣ καλουμένης αἱρέσεως καὶ Ἀπολλώνιος ἐκκλησιαστικὸς συγγραφεὺς ἀκμαζούσης εἰσέτι τότε κατὰ τὴν Φρυγίαν ἔλεγχον ἐνστησάμενος, ἴδιον κατ᾽ αὐτῶν πεποίηται σύγγραμμα, τὰς μὲν φερομένας αὐτῶν προφητείας ψευδεῖς οὔσας κατὰ λέξιν εὐθύνων, τὸν δὲ βίον τῶν τῆς αἱρέσεως ἀρχηγῶν ὁποῖός τις γέγονε διελέγχων. “While the heresy called ‘that of the Phrygians’ was still flourishing in Phrygia at that time, the ecclesiastical writer Apollonius undertook its refutation and composed a special work against them, examining word for word the prophecies circulated by them and showing them to be false, while also exposing what sort of life was led by the leaders of that heresy.” Book V, *Ecclesiastical History*, chap. 18]:

> A writer who undertook to refute the Cataphrygian heresy [Col. 0138A], which was still flourishing in his own age, composed a special volume against them, both examining word for word the false prophecies circulated by them and investigating the life and conduct of those who were the authors of that heresy.

He then presents several fragments from this work in which Apollonius describes the depraved conduct of Montanus and his little women, and also that of Themison and Alexander. Afterward he adds [Note: [Col. 0138D] Δεῖ γὰρ τοὺς καρποὺς δοκιμάζεσθαι τοῦ προφήτου· ἀπὸ γὰρ τοῦ καρποῦ τὸ δένδρον γινώσκεται. “For the prophet’s fruits must be examined; the tree is known by its fruit”]:

> A prophet’s deeds must be examined as his fruits. For the tree is known by its fruits.

And a little later [Note: [Col. 0138D] Ἐὰν ἀρνῶνται δῶρα τοὺς προφήτας αὐτῶν εἰληφέναι, τοῦτο ὁμολογησάτωσαν, ὅτι ἐὰν ἐλεγχθῶσιν εἰληφότες, οὐκ εἰσὶ προφῆται, καὶ μυρίας ἀποδείξεις τούτων παραστήσομεν· ἀναγκαῖον δέ ἐστι πάντας καρποὺς δοκιμάζεσθαι προφήτου· προφήτης, εἰπέ μοι, βάπτεται; προφήτης φιλοκοσμεῖ; προφήτης, τάβλαις καὶ κύβοις παίζει; προφήτης δανείζει; ταῦτα ὁμολογησάτωσαν, πότερον ἔξεστιν ἢ μή; ἐγὼ δὲ ὅτι γέγονες παρ᾽ αὐτοῖς δείξω. “If they deny that their prophets accepted gifts, let them concede this: if they are proved to have accepted them, they are not prophets; and we shall present countless proofs of these things. It is necessary that every fruit of a prophet be examined. Tell me: does a prophet dye his hair? Does a prophet delight in adornment? Does a prophet play at tables and dice? Does a prophet lend money at interest? Let them acknowledge and answer whether these things are permissible or not. I shall show that they have occurred among them”]:

> If they deny that their prophets accepted gifts, let them therefore admit that they are not prophets if they are proved to have accepted gifts. Then at last we shall produce countless proofs and testimonies of the fact. Moreover, all the fruits and deeds of a prophet must be tested. [Col. 0138B] Tell me: does a prophet dye his hair? Does he paint his eyes with antimony? Does he strive to adorn himself? Does a prophet play at tables and dice? Does he lend money at interest? Let them candidly admit and answer whether it is permissible to do these things or not. I, for my part, shall prove that these things have been done among them.

II. But in these Acts of Perpetua, Felicitas, and their fellow martyrs, marvelous examples of every Christian virtue shine everywhere. Thus one may rightly affirm that for every vice Apollonius censures in Montanus, Maximilla, Themison, and Alexander, an equal number—and indeed many more—adornments of every virtue shine forth in these holy martyrs, and especially in Perpetua. As examples, I shall indicate several passages of the Acts that bear more directly on the matter.

Chapter I, § 2:

> While we were still with our persecutors, she says, and my father persisted in trying to turn me away and [Col. 0138C] cast me down because of his affection, etc., I said to him . . . “I cannot call myself anything other than what I am: a Christian.” Then my father, provoked by this word, threw himself upon me as though he would tear out my eyes; but he merely tormented me and went away, defeated along with the devil’s arguments. Then, because I was without my father for a few days, I gave thanks to the Lord, and his absence brought me relief. During that very interval of a few days we were baptized; but the Spirit instructed me to ask for nothing else in the water except endurance of the flesh. After a few days we were taken into prison, and I was terrified because I had never experienced such darkness. . . . I was nursing my child, who was already faint from hunger. In my anxiety for him, I spoke with my mother, encouraged my brother, and commended my son to them. I wasted away because I saw them wasting away on my account. [Col. 0138D] I endured such anxieties for many days, and obtained permission for my child to remain with me in prison. At once I recovered my strength and was relieved of my distress and anxiety for the child; and the prison suddenly became like a palace to me [Col. 0139A], so that I preferred to be there rather than anywhere else.

How many virtues shine here! Constancy against her father’s threats and entreaties; constancy likewise against every human affection; devotion toward her parents; a mother’s concern for her son; invincible patience in enduring the hardships of prison. She does not, after the fashion of hypocrites, conceal human affections beneath a Stoic solemnity, but overcomes and moderates them through Christian virtue. She gives thanks to the Lord, implores divine assistance, and grieves more over the distress of others than over her own—a marvelous testimony to her religious devotion toward God and charity toward her neighbor.

The same virtues shine in other passages also. Chapter II, § 1:

> After a few days a report spread that we were to be given a hearing. My father also arrived from the city, worn out with grief, and came up to me in order to cast me down, saying: “Have pity, daughter, on my gray hairs,” etc. [Col. 0139B] My father said these things out of his affection, kissing my hands, throwing himself at my feet, and with tears calling me not his daughter but his lady. And I grieved for my father’s gray hairs, because he alone of my whole family would not rejoice in my suffering. I encouraged him, saying: “On that platform, whatever God wills shall happen. For know that we have not been placed in our own power, but in God’s.”

Similar examples both of filial respect for her father and of Christian fortitude occur in § 2. Although the whole passage deserves to be transcribed, I shall append only these few words from it:

> And the procurator Hilarianus . . . said: “Spare your father’s gray hairs; spare the tender years of your child. Offer sacrifice for the safety of the emperors.” And I answered: “I will not.” Hilarianus said: “Are you a Christian?” And I answered: “I am a Christian.” And when my father stood there trying to cast me down [Col. 0139C], Hilarianus ordered him to be cast down, and he was struck with a rod. My father’s misfortune grieved me as though I myself had been struck; so deeply did I grieve for his wretched old age. Then he pronounced sentence upon us all and condemned us to the beasts, and we went joyfully down to the prison.

Saint Augustine commends Perpetua’s filial respect toward her father in these words [Note: [Col. 0139D] Sermon 281, otherwise *On Various Subjects* 104]:

> She grieved at the outrage done to her aged parent; and although she did not give him her assent, she preserved her affection for him. For in him she hated his folly, not his nature; his unbelief, not her own origin. With all the greater glory, therefore, did she resolutely reject the evil counsel of a father whom she loved so deeply that she could not see him beaten without sorrow. Accordingly, that sorrow neither diminished the strength of her courage nor failed to add something to the praises of her suffering:

“For all things work together for good for those who love God.”

[Col. 0139D] Another example of the same virtues occurs in chapter III, § 1:

> When the day of the games drew near, my father entered to see me, worn out with grief. He began to tear out his beard, cast himself upon the ground, prostrate himself upon his face, reproach his own years, and utter such words as would move the whole creation. I grieved for his unhappy old age.

Here Saint Augustine must again be heard [Note: [Col. 0139D] *Exposition of Psalm* XLVII, no. 13]:

> Through charity many have died to the world in order to live to God. The martyrs were set aflame by this charity—not pretenders, not people blown about by vainglory, not such as those of whom it was said, “If I hand over [Col. 0140A] my body to be burned,” etc., but such as were truly brought to suffering by love of Christ and of the truth. What did the persecutions of their raging assailants do to them? The eyes of their weeping loved ones exerted greater violence than the persecutions of those who pursued them. How many were held back by their children, lest they suffer! At the knees of how many did their wives prostrate themselves, lest they be left widows! How many parents did their children try to prevent from dying, as we know and read in the Passion of BLESSED PERPETUA? These things happened. Yet however many tears flowed, and however violently, when could they extinguish the ardor of charity?

Chapter V, § 2, presents us with numerous examples at once of mutual charity, hope, and magnanimity:

> As for Felicitas—for the Lord’s grace also befell her in this manner—she was already eight months [Col. 0140B] pregnant, since she had been pregnant when arrested. As the day of the spectacle approached, she was in great sorrow lest she be postponed because of her pregnancy, since pregnant women are not permitted to be presented for punishment, and lest she afterward shed her holy and innocent blood among some criminals. Her fellow martyrs also were deeply grieved lest they leave so good a companion behind, alone, as it were, upon the road of the same hope. Therefore, joining together in one united groan, they poured forth prayer to the Lord three days before the games. Immediately after the prayer, labor pains seized her. And when she suffered in childbirth because of the natural difficulty of the eighth month, one of the servants of the prison guards said to her: “If you are suffering so much now, what will you do when you are thrown to the beasts which you scorned when you refused to sacrifice?” And she answered: “Now it is I who suffer [Col. 0140C] what I suffer; but there another will be within me who will suffer for me, because I too am to suffer for him.” Thus she gave birth to a girl, whom one of the sisters raised as her own daughter.

No less elevated, and deserving of no less admiration, are the proofs of Perpetua’s and Saturus’s unbroken and exalted courage described in §§ 3 and 4. But chapter VI, § 1, must not be omitted, since it presents a connected tissue and variety of all the virtues:

> The day of their victory dawned, and they proceeded from the prison into the amphitheater as though into heaven—joyful and lovely in countenance, trembling, if at all, with joy and not fear. Perpetua followed with a serene face and measured step, like a matron of Christ, beloved of God, lowering the vigor of her gaze before the eyes of all. Felicitas likewise rejoiced that she had safely given birth and so could fight the beasts, passing from blood [Col. 0140D] to blood, from the midwife to the net-fighter, to be washed after childbirth in a second baptism. When they had been brought to the gate and were being compelled to put on costumes—the men those of the priests of Saturn, and the women those of women consecrated to Ceres—that noble woman resisted with steadfastness to the very end. For they said: “We came to this voluntarily precisely so that our freedom should not be taken from us. We pledged our souls to God so that we would do no such thing; this was our agreement with you.” Injustice acknowledged justice: the tribune permitted them to be brought in simply dressed as they were. Perpetua sang psalms, already treading upon the Egyptian’s head. Revocatus, Saturninus, and Saturus threatened the watching populace with judgment for this. When they came within Hilarianus’s sight [Col. 0141A], they began to say to him by gesture and sign: “You judge us,” they said, “but God will judge you.” At this the infuriated populace demanded that they be scourged by a line of beast-fighters. And they rejoiced because they had obtained a share in the Lord’s sufferings.

Chapter VI, § 3, should also be consulted, so that, besides the invincible fortitude with which the holy women offered themselves to the most savage cow, Perpetua’s modesty may also receive its due:

> For when she had been tossed by the savage beast, she fell upon her loins; and when she saw that her tunic had been torn at the side, she drew it over her thighs as a covering, more mindful of modesty than of pain.

### III

Nothing in these acts of the martyrs can be observed as proceeding from the school and training of Montanus: nothing superstitious, nothing disorderly, nothing tumultuous, nothing confused, nothing, finally, irregular [Col. 0141B]—all of which, as is evident from Asterius Urbanus, Apollonius, Miltiades, Serapion, Aelius Publius, and other Fathers [Note: [Col. 0141D] In Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book V, ch. 16 and following], are characteristics of the Montanist spirit. On the contrary, throughout there shine forth a marvelous modesty, composure, prudence, piety, reverence, charity, courage, faith, and wisdom; so that there is no other martyrdom of holy women attended by more illustrious ornaments of every virtue.

It seems altogether impossible that a woman driven by madness and frenzy, and impelled by a demonic spirit—such as the Montanist pseudo-prophetesses were—could have guarded herself so carefully in everything and conducted herself in such a way that even the strictest censor could find nothing insolent in her words, nothing arrogant, nothing shameless in her movements, and nothing irreligious in her actions. The Montanists did indeed make a display [Col. 0141C] of a certain outward gravity of conduct; they boasted of the severity of their discipline and greatly vaunted their abstinence, chastity, and endurance of persecutions. Yet those who proclaimed in the most presumptuous language that they had added stricter ordinances to the teachings of the Gospel afterward failed utterly to reflect in their conduct the sanctity of the evangelical law, but departed from it as far as possible. Perpetua and her fellow martyrs, by contrast, reproduce the Gospel in their conduct and express it with the utmost exactness.

There is also something else worthy of observation in the virtues of these martyrs, and especially of Perpetua, by which they can readily be distinguished from the counterfeit virtues of hypocrites and pseudo-prophets: they commend themselves by a certain native simplicity. Just as clear signs of a kind of divine wisdom, of a lofty spirit, and of a mind thoroughly detached from human affairs are discerned in them, so too they please by a certain natural candor [Col. 0141D]; nothing in them is artificial, and nothing is found to have been done through pretense or hypocrisy. This simplicity and the beauty of a candid heart shine even in Perpetua’s own words and manner of writing: she does not conceal her human emotions, as was observed above; she does not exalt herself above others; she does not exaggerate her circumstances; she refers everything to God; in faith, in hope of divine mercy, and in the bosom of Providence she rests with complete serenity; she despises every misfortune, fears nothing, hopes for everything, and dares anything.

Such flowers of virtue assuredly do not grow among the thickets of heresies; a bad tree does not produce such fruits. It can indeed happen that a wicked spirit affects some outward shadow [Col. 0142A] of holiness and eagerly attempts to imitate such acts of virtue; but it cannot present an image of Christian perfection that is complete in every respect and wholly sincere in every part. Hypocrisy cannot guard itself so carefully that nothing slips out by which it betrays itself. Some vice is readily mingled with false virtues, and that spirit of pride is especially recognized when it feigns humility of mind and composes itself into a certain outward appearance of modesty.

But what does Basnage find to censure in matters of conduct in Perpetua and her companions? Absolutely nothing. It can surely be affirmed that, just as no image is more like the discipline of the Gospel, so none is more at variance with heretical training. Let Perpetua and Maximilla be compared with one another: their characters will differ [Col. 0142B] as widely as vice is separated from virtue, and darkness from light. It cannot therefore be that they were impelled by the same spirit of frenzy and madness.

Indeed, if so illustrious a martyrdom, adorned with the embellishments of so many virtues, was or could have been perfected among heretics, then the argument for the Christian religion which arises—and arises most effectively—from the constancy and virtue of the martyrs either perishes altogether or is greatly weakened. For Christian martyrdom is commended not so much by death undertaken for the faith—since many others from every sect have voluntarily surrendered themselves to death for their superstitions—as by the array of the other virtues with which Catholic martyrs adorned their contest: namely faith, hope, charity, reverence, piety, modesty, and the invincible strength of a lofty spirit, all of which, as we have shown, [Col. 0142C] shone marvelously in Perpetua and her fellow martyrs.

### IV

But so that I may neglect nothing, or leave without refutation anything from which some captious faultfinder or shameless slanderer might manufacture ill will against the holy martyrs, I shall examine two passages in the Acts in which they seem to violate the laws of nature. By these laws each person is commanded to preserve his own life, and we are forbidden either to desire death for ourselves or others, or to urge others toward our destruction.

Our martyrs seem to have sinned against these laws of nature, first in chapter V, § 2, where they prayed with common supplications that Felicity might give birth prematurely, “since the day of the spectacle was already at hand,” “lest she be delayed because of her pregnancy, since it is not lawful for pregnant women to be presented for punishment.” More seriously, they seem to have done so in the last section of chapter VI, where Perpetua herself, with her own hands, positioned the instrument of death so as to hasten her martyrdom: “Perpetua, however, so that she might taste something of pain, cried out when she was pierced between the ribs, and herself placed the wandering right hand of the novice gladiator upon her throat.”

No one who has attended to what Daillé poured forth against the martyr Ignatius for an altogether similar reason will be surprised that these things could be censured in Perpetua and her fellow martyrs. Because that most holy martyr had warned the Romans by letter not to delay his desired martyrdom through their prayers to God or their services, and had declared that he would drive even reluctant and resisting beasts to destroy him, Daillé arraigns him as guilty of violating piety and modesty.

But so that it may be understood more clearly how well Ignatius and Perpetua [Col. 0143A] and her fellow martyrs harmonize with one another in such desires, I shall set down Ignatius’s own words here [Note: [Col. 0143D] “I entreat you, do not become an untimely kindness to me. Allow me to be food for the beasts, through whom it is possible to attain to God. I am God’s wheat, and I am ground by the teeth of beasts, so that I may be found pure bread of Christ. Rather entice the beasts, so that they may become my tomb and leave nothing of my body behind, lest, once I have fallen asleep, I become a burden to anyone. . . . Entreat Christ on my behalf, so that through these instruments I may be found a sacrifice.” From the Epistle to the Romans, in Ruinart, *Acts*, at the end, etc.]:

> I beseech you not to show me an untimely kindness. Allow me to be food for the beasts, through whom it is possible to attain to God. I am God’s wheat and am ground by the teeth of beasts, that I may be found pure bread of Christ. Rather entice the beasts, that they may become my tomb and leave nothing of my body behind, lest, after I have fallen asleep, I become a burden to anyone. . . . Entreat Christ on my behalf, that through these instruments I may be found a sacrifice.

What Ignatius wished the Romans to do for him, our martyrs performed as a duty toward Felicity. He wished united prayers to be poured forth to God by the Romans so that he might be ground by the teeth of beasts and through these instruments be made a sacrifice of Christ. This likewise was what Felicity’s companions [Col. 0143B] desired, and in prayers poured forth to God they asked that she might deliver the child prematurely, lest her martyrdom be delayed, but that she might be cast to the beasts together with the others.

Ignatius continues and displays not only his burning desire for martyrdom, but says that he will provoke even unwilling and resisting beasts to kill him [Note: [Col. 0143D] “May I have the enjoyment of the beasts prepared for me; and I pray that they may be found ready for me. I shall even entice them to devour me swiftly, and not, as in the case of some whom they feared and did not touch. But even if, against their will, they should refuse, I shall force them.” Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book V, ch. 16 and following]:

> May I have the enjoyment of the beasts prepared for me, and I pray that they may be found ready for me. I shall even entice them to devour me swiftly, and not, as in the case of some whom they feared and did not touch. But if they should resist and refuse, I shall force them.

It makes no difference whether someone places a gladiator’s right hand upon his own throat, as Perpetua did, or drives beasts to devour him, as Ignatius wrote that he would do. Hence either both are open to the same censures or both must be attended by the same praises. [Col. 0143C] Meanwhile, just as Pearson shows by the example of our martyrs that Ignatius’s desires were not unworthy of a holy martyr, so we shall defend those martyrs’ prayers for Felicity by the example of Ignatius. For why, to use the words of Pontius the deacon, should we condemn ordinary martyrs, newly come from baptism, for that for which we hold the wisest bishop and disciple of the Apostles in honor and admiration?

### V

But since no small number from the Protestant body, including Basnage, reject the epistles of Ignatius as a pseudepigraphal and adulterated work, and among other things which they mark in them as alien to Ignatius’s virtues they censure that burning desire for martyrdom, I shall, with Pearson, defend both the epistolary Ignatius and our martyrs by other examples.

Celerinus the confessor, writing [Col. 0143D] to Lucian the confessor in Epistle 21 among the Cyprianic letters:

> When I wrote these things to you, my lord and brother, I was both joyful and sorrowful: joyful because I had heard that you were arrested for our Lord Jesus Christ, our Savior, [Col. 0144A] and had confessed his name before the magistrates of this world, etc.

And below:

> May he whose name you confessed crown you. . . . Ask that I may be worthy to be crowned among your company.

And again:

> O happy man! You receive your desires, which you always longed for; even while sleeping on the ground you wished to be cast into prison for his name, and this now happens to you, as it is written: “May the Lord grant you according to your heart.”

So wrote Celerinus, commended by Saint Cyprian [Note: [Col. 0144D] Epistle 27, otherwise 23] especially for moderation, humility, fear, caution, and modesty.

Likewise, the martyrs of Lyons—the chief ornament of the Christian religion, distinguished no less by faith and wisdom than by invincible courage—“with abundant tears,” as Eusebius reports [Note: [Col. 0144D] “With tears they besought the brethren, begging that earnest prayers be made that they might be perfected.” Book V, *Ecclesiastical History*, ch. 2], “besought the brethren that continual prayers be made to God [Col. 0144B] so that they themselves might at last be perfected.”

Pontius, Saint Cyprian’s deacon, writes concerning him:

> Meanwhile, many men of eminent and most distinguished rank, noble also by the nobility of the world, gathered together. Because of their friendship, they repeatedly advised him to withdraw; and lest bare persuasion seem insufficient, they also offered him places to which he might withdraw. But he, with his mind now lifted up to heaven, had disregarded the world and did not assent to their flattering counsels. Perhaps even then he would have done what many faithful persons requested, had he also been commanded by a divine order.

For, as Pontius himself teaches, during the earlier withdrawal, “when the Lord then commanded him to hide, he obeyed.”

But when Saint Cyprian was being led to execution, the faithful people were so far from praying to God that he might be spared, or from impeding his martyrdom in any way, that they desired rather to die together with him [Col. 0144C]:

> Although what their common desires sought could not come to pass—namely that the whole people might suffer together in fellowship of equal glory—whoever, under the eyes of Christ looking on and within the hearing of the bishop, sincerely wished to suffer, sent, through a suitable witness of his desire, what were in a sense letters of embassy to God.

Saint Jerome, *Life of Paul the Hermit*:

> Under the persecutors Decius and Valerian, at the time when Cornelius at Rome and Cyprian at Carthage were condemned to shed their blessed blood, a savage storm devastated many churches throughout Egypt and the Thebaid. The desire of Christians then was to be struck down by the sword for Christ’s name. But the cunning enemy, devising protracted tortures leading to death, wished to slaughter souls, not bodies; and, as Cyprian himself, who suffered from him, says: “Those who wished to die [Col. 0144D] were not permitted to be killed.”

Well known also are the words of the holy martyr Polycarp to the proconsul who was threatening him first with beasts and then with flames: ἀλλὰ τί βραδύνεις; φέρε ὃ βούλει, “But why do you delay? Bring whatever you wish.” Ταῦτα καὶ ἄλλα πλείονα λέγων θάρσους καὶ χαρᾶς ἐνεπίμπλατο, “As he said these and many other things, he was filled with confidence and joy,” as his very ancient Acts testify. And what, I ask, were those “many other things” which he pronounced full of courage and exultation, if they were not like the desires of Ignatius, Perpetua, Felicity, and their fellow martyrs? If they did not accord with that voice which he heard from heaven, Ἴσχυε, καὶ ἀνδρίζου, Πολύκαρπε, “Be strong and act manfully, Polycarp”?

Also very well known are the words of Romanus, the deacon of Caesarea, heard at Antioch: ποῦ μοι τὸ πῦρ; “Where is the fire for me?”

To the examples which Pearson adduces in defense of Ignatius I shall add another, no less remarkable than the preceding ones, from the authentic Acts of Saints Montanus, Lucius, and the others. When the rest had been condemned, Flavian was recalled to prison and his martyrdom was postponed. He endured this no less reluctantly than did his companions. Hence Montanus, when, as the Acts say,

> the executioner was already standing over him and the sword hung poised above his neck, stretched out his hands toward heaven and prayed in a clear voice, so that its sound struck not only the ears of the people but even the pagans themselves, asking and entreating that Flavian, who through the people’s vote had been left behind from their company, might follow on the third day.

The feelings and desires of Flavian’s own mother were no different. The Acts add concerning her:

> At his side clung his incomparable mother, who, besides the faith by which she belonged to the patriarchs, proved herself a daughter of Abraham in this also: that she desired her son to be killed and was deeply grieved that he had meanwhile been left behind.

Flavian himself consoled his afflicted mother with these words:

> You know, mother deservedly most dear, how I have always tried, if the opportunity for confession should arise, to enjoy my martyrdom, to be seen frequently in chains, and repeatedly to be postponed. If, therefore, what I desired has happened, it is a cause for glory rather than sorrow.

Such were the martyrs’ desires. If these are made a charge against them, there will be innumerable martyrs from whom the crown of martyrdom must be taken away.

### VI

Greater ill will might be manufactured against Perpetua on the second ground; but that too, as I said, is dispelled by Ignatius’s example. For Perpetua did nothing other than what Ignatius writes that he would do. But since controversy is raised concerning his Acts and epistles, other examples are not lacking, examples Pearson gathered with a full hand in his defense of the epistles of Ignatius.

In the very ancient letter of the Church of Smyrna, Germanicus is represented as though he were a noble and distinguished combatant against beasts, ἐπισήμως θηριομαχῶν, “fighting the beasts with distinction.” But what, in the judgment of the most ancient Church, is found to be ἐπίσημον—distinguished or noble—in the brief account of his martyrdom? This one thing, from which Perpetua might perhaps be charged with violating the law of nature [Note: [Col. 0145D] “For when the proconsul wished to persuade him and told him [variant: λέγοντος, ‘was telling him’] to have pity upon his age, he forcibly drew the beast toward himself, desiring to be delivered more swiftly from their unjust and lawless life. From this, therefore, the whole multitude, marveling at the courage of the God-loving and God-fearing race of Christians, etc.”]:

> For [Col. 0145D] when the proconsul wished to sway him and told him to have pity upon his own age, he voluntarily drew the beast toward himself and forced it upon himself.

He is said to have done this in order to hasten his martyrdom:

> Desiring to escape more swiftly from the unjust and lawless life of those people. From this it came about that the whole multitude, marveling at the courage of the pious and religious race of Christians, etc.

Germanicus, therefore—whom the ancient and celebrated Church of Smyrna presented as an especially distinguished and noble martyr, and because of whose remarkable deed the pagans themselves admired the nobility and high courage of the Christian people—did toward the beasts what Perpetua did with the gladiator. Burning with desire for martyrdom, he “voluntarily drew the beast toward himself”; while she, burning with the same desire, “herself placed the right hand of the novice gladiator upon her throat.”

Dionysius, bishop of Alexandria, greatly praises the virgin Apollonia because, after all her teeth had been knocked out by blows to her jaws and the flames had been brought near [Note: [Col. 0146D] Συντόνως ἐπεπήδησεν εἰς τὸ πῦρ, καὶ καταπέφλεκται, “She leapt vigorously into the fire and was burned up.” Letter to Fabius of Antioch, in Eusebius, Book VI, ch. 41], “she swiftly leapt into the fire and was consumed.”

Saint Hilary, *Commentary on Psalm 65*:

> Some glory in the chains of prisons; others rejoice at being struck with blows; others submit the necks of their blessed heads to be severed by the power [Col. 0146B] of the irreligious; many run toward the constructed pyres and, while the ministers of punishment tremble, leap into the fire with the devoted haste of their resolve.

Saint John Chrysostom describes this ardor for suffering in the martyrs most excellently in his discourse on Romanus, introducing the devil as speaking thus [Note: [Col. 0146D] “I spread burning coals beneath them, but they ran toward them as toward roses. I kindled fire, but they cast themselves into it as into springs of cold water. . . . And as though dancing in a sacred procession and playing in a green meadow, each seized the punishments for himself—not receiving them as penalties but as spring flowers, being crowned and, by the excess of their own eagerness, forestalling my punishments”]:

> I spread burning coals beneath them, but they ran toward them as toward roses. I kindled fire, but they cast themselves into it as into springs of cold water. . . . And as though dancing in a sacred procession and playing in a green meadow, each seized the torments—not receiving them as punishments but as spring flowers, being crowned and, through the excess of their own eagerness, forestalling my torments.

### VII

Nor is it strange that some provoked beasts already prepared [Col. 0146C] to kill them, or voluntarily employed instruments of cruelty placed at hand in order to hasten martyrdom, since it is most certainly established—something much greater—that very many sought death for Christ’s name when they were not in the power of their enemies, disclosed themselves, and provoked their enemies themselves to inflict punishment.

Lucian says of the Christians of his own time in *Peregrinus* [Note: [Col. 0146D] “For the wretched people have persuaded themselves that they will be altogether immortal and live forever. Therefore they despise death, and many voluntarily surrender themselves”]:

> The wretched people, having persuaded themselves that they will be altogether immortal and live forever, despise death, and many voluntarily surrender themselves.

Justin Martyr acknowledges that he became a Christian because no wicked person seemed to him [Note: [Col. 0146D] Θάνατον ἀσπάζεσθαι, οὐχ’ ὅτι ἑαυτὸν κατήγγελλε φονευθησόμενον] “to welcome death—much less voluntarily to disclose and denounce himself so that he might be killed,” as Christians did at that time.

Tertullian, *To Scapula*, ch. 1:

> We contend against all your savagery, even bursting forth voluntarily, and we rejoice more when condemned [Col. 0147A] than when acquitted.

And chapter 4:

> Take care only lest, by the very fact that we endure such things, we appear to burst forth for this single purpose: to prove precisely that we do not fear these things but voluntarily summon them. When Arrius Antoninus was persistently persecuting in Asia, all the Christians of that city, having formed a band, presented themselves before his tribunal. After ordering a few to be led away, he said to the rest: Ὦ δειλοί, εἰ θέλετε ἀποθνῄσκειν, κρημνοὺς ἢ βρόχους ἔχετε, “O wretches, if you wish to die, you have cliffs or nooses.” If it should please them that the same be done here, what will you do with so many thousands of people—so many men and women of every sex, every age, and every rank—presenting themselves to you?

Concerning the ninth persecution, Sulpicius says:

> People rushed competitively into glorious contests, and martyrdoms by glorious deaths were then sought far more eagerly than bishoprics are now pursued by headlong ambitions.

The same author, Letter XI, concerning Blessed Martin:

> What if it had been granted to him, in the times of Nero and Decius, to fight in the contest that then existed? I call the God of heaven and earth to witness: he would voluntarily have mounted the rack and of his own accord cast himself into the flames. . . . But if, after the example of the teacher of the Gentiles, he had been assigned to the sword and led among other victims, as often occurred, he would have been the first of all—compelling the executioner—to seize the palm of blood.

Saint John Chrysostom observes that under Julian’s rule [Note: [Col. 0147D] Πᾶσαν ἡλικίαν ἁπλῶς καὶ φύσιν ἑκατέραν πηδῶσαν ἐπὶ τὰς ὑπὲρ τῆς εὐσεβείας σφαγάς] “every age without distinction, and both sexes, leapt forward to undergo slaughter for the true religion.” He gives this reason why Julian the Apostate refused to devise an open persecution against the Christians [Note: [Col. 0147D] “For he knew, he knew clearly, that if he dared this, all would surrender their souls for Christ. ‘For all,’ he says, ‘will come like bees to the honeycomb, flying toward martyrdom’”]:

> For he knew, he knew clearly, that if he dared this, all would surrender their souls [Col. 0147C] for Christ. “For all,” he says, “will come like bees to the honeycomb, flying toward martyrdom.”

Nor did the Christians of the ancient Church merely speak courageous words; they also acted and suffered. Especially celebrated was the name of the martyr Phocas. When by chance he had received as guests the officers who said that they had been sent to kill Phocas, he promised that on the next day he would show Phocas to them. After first preparing a place for burial, he stood before them and said, “I am that Phocas.” When they began to hesitate, he encouraged them by exhortation to kill him [Note: [Col. 0147D] Εἶπεν, ἔπεισεν, ἔπαθεν, καὶ, τὴν κεφαλὴν ἀποτμηθείς, ἱερεῖον τῷ θεῷ κεχαρισμένον προσήχθη]:

> He spoke, persuaded them, and suffered; and, having been beheaded, he was offered as a sacrifice pleasing to God,

as Asterius of Amasea, Epiphanius’s contemporary, says.

During Valerian’s persecution [Col. 0147D], Priscus, Malchus, and Alexander mutually accused one another of cowardice and idleness because, although an opportunity had presented itself, they had still held back, μὴ οὐχὶ προαρπάζοντες τὸν τοῦ μαρτυρίου στέφανον, “and had not seized the crown of martyrdom beforehand.” They therefore approached the judge, were condemned to the beasts, and θείῳ κατεκοσμήθησαν μαρτυρίῳ, “were adorned with divine martyrdom,” as Eusebius relates [Col. 0148A] in Book VII, ch. 12.

Romanus, the deacon of Caesarea, seeing many people sacrificing, ζήλῳ θεοσεβείας πρόσεισι, “approached more closely, impelled by zeal for divine worship,” and, rebuking them with a loud voice, forced himself upon the judge. Arrested for his boldness [Note: [Col. 0148D] Γενναιότατος, εἰ καί τις ἄλλος, ἀποδέδεικται μάρτυς τῆς ἀληθείας, “He proved himself, if anyone ever did, a most courageous martyr of the truth.” Eusebius, *The Martyrs of Palestine*, ch. 2], “he was adorned with a courageous martyrdom, if anyone ever was.”

Indeed, when the persecution was raging, Apphianus, without the knowledge of everyone living in the same house and even of the cohort of soldiers, seized the right hand of the governor Urbanus, compelled him to cease sacrificing, and, surrendering himself to most grievous torments, suffered. Eusebius, who knew him personally, judged that he had done this [Note: [Col. 0148D] Τῆς ἐπὶ τοῦτ’ αὐτὸν προαγούσης ἐνθέου δυνάμεως μονονουχὶ βοώσης διὰ τοῦ γενομένου, etc., ibid., ch. 4], “because divine power impelled him to this very act and all but cried aloud through what occurred, etc.” Eusebius also relates that Aedesius attempted to do the same thing his brother had done and suffered in the same way [Col. 0148B].

It would take too long to enumerate all those whom Eusebius and others commemorate as having voluntarily and deliberately presented themselves for martyrdom. These are Pearson’s arguments for Ignatius; no one fails to see how well they apply to our martyrs.

### VIII

But to the many examples he records, I think that the remarkable and daring deed of Andronicus and Tarachus must certainly be added. Of these, one incited a bear and the other a lioness—both rendered tame by divine power—to devour him, as is read in their Acts [Note: [Col. 0148D] “They released a man-killing bear, which, as some said, had killed three men that day. When it had been released and had come near them, it passed by the other bodies and ran toward the holy martyr Andronicus; sitting beside him, it licked the fluid from his wounds. . . . Holy Andronicus placed his head against it and tried forcibly to enrage the beast so that it might seize him and release him from life; but the bear remained beside him and lay down together with the saint. . . . When the lioness saw the holy bodies cast down, she came to blessed Tarachus, bent down, and did homage at his feet. The holy Tarachus stretched out his hand, grasped her mane and ears, and drew her toward himself; but she was like a sheep being led, etc.” In Ruinart, *Authentic Acts of the Early Martyrs*]:

> They released a most savage bear, which they said had killed three men that very day. It approached the bodies of the saints and harmed no body. After passing by, it came to Saint Andronicus and, sitting down, licked his wounds. Saint Andronicus [Col. 0148C] placed his head upon the bear and provoked it to become angry and make him surrender his spirit more quickly. But the bear suddenly became as though tame.

And a little later:

> When the lioness came out, she saw the bodies of the saints lying there and came to blessed Tarachus. She lowered herself before his feet as though adoring him. Saint Tarachus drew her toward himself with his hand so that the beast might become angry and he might be perfected more quickly. But the lioness was like a sheep, etc.

Besides the natural law by which we are forbidden either to seek or to hasten our own death, there seemed also to be present a manifest indication of the divine will, which was taming the most savage beasts so that they would not harm the saints. Yet the holy martyrs, thinking of none of these things and burning only with desire for martyrdom [Col. 0149A], rushed headlong toward death—if it is permissible to speak thus. That they longed for it under the inward inspiration of the divine Spirit is evident even from the miracle. For since no one is permitted to proceed toward his own destruction unless God commands it, God would never have confirmed a rash and daring deed by miracles unless it had been undertaken by his authority.

We must hold it certain that the same Spirit impelled those who voluntarily presented themselves to tyrants or, employing greater freedom than they ought to have done, inflamed them more and more to cruelty, and whose memory the Church afterward always honored among the holy martyrs—unless we wish, at our own discretion, to expunge innumerable martyrs from the sacred calendars. From the beginning, and throughout the subsequently uninterrupted succession [Col. 0149B] of so many centuries, Perpetua held a place among these martyrs. Hence the fact that she presented her throat to the gladiator and guided the wandering sword toward herself must not be counted as a fault in her, but that noble deed must be referred to the divine Spirit by whom she was inwardly impelled.

For it is beyond controversy that Perpetua was impelled by some spirit. The only question is whether she was led by a good or an evil spirit. But since nothing worthy of censure occurs in her actions and, rather, everything was done with wisdom and virtue, it seems there can be no doubt that the Holy Spirit dwelling in her breast was the author of her visions and revelations, and that, under his inward impulse, she therefore hastened toward martyrdom.

### IX

But so that every ground for uncertainty in this matter may be removed [Col. 0149C], I wish us to examine not only the virtues of Perpetua and her fellow martyrs in general, as we have done thus far, but especially those virtues that were the fruits of the spirit dwelling in her and of her visions and revelations. For if a tree’s nature is known from its fruits, then from the fruits we shall certainly discover the nature of the spirit that was in Perpetua.

When she was baptized, she was taught by this spirit’s instruction that a Christian should seek nothing other than patience and endurance of sufferings:

> During the interval of a few days we were baptized; but the Spirit directed me to ask for nothing else in the water except endurance of the flesh.

What surer proof of a good and divine Spirit could there be than this?

Certainly Montanus’s spirit did not teach him this, perhaps even when he was baptized; for Asterius relates that, though newly baptized, Montanus burned with ungoverned ambition and an immoderate desire for first place [Note: [Col. 0149D] “There is said to be a village in Mysia bordering upon Phrygia named Ardabau. There, they say, a certain Montanus, one of those newly enrolled among the faithful, first, under Gratus, proconsul of Asia, being seized by an immoderate desire of soul for preeminence, gave the opposing spirit entrance into himself; he then began to prophesy and, suddenly falling into a kind of possession and ecstasy, began to rave, speak, and utter strange words.” In Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book V, ch. 16]:

> There is said to be a village in Mysia adjoining Phrygia named Ardabau. There, they say, a certain Montanus, one of those recently enrolled among the faithful, under Gratus, proconsul of Asia, was seized by an immoderate desire for first place [Col. 0150A], gave the adversarial spirit entrance into himself, and, filled with a demon, began to be shaken by a sudden frenzy and mental derangement, and to utter certain novel and unheard-of things, etc.

Tertullian does indeed say of his Paraclete [Note: [Col. 0150D] Book *On Flight in Persecution*, at the end] that he was the exhorter “to every kind of endurance.” But here we seek not the leaves of words but the fruits of deeds. How widely these differed from one another among the Montanists is most clearly evident by comparing this passage of Tertullian with another from Apollonius.

Tertullian speaks thus:

> And therefore the Paraclete is necessary, the guide into all truth and exhorter to every kind of endurance. Those who have received him know neither how to flee persecution nor how to buy themselves free, since they possess him who will act on our behalf—speaking during interrogation and assisting during suffering.

[Col. 0150B] But what does Apollonius say about Themison and Alexander, leading disciples of Montanus and, as they boasted, martyrs of that sect? Did he not hand down to memory in Eusebius things wholly contrary to these?

“And a little later,” says Eusebius [Note: [Col. 0150D] “Again, descending to the case of one of those whom they number among their confessors, he says: ‘Moreover, there is Themison, clothed in plausible covetousness, who did not bear the token of confession but cast off his bonds by paying a large sum of money. Although for this reason he ought thereafter to have behaved humbly, he boasted as though he were a martyr, etc. . . . And so that the facts concerning Alexander may be known to those who wish to know them: he was judged by Aemilius Frontinus, proconsul at Ephesus, not on account of the Name but because of the robberies he had dared to commit, being already a transgressor. Then, falsely invoking the Lord’s name, he was released after deceiving the faithful there. His own local church, from which he came, did not receive him because he was a robber; and those who wish to learn the facts concerning him have the public archives of Asia.’ Book V, *Ecclesiastical History*, ch. 18], “he says the following concerning one of those whom they number among their confessors”:

> Moreover, Themison, clothed in plausible covetousness, did not bear the token of confession but cast off his bonds by paying out a large sum of money. Although for this reason he should thereafter have conducted himself more modestly and humbly, he boasted as though he were a martyr, etc. . . . As for Alexander, so that the truth may become known to all who desire to know it, he was tried by Aemilius Frontinus, proconsul of Asia, not for the name of Christ but for the robberies he had committed, since he was already [Col. 0150C] a deserter from the faith. Then, falsely assuming the name of Christ, he was released after deceiving the faithful of that city. But the church of the place from which he originated did not receive him, because he practiced robbery. If anyone desires to know his entire affair, the public archives of Asia are available.

These are the martyrs and confessors of the Montanist sect; these are the men upon whom the Paraclete had breathed his spirit and whom Tertullian proclaims with puffed-out cheeks as knowing neither how to flee persecution nor how to buy themselves free.

The spirit of Prisca—or Priscilla—and Maximilla was likewise very far from suggesting such endurance of sufferings to his prophetesses. Concerning them we must again hear Apollonius, who, according to Eusebius [Note: [Col. 0150D–0151D] “Proceeding to the prophetesses of Montanus, he writes thus: ‘We therefore demonstrate that these very first prophetesses, from the moment they were filled with the spirit, abandoned their husbands. How greatly, then, did those lie who called Prisca a virgin!’ Then he adds: ‘Does not all Scripture seem to you to forbid a prophet to receive gifts and money? When, therefore, I see that the prophetess has received gold, silver, and costly garments, how can I fail to reject her?’ At the place cited above], speaks of Montanus’s [Col. 0151A] prophetesses in this manner:

> We therefore demonstrate, he says, that these leading prophetesses, as soon as they were filled with the Spirit, abandoned their husbands. How greatly, then, did those who called Prisca a virgin lie!

He then adds these words:

> Does not the whole of Scripture appear to you to forbid a prophet to receive gifts and money? When, therefore, I see that the prophetess has received gold and silver and costly garments, how can I fail to reject her?

These were the actual fruits of the Montanist spirit, not those which Tertullian falsely alleges in ambitious and inflated language.

### X

But we must return to Perpetua and her fellow martyrs. The fruit of the vision by which Perpetua and Saturus understood that death was imminent—and concerning which Basnage [Col. 0151B] cavils so greatly—was that disdain for all human affairs which is so necessary to candidates for martyrdom, so that they may proceed toward God with greater freedom:

> We understood, she says, that suffering was going to occur, and we began thereafter to place no hope in this world.

From the other vision, in which she saw Dinocrates in punishment, this good resulted: endowed with marvelous confidence in God, Perpetua wearied heaven with prayers and tears until she earned the removal of her brother from punishment and his transfer into rest:

> I trusted that my prayer would benefit his suffering, and I prayed for him every day until we were transferred to the military prison. . . . And I prayed for him day and night, groaning and weeping, that he might be granted to me.

Saturus too saw his own vision and committed it to writing [Col. 0151C] with his own hand. This vision likewise was not without fruit and testimonies of the divine Spirit. Through it a reconciliation was arranged between Optatus and Aspasius. Optatus was admonished to correct the people and reform their conduct. Saturus awoke and rejoiced concerning the coming suffering.

When Perpetua was being mauled in the amphitheater by the most savage cow, she was in ecstasy. After awakening, she remembered modesty rather than pain and was more concerned for her companion than for herself:

> When she saw that Felicity had been thrown down, she approached, gave her a hand, and raised her up.

Finally, she addressed her brother with these words, than which none could be more fitting for a most courageous and holy martyr:

> Stand firm in the faith, and all love one another; and do not be scandalized by our sufferings.

If, as has been said repeatedly, we must recognize and judge the Spirit by which a prophet was inspired from the fruit of visions and revelations, just as we recognize the nature of a tree from its fruits [Col. 0151D], who will any longer doubt that Perpetua was filled with the Holy Spirit, and that this divine Spirit was for her the cause and abundant source of heavenly revelations?

For an evil spirit would not have introduced into her such visions as greatly inflamed her to endure martyrdom, to despise the world, and to perform acts of every Christian virtue; visions from which there sprang the most abundant harvest of faith, hope, charity, reverence, modesty, and patience [Col. 0152A]; from which nothing flowed that was not holy, and nothing, finally, that was not altogether joined to the benefit of the Church.

> “Do people gather grapes from thorns, or figs from thistles? Thus every good tree bears good fruit, but a bad tree bears bad fruit. A good tree cannot bear bad fruit, nor can a bad tree bear good fruit” (Matthew, ch. VII, v. 16 and following).

## CHAPTER VII  
## THAT PERPETUA AND HER FELLOW MARTYRS WERE INSPIRED BY THE PROPHETIC SPIRIT IS DEMONSTRATED FROM THE FULFILLMENT OF THEIR PROPHECIES AND FROM MIRACLES; AND THAT THEIR TEACHING AND CONDUCT WERE ENTIRELY ALIEN TO THE DOCTRINES AND PRACTICES OF THE MONTANISTS

[Col. 0152B] I. Events corresponded in every respect and with complete exactness to Perpetua’s revelations. II. Concerning the miracles related in the Acts of our martyrs. III. Perpetua and Saturus saw in Paradise the souls not only of martyrs but also of other faithful persons. IV. They were in communion with Catholic martyrs. V. Dinocrates’s soul was transferred to eternal glory through Perpetua’s prayers. VI. The bishop Optatus mentioned in the Acts presided over Catholics. At that time there was no Montanist bishop at Carthage. VII. Our martyrs’ ordinary and customary food in prison was utterly inconsistent with the Montanist laws concerning fasting. [Col. 0152C] VIII. Concerning the Catholic Church’s solicitude in feeding and supporting its confessors. IX. Catholic martyrs by no means rejected food prepared for them by the devotion of the faithful—or even delicacies. X. Recapitulation (ἀνακεφαλαίωσις) of the argument.

I. After the character of prophets and the fruits of their visions—from which, in controversies of this kind, the strongest presumption has always arisen—the first indication of a prophetic Spirit is derived from the fulfillment of oracles. For if oracles lack fulfillment, doubt immediately enters the mind as to whether the Holy Spirit inspired the prophet’s mind, or whether there was instead either a deception by a malignant spirit or an error of human perception. The frequently mentioned Asterius convicts the spirit of Maximilla [Col. 0152D] of falsehood chiefly by this argument: that the outcome did not correspond to the prophecies. For although she had predicted that wars and disturbances would be imminent after her death, both the empire and the Christian commonwealth enjoyed a long peace. In the same book also, says Eusebius, speaking of Asterius’s writings against the Montanists [Note: [Col. 0152D] “Again in the same work, after interposing various other remarks to refute Maximilla’s false prophecies, he indicates both the time at which he wrote these things and recalls her predictions, by which he censures her falsehood, speaking as follows: ‘And how has this lie not already become manifest? For more than thirteen years have passed, down to the present day, since the woman died, and neither a local nor a universal war has occurred in the world; rather, by the mercy of God, a lasting peace has prevailed especially for Christians.’ These things, too, come from the second treatise.” Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book V, chapter 16.], “[Col. 0153A] After inserting several remarks to refute that false prophecy of Maximilla, he both specifies the very time at which these things were written and recalls that woman’s predictions, in which she had foretold that wars and disturbances were imminent. He refutes the falsehood of those predictions in these words: ‘Has not,’ he says, ‘this lie also become manifest to everyone? For from Maximilla’s death until the present day more than thirteen years have now elapsed; and yet there has been no war on earth, either local or universal. On the contrary, by a certain exceptional mercy, a stable and enduring peace has remained for Christians.’ And these words are found in the second book.”

By contrast, the Church of Smyrna demonstrates that Polycarp [Note: [Col. 0153D] “An apostolic and prophetic teacher . . . for every word that he uttered from his mouth both was fulfilled and will be fulfilled.” Encyclical Epistle on the Martyrdom of Polycarp.] “was an apostolic and prophetic teacher” from the fact that “every word which he uttered from his mouth [Col. 0153B] either had been fulfilled or awaited fulfillment.” By the same argument we too shall demonstrate that our martyrs were filled with a prophetic spirit. For everything revealed to them, and every word which they uttered from their mouths, *was fulfilled* (ἐτελειώθη), although these things belonged to the class whose foreknowledge pertains to divine wisdom alone—namely, future contingencies, especially those which depend upon the free will of God himself or of human beings.

While the matter was still uncertain—whether there would be a passion or a reprieve—Perpetua understood from her first revelation that there would be a passion; and the passion actually followed. Nor did the martyrs merely suffer; they suffered also in the order in which Perpetua had foreseen that they would. For Perpetua saw Saturus ascend the ladder first [Col. 0153C]; and Saturus was in fact the first to complete his martyrdom, as the author of the Passion observes: “Saturus, who had also ascended the ladder first, was the first to render up his spirit. For he was also waiting for Perpetua.”

The procurator Hilarianus had already pronounced sentence upon them all and condemned them to the beasts when, in another revelation, the same holy Perpetua learned that she would fight, as she says, not against the beasts but against the devil; that is, her final and most severe contest would not be against the beasts, but against the devil, with whom she had seemed to wrestle in the arena. The event occurred just as it had been foreseen. When exposed to the beasts, she experienced no pain from them; but she suffered most bitterly when, pierced between the ribs by the gladiator, she cried aloud. Afterward, by offering him her throat, she triumphed over the devil, who had attacked her through the agency [Col. 0153D] of the gladiator.

Now I ask whether Basnage concedes that Perpetua wrote these revelations in her own hand, as the Acts state, or whether he denies it altogether. For if he does not believe that they were written by Perpetua, why does he not attribute to the author of the Passion, as to an impostor, everything in them that offends his mind, instead of accusing the holy martyrs themselves on account of things fraudulently attributed to them by another? But if he concedes that Perpetua committed her revelations to writing, then, since he sees that they were confirmed by the outcomes [Col. 0154A] of subsequent events, why does he call into doubt that the Holy Spirit was their author?

And not only Perpetua, but also the other fellow-soldiers in the same contest, can readily be shown by the same argument to have been illumined by prophetic light. For each obtained the kind of contest which he had desired and perhaps had foreknown would occur. On this matter the writer of the Acts must be heard:

“But he who had said, ‘Ask, and you shall receive,’ gave to those who asked the end that each had desired. For whenever they spoke among themselves about what they wished for in their martyrdom, Saturninus declared that he wished to be exposed to all the beasts, so that he might wear a more glorious crown. Accordingly, at the opening of the spectacle, he and Revocatus encountered the leopard [Col. 0154B], and on the platform they were also mauled by the bear. Saturus, however, detested nothing more than a bear; but he already felt confident that he would be finished by a single bite of the leopard. Accordingly, when a boar was brought out, it was instead the huntsman who had supplied that boar who was gored by the same beast, and he died after the days of the games. Saturus was merely dragged about. And when he had been tied down on the bridge for the bear, the bear refused to come out of its cage. Thus Saturus was recalled unharmed for a second time.”

These desires of the martyrs were not merely ordinary wishes, but, so to speak, prophetic wishes, as the words of Saturus which the author adds shortly afterward plainly demonstrate:

“Likewise Saturus, at another gate, was exhorting the soldier Pudens, saying: ‘Here I am, just as I promised and predicted. Up to this moment I have felt no beast at all. And now believe with your whole heart. See, I go forth [Col. 0154C] there, and I am finished by a single bite of the leopard.’”

The event corresponded to the prophecy. For, as the author of the Passion adds:

“Immediately, at the end of the spectacle, he was exposed to the leopard, and by a single bite he was so drenched in blood that, as he returned, the people shouted back to him in testimony of a second baptism: ‘Saved and washed! Saved and washed!’ Plainly he was indeed saved, who had become illustrious through this spectacle.”

But even if nothing prophetic had occurred here, who, upon attending to that marvelous providence of God toward the martyrs and toward the fulfillment of their wishes, does not immediately understand how pleasing to God their confession was, and therefore their faith as well—since, as the Apostle says, without faith it is impossible to please God?

II. There is also another argument of very great weight, from which the highest authority accrues to prophets. It is drawn [Col. 0154D] from the miracles which divine omnipotence manifested either through them or, on their behalf, directly by itself. These miracles—with which there are no Acts of martyrs that do not abound—were not lacking for our martyrs either, as is already evident from what has just been said. For it did not occur without a miracle that the boar sent against Saturus turned its rage and attack instead upon the huntsman himself, or that the bear incited against Saturus refused to come out of its cage.

Here there is less reason to doubt the reliability of the Acts than in passages dealing with visions, since they report events performed openly and in the middle of the amphitheater—events which no writer of those times, however shameless, would have dared to fabricate.

It must also be counted among the miracles that, while Perpetua [Col. 0155A] was being mauled by a most savage cow, she was so deeply in ecstasy that she experienced no sensation of pain. Hence she “did not believe that what had already occurred had occurred until she recognized certain marks of the assault upon her body and clothing.” This too happened openly, in the middle of the arena, while everyone looked on in amazement.

Nor—lest perhaps Basnage draw so marvelous an event into suspicion of Montanism—is the event without parallel in other martyrs who are free from every suspicion of that kind. Entirely parallel to this passage of our Acts is another concerning the blessed Blandina in the Epistle of the Christians of Lyons, where they relate how she too [Note: [Col. 0155D] “At last she was enclosed in a net and thrown before a bull. After she had been tossed high into the air for a considerable time by the animal, she no longer had any perception whatever of what was happening, because of her hope and possession of the things believed, and because of her communion with Christ; and she too was finally sacrificed.”] “was enclosed in a net and exposed to a bull. After being tossed high into the air by it for a long time, she no longer felt anything at all of what was being done, both because of her hope and apprehension of the good things in which she believed, and because of the intimate communion [Col. 0155B] which she had with Christ in prayer; at last she too was slain like a sacrificial victim.”

We have another remarkable example, in the same Blandina, of the removal of the sensation of pain amid punishments. As it is written in the aforementioned Epistle of the Christians of Lyons [Note: [Col. 0155D] “But the blessed woman, like a noble athlete, renewed her youth in the confession; and her recovery, rest, and freedom from pain amid what was happening consisted in saying, ‘I am a Christian, and among us nothing wicked is done.’”], “Like a noble athlete, she recovered her strength and courage in the very act of confession. Her refreshment and rest, and the thing that removed every sensation of her present pain, was the utterance of these words: ‘I am a Christian, and among us nothing evil is done.’”

No less remarkable is what ecclesiastical histories have handed down concerning Theodore [Note: [Col. 0155D] Rufinus, *Ecclesiastical History*, book X, chapter 36. Saint Augustine, *The City of God*, book XVIII, chapter 52. Socrates, *Ecclesiastical History*, book III, chapters 18 and 19. Sozomen, book V, chapters 19 and 20. Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History*, book III, chapters 10 and 11.]. By order of Sallustius, praetorian prefect under Julian, he was tortured for a long time and with extreme cruelty; yet amid the torments, with a cheerful and serene countenance, he repeatedly recited that verse of the Psalm: “Let all who worship carved images and who trust in their idols be confounded.”

“We ourselves,” says Rufinus, “later saw this [Col. 0155C] Theodore at Antioch; and when we asked him whether he had felt the pain, he said plainly that he had indeed felt the pains only slightly, but that a certain young man had stood beside him and, as he perspired, wiped away his sweat with a cloth of dazzling whiteness and frequently poured cold water upon him. He had been so delighted by this that he became sadder at the moment when he was ordered to be taken down from the rack.”

Finally, Saint Flavianus, of whom mention has been made more than once above, himself relates this revelation of his [Note: [Col. 0155D] In Ruinart, *Acts of Saints Montanus, Lucius, etc.*, § 21.]:

“When our bishop alone had thus far suffered, this was shown to me: it was as though I were asking Cyprian himself whether it was painful to endure the blows. Since I was to become a martyr, I was seeking his advice about enduring the passion. He answered me and said: ‘It is another flesh that suffers [Col. 0155D] when the mind is in heaven. This body feels nothing at all when the whole mind has devoted itself to God.’”

To these [Col. 0156A] words of the holy martyr, the compiler of the Acts adds:

“O words of a martyr encouraging a martyr! He denied that there was pain in the blow of the passion, so that the one who himself was destined to be killed might be animated with greater constancy, because he need not fear even the slightest sensation of pain in the blow of the passion.”

Saint Augustine readily persuaded himself that Perpetua’s mind, no less than Cyprian’s, was in heaven when, exposed to the beasts and mauled by them, she experienced no sensation of pain. He illuminates this passage of the Acts in these words [Note: [Col. 0156D] Sermon 280, formerly 103, *On Various Subjects*.]:

“Where was that woman when she did not feel herself fighting against the most savage cow, and when she asked whether that which had already happened was still going to happen? Where was she? What was she seeing, that she did not see these things? What was she enjoying, that she did not feel these things?
