By what love was she carried away from herself, by what spectacle was she drawn aside, by what cup was she made drunk, etc.?”

[Col. 0156B] The premature delivery of Felicitas must also be numbered among the miracles. For although it is not absolutely a miracle for a woman to bring forth her child in difficult labor, the circumstances accompanying Felicitas’s delivery plainly suggest that it occurred through the special providence of God, and not according to the common and ordinary laws of nature. For immediately after the prayer which the martyrs had poured out to God that he might hasten the delivery, “the pains came upon her.” On this subject the same celebrated Saint Augustine must be heard [Note: [Col. 0156D] Sermon 281, otherwise *On Various Subjects*, 104.]:

“Finally, the delivery was timely though the month was untimely. For it was divinely brought about that the burden of her womb should be laid down before its proper time, lest the honor of martyrdom be postponed beyond its proper time. It was divinely brought about, I say, that the child should be brought forth on a day not due to it, provided that Felicitas, who was due to so great a company, [Col. 0156C] should be restored to it, etc.”

Finally, it does not appear to have occurred without a miracle that, when her father, enraged beyond measure, refused to return Perpetua’s infant so that he might remain with her in prison as before and be nursed by her, no pain came either upon the child through the withdrawal of milk or upon the mother through the inflammation of her breasts:

“Then, because the infant had been accustomed to take the breasts from me and to remain with me in prison, I immediately sent the deacon Pomponius to my father, asking for the infant. But my father refused to give him. And as God willed, neither did the child desire the breasts any longer, nor did they cause inflammation in me, so that I should not be tormented by anxiety for the infant and by pain in my breasts.”

If anyone is unwilling to regard all these things as true miracles, he must at least admit that they display the special [Col. 0156D] providence of divine goodness toward God’s martyrs. As for the credibility of the events, the very simplicity of the narrative—which is especially evident in Perpetua’s words—does not permit doubt.

III. The arguments which we have pursued thus far show generally that Perpetua and her fellow martyrs were by no means lacking in the prophetic spirit. Those which I shall now add plainly demonstrate how exceedingly far those same holy martyrs stood from the doctrines and institutions of the Montanists.

The opinion of the Montanists, as has frequently been stated from Tertullian, was that before the day of the solemn judgment, martyrs alone are received into heaven. Tertullian confirms this opinion [Col. 0157A] in his book *On the Soul* by the authority of Perpetua, “that most courageous martyr,” who, he says, “as the day of her passion approached, in a revelation of the glory of Paradise, saw there only her fellow martyrs.”

But Tertullian either is plainly mistaken or is misleading his readers. For Perpetua does not say that she saw only martyrs in Paradise; indeed, she clearly and openly testifies to the opposite: “And there we began to recognize many brethren, and martyrs as well.” Thus Perpetua—or rather Saturus—saw there not only fellow martyrs, but also fellow Christians, and not a few of them. For Saturus received this revelation and committed it to writing in his own hand.

The reason why they make special mention of martyrs is readily apparent. At the very threshold of Paradise they had encountered four martyrs who had been consummated shortly before in the same persecution under Severus [Col. 0157B]. When they asked them about the others, they were admonished by the angels that they should first enter and greet the Lord:

“There we found Jocundus, Saturninus, and Artaxius, who had suffered in the same persecution and had been burned alive; and Quintus, who had also departed from prison as a martyr. And we asked them where the others were. But the angels said to us: ‘Come first, enter, and greet the Lord.’”

When these things had been done, they testify that they saw many brethren, and specifically martyrs as well, in order to declare more plainly and clearly that their desire had been fulfilled. Nor should it seem surprising if a mind rejoicing in the martyr’s robe of white and itself approaching martyrdom speaks particularly and distinctly of the reward of martyrs. For the mind gladly recalls those things toward which it is affectionately disposed, and employs them often [Col. 0157C] and repeatedly.

IV. There is another feature which I would note in this vision of Saturus, and it seems to carry no small weight in vindicating the orthodoxy of our martyrs against Basnage. He maintains that the Montanists had no association with Catholics, even with Catholic martyrs, but shunned all communion with them because they held them up to mockery and contempt and denounced them as “psychics.”

If that is so, we shall have to accuse of Montanism not only Saturus, Perpetua, and their fellow martyrs, but also Jocundus, Saturninus, Artaxius, Quintus, and the other martyrs for whom they were asking and whose glory they afterward saw, who had already suffered in the same persecution under Severus. For Saturus and Perpetua [Col. 0157D] would have asked only for martyrs belonging to their own communion. We must therefore either say that all the aforementioned martyrs belonged to the flock of the Montanists, or enroll them all alike in the list of Catholic martyrs. But who could patiently and calmly endure that, on account of certain slight conjectures which occurred to Basnage, so many martyrs should be erased from the Catholic diptychs and the Montanist rolls enriched with their names?

V. But to continue the argument begun above and to demonstrate still more clearly from Perpetua’s revelations that, contrary to Montanist teaching, it was not only martyrs who were placed in heaven, we must recall that vision of the holy martyr in which she understood that her brother Dinocrates had been transferred [Col. 0158A] out of punishment. For Perpetua describes the place and glory to which he had been transferred in words which plainly indicate that he was received into the same place and glory in which Saturus afterward saw the martyrs, as is manifestly evident from a comparison of the two visions.

Perpetua speaks thus of her vision:

“I see that the place which I had seen as dark is now bright, and Dinocrates is there, with a clean body, well clothed, and taking refreshment. And where the wound had been, I see a scar. The pool which I had seen before had its rim lowered as far as the boy’s navel, and he drew water from it without ceasing. Above its rim was a bowl full of water. Dinocrates approached and began to drink from it, and the bowl did not become empty. When he had drunk his fill, he departed from the water and began joyfully to play in the manner of children [Col. 0158B].”

Entirely consonant with these things is what Saturus afterward saw:

“And we saw,” he says, “nearby a place whose walls were as though built of light. Before the entrance of that place stood four angels, who clothed those entering with white robes. And when we had been clothed, we entered and saw an immeasurable light, etc. And the elders said to us: ‘Go and play.’ And I said: ‘Perpetua, you have what you desire.’ She said to me: ‘Thanks be to God; just as I was cheerful in the flesh, I am even more cheerful here now.’”

And below:

“And while we were speaking with them, the angels said to them: ‘Allow them to refresh themselves. . . .’ We were all nourished by an indescribable fragrance which satisfied us.”

How well Perpetua’s revelations concerning the glory of Dinocrates and Saturus’s concerning that of the martyrs harmonize with one another! The place in which Perpetua saw Dinocrates was bright; the walls of the place [Col. 0158C] in which Saturus saw the martyrs were as though built of light. Dinocrates had a clean body and was well clothed; the angels clothed the martyrs in white robes. Dinocrates, having drunk his fill, played in the manner of children; the elders encouraged Perpetua and Saturus to play. Perpetua saw Dinocrates refreshing himself; of Perpetua and Saturus the angels said: “Allow them to refresh themselves.” Dinocrates drank from the water without ceasing and was, as it were, made drunk by that draught; Perpetua and Saturus were nourished by an indescribable fragrance which marvelously satisfied them.

Who can deny that the same glory was represented under such closely corresponding symbols and figures? Who can deny that the water for which Dinocrates at first panted, which he afterward drank without ceasing, by which he was satisfied, and which never failed him, foreshadowed that perennial fountain of eternal life and the torrent of delight of which the prophet once sang [Note: [Col. 0158D] Psalm XXXIII, 10.]:

“They shall be made drunk from the abundance of your house, and you shall give them drink from the torrent of your delight; for with you is the fountain of life, and in your light we shall see light”?

By these words he surely described no other glory and happiness than that of heaven—that is, the glory and happiness of blessed eternity and the clear vision of God.

Since, therefore, Dinocrates did not die a martyr, it is entirely false when Tertullian says that Perpetua saw only martyrs in Paradise. It is false when Basnage says that, in accordance with Montanist opinion, Perpetua placed all souls except those of martyrs [Col. 0159A] outside Paradise, in a dark place. And finally it will be false that Perpetua and those martyrs who joined her as companions in death had come from the school of the Montanists and were imbued with their doctrines and discipline.

VI. From the same vision of Saturus there arises another inference by which I may readily establish that Perpetua and her fellow martyrs were exceedingly far removed from communion with the Montanists, but both lived in the peace and unity of the Catholic Church and shed their blood gloriously for Christ:

“And we went out,” says Saturus, “and before the doors we saw Bishop Optatus on the right and Aspasius, the presbyter and teacher, on the left, separated and sorrowful. They threw themselves at our feet and said to us: ‘Reconcile us, because you have departed and leave us thus.’ And we said to them: ‘Are you not our pope, [Col. 0159B] and are you not a presbyter? Why do you cast yourselves at our feet?’ And we threw ourselves down and embraced them. . . . And while we were speaking with them, the angels said to them: ‘Allow these people to refresh themselves; and if you have any disagreements among yourselves, forgive one another.’ And they disturbed them. And they said to Optatus: ‘Correct your people, because they assemble before you as though returning from the circus and quarreling over their factions.’”

Basnage makes this Optatus a bishop of the Carthaginian Montanists and Aspasius a presbyter of the same sect, and he believes that one or the other composed the Acts of our martyrs.

By contrast, the most learned Pagi, drawing upon an observation supplied to him by the distinguished abbé Louis de Four, teaches that Optatus was bishop of the Carthaginians—that is, of course, of the Catholics—and the successor [Col. 0159C] of Agrippinus, and that the list of those bishops in Schelstrate’s dissertation *On the African Church* must be supplemented from these Acts. I consider this opinion altogether to be followed, and I confirm it from the fact that there appears to have been no Montanist bishop at Carthage at that time. Tertullian certainly never mentions any such person in his books; indeed, in several passages he indicates most clearly that there was then none.

I seem to myself to infer this with the greatest clarity from all those passages in which he presses the authority of traditions against heretics. For he maintains that Christ communicated his doctrine to the Apostles; that the Apostles communicated it to apostolic men whom they appointed bishops in the individual cities; and that these men communicated it to their successors—that is, to those who afterward succeeded the apostolic men by legitimate ordination. [Col. 0159D] He lays down that only those churches should be regarded as true and apostolic which, in compiling their records, carried the catalogue of their bishops back either to one of the Apostles or to one of the apostolic men who had nevertheless persevered with the Apostles; or which, if founded later, had received the transmission of the faith from apostolic churches and had never thereafter fallen away from their communion. Of this kind were the African churches, which traced their origin back to the Roman Church.

He challenges the heretics to disclose the origins of their churches and either carry the catalogue of their bishops back to the Apostles or to apostolic men, or show that their first bishop was given to them by apostolic churches together with the seed of the faith. Thus he argues against the heretics [Col. 0160A] both in his book *On Prescription against Heretics* [Note: [Col. 0160D] Chapter 32 and following.] and in the fourth book *Against Marcion*, where, among other things, he assails the Marcionites in these words [Note: [Col. 0160D] Chapter 5.]:

“He certainly has churches too, but churches of his own, as late as they are adulterous. If you inquire into their register, you will more readily find it apostatic than apostolic, with Marcion, of course, as founder, or someone from Marcion’s swarm. Wasps too make honeycombs; the Marcionites too make churches.”

Tertullian certainly would never have used this argument if the Carthaginian Montanists had possessed at that time a single bishop separated from the Catholic bishop. For nothing would have been more straightforward and easy than to turn that argument back upon its author and press the Montanists to publish the catalogue of their bishops, so that it might be seen whether they perhaps owed their origin to the Apostles, to apostolic men, or at least [Col. 0160B] to apostolic churches, or rather to Montanus or someone from Montanus’s swarm.

But Tertullian, as we have shown above, did not yet consider himself cut off from the communion of the apostolic churches, and he thought that Catholics and Montanists were combined into one body of the Church, governed in its different members by different institutions. Nor did he believe that diversity of disciplines, provided the rule of faith remained intact, harmed the unity of the churches. Hence those words of his when speaking of the apostolic churches: “We are one Church [Note: [Col. 0160D] *On the Veiling of Virgins*, chapter 2.].” But how could they be one Church if they had erected chair against chair and appointed bishop against bishop?

Yet just as Tertullian, when disputing against heretics, exalts the order of bishops, so in [Col. 0160C] his books against Catholics he depreciates it and places it almost on a level with the laity. When disputing against heretics, he recognizes no true Church without apostolic bishops; yet in his books against Catholics he locates the Church in three laymen. Thus, in the book *Exhortation to Chastity* [Note: [Col. 0160D] Chapter 7.]: “Where three are, there is a Church, even though they are laymen.” And in the book *On Flight in Persecution* [Note: [Col. 0160D] Chapter 14.]: “You cannot go about to every individual; let the Church for you consist even in three.” And in the book *On Modesty* [Note: [Col. 0160D] Chapter 21.]: “The Church is not the number of bishops.”

As I considered why he blurted out propositions so contrary to one another in these books, only one explanation occurred to me. Since the Catholic bishops were repelling the Montanists from communion, while they themselves had no other bishop of their own sect, he devised this for his own consolation: that by divine law the clergy possess no authority over the laity [Col. 0160D], no authority which could bind laymen in a case of necessity. In this way laymen separated from communion by the clergy became clergy for themselves, priests for themselves, and could both baptize and offer for themselves. Consequently, no obligation remained to subject themselves thereafter to the discretion of the clergy for the sake of receiving the sacraments.

“Are not we laymen also priests?” he says in the cited passage of the *Exhortation to Chastity*. “It is written: ‘He has also made us a kingdom and priests to God and his Father’ [Col. 0161A]. The authority of the Church has established the distinction between the order and the people, and the honor has been sanctified by the assembly of the order. Thus, where there is no assembly of the ecclesiastical order, you both offer and baptize, and you alone are a priest for yourself. But where three are, there is a Church, even though they are laymen. For each person lives by his own faith, and there is no partiality with God, etc. Therefore, if you possess the right of a priest within yourself wherever necessity exists, you must also possess the discipline of a priest wherever it is necessary to possess the right of a priest. Do you, being twice married, baptize? Do you, being twice married, offer? How much more is it a capital offense for a layman who has married twice to act as a priest, when even a priest himself, after marrying twice, is denied the exercise of the priesthood?”

Is this not an excellent indication that there was then no bishop of the Montanists at Carthage? For if the authority of the episcopal order must be pressed [Col. 0161B] against heretics, the registers of the Catholics are brought forward. But if battle must be joined on behalf of the Montanists against the Catholics, the authority of bishops is despised and the Church is located in three laymen.

Therefore, Bishop Optatus, who is mentioned in the Acts of our martyrs, is wrongly said to have been bishop of the Carthaginian Montanists; rather, he presided over the Catholic communion. This is also confirmed by those words of the angels in which he is ordered to correct his people: “Because,” they say, “they assemble before you as though returning from the circus and quarreling over their factions.” These words do not properly apply to someone who presided over a sect consisting of a few people, as that of the Montanists then was in Africa, but to one who governed a people and a multitude, in which [Col. 0161C] the Catholics justly gloried, as we learn from Tertullian himself [Note: [Col. 0161D] *On Fasts*, chapter 11.].

I now think it is clear from this argument that Perpetua, Saturus, and their fellow martyrs belonged to the Catholic communion and not to the flock of the Montanists: for their Catholic bishop cares for them, hastens to them, communicates with them, casts himself at their feet, converses with them, and finally implores their aid; and the martyrs themselves expressly call him their pope and bishop.

VII. Finally, an inference in favor of the holy martyrs arises both from the Church’s concern that they should be treated splendidly and generously in prison, and from the readiness with which the martyrs themselves accepted the refreshment offered to them. They were entirely free from that moroseness which is generally especially conspicuous in hypocrites and heretics—particularly [Col. 0161D] those who boast of the severity of their morals and the harshness of their discipline, as the Montanists did.

The passages of the Acts which bear upon this matter should be noted. Chapter I, § 2:

“Thereupon Tertius and Pomponius, the blessed deacons who ministered to us, arranged by payment that, after being released for a few hours, we might refresh ourselves in a better part of the prison.”

Chapter III, § 1:

“Then, after a few days, Pudens, the soldier who was an *optio* and was in charge of the prison, began to hold us in great esteem, understanding that there was great power in us. He admitted many brethren to us, so that both we and they might refresh one another.”

Chapter V, § 3:

“When they were being treated more harshly by the tribune because, [Col. 0162A] owing to the warnings of exceedingly foolish men, he feared that they might be removed from prison by some magical incantations, Perpetua answered him to his face and said: ‘Why, in any case, do you not permit the most illustrious condemned persons—Caesar’s prisoners, of course, who are to fight on his birthday—to refresh themselves? Is it not to your glory if we are brought out in better condition on that occasion?’ The tribune shuddered and blushed, and therefore ordered that they be treated more humanely, so that her brethren and the others should be given permission to enter and refresh themselves with them, the *optio* of the prison himself now also being a believer.”

And chapter V, § 4:

“On the preceding day also, at that final supper which they call the free meal, so far as it lay in their power, they celebrated not a free meal but an *agape*, etc.”

### VIII

How consonant these things are with the discipline of the most ancient Catholic Church, which always showed the greatest [Col. 0162B] and maternal solicitude toward confessors held in chains; and how foreign they appear to the seemingly most rigorous institutions of the Montanists. Lucian, in his letter *On the Death of Peregrinus*, graphically and clearly describes in the following words the duties of piety and charity performed by the ancient Christians toward their brethren imprisoned for the faith, although he wickedly mocks them:

[Note: [Col. 0162D] “Those of them who held positions of authority even slept inside with him, after bribing the prison guards. Then various meals were brought in, and their sacred discourses were delivered.… Moreover, some came from certain cities in Asia, sent at the common expense of the Christians, to assist, defend, and console the man. They display an extraordinary speed whenever anything of this kind becomes public, for in a short time they spare no expense. Thus a great deal of money then came to Peregrinus from them on the pretext of his imprisonment, and he made no small income from it.”]

“Their magistrates even slept inside with him, after the guards had been bribed. Then various meals were brought in, and their sacred discourses were delivered.… Some also came from certain cities of Asia, sent at the common expense of the Christians, to bring aid to the man, defend him, and console him. They display a certain incredible speed if anything of this kind [Col. 0162C] becomes public. For they immediately spare no expense. Accordingly, much money was then sent to Peregrinus, and he made no small profit from this.”

But let us hear the Christians themselves discussing this subject. Saint Cyprian mentions this ancient custom of the Church in many passages of his letters, and he applied himself diligently and intelligently to this no less than to the other duties of pastoral care. For in his fifth letter, written from his place of retirement to the clergy, he gives the following instruction on this matter:

“As regards supplying expenses, whether for those who, having confessed God with a glorious voice, are being held in prison, or for those who suffer in poverty and want, I ask that nothing be lacking. For the entire sum that has been collected is there, distributed among the clergy for cases of this sort, so that several may have the means [Col. 0162D] to provide for the necessities and afflictions of individuals.”

Indeed, such was the Christian people’s affection toward the confessors that there was no need to spur them on in this respect; rather, it was necessary, according to the dictates of prudence, to regulate the brethren’s rush to the prisons to cherish and refresh the confessors. [Col. 0163A] Hence he immediately adds:

“I also ask that your skill and solicitude not cease to make provision for peace and quiet. For although the brethren, in their affection, eagerly desire to assemble and visit the good confessors, whom divine favor has already distinguished by glorious beginnings, I nevertheless think that this should be done cautiously—not in crowds, nor with a large multitude gathered at once—lest resentment be aroused by that very fact, access be denied, and, while in our insatiability we desire too much, we lose everything. Therefore take counsel and make provision so that this may be done more safely and with moderation. Thus also the presbyters who offer there among the confessors should take turns, each accompanied by a single deacon; for both a change of persons and the rotation of those assembling [Col. 0163B] diminish resentment.”

And in Letter 12—number 37 in Pamelius’ arrangement—he again writes to the clergy on the same subject:

“Although I know, dearest brethren, that you have frequently been admonished by my letters to show every diligence toward those who, having confessed the Lord with a glorious voice, are being held in prison, I nevertheless repeatedly press this duty upon you, lest anything be lacking in the care of those to whom nothing is lacking for glory. And would that the circumstances of my location and rank permitted me to be present there myself now. Eagerly and gladly would I fulfill, with solemn ministry, every affectionate duty toward our most steadfast brethren. But let your diligence represent my office and do all that ought to be done for those whom divine favor has distinguished by such merits of faith and courage.”

And farther on in [Col. 0163C] the same letter, he praises Tertullus’ diligence and solicitude in these duties of piety:

“Although Tertullus, our most faithful and devoted brother, in accordance with the rest of the solicitude and care that he devotes to the brethren in every service of active charity, is not lacking there either in the care of their bodies, etc.”

This care pertained especially to the deacons, as is evident not only from the Acts of our martyrs, but also from the letters of Cyprian himself and from the letter of Dionysius of Alexandria to Domitius and Didymus. There Dionysius commends the diligence of the deacon Eusebius, who devoted to the Alexandrian martyrs the care that Tertullus devoted to the Carthaginian martyrs:

[Note: [Col. 0163D] “Eusebius, whom God strengthened and prepared from the beginning vigorously to fulfill the ministries owed to the confessors held in prison, and, not without danger, to perform the burial rites for the bodies of the perfected and blessed martyrs.” In Eusebius, book VII, chapter 2.]

“Eusebius, whom God strengthened from the very beginning and impelled vigorously to render service to the confessors held in custody, [Col. 0163D] and to bury the bodies of the perfected and blessed martyrs, not without danger to his own life.”

Before Tertullian had completely estranged himself from the Church and begun to argue against it more violently, he spoke with praise of the same custom in his book *To the Martyrs*:

“Among the nourishment of the flesh, blessed designated martyrs, which both our lady mother the Church supplies to you in prison from her own breasts and individual brethren from their own private resources, receive [Col. 0164A] also something from us that may nourish the spirit. For it does no good that the flesh should be fattened while the spirit hungers.”

And farther on, in chapter two:

“Meanwhile, let us compare the very mode of life of the world with that of prison, and see whether the spirit does not gain more in prison than the flesh loses. Indeed, through the care of the Church and the brethren’s *agape*, the flesh does not lose even those things that are its rightful due.”

But after he had surrendered himself entirely to the discipline of Montanus and had begun to conduct his quarrels with the Catholics more bitterly and shamelessly, he represented the Church’s charity toward confessors far more spitefully than Lucian had done. At the same time, in his book *On Fasts*, he set forth in the following words the rigor of diet and discipline that Christians in chains were to observe under the laws and institutions of the Montanists:

[Note: [Col. 0164D] Chapter twelve.]

“Certainly it is your practice to set up taverns in prisons for martyrs whose fate is still uncertain, lest they miss their accustomed way of life, grow weary of life, or be scandalized by a novel discipline of abstinence. Even that Pristinus of yours, a martyr who was no Christian, would not have touched it. For some time, under the privilege of open custody, he had been stuffed with every indulgence—with every bath, as though baths were better baptisms; with every retreat of luxury, as though they were the more private sanctuaries of the Church; and with every enticement of this life, as though these were worthier of eternal life. He was, I suppose, bound by these things so that he would not wish to die. Finally, on the very day of his trial, you premedicated him with wine, as though with an antidote, and so enervated him that, when the governor questioned him, he could no longer answer which Lord he confessed, though merely tickled by a few claws—for this was all his drunkenness could feel. Thus, after the confession had already been wrenched from him, having nothing left but hiccups and belches, he digested his denial on the spot.”

These are Tertullian’s words about the Catholics. Although they are exaggerated beyond all measure in order to bring them into disrepute, [Col. 0164C] they nevertheless clearly show that Catholic martyrs in chains were treated splendidly and generously, insofar as the soldiers and guards permitted it.

Concerning the severity and strictness of the Montanists, however, he had previously prefaced the following:

“Even if the Paraclete had fallen silent from the time of John onward, we ourselves ought especially for this cause to have arisen as prophets … enjoining every *tapeinophrosynē* (ταπεινοφρόνησις, humility or self-abasement), since prison must be learned beforehand, hunger and thirst must be practiced, and endurance of both starvation and meager rations must be adopted, so that a Christian may enter prison in the same condition in which he would emerge from it—not to suffer punishment there, but discipline; not the torments of the world, but duties—and may thereby proceed from custody to the contest with greater confidence, having nothing left of the flesh: armored, as it were, in skin alone, dry and hardened against the claws, the fluid of the blood having already been discharged as though it were an impediment to the soul; while the soul itself is already hastening onward, since through frequent fasting it has learned to know death at close hand.”

This austerity of diet, which Tertullian here describes from the discipline of the Montanists, not only appears nowhere in the Acts of our martyrs; on the contrary, we saw above that they freely used food and drink. And when they were treated more harshly, we heard Perpetua rebuke the tribune in these words, saying to him with holy confidence:

“Why, then, do you not permit the most noble condemned persons to be refreshed—Caesar’s prisoners, that is, who are to fight [Col. 0165A] on his birthday? Or is it not to your glory if we are brought out for him in better flesh?”

These words certainly display not only a lofty confidence of spirit and character, but also demonstrate that Perpetua’s mind was entirely alien to the institutions of the Montanists and was occupied with thoughts different from Tertullian’s. For what could be more contrary than the views and words of Perpetua and Tertullian on this matter? He wishes the Christian to proceed from custody to the contest with nothing left of the flesh, armored in skin alone, dry and hardened, the fluid of the blood already discharged, and so forth. Perpetua, however, protests to the tribune about the meagerness of their diet and says—although playfully—that she wishes to be brought into the amphitheater in better flesh. He reproaches the Catholics because they prepared a richer banquet for Pristinus [Col. 0165B] on the very day of his trial. Perpetua and her fellow martyrs, however, on the day before they were exposed to the beasts, by no means rejected the supper that they called “the free meal,” and which was prepared most lavishly for those condemned to fight the beasts.

### IX

In this they certainly followed the custom of Catholic martyrs, who were accustomed to receive with thanksgiving the food brought to them. Alcibiades, one of the martyrs of Lyons, retained in prison the austere manner of life that he had followed before he was arrested for the faith. But it was shown to Attalus through a vision that Alcibiades was not acting rightly or in good order by practicing that harsh, austere, and singular manner of life.

We have witnesses of the greatest possible weight for this fact: the Christians of Lyons and Vienne themselves, in their encyclical letter concerning the martyrdom of their people, preserved in [Col. 0165C] Eusebius:

[Note: [Col. 0165D] “For a certain Alcibiades, one of their number, lived a very austere life and previously partook of nothing at all, but used only bread and water; and he attempted to continue living in this way even in prison. But after the first contest that Attalus completed in the amphitheater, it was revealed to him that Alcibiades was not acting rightly by refusing to use the creatures of God and by leaving to others an occasion of stumbling. Alcibiades was persuaded and thereafter partook freely of everything and gave thanks to God. For they were not left without the visitation of God’s grace, but had the Holy Spirit as their counselor.” In Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book V, chapter 3.]

“A certain Alcibiades, one of the number of those martyrs, followed a harsh and squalid manner of life. Taking no other food at all, he had until that time been accustomed to live on bread and water alone. When, after being placed in prison, he wished to retain the same way of life, it was revealed to Attalus, after the first contest that he had completed in the amphitheater, that Alcibiades was not acting rightly or in good order, since he neither used the creatures of God nor avoided becoming an example of scandal to others. Alcibiades therefore obeyed, and from that time onward began to partake freely of every kind of food, giving thanks to God. For divine grace had not deprived them of its presence; rather, they had the Holy Spirit as their counselor.”

Accordingly, our martyrs, obeying this same Spirit, practiced even in chains the common and ordinary mode of life [Col. 0165D] of which we have spoken—a way of life plainly different from that which the Montanists prescribed for their own martyrs.

[Col. 0166A]

### X

Now, although it already seems to me that I have presented all that could be argued on either side concerning our martyrs, bear with me nevertheless, reader, and allow me to detain you a little longer, until I place under a single view, as it were, everything that has perhaps been discussed at excessive length. I shall reduce to a few words the grounds supporting each opinion—both that which represents the holy martyrs as Montanists and that which has undertaken their defense—by comparing the institutions of the two parties.

But first we must recall that this is one of those controversies concerning which no judgment can safely be pronounced unless we attend to every indication and all the circumstances that either arise from the very matter under dispute or accompany it externally. [Col. 0166B] Concerning such questions, the following most wise rule has been established:

[Note: [Col. 0166D] See *Logic, or the Art of Thinking*, part IV, chapter 13.]

If all the circumstances are such as are only very rarely found conjoined with falsehood, it is the part of a prudent man to show himself compliant and readily to give assent. But if, on the contrary, these circumstances are of the kind that very frequently have falsehood attached to them, reason demands that we either withhold our assent or judge the report to be false, since it does not in any way appear to be true—even though, from another point of view, it may not be absolutely impossible for it to have happened, nor may it be certain, with what is called metaphysical certainty, of the kind enjoyed by the mathematical sciences, that it did not actually happen. For it would be the mark of an exceedingly imprudent man, devoid of judgment, to demand evidence and certainty of this kind in contingent matters [Col. 0166C] and particular events narrated in histories, which rest upon human testimony and human faith.

These principles being established, let us compare Basnage’s arguments with ours, reasons with reasons. It will be the task of a fair and prudent reader to award the case to the party whose reasons are very rarely—or at least less frequently—conjoined with falsehood than those produced by the opposing side. And since the contest on both sides has been waged with both external and internal arguments, we shall compare external arguments with external, and internal arguments with those of the same kind.

As regards the former, or external arguments, I have no doubt whatever that, according to the rule laid down and approved by the judgment of wise men, the case must be awarded to us—or rather to the holy martyrs. [Col. 0166D] For the external testimonies that we possess concerning the sound faith of our martyrs are of such a kind that, although one or another may be mistaken, or may even sometimes have been mistaken, they are all together found conjoined with falsehood not merely very rarely, but never at all. No example can be produced of any martyr or confessor whom the Church entered in the roll of the saints with the same solemnity as Perpetua and her fellow martyrs, but who was subsequently found, fifteen centuries after his death, to have been alien to the sound faith.

We therefore find Basnage lacking in prudence when, to diminish the force of the argument proposed, [Col. 0167A] he points to examples of certain heretics whose names some compilers of works of this kind inserted in their martyrologies on their own private judgment. For to weaken an argument drawn from the public and universal veneration of the saints, never interrupted through so many centuries, it would have been necessary to produce some heretic whose veneration in the Church was no less widespread than that of our martyrs.

In his apologetic letter on behalf of Saint Dionysius of Alexandria, defending Dionysius’ orthodoxy against the Arians, the great Athanasius uses this argument above all, regarding it as great and exceedingly evident:

[Note: [Col. 0167D] “It is therefore a great proof that they do not speak the truth even in this matter, but slander the man, that he was neither condemned for impiety by other bishops and expelled from the episcopate, as these men were from the clergy, nor did he himself leave the Church in defense of a heresy; rather, he fell asleep in it with a good reputation, and to this day his memory is ranked with that of the Fathers and is inscribed among them. For if he had held the same opinions as these men, or had not defended what he wrote, there is no doubt that he would certainly have suffered the same things as they did.” Montfaucon edition, no. 3.]

“It is certainly a weighty argument that in this matter they do not speak the truth, but slander the man: he was never condemned by other bishops for detected [Col. 0167B] impiety and expelled from his episcopate, as they were ejected from the clergy; nor did he withdraw from the Church for the sake of defending a heresy. Rather, he fell asleep piously within it, and his memory has been celebrated to the present day together with that of the Fathers, and has been entered with theirs in the roll. For if he had held the same views as they, or if he had not given an account of his writings, there is no doubt whatever that he would have been punished with the same penalty as they.”

Would Basnage also have disposed of this argument of Athanasius on behalf of Dionysius with the feeble answer that heretical bishops had sometimes slipped into martyrologies or sacred diptychs? Indeed, that would be a futile answer and wholly unworthy of a prudent man. Rather, an example should have been established in the case of a man in whom all these indications of orthodoxy were simultaneously combined, but who was nevertheless discovered to be a heretic after an interval of many centuries following his [Col. 0167C] death. Yet absolutely no example of such a thing exists in the ecclesiastical records.

The conjectures that Basnage derives from the authority of Tertullian and from the compiler of the Acts against Perpetua and her fellow martyrs, however, are of such a kind that they are not infrequently and most manifestly conjoined with falsehood. For, as we have shown, Tertullian very often praised Catholic martyrs and aspired to their communion; and the Novatians, finally, no less exiled from the Catholic Church than the Montanists, published the Acts of Catholic martyrs and commended them to remote posterity, and so forth.

The comparison of the internal arguments yields the same result. Our arguments are drawn from the holiness of the martyrs, from their virtues, [Col. 0167D] miracles, and prophecies, and from the fulfillment of those prophecies—all of which together are never found to have been conjoined with heresy. The arguments advanced by Basnage, however, arise from what appears to him to be the awkwardness of certain visions. Considered by themselves, such things could at most be interpreted either favorably or unfavorably. [Col. 0168A] But when they are found conjoined with holiness and simplicity of life, with miracles and the fulfillment of prophecies, reason demands that, so far as possible, we understand them in the most favorable sense.

From this arises an argument from which, as it seems to me, the adversary cannot escape by any reasoning. For he must either give credence to what is reported in the Acts concerning the virtues, prophecies, and miracles of our martyrs, or rather deny it. If he gives credence to it, the orthodoxy of the holy martyrs is certainly secure, since those virtues—in which nothing feigned, nothing adulterated, and nothing done through dissimulation or hypocrisy is found—together with those miracles and prophecies, do not suit heretical martyrs. Much less do the things contained in the Acts suit Montanists, [Col. 0168B] since, as we have shown, they are thoroughly alien to Montanist dogmas and discipline. In that case, as I have said, reason demands that we interpret the visions and revelations in the most favorable sense, just as we have done, and as before us Saint Augustine and other very learned men did.

But if Basnage denies credence to what is reported concerning the virtues of Perpetua, Felicity, and their fellow martyrs, and so forth, he will for the same reason also have to deny credence to what in the Acts pertains to the martyrs’ visions and revelations. For no principle permits him to believe the Acts when they speak against the martyrs while refusing them credence when they speak on their behalf. This is especially so because it would be far easier to suppose that the compiler of the Acts lied in what he narrates concerning visions than in what he reports concerning signs and miracles. [Col. 0168C] For God alone and the martyrs themselves were witnesses of the visions and revelations, and the martyrs had already been driven from the number of the living by the savagery of the executioners. But as regards the miracles, some of them are said by a contemporary writer to have taken place openly, in the middle of the amphitheater, where certainly there could have been no room in a contemporary author for fraud or suspicion.

Especially relevant here is Dodwell’s excellent observation concerning miracles of this kind:

[Note: [Col. 0168D] *Cyprianic Dissertation XII, On the Fortitude of the Martyrs*, § 45.]

If atheists are willing to approve such things according to the capacity and nature of historical evidence, there is absolutely nothing they could require here to prevent such accounts from appearing entirely true:

“For first of all,” he says, “they relate that the events were performed not in corners or before a few persons privy to them, whose interests might have been involved, but openly and in the sight [Col. 0168D] of everyone, enemies as well as friends—or rather especially enemies, who held the foremost places in the theaters. Thus it came about not only that those who wrote of the events could know them with certainty, but also that those who held a different opinion could easily and decisively refute them.

“Secondly, these events were of such a kind that it was in the highest degree to the interest of very many that the truth should not remain hidden, but should instead become as fully known as possible. It was in the persecutors’ interest that these things should not be believed true, since by them the persecutors would be burdened among those absent—both the living and posterity—with the gravest infamy of cruelty, and would also seem to have been condemned by divine [Col. 0169A] judgment. It was likewise, above all, in the interest of the Christians, if these things had been false, that they should not be believed true, since on their account the Christians would have had to endure such great torments in this life while gaining no recompense at all in the form of future rewards. There is therefore no reason to suspect that these narratives were disregarded. On the contrary, we should expect that both sides would have applied every diligence to investigating them.”

But if Basnage denies that the Acts of Perpetua were compiled by a contemporary author, the matter now comes down to this: we must deny credence not only to the miracles but also to the visions, and the whole controversy must be referred back to the external arguments, in which we have seen how greatly Perpetua’s case triumphs.

[Col. 0170A] Let us grant, nevertheless, that the arguments now advanced on both sides are equal. Since it is the part of a good man and an equitable judge to interpret doubtful matters in a favorable rather than an unfavorable sense, and since no one should be deprived of the possession of a good name and reputation that he enjoys unless he is shown by certain indications and clear arguments to be guilty, it was in no way permissible for Perpetua and her fellow martyrs—who for fifteen centuries had enjoyed a reputation for sound faith and holiness—to be deprived of it on account of a few slight conjectures. This indeed was the reason why I voluntarily assumed the role of defender in this controversy and published this dissertation of mine, such as it is. May the whole of it, in all its extent, redound to the honor of God and the glory of the martyrs!

## [HEADLESS FRAGMENT]

[Col. 0169]

## ANNOTATIONS ON THE FRAGMENT OF AN UNKNOWN AUTHOR CONCERNING THE CANON OF HOLY SCRIPTURE

(L. A. Muratori, *Antiquities of Medieval Italy*, vol. III, col. 854. Gallandi, *Library of the Ancient Fathers*, vol. II, p. 208. Routh, *Remains of the Sacred Writers*, vol. IV, p. 3. Everard Stosch, *Commentary on the Canon of the Books of the New Testament*, § 63, p. 199. Freindaller, *Commentary*, Linz, 1802. Kirchnoser, *Collection of Sources for the History of the New Testament Canon*, Zurich, 1842, pp. 1–2.)

[Col. 0169B] Muratori was the first to publish this most ancient fragment, which treats of the canon of the New Testament. In *Antiquities of Medieval Italy*, volume III, Milan, 1740, he prefaced the following remarks concerning the manuscript codex from which it was taken:

“But since we have begun to examine the wounds inflicted upon literature during the course of the uncultivated centuries, this fact too must not be passed over in silence: men of the greatest inexperience and ignorance were more frequently employed than before to copy manuscripts, which one consequently sees filled to the point of nausea with errors and filth. I have had no small number of these before me, and it is helpful to offer an example that, in more than one respect, unless I flatter myself too readily, appears to call for publication.

“The Ambrosian Library at Milan preserves a parchment codex received [Col. 0169C] from Bobbio, whose age seemed to me to approach a thousand years. For it was written in large, square letters. The title prefixed to it attributes everything to John Chrysostom, but wrongly.” Page 851.

Then, after mentioning the other treatises contained in the codex, the distinguished man continues:

“From the same codex, therefore, I extracted a most ancient fragment relating to the canon of the divine Scriptures. I spared no effort to discover its author and at the same time to learn whether it had previously been published. Unless my eyes deceived me, or unless I was hindered by the lack of many books—a lack that I have more than once lamented—I nowhere found that it had been published. [Col. 0170B] I therefore retain the hope that readers will receive it all the more gladly, particularly because it breathes an antiquity worthy of the highest veneration.”

Muratori then shows that he believes the fragment should be attributed to Caius, a presbyter of the Roman Church who flourished at the end of the second century. The distinguished Gallandi held the same opinion in the prolegomena to volume II of his *Library of the Fathers*, p. 23. Because the author of the fragment introduced mention of a certain heretic named Miltiades—or, as the name is written here, Miltiadis—Gallandi maintains that this excerpt belonged to the disputation that Caius composed against Proculus, or Proclus, a follower of the Cataphrygians.

For the anonymous writer in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book V, chapter 16—or above, in my volume II, p. 73—at the very beginning [Col. 0170C] of the work he composed against the Cataphrygians, names the heresy of Miltiades. Yet Gallandi’s argument, even if the reading *Miltiades* were sufficiently established—some wish to substitute *Alcibiades* in its place—would not be sufficiently strong to vindicate this fragment for Caius.

Furthermore, the Very Reverend Everard Stosch opposed Muratori’s conjecture concerning Caius. Stosch himself reproduced the fragment after Muratori in his *Dissertation on the Canon of the Books of the New Testament*, published at Frankfurt an der Oder in 1755. In § 63, p. 199, he says that the arguments Muratori advances in support of his conjecture lend it little probability:

[Col. 0171A] “For the fact that Caius rejected the Epistle to the Hebrews as noncanonical was shared by him with several others—Irenaeus and Hippolytus, for example—and indeed, according to Eusebius, book VI, chapter 20, and Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 60, with several other doctors of the Roman Church. And the statement that Hermas composed the *Shepherd* in the author’s own time can be applied to any other person who lived in that age.”

Yet although the distinguished Stosch, in §§ 61 and 62, judges that this fragment should not be attributed to Caius because Caius, according to Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book III, chapter 28, regarded the Apocalypse of John as a work of Cerinthus, whereas the author of the fragment regards it as canonical, we must remember that the question whether Caius’ words pertain to the Apocalypse of Saint John is still under judgment. [Col. 0171B] We made some annotations on this matter among Caius’ fragments in volume II of the *Remains*, p. 16; and the distinguished Freindaller, the recent editor of this fragment, whom I shall mention presently, discussed it in §§ 9 and 10.

Stosch also proposed another argument against Caius: the author of the fragment either entirely failed to know, or at least failed to notice, that Paul’s epistles had been written long before the Apocalypse was seen and published by the apostle John. Such an error and lack of reflection could only with difficulty be conceived of Caius, whom Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* VI.2, calls “a most learned man” (ἄνδρα λογιώτατον), and whose disputation against Proclus Photius, codex 48, calls “an earnest discourse” (σπουδαίαν διάλεξιν).

Thus Stosch. Yet this would merely be a “chronological error” (*para ton chronon hamartēma*, παρὰ τὸν χρόνον ἁμάρτημα). Meanwhile, those learned men who, as the distinguished author himself also notes, refer John’s Apocalypse to the reign of the emperor Claudius would deny, together with Epiphanius, *Heresy* LI, chapters 12 [Col. 0171C] and 36, that the matter must be understood in that way. Compare also Thomas Newton, Bishop of Bristol, *Dissertations on the Prophecies*, written in English, volume III, § 24, chapter 1, and J. D. Michaelis, *Lectures on the Books of the New Testament*, final section.

For my part, I would be more troubled by the blemish found at the end of this fragment, where Basilides appears to be presented—if it please the gods—as the founder of the Cataphrygians. For if the passage is to be read and construed in that way, I fear that an argument for gross ignorance on the part of this author would have to be drawn from it.

Although the distinguished Stosch does not wish these words to be regarded as Caius’, an opinion shared both by the distinguished Keil in his additions to Fabricius’ *Greek Library*, volume VII, p. 285, and by [Col. 0171D] other learned men whom Keil mentions there, Stosch nevertheless regards it as highly probable that the fragment is altogether very ancient and was composed around the end of the second century or the beginning of the third. To confirm this opinion he appended many arguments, and very strong ones. So far as I know, all writers who have mentioned this short fragment agree in this judgment.

I shall subsequently present Stosch’s arguments in connection with the individual books of Holy Scripture named in the fragment, since they not only confirm its antiquity but also illuminate the fragment itself admirably.

Nor had the celebrated Mosheim, before Stosch, judged differently concerning the date of the work. In his *Commentary on the Affairs of the Christians before Constantine the Great*, [Col. 0172A] under the first century, § 54, p. 164, he wrote the following concerning it:

“The author is unknown. Muratori thinks that he was Caius, a Roman presbyter who flourished as the second century drew to its close. This is doubtful; but from the little work itself it is certain that he wrote in the second century, and specifically at the time when Hermas was alive. Thus, in this fragment of great value, the following is written concerning Hermas: ‘But very recently, in our own times, in the city of Rome, Hermas composed the *Shepherd*, while his brother Pius, the bishop of the Church of the city of Rome, occupied its chair.’”

Thus Mosheim. Accordingly, the author appears either to have lived near the middle of the second century, when the episcopate of Pius had indeed come to its end, or at least it is certain that he wrote before the century was over, even if a different judgment is made concerning the true date of the little work called the *Shepherd*.

How it happened that this fragment—which, unless I am mistaken, no one at all has rejected or disapproved—escaped the diligence of the distinguished Lardner, I confess I do not know, since the fragment had been communicated to the learned world long before Lardner himself again committed to print his altogether excellent work *On the Credibility of the Gospel History*. [Col. 0172B] Since its author must be placed among those writers who were the very first, with the exception of Papias, either to mention the evangelists themselves or expressly to cite their writings, it is impossible that this first catalogue of the books of the New Testament should not be judged worthy of our attention.

Nevertheless, to our great astonishment, he omitted an epistle that was always and universally received, namely the First Epistle of Saint Peter, [Col. 0172C] whose authority no one had doubted from the time of Polycarp and Papias onward. This omission was made by an author who acknowledged three of the seven “disputed” (ἀντιλεγόμεναι) writings, while admitting no “spurious” (νόθον) book into the canon of the New Testament, with perhaps one exception. I have already spoken of the other blemish in his work concerning the heretic Basilides.

Very recently, after I had stated on page XXI of the preface to my work that I had postponed presenting this fragment concerning the canon because its latest edition had not yet come into my hands, a small work was sent to me from Germany by a nobleman traveling abroad. It had previously appeared at Linz in 1802, with a commentary by Francis Freindaller, canon and public professor of theology.

[Col. 0172D] Freindaller nowhere mentions Stosch’s book on the canon. On the contrary, he maintains that the fragment should be vindicated for Caius the presbyter, although in § 8, p. 13, he says:

“It is highly probable that Caius’ conference with Proclus was conducted and written down in Greek. For Eusebius, Photius, and Theodoretus—who in book III of his *Heretical Fables* entitled it *Against Patroclus* (κατὰ Πάτροκλον)—read it in that form. I add that Valesius argues, on grounds by no means negligible, that this Proclus, one of the leaders of the Montanist sect, was a Greek from Asia. Caius therefore conferred in Greek with a Greek man. Yet our fragment has the stylistic flavor of a Latin rather than a Greek original. [Col. 0173A]

“This difficulty can be met only if one says that the disputation was immediately translated into Latin, or that Caius himself simultaneously composed it in Latin for the benefit of the Romans. Neither conjecture is, to be sure, discordant with the truth. For in this manner most of Saint Irenaeus’ works have come down to us in a very ancient Latin translation, as have very many other works of this kind.”

Thus Freindaller. Meanwhile, I myself seem to have detected from sufficiently clear traces that behind these Latin words lies a man who wrote in Greek, for the evidence is that their construction is so thoroughly Greek that they appear to have been translated from that language.

Freindaller continues in § 13 as follows, after having observed in § 11 that this Caius—Valesius and Ruinart agreeing—was the person of whom it is written at the end of the Acts of Saint Polycarp, “Caius copied these Acts from the manuscripts of Irenaeus, the disciple of Polycarp, with whom he was contemporary”; and that one should therefore not believe that a man who had long associated with Irenaeus despised the Apocalypse of the apostle John:

[Col. 0173B] “If arguments were available from which we could securely conclude that this fragment belonged to the same *Disputation with Proclus* from which Eusebius borrowed his material, and which is undisputedly the work of Caius, then indeed our vindication of it for Caius would rise to the level of fully established certainty.

“Muratori himself, in the passage cited, has already advanced a consideration favorable to this opinion, when he conjectures that Caius seized upon the occasion furnished by his adversaries’ shameless audacity in fabricating new writings to discuss the canon of the books of the New Testament, as is done in the fragment. [Col. 0173C]

“To this it may most appropriately be added that the fragment itself indicates a certain trace of continuity with a disputation—something that it is truly astonishing should have escaped the eyes of so acute a man. [Col. 0174A] For after mentioning Paul’s Epistle to the Romans and its subject, the author appended these words: ‘Concerning each of these matters, it is necessary for us to dispute.’

“Moreover, since nowhere else in the fragment’s entire argument does anything occur discordant with such a disputation, and since everything in it can instead be most readily reconciled with one, what can further delay us from once again restoring this most venerable monument of ecclesiastical antiquity to the ancient Caius, to whom so many arguments vindicate it, now that the opposing difficulties have, as I believe, been sufficiently resolved?”

Thus Freindaller.

“Come now,” says Muratori, “let us produce [Col. 0174B] the fragment itself, extracted from a very ancient Ambrosian codex, and submit it to the examination of all scholars, removing none of the errors with which the ignorance of copyists has saturated and disfigured the text, although these errors do not prevent us from understanding the value of the work.” Thus he writes; and in the same way the distinguished Stosch presented the fragment with all its faults and errors, as did Gallandi in volume II of his *Library of the Fathers*, where he placed it among the Fragments of Caius. Would that learned men had undertaken the task of correcting it. Since this was not done—except that in some passages where emendation is easier, the distinguished Freindaller, treating the fragment section by section, restored the true reading—I have taken up the allotted task (τὴν στάρταν, a corrupt or transliterated form alluding to the proverbial “allotted province/task”), which those earlier scholars had left still to be adorned [Col. 0174C]. Whether I have succeeded in extracting anything worthwhile from these letters so shamefully corrupted must be left to the judgment of others.

[Col. 0173]

## Headless Fragment of an Uncertain Author on the Canon of Holy Scripture (S)

[Col. 0173C]

[Note: [Col. 0173D] **I.—At which, nevertheless, he was present.** If the deeds of Christ the Lord, rather than those of the Apostles themselves, are meant here, the author of the fragment would contradict the words of Papias. As we saw above, Papias, following the ancient presbyter, denied this of Mark—namely, that Mark had either heard the Lord himself or followed him. Papias received this from the presbyter’s own lips, and you have Jerome subsequently confirming it by his own testimony in the preface to his *Commentary on Matthew*. I pass over the other Fathers in silence.

Nevertheless, the contrary tradition concerning Mark is very well known—although I doubt whether it is also entirely certain—which Epiphanius records in *Heresy* LI, § 6, according to which Mark is said to have been [Col. 0174D] one of the seventy-two disciples. The same Epiphanius also relates this of Saint Luke in § 11, just as he had earlier asserted it of both evangelists in *Heresy* XX, § 4, following Hippolytus, if the testimonies placed by Mill before the Gospels are to be trusted.

Many very learned men have considered this scarcely reconcilable with the beginning of Saint Luke’s Gospel, nor do I wonder at that. If Luke had ever been a disciple of the Lord, he certainly does not appear to have been one of “the eyewitnesses from the beginning” [τῶν ἀπ᾽ ἀρχῆς αὐτοπτῶν] who would write as follows: “just as those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and became ministers of the Word delivered them to us” [καθὼς παρέδοσαν ἡμῖν οἱ ἀπ᾽ ἀρχῆς αὐτόπται καὶ ὑπηρέται γενόμενοι τοῦ Λόγου].

The author of the fragment agrees with those learned men, as you will shortly see, by denying that Luke was a disciple; Eusebius also agrees in book III of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapters 4 and 24. In book I, chapter 12 of the same work, he says that no catalogue of the seventy disciples [τῶν ὅ] survives, although it has been handed down that Barnabas was one of them.

After I had written these notes, I saw that the distinguished Freindaller, in his recent edition of this fragment, judged that the passage should be interpreted as meaning that Mark had attended Peter’s discourses. Yet he afterwards says:

> “Perhaps someone might form the opinion that Mark had associated with Christ and later committed to writing those things at which he himself had been present, and that this is what the author of the fragment meant by those words. But the most ancient presbyter Aristion expressly denies this in Papias; nor is it permissible to confuse Mark the evangelist with that other John Mark who is mentioned in chapter XII of the Acts of the Apostles. With regard to the latter, however, there might appear to be some ground for holding such an opinion.”

Thus Freindaller.

Nevertheless, whatever conclusion is reached concerning Mark’s discipleship or concerning John Mark, it may still be that the author of the fragment actually wrote something of this sort:

> Mark, the disciple and interpreter of Peter, set in order the deeds done by the Lord—according to what he had heard Peter relate—at which he himself nevertheless had been present, and thus committed them to writing.

(Up to this point I have reproduced Jerome’s words, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 8.)

Besides John the presbyter in Papias, Irenaeus, Clement of Alexandria, Origen, Eusebius, and Epiphanius say the same thing about Peter and Mark. Tertullian likewise says in book IV *Against Marcion*, chapter 5:

> What Mark published is affirmed to belong to Peter, whose interpreter Mark was.

Furthermore, Eusebius, book III of the *History*, chapter 24, relates that this Gospel was approved by the apostle John. As for Eusebius’s statements about Mark’s Gospel in book II of the *History*, chapter 15, and book IV, chapter 14—which in both places are taken from one and the same Clement, if indeed those *Hypotyposes*, which contained at least many frivolous and absurd things, were Clement’s—they seem to me to be reconciled and interpreted in the following manner. The Romans asked Mark, who had long been Peter’s follower, to write down the things Peter had said and afterward to communicate them to them. When Peter learned of this request, he neither prohibited it from being done nor encouraged its execution. But when the work had been completed and Peter learned that the Gospel had been composed, he willingly approved the book by his own authority so that it might thereafter be read in the churches.

For the rest, I noted above, in connection with the Fragments of Papias, vol. I, p. 36, how highly the testimony concerning Mark’s Gospel, which Papias received from the lips of John the presbyter, ought to be valued. Papias was also the first of all writers expressly to mention Saint Matthew’s Gospel.

**And thus committed it to writing.** That is, he committed it to letters, or composed it.

**Book according to Luke.** Or should this be the nominative, “The book according to Luke”? Freindaller likewise restored *according to* [*secundum*], and rightly observed that the antiquity of this inscription or title of the Gospels is demonstrated by the fragment.]

**I. . . . . AT WHICH**, nevertheless, he was present, and thus committed it to writing. Third, [Col. 0174C] the Gospel book according to [Note: [Col. 0173C] Perhaps, “The book according to.” Routh.] Luke. This Luke, a physician, [Col. 0175A]

[Note: [Col. 0175D] **When Paul had taken him along with himself, as though a student of law, according to, he composed it under his own name from opinion.** The separating strokes—the lines after the words *according to*, *had taken along*, *his own*, and *had written* (*concriset*)—were added by Freindaller and indicate my suspicion that words have been omitted in gaps. The grammatical errors are *eo* for *eum*, *numeni* for *nomine*, and *conscrisset* for *conscripsisset*. The following proposition, which would complete the sentence, is entirely missing.

But how is this passage to be explained? In Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book II, chapter 8, after mentioning the Gospels of Mark and Matthew, Irenaeus writes:

> Luke also, the follower of Paul, committed to writing the Gospel preached by Paul.

Might our fragmentary author perhaps have intended to say the same thing—namely, that Luke, in his own name, gave the Gospel deeds preached by Paul written form, according to the opinion of most writers, for example Irenaeus? The ancients commonly reported that Luke was a physician, and some also said that he was a painter. Finally, Callistus Nicephorus relates a great many things about him in the *Historical Breviary*, book II, chapter 45. But I do not remember ever reading anywhere that he was also a student of law and that, in that capacity, he was attached to Paul as a companion, as the cited passage of the fragment says. Perhaps the Apostle did this so that, with a legal expert as his associate, he might obtain easier access either to learned men or to magistrates.

Above all, however, the genuine meaning of the added word *according to* [*secundum*] is difficult to divine. Does it mean “on a second occasion”? The resulting interpretation would then be that after Paul had associated Luke with himself a second time as a legal expert, Luke wrote this Gospel. Or has some other word, either preceding or following this expression, been lost? I think this last possibility comes closest to the truth. Thus Freindaller.

The passage is exceedingly corrupt, but perhaps it should be cleansed as follows:

> When Paul had taken him along with himself as one also devoted to law [καὶ τοῦ δικαίου, “and to justice”], he composed it under his own name in order [καθεξῆς σοι γράψαι, Saint Luke 1:3, “to write to you in order” in the Vulgate translation; see also below, where it is said of John that “he professes himself the writer, in order, of all the Lord’s wonders”].

Many ancient writers handed down that Luke, Paul’s follower, committed to writing the Gospel preached by Paul, including Irenaeus, book III *Against Heresies*, chapter 1, Origen, Eusebius, and Jerome. “For they are also accustomed to ascribe Luke’s arrangement to Paul,” says Tertullian, *Against Marcion* 4.5, wisely adding that what disciples published could be regarded as belonging to their teachers.

As for the words “also devoted to law,” it may be that some comparison is made here between jurisprudence—the knowledge of what is equitable and good—and the medical art that Luke practiced. Certainly the beginning of the *Commentary on the Deeds of Luke*, first published by Combefis in his *Supplement to the Fathers*, tends to confirm the integrity of the words. There the Metaphrast says:

> “Although a certain divine man, wise in divine matters, lays down that the memory of a righteous man should be celebrated with praises” [Εἰ καὶ δικαίῳ μνήμη μετ᾽ ἐγκωμίων τελεῖσθαι, θεῖός τις ἀνὴρ καὶ σοφὸς τὰ θεῖα νομοθετεῖ] (Prov. 10:7), “how great a tribute of praise, then, ought to be offered to the Apostle? For RIGHTEOUSNESS [Ἡ ΔΙΚΑΙΟΣΥΝΗ] made him both worthy of the apostolate and worthy TO APPEAR BELOVED TO THE PREEMINENT PAUL [ΤΟΥ ΑΓΑΠΗΤΟΝ ΟΦΘΗΝΑΙ Τῼ ΠΑΥΛῼ, διαφέροντος].”

One may add that the ancient Glosses have δίκαιον, “law,” “just.”

My emendation of *secum* (“with himself”) for *secundum* (“according to”) may perhaps be confirmed from Acts 15:37: “But Barnabas wished to take along with them [*secum assumere*] also John, who was surnamed Mark.”

Concerning the restoration of *nomine* for *numeni*, it should be noted that the author writes a little below: “John should describe everything under his own name.”

**Yet he himself did not see the Lord**, etc. See what I noted a little above concerning this matter.

**Committed it to writing.** Perhaps a semicolon, as I have supplied, should replace the full stop; for it should not be supposed, with Freindaller, that something is missing here.

**Thus also from the birth of John he will begin to speak.** A scribal error for “he begins.” Freindaller.

The earlier chapters of Luke’s Gospel, which heretics both ancient and modern have eagerly sought to deny to him, are meanwhile confirmed by this. It is also worthy of note that this same portion of the Gospel was acknowledged not only by all the writers whom I shall mention here—Justin Martyr, Irenaeus, Clement of Alexandria, Tertullian, Julius Africanus, Origen, Cyprian, Novatian, the author of the *Computation concerning Passover*, Victorinus, and Peter [Col. 0177A] of Alexandria in Canon V—but also, during Hadrian’s reign, by Celsus in Origen, book II, chapter 32, and, in the middle of the third century, by the anti-Trinitarians, according to Novatian in his book *On the Trinity*, chapter 24. Add what Eusebius reports from other writers: Luke’s Gospel itself, together with the other two Gospels, was approved by the apostle John. See book III of the *History*, chapter 24.]

after Christ’s ascension, when Paul had taken him [Note: [Col. 0175A] *Him*, as Freindaller has already restored.] along with himself as though [Note: [Col. 0175A] Perhaps “also.” Routh.] a student of law, according to, under his own name [Col. 0176A] from opinion he wrote [Note: [Col. 0176A] Perhaps: “had taken him along with himself; under his own name he composed it in order.” Routh.]. Yet he himself did not see the Lord in the flesh; and, according as he was able to ascertain matters, so also [Col. 0177A]

[Note: [Col. 0177A] **Of the Gospels.** Freindaller says that one should read “Gospel,” or rather “Gospel book,” as above.

**From the disciples**, ἐκ τῶν μαθητῶν; see also below. Perhaps immediately afterward one should read: “He, when his fellow disciples and bishops exhorted him,” etc., since the pronoun *he* [*is*] appears to have been absorbed by the preceding word.

Clement of Alexandria confirms this in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* VI.14. Clement had written in his *Hypotyposes* that John, the last of all the evangelists, seeing that the matters pertaining to Christ’s body had been handed down in the other Gospels, was himself inspired by the divine Spirit and composed a spiritual Gospel at the request of his intimate associates. Eusebius himself likewise relates in the passage just cited, book III of the *History*, chapter 24, that after approving the other Gospels, John, when requested, handed down in his Gospel the deeds done by Christ before the Baptist’s imprisonment. Thus Clement and Eusebius.

Victorinus, who flourished toward the end of the third century, comes very close to this account. In the commentary attributed to him on the Apocalypse, p. 1253, in vol. I of the Paris *Library of the Fathers*, he writes concerning the apostle John:

> For he also wrote the Gospel afterward. [Col. 0177C] When Valentinus, Cerinthus, Ebion, and the others of Satan’s school had spread throughout the world, they all came to him from the neighboring provinces and compelled him to write down his own testimony.

Epiphanius also, *Heresy* LI, no. 12, while mentioning this purpose of establishing Christ’s divine nature, continues:

> Therefore, afterward, the Holy Spirit compelled John—who declined to evangelize out of reverence and humility—to do so in his advanced old age. [Διὸ ὕστερον ἀναγκάζει τὸ ἅγιον πνεῦμα τὸν Ἰωάννην παραιτούμενον εὐαγγελίσασθαι δι᾽ εὐλάβειαν καὶ ταπεινοφροσύνην, ἐπὶ τῇ γεραλέᾳ αὐτοῦ ἡλικίᾳ.] … After he had spent many years in Asia, he was compelled to set forth the Gospel. [Μετὰ ἱκανὰ ἔτη τοῦ διατρῖψαι αὐτὸν ἐπὶ τῆς Ἀσίας, ἀναγκάζεται ἐκθέσθαι τὸ εὐαγγέλιον.]

P. 434, Petavius’s edition.

Jerome also says in *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 9, that John wrote the Gospel last of all, at the request of the bishops of Asia, against Cerinthus and other heretics, and especially against the then-rising doctrine of the Ebionites, who assert that Christ did not exist before Mary. Jerome has the same and more in the preface to his *Commentary on Matthew*, which is very closely related to this brief fragment. There he adds that ecclesiastical history relates that when John was compelled by the brethren to write, he answered that he would do so if all would proclaim a fast and pray to God in common. When this had been completed, filled with revelation, he poured forth that prologue coming from heaven:

> In the beginning was the Word; and the Word was with God; and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God.

As for the proclaimed fast, which some have regarded as suspect because no one before Jerome had mentioned it, this author, who preceded Jerome by nearly two centuries, has now at last become a witness to it for us. Indeed, Acts of the Apostles 14:22 provides an example of this apostolic custom observed in matters of great importance:

> And when they had appointed presbyters for them in each church and had prayed with fastings, they commended them to the Lord.

**Let us relate it to one another.** That is, whether or not the Gospel was to be written at their request.

**That same night it was revealed to Andrew**, etc. An extraordinary subject for the narrative. Saint Jerome relates something similar concerning John’s Gospel; and Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book III, chapter 24, is no less worthy of reading on this matter. The one feature found nowhere else, however, is Saint Andrew’s participation in this evangelical labor.

Did Andrew survive so long? According to Eusebius and Jerome, John wrote his Gospel very late, after his return from exile, under the emperors Nerva or Trajan. Yet that chronological indication is not so firmly attested that it leaves no room for another, shorter interval after John’s banishment to the island of Patmos under Domitian. Who will deny that Andrew could have survived into these years? The many very extensive journeys of this Apostle, which are recorded in the most ancient histories, provide reason to suppose that he reached an extremely advanced age, until Aegeas, proconsul of Achaia, condemned him to be suspended upon a cross. **Freindaller.**

That Andrew preached the Gospel in regions not far removed from Asia is attested by the competent authority Gregory of Nazianzus, *Oration* XXV, p. 438, Paris edition, where he says that Epirus was the province assigned to this Apostle. Jerome further relates, chapter 7 of *On Illustrious Men*, that Saint Luke’s bones were transferred to Constantinople together with the relics of the apostle Andrew in the twentieth year of Constantius. On this passage Fabricius noted from Philostorgius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book III, chapter 2, that the relics of Saints Andrew and Luke were transferred from Achaia.

**John should describe everything under his own name.** Clearly “John.” **Freindaller.**

Concerning this divine Gospel, it is worthy of note that words drawn from it appear to have been cited by Ignatius at the beginning of the Church’s second century, in the *Epistle to the Philadelphians*, § 7. Papias relates that the same was done by presbyters who had been disciples of the Apostles—or at least Irenaeus himself does so in book V, the final chapter, *Against Heresies*. Likewise, in two passages of Celsus preserved by Origen, book II, chapters 37 and 54, John’s Gospel is either indicated or cited during Hadrian’s reign. Add Justin Martyr, who in the middle of the second century cites the same Gospel in his *Apology to Antoninus Pius*, Hadrian’s successor, § 61, p. 71, Benedictine edition. There is no need to proceed further in this matter.

**The beginnings are taught.** “Let it be seen,” says Tertullian, “whether the arrangement of the narratives varies”—that is, among the evangelists—“provided that they agree concerning the chief point of faith,” book IV *Against Marcion*, chapter 2. For I would be more inclined to think that the word *beginnings* [*principia*] means chief points or propositions, since everyone commonly speaks of being taught the principles or chief points of faith, rather than prologues or prefaces.
