Nevertheless, chapter 3 of the *Responses* attributed to Saint Polycarp by Victor, bishop of Capua, seems to suggest the contrary:

> The evangelists reasonably employ different beginnings, although their one and identical purpose in evangelizing is established. Matthew, writing to the Hebrews, traced the order of Christ’s genealogy in order to show that Christ descended from that lineage from which all the Prophets had sung that he would be born. John, however, established at Ephesus among those who, being of Gentile origin, were ignorant of the law, took the beginning of his Gospel from the cause of our redemption, etc., etc. Nothing contrary is therefore found where, though the writings are different, the same homeland is nevertheless reached.

P. 32 of the Appendix to the *Ignatian Writings*, edited by Ussher at London in 1647. These words attributed to Polycarp had first been transferred by Feuardentius, in his notes on Irenaeus, book III, chapter 3, from a very ancient Catena on the four Gospels.

Freindaller also notes:

> “This is indeed an outstanding testimony for posterity to the inspiration conferred upon these evangelical writers. Although they employed different beginnings in developing their histories, they were nevertheless directed so harmoniously by their common mover—namely, the one sovereign Holy Spirit—that almost all the principal deeds are found recorded without discordance in each of their books. The author lists them in such an order that he reduces everything to the history of the birth of Jesus Christ, his Passion, his Resurrection, his association with the disciples—namely, after the Resurrection—and his twofold advent, as the principal heads.”

Thus Freindaller.

Meanwhile, as I think, Saint Jerome speaks in agreement with the author of this Fragment on the Canon of the New Testament when he writes in his *Letter to Pammachius*, concerning the best method of translation: “Diversity of expression agrees in the unity of the Spirit”; p. 373, Froben edition.]

(Luke, chapter 1) begins [Note: [Col. 0177A] Freindaller restored “begins.”] to speak from the birth of John. Of the fourth of the Gospels [Note: [Col. 0177A] Perhaps: “Fourth, the Gospel.” Routh.], John, one of the disciples. When his fellow disciples and bishops exhorted him [Note: [Col. 0178A] Perhaps: “He, when they exhorted him.” Routh.], he said:

> Fast together with me for three days beginning today, and let us relate to one another whatever shall have been revealed to each.

That same night it was revealed to Andrew, one of the Apostles, that, after all had reviewed it, John [Note: [Col. 0178A] “John.” Freindaller.] should describe everything under his own name. And therefore, although different beginnings are taught in the individual books of the Gospels, [Col. 0179A]

[Note: [Col. 0179B] **Of the faith.** Correction: “faith.” **Freindaller.**

**Sovereign.** Perhaps it had been written in Greek. The Philoxenian gloss is ἡγεμονικόν, “sovereign” or “principal.”

**Concerning the association.** The word “Lord” appears to have fallen out.

**First, despised in humility, which ro—.** Freindaller says, “This cannot be restored even by conjecture”; nor do I see any basis for supplying the passage. One might nevertheless conjecturally read either “which was prophesied,” since this verb was sometimes employed by ecclesiastical writers, or “which was fulfilled” [ἐπληρώθη]. The latter word occurs below, if that is of any relevance.

Read further Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, chapter 21:

> For since two advents of his were signified—the first, which has already been accomplished in the humility of the human condition; the second, which threatens at the close of the age in the sublimity of revealed divinity—they did not understand the first, but, hoping for the second because it had been more plainly foretold, regarded it as the only one.

That is, the Jews.

Cyprian imitated this passage of Tertullian when, not far from the end of his work *On the Vanity of Idols*, he wrote:

> But since his twofold advent was signified—one in which he would discharge the role and furnish the example of a man, the other in which he would confess himself God—they failed to understand the first advent, which preceded hidden in the Passion, and believe in only one, which will be manifested in power.

Thus Cyprian. Compare also what his teacher Tertullian wrote in the final chapter of his book *Against the Jews*.

**Second, splendid in royal power.** Correction: “second … splendid.”

**So steadfastly.** That is, so confidently and assertively. Ancient Glosses: *constanter*, εὐσταθῶς, θαρρούντως, “steadfastly, confidently.”

**Saying in himself.** I had conjectured, as did Freindaller, that *concerning* [*de*] should be restored for *in*. But the words may perhaps mean the same as Tertullian’s statement in *On Modesty*, chapter 18:

> For the Apostle also laid this down in his own person.

For after affirming that Christ came for this purpose, to save sinners, of whom he himself had been the first, what does he add?

> “And I obtained mercy, because I acted ignorantly in unbelief” (1 Tim. 1).

Compare the anonymous author *On Rebaptism*:

> … and therefore his disciples believe that he would furnish eternal life to them in no other way unless he had first joined this temporal life with that eternal life in himself.

P. 359 of the Benedictine edition of Saint Cyprian’s works.

**But a hearer.** Perhaps one should read, “himself both a hearer.”

**In order.** That is, “orderly,” as better authors customarily write. Yet just as this author employed a scarcely sound expression here, so too did Tertullian, *On the Shows*, chapter 5; Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 9; Optatus, *On the Donatist Schism*, book III, pp. 62 and 64 of Du Pin’s edition; and other writers.

For the rest, Freindaller says:

> “We are not without indications that John’s Epistles are later than his Gospel, and that the author of our fragment, perhaps relying upon an ancient tradition, used verses 1–4 of the First Epistle to confirm the authority of that Gospel, insofar as the Apostle himself in these words referred to the Gospel written by him. This could indeed have happened in precisely this way, although the words ταῦτα ἀπαγγέλλομαι ὑμῖν, ‘these things I proclaim to you,’ can equally be understood of the Gospel that had been preached.”

**But the Acts of all the Apostles were written in one book. Luke compiled them, most excellent Theophilus, because**, etc. Freindaller says:

> “Who does not see the numerous gaps caused by corruption of the sense in this passage? But what remedy is there for this evil?”

Thus Freindaller. Perhaps, however, either the word *were* should be deleted, or the word *them* should be inserted after *excellently*; likewise, *to Theophilus* should be written instead of *O Theophilus*.

Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 7, following Eusebius, has a similar account concerning Luke:

> He wrote the Gospel as he had heard it, but composed the Acts of the Apostles as he had seen them.

Moreover, since Polycarp, a disciple of the apostle John, cited this sacred book in so many words in his Epistle, § 1—compare also § 6—it was accepted and ascribed to Luke before the Council of Nicaea by Irenaeus, Clement of Alexandria, Tertullian, and Origen. Of these, Irenaeus drew solely from this book his proofs of the teaching of those Apostles who did not write Gospels, book III, chapter 12. Tertullian also says:

> Those who do not receive this Scripture cannot belong to the Holy Spirit, since they are unable to acknowledge that the Holy Spirit was sent to the disciples; nor can they defend the Church, since they have no means of proving when and from what beginnings this body was established.

*On the Prescription of Heretics*, chapter 22.

Furthermore, this book—although its author is not named—is cited as sacred by the churches of Lyons and Vienne, by Polycrates, by the author writing against the Cataphrygians, by Firmilian, Cyprian, and his deacon Pontius, as well as by the author of the *Computation concerning Passover*, Victorinus, and Lactantius; and Eusebius placed it “among the acknowledged books” [ἐν τοῖς ὁμολογουμένοις].

**Just as, separately, he clearly declares Peter’s passion to the Father, but Paul’s completion**, etc. But how are the words that immediately follow to be explained?

**And separately [*semote*] he clearly declares Peter’s passion.** Perhaps these words indicate Peter’s imprisonment and miraculous deliverance (Acts 12); for these could in every respect be regarded as a kind of prelude to Peter’s impending martyrdom.

**But Paul’s journey from the city as he set out for Spain.** The Acts in our Bibles are entirely silent about this journey of Paul from Rome to Spain. But the unquestionably mutilated passage prevents us from knowing whether this reference inserted there pertains to the Acts of the Apostles or rather to another book. Nevertheless, these words assure us that Paul departed from the city of Rome for Spain, undoubtedly after he had been acquitted by Nero—that is, after the first imprisonment whose history is read in the final chapter of Acts. Was it perhaps our fragmentary author’s intention to indicate that the book of Acts ended with this event, just as it was designated as beginning with the words, “Most excellent Theophilus”? **Freindaller.**

Perhaps instead of *semote* one should read *semota*, “separate things,” so that the word is understood of narratives placed separately and apart—that is, elsewhere than in the Acts of the Apostles. The passage would consequently be restored as follows:

> Just as separate writings clearly declare Peter’s passion—namely Saint John 21:18–19—and also Paul’s journey from the city as he set out for Spain.

Concerning this journey, the Apostle writes in his Epistle to the Romans, chapter 15, verse 24:

> “When I travel to Spain, I shall come to you” [ὡς ἐὰν πορεύωμαι εἰς τὴν Σπανίαν, ἐλεύσομαι πρὸς ὑμᾶς];

and again in verse 28:

> “Therefore, when I have completed this and have securely delivered this fruit to them, I shall depart through you for Spain” [τοῦτο οὖν ἐπιτελέσας, καὶ σφραγισάμενος αὐτοῖς τὸν καρπὸν τοῦτον, ἀπελεύσομαι δι᾽ ὑμῶν εἰς τὴν Σπανίαν].

A certain scholium published by the distinguished Matthaei at the final chapter of Acts in his edition pertains to this:

> After the two-year period mentioned in verse 30, Paul went to Spain and preached; and after returning to Rome, he suffered martyrdom. [Μετὰ τὴν διετίαν εἰς Σπανίαν ἀπελθὼν ἐκήρυξε, καὶ ὑποστρέψας εἰς Ῥώμην ἐμαρτύρησεν.] He himself wrote to the Romans: “I am hastening to Spain, and I hope to see you as I pass through”; and to Timothy: “At my first defense no one stood with me.” [Αὐτὸς Ῥωμαίοις ἔγραψεν· Εἰς Σπανίαν ἐπείγομαι, καὶ ἐλπίζω διαπορευόμενος θεάσασθαι ὑμᾶς· καὶ πρὸς Τιμόθεον· Ἐν τῇ πρώτῃ μου ἀπολογίᾳ οὐδείς μοι συμπαρεγένετο.] It should be known that Luke records the affairs of the blessed Paul in the Acts of the Apostles only up to this point, since he wrote the book at that time and had scarcely any knowledge of the subsequent events. Nor did he include Paul’s martyrdom in the book; for Luke and Aristarchus left him there and departed. [Ἰστέον δὲ ὅτι μέχρι τούτου ἱστορεῖ Λουκᾶς τὰ περὶ τὸν μακάριον Παῦλον ἐν ταῖς Πράξεσι τῶν ἀποστόλων, κατ᾽ ἐκεῖνο καιροῦ τὸ βιβλίον συγγραψάμενος, καὶ τὰ καθεξῆς ἥκιστα γινώσκων· οὐδὲ τὸ μαρτύριον τούτου ἐγκατέθετο τῇ βίβλῳ, καταλιπόντες γὰρ αὐτὸν ἐκεῖσε Λουκᾶς τε καὶ Ἀρίσταρχος ἐξῆλθον.]

P. 436.

The same learned man observed that the latter words, or second scholium, beginning “It should be known,” etc. [Ἰστέον δὲ κ.τ.λ.], are also presented by Oecumenius in his *Commentary*, p. 197. Nevertheless, concerning Saint Paul’s journey to Spain, Samuel Basnage’s *Historical-Critical Exercises*, pp. 511–516, deserve comparison.]

there is nevertheless no difference for the faith [Note: [Col. 0179A] “Faith,” Freindaller.] of believers, since by one sovereign Spirit everything has been declared in all of them concerning the birth, the Passion, the Resurrection, the association [Note: [Col. 0179A] Perhaps “of the Lord” should be added. Routh.] with his disciples, and his twofold advent: the first, despised in humility, which was pro— . . . . . . . . . [Note: [Col. 0179A] Perhaps, “which was prophesied.” See the note. Routh.]; the second [Note: [Col. 0179A] Perhaps, “secondly.” Routh.], splendid in royal power [Note: [Col. 0179A] Perhaps, “splendidly.” Routh.], which is yet to be.

What wonder, then, if John so steadfastly presents each matter also in his Epistles, saying of himself (1 John 1:1–4): [Col. 0180A]

> What we have seen with our eyes, and heard with our ears, and our hands have touched, these things we have written.

For in this way he professes himself not only an eyewitness but [Note: [Col. 0180A] Perhaps, “himself both.” Routh.] also a hearer, and also the writer, in order, of all the Lord’s wonders.

The Acts of all the Apostles, however, were written in a single book. Luke compiled them for the most excellent Theophilus [Note: [Col. 0180A] “They were written. Luke,” in the editions of Kirchnoser, perhaps through a typographical error. Editors. Perhaps: “Luke compiled them very well for Theophilus.” Routh.] (Acts 1:1), because the individual events took place in his presence; as he also plainly shows by omitting [Note: [Col. 0180A] Perhaps *semota*, “having been omitted.” Routh.] (John 21:18–19) Peter’s passion [Col. 0181A] [Note: [Col. 0181A] Perhaps “they indicate.” Routh.] and Paul’s departure from the city as he set out for Spain [Note: [Col. 0181A] Freindaller restored “and also” in place of “but.”] (Rom. 15:24, 28).

[Note: [Col. 0181D] “But the Epistle of Paul—which ones, from what place, or for what reason they were sent—he himself makes clear to those wishing to understand.” Freindaller corrects this, as I later saw, to “the epistles,” “sent,” “to those wishing,” and “they themselves.” I myself would prefer to restore “he makes clear” in place of “they make clear,” on account of the verb “forbidding” in what follows.

“A schism of heresy.” A rather unusual verbal expression. [Col. 0182B] In Greek, σχίσμα τῆς αἱρέσεως, “a schism of the heresy.” Shortly afterward, Freindaller restored “Galatians,” which is indeed read below, in place of “Callactians.”

“In the order of the Scriptures.” That is, unless I am mistaken, he interpreted the Scriptures of the Old Testament in their order, one after another. Freindaller says: “The words ‘in the order of the Scriptures’ do not appear to suggest anything other than that Paul here advanced his arguments from the old Law in order to establish the new, and subordinated the former to the latter in due order.”

“Beginning.” That is, ἡ ἀρχή, “the beginning, foundation.”

“Following the order of his predecessor John.” This is ineptly written, if the author means—as is nevertheless far from certain—that Paul imitated the Apocalypse; for, as Stosch plausibly determined in his *Commentary on the Canon of the Books of the New Testament*, chapter V, §62, the Apocalypse was published under Domitian and must not be carried back to the time of Claudius or [Col. 0182C] Nero—although, as I have said, some distinguished men have indeed maintained this. Freindaller further says that he believes John was called Paul’s predecessor by the author “because he preceded him in his calling to the apostolate; and that this designation corresponds in meaning to the other term, ‘Elder,’ which John himself employed in his epistles. That interpretation, certainly not discordant with the truth, plainly restores the order of the whole passage, since the comparison between the Pauline and Apocalyptic epistles now concerns not the date of each group, but only the number seven.”

“First . . . second,” etc., etc. Perhaps one should read “firstly . . . secondly,” and so thereafter.

*Correbtione*. Thus in the old manner for *correptione*, “correction.”

“Nevertheless, it is recognized that there is one Church throughout the whole world.” Tertullian, *On the Prescription of Heretics*, chapter 20: “Every kind must necessarily be classified according to its origin. Accordingly, so many and such great churches are one: that first Church from the Apostles, from which all derive. [Col. 0182D] Thus all are first, and all are apostolic, while they are one; all demonstrate unity.”

“Although he writes to seven churches,” etc. Stosch, in the work cited a little above, §59: “I seem to myself to have found in this yet another trace of the second century, or of the beginning of the third: the author of the fragment, in imitation of John’s epistles to the seven churches of Asia, similarly reduces to seven the number of churches to which the apostle Paul wrote epistles. For one may see from Cyprian, book I of the *Testimonies against the Jews*, chapter 20, that at the beginning of the third century there were people who sought some mystery in this. Likewise, Cyprian writes, in the first book of *Kings*: ‘The barren woman bore seven, and she who had very many children grew weak. The seven sons, however, are the seven churches. Hence Paul also wrote to seven churches, and the Apocalypse sets forth seven churches, so that the number seven might be preserved: like the seven days in which God made the world, and like the seven angels [Col. 0183A] who stand before the face of God.’” See also the same Cyprian’s *Exhortation to Martyrdom*, p. 270, Benedictine edition. “Nor perhaps will the thought be inept if we say that the reason why doubts raised against the Epistle to the Hebrews gained weight among some of the ancients was this alleged mystery of the number seven, which they wished by every means to preserve intact with respect to the churches to which Paul [Col. 0183B] wrote. Hence also others, who did not doubt the Epistle to the Hebrews, preferred to say that Paul wrote twice seven epistles rather than that he wrote fourteen.” Thus Stosch.

Freindaller says that “perhaps the Epistle to the Hebrews is found to have been omitted for this reason, lest the excess offend against that number. He could, moreover, rightly leave it unmentioned here even if he attributed it to Paul, because the Hebrews, or Jewish Christians, to whom it was sent were indeed intermingled with the individual communities, but did not constitute a distinct community.” Thus he argued, and plausibly.

But more on this Epistle below. Freindaller also rightly observed that by the second century the Apocalyptic epistles were already regarded as catholic—that is, as epistles directed to the universal (ὅλην, “whole”) Church. The Church is called “sevenfold” by Optatus in book II of *On the Donatist Schism*, chapter 3, p. 93, Dupin’s edition. But, to omit the passages of other ancient writers [Col. 0183C] who, with Augustine in book VII of *The City of God*, chapter 4, maintain that the perfection of the universal Church was signified by the number seven, I shall note only this: Jesus Christ, who undoubtedly abides perpetually in the midst of all the churches, was seen by John in the Apocalypse, chapter 1, verse 13, in the midst of seven lampstands—that is, churches.

I must now present words of Victorinus very closely related to this passage of our fragment, which I have taken from the commentary on the Apocalypse attributed to him: “Paul taught that throughout the whole world all seven churches—and the seven that are named—are one catholic Church. And first, indeed, so that he too might preserve the pattern of seven churches, he did not exceed the number. But he wrote to the Romans, to the Corinthians, to the Galatians, to the Ephesians, to the Thessalonians, to the Philippians, and to the Colossians. Afterward he wrote to individual persons, so that he would not exceed the measure of seven churches. And, condensing his preaching into a brief statement, he says thus to Timothy: ‘That you may know how you ought to conduct yourself in the Church of the living God’ (1 Tim. 3:15).” Thus [Col. 0183D] Victorinus, chapter 1.

Finally, since this number seven was regarded among the ancient Pythagoreans as both perfect and especially suited to religion—whence the *Etymologicum Magnum*: Ἑπτὰς, ἀπὸ τοῦ σέβω, σεπτάς τις οὖσα, ὡς θεία, καὶ ἀμήτωρ, καὶ πάρθενος, “*Heptas* (‘seven’), from *sebō* (‘I revere’), being something august, as divine, motherless, and virgin”—Glycas, pursuing similar ideas in his *Annals*, maintains that the Holy Spirit descended from heaven on the tenth day after Christ had risen because the number ten is also perfect; part 3, p. 225, Labbe’s edition.]

But the Epistles of Paul—which ones they are, from what place, or for what reason they were sent—he himself makes clear to those wishing to understand [Note: [Col. 0181A] “Epistles,” Freindaller.] [Note: [Col. 0181A] “Sent,” Freindaller.] [Note: [Col. 0181B] “To those wishing,” Freindaller.] [Note: [Col. 0181B] Routh omitted “to understand” from the text but restored it in a note. Editors.] [Note: [Col. 0182A] Perhaps “he makes clear.” Routh.]: first of all, to the Corinthians, forbidding a schism of heresy; next, to the Callactians [Note: [Col. 0182A] “Galatians,” Freindaller.] concerning circumcision; and to the Romans he wrote at greater length, setting forth in due order the Scriptures, yet also intimating that Christ is their beginning. It is necessary for us to discuss each of these individually, [Col. 0182A] since the blessed apostle Paul himself, following the order of his predecessor John, writes by name to no more than seven Churches, in the following order: to the Corinthians, first [Note: [Col. 0182A] Perhaps “firstly,” and in what follows “secondly,” and so thereafter. Routh.—More correctly, the word “Epistle” should be understood. Editors.]; to the Ephesians, second; to the Philippians, third; to the Colossians, fourth; to the Galatians, fifth; to the Thessalonians [Note: [Col. 0182B] “Thessalonians” here and below. Freindaller.], sixth; to the Romans, seventh. Yet although the Epistle is repeated to the Corinthians and Thessalonians by way of correction [Note: [Col. 0182B] “Correction,” Kirchoser.], it is nevertheless recognized that there is one Church spread throughout the whole world [Note: [Col. 0182B] “It is discerned,” Freindaller.]. For John too, in the Apocalypse, although he writes to seven Churches (Rev. 1–2), [Col. 0183A] nevertheless speaks to them all.

[Note: [Col. 0183D] “Two.” “Two” must be restored with Freindaller. It should similarly be corrected a little below.

“They have been sanctified in the ordering of ecclesiastical discipline.” Tertullian says at the end of the last book *Against Marcion*: “This Epistle alone—namely, that to the Philippians—was aided by its own brevity, so that it escaped Marcion’s falsifying hands. Yet I marvel that he accepted a letter written to one man, Philemon, but rejected the two to Timothy and the one to Titus, composed concerning ecclesiastical order.” Thus he. Note that at least one of these epistles was sent to several people.

Moreover, to speak of all the Pauline epistles: since all his epistles were either written or signed by Paul’s own hand (see Gal. 6:11 and 2 Thess. 3:18), and most of them were sent to very populous churches that continued flourishing for a long time afterward, in which it was customary for those very epistles to be read aloud (compare Col. 4:16 with the fragments of Dionysius of Corinth, p. 168, vol. I of the *Reliquiae*), [Col. 0184A] and since Paul [Col. 0184B] himself later visited most of those same churches, there can be no doubt that no other author—not even among more recent writers who have already died—can have his own work attributed to him on weightier and more certain evidence. Add that, from apostolic times onward, all the Fathers who survive have cited these thirteen epistles as witnesses and a rule of faith and religion. The matter of Paul’s Epistle to the Hebrews, which the author of the fragment omits, must be discussed presently.

“To the Laodiceans, another to the Alexandrians.” Perhaps it should be written: “To the Laodiceans one, another to the Alexandrians.”

Stosch writes as follows in *On the Canon of the Books of the New Testament*, §56: “First, then, there is mentioned a certain epistle of Paul to the Laodiceans, which pertains to the heresy of Marcion. Now it is established from Tertullian, *Against Marcion*, book V, chapters 11 and 17, and Epiphanius, *Heresy* XLII, that Marcion, who disseminated his heresy in the middle of the second century, had in his canon some epistle to the Laodiceans. And although it should almost be inferred from Tertullian’s words that it differed from the Epistle to the Ephesians only [Col. 0184C] in title, nevertheless, from the testimony of Epiphanius and from the fact that it was almost invariably Marcion’s custom to corrupt the genuine writings of the Apostles, there can scarcely be any doubt that Marcion’s epistle to the Laodiceans differed from Paul’s genuine Epistle to the Ephesians, and that it is the one intended by the author of the fragment.

“Joined to this Epistle to the Laodiceans is another of Paul to the Alexandrians, of which, says the celebrated Muratori, I do not know whether anyone else has made mention. Nor have I been able to find any mention of it among the ancients. It has therefore either completely perished, or perhaps was mentioned by the ancients under another title, since it is certain that several titles were often given to one and the same apocryphal book. See the celebrated Beausobre’s *Dissertation on the Apocryphal Books of the New Testament*, §10; or perhaps it still lies somewhere unpublished. Kirsten certainly testifies that several epistles of Paul, still unknown to us, are found among the Arabs. See Fabricius, *Apocryphal Codex of the New Testament*, part II, p. 920.” Thus Stosch.

Jerome says at the end of chapter 5 of *On Illustrious Men*: “Some also read the Epistle to the Laodiceans, but it is rejected by everyone.” [Col. 0184D] Philastrius, however, has material concerning this epistle worthy of being presented here, in his *Heresy* LXXXIX: “Others, however, say that the Epistle to the Hebrews is by Luke the Evangelist; and that an Epistle to the Laodiceans was also written. And because some people with unsound opinions added certain things to it, it is therefore not read in the Church. And although it is read by some, nevertheless only thirteen Epistles of Paul himself are read publicly in the Church, and occasionally the Epistle to the Hebrews”; p. 169, Fabricius’s edition.

Meanwhile, a singular instance occurs in Abbot Ælfric’s treatise on the Old and New Testaments, composed in the time of Edgar, king of England: after Ælfric had placed each and every book of the New Testament in the canon of Scripture, he added to them only Paul’s Epistle to the Laodiceans. See p. 28, Lisle’s edition, 1623.

Finally, there exists a certain very brief epistle called Paul’s Epistle to the Laodiceans, but it differs from the ancient work and is pieced together from the other Pauline epistles; it was reprinted by Fabricius in the *Apocryphal Codex of the New Testament*, vol. II, p. 873.

“According to the heresy of Marcion.” In Greek, κατὰ τὴν αἵρεσιν τοῦ Μαρκίωνος, “according to the heresy of Marcion.” Ancient Glosses: “according to,” “toward,” κατά. [Col. 0185A]

“Here, moreover,” says Freindaller, “there occurs another spurious Epistle of Paul bearing the superscription ‘To the Alexandrians’; what judgment should be made concerning it was indeed unknown to Muratori himself, nor do I remember ever having encountered anything about a similar Epistle. Our author further records that these letters, both to the Laodiceans and to the Alexandrians, were fabricated for the sake of confirming the heresy of the Marcionites, with the result that a definite date can be assigned to their origin. What is more, Epiphanius’s [Col. 0185B] testimony also agrees with this, since in *Heresy* XLII he writes expressly that Marcion borrowed support from the Epistle to the Laodiceans in order to reinforce his errors.”]

But one Epistle to Philemon, one to Titus, and two to Timothy [Note: [Col. 0183A] “Two.” Freindaller.], written from affection and love, have nevertheless been sanctified in honor of the catholic Church, for the ordering of ecclesiastical discipline. [Col. 0184A] There is also in circulation an epistle to the Laodiceans, and another [Note: [Col. 0183A] Perhaps: “other epistles to the Laodiceans.” Routh.] to the Alexandrians, forged in Paul’s name for the heresy [Note: [Col. 0184A] Perhaps *haeresim*. Routh.] of Marcion, as well as several others, which cannot be received into [Col. 0185A] the catholic Church. For it is not fitting that gall be mixed with honey.

[Note: [Col. 0185B] “Cannot be received.” According to the form of the Greek expression, παραλαμβάνεσθαι οὐ δυνατόν ἐστι, “it is not possible for it to be received.” Freindaller wishes to restore “they cannot” in place of “it cannot.”

“For it is not fitting that gall be mixed with honey.” The elder mentioned by Irenaeus, p. 42, vol. I of the *Reliquiae*, employed a similar metaphor: “Plaster is badly mixed with the milk of God.”

“And two of the above-mentioned John.” Read “two,” as above at line 8.

Stosch writes as follows in *On the Canon of the Books of the New Testament*, §53: “I infer that the author of this fragment should be assigned to the end of the second century or the beginning of the third, because in it there occur quite a few statements concerning the books of the New Testament that conform perfectly to the opinions of certain Christians of that period. Namely:

“[Col. 0185C] I. In this canon of the sacred books, the Epistle to the Hebrews and the Epistle of James are omitted, and only two Epistles of the apostle John are mentioned. Now the clearest testimonies establish that, toward the end of the second century, both the Epistle to the Hebrews and that of James, and even John’s third Epistle, were not included in the canon by some. For, as regards the Epistle to the Hebrews, Stephen Gobarus, in Photius, *Library*, codex 232, testifies that Irenaeus and his disciple Hippolytus did not regard it as a genuine work of Paul: Ὅτι Ἱππόλυτος καὶ Εἰρηναιοῖς τὴν πρὸς Ἑβραῖους ἐπιστολὴν Παύλου, οὐκ ἐκείνου εἶναι φασίν, ‘Hippolytus and Irenaeus say that Paul’s Epistle to the Hebrews is not his.’ In the same work, codex 121, from Hippolytus’s book *Against Heresies*: Λέγει δὲ ἀλλά τέ τινα τῆς ἀκριβείας λειπόμενα, καὶ ὅτι ἡ πρὸς Ἑβραίους ἐπιστολὴ οὐκ ἔστι τοῦ ἀποστόλου Παύλου, ‘He also says certain other things deficient in accuracy, and that the Epistle to the Hebrews is not by the apostle Paul.’

“Concerning Gaius, the Roman presbyter, as Muratori already observed, Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VI, chapter 20, [Col. 0185D] likewise reports that, in his disputation against Proclus, a defender of the Cataphrygian heresy, he mentions only thirteen Epistles of the divine Apostle, not numbering among the rest the one inscribed to the Hebrews. What Origen thought of it, see above, §48”—where Stosch shows that Origen regarded this Epistle as a little work conveying Paul’s thought.

“That the Epistle of James, moreover, was not included in the canon by everyone at about the same time is attested by Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book II, chapter 23, at the end. Certainly very few of the earlier writers made mention either of this Epistle or of that of Jude, which is itself numbered among the seven catholic epistles. As for John’s third Epistle, it is established that it too was regarded as doubtful by some. Irenaeus certainly cites John’s first and second Epistles, but makes no mention of the third. See Lardner, *Credibility of the Gospel History*, part II, vol. I, chapter 17, pp. 301–302.” Thus Stosch.

[Col. 0186A] I. Concerning the Epistle to the Hebrews, however, I should like to add the following: Tertullian attributed it to Barnabas, not Paul, in *On Modesty*, chapter 20; Jerome also records this concerning Tertullian in *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 5. Nor had that Epistle been received into the Latin canon even in Jerome’s time. Among other passages, his Epistle to Dardanus, p. 69, Froben’s edition, should be consulted.

Nevertheless, it is not established that Irenaeus or his disciple Hippolytus, whom Stosch names above, cast this Epistle out of the number of sacred books, since, according to the testimony of [Col. 0186B] Eusebius, book V of the *History*, chapter 26, that same Irenaeus cited certain passages from it in his work *Various Discussions*. Origen too wrote commentaries on this Epistle.

Moreover, in the passage just cited, Jerome shows Dardanus that it was accepted as the Epistle of the apostle Paul by the churches of the East and by all writers in the Greek language. During my reading, I have certainly seen this done clearly and openly by the authors whom I shall name here, all of whom, except St. Peter, bishop of Alexandria, and Eusebius, lived before the end of the third century: namely, Clement of Alexandria—although the Epistle was also cited by Clement of Rome, who lived in the first century, in chapters 17 and 36; furthermore, by the ancient presbyter in the same Clement of Alexandria, whom I placed at p. 472, vol. I of the *Reliquiae*; by Origen, both elsewhere and in his *Epistle to Africanus*, chapter 9; by Dionysius of Alexandria; by the bishops of Antioch in their Epistle to Paul of Samosata, placed at pp. 473–474 of vol. II; by Peter of Alexandria [Col. 0186C] in his ninth Canon; and finally by Eusebius himself in *The Martyrs of Palestine*, chapter 11.

To Clement of Rome, who did not append Paul’s own name, should be added Pinytus in his Epistle to Dionysius of Corinth, p. 132, vol. I of the *Reliquiae*; Theognostus, head of the catechetical school in the city of Alexandria; St. Methodius, in the *Banquet of the Virgins*, pp. 90 and 96, Combefis’s edition; and Manes and Archelaus in the *Disputation*, chapters 5, 34, 41, and 53.

II. As regards the Epistle of James—which Origen, like that of Jude, omitted at least from his catalogue of the sacred books in Eusebius, book VI, chapter 25—I must point out that the words of Eusebius mentioned by Stosch are, in Greek, οὐ πολλοὶ τῶν παλαίων αὐτῆς ἐμνημόνευσαν, “not many of the ancients made mention of it.” Valesius translated them “very few of the earlier writers,” but scarcely accurately, although perhaps one might have spoken in that way even in Eusebius’s time. For, if there are any besides Irenaeus, book IV, chapter 16 or 30, there are few surviving writers earlier than Eusebius who expressly cited this Epistle; [Col. 0186D] nevertheless, some other surviving writers among them may allude to it, especially where passages of the Old Testament are quoted in it.

Cosmas Indicopleustes certainly reports, in *On the World*, book VII, p. 292, Montfaucon’s edition, that the Epistle of James was received by the Syrians; and that same Epistle always existed in the Syriac version, as did one other of the seven ἀντιλεγόμεναι γραφαί, “disputed Scriptures,” namely the Epistle to the Hebrews.

III. Finally, concerning the Third Epistle of St. John, I shall add the following. Clement did indeed comment on the first two Epistles of this apostle, as Cassiodorus testifies in book I of the *Divine Readings*, chapter 8; indeed, the *Adumbrations* on these two Epistles attributed to Clement of Alexandria still survive, but not on the third. Nevertheless, Eusebius, book VI of the *History*, chapter 14, reports that in the books of the Ὑποτυπώσεις, or *Outlines*, Clement composed a concise exposition of all the Scriptures of both Testaments, not even omitting those writings concerning which many were in doubt: the Epistle of Jude, that of Barnabas, and the remaining catholic Epistles. [Col. 0187A] Therefore Clement, if Eusebius is an accurate witness, wrote commentaries on John’s third Epistle just as he did on the Epistle of James.

However the matter stands, this at least must certainly be inferred from the fact that the same Clement, in book II of the *Stromata*, chapter 15, when citing John’s first Epistle—which everyone had received from the time of Polycarp onward—described it as ἐν τῇ μείζονι ἐπιστολῇ, “in the longer Epistle”: [Col. 0187B] at least that second Epistle, in Clement’s judgment, must be attributed to John the apostle, not to the presbyter, to whom many in antiquity, according to Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 9, and Eusebius, book III of the *History*, chapter 35, were accustomed to assign the two latter Epistles. Jerome himself, however, did not agree; for, as is clear from his Epistles to Paulinus, p. 9 of Froben’s edition, and to Evagrius, p. 334, he attributed both to John the apostle.

Meanwhile, I showed above, at the Seventh Council of Carthage, p. 166, vol. III of the *Reliquiae*, which writers before Cyprian’s time accepted the second Epistle. To these I shall now add Alexander of Alexandria, an author before the Council of Nicaea, who wrote in his Epistle preserved by Socrates, book I of the *History*, chapter 6.

It must, however, be admitted that I have encountered no pre-Nicene writer—perhaps because of the Epistle’s brevity—who cited the third Epistle, except one who, after mentioning it, also added either his own doubt or at least that of others concerning the γνησιότης, “genuineness,” of both this and the second Epistle. But enough of this.

[Col. 0187C] Meanwhile, how does it happen—and this is more surprising—that the author of this fragment is silent concerning the First Epistle of St. Peter? According to Eusebius, and according to Origen himself as quoted by Eusebius, it is reckoned among the ὁμολογούμεναι γραφαί, “acknowledged Scriptures”; that is, it was received by everyone, always, and everywhere. So many Fathers, from the time of Polycarp and Papias onward, cited it in their works. Both Stosch and Muratori pass over the matter in silence, leaving it entirely untouched.

I can scarcely think anyone would say that the Church in which this anonymous writer on the canon lived did not yet know St. Peter’s Epistle, for he flourished in the middle of the second century. The celebrated Freindaller does indeed say, as I now find: “The two Epistles of Peter are passed over here, although the first is already found to have been generally received in the author’s own time; likewise the Epistle of James, which could not have been unknown to an author living at Rome; and finally John’s third Epistle is left entirely unmentioned. But, on the one hand, it must be considered that we are dealing here with a fragment which in a great many places lacks completeness of sense, [Col. 0187D] and that for this very reason the question is still unresolved whether these portions of the Bible were mentioned in a preceding or following part of the text, and whether mention of them is missing today solely because of the mutilated condition of the work. On the other hand, it must not be concealed that not all the divine books were received in all churches at the same time, and that Eusebius himself individually numbers the Epistle of James, the Second of Peter, and the Third of John among the disputed writings.”

Thus he. Here I shall note only that Eusebius, who more than once calls the aforesaid books of Holy Scripture τοὺς ἀντιλεγομένους, “the disputed books,” adds γνωρίμους δ` οὖν ὅμως τοῖς πολλοῖς, “yet nevertheless known to most,” and ὅμως δὲ ἐν πλείσταις ἐκκλησίαις παρὰ πολλοῖς δεδημοσιευμένους, “nevertheless publicly circulated by many in most churches.”

However the matter stands, and for whatever reason St. Peter’s Epistle was omitted, the author certainly mentioned the Epistle of Jude, although everyone knows that Eusebius counted it among the ἀντιλεγόμεναι γραφαί, “disputed Scriptures.” In book II of the *History*, chapter 23, in the passage cited above by Stosch, Eusebius also says that not many of the earlier writers made mention of this Epistle.

[Col. 0188A] Among those few I have seen Tertullian, Clement of Alexandria, and Origen cite it as a book of Holy Scripture; perhaps also the Council of Antioch held against Paul of Samosata, and the author against Novatian, who at least repeats statements that Jude himself had made. To these writers must now at last be added the author of this fragment, who also confirms by his own approval, as you have seen, two further books among those same seven disputed books of Holy Scripture: the Apocalypse and the Second Epistle [Col. 0188B] of John.

Moreover—and this is more important—as I have already observed, this same writer has intruded no ὑποβολιμαῖον, “supposititious,” work into the canon of the New Testament except the Revelation of Peter, while at the same time recording the mark of νοθεία, “spuriousness,” which others had affixed to that book. Furthermore, this writer of ours has enumerated all the ὁμολογούμεναι γραφαί, “acknowledged Scriptures,” with only one omitted, namely that Epistle of St. Peter.]

[Col. 0186A] Certainly the Epistle of Jude and two of the above-mentioned John [Note: [Col. 0185A] “Two.” Freindaller.], [Col. 0187A] cannot be received into the catholic Church.

[Note: [Col. 0188B] “In the catholic.” In Greek, τῇ καθολικῇ, “in the catholic,” with the word ἐκκλησίᾳ, “Church,” understood, as sometimes happens. Examples occur both in Tertullian’s *On the Prescription of Heretics*, chapter 30, and frequently elsewhere in writers later than Tertullian, such as Optatus and Augustine. See also the notes on the fragments of St. Cornelius, p. 30, vol. III.

In the Theodosian Code too, book XVI, title II, *On Bishops*, law 4, the emperor Constantine has the expression “the most holy council of the catholic.” Likewise, in the *Code of the African Canons*, no. 109, the following occurs: “Likewise, if a bishop has been converted from the party of Donatus to the catholic,” etc.; the Greek translation reads: Ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ ἐὰν ἐπίσκοπος ἐκ τῶν τοῦ Δονάτου μερῶν πρὸς τὴν καθολικὴν ἐπιστρέψῃ, “Likewise, if a bishop from the party of Donatus should turn to the catholic,” [Col. 0188C] etc.

“Wisdom, written by the friends of Solomon . . . .” Since this work was included in the Version of the Seventy [the Septuagint], and was designated by the name *Wisdom* not only by Methodius—cited among the fragments of Melito, p. 128, vol. I—but also by Clement of Alexandria and others more ancient than Methodius, the earliest Christians, like our author, cited the same book at least as ecclesiastical and useful, although of uncertain origin and unknown to the Jewish canon.

Yet the statement of the fragment’s author that the book was composed by the friends of Solomon is certainly somewhat improbable, novel, and unheard of; according to Jerome’s testimony in the Preface to Proverbs, this book is nowhere found among the Hebrews; p. 26.

Meanwhile Freindaller observed: “By what reasoning the Book of Wisdom—unless perhaps a different work is meant here—obtained a place among the Scriptures of the New Covenant escapes the acuity of criticism. But the Psalms too are mentioned a little below in this fragment, although touched upon only in the most cursory fashion.”

“Apocalypse.” Perhaps *Apocalypses*, but Freindaller prefers to rewrite it as *Apocalypsim*.

“And only that of Peter do we receive, which some of our people do not wish to be read in the Church.” “These words,” says Muratori in the passage cited above, p. 853, “fit well with the time of Gaius. For Eusebius, book III, chapter 25, numbers the Apocalypse of Peter among the disputed books, but does not reject it as the offspring of heretics. According to the same witness, book VI, chapter 14, Clement of Alexandria also used this Apocalypse, just as he did the Epistle of Barnabas and the catholic Epistles. Sozomen likewise informs us, book VII, chapter 19, that this Apocalypse was still read once every year in certain churches of Palestine.”

Thus Muratori. In a certain catalogue of Holy Scriptures, first published by Cotelier in his *Judgment on the Epistle of St. Barnabas*, I see four other books mentioned outside the canonical books of the New Testament: the Epistle of Barnabas, the *Shepherd*, the *Acts of Paul*, and the *Revelation of Peter*. Eusebius, in the passage previously cited by Muratori, placed these same works—[Col. 0189A] with the addition of the book entitled *The Teaching of the Apostles*—after the acknowledged and disputed Scriptures, as books indeed νόθοι, “spurious,” while wholly omitting that immense heap of ψευδεπίγραφα, “falsely attributed writings,” composed by heretics.

Nevertheless, the brief passages translated from the *Apocalypse of Peter* in the *Eclogues* attributed to Clement of Alexandria are too frivolous for the book to possess even the slightest claim to reverence. See §§49–50, p. 207, Combefis’s *Latest Supplement to the Fathers*.

Perhaps, meanwhile, some may think that the relative *quas*, “which” in the plural, should be restored here in place of *quam*, “which” in the singular, so that the Apocalypse of John might also be included. It is well known that at that time there were some people unfavorably disposed toward this book. [Col. 0189B] The words concerning the *Shepherd* of Hermas that immediately follow persuade me that the subject here is reception by the Church among the divine Scriptures, not merely reading in sacred assemblies, as in the final canon of the Council of Laodicea, where the Apocalypse is omitted. Compare throughout the passage of Philastrius that I cited above.

I stated earlier, in connection with the fragments of Gaius, p. 16, vol. II, how many writers either older than Gaius the presbyter or at least of his own time accepted the book of the Apocalypse; I shall now append their names. They are Papias, Justin Martyr, the brethren of Vienne and Lyons together with Irenaeus, Melito, Theophilus of Antioch, Apollonius, Hippolytus, Tertullian, and Clement of Alexandria.

It is fitting to show from Clement’s little work entitled *Who Is the Rich Man That Shall Be Saved?* that this last Father attributed the Apocalypse to John the apostle. For in its final section it is reported that John the apostle, after the tyrant’s death, returned from the island of Patmos to Ephesus; and John, the author of the Apocalypse, himself mentions this very exile in chapter 1, verse 9.

[Col. 0189C] I omit the other writers down to Dionysius of Alexandria, who indeed attributed the book to John the presbyter rather than to the apostle, yet by no means excluded this divine work from the sacred books; see Eusebius, *History*, book VI, chapter 22. Indeed, in the fragment of his Epistle to Hermammon preserved by the same Eusebius, book VII, chapter 20, Dionysius cited words from it as from that prophetic and Θεόπνευστος, “divinely inspired,” book. Καὶ τοι Ἰωάννης, he says, ὁμοίως ἀποκαλύπτεται, etc., “And indeed John is similarly given a revelation,” etc.

“The *Shepherd*, however, was written very recently in our own times,” etc. Against the opinion of those who would have Hermas, the author of the book called the *Shepherd*, be the Hermas whom St. Paul mentions at the end of the Epistle to the Romans, chapter 16, verse 14—or at least an exceedingly ancient writer who lived before the destruction of Jerusalem—the celebrated Mosheim, in *On the Affairs of the Christians before Constantine the Great*, century I, §54, adduces an argument from the very ancient author of the poem *Against Marcion*, which is attributed to Tertullian. Near the end of book III are these lines:

> And now, in the ninth place, Hyginus received the chair;
>
> [Col. 0189D] Then after him came Pius, to whom Hermas was a brother by birth.

Angelic Shepherd, because he spoke the words delivered to him.

In this final verse Mosheim wishes to read *cui* (“whose”) in place of *quia* (“because”), while others have perhaps more appropriately printed *qui* (“who”). But, leaving this matter aside, the distinguished scholar continues:

> “It is unnecessary for me to cite the remaining passages of the ancients concerning Hermas, the brother of Pius, in order to show that they agree entirely with Tertullian and attribute the book of the *Shepherd* to him.”

(Mosheim has the *Liber Pontificalis* and the Martyrologies in mind.)

> “For good fortune brought forward for us, only a few years ago, a witness beyond exception and contemporary with our Hermas, who places it entirely beyond controversy that the *Shepherd* which we possess was composed in the second century by the brother of Pius, bishop of Rome. . . .” (See above, col. 172.)
>
> “In this fragment of great value, therefore, the following is written concerning Hermas: ‘But very recently, in our own times, in the city of Rome, Hermas composed the *Shepherd*, while his brother Pius, the bishop, was occupying the chair of the Church of the city of Rome.’ These words are unmistakable [Col. 0190A] and bring to an end every dispute among learned men concerning the age, place, and condition of Hermas. Other words no less worthy of notice follow, from which it is evident what place and rank Hermas formerly held in the Latin Church. He is excluded from the canon, or number, of the divine books—not, indeed, in very elegant or well-formed language, but nevertheless plainly and manifestly: ‘And therefore it ought indeed to be read, but it cannot be published to the people in the Church, either among the Prophets, whose number is complete, or among the Apostles, at the end of the times.’ The writer says that the *Shepherd* may indeed be read privately by devout persons, but denies that it ought to be read in the assembly of the Christian people or that it may be added to the books of either the Prophets or the Apostles. This passage is honorable [Col. 0190B] to the Latin churches and demonstrates that there was more wisdom and caution among them than among the Greeks, to most of whom Hermas appeared no less authoritative than the Prophets and Apostles. . . .
>
> “I shall add a word concerning the argument by which learned men say they are chiefly moved to distinguish Hermas, the author of the *Shepherd*, from Hermas, the brother of the pontiff Pius. In the *Liber Pontificalis* and in some other ancient writings, a certain passage is quoted from the book of Hermas, the brother of Pius, to which he had given the title *Shepherd*, concerning the celebration of Easter on the Lord’s Day; this passage we seek in vain in the *Shepherd* of Hermas which has come down to us. See Johann Albert Fabricius, *Codex Apocryphus Novi Testamenti*, vol. III, p. 761. From this they infer that Hermas, the brother of Pius, left a book distinct from our *Shepherd*. If the Greek *Shepherd* of Hermas still existed today, and if it were beyond doubt that this little book had reached us intact, this argument would not be contemptible. But since we possess only a Latin translation, and perhaps a mutilated one at that, the argument must be regarded as wholly devoid of force. It is probable [Col. 0190C] that those Eastern and Greek Christians called Quartodecimans removed this passage concerning the date of Easter from the *Shepherd* because it opposed their view.”

P. 164.

Thus this most eminent man argues against that widespread opinion concerning Hermas, the author of the *Shepherd*. Yet that opinion can scarcely—indeed, cannot at all—be called an invention of modern writers; for Origen, in book X of his *Commentary on the Epistle to the Romans*, at the passage where Hermas is mentioned by the Apostle, determined that the book of the *Shepherd* should be ascribed to the Pauline Hermas; and other authors besides, as is evident from Eusebius and Jerome, handed down the same view. Moreover, some learned men in Germany still believe that this writer should be assigned to the first century; whether, however, they support their opinion with any new arguments, I have not yet had occasion to see.

Gallandi, however, in the *Prolegomena concerning Caius the Presbyter*, § IV, p. XXXI of vol. II of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, wishes to distinguish the works of the Pauline Hermas and of Hermas, or Hermes, the brother of Pius; and he says that Justus Fontanini clearly [Col. 0190D] demonstrated the same thing in *Historia Litteraria Aquileiensis*, book II, chap. 1. Gallandi himself writes the following, which is well worth reading:

> “Just as the work of the apostolic man was called by the ancient Fathers the *Shepherd*, or *Book of the Shepherd*—a designation perhaps derived from the fact that throughout almost the entire work a Shepherd is introduced speaking to and instructing Hermas—so too it may have happened that the book of Hermes concerning Easter was called, at least by some, the *Shepherd*, because its author wrote about the things commanded him by an angel when the angel came to him in the garb of a shepherd, as the Second Henschenian Catalogue states. Hence the name *Shepherd* became attached not only to the writer but also to his book.”

Gallandi and Fontanini think that the book published by Hermes, the brother of Pius, was lost through the ravages of time; and Fontanini indeed denies that this Hermes ought to be called Hermas. Yet we see that the author of this fragment calls him Hermas, not Hermes, just as pseudo-Tertullian [Col. 0191A] has “Hermas.” Conversely, Usuard calls that Pauline Hermas “Hermes” in his *Martyrology* under May 9, fol. 70, Louvain edition.

Moreover, the author of the fragment may have had in mind the extant book called the *Shepherd* of Hermas; and even if you suppose that he mistakenly ascribed the work to Hermas, or Hermes, the brother of Pope Pius, nevertheless, as Freindaller rightly says—though in another place:

> “This writer speaks confidently here about the matter, in the way one ordinarily speaks about any well-known and recent events.”

Meanwhile, against Gallandi, who maintains that the fragment’s words should not be understood of the book of the *Shepherd* known to us, but of some more recent book now lost, Freindaller acutely replies as follows:

> “Nowhere throughout the whole of antiquity is there any trace that the question was ever raised whether this later book of the *Shepherd* belonged among the canonical books of the New Covenant and ought to be read in the Church. Caius, therefore, could by no means have been referring to Gallandi’s Hermas, since everything he brought forward concerning the book of the *Shepherd* applies to the other, familiar and more ancient book, which accordingly, for this very reason, was composed not by the earlier Hermas of the first century, but in the second century by the brother of Pius I.”

] are held as catholic. And *Wisdom* was written by friends of Solomon in his honor. We receive only the Apocalypses [Note: [Col. 0187A] Perhaps “Apocalypses.” Routh.] [Col. 0188A] of John and Peter, although some of our people are unwilling that the latter be read in the Church.

[Col. 0189A] But very recently, in our own times, in [Col. 0191A] [Note: [Col. 0191B] “Herma.” Perhaps it should read “Hermas.” “While Pius, the bishop, was occupying the chair of the Church of the city of Rome.” Freindaller agrees with me that the particle *in* must be added after *sedere* (“to sit”). It should furthermore be noted that Pius occupied the chair of the city of Rome for ten years after the year of Christ 140.

“But to publish himself.” Perhaps: “but to be published.” In Greek, δημοσιεύσθαι δὲ, “but to be made public.” Yet Freindaller too printed *se* (“himself”) in place of *sed* (“but”). Meanwhile, published books are contrasted with τοῖς ἀποκρύφοις (“the apocryphal books”). Eusebius, *History*, book III, chap. 3, speaking of his own time and region, says that this very work of Hermas was customarily δημοσιεύσθαι, “published,” or read publicly, even though it should not be placed ἐν ὁμολογουμένοις, “among the acknowledged books.”

> “This book of the *Shepherd*,” says Freindaller, “was held in greater honor among the Greeks than among the Latins, perhaps because Greek is the original language of this work, from which it was afterward rendered into Latin.”

Later the same man also observed that, among the Greeks more readily than among the Latins, the opinion could have gained acceptance that the book of the *Shepherd* belonged to the earlier Hermas—the one, namely, greeted by Paul—because the writer was known to the Latins; and that from this [Col. 0191D] the reason is apparent why this volume was held in greater honor among the Greeks than among the Latins. For St. Jerome says of it in *On Illustrious Men*, chap. 10: “Among the Latins the book is almost unknown.” Compare Mosheim above at p. 32.

*Completum*: read *completos*. *Potest*: in Greek, δυνατόν ἐστι, “it is possible.” The author against the Cataphrygians says in Eusebius: Δεδιὼς δὲ καὶ ἐξευλαβούμενος, μή τῃ δόξω τισὶν ἐπισυγγράφειν ἢ ἐπιδιατάσσεσθαι τῷ τῆς τοῦ εὐαγγελίου καινῆς διαθήκης λόγῳ· ᾧ μήτε προσθεῖναι μήτ᾽ ἀφελεῖν δυνατόν, τῷ κατὰ τὸ εὐαγγέλιον αὐτὸ πολιτεύεσθαι προῃρημένῳ—“But fearing and carefully guarding against appearing to some to write additions or append further ordinances to the word of the New Covenant of the Gospel, to which one who has chosen to conduct his life according to the Gospel itself may neither add nor take away,” p. 73, vol. II of these *Reliquiae*.

“Of Arsinoüs, however, or Valentinus,” etc. No mention of Arsinoüs exists elsewhere, so far as I know; but he appears to have been Egyptian by nationality and Gnostic by sect. Both Muratori and Stosch report, from Tertullian’s book *On the Flesh of Christ*, that Valentinus fabricated a book of Psalms. Moreover, in the manuscript Catena on Job preserved in the Bodleian Library, [Col. 0192A] at chap. 21, verse 12, as Grabe informs us in vol. II of his *Spicilegium Patrum*, p. 38, Origen mentions the *Psalms of Valentinus* and the *Odes of Basilides*. In the Catena on Job translated into Latin by Paulus Comitolus and published at Venice in 1587, p. 345, Origen likewise cites these same minor works.

That any work of this kind belonged to Marcion or the Marcionites has, so far as I know, been related by no one except this writer. Epiphanius merely says, after mentioning Marcion’s Gospel and Apostolic collection, ἄλλα δὲ συντάγματα ἀφ᾽ ἑαυτοῦ συνέταξε (Marcion) τοῖς αὐτοῦ πλανωμένοις—“Marcion also composed other treatises of his own for those led astray by him”: *Heresy* XIII, chap. 9, p. 309, Petavius’s edition. Of these works, Tertullian frequently cited one called the *Antitheses*.

A passage of Origen in Macarius’s *Orations on Luke*, p. 981 of Delarue’s edition of Origen’s works, is noteworthy: Ταῦτα δὲ εἴρηται πρὸς τοὺς ἀπὸ Οὐαλεντίνου, καὶ Βασιλίδου, καὶ τοὺς ἀπὸ Μαρκίωνος· ἔχουσι γὰρ καὶ αὐτοὶ τὰς λέξεις ἐν τῷ καθ᾽ ἑαυτοὺς εὐαγγελίῳ—“These things have been said against the followers of Valentinus and Basilides, and those of Marcion; for they too have these words in the Gospel peculiar to themselves.” From this, it seems to me, one must infer that some common gospel existed among the disciples of those heresiarchs, as I noted earlier under AGRIPPA CASTOR, p. 85, vol. I of the *Reliquiae*. Irenaeus, book III *Against Heresies*, chap. 11, and the author of the Appendix to Tertullian’s *Prescription against Heretics*, chap. 49, attest that Valentinus possessed a gospel; Origen himself likewise states in his *Homily on Luke*, p. 932, that Basilides possessed one—to say nothing [Col. 0192C] of Jerome and Ambrose at the beginning of their commentaries on the same Gospel. Marcion’s Gospel, compiled from the work of St. Luke, is too celebrated to require a witness.

What, therefore, prevents us from thinking that some book of Psalms was common to those three sects, which held opinions in common? Not only in the passage cited above, but elsewhere as well, Origen joined Valentinus, Basilides, and Marcion together in his account. See the Catena on Job translated into Latin by Comitolus, p. 237. Other authors did no differently, as, for example, Clement of Alexandria in the celebrated passage of *Stromata*, book VII, chap. 17. Indeed, Jerome seems to write about Priscillian in chap. 121 of *On Illustrious Men* in such a way that one may recognize their heresy as one and the same, or at least similar:

> “To this day he is accused by some of the Gnostic heresy—that is, the heresy of Basilides and Marcion, about whom Irenaeus wrote—while others defend him, saying that he did not hold the opinion imputed to him.”

Thus Jerome.

It remains to speak about Mitiades, an unknown man mentioned in this passage. He appears to have had no connection with Miltiades the Cataphrygian, or disciple of Montanus, whom the anonymous author against the Cataphrygians opposed. See p. 73, vol. II of the *Reliquiae*. Freindaller writes as follows:

> “A doubt will arise as to how that man composed a book of psalms in support of Marcion, as did Arsinoüs and Valentinus. Miltiades, certainly, or Alcibiades”—

(for Lang, in his notes on Nicephorus, and Valesius, in his notes on Eusebius, thought that it should be read thus)—

> “had adhered to the sect of Montanus, whereas the heretic Marcion preceded him by forty, if not fifty, years according to chronological reckoning. What business, I ask, would he have undertaken to advance the errors either of Marcion or of his followers, with whom the Montanist heresy had either no common cause or almost none?”

Finally, as regards that monstrosity in this fragment—Basilides as the founder of the Asian Cataphrygians—who has ever heard that Basilides [Col. 0193A] of Alexandria, the celebrated teacher of the Gnostic heresy, was the founder or originator of the Cataphrygians, or Montanists, a most familiar sect of later date? The Montanists, moreover, had no similarity or kinship with the Gnostics or Marcionites, although Tertullian, a follower of Montanus, refuted those heresies in so many books.

Only one passage occurs to me in which something of this sort might be intimated: namely, one containing Epiphanius’s error concerning the reason for the Montanists’ abstinence from foods, which I indicated above at vol. I, p. 331. Moreover, it must be noted here that, since the Montanists ordinarily treated penitents more severely, Clement of Alexandria wrote the following concerning Basilides in *Stromata* IV, chap. 24: πλὴν οὐδὲ πάσας (ἁμαρτίας) ὁ Βασιλείδης φησὶ, μόνας δὲ τὰς ἀκουσίας καὶ κατ᾽ ἄγνοιαν, ἀφίεσθαι—“Yet Basilides says that not all sins are forgiven, but only those committed involuntarily and through ignorance.”

Could it therefore be—though I would affirm nothing on this matter—that, if not through the ignorance of our author, then perhaps through the malice of certain persons, the Montanists, or Cataphrygians, were said to have Basilides the Gnostic heretic as their founder? Nor would the matters I have assembled here be irrelevant if the words “founder of the Asian Cataphrygians” could be understood of that book of Psalms rather than of Basilides [Col. 0194A] himself. By that interpretation we could defend our author’s reputation more readily. But after citing the words “the Asian founder of the Cataphrygians,” for which he printed “with the Asian founder of the Cataphrygians,” Freindaller says that this person might lie concealed under the name Miltiades or Alcibiades; “nevertheless, he judges that this final section suffers from a defect of sense and that its restoration is hopeless.”

Concerning the age of Basilides and Valentinus, who appear to have arisen shortly after all the Apostles had died, I spoke earlier at p. 135 of the first volume of the *Reliquiae*. Clement of Alexandria also attests that these same heretics [Col. 0194B] lived around the reign of Emperor Hadrian, as he states concerning them in the passage of *Stromata* VII, chap. 17, p. 898 of Potter’s edition, which I mentioned just now.]

the city of Rome, Hermas [Note: [Col. 0191A] Perhaps “Hermas.” Routh.] composed the *Shepherd*, while his brother Pius, the bishop, occupied the chair [Note: [Col. 0191A] “In the chair.” Freindaller.] of the Church of the city of Rome. And therefore it ought indeed to be read, but it cannot be published [Note: [Col. 0192A] Perhaps “but be published.” Routh.] to the people in the Church, either among the Prophets, whose number is complete [Col. 0192A] [Note: [Col. 0192A] Perhaps “completed.” Routh.], or among the Apostles, at the end of the times.

But we receive absolutely nothing of Arsinoüs, or Valentinus, or Mitiades, [Col. 0193A] [Note: [Col. 0194B] “Who also composed a new book of Psalms for Marcion.” Epiphanius uses the same construction in the passage transcribed above at p. 35: ἄλλα δὲ συντάγματα ἀφ᾽ ἑαυτοῦ συνέταξε (Marcion) τοῖς ἀπ᾽ αὐτοῦ πλανωμένοις—“Marcion also composed other treatises of his own for those led astray by him.” So too Cornelius Nepos, *Lysander*, chap. 3: “Cleon of Halicarnassus is said to have written this speech for him.” Above, the author had spoken of pseudepigraphical epistles attributed to Paul, fabricated in support of Marcion’s heresy.] who also composed a new book of Psalms for Marcion, together with Basilides, [Col. 0194A] the founder of the Asian Cataphrygians [Note: [Col. 0193A] Perhaps “together with the founder of the Asian Cataphrygians,” or “the founders.” Routh.].

## AT THE BEGINNING OF THE THIRD CENTURY  
## MARCUS MINUCIUS FELIX, ADVOCATE AND APOLOGIST

[Col. 0193]

## PROLEGOMENA  
## ON THE LIFE, HISTORY, AND WRITINGS OF M. MINUCIUS FELIX THE APOLOGIST, BY DOM GOLHASR. LUMPER, O.S.B.

[Note: [Col. 0193C] *Critical Theological History of the Life, Writings, and Doctrine of the Holy Fathers*, part VII.]

### I

[Col. 0193C] *Minutius*, or *Minucius*, was Marcus’s family name; for Octavius addressed him in these words [Note: [Col. 0193C] Minucius, *Dialogue*, chaps. 2 and 5.]:

> “It is not the part of a good man, brother Marcus, [to …] a man,” etc.

Caecilius, likewise:

> “Although for you, brother Marcus,” etc.

Yet, just as the consular family of the Minucii was familiar to everyone and distinguished among the Romans, so it has remained unknown to everyone up to the present whether our Minucius derived his origin from it or from some other family. Nor is anyone better informed about what his native country was [Note: [Col. 0193C] Gallandi, vol. II, *Prolegomena*; Ceillier, [Col. 0193D] *Histoire des Auteurs*, vol. II, p. 222.]. Nevertheless, some suspect from the style of his book that he was born in Africa [Note: [Col. 0193D] Tillemont, *Mémoires*, vol. III, *Histoire ecclésiastique*, p. 71; Basnage, at the year 210, § 3. Dupin, following Rigaltius, reasons as follows: “Jerome, in his Catalogue, in which he observes chronological order, places him between Tertullian [Col. 0194C] and Cyprian.” It is evident that Minucius took not a few things from Tertullian, and that Cyprian copied Minucius’s words in more than one passage of his book *On the Vanity of Idols*. From this it is presumed that he was African; and his writing approaches the African style.]. But they neither prove nor can prove that anything characteristic of the harsher African manner of speech is found in him.

Might it not be said with better right that Caecilius and Octavius, who were bound to Minucius by so strong a tie of affection, were in fact Africans and his fellow-countrymen? Yet, as we shall see shortly, this is not so certain, nor can it be inferred beyond doubt from however close a bond of friendship they had with him.

### II

We believe, however, that no one will deny that Minucius lived for a long time at Rome, which was then the capital of all the other cities of the world, and there discharged the office of an advocate, as Lactantius [Note: [Col. 0194D] Lactantius, *Institutes*, book V, chap. 1.] and [Col. 0195A] Jerome [Note: [Col. 0195D] Jerome, *Catalogue*, chap. 58, and Letter 83 to Magnus.] plainly and explicitly assert.

Minucius himself writes at the beginning of his book [Note: [Col. 0195D] Minucius, *Dialogue*, chap. 2.] that Octavius came to him at Rome, and that shortly afterward he traveled to Ostia with him and another companion:

> “When,” he says, “the vintage holidays had relaxed my judicial responsibilities”—

that is, when during the vintage season he was free from the forensic labor that occupied him throughout the entire year.

Did not Octavius also say of himself and Minucius—or rather solely in Minucius’s name:

> “Nevertheless, we undertook to defend and protect certain sacrilegious and incestuous persons, even parricides; but these men,”

that is, the Christians,

> “we thought ought not to be heard at all” [Note: [Col. 0195D] Ibid., chap. 28.]?

From these words it is evident that, while he was still a pagan, Minucius performed the office of an advocate.

### III

In our own age, however, Heumann, a man of exceedingly acute intellect, thought that Minucius’s status should be questioned and that he ought to be removed from the number of advocates or jurisconsults [Note: [Col. 0195D] Heumann, *Parerga Gottingensia* X, pp. 208–212.].

Heumann says, namely, that Lactantius—who is believed to be the first of all the more ancient writers to report that Minucius exercised that profession—does indeed call him a “causidicus,” or advocate, but in that elegant sense in which he indicates an advocate not “of the forum,” but “of the Christian religion.” Once this is assumed, Heumann thinks that Jerome misunderstood Lactantius’s words. He goes so far as almost to persuade himself that Lactantius did not write, “Minucius Felix held a not undistinguished place among advocates,” but “held a not undistinguished place among the advocates of the Church.” That is, he says, from the abbreviated spelling *Ecce* for *Ecclesiae* (“of the Church”), *loci* (“of a place”) could easily have arisen.

But [Col. 0195C] the critic is found to have wasted his effort. I pass over the passage from Minucius just cited, which alone Heumann saw and twisted into another meaning. For even if, in his opinion, the words of that passage are judged insufficiently suited to settle such a dispute, elsewhere our “advocate,” and indeed an advocate “of no undistinguished standing,” argues his own case so clearly that there will be absolutely no one who, assuming the role of an impartial judge, will refuse to deliver judgment in accordance with his pleas. He speaks as follows [Note: [Col. 0195D] Minucius, *Dialogue*, chap. 28.]:

> “When we undertook to defend and protect certain sacrilegious and incestuous persons, even parricides, we thought that these men”—the Christians—“ought not to be heard at all.”

Here particular notice should be taken of the word *suscipiebamus*, “we undertook,” which is drawn from the forum, as Wowerius observed on this passage. Clients who had been taken under an advocate’s protection were called *suscepti*. Thus Servius, on the Virgilian line [Col. 0195D] [Note: [Col. 0195D] Virgil, *Aeneid* VI.609.]:

> And fraud fastened upon a client,

says:

> “He wishes us to understand corrupt advocates who are patrons of clients, whom we now call *suscepti*.”

The remainder of the context in Minucius which we have transcribed is moreover known to agree so closely with this meaning of the word that whoever examines the author’s complete statement must admit that, at least at one time—[Col. 0196A] namely, while he was still devoted to pagan superstition—he had performed the office of an advocate.

Nor could anyone rightly reply that Minucius introduces Octavius as speaking in this way, and that all that can at most be inferred from the passage is that Octavius, but not Minucius, acted as a forensic patron. For who, asks a learned man [Note: [Col. 0196D] Le Nourry, *Apparatus*, vol. II, p. 11.], does not clearly understand that Octavius said, either about himself and Minucius together or rather solely in Minucius’s name, “that he had once undertaken to defend and protect sacrilegious and incestuous persons, even parricides, but had thought that Christians ought not to be heard at all”?

### IV

But if it is evident that the matter stands thus, it will also follow that our Minucius continued to discharge the same office even after professing the Christian religion. For he writes [Note: [Col. 0196D] Minucius, *Dialogue*, chap. 2.] that Octavius came to him at Rome,

> “when the vintage holidays had relaxed his judicial responsibilities”—

that is, when, with the autumn holidays beginning, he was free from the forensic labor that occupied him during the remainder of the year.

Nor, finally, is there any reason for anyone to wonder, with Baudouin [Note: [Col. 0196D] Baudouin, *Dissertation on Minucius Felix*, § 5.], “how a devout advocate could have maintained his position in so profane and hostile a forum”; and consequently there is no reason for Heumann to infer from this [Note: [Col. 0196D] Heumann, passage cited, p. 212.] that Minucius was by no means an advocate in the Roman forum.

> “For if they consider,”

to use the words of the distinguished Mamachi [Note: [Col. 0196D] Mamachi, *Origins and Antiquities of Christianity*, vol. III, p. 299 ff.],

> “both that the emperors did not always take precautions to prevent any of our people from exercising public offices, and that not all emperors did so, they will certainly readily admit that in the third century—when our people had obtained Septimius Severus, who was at times more equitable toward them than his predecessors had customarily been [Col. 0196C] [Note: [Col. 0196D] Tertullian, *To Scapula*, chap. 4.], and Alexander [Note: [Col. 0196D] Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VI, chaps. 16 and 28.] and the two emperors named Philip, who judged that nothing should be decreed against us [Note: [Col. 0196D] Ibid., chap. 34.]—it was permissible for a Christian man to enter the forum and undertake the representation of those whom he judged to have suffered injury or to have been unjustly deprived of their property.”

Arnobius indeed testifies [Note: [Col. 0196D] Arnobius, *Against the Nations*, book II, p. 21, Paris edition, 1656.] that

> “orators endowed with great talents and men learned in the law sought Christian instruction, scorning the things in which they had trusted shortly before.”

And who can doubt that in these words Arnobius was referring to our Minucius—indeed, to his own Minucius—whom he knew perfectly well to have held the foremost place among such orators and jurisconsults?

Moreover, Tertullian said [Note: [Col. 0196D] Tertullian, *Apology*, chap. 37, Migne ed., vol. I, col. 462.]:

> “We are but of yesterday, and we have filled everything that belongs to you: cities, islands, fortresses, towns, meeting places, the very camps, tribes, decuries, the senate, and the forum. We have left you only the temples.”

Heumann should therefore erase from his *Parerga* that observation in which he determined that Minucius must be struck from the roll [Col. 0197A] of jurisconsults; and let the authority of Firmianus and Jerome prevail, who assert that Minucius Felix held a position of no small distinction—indeed, an eminent position—among the advocates at Rome [Note: [Col. 0197D] See *An Apologetic Letter of M. Minucius Felix on Behalf of Himself and His Status, to F. O. M.*, that is, Friedrich Otto Mencke, in which, against Heumann’s observation, it is demonstrated that Minucius Felix rightly and deservedly retains his place among jurisconsults and advocates. This letter was reproduced in the *Nova Acta Eruditorum*, 1738, p. 210.].

### V

Minucius had been raised in paganism from infancy, but at a more advanced age he abandoned the superstition of the gentiles and embraced the Christian faith. He testifies to this about himself when he says the following concerning Octavius [Note: [Col. 0197D] Minucius, *Dialogue*, chap. 1.]:

> “When, after the mist had been dispersed, I emerged from the depth of darkness into the light of wisdom and truth, he did not reject me as a companion, but—what is more glorious—went before me”—

that is, Octavius preceded me in professing the Christian faith.

Caecilius too intimates this when, at the beginning of the *Dialogue*, he asks Minucius:

> “Although you have moved in both ways of life, have rejected the one [Col. 0197B] and approved the other”—

that is, although you have rejected the superstition of the gentiles, yet have approved the Christian faith—

> “nevertheless, for the present your mind must be so disposed that you hold the balance of a perfectly impartial judge and do not lean with partiality toward either side, lest the judgment appear not so much to have arisen from our arguments as to have been brought forward from your own sentiments” [Note: [Col. 0197D] Ibid., chap. 5.].

Eucherius, bishop of Lyons, teaches in the following words how devoutly and holily Minucius lived after his conversion [Note: [Col. 0197D] Eucherius of Lyons, *Letter to Valerian*, vol. V, *Bibliotheca Patrum*, p. 771.]:

> “And when shall I unfold from that catalogue of great numbers Firmianus, Minucius, Cyprian, Hilary, John, and Ambrose, men most illustrious for eloquence? They had said, I believe: ‘What is this? The unlearned arise and seize heaven, while here we, with all our learning, wallow in error and blood!’ They had said this, and therefore afterward they themselves took the kingdom by force.”

### VI

After Minucius gave his name to Christ and had been “instructed in the mysteries of this name,” to speak with Arnobius [Note: [Col. 0197D] Arnobius, passage cited.], he presented himself as a vindicator and champion of the truth [Note: [Col. 0197D] Le Nourry, *Apparatus to the Bibliotheca Maxima Patrum*, vol. IV, p. 19.].

He therefore composed a dialogue divided into two parts, one of which contains Caecilius’s speech on behalf of the pagans and the other Octavius’s speech on behalf of the Christians. He entitled it *OCTAVIUS*, as Lactantius and Jerome report, plainly in imitation of Plato, Cicero, and other ancient authors who prefixed to books of this kind, composed in dialogue form, the name of the person who plays the principal role in them.

The distinguished Blackwall says:

> “Minucius’s dialogue is arranged with acuteness, elegance, and clarity. You find in it almost as many weighty thoughts as periods, and these thoughts, flowing naturally from the subject, are skillfully woven into the discourse. He both fights and conquers by argument; and he possesses as much wit [Col. 0198A] as penetration. His natural genius was given to him not for invention, but for speaking the truth, which he does not know how to adulterate. He clears Christian doctrine of the charges brought against it by the pagans and turns his opponents’ calumnies back against their own religion so aptly and manifestly that he shows himself at once the strongest and most formidable assailant of a bad cause and the noblest advocate of a good one” [Note: [Col. 0198D] Blackwall, *On the Excellence of the Classical Authors*, chap. 10, § 5, p. 193.].

### VII

As for the other events of Minucius’s life, how long he lived, and how he died, there is profound silence among both ancient and modern writers. Nor is there agreement among writers concerning the age in which Minucius Felix lived.

Henry Dodwell [Note: [Col. 0198D] Dodwell, *Cyprianic Dissertations* III, § 16, p. 12.] persuaded himself that Minucius flourished near the end of the reign of Marcus Antoninus; and David Blondel [Note: [Col. 0198D] Blondel, *On the Eucharist*, p. 119.] made him a contemporary of Fronto, [Col. 0198B] who taught Marcus Antoninus around the year of Christ 160.
