Most scholars, not without reason, number him among the ecclesiastical writers of the third century. It is nevertheless insufficiently certain and clear during which years of that age he flourished and, especially, during which emperor’s reign he lived at Rome.

William Cave [Note: [Col. 0198D] Cave, *Literary History of Ecclesiastical Writers*, vol. I, p. 101.] says:

> “Concerning the age in which he lived, I have nothing that I would venture to affirm as certain. Yet if conjecture is permissible in an obscure and doubtful matter, I would surmise that, as a contemporary of Tertullian and older than Cyprian, he was famous around the year 220.”

Johann Albert Fabricius [Note: [Col. 0198D] Fabricius, notes on Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*, chap. 58, p. 133, *Bibliotheca Ecclesiastica*.] observes that all agree that Minucius was not far removed from the reigns of Antoninus, Commodus, and Severus.

Ceillier [Note: [Col. 0198D] Rémi Ceillier, *Histoire des Auteurs ecclésiastiques*, vol. II, chap. 23, p. 222.] conjectures from Jerome that Minucius lived at Rome during the pontificate of Zephyrinus, since Jerome, in his catalogue [Col. 0198C] *On Illustrious Men*, listed Minucius among the writers who existed at that time. The very learned Baronius [Note: [Col. 0198D] Baronius, at the year 211, §§ 3–4.] and Tillemont [Note: [Col. 0198D] Tillemont, *Mémoires*, vol. III, “Note on Minucius,” p. 295.] held the same opinion.

In our own age, the distinguished Johann Daniel van Hoven, in a letter to Gerard Meerman, endeavored to show that Minucius was a contemporary of Athenagoras and to claim for him the leading place among Latin Christian writers [Note: [Col. 0198D] This letter occupies first place in the *V.D. Campenses*, or *Critical-Antiquarian Gleanings*. Kampen, 1766. It also appears in Lindner’s second edition of Minucius Felix, 1773.].

### VII

In addition to this dialogue, Jerome, in *On Illustrious Men*, chap. 58, describes another book by Minucius, *On Fate*, or *Against the Astrologers*, as follows:

> “Another work, *On Fate*, or *Against the Astrologers*, is also circulated under his name. Although it too is the work of an eloquent man, it does not appear to me to agree with the style of the preceding book.”

This book, which Jerome also mentions in his letter to Magnus [Note: [Col. 0198D] “In the book entitled *Octavius* [Col. 0199A] and in the other *Against the Astrologers*—if, however, its attribution does not falsely represent its author—what part of pagan literature did Minucius Felix leave untouched?” Jerome, Letter 83 to Magnus.], is no longer extant [Col. 0199A].

That Minucius was its author is not certain, although it is probable. For he himself indicates in the following words [Note: [Col. 0199A] Minucius, *Octavius*, chap. 36.] that he intended to write on fate:

> “And enough concerning fate—even if, in view of the occasion, it has been but little; we shall discuss it elsewhere more richly and fully.”

But, as the distinguished Dupin observes [Note: [Col. 0199A] Dupin, *Bibliothèque des Auteurs*, vol. I, p. 189.], it is uncertain whether he discussed fate more extensively in another book and whether the treatise extant in Jerome’s time was the one he had promised, or whether some author instead seized upon this passage as an opportunity to put forward a work falsely under Minucius’s name.

Since it is sufficiently evident that this monument of his genius has perished, it is truly surprising that Sébastien Le Nain de Tillemont [Note: [Col. 0200A] Tillemont, *Mémoires*, vol. III, p. 73.], while discussing Minucius and his *Dialogue* learnedly, should add that the work may be read in print in a certain edition of Arnobius.

[Col. 0199]

## A DISSERTATION BY FRANCIS BAUDOUIN, JURISCONSULT, ON THE *OCTAVIUS* OF MINUCIUS FELIX
[Col. 0199B] Two good, ancient, and weighty witnesses and authorities, Lactantius and Jerome, readily persuaded me both to entitle this work—whether booklet or dialogue—which for many centuries has falsely been believed and called Arnobius’s eighth book *Against the Nations*, and to affirm plainly and unequivocally that it is the *Octavius* of Marcus Minucius Felix. For Lactantius, in Book I, chapter 11, of his *Institutes*, cites “Minucius Felix in that book which,” as he says, “is entitled *Octavius*.” And he quotes from it certain words which do not permit us to imagine either some other *Octavius* or an *Octavius* belonging to anyone else. The same author, in Book V, chapter 1, when speaking of the eloquence of the Christians whom he had read, praises this Minucius first: “Minucius Felix,” he says, “held no undistinguished place among advocates. His book, [Col. 0199C] entitled *Octavius*, shows how capable a champion of the truth he could have been, had he devoted himself wholly to that pursuit.”

The other witness is Jerome, who, following Lactantius in this matter, as he himself acknowledges, says in his catalogue of ecclesiastical writers: “Minucius Felix, a distinguished advocate at Rome, wrote a dialogue between a Christian and a pagan engaged in debate, which is entitled *Octavius*.” Likewise, in his letter to Magnus, the Roman orator, he says: “Minucius Felix, an advocate of the Roman forum, in the book entitled *Octavius*, what part of pagan literature did he leave untouched?”

Now that this book is not by Arnobius is sufficiently evident, since it appears to be by Minucius. Indeed, what Jerome adds in the same letter could otherwise have shown that it was not Arnobius’s, since [Col. 0199D] he testifies that Arnobius wrote only seven books *Against the Nations*, the same seven that still survive. And since Jerome relates that another book had been falsely inscribed with the name of our Minucius, I am all the more astonished and grieved that this work, which was his sole and authentic work (*καὶ γνήσιος*, “and genuine”), should have been stolen from him [Col. 0200B] and unjustly attributed to another, who was not its owner; thus our Minucius appears to have suffered a double injury, both by plagiarism and by the substitution of a spurious offspring. But this is a frequent complaint concerning the misdeeds of copyists, who rashly mix up everything. Perhaps a certain resemblance of style and argument—which very often deceives the unlearned—caused some to attribute this booklet to Arnobius; and when they read “Octavius,” they immediately dreamed that it was some “eighth” book. Ridiculous and foolish indeed! At least they ought to have considered that a dialogue should not rashly be attributed to Arnobius, who employs continuous discourse. But ignorance possesses an audacity as blind as it is confident.

Jerome, indeed, writes that his Nepotian was so diligently versed in ecclesiastical writers that, if anything from them were produced, [Col. 0200C] he immediately recognized and distinguished what belonged to Tertullian, what to Cyprian, what to Lactantius, what to Minucius, what to Victorinus, and what to Arnobius. All the more, therefore, am I astonished that Erasmus—in that passage, I mean Erasmus, a man endowed with extremely acute judgment and by no means an obtuse critic of such writers—observed that nothing by this Minucius now survived.

Under which emperor our Minucius lived at Rome is not yet sufficiently clear to me. In his catalogue, in which he appears to enumerate ecclesiastical writers in the order in which they lived, Jerome obscurely indicates that Minucius was close in time to Origen and earlier than Cyprian. Yet elsewhere he indicates neither his century nor his period of life. Certainly, in Cyprian’s booklet *On the Vanity of Idols*, many things are found which are read in precisely the same [Col. 0200D] words in Minucius’s *Octavius*; it must therefore be the case either that Minucius took them from Cyprian or that Cyprian took them from Minucius. Jerome, however, in his letter to Magnus, when speaking of the Latin writers of the Church, although he praises Minucius before Cyprian, nevertheless appears to attribute that discourse on idols [Col. 0201A] to Cyprian. Yet in his *Apology for His Books Against Jovinian*, he mentions Tertullian first, Cyprian second, and Minucius third.

Sabellicus, though without citing a witness, affirms that Minucius flourished at Rome when Urban was bishop there—that is, in the reign of the emperor Alexander Severus. If that were so, Minucius would be earlier than Cyprian, contemporary with Tertullian, and thus also contemporary with our jurists Ulpian and Paul. But although I believe him to have been later, I nevertheless think that he followed closely upon that period, whereas he does not approach our own except across the vast interval of nearly thirteen hundred years.

I recall that the Minucian clan was once noble at Rome, and that within it four consuls named Minucius Augurinus may be counted within forty years. I also read of the Minucii Rufi [Col. 0201B] and the Minucii Thermi in the consular fasti. Finally, Minucius Fundanus was a distinguished governor of Asia, to whom the emperor Hadrian sent a law concerning the Christians that was not unjust—to say nothing now of the Minucius whom Pliny mentions in his *Letters*, or the one praised by our Julian, whose books on civil law addressed to Minucius Natalis are commended.

Yet before all these I readily place one Minucius Felix, even if he was not of the same clan or family: later than they in age, certainly, but far superior in learning, virtue, and—what must be reckoned first—in piety. For he was not only a great jurist and an outstanding orator in his time; what is greater, he was a Christian in earnest. I suspect that he was African, although I dare not affirm it. [Col. 0201C] Certainly, he mentions Fronto of Cirta—Cirta was a most celebrated city of Numidia, also mentioned in the *Pandects*—in such a way as to indicate that he himself had spent time in Africa. Moreover, he adopted the kind of speaking and writing characteristic of those Africans Tertullian, Cyprian, and Arnobius—not to speak now of later authors nourished by that same Africa: that happy and fruitful Africa, I say, which, just as it was said always to produce something new, also produced the most learned and vigorous champions and defenders of our religion, and sent them even to support and defend the Roman Church itself. For from that same Africa also came enemies who were by no means inactive, and slanderers no less depraved than violent, such as—to go no farther—the Fronto whom I have just mentioned. From Minucius we shall learn that he was as shameless a rhetorician as he was an impious adversary of the Christians. [Col. 0201D] I should not like this man to have been Papirius Fronto, the jurist praised in the *Pandects*. I rather suspect that he was the rhetorician Cornelius Fronto, whom Capitolinus relates to have been the teacher of Marcus Antoninus, the philosopher-emperor. From his school of rhetoric we are also told that our [Note: [Col. 0201D] Bishop of Sardis and author of an *Apology for the Christians*. Jerome, *Catalogue*.] Melito emerged; he turned his eloquence to the defense of the Christians, so that by replying the good pupil might wipe away the reproach which his impious teacher had cast upon them through abuse.

[Col. 0202A] That our Minucius pleaded cases at Rome has already been stated above from Lactantius and Jerome. Nor does he himself conceal it, since he relates that during the vintage holidays he had been released from judicial business. Thus Ulpian too, in the *Pandects*, Law I, *On Holidays*, writes that it was expressly provided by a speech of the emperor Marcus Antoninus “that no one should compel an opponent to come to court during harvest or vintage.” Similarly, Suetonius (chapter 35) relates that Augustus ordained “that it should not be necessary” to attend the Senate “in September or October.” Indeed, Cyprian himself, as though another Minucius, in his *Letter to Donatus* (Oxford edition, treatise *On Grace*, p. 1), recalls that season in which, as he says, “with the vintage granting indulgence, the mind, released into repose, obtains the customary and appointed respite from the weariness of the year.” [Col. 0202B] At that time, he says, he sought pleasant retreats in which to reflect on divine matters. The narrative of our Minucius is not dissimilar.

Happy indeed were those holidays by which that most distinguished advocate, led away from the forum and its benches, was brought to religious reflection or debate. Cicero, reporting what he learned from our Scaevola, relates (*On the Orator*, II.6) that “Laelius was accustomed to spend time in the country with Scipio, and that they used incredibly to become boys again when they had flown from the city into the countryside as though from chains;” that they were even accustomed “to gather shells and smooth pebbles at Caieta and Lake Lucrinus, and to descend to every kind of mental relaxation and play.”

This example immediately came to mind when I heard that Minucius, having left the din of the forum, went into the country with his Octavius [Col. 0202C] and pleasantly watched on the shore at Ostia the childish game which he describes. But when I then hear how weighty and serious a debate concerning religion took place in that retreat, and what sort of council was held within a deserted vault, I perceive that no senate was ever convened at Rome concerning a greater matter. I would prefer no forum, no city, and no business to that leisure or solitude; and I am repeatedly compelled to wish that jurists might sometimes be willing to take holidays, retire, and go into the country in this manner. Can no holy and religious meditation on divine things, worthy of their privacy, enter their minds?

Lactantius intimates that Minucius did not devote himself wholly to the study of ecclesiastical matters. Yet all the nobler for that reason was his jurisprudence: it existed in the commonwealth as jurisprudence ought to exist, and united concern for and knowledge of divine and human things. For that reason, I commend his example all the more to men of our profession, so that at least on days when legal business is forbidden they may cultivate in leisure the calendar of a better religion and give and dedicate themselves to it.

When the Romans took holidays, they once had their “Tiber excursion,” mentioned by Cicero (*On Ends*, V.24), and also what our laws [Note: [Col. 0202D] Under the title *On the Maiuma* in both Codes. The *Suda* adds that these games were celebrated at Ostia; their chief feature was “to revel voluptuously in the waters of the sea, throwing one another in” (*ἡδυπαθεῖν ἐν τοῖς θαλαττίοις ὕδασιν, ἀλλήλους ἐμβάλλοντες*).] call their “Maiuma” at Ostia. But how completely free from idleness or play was the excursion of our Minucius! It was assuredly worthy [Col. 0203A] of having Augustine gladly behold its traces and salute the retreat in which the debate had taken place when he buried his mother Monica in the church at Ostia. For my part, whenever I read this Minucian dialogue, I am accustomed to recall the religious conversation which that holy matron held with her son at those mouths of the Tiber, as he himself recounts in Book XI of the *Confessions*.

What the condition of the Roman forum was when Minucius practiced there, and what appearance the Church then presented in that city, are plainly shown by the record of his age; and what I once wrote on the edicts of the ancient Roman emperors concerning the Christians illuminates the matter. Nor is the history of the times in which Decius or Valerian ruled unknown.

It is truly gratifying that a Christian advocate succeeded jurists whose opinions on civil law we read, men not only alien to religion but also its bitterest adversaries; and that the Roman forum or college of the toga and advocacy, which for so many years had been sprinkled with the blood and ashes of pious men, was at last purified and consecrated by the voice and footsteps of a Christian legal expert. [Col. 0203B] Arnobius boasts in his first book that both orators and jurists, men endowed, as he says, with great talents, had passed over to the Church. I indeed believe that, when he wrote this, he was thinking of his Minucius. He could perhaps scarcely have enumerated many of that profession. Yet I believe that some followed Minucius’s example, just as Minucius had men whom he himself followed [Col. 0203C] in the same course.

At any rate, when praising Minucius in his letter to Magnus, Jerome mentions two senators of the city of Rome, Hippolytus and Apollonius, who deserved to be included among the ecclesiastical writers. What shall I say of that [Note: [Col. 0203D] A martyr at Lyons under Marcus Antoninus and Lucius Verus. The witnesses are Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, V.1, and Gregory of Tours, I.29.] Vettius Epagathus of Lyons, who lived many years before Minucius and was publicly called—partly as a term of reproach and partly as an honor, since judgments about names arising from religion then varied—[Note: [Col. 0203D] *παράκλητος Χριστιανῶν*, “advocate of the Christians.” Eusebius, passage cited.] THE ADVOCATE OF THE CHRISTIANS?

Whether Minucius ever pleaded their cause in the Roman forum I do not know. Tertullian certainly indicates that this was scarcely permitted. So hateful then was their religion or Church, to which the constitution of the Roman state and empire was opposed, and so thoroughly had it already been pierced by public prejudgments, that the mere confession of the Christian name was sufficient for condemnation. So far was the defense of this religion from enjoying the defense of liberty. Meanwhile, I marvel all the more that a pious advocate could maintain his position in so profane and hostile a forum.

But it is astonishing that, when for nearly two hundred years the Roman world had openly, publicly, and freely given its allegiance to Christ, under the emperors’ own authority, a law was thought necessary—and was at last enacted—providing that in no court should anyone be an advocate or pleader, or possess the right to plead, unless he were a Christian. (Law VIII, Code, *On Pleading*.) [Col. 0204A] How noble, therefore, was the example of our Minucius, who was at Rome a champion of the good cause so far as he could be, at a time when this was not yet permitted with impunity! Christians were then certainly barred from the forum, and the praetor did not grant them the right to plead.

Yet although they were generally men of the cloak rather than of the toga, because the commonwealth often could not do without them, pagan emperors from time to time permitted them to wear the toga and some of them to perform public office. Christian emperors were afterwards far more indulgent, for they sometimes appointed as consuls, prefects of the city, and even praetorian prefects men whom they otherwise knew to be the bitterest enemies of religion, as may be understood even from the circumstances of Symmachus alone. But at last they became more severe, thoroughly purged the Roman Senate and forum, and ordered that all who either administered justice or pleaded cases should be Minuciuses, as it were.

They had long before overthrown the altar of Victory which stood in the vestibule of the senate-house and at which the Senate was accustomed to swear and sacrifice, despite the protests of both Symmachus himself [Note: [Col. 0204D] Symmachus, Book X, Letter 54 in Juretus’s edition, or 61 in Scioppius’s, to the Augusti Valentinian, Theodosius, and Arcadius.] and the Senate. But in the end they brought it about not only that all wearers of the toga were free from such superstition, but also that no jurisprudence existed in the forum except that Christian jurisprudence of which some likeness had already appeared long before in our Minucius.

[Col. 0204C] The title of this Minucian booklet and its dialogue form reproduce an ancient and learned manner of writing. Its style is pointed, keen, and vehement; compressed, dense, vigorous, compacted with frequent maxims, filled with the memory of every kind of antiquity and history, and such that one may count more thoughts than periods in it. For the early Christians were not verbose, since they had not yet learned to deceive with words; and their defenders were learned men—in a word, polymaths. As for the false charges against them, they refuted their adversaries not so much by words and pamphlets as by their life and by the reality itself.

The question proposed here and the case at issue are great: namely, whether religion is true or false. The pleading and contention on both sides are extremely sharp. [Col. 0204D] The outcome and victory are what they ought to be when truth conflicts with falsehood. Caecilius Natalis is the vehement advocate of the bad cause and a formidable enemy of the good. Octavius Januarius, by contrast, is the champion of the good and the most vigorous and just accuser of the bad. Between them sits Minucius Felix, the good judge and arbiter.

The occasion of the dispute was this: while Minucius was walking with the other two men I have named on the shore at Ostia, the pagan Caecilius encountered an image of Serapis and indicated his worship of it; for this he was reproved by the Christian Octavius. Long before, in the consulship of Piso and Gabinius, [Col. 0205A] the rites of Serapis had been expelled from the Capitol and the city; but they were afterwards restored and easily took root in the suburbs. Caecilius, having been reproved, fumes and, as though provoked, launches a fierce attack upon the Christian religion; while simultaneously defending his own superstition, he challenges Octavius, as it were. But unwittingly he encounters a strong and keen adversary, and, as the poet says:

> Desiring to drive his tooth into something fragile,  
> He broke it upon something solid.

(Horace, *Satires*, II.1.)

The posture of the case is not a single one. Caecilius argues variously and confusedly about many matters. Octavius repels most of them by simple denial and turns them back by a just counteraccusation. Some things he candidly admits, but legally defends. Thus this dispute consists partly of questions of fact and partly of questions of law. [Col. 0205B]

Tertullian before him—and before Tertullian, Justin and Athenagoras, whose apologetic booklets survive—and afterwards Cyprian, partly *Against Demetrian* and partly in his booklet *On the Vanity of Idols*, and later, much more extensively, Arnobius and Lactantius, pleaded this same case. They generally employed not merely the same thoughts and arguments, but even the same words and formulas. For thus our forefathers were accustomed to say, as that ancient author put it, “the same things about the same subjects.”

Would that posterity had observed such an example and ambitious novelty had not defiled sound antiquity. I should certainly like the *Apologies* of the authors whom I have named to be compared with this Minucian booklet, so that it may not now be necessary to compile another commentary. Many things from the disputations of ancient philosophers, the fables of poets, and Roman and Greek history [Col. 0205C] are subtly and learnedly rehearsed here. But it would be foolish to heap up many idle annotations on those subjects in this place.

I would rather explain fully the matters pertaining to the record of Christian antiquities. But for commentaries upon these too, another, freer occasion will be given, for I shall at some point devote myself to completing those which I have already begun. For now, besides the booklets I have named, I should very much like the opposing orations of Symmachus and Ambrose also to be read and compared here. Thus we shall hear from Minucius that this case was argued sharply but privately, at a time when Christians were scarcely permitted to exist openly; and we shall hear the same case argued publicly many years later, again and again, in the imperial consistory. In it, the distinguished champion of the Roman rites, who was both pontifex maximus and prefect of the city, engaged in combat with the greatest and keenest prelate of the Christian religion, at a time when our people were free and enjoyed a fair and equitable condition. [Col. 0205D] Most importantly, the judge and arbiter who sat over the case was not merely as religious as Minucius but possessed far greater authority, and could execute a sound judgment and restrain and punish the insolence of the slanderous adversary.

Finally, if anyone should add here Augustine’s books *On the City of God*, he would add much light and splendor to Octavius’s disputation. I shall not linger now over the writing out of such commentaries, but shall merely touch briefly upon certain chapters of the Minucian booklet, to prepare the reader.

[Col. 0206A] At the outset Caecilius praises some sort of Academic *ἀκαταληψία* (“inapprehensibility”) or Pyrrhonian *ἐποχή* (“suspension of judgment”), as though there were no knowledge of religion; and with Epicurean audacity he attacks the providence of God, almost as that [Note: [Col. 0206D] The names have been transposed and confused. For Gaius Velleius, a senator, is the Epicurean in Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, Book I, chapter 6, who attacks Providence from chapter 8 to chapter 21; Gaius Cotta, the Academic, replies to him from chapter 21 to the end of the book. Add the beginning of Book II. (LINDNER.)] Cotta does in Cicero’s books *On the Nature of the Gods*. Octavius defends Providence; nor does he disdain to use even those arguments by which Velleius in the same work of Cicero refutes Cotta’s vanity.

Caecilius reproached the Christians for assigning to God, as some assign to Fate, whatever is done or comes to pass. Octavius does not shrink from the word “Fate,” although it was odious because of the follies of the Stoics, who misused that term. But he postpones a longer discussion of the matter to another occasion, and cautiously avoids it as though it were a reef.

Jerome, in his *Catalogue* and in his letter to Magnus (Letter 84), testifies that a certain book *On Fate* was once inscribed with Minucius’s name, but warns that the attribution was false. [Col. 0206B] I believe that some attributed it to him because he appeared here to have promised something of that kind.

Arnobius, whom I am accustomed to call Minucius’s disciple and imitator, at one moment accuses his opponents concerning fate and at another shows that the Christians themselves were accused under that same name; yet in both cases, when he comes to the heart of the matter, he falters and somehow, as though stunned, *ἐπέχει* (“suspends judgment”). For—it is helpful, on account of Minucius and certain others, to note this here in passing—after attacking fate in Book VII, especially as the Stoics fashioned it, he says: “Yet these aspects, because the subject requires an excessively long and extensive discourse, we pass over unexplained and untouched.”

Likewise in Book II, when writing that the Christians were pressed with the question whether anything happened without God’s will, he feels himself so constricted on both sides that, in order to escape, he appeals to a kind of plea of ignorance:

> If all things are accomplished by his will, and nothing in the world can either arise or fail without his assent, it necessarily follows that all evils too must be understood to spring from his will. But if, rejecting from him the causes of the worst things, we wish to say that he is conscious of evil but the author of none, the worst things will begin to appear to occur either against his will or—what is monstrous to say—without his knowing them, while he is ignorant and unaware.

[Col. 0206C]

What, then, does he finally answer to the question when confined between these, as it were, clashing rocks? “We must answer,” he says, “that we do not know these things, etc.”

Before him, Justin in his *Apology* had not hesitated openly to deny and wholly reject what he calls *τὴν τῆς εἱμαρμένης ἀνάγκην* (“the necessity of destiny”), wishing thereby to escape one reef which he thought otherwise threatened him. Yet he then runs into another which Minucius and Arnobius seem to have feared no less.

At last Augustine, in that same Africa, wishing, as it were, to discharge what Minucius was said to have promised, and to pay in full what Minucius might perhaps scarcely have been able to furnish, [Col. 0207A] subtly expounded a middle position on this question, by which he judged that both difficulties could be satisfied.

Both Minucius and Arnobius knew what dispute and disagreement had once existed between Chrysippus and Diodorus *περὶ δυνατῶν καὶ εἱμαρμένης* (“concerning possibilities and destiny”), or *On Fate*. For we too possess some knowledge of it from Cicero and Plutarch. Yet even among its judges and arbiters our authors found nothing which they could follow unreservedly. Therefore, so long as the matter was unclear, they preferred to pronounce that further inquiry was needed rather than rashly define something else at once.

I return to Caecilius. He defends as far as he can the antiquity of his deities and their authority, which had been received everywhere. He attacks the true and unique God of the Christians, while abusing them as *ἄθεοι* (“atheists”). [Col. 0207B] Octavius wittily exposes the fiction and emptiness of the idols, even using the same words which Cyprian employs in the same argument. Nor was the refutation difficult, since Cicero’s own books *On the Nature of the Gods* seemed, as it were, to cast their vote in its favor. For Arnobius too, near the beginning of Book III, testifies that on this account certain enemies of the Christians had once “muttered that those books ought to be abolished and burned by order of the Senate.”

What more? The thing itself, which even its own worshippers mocked—for no tale belonging to any superstition was ever more foolish or absurd—refuted itself of its own accord. Moreover, Minucius could easily have copied what was relevant here from Tertullian, Justin, Athenagoras, and Theophilus, just as Arnobius, [Col. 0207C] Lactantius, Ambrose, and Augustine afterwards drew from Minucius when pleading the same cause. Certainly, Lactantius repeats what Octavius relates about Saturn, citing Minucius himself as his authority, and expounds it more fully in Book I, chapter 11.

Just as Octavius wittily mocks the entire fiction of Roman superstition, so too he elegantly demonstrates the emptiness of the very oracles in which the pagans so greatly gloried. He indicates that even before his own time the oracle of Pythian Apollo had ceased, just as Plutarch acknowledges that in the reign of the emperor Hadrian it had utterly failed. For as the truth of the Christian religion grew strong, the deception of those *χρηστήρια* (“oracles”) necessarily vanished.

Furthermore, Octavius speaks of demons and of their trembling when adjured by Christians, just as Justin and Tertullian had previously done in their *Apologies*, Cyprian in *Against Demetrian*, and Lactantius later in Book IV, chapter 27. [Col. 0207D] Thus he readily refutes Ulpian himself, who in Law I, *On Extraordinary Proceedings*, mocks Christians as impostors because of what is called this exorcism. That exorcisms were not ineffectual even in later times, and were frequent in the Church, may also be understood from Optatus the African and Augustine, writers by no means remote from Minucius.

Octavius also repeatedly presses many points concerning the one God, not unlike those collected by Justin *περὶ μοναρχίας* (“On the Sole Sovereignty [of God]”) and Clement of Alexandria. For our author could have read them both. Nor does he overlook what Cyprian emphasizes: that even the common people naturally call God one and singular when they invoke the Deity. Similarly, Lactantius says in Book II, chapter 1, that when the pagans swore, they named “God” rather than Jupiter.

In the ancient Roman formula of oath, Diespiter is named. But Cicero, in Book VII of his *Letters to Trebatius*, said, “to swear by Jupiter the Stone.” [Col. 0208A] It is also established that those taking oaths in ancient times often mentioned Jupiter; among the Greeks he was called *Ζεὺς ὅρκιος* (“Zeus, guardian of oaths”).

It is astonishing that Caecilius boasts that the Romans erected altars even to unknown deities. For what is this but an admission of error? Paul says that he saw such an altar at Athens and from it draws an argument for convicting this ignorance and instructing the Athenians. Pausanias testifies that altars bearing such an inscription existed not only in Attica but also in Elis. [Note: [Col. 0208D] Pausanias, *Elis* I.14: *ἀγνώστων θεῶν βωμός*, “an altar of unknown gods.”] Perhaps, when Octavius afterwards undertook to instruct Caecilius, he likewise followed Paul’s example and derived from this the beginning of his catechesis concerning knowledge of the true God. [Col. 0208B]

It might also seem astonishing that Caecilius boasts that “all the deities worshipped individually among other peoples are worshipped at Rome,” so that nothing remains except for him proudly to display his Pantheon. Yet Romulus’s law stood in the way, for it forbade the worship of foreign gods. Cicero’s judgment also stood in the way, for he declared that otherwise a confusion of religions would arise. But perhaps they did not regard them as foreigners, because they had now been officially invited and, as it were, granted citizenship.

Thus that city which Athenaeus (I.17) aptly called *ἐπιτομὴ τῆς οἰκουμένης* (“an epitome of the inhabited world”) was wittily called by our Theophilus, before Minucius’s age, *ἐπιτομὴ τῆς δεισιδαιμονίας* (“an epitome of superstition”). For Tertullian too (*On the Spectacles*, chapter 6) had said that “an assembly [Col. 0208C] of demons” and a senate-house of gods had settled there. Meanwhile, he did not rashly add that in that city it was lawful to worship anything whatever except the true God.

What Augustine writes in Book I, chapter 18, of *The Harmony of the Evangelists* is certainly memorable: why did the Romans, who worshipped all the others, not worship that one God? Because, he says, he wished to be worshipped alone and forbade the worship of those gods of the nations whom they were already worshipping. When the question concerned Christ himself, moreover, there was another reason for the Senate’s opposition.

And just as Augustine in that book repeatedly presses many points which might seem to have been taken from our *Octavius*, so too his elegant answer concerning the destruction of Jerusalem confirms Octavius’s answer on the same matter. But there is no reason now to set out every particular. I return to the Minucian courtroom.

[Col. 0208D] Caecilius accuses the Christians because they “despise temples as though they were funeral pyres.” Octavius admits it. For Clement of Alexandria had earlier proved in his *Protrepticus* that they were [Note: [Col. 0208D] Clement, *Protrepticus to the Nations*, p. 58: *δεικνύντες, τῶν εἰδώλων τὰ τεμένη, τάφους τινὰς ἢ δεσμωτήρια*, “showing that the sacred precincts of the idols are certain tombs or prisons.”] tombs. Arnobius, however, says in Book VI that “temples had been raised above funeral pyres.”

Yet Christians afterwards, on a different principle, made not only churches but also altars from the tombs of their martyrs. Minucius himself could well have seen such things. The matter is certainly thus: although our forefathers did many things in the name of religion which outwardly resembled what the pagans did, [Col. 0209A] nevertheless, because the purpose and use were different, they knew that their own sacred practices could be defended even while they condemned the *κακοζηλία* (“misguided imitation”) of others. How vigorously they mock the rites of Roman sacrifices! Yet their form was once not unlike that of the rites commanded to the Jews by divine law.

Although the Christians in the age of our Minucius could not proudly raise their own temples after the pagan model, they nevertheless possessed at least their crypts and even certain sacred buildings and houses in open and elevated places, as Tertullian says. They gladly assembled at the tombs of their martyrs, which they called *κοιμητήρια* (“sleeping places,” cemeteries). Eusebius writes that the emperor Gallienus, who was separated from Minucius’s age by no long interval, permitted them to have these.

Caecilius mocks the Christians because they said and believed that their people who had departed this life were not so much dead as asleep, and because they vaunted the resurrection of bodies. [Col. 0209B] Yet in his own Homer (*Iliad* XXIV.344) he had read *ὑπνώοντας ἐγείρειν* (“to awaken those who sleep”), and in Virgil (*Aeneid* IV.244), “to take away sleep,” when the subject is recalling the dead to life. What Octavius further answered here may be compared with what Theophilus, Athenagoras, Justin, and Tertullian had previously written on the same matter, for Minucius followed them.

Caecilius mocks the Christians (chapter 12) because they anoint corpses but do not crown them. Yet the Romans too, although they did not understand what they were doing, possessed funeral ointments. That little verse of Ennius is well known:

> A good woman washed and anointed the body of Tarquinius.

And although the Laws of the Twelve Tables abolished the anointing of corpses by slaves, as Cicero says (*On the Laws*, II.24), they nevertheless allowed another kind of anointing; and the jurists themselves include ointments among the legitimate expenses of a funeral (Law 37, *On Religious Matters and Funeral Expenses*). [Col. 0209C]

As regards “crowns for corpses,” Octavius admits that they seem foolish to Christians and that Christians therefore refuse to imitate the pagans in this practice. Tertullian, in *On the Crown* (chapter 13), says that “even the undertakers’ establishments are crowned by the world.” Cicero himself, in *For Flaccus* (chapter 31), mentions “a golden crown placed upon the dead body” of a certain Castricius. What the ancient Roman laws ordained concerning crowns for corpses, however, I have explained in my work on the Twelve Tables.

Finally, Caecilius mocks and resents the fact that among Christians “corpses are buried,” not “burned.” But that ancient saying is true: “Nothing is more foolish than foolish laughter.” What does Octavius say? [Col. 0209D] He answers simply that his custom of burial is ancient and better. Arnobius too gave this answer, for even after Minucius the question was raised again.

Yet the Romans could at least have read the second book of their own Cicero’s *On the Laws* (chapter 22), in which he defends and confirms this custom. Pliny too says in Book VII, chapter 54: “Cremation itself was not an ancient institution among the Romans; bodies were buried in the earth.” Tertullian, in *On the Crown* (chapter 12), says that it was not lawful for a Christian to cremate a body; and at the beginning of *On the Resurrection of the Flesh* he mocks those who, as he says, “burn the dead with the utmost cruelty.”

Furthermore, Augustine in Book XI of the *Confessions* indicates that some peculiar custom for the burial [Col. 0210A] of bodies existed in the church at Ostia. Whether it was already in use when Minucius was active there, I do not know.

It is ridiculous that Caecilius, a stern censor indeed, accuses the Christians because they were neither drenched in perfumes nor wreathed with garlands. It is astonishing that he does not meanwhile marvel that they nevertheless already used oil and chrism. The pagans themselves were accustomed to praise a sober, austere, and frugal life—that is, one free from perfumes. In the ideal commonwealth which Plato fashioned according to his own judgment, he expels Homer only after having drenched him in perfume, bound him with ribbons, and, as our Octavius says here, “crowned” him; by this he indicated that he did not wish to have citizens so effeminate.

And, not to go farther afield, Vespasian turned away from a certain man drenched in perfumes who was thanking him for obtaining a prefecture, and said: [Col. 0210B] “I would rather you smelled of garlic.”

But what would Caecilius not make into an accusation, since he even charges the Christians with holding flowers to their noses rather than placing them upon their heads as crowns? Yet Lucian himself, in his *Nigrinus*, more justly mocks the Romans themselves because they do not imitate the Christians in this respect, but act contrary to nature and plainly possess neither taste nor sensation. Add Tertullian, *On the Soldier’s Crown*.

Moreover, Caecilius, like another Lucian in the *Peregrinus*, ridicules the Christians because they worship a crucified man. Octavius briefly denies that the one whom they worship is merely a man, and retorts that their adversaries are rather “worshippers of men” (*anthrōpolatrai*, ἀνθρωπολάτραι), since they worship kings as gods and even swear by their genius; indeed, they punish someone who perjures himself in this way more severely than if anyone knowingly [Col. 0210C] deceived his own Jupiter by swearing an oath. I suspect that a certain constitution of Alexander Severus is being noted here; it has, however, been incorporated into the books of law, Law II, Code, *On Things Lent*. Tertullian, in the *Apologeticum*, certainly bears witness that Christians of old were unwilling to use such a formula of oath. But I am all the more surprised that it is commended in the laws of the later Christian Caesars.

Caecilius insultingly charges the Christians with “worshipping the cross itself.” Octavius denies it. Their adversary curses them as “gallows-bearers.” Our author—for he is not ashamed of the Christian cross—does not refuse to be called a cross-bearer in his own fashion, and, concerning the religious sign of his cross—which was certainly familiar to our ancestors of old—he replies with what Justin and Tertullian had written before him, and Lactantius afterward in Book IV, chapter 27. [Col. 0210D] For it is well known how highly Constantine valued it; certainly, in order that the matter might be less disgraceful in common estimation, he decreed that criminals should no longer be fastened to a cross. Julian the Apostate nevertheless did not cease, like Caecilius, to reproach the Christians with the worship of the cross in order to disgrace them, as may be understood from Cyril.

The shamelessness of the slander is astonishing. It eventually reached such a point that their adversaries charged the Christians with I know not what monstrous rites, “such portents as mad [Note: [Col. 0210D] Juvenal, *Satire* 15, at the beginning.] Egypt worships,” as a certain poet said. Caecilius even dares to pretend that they “worship the head of an ass,” although he was not the first to invent this. Octavius repels so foul a slander by denying it, and proves by recrimination that it could more truly be said of their adversaries, following his Tertullian (*Apologeticum*, ch. XVI), who relates both that Christians were commonly called ass-worshippers and that Christ himself had been portrayed by an impious painter with ass’s ears, like another Midas. [Col. 0211A] He indicates, however, that it was a fabricated tale, since Cornelius Tacitus had mendaciously related something of the kind about the Jews. Yet many years before Tacitus, Apion of Alexandria, in the time of Caligula, had accused the Jews of a certain “ass-worship” (*onolatreia*, ὀνολατρεία). Moreover, since Josephus had already refuted such a lie, Tacitus, who persists in it, is less deserving of pardon—and least of all are those who, with still greater shamelessness, bespatter the Christians with this reproach.

More disgraceful still is the fact that Caecilius, with the same lack of shame, cries out [Col. 0211B] that they “worship certain shameful parts, I know not what.” To what depths does his filthy abuse rush? Octavius considers it consistent with his own modesty not to refute this at greater length. Meanwhile, he is compelled to hear other charges no less abominable, as Caecilius declaims that the Christians’ meetings before dawn are criminal assemblies, polluted by incest and parricide, almost as the Bacchanalia once were at Rome. Octavius not only repels such charges from his own people but also turns them back upon their adversaries. How incestuous the rites of the Romans were is not unknown. For even their poet says, [Note: [Col. 0211D] Juvenal, *Satire* 6, verse 313.] “The secrets of the Good Goddess are well known.” They also sacrificed human victims for a long time, although among other nations they condemned this ferocity, which I will no longer call sacred but bloodthirsty and criminal. It is memorable, moreover, that Plutarch relates in his *Problems* that they advanced this as a pretext for [Col. 0211C] excusing their own conduct and condemning that of others. Yet it is astonishing that such rites were imputed to the Christians. This slander, however, was ancient and long-lived. The suspicion of promiscuous lust was readily increased by the credulity of certain people, who judge others according to their own character; by the nocturnal gathering of a mixed multitude; by the Christians’ calling one another brothers and sisters; and also by their greeting one another with a kiss. What am I to say of the fact that some shamelessly abused the kiss, as Clement of Alexandria both admits and laments in the *Paedagogus*? The Christians opposed to these charges many sufficient testimonies to their own most chaste modesty. But shameless malevolence listens to nothing: just as its tongue is unrestrained, so it has neither brow nor ears. Josephus indeed relates that Apion had long before fabricated something similar concerning the assemblies of the Jews. [Col. 0211D] Thus nothing remained for our people, oppressed by such infamy, except what Aeschylus aptly and elegantly says: “to commit the truth to time” (*tēn alētheian anatithenai tō chronō*, τὴν ἀλήθειαν ἀνατιθέναι τῷ χρόνῳ). They were not impostors who deceived people with words, nor clamorous and violent men who wished in turn to overwhelm their adversaries with taunts, curses, and defamatory pamphlets. They preferred to refute falsehood by the facts themselves and at last to conquer in this way, by sitting still and remaining silent; meanwhile, they sustained and consoled themselves with a good conscience. Thus they conducted a good cause well.

It is again astonishing that Caecilius regarded that “sharing of the name of brother” among them as so extraordinary, [Col. 0212A] since Ulpian himself wrote that one who is loved with brotherly affection, although he is not a brother, may nevertheless rightly be called simply “brother”; and this too has been incorporated into the books of law, Law 58, *On the Institution of Heirs*. Indeed, I have learned from a certain fragment of Philo, preserved in Eusebius’s *On Preparation* (*Peri proparaskeuēs*, περὶ προπαρασκευῆς), Book VIII, chapter 12, that even the Essenes of old, before the age of the Christians, addressed one another in this way.

More horrible is the other charge brought against them, “the crime of infanticide.” This slander began shortly after the age of Trajan and endured until the time of Constantine, together with the tragic suspicion of some Thyestean banquet. But whence came this suspicion? Was it because Christians were accustomed to say that they fed upon the body and blood of Christ? Augustine, by contrast, relates that some once believed that Ceres and Bacchus were worshipped by the Christians, because they heard that bread and wine were held in such importance in their mysteries and otherwise did not understand the matter. [Col. 0212B] What am I to say of Epiphanius’s account [Note: [Col. 0212D] Epiphanius, Heresy XLVIII, section XIV, p. 416.] that certain heretics once called Gnostics, Cataphrygians, and Pepuzians, who falsely claimed that they were Christians, committed the very thing that Caecilius here imputes to all Christians? But was it just that good men should therefore be accused of what was utterly foreign to them? In place of proof, their adversaries advanced reputation and rumor. Yet the civil laws answered on behalf of our people that this too was done without any right, and Quintilian himself [Note: [Col. 0212D] Quintilian, Book V of the *Institutio Oratoria*, chapter 3.] said that “it can befall anyone, even the most innocent, through the deceit of enemies spreading falsehoods, that he suffers under adverse rumor.” Octavius sufficiently shows how far removed the Christians were [Col. 0212C] from every kind of homicide when he relates that their religion did not permit them even to watch killings in gladiatorial games. Theophilus had previously said the same to Autolycus; Athenagoras said it at the same time in his *Apology*; Tertullian discussed it more fully in his book *On the Spectacles*; and Lactantius did so afterward in Book VI, chapter 20. Minucius also affirms, as does Tertullian, that our people did not taste the blood of a slaughtered animal. For through many centuries our people diligently observed the law of Noah, which the Apostles had reiterated and enacted anew, no less than the apostolic decree concerning fornication (*peri porneias*, περὶ πορνείας) from the same council. Certainly, if Caecilius had preferred to tell the truth frankly rather than to lie wickedly, he could have learned how honorable, religious, modest, and chaste was the Christians’ solemn meal, which they called the *agapē* (ἀγάπη), not only from our Tertullian’s *Apology* but also from a certain letter of his own Pliny to Trajan. [Col. 0212D] But what could restrain the insolence of abandoned abuse? I have said more about that meal in my annotations on that letter, and there is no need to repeat it now. Yet however innocent the Christians’ nocturnal assemblies were, the Law of the Twelve Tables, confirmed by many decrees, nevertheless stood in their way, and the judgments against unlawful associations were severe. Our people replied that the republic faced no danger from their gatherings, because they were utterly foreign to all ambition and to every thought of holding office; there was nothing in the republic to which they aspired, [Col. 0213A] but they were content with their own private condition, as Tertullian replies in the *Apologeticum*.

But to pass over now the remaining heads either of Caecilius’s accusation or of Octavius’s defense, it is helpful to observe this: although this ingenious and bitter slanderer either invents or exaggerates everything and adds certain lesser crimes against majesty, he nevertheless passed over the crime of high treason, which others had previously charged against the Christians and which seemed especially suited to crushing the accused at once. Did he conceal it because there was not even the slightest suspicion of it? This, at least, was the perpetual glory of our ancestors: no injuries could so provoke them that they became hostile in spirit toward princes or tyrants, although they were treated most outrageously by them; nor did they consent to any conspiratorial plots against them, though such plots were otherwise both plausible and frequent at that time; nor did they forget what was worthy of their patience, endurance, moderation, and self-restraint. [Col. 0213B] So far were they from being turbulent or seditious, or from being swept away by a monstrous desire for vengeance. For although they were surrounded by such multitudes that they could easily have accomplished whatever they undertook in this regard, they nevertheless considered it unlawful. Indeed, otherwise they would have abolished the very principles of their religion and overturned its foundations. More than that, they would have dissolved all the bonds of human society. It was well known what many philosophers ostentatiously proclaimed about tyrannicides. But our people did not allow themselves to be inflamed by such bellows—so far were they from being incited in the name of religion [Col. 0213C] to public parricide. Nothing was omitted that could have inflamed them, and patience repeatedly wounded is said to become madness. But religion restrained them and armed them only for invincible endurance. On this matter, which I hear is being debated even in the present age—and am astonished that it is—we shall elsewhere confirm our case from the continuous history of several centuries. For now I shall touch only briefly upon what Minucius could have said and what happened shortly before his lifetime.

Tertullian says to Scapula (ch. 2): “We are defamed in matters concerning the majesty of the emperor; yet Christians could never be found among the Albinians, the Nigrians, or the Cassians.” It is useful to append another passage from the same Tertullian, the ancient recollection of which it is of the greatest importance to revive in our own times. [Col. 0213D] “Whence,” he says in the *Apologeticum* (ch. 35), “came the Cassii, the Nigri, and the Albini? Whence those who lie in wait for Caesar between the two laurels? Whence those who practice wrestling so as to throttle him? Whence those who burst armed into the palace, more audacious than all the Stephani and Parthenii? From the Romans, unless I am mistaken—that is, from non-Christians.” I shall not be reluctant to illustrate even this passage from history. Avidius Cassius, governor of Syria, had risen against the emperor Marcus Antoninus, under the pretext that he wished to restore and preserve the republic, which Marcus’s lax indulgence was ruining. Yet none of the Christians, who were so numerous in Marcus’s army against the Marcomanni, belonged to the Cassian faction. Romans who were especially intimate with Commodus arranged for that impure tyrant, and most hostile enemy of our people, to be strangled at home. [Col. 0214A] Was any Christian present among them? Pescennius Niger in Syria, and afterward Clodius Albinus in Britain and Gaul, opposed Septimius Severus, who was striving toward imperial power with the spirit of a gladiator, since each believed himself armed with as good a right as Severus. For Tertullian himself, in his book *On the Pallium* (ch. 2), once acknowledged and called these men “Augusti” no less than Severus. Yet no Christians were found either in their army or in their faction. Plautianus, who stood nearest to the prince and possessed the greatest authority after him, sent his own prefect into the council chamber in order that Severus and Caracalla, by whom many cruel deeds were being committed, might be slain; and shortly afterward he himself burst into it. [Col. 0214B] Did the Christians follow Plautianus, though it seemed to be in their interest that those tyrants be removed? On the contrary, they treated and healed Severus, when he was already confined to bed, with their own oil, as Tertullian bears witness in *To Scapula*, where he also commemorates the Church’s solemn prayers for rulers. He then adds: “That we act according to the rule of divine patience is sufficiently evident, since, although we are so great a multitude of people—almost the larger part of every city—we conduct ourselves in silence and moderation. Far be it from us to resent suffering those things which we desire, or to contrive any vengeance for ourselves when we await it from God.” The things he repeats in the *Apologeticum* are not dissimilar, and they deserve to be impressed upon people in these times as well. He certainly says that the Christians could easily [Note: [Col. 0214D] Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, chapter XXXVII: “Even a single night, with a few small torches, could amply effect vengeance, if it were permitted among us to repay evil with evil.” Baldwin expressed Tertullian’s thought rather than his words; but in what immediately follows, the words themselves are taken from the same passage of the *Apologeticum*. (LINDNER.)] have avenged themselves “in a single night with a few small torches,” [Col. 0214C] if they had either been, or had wished to be, incendiaries—as they had nevertheless been called ever since the time of Nero. “But far be it,” he says, “that a divine sect should be vindicated by human fire, or should grieve to suffer that by which it is proved.” He says that, if they had wished to act openly and repel force with force, they certainly did not lack “the strength of numbers and troops.” But, he says, “under this discipline it is more lawful to be killed than to kill.” He says that they could even have conquered without arms by withdrawing and leaving the Roman world empty, had they wished to migrate elsewhere. For then there would have been no one left for the Roman emperor to rule. So few remained who were not Christians. But he indicates that our people wished both to remain citizens and not to pass over to the enemies of the Romans, while nevertheless [Col. 0214D] being called by the Romans not merely enemies, but enemies of the rulers and of the human race. Yet this injury was so manifestly unjust that even the enemies of the Christians were at last ashamed to act with such ingratitude and to speak so shamelessly.

Thus Caecilius, however shameless he was, blushed to fabricate against them any charge of high treason. He preferred to object to, carp at, lie about, and slander them in every other way. [Col. 0215A] Nor does he “ascribe to the Christians the cause of public calamities,” although at that time other adversaries were especially accustomed to do so maliciously. In Minucius’s most sorrowful age, the condition of the Roman Empire was indeed dreadful, and its dismemberment and confusion were horrifying. What need is there to say that every kind of evil then flooded in, and that the world was shaken and thrown into confusion by wars, fires, floods, earthquakes, the ruin of cities, and the destruction of peoples and kingdoms, and was finally exhausted by famine and a public plague? Yet Caecilius does not go so far as to slanderously declare—as the common people cried out at that time, and as was vaunted for many centuries both before and afterward—that this whole chaos ought to be charged to the Christians’ account and expiated with their blood. Before the age of Minucius, Tertullian said: “If the Tiber rises into the fields, if the sky [Col. 0215B] stands still, if the earth moves, if there is famine, if there is pestilence, immediately the cry goes up: ‘The Christians to the lion!’” [Note: [Col. 0215D] Certain words are missing from Tertullian’s *Apologeticum*, chapter 40, and should be supplied as follows: “If the Tiber rises to the walls, if the Nile does not rise over the fields, if the sky stands still,” and so forth. (LINDNER.)] The cry was no less hateful and monstrous in the time of Cyprian, as is sufficiently evident from his letter *To Demetrianus*. It was the same in the time of Arnobius. For in his books *Against the Nations* he too labors to free our people from this flame of public hatred and odium. What of Symmachus himself afterward? Does he not dare to sing the same refrain again? He certainly deserved to hear the cry once raised at Rome after the death of Commodus: [Note: [Col. 0215D] Lampridius, *Life of Commodus*, chapter 18, has transmitted both this and similar acclamations. (LINDNER.)] “The informers to the lion!” But our people were foreign to bloodshed and the desire for vengeance. Ambrose did not permit him to exult any longer over so false a charge. Yet when the city itself was captured and plundered not long afterward, the impious slanderers were not ashamed finally to ascribe even such a calamity to the Christian religion; and Augustine was once more compelled to confront so foul an accusation. For he admits that this was one reason why he wrote his books *On the City of God*. Caecilius therefore acts less maliciously: unlike the others, he does not hurl such a torch against our people, nor does he so outrageously burden their innocence. Rather, as though exalted by great victories and crowned with supreme prosperity, he arrogantly insults them as wretched, conquered, and enslaved; on this account he contemptuously depresses their religion as much as he gloriously exalts his own superstition. [Col. 0215C] For profane men depend in this way upon fortune and the success of events. Thus Cicero himself, in his speech *For Flaccus*, insultingly attacks both the nation and the rites of the Jews. From Josephus we also learn that Apion confidently reproached the Jews with their servitude and miseries [Col. 0215D] as testimonies of a false religion. It is astonishing, however, that even after the age of Constantine the emperor Julian attacked our people on the same grounds, as we learn from Cyril’s replies. How much more readily could Caecilius do this, who had seen Christians only as afflicted, wretched, poor, and insignificant? Thus, with great arrogance, haughtiness, and contempt, he spits upon them and tramples them down as “refuse and offscourings” (*katharmata kai peripsēmata*, καθάρματα καὶ περιψήματα)—to use the Apostle’s [Col. 0216A] words. But Octavius looks down upon his boastful spirit from a loftier elevation and opposes to it a certain holy pride, by which our people were rich even in poverty, free even in servitude, and, finally, victorious in the midst of death. Yet although Caecilius began by foaming at the mouth, intemperately pouring forth abuse, breathing threats, casting out bombastic horrors, and finally insulting Christ, he nevertheless yields soon afterward, conquered by the truth. Nor does he await the judgment of Minucius as arbiter and judge, but anticipates it of his own accord. This conversion is truly admirable, especially because it was so sudden. But it shows that many at Rome were capable of being healed, although they otherwise seemed abandoned and beyond hope, and that error readily yields to truth. Thus Caecilius could, as though by a formal surrender in law, be adjudged to Octavius when the latter claimed him. [Col. 0216B] He certainly does not refuse to be conquered and to surrender; struck, as it were, by a thunderbolt from Octavius’s speech, like another Paul he suddenly embraces, once admonished, the religion that he had attacked in ignorance.

I wish, however, that Minucius had also set forth for us the whole history of this *metanoia* (μετάνοια), or change of mind, so that we might understand by what rule, on what condition, with what sponsors, by what rite, and with what ceremony Caecilius, after returning to Rome, was enrolled in the association and communion of the Church. For the memory of that ancient custom is also worth seeking. But let us suppose that what Jerome, in his additions to Eusebius’s *Chronicle*, and Augustine, in Book VIII of the *Confessions* (ch. 2), relate concerning two other men—Arnobius and Victorinus—of the same condition, rank, nation, and ability, also happened to Caecilius. Indeed, [Col. 0216C] this Caecilius admits that, after he had understood what true religion is not, he desired an understanding, knowledge, and instruction in true religion; Minucius writes that this catechesis was postponed until the following day. But for that very reason I grieve all the more that this second lesson—which would have been the best and largest part of Minucius’s book—was not published, or at least is no longer extant. For it is not enough to refute falsehood; one must also teach the truth, so that both what God or religion is not and what God or religion is may be explained. But all is well: what we miss here can be supplied by Augustine’s book *On Catechizing the Uninstructed*, which elegantly describes both the rules and the form of ancient catechesis and also advises how one must deal with learned and literary people. I believe that catechesis in Minucius’s age was not dissimilar, and I wonder that it is not observed in our own times as well. [Col. 0216D] It is pleasing, moreover, now that we have heard Caecilius as accuser and adversary, to behold him, with circumstances reversed, as a catechumen. Catechumens were then also called “hearers” or “those hearing,” as is evident from many passages of Tertullian; they were especially teachable and by no means obstinate, as Lucian himself indicates in the *Philopatris*. Consequently, there were no contentious disputations with them; religion was taught by calm admonitions. After catechesis, those who had now given their names to the Church so that they might be initiated through Baptism were called “competentes,” or candidates; and it is pleasing to behold our Caecilius now in their order as well. After Baptism, the candidate finally became a participant in the “mysteries” (*tōn mystēriōn*, τῶν [Col. 0217A] μυστηρίων), from which he had previously been commanded to remain far away. Our ancestors certainly were not accustomed either to debate those mysteries indiscriminately or to discuss them in the presence of profane persons. Theodoret is a witness [Note: [Col. 0217D] Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus, in the *Dialogues* to which he gives the title *Eranistes*, Dialogue 2, p. 159, Leipzig edition, introduces the Orthodox speaker replying as follows to Eranistes when questioned about the Holy Eucharist: οὐ χρὴ σαφῶς εἰπεῖν· εἰκὸς γάρ τινας ἀμυήτους παρεῖναι. “It is not proper to speak openly, for perhaps some are present who have not yet been initiated into the mysteries.” Eranistes replies: αἰνιγματώδως ἡ ἀπόκρισις ἔστω. “Then let the answer be set forth in the form of an enigma.”] in the *Eranistes*. For they believed that such matters should be treated with greater reverence and even with greater caution, and they foresaw far in advance what the matter might otherwise come to. Thus, although, when their “assemblies” (*synaxeis*, συνάξεις) were accused, there seemed to be a strong reason why they should explain everything done in them, they nevertheless said nothing about the mysteries in court, nor did they dispute or litigate about them with their adversaries.

These, then, are the matters that I thought fit to mention briefly by way of preface, in order to prepare, as it were, a road toward reading Minucius’s *Octavius*—a reading that both commends to us the memory of Christian antiquities and rouses us to renew it, since we otherwise pursue Roman antiquities with such zeal. Would that the learned men at Rome, who leave no stone unturned and overlook no letter even upon the stones themselves in order to unearth something belonging to the ancient republic, would also collect the monuments of the ancient Church, in which that same city abounds, and raise up more Minuciuses who both lived and were buried there. [Col. 0217B] Enough—enough now—of new little books about religion. Let us labor instead to restore to the light the ancient remains of this kind; let us at last be students of learned antiquity rather than empty novelty; and let us both contemplate the portraits of our ancestors and display them to others, lest perhaps we seem to be new men. Yet although their religion and spirit were the same, their outward appearance and condition were not always the same as well. For they did not always lie harassed and cast down, nor were they either so ungrateful or so foolish as to refuse to enjoy the best legal status and condition when this was permitted them through Christian princes; nor were they so witless as not to use this benefit; nor so unjust as to regard their own emperors as equivalent to pagan tyrants—as we say—if they found something wanting in them; nor so peevish as to concede absolutely nothing to the public peace. I speak of those who were not degenerate. But Minucius did not see the splendor of a free Church; he saw only the squalor of an enslaved one. It is our duty, however, rightly to consider and distinguish both conditions and the circumstances of both periods, and prudently to observe this difference in their external form [Col. 0217D] and historical setting, so to speak, so that we may rightly use both the memory of antiquity and the examples of our ancestors. [Col. 0217C]

For here, I admit, [Col. 0218A] great prudence and the utmost caution are necessary. When a new law is proposed, the vote “As you propose” is often cast, but “I reject it” still more often; it is necessary, and the situation requires, that these formulas occur to us and meet with our approval. It is said that these words are carved upon an ancient marble at Rome:

> HAPPY ANTIQUITY, MORE NOBLE IN ITS WHITE PURITY THAN YELLOW GOLD.

But we would misuse its precedents disastrously unless we applied free and impartial judgment in distinguishing and choosing among them, lest either we confuse everything indiscriminately, or maliciously pass over what we ought to imitate, or intemperately insist upon things that do not suit the present age. When wills were once under discussion, a certain civil law replied that “the custom of most trustworthy antiquity must be retained.” Law XVIII, Code, *On Wills*. And when the boundaries and order of ecclesiastical government were under consideration, that declaration was heard at the Council of Nicaea: ΤΑ ΑΡΧΑΙΑ ΕΘΗ ΚΡΑΤΕΙΤΩ—“Let the ancient customs prevail.” [Col. 0218B] There was nevertheless no superstition that intemperately and violently insisted upon what the welfare of the republic rejected. And just as wise jurists, when a question arose concerning the right of magistrates, solemnly replied that one must consider not only what had been done at Rome but also what ought to be done—see Law XII, *On the Office of the Governor*—so too we must consider not merely what our ancestors did, but also at what time, under what circumstances, and for what purpose. Nor must we forget the warning of a certain law, that judgment should be made not so much according to examples as according to laws. I therefore act with the greatest willingness when I either cultivate jurisprudence and history in conjunction or at least frequently profess that they ought to be cultivated together—and indeed both of them in each domain: I mean human and divine affairs, or civil and ecclesiastical affairs. For their understanding and recollection require such a conjunction of these studies. Thus, if the emperor Tiberius rightly judged that military discipline—as [Note: [Col. 0218D] Suetonius, *Tiberius*, chapter 19: “He enforced discipline most rigorously, reviving from antiquity various forms of punishment and disgrace.”] Suetonius says—should be recovered from antiquity, we should much more strongly believe, and more correctly say, that civil and ecclesiastical discipline ought to be recovered from it in good faith and with sound judgment. [Col. 0218C] Meanwhile, because I perceive that one can err here in many dangerous ways, I shall again and again entreat all good and prudent men that, turning away from factions and remaining foreign to partisan zeal, they should first assign to antiquity only as much authority as is owed to it; and then calmly consider and observe not only what the ancient Christians in the time of Minucius did when they could do nothing else, but also what they desired, what they determined should be done when they had the power, and, indeed, what they finally did when they became free, in order rightly to establish both the republic and the Church. [Col. 0218D]

[Col. 0219]

# JOHN AUGUSTINE ERNESTI’S PREFACE TO LINDNER’S FIRST EDITION

[Col. 0219A] Greetings to the learned and Christian reader.

In the institutions of those through whom God restored to the human race the understanding and knowledge of all good literature, and especially of sacred literature, I find this principle: that they themselves joined sacred learning with humane learning, were no less zealous in reading the writers of the ancient Church, both Greek and Latin, than in preserving what they had received from the more ancient Greeks and Romans, and were the authors and advocates of the same conjunction for those who committed themselves to their discipline and authority. Not to seek examples from afar and among foreign peoples: Erasmus, whom everyone numbers among the foremost restorers of learned humanism, took no less care to be thoroughly versed in the writings of the ancient Doctors of the Church than in the profane writings of the Greeks and Latins. Greek and Roman antiquity owes him no more than ecclesiastical antiquity does, since he reviewed, corrected, and elucidated according to the evidence of manuscripts considerably more volumes by the Doctors of the ancient Church than by classical authors. [Col. 0219B]

In our own lands, however, the first man who emerged as a founder of humane learning here in our own Leipzig, Peter Mosellanus, interpreted Greek and Latin writers in such a way that, by interpreting the Holy Scriptures and lecturing upon ecclesiastical poets, he also led the young men who emulated his studies—that is, the flower of youth—to the understanding and reading of the Fathers. Caspar Borner retained this form of instruction received from him and handed it down to his own pupils. He too was a man, in the judgment of Joachim Camerarius (*Life of Philip Melanchthon*, p. 71), born to establish branches of learning, and Luther and Melanchthon accorded him as much authority in this Academy as they did to anyone. We have a suitable witness to this in Georg Fabricius, a pupil of Borner’s school, who received from him the same form of instruction. For in the letter in which he commends a corpus of Christian poets to Alexander, administrator of the bishopric of Merseburg, he says:

> At Leipzig he had heard Caspar Borner interpreting the hymns of Prudentius with the greatest learning; and Borner had for many years faithfully preserved for public use that course of reading, which had been handed down to him, as it were, from hand to hand by the most illustrious Peter Mosellanus. [Col. 0219D]

[Note: [Col. 0219D] You may also learn from the beginning of p. 30 of G. Fabricius’s *Commentary on the Christian Poets* that Prudentius was edited by Borner at Leipzig.]

Nor did Joachim Camerarius depart from this method. He was the third among those who established literature among us; both his training under Mosellanus and the *Notes on the Figures of Speech of the Lord Jesus Christ and the Apostles*, together with other little works concerning ecclesiastical matters, show clearly that he treated ecclesiastical writers studiously and diligently. [Col. 0220A]

What am I to say of Philip, that teacher of Germany? Who does not know that, although he was preeminent in Greek and Latin literature insofar as it is learned from non-Christian poets, orators, historians, and philosophers, he was likewise the foremost scholar of ecclesiastical literature in those times, especially in these lands, and so thoroughly versed in every class of writers of the ancient Church that he might have seemed to have studied nothing but them? And, what is more astonishing, while still almost a young man he had advanced so far in that field that, at the disputation on religion held in this city in the year 1519 under the authority of Duke George, when the theologians Carlstadt and Luther disputed with Eck, he even supplied passages from the Fathers during the debate for them to use against Eck. [Col. 0220B] From this it may be understood that the form of instruction then prevailing in those parts of Germany that attached the greatest importance to humane learning was to join both kinds of literature almost from earliest childhood.

Our native land thereafter possessed in Georg Fabricius a diligent guardian, advocate, and promoter of this course of instruction, as the very letter mentioned above declares. In it he gravely complains that those who wish to be, and to appear, devoted to Latin elegance generally neglect the writings of the ancient Doctors of the Church, although reading them supplies excellent learning useful to the Church and nourishes piety, for which one ought to have considerably greater concern than for elegance.

What of Barthius, Reinesius, [Col. 0220C] Rivinus, Rittershusius, and no small number of others? Who can possess any adequate acquaintance with them and yet not know that, in addition to their other learning—especially their knowledge of Latin literature—they treated, cultivated, and adorned this class of writings with the greatest diligence? How many others among more recent literary scholars could I mention who devoted very great attention to reading this class of writers? Among them was Johann Friedrich Gronovius, the most elegant interpreter of Roman authors of them all, who elucidated and corrected the ancient ecclesiastical writers with good observations no less than he did the Roman authors. [Col. 0220D]

That method, moreover, can readily be shown to possess many great advantages, and also a very considerable measure of refined enjoyment. First of all, the fact that the restoration of Greek and Latin letters contributed to restoring the purity and integrity of sacred doctrine—a fact proclaimed with one unanimous voice by scholars and learned theologians alike—came about chiefly because the study of those languages [Col. 0221A] was joined first with the reading and interpretation of the divine books, and afterward with that of the ancient books of the Church as well. For although those languages could sharpen minds to a sense of elegance and kindle a love of it, nevertheless, if their students had confined themselves to them—that is, to reading pagan books—they could have acquired nothing but contempt for those who transmitted knowledge of divine matters, because their teaching was contaminated and obscured by the filth of barbarism.

As for the report handed down concerning certain scholars of that period, that they recoiled from religion and despised and ridiculed divine things—if this is true, rather than a fabrication devised at the time by barbarous men for the purpose of accusation and odium, because they wished to avenge [Col. 0221B] the contempt shown them, as certain very learned men believe—I wonder whether this befell them because they rested content with reading and treating the books of the pagans, and were so captivated by their elegance and charm that they wished, or could bear, to touch nothing else. In such circumstances it could easily happen that they judged the discipline of religion from the dullness and folly either of the men who then professed it or of the books about religion that were in people’s hands. But when some men imbued with these languages devoted themselves to understanding the ancient Greek and Latin books of the Doctors of the Church—a capacity for understanding which their knowledge of those languages had given them—then they learned to understand the sacred books themselves more correctly, and realized that whatever folly and ignorance the ordinary discipline [Col. 0221C] of theology contained had been added to it through the fault of unlearned and barbarous men. By this their minds were kindled to the effort of freeing divine doctrine from the filth of scholastic errors and absurdities beneath which it had lain contaminated and oppressed for so many centuries.

And just as humane letters benefited religion in this way, so religion in turn, and the union of those letters with the reading of ecclesiastical writers, benefited them very greatly. For the barbarous Sophists and Theologasters had previously cried out that those letters were injurious to religion, or at least were wholly occupied with words, fables, and empty histories; that they contributed nothing to the higher disciplines; that they were devoid of matters great and useful for religion; and that for this reason they were useless and unworthy of the study [Col. 0221D] of youth.
