It is reported that this boast was made even in this Academy when Rhagius Aesticampianus began to teach them, Andreas Delitianus calling him “a fifth wheel on a wagon.” But their mouths were stopped when those languages were applied to the understanding of the sacred books and the Fathers of the Church, and it was understood that through them access was given to the true interpretation of the sacred books and to the true knowledge of theology.

Accordingly, when Peter Mosellanus began to interpret the Epistles of Paul—in which undertaking, especially given the circumstances of the time, he was assisted by reading the Greek and Latin Fathers—such crowds of young men gathered both for those very lectures and for his other lectures that those who had previously opposed humane letters now lay defeated. [Col. 0222A] And I wonder whether even now the excellent wares of humane letters would not be more marketable in the universities if their teachers—who in most places sit almost alone in their classrooms—were to unite their instruction with sacred studies in this manner. For the discipline of the humanities would both become more useful in itself, and young men would readily understand that these languages would benefit them not merely, as is now commonly believed, by giving them some ability to write Latin—an ability very many do not even seek, because they foresee little or no use for it under the plan of life they have adopted—but also, and much more, by furnishing an abundance of useful learning. They would gradually be attracted to desire that very learning and be led to acquire it.

For it certainly cannot truthfully be said that the books of the Doctors of the ancient Church [Col. 0222B] contain nothing from which we may derive assistance in every kind of learning that has some connection either with religion or with the proper treatment of sacred scholarship. It would take too long to demonstrate what assistance may be sought from them, and how, for theology, the interpretation of Holy Scripture, sacred and civil history, both branches of geography, and other arts and disciplines. This subject would require an entire commentary, which we are not now writing.

As for the eloquence appropriate for use in churches, how great a wealth of subject matter, arguments—especially arguments suited to the people—and excellent, even pointed and graceful, maxims will a properly directed reading of these works supply, provided that a teacher experienced in this class of books indicates [Col. 0222C] what is useful for this purpose in each one. In this class there are certainly many excellent and abundant writers. To say nothing of Chrysostom and other Greeks renowned for eloquence, there are Tertullian, Cyprian, Augustine, and especially Ambrose, together with Salvian, Peter Chrysologus, and Bernard. So far as concerns an abundance of good, pointed, and graceful maxims useful in ecclesiastical eloquence, Bernard is chief of them all; it is for no other reason that he was called “honey-flowing.”

Students will draw this abundance of maxims from such writers all the more beneficially because their works were written about true religion; by reading them, moreover, their sense of piety will be awakened, nourished, and strengthened. This is what Georg Fabricius chiefly sought in reading the ancient Christians, including their poets:

> “For,” he says (*Preface to the Christian Poets*, p. 4), “the sole end of study and learning is not that you should possess a polished and fluent tongue, but that the mind should be cultivated and abound in knowledge of great and useful things. Yet there are assuredly no subjects greater, more fruitful, or worthier than the knowledge of piety and religion that may be sought from these writers. Even if other qualities do not excel in them, they can nevertheless send their reader away a better and holier person.”

But in truth, the ignorance and indolence of our times—which reigns far and wide in this respect even among theologians—holds far too low an opinion of this entire class of writers, although it either does not know it at all or has scarcely ever glanced at it on a few slight and rare occasions [Col. 0223A]—that is, for the purpose of citing a testimony, and generally upon the indication of more recent writers.

To confine myself to the part most closely related to the study of eloquence: take one of Cyprian’s longer and more carefully written letters, such as the second; or Ambrose’s letter replying to Symmachus, who had requested in a most eloquent epistle that the emperors preserve the pagan religion; or Bernard’s letter to William, Abbot of Saint-Thierry, before whom he had been accused of zealously disparaging the Cluniac monks, in which he so clears himself that he portrays every one of their vices. These letters, to say nothing of other similar works, I would far prefer to all the Latin panegyrics appended to Pliny’s; indeed, I come very close to preferring them even to the ambiguous subtleties and learned flatteries of Pliny himself, on account of which [Col. 0223B] his *Panegyric* is admired.

While mentioning Bernard, I am reminded of his books *On Consideration*, written to Pope Eugene III, which I recently recommended to students in my lectures on ecclesiastical history. Those books, like the other writings of that man and of almost all the Fathers of the Church, are—as Luis Vives judged with perfect truth—not water that is clear, but water somewhat turbid; that is, their Latin and style are not entirely pure and elegant. Yet they were written, I think, in imitation of Cicero’s most famous letter to his brother Quintus on the proper administration of a province, and even contain certain thoughts from it, though dressed in different clothing. In them Bernard handles Eugene with no less skill and no less delicate a touch than Marcus handles his brother: he exhorts him by praising him, and so prescribes the proper manner of administering the pontificate that he gives the clearest description of all the vices of the pontiffs as they existed in those times, of Eugene himself, of the papal court, and of the whole clergy, everywhere observing propriety and avoiding offense. [Col. 0223C] Accordingly, when I first began to read those books, although accustomed to purer and more elegant authors, they nevertheless held me so firmly that I did not leave them until I had read them to the end. If I myself could be held by reading such works—although I was treating the chief masters of Greek and Latin eloquence with such zeal and, I think, not without a sense of elegance—and could derive from them a profit in learning that seemed by no means contemptible to me, should I suppose that others, less devoted to those humanistic studies and less advanced in them, could neither enjoy nor be assisted by them in their learning?

[Col. 0223D] But just as teachers of the humanities customarily prescribe a certain order, suited to the age and progress of students, among the older Greek and Latin authors whom we call classical, so also some such method must be employed in this class of writings. For not everything is suited to everyone, or to every period and every course of study. Youth requires one sort of work when it is chiefly occupied with Greek and Latin letters, another when engaged in the higher studies of theology; one sort at the beginning, and another when it has advanced farther in them and aspires to a certain perfection and abundance of learning.

My present purpose is not to discuss the entire method and complete order in which the Fathers should be read; it will be enough to offer some advice about the beginnings of that study. In these beginnings it seems to me most correct [Col. 0224A] that those books should be presented and recommended which have the closest connection with the other studies of that age, whether in subject matter or in style. There can be no doubt that the books especially belonging to this class are those which demonstrate the truth of the Christian religion and attack pagan superstition. For, first, a large part of their subject matter is either already known to that age from reading pagan writers, especially poets—which makes those books easier to understand—or in turn sheds light upon the books with whose study the student ought then chiefly to be occupied. This class of writings is also very closely connected in date with the classical authors, since the greater part of it comes from the period when pagan superstition was dominant. The authors of these books themselves, even those who lived later, such [Col. 0224B] as Augustine, Orosius, and others, were either teachers of eloquence—as is reported of most of them—or particularly devoted to eloquence and to humane letters of every kind. Accordingly, attention to diction and skill in speaking and argumentation generally appear in these more than in the others.

For if some contain a certain impurity of vocabulary, or are harsh and rough in style, as is Arnobius, they generally derived this from their native country. Young people may be protected from acquiring anything of the kind if such writers are deferred until the time when they have acquired some firmness in the art of writing well, at least with respect to purity of vocabulary.

My own reading of such books began with Minucius’ *Octavius*, which I first encountered at the school of Pforta. At that time some attention was given there to this reading, upon the recommendation of the teachers; and it was not easy to find one among the more advanced students [Col. 0224C] who did not possess one, and then another, such writer—even several Christian poets—to read on Sundays and other feast days. From this there was first instilled in me a love of ecclesiastical writers. It was afterward further confirmed when I saw that the greatest scholars had valued them highly, and when I first heard from my teachers, and then saw for myself, that the foremost theologians, from Luther’s time onward, had devoted very great effort to understanding the writings of the Fathers.

I therefore approved all the more highly the plan of the most learned Johann Gottlieb Lindner, most worthy vice-rector of the school at Salza in Thuringia, to publish Minucius once again and to elucidate him with such observations both by other learned men and by himself as would make the work easier and more profitable for school pupils to read. Upon examining the man’s notes themselves, I saw not only that many things had been well explained concerning words and subject matter, but also that he had employed a modest and exact criticism, occupied more with defending and explaining the received reading than with exercising conjecture, of which Minucius has experienced far too much. [Col. 0224D] Accordingly, I am confident that this little book will in many respects be useful and suitable for young people; and I earnestly hope that the most learned man, in addition to receiving other rewards for this learned labor and for his scholarship generally, may receive this above all: the knowledge that by it he has rendered useful service to Christian youth. I am confident that this very aim was foremost in his undertaking of this labor.

Written at Leipzig, on the fourth day before the Kalends of March.

[Col. 0226]

# JOHANN GOTTLIEB LINDNER’S LOGICAL ANALYSIS OF THE DIALOGUE

> **Note:** [Col. 0225B] Abraham Scultetus has already provided an analysis of this dialogue [Col. 0225C] in *The Marrow of the Theology of the Fathers*, Part I, Book X, chapter 9, p. 357. Various reasons, however, persuaded me not to retain it. I could never bring myself to believe that Caecilius was so changeable and so little consistent with himself that he advanced arguments which had little coherence and could not be reduced to some definite proposition. I therefore considered reducing Caecilius’ arguments to syllogistic forms. This was not a task of great labor once I reflected that almost two things were required of him: first, that he should relinquish the superstition in which he had been reared; second, that he should submit himself for initiation into the rites of the Christians. [Col. 0225D]
>
> He endeavored to reject the Christian religion by the following reasoning: Whatever religion is uncertain and less advantageous is certainly not to be embraced. But the Christian religion is neither certain nor advantageous. Therefore the Christian religion is not to be embraced.
>
> In favor of retaining his native religion, he formed this syllogism: Whatever religion is certain and useful must certainly be retained. But the religion received by the Romans is certain and useful. Therefore one must remain in the religion handed down by tradition.
>
> Caecilius’ entire disputation is contained in these two arguments.

## ΠΑΡΑΣΚΕΥΗ — PREPARATION

### THE WORK CONSISTS OF:

[Col. 0225A]

1. **What precedes**, where the author digresses into praise of Octavius the Christian. Caecilius, a worshipper of the gods who had come to Rome to visit Minucius, was recalled to the true religion by Octavius while they were walking. Chapters I–II.

2. **The accompanying circumstances**, where he explains what occurred on the way and how Octavius admonished Minucius not to permit his intimate friend to remain in error any longer. Chapters II–III in their entirety.

3. **What follows**, which explains the occasion for the disputation about religion arising from the rebuke just mentioned. Chapter IV.

## ΑΓΩΝ — THE CONTEST

The **TRANSITION** contains Caecilius’ admonition to Marcus [Col. 0225B] Minucius, the presiding judge, that he duly observe the obligations of his office. Chapter V.

> **Note:** [Col. 0225B] In Migne, the sections headed *Thesis* and *Antithesis* are printed in parallel.

# THESIS

## I

**Christians cannot possibly advance anything certain when introducing a new religion.**

### I.—Not in the article concerning God. This is proved:

a. From the condition of truth, which is uncertain, chapter V.

[Col. 0226A]

b. From the condition of the subject, which is ill-suited to investigating that truth, chapter V; for it lacks:

1. The causative means: instruction and learning;

2. The means of rank: wealth and resources.

c. From uselessness. For knowledge of oneself is sufficient for a blessed life, chapter V.

d. From the natural condition of man, who is lowly and cast down toward the earth, [Col. 0226B] ibid.

### II.—Nor in the article concerning creation,

which Christians wrongly attribute to God, because all things have been assembled by fortune and a certain chance in the form in which they are now seen, chapter V.

### III.—Nor in the article concerning Providence:

a. Because things once begun are continued by the law of necessity; and thus everything may more suitably be derived from the mechanical structure of bodies, chapter V.

[Col. 0226C]

b. Because of the absence of order:

1. In natural things, [Col. 0226D] chapter V;

2. In moral things, ibid.

## II

[Col. 0227A]

**One must remain in the religion handed down by one’s ancestors,** [Col. 0227B]

### I.—Because it is certain:

a. On account of the uncertainty of truth, which is evident from the preceding arguments, chapter VI;

b. On account of its antiquity: for we possess religions received through tradition, ibid.;

c. On account of the trust owed to our ancestors: for the nearer anyone approaches to the age of the gods, the greater the trust that must be placed in him, ibid.

[Col. 0227D]

### II.—Because it is useful.

For the Romans owed the greatness of their empire to the gods.

a. That the Romans were religious is evident from their reverence for:

1. Their native gods, chapter VI;

2. Foreign gods, ibid.;

3. Their institution of chaste virgins and priestly offices, ibid.

[Col. 0228A]

b. That this religion secured empire for them [Col. 0228B] is evident:

1. From its institution, because the Roman rites were instituted upon an excellent plan, chapter VII:

   a. To repay divine favor, ibid.;

   b. To avert wrath, ibid.;

2. From the outcome, because auspices neglected were followed by disaster, and those observed by success, ibid.;

3. From oracles and prophecies, not only of the most ancient times [Col. 0228C] but also of more recent times, ibid.

## III

[Col. 0228D]

**The Christian religion is not useful:**

1. Because of the utterly wicked morals of Christians. For if it were useful, it would surely display its first usefulness in correcting morals, chapter VII. But in fact Christians are:

[Col. 0229A]

a. From the lowest dregs of the populace, chapter VII;

b. Seditious, ibid.;

c. Silent in public, ibid.;

d. Increasing in number daily, chapter IX, like darnel;

e. Recognizable to one another by secret signs, ibid.;

[Col. 0229B]

f. Committing incest through the appellation “brother,” ibid.

2. Because of their far worse rites; for they:

a. Worship the head of an ass, chapter IX;

b. Adore the genitals of their priest, ibid.;

c. Supplicate a man hanging from a cross, ibid.;

d. Are initiated through the killing of an infant, ibid.;

e. Celebrate incestuous banquets, ibid.;

f. Conceal their rites, chapter X.

[Col. 0229C]

3. Because of several other monstrous beliefs:

### A.—In the article concerning God; for they worship:

a. A solitary God, and one who is also powerless, as is evident from the example of the Jews, chapter X;

b. An invisible God, which is absurd, ibid.;

c. An omniscient God, which is impious, ibid.

### B.—Concerning the end of the world.

They maintain that the world will someday perish, an opinion contrary to the law [Col. 0229D] of nature once established and eternal, chapter X.

### C.—Concerning the resurrection of the dead,

which he attacks with arguments:

1. **Κατ’ ἄνθρωπον — *ad hominem***: because, to establish the resurrection, many other absurdities must be assumed at the same time; for example:

a. That burial by fire must be rejected, lest the body intended for resurrection perish, chapter XI;

[Col. 0230A]

b. That punishments and rewards after death must be posited, because one error readily engenders another, ibid.;

c. That Christians themselves deserve punishment, since they are wicked, ibid.;

d. That God is unjust because he punishes a person’s lot, although all things are subject to fate, ibid.

2. **Κατ’ ἀλήθειαν — according to the truth**, by demonstrating its impossibility:

a. Through a dilemma, ibid.;

b. Through the absence of an example, ibid.

[Col. 0230B]

3. Because of the many evils to which it exposes its worshippers. For the worship of one God does not lead to happiness:

a. Because his worshippers are poor, chapter XII;

b. Because they are weak and afflicted by calamities, ibid.;

[Col. 0230C]

c. Because they are exposed to tortures inflicted by others, ibid.;

d. Because they are forsaken by God, ibid.;

e. Others are happy without God, ibid.;

f. It calls them away from honorable pleasures, such as:

1. Processions and spectacles, ibid.;

2. Foods tasted beforehand and drinks poured as libations, ibid.;

g. It condemns the use of lawful things, such as flowers, [Col. 0230D] ibid.;

h. It deprives the dead even of the honor owed them by forbidding them to be crowned, ibid.;

i. Nor does it compensate for the loss of the present life with future happiness, ibid.

## IV

**Summary of the entire disputation.**

1. One must abstain from investigating divine matters:

a. Because truth is above us, chapter XII, ibid.;

b. Because of the indolence and rudeness of those who devote themselves to this [Col. 0231A] study, chapter XII;

c. From the examples of Socrates, Arcesilaus, Carneades, the Academics, and Simonides the lyric poet, chapter XIII.

2. Matters that are doubtful should therefore rightly be left alone, ibid.

## V. EPILOGUE

It contains:

1. Caecilius’ challenge [Col. 0232A] to Octavius, inviting him to reply, chapter XIV;

2. Minucius’ address to Caecilius, warning him not to exult before both sides have concluded their speeches, ibid.;

3. Caecilius’ reply, in which he reproaches Minucius for interrupting him with a most weighty address, and promises that he will be an attentive hearer of Januarius, chapter XV in its entirety.

# ANTITHESIS

[Col. 0225B]

## I

**The path to attaining certainty is readily accessible, because:**

### I.—That uncertainty does not lie in truth,

but in the judgments of men investigating truth; and it arises from an obscurity that is not objective but subjective, chapter XVI.

[Col. 0226A]

b. The external condition of human beings in no way impedes truth, chapter XVI:

1. We can acquire certain truths even without learning;

2. Wealth draws people away from wisdom more than poverty does.

c. I grant that knowledge of oneself is salutary, but without investigation of the universe it makes less progress, chapter XVII.

d. Man’s natural condition, since he stands erect, commands him rather to look toward heaven.

[Col. 0226B]

### II.—God is the creator of this universe.

This is evident from the order of things established toward a definite end, which assuredly cannot be the product of fortuitous chance, chapter XVII.

### III.—Providence exists. This is proved:

a. From perfection in every respect, chapters XVII–XVIII, which is observed:

1. In the universe, for example:

   α. In the four seasons of the year;

   β. In the waters;

   γ. On dry land; [Col. 0226C]

   δ. In living creatures;

   ε. In man;

   ζ. In the manner of birth.

2. In the individual parts of the universe, § 3:

   α. Britain;

   β. Egypt;

   γ. Mesopotamia;

   δ. The East.

b. From the analogy of a well-built house, chapter XVIII.

[Col. 0226D]

## DIGRESSION I

### On the Unity of God

This is proved:

1. By Socratic induction, with examples drawn:

a. From earthly governments, chapter XVIII;

[Col. 0227A]

b. From social animals, ibid.;

2. From God’s eternity, ibid.;

3. From his omnipotence, ibid.;

4. From his other perfections, which belong to one, not to many, ibid.;

5. From the absence of a name for him, ibid.;

6. From the testimony of the common people, ibid.; of the poets, chapter XIX, ibid.; and also of the philosophers, ibid.

## II

**It is foolish to wish to remain in a religion that is indeed false, merely because it was handed down by one’s ancestors.** [Col. 0227B]

This is proved:

a. By denying that all things are uncertain; Providence is proved, chapter XX;

b. By distinguishing between a fabulous antiquity and one that loves truth: the latter, not the former, must be followed, ibid.;

c. From the doubtful credibility of the ancestors, ibid.

## DIGRESSION II

### That Those Whom the Pagans Worshipped as Gods Were Human Beings

[Col. 0227C]

This is proved:

1. By showing how this came about, tracing the origin of the gods farther back from historical accounts, chapter XX;

2. From the testimonies of philosophers and historians, chapters XXI–XXII;

3. From human passions, chapter XXI;

4. From the testimonies of poets, chapter XXII;

5. From their birth and death, chapter XXIII.

## DIGRESSION III

### On the Origin and Vanity of Idols

[Col. 0227D]

1. Their origin, chapter XXIII;

2. Their vanity, chapter XXIV.

### II.—It is utterly false that the Romans owed their empire to the gods, chapter XXV.

a. Because the Romans were not so much religious as sacrilegious with impunity.

This is proved indirectly, by a disjunctive argument. If the Romans received and possessed their kingdoms from the gods, they had them:

1. Either from foreign gods;

2. Or from their native gods;

3. Or because of their more religious worship.

[Col. 0228A] But not from foreign gods, who would rather have protected their ancient worshippers if they possessed any power, chapter XXV;

Nor from their native gods, who are diseases and obscenities rather than gods, ibid.;

Nor because of purer worship, since for virgins unchastity proved more fortunate than chastity was secure, ibid.

Therefore the Romans in no way owe their empire to the gods; rather, it is the spoil of audacity, ibid.

b. Foreign nations possessed empires [Col. 0228B] even without Roman superstition, ibid.

2. Auspices failed many times; therefore the fallacy of treating a non-cause as a cause is committed, chapter XXVI.

3. Oracles very often lied; therefore the outcome must be attributed not to design [Col. 0228C] but to chance, ibid.

## DIGRESSION IV

### On the Existence and Machinations of Demons

Here are described:

1. Their existence, chapter XXVI:

a. By description, ibid.;

b. By testimonies, ibid.

2. Their machinations, chapter XXVII in its entirety.

## DIGRESSION V

### On the Perverse Judicial Examination of Christians

This examination, instigated by demons, is perverse because it is conducted:

1. Concerning things unknown and uninvestigated, chapter XXVIII;

2. Because it does not admit a defense, [Col. 0228D] ibid.;

3. Because it compels the accused not to confess but to deny, ibid.

## III

1. **The reports circulated about the crimes of Christians are partly manifestly false and disseminated by certain malicious persons at the instigation of demons; others are indeed partly true, but corrupted by hostile interpretation and by the intermixture of falsehoods.**

[Col. 0229A]

a. He denies that this follows from the fact that Christians refuse the honors and purple robes of the pagans, chapter XXXI;

b. He denies it by explaining that Christians gathered together behave with the same quietness as they do individually, ibid.;

c. He concedes it, but points out that this happens because the pagans would be ashamed to hear them publicly, ibid.;

d. He concedes it, but teaches that this is grounds for praise, not accusation, ibid.;

e. He concedes it, but removes the charge because they recognize one another not by a mark on the body but by a sign of innocence, ibid.;

[Col. 0229B]

f. He denies it and defends the innocence of the fraternal appellation, ibid.

2. **Most of the things you spread abroad about our rites are false; not a few are distortions.**

a. He denies and turns the charge back upon them, chapter XXVIII;

b. He denies it and returns the insult, chapters XXVIII–XXIX;

c. He denies and turns the charge back upon them, ibid.;

d. He denies and turns the charge back upon them, chapter XXX in its entirety;

e. He denies and turns the charge back upon them, chapter XXXI;

f. He concedes it, but points out that it is done justly, chapter XXX.

[Col. 0229C]

3. **The teaching of the Christians is entirely sound. Hence:**

### A.—In the article concerning God:

a. He advises that a distinction be made between the ancient Jews, obedient to the divine law, and the more recent, disobedient Jews, chapter XXXIII;

b. He teaches that God’s invisibility is rightly affirmed, chapter XXXII;

c. He asserts that God’s omniscience rests upon the strongest arguments, chapters XXXII–XXXIII.

### B.—The doctrine concerning the end of the world

is contrary neither to the law of nature nor to the opinions of the philosophers, chapter XXXIV.

[Col. 0229D]

### C.—A reply is given to the objections concerning the resurrection of the dead.

a. Burial by fire is rejected not to facilitate resurrection, but so that the ancient custom of burying bodies may be followed, chapter XXXIV;

[Col. 0230A]

b. The pagans also posit punishments after death, but dread those same punishments, ibid.; chapter XXXIV;

c. Christians are nevertheless much better than pagans, ibid.;

d. He concedes that fate exists, but that it is free, because of God’s omniscience, by which he foreknows future events, chapter XXXVI.

2. **The possibility of resurrection is affirmed:**

a. Both by the opinions of philosophers and by arguments drawn from reason, chapter XXXIV;

b. To wish to see the example of a man who has risen from the dead [Col. 0230B] is just as absurd as it would be to demand that the sun rise at nightfall and that trees blossom in winter. Examples of those rising will certainly appear, but in their proper time, ibid.

3. **Christians and pagans do not agree about what is good or evil.**

a. This poverty is not a matter of disgrace but of glory; it is not forced but voluntary, chapter XXXVI;

b. Courage is strengthened by infirmities, virtue by calamities, [Col. 0230C] § 8;

c. We glory when subjected to punishments, trusting in God’s assistance, chapter XXXVII;

d. We are not abandoned by God but tested, ibid.;

e. Happiness without God cannot be secure, ibid.;

f. The pleasures from which we abstain are not honorable but corrupt and unlawful, ibid.; this is proved there with regard to:

1. Processions and spectacles, §§ 12–13;

2. The remnants of sacrifices, which are offered as libations to demons, chapter XXXVIII;

g. Not the use but the abuse of flowers is condemned, [Col. 0230D] ibid.;

h. The custom of crowning the dead is contrary to reason, ibid.;

i. Christians not only live in tranquillity but are also blessed in the hope of future happiness, ibid.

## IV

1. **No one should be deterred from investigating divine matters, because:**

a. Truth is not above us but in our possession, ibid.;

b. We display wisdom not by our garb but by our mind, [Col. 0231A] chapter XXXVIII;

c. The examples of the philosophers teach us nothing, ibid.

2. Things that were once doubtful are no longer doubtful, since the truth of the divinity has now come to maturity.

## V. EPILOGUE

It shows:

1. What impulses Octavius’ speech [Col. 0232A] left in the minds of his hearers, chapter XXXIX in its entirety;

2. Caecilius’ confession, in which he acknowledges that he has been defeated, chapter XL;

3. The postponement of the question concerning matters for which fuller instruction was required, ibid.;

4. Minucius’ congratulations, joined with thanksgiving to Octavius, chapter XLI, §§ 1–2;

5. The joyful departure of them all, ibid.

[Col. 0231]

# MARCUS MINUCIUS FELIX’S *OCTAVIUS*

> **Note:** [Col. 0231C]
>
> **M. Minucius Felix.** The Minucian clan possessed several surnames: Rufus, Thermus, Faustus, Macer, Fundanus, and among them also Felix. An ancient Roman inscription in Gruter, p. 918, reads:
>
> **SACRED TO THE DIVINE SPIRITS OF THE DEAD. QUINTUS MINUCIUS FELIX.**
>
> It is written with a *c*, because it is not derived from *minutus* (“diminished”); the short quantity of the syllable also requires this. Silius Italicus VII.523:
>
> > Without delay, once the rampart was demolished, Minucius’ madness  
> > Burned with the desire at once to destroy and to perish.
>
> **CELLARIUS.**
>
> **Octavius.** This is the title of the dialogue, taken from its principal interlocutor, just as Cicero entitled his dialogues *Cato*, *Lucullus*, *Brutus*, and *Laelius*, in imitation of Plato, whose *Phaedo*, *Alcibiades*, *Socrates*, and other books bear the names of their principal speakers. Who Octavius was may be learned from chapters I and II, to the extent that information about him has been handed down to us. Below, [Col. 0232C] in chapter XV, he is called by his full name, Januarius Octavius. The other interlocutors are Caecilius Natalis, still a pagan at the time but a Christian after the conversation, and our own Marcus Minucius Felix, who in this dialogue is sometimes called merely by his praenomen, Marcus. See chapters III and V. **CELLARIUS.**

(C)

# PROEM

[Col. 0231B] In this dialogue Caecilius is introduced as a man devoted to pagan superstitions. By various arguments he attempts to prove that no one should abandon the ancestral worship of the gods; that no one should make an anxious inquiry into religion, but that the ancient religion should be retained and the new rejected. Octavius, on the other hand, had rejected that impious worship and, together with Minucius Felix, enrolled himself in the Christian profession. He so completely overturns every argument of Caecilius, and demonstrates the truth of the Christian religion with arguments of such weight, that Caecilius, broken and wholly convinced by the most serious disputation, embraces the true religion with a joyful and grateful heart. The author first presents Caecilius’ speech in defense of the worship of the gods. [Col. 0232B] He then supplies Octavius’ reply to each individual part of Caecilius’ discourse.

# CHAPTER ONE

> **Note:** [Col. 0232C]
>
> **Most faithful companion.** Buzelius interprets this in a military sense, namely, that our Minucius, in accordance with Roman custom, had as a young man shared Caecilius’ military quarters. It is incumbent upon him to prove whether that custom remained so consistently in use in later centuries; for we impose upon no one this burden of proof concerning Minucius himself. It is better to understand the expression generally as a companion in labor and study. **LINDNER.**
>
> **So great a sweetness.** Wopkenius thinks the text should be emended to “only sweetness,” but with insufficient justification. **LINDNER.**
>
> [Col. 0233A] **Departing.** From the entire context of the discourse it is perfectly clear that our Felix committed this dialogue to writing after Octavius’ death; therefore the reading should be *decedens*, “dying.” [Col. 0233B] Cicero and other excellent writers use the word in this way very frequently. Phaedrus, Book IV, fable 4: “A certain man, when dying, left three daughters.” Sulpicius Severus, *Sacred History*, Book I, chapter 7: “When Sarah was one hundred and twenty-seven years old, she died.” The same historian uses it everywhere else in the same way.
>
> Claudian, however, writes in *Against Rufinus*, Book II.10:
>
> > As consolation for death,  
> > A common destruction will suffice; nor shall I depart in terror beforehand:  
> > Together with life, power must be relinquished.
>
> But in that passage certain manuscripts read “I shall die”; correctly, indeed. **DAVIS.**
>
> —If you listen to Gruner in the *Transactions of the Latin Society of Jena*, vol. IV, p. 209, the editors’ reading must be retained in the same sense. But the learned man appears to establish this with examples that are not sufficiently apposite, such as “departing from life,” “I depart from life,” and “the departure from the body.” Passages should have been produced in which the verb *discedo* (“depart”) is used by itself and is understood absolutely and beyond dispute of death, as is certainly established for the verb *decedo* (“die”). [Col. 0233C] **GALLAND.**
>
> —There is nothing that compels us to think of death, as Gronovius does, merely because of a slight imitation of Cicero, who says at the beginning of the *Brutus*: “Because that excellent man was cut off at a most unfavorable time for the republic, and left us with a sorrowful longing for both his authority and his wisdom.” For:
>
> 1. Minucius could have written these words just as readily after Octavius’ departure from Rome as after his death.
>
> 2. There is remembrance of the absent no less than of the dead.
>
> 3. Longing for an absent friend is immeasurable; longing for a dead friend is sorrowful and not easily endured.
>
> 4. Octavius was still young at the time, since his children were infants.
>
> 5. I doubt whether *discedere* by itself is used to mean “to die.”
>
> **LINDNER.**
>
> **An extraordinary and holy man.** Even pagans called a man or woman “holy” when distinguished in morals and virtue. Among Christians, one who kept the faith pledged to Christ and preserved his Baptism inviolate was called holy. This designation denotes both religion and morals. But if anyone was marked by wicked conduct, he then ceased both to be and to be regarded [Col. 0233D] as a Christian. **RIGALTIUS.**
And in playful and serious matters. The distinguished Heumann reads: “and in serious matters.” But no alteration is needed. Those ancient authors of the second and third centuries certainly favor such verbal abbreviations, especially those who employ a brief and concise style and pursue abundance of substance rather than words. I would not hesitate to say that sufficiently numerous examples could be sought from Tacitus, Pliny, Suetonius, and other writers of that period. MENCKEN.—Thus Livy, 34.7.14: “And you ought to keep them in your power and guardianship.” Tacitus, *Histories* 4.36: “Abandoning themselves to luxury and banquets and nocturnal gatherings.” Pliny, *Panegyric* 21.3: “In our hearts and judgments you were father of the fatherland.” LINDNER.

Would will or reject the same things. Thus Heraldus printed it, on the authority, unless I am mistaken, of the Royal manuscript. Rigaltius and Sigismund Gelenius, however, have “to will or reject the same things,” which the distinguished Gruner explains as infinitives possessing the nature of nouns. Wopkenius, to whom these four words seem to savor of a gloss, should by no means be heard. Yet he himself, as though placing little confidence in this conjecture of his, immediately adds: [Col. 0234A] “Not infrequently the same or nearly the same thing is thus reiterated in different words, without necessity, and that by asyndeton [ἀσύνδετον]”; and on this point he appeals to chapter 3, “would dart up, would emerge”; 5, “a matter for indignation, for grief”; 11, “dead, extinct”; 37, “be burned, be cremated”; 24, “they know, they are aware.” The distinguished Heumann wishes the text to be read thus: “would harmonize, and would will the same things whether he wished or not.” But F. O. Mencken proves with sufficiently numerous examples that ancient authors very frequently employed this manner of expression; to these I add Pliny, book X, Letter 50: “It remains for you to send a surveyor or architect.” Plorusi [?], 9.10: “Lest power be corrupted by isolation or delay.” Our Minucius, 20: “Antiquity, delighted or captivated by fables.” The same, 25: “By whose food or disgust.” There can therefore be no doubt that Felix could have spoken as the text is commonly read. I would, however, more readily believe that he deliberately did so, the more clearly he himself understood that care had to be taken lest refined ears be offended by the repetition of those two little words of the same form and sound. LINDNER.

You would have believed that one mind . . . had been divided. There is no fault in these words. Lactantius, *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, chapter 8: “For they could not have remained united in such faithful friendship unless there had been one mind in both.” See Persius, *Satire* V.23 and the scholia there; and Jerome, Letters I and XV, [Col. 0234C] ed. BB. DAVIS.

Thus, he alone privy to my affections, himself my companion. I understand this as follows: “Thus he who alone shared my affections—as that most trustworthy companion himself can testify—also shared my errors.” Here is a similar passage in Cicero, who writes of Curio in book VII, Letter 32: “He is, as you know, among those dear to me.” Minucius might perhaps have expressed this as follows: “He himself shares my confidence, among those dear to me.” Scheffer deletes *conscius* (“privy”) and thinks the text should be read: “Thus my companion in affection himself was my companion in error.” Gronovius reads: “Thus he alone was privy to my affections, himself my companion in errors”; and he maintains that in these words Octavius confesses concerning himself that they scattered their sexual favors indiscriminately, when he acknowledges that his youth was spent according to their fashion. Heumann reads: “Thus he alone shared his affections, a companion in errors, when, after the mist had been dispelled, . . . I emerged.” The reasons why I cannot accept this emendation are, first, that several words must be thrown out, and I do not see how that can be justified; and, second, that an excellent part of the discourse [Col. 0234D] disappears. For Minucius affirms three things about his Octavius: first, that he was his friend; second, that through love for him he likewise adhered to his error; third, that together with him he returned from error into the light of truth. In Heumann’s emendation, however, the second member is absent. Let the reader observe besides the elegant play on words: *conscius* and *socius* (“privy” and “companion”), *amoribus* and *erroribus* (“affections” and “errors”). LINDNER.

Of wisdom and truth. That is, of true wisdom, namely Christian wisdom. Thus Tertullian called women who had attained wisdom “Christian women”; and he said that Socrates was wise “in relation to the truth” when he approached more closely to Christian doctrines. RIGALTIUS.

Went on ahead. So it stands in the manuscript; but the Roman edition, which is the earliest of all, has “went ahead.” Nothing, however, should be altered against the authority of the manuscript. Plautus has this form in *Menaechmi* 5.8.8. Compare, concerning *concurrere*, *decurrere*, and *procurrere* in the same form, Freinsheim’s index to Florus, s.v. *concurrere*. LINDNER.

Still clinging even now. Minucius speaks thus with reference to the time or event being described here. [Col. 0235B] LINDNER.—A sound reading, which various editors had corrupted, some printing *etiamnum* (“still”), others *etiam tunc* (“even then”). Apuleius, *The Golden Ass* 4: “And after dragging him a little way back from the road, they cast him down a very high precipice onto the nearest road, still breathing even now.” Here “even now” is Greek *eti* (ἔτι), “still.” HERALDUS.

**SUMMARY.—From the very opening of the dialogue, Minucius relates how pleasantly he was entertained by the recollection of the things that had happened to him with Octavius while the latter was staying with him at Rome, and especially by the memory of this debate.**

## I

### (I) 1

[Note: [Col. 0232C] To present a more exact collation and truer representation of the one surviving manuscript of the dialogue *Octavius*, numbers have been inserted into the text. Some of them, namely the Roman numerals, indicate the chapters or divisions of the manuscript; the others, that is, the ordinary numerals, indicate its folios. EDD.]

As I reflected and reviewed in my mind the memory of Octavius, my good and most faithful companion, such sweetness and affection for the man took possession of me that I myself seemed somehow [Col. 0233A] to return to the past, rather than to recall through memory things already completed and run their course. Thus, the more the sight of him was withdrawn from my eyes, the more deeply it became entwined with my heart and almost with my innermost senses.

### (II)

And not without reason did this excellent and holy man, when he departed, leave us with an immense longing for him, seeing that he himself had always burned with such great love for me that in both playful and serious matters his will harmonized equally with mine: he would will or reject the same things. You would have believed that one mind had been divided between two persons. 2 Thus, he alone was privy to my affections, himself my companion in errors; and when, after the mist had been dispelled, I emerged from the depth of darkness into the light of wisdom and truth, he did not reject me as a companion but—what is more glorious—went on ahead. And so, as my thought ranged over the whole period of our shared life and intimacy, my mind’s attention came to rest especially upon that discourse of his by which, through a most weighty debate, he restored Caecilius, who even then still clung to superstitious vanities, to true religion.

## CHAPTER II

[Col. 0235A] [Note: [Col. 0235B]

**CHAPTER II.—While their years were still innocent.** This refers to their tender years, which are generally ignorant of crimes; for Fulvius Ursinus dealt badly with the passage when he judged that the word “years” should be expunged. DAVIS.—Prudentius speaks of “innocent little age” in the contest of the martyr Romanus; Tacitus, book III, of “guiltless age.” HERALDUS.—Lactantius, book I, chapter 20: “When,” he says, “without any regard for natural affection, they destroyed tender and innocent souls—the age that is especially dear to parents,” etc. WOWER.—“While their years were still innocent.” Wopkenius thinks that the children must certainly be understood as those who are “still by reason of, or amid, their innocent years,” with the participle “existing” left understood by a conventional ellipsis. Minucius called the years “innocent,” just as Seneca called years “weary,” *Hippolytus* 267, and Quintilian “untrained years,” *Institutes of Oratory* I, chapter n. BURMAN.—Thus, I believe, the received reading [Col. 0235C] stands sufficiently confirmed, and there was no reason for Heumann to rewrite it: “and, what is more lovable, with their children still innocent.” I add that these words can be explained more conveniently as follows: “with the children still innocent through their years,” that is, during or because of their years. Cortius, on Cicero, *Letters* II, Letter 10, §5, certainly teaches that the ablative must sometimes be explained in this manner. Mencken interprets “children innocent in years” as “children whose years are innocent.” LINDNER.

**Speech . . . sweeter.** Meursius thinks that the text should be restored to: “speech, sweeter through the very brokenness of a stumbling tongue,” and Chr. Cellarius indeed printed it thus. But, to say nothing of the cacophony [κακοφωνία], the common reading, confirmed by the Royal manuscript, does not demand a physician’s hand; for it is the not uncommon construction known as apposition, concerning which G. J. Vossius, *On Construction*, chapter 2, may be consulted. See also Caspar Barthius, *Adversaria* XLIII.25. DAVIS.—The celebrated Heumann endeavors to evade the charge of cacophony brought against this emendation by citing for that purpose a passage [Col. 0235D] from Jerome, *Letters*, p. 49: “A chattering and stammering tongue becomes sweeter through its stumbling.” But who does not see that this passage is very different from one in which the ablative case is repeated five times? LINDNER.

**With uncontrollable joy.** I read “unrestrained.” Catullus, *Epigram* 36, and Tacitus, *Histories* IV.44, likewise spoke of “unrestrained” love—that is, love that is immoderate and renders a man no longer master of himself. In Lactantius, book V, chapter 1, scribes likewise wrote “uncontrollable” in place of “unrestrained.” HEUMANN.—I do not understand what reason Heumann has for demanding that “unrestrained” be read in place of “uncontrollable.” The word *impatient* is of the kind used especially of violent emotions, and so can correctly be used of joy. For if the ancients called grief “impatient,” I do not see why it should be thought less appropriate to attribute this word to joy, which possesses the same power to agitate the mind. Thus Justin, speaking of grief, 12.15: “He consoled some who were grieving rather uncontrollably”; and 32.33: “Offended by these events, Philip grieved day by day more uncontrollably over Demetrius’s death”; Aurelius Victor, *On the Caesars*, chapter 6: “Grieving rather uncontrollably because Piso had been preferred to him for adoption”; and in the *Epitome*, chapter 14: “Burning with grief and unable to endure it”; Pliny, book IX, Letter 22: “He grieves as one who does so most uncontrollably”; and Tacitus, *Annals* IV.17: “Then indeed he grieved uncontrollably that young men should be placed on a level with his old age.” MENCKEN.—Even if I were to concede as fully as possible that joy can be called “impatient” just as grief can—which I could scarcely believe—I nevertheless very much doubt whether unexpected, sudden, and present joy is so called. LINDNER.

**For my body.** Heumann writes “of my body.” But the construction of the substantive verb with the dative case is sufficiently worn smooth by usage. See, however, Bunemann on Lactantius V.2.5. LINDNER.

**For drying the humors**, in place of “in order to dry the humors.” For they used sea baths whenever they had contracted weakness because of unhealthy internal humors, with their sinews rendered too relaxed and lax. Suetonius, *Augustus* 82.5. Add Scriverius’s notes on Martial 10.13. GRONOVIUS.—Vitruvius also mentions this treatment, book V, [Col. 0236C] chapter 9. I also refer here to Symmachus, book VIII, Letter 46. Jacob Heinrich Christian Adami interpreted that passage in a special dissertation published at Leipzig in 1734 and reviewed there the following year in the *Acta Academica*, p. 120 ff. HEUMANN.

**At the vintage.** Heumann writes “because of the vintage.” This injury is inflicted upon an innocent little word. No one sufficiently acquainted with the many passages in authors—a large portion of which were collected by Johann Friedrich Gronovius on Seneca, *On Benefits* IV.6—in which *ad* denotes “at that time” or “about that time,” will judge it to have been less appropriately placed here. “Holidays at the vintage” are those held at vintage-time, namely vintage holidays; and, to tell the truth, the expression is more elegant with *ad* than it would be if *ob* were substituted for it. MENCKEN.—Compare also Cortius on Cicero, *Letters* III, Letter 5, note 9. There is another explanation, no less elegant and concise, according to which the holidays are said to relax judicial business “for the enjoyment of the vintage.” LINDNER.

[Col. 0236D] **For at that time.** Minucius sets forth two things that especially recommended this treatment, namely the vintage holidays and the mildness of autumn. The treatment was pleasant because of autumn’s mildness and suitable because of the vintage holidays. LINDNER.

**Autumn was moderating itself.** The most learned Meursius raised a difficulty here to no purpose, as though some words were missing about Caecilius being taken along as their companion on the walk. Accordingly, he found none of the learned men who subsequently edited the text agreeing with him. This was doubtless not because they thought certain circumstances could be omitted as though by a privilege that historians do not shun, but because they believed Caecilius’s companionship could sufficiently be gathered partly from the preceding words, where the author shows that he intends to discuss the discourse of Octavius by which the latter restored Caecilius to true religion through a most weighty debate; and partly from what follows, where Octavius describes Caecilius as clinging to Minucius’s side at home and abroad. The author arranged these two passages so aptly that from them the reader cannot suppose anything other than that Caecilius went out together with them. GRONOVIUS.

[Col. 0237A] **By walking along the shore.** Cellarius, with the distinguished Heumann as his supporter, printed “along the shore” in the dative. Yet the expression “to walk along” with a dative is unknown to ancient writers, nor do I find this verb joined with the dative case anywhere. Consequently, *inambulando* has the force of a gerund, not a participle; while “the shore” is placed in the ablative for “on the shore,” in the same way as in Livy XXIII.21: “Those who had fallen in the battle of Cannae”; Florus III.16: “Annius having been openly killed at the elections”; Curtius VII.7: “Two thousand infantrymen fell in that battle”; and Ovid, *Heroides* I.21:

> In short, whoever had been slaughtered in the Achaean camp;

and many other passages, some of which are cited by the distinguished Drakenborch on Livy IX.32. MENCKEN.

**So that both the breeze.** Heumann deletes “so that,” perhaps because he was offended that the sand’s sinking as it yielded to their footsteps would in this way be made a reason for walking, which he did not approve. LINDNER.

**To the gentle footprint.** “Footprint” here denotes the sole of the foot. Gellius, *Attic Nights* IX.4: “Having the soles of their feet extended backward, not pointing forward like those of other human beings.” Prudentius, *Against Symmachus*, book II, preface, verse 33:

> But he had begun to dip  
> The soles of his feet in the surface of the waves.

Caspar Barthius will supply further examples in *Adversaria* XLIII.25. There, however, he wrongly restores the text to: “would refresh their limbs with exceptional pleasure, and the sand, yielding to the gentle footstep, would sink down,” as though sand yielding beneath the feet afforded no pleasure at all to the walker. DAVIS.—“The sand yielding to the gentle footprint.” This passage has been variously assailed by interpreters. Ouzel, and with him Scheffer and Davis, understand “footprint” to mean the sole of the foot. Scheffer, however, could not stomach the question of how the soles, especially of people who do not wear shoes very often, could be called gentle. Moved by this difficulty, he threw out “gentle” altogether. Gruner, who with Wopken and Gronovius understands it metonymically of the impression made by the footprint or foot, resolves the matter thus: “The yielding sand was gentle to the footprint, because by yielding it made the place being trodden by the foot softer.” In this sense the ablative describes a quality, as in “a soft journey” in Quintilian, *Institutes of Oratory* 4.2, p. 350; “a soft path”; and Ovid, *Fasti* 3.15, “a soft and yielding vineyard.” Neither Davis nor Le Clerc, in *Bibliothèque choisie*, vol. XXIV, p. 124, ought to have agreed with Wower, who restored “soft,” which he claimed to have found in the Roman edition. I applaud Heumann, who says that Minucius meant that the sand yielded even when only lightly impressed by the walkers. One may say in the same way: “The pillow, yielding to a soft neck, sinks down”; German, *Es liegt sich weich*, “It is soft to lie upon.” LINDNER.

**The superstitious populace is accustomed.** I would prefer to read “is superstitiously accustomed.” HEUMANN.—Perhaps because he does not want the masculine gender joined to the word *vulgus* (“populace”). Yet Horace has this word in the same gender, *Satires* II.3.62:

> I shall show him that the whole populace  
> Is insane with an error like his.

So Mencken, who also prefers the comparative “more superstitious.” LINDNER.

**Bringing his hand to his mouth . . . pressed.** The Roman edition has “impressed.” HERALDUS.—Pliny, book XXVIII, chapter 11: “In worship we bring our right hand to our lips for a kiss.” Jerome, vol. VI, on Hosea 13, fol. 72: “Those who worship are accustomed to kiss their own hand, which Job denies that he did, saying: ‘If I kissed my hand while placing it against my mouth, this too would be accounted to me as the greatest iniquity.’” On the gesture, posture, movement, and bending of the body among worshippers, see Barnabé Brisson, *On Formulas* I, p. 35, and Pierre Pithou, *Adversaria* I.3. ELMENHORST.—The material Elmenhorst has just advised the reader to compare and consult may be seen most learnedly and concisely collected in the note J. G. H. Greppo appended to the Lyon edition and translation of the *Octavius*, pp. 193–199. EDD.]

**SUMMARY.—Octavius’s arrival at Rome during the judicial holidays was most welcome to Minucius. They both decided to go to the sea baths at Ostia, taking Minucius’s companion Caecilius with them. As they proceeded together toward the sea, Caecilius caught sight of an image of Serapis, brought his hand to his mouth, and worshipped it.**

For he had hastened to Rome on account of business and to see me, leaving behind his home, wife, and children—and what is especially lovable in children, while their years were still innocent and they were still attempting half-formed words, their speech made sweeter by the very brokenness of a stumbling tongue. On his arrival [Col. 0236A] I cannot express in words with what great and uncontrollable joy I exulted, especially since the unexpected presence of my dearest friend heightened my delight. And so, after one or two days, when frequent and constant association had already satisfied the eagerness born of longing, and we had learned by exchanging accounts all that our mutual absence had kept us from knowing about one another, we decided to make for Ostia, a most delightful city, because bathing in the sea offered a pleasant and suitable treatment for drying the humors of my body. Besides, at the vintage season the holidays had relaxed the demands of judicial business. For at that time, after the heat of summer, autumn was moderating itself toward mildness. And so, when [Col. 0237A] at dawn we proceeded toward the sea, walking along the shore, so that both the gently breathing breeze might refresh our limbs and, to our exceptional pleasure, the sand might sink as it yielded beneath a light footfall, Caecilius, upon noticing an image of Serapis, brought his hand to his mouth in the manner customary among the superstitious populace and pressed a kiss upon it with his lips.

## CHAPTER III

[Note: [Col. 0238B]

**CHAPTER III.—It is not the act of a good man, brother Marcus.** Octavius calls Marcus Minucius “brother,” as one Christian calls another Christian. But in chapter V Caecilius, while still a pagan, will likewise address the same Minucius thus: “although, brother Marcus, you . . .” This form of address was therefore one both of affection and of religion: certainly of both in Octavius, and of affection in Caecilius. RIGALTIUS.

**In the blindness of common ignorance.** That is, to permit him to remain in the religion [Col. 0238C] of the pagans. He calls the ignorance “common” because at that time those who were somewhat more discerning gradually perceived the deceptions of pagan religion and followed Christ, so that only the populace remained in pagan superstition. LINDNER.

**Fashioned into images.** Savaro says much about the verb *effigiare* (“to fashion into an image”) on Sidonius Apollinaris VI, Letter 12; to his material the following passages may be added. Papias: “*Effigiare*: to give form.” Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* II, p. 11: “Fashioned externally with marvelous images.” Martianus Capella, *The Marriage of Philology* VI, p. 130: “For it is recorded as being able to fashion all things into images.” Page 228: “Fashioned into marvelous forms.” Augustine, *On Heresies*, chapter 86: “Tertullian says that the soul is a body fashioned into a form . . . and that God is corporeal, though not fashioned into a form.” ELMENHORST. Differently in ed. BB, vol. VIII, p. 25.

**Anointed and crowned.** Both customs have been sufficiently illustrated by Jean Le Clerc on Genesis 28:18 and Carlo Pasquali, *On Crowns* IV.4. DAVIS.—It is entirely unknown how the Lyon edition came to assert that this reading, “anointed and crowned,” arose from a sound correction by very learned men and that the Royal manuscript reads nothing other than “arranged with ointments.” We testify that we have seen with our own eyes: “anointed and crowned.” EDD.

**The intervening distance from the city.** This is not the distance from Ostia to Rome, as Wopkenius supposed, since the interval between Rome and the shore—sixteen stadia—would be enough to weary even runners, much less allow bookish men out for a stroll either to be able or willing to complete such a distance. Nor is it an intervening distance through the city of Ostia, which on the side facing the sea was free of walls, a view that commended itself to Barthius, *Adversaria* XLIII.25, since upon completing this distance they would have reached not the open shore but fields and farmland. Rather, it is the distance lying between the city of Ostia and the place sought by the walkers, that is, the sea. This was rightly observed by a certain learned man in *Miscellaneous Critical Observations*, vol. X, part I, p. 13. Romans, after all, resorted to Ostia as our people resort to baths, mineral springs, or even vineyards. After staying there for some time, they took daily pleasure [Col. 0239B] in proceeding to the sea by walking along the shore. The sea is three stadia from the city of Ostia, a distance that could easily be completed within the space of an hour. Given these observations, we must agree neither with Davis, who deletes the word “city,” nor with Heumann, who restores “journey,” nor with Mencken, who rewrites it as “the distance of the road and journey.” LINDNER.

**Stretched.** So the manuscript; the Roman edition reads “beat,” as does Wower. Here “stretched” means “extended,” according to all the interpreters. For Heumann, however, it is not transitive but intransitive: overflowing water is said to “stretch” across the ground it has occupied, like an army on a field. The accusative “sands” is governed by the participle “washing over.” LINDNER.

**And, as the sea is always, etc.** I understand and supplement this as follows: “As the sea is always restless even when the winds have fallen (so it was then also, and), although it did not go out to land in white and foaming waves, nevertheless it went out in rippling and swelling waves”—the verb being supplied by zeugma. Zeugma is familiar from Sallust, *Jugurtha* 3, note 2; the other thing I supplied, namely the consequent clause in a comparison after its antecedent, is not equally familiar. Yet Cicero writes in book VII, Letter 28.6: “The republic was dearer to me than it is now”—with “it is” understood; Sidonius, II, Letter 8: “When brought to her perpetual resting place, she seemed more like one sleeping”—with “than one dead” understood. There was therefore no reason for the distinguished Heumann to emend the passage thus: “And, as the sea is always restless even when the winds have fallen, although it does not surge toward the land in white and foaming waves, it nevertheless licks the shore with rippling and twisting ones. We were exceedingly delighted when,” etc. LINDNER.

**Rippling and swelling.** So it is written in the Royal manuscript, not “twisting.” Note Jerome to Heliodorus: “Although the expanse of sea may smile, spread out like a pond, although scarcely the slightest breath may ripple the surface of the recumbent element.” And in the *Epitaph of Paula*: “Thus far we have sailed with favorable winds, and the gliding keel has furrowed the rippling surface of the sea.” HERALDUS.—The first man who reported from the Royal copy that it read “twisting” had inspected it with insufficiently attentive eyes. For in that book there had first been written *srispis tororisisque*, and the corrector intended it to be read *crispis torosisque*, “rippling and swelling.” Physicians have spoken of the “swellings” of veins, and poets of the “swellings” of manes. RIGALTIUS.

**Which in turn it would now draw back in.** Following the distinguished Gruner, I punctuate the passage in this manner. The sea is said to draw its waves back in by Ovid, *Heroides* XII.125:

> And vomits forth as many waves as it draws back in.

There Burman reads, “The Sabaean edition has ‘would dash against.’” Wower wishes “would dash against” to be read in the manuscript; in this, however, the most learned man is mistaken, for he did not inspect the manuscript himself but rashly trusted another man’s testimony, whereas Heraldus and Rigaltius defend the received reading. Gronovius prefers “would play against with its wave.” Davis reads “would dash the waves against,” in order to straighten out the syntax [σύνταξις]. [Col. 0240B] Barthius, *Adversaria* XLIII.25: “by its impact, and changes itself into itself.” LINDNER.

**These stories.** This is the full form of expression. Cortius supplies several examples on Cicero, book IX, Letter 25, section 13, note 2, and still more could be collected from Caesar. LINDNER.

**About the voyage**, namely his own. In familiar conversations, the time, place, persons, business, and finally anything set before the eyes supply occasions for discussion. LINDNER.

**Having traversed the path.** Heumann removes “having traversed,” on the ground that it was repeated from chapter 2; he does so without necessity. LINDNER.

**Raised above the earthy corruption.** By “corruption” he means the muddy dampness by which the boats would rot if left standing for a long time. RIGALTIUS.

**We see.** Berger, citing Longinus, proves that the present is used with force in narratives in place of the imperfect: *On the Natural Beauty of Oratory*, p. 203. LINDNER.

**That shard.** This is the full form of expression. See V, note. LINDNER.

**Or would swim out.** Unless I am mistaken, a corruption lies hidden in these words of Minucius, though perceptive scholars have not noticed it. I believe we should read “and would not swim out.” Sometimes the shard skimmed the surface of the sea without leaping, but at other times it was carried into the air by repeated bounds. Hence the author: “so that the missile would either skim the sea’s surface and not swim out, or, grazing the crests of the waves, would dart up and emerge.” Unless this emendation is accepted, Felix must be judged tautologous [ταυτολόγος]. Eustathius describes the former manner on *Iliad* Σ, p. 1219; Pollux the latter, *Onomasticon* IX §119. DAVIS.—“Would skim, or would swim out.” “Or” is altogether foreign to this passage and should therefore be deleted. For “would skim” and “would swim out” are synonymous expressions, just as are the following verbs, “would dart up” and “would emerge.” The former concern the shard’s course, the latter its leap. Wopken writes “would swim upon,” with Heumann’s approval. Davis emends to “would skim and not swim out.” LINDNER.

[Col. 0240D] **Would dart up, would emerge.** Minucius likes to join several words of the same meaning; hence errors [σφάλματα] have crept in, which we shall observe later. We therefore do not venture to condemn “would emerge,” as the man of most refined intellect, Johann Wower, did. In place of “would rebound,” which follows later, we have printed “would leap up,” following the Royal manuscript and the Roman edition. HERALDUS.—“Would dart up, would emerge.” The latter verb was thrown out by Wower, but is retained with better reason by Heraldus, who at the same time lays down this rule for editors of Minucius: “Minucius likes to join several words of the same meaning”—and that without conjunctions [ἀσυνδέτως]. LINDNER.

**Would leap up.** So it stands in the manuscript and the Roman edition; certain editors should not have printed “would rebound” in its place. For although that verb is not unsuitable here—Ovid too said in *Metamorphoses* XII.480, “Hail rebounds from the roof’s peak”—there is nevertheless no reason to reject “would leap up,” which is also more similar to the preceding “would dart up.” HEUMANN.]

**SUMMARY.—Indignant at the superstitious man’s act, Octavius sharply reproaches Minucius, declaring that the disgrace of this impious deed rebounds no less upon Minucius himself, as Caecilius’s host, than upon Caecilius.**

Then Octavius said: “It is not the act of a good man, brother Marcus, to abandon a man who clings to your side at home and abroad in such blindness of common ignorance that, in such broad daylight, you permit him to stumble against stones—fashioned into images, to be sure, and anointed and crowned—although you know that the disgrace of this error rebounds no less upon you than upon the man himself.”

While he was saying this, we traversed the intervening distance from the city and were already upon the open shore. There a gentle wave, washing over the outermost sands as though spreading them beneath a promenade, stretched across them. And, as the sea is always restless even when the winds have fallen, although it did not come out upon the land in white and foaming waves, it nevertheless did so in rippling and swelling ones. There we were exceedingly delighted by the wandering waves as we dipped the soles of our feet at the very edge of the sea: now, as the sea washed in, it played against our feet; now, flowing back and withdrawing our footprints, it reabsorbed its waves into itself. And so we proceeded gradually and quietly, tracing the gently curving shoreline and beguiling our journey with conversation. The conversation consisted of Octavius’s account of his voyage. But when we had spent a sufficiently substantial stretch of our walk in conversation, we turned our steps and once again retraced the same path. And when we reached the place where small boats, drawn ashore and resting upon timbers placed beneath them, lay raised above the earthy corruption, we saw boys exultantly competing with one another in a game of throwing shards into the sea. 4

This is the game: one picks up from the shore a rounded shard smoothed by the tossing of the waves; grasping that shard flat between the fingers, one bends forward as low as possible and spins it over the waves, so that the missile either skims the sea’s surface and swims out while gliding with a gentle impulse, or, grazing the crests of the waves, darts up and emerges as it is lifted by repeated leaps. The boy whose shard both sped farther and leapt up more frequently claimed the victory.

## CHAPTER IV

[Note: [Col. 0240D]

**CHAPTER IV.—To pay attention to nothing.** Whether you explain these infinitives as an interchange of moods or by the ellipsis [Col. 0241B] of the verb “began,” you will find that they nearly always possess a certain disjointed quality and are used in states of sadness, confusion, or alarm. Caesar, *Gallic War* 1.32: “The Sequani answered nothing but remained silent in the same sadness.” The same author, chapter 16: “The Aedui kept putting him off from day to day, saying that the grain was being collected, conveyed, and was close at hand.” The principle is the same as with asyndeton. LINDNER.

**Silent, anxious, withdrawn.** He describes a man tormented by grief and enormous cares, such as Homer’s Bellerophon, *Iliad* Ζ.201. RIGALTIUS.

**Withdrawn, his expression confessed that he was grieving over something or other.** The Royal manuscript and the editions present the wholly inappropriate reading: “withdrawn through grief, his expression confessed something or other.” For the face is an indicator of the emotions, and for that reason Cicero, *Against Piso*, called it “a kind of silent speech of the mind.” See also *On Duties* I.29. DAVIS.—**To be grieving.** The manuscript has “through grief,” from which Heumann produces “of grief.” It is elegant, certainly; but there is no less elegance in the received reading. “To grieve over something or other” means “to grieve because of something.” LINDNER.

**That characteristic liveliness of yours.** Lest anyone be offended by the conjunction of the words “that . . . of yours” and “that,” I shall show that this accords with the author’s usage. Thus our author, 21.5: “the rites themselves and the mysteries themselves”; 35.4: “the parent of all and lord of all”; 9.8: “people of every sex and of every age”; 10.2: “no temples, no known images”; 10.5: “to investigate the conduct of all, the actions of all”; 10.6: “he stands beside every deed, wanders through every place”; 7.4: “the established witness is, and a witness also”; 5.5: “sufficiently blessed and sufficiently wise”; 28.8: “heads of oxen and heads of rams”; 32.8: “he is present in darkness, present in our thoughts”; 23.8: “by what tortures and by what machines”; 24.4: “how many things are laughable, and many things too are pitiable.” Once this is settled, it remains to warn the reader that the interrogative “why?” must be repeated before the verb “I ask,” by zeugma. If anyone wishes to receive it into the text, he may do so with my leave. It is certainly clear that Heumann’s emendation is superfluous: [Col. 0241D] “Why, Caecilius, do I not recognize that characteristic liveliness of yours, and that cheerfulness of your eyes even in serious matters?” Nor should Cellarius be heard, who changes “that?” into “and why?” LINDNER.

**Rebuked.** Supply “you.” The pronoun is similarly omitted in Cicero VII, Letter 28.5: “For I understood from your conversation that you said you missed my spirit in my books.” LINDNER.

**A man of that very sect.** This is opposed to a fictitious and, as it were, shadowy adversary who assumes an opponent’s role merely for the sake of practice, as happens when companions debate among themselves. By what right, then, Heumann rewrites the passage, “So that I may debate with him today concerning his own sect,” others may judge. Wopken likewise misunderstood it when he thought of a sect shared with Octavius. Cellarius is plainly better, understanding the pagan sect to which Caecilius was still devoted. LINDNER.

**Than to join issue in the manner of wise men.** Thus we readily restore Minucius’s very own wording, corrupted in the copy by one transposed letter: “It is easier to debate among companions than to join issue in the manner of wise men. Among those structures for the protection of the baths,” etc. All editions until now had destroyed the sense through faulty punctuation. And those interpreters who assert that the manuscript reads otherwise than we have reported here are mistaken. Caecilius says that he will make Octavius understand that it is easier to debate and quarrel among companions with vulgar taunts and insults than to join issue in the manner customary among wise men. He then begins another sentence: “Among those structures for the protection of the baths,” etc. RIGALTIUS.—“To join issue in the manner of wise men,” that is, to debate precisely, as befits philosophers such as we profess ourselves to be. “To join,” with “arguments” understood, means “to debate”; “manner,” moreover, is used for “fashion.” Thus Lactantius 7.7.9: “Democritus therefore erred when he thought that human beings had been poured forth from the earth in the manner of little worms.” See also *On the Anger of God* 20.10. Some editions have: [Col. 0242C] “To creep upon the ground in the manner of cattle.” In the manuscript, according to the testimony of Heraldus and Rigaltius, the text reads: “than to join wisdom in the manner among those,” etc. From this Rigaltius was the first to produce: “to join issue in the manner of wise men. Among those,” etc. In this emendation I miss only one thing: the next clause begins too abruptly. Hence I suspect that the preceding clause ended with “manner” and the following one began with “just now,” examples of which construction I gave at note 3 of this chapter. The reason why the word was omitted in one clause or the other is readily apparent. No one, I believe, will agree with Heumann when he rewrites the passage: “If you please, let me debate with him; let me debate more intently among those structures for the protection of the baths. He will surely now understand that it is easier to discourse among companions”—I write “discourse” in place of “join”—“than to debate in the manner of wise men.” Heraldus reads: “than to join a wise hand.” LINDNER.

“Or of rank.” WOW. is mistaken in supposing that these words are absent from the manuscript codex. Heraldus, who saw it with his own eyes (αὐτόπτης), testifies to the contrary; at chap. 9, §3 he also shows that WOW. repeatedly cites a reading as though it belonged to that ancient codex, although it is not found there. Evidently he had been deceived by [Col. 0242D] a friend who falsely claimed to have inspected the codex himself. HEUMANN.—“Nor was this a matter of deference, or rank, or honor.” The Royal manuscript changes nothing. For those who say that the words “or of rank” appear nowhere in it are mistaken; nor should they have so readily trusted the observations of others. Certainly, if some persons were more distinguished or of higher rank, the more honorable place was given to them, and for that reason it was the middle one. Appian, *Civil Wars*, book IX: “And the three sat together, Caesar having taken the central seat of precedence because of his office” (Καὶ συνήδρευον οἱ τρεῖς, Καίσαρος ἐν μέσῳ διὰ τὴν ἀρχὴν προκαθίσαντος). HERALDUS.

“Disputing.” The Oxford edition has “disagreeing.” OUZELIUS.]

**ARGUMENT.—**Caecilius, somewhat saddened by the rebuke in which Octavius had censured Minucius on Caecilius’ account, asks permission to dispute with Octavius about the truth of his own religion. Octavius agrees, together with his companion, [Col. 0240B] and Minucius sits between Caecilius and Octavius.

Accordingly, while all of us were absorbed in the pleasure of this spectacle, Caecilius paid no attention and did not [Col. 0241A] laugh at the contest; instead, silent, anxious, and withdrawn, he confessed by his expression that something—I knew not what—was troubling him. I said to him: “What is the matter? Why, Caecilius, do I not recognize that liveliness of yours? I miss even that cheerfulness in your eyes which you retain amid serious matters.”

Then he replied: “For some time now the speech of our Octavius has been sharply troubling and tormenting me. In assailing you, he rebuked you for negligence, so that indirectly he might accuse me more gravely of ignorance. I shall therefore go further: I have an entire controversy to pursue with Octavius. If you consent to my disputing with him as a man of his own sect, he will certainly now understand that it is easier to debate among companions than to join arguments in the manner of the wise. Only let us sit down upon those stone barriers thrown out to protect the baths and projecting into the deep, so that we may both rest after our walk and debate more attentively.”

At his word we sat down [Col. 0241B] in such a way that, of the three, they enclosed me in the middle by occupying either side. [Col. 0242A] This was not a matter of deference, rank, or honor—for friendship always receives or makes equals—but was so that, as an arbiter situated equally close to each, I might lend them my ears and, seated between them, keep the two disputants apart. Then Caecilius began as follows:

# CHAPTER V

[Note: [Col. 0242D]

**CHAP. V.—“Although to you, my brother Marcus.”** The pagan Caecilius calls the Christian Minucius “brother,” since he was most closely joined to him by intimate friendship, as is indicated by Octavius’ words to Minucius concerning Caecilius in chap. 3: “A man who clings to your side at home and abroad.” RIGALTIUS.—“Concerning that which.” It must be *id, de quo scripserit* (“that concerning which he wrote”), Minucius. For so harsh an ellipsis does not befit an author so learned in Latin and so devoted to elegance. HEUMANN.—Yet such an ellipsis befits Cicero, *Letters*, book III, Ep. 6, §7: “So that your action may appear, to those who do not know on what terms we stand with one another, to be that of an estranged man …,” on which Cortius has more. It befits Lactantius 6.12.39: “But may you divert to better purposes what you would have spent upon superfluities.” Caesar, *Gallic War* I.1: “The third, who in their own language are called Celts.” LINDNER.

[Col. 0243B] **“Rejecting the one, approving [the other].”** Thus the manuscripts of R. read, apparently corruptly. Gronovius therefore rightly judges that τὸ *alterum*, the word “other,” should be inserted twice between the two verbs “rejecting” and “approving”; nearly all printed editors have followed him. EDD.

**“For the present.”** Gronovius appears plainly to condemn the expression *in praesentiarum* (“for the present”), not only in Minucius but also in Tacitus and Cornelius Nepos, as though scribes had corrupted it. But I consider that argument futile. *Inpraesentiarum* is thoroughly Latin and formed according to the analogy of the Latin language, arising from *in praesentia rerum* (“in the present state of affairs”), just as *illicet* comes from *ire licet*, and so forth. GRUNER, work cited, p. 212.

**“Of a most impartial judge.”** Heumann wonders that *judicii* (“judgment”) had not long since been substituted. I, for my part, wonder rather at that most learned man, who dared alter anything in so sound a passage. It plainly alludes to the representation of judges, who were depicted holding a balance in their hand. Arnobius praises the “balance of the just judge” in Psalm 139. [Col. 0243C] LINDNER.

**“Inclined.”** With equal facility Heumann substitutes *propensius* (“more inclined”). But the received reading can be defended just as readily.
