Certainly, the formula *propensus in alteram partem* (“inclined toward one side”) is a formula employed by Cicero himself in *To Atticus*, book VIII, Ep. 3: “The multitude, and especially every person of the lowest station, was inclined toward the other side.” As for Minucius’ joining the two words *propensus* (“inclined”) and *incumbas* (“lean”), to either of which the phrase “toward either side” may refer, this can seem strange and unusual only to someone who has not read Minucius in full, for he uses this mode of expression very frequently. Thus above, chap. 3: “The gentle wave, bathing us, stretched out”; and chap. 5: “Retracing the same road, we trod it again with our steps reversed.” In the same place: “The things suspended above us in heaven have been raised aloft.” Cortius noted similar prolix expressions on Cicero, book V, Ep. 7, n. 2, and likewise book XVI, Ep. 26, n. 1.

**“Lest not so much.”** As we once observed elsewhere, he imitates Cicero, *Paradoxes* 1.2: “I fear that this speech may appear to some of you to have been drawn from the disputations of Stoic philosophers, rather than from my own judgment.” WOPKENSIUS.

[Col. 0243D] **“If you … take your seat for me.”** From a certain Oxford edition Jacob Ouzelius restores: “If you … trust me” (*confidas*). I am indeed surprised at this, since, if that reading is accepted, no meaning arises except one that is exceedingly foolish and unsuitable. But that good man encountered difficulty in resolving the syntax because he did not recall that pronouns of this sort are not infrequently redundant (παρέλκειν) in the best authors, as very learned men have demonstrated with many examples: Dionysius Lambinus on Lucretius, book III, p. 292, and Peter Burman on Phaedrus, book I, fable 22.3. Observe the same thing also in Greek writers. Athenagoras, *Embassy for the Christians*, chap. 9: “And let no one, I pray, think it ridiculous that God should have a Son” (Καὶ μή μοι γελοῖόν τις νομίσῃ τὸν υἱὸν εἶναι τῷ θεῷ). So too Tatian in the *Address to the Greeks*, and others. DAVIS. VECHNERUS, *Hellenolexia*, book I, chap. 6, §5. I add that the Hebrews are not without this kind of pleonasm either—for example, Genesis 12:1 and 22:5—and indeed neither are we Germans. HEUMANN.

**“Some new man.”** The common editions, contrary to the manuscript’s authority, read *aliquis*, without any compelling reason. Cicero, *Academic Questions*, book IV, chap. 7: “Let some god inquire.” The same author, *On Duties*, book IV, chap. 7: “Unless some accident or occupation had destroyed his plan.” Tertullian, *Apology*, chap. 19: “A certain Egyptian Manetho.” Aulus Gellius, *Attic Nights*, book I, chap. 13: “Even if some sudden accident”—so the manuscript—“promised that the matter could be accomplished more advantageously.” The same author, book XI, chap. 13: “And let some one of you, I pray, tell me”; and [Col. 0244B] shortly afterward: “Lest some modulated sound of fluent eloquence readily dazzle you.” See also G. J. Vossius, *Annals*, book IV, chap. 8. DAVIS.—The recently mentioned Lyon edition states that it read in the manuscript codex *novus aliqui eo loci*, saying in a note: “Thus the manuscript as edited by Heraldus, not *aliqui*, as Wouw., Gronov., and Davis maintain.” Yet, with the Lyon editor’s leave, it must be asserted that this reading belongs neither to the Royal manuscript nor to Heraldus. EDD.

**“Doubtful, uncertain.”** He joins the same words as Cicero does in *On the Orator*, book I, chap. 20. GRONOVIUS.

**“And that everything is more probable.”** Thus it stands in the manuscript; the printed editions omit “everything.” LINDNER.

**“All the more.”** The manuscript has *quo magis* (“all the more”). But the Roman edition’s reading, which, according to WOW., has *minus* (“less”), is preferable. LINDNER.

**“Of thoroughly investigating … to succumb.”** Thus the manuscript unquestionably reads. Yet this did not prevent Fulvius Ursinus from restoring: “rather of investigating the truth.” Jacob Ouzelius and Christopher Cellarius, however, [Col. 0244C] printed: “of thoroughly investigating the truth, rashly rather to succumb to any opinion.” Entirely wrongly, since the word “rather” is often understood without being expressed. Cornelius Nepos, *Datames* 8.1: “He determined to engage, rather than retreat with so great a force.” Livy 23.43.13: “That it was in their own interest rather than Hannibal’s.” Aulus Gellius, *Attic Nights* II.7: “They say that they should be gradually avoided and abandoned, rather than rejected outright.” Among the Greeks, however, the particle μᾶλλον (“rather”) is understood. Porphyry, *On Abstinence*, book II, §15: “Experience indeed testifies that the gods rejoice in this rather than in what is extravagantly costly” (Καὶ μαρτυρεῖ γε ἡ πεῖρα, ὅτι χαίρουσι τούτῳ οἱ θεοὶ ἢ τῷ πολυδαπάνῳ). Tatian, *Address to the Greeks*, chap. 61: “One ought to believe him who has precedence in age rather than Greeks who have drawn from the spring” (Χρὴ τῷ πρεσβεύοντι κατὰ τὴν ἡλικίαν πιστεύειν, ἤπερ ἀπὸ τῆς πηγῆς ἀρυσαμένοις Ἕλλησιν). Eusebius, however, *Preparation for the Gospel* X.2, reads there: μᾶλλον ἤπερ, “rather than.” See also Justin Martyr, *Apology* I, chap. 18. DAVIS.—Add those cited by J. H. Maius the Younger, *Sacred Observations*, book I, p. 26; Grabe on Irenaeus, book IV, chap. 23, fol. 309, note s, and likewise fol. 325, note B; Gronovius on book V, 21; Sanctius and Perizonius on *Minerva* IV.7, p. 692. LINDNER.

**“All must be indignant and must feel grief.”** This reading of the ancient exemplar ought not to have been disturbed. [Col. 0244D] It is sound, and is confirmed by the disputation of Octavius, who repeats Caecilius’ words in chap. XVI: “And since my brother burst out that he took it ill, was vexed, indignant, and grieved,” etc. RIGALTIUS.

All printed editions have “one must feel grief, and must feel grief,” wrongly claiming the manuscript codex as their authority. Similarly, a little below the same codex reads *audere* (“to dare”), which Heraldus and many after him accepted; but the Lyon editor again wrongly attributes *audire* (“to hear”) to the codex and, without consulting it, adds the following note to the word *audere*: “Thus Heraldus correctly printed it in place of the manuscript’s *audire*.” EDD.

**“That certain men should dare, and these untrained in learning.”** Thus we have printed, following the authority of the Royal manuscript. Previously the reading was “to hear certain men.” In the same manuscript, *rude* is wrongly written for *rudes*. We had observed, on the following passage of Arnobius, book III, that Christians were regarded as untrained in learning: “Is this that disdain of yours, this arrogant wisdom, by which you spurn us as uncultivated?” etc. HERALDUS.

**“And these.”** I do not understand how learned men could have altered this: Sabaeus to *horum* (“of these”), and another to *hos* (“these men”). It is precisely the construction in Hebrews 11:12: “From one man were born—and he as good as dead” (Ἀφ’ ἑνὸς ἐγεννήθησαν, ΚΑΙ ΤΑΥΤΑ νενεκρωμένου), where the Old Translator renders it correctly, though hesitantly, “and this one as good as dead,” but Beza corruptly, “and he now being dead.” For that is not what stands in the Greek. Achilles Tatius VII, p. 427: “And will you dare to die in this way on the most shameful charges, believed to be a murderer—and of Leucippe, at that?” (Καὶ τολμήσεις οὕτως ἐπὶ τοῖς αἰσχίστοις ἀποθανεῖν, νομιζόμενος φονεὺς, καὶ ταῦτα Λευκίππης). GRONOVIUS.

**“Unacquainted even with the meanest arts.”** This passage must be corrected by changing the punctuation. It had certainly been written: “strangers to literature, unacquainted even with the meanest arts.” He thus says that Christians are strangers and unacquainted with literature; concerning this reproach we made several observations on Arnobius. He added “even with the meanest arts.” Christians, therefore, were not only regarded by them as strangers to and unacquainted with literature, but also as enslaved to mean crafts; and even the teachers of the Church themselves were considered wool-workers, cobblers, and fullers—ἐριουργοί, σκυτοτόμοι καὶ κναφεῖς—as Origen observes in book III [Col. 0245C] *Against Celsus*. In Minucius, moreover, several words are found signifying one and the same thing, except that those which follow are clearer and serve, as it were, in place of an interpretation. One might therefore not unreasonably suspect them to be glosses, were this not almost constant throughout the whole work. Thus earlier, on chap. 3, we observed *emicaret, emergeret*: “gleamed forth, emerged.” HERALDUS.

**“Concerning the highest reality and its majesty.”** Heumann reads “the majesty of the highest reality,” that is, God. But, to conceal nothing of my judgment, the common reading pleases me more. I think that the expression in the common editions possesses a stronger and more vigorous meaning than Heumann’s. Minucius elegantly calls nature itself *summa rerum*, “the highest reality”; Cicero does the same in *On the Orator*, book II, chap. 31. “Majesty,” however, is that divine power itself by which all things are most wisely governed and through which the highest reality is administered. See the passages I collected in *Leipzig Miscellanies*, vol. I, part III, p. 532, and Graevius on Cicero, *For Milo*, chap. 30. MENCKENIUS.

[Col. 0245D] **“Throughout all those ages.”** Terence, *The Woman from Andros* I.1.28: “What nearly all young men do.” Likewise *The Eunuch* I.2.5: “Now you will grow warm more than enough.” The Greeks speak similarly: πλείονες δὴ πάντες, “very nearly all,” and πάμπολλα, “very many things.” Pareus in his Plautine lexicon and Pricaeus on Apuleius, p. 346, observe that the Latins also sometimes said *universos omnes*, “all without exception.” Wopkensius’ punctuation also pleases me: “Concerning which so many, throughout all ages, of very many schools,” that is, “so many of very many schools.” I prefer it to the emendation he formerly proposed, “through whole, through all ages,” with asyndeton. Heumann’s conjecture is more licenseful—“after the inquiry of so many schools of every age”—and must therefore be rejected. LINDNER.

**“Philosophy itself,”** that is, philosophers themselves: the abstract for the concrete. See Cortius on Cicero, book VIII, Ep. 4.5. LINDNER.

**“From investigation of the divine,”** that is, of God. Heumann does not hesitate to write: “From the investigation of divine things.” LINDNER.

**“The things suspended above us in heaven have been raised aloft.”** This entire passage has been printed according to the exemplar. Those who order *sublimata* (“elevated”) to be written in place of *sublata* (“raised aloft”) labor in vain. Things are “raised” when they are carried *sus* or *sursum*, that is, upward and on high. Thus *sublata sunt* means τὰ ὑψωθέντα, “things raised on high.” More refined writers used *sublata* for *suslata*. Here “raised aloft” is opposed to “submerged,” just as “suspended” is opposed to “deep beneath.” Minucius therefore rightly says that it is not permitted to scrutinize the things suspended above us in heaven, and that it is not religiously lawful to violate those that lie deep beneath the earth—as though those who dare penetrate its entrails inflicted a sexual violation upon the earth. Pliny has some most elegant remarks to this effect in book II, chap. 63, and in the preface to book XXXIII. RIGALTIUS.—**“Have been raised aloft.”** *Sustollere* is used of machines by which something is raised on high. Lucretius IV.904: “A machine raises it with a light effort”; Avienius likewise uses it of the stars in his *Aratus*, verse 631: “Where the stars then raise themselves.” Its opposite is “to submerge.” LINDNER.

**“Or it is granted to know.”** These words are read thus in the Royal manuscript: “That to scrutinize is permitted, or to *struprari* religiously lawful.” Hence Heraldus: “or to scrutinize is permitted, or to *struprari*”—through a printer’s error, [Col. 0246C] I believe, for *stuprari*, “to violate”—“is religiously lawful.” Joseph Scaliger thought it might be read *ruspare* or *ruspari*, which seems to approach the manuscript most closely. Cellarius reads “to inquire … religiously lawful”; Heumann, “to learn is permitted, or to scrutinize is religiously lawful.” That *stuprare*, “to violate,” can be explained as “to corrupt,” or to involve in error by empty and fearful opinions, as our author says, I do not doubt at all. Cicero himself, *To Atticus* 1.18, speaks of *stupratum judicium*, “a violated,” that is, corrupted judgment. LINDNER.

**“Let seeds be the origin of all things, compacted as nature coalesced within itself.”** Thus we printed the passage, following the authority of the Royal manuscript. Indeed, Epicurean teaching, from which these statements were drawn, demanded this reading, *principio* (“as the origin”), not *principia* (“first principles”), which was the common reading. HERALDUS.

**“What god is the author here?”** Heumann suspects that *his* (“of these”) should be read for *hic* (“here”). But this interchange is frequent, even in Cicero, book II, Ep. 5: “How these affairs stand,” that is, “how the affairs stand here.” LINDNER.

**“Its own matter.”** Thus the Royal manuscript, according to Heraldus. WOW. is mistaken in saying that it has “pure matter” and in judging that the text should read [Col. 0246D] “the lightest matter.” LINDNER.

**“Though it founded the earth by its weight.”** Thus we presented the text, scrupulously following the reading of the sole codex and the example of the most learned Heraldus. Although he made an excellent choice when he restored Sabaeus’ first reading, Rigaltius immediately did not hesitate to alter it, writing: “though weights founded the earth”—entirely unsuccessfully. GRONOVIUS.—Barthius thought it should be rewritten: “founded itself by its weight.” Cellarius, with others: “though its weight founded it.” Heumann: “though its own weight founded the earth.” LINDNER.

**“And though the sea flowed in from liquid.”** This is certainly not Latin, and Rigaltius’ conjectural restoration, “and though liquid—or *eliquor*—flowed into the sea,” seems to depart too far from the exemplar. I think we should restore: “though the sea flowed together from fluid.” Novatian, *On the Trinity*, chap. 5: “Let us believe in God the Father … who suspended heaven at a lofty height, made the earth firm in its low-lying mass, and spread out the seas in unconstrained fluid.” That passage is a twin to this one in Minucius. DAVIS.—Gronovius, however, retains the manuscript codex’s reading with Heraldus. GALLAND.—The sense is: “Though its own matter flowed from liquid into the sea.” Hence Rigaltius introduces this reading: “and though *eliquor* flowed into the sea,” [Col. 0247B] taking the last word as a substantive noun. Others read: “liquid flowed in.” Heumann: “it flowed together from liquid”; Menckenius approves this emendation on the basis of Tibullus, book IV.20:

> Just as the sea flowed together into the curving globe.

Menckenius, defending the manuscript reading, teaches that the verb *influere* (“flow in” or “swell”) properly applies to the sea as it rises and, as it were, mounts on high, and that it signifies the same as the German *anflüssen, anwachsen*, “to swell, increase.” LINDNER.

**“What superstition is there?”** Heumann reads: “and it is superstition.”

**“And is nourished.”** The Roman edition and WOW. read “and is nourished.” The manuscript has “is raised up.” Neither Cuper’s correction nor his interpretation—the former presented by Clericus in *Bibliothèque choisie*, vol. XXIV, p. 128, the latter in vol. XXVI, p. 459—deserves assent. HEUMANN.—After so many conjectures by the greatest scholars, I shall offer my own, such as it is, which can be reconciled with the manuscript very well: “Man and every animal that is born is given breath and taken away, as the elements,” etc. One that “is given breath” receives life; one “is taken away” is deprived of life. “Man and every animal” is the subject; “is given breath and taken away” is the predicate. Gronovius punctuates interrogatively [Col. 0247C] as follows: “Is it a voluntary combination of the elements?” LINDNER.—Surely this is no surprising example of commentators voluntarily entangling themselves in perplexities! In the codex it is read in the clearest possible light as “and is nourished,” not at all “is raised up.” Thus this heap of itching scholars’ conjectures collapses utterly; yet the Lyon editor stumbled into it again when, after writing “and is nourished,” etc., he added the following—which it is irksome even to repeat: “Thus the Roman edition, but the manuscript has ‘is raised up.’ Perhaps one should read: ‘and is taken away,’ that is, it receives and loses life.” P. 18. EDD.

**“As the elements are voluntarily combined … so they flow back into their source.”** The distinguished Gruner, work cited, p. 212, restored this passage—which learned men had disturbed in various ways—to its integrity solely by punctuation of this kind. This, he says, is unquestionably correct: for τὸ *ut*, the word *ut*, is placed for *uti* or *quemadmodum*, “as” or “in the manner in which,” and the following word *ita*, “so,” answers to it.

**“A voluntary combination.”** Heumann says that the true reading is “a fortuitous combination.” But I do not know whether the common reading may not be retained with equal right, especially since *casus voluntarius* (“a voluntary occurrence”; Cicero, *On Ends* 65) is the same as one that is [Col. 0247D] fortuitous. LINDNER.

**“Is dissolved.”** It should undoubtedly read “is resolved.” HEUMANN.—Yet simple verbs are often used in place of compounds. LINDNER.

**“All things return upon themselves.”** Heumann orders the words to be transposed: “return all things.”

**“With no judge.”** Because Heumann did not grasp the force of the word, he reads “with no directing auspice.” Menckenius likewise admits that he does not know what “judge” means here. What “judge” signifies in this passage will be demonstrated by Ovid, *Metamorphoses* I.19:

> God and a better nature settled this dispute.

LINDNER.

**“When these have been compacted.”** There was no reason for Heumann to rewrite it: “and when these have been compacted.” LINDNER.

**“Falling.”** Thus it stands in the manuscript from the Roman edition, the same Heumann testifies. Sabaeus and Balduinus, however, read “tottering.” LINDNER.

**“Flash brilliantly.”** I am not at all moved to read *promicare* instead, with the learned Heusinger. For *praemicare* itself has a very suitable meaning, well adapted to Minucius’ thought, since he wished by this word to signify the supreme and marvelous brilliance of thunderbolts. *Praemicare* means “to flash intensely,” since [Col. 0248B] the prefix *prae-* in compounds very frequently intensifies the meaning of the simple verb. It is an Apuleian word; that author writes in *Metamorphoses*, book V: “And an elegant lamp, filled with oil and brilliantly flashing with a clear light.” And in book X: “For also a helmet brilliantly flashing with splendor.” Book XI: “I see the orb filled with the exceedingly bright radiance of the brilliantly flashing moon.” And in the same book: “The first of them held out a brilliantly flashing lamp with a clear light.” MENCKENIUS.

**“So extensively.”** The distinguished Heumann should not have altered *adeo* (“so”) to *atque* or *ac ea* (“and those”). For this is a familiar Latin form of expression in which *adeo* is placed at the beginning of a clause, while the *ut* (“that”) which ought to follow and to be construed with what preceded is omitted. In full it would read: “So extensively do they fall … that it is readily apparent from this that the author of these things is not a god.” Here is a similar passage in Lactantius III.9.12: “If someone invited you to dinner and you were very well received there, would you seem sane if you valued the pleasure itself more highly than the author of the pleasure? So do philosophers relate everything to the body and absolutely nothing to the mind”; supply: “that it is readily apparent from this that they [Col. 0248C] value the pleasure more highly than its author.” Compare the same author II.1.12; II.6.6; V.1.17. LINDNER.

**“They crash into mountains.”** The Roman edition has “they demolish,” according to W. “They crash into,” which stands in the manuscript, is correct; for *irruere* means to rush or fall against something. Claudian, *Consulship of Mallius Theodorus*, verse 195, in the best manuscripts and editions:

> Undaunted, he will rush into the flames.

Prudentius, *Apotheosis*, verse 414:

> Behold, the savage legion rushed into the Gadarene swine.

Ammianus XVII.28: “The Parthiscus, rushing into these lands along winding courses, mingles with the Danube.” Avienius, *Description of the World*, verse 594, concerning the Achelous:

> It rushes into the surface of the Adriatic Sea.

These passages, assembled by Cellarius at Gronovius’ suggestion, were taken from Nicolaus Heinsius’ notes on Claudian’s *Consulship of Mallius*, verse 194. LINDNER.

**“They strike guilty men, and often also”—**that is, “often even.” [Col. 0248D] Caesar, *Civil War* I.9: “So that these things may be done more easily, may be settled on definite terms, and may be confirmed by an oath.” Lactantius 1.18.13: “For the very same gate stood open to Hercules also.” Others may judge by what right Heumann believes that Minucius wrote: “They strike not only guilty men but often religious men.” I add that the manuscript has “and often.” LINDNER.—Lest you trust his overly confident assertion: the manuscript in fact reads “often also.” EDD.

**“Or examination,”** that is, judgment. Heumann could have spared himself the labor by which he substitutes “discrimination.” LINDNER.

**“The onset of all things,”** that is, by periphrasis, all things; for the distinguished Ernesti shows in his *Key to Cicero* that the ancients used this word in periphrases. Wopkensius takes it to mean “the mass.” LINDNER.

**“To befall.”** Because Heumann thinks a verb is missing upon which the accusatives joined to infinitives might depend, he writes *constat evenire*, “it is established that it happens.” But someone might more suitably say that these constructions depend upon the verb “shall I speak,” provided the words are punctuated in the manner Gronovius showed us. LINDNER.

[Col. 0249B] **“When the fury rages.”** Heumann says there is no doubt that our author’s true reading is: “when the heat of war rages.” Yet I do not see why that most learned man is more offended by this impersonal passive, formed from a neuter active, than by such expressions as “there is going” and “there is standing,” especially since, besides “it has been raged,” there occurs in Velleius, book II, chap. 74: “The soldiers’ anger raged more fiercely against the Perusians than their commander’s intention did.” Curtius, book VIII, chap. 19.6: “The fury raged even against the houses.”

**“But it is also honored.”** This is the exemplar’s reading. Others have “but it is raised up”; Davisius, “but it is preferred”; Wopkensius deletes “but.” In my view absolutely nothing should be altered. Those who judged that “is honored” must be changed do not appear to have perceived the force of the word. For if wickedness is placed on a level with better men, it is not therefore immediately honored as well. Wickedness is already placed on a level with better men if it is permitted to be wicked with impunity. But it is honored as well if wicked men are placed in such a condition of fortune that others are compelled to venerate them as though they deserved it and to hold them in great honor. This is what the word *colere* means. Cicero several times joins *colere* (“honor”) and *observare* (“respect”), [Col. 0249C] as in *Letters to Friends* XIII.78: “He honors and respects me above all others.” And *On Duties* I.41: “Those whose lives have been proved honorable in worthy and important affairs … we ought to respect and honor as persons invested with some distinction and authority.” GRUNER, work cited.—By a rather harsh ellipsis, “in preference to them,” namely, “to better men,” would have to be understood. Therefore Davis’ conjecture “but it is preferred” should not be rejected—unless perhaps, with a lighter alteration, we prefer: “In peace also, wickedness is equated with better men to such a degree and is honored, that among the majority…”; or perhaps: “In peace also, wickedness is not only equated with better men, but is honored to such a degree that among the majority…”—that is, so that more evil people than good are prosperous. WOPKENSIUS.—Pliny VII.30 also has *sed et*: “But let us also review our own glory.” LINDNER.

**“Phalaris and Dionysius.”** He derives this from Cicero, who treated these matters at greater length in *On the Nature of the Gods*, book III, chaps. 32–33. DAVIS.

**“Now the wine-heavy vintage.”** Very near to *temetum*, “wine,” concerning which shortly afterward: “let wine be made”; hence also *temulenti*, “drunken” or “wine-soaked.” RIGALTIUS.

**“Now the crop is white.”** Heumann rewrites “now the white crop,” [Col. 0249D] but wrongly. For our author indifferently sometimes places adjectives before their nouns and sometimes after them: “Since fortune is either certain or nature uncertain”; chap. 7: “they provide caution against dangers, a remedy for diseases”; chap. 31: “he did not provide testimony as an affirmer, but sprinkled abuse as an orator.” WOW. notes that the manuscript has “golden,” but it does not; Herm. and Rig. testify to this. LINDNER.

**“So either.”** This reading is not Meursius’ emendation of the common *adeo ut* (“so that”), but the manuscript reading itself. LINDNER.]

**ARGUMENT.—**Caecilius begins his disputation. He first argues that everything in human affairs is doubtful and uncertain, and therefore that it is deplorable that Christians—generally uncultivated and illiterate—dare to determine anything with certainty concerning the highest reality and divine majesty. From this he argues that no providence governs the world and concludes that it is better to adhere to the religions handed down by tradition.

[Col. 0242B] Although to you, my brother Marcus, the point chiefly under investigation [Col. 0243A] is not doubtful, since you have carefully engaged in both ways of life, rejecting the one and approving the other, nevertheless for the present you must so frame your mind that you hold the balance of a most impartial judge and do not lean with an inclination toward either side, lest your verdict appear not so much to have arisen from our arguments as to have been produced from your own convictions.

Accordingly, if you take your seat for me as though you were some newcomer and ignorant of either side, it will be no difficult matter to reveal that everything in human affairs is doubtful, uncertain, and unresolved, and that everything is more probable than true. All the more astonishing, therefore, is it that some, out of weariness with thoroughly investigating the truth, should rashly succumb to any opinion rather than persevere in their inquiry with unyielding diligence.

Everyone must therefore be indignant and feel grief that certain men should dare—and these untrained in learning, [Col. 0245A] strangers to literature, unacquainted even with the meanest arts—to determine anything with certainty concerning the highest reality and its majesty, a question upon which, throughout all those ages and among very many schools, philosophy itself continues deliberating to this very day. And rightly so: human mediocrity is so far removed from the investigation of the divine that, concerning neither the things suspended above us in heaven and raised aloft nor those sunk in the depths below the earth, is it granted to us to know them, permitted to scrutinize them, or religiously lawful to violate them. We may justly regard ourselves as sufficiently fortunate and sufficiently wise if, in accordance with that ancient oracle of the Sage, [Col. 0245B] we know our own selves more intimately.

But since, by indulging in an insane and foolish labor, [Col. 0246A] we wander beyond the limits of our low estate and, though cast down upon the earth, transcend heaven itself and the very stars through our audacious desire, let us at least not entangle this error in empty and fearful opinions.

Let seeds be the origin of all things, compacted as nature coalesced within itself: what god is the author here? Let the members of the whole world have come together, been arranged, and taken form through fortuitous collisions: what god is their architect? Granted that fire kindled the stars, that heaven was suspended by its own matter, that the earth was founded [Col. 0246B] by its weight, and that the sea flowed in from liquid: whence comes this [Col. 0247A] religion, whence this fear? What superstition is there?

Man, and every animal that is born, receives breath and nourishment. Just as it is a voluntary combination of the elements, into which man and every animal is in turn divided, dissolved, and dispersed, so those elements flow back into their source and all things return upon themselves, with no craftsman, judge, or author.

Thus, when the seeds of fire are gathered together, ever-new suns shine; thus, when vapors are exhaled from the earth, mists continually grow; when these are compacted and massed together, clouds rise higher; when these same clouds descend, rains flow, winds blow, and hailstorms rattle; or when storm clouds [Col. 0248A] collide, thunder bellows, lightning flashes red, and thunderbolts flash brilliantly. So extensively do they fall: they crash into mountains and strike against trees; without discrimination they touch sacred and profane places; they strike guilty men, and often religious men also.

(III) Why should I speak of the variable and uncertain storms, by which, without order or examination, the course of all events is tossed about? In shipwrecks, the fates of the good and evil are mingled and their deserts confused; in fires, the same destruction befalls the innocent and the guilty; when a pestilential blight infects a region of the sky, all perish without distinction; and when the fury of war rages, [Col. 0249A] it is rather the better men who fall.

Even in peace, wickedness is not only equated with better men but is also honored, so that, in most cases, you do not know whether their depravity should be detested or their good fortune desired.

(IV) But if the world were governed by divine providence and the authority of some divinity, Phalaris and Dionysius would never have deserved a kingdom, Rutilius and Camillus would never have deserved exile, and Socrates would never have deserved poison.

(V) Behold the fruit-bearing plantations; behold, now the crop is white, now the wine-heavy vintage—and it is ruined by rain and beaten down by hail. So either the truth, uncertain to us, is hidden and suppressed, or else, as is more credible, Fortune, released from laws, rules through variable and slippery accidents.

# CHAPTER VI

[Col. 0250A] [Note: [Col. 0249D]

**CHAP. VI.—“How much more venerable.”** The common editions had *quando*, “when.” But the laurel for this emendation is owed not to Meursius but to Heraldus, who printed it thus. LINDNER.

**“Priests of truth.”** This is the genuine reading of the Royal codex. The printed editions have the singular “priest.” EDD.

**“Fear was instilled in you beforehand.”** This reading of the ancient book is entirely correct. It evidently must be taken impersonally. RIGALTIUS.—The common editions wrongly read: “imbued to suppose rather than to know.” LINDNER.

[Col. 0250B] **“While the age was still uncultivated.”** These words are absent from Gronovius’ edition, through a printer’s error, I think. LINDNER.

**“At the very birth of the world.”** I do not think that the pronoun supplies the emphasis which Minucius wished to place in it if one prints “at the birth of the world itself,” as the manuscript would have it. It will supply the emphasis, however, if you write “at the very birth of the world,” just as below, “from the very cradle of the nascent empire.” Certainly, WOW. and Elmenhorst also printed it thus long ago, although an interchange of cases could be acceptable. What the author now puts forward in the person of Caecilius is found in its entirety as an opinion once accepted and approved by the Germans in Tacitus, *Germania*, chap. 34: “It seemed more reverent to believe the deeds of the gods than to know them.” GRONOVIUS.

**“They deserved to have either benevolent gods or kings.”** He calls them *faciles*, “benevolent,” meaning beneficent and deserving well of others. Pliny, book II: “This is the most ancient custom of returning gratitude to benefactors: that such persons should be enrolled among the divinities.” RIGALTIUS.—I wonder how it happened that the most learned Jacob Perizonius restored in this passage: “they had either fathers or kings,” since not [Col. 0250C] all those immediately enumerated were either fathers or kings. *Faciles* means mild and propitious, and therefore beneficent. Virgil, *Eclogues* III.9:

> The benevolent nymphs smiled.

Here Servius comments: “The nymphs,” he says, “indulged them because they are gentle and readily entreated”; so too in the *Georgics*: “And worship the benevolent Napaeae.” Prudentius, *Against Symmachus*, book II, verse 804:

> Thus the upright man and the defendant accused of a capital crime alike  
> Enjoy the same stars and the benevolence of a kindly heaven.

Hence Arnobius, book I, p. 5: “It follows that in a time of abundance the gods are not angry and unaccommodating.” No one is unaware, moreover, that among the pagans many persons were regarded as gods because of their services and inventions in the arts. See Clement of Alexandria, *Exhortation to the Greeks*, p. 13A, Lyon edition of [Col. 0250D] 1616, and our author, chap. XX. DAVIS.—Scheffer restores “companions or associates,” supposing the word *familes* to have been written in abbreviated form with a small line above it. Heumann proposes “citizens,” because of what follows in chap. 20. But these corrections are of such a kind that one could suspect the weakness of the case merely from the disagreement among the parties. What is objectionable in the received reading? It coheres perfectly with Minucius’ remaining words. In chap. 21 our author says that men were regarded as gods because of the merit of their valor—there are the kings—or of their service—there are the benefactors. It is true that the preceding chapter mentions citizens, but not citizens in an absolute sense; rather, it calls them “citizens of good memory,” that is, persons who made themselves beneficent toward their fellow citizens by inventing some useful service or art and thereby obtained a good remembrance. It is also true, as Scheffer objects, that the opposition apparently demanded by the conjunction *vel*, “either,” is insufficiently exact. But Wopkensius rightly observes that no opposition has a place here, and that *vel* in both instances has the force of “and”; he adduces Severus, *Sacred History* I.53: “both sacred ornaments, public and private.”

[Col. 0251B] **“To worship gods belonging to their own communities.”** Minucius Felix calls those gods *municipes*, “members of the municipality” or “local gods,” who were consecrated with a special cult in individual cities or provinces. Tertullian, *Apology*, chap. 24; Lactantius, book I; and Prudentius, *Against Symmachus* II likewise draw up catalogues of these. Sidonius Apollinaris, with his characteristic brevity, included two in each verse (*Poem* IX, verses 165 ff.); an ancient epigram assigns one to each line, in this manner:

> Dodona, Jupiter, is consecrated to you, etc.

Compare D. Martin, *Religion of the Gauls* II, p. 210; Burmann, *Latin Anthology*, pp. 147 ff. EDD.

**“The Eleusinians worship Ceres.”** The Eleusinians, in worshiping Ceres, cannot be celebrated as though they worshiped a goddess belonging to their own municipality, however much they may possess native rites of worship, since the ancient myths derive her from Sicily—or, if one wishes to indulge so fabulous a people, from Crete. Moreover, in the passages immediately following, he produces either great nations or famous cities. What reason is there for preferring the Eleusinians to them, even if they boasted that their city had been ruled by Celeus? One might suspect that the strokes of the letters in that [Col. 0251C] word were confused and that Minucius wrote: “the people of Henna worship Ceres.” Perhaps it was written *Henneios*, just as in chap. 51 the manuscript had *Henneis*, for which the editors restored “the people of Oeta.” GRONOVIUS.

**The Phrygians, the Mother.** There is no need, with Sigismund Gelenius, Laurentius Barrensis, Fulvius Ursinus, and Christian Cellarius, who followed them, to restore “the Phrygians, the Great Mother”; for the sole manuscript resists this, and Cybele is sometimes called “Mother” *par excellence* (κατ’ ἐξοχήν). Virgil, *Georgics* IV, 64:

> Raise the clashing din, and shake the Mother’s cymbals all around.

And *Aeneid* III, 3:

> Hence the Mother, dweller on Cybele, and the Corybantian bronze.

For thus, with Servius, I think the passage should be read, not “Cybele,” as the more recent editions have it. So too Arnobius, book V, p. 167. **DAVIS.**

**The Romans, all.** Shortly afterward he will say: “They adopted the rites of all nations.” And a little later: “They initiated the rites of all religions.” **RIGALT.**

**Extended.** It must certainly be written *propagarunt*, “they extended.” **HEUM.** There is no need, since the singular refers back to “their power and authority.” **LINDNER.**

**While they exercise.** That is, the Romans; it ought to be *exercet*, “it exercises,” like the preceding *propagavit*, “it extended.” But the best authors are accustomed to speak in this way. Caesar, *Gallic War* VI, 24: “That nation down to the present time confines itself within those territories and possesses the highest reputation for justice and military renown, and now remains in the same poverty, want, and endurance as the Germans.” **LINDNER.**

**While they fortify the city.** Thus the royal manuscript. Others read “the world.” **LINDNER.**

**Gods whom another would already have despised when angry.** Thus the manuscript, as it seems; and from it Sabaeus, Gelenius, Heraldus, Rigaltius, and others. But Wouwerius and Elmenhorstius read, “gods whom another, now angry, would have despised,” a reading that greatly pleases both me and Gronovius. For what Livy says in book I, chapter 31, has often occurred: people angered by their fortune have abandoned the worship of their gods. **DAVIS.**—Some have wrongly printed “angry” in the singular. The first edition correctly has “angry” in the plural. Yet even those who print the plural have erred by failing to put a comma before this word. The gods, of course, were said to be angry when some city fell into the enemy’s power. [Col. 0252B] Hence Florus II, 6, 20 called the gods “turned away from Carthage.” At such a time the pagans used to despise their own gods, and even to inflict “savage blows upon the sacred gods,” to use Ovid’s words from *Amores* I, 7, 6. On this custom see Pitiscus on Suetonius, vol. I, p. 767, and Bayle in his book on comets, chapter 132. **HEUM.**

**While captured, within hostile walls.** While the Romans were on the Capitol, how narrowly did they escape being captured and falling under enemy dominion? Yet even there, within walls that had now become hostile—that is, occupied by the enemy—they worshipped conquered divine powers. This yields an excellent sense. The word “captured” now advances beyond what he had said above, “captured except for the Capitol alone,” making clear that by this distinction he wished to imitate Virgil’s line from *Aeneid* VII: “Could the captured be captured?” **GRON.**—The penultimate word is due either to a sleepy copyist, or the text should read: “while at last they erect altars even to unknown divine powers.” **DAVIS.**—Davis successfully changed *in* to *vir*; but *hostilibus* should also have been changed to the singular *hostili*. Thus chapter VII, “through fear of the enemy.” **HEUM.**—Lindner followed Davis’s reading. The sense, he says, is this: after violently capturing the cities of their enemies, the Romans, even amid the savagery of victory, where all other piety is ordinarily banished, nevertheless revered the conquered divine powers. **ERIC.**

**While they erect altars, while even.** Perhaps it should be read: “sometimes even to unknown divine powers.” For the rest, I confess that I do not adequately understand why he adds “and to the shades.” The subject of unknown gods is well worn. Even children know that the shades were regarded as gods; but why are they mentioned here? I therefore wondered whether the text should read: “to unknown and empty divine powers.” **HERALD.**—Gronovius defends the reading and holds that *dum* means *etiamdum*, “still”; or else that one should read: “long ago, even to unknown divine powers.” **LINDNER.**

**To divine powers and to the shades.** Caecilius appropriately joins the divine Shades with unknown divine powers. Appropriately, I say, from the standpoint of Epicurus, who denied that there were any Shades or subterranean kingdoms. For “Shades” is the name given to those who have already ceased to exist and therefore are nothing. Caecilius despises unknown gods because they are unknown, and the Shades, or the dead, because they are dead and now nothing. **RIGALT.**

**Earned.** Supply “to receive.” This zeugma was not unknown even to Cicero, book XI, Letter 18: “But if he should by chance collect any strength, he will perceive that neither the senate lacks judgment, nor the Roman people courage, nor, while you live, the republic a commander”—supply “lacks.” Or rather it is syllepsis, as in the same author, book XIII, Letter 10: “See to it, then, if you value me as highly as Varro thinks”—supply “you value me.” Likewise book IX, Letter 8: “But now what is there for whose sake we should wish to live without these things? For my part, even with them I scarcely wish to live; but if they are taken away, not even scarcely”—supply “do I wish to live.” That this is indeed the manuscript reading is inferred from the silence of Heraldus and Rigaltius. Meursius, however, indicates that *merunt* is read instead of *meruerunt*, and from this corrects it to *inierunt*, “entered upon,” or even *regnaverunt*, “reigned.” Gronovius reads *iverunt*, “went,” namely into their power, as though accompanying the gods. Heumannus wants: “they even earned the right to reign over them.” Davis reads *merent*, “they earn.” Heumannus informs us that the reading adopted by us—*meruerunt*, “earned”—appears in the Roman edition. **LINDNER.**

**Has remained.** Lindner reads *mansit*, “remained,” with nearly all the printed editions. The Roman edition has *maneat*, “may remain.”

**Antiquity … added antiquity.** It is somewhat inelegant to say that antiquity “adds age” to ceremonies. Yet expressions of this sort occasionally escape even the most elegant writers. Cicero, *On Divination* II, 33: “For antiquity erred in many matters, and we see it now transformed either by practice, learning, or age.” Velleius Paterculus I, 4 uses a similar form: “In the ensuing period a great mass of Greek youth, seeking settlements because of its abundance of strength, poured into Asia.” Other examples may be found there and in *Readings from Cicero* II, 5. **WOPK.**—Heumannus accordingly rewrites the passage: “It was accustomed to attribute to sanctified shrines as much [sanctity] as age had added to them.” Even earlier Fulvius Ursinus had rewritten it with *adstruxerat*, “had added.” **LINDNER.**

**ARGUMENT.—Every nation, and afterward the Romans, worshipped its own divine powers in such a way that through their worship the Romans attained supreme dominion over the whole world.**

Since, therefore, fortune is either certain or nature uncertain, how much more reverent and better it is, O guardians of truth, to accept the teaching of our ancestors, to cultivate the religious practices handed down to us, and to fear the gods with whom you were first imbued by your parents rather than to know them too familiarly; not to pass judgment upon the divine powers, but to trust our predecessors, who, while the age was still unsophisticated, at the very birth of the world, deserved to have the gods either gracious or as kings! [Col. 0251A] Hence throughout all empires, provinces, and towns we see individual peoples possessing their own rites and worshipping local gods: the Eleusinians Ceres, the Phrygians the Mother, the Epidaurians Aesculapius, the Chaldaeans Bel, the Syrians Astarte, the Taurians Diana, the Gauls Mercury, and the Romans all the gods.

Thus their power and authority occupied the whole circuit of the world; thus it extended their empire beyond the paths of the sun and the bounds of Ocean, while they exercised religious courage in arms, while they fortified the city with the sanctity of rites, with chaste virgins, and with the many honors and titles of priests; while [Col. 0252A] besieged and captured except for the Capitol alone, they worshipped gods whom another would already have despised as angry; and, through the battle lines of the Gauls, who marveled at the audacity of their religious devotion, they advanced defenseless against weapons but armed with religious observance; while captured, within hostile walls and while victory was still raging, they revered conquered divine powers; while they sought foreign gods everywhere and made them their own; while they erected altars, even to unknown divine powers and to the shades.

Thus, while adopting the rites of all nations, they also [earned] kingdoms. Hence the uninterrupted course of their veneration has remained, and is not broken but increased by the passing of a long age; for antiquity has been accustomed to attribute as much sanctity to ceremonies [Col. 0253A] and shrines as age has added to them.

# CHAPTER VII

> **Note: [Col. 0253B]**
>
> **CHAPTER VII.—Better to err.** Caecilius says that it is better for him to err than for Octavius, if he appears to approve the superstitions of the Romans as being so useful and favorable to their worshippers. **RIGALT.**—The Roman edition has “that it is better.” **WOW.**
>
> **Memory.** Lindner reads: “Look to the memory derived from books,” that is, look to the record that must be drawn from books. The manuscript has *memoria*, from which La Cerda absurdly makes *memoriai*. Gronovius follows him. Rigaltius thinks either that the true reading is [Col. 0253C] “Look to the books of records,” or “Look to the records from books.” Wopkenius conjectures “concerning these matters” instead of “from books,” or rather thinks that “from books” arose through a copyist’s error from the word *delubris*, “shrines,” which occurs in the preceding line. Davis reads: “Look to the books; memory will now….” Heumannus, because “look” generally refers to external objects, reads: “Inspect the acts and books of records”; and he understands *acta* as public monuments recording deeds. **LIND.**
>
> **The Idaean Mother.** This is the entirely genuine reading, traces of which we recognized in the royal manuscript, where *Idaea* had certainly been written. But because the letter *I* was only loosely attached and had been joined to the preceding word, they had therefore almost erased it, so that only some faint semblance of that little letter remained. Others therefore printed “the Mother of the Gods”; Fulvius Ursinus printed “the Mother-goddess,” but added a note indicating that he wanted “the Idaean Mother” to be read. Cicero provides support in *On the Responses of the Haruspices*: “And that Idaean Mother.” **HERALD.**
>
> **Witnesses are the equestrian brothers.** Heumannus’ emendation is: “the equestrian statues of the brothers, just as they had shown themselves.” It is indeed a good one, but should not be preferred to the manuscript reading. Barth, *Adversaria* LXIII, chapter 25, eliminates the words τὸ “in the lake.” **LINDNER.**
>
> **Just as they had shown.** Thus also the older printed editions. Fulvius Ursinus, however, thinking that something was missing, printed “just as they had shown themselves”; and Caspar Barth, *Adversaria* XLIII, chapter 25, says that there can be no doubt that those very learned men correctly conjectured “just as they had shown themselves”—as though, of course, a reflexive pronoun could not be understood. Cornelius Severus, *Aetna*, verse 317:
>
> > And, driven together deep within,  
> > the winds agitate them.
>
> Sedulius, *Poem* IV, 80:
>
> > Washing his own tears in the flood.
>
> The author of *Panegyric* V, chapter 12, §8: “The winds ceased; the clouds fled,” etc. G. J. Vossius will supply many such examples in *Annals* III, chapter 3, and *On Construction*, chapter 58. **DAVIS.**—Scheffer’s “as they showed themselves” is not bad. **LIND.**
>
> **Who with panting**, that is, horses panting from their course. For it was not the riders seated upon the horses who were panting, but the horses burdened with riders and exhausted by the length of the road. The manuscript and both Roman editions have the text as we have printed it; Ursinus was the first to add *anheli*, “panting,” in the margin, and the others afterward followed him. **LINDNER.**
>
> **Which they had brought about**, namely victory for the Romans, or “had furnished.” [Col. 0254B] This sense accords both with historical reliability and with acceptable Latin usage, contrary to Meursius, who thought that no Latin author had ever said “to make a victory,” and therefore rewrote it as “which they had won.” Vegetius, *Military Matters* I, 20: “by whom it is agreed that victory was often achieved.” The anonymous panegyrist of Maximian and Constantine, chapter 13: “If Agrippa, his son-in-law, alone accomplished the victory at Actium for the deified Augustus, the rest….” **WOPK.**—Heumannus deletes both words as a gloss. **LINDNER.**
>
> **The offense given to Jupiter.** In some primary copy it had been written in the ancient copyists’ manner as *offens Jovis*. From this it was copied in the royal codex as *offensio Jovis*. It should be read *offensi Jovis*, “of offended Jupiter.” And correctly so: the games belonged to Jupiter. For the Circus Games—the great votive games—were dedicated to Jupiter and were then held for the first time during the Latin War. Arnobius VII: “It is so that we should acknowledge that, when Jupiter was indignant, insufficiently solicitous care had been devoted to the Circus Games that were his own.” His own, that is, dedicated to Jupiter himself. Rigaltius corrects it to “with Jupiter offended.” Meursius likewise reads “with Jupiter offended.” **CELLAR., LINDNER.**
>
> **From sleep.** Thus the manuscript, although Wouwerius testifies that it has “from a dream,” which Meursius also restores. Thus Cicero, *On Divination* I, 42: “Hecuba appeared in dreams”; and II, 27, “during sleep.” Virgil, *Aeneid* VII, 270. **LINDNER.**
>
> **Repetition.** That is, a renewed performance. Arnobius pursues this entire story at greater length, certainly, but also with greater scrupulousness, book VII, p. 244. **RIGALT.**
>
> **Of the Decurii.** Thus it is plainly read in the royal manuscript, presumably through an antiquarian copyist’s error for “of the Decii,” which the printed editions have. **EDD.**
>
> **Is a witness.** Gronovius reads “and a witness.” He called this repetition rough and unpleasant, though he changed his mind in the Addenda, p. 494. See what we noted [Col. 0254D] on chapter IV. **LINDNER.**—**Of his rider.** “Rider” for “horse.” The expression is rare, indeed, but belongs to good Latin. Nonius, chapter 2, gives “rider” for “horse.” Virgil, *Georgics* III, 11:
>
> > And they taught the rider, beneath arms,  
> > to bound over the ground and gather up his proud steps.
>
> Orosius II, chapter 7: “When one of the royal riders, outstanding in whiteness and beauty,” etc. **DAVIS.**
>
> **Either in mass or in honor.** We have reproduced the manuscript reading. The story to which our author refers appears in Livy VII, 6. Whether because of an earthquake or some other force, nearly the whole middle of the Forum had collapsed into a vast cavern. After this event, the prophets proclaimed that the thing in which the Roman people had the greatest power must be dedicated at that spot if they wished the republic to endure forever. They hesitated, and Marcus Curtius is said to have rebuked them by asking whether there was any Roman good greater than arms and courage. He then mounted a horse adorned as splendidly as possible and, fully armed, plunged into the chasm, while the crowd heaped gifts and produce over him. We may now undertake the explanation of the individual words. “Of his rider” stands in apposition to “with his mass”: his own mass, as one who was a horseman. *Moles* is used of display, majesty, strength, and power. See Gronovius, *Observations* I, 20. Behold “arms,” in which all power consisted. “Honor” is the reward of courage conferred upon someone by the judgment and zeal of the citizens; Cicero, *On Famous Orators* 280, chapter 81. Behold “Courage”—the two things the oracle required if they wished the republic to be saved. Cellarius therefore errs in understanding “Curtius” of the lake and “rider” of the horse. Heumannus thinks that the true reading was: “Curtius, who, as a horseman, once by his self-devotion closed the chasm,” etc.; that *equitis* arose from *eques sui*; that *ole vel honore* was written for *devotione*, whence arose *vel mole vel honore*; and finally that *olim* arose from *velim*. Let whoever wishes believe it. **LINDNER.**—**Or in honor.** Heraldus rewrote this as “or in burden.” Less correctly, it seems. For who could think that Minucius wrote “either in mass or in burden”? Rigaltius confirms the common reading from Valerius Maximus V, chapter 6, who writes to this effect: “Upon him all the citizens, competing to show him honor, threw produce.” See also Livy VII, chapter 6. **GALLAND.**
>
> **It is a deadly shipwreck.** The laws of grammar require the deletion of the final word. For Minucius is speaking not of the then-present time, but of the distant past. **DAVIS.**
>
> **That we may demand back the standards from the Parthians.** No one doubted that *reposcamus*, “demand back,” should be restored, since Minucius had before his eyes his Virgil, *Aeneid* VII, 606:
>
> > And to demand back the standards from the Parthians.
>
> If either Heumannus or Heusinger, whom he praises as the inventor of the emendation, had had this passage at hand, they certainly would not have rewritten it as “from the Parthians.” **LINDNER.**
>
> **And, concerning the births of the gods, etc.** The passage suffers from faulty punctuation. It should be divided thus: “And, concerning the births, gifts, and offerings of the gods, I disregard the poets’ songs”; for no one is unaware how frequently poets sing of these subjects. **DAVIS.**—Heumannus reads: “I omit the ancient matters, which are many—the poets’ songs concerning the births, gifts, and offerings of the gods.” But one does not say that “much exists concerning a subject,” but “in a subject.” **LINDNER.**
>
> **Antiquity excessively fabulous.** For they certainly knew that all antiquity was fabulous; and perhaps at this very time of Minucius, Justin wrote of it in precisely these terms, XI, 6: “As all antiquity is fabulous.” **GRONOV.**
>
> **Than rich in the insignia of worship.** This is what the royal codex once had. Today it offers “than rich in the insignia by worship.” From this the critics seized the opportunity to correct it to “insignia in worship.” But traces of an erased letter *s* are visible, which we bring back to light in this edition, thereby restoring Minucius’ genuine meaning: Roman temples and shrines are more majestic through titles of divine beneficence than they are wealthy in the insignia and gifts of worship. The titles of beneficence [Col. 0256B] are those majestic inscriptions:
>
> > TO THE INDIGENOUS DIVINE POWERS.  
> > TO THE PRESENT DIVINE POWERS.  
> > TO THE SOJOURNING DIVINE POWERS.
>
> The costly insignia of worship are golden statues, sacred carriages, incense caskets, banquets of the gods, couches for the gods, chariots, and other precious objects of this sort. **RIG.**—Heraldus thinks it should be punctuated: “than wealthy in worship, insignia, and gifts.” **LINDNER.**
>
> **Hence indeed.** “Do not, I beg you, hesitate to read with me, ‘filled with God,’” says Heumannus; but I do not know whether he will persuade everyone. **LINDNER.**
>
> **We deny, refuse, perjure.** This is the reading of the royal manuscript. The Roman edition has “we wish”; Gelenius has “we violate” (compare chapter XXIX), a reading that would not displease me if it rested on manuscript authority. **HERALD.**—It does not seem doubtful to me that the great J. F. Gronovius, *Ecclesiastical Observations*, chapter VII, correctly amended the text to: “we deny that we see, refuse to hear, and disavow”—*ejeramus*, which is equivalent to “we do not acknowledge.” **DAVIS.**—What stands both in the manuscript and in the Roman edition, *pejeramus*, must certainly be retained. Minucius said “to perjure the gods” by the same right as one commonly says “to swear the gods.” The familiar expression is “to swear Jupiter the Stone,” that is, to swear by Jupiter:
>
> > Whose divine power they fear to swear by and deceive.  
> > (Virgil VI, 324.)
>
> > I swear by the harsh seas.  
> > (*Ibid.*, verse 351.)
>
> > We have sworn by the Stygian waters.  
> > (Ovid, *Metamorphoses* II, 101.)
>
> > The marsh by which the gods swear.  
> > (*Ibid.*, verse 46.)
>
> One also says “to swear falsely,” or “to perjure, the gods,” that is, to swear falsely by the gods. Here is a passage from Ovid, *Amores* III, 10, 22:
>
> > [Col. 0256D] And the gods falsely sworn by to my injury.
>
> **HEUMAN.**

**ARGUMENT.—Roman auspices and auguries, when omitted, brought repentance; when observed, success.**

Yet our ancestors did not act rashly—for meanwhile [9] I myself would dare to concede this, and thus to err in the better direction—when they devoted their efforts to observing auguries, consulting entrails, instituting rites, or dedicating shrines. Look to the record in the books: you will find that they initiated the rites of all religions either so that divine indulgence might be repaid, or impending wrath averted, or wrath already swelling and raging appeased.

Witness is the Idaean Mother, who by her arrival both established the chastity of a matron and freed the city from fear of the enemy. Witnesses are the consecrated statues of the equestrian brothers at the lake, just as they had shown themselves: on panting horses, foaming and steaming, they announced the victory over Perseus on the very day on which they had brought it about. Witness is the renewed performance of the games because Jupiter had taken offense, as revealed through the sleep of a common man. The duly accepted self-devotion of the Decii is also a witness. Curtius too is a witness: by the mass or honor of his rider he leveled the yawning chasm of the deep abyss. [Col. 0255A]

More often than we wished, the presence of the gods has also been attested by auspices that were disregarded. Thus the Allia became a name of ill omen; thus the expedition of Claudius and Junius against the Carthaginians became not a battle but a deadly shipwreck. Flaminius despised the auguries so that Lake Trasimene might become both swollen and discolored with Roman blood; and Crassus both earned and mocked the curses of the Furies, so that we might demand back the standards from the Parthians.

I omit ancient matters, which are numerous; and I disregard the poets’ songs concerning the births, gifts, and offerings of the gods. I also pass over the destinies foretold by oracles, lest antiquity appear excessively fabulous to you. Direct your attention to the temples and shrines of the gods by which the Roman state is both protected [10] and armed: they are more majestic through the indwelling, present, and sojourning divine powers than wealthy in the insignia and offerings of worship. [Col. 0255B]

Hence, filled and mingled with God, seers anticipate the future, provide caution against dangers, remedies for diseases, hope for the afflicted, aid for the wretched, consolation in calamities, and relief in hardships. Even in sleep we see, hear, and acknowledge the gods whom by day we impiously deny, refuse, and perjure. [Col. 0256A]

# CHAPTER VIII

> **Note: [Col. 0256D]**
>
> **CHAPTER VIII.—So ancient, so useful.** In some copy it had been written in the antiquarian manner as *tam vetus tam utilem*, meaning “so ancient, so useful.” Immediately repeated syllables were written only once, as we see in the edition of the *Digest* of law made after the Florentine manuscript. This mode of writing occurs several times in the manuscript of Minucius. **RIGALT.**
>
> **Thus though.** I write “Let him be, though.” **MEURS.**—And thus it stands in the royal manuscript. **LINDNER.**
>
> **Diagoras of Melos.** The manuscript has “Diagoras of Miletus”; and indeed not only Eusebius and Theodoret, as the very learned Richard Bentley noted on fragment 86 of Callimachus, but also Chrysostom, Homily IV on 1 Corinthians, chapter I, called him this, so that I am uncertain whether we owe this reading to the author or to the copyists. However that may be, this atheist was born on the island of Melos. See Aelian, *Various History* II, 23, and the *Suda*. **DAVIS.**
>
> **The surname Atheon.** Heumannus, both at this passage and in *Acts of the Philosophers*, vol. I, p. 43, judged that the Greek ἀθέου, “of the atheist,” should be restored. But Cicero gives the surname of this perverse philosopher not only in Greek but also in Latin—for example, *On the Nature of the Gods* I, 23: “What of Diagoras, who was called *atheos*, ‘the atheist’?” Likewise III, 37: “But Diagoras, that *atheos*, as he is called.” Similarly, the surname of Heraclitus, which in Cicero, *On Ends* II, chapter 5, is the Greek σκοτεινόν, “the Obscure,” is translated into Latin by Livy—though of a different person—XXIII, 39: “Heraclitus, whose surname was Scotinus.” **LINDNER.**—This reading should not be suspected of corruption. Aulus Gellius, *Attic Nights* XV, 29:
>
> > These two forms of speech are sufficiently familiar and customary: “My name is Julius,” and “My name is Julio.” By Hercules, I have found a third and novel construction in the second book of Piso’s *Annals*. Piso’s words are these: “He feared his colleague Lucius Tarquinius because his name was Tarquinius, and asked him to proceed to Rome of his own accord.” “Because his name was Tarquinius,” he says; this is just as if I were to say, “My name is Julium.”
>
> Livy too used this construction more than once. Many manuscripts certainly display the corrupt reading, “because his name was Tarquinio”; but this wording is entirely contrary to Gellius’ meaning and should not be accepted, although Jacob Gronovius remains uncertain whether it should be received. **DAVIS.**
>
> **By which humanity is governed.** “Humanity” here denotes the human race. Our author, chapter XXVI: “He likewise revealed that demons are earthly, wandering, and hostile to humanity.” Arnobius II, p. 75: “An obscure credulity, whatever it may be, hostile to humanity, fed upon their torments.” **DAVIS.**
>
> **They will prevail.** Davis read “he will prevail” and explained: Let the man who attempts to dissolve this religion be Theodorus or Diagoras; nevertheless he will never succeed in accomplishing it. But I would change nothing in the common reading. The sense is: Theodorus may have done this—or attempted it—and Diagoras even earlier; nevertheless, among posterity, they will never prevail greatly through the name and authority of counterfeit philosophy. Thus the plural verb “they will prevail” is correctly referred to two singular subjects. Or *vel* here must be understood as “and,” as above in chapter I: “that he might harmonize with me in equal goodwill, wishing and not wishing the same things.” See what I noted on chapter V. **WOPK.**
>
> **The Athenian men.** Fulvius Ursinus expunged the final word altogether rashly, for good authors everywhere speak in the same way. Caesar, *Gallic War* I, chapter [Col. 0257D] 31: “Twenty-four thousand men of the Harudes had come to him.” Prudentius, *Against Symmachus* I, 550:
>
> > Into the pure sanctuaries of the men of Nazareth.
>
> And book II, 541:
>
> > And the victorious standards of the men descended from Aeneas advanced of themselves.
>
> Rufinus, in his translation of the *Recognitions of Clement* I, chapter 65: “Be silent a little while, [10] men of Israel.” See also chapter 20. **DAVIS.**—The Greeks too customarily speak in the same way: ἄνδρες Νινευῖται, “men of Nineveh” (Matthew VII, 24); ἄνδρες Γαλιλαῖοι, “men of Galilee” (Acts I, 11). Xenophon, *Cyropaedia* II, p. 33: ἄνδρες Πέρσαι, “men of Persia”; and Demosthenes frequently: ἄνδρες Ἀθηναῖοι, “men of Athens.” **LINDNER.**
>
> **With deliberation rather.** Cellarius admitted into the text Meursius’ emendation *inconsulte*, “without deliberation,” which Heumannus approved, and I retained it because Protagoras had certainly behaved rather imprudently—not because he held such an opinion, but because he discussed it publicly. Many things are prudently advanced in private from an academic chair which another imprudently discusses in public from the rostrum. **LIND.**—Johannes Meursius, who prefers *inconsulte* to *consulte*, behaved in a manner that Christian Cellarius followed incautiously. For what is surprising if Caecilius calls Protagoras’ ἐποχή, “suspension of judgment,” deliberate, when in chapter V he played the Academic, and in chapter XIII enthusiastically praised the cautious doubt of Carneades and of very many Academics concerning the highest questions? **DAVIS.**
>
> **Burned.** This is the entirely genuine reading supplied by the Roman edition and the royal manuscript. Gelenius had printed “mocked,” yielding an absurd meaning. **HERALD.**—The Roman edition has “mocked.” But the true wording was restored by Leopardus, *Emendations* XI, chapter 11, and Ludovicus Carrio, *Emendations* II, chapter 18. Minucius is plainly saying the same thing as Diogenes Laertius IX, 52: Ἐξεβλήθη πρὸς Ἀθηναίων, καὶ τὰ βιβλία αὐτοῦ κατέκαυσαν ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ, “He was expelled by the Athenians, and they burned his books in the marketplace.” **HEUM.**—Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* I, chapter 23: “And his books were burned in the assembly.” **RIGALT.**
>
> **Men, I say.** This is epanalepsis, extremely common in Cicero; book I, Letter 9, §67: “I have also written—for I am even withdrawing from speeches to the gentler Muses—I have therefore written three books in the Aristotelian manner.” See Cortius on Cicero XV, Letter 10, §1. **LINDNER.**
>
> **Of an unlawful, deplorable, unlawful, and desperate faction.** They say that the manuscript reads “defiled” (Wouwerius, namely—a suspect witness, openly unreliable now as often elsewhere. **EDD.**). But no one has yet produced any ancient codex other than the royal copy. The royal manuscript very clearly reads “unlawful.” What Ferrarius and Priscianensis printed, “renowned,” is rightly rejected. Yet “unlawful,” though defended by the antiquity of the manuscript, nevertheless falls flat between “deplorable” and “desperate.” Therefore, if conjecture is permissible, I would read *incitae*, “frenzied,” meaning excited, furious, rabid. Catullus in his *Galliambic Poem*: “Drive some into frenzy, drive others rabid.” *Incitus* is formed like *percitus*. In Prudentius’ *Vincent* concerning unclean spirits:
>
> > Who secretly drive you, frenzied, into every crime.
>
> **RIGALT.**—Wopkenius reads “incestuous.” For my part, I have no doubt that the text ought to read “of deplorable ignorance.” Below too, in chapter XII, the Christians are called by the pagan Caecilius “unlearned, uncultivated, coarse, rustic”; and above, in chapter V, “untrained in studies, strangers to literature, inexperienced in the arts.” Livy VII, 2 also uses *inscitia* for ignorance or lack of knowledge. **HEUM.**—Gronovius makes *incultae*, “uncultivated,” as though Δρυχαρνεῖς [uncertain Greek reading], from *incilitae*, which according to Rigaltius stands in the manuscript. Others read “declining.” **LINDNER.**
>
> **Which in nightly.** Because of the anaphora, Heumannus reads “who in nightly.” **LINDNER.**
>
> **[Col. 0258D] With solemn fasts.** Davis, in his second edition of our Minucius, rightly called Jacob Gronovius’ correction—which substitutes *olentibus*, “foul-smelling”—itself foul. **HEUM.**—No one will doubt that, at the time when Minucius wrote, Christians already observed solemn fasts. Tertullian, *To His Wife* II, p. 128, *Works*, vol. II, Paris edition, 1566–68: “If fasts are to be observed, the husband may hold a banquet on that same day.” But to understand this passage of our Minucius correctly, the following points must also be observed. The Romans regarded Christian rites as most criminal mysteries, like the Bacchanalia they had formerly experienced, concerning which see Livy XXXIX, 10. They slanderously alleged that Christians celebrated those mysteries in their nightly gatherings. Thus they claimed that Christians met on an appointed day and, through the eating of human flesh and promiscuous intercourse after the feast, conspired together and bound themselves to every crime. Caecilius calls that human flesh “inhuman food.” He says that the Christians “bind themselves in a covenant,” using a term drawn from the character of mystery rites; but they are bound together not through sacred rites, like initiates in the mysteries of Roman religion, but through abominations—namely, the eating of human flesh [Col. 0259A] and promiscuous intercourse. We discuss at greater length this malicious Roman slander against the Christians in the *Historical Exercise on the Hatred of the Human Race Formerly Charged against Christians by the Romans as a Cause for the Persecution of the Christian Name*, chapter 2, §7. [Col. 0259B] **GRUNER.**
>
> **Inhuman food.** I read “human food.” Florus III, 5, 10, concerning Lucius Sulla: “And first, by siege and famine, he drove Athens—a city, who would believe it, the mother of produce—to human food.” **LINDNER.**
>
> **A light-shunning nation.** Thus the manuscript and, according to Rigaltius, the first Roman edition—not *lucifuga*. Gesner’s *Thesaurus of the Latin Language*, vol. III, p. 154, must therefore be corrected, since it falsely testifies that the manuscript and old books have *lucifuga*, while the common editions have *lucifugax*. **LINDNER.**—By “nation” Minucius means a sect or class. Thus Phaedrus II, Fable V, 1: “There is at Rome a certain nation of busybodies.” Cicero likewise used “nation” for the sect of the Epicureans, *On the Nature of the Gods* II, chapter 29. **DAVIS.**
>
> **Mute in public.** Thus the manuscript. Some correctly restored “mute in a public place,” which already appears in Sabaeus’ Roman edition. The cause of the error is obvious. **HEUM.**—Thus chapter 19, “to speak in public”; chapter 28: “We thought that these men should not be heard at all.” Quintilian, *Declamation* 13: “Life is lived in public, and all resources are gathered into a common fund.” I do not know why Heraldus retained “in a public place.” Gronovius cites Gellius VI, 14, “to leave in the common space”; Plautus, *Bacchides* I, 2, 53:
>
> > It has now come into my mind.
>
> **LINDNER.**
>
> **As they despise tombs.** Tertullian, *On the Spectacles*, chapter 13: “We spit upon temples no less than upon tombs.” Since the bodies of the dead had been placed and buried in very many pagan temples—a fact demonstrated extensively by Clement of Alexandria, Arnobius, Eusebius, and others—the Christians, because of that practice, frequently both called and regarded them as tombs. Hence also Ammianus Marcellinus XXII, concerning Gregory, bishop of Alexandria: “Returning from the emperor’s court, when he was passing a splendid temple of the Genius, surrounded as usual by a crowd, he turned his eyes toward the building itself and said, ‘How long will this tomb stand?’” Pertinent to this argument too are Tiberius’ words in Tacitus, *Annals* IV: “These are my temples in your minds; these are the most beautiful and enduring images. For structures built of stone, if posterity’s judgment turns to hatred, are despised as tombs.” **HERALD.**—Because *despiciunt*, “despise,” occurs again immediately afterward, Rigaltius rightly suspected a copyist’s error. The passage he cites from Tertullian, *On the Spectacles*, chapter 13, opens the way to an emendation. Christians knew that temples had been erected at the places where those worshipped as gods had been buried. Since scholars agree that our Minucius had Tertullian before his eyes, it is readily apparent that he wrote: “They spit upon temples as tombs.” Therefore remove “despise,” and join “the gods” with what follows: “They ridicule the gods and their rites.” Continue now: “Wretched themselves, they pity….” The Roman edition—and the royal codex—has *miserentur*, not *miserantur*. The inserted *fas est*, “if it is right,” seems to have arisen because the copyist wrote *sacer* twice and then did not wish to delete the first occurrence. **HEUM.**—These alterations arose because very learned men could not endure the repetition of *despiciunt*. Yet one must endure the word “part” six times in Caesar, *Gallic War* I, 12; five times in chapter 49 of the same book; and four times in chapter 1 of book IV. **LINDNER.**
>
> **Wretched themselves, they pity.** Thus Heraldus punctuates. The common punctuation is: “Wretched themselves, they pity, if it is right to say so, the priests….” Heraldus’ punctuation alone is correct. It is well known that “honor” is used for a magistracy; see Rittershausen on Pliny, Letter XI, 11, 2. Purple, moreover, is an insignia of magistrates. See Andreas Steyer, *Dissertation on Purple as an Insignia of Sacred Rank*. **GRUNER.**—He aims at wordplay, as in “to die after death,” 9, 8; “rites more hideous than every sacrilege,” 27, 2; “they are deceived and deceive,” 10, 2; and “either it must be punished or one must be ashamed.” **LINDNER.**
>
> **With astonishing folly and incredible audacity they despise.** The royal codex inserts no interjection or punctuation, whereas the printed editions have: “Oh, astonishing folly and incredible audacity! They despise….” **EDD.**
>
> **Present things.** “And therefore certain” must be supplied from the second clause. John 1:18 must be supplemented in the same way. **LINDNER.**
>
> **Thus for them fear … soothes.** The manuscript has “renewed consolations.” Here “to soothe” means to soften, alleviate, or mitigate, as in Columella VII, 16: “Goat’s milk soothes the fiery savagery of erysipelas.” This passage also makes clear the construction of the verb “to soothe” with the accusative. “Fear” is fear of present death and tortures. “Renewed consolation” is the sort hoped for by those who are to live again in another life. He said “to soothe with renewed consolation,” as Ovid, *Metamorphoses* X, 555:
>
> > The poplar soothes with its shade.
>
> The sense is therefore: that false hope that they will one day live again mitigates their fear of present death and tortures. Indeed, Lactantius VII, 22, 8 says “the souls of the righteous brought back to life” for “the righteous brought back to life,” or “the souls of righteous persons brought back to life”; for Latin authors often attach an adjective to a different noun, as Virgil, *Aeneid* II, 713:
>
> > And the ancient temple  
> > of deserted Venus.
>
> That is, an ancient and deserted temple.—Having explained my own opinion concerning this passage, I shall append in order the conjectures and emendations of the most learned men, so that each may choose whichever he wishes. Heraldus printed: “Thus for them fear, and false hope, soothes with renewed consolation.” Gronovius interprets the manuscript reading by assigning a pregnant sense to the verb: “False hope, by soothing or in the act of soothing, gives them renewed consolations against fear.” Davis reads: “Life soothes their fear; false hope, their renewed consolations.” Wopkenius: “Thus for them a perverse and false hope promises ridiculous consolations,” that is, foretells or pledges them, as in chapter XI, “foolish consolations.” Heumannus: “Thus for them, amid fear, the false hope of a restored consolation offers soothing promises.” For *recidivum* denotes what is restored and, as it were, reborn after it has vanished and perished. Grunerus: “Thus false hope deceives his fear and promises renewed consolations.” Ovid, *Tristia* V, 7, 39:
>
> > I occupy my mind with studies and beguile my sorrows.
>
> **LINDNER.**

**ARGUMENT.—By no means tolerable is the impious rashness of Theodorus, Diagoras, and Protagoras, who wished either wholly to abolish the religion of the gods or at least to weaken it; but far less tolerable is the secretive and light-shunning nation of the Christians, who spit upon the gods and, while fearing death after death, do not meanwhile fear to die.**
Thus, although among all nations the account or origin of the immortal gods may be uncertain, a firm consensus concerning them nevertheless remains; accordingly, I cannot tolerate anyone swelling with such audacity and with some sort of prudence—though I know not what sort—so irreligious that he attempts to dissolve or weaken this religion, so ancient, so useful, so [Col. 0256B] salutary. Let him be Theodorus of Cyrene, if you please, or the earlier Diagoras of Melos, to whom antiquity gave the surname “Atheist” [Col. 0257A]: both of them, by asserting that there were no gods, utterly abolished all fear by which humanity is governed, and all reverence. Yet they will never enjoy influence in this school of impiety under the name and authority of counterfeit philosophy, seeing that the men of Athens expelled the Abderite Pythagoras [Protagoras] from their territory and burned his writings [Col. 0258A] in the assembly, merely because he discussed the divine more cautiously than profanely. Why, then—permit me to express more freely the vehemence of the case I have undertaken—why, I say, should we not groan that men belonging to a ruinous, unlawful, and desperate faction are assailing the gods? Gathering the more ignorant from the dregs of the populace, together with credulous women who, through the susceptibility of their sex, [p. 11] readily fall, they organize a rabble of profane conspiracy, bound together by nocturnal gatherings, solemn fasts, and inhuman [Col. 0259A] foods—not by some sacred rite, but by an act of sacrilege. A skulking, light-shunning tribe, mute in public but talkative in corners: they despise temples as though they were tombs; they spit upon the gods and ridicule sacred rites. Miserable themselves, they pity—if one may say so—the priests; half-naked themselves, they despise offices of honor and robes of purple. What astonishing folly and incredible audacity! They scorn present torments while fearing torments uncertain and yet to come; and while they fear to die after death, meanwhile they do not fear death. Thus a deceptive hope soothes their fear with the comfort of renewed life.

## CHAPTER IX

[Col. 0260A]

[Note: [Col. 0260D]
