**CHAP. IX.—“Shrines . . . increase.”** A *sacrarium* is a small temple, or even a place where sacred objects are stored. Here the term is applied to a house in which Christians assembled to pray. Places “increase” when they are frequented and a great number of people gathers there. Thus Velleius, II.30.6: “The number increased to such an extent.” Tacitus, *Histories* II.34: “Cremona increased through the number of its colonists, the advantageous position of its rivers, the fertility of its soil, and its connections and intermarriages with other peoples.” Behold [Col. 0261B] the Church of Christ disseminated throughout the world even before the age of Christian emperors! LINDNER.

**“Must be utterly uprooted.”** Heumann suspects that *ejicienda* (“must be cast out”) was written, and that Minucius had before his eyes Cicero, *On Duties* I.41: “Indeed, the entire tribe of Cynics must be cast out.” But why may one not speak of “uprooting a consensus” with the same propriety with which we say: to uproot weeds, a tree, eyes, or a city? LINDNER.

**“They recognize one another by secret marks and signs.”** On this passage see Dodwell, *Dissertations on Cyprian* II, §11, p. 19.

**“And indiscriminately call one another.”** I have printed this reading at the manuscript’s direction. All printed editions have *promiscue*, as though the alternative form were not Latin. Gellius, in the preface to the *Attic Nights*: “I used to make notes without distinction and indiscriminately”; hence the same writer spoke of “miscellaneous reflection” in Book XI, chap. 16, and “miscellaneous questions” [Col. 0261C] in Book XIII, chap. 9. DAVIS.—*Promisce* is the manuscript reading, which Davis supports by Gellius’s authority. Heumann, however, observes that Gellius’s manner of speaking is one thing and Minucius’s another: the former is marked by an antiquarian affectation, whereas the latter avoids every affectation. LINDNER.

**“Especially abominable in the highest degree.”** Fulvius Ursinus correctly restored this reading, since the manuscript has *maxima et varia* (“very many and of many kinds”). LINDNER.—Since the copyist’s error is manifest, I wonder that Davis retained this reading. Wopken rightly rejects Burmann’s correction, *maxima et valida*, that is, “certainly true,” which Burmann directed to be written in his note on Suetonius, while at the same time approving Ursinus’s emendation. HEUMANN.

**“The head of an ass.”** The most learned Davis thought that the order of the words recommended deleting, with Cuper (*On Caesar*, Book III, *Gallic War*, chap. 1), the word *asini* (“of an ass”) as a gloss. The distinguished Heumann likewise deletes it, supposing that someone wrote the word in the margin from chap. 28.8. Wrongly, as we saw in *Tullian Readings* II.6, *Prodigies*, chap. [Col. 0261D] 128: “before the house of Lepidus the Pontifex Maximus.” Thus this manuscript reading seems worthy of emphatic approval. Valerius Maximus III.2.3: “and, after routing the enemy, he brought back to the god the *spolia opima*, to Jupiter Feretrius”; where the common reading is *de eo*. Nor should the reading in Florus IV.1 be rejected: “Then the consul, after holding a meeting of the senate, Cicero delivered a speech against the man while he was present.” Here the word *Cicero* seemed to Graevius to have crept in from a gloss, or at least to have been put in the wrong place. Compare Book II.2: “The other consul, Asina Cornelius, was intercepted.” WOPKEN.—Thus our author in chap. 26 has “the blind Tiresias”; 19.2, “God, the parent of all”; 28.9, “the bull Apis”; 31.9, “the one God and Father”; 34.3, “the craftsman himself, God alone”; 35.3, “the fires of Etna and Mount Vesuvius.” LINDNER.

**“A religion worthy of and born for such morals.”** Heumann thinks that Minucius wrote: “Surely such a religion is worthy of such animals.” But take care not to alter anything in a perfectly sound passage. Caecilius had branded the Christians as lustful fornicators and incestuous persons. He therefore says most appropriately that the worship of the ass, an exceedingly lustful animal, accords with these morals. Phaedrus, Book I, Fable 29. He then alludes to the asinine patience of Christians. For the ass treats [Col. 0262B] with honor and dutiful service the very person by whom it is beaten and held in contempt; hence the rabbinic proverb: [Hebrew text absent in the supplied source]. See Buxtorf’s *Chaldaic-Talmudic Lexicon*, p. 788. It is noteworthy that from the Hebrew [word absent], “ass,” derives [word absent], “shameful.” LINDNER.

**“Nature.”** Jerome, Letter LXI: “The more private part of our body is called by us ‘nature,’ *physis* (φύσις).” WOWER.

**“Who [say] that a man.”** Behold the nature of slander and falsehood! They omit certain essential things and add others of their own invention: they say “a man” but omit “God,” or *God-man* (θεάνθρωπος). They speak of the supreme punishment as though it were infamous and servile, not as foretold by prophets and necessary. They say that he was punished for a crime, but omit whose crime, so that his own crimes may be understood, whereas they ought to have said the crimes of others. LINDNER.

[Col. 0262C] **“They tell tales that their rites are such.”** This indeed is the reading of the royal manuscript; but one must read *caerimonias fabulatur* in the singular, as Sigonius, Gelenius, Desiderius Heraldus, and others printed it, for without a singular verb the syntax (σύνταξις) does not hold together. J. Meursius, however, labors in vain when he substitutes *caerimonia fabulantur*. For among the Latins *caerimoniae* means all sacred rites, as Isidore says in *Origins* VI.19, and Servius before him on Virgil, *Aeneid* IV.302. Caecilius therefore reproaches the Christians for worshiping both Christ and the cross. DAVIS.—Octavius himself below, in chaps. 28 and 30, certainly seems to indicate that someone in particular is being named. HERALD.

**“Is to be initiated.”** Thus Heraldus from the royal manuscript. Others have *imbuitur* (“is initiated”), including Lindner, who cites Heraldus’s reading and says: “I do not know whether it comes from the manuscript or from a printer’s error.” We therefore present both readings of the codex. EDITORS.

**“That infant.”** On this repetition, compare chap. VIII. LINDNER.

**“It is known; everyone everywhere talks of it; even . . . a speech.”** The distinguished Heumann should not be followed in thinking that one must read: “Is not that of which everyone everywhere speaks also . . . a speech?” For the broken-off sentence most effectively expresses the emotion of indignation. Thus chap. XI: “Many things are available in reply to this—let my speech not hurry.” “That they themselves are more unjust I no longer labor to prove; I have already demonstrated it.” LINDNER.

**“Our fellow citizen of Cirta.”** No one doubts that our author has here indicated Marcus Cornelius Fronto, born at Cirta in Numidia, an orator by no means contemptible among the Latin writers of that age and a most bitter enemy of the Christians, whom the author mentions again in chap. XXXI. From this and other evidence it is established that he wrote a speech against the Christian sect. I would not have you rashly suppose him to be the other Fronto praised by Juvenal, *Satires* I.12; Pliny the Younger, *Letters* II.11; and Martial, *Epigrams*. According to Eutropius VIII.6, Fronto of Cirta himself was the instructor in Latin literature of the emperors Marcus Antoninus and Lucius Verus. Eumenius extols him with great praise and proclaims him not the second but the other glory of Roman eloquence. If any credit is due to John of Salisbury, *Policraticus* VIII.19, on his mother’s side he descended [Col. 0263B] from the eminent Plutarch of Chaeronea. Nearly all his works had seemed lost, with the exception of a few fragments concerning grammar, when the most illustrious Angelo Mai, cardinal-priest of the Holy Roman Church, successfully brought most of Fronto’s works back to light from within a very ancient palimpsest codex (παλίμψηστος) in the Ambrosian Library, and published them under this title: *Unpublished Works of M. Cornelius Fronto, together with Unpublished Letters of Antoninus Pius, Marcus Aurelius, Lucius Verus, and Appian, as well as Fragments of Other Ancient Authors*. Milan, 1815, octavo. The declamation against the Christians is missing. EDITORS.

**“With all their children.”** This passage should be noted: from its mention of a light it indicates that there was a supper; and, since it attests that all the children and persons of every age were present, are we to believe that none of those children had been baptized? To me, certainly, the narrative seems instead manifestly to imply that baptism was administered even in earliest childhood. [Col. 0263C] GRONOVIUS.—This reflection is pious, but I doubt whether it is also sound. From the presence of persons at the supper, the very learned man concludes that they had all been baptized. Many—including Constantine the Great—deferred baptism until death, yet it is hardly probable that throughout all that time they abstained from the Christians’ love-feasts. Furthermore, the very word *missa* directs us to think of the dismissal of the people. But grant that matters are as the learned gentleman wishes, and that Justin, *Apology* I, chap. 85, attests: “Those called deacons among us give to each of those present a share of the bread, wine, and water over which thanksgiving has been offered, and carry portions to those who are absent” (Οἱ καλούμενοι παρ’ ἡμῖν διάκονοι, διδόασιν ἑκάστῳ τῶν παρόντων μεταλαβεῖν ἀπὸ τοῦ εὐχαριστηθέντος ἄρτου καὶ οἴνου καὶ ὕδατος, καὶ τοῖς οὐ παροῦσιν ἀποφέρουσι). The same, chap. 86: “No one else is permitted to partake of the Eucharist except one who believes and has been washed with the washing for the forgiveness of sins and for regeneration” (τῆς εὐχαριστίας οὐδενὶ ἄλλῳ μετασχεῖν ἐξόν ἐστιν, ἢ τῷ πιστεύοντι καὶ λουσαμένῳ τὸ ὑπὲρ ἀφέσεως ἁμαρτιῶν καὶ εἰς ἀναγέννησιν λουτρόν). Nevertheless, testimony from the mouth of an enemy remains weak, since he did not himself witness what he attests, but knew it only by report—and that uncertain and doubtful. For if this passage could prove that children were present during the administration of the sacred supper, I do not see why it could not with equal right prove that a dog was [Col. 0263D] truly tied to the lampstand. With children present, I believe, the mysteries of the Christians would not long have remained secret. Nor can the use of a supper properly be inferred from the lighting of a lamp, since during times of persecution they generally held their meetings at night. LINDNER.

**“The banquet grew heated.”** Sulpicius Severus also uses the same expression, *Sacred History* II.13: “Therefore, when after the meal and many cups the banquet had begun to grow heated.” WOPKEN.—I do not doubt that *incaluit* (“became heated”) should be restored. Curtius V.7.5; VIII.1.22: “When the king had become heated with much wine.” Nor am I moved by the passage from Sulpicius that Wopken adduces; for the preceding *m* easily persuades me that here too a copyist wrote *calere* for *incalere*. HEUMANN.—But what will he do with Horace, *Odes* III.21.12:

> It is told that even old Cato’s virtue often grew heated with wine.

LINDNER.

**“The heat of incestuous lust blazed up.”** The manuscript has: “the heat of the drunkenness of incestuous lust [Col. 0264B] blazed up.” Gelenius: “Through the drunkenness of incestuous lust, the heat blazed up.” Meursius substitutes *ebriatis* (“when they had become drunk”). Rigaltius: “And the heat of drunkenness blazed up for incestuous lust.” Gronovius: “And the heat of drunkenness blazed up into blind lusts.” Valerius Maximus II.1.5: “The step nearest to Father Liber in intemperance was customarily toward forbidden sexual intercourse.” Hence Isidore, *Origins* VIII.8, attests that wine was attributed to Liber because it arouses lust.

**“The dog is provoked.”** *Carnis* (“of flesh”) is unquestionably an old antiquarian’s error for *canis* (“dog”). EDITORS.—It is difficult to conjecture whence the pagans obtained this slander. Yet I would believe that its origin was as follows. Those employed to track and sniff things out were called “dogs,” as the venerable Ernesti teaches in his *Key to Cicero*; Plautus likewise used the word for a watchman. Since in the early Church there were many who plotted against the Christians, they also maintained certain persons who would inspect gatherings [Col. 0264C] to see whether a spy was present to eavesdrop upon their discussions and mysteries. They called such a person a “dog.” Perhaps it was his task to extinguish the lamps whenever they feared an ambush, or at least to block the windows through which those unwelcome observers might look in. LINDNER.

**“By deed.”** The reading is sound; the distinguished Heumann should not have troubled it and restored *opere*. Cicero, *On Duties* I.35: “To devote one’s effort to children is honorable in fact but obscene in name.” Plautus, *The Merchant* IV.5.10: “By Pollux, I did not think their father was engaged in such activities.” LINDNER.]

**ARGUMENT.—**The religion of the Christians is foolish, since they venerate a crucified man and the very instrument of his punishment. They are said to worship the head of an ass and to adore the “nature” of their own father. They are initiated by the murder and blood of an infant, and in shameless darkness they all mingle together by an uncertain lot.

And now, just as the worse things grow more prolific, with corrupt morals spreading daily, those most loathsome shrines of an impious association are increasing throughout the entire world. [Col. 0261A] This confederacy must be utterly uprooted and accursed. They recognize one another by secret marks and signs, and love one another almost before they know one another. Everywhere among them, moreover, something like a religion of lust is intermingled; and they indiscriminately call one another brothers and sisters, so that even an otherwise ordinary act of fornication, through the intervention of the sacred name, becomes incest. Thus their empty and insane superstition glories in crimes. Nor would shrewd rumor speak about them—unless truth had some foundation—of numerous and various deeds, especially abominable in the highest degree and to be mentioned only after an apology. I hear that, by some absurd persuasion or other, they venerate the consecrated head of that most disgraceful beast, the ass: a religion worthy of and born for such morals. Others report that they worship the genitals of their own presiding minister and priest and adore, as it were, their father’s “nature.” [Col. 0261B] I do not know whether this is false; [p. 12] it is certainly a suspicion suited to secret and nocturnal rites [Col. 0262A]. And whoever tells the tale that their rites center on a man punished with the supreme penalty for a crime, and on the deadly wood of the cross, assigns to abandoned and criminal people altars suited to them, so that they may worship what they deserve. (VI) The story concerning the initiation of novices is as detestable as it is well known. An infant covered with meal, to deceive the unwary, is placed before the person who is to be initiated into the rites. The novice is induced, by the surface of the meal, to strike what seem to be harmless blows; the infant is killed by unseen and concealed wounds. Then—horrible!—they thirstily lick up its blood and eagerly divide its limbs among themselves. By this victim they are bound in covenant; by this shared consciousness of crime they mutually pledge themselves to silence. These rites are fouler than every sacrilege. (VII) And their banquet—it is known; everyone everywhere talks of it; even [Col. 0262B] a speech by our fellow citizen of Cirta attests it. On a solemn [Col. 0263A] day they assemble for a feast with all their children, sisters, and mothers—persons of every sex and every age. There, after many courses, when the banquet had lacked heat [had grown heated], and the heat of the drunkenness of incestuous lust had blazed up, a piece of food is thrown beyond the reach of the line by which the flesh [dog] tied to the lampstand is bound, provoking it to charge and leap. Thus, when the witnessing light has been overturned and extinguished, in the shameless darkness they envelop themselves in the bonds of unspeakable desire according to the uncertainty of chance. And even if not all are incestuous in deed, all are nevertheless equally so in complicity, since whatever can occur in the act of individuals is sought by the desire of all.

## CHAPTER X

[Note: [Col. 0264C]

**CHAP. X.—“Most of all things.”** Wopken proposes *pleraque omnia* (“almost everything”), like *plerique omnes* in Terence and Nepos. Heumann proposes *pleraque omnino* (“almost everything altogether”). I think either the received reading should be retained or *omnium* (“of all things”) deleted. LINDNER.

**“Whatever that is which they worship.”** Heumann restores: “whatever it is that they worship.” To me, *illud* (“that”) seems to have been used pleonastically. LINDNER.

**“Why do they have no altars?”** Thus there is profound silence concerning the sacrifice of the Mass in those times! LINDNER.

[Col. 0264D] **“No known images.”** Nicolaas Heinsius thinks that *vota* (“vowed”) should be written for *nota* (“known”): *Adversaria* I.18, p. 185. But nothing should be changed. The pagan implies that Christians have some image which they worship but which is generally unknown; for shortly before, he said that they conceal and hide what they worship. HEUMANN.

**“Endure.”** Cellarius inserted this verb, which is absent from the manuscript, and because it is absent placed it in brackets. Certainly either this or a similar verb has fallen out. HEUMANN.

**“Whence, moreover, or who is he, or where?”** Unknown persons are customarily questioned in this way. Florus I.18.5: “For who, or from where, were the Romans?” Seneca, *The Death of Claudius Caesar*, p. 811 of my edition, from Homer, *Odyssey* I: “Who are you among men, and whence? Where is your city?” (Τίς, πόθεν εἶς ἀνδρῶν, πόθι τοι πτόλις . . .). LINDNER.

**“A free nation, Roman superstition, have known.”** With great confidence I restore “free nations”; for “kingdoms” follows, and then the plural “have known.” Therefore I also restore, without hesitation, “Roman superstitions.” HEUMANN.—For my part, I interpret this passage through the customary syllepsis as follows: “a free nation [Col. 0265B] has known him; kingdoms have not known him; at least Roman superstition has not known him.” Singulars and plurals are thus interchanged: “Wealth, honor, and glory are situated before the eyes.” What wonder is it if a verb referring to several preceding subjects is put in the plural? LINDNER.

**“The Jewish . . . nation.”** *Gentilitas* here denotes a nation. Tertullian, *On the Soul*, chap. 30: “Aborigines now remain in their own settlements and elsewhere have lent out their nation at interest more extensively.” In the same sense Prudentius wrote “the nation of the Vascones,” *On Crowns* (περὶ στεφάνων), Hymn I.94. DAVIS.

**“To Roman divinities.”** The manuscript has *nominibus* (“names”), which Wower, Rigaltius, Heumann, Cellarius, and many others emend to *numinibus* (“divinities”). Thus Heumann restored *numinis* for *nominis* at Lactantius III.29.14. But the Roman edition has *hominibus* (“men”), which Wopken retains and defends, because otherwise [Col. 0265C] the statement would seem far too feeble and, according to Caecilius’s thinking, would not demonstrate the weakness of the Jews’ God as forcefully if he were captive to Roman divinities as if he were captive to Roman men; compare chap. 33.6. Livy III.17.3 also supports this opinion: “But would you fear your ancestral gods after their capture by the enemy?” LINDNER.—I side with those who regard “to Roman men” as genuine. The preceding words, “whose power and might are so utterly nonexistent,” absolutely require it. Furthermore, nowhere will you find it said that the gods of a conquered nation were held captive with their nation by Roman divinities. But it is often said that a victorious people captured and led in triumph the gods of a defeated people. Tertullian, *Apology* 25: “There are as many triumphs over gods as over nations, as many spoils as there remain images of captive gods.” Minucius himself speaks in the same sense below, chap. 25. GRUNER, cited work, pp. 222 ff.

**“But even indeed.”** Cellarius placed brackets around this word to indicate that it would be better omitted. But since it occurs both in the manuscript and in the Roman edition, I restore *enim* (“indeed”). HEUMANN.—Terence combines these particles under the influence of indignation, *The Eunuch* V.7.10: “But indeed at first I believed the man clever and eloquent.” Cicero, *Philippics* II, p. 438C of my edition: “But indeed he read out letters.” Likewise p. 442A: “But indeed at one point you wished to be witty.” Likewise p. 441: “But indeed you dared to say.” The same, *On the Nature of the Gods* I.41: “But indeed Epicurus wrote books about holiness and piety toward the gods.” LINDNER.

**“What monstrous things.”** The old copy has *quam ta nra*. RIGALTIUS.—Here Rigaltius, too attentive to the obscure writing of the manuscript codex, printed *qua in tam nostra* and, scarcely credibly, even defended it vigorously, explaining: “Christians, insofar as they are spread into the cities of Italy and into the provinces of the Roman people, into so much of our territory.” To such an extent is he held by blind love of that codex. Scheffer recognizes the copyist’s error but is less successful as an emender, judging that the passage should be restored thus: “But now the Christians—what, astonishingly, monstrous things . . .” Yet “astonishingly” before “monstrous things and prodigies” is remarkably feeble and vulgar. I subscribe to DAVIS, who thinks one should read “what monstrous things”; for this comes closest to the writing of that ancient codex. HEUMANN. [Col. 0266B] According to Rigaltius, Ferrarius and the Priscian manuscript read: “what sort of monstrous things?” Ouzel: “But the Christians—what monstrous things?” Gronovius: “How empty are the things, what prodigies, that Christians fabricate?” He appeals to Prudentius on Cassian: “It is no empty or old-womanish tale.” Gruner: “What things contrary to nature, what prodigies they fabricate,” and supports this from Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* II.5: “Cleanthes posited a third conception of the gods, the one that terrifies human minds through prodigies contrary to the nature of human beings and animals.” LINDNER.

**“Into the conduct of all.”** Gronovius wonders how Caecilius, a pagan, could have said this, since “the eye of Justice that sees all things” (Δίκης ὀφθαλμὸς τὰ πάνθ’ ὁρῶν) was celebrated throughout pagan literature. But I know very well how he could say it: he spoke, namely, as an Epicurean, not as a pagan. He attacked providence in the same manner as Velleius in Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* I.20. LINDNER.

[Col. 0266C] **“For the whole world.”** Other editions have *toti orbi*, but the reading we adopt, *toto orbi*, occurs in the royal manuscript, as Nicolas Rigaltius attests; nor ought it to have been altered, since Apuleius and others used the same form. Propertius, Book III, Elegy IX.57:

> The city high upon seven hills, which presides over the whole world.

Lactantius, *The Phoenix*, verse 139:

> A radiant crown is fitted evenly to the whole head.

Hyginus, *Fables* V: “For this reason Juno was hostile to his whole race.” G. J. Vossius collected many similar examples involving other words of this form in *Analecta* IV.6. See also Janus Gulielmus on Cicero, *For Quinctius*, chap. 1. DAVIS.

**“The fabric divided.”** Wopken rightly refutes Burmann, who at Valerius Flaccus I, p. 139 directed that *divulsa* (“torn apart”) be written, by adducing passages from Hegesippus II.9, at the end: “Having demolished and divided the colonnades, you separated the temple”; Cyprian, *On the Unity of the Church*, p. 110: “He who rends and divides the Church of God”; Firmicus, *On the Error of Profane Religions*, p. 19: “Who tore him? Who divided him? Who feasted upon his limbs?” [Col. 0266D] Thus Prudentius, *Peristephanon*, Hymn X.494 and XI.93, and others everywhere; and above, chap. IX, *dispertire* is similarly used for “to pull apart, lacerate, tear to pieces.” LINDNER.

**“By which it is held together and encircled.”** Supply from the preceding words “the whole world and the cosmos itself.” Thus Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* II.57: “Nature first clothed and enclosed the eyes with the thinnest membranes; she first made these transparent, so that one could see through them, but firm, so that they might be held together”—supply “the eyes by those membranes.” Compare Wopken, *Tullian Readings* II.17. Caecilius concludes that it is impossible for the whole world to collapse from the fact that it is not open and exposed to ruin on every side, but rather, like a most strongly fortified citadel, is held together and encircled on every side by so vast a mass. LINDNER.—**“By which it is held together and encircled.”** Meursius emends this to “by which we are held together and encircled.” Cellarius printed it thus. We, however, prefer the slighter alteration, “which is held together and encircled.” Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* II.36: “Earth, situated in the central part of the world, is surrounded on every side by this animate and breathable substance whose name is air”; [Col. 0267A] and chap. 40: “That which surrounds and restrains everything is called the embrace [Col. 0267B] of heaven.” Lucretius V, p. 614:

> Finally, look now upon this around and above us, which  
> Holds the whole earth in its embrace.

DAVIS.]

**ARGUMENT.—**Whatever they worship, they strive with great effort to conceal. They have no altars, no temples, [Col. 0264A] no known images. Their God, like that of the Jews, is said to be unique; although they can neither see nor display him, they nevertheless consider him meddlesome, restless, and perversely inquisitive.

I deliberately pass over many things, for even these are far too many; and the very obscurity of their depraved religion declares that either all or most of them are true. For why do they strive so greatly to conceal [p. 13] and hide whatever that is which they worship, when honorable things always rejoice in publicity, while crimes are secret? Why do they have no altars, no temples, no known images? Why do they never speak openly and never [endure] assembling freely, unless that which they worship and suppress is either punishable or shameful? Whence, moreover, or who is he, or where is this one, solitary, forsaken God, whom no [Col. 0265A] free nation, no kingdoms, not even Roman superstition have known? The sole and wretched Jewish nation also worshiped one God—but openly, with temples, altars, victims, and ceremonies. His power and might are so utterly nonexistent that he is captive to Roman divinities together with his own nation. But indeed, what monstrous things, what prodigies do the Christians fabricate? They maintain that this God of theirs, whom they can neither show nor see, diligently investigates the conduct of all people, everyone’s actions, and even their words and secret thoughts—running to and fro, of course, and present everywhere. They would have him be meddlesome, restless, and even shamelessly inquisitive, since he stands by every deed and wanders through every place, though he can neither attend to individuals while distracted throughout the universe [Col. 0266A], nor suffice for the universe while occupied with individuals. (VIII) What of the fact that they threaten the whole world, and the cosmos itself with its stars, with fire, and devise its destruction? As though the eternal order established by the divine laws of nature could be disturbed; or, when the compact of all the elements had been broken and the fabric of heaven divided, this mass [p. 14] by which it is held together and encircled could collapse.

## CHAPTER XI

[Note: [Col. 0267B]

**CHAP. XI.—“Both ashes and cinders.”** That is: although after death they are ashes and cinders, by apposition. For in that persecution by tyrants many were either burned alive or, after a violent death, cast into the fire and reduced to ashes and cinders. What appeared so astonishing to the pagans was that Christians believed they would be raised again even after being reduced to ashes. Heumann does not hesitate to write “from ashes and cinders,” but he does so without necessity. I have therefore also placed a comma after “they assert.” LINDNER.

**“You would think they had already returned to life.”** The French translator renders this: *Vous diriez qu’ils sont déjà ressuscités* (“You would say that they have already risen again”). Appel, however, in his German translation blindly followed the Frenchman and rendered it: *Woltet ihr sagen, es waren bereits etliche Wieder auserwecket* (“Would you say that some had already been raised again?”). By this very rendering he declares that he understands neither French nor Latin. [Col. 0267C] LINDNER.

**“For themselves when dead, extinguished.”** There is no need to substitute, with Fulvius Ursinus and Christoph Cellarius, “for themselves when dead and extinguished.” For our author speaks in the same manner in chap. 3.7: “Would flash out, would emerge, after the waves had been shorn,” where J. Wowerus vainly suspects the final word of being a gloss. Arnobius I, p. 8: “It is accustomed to freeze and constrict the heat of its blood.” And shortly afterward: “You cannot endure and withstand the most blazing suns.” Also p. 11: “They are able to repel and defend themselves against insults.” Thus that writer everywhere heaps up synonyms (συνώνυμα). DAVIS.—Heumann thinks Minucius wrote “extinguished by death,” as in Curtius III.5.10: “to be extinguished by an ignoble death.” LINDNER.

**“With years and ages.”** That is, “with the passage of years and ages”—*mit der Zeit und mit den Jahren*. Nicolaas Heinsius, *Adversaria* II.19, p. 366, wrote “by the force of age” in place of “with ages.” LINDNER.

**“Is dissolved into earth.”** Gronovius says one should consider whether the author published “is dissolved into air,” because this discussion does not concern the material into which the corpse is dissolved, but rather its reduction to nothing, so that nothing can be hoped for from it. But who does not see that this is far too remote? LINDNER.—There is no reason to alter anything, for many pagans maintained that the bodies of the dead become earth. Thus Sophocles, *Electra* 246. Epicharmus, in Plutarch, *Consolation to Apollonius*, p. 110, says: “Earth indeed departs into earth” (γᾶν μὲν εἰς γᾶν ἀπελθεῖν). Euripides, *Hypsipyle*:

> He himself dies, and mortals grieve at these things,  
> Bearing earth into earth  
> (Αὐτός τε θνήσκει καὶ τάδ’ ἄχθονται βροτοί,  
> Εἰς γῆν φέροντες γῆν).

Cicero rendered those verses into Latin in *Tusculan Disputations* III.25. See Lactantius, *Divine Institutes* VII.12. DAVIS.

**“Nor does it matter.”** Davis thought that one absolutely had to read “and it matters,” because of the preceding “as though . . . not.” No wonder. Yet he would have thought differently if he had observed our Minucius’s mnemonic error (ἁμάρτημα μνημονικόν), examples of which I long ago warned critics must be observed in my *Critical Art*, §§40–43 [Col. 0268A]. Minucius evidently thought that he had previously [Col. 0268B] written, “although every body . . . is dissolved.” Wopken therefore rightly declined to subscribe to Davis’s view. HEUMANN.—The learned gentleman’s observation is indeed highly erudite, but it is less necessary in this passage. For in a question “as though . . . not” produces the affirmative proposition that Heumann supposed Minucius to have had in mind. LINDNER.

**“Every burial.”** I once thought one should read “burial by fire,” because of its speed in consuming the body, since no form of burial consumes a body more rapidly than fire. It was indeed an obstacle that “burials by fire” had already occurred in §3. It was an obstacle that *quidem* had then to be supplied after *paena*, and the adversative *sed* before *si*. It was also an obstacle that I saw “every burial” included burial in the bellies of wild beasts, at sea, in the ground, and in flames. But these objections were too slight to suppress the memory of so fine an emendation. Now, however, I see that “every burial” is here contrasted with the preservation of corpses by spices and ointments according to Egyptian custom, which caused corpses to be consumed only very late, although, as our author said above, they were dissolved into earth [Col. 0268C] over years and ages. LINDNER.

**“Unending life.”** *Perpetuam*, as some editions have, comes from a gloss. Festus: “The poets said *perpetem* for *perpetuo*.” Plautus certainly speaks thus not infrequently; nor did only poets do so, but prose writers as well. Claudius Mamertinus, *Panegyric* I.3.4: “To pass all nights and days in unending anxiety for the safety of all.” And *Panegyric* II.3.4: “Though the empire has been brought into order, he governs it with unending care.” See also Tertullian, *Apology*, chap. 18. DAVIS.

**“That they themselves are more unjust I no longer labor to prove.”** These words yield a double meaning according as *magis* (“more”) is connected with what precedes or with what follows. *Injustus magis* means “more unjust,” a manner of speaking sufficiently [Col. 0268D] familiar even from the lexicons. Hence the sense is: “I shall not further demonstrate that Christians are more unjust than pagans, since I have already shown it.” This explanation accords very well with Octavius’s reply in chap. 35: “Yet if Christians are compared with you . . . we shall be found much better than you.” Furthermore, *magis nec laboro* means “I labor no longer,” namely to demonstrate that they themselves are unjust. Heumann thinks the author’s true text was: “I have already shown that they themselves are unjust and by no means good.” LINDNER.

**“Yet the guilt or innocence is attributed to fate by the opinions of most people, and this is your consensus.”** This is the reading of the royal manuscript. Gelenius had printed: “This is also your consensus.” The Roman edition has: “And this your . . .” He thus says that neither good nor evil deeds should be imputed to anyone, since they are attributed to fate. On this matter we made several observations at Tertullian, *Apology*, chap. 2. HERALD. Heumann reads: “The opinion of most people attributes it. And this is also your consensus.” LINDNER.

**“Thus you assign to God.”** Cellarius, following others, printed *addicitis* (“you consign”) instead of *dicitis*. With a slighter alteration one might substitute *dicatis* (“you dedicate”), that is, “you attribute.” Tertullian, [Col. 0269A] *Apology*, chap. 13: “You dedicate the honor of divinity to deceased emperors.” Again, chap. 21: “Yet the Romans did not dedicate so much honor to the Fates.” See, if you please, chaps. 28 of the same book and Sedulius, *Poem* III.88. But there is no reason to depart from the manuscript reading, as will be shown by what Heinsius noted concerning the verb *dicere* at Ovid, *Fasti* VI.594, and Graevius at Cicero, [Col. 0269B] *For Flaccus*, chap. 34. DAVIS.—Let no difficulty be raised against excellent Minucius because he preferred to use the simple verb with the meaning of the compound; the paternal *Observations*, chap. 3, “To Ecclesiastics,” prove that Cyprian likewise favored this usage. Cicero had already published in *For Flaccus*: “Valeria, he says, had assigned all the money as dowry.” And Plautus, *The Pot of Gold* IV.9.14: “Surely he assigns half to this man.” GRONOVIUS.—I do not see how Davis could defend *dicatis* by adducing passages from Tertullian, *Apology* 13, 25, and 27, nor how Heumann, with Cellarius and others, could defend *addicitis* from chap. 14 of the same Tertullian. LINDNER.

**“Thus you say that those who desire your sect are not volunteers.”** Rigaltius says this is a Hellenism, and for this purpose adduces the following words as though from the Suda: “Desiring, with the genitive, means having a deliberate inclination” (Ἐπιθυμῶν γενικῇ προαιρετικῶς ἔχων). But, apart from the fact that the antepenultimate word does not occur in that writer, the phrase is thoroughly Latin and governs not the genitive but the dative. Caesar, *Gallic War* I.18: “To favor and support the Helvetii.” [Col. 0269C] Tullius Tiro in Gellius, *Attic Nights* VII.3: “They were accused because, against the Roman people, they had supported and favored the king instead.” Likewise Terence, *The Woman of Andros*, Act V, scene IV.2. DAVIS.

**“But chosen.”** Paul, *To the Romans* IX.16: “It depends not on the one who wills nor on the one who runs, but on God who shows mercy” (Οὐ τοῦ θέλοντος οὐδὲ τοῦ τρέχοντος, ἀλλὰ τοῦ ἐλεοῦντος θεοῦ). RIGALTIUS.—He recasts this entire passage as follows: “Thus, fabricating that those who desire your sect are not volunteers but chosen, you fabricate an unjust judge,” etc. But there is no need, provided that after “chosen” you understand from what precedes “you say,” though with a different sense. Thus Cicero, *Letters* IX.17.6: “We serve him [Caesar], he the circumstances”—supply “serves.” The verb has one meaning when one says “to serve Caesar,” and another when one says “to serve the circumstances.” LINDNER.

**“Whether without a body, or.”** Heraldus, from the royal manuscript, printed: “Whether people rise again with bodies—and with what bodies: the same ones, or renewed ones? Without a body? Without this body . . .,” etc. Here the twice-repeated “without a body” indicates that the first occurrence was placed where it does not belong. Thus [Col. 0269D] Fulvius Ursinus, by inserting these two words between “whether” and “with,” restored them to the place from which they had been moved; he did not supply them from his own conjecture. LINDNER.—**“Whether with bodies?”** More recent editors have: “Whether without a body, or with bodies?” The sentence thereby indeed becomes fuller and more rounded. But since that reading rests solely on Fulvius Ursinus’s conjecture, we have decided that the manuscript’s authority should be followed. DAVIS.

This, so far as I know, etc. He speaks thus because he could conceive in his mind nothing that was not embodied. Velleius speaks in the same way in Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* I.12: “As for his claim that God is without any body—ἀσώματον (*asōmaton*, ‘incorporeal’), as the Greeks say—it is impossible to understand what such a being could be; for he must necessarily lack sensation, and also lack intelligence and pleasure.” And in chapter 11: “But when he likewise maintains that God is without a body, he deprives him of every sensation, including intelligence.” Yet the sounder philosophers also held that inferior natures endowed with reason were furnished with bodies; Origen and others among the Fathers shared this opinion, as P. D. Huet has shown, *Origeniana* II, Question 5, §3 ff., and Question 6, §13. DAVIS.

*And yet so great an age has passed . . . countless ages have flowed by.* Heumann confidently rewrites this: “But since so great an age *has passed* . . . and countless ages *have flowed by*.” Yet there is no need. So chapter 36: “And yet, if we thought resources useful, we would ask them from God”; chapter 37: “And yet even an emperor does not give what he does not possess”; chapter 36: “And yet who can be poor?” And: “Yet these things were born for us.” LINDNER.

*What single person whatsoever from the dead.* Lactantius takes this from Minucius in *Divine Institutes* VII.22, omitting the word *ullus* (“whatsoever”). But it is read in the manuscript, despite the contrary assertion of those who peddle their excerpts to the excessively credulous. RIGALTIUS.—If what Wower testifies were true—namely, that the manuscript does not recognize the word *ullus*—everything would be straightforward and would agree exactly with the passage of Lactantius. But Heraldus and Rigaltius are so far from agreeing with him that Heraldus instead supposes a defect here in Lactantius and says that the word *ullus*, omitted in Lactantius, is found in the Royal Paris manuscript. Yet since Bonemann, a most diligent investigator of books and manuscripts, declares that he found nothing of the sort, we have reason to doubt. The expression *quis unus* (“what single person”) is frequent in Livy and Cicero. (Wower is mistaken in his customary fashion: Her[aldus] and Rigal[tius] correctly testify that *ullus* is present in the manuscript. EDD.) On this pagan argument against belief in the resurrection, see, besides Lactantius VII.22.10, also Theophilus, *To Autolycus* I.18: φὴς γὰρ δεῖξόν μοι κἂν ἕνα ἐγερθέντα ἐκ νεκρῶν, ἵνα ἰδὼν πιστεύσω, “For you say: ‘Show me even one person raised from the dead, so that upon seeing him I may believe.’” Compare Luke 16:27 ff. LINDNER.

*At least of hours.* Broukhusius, on Propertius I, Elegy XIX.10, thought that something had fallen out and emended the text to: “with a leave of absence permitted for at least a few hours.” Davis, however, proposed “at least three hours,” as reported by Hyginus, *Fables* CIII; he proves that this corruption could easily have arisen from the resemblance of the numeral sign to the preceding letter. Gronovius nevertheless ably defends the received reading. Here are his very words:

“Although everyone now understands the very pleasing transferred sense of the word *commeatus* (‘leave of absence’), drawn from either a military camp or the imperial court, nevertheless the genitive *horarum* (‘of hours’), standing by itself, expresses the fullest completeness. In Roman calculations of time, the number of hours did not extend beyond twelve; hence, to designate merely a small portion of time—one that did not extend beyond a single day and indeed did not fill even one day—the author rightly calls for *hours*, not days, weeks, or months. [Col. 0270D] Lucian plainly exhibits this ancient meaning in the *Downward Journey*, where Megapenthes says, οὐ πολὺν χρόνον, ὦ Μοῖρα, αἰτῶ, ‘I do not ask for much time, O Fate’; and the scholiast of our Academic Library aptly explains, εἰς Πρωτεσίλαον ἀποσκώπτει, ‘he is jesting at Protesilaus.’ Thus what the Greeks commonly called ‘a leave of no great duration’ is described by Minucius as a leave ‘of hours’—a wholly sound expression, especially since military leaves of this kind could also be specified in hours according to the distance involved, and not only in days or weeks. The distinguished Price likewise observed that those very words were perfectly complete, in his illustration of Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* II, p. 114. To be sure, when the Latins say simply *horarum*, according to the grace of Latin idiom, it is not the word ‘all’ that is understood, but ‘some’ . . . . . Not that they did not sometimes choose to express this in full—for thus Cicero, *On the Orator* II.18: ‘The eloquent man is said to have spoken for some hours’; Suetonius, *Augustus* 56: ‘He sat on the benches for some hours,’ and the reason for the difference is sufficiently evident—or that they were not permitted to define them by adding a specific number within which they were comprised. But they preferred to do this with intervals of time whose exact duration it mattered to know, as the same Suetonius does in *Nero* 33 concerning a kid, after Nero prolonged the affair for five hours. This cannot be applied to the present story, in which, as commonly happens, the accounts vary.”

Our author likewise disliked an exact determination of time below, chapter 18: “I omit the Persians. But who has not eagerly desired and exulted to celebrate those seven Persians . . .?” DAVIS cites Justin II.14: “the news of the victory was reported within so brief a span of hours.”

*In sweetness.* *Into sweetness* would be preferable; and I do not believe that the Latins, especially the more elegant writers, used the ablative in place of the accusative as often as these cases were confused by copyists. Thus Justin IV.1: “This was composed by the ancients to add sweetness to the tale.” WOPKENS.

*By you, namely the credulous.* Thus the manuscript and the Roman editions, Rigaltius, Gronovius, and Davis. But Gelenius and Cellarius read “the excessively credulous,” which Heraldus thought the sense required. Punctuate: “by you—namely, the credulous—they were shamefully remade with reference to your God.” Nothing then remains that could give offense. GRUNER.

**SUMMARY.—They also assert that the whole world will one day be consumed by fire; and after the resurrection of our bodies they promise the righteous an eternity of most blessed life, but the unrighteous an eternity of the greatest punishments.**

Not content even with this frenzied opinion, they construct and append old women’s tales. They maintain that after death, ashes, and cinders they are born again; and with some inexplicable confidence they mutually believe one another’s lies—you would think they had already come back to life. A twofold evil and a double madness! They announce destruction for heaven and the stars, which we leave exactly as we found them; but for themselves, when dead and extinguished—for we perish just as we are born—they promise eternity in return. That, of course, is why they curse funeral pyres and condemn burial by fire, as though every body, even if withdrawn from the flames, were not nevertheless dissolved into earth by years and ages; and as though it made any difference whether beasts tear it apart, the seas consume it, the soil covers it, or flame carries it away. For if corpses possess sensation, every burial is punishment; if they do not, the very speed of their destruction is a remedy.

Deceived by this error, they promise themselves, as good people, a blessed and everlasting life after death, but all others, as unrighteous, eternal punishment. Many replies to this occur to me, were my speech not hastening onward. That they themselves are the unrighteous is a point on which I need not labor further: I have already proved it. Yet even if I granted that they were righteous, nevertheless guilt—or innocence—is attributed to fate in the opinions of very many, and this is also your own position. For whatever we do, just as others assign it to fate, so you assign it [Col. 0269A] to God: thus you maintain that the members of your sect do not desire it of their own accord, but are chosen. You therefore imagine an unjust judge, who punishes fortune in human beings rather than will.

Yet I should like to ask whether resurrection occurs with bodies—and with what bodies: the same or renewed ones? Without a body? Without a body, so far as I know, there is neither mind, soul, nor life. With the same body? But it has already dissolved. With another body? Then a new person is born; the former person is not restored. And yet so great an age has passed, countless centuries have flowed by: what single person whatsoever has returned from the dead—even by the fortune of Protesilaus—with leave for at least a few hours, so that we might at least believe on the strength of an example? All these fabrications of a diseased opinion and foolish consolations, playfully fashioned [Col. 0271A] by deceitful poets to add sweetness to their verse, have been shamefully remade by you—credulous people indeed—with reference to your God.

## CHAPTER XII

> **Note: [Col. 0271C]**
>
> **CHAPTER XII.—*Judge*.** Cellarius wrongly printed *aestimatis* (“you judge”). Ouzelius, Davis, and Gronovius correctly give *aestimate* (“judge”), which is also the reading of the Roman edition. HEUMANN.—I add that the manuscript has it as well. LINDNER.
>
> *You are in need, you are cold,* etc. The manuscript does indeed have *opere* as a single word, but it must be pronounced separately, as most editors have printed it. Moreover, the passage is perfectly sound and clear. James 2:15–16 also joins being in need with being cold. *Ope laborare* means to lack assistance, or, as Cicero expresses it, *egere ope*, “to be in need of aid.” *Re laborare* means to lack property. Columella has *fame laborare*, “to suffer from hunger,” in his first preface. The pagan Caecilius intensifies the Christians’ poverty through *exergasia*, or elaboration. [Col. 0271D] I am astonished that learned men have tampered with this passage: Davis rewrites it, “you are sick, you are cold, you suffer from poverty and hunger”; Wopkens reads, “you are in need, you are cold, you labor at a futile work”; Heumann restores the passage thus: “you suffer in body and mind. While God tolerates and disregards this, he either does not wish or is unable to aid his own.” LINDNER.
>
> *Does not wish or cannot.* For “or does not wish.” See what we note above on chapter 1, and likewise chapter 34. LINDNER.
>
> *When you are shaken by danger.* Heraldus, Rigaltius, the Baluze manuscript, Ursinus, Wower, and Lindner read *cum querquero quateris*, “when you are shaken by a feverish chill,” that is, by cold and trembling. Pompeius Festus, or his interpolator Paulus, says: “It is certain that *querquera*, a chill accompanied by trembling, is so called from the Greek κάρκηρα.” He adds from Lucilius: “A shivering fever follows, and pains of the head.” Gellius XX.1: “a serious illness with a raging and shivering fever.” Apuleius also has *querquerum* in the *Apology*. Fr. Balduinus, Fulvius Ursinus, and Joannes Wowerus accordingly read *querquero* in Minucius; by contrast, Heraldus and Rigaltius read *periculo* (“danger”) from ancient books. I would follow them if “to be shaken by danger” seemed a convenient expression, especially in this passage and in such a sequence of words. CELLARIUS.—On this disease consult Keuchenius on Serenus Sammonicus, p. 269; he nevertheless supports Ludovicus Carrio, *Emendations* II.18, who rewrites our Minucius as *querquera*, when he maintains that the form is *querqueram*, not *querquerum*. HEUMANN.
>
> *And now no longer.* Some editions wrongly have “also not to be worshipped.” *Jam* (“now”) thus frequently intensifies the force of the negative *non*. Below, chapter 21: “These are now no longer sacred rites; they are tortures.” Lactantius, *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* 19: “now no longer a shepherd of cattle, but of soldiers.” Salvian, *On the Governance of God* I, p. 17, Bremen edition: “For in Egypt at that time, no longer merely a single but a manifold . . .” I would read there with the common text, “for at that time not . . .” Paulinus, *Letter to Aper*: “Nor now in scholastic rather than divine speech.” Justin, *Preface*: “Which I sent to you, no longer so much for the sake of learning as of correcting.” WOPKENS.
>
> *You deny even garlands to tombs.* The earliest Christians abstained from this rite so as to have nothing in common with the nations. Pagans decorated tombs with wreaths. Propertius III, Elegy 16:
>
> > She will bring perfumes here for me, and adorn my tomb  
> > With a wreath, sitting as guardian beside my ashes.
>
> And the ancient poet in *The Barmaid*:
>
> > Why preserve fragrant wreaths for ungrateful ashes?  
> > Do you wish them to cover a stone crowned with flowers?
>
> Hence, among the charges brought against Christians, Justin Martyr reports in *Apology* II, p. 68: μὴ τοῖς ἀποθανοῦσι χοὰς καὶ κνίσας, καὶ ἐν ταφαῖς (as Meursius emends it) στεφάνους καὶ θυσίας φέρειν, “that they do not bring libations and the savor of burnt offerings to the dead, nor garlands and sacrifices at burials.” Later Christians, however, departed from this simplicity. Prudentius, *Cathemerinon*, Hymn X, at the end of the funeral hymn:
>
> > We shall cherish the covered bones  
> > With violets and abundant foliage,  
> > And sprinkle the inscription and cold stones  
> > With liquid perfume. CELLARIUS.
>
> *Worthy of pity, but of our gods.* In place of *sed* (“but”), J. F. Gronovius, *Observations on Ecclesiastical Writers* 7, p. 75, rewrote *et* (“and”), while Davis proposed *vel* (“or”). Yet the manuscript reading is sound. If anyone is offended by the word order, let him read: “worthy of the gods’ pity, but of our gods’.” Thus below, chapter 26: “angels, that is, servants and messengers of God—but of the true God,” which could also be phrased: “messengers—but of the true God.” Florus I.1.6: “The former first sees six vultures; the latter afterward—but twelve.” Pliny 33.3: “Among us Antonius, as an insult to nature, made cheapness worthy of proscription by means of gold—but the cheapness of Spartacus.” LINDNER.
>
> [Col. 0273A] *Before your feet.* That is, the things that lie before your feet. Cicero, *On Divination* II.13: “No one observes what is before his feet; they scrutinize the regions of the sky.” [Col. 0273B] LINDNER.
>
> *To discuss divine things.* That is, “to discuss concerning divine things.” Thus Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* III.40: “I have preferred to discuss rather than judge the matters I have debated”; Sulpicius Severus, *Sacred History* II.28: “As for the remainder concerning him, it is uncertain whether one should feel more regret or shame in discussing it”; Jerome, *Against Jovinian* I, col. 147, Benedictine edition: “My teacher Gregory of Nazianzus, discussing virginity and marriage, explained them in Greek verses.” The same author, *Letter XXXI to Pammachius*: “You are compelled to discuss that passage [περιοχήν, *periochēn*] of the Apostle differently.” Tacitus and other very celebrated writers use the construction likewise. DAVIS.

**SUMMARY.—What is destined to happen to the Christians themselves after death may be inferred from the fact that they are now deprived of every resource and oppressed by the greatest calamities and miseries.**

Yet you do not draw a lesson even from present circumstances about how the empty hopes of a futile promise deceive you. While you still live, wretches, judge what threatens you after death. Behold: a part of you—and the greater and better part, as you say—are needy and cold; you suffer from lack of aid and from hunger. Yet God permits it and disregards it: he either does not wish or [Col. 0271B] is unable to help his own. Thus he is either powerless or unjust.

You who dream of immortality after death: when danger shakes you, when fevers burn you, when pain tears you apart, do you not then perceive your condition? [Col. 0272A] Do you not then acknowledge your frailty? Against your will, wretch, you are convicted of weakness, yet you will not admit it. But I pass over what is common to all. Behold what awaits you: threats, punishments, tortures, and crosses now no longer to be worshipped but to be endured; fires as well, which you both foretell and fear. Where is that God who can assist people when they come back to life, but cannot assist them while they are alive?

Do not the Romans rule, reign, enjoy the whole world, and exercise dominion over you without your God? Meanwhile, you live in suspense and anxiety, abstaining from respectable pleasures. You do not attend public shows or take part in processions; public banquets go on without you. You abhor sacred contests, foods from which a portion has first been taken, and drinks first poured in libation upon altars. Thus you dread the gods whose existence you deny. You do not bind your heads with flowers or honor your bodies with perfumes; you reserve ointments for funerals and deny even garlands to tombs—pale and trembling, worthy of pity, but of our gods’ pity. Thus, wretches, you neither rise again nor live in the meantime.

(IX) Accordingly, if you possess any wisdom or modesty, cease examining the regions of heaven, the destinies of the world, and its secrets. It is enough to look at what lies before your feet—especially for the unlearned, uncultivated, ignorant, and rustic. Since it has not been granted to them to understand civil matters, much more has it been denied them to discuss divine things.

## CHAPTER XIII

> **Note: [Col. 0273B]**
>
> **CHAPTER XIII.—*Whoever among you is so great*.** Thus the manuscript. Yet there have been editors who emended it to “whoever among you is so great,” using a different Latin construction; and Chr. Cellarius indeed printed it so. But there is no need to depart from the manuscript’s reading. Prudentius, *Peristephanon*, Hymn X.214:
>
> > Whoever consecrates Hercules as a god  
> > By statue or shrine shall feel Juno’s anger.
>
> Juvencus, *Gospel History* I, p. 35, Lyons edition of 1553:
>
> > Whoever devotes his ears and deeds to my admonitions.
>
> And II, p. 45:
>
> > Whoever, therefore, seeks the first beginnings of a righteous life,  
> > He is like, etc.
>
> Symmachus I, Letter 52: “Whoever is of good character is claimed for the public benefit.” See Fr. Juretus there, and also on Ambrose, *Against Symmachus* I, p. 318. THE SAME.
>
> *If he shall have been able.* I first see *si poterit* (“if he will be able”) in Rigaltius’ edition; if its editor adopted this on the authority of the manuscript, it is correct. But all earlier editions, beginning with Sabaeus’ own, have *si potuerit*. To be sure, chapter 15 has “if it can be refuted,” while chapter 27 has “attack, if you can.” And although you will scarcely have moved a finger, Cicero nevertheless preferred the same form in *On the Orator* II.20, “if I shall have been able,” and III.22, “if you shall not have been able.” GRONOVIUS.
>
> *What is above us is nothing to you.* Lactantius III.19 and Jerome, *Apology Against Rufinus* 8, record this saying of Socrates. See Xenophon, *Memorabilia* I, fol. 710; Theodoret, *Against the Greeks*, Oration IV, *On Matter and the World*, fol. 60; and Gellius XIV.3. ELMENHORST.—*Deservedly,* etc. That is: Socrates deservedly said, “What is above us is nothing to us.” RIGALTIUS.—This was Apollo’s response concerning Socrates:
>
> > Ἀνδρῶν ἁπάντων Σωκράτης σοφώτατος.  
> > Of all men, Socrates is the wisest.
>
> Very many ancient authors record it; Aegidius Menagius collected their testimonies in his notes on Diogenes Laertius II.§37. DAVIS.
>
> *Which oracle he himself perceived, and therefore to have been placed before all.* We have presented the exact words of the Royal manuscript and understand them in this way: “The oracle—namely, Socrates himself—perceived, therefore,” etc. It is not so absurd for a wise man to be called an oracle, since Cicero himself, *On the Orator* I.45, called the jurist’s house “the oracle of the entire state.” Before the infinitive *esse* (“to be”), *se* (“himself”) must be supplied, as also commonly happens in Latin usage. Let us now examine the commentators’ conjectures about this passage. Rigaltius: “What is above us is nothing to us. Deservedly. He therefore earned from the oracle testimony to his singular wisdom—which oracle he himself perceived—and was therefore placed before all, not because,” [Col. 0274B] etc. J. F. Gronovius, *Observations on Ecclesiastical Writers* 6, p. 76: “He himself perceived what the oracle meant; for that reason he was placed before all,” etc. The younger Gronovius: “What of the oracle? He himself perceived it, therefore,” etc. Ouzelius: “By this oracle he himself perceived that he was therefore placed before all, not because,” etc. Wopkens: “Therefore he himself was placed before all,” and explains it thus: “He himself rightly understood the meaning of that oracle—namely, that by it he was placed before all for this reason, not because,” etc. Davis: “Through this oracle he himself thoroughly perceived that he was therefore placed before all,” etc. Gruner: “Which oracle he himself perceived, therefore,” etc.; he adds that Minucius wished to remove every trace of dissimulation from Socrates, as Justin also did in the words cited by Heraldus. Heumann deletes the words “which oracle . . . placed before all” as a gloss and wishes the text to read: “Deservedly . . . singular wisdom: not because . . . he had learned,” etc. LINDNER.
>
> *Thus of confessed.* Read: “Thus confession.” So also below, chapter 38.1, “a confession of fear.” The matter itself shows that the copyist erred. HEUMANN.
>
> [Col. 0274C] *Of very many Academics* means numerous and diverse Academics. Pliny 9.12: “Aquatic creatures have numerous coverings.” And the Academic school was indeed numerous: the Old, Middle, New, Fourth, and Fifth Academies are counted. These classes, as though separate heads, likewise included several persons. Davis conjectured: “of Academics and Pyrrhonists in the highest,” etc.; yet, as Wopkens correctly observes, the Pyrrhonists may readily be understood as included among the Academics. Heumann preferred to rewrite: “of the younger Academics.” Is this meant in apposition? But Arcesilaus was head of the Middle Academy. Or are younger Academics other than the two leading figures named by Caecilius being mentioned? But Carneades was a follower of the New Academy. And did not the Old Academy equally approve of doubting individual matters, just as the New or Younger Academy did? LINDNER.
>
> *Simonides of Meles.* It is unclear how every editor without contradiction, down to the most recent, came to read “Simonides the lyric poet.” Nor did Lindner himself write more soundly, although he has these remarks in his Notes. “Simonides of Meles” is the reading of the Royal manuscript. Minucius certainly likes to repeat expressions in this manner, as below in chapter 19: “Let Thales of Miletus be first of all to have debated celestial matters. This same Thales of Miletus said that water was the beginning of things.” Thus Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* I: “Thessaly—for there the foundations of our maternal ancestry, transmitted by the celebrated Plutarch and shortly afterward by his grandson Sextus the philosopher, bring us glory—that Thessaly I was making for on business.” I remember having observed such repetitions quite frequently even in Caesar. HERALDUS.—Thus chapter 22: “For all ancient writers, Greek and Roman, have handed down that Saturn, the chief of this class and swarm, was a man.—This Saturn, therefore, an exile from Crete,” etc. Chapter 26: “They are impure spirits, wandering, weighed down from heavenly vigor by earthly stains and desires. These spirits, therefore, after,” etc.; chapter 27: “These unclean spirits, therefore”; chapter III.7: “to pick up from the shore a rounded potsherd smoothed by the tossing of the waves, and to hold that potsherd with its flat side between the fingers,” etc.; Cornelius Nepos, *Eumenes* III.3: “Since Eumenes had neither large nor reliable forces.—Eumenes therefore understood.” On that passage see Boeclerus. LINDNER.
>
> *What and of what kind.* Thus above, chapter 17: “A human being ought to know himself and look about him: what he is and why he exists.” LINDNER.
>
> *Toward the other side.* There is no reason to substitute *alterutram* (“either of the two”) for *alteram* (“the other”), as Davis did; the latter is very frequently used by the Latins for the former. Above, chapter 5: “So that you may hold the balance of a perfectly impartial judge and not lean with partiality toward either side.” Cicero, *Academics* II.43: “Therefore both cannot be wise . . . but one or the other.” Many more examples may be drawn from Faber’s *Thesaurus*, Tursellinus *On Particles*, Freinsheim’s index to Florus, and elsewhere. WOPKENS.
>
> *A man of Plautine lineage.* Caecilius’ mind is still rankled by Octavius’ jest that in the clearest daylight he had stumbled against stones, because on the shore at Ostia he had worshipped a stone that the pagans had anointed and fashioned into an image. Caecilius therefore rubs down his Octavius with a different salt and calls him “a man of Plautine lineage.” At first sight this might seem to refer only to Plautine jokes. But immediately afterward he drives that very Plautine man into a mill, where Varro and most other authorities report that Marcus Accius Plautus wrote three plays. Caecilius turns the disgrace of this service in the mill against Octavius because of the simplicity of the Christian religion, a great part of whose adherents were uneducated laborers, such as bakers, shoemakers, and others of that kind. He therefore says that Octavius is preeminent among Christian bakers, but last among philosophers. RIGALTIUS.—The following expressions, frequent enough in St. Jerome, attest that this proverbial formula was once well worn: “members of the Plautine family have been discovered,” Letter XXVII . . . “the pillar of the Plautine family,” Letter XLVII. EDD.
>
> *Refrain from applauding against him.* Minucius now strikes Caecilius back with the phrase “Plautine lineage.” “Refrain,” he says, “from applauding against him”—as though he said: “Do not bark at our Octavius with that Plautine, or barking, lineage of yours.” The jest is double, for after a comedy is completed the actors customarily ask for applause. Here Caecilius applauds himself to Octavius’ disparagement and disgrace. Applause is given by striking or clapping the hands together; shells suited particularly well for clapping are called *plautiores*, and dogs whose hanging, flaccid, and rather broad ears flap against their heads are called *plauti*. RIGALTIUS.

**SUMMARY.—Caecilius finally concludes that the new religion must be rejected and that one must not pronounce rashly upon doubtful matters.**

Yet if you have a desire to philosophize, let whoever among you is so great imitate Socrates, the foremost figure in wisdom, if he can. Whenever that man was asked about heavenly matters, his well-known response was: **WHAT IS ABOVE US IS NOTHING TO US.** Deservedly, therefore, did he earn from the oracle testimony to his singular wisdom. That oracle he himself understood to mean that he had been placed before everyone for this reason: not because he had discovered everything, but because he had learned that he knew nothing. Thus confession of ignorance is the highest wisdom.

From this source flowed the cautious doubt of Arcesilaus, and much later of Carneades, and of very many Academics in the highest questions—a mode of philosophizing in which the unlearned can engage cautiously and the learned gloriously.

(X) What then? Is not the hesitation of Simonides of Meles something for everyone to admire and all to follow? When the tyrant Hiero asked Simonides what he thought the gods were and of what nature, Simonides first requested one day for deliberation; on the following day he extended it to two days; soon afterward, when reminded, he added as much again. Finally, when the tyrant asked the reason for so great a delay, Simonides replied that the longer his inquiry continued, the more obscure the truth became to him.

In my opinion also, matters that are doubtful should be left as they are. While so many eminent men remain in deliberation, judgment should not rashly and boldly be delivered in favor of either side, lest either an old woman’s superstition be introduced or all religion be destroyed.

## CHAPTER XIV

> **Note: [Col. 0275D]**
>
> **CHAPTER XIV.—*More fully*.** Gronovius wishes to read *penitus* (“thoroughly”), but without reason. The Latins call that *plenum* (“full”) which lacks nothing; concerning this meaning of the word, we give further material in our note on Aurelius Victor, *Origin of the Roman People* XII.12. Hence *plene* means “entirely.” Cicero, *Letter to Quintus* I.1.13: “You cannot entirely avoid this”; Justin XI.11.9. Hence in Minucius, “until the case has been argued more fully on both sides,” means “entirely.” As for the comparative, it can be explained as having the force of the positive. More exacting scholars, however, maintain that one or more words must always be understood. See Sanctius and Perizonius on *Minerva* II.10, p. 219 of my edition. In Minucius’ words one could understand “than hitherto.” GRUNER.
>
> *Not on praise and truth,* Royal manuscript. From this Heraldus produced “on praise, but on truth.” Others read, “by praise, but by truth.” EDD. Heumann reads “on applause,” because shortly before Minucius had said, “Refrain from applauding against him.” But applause is a sign of praise. LINDNER.
>
> *Your speech has delighted me with its subtle variety.* Minucius calls Caecilius’ variety “subtle”; shortly afterward Octavius will call it a “subtle variation and wavering,” which comes very close to sophistry and cunning. RIGALTIUS.
>
> [Col. 0276C] *According to the abilities of those debating.* I write “according to the powers of debate,” because “the power of eloquence” follows. HEUMANN. According to the abilities of the debaters, a good case is sometimes defended badly and a bad case well. All this force resides in the weight of arguments and opinions. Yet arguments neither alone nor everywhere exercise their force unless elegance of language is also joined to them. Eloquence has such power that it moves the hearer’s mind and, through a splendid style of speaking, readily sweeps it away—uplifted and struck with astonishment—into admiration and assent. LINDNER.
>
> *Without discrimination.* Thus the Royal manuscript and the Roman edition. Others read a variant spelling, *dilectu*. LINDNER.
>
> *From what is right.* I consider the word *rectis* (“right things”) sound, contrary to the judgment of Jacobus Gronovius when he emends it to *certis* (“certain things”). For statements are called “right” when they are true and sincere, containing nothing fabricated, and thus opposed to falsehoods. So below, chapter XVI.9: “Speech . . . is not painted with the pomp of eloquence, but is sustained, just as it is, by the rule of what is right.” Plautus, chapter 5: “Speak right and true things.” WOPKENS. Cicero, *On Friendship* 10: “to ask of friends what is not right”; and chapter 11: “if we have determined that it is right to grant friends whatever they wish.” The same author, *On Duties* III.11: “It is right”—that is, “it is true”—“that this is not permitted.” Ovid, *Metamorphoses* VII.72: “right, piety, and shame.” It is evident from this that both what is morally honorable and what is true are called *rectum*. Indeed, does not our own Minucius say at the conclusion of this chapter that we ought to select and approve those things that are right? HEUMANN.
>
> *Within the incredible.* The manuscript reads “and incredible.” But the author’s meaning requires us to understand that the two syllables were contracted into one in the copyist’s manner noted above. Just as Minucius said that falsehood is present “within the probable,” he surely said that truth is present “within the incredible.” It is incredible that God became man and was crucified. It is incredible that the bodies of the dead, whether cremated or buried, will return to life even after many centuries. Yet these things, although incredible, are true. Conversely, it appears probable that there is no god; or that he takes no care for human affairs; or that, if he did, he would be polluted by so sorrowful and manifold a ministry. Likewise, it appears probable that death ends all human things. Yet although these claims are probable, they are utterly false. RIGALTIUS.
>
> *They transfer the judge’s fault to a complaint about uncertainty.* This reading is unsound, for Minucius is speaking of many judges. Wower therefore restores “the fault of the judgment.” Meursius and Cellarius emend: “the judges transfer the fault to a complaint about uncertainty.” The sentence seems feeble to me unless the pronoun is added, so that it reads: “The judges transfer **their own** fault to a complaint about uncertainty.” Ausonius, *The Crucifixion of Cupid*, verse 64:
>
> > So they transfer their own faults to another’s crimes.
>
> Sallust, *Jugurtha* 1: “The authors themselves transfer **their own** fault to their occupations.” The same author likewise said in chapter 34, “to transfer fear from his own crime to your cowardice.” DAVIS.—[Col. 0277C] Heumann explains it thus: “Although they ought to accuse their own rashness in judging, from the fact that they are so often mistaken they conclude that nothing is right, but that everything must perpetually remain in doubt.” Yet the manuscript has *judicis* (“of the judge”), which is sound, as Gronovius explains on this passage. For it is “the judge’s fault” that the judge commits when his attention slackens during the hearing, or when in listening his mind is disengaged or becomes more disengaged from the pleader’s case, to use Terence’s expression as noted by Gronovius’ father in *Observations* III.7. Consequently, instead of avoiding the fault committed solely in the judge’s own person, they transfer it to the subject matter, which they complain was full of darkness, obscurity, and uncertainty, although the cause of the difficulty or darkness lies with the judge himself. It is precisely the same expression that Sallust uses in the passage cited. LINDNER.
>
> *So that, after condemning everything.* I read, “so that, after adjourning everything.” MEURSIUS. But “adjourning” means the same as “suspending,” whereas that participle ought to have had some force different from the meaning of the verb *suspendere*. Indeed, why would the author wish to be so foolishly redundant as to say, “after adjourning everything, they prefer to suspend everything”—that is, “they prefer to adjourn everything,” or “they prefer to suspend everything”? “Condemning,” however, means rejecting, alienating, and setting aside because of the difficulty of penetrating the matters, not for a time but permanently. GRONOVIUS.—If anything must nevertheless be changed, I would prefer: “after condemning opinions.” For opinions are uncertain and fallacious, and they are properly opposed to certainty. LINDNER.
>
> *Let us labor; so that,* etc. I read and punctuate: “let us labor in such a way that, as an object of execration,” etc. Aulus Gellius, *Attic Nights* IV.8: “But as for what I wrote above concerning what Fabricius said about Cornelius Rufinus, he said it in the form in which it is recorded in most historical works.” And IX.14: “I found it written in rather numerous books in the form stated by Caesellius.” Our author speaks in the same way below. DAVIS.
>
> *Are made savage.* Davis changes this to “are carried forth.” Wrongly; for the verb is *efferare* (“to make savage”), not *efferre* (“to carry forth”). Here is a parallel passage from Livy V.27: “made savage by hatred and anger.” Had Wopkens noticed this, he would not have wasted so many words in refuting Davis and showing that indirect discourse, which properly ought to be direct, is not infrequently shifted in this way into the subjunctive after an infinitive. HEUMANN.
>
> *For incautiously credulous.* Heumann has no doubt that Minucius wrote: “For **while** incautiously,” etc. This emendation is not particularly necessary; at most the particle “while” can be understood. LINDNER.
>
> *Anxious.* Since this word is foreign to the present context, I write “accustomed”; and because an infinitive verb is now required, I read: “We, accordingly, are accustomed to hear.” The sense is: “We who plead cases in the forum are accustomed to hear that on both sides,” etc. HEUMANN. The manuscript’s received reading is sound, for *sollicitus* means doubtful or attentive. Cicero, *For His House* 96: “the whole community being in suspense and anxiety.” The same author, *On Friendship* 52: “Everything in the lives of tyrants is always suspect and anxious.” Livy V.47: “dogs, an animal alert to noises in the night.” LINDNER.
>
> *From the other side.* Thus the manuscript. The Roman edition has “may lie concealed.” Supply “may be.” “From the other side, there may be marvelous subtlety.” Heumann, though hesitantly, writes “may shine forth.” The emendation of Fulvius Ursinus, which appears in the Roman edition, is, I confess, highly pleasing to me. LINDNER.
>
> *To look up to.* Perhaps “to undertake.” Thus chapter 6.7: “While they undertake the rites of all nations.” Yet the progression is sufficiently sound even as it stands, for “to look up to” is more than “to approve.” But I now see that Heraldus printed it thus from the Royal manuscript, so that I do not know where Cellarius obtained the verb “to look up to”; it must be entirely removed. LINDNER.

**SUMMARY.—With the disdain of a proud spirit, Caecilius challenges Octavius to answer his arguments. Minucius replies modestly that Caecilius should not exult over his own by no means inconsiderable eloquence or over the harmonious variety of his speech.**
[Col. 0276A] Thus Caecilius spoke, and then, smiling—for the vehemence of his outpouring had relaxed the swelling of his indignation—said: “Does Octavius dare make any reply to this—a man of Plautine lineage, foremost among millers, but last among philosophers?”

“Refrain,” I said, “from applauding him; for you have no right to exult in the elegance of your discourse before both sides have argued their cases more fully, especially since your debate rests not upon praise but upon truth. And although your speech, with its subtle variety, has delighted me exceedingly, I am nevertheless more deeply troubled—not by the present pleading, but by the whole manner of conducting debate—because the standing even of manifest truth is generally altered according to the abilities of the disputants and the power of their eloquence.

“It is well known that this happens through the pliability of audiences: while the enticement of words distracts them from attention to the facts, they assent indiscriminately to everything that is said and do not distinguish falsehood from truth, [18] unaware [Col. 0276B] that truth may be found even in the incredible and [Col. 0277A] falsehood in the plausible. Accordingly, the more often they trust confident assertions, the more frequently they are refuted by those of greater expertise, and so are continually deceived by their own rashness. They transfer the judge’s fault into a complaint about uncertainty, preferring, after condemning everything, to suspend judgment universally rather than to pass judgment upon deceptive claims.

“We must therefore take care that we do not repeatedly become afflicted with hatred for every discourse, as many of the more simple-minded are carried away into loathing and hatred of humankind. For in their incautious credulity they are deceived by those whom they believed good; presently, through a similar error, they become suspicious of everyone and fear as wicked even those whom they might have recognized as excellent.

“We, therefore, are apprehensive because in every matter arguments are presented on both sides, and because on the one side the truth is generally obscure, while on the other [Col. 0277B] there is remarkable subtlety, which sometimes, through copious eloquence, [Col. 0278A] imitates the credibility of demonstrated proof. Let us weigh each point as carefully as possible, so that we may indeed praise ingenuity, but choose, approve, and embrace what is right.”

## CHAPTER XV

> **Note: [Col. 0278C]**
>
> **CHAPTER XV.—“If he can,” etc.** The Royal manuscript has *reputare* (“reconsider”). The passage does not appear sound; perhaps it was written: “Since Octavius has every point whole and unimpaired, if he can refute them. That which,” etc. HERALDUS.—I would punctuate it: “. . . has every point, if he can, to refute,” that is, “has points that must be refuted.” Unless perhaps the author used *habere* (“to have”) for *debere* (“to have to”), or—as I should prefer—we ought to read *debeat*.
