For Pythagoras, too, God is the mind that passes through and pervades the whole nature of things, from which the life of all living creatures is also derived. Xenophanes is well known for teaching that the entire infinite together with mind is God; Antisthenes, that the gods of individual peoples are many, but that the one natural God is supreme; and Speusippus [printed: Zeuxippus], that God is the natural, animate power by which all things are governed.

What of Democritus? Although the first inventor of atoms, [p. 26] does he not very often call God the nature that emits images, and intelligence? Strato likewise calls nature itself God. Even that Epicurus who imagines the gods either idle or nonexistent nevertheless places nature above all. Aristotle varies, yet still assigns sovereignty to a single power. For at one time he calls mind God, at another the world, and at another places God over the world. Aristotle of Pontus varies, assigning sovereignty at one time to the world and at another to the divine mind. Heraclides of Pontus likewise attributes divine mind to God, though in varying ways.

Theophrastus, Zeno, Chrysippus, and Cleanthes are themselves diverse in their accounts, yet they all return to the unity of providence. For Cleanthes discussed God now as mind, now as soul, now as ether, but most often as reason. Zeno, his teacher, holds that natural and divine law, and at one time ether [Col. 0295B] and at another reason, is the origin of all things. Likewise, by interpreting Juno as air, Jupiter as heaven, Neptune as the sea, Vulcan as fire, and similarly demonstrating that the other gods of the common people are elements, he gravely exposes and refutes the general error.

[Col. 0296A] Chrysippus says almost the same: he believes that God is divine power, rational nature, at one time the world, and also the necessity of fate; and in his physical interpretation of the poems of Hesiod, Homer, and Orpheus, he imitates Zeno.

(XIII) Diogenes of Babylon also makes it his discipline to expound and discuss how Jupiter was born and Minerva came into being, and how terms for the other things of this kind are names of things, not of gods.

(XIV) Xenophon the Socratic denies that the form of the true God can be seen, [p. 27] and therefore says that it ought not to be sought. Aristo of Chios [printed: “the Stoic”] says that it cannot be comprehended at all. Both perceived the majesty of God through their despair of understanding him.

Plato’s discourse concerning God is clearer, both in the realities themselves and in their names; it would be wholly heavenly if it were not sometimes sullied by an admixture of civic persuasion. Thus, in Plato’s *Timaeus*, God is, by his own [Col. 0296B] name, the parent of the world, the craftsman of the soul, and the maker of things heavenly and earthly. Plato first declares that to discover him is difficult because of his exceedingly great and incredible power, and that, once you have discovered him, to speak of him publicly is impossible.

[Col. 0297A] (XV) These things are almost the same as ours: for we both know God and call him the parent of all, and we never proclaim him publicly unless we are questioned.

## CHAPTER XX

[Note: [Col. 0297B]

**CHAPTER XX.—One God . . . names.** The celebrated Heumann regards these words as suspect of being a gloss; but they cohere well if one interprets them to mean that those philosophers designated one God, although by many names. In the same way we explained the words of this chapter: “Chrysippus says almost the same,” namely, divine power, and so forth. Lactantius I.5: “For whether you call him nature, ether, reason, mind, fatal necessity, divine law, or anything else, it is the same as that which we call God. Nor is the diversity of appellations an obstacle, since in their very signification all things return to one.” LINDNER.

**The antiquity of the unlearned.** So far as I know, [Col. 0297C] virtually all the interpreters translate these words as though it made little difference whether the word “unlearned” were absent or present. Thus the French translator: “We must not allow ourselves to be carried away by the fables of antiquity.” Yet that word was by no means to be neglected. For Octavius distinguishes between the antiquity of the unlearned and that of the learned, or philosophers. His purpose is to teach that those who rashly follow antiquity because of some preconceived opinion should listen to the philosophers rather than to the unlearned, since both parties equally possess the authority of age, while the philosophers possess in addition the authority of reason. LINDNER.

**Delighted or captivated.** Cicero similarly joins “rejoice” and “be captivated” in *Letters to Friends* VI, letter 7: “With your prudence, you understand what things Caesar rejoices in and by what he is captivated.” Our author is much given to joining synonyms, such as “more sublime and loftier,” “inventions and lies,” “defend and protect,” and “err and be mistaken,” in chapters 19, 22, 28, 32, and elsewhere. Moreover, synonyms of this kind are rather often joined by the conjunction *vel* (“or”) in place of *et* (“and”). Sulpicius Severus, *Sacred History* II.15: [Col. 0297D] “That he had paid the Lord sufficient penalties for his sins or crimes,” where we accumulate several expressions. Compare what was said above on chapter VIII. There was therefore no reason for Davis to banish the words “delighted or” and read only “captivated by its fables.” For he objects without justification that this is not the place to discuss the delight or charm of fables. We are quite appropriately said here to be “delighted” by fables of any kind if we readily lend them our ears and highly esteem them. Similarly, in Lactantius I.7 the multitude of gods is said to delight people; and below, in chapter 22, the inventions and lies by which people readily permit themselves to be captivated are called sweet. Compare Cicero, *On Divination* I.55. WOPKENS.

Heumann, on Lactantius I.20 and IV.15, shows that copyists often wrote *monstruosa* for *monstrosa*, following popular pronunciation. But Bünemann has already observed that Scheffer, Heinsius, Goes, and Burmann more correctly use *monstruosus* in prose than *monstrosus*, which is more familiar to poets. Gronovius proves from a fragment of Varro cited by Nonius that *mira miracula*, “marvelous marvels,” can be said: “To the same place they had gathered I know not what marvelous marvels.” As regards emendations, Meursius proposes “monstrous marvels”; Heraldus, “monstrous, marvelous marvels”; Davis, “dreadful marvels”; Cellarius and Heumann, “monstrous marvels”; and Gruner, “other monstrous, marvelous marvels.” LINDNER.—“Marvelous marvels.” Nothing should be changed. It is a play on words, like “the wretched take pity” above and “to die after death.” GRUNER, work cited, p. 226.—So too Davis in his second edition, where he also observes that the ancients used similar expressions. Apuleius, *Metamorphoses*, book I, p. 15, and book II, p. 185, said *gratas gratias*, “welcome thanks.” Ausonius, *Epigram* 20: “Accustomed to drink wine unmixed and wine that was pure wine,” etc. See the notes above at the end of chapter 8. GALLAND.

[Col. 0298C] **Horses entwined with their human beings.** The learned J. Wower is mistaken in conjecturing that one should restore “horses entwined with half-human beings”; for the common reading must be retained. Arnobius, book I, near the end: “The destroyer of death itself permitted his human being to be slain.” For the force and meaning of this pronoun one should consult J. F. Gronovius, *Observations*, book I, chapter 11. DAVIS.

**It is permitted.** Without doubt *libet*, “it pleases,” must be restored. HEUMANN.

**It was pleasing for them to hear.** So the German: *Es war ihnen lieb zu hören*, that is, “they heard willingly.” Propertius I.20.13:

> May it not be for you to approach harsh mountains and cold rocks,  
> Gallus, nor always lakes devoid of life.

Here “may it not be for you to approach” means “may you not approach,” “may you not wish to approach”; see Passeratius in his notes. There was consequently no reason for Heumann to restore: “It was for them, being willing, to hear.” LINDNER.

**Birds from human beings.** In place of “out of human beings.” This is Tertullian’s style, as I observed on Lactantius V.9. This reading is therefore entirely sound, contrary to the opinion of an anonymous writer in *British and Dutch Critical Observations*, vol. I, p. 29. HEUMANN.—“Birds from human beings, and wild beasts human beings” [a corrupt reading]. Wower’s edition has “birds from human beings, and human beings from wild beasts.” This is indeed a little better, yet I think something is missing, for in this form Minucius does not mention the transformation of human beings into wild beasts. I therefore think one should restore: “Birds and wild beasts from human beings, human beings from wild beasts, and trees and flowers from human beings”? Clement, *Recognitions*, book X, chapter 26: “They say that from human beings come stars, trees, animals, birds, springs, and rivers.” DAVIS.

**Birds and wild beasts.** The manuscript has “and wild beasts, human beings.” But who, even without a warning from me, fails to see that the word *homines*, “human beings,” is a most disgraceful gloss? For Minucius establishes two classes of things into which fables report that human beings were transformed: one animate, namely birds and wild beasts; the other inanimate, namely trees and flowers. Wower, with some openly and Gronovius hesitantly agreeing with him, had published “birds from human beings, and human beings from wild beasts.” Scheffer’s reading is bad: “birds and all wild beasts from human beings.” In my judgment, however, it is utterly wrong. LINDNER.

**Because they cannot occur.** The manuscript codex correctly reads thus. Several editors had printed, very badly: “If they had happened, they would happen—things which cannot happen; therefore they did not happen.” I add that “they would happen” is expressed briefly for “they would happen even now,” and “because they cannot happen” for “because they cannot happen in our own time.” For the rest, I stated in *Poecile*, vol. II, p. 282, what ought to be thought of this argument of Minucius. HEUMANN.

**Similarly indeed, also regarding the gods.** German: *Gerade so, wie sie auch in Ansehung der Götter*, etc., “Just as they also did in regard to the gods.” In the manuscript the words are transposed: *similiter ac vero*. Since this is foreign to Latin usage, Rigaltius punctuated it: *Similiter ac vero.* [Col. 0299C] Wower and Elmenhorst published “similarly indeed regarding the gods,” omitting the particle *ac*; Gronovius, absurdly, *simili veratro*; Scheffer, “similarly and truly”; Heumann, “by a similar error.” None of these emendations seems to present us with the true text of Minucius. *Similiter vero* means “similarly, certainly.” Cicero, *To Quintus his Brother* I.1: “For you this both always was very easy and certainly ought to have been so.” *Ac* follows *similiter* in Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* III.3: “But you, who ask this, act just as if you were to ask me.” LINDNER.

**Improvident, credulous.** We have several times noted such asyndetic expressions above. Heumann reads *improvide creduli*, “improvidently credulous,” as above in chapter 14: “incautiously credulous.” LINDNER.

**They believed out of their primitive simplicity.** Heumann prefers “they believed primitive simplicity,” that is, they believed the ancients, who were conspicuous for great simplicity and ignorance. But who are those simple ancients in relation to the forefathers, unless they are the forefathers themselves? And those forefathers did not believe primitive simplicity because the ancients were to be preferred to their own predecessors, but rather believed *out of* primitive simplicity. LINDNER.

**Memories in statues.** Louis Carrion, *Emendations*, book II, chapter 18, was the first to restore this in place of the printed “more insistently.” Heraldus teaches that “in statues” is also read in the manuscript. For plural “memories” Heumann reads the singular “memory.” LINDNER.

**In short, also.** I have printed it thus, following Heraldus and Rigaltius; from this I suppose it stands thus in the manuscript, although the other editions delete the second word without cause. GRONOVIUS.

**Stronger than her sex.** For women can easily be deceived, as Ovid says, *Heroides* II.63:

> To deceive a trusting girl is no laborious glory.

Likewise:

> Both loving and a woman, I was deceived by your words.

She who therefore did not allow herself to be deceived was stronger than her sex. Heumann restores “or than her sex.” LINDNER.]

**SUMMARY.—But if the world is ruled by Providence and governed at the command of one God, the ignorant past must not drag us into the error of mutual agreement, since it was delighted by its own fables and introduced ridiculous traditions. It is no less clearly demonstrated that the worship of the gods was always foolish and impious, since the earliest mortals venerated their kings, illustrious leaders, and inventors of arts, on account of their notable deeds, just as though they were gods.**

I have set forth the opinions of almost all the philosophers [Col. 0297B] whose more distinguished glory lies in having designated one God, although by many [Col. 0298A] names. Thus anyone might suppose either that Christians are now philosophers, or that philosophers were already Christians then.

But if the world is ruled by Providence and governed at the command of one God, the antiquity of the unlearned, delighted or captivated by its own fables, ought not to carry us away into the error of mutual agreement, since it is refuted by the opinions of its own philosophers, whose authority rests upon both reason and antiquity.

For our forefathers possessed such ready faith in falsehoods that they rashly believed even other monstrous, marvelous marvels: Scylla with her many forms, the multiform Chimaera, the Hydra reborn through its fruitful wounds, the Centaurs—horses entwined with their human beings—and whatever rumor is permitted to invent, [p. 28] they were pleased to hear. What of those old women’s tales about [Col. 0298B] birds and wild beasts arising from human beings, human beings, and trees and [Col. 0299A] flowers arising from human beings? If these things had happened, they would still happen; because they cannot happen, they therefore did not happen.

Similarly, indeed, our forefathers were improvident and credulous also regarding the gods, and believed out of their primitive simplicity. While they reverently worshiped their kings, while after their deaths they longed to see them in images, while they eagerly sought to preserve their memories in statues, things assumed as consolations became sacred rites.

In short, both before the world lay open to commerce and before nations mingled their rites and customs, each nation venerated its own founder, or an illustrious leader, or a chaste queen stronger than her sex, or the discoverer of some function or art, as a citizen of good memory. Thus both a reward was given to the dead and an example to those yet to come.

## CHAPTER XXI

[Note: [Col. 0299D]

**Read the writings of the Stoics.** *Lege*, “read,” is imperative. If anyone should happen to be surprised that I give this warning, let him know that in Cellarius’s index these words are entered under the heading *Lex Stoicorum scripta*, “Law of the Stoics written.” LINDNER.

[Col. 0300B] **Or the writings of the wise.** Cellarius judged that these words should be deleted. Others restore: “Read the writings of the historians, or the writings of the wise.” But nothing should be changed, for among the best authors a genus is placed beside a species. Ovid, *Metamorphoses* V:

> Daulian fields and Phocian fields, with a Thracian soldier,

although Daulis is a town of Phocis. DAVIS.—It pertains to the boastfulness of the Stoics that they claimed for themselves above all others the title of “wise men,” a fact that escapes no one even slightly acquainted with Seneca’s writings. Thus “the wise” κατ’ ἐξοχήν, “preeminently,” are the Stoics. But why was mention of the Stoics made before? Was it so that a genus might be placed beside a species? I do not think so. What, then? One must read “historians,” not “Stoics.” This is proved:

1. Because Heumann observed that even in a certain passage of Jerome some copyists wrote “Stoics” and others “historians”: *Poecile*, vol. II, p. 344.
2. Because Lactantius speaks similarly, V.4: “Human testimonies first had to be adduced, that is, those of philosophers and historians.”
3. Because Minucius actually did adduce the testimonies of Stoics and historians. Euhemerus, Prodicus, and Persaeus are included under “the wise”; Alexander the Great, Nepos, Cassius, Thallus, and Diodorus under “the historians.”
4. Because the gloss “Stoics” could easily have displaced the word “historians,” since copyists did not notice that *vel*, “or,” was used adversatively, as in chapter I.

Gronovius thinks that Minucius wrote “or the maxims [constitute] wisdom” (*vel scita sapientiam*) [an uncertain conjectural reading]. LINDNER.

**Considered gods because of the merit of their virtue or service. Euhemerus brings out**, etc. The passage suffers from its punctuation and must be divided thus: “You will recognize. Euhemerus traces how they were considered gods because of their merits, and,” etc. For this is what that ancient writer accomplished. Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, book I, chapter [Col. 0300D] 42: “Those who teach that brave, famous, or powerful men attained to the gods after death—are they not devoid of every form of religion? This line of reasoning was especially developed by Euhemerus.” Consult Lactantius, *On the Wrath of God*, chapter 2. See also *Divine Institutes*, book I, chapter 11. DAVIS.

**By prodigies.** From this Desiderius Heraldus restores “Posidippus”; but Nicolas Rigaltius very well restored the text from Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, book I, chapter 42: “What,” he says, “of Prodicus of Chios, who said that those things which benefited human life were counted among the gods?” Here one must read: “What of Prodicus of Ceos?” The *Suda*: Πρόδικος Κεῖος ἀπὸ Κείου τοῦ νήσου, “Prodicus of Ceos, from the island of Ceos.” In Plato, too, he is everywhere called Κεῖος, “Cean.” Erasmus, however, in the *Adages*, and J. A. Fabricius, *Bibliotheca Graeca*, book II, chapter 18, falsely call this sophist “Cian,” although Fabricius correctly identifies him as Cean in book XXIII, chapter 41 of the same work. DAVIS.—Accordingly Sevin should not be heard either; in the *Memoirs of the Royal Academy of Inscriptions*, vol. VIII, p. 2, he proposes changing “by prodigies” to “he betrays.” The source then breaks off with *Is*, “he.” HEUMANN.

**With new [crops].** Delete “crops,” which, if Wower is to be believed, does not appear in the Roman edition either; he very aptly adduces this statement of Pliny: “Individual discoveries added certain persons to the number of the gods.” Fulvius Ursinus likewise deleted “crops.” HEUMANN.

**That Alexander the Great, the Macedonian.** To Wower the last of these words seemed spurious; to me the penultimate one does. For our author did not mean to praise “that Alexander,” but to distinguish him from other Alexanders. HEUMANN.—“That Alexander the Great, the Macedonian.” Nicolas Rigaltius, followed by Christopher Cellarius, maintains that Minucius made a mistake and that Alexander surnamed Πολυΐστωρ, “the Polymath,” rather than Alexander the Great, must be meant. Yet Athenagoras, *Embassy for the Christians*, chapter 24, says: Ἡρόδοτος μὲν οὖν . . . καὶ Ἀλέξανδρος ὁ τοῦ Φιλίππου, ἐν τῇ πρὸς τὴν μητέρα ἐπιστολῇ . . . φασὶ παρ’ ἐκείνων (ἱερέων) ἀνθρώπους αὐτοὺς γενέσθαι μαθεῖν, “Herodotus, then . . . and Alexander the son of Philip, in his letter to his mother . . . say that they learned from those priests that these gods had been human beings.” So too Augustine, *City of God*, book VIII, chapters 3 and 27. Indeed, the excellent and most learned bishop John Fell, in his notes on Cyprian’s *On the Vanity of Idols*, p. 12 of the Oxford edition, demonstrates by many arguments that this suspicion of those learned men is wholly groundless. DAVIS.—The very learned Sablonsky, however, strives with all his might to prove that the letter of Alexander the Great was spurious: *Egyptian Pantheon*, Prolegomena 15–16. See our annotations on Tertullian’s *Apology*. EDITORS.

**There Vulcan.** The Royal manuscript has “to him.” HERALDUS and RIGALTIUS.—What then? Do Heraldus and Rigaltius so despise the manuscript codex that they reject what they themselves saw in it? They mentioned it, however, because of Ursinus, who printed “he,” while they themselves lapsed into something worse. Or did they not know that this particle, in precisely the sense “while I sit there,” has been so carefully noted in Plautus and Terence? I therefore did not hesitate to restore to Minucius what is his own, for I know that it is read thus in the sole manuscript. GRONOVIUS.—Rigaltius correctly restored *illic*, “there,” in place of the manuscript’s *illi*, “to him.” Below, chapter 22: “There he died; there he had sons.” HEUMANN.—**Uranus.** I did not hesitate to restore this in place of what appears in the common editions—and also in the sole Royal manuscript, EDITORS—namely, “Vulcan.” See Lactantius discussing the same subject, I.13: “Ennius, to be sure, in his *Euhemerus*, says that Saturn did not reign first, but Uranus, his father. Although Uranus had several sons, Ennius mentions none of them except Cronus, that is, Saturn; and, passing over Saturn’s sons, he records only the family of Jupiter.” Thus everything becomes very easy. How convoluted, by contrast, is Heumann’s emendation: “He makes Vulcan prince of the Lemnians, born of Vesta and Jupiter.” LINDNER.

**You look down upon.** I hold it certain that the order of the argument has been interrupted by an exchange of several pages in the codex or by some other accident. I do not think it can be restored except by rearranging the dislocated parts. The words of Minucius appear to me to cohere as follows:

Chapter XXI.4: “There he makes Vulcan the prince of all, and afterward the race of Jupiter. For Saturn is the prince of this lineage and swarm,” etc.

Chapter 22 as far as chapter 23: “From this it is evident that those were human beings whom we both read were born and know to have died. Examine the sistrum of Isis beside the swallow, of course, and you will discover that those whom we read were born also died.”

Chapter 21 as far as chapter 23: “And in those same opinions the wretched grow old, though the truth is readily accessible—but only to those who seek it. Who therefore doubts,” etc., chapter 23.

Compare also the *Arrangement* prefixed by me to this work. LINDNER.—Rigaltius testifies that the manuscript very clearly reads not *dispice*, “examine,” but *dispicis*, “you perceive,” which he also attempts to interpret; Jacob Gronovius does the same out of his superstitious veneration for the manuscript codex. Davis, however, rightly calls this interpretation exceedingly harsh and convoluted; following Salmasius, he judges that the text should be restored as: *Respice sis Isidis ad hirundinem sistrum*, “Pray look at the sistrum of Isis beside the swallow.” But even this phrasing is not fluid and elegant. Worse still is the correction he offered in his second edition: “It laughs at the ears of grain of Isis and the swallow.”

Nor can I approve Wower’s conjecture, in his note on Sidonius Apollinaris, book II, letter 9, p. 418, restoring *dispicis*, supposedly the genitive of *dispex*. I confess that the divinations of a certain British critic in *Miscellaneous Critical Observations*, vol. II, pp. 54 ff.; vol. IV, p. 442, do not please me; indeed, I doubt whether they will please anyone. He thought that Minucius’s words “and concerning the ears of grain of Isis” could cohere with what precedes if one assumed that the preceding verb *facit*, “he makes,” was understood here in the sense “he represents.” LINDNER.—Elsner too, I hope—a man flourishing in singular talent and learning—will pardon me for confessing that not one of his conjectures appears successful to me. In his *Critical Essay*, published in 1744, chapter 11, pp. 111 ff., he judges that one should read either, with certain scholars, *Despice Isidis ad hirundinem sistrum*, “Look down upon the sistrum of Isis beside the swallow,” or *Despice Isidis hirundinum sistrum*, “Look down upon the swallow-sistrum of Isis.” On p. 114 he also interprets *despice* as “look at in passing” or “look upon with contempt.” But since he thinks that *ad hirundinem* can be said for “in the likeness of a swallow,” a certain critic in the *Literary News*, published at Hamburg in 1744, p. 8, rightly denies that the character of the Latin language permits such an expression.

The best μάντις, “diviner,” appears to me to be J. Huber, a doctor of law from Basel and a man highly skilled in textual criticism. While residing for several years at the University of Göttingen, he recast these words in private conversation as follows: *Aspice Isidis ac Anubidis sistrum*, “Look at the sistrum of Isis and Anubis.” It is agreed that Anubis was the son of Isis. HEUMANN.—I, however, retain Cellarius’s reading and explain it thus: *Dispice*, that is, “consider the sistrum of Isis beside (*ad*, that is, next to) the swallow.” For Isis was depicted with a small swallow and a sistrum. Just as the sistrum was a querulous instrument, so too the swallow was a querulous creature suited to lamentation. Hence it is easy to infer funerals and deaths. Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 15: “Look closely at the beauties of the Lentuli and Hostilii,” etc. LINDNER.—Others, freely tearing apart and rearranging this mutilated passage this way and that, have gone off into different opinions. It will therefore suffice merely to indicate the most recent attempts, namely those of the Lyons editor, who might perhaps favor these:

“Separate Isis’s sistrum from the swallow . . .”

or:

“Look at the ears of grain of shaggy Isis, and the sistrum,”

or, if preferred:

“The barley ear of Isis and the sistrum,”

or finally—spare us, reader!—

“From the asp of Isis to the resounding sistrum.”

[Col. 0302D] “Now close the channels, boys!” EDITORS.

**And sprinkled.** I read “and scattered.” I shall append the words of the scholiast on Lycophron, which shed no little light on this passage:

> Ὄσιρις ὁ καὶ Διόνυσος, βασιλεὺς ὑπάρχων Αἰγύπτου ὑπὸ Τυφῶνος τοῦ ἀδελφοῦ καὶ τῶν συνωμοτῶν μεληδὸν κατετμήθη, καὶ ἐξετέθη πολλαχοῦ. Ἶσις δὲ ἡ καὶ Δήμητρα, γυνὴ Διονύσου, μετὰ Ὥρου τοῦ υἱοῦ τὸν Τυφῶνα καὶ πάντας τοὺς σὺν ἐκείνῳ φονεῖς ἀναιρεῖ· τὰ δὲ τοῦ Διονύσου μέρη καὶ μόρια συλλέξασα, ἑκάστῳ ναὸν καὶ ἱερὰ ᾠκοδόμησεν.
>
> Osiris, who is also Dionysus, while king of Egypt, was cut limb from limb by his brother Typhon and the conspirators, and his pieces were exposed in many places. Isis, who is also Demeter, the wife of Dionysus, together with her son Horus, killed Typhon and all the murderers who were with him. After gathering the parts and limbs of Dionysus, she built a temple and sacred precincts for each one.

I refrain from transcribing passages from other authors, of which there are abundant numbers. MEURSIUS.

**Your Serapis.** Here Octavius again taunts Caecilius derisively because, when he encountered and noticed an image of Serapis, he had brought his hand to his mouth and pressed a kiss upon his hand with his lips—that is, had worshiped it. RIGALTIUS.

**Deaths and funerals.** So it stands in the manuscript. Julius Firmicus, *On the Error of Profane Religions*, p. 408: “But in these funerals and lamentations, which truly are funerals that happened”; where I read “that happened,” while Heumann reads “and shameful funerals.” LINDNER.

[Col. 0303B] **Bald priests.** An elegant reading presented by the Royal manuscript. Previously all editions had “and other priests.” It is well known that the priests of Isis shaved their heads, and in our youthful notes on Martial, *Epigrams* XII.29, we made several observations on these words:

> The bald linen-wearers flee, and the sistrum-bearing throng.

Artemidorus I.23:

> Ξυρᾶσθαι δὲ δοκεῖν τὴν κεφαλὴν ὅλην, πλὴν Αἰγυπτίων ἱερεῦσι καὶ γελωτοποιοῖς, καὶ τοῖς ἐξ ἔθους ἔχουσι ξυρᾶσθαι, ἀγαθόν, πᾶσι δὲ τοῖς ἄλλοις πονηρόν.
>
> To dream that one’s entire head is being shaved is good for Egyptian priests, jesters, and those who customarily shave, but bad for everyone else.

Prudentius, in the first book *Against Symmachus*:

> The rites of Isis, always mourning the lost Osiris,  
> Farcical and laughable, with their bald men.

HERALDUS.

**Cynocephalus.** He is also Anubis; Mercury, according to Plutarch’s *On Isis*. He was worshiped by the Egyptians with a dog’s face. Apuleius: “Anubis, raising aloft a dog’s high-stretched neck, bearing a caduceus in his left hand.” WOWER.

**Yet these Egyptian rites were once.** Jacob Ouzel supposes that nothing prevents us from saying that Minucius refers to the fact that, just as the Egyptians worshiped Isis, so the Romans worshiped Cybele with the same solemnities and ceremonies. In this the learned man is greatly mistaken, for it was the custom of the Romans to worship no gods unless they had been publicly adopted. See the learned J. Le Clerc on Pedo Albinovanus, *Elegy* I.24. Hence, when Piso and Gabinius were consuls, the rites of Isis were expelled from Rome, although the superstitious populace afterward received them again.

Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 6: “Serapis, Isis, and Harpocrates, together with their Cynocephalus, were prohibited from the Capitol—that is, expelled from the senate-house of the gods—by the consuls Piso and Gabinius, who certainly were not Christians. After demolishing even their altars, they renounced them. You restored them and bestowed upon them supreme majesty.” See also the same author, *To the Nations*, book I, chapter 10. Arnobius, book II, p. 95: “Did you not, after the consulships of Piso and Gabinius, enroll among the number of your gods the Egyptian deities named Serapis and Isis?” It is clearer than the midday sun that Minucius had this in view. DAVIS.

**And surrounded by a serpent.** According to Heraldus, the Royal codex has “surrounded,” but “carried about” is preferable. Ovid, *Fasti* IV.497, on Ceres:

> She yoked bridled serpents to her chariot,  
> And thus passed dry-shod across the waters of the sea.

Hieronymus Alexander also defends this reading in his *Explanation of an Ancient Tablet Engraved with the Image and Symbols of the Sun*, p. 754 of Graevius’s edition. The riddle Gronovius adduces—namely, torches surrounded by a serpent—does not prove the manuscript reading. For because Ceres is not represented on that coin as seated in a chariot, the serpents cannot be shown yoked to her chariot; instead, the torches are depicted simply as surrounded by a serpent. LINDNER.

**Libera.** Proserpina was so called. Cicero, *Against Verres*, [Col. 0304B] book IV, p. 1281 in Lambinus’s edition: “Libera, whom they also call Proserpina, was carried off from the grove of Enna.” And *On the Nature of the Gods*, book II, chapter 24: “Because we call those born from us *liberi*, ‘children,’ those born of Ceres were therefore named Liber and Libera; this is preserved in the case of Libera, but not likewise in that of Liber.” See also Arnobius, book V, pp. 171, 182. DAVIS.

**And which.** So the manuscript and the Roman edition.

**The ringing is drowned out.** I infer from Heraldus’s silence that this stands in the manuscript, since, had he read something different, he certainly would not have left the passage untouched. Meanwhile, Rigaltius testifies that the text there is *initus eliditur*, “the entrance is drowned out.” How these accounts can be reconciled I cannot see. I do see, however, that *tinnitus*, “ringing,” could easily have arisen from *initus*, and I approve it. Just as our author says “to drown out a ringing,” so Celsus IV.4 said “to drown out a whistling,” [Col. 0304C] and Pliny XI.51, “to drown out a sound similar to sneezing.” That ringing, however, was drowned out by the cymbals of the Corybantes so that the father would not hear the crying—that is, the frequent and unceasing crying. Rigaltius prefers *intus eliditur*, “it is drowned out within”; Wower, *tinnitus editur*, “a ringing is produced”; Heumann, *vagitus tinnitu eliditur*, “the crying is drowned out by the ringing.” LINDNER.

**Cybele Dindymena.** This emendation is owed to the celebrated Heumann and is far preferable to all others that have yet seen the light. Rigaltius wished to read “the Dindyma of Cybele”; Davis, “Cybele Dindymena’s”; Cellarius, “Cybele Dindymena” in the accusative. According to Meursius, the manuscript has: “Cybele Dindyma—it is shameful to say what,” etc. LINDNER.—**Cybele Dindyma.** Τὰ Δίνδυμα, “the Dindyma.” Nothing needed to be changed here. Virgil: “Go through the lofty Dindyma.” Servius: “The mountains of the Mother of the Gods.” Catullus called her the goddess of Didymus, or Dindymus. RIGALTIUS.—The manuscript presents “Cybele Dindymena,” whence the old editions exhibit “concerning Cybele Dindymena.” John Meursius, however, judged that the accusative “Cybele Dindymena” should be restored, and Christopher Cellarius printed it thus. [Col. 0304D] To me it appears scarcely doubtful that one should read *Cybelae Dindymena*, “the Dindymena of Cybele”; for the rites of Cybele were named thus from the frenzy by which their participants were driven. DAVIS.

**And she herself.** It is clearly apparent that “she herself also” must be restored. HEUMANN.

**And half-men.** Who, pray, besides the Galli, worshiped Cybele by inflicting punishment upon their own bodies? No one. One must certainly read: “The Galli, half-men, worship her”; the copyists’ stupidity introduced the conjunction after it had been deleted. DAVIS.—What if Minucius added that conjunction emphatically? Namely, with this sense: “The Galli worship Cybele to such an extent that, even as half-men, they worship her through punishment of their own bodies.”

**And disgraces.** Correctly restored thus in place of the manuscript’s “and honors.” Heumann. Heraldus thinks “mockeries and disgraces” was written. LINDNER.

**As though turned backward.** So it stands in the manuscript, and so Heraldus, Rigaltius, Davis, and Gronovius printed these words, although the last suspects that they contain some corruption and that one should read “as though he proceeds in either direction.” But I cannot approve that correction, however the most learned man may defend it in *Le Clerc’s Malicious Mockery*, p. 47. Nor am I any more pleased by the conjecture of Ursinus, Wower, and Elmenhorst, “as though also turned backward.”

A passage of Plautus, *The Merchant* I.1.90, defends the manuscript reading as uniquely correct: “She sends a slave along with me, who formerly, when I was a very small boy, had been my tutor, as though so that he might serve as my guardian.” In these words *ut*, “so that,” is redundant, as *quod*, “that,” not infrequently is. *Aversus*, moreover, means the same as “from behind.” Livy XXXIII.8: “because they were cut down from behind.” Aurelius Victor, *Origin of the Roman People* VI.2, on Cacus, the slave of Evander: “He stole the cattle of his guest Recaranus and, to prevent any evidence, dragged them backward into the cave.” It is well known that the ancients gave Janus two faces. Ovid, *Fasti* I.89 ff.:

> And let there be a face that sees what is behind,  
> And one that sees what is before him.

The reasons why the ancients imagined him two-faced are given by Vossius, *On the Origin and Progress of Idolatry* I.19, and Everard Otto, *On the Guardianship of Public Roads*, part I, chapter 7, p. 126. GRUNER.—I add Lactantius III.24: “I do not know what to say [Col. 0305C] about those who, once they have gone astray, persist steadfastly in folly, except that I think prudent and knowledgeable men undertake to defend falsehoods as though so that they may exercise their talents upon evil subjects.” Compare Bünemann there. LINDNER.

Built with Spits. Others read *with breasts* (*uberibus*); here it is not a substantive—as everyone has believed—but an adjective. Our author calls breasts *abundant* (*uberes*) when they are full of much milk (something that can perhaps be inferred from the size of the breasts, although otherwise abundance of milk is inferred from breast size with less accuracy). LINDNER.—Thus *uber ager*, “fertile field,” in Livy XXIX, 25 and XXXIV, 62; *uber solum*, “fertile soil,” in Tacitus, *Histories* V, 6, and Curtius VI, 4. In the manuscript codex of Minucius the reading is *veribus*. Rigaltius acutely conjectures that this arose from *uveribus*—for scribes often wrote it so, interchanging the letters *b* and *u*—and therefore does not hesitate to restore *uberibus*. Heraldus also approved this. Lipsius emended this passage in the same way in his notes on Tacitus, *Annals* III, 61. Above too, in chapter 19, the manuscript codex has *verius* for *uberius*; and below, in chapter 36, the Roman edition has *verius* for [Col. 0305D] *uberius*. It is now apparent that the correction of Lucas Holstenius is entirely false: in his *Letter on the Spits of Diana of Ephesus*, first published at Rome in 1688, reviewed in the *Acta Eruditorum*, supplement I, p. 350, and afterward reprinted in volume VII of Gronovius’s *Greek Antiquities*, he judged that *verubus*, “with spits,” should be restored. I find that reading also in the Roman edition. Davisius, however, likewise rejects this correction, although it had found favor with Jacob Gronovius. HEUM.—Heumannus was not the first author of this explanation, but J. Tristanus, according to Lucas Holstenius, whose *Letter on the Spits of Diana* I have appended to the end of this book. LINDN.—See the same letter in this volume a little below, after the dissertation of Dom Nicolas Le Nourry, col. 365. EDD.

**The bearded one is placed.** Heumannus judges that the verb *locatur*, “is placed,” should be removed, but it is more suitably retained. It stands for the compound *collocare*, “to set up,” which Phaedrus uses in the epilogue to book II:

> The Athenians set up an enormous statue to Aesop,  
> And placed a slave upon an everlasting pedestal.

LINDNER.

**Then he bears thunderbolts.** Gronovius was troubled by the particle [Col. 0306B] *tunc*, “then”; yet it should trouble no one here any more than *tum*, “then,” in Cicero, *For the Manilian Law*, ch. 6: “When disaster comes, then loss is suffered”; and in Plautus: “I shall then be present when I have an opportunity to see you.” A similar redundancy occurred in chapter 17: “which from the earth,” etc. LINDNER.

**He is not approached.** That is, by those intending to make supplication. For those intending to supplicate or give thanks, says Broukhusius on Tibullus I, 593, p. 104, were in the proper idiom said “to approach the gods” and “to approach unto the gods.” Jupiter Feretrius did not exist in order to be approached by suppliants—an honor paid rather to Capitoline Jupiter—but so that the *spolia opima*, the choice spoils won from defeated enemies, might be brought to him. Thus Wowerus and Rigaltius read *non aditur*, “is not approached,” in place of the manuscript’s *non auditur*, “is not heard,” but explain it differently. Wowerus says that in slightly fewer than 530 years, according to Festus, only three sets of *spolia opima* were hung up for Jupiter Feretrius. Rigaltius writes that Jupiter Feretrius was not approached because the *spolia opima* were brought not to Feretrius but to Mars and Quirinus. Jacob Gronovius: “The name is heard, but no statue or form is seen.” J. F. [Col. 0306C] Gronovius: “He is clothed in the choice spoils.” Schefferus: “He is not shut up,” supposing that his temple, like that of Peace, always stood open because Feretrius also was believed to bring peace. Withofius, in his *Critical Dedication-Festival*, published in 1741: “He is approached with vows”; but this is something he shares with Hammon, Capitolinus, and Latiaris. Perizonius: “He is approached in procession”; Heumannus: “He is approached with a procession.” But they also approached Capitoline Jupiter with a procession. LINDNER.—“When he is Feretrius, he is not heard.” The passage has been assailed by various scholars. Davisius reviews and rejects their conjectures, and finally concludes as follows: “It is indeed much easier to refute false readings than to discover the true one; yet perhaps I might not unsuitably correct it to: ‘When he is Feretrius, he does not hear.’ Minucius covertly mocks the Romans because for so long a time they had not carried off any *spolia opima*.” GALLAND.

**And, lest at greater length.** I greatly approve Heumannus’s opinion that the words “many Jupiters” crept in from the margin, and his advice to read *et ne longius abeam*, “and, lest I go farther,” as in Cicero, *On Ends* II, ch. 30: “Lest I go farther, what does Epicurus say?” But [Col. 0306D] I was unwilling to alter anything in a matter still uncertain, especially since Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* III, ch. 16, mentions several Jupiters, and since *obire terram* in the sense “to traverse the earth” is well known. Thus Pallas in Virgil, *Aeneid* X, 446:

> Across his massive frame she rolls her eyes,  
> And surveys everything afar with a savage gaze.

**Kindled.** All editors except Jacob Gronovius have followed Rigaltius and Heraldus in writing *ignita*, “kindled,” for the manuscript’s *ignata*. Gronovius thought that *signata*, “marked out,” should be restored—surely against the will of the critical Minerva. Yet he correctly perceives that the word *ignata* must be joined not with “stars” but with “maiden.” Minucius could certainly have spoken more clearly: “So that, as a kindled maiden, she might be among the stars.” HEUM.

**In the fires of Oeta.** The manuscript has *Henneis*. It had been dictated as *Aetnaeis*, “of Etna,” incorrectly for *Oetaeis*, “of Oeta.” RIGALT.]

[Col. 0299B] **SUMMARY.—**Octavius confirms that mortals were taken up among the gods by the testimony of Euhemerus, Prodicus, Perses, and Alexander the Great, who enumerate the gods’ native countries, births, and tombs. He further sets forth the gods’ sorrowful ends, deaths, and funerals. In addition, he exposes the foolish and noisome nonsense that the pagans peddle concerning the form and appearance of their gods.

Read the writings of the Stoics, or the writings of the wise, and you will acknowledge the same things together with me. Euhemerus [printed: *Erueret*] pursues the theme that men were regarded as gods because of the merit of their virtue or service; he enumerates their births, native countries, and tombs, and points them out province by province: Dictaean [printed: *dicta*] Jupiter, Delphic [printed: *Delphiciae*] Apollo, Pharian [printed: *Pariae*] Isis, and Eleusinian Ceres. Prodicus [printed: *Prodigiis*] says that those who, in their wanderings, benefited human welfare by discovering new things were taken up among [Col. 0300B] the gods. [Col. 0301A] Persaeus philosophizes in the same sense, and connects the crops that were discovered and the discoverers of those very crops under the same names—as the comic saying has it, “Without Liber and Ceres, Venus grows cold.”^29 Alexander the Great, the Macedonian, wrote in a celebrated volume to his mother that a priest, out of fear of Alexander’s power, had revealed to him the secret that the gods were men. The priest makes Vulcan the first of them all, and afterward the race of Jupiter. And you may look down upon Isis’s swallow, rattle, and the empty tomb of your Serapis or Osiris, with its scattered limbs. (XVI) Finally, consider the sacred rites themselves and the mysteries themselves: you will find the sorrowful ends, deaths, and funerals, [Col. 0303A] and the mourning and lamentation of wretched gods. Isis, together with her dog-headed attendant and bald priests, mourns, laments, and searches for her lost son; the wretched devotees of Isis beat their breasts and imitate the grief of the most unhappy mother. Soon, when the child has been found, Isis rejoices, the priests exult, and the dog-headed discoverer boasts. Every year they never cease either losing what they find or finding what they lose. Is it not ridiculous either to mourn what you worship or to worship what you mourn? Yet these rites, once Egyptian, are now Roman rites as well. Ceres, with torches lit and encircled by a serpent, wanders anxiously and solicitously in search of Libera, who was stolen away and violated. These are the Eleusinian mysteries.

And what are the rites of Jupiter? His nurse is a she-goat, and the infant is snatched from his ravenous father lest he be devoured; the clang of the Corybantes’ cymbals drowns out his crying so that his father will not hear it. Cybele [Col. 0304A] of Dindymus—it is shameful to say it—castrated the lover who had unhappily pleased her, because she herself, deformed and aged though she was, as the mother of many^30 gods, could not entice him to debauchery; thus, of course, she made the god a eunuch. Because of this fable, her Galli and half-men worship her by inflicting punishment upon their own bodies. These are no longer sacred rites; they are tortures.

What of their very forms and appearances? Do they not reveal the mockeries and ornaments [printed: “disgraces”] of your gods? Vulcan is a lame and disabled god; (XVII) Apollo remains smooth-cheeked through so many ages; Aesculapius is fully bearded, although he is forever the son of the youthful Apollo; Neptune has sea-green eyes, Minerva gray-blue eyes, Juno ox-like eyes; Mercury has winged feet, Pan hoofed feet, Saturn fettered feet; (XVIII) Janus indeed bears two faces, as though to walk backward. [Col. 0304B] Diana, meanwhile, is the huntress with her tunic girded high; the Ephesian Diana [Col. 0305A] is built with many full breasts; Trivia is terrifying with three heads and many hands. What then? Your Jupiter himself is at one time erected without a beard, at another installed bearded; when he is called Hammon, he has horns; when Capitolinus, then he carries thunderbolts; when Latiaris, he is drenched with blood; and when Feretrius, he is not approached. (XIX) And, lest I traverse the many Jupiters at greater length, there are as many monstrosities of Jupiter as there are names. Erigone hanged herself with a noose so that, as the Maiden, she might be kindled among the stars. The Castors die by turns so that they may live; Aesculapius is struck by lightning so that he may rise into godhood; Hercules is consumed in the fires of Oeta [manuscript: *Henneis*] so that he may put off the man.

## CHAPTER XXII

[Note: [Col. 0306D]

**CHAPTER XXII.—We learn.** Thus the royal manuscript, better than the common reading *we have learned*. HERALD. Ludovicus Carrio also defends the manuscript reading, *Emendations* II, ch. 18. HEUM.

**We elaborate.** *Elaborare* means “to adorn, to polish.” Cicero [Col. 0307B], *Orator* 84: “Elaborate symmetry.” Heumannus reads *corroboramus*, “we strengthen.” LINDNER.

**Very greatly.** Cellarius and several others printed *wonderfully greatly* (*permirum quantum*), which is also found in the Roman edition. But the manuscript has *very greatly* (*plurimum quantum*), which Carrio correctly defends in the chapter just cited. The phrase *plurimum quantum* occurs again below, in chapter 40, and that Roman edition has it there as well. HEUM.

**By their own authority.** Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* I, 16: “For the things poured forth in the voices of the poets are not much more absurd, and they have done harm by their very charm.” And our author below: “By these and similar fictions and sweeter falsehoods the minds of boys are corrupted.” Consider whether the reading ought to be: “by their very own charm.” LINDNER.

**Praised and crowned.** In a brief summary Minucius has reported what Plato said at greater length in this discourse in book III of the *Republic*: “If anyone in our city should wish to display his poems, we shall indeed venerate him as sacred, marvelous, and delightful; but we shall say that it is not lawful for such a man to be in our commonwealth, and we shall send him away to another city after pouring perfume upon his head and placing a woolen crown upon him.” Behold the poet first praised, then crowned, and finally expelled from the city! HEUM.

**In his discourse.** R. Bentley, on Horace, *Odes* III, 8, verse 5, p. 110, proves that *sermo*, “discourse,” is elegantly used for a book, treatise, dialogue, or history. Likewise Cicero, *Letters* IX, 8: “I therefore composed the conversation held between us at Cumae, when Pomponius was with us.” LINDNER.

**By Venus’s strap.** This is the reading in the manuscript codex of Minucius, not “by Venus’s girdle”; in place of it the Roman edition incorrectly prints *toro*, “couch,” which Gronovius also printed. HEUM.—In the royal codex it is clearly written *thoro*. EDD.

[Col. 0307D] **Constructed.** Heusingerus, according to Heumannus, reads “equipped.” I alter nothing and adopt the position of Burmannus, who, on seeing variation between these words in Quintilian, *Institutes* I, 1, p. 17, says: “I think it matters little, since either reading can readily be defended.” I would not suppose that the other should perhaps be preferred because “unhappy builder” follows. LINDNER.

**There [Vulcan].** Delete the latter word, since it is not found in the manuscript but only in the Roman edition. Rigaltius, Davisius, and Gronovius therefore rightly omitted it from their editions. HEUM.

**The sky and thunderbolts.** We have added the conjunction from the royal manuscript. HERALD.

**Against Ganymede.** More idiomatically, “in Ganymede”; or *in* should be deleted, so that the sense is: “Why should I speak of Ganymede, Jupiter’s sexual outrage,” etc. LINDNER.

**So that for the vices of men.** Heraldus printed this without mentioning any variant. Rigaltius, however, declares that “so that by men’s judgments” is plainly the reading of the ancient copy. I have retained Heraldus’s reading, which Sabaeus also has; that is:

> Why should I think shameful for myself  
> What was becoming for the gods?

as someone says in the words of Ovid, *Amores* II, 8.—Rigaltius approves the reading of the ancient copy. For, he says, through corrupted judgment—when men judge badly—the vices they read were perpetrated by the gods are regarded as virtues. But Gelenius and Cellarius printed “so that for the vices of men.” Davisius, coming somewhat closer to the traces of the manuscript, thinks that *uti vitiis hominum* should be read. That is good enough. For I approve less of another conjecture by the learned man, who in his second edition reads: “so that a certain authority might be secured for the crimes of men.” GALLAND.

**Are corrupted.** Bayle, in his *Dictionary*, under the entry JUPITER, letter D, teaches that the system of paganism is exceedingly well suited to corrupting morals. LINDNER.

**By these same.** The manuscript has *hisdem*; nevertheless, that form means *iisdem*, “by these same.” See Bünemannus on Lactantius, *Deaths of the Persecutors* XXIII. LINDNER.

**Clinging.** That is, clinging in the mind. Nor would “while they cling” be a bad reading. Above, chapter 1: “whereby Caecilius was still clinging to superstitious vanities.” Lactantius I, 1: “For many, stubbornly clinging to empty superstitions.” LINDNER.

**Swarm.** Pacatus, Pliny, and others used *examen*, “swarm,” for a multitude or flock. Tertullian likewise does so in a passage corresponding to this one, *Apology* ch. 10: “Enough now about Saturn, although only a little has been said. We shall also show that Jupiter was as much a man as he was born from a man, and thereafter that the whole swarm of his line was as mortal as the father of its stock.” Minucius appears to have had this passage before his eyes. [Col. 0308D] LINDNER.

**And by Janus.** This is the entirely correct reading from the royal manuscript. Previously: “and he too was received as a guest.” HERALD.

**To imprint letters.** Compare Cyprian, *On the Vanity of Idols*, ch. 2. From this Pomponius Laetus divined that the art of typography was born in Italy in Saturn’s age, an opinion sharply attacked by Peutinger in his *Conversational Discourse on the Marvels of Germany*. Meanwhile, see Cicero discussing the following, with Balbus as speaker, in *On the Nature of the Gods* II, 37: “Why should he not likewise suppose that, if innumerable shapes of the twenty-one letters, whether of gold or any material one pleases, were thrown together somewhere, the *Annals* of Ennius could be produced when they were shaken out onto the ground, so that they could then be read in sequence? Yet I do not know whether chance could accomplish so much even in a single verse.” Indeed, even before Saturn’s age, if the most learned Grotefend is to be believed, a genuine art of printing characters from bronze types already existed in the East, as Babylonian tablets attest. Compare Lambinet, *Origins of Printing*, vol. I, p. 359; Prosper Marchand, *History of Printing*, pp. 3–5; Porthmann, *Essay on Printing*; Cicero, ed. Leclerc, vol. XXV, p. 328. EDD.

**And he gave the city Saturnia from his own name.** Thus the manuscript. Fulvius Ursinus was the first to print: “the city Saturnia from his own name,” omitting the word “gave.” Some editions have: “he gave the city Saturnia his own name,” omitting “from.” Arntzenius, on Aurelius Victor, thought that *founded* should be read for *gave*. But Barthius, on Statius, *Thebaid* III, 16, showed that *give* is commonly used for “found,” so that no change is necessary. Two verbs are present here, *gave* and *left*, one of which must be absent. If you delete the latter, the words run thus: “He gave the city Saturnia from his own name, as Janus did the Janiculum, each as a memorial for posterity.” The latter method, however, in which “gave” is absent, has found more supporters. LINDNER.

**Because among the Italians.** Not likewise among the Cretans. “To be of unknown parents” means “to have unknown parents.” Heumannus does not doubt that the true reading is: “because among the Italians his parents were unknown.” LINDNER.

**Those seen unexpectedly.** Barthius, on Statius, *Thebaid* X, 752, inferred that there was a lacuna containing certain words here, because persons appearing unexpectedly were also called “sons of the earth” or “earth-born”; once these words were expressed, there would be a more suitable opposition between “those seen unexpectedly” and “the lowborn and unknown.” But the author appears to have made his distinction such that by the former he means specifically men who are distinguished or outstanding in some respect, and by the latter those who, besides being of obscure birth, do not greatly distinguish themselves by deeds or virtues. Lactantius also appears to have understood it thus at I, 11. The designation “sons of the earth” is generally applied to persons of lower station. WOPK.

**A cave still.** Read: “There a cave still.” HEUM.]

**SUMMARY.—**These fables, first handed down by uneducated men, were afterward celebrated by others, and especially by the poets, who did no small harm to truth through their authority. By such fictions and sweeter falsehoods the minds of boys are corrupted, and consequently the wretches grow old in them, although truth is readily accessible—but only to those who seek it.

(XX) We learn these fables and errors from ignorant parents and—what is more serious—we elaborate them through our very studies and disciplines, especially through the poems of the poets, who [Col. 0307A] very greatly harmed truth itself by their own authority.^31 And for this reason Plato acted splendidly when he expelled that illustrious Homer, after praising and crowning him, from the city he was establishing in his discourse. For Homer, chiefly in the Trojan War, although he made sport of your gods, nevertheless involved them in human affairs and actions. He matched them against one another, wounded Venus, bound, wounded, and routed Mars. He relates that Jupiter was freed by Briareus lest he be bound by the other gods; that he wept bloody showers for his son Sarpedon because he could not rescue him from death; and that, enticed by Venus’s couch [printed: “cord”], he lay with his wife Juno more ardently than he was accustomed to lie with adulteresses. Elsewhere Hercules carries off dung, and Apollo tends Admetus’s flock. Neptune, meanwhile, constructs walls for Laomedon, yet the unhappy builder receives no payment for his work. There [Col. 0307B] Jupiter’s thunderbolt is fashioned upon the anvil together with Aeneas’s arms, although the sky, thunderbolts, and lightning had existed long before Jupiter was born in Crete, and neither could a Cyclops imitate the flames [Col. 0308A] of a real thunderbolt, nor could Jupiter himself avoid fearing them.

Why should I speak of the discovered adultery of Mars and Venus, or of Jupiter’s sexual outrage against Ganymede, consecrated in heaven? All these things were handed down so that a certain authority might be secured for the vices of men. By these and similar fictions and sweeter falsehoods the minds of boys are corrupted; with these same fables clinging to them, they grow up even to the full strength of mature age, and in these same opinions the wretches grow old, although truth is readily accessible—but only to those who seek it.

For all the writers of antiquity, Greek and Roman, have represented Saturn,^32 the founder of this race and swarm, as a man. Nepos and Cassius know this in their historical writings, and Thallus and Diodorus say it. Accordingly, Saturn, a refugee from Crete, had come to Italy in fear of his raging son and, having been received as a guest by Janus, taught those rude and rustic men many things, since he was a polished little Greek: how to imprint letters, stamp coins, [Col. 0309A] and fashion implements. He therefore preferred that his hiding place, because he had lain there safely concealed, be called Latium; and from their own names Saturn and Janus left behind the city Saturnia and the Janiculum, each as a memorial for posterity. He was therefore surely a man who fled, surely a man who lay hidden, both the father of a man and born from a man. For he was represented as the son of earth or [printed: “and”] heaven because among the Italians his parents were unknown, just as to this very day we call those who appear unexpectedly “sent from heaven,” and those of low or unknown birth “sons of the earth.” His son Jupiter reigned in Crete after driving out his father; there he died, there he had children. A cave of Jupiter is still visited, his tomb is pointed out, and by his own sacred rites he is convicted of humanity.

## CHAPTER XXIII

[Note: [Col. 0309D]

**CHAPTER XXIII.—And when Proculus swore falsely.** Meursius wished, not unsuitably, to restore “as Proculus swore falsely.” But since this correction is unnecessary, I do not endorse it. The Roman edition has “and when he swore falsely,” perhaps written for “and when he committed perjury.” See what I wrote on Lactantius, *On Anger*, ch. 16. HEUM.—Cyprian 2, 5 has *pejerante*, “swearing falsely.” LINDNER.

**And Juba.** Scholars dispute whether he was king of Numidia or Mauretania. Cellarius proves from Dio that he was king of Numidia; Dio at the same time attests that during Pompey’s civil war the kingdom of Mauretania was divided, Bocchus reigning in the nearer part and Bogud in the farther. Lucan, IV, 672, meanwhile extends Juba’s kingdom to the sea of Gades. But grant that this was poetic license; he is nevertheless expressly called king of Mauretania by Florus IV, 2, and Eutropius VI, 18. Tacitus likewise says in *Annals* IV, 5: “Juba received the Moors as a gift from the Roman people.” The same author, *Histories* II, 58, says there was a report that Albinus, scorning the title of procurator, had assumed the insignia of royalty and the name of Juba. Albinus, however, was procurator [Col. 0310C] of Mauretania. As for Cellarius’s further claim that it is improbable that Juba—defeated by Caesar at Thapsus and, when his cause was hopeless, laying violent hands upon himself—was readily deified by his own people: this, so far as I see, presents no difficulty, because the Moors regarded all their kings indiscriminately as gods, whatever kind of death they suffered. Perhaps Minucius selected this man in preference to the others so that the absurdity of his deification might be more evident. LINDNER.

**They desire to persist as men.** Heumannus restores: “men desire to be preserved.” I alter nothing. The expressions “to put on the man” and “to put off the man,” that is, human nature, are well known; on these see Bünemannus on Lactantius IV, 10. Paul himself, 1 Corinthians 15:53: “For this corruptible thing must put on incorruption, and this mortal thing must put on immortality” (*Δεῖ γὰρ τὸ φθαρτὸν τοῦτο ἐνδύσασθαι ἀφθαρσίαν, καὶ τὸ θνητὸν τοῦτο ἐνδύσασθαι ἀθανασίαν*). Lactantius IV, 25: “So that it might appear that even as a man he was heavenly.” Therefore, “they desire to persist as men” means “they desire to remain men longer.” LINDN.

**And if already old.** J. Meursius corrected this to: “Although already old, they therefore are not …” But there is no need to alter anything except to combine two words into one and read: “although already old, they are unwilling”; in this way the passage will be complete. DAVIS.—I read: “and, although already old.” HEUM.

**And childbearing has failed in Juno.** This could appear all the more remarkable because she possessed a mystery for annually renewing her virginity by washing herself in the Canathus, a river of the Peloponnese. Pausanias, *Peloponnese*, book II, at the end. She also conceived partly by the breath of a breeze, partly by touching a flower, and partly by eating lettuce. LINDNER.

**If the gods could beget.** Thus the manuscript correctly, although Jacob Ouzelius thought otherwise and preferred “could be begotten.” But the good man did not recall that this verb contains the meaning “to beget”; being, I suppose, more skilled in theology than in textual criticism, he immediately dreamed of creation from nothing. Ovid, *Metamorphoses* VII, 666:

> At once those begotten with Pallas  
> Assemble.

And book XIII, 22:

> I should be powerful in nobility, begotten by Telamon.

[Col. 0311B] Lucretius I, 734:

> So that he scarcely seems begotten from human stock.

And again V, 1012:

> And to see offspring begotten from himself.

Lactantius, *Epitome*, ch. 5: “Let desire … serve for the begetting of children.” More examples could readily be assembled, but I shall not linger over a familiar matter. DAVIS.—Compare also Burmannus on Phaedrus I, [uncertain chapter number] 6: “If he has begotten children”; and Torrenius, with others, on Valerius Maximus VII, 7: “because the marriage had not been contracted for the sake of begetting children.” LINDNER.

**Is dazzled.** Dionysius Lambinus, on Lucretius III, p. 411, writes: “is blinded by the gleam of gold”; and on Horace, *Epistles* II, 1, p. 234, says that wherever one reads *praestringere*, whether “to dazzle the eyes” or “the eyesight,” *praestinguere*, “to extinguish,” should be read. But this opinion is excessively dogmatic. Lactantius II, ch. 6: “Their beauty and splendor dazzle the eyes.” Nonius Marcellus, p. 695: “*Praestringere*: to darken.” Plautus, *The Braggart Soldier*:

> Let him dazzle the eyesight of enemies in the battle line.

The passage is found at act I, scene 1, line 4. There the learned man not only repeated the same error in his notes, but also wrongly printed “let him extinguish the eyesight”—an exceedingly rash act, since it is established that Cicero, Livy, and others spoke in precisely the former way, quite apart from the fact that Apuleius also quotes that verse in this form in *On the God of Socrates*, p. 77, Lyon edition. DAVIS.—Compare also Bünemannus on Lactantius II, 6. LINDNER.

**By what instruments of torment.** Read “by what lathes”; for the word *tormentum* denotes: first, a military engine; second, punishment and torture; third, a stretched rope. The first meaning is wholly unsuitable here. The second could indeed be applied in some fashion if you understood it to mean that statues are imagined to suffer pain when cut, hewn, planed, and rasped. So too could the third, since the statue is suspended by ropes, though I believe this was done rather by inserting hooks. But a *tornus* is a craftsman’s lathe, invented, according to Pliny VII, 56, by Theodorus of Samos. LINDNER.—Lindner wishes to read “by what lathes,” but the word *tormentum*, “instrument of torment,” appears better and more suitably adapted to the sense and context of the passage. RUSWUM.

**To fear material.** We have printed this on the authority of the royal manuscript. The former reading was: “He will blush at having rashly been mocked by material so as to make a god,” which has no meaning. Everything Minucius discusses in this passage has been explained in the notes on Tertullian’s *Apology*. HERALD.

**Golden.** The Roman edition wrongly reads: “A god of wax or silver.” HERALD.—Gatakerus, in his *Adversaria Miscellanea* II, ch. 19, p. 371, restores “golden,” though hesitantly. He would have made this emendation with greater confidence had he read in Minucius, ch. 24, that avarice was consecrated by the pagans “in gold and silver, from which the gods are fashioned.” The same scholar correctly observes that “more often” must be emended here, since that Egyptian king did it not more often, but only once. He therefore thinks that Minucius wrote either “we read” or “we know” in place of “more often.” I have at hand an easier and therefore more probable correction. By transposing the words I write: “from an unclean vessel more often, as was done by the Egyptian king.” I now see that Jacob Gronovius also thinks it should be restored in this way. HEUM.

**From an unclean vessel, as was done by the Egyptian king.** Minucius has in mind the deed of Amasis, related by Herodotus II, ch. 172, and from him by Athenagoras, *Embassy for the Christians*, ch. 23. Cotelerius, on the *Clementine Homilies* X, ch. 8, punctuates this passage differently; Gatakerus, *Adversaria Miscellanea* II, ch. 19, p. 371, reads it differently, but without compelling reason. DAVIS.

[Col. 0312C] **And with anvils.** I write “and upon anvils.” MEURS.

**By an impure man.** The manuscript correctly has this, not “by an unskilled man,” as the Roman edition and therefore several others have it. Pareus presents in his *Critical Lexicon* the passages of Plautus in which the same word occurs. Elmenhorstius adduced at this passage a text from Justin Martyr very similar to this one in Minucius, and Heraldus another from Origen. HEUM.

**The stone is not yet a god.** Davisius says that these words contain not merely no wit but not even any meaning unless the word is divided and one reads: “Unless perhaps it is not stone while it is a god.” There is no need. The sense is: “Unless perhaps stone, wood, or silver is not yet a god”—that is, the raw and unworked material of stone, wood, or silver is not yet a god, something our author assumes hypothetically. He then continues: “When, therefore, is it born?” That is, “When, therefore, does the stone, wood, or silver become a god?” LINDNER.

**When a man willed it.** The most learned Rigaltius and Heraldus rightly vindicated this manuscript reading, which has been attacked in vain with conjectures ever since the first edition. For *voluit*, “willed,” is Minucius’s expression, just as conversely he said, “those whom we deny by day, whom we reject”; and, “on my birthday I reject this trickery—I do not believe it.” Does he not derive it from Cicero’s most pleasing *On the Orator* II, ch. 6, where it is supplied from Lucilius: “I want Decimus Laelius,” which Lucilius in his own context understands both before and afterward as meaning “according to his judgment”? GRONOV.—Previously the reading was “that man willed,” as Cellarius printed it. Meursius corrects it to: “when the man vowed it”; Heumannus: “when the man willed and dedicated it as the one whom he wished to be God.” LINDNER.—“When a man willed it”—namely, willed it to be God, says Rigaltius, maintaining that the manuscript reading is sound. Cellarius: “when that man willed.” Meursius: “vowed.” Davisius, however: “worshiped,” a word that, in his judgment, fits this passage well, whether one adopts the common meaning “to adore” or the less ordinary meaning “to adorn.” GALLAND.]

**SUMMARY.—**Although the pagans acknowledge that their kings are mortal, they nevertheless fashion them into gods, even against their will—not from belief in their divinity, but to confer the honor of a meritorious posterity. Yet the true God has neither rising nor setting. Octavius next attacks the gods’ images and statues.

It is idle to go through them individually and unfold the whole succession of that race, since mortality, once proved in the case of the earliest ancestors, has passed into all the others by the very order of succession—unless perhaps you fashion gods after their death: Romulus became a god when Proculus swore falsely, and Juba is a god because the Moors willed it, as are the other deified kings who are consecrated, not from belief in their divinity, but in honor of their power after it has run its course. In the end, this name is assigned to them against their will:^33 they desire to persist as men; they fear being made gods, and although already old, they are unwilling. Therefore the dead are not gods, since God could not [printed: “cannot”] die; nor are those who have been born gods, since everything born dies, whereas the divine is that which has neither rising nor setting.

For if they were born, why are they not still being born today? Unless perhaps Jupiter has now grown old, childbearing has failed in Juno, and Minerva grew gray before she gave birth. Or has this generation ceased because no assent is offered to fables of this kind? Besides, if the gods could beget, they could not perish; we would have more gods than [printed: “born”] all mankind, so that by now neither heaven could contain them, nor air hold them, nor earth sustain them. Hence it is manifest that they were men, whom we both read were born and know to have died.

Who, then, doubts that the common people pray to the consecrated images of these men and publicly worship them, while the opinion and mind of the ignorant are deceived by artistic symmetry, dazzled by the gleam of gold, and blunted by the luster of silver and the whiteness of ivory? But if anyone were to consider with what instruments of torment and by what machinery every statue is formed, he would blush to fear material that the craftsman mocked in order to make a god. For a wooden god—perhaps a portion of a funeral pyre or an ill-omened log—is hung up, cut, hewn, planed, and rasped; and a god of gold or silver, often made from an unclean vessel, as was done by the Egyptian king, is melted, beaten with hammers, and shaped upon anvils; and a stone god is cut, carved, and polished by an impure^34 man. It does not feel the injury of its own birth, just as [Col. 0312A] it afterward feels no worship arising from your veneration—unless perhaps stone, wood, or silver is not yet a god.

When, then, is it born? Look: it is cast, fashioned, and carved; it is not yet a god. Look: it is soldered with lead, assembled, and erected; it is still not a god. Look: it is adorned, consecrated, and prayed to. Only then, finally, is it a god, when a man has willed and dedicated it.

## CHAPTER XXIV

[Note: [Col. 0312D]

**CHAPTER XXIV.—How much more truly.** The manuscript has “how great, however,” for which Fulvius Ursinus was the first to restore “how much more truly.” LINDNER.

**By nature.** This is not a gloss. By this adverb our author meant that animals, under nature’s guidance, judge much more truly concerning the gods than do pagans endowed with the use of reason. LINDNER.

**They know, they recognize.** Thus the manuscript correctly, and it must be punctuated as we have done. There is no need to follow Wowerus, Ouzelius, Cellarius, and others, who prefer “they know, they gnaw.” The learned men should have remembered that African writers frequently join synonyms (*συνώνυμα*). Arnobius III, p. 106: “To judge, to believe far more honorably than you concerning the dignity of his own name.” And p. 109: “How great, I say, were the flames of anger that they would kindle, arouse.” We have assembled further examples in the notes on chapter 11 of this book. DAVIS.—Wowerus correctly restored “they recognize,” and Ouzelius and Cellarius followed him. For “gnaw” belongs to the mice; “leap repeatedly upon” to the swallows; and “perch upon” to the kites. Moreover, this whole passage appears to me to require the following punctuation and reading: “How much more truly do dumb animals judge concerning your gods! Mice, swallows, and kites—for they know that the gods do not feel—gnaw, leap upon, and perch upon them.” HEUM.—I do not think this parenthesis is needed in a concise style, which must be supplied as follows: “Because they know that the gods do not feel, they therefore gnaw,” etc. In a connection of words such as this, those particles are understood rather than expressed. Gronovius, defending the word “recognize,” says that “gnaw” is inept, although all lexicographers unanimously affirm that this action properly belongs to mice, which wear something away—and false in regard to objects that are cast and soldered with lead. But is it also false in regard to objects made from wood, which are cut, fashioned, and carved? LINDNER.

**They trample upon.** They tread on, trample underfoot. Tertullian, *On Repentance*, ch. 7: “They fear to appear to trample upon what they have attained.” The same author, *To the Nations* I, ch. 10: “Those Lares and Penates whom you claim to consecrate by domestic devotion, you trample upon with domestic license.” Wowerus’s and Cellarius’s conjecture “leap upon” is therefore unnecessary. DAVIS.

**You protect and fear them.** That is, “and yet you fear them.” Below, chapter 26: “Regulus observed the auspices and was captured”; chapter 28: “You both sacrifice and worship the heads of wethers”; chapter 35: “You prohibit and commit adulteries.” Lactantius IV, 2: “Nowhere have they grasped wisdom, and yet it must exist somewhere.” There was therefore no reason for Wopkenius to read: “and you fear those whom you make and protect.” That reading indeed yields a sufficiently convenient sense, but it is not merely inferior to the former sense produced by the received reading; it cannot even be regarded as equal to it. It is indeed absurd to fear what one has made—to speak with Lactantius, *Epitome* XXV, 5—but this could still be tolerated in some fashion, provided that, after being made, the gods ceased to remain under human protection. Yet when the gods continually require human protection, who could endure the fact that these same gods are feared? Meanwhile, the nations are so empty-headed that they protect the gods they have made and nevertheless fear them. LINDNER.

“Thus in gold . . . has been consecrated.” Below, ch. 25, our author said “to consecrate sacrilege,” as Nicolas Rigault observed; but the words of Lactantius, book II, ch. 6, are especially useful for explaining Felix’s meaning: “The beauty and brilliance of images dazzle their eyes, and they suppose that there is no religion wherever such images do not glitter. And so, under the pretext of the gods, avarice and cupidity are worshipped.” DAVIS.

“Whose rites.” Supply “of the Romans.” Minucius evidently thought that he had written not “Roman superstition” but “the superstition of the Romans” [Col. 0314A], as Jacob Gronovius acutely observed. For my part, I have said enough about this critical discretion—the practice, namely, of not correcting errors that the authors themselves committed through a lapse of memory—in my little book *On the Art of Criticism*, published in 1712, §§ 40–43. HEUM.—Similarly [Col. 0314B] in ch. 25: “The distinguished Roman justice familiar to us was inaugurated.” “Were not those just men—the Romans—gathered together at their very origin in crime?” LINDNER.

“How many things are laughable, [many] even pitiable.” There is no need to read with Heumann, “How many things are laughable, and even pitiable!” Compare what we noted above at ch. 4. LINDNER.

“They run about.” I readily recognized that the text had been written thus: “some run about; others march.” HEUM.

“They beat skins.” J. Wower and Christopher Cellarius think that these words have been displaced from their proper position and should be placed before the preceding three words, so that they may be understood of the Luperci. But the distinguished Cuper restores *peltas* (“small shields”), while Stephen Le Moyne, in his notes on the Epistle of Polycarp, vol. II of *Varia Sacra*, p. 366, rewrites it as *peltes*, a term under which cymbals might be included. Yet, as Franz Adolf Lampe rightly saw in the additions to his work *On the Cymbals of the Ancients*, book III, ch. 14, the received reading should not be rejected, for [Col. 0314C] *pelles* are drums made from skins. DAVIS.—Phaedrus, book III, 20.7, speaking of the Galli, priests of Cybele: “Having stripped off the ass’s hide, they made drums for themselves.” I observe in addition that *alii* (“others”) must be inserted between *pelles* and *caedunt*. Minucius, in fact, presents three kinds of priests: the Luperci, the Salii—whose *ancilia* he calls “ancient shields”—and the Galli. The sentence must therefore have flowed from Minucius in this form: “Some run about naked in the bitter winter; others march wearing caps and carry ancient shields around; others beat skins and lead their gods, as beggars, from street to street.” It must also be pointed out that *mendicantes* is not nominative but accusative, and refers to the gods. Tertullian, I think, will establish this, for in ch. 42 of his *Apology* he speaks thus: “We do not have sufficient means to bring aid both to human beings and to your gods, who are beggars.” HEUM.

“From street to street as beggars.” Jacob Gronovius, at the end of the preface to his edition of Minucius Felix published in 1709, believes that a corruption lies hidden here. But the passage is perfectly sound, and I do not fear that anyone else will judge [Col. 0314D] otherwise. HEUM.

*Vicantes*, in the same sense as *vicatim* (“from street to street”), which the printed editions commonly have. EDD.

“They permit certain shrines to be visited once a year.” At the shrine of Ceres and Proserpina among the Arcadians, women had access “throughout the whole period,” that is, at all times: “but the men enter it no more than once in each year”—for men, therefore, only once annually. Pausanias, *Arcadia*, ch. 31. At Thebes also they regarded it as lawful to open the sanctuary of Dindymene, who is the Mother of the Gods, “on one day in each year” only. The same author, *Boeotia*, ch. 25. CELLARIUS.

“It is altogether forbidden to visit [throughout the year].” Such was the temple of Neptune at Mantinea: “Entrance into it was never available to human beings, nor is it so down to our own time.” Pausanias, *Arcadia*, ch. 5. CELLARIUS.
