“There is a place where a man is not permitted.” The rites of the Good Goddess, Ceres, and Vesta. Lactantius, book III, ch. 20, §4, where he joins these three goddesses together. On the Good Goddess separately, Cicero, *Response Concerning the Haruspices*, ch. 17; on Ceres at Catana and Enna, *Against Verres* VI, chs. 45 and 49. CELLARIUS.—Heraldus printed it thus, without saying anything at all about a variant reading in the manuscript. Rigault, however, attests that it was written: “There is a place where a man is not permitted.” If this reading is genuine, it must certainly be explained as Wopkens directs. Arguing against Davis, who conjectured, “There is a place where a man is not permitted to go,” Wopkens supplies *visere* (“to visit”) ἀπὸ κοινοῦ, that is, as shared by both clauses, because Latin authors say not only “to visit a place” but also “to visit to a place.” Plautus, *Casina* III.4: “I shall go over here to see whether the lover has returned home from the forum”; and in *Rudens* V.1: “I shall go over here to see her in Venus’s shrine.” Lucretius II.360: “and frequently she returns to visit the stall.” Juretus gives more examples on Symmachus IV, epistle 52, and [Col. 0315C] Heinsius on Ovid, *Amores* II.2. LINDNER.

“Some rites are without women.” Those of Hercules, evidently. Gellius XI.6: “Women abstain from the sacrifice to Hercules.” Macrobius supplies the reason in *Saturnalia* I, ch. 12. CELLARIUS.

“For a slave to take part in certain ceremonies.” The ceremonies of the rites of Hercules; Livy IX, ch. 29, and Valerius Maximus I, ch. 1, no. 17, relate that neglect of this matter was punished in the case of Appius and the Potitii.

“A once-married woman crowns one set of rites.” Tertullian, *On Monogamy*, ch. 17: “No woman places the crown upon Fortuna Muliebris unless she has been married only once; and likewise with Mater Matuta.” CELLARIUS.

“He who makes a libation of his own blood.” Dougtaeus quoted these words freely in *Sacred Analecta*, part I, excursus 102: “He who makes propitiation with his own blood and makes supplication with wounds would perhaps be better irreligious than religious in this fashion.” LINDNER.

“Not irreligious.” *Non* is used in the sense of *nonne* (“would he not?”). Gronovius collected many examples of this kind in his notes on Seneca, *On Anger* III, ch. 33; Epistle 58; and *Natural Questions* IV, preface. LINDNER.

“Or he whose shameful entrails have been reaped away.” This is the reading of the Roman edition and the royal manuscript. From it Gelenius produces *testa* (“with a potsherd”). And indeed, some have related that the Galli cut off their own genitals with a Samian potsherd. Ramírez produced the passages in ch. 4 of his *Pentecontarchus. HEUM.* Nevertheless, I think Minucius wrote, “or he whose shameful parts have been cut out, reaped away”; this has more of the flavor of Minucius’s style. Lactantius indicates that this “harvest” was made not only with a potsherd but also with iron, book V, ch. 9: “Those who reap their own male organs with iron—and, what is more criminal, do so in order to be ministers of religion.” HERALDUS.—Some think that *exta* should be corrected to *testa*. Yet it does not seem to have been necessary here to show how that cutting was performed. I would rather believe that *exta* arose from an abbreviation of the word *exsecta* (“cut out”), with which someone had explained the following word *demessa* (“reaped”), and that it should therefore be deleted. Unless perhaps we suppose that he decorously called the male organs *extra* because they “stand out” (*exstant*), as Rigault thought; in that case *obscoena* (“shameful”) would appear to be a gloss, and should not be joined with *exta*. Since, however, *exta* appears to be used elsewhere in this sense, I prefer to retain the former opinion. SCHEFFER.—Ramírez likewise reads *testa* in ch. 4 of his *Pentecontarchus*, where he illustrates this passage at greater length. GALLAND.

“How does he outrage God?” Jacob Perizonius, thinking that the negative particle had fallen out, emends: “How does he not outrage God?” But there is no need for this most learned man’s correction if an exclamation mark is placed at the end of the sentence. DAVIS.—Heumann ought to have rested content with this interpretation, rather than rewriting it: “How impiously does he outrage God who appeases him in this way!” Cicero, *On Friendship*, ch. 2: “How, for example—to omit other matters—did he bear the death of his son!” LINDNER.

“Could create them so, not make them so.” *Could* cannot be carried over before the infinitive *facere* (“make”); another verb must be supplied, for example “would have had to.” Something is ascribed to God that ought to have been ascribed to human beings. Besides, the argument is exceedingly weak. We could argue in precisely the same fashion: “If God wanted beardless men, he could create them so, not make them so.” LINDNER.

“Of both an empty and a ruined mind.” Supply “human beings,” which also had to be understood with “mentally unsound.” Heumann emends: “that unsound and ruined minds are thus mad about these things.” But *desipere in ista* means “to disclose one’s madness in those things,” just as Latin authors say *desipere intra verba*, “to be mad within one’s words.” The verb may also contain a pregnant sense, such as Gronovius noted in the verb *alludere* at ch. 3, and may be explained as “to lose one’s senses and lapse into these things.” LINDNER.

“Here the defense.” There is no reason either to read “such is the defense” with Wopkens or, with Heumann, to eject the words “here the defense . . . multitude.” The words cohere, are Latin, and express a sentiment sufficiently common in other authors. LINDNER.

**ARGUMENT.—By a further brief survey, he demonstrates how many ridiculous, obscene, and cruel rites were observed in celebrating the mysteries of certain gods.**

But how many things do dumb animals naturally discern about your gods? Mice, swallows, and kites know and understand that they have no sensation; they tread upon them and settle on them; and unless you drive them away, they build their nests in the very mouth of your god. Spiders weave over his face and suspend their threads from his very head. You wipe, clean, and scrape them; and those whom you make, you protect and fear.

Each one of you does not reflect that he ought to know God before worshipping him; you are thoughtlessly eager to obey your parents; you prefer to become an appendage to another person’s error rather than trust your own judgment; and you know nothing of those things that you fear. Thus avarice has been consecrated in gold and silver; thus the form of empty statues has been formally authenticated; thus Roman superstition was born.

If you were to review its rites, how many things are laughable, and [many] even pitiable! They run about naked in the bitter winter; others march wearing caps and carry ancient shields around; they beat skins and lead begging gods from street to street. They permit certain shrines to be visited once a year, while others it is altogether forbidden to visit. There is a place where a man is not permitted to go; some rites are performed without women. For a slave even to take part in certain ceremonies is a sin requiring expiation. A once-married woman crowns one set of rites, a many-married woman another; and with great religious scruple they seek out a woman able to count the largest number of adulteries.

What of the man who makes a libation of his own blood and makes supplication with his wounds? Would he not be better irreligious than religious in this fashion? Or the man whose shameful parts have been reaped away—how he outrages God by appeasing him in this way! For if God wanted eunuchs, he could create them, not have men make themselves so.

Who does not understand that the mentally unsound, people of both empty and ruined minds, rave over such things, and that the very crowd of those in error furnishes mutual protection to its members? Here the common madness finds its defense in the multitude of the mad.

## CHAPTER XXV

> **Note: [Col. 0316C]**
>
> **CH. XXV.—“Yet nevertheless.”** Heumann reads, “But indeed.” I change nothing: it means “And yet.” Below, §13: “And yet before them, by God’s ordering, the Assyrians long held their kingdoms” [Col. 0316D]; ch. 20: “Yet nevertheless auspices or oracles have sometimes touched upon the truth”; ch. 35: “And yet they are admonished by the books of the most learned men.” LINDNER.
>
> **“Was inaugurated.”** That is, “began.” Thus in §3: “These are the first auspices of a religious state.” Florus I.1.6: “To determine which of them should inaugurate and rule the city, they employed expiatory rites.” The reading must therefore be retained against Heumann, who wished to delete it. LINDNER.
>
> **“Had flowed together.”** I write, “to which they had flowed.” MEURSIUS. But just as our author’s style is rather abrupt in many other passages, so nothing is more customary than for words such as “there” or “to that place” to be omitted in this fashion. We see this in Velleius II.51: “He allowed nothing to delay his proceeding [there]”; and Justin VII.1: “He occupied the city of Edessa . . . and, having been recalled . . . established the seat of his kingdom [there].” Moreover, the verb “flow together” is more appropriate here than simply “flow.” WOPKENS.
>
> **“He abducted, without precedent.”** This alludes to the Virgilian line, *Aeneid* VIII.635:
>
> > The Sabine women, abducted without precedent.
>
> “Without precedent” means without an example: something that had never been done before and was previously unheard of and unusual. By contrast, Virgil, *Aeneid* IV.57:
>
> > Ewes chosen according to custom.
>
> RIGAULT.
>
> **“That is, with his own fathers-in-law.”** Johann Wower suspects these words of being a gloss, and Christopher Cellarius enclosed them in brackets for that reason. In my opinion this is not quite right, since good authors everywhere speak in the same fashion. Arnobius, book VI, p. 203: “That the gods, after leaving their own abodes, that is heaven, do not refuse or flee from entering earthly dwellings.” Julius Firmicus, *On the Error of Profane Religions*, p. 1: “No one doubts that the four elements are the principles of created things, that is, fire, water, air, and earth”; there Wower wrongly rejected the final words. Lactantius, *Divine Institutes* II, ch. 12, uses the same manner: “Empedocles . . . established four elements, that is, fire, air, water, and earth.” This is common among those who take pains to make their discourse transparent and not entangled in any ambiguities. DAVIS.—Take care not to agree with Wower when he banishes these words as a gloss. They possess both elegance and a certain emphasis. In the same fashion our author writes at no. 5 [Col. 0317C]: “from spoils, that is, from the ruins of cities.” So too in ch. 36: “angels, that is, the ministers and messengers of God.” HEUMANN.—Lampridius, *Severus*, ch. 6: “When the senate had assembled in full numbers in the senate house, that is, the Temple of Concord. . . .” LINDNER.—The words “that is, with his own fathers-in-law” are necessary here because they render Romulus’s crime more manifest. They therefore increase the force of the sentence. GRUNER.
>
> **“More securely.”** A person who acts more fearfully is generally less secure than one who acts with confidence, since the latter is believed to act in this way because he relies upon the justice of his cause. “More securely” says more than “more boldly.” Thus ch. 29: “It is more secure for them to swear falsely by the genius of Jupiter.” Below, no. 11: “It was not greater security in chastity.” LINDNER.
>
> **“To compel the captives.”** Florus I.15.3: “By this victory so many people and so much territory were brought under his power that even the victor himself could not determine in which category the amount was greater.” Heumann reads “to heap together plunder.” LINDNER.
>
> **“And the latest commanders.”** Read: “later-born commanders.” WOWER.—I think Davis was right to be displeased with “latest,” though he attempted “their descendants.” With a smaller change one might also conjecture “after the kings.” WOPKENS.—I do not think any alteration necessary. I do not see why all Roman commanders after the kings may not be called “the later ones.” GRUNER.
>
> **“An act of pollution was committed.”** Impersonal. *Impiare* means “to pollute.” Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* I: “Sprinkled and polluted with human blood.” Prudentius, *Cathemerinon* VI, hymn before sleep, verse 35:
>
> > But he who has polluted  
> > A heart stained by vices.
>
> CELLARIUS.—*Impiatum*, just as Tertullian, *Against the Gnostics*, has *victoriatum* and *injuriatum*. WOWER.—Christopher Cellarius printed “by the Romans.” But there is no need; ch. 23: “As was done to the Egyptian king”; ch. 27: “The things said to you a little earlier.” LINDNER.
>
> **“And trophies.”** Do not hesitate to delete “and.” HEUMANN.
>
> **[Col. 0318B] “Took up arms.”** “To seize arms” in the sense “to take up arms” is a phrase frequently used by Florus; see Freinsheim’s index. LINDNER.
>
> **“And those whom they had demanded.”** “And those whom, after winning the laurel, they had triumphed over,” etc. We think the text may be emended thus, since “and those whom they had demanded,” as read in the manuscript, makes no sense. Traces of the former writing are apparent: “what they had demanded,” but the letter *d* was erased and an *s* was written above it, likewise by an ancient hand. RIGAULT.—Following Sigismund Gelenius, Christopher Cellarius and others printed “and those whom they had led in triumph after their defeat.” Jacob Ouzel did likewise, except that he printed *detriumphatos* (“stripped of triumph”), from which Jacob Perizonius restored “finally led in triumph”—without any compelling reason, since Tertullian employs the other word in *Apology*, ch. 27. Fulvius Ursinus comes much closer to the traces of the manuscript by reading, “and those whom they had laid waste.” My own conjecture pleases me: I think the text should be rewritten, “and after triumphing over them, they began to worship what they had demanded.” Justin 2.15: “As though a triumph had been won over the Spartans, he is received by the citizens.” DAVIS.—I suspect that someone wrote “after victory” in the margin from the words just quoted [Col. 0318C], and that from this afterward arose the absurd *postulaverant*. The text ought therefore to read: “and those over whom they had triumphed,” etc. HEUMANN.—I understand this verb as referring to the ritual summoning of gods. To summon gods means nothing other than to request that they abandon the people by whom they had hitherto been worshipped and pass over to the Romans. LINDNER.—The Lyons edition, following an anonymous restoration, reads: “Or those whom they perversely assisted began to be worshipped after they had been defeated.” Whether M. Caillau is more successful when, following Fulvius Ursinus, he offers “those whom they had laid waste,” or when he proposes on his own “in accordance with what they had vowed” (*Apostolic Fathers*, vol. II, p. 92, 1842), let the experts judge. EDD.—Gronovius considers the old manuscript reading, “what they had demanded,” unquestionably genuine. At the beginning of a war, he says, vows were pronounced on the Capitol so that a triumph might result from it, together with a promise that the enemy’s divinities would be transferred. Others explain it otherwise. GALLAND.
>
> **“Picus.”** I do not know what error led Cellarius [Col. 0318D] to believe that Picus was the son of Faunus and grandson of Saturn, since the passage of Virgil that he himself cites plainly attests that Picus was Faunus’s father, not his son. And Cellarius himself, in his notes on Prudentius, book I *Against Symmachus*, verse 244, writes that Picus was Saturn’s son and Faunus’s father. LINDNER.
>
> **“Polumnus.”** In the manuscript, Tertullian, *To the Nations* II, has: “Likewise the gods of Will: Volumnus and Voleta.” RIGAULT.—I prefer “Pilumnus and Picumnus” to Rigault’s substitution “Volumnus.” For Pilumnus and Picumnus, as Servius says on *Aeneid* IX.4, were brothers and gods. OUZEL.
>
> **“Cloacina . . . Fear . . . Pallor . . . Fever.”** On the worship of these ancient divinities of Rome at its birth, compare M. Greppo’s excellent dissertation in the notes to the Lyons edition of the *Octavius*, pp. 261–270. EDD.
>
> **“This superstition is the foster-child of that city.”** That is: these are divinities fostered by the city of Rome. The foster-divinities of a nation are those raised and nourished by it; they are opposed to foreign gods whom a people makes its own by adopting their cult and religion. Heumann writes “of that nurturing city.” LINDNER.
>
> **“Acca Larentia.”** The Roman edition—and the manuscript—has *Laurentia*. J. F. Gronovius contends that the former spelling is correct in his note on Livy I.4. HEUMANN.
>
> **“Among the diseases of the Romans.”** Heumann rewrites: “among the disgraces and gods of the Romans.” There is no need for this if one punctuates: “This superstition is the foster-child of that city—Fear, Pallor, and Fever—diseases, that is, and certainly forms of ill health; and”—that is, likewise—“Acca Larentia and Flora, prostitutes notorious for their debauchery.” LINDNER.
>
> **“Or Taurian Diana.”** I printed this with Sigismund Gelenius and Christopher Cellarius; Jacob Perizonius conjectured that the text should be rewritten thus, and very correctly. Desiderius Heraldus, Nicolas Rigault, and Jacob Ouzel arranged to have “now Taurian Diana” printed, as though Juno had been distinguished by that name. DAVIS.—The error and its cause are so obvious that I am amazed Jacob Gronovius ventured to defend it. LINDNER.—Nevertheless, the manuscript reads “now.” EDD.
>
> **“As those who.”** This has been not badly rewritten for the manuscript’s “and those who.” LINDNER.
>
> **“Certainly without Vesta’s knowledge.”** If Vesta had been a goddess, she ought not to have been ignorant of what was done in her own temple, and she ought to have disclosed it even if it had been concealed. Yet in fact the crimes of those virgins were never detected through Vesta, but always through human beings. They therefore had no reason to fear Vesta as a witness, provided that they deceived human beings; but deceiving her was so easy, as Ovid says in the passage cited by Rigault:
>
> > Vesta’s images are said  
> > To have placed maiden hands before their eyes.
>
> LINDNER.
>
> **“Acts of debauchery are hired.”** The Roman edition has “acts of debauchery are contracted for.” WOWER.—That is unquestionably how it should be read: it is not the acts of debauchery, but the women who are to be debauched, who are hired for money; but among the altars, men and women bargain and reach agreements about debauchery. DAVIS.
>
> **“Adulteries are premeditated.”** This verb, commonly considered deponent, has a passive force here, as it does elsewhere, according to the observation of G. J. Vossius, *Analecta* III, ch. 6. To the examples he produced may be added the following. Cicero, *Response Concerning the Haruspices*, p. 1990: “Nothing that had not been considered for a long time and premeditated far in advance.” Ovid, *Metamorphoses* VII.727:
>
> > And I almost abandoned the provisions  
> > Of the will I had prepared in good faith.
>
> [Col. 0320B] Pliny, *Panegyric*, ch. 3: “And that he is considered more welcome who brings to their shrines a pure and chaste mind than one who brings a premeditated poem.” Latinus Pacatus, *Panegyric* XII, ch. 2: “The passions were meditated long beforehand and foreseen from afar.” So too Rufinus in his translation of the *Recognitions of Clement* II, ch. 26. DAVIS.
>
> **“The entire state.”** There is no need to restore either Wower’s “the sum of the state” or Elmenhorst’s “the supreme matter.” Cicero, *For Sextus Roscius of Ameria*, ch. 51: “Because the entire state is put to the test in his danger.” The excellent J. F. Gronovius established this expression with many examples in his note on Livy XXVI, ch. 10. DAVIS.

[Col. 0315B] **ARGUMENT.—He next shows that Caecilius wrongly boasts that the Romans gained dominion over the whole world by duly observing superstitions of this kind [Col. 0316A]. On the contrary, the Romans were gathered together in crime at their origin and grew through the terror produced by their savagery. The Romans therefore became so great not because they were religious, but because they committed sacrilege with impunity.**

Yet nevertheless it was this very superstition that gave, enlarged, and founded the Romans’ empire, since they excelled not so much in courage as in religion and devotion! No doubt the distinguished and noble justice of Rome was inaugurated from the very cradle of its nascent empire. Were not its people, at their very origin, gathered together in crime, fortified by the terror of their own savagery, and increased in number? For its first populace was assembled through an asylum: ruined men, criminals, the incestuous, assassins, and traitors had flowed together there. And so that Romulus himself, their commander and ruler, might surpass his people in crime, he committed parricide. (XXI) These are the first auspices of a religious state.

Soon afterward he abducted, violated, and mocked other men’s maidens—some already betrothed, some already promised—and even some young married women, without precedent; and he joined battle with their parents, that is, with his own fathers-in-law, and shed the blood of his relatives. What could be more irreligious, what more audacious, what, through sheer confidence in crime, more secure?

Thereafter, to drive neighboring peoples from their land; to overthrow nearby cities together with their temples and altars; to compel captives; and to grow powerful through the losses of others and their own crimes—this was the common discipline practiced by Romulus, the other kings, and the later commanders. Thus, whatever the Romans hold, cultivate, and possess is the spoil of audacity. All their temples were built from war-spoils, that is, from the ruins of cities, the plunder of gods, and the slaughter of priests.

This is to taunt and mock: to serve conquered religions and, after victories, to adore them as captives. For to adore what you have captured by your own hand is to consecrate sacrilege, not divinities. An act of pollution was therefore committed by the Romans as many times as a triumph was celebrated; the spoils taken from gods were as numerous as the trophies taken from nations. The Romans therefore became so great not because they were religious, but because they committed sacrilege with impunity.

For they could not have had as helpers in those very wars the gods against whom they had taken up arms; and those whom they had summoned, after triumphing over them, they began to worship. But what can those gods do for the Romans, when they were powerless to do anything for their own peoples against Roman arms?

We know the native-born gods of the Romans: Romulus, Picus, Tiberinus, Consus, Pilumnus, and Polumnus. Tatius both discovered and worshipped Cloacina; Hostilius worshipped Fear and Pallor; afterward Fever was dedicated by someone or other. This superstition is the foster-child of that city: diseases and forms of ill health. (XXII) Acca Larentia and Flora too—prostitutes notorious for their debauchery—should certainly be counted among the diseases and gods of the Romans.

These gods, presumably, extended the Roman Empire against all the other gods worshipped among the nations! For neither Thracian Mars, Cretan Jupiter, Juno—now Argive, now Samian, now Punic—nor [printed: “or”] Taurian Diana, the Idaean Mother, or that Egyptian goddess, all of them not divinities but monstrosities, assisted their own peoples against the Romans.

Unless perhaps among the Romans the chastity of virgins was greater or the religious observance of priests holier! Yet violation of chastity has been punished in the case of nearly all the virgins who had rather heedlessly joined themselves to men—certainly without Vesta’s knowledge—while in the remaining cases it was not greater security in chastity but greater success in unchastity that produced impunity. (XXIII)

Where, moreover, are acts of debauchery hired, procuring arrangements negotiated, and adulteries premeditated more than by priests among altars and shrines? Indeed, blazing lust is satisfied more frequently in the little chambers of temple attendants than in the brothels themselves.

And yet before the Romans, by God’s ordering, the Assyrians, Medes, Persians, Greeks, and even the Egyptians long held kingdoms, although they had no Pontiffs, Arval Brethren, Salii, Vestal Virgins, or Augurs, nor chickens enclosed in a cage, by whose eating or refusal of food the entire state was governed.

## CHAPTER XXVI

> **Note: [Col. 0320C]**
>
> **CH. XXVI.—“You have attested.”** Heraldus, perhaps through a typographical error, incorrectly prints “he has attested.” LINDNER.
>
> **“The most solemn dance”** is the reading of the Roman edition and the royal manuscript; in its place Gelenius printed *solistimum*. But although *solistimum tripudium* is properly the name for a favorable augury—a fact known even to schoolboys—it is nevertheless possible that Minucius wrote *solemnissimum*, because it was in fact a customary and commonly used augury. By Cicero’s own time, taking auspices from the flight of birds had already fallen into disuse, as Cicero himself teaches in his books *On Divination*. HERALDUS.—Brissonius also quoted and annotated this passage of Minucius in book I of *On Formulae*, where he examines the entire discipline of the *solistimum tripudium* on p. 124. And although the French translator likewise renders it *le trépignement solennel des poussins* (“the solemn stamping of the chicks”), no such expression was ever used or can be understood, since there was only one kind of *tripudium*, namely the *solistimum*. This, therefore, is what Minucius meant, not *solemnissimum*. GRONOVIUS.
>
> **“And Paulus at Cannae; nevertheless.”** Learned men punctuate: “and Paulus, nevertheless, at Cannae, together with,” etc. But I scarcely doubt that the conjunction should be transposed thus: “Paulus had them, and nevertheless at Cannae,” etc. “And” is used in this same fashion in the preceding sentences: “What of Regulus? Did he not observe the auguries and was captured?” etc. Add the fact that Cyprian reproduces Minucius in this fashion in *On the Vanity of Idols*: “He was sent away; and Paulus had voracious chickens, and nevertheless he was slain at Cannae.” WOPKENS.—This very fact persuades me that we should refrain from an unnecessary correction. For Cyprian occasionally alters Minucius’s wording somewhat. Thus a little later, instead of “and the more easily for that reason he both sailed and conquered,” Cyprian has: “and the more easily for that reason he sailed and conquered.” HEUMANN.
>
> **“Of the Roman people.”** The manuscript has “with the greater part of the state.” The text had been written *cum majore R. P. parte*. From this the error arose. MEURSIUS.
>
> **[Col. 0321B] “Gaius Caesar.”** Supply: “Gaius Caesar, having been warned not to send ships to Africa before winter . . . disregarded the warnings.” LINDNER.
>
> **“To send ships to Africa.”** Either the penultimate word must be omitted, as Cicero did in *On Divination* II, ch. 24, which Minucius copied, or *navigio transmitteret* (“to cross by ship”) must be read; for Latin usage rejects *navigia transmittere* in the sense “to cross over.” DAVIS.
>
> **“The more easily for that reason.”** I write “the more successfully.” HEUMANN.
>
> **“Who did not know that he would be betrayed.”** This is the entirely correct reading, which we owe to the royal manuscript. Previously the text read: “who, having himself been betrayed for a necklace, was unaware of it.” HERALDUS.
>
> **“Blind Tiresias.”** Davis thought that *caecus* (“blind”) should be scraped away. Yet this pleonasm is no more objectionable than the one he illustrated at ch. 16: “I at any rate shall speak as best I can, according to my powers.” A great quantity of other examples could very easily be amassed. WOPKENS.
>
> **“Who.”** After *qui* the antithesis to *caecus* (“blind”) is necessarily missing. MEURSIUS.—This judgment of that most learned man, unless I am mistaken, led Davis into error and induced him to delete *caecus*. But *caecus* is not an adjective to be joined with the verb “saw”; it is an epithet of Tiresias. It is therefore clear that the comma should be placed not after “Tiresias,” but after “blind.” LINDNER.
>
> **“Whose guarded saying then.”** Gelenius correctly printed it thus [Col. 0321D]. But the Roman edition has the meaningless “that guarded place.” HERALDUS.
>
> **“Chance imitated skill.”** Our author repeated this from Cicero, who says in *On Divination* II, ch. 21: “Chance can therefore imitate truth.” Relevant too is the saying of the philosopher Favorinus in Gellius XIV, ch. 1: “By trying many things, they sometimes stumble inadvertently upon the truth.” HEUMANN.
>
> **“Or sought.”** Heumann prefers “conducted.” If I thought anything needed changing, I would prefer “carried through,” which Cicero has in *Letters* XIII.31. But no change is necessary. The simple *petere* is used for the compound *appetere* (“seek”). Observe Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* III.23: “Things in accordance with nature are sought; their opposites are avoided.” LINDNER.
>
> **“Or for things that do not exist to appear.”** That is, “so that even things that do not exist may appear.” Nepos likewise construes words that ought to be followed by *ut* with a subsequent infinitive. Johann Joachim Ungnad produces passages in his note on *Miltiades* 7.1. Heumann thinks our author wrote: “They perform illusions, so that even things which do not exist may appear to be seen.” LINDNER.
>
> **“Both in speech and in deed.”** Heumann deletes these words. I think our author had in view Luke 24:19: “Who proved to be a prophet, mighty in deed and word” (ὃς ἐγένετο ἀνὴρ προφήτης, δυνατὸς ἐν ἔργῳ καὶ λόγῳ). LINDNER.
>
> **“Sosthenes.”** Thus the royal manuscript and the early editions of Cyprian; *Sostanes* in the Baluze and Grenoble manuscripts; *Hostanes* in Pamelius and the Tours manuscript; *Ostanes* in Pliny and Apuleius. He was a distinguished Magus, “the foremost of the Magi,” as Augustine says in *On Baptism Against the Donatists* VI, final chapter. He denies that the form of the true God can be seen and says that true angels stand beside his throne. Pliny first mentions him in book XXX, ch. 1, and relates that he accompanied Xerxes, king of the Persians, when he brought war into Greece, sowed the seeds of the magical art, and infected the whole world wherever he went. Compare, together with Pliny and Augustine in the passages cited, Apuleius, *Apology*, pp. 449 and 554 of the edition *ad usum*; Tertullian, *On the Soul*, ch. 57; Tatian, *Address to the Greeks*; Suidas, s.v. *Astronomy*; Diogenes Laertius; Selden, book V, ch. 11, and Proem, ch. 2; Adrianus Junius. Compare the notes on Tertullian, vol. II, cols. 748 ff. EDD.
>
> **“But of the true.”** Supply “that they exist,” and “he knows that they attend upon his worship.” Hostanes therefore transmitted not only the existence of angels but also their functions. It will now be easy to recognize that the learned Ursinus, Davis, and Heumann deleted the conjunction *and* without cause and wrote: “and that angels . . . attend upon his worship.” LINDNER.
>
> **“Even demons.”** Davis is eager to rewrite this as “or demons,” a correction manifestly false. HEUMANN.
>
> **“From which he also informs us of a predisposition to love” [the manuscript wording is uncertain].** Thus the manuscript, whose traces Rigault followed when he printed: “from which it moves also into us a predisposition to love.” Gelenius and Heraldus read: “from which, he says, a predisposition to love also flows into us, and is formed and slips into human breasts.” Others read: “a desire for love continues further into us.” Less suitably. Davis, however, reads: “he advises that an itching for love is also born from it”; for *procupido*, he says, is a new and unheard-of word. This certainly pleases me more. GALLAND.—Davis reads: “from which he also moves us through the desire of love.” Heumann: “from which loves also continue into us through desire.” But these readings can scarcely stand without the fault of tautology. For what else is “to fashion affections and infuse the heat of desire” than to prompt love? We have therefore retained Heraldus’s reading, observing only that we wish *in eos* (“into them”) to be read in the following sense: Plato holds that from that admixture of earthly weight there flows into those spirits or demons a *procupido*, that is, a certain πρόληψις (“prior disposition” or “preconception”), toward love. He speaks in accordance with the opinion of the Fathers, who maintained that certain angels, having been captivated by love of women, had intercourse with them. Therefore, lest anyone wonder that angels were contaminated by so impure a love, he affirms that this happened because demons were not complete spirits but a substance intermediate between body and spirit; and that from this admixture of earthly weight there flowed into them a predisposition toward love, which could not have existed if they had been formed wholly from celestial lightness. LINDNER.
>
> **“Slip into.”** Thus the critics rewrote the manuscript’s simple “slip.” LINDNER.

**ARGUMENT.—Octavius next turns against Caecilius himself, by the examples of Regulus, Mancinus, Paulus, and Caesar, the weapon that Caecilius had lightly brandished from the auspices and auguries of birds. By other examples he demonstrates that an argument drawn from oracles is no more valid.**
For now I come to those Roman auspices and auguries which, you declared, were collected with the greatest diligence, omitted to one’s regret, and observed with happy results. Clodius, Flaminius, and Junius, we are to suppose, lost their armies [Col. 0320B] because they did not think it necessary to await the chickens’ most solemn ritual dance? What of Regulus? Did he not observe the auguries—and was he not captured? Mancinus respected the religious rites, yet he was sent under the yoke and handed over to the enemy. Paulus too had chickens that fed greedily at Cannae; nevertheless, he was struck down together with the greater part of the republic. [38] C. Caesar disregarded the auguries and auspices that sought to prevent him from sending ships to Africa before midwinter; and thus he sailed and conquered all the more readily. [Col. 0321A]

What, then, and how much am I to recount about oracles? After his death Amphiaraus gave answers concerning things to come, although he did not know that his wife would betray him for a necklace. The blind Tiresias could see the future, though he could not see the present. Ennius fabricated the responses of Pythian Apollo concerning Pyrrhus when Apollo had already ceased composing verses; and that guarded and ambiguous oracle of his failed precisely when people began to be more refined and less credulous. And Demosthenes, because he knew the responses were contrived, complained that the Pythia was “Philippizing” (*philippizein*, φιλιππίζειν), that is, taking Philip’s side.

Yet auspices or oracles have sometimes touched upon the truth. Although among so many falsehoods chance might appear to have imitated deliberate skill, [Col. 0321B] I shall nevertheless approach the very source of error and depravity from which all this darkness has flowed, and shall dig more deeply and disclose it more plainly.

There are impure, wandering spirits, weighed down from their heavenly vigor by earthly stains and desires. After these spirits, burdened and submerged in vices, had lost the simplicity of their own substance, they did not cease—in consolation for their own calamity, being themselves already ruined—to ruin others; being depraved, to instill the error of their depravity; and being estranged from [Col. 0322A] God, to separate others from God by introducing corrupt religions.

The poets know that these spirits [39] are demons; philosophers discuss them; Socrates knew them, for at the nod and discretion of the demon that attended him he either avoided or undertook particular affairs. The magi likewise not only know demons but also perform through demons every marvel with which they make sport: through the demons’ inspiration and influence they produce illusions, causing things that do not exist to appear, or things that do exist not to appear.

Sosthenes, foremost among those magi both in eloquence and practice, proclaims the true God with the majesty he deserves. He also knows that angels—that is, the ministers and messengers of the true God—attend upon his worship, so that they tremble in terror at the Lord’s mere nod and countenance. The same Sosthenes also revealed that demons are earthly, wandering, and hostile to humanity. [Col. 0322B]

What of Plato, who believed it a difficult task to discover God? Does he not speak without difficulty about both angels and demons? In his *Symposium* he even endeavors to define the nature of demons. He maintains that their substance is intermediate between mortal and immortal—that is, between body and spirit—formed from a mixture of earthly weight and heavenly lightness. From this, he warns, a certain predisposition to love (*procupidinem amoris*) is also formed and glides into human hearts, stirring sensation, shaping affections, and infusing the ardor of desire. [Col. 0323A]

## CHAPTER XXVII

> **Note: [Col. 0323B]**
>
> **CHAP. XXVII.—“Demons.”** I expel this as a gloss. For the word “demons” (*daemones*), written in the margin by some reader as an interpretation, was afterward admitted into the text by others. [Col. 0323C] **MEURSIUS.**—Fulvius Ursinus and Johannes Meursius wrongly reject this word as a gloss, and Chr. Cellarius, following them as his guides, eliminated it altogether. It must certainly be retained, however, and authors frequently speak in this manner. Justin Martyr, *Apology* I, 71, Oxford ed.: Ἤκουσαν διὰ τοῦ ἄλλου προφήτου ΗΣΑΙΟΥ λεχθέν, “They heard what was spoken through the other prophet, ISAIAH.” And *Apology* II, 6: πολλοὶ τῶν ἡμετέρων ἀνθρώπων ΤΩΝ ΚΡΙΣΤΙΑΝΩΝ, “many of our people, THE CHRISTIANS.” See also Athenagoras, *Embassy for the Christians*, chap. 22, p. 101. **DAVIS.**
>
> **“By philosophers.”** Heumann says that this should be removed as a gloss. But it deservedly maintains its place, since mention is made not only of the magi and Plato but also of Socrates in § 8. I add that “and by Plato” must be explained as “and especially by Plato.” Mark 16:7: Εἴπατε τοῖς μαθηταῖς αὐτοῦ ΚΑΙ Πέτρῳ, “Tell his disciples, AND Peter.” Acts 1:14: Σὺν γυναιξὶ ΚΑΙ Μαρίᾳ, “With the women, AND Mary.” **LINDNER.**
>
> **“Lie hidden, consecrated.”** Cyprian, *On the Vanity of Idols*, chap. 4, reads “lie hidden beneath consecrated things” (*consecratis delitescunt*). Johannes Meursius thought that Cyprian’s manuscripts should be corrected according to the text of Minucius; but Fulvius Ursinus emends Felix from the Bishop of Carthage, and he has my agreement, for statues had to be consecrated in a particular manner if they were to possess any power. Related are the things Eastern writers relate about talismans. See Thomas Stanley, *Philosophy of the East*, book I, section 2, chap. 27, Le Clerc’s edition. **DAVIS.**—For my part, I think neither text should be corrected from the other. For who, other than demons, is consecrated beneath statues? In the same way I can say: “Poison, swallowed under cover of food, lies hidden,” and “Poison lies hidden beneath food that has been eaten.” **LINDNER.**
>
> **“While they are inspired . . . prophets.”** Read, without doubt, “while they inspire.” Thus chap. 16: “When demons inspire and influence them, the magi produce illusions.” Lactantius II, 14, 10: “All the art and power of the magi consists in the inspirations of demons.” Apuleius, *On the God of Socrates*, p. 45: “Demons take care either to fashion dreams . . . or to instruct omens from birdsong, or to inspire prophets.” **HEUMANN.**—From these passages it is likewise clear that the reading should be: “while in the meantime they inspire prophets.” But if so, I do not see why the passive cannot stand just as well: “while prophets are inspired”—by them. [Col. 0324B] **LINDNER.**
>
> **“So that both, not knowing.”** I am surprised that, among so many interpreters, no one saw that the particles *ut et* must be transposed. The sense is: the demons are deceived and deceive others—deceived as not knowing the unadulterated truth, that is, as beings who do not know it; and deceiving others because they do not confess what they do know, to their own destruction. The Fathers attributed to demons a knowledge not only not superior to human knowledge but not even equal to it. Augustine, book I, *Against the Academics*, chap. 6: “I grant that we can be surpassed in acuteness and subtlety of sense by certain utterly base creatures of this air, whom they call demons; but in reason, I deny it.” And elsewhere: “Far be it from a genuinely religious mind, subject to the true God, to consider demons better than itself merely because they have better bodies. . . . But just as we are better than all these animals in reasoning and understanding, so too ought we to be better than demons in living well and honorably.” We infer from this chapter that demons take great care not to do anything leading to their own ruin and disgrace: “The demons, overcome by pain, declare what they are; and certainly they do not lie to their own disgrace, especially when some of your own people are present.” [Col. 0324C] **LINDNER.**
>
> **“They weigh men downward from heaven.”** By the earthly weight of vices implanted in the soul, they drag it down so that it cannot rise to God. **CELLARIUS.**
>
> **“They divert them to material things.”** Thus Heraldus printed it, and it is believed that he found this reading in the Royal manuscript. Heumann falsely testifies that the manuscript has the singular *materiam* (“matter”); indeed, I do not know his source—unless, perhaps, he derived it from Rigaltius. **LINDNER.**
>
> **“They disturb everyone.”** So the ancient parchments read, as Nicolas Rigaltius testifies. But Cyprian, *On the Vanity of Idols*, p. 14, reads “they disturb dreams” (*somnios inquietant*), with whom Meursius, Ouzelius, and Cellarius agree; and apparently quite correctly, for Lactantius, who modeled his own words upon our author’s, says in *Divine Institutes*, book II, chap. 14: “Because they”—the demons—“are subtle and imperceptible spirits, . . . they cause diseases and terrify minds through dreams.” [Col. 0324D] **DAVIS.**
>
> **“By releasing what they had constricted.”** They cease doing harm so that they may appear to have cured the victims. Tertullian, *Apology*, chap. 22. Thus Cyprian read it in his manuscript—not *remissus*—as Sigismund Gelenius and others also printed it. **RIGALTIUS.**
>
> **“These are also the frenzied,” etc.** Minucius did not mean the demons themselves, but people possessed and tormented by those foul spirits. Perhaps, therefore, the reading should be: “Hence come also the frenzied.” Our author afterward calls them “prophets outside a temple,” because, just as prophets raved in temples, so these people went mad and whirled about in streets and public squares. See the *Recognitions of Clement*, book V, chap. 13; the *Homilies*, IX, chap. 7; [Col. 0325A] Origen, *Against Celsus*, book VIII, pp. 333 ff.; and Prudentius, *Peristephanon*, v. 1063. **DAVIS.**—**“These are also the frenzied.”** This is an exceedingly vexed passage, for which I offer the following remedy: “These”—of whom I have thus far spoken, whose limbs the demons contort—“are the frenzied whom you see rushing out in public”—he means the possessed, but they are not the only people driven by demons. “The prophets themselves in a temple”—who do not rush out in public—“likewise rave, revel madly, and whirl around”—that is, they behave in the same manner as the possessed. “The instigation of the demon is alike in both, but the purpose of their frenzy is different.” In the possessed its purpose is that, by releasing what they had constricted, they may appear to have cured them; in inspired prophets, that by their breath they may obtain the authority, as it were, of a present divinity and accustom to themselves people curious about the future. [Col. 0325B]
>
> Come, let us examine the interpretations of others. Heumann reads: “They themselves are also prophets, although they grow heated in a temple under the demon’s agitation.” A most elegant jest; but you should know, reader, that the punctuation here must be corrected, placing a comma after “rush out” and a colon after “temple.” **WOPKENIUS.**—I think it should be punctuated: “prophets. They themselves, even without a temple, . . . whirl around.” Furthermore, because Minucius is speaking not of the demons themselves but of possessed people, Davis read: “Hence come also the frenzied,” etc. But I think the author is plainly speaking about the demons themselves, and that the words “they themselves, even without a temple,” etc., can refer to nothing else. Nothing is more customary than for authors to speak about spirits and demons as though speaking about the people whom they drive; see Mark 3:3. Cellarius says: “If demons who lie hidden beneath statues in temples, and agitate their people and move their priests—or if the latter pretend to be moved by them—are regarded as gods, then all madmen who do the same thing outside temples by whirling and tossing themselves about could equally be regarded as gods.”
>
> Heraldus: “I should think that one must read, ‘The prophets themselves in a temple.’ For we noted agitation of prophets of this kind within the temples themselves, in our remarks on Tertullian’s *Apology*, from Julius Firmicus.”
>
> Grunerus: “I change only the punctuation, as follows: ‘These are also the frenzied whom you see rush out in public; the prophets themselves are without a temple: thus they rave,’” etc. [Col. 0325C] **LINDNER.**
>
> **“Most of you—a part.”** I am thoroughly dissatisfied with Rigaltius’ conjecture, which reads: “Most people know all these things; a portion of your own people know that the demons,” etc. Gelenius, Heraldus, and Cellarius printed: “Most of you know everything.” Badly, for they omit a useful word. The text must certainly be restored: “The greater part of you knows all these things” (*Haec omnia sciunt pleraque pars vestrum*). Sallust, *Jugurtha*, chap. 18: “The greater part of Lower Africa is possessed by the Numidians.” So too Juvencus, *Gospel History*, book I, p. 9:

> This man will persuade the greater part of that people to return  
> To the true path.

> Nor should anyone be surprised at the construction, for “part” is a collective noun. Virgil, *Aeneid* I, 212:
>
> Some cut them into pieces.
>
> Ovid, *Metamorphoses* I, 244:
>
> Some approve Jupiter’s words aloud.
>
> See Adsonius on Thales VI, 27. [Col. 0325D] **DAVIS.**—The ordinary construction of these words is: “Most of you know that the demons themselves confess all these things about themselves.” Such interweaving of two clauses is not uncommon among the best writers. Yet since the manuscript reads *plerique pars vestrum*—which no one who knows Gronovius will be surprised that he defended—[Col. 0326A] Davis directs that it be read *pleraque pars vestrum*, “the greater part of you.” But this produces an excessively harsh expression, which ought not to be attributed to our Minucius. Perhaps Rigaltius was mistaken when he taught that the manuscript reads so. Certainly Heraldus, who inspected the same codex with his own eyes, did not see the little word *pars* there—unless perhaps he was unwilling to report an obvious error. [Col. 0326B] **HEUMANN.**
>
> **“Tortures of words.”** The earlier reading was “and by the merits of words,” which presented no difficulty. But besides appearing more suitable, the reading of the Royal manuscript also has Cyprian as a supporter, since he imitates Minucius in this matter. *To Demetrianus*: “When they are adjured by us and tortured with spiritual scourges and tortures of words, they are cast out of possessed bodies.” Lactantius V, 22: “Thus, wrenched and tortured by the power of the divine majesty, they howl.” **HERALDUS.**
>
> **“With themselves as witnesses.”** According to a learned man in *Miscellaneous Observations*, 1734, vol. IV, p. 423, the manuscript has *credite f:ssis* [uncertain reading], although this *f:ssis* has been partly erased; and the words “confessing the truth about themselves” occur only between the lines—although, certainly, in the same hand. From this he conjectured: “Believe, with themselves as witnesses, that they are those demons who have confessed.” But in such a reading *testibus*, “as witnesses,” would be far better omitted, for it seems excessively tautological and harsh. I therefore prefer: “Believe, with themselves as witnesses, that they are demons who have confessed the truth about themselves.” [Col. 0326C] **WOPKENIUS.**—“That they are demons” is an obvious gloss. **HEUMANN.**
>
> **“Unwillingly, the wretches shudder within bodies.”** Thus the manuscript: demons, when adjured, shudder within bodies. This is the same as what James 2:19 says: Καὶ φρίσσουσι, “And they shudder.” This is the first effect of exorcism. Then they leap out, and do so unwillingly, as in Luke 9:39: Καὶ ἐξαίφνης κράζει καὶ σπαράσσει αὐτὸν μετὰ ἀφροῦ καὶ ΜΟΓΙΣ ἀποχωρεῖ, “And suddenly it cries out and convulses him with foam, and SCARCELY departs.” And our author, chap. 12: “Unwillingly, wretch, you are convicted of weakness, yet do not confess it.” **LINDNER.**—I should prefer: “Unwillingly they shudder within the wretched bodies.” Cyprian spoke of “possessed bodies.” It is also surprising that the learned man in *Miscellaneous Observations*, at the place cited, thought the text should read: “the wretches shudder and either leap out of the bodies,” etc. For just as the phrase “shudder within bodies” is used here in a plain and natural sense, so in the words “and either leap out,” etc., “from there” or “from them” is very conveniently understood; nor did Cyprian IV, 7 prefix anything of the kind. [Col. 0326D] **WOPKENIUS.**—It should be read thus: “Overcome, they shudder within the wretched bodies.” **HEUMANN.**—Others read *inhaerescunt*, “cling within.” **LINDNER.**
>
> **“And to attack one whom you fear.”** The sentence lies utterly limp unless it is restored as: “and to attack one whom you hate,” as Johannes Freinsheim conjectured in his note on Curtius, book X, chap. 8. This emendation is deservedly approved by Jacob Gronovius. Consult Hieronymus Columna on the *Fragments of Ennius*, p. 298, and Janus Gruter on Publilius Syrus, v. 37. **DAVIS.**—I agree. The origin of the error is obvious. Observe a nearly similar maxim of Tacitus in the *Life of Agricola*, chap. 42: “It is peculiar to human nature to hate the person whom one has injured.” Ennius speaks in precisely the same manner as our Minucius in Cicero, *On Duties*, book II, [Col. 0327B] chap. 7: “Whom they fear, they hate; and each person desires the death of the one he hates.” **HEUMANN.**

**SUMMARY.—**In order to establish this point firmly, Octavius traces the matter more deeply, back to its first origin. The source of the error, namely, is this: demons lie hidden beneath statues and images, dwell in shrines, animate the fibers of entrails, govern the flights of birds, direct lots, and utter oracles wrapped in false responses. Nevertheless, when adjured by Christians through the true God and driven from possessed bodies, they are compelled to confess that these things were done not by God but by themselves. Hence they flee from Christians when nearby, and stir up so much hatred against them among the pagans that the latter begin to hate them before knowing them, lest, once they know them, they should either be able to imitate them or be unable to condemn them.

[Col. 0323B] These impure spirits, then—the demons, as has been shown [Col. 0324A] by the magi, by the philosophers, and especially by Plato—lie hidden, consecrated beneath statues and images. By their breath they obtain the authority, as it were, of a present divinity: meanwhile prophets are inspired by them; they dwell in shrines; they sometimes animate the fibers of entrails; govern the flights of birds; direct lots; and produce oracles wrapped in many false responses.

For they are both deceived and deceivers: they do not know the unadulterated truth, and what they do know they do not confess, to their own [40] destruction. Thus they weigh men downward from heaven, divert them from the true God to material things, disturb life, and trouble everyone. Secretly creeping even into bodies, subtle spirits as they are, they fabricate diseases, terrify minds, and contort limbs, in order to compel people to worship them. Then, fattened by the smoke of altars or by animal victims, they release what they had constricted [Col. 0324B] so that they may appear to have cured it.

These are also the frenzied whom you see [Col. 0325A] rushing out in public; the prophets themselves, even without a temple, rave in this way, revel madly in this way, and whirl around in this way. The demon’s instigation is alike in both, but the purpose of the frenzy is different.

Those incidents mentioned to you shortly before also concern these spirits: that Jupiter ordered the games to be repeated because of a dream; that the Castors appeared with their horses; and that the little ship followed the matron’s girdle.

Most of you know all these things: the demons themselves confess them about themselves whenever they are driven from bodies by us, through the tortures of words and the fires of prayer. Saturn himself, [Col. 0326A] Serapis, Jupiter, and whatever host of demons you worship—overcome by pain—declare what they are. And surely they do not lie to their own disgrace, especially when some of your people are present. Believe the truth about them on the testimony of the demons themselves, who confess it concerning themselves.

For when adjured through the true and only God, they unwillingly shudder within the wretched bodies and either leap out immediately or vanish gradually, according as the sufferer’s faith assists or the healer’s grace inspires. Thus they flee from Christians when close at hand, though at a distance they attacked them in your assemblies through your agency.

Therefore, once they have implanted themselves [Col. 0327A] in the minds of the ignorant, they secretly sow hatred of us through fear; [41] for it is natural both to hate the person whom you fear and, if you can, to attack the person whom you dread. Thus they preoccupy minds and obstruct hearts, so that people begin to hate us before they know us—lest, once they know us, they should either be able to imitate us or be unable to condemn us.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

> **Note: [Col. 0327B]**
>
> **CHAP. XXVIII.—“How unjust it is.”** Thus, most excellently, in the Royal manuscript. The earlier reading was: “How great a fault it is.” Minucius touches upon the injustice which Tertullian attacks at greater length in the *Apology*. **HERALDUS.**
>
> **“Things unknown and unexamined,”** that is, the matters themselves. The expression occurs in full in Cicero, *For Caecina* 29: “When he had wished to judge the matter without examining it.” Virgil, *Aeneid* I, 519: “But the unknown circumstance disturbs their minds.” Accordingly there was no reason for Ludovicus Carrio, *Emendations* II, chap. 18, to restore *de incognitis*, “concerning unknown things,” or for Meursius to write *in incognitis*, “among unknown things.” [Col. 0327C] **LINDNER.**
>
> **“We did the same.”** Thus the manuscript; the printed editions have “We were.” **EDITORS.**—I write *iidem*, “we, the same people.” **MEURSIUS.**—Write “We did the same.” For “what you do” precedes. **WOPKENIUS.**
>
> **“Circulated.”** Heumann writes *venditari*, “offered for sale,” and deletes the following “and.” **LINDNER.**
>
> **“The reward for information.”** Gelenius had printed this reading, most correctly. But the Roman edition has *judicii*, “of judgment.” Badly. The Royal manuscript confirms Gelenius’ edition. Is this, however, what Tertullian meant in *Apology*, chap. 7: “Who, after discovering such crimes, concealed them, or sold them while dragging the people themselves forward?”—so that “sell” there means “to inform in exchange for payment”? We have said that this is not clear to us. **HERALDUS.**
>
> **“The evil, however.”** That is: “nor did we understand that the evil was so far from existing that, on the contrary, a Christian on trial neither blushed,” etc. For bad actions possess a certain natural shame joined with fear. [Col. 0327D] **LINDNER.**
>
> **“Regretted only one thing . . .”** Although this construction may seem unusual, it is not unknown among good authors. Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations*, book V, chap. 28: “For it is peculiar to the wise man to do nothing that he could regret.” The same author, *On Invention*, book II, p. 66: “Whether that is a deed which it was necessary to regret.” See Aulus Gellius, *Attic Nights*, book XIII, chap. 2. **DAVIS.**
>
> **“Some persons.”** This word apparently should be deleted. Lactantius V, 1, 2. **HEUMANN.**
>
> **“We undertook.”** A forensic term. For clients were “undertaken.” Servius, on *Aeneid* VI, 609:
>
> And fraud entwined around a client:
>
> “He wishes,” Servius says, “us to understand prevaricators who are patrons of clients, whom we now call those ‘undertaken’ (*susceptos*).” **WOWER.**
>
> **“Taking pity on them.”** Moved by compassion toward those [Col. 0328B] whose lives we were striving to preserve. Heumann writes *miserentes*, “pitying.” **LINDNER.**
>
> **“So that we might torture them.”** Thus the manuscript. But already in the Roman edition it was restored as “so that we pressed them.” Correctly; and immediately afterward this verb “to press” is used again. **HEUMANN.**
>
> **“Of course, lest they should perish.”** He indicates the benefit which ought to accrue to them from that denial. A surgeon too, taking pity on the sick person, amputates, cuts, and cauterizes his limbs—of course, lest he perish. [Col. 0328C] **LINDNER.**
>
> **“Pressed and overcome by suffering.”** There is no need to restore with Heumann “oppressed and overcome by pain.” The learned man was evidently thinking of evil not in the physical but in the moral sense. Yet all dictionaries attest that *malum*, “evil,” can mean punishment and pain. Quintilian too used *premere*, “press,” for *opprimere*, “oppress,” in *Institutes of Oratory*, book III, chap. 2, p. 407 of my edition: “Varenus, who was oppressed amid every public calamity; for he was also condemned.” Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* 2, 17: “But who is not wretched precisely when he is pressed by the greatest pains, if the highest evil consists in them?” **LINDNER.**
>
> **“That we thought and acted as you think and behave.”** Either *gessisse*, “behaved,” must be restored with the anonymous Parisian because *geritis*, “behave,” follows; or—and I prefer this—*agitis*, “act,” must be written instead of *geritis* because *egisse*, “acted,” precedes. **HEUMANN.**—One or the other would indeed be necessary if one equivalent verb could not be substituted for another. [Col. 0328D] **LINDNER.**
>
> **“When, if reason and not the instigation of a demon were judging, they ought rather to be pressed.”** The manuscript has *urguendi*, “to be pressed”; it had wrongly been printed *arguendi*, “to be accused.” Supply: “when Christians were—or had—to be pressed.” **CELLARIUS.**—Heumann expels *magis*, “rather,” which has the force of “more properly,” as in chap. 5, and writes *urgendum esset*, “it would have been necessary to press.” **LINDNER.**
>
> **“Nor is it, however, surprising, since everyone’s report.”** If nothing has been omitted here from the exemplar, the entire period must be arranged in the following way if any sense is to be extracted: “For with these and similar tales the same demons have filled the ears of the ignorant against us, to produce the horror of execration. Nor, however, is this surprising. Just as the reputation of human beings, which is always nourished by falsehoods scattered into it, is destroyed when the truth is disclosed, so is the business of demons; for false rumor is both sown and fostered by them.” The words “since human reputation” must be joined to “so is the business of demons,” so that the conclusion is understood thus: “Nor, however, is it surprising. Such is the business of demons with the reputation of human beings, which,” etc. [Col. 0329A] By “human beings” understand Christians. The manuscript reads “everyone’s.” **RIGALTIUS.**—Rigaltius rightly replaces *omnium*, “everyone’s,” with *hominum*, “human beings”; but he wrongly wishes this to be understood of Christians, as the distinguished Johannes Fredericus Gronovius has already observed in *Observations on Ecclesiastical Writers*, chap. 7. There he judges that the entire passage should be restored thus: “Nor, however, is it surprising, since the reputation spread by people’s mouths, which is always nourished by falsehoods scattered into it and is destroyed when the truth is disclosed, is also the business of demons; for false rumor is both sown and fostered by them.” [Col. 0329B]
>
> According to his interpretation, this means: “That report, tossed about and propagated by human mouths, which is always nourished and enlarged by falsehoods and disappears when the truth is revealed—that same human report is the business and work of the demons themselves. The authority and instigation belong to the latter; the service belongs to the former.” **OUZELIUS.**—**“Nor, however, is it surprising.”** Rigaltius was the first to apply a healing hand to this passage when, for *omnium*, which is in the manuscript, he restored *hominum*, meaning Christians, in this sense: “Nor, however, is it surprising. Such is the business of demons with the reputation of human beings, which,” etc. J. F. Gronovius came closer to the truth in chap. VII of his *Ecclesiastical Observations*, p. 81. He likewise restores *hominum* for *omnium*, but understands it not of maliciously disposed pagans but of human beings universally, which I approve. Yet when he restores *sit et*, “is also,” for *sic est*, “so it is,” he does not have my agreement. I therefore think *si est*, “if it is,” was written.
>
> For in Terence especially, *si*, “if,” regularly follows “it is not surprising.” Thus *Hecyra* IV, 4, 87: “The wife acted unsurprisingly, if she took this badly.” *Andria* IV, 1, 27: “What is so surprising in that, if he takes his example from you?” The sense is: If it were only human report that spoke such abominations about us, someone might perhaps wonder how it came about that it was not at some point destroyed when the truth was disclosed. But it is not surprising. For it is the business of demons, by whom false rumor is not only sown—as we know also happens in human report—but fostered as well, lest it ever be destroyed. [Col. 0329C]
>
> Heumann restores: “Since common report, which is always nourished by falsehoods scattered into it and is destroyed when the truth is disclosed, is the business of demons.” Grunerus: “Since the report of everyone, which is always nourished by falsehoods scattered into it, is likewise destroyed when the truth is disclosed, so is the business of demons.” **LINDNER.**
>
> **“Even with your Epona”:** thus it is written in the Royal manuscript. The Roman edition has “or Hippona.” I certainly think Minucius wrote “with your Epona,” and that someone noted “or Hippona” in the margin. Adrianus Turnebus shows by many examples in his *Adversaria* that the ancients wrote Epona. [Col. 0329D] **HERALDUS.**—Gronovius the younger therefore ought not to have written *Vesta* for *vestra*, “your.” That Minucius mentioned Epona alone here is readily established by the passage of Tertullian just cited, which he had before his eyes. Examine also another very similar passage in Tertullian, *Apology*, chap. 16. On Epona see also Tomasini’s book *On Votive Gifts*, chap. 1. Barthius, with intolerable audacity, maintained that this goddess was called not Epona but Equona, in *Adversaria*, book XXVI, chap. 2, and book XXXVII, chap. 1. **HEUMANN.**—Because the interpreters failed to perceive the force of the particle *vel*, “even,” they indulged their ingenuity in various ways. The following examples will make its force clear. Tertullian, *Apology* 23: “This ought to be understood even from their fodder. . . .” Terence, *The Self-Tormentor* III, 3, 7: “Even yesterday, in your wine, how immoderate you were!” Cicero, *Letters to Friends* VII, 15: “How captious lovers are can be understood even from this.” Perhaps no one would have doubted the integrity of the passage if Minucius had written: “even with Epona, your goddess.” But this word order ought not to detain us, since above, chap. 11, he similarly writes “even so that we might believe from an example” in place of “so that we might believe even from an example.” Cicero speaks almost so in *On the Orator* II, 27: “These things all belong to talent even of a moderate degree,” in place of “even to talent of a moderate degree.” [Col. 0330A–B] **GRUNERUS.**—Johannes Georgius Keyssler, *Travels*, letter 19, p. 123, supplies an inscription concerning this goddess found at Solothurn in Switzerland. **LINDNER.**—Whatever survives concerning the goddess of the stable, whether in ancient testimonies or in monuments—inscribed, painted, cast in bronze, or numismatic—has been collected most learnedly by the same already deservedly praised Dr. Greppo, in his notes to the Lyon edition, pp. 275–288. **EDITORS.**
>
> **“Consecrated.”** The manuscript has *devoratis*, “devoured,” which could have a place if anyone showed that Isis devoured asses, or that asses were used in sacrifices, since those performing sacrifices ate a portion of the offerings. Since, so far as I know, no one has done this, Meursius restored *devotatis*, which means either to consecrate or to show oneself devoted to the asses and to Isis. Heraldus reads *denotatis*, “marked out”—that is: “You worship the ass, Isis’ bearer, together with Isis, by a religious mark of distinction.” Nicolas Heinsius, *Collection of Letters*, vol. IV, p. 260, reads *adoratis*, “worshiped.” Wopkenius reads *religione decoratis*, “honored with religious observance”—that is, “you deem them worthy; you honor them.” [Col. 0330C] Rigaltius and Heumann read *decoratis*, “adorned,” because less costly ornaments were placed around the ass that bore the richly adorned Isis; Ovid too, *Fasti* VI, 311 and 317, mentions such asses crowned and adorned. **LINDNER.**
>
> **“Heads of oxen.”** This is not in foreign and Egyptian religions but in Roman rites, whence we see all altars covered with these heads, and indeed garlands fashioned from them, as it were, between the columns of temples. Thus we see the head of a ram, eagle, or lion used to adorn fasces, and that of an ox for other decorations, in the tomb of Marcus Antonius Antius Lupus reproduced by Bellori in *Tombs*. Such an ox-head also appears stamped on a coin of the Sardinians under Gordian, in Erizzo, p. 512. But the Roman practice is confirmed by the appearance of the monument of Caecilia Metella, daughter of Creticus, which is well known. **GRONOVIUS.**
>
> **“Faces.”** Thus the manuscript reads, and it can be explained as an apposition. For Anubis, or Cynocephalus, had a canine face. The “Frugifer” mentioned by Arnobius, book VI, p. 196, in the passage cited by Cellarius, had a lion’s face. [Col. 0330D] Others read “combined with the face of lions and dogs,” supplying “faces.” Tertullian, *Apology*, chap. 16, supports this emendation: “They ought immediately to have worshiped a two-formed divinity, since they accepted gods combined with both canine and leonine heads, horned from both goat and ram,” etc. **LINDNER.**
>
> **“The same Egyptians, together with most of you.”** I am surprised that they wished to publish this passage in so shamefully corrupt a form, when other editions are correct here—for example, the Paris edition, which reads “together with most of you” (*cum plerisque vobis*), not *vobiscum*. **SCHEFFER.**
>
> **“Noises expressed through the shameful parts of the body.”** The Roman edition has *crepitus*, “breaking of wind.” Petronius, however, called an obscene noise a *strepitus*. Alexander of Aphrodisias, book I, *Problems* 164: ἀποπορδή, “the breaking of wind.” This ridiculous superstition is also known from Cato’s words quoted by Festus under “To prohibit the assemblies.” **WOWER.**
>
> **“They tremble.”** The Roman edition has *extremiscunt* [a corrupt form]. Badly. **HEUMANN.**
>
> **“This much shamelessness,”** for “this shamelessness.” A little below: “they admit into themselves that degree of the worst crime”; chap. 2, § 4: “that time”; chap. 3, § 6: “that place.” Heumann declares that *impudicitiae*, “of shamelessness,” should be removed. [Col. 0331B] **LINDNER.**
>
> **“Every sex.”** I delete “every,” which easily crept in because “all” follows. Take care not to change “every” to “female,” for our author is speaking of both sexes. **HEUMANN.**—Lactantius VI, 23, 10: “The sex given by God does not suffice unless they also profanely and wantonly mock their own sex.” The same author I, 20, 25: “There is no chastity, since unbridled lusts pollute every sex and every part of the body.” **LINDNER.**
>
> **“Shamelessness is called refinement.”** Similarly Curtius V, 1, 38: “Among Persian matrons and maidens, the promiscuous degradation of the body is regarded as affability.” **HEUMANN.**
>
> **“Crime.”** Rigaltius testifies that the exemplar has *mali*, “evil.” Heraldus, however, notes nothing. Heumann approves neither reading and writes: “they admit into themselves that degree of crime.” **LINDNER.**
>
> **“Nor is a harsher servitude imposed.”** Ulpian, Digest, law 2, *Concerning Those Who Are Under Their Own or Another’s Jurisdiction*, etc.: “If a master has raged against his slaves or compels them to shamelessness and degrading violation, the duty of the governor will be made clear from the rescript of the deified Pius to Aelius Marcianus, proconsul of Baetica. The words of that rescript are as follows: [Col. 0331D]
>
> > ‘The power of masters over their slaves ought indeed to remain unimpaired, nor should any person be deprived of his right; but it is in the masters’ own interest that assistance against cruelty, starvation, or intolerable injury not be denied to those who justly petition for it. Therefore investigate the complaints of those from the household of Julius Sabinus who fled to the statue; and if you find that they were either treated more harshly than is just or subjected to a disgraceful injury, order them to be sold, on the condition that they do not return into their master’s power.’
>
> See Justinian Code, law 14, *On Episcopal Jurisdiction*; Seneca, *On Benefits*, book III, chap. 20; Photius, *Nomocanon*, title 13, chap. 22. **ELMENHORST.**

**SUMMARY.—**They not only inflict hatred upon Christians but also charge them with abominable crimes which no one has yet been able to prove. Such is the business of demons, for false rumor is both sown and fostered by them. Octavius then demonstrates with unanswerable force that Christians are falsely accused of sacrilege, incest, sexual outrage, and parricide, just as it was certain and true that precisely the same crimes—or deeds altogether [Col. 0327B] similar and even worse—were actually committed by the pagans themselves.

But how unjust it is to judge matters unknown and unexamined, as you do, believe us on the testimony of our own repentance. For we too once did the same: while still blind and obtuse, we shared your opinions, supposing that Christians worshiped monsters, devoured infants, and mingled in incestuous banquets. We did not understand that these stories were continually being circulated by those men, yet were never either investigated [Col. 0328A] or proved; nor that throughout so long a time anyone had ever appeared who would betray them, though he would have obtained not merely pardon for his own deed but also a reward for giving information; nor that the evil was so far from existing that a Christian on trial neither blushed nor feared, and regretted only that he had not been a Christian before.

Yet although we undertook to defend and protect certain sacrilegious and incestuous persons, even parricides, we thought that Christians should not be heard at all. Sometimes, indeed, out of pity for them, we treated them with greater cruelty: we tortured those who confessed, to make them deny—evidently so that they should not perish—employing against them a perverse interrogation designed not to elicit the truth but to compel a lie. And if anyone weaker, overwhelmed and conquered by suffering, denied that he was a Christian, we favored him, as though by abjuring the name he had cleansed away all his deeds through that denial [Col. 0328B]. Do you recognize that we held and acted upon the same opinions, 42 which you now hold and act upon? Yet if reason, rather than the instigation of a demon, were judging, they should instead have been pressed, not to deny that they were Christians, but to confess to incestuous debauchery, impious rites, and the sacrifice of infants.

For with these and similar tales those same demons have filled the ears of the ignorant against us, inspiring the horror of execration. Nor is that surprising, since human rumor, which is always nourished by lies scattered abroad, is consumed when the truth is disclosed [Col. 0329A]. Such is the business of demons: by them false rumor is both sown and fostered.

Hence comes what you say you have heard: that an ass’s head is an object of worship to us. Who is foolish enough to worship this? Who is more foolish than one who believes it is worshiped? Unless it is because you consecrate even whole asses in your stables, together with your Epona, and religiously devour those same asses together with Isis. Likewise you both sacrifice and worship the heads of cattle and rams; you dedicate as gods beings compounded of goat and man, and faces of lions and dogs. Do you not also worship and feed the bull Apis [Col. 0330A] along with the Egyptians? Nor do you condemn their rites established in honor of serpents, crocodiles, other beasts, birds, and fish—if anyone kills one of these gods, he is even punished with death. Those same Egyptians, together with most of you, fear the pungency of onions no less than Isis, and tremble at noises expelled through the body’s private parts no less than at Serapis.

The man who fabricates against us the story that we worship a priest’s genitals is likewise trying to transfer to us 43 what belongs to his own people. For perhaps those things are rites of their shamelessness [Col. 0331A], among men for whom every sex is prostituted through every bodily member, among whom utter obscenity is called sophistication; who envy prostitutes their license; who lick men about the middle and cling with lustful mouths to their groins—men of evil tongue even when silent, who become weary of their obscenity before they become ashamed of it. Monstrous wickedness! They perpetrate upon themselves an evil deed that neither tender age can endure nor the harshest slavery compel.

## CHAPTER XXIX

> **Note: [Col. 0331D]**
>
> **CHAP. XXIX—“Believed to be God.”** Construe: “either that a guilty man deserved to be believed God, or that an earthly being could be believed God.” LINDNER.
>
> **“The Egyptians indeed.”** For *sane* Jacob Gronovius wishes to restore *Saitae* (“the Saïtes”). Whoever wishes may agree. HEUMANN.
>
> **“Honor more truly.”** Do not delete *verius* with Heumann; it is indispensable here. Two propositions are connected by one and the same verb:
>
> [Col. 0332B] “since honor is bestowed more truly upon an illustrious man;
>
> “since love is bestowed more sweetly upon an excellent man.” LINDNER.
>
> **“We neither worship nor desire crosses.”** There is no reason to abandon the manuscript, which reads *optamus* (“desire”). For just as the ancient Christians did not desire to be subjected to crosses, so they did not refuse to undergo that punishment rather than renounce their religion. Ausonius, *Morning Prayer*, v. 73:
>
> “Let a life with a good conscience neither fear nor desire death.”
>
> The same author, *Periander*, v. 3, p. 290:
>
> “To desire death is evil; to fear it is worse.” DAVIS.—Read *ornamus* (“adorn”). He is arguing against the gentiles, whom he presently confronts with adorned crosses. GRUNER, loc. cit., p. 246.—**“We do not worship crosses.”** Caecilius reproached the Christians for worshiping the cross. Hence above, chap. 9, he called the funereal wood of the cross part of Christian ceremonial. [Col. 0332D] And in chap. 12, objecting still more plainly that Christians worshiped the cross, he says: “See, here are crosses for you, no longer to be worshiped but to be endured.” Accordingly, when Minucius answers Caecilius’s objection by saying, “We do not worship crosses,” his words must clearly be understood of worship in the absolute sense conveyed by Caecilius’s accusation. It is as though Minucius had said: “We Christians do not worship crosses in such a way as to render honor and worship to the crosses themselves, as you gentiles worship your images.” That this is our author’s meaning is clear from what he immediately adds, turning this very accusation back against the gentiles: “But you, who consecrate wooden gods, perhaps worship wooden crosses as components of your gods.” See *Giornale de’ Letterati d’Italia*, vol. XXVII, p. 391 ff.; and add the distinguished Orsi, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VI, § VII, and Trombelli, *On the Worship of the Saints*, vol. II, part III, p. 373. GALLAND.
>
> **“Cantabra, soldiers’ standards.”** See Tertullian, *To the Nations* I, the notes there, and the dissertation by Dom Le Nourry elsewhere in the same volume. EDD.
>
> [Col. 0333B] **“With a pure mind.”** These words have plainly nothing to do with the point. A man forms the sign of the cross when he stretches out his hands and worships God, whether this is done with a pure or an impure mind. LINDNER.

**ARGUMENT.—** Nor is it any more true that they worship a mere man affixed to a cross for his crimes; for they rightly believe him to have been not merely innocent but also God. The gentiles, by contrast, invoke the divine powers of kings whom they themselves have enrolled among the gods, supplicate their images, and implore their guardian spirits [Col. 0331B].

Such disgraces and the like it is not lawful for us even to hear; and to defend them at greater length is shameful. For you invent against the chaste and modest things that we would not believe could be done, had you not proved them of yourselves.

As for your ascribing to our religion a guilty man and his cross, you wander far from the neighborhood of truth in supposing either that a guilty man deserved to be believed God or that an earthly being could be so believed. Truly [printed *nec*, “not”] pitiable is the man whose entire hope rests upon a mortal man, for all his aid ends when that man dies [Col. 0332A].
