The Egyptians, indeed, choose a man for themselves to worship; they propitiate him alone, consult him concerning everything, and slaughter victims to him. Yet the man who is a god to everyone else is certainly a man to himself, whether he likes it or not; for though he deceives another’s conscience, he does not deceive his own. Even toward princes and kings, false adulation shamefully fawns upon them not as great and eminent men, as is proper, but as gods [printed *de eis*, “concerning them”], 44 although honor would be rendered more truly to an illustrious man and love more sweetly to an excellent one. Thus they call upon their divinity, supplicate their images, and implore their *genius*—that is, their demon; and among them it is safer to perjure oneself by Jupiter’s genius than by the king’s.

We neither worship nor desire crosses. But you, who consecrate wooden gods, perhaps worship wooden crosses as components of your gods. For what else are the standards themselves, the *cantabra*, and the military banners but gilded and ornamented crosses [Col. 0332B]? Your victorious trophies imitate not merely the appearance of a simple cross but also that of a man affixed to it. We naturally see the sign of the cross in a ship when it is driven along with swelling sails or glides forward with its oars outspread. When a yoke is raised, it is the sign of a cross; and so it is when a man worships God with a pure mind and outstretched hands. Thus either natural reason rests upon the sign of the cross, or your own religion is fashioned by it.

## CHAPTER XXX

> [Col. 0333A] **Note: [Col. 0333B]**
>
> **CHAP. XXX—“Concerning the slaughter.”** I delete *de* (“concerning”), for it is un-Latin. HEUMANN.
>
> **“The fates of wounds.”** I restore *tanta* (“so many,” that is, “so numerous”) *vulnera*. HEUMANN.—Since Valerius Flaccus, *Argonautica* VI.652, said *fatale vulnerum* (“a fatal wound”), I think our author could correctly have said *fata vulnerum*. LINDNER.
>
> **“No one can believe this.”** Tertullian, *Apology*, chap. 9: “You who believe such things of a human being are also capable of doing them.” ELMENHORST.
>
> **“Fresh blood.”** Without offering even the slightest reason, the Lyon editor smoothly introduced what he regarded as the more delicate reading, *roseum sanguinem* (“rosy blood”)! EDD.
>
> **“Children they have begotten.”** Not foolishly, Nicolaus Heinsius, *Adversaria*, book III, chap. 2, p. 409, suspects that one little word has fallen out here, and reads: *modo procreatos*, “children only just begotten.” HEUMANN.—Lactantius V.9.15: “Who either strangle the children born from themselves or, if they are excessively dutiful, expose them.” LINDNER.
>
> **“By drugs and potions.”** So the Royal manuscript reads, not *epotis* (“drunk down”), as in most common editions. Whether *et potis* is one word or the same expression, let experts determine. EDD.
>
> **“To the Taurians of Pontus.”** Heraldus printed *Pontificis* (“of the pontiff”). LINDNER.
>
> **“And to Mercury the Gauls.”** The word *constat* (“it is established”), or something similar, has dropped out. It is harsher to restore *Gallis* (“among the Gauls”) with Wopken and understand *ritus fuit* (“it was the custom”) ἀπὸ κοινοῦ, “in common,” from the previous clause. HEUMANN.—In his notes on these words, Wower cites the dialogue of Aeneas of Gaza entitled *Theophrastus* to show that the Getae sacrificed their servants to Zalmoxis. But since nothing of the kind is found there, Caspar Barth, in his notes on that dialogue, p. 125b, believes that Wower’s memory failed him. LINDNER.
>
> [Col. 0333D] **“Human or inhuman victims.”** Either *vel inhumanas* is a gloss, or *vel* is used for “or rather.” Thus Cicero, *Philippic* II, chap. 12: “But observe the insensibility of the man—or shall I say, of the beast?” The same author, *On Friendship*, chap. 12: “Gracchus attempted to seize the kingship—or rather, he actually reigned for a few days”; and *Letters to Friends* IV.13, at the end: “But you understand all this better than anyone.” HEUMANN.
>
> **“To bury them alive for the sacrifice.”** Gelenius printed *sacrifici viventes obruere*; but the manuscript has *sacrificii*, as Rigaltius testifies, and this is the true reading, for *causa* (“for the sake”) is understood. Terence, *The Brothers* IV.4.6: “Nor do I say this more for the sake of flattery than because I have reason for you to think me grateful.” Apuleius, *Apology*, p. 187: “So that, under cover of his tender age, he himself might not be punished for the sake of the false accusation.” See also the commentators on Sallust, *Catiline*, chap. 6. DAVIS.—**“For the sacrifice.”** Since the manuscript had *sacrificii*, Davis accepted this reading, understanding *causa*. But his examples do not appear by any means to have proved this ellipsis sufficiently Latin. Jacob Gronovius read *sacri vice* (“in place of a sacred offering”). An easy change with a plain sense would be *sacrificiis* or *in sacrificiis* (“at sacrifices”). Tacitus, *Annals* XV [Col. 0334B].47: “Two-headed offspring … were found in sacrifices at which it is customary to slaughter pregnant victims.” Paulinus of Nola, *Letter* XI.7: “Let us slaughter as sacrifices, in our vices, those animals which were commanded by the Law.” In the same way *lustratione, ludis, comitiis*, and so forth, are used of the time when such things occur, as critics long ago noted from *Observations on Prodigies*, chap. 130, Livy II.36, and elsewhere. WOPKEN.—This word seems to me to have proceeded from another hand and therefore should be expelled. Indeed, since the Roman edition—which Heraldus also followed—has *sacrifici*, it will readily be believed that someone wrote this word in the margin as a gloss on *Romani*. HEUMANN.—I greatly prefer the Roman edition’s reading, taking *Romani* as an adjective and *sacrifici* as a substantive. A *sacrificus* is one who performs sacred rites. Ovid, *Fasti* VI:
>
> “Martia—a name derived from Ancus the sacrificer.” LINDNER.
>
> [Col. 0334C] **“Buried.”** This is not an infinitive but the indicative perfect. HEUMANN.—In the Royal manuscript most paradigms of this kind are represented only by the abbreviation *er*, *obruer*; hence the abbreviated word *ere*, *obruere*, is commonly introduced in printed editions. EDD.
>
> **“Of a wicked and guilty man.”** That is, of a condemned combatant with beasts. Tertullian, *Apology*, chap. 9: “Look: in that most religious city of the pious descendants of Aeneas there is a Jupiter whom at his games they drench with human blood. ‘But it is the blood of a bestiary,’ you say. This, I suppose, is less than the blood of a man. Or is it more disgraceful because it is the blood of an evil man?” LINDNER.
>
> **“Bellona her sacred servant.”** So the exemplar reads. Minucius attributes to Bellona’s rite what Tertullian, *Apology*, had said of those consecrated to and serving Bellona. RIGALTIUS.—Salmasius, *Plinian Exercises*, p. 130, likewise retains the Royal manuscript’s reading and confirms that *sacrum* is used for “sacrifice.” I do not accept the very learned man’s opinion, since Minucius would have been guilty of ἀκυρολογία, “improper diction,” if he spoke in this way. For mention of the person who is initiated by drinking blood seems altogether necessary [Col. 0334D]. Here, therefore, *sacer* has the force of *sacratus*, “consecrated.” Virgil, *Aeneid* VI.484:
>
> “Polyboetes, sacred to Ceres.”
>
> On which Servius comments: “*Sacrum*, ‘consecrated’: a noun for a participle.” Prudentius, *Peristephanon*, Hymn XI.2:
>
> “We have seen you, Valerian, consecrated to Christ.”
>
> There is therefore no need to substitute either *servum* (“servant”) with Gelenius or *sacratum* (“consecrated”) with Heraldus. DAVIS.—**“Bellona her sacred rite by a draught.”** *Sacrum* comes from the manuscript; the common text has *servum*. But *sacrum* means “sacrifice,” and the entire cult of the savage goddess, whose celebrants bloodied their forearms and arms. Lucan, book I, v. 565:
>
> “Then those whom savage Bellona rouses by their slashed arms  
> prophesied of the gods.” CELLARIUS.—The remarks of a learned man in *Miscellaneous Observations*, vol. IV, tome II, p. 224, on Aelius Lampridius’s *Commodus*, chap. 9, deserve notice: “In his eagerness for cruelty he commanded those serving Bellona actually to cut their arms.” Casaubon says: “Observe the word ‘actually’; from it we learn that the wounds of Bellona’s devotees were generally only feigned and simulated.” It is clear from a thousand testimonies that the Bellonarii were accustomed truly to cut their arms. But they skillfully gave themselves slight wounds, as Seneca says in *On the Happy Life*, chap. 27. That monster compelled the wretched men to inflict deep wounds upon their bodies. LINDNER.
>
> **“Not unlike them.”** That is: “Not unlike these devotees of Bellona are those who,” etc. LINDNER.
>
> **“Nor hear.”** Delete this disgraceful addition. Minucius says: “For us it is unlawful even to see a killing”—that is, to see one at all. HEUMANN.—I read *audere* (“dare”). For Caecilius had accused Christians of being initiated through the killing of an infant. Octavius answers this slander by saying that a Christian is so far from daring to commit a killing that he thinks it unlawful even to see one. I could defend here the construction of *audere* with the accusative, were I not aware that every dictionary has already done so. I add only two passages. Lactantius, *Divine Institutes* VI.20.25: “If it is in no way permissible to commit homicide, neither is it at all permitted to be present at one.” The same author, *Epitome* (IV), LXIII.4: “But if to be present at homicide is complicity in crime, and the spectator is bound by the same guilt as the perpetrator, then at these gladiatorial slaughters the man who watches is no less drenched in blood than the man who does the deed.” LINDNER.
>
> **“Edible livestock.”** He calls livestock that may be eaten *edulia pecora*, just as Horace, *Satires* II.4.43, called roe deer *edules*, “edible.” Tertullian, *Apology*, chap. 9, calls them “edible meals,” and Pliny VIII.55, “edible animals.” HEUMANN.

**ARGUMENT.—** Octavius also proves utterly shameless the slander that Christians drink the blood of an infant whom they themselves have killed. Gentiles, however, he says, cruelly expose newborn children and, before they are born, kill them by cruel abortion. Christians are not permitted even to see or hear a killing.

I should now like to confront the man who says or believes that we are initiated through the slaughter and blood of an infant. Do you think it possible that so tender, so tiny a body could sustain fatal wounds? That anyone could slaughter, pour out, and drain the fresh blood of a newborn and scarcely human creature? No one can believe this unless he is capable of daring it.

For I see you now exposing the children you have begotten to wild beasts and birds, now strangling and crushing them to death by a miserable kind of death [Col. 0333B]. There are women who extinguish in their very wombs, by drugs and potions [Col. 0334A], the origin of the human being to come and commit parricide 45 before they give birth.

These practices assuredly descend from the teaching of your gods. Saturn did not expose his sons but devoured them. With good reason, therefore, in certain parts of Africa infants were sacrificed to him by their parents, while caresses and a kiss suppressed their wailing, lest a weeping victim be sacrificed. The Taurians of Pontus and the Egyptian Busiris likewise had a rite of sacrificing guests; and the Gauls slaughtered human—or rather inhuman—victims to Mercury. The Romans buried a Greek man and Greek woman, and a Gallic man and Gallic woman, alive as a sacrifice. Even today Jupiter Latiaris is worshiped by them through homicide and, in a manner worthy of Saturn’s son, is fattened on the blood of a wicked and guilty man.

It was he, I suppose, who taught Catiline to bind his conspiracy by a covenant of blood, and Bellona to initiate her consecrated servant [Col. 0334B] with a draught of human gore; and to cure epilepsy [Col. 0335A] with a man’s blood—that is, with a more grievous disease. Not unlike them are those who devour beasts from the arena, smeared and saturated with blood or fattened on human limbs and entrails. For us it is unlawful even to see or hear a killing; and we are so wary of human blood that we do not even regard the blood of edible livestock as food.

## CHAPTER XXXI

> **Note: [Col. 0335C]**
>
> **CHAP. XXXI—“Conspiracy.”** The manuscript has *cotio*. Minucius wrote *coitio*, that is, faction or conspiracy. HERALDUS.—The Roman edition, according to Heumann, has *concio* (“assembly”).
>
> [Col. 0335D] **“Deflection.”** I restore *adspersione*, or, as monks wrote it, *aspersione* (“bespattering”). Wower has already emended it thus. Cornelius Nepos, *Alcibiades*, chap. 3.6: “He was also bespattered with the infamy that,” etc. Cicero, *For Caelius*, chap. 10: “He was not bespattered even by suspicion of that deed, much less by infamy.” Similarly Curtius X.10.18: “Those whom rumor had bespattered.” Again Cicero, *Against Vatinius*, final chapter: “Lest any stain from your supreme unworthiness be spattered upon his dignity.” Jacob Gronovius, who thought Minucius had undoubtedly written *accessione* (“addition”), was undoubtedly mistaken. HEUMANN.—I agree with the very learned man. Someone wrote *aversione* because the verb *averteret* follows. But *aspersione* is preferable because the subsequent phrase is “as an orator, he bespattered.” LINDNER.
>
> **“By terror.”** I see that, if one attends to grammatical rules, Heumann rightly restores *terror*; whether he does so rightly if one attends to the author’s thought, I doubt. Minucius surely wrote *errore* (“by error”) and intended “the conspiracy of demons” to be repeated ἀπὸ κοινοῦ, “in common.” For the demons’ conspiracy turns men away from Christians through terror at the abominable opinion. By an equal right I can say [Col. 0336B]: “The cunning of demons turns men away from virtue through terror at its difficulty”; and: “Terror at difficulty turns men away from virtue.” LINDNER.
>
> **“Your Fronto.”** From the word “your,” Dallaeus sought to prove that Minucius was Fronto’s contemporary, against Bellarmine, who had maintained that Minucius was later than Tertullian. But that otherwise learned man is mistaken. For “your” signifies not merely a contemporary but also a fellow citizen, an adherent of the same religion, and one whom somebody cites as a witness to prove his opinion. LINDNER.—See the note above on chapter 9. EDD.
>
> **“Have arisen.”** Read *nota sunt*, “are well known.” HEUMANN.
>
> **“Among the Egyptians and at Athens.”** Read either “among the Egyptians and Athenians” or “in Egypt and at Athens.” LINDNER.
>
> **“Your records and tragedies glory in acts of incest.”** *Memoriae* are writings and books by which things are handed down to memory, or literary monuments, as above, chap. 7: “Examine the records in your books.” Gellius IV.6: “We read it written in ancient records.” The same author V.5, at the beginning: “It is written in books of ancient records.” Tertullian, *Against the Jews*, chap. 1: “According to the records of the divine Scriptures, the elder—that is, more ancient—Jewish people abandoned God and served idols.” There is therefore insufficient reason to substitute *comoediae* (“comedies”) with Fulvius Ursinus and Wower. CELLARIUS.
>
> **“With his mother.”** This refers to Jupiter, to whom Juno was both sister and wife, as Virgil says, *Aeneid* I.51. But that is well known; less well known is that this common king of the gods also had intercourse with his mother and daughter. The commentators are silent about this—not, I suppose, because the enormity of the crime has struck them speechless. We shall demonstrate what we have said by ancient testimonies. Clement of Alexandria, *Protrepticus*, p. 8D: Δηοῦς δὲ μυστήρια καὶ Διὸς πρὸς μητέρα Δήμητραν ἀφροδίσιοι συμπλυκαί, “The mysteries of Deo, and Zeus’s sexual embraces with his mother Demeter.” Athenagoras, *Plea for the Christians*, chap. 27: Χρῆν δ᾽ αὐτοὺς … τὸν Δία μεμισηκέναι ἐκ μητρὸς μὲν Ῥέας θυγατρὸς δὲ Κόρης πεπαιδοποιημένον, “They ought … to have hated Zeus, who fathered children by his mother Rhea and by his daughter Kore.” [Col. 0336D] The same author in chap. 16 mentions θυγατέρα τοῦ Διὸς ἣν ἐκ τῆς μητρὸς Ῥέας ἢ Δήμητρος ἐπαιδοποιήσατο, “a daughter of Zeus whom he begot by his mother Rhea or Demeter.” Arnobius also relates the matter at length in book V, p. 170 ff. DAVIS.
>
> **“You scatter promiscuously.”** So the manuscript reads both here and above in chap. 9; for the ancients said both *promiscus* and *promiscuus*. Gellius XI.16: “It deters us from varied and promiscuous thought”; II.24: “To distribute promiscuously and without limit”; and VI.14: “As it is commonly said.” CELLARIUS.
>
> **“While you even expose children born at home.”** By all means consult the highly learned jurist Gerard Noodt’s *Julius Paulus, or Commentary on Law IX of the Digest, Concerning the Acknowledgment and Support of Children*. GALLAND.—**“Born at home.”** Heraldus wrongly reads *dominatos*. LINDNER.
>
> **“Return among your own.”** Johannes Pricaeus, on Apuleius’s *Metamorphoses* VII, p. 379, substitutes *incurrere* (“run into”), and Jacob Ouzel followed him. But there is no need to listen to them. DAVIS.
>
> [Col. 0337B] **“Stray unwittingly among your sons.”** The very learned Jacob Perizonius prefers *in filias inerrare*, “stray among your daughters.” I do not agree, since *filii* denotes children of either sex. Tertullian, whom our author follows, *Apology*, chap. 9: “First of all, you expose your children.… The memory of an alienated family line must eventually be dispersed. And once error has caused a collision, thereafter the offshoot of incest will advance, as the family line creeps onward together with the crime.” Arnobius IV, p. 137, after speaking of Minerva’s birth from Jupiter’s head, adds: “He begets children conceived from his head.” Javolenus, *Digest* I, title XVI.84: “Under the designation ‘sons’ we understand all children.” Add Laws 116, 121, and 201. DAVIS.—Perizonius proposed *in filias inerrare*, “stray among your daughters,” while Davis defended the other reading because daughters are commonly included under the name “sons.” But Perizonius himself had already noted that very point on Sanctius, *Minerva* IV.10.5, as had many others. Since the matter is thus so commonplace, that celebrated scholar seems to have employed this emendation to give the sentence a more elegant variation, making Minucius refer *recurrere* to females and *inerrare* to males. Yet we have seen in chap. 1 and elsewhere that Minucius was by no means averse to the appearance of this kind of ταυτολογία, “repetition.” WOPKEN.—Unless I am greatly mistaken, our Minucius wrote: *Necesse est vos vestras incurrere in filias, in sorores*, “You must run into your own daughters and sisters.” Pricaeus had already restored *incurrere*, and Ouzel followed him, supporting Pricaeus’s emendation sufficiently by producing other authors who spoke in this way. HEUMANN.—Pricaeus ought not so violently to have introduced here the verb *incurrere*, used by others of lustful frenzy, because Minucius sometimes favors compounds such as *recurrere* even though the prefix’s meaning contributes nothing and wholly disappears, as above in *recognoscere*, and shortly afterward in *vera religio reservetur*. Elsewhere he has *refidamus*, where the expression is likewise strained and grating [Col. 0337D]. Here, however, the prefix’s full meaning is required, as though he said that while you drive away some of your blood in this fashion and retain others, these, ignorant of their kinship, form love affairs with one another; and Venus thus returns upon your own, overflows, and circles back among them. GRONOVIUS.
>
> **“Thus you weave the story of incest.”** He means the story of Oedipus, of whom Lactantius VI.20.23 says: “Who does not understand, who does not know, what may or commonly does happen to either sex through error? The example of Oedipus alone, confounded by a double crime, makes this clear.” He could have said “you enact the story,” but preferred “weave” because above, chap. 9, Caecilius had said: “The bonds of unspeakable lust entwine them.” Wower’s conjecture *fibulam nectitis*, “you fasten a clasp,” departs too far from the truth for us to assent to it. LINDNER.—The Lyon editor likewise strays in conjecturing *labem nacti estis*, “you have incurred a stain.” EDD.
>
> **“By the desire of procreation.”** So all editions and the Royal manuscript read. The sense, however, requires *cupiditatem*, “as regards the desire.” HERALDUS.—Jacob Gronovius rightly rejected Heraldus’s correction. John Davis printed *cupiditatem* in the text, but in his notes more correctly judged the manuscript reading sound. *Unam, nullam* (“one, none”) depend upon the understood word *mulierem* (“woman”) or something similar, just as in Ovid, *Art of Love* II.399:
>
> “While Atreus’s son was content with one, and she  
> Was chaste.”
>
> Plautus spoke more fully, *The Merchant* IV.6.8:
>
> “For a good wife is content with one man;  
> Why should a man be less content with one wife?” GRUNER.
>
> **“Disdainful.”** Almost all printed editions and the Royal manuscript have this. We nevertheless dare affirm that one must read *nec factiosi sumus*, “nor are we factious.” For Christians were accused especially on the ground that they entered into conspiracies and factions, a charge Caecilius had not omitted in chap. 8. Octavius now refutes that accusation in the same manner as Tertullian in the *Apology*, from which this material is taken, chap. 39: “We are the same when assembled as when dispersed; the same all together as individually,” etc. See our observations there. HERALDUS.
>
> **“We are of one mind concerning the good.”** Fulvius Ursinus rejects *bonum* (“the good”) as a gloss. CELLARIUS.—He repeated, that is, the words of Paul in Romans 15:5 and Philippians 2:2, τὸ αὐτὸ φρονεῖτε, “think the same thing,” rendered thus in the Old Latin version: *Idem sapiatis*, “Be of the same mind.” HEUMANN.
>
> **“Our number.”** I write *noster numerus*. HEUMANN.—There is no need. Thus chap. 32: “Shall I offer the Lord sacrifices and victims which he produced for my use?” Chap. 34: “See how all nature contemplates the future resurrection for our consolation.” LINDNER.
>
> **“In this way of life one of its own both excels and perseveres.”** I emend thus: *viventibus et perstat suus*, “among those living thus, one of their own persists.” Someone had explained τὸ *perstat* in the margin by *perseverat*. An “outsider” is one who was not yet a Christian. Now it is also clear who is called “one of their own.” HEUMANN.
>
> [Col. 0338D] **“Not by a bodily mark.”** So the books read, using an unusual word. Yet the old glosses have: “*NOTACULUM*: mark, sign.” The Roman book has *nota occulta*, “a secret mark,” as Caecilius said above, chap. 9: “They recognize one another by secret marks and tokens.” WOWER and CELLARIUS.
>
> **“By mutual love, which pains you.”** *Amore* should not, it seems, be removed. Horace, *Epodes* XV.10:
>
> “That this love would be mutual.”
>
> Terence: “The prostitute excluded the young man by whose mutual love she was held.” LINDNER.—The words of Terence which Lindner cites here are incorrectly assembled from an old lexicographer and are given only with a mark of doubt in Robert Estienne’s *Thesaurus*, under *MUTUUS*. EDD.
>
> **“As human beings under the one God as Father.”** Cast *Dei* (“of God”) into the margin, from which it was transferred into the text. HEUMANN.—Cellarius printed *omnes* (“all”), from what source I do not know. LINDNER.
>
> **“For parricide.”** Rigaltius interprets this, following Petronius’s Crito, of the destruction of a human being who exists in the seed; Heumann, of Romulus and Remus, Eteocles and Polynices. I approve the latter. LINDNER.

**ARGUMENT.—** The charge that Christians pollute their banquets with incest is as wholly removed from every appearance of truth as it is certain that the gentiles are themselves truly guilty of incest. Christian banquets are not merely chaste but also sober. Finally, they are so far from desiring incest that some are ashamed even of a chaste union.

[Col. 0335B] Concerning an incestuous banquet, moreover, the demons’ conspiracy [Col. 0336A] has fabricated an enormous tale against us, so that it might stain the glory of chastity by bespattering it with hideous infamy, and turn people away from us through terror at this abominable belief before the truth had been examined. Thus, concerning this matter, 46 even your Fronto bore witness not as one making an assertion but, as an orator, cast an insult upon us.

Such things have instead arisen among your own nations. Among the Persians it is lawful to unite with one’s mother; among the Egyptians and at Athens marriages with sisters are legitimate. Your records and tragedies glory in acts of incest, and you gladly both read and hear them. Thus too you worship incestuous gods joined with mother, daughter, and sister. With good reason, therefore, incest is often detected among you and always committed.

Even unknowingly, wretched people, you can rush into unlawful unions: while you scatter Venus promiscuously, while you sow children everywhere, and while you frequently expose even children born at home to another’s compassion [Col. 0336B], Venus must inevitably return among your own people [Col. 0337A] and stray among your children. Thus you weave the story of incest even when you have no consciousness of it.

Among us, modesty is displayed not merely in the face but in the mind. We gladly adhere to the bond of a single marriage; for the purpose of procreation, we know either one woman or none. The banquets we celebrate are not merely chaste but also sober. We neither indulge in feasts nor prolong the banquet with unmixed wine, but temper merriment with dignity, with chaste conversation and a still chaster body. Most enjoy rather than boast of the perpetual virginity of an inviolate body. Finally, the desire for incest is so far removed from us that some are ashamed even of a chaste union.

Nor do we consist solely of the lowest dregs of the people merely because we refuse your offices and purple robes. Nor are we disdainful [printed correction: “factious”] because, assembled together, we are of one mind concerning the good, with the same peace that we possess individually. Nor are we chatterers in corners merely because you are either ashamed or afraid to hear us publicly.

The daily increase of our number [Col. 0338A] is not proof of error but testimony to merit. For in a noble manner of life one of its own both excels and perseveres, while an outsider joins and increases it. Finally, we are readily recognized not by a bodily mark, as you suppose, but by the sign of innocence and modesty. Thus we love one another with mutual love—which pains you—because we do not know how to hate. Thus, to your envy, we call ourselves **BROTHERS**, as human beings under the one God as Father, as partners in faith, and as coheirs of hope. For you neither acknowledge one another nor cease raging in mutual hatreds; nor do you recognize yourselves as brothers except, indeed, for the purpose of parricide.

## CHAPTER XXXII

> **Note: [Col. 0339B]**
>
> **CHAP. XXXII—“I may dwell more widely.”** Heumann wishes to read *laxius habeam*, “I may have more spaciously,” an opinion he advanced in his *Critical Byworks*, published in 1712, p. 47, and in the new *Leipzig Miscellanies*, vol. VIII, part I, p. 127. But Davis and Wopken defend the manuscript reading which we have had printed.—For *latius* is used of things that are broad or extended, whether they are such through breadth properly so called or even through length, as Davis proves on Lactantius, *Epitome*, chap. 58, and Cicero, *On the Laws* II.1. Wopken proves *manere* in the sense “to dwell,” as do all dictionaries and the Greek μένω, which occurs in the same sense in John 1:38 and Matthew 10:11. But the strongest argument is drawn from Cyprian, Minucius’s epitomator, who writes in *On the Vanity of Idols*, chap. 5: “And although man dwells more widely.” LINDNER.
>
> **“Within.”** Cellarius incorrectly prints *inter*, “among.” LINDNER.
>
> **“Indeed, in our.”** Heumann, who understood *immo* as “innermost,” deletes *nostro*. I take it as an adverb and am confirmed in my conjecture by the authority of the Roman edition, which gives *immo*. LINDNER.
>
> **“Victims … with an uncorrupted conscience.”** Jacob Gronovius did not understand Minucius’s meaning and wrote the following on these words: “He plainly alludes to Paul’s words in 1 Timothy 4:4: οὐδὲν ἀπόβλητον μετ᾽ εὐχαριστίας λαμβανόμενον, ‘nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving.’ Here *rejicere* does not mean ‘disapprove’ but must be taken in its proper sense, ‘throw back’ or ‘return.’ For to offer sacrifices and victims to God is the same as wishing thoughtlessly to return to him what he himself gave us. This, however, is ungrateful, because God gave us animals so that we might use them to the glory of his name, not misuse them to his dishonor—as those certainly do who suppose that God needs victims and can be appeased by their slaughter.” GRUNER.—Heumann rejects *ingratum est*, “it is ungrateful,” as a manifest gloss. LINDNER.
>
> **“Since it is a propitiatory victim.”** Lactantius also uses *victima litabilis* in *Divine Institutes* I.21, that is, a victim pleasing and acceptable to God; and in the *Epitome*, chap. 5, *victima litabilior*, “a more propitiatory victim.” CELLARIUS.—Cellarius is right as to the meaning, but not as to the force of the word. A *litabilis hostia* is a victim by which God can be propitiated. For *litare*, a pontifical term, means “to have appeased the divinity by offering sacrifice,” as Macrobius says in *Saturnalia* III.5. Add Servius on Virgil, *Aeneid* II.118. Minucius appears to have Psalm 50:18–19 in view. GRUNER.
>
> **“An uncorrupted judgment.”** The Roman edition has *conscientia*, “conscience.” WOWER.
>
> **“Justice.”** Heraldus incorrectly prints *injustitiam*, “injustice.” LINDNER.
>
> **“The best victim.”** Isaac Vossius, on Mela III.2, emended this to *optimam victimam* (“the best victim”), as Heraldus also printed it. LINDNER.—But one must by all means adhere to the alternative reading. For in the preceding clauses, “to supplicate,” “to pour a libation,” [Col. 0340B] and “to propitiate” mean doing fully and perfectly what was done imperfectly by literal supplications and the like; *opimam victimam caedere*, “to slaughter a choice victim,” must therefore be understood in precisely the same manner. And who does not know that choice victims were commonly regarded as most pleasing to God? Lactantius VI.2: “They therefore slaughter the finest and fattest victims for God, as though he were hungry.” WOPKEN.—By a similar error, Lactantius, *Epitome* 25.7, used to be read: “Can the man who slaughters the finest victims for such beings be thought to be in his right mind?” But Pfaff, Davis, and Bünemann vindicate *opimas*, “choice,” in that passage. LINDNER.
>
> **“Before the eyes.”** Read *sub oculos*, “before one’s eyes.” Seneca, *On Benefits* I.5: “A benefit is not that which comes before the eyes.” Lactantius III.9.12: “Nor do they see more than what comes before their eyes.” The same author, VII.9.2, uses the same argument as our Minucius and at the same time—even the same distinction, as I believe may perhaps have happened: “God,” he says, “does many things whose force is apparent although their substance is not seen, as with the voice, scent, and wind; so that by the proof and example of these things we might perceive God also from his power, effect, and works, even though he did not come before our eyes.” HEUMANN.—Add the same author VII.1.9; chap. 9.27; chap. 11.9. LINDNER.

In the sun. So the manuscript. Heumann wishes the preposition deleted and accepts Gelenius’ emendation, who rewrote it as *the sun*. But Gifanius noted in his *Index to Lucretius* that this preposition is joined indiscriminately either with the accusative or with the ablative. Horace, *Satires* I, Satire 3, 26:

> Why are you so sharp-sighted toward the faults of friends?  
> —LINDNER.

To see. Thus the Roman edition and the manuscript, and so Heraldus printed it.

[Col. 0340D] What? the very. The Roman edition has *What the very*, without an intervening question mark. I now rewrite it thus: *How [qui] the very* (that is, *in what manner*). Thus below, chapter 36: “How [qui] can one be poor who lacks nothing?” (the manuscript has *quis*).  
—HEUMANN.

Flashes. Write *lightning-flashes [fulguribus]*. He is accustomed to join *fulgura* and *fulmina*. Thus above: “Lightning gleams red; thunderbolts flash forth.” And afterward: “Since the sky, thunderbolts, and lightning-flashes existed long before Jupiter was born in Crete.”  
—MEURSIUS.

Take care not to change anything. Cicero, *On Divination* II, chapter 19: “Then both flashes and thunder arise.” For this is how the passage should be read from the Cambridge and Victorian manuscripts, not *lightning*, as in the common editions. Again, in chapter 39, where he interprets a verse from the *Iliad*, line 236. Lucretius VI, 755:

> Thus too we see the flash before  
> We hear the thunder.

Ovid, *Metamorphoses* VII, 619:

> He gave the appointed sign by a flash and then by thunder.

See Aurelius Victor, chapters 14 and 23.  
—DAVIS.

[Col. 0341B] Nor grasp. Davisius, failing to see how *grasp* was relevant, read *discern*; another learned man, in the *Leipzig Acts* for October 1733, read *behold*. Tacitus indeed uses such a construction in *Agricola* 40: “When Agricola had been seen and beheld”; and chapter 45: “The chief part of our miseries under Domitian was to be seen and observed.” Colerus there attacked this construction without justification. But I do not think *grasp*, in the sense of *comprehend*, should be disturbed here. Ambrose, *Duties* I, 29: “And they saw Elisha, whom they were eager to seize, yet although they saw him, they could not grasp him.” In this way *grasp* is customarily joined with the verb *see*. Paulinus of Nola, Letter XVIII, 1: “So that … we might enjoy some share of your grace, seeing and grasping him whom faith in the truth has approved.” [Col. 0341C] Paulinus of Périgueux, *Life of Martin* VI, 4:

> Surviving your flesh without flesh,  
> You are discerned, sought, touched, and grasped.

Novatian, *On the Trinity*, chapter 11: “For no blindness of heretics will prejudice the truth; nor, because they grasp something in Christ and do not grasp something else, see the one and do not see the other, will that which they do not see be wrested from us by that which they see.” Here what was first signified by the verbs *seeing* and *grasping* is afterward comprehended under the single verb *seeing*, since the two ideas plainly did not differ greatly. A learned man in *Miscellaneous Observations*, 1732, vol. I, p. 32, also vindicates *grasp* for this passage, because *grasp* in our author appears to mean the same as *touch* in Lactantius, *On the Blessed Life*: “The soul is immortal for this reason, because it can neither be touched nor seen.”  
—WOPKEN.

Known to God and filled with God. Those who emended this to “all things are filled with God,” or “all things are fully known to God,” appear to have been offended because the same word *God [Deo]* depends in such different ways upon the adjectives *known* and *filled*, being understood as an ablative with the latter and a dative with the former [Col. 0341D]. But this construction is sufficiently common. Thus chapter 26: “burdened with and immersed in vices”; chapter 36: “who lacks nothing, who does not covet another’s property.” Arnobius I, p. 25: “It would have been fitting and worthy of God.” Pliny VII, Letter 26: “Nor indeed does he attend to or nourish himself upon malicious conversation.” Lactantius, *On the Anger of God*, chapter 4: “What is so worthy of and so proper to God as providence?” Anonymous *Panegyric* VIII, 22: “So that they may promise things worthy of and near the stars and heaven.” Ausonius, *Thanksgiving*, chapter 3: “Not ungrateful for his benefits, but overwhelmed by them.” Ambrose, *Duties* I, 21: “We ought not merely to believe in intercessions, but also to delight in them.” Hegesippus I, 34: “We do not see virtues, but delight in them.” Boethius, *Consolation of Philosophy* I, 1: “They accustom human minds to illness but do not free them from it”; and III, 4: “So that they may implant virtues in the minds of those who use them and expel vices.” Dictys of Crete V, 8: “That he was neither moved by these things nor indignant at them.” I knowingly omit many more examples.  
—WOPKEN.

For the brightness. Gronovius thinks the author wrote *its brightness*.  
—LINDNER.

From whom no secret can be kept. Heumann believes these to be the true words of Minucius: “How much more does God, the author and observer of all things, [Col. 0342B] from whom nothing can be hidden by any darkness” (that is, separated from him), “enter into our thoughts.” I change nothing. God enters into darkness without any diminution of his brightness.  
—LINDNER.

But also with him. Thus the manuscript. I, however, am persuaded that Minucius wrote *but with him*, which I also find in the Roman edition.  
—HEUMANN.

I change nothing; chapter 4: “Even in peace wickedness is not only placed on an equality with better men, but is also honored.” Chapter 31: “We maintain banquets that are not merely chaste, but also sober.” Ovid, *Metamorphoses* IV, 330:

> He does not know what love is; but it was also fitting that he blushed.  
> —LINDNER.

[Col. 0342C] So to speak, almost. Wopkenius defends this manuscript reading in *Miscellaneous Critical Observations*, vol. X, book I, p. 48, though he afterward prefers to read *so to speak, properly*. But, for my part, that most learned man has persuaded me of neither reading.  
—HEUMANN.]

**SUMMARY.—** Nor can it be said that Christians conceal what they worship because they have no shrines or altars [Col. 0338B]. For they are persuaded that God cannot be confined within any temple, nor can an image of him be fashioned. [Col. 0339A] Present everywhere, however, he sees all things, even the more secret thoughts of our minds; and we live almost with him and in his bosom.

**(XXVI)** Do you suppose that we conceal what we worship because we have no shrines and altars? For what image shall I fashion for God, when, if you judge rightly, man himself is God’s image? What temple shall I erect for him, when this entire world, constructed by his work, cannot contain him? And when I, a human being, dwell more spaciously, shall I enclose the power of such majesty within one little building? Is he not better dedicated in our mind—indeed, consecrated in the innermost part of our breast? Shall I offer to the Lord sacrificial animals and victims which he has brought forth for my use, so that I may cast his own gift back to him? That would be ingratitude, since an acceptable victim is a good disposition, a pure mind, and a sincere judgment. [Col. 0339B] Therefore, [p. 48] he who cultivates innocence makes supplication to the Lord; he who cultivates justice pours a libation to God; he who abstains from fraud [Col. 0340A] propitiates God; he who rescues a person from danger slaughters the choicest victim. These are our sacrifices; these are God’s sacred rites. Thus among us the more religious man is the more just.

But, you say, we neither display nor see the God whom we worship. On the contrary, we believe him to be God precisely because we can perceive him but cannot see him. For in his works and in all the movements of the world we behold his power continually present: when it thunders, flashes, and hurls thunderbolts; when it becomes serene. Do not be surprised that you do not see God: everything is driven, shaken, and agitated by wind and gusts, yet neither wind nor gust comes before the eyes. Even in the sun, which is the cause of sight for everyone, we cannot see: its rays drive back our vision, the gaze of one looking at it is dulled, and if you look longer, all sight is extinguished. [Col. 0340B] What, then? Could you endure the very maker of the sun, that fountain of light, when you turn away from his flashes and hide from his thunderbolts? Do you wish to see God with [Col. 0341A] fleshly eyes when you cannot behold or grasp even your own soul, by which you are given life and speech?

**(XVII)** But, you say, God is ignorant of human conduct and, being stationed in heaven, can neither visit everyone nor know individuals. You err, human being, and are deceived. For how is God far away, when all things in heaven and on earth, and those beyond this province of the world, are known to God and filled with God? Everywhere he is not merely very near us but infused within all things. Consider the sun once again: fixed in heaven, it is nevertheless diffused over every land; equally present everywhere, [p. 49] it enters into and mingles with everything, yet its brightness is nowhere impaired. How much more does God, the author and observer of all things, from whom no secret can be kept, enter into darkness and enter into our thoughts, which are like a second darkness. We do not merely act [Col. 0341B] beneath him; we live also with him, so to speak, almost.

# CHAPTER XXXIII

[Col. 0342A] [Note: [Col. 0342C]

**CHAPTER XXXIII.—Flatter ourselves.** Here, if nowhere else, one may see how full of hazard is the task of emending ancient authors. Cellarius had noted at these words: “He answers the objections of chapter 9.” Since the distinguished Heumann believed this and emended the text to “we flatter ourselves: we seem numerous to you,” he suffered a human lapse. For the author is not referring to the passage cited by Cellarius, but to chapter 10, where Caecilius had attacked divine providence with an argument drawn from the frequency and multitude of human beings. It is exactly like the man in Juvenal, Satire 13:

> If they are therefore concerned to punish every guilty man,  
> When will they reach me?

Octavius now replies that human beings have no reason to flatter themselves about their great numbers, and so forth. For he already answered chapter 9 [Col. 0342D] in chapter 31. Compare, if desired, the *Arrangement of This Dialogue* prefixed to this edition.  
—LINDNER.

Kings only. Johannes Meursius emended this to: “Kings know the condition of their kingdom through the various duties of their ministers.” But the learned man departed from the manuscript reading because he did not understand its construction (*syntaxis*, σύνταξις), which will be sufficiently clear if the sentence is punctuated thus: “Kings alone know all that pertains to their kingdom through the duties of their ministers.” He said “all things of their kingdom” for “all the affairs of their kingdom,” or “their entire kingdom,” as in “the shaded parts of the roads,” “the expanses of the fields,” and similar expressions. Tacitus, *Histories* III, 4: “They looked to the foremost measures for peace”; and V, 10: “He held all the plains … with his victorious army.” So frequently elsewhere.  
—DAVIS.

I agree with the learned man. For only kings—because, distracted among all things, they cannot attend to individuals, and, occupied with individuals, cannot meet the needs of all—know everything in their kingdom through the duties of ministers. God, however, has no need of informants.  
—LINDNER.

Informants. Understand “of others.”  
—HEUMANN.

There is no need. For *indicium* is used substantivally for *index*, “an informer.” Lactantius, *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* VIII, 4: “There was no lack of very wealthy [Col. 0343B] senators who, after informers had been secretly suborned, were accused of having aspired to imperial power.”  
—LINDNER.

So long as they worshiped him chastely…. According to Meursius, the manuscript presents “for so long then chastely.” I think it should be read: “so long as they worshiped him chastely….” For authors customarily insert pronouns of this kind after a parenthesis (*parenthesis*, παρένθεσις). Cicero, *Academica* IV, chapter 7: “But if the conceptions were false” (for you seemed to call concepts [ἐννοίας] “conceptions”), “if, therefore, these were false.” The same author, *On Fate*, chapter 16. So also Caesar, *Gallic War* III, chapter 22. J. F. Gronovius collected many passages of the ancients concerning this usage in his notes on Livy XXV, 27, and Seneca, *On Anger* I, 3.  
—DAVIS.

And with the elements. A comma has been placed most wrongly after *command* in every edition I have seen, and thus it has not been possible to recognize that *and* means *also*. Read: “at God’s command, with even the elements striving in their support.” Among other things, our author has in view the history of Joshua, who obtained the sun and moon, and even rainstorms and hailstones, as though they were [Col. 0343C] auxiliary forces. In place of *overwhelmed*, which hardly suits this passage, I would write *defeated*. Nor does *striving in their support* quite satisfy me. Did Minucius perhaps write *assisting* or *fighting alongside them*?  
—HEUMANN.

*Overwhelmed* is well said of the few, since Virgil, *Aeneid* II, 424, said of the many, “We are overwhelmed by their number”; and Ovid, *Fasti* I, 488:

> That storm overwhelmed mighty men.  
> —LINDNER.

Flavius Josephus, or Antonius Julianus. The manuscript reads *Flavi Josaepi*, and the scraped surface of the parchment shows that *Antoninus Julianus* had been written.  
—RIGALT.

Apart from our author, no one mentions an Antonius Julianus as a writer on Jewish affairs. Aulus Gellius does several times mention a rhetorician of that name in *Attic Nights* I, 4, and IX, 1 and 15. But whether that man was or was not different from the one in Minucius is unclear to me and immaterial to our present purpose. The point of somewhat greater importance to antiquarians (*philarchaioi*, φιλαρχαίοις) arises when we ask how Flavius Josephus came to be mentioned here. For our author sets Jews in opposition to Romans “from the contrary side” (*ex enantias*, ἐξ ἐναντίας) [Col. 0343D]. Accordingly, although Josephus had been granted Roman citizenship, it seems entirely inappropriate for him to be cited here, since he was a Jew both by nationality and religion. Moreover, Josephus wrote in Greek, and his works had not yet assumed Roman dress in the time of Minucius. See Jerome, Letter XXVIII to Lucinius, Victor’s edition, and Cassiodorus, *Divine Readings*, chapter XVII. I would therefore read the passage thus: “Read their writings again; or, if you take greater pleasure in Roman writers, let us pass over the ancients and consult Antonius Julianus concerning the Jews.” Unless I am mistaken, the name of Flavius Josephus invaded the body of the discourse after a copyist had inserted it in the margin of his manuscript. This happened because Josephus was a very celebrated author and treated the same subject as Julianus.  
—DAVIS.

Lindner proposes rearranging the words thus: “Read again, so that we may pass over the ancients, either Flavius Josephus; or, if you take greater pleasure in Roman writers, Antoninus Julianus.”  
—EDITORS.

Here I read “without hesitation.”  
—HEUMANN.

You will understand. There is no reason for us to hesitate to read *you will discover*.  
—HEUMANN.

[Col. 0344B] Captured with their God. Rigaltius alone reads thus, and several later editors follow him, although he offers not one word to explain why he omitted *to have been*, which is found in Sabaeus, Wowerus, Heraldus, and even Cellarius, who present “to have been captured with their God.” I mention this so that the truth may be investigated.  
—GRONOVIUS.

False.  
—EDITORS.]

**SUMMARY.—** But if it is nevertheless said that God was of no benefit to the Jews, the writers of Jewish annals are certainly most trustworthy witnesses that the Jews first deserted God before they were themselves deserted by him.

Nor should we flatter ourselves because of our numbers: we seem numerous to ourselves, but to God we are very few. We distinguish peoples and nations; to God this entire world is one household. Kings alone know all that pertains to their kingdom through the duties of their ministers; God has no need of informants: we live not merely under his eyes but also in his bosom.

But, you say, it did the Jews no good that they too worshiped one God with the greatest superstition, at altars and temples. You slip into ignorance if, forgetful or unaware of earlier [Col. 0342B] events, you remember only the later. For they too worshiped our God [Col. 0343A]—for the same God belongs to everyone. So long as they worshiped him chastely, innocently, and religiously, so long as they obeyed his salutary commands, they grew from a few into a countless people, from needy men into the rich, from servants into kings. Though few, they overwhelmed many; though unarmed, they overwhelmed the armed men pursuing them as they fled, at God’s command and with even the elements striving in their support. Read their writings again; or, if you take greater pleasure in Roman authors, let us pass over the ancients and consult Flavius Josephus or Antoninus Julianus concerning the Jews. Then you will know that by their own wickedness they deserved this fate, and that nothing happened to them which had not [p. 50] previously been foretold should they persist in their obstinacy. Thus you will understand that they deserted God before they were deserted by him, and that they were not, as you impiously say, captured with their God, but were surrendered by God as deserters from his discipline.

# CHAPTER XXXIV

[Col. 0344A] [Note: [Col. 0344B]

**CHAPTER XXXIV.—Or difficult not to believe.** That is, “to believe with difficulty or not at all.” The distinguished Gruner explains it in almost the same way, except that he reads “either difficult or not to believe.” I, however, would merely transpose the words: “difficult or not.” Thus chapter 12: “And God endures it, disregards it, (or) either does not wish or is unable to assist his own.” In this way, I think, the least violence is done to the manuscript, which reads: “or difficult not to believe.” We could also read “that it is difficult,” but the former reading is preferable. Some editions have: “Either that an unforeseen fire should fall, or to believe it difficult.” Rigaltius thinks the true reading can be restored thus: “either to believe that an unforeseen fire should fall, or that it is difficult for it not to fall.” Boxhorn [Col. 0344C] finds it far more pleasing if it is rewritten: “Either that an unforeseen fire should fall, or not to believe that it is sufficient.” Gronovius restores: “Either that an unforeseen fire should fall or burst apart.” Wopken thinks the author wrote with less constraint: “But for you to find it difficult or impossible to believe that conflagrations of the world or an unforeseen fire will fall is a common error.” In Heumann’s judgment the words of Minucius are: “But not to believe in the world’s conflagration is a common error.”  
—LINDNER.

Who does not know? Under Heumann’s hypothesis, by which he expels “or difficult,” these words also had to be deleted. He who doubts believes with difficulty; he who does not know does not believe.  
—LINDNER.

As to have begun. Thus the manuscript, for which the Roman edition rewrote *had begun*, although it should be rewritten *began to exist*.  
—HEUMANN.

The fresh water of springs to nourish the seas, destined to pass into the force of fire. An old copy has suggested to us a splendid emendation of this formerly very corrupt passage. For it reads exactly thus: “The fresh water of springs to nourish the seas, destined to pass into the force of fire.” This reading must be understood as follows: “that the act of nourishing is destined to pass into the force of fire” is an established Stoic opinion. But the words that follow—“that, once the moisture has been consumed, this entire world catches fire”—are superfluous and savor of a note carried over from the margin. They say nothing other than what was already stated more elegantly: “the fresh waters of springs nourish the seas, destined to pass into the force of fire”; that is, the seas will no longer nourish the springs with fresh waters, but that nourishment will pass [Col. 0344D] into the force of fire: that sustenance will be transformed into flames, and torrents of fire will boil up from the source of the springs.  
—RIGALT.

Gelenius printed “to be nourished by the fresh water of springs, or by the sea”; Cellarius did not differ. But, as it seems to me, Nicolaus Rigaltius made an elegant emendation from the Royal manuscript. It is certainly not rare for an infinitive to be used as a noun. Aulus Gellius, *Attic Nights* I, chapter 8: “I do not purchase the act of repenting at so high a price.” Arnobius II, p. 27: “Not knowing what the very act of fearing is.” So too Sulpicius Severus, *Sacred History* II, chapter 3.

I think it should further be noted that this passage still suffers from defective punctuation. Since [Col. 0345A] Nicolaus Rigaltius did not notice this, he wrongly [Col. 0345B] expelled seven words as a gloss. Punctuate: “The fresh waters of springs—the seas’ act of nourishing destined to pass into the force of fire?” For these words depend upon what precedes. The author then continues: “It is an established Stoic opinion that, once the moisture has been consumed, this entire world catches fire.” These are nearly the words of Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* II, 46: “From this our philosophers think that what Panaetius, they used to say, doubted will occur: that in the end the entire world will catch fire, since, once the moisture has been consumed, the earth could no longer be nourished, nor could the air return, whose origin could not exist once all water had been exhausted.” The same author, III, 14: “What then? Do you not also hold that every fire needs sustenance and cannot possibly continue unless it is nourished? And that the sun, moon, and remaining stars are nourished, some by fresh waters and others by seawater?” Lucretius I, 231:

> Whence do the sea, its native springs, and rivers flowing  
> Far away maintain their supply? Whence does the ether feed the stars?

There are therefore three things about which no wise man doubts: first, that all things—and heaven foremost among them—began; [Col. 0345C] second, that they will sometime cease; and third, that meanwhile they are nourished. The hinge of the entire argument also turns upon these three divisions. Heaven began; therefore God exists. Heaven will cease; therefore there is an end of the world and punishment after death. Heaven is nourished; therefore providence exists.  
—DAVIS, RIGALTIUS.

Boxhorn, whose words are quoted by Ouzelius, reads: “the fresh waters of springs nourish the seas,” etc. Gronovius reads: “of springs, of fresh water, the sea’s nourishment into force,” etc. Heumann, rejecting the words “passes into the force of fire,” reads: “that it” (that is, heaven) “is nourished by the fresh water of springs or by the sea is established among the Stoics,” etc.  
—LINDNER.

Plato speaks. He says that portions of the world are now flooded. The passage must be punctuated thus if this ancient reading seems worth retaining. For the rest, I would rather preserve the familiar form of expression well known in Minucius, removing the useless verb *says*, as follows: “Plato speaks of portions of the world now being flooded and, at alternating intervals, catching fire.”  
—RIGALT.

The remedy will be milder if, with the addition of a connective particle [Col. 0345D], we read: “Plato speaks, and says that portions of the world are now flooded.” Cyprian, *On the Unity of the Church*: “Divine Scripture speaks and says.” Jerome, *Against Vigilantius*, vol. IV, col. 288: “Concerning which you argue and say.” The ancient ecclesiastical writers frequently use the same construction.  
—DAVIS.

It is much more probable, however, that *speaks* slipped into the text and must accordingly be expelled. I now change “and says” into *teaches*, with all the more confidence because “would say” follows shortly afterward. For it is not credible that a writer so devoted to elegance used the same verb twice in the same sentence. Finally, following Wopken in *Miscellaneous Critical Observations*, vol. X, book I, p. 49, I write *to be flooded* in place of *to flood*.  
—HEUMANN.

To God alone. I rewrite this as *to the maker alone*, relegating “to God himself” to the margin.  
—HEUMANN.

To God alone, both dissoluble and to be mortal. Transpose one word and read: “to God alone both to be dissoluble and mortal.”  
—DAVIS.

And to be mortal. The manuscript has “and to be mortal.” Wopkenius defends this reading.  
—LINDNER.

By him by whom. Heumann defends this reading in *Tullian Readings* I, chapter 1, p. 4, [Col. 0346A] teaching by many examples that the second *by* is not infrequently omitted [Col. 0346B] by the best authors.  
—HEUMANN.

What we say. I read: “What we teach, we do not….” Lactantius VII, 25, 1: “So that I might teach that the truth which they refuse to acknowledge is held under seal not only among us, but even among those very men who persecute us.”  
—HEUMANN.

To distort. That is, to obscure or divert. Pythagoras handed down the doctrine of resurrection, but of the soul alone and not also of the body, and thus with a halved faith; but so that the truth might be distorted still further, he adds that human souls return into animals, when he should have said that they return into their own bodies. Heumann thinks Minucius wrote: “They also add, in order to turn savagery back, that human souls return into beasts, birds, and wild animals.” “To turn savagery back” means to transfer savagery into gentleness, as Cicero speaks in *For Sestius*, chapter 42.  
—LINDNER.

That opinion is worthy of a mime’s vice. Thus the exemplar. “A mime’s vice” means “in the manner of a mime,” namely, seeking laughter from every possible source. Minucius, from Christian austerity, calls this manner a vice and contrasts the mime’s vice with a philosopher’s study. What is found in some [Col. 0346C] editions, “the abuse of a mime,” might appear to answer “a philosopher’s study” more aptly. But Minucius rightly says that the opinion that human souls will return into the bodies of cattle and beasts is worthy of a mime’s vice. For among the other vices of the mimetic art, surely this is the most disgraceful: mimes often assume the forms of cattle and beasts. Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 48: “There will also be need of many idle jests if we wish to be wanton on this subject: who might appear to be transformed into which beast.”  
—RIGALT.

Rigaltius labors in vain when he strives to vindicate this reading for Minucius. The entirely true reading is “the abuse of a mime,” which is presented by the Roman edition, Elmenhorstius, Wowerus, and Cellarius, and approved by Jacob Gronovius. Minucius means that the opinion concerning the transmigration of souls is unworthy of a philosopher’s serious reflection, but so ridiculous that it could provide even a theatrical mime with material for entertaining people. Elmenhorstius appropriately cited here Lactantius VII, 12: “The opinion of a madman was ridiculous, more worthy of a mime than of a school.” [Col. 0346D] The word *abuse* will seem extremely appropriate here if you read Manucius’ observation on Cicero, *Letters to Friends* IX, 16: “Now I come to your jests, since, following Accius’ *Oenomaus*, you introduced not, as was formerly customary, an Atellan farce, but, as is now done, a mime.”  
—GRUNER.

Critics long ago saw that Minucius wrote “the jeering of a mime.” They are aided by the Roman edition, which, according to Heraldus, has “hostile vice,” but according to Wowerus “a mime’s jeering.” On this word see the observations of philologists on Phaedrus I, 6, 5. Add Ovid, *Metamorphoses* V, 675, and Cicero, *Letters to Quintus* II, Letter 1, where jeering is contrasted with silence, as it also is in *For Archias*, chapter 6. The same author, *Letters to Friends* I, Letter 5: “When Pompey spoke for Milo, he was assailed by shouting and jeering.” And *Against Verres* V: “The banquets were conducted not with that silence … nor with that modesty … but with the greatest shouting and jeering.” You see that in Minucius “a mime’s jeering” does not mean serious insults but mockery and ridicule, customarily delivered with loud shouting. Hear [Col. 0347B] Lactantius speaking similarly in VII, 12, 31: “Since this opinion of a madman was ridiculous and more worthy of a mime than of a school, it did not even deserve a serious refutation.”  
—HEUMANN.

As at first to have been capable of being fashioned. Wowerus [Col. 0347C] substituted “as at first he could be fashioned” entirely in vain, as we observed earlier in the *Tullian Readings*. A similar infinitive appears just above: “Who does not know that heaven, just as to have begun, will cease?” in place of “as it began”; chapter 33: “Thus you will understand that they deserted him before themselves to have been deserted,” that is, “before they were deserted.” Orosius III, 2: “Whoever does not know that these peoples now grow old in theaters just as they then to have wasted away in military camps.” See V, 1, and frequently elsewhere.  
—WOPKEN.

To be nothing after death … to have been nothing. Heumann expels these words, evidently to free the author from the error of which Dupin accuses him in his *Ecclesiastical Library*: maintaining that souls die together with the body. If this is the true method of vindicating the Fathers from the stain of error, there is hope that the Fathers will shortly appear immune from every error. It is manifest that Minucius speaks of the body alone. God first fashioned it and will form it anew. What is being born from nothing other than having been nothing before one’s origin? And what is restoration from nothing after [Col. 0347D] death other than being nothing after death? I detect no error here. He speaks in the same manner as our Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 48: “Consider again what you were before you existed: certainly nothing, for you would have remembered if you had been anything. You, therefore, who were nothing before you existed, after becoming that same nothing when you have ceased to exist—why could you not exist again from nothing by the will of that same author who willed you to exist from nothing?” etc.  
—LINDNER.

Every body. Wopkenius is eager to rewrite it as “the body altogether” in *Tullian Readings* I, chapter 11, p. 65. For my part, I do not subscribe to his view.  
—HEUMANN.

Keeping. This comes from Wowerus’ emendation. Heraldus undoubtedly printed *keeping-place* from the manuscript.  
—LINDNER.

The sun sinks. I read: “The sun sinks itself.”  
—HEUMANN.

In the age. You will readily believe me, I think, that it must be rewritten “in the grave.”  
—HEUMANN.

In the wintry. That is, “season.” More fully, Caesar, *Alexandrian War*, chapter 43: “in the wintry season of the year.” Heumann prefers to write “like wintry trees.”  
—LINDNER.

[Col. 0348B] With feigned dryness. The dryness of trees in winter is not real but merely feigned, because their greenness is not wholly absent but only concealed. In full: “As trees in the wintry season conceal their greenness with feigned dryness, so the body in the grave conceals life with feigned mortality.” [Col. 0348C] Heumann believes that Minucius wrote: “Thus the body is concealed in the grave like wintry trees, with greenness destined to follow dryness.”  
—LINDNER.

The more delayed the judgment. Here *more* [magis] should be understood, not, against the author’s will, written into the text with Heumann. Tacitus, *Annals* III, chapter 46: “The more wealthy in money and rich in pleasures”—the words “the more cowardly” must be supplied—“defeat the Aedui.”  
—LINDNER.]

**SUMMARY.—** There is nothing astonishing if this world is finally to be consumed by fire, since all things that have a beginning also have an end. Nor do the ancient philosophers dissent from the doctrine of a conflagration of the world. It is nevertheless certain that God can raise from death to life the human being whom he fashioned from nothing. All nature, moreover, rehearses the resurrection to come.

But regarding the conflagration of the world, to believe either that an unforeseen fire will fall, or to find it difficult not to believe this, is a common error. For which of the wise doubts, who does not know, that all things which have arisen perish, and that things which were made pass away? That heaven too, together with everything contained in heaven, will cease just as it began? That the fresh water [Col. 0345A] of springs nourishes the seas, which nourishment is destined to pass into the force of fire? It is an established Stoic opinion that, once the moisture has been consumed, this entire world catches fire; and the Epicureans hold precisely the same opinion concerning the conflagration of the elements and the destruction of the world. Plato speaks of portions of the world now being flooded and says that, at alternating intervals, they now catch fire; and although he said that the world itself had been fashioned eternal and indissoluble, he nevertheless adds that to its own maker, God alone, it is both dissoluble and mortal. Thus there is nothing astonishing if that mass is destroyed by him by whom it was constructed.

You observe that the philosophers argue [Col. 0346A] the same things that we say—not because we have followed in their footsteps, but because, from the divine proclamations of the prophets, they imitated the shadow of a corrupted truth. Thus also the more renowned of the wise—Pythagoras first, and Plato chiefly—handed down, with a corrupted and halved faith, the condition of being born again. For, once bodies have been dissolved, they hold that souls alone both remain perpetually and repeatedly pass into other, [p. 51] new bodies. To these doctrines they add the following in order to distort the truth: that human souls return into cattle, birds, and wild beasts. This opinion is worthy not of a philosopher’s study but of a mime’s vice.

Yet [Col. 0347A] for the present purpose it is enough that your wise men agree with us to some degree even on this point. Besides, who is so foolish or brutish as to dare deny that, just as a human being could at first be fashioned by God, so he can be formed anew? That he is nothing after death and was nothing before birth? That just as it was possible to be born from nothing, so it is possible to be born anew and restored from nothing? Furthermore, it is more difficult for that which does not exist to begin than for that which once existed to be repeated.

Do you believe that anything perishes even for God if it is withdrawn from our dull eyes? Every body—whether it dries into dust, is dissolved into moisture, compressed into ashes, or attenuated into vapor—is withdrawn from us, but is reserved for God in the keeping of the elements. Nor, as you believe, do we fear any injury from burial; rather, we follow the ancient and better custom of interment.

Consider [Col. 0347B], then, how all nature, for our consolation, rehearses the resurrection to come. The sun sinks and rises; the stars fall and return; flowers die and revive; after old age the shrubs put forth leaves; seeds grow green again only after they have decayed. Thus the body conceals its greenness in the age, as trees do in the wintry season, with a feigned dryness. Why are you impatient for it to revive and return while winter is still unripe? We too must await [p. 52] the springtime of the body.

Nor [Col. 0348A] am I unaware that most people, conscious of their deserts, desire rather than believe that they will be nothing after death. For they prefer to be utterly extinguished rather than restored for punishment. Their error is increased both by the unrestricted freedom allowed in this age and by God’s very great patience: the more delayed his judgment, the more just it is.

# CHAPTER XXXV

[Note: [Col. 0348C]

**CHAPTER XXXV.—Of human beings.** The manuscript has *human beings*. In that case, “men” must be supplied.  
—LINDNER.

Concerning the Stygian marsh. Why, I ask, does our author not express the fiery river by its proper name when he has thought the Stygian marsh worthy of being named? The matter can readily be placed in its proper light. The words “concerning the Stygian marsh” must be regarded as a gloss. Minucius had written: “Human beings are reminded … of that fiery river” (he means Pyriphlegethon) “and of the fire more frequently encircling it.” Lest the reader fail to recognize what that more frequently encircling fire was, a copyist wrote in the book’s margin that the Stygian marsh was under discussion. [Col. 0348D] As commonly happens, these words were afterward received into the body of the discourse. On the rivers of the underworld see Plato’s *Phaedo*, p. 400, and Arnobius II, p. 52.  
—DAVIS.

By an extremely familiar explanatory construction, he afterward describes the fiery river in respect both to its origin and its shape. I certainly do not see why, with Davisius, we should regard that set of three words as a copyist’s insertion any more than the following phrase, “the fire more frequently encircling it.”  
—WOPKEN.

More frequently encircling. He appears to have written “always bursting forth.” Cicero, *Against Verres* VI, chapter 48, says that fires burst forth from Etna’s summit.  
—HEUMANN.

Prepared. Understand “to be.”  
—HEUMANN.

Reports. The Roman edition has *judgments*.

Recognized and handed down. That is: the most learned men and poets learned from the reports of demons and from the oracles of the prophets that these things had been prepared for eternal torments, and handed them down.

Burning banks—that is, blazing banks. Virgil, *Aeneid* IX, 104:

> He had spoken; and by his Stygian brother’s streams  
> [Col. 0349B] And banks burning with pitch amid the black abyss,  
> He confirmed it with a nod.  
> —LINDNER.

Fires. The manuscript has “of Mount Henneus and Mount Lesuus.” These forms are corrupt and entangled with superfluous explanations.  
—RIGALT.

No one should doubt that the author could have written “the fires of Mount Etna and of Mount Vesuvius,” and that the nature of a thing, though extremely well known, may nevertheless be added and explicitly stated. Yet this repetition is altogether inelegant and presumes very poorly upon the reader’s progress. I am surprised that Heraldus noted nothing here, since, choosing a kind of middle course, he printed “of Etna and Mount Vesuvius.” But since this noun occurs twice in the manuscript [Col. 0349C], it is evident that it has been displaced and that Minucius wrote “of Mount Etna and Mount Vesuvius.” For this is his customary arrangement, as shortly afterward: “the parent of all and lord of all”; chapter 5: “heaven itself and the stars themselves”; and several times earlier.  
—GRONOVIUS.

Source/review notes: Two inherited source passages remain textually corrupt or incomplete: the sentence beginning “Indeed, some are exalted…” in Chapter XXXVII and the clause concerning Simonides in Chapter XXXVIII. The proposed edits mark both explicitly without inventing missing text.

And although. I change nothing in a sound passage. In chapter XI Caecilius could not stomach the Christians’ promising themselves perpetual life after death—and this as the just—while promising all others, as unjust, eternal punishment. Octavius replies to this: (1) the Gentiles deserve eternal punishment precisely as Gentiles, because ignorance of God is sufficient for punishment, even if in other respects one’s life is conducted honorably; Christians, however, are rendered worthy of pardon precisely as Christians, because knowledge of God conduces to pardon even if one’s life is not entirely without fault; (2) the Gentiles also deserve eternal punishment as criminals, whereas Christians deserve eternal life because they are far better than the Gentiles. Meursius emends: “And although ignorance of God may be sufficient for punishment, knowledge may conduce to pardon.” Heumann [Col. 0349D], however, reads: “And even if” (that is, “even supposing that”) “ignorance of God is sufficient for pardon, and knowledge conduces to punishment; nevertheless”; and he illustrates this from Luke 12:47. But I know of no one who has said “conduces to punishment.” LINDNER.

Although among some. That is, although some of our people observe our discipline less carefully. HERALDUS.—I read: “our discipline falls short of what is just.” Relevant here is that statement of Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 46: “But someone will say that even among our people some depart from the rule of discipline.” HEUMANN.

We are born husbands. Davisius and Jacob Gronovius rightly defend this verb against Meursius (I believe he meant to write Wowerius), who was eager to substitute “we are known.” Recently, however, Arntzenius, on chapter 6, page 34 of Pliny’s *Panegyric*, following Pricaeus as his guide, maintained that “we are known” should be restored. He evidently believes that, if Minucius had written “we are born,” it would follow that he denied original sin and believed that we were already Christians when we came forth from our mother’s womb. Whoever wishes may judge this judgment. For my part, I am not so sharp-sighted as to perceive the force of this argument. That Minucius certainly wrote “we are born” may be shown by Tertullian, whom he so frequently imitates, writing thus in *Apology*, chapter 46: “For his own wife alone, a Christian is born a male.” HEUMANN.—Pricaeus adduces these words in connection with Luke 1:34, where Mary uses the verb γινώσκω (*ginōskō*, “know sexually”); he therefore judged that Minucius, treating almost the same subject, ought to have written “we are known,” as he confidently alleges. This is by no means probable. Octavius is alluding to 1 Timothy 3:2: μιᾶς γυναικὸς ἄνδρα (*mias gynaikos andra*), “the husband of one wife.” GRONOVIUS.

Or a deserter. Here “deserter” does not mean one who crosses over from profane rites to Christianity; for in that sense all Christians could in some fashion be called deserters, since before professing allegiance to the true religion they were profane. Rather, it means ἀποστάται (*apostatai*, “apostates”), who, impatient of the yoke imposed by Christ, have relapsed into their former sins and by that very fact have ceased to be Christians. LINDNER.]

**SUMMARY.—Octavius then shows that just and devout persons are to be endowed with everlasting happiness, while the unjust are to be afflicted with eternal punishments. He next demonstrates clearly that the morals of Christians are far holier than those of the pagans.**

And yet men are warned by the writings of the most learned [printed text: “books”] and by the songs of the poets about that fiery river and the heat repeatedly encircling the Stygian marsh, [Col. 0348B] which they have handed down as prepared for eternal torments, having learned this both from the disclosures of demons and from the oracles of the Prophets. And for that reason even their king Jupiter himself swears solemnly by the burning banks and the black abyss; for, foreknowing it, he shudders at the punishment appointed for himself together with his worshipers. Nor is there any measure or end to those torments. There an intelligent fire burns the limbs and restores them; it consumes and nourishes them, just as the fires of lightning strike bodies [Col. 0349A] but do not consume them; just as the fires of Mount Henna and Mount Lesui [printed: Mount Etna and Mount Vesuvius] and of burning lands everywhere blaze yet are not exhausted: so that penal conflagration is not fed by the destruction of those who burn, but is sustained by the unconsumed laceration of their bodies.

No one but a profane person questions that those who do not know God are deservedly tormented as impious and unjust, since it is no lesser a crime to be ignorant of the Parent of all and Lord of all than to injure him. And although ignorance of God is sufficient for punishment, just as knowledge conduces [53] to pardon, nevertheless, if Christians are compared with you, although in some of us our discipline falls short, we shall still be found far better than you. For you forbid adulteries and commit them; we are born husbands solely for our own wives. You punish crimes [Col. 0349B] once committed; among us even to contemplate one is to sin. You fear accomplices; we fear even conscience [Col. 0350A] alone, without which we cannot exist. Finally, the prison seethes with people from your number; no Christian is there unless he is either accused because of his religion or has deserted it.

## CHAPTER XXXVI

[Note: [Col. 0350C]

**CHAP. XXXVI.—May it be the lot of fortune.** The manuscript reading makes no sense, and therefore I did not hesitate to replace the singular *sit* with the plural *sint*. Fortunes, that is, are the work of lot. Phil.: *On the Creation of a Prince*: “Lot concerns happiness, not virtue. Fortunes and rank are not judged, because they belong to lot; a person’s mind and actions are judged, because they are free.” Gronovius proposes: “Let lots belong to Fortune.” Meursius reads: “of Strong Fortune,” because Chance-Fortune was a goddess distinct from Fortune, had a temple across the Tiber, and was worshiped by those who sustained life without any trade. Heumann reads: “Let the lot belong to fortune,” that is: “I grant that lot is the work of fortune and that to fortune it is owed that one person is born in an illustrious station and amid great wealth, another lowly and poor.” LINDNER.—“Let the outcome belong to the lot of Fortune.” So reads the manuscript, and far better than those who read “of Strong Fortune.” For this is no place for that Roman goddess. Minucius is now speaking from the perspective of those who assigned to each person his own fortune on the basis of ἀποτελεσματική (*apotelesmatikē*, “astrological”), or judicial, astrology, by which the whole course of human life was supposedly governed. This was called the Lot of Fortune, or ὁ κλῆρος τῆς τύχης (*ho klēros tēs tychēs*), “the lot of fortune.” On the Lot of Fortune, see Scaliger on Book II of Manilius’ *Astronomica*; likewise Selden, *On the Syrian Gods*, treatise I, chapter 1, and Salmasius, *On Climacteric Years*. OUZELIUS.

[Col. 0350D] **Rank is not judged.** I do not understand what rank has to do with this. Minucius is arguing against astrologers, who maintained that the fates of persons at birth had been fixed by the various aspects and conjunctions of the planets. I restore what long ago pleased the distinguished Ferrerius: “Nativity is not judged.” Shortly afterward: “In us it is not birth that is punished, but the nature of our disposition.” See Petrus Faber, *Semestria*, Book III, chapter 33. DAVISIUS.

**Matter.** It is quite evident that “the future” ought to be written. HEUMANN.

[Col. 0351B] **Birth.** By which one person is noble or ignoble, rich or poor, and so forth. LINDNER.

**More truly and fully.** In the manuscript it is written *verius*, which represents *uverius* for *uberius* (“more abundantly”), just as in chapter 21 *veribus* stands for *uberibus*.
