[Col. 0351C] RIGALTIUS.—See the notes on chapter 19: “more nearly and more truly.” LINDNER.—Minucius, or Octavius, was permitted to proceed thus in this part, since Caecilius had dismissed these matters in so cursory a fashion. Chapter 11: “Many points are available for this, were the discourse not hastening onward.” GRONOVIUS.

**Who can.** In place of “how can.” The Roman edition wrongly reads: “who is able?” HEUMANN.—So too the manuscript. EDITORS.

**And pastures are fed from day to day.** I correct this to “pastures [feminine] from day to day are fed.” The use of *pascua* in the feminine gender was not unusual in that age. The glosses give: “Pasture, Νομή. Νομαί.” Arnobius on Psalm 22: “This, then, is the voice of the perfect which the Church received from the Lord’s Passion. Placed in a place of pasture, raised beside the water of refreshment.” Likewise on Psalm 106: “Appointing shepherds and pastures for them.” MEURSIUS.—“Livestock is fed.” The manuscripts read: “pastures are fed.” I think *pecua*, that is, “livestock,” was written. Prudentius in the *Passion of Romanus*:

> Draft animals, livestock, beasts beneath the yoke.

HERALDUS.—The manuscript reads “pastures are fed,” from which [Col. 0351D] Desiderius Heraldus extracted the received reading and, as it seems to me, quite correctly; for the ancients said *pecua* and *pecuda* just as they said *pecora* (“livestock”), as Nonius Marcellus shows by examples in chapter 2. Hence Cato in Gellius, *Attic Nights*, Book VII, chapter 3: “If anyone should wish to possess a larger number of livestock.” Livy, Book XXXV, chapter 20: “As the fields were flooded everywhere, livestock was swept away.” See also Prudentius, *Peristephanon*, Hymn X, 333. DAVISIUS.

**All of which.** Perizonius correctly restored “who possesses all things.” Minucius seems to have had before his eyes Paul’s statement in 2 Corinthians 6:10: “As having nothing and yet possessing all things.” HEUMANN.—The forcefulness in the words “all of which” ought not to be altered: it is as though someone were saying to us, “All these things that you see are yours,” a formula used by Apuleius, Book II of the *Milesian Tales*. GRONOVIUS.

**The defects of a human body.** This is equivalent to “the defects of the human body.” Lucretius, Book II, page 109:

> And the gleaming Meliboean  
> Purple dyed with the Thessalian blood of shellfish—

that is, with the blood of Thessalian shellfish. [Col. 0352B] Propertius is no different in Book IV, Elegy VIII, 23, nor Statius in the *Epithalamium of Stella and Violentilla*, verse 191. Prose writers use the construction similarly. Novatian, *On the Trinity*, chapter XXII (otherwise XVII): “God did not refuse to assume the human frailty of condition,” for “the frailty of the human condition.” [Col. 0352C] Cyprian, *On Mortality*, page 164, Oxford edition: “To the heavenly splendor of kingdoms,” for “to the splendor of heavenly kingdoms.” DAVISIUS.

**Nor can he fail to assist.** The matter itself declares that Minucius wrote: “Nor does he fail to provide.” HEUMANN.—For my part, I think it should read: “And can God fail to assist us, and does he despise us?” Jeremiah 14:8: “O hope of the Israelites and their savior in time of adversity, why should you be like a stranger in the land, and like a traveler turning aside to spend the night? Why should you be like a drowsy man, like a soldier unable to defend?” LINDNER.

**In adversities.** Delete “in,” which ought to be absent here just as it is absent from the following “dangers.” HEUMANN.

**The will.** David prays in a suppliant voice that God may do this in Psalm 139:23. Above he had said, “he weighs the disposition of each person”; now he adds, “he investigates the will.” Heumann restores “virtue,” which also depends upon the will and spontaneous choice. LINDNER.

[Col. 0352D] **Confident that nothing belonging to him can perish.** That is, knowing that those who are true Christians will be conquered by no calamity or torture so as to fall away from him—that is, from God. HEUMANN.]

**SUMMARY.—No less clearly does he teach that fate is nothing other than what God has decreed. The mind is free, and therefore a person’s action, not his birth, is judged. After this he makes it perfectly clear that the poverty reproached against Christians is not a disgrace but a glory, and that their suffering bodily evils is not punishment but military service.**

Let no one either derive consolation from fate or use it to excuse an outcome. Let the lot belong to fortune; nevertheless, the mind is free, and therefore a person’s action, not his rank, is judged. For what else is fate but what God has decreed concerning each one [Col. 0350B] of us? Since he can foresee the material circumstances, he also determines destinies in accordance with the merits and qualities of individuals. [Col. 0351A] Thus, in us it is not birth that is chastised, but the nature of our disposition that is punished.

Enough about fate—or, if only a little has been said because of present constraints, we shall discuss it elsewhere more richly and fully. As for the fact that most of us are called poor, it is not our disgrace but our glory; for just as the spirit is enervated by luxury, so it is strengthened by frugality. And yet how can anyone be poor who is not in need, who does not covet what belongs to another, who is rich toward God? The poorer man is rather he who, although he possesses much, desires still more.

Nevertheless, I shall say what I think: no one can be as poor as he was when born. Birds live without [54] an inheritance, and livestock is fed from day to day; yet these things have also been born for us, and if we do not covet them, we possess them all. Therefore, just as a traveler is happier the lighter he walks, so in this journey of life the person who lifts himself by poverty is more blessed than one who groans beneath the burden of riches. And yet, if we considered wealth useful, we would ask it from God; surely he whose is the whole could grant a portion. But we prefer to despise riches rather than possess them; we desire innocence more, we demand patience more earnestly; we prefer to be good rather than extravagant.

And the fact that we experience and suffer the defects of the human body is not punishment; it is military service. For courage is strengthened by infirmities, and calamity [Col. 0352A] is very often the training ground of virtue. Indeed, the powers both of mind and body grow sluggish without the exercise of labor. Thus all your brave men whom you proclaim as examples flourished in renown through their afflictions. Accordingly, God cannot fail to assist us and does not despise us, since he is both ruler of all and lover of his own; but amid adversities he tests and examines each person. He weighs the disposition of each amid dangers; right up to the final moment of death he investigates the human will, confident that nothing belonging to him can perish. Thus, just as gold is tested by fire, so are we proved by ordeals.

## CHAPTER XXXVII

[Note: [Col. 0352D]

**Mocking, he taunts?** The manuscript reads “snatching, he drives home.” Hence Gelenius emended it to “mocking, he drives home.” The verb occurred in this sense in chapter 24: “they know them, drive them home, and press them.” Rigaltius and other more recent editors, however, preferred “mocking, he taunts,” which is better known and more approved. Jacob Gronovius, for his part, carves out the reading “filling, he drives home,” that is, while occupied and engrossed in filling out and satiating the noise of the deadly instruments and the horror of the executioner, he also drives it home. Heumann deservedly called this opinion a waking dream; yet Heumann himself, who reads “exults,” does not have my assent. For in the exemplar, according to Rigaltius, it reads *stultat* (“plays the fool”; not here, but below. EDITORS). The Roman edition, however, plainly presents *insultat* (“taunts”). What it means to “taunt the noise of death and the horror of the executioner” is shown by Prudentius, among many other passages, especially *Peristephanon* II, 313 following and 397–409. LINDNER.

**Raises.** He imitates Florus, Book I, 21: “They who had raised their liberty against their masters themselves.” Firmicus, *The Error of Profane Religions*, [Col. 0353B] page 6: “And then, with freedom of speech raised aloft, he proclaims.” WOPKENS.

[Col. 0353C] **Mucius Scaevola.** Read: “as Mucius.” HEUMANN.—I, however, conjecture that some words have fallen out and should be supplied from the following paragraph: “You yourselves exalt afflicted men to heaven: Regulus, Aquilius, Mucius Scaevola, who,” etc. LINDNER.

**Against the king.** I write “in regard to the king.” HEUMANN.

**To be burned, to be consumed by fire.** “To be burned” has been displaced from its proper position. I restore it thus: “Not merely for their right hand to be burned, but for their whole body to be consumed by fire.” HEUMANN.

**Inspired.** So it stands in the manuscript. Although Heraldus defends it from Lactantius V.13.12, I have no doubt that “unexpected patience” is preferable. The passage in Lactantius is very different from ours. There “inspired patience” is required because it is greater than that of robbers; here “unexpected,” because no one would have expected such patience from children and little women. LINDNER.

**So that their disposition.** This passage has always seemed desperate to me. I restore it as follows, conveniently enough, though I do not know whether successfully as well. Two contraries are always opposed to one another: they are raised up and fall down; they are fattened and suffer [Col. 0353D] punishment; they are crowned and slaughtered; they are exalted and cast down. The manuscript has: “so that their disposition may freely be sold by the license of a ruined mind of power,” words that yield absolutely no sense. I reject “their disposition,” as Heumann already saw (or did?); I render “mind” as a nominative plural and “power” as an accusative. “Minds of ruined license” are the Praetorian soldiers, who freely sold powers—that is, commands and magistracies. They could not do this unless a predecessor had first been removed. An illustrious example of this occurred after Pertinax was removed by the soldiers through a violent death. Who can doubt that Minucius—who, according to Daniel Heinsius on Seneca’s *Hercules Oetaeus*, lived in those times—had this in view? I adduce Herodian’s passage on the subject, Book II, chapter 6:

> The soldiers brought the loudest-voiced among them up onto the wall and proclaimed that the imperial power was for sale. They promised to entrust the sovereignty to the man who would give the most money and to conduct him safely under arms into the imperial palace. … Then, for the first time, the character of the soldiers was corrupted, and they were taught an insatiable and [Col. 0354B] shameful greed for money and contempt for the reverence due to their rulers. … For the absence of anyone to prevent the sovereignty from being so indecently proclaimed and sold for money [Col. 0354C] became thereafter the origin and cause of a disorderly and insubordinate condition, as greed for money itself and contempt for rulers continually increased to the point of bloodshed.

Heumann emends the passage thus: “So that their ruined minds may be severely punished for the license of their power.” LINDNER.

**Since death is.** I punctuated this passage in this way long ago. I now see that Wopkens also approved the same punctuation. Nor am I surprised that Heumann did not subscribe to it, for he preferred to restore: “Which is not like a dream and slips away before it is grasped.” LINDNER.

**Are you a king?** The author now establishes in order that no one should be deceived by the three things he discussed above—riches, honors, and powers. (1) He speaks of powers: “Are you a king?” (2) Of riches: “Are you rich?” (3) Of honors: “Do you glory in the fasces and purple?” LINDNER.

**Nevertheless.** I do not assent to Heumann when he substitutes “for.” It has the force of “but,” which occurred in the same syntactical structure. LINDNER.

[Col. 0354D] **Against itself.** Read “among themselves.” HEUMANN.—Or rather interpret it in this way. LINDNER.

**No less the frenzy; and more protracted the disgrace.** The royal manuscript reads “with frenzy”; perhaps: “the frenzy is no less, the disgrace more protracted.” HERALDUS.—The exemplar reads “with frenzy.” This reading should by no means be scorned, although syllables of this kind frequently coalesce in the same manuscript: “disgrace with frenzy,” for “frenzy and disgrace.” RIGALTIUS.

**While the actor feigns love, he inflicts it.** Cyprian, *On Grace*, page 6 (Commelinus, Letter II, chapter 3): “Adultery is learned while it is watched; and because the evil of public authority acts as a procurer for vice, the matron who had perhaps gone to the spectacle chaste returns from the spectacle unchaste. Then too, how great is the corruption of morals, what incitements to disgrace, what nourishment of vice—to be defiled by actors’ gestures?” CELLARIUS.—Lactantius VI.20: “What else do the actors’ most shameless movements do but teach and inflict lusts?” ELMENHORST.—Remarkable indeed is the acumen of the anonymous Parisian editor, who restores “fixes within.” Minucius cleverly says that love is simultaneously feigned and fixed—indeed, implanted. HEUMANN.

[Col. 0355B] **Clothing them in sexual crimes.** Heumann restores “introducing,” which is a word proper to the theater, as may be learned even from Faber’s lexicon. But from that same book I also learn that the meanings of these verbs are used interchangeably. And just as one commonly says to “put on” flattery, different things, mortal form, chaste manners, another person’s character, and so forth, one may similarly clothe gods in sexual crimes, sighs, and hatreds. LINDNER.

**In reality … in fiction.** That is, at gladiatorial spectacles you demand that one person pierce another through, but when a simulated murder occurs on the stage, you shed tears. There is a similar passage in Lactantius V.20.12, most worthy of reading. HEUMANN.]

**SUMMARY.—Spectacles worthy of God are the torments most unjustly inflicted for the confession of Christ. Octavius demonstrates this clearly by comparing certain exceptionally brave [Col. 0352B] pagans with the holy martyrs. He further explains that Christians do not attend spectacles and processions because they know with utter certainty that these are no less impious than cruel.**

How beautiful a spectacle it is for God when a Christian grapples with pain; when he arrays himself against threats, punishments, and tortures; when, seizing upon the noise of death [55] and the horror of the executioner, he drives them home; when [Col. 0353A] he raises his liberty against kings and princes and yields to God alone, to whom it belongs; when, triumphant and victorious, he taunts the very man who pronounced sentence against him! For he has conquered who has obtained the object for which he contended.

What soldier would not challenge danger more boldly beneath the eyes of his commander? For no one receives the prize before the trial. And yet a commander does not give what he does not possess: he cannot prolong life, though he can honor military service. But God’s soldier is neither abandoned in pain nor ended by death. Thus a Christian can appear wretched, but cannot be found to be so.

You yourselves exalt afflicted men to heaven: Mucius Scaevola, who, when he had made a mistake concerning the king, would have perished among the enemy had he not lost his right hand. Yet how many of our people have endured, without any wailing, not merely for their right hand but for their whole body to be burned and consumed by fire, [Col. 0353B] although it was especially within their power to be released? Shall I compare men with Mucius, Aquilius, or Regulus? Our children and little women mock crosses and torments, wild beasts and all the terrors of punishment, with inspired endurance of pain. Do you not understand, you wretched people, that no one would wish to undergo punishment without a reason or could endure torture without God?

Unless, perhaps, you are deceived because people who do not know God abound in riches, flourish in honors, and possess great power. Wretched people! They are raised higher for this purpose: that they may fall farther. For these men are fattened like sacrificial animals [Col. 0354A] [56] for punishment; like victims destined for penalty, they are crowned. Indeed, some are exalted to commands and dominions precisely so that—[the transmitted text is corrupt]—their disposition may be freely sold by the license of a ruined mind and of power. For without knowledge of God what happiness can be secure, since death is like a dream? It slips away before it can be grasped.

Are you a king? You fear as much as you are feared; and however large the retinue surrounding you, nevertheless you face danger alone. Are you rich? It is unwise to trust fortune, and a great stock of provisions does not equip but burdens life’s brief journey. Do you glory in the fasces and purple? What an empty human error and hollow cult of rank—to glitter in purple while being filthy in mind. Are you nobly born? Do you praise your ancestors? Yet we are all born to an equal lot; we are distinguished by virtue alone.

We, therefore, who are judged by our morals and modesty, [Col. 0354B] deservedly abstain from your wicked pleasures, processions, and spectacles, whose origin in your sacred rites we know and whose harmful enticements we condemn. For at the chariot games, who would not shudder at the madness of a populace quarreling against itself? At the gladiatorial games, who would not shudder at the schooling in murder? At theatrical performances, too, the frenzy is no less and the disgrace more protracted. Now the mime either displays adulteries or represents them; now the effeminate actor, while feigning love, inflicts it. He dishonors your gods by clothing them [Col. 0355A] [57] in sexual crimes, sighs, and hatreds. By simulated sorrows he likewise provokes your tears with empty gestures and nods. Thus you demand murder in reality but weep over it in fiction.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII

[Note: [Col. 0355C]

**God’s inviolable gift.** That is, a gift given by God to humankind which human beings cannot violate—that is, cannot make it unlawful to touch or eat—when they turn it into a victim dedicated to demons. Our author has in view the principle stated by the Apostle in 1 Corinthians 10:25 and 8:7 and Romans 14:14, where he teaches that Christians may eat any food, even food sacrificed to idols, provided, however, that if a brother is present who doubts this freedom, they abstain from it for the time being. HEUMANN.

**Lest anyone suppose.** “Us” must be understood, but should not, as Heumann does, be inserted into the text.

**Yield.** I read “believe.” So in chapter 40, “believe God.” Meursius had already corrected this passage in that way. “To believe” is a Christian formula: Christians are said to believe God, while idolaters believe demons. HEUMANN.—I once thought “eat” should be read, as in Paul, 1 Corinthians 10:20, δαιμονίοις θύει (*daimoniois thyei*), “he sacrifices to demons.” But I now see that the common reading must be retained. For not yielding is an exercise of liberty; Christians “yield to God alone,” chapter 37. LINDNER.

[Col. 0355D] **We take.** Stewechius, on Apuleius’ *Metamorphoses*, Book X, page 382, restores “we pluck.” Davisius reports this but does not approve it; I agree with Stewechius. Virgil, *Georgics* IV, 134:

> To pluck the rose in spring and apples in autumn.

Indeed, this very passage seems to have been present to Minucius’ mind. HEUMANN.

**We use both scattered flowers and garlands.** Christians used flowers scattered, garlanded, and loose for simple enjoyment, but scrupulously abstained from that use and manner of arrangement which belonged to Gentile rites. CELLARIUS.—Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* IV: “flowers garlanded and loose”; I.10, page 406: “with flowers cast about, garlanded and loose.” Tertullian, *On the Soldier’s Crown*, chapter 5: “flowers both inserted and interwoven, both free and loose.” ELMENHORST.

**The fragrance of a good flower.** Tertullian, *On the Crown*, chapter 5: “What enjoyment of a flower is there on the head? It is as contrary to nature to seek a flower with the head as food with the ear or sound with the nose.” And in chapter 42 of the *Apology*: “We know the garland with our nostrils. Let those who smell through their hair see to it.” [Col. 0356B] HEUMANN.

**Nor do we crown the dead.** The Laws of the Twelve Tables forbid elaborate garlands at funerals, according to Cicero, *On the Laws*, Book II, chapter 24; they therefore appear to have permitted others. Tertullian, *On the Crown*, chapter 10: “What is as worthy of an idol as that which is also given to a dead person? For it also belongs to the dead to be crowned in this manner, since they immediately become idols themselves through the garb and observance of consecration.” For this reason the early Christians abstained from the use of garlands at funerals. We noted above, on chapter 12, that they later cast flowers upon tombs. CELLARIUS.

**How you assign to a lifeless person either a torch when he does not feel [Col. 0356C], or a garland when he does not feel.** So reads the manuscript; but Gelenius published: “to a lifeless person either a torch when he feels.” Meursius conjectured: “to a lifeless person, or one who does not feel, a garland as though he felt.” Desiderius Heraldus emends: “to a lifeless person, as one who does not feel, a torch; as one who feels, a garland.” Finally, the distinguished Salmasius, *Plinian Exercises*, page 963, Paris edition, pronounces that it must be written: “you assign either a torch to one who feels or a garland to one who does not feel.” Yet all of them have missed the mark. With the negative particle deleted, it should be corrected to “a torch to a lifeless person or one who does not feel” (for a torch affords no use except to one who sees and therefore feels), “or a garland to one who feels.” Minucius himself adds the reason: since the blessed person does not need flowers and the wretched person does not rejoice in them. Of what benefit, then, are they placed upon the dead, even if the dead feel? DAVISIUS.—Gutherus, Book III, *On the Law of the Shades*, while preserving the authority of the ancient manuscripts, thinks that it was written: “either a torch to one who does not feel or a garland to one who does not seek it.” Gronovius adheres to the manuscript reading and explains it thus: “either a torch for one who does not feel, to dispel the darkness, or a garland for one who does not feel its sweet breath or fragrance.” Grunerus says this to be the author’s meaning: “I am [Col. 0356D] more astonished at you precisely because you crown the dead: how you assign this to a lifeless person—who must either feel the torch with which you customarily burn him or fail to feel the garland with which you think you honor him—since if the dead person is blessed, he does not need flowers, while if wretched, he does not rejoice in them.” For my part, I have always believed the sense of the passage to be this: it is unsurprising that we do not crown the dead, because we know that they do not feel. But why do you crown a lifeless person? Perhaps because he feels? Then why do you place a torch beneath one who feels? But the dead person does not feel. Therefore he should not be crowned. It is a dilemma of the kind Caecilius had presented above in chapter 11, and ought to be formulated thus: “A lifeless person either feels or does not feel: if he feels, why do you place a torch beneath him? If he does not feel, why do you give him a garland?” LINDNER.

**But we adorn funerals.** So Heraldus reads from the royal manuscript, as does Meursius. The common reading is “we perform funeral rites,” which is interpreted as “we conduct them,” because Festus says: “Among the ancients *adorare* meant ‘to perform.’” But Festus did not prove this by examples; and even had he done so, it would not follow with certainty that Minucius preferred to speak [Col. 0357B] ἀρχαϊκῶς (*archaikōs*, “in an archaic manner”) rather than with the Latins of his own and the immediately preceding age, with which he was thoroughly familiar. CELLARIUS.

**The hope of future happiness.** That is, “we are confidently encouraged toward the hope of future happiness because we believe in his present majesty.” Thus Claudian, *The Rape of Proserpina* III, 386: [Col. 0357C] “to encourage toward crimes.” I formerly emended it thus: “we await it calmly: modest, through our God’s generosity; confident, through the hope of future happiness; encouraged, through faith in the presence of his majesty.” Rigaltius published: “we await it, calm, modest, secure in our God’s generosity; we are encouraged in the hope of future happiness by the presence of his majesty.” Heumann writes that Minucius’ text was: “We who, secure in the power and generosity of our God, are encouraged toward the hope of future happiness by faith in his present majesty.” LINDNER.

**In the age of our time.** The expression is good Latin. Propertius, Book I, Elegy IV, 7:

> And every woman whom the age of a beautiful time has produced.

See Janus Broukhusius there. Sulpicius Severus, *Life of St. Martin*, chapter 20: “As is the age of our times.” Arnobius, Book II, page 58: “The longevity of past time has run its course.” Conversely, Aulus Gellius said “in the times of his age,” Book IX, chapter 4. DAVISIUS.—The learned Davisius rightly defends “in the age of our time”; but I doubt whether he changes “came to maturity” into “became known” without necessity. For the evangelical revelation, or the truth of the Divinity, is quite aptly said to have come to maturity around that time, insofar as it then, and not earlier or later, seemed to God fit to be brought into the light. Thus a thing is said to mature, or become mature, when it reaches the time appointed or appropriate for it. Quintilian, *Letter to Trypho*: “For I myself did not yet think that the books had sufficiently matured.” Compare Cicero, *First Oration against Catiline*, chapter 13: “The maturity of all your crimes and of your long-standing frenzy and audacity has erupted in the time of my consulship.” The metaphor seems to be derived from crops appearing in their proper season. WOPKENS.

**Let us regulate.** So that it degenerates neither into superstition, by which someone believes everything, nor into impiety, by which someone believes nothing. This middle way is called true religion. Heumann restores: “Let us obey those who think rightly.” LINDNER.

**Let it be preserved.** Heumann restores “let it be restored.” But “let it be preserved” is equivalent to “let it be kept,” and our author customarily employs compounds with the syllable *re-* in the sense of their simple forms. [Col. 0358B] LINDNER.]

**SUMMARY.—The Christians likewise abstain from food sacrificed to idols, lest anyone suppose that they either yield to demons or are ashamed of their own religion. Yet they do not reject every color and fragrance of flowers. They customarily use scattered, loose, and soft flowers and encircle their necks with garlands; but they consider it superfluous and useless to crown the head of a dead person. They bury their dead with the same tranquility with which they live, awaiting the crown of eternal happiness with the surest hope. Their true religion, therefore, once Gentile superstitions have been rejected, ought to be embraced by everyone.**

[Col. 0355B] As for our scorning the remnants of sacrifices and cups from which libations have been poured, [Col. 0356A] this is not an admission of fear but an assertion of true liberty. For although everything that comes into being, as an inviolable gift of God, is corrupted by no act, we nevertheless abstain, lest anyone suppose either that we yield to the demons to whom the libation was offered or that we are ashamed of our own religion.

Who doubts that we enjoy the flowers of spring, since we take both the spring rose and the lily, and whatever else among flowers possesses an enticing color and fragrance? We use them both scattered, soft and loose, and we encircle our necks with garlands. As for our not crowning the head, forgive us. We are accustomed to draw in the breath of a fragrant flower with our nostrils, not to inhale it with the back of the head or the hair.

Nor do we crown the dead. In this I am more astonished at you: how you assign to a lifeless person either a torch when he does not feel, or a garland when he does not feel, since the blessed person does not need flowers and the wretched person does not rejoice in them. But we [Col. 0356B] adorn funerals with the same tranquility with which [Col. 0357A] we live. We do not attach a withering garland, but await from God one living with eternal flowers; for, modest and secure in our God’s generosity, we are encouraged toward the hope of future happiness by faith in his present majesty. Thus we both rise again in blessedness and, through contemplation of the future, live out our present course.

Therefore [58] let Socrates, the Attic buffoon, look to it—glorious though he was through the testimony of a most deceitful demon after confessing that he knew nothing. Let Arcesilaus too, Carneades, Pyrrho, and the whole multitude of Academics remain in doubt. As for Simonides too: “forever … not to be comprehended” [the transmitted reading is incomplete; common text: “let him defer it forever”]. We despise the superciliousness of philosophers, whom we know to be corrupters, adulterers, and tyrants, and always eloquent against their own vices. We profess wisdom not in our clothing but in our mind; we do not utter grand things but live them. [Col. 0357B] We glory in having attained what they sought with the utmost exertion but could not find.

Why are we ungrateful? Why are we begrudged this, if the truth of the Divinity has come to maturity in the age of our time? Let us enjoy our good, and let us regulate right judgment: let superstition be restrained, impiety expiated, and true religion preserved.

## CHAPTER XXXIX

[Note: [Col. 0358B]

**We held our faces intent.** So it stands in the manuscript, and rightly. Caesar, *Gallic War* VII, chapter 80: “The intent minds of all the soldiers awaited the outcome of the battle.” [Col. 0358C] Johannes Meursius restores “we, intent, held our faces,” and Ouzelius, Cellarius, and Gronovius follow him in their editions. Virgil indeed said in *Aeneid* II.1:

> All fell silent and, intent, held their faces fixed.

There Servius says: “*Held* means ‘had,’ so that the construction is: ‘they had their faces intent.’” Minucius should therefore not be blamed for employing the more familiar manner of speech. DAVISIUS.—“We, intent, held our faces.” According to Meursius, the manuscript has “intent faces,” which is not bad. Yet our author seems to have reproduced the expression of the prince of poets at the beginning of *Aeneid* II:

> All fell silent and, intent, held their faces fixed.

CELLARIUS.—Meursius must be mistaken, since neither Heraldus nor Rigaltius, both of whom inspected that manuscript, supports his testimony. HEUMANN.

**As far as concerns me.** Only a barbarian would have spoken thus instead of “as far as I am concerned.” Yet I do not reject the phrase, but change “in” to “from”: “I vanished from the greatness of my astonishment,” says [Col. 0358D] Minucius. Now “as concerns me,” so far as I know, does not occur elsewhere; it is nevertheless sufficiently clear. Cicero similarly used the concise “about me” for “as far as I am concerned” in his letters. HEUMANN.—Cicero said, “As concerns Caesar,” with “concerns” understood, Book VIII, Letter I.8; compare Cortius on that passage. LINDNER.]

“I fainted away” (*evanui*). A harsh and novel expression. Yet it is readily understood that our Minucius spoke thus in place of “I was seized by a kind of ecstasy,” or, as Lactantius, I.4.3, puts it, “my mind had been displaced,” or, as Apuleius says, Book V, p. 166, Frankfurt ed., 1621: “I had been placed beyond the bounds of my mind.” HEUMANN.]

ARGUMENT.—After Octavius had thus concluded his speech, [Col. 0358A] Minucius and Caecilius remained for some time stunned into silence, their faces fixed in attention. Minucius, indeed, carried away in admiration of Octavius, remained silent, inwardly and wordlessly pondering what he had heard.

When Octavius had finished speaking, for some time we remained stunned into silence, our faces fixed in attention; and, as for me, I fainted away from the greatness of my admiration, because he had embellished with arguments, examples, and the authority of his reading matters that are easier to feel than to express; because he had beaten back the malevolent with those very missiles of the philosophers with which they arm themselves; and because he had also shown that the truth was not merely easy, but attractive as well.

## CHAPTER XL

[Note: [Col. 0358D]

CHAP. XL.—“Caecilius burst out.” Without awaiting the arbiter’s judgment, he spoke unexpectedly; stirred by the disposition of his newly transformed mind, he could contain himself no longer. See chap. 16. CELLARIUS.—The Roman edition has “thus burst out.” This addition is rightly rejected; above also, in chap. 16, the simple phrase “burst out” is used. HEUMANN.

“Very greatly indeed” (*plurimum quantum*). After these words the following are added in the Roman edition [Col. 0359B]: “with the same tranquility with which we live.” They are not found in the manuscript, but were transferred here through a printer’s error from chap. 38, where these same words occur. Heraldus therefore already ordered them deleted. HEUMANN.—Heumann himself is mistaken, for we read these four words in the royal manuscript. EDITORS.

“And so, as I shamelessly appropriate the victory.” The common editions read: “and so, as a shameless man” (*et ita, ut improbus*). We, however, have retained the manuscript reading. Petrus Scriverius emended it: “We have won—hurrah!—as I shamelessly appropriate the victory.” Jacobus Gronovius ingeniously proposed: “We have won, and thus not shamelessly”; I would readily assent to that emendation, were it not that the word “thus” seems entirely superfluous. I prefer: “We have won, and I do not shamelessly appropriate the victory.” DAVIS.—Heumann, *Dissertationum Sylloge*, vol. I, part II, p. 483: “We have won. And so, not shamelessly, I appropriate the victory.” GALLAND.—“Not shamelessly.” In the sole manuscript it is evident that *ita ut* was written because the copyist overlooked the repetition of the first vowel, when he ought to have restored *ita aut*; or, as I think, in the exemplar he used there was written something which, when another person dictated and pronounced it too softly, he set down in place of *ita haut*. For I think it evident that Minucius wrote: “We have won, and thus not shamelessly do I appropriate the victory”; for he has in view the Greek expression κοινὸν ἑρμῆν, “a shared windfall,” and brings this gain into common ownership. GRONOVIUS.—It must certainly be read thus: “We have won. And so, not shamelessly, I appropriate the victory.” HEUMANN.

“Insofar as it may concern” (*quod pertineat*). I write “insofar as it concerns” (*quod pertinet*). HEUMANN.

“I yield to God.” Others want “I believe in God”; but we have retained the reading of the exemplar, which is correct. Our author above, chap. 38: “lest anyone suppose that we yield to the demons to whom a libation has been made”; there too Joannes Meursius wrongly emends “yield” to “believe.” Prudentius, *Peristephanon*, Hymn X, 960:

> Yield now to the miracles that have been proved.

Again, *Against Symmachus*, Book II, verse 3:

> We have spoken, and now Rome yields to our Christ.

Likewise Arnobius, Book VI, p. 197, said “to believe the truth that has been confessed.” DAVIS.

“Settle down together” (*consubsidunt*). The word is not Latin and was undeservedly inserted [Col. 0359D] into Faber’s lexicon. I reject the prefix *con-* and take the following *non* to have arisen from it; the copyist, who had written it prematurely, was unwilling to delete it. [Col. 0360B] “Settle down” (*subsidunt*), however, gives excellent sense. For in a vessel that part of a liquid which is turbid, and consequently somewhat heavier, is said to settle. “Some things settle down,” he says—that is, they still reside and remain at the bottom of his breast. Caecilius is therefore saying that certain questions for deliberation remain in his mind. They do not have such force as to compel him to doubt the truth of the Christian religion, but he nevertheless wishes them removed so that his knowledge of the truth may become more perfect. HEUMANN.

“Concerning the whole” (*ut de toto*). I delete *ut* and emend the text to “throughout the whole day” (*die toto*); and I now see with some pleasure that the anonymous Parisian also made this emendation. HEUMANN.—“Concerning the whole,” that is, concerning a complete subject supplying material for a proper disputation. *Ut* is not a conjunction but an adverb of comparison. LINDNER.

“More readily” (*promptius*). Delete this word as a variant reading admitted into the text from the margin by an ignorant copyist. HEUMANN.]

[Col. 0358B] ARGUMENT.—Caecilius, however, exclaimed that he had been defeated by Octavius, that he was now the conqueror of error, and that he henceforth professed the Christian religion; fuller instruction in the mysteries of the faith was meanwhile postponed until the following day.

While, therefore, I was silently turning these matters over within myself, Caecilius burst out: “I congratulate my Octavius very greatly indeed—with the same tranquility with which we live—but I congratulate myself as well, [Col. 0359A] and I do not await the judgment. We have won, and so I shamelessly appropriate the victory; for just as he is the conqueror of me, so I am the triumphant conqueror of error. 59 Accordingly, as regards the principal question, I both acknowledge providence, yield to God, and assent concerning the sincerity of the sect that is now ours. Nevertheless, some matters still settle together in my mind—not matters that contradict the truth, but matters necessary for complete instruction. Concerning these we shall inquire tomorrow, since the sun is now sinking toward its setting, when it will be more fitting and more convenient to deal with the whole subject.”

## CHAPTER XLI

[Note: [Col. 0360B]

CHAP. XLI.—“On behalf of all of us” (*omnium nostrum vice*). It should be emended to *vicem*. Curtius VII.2.5: “Sorrowful not for his own lot, but [Col. 0360C] for that of his brothers”; and in chap. 11.20 of the same book: “anxious for their lot.” The same author, X.5.21, concerning Queen Sisygambis: “She mourned her own lot, she the lot of her granddaughters.” Gronovius the elder, in his notes on Livy, Book I, chaps. 9 and 25, will also teach you that Livy often speaks thus, and that in Livy too ignorant copyists changed *vicem* to *in vice*. HEUMANN.

“And inspired.” The “and” may conveniently be absent. LINDNER.

“Octavius rejoiced because he had conquered.” In some books this is inserted in the following form: “Octavius rejoiced because he had conquered.” But even if “began” is understood, it will nevertheless repeat what was already expressed in “glad and cheerful.” CELLARIUS.—“Octavius rejoiced.” Either the final word must be deleted altogether with Fulvius Ursinus, or, by transposing the words, the text must be read: “Caecilius rejoiced because he had believed; Octavius because he had conquered.” Those more skilled in the refinements of Latin will readily admit this. DAVIS.

“And because this man.” Only the briefest attention is needed to see [Col. 0360D] that the text should very clearly be written: “Because this man too had believed” (*quod et hic crediderit*). HEUMANN.]

ARGUMENT.—At last they all depart glad and cheerful: Caecilius because he had believed; Octavius because [Col. 0360A] he had conquered; and Minucius because the former had believed and the latter had conquered.

“But I,” I said, “rejoice more fully on behalf of all of us, because Octavius has conquered for me as well, since the very great unpopularity involved in passing judgment has been removed from me. Yet I cannot repay his merit with praises expressed in words. The testimony of a man—and of one man alone—is weak. He possesses the extraordinary gift of God, by whom he was both inspired when he spoke and assisted when he prevailed.”

After this we departed glad and cheerful: Caecilius because he had believed; Octavius, rejoicing because he had conquered; and I because the one had believed and the other had conquered.

# INDEX OF THE CHAPTERS OF THE DIALOGUE ENTITLED *OCTAVIUS*, BY MARCUS MINUCIUS FELIX

[Col. 0359]

## ARGUMENT

In this dialogue Caecilius is introduced as a man devoted to pagan superstitions. By various arguments he attempts to prove that no one should abandon the ancestral worship of the gods inherited from his forefathers; that no one should anxiously inquire into religion, but that the ancient religion should be retained and the new rejected. Octavius, by contrast, had rejected that impious worship and, together with Minucius Felix, had enrolled himself in the Christian profession. He so completely overthrows all Caecilius’ arguments, and demonstrates the truth of the Christian religion with such weighty reasoning, that Caecilius, broken and completely convinced by the most serious disputation, embraces the true religion with a glad and grateful mind. The author first sets forth Caecilius’ speech in defense of the worship of the gods. He then introduces Octavius’ response to every part of Caecilius’ address.

[Col. 0359D] **CHAP. I.** At the very beginning of the dialogue Minucius relates how delightfully he was entertained by the recollection of the things that had happened to him with Octavius [Col. 0360D] while the latter was staying with him at Rome, and especially by the memory [Col. 0361A] of this disputation. col. 232

**CHAP. II.** Octavius’ arrival at Rome during the holidays of the courts is most welcome to Minucius. The two decide to go to the seaside baths at Ostia, accompanied by Caecilius, Minucius’ companion. As they proceed together toward the sea, Caecilius sees an image of Serapis, puts his hand to his mouth, and venerates it. 235

**CHAP. III.** Indignant at the superstitious man’s action, Octavius sharply reproaches Minucius, declaring that the disgrace of this impious deed redounds no less upon Minucius himself, as Caecilius’ host, than upon Caecilius. 237

**CHAP. IV.** Caecilius, somewhat saddened by this rebuke, in which Octavius censured Minucius [Col. 0361B] on his account, asks permission to debate with Octavius concerning the truth of his religion. Octavius agrees with his companion, and Minucius sits between Caecilius and Octavius. 240

**CHAP. V.** Caecilius begins his disputation. First, he asserts that everything in human affairs is doubtful and uncertain, and therefore that it is regrettable that Christians, generally uneducated and illiterate, dare to make any certain determination concerning the sum of things and the divine majesty. From this he argues that no providence governs the world and concludes that it is better to adhere to the ancient religions handed down by tradition. 242

[Col. 0361C] **CHAP. VI.** Every nation, and afterward the Romans, so worshiped its own divinities that through their worship they attained supreme dominion over the whole world. 250

**CHAP. VII.** When Roman auspices and auguries were omitted, the omission brought regret; when observed, they brought success. 253

**CHAP. VIII.** Intolerable is the impious audacity of Theodorus, Diagoras, and Protagoras, who wished either to abolish the religion of the gods entirely or at least to weaken it. Yet even less tolerable is the secretive race of Christians, which shuns the light and despises the gods; while they fear death after death, they meanwhile do not fear to die. 256

[Col. 0361D] **CHAP. IX.** The Christians’ religion is foolish: for they venerate a crucified man and the very instrument of his punishment. They are said to worship an ass’s head and adore the very nature of their father. They are initiated by the slaughter and blood of an infant, and in shameless darkness they all mingle indiscriminately as chance determines. 260

**CHAP. X.** Whatever they worship, they strive diligently to conceal. They have no altars, no temples, and no recognized images. Their God, like that of the Jews, is said to be one; although they can neither see nor display him, they nevertheless consider him troublesome, restless, and perversely inquisitive. 263

[Col. 0362A] **CHAP. XI.** They also assert that the whole world will one day be consumed by fire; and after the resurrection of our bodies they promise the righteous an eternity of most blessed life, but the unrighteous an eternity of the greatest punishments. 266

**CHAP. XII.** What will happen to the Christians themselves after death may be inferred from the fact that they are now bereft of every resource and oppressed by the greatest calamities and miseries. 271

**CHAP. XIII.** Caecilius finally concludes that the new religion must be rejected and that one must not pronounce rashly upon doubtful matters. 273

**CHAP. XIV.** With the disdain of a haughty spirit, Caecilius challenges Octavius to answer his arguments. [Col. 0362B] Minucius modestly replies that Caecilius should not exult in his own considerable eloquence or in the harmonious variety of his speech; rather, each of his arguments must be weighed carefully. 275

**CHAP. XV.** Caecilius responds to Minucius, not without some indication that his feelings have been wounded, saying that Minucius has departed from the duty of an impartial judge by weakening the force of his disputation. Octavius is entirely free to refute everything that he had brought forward for consideration. 278

**CHAP. XVI.** Octavius therefore begins his reply and expresses confidence that he will wash away the most bitter stain of their reproaches with a flood of truthful words. He then proceeds to weaken each of Caecilius’ arguments. [Col. 0362C] First, therefore, he establishes that no one should resent the fact that Christians, however unlearned, discuss heavenly matters; for it is not the authority of the disputant but the truth of the disputation itself that must be considered. 279

**CHAP. XVII.** He admits that a person ought to know himself, but utterly denies that this knowledge can be acquired unless he first recognizes the universe and God himself. From the structure and adornment of the world itself, everyone endowed with reason knows for certain that it was created by God and is ruled and administered by him. 284

[Col. 0362D] **CHAP. XVIII.** God exercises care not only for the whole world, but also for each of its parts. That all things are governed by the will of one God is proved by the example of earthly empires. Although he is infinite and immeasurable and, in the fullness of his being, known to himself alone, and although he can neither be seen nor named by us, his radiance is nevertheless perceived if supplementary additions to his name are removed. 287

**CHAP. XIX.** Moreover, the poets called him the father of gods and human beings, the creator of all things, mind, and spirit. Indeed, even the more eminent philosophers themselves held almost the same views as the Christians concerning the one God. 292

[Col. 0363A] **CHAP. XX.** But if the world is ruled by Providence and governed by the will of one God, ignorant antiquity must not carry us away into the error of mutual agreement—an antiquity which, delighted with its fables, introduced ridiculous traditions. It is demonstrated no less clearly that the worship of the gods was always foolish and impious, since the earliest mortals venerated their kings, renowned leaders, and inventors of the arts for their illustrious deeds just as if they were gods. 297

**CHAP. XXI.** Octavius confirms this by the testimony of Euhemerus, Prodicus, [Col. 0363B] Persaeus, and Alexander the Great, who enumerate the homelands, birthdays, and tombs of the gods. He further describes the gods’ miserable ends, deaths, and funerals. In addition, he ridicules the absurdities and foul nonsense that pagans retail concerning the form and appearance of their gods. 299

**CHAP. XXII.** These fables, first handed down by ignorant people, were afterward celebrated by others, especially by the poets, whose authority did considerable harm to the truth. Children’s minds are corrupted by such inventions and seductive falsehoods, and so the poor creatures grow old in them, although the truth is readily accessible—but only to those who seek it. 306

[Col. 0363C] **CHAP. XXIII.** Although pagans acknowledge their kings to be mortal, they nevertheless fashion them into gods, even against their will—not to establish belief in their divinity, but to honor their merits in posterity. Yet the true God has neither rising nor setting. Octavius then assails the images and statues of the gods. 309

**CHAP. XXIV.** By a brief survey he demonstrates how ridiculous, obscene, and cruel the rites observed in celebrating the mysteries of certain gods were. 312

**CHAP. XXV.** He then shows that Caecilius is wrong to boast that the Romans obtained dominion over the whole world [Col. 0363D] by duly observing superstitions of this sort. In fact, at their origin the Romans were assembled through crime and grew through the terror of their savagery. The Romans were therefore great not because they were religious, but because they committed sacrilege with impunity. 315

**CHAP. XXVI.** Octavius turns against Caecilius the weakly hurled missile drawn from the auspices and auguries of birds, using the examples of Regulus, Mancinus, Paulus, and Caesar. By other examples he demonstrates that the argument drawn from oracles is no more valid. 320

**CHAP. XXVII.** To establish this securely, he takes the matter up from further back, from its first origin. [Col. 0364A] This, indeed, is the source of the error: demons hide beneath statues and images, dwell in shrines, animate the fibers of entrails, govern the flight of birds, direct the lots, and pour forth oracles wrapped in false responses. Nevertheless, when adjured by Christians through the true God and driven from the bodies they possess, they are compelled to confess that these things were performed not by God, but by themselves. Hence they flee from Christians whenever they are near; and they stir up such hatred of Christians among the pagans that the latter begin to hate them before knowing them, lest, once they know them, they should either be able to imitate them or be unable to condemn them. 323

**CHAP. XXVIII.** They not only inflict hatred upon Christians, but also charge [Col. 0364B] them with unspeakable crimes, which no one has yet been able to prove. Such is the work of demons, for by them false rumor is both sown and fostered. Octavius demonstrates with the utmost force that Christians are as falsely accused of sacrilege, incest, fornication, and parricide as it is certain and true that precisely those crimes—or ones altogether similar and even greater—are actually committed by the pagans themselves. 327

**CHAP. XXIX.** Nor is it any more true that Christians worship a man affixed to a cross for his crimes. For they rightly believe him to be not merely innocent but also God. [Col. 0364C] Pagans, by contrast, invoke the divine powers of kings whom they themselves have enrolled among the gods, make supplication before their images, and implore their guardian spirits. 331

**CHAP. XXX.** Octavius also proves utterly shameless the slander that Christians drink the blood of an infant whom they have killed. Pagans, he says, both cruelly expose newborn children and kill them by cruel abortion before they are born. Christians are not permitted even to witness or hear of homicide. 333

**CHAP. XXXI.** The polluted incestuous banquet alleged against Christians is as remote from every probability as it is certain [Col. 0364D] that pagans are in fact guilty of incest. Christian banquets are not merely chaste, but sober as well. So far removed, indeed, are Christians from a desire for incest that for some even a chaste union is a cause for modest embarrassment. 335

**CHAP. XXXII.** Nor can it be said that Christians conceal what they worship merely because they have no temples or altars. For they are persuaded that God cannot be confined within any temple, nor can an image of him be fashioned. Present everywhere, he sees everything, even the more secret thoughts of our mind; we live near him [Col. 0365A] and in his bosom. 338

**CHAP. XXXIII.** But if it is nevertheless said that God was of no benefit to the Jews, the writers of Jewish annals are certainly most substantial witnesses that the Jews first abandoned God before they themselves were abandoned by him. 342

**CHAP. XXXIV.** There is nothing surprising if this world is ultimately to be consumed by fire, for all things that have a beginning also have an end. Nor do the ancient philosophers reject the doctrine of a conflagration of the world. It is nevertheless certain that God can raise from death to life the human being whom he fashioned from nothing. All nature, moreover, rehearses the resurrection that is to come. 344

[Col. 0365B] **CHAP. XXXV.** Octavius then shows that righteous and devout people are to be granted everlasting happiness, but the unrighteous are to be afflicted with eternal punishments. He then clearly demonstrates that the morals of Christians are far holier than those of pagans. 348

**CHAP. XXXVI.** No less clearly, he teaches that fate is nothing other than what God has spoken. The mind is free, and therefore a person’s conduct, not his birth, is judged. He next makes perfectly clear that the poverty for which Christians are reproached is not a disgrace but a glory, and that their suffering bodily evils is not punishment but military service. 350

[Col. 0365C] **CHAP. XXXVII.** Torments most unjustly inflicted for the confession of Christ are spectacles worthy of God. Octavius clearly demonstrates this by comparing certain exceptionally brave pagans with the holy martyrs. [Col. 0366A] He further declares that Christians do not attend public shows and processions because they know with absolute certainty that these are no less impious than cruel. 352

**CHAP. XXXVIII.** They likewise abstain from food sacrificed to idols, lest anyone suppose that they either yield to demons or are ashamed of their religion. Yet they do not reject every color and fragrance of flowers. They customarily use flowers scattered, loose, and soft, and encircle their necks with garlands; but they consider it superfluous and useless to crown the head of the dead. They bury their dead with the same tranquility with which they live, awaiting with absolutely certain hope the crown of eternal happiness. Their true religion, therefore, after the superstitions of the pagans have been rejected, must be adopted by everyone. 355

**CHAP. XXXIX.** After Octavius had thus concluded his speech, Minucius and Caecilius remained for some time stunned into silence, their faces fixed in attention. Minucius, indeed, carried away in admiration of Octavius, remained silent, wordlessly turning over within himself what he had heard. 357

**CHAP. XL.** Caecilius, however, exclaimed that he had been defeated by Octavius, that he was now the conqueror of error, and that he henceforth professed the Christian religion; fuller instruction in the mysteries of the faith was meanwhile postponed until the following day. 358

[Col. 0366C] **CHAP. XLI.** At last they all depart glad and cheerful: Caecilius because he had believed; Octavius because he had conquered; and Minucius because the former had believed and the latter had conquered. 359

[Col. 0365]

# LETTER OF LUCAS HOLSTENIUS ON THE SPITS OF DIANA OF EPHESUS, IN CONNECTION WITH MINUCIUS XXI

[Note: [Col. 0365D] Above, chap. 21, col. 305.]

[Col. 0365D] Lucas Holstenius wishes prosperity to Francesco Cardinal Barberini, the finest patron of learning.

Since, by a singular act of generosity, you ordered the learned little work of Claude Menestrier—formerly a member of your household and a most skillful investigator of antiquarian matters—to be brought before the public, a work in which he lucidly explained the statues of Diana of Ephesus inscribed with recondite enigmas, [Col. 0366D] I thought it would not be unwelcome to you if I took the same opportunity to submit to you a thought that occurred to me long ago concerning ancient coins of that same Diana. I have done this all the more willingly and, I hope, with all the more justification because it embraces a subject left untouched by Menestrier and so far unnoticed by any antiquarian. I submit this writing to your judgment because no one understands more correctly than you the manifold [Col. 0367A] service that an exact knowledge of antiquity renders in adorning and enlarging every other branch of study. For since you rightly judged that nothing lies so deeply hidden or obscure in the writings of the ancients that it cannot borrow some light from ancient monuments, that was your reason for adding to the most celebrated library you assembled an abundant collection of ancient tablets, statues, coins, and inscriptions, so that you might place the whole memorial record of learned antiquity before the eyes of scholars. Now learn the matter itself.

Ancient coins stamped with the image of Diana of Ephesus, some of which are shown on the accompanying plate, differ from the statues produced through Menestrier’s industry in this respect: they support the goddess, burdened by the weight of her breasts, on either side with certain props or supports that one might take for knotted staffs. [Col. 0367B] All the examples I have seen—and I have seen very many—agree so consistently on this point that I think it must be affirmed beyond doubt that the Ephesian image was once supported in the same manner. Nor does a passage of Minucius Felix, a most learned writer, permit us to doubt the matter; there he mentions the image of Diana of Ephesus as built up with many breasts and iron spits (*verubus*). But the acumen of critics has thus far exercised itself wonderfully in corrupting that passage—so much so that, unless a defense is opportunely supplied from ancient books and monuments, it will hereafter be rendered inadmissible as testimony.

I shall explain the matter more clearly, so that it may be thoroughly perceived how unhappily Felix has been received and treated by his editors. The first Roman edition, prepared by Faustus Sabaeus [Col. 0367C] according to the Vatican manuscript, presents the passage I have mentioned as follows:

> Diana, meanwhile, as huntress, is girt up high; the Ephesian Diana is built up with many breasts and spits; and Trivia is rendered terrible with three heads and many hands.

Thus the learned writer accurately distinguished, by their peculiar marks and emblems, a threefold divinity of the single Diana, in accordance with the fabulous theology of the pagans. The Basel edition and the Heidelberg edition of Franciscus Balduinus scrupulously preserved the reading of the first edition, as did the later Roman edition, which appeared according to the recension of Fulvius Ursinus—except that this extremely precise scholar appended his own conjecture in the margin, advising that the text should read not “spits” (*verubus*) but “udders” (*uberibus*). The two editions of Desiderius Heraldus, an advocate of Paris, then reproduced the Roman reading; but one of them, changing a single letter, presents *veribus* in place of *verubus*, following, as he notes, the ancient manuscript itself [Col. 0367D] which, through the munificence of Leo X, passed from the Vatican Library into the royal library. That unique manuscript had been sent to King Francis together with a printed copy that the Roman editors had dedicated to him. This slight change induced Heraldus to judge that the reading should be either “udders” (*uberibus*), with Ursinus, or “swellings” (*tuberibus*), with Joseph Scaliger; he nevertheless inclined more toward the former conjecture.

These men, indeed, indulged in conjecture only so far as to keep their hands off Minucius’ text itself. But the others afterward were not equally scrupulous. For Joannes Wowerius, my fellow citizen, otherwise excellently furnished with learning and judgment, embraced Ursinus’ conjecture so completely that [Col. 0368A] he did not hesitate to admit it into Minucius’ text as unquestionably genuine. Rigaltius at Paris subsequently followed his example, as have, most recently, the Dutch editors in a repeated edition. The authority of Justus Lipsius seems to have lent no small support to this confidence, since they knew that he had approved this correction in his notes on Tacitus, *Annals*, Book III. All these men followed exactly in Ursinus’ footsteps. Geverhart Elmenhorst, however, a man certainly not lacking in diligence, took a different path. Not daring to change the Roman reading, he wretchedly dislocated the passage by transposing the words in the larger Hamburg edition, where Minucius’ words are read in this deformed state:

> Diana, meanwhile, as huntress, is girt up high and built up with spits; the Ephesian Diana has many breasts; and Trivia has three heads, etc.

Yet these things are comparatively slight beside what Petrus Faber, a celebrated authority on law, had already devised concerning [Col. 0368B] the same passage of Minucius in Book III, chap. 3, of his *Semestria*. Sharply assailing St. Jerome for distinguishing the many-breasted Diana of Ephesus from the huntress who holds a bow and is girt up high, he attempts, with great but fruitless effort, to prove that the ancients knew a many-breasted Ceres but were ignorant of a many-breasted Diana. Therefore, lest Minucius’ words support Jerome’s case, he distorts, corrects, and interpolates them as follows:

> Diana, meanwhile, is the Ephesian huntress girt up high, and Ceres is built up with many breasts.

But this is not, as he proclaims of himself, to correct a corrupted passage, but to corrupt one that was sound. So great a man would surely have refrained from this unfortunate controversy if he had, even through a lattice, [Col. 0368C] inspected an ancient image of Diana of Ephesus or her coins.

To the foregoing I shall add a man now celebrated in France, the king of this antiquarian court, Jean Tristan. In volume I he presents a coin of the ΚΑΔΟΗΝΩΝ, “of the Cadueni” (for I shall show that they are so named by Stephanus, Pliny, and himself elsewhere), stamped with the image of Diana of Ephesus; and, in illustrating it, he adduces Minucius’ much-abused passage, intending to make his own trial of ingenuity upon it. He therefore rejects “spits” (*verubus*), which he considers not a genuine word of Minucius but an invention of Wowerius—although Wowerius’ actual view was entirely different—and judges that the reading should indeed be “udders” (*uberibus*), but in a sense far removed from that of all the others. For he had very correctly perceived that grammarians establish either no distinction at all, or only a thoroughly foolish one, between breasts (*mammae*) and udders (*ubera*), and that this tautology [Col. 0368D] could therefore scarcely be attributed without fault to a writer of exact and concise diction. He accordingly proposed, with considerable ingenuity, that the many, milk-rich breasts of Diana of Ephesus should be explained as breasts swollen and distended with much milk. By this interpretation he plainly destroys the corruption introduced by Ursinus and all the critics who subsequently followed in his footsteps. Yet he did not attain Minucius’ meaning, because he rashly put his trust in the recent and interpolated edition that he appears to have used.

But all these men had their eyes and minds clouded as if by glaucoma when dealing with this perfectly clear passage of Minucius, because they had not investigated the precise meaning in which *verua* were properly named and understood by the ancient authorities on the Latin language. For since the roasting-spits—or “transfixing implements,” as Papias calls them—used in the kitchen, [Col. 0369A] and rightly ridiculed by Tristan in the French translation of Minucius, seemed to contribute nothing at all to the construction of Diana of Ephesus, they all agreed—astonishingly—that Minucius’ *verua* could only be understood and explained as the darts or javelins of Diana the huntress. Hence so many supreme and incomparable men conspired in rivalry to interpolate that word. Against this united host, however, I affirm that these *verua* are free from corruption, and I insist that they must be taken away neither from Diana of Ephesus nor from Minucius. For the *verua* with which the Ephesians constructed their Diana are not spears or javelins, but elongated iron supports which, placed beneath her arms, sustained the entire mass of her breast-laden chest.

[Col. 0369B] Since this extremely ancient image, in the manner of Egyptian statues, had its feet tightly pressed together, its very small base was unequal to bearing the weight of the body placed upon it and had to be reinforced with supports. If those were removed, the whole mass would necessarily weaken and collapse. Because those props or supports were extended at some length in iron, Minucius called them *verua*, using an exact and elegant word and following the usage not of the later age in which he lived, but of the Augustan age. For a Latin glossary of the highest quality, extant in three extremely ancient Vatican manuscripts, explains *verua* as iron rods and little rods.

Experience itself taught me that this explanation is true and genuine; and I think that even now you remember that experience, Most Eminent Cardinal, because you once witnessed it together with me. It was [Col. 0369C] fifteen years ago, unless I am mistaken, when the Society of Jesus at St. Andrew’s on the Quirinal, while laying the foundations of a new building, encountered several very large stones of Tiburtine limestone arranged in a square. Two of them were inscribed as follows, as I copied the inscription from the rough and poorly polished stone at your command and with your assistance:

> THIS AREA, ENCLOSED WITHIN THIS BOUNDARY OF TERMINAL STONES BY IRON RODS, TOGETHER WITH THE ALTAR BELOW, WAS DEDICATED BY THE EMPEROR CAESAR DOMITIAN AUGUSTUS GERMANICUS, IN FULFILLMENT OF A VOW THAT HAD BEEN UNDERTAKEN BUT HAD LONG BEEN NEGLECTED AND NOT DISCHARGED, FOR THE PURPOSE OF PREVENTING FIRES.

[Col. 0369D] Those boundary stones preserved two holes on either side and traces of the *verua*, or iron rods, surrounded with lead. By these rods they had formerly been joined to one another and had enclosed the inner area so that access was not generally open. I then perceived from the physical objects themselves how remarkably mistaken was N. Rigaltius, a man otherwise of the keenest discernment, when, in his notes on the writers *On the Demarcation of Boundaries*, he explained these *verua* as stakes sharpened to points like awls; I had learned with my own eyes and hands that they possessed no sharpness or point. In the same ancient sense, Marcellus, an early medical author, prescribes the following in chap. 10 for stopping a flow of blood from the nostrils:

> Continually quench a glowing iron *veru* in vinegar, and draw its smoke into the nostrils.

[Col. 0370A] Who does not see that what is meant here, simply and without qualification, is a mass of iron drawn out into a long rod—the form in which nearly all rough and unworked iron commonly comes?

Yet nothing more suitable for illuminating Minucius’ meaning and the matter at issue can be adduced than the verses of Prudentius from the first poem *Against Symmachus*. In them he describes the statues of the twin brothers Castor and Pollux in the bearing and posture in which they could then be seen in their temple beside the Sacred Way. These are the verses:

> The twin brothers too,  
> Bastard sons of a corrupted mother, offspring of Leda,  
> Riders of the night and two divinities of lofty Rome,  
> Loom overhead, held back by an iron rod, and fix in place  
> With poured lead the footprints that announce their mighty triumph.

He graphically depicts the Dioscuri represented in the posture of men running, [Col. 0370B] projecting beyond the perpendicular line and the base, so that they appeared to loom over those who saw them, not without horror and fear. For objects “loom overhead” when they hang above one’s head and seem on the very point of falling, as Valla rightly says. Fear and wonder, moreover, produced an impression of religious awe among the rude and superstitious populace. The Christian poet mocks that fear, since there was no danger that the statues would fall or run away: a *veru*—that is, an iron bar or hook fixed into their backs—held them in place, and their feet, lead-fastened to their bases, could not move.

This twofold kind of restraint, by which the images of the gods were fixed fast as though bound with chains, is similarly reproached by Arnobius in Book VI *Against the Nations*: “If,” he says, “they are subject to the necessity of remaining in place, what could be more wretched or more unfortunate than they, if hooks and leaden fastenings thus hold them upon their bases?” [Col. 0370C] Both kinds are also joined together in Law II of the *Digest*, *On the Violation of a Tomb*: “Celsus asks whether, if a statue was neither secured with lead nor fastened down, it became part of the monument, or whether it remains among our possessions.”

But Prudentius, too, was made to experience Minucius’s fate and the critics’ heavy hand because the meaning of the same word was not sufficiently well observed. Hence in the very ancient manuscripts of the Vatican Library one may see *retinente solo* (“held by the ground”) substituted for *retinente veru* (“held by the iron bar”); Aldus and others who followed the authority of his text printed that reading. George Fabricius, however, finding *retinente veru* consistently written in his copies, but not having adequately understood the word’s proper usage among the ancients, resorted to emendation, that sacred anchor of critics. [Col. 0370D] Accordingly, since he knew that the Dioscuri were commonly armed with spears or javelins for a cavalry exercise, he sharpened this *veru*, made from rough and blunt iron, with the point of a javelin, and, by altering the wording, forged from his own abundant ingenuity the reading *impendent retinentque veru*—“they overhang and hold a spear.” From that time onward this reading established itself in most of the more recent editions. Yet I am so far from approving it that, on the contrary, I do not hesitate to defend the ancient and genuine reading tenaciously, relying both upon the evident nature of the thing itself and upon the authority of the old books. Among these I readily assign first place to the excellent manuscript of the Urbino Library, which recently, through the immortal benefaction of the most wise Pope Alexander VII, was added to the Vatican Library; in it I found the text written thus.

[Col. 0371A] I have written these observations to elucidate the statues of Diana of Ephesus and ancient coins, so that, with their mutual assistance, I might rescue from the corruptions of critics two passages of ancient authors that have hitherto been less than correctly understood; and also [Col. 0372A] so that I might show by a distinguished example that the study of antiquity is not to be measured by empty pleasure, but yields its own proper fruit if rightly cultivated.

[Col. 0371]

# DISSERTATION ON THE BOOK OF MARCUS MINUCIUS FELIX ENTITLED *OCTAVIUS*

By Dom Nicolas Le Nourry, Monk of the Order of Saint Benedict, of the Congregation of Saint Maur

## CHAPTER ONE

### ANALYSIS OF THIS BOOK; WHO ITS AUTHOR WAS; AND WHO WERE CAECILIUS AND OCTAVIUS, WHO ARE INTRODUCED IN IT AS DISPUTANTS

[Col. 0371B]

## ARTICLE I

### Analysis of This Book

This book contains nothing other than a dialogue in which Caecilius, devoted to the superstitious vanities of the pagans, endeavors by various arguments to prove that no one should abandon the ancestral worship of the gods handed down by his forefathers, and that everyone should persevere in it. Octavius, on the other hand, who, after rejecting that impious worship, had enrolled himself together with Minucius Felix in the Christian profession, so thoroughly overturns all [Col. 0371C] Caecilius’s arguments, and demonstrates the truth of the Christian religion with such weighty reasons, that Caecilius, fully convinced by them, embraced it with a joyful and grateful heart.

At the very beginning of the book Minucius relates how greatly he delighted in the pleasant recollection of the things that had happened to him with Octavius while the latter was staying with him in Rome, and especially in the memory of this disputation. For Octavius had unexpectedly come to him on certain business during the vintage holidays and the recess of the courts. Octavius’s arrival was as welcome to Minucius as it was unexpected. After they had satisfied for a day or two the eagerness born of their intense longing, they decided to go together to the seaside baths at Ostia, taking with them Caecilius, Minucius’s companion. Accordingly, at daybreak, as they proceeded toward the sea “walking along,” [Col. 0371D] as he says, upon the shore, Caecilius, “upon noticing” an image of Serapis, raised his hand to his mouth and pressed a kiss upon it with his lips. Octavius at once sharply reproached Minucius, saying that the disgrace of this impious act reflected no less upon him, as Caecilius’s host, than upon Caecilius himself. Nevertheless, after traversing [Col. 0372B] the remainder of their route, they walked along the seashore conversing about voyages.

There, moreover, while Minucius and Octavius watched with some pleasure the boys playing at throwing shells into the sea, Caecilius, by contrast, paid no attention to so pleasing a spectacle and displayed a rather gloomy frame of mind. Minucius therefore missed his customary cheerfulness. Caecilius frankly confessed that Octavius’s words had struck him deeply, and for that reason asked to be allowed to debate with Octavius concerning the truth of his religion. Octavius agreed, together with his companion; and, after a somewhat elevated spot had been selected, Minucius sat between Caecilius and Octavius.

Before Caecilius entered upon this disputation, however, he asked Minucius to hold the scales of a perfectly impartial judge, [Col. 0372C] just as if nothing whatever had yet become known to him about either religion. He then confidently asserted that it could very easily be proved that everything in human affairs is doubtful, unresolved, uncertain, and less true than plausible. It was therefore deplorable, he said, and deserving of everyone’s indignation, that certain uneducated men, ignorant of the sciences and arts, did not hesitate to make pronouncements about the supreme order of things and the divine majesty, concerning which the philosophers had not dared to establish anything certain down to that very day. Nor was this without reason, since they were persuaded that weak human beings were forbidden to investigate heavenly matters and ought to be satisfied if they came to know themselves more intimately. He then attempted by a brief induction to demonstrate that it was uncertain whether all things had been made by some God as their author. From the prosperous fortune [Col. 0372D] of wicked men such as Phalaris and Dionysius, the adverse fortune of good men such as Rutilius, Camillus, and Socrates, and the varied and unstable accidents of earthly affairs, he strove to prove that it had not yet been established for us whether the world is governed by God’s providence or whether fortune, unbound by laws, rules over all things.

[Col. 0373A] From this, therefore, he concluded that it was better to adhere to the religions handed down from antiquity and to fear and adore the gods than to pass any judgment about them. For from the very beginning of the world our ancestors had regarded these gods either as propitious beings or as kings. Every nation, and afterward the Romans, had so worshiped its own divinities that the Romans, through their pious worship, deserved to obtain supreme dominion over the whole world. He then did not hesitate to assert that this worship of the gods—which is holier in proportion as it is older—was sufficiently proved by certain miracles and had not been scorned and mocked with impunity by certain impious persons. After declaring that he had passed over many other things concerning the gods’ natural attributes and gifts, the songs of the poets, and the oracles that foretold the future, he confidently pronounced that the gods’ presence became manifest to anyone [Col. 0373B] from the temples they inhabited; from the seers who knew what was to come; from the benefits by which the gods themselves were accustomed to render good service to human beings; and, finally, from dreams, through which they were most clearly recognized. Although, therefore, the nature or origin of these gods might be uncertain, the consensus of all nations concerning them ought nevertheless to remain firm. Hence he said that the impious temerity of Theodorus, Diagoras, and Protagoras, who wished utterly to abolish or at least to weaken this religion, was by no means to be tolerated.

Yet far less, he said, should that unlawful and desperate faction of Christians be tolerated—their light-shunning nation, gathered from the lowest dregs of humanity and bound together by nocturnal assemblies, solemn fasts, and inhuman foods. They indeed regard temples [Col. 0373C] as tombs, reject the gods, mock sacred rites, set honors at naught, and finally despise tortures in such a way that, although they fear to die after death, they meanwhile do not fear to die. Nevertheless, though scattered throughout every region of the earth, they recognize one another by secret signs and love one another almost before becoming acquainted. They are said to adore the head of an ass, to worship the genitals of their priest, and to venerate a crucified man and the very instrument of his punishment. What more need be said? On a solemn day they gather for a feast, and there, after drinking the blood of an infant most cruelly slain, they ratify the covenant they have struck, and their novices are initiated. After this banquet of utterly monstrous savagery, when the lamps have been extinguished by a dog, they all mingle indiscriminately, as chance determines, amid shameless darkness; and thus they become incestuous either in deed or in conscience. Moreover, [Col. 0373D] whatever they worship, they strive with great care to conceal: they have no altars, no temples, no publicly recognizable images.

Their God, moreover, is said to be one, as is that of the Jews. Though they can neither see nor display him, they nevertheless suppose him to be thoroughly restless in mind, perversely inquisitive, present everywhere, and carefully investigating all human deeds and the innermost thoughts of the mind, even though he cannot attend to every individual.
