They also assert that the whole world will one day be consumed by fire and promise, after the resurrection of our bodies, a supremely blessed eternity of life to the just and an eternity of the greatest punishments to the unjust. For this reason they condemn funeral pyres and burial by fire, and ascribe everything to the divine will or to fate. Yet no dead person can be raised [Col. 0374A] from the underworld, and no one has ever, by the fortune of Protesilaus, been recalled to life even for a single hour. What will happen to these Christians after death they ought to infer from the fact that now, deprived of all divine assistance and subjected to the Romans, they are crushed by the greatest calamities and miseries. They abstain from respectable pleasures, spectacles, processions, public banquets, food offered to idols, flowers, and crowns, and reserve ointments for funerals.

Caecilius therefore urged his companions to stop probing the regions of heaven and the secrets of the universe and to follow this maxim of Socrates: “What is above us is no concern of ours.” And Socrates certainly deserved to be praised by the divine oracle for this reason: “Because he had learned that he knew nothing.” From this source flowed the prudent doubt of Arcesilaus, Carneades, and very many Academics regarding the highest questions, [Col. 0374B] as well as the hesitation of Simonides when questioned about the gods by the tyrant Hiero—a hesitation that all should imitate. Finally, Caecilius declared that he gladly subscribed to their opinion and, not without the disdain of an exalted spirit, challenged Octavius to answer his arguments; with this he ended his speech.

Minucius then answered Caecilius calmly that he should not exult in the elegance of his discourse, the subtle variety of his speech, or his considerable eloquence; rather, each of his arguments must be carefully weighed, so that whatever was true and valid in them might be selected, approved, and accepted. But Caecilius, with some indication that his feelings had been wounded, said that Minucius, by weakening the force of his argument, was departing from the office of a conscientious judge. For Octavius was entirely free [Col. 0374C] to refute, if he could, everything Caecilius had brought forward, and Caecilius was now fully prepared to listen to him in profound silence.

“I shall indeed speak,” Octavius replied, “and shall strive according to my powers to wash away the most bitter stain of abuse with a flood of truthful words.” Before all else, he declared that it was not right for him to conceal the doubtful, divided, wandering, and fluctuating character of Caecilius’s mind and opinion. Yet he acknowledged that this should be attributed neither to any malicious deceit on Caecilius’s part nor to a crafty and cunning disposition—something entirely foreign to his sincerity—but to ignorance of the truth.

Then, proceeding to weaken each of Caecilius’s arguments, he taught that no one should resent the fact that [Col. 0374D] Christians, however unlettered and poor, discuss heavenly matters. For such were not only the philosophers and other inventors of the arts, but also men of our own people who, although poor and needy, imparted wisdom and learning to others. And since ability is bestowed neither by fortune nor by wealth, but is implanted in us by nature, any human being of either sex and of any condition can investigate divine matters and form a judgment about them.

He indeed acknowledged that a person ought to know himself—who he is, whence and why he came, by whom and from what elements he was made—but he wholly and utterly denied that this knowledge could be acquired without first knowing the universe [Col. 0375A] and God himself. For no one, unless entirely bereft of reason, can observe the ordered beauty of the whole world without being immediately persuaded that it was not founded by a chance collision of atoms, but was created by God and is ruled and administered by him. Octavius confirms and establishes this from the motions and usefulness of the heavens, the sun, the moon, and the stars; from the cycle of the months; the alternation of darkness and light; the marvelous order of the seasons; the constant variation of crops; the bounds of the sea; the manifold armor naturally bestowed upon living creatures for their defense; the human form and figure; and the manner of generation and birth. For none of these things can come about without the providence of almighty God. God, moreover, takes thought not only for the whole world, but for each [Col. 0375B] of its parts. For who doubts that at his command Britain is made fruitful by the warmth of the sea, Egypt by the Nile, Mesopotamia by the Euphrates, and the East by the river Indus? Finally, just as we see that someone presides over a house arranged with splendid ornament, so we see that this Lord presides over the whole world.

Octavius further proved that God himself is one by the example of earthly empires—those of the Persians, Thebans, and Romans—where, he says, neither brother could ever tolerate his brother nor father-in-law his son-in-law as a partner in sovereignty. And what of the fact that, just as bees, flocks, and herds have only one king or leader, so there is one God, who, lacking beginning and end, governs all things?

Although he is infinite and immeasurable, and known in his full magnitude [Col. 0375C] to himself alone, and although he can neither be seen nor named by us, nevertheless, if you remove the earthly additions made to names, you will clearly recognize him. Indeed, Octavius argues that there is unanimous agreement among all concerning him from the fact that ordinary people invoke him while stretching their hands toward heaven. Moreover, the poets called him the father of gods and humans, and Virgil called him the creator, mind, and spirit of all things. Indeed, the more distinguished philosophers themselves—as Octavius shows individually—Thales, Anaximenes, Diogenes of Apollonia, Anaxagoras, Pythagoras, Xenophanes, Antisthenes, Speusippus, Democritus, Strato, Aristotle, Heraclides, Theophrastus, Zeno, Chrysippus, Cleanthes, Diogenes of Babylon, Xenophon, Aristo, and Plato, although [Col. 0375D] differing from us in words and expression, nevertheless adopted our view concerning that same one God, some more obscurely and others more plainly.

Having thus argued, Octavius clearly convicts of falsehood the ridiculous old wives’ tales and absurd traditions concerning Scylla, the Chimera, the Hydra, the Centaurs, and others, which our ancestors had retailed as miracles. No less clearly does he show that the worship of the gods was always foolish and impious. For the most ancient people first venerated as gods their kings, illustrious leaders, queens who were chaste and possessed of courage beyond that usual for their sex, and inventors of the arts, because of their splendid deeds or the benefits received from them. This is proved by Octavius [Col. 0376A] from the testimony of Euhemerus, Prodicus, Persaeus, and Alexander the Great, who recount the homelands, birthdays, tombs, or benefactions of the gods and the secrets of their priests. The pagans could not therefore deny these things, any more than they could deny that the sistrum of Isis, the tomb of Serapis or Osiris, and their sacred mysteries disclose nothing other than the sorrowful ends, deaths, and funerals of wretched gods. Who, moreover, does not see that the Eleusinian rites of Ceres and the other rites of Jupiter and Cybele are no less absurd than disgraceful?

What great absurdities and foul nonsense, besides, do the pagans retail about the form and appearance of their gods! They fashion Vulcan as lame; Apollo as beardless; his son Aesculapius as bearded; Neptune with sea-green eyes; Minerva with gray-blue eyes; Juno with bovine eyes; [Col. 0376B] Mercury with winged feet; Pan with hooves; Saturn in fetters; Janus with two faces; Diana with her robe girded high; the Ephesian Diana with many breasts; Trivia with three heads and many hands; Jupiter hideous with as many monstrous forms as the names by which he is called; Erigone hanging from a noose; the Castors living and dying on alternate days; Aesculapius struck by lightning; and Hercules burned in the fires of Mount Oeta.

These tales, first handed down by impious men, were afterward celebrated by others, and especially by the poets, who did no small harm to truth through their authority. Plato therefore not undeservedly expelled Homer from his city, for Homer sang in shameless mockery of Venus wounded, Mars driven into flight not without wounds, Jupiter freed by Briareus, Jupiter weeping over Sarpedon’s [Col. 0376C] fall in showers of blood, and Jupiter ensnared by the girdle of Venus; of Hercules carrying away dung; Neptune building Laomedon’s walls without any payment; Apollo pasturing Admetus’s flock; Vulcan forging the thunderbolts of Jupiter, who was born in Crete; the adultery of Mars and Venus; and Ganymede’s abduction by Jupiter himself. Yet by those ridiculous and obscene inventions the minds of children are corrupted, and finally they grow shamefully and wickedly old in them.

From Diodorus Siculus, Thallus, and Nepos, whom Octavius cites, everyone could nevertheless have learned very easily that Saturn was the foremost of these gods. Fleeing from Crete through fear of his son and received in Italy by Janus, he taught many things to uncivilized people; and, by imposing his own name upon various places, he proved [Col. 0376D] himself to have been a human being. Jupiter, moreover, who reigned in Crete after driving Saturn from it, died on that island, where his tomb is shown. Furthermore, Romulus after his death—through Proculus’s perjury—Juba at the wish of the Moors, and others as well, although unwilling and resistant, were proclaimed gods. Yet the true God can neither be born nor die.

Octavius next attacks the images and statues of the gods and makes it plain that, whether fashioned from cheap and filthy material or from precious matter, made in one way or another by the hands and skill of craftsmen, and very often befouled by birds and other animals, they are impiously worshiped by the pagans and wearied with prayers to no purpose and without effect. He also demonstrates by a brief survey how many ridiculous, obscene, and cruel rites were observed in celebrating [Col. 0377A] the mysteries of certain gods.

He then shows that Caecilius falsely boasted that the Romans gained dominion over the whole world by duly observing superstitions of this kind. For that kingdom began with fratricide and grew through crimes, impiety, and sacrilege. And what of the fact that their native gods—Romulus, Picus, Tiberinus, Consus, Pilumnus, Picumnus, Cloacina, Fear, Pallor, Fever, Disease, Acca Larentia, and Flora—could offer the Romans no assistance? Still less could the gods of other nations, whom the Romans did not worship until they had first defeated them in war and celebrated a triumph over them. Finally, no one is unaware that the Assyrians, Medes, Persians, Greeks, and Egyptians ruled before any of the Roman superstitions, [Col. 0377B] which are worse than all the rest.

The weapon lightly hurled by Caecilius from the auspices and auguries of birds is turned back against him by Octavius through the examples of Regulus, Mancinus, Paulus, and Caesar. By the similar examples of Amphiaraus, Tiresias, and the Pythian Apollo, Octavius also demonstrates that the argument drawn from oracles is no more valid. But because someone might press the objection that at least some oracles had been true, Octavius judged that the matter must be taken up at a deeper level and traced back to its first origin. He therefore says that there are certain impure spirits who, through lust and vice, lost the simplicity of their substance. Nor could the pagans deny this. For the poets call them *daemones* (“demons”), and they were known to the Magi and to Socrates, [Col. 0377C] who had one of them as guardian and counselor. Hostanes and Plato explain who these spirits are. Now the Magi and others, by the breath and inspiration of these ruined angels, who strive to ruin human beings together with themselves, perform various magical deceptions.

Those same demons lurk beneath statues and images, dwell in shrines, or creep into human bodies; they disturb the natural order of certain things, pour forth oracles wrapped in false responses, and bring about other extraordinary events—such as those Caecilius had recounted concerning Jupiter, the Castors, and Claudia—in such a way that they appear to the pagans to have performed true miracles. Yet they are then compelled to confess that these things were done not by God but by themselves, when they are adjured by Christians through the true God and driven by sacred exorcisms [Col. 0377D] from the bodies they possess. For this reason they flee Christians when they draw near and stir up such hatred against them among the pagans that the latter begin not only to hate them before knowing them, but also to impute to them unspeakable crimes that no one has yet been able to prove. Octavius indeed clearly testifies that he had learned this from his own experience: when he and his associates were still pagans, they tried by various tortures to compel Christians, not so much to confess those fictitious crimes as to renounce the faith of Christ.

There Octavius demonstrates with irresistible force that Christians were as falsely accused of sacrilege, incest, debauchery, and parricide as it was certain and true that precisely the same [Col. 0378A] crimes, or others entirely similar and even greater, were actually committed by the pagans themselves. First, he says, those who perversely clamored that Christians worshiped the head of an ass consecrated asses together with Epona and Isis, venerated the heads of oxen and rams, and dedicated gods represented either in goat or human form, or with the face of an ox or dog. Moreover, the Romans themselves worshiped the bull Apis, and others worshiped animals, serpents, birds, beasts, and fish, as did the Egyptians, who revered Isis and Serapis no more than the sharpness of onions and the breaking of wind from the belly.

As for Caecilius’s further objection that Christians worshiped the genitals of their priest, Octavius asserts that this was as false as it is certain that the pagans were defiled by utterly obscene acts of debauchery that we were never permitted either to name or to hear.

Nor was it any truer that we worship a man affixed to a cross for his crimes. For we rightly believe him not only innocent but God. The Egyptians, by contrast, slaughter victims and offer sacrifices to a man whom they themselves have chosen. Others invoke the divine powers of kings whom they have enrolled among the gods, supplicate their images, and implore their guardian spirits.

“We neither worship nor desire crosses,” Octavius continues. But perhaps the pagans venerate them as parts of their gods. For the shape of the cross is visible in the emblems, cantabrian standards, banners, trophies, and many other natural objects that they worship and that he enumerates.

[Col. 0378C] He also says that the accusation that Christians drink the blood of an infant killed by themselves is utterly shameless. The pagans, however, as he argues, both cruelly expose newborn children and, before they are born, kill them by the most cruel abortion. Saturn is said to have devoured his sons; infants are sacrificed by certain inhabitants of Africa, just as guests were sacrificed by the Taurians and the Egyptian Busiris, and human beings by the Gauls and Romans; and Jupiter himself is worshiped with this victim also—horrible to tell. What more? Catiline sealed his conspiracy with human blood; Bellona is propitiated with it; and epilepsy is cured by it. Finally, athletes devour beasts still fattened with human blood and limbs. Christians, however, are not permitted even to hear of or witness homicide, and are forbidden animal blood.

[Col. 0378D] The charge that Christians hold a banquet polluted by incest is as remote from all plausibility as it is certain that the pagans themselves are in fact guilty of incest. For the Persians have intercourse with their mothers, and the Egyptians and Athenians with their sisters. The poets, moreover, sing of the gods’ various execrable adulteries, of which very many pagans were themselves also aware. Christians, by contrast, bound by the bond of a single marriage, were always chaste outside it, or persevered in virginity, and held banquets marked by a chaste, sober, and dignified cheerfulness.

Although Christians reject purple robes and honors, they did not arise from the lowest dregs of the common people, nor are they factious or babblers in corners. The complaint repeatedly [Col. 0379A] made that their number was increasing daily was no uncertain testimony to their proven manner of life. They recognize one another, certainly, not by a mark upon the body but by the sign of innocence; and to the same degree that they love one another and rightly and deservedly call one another brothers, the pagans, though unknown to one another, rage more cruelly against their own selves in mutual hatred.

Nor can it be said that these Christians conceal what they worship because they have no shrines and no altars. For they were persuaded that God cannot be confined within any temple, that no image of him can be fashioned, and that no victim is more pleasing and acceptable to him than a person’s pure and sincere conscience.

Although we do not see this God with our eyes—just as we do not see the winds, the sun, or our own soul—we nevertheless clearly [Col. 0379B] recognize him from his works. Present everywhere, he sees all things, even the most secret thoughts of our mind, and we live near him and, as it were, in his bosom. But if it is said that God was of no benefit to the Jews, the writers of the Jewish annals were certainly most ample witnesses that they abandoned God before they were abandoned by him.

Moreover, since all things that have a beginning also have an end, it is no wonder if this world is ultimately to be consumed by fire. Octavius indeed shows that the Stoics, Epicureans, and Plato held this opinion concerning the conflagration of the world. But Plato, like Pythagoras, acknowledged only a partial restoration of a dead person to life. It is nevertheless certain that God can raise from death to life the human being whom he fashioned from nothing. [Col. 0379C] By certain examples Octavius proves that this resurrection of bodies will occur; Christians buried those bodies according to the ancient and better custom. In a manner not very different, he shows that after this life just and pious people are to be rewarded with eternal happiness, but the unjust with everlasting punishments. He then clearly demonstrates that the morals of Christians are far holier than those of the pagans. No less plainly does he teach that fate is nothing other than what God has spoken—*fatum* from *fatus est*—for God determines destinies in accordance with each person’s deserts. There he promises that he will at some time discuss fate more fully.

After this he makes it perfectly clear that the poverty reproached in Christians is not a disgrace but a glory; likewise, their adversities and the tortures inflicted upon them most unjustly, however horrifying, for their confession of Christ, and death itself, are not punishments but trials of virtue, triumphs, and spectacles worthy of God. [Col. 0379D] Octavius clearly shows this by comparing the deeds of certain most courageous pagans with those of our martyrs. But if any who do not know God abound in riches and honors or are raised to the highest pinnacle of rank and power, he asserts that these are victims fattened and crowned for punishment, who are lifted all the higher precisely so that they may fall with a heavier crash. For without the knowledge of God there can be no solid happiness.

Octavius further declares that Christians do not attend spectacles and processions because they had come to know with absolute certainty that these were no less impious than cruel. They likewise abstain from food offered to idols, [Col. 0380A] lest anyone think that they either yield to demons or are ashamed of their religion. Yet they do not spurn every color and fragrance of flowers. They are accustomed to use flowers scattered, loose, and soft, and to encircle their necks with garlands; but they consider it superfluous and useless to crown the head of a dead person. With the same tranquility with which they live, they also bury their dead, awaiting with the surest hope the crown of eternal happiness. Hence, however much Socrates, Arcesilaus, Carneades, Pyrrho, the Academics, and Simonides may assert that they know nothing for certain, Christians nevertheless rightly glory in having found the truth that those men sought in vain. Their true religion, therefore, once the superstitions of the pagans have been rejected, ought to be embraced by all.

When Octavius had concluded this speech and Minucius, [Col. 0380B] carried away in admiration of him, remained silent, Caecilius exclaimed that he had been defeated by Octavius, that he was now the victor over his own error, and that he already professed the Christian religion. Finally, a clearer explanation of our mysteries having been deferred until the following day, they all returned home joyful and cheerful.

## ARTICLE II

### Whether Minucius Felix Was the Author of This Book, and Who He Was

That Minucius Felix was the author of this book or dialogue is proved by such irresistible authority on the part of writers whose trustworthiness is beyond all question that no room for doubt on the matter can remain for anyone. For Firmianus Lactantius, who flourished under the emperor Diocletian, as Jerome notes (*Jerome, Catalogue of Writers*, § 80), and not long after Minucius, has these words concerning him (*Lactantius, Book I, On True Religion*, ch. 11): “Minucius Felix argued as follows in the book entitled *Octavius*: Saturn, when he had been driven away by his son and had come to Italy, etc.” These words we do indeed read in this book of Minucius. Afterward the same Lactantius says: “Among those known to me, Minucius Felix held no obscure place among advocates. His book, entitled *Octavius*, shows how capable a defender of the truth he might have been, had he devoted himself wholly to that study” (*Lactantius, Book V, On Justice*, ch. 1).

[Col. 0380D] Jerome, moreover, says in his *Catalogue of Illustrious Men*, or *Ecclesiastical Writers*: “Minucius Felix, a distinguished advocate at Rome, wrote a dialogue of a Christian and a pagan disputing”—the most ancient manuscript of Saint-Germain-des-Prés reads “of one disputing”—“which is entitled *Octavius* . . . Lactantius also mentions this Minucius in his books” (*Jerome, On Ecclesiastical Writers*, ch. 58), namely in those that, as you see, we have cited. To Magnus he further wrote the following concerning him (*Jerome, Letter to Magnus*): “Minucius Felix, an advocate of the Roman forum, in the book entitled *Octavius*, and in another *Against the Astrologers*—if, indeed, the title does not misrepresent the author—what portion of pagan literature did he leave untouched?” To Heliodorus also he writes the following concerning Nepotian [Col. 0381A] (*Jerome, Letter to Heliodorus*): “He used to say that saying of Tertullian . . . Thus Minucius Felix spoke, thus Victorinus, and in this manner Arnobius.” Finally, in the *Apology Against Jovinian* (*Jerome, Letter 30 to Pammachius*, or *Apology Against Jovinian*), he says: “I pass over the Latin writers Tertullian, Cyprian, Minucius, Victorinus, Lactantius, and Hilary.”

It would certainly be lengthy and useless to present all the testimonies of more recent writers concerning the author of this book. For it is sufficiently established that, with no one objecting, it is attributed by everyone to our Minucius and claimed for him with complete justice.

The additional name of the man who is called by some *Minutius*, with the letter *c* changed to *t*, was Marcus. For Octavius addressed him in these words: “It is not the part of a good [Col. 0381B] man, brother Marcus, to leave a man, etc.” Caecilius likewise said: “Although to you, brother Marcus, etc.”

How well known to all and how noble the consular family of the Minucii was among the Romans is plain; yet it has remained entirely unknown to everyone down to the present whether our Minucius derived his origin from that family or from some other. Nor has anyone more certainly ascertained what his native country was. Some nevertheless conjecture from the style of the work under discussion that he was born in Africa. But they neither prove nor can prove that any trace of the harsher African style is found in it. Could it not be said with better right that Caecilius and Octavius, who were bound to Minucius by so great a bond of affection, were actually Africans and his fellow countrymen? Yet, as we shall see shortly, this is neither certain nor can it be inferred without any doubt from even the closest intimacy of their friendship. [Col. 0381C]

We think, however, that no one will deny that Minucius lived for a long time at Rome, which was then the capital of all the other cities of the whole world, and that he discharged the office of an advocate there. Lactantius and Jerome, whom we have cited, openly and expressly assert this. Minucius himself writes at the beginning of this book that Octavius came to him at Rome and shortly afterward went with him and another companion to Ostia: “When,” he says, “the vintage holidays had relaxed the care of judicial business”—that is, when, during the vintage season, he had leisure from the forensic labor with which he was occupied throughout the year. Did not Octavius also say of himself and Minucius—or rather in the name of Minucius alone—“Nevertheless, we undertook to defend and protect some men accused of sacrilege and incest, and even parricides; but these men,” namely Christians, “we thought should not be heard at all”? From these words it is clear that, while he was still a pagan, he had discharged the office of an advocate.

We have Minucius himself, however, as witness that from early youth until he was already well into adulthood he had been bound by all the superstitions of the pagans, and that at last, having renounced them, he embraced the Christian faith. For he committed the following to writing about himself and Octavius: “He alone was privy to my affections and himself my companion in errors; and when, after the mist had been dispelled, I emerged from the depths of darkness into the light of wisdom and truth, he did not reject me as a companion but—what is more glorious—ran ahead of me.” Caecilius, moreover, addresses him thus from the very beginning of his speech [Col. 0382A]: “For you, Marcus my brother, there can be no uncertainty concerning the very matter we are now investigating”—that is, the truth of the pagan and Christian religions—“since, having carefully experienced both ways of life, you rejected the one and approved the other.” Indeed, Octavius, speaking perhaps not so much about himself, as we have said, as about Minucius Felix, again expresses himself in this manner: “How unjust it is to pass judgment upon what is unknown”—namely, the Christians—“and unexamined, as you do, believe us who ourselves repent of having done so. For we too were once the same, and, while still blind and dull-witted, held the same opinions as you: that Christians worshipped monsters, devoured infants, and mingled in incestuous banquets. Nor did we understand that these tales were always being bandied about by those men and [Col. 0382B] were never either investigated or proved. . . . We thought that they ought not even to be heard at all. Sometimes, even while taking pity on them, we raged against them all the more cruelly, torturing those who confessed in order to make them deny—ostensibly so that they might not perish—subjecting them to a perverse interrogation designed not to elicit the truth but to compel a lie. And if anyone weaker, crushed and overcome by suffering, denied that he was a Christian, we favored him, as though by abjuring the name he had now cleansed all his deeds through that denial. Do you recognize that we once thought and acted exactly as you now think and act?”

But someone may perhaps further ask us whether Minucius Felix, after professing the Christian faith, still devoted himself to discharging the office of advocate. Let him, I beg, attend to what [Col. 0382C] we observed shortly before: Minucius came with Caecilius and Octavius to Ostia, where the debate presented in the book under discussion was held, at the time when “the vintage holidays had relaxed his judicial duties.” Yet at that time, as we have shown from the words of Caecilius cited shortly before, Minucius professed the Christian religion. Therefore, when Caecilius had worshipped an image of Serapis that they encountered, Octavius immediately assailed Minucius in these words: “It is not the conduct of a good man, Marcus my brother, to abandon in such blindness of common ignorance a man who cleaves to your side at home and abroad, so that in the full light of day you allow him to stumble against stones . . . when you know that the disgrace arising from this error reflects no less upon you than upon him.” There, as you see, Octavius rebukes Minucius precisely because, although then professing the Christian religion, he had allowed the image of Serapis to be worshipped by Caecilius, his inseparable companion, during the journey he was making to the shore at Ostia. [Col. 0382D]

Nor should this seem surprising to anyone. For Christians at that time were not accustomed to resign their posts, dignities, or other offices together with the pagan religion. Rather, as we have said and shall explain more fully below, they were then dispersed throughout the whole world and intermingled with pagans, and were accustomed to conduct every kind of duty and business with them, excepting only the worship of the gods. Hence Tertullian says (Tertull., *Apologeticum*, ch. 37, p. 33): “We are but of yesterday, and we have filled everything that is yours: cities, islands, fortresses, municipalities, [Col. 0383A] meeting places, the camps themselves, tribes, decuries, the palace, the senate, and the forum; we have left you only the temples.” And below (the same, ibid., ch. 42): “And so we inhabit this world together with you, not without the forum, not without the meat market, baths, shops, workshops, inns, your markets, and other commercial dealings. We too sail with you, serve as soldiers with you, till the land, and trade; likewise, we combine our crafts with yours and make our labor available for your use. How we can appear unprofitable for your business, when we live both with you and by means of you, I do not know. But I do not attend your rites, etc.”

How piously and holily Minucius lived afterward is taught by Eucherius, bishop of Lyons, in these words (Eucher. Lugdun., Epistle to Valerian): “And when shall I unroll from that volume of harmonious eloquence the most illustrious Firmianus, Minucius, Cyprian, Hilary, John, and Ambrose? They had said, I believe: ‘What is this? The unlearned arise and seize heaven, while behold where we, with all our learning, wallow—in error and blood.’ They had said this, and therefore they afterward took the kingdom by force.”

## ARTICLE III. Who Caecilius and Octavius Were, Who Are Introduced as Disputants in This Book

Since this book, as we have seen, contains nothing other than a dialogue between Caecilius and Octavius debating the pagan and Christian religions, someone will doubtless ask us who these men were. But [Col. 0383C] we shall candidly reply that nothing more certain can be asserted about them than what may be drawn from this book. Caecilius, who pleads the pagans’ case, is also called Natalis there by Octavius: “Nor shall I conceal,” he says, “that at first my dear Natalis’s judgment wavered—erring, wandering, and unstable. . . . But in my Natalis I neither desire nor believe there to be cunning; subtle sophistication is far removed from his simplicity.” From these words we further gather that he was a good, upright, sincere man and a friend of unadorned truth.

Nor can anyone doubt that he was initially enslaved to the religion of the pagans, which in this book he strives in good faith and with all the powers of his intellect to defend. Indeed, when he understood that Octavius was striking at him through Minucius because, in the pagan manner, as has been said, he had saluted an image of Serapis, he was seized by such pain that he burst out in these words [Col. 0383D]: “For some time now the speech of our Octavius has sharply tormented and gnawed at me: in attacking you, he rebuked you for negligence so that, indirectly, he might accuse me more gravely of ignorance.” Finally, such were his integrity and candor, and such the sincerity of his mind, that after listening most attentively to Octavius’s speech, he immediately confessed himself vanquished on both points, abjured his former errors, and embraced the Christian faith.

Some think it can be gathered that his native city was Cirta—that is, that he originated from Cirta, the most famous town in Numidia—from the words in which he calls Fronto the orator “our man of Cirta”: “The speech of our fellow citizen of Cirta also bears witness to this.” Because Octavius knew perfectly well that this was true, he replied to him thus [Col. 0384A]: “Thus concerning this matter your Fronto too did not give testimony as one affirming a fact, but hurled abuse as an orator.” Nevertheless, since Caecilius could have called Fronto “his” for some other reason, let others judge how much weight this argument possesses.

Whatever may be decided about his native country, we do know that he lived for a long time in Rome and in the same house as Minucius. So close a bond of friendship existed between them there that Caecilius never left Minucius’s side. For Octavius openly declares that he was “a man who cleaved to the side” of Minucius Felix “at home and abroad.” Therefore, when Caecilius had worshipped an image of Serapis, Octavius immediately rebuked Minucius [Col. 0384B], saying: “You should know that the disgrace arising from this error reflects no less upon you than upon him.”

Moreover, he appears to have been a philosopher and a follower of the sect of the Academics, who asserted that everything was doubtful and uncertain and that they themselves knew nothing. In his speech he plays no other part than that of an Academic of this kind, as is most manifest to everyone not only from its beginning but also from its conclusion. What of the fact that in the same speech he endeavors to prove that it is entirely uncertain and has thus far been ascertained neither by himself nor by any human being whether there is one god or several, and that it is therefore better, in a matter so doubtful, to follow the traditions concerning those gods and their worship received from one’s ancestors? But when the light of truth shone upon him, he immediately rejected his former errors, as we have seen, [Col. 0384C] acknowledged and believed in one God, and professed the Christian religion.

Some have thought that it could be established from the writings of Lampridius that this Caecilius was an African by nationality, a rhetorician by profession, and the teacher of Diadumenianus, the son of Macrinus. But this opinion rests upon absolutely no reasoning, not even plausible reasoning—indeed, not even upon the name itself. For those who have been permitted to read the manuscript codices of Lampridius assert that in all of them the teacher of Diadumenianus is called neither Caecilius nor Caecilianus, but Caelianus. As for the suspicion of some others that he was the Natalis who, under the reign of Severus, confessed Christ but afterward defected to the Theodotian heretics, they plainly rely upon mere and utterly feeble conjecture—namely, only a similarity of name. [Col. 0384D]

Those, however, are thought to come closer to the truth who judge him to be the man who returned to Africa, was afterward ordained a presbyter, and brought Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, to the Christian religion itself. For Pontius the Deacon relates the following about him in his *Life of Cyprian* (Pont., *Vita Cypriani*): “He also had living with him one of our people, Caecilius, a righteous man of praiseworthy memory and at that time a presbyter both in age and rank, who had corrected him from secular error and brought him to the knowledge of the true divinity. He loved this man with every honor and all respect, receiving him with dutiful veneration, no longer as a friend equal to his own soul, but as the parent of his new life.” [Col. 0385A] In remembrance of so great a benefit, Cyprian doubtless assumed the additional name Caecilius. For what else, I ask, do these words of Jerome mean (Jerome, *De Scriptoribus Ecclesiasticis*, ch. 67): “Thereafter, at the persuasion of the presbyter Caecilius—from whom he also obtained his additional name—he became a Christian”?

Caecilius, in turn, treated Cyprian with such love and honor that, as Pontius further attests, when dying he entrusted his wife and children to him. “Won over by Cyprian’s devoted services,” says Pontius (Pont., *Vita Cypriani*), “he was deservedly moved to such immeasurable affection that, when departing from the world and with his summons now close at hand, he entrusted to him his wife and children; and the man whom he had made a sharer in the fellowship of the sect, he afterward made the heir of his familial duty.” They consider it not unreasonable to confirm that this was the Caecilius under discussion [Col. 0385B] from the fact that he and Cyprian belonged to the same period and, apparently, had the same native country, to which Caecilius had returned after professing the name of Christ. Added to this is the fact that Cyprian copied verbatim several passages from this book, which we shall discuss below. Yet even if you prove that nothing in these considerations conflicts with this opinion, you will nevertheless never persuade anyone that anything altogether certain and indubitable can be concluded from them.

Octavius, who is also called Januarius by Caecilius, was, as Minucius says, an excellent and holy man and his closest friend. Certainly each burned with such love for the other that “you would have believed,” says Minucius himself, “that a single mind had been divided between two men.” [Col. 0385C] Both, as we have noted, had also been advocates in legal cases and pagans, and both together, after abjuring the impious worship of the pagans, were initiated into the Christian religion. At that time Octavius was Minucius’s most faithful *contubernalis*, as Minucius himself calls him—that is, he lived with him in Rome. Afterward he returned to his native country, married there, and had several children. But while they were still infants, merely attempting half-formed words, he left them and came again to Rome on business and to visit Minucius, who received him with the greatest joy. His piety and holiness are sufficiently revealed by the fervor and zeal of mind with which he was carried against pagan superstitions, rebuking Caecilius, and even Minucius himself, so sharply because Caecilius had worshipped an image of Serapis, as we have seen. [Col. 0385D] We know, indeed, that in Cyprian’s time there were certain bishops in Africa, one of whom was called Natalis and the other Januarius. But whoever says that they were the same men who debate in this book of Minucius will be guessing at will, supported by absolutely no reasoning, however slight.

At the beginning of this book, moreover, Minucius seems to indicate that Octavius had departed this life when he committed to writing the latter’s dialogue with Caecilius. For there he explains how dear the memory of Octavius was to him and how deeply Octavius was lodged in his innermost feelings, and immediately adds: “Nor without reason did that excellent and holy man, in departing, leave us an immeasurable longing for him.” [Col. 0386A] Nevertheless, because he uses the simple word “departing,” it does not seem so easy for us to say whether it should be understood of Octavius’s death or of his departure from Minucius and Rome. We are not unaware, however, that certain learned men explain these words in the former sense, doubtless because Minucius added: “He left us an immeasurable longing for him.” Yet whether he could not have said this of a man most closely bound to him and his dearest friend—with whom he shared one mind and soul, and who had now been separated from him by a long distance over land—is for you, learned reader, to judge.

However the matter may stand, there are some who suspect that Octavius and Caecilius were fictitious, assumed personae introduced as disputants by our Minucius in this book. [Col. 0386B] Yet these men too offer absolutely no, not even the slightest, confirmation of their conjecture. We are well aware that various writers—from whom our author doubtless borrowed this dialogical form—quite often introduce invented figures of this kind in their books. But they generally alert their readers to this fiction in explicit words, or it is easily understood from their discourse. In our author’s book, by contrast, nothing whatever occurs that would lead us to believe either that real men did not conduct the debate or that all the events narrated are not true. Moreover, whatever one may say on this matter, Minucius’s arguments against pagan rites and in defense of the Christian religion will always remain intact and carry the same weight.

# CHAPTER II. ON THE DATE, STYLE, TITLE, SUBJECT, DIVISIONS, MANUSCRIPT CODICES, AND EDITIONS OF THIS BOOK; ON THE OBSERVATIONS OF VARIOUS SCHOLARS UPON IT; ON CORRUPT PASSAGES; AND ON WHAT MINUCIUS DREW FROM OTHERS AND OTHERS FROM HIM

[Col. 0386C]

## ARTICLE I. At What Time This Book Was Published

The time at which Minucius committed the conversation between Caecilius and Octavius to writing and fashioned it into the form of a book that it now displays is disputed among the most learned writers of the present age. Some believe that Minucius wrote this book around the year of Christ 160. [Col. 0386D] But they are led by no other reason than that they have persuaded themselves that the orator Fronto of Cirta, whom they call the teacher of the emperor Marcus Aurelius, is cited in this book. Yet it is entirely uncertain whether the Fronto praised by Minucius was really Aurelius’s tutor. Furthermore, what prevents Fronto, though previously deceased, from having been cited afterward by our author? Finally, in his *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers* (Jerome, *Catalog.*, §§ 53 and 58 [OCR: “584”]), Jerome assigns to Tertullian—whom he, like others, reports to have flourished under the emperors Severus and Caracalla—a place considerably earlier than Minucius.

Some, on the contrary, have thought that Minucius was later [Col. 0387A] than Cyprian, who ended his life in martyrdom in the year of Christ 258. For Jerome, they say, in his *Apology against Jovinian*, or *Epistle to Pammachius*, named our Minucius after that same Cyprian. From this they think two things can be established: first, that when Minucius discusses the persecution of Christians he indicates the persecution stirred up by the emperor Decius; and second, that in this book Minucius excerpted many things from Cyprian’s treatises.

But this entire argument rests solely upon Jerome’s *Apology*. There, however, when naming various writers, he does not follow chronological order. Once the foundation of this opinion has been overturned, therefore, the opinion itself must necessarily collapse as well. Nor does Minucius seem to speak of the Decian persecution [Col. 0387B], but of another and earlier one. Cyprian also undoubtedly excerpted his material from Minucius rather than Minucius from him.

For this reason, others judge that this book of our Minucius was published at the beginning of the Church’s third century, when, after the edicts issued by the emperor Severus, the pagans were raging against Christians. For in the *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers* (the same, *Catalog. Script. Eccles.*, §§ 58 and 59), where Jerome observes chronological order more carefully, he placed our Minucius immediately before Caius, as in all printed editions of that *Catalogue*, or immediately after him, as in our very ancient Saint-Germain codex, copied in Lombardic script a thousand years ago. But in all the codices of that work, whether printed or unprinted, Cyprian is placed considerably after both of them [Col. 0387C]—namely, after seven other writers. May one not infer from this that Minucius and Caius were contemporaries and older than Cyprian?

Now “Caius, under Zephyrinus, bishop of the city of Rome,” says Jerome, “that is, under Antoninus, the son of Severus, held a very notable disputation against Proculus, an adherent of Montanus.” Eusebius had already said more than once that this Caius lived during the pontificate of Zephyrinus (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, bk. II, ch. 25, and bk. VI, ch. 20). Zephyrinus is reported to have presided over the Roman Church from the year 201 or 202. The son of Severus, or Caracalla, whom Jerome mentions, ruled after his father Severus from 211 to 217. May it not therefore be concluded that the book of our Minucius was brought to light [Col. 0387D] under the rule of Caracalla, while the pagans were still committing outrages against Christians?

But learned men object that Caecilius reproached Octavius with the fact that Christians then had no temples, and that Octavius certainly did not deny it. Yet Origen, they say, in his commentaries on Matthew—which are reported to have been composed during the reign of Philip, that is, around the year 244—has testified to us that Christian churches had been burned (Origen, *Tractate on Matthew*, ch. 28). They had therefore previously been erected in public places, but not long before, and only when Alexander Severus ruled the Romans, around the year 222. For he, according to Lampridius, “wished to build a temple to Christ and receive him among the gods, something that Hadrian also is reported to have contemplated, since he had ordered temples without images to be constructed in every city” (Lampridius, *Life of Alexander Severus*, after the middle). [Col. 0388A] The Christians, therefore, doubtless did not lose the opportunity Alexander offered them to construct churches. But why, I ask, would they have failed to use a similar opportunity previously granted them by Hadrian, as Lampridius relates in the same passage? This argument therefore wavers, and absolutely nothing certain can be established from it.

They nevertheless press the point that Caecilius boldly asserted that Christians were people from the very dregs of the populace and were everywhere oppressed by the greatest misery and poverty. But this, they say, could not have been said except shortly before the reign of Alexander Severus, whose palace was filled with Christians—people who doubtless did not live in the greatest misery and [Col. 0388B] poverty.

But this argument certainly has no greater weight or force. For we have already heard Tertullian saying that the cities, fortresses, forum, senate, and palace had been filled with Christians, who had left nothing to the pagans except the temples of their false gods. Who will deny that these Christians, like the pagans, were not all of the lowest rank but belonged to every social condition?

Indeed, what of the fact that our Minucius himself, after professing the Christian religion, was of no lower status than before, but was, as we observed above, a distinguished advocate in legal causes? Although Caecilius and others as well, as we shall explain below, said that many Christians were poor and needy, they nevertheless do not deny that a considerable number of them abounded [Col. 0388C] in great wealth and resources. Hence Octavius replies to Caecilius, when the latter reproaches Christians with their poverty, obscurity, and lowliness: “We do not therefore consist of the lowest populace merely because we reject your offices and purple robes”—that is, when those things were contrary to Christian holiness.

“What then?” someone will ask. “Can nothing certain be determined about the date of this book?” We shall reply that Minucius rather clearly denies that, when he wrote these things, Christians had built public churches or, as he himself puts it, that there were any public temples in which they could assemble openly. From this it may not unreasonably be inferred that this book was published before Alexander Severus obtained the Roman Empire, since his palace, as we have said, was full of Christians and he himself had resolved to construct a temple [Col. 0388D] to their God.

The particular time at which that book was published can, in our judgment, be ascertained with greater certainty from no other source than Jerome’s aforementioned *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*. For even if it were proved that not absolutely all the writers mentioned by him are there enumerated in exact chronological order, nevertheless more writers are listed from Tertullian to our Minucius, and from that same Minucius to Cyprian, than would permit one unreasonably to refuse the conclusion that this book was published by Minucius after Tertullian’s writings on the same subject and before Cyprian’s (Jerome, *Catalog. Script. Eccles.*, § 53, p. 115; § 58, p. 117; and § 67, p. 119). Now Tertullian brought his *Apologeticum* [Col. 0389A], which must be discussed below, to light around the year 200, while Cyprian is reported to have written his work *To Demetrianus* around the year 257. Minucius must therefore be said to have made this book public sometime between those years.

Furthermore, if he really asserts, as we were saying shortly before, that there were then no public Christian churches, it will further follow that this book appeared before the year 220, when Alexander Severus was raised to imperial power. If all these points, moreover, are reconciled with one another, may it not be said with greater probability that this book was published by Minucius around the year of Christ 217, when Caracalla was killed, or during the reign of Elagabalus, while Christians were harassed with impunity by pagans amid the various upheavals of the Roman Empire? Nevertheless, we shall not begrudge anyone more expert who may suggest something better. [Col. 0389B]

## ARTICLE II. In Whose Words and in What Style This Book Was Composed; What Its Title Is; What Aim Minucius Felix Had in It; and Whether He Pleaded the Christians’ Case Fully and Perfectly

Although Minucius Felix most openly declares that the book he published arose from the debate instituted, as was said above, between Caecilius and Octavius, no one should doubt that he composed it not so much in their words as in his own. For what they said was all the more difficult for him to retain in memory because he attests that he reduced it to the book form we now see not immediately, but after some time had elapsed and after Octavius had departed from him. [Col. 0389C] Moreover, the style of this entire book is plainly uniform. Who could easily be persuaded that Caecilius and Octavius, debating extemporaneously, spoke in precisely the same manner? In addition, the mode of expression and manner of speaking are the same in the preface placed before this debate by Minucius himself as throughout the whole book. Those who consider Caecilius and Octavius to have been assumed personae will concede far more readily that the book was composed by Minucius.

Furthermore, all confess with remarkable consensus and in a single voice that Minucius’s manner of expression in this dialogue is dignified, acute, elegant, polished, vigorous, vehement, compact, and concise, and everywhere filled throughout with excellent and weighty reflections. Certain elegant and harmonious descriptions also occur in it, especially pleasing through their very brevity—above all that universally celebrated description of the game in which boys amuse themselves by skipping shells over the sea. [Col. 0389D]

There is also no one who does not see that this book is divided into two parts, the first of which comprises Caecilius’s speech for the pagans and the second Octavius’s speech for the Christians. But everything in it has always been written continuously and without any divisions in the discourse, both in the manuscript codex and in the printed editions. In only the latest edition were certain signs or numbers for dividing the text into chapters placed in the margins. [Col. 0390A] But these divisions often do not appear sufficiently accurate. For the greater convenience of readers, however, the entire book can easily be distinguished into various chapters.

The true and genuine title of this book is *Octavius*, which the highly authoritative witnesses cited by us, Lactantius and Jerome, explicitly declare was imposed upon it by Minucius himself. In giving it this title, Minucius imitated Plato, Cicero, and others, who prefixed to books of this kind, composed in dialogue form, the name of the person who plays the principal role in them. Octavius is represented as such a person in this book: he triumphed over his opponent, namely Caecilius, and finally brought him to acknowledge as true the Christian religion that he had attacked [Col. 0390B] and immediately to embrace it.

Minucius’s only aim and purpose throughout this book was to demonstrate the falsity of the pagan religion and the truth of the Christian. But because this demonstration can be made by various arguments and in different ways, Minucius undertook to prove only the following: that the gods of the pagans were false and fictitious, and their forms of worship altogether impious and absurd; that there was only one God, present everywhere and exercising providence over all collectively and each individually; that the morals and assemblies of Christians were holy and undefiled; and that the pagans themselves were guilty of the crimes of which they falsely accused the Christians, whom, against all justice and divine law, they tortured and slaughtered with every most dreadful kind of punishment merely on account of their name. [Col. 0390C] He proves these things most invincibly either by arguments, as they say, *ad hominem*—that is, by the testimony of the pagans’ own writers—or by others drawn from natural reason and equity themselves.

“But if the matter stands thus,” someone will ask, “for what reason does Lactantius say that our Minucius was one of those defenders of the Christian religion who ‘were unequal to its defense’?” (Lactantius, *Divine Institutes*, bk. V, ch. 1). Why does he also unhesitatingly assert that Minucius’s work reveals “how capable a champion of the truth he would have been, had he devoted himself wholly to that pursuit”? Do these words not indicate clearly enough that Minucius treated this subject either very superficially or only for the sake of relaxing and refreshing his mind? [Col. 0390D] By no means. For the debate was conducted by him with such seriousness and zeal that Caecilius openly professed himself vanquished by it alone and compelled to abjure the errors of the pagans and embrace the Christian religion.

Lactantius therefore seems to have meant nothing other than that the defense of the Christian religion was not presented in this book of Minucius as whole, complete, and perfected and finished in every aspect possible. For, as we have already remarked and as all readily acknowledge, the truth of the Christian religion can be demonstrated by various arguments, each of which is independently sufficient. No one, therefore, could ever justly and deservedly fault Minucius for selecting, from among numerous arguments for utterly overthrowing pagan errors, repelling their utterly false accusations against Christians, and establishing the truth of the Christian religion, those by which these things are demonstrated more than sufficiently. [Col. 0391A] Thus certain by no means undistinguished defenders of the Christian religion demonstrated its truth from the fulfillment of the oracles of the divine prophets; others from the miracles of Christ and his disciples; and still others by other arguments that there is no need to enumerate here. Yet who has ever dared to say that they did not duly discharge their office as defenders?

## ARTICLE III. On the Manuscript Codices and Various Editions of This Book

[Col. 0391B] For a long time now only a single manuscript codex of this book has remained to us, copied eight hundred years ago in an elegant hand, certainly, but by an unskilled scribe. It is presented under Arnobius’s name after the seven books of his work *Against the Nations*, with this title: “The seventh book of Arnobius ends; the eighth book auspiciously begins.” The Supreme Pontiff gave this codex, discovered at Rome in the Vatican Library, together with a copy of that first edition, as a gift to Francis I, king of France. It is now preserved in the Royal Library at Paris, formerly catalogued under number 1344 and now under number 3975.

Deceived by the false title of this codex, Faustus Sabaeus of Brescia caused it to be printed in 1542 under the name of Arnobius and as his eighth book. [Col. 0391C] Three years later, that is, in 1545, Sigismund Gelenius made public at Basel a new edition of this book, under the same title and name, from the press of Froben.

The same error afterward misled those by whom this book was again printed and circulated in Germany in the same manner.

Thus this book, wrongly ascribed to Arnobius, circulated for so long without anyone noticing the error in various parts of the world—Italy, France, and Germany. This error had so thoroughly taken possession even of all other and more learned men that Erasmus himself, well practiced in reading the books of the holy Fathers of the Church, asserted that the true *Octavius* of Minucius no longer survived. But if he had read both this work of our author [Col. 0391D] and the other books of Arnobius with a more attentive mind, it would have been no less easy and ready for him than it once was for Nepotian, as Jerome attests (Jerome, Epistle 35, to Heliodorus, p. 271), to distinguish the utterly different styles of expression of the two authors. Indeed, what could have been easier for Erasmus and all the rest than, upon examining this book, immediately to perceive that the books of Arnobius were not composed in dialogue form, as this *Octavius* of Minucius was, and were written in a very different style?

Franciscus Balduinus, however, understood this perfectly well and, for this very reason, relying upon the authority of Lactantius and Jerome, whom we cited above, restored this *Octavius* to its genuine author, Minucius Felix. Accordingly, in 1560 he caused it to be printed at Heidelberg by Ludovicus Lucius [Col. 0392A], bearing the name of Minucius himself.

Thirteen years later, however—namely, in 1583—a new edition of this book together with the seven books of Arnobius was prepared at Rome by Fulvius Ursinus. In it, *Octavius* was separated from those books in such a way as to suggest that Ursinus had been the first of all to do this and that no one had previously thought of separating this work of Minucius from those of Arnobius. But if he had seen Balduinus’s edition, one may quite reasonably find his good faith wanting; if he had not known it, his diligence.

Thereafter, however, the book was published by all others under the name of Minucius. For subsequently it appeared at Basel from the Froben press in 1603, through the study and care of Johannes a Wower. He informs us [Col. 0392B] that he corrected the errors of Minucius’s text from the edition of Fulvius Ursinus and from another volume, in whose margin Petrus Daniel had collected variant readings from the Royal manuscript and from other books.

At Hamburg, moreover, this same book of our Minucius was published together with the seven books of Arnobius, once and again, in 1610 and 1612, by Gebhart Elmenhorst.

In like manner, another edition of it was prepared at Paris in 1613 by Desiderius Heraldus and brought before the public, but without any observations on the *Octavius*, as will presently be stated.

Ouzelius informs us of another edition of this book, issued from the press of the Oxford printers but differing little from the others.

[Col. 0392C] Afterward, Nicolaus Rigaltius once again brought it before the public at Paris, from the press of the widow of Mathurin Dupuis, revised according to the authority of the Royal codex and, as he himself says, corrected and emended in various places. Indeed, in this Royal manuscript codex we found Rigaltius’s marks, by which he separated and corrected Minucius’s words, and various punctuation marks by which he believed clauses and phrases ought to be distinguished. From this edition the same book was afterward printed at Amsterdam in 1645, and among the works of Cyprian in 1666. But the edition prepared by Rigaltius could not escape the censure of many.

For although Jacobus Ouzelius extols it with considerable praise, he nevertheless published another edition, which he considered better, while still a young man, at Leiden in 1652, through Johannes le Maire. [Col. 0392D] In its preface he informs the reader that he retained the author’s words where others had correctly emended them from the Royal codex, but elsewhere preferred the commonly received reading. He inserted his own conjectures—which, as he says, were entirely certain—into Minucius’s text only once or twice, consigning the rest to his annotations. Finally, he attests that he altered a very great deal in the faulty punctuation and division of the words.

That edition of Ouzel was reprinted at the Hackius press in Leiden in 1672; but its author, and by whose care and labor it was produced, are left entirely unmentioned. [Col. 0393A] For in merely a brief notice, the printers declare that they had remained uncertain and anxious as to which writer’s work they should above all print in new type, and that at last, on the advice of learned men, they had published this *Octavius* of Minucius Felix—complete, as they say, in every respect, and illustrated with all the notes and observations of the various scholars that had appeared up to that time.

But Gronovius, as will be said a little later, took a very different view. Indeed, he thinks that there is no edition worse or less worthy of approval than this very one, precisely because of those same notes of Ouzel. Moreover, although it appears to have been printed in more elegant type than all the others, we have nevertheless detected numerous typographical errors, especially in the observations and notes where authors’ books are cited. [Col. 0393B] We have thought it necessary to give this warning so that no one in the future may be led into error by failing to examine them carefully enough.

In addition, Christoph Cellarius arranged for another edition of this work of Minucius to be produced at Halle in 1699 for the benefit of Christian youth. For this was his conviction—and would that it were everyone’s—that the best authors of Latin, Cicero and others who present nothing but what is modest and honorable, certainly ought to be read by Christian youths, but that with them should be joined the most ancient writers of the Christian Church who wrote in purer Latin. For he was persuaded, and not without reason, that through such reading young people could at once be imbued and formed by the splendor and elegance of the Latin language, by proofs of our faith, [Col. 0393C] by holiness of conduct, and by ecclesiastical history.

Finally, in 1709 this book was committed to print at Leiden “according to the recension of Jacob Gronovius.” The reasons that led him to publish it again are explained by him in these words at the very beginning of his preface:

> An edition of M. Minucius Felix had to be repeated in this city, when, through various conversations, the booksellers learned of my frequent recommendation of this little work and of my reading it both long ago and continually, so that it was impossible that they should not approach me.

The republic of letters is therefore undoubtedly indebted to him on many counts for not denying these booksellers—or rather printers—his assistance. Without it, indeed, there would have been no new edition of the *Octavius*, [Col. 0393D] or it would have appeared defiled rather than cleansed by less learned hands.

He censures all the earlier editions of this book, asserting that there is none in which much is not lacking. But he attempts above all to discredit those prepared by Rigaltius and Ouzel in the years 1645, 1652, and 1672. Yet he criticizes nothing except that the notes published in them “are,” as he says, “either excessively abundant and verbose, or too few.” For the longer notes not only obscure and cause the entire charm of Minucius’ style to vanish, but his text itself, submerged in them, can scarcely be read through by anyone without great weariness. He further believes that many passages still remain which, although requiring correction, [Col. 0394A] were nevertheless left entirely untouched and passed over by the authors of those observations.

Yet Gronovius certainly seems to exaggerate the faults of these and other editions for no other purpose than to persuade everyone that his own is superior to all the rest and complete in every respect. Nevertheless, those places in the text of our Minucius which he judges still to be disfigured by numerous errors or to be rather obscure, he endeavors to elucidate—or, more rarely, to correct—not on the authority of any manuscript codex, but solely by his own conjectures or those of others. How much weight these conjectures possess we shall show below in the appropriate place. And we shall presently make it plain that in his own notes he fell into the very faults that he dared to rebuke in others with such confidence.

[Col. 0394B] It must also be observed that some of the editions of this work of Minucius reviewed thus far were printed not merely once, but a second and third time, and even more often. But because nothing new was added to them, it seems to us of little use—or rather wholly superfluous—to enumerate and review them here.

## ARTICLE IV. On the Notes and Observations of Various Scholars upon This Book

Of all those through whose efforts, as we have said, this book was published in print, there are few who did not publish numerous notes and observations upon it. We must therefore now [Col. 0394C] explain what these are, what their quality is, and of what kind they are. First, Johannes Meursius produced several notes on this *Octavius*, which we possess in print in a certain little work entitled *Hypocriticus Minucianus, or A Critic in His Spare Hours*. In them he attempted to correct by his own conjectures certain passages of our author that seemed corrupt to him, but very often with little success or appropriateness. He also explains and interprets a few other passages by means of the words of other writers.

Franciscus Balduinus, in his *Prolegomena* to this book, after vindicating it for Minucius Felix, first makes some preliminary remarks about his period, family, native country, profession, advocates, and the Roman forum. He then discusses the style and subject of this book, the different methods of argument employed by Caecilius and Octavius, and briefly expounds several [Col. 0394D] topics in their debate. He confirms them from certain other writers, especially defenders of the Christian religion—Justin Martyr, Athenagoras, Theophilus of Antioch, Clement of Alexandria, Arnobius, Lactantius, Ambrose, and Augustine—but almost nowhere indicates in which books, or in what part of those books, the passages he cites are to be found. Finally, at the close of his preface, he exhorts Christians to the study of venerable ecclesiastical antiquity.

Wower, for his part, paid sufficient regard to brevity in his notes. In them he either attempts to correct errors in the text or to explain or [Col. 0395A] confirm the words and statements of Minucius Felix by certain testimonies of other writers. Yet one may certainly and rightly demand greater diligence from him in citing them. For in some places he mentions only the writer’s name but takes no care to indicate either his book or the place in the book where the words cited by him occur. We have noticed that he does this especially when he sends us to the works of Tertullian, and above all to his *Apologeticum*. At times he also wanders beyond the subject. An example is the passage where Octavius is insultingly called by Caecilius “the foremost of the bakers.” There Wower improperly accumulated much that contributes absolutely nothing to the author’s purpose.

Elmenhorst’s notes, however, are more extensive than Wower’s, and in them he records the passages of the authors he cites much more accurately than Wower does. [Col. 0395B] Yet in observations so lengthy you will search in vain for anything pertaining to the integrity or correction of Minucius’ text; for in them his only aim is to assert and establish many of the author’s statements by the testimony of others. Finally, he occasionally refers us to his own observations on Arnobius, or to Wower’s observations on this work of our Minucius. Gronovius, moreover, treats all those notes of Elmenhorst with his customary contempt and asserts that the judgment previously pronounced upon them by Scaliger was true (Scaliger, *Epistles* 260 and 261).

As for the notes originating with Heraldus, in most of them he discusses either the emendation of our author’s text on the authority of the Royal manuscript, or its correction by his own conjectures. In others, however, he refers us either to his own notes on the works of Arnobius or to Tertullian’s *Apologeticum*, though he scarcely ever cites any of its chapters. [Col. 0395C] In the remainder of his notes, finally, he attempts to confirm the opinions of Minucius from other writers. But these pertain more to the first part of the book—namely, Caecilius’ speech and his calumnies against the Christians. Very few of this kind relate to Octavius’ reply and his rejection and denunciation of the impious rites of the pagans.

To some, Rigaltius’ observations on this book seem learned and quite curious. To omit others, Ouzel admits in his preface to the book that many excellent things are found in them and that Rigaltius restored the *Octavius* to soundness more than all the rest. [Col. 0395D] Yet he reproaches Rigaltius for indulging excessively in his own conjectures and, by intermingling them with Minucius’ words, making him say things that had never entered his mind. But if Gronovius is to be believed, this disputation of Minucius Felix deserved “to proceed more reverently, and to be more sharply polished and placed in a better light” than it was in Rigaltius’ edition.

Yet certainly whoever reads his observations will plainly discover that they sometimes provide a rationale for the emended text, explain certain rather obscure expressions, and support many passages of Minucius by the authority of other authors. Nevertheless, he will perceive no less clearly that often neither their books nor the chapters of those books are cited, but only the author’s name. He will also discover that Rigaltius entirely passed over [Col. 0396A] many things that appear to require explanation no less than the rest. Finally, from what will be said later, anyone will be able to recognize upon what slight conjectures he often wished to emend the text of Minucius.

Although Ouzel’s observations on this book are exceedingly lengthy, he nevertheless admits that he composed them “in his youthful years” and “while the press was running.” He further declares that in them he occasionally departed from the opinion of other men, though very learned, but without insult. Yet no one will deny that they are excessively long. For he often digresses entirely from the author’s text under discussion and accumulates to the point of nausea a great deal that contributes absolutely nothing to it. Would you like some examples of these digressions to be presented? [Col. 0396B] Consider, I ask, how irrelevant to the subject are the things he reported about the idols set up in the Turks’ temple at Mecca in order to explain Minucius’ discourse about stones that had been shaped and anointed. And how does Ouzel’s lengthy investigation contribute to Minucius’ purpose—his inquiry into the care devoted by Romans to dedicating shrines, or by certain others to observing auguries, and into the first inventor of augury and the etymology of *delubrum* (“shrine”)? Why, too, when merely presented with an opportunity to speak of the birthdays of the gods, does he range at very great length through explanations of the birthdays of men, both princes and private persons, and even of cities, and the various rites by which they were celebrated? No smaller are his digressions concerning Mercury’s name and offices, where Minucius simply says that he was depicted with [Col. 0396C] winged feet; concerning sneezing, where Socrates’ *daimonion* is mentioned; and—to pass over a great many others—concerning the dog and other animals worshiped by the Egyptians, of which Minucius had made no mention.

But perhaps these things will seem more readily pardonable in a young man who, since he wished to make a show of his empty learning, could not make his observations—published, as he says, “while the press was running”—any shorter. Gronovius, however, could grant him no pardon at all. For he calls him a wild and iron-hearted man, and an impious commentator who falsely peddles the claim that his observations were born “while the press was running.” They are, Gronovius says, a wicked repository in which he stored his thefts, which should rather have been consigned to curses, had he not derived some things from Gronovius’ own father, [Col. 0396D] from Boxhorn, Vossius, and Elias Schevius. But who will not admit that this is the judgment of a harsh and iron-hearted man rather than of an equitable judge?

Cellarius states that he accomplished three things in his notes. First, he gave an account of his emendation of the text. Second, obscure histories and fables, if there were any, were elucidated; and finally, Minucius’ Latin words, whenever less common or more difficult ones occurred, were explained more clearly. Yet in these observations he either repeats much that others had said or leaves unmentioned many things that required exposition no less than the rest.

Furthermore, Jacob Gronovius asserts that this entire collection of notes and observations with which we have dealt thus far is nothing but an undigested [Col. 0397A] mass, an infinite heap of filth, and insane digressions from Minucius’ text. Yet although he admits that the same text of Minucius is utterly and perversely overwhelmed and submerged beneath that absurd and useless profusion of observations, he nevertheless laments that many things were omitted from them—things by which Salmasius, Brummerus, Ernestius, and especially Johannes Pricaeus had attempted, in works on other subjects, to emend or elucidate certain obscure passages of our author.

For that reason Gronovius himself, in his edition of this book—the last of all its editions—added to those earlier observations, apart from certain ones of Ouzel, the notes of Salmasius and others, as well as his own. Yet he carelessly slips into precisely the same deviations that he condemns in others with such confidence. For Minucius’ text is far more thoroughly submerged than in the earlier editions beneath the lengthier notes [Col. 0397B] of Gronovius himself and of the others whom he transcribed. Indeed, one may see numerous pages on which not a single word of Minucius appears; on others there are only one, two, or three lines, and on the remainder very few lines of his text. Who, then, will deny that Ouzel himself—whose notes Gronovius thinks deserving of such disdain—was far more prudent, since in his edition he presents the whole and complete text of Minucius and relegates all his observations to its end?

If you wish to know how weighty and how much superior to the rest Gronovius’ notes are, this must be shown to you by several examples. First, upon these words of Minucius, “to return to things past,” [Col. 0397C] he notes that they present a most effective description of true pleasure derived from past joys. He attempts to prove this by the examples of Tullius and Vespasian, which are no more relevant to the subject than countless others would be. Then he immediately continues as follows:

> Certainly what the eyes accomplish here, reflection can accomplish in other matters; indeed, may I not live if this happiness does not accompany me throughout my years, so that domestic happiness may console me and I may live at Cambridge with John Pearson, at Paris with Henri Valois, and at Florence with Antonio Magliabechi, men blessed forever with every distinction of learning.

Good heavens, how excellent, how learned, how necessary this observation was! Who could ever have heard Minucius, who speaks perfectly clearly and plainly, if it had been omitted?

[Col. 0397D] Where Caecilius said that “mists always arise,” Gronovius heaps up numerous remarks about the Greek nouns ἀνεφέλη (*anephélē*, “cloudlessness” or “clear sky”) and νέφος (*néphos*, “cloud”), not in order to explain his author’s text, but to refute Pricaeus and the French translator of this book.

But he wanders still further afterward, where Caecilius objects to the Christians that no one had returned from the underworld, even with Protesilaus’ lot, “with leave granted for hours at least.” First Gronovius warns us that nothing in Latin is either more charming than this expression or more pleasing to himself. He then proves at great breadth that the single elegant genitive “of hours” signifies a short portion of time that did not extend beyond one day. Who, I ask you, could ever have understood this [Col. 0398A] without Gronovius’ warning? Finally, he sharply chastises Jan Broukhusius, who wished to write “of a few hours,” adding the word “few” before “hours,” and adds that he had been harassed by him with every kind of lie and calumny. Was it therefore permissible for Gronovius rather than for others not only to digress in lengthy notes from his author’s purpose, but also to avenge private injuries?

But come now: who in any edition of this book ever produced an observation longer than the one he wrote on these few words of Minucius concerning the statue of Diana: “constructed with many breasts and spits”? For this note fills six or more pages of his book, and an entire letter of Holstenius, which had already been published more than once, is transcribed there. Could he not, if this were necessary, either have relegated it to the end of the book or [Col. 0398B] selected from it—as he did from the observations of Wower, Elmenhorst, and others—certain matters more conducive to the explanation of our author?
