But we ourselves would certainly become too lengthy if we wished to review individually Gronovius’ other notes resembling these, especially those in which he inserts the testimony of a certain more recent writer composed in French and everywhere points out Ouzel’s thefts and compilations—as though Minucius’ text could not have been understood if these things had been omitted.

Yet neither are we among those who, like Gronovius, scorn the notes and observations of everyone else or judge that they ought to be rejected entirely. For it must be admitted that in them one repeatedly finds varied learning, both that of Gronovius himself and of others, and that by them [Col. 0398C] certain of Minucius’ more obscure expressions and some words badly corrupted by the copyist are explained. Yet other passages still remain that call for a physician’s hand and undeniably require explanation. A new edition of this book, more accurate and complete than the rest, could therefore undoubtedly be prepared by some learned and sincere lover of truth who is not excessively devoted to his own party.

## ARTICLE V. On Certain Passages of This Book That Are Corrupt or Suspected of Corruption

Since only one manuscript of this book, the Royal codex, survives for us, it is certainly no wonder if various errors by an unskilled copyist ignorant of Latin occur in the author’s [Col. 0398D] text—errors which the editors of so many scholia and notes have either passed over untouched or attempted to correct by conjectures that were either insufficiently certain or false. Something must therefore be said here concerning these corrupt or suspect passages, apart from the matters to be discussed below when a more suitable opportunity presents itself; and, if possible, a physician’s hand must be applied to them.

First, then, Meursius suspected that in this passage of the *Octavius*, where Minucius said, “While walking by the sea at daybreak, etc.,” the name of Caecilius, the companion of the others, had been omitted. But this is mistaken. For Minucius soon afterward calls him by his own name, and a little later Octavius calls him “a man who at home and abroad clings to the side” [Col. 0399A] of Minucius. From this it is sufficiently clear that in the earlier passage everyone can easily supply Caecilius’ name.

Rigaltius observed that Minucius, when speaking of the sea’s waves, said: “delighted there by curling and swelling windings.” But in the Royal manuscript the first letter *C* of the first adjective *crispis* (“curling”) had been corrected, and another letter that preceded it appears to have been erased, as does one that stood in the middle of the word *torosis* (“swelling”). For this reason, some thought that *tortuosis* (“winding”) should be read there; others thought that the copyist had correctly changed it to *torosis*. Rigaltius approves this latter reading. Physicians, he says, spoke of the *tori* (“swellings”) of veins, and poets of the *tori* of manes. But he could have cited as more relevant to Minucius’ purpose this verse of Virgil:

> The swelling banks, and meadows fresh with streams,  
> We inhabit.  
> —Virgil, *Aeneid* VI.674

[Col. 0399B] Later, however, we read in the Royal codex: “It is easier to debate among messmates than to engage in the manner of wise men in those matters, etc.” These words appear corrupt to many. Accordingly, some thought that one should read “than to join hand with a wise man”; others, “than to engage in the manner of wise men,” that is, as wise men are accustomed to converse and debate among themselves. But because this verb *conserere* (“to join” or “engage”), standing alone and without the addition of some noun—such as “hand,” “battle,” “war,” or something similar—is scarcely ever used by good writers, nothing certain can undoubtedly be determined without the aid of another manuscript.

A little later Caecilius asks Minucius to hold the balance of a perfectly impartial judge in his debate with [Col. 0399C] Octavius. “And sit as judge for me,” he addresses him, “as though ignorant of either side.” But Ouzel, against the evidence of the Royal codex, thinks that the passage should be corrected, as in the Oxford edition, to “trust me,” since the expression “sit as judge for me” is said by grammarians to be unusual. Yet is it not often written in Virgil that one “sits upon” fields, tables, or benches? Why, then, was Minucius not permitted to write “sit as judge for me,” when Cicero and other highly polished writers likewise said, “he sits beside me,” and “he sits beside Jupiter”?

Moreover, what is written in the manuscript—“the things above us, suspended in heaven, have been raised up”—seems to some suspect of error. They therefore think that *sublimata* (“raised aloft”) should be restored in place of *sublata* (“raised up”). To confirm this, [Col. 0399D] Rigaltius cites these words from a certain book wrongly ascribed to Ambrose: “In what manner this entire heaven that we behold was suspended at a lofty height” (*On Solomon*, Appendix). Yet with better right we may cite the genuine Cicero in support of the Royal manuscript’s reading; speaking against Rullus in his speech on the Agrarian Law, he said: “Rome, situated among mountains and valleys, raised up and suspended upon upper stories” (Cicero, *Speech 2 on the Agrarian Law*, p. 309).

In some editions one may read these words: “although weights established the earth.” In others: “although weight established the earth.” But the manuscript’s reading should not have been altered on the basis of mere conjecture: “although it established the earth by weight.” For there the two words “its own matter” must be understood and supplied from the words that immediately precede: [Col. 0400A] “although it suspended the heaven by its own matter, although it established the earth by weight”; that is, it suspended heaven by its own matter and also established the earth by the weight of its own matter, which is dense and heavy.

This passage, however, is extremely corrupt; it is written as follows in the Royal manuscript: “But even κρῖani quantᾶ nrᾶ, what prodigies do they invent?” [The manuscript’s mixed Greek and abbreviated forms are materially uncertain.] For it is extremely difficult to say what these words mean. Rigaltius rendered them thus: “But even the Christians—where in so much that is ours—what prodigies do they invent?” He explained them as follows: “The Christians, insofar as they are dispersed through the cities of Italy, through the provinces of the Roman people, through so much territory of ours—what prodigies do they invent?” But no one followed this reading and conjecture. [Col. 0400B] Accordingly, all others wished to emend it to: “What monsters, what prodigies do they invent?” These words indeed accord better with what precedes and follows. But what can one dare to determine when there is only a single manuscript, and it plainly corrupt, unless a second and better one is discovered?

Where Minucius demonstrates from created things that God the Creator exists, he said: “the winter olive harvest is necessary.” “But how does this pertain to Minucius’ purpose?” asks Rigaltius. For olive trees do not grow in most regions. It would have been better, he continues, to write “winter moisture,” by which the soil rests in winter as though drenched with oil. Yet he did not sufficiently notice what we read in Columella: “The middle olive harvest generally falls at the beginning of December; for before that time bitter oil is produced” (Columella, book XII, chap. 50, beginning, p. 484). [Col. 0400C] Although this occurs only in certain regions, these words of Columella were nevertheless entirely sufficient to prove our author’s reading. For if the olive harvest is in December, could it not be called a winter harvest? Moreover, Cicero argues in precisely the same manner as Minucius from vines and olive groves, which do not grow in every part of the earth (Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* II, p. 238, line 16). But Gronovius divines that Minucius wrote *hyberni*, “of winter,” that is, “the olive harvest of winter”; yet this is a wholly futile and empty conjecture, contrary to the evidence of the manuscript.

After this we read these words of Octavius in the printed editions: “Birds live without patrimony, and cattle are fed from day to day.” [Col. 0400D] But in the Royal codex it is written: “they feed upon pastures from day to day.” This reading of the author certainly should not have been altered with such ease. For *pascua* are places in which cattle graze. Why, then, could Octavius not have said “they feed upon pastures,” just as Virgil wrote:

> Indeed, they graze the forests and the heights of Lycaeus.  
> —Virgil, *Georgics* III.314

No less obscure than corrupt is this passage, which the manuscript presents as follows: “Some are raised up to commands and dominions to such a degree that their talent is freely put up for sale by the license of a ruined mind’s power.” Since these words seemed to have scarcely any meaning, they were emended in the printed editions as follows: “Some are raised up to commands and dominions [Col. 0401A] to such a degree that ruined minds may freely put their talent up for sale through the license of power.” Rigaltius thinks that “ruined minds” means the same as slanderers, flatterers, and other such plagues of the human race. He observes nothing more there. The words of Minucius as thus corrected yield this sense: flatterers or slanderers freely put the character of princes and kings up for sale by the license of the power that they possess over them.

Others, however, would prefer to read: “so that the character of their ruined mind may freely sell the license of power”; that is, they are raised up for the purpose that the character of their ruined mind may sell the license of unrestricted power. Finally, Gronovius, retaining the words “license” and “of unrestricted power,” explains the entire passage thus: “Dominions and commands are sold by their character of a ruined mind, through the license of unrestricted power.” [Col. 0401B] But who would dare assert that Minucius, who everywhere speaks with such clarity and elegance, fell into such obscurity of expression? It is therefore better to await the aid of a superior manuscript in healing this passage than to indulge in empty and frivolous conjectures.

Octavius then immediately continues: “Without knowledge of God,” he says, “what solid happiness can there be, when death is like a dream? Before it can be grasped, it slips away.” Some suspect that the word “death” is superfluous there. Others wish to substitute the noun “thing” for it. But prudently, nothing has been changed in the text. For our author’s meaning is sufficiently plain and clear: without knowledge of God there can be no solid happiness, [Col. 0401C] but only fleeting and empty happiness, since such happiness is death, which Cyrus in Xenophon said was like a dream or sleep: ἐγγύτερον μὲν τῷ ἀνθρωπίνῳ θανάτῳ οὐδέν ἐστιν ὕπνου, “Nothing is nearer to human death than sleep” (Xenophon, book VIII, *The Expedition of Cyrus*, p. 237).

Finally, some will perhaps suspect one of the following two passages. The earlier one, at the beginning of the book, reads: “And so, while proceeding along the shore at daybreak, etc.” By these words Minucius indicates that very early in the morning he proceeded with his two companions to the sea while walking, and that after a walk of no great length they all sat down in the same place to debate. The other passage, which appears to conflict with this one, occurs at the end of the book: “Yet even now some matters remain unsettled . . . concerning which we shall speak tomorrow, since the sun is now [Col. 0401D] declining toward its setting.” Did the walk and debate of Caecilius and Octavius, someone will ask, which are contained in this short book of Minucius, last throughout the entire day? Apart from this debate and a not very lengthy walk, did Minucius do nothing else with his companions, and did they all spend the entire day alike either walking or debating, without lunch and while fasting? Perhaps, then, the final words of the latter passage should be deleted, or the word “at daybreak” in the earlier one.

But this manner of speaking must not be taken altogether according to what are called the fine points of law. For Minucius did not commit to writing everything that was done that day by him and his companions. Indeed, since he testifies that he wrote down this debate at a time other than that at which it took place, [Col. 0402A] he thought that only the matters relevant to it should be narrated, with the rest omitted. Finally, Tertullian clearly declares, in the opening words of his book *Against the Jews*, that an entire day down to evening was consumed in a similar debate between a Christian and a Jewish proselyte:

> It happened recently that a debate was held between a Christian and a Jewish proselyte. Each in turn, tugging upon the contentious rope, drew the day into evening.  
> —Tertullian, *Against the Jews*, chap. 2

Yet no one has ever dared to argue from this either against the integrity of the text or against the truth of the debate. If there are other corrupt words of Minucius, or words suspected of corruption, we shall discuss them below when the occasion presents itself.

## ARTICLE VI. What Minucius Excerpted from Other Writers—Cicero, Seneca, and Tertullian—and, Conversely, What Cyprian and Others Excerpted from This Same Book of Minucius

[Col. 0402B]

Just as we observe that much in this book of Minucius was excerpted from other writers—namely Cicero, Seneca, and Tertullian—so too we observe that Cyprian transferred many passages from it, in precisely the same words, especially into his own book *On the Vanity of Idols*. We shall now select some of these; the rest, to avoid repeating the same material, we shall more conveniently reserve for their appropriate places, where the doctrines presented by Minucius will have to be examined.

First, then, Minucius proves that one God truly exists by this argument:

> What can be so manifest, so generally acknowledged, and so evident, when [Col. 0402C] you raise your eyes to heaven and survey the things below and around it, as that there exists some divine power of surpassing intelligence by which all nature is inspired, moved, nourished, and governed?

Cicero urges the same argument in precisely the same manner, but more briefly:

> What can be so manifest and so evident, when we look up at heaven and contemplate the heavenly things, as that there exists some divine power of surpassing intelligence by which these things are governed?  
> —Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* II, beginning, p. 214, line 10

Do you see how most of Cicero’s very words were expanded by Minucius?

Then Minucius says:

> A more extended discourse about the stars must be left to the astrologers . . . . Each individual thing required the supreme [Col. 0402D] craftsman and perfect reason not merely in order to be created, brought into being, and arranged; indeed, they cannot even be perceived, discerned, or understood without the highest skill and reason.

Tullius, however, says:

> This entire arrangement of the stars . . . . What other nature devoid of mind could have produced these things, which not only required reason in order to come into being, but cannot be understood for what they are without the highest reason?  
> —Cicero, in the same book, p. 231, line 41

Again Minucius:

> Why should I speak of the manifold protection that living creatures possess against one another? Some are armed with horns, others fenced about with teeth, supported by hooves and bristling with stings; some escape by speed of foot, others by raising their spines.

Cicero speaks more explicitly:

> We now also observe how each creature defends itself against fear and violence with its own weapons: bulls with horns, boars with tusks, lions with their bite; some protect themselves by flight, others by concealment.  
> —Cicero, ibid., p. 233, line 39

[Col. 0403A] Moreover, Minucius sometimes makes by compression a briefer statement of what Cicero had treated at greater length. Thus Minucius says:

> The Nile tempers the drought of Egypt; the Euphrates cultivates Mesopotamia; the Indus is said both to sow and to water the East.

Cicero, however, writes more fully:

> The Nile waters Egypt, and after it has kept the whole country buried and flooded throughout the summer, it then recedes and leaves the fields softened and covered with silt for sowing. The Euphrates makes Mesopotamia fertile, carrying into it each year what are, as it were, new fields. The Indus, which is the greatest of all rivers, not only enriches and softens the fields with water, but even sows them; for it is said to carry down with it a great quantity of seeds of grain and similar crops.  
> —Cicero, ibid., p. 234, line 20

Minucius then immediately continues:

> If, upon entering some house, you saw everything cultivated, arranged, and adorned, you would surely believe that a master presided over it and was much better than those good possessions. So too in this house of the world, when you behold heaven and earth, [Col. 0403B] its providence, order, and law, believe that there is a lord and parent of the universe, more beautiful than the stars themselves and all the parts of the world.

Cicero had anticipated these words:

> Just as, if someone entered a house, a gymnasium, or a forum, and saw the rational arrangement, measure, and discipline of everything, he could not judge that these things came about without a cause, but would understand that there was someone who presided and whom others obeyed; so, much more, amid such great movements and such great alternations, and amid the ordered courses of so many and such great things, in which immeasurable and infinite antiquity has never proved false, he must conclude that such great motions of nature are governed by some mind.  
> —Cicero, ibid., p. 216, line 3

It is also easy to prove that Minucius excerpted much from Seneca. For he introduces Caecilius assailing as follows the Christians who were unwilling for the dead bodies of human beings to be burned upon funeral pyres:

> As though it made any difference whether wild beasts tear them apart, seas consume them, earth covers them, or flame carries them away.

[Col. 0403C] Seneca, however, had said:

> When that divine spirit is about to depart from the human being, it judges the place to which its receptacle is consigned—whether fire burns it, wild beasts tear it apart, or earth covers it—to concern itself no more than the afterbirth concerns the child once it has been born.  
> —Seneca, *Epistle* 92, p. 381

Octavius, moreover, responds to the charge of Christian poverty:

> No one can be as poor as he was when born.

Seneca says in precisely the same manner:

> No one lives as poor as he was when born.  
> —Seneca, *Why Misfortunes Befall Good Men*, etc., or *On Providence*, chap. 6, p. 504
The same Octavius says a little later: “That we experience the defects of the human body is not punishment, but military service . . . adversity is very often the training-ground of virtue.” Seneca, however: “Fortune beats and lacerates us. Let us endure it: it is not cruelty, but a contest.” And shortly before these words: [Col. 0403D] “Adversity is the opportunity of virtue” (Senec. ibid., ch. 4, p. 409).

Octavius continues: “God . . . in adversity tests and examines each person; [Col. 0404A] he weighs the character of each through dangers; he investigates him even to the point of death, secure in the knowledge that nothing belonging to him can perish.” Now, I ask you, listen to Seneca: “Therefore, those whom God approves and loves he hardens, scrutinizes, and exercises; but those to whom he seems indulgent and whom he seems to spare, he keeps soft for evils to come. For you are mistaken if you judge anyone exempt. His share will come to the man who has long been fortunate. Whoever appears to have been dismissed has merely been deferred” (Senec. ibid., ch. 4, p. 408).

Octavius adds: “Therefore, just as gold is tested by fire, so are we proved by ordeals.” And Seneca, after the words of his that we have cited: “Fire tests gold; misery tests brave men” (Senec. ibid., ch. 5, p. 391).

Why say more? Octavius proceeds and says: “What a beautiful spectacle it is for God when a Christian grapples with pain, when he sets himself against threats, punishments, and tortures!” Earlier Seneca had said in the same book: “Behold a spectacle worthy of God’s turning his gaze from his work to look upon. Behold a contest worthy of God: a brave man matched against ill fortune” (Senec. ibid., ch. 2, p. 492). Do you see how aptly [Col. 0404B] Minucius turned the things written by Seneca—the best and most honorable man among the pagans—against the pagans themselves and toward the defense of Christian teaching, which is far holier than pagan teaching?

If we pass from pagan writers to Christian ones, we shall also notice many things that Minucius excerpted from Tertullian’s books, especially from his *Apologeticum*. To prove this, it will suffice for now to adduce only some of them. Thus Octavius said this concerning God: “Whatever things exist, he commands by his word, orders by reason, and brings to completion by power.” Tertullian likewise says of him: “That which we worship is one God, who produced this entire mass . . . from nothing, by the word with which he commanded it, the reason with which he ordered it, and the power by which he was able” (Tertull., *Apologet.*, ch. 17, p. 18).

Again Octavius says of the same God: “What of the fact that [Col. 0404C] I have the agreement of everyone concerning him? I hear the common people, when they stretch their hands toward heaven, say nothing other than ‘God’; and ‘God is great,’ and ‘God is true,’ and ‘If God grants it.’ Is this the natural speech of the common people, or the confession of a Christian?” Tertullian similarly: “The soul . . . calls God by this name alone, because it is the proper name of the true God: ‘God is great,’ ‘God is good,’ and ‘Whatever God grants’; this is the voice of all. It also appeals to him as judge: ‘God sees’; ‘I entrust it to God’; and ‘God will repay me.’ O testimony of the soul naturally Christian! Finally, when pronouncing these words, it looks not toward the Capitol but toward heaven” (Tertull., ibid.). He said the same thing, though more briefly, in two other books (the same author, *On the Testimony of the Soul*, ch. 2, p. 81, and *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, ch. 3, p. 381). No one should doubt that Minucius, in the statements we have quoted, had in view these words of Tertullian himself.

Was he not also aiming at other words of Tertullian when [Col. 0404D] he justly and deservedly cast this charge against the pagans: “Where are acts of fornication arranged more often by priests than among altars and shrines, procuring is negotiated, and adulteries planned? [Col. 0405A] Indeed, blazing lust is satisfied more often in the chambers of temple-keepers than in the brothels themselves.” For Tertullian had earlier cast precisely the same charge against those same pagans: “The consciences of all will acknowledge that adulteries are arranged in temples, procuring negotiated among altars, and lust discharged, often in the very chambers of temple-keepers and priests, beneath the same sacred bands, priestly caps, and purple robes, while incense burns” (Tertull., *Apologet.*, ch. 15, p. 16).

Moreover, concerning the utterly cruel savagery of gladiators, these are the words of Octavius: “No different are those who devour beasts from the arena, smeared and steeped in blood, or fattened on human limbs and entrails.” Tertullian says of the same people: “Those who dine on wild-beast dishes from the arena, who ask for some of the boar and some of the stag. The boar [Col. 0405B] wiped away, in struggling, the blood of the man it had bloodied. The stag lay in a gladiator’s blood. The bellies of the bears themselves are sought after, while they still belch with human entrails. Thus man belches up flesh that was fed upon man” (Tertull., *Apologet.*, ch. 9, p. 10).

Octavius also says: “Nor are we seditious, if we all share the knowledge of the one good, gathered together in the same peacefulness in which we live as individuals.” Tertullian, however: “This assembly of Christians . . . if anyone complains of it under the same charge by which complaint is made against factions: for whose destruction have we ever assembled? Gathered together, we are the same as when dispersed; all together, the same as individually—injuring no one, grieving no one” (Tertull., *Apologet.*, ch. 39, p. 36).

Finally, to pass over for now the many other passages that must be cited below, [Col. 0405C] Octavius says: “The victor is the one who has obtained what he contended for.” Tertullian, however: “Victory is to obtain that for which you have contended” (Tertull., *Apologet.*, ch. 50, p. 44).

Let us now come to the passages that Cyprian copied from our Minucius: “When,” says our author, “has a partnership in kingship ever begun in good faith, or ended without blood?” Cyprian in exactly the same words: “When has a partnership in kingship ever begun in good faith, or ceased without blood?” (Cyprian, *On the Vanity of Idols*, p. 14). From this one may perhaps conclude that in Minucius’s text too *desiit* (“ceased”) should be read instead of *discessit* (“ended”), since it is better opposed to *coepit* (“began”).

Minucius: “Bees have one king, flocks one leader, and herds one ruler.” Cyprian: “Bees have one [Col. 0405D] king, flocks one leader, and herds one ruler” (Cypr., ibid.).

Minucius: “He who commands whatever things exist by his word, orders them by reason, and brings them to completion by power, cannot be seen, for he is brighter than sight; cannot be comprehended, for he is purer than touch; cannot be estimated, for he is greater than the senses . . . and therefore we estimate him worthily when we call him inestimable.” Cyprian, however: “He who commands whatever things exist by his word, orders them by reason, and brings them to completion by power, cannot be seen, for he is brighter than sight; cannot be comprehended, for he is purer than touch; cannot be estimated, for he is greater than sense; and therefore we estimate him worthily when we call him inestimable” (Cypr., loc. cit.). There, however, Cyprian omitted certain words of Minucius—omitted by us and marked [Col. 0406A] by dots—doubtless for brevity’s sake.

Minucius: “Do not seek a name for God: ‘God’ is his name. Names are needed where a multitude must be distinguished person by person through the particular marks of appellations. For God, who alone exists, the word ‘God’ is his whole designation . . . I hear the common people . . . say ‘God is great,’ and ‘God is true,’ and ‘If God grants it’; this is the natural speech of the common people.” Cyprian: “Do not seek God’s name: ‘God’ is his name. Names are needed where a multitude must be distinguished through the particular marks of appellations. For God, who alone exists, ‘God’ is his whole designation . . . In many sayings the common people naturally confess God . . . We frequently hear it said: ‘O God!’ and ‘God sees’; and ‘I entrust it to God’; and ‘God will repay me’; and ‘What God wills’; and ‘If [Col. 0406B] God grants it’” (Cypr., ibid., p. 15). Do you see how Cyprian inserted his own words among those of Minucius? Minucius had furthermore committed this to writing concerning images of the dead: “Those things that had been adopted as consolations became sacred rites.” Cyprian says of the same things: “Those things that had first been adopted as consolations became sacred rites” (Cypr., ibid., p. 11).

Minucius: “That great Macedonian Alexander wrote to his mother in a notable volume that, through fear of his power, a priest had disclosed to him the secret that the gods were men.” Cyprian: “Alexander the Great writes to his mother in a notable volume that, through fear of his power, a priest had disclosed to him the secret that the gods were men” (Cypr., ibid., p. 12).

Minucius: “The Castors die by turns so that they may live; [Col. 0406C] Aesculapius is struck by lightning so that he may rise into godhood; Hercules is burned in the fires of Oeta so that he may cast off the man.” Cyprian, still in the same words: “Castor and Pollux die by turns so that they may live; Aesculapius is struck by lightning so that he may rise into godhood; Hercules is burned in the fires of Oeta so that he may cast off the man” (Cypr., ibid., p. 11).

Minucius: “Apollo pastures the flock of Admetus. Neptune constructs walls for Laomedon, and the unfortunate builder receives no payment for his work.” Cyprian: “Apollo pastured the flock of Admetus. Neptune constructed walls for Laomedon, and the unfortunate builder received no payment for his work” (Cypr., ibid.).

Minucius later records this concerning Saturn and Janus: “He taught men to stamp letters and coin money . . . Accordingly he preferred Latium to be named from his hiding place (*latebra*) . . . and the Janiculum [Col. 0406D] from Janus.” Cyprian: “Hence Latium received its name from his hiding place. He was the first in Italy to institute the stamping of letters and the coining of money . . . From the name of Janus the Janiculum was named” (Cypr., ibid.).

Minucius: “The cave of Jupiter is visited, and his tomb is shown.” Cyprian reproduced this in exactly the same words: “The cave of Jupiter is visited in Crete, and his tomb is shown” (Cypr., ibid.).

Minucius: “Through Proculus’s perjury, Romulus is a god.” Cyprian, however: “There is Romulus, made a god through Proculus’s perjury” (Cypr., ibid., p. 12).

Minucius, concerning the gods: “Why, if they were born, are they not still being born today, unless perhaps Jupiter has now grown old and Juno’s childbearing has failed?” Cyprian, concerning the same: “But if [Col. 0407A] the gods were once born, why are they not still being born today, unless perhaps Jupiter has grown old or Juno’s childbearing has failed?” (Cypr., ibid.).

Minucius: “We know the native-born gods of the Romans: Romulus, Picus, Tiberinus, Consus, Pilumnus, and Picumnus are gods. Tatius both discovered and worshiped Cloacina; Hostilius, Fear and Pallor; soon Fever was consecrated by someone or other . . . and, of course, Acca Larentia and Flora were prostitutes.” Cyprian: “We know the native-born gods of the Romans. There is Romulus . . . Picus, Tiberinus, Pilumnus, and Consus . . . Tatius also both discovered and worshiped the goddess Cloacina; Hostilius, Fear and Pallor; soon Fever was consecrated by someone or other; and Acca and Flora were prostitutes” (Cypr., ibid., p. 12).

[Col. 0407B] Minucius: “Thracian Mars, Cretan Jupiter, Juno now Argive, now Samian, now Punic, now Taurian Diana, or the Idaean or Egyptian Mother—these are not divine powers but monstrosities.” Cyprian: “Thracian Mars, Cretan Jupiter, Juno either Argive or Samian or Punic, Taurian Diana, and the Idaean and Egyptian Mother of the Gods are monstrosities, not divine powers” (Cypr., ibid., p. 13).

Minucius: “Before them, by God’s ordering, the Assyrians, Medes, and Persians long held kingdoms, as did also the Greeks and Egyptians.” Cyprian: “Before them the Assyrians, Medes, and Persians held empire; and we know that the Greeks and Egyptians reigned” (Cypr., ibid.).

Minucius: “What of Regulus? Did he not observe the auguries and yet was captured? Mancinus kept the religious observances, and was sent [Col. 0407C] under the yoke and surrendered. Paulus had chickens that ate greedily at Cannae; nevertheless he was laid low with the greater part of the commonwealth. Gaius Caesar disregarded the resistance of the auguries and auspices against sending ships to Africa before midwinter; and for that very reason he sailed and conquered more easily.” Cyprian: “Regulus observed the auspices and was captured. Mancinus kept the religious observances and was sent under the yoke; Paulus had chickens that ate greedily, and yet was slain at Cannae. Gaius Caesar disregarded the resistance of the auguries and auspices against sending ships to Africa before midwinter, and for that very reason sailed and conquered more easily” (Cypr., ibid.).

Minucius, concerning demons: “Impure and wandering spirits, weighed down from heavenly vigor by earthly stains and desires . . . Already ruined, they do not cease ruining others; depraved, they infuse [Col. 0407D] the error of their depravity.” Cyprian similarly: “Impure and wandering spirits, who, after being immersed in earthly vices and withdrawing from heavenly vigor through earthly contagion, do not cease, though ruined, to ruin others, and, though depraved, to infuse the error of their depravity” (Cypr., ibid.).

Minucius, still concerning the same: “These impure spirits, therefore . . . hide beneath consecrated statues and images, and by their breath . . . prophets are inspired . . . Sometimes they animate the fibers of entrails, govern the flight of birds, direct lots, and produce oracles wrapped in many falsehoods. For they are both deceived and deceive others . . . They disturb life and trouble sleep; secretly creeping even into bodies . . . they terrify minds and contort limbs, [Col. 0408A] so as to compel people to worship them; so that, fattened by the stench of altars or by animal victims, they may release what they had constricted and appear to have effected a cure.” Cyprian: “These spirits, therefore, hide beneath consecrated statues and images; by their breath they inspire the breasts of prophets, animate the fibers of entrails, govern the flight of birds, direct lots, and produce oracles, always wrapping falsehoods in truths. For they are both deceived and deceive others; they disturb life and trouble sleep. Secretly creeping even into bodies, they terrify minds and contort limbs . . . so as to compel people to worship them; so that, fattened by the stench of altars and the pyres of cattle, they may release what they had constricted and appear to have effected a cure” (Cypr., ibid., p. 14).

Minucius, again concerning these same demons: “Thus they seize minds, so that people begin to hate us [Col. 0408B] before they know us, lest, once they know us, they should either be able to imitate us or be unable to condemn us.” Cyprian likewise: “Hence they drive the common people to hatred of our name, so that people begin to hate us before they know us, lest, once they know us, they should either be able to imitate us or be unable to condemn us” (Cyprian, ibid.).

Minucius: “What temple shall I build for him, God, when this whole world, fashioned by his works, cannot contain him? And when I, a human being, dwell more spaciously, shall I enclose the power of such majesty within a single little shrine? Is he not better dedicated in our mind, consecrated in the depths of our heart?” Cyprian, however: “What temple could God have, when the whole world is his temple? And when a human being dwells more spaciously, shall I enclose the power of such majesty within a single little shrine? He must be dedicated [Col. 0408C] in our mind, consecrated in our heart” (Cypr., ibid., p. 15).

Still other passages occur in this book of Minucius that resemble things Cyprian wrote either in the book already cited by us so often, or in his works addressed to Donatus and Demetrian, and elsewhere; to transcribe them now would take too long. We shall therefore adduce them below whenever they are needed to confirm our author’s opinion.

Yet it will doubtless seem astonishing that Cyprian, so eloquent and learned a man, copied word for word so many passages from a single little book composed by Minucius. Many, therefore, will readily persuade themselves that Minucius borrowed his material from Cyprian rather than Cyprian from Minucius. But if Minucius published [Col. 0408D] his book earlier, as we have already shown, then certainly he did not take his material from Cyprian; Cyprian took his from him. What, moreover, of the fact that our Minucius was neither of the lowest nor of an obscure reputation? For Lactantius calls him a distinguished advocate endowed with no inconsiderable learning, as was observed above, and did not hesitate to draw many things from his book. Why, then, should Cyprian not have done so as well?

# CHAPTER III  
## NEW ANNOTATIONS ON THE BOOK OF MINUCIUS FELIX; AND FIRST, AN EXAMINATION OF THE ARGUMENTS BY WHICH CAECILIUS DENIES THAT GOD EXISTS AND OCTAVIUS PROVES IT

[Col. 0409A]

## ARTICLE I  
### What Will Be Treated in These Notes and How; and First, Whether Christians Should Be Excluded from This Disputation

As we have already said, nothing else occurs throughout this whole book of Minucius—if one excepts the prologue, the epilogue, and Minucius’s own judgment—except the disputation of Caecilius and Octavius, in which the former strives with all the powers of his intellect to defend [Col. 0409B] and uphold the religion of the pagans, and the latter that of the Christians. But the arguments of each, and especially Octavius’s answers to Caecilius’s unjust accusations, are separated from one another by such long intervals of discourse that they may so confuse the reader’s mind that he can scarcely perceive their force and weight unless he reads and rereads the same things repeatedly. Moreover, several matters are touched upon briefly and summarily in them that, although clear and evident in Minucius’s time, are now obscure to many and must therefore be explained by us.

Accordingly, we have judged that three things must be accomplished in our observations. First, we shall present and examine together, in connected form, each argument of Caecilius and Octavius’s answers and refutations, which are separated from one another. Second, we shall show [Col. 0409C] what in them is sound or invalid, true or false. Third, we shall attempt to explain what has been stated too briefly and compactly, or too obscurely.

In his first argument against the Christians, Caecilius contends that they should in no way whatsoever be admitted to this disputation concerning the gods, and should be heard by no one. He thinks that his argument can be derived from two conditions of those same Christians, one peculiar to them and the other common to them with the rest of humankind. For he says that they were gathered from the lowest dregs of the populace, wholly ignorant of the liberal arts, illiterate, altogether unlearned, and mere simpletons, and therefore entirely unworthy to be heard when they dispute and decide “concerning the highest principle of things and its majesty,” that is, concerning whether God exists and who and what sort of being he is. [Col. 0409D] What is more, it is not merely unworthy but even, as he himself says, “a matter for indignation” that men of this kind have arrived at such audacity that they should determine something certain concerning God, about whom the most learned philosophers had thus far dared to determine nothing. Do you wish Caecilius’s own words to be presented to you? Here they are: “All should be indignant and deeply grieved that certain persons should dare—even persons so ignorant of learning, strangers to literature, and inexperienced even in the meaner arts—to decide anything certain concerning the highest principle of things and its majesty, concerning which philosophy itself, among very many schools, has continued to deliberate through all the centuries down to the present.” Again, he presses the charge that Christians were “men of a deplorable, unlawful, and desperate faction, who, gathering the more ignorant from the lowest dregs [Col. 0410A] and women who, through the weakness of their sex, easily slip, establish a rabble of profane conspiracy”; and finally, he says, “a furtive, light-shunning nation, mute in public and chattering in corners.”

Nor, moreover, was Caecilius alone in reproaching Christians with this condition—the lowest of all mankind—of being last in rusticity and ignorance. For Celsus too, himself a pagan, inveighs against them in Origen as though they were the vilest and lowest of all and dared to teach anything only before children, petty women, and fools:

> Ὁρῶμεν δὴ ποῦ καὶ τοὺς ἐν ταῖς ἀγοραῖς ἐπιῤῥητότατα ἐπιδεικνυμένους, καὶ ἀγείροντας, εἰς μὲν φρονίμων ἀνδρῶν σύλλογον οὐκ ἄν ποτε παρελθόντας, οὐδ` ἐν τούτοις τὰ ἑαυτῶν κατατολμήσαντας ἐπιδεικνύειν· ἔνθα δ` ἂν ὁρῶσι μειράκια [Col. 0410B] καὶ οἰκοτρίβων ὄχλον, καὶ ἀνοήτων ἀνθρώπων ὅμιλον ἐνταῦθα ὡθουμένοὺς τε, καὶ καλλωπιζομένους.

“We certainly see those itinerant mountebanks displaying their much-vaunted wares in the marketplaces and gathering crowds—not before assemblies of prudent men, for they would never dare to enter them or venture to display their teachings among them; but wherever they notice a crowd of youths, household drudges, and foolish people, there they thrust themselves in and make a show of themselves.”

And a little later:

> Ὁρῶμεν καὶ κατὰ τὰς ἰδίας οἰκιας ἐριουργοὺς, καὶ σκυτοτόμους, καὶ κναφεῖς, καὶ τοὺς ἀπαιδευτοτάτοὺς τε καὶ ἀγροικοτάτους, ἐναντίον μὲν τῶν πρεσβυτέρων, καὶ φρονιμωτέρων δεσποτῶν οὐδὲν φθέγγεσθαι τολμῶντας· ἐπειδὰν δὲ τῶν παίδων ἰδίᾳ λάβωνται, καὶ γυναίκων τινῶν σὺν αὐτοῖς ἂν ἁνοήτων, θαύμασι` ἄττα διεξιόντας, ὼς οὐ χρὴ προσέχειν τῷ πατρὶ καὶ τοῖς διδασκάλοις, σφίσι δὲ πειθεσθαι.

“One may see wool-workers, [Col. 0410C] shoemakers, fullers in their own houses, and every most uneducated and rustic person, daring to say nothing in the presence of the older and more prudent masters of the household. But whenever they get their children alone, together with certain ignorant women, they expound marvelous claims: that parents and teachers should not be heeded, but that they themselves should be believed” (Origen, bk. III, *Against Celsus*, pp. 141, 144, quarto ed.).

For this reason Gregory Nazianzen thus mocks the emperor Julian the Apostate: “These are our tales—that is, the tales of the Galileans, those despised and abject men. This is what we are, we who adore Christ. This is what we are, disciples of fishermen and, as they themselves say, of uneducated men. This is what we are, we who sit with old women and sing psalms. This is what we are, wasted by long fasts and half-dead. [Col. 0410D] This is what we are, we who keep vigils in vain and babble during nocturnal watches, and yet we overthrow you. Where are the grammarians? Where are the counselors? For I am pleased to borrow a triumphal hymn from one of our uneducated people, as indeed you regard them” (Gregory Nazianzen, Orat. 4, *Against Julian*, p. 298 ff.).

Nevertheless, Julian himself, in Cyril of Alexandria, reproaches not so much the Christians of his own age as those of the Church’s first century with these things:

> μηδὲ ἤλπισαν εἰς τοῦτο ἀφίξεσθαί ποτε δυνάμεως ὑμᾶς. ἡγάπων γὰρ εἰ θεραπαίνας ἐξαπατήσουσι καὶ δούλους, καὶ διὰ τούτων τὰς γυναῖκας, ἄνδρὰς τε ὄιους Κορνήλιος καὶ Σέργιος, ὧν εἶς ἐὰν φανῇ τῶν τηνικαῦτα γνωριζομένων ἐπιμνήσθεις, ἐπὶ Τιβεριου γὰρ ἤτοι Κλαυδίου ταῦτα ἑγένετο, περὶ πάντων [Col. 0411A] ὅτι ψεύδομαι νομίζετε.

“Nor did they ever hope,” he says, “that you would attain such power. For they were content if they could deceive maidservants or slaves, and through them wives, and men such as Cornelius and Sergius. If even one of these should appear among the notable men of that age—remember that these things occurred in the time of Tiberius or Claudius—then consider me a liar about them all” (Cyril of Alexandria, bk. VI, *Against Julian*, p. 206). But Caecilius does not hesitate to assert that Christians in his own day were still illiterate and uneducated men of the vilest populace.

Yet it is absurd, he says—or, if you prefer, a matter for indignation—that they should decide something concerning God without hesitation, while very many philosophers are still deliberating about him. Nor should you say that Caecilius gratuitously invented this claim about so many philosophers. For Cicero asserts not only that the opinions of these most learned men, as he calls them, concerning God were various and [Col. 0411B] widely divergent: “But,” he says, “those who declared that gods exist are found in such variety and disagreement that it would be troublesome to enumerate their opinions.” And a little later: “Surely so great a doubt among the most learned men concerning the greatest matter will compel even those who think that they possess some knowledge to entertain doubt” (Cicero, bk. II, *On the Nature of the Gods*, pp. 195, 197).

Octavius—or rather Minucius under Octavius’s name—dissolves this argument of Caecilius and the other pagans by two lines of reasoning and utterly overturns it. First, he grants Caecilius freely, and concedes, that all Christians were poor, illiterate, and unskilled, as Caecilius nevertheless falsely contended. But he demonstrates by multiple arguments that the argument [Col. 0411C] derived from this is utterly feeble and weak. For all human beings whatsoever, of every age, sex, and rank, are naturally capable of sense and reason, and wisdom is implanted in them not by chance but by nature.

Next, the pagan philosophers themselves, as well as other inventors of the arts, had at first been commoners, uneducated, and half-naked. Indeed, says Octavius, our own people, however poor, devised practical wisdom and afterward transmitted instruction to others. Therefore, intellect is neither given by resources and riches nor acquired by study and labor, but is engendered in a human being together with his very mind.

Finally, in debates and controversies what is sought is not so much the authority of the disputant as the weight and truth of his reasons. This indeed, to note it in passing, is asserted by Cicero in these words: “For in disputation it is not so much authority [variant: authorities] that should be sought as [Col. 0411D] the weight of reason” (Cicero, bk. I, *On the Nature of the Gods*, near the beginning, p. 197). Therefore, whoever disputes concerning God and divine matters persuades everyone the more effectively that he is defending the truth insofar as his speech is more unpolished and less adorned with the display of empty eloquence. But it is better to hear Octavius disputing against Caecilius in his own words:

> “Let all know,” he says, “that human beings, without distinction of age, sex, or rank, were created capable and fit for reason and perception, and that they did not obtain wisdom by fortune but possess it implanted by nature. Indeed, even the philosophers themselves, or any other [Col. 0412A] inventors of arts who became renowned in human memory, were regarded as commoners, uneducated, and half-naked before the ingenuity of their minds gained them a celebrated name. But the rich, bound to their possessions, have been accustomed to look up to gold rather than heaven. Our poor people both devised practical wisdom and transmitted learning to others. Hence it is apparent that intellect is not bestowed by wealth or procured by study, but is generated together with the very formation of the mind. There is therefore nothing for indignation or grief if anyone investigates, perceives, and declares something concerning divine matters, since it is not the authority of the disputant but the truth of the disputation itself that is required; and indeed, the more unskilled the speech, the more evident it is, since it is not embellished by the pomp and charm of eloquence, but is sustained, just as it is, by the rule of what is right.”

Cyril of Alexandria argues in precisely the same way [Col. 0412B] against Julian when he makes the same objection:

> “As for the fact that petty women believed, and servants and certain obscure persons were called, he uses this to reproach the Savior’s clemency. But is it not better to hold that a human being, insofar as he is born human, is in no way superior to another human being, but that one rational principle of being extends through all? For all have one entrance into the world and an equal departure, as it is written . . . All human beings indeed have one nature. And that nature is so constituted as to be capable of everything worthy of praise. For it is intelligent and able to distinguish better things from worse. Nothing, therefore, prevents a man of the lowest station from being wise, one deprived of money from cultivating justice, and one of servile [Col. 0412C] condition from appearing fair and honorable . . . For my part, I would say that a poor man, if he has adopted a right and honorable manner of life, is beyond comparison superior to a rich miser, and a wise slave to an insane master . . . Moreover, one may see that those among the Greeks who surpassed others most greatly in the praise of virtue were artisans at first and practiced common and menial trades received from their parents, yet not without admirable wisdom. I pass over many. I come to Socrates himself, the son of Sophroniscus, who was born of a mother who was a midwife and a father who was a sculptor; he became highly skilled in that art and did not consider it a disgrace to himself” (Cyril of Alexandria, bk. VI, *Against Julian*, p. 207).

Because it would be too long to reproduce Cyril’s Greek words here, you may read them in his book, where, after proving the point most clearly both by the authority and [Col. 0412D] the words of Porphyry, copied from the third book of the *History of Philosophers*, he confirms it by the testimony of Timaeus. To these may be added Laertius, who in the *Life of Socrates* cites Plato, who relates that Socrates was born to Sophroniscus, a stonecutter, whose craft he afterward practiced, and to Phaenarete, a midwife (Laertius, bk. II, §18). Valerius Maximus, Suidas, Timon—who will be cited by us in the following article—and others support him (Valerius Maximus, bk. III, ch. 4).

What, moreover, of the fact that Cyril in the same place, still with Porphyry as witness, demonstrates that Plato was first exercised for a long time in wrestling schools and athletic exertions, or, as some say, that he passed from the Isthmian and Pythian games, or other contests, [Col. 0413A] to philosophy (Cyril of Alexandria, bk. VI, *Against Julian*, p. 208)?

He adds, moreover, that Zalmoxis the Thracian had been Pythagoras’s slave, and that Pythagoras instructed many women in philosophical disciplines, just as Plato instructed Marcella. To this may further be added what we have discussed elsewhere concerning women philosophers, painters, and poets (vol. I, *Apparatus*, bk. III, diss. II, ch. 18, art. 4, p. 1155; and ch. 24, art. 3, p. 25 ff.).

Finally, if by the designation “our own people” Minucius meant the Hebrews, who transmitted arts and disciplines to the pagans, this has already been proved by us from Justin Martyr and Clement of Alexandria in vol. I, *Apparatus*, bk. II, dissertation 2, ch. 7, §2, p. 387. Likewise, bk. III, diss. 2, ch. 1, art. 1, [Col. 0413B] p. 834; ch. 15, art. 1 ff.; and from what was said concerning Thales, ch. 17, art. 1, p. 1121; concerning Pythagoras, ibid., ch. 17, art. 2; concerning Plato, ibid., art. 4; concerning the philosophers’ thefts and plunderings from our sacred Scripture, ch. 16, art. 2; and finally concerning the inventors of the arts and sciences, ibid., ch. 31, art. 1, p. 1187 ff.

Although this answer of Minucius, which utterly overturns Caecilius’s frivolous argument, should have fully satisfied both Caecilius himself and anyone else, however difficult to please, he nevertheless adds a second answer. For he plainly and utterly denies that the Christians of his time were such people as Caecilius so boldly asserted: poor and uneducated men of the lowest station of all. “For we do not,” he says, “necessarily belong [Col. 0413C] to the lowest class merely because we reject your offices and purple robes.” This, certainly, and no more, is what this exceedingly modest man says to deny in very few words the truth of Caecilius’s reckless assertion.

But what Minucius denies with such modesty, Origen, in answering Celsus, openly declares to be a gross insult and an impudent slander (Origen, bk. III, *Against Celsus*, p. 142 ff.). Nor is this surprising. For Tertullian, a little older than Minucius, left this account of himself and all the Christians of his age: “We are but of yesterday, and we have filled everything you possess—cities, islands, fortresses, municipalities, council chambers, the camps themselves, tribes, wards, palace, senate, forum. We leave you only your temples” [Col. 0413D] (Tertullian, *Apologet.*, ch. 37, p. 33). Yet surely among those who filled cities, the forum, camps, wards, the palace, the senate, and so many other places, very many, as we have already said, were neither persons of the lowest station, nor poor, nor uneducated and illiterate.

But why, someone will object, did Minucius pass over these and other matters to be cited by us below in such profound silence? Why, we too ask, did he not at once stop the mouth of Caecilius, who lied so shamelessly, by his own example alone? For a man could not be called one of the dregs of the lowest populace who, as we have already observed from the highly reliable witnesses Lactantius and Jerome, was a distinguished advocate at Rome. We shall therefore not find it difficult to believe that he thought he ought to employ so modest and restrained a response [Col. 0414A] so that by such gentleness and moderation he might more easily entice his opponent to renounce his errors and embrace the Christian religion.

Nothing, moreover, was more foolish than Caecilius’s insistence that Christians were a furtive, light-shunning nation, chattering in corners. For they proclaimed their teachings publicly; but the pagans blushed and were afraid to hear them, lest they should be unable to deny that they were true. More on this below.

Lastly, from what has been said it is still clearly demonstrated that, however various and divergent the opinions of the pagan philosophers concerning God were, however much they doubted concerning him, and even if, as you please, some denied that he existed, Christians—even if poor and [Col. 0414B] illiterate—could nevertheless dispute concerning him, determine something certain, and render a true judgment.

In vain, therefore, does Caecilius exhort them at the end of his speech to cease “probing the regions of heaven and the destinies and secrets of the world. For it is enough to look at what is before one’s feet, especially for the uneducated, uncultivated, and rude.” Cicero’s words show that this was drawn from Democritus, from whose spring Epicurus watered his little gardens with empty and false opinions: “Democritus, as a natural philosopher—a class of men than which none is more arrogant—talks nonsense not without wit: ‘No one looks at what lies before his feet; he scrutinizes the regions of heaven’” (Cicero, bk. II, *On Divination*, p. 282, line 30). For this argument of a proud man, intemperately abusing learning and leisure, has been utterly overturned by what has thus far been said.

## ARTICLE II  
### Examination of the Arguments by Which Caecilius Attempts to Prove That Christians and Others May Not Lawfully Dispute Concerning God

[Col. 0414C]

Caecilius proves by another line of reasoning that Christians should be barred from every disputation concerning God, one that is entirely common to them with the rest of humankind. For he objects that the weakness of human nature is such that no one is permitted to know or investigate what hangs in heaven above us or lies below in the bowels of the earth: “Let human mediocrity,” he says, “keep away from the investigation of divine things, since it is neither given to us to know nor permitted to investigate what hangs in heaven above us . . . or what lies beneath the earth.” For it is enough for each person [Col. 0414D] if, “according to the ancient oracle of the sage, we know ourselves.” He alludes to that most celebrated maxim, γνῶθι σεαυτόν, “Know yourself,” which we have noted elsewhere was ascribed by some to Thales, by others to Chilon, and also to the Pythia (vol. I, *Apparatus*, bk. III, diss. 2, ch. 14, art. 3, p. 1097; and ch. 19, art. 4, p. 1170).

Caecilius adds that if at any time, indulging in mad and foolish labor, we wander beyond the bounds of our lowly condition, this error must not be entangled with the empty and fearsome opinions of Christians. He therefore wishes no disputation concerning God and divine matters to be undertaken by Christians, and holds it sufficient for them to know themselves.

[Col. 0415A] He attempts to establish and confirm this, as it seemed to him, by the great authority and testimony of Socrates, who was declared by a divine oracle to be the wisest of men: “If there is a desire to philosophize,” he says, “let any one of you who is great enough imitate Socrates, the prince of wisdom, if he can. Whenever that man was questioned concerning heavenly matters, his familiar reply was: **WHAT IS ABOVE US IS NO CONCERN OF OURS**. He therefore deservedly obtained from the oracle its testimony to his singular prudence. He himself perceived why the oracle had placed him above all others: not because he had discovered everything, but because he had learned that he knew nothing. Thus the confession of one’s ignorance is the height of prudence.”

These statements were not made thoughtlessly by Caecilius, as is proved by the fact that Cicero likewise committed to writing the following concerning the same Socrates [Col. 0415B]:

> Socrates seems to me—as is universally agreed—to have been the first to call philosophy away from hidden matters and from things veiled by nature itself . . . and to have brought it into ordinary life, so that it might inquire into virtues and vices, and generally into good and evil things; while he judged that heavenly matters either lay far beyond our consideration or, even if they were fully known, nevertheless contributed nothing to living well. In nearly all the discourses variously and copiously recorded by those who heard him, he argues in such a way that he himself affirms nothing and refutes others; he says that he knows nothing except that very fact, and that he surpasses others because they think they know what they do not know, whereas he knows this one thing, that he knows nothing. For this reason he believed that Apollo had declared him the wisest of all, because [Col. 0415C] all wisdom consisted in this alone: not thinking oneself to know what one does not know.  
> (Cicero, *Academic Questions*, Book I, p. 5, line 41 ff.)

Who would not readily allow himself to be persuaded that these and other words of Cicero—quoted by us elsewhere when we were discussing the same Socrates—agree so closely with Caecilius’s statements that we seem to have grounds for the by no means wholly absurd suspicion that Caecilius drew his own material from them? (*Apparatus*, vol. II, Book III, dissertation 2, chapter 17, article 5, p. 1133 ff.)

Moreover, Cicero again mentions this oracle of Apollo in praise of Socrates in other books (Cicero, *On Old Age*, p. 417, line 12; *On Friendship*, p. 419, line 43, and p. 429, line 22), as do Pausanias (Book I, p. 20), Pliny (*Natural History*, Book VII, chapter 31), Solinus (chapter 1, p. 11), Valerius [Col. 0415D] Maximus (Book III, chapter 4), and very many others. Laertius, indeed, testifies that it was delivered by the Pythia in these words:

> Ἀνδρῶν ἁπάντων Σωκράτης σοφώτατος·  
> “Of all mortals, Socrates is the wisest.”  
> (Laertius, Book II, *Life of Socrates*, §37.)

The martyr Justin (*Exhortation to the Greeks*, p. 33) offered the same explanation of this oracle as Caecilius and Cicero. Lucian, however (*On Dancing*, p. 507; *Dialogues of Love*, p. 583; and *Dialogue on the Sects*, p. 304), after mentioning it more than once, speaks of Socrates himself in these words:

> Ὃς ἐκεκράγει πρὸς ἅπαντας, οὐχ ὅπως μὴ πάντα ἀλλὰ μηδ’ ὅλως εἰδέναι τι, ἢ τοῦτο μόνον, ὅτι οὐκ οἶδε.  
> [Col. 0416A] “He proclaimed before everyone that he knew not merely not everything, but absolutely nothing at all—or only this, that he did not know.”

Theodoret, moreover (*Cure of the Greek Maladies*, discourse 2, p. 488; discourse 4, p. 531), who attributes this oracle to the Pythia, somewhere quotes Xenophon’s words (Xenophon, *Memorabilia*, Book I, p. 710; Book IV, p. 815), in which he relates how Socrates discouraged all men from investigating heavenly and divine matters, and asserted that those who attempted to scrutinize them were either fools or in the greatest danger of folly. You will find Xenophon’s complete words in his own books, and also cited by Cyril of Alexandria (Book V, *Against Julian*, p. 180) and Gellius (Book IV, *Attic Nights*, [Col. 0416B] chapter 4). Nevertheless, Laertius (Book II, §§37 and 45) proves from the testimony of the same Xenophon (Xenophon, *Memorabilia*, Book I, p. 726) that Socrates sometimes discussed the providence of God; and the passage of Xenophon cited by him is indeed found in Xenophon’s own books.

Finally, the saying of Socrates cited by Caecilius, “What is above us is nothing to us,” is given by Lactantius (*On False Wisdom*, Book III, chapter 20, p. 308) in these words:

> Socrates had this celebrated proverb: “What is above us is nothing to us.”

Jerome, however, employs it against Rufinus as follows:

> You set the whole of natural philosophy against me, so that Socrates passed over to ethics in vain when he said: “Things above us are nothing to us.”  
> (Jerome, *Apology Against Rufinus*, Book II, [Col. 0416C] well past the middle.)

Caecilius concludes from these considerations that the safe suspension of judgment practiced by Arcesilaus, Carneades, Simonides, and the Academics in the highest questions—and especially concerning the gods—must be imitated. You can certainly see the foundations on which this argument of Caecilius, or of the pagan spokesman, rests. Let us now examine Octavius’s response to it.

## ARTICLE III  
### The Replies by Which Octavius Dissolves and Overthrows Caecilius’s Foregoing Arguments Are Set Forth

Octavius indeed admits, and concedes to Caecilius, that a man [Col. 0416D] ought to know himself and carefully consider what he is and whence he comes: whether he has been compounded from elements or atoms, or was made and created by God. But this, he says, cannot be known by him unless he knows God. Furthermore, just as other animals are bent toward the earth and so formed as to look upon the ground and their food, man has an uplifted and erect countenance so that he may not crawl upon the ground, but, by raising his eyes to heaven and contemplating the entire adornment of the world, may attain to knowledge of God. What, moreover, of the fact that it is not right for him to remain ignorant of the divine splendor that thrusts itself upon our eyes and senses? For if he surveys the things below, around, and above himself, the things set before his feet and in the regions of heaven, [Col. 0417A] he will immediately discover with perfect clarity that there exists a divine power of surpassing intelligence, by which all nature was created and is moved, nourished, and governed. We have already seen that Octavius excerpted this from Cicero’s first book *On the Nature of the Gods*. Christians, therefore, in asserting this with the greatest constancy, were entangling themselves in no vain or fearful opinions.

He very easily extricates himself from the authority of Socrates advanced against him, diminishing it in very few words and utterly disposing of it. For after he had shown that the many arguments by which he had proved God’s existence were certain, he immediately added:

> Let Socrates, then, that Attic buffoon, look to it: he confessed that he knew nothing, although he gloried in the testimony of a most deceitful demon.

He says no more there, but enough to destroy completely [Col. 0417B] everything drawn from Socrates’ authority. For he freely grants Caecilius that Socrates did indeed confess that he knew nothing, but in the same place asserts that he was “an Attic buffoon.” If you ask on whose authority he said this, he will answer that Cicero reports that Zeno called him so:

> Zeno, he says, assailed with abuse not only those then living—Apollodorus, Syllus, and the rest—but Socrates himself, the father of philosophy, whom, employing a Latin expression, he used to call an Attic buffoon.  
> (Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, Book I, p. 209, line 9.)

Accordingly, Lactantius, on this very subject and citing the same Zeno, attacks Socrates in these words:

> He used to swear by the dog and the goose. What a buffoon the man was—as Zeno the Epicurean says—what a foolish, ruined, desperate man, if he intended to mock religion; what a madman, if he did this [Col. 0417C] seriously, so as to regard a most shameful animal as God!  
> (Lactantius, *On False Wisdom*, Book III, chapter 20, p. 309.)

He thus plainly proves that Socrates was rightly and deservedly called a buffoon by Zeno, although Zeno was an Epicurean: for if Socrates playfully swore by the dog and the goose, he ridiculed and mocked religion; but if he did so seriously, he was certainly insane, since, no differently from the Egyptians, he regarded a most shameful animal as God. Hence, without doubt, Timon portrayed this philosopher in his *Silloi* in the following verses:

> Ἐκ δ’ ἄρα τῶν ἀπέκλινε λιθοξόος, ἐννομολέσχης,  
> Ἑλλήνων ἐπαοιδός, ἀκριβολόγους ἀποφήνας,  
> Μυκτὴρ ῥητορόμυκτος, ὑπαττικός, εἰρωνευτής.
>
> From these there issued the stone-polisher, the chatterer about laws,  
> The prophet of the Greeks and master of imposture,  
> A scoffer, a snuffling rhetorician, sub-Attic, and a dissembler.  
> (Laertius, Book II, *Life of Socrates*, §19.)

[Col. 0417D] Nor is there any ground for someone to object that, as Cicero testifies, Socrates was called εἴρων (*eirōn*) by the Greeks—that is, witty, humorous, and elegant (Cicero, *On the Orator*, Book II, p. 167; *Brutus*, p. 240; *Academic Questions*, Book II, p. 14; *On Duties*, Book II, p. 365)—because with Attic wit, or words seasoned with gravity, he constantly attacked other philosophers who boasted that they had laid claim to wisdom for themselves; whereas the Epicureans, taking greater offense at this, struck him with the most insulting reproach of “buffoon.” For who would deny that a man who professed to know nothing—not even God himself—was rightly called by other pagan philosophers, and by Minucius and Lactantius, a “buffoon,” or, more mildly, an “Attic buffoon”?

[Col. 0418A] Furthermore, Minucius rebukes with great sharpness and wit that Socrates who gloried in Apollo’s testimony. For it was the oracle of a most deceitful demon—an oracle which, like the others vaunted by the pagans, he demonstrates, as we shall see below, to have been delivered and produced by impious demons. Hence Tertullian speaks exceedingly well against this very oracle of Apollo, by which, he says, “Apollo proclaimed Socrates the wisest of all,” exclaiming:

> O thoughtless Apollo! He gave testimony of wisdom to the man who denied that the gods existed.  
> (Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 46, p. 40.)

Once Socrates’ authority has thus been overthrown, the testimony of Arcesilaus, Carneades, and the other Academics subsequently cited by Caecilius must necessarily collapse completely [Col. 0418B] as well. For these men, as Caecilius himself admits, were Socrates’ disciples and proponents of the same opinion:

> From this source—these are Caecilius’s words—flowed the safe suspension of judgment practiced by Arcesilaus, and much later by Carneades and very many Academics, in the highest questions—a kind of philosophizing by which the unlearned may proceed cautiously and the learned gloriously.

Cicero explains this opinion of Arcesilaus, Carneades, and the other Academics with the greatest clarity in *On the Orator*, Book III, p. 193; *On Ends*, Book II, p. 58; *On Duties*, Book III, p. 390; *On Divination*, Book II, p. 301; and especially *Academic Questions*, Book I, p. 10, and Book IV, pp. 15, 14 ff. So too does Diogenes Laertius in Book IV of *Lives and Doctrines of the Philosophers*, where he wrote the lives of both Arcesilaus and Carneades; Augustine in *The City of God*, Book XIX, chapter 18, and *Against the Academics*, Book III, [Col. 0418C] p. 284; Gellius in *Attic Nights*, Book XI, chapter 5, where he clearly elucidates the difference between the Academics and the Pyrrhonists; and Vossius, Jonstonus, and others who committed many observations about the philosophers and their schools to writing. We ourselves discussed the vain school of the Academics, and Arcesilaus and Carneades by name, in volume I of this *Apparatus*, Book III, dissertation 2, chapter 17, article 5, p. 1134. Who, moreover, does not understand by what right Minucius, after refuting and rejecting Socrates, regards the opinions and testimony of all these men as worthless and utterly spurns them?

The point that Caecilius presses at somewhat greater length from Simonides is of no greater value in Minucius’s estimation:

> What of Simonides the lyric poet? Is not his hesitation admirable to all and worthy of everyone’s imitation? When the tyrant Hiero asked Simonides [Col. 0418D] what and of what sort he believed the gods to be, he first requested one day for deliberation; on the next day he extended it to two; then, when reminded, he added an equal period; and at last, when the tyrant inquired into the reasons for so long a delay, Simonides answered that the longer his inquiry proceeded, the more obscure the truth became to him.

He appears to have borrowed this from Cicero, for the Latin orator relates the same matter as follows:

> You ask me what or of what sort God is? I shall employ the authority of Simonides. When the tyrant Hiero asked him this same question, Simonides requested one day for deliberation. When Hiero asked him again the next day, he requested two days; and when he repeatedly doubled the number of days, Hiero asked in amazement why he did so. “Because,” he said, [Col. 0419A] “the longer I consider it, the more obscure it appears to me.”  
> (Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, Book I, p. 204, line 12 ff.)

In that passage Simonides is called by the same Cicero “a charming poet”; and hence, as Suidas says, he was called Μελικέρτης, *Melicertes*, because of his sweetness. Accordingly, the royal manuscript of our Minucius corruptly reads *Simonidis Melchi*, and the restoration *Melici* in the printed editions is not incorrect. Pausanias mentions him, and Aelian testifies that his native land was Ceos. We have already discussed him (Pausanias, *Attica*, Book I, p. 2; Aelian, *Various History*, Book IV, chapter 15; Book IX, final chapter; and Book XII, chapter 25; our *Apparatus*, vol. I, Book III, dissertation 2, final chapter, final article, p. 1284).

How cheaply Minucius values not only this Simonides, or Arcesilaus and Carneades, but [Col. 0419B] also Pyrrho and all the other Academic and pagan philosophers, may be gathered from these words of his:

> Let Arcesilaus, Carneades, and Pyrrho deliberate—as to Pyrrho, see Laertius, Eusebius, and others, as well as our discussion elsewhere—and let the entire multitude of Academics deliberate; let Simonides even postpone his decision forever. We despise the haughty brows of the philosophers, whom we know to be corrupters, adulterers, tyrants, and eloquent against their own vices. We display wisdom not in our attire but in our minds; we do not utter great things, but live them. We glory that we have attained what they sought with the utmost exertion and could not find.  
> (Laertius, Book IX, *Life of Pyrrho*; Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, Book XIV, chapters 17 and 18, p. 350.)

Cyprian similarly transferred some of these words [Col. 0419C] into his book *On the Good of Patience*:

> We see that philosophers are neither humble nor gentle, but highly self-satisfied; yet by the very fact that they satisfy themselves, they displease God. . . . But we, who are philosophers not in words but in deeds, display wisdom not in clothing but in truth; we know the consciousness of virtues rather than ostentation; we do not speak great things, but live them.  
> (Cyprian, *On the Good of Patience*, shortly after the beginning, p. 210 ff.)

Tertullian, moreover—whom we discuss in his proper place (*Dissertation on Tertullian*, chapter 4, article 4)—relates about Thales the same story that Minucius tells about Simonides:

> What certain answer did that Thales, the chief of the natural philosophers, give to Croesus when questioned about the Divinity, after repeatedly failing to make use of the periods granted him for deliberation?  
> (Tertullian, *Apology*, [Col. 0419D] chapter 46, p. 40.)

Minucius therefore rightly concludes that neither human weakness nor the philosophers’ professed ignorance could ever prevent Christians from discussing God and heavenly matters. For before our Minucius, Tertullian had said in the passage already cited:

> Any Christian artisan both finds God and demonstrates him, and from that point assigns in fact everything that is sought concerning God, although Plato declares that the maker of the universe is not easy to find and, once found, is difficult to explain to everyone.

Finally, Tertullian there proves, as we shall demonstrate more fully in its proper place, what Minucius said concerning the vices of the philosophers.

## ARTICLE IV  
### The Arguments by Which Caecilius Denies That God Exists and Octavius Demonstrates His Existence Are Examined

[Col. 0420A]

Since Caecilius, as we have said, sustains in his disputation the role and office of the Academics, it is no wonder that from the very beginning of his speech he confidently affirms that it can be proved with no difficulty at all that “all things in human affairs are doubtful, uncertain, and unresolved, and that all things are more probable than true.” Although the falsity of so absurd and foolish a proposition has been amply demonstrated by us, following Octavius, in the preceding articles, Caecilius nevertheless attempts to infer from it that no one thus far has possessed certain and established knowledge whether God exists:

[Col. 0420B]

> Suppose that in the beginning the seeds of all things, as nature gathered into itself, were compressed together: what God was the author here? Suppose that the members of the whole world were joined, ordered, and formed through accidental collisions: what God was their craftsman? Suppose that fire kindled the stars, that heaven was suspended by its own material, that the earth was established by its weight, and that the sea flowed in as liquid: whence comes this religion, whence this fear, what is this superstition?

Yet with these words Caecilius, after the opinion of Democritus and Epicurus had been rejected by other philosophers—an opinion according to which, as Cicero and others say, they believed that all things were formed by the motion and collision of atoms—endeavors to undermine the true Christian teaching about God (Cicero, *On Ends*, Book I, p. 41 ff.; *Academic Questions*, Book I, p. 4; *On the Nature of the Gods*, Book I, pp. 203, 204 ff.; Laertius, Books IX and X, *Lives of Democritus and Epicurus*; Theodoret, [Col. 0420C] discourse 2, p. 487, and discourse 4, p. 528; Gassendi, vol. I, p. 256 ff.; *Syntagma of Epicurean Philosophy*, part 2, §1, chapter 15; and our *Apparatus*, vol. I, pp. 435 and 1136). For in Cicero himself, the Epicurean Velleius tried to refute Plato’s position concerning God by the same argument:

> With what eyes could your Plato have beheld the construction of that mighty work by which he makes the world be constructed and built by God? What was the method of construction? What tools, what levers, what machines, what assistants were employed in so great a task? How, moreover, could air, fire, water, and earth obey and submit to the architect’s will? And whence arose those five forms from which the remaining things are formed, so aptly suited to fashioning the mind and producing the senses? It would take too long to proceed through all such matters, which make them appear to have been wished for rather than discovered.  
> (Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, p. 198, line 22.)

[Col. 0420D] Caecilius undoubtedly believed that by this mine of Cicero’s all the philosophers’ opinions concerning God could be demolished. For if everything was composed by the accidental motion and collision of atoms, and the elements flow and revolve back into themselves without any craftsman or author, then assuredly no God exists—or at least his existence is doubtful and uncertain.

Octavius rightly replies that those who think the world and all its adornment were massed together out of certain fragments or atoms adhering to one another blindly and accidentally appear to possess neither mind, perception, nor eyes. [Col. 0421A] Cicero had previously said:

> Should I not therefore wonder that anyone exists who persuades himself that certain solid and indivisible bodies are borne along by force and weight, and that this most orderly and beautiful world is produced from their accidental collision? If someone thinks that this could have happened, I do not understand why he should not likewise think that, if innumerable letters in the twenty-one forms of the alphabet, whether made of gold or of any material, were thrown together somewhere and shaken out upon the ground, the *Annals* of Ennius could be produced from them in a form that might subsequently be read. I doubt whether chance could accomplish so much even in a single verse. . . . But if a collision of atoms can produce the world, why can it not produce a colonnade, a temple, a house, or a city, which are less laborious works and indeed much easier? Certainly they so recklessly [Col. 0421B] babble about the world that they seem to me never to have looked up at this marvelous adornment of heaven, which is nearest at hand.  
> (Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, Book II, p. 228, line 6.)

Not content to say this only once, he repeats it in another book more briefly, indeed, but no less clearly:

> The beauty of the world and the order of heavenly things compel mankind to confess that there exists some surpassing and eternal nature which must be revered and admired.  
> (Cicero, *On Divination*, p. 301, line 22.)

Nor is there any reason for some atheist or obstinate unbeliever to object that Cicero followed the Academic school, which held that all things were uncertain, and that he actually doubted whether the true God or the other gods of the pagans existed. For we are not asking [Col. 0421C] what he himself believed, nor whether some fear prevented him from openly confessing the true God whom he knew. Rather, we are weighing the force of his argument. Yet no man of sound mind can deny that it proves most invincibly the existence of one God, the creator and ruler of all things. For wherever Octavius says a man turns his eyes—upward or downward, this way or that—he will discover as easily as certainly that there exists a divine power of surpassing intelligence, by which all things were made and are governed.

Both Cicero and Octavius demonstrate this most plainly through a by no means brief enumeration of created things.
