Octavius does so from heaven and its swift motion, and from the fixed and settled movements of the sun and moon; from the moon’s old age and travail—that is, its various wanderings [Col. 0421D] or increases and decreases, as may be understood from Cicero, whom we shall cite presently, and from Virgil (*Georgics*, Book II, verse 478); likewise from the continuous alternation of light and darkness; the order and arrangement of the stars; the stable variety of crops and of the four seasons of the year; the sea enclosed within the bounds of its shores and coasts; the ebbing and flowing tides of the Ocean; the perpetual course of rivers and streams; straight-rising mountains, curving hills, and outstretched plains; the natural protection afforded to living creatures; and especially the beauty of man and his limbs, none of which was formed except for the sake of necessity or adornment; and from the very appearance of all human beings, by which, although they seem similar to one another, each is nevertheless found dissimilar in particular features; [Col. 0422A] and finally from the principle of birth or the desire to reproduce implanted in each creature.

Cicero pursues this induction at far greater length and devotes a very large part of the whole second book *On the Nature of the Gods* to explaining and elucidating it (Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, Book II, p. 228 ff.). It would indeed be too lengthy and of little use to transcribe here everything that he stated with his customary elegance and that our Minucius excerpted, especially since anyone may easily consult it in Cicero himself. It will therefore suffice for us to observe that Cicero, although a follower of the Academic school, advises us there that this argument was not only handled by certain philosophers, and by Cleanthes in particular, but ought also to have convinced all philosophers completely:

> For the philosophers, if perhaps they had initially been bewildered by the first sight of the world, ought afterward, when they had observed its finite and regular motions, [Col. 0422B] and all things governed by settled orders and immutable constancy, to have understood that in this heavenly and divine house there dwells not merely an inhabitant, but also a ruler and governor, and, as it were, the architect of so great a work and so great a task.  
> (*On the Nature of the Gods*, Book II, p. 227; ibid., p. 216.)

He had already made other entirely similar statements in the same book. But you may also consult Philo the Jew, author of the book *On Monarchy* and of the *Greek Questions*, as well as Athenagoras, Theophilus of Antioch, Irenaeus, Lactantius, Athanasius, and others.

What of the fact that not only these pagan, Jewish, [Col. 0422C] and Christian writers, but also the more recent scholastics—and especially St. Thomas—employ this argument to demonstrate, as they say, the existence of God, and regard it as more compelling than others insofar as it may be more easily perceived and understood by everyone? Accordingly, the Apostle confidently declares from it that no man can have any excuse whatever for his ignorance of God:

> For his invisible things, from the creation of the world, are perceived and seen through the things that have been made; his eternal power also and divinity, so that they are without excuse.  
> (Romans 1:20.)

Hence Tertullian says:

> And this, he says, is the culmination of the sin of those unwilling to acknowledge what they cannot fail to know.  
> (Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 17, p. 18.)

Cyprian says in almost the same words:

> [Col. 0422D] And it is the culmination of sin to be unwilling to acknowledge him whom you cannot fail to know.  
> (Cyprian, *On the Vanity of Idols*, p. 14.)

We have seen that this was asserted before both of them by Clement of Alexandria (*Apparatus*, vol. I, dissertation 2, chapter 6, article 1, p. 948).

## ARTICLE V  
### Another Argument of Minucius Is Considered, by Which He Demonstrates That God, Known Through the Innermost Sense and Very Conscience of Human Beings, Truly Exists

Our Minucius recalls the pagans from created things and the altogether marvelous adornment of the whole world to themselves, to their innermost sense, and to the individual conscience of each person. [Col. 0423A] For the idea and knowledge of a God who truly exists, he says, is so deeply planted and innate in their minds that not only philosophers and educated people, but even common and uneducated people, with nature as their guide, openly and plainly confess on various occasions that he exists:

> What of the fact that I have universal agreement on this matter? I hear the common people, when they stretch out their hands toward heaven, say nothing other than “God”; and “God is great”; and “God is true”; and “If God grants it.” Is this the natural speech of the common people, or the utterance of a Christian making confession?

Furthermore, he immediately added there that the pagans, under the false name of Jupiter and of their gods, in reality invoke the true God himself:

> Those who would have Jupiter as chief are mistaken in the name, but [Col. 0423B] agree concerning the divine power.

Cyprian, as we have seen above, committed precisely the same thought to writing. But both were preceded by Tertullian, who argues against the same pagans in an entirely similar manner:

> Do you wish us to prove from the testimony of the soul itself

—that is, that only one God of all things exists?—

> which, although confined in the prison of the body, although hemmed in by corrupt training, although enervated by lusts and desires, although enslaved to false gods, nevertheless, when it comes to its senses as though from drunkenness, sleep, or some illness, names God for this reason alone: because properly speaking this one God is true, good, and great—

so the older and better manuscripts read, as we shall see in the proper place—

> and “What God grants” is the voice of all. It also calls him to witness as judge: “God sees”; and [Col. 0423C] “I commend myself to God”; and “God will repay me.” O testimony of a soul naturally Christian! Finally, in making these declarations, it looks not toward the Capitol but toward heaven. For it knows the dwelling place of the living God. From him and from there it descended.  
> (Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 17, p. 18.)

He pursues these matters still more fully in another book. Since it would be too lengthy to transcribe them all, we shall present some, especially those relevant to our Minucius’s second passage:

> I hear you publicly and with all the freedom that is not permitted to us, at home and abroad, pronounce these words: “What God grants,” and “If God wills.” By that expression you both indicate that someone exists and confess all power to belong to him, upon whose will you wait. At the same time, you deny that the others are gods, since you call them by their own names—Saturn, Jupiter, [Col. 0423D] Mars, and Minerva. You affirm God alone when you call only him “God,” so that, when you sometimes call those others gods, you appear to use a designation belonging to another, as though on loan. Nor are you ignorant of the nature of God which we proclaim. “God is good”; “God does good”: these are your words.  
> (*On the Testimony of the Soul*, chapter 2, p. 81.)

Likewise, in his book *To Scapula*:

> The people, acclaiming the God of gods, who alone is mighty, bore testimony under the name of Jupiter to our God.  
> (*To Scapula*, chapter 4, p. 87.)

Yet this, he says, is “the testimony of a soul naturally Christian,” namely, inasmuch as it possesses by nature an implanted knowledge of the true God of the Christians. For elsewhere, as we shall see in the proper place, he affirms no less clearly that Christians are made, not born. [Col. 0424A] Accordingly, our Minucius said:

> Is this ordinary natural speech, or the utterance of a Christian confessing—

namely, confessing that God exists? After proving this first and principal teaching of the true religion by various testimonies of pagan philosophers, he concludes from them that “either the philosophers are now Christians, or the philosophers were Christians even then”—insofar as they acknowledged the true God, but not the other tenets of the Christian religion. More on this, however, in our dissertation on Tertullian’s *Apology*.

Arnobius, moreover, argues in exactly the same manner as Tertullian and our Minucius:

> Render a true judgment: as you look about upon all these things that we see, [Col. 0424B] you will sooner doubt whether the other gods exist than hesitate concerning God, whom we all know by nature—whether when we exclaim, “O God!” or when we appoint him witness of the wicked and, as though he saw us, raise our faces toward heaven.  
> (Arnobius, *Against the Pagans*, Book II, beginning, p. 43.)

Finally, Lactantius similarly argues against the pagans:

> For when they swear, he says, and when they make wishes and give thanks, they name not Jupiter or many gods, but God: so completely does truth itself, under nature’s compulsion, burst forth even from unwilling hearts. . . . But if some grave necessity presses upon them, then they remember God. If the terror of war roars, if a long drought denies nourishment to the crops, if a savage storm or hail bears down upon them, they flee to God; help is sought from God; God is entreated to bring aid. If anyone is tossed upon the sea [Col. 0424C] while the wind rages, he invokes him. If anyone is afflicted by some violence, he immediately implores him. If anyone, reduced to the extremity of begging, seeks sustenance through entreaties, he calls upon God alone and appeals by his divine and unique power.  
> (Lactantius, *Institutes*, Book II, chapter 2, p. 138.)

Moreover, that knowledge of God is so deeply engendered in the human mind and innermost senses that no one can be ignorant of him without great guilt. For “it is neither right nor lawful,” our author says, “to remain ignorant of the heavenly splendor that thrusts itself upon our eyes and senses.” Accordingly, he afterward confidently asserts that all who are ignorant of God must, like the impious, be punished with the penalties and torments they deserve. If you wish to hear him speak, here are his very words:

> No one who is not profane deliberates whether those who [Col. 0424D] do not know God ought deservedly to be punished as impious and unjust, since it is no lesser crime to be ignorant of the Parent and Lord of all than to injure him.

But you have already heard Paul the Apostle, Tertullian, and Cyprian, cited by us, making the same pronouncement concerning those who neither recognize nor wish to recognize him from created things or from that knowledge of God implanted in their minds.

How greatly even pagan philosophers favor this opinion concerning the knowledge of God innate in man may be learned from their Latin Orator:

> What nation or what race of men is there that does not possess, without instruction, a certain anticipation concerning the gods, which Epicurus calls πρόληψις (*prolēpsis*), that is, a certain conception of a thing grasped beforehand by the mind, [Col. 0425A] without which nothing can be understood, investigated, or discussed? . . . For since this belief was established by no institution, custom, or law, and the firm and unanimous agreement of all remains, it must be understood that gods exist, because we possess implanted—or rather innate—knowledge of them. But that on which the nature of all agrees must necessarily be true. It must therefore be confessed that gods exist.  
> (Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, Book I, p. 202, line 5 ff.)

What could be truer than this confession and argument of a pagan man, had he only said “the true and one God” in place of his gods? But consider, I ask, whether he corrected this error when, on the testimony of Ennius, he shows that this true God, as Minucius and Tertullian say, is invoked by everyone under the name of Jupiter:

> For if this were not [Col. 0425B] so, how could Ennius, with the assent of all, have said:
>
> Behold this  
> Lofty, gleaming vault, which all invoke  
> As Jupiter.
>
> And indeed call him Jupiter, ruler of things, governing all by his nod, and, as the same Ennius says,
>
> Father of gods and men,
>
> and the present and supremely powerful God? Whoever doubts this, I truly do not understand why he could not likewise doubt whether there is a sun or no sun at all.  
> (*On the Nature of the Gods*, Book II, p. 214, line 12 ff.)

# CHAPTER IV  
## ON THE ONE GOD

## ARTICLE I  
### The Argument Is Examined by Which Octavius Shows, on the Authority of the Pagan Poets Homer and Virgil and of the Philosophers Thales, Anaximenes, Diogenes of Apollonia, Anaxagoras, Pythagoras, and Xenophanes, That There Is Only One God

[Col. 0425C]

Just as Minucius demonstrates by the strongest arguments of reason and by the common agreement of all peoples that God truly exists, so too he clearly shows, from the testimony of the pagans’ own poets and philosophers alike, that God is plainly one. He begins with the poets as follows:

> I hear the poets also proclaiming one Father of gods and men, and saying that the mind of mortals is such as the Parent of all has declared it to be.

[Col. 0425D] Someone may perhaps ask us whether these are the words of one Greek or Latin poet, or of several. Yet at the end of the preceding article we saw that Jupiter, whom all invoke, is called by the poet Ennius “the Father of gods and men.” Cicero there introduces the Stoic Balbus citing these very words to affirm the existence of a divine power of surpassing intelligence. Augustine further testifies that the same Cicero (*The City of God*, Book V, chapter 8, p. 121), when proving that the Stoics called Jupiter “the supreme God,” as they thought him to be, cited the following verses of Homer and translated them into Latin thus:

> Such are the minds of men as the Father himself,  
> Jupiter, when he has surveyed with his light the fruit-bearing earth.

[Col. 0426A] These verses are presented in Greek by Homer himself as follows:

> Τοῖος γὰρ νόος ἐστὶν ἐπιχθονίων ἀνθρώπων,  
> Οἷον ἐπ’ ἦμαρ ἄγησι πατὴρ ἀνδρῶν τε θεῶν τε.  
> (Homer, *Odyssey* XVIII, verse 135.)

A Latin translator rendered them thus:

> For such is the mind of earth-dwelling men  
> As the Father of men and gods directs it each day.

We know, indeed, that Lactantius declared that nothing pertaining to truth could have been supplied by Homer, since he wrote about human rather than divine matters (Lactantius, *Divine Institutes*, Book I, chapter 5, p. 21). But apart from the fact that Cicero cited these verses as accepted by the Stoics, they agree so closely with our Minucius’s purpose [Col. 0426B] that he plainly seems to have aimed at them. Yet if anyone properly proves to us that Minucius cited either Ennius or other poets there, we shall immediately assent to him.

The other poet is thus called by his proper name by Minucius, just as he was later by Lactantius (Lactant., *Divine Institutes*, book I, chap. 5, p. 22): “What of Maro of Mantua? Does he not speak more openly, more nearly, and more truly?”—that is, does he not approach more closely to the true doctrine concerning God, and declare it more openly and truly? Yet our author does not give his verses in full, nor say in which book they occur, but presents only their sense and certain words, although excerpted from two of his books, in this form: “In the beginning, a spirit nourishes from within heaven and the earth and the other members of the world, and an infused [Col. 0426C] mind moves them; thence comes the race of men and cattle, and whatever else belongs to living creatures.” Elsewhere he calls this same mind and spirit “God.” For these are his words: “For God passes through all the lands, the expanses of the sea, and the profound heaven; from him come men and cattle, rain and fires.” It will therefore not be wholly useless—and for some will be worth the effort—to transcribe those verses in full and indicate where they are found. The former are read thus in the sixth book of the *Aeneid*:

> In the beginning, a spirit nourishes from within the heaven, the earth,  
> The liquid plains, the shining globe of the moon, and the Titanian stars;  
> And a mind, infused throughout its limbs, moves the whole mass  
> And mingles itself with the mighty body.  
> Thence come the race of men and cattle, the lives of flying creatures,  
> And the monsters that the sea bears beneath its marble surface.  
> (Virgil, *Aeneid*, book VI, v. 719 ff.)

The latter occur thus in the fourth book of the *Georgics*:

> [Col. 0426D] For God passes through all  
> The lands, the expanses of the sea, and the profound heaven.  
> From him come cattle, herds, men, and every race of wild beasts;  
> And each at birth summons from him its slender life.  
> (The same, *Georgics*, book IV, v. 220 ff.)

On these verses, and especially the former, Servius’s observations should be read. Minucius could have cited several other poets, especially Greek poets, whom we discussed in the preceding volume (vol. I, *Apparatus*, p. 784). But because, as is evident, no one denies that Homer was the leader and chief of all Greek poets and Maro of the Latin poets, he therefore considered their testimonies more than sufficient to prove that principal [Col. 0427A] dogma of the Christian religion.

He accordingly passes to the more celebrated philosophers and proves that, although not in the same words, they agreed in substance upon the same doctrine. He begins his account with Thales: “Thales of Miletus, who was the first of all to dispute about heavenly things, said that the origin of things was water,” as we saw elsewhere, “but that God was the mind which formed all things from water” (vol. I, *Apparatus*, pp. 434 and 776). These words appear to have been excerpted from Cicero, where he discusses the same question as our Minucius. For there, like Minucius, he reviews the philosophers’ opinions and likewise begins with Thales: “Thales of Miletus, who was the first to inquire into such matters, said that water was the origin of things, but that God was the mind which fashioned all things from water” (Cic., *On the Nature of the Gods*, book I, p. 199, line 20). Lactantius later reported the same thing in almost exactly the same words as Minucius (Lactant., *Divine Institutes*, book I, chap. 5, p. 24).

But Minucius immediately added the following words, which have been so corrupted by the carelessness of scribes and copyists that, without some new manuscript codex, their true reading can scarcely be discovered by anyone. In our printed editions they are presented thus: “And (*et*; royal ms. *eo*; Rigaltius *eho*) the account of water and spirit is higher and more sublime than could have been (*potuerit*; royal ms. *poterit*, wrongly) discovered by man, having been handed down by God (*a Deo tradita*; royal ms. *traditum*).” At the beginning of these words, should we not read *sed* (“but”), or something of that kind, in place of *eo*? However that may be, Minucius’s meaning appears to be that the account of water and spirit—as, they say, the material and efficient causes of all things—is too high and sublime to have been discovered by man unless he were instructed by God himself. Thales therefore could not have discovered what was handed down by God alone. Nevertheless, he could have learned it from the Egyptians, with whom, as we have said elsewhere, he had associated. The Egyptians had received it from Moses, and Moses from God (vol. II, *Apparatus*, p. 1120 ff.).

“Next Anaximenes,” Minucius continues, “and after him Diogenes of Apollonia, held that the infinite and immeasurable air” [was God]. Cicero, however, explains the opinion of each separately. First, these are his words concerning Anaximenes: “Anaximenes established air as God, saying that it is generated, immeasurable and infinite, and always in motion” (Cic., *On the Nature of the Gods*, book I, p. 199, [Col. 0427D] line 25). Minucius deliberately omitted the words “that it is generated”; for by the former words Anaximenes strayed all the farther from our true doctrine concerning God, the nearer he appears to approach it in the following words, “infinite and immeasurable.”

Concerning Diogenes of Apollonia, Tullius later says: “But what perception, or what form of God, can the air possess which Diogenes of Apollonia employs as God?” (The same Cicero, ibid., p. 200, line 10.) That Latin orator is indeed silent about what sort of air it was that Diogenes of Apollonia employed as God; but Augustine explains it in these words: “Diogenes, another pupil of Anaximenes, said that air was indeed the matter of things, from which all things were made, but that it was endowed with divine reason, without which nothing could be made from it” (Aug., *City of God*, book VIII, chap. 2). You surely see how rightly Minucius said that Anaximenes and Diogenes held the same opinion concerning God, and that it was not altogether repugnant to the Christian view. For although Diogenes differs from others in saying that air was the matter of things, he nevertheless agrees with Christians in this: he appears to have held it certain that air, endowed with divine reason, was the efficient cause of all things.

There are indeed writers who suspect that by the term “infinite and immeasurable air” these philosophers understood not the air we breathe, but a certain divine spirit by which, as we heard Virgil sing, the entire machinery of the world [Col. 0428B] is nourished and animated. This suspicion appears to be supported by the following words of Plutarch, quoted by Eusebius, concerning Anaximenes’ opinion: “Anaximenes of Miletus taught that air was a principle of this kind; for from it all things arise, and into it in turn all things are dissolved. For our soul (*psychē*, ψυχή), for example, is air and sustains and preserves us; and likewise spirit and air (*pneuma kai aēr*, πνεῦμα καὶ ἀήρ) encompass the whole world. ‘Spirit’ and ‘air’ have the same meaning (*legetai de synōnymōs aēr kai pneuma*, λέγεται δὲ συνωνύμως ἀὴρ καὶ πνεῦμα)” (Euseb., *Preparation for the Gospel*, book XIV, chap. 14, p. 74). These words are found in the first book of Plutarch’s *Opinions of the Philosophers* (Plutarch, book I, *On the Opinions of the Philosophers*, chap. 3, p. 876, vol. 2). But there Anaximenes is reproved by him for assigning merely the matter of things and not their efficient cause. Earlier, however, Eusebius relates from another work of Plutarch, the *Stromata*, that Anaximenes asserted nothing beyond air—which he regarded as infinite—to be the principle of all things. But Laertius explains these matters as though Anaximenes had thereby established the first principles of things (Laert., book II, § 3, and book IX, § 57). Yet perhaps these writers either did not set forth the whole opinion of Anaximenes and Diogenes of Apollonia, or by “infinite” an immeasurable spirit must be understood. On the opinions of both, see the other authors cited by us elsewhere, and Augustine, Epistle CXVIII to Dioscorus, p. 338 (vol. I, *Apparatus*, book II, diss. 2, § 29, p. 435; and book III, diss. 3, chap. 1, art. 1, p. 776).

Minucius continues: “For Anaxagoras, God is said to be the ordering and motion [Col. 0428D] effected by an infinite mind.” Cicero likewise says: “Next Anaxagoras, who received instruction from Anaximenes, was the first to maintain that the ordering and motion of all things were designed and accomplished by the power and reason of an infinite mind” (Cic., *On the Nature of the Gods*, book I, p. 199, line 22). Elsewhere he puts it somewhat differently: “Anaxagoras held matter to be infinite, but its particles to be mutually similar and minute; these were at first confused and were afterward reduced to order by the divine mind” (*Academic Questions*, book IV, p. 33, line 12). But Laertius expounded his opinion much more clearly and reliably from Anaxagoras’s own books and on the authority of Timon:

> He was the first to set mind over matter, beginning his work in this manner, in language pleasingly and nobly expressed: “All things were together; then mind came and ordered them.” For this reason he was also surnamed “Mind” or “Intellect” (*ho nous*, ὁ νοῦς). Timon also celebrated this very point about Anaxagoras in the *Silloi*:
>
> And somewhere, they say, is Anaxagoras, that valiant hero,  
> Mind—for truly he had a mind—which suddenly arose  
> And compacted together all things formerly confused.

The Latin rendering is:

> This man was the first to add mind to matter, writing thus at the beginning of his work in pleasant and magnificent language: “All things were together; then mind approached and arranged them; for which reason it is called mind or intellect, ὁ νοῦς.” Timon sang this very thing about Anaxagoras in the *Silloi*:
>
> Now where Anaxagoras is, there is Mind, the most valiant hero,  
> Who thinks that Mind—for mind was not lacking to him—suddenly  
> Arranged those things which once had been disordered together.

Lucretius, Augustine, and we ourselves also say more about him in the places already cited (Lucret., book I, near the end).

Minucius next says: “For Pythagoras, God is the mind that passes through and pervades the whole nature of things, from which the life of all living creatures is also derived.” Our author excerpted this too from Cicero: “Pythagoras,” says Cicero, “held that mind pervades and passes through the nature of things, and that from it our souls are taken” (Cic., *On the Nature of the Gods*, book I, p. 199, line 37). Lactantius undoubtedly followed both. What Laertius and Plutarch record concerning the unity and duality asserted by Pythagoras also comes to the same point, as is clear from what we observed concerning that philosopher at the places already cited in the preceding volume of our *Apparatus* (Lactant., *Divine Institutes*, book I, chap. 5, p. 24; and *On the Anger of God*, chap. 11, p. 796; Laert., book VI, *Life of Pythagoras*; Plutarch, *On the Opinions of the Philosophers*, book I, p. 876; vol. I, *Apparatus*, p. 783).

After this Minucius says: “It is well known that Xenophanes taught that the whole infinite, together with mind, is God.” These are Cicero’s very words: “Then Xenophanes, adding mind, held that everything else which was infinite was God” (Cic., *On the Nature of the Gods*, book I, p. 199, line 4). Laertius, however, relates his view somewhat differently, though not in an altogether different sense: “The substance of God is spherical and has nothing in common with human beings. He sees wholly and hears wholly, yet does not breathe. He is at once all things: mind, wisdom, and eternity” (Laert., book IX, § 15). Here the word *sphairoeidē* (σφαιροειδῆ), “spherical” or “round” in substance, signifies nothing other than “infinite.” He used it because a round figure has neither beginning nor end. Cicero therefore reports the same opinion of Xenophanes elsewhere in these words: “Xenophanes said that all things are one, that this one is immutable and is God, never born, everlasting, and spherical in shape” (*Academic Questions*, book IV, p. 33). Before Minucius’s time, moreover, Clement of Alexandria openly taught that this opinion of Xenophanes agreed with Christian doctrine and with these words of Isaiah: “To whom have you likened me? says the Lord.” He proves it in this manner:

> Xenophanes of Colophon therefore rightly teaches that God is one and incorporeal, and adds:
>
> One God, greatest among gods and men,  
> In bodily form and in thought wholly unlike mortals.

The Latin rendering is:

> Xenophanes of Colophon, rightly teaching that God is one and incorporeal, adds:
>
> Greatest in the race of gods and men  
> Is the one God,  
> Who neither in body nor in mind is like  
> Any mortal.

Eusebius transcribed in full this passage, which we briefly touched upon elsewhere; yet in another place he gives words of Plutarch which represent Xenophanes’ opinion concerning God very differently. See Epiphanius and Theodoret (vol. I, *Apparatus*, [Col. 0430B] p. 1113; Euseb., *Preparation for the Gospel*, book XIII, chap. 13, p. 679, and book I, chap. 8, p. 23; Epiphan., *Exposition of the Faith*, p. 1087; Theodoret, Discourse 2, *On the Cure of the Greek Maladies*, p. 486).

## ARTICLE II  
### On the Other Gentile Philosophers: Antisthenes, Speusippus, Democritus, Strato, Epicurus, Aristotle, Heraclides of Pontus, Theophrastus, Cleanthes, Zeno, Chrysippus, Diogenes of Babylon, Xenophon, Aristo, and Plato

Let us, if you please, proceed with our Minucius to the other gentile philosophers. He relates as follows what Antisthenes and Speusippus thought concerning God: “Antisthenes knew many popular gods, but one principal natural God; Speusippus, however, knew God as a natural, animate power by which all things are governed.” He undoubtedly borrowed this from Cicero, who had spoken of both in almost the same words: “Antisthenes, in the book entitled *The Natural Philosopher*, says that there are many popular gods, but one natural God.... Nor does Speusippus speak very differently (*Seuxippus* in the royal manuscript, but wrongly), for, following his uncle Plato, he says that there is a certain power by which all things are governed, and that it is animate” (Cic., *On the Nature of the Gods*, book I, p. 200, line 22). Lactantius later committed the same opinion of Antisthenes to writing (Lactant., *Divine Institutes*, book I, chap. 5, p. 24; and *On the Anger of God*, chap. 11, p. 796). We have discussed this philosopher and Speusippus elsewhere (vol. I, *Apparatus*, pp. 1113, 1122, and 1134). Laertius [Col. 0430D], in Speusippus’s *Life*, asserts that he remained within the doctrines of his uncle Plato. But Numenius, quoted by Eusebius, complains that Speusippus undermined those doctrines. Finally, Laertius observes that Speusippus wrote a book of *Definitions*, which some think to be the work published among the acknowledged writings of Plato. At the beginning of that book the following definition of God is read: “God is an immortal living being, self-sufficient for happiness, an everlasting essence, and the cause of the nature of the good” (*Theos zōon athanaton, autarkes pros eudaimonian, ousia aidios, tou agathou physeōs aitia*; Θεὸς ζῶον ἀθάνατον, αὐτάρκες πρὸς εὐδαιμονίαν, οὐσία ἀΐδιος, τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ φύσεως αἰτία) (Laert., book IV, §§ 1, 5; Euseb., *Preparation for the Gospel*, book IV, chap. 5, p. 727; in Plato, vol. 3, p. 411).

Again, Minucius had excerpted from Cicero [Col. 0431A] what he next added about Democritus: “What of Democritus? Although the first inventor of atoms, does he not frequently speak of the nature which pours forth images, and of intelligence, as God?” Cicero similarly says of him: “What of Democritus,” he asks, “who at one time numbers images and their circuits among the gods, at another that nature which pours forth and emits the images, and at another our knowledge and intelligence?” (Cicero, cited book, p. 200, line 5). Augustine therefore writes the following to Dioscorus concerning that opinion of Democritus:

> How much better it would have been had I never even heard the name of Democritus than that I should reflect with grief upon some man, regarded as great in his own time, who thought that the gods were images flowing from solid bodies, although not themselves solid, and that by moving about this way and that through their own motion and gliding into human minds, they caused divine power to be conceived—although certainly the body from which the image flowed would be judged all the more excellent in proportion as it was more solid. And so, as these men say, his opinion fluctuated and wavered, so that at times he said that a certain nature from which the images flowed was God; yet this God could not be conceived except through those images which it pours forth and emits—that is, images which were borne, came, and entered our minds as though by a continuous emanation, in the likeness of a body, from that nature which he regards as somehow corporeal and everlasting, and therefore also divine—in order that we might conceive God or gods.  
> (Augustine, Epistle 118, p. 340)

But however much Democritus fluctuated and wavered, from what Augustine himself and Cicero handed down in writing concerning his opinion, who does not see that Minucius rightly and deservedly said that in at least some manner Democritus acknowledged the divine nature and that God is truly one? And that was sufficient for Minucius’s purpose.

He next sets forth Strato’s opinion in these few words: “Strato likewise [held] nature itself.” Yet the fewer these words are, the less clear they are. Cicero, whom we have so often praised, will therefore furnish you with their explanation: “Nor should we listen,” he says, “to Strato, the pupil of Theophrastus, who is called the natural philosopher and who holds that all divine power resides in nature, which possesses the causes of generation, growth, and diminution, but lacks all sensation and form” (Cic., [Col. 0431D] cited book, p. 200, line 45). Do you want more? Hear the same orator speak of him again:

> You deny that anything can exist without God. Here, coming at you from the other side, is Strato of Lampsacus, who grants this God exemption from a very great task indeed. But since the priests of the gods enjoy exemption from duties, how much more equitable is it that the gods themselves should enjoy it? He denies that he employs the gods’ workmanship in constructing the world. He teaches that all things, whatever they may be, were produced by nature—not as the philosopher does who says that these things are compounded of rough and smooth bodies and of hooked and barbed bodies, with void interposed. He judges these to be dreams of Democritus, who was not teaching but merely wishing. Strato himself, however, pursuing the individual parts of the world, teaches that whatever exists or comes to pass does so, or has done so, through natural weights and motions. [Col. 0432A] Thus he frees God from a great task, and me from fear.  
> (*Academic Questions*, book IV, p. 33, line 46)

If you desire another author to be cited, here at hand is Plutarch, who left the following written concerning Strato’s opinion:

> Indeed Strato, the foremost of the other Peripatetics, disagrees with Aristotle on many matters and maintains opinions contrary to Plato concerning motion, mind, soul, and generation. Finally, he denies that the world itself is a living being and says that what occurs by nature follows what occurs by chance.

The Latin version continues: “Chance supplies the beginning of motion to nature, and physical motions are then completed by nature in this way” (Plutarch, *Against Colotes the Epicurean*, p. 1115). We have already seen Cicero explain what Strato called “nature.” But we shall still have something to say about this opinion of his when we attempt to make clear to everyone how Lactantius refutes it.

Meanwhile, let us follow our Minucius: “Even that Epicurus,” he says, “who imagines the gods either idle or nonexistent, nevertheless sets nature above them.” Velleius the Epicurean, however, explains at length in Cicero this opinion of Epicurus concerning God. After proving by many arguments that the life of God is such that nothing happier or more wholly abounding in every good can be conceived, he gives this reason for his opinion: “For he does nothing, is entangled in no occupations, and undertakes no labors; he rejoices in his wisdom and virtue, and is assured that he will always possess both the greatest and everlasting pleasures.” Later, in the same place, he declares that Epicurus falsely taught that the world was produced by nature: “There was no need for craftsmanship, and that matter is very easy for nature” (Cic., *On the Nature of the Gods*, book I, p. 203, line 8). For, as we have already said, he babbled that all things had been made by a fortuitous collision of atoms. Finally, in the same place, Tullius said in the person of Velleius, or of the Epicureans: “And we piously and reverently worship the excellent and preeminent nature.” Our Minucius distinguishes the things Epicurus taught falsely from those by which, willing or unwilling, he confessed a nature more excellent than all others and therefore divine. Consult, if you please, Laertius and the notes of Ménage and Gassendi upon him, and another book by the latter (Laert., book X, § 123; notes of Ménage and Gassendi on the latter’s book IV, *On the Life and Character of Epicurus*, chaps. 1, 2, 3).

Next Minucius transcribed many of Cicero’s words reporting Aristotle’s opinion concerning God. For behold how he speaks: “Aristotle varies, yet nevertheless assigns a single power. For at one time he calls mind God, at another the world, and at another he sets God over the world.” Tullius says: “Aristotle, in the third book *On Philosophy*, throws many things into confusion, disagreeing with his master Plato alone. For at one moment he ascribes all divinity to mind, at another says that the world itself is God, and at another places some other being over the world” (Cic., cited book, p. 200, line 26 ff.). Minucius excerpted these words but omitted [Col. 0433A] the following: “And he assigns such functions to that being that it governs and preserves motion by a certain revolution of the world; then he says that the heat of heaven is God.... But when he also wishes God to be without a body, he deprives him of every sensation and of wisdom.” Lactantius nevertheless reported fewer details than either author concerning Aristotle’s opinion, in this manner: “Although Aristotle disagrees with himself and both says and thinks contradictory things, he nevertheless testifies that one supreme mind presides over the world” (Lactant., *Divine Institutes*, book II, chap. 25, p. 25; and *On the Anger of God*, chap. 11, p. 796). In another book he is briefer still: “Aristotle and his Peripatetics,” he says, “held nearly the same views as Antisthenes,” of whom we spoke shortly before. See Plutarch and Lescalopier, and, if you wish, what we have observed elsewhere (Plutarch, *On the Opinions of the Philosophers*, book I, chap. 7, p. 881; Lescalopier on the cited passage of Cicero, § 33, p. 54, and *On Aristotle’s Theology*, p. 184 ff.; vol. I, *Apparatus*, p. 781).

Furthermore, Minucius says, “Heraclides of Pontus, though in varying ways, ascribes divine mind to God, assigning supremacy at one time to the world and at another to the divine mind.” Cicero reports this and still more concerning him: “Heraclides of Pontus, from the same [Col. 0433B] school of Plato, filled his books with childish tales; and yet at one time he thinks the world is God, at another a divine mind. He also ascribes divinity to the wandering stars, deprives God of sensation, and wishes his form to be mutable; and in the same book he again numbers earth and heaven among the gods” (Cic., *On the Nature of the Gods*, book I, p. 200, line 39 ff.). Minucius therefore, as you see, reports only those elements of Heraclides’ opinion which served his purpose. Laertius wrote his life, and we discussed him in the passage cited shortly before in the preceding volume (Laert., near the end of book V; vol. I, *Apparatus*, p. 779).

Minucius then joins four other philosophers together: “Theophrastus, Zeno, Chrysippus, and Cleanthes are themselves manifold in their views, but all return to the unity of providence.” Immediately thereafter he reviews individually the opinions of the latter three, but says nothing further about the first. Who would dare assert whether this was omitted by Minucius himself or through a copyist’s drowsiness? If you wish to know Theophrastus’s opinion, these words of Cicero will disclose it to you: “Nor indeed is the inconsistency of Theophrastus to be tolerated; for at one time he assigns divine supremacy to mind, at another to heaven, and then to the signs and heavenly stars” (Cic., ibid., p. 200, line 42). See, if you please, what we have observed concerning him elsewhere (vol. I, *Apparatus*, p. 781).

Having made these observations, let us now examine what Minucius determines concerning the other three. He begins with Cleanthes: “Cleanthes asserts that God is at one time mind, at another soul, at another ether, and most often reason.” Thus he began with the last, although he acknowledges, as does Cicero, whose footsteps he follows in his usual manner, that Cleanthes was Zeno’s pupil. Cicero committed the following account of his opinion to writing: “Cleanthes, who heard Zeno, at one time says that the world itself is God; at another he gives this name to the mind and soul of the whole of nature; while at another he judges the outermost and highest heat, poured around everything on every side, enclosing and embracing all things at the boundary—which is called ether—to be most certainly God” (Cic., cited book, p. 101, line 10). Cicero explains this still more fully, as we have noted elsewhere (vol. I, *Apparatus*, p. 782).

Minucius next assigns the second place to Zeno, Cleanthes’s master, and sets forth his opinion concerning God as follows: “Zeno, his master, holds that the natural and divine law, at one time the ether, and at another reason, is the principle of all things. The same man, by interpretation—showing that Juno is air, Jupiter heaven, Neptune the sea, Vulcan fire, and similarly that the other gods of the common people are the elements—sternly accuses and refutes the public error.” Have not these words also been excerpted from the following passage of Cicero?

> Zeno holds that natural law is divine, and that it possesses the power of commanding what is right and forbidding the contrary.... Elsewhere he says that the ether is God.... In other books, however, he thinks that a certain reason extending throughout the whole of nature is endowed with divinity. He ascribes the same to the stars, and then to the years, months, and changes of the years. But when he interprets Hesiod’s *Theogony*, he wholly abolishes the customary and accepted conceptions of the gods. For he does not number Jupiter, Juno, Vesta, or anyone else called by such a name among the gods, but by a certain mode of signification assigns these names to inanimate and mute things.  
> (Cic., cited book, p. 200, line 47 [Col. 0434C] ff.)

Laertius testifies that Zeno’s opinion was: “There is one God, who is also mind, fate, and Zeus, and is called by many other names” (*Hena te einai Theon, kai noun, kai heimarmenēn, kai Dia, pollais te heterais onomasiais prosonomazesthai*; Ἕνα τε εἶναι Θεὸν, καὶ νοῦν, καὶ εἱμαρμένην, καὶ Δία, πολλαῖς τε ἑτέραις ὀνομασίαις προσονομάζεσθαι) (Laert., book VII, *Life of Zeno*, §§ 135 and 147). He later enumerated those names. Hence Tertullian says: “Among your own sages also it is agreed that the *Logos* (λόγος), that is, Speech and Reason, is regarded as the artificer of the universe. For Zeno defines him as the maker who formed all things in their ordered arrangement, and says that the same is called Fate, God, the mind of Jupiter, and the necessity of all things” (Tertull., *Apology*, chap. 21). Lactantius follows Tertullian (Lactant., *Divine Institutes*, book IV, chap. 7, p. 373). But we have already touched upon some of these matters [Col. 0434D] in the preceding volume of our *Apparatus* (vol. I, *Apparatus*, p. 780). We shall show in the following dissertation in what manner Zeno and the Stoics regarded the gods of the common people as elements (*Dissertation on Arnobius*, chap. 17, art. 5).

The third named by Minucius is Chrysippus, who, he says, “holding almost the same doctrines, believes divine power, rational nature, and fatal necessity to be God; and he imitates Zeno in the physiological interpretation of the poems of Hesiod, Homer, and Orpheus.” Cicero pursues these matters much more fully (Cic., cited book, p. 201, line 27). For he records the following as committed to writing in the first book of Chrysippus’s *On the Nature of the Gods*: “He says that divine power resides in reason and in the soul and mind of universal nature; he also says that the world itself is God, as is the universal diffusion of its soul; then also its ruling principle, which consists in mind and reason; and the common nature of things, containing the universe and all things; and further the force of fate and the necessity of future events.” After adding other things which you may read in the same place, Cicero reports the following from Chrysippus’s second book, likewise *On the Nature of the Gods*: “In the second book, however, he wishes to adapt the fables of Orpheus, Musaeus, Hesiod, and Homer to what he himself had said in the first book concerning the immortal gods, so that even the most ancient poets, who did not so much as suspect these doctrines, may appear to have been Stoics.” Concerning these and the other Stoics, see Laertius, who published their lives; Plutarch; Lipsius; and the observations made by us in the preceding volume (Laert., book VII, *On the Lives and Doctrines of Illustrious Philosophers*; Plutarch, *On the Opinions of the Philosophers*, book I, chaps. 7 and 8, and *On the Contradictions of the Stoics*; Lipsius, *Stoic Physics*, book I, diss. 3 ff.; vol. I, *Apparatus*, p. 780).

Our Minucius continues and says: “For Diogenes of Babylon also, the method is to explain and discuss the birth of Jupiter, the origin of Minerva, and other matters of this kind as names of things, not of gods.” Cicero had preceded him in these words: “Diogenes of Babylon,” whom elsewhere he calls a great and weighty Stoic, “in the book entitled *On Minerva*, translates Jupiter’s giving birth and the virgin’s origin into philosophical terms, separating them from the fable” (Cic., *On the Nature of the Gods*, book I, p. 220, line 41; and *On Duties*, book III, p. 394). You will find other books of his—*On Divination*, *On Nobility*, and *On Laws*—cited by the same Cicero, by Athenaeus, and by Plutarch. If Laertius is to be believed, “he was a Stoic from Seleucia and was called the Babylonian because of the proximity of the cities.” If Gellius is to be trusted, he lived in the time of the poet Plautus and Carneades the Academic; if Lucian, he prolonged his life to the age of ninety-two (Cic., *On Divination*, book I, p. 255; Athenaeus, *Deipnosophists*, book IV, p. 168, and book XII, p. 526; Plutarch, *On Exile*, p. 605; Laert., book VI, near the end of the *Life of Diogenes*, § 81; Gellius, *Attic Nights*, book XVII, chap. 21; Lucian, *The Long-Lived*, p. 916).

Why say more? Minucius brings forward two other men who utterly denied that God’s majesty could be understood by human beings. The one, to use Minucius’s words, was “Xenophon the Socratic, who denies that the form of the true God can be seen and therefore says that it ought not to be investigated.” The other was “Aristo of Chios, who says that it cannot be comprehended at all.” Cicero explains the former more clearly: “In the writings in which Xenophon reported the sayings of Socrates, he makes Socrates argue that the form of God ought not to be investigated; he also calls both the sun and the mind God, and at one time speaks of one God, but at another of several gods.” What Cicero relates concerning him is in fact found in the fourth book of Xenophon’s *Memorabilia*. Our Minucius appropriated for his own purposes the first part of this proposition, and after him so did Lactantius and Theodoret. We have discussed it elsewhere (Cic., *On the Nature of the Gods*, book I, p. 200, line 18; Xenoph., *Memorabilia*, book IV, p. [Col. 0436A] 802; Lactant., *On the Anger of God*, chap. 11, p. 795; Theodoret, vol. 4, discourse *On Faith*, p. 477).

Cicero explained Minucius’s few words concerning Aristo’s opinion in the following fuller and clearer terms: “He holds that the form of God cannot be understood, says that there is no sensation in the gods, and is altogether uncertain whether God is animate or not” (vol. I, *Apparatus*, p. 782; Cic., *On the Nature of the Gods*, book I, p. 201, line 8). It should be observed in passing that the royal manuscript codex of Minucius does not read “Aristo of Chios,” as the printed editions do, but “Aristo the Stoic.” You may therefore perhaps ask whether “Stoic” ought to be read there rather than “of Chios.” But however one reads it, the difference is slight. Aristo was from Chios by birth and a Stoic by philosophical sect. This is sufficiently clear from what we have observed about him elsewhere (vol. I, *Apparatus*, diss. 3, [Col. 0436B] chap. 2, art. 18, p. 1145 ff.).

Plato, finally, deservedly closes the ranks of these philosophers, being easily the chief of all the others. Minucius relates his opinion concerning God as follows: “For Plato in the *Timaeus*, God is, by his very name, the parent of the world, the artificer of the soul, and the maker of heavenly and earthly things; he prefaces his account by saying that God is difficult to discover because of his exceedingly great and incredible power and, when discovered, impossible to declare publicly.” Minucius therefore openly states that this opinion of Plato is clearer than all the others and almost wholly heavenly, “were it not that it is sometimes sullied by an admixture of civic accommodation”—that is, if Plato, fearing the hemlock and death of his teacher Socrates, had not sometimes been compelled cravenly and slavishly to flatter the false and empty opinions of the ignorant populace. Hence Justin Martyr says: “Here Plato, fearing those who embraced the worship of many gods, introduces his creator-god speaking things contradictory to himself” (*Enthaûtha ho Platōn tous tēn polytheotēta aspazomenous dediōs, ta enantia heautō ton kat’ auton dēmiourgon eisagei legonta*; Ἐνταῦθα ὁ Πλάτων τοὺς τὴν πολυθεότητα ἀσπαζομένους δεδιὼς, τὰ ἐναντία ἑαυτῷ τὸν κατ’ αὐτὸν δημιουργὸν εἰσάγει λέγοντα) (Justin, *Exhortation to the Greeks*, p. 21; Plato, *Timaeus*, p. 41, vol. 3), namely when speaking to the other gods, whom in the same place he had said were begotten by him.

When Cicero relates Plato’s opinion, however, he first reproaches his inconsistency: “It would take too long,” he says, “to speak now of Plato’s inconsistency: in the *Timaeus* he says that the father of this world cannot be named, while in the books of the *Laws* he thinks that one ought not to inquire at all what God is” (Cic., *On the Nature of the Gods*, book I, p. 200, line 11). Lactantius cited the same book and opinion of Plato (Lactant., *Divine Institutes*, book I, chap. 8, p. 41; and *On the Anger of God*, chap. 11, p. 795). Cicero, however, and afterward Eusebius record more there concerning Plato himself and his inconsistency, to which Lescalopier attempted to respond (Euseb., *Preparation for the Gospel*, book XIII, chap. 14; Lescalopier, *Exposition of Book I of Cicero’s On the Nature of the Gods*, § 30, p. 50). Minucius omitted these matters because they did not conduce to his purpose.

The words of Plato cited by Minucius and others are in fact read thus in his *Timaeus*: “It is difficult to discover the father of this universe, and, when he has been discovered, impossible to declare him to the multitude” (*eis pantas adynaton legein*; εἰς πάντας ἀδύνατον λέγειν) (Plato, vol. III, p. 28). Athenagoras transcribed the same words where, like our Minucius, he plainly demonstrates that the gentile philosophers acknowledged one supreme God (Athenag., *Embassy for the Christians*, p. 6 ff.). Cicero, in the *Fragments*, and Tertullian likewise cited those words of the philosopher, and we reported them elsewhere (Cic., *Fragments*, p. 26; Tertull., *Apology*, chap. 46, p. 40; vol. I, *Apparatus*, pp. 781 and 948, p. 155).

Minucius then adds the following: “These things are almost the same as our own. For we too know God and have called him the parent of all things.” Athenagoras similarly says:

> If, then, Plato is not godless when he conceives one unbegotten God as the creator of the universe, neither are we godless, since we know and hold fast to that God by whose Word all things were created and by whose Spirit they are sustained.

(*Ei toinyn ouk estin atheos Platōn, hena ton dēmiourgon tōn holōn noōn agennēton Theon, oude hēmeis atheoi, hyph’ hou logō dedēmiourgētai, kai tō par’ autou pneumati synechetai ta panta, touton eidotes kai kratountes Theon*; εἰ τοίνυν οὐκ ἔστιν ἄθεος Πλάτων, ἕνα τὸν δημιουργὸν τῶν ὅλων νοῶν ἀγέννητον Θεόν, οὐδὲ ἡμεῖς ἄθεοι, ὑφ’ οὗ λόγῳ δεδημιούργηται, καὶ τῷ παρ’ αὐτοῦ πνεύματι συνέχεται τὰ πάντα, τοῦτον εἰδότες καὶ κρατοῦντες Θεόν.)

The accompanying Latin rendering is:

> If, then, this opinion of Plato concerning the one unbegotten God of the universe is not impious, neither shall we be impious, since we acknowledge and worship that God by whose Word all these things were fashioned, just as by his Spirit they are held together.

From all these opinions of the philosophers, thus explained, Minucius draws this conclusion: “I have set forth the opinions of nearly all the philosophers who enjoy the greatest renown; although under many names, they have designated one God, so that anyone might suppose either that Christians are now philosophers, or that the philosophers were already Christians then”—in precisely the sense explained above. But consider, I ask, whether Augustine departed very far from this conclusion when he pronounced the following judgment concerning those same philosophers: “And so, if those men could have lived this life again together with us, they would assuredly have seen by whose authority provision could more readily be made for humankind; and, with a few words and opinions changed, they would have become Christians, as most Platonists of recent times and of our own age have done” [Col. 0437C] (Augustine, *On True Religion*, ch. 4, vol. 7, p. 750). One further point may be added: most of those philosophers are cited for the same reason by Tertullian, Lactantius, and others, and precisely the same result is established and conclusion drawn from their opinions. But we shall discuss them later.

## ARTICLE III. Another argument of Octavius concerning the one God, drawn from examples of earthly kingdoms and natural phenomena, is examined

From earthly empires, where no one can tolerate a partner in kingship, [Col. 0437D] Minucius derives another argument, by which he confirms and demonstrates not only that there is but one God, but also that all things are governed by the sovereignty of that one alone: “For when,” he says, “has a partnership in kingship ever begun in good faith, or endured without bloodshed?” Ennius had previously written, as quoted by Cicero:

> No partnership in kingship is sacred, nor does it admit good faith.  
> (Cicero, *On Duties*, I, p. 354, line 9.)

Our Minucius proves this with four examples, the last of which is presented by Cicero in the same place. But the more briefly our author reported them, the more obscurely he did so. For he never even calls by their own names the persons under discussion. It will therefore be appropriate to explain these matters somewhat more clearly.

[Col. 0438A] He thus began with the Persians in these words: “I pass over the Persians, who divined the sovereignty from the neighing of horses.” Yet who will understand this unless he knows, or recalls, the history of Darius, king of the Persians? For after the Magi had been killed and their base domination, as Valerius Maximus calls it, had been overthrown, Darius was appointed sole king by compact and agreement, after his horse, through the trickery of Oebares, had neighed just at sunrise (Valerius Maximus, book VII, ch. 2, Foreign Examples, § 2). See Herodotus, Justin the historian, Valerius Maximus, and others (Herodotus, book III, §§ 82, 85 ff.; Justin, toward the end of book I; Valerius Maximus, loc. cit.).

Nor are the following words of Minucius any clearer: “And I pass over, as a fable, the Theban pair who died”; or, still more obscurely and corruptly in the royal manuscript, [Col. 0438B] “through the dead fable.” In these few words Minucius briefly touches upon the celebrated tale, sung by Statius, of the brothers Polynices and Eteocles, sons of Oedipus, king of Thebes (Statius, books XI and XII of the *Thebaid*). The story is told as follows. When Oedipus voluntarily departed into exile, he surrendered his kingdom to those same sons on the condition that they should rule in alternate years. But after the elder, Eteocles, had reigned for the first year, he refused Polynices his turn to rule in the following year. Having been rejected, Polynices went to Adrastus, king of the Argives, and became betrothed to his daughter Argia. Then, after raising an army, together with Tydeus, Adrastus’ other son-in-law, he made war upon the Thebans. In that war the two brothers, Eteocles and Polynices, engaged in single combat and killed one another by mutually inflicted wounds. Finally, [Col. 0438C] when their bodies were placed upon the funeral pyre, the flame is said to have divided itself into two parts as a sign of their implacable hatred. Hear, if you please, Ovid sing of it in these verses:

> When, by design, a common sacrifice is made upon the altar  
> For the brothers who perished each by the other’s hand,  
> The dark ash, itself at variance, as though commanded by them,  
> Splits apart into two divisions.  
> (Ovid, *Tristia* V, elegy 5, lines 33 ff.)

There are Greek verses on this subject by Branor, which Ausonius rendered into Latin (Ausonius, *Epigram* 129). And, to omit Pausanias, Diodorus Siculus, Seneca, and others, Lucan alluded to it in these verses:

> A flame, showing that Latin affairs were at an end [“affairs” supplied; the source text appears defective],  
> Splits apart and rises with a twin summit,  
> Imitating the Theban pyres.

[Col. 0438D] Minucius then says: “The best-known memory of the twins concerns a kingdom of shepherds and a hut.” Correctly indeed, but much more clearly had he added the names of Romulus and Remus. For no one is unaware that Remus, because he had leapt over the new walls of Rome in mockery of his brother, was killed by his enraged brother Romulus—or at least on Romulus’ orders (Livy, book I; Florus, book I; and others).

He also withheld the names of those whom our author presents as his final example: “The wars,” he says, “of son-in-law and father-in-law spread throughout the whole world, and fortune could not contain two men within so great an empire.” But Cyprian, who compiled these latter three examples, as well as many others, from Minucius, as we have said, calls both men by name: “Pompey,” he says, “and Caesar were related by marriage, yet in their rivalry for power they did not preserve the bond of kinship” [Col. 0439A] (Cyprian, *On the Vanity of Idols*, p. 14). How they were related by marriage, and how one was father-in-law and the other son-in-law, you may learn from these words of Suetonius concerning Caesar: “In order to retain Pompey’s attachment and goodwill, he offered him in marriage Octavia, his sister’s granddaughter, who was married to Gaius Marcellus, and asked Pompey’s daughter in marriage for himself” (Suetonius, *Life of Caesar*, § 27), although she had been promised to Faustus Sulla. Earlier, however, he had said: “At about the same time he married Calpurnia, daughter of Lucius Piso, who was to succeed him in the consulship, and gave his own daughter Julia in marriage to Gnaeus Pompey, after breaking her prior engagement to Servilius Caepio” (§ 21). See also, if you please, Plutarch’s *Life of Pompey*, and other writers of Roman history (Plutarch, [Col. 0439B] vol. I, p. 644).

Furthermore, as Minucius proceeds, not only have human beings been unable to tolerate a kingdom divided between two persons, even when joined by the closest natural bonds; nature itself has been unable to tolerate it as well. “Look,” he says, “at the other creatures: among bees there is one king; among flocks, one leader; among herds, one ruler.” Cyprian repeated these words verbatim (Cyprian, *On the Vanity of Idols*, p. 14). From this both conclude that supreme power in heaven cannot be divided either, and therefore that there is but one God. After Lactantius—whom we shall discuss in his proper place—Jerome supplies several further examples of this sort, by which he undertook to prove that there ought to be one superior in a monastery: “Even dumb,” he says, “animals and herds of wild beasts follow their leaders. Among bees there are rulers. Cranes follow one bird in a letter-shaped formation. There is one emperor; one judge of a province. When Rome was founded, it could not have two brothers as kings at once, and it was consecrated by parricide. In Rebecca’s womb Esau and Jacob waged war. . . . On a ship there is one helmsman; in a household, one master. In even the greatest army, the signal of one commander is awaited” [Col. 0439C] (Lactantius, *Divine Institutes* I, ch. 3 ff.; *On the Anger of God*, ch. 11, p. 793; Jerome, Epistle 95, *To Rusticus the Monk*, p. 775).

From these examples Octavius, in the name of Minucius, argues thus against the pagan Caecilius: “Do you believe that supreme power is divided in heaven, and that the entire power of that true and divine sovereignty is split apart?” Cyprian puts it more briefly: “Much more,” he says, “is there [Col. 0439D] one ruler of the world” (Cyprian, ibid.). And Athanasius presses this argument in the following manner, so that everyone may perceive its force and weight even more readily: “The very order of its arrangement, and the harmonious cooperation of all its parts, clearly shows that there are not many leaders and governors of the world, but one. For if several ruled the world, that order could not be preserved; rather, everything would be full of confusion and disorder, as each drew all things according to his own will and fought against the other. For just as we held that many gods are no gods—*tēn polytheotēta atheotēta einai*, ‘polytheism is atheism’—so we must say that many rulers are no rulers. For when one overthrew the sovereignty of another, there would assuredly be no one [Col. 0440A] who exercised command and dominion, no one who ruled and governed” (Athanasius, *Oration Against the Gentiles*, § 38, p. 37).

Who, moreover, does not see that precisely the same point is proved by our Minucius through this reasoning? “Since it is evident that God, the parent of all, has neither beginning nor end; that he bestows birth upon all things, but perpetuity upon himself; that before the world existed he was himself a world unto himself; that he commands by his word all things whatsoever that exist, orders them by reason, and brings them to completion by his power.” We have seen, moreover, that the same things were said earlier by Tertullian and later by Cyprian. Do you see how powerful is this argument, by which those most learned men clearly demonstrate that, if there are several gods, there can in fact be no gods at all, and that it is therefore absolutely necessary that there be only one God and not many?

# CHAPTER V. ON THE NAME, NATURE, AND ATTRIBUTES OF GOD

[Col. 0440B]

## ARTICLE I. Who and what God is, what his name is, and how he is known by humankind, although he cannot be seen with bodily eyes

Although Octavius proved by arguments both certain and evident that God exists and that he is one, Caecilius nevertheless, still wavering with the customary obstinacy of the pagans, attempts to weaken their force and weight—if indeed he could ever have done so—by this question: “Whence, or who, or where is that one solitary and forsaken God, whom no free nation, no kingdoms, [Col. 0440C] not even Roman superstition knew? The Jews alone, a wretched people, themselves also worshipped one God.” To these questions of Caecilius and the other pagans, Minucius steadfastly replies that the God of the Jews and of the Christians is wholly the same; and Caecilius himself had already declared that the Christians were then dispersed throughout the whole world, while Tertullian, as we observed, had declared that they filled every place.

When asked who that God is, Octavius replies: “Do not seek a name for God: ‘God’ is his name. There is need of designations when a multitude must be distinguished individual by individual through the distinctive marks of proper names; for God, who alone exists, the word ‘God’ is the whole of his name. If I call him father, you may think him earthly; if king, you may suspect him to be fleshly; if lord, you will certainly understand him as mortal. Remove the additions made to the name, and you will perceive his radiance.” In Cyprian, who transcribed the opening phrase verbatim, the two words “individual by individual” are omitted, and the passage there reads: “God is his name; there is need of designations where a multitude must be distinguished through the distinctive marks of proper names” [Col. 0440D] (Cyprian, *On the Vanity of Idols*, p. 15). He adds no more there.

Lactantius, however, says of Trismegistus: “He wrote books, and indeed many of them, in which he affirms the majesty of the supreme and sole God, and calls him by the same names that we use, God and Father; and lest anyone should seek his name, he said that he is *anōnymos* (ἀνώνυμος), ‘nameless,’ because, by reason of his very unity, he has no need of the identifying property of a name” (Lactantius, book I, ch. 6, p. 30). Trismegistus’ words are cited by Lactantius as follows: *Ho de Theos heis, ho de heis, onomatos ou prosdeetai; esti gar ho ōn anōnymos* (Ὁ δὲ Θεὸς εἷς, ὁ δὲ εἷς, ὀνόματος οὐ πρὸσδέεται· ἔστι γὰρ ὁ ὢν ἀνώνυμος): “God is one, and the one has no need of a name; for he who is, is nameless.” [Col. 0441A] Lactantius himself then argues as follows: “God therefore has no name, because he is alone. Nor is there need of a proper designation except when a multitude requires differentiation, so that you may designate each person by his own distinctive mark and appellation. But for God, because he is always one, the proper name is ‘God.’” What he adds there after Trismegistus’ Greek words, he certainly seems to have drawn from our author, as he did many other things, and he rendered the author’s meaning clearer.

Minucius therefore teaches, first, that God’s nature is supremely simple and cannot be divided in any way whatsoever; that God himself is neither earthly, corporeal, nor mortal, and is therefore of a spiritual and immortal substance.

[Col. 0441B]

Second, God as he is in himself—in his nature and greatness—cannot indeed be known by us; nevertheless, any person may arrive at a manifest knowledge of him by removing from one’s conception of him everything earthly and imperfect.

Third, names are imposed only upon things that are distinct and different from one another, so that each individual thing may be designated. Therefore, he says, no name can be given to God, who is supremely simple and, alone before all creatures, has always existed—just as Trismegistus, cited a moment ago by Lactantius, said. Justin Martyr speaks in a wholly similar manner: *Theō de oute ho titheis onoma proypērchen, oute autos heauton onomazein ōēthē dein, heis kai monos hyparchōn* (Θεῷ δὲ οὔτε ὁ τιθεὶς ὄνομα προϋπῆρχεν, οὔτε αὐτὸς ἑαυτὸν ὀνομάζειν ᾠήθη δεῖν, εἷς καὶ μόνος ὑπάρχων): “It is altogether impossible [Col. 0441C] that any proper name should be attributed to God, because names are imposed to designate and distinguish the things that underlie them, which are various and many. But no one existed before God to give him a name; nor did he himself consider it necessary to designate himself by any name, since he exists as one and alone” (Justin, *Exhortation to the Greeks*, p. 19). Elsewhere too, more than once, he, like the other Fathers of the Church, denies that any proper name of God can be devised.

Nor is this contradicted by Origen’s response when Celsus objects that God is unnameable:

*Diastolēs deitai. Ei men gar, hoti ouden tōn en lexesi kai sēmainomenois dynatai parastēsai tas idiotētas tou Theou, alēthes esti to legomenon, ei ge kai pollai poiotētes ouk eisin onomastai. Tis gar dynatai onomasi diaphoran dounai poiotētos phoinikos, kai glykytētos ischados . . . ouden oun thaumaston ei ouk onomastos houtōs ho Theos. Ei de to onomaston lambaneis, kath’ ho hoion te estin onomasi parastēsai ti tōn peri autou, eis to cheiragōgēsai ton akroatēn, kai poiēsai noēsai peri Theou, kata to ephikton tē anthrōpinē physei, tina tōn peri autou, ouden atopon legein auton onomaston* (Διαστολῆς δεῖται . εἰ μὲν γὰρ, ὅτι οὐδὲν τῶν ἐν λέξεσι καὶ σημαινομένοις δύναται παραστῆσαι τὰς ἰδιότητας τοῦ Θεοῦ, ἀληθές ἔστι τὸ λεγόμενον, εἴ γε καὶ πολλαὶ ποιότητες οὐκ εἰσὶν ὀνομασταί . [Col. 0441D] τίς γὰρ δύναται ὀνόμασι διαφορὰν δοῦναι ποιότητος φοίνικος, καὶ γλυκύτητος ἰσχάδος . . . . οὐδὲν οὖν θαυμαστὸν εἰ οὐκ ὀνομαστὸς οὕτως ὁ Θεός . εἰ δὲ τὸ ὀνομαστὸν λαμβάνεις, καθὸ οἷον τέ ἐστιν ὀνόμασι παραστῆσαι τι τῶν περὶ αὐτοῦ, εἰς τὸ χειραγωγῆσαι τὸν ἀκροατὴν, καὶ ποιῆσαι νοῆσαι περὶ Θεοῦ, κατὰ τὸ ἐφικτὸν τῇ ἀνθρωπίνῃ φύσει, τινὰ τῶν περὶ αὐτοῦ, οὐδὲν ἄτοπον λέγειν αὐτὸν ὀνομαστόν):

“A distinction is needed. If he means that nothing contained in verbal expressions and significations can represent the distinctive properties of God, the statement is true, since many qualities are themselves unnameable. For who can give names distinguishing the quality of a date’s sweetness from that of a dried fig? . . . It is therefore no wonder if God is unnameable in this sense. But if ‘nameable’ is understood insofar as it is possible through names to represent something about him, so as to guide the hearer and enable him to understand certain things about God, as far as human nature is capable of attaining them, then it is not absurd to call him nameable” [Col. 0442A] (Origen, book LXI [source reading, apparently corrupt], *Against Celsus*, p. 320, quarto).

For Origen admits that no one can impose a proper name upon God, nor can God be named by anyone except insofar as this has been granted to human frailty.

Yet with these points established as entirely true and correct, our Minucius—and with him Cyprian and Lactantius—asserts that the word “God” is truly, insofar as it is permissible for a human being to name him, as Origen says, the complete and proper name of the true God. We earlier read this point confirmed by Tertullian in these words: The soul, “though weighed down by the body, though . . . it names God for this reason alone: because this God is properly the true, good, and [Col. 0442B] great God” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 17, p. 24). Therefore he asserts that this name “God” must be given to him alone and to no other.

But if anyone should inquire of our Minucius, as Caecilius did, who that God is, he will immediately receive this answer from him: “He cannot be seen, for he is brighter than sight; nor comprehended, for he is purer than touch”—although these last three words, transcribed by Cyprian, are absent from the royal manuscript—“nor appraised, for he is greater than the senses (infinite, immeasurable, and known in his greatness to himself alone. Our heart, however, is too narrow for understanding him), and therefore we appraise him worthily when we call him beyond appraisal” (Cyprian, *On the Vanity of Idols*, p. 14). Cyprian reproduced all these words verbatim, except only those enclosed in parentheses. [Col. 0442C] But before both of them Tertullian had said the same thing in other words, in the following manner: “He is invisible, though he is seen; incomprehensible, though represented through grace; beyond appraisal, though appraised by human senses; therefore he is true and so great. For what can ordinarily be seen, comprehended, and appraised is less than the eyes by which it is occupied, the hands by which it is contaminated, and the senses by which it is discovered. But what is immeasurable is known to itself alone; this is what causes God to be appraised, while he does not admit of appraisal. Thus the force of his greatness presents him to human beings as both known and unknown.” Who is unaware that the same teaching was handed down again and again by Theophilus of Antioch, Gregory Nazianzen, and other Fathers of the Church? (Theophilus of Antioch, book I *To Autolycus*, shortly after the beginning, p. 71.)

[Col. 0442D] Yet against these so certain and true teachings some pagan will still rise up and, with Caecilius, insist that these are monstrosities and prodigies of Christian doctrines, by which Christians vainly affirm that they possess God. For they are compelled to confess that he can neither be shown nor seen. But what wonder is it, says Minucius, if Christians profess that they do not see with bodily eyes their God, whom they clearly recognize from his works? Do you yourself, whoever you are, pagan man, see with your eyes the wind and the blasts by which everything is driven? Is not the gaze of your eyes weakened and dulled when looking upon the sun, which enables all things to be seen? Do you see and behold your own soul, by which you live, are animated, and speak?

[Col. 0443A] And let no one, I ask, persuade himself that the vain subtleties and cavils of the pagans were refuted through these comparisons by our author alone. For the same comparisons were employed not only by the most ancient Fathers of the Church and others, but also by certain of the most learned pagan writers. To select a few from the many, Theophilus of Antioch says: “God created all things when they did not exist, so that through his works it might become known to humankind how excellent he is. The human soul exists in the human body; it is not seen, being invisible, but is known through the body’s movements. In the same way God cannot be seen by human and bodily eyes. . . . Just as, if someone sees a ship equipped with its rigging, ploughing the sea and putting into harbor, he assuredly believes that someone who governs it—a helmsman—is aboard it. . . . If a human being cannot fix his eyes upon the sun, which is indeed the least element”—in comparison with God, that is—“because of the excellence of its heat and power, much less can a mortal human being behold the glory of God, which is ineffable to humankind” [Col. 0443B] (Theophilus of Antioch, book I *To Autolycus*, p. 72). He says still more there; if you wish to see it written in Greek, you will readily be able to read it in his book.

Later Lactantius argues in precisely the same manner and also employs several comparisons of this kind: “Above all, since God cannot be seen by a human being, yet lest anyone for that very reason suppose that God does not exist because he is not seen by mortal eyes, among the other wonders of his ordinances he also made many things whose force is indeed apparent, although their substance is not seen, such as voice, smell, and wind; so that from the argument and example of these things we might also perceive God, even though he did not come before our eyes, from his power, effect, and works. What is clearer than a voice, stronger than wind, or more penetrating than an odor? Yet although these things are carried through the air, reach our senses, and strike them with their power, they are not perceived by the gaze of the eyes, but are sensed by other parts of the body. Similarly, God is not to be comprehended by our sight or by any other frail sense, but must be beheld with the eyes of the mind, when we see his glorious and marvelous works” [Col. 0443C] (Lactantius, book VII, *On the Blessed Life*, ch. 9). You may consult Irenaeus and others who set forth the same things; their discussions are too lengthy for us to transcribe them all.

[Col. 0443D] Moreover, Cicero himself—to oppose a pagan writer even to pagan people—spoke in a wholly similar manner: “Thus, although you do not see the human mind, just as you do not see God, nevertheless, just as you know God from his works, so from its memory of things, its inventiveness, the speed of its movement, and all the beauty of virtue, recognize the divine power of the mind” (Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* I, p. 126, line 38).

By these arguments, therefore—arguments confirmed with equal authority by pagan and Christian writers—Minucius answers Caecilius most completely and utterly demolishes his reasoning. Accordingly, he rightly concludes: “From this we believe in God: because we can perceive him, though we cannot see him. For in his works and [Col. 0444A] in all the movements of the world we behold his power as always present: when it thunders, flashes, hurls lightning, and when it clears the sky,” as we showed above.

## ARTICLE II. By what arguments Minucius proved that God is infinite, eternal, immeasurable, and knows all things

Many of God’s attributes, or his supreme and divine perfections, are clearly explained by our Minucius. For he declares God infinite because he lacks beginning and end. Nor could Caecilius deny this, since he ought to have known the saying of Thales recorded by Laertius: *Ti to Theion?* (Τί τὸ Θεῖον;) Thales asked: “What is the divine?” *To mēte archēn echon mēte teleutēn* (τὸ μήτε ἀρχὴν ἔχον μήτε τελευτὴν): “That which has neither beginning [Col. 0444B] nor end” (Laertius, book I, *Life of Thales*, § 36).

Minucius then asserts that God is eternal, since he “bestows birth upon all things, but perpetuity upon himself,” and himself existed before the world. Tertullian appears to derive this eternity of God from Minucius’ foregoing argument, by which God is proved infinite. For he argues against Hermogenes as follows: “What other origin can be assigned to God than eternity? What other condition belongs to eternity than always to have existed and always to exist in the future, by virtue of having neither beginning nor end?” (Tertullian, *Against Hermogenes*, ch. 4, p. 267). But those two attributes, infinity and eternity, are so connected with one another that either can equally be proved from the other. Yet hear, if you please, Gregory Nazianzen arguing further concerning God’s eternity: [Col. 0444C] “God both always was,” he says, “and is, and will be—or, to speak more correctly, he always is; for ‘was’ and ‘will be’ are portions of our time and of our transitory nature. But he always is, and in this manner he names himself when he gives his oracle to Moses on the mountain. For he embraces within himself the totality of that which is, having no beginning and destined to have no end” (Gregory Nazianzen, Oration 38, p. 811). These same words occur in his second Oration above the fortieth [i.e. Oration 42] (ibid., Oration 42, p. 898). Therefore, since God receives neither his being nor whatever he is from another, but from himself, he must consequently be both infinite and eternal.

Caecilius also contended that another novel monstrosity of Christian doctrine was that its adherents proclaimed God to be immeasurable and present everywhere. For how, he asked, can one who is stationed in heaven be present in all places and at the same time “stretched throughout all things”? [Col. 0444D] What then? Minucius replies. Is not the sun, though fixed in heaven, present everywhere? Does it not mingle with all things without corruption of its light, which always remains whole and unimpaired? Yet far more is God not merely present to each individual thing, but also very near to us and infused within us. Indeed Minucius adds: “We do not merely act beneath him, but, as I might almost say, live with him.” From these words some may perhaps suspect that he had in mind the saying of the Apostle: “In him we live, move, and have our being” (Acts ch. XVII, v. 28).
