But since throughout the whole disputation against the pagans he drew nothing, as we observed, from our sacred Scripture, he surely advanced this reasoning because the pagans could neither weaken nor reject it. Seneca, certainly, though a pagan, had written in one of his Epistles: “He himself—God—renders service to the human race: he is everywhere and present to all.” Elsewhere he says: “Wherever you turn, there you will see him meeting you. Nothing is empty of him” [Col. 0445A] (Seneca, Epistle 95, p. 397 ff.; *On Benefits* IV, ch. 8). Finally, to omit further passages, he says again in another Epistle: “God comes to human beings; indeed, what is still nearer, he comes into human beings” (Epistle 73, p. 305). Since, therefore, all things are full of God, as Minucius rightly teaches after Thales and Aratus, all things must also be known to him [Col. 0445B] (Thales, in Aristotle, *On the Soul* I, ch. 5). Accordingly, he, the observer of all, knows all human actions and thoughts.

But Caecilius stubbornly insisted against all this that God was vainly and gratuitously imagined to be present in every place, deed, and thought. For what else, he says, did the proponents of this opinion thrust upon us by these words, except a God who is “troublesome, restless, and even shamelessly inquisitive”? Yet this was the very impious complaint of the Epicurean philosopher quoted by Cicero: “You have imposed upon our necks,” he says, “an everlasting master whom we must fear by day and night. For who would not fear a God who foresees, considers, and observes everything, thinks that everything concerns himself, and is inquisitive and full of business?” (Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* I, p. 203, line 29). Hence Lucretius both gives Epicurus the greatest thanks for driving away this fear and congratulates him most warmly. What of the fact that Cicero, when recounting Strato’s teaching that “all things were produced by nature,” afterward adds: “Thus he frees God from a great labor, and me from fear. For who, when he believes that he is watched over by God, can fail to dread the divine power by day and night, and, if any adversity occurs—as happens to everyone—to fear that it has justly befallen him?” [Col. 0445C] (Cicero, *Academica*, p. 33, line 47).

But those philosophers, and the Epicureans above all—men wholly given to pleasure—made these objections. For they were persuaded that, if God knew the actions and thoughts of human beings, he must be feared, [Col. 0445D] and that by this fear their pleasure and happiness would be disturbed. Nevertheless, God is in no way like other kings, who, as Minucius says, “know everything in their kingdom through the services of ministers”; rather, he knows all things through himself. Nor does he “need informers” in order to know them. The most ancient philosophers freely acknowledged this. For Thales of Miletus, as we learn from Laertius, “when asked whether a human being doing wrong escaped the gods’ notice, replied, *All’ oude dianooumenos* (ἀλλ᾽ οὐδὲ διανούμενος), ‘Not even when thinking of it’” (Laertius, book I, *Life of Thales*, § 36). Valerius Maximus likewise handed this down to posterity and gave the following reason for the pronouncement: “Thales spoke marvelously; for when asked whether human deeds escaped the gods, [Col. 0446A] he replied: ‘Not even their thoughts.’ Thus we should wish to possess not only pure hands, but pure minds as well, since we believed that the divine power was present to our secret thoughts” (Valerius Maximus, book VII, ch. 2, § 8, Foreign Examples). The fear that arises in human beings from this conviction, therefore, though it may be inconvenient to Epicureans and wicked persons, is rightly and deservedly judged by everyone else to be supremely good and just. See the authors cited on this passage of Laertius—Lucan, Euripides, and Theon the Sophist, who attributes the saying not to Thales but to Pittacus.

# CHAPTER VI. ON DIVINE PROVIDENCE

## ARTICLE I. The arguments by which Minucius shows that the world and all things, both collectively and individually, are governed by God’s providence are examined; with a discussion of Britain, the Nile, the Euphrates, and the Indus

[Col. 0446B]

From the same arguments by which Minucius proved that God exists, he infers that all things, both collectively and individually, which were first created by God’s command and will, and the whole world, are ruled and governed by his divine Providence. We have already set forth and examined those arguments above. No one can deny their supreme force and very great weight. Cicero, as we have said, in the principal portion of the second book of his *On the Nature of the Gods*, demonstrates against the Epicureans by the same lines of reasoning, though much more copiously than our author, that the world is administered by divine providence.

[Col. 0446C] Cicero, and after him Minucius, affirms and illustrates this teaching concerning divine Providence by the familiar comparison of a house. Our Minucius says: “If, upon entering some house, you saw everything cultivated, arranged, and adorned, you would surely believe that a master presided over it and was better than those good things. So too, in this house of the world, when you behold providence, order, and law in heaven and earth, believe that there is a lord and parent of the universe, more beautiful than the stars themselves and all the parts of the world.” Earlier, however, the Orator had said: “Just as, if someone entered a house, a gymnasium, or a forum, and saw the rational arrangement, measure, and discipline of everything, he could not judge these things to occur without a cause, but would understand that there was someone who presided and was obeyed; much more, amid such great movements, such great alternations, and the orderly arrangements of so many and such great things, in which immeasurable and infinite antiquity has never proved false, must he conclude that such great movements of nature are governed by some mind” [Col. 0446D] (Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* II, p. 216, line 3 ff.).

God’s Providence provides not only for the totality of things, within which all things are contained, but also for the individual parts of the world. But let us hear, if you please, Minucius demonstrating this by several examples as well: “Britain,” he says, “is deprived of the sun, but is refreshed by the warmth of the sea that flows around it. The Nile moderates Egypt’s drought. The Euphrates cultivates Mesopotamia. The Indus is said both to sow and irrigate the East.” [Col. 0447A] In the royal manuscript, however, after the word “Nile” these words are read: “The river Euphrates serves Mesopotamia in place of rains.” Why these were altered in the printed editions is certainly unknown to us.

We have no doubt that these statements were excerpted from the second book of Cicero’s *On the Nature of the Gods*, where he likewise uses the same examples of the Nile, Euphrates, and Indus to prove God’s Providence. We have considered it unnecessary to repeat here Cicero’s words, which we transcribed above (Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* II, p. 234, line 20; see above, ch. 2, art. 6).

But did not Minucius, you will say, wrongly and perversely present Britain first as an example? From where did he derive the claim that it is deprived of the sun? But tell me, I ask: did not Strabo similarly record the following concerning the Britons? *Epombroi d’ eisin hoi aeres mallon ē niphitōdeis; en de tais aithriais homichlē katechei polyn chronon; hōste di’ hēmeras holēs, epi treis monon ē tettaras hōras tas peri tēn mesēmbrian, horasthai ton hēlion; touto de kan tois Morinois symbainei, kai tois Menapiois, kai hosoi toutōn plēsiochōroi* (Ἔπομβροι δ` εἰσὶν οἱ ἀέρες μᾶλλον ἢ νιφιτώδεις . ἐν δὲ ταῖς αἰθρίαις ὁμίχλη κατέχει πολὺν χρόνον· ὥστε δι` ἡμέρας ὅλης, ἐπὶ τρεῖς μόνον ἢ τέτταρας ὥρας τὰς περὶ τὴν μεσημβρίαν, ὁρᾶθαι τὸν ἥλιον· τοῦτο δὲ κἀν τοῖς Μορινοῖς συμβαίνει, καὶ τοῖς Μεναπίοις, καὶ ὅσοι τούτων πλησίοχωροι): “Their air is more subject to rain than to snow; and even under clear skies a kind of mist persists for a long time, so that throughout the whole day the sun can be seen for no more than three or four hours around midday. The same thing also happens among the Morini, the Menapii, and those who live near them” [Col. 0447B] (Strabo, *Geography* IV, p. 200).

Would you like another witness to be produced? Tacitus is at hand, and these are his words: “The sky is disfigured by frequent rains and mists; severe cold is absent. The spans of daylight exceed the measure found in our part of the world, and the night is bright and, in the furthest part of Britain, short, so that you can distinguish the end and beginning of daylight by only a slight interval. They affirm that, if clouds do not obstruct it, the sun’s radiance is seen during the night, and that it does not set and rise, but passes across; evidently the level extremities of the lands, casting only a low shadow, do not raise up darkness, and night falls beneath the sky and the stars” [Col. 0447C] (Tacitus, *Life of Julius Agricola*, well after the beginning).

But if you should desire a third witness besides these, Caesar too is still ready to hand, for he crossed over to this island. He writes of it in the following manner: “The regions are more temperate than in Gaul, with less severe cold. . . . Halfway across this passage lies an island called Mona; several smaller islands besides are believed to lie opposite, concerning which some have written that at the winter solstice night lasts continuously for thirty days” [Col. 0447D] (Caesar, *Gallic War* IV, p. 743). But these writers, like Herodian, Servius, and Jornandes, were either deceived by a false report or are speaking of the furthest northern limits of Scotland. For Tacitus, already cited, says in the *Life of Julius Agricola*: “The night is bright and, in the furthest part of Britain, short, so that you can distinguish the end and beginning of daylight by only a slight interval” (Herodian, *History* III, p. 84; Servius, on Virgil’s *Georgics* I, p. 81; Jornandes, *On the Affairs of the Getae*, ch. 2).

Granted, another will say, let the matter be so; I concede it. But on what grounds, he will ask, does Minucius confidently affirm [Col. 0448A] that Britain is refreshed by the warmth of the sea? We shall therefore answer him in Cicero’s words: “The seas,” he says, “when stirred by the winds, grow so warm that it can readily be understood that heat is contained within those vast masses of moisture. For that warmth must not be regarded as external and adventitious, but as aroused by agitation in the innermost parts of the sea. This also happens to our bodies when they grow warm through movement and exercise” (Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* II, p. 217, line 42 ff.). Yet he is speaking generally about every sea. What wonder, then, if Britain grows warm from the heat of the sea that surrounds it on every side? But perhaps it would have been better to say that this warmth is produced not from heat enclosed within the sea, but merely from the agitation of its saline particles and from its vapors.

[Col. 0448B] As for the three rivers mentioned by Minucius, if you seek the testimony of writers other than Cicero, many examples can quickly be produced for you. First, Diodorus Siculus clearly shows not only how the Nile moderates Egypt’s aridity, as Minucius says, but also how it renders the country fruitful and fertile. Since his Greek words are rather lengthy, we shall give them only in the Latin translator’s rendering:

> “Its inundation,” he says, “beginning at the summer solstice, increases until the autumnal equinox. Meanwhile, continually bringing in fresh silt, it waters both untilled ground and soil cultivated with crops and plants for as long as the farmers wish. For they easily divert the gently advancing waters with modest embankments; and, by opening these, they let the water in again with no great labor, if that seems useful. [Col. 0448C] It brings so great a saving of labor and benefit to the inhabitants that most of the country people, after casting seed upon the fields once the ground has dried, drive in their livestock to tread it down and return after four or five months to reap the harvest. Others, lightly breaking the upper surface of the soil with small plows after it has been moistened, gather from it enormous heaps of produce without great expense or the hardships of labor” (Diodorus, *Library*, book I, p. 22).

Saint Ambrose likewise writes no less clearly:

> “In springtime among the Egyptians,” he says, “the Nile overflows, so that the earth may be softened for the sowing of seed and the seed cast upon it may be received in a gentler fold and a more kindly bosom” (Ambrose, *On Noah and the Ark*, ch. 14, § 48, p. 247).

Anyone who desires more may consult Strabo, Mela, [Col. 0448D] Pliny, Solinus, and others (Strabo, *Geography*, book V, p. 694, and book VII, p. 788; Mela, *On the Situation of the World*, book I, ch. 9; Pliny, *Natural History*, book I, ch. 9, p. 557, and book XVIII, ch. 8, p. 490; Solinus, ch. 32).

The same authors testify that, just as Egypt is made fertile by the Nile, so Mesopotamia, as Minucius says, is made fertile by the Euphrates. Concerning this river Pliny relates:

> “It too rises, like the Nile, on fixed days, though with a slight difference, and inundates Mesopotamia when the sun occupies the twentieth degree of Cancer. It begins to diminish in Virgo, after the sun has passed through Leo. It returns completely to its bed at the twenty-ninth degree of Virgo” (Pliny, *Natural History*, book V, ch. 27, p. 584).

Solinus, Pliny’s intermediary and imitator, says:

> [Col. 0449A] “It enriches Mesopotamia by the overflow of its annual inundation, covering the land after the fashion of the Egyptian river—that is, the Nile—and carrying fertility into the soil at almost the same times as the Nile” (Solinus, ch. 38).

See Strabo, Arrian, Quintus Curtius, and other geographers (Strabo, *Geography*, book XVI, p. 740; Arrian, *Expedition of Alexander*, book VII, pp. 453 and 489; Q. Curtius, book V, shortly after the beginning).

Furthermore, after the same Strabo has first said certain things about the rivers that flow into the Ganges and the Indus, he confirms on Eratosthenes’ authority what Minucius recorded in writing about the Indus:

> Ἐκ δὲ τῆς ἀναθυμιάσεως τῶν τοσούτων ποταμῶν, καὶ ἐκ τῶν ἐτεσίων, ὡς Ἐρατοσθένης φησι, βρέχεται τοῖς θερινοῖς ὄμβροις ἡ Ἰνδικὴ καὶ λιμνάζει τὰ πεδία· ἐν μὲν οὖν τούτοις τοῖς ὄμβροις λίνον [Col. 0449B] σπείρεται, καὶ κέγχρον· πρὸς τούτοις σησάμην, ὄρυζα, βοσμορον· τοῖς χιμερινοῖς δὲ καιροῖς πυροὶ, κριθαὶ, ὄσπρια, καὶ ἄλλοι καρποὶ ἐδώδιμοι, ὧν ἡμεῖς ἄπειροι.
>
> “Eratosthenes states that, through the exhalations from so many rivers and the blowing of the Etesian winds, India is drenched by summer rains and its plains are turned into standing pools; during these rains flax and millet are sown, together with sesame, rice, and *bosmoron* [the precise crop-name is uncertain]. In wintertime, however, wheat, barley, pulses, and other edible crops with which we are unacquainted are sown” (Strabo, *Geography*, book XV, p. 690).

Do you see how rightly Minucius concludes from all these things that all things, collectively and individually, are governed by God’s Providence? For it makes lands naturally barren, scorched by the sun, and not moistened by rain fertile through the inundations of these rivers. In precisely the same manner, [Col. 0449C] he had previously shown that, through this divine Providence, the fertility of other parts of the world was wonderfully provided for by the regular succession of the four seasons of the year:

> “How great, moreover, is the providential care,” he says, “that autumn and spring have been inserted as temperate intervals, lest winter alone should burn with frost or summer alone scorch with heat, so that, as the returning year retraces its course, the transitions too may return unnoticed and harmless.”

There, moreover, he said, “Winter burns with frost,” just as Virgil wrote:

> . . . Or the piercing cold of Boreas burn.  
> (Virgil, *Georgics*, book I, v. 93.)

## ARTICLE II. Caecilius the pagan’s arguments against divine Providence, drawn from the prosperity of the wicked and the adversity of the good, are examined; with a discussion of the tyrants Dionysius and Phalaris, Rutilius, Socrates, Camillus, and the misery of the Jews and Christians

[Col. 0449D]

Caecilius raises several objections against divine Providence, some of which concern all human beings universally, others particular individuals, others the Gentiles, others the Jews, and still others the Christians. First, he asked, if God’s Providence exists, how is it that sacred and profane places, just like pious and impious people, are struck equally and indiscriminately by lightning and other accidental disasters? Why are the guilty as well as the innocent, the good and the wicked, overwhelmed without any distinction by storms and shipwrecks? Finally, why are the most wicked men so very often more prosperous and fortunate than the best?

[Col. 0450A] He then undertakes to prove by certain examples that it is false that the world is governed by divine Providence, or that provision is made for each and every thing. But it is better to hear Caecilius himself presenting them:

> “For if the world,” he says, “were ruled by divine Providence and by the authority of some deity, Phalaris and Dionysius would never have deserved a kingdom, Rutilius and Camillus would never have deserved exile, nor Socrates poison.”

By precisely the same argument, Cotta the Academic attempted in Cicero to undermine God’s Providence (Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, book III [the printed “V” is evidently erroneous], p. 252, line 4 ff.). He treated as certain what Telamon repeatedly declared about the gods in this single verse:

> For if they cared, it would go well with the good—which now it does not.

That Academic endeavors to confirm this by the same examples as Caecilius and by several others, [Col. 0450B] although omitting Camillus. There he presses them as follows:

> “Why is my uncle, P. Rutilius, a man of perfect innocence and also of the greatest learning, in exile? . . . For thirty-eight years Dionysius was tyrant of a most wealthy and fortunate city. How many punishments before him did Pisistratus, Phalaris, and Apollodorus suffer amid the very flourishing of Greece, though they had first tortured and killed many? . . . What shall I say about Socrates, whose death makes me weep whenever I read Plato?”

Finally, after recounting many impious and sacrilegious deeds of Dionysius—later also noted by Valerius Maximus (book I, ch. 1, Foreign Examples, § 3)—he concludes his narrative with these words:

> “Thus neither did Olympian Jupiter strike him with lightning, nor did Aesculapius destroy him by wasting him away through a miserable and lingering disease. He died in his own bed, was borne to the pyre of Tympanidis, and handed on to his son as though just and legitimate, by way of inheritance, the power that he himself had obtained through crime” (Cicero, passage cited).

[Col. 0450C] Yet neither Caecilius nor the other Gentiles could conceal the fact that this Dionysius—whose various and extraordinary crimes both Cicero and Valerius Maximus also recount elsewhere—was utterly miserable amid such blessed and prosperous circumstances (Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations*, book V, p. 186, line 3 ff.; Valerius Maximus, book IX, ch. 13, Foreign Examples, § 4). For Cicero himself recorded the following about him in another book:

> “What are we to think of that elder Dionysius? By what torment of fear was he habitually distressed, when, fearing the barber’s razor, he used to singe his own hair with a glowing coal?” [Col. 0450D] (Cicero, *On Duties*, book II, p. 377, line 17 ff.).

Valerius Maximus relates in the following manner how Dionysius paid the penalty for his crimes in another way:

> “Although he did not discharge the punishments he owed, nevertheless, after death, through the disgrace of his son, he paid the penalties that he had escaped while alive. For the divine wrath advances with a slow step toward its vengeance, and compensates for the delay of punishment by its severity” (Valerius Maximus, book I, ch. 1, Foreign Examples, § 5).

Concerning the death of Phalaris, Cicero handed down the following to posterity:

> “Phalaris is a witness, whose cruelty has become notorious above that of all others. He did not perish by treachery, as did the man whom I just mentioned, Alexander; nor at the hands of a few, as did this man of ours; rather, the entire multitude of the Agrigentines launched an attack against him.”

From Valerius Maximus [Col. 0451A] you may learn on whose advice and in what manner this tyrant was killed by the Agrigentines (Valerius Maximus, book III, ch. 3, Foreign Examples, § 2).

The story of P. Rutilius Rufus, whom Paterculus calls the best man not merely of his own age but of every age, is known to everyone (Paterculus, *History*, book II). For who does not know that he was driven into exile by a conspiracy of the tax-farmers, whose depredations he had restrained, although, as Cicero testifies, he was entirely innocent (Cicero, Oration II, *For Fonteius*, p. 227 ff., and Oration 37, *Against Piso*, p. 544)? Valerius Maximus speaks of him as follows:

> “What is more wretched than condemnation, what more wretched than exile? Yet when P. Rutilius was struck down by a conspiracy of the tax-farmers, they could not deprive him of his authority. When he made for Asia, all the cities of that province [Col. 0451B] sent envoys to meet him, awaiting his arrival among them. Would one more rightly call this exile or a triumph?” (Valerius Maximus, book II, ch. 10, § 5.)

Seneca said similar things more than once (Seneca, *Why Misfortunes Befall Good Men*, etc., ch. 3; *On Benefits*, ch. 17; and Letters 24 and 69). Nor should these verses of Ovid concerning the same Rutilius be omitted:

> And marvel at the stern resolve of great-souled Rutilius,  
> Who did not accept the offered terms of return.  
> Smyrna detained the man, not Pontus and an enemy land.  
> (Ovid, *Letters from Pontus*, book I, Elegy IV, v. 65.)

Finally, Vossius mentions him; if you wish to consult him, you will have no difficulty doing so (Vossius, *On the Greek Historians*, book I, ch. 22).

[Col. 0451C] The book of Plato concerning the death of Socrates, which Cicero testifies he never read without tears, is the very work entitled *Phaedo, or On the Soul*. At its conclusion Plato laments, with no less eloquence than grief, how Socrates ended his life after drinking poison (Plato, *Phaedo*, vol. I, p. 116 ff., and *Apology of Socrates*, vol. I). Concerning the killing of so great a philosopher, however, one may read his *Apology*, composed by Plato, Xenophon, and Apuleius, as well as the books and discussions of Seneca, Origen, Augustine, and many others (Xenophon, *Apology of Socrates*, p. 705, and *Memorabilia*, book II; Apuleius, *Apology of Socrates*; Laertius, *Life of Socrates*, book II, § 42; Seneca, *On Providence*, p. 272; *On the Happy Life*, book I, chs. 26 and 27; and Letter 74; Origen, *Against Celsus*, book II, p. 71; Augustine, *City of God*, book VIII, ch. 3, [Col. 0451D] p. 192; Laertius, passage cited; Origen, *Against Celsus*, book I, p. 5; Seneca, *On Providence*, ch. 3, p. 495). Moreover, the writers we have cited relate how false and fictitious were the charges for which he was condemned to death by utterly unjust judges. Lastly, Laertius and, later, Origen recorded that the Athenians repented of their unjust condemnation as soon as he was dead. Accordingly, Seneca asserts that this death was as glorious for him as the life of many others was infamous:

> “Do you judge Socrates badly treated because he drank the publicly mixed potion just as though it were a medicine of immortality, and discussed death right up to death itself? Was he badly dealt with because his blood [Col. 0452A] congealed and, as the cold gradually spread, the vitality of his veins ceased? How much more is he to be envied than those who are served from jeweled cups, for whom some effeminate youth, trained to submit to every abuse, melts snow suspended in gold? Whatever these men drink, they will measure out again in vomit, wretched and tasting their own bile once more; but he will drain the poison gladly and willingly.”

Concerning Camillus, finally, whom Caecilius—but not Cicero—mentions, you will find the following written by Valerius Maximus:

> “Furius Camillus, both the most joyful source of the growth of Roman power and its surest safeguard, was unable to protect his own security in the City whose safety he himself had established and whose prosperity he had increased. For L. Apuleius, tribune of the plebs, charged him with embezzlement of the booty of Veii, and he was sent into exile by harsh and, so to speak, [Col. 0452B] iron sentences. This happened, moreover, at the very time when he had been deprived of his excellent young son and ought rather to have been relieved by consolations than burdened with disasters. But his homeland, forgetful of so great a man’s immense services, joined the father’s condemnation to the son’s funeral. ‘Yet,’ he says, ‘the tribune of the plebs complained that fifteen thousand asses were missing from the treasury, for his penalty was fixed at that amount—an unworthy sum, on account of which the Roman people were deprived of such a leader’” (Valerius Maximus, book V, ch. 3, § 2).

Plutarch described these events at greater length; you may consult him, as also Seneca, Diodorus Siculus, Livy, Florus, and others (Plutarch, *Life of Camillus*, vol. I, p. 334 ff.; Seneca, *On Benefits*, book IV, ch. 27, and book V, ch. 17; Diodorus Siculus, *Library*, book XIV, p. 456; Livy, book V, § 32).

[Col. 0452C] Caecilius passes from the Gentiles to the Jews and Christians, and thus attempts to abolish divine Providence by their example:

> “I know indeed,” he said, “that one God is openly and publicly worshiped by the Jews. But what assistance or aid has he brought them? Is not that nation utterly miserable, since it and its God are captives of the Roman deities?”  
> (*cod. reg.* “names”; Rigault’s edition, “men.”)

He presses the Christians still more sharply:

> “Behold, the greater and better part of you, as you say, are needy, cold, and afflicted by toil and hunger; and God permits and disregards it. He either does not wish or is unable to assist his own; thus he is either powerless or unjust.”

“But these things,” he continues, “are few and are shared with others. In addition, however, we see that you always have evils peculiar and proper to yourselves: threats, punishments, tortures, [Col. 0452D] crosses, and fires. Where, then, is your God? Why does he not come to your aid and assist you?”

But not only Caecilius: all the pagans were accustomed to assail Christians with this very complaint and remonstrance. For, as Clement of Alexandria reports, they objected to them:

> Εἰ κήδεται ὑμῶν ὁ Θεὸς τὶ δήποτε διώκεσθε, καὶ φονεύεσθε; ἢ αὐτὸς ὑμᾶς εἰς τοῦτο ἐκδίδωσι;
>
> “If God cares for you, why are you persecuted and put to death? Or does he himself surrender you to this?” (Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata*, book IV, p. 504.)

And shortly afterward:

> Διατί δὲ οὐ βοηθεῖσθε διωκόμενοι . . . .
>
> “Why, then, when you are persecuted, is no assistance brought to you?” (*Ibid.*, p. 505.)

In Eusebius too, the Church of Lyons and Vienne wrote:

> Οἱ [Col. 0453A] δὲ ἐπιεικέστεροι, καὶ κατὰ ποσὸν συμπαθεῖν δοκοῦντες, ὠνείδιζον πολὺ, λέγοντες ποῦ ὁ Θεὸς αὐτῶν, καὶ τί αὐτοὺς ὤνησεν ἡ θρησκεία, ἣν καὶ πρὸ τῆς ἐαυτῶν εἵλοντο ψυχῆς;
>
> “Some who were rather more moderate, and who seemed in some measure to sympathize with our plight, repeatedly reproached us, saying: ‘Where is their God, and what benefit did they receive from this religion, which they preferred even to their own lives?’” (Eusebius, *History*, book V, ch. 2, p. 165.)

Thus Caecilius himself, as well as very many other Gentiles—especially Epicureans and Academics—used all these arguments, as we have shown from Cicero’s books *On the Nature of the Gods*, to attack divine Providence. By them they attempted to prove that God, if there is one, enjoys supreme repose and happiness, does nothing, is distracted by no occupations, undertakes no works, and [Col. 0453B] is blessed because he holds it as certain and established that he will always enjoy the greatest and eternal pleasures. Accordingly, they rejected the Providence of God asserted by the Stoics as though it were a prophetic old woman, and denied that God cared for anything or that the world was governed by any Providence of his. But they raised these objections as impiously as they did in defiance of the promptings of their own conscience, so that they might sin with impunity and do whatever they pleased. But let us hear Octavius, if you wish, refuting and overturning those various arguments.

## ARTICLE III. How Octavius weakens and demolishes Caecilius’s preceding arguments

Octavius answers the arguments raised against divine Providence by Caecilius with as much ease as solidity, and utterly demolishes them. [Col. 0453C] For you have already observed that the examples advanced by the pagans—the tyrants Phalaris and Dionysius, and also Socrates, whom they called the greatest and most admirable of philosophers—were overturned by the pagans themselves.

To the argument drawn from lightning bolts, which strike sacred and profane places, and pious and impious people, either with vain and ineffectual strokes or without any distinction, Octavius replies that we are so far from denying God on that account that, rather:

> “In all the movements of the world,” he says, “we behold his power always present: when it thunders, flashes, and hurls lightning, and when it clears the sky.”

For just as we recognize God and his omnipotent power in the serenity of the heavens, so too do we recognize them amid their greatest and most turbulent storms. And surely, although no one then sees God with bodily eyes, [Col. 0453D] who can doubt that the one whom he then fears and dreads is the first author of such great movements? Thunder therefore roars, Tertullian says, “so that human beings may be terrified,” and so that through this terror the wicked may return to a sounder mind and implore God’s mercy (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 17, p. 18). But we shall discuss Tertullian in his proper place.

Caecilius’s second argument against God’s Providence—repeated rather frequently and tediously by other pagans and atheists—is drawn from the prosperity of certain wicked people and the misery of the good. For how, they ask, could a God equally just and powerful have tolerated these things? But Minucius easily and clearly shows that only the person who knows the true [Col. 0454A] God, and serves and obeys him piously and faithfully, is happy. To weaken Caecilius’s argument, he generally employs the same reasons and words as Seneca, although Seneca was a pagan (Seneca, *Why Misfortunes Befall Good Men*, etc., p. 488 ff.).

First, therefore, he utterly denies that those who abound in riches or have attained the most exalted ranks of honor and dignity are happy. For they are raised higher so that they may fall more heavily; or, as Claudian sang:

> They are raised on high  
> So that they may fall with a heavier plunge.  
> (Claudian, *Against Rufinus*, book I.)

Moreover, like victims they are fattened for punishment and, like sacrificial animals, garlanded for execution. What is more, do not flatterers very often misuse the power of others through feigned blandishments [Col. 0454B] and obsequiousness?

Furthermore, is not the rich man, as Minucius says, “wrongly entrusted to fortune” and committed to her inconstancy? Is he not less enriched than burdened by his wealth, as though it were traveling money for completing life’s short journey? A king, moreover, is as much afraid as he is feared, and he alone stands exposed to danger. For Labienus, quoted by Seneca, rightly sang:

> He whom many fear must fear many.

The man who proclaims the nobility of his family praises not himself but his ancestors. Finally, the man who glories in the fasces and purple is sordid in mind. For all human beings, whether poor or rich, [Col. 0454C] are born with an equal lot and are distinguished by virtue alone.

Cyprian, in his Letter to Donatus, pursues this matter far more fully than our author (Cyprian, Letter 2 to Donatus, pp. 7–8). We do not venture to reproduce his rather lengthy discourse here in full, though you will doubtless not regret having read it. We shall therefore add what we find written more briefly by Apuleius:

> “Is he nobly born? You are praising his parents. Is he rich? I do not trust fortune. I count such things as disadvantages instead. Is he strong? He will be worn down by sickness. Is he swift? He will pass into old age. Is he handsome? Wait a little while, and he will not be” (Apuleius, *On the God of Socrates*, near the end).

See, if you wish, the book of Seneca cited by us, *On Providence, or Why Misfortunes Befall Good Men Although Providence Exists*, together with Muretus’s *Disputation* on this book [Col. 0454D] and the *Observations* of Morellius and others.

Minucius proceeds and similarly rejects the argument drawn from the poverty and adversities of upright people. For that poverty, he says, is neither disgrace nor misery, but glory and an opportunity to acquire and establish virtue. For “just as our spirit is weakened by luxury, so it is strengthened by frugality.” Moreover, amid want, the person who desires nothing is rich; conversely, the person who abounds in riches yet desires still more is poor. Accordingly, Pomponius Rufus said in Valerius Maximus:

> “He who desires nothing possesses everything, and more surely than one who possesses all things” (Valerius Maximus, book IV, ch. 4, preface).

[Col. 0455A] To this is added that no one, as Minucius says after Seneca, “lives so poor as he was born.” Seneca infers from this that poverty should be despised (Seneca, *On Providence*, ch. 6, p. 504). Then, so far as Christians are concerned, Minucius unhesitatingly declares that they could obtain riches and resources from God if these were useful to them, but that riches are disdained by them and innocence and piety preferred.

The point Caecilius presses from the utterly miserable condition of the Jews is of far less—or rather, of no—weight. For as long as they worshiped God piously and devoutly, and as long as they diligently obeyed his commandments, it is established that they enjoyed favorable circumstances and every kind of prosperity, accompanied by great miracles. But after they abandoned God through their impiety and [Col. 0455B] crimes, they were in turn abandoned by him and paid the penalties owed for their impiety and crimes. Hear, I ask you, the words of Minucius:

> “As long as they worshiped chastely, innocently, and devoutly, and as long as they obeyed his saving precepts, from a few they became innumerable, from needy they became rich, and from servants they became kings. Though few, they overwhelmed many; though unarmed, they overwhelmed the armed; while fleeing, they overwhelmed their pursuers, at God’s command and with the elements assisting them. . . . Thus you will understand that they first deserted him before they were deserted; that they were not taken captive together with their God, but were surrendered by God as deserters from his discipline.”

Neither Caecilius nor anyone else could reply that Minucius had fabricated this without foundation, since it was handed down to everlasting remembrance in the writings of these same Jews and is read everywhere throughout them. For they wrote nothing in them against themselves [Col. 0455C] and their own ancestors except what they could neither suppress nor conceal. Minucius adds that the Jews were all the more guilty because all these events had been foretold in those same books long before they occurred.

Moreover, he names two witnesses explicitly: Josephus and Antonius Julianus. The former was certainly beyond all suspicion in this matter. For he was a Jew, and anyone can very easily read the matters reported by Minucius in the books that he wrote about his own nation and the Jewish War, works that are in everyone’s hands. The latter too, as Minucius indicates quite plainly, had published commentaries concerning the Jews. But we lost them so long ago that scarcely anyone besides our author can be found who remembers either those works or Julianus himself. [Col. 0455D] Yet no one who is not altogether incredulous can deny that the things advanced by our Minucius are true.

If anyone more exacting than Caecilius should demand that another witness be cited to him in place of Julianus, we shall immediately give him Tertullian, whose words are as follows:

> “So great was the favor enjoyed by the Jews before God, on account of the extraordinary righteousness and faith of their original ancestors, that among them both the greatness of their nation and the elevation of their kingdom flourished; and so great was their happiness that they were forewarned by God’s utterances how to merit God’s favor and not offend him. Yet how greatly they sinned—swollen with confidence in their fathers and deviating from his discipline in a profane manner—even if they themselves would not confess it, their present condition would prove. Scattered, wandering, exiles from both their heaven [Col. 0456A] and their land, they roam the world without man, without God as king; they are not permitted, even under the law accorded to strangers, so much as to greet their native land with the sole of their foot” (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. I, p. 20).

You will find the same things in Cyprian, who, excerpting this entire passage of Tertullian, sometimes borrowed his very words as well (Cyprian, *On the Vanity of Idols*, p. 15). But these matters must be treated more fully in another of our dissertations.

Caecilius nevertheless insisted that God’s Providence was proclaimed in vain, since God permits upright people to be afflicted with every kind of adversity without punishment, and especially permits Christians to be tormented, mangled, and killed by the greatest and most exquisite tortures. Minucius admits that this is indeed true, but contends that these things are the surest indications not only [Col. 0456B] of God’s Providence, but also of his compassion—indeed, of his love and benevolence. For God, as he says after Seneca, tests and examines each person in adversity; or, to use Seneca’s own words:

> “Those whom God approves and loves he hardens, scrutinizes, and trains. But those toward whom he seems indulgent, whom he seems to spare, he keeps soft for evils still to come. For you are mistaken if you believe anyone exempted. His own share will come to the person who has long been fortunate: whoever seems to have been released has merely been deferred” (Seneca, *On Providence*, ch. 4, p. 498).

Accordingly, just as gold is tested by fire, say both Seneca and Minucius, so a brave, pious, and upright man is tested by miseries and calamities. He may therefore appear wretched, but in reality he is not wretched. For all bodily evils and torments [Col. 0456C] are not punishments but military service, and quite often the training of virtue—or, as Seneca puts it, “It is not cruelty; it is a contest,” and an opportunity for virtue (*Ibid.*, ch. 5, p. 501; ch. 3, p. 494; ch. 4, p. 498). Minucius further adds what is confirmed not only by the same Seneca but also by Plato and Xenophon: that without the exercise of labor our powers become altogether sluggish (Plato, *Theaetetus*, vol. I, p. 153; Xenophon, *Expedition of Cyrus*, book VII, p. 198).

Above all others, moreover, we praise Seneca here and have quoted his words because Minucius drew many things from him, as we showed above. On all these matters you may also read Cicero’s *Paradoxes*; Valerius Maximus, book IV, ch. 4, *In Praise of Poverty*; Justin Martyr, *Apology* 76, [Col. 0456D] p. 43 ff.; Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata*, book IV, p. 504 ff.; Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 41; Cyprian, treatise *On Mortality*, p. 158; Arnobius, *Against the Gentiles*, book II, p. 97; Lactantius, book V, chs. 21–22, p. 529 ff.; Ambrose, Sermon 11 on Psalm 118, p. 1110 ff., and *On Jacob and the Happy Life*, book II, ch. 9, p. 473 ff.; Augustine, *City of God*, ch. 29, p. 27; Theodoret, Oration 6, *On Providence*, p. 378 ff., and *Cure of the Greek Maladies*, Discourse 6, likewise *On Providence*, p. 573 ff.; and very many others. Meanwhile, however, let us follow our author as he turns this feeble weapon of the pagans back against them with the utmost force.

## ARTICLE IV. How Octavius answered Caecilius’s argument drawn from the sufferings and death of the martyrs; with an exposition of the examples of Scaevola, Regulus, and Aquilius, and a discussion of the great number of martyrs and the necessity of divine grace for undergoing martyrdom

[Col. 0457A]

Minucius proceeds and clearly shows Caecilius and the other pagans that the cruelest tortures of the Christian martyrs not only do no injury to God’s Providence, but commend it in a truly wonderful manner. For he is so far from regarding a Christian who is mangled by the most dreadful agonies and torments for professing his religion, and who gives up his life amid them, as miserable [Col. 0457B] and unfortunate, that he considers him a spectacle worthy of God. For is not that most holy martyr worthy of the gracious gaze of the supreme Majesty, and most acceptable to him, who, because of his public confession of the Christian faith, has endured innumerable and exceedingly atrocious punishments and, after finally shedding his blood, triumphs over executioners and tyrants?

Certainly no pagan, however obstinate, can rightly deny this if he has read Seneca’s words concerning the brave man:

> “Behold a spectacle worthy of God’s looking upon while intent upon his work. Behold an encounter worthy of God: a brave man matched against evil fortune, especially if he himself challenged it. I see, I say, nothing on earth more beautiful for Jupiter to behold, should he wish to turn his attention to it, than Cato standing upright amid the ruins of the commonwealth, although his party had already been [Col. 0457C] shattered more than once. . . . It is clear to me that the gods watched with great joy when that man, the sternest avenger of himself, provided for the safety of others and organized the escape of those departing; when even on his final night he pursued his studies; when he drove the sword into his sacred breast, scattered his entrails, and drew forth with his own hand that most holy soul, unworthy to be defiled by steel” (Seneca, *On Providence*, ch. 2, p. 492).

If Seneca could say these things about a brave pagan man placed amid so many adversities and uncertain of his lot after this life, what ought he to have said of a Christian martyr, who knows with absolute certainty that by his death he will attain eternal happiness?

Lest Caecilius or some other pagan object [Col. 0457D] that this was indeed Seneca’s opinion, or that of some Stoic philosopher, but not the opinion of others, Minucius presses his case further and sets before the eyes of Caecilius and the rest the examples of Mucius Scaevola, Regulus, and Aquilius. Although they appeared afflicted by calamity, all the pagans nevertheless extolled them to heaven with the highest praises because of their unconquered steadfastness amid the most bitter torments.

Minucius says nothing of the punishments endured by Aquilius and Regulus, doubtless because in his time they were unknown to no one. But lest they perhaps be unknown to someone, we shall recount them briefly. Concerning the ordeal of Mucius Scaevola, Arnobius added the following in the same place:

> “Since he had mistaken his target in attacking the king, he would have perished among the enemy had he not sacrificed his right hand.”

[Col. 0458A] For when Porsenna, king of the Etruscans, was besieging Rome in a severe and protracted war, Scaevola boldly entered the enemy camp without any hope of safety, as Cicero says, and there inadvertently killed the king’s secretary instead of the king himself, whom he intended to kill (Cicero, *Paradoxes*, p. 434). Consequently, when captured and brought before the king’s tribunal, he fearlessly thrust his right hand into a fire kindled for sacrifice. Terrified by such boldness, Porsenna granted him his freedom and released him (Livy, Decade I, book II, p. 22 ff.). We have, however, discussed this deed of his elsewhere.

Marcus Atilius Regulus, whom our author later mentions, was consul for the second time during the First Punic War. He was captured by enemies whom he had crushed and defeated in various disasters, and was sent [Col. 0458B] to Rome to negotiate an exchange of prisoners after swearing that he would return:

> “When he arrived,” says Cicero, “he advised in the senate that the captives should not be returned. Then, although his relatives and friends tried to detain him, he nevertheless preferred to return to certain punishment rather than violate the pledge he had given the enemy” (Cicero, *On Duties*, book I, p. 356, line 16 ff.).

Accordingly, after returning to them, he was killed by sleep deprivation and starvation. See the same Cicero, *On Ends*, book V, p. 112, and especially *On Duties*, book III, p. 401 ff.; Valerius Maximus, book I, ch. 1, § 14, p. 13; Eutropius, *Roman History*, book II; Aurelius Victor, *On Illustrious Men*, p. 605; Aulus Gellius, *Attic Nights*, book VI, ch. 4; Florus, book II, ch. 2; Seneca, *On Providence*, ch. 13, p. 272; Augustine, *City of God*, book I, ch. 13, p. 15; ch. 24, p. 23; book II, ch. 23, p. 52; and book III, ch. 18, p. 76. [Col. 0458C] On both Scaevola and Regulus, see Cicero, *On Duties*, book III, p. 252; Lactantius, book V, ch. 13, p. 496; Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 50, and *To the Martyrs*, ch. 4; and others. We shall note only one point: these writers held varying opinions about the punishments inflicted upon Regulus and the manner of his execution.

Moreover, the more frequent the mention of this Regulus and Mucius Scaevola among various writers, the rarer is the mention of Aquilius, whom our author records in the same place. For this reason some suppose that a copyist erred in writing his name and that *Atilius* or *Acilius* should be read there instead of *Aquilius*. After making this emendation, they believe this to be the man whom Dionysius of Halicarnassus called Ἀτύλιον (*Atylion*), or rather, as they prefer, Ἀκύλιον (*Akylion*) (Dionysius of Halicarnassus, *Antiquities*, book III, p. 259 ff.). [Col. 0458D] But these conjectures are futile and vain. For Minucius is speaking about entirely innocent men who were killed by various kinds of exceedingly dreadful punishment. Atilius, however, according to the same Dionysius of Halicarnassus, paid the penalties deserved by his crime.

What, I ask you, prevents us from saying that Minucius is speaking of Marcius Aquilius, whom Appian describes as having been delivered over by Mithridates to a most cruel death in these words?

> “Not long afterward he took Manius Aquilius, the principal instigator of this embassy and war, and carried him around bound upon an ass, compelling him to proclaim in his own voice before the spectators that he was Marcius, until at Pergamum he poured molten gold into his mouth, reproaching the Roman [Col. 0459A] name for the corruptions caused by bribery” (Appian, *The Mithridatic War*, well after the beginning, p. 123).

Pliny likewise says:

> “And now, to the disgrace not of any single Roman citizen but of the Roman name as a whole, King Mithridates poured gold into the mouth of the captured commander Aquilius” (Pliny, *Natural History*, book XXXIII, ch. 3, p. 32).

We are indeed not unaware that Valerius Maximus records in writing that M. Aquilius preferred to serve Mithridates shamefully rather than to die gloriously and courageously. But Valerius himself there passes over in complete silence the manner of his death (Val. Max., book IX, chap. 13, § 1). Yet even if he held a different opinion concerning Aquilius’ death from Appian and others, that certainly could not prevent Minucius from following their opinion rather than that of Valerius Maximus. To this may be added that this Aquilius is believed to be the man of whom Cicero speaks as follows in one of his speeches: [Col. 0459B] “Will you allow that king Mithridates to go unpunished, who killed a consular legate of the Roman people after torturing him with chains, scourging, and every kind of torment?” (Cic., Speech 13, *For the Manilian Law*, p. 243.) Finally, Arnobius, whom we shall discuss in the appropriate place, employed the example of this same Aquilius against the pagans, just as our Minucius did (Arnob., book I, p. 23).

Now, I ask you to consider how correctly our author argues against the pagans from these examples. First, he reasons from the example of Scaevola as follows: “And how many of our people have endured not merely having their right hand burned, but having their entire body set on fire and consumed, without uttering any cries, especially when it lay within their own power to be released?” Then, more forcefully, gathering all the examples together, he presses the point in this manner: “I compare men with Mucius, [Col. 0459C] or with Aquilius or Regulus. Our boys and little women, through divinely inspired endurance of pain, make sport of crosses and tortures, wild beasts, and all the terrors of execution.” Lactantius reasons in precisely the same way, and from the same examples of Mucius and Regulus: “Not to speak of our men,” he says, “our boys and little women silently overcome their torturers, and not even fire can force a groan from them. Let the Romans go and boast of Mucius or Regulus. . . . Behold, the weaker sex and fragile youth willingly endure being torn throughout their entire bodies—not from necessity, since they could avoid it if they wished, but voluntarily, because they trust in God” (Lactant., book V of the *Divine Institutes*, chap. 13, p. 495 ff.). Other pagans, however, though vigorous in body, cried aloud and uttered groans when tortured, because, as he says, [Col. 0459D] “they lack divinely inspired endurance.” As you see, our Minucius had already used these very words. Lactantius therefore reproduced not only our author’s sense and thought, but even some of his actual words.

Furthermore, we think that no one will find it unwelcome or disagreeable if, from those two passages of Minucius and Lactantius, we observe that the number of martyrs in their time was not small, as some falsely suppose. Do they not plainly and openly declare that there was a great multitude of them when they say that not only men but even boys and little women, with the greatest endurance and without any groan, suffered their bodies to be burned and consumed? And what must be said of the various other kinds of torment about which they were silent—crosses, [Col. 0460A] wild beasts, and, as Minucius himself says, “all the terrors of execution”? Were not Christians, by no means few in number, cruelly killed by so many and such diverse torments, and did they not thereby obtain the palm of martyrdom?

It must further be noted that Minucius, like Lactantius, was persuaded that without the divine aid of victorious grace no one could, in confessing Christ, endure those most cruel torments all the way to death with such great steadfastness (Lactant., passage cited). For first, both expressly affirm that endurance was inspired in them. But how was it inspired except by the assistance of divine grace? Minucius then adds that “there is no one who would wish to undergo punishment without reason, or who could endure tortures without God.” Lactantius subsequently wrote: “Nor can endurance itself, [Col. 0460B] without God, overcome such great tortures” (Lactant., passage cited). Does he not in these words most clearly assert and vindicate the necessity of divine grace itself for undergoing death amid so many and such great torments? Something more concerning Lactantius must still be said below. (*Dissertation on Lactantius*, chap. 28, art. 1.)

## ARTICLE V. How Octavius answers Caecilius’ final argument against divine Providence, an argument drawn from the Christians’ opinion concerning fate

Caecilius’ final bulwark against divine Providence was, as he claimed, the common opinion not only of the pagans but also of all Christians, [Col. 0460C] who believed that everything happened by fate. What then? How could Caecilius so confidently assert that this was the common position of all Christians? Did they not oppose it with all the powers of mind and intellect? If he had said this of certain heretics, we would readily concede the point to him. But who can tolerate his asserting it universally of all Christians? Listen, however, I beg you, to the reasoning by which he attempts to prove it. “Whatever we do,” he says, “just as others ascribe it to fate, so you ascribe it to God; thus you say that the members of your sect act not of their own accord, but as chosen persons”—that is, you Christians embraced your sect and religion not voluntarily and of your own accord, but by divine election. In making this objection, he appears to have had in view the words of Christ which he had either heard from Christians [Col. 0460D] or read in John’s Gospel: “You did not choose me, but I chose you” (John 15:16). From these words he concludes: “You therefore represent God as an unjust judge, who punishes men’s lot, not their will.”

But Minucius quickly and easily overturns this futile and inept argument. For although we have indeed been chosen by God, it is nevertheless certain that the human will always remains free and that, consequently, men are punished for their own free acts, if those acts are wicked, rather than for a lot assigned them by God. “The mind,” as he says, “is free, and therefore it is a person’s action, not his condition, that is judged.” God is therefore a just and equitable judge, who rewards men for good actions and punishes them for evil ones.

[Col. 0461A] Yet Octavius deals more generously with Caecilius. He grants him what he wants: that all Christians believed everything to happen by fate. But what, he asks, is fate? “Fate (*fatum*) is what God has pronounced (*fatus est*) concerning each one of us.” Augustine does not disagree with this definition of fate. For he says: “We neither deny the order of causes, in which the will of God has the greatest power, nor call it by the name ‘fate,’ unless perhaps we understand *fatum* as derived from *fando*, that is, from speaking” (August., *City of God*, chap. 9, p. 123). You will find more on this subject in Vossius’ *Etymologicon*.

Having established this definition of fate, Octavius maintains that God imposes no fatal necessity upon a person’s actions. For God, he says, “since he can foreknow the material”—that is, all future works of men, whether good or evil—[Col. 0461B] “determines their fates according to the merits and qualities of each.” By these words he plainly teaches that God, who through his divine foreknowledge knows perfectly all future things and whatever each individual will do either well or badly, yet always with great freedom, determines the fates of each according to their merits, whether good or bad—that is, determines eternal punishments or rewards, or establishes and decrees them by his eternal decree. From this he concludes as follows: “Thus in us it is not our birth that is punished, but the character of our disposition”; that is, it is not our birth or manner of being born, but our vices and all the sins we have committed by disobeying God’s commands, that are most justly punished by him.

Moreover, because Caecilius openly asserts that many pagans defended the impious opinion concerning fate or fatal necessity, someone will doubtless ask us who those pagans were. We believe that anyone who asks this will be fully satisfied by the following words of Cicero: [Col. 0461C] “It seems to me,” he says, “that, although there were two opinions among the ancient philosophers—one belonging to those who thought that everything happened by fate in such a way that fate imposed the force of necessity, an opinion held by Democritus, Heraclitus, Empedocles, and Aristotle; the other belonging to those who thought that the voluntary motions of minds occurred without any fate—Chrysippus wished to take a middle position, like an honorary arbiter. Yet he inclines rather toward those who wish the motions of minds to be freed from necessity. But while employing his own terminology, he slips into such difficulties that he unwillingly confirms the necessity [Col. 0461D] of fate” (Cic., *On Fate*, p. 307, line 48 ff.). Whoever wants more should consult Cicero’s own book *On Fate*, from which these words were taken. He should also read, among the more recent Christian writers, Lipsius and Vossius; and, among the ancient Fathers of the Church, Augustine, Eusebius, and Tatian, who in his *Address to the Greeks*, as we have observed elsewhere, thoroughly attacks and refutes this error (Voss., book II, *On the Origin and Progress of Idolatry*, chap. 45 ff.; Lips., *On Constancy*, chap. 29 ff.; August., book V of *The City of God*, chaps. 2 and 20; Euseb., book VI of the *Preparation for the Gospel*, chaps. 1, 2, 3 ff.; and Tatian, vol. I of our *Apparatus*, p. 543).

# CHAPTER VII. ON OTHER DOGMAS OF THE CHRISTIAN RELIGION

[Col. 0462A]

## ARTICLE I. The arguments by which Caecilius attacks the resurrection of our bodies and Octavius defends it are examined; with a discussion of metempsychosis and of Pythagoras and Plato, the authors and defenders of this opinion

Caecilius attempts to overthrow certain other teachings of the Christian religion, but with no greater success. One of the chief among them is undoubtedly the teaching which asserts that our bodies will in the future return to life. For if this is removed, our faith, as the Apostle says, will be vain [Col. 0462B] and empty. Caecilius sought to overturn this foundation of our faith and hope by the following dilemma: Either, he says, we shall rise without a body, or with a body. Not the former, certainly; for without a body there is neither mind, nor soul, nor life. This was how the pagans argued, since they prattled that nothing could exist unless it were corporeal. Nor, Caecilius continues, shall we rise with a body, whether with our very own or with another. Certainly not with our own, for it will have been dead for so long that absolutely no remnant of it could remain. Nor with another, since in that case the person restored to life would not be numerically the same but another person than the one who died.

Caecilius next continues his attack upon the raising of our dead body to life with a second argument: [Col. 0462C] “What single person has ever returned from the underworld, even with the grant of a few hours’ leave, as befell Protesilaus, so that we might at least believe on the basis of an example?” We have already observed that certain persons conjecture, without reason, that in this text of Minucius the adjective “few” must be added after the word “hours.” It is sufficiently understood there, since the matter concerns the fate of Protesilaus, who is said to have been the first of the Greek princes killed by Hector in the Trojan War. His wife Laodamia, as soon as she learned that he was dead, is said to have obtained from the gods, through earnest prayers, permission to enjoy conversation with him for three hours after he had been restored to life. See Propertius, Hyginus, Catullus, and Ovid, who wrote an epistle to this Protesilaus in the name of his wife (Propert., book I, Elegy 19; Hygin., *Fable* 103; Catull., [Col. 0462D] Epistle 63 to Mallius; Ovid, Epistle 13).

This line of pagan argument was common and frequently repeated. Justin Martyr presents it as follows: διὰ τὸ μήπω ἑωρακέναι ὑμᾶς ἀναστάντα νεκρὸν, ἀπιστία ἔχει. “Because you have not yet seen a dead man rise, disbelief in the resurrection possesses you” (Justin, *Apology* II, p. 65). Theophilus of Antioch similarly writes: ἀλλὰ καὶ τὸ ἀρνεῖσθαί σε νεκροὺς ἐγείρεσθαι φὴς γὰρ, Δεῖξόν μοι κᾄν ἕνα ἐγερθέντα ἐκ νεκρῶν, ἵνα ἰδὼν πιστεύσω. “But you also deny that the dead are raised. For you say: ‘Show me at least one person raised from the dead, so that, when I have seen him, I may believe your words’” (Theoph., book I *To Autolycus*, p. 77). To these, apart from the others whom it would take too long to cite, [Col. 0463A] may be added Lactantius, who likewise introduces the pagans making this objection: “So many ages have now passed; what single person has ever risen from the underworld, so that we might believe on the basis of his example?” (Lactant., book VII, chap. 22, p. 719).

But why, Minucius asks, do you, Caecilius, a pagan, dare to reject as an old woman’s tale this Christian teaching concerning the resurrection of our bodies? Why do you demand that it be proved to you by the example of one person? Have you perhaps forgotten that at least half of it is steadfastly defended by Pythagoras and Plato, who asserted that our souls migrate from dead bodies into others? But if this has slipped from your memory, read, I ask you, the first book of Diodorus Siculus, and there you will find it written that Pythagoras received this opinion from the Egyptians (Diod. Sic., [Col. 0463B] book I of the *Library*, p. 62). Turn through the books of Herodotus, and there you will see that he likewise said that the Greeks—under whose name he undoubtedly includes Pythagoras and Plato—drew that doctrine from the same Egyptians (Herod., book II, § 123). Consult Laertius, and from the writers cited by him you will learn what Pythagoras proclaimed concerning the various transmigrations of his own soul (Laert., book VIII, §§ 4–5). If all this is not sufficient for you, you will doubtless not withhold credence from Laberius, who, as quoted by Tertullian, openly testifies that this very doctrine of metempsychosis was defended by Pythagoras (Tertull., *Apologeticum*, chap. 48, p. 42). Tertullian himself, Ambrose, and others, however, just like our Minucius, rightly conclude from this that the Christian teaching concerning [Col. 0463C] the resurrection of our body ought not to appear incredible to the pagans (Ambrose, book II *On Faith in the Resurrection*, § 65, vol. II, p. 1151).

What is more, this same Tertullian elsewhere unhesitatingly asserts that this absurd dogma concerning the transmigration of souls was defended not only by Pythagoras, but also by Plato, as our Minucius said (same author, *On the Soul*, chap. 28). But as far as Plato is concerned, no witness at all is needed to prove the point. For he may be read to have taught it clearly and more than once in his books (Plato, at the end of the book *On the Soul*, vol. III, p. 104, and book X of the *Republic*, vol. II, p. 620).

Before we proceed further, two matters must be noted here. First, concerning this ridiculous error of the philosophers, Minucius said: “This opinion deserves not philosophical [Col. 0463D] study, but a mime’s reproach.” It is truly astonishing how zealously no small number of learned men have attempted to emend this passage, which they consider corrupt, and how many different corrections they have devised for it. But they offer no certain reason why the authentic reading of the royal manuscript should be changed. Retaining it, therefore, Rigaltius conjectures that by these words Minucius was aiming at mimes who sometimes transformed themselves into beasts upon the stage and assumed their forms. Others think that Minucius is referring to Laberius, whom Tertullian praised, as we noted shortly before, and to the following verses of his transcribed by Crinitus:

> And I hear that many evils arise even from good things  
> [Col. 0464A] through that doctrine by which the philosophers transform us,  
> making now a human being from a mule, a snake from a woman,  
> and various other things from different forms.  
> (Crinit., book XI, *On Honourable Learning*, chap. 3.)

Laberius, moreover, was both a poet and a mime. Among others, Macrobius says of him: “Caesar induced Laberius, a Roman knight of uncompromising independence, by an offer of five hundred thousand sesterces, to appear upon the stage and personally perform the mimes which he habitually wrote” (Macrob., book II of the *Saturnalia*, chap. 7). There Macrobius quotes several verses by Laberius, who was compelled to perform the mimes he himself had written. Horace too sang of him:

> And the mimes of Laberius, which I am expected to admire as beautiful poems.  
> (Horat., book II, *Satires*, Satire 10.)

Laberius therefore had undoubtedly ridiculed these philosophers’ ravings about metempsychosis [Col. 0464B] not only in the writings cited shortly before, but also in his mimetic performances. Minucius could accordingly infer that this error was worthy of “a mime’s vice” (*mimico vitio*), or “a mime’s reproach” (*mimico convitio*), or “the reproach of the mime” (*mimi convicio*)—namely Laberius—or, if you prefer, of any pantomime.

Second, it must be noted that Pythagoras is called by Minucius the first person to introduce this opinion, or rather this delusion. But by what right, or on whose testimony, did he affirm this so confidently? For Diodorus Siculus, quite explicitly, as we have already said, and Herodotus somewhat less clearly, testify that the first authors of this opinion were the Egyptians, from whom Pythagoras received it. Consequently, either Minucius was mistaken, or, more probably, he meant nothing more than that this doctrine was disseminated [Col. 0464C] by Pythagoras as its first inventor and author among the Greeks. If he meant only the latter, he will undoubtedly have Herodotus himself as his witness, whose words are these: Τούτῳ τῷ λόγῳ εἴσι οἳ Ἑλλήνων ἐχρήσαντο, οἱ μὲν πρότερον, οἱ δὲ ὕστερον, ὡς ἰδίῳ ἑαυτῶν ἐόντι· τῶν ἐγὼ εἰδὼς τὰ οὐνόματα, οὐ γράφω. “There are some among the Greeks who have employed this doctrine as though it were their own, some earlier and others later; though I know their names, I do not think they should be written down” (Herod., book II, § 123). Jerome, however, wrote much more clearly: “And because I had said that I had read the Pythagorean doctrines, hear what Pythagoras was the first among the Greeks to discover: that souls are immortal and pass from some bodies into others” (Jerome, *Apology Against Rufinus*, book III, near the end, p. [Col. 0464D] 470; vol. I of the *Apparatus*, pp. 522, 620, and 1136; *Dissertation on Lactantius*, chap. 29, art. 1; *Dissertation on Tertullian’s Apologeticum*, chap. 11, art. 2). We have already spoken of this opinion of his and Plato’s, and shall discuss it further below.

## ARTICLE II. Other arguments of Octavius for proving the resurrection of our bodies, and the contrary arguments of Caecilius, are examined

Against Octavius’ first line of argument, Caecilius and other pagans objected that they could never assent to the utterly ridiculous opinion either of Pythagoras and Plato or of the Christians concerning the restoration of our body to life, [Col. 0465A] since, by whatever reasoning might be devised, it could never happen. But Octavius checks the foolish rashness of his adversary, who doubts the divine power, as follows: “Who is so foolish or brutish that he dares deny that a dead man could be restored to life by God?” For just as God fashioned and created a human being from nothing, so he can just as easily raise him from the dead. Justin Martyr, however, presses this argument more forcefully:

“If anyone, when you did not yet exist in your present form or originate from such things, had pointed to human seed and to a painted image and asserted that from that very seed a nature of this kind could arise, would you have believed him before it happened? I certainly do not think anyone would dare say that he would. But [Col. 0465B] just as in the beginning you would not have believed it possible that people such as yourselves could arise from a tiny drop, although you now see that they have arisen, in the same way consider it not impossible that human bodies, after being dissolved and cast into the earth like seeds, should at the proper time, by God’s command, arise and put on an incorruptible nature” (Justin, *Apology* II, p. 65).

With the same weapon not only Tatian and Athenagoras, whom we shall cite shortly, but also Tertullian strikes the pagans as follows:

“Consider yourself, O human being, and you will discover confidence in the fact. Think back upon what you were before you existed—nothing, certainly; for you would remember if you had been anything. You, therefore, who were nothing before you existed, and who will likewise have become nothing when you cease to exist, why could you not exist again from nothing by the will of the same author who willed you to exist [Col. 0465C] from nothing? You who did not exist were made; when you do not exist again, you will be made. Explain, if you can, the manner in which you were made, and then demand to know the manner in which you will be made. And yet you will certainly be made more easily, since you once existed, seeing that you were just as easily made when once you had never existed. Doubt will be cast, I suppose, upon the powers of God, who composed this vast body of the world from that which had not existed—from no less than the deathlike absence and emptiness of being—and animated it with the spirit of all living things” (Tertull., *Apologeticum*, chap. 48, p. 42).

He pursues these matters more fully in that book (same author, *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, chap. 11 ff.). Lactantius later states it more briefly: “If in the beginning God formed man in some ineffable manner unknown to me, let us believe that he who made a new man can restore the old one” (Lactant., book VII of the *Institutes*, chap. 23, p. 721).

[Col. 0465D] The pagans nevertheless insisted that it was absolutely impossible for a human body that had been swallowed by water, consumed by fire, reduced to dust, ashes, and embers, or transformed into another body to be raised, restored, and reconstituted as numerically the same body. Minucius replies, however, that although that body “is withdrawn from us, it is nevertheless preserved for God, the guardian of the elements.” Minucius states this briefly, while Tatian treated it at greater length and pressed the point as follows:

“We believe that this will happen, caring nothing meanwhile for however much you may suppose us to jest and babble. For just as I did not know what I was before I was born, when I did not yet exist at all but existed only in the underlying matter of the flesh, and then, once born, though formerly I had not existed, possess in that very generation assurance of my being; [Col. 0466A] so, having been born and then reduced through death to non-being, I shall again come into existence and once more become visible to the eyes. For even if all my flesh is consumed by fire, the world nevertheless receives its evaporated matter; although I dissolve in rivers or the sea, or am torn apart by wild beasts, I am still stored in the treasury of a most wealthy master. Although the poor and impious do not know this, God who reigns nevertheless will, whenever he wishes, restore to its former integrity the substance visible to him alone” (Tatian, *Address Against the Greeks*, p. 146).

Tertullian likewise answers in the same manner: “Wherever you may have been dissolved, whatever material may have destroyed, swallowed, abolished, and reduced you to nothing, it will return you. Nothingness itself belongs to him to whom [Col. 0466B] the whole belongs” (Tertull., *Apologeticum*, chap. 48, p. 43).

Athenagoras presses and explains these points against the pagans at far greater length. There he himself, like the other writers already cited by us, says: Εἰ μὴ ὄντα κατὰ τὴν πρώτην σύστασιν, ἐποίησε τὰ τῶν ἀνθρώπων σώματα, καὶ τὰς τούτων ἀρχὰς, καὶ διαλυθέντα, καθ’ ὃν τύχῃ τρόπον, ἀναστάσει μετὰ τῆς εὐμαρείας· ἐπίσης γὰρ αὐτῷ καὶ τοῦτο δυνατόν. “If God made human bodies when they did not exist at their first constitution, and created the principles from which they derive their origin, he will also restore them with the same ease after they have been dissolved, in whatever manner that may happen. For this too is equally possible for him” (Athenagor., *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, p. 43 ff.). You should not begrudge the effort of reading in his book the remainder, which it would take too long to transcribe here.

[Col. 0466C] Although Minucius utterly overturned the pagans’ frivolous quibbles with so many arguments of such great weight, he nevertheless further refutes and destroys them with various examples:

“See, then, how all nature rehearses the future resurrection for our consolation. The sun sinks and rises; the stars pass away and return; flowers die and revive; after old age the trees put forth leaves; seeds become green again only after decay. Thus the body in this present age is like trees in winter: it conceals a vitality not yet apparent, under the false appearance of dryness. Why are you in haste for it to revive and return while winter is still unripe?”

Theophilus of Antioch uses the same method to prove the future resurrection of our body:

“God,” he says, “supplies arguments from very many things by which he may drive away our unbelief in the matter of the resurrection. [Col. 0466D] Observe, if it is not troublesome, the passing away of seasons, days, and nights. Do you not notice how these things die and rise again? Why, moreover, should I mention the resurrection of fruits and seeds, all of which serve our will? For if, by way of example, you scatter a grain of wheat or of some other crop upon the earth, it first dies and is dissolved, and only then is born and rises into a fruit-bearing stalk. The nature of trees and oaks, in accordance with the Lord’s command, brings forth fruit at appointed times by a certain hidden power invisible to us. Sometimes a sparrow or another little bird devours the seed of an apple, a fig, or some other thing, flies to some elevated, rocky place, and expels it into [Col. 0467A] some hollow through another part of its body. What happens? That seed grows up and becomes a great tree, although it was swallowed and passed through such great heat. . . . But if you wish to behold a more wonderful spectacle, one suited to proving the resurrection of the dead with greater clarity, I bid you raise your face not only toward earthly things but also toward the resurrection of heavenly things. Look at the moon, which dies and is reborn every month, and consider the other stars as well. Moreover, recognize in yourself the operation of resurrection, O human being, although you do not understand it. I do not doubt that, when at some time afflicted by illness, you lost your flesh, appearance, and strength; yet God, showing you mercy and granting healing, [Col. 0467B] caused you to recover the flesh, appearance, and strength you had lost. Just as you do not know where your flesh went when it left you, so you do not know where it returned from or whence you received it. ‘But in truth,’ you say, ‘my flesh grew again from nourishment and flavours converted into blood.’ Well said; but do not be mistaken: this is God’s benefaction and must not be credited to another” (Theoph., book II *To Autolycus*, p. 77 f.).

Many of the most learned Fathers of the Church also confirmed the future resurrection of our bodies by these same, or very similar, examples. But because their words are too lengthy to be reproduced here in full, we shall indicate them for all curious readers who wish to inspect everything with their own eyes. Let them therefore read Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, chap. 48, and [Col. 0467C] *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, chap. 12; Ambrose, book V of the *Hexaemeron*, chaps. 22–23, p. 109 ff., and especially book II *On Faith in the Resurrection*, § 53 ff., p. 1147 ff.; Theodoret, Oration 9, *On Providence*, near the end, p. 436 ff.; Nilus, Oration 1, *On Easter*, in Photius, *Bibliotheca*, p. 1530. They should also consult Augustine, book XXII of *The City of God*, chap. 21 ff., p. 676 ff., where he explains whether and how bodies are to be restored to life, whether those which have been reduced to embers and ashes, those eaten by other people, or even the bodies of infants. If they have the leisure and inclination, let them also turn through the pseudonymous work *Questions and Answers to the Greeks*, ascribed to Justin Martyr, p. 208 ff., published among the works of Justin himself.

[Col. 0467D] But some pagan, or some unbeliever or other, will rise up and object that the examples thus far proposed to prove the resurrection of our body are of little, or rather of no, weight. For neither the sun nor the stars die, nor do the numerically identical flowers and fruits that have died revive. Yet the most learned men praised by us were not so dull and obtuse as either to be ignorant of these points or fail to notice them. They certainly knew that all comparisons, as the saying goes, limp in some respect. Accordingly, they set forth these comparisons in order to make plain that many examples are available to us which have something in common with, and similar to, our dead bodies when they are someday restored to life, and by which [Col. 0468A] God’s power to restore them—the only matter at issue—is clearly and distinctly proved. For do not the setting and rising of the sun and stars, and fruits and other things of this kind growing again from their decaying grains, present us with some likeness of our rising body? But if these things continually happen by God’s customary power, how did the pagans dare deny that our dead bodies could be raised to life by the same divine power? Therefore, for them to return to the breezes of the light they have lost, nothing is required except God’s own will. That God wills this is gathered most clearly from our sacred Scriptures, as we shall show below from other writers of ours. Since, however, the pagans’ dispute concerned not this will of God but only his power, Minucius [Col. 0468B] and the others thought it sufficient to have demonstrated that power by various examples and even by certain arguments *ad hominem*, as they call them.

Moreover, once these points had been established and confirmed, our author thought that nothing further needed to be said in answer to Caecilius’ inept quibble, by which he demanded that some dead person be produced who had ever returned to us alive. For what need was there to prove the divine power to raise the dead by the example either of Protesilaus or of anyone else, when that power had already been demonstrated by the most certain force of reasoning? Theophilus of Antioch, however, in order to blunt that dull and feeble pagan weapon, presents examples other than that of Protesilaus—examples handed down by the pagans themselves—in the following manner:

“But what remarkable thing do you do if you see and then believe? Εἴτε [Col. 0468C] πιστεύεις τὸν Ἡρακλέα καύσαντα ἑαυτὸν ζῆν, καὶ Ἀσκλήπιον κεραυνωθέντα ἐγηγέρθαι, τὰ δὲ ὑπὸ τοῦ Θεοῦ σοὶ λεγόμενα ἀπιστεῖς, ἴσως κἂν ἐπιδείξω σοι νεκρὸν ἐγερθέντα, καὶ ζῶντα, καὶ τοῦτο ἀπιστεύσεις.
