If you believe that Hercules, who burned himself, is alive, and that Asclepius, who was struck by lightning, was restored to life, what madness is it to refuse belief to the things God tells you? Doubt would still possess you even if I presented to you someone summoned back from the dead and alive; could I obtain credence from you?” (Theoph., book *To Autolycus*, p. 77.)

He might further have adduced the example, presented by Plato, of Er the Armenian, whom we discuss elsewhere, and many other such stories circulated by the pagans; but our writers rejected them as superfluous. If, however, anyone desires still more concerning the future resurrection of the dead than what we have related [Col. 0468D] from the authors cited, let him consult Tatian, Ambrose, and others who published entire treatises on this subject (vol. I of the *Apparatus*, book III, dissertation 2, chap. 16, art. 1, p. 1116).

## ARTICLE III. The arguments are considered by which it is shown that wicked people will be tormented with eternal punishments and everlasting fire, while the devout and righteous will be endowed with perpetual happiness; with a discussion of the fires of Mount Etna and Vesuvius, the Stygian marsh, and the fiery river of hell

Just as Caecilius rejects and repudiates, not without mockery, the dogma of the Christian faith concerning dead people’s return to life, so too does he reject its teaching concerning the everlasting punishments of the wicked [Col. 0469A] and the eternal happiness of the devout. “Deceived,” he says, “by this error”—the future return from death to life—Christians “promise themselves, as good people, a blessed and perpetual life after death, but everlasting punishment to all others as unrighteous. . . . While you live in misery, judge what awaits you after death. . . . You who dream of posthumous immortality: when you are shaken by danger, consumed by fevers, and torn by pain, do you still not perceive your condition?” Finally, with equal boldness and impiety, he declares: “As we are born, so we perish”; that is, just as we were nothing before we were born, so after death, reduced to the same nothingness, we shall be absolutely nothing. Such, then, was Caecilius’ argument. But it must incidentally be noted [Col. 0469B] that in this text the words *periculo quateris*, “you are shaken by danger,” have displeased some, who conjecture that one should read *querquero*, that is, “you are shaken by cold and trembling,” or by a chill fever. But the royal manuscript contradicts this conjecture, and the words that follow also prevent its acceptance.

Octavius, however, modestly replies to Caecilius, who casts these objections—or rather these arrogant reproaches—at the Christians, that very many people, “because of the consciousness of their deserts,” that is, because their sins and vices condemn their conscience, more strongly wish than actually believe that a person is extinguished utterly by death and is not preserved for any subsequent punishment. There can indeed be no doubt that the more slowly God’s most just judgment is brought against those who deceive themselves by this error and sin with greater licence, the more severely it will come. [Col. 0469C] Hence Valerius Maximus says concerning Dionysius, tyrant of Syracuse: “Divine wrath proceeds with a slow step toward exacting vengeance for itself, and compensates for the delay of punishment by its severity” (Val. Max., book I, chap. 1, Foreign Examples § 3, p. 21).

But if, by the admission of a pagan, divine vengeance does not permit those guilty of more serious crimes to go unpunished, others certainly cannot deny that wicked, criminal, and impious people who die still stained by their crimes must undergo their due punishments after death. For then, in the other life, which will be eternal, they will pay with everlasting fire the penalties they did not pay in this life. For, Minucius says, “a discerning fire burns and restores the limbs, consumes and nourishes them.” Nor could the pagans answer that this was a fabrication invented by certain persons who wished [Col. 0469D] to frighten others. For this is no more difficult for almighty God than raising a dead person to life. It is therefore sufficient that he should will it. That he does so will is declared not only by sacred Scripture, but also by his divine justice, which can leave no crime unpunished.

But to persuade the pagans of this more readily, Minucius adduces, in confirmation of this teaching, certain examples drawn from fires, lightning bolts, Mounts Etna and Vesuvius, and lands burning everywhere—phenomena that were doubtless not unknown to them. Listen, if you will, to his words:

> “Just as the fires of lightning,” he says, “touch bodies without consuming them; just as the fires of Etna and Vesuvius, and of lands burning everywhere, [Col. 0470A] blaze without being exhausted; so that penal conflagration is not fed by the destruction of those who burn, but is sustained by the unconsumed torment of their bodies.”

But he seems to have excerpted this from the following passage of Tertullian, who is discussing the same eternal fires:

> “The philosophers too recognize a difference between hidden and ordinary fire. Thus the fire that serves human use is far different from that which appears in the judgment of God, whether it strikes with lightning from heaven or erupts from the earth through the summits of mountains. For it does not consume what it burns; rather, while it expends, it restores. Thus mountains remain forever burning, and one who is struck from heaven remains intact, so that thereafter he cannot be reduced to ashes by any fire. And this will be testimony to eternal fire, an example of the continual judgment that sustains punishment. Mountains burn and endure. What, then, of the guilty and the enemies of God? [Col. 0470B] These are the things that, when asserted by us alone, are called presumptions, but in philosophers and poets are regarded as the highest knowledge and distinguished judgments” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 48, p. 43).

In the same way Lactantius, after both Tertullian and Minucius Felix, argued as follows, in words plainly somewhat different from theirs (Lactantius, *Divine Institutes*, VII.21, p. 715 ff.):

> The nature of eternal fire “differs from that fire of ours which we use for the necessities of life and which, unless fed by the fuel of some material, is extinguished. But that divine fire lives and flourishes forever by itself, without any nourishment; nor does it contain an admixture of smoke, but is pure and clear, and fluid like water. For it is not driven upward by any force, as ours is.... Therefore that same divine fire, by one and the same [Col. 0470C] force and power, will both burn the impious and restore them; and as much as it consumes from their bodies, so much it will replace”—our manuscript reads “resume”—“and it will provide itself with everlasting fuel. What the poets transferred to the vulture of Tityus: thus, without any loss to the bodies that grow fresh again, it will merely burn them and afflict them with the sensation of pain” (*Dissertation on Lactantius*, ch. 29).

But we shall say something more, in its proper place, about this argument of Lactantius and Tertullian, and shall show in what sense both he and Minucius understood the verb *erogare* (“to expend”) here (*Dissertation on Tertullian*, ch. 11).

Meanwhile, let us proceed and meet those who may perhaps object to us in the name of the pagans that comparisons between the fire of hell and lightning, mountains, and perpetually burning lands are utterly inept. “For,” someone will say, [Col. 0470D] “is not some part of the substance of a person struck by lightning consumed by its heat? Is not fresh material continually supplied to the fires of Etna and Vesuvius”—in the manuscript the reading is corrupt, “of Henneus and Jesu,” as you see—“or of other mountains or burning lands? Christians, by contrast, maintained that the fire of hell would always remain the same and that absolutely nothing would perish from the human body burned by it.”

Tertullian, however, whom our Minucius follows, as we have already observed, completely cuts off the force of this objection from the pagans. For he shows that the chief strength of this argument lies in the fact that the pagans admitted, without anyone contradicting them, that certain fires of lightning, mountains, and lands are [Col. 0471A] altogether extraordinary. Could he not then infer from this that those same pagans were wrong to deny that, by God’s infinite power, another fire could be kindled—one that would always remain the same and, without consuming the bodies of the impious, would burn and torment them forever?

Nor did Minucius stop there. By another comparison—or, as they say, another *argumentum ad hominem*—he further confirms how foolishly Caecilius and the other pagans denied this:

> “Men,” he says, “are reminded by the books of the most learned and by the poems of the poets of that fiery river and of the burning heat that repeatedly encircles the Stygian marsh, which they have handed down as prepared for eternal torments, known both from the declarations of demons and from the oracles of the Prophets.”

Here Minucius undoubtedly cited both secular and sacred writers. By the name “Prophets,” [Col. 0471B] he designates the books of the Old Testament and also, if you prefer, the utterances of the Sibyls and of others whom the pagans regarded as prophets; but by “the declarations of demons,” he means the sacred books of the New Testament, where we read that demons openly confessed, in the hearing of all, that they were to be tormented in eternal fires. He therefore confronts the pagans with that public confession of the demons, which neither they nor anyone else could deny.

He appeals to secular, or pagan, writers as witnesses to “the fiery river” and “the Stygian marsh”—namely Acheron, which those same pagans imagined to be one of the four most celebrated rivers of the underworld and, as Servius says, full of fire, receiving the waters of Pyriphlegethon (Servius on Virgil, [Col. 0471C] *Aeneid* VI, p. 404). Anyone may very easily learn from Plato, who described them, and from a great many other authors, what this and the other two rivers of the underworld were (Plato, *Phaedo*, vol. I, p. 112 ff.).

From that same Plato one may learn with equal ease why Styx is called a marsh by Minucius and is said to be repeatedly encircled by burning heat, although others have handed it down as a river whose water is so cold that anyone who drinks it dies immediately. For Styx, he says, falls into a dreadful and immense place and forms a marsh (ibid., p. 113). It then enters the earth and, circling around, flows into fire-burning Pyriphlegethon; yet its water does not mingle with that river or with any other. After completing its circuit, it pours itself into Tartarus. That entire passage of Plato [Col. 0471D] is reproduced by Eusebius (Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, XI.23, p. 567).

Who would not readily persuade himself that it is above all this very Plato whom our Minucius cites under the name of “the most learned men,” or, as Tertullian says, “the philosophers,” and that he is citing this book of Plato? Perhaps no one will deny, either, that among the poets praised by Minucius and Tertullian, first place must be given to Homer and second to Virgil. For Homer sang:

> There Pyriphlegethon and Cocytus flow into Acheron,  
> Cocytus, which indeed is an offshoot of the water of Styx,  
> And there are the rock and the meeting of the two loudly roaring rivers.

The accompanying Latin rendering reads:

> Here indeed Pyriphlegethon and Cocytus flow together into Acheron,  
> And Cocytus, which surely is an outflow of the water of Styx,  
> [Col. 0472A] And the rock and the confluence of the two loudly roaring rivers.  
> (Homer, *Odyssey* X.145.)

Later Virgil wrote:

> From here lies the road that leads to the waters of Tartarean Acheron.  
> Here a whirlpool, turbid with mud and vast in its abyss,  
> Seethes and disgorges all its sand into Cocytus.  
> (Virgil, *Aeneid* VI.295 ff.)

On these verses Servius observes:

> “He intends Acheron, as it were, to arise from the lowest Tartarus; its estuaries to create Styx; and Cocytus in turn to arise from Styx.”

See also, if you wish, what he had previously annotated on verse 107 of the same book. The Stygian marsh, however, is frequently mentioned by various writers.

Minucius then continues:

> “And therefore,” he says, “among them even King Jupiter himself swears religiously by the rushing banks and the black [Col. 0472B] abyss,”

that is, undoubtedly, by the waters of Styx, of which Homer says:

> Come now, swear to me by the inviolable water of Styx.  
> (Homer, *Iliad* XIV.271.)

In another book he also sang:

> And by the water of Styx flowing beneath, which is the greatest  
> And most dreadful oath among the blessed gods.

The accompanying Latin rendering reads:

> And by the water of Styx itself lying below, which is held to be  
> The greatest and most solemn oath among the blessed gods.  
> (Homer, *Odyssey* V.185 ff.)

Virgil plainly agrees with Homer in these Latin verses:

> You see the deep pools of Cocytus and the Stygian marsh,  
> By whose divinity the gods fear to swear falsely.  
> (Virgil, *Aeneid* VI.323 ff.)

[Col. 0472C] If you desire more, consult Apollonius, *Argonautica* II.290; Hesiod, *Theogony* IV.383 ff. and 775 ff.; Ovid, *Metamorphoses* I.184 ff.; Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* VII, around the middle; Natalis Comes, *Mythology* III.1 ff.; and Vossius, *On the Origin and Progress of Idolatry* II.81, p. 359 ff.

Moreover, just as it is certain that wicked people who depart this life conscious of their crimes are subjected to eternal punishments by a just and omnipotent God, so it must be regarded as established that the righteous, dying in righteousness, are endowed by that same God with everlasting happiness. Minucius thought that, by proving the former, he had sufficiently demonstrated the latter as well. He therefore did not consider it necessary to prove it further, and does not hesitate openly to declare:

> “These pious people, namely, live secure in the hope of future happiness.” [Col. 0472D]

## ARTICLE IV  
### The arguments by which Octavius proves against Caecilius that the world will someday perish by fire are examined, together with the opinions of the Stoics, Epicureans, and Plato on this subject

Christians continued to hold it as a certain and settled decree that this entire world and everything in it was to be consumed by fire. But Caecilius assails this in the following few words:

> “As though either the eternal order established by the divine laws of nature were to be disturbed, or, once the compact [Col. 0473A] of all the elements had been broken and the heavenly structure divided, this mass, which is held together and enclosed by it, were to collapse.”

Octavius, however, rebukes him in these words:

> “It is a common error either not to believe that an unforeseen fire may fall or to believe that this is difficult.”

These words, however, seem obscure to many. Rigaltius and certain others therefore wished them to be corrected in printed editions by transposing two words, as follows:

> “It is a common opinion either to believe in an unforeseen fire or not to believe that it is difficult for it to fall.”

Ouzel, by adding one word, thought the corruption should be repaired thus:

> “It is a common error either not to believe that an unforeseen fire may fall or that it is sufficient.”

But this is wrong and contrary both to the authority of the manuscript and to Minucius’s meaning. For his sense is sufficiently clear to everyone: it is a common [Col. 0473B] error to believe either that an unforeseen fire cannot fall or that this is difficult—namely, difficult for God, who can destroy all things with precisely the same ease with which he created them. That this is his true meaning is plainly evident from his subsequent words and argument.

He proves his proposition by the following arguments. First:

> “Who among the wise,” he says, “does not know that everything that has arisen dies, and that everything that has been made perishes? The heaven too, together with everything contained in heaven, will cease just as it began.”

Here he undoubtedly opposes the wise to the uneducated multitude—or else by that name he designates philosophers, or any others who do not allow themselves to be led by the opinions of the ignorant populace. Earlier [Col. 0473C] Cicero had introduced the Epicurean Velleius arguing as follows:

> “Do you suppose that he”—Plato—“had merely tasted natural philosophy with the tips of his lips, as the saying goes, when he thought anything that had arisen could be eternal? For what joining is incapable of being dissolved? Or what is there that has a beginning but no end?”  
> (Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* II, p. 198, line 31 ff.)

Cyprian, writing to Demetrianus, says that this law was established by God himself: everything that has arisen must die and at some time come to an end:

> “This sentence,” he says, “has been given to the world; this is God’s law: that all things which have arisen should die, things that have grown should grow old, strong things should become weak, great things should diminish, and, once they have become weak and diminished, should come to an end.”  
> (Cyprian, *To Demetrianus*, vol. I, p. 187.)

[Col. 0473D] He develops these points at greater length, and you may read them in his book, as also almost countless other statements handed down on the same subject by other writers, which there is no need to collect here.

Our Minucius, moreover, confirms that most true Christian belief concerning the end of the world and its future conflagration not only by the common opinion of the wise, but also by the testimony of certain philosophers, although they did not belong to the same school. For immediately after the words cited above, he added:

> “That [heaven] is nourished by the fresh water of springs or by sea-water”—the manuscript reads *dulcis* and *maria nutrire*—“and will pass into the force of fire is the settled opinion of the Stoics, because, once the [Col. 0474A] moisture has been consumed, this whole world will catch fire.”

It is remarkable how greatly learned men disagree with one another in emending this passage, which they regard as corrupt. Some think the manuscript reading should be retained, but entirely reject the words following “it is the settled opinion,” as a superfluous addition that crept from the margin into the text. They say Minucius’s meaning is this: springs will no longer nourish the waters of the sea with their sweet waters; rather, that nourishment, or the sea’s supply, as the Stoics believed, will pass into a mass of fire—or will be consumed by fire. Others suspect that nothing in the manuscript text should be changed except “sweet waters” for “sweet water,” and that our author’s meaning is: the nourishment, or [Col. 0474B] supplies, which springs and seas owe to heaven will, together with heaven, pass into the force of fire.

Gronovius, however, rejecting all these conjectures, thinks that Minucius’s words embrace three distinct kinds of liquids. He therefore believes the text should be corrected thus:

> “The nourishment of springs, fresh water, and the sea will pass into the force of fire.”

But apart from the fact that this correction is supported by no authority, what distinction, I ask, is there between the nourishment of springs and that of fresh water?

Yet however obscure and difficult to emend our author’s words may be, it seems entirely certain that he was looking to the following words of Cicero:

> “The stars are fiery by nature; therefore they are nourished by the vapors of the earth, the sea, and the waters, which are raised by the sun from the warmed fields [Col. 0474C] and from the waters.... From this our philosophers”—that is, the Stoics—“think that the event will follow concerning which they said Panaetius had doubts: that in the end the whole world would catch fire when its moisture had been consumed, since the earth could no longer be nourished, nor could the air return, whose production, once all the water had been exhausted, would be impossible. Thus nothing would remain except fire; and from this fire, again, as animate and divine, the renewal of the world would take place and the same ordered structure would arise.”  
> (Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* II, p. 232, line 12 ff.)

For you see that some of these words are the same as those found in Minucius, who accordingly wished to reproduce Cicero’s meaning. That meaning appears to be this: none of the wise is unaware that heaven and everything contained in it are nourished by both the fresh water of springs and the water of the sea; and that this very heaven and the whole world, when their moisture has been consumed—[Col. 0474D] as the Stoics believed—will pass into that force of fire from which they began. If, however, anyone offers something more certain, we shall not oppose him.

Besides the Cicero whom we have cited, Philo committed the following account of this Stoic doctrine to writing:

> “The Stoics assert that there is one world, and that God is the cause of its generation; but that the cause of its corruption is no longer God, but the tireless power of fire inherent in existing things, which, after long revolutions of time, dissolves all things into itself, and from which, in turn, a renewed generation of the world is established by the providence of the Craftsman.”

The accompanying Latin rendering reads:

> “The Stoics assert one world, and God as the author of its generation; but not likewise God as the author of its corruption, but rather the unwearied force of fire, implanted in things, which, after long circuits of time, will consume all things and transform them into itself, and from which [Col. 0475A] the Craftsman’s providence will restore the world anew.”  
> (Philo, *On the Incorruptibility of the World*, p. 940.)

Yet he afterwards added:

> “Boethus, Posidonius, and Panaetius, men highly accomplished in Stoic teaching, as though seized by divine inspiration, abandoned conflagrations and restorations and deserted to the more divine doctrine of the incorruptibility of the world.”

The Greek expression is: “They deserted to the more divine doctrine, that of the incorruptibility of the entire world.”

Consider, I ask, whether these words can confirm what we saw stated by Cicero: that not only Panaetius but also other Stoics had doubted whether the opinion of their fellow Stoics concerning the future conflagration of the world was true. For our Minucius, however, it was sufficient that this was the opinion of by far the greater number. See, if you wish, Lescalopier’s observations on the cited passage of Cicero, and Origen’s argument against Celsus [Col. 0475B] (Origen, *Against Celsus* V, p. 244), and also what we observed in the preceding volume of our *Apparatus* (vol. I, *Apparatus*, III, dissertation 2, ch. 16, art. 1, p. 1117).

Nor does our Minucius assert that this view concerning the conflagration of the elements and the ruin of the world belonged only to the Stoics. Rather, he says:

> “The Epicureans hold this very same opinion.”

There is, however, considerable room for doubt as to whether he should be understood there as referring to all Epicureans or only to some, and whether he believed that Epicurus had received it from his teacher Democritus. For Epicurus wrote the following to Pythocles (in Laertius, X §88):

> “A world is a certain enclosure of heaven containing the stars and all visible things, having a section cut off from the infinite [Col. 0475C] and terminating at a boundary, whether rare or dense; when this is dissolved, all things within it will fall into confusion ... in which it is impossible to apprehend an end.”

The accompanying Latin rendering reads:

> “The world is a certain enclosure of heaven, containing the stars, the earth, and everything visible, having a division from the infinite and terminating at a boundary, whether rare or dense; when this is dissolved, all things within it will fall into confusion: either terminating, or in that which is turned about, or in that which possesses stability ... in which we are unable to apprehend the boundary.”

Plutarch, whose words Eusebius reproduced, relates the following in the second book of *The Opinions of the Philosophers*:

> “Epicurus said that the world was perishable because it had come into being, like an animal or a plant.”

The accompanying Latin rendering reads:

> “Epicurus said that the world would perish because it had been generated, like a living creature and a plant.”  
> (Plutarch, *Opinions of the Philosophers* II.4, [Col. 0475D] p. 886; Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel* XV, p. 842.)

Lactantius testifies that these ideas were drawn by Epicurus from the sources of Democritus:

> “Epicurus, on the authority of Democritus, says that the world both had a beginning and will someday perish.”

He later explains Epicurus’s opinion more fully:

> “Epicurus,” he says, “or Democritus, said that it arose spontaneously when seeds came together with one another, and that when these were again dissolved, separation and destruction would follow.”  
> (Lactantius, *Divine Institutes* VII, ch. [text uncertain], p. 647, and ch. 3, p. 657.)

And rightly so. For a little above we heard the Epicurean in Cicero assert that everything which has arisen must necessarily perish.

But we have not yet sufficiently ascertained in what [Col. 0476A] manner Epicurus or his followers said the world would perish: whether by water, fire, the dissolution of atoms or corpuscles, as Lactantius says, or by their collisions and impacts, as Philo indicates concerning Democritus and Epicurus in the following words:

> “They imagine many worlds, whose generation they attribute to the collisions and interlockings of atoms, and whose corruption to impacts and separations of the things that have come into being.”

The accompanying Latin rendering reads:

> “They imagine many worlds, whose generation they attribute to the collisions and connections of atoms, and whose corruption to impacts and dispersions.”  
> (Philo, *On the Incorruptibility of the World*, p. 940.)

For if Epicurus thought that many worlds could be destroyed by various collisions and impacts of this kind, why not all of them? Gassendi, however, considers it more [Col. 0476B] probable that he taught that this world was to be utterly consumed by fire, since fire is more active than all the other elements (Gassendi, *Syntagma of Epicurean Philosophy*, §2, ch. 7, vol. III, p. 32). But if he had either read, or remembered having once read, our author’s words cited shortly above, he could undoubtedly have offered them as a by no means entirely weak confirmation of his conjecture.

Finally Minucius comes to Plato, who, as he reports:

> “Plato speaks; he says that parts of the world now flood”—some either reject this last word or retain it if “says” is added after “Plato”—“and now, in alternating cycles, [Col. 0476C] catch fire; and although he said that the world itself had been fashioned perpetual and indissoluble, he nevertheless adds that to God alone, its Craftsman, it is both dissoluble and mortal. Thus it is no wonder if this mass should be destroyed by him by whom it was constructed.”

Minucius here reports two assertions made by Plato. First, that the world was created “indissoluble” by God, yet in such a way that it could be dissolved and destroyed by him. Second, that parts of the world, in alternating cycles, either flood—that is, are overwhelmed by water—or “catch fire,” that is, are consumed by fire.

Plato stated the first point very explicitly:

> “Since God wished to produce the most beautiful offspring, the world, he made it a generated god, never to be corrupted by any cause other than God, who composed it, should he ever wish to dissolve it.”

The accompanying Latin rendering reads:

> “Since God therefore wished to produce the most beautiful offspring, the world, he made it a generated god, never to be corrupted by any other cause except God, who composed it, if ever he should wish to dissolve it.” [Col. 0476D]  
> (Plato, *Timaeus*, vol. III, p. 94.)

For precisely this reason we read the following committed to writing by Arnobius:

> “That divine Plato, entertaining many thoughts about God that were worthy of him and not common among the multitude, says in the discourse and book entitled *Timaeus* that the gods and the world are corruptible by nature and not wholly exempt from dissolution, but are held in perpetual union by the will of God, the king and ruler.”  
> (Arnobius, II, p. 68.)

Philo the Jew testified that this truly was Plato’s opinion concerning the created and incorruptible world, since Plato introduces the supreme God as speaking the following words to the other gods (Philo, *On the Corruptibility of the World*, p. 950):

> “Gods of gods, whose Craftsman [Col. 0477A] and Father I am: [these works are] indissoluble unless I will it. Now everything that has been bound is capable of dissolution; yet only an evil being would wish to dissolve what has been beautifully fitted together and is in a good condition. Therefore, although you have come into being, you are not immortal nor altogether indissoluble; nevertheless you shall not be dissolved, nor shall you meet the fate of death, because my will has obtained a bond still greater and more sovereign than those bonds by which you were joined together when you came into being.”  
> (Plato, *Timaeus*, vol. II, p. 41.)

These words are indeed found in Plato’s *Timaeus*, apart from some variant readings. The opening words were cited by Athenagoras (Athenagoras, *Embassy for the Christians*, p. 7); the whole passage is presented in Latin in a fragment of Cicero’s works as follows:

> “Attend to these things, you who have sprung from the stock of gods. Of the works whose parent and maker I am, those which were made by me are not dissolved against my will, [Col. 0477B] although everything joined together can be dissolved; yet it is by no means the act of a good being to wish to dissolve what has been bound together according to reason. But because you have come into being, you cannot indeed be immortal and indissoluble; nevertheless you shall by no means be dissolved, nor shall any fate of death destroy you, nor shall any power prove stronger than my purpose, which is a greater bond for perpetuity than those by which you were joined when you were generated.”  
> (Cicero, *On the Universe*, Appendix, p. 29, line 6 ff.)

But these authors do not explain whether Plato believed that the world was to be destroyed in alternating cycles by fire and water. Clement of Alexandria, however, set this forth in the following words:

> “Plato says that at certain times the earth is purified by fire and water, in approximately these terms: ‘There have often been many destructions of humankind, and there will be again—the greatest [Col. 0477C] by fire and water, and other, lesser ones by countless other means.’ A little later he adds: ‘The truth is that a deviation occurs among the things that move around the earth and through heaven, and after long intervals there is a destruction by much fire of the things upon the earth.’ He then adds concerning the flood: ‘But whenever the gods again purify the earth with water and flood it, the herdsmen and shepherds in the mountains are preserved, while those in the cities among us are carried by the rivers into the sea.’”

The accompanying Latin rendering reads:

> “Plato says that at certain times the earth is purged by fire and water in this manner: ‘There have often been many destructions, and there will be again—the greatest by fire and water; indeed there will also be other, shorter destructions by countless other causes.’ A little later he adds: ‘In truth, there is a change among the things that pass around the earth and through heaven, and after long intervals a destruction by much fire occurs among the things on earth.’ [Col. 0477D] He then adds concerning the flood: ‘But when the gods again purge the earth with water and flood it, the herdsmen and shepherds in the mountains are preserved, while those in the cities among you are carried by the rivers into the sea.’”  
> (Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata* V, p. 549 ff.)

Consider, I ask, whether our Minucius was aiming at this passage of Clement of Alexandria, and whether on the basis of what has been said those authors can be reconciled who, like Lactantius (*Institutes* VII.1, p. 646; VII.3, p. 656), say that Plato taught that the world would remain forever, and those who, like Epiphanius (*Against Heresies* I, p. 12; *Exposition of the Faith*, p. 1088), say that it is subject to corruption and [Col. 0478A] will be dissolved in time. For Plato taught, as we have seen, that the world could be dissolved by God’s will alone, and therefore that in itself, and unless God willed otherwise, it would remain forever.

See also whether Cicero, cited shortly above, was justified in criticizing him because he believed that the world had come into being but would nevertheless be eternal in the manner we have described. Whatever judgment you make, you cannot deny that Minucius, from this opinion of Plato and others concerning the eventual destruction of the world, not unreasonably concluded that the pagans could not deny the truth of the Christian doctrine that the world would someday perish by fire. We noted something concerning this in the preceding volume of our *Apparatus*, and shall say more in our subsequent dissertations (vol. I, *Apparatus*, [Col. 0478B] p. 1117).

# CHAPTER VIII  
## ON THE THREE ABOMINABLE CRIMES—INFANTICIDE, THE EATING OF HUMAN FLESH, AND INCEST—OF WHICH CHRISTIANS WERE ACCUSED BY CAECILIUS AND OTHER PAGANS

## ARTICLE I  
### What was the nature of this accusation, what occasions gave rise to it, and how long did it persist?

Thus far we have seen with how vain and ineffectual an effort Caecilius attempted to undermine certain principal teachings of the Christians, and by what arguments they were established by Octavius—or rather, Minucius Felix. [Col. 0478C] Let us now turn to the accusations by which Caecilius and other pagans, with plainly reckless audacity, attempted to defame the Christians’ sacred rites and most holy morals.

First, Caecilius accuses all Christians of utterly dreadful crimes committed at their *synaxes*—their assemblies—and nocturnal gatherings. He says that on a certain solemn day they assemble somewhere for a banquet to be held at those nocturnal gatherings. Once a lamp has been lit there, an infant is most cruelly killed by them; with a savagery greater than that of wild beasts, they eat its flesh and lick its blood; finally, when the torches have been extinguished, they all defile themselves with every sort of fornication, adultery, and incest.

In the preceding volume of our *Apparatus*, we already observed that certain writers of the second century of the Church [Col. 0478D], especially Justin Martyr, Athenagoras, and Theophilus of Antioch, recorded that Christians had been accused of these crimes by the pagans. But even though these and other Christian authors conceded that certain heretics noted by us in that same place—namely, the Cataphrygians, or Basilides, Carpocrates and his followers, or the Gnostics, as Irenaeus (Irenaeus, *Against Heresies* I.24), Eusebius (Eusebius, *History* IV.7, p. 120), and Epiphanius testify (Epiphanius, *Heresies* 26 §5, p. 87, and 27 §3, p. 104)—had provided some occasion for this slander, they nevertheless openly and most steadfastly assert that the accusation was utterly false. Indeed, they publicly protest that the pagans never investigated, [Col. 0479A] or dared to investigate, whether those alleged Christian crimes were true, lest they should eventually discover them to be false. Nor could they ever find any person of any station, as will be stated later, except a very few lying Christian slaves, from whom the most cruel tyrant of all, even by the most exquisite tortures, could extort a confession that these crimes were true and had been committed by Christians.

Although this testimony, as certain as it was public, would suffice to explain and confirm the judgment of our Minucius, who rightly and resolutely denies these abominable crimes, it is worthwhile to hear Caecilius, since he frames the accusation somewhat differently from the writers cited by us. [Col. 0479B] He explains as follows the manner in which the pagans then shamelessly exploited that detestable falsehood:

> “The story concerning the initiation of novices is as detestable as it is well known. An infant covered with meal, so as to deceive the unwary, is placed before the person being initiated into their rites. The novice, induced by the surface of the meal to strike what seem to be harmless blows, kills the infant by blind and hidden wounds. They thirstily lick its blood—what an outrage!—and eagerly divide its limbs among themselves.... Their banquet too is well known.... On a solemn day they gather for a feast with all their children, sisters, and mothers—people of every sex and every age. There, after much feasting, when the banquet has grown heated and the frenzy of incestuous lust has been inflamed by drunkenness, a dog tied to the lampstand is incited by the toss of a morsel to rush and leap beyond the length of the cord by which it is bound. [Col. 0479C] Thus the witnessing light is overturned and extinguished, and in the shameless darkness they become entangled in the bonds of unspeakable desire, as chance indiscriminately determines; and even if not all commit incest in deed, all nevertheless share consciousness of it.”

What could be more cruel, impious, inhuman, and horrible than these crimes?

Before proceeding further, however, it must be observed that the manuscript reads, “the heat of drunkenness belonging to incestuous lust”; but this, as most have judged, arose from a copyist’s carelessness. Accordingly, several editions adopted “by drunkenness,” yielding a sufficiently clear and evident sense. This emendation did not please Gronovius, however, who suspected that the words “of incestuous lust” were corrupt and that the text should read:

> “the heat of drunkenness blazed forth into blind lusts.”

For incest, he says, is mentioned shortly [Col. 0479D] afterward: “all nevertheless equally share consciousness of incest.” But those last words are so far from excluding the earlier phrase “incestuous lust” that they appear instead to refer back to something already stated. The alternative reading therefore comes closer to the truth, although it must still be confirmed by the authority of a better manuscript.

What Gronovius adds in the same place, however, is altogether improbable: that Caecilius’s words concerning Christian assemblies refer to the baptism of infants. Could Caecilius, arguing against Christians in the name of the pagans, not speak about their sacred gatherings unless he mentioned baptism? Did he and the pagans know everything that was done in those assemblies? Were infants initiated by sacred baptism [Col. 0480A] as often as Christians held their solemn but secret gatherings? It is nevertheless welcome that Gronovius freely acknowledges that infants were washed in the sacred waters of baptism in the age of Minucius Felix.

As for the crimes of which Christians were accused as falsely as they were rashly, Tertullian left us the following written statement:

> “We are called the most criminal of men because of the sacrament of infanticide, the meal made from it, and incest after the banquet, which dogs—the overturners of the lamps, procurers, of course, of darkness—are said to facilitate, together with shameless indulgence in impious lusts.”  
> (Tertullian, *Apologeticum* 7, p. 8.)

Here he gathers in a few words all the crimes that Caecilius, or Minucius, stated at greater length: namely, infanticide; a banquet prepared from the flesh and [Col. 0480B] blood of the infant most inhumanly slain; then dogs overturning the lights; and indiscriminate sexual intercourse and incest. Yet Tertullian does not explain with complete clarity how the infant was said to be killed by Christians.

He later plainly declares that the pagans truly believed that the infant’s fresh, or raw, blood was collected by Christians, that bread was dipped into it, and that they then ate both the bread and the flesh of the same infant (ibid., ch. 8, p. 9). In another book, however, he speaks more obscurely and mentions nothing except “infanticide, the appointed hour of the lamps, the service of the dog, and the contrivances of darkness,” with whose aid Christians were said to defile themselves by every kind of fornication, adultery, and incest (Tertullian, *To the Nations* I [Col. 0480C].15–16, p. 60). But we shall explain these matters more fully in their proper place (*Dissertation on Tertullian*, ch. 20, art. 1).

When Origen rebukes Celsus as he deserved for continuing to level these crimes against Christians with his customary insolence, he testifies that the originators of this slander—which had been directed against Christians from the very beginning of the nascent Church—were not pagans or heretics, as we saw others say shortly above, but Jews. He adds that even in his own time some people were deterred by these utterly false rumors from embracing the Christian religion and avoided all conversation with Christians:

> “Celsus seems to me to have acted similarly to the Jews who, at the beginning of Christianity, spread a slander against the doctrine: that those belonging to this sect sacrifice a child and partake of its flesh; [Col. 0480D] and again, that whenever the adherents of the doctrine wish to engage in deeds of darkness, they extinguish the light, and each man has intercourse with the first woman he happens upon. This irrational slander long prevailed over very many, persuading those alien to the doctrine [Col. 0481A] that Christians are such people; and even now it still deceives some, who because of such charges are deterred from approaching Christians even for the simplest exchange of words.”

The accompanying Latin rendering reads:

> “Celsus, he said, seems to me to have done the same thing as the Jews, who at the beginning of Christian teaching spread the rumor that the members of that sect ate the flesh of a slaughtered child; and also that whenever they wished to devote themselves to secret lusts, after extinguishing the light, each violated the first woman he encountered. This false and unjust opinion long held very many who were alien to our religion, persuading them that Christians were such people; and down to the present time it deceives some, because for this reason they so abhor Christians that they are unwilling even to have a simple conversation with a Christian.”  
> (Origen, *Against Celsus* VI, p. 293 ff.)

Nevertheless, if the Jews were the originators of this slander, it was undoubtedly enlarged by certain pagan slaves of Christians mentioned in the letter of the Churches of Lyons and Vienne reproduced by Eusebius. Having been arrested by the governor, these slaves feared torture and, at the instigation of demons and the urging of the soldiers, falsely attributed to the Christians “Thyestean banquets and Oedipal unions,” that is, “the feasts of Thyestes and the incestuous intercourse of Oedipus,” which will be explained by us shortly below (Eusebius, V.2, p. 156).

[Col. 0481B] Yet afterward this slander persisted only for a short time. For Eusebius further testifies that, once the innocence of the Christians had become known to all, that utterly shameless accusation was completely extinguished:

> “But these devices of the demon,” says that learned man, “did not succeed for him for any great length of time, since truth itself established and commended itself, and with the passage of time shone more brightly from day to day.... At the same time, as time passed, that slander which had been fabricated against our religion was also extinguished.”  
> (Eusebius, *History* IV.7, p. 120.)

It must now be examined how Minucius refutes these crimes, which were as false as they were horrible.

## ARTICLE II. An Examination of the General Arguments by Which Octavius Refutes the Crimes Charged against Christians by Caecilius and the Gentiles

[Col. 0481C]

By a twofold reply, Octavius makes it clear to everyone that nothing whatever is more foul than these calumnies, or more remote from truth itself and from every semblance of probability. The first reply is general and embraces together all those crimes which Octavius demonstrates to be utterly false and wholly incredible. The second refutes each individual charge and clearly shows that each was imputed to the Christians just as falsely as it was shamelessly and with impunity perpetrated by the Gentiles. The former reply is to be examined in this article, the latter in those that follow.

Octavius, therefore—that is, Minucius—confidently replies that it came about through the evil arts of demons that the pagans “begin [Col. 0481D] to hate us before they know us, lest, once they know us, they should either be able to imitate us or be unable to condemn us.” Cyprian repeats this in precisely the same words (Cypr., *On the Vanity of Idols*, p. 14). Accordingly, he very justly protests against Caecilius and the other Gentiles because they condemned Christians whom they did not know, had not investigated, and had never heard. And lest the pagans should dare deny this, he firmly affirms that he had not merely learned it with certainty from others, but knew it thoroughly from his own most grievous experience, of which he was then deeply repentant. If you do not believe us, here are his own words:

“How unjust it is to pass judgment upon persons unknown and unexamined, as you do—believe us, for we ourselves repent of it. We too were once the same as you, and, still blind and dull, entertained the same opinions: that Christians worshipped monsters, devoured infants, and joined in incestuous banquets. Nor did we understand that these tales were always being circulated by the same persons, yet were never either investigated or proved; and that throughout so long a time no one had appeared to betray the deed, though he would have obtained not only pardon for the act but also a reward for giving information.”

We have already seen that this was the entirely just complaint of Justin Martyr and of the others cited by us shortly before. But Tertullian presses it still more sharply and fully against the pagans, and after him Lactantius and others do the same, as we must demonstrate in the appropriate place (Tertull., *Apology*, chs. 1 and 2, and *To the Nations*, bk. I, ch. 7; Lactant., bk. V, ch. 1).

Nor did the extreme injustice of the Gentiles against [Col. 0482B] the Christians, contrary to every principle of right, stop there. For Minucius and Octavius, while they were still devoted to Gentile superstitions and were discharging, as we have said, the public office of advocates, defended before the judges all manner of sacrilegious men, parricides, and persons accused of other most serious crimes, and undertook their legal defense. By contrast, when they raged against Christians with an utterly impious and hitherto unheard-of kind of “compassion,” they tried, by dreadful interrogation under torture and the most bitter punishments, to compel them—if that were possible—not to confess those crimes, but to deny that they were Christians. “They employed against them,” he says, “a perverse judicial examination, not one that would elicit the truth, but one that would compel a lie.”

Tertullian likewise denounces the same grossly unjust [Col. 0482C] cruelty of the Gentiles in these words:

“Thus, in our case, you do not even proceed according to the regular form for judging criminals: in the case of others who deny, you apply torture to make them confess; to Christians alone you apply it to make them deny. Yet if Christianity were an evil, we for our part would deny it, while you would compel us by torture to confess it. . . . A man cries out, ‘I am a Christian.’ He says what he is; you wish to hear what he is not. You governors, whose duty it is to extort the truth, labor to hear a lie from us alone. ‘I am,’ he says, ‘what you are asking whether I am. Why do you torture me into perversity? I confess, and you torture me; what would you do if I denied?’ Clearly, when others deny, you do not readily believe them; if we deny, you believe us at once. Let this perversity be suspect in your eyes, lest some hidden force lie concealed beneath it, which makes you act contrary to regular procedure, contrary to the nature of judicial inquiry, and [Col. 0482D] contrary even to the laws themselves” (Tertull., *Apology*, ch. 2, p. 3; and *To the Nations*, bk. I, ch. 2, p. 46 ff.).

Nor was he content to say this once; later he presses the pagans again and says: “You assign the executioner a very different duty in the case of Christians: not to make them say what they do, but to make them deny what they are.”

Cyprian, moreover, argues in a similar manner against the same Gentiles and refutes and confounds them with this dilemma:

“To be a Christian either is a crime or is not. If it is a crime, why do you not kill one who confesses it? If it is not a crime, why do you persecute an innocent man? I ought to have been tortured if I denied it—if, fearing your punishment, I concealed by a deceptive lie what I had formerly been and the fact that I had not worshipped your gods. [Col. 0483A] Then I ought to have been tortured; then I ought to have been driven by the force of pain to confess the crime, just as in other judicial examinations accused persons are tortured when they deny that they are guilty of the crime charged against them, so that the truth of the deed, which is not brought forth by a revealing voice [reading *promitur* for source *premitur*], may be wrung from bodily pain. But now, when I confess voluntarily and cry aloud, and repeatedly attest again and again that I am a Christian, why do you apply torture to one who confesses?” (Cypr., *To Demetrianus*, p. 190 ff.).

Another aspect of the Gentiles’ grossly unjust judgment against Christians was this: if anyone, finally overcome by the violence of torture, denied that he was a Christian, they then showed him favor, extolled him with praises, and increased his honors. As though it were lawful for them, under the guise of this false piety, not only to acquit persons accused of so many and such great crimes—who did not deny having committed them [Col. 0483B]—but even to heap every benefit upon them merely because they had denied the Christian name! Thus they acknowledged, as Tertullian says, that all their charges against Christians were founded solely upon the Christian name (Tertull., *Apology*, chs. 2 and 3, p. 4; and *To the Nations*, bk. I, chs. 3, 5).

In truth, by this deceit and cunning those impious men wished more readily to entice others into abjuring the Christian faith. Do not suppose that we have invented this without evidence. Minucius confesses, with the deepest anguish of a contrite heart, that he himself had acted in this way:

“And if anyone weaker than the others, oppressed and overcome by suffering, denied that he was a Christian, we showed him favor, as though, once the name had been abjured, his denial cleansed all his deeds. Do you recognize that we felt and acted in the same way as you now feel and act? [Col. 0483C] Yet if reason, and not the instigation of a demon, governed your judgment, they ought rather to have been pressed, not to deny that they were Christians, but to confess to incest, sexual outrages, impious—that is, polluted—rites, and the sacrifice of infants.”

Lactantius later likewise recorded the same thing in precisely these words: “But if any, through fear of pain or death, or through their own perfidy, abandon the heavenly sacrament or consent to the deadly sacrifices, they praise them and honor them with distinctions, so that by their example they may entice the others” (Lactant., bk. I, ch. 9, p. 483).

Another entirely certain indication of the integrity and innocence of Christians was this: if they had committed such great outrages, at least some of them would at some time have repented, or feared to pay the penalties due for their crimes, or finally have been ashamed to have given their names to a religion [Col. 0483D] that compelled them to perpetrate such acts. “But Christianity is so far from being an evil,” says Minucius, “that the Christian accused of it neither blushed nor feared, and repented of one thing only—that he had not been a Christian before.”

We read, however, that Tertullian had already stated this more fully. These are his own words:

“But what of this sort is found in the Christian? No one is ashamed; no one repents, except of not having been a Christian before. If he is denounced, he glories in it; if accused, he offers no defense; when questioned, he confesses even of his own accord; when condemned, he gives thanks. What kind of evil is this, which lacks the natural characteristics of evil—fear, shame, evasion, repentance, and lamentation? What kind of evil is this, whose accused rejoices, whose accusation is his desire, and whose punishment is his happiness?” (Tertull., [Col. 0484A] *Apology*, ch. 2, p. 4).

The weight and force of this argument may be gathered from the fact that it cannot happen that a man conscious of so many crimes should not blush, even if conscience alone were his avenger; or that he should not repent of having given his name to a sect that drove him to such crimes; or finally that, when accused of so many execrable outrages, he should not fear to undergo punishment. Yet nothing of this sort happened to the Christians. On the contrary, they always gloried both in their name and in their profession, and for the defense of both they most steadfastly endured every kind of torture, even the most cruel, unto death.

Furthermore, our Minucius cannot endure the Gentiles’ objection that Christians were convicted by the report, everywhere circulated, of so many and such great crimes. First, he maintains that these false [Col. 0484B] rumors had been spread by the wicked arts of demons. Then he says: “Rumor is always nourished by disseminated lies and consumed when the truth is disclosed.” Tertullian, however, pursues this argument at much greater length and, even citing a verse of Virgil, demonstrates unanswerably that nothing could be more frivolous, feeble, and absurd than this argument (Tertull., *Apology*, ch. 7; and *To the Nations*, bk. I, ch. 7). How he presses this and the other points explained by us will be examined in the appropriate place (*Dissertation on Tertullian*, ch. 20, art. 1).

## CHAPTER IX. IT IS DEMONSTRATED HOW FALSE ARE THE FIRST TWO CRIMES CHARGED AGAINST CHRISTIANS—THAT AN INFANT WAS KILLED BY THEM AMID THEIR SACRED MYSTERIES, AND THAT HIS FLESH WAS THEN DEVOURED—AND THAT THE PAGANS, BY CONTRAST, WERE THEMSELVES IN FACT GUILTY OF THESE THINGS

[Col. 0484C]

## ARTICLE I. An Examination of the Arguments by Which Minucius Entirely Acquits the Christians of Both Charges

Although by his general replies Minucius had more than sufficiently refuted the three horrible and unspeakable crimes branded upon the Christians by Caecilius and the other Gentiles, he nevertheless proceeds to each one and refutes and destroys it individually by a twofold argument. First, he demonstrates that it is wholly false. Then he proves with complete clarity that the Gentiles themselves—the Christians’ hateful accusers—were in fact guilty of and privy to it.

He begins with the slain infant, whose flesh was eaten and whose blood was drunk, in these words:

“I should now like to confront the man who says [Col. 0484D] or believes that we are initiated by the slaughter or blood of an infant. Do you think it possible that so tender and tiny a body could receive fatal wounds, or that anyone could cut, shed, and drain the fresh blood”—Tertullian uses the same word—“of a newborn and scarcely yet born human being? No one can believe this except one who could dare to do it” (Tertull., *Apology*, ch. 8, p. 9).

He therefore says that this accusation is so utterly abhorrent to every truth that it could be believed only by those who themselves perpetrated the same crime. Justin Martyr, moreover, gives us reasons why it surpasses all human credibility (Justin Martyr, *Apology*, p. 50). For, he says, no one can believe that men devoted to the most disgraceful pleasures and accustomed to feeding upon the flesh of slain human infants—as the Christians were represented by the [Col. 0485A] pagans—would voluntarily deprive themselves of every good, of wealth and property; would allow themselves, solely for confessing so cruel a religion, to be killed by the most exquisite tortures; and would sometimes even offer themselves voluntarily for death.

What, moreover, of the fact that Trypho the Jew, when asked by the same Justin Martyr whether he considered true this and the other outrage habitually fastened upon the Christians—“that they devoured human beings and, after the banquet, when the lamps had been extinguished, became promiscuously entangled in unlawful intercourse”—answered without any hesitation:

Περὶ δὲ ὧν πολλοὶ λέγουσιν, οὐ πιστεῦσαι ἄξιον· πόῤῥω γὰρ κεχώρηκε τῆς ἀνθρωπίνης φύσεως.

“As for the things that many people say, they are unworthy of belief, for they are far removed from human nature” (Justin, *Dialogue against Trypho*, p. 227).

[Col. 0485B] Do you hear the Jew not only admitting of his own accord that these things were incredible, but also giving the reason why he was convinced that they were entirely false and could not be believed?

Tertullian, moreover, not without reason asserts that it is wholly beyond all credibility, and beyond the opinion of any man not entirely deprived of his senses, that the Christians should have reached such madness as to promise eternal life and its reward to persons who polluted themselves with such great and horrible crimes, not once or rarely, but throughout almost the whole course of their lives. It is better, however, to hear him speak:

“To appeal to the testimony of nature itself against those who presume that such things ought to be believed, see: we set before you the reward of these crimes. They promise eternal life. Believe it for the moment. For on this point [Col. 0485C] I ask whether even you who have believed it would consider it worth the cost to reach eternal life with such a conscience. Come, plunge the blade into an infant—enemy to no one, guilty before no one, the child of all; or, if that is another’s office, merely stand beside a human being dying before he has lived. Await the flight of the fresh young soul. Receive the fresh blood; saturate your bread with it; eat freely. Meanwhile, as you recline, count the places carefully; note where your mother lies and where your sister, so that when the dogs’ darkness descends you make no mistake. For you will have committed sacrilege unless you commit incest. Initiated and sealed by such rites, you live forever. I want you to answer: is eternity worth so much? Or, if it is not, for that very reason the story ought not to be believed. Even if you believed it, I deny that you would wish to do it; even if you wished it, I deny that you could. Why, therefore, could others do it if you cannot? Why could you not do it if others can?” [Col. 0485D] (Tertull., *Apology*, ch. 8, p. 9; the same Tertullian, *To the Nations*, bk. I, ch. 7, p. 52; *Dissertation on Tertullian*, ch. 20, art. 1 ff.).

But there and elsewhere he expounds these matters still more fully; they must be explained by us in the appropriate place.

To this reply Minucius adds a second: that the alleged infanticide was as alien to the truth itself as it was to Christian morals and institutions. For how could either the custom or precept of their Church permit Christians to kill an infant with impunity, when, as he argues, “it is not lawful for them even to see or hear of homicide”?

Athenagoras likewise turns the same weapon against those public and wicked accusers:

“How,” he says, “could anyone accuse of either homicide or the eating of human flesh those whom he knew to be unwilling or unable even to look upon the execution of a man who had been justly condemned?”

Οὓς γὰρ ἴσασιν οὐδ’ ἰδεῖν, κἂν δικαίως φονευόμενον ὑπομένοντας, τούτων τίς ἂν κατείποι, ἢ ἀνθρωποφονίαν, ἢ ἀνθρωποβορίαν;

[Col. 0486A]

He continues:

“Who does not set the highest value upon those spectacles in which you—especially you emperors—exhibit gladiators and wild beasts to the people? But we, judging that there is no very great difference between being a spectator of slaughter and causing it, keep our minds alien from such spectacles. How, therefore, shall we ourselves commit homicide, when we cannot endure even to see it done by others, lest some part of the guilt and sacrilege arising from it should fall upon us?” (Athenag., *Embassy for the Christians*, p. 38).

[Col. 0486B] Theophilus of Antioch argues in precisely the same manner against the Gentiles. For he wrote to Autolycus in these words (Theoph., *To Autolycus*, bk. III, p. 126):

“Now consider whether those who are taught such things”—that is, the most holy laws of Christ that he had mentioned—“and learn such things can live like brute animals and be polluted by unlawful unions, or can touch what is most savage of all: human flesh, namely that of an infant whom they themselves have killed.”

Ὅπου γε καὶ τὰς θέας τῶν μονομάχων ἡμῖν ἀπείρηται ὁρᾶν, ἵνα μὴ κοινωνοὶ καὶ συνίστορες τῶν φόνων γενώμεθα. Ἀλλ’ οὐδὲ τὰς λοιπὰς θεωρίας ὁρᾶν χρή, ἵνα μὴ μολύνωνται ἡμῶν οἱ ὀφθαλμοί, καὶ τὰ ὦτα, γενόμενα συμμέτοχα τῶν ἐκεῖ φωνῶν ᾀδομένων· εἰ γὰρ εἴποι τις περὶ ἀνθρωποβορίας, ἐκεῖ τὰ Θυέστου καὶ Τηρέως τέκνα ἐσθιόμενα.

“Especially since [Col. 0486C] we are forbidden even to watch gladiatorial combats, lest we become participants in and witnesses to the killings. Nor should we watch the other spectacles, lest our eyes be polluted and our ears become participants in the words sung there. For if one were to speak of anthropophagy, there the children of Thyestes and Tereus are eaten.”

There is no one who does not know what those most savage tragic crimes of Thyestes and Tereus were, which the pagans represented in public spectacles. For Thyestes is said to have violated in adultery the wife of his brother Atreus. In vengeance for this outrage, Atreus served Thyestes’ son to him as a meal; and they tell the story that the sun reversed its course so that it might not see those crimes. Tereus, moreover, king of the Thracians, after violating Philomela, [Col. 0486D] the sister of his wife Procne, cut out her tongue and confined her under the closest guard. But Procne rescued her from there, and the two women served Itys, the child begotten of the adulterous union, to his father Tereus to be eaten at a banquet. Besides Ovid and others, Martial sang of so many crimes in these two verses:

> The man who writes of savage Tereus’ meals  
> Or of thy banquet, cruel Thyestes, is more sportive still.

(Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, bks. VI and XIV; Martial, *Epigrams*, bk. I, epigr. 19).

You therefore see how rightly and deservedly our Minucius and the other most ancient Fathers of the Church asserted that the Christians were most falsely accused by the pagans of homicide, since they so greatly abhorred it that they never wished even to see or hear it represented in public spectacles. [Col. 0487A] You see no less clearly that the charge of eating human flesh was imputed to them falsely, while certain pagans were charged with it truly. If anyone should wish still more authors who argue in the same way to be adduced, we shall cite Tertullian, *On the Spectacles*, chs. 19 and 20; Cyprian, *Letter to Donatus*, ch. 15; Lactantius, bk. VI, ch. 20, p. 619, and *Epitome*, ch. 6, p. 743.

Furthermore, Minucius refutes that calumny not only by this argument, but also by another: “So greatly,” he says, “do we guard against human blood that we do not even recognize the blood of animals as an edible food.” Tertullian presses this argument still more sharply and forcefully against the same pagans. His words are certainly worthy of being transcribed here:

[Col. 0487B]

“Let your error blush before the Christians, for we do not even regard the blood of animals as food at our meals; for this reason we also abstain from things strangled and from animals that have died naturally, lest we should in any way be contaminated by blood, even when it is buried within the entrails. Finally, among your tests of Christians you also offer them sausages swollen with blood, because you are, of course, entirely certain that the very thing by which you wish to make them transgress is unlawful among them. Furthermore, what sense does it make that you should believe those whom you trust to abhor the blood of cattle to be panting after human blood?” (Tertull., *Apology*, ch. 9, p. 10).

Not only men, but women too, acquitted Christians of this plainly fictitious charge by this compelling argument. Eusebius relates that Biblias, a Christian woman, overcome by the most dreadful punishments, at first abjured the faith of Christ and said before the tyrant many things about Christians that were both impious and false:

[Col. 0487C]

Ἡ δὲ ἐν τῇ στρεβλώσει ἀνένηψε, καὶ ὡς ἂν εἰπεῖν, ἐκ βαθέος ὕπνου ἀνεγρηγόρησεν· ὑπομνησθεῖσα διὰ τῆς προσκαίρου τιμωρίας τὴν αἰώνιον ἐν γεέννᾳ κόλασιν, καὶ ἐξ ἐναντίας ἀντεῖπε τοῖς βλασφήμοις φήσασα· Πῶς ἂν παιδία φάγοιεν οἱ τοιοῦτοι, οἷς μηδὲ ἀλόγων ζώων αἷμα φαγεῖν ἐξόν;

“But,” in the words of Eusebius, “she came to her senses amid the tortures and, so to speak, awoke from a deep sleep, the present punishment reminding her of the eternal torments of Gehenna. She contradicted the impious men, saying: ‘How could such people eat infants, when they are not permitted even to taste the blood of irrational animals?’” (Euseb., *Ecclesiastical History*, bk. V, ch. 1, p. 159).

[Col. 0487D] What could be stronger and more effective than this woman’s testimony for disproving the pagans’ calumny? Biblias, a Christian woman tortured with the most savage punishments, affirms that the crime fastened upon Christians is false; but, overcome by the greatest pains and wishing to be freed from them, she admits—falsely and against her will—that it is true. Then she returns to a sounder mind and openly declares that she had been forced by the violence of torture to speak falsely; and finally, mangled by still more dreadful torments, she perseveres in this final confession and dies. What man of sound mind, therefore, will refuse credence to this testimony? We have discussed elsewhere the Christians’ prohibition against consuming animal blood (vol. I, *Apparatus*, bk. III, diss. 1, ch. 3, art. 5, p. 680 ff.).

## ARTICLE II. It Is Shown How Certainly Minucius Convicts the Pagans of Homicide, Since They Exposed Their Newborn Children or Killed Them by Abortion, and Since the Carthaginians Even Sacrificed Their Own Children to Saturn, the Devourer of His Children, Attempting at the Time to Suppress Their Cries with Caresses and Kisses—and for What Reason

[Col. 0488A]

No greater calumny can be devised by utterly depraved men than when they charge others, who are wholly innocent, with the gravest crimes of which they themselves are guilty. Minucius proves that the pagans were such men. For he makes it openly clear to everyone that the homicide of which, as was said in the preceding article, they most falsely accused the [Col. 0488B] Christians was in fact committed by themselves—not once, nor in only one manner, but repeatedly and in various ways. For, besides the things we reported from Theophilus of Antioch in the preceding article, our Minucius reproaches them with two kinds of homicide: the exposure of newborn children and abortion before their birth:

“I see you,” he says, “at one time exposing your newborn children to wild beasts and birds, at another destroying them by strangulation, a pitiable kind of death. Some women, by drinking drugs, extinguish in their very wombs the beginning of the future human being and commit parricide before they give birth.”

Athenagoras had previously argued in the same way. By what reasoning, he says, could we slaughter human beings?

Οἱ τὰς τοῖς ἀμβλωθριδίοις χρωμένας ἀνδροφονεῖν τε καὶ λόγον ὑφέξειν [Col. 0488C] τῆς ἐξαμβλώσεως τῷ Θεῷ φαμέν.

“We who say that women who use abortifacient drugs are guilty of homicide and will render an account to God for the abortion” (Athenag., *Embassy for the Christians*, p. 38).

For, he continues, is not the person who extinguishes a fetus in its mother’s womb, or exposes a newborn to certain death, guilty of the same crime as one who kills a human being advanced in age? Yet Christians, he says there, abhorred these crimes as greatly as they were frequently and with impunity perpetrated by the pagans. But let us hear Tertullian, who openly and boldly reproaches them with these deeds and argues against them as follows:

“But since, in respect of infanticide, it makes no difference whether it is perpetrated as a sacred rite or at one’s own discretion—though there is a difference in respect of parricide—I shall turn to the people. How many of those standing around, panting for Christian [Col. 0488D] blood, and even of you, most just and most severe governors against us, should I assail in their consciences as persons who kill their own newborn children? And since there is indeed a difference in the manner of killing, you certainly wring the breath out more cruelly in water, or expose them to cold, hunger, and dogs; for even one of more advanced age would choose to die by the sword. But as for us, since homicide has once for all been forbidden, it is not lawful even to dissolve what has been conceived in the womb, while the blood is still being formed into a human being. To prevent birth is a hastening of homicide; nor does it matter whether one snatches away a life already born or disrupts one in the process of birth. He who is going to be a human being is already human; indeed, every fruit is already present in the seed” (Tertull., *Apology*, ch. 9, p. 10).

But we discuss these matters more fully in our dissertation on this book [Col. 0489A] (*Dissertation on Tertullian*, ch. 20, art. 3).

No less sharply, and not without irony, Lactantius repels this shameless calumny, which the guilty themselves did not shrink from employing against the innocent:

“They call them impious—they themselves, of course, being pious and abhorring human blood! Yet if they considered both their own actions and those of the persons whom they condemn as impious, they would then understand how mendacious they are, and how much more deserving they themselves are of all the things they either say or do against the good. For it is never from our number, but always from theirs, that men arise who lie in wait armed upon the roads . . . who secretly prepare poisons; who kill their wives in order to obtain their dowries, or their husbands in order to marry their lovers; who either strangle the children born to them or, if they are excessively pious, expose them” (Lactant., [Col. 0489B] *Institutes*, bk. V, ch. 9, p. 483; *Dissertation on Lactantius*, ch. 27, art. 2).

He says certain other things about these matters elsewhere, as we shall see in the appropriate place. Anyone who wants more should consult Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Plato as cited by Theodoret, Philo the Jew, Clement of Alexandria, and what we have observed elsewhere concerning the exposure of children (Dionys. Halicarn., *Roman Antiquities*, bk. II, p. 88; Theodoret, vol. IV, serm. 9, p. 678; Philo, *On the Special Laws*, p. 793 ff.; Clem. Alex., *Paedagogus*, bk. III, p. 226, and *Stromata*, bk. II, p. 400; vol. I, *Apparatus*, p. 805).

Moreover, by other examples Minucius proves unanswerably that the most cruel parricide and other homicides were formerly, and were still in his own time, customarily committed by the pagans not only with impunity but with public praise and applause. [Col. 0489C] For the pagans, he says, were convinced that Saturn had devoured his children. Accordingly, credulous people in certain regions of Africa considered it an act of piety to sacrifice their own children to him as well. Human victims were also slain by the Taurians of Pontus and by the Egyptian Busiris; by the Gauls to Mercury; and by the Romans, a Greek man and woman and a Gallic man and woman. Moreover, the same Romans believed that Jupiter Latiaris was appeased by the blood of a man cruelly slain. Our author considers it to have resulted from the example of such horrible savagery that Catiline entered into his conspiracy with human blood; that others sacrificed to Bellona by drinking human blood; and that many cured the epileptic disease with the same human blood—that is, as Minucius rightly observes, with a more grievous disease. Finally, he says that [Col. 0489D] not unlike this utterly savage cruelty was that whereby certain combatants in the arena greedily licked and devoured wild beasts fattened on human blood and limbs. With what effrontery, therefore, Minucius concludes, could the Gentiles, guilty of so many crimes, charge in shameless calumny that an infant was killed by Christians, that his flesh was devoured, and that his blood was drunk?

But Tertullian had earlier refuted that utterly false accusation still more sharply, in this manner:

“To refute these things more fully, I shall show that they are done by you, partly openly and partly in secret—and perhaps this is the very reason you believed them of us. In Africa infants were openly sacrificed to Saturn down to the proconsulship of Tiberius, who exposed the priests themselves upon votive crosses amid the very trees of their temple, which overshadowed their crimes. [Col. 0490A] The soldiers of my own country bear witness, for they performed that very duty for the proconsul. Yet even now this sacred crime continues in secret. . . . Since Saturn did not spare his own children, he certainly persisted in not sparing those of others; and their own parents offered them, willingly replied when addressed, and caressed the infants so that they would not be sacrificed while weeping. And yet parricide differs greatly from homicide. Persons of more advanced age were slaughtered among the Gauls for Mercury. I leave the Taurian tales to their own theaters. Behold, in that most religious city of the pious descendants of Aeneas—Rome, of course—there is a certain Jupiter whom, during his games, undoubtedly dedicated to Jupiter Latiaris, they drench with human blood. . . . Concerning the nourishment of blood and tragic dishes of that sort, [Col. 0490B] read whether it is not related somewhere—I believe in Herodotus—that certain nations established a treaty by tasting the blood poured from one another’s arms. Something of the kind, I know not precisely what, was also tasted under Catiline. They say that among certain Scythian Gentiles each dead person is eaten by his relatives. But I am wandering too far. Today, in this very place, blood taken from a thigh cut open, received in the hollow of the hand, and given as food marks the devotees of Bellona [the manuscript reads singular *sacratus*]. Again, where are those who, seeking a cure for epilepsy, carry off with greedy thirst the fresh blood of criminals slaughtered in the arena? Likewise those who feast upon the wild beasts’ dishes from the arena—those who ask for some from the boar, others from the stag! That boar wiped away, in its struggle, the blood of the man whom it had wounded. That stag lay in a gladiator’s blood. The entrails of the very bears are eagerly sought while they are still belching up human viscera. Thus a man belches the flesh of an animal that fed upon a man” [Col. 0490C] (Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 9, p. 9).

We judged that this entire passage of Tertullian should be presented because in it he adduces certain examples untouched by our author, and explains others more clearly and abundantly; of these our Minucius himself appears to have made a compendium. Yet we cannot deny that Tertullian’s earlier words are not free of certain difficulties. In the appropriate place, however, we shall endeavor to explain and resolve them to the best of our ability (*Dissertation on Tertullian’s Apology*).

Meanwhile, something must be said about those horrible sacrifices of human beings slaughtered by other human beings. There is no need to accumulate more material concerning the famous pagan belief, unknown to few, according to which Saturn [Col. 0490D] is said to have devoured his children. Passing over, therefore, Pausanias, Strabo, Diodorus Siculus, Lucian, Apollodorus, Theophilus of Antioch, and very many others (Pausan., bk. VII, p. 242; Strabo, *Geography*, p. 468; Diod. Sicul., *Library*, bk. V, p. 235; Lucian, *On Sacrifices*, p. 73; Apollod., *Library*, bk. I, beginning; Theoph. Antioch., *To Autolycus*, bk. I, p. 75, and bk. III, p. 118), let it suffice to note that Hesiod celebrates this belief in these verses (Hesiod, v. 463 ff.):

> Πεύθετο γὰρ γαίης τε καὶ οὐρανοῦ ἀστερόεντος  
> Οὕνεκά οἱ πέπρωτο ἑῷ ὑπὸ παιδὶ δαμῆναι,  
> Καὶ κρατερῷ περ ἐόντι, Διὸς μεγάλου διὰ βουλάς.  
> Τῷ ὅγε οὐκ ἀλαοσκοπίην ἔσχεν, ἀλλὰ δοκεύων  
> Παῖδας ἑοὺς κατέπινε.
>
> For he had heard from Earth and starry Heaven  
> That it was fated for him to be overcome by his own son,  
> Mighty though he was, through the counsels of great Zeus.  
> Therefore he did not keep blind watch, but, lying in wait,  
> Devoured his own children.

[Col. 0491A]

Accordingly, Nonnus calls the same Saturn “the devourer of his own children,” ἑῶν θοινήτορα παίδων (*heōn thoinētora paidōn*) (Nonnus, bk. XXI; *Dionysiaca*, verse 249).

Let us be permitted to add to these Tatian, who, from the examples not only of Saturn but also of other gods, charges the pagans in these words with the anthropophagy of which they falsely accused the Christians:

“Among us,” he says, “there is no anthropophagy. You who have fabricated this charge against us have been exposed as false witnesses. Among you, however, Pelops becomes a meal for the gods and is the boy beloved by Neptune; Saturn consumes his sons, and Jupiter swallows Metis.”

[Col. 0491B]

Παρ’ ἡμῖν οὐκ ἔστιν ἀνθρωποφαγία· ψευδομάρτυρες οἱ ἐπιτηδευόμενοι γεγόνατε. Παρ’ ὑμῖν δὲ ὁ Πέλοψ δεῖπνον τῶν θεῶν γίνεται, καὶ Ποσειδῶνος ἐρώμενος, καὶ Κρόνος τοὺς υἱοὺς ἀναλίσκει, καὶ ὁ Ζεὺς τὴν Μῆτιν καταπίνει.

(Tatian, *Oration against the Greeks*, p. 162).

The Carthaginians, moreover, wishing to gratify Saturn, the devourer of his children, sacrificed their own children to him, as our Minucius rightly says. For although Plato openly denied that human beings had actually been slaughtered by his own countrymen according to this barbarous custom, he nevertheless added in the same place:

“The Carthaginians, by contrast, customarily perform such sacrifices, since among them this is considered holy and lawful,” Καρχηδόνιοι δὲ θύουσιν, ὡς ὅσιον καὶ νόμιμον αὐτοῖς. [Col. 0491C] “Indeed, it is customary among them for some to sacrifice their own sons to Saturn. . . . But even those Greeks who dwell in Lycia and are descended from Athamas offer victims of the same kind” (Plato, vol. II, bk. *Polit.*, p. 315).
