In Eusebius, too, we read these words of Diodorus Siculus concerning the Carthaginians when besieged by Agathocles, tyrant of Sicily:

“They suspected that Saturn was angry with them for this reason: whereas formerly they had sacrificed the flower of their own children, in later times they offered for sacrifice only certain boys who had been secretly purchased and raised by them. An investigation was therefore conducted, and some of those who had been killed according to the sacred and solemn rite were found to have been substituted children. When they considered these things among themselves and saw the enemy’s camp threatening their walls, they were seized with a great religious dread, as though they had abolished the ancestral [Col. 0491D] honors due to the gods. To make expiation for this error without delay, they first publicly sacrificed two hundred exceptional youths, chosen by the common vote. Then others besides, who were commonly suspected of having violated the religion, offered themselves voluntarily and of their own accord, no fewer than three hundred” (Euseb., *Preparation for the Gospel*, bk. IV, ch. 16, p. 161).

These words were taken from the twentieth book of the same Diodorus’ *Library*, and you may compare the Greek wording of Diodorus and Eusebius with one another. In another book, moreover, Diodorus had said concerning Hamilcar:

“Performing supplications to the gods according to the ancestral rite, τῷ μὲν Κρόνῳ παῖδα σφαγιάσας, τῷ δὲ Ποσειδῶνι πλῆθος ἱερῶν καταποντίσας—he slaughtered a boy for Saturn and submerged a multitude of sacred victims in the sea for Neptune” (Diodorus, *Library*, bk. XX, p. 739 ff.; the same, bk. XIII, p. 377).

[Col. 0492A]

What, moreover, of Plutarch’s account that Gelon, after defeating the Carthaginians in a great battle, granted them the peace they sought only on the condition that they should no longer sacrifice their children to Saturn? To this may be added what we read in Dionysius of Halicarnassus:

“It is reported that the ancients were accustomed to appease Saturn with human victims, just as the Carthaginians did while their city stood; and the same thing is still done even now among the Gauls and other peoples nearest the West” (Dionys. Halicarn., *Roman Antiquities*, bk. I, p. 30).

Anyone for whom these testimonies are insufficient may also read Justin Martyr, Origen, and Augustine, who cited Varro as his witness (Justin, *Second Apology*, p. 50; Origen, *Against Celsus*, bk. V, [Col. 0492B] p. 249; Augustine, *City of God*, bk. VII, chs. 19 and 26).

But consider, I ask, what human beings are capable of when deceived by the mere semblance of false piety. “Infants,” Minucius says, “were sacrificed by their parents, who stifled their crying with caresses and kisses, lest a weeping victim be sacrificed.” Here he follows Tertullian, who, as we have already noted, had said: “Parents offered their own children; they responded willingly and caressed the infants, lest they should be sacrificed while weeping” (Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 9). But if they then suppressed their children’s crying and tears, how could they themselves, while killing them, restrain their own sighs, groans, and every feeling of a father’s heart? Yet with that wholly perverse fortitude they stifled their children’s groans and tears, [Col. 0492C] lest a mournful and tearful victim—and therefore one by no means pleasing to the gods—be slaughtered. For it was indeed an evil omen if a victim was sacrificed while resisting and unwilling. If you desire a witness, hear Macrobius: “Those performing sacrifices observed the rule that, if the victim being led to the altars resisted too violently and showed itself unwilling to be brought to them, it should be removed, because they believed it was being offered to an unwilling god.” Or, as Pliny says: “The gods are not appeased by a victim belonging to another, nor by one that draws back from the altars” (Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, bk. III, ch. 5; Pliny, *Natural History*, bk. VIII, ch. 45, p. 221). For this reason, according also to Ammianus Marcellinus, they considered it an ill omen that, during the sacrifice of Julian the Apostate, the tenth bull broke its bonds and escaped, and was recovered only with difficulty (Ammianus Marcellinus, bk. XXIV, [Col. 0492D] ch. 6, p. 409). Likewise, “the flight of the victims from the very altars,” as Valerius Maximus says, appeared to portend some disaster for Pompey (Valerius Maximus, bk. I, ch. 6, § 12); or, as Lucan sang:

> Brought near the gods, the bull broke loose and fled the altar,  
> And headlong cast itself upon the Emathian fields;  
> Nor was any victim found for the ill-omened rites.  
> (Lucan, bk. VII, v. 156)

Yet it was not only by these examples that the Gentiles were convicted of homicide and parricide, but by many others still, which we must examine.

## ARTICLE III. In What Further Manner Minucius Shows That Guests Were Sacrificed by the Taurians of Pontus and by Busiris the Egyptian; Human Beings to Mercury by the Gauls; and a Greek Man and Woman, a Gallic Man and Woman, and Others to Jupiter Latiaris by the Romans

[Col. 0493A]

Just as it was a most inhuman custom among certain peoples of Africa to sacrifice infants to Saturn, so, Minucius says, “among the Taurians of Pontus and under Busiris the Egyptian, guests were sacrificed to their fictitious gods.” Concerning the Taurians, Clement of Alexandria committed the following to writing in Greek: “The Taurians, the people who inhabit the region about the Tauric Chersonese, immediately sacrifice to Tauric Artemis any strangers whom they capture among those who have lost their way at sea.” [Col. 0493B] (Clement of Alexandria, *Exhortation to the Gentiles*, p. 27). You will find these words of Clement of Alexandria copied by Eusebius. Athenagoras relates precisely the same thing more briefly, Origen more clearly, and Athanasius more fully than either of them (Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, bk. IV, ch. 16, p. 157; Athenagoras, *Embassy for the Christians*, p. 29; Origen, *Against Celsus*, bk. V, p. 249; Athanasius, *Oration Against the Greeks*, § 25, p. 2). Before all these, however, Naso thus sang of that utterly savage cruelty, more characteristic of wild beasts than of human beings:

> Those whom you hear delighting in human blood  
> Dwell almost beneath the same zone of cold.  
> [Col. 0493C] Nor far from us is the place where the dread Tauric altar  
> Of the quiver-bearing goddess is sprinkled with slaughter.  
> (Ovid, *Tristia*, bk. IV, Elegy IV, v. 325 ff.)

Juvenal harmonizes with Ovid in these verses:

> What comparable excuse does Egypt have, more savage than the Maeotian altar?  
> For Taurica, the inventor of that unspeakable rite,  
> Nevertheless sacrifices human beings—if now you believe  
> The trustworthy testimony handed down by poems. . . .  
> (Juvenal, *Satires*, XV, v. 115 ff.)

Prudentius likewise subscribed to both writers in these words:

> In vain do we now habitually condemn the Tauric rites:  
> Human blood is shed in the service of Jupiter Latiaris.  
> (Aurelius Prudentius, *Against Symmachus*, bk. I, on the spectacles, etc.)

Lucan too, and others soon to be cited, [Col. 0493D] relate things not unlike these. But Diodorus Siculus gives the reasons for this most dreadful custom; you may read them in his work if you wish, and may in addition consult Seneca and Gregory Nazianzen (Diodorus Siculus, *Library*, bk. IV, p. 173; Seneca, at the end of *Octavia*; Gregory Nazianzen, Oration 39, *On the Holy Lights*, p. 829).

But as much as Diodorus supports Minucius in that case, so much does he appear to disagree with him concerning Busiris. For he declares that it is a mere fable that foreigners were slaughtered through the cruelty of Busiris. Hear, I ask, his words: “They say that in ancient times human beings of the same color as Typhon—that is, red-haired—were sacrificed by the kings at the tomb of Osiris. Now only a few Egyptians are found to be red-haired, but many foreigners are. Hence the tale about Busiris’s cruelty in slaughtering foreigners [Col. 0494A] gained strength among the Greeks—not because any king was named Busiris, but because the tomb of Osiris bore that designation in the native language” (Diodorus, bk. I, p. 53 ff.). Yet in the same book he does not entirely deny that there were Egyptian kings called by the name Busiris, for he mentions two who bore that name (ibid., bk. I, p. 29). Accordingly, he appears to assert only that not human beings but cattle were sacrificed at the tomb of Osiris, and not by Busiris.

[Col. 0494B]

Strabo appears to support Diodorus in these very words: “In the Busirite nome are the city of Busiris and Cynopolis. Eratosthenes says that the custom of expelling foreigners is common to all barbarians; but that the Egyptians are accused because of the fables told about Busiris in the Busirite nome, later writers wishing to malign the inhospitality of this region, although, by Zeus, there was neither a king nor a tyrant named Busiris.” [Col. 0494C] (Strabo, *Geography*, bk. XVII, p. 802).

But although these writers denied the matter, Minucius nevertheless has more numerous supporters, foremost among them Ovid, who sings in these verses:

> Egypt is said to have lacked the rains that aid the fields,  
> And to have been dry for nine years.  
> When Thrasius approaches Busiris and shows that Jupiter  
> Can be appeased by the shedding of a guest’s blood.

And elsewhere:

> Therefore I subdued Busiris, who defiled his temples  
> With the blood of foreigners.  
> (Ovid, *Art of Love*, bk. I, v. 650; *Metamorphoses*, bk. IX, v. 293)

Virgil spoke no less clearly:

> [Col. 0494D] Who does not know of harsh Eurystheus,  
> Or the altars of the infamous Busiris?  
> (Virgil, *Georgics*, bk. III, vv. 4–5)

Servius observes on this passage: “Busiris was a king of Egypt who used to sacrifice the guests he received. He was killed by Hercules when he wished to kill Hercules also. Isocrates wrote an encomium of him.” For this reason Statius somewhere called them:

> The pitiless altars of Busiris.

Eusebius transmitted the following concerning Busiris: “Busiris, son of Neptune and Libya, the daughter of Epaphus, exercises tyranny in the regions neighboring the Nile, killing passing guests in a cruel crime” (Eusebius, *Chronicle*, at the year 546). Augustine, among others, supported him: [Col. 0495A] “At that time,” he says, “that is, in the time of Hercules, Busiris, whether king or tyrant, sacrificed his guests to his gods. He is said to have been the son of Neptune by his mother Libya, daughter of Epaphus” (Augustine, *City of God*, bk. XVIII, ch. 12). You see that several authorities have voted with Minucius concerning that savage ferocity of Busiris.

We likewise possess very many reliable witnesses confirming what Minucius adds afterward: “The Gauls slaughter human—or rather inhuman—victims for Mercury.” Cornelius Tacitus is guarantor and witness of so great an inhumanity, when, among many other statements concerning the customs of the Gauls, he relates the following: “Of the gods they worship Mercury above all; on certain days they consider it lawful to propitiate him even with human victims.” Caesar, moreover, to whom the Gallic nation was especially well known, [Col. 0495B] writes that when afflicted by more serious illnesses or engaged in battles, they sacrificed human beings as victims, or vowed that they would sacrifice them, and employed Druids as ministers at these sacrifices (Tacitus, *On the Customs of the Germans*, shortly after the beginning; Caesar, *Gallic War*, bk. I, shortly after the beginning). Caesar does not, however, explain there to which god they presented these victims. But since he, like Strabo, asserts in the same place that the Gauls especially worshiped Mercury, can it not be said with our Minucius that this cruel sacrifice was made chiefly to that god, and also to Hesus, as will soon be stated? (Strabo, *Geography*, bk. IV, p. 198). The same judgment must undoubtedly be passed concerning Diodorus Siculus, Mela, Strabo, Cicero, and Solinus, who likewise testify generally that the Gauls sacrificed human beings to the gods [Col. 0495C] (Diodorus, *Library*, bk. V, p. 214; Mela, bk. VI, where he treats Gaul; Strabo, *Geography*, bk. IV, p. 193; Cicero, *Oration for Marcus Fonteius*, p. 222; Solinus, ch. 21, p. 41). Finally, Lucan sang the following about them and about Tauric Diana, whom we discussed a little earlier (Lucan, *Pharsalia*, bk. I, v. 444 ff.):

> And you, by whom pitiless Teutates is appeased with dreadful blood,  
> And Hesus, grim at savage altars,  
> And Taranis, whose altar is no gentler than that of Scythian Diana.

Lactantius supports Lucan. Suetonius further attests that this impious and detestable sacrifice was prohibited by the emperor Augustus and afterward abolished by Claudius: “He utterly abolished,” Suetonius says, “the religion of the Druids among the Gauls, a religion of dreadful cruelty, which under Augustus had been forbidden only to citizens” (Lactantius, *Divine Institutes*, [Col. 0495D] bk. I, ch. 21, p. 112; Suetonius, bk. V, § 25).

Undoubtedly no less cruel was the Roman sacrifice next mentioned by our Minucius, in which they buried alive beneath the Forum Boarium a Greek man and woman and a Gallic man and woman. We have received from Livy the following written account of this utterly inhuman sacrifice: “On the authority of the Books of Fate, several extraordinary sacrifices were performed. Among them a Gallic man and woman and a Greek man and woman were lowered alive beneath the earth in the Forum Boarium, into a place enclosed by stone, which had previously been drenched with human victims in a rite particularly alien to Roman religious practice” (Livy, third decade, bk. II, p. 195). Plutarch relates the same things, adding, however, that those rites were performed in November. Pliny openly declares that they persisted even to [Col. 0496A] his own age (Plutarch, vol. I, *Life of Marcellus*, p. 299; vol. II, *Roman Questions*, p. 283; Pliny, *Natural History*, bk. XXVIII, ch. 1, p. 537).

Indeed, as our author continues, Jupiter Latiaris is honored by these same Romans with homicide; or, as he wrote earlier: “When Jupiter is Jupiter Latiaris, he is drenched with blood.” Tatian firmly asserts that he was an eyewitness of this horrible sacrifice and of another offered to Diana: “When I saw these things . . . among the Romans, Jupiter Latiaris being appeased by human gore and by blood shed through acts of homicide, and Diana, not far from Megalopolis, delighting in similar sacrifices” (Tatian, *Oration Against the Greeks*, p. 165). For this reason Theophilus of Antioch was wholly justified in reproaching the Gentiles [Col. 0496B] with the wantonness of the Mother of the Gods and the cruelty “of Jupiter Latiaris, who thirsts”—*dipsōntos* (διψῶντος)—“for human blood” (Theophilus, *To Autolycus*, bk. III, p. 122). Tertullian not only expressly confirms this in his *Apology*, as has been noted, but repeats it in another book in these words: “The age permitted the Scythians’ Diana, the Gauls’ Mercury, and the Africans’ Saturn to be appeased with human victims; and in Latium, even to the present day, human blood is given to Jupiter to taste in the middle of the City” (Tertullian, *Scorpiace*, ch. 7, p. 624). Thus, in his time that horrible custom persisted, and it continued still later. For Lactantius similarly writes: “Nor indeed were the Latins free from this cruelty, since even now Jupiter Latiaris is worshiped with human blood” (Lactantius, [Col. 0496C] bk. I, ch. 21, p. 113). Who would dare to deny credence to so many and such reliable witnesses?

Whether so monstrous a sacrifice was performed long afterward is not so well established. Athanasius certainly did not believe that it was, since he speaks of it as follows: “The Romans of old likewise worshiped the one they call Jupiter Latiaris with human sacrifices” (Athanasius, *Oration Against the Greeks*, § 25, p. 23).

We have elsewhere discussed this detestable rite and custom of slaughtering human beings for the gods. In addition to the writers cited by us there, you may also read Philo Judaeus, Cornelius Tacitus, Pliny, Suetonius, Porphyry, Eusebius, and Cyril of Alexandria, to whom Tertullian and [Col. 0496D] Lactantius may be added; but we shall treat them in their proper place (vol. I, *Apparatus*, bk. III, dissertation 1, ch. 9, art. 2, p. 757; Philo, *On the Offering of Victims*, p. 853; Tacitus, *Annals*, bk. XIV, around the middle; Pliny, *Natural History*, bk. XXX, ch. 1, p. 728; Suetonius, *Life of Claudius*, § 25; Porphyry, *On Abstinence from Animals*, bk. XII, p. 223; Eusebius, *Oration in Praise of Constantine*, p. 646; Cyril of Alexandria, *Against Julian*, bk. IV, p. 128; *Dissertation on Lactantius*, ch. 34, art. 1; and *On Tertullian*, ch. 20, art. 2 ff.).

## ARTICLE IV. On Other Crimes Arising from That Savage Custom of Slaughtering Human Beings: Namely, Catiline’s Conspiracy Sealed with Human Blood; the Rites of Bellona Drenched in Human Gore; the Remedy for Epilepsy Sought by Drinking It; and Beasts Fattened on It and Then Devoured by Human Beings in the Arena

[Col. 0497A]

Minucius suspects that three horrible crimes flowed, as from a most corrupt fountain, from the custom thus far explained of sacrificing human beings to fictitious gods: namely, Catiline’s criminal conspiracy, sealed by a compact of human blood; the rites of Bellona drenched by the drinking of human blood; and a remedy for epilepsy sought in that same human blood. Would you like to hear him [Col. 0497B] speak? “It was this practice itself, I believe,” he says, “that taught Catiline to conspire under a covenant of blood; taught Bellona to drench her rite by drinking human gore; and taught men to cure epilepsy with blood—that is, to cure one disease with a still more grievous disease.” You have already heard the words of Tertullian cited by us, in which he had previously committed the same matters to writing.

Not everyone, however, relates in the same way how Catiline’s conspiracy was formed. Sallust transmitted the following concerning it to posterity: “At that time there were some who said that, after delivering a speech, when Catiline was binding the associates in his crime by an oath, he passed around in a bowl human blood mixed with wine. Then, after an imprecation, when all had tasted it, as was customary in solemn rites, he is said to have disclosed his plan” (Sallust, *The Conspiracy of Catiline*, [Col. 0497C] ch. 8). Sallust therefore reports that this was the opinion not of everyone, but only of certain persons, and he himself pronounces nothing definite about it. Florus, however, asserted without hesitation that the event occurred in this way (Florus, *Roman History*, bk. IV, ch. 1).

Cassius Dio, however, testifies in these words that it occurred differently: “He compelled them to bind themselves by an unlawful oath. For he sacrificed a certain boy and, after swearing the oath over his entrails, then ate them together with the others” (Cassius Dio, *Roman History*, bk. XXXVII, p. 48 ff.). Plutarch transmitted that they tasted the flesh of the sacrificed man (Plutarch, *Life of Cicero*, p. [Col. 0497D] 866). Yet the authority of these latter writers, being Greek, will perhaps undoubtedly appear to some less weighty than that of the former. Not without reason, therefore, our author and Tertullian support these Latin writers (Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 9, p. 10).

Concerning the rites and festivals of Bellona customarily celebrated in her honor, Lactantius gives the following words, describing the bloody human sacrifice: “There are other rites of Valor, whom they also call Bellona, in which the priests sacrifice not with another’s blood, but with their own. For, cutting their shoulders and brandishing swords in both hands, they run, are carried into frenzy, and rave” (Lactantius, bk. I, ch. 21, p. 116). Lampridius [Col. 0498A] says of the emperor Commodus: “In his zeal for cruelty, he ordered the servants of Bellona actually to cut their arms” (Lampridius, *Commodus*, p. 49). For this reason Lucan sang:

> . . . Those whom Bellona’s rite excites  
> When they have cut their arms.  
> (Lucan, *Pharsalia*, bk. I, after the middle)

And again in another book:

> . . . Wherever she wanders,  
> Bellona seems to brandish a bloodstained scourge.  
> (Ibid., bk. VII, after the middle)

You may consult Montfort’s observations on these verses of Lucan, Casaubon’s on Lampridius, and Caecilius’s scholia on these verses of Juvenal: [Col. 0498B]

> . . . Behold, the chorus of raging Bellona  
> And of the Mother of the Gods enters.  
> (Juvenal, *Satires*, VI, around the middle)

You have surely observed that some authorities transmitted that the shoulders were cut in these mysteries, others the upper arms, and others the arm. Seneca, however, mentions all these parts of the body together in these words: “When someone skilled in cutting his own upper arms makes his arms and shoulders bleed with suspended hand” (Seneca, *On the Happy Life*, ch. 27). Who does not see that he is there alluding to the rites of Bellona?

Why, then, someone will ask, did Tertullian mention only the cutting of the thigh? “Today,” he says, “in this very place, blood caught in the hollow of the hand from a cut thigh and given as food marks those consecrated to Bellona”—the manuscripts read “one consecrated”— (Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 9, p. 10). Why should he not have been permitted to mention only [Col. 0498C] the thigh, just as others mentioned only the shoulders or upper arms? For neither he nor the others thought that all the limbs cut during Bellona’s rites had to be enumerated. But something more must be said below about these mysteries and that passage of Tertullian (below, ch. 20, art. 3).

Yet I would have you observe that our Minucius did not merely say that blood was drawn from the initiates’ limbs in these rites, but that these rites were drenched by drinking human gore. He mentions only this second act because it was more grievous, although the initiates did not drink human blood unless it had first been drawn from their limbs. You have just heard Tertullian, who appears to have mentioned both the drawing and the drinking of the blood on that occasion. But we shall discuss it later (*Dissertation on Tertullian*, [Col. 0498D] ch. 20, art. 4).

Finally, our author justly rebukes those who, when suffering from epilepsy, eagerly drank the blood of gladiators wounded in the arena, believing they could be cured by it. For Pliny himself, although a Gentile, inveighs no less sharply against them: “Epileptics drink the blood of gladiators, as though from living cups—a sight that horrifies us even when wild beasts do the same in that very arena. But, by Hercules, they consider it most effective to suck from the human being himself while the blood is warm and steaming, and to drink the very life from the wound by placing their lips upon it, though it is not considered lawful for human mouths to be brought even to the wounds of wild beasts. . . . As though it could be regarded as health to turn from a human being into a beast, and as though a person were not deserving of disease in the very remedy—[Col. 0499A] an excellent frustration, by Hercules, if it does no good. It is considered impious to look upon human entrails; what, then, of eating them? Who invented these portents? My dispute is with you, destroyer of human law and craftsman of monstrosities, whoever you were who first devised them, I suppose so that human life would not forget you. Who invented the eating of human limbs one by one? By what conjecture was he led to it? What origin could this medicine have had? Who made poisons more innocent than remedies? Grant that barbarous and foreign rites invented them; did even the Greeks make these practices their own?” (Pliny, *Natural History*, bk. XXVIII, ch. 1, p. 54). You may also consult Celsus, the already cited Tertullian, and others (Celsus, bk. III, ch. 23, on epilepsy; Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 9, p. 10).

Finally, anyone may readily learn from Apuleius and the already cited Tertullian that wild beasts fattened on the blood, entrails, and limbs [Col. 0499B] of human beings were devoured by other human beings who fought against them in the circus, as we shall demonstrate in the following dissertation on Tertullian’s books (Apuleius, *Metamorphoses*, bk. IV, before the middle, p. 58 ff.; *Dissertation on Tertullian*, ch. 20, arts. 4–5).

# CHAPTER X. ON THE THIRD CHARGE, NAMELY THE INFAMOUS FORNICATION, ADULTERY, AND INCEST AFTER THE BANQUET OF WHICH CHRISTIANS WERE ACCUSED

## ARTICLE I. How Greatly Christians Abhorred This Crime, How Chaste Their Marriage Was, and How Many Persevered in Perpetual Virginity

[Col. 0499C]

In another slander no less shameless than the former, the Gentiles attacked the Christians, accusing them of infamous fornication, adultery, and incest after their banquets and feasts. Caecilius pursued this charge with a disposition no fairer and with no less vehemence than the preceding one. For although this charge was plainly fictitious and fabricated, he nevertheless attempts to prove it by two arguments. He derived the first from the testimony and authority of Fronto; the second from the fact that, as he said, “honorable things always rejoice in publicity,” whereas Christians always concealed their mysteries with great care.

[Col. 0499D] But Octavius crushes and refutes both this entire slander and the argument for it with two replies. For he boldly and openly declares that this crime attributed to the Christians was fabricated by the customary lies of the demons and was never proved by anyone. Secondly, he shows that the Gentiles themselves were in fact guilty of this very detestable offense that they wrongly charged against Christians.

He therefore emphatically pronounces: “It is a monstrous fable which the conspiracy of demons has falsely devised against us for a twofold reason: first, that it might stain the glory of chastity by directing foul infamy against it.” But several scholars consider the word *aversione* (“by aversion” or “by directing away”) corrupt: some suspect that *aspersione* (“by aspersion” or “by besmirching”) should be read, others *accessione* (“by accession”). [Col. 0500A] Yet who would dare to decide anything certain without consulting another, more accurate manuscript? For what if Minucius took the word *aversione*, or *adversione*, in the sense in which it is used only by jurists, for deflecting something onto another person, or for action taken without the matter being properly perceived or investigated? The meaning of our Minucius, the advocate, would then be: the demons devised this fable so that, by casting foul infamy upon Christians—or by allowing it to go unexamined and uninvestigated among the Gentiles—they might stain the glory of Christian chastity. Whether we have struck the mark must be left to the judgment of others. Our author’s second reason, by which the first appears to be confirmed, is this: “That before the truth had been investigated, the demons might, through terror inspired by an unspeakable belief, turn people away from us and from examining the Christian religion.”

[Col. 0500B] Octavius then very easily weakens the authority of Fronto that had been interposed: “Your Fronto,” as he continues, “did not give testimony as one affirming a fact, but hurled abuse as an orator.” Who does not see that the word “your” clearly declares that the Fronto of whom we spoke above was a Gentile orator, whose testimony against Christians could therefore carry no weight?

But so that this might appear more clearly, Octavius exposes that shameless slander of the Gentiles and the exceptional innocence of Christians from their sober banquets and especially from their supreme chastity, which he sets forth as truthfully as simply in the following manner: [Col. 0500C] “We preserve modesty not merely in the face, but in the mind. We willingly adhere to the bond of a single marriage; in the desire for procreation, we know either one wife or none.” Such, therefore, was the chastity of Christian spouses in Minucius’s time, and such, by Christ’s command, it should always have been. But, from zeal for greater perfection, many who were never bound by any marriage bond remained in perpetual virginity. Yet it is better again to hear our author speaking about it: “Very many enjoy, rather than boast of, the perpetual virginity of an undefiled body. So far removed are they from the desire for incest that, for some, even a chaste union is a cause for shame.” In the words “They enjoy, rather than boast of,” he incidentally censures the Gentiles, among whom the Vestal Virgins and the priests of the Mother of the Gods boasted of their virginity more than they actually enjoyed it. [Col. 0500D] But of these matters below.

Tertullian likewise answers that utterly false accusation by the Gentiles in a similar manner: “A most careful and faithful chastity has fenced us off from that eventuality; and just as we are kept from fornication and from every excess after marriage, so are we kept from the chance of incest. Some, much more securely, repel the whole force of this error by virginal continence—boys grown old” (Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 9, p. 10). By “boys grown old” he means those who preserved the virginity of childhood even to old age. Justin Martyr had earlier declared the same in these words: “Indeed, very many men and women sixty and seventy years old, who were instructed in Christ from childhood, remain incorrupt and celibate; and I boast that I can point out such persons [Col. 0501A] among every race of humankind” (Justin Martyr, *First Apology*, p. 62).

Moreover, concerning not only these virgins but also Christian spouses, Justin afterward transmitted the same teaching as Tertullian and our Minucius: that Christians either entered marriage solely for the sake of procreating and educating children or, having rejected it, remained in a state of perpetual continence. Athenagoras repels the unjust accusation of the Gentiles in the same manner and by an equally public declaration: “Each of us regards the wife whom he has married according to the laws approved among us [Col. 0501B] as intended for no purpose other than the procreation of children. For just as the farmer, after entrusting seed to the earth, awaits the time of harvest and does not sow more upon it, so among us the measure of desire is defined by the procreation of children. You may find many among us, both men and women, who grow old in celibacy because they know that in this state they will be more closely united with God” (Athenagoras, *Embassy for the Christians*, p. 36 and [Col. 0501C] following).

Finally, to omit others, Origen, in refuting the frivolous quibbles of Celsus, plainly shows that men and women, after professing the Christian religion, became as much more chaste as they had formerly been impure and unchaste: “From the time when they received the Word, they have in some measure become more equitable, more dignified, and more steadfast; so much so that some of them, through love of surpassing purity and in order to worship God more purely, do not engage even in the sexual relations permitted by the law” (Origen, *Against Celsus*, [Col. 0501D] bk. I, p. 21).

In another book, after showing that Gentile philosophers had wallowed in every mire of impurity, wantonness, and disgrace, he adds the following about Christians: “But those whom they despise as uneducated, and call fools and slaves, if only they entrust themselves to God and receive the teaching of Jesus, are so far removed from wantonness, uncleanness, and every indecency in sexual intercourse that, after the manner of perfect priests who turn away from all intercourse, many of them live wholly chastely and purely, refraining even from lawful intercourse with women . . . Among Christians, complete virginity is practiced not for honors among human beings, not for monetary rewards, nor for petty glory; and because they have determined to retain God in their knowledge, they are preserved by [Col. 0502A] God in a sound mind and in the performance of their duties, filled with all righteousness and goodness” (ibid., bk. VII, p. 364 ff.).

[Col. 0502B] There he contrasts Christians living in chastity or perpetual virginity with the Athenian high priest, who used hemlock in order to perform solemn ceremonies chastely, and with certain—but very few—Gentile virgins, who, like that high priest, appeared to remain virgins for the sake of religion, honor, or reward. In other dissertations we have discussed the continence and virginity preserved by very many Christians throughout the entire course of their lives, and the most chaste use of marriage among all the rest (vol. I, *Apparatus*, bk. III, dissertation I, ch. 5, art. 3, p. 708; ibid., dissertation II, ch. 10, art. 4, p. 1021). But something more will have to be said below about each of those Christian virtues (*Dissertation on Lactantius*, ch. 27, arts. 5–6).

Furthermore, when our author said, “We willingly adhere to the bond of a single marriage,” [Col. 0502C] do not, I ask, allow yourself to suppose that he condemns a second marriage. For he added “willingly” to signify that a Christian man could indeed marry a second wife, but that this was conceded to him by the Apostle as an indulgence. See, if you wish, what we have observed elsewhere on this subject (vol. I, *Apparatus*, loc. cit., p. 2015 ff.).

## ARTICLE II. How Minucius Turns Caecilius’s Argument Back Against the Gentiles and Demonstrates from Their Own Records That They Contract Marriages with Their Mothers and Sisters and That Their Gods Are Defiled by Fornication, Adultery, and Incest

[Col. 0502D]

It was not enough for our Minucius to repel the Gentiles’ slander and disclose the innocence of the Christians. He proceeds and demonstrates, by arguments of the greatest force, that the Gentiles themselves are truly guilty of the fornication, adultery, and incest of which they maliciously accused Christians. For, as he says, “among the Persians it is lawful to have intercourse with their mothers; among the Egyptians and Athenians, marriages with sisters are legal.”

Concerning the Persians, in addition to Tertullian (*Apology*, ch. 9, p. 11), Tatian writes that the Greeks consider it abominable for sons to be joined to their mothers, but that among the Persian Magi this is regarded as especially praiseworthy (Tatian, *Oration Against the Greeks*, p. 164). Origen asserts that there are many laws by which the Persians [Col. 0503A] are not restrained, “neither mothers from marriage with their sons nor fathers from marriage with their daughters”: “They do not prohibit mothers from marrying their sons, nor fathers from marrying their own daughters” (Origen, *Against Celsus*, bk. V, p. 248). How greatly that which appears wholly execrable to other human beings was regarded as praiseworthy and approved among the Persians you may learn from these words of Philo Judaeus: “Persians of the highest rank marry their own mothers, and they consider the offspring born from these unions to be of the noblest birth and worthy, as they say, of the highest kingship” (Philo, *On the Special Laws*, p. 778).

Besides these witnesses, after Eusebius (Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, bk. I, ch. 4, p. 11), we have Theodoret, [Col. 0503B] who testifies that this most impious law was enacted by Zaradas and was immediately abolished after those same Persians received the Christian faith: “The Persians,” he says, “who formerly lived according to the laws of Zaradas, had intercourse with their mothers, sisters, and even daughters, and regarded the grossest violation of law as a lawful ordinance. But after they obeyed the laws of the fishermen, they trampled upon the laws of Zaradas as lawless and embraced evangelical continence” (Theodoret, vol. IV, discourse IX, *On Laws*, p. 614). We have already discussed this abominable law and custom of the Persians (vol. I, *Apparatus*, bk. III, dissertation II, ch. 24, art. 1, p. 1239 ff.).

[Col. 0503C]

If we turn to the Egyptians and Athenians, Philo Judaeus declares the marriage practices of both to be utterly depraved: “It is commanded that not even a sister is to be married—a truly honorable precept and one suited to continence—although among the Athenians Solon permitted marriage with sisters who had the same father, but prohibited marriage with those who had the same mother. The Spartan lawgiver, conversely, permitted marriage with sisters born of the same mother but prohibited it with those born of the same father. The Egyptian, however, mocking the scruples of both as though their regulations were only half-complete, gave free rein to lust and lavishly increased in bodies and souls the incurable evil of intemperance, granting permission to marry all sisters: those related through [Col. 0503D] either one parent or the other, and those related through both; not only younger sisters but elder and same-aged sisters as well. For twins too have often been born, whom nature separated and divided from each other at the very moment of birth, but whom licentiousness and sensuality summoned into an association that admits no association and into an inharmonious union.” [Col. 0504A] (Philo, loc. cit., p. 779 ff.).

Diodorus Siculus had previously said that the laws of the Egyptians permitted marriage between sisters and brothers, since this had turned out happily for Isis: “They marry their sisters because of the success Isis experienced in such a union” (Diodorus Siculus, *Library*, bk. I, p. 16).

Pausanias mentions the same most unjust law where he speaks of Ptolemy as follows: “This Ptolemy, having fallen in love with Arsinoë, his full sister, joined her to himself in marriage. In doing so he acted not at all according to Macedonian custom, but according to the law of the Egyptians over whom he ruled” [Col. 0504B] (Pausanias, bk. I, p. 6). Aemilius Probus—or the author of the little book *On Illustrious Men* addressed to Atticus—is likewise said to have related the same thing concerning Cimon’s marriage at Athens to his sister Elpinice. Plutarch, however, says that Cimon married her because he had not found a bride equal to the dignity of his family (Plutarch, vol. I, *Life of Cimon*, p. 481). Athenaeus, by contrast, asserts that this was done contrary to the laws (Athenaeus, *Deipnosophists*, bk. XIII, p. 589). But we believe we have thus far sufficiently proved what our author transmitted concerning these criminal and abominable marriages of both the Athenians and the Egyptians.

Yet he presses the matter more vigorously, and argues thus against Caecilius and the pagans: “Your records and tragedies [Col. 0504C] glory in acts of incest, which you gladly both read and hear. Thus you also worship incestuous gods.” He had used the term “records” above: “Look at the records in the books.” This word was frequently employed by Aulus Gellius. For in one place he says, “It is written in books of records” (A. Gellius, *Attic Nights*, book V, chap. 5); and elsewhere, more simply, “We read it written in ancient records” (book IV, chap. 6). “Records,” therefore, means the same as writings, commentaries, and things committed to writing in order to preserve the memory of events. Tertullian likewise used the word in this sense: “Among the other records” (Tertullian, *Apology*, chap. 18); and shortly afterward, “the hoary records” (chap. 19, p. 19). Elsewhere he says: “According to the records, the Jewish people—that is, the more ancient people—forsook God [Col. 0504D] and served idols” (*Against the Jews*, book I, chap. 1, p. 205). Octavius therefore rightly reproaches Caecilius because pagans gladly read and listened to “Records”—that is, writings and books, whether histories or works of poets, in which the incestuous acts of their gods were represented in writing—and tragedies, in which they were represented through voice and gesture. For no one is unaware that in the comedies and tragedies of both Greek and Latin poets, and in the histories of other pagans, the gods’ acts of fornication, adultery, and incest are celebrated no less frequently than shamelessly. If you have the leisure and inclination, see what Lactantius (*Divine Institutes*, book VI, chap. 20, p. 19; and *Epitome*, chap. 63), Cyprian (Cyprian, *Epistle to Donatus*, [Col. 0505A] p. 5), Augustine (Augustine, *City of God*, book II, chap. 8 ff.), and others said about these comedies and tragedies. But we shall have more to say about them in this and the following dissertations.

Finally, Octavius charges the pagans with incest in another way: because newborn children, as he had already said and as we observed above (preceding chapter, art. 3), were very frequently exposed by their parents. For it happened not infrequently that those utterly depraved and lustful parents polluted themselves through abominable incest with their now-grown sons or daughters, who had been reduced to slavery or were living as prostitutes, either without recognizing them or while pretending not to recognize them. Hence Clement of Alexandria says: Παιδὶ πορνεύσαντι, καὶ μαχλώσαις θυγαθράσιν ἀγνοήσαντες πολλάκις μίγνυνται πατέρες, οὐ μεμνημένοι τῶν ἐκτιθέντων παιδίων, καὶ ἄνδρας δείκνυσι τοὺς [Col. 0505B] γεγενηκότας ἀκρασίας ἐξουσία· ταῦτα οἱ σοφοὶ τῶν νόμων ἐπιτρέπουσι: “Fathers often have intercourse with a son who has become a prostitute and with daughters practicing prostitution, without recognizing them. Unmindful of the children they exposed, fathers are made into their daughters’ husbands by unrestrained license in lust. These things the wise lawgivers permit” (Clement of Alexandria, *Paedagogue*, book III, chap. 3, p. 226). Thus he assails the pagans, and their monstrous savagery and cruelty in exposing their children, with biting irony. Nor is it without cause that he complains that incest frequently resulted from this practice. Nevertheless, Tertullian (*Apology*, chap. 9) and Lactantius (*Divine Institutes*, book VI, chap. 20, p. 618 ff.) develop at greater length and more explicitly our Minucius’ argument against them. To avoid undue length, we have thought it best to refer you to them until we undertake a new discussion of their books. [Col. 0505C]

# CHAPTER XI  
## ON THE ABSURD WORSHIP WHICH CAECILIUS MOST FALSELY ALLEGES THAT CHRISTIANS RENDERED TO AN ASS’S HEAD AND TO A PRIEST’S GENITALS

### ARTICLE I  
#### How false this accusation is; whether the Jews or Gnostics gave occasion for it; and whether they were the first of all actually to worship an ass’s head

The pagans brought against the Christians another charge, as absurdly fabricated as it was impious, which Caecilius puts to Octavius in these words: “I hear that, through some persuasion unknown to me, they venerate the consecrated head of an ass, that most shameful [Col. 0505D] animal.” Tertullian explains this ridiculous accusation more clearly and discloses its occasion and cause in these words: “You have dreamed,” he says, addressing the pagans, “that an ass’s head is our god. Cornelius Tacitus first introduced this sort of suspicion. For in the fifth book of his *Histories*, beginning his account of the Jewish War from the origin of the nation, and arguing as he pleased about that nation’s origin, name, and religion, he relates that the Jews, having departed from Egypt—or, as he thought, having been driven from it—and being tormented by thirst in the vast and extremely waterless regions of Arabia, used wild asses as guides to a spring, because those animals happened to be thought to be seeking water after grazing; and that, in gratitude for this, they consecrated the likeness of such a [Col. 0506A] beast. And thus, I suppose, it was inferred that we too, as near relatives of the Jewish religion, are initiated into the same image” (Tertullian, *Apology*, chap. 16, p. 17). He repeats this in another book as well (idem, *To the Nations*, book I, chap. 11, p. 57 ff.). How rightly Tertullian said that this absurd slander should be laid at Cornelius Tacitus’ door may be judged from Tacitus’ own words in the cited fifth book of the *Histories*: “But nothing distressed the Jews as much as the scarcity of water. They were already lying prostrate over the whole plain, not far from destruction, when a herd of wild asses left their pasture and withdrew to a rock shaded by woodland. Moses followed them and, inferring from the grassy ground, uncovered abundant veins of water. . . . They consecrated in their sanctuary the image of the animal by whose guidance they had dispelled their wandering and thirst [Col. 0506B], sacrificing a ram, as if in insult to Ammon” (Cornelius Tacitus, *Histories*, book V, beginning). Although Tertullian calls Tacitus “the most loquacious of liars”—at least in this matter not without justification—Plutarch nevertheless subscribed to that false opinion when speaking about the same Jews as follows: “They now regard it as a religious prohibition both to kill and to eat a pig. And perhaps this accords with reason: Ὡς τὸν ὄνον δὲ ἀναφήναντα πηγὴν αὐτοῖς ὕδατος τιμῶσι, ‘Just as they honor the ass that revealed to them a spring of water,’ so they revere the pig as their teacher in sowing and ploughing” (Plutarch, vol. II, *Table Talk*, book IV, p. 670).

What of the historian Democritus, who, according to the account of the *Suda*, handed down these assertions about the Jews: Χρυσῆν ὄνου [Col. 0506C] κεφαλὴν προσεκύνουν κατὰ τριετίαν ξένον ἀγρεύοντες προσέφερον, καὶ κατὰ λεπτὸν τὰς σάρκας δίεξαινον, καὶ οὕτως ἀνῄρουν: “They worshipped a golden ass’s head; every third year they captured and offered a foreigner, sliced his flesh into small pieces, and thus killed him” (*Suda*, s.v. Ἰούδας, “Judas/Jew”). Perhaps this is why Zeno of Alexandria, formerly a Jew, as the same *Suda* reports (idem, s.v. Ζήνων, “Zeno”), renounced his religion and, in mockery of this absurd though wholly fictitious cult, led a white ass through their synagogue on the Sabbath day.

Josephus, however, replying to Apion when he advances the same slander, demonstrates its falsity by various arguments. His words should be quoted; although absent from the Greek text, they nevertheless appear in the printed editions in Latin [Col. 0506D] as follows: “Apion presumed to declare that the Jews had placed an ass’s head in the sanctuary, worshipped it, and deemed it worthy of such great religious reverence. He affirms that this was exposed when Antiochus Epiphanes plundered the temple and found that head fashioned from gold and worth a great sum of money. To this, then, I reply first that, since he was an Egyptian, even if there had been anything of the sort among us, he ought by no means to have reproached us, because an ass is no worse than the shrews, goats, and other creatures that are gods among them. Next, how did he fail to understand that his incredible lie was refuted by the facts? For we have always followed the same laws, in which we have steadfastly remained. And although various disasters have afflicted our city, as they have others, [Col. 0507A] and Theos, Pompey the Great, Licinius Crassus, and finally Titus Caesar conquered it in war and took possession of the temple, they found nothing of this sort” (Josephus, *Against Apion*, book II, p. 1065). Josephus therefore makes two replies to this tasteless falsehood, so often repeated and refuted. First, he turns the argument against Apion himself, an Egyptian, and shows that his complaint about this charge is grossly unjust: for the Egyptians worshipped and venerated beasts with no less absurd and impious a cult. Second, he proves that the allegation is not merely false but utterly incredible: for the Jews, who always held every form of idolatry—and consequently the worship of an ass’s head, however golden—in the highest hatred, always lived under the same laws. [Col. 0507B] Then Josephus shows that what Apion records about Antiochus Epiphanes is wholly at variance with the truth. For neither Pompey the Great nor any other Roman commanders, upon entering the Temple at Jerusalem after winning victories over the Jews, ever found in it any image of an ass’s head.

Nor could Tacitus deny this. Tertullian refutes and assails him as a liar forgetful of his own testimony: “But indeed this same Cornelius Tacitus”—these are Tertullian’s own words—“that most loquacious of liars, relates in the same *History* that Gnaeus Pompey, after capturing Jerusalem and consequently entering the temple to inspect the mysteries of the Jewish religion, found no image there. [Col. 0507C] And surely, if the object worshipped was represented by some image, it would be displayed nowhere more than in its own sanctuary; all the more so because that worship, however vain, had no fear of foreign observers: for only the priests were permitted to enter, and even the sight of it was forbidden to all others by a curtain drawn before it” (Tertullian, *Apology*, chap. 16, p. 17). We read the same points transmitted by him again, though in other words, in the first book *To the Nations* (chap. 11). And rightly so; for Cornelius Tacitus had actually written the following in the book cited: “Gnaeus Pompey was the first of the Romans to subdue the Jews, and by right of victory he entered the temple. It then became generally known that there was no image of God within”—that is, none painted or fashioned—“and that the seat was empty and the mysteries void” (Tacitus, *Histories*, book V, shortly after the beginning).

[Col. 0507D] From what has been discussed thus far, who does not see that no credence whatsoever should be given either to this Cornelius Tacitus or to the other wicked slanderers who most shamelessly lied that divine worship had been accorded to an ass’s head, first by the Jews and then by the Christians?

Besides the explanation already offered by us, Bochart (*Sacred Animals of Scripture*, vol. I, chap. 18, p. 221 ff.) and Vossius (*On the Origin and Progress of Idolatry*, book III, chap. 75, p. 565) have given various accounts of the origin of so foul a fable. Since anyone may easily read these in their books, we shall add only what Tertullian records concerning a certain Jew, a thoroughly depraved man. [Col. 0508A] For after renouncing the Jewish religion, this man, says that learned African writer, “displayed a picture bearing an inscription of this kind: THE GOD OF THE CHRISTIANS ONOCHOETES” (Tertullian, *To the Nations*, book I, chap. 11, p. 57 ff.). He then adds that this fictitious god was represented with ass’s ears, one hoofed foot, carrying a book, and wearing a toga (idem, *Apology*, chap. 16, p. 17), as we shall explain in its proper place. Moreover, Epiphanius, when discussing the Gnostics, those most notorious Christian heretics, committed the following to written record: “As regards Sabaoth, some consider him to have the form of an ass, others that of a pig” (Epiphanius, *Heresy* XXVI, § 40, p. 91). But whether this or any other fabricated story gave any occasion for accusing Christians of so wicked a [Col. 0508B] cult, our Minucius certainly denies utterly and completely that either the malicious imposture of that apostate from the Jewish religion or the supremely absurd cult of the Gnostics pertained in any way whatsoever to true Christians. For he openly and steadfastly asserts that this false rumor concerning the worship of an ass’s head was scattered and spread abroad by demons, and that no sane person could ever have believed it. “For who,” he says, “is so foolish as to worship this? Who is more foolish still as to believe that it is worshipped?” He therefore declares it to be mere slander and a most shameless lie, utterly incredible to anyone unless he is wholly bereft of sense. He does not refute it in more words, since he considered that by denying it once he had sufficiently confuted it.

### ARTICLE II  
#### How Minucius proved that the pagans were guilty of this same crime, or one similar or worse, since they impiously worshipped and venerated asses together with Epona and Isis, as well as the heads of cattle and wethers

[Col. 0508C]

Our author makes manifest the extent of the madness of the pagans who accused Christians of ass-worship by showing that they themselves could most certainly be convicted, not once but very frequently, of the same or a similar offense. He proves this by so many examples that the pagans dared neither answer anything in reply nor even open their mouths. He therefore begins with the very worship they rendered to asses and Epona: “You consecrate even whole asses [Col. 0508D] together with your”—the Royal manuscript adds “or”—“Epona.” Most scholars, however, believe that a scribal error lies here, which each has attempted to correct according to the sharpness of his own ingenuity. Some have removed the word “or” and wished the printed editions simply to read “together with your Epona.” Yet some of these have suspected that someone wrote “with Hippona” in the margin. These, however, are mere conjectures supported by no authority or testimony. Others directed their edition to read, “with your or its Epona.” Although contrary to the manuscript’s authority, they try—wrongly—to confirm this conjecture by words of Tertullian soon to be cited. Finally, some think it should be emended to “with Vesta, or Epona,” [Col. 0509A] because the pagans were persuaded that the ass was Vesta’s favorite. Yet even if the ass truly had been Vesta’s favorite, it would still have to be proved that asses were consecrated to her, and why Minucius said “or Epona.” Moreover, he ought to have written “and Epona,” especially since he immediately added that asses were sacrificed to Isis. What, then, if the particle *vel* (“or”) is used by our author, as by many others, to mean “also”? Would not his expression then be Latin and clear, with nothing requiring alteration in his text?

Plutarch, following Agesilaus (Agesilaus III Italicus), explains who Epona was in these words: “Fulvius Stellus, estranged in mind from women, had intercourse with a mare. In due time she gave birth to a most beautiful daughter, to whom her father gave the name Epona, ὠνόμασεν Ἱππώναν, ‘he named her Hippona’; [Col. 0509B] and she is the goddess who presides over the breeding of horses” (Plutarch, vol. II, *Parallel Stories*, p. 312).

That her image was customarily placed in stables is inferred from these words of Juvenal:

> . . . He swears  
> Only by Hippona and the faces painted by the foul-smelling mangers.  
> (Juvenal, *Satires* VIII, v. 157.)

Some, however, wish *Epona* to be read there instead of *Hippo*. Apuleius also says the following of the image of Epona, or Hippona, placed in stables: “I looked toward the central pillar supporting the stable’s beams, and almost exactly at its midpoint there was an image of the goddess Hippona, or Epona, resting in a shrine, which had been carefully crowned with garlands of roses—and fresh ones at that” (Apuleius, *Metamorphoses*, book III, near the end).

[Col. 0509C] Moreover, when our Minucius reproaches the pagans with that impious worship of Epona, he appears to follow in the footsteps of Tertullian, who had argued similarly against them: “Yet you will not deny that all beasts of burden, and even whole geldings along with their Epona, are worshipped by you. Perhaps we are reproved for this: that among the worshippers of all livestock and wild beasts, we alone are worshippers of asses” (Tertullian, *Apology*, chap. 16, p. 17; and *To the Nations*, chap. 11, p. 58). He also repeats the same point in another book, for the most part in the same words. Accordingly, Prudentius rejects this asinine divinity in these verses:

> No one grants the goddesses Cloacina or Epona  
> A throne above the stars, although he pays out a solid incense-box  
> And, with sacrilegious hands, probes the meal and entrails.  
> (Prudentius, *Apotheosis*, § II.)

[Col. 0509D] After this Octavius continues to rebuke Caecilius and the other pagans as follows: “You devoutly consecrate [*devotatis*] the same asses together with Isis.” The Royal manuscript has “devour [*devoratis*],” but nearly everyone considers this a scribal error. Some therefore thought that *devotatis* should be read—that is, “you show them to be consecrated.” But they ought to have proved where the verb *devotare* is used in that sense. Others conjectured that *denotatis* (“you designate”) had been written. But what would that contribute to Octavius’ purpose? Others maintained that it should be emended to *devocatis* (“you call down”), in the sense in which good authors say that Socrates “called philosophy down” from heaven. But what, pray, would be the point of calling asses down together with Isis? Finally, others judge that it should be corrected to [Col. 0510A] *decoratis* (“you adorn”), because they simultaneously worshipped both the image of the ass carrying the goddess Isis and that of Isis herself, adorned with various ornaments. This conjecture does not seem wholly inept; for we have just heard Apuleius say that the image of the goddess Epona had been carefully crowned with fresh rose garlands. In another book he declares no less clearly that the image of Isis was customarily carried by her priests through huts, villages, and camps, covered with a silken mantle, and was worshipped by every pagan who met it (Apuleius, *Metamorphoses*, book VI, near the end). Consider, therefore, whether this is our Minucius’ meaning and whether *decoratis* should be read in his text. For we believe that nothing should be decided with certainty without the authority of a complete manuscript.

[Col. 0510B] Let us therefore pass to other matters. “You both sacrifice,” he adds, “and worship the heads of cattle and the heads of wethers.” Herodotus speaks as follows concerning the worship and sacrifice of cattle: “All Egyptians θύουσι, ‘sacrifice,’ clean bulls and bull-calves. But they are not permitted θύειν, ‘to sacrifice,’ the females, since these are consecrated to Isis. For the image of Isis is female and provided with bovine horns, just as the Greeks portray Io. Καὶ τὰς βοῦς τὰς θηλείας Αἰγύπτιοι πάντες ὁμοίως σέβονται προβάτων πάντων μάλιστα, ‘And all Egyptians alike venerate female cattle far more than all other livestock’; hence no Egyptian man or woman would kiss a Greek man on the mouth, or use his knife, spit, or pot, or eat the flesh even of a clean ox cut with a Greek knife” [Col. 0510C] (Herodotus, book II, § 41).

What then, someone will argue? Is it not entirely false that the Egyptians displayed any veneration toward the ox, since they sacrificed it to the gods? Eusebius, indeed, most explicitly denied that the Egyptians regarded oxen as gods, since they sacrificed those same oxen to the gods. These are his words: Ὅτι δὲ οὐδὲ τὰ ζῶα θεοὺς ἡγοῦνται, δηλοῖ τὸ πολλαχοῦ βοῦς ἀναχθέντας θεοῖς ἐν ταῖς ἱερομηνίαις: “That they—the Egyptians—did not regard brute animals as gods is clear even from the fact that in many places they customarily sacrificed oxen consecrated to the gods during solemn festivals and religious observances” (Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, book III, chap. 12, p. 117). Yet one should consider whether the knot of this difficulty is not untied by Herodotus’ distinction [Col. 0510D] between male and female cattle.

For no one will deny that the Egyptians sometimes showed reverence and honor to the ox, since, besides many others, Philo the Jew left this written concerning them: Ἐκλαθόμενοι τῆς πρὸς τὸ ὃν ὁσιότητος, ζηλωταὶ τῶν αἰγυπτιακῶν γίνονται πλασμάτων· εἶτα χρυσοῦν ταῦρον κατασκευασάμενοι, μίμημα τοῦ κατὰ χώραν ἱερωτάτου ζώου δοκοῦντος εἶναι, θυσίας ἀθύτους ἀνήγαγον: “The Israelites, forgetting the piety owed to the One who is, began to emulate Egyptian fabrications; then, having made a golden bull in imitation of the animal regarded as most sacred in that country, they offered unhallowed sacrifices and performed dances, and so forth” (Philo, *Life of Moses*, book III, p. 677). Jerome likewise says: [Col. 0511A] “It seems to me that the people of Israel made for themselves in the wilderness a calf’s head to worship, and that Jeroboam son of Nebat fashioned golden calves, so that they might preserve in their superstition what they had learned in Egypt: that Apis and Mnevis, worshipped in the form of oxen, were gods” (Jerome, on chap. XLVII of Hosea, v. 15 [citation as printed]). Earlier Lactantius likewise said of the same Israelites: “Having fallen into luxury, they turned their minds to the profane rites of the Egyptians. For when Moses their leader had ascended the mountain and remained there forty days, they fashioned a golden head of the ox called Apis, to precede them as a standard” (Lactantius, book IV, chap. 10, p. 376). But we shall discuss the ox Apis a little below.

[Col. 0511B] Nor should anyone be troubled because both Lactantius and Jerome said “a calf’s head,” just as our Minucius speaks of “heads of cattle.” For by this manner of speaking they signify nothing other than the whole calf or oxen themselves. If you wish, you may consult Bochart on this subject (*Sacred Animals of Scripture*, book II, chap. 34, p. 346).

In precisely the same sense our author added “and heads of wethers.” No one, surely, is unaware that a wether is a castrated male sheep. Elsewhere we have noted that the Samians actually rendered worship to a sheep, and for what reason (vol. I, *Apparatus*, book III, dissertation 1, chap. 9, art. 3, p. 768). But that did not prevent others from sacrificing wethers to the Lares, as Cicero testifies: “Nor [Col. 0511C] is it necessary,” he says, “for us to explain . . . what kind of sacrifice is made to the Lar with wethers” (Cicero, *On the Laws*, book II, p. 340). Lambinus confirms this in his observations on this passage of Cicero with the following inscription of the Larval Brethren: LARIB. VERB. N. II. MATRI. LAR. OV. N. II. [“To the Lares, two wethers; to the Mother of the Lares, two sheep.”]

He then relates that, because the name Augustus had been conferred upon Octavian Caesar and in commemoration of that event, “a wether” was sacrificed in the temple of Jupiter by the flamen on the Ides of January. For this reason Ovid sang:

> On the Ides, in the temple of mighty Jove, the pure priest  
> Offers in the flames the entrails of a half-male sheep.  
> Every province was restored to our people,  
> And your grandfather was given the name Augustus.  
> [Col. 0511D]  
> (Ovid, *Fasti*, book I, v. 346 ff.)

### ARTICLE III  
#### How Minucius further proved that the pagans worshipped and adored gods compounded of goat and man and bearing the faces of lions and dogs; likewise the ox Apis, serpents, crocodiles, and other birds and beasts, and even onions and the breaking of wind

Minucius continues and, in order to shame the pagans for the utterly senseless slander by which they falsely charged Christians with ass-worship, says: “You dedicate as gods beings compounded of goat and man, and faces of lions and dogs as gods.” Of the first kind he mentions, Pan undoubtedly belonged; Herodotus relates that he was represented as follows by painters and sculptors [Col. 0512A]: Γράφουσι δὲ δὴ καὶ γλύφουσι οἱ ζωγράφοι, καὶ οἱ ἀγαλματοποιοὶ, τοῦ Πανὸς, καθάπερ Ἕλληνες, τὤγαλμα αἰγοπρόσωπον, καὶ τραγοσκελέα: “Painters paint and sculptors carve the image of Pan, as do the Greeks, with a goat’s face and a he-goat’s legs” (Herodotus, book II, § 46). He adds, however, that they believed Pan resembled the other gods, but that they depicted him in this manner for certain reasons which, he declares, it was by no means agreeable for him to relate. Satyrs too were imagined with a human but horned head, goats’ feet, and a hairy body. Lucian says that they, like Pan and Silenus, were remarkable for their monstrous appearance: Ὧν ὁ μὲν κέρατα ἔχων, καὶ ὅσον ἐξ ἡμισείας, ἐς τὸ κάτω αἰγὶ ἐοικὼς, καὶ γένειον βαθὺ καθειμένος . . . . . οἱ δὲ σάτυροι ὀξεῖς [Col. 0512B] τὸ ὦτα, καὶ αὐτοὶ φαλακροὶ, κεράσται, οἷα τοῖς ἄρτι γεννηθεῖσιν ἐρίφοις τὰ κέρατα ὑποφύεται: “The one, bearing horns, resembling a goat from the waist downward, and letting a deep beard hang down, differs little from a he-goat. . . . The satyrs have pointed ears, are themselves bald and horned, with horns like those that begin to sprout on newborn kids” (Lucian, *The Council of the Gods*, p. 1096). Hence Propertius, book III, Elegy 16:

> Goat-footed Pans will sing through the open reed.

And Lucretius, book IV, before the midpoint:

> The neighboring peoples imagine that goat-footed Satyrs and Nymphs  
> Possess these places, and they say that Fauns exist.

If you desire other witnesses to a matter not unknown, you may consult Eusebius, Servius, Vossius, Natalis Comes, and not a few others (Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, book [Col. 0512C] III, chap. 4, p. 124; Servius on Virgil, *Eclogue* 2, v. 31; Vossius, *On the Origin and Progress of Idolatry*, book I, chap. 8, p. 31, and book VII, chap. 3, p. 359).

Those gods who bore the faces of lions and dogs, and other monstrous figures of gods, are mentioned not infrequently by various writers. First, we read the following report from Porphyry in Eusebius: “In fashioning images of the divine powers, they used every kind of animal, sometimes mingling wild beasts with human beings, and sometimes combining the bodies of birds and humans.” Εἴκασται γάρ τις παρ᾽ αὐτοῖς μέχρι τραχήλου ἀνθρωποειδής, τὸ δὲ πρόσωπον ὀρνέου, ἢ λέοντος, ἢ ἄλλου τινὸς ζώου κεκτημένος· καὶ πάλιν αὖ κεφαλὴ [Col. 0512D] ἀνθρώπειος, καὶ ἄλλων τινῶν ζώων μέρη, πῇ μὲν ὑποκείμενα, πῇ δὲ ἐπικείμενα: “Among them one may see certain images human in form as far as the neck, but with a face resembling now a bird, now a lion, or any other animal; and others again with a human head, while the remaining parts of the body, whether lower or upper, display the form of other living creatures” (in Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, book III, chap. 4, p. 93). Eusebius had borrowed this from the fourth book of Porphyry’s Περὶ ἀποχῆς ἐμψύχων (*On Abstinence from Animal Food*), and from it, while combating the pagans, turns back against them the same weapon they had directed against the Christians, as Minucius does (Porphyry, book IV, before the midpoint, p. 372).

[Col. 0513A] Tertullian too, arguing in the same way against those same pagans, had carried the torch before our author in these words: “But they ought immediately to have worshipped a two-formed deity, since they have accepted gods compounded with dogs’ and lions’ heads, horned from goat and ram, goats from the loins, serpents from the legs, and winged on sole or back” (Tertullian, *Apology*, chap. 16). Again in another book: “Among you—that is, the pagans—there are gods with goats’ heads and lions’ heads, derived from ox, ram, and he-goat; caprine gods, goat-born or serpent-shaped, and winged on sole, forehead, and back” (idem, *To the Nations*, book I, chap. 14).

These points may be further confirmed from other authors, and especially by the following very words of Macrobius: “A city adjoining Egypt, which boasts Alexander the Great of Macedon as its founder, [Col. 0513B] observes the worship of Serapis and Isis with a veneration bordering on stupefaction. Yet it declares that all this veneration is rendered to the sun under that name, whether when they attach to his image a three-headed creature, whose central and largest head presents the likeness of a lion; on the right rises that of a dog, with the gentle appearance of one fawning; while the left side of the neck ends in the head of a ravening wolf. A serpent connects these animal forms with its coils, its head returning toward the god’s right hand, where the monster is seen” (Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, book I, chap. 20).

But let us, if you please, follow our author: “Do you not both worship and feed the ox Apis together with the Egyptians?” If you seek a witness to the feeding and worship of this prodigious divinity, you will find Strabo, [Col. 0513C] who relates that Memphis was the royal city of the Egyptians, where there was a temple of Apis, who was the same as Osiris, and of the Sun [the transmitted Latin syntax is uncertain]: Καὶ τὸν βοῦν τὸν Μνευῖν, ἐν σηκῷ τινι τρεφόμενον, ὃς παρ᾽ αὐτοῖς νενόμισται Θεὸς, ὥσπερ καὶ ἐν Μέμφει ὁ Ἄπις: “And the ox Mnevis, which is fed in a certain enclosure and is regarded by the Heliopolitans as a god, just as Apis is by the Memphites” (Strabo, *Geography*, book XVII, p. 803 ff.). He adds that certain marks indicate which other ox, when this one dies, is fit to succeed it. If you want still more, consult Diodorus Siculus, who also relates how that ox Apis was buried after death and another installed in its place, by whom it was fed, and where it was stationed and honored. You may also consult Herodotus, Aelian, Mela, Porphyry as cited by Eusebius, Cicero, and, if you wish, what we reported in the first volume of our *Apparatus* (Diodorus Siculus, *Library*, book I, p. 53 ff.; Herodotus, book III, § 27; Aelian, *On Animals*, book X, chap. 28; Mela, *Description of the World*, chap. 9; Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, book III, chap. 13, p. 117; Cicero, *Nature of the Gods*, book I, p. 207; vol. I, *Apparatus*, p. 1090 ff.).

[Col. 0513D] Minucius further faults the Romans because they not only worshipped the ox Apis together with the Egyptians, but also did not condemn the laws those Egyptians had established concerning beasts, birds, crocodiles, and serpents—namely, that anyone who killed one of them should be punished with death. Very many writers have mentioned this impious Egyptian custom. To select a few from their great number, let [Col. 0514A] Cicero come first; in these few words he explains how great the superstition of those peoples was: “The Egyptians consecrated nearly every kind of beast” (Cicero, *Nature of the Gods*, book III, p. 245, line 25; ibid., book I, p. 207, line 18). Elsewhere he records that this superstition went so far that it had never even been heard said that they harmed a crocodile, ibis, or cat. Indeed, “Even if they have inadvertently done any harm to one of them,” as he says in another book, “they refuse no punishment” (*Tusculan Disputations*, book V, p. 189, line 25). Herodotus speaks no less clearly about the penalty for harming a sacred animal: “If anyone kills one of these beasts,” he says, “if intentionally, he is punished with death; if unintentionally, he pays whatever penalty the priests have determined” (Herodotus, book II, § 65). [Col. 0514B] Tertullian, in whose footsteps our author still seems to stand, attests this concerning the same Egyptians: “No one, not even a human being, will wish to be worshipped against his will. And therefore even the Egyptians have been permitted the power of so vain a superstition: consecrating birds and beasts, and condemning to death those who kill any god of this kind” (Tertullian, *Apology*, chap. 24, p. 26).

We briefly touched upon this ridiculous Egyptian worship in the preceding volume of our *Apparatus*. But if this does not suffice for you, we shall refer you to Herodotus, Diodorus Siculus, Strabo, Aelian—who gave Plutarch as his guarantor—Cyril of Jerusalem, Jerome, and Theodoret (vol. I, *Apparatus*, pp. 496 and 636; Herodotus, book II, § 65 ff.; Diodorus Siculus, *Library*, book I, pp. [Col. 0514C] 52, 54 ff.; Strabo, *Geography*, book XVII, p. 811 ff.; Aelian, *On Animals*, book X, chap. 13, and book XVII, chap. 5; Cyril of Jerusalem, *Catechesis* 6, p. 61; Jerome, *Against Jovinian*, book II, p. 59; Theodoret, Discourse 4, *On Angels and Demons*, p. 521). As for Minucius’ additional assertion that these Egyptian superstitions were not condemned by the Romans, anyone will readily concede it who remembers that the Romans either adopted or tolerated the religions of all other nations, however absurd. For, as Caecilius himself said: “By adopting the sacred rites of all nations, they also earned dominion.”

[Col. 0514D] Still more absurd was what Minucius next adds: that the Egyptians, together with very many Romans, feared the pungency of onions and the noises of the belly. That this was no less true and certain than the foregoing may be learned from these verses of Juvenal:

> Who does not know, Volusius Bithynicus, what monsters  
> Mad Egypt worships? One district adores  
> The crocodile; another fears the ibis gorged with serpents.  
> The golden image of the sacred long-tailed monkey gleams;  
> . . . . . . . . . .  
> Some towns worship blue fishes, others a river fish; elsewhere  
> Whole cities venerate a dog, but no one Diana.  
> It is sacrilege to violate the leek and onion or break them with a bite.  
> O holy peoples, in whose gardens such  
> Divinities grow!  
> (Juvenal, *Satire* XV, beginning.)

We read similar lines sung later by Prudentius:

> Do you pray to Venus? Pray also to the ape.  
> Does the sacred asp of Aesculapius please you?  
> Why then do the crocodile, ibis, and dogs displease you?  
> Set religious little altars beside your couches;  
> [Col. 0515A] Venerate the bitter onion and pungent garlic.  
> (Prudentius, Hymn in Honor of Saint Romanus, v. 256 ff.)

Accordingly, Pliny had said without hesitation concerning the onion: “Egypt includes garlic and onions among its gods when taking an oath” (Pliny, *Natural History*, book XIX, chap. 6, p. 593).

If you ask the causes of this ridiculous veneration and worship, we shall give them in Plutarch’s words: Οἱ δὲ ἱερεῖς ἀφοσιοῦνται, καὶ δυσχεραίνουσι, καὶ τὸ κρόμμυον παραφυλάττοντες, ὅτι τῆς σελήνης φθινούσης μόνον, εὐτροφεῖν τοῦτο καὶ τεθηλέναι πέφυκεν· ἔστι δὲ πρόσφορον οὔτε ἁγνεύουσιν, οὔτε ἑορτάζουσιν· τοῖς μὲν, ὅτι διψῆν, τοῖς δὲ, ὅτι δακρύειν ποιεῖ τοὺς προσφερομένους: “The priests religiously abstain from the onion and regard it with aversion, taking care to avoid it because this plant alone naturally thrives and flourishes while the moon is waning. The use of onions is appropriate neither for those practicing ritual purity nor for those celebrating festivals: for the former, because it creates thirst; for the latter, because it causes those who partake of it to shed tears” (Plutarch, *On Isis and Osiris*, p. 853). [Col. 0515B] Aulus Gellius indeed reported the first of these explanations from the same Plutarch, but asserts that the Egyptian priests said this about the people of Pelusium (Gellius, *Attic Nights*, book XX, chap. 8). And not entirely without good reason. For Lucian relates that the Pelusians were devoted to this ridiculous and absurd cult, just as others were devoted to another: Μεμφίταις μὲν ὁ βοῦς Θεὸς, Πηλουσιώταις δὲ κρόμμυον, καὶ ἄλλοις ἴβις, ἢ κροκόδειλος, καὶ ἄλλοις κυνοκέφαλος, ἢ αἴλουρος, ἢ πίθηκος: “For the Memphites the ox is a god; for the Pelusians, the onion; for others, the ibis or crocodile; and for still others, the dog-headed ape, cat, or monkey” (Lucian, *Jupiter Tragoedus*, p. 699 ff.). [Col. 0515C] Hence Jerome says: “Compel a Pelusian, if you can, to eat an onion” (Jerome, *Against Jovinian*, p. 59).

Elsewhere the same Jerome speaks as follows both of that same onion and of the breaking of wind, which our author mentions second: “Most of their towns—the Egyptians’—derive their gods from beasts . . . not to mention the fearsome and horrible onion and the breaking of a swollen belly’s wind, which is the religion of Pelusium” (idem, on Isaiah 46). Pseudo-Clement supports Jerome, speaking as follows about these and the other matters discussed by our author: “Some of the Egyptians handed down the ox called Apis as an object of worship; others, the he-goat; others, cats; some, the ibis; certain people, a serpent; also a fish and onions, the breaking of wind, sewers, and the limbs of brute animals—and [Col. 0515D] they submitted themselves to a thousand other most loathsome obscenities” (Pseudo-Clement, *Recognitions*, book V, § 20, p. 466). He mentions similar things elsewhere; if you have the leisure, you may consult him (idem, *Homilies* 10, p. 657). What, then, must be said of the Romans, who, as we have stated, either did not condemn or actually followed those insane rites, yet patiently endured their ridicule by the poets?

## ARTICLE IV. That it is false that Christians worship the genitals of a priest; that the pagans are convicted of fouler enormities; and what occasion gave rise to the accusation that Christians practiced that most shameful veneration

Caecilius further charges the Christians with another deed, full indeed of infamy and disgrace, yet in such a way that he does not venture to accuse them positively of so great an outrage: “Others,” he says, “report that they worship the genitals of their own bishop and priest, and adore his sexual nature as though he were their parent.” [Col. 0516A] Certainly nothing is more frivolous than this calumny, or less grounded in truth. Caecilius, moreover, says that it was practiced, not according to everyone, but only according to certain persons who circulated as a false rumor what they did not dare to affirm.

Octavius therefore refutes this wholly fictitious charge, most unjustly branded upon the Christians, by his customary twofold reply. First, he denies that they ever did such a thing and declares it a ridiculous tale and sheer calumny. He then asserts that the pagans were defiled by obscenities far fouler—things which it was unlawful for chaste ears either to name or to hear. But it is better that these matters be expressed in his words rather than ours:

> “He who invents tales against us about the worship of a priest’s male organs is trying to transfer his own practices to us. For such things may perhaps be sacred rites of their lewdness, among people with whom every sex prostitutes itself through every member; among whom utter impurity is called sophistication; who envy the license of prostitutes; who lick men about the waist, fastening their lustful mouths upon their groins—men of evil tongue even when silent, who grow weary of their impurity before they become ashamed of it. What wickedness! They perpetrate upon themselves a deed of the utmost depravity, such as neither a more tender age can endure nor a harsher slavery compel. We are not permitted even to hear of these and similar outrages; to defend them at greater length is itself shameful.”

Although he said that it was unlawful to explain these utterly shameful pagan enormities more explicitly, or for any Christian to hear them, or for any other person to defend them, [Col. 0516B–C] they were nevertheless no less true and well known to everyone. For, besides the various testimonies concerning them given by poets and other writers, especially Martial, the most holy Apostle, in his Epistle to the Romans alone, reproached the Gentiles with several extremely serious offenses, with all the greater justice because he knew with absolute certainty that they were true. (St Paul, *Epistle to the Romans*, chap. I, verses 16 ff.)

Our author therefore rightly turns the pagans’ argument back upon them. No one, indeed, was ever able to prove that the Christians were guilty of the great crime of which they were suspected. On the contrary, their most devout manner of life entirely and utterly dispelled so ridiculous a suspicion. The Gentiles, however, were certainly convicted of this and still greater crimes by their own authors, as has been said, and by other witnesses whose credibility was beyond all question. [Col. 0516D]
