Yet someone will object: although the claim that Christians worshiped a priest’s genitals was wholly at variance with the truth, it is nevertheless incredible that a public rumor concerning so horrible a crime could have been spread unless at least some occasion for it had been given. To anyone wishing to know what that occasion was, we reply that Christians who, during the earlier centuries of the Church, performed public penance for their sins and graver offenses prostrated themselves outside the doors and upon the threshold of the church at everyone’s feet, especially those of the priests, so that they might obtain their pardon. When the Gentiles heard of this through vague and uncertain rumor, they fabricated from it the tale that Christians worshiped a priest’s genitals. [Col. 0517A]

For concerning penitents of this sort, whom we have discussed more fully elsewhere, Tertullian writes above all:

> “Exomologesis is a discipline for prostrating and humbling a person. . . . It generally consists in sustaining prayers by fasts, groaning, weeping, and crying aloud day and night to the Lord one’s God; falling at the feet of the presbyters and kneeling before those dear to God; and enjoining upon all the brethren the office of intercession on one’s behalf.”  
> (Tertullian, *On Penance*, chap. 6, p. 146.)

Again, although at that time he had become entangled in the errors of the Montanists and had departed from the true doctrine of the Church, he says:

> “And indeed, when bringing the repentance of an adulterer into the church to entreat the brotherhood, you prostrate him in the midst, clothed in sackcloth and covered with ashes, composed in shame and horror, before the widows and before the presbyters, grasping the hem of everyone’s garment, licking everyone’s footprints, and clinging to everyone’s knees.”  
> (The same, *On Modesty*, chap. 13, p. 729.)

Eusebius also relates that Natalis the confessor, after being thoroughly deceived by the heretics Asclepiodotus and Theodotus the money-changer, had accepted a salary and been made bishop of their sect. But after he had often been warned of so great a crime by nocturnal visions and had disregarded them, he was most severely scourged throughout the night by holy angels:

> Ὥστε ἕωθεν ἀναστῆναι, καὶ ἐνδυσάμενον σάκκον, καὶ σποδὸν καταπασάμενον μετὰ πολλῆς σπουδῆς, καὶ δακρύων προσπεσεῖν Ζεφυρίνῳ τῷ ἐπισκόπῳ, κυλιόμενον ὑπὸ τοὺς πόδας οὐ μόνον τῶν ἐν τῷ κλήρῳ, ἀλλὰ καὶ τῶν λαικῶν, συγχέαι τε τοῖς δάκρυσι τὴν εὔσπλαγχνον ἐκκλησίαν τοῦ ἐλεήμονος Χριστοῦ.
>
> “So that, rising at first light, putting on sackcloth, and sprinkling himself with ashes, he hastened with many tears and fell at the feet of Bishop Zephyrinus; rolling at the feet not only of the clergy but also of the laity, he moved and profoundly stirred by his tears the compassionate Church of the merciful Christ.” [Col. 0517B–C]

Who, then, will deny that it is extremely probable that the pagans seized upon this pious and holy custom—which they either did not sufficiently understand or maliciously interpreted—as an opportunity falsely to accuse the Christians of the shameful worship of which our author speaks?

# CHAPTER XII. OTHER ACCUSATIONS MADE BY CAECILIUS, AND OCTAVIUS’ ANSWERS TO THEM, ARE EXAMINED

[Col. 0517D]

## ARTICLE I. How undeservedly Caecilius condemns the Christians’ assemblies and fasts, and calls them men of a desperate faction, a light-shunning nation, recognizing one another by secret signs and loving one another before they are acquainted

By means of insults rather than legitimate accusations, the pagans endeavored to bring the Christians into disrepute. For the things which the former charged as abominations and crimes, the latter maintained to be excellent, commendable, and properly instituted. Such, beyond doubt, is that practice which Caecilius imputes to the Christians as though it were some crime: namely, that through nocturnal gatherings and solemn fasts “they are bound together not by some sacred rite, but by an expiatory crime.” [Col. 0518A] Yet they readily acknowledged that this was just as true as it was false that anything other than the holiest actions took place in those assemblies, which, as Caecilius says, they were accustomed to hold on a solemn day. This is most clearly proved by the passages concerning them which we have cited elsewhere from the *Apology* of Justin Martyr and which will be produced below from Tertullian. Indeed, that point has already been sufficiently demonstrated by what we have thus far advanced against the shameless calumnies of Caecilius, through which he wrongly alleged that crimes as unspeakable as they were incredible were committed in those assemblies.

Would you like another witness, in this matter above every possible objection, to be presented to you? We shall produce Pliny, certainly a pagan, to whom the emperor Trajan had assigned the task of diligently investigating the crimes of which the Christians were accused. After examining everything with the greatest diligence he could employ, he wrote to Trajan that those Christians who, as he says, had abandoned the Christian faith affirmed:

> “That this had been the sum of either their guilt or their error: that they had been accustomed to assemble on a fixed day before dawn and to recite responsively among themselves a hymn to Christ as to a god; and to bind themselves by an oath, not to commit any crime, but not to commit theft, robbery, or adultery, not to break their word, and not to refuse to return a deposit when called upon. When these things had been completed, it was their custom to depart and then to assemble again to take food—ordinary food, however, and harmless.”  
> (Pliny, book X, *Letter to Trajan*, [Col. 0518B–C] p. 376.)

What could be clearer or more effective than this testimony—which we shall see transcribed by Tertullian—for proving the sanctity of Christian assemblies? (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, chap. 2.)

Thus no Christian was ashamed not only of these gatherings, but also of “the solemn fasts, worthy of every commendation”; rather, he gloried in them. For this reason Gregory of Nazianzus said in one of his orations against Julian the Apostate:

> “Such are we, worn out by long fasts and half-dead. Such are we who keep vigils in vain and trifle at nocturnal stations, yet nevertheless overthrow you.”  
> (Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 4, p. 299.)

Someone, therefore, will doubtless be astonished at Gronovius, who suspects that in the text of Minucius, instead of *solemnibus jejuniis*, “solemn fasts,” one should read *olentibus jejuniis*, “malodorous fasts.” [Col. 0518D] Were not the Christians’ fasts—and above all the fasts of Lent—solemn at that time? Did Tertullian not write concerning them, “On Easter Day the observance of fasting is common and, as it were, public”? (Tertullian, *On Prayer*, chap. 14.) But if the observance was common and public, why was it not also solemn?

Gronovius continues: But these Christian fasts are taken in a bad sense by Caecilius, who plays the part of the pagans. Yet what prevents that pagan from having called them “solemn,” either in mockery or because he was speaking the truth? Anyone who desires more information about these and other Christian fasts should consult Irenaeus, cited by Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book V, chap. 24, p. 192; Tertullian, cited just above, *To His Wife*, book II, chap. 4; *On Baptism*, chap. 20; *On Flight*, chap. 1; *On Fasting*, chaps. 13 and 14; Athanasius, *Apology to the Emperor Constantius*, p. 310, and *Apology for His Flight*, p. 334; Cotelerius’ notes on Hermas, pp. 72 ff., and on book V of the *Apostolic Constitutions*, chap. 15, pp. 245 ff. We have discussed Christian vigils in vol. I of the *Apparatus*, book III, dissertation 1, chap. 6, article 3, pp. 712 ff.; fasting in the same work, book I, dissertation 4, article 5, p. 53, and article 23, p. 67; also book II, dissertation 1, chap. 7, article 2, p. 330; and book III, dissertation 1, chap. 1, article 7, p. 884; chap. 11, article 7, pp. 1038 ff.; and chap. 12, article 4, p. 1049.

Utterly intolerable, therefore, was the shamelessness of Caecilius and the other Gentiles, who dared to call Christians—adorned with the chastest conduct and assiduously devoted to virtue—men of a deplorable, unlawful, and desperate faction; a secretive, light-shunning nation, mute in public and babbling in corners; men who recognized one another by secret marks and tokens before they were acquainted, and who finally despised present torments and death altogether. [Col. 0519A–B] For, Tertullian said, precisely because we Christians, by merely repudiating our name, can immediately escape every kind of punishment and death, “we are regarded as desperate and ruined,” as Lactantius likewise stated. (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, chap. 50, p. 44; Lactantius, *Institutes*, book V, chap. 9, p. 463.)

Yet the more shameless was the insolence and effrontery of Caecilius and the other Gentiles, the greater certainly was the moderation of Octavius in answering on behalf of the Christians. For what, I ask you, could be more moderate than his reply?

> “Nor are we disdainful, if we all hold to the one good; gathered together, we are as peaceful as we are individually. Nor do we babble in corners, if you are either ashamed or afraid to hear us publicly.”

In this way he attenuates and refutes each particular head of the accusation. First, he denies that Christians are members of an unlawful faction because, he says, they all hold to the one good. But there can be no unlawful faction without opposing parties that contrive something against the public good. For this reason some suspect that instead of *fastidiosi*, “disdainful,” one should read *factiosi*, “factious.” The emendation would indeed not be a bad one if supported by the authority of some manuscript. [Col. 0519C–D] For who knows whether Minucius did not connect the word *factiosi* with the statement “we hold to the good”? What if he refutes the accusation of an unlawful faction with the words “we are all gathered together with the same peacefulness as when alone”? Yet if there is any room to doubt the true reading, our author nevertheless declares and proves most clearly that Christians cannot be called members of an unlawful faction.

Moreover, in this passage he follows closely in the footsteps of Tertullian, who demonstrates much more plainly, in the following words, that the unlawful faction was not that of the Christians but of the Gentiles themselves:

> “This association of Christians is certainly deservedly unlawful—if it is comparable to unlawful associations; deservedly to be condemned—if it is not unlike associations that deserve condemnation. If anyone complains about it on the charge ordinarily made against factions, for whose destruction have we ever assembled? We are the same when gathered together as when scattered, the same collectively as individually, injuring no one and grieving no one. When upright and good people meet, when the devout and the chaste assemble, it must not be called a faction but a council. Conversely, the name ‘faction’ must be applied to those who conspire in hatred of good and upright people, who clamor for the blood of the innocent—that is, of Christians.”  
> (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, chaps. 39 and 40, p. 36.)

But more will be said about these matters when we discuss this book of Tertullian.

If the Christian community could not be called an unlawful faction, much less could it be called a “desperate” one, since, as Minucius says, “secure in the hope of future happiness, we are animated by faith in the present majesty of God.” [Col. 0520A–B] Thus it was not through any despair, but through the surest hope of eternity, that they most steadfastly endured every kind of torment for professing their religion; indeed, as we have said, they gloried in such torments. Lactantius presses the point more sharply: it was by no means the Christians, who “do not spare their bodies,” but the Gentiles themselves who ought to have been called desperate, since “nothing can be more desperate than to torture and tear apart someone whom you know to be innocent.” (Lactantius, *Institutes*, book V, chap. 9, p. 485.) Something more must be said about these matters later.

The pagans had no better right to object that the Christians were a secretive and light-shunning nation, mute in public and babbling in corners. For they preached their doctrine openly, and the pagans could readily “hear them publicly,” unless they were either ashamed that their own impiety and crimes should be exposed or afraid that the true religion should be demonstrated to them. [Col. 0520C]

Caecilius next objects that Christians recognize one another by secret marks and tokens. Octavius answers as truthfully as simply:

> “We readily recognize one another, not by a mark upon the body, as you suppose, but by the sign of innocence and modesty.”

We have nevertheless observed that the Carpocratians imprinted a certain mark upon the rear part of their adherents’ right ear, by which they doubtless distinguished them from other people. (*Apparatus*, vol. I, book II, dissertation 3, chap. 3, article 3, §12, p. 293.) But neither Caecilius nor Octavius is speaking of these or other heretics; they are speaking of Christians in general, who recognized one another, as our author says, by no sign other than that of innocence and modesty. Their innocence is established by what has been said thus far and by what will be said below; likewise their modesty, especially as they stood in the church or approached it, is clear from our annotations on the books of Clement of Alexandria. (*Apparatus*, vol. I, book III, dissertation 1, chap. 6, article 4, p. 713.) [Col. 0520D]

Finally, in answer to Caecilius’ last taunt concerning the Christians’ mutual affection, Minucius replies that Christians loved one another with mutual and sincere love both because they did not know how to hate others and because they were brothers who had one Father, as Tertullian had also said, partners in faith and coheirs of hope. Octavius further insists that the pagans reproached them for this mutual love, which surely ought to be esteemed most highly, because, as he declares in addressing them, “you rage in mutual hatred and recognize one another as brothers only when it comes expressly to parricide”; or, as Tertullian, whom we cited just above, says, “you are more ready to kill one another . . . because among them every name of blood-kinship is a mere pretense of affection.” [Col. 0521A] (Tertullian, loc. cit.) But these matters are treated more fully in our dissertation on this book of Tertullian. (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, chap. 39, p. 35.) Meanwhile, concerning that brotherly charity of the Christians and the name “brethren,” see Lucian, *The Death of Peregrinus*, p. 996, and, if you please, our observations in the preceding volume, pp. 473 and 999.

## ARTICLE II. By what right Caecilius said that Christians despised temples as though they were tombs, and that they had no temples, no altars, and no known images; and the foolish cavils of the more recent Iconoclasts are refuted

[Col. 0521B]

It certainly appeared to Caecilius a most serious crime that Christians despised temples dedicated to the gods of the Gentiles just as they did tombs. “They scorn temples,” he said, “as though they were *busta*,” that is, tombs of dead men. For although the word *bustum* is derived from the verb *uro*, “I burn,” and originally signified the place in which the bodies of the dead were customarily burned, it is nevertheless commonly used by reputable authors to mean a tomb, as it is here by our author. [Col. 0521C]

If you ask for a witness, we shall immediately produce Tertullian, from whom Minucius appears to have drawn his material. He had previously said to the pagans: “We despise temples no less than tombs.” (Tertullian, *On the Shows*, chap. 13.) You see that the meaning of *busta* is clearly explained by Tertullian, who also confirms that Christians despised the temples of the gods as tombs of deceased human beings. Why should they not have despised them in this way, when Clement of Alexandria and others demonstrated, as we have noted elsewhere, that the temples of the gods were in fact the tombs of dead human beings? (*Apparatus*, vol. I, book III, dissertation 1, chap. 7, article 3, pp. 72 ff.)

Caecilius’ second complaint and accusation was that Christians not only despised the temples of the gods, but, in order to conceal their mysteries more securely, had no temples, no altars, and no images. Listen, I ask you, to the manner in which he complains about them:

> “Why do they have no altars, no temples, no known images? . . . Unless it is because whatever it is that they worship and conceal is either punishable or shameful.” [Col. 0521D]

Is this not the same complaint made in Origen by the pagan Celsus, who accused the Christians of avoiding the dedication—or rather the erection and installation—of altars, statues, and temples: βωμοὺς, καὶ ἀγάλματα, καὶ νεὼς ἱδρύσθαι φεύγειν, “of avoiding the erection of altars, cult-images, and temples”? (Origen, *Against Celsus*, book VIII, p. 389.)

What, then, do you suppose Minucius answered to this accusation? He freely concedes that Christians had no altars and no images—indeed, not even any temples or shrines. He gives the following reason why they did not possess any of them:

> “Do you think that we conceal what we worship because we have no shrines and altars? For what image could I fashion for God, when, if you judge rightly, the human being himself is God’s image? What temple could I build for him, when this entire world, fashioned by his workmanship, cannot contain him? And when I, a human being, dwell more spaciously, should I confine the power of so great a majesty within a little sanctuary?”

Cyprian transcribed from this passage of our author—and thereby approved—these final words concerning a temple. (Cyprian, *On the Vanity of Idols*, p. 15.) [Col. 0522A]

A little sanctuary (*aedicula*), as we may observe in passing, was a small chapel, an annex to some sacred building, or a niche in which the statue or image of some god was placed. Thus Cicero says: “What of the fact that Licinia, a Vestal Virgin, . . . dedicated an altar, a little sanctuary, and a sacred couch beneath the Sacred Rock?” (Cicero, Oration 29, *For His House*, p. 427.) Apuleius, for his part, says: “In the very center of the little sanctuary sat an image of the goddess Hippona.” (Apuleius, *Metamorphoses*, book III, near the end.) Finally, to omit Pliny, Tertullian certainly distinguished temples or shrines, altars, and little sanctuaries in the following words, just as our author did: “For it makes no difference whether you build it or adorn it, if you have furnished his temple, his altar, or his little sanctuary.” (Tertullian, *On Idolatry*, chap. 8, p. 107.) Nevertheless, both authors use the name *aedicula* to designate any temple whatsoever, precisely in order to show more clearly how much smaller and less august it is than God’s infinite majesty. [Col. 0522B–C]

Minucius therefore testifies that the Christians had other and far more excellent temples, shrines, altars, sacrificial altars, and victims than the pagans, as well as other and far more sacred sacrifices:

> “Should not God,” he says, “rather be dedicated in our mind and consecrated in our innermost heart? Shall I offer to the Lord sacrificial animals and victims which he produced for my use, so that I may cast his own gift back to him? That would be ingratitude, when the acceptable victim is a good disposition, a pure mind, and a sincere conscience. Thus he who cultivates innocence makes supplication to the Lord; he who cultivates justice pours a libation to God; he who abstains from fraud propitiates God; he who rescues a human being from danger slaughters the best victim. These are our sacrifices; these are God’s sacred rites.”

Just as Octavius answers Caecilius, so Origen likewise answers the pagan Celsus, who, as we said shortly before, raised the same objection. Celsus fails to see:

> ὅτι βωμοί, “that the altars” of each one of us are “our own minds, from which” truly spiritual and sweet-smelling incense rises upward, together with prayers from a pure conscience:
>
> Ἀγάλματα δὲ καὶ πρέποντα Θεῷ, οὐκ ὑπὸ βαναύσων τεχνιτῶν κατεσκευασμένα.
>
> “The images to be dedicated to God and worthy of him are not works made by mechanical craftsmen, but virtues carved and formed within us by the Word of God, in imitation of the Firstborn of all creation, in whom are the exemplars of justice, temperance, courage, wisdom, and the other virtues. These are the statues—ἀγάλματα, ‘cult-images’—to be dedicated to God in the souls of those who, in accordance with God’s command, practice justice, courage, piety, and the remaining virtues.”  
> (Origen, *Against Celsus*, book VIII, p. 389.) [Col. 0522D–0523A]

In the same manner, therefore, our Minucius, Origen, and other Christian writers of the same period openly declare that Christians had no temples or shrines, no sacred buildings, no altars, and no images. They all speak of these things in one and the same manner. Indeed, if there is any distinction, it is that Minucius added the word “known” to “images,” as though wishing to signify that Christians did possess some images, but that these were not known and were kept secretly and in concealment.

But observe, I ask you, the foolish cavils of the Calvinists and other Protestants, who admit whatever pleases them in the writings of the most ancient Fathers and reject whatever displeases them. For they openly acknowledge with Dallaeus that in the time of our Minucius, and from the first centuries of the Church, Christians did indeed have their own temples, but no altars and no images. Let us consider for a moment with what temerity they distinguish things which those most ancient writers did not distinguish. [Col. 0523B]

It is well that Dallaeus and other Protestants concede that Christians had their own temples in the earliest age of the Church. But with what effrontery could they have denied what those Fathers of the Church assert with absolute certainty? Tertullian, as we have seen elsewhere, expressly declares that they possessed temples, which he called “churches,” following the Apostle, although the Calvinists reject that designation. Would you like another testimony from him, written even against the Catholic Church?

> “The remaining frenzies of lust, impious against both bodies and sexes beyond the laws of nature, we exclude not merely from the threshold but from every roof of the church.”

We have already noted that Clement of Alexandria likewise called them by the Greek name ἐκκλησίαν, “church.” (*Apparatus*, p. 741; Tertullian, *On Idolatry*, chap. 7, p. 107; *On the Veiling of Virgins*, chap. 13, p. 201; *On Modesty*, chap. 4, p. 718; *Apparatus*, vol. I, p. 713; Clement of Alexandria, *Paedagogus*, book III, chap. 11, p. 255.) [Col. 0523C]

This is proved no less clearly by the Christian assemblies which, as we have often seen, they were accustomed to hold in buildings and temples; and, moreover, by the public penance of offenders who, prostrate at the doors of the church, implored the prayers of the faithful and the mercy of the priests. Finally, it is demonstrated most manifestly by the authority of Arnobius and Lactantius, who reproached the pagans for destroying or burning the Christians’ meeting places and churches.

Eusebius relates more concerning the destruction and restoration of those churches, calling them προσευκτηρίων τοὺς οἴκους, “houses of prayer” or “sacred buildings,” and ἐκκλησίας, “churches”; elsewhere, τοὺς οἴκους ἐν οἷς συνήγοντο, “their buildings in which they held their assemblies”; and finally, οἴκους ἐκκλησιῶν, “buildings of the churches.” (Arnobius, *Against the Gentiles*, book IV, p. 152; Lactantius, *Institutes*, book V, chap. 11; Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VIII, chap. 2, pp. 293–294; ibid., chap. 17, p. 316; ibid., book IX, chap. 9, p. 362.) [Col. 0523D]

But why is there any need to prove at greater length something that is entirely certain and that our adversaries have never been able to deny? I would therefore have you observe their changeable and cunning disposition. They confess that Christians did indeed have their own temples, yet temples fashioned not like ours, but only like theirs. If you do not believe us, here are Dallaeus’ exact words:

> “For Minucius’ statement must not be understood as though at that time there were no buildings in which members of the Christian communion held sacred assemblies, both to be instructed concerning divine matters and to make common supplication to God—buildings such as those which today are called Protestant temples.”  
> (Dallaeus, *On Images*, book I, chap. 3, p. 52.)

But by what argument, I ask you, have he and others of the same sect ever proved that the temples of the most ancient Christians resembled theirs rather than ours? [Col. 0524A–B] By not even the slightest argument. Is it therefore because they have utterly removed altars, sacrificial altars, statues, and images from their temples, just as they have removed the sacrifice of the Mass, that they proclaim the most ancient Christian temples to have resembled their own?

Yet the same plain evidence that proves that the Christians built temples can demonstrate that altars were placed and sacrificial altars erected in those ancient temples and churches. For Tertullian declares it most explicitly in the following words:

> “Will your station not be solemn if you have stood at the altar of God?”  
> (Tertullian, *On Prayer*, chap. 14, p. 155.)

Cyprian, moreover, wrote to the people of Furni concerning not only an altar but also a sacrifice, which our adversaries so insolently reject:

> “It was established long ago in a council of bishops that no one should appoint any cleric or minister of God as a guardian or administrator in his will, since those who have individually been honored with the divine priesthood and appointed to clerical ministry ought to serve only the altar and sacrifices and to devote themselves to prayers and supplications.”

He then says that his episcopal predecessors had decreed:

> “That no brother departing from this life should name a cleric as guardian or administrator; and that if anyone did so, no offering should be made for him, nor should a sacrifice be celebrated for his falling asleep. For he does not deserve to be named at the altar of God in the priests’ prayer who wished to call priests and ministers away from the altar. And therefore, since Victor dared to appoint a presbyter as guardian, no offering for his falling asleep is to be made among you, nor is any supplication in his name to be frequently offered in the church.”  
> (Cyprian, Epistle 1, *To the Presbyters*.) [Col. 0524C–D]

You see clearly that he distinguishes the altar and sacrifice from the Christians’ prayers, supplications, and petitions. In their churches, therefore, there were altars in the true and proper sense, and at that time sacrifice was customarily offered for the dead.

In another letter to Pope Cornelius, Cyprian writes that a document of the Novatians, who falsely accused Cornelius, was rejected “while God’s priests sat in council and the altar had been set in place.” (The same, Epistle 45, p. 87.) And, to omit many other passages readily found by anyone in his writings, he congratulates Pope Lucius on his return from exile, since “the authority of the priesthood has increased all the more, so that its bishop might stand beside the altar of God.”

We have now proved something that even the very celebrated editor of these works of Cyprian, although an adherent of the Church of England, freely and openly acknowledges. It is therefore just as certain that altars were placed in Christian churches or temples as it is that Christians built churches in which, as Dallaeus admits, they held their sacred assemblies. For, as he says:

> “It is sufficiently clear not only from Eusebius’ *History* but also from several other monuments of the ancient Church that Christians already possessed sacred buildings of this kind. If they lacked them anywhere, this resulted from the violence and injustice of the pagans, who unlawfully begrudged devout people this opportunity and freedom, not from any religious principle of the Christians themselves.”  
> (Dallaeus, *On Images*, book I, chap. 3, pp. 52 ff.) [Col. 0525A]

But tell me, I ask you, my dear Dallaeus: you admit what you could no longer conceal—that Christians possessed their own sacred buildings; you deny that they had altars; you deny that they had images. Where is your good faith? Did Minucius not say all these things in exactly the same manner: “Why do they have no altars, no temples, no known images?” Why, therefore, do you concede one and deny another? Has there ever been, to use your own words, “any greater or more unjust exercise of force than to assume for yourself the right and authority to alter at your pleasure the very thoughts of men—and indeed of men who died many centuries ago”? (Dallaeus, *On Images*, book I, p. 52.)

For Minucius appears less completely to deny that Christians had temples and altars than that they had images. Caecilius did not thoughtlessly add the phrase “known images,” meaning, as we have said, images that were public and known to others. We have sufficiently demonstrated that Christians constructed temples and altars in which they customarily offered a true sacrifice. [Col. 0525B–C] Let us now see by what argument the same Dallaeus contends that they had no statues or images.

He replies that “it is possible” that Caecilius, like any other Gentile, remained uncertain whether Christians “secretly worshiped a deity of shameful and dishonorable form.” For Caecilius himself said in the same passage: “They make every effort to conceal whatever it is that they worship.”

Is it truly because you think this “possible” that you assume the right to conclude from it that neither this Gentile nor the Christian Minucius denied that Christians possessed their own temples and altars, but only denied that they possessed images, although they speak of all these things in one and the same manner? And from where did you learn that the Christians’ images were less known to the pagans than their sacred buildings, which they were accustomed to enter only in secret? [Col. 0525D]

Dallaeus nevertheless insists that it would have been easy and obvious for Octavius to answer that Christians possessed certain images and altars, but ones very different from the images and altars of the pagans. So far is Octavius from giving such an answer that, on the contrary, he says that no temple should be built for God, whom the entire world cannot contain, much less a single little sanctuary; but that a good disposition, a pure mind, and a sincere conscience are the best and most acceptable sacrificial offerings and victims to God; and, finally, that the human being is God’s image.

Yet nothing is more insubstantial or frivolous than this reply. For Jews and Gentiles, among whom no one is unaware that many altars, victims, and sacrifices existed, use the same manner of speaking as Minucius. Thus, in Philo the Jew’s book *On Victims*, we read:

> Τοῦ Θεοῦ θυσιαστήριον ἐστιν ἡ εὐχάριστος τοῦ σοφοῦ ψυχή, παγεῖσα ἐκ τελείων ἀριθμῶν ἀτμήτων καὶ ἀδιαιρέτων.
>
> “The altar of God is understood to be the grateful soul of the wise person, compacted from perfect numbers that cannot be cut or divided.”

He had written much more to the same effect shortly before. (Philo, *On Victims*, p. 851.) [Col. 0526A]

The pagan Seneca, cited by Lactantius, says:

> “The benefit itself is not what is counted out or handed over. So too, even in the case of victims, although they be fat and gleam with gold, the honor paid to the gods does not lie in them, but in the devout and upright mind of those who worship.”  
> (Seneca, *On Benefits*, book I, chap. 6; Lactantius, *Institutes*, book VI, chap. 25, p. 638.)

Even earlier Cicero had said:

> “The best worship of the gods, and likewise the purest and fullest of piety, is that we should always venerate them with a pure, whole, and uncorrupted mind and voice.”  
> (Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, book II, p. 224, line 42.)

If you wish for more, consult Porphyry and the many other authors cited by Lescalopier on this passage of Cicero. But who has ever said that by these words the Jews or Gentiles denied that true altars, sacrificial altars, victims, and sacrifices existed among them? (Porphyry, *On Abstinence from Animals*, book II, near the end; Lescalopier, on *On the Nature of the Gods*, book II, §72, p. 347.) [Col. 0526B]

What, moreover, will you do with Tertullian, whom Minucius follows so closely? Did he not also write:

> “We despise temples no less than tombs; we recognize neither kind of altar; we worship neither kind of image”?  
> (Tertullian, *On the Shows*, chap. 13, p. 96.)

Does he not there deny, just as openly as Minucius, that Christians possessed any temples, altars, or images whatsoever? Does he not also elsewhere answer the pagan Scapula:

> “We sacrifice for the emperor’s welfare, but to our God and his, and in the manner God has commanded—with pure prayer”?  
> (The same, *To Scapula*, chap. 2, p. 86.)

Did he on that account deny that Christians possessed any temples, altars, or sacrificial altars at all? By no means, as has been proved from his other words cited shortly before and as Dallaeus himself concedes. [Col. 0526C]

We must therefore say that our Minucius, Tertullian, and others who speak in the same manner concede the point in one sense and deny it in another. For since they were disputing against the pagans, they therefore denied that Christians [Col. 0526D] possessed temples after the manner of the Gentiles, in which they worshipped fictitious gods and believed them to dwell, or altars and sacrificial tables for slaughtering and offering victims to them; but they did possess sacred buildings and altars in which they worshipped the true God according to the Christian rite and offered an unbloody sacrifice. Nothing, therefore, could be more absurd than to claim, as Dallaeus prattled, that the quoted words of Minucius excluded the altars of “Roman men”—the spiteful name by which that heretical man designates Catholics—because he and his associates had decided, on their own authority, to reject the Eucharistic sacrifice. For we have already shown, by the entirely certain testimony of the ancient Fathers, that in Minucius’s time altars were set up in Christian temples or churches, and that the sacrifice of the holy Eucharist [Col. 0527A] was offered. Augustine later asserts this most explicitly (Augustine, *City of God*, book VIII, ch. 27, p. 217; and book X, ch. 20, p. 255).

Moreover, since Minucius’s and Tertullian’s words concerning temples, altars, and images are the same, they must certainly be explained in the same way. They therefore deny that Christians possessed any images of the kind that the pagans had constructed of their gods. That this was Minucius’s meaning is gathered not only from what has been said thus far, but also from the entire dispute between him and Caecilius. Caecilius, indeed, objected that Christians, unlike the Gentiles, possessed neither temples nor images of false gods. Minucius acknowledges that this is certainly the case. But just as he does not deny that they possessed temples other than those of fictitious gods, [Col. 0527B] so too he does not deny that they possessed images other than those which the pagans had made of those gods.

Nor should you insist that Minucius excludes absolutely all statues and images, since he replies: “What image shall I fashion for God, when, if you judge rightly, man himself is God’s image?” For he had spoken similarly about temples, as we have noted: “What temple shall I build for him, when this whole world, fashioned by his work, cannot contain him?” Yet Dallaeus and other men of the same sect are compelled to confess that these latter words do not exclude actual Christian temples. They must therefore confess likewise that the former words of the same Minucius exclude only the statues and images of false gods, which Christians could not tolerate without idolatry. [Col. 0527C] We have discussed these Christian images and statues, and their use, in our preceding dissertations; and you may read much that has been handed down by Petavius, Thomassin, and many others (vol. I, *Apparatus*, p. 747 ff.; Petavius, vol. V, *Dogmatic Theology*, book XV, ch. 11; and Thomassin, book XII, *Dogmatic Theology on the Incarnation*, ch. 7 ff.). What our author held concerning the worship and honor shown by Christians to Christ’s cross must be investigated in the fourth article below.

## ARTICLE III. How Octavius refutes Caecilius’s charge that Christians worship a man fastened to a cross for a crime; the supreme divinity of Christ; how clearly the same Octavius shows that a criminal man was honored with divine worship by the Egyptians, and kings and emperors by the Romans, and that oaths were sworn by their guardian spirits; and whether Christians were permitted to swear by their welfare

[Col. 0527D]

Caecilius further accuses Christians of a twofold crime: “Those,” he says, “who tell—or rather, one tells—of a man punished for a crime by the supreme penalty, and of the deadly wood of the cross, as objects of their rites, assign altars appropriate to abandoned and criminal men, so that they may worship what they deserve.” You hear, surely, how the Gentiles condemned Christians for two further forms of impious worship, as they regarded them: first, because they worshipped a man subjected to the punishment of the cross for his crimes; and second, because [Col. 0528A] they worshipped and venerated the cross, the deadly instrument of that punishment.

But Minucius shows separately that both charges are false. As regards the former, he openly and steadfastly asserts that the Gentiles are completely deceived and have gone utterly astray in persuading themselves that an earthly man, fastened to the cross for his own crimes, could have been deemed God by Christians, or could have deserved to be so deemed, and on that account be accorded divine honor by them. For those same Christians were fully convinced that those who place their hope in a mortal man are utterly pitiable, since when that man dies, all the help they could expect from him comes to an end.

But Minucius himself must be heard: “In ascribing to our religion a guilty man and his cross, [Col. 0528B] you stray far from the neighborhood of truth when you suppose either that a guilty man deserved to be believed God, or that an earthly man could be. Truly pitiable is the man whose entire hope rests upon a mortal man; for all his assistance ends when that man has died.” He therefore categorically denies that Christians worship a guilty man deservedly punished with death.

What, then? Could Minucius have affirmed so certainly that Christians denied Christ the Savior absolutely all worship and veneration, and placed no hope whatever in him? Surely no human being has ever believed that. Since it is certain and established that Christians both worshipped Christ and placed their hope in him who had died for them, what can you infer from this except that Minucius took it as fixed and certain that [Col. 0528C] Christ was indeed worshipped by his followers—not as a man, from whom nothing more could be hoped after his death, but as God, in whom, as the true and immortal God, they always placed their greatest hope? And may it not rightly be inferred from this, to observe the point in passing, that Minucius was thoroughly persuaded that Christ is the true and supreme God, and of the same substance as his eternal Father? For, as we showed above, he taught with the greatest constancy that there is only one God. Therefore, when he acknowledged Christ as God, he certainly confessed him to be the one and same God with his Father.

Petavius therefore attempts to prove from these same words of Minucius, though by another line of reasoning, that Minucius acknowledged the supreme divinity of Christ (Petavius, vol. II, *Dogmatic Theology*, [Col. 0528D] preface, ch. 5, § 3). The learned man judges that Minucius confesses Christ to be true God and, under that name, to be worshipped by Christians, just as the Gentiles venerated their gods. But, with the most learned man’s permission, we may say that it must be explained somewhat more clearly how this can be inferred from the few words of Minucius that we have quoted in full. His argument, however, appears to be this: “You err, pagans, when you suppose that we believe a merely earthly and guilty man to be God. For we believe Christ to have been not only an innocent man, but also true God, upon whom our hope most firmly rests.”

For when Christians were interrogated by pagan judges, undeterred even by fear of the impending punishments, [Col. 0529A] they steadfastly replied, as Pliny wrote to the emperor Trajan, that they “sang a hymn together to Christ as to a god”—that is, to Christ, whom they asserted to be true God, and such as, in Petavius’s view, the pagans believed their own gods to be (Pliny, *Letters* 101).

Minucius then turns the pagans’ argument back upon them and demonstrates that they themselves actually rendered to a mere man the very religious worship which they falsely reproached Christians for rendering. For the Egyptians, he says, consulted one man selected from among them all, “propitiated him,” and slaughtered victims to him, whom they declared to be God. How true this is Porphyry will teach you, who wrote the following to Anebo, as Eusebius reports: [Col. 0529B] “They also worship a man near the village called Anabis, where sacrifice is offered to him and the sacred victims placed upon the altars are burned”—Ἂνθρωπον σέβουσι, κατ’ Ἄναβιν κώμην, ἐν ᾗ καὶ τούτῳ θύεται, καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν βωμῶν τὰ ἱερὰ ἐκκαίεται. “He himself, however, later eats only what has been prepared and set before him from his private store, as for a private man” (Eusebius, *Preparation of the Gospel*, book III, ch. 3, p. 94). Eusebius repeats the same account elsewhere without citing an author, as does Theodoret later; Theodoret does indeed cite Porphyry’s *Letter*, but gives its sense rather than its words (Theodoret, vol. IV, Sermon 3, *On Angels and Demons*, p. 516).

By yet another argument Minucius convicts the pagans, and especially the Romans, of the same impiety. For they not only shamefully flattered their own rulers and kings as [Col. 0529C] gods, but also invoked their divinity, supplicated their images, implored their guardian spirit, and found it safer to swear by Jupiter’s genius than by that of their king.

Concerning that criminal flattery by which the Romans enrolled their dead emperors among the gods, we read the following in Justin Martyr: Καὶ τί γὰρ ἀποθνήσκοντας παρ’ ὑμῖν αὐτοκράτορας ἀπαθανατίζεσθαι ἀξιοῦντες, καὶ ὁμνύντα τινὰ προάγετε ἑωρακέναι ἐκ τῆς πυρᾶς ἀνερχόμενον εἰς τὸν οὐρανὸν τὸν κατακαέντα Καίσαρα. “For why is it that you always deem emperors who die among you worthy of being made immortal, and produce someone who confirms under oath that he saw the Caesar who was burned ascend from the funeral pyre into heaven?” And later: “And when emperors among you die, you consecrate images of them in [Col. 0529D] this fashion and call them gods in the inscriptions” (Justin Martyr, *First Apology*, pp. 67–90). But this impious apotheosis of Roman emperors can be unknown to no one who has even tasted their history with the tips of his lips. Yet the utterly detestable flattery of the pagans did not stop there: they erected temples and altars and appointed priests for these same emperors while they were still alive, as they did for Julius Caesar, Augustus Octavian, and others (Suetonius, *Life of Julius Caesar*, § 76; *Life of Augustus*, § 52; Cornelius Tacitus, *Annals*, book III, around the middle).

They held their own emperors—whether still living or, after death, proclaimed gods by them—in greater awe than the more ancient gods, consecrated long before by their [Col. 0530A] ancestors. Why, then? Because, Octavius says, it was “safer for them to swear falsely by Jupiter’s genius than by the king’s.” Here he undoubtedly followed Tertullian, who went before him and whose very words he seems to have read: “Among you Gentiles, perjury is committed more readily by all the gods than by the one genius of Caesar” (Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 28).

It is more certain than certainty itself that from the time of the emperor Augustus the custom prevailed of swearing by the emperor’s name or genius. For Horace, addressing Augustus himself, sang:

> While you are still with us, we lavish timely honors upon you,  
> And set up altars on which men swear by your name.  
> (Horace, *Letters*, book II, epistle 1, vv. 15–16.)

You hear clearly both that altars were erected, as we just said, to Augustus [Col. 0530B] while he was still alive, and that pagans swore by his name—that is, by his genius. After he had died, Claudius Caesar, according to Suetonius, “established no oath for himself more sacred or more frequent than that sworn by Augustus” (Suetonius, *Life of Claudius*, § 11), that is, by his genius and name. If you still desire proof of how sacred and religious this oath was, you will learn it from these words of Tacitus: “Aubrius was charged with the crime of having violated the name of Augustus by perjury. When this became known to Tiberius, he wrote to the consuls . . . . . . . . . that the oath must be regarded just as if he had deceived Jupiter” (Tacitus, *Annals*, book I, near the end).

Moreover, the Gentiles were accustomed to swear not only by Augustus’s genius but also by those of other emperors. [Col. 0530C] Apuleius is for us a most substantial witness to this most perverse custom. For when magistrates were searching for a certain gardener and asking where he was, “the soldiers,” he says, “insisted, swearing by the genius of the emperor, that he was neither there nor hiding anywhere” (Apuleius, *Metamorphoses*, book IX, near the end). Caligula, moreover, according to Suetonius, subjected many men to severe punishments “because they had never sworn by his genius” (Suetonius, book IV, § 27). Finally, to omit further examples, Tertullian relates that the rebels who supported the parties of Cassius and Albinus swore falsely by the genii of the emperors (Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 35; and *To Scapula*, ch. 2, p. 85).

But Christians detested that impious oath. Hence Polycarp, as [Col. 0530D] Eusebius relates, could never be compelled by the tyrant to swear by Caesar’s genius (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book IV, ch. 15, p. 131 ff.). Other Christians, as the same Tertullian testifies, were therefore proclaimed irreligious and enemies of the people because they refused to propitiate the images of the Caesars or to swear by their genii. But something further must be said about Tertullian in its proper place (Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 32, p. 31; and *To the Nations*, book I, ch. 17, p. 61).

Some may perhaps ask us why Minucius so confidently declares that the pagans swore “more safely,” or, as Tertullian says, “more readily,” by Jupiter’s genius than by the emperor’s (*Apology*, ch. 28). We shall therefore give them two reasons. [Col. 0531A] The first, which Tertullian suggests to us, is that the Gentiles feared their gods less than the present power of the emperors. The second is that, according to Zosimus, forgiveness for an oath made to God was left to divine kindness (Zosimus, *History*, book V, at the end). But anyone who swore falsely by the emperor’s genius, even in a relatively trivial matter—for example, a financial one—was, as Ulpian noted, ordered to be beaten with clubs (Ulpian, book II, title 2, law 13, § *Si quis*). Anyone who desires more should consult Brissonius, Hansenius, Trelierus, and others who wrote on the oaths of the ancients, and Taffinus, who wrote on the worship of the genius and the custom of swearing by it (Brissonius, *On Formulae*, book VIII, p. 809; Hansenius, *On the Oaths of the Ancients*, ch. 16; Taffinus, *On the Secular Year*, etc., ch. 13).

## ARTICLE IV. In what sense Minucius said that crosses were neither worshipped nor desired by Christians

[Col. 0531B]

Octavius also responds in two ways to Caecilius’s second reproach concerning the worship of the cross. His first answer is contained in these words and no more: “We neither worship nor desire crosses.” But the briefer it is, the more obscure it will seem to many. Is it really so, you will say, that Christians worshipped neither the very cross of Christ nor any image whatever of it? Is not Christ’s cross called by Cyril of Jerusalem τὸ σωτήριον τοῦ σταυροῦ ξύλον, “the saving wood of the cross”; and by Eusebius σωτήριον σημεῖον, “the saving sign,” σωτήριον καὶ ζωοποιόν, “saving and life-giving,” [Col. 0531C] and also σωτήριον τροπαῖον, “the saving trophy”—the safeguard of the city of Rome, the empire, and the whole world, whose divine power the pagan emperor Licinius acknowledged? (Cyril of Jerusalem, *Letter to the Emperor Constantius*, p. 247.) Who, moreover, doubts that such a sign of the cross was honored by Christians with sincere veneration? Yet if anyone resists, let him hear Eusebius, who extols Constantine the Great with the highest praises because he honored that triumphant sign—τὸ νικοποιὸν ἐτίμα σημεῖον, “he honored the victory-making sign”—in which he had repeatedly experienced the power of divinity and the marvelous effects recorded there by Eusebius himself (Eusebius, *Life of Constantine*, book I, ch. 31, p. 423; book II, ch. 16, p. 451; book IV, ch. 21, p. 535; and *Oration in Praise of Constantine*, pp. 627–628). Ambrose, moreover, declares without hesitation that the cross of Christ was placed by Helena, the same Constantine’s mother, upon the head of kings, “so that it might be adored in kings” (Ambrose, *Oration on the Death of Theodosius*, § 46, p. 1211). Jerome says that Paula, “prostrate before the cross, worshipped as though she saw the Lord hanging upon it” (Jerome, Letter 86, or *Epitaph of Paula*, p. 673).

Why say more? Julian the Apostate, like Caecilius, reproached Christians because, while mocking and despising the shield of Jupiter and Mars said to have fallen from heaven, they venerated the sign of the cross. Cyril of Alexandria replies to him that τὸ σωτήριον ξύλον, “the saving wood,” τοῦ τιμίου σταυροῦ, “of the honorable cross,” revives the memory of all the benefits conferred upon us by Christ’s death [Col. 0532A] (Cyril of Alexandria, *Against Julian*, book VI, p. 194 ff.). Who can doubt that it is far more equitable and just to honor this saving sign than the images painted upon walls of the dreadful and most shameful crimes committed by the gods?

But if this is so, how could Minucius say: “We neither worship nor desire crosses”? Some have wrongly read *oramus*, “we pray to,” here. Others, who did not sufficiently grasp our author’s meaning, thought it should be emended and wished the actual reading to be *horremus*, “we shudder at them.” But all this is contrary to the authority of the manuscript codex and yields no better sense.

What, then, you will say, did Minucius mean by the words “We neither worship nor desire crosses,” or how can they be explained? It appears certain [Col. 0532B] that they cannot be understood of the actual beam and wood of Christ’s cross itself, of which Ambrose and Jerome, already cited by us, speak. For in his time that true cross of the Lord had not yet been discovered by Helena, the mother of Constantine the Great.

Accordingly, he is undoubtedly speaking either of the sign and image of this sacred cross, or of the crosses of other criminal men. That his words can be taken in this second sense may be inferred, not unreasonably, from the fact that, just as “the pagans,” according to Origen, on “reading” the history of Christ, supposed that Christians showed some veneration to everyone put upon a cross, so they also falsely believed that Christians revered crosses of every kind (Origen, *Against Celsus*, book II, p. 87). [Col. 0532C] Both Caecilius’s reproach and Minucius’s response appear to favor this explanation. For neither of them spoke of one particular cross, but of crosses in general. Minucius could therefore say with complete correctness that Christians neither worshipped nor desired the crosses of men condemned to death for their crimes.

But if anyone thinks that these words must be explained as referring to images of Christ’s true cross, he will undoubtedly suppose this to be Minucius’s intention and meaning: “We do not worship crosses, whether made of wood or of any other material, because we do not honor the wood itself or any similar material; rather, when we see the cross, we direct all our worship to Christ himself, who hung upon the cross.” Nor will this explanation seem excessively forced to some. For Ambrose, who, [Col. 0532D] as we observed, said that the true cross of Christ was adored in kings, had written a little earlier of that very cross: Helena “found the inscription” of the cross; “she adored the King, certainly not the wood, for that is pagan error and the vanity of the impious; rather, she adored him who hung upon the wood and was named in the inscription” (Ambrose, *Oration on the Death of Theodosius*, § 46, p. 1211).

But if that is our author’s meaning, by what right did he add, “nor do we desire them”? For what could be more desirable to Christians than to see an image of Christ’s cross, or to undergo the punishment of the cross for Christ? It may be answered that Minucius’s word “worship” refers to Caecilius’s earlier phrase “to be adored,” and “desire” to the words “crosses to be undergone,” so that the sense is: “We do not desire or seek crosses; [Col. 0533A] but if we are seized by tyrants and compelled to undergo them, we suffer with a willing spirit and desire to end our life by the punishment of the cross.” Tertullian speaks in the same sense: “Certainly we desire to suffer, but in the same way that no one willingly suffers war, since it is necessary both to fear and to incur danger; nevertheless, he fights with all his strength, and the man who complained of the battle rejoices when he conquers in it” (Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 50). But we cannot conceal that this second interpretation does some violence to Minucius’s words. For one and the same word will signify at once the mere sign of the cross and an actual cross. Consider, therefore, why the other interpretation should be preferred to this one.

Yet whatever judgment may be made concerning the meaning of these words of Minucius, it certainly cannot be denied that Christians [Col. 0533B] in his time rendered some honor to the sign of the Lord’s cross. For they placed it very frequently upon their foreheads; and Jerome exhorts the virgin Eustochium: “At every action, at every step, let your hand trace the Lord’s cross”; and another virgin: “Frequently fortify your forehead with the seal of the cross, lest the destroyer of Egypt find a place in you, but so that the firstborn who perish among the Egyptians may be preserved in your mind” (Jerome, Letter 18 to Eustochium, p. 46; and Letter 97 to Demetrias, p. 790). In our following dissertations we shall demonstrate that this Christian custom was far older, and we shall also note later, in another dissertation, that demons were very frequently driven away by Christians through this same sign of the cross ([Col. 0533C] *Dissertation on the Book of Lucius Caecilius, On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, ch. 5, arts. 2–3). What man of sound mind, therefore, will deny that Christians paid honor to the sign of Christ’s cross, with which they marked themselves very frequently, almost every hour, and by whose power they marveled that so many and such great miracles were wrought? Away, then, with Gronovius’s foolish comment on this passage of Minucius, in which he absurdly asserts that no honor should be paid to Christ’s cross. This matter must be treated again later; meanwhile you may consult Petavius, Thomassin, Gretser, and other theologians, whether scholastic theologians or controversialists (Petavius, vol. V, *Dogmatic Theology*, book XV, ch. 8; Thomassin, book XII, *Dogmatic Theology on the Incarnation*, ch. 8; *Theology on the Master of the Sentences*, book III, diss. 9; and *On St. Thomas*, part III, question 25).

## ARTICLE V. How Minucius turns back upon the pagans the weapon of those who charged Christians with worshipping the cross, since they honored crosses in the images of their gods, their *cantabra*, standards, and trophies; and how the sign of the cross is represented in ships’ swelling sails, in the yoke, and in a man praying with outstretched arms

[Col. 0533D]

Minucius was not satisfied merely to refute the pagans who reproached Christians for worshipping the cross; he also turns back upon them the very weapon they fashioned from that accusation: “You certainly consecrate wooden gods; perhaps you worship wooden crosses as parts of your gods. For your standards themselves, your *cantabra*”—some wrongly wish *labara* to be read [Col. 0534A]—“and your military banners: what else are they but gilded and decorated crosses? Your victorious trophies imitate not only the appearance of a simple cross, but even that of a man fastened to one.” Our author seems to have drawn this from Tertullian, who refutes in precisely the same way that empty pagan argument concerning the worship rendered by Christians to the cross: “He who considers us,” he says, “devotees of the cross will be our fellow-worshipper when he propitiates some piece of wood. Never mind its outward dress, so long as the material has the same quality; never mind its form, so long as it is the very body of a god. And yet how greatly are Attic Pallas and Pharian Ceres distinguished from the beam of a cross, when they stand without an image as a rough stake and shapeless piece of wood? Every piece of timber fixed upright is part of a cross; we, if anything, worship a whole [Col. 0534B] and complete god. We have said that the origin of your gods is fashioned by the modelers upon a cross. But you also adore Victories, since in trophies crosses are the inner framework of the trophies. The whole religion of the camp venerates the standards, swears by the standards, and sets the standards above all the gods. All those prominent arrangements of images are necklaces of crosses; those hanging cloths of the standards and *cantabra* are robes of crosses. I commend your diligence: you did not wish to consecrate naked and undecorated crosses” (Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 16, p. 17). The same points, repeated in different words in another book, may be read by everyone (ibid., *To the Nations*, book I, ch. 12, p. 58).

Why Minucius said that wooden crosses were worshipped by pagans as parts of their gods you will understand from these words of the same Tertullian: “The image of any god,” [Col. 0534C] he says, “is first molded in clay built up around a cross and stake. Upon a gibbet”—that is, a cross—“the body of your god is dedicated” (ibid., *Apology*, ch. 12, p. 14; *To the Nations*, book I, ch. 12, p. 58 ff.). He explains this more plainly and clearly in another book; but because his discussion there is rather long, we thought it better to refer you to the book itself. Yet it should not be passed over without observation that Minucius added the adverb “perhaps” before “you worship.” Did he perhaps refrain from asserting it absolutely because the pagans, while worshipping the images of their gods, did not direct their attention to the crosses placed beneath them? Or what if he said it ironically, and therefore affirmatively, as Tertullian did?

Before both of them, however, Justin Martyr [Col. 0534D] similarly charged the pagans that “military standards and victorious trophies” were crosses, as Minucius says, or, as Tertullian put it, “robes of crosses” (Justin, *First Apology*, p. 90). Since this is sufficiently well known to everyone, we shall add nothing further except these words of Jerome to Laeta: “The standards of soldiers bear the emblems of the cross” (Jerome, Letter 57 to Laeta, p. 591).

The *cantabra* mentioned by our author and Tertullian were standards adorned with purple and gold, which were carried through the city with images of the gods in processions and solemn ceremonies. There was no other distinction between *cantabra* and banners except that the latter were merely pieces of cloth, readily distinguished by their color; *cantabra*, however, were distinguished from them both by their color and by some verse [Col. 0535A] or name signifying something agreeable and pleasant.

“Trophies,” moreover, were captured spoils of the enemy, customarily hung upon two poles, one upright and the other transverse, and thus presenting the form of a cross. Those appointed to carry trophies were called *cantabrarii*, who are mentioned in the Theodosian Code; Gothofredus’s notes upon that passage should be read, along with Bullinger’s observations *On Gallic Spoils* (Theodosian Code, law 2, *On Guild Members*, vol. V, p. 192; Bullinger, *On Greek Spoils*, ch. 3).

Minucius continues and says that the sign of the cross is naturally seen in a ship driven along by swelling sails and in the yoke with which the earth is customarily plowed. Justin Martyr explains these points still more fully. Tertullian and Jerome likewise observed that a ship’s yardarm [Col. 0535B] is a sign of the cross (Tertullian, *Against the Jews*, ch. 11; Jerome, *Letter to Heliodorus*).

Another natural sign of the cross is a man “with outstretched hands,” as Tertullian says, or, as our Minucius puts it: “A man who, with hands extended, worships God with a pure mind” (Tertullian, *To the Nations*, book II, ch. 12).

But to what purpose, you will ask, did he argue against the pagans from this example? Did those pagans also pour out prayers with outstretched hands? Indeed they did; and not only prayers but also their vows in this rite, as may very easily be proved by very many testimonies from writers of every kind. Virgil, for example, sang of Anchises:

[Col. 0535C]

> But father Anchises joyfully raised his eyes  
> To the stars, and stretched his palms toward heaven with his voice:  
> “Almighty Jupiter, if you are moved by any prayers,” etc.  
> (Virgil, *Aeneid*, book II, v. 687 ff.)

And in the following book:

> I snatch my body from the bed, and stretch up  
> My upturned hands toward heaven with my voice, and offer  
> Untainted gifts upon the hearths.  
> (Virgil, *Aeneid*, book III, v. 176 ff.)

A little later he says that the divine powers were invoked by the same Anchises with open—that is, extended—hands:

> But father Anchises, from the shore with open palms,  
> Invokes the mighty divine powers.  
> (Ibid., v. 263.) [Col. 0535D]

Why say more? Elsewhere he sang of another:

> Unaware of events and ungrateful for his deliverance, he looks back,  
> And stretches both hands toward the stars with his voice:  
> “Almighty Father,” etc.  
> (Ibid., book X, v. 666 ff.)

Ovid likewise writes of a ship’s captain during a storm:

> The helmsman himself, lifting his palms toward the stars,  
> Forgetful of his art, sought help through vows.  
> (Ovid, *Tristia*, book I, elegy 10.)

And elsewhere:

> . . . . . . . . Here he adores the divine power with vows,  
> And, lifting ineffectual arms toward the heaven he cannot see,  
> Begs for help.  
> (Ibid., *Metamorphoses*, book II, 58.)

If you desire more, Brissonius will supply it for you (Brissonius, [Col. 0536A] *On Formulae*, book II, pp. 44 and 118). Not only the Gentiles, however, but Moses also, while the Israelites were fighting against the Amalekites, “when he raised” his hands, namely toward heaven, and prayed to God for them, “Israel prevailed” (Exodus 17:11).

Tertullian plainly teaches that Christians had the same custom: “Looking up there”—that is, to heaven—“Christians,” he says, pray “with hands outstretched, because they are innocent; with head uncovered, because we are not ashamed; finally, without a prompter, because we pray from the heart” (Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 30). In another book he also writes: “We, however, not only raise our hands but even spread them out, shaping them after the Lord’s Passion, and in prayer we confess Christ” (ibid., *On Prayer*, ch. 11). But these words of Tertullian will be discussed in their proper place.

[Col. 0536B] Ambrose also, when describing the martyrdom of the most holy Agnes, says: “If she were dragged unwillingly to the altars, she would stretch out her hands to Christ amid the flames and, upon the very sacrilegious hearths, trace the trophy of the victorious Lord”—that is, the sign of the Lord’s cross, as we have noted there (Ambrose, *On Virgins*, book II, ch. 2, § 7, p. 148).

Finally, to pass over many others, Prudentius sang that the bonds fell from the hands of the martyrs Fructuosus, Aurelius, and Eulogius as they raised them to God amid the flames:

> The punishment did not dare restrain the palms  
> That were to be raised to the Father in the form of a cross;  
> It released the arms that they might pray to God.  
> (Prudentius, *Hymn on Fructuosus*, etc., p. 187.)

[Col. 0536C] Nor is this surprising, since Paul had written in his First Letter to Timothy: “I desire men to pray in every place, lifting up pure hands” (Paul, First Letter to Timothy 2:8).

Our author therefore rightly concludes from these things: “Thus either natural reason rests upon the sign of the cross, or your”—that is, the Gentiles’—“religion is fashioned by it.”

# CHAPTER XIII. FURTHER HEADS OF CAECILIUS’S MOST UNJUST ACCUSATIONS ARE EXAMINED

## ARTICLE I. With what great injustice Caecilius blamed Christians for abstaining from respectable pleasures, spectacles, processions, circus and gladiatorial games, and the shameful scenes of the theater

[Col. 0536D]

Caecilius charges Christians with other things as though they were disgraces and crimes, although these should have been imputed to them as reproach and fault all the less precisely because they made their piety and holiness all the more manifest to everyone. Yet no one will wonder at the extraordinary insolence of an accusation of this kind if he observes that impious men have always found it difficult to endure having their wicked and utterly shameful works reproved and condemned by the outstanding and exceptional holiness of Christians. But come, let us see what Caecilius dared to reproach them for.

Christians, he said, abstain from respectable pleasures. [Col. 0537A] O great crime! What wonder is it, I ask you, if a Christian, who must carry his cross daily in following his crucified Lord, flees every pleasure? Have we not learned from Clement of Alexandria that pleasure, ἡδονή (*hēdonē*), is defined by the pagan philosophers themselves as ἔπαρσιν ψυχῆς ἀπειθῆ λόγῳ, “an elevation of the soul disobedient to reason” (Clement of Alexandria, *Paedagogus*, book I, ch. 13, p. 135)? We have also observed that Clement taught that desire is the beginning of every pleasure and that, conversely, desire is generated by pleasure (vol. I, *Apparatus*, book III, diss. 2, ch. 21, art. 2, p. 1024). Therefore, every Christian must always flee it as far as possible. What of the fact that Cicero, although a pagan, concludes the books in which he instructs his son in the cultivation of duty [Col. 0537B] as follows? “We say that every pleasure is contrary to moral worth . . . . For even if we grant something to pleasure, it will perhaps possess a little of seasoning, but certainly nothing of usefulness” (Cicero, *On Duties*, book III, p. 404 ff.).

Nevertheless, so as not to irritate Caecilius’s mind too greatly, our Minucius modestly replied that Christians “abstain from evil pleasures,” which the pagans indulged as though they were respectable and lawful.

Tell us, then, Caecilius, what are those respectable pleasures from which you contend it is wicked for Christians to abstain? “You do not attend spectacles,” he addresses them, “you take no part in processions; public banquets proceed without you; you abhor sacred contests, food previously tasted, [Col. 0537C] and drinks poured as libations upon altars.” But this truly novel and extraordinary kind of charge did not in the least dismay or disturb Minucius. For he freely acknowledges that Christians flee and abhor all these things as harmful, impious, and opposed to modesty and chaste morals.

As regards spectacles and processions, he says: “We, who are judged by our modesty and morals, abstain from evil pleasures, from your processions and spectacles, whose origin in sacred rites we know, and whose harmful allurements we condemn.” Tertullian had earlier spoken in an entirely similar manner: “We likewise renounce your spectacles to the same extent that we renounce their origins, which we know were conceived from superstition. Indeed, we also take no part in the very matters represented in them” (Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 38, p. [Col. 0537D] 34). What those origins of the spectacles were, and how they arose from idolatry and the impious worship of false gods, he clearly explained in his book *On Spectacles* (Tertullian, *On Spectacles*, ch. 5 ff., p. 91 ff.), where you may read more about those same spectacles and their prohibition, as also throughout other works of the holy Fathers.

Someone may well say so. But what are the “processions” (*pompae*) mentioned afterward by Minucius, which Christians avoided no less than the spectacles? *Pompa* is called πομπή in Greek, from the verb πέμπω, which in Latin means “I send,” “lead forth,” or “convey.” It was a solemn public procession and conveyance through the streets of cities, customarily held at triumphs, supplications, and other solemnities, especially the circus games. [Col. 0538A] In it, chosen men advanced, each in his proper order, together with flute-players and others; at the very end, images of the gods were carried. Hence Macrobius says: “Images of the gods are borne on a carrying-frame in the procession of the circus games” (Macrob., *Saturnalia*, book I, ch. 23). Tertullian likewise says: “The ceremonial apparatus of the circus games is somewhat more pompous. These games, to which this name properly belongs, are preceded by a procession; whose procession it is, it proves in itself by the sequence of idols, the train of images, the chariots, the sacred cars, the covered wagons, the seats, the crowns, and the spoils. Moreover, how many rites and sacrifices precede, intervene, and follow; how many colleges, priesthoods, and offices are set in motion—the people of that city know, in which the assembly of demons has established its seat” (Tertullian, *On the Spectacles*, ch. 7, p. [Col. 0538B] 93). He reported certain further details elsewhere. But you will find all these matters described individually and graphically by Dionysius of Halicarnassus (the same, *On Idolatry*, ch. 11, p. 110; Dionysius of Halicarnassus, *Roman Antiquities*, book VII, p. 475 ff.). We have also made some notes on them in our annotations on certain books of Ambrose (Ambrose, *Exposition of Psalm 118*, sermon V, and *On Duties*, book I, ch. 18, § 73, p. 21).

Although from this, and especially from Tertullian’s words, it is easy to understand why those spectacles of the pagans were forbidden to Christians, our author nevertheless gives certain specific reasons for this prohibition: “For at the chariot games,” he says, “who would not shudder at the madness of the people quarreling among themselves; at the gladiatorial games, [Col. 0538C] the training in homicide; and even on the stage, no less frenzy and more protracted obscenity?” In the royal manuscript the reading is “no less in frenzy” (*non minor furore*), a sense by no means absurd. However that may be, Tertullian had preceded our author in his *Apologeticum*, where we similarly read: “We have nothing to do with the madness of the circus, the shamelessness of the theater, the savagery of the arena, or the vanity of the wrestling-ground.” Again elsewhere he said: “Why do you not frequent those solemn pleasures—the raging circus, the savage amphitheater, and the wanton stage?” Finally, in yet another book: “Even the faithful man perishes when he slips away into the spectacle of chariot-racing frenzy, gladiatorial bloodshed, theatrical foulness, and athletic vanity; into the games and banquets of a secular solemnity; into the service and ministry of another’s idolatry” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, [Col. 0538D] ch. 38, p. 34; the same, *Against Marcion*, book I, ch. 27, p. 451; *On Modesty*, ch. 7, p. 722). Hence Jerome writes the following to Marcella: “Let Rome keep her riots to herself; let the arena rage, the circus run mad, and the theaters luxuriate.” For “one who believes in the Lord Jesus,” as he said elsewhere of Saint Hilarion, “takes no delight in the frenzies of the circus, the blood of the arena, or the licentiousness of the theater” (Jerome, Epistle 45, to Marcella, p. 554; and *Life of Hilarion*, p. 75).

Moreover, in the already cited book *On the Spectacles*, after Tertullian had made clear to everyone what the circus was, why it was so named, and what took place there, he then clearly explained what these words of our author—“the madness of the people quarreling among themselves”—mean: [Col. 0539A] “When frenzy,” he says, “is forbidden to us, we are excluded from every spectacle, even from the circus, where frenzy properly presides. Look at the people coming to the spectacle already in a frenzy, already tumultuous, already blind, already excited by their wagers. The praetor is too slow for them; their eyes are forever rolling about with the lots in his urn. Then they hang anxiously upon the signal; one cry comes from a single madness. I recognize madness from its vanity: ‘He has sent it!’ they say, and they announce to one another what was seen simultaneously by everyone. I have proof of their blindness. They do not see what has been sent: they think it is the napkin, but it is the figure of the devil cast down from on high”—another reading has “gluttony” (*gula*). “From that point they proceed into rages, passions, dissensions, and everything forbidden to the priests of peace. Hence curses and insults [Col. 0539B] without justice, and even votes of hatred without any deserved ground for love” (Tertullian, *On the Spectacles*, ch. 8, p. 93; ibid., ch. 16, p. 97). He adds more, which you should not begrudge the effort to read. You may also consult what he added about those same spectacles, where, like Martial, Suetonius, and others, he mentioned the napkin (*mappa*), which, according to some, the praetor customarily sent to the victor, or, as others prefer, which served as the signal for beginning the games (Juvenal, end of Satire 11; Martial, book XII, Epigram 29; Suetonius, *Life of Nero*, § 22). The author of the iambic poem published among the works of Gregory Nazianzen describes in detail the frenzy of the circus—its anger, quarrels, insults, hatred, fights, wounds, and killings (Gregory Nazianzen, *Iambic Poem* 3, p. 292).

[Col. 0539C] The “training in homicide” which Minucius next notes “at the gladiatorial games” is explained more clearly by Cyprian: “A gladiatorial show,” says that most holy martyr, “is prepared, so that blood may delight the lust of cruel eyes. The body is filled out into flesh with richer foods, and the robust mass of its limbs grows fat with layers of grease, so that, fattened for punishment, the man may perish at a higher price. A human being is killed for a human being’s pleasure; and the ability to kill is a skill, a practice, an art. Crime is not merely committed but also taught. What can be called more inhuman or more cruel? It is training, so that someone may be able to perish; and glory, because he kills” (Cyprian, *To Donatus*, p. 5). See further, if you please, Tatian, Arnobius, Lactantius, Prudentius, and what we have observed elsewhere about those gladiatorial contests [Col. 0539D] (Tatian, *Oration Against the Greeks*, p. 161; Arnobius, book II, p. 72; Lactantius, book VI, ch. 20, p. 617; Prudentius, *Against Symmachus*, book II, p. 429; in the hymn on Saints Fructuosus, Augurius, etc., p. 135; and *Hamartigenia*, p. 322; vol. I of the *Apparatus*, p. 800).

Finally, concerning theatrical obscenities, Cyprian likewise expounds somewhat more fully what our author said: “In the theaters,” he says, “you will see what must cause you both grief and shame. The tragic buskin recounts the crimes of ancient poems: the old error concerning parricides and incest is reenacted in a performance fashioned after the likeness of reality, lest the crime once committed fade from the memory of passing generations. Every gathering is reminded by hearing that what was done can be done. . . . Then, in the mimes, one delights, under the instruction of obscenities, [Col. 0540A] either to recognize what he has done at home or to learn what he might do. Adultery is learned while it is watched; and through the evil of public authority acting as a procurer for vice, the matron who perhaps went to the spectacle chaste returns from the spectacle unchaste. . . . They portray a shameless Venus, an adulterous Mars, and that Jupiter of theirs, chief no more in sovereignty than in vices. . . . They imitate the gods whom they venerate; and for these wretched people, crimes become religious acts as well” (Cyprian, ibid., p. 5 ff.).

Earlier, however, Tertullian had said: “We separate ourselves from the theater,” he says, “because it is the private council-chamber of shamelessness. . . . Its highest appeal has been elaborately fashioned chiefly from filthiness: such filthiness the Atellan farce acts out; the mime even represents it through women, destroying the shame proper to their sex, [Col. 0540B] so that they blush more readily at home than on stage; and the pantomime suffers it in his body from childhood, so that he may become an artist. Even prostitutes themselves, victims of public lust, are brought forward on the stage, etc.” (Tertullian, *On the Spectacles*, ch. 17, p. 98). Before both of them, Theophilus of Antioch and Clement of Alexandria—and afterward Lactantius, Jerome, the author of the iambic poem ascribed to Gregory Nazianzen, and others—rightly and deservedly inveighed against these theatrical obscenities. Who, moreover, does not know that the tragedies and comedies of pagan poets, both Greek and Latin, teem with such things, and that, to the ruin of many, they have remained in print far longer than many extremely useful works of the ancient Fathers of the Church? (Theophilus, *To Autolycus*, book III, [Col. 0540C] p. 126 ff.; Clement of Alexandria, *Paedagogus*, book II, ch. 6, p. 169, and book II, ch. 11, p. 254; Lactantius, *Institutes*, book VI, ch. 20, p. 619 ff.; Jerome, Epistle 18, to Marcella; in Gregory Nazianzen, vol. II, p. 191.)

## ARTICLE II. How Minucius replies to Caecilius’ other reproaches—that Christians did not take part in public banquets and sacred contests, and abstained from foods offered to idols—where it is shown what those public banquets of the pagans were and how greatly they differed from those of the Christians
