Caecilius reproaches the Christians for three further reasons: because they refused to celebrate public banquets with the pagans, to take part in their sacred contests, and to taste beforehand foods and drinks from which portions had been offered [Col. 0540D] to the gods. If you wish to know what those pagan banquets were and why they were instituted, these words of Tertullian will instruct you: “A great duty indeed—to bring hearths as well as couches out into public, to feast street by street, to make the city reek with the atmosphere of a tavern, to turn mud into mire with wine, and to run about in gangs committing outrages, shameless acts, and enticements to lust. Is public joy expressed in this fashion through public disgrace? Are such solemn days becoming to emperors, when they are unbecoming to everyone else? Will those who observe discipline out of respect for Caesar abandon it on Caesar’s account? Will license for bad behavior count as loyalty, and an occasion for extravagance be reckoned religion?” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 35).

From these and other words of his, anyone may readily understand [Col. 0541A] that those banquets were celebrated with the utmost disgrace on the solemn days of emperors and Caesars—namely, their birthdays, as he relates elsewhere; likewise their quinquennial celebrations, which we have touched upon briefly; their decennial and vicennial celebrations; at the beginning of each year, as will be explained in its proper place; and with the greatest solemnity at triumphs (Tertullian, *To His Wife*, book II, ch. 6; *On the Spectacles*, ch. 6; *Dissertation on Lucius Caecilius*, chs. 8 and 13, arts. 7 and 3).

With no less corruption of morals, the pagans also held other banquets on certain fixed festivals of the gods. Such indeed were those of which the same Tertullian says: “I do not recline at a public banquet during the Liberalia, as is customary for beast-fighters taking their final meal” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 42, p. 38). [Col. 0541B] For this reason Christians utterly abhorred them as impious and polluted by the vice of idolatry. Indeed, Bishop Martialis, as Cyprian attests, was convicted of idolatry because he had frequented the shameful and filthy banquets of the pagans (Cyprian, Epistle 67, p. 173).

Accordingly, since Minucius well knew that no pious person could be ignorant of these matters, he judged that no other reply need be made to Caecilius’ unjust rebuke than to demonstrate to him and all other pagans how greatly our banquets differed from theirs: “The banquets we hold,” he says, “are not merely chaste but also sober. For we neither indulge in feasting nor prolong the banquet with unmixed wine, but temper our cheerfulness with gravity.” We have already touched somewhat upon these matters and shall discuss them more fully in the following discourse on Tertullian’s *Apologeticum* [Col. 0541C] (vol. I of the *Apparatus*, book II, dissertation 1, ch. 6, art. 4, p. 715).

We have discussed the “sacred contests,” as Caecilius calls them, in the first volume of our *Apparatus* and in the preceding article, where we dealt with gladiators and spectacles (vol. I of the *Apparatus*, pp. 774 and 800). Minucius, moreover, seems to have answered this reproach with nothing beyond what we observed in the cited passage of that same *Apparatus*. What has been said sufficiently shows how dreadful their cruelty was.

The third heading of Caecilius’ reproach is that Christians refused to taste foods from which portions had been offered to the gods. Minucius readily admits this and at the same time gives the reason for such abstinence: “As for the fact,” he says, “that we disdain the remains of sacrifices [Col. 0541D] and cups from which libations have been made, it is not a confession of fear but an assertion of true liberty. For although everything that comes into being, as the inviolable gift of God, is corrupted by no act, we nevertheless abstain, lest anyone think either that we are yielding to the demons to whom the libation was made or that we are ashamed of our religion.”

Although Minucius, as we have already noted, never argued against the pagans who despised our Sacred Scripture by expressly appealing to its authority, and therefore passes over entirely in silence the law enacted by the Apostles concerning abstention from things offered to idols, he nevertheless seems to allude to what Paul taught concerning it and the reason for this abstinence in the First Epistle to the Corinthians (1 Cor. 8:1 ff.; 10:19 ff.). Tertullian, however, did not hesitate to cite Paul’s very words [Col. 0542A] on this matter: “Nor,” he says, “do we eat food offered in sacrifice or at funeral rites, because I cannot eat the Lord’s supper and the supper of demons” (Tertullian, *On the Spectacles*, ch. 13). Finally, Clement of Alexandria had earlier handed down much that is entirely consonant with what our author said (Clement of Alexandria, *Paedagogus*, book II, ch. 10, p. 213).

Celsus, however, in Origen pressed the Christians more sharply with this so-called *argumentum ad hominem*: “If idols are nothing,” as the Christians maintained, “what harm is there in enjoying the feasts?” But Origen completely overturned that futile argument by means of the words of Paul’s Epistle to the Corinthians already cited by us, and added: “Even if there are demons to whom the victims are sacrificed, we ought not to become participants in their sacrifices, [Col. 0542B] ἐπισταμένους διαφορὰν τραπέζης Κυρίου, καὶ τραπέζης δαιμονίων· καὶ διὰ τὸ ἐπίστασθαι, πάντα μὲν πράττοντας, ἵνα τραπέζης Κυρίου ἀεὶ μετέχωμεν· παντὶ δὲ τρόπῳ φυλαττομένους, ἵνα μηδέ ποτε κοινωνοὶ γινώμεθα τραπέζης δαιμονίων—knowing the difference between the table of the Lord and the table of demons; and, because we know it, doing everything so that we may always partake of the Lord’s table, while guarding ourselves by every means lest we ever become sharers in the table of demons” (Origen, *Against Celsus*, book VIII, p. 394). See Cyril of Alexandria replying to a similar argument advanced by Julian the Apostate, and Cyril of Jerusalem, Oecumenius, Estius, and other interpreters of Scripture on the cited words of the Apostle (Cyril of Alexandria, *Against Julian*, book VII, [Col. 0542C] p. 233; Cyril of Jerusalem, *Catechesis* 4, p. 34).

## ARTICLE III. An examination of Caecilius’ other reproaches, in which he censures Christians because they did not adorn their heads with flowers or their bodies with perfumes, reserved ointments for funerals, denied crowns to the dead, and did not cremate but buried their bodies; including a discussion of the custom of burying bodies and its antiquity

Caecilius reproaches Christians for other practices that were far more worthy of praise than blame: “You do not,” he says, “bind your heads with flowers; you do not adorn your bodies with perfumes; you reserve ointments for funerals; you deny crowns even to tombs.” That accusation is threefold, [Col. 0542D] as you see. Minucius replies to the first charge that Christians rightly and deservedly reject not the legitimate use of flowers, but the abuse of crowns. Hear, I ask, his words: “Who is there who doubts that we enjoy the flowers of spring, since we gather both the spring rose and the lily and whatever other flower possesses an attractive color and fragrance? We use them both scattered, soft and loose, and woven into garlands with which we encircle our necks. As for the fact that we do not crown our heads, pardon us: we are accustomed to draw in the breath of a lovely flower through our nostrils, not to inhale it through the back of the head or the hair.”

Here, however, he seems to follow Tertullian as a predecessor, who had dispelled this absurd pagan accusation with a precisely similar answer: “I do not care for a crown upon my head,” he says; “what concern is that of yours? Having bought the flowers all the same, how shall I use them? I think they are more pleasing free, loose, and [Col. 0543A] wandering everywhere; but even if gathered into a crown, we know the crown by our nostrils. Let those who smell through their hair see to it” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 42, p. 38). But in another book he pursued the matter more fully, showing that the use of flowers is lawful, provided their color and fragrance are perceived by no senses other than sight and smell, which divine Providence appointed for this purpose: “Use flowers,” he says, “by sight and smell, for that is the fruit proper to those senses. . . . But what savor of a flower is there in the head? What perception does a crown afford except only that of a bond, by which neither the color is seen, nor the fragrance inhaled, nor even the rashness approved? It is as contrary to nature to pursue a flower with one’s head as food with one’s ear or sound with one’s nose. Everything contrary to nature deserves among all people the designation of monstrosity, but among us also the verdict [Col. 0543B] of sacrilege against God, the Lord and Author of nature” (the same, *On the Crown*, ch. 5, p. 123). Indeed, even in Lucian, though he was a pagan, those who wore crowns are censured, ὅτι μὴ ἴσασι τοῦ στεφάνου τὸν τόπον, “because they did not know the proper place for the crown”—where it should be put (Lucian, *Dialogue on the Conduct of Philosophers*, p. 24).

Justin Martyr, however, gave another reason why Christians disapproved of the use of crowns: because pagans customarily bestowed them upon lifeless images of the gods (Justin, *Apology* 2, p. 57). Moreover, Tertullian, whom we have just commended, proves by various arguments that the origin of that custom derived from the impious worship of those gods. He later added: “By this we may be sufficiently instructed how alien we ought to judge the [Col. 0543C] institution of the crowned head, approved by them and thereafter administered in their honor,” just as he shows in yet another book, “whom the world believed to be gods” (Tertullian, *On the Crown*, chs. 7 ff., pp. 124 ff.; and *On the Spectacles*, chs. 7, 11, and 12, pp. 93 and 95). Therefore Cyprian, his follower, congratulated Christ’s confessors with these words: “Your head remained free from the impious and criminal covering with which the captive heads of those sacrificing there were veiled. The forehead made pure by the sign of God could not bear the devil’s crown; it reserved itself for the Lord’s crown” (Cyprian, *On the Lapsed*, p. 122). Consult further, if you please, Mader’s special book *On Crowns*, and, if you wish, what we said about them in the preceding volume of our *Apparatus*, as well as what must still be said later (vol. I of the *Apparatus*, p. 801 [Col. 0543D] ff.; and below, ch. 19, art. 2).

But Caecilius and other pagans blamed Christians on this ground not only because they denied crowns to the living, but also because they denied them to the dead: “You deny crowns,” he said, “even to tombs.” What, then, does Octavius say to this? He readily concedes that it is entirely true and marvels that the dead are crowned by the pagans: “I marvel at you all the more in this,” he says, “how you bestow upon a lifeless person either a torch, or upon one who does not feel a crown, since the blessed person does not need flowers and the wretched person cannot rejoice in them” (ibid., p. 341). But many consider the text of our author corrupt here; in some editions the particle *non* (“not”) and the noun *exanimi* (“lifeless person”) have been omitted. This correction, however, conflicts with the manuscript codex [Col. 0544A] and increases the difficulty rather than removing it. It appears contrary to Minucius’ thought. For it is not remarkable that a torch should be given to one who “feels,” but that it should be given to a dead person, who can see nothing. If the codex’s reading is preserved, our author’s meaning seems to be: “I indeed wonder why you bestow crowns upon one who does not feel and is dead.” For that is no less absurd than bringing a torch to one “lifeless,” and therefore insensible. A dead person is either “blessed” or “wretched”: if blessed and enjoying eternal felicity, he has no need of flowers; if wretched and tormented by eternal punishments, he cannot rejoice in flowers, since he can be affected by no sensation of joy.

By this argument he assails the pagans, who not only customarily crowned the dead, [Col. 0544B] but had even been commanded to do so by a most ancient law. If you wish, you may have Cicero as witness, where he discusses the laws of the Twelve Tables: “That provision,” he says, “is already an indication that the ornaments of praise pertain to the dead, since the law commands that a crown won by valor may without penalty be placed both upon the man who had not won it and upon his parent” (Cicero, *On the Laws*, book II, p. 341, line 39). Pliny teaches when it was to be placed: “What honor, then,” he says, “was it that it might without penalty be placed upon the dead man himself and his parents, while he was laid out indoors or was being carried outside?” (Pliny, *Natural History*, book XXI, ch. 3, p. 107)—that is, while the dead man’s body was kept at home and was then carried out and the funeral procession held. Lucian also wrote of all the dead: Στεφανώσαντες ὡραίοις ἄνθεσι προτίθενται λαμπρῶς ἀμφιέσαντες, [Col. 0544C] “Having crowned them with the loveliest flowers and splendidly clothed them, they lay them out” (Lucian, *On Mourning*, p. 810). But he ridicules and rejects this custom and other pagan burial rites. Why, then, should Christians not have rejected that use of crowns, which we have discussed elsewhere? (Vol. I of the *Apparatus*, book III, dissertation I, ch. 19, art. 6, p. 802 ff.) Minucius gives this reason why they rejected it: “But we adorn funerals with the same tranquility with which we live; nor do we attach a withering crown, but await from God one living with eternal flowers” (Minucius, p. 342); that is, we expect it.

Although Christians did not encircle the heads of the dead with any crown, they nevertheless customarily anointed their bodies with ointments (ibid., p. 98). For what could be more fitting than that they should imitate the example, set before them by the Evangelist, of Christ’s anointed body [Col. 0544D] (John 19:39 ff.)? Nor did Caecilius dare to condemn this custom. For when, as Pliny says, the use of ointments had reached them in the time of Darius, “then the honor began to be extended to the dead as well” (Pliny, *Natural History*, book XIII, ch. 1, p. 56). Let us hear, then, what Caecilius himself censures in Christians: “You do not adorn the body with perfumes; you reserve ointments for funerals” (Minucius, p. 97). Thus he reproaches them not because they poured ointments over the dead, but because they did not anoint themselves while still alive. Octavius, however, scorning this wholly perverse accusation, appears to have made no reply to it, unless perhaps in what he had said in the same passage: that Christians did not reject the lawful use of flowers and therefore also of ointments, but rather the intolerable pagan abuse of them, as we have shown elsewhere [Col. 0545A] (vol. I of the *Apparatus*, pp. 803 ff.). Tertullian, moreover, related more concerning the pious and praiseworthy Christian rite of anointing dead bodies; this must be examined by us in its proper place.

Lastly, Caecilius attacks Christians for still observing the ancient custom of burying the dead: “They execrate funeral pyres and burials by fire, as though every body, even if withdrawn from the flames, were not nevertheless dissolved into earth through years and ages; and as though it made any difference whether wild beasts tear it apart, the seas consume it, the soil covers it, or flame removes it. If corpses possess feeling, every burial is a punishment; if they do not, the very speed with which they are destroyed is a remedy” (Minucius, p. 97 [Col. 0545B] ff.). We have already observed that these words were drawn from Seneca (above, ch. 2, art. 5).

What does Minucius reply to such insipid mockery? “Nor, as you believe,” he says, “do we fear any harm from the mode of burial; rather, we maintain the ancient and better custom of interment” (Minucius, p. 255). If you doubt that the custom of burying corpses was indeed the most ancient and best, Cicero will teach you in these words: “For my part, the most ancient kind of burial appears to me to have been that which Cyrus uses in Xenophon. The body is returned to the earth, and when thus placed and laid out it is covered, as it were, by the covering of its mother. We have learned that our King Numa [Col. 0545C] was laid to rest by the same rite in that tomb not far from the altar of Fontus; and we know that the Cornelian clan practiced this burial by interment down to our own memory. Sulla, when victorious, ordered the remains of Gaius Marius, laid beside the Anio, to be scattered. . . . Perhaps fearing that this might happen to his own body, he was the first of the patrician Cornelii who wished to be cremated by fire” (Cicero, *On the Laws*, book II, p. 340, line 45 ff.).

Concerning Numa, Plutarch also handed down the following for remembrance: “His body, in accordance with his command, as the report goes, πυρὶ μὲν οὐκ ἔδοσαν τὸν νεκρὸν, αὐτοῦ κωλύσαντος· δύο δὲ ποιησάμενοι λιθίνας σορούς, ὑπὸ τὸν Ἰανικλὸν, τὴν μὲν ἑτέραν ἔχουσαν τὸ σῶμα—they did not give the corpse to the fire, since he himself had forbidden it; instead, they made two stone chests and buried them beneath the Janiculum, one of which contained his body” (Plutarch, *Life of Numa*, p. 74). From these accounts, therefore, [Col. 0545D] it is clear that the custom of burying corpses was extremely ancient. Pliny likewise subscribed to this view, as is evident from these words of his: “Cremation itself was not an ancient institution among the Romans: the dead were buried in the earth. But after they learned that those buried in distant wars were being dug up, cremation was then instituted. And yet many families preserved the ancient rites; thus, in the Cornelian family, no one is reported to have been cremated before the dictator Sulla. He wished this because he feared retaliation after Gaius Marius’ corpse had been dug up. But *sepultus* should be understood of one laid to rest in any manner whatever; *humatus*, of one covered with earth” (Pliny, *Natural History*, book VII, ch. 54, pp. 91 ff.). As you see, he follows Cicero κατὰ πόδα, “step by step,” and clearly explains the difference between *sepultura* (“burial” in the general sense) and *humatio* (“interment in earth”).

The same Cicero bears witness that this custom prevailed not only among [Col. 0546A] the Romans but also among other nations. He committed the following concerning the Egyptians, Persians, and Magi to writing and memory: “The Egyptians embalm the dead and keep them at home. The Persians also preserve them after coating them with wax, so that the bodies may endure as long as possible. It is the custom of the Magi not to bury the bodies of their people unless they have first been torn by wild beasts” (Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations*, book I, p. 133, line 23). He adds that the Hyrcanians considered it the best burial when the corpses of the dead were torn apart by dogs.

Concerning the Athenians, he records the following in the second book *On the Laws* cited by us: “At Athens, that custom, as they say, endured from Cecrops: the established practice of burying in the earth. After the nearest relatives had done this and the earth had been drawn over the body, it was sown with crops, so that the bosom and lap, [Col. 0546B] as it were, of a mother might be granted to the dead person; while the ground, purified by the crops, might be restored to the living” (ibid., *On the Laws*, book II, p. 342, line 9). Nor should Servius be passed over, who observes the following in his commentary on the sixth book of the *Aeneid*: “Those who have written on the kinds of piety wished the first place to belong to burial. Hence, although it was unlawful for pontiffs to look upon a corpse, it was nevertheless a greater violation if, after seeing one, they left it unburied. One kind of burial was the casting of dust upon it. Hence the verse: ‘Or cast earth upon me, for you can.’ Horace says: ‘There is no long delay; you may run on after casting dust three times’” (Servius on *Aeneid* VI.175 ff., p. 409; and on book II, pp. 618–19). But he discusses the matter elsewhere as well; consult him, together with [Col. 0546C] Macrobius, who openly testifies that in his own age there was no custom of burning the bodies of the dead (Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, book VII, ch. 7). In another book, however, he wrote that the institutions of very many nations or regions ordained that the bodies of the dead should not be carried to burial without song (*Commentary on the Dream of Scipio*, book II, ch. 3). Lilius Gyraldus discusses at greater length the various rites of burial in a special book written on that subject; Alexander ab Alexandro in the sixth book of his *Days of Genius*; and Tiraquellus in his annotations on that book.

## ARTICLE IV. How holy the morals of Christians were and how corrupt those of the pagans; why Caecilius calls the Christians’ discipline inferior; how greatly those same Christians surpassed the pagan philosophers in piety and learning; yet that pagans and Christians were friends and addressed one another by the name of brothers

[Col. 0546D]

From what has thus far been said, it can be obscure to no one how falsely Caecilius boasted—as he himself later rightly acknowledged—that throughout his entire speech he had proved Christians to be people not merely rude and uneducated, but also impious and defiled by the greatest crimes, hitherto unheard of. Octavius, however, further refutes this great calumny, already more than sufficiently answered, with these words: “If we Christians are compared with you”—that is, the pagans—“although in some respects our discipline is inferior, we shall nevertheless be found far better than you.” By these words [Col. 0547A] he confidently asserts that Christian morals were far purer and holier than those of the pagans.

But someone will ask: what does Octavius mean when he says, “In some respects our discipline is inferior” to that of the pagans? These words may have a twofold meaning. First: although among certain indolent and slothful Christians our discipline is inferior, these Christians are nevertheless better than the pagans. The second meaning is this: Christians are found better than the pagans, although in certain matters their discipline is inferior to that of the pagans—for example, in the multitude of laws, ceremonies pertaining to the worship of the gods and to religion, temples, altars, sacrifices, processions, the use of crowns, and other rites that we have discussed above. Consider whether this latter meaning may appear better than the former, because Minucius compares Christians with pagans, not Christians with themselves.

[Col. 0547B] How upright, chaste, and religious the morals of Christians were, and how corrupt, depraved, and wicked those of the pagans, Minucius—or Octavius in his name—shows by a brief comparison, which Tertullian pursues at greater length (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 46, p. 39 ff.): “You,” he says, “forbid adultery and commit it; we are born as men only for our own wives.” Tertullian, whom we have just cited, confirms this by the example of Speusippus: “I hear,” he says, “that a certain Speusippus of Plato’s school perished in the act of adultery; the Christian is born a male for his own wife alone” (Tertullian, passage cited, p. 40). But we have already related certain matters concerning the chastity of Christians and the infamous [Col. 0547C] shamelessness of the pagans (above, ch. 10, arts. 1 and 2; and ch. 16, art. 2), and shall say more below.

Minucius then continues: “You punish crimes once committed; among us, even to think of sin is to sin. You fear witnesses; we fear even conscience alone, without which we cannot exist.” Tertullian, however, says: “Democritus, by blinding himself because he could not look upon women without desire and suffered pain if he did not possess them, confesses his incontinence by his correction of it. But the Christian, while keeping his eyes unharmed, does not see women: he is blind in mind against lust” (Tertullian, passage cited, p. 40). This requires no proof. For who does not know the law established by Christ: “Everyone who looks at [Col. 0547D] a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. 5:28)? From this Tertullian concludes that divine law is more perfect than human law: “Which is more perfect,” he says, “to prohibit adultery, or to restrain even from the solitary lust of the eyes?” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 44, p. 39). But more on these matters in the following dissertations (*Dissertations on Tertullian*, ch. 12, art. 4).

Finally, our author added the following concerning accused persons cast into prison: “The prison seethes with people of your number; no Christian is there unless he is either accused on account of his religion or a deserter from it.” These words agree so closely with Tertullian’s that they appear to have been excerpted and transferred from him. For he says: “So many criminals are enumerated among you under the indictments of various crimes: what murderer there, [Col. 0548A] what cutpurse, what temple-robber, what corrupter, or what thief among bathers, is also recorded as a Christian? Or, when Christians are brought forward under their own designation, which of them is also such as all those criminals? It is always from your people that the prison seethes; always from your people that the mines groan; always on your people that the beasts are fattened; always from your people that the providers of public shows feed their herds of condemned criminals. No Christian is there unless for this alone; or if for something else as well, he is now no longer a Christian” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 45, p. 39). That is: no Christian was cast into prison on account of any crime whatsoever, but solely on account of the name “Christian” and the profession of the Christian law. But if he was imprisoned for some crime, he was no longer a Christian—that is, he had fallen away from Christian profession. [Col. 0548B] This is precisely what we have seen stated by our Minucius. In another dissertation (*Dissertations on Tertullian*, ch. 12, arts. 3–4), we shall show how much more extensively Tertullian develops this comparison between Christians and pagans. Meanwhile, you may read what Tertullian, Lactantius, and Eusebius committed to writing in confirmation of these points (Tertullian, *To Scapula*, ch. 2; Lactantius, *Institutes*, book V, ch. 9, p. 383; Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book V, ch. 2, p. 160).

Our Minucius proceeds and establishes another comparison between Christians and pagan philosophers in the following manner: “We despise the haughty brows of the philosophers, whom we know to be corrupters, adulterers, and tyrants, and always eloquent against their own vices. We profess wisdom not in outward dress but in the mind; [Col. 0548C] we do not speak grandly, but live so. We glory that we have attained what they sought with the utmost exertion and were unable to find.” Cyprian undoubtedly borrowed this very comparison from this passage of our author, as well as several of his words that we quoted above (above, ch. 2, art. 39, p. 4).

But Tertullian had treated this much more fully before: “Philosophers affect truth, and in affecting it they corrupt it, since they seek glory. Christians both necessarily desire it and present it in its integrity, since they are concerned for their salvation. Thus we are not on an equal footing, as you suppose, either in knowledge or in discipline” (Tertull., *Apology*, chap. 46, p. 40). He discusses many more matters on this subject there, which must be examined by us in their proper place [Col. 0548D] (*Dissertation on Tertullian*, chap. 12, arts. 3 and 4; and chap. 13, arts. 2 and 3).

Moreover, Minucius says, when the pagan philosophers uttered grand things with the cosmetic coloring of empty eloquence, they were eloquent against their own vices. Earlier, however, they had been called by the same Tertullian “men lustful for glory and eloquence” (Tertullian, ibid., chap. 47, p. 41), because they abused these things to serve their lust. They therefore sold nothing but a cosmetic coloring of words. Nor was unknown even to the pagans themselves what Anaxippus sang in these verses preserved by Athenaeus:

> Alas! You philosophize; but I find philosophers  
> Wise only in their words,  
> [Col. 0549A] While in their deeds I see that they are foolish.

(Athen., bk. XIII, *Deipnosophistae*, chap. 9, p. 610 ff.)

Would you like a celebrated example of this? Rufinus will give you an eminent philosopher who, although he surpassed all the others in eloquence and learning, was nevertheless confounded by a single bishop of the Council of Nicaea through the plain and simple exposition of Christian doctrine, and openly confessed himself defeated (Rufinus, bk. X, *Ecclesiastical History*, chap. 13).

Although Minucius said that truth had neither been sought nor discovered by the pagan philosophers, we nevertheless read that a little earlier he had written: “From the divine proclamations of the Prophets they imitated a shadow of truth that had been adulterated.” By these words, however, he means nothing other than that the philosophers pursued a shadow of the truth drawn from the sacred proclamations of our [Col. 0549B] Prophets, whether handed down in writing or orally, since they corrupted the truth found there with their various errors. This, unless we are mistaken, has already been demonstrated quite clearly more than once in our other dissertations (vol. I, *Apparatus*, pp. 327, 423, 1104, 1112), and will be demonstrated further in those that follow.

Furthermore, the profound difference in doctrine and morals between Christians and pagans did not prevent them from sometimes living in the same house and addressing one another by the name “brother.” For we have seen that the pagan Caecilius lived at Rome with Minucius Felix, and that he was called brother by Octavius, just as Octavius was called brother by him (above, chap. 3, art. 2, pp. 11 [Col. 0549C] and 12).

Nor should you say that Caecilius and Octavius were not real but fictitious persons; for even if that were so, it must nevertheless be certain that Minucius would not have said these things unless this custom of address and shared residence had become established in his own time.

# CHAPTER XIV

## THE ARGUMENTS BY WHICH CAECILIUS ATTEMPTS TO PROVE THAT HIS GODS REALLY EXIST, AND CONSEQUENTLY THAT THE RELIGION OF THE PAGANS IS TRUE, ARE EXAMINED

### ARTICLE I

#### Caecilius’ first argument is explained, by which he attempts to prove that his gods are true gods from ancestral tradition and the most ancient worship of the gods—namely, Eleusinian Ceres, the Phrygian Mother or Cybele, Epidaurian Aesculapius, Chaldaean Bel, Syrian Astarte, Tauric Diana, and Gallic Mercury

[Col. 0549D]

Thus far we have heard Caecilius arguing, always in vain, against the Christian religion, and Octavius triumphing over him. We must now see whether he fought with greater success in defense of his own pagan religion. His first argument, which he considers the strongest, is drawn from its antiquity. For from the very beginning of the world—or, as Caecilius himself says, “while the age was still uncultivated and at the very birth of the world”—our ancestors were privileged to have either “gracious” gods or [Col. 0550A] “kings.” He said “gracious,” following Ovid, who sang:

> You made your wishes, and had gracious gods;

(Ovid, bk. V, *Metamorphoses*, penultimate section), that is, gods who were favorably disposed, benevolent, and readily granted what was desired. From there their worship spread into every part of the earth. The Eleusinians worshiped Ceres; the Phrygians, the Mother, that is, Cybele; the Epidaurians, Aesculapius; the Chaldaeans, Bel; the Syrians, Astarte; the Taurians, Diana; the Gauls, Mercury; and the Romans, all the gods. And because the Romans fortified their city with the sacred rites of every nation, with chaste virgins, and with honors paid to priests, they obtained dominion over the whole world. From these considerations Caecilius concludes that, since everything is uncertain, it is better to follow those religions, rites, and forms of divine worship handed down by our ancestors from the cradle of the world [Col. 0550B] and enduring down to his own age than, with blind fickleness, to surrender oneself to a new religion defiled by secret and utterly corrupt crimes. This is the conclusion of Cotta the Academic in Cicero, of Celsus in Origen, of Symmachus in Ambrose, and of other pagans, as Arnobius and Lactantius attest (Cic., bk. III, *On the Nature of the Gods*, beginning, p. 240; Origen, bk. V, *Against Celsus*, p. 254 ff.; Symmachus, *Memorial*, in Ambrose, §§ 3, 5, and 8, p. 829; Arnobius, bk. II, *Against the Pagans*, p. 30 f.; Lactantius, bk. II, chap. 6, p. 171).

Because Caecilius believed that none of the things concerning his gods which we have just reviewed and which he put forward were unknown to anyone, he did not trouble to prove them individually. But if anyone should wish to know something about them, since they may now perhaps be unknown to him, [Col. 0550C] we shall observe that Eleusis was a city of Attica situated not far from Athens. There Ceres, mentioned by Caecilius, while searching for her daughter, was most kindly received as a guest by Eleusis, who was ruling there. In memory of these events the Eleusinians celebrated rites called the Eleusinian Mysteries, which we have discussed elsewhere (vol. I, *Apparatus*, bk. III, diss. I, chap. 9, art. 2, p. 789 ff.). Herodotus attests that the temple of Eleusinian Ceres there was founded by Philistus, son of Pasicles. You may read more in Diodorus Siculus, Strabo, Mela, and Pausanias, as well as, if you wish, what we have noted elsewhere (Herodotus, bk. IX, §§ 64 and 96; Diodorus Siculus, bk. I, *Library*, p. 117, and bk. V, p. 200; Strabo, bk. IX, *Geography*, p. 395; [Col. 0550D] Mela, *On the Situation of the World*, chap. 3; Pausanias, bk. VI, p. 103, and bk. VIII, pp. 249 and 256; vol. I, *Apparatus*, p. 759 f.).

From the already cited Pausanias you will learn why “Aesculapius,” as Caecilius says, was worshiped by the Epidaurians and where his temple was situated. Livy writes: “Epidaurus did not equal Sicyon and Argos in resources, but was famous for the renowned temple of Aesculapius, which stood five miles from the city. Now it is rich in traces of offerings that have been torn away; at that time it was rich in the offerings that the sick dedicated to the god as payment for healing remedies.” We have noted something elsewhere about the inscription of this temple (Pausanias, bk. II, p. 68; Livy, bk. XLV, § 18; vol. I, *Apparatus*, p. 1093).

The Phrygians, Caecilius further says, venerated the Mother, [Col. 0551A] as Strabo attests in these words: “The Berecyntes, a Phrygian people, and the Phrygians generally, as well as those of the Trojans who live around Ida, themselves honor Rhea and celebrate orgiastic rites for her, calling her the Mother of the Gods, and Agdistis, and the Phrygian and Great Goddess; and, from places, Idaean, Dindymene, Bylene, Pessinuntian, and Cybele” (Strabo, bk. X, *Geography*, p. 469). See also what we have noted elsewhere (vol. I, *Apparatus*, bk. III, diss. I, chap. 9, art. 2, p. 758).

How great was the reverence with which the Chaldaeans honored Bel may easily be gathered from the enormous size of the temple built in his honor. Herodotus, in his account of Babylon, reports the following about it:

[Col. 0551B]

> In the other enclosure is the temple of Zeus Bel, with gates of bronze; it still existed in my own time. It is a square measuring two stades on every side. In the middle of the sanctuary a solid tower has been built. . . . No human being spends the night there except one woman of the native population, whom the god has chosen from them all, as the Chaldaeans, the priests of this god, relate.

(Herodotus, bk. I, § 181.)

Diodorus Siculus also says more about this temple, which he reports to have been built by Semiramis but to have collapsed from age (Diodorus, *Library*, [Col. 0551C] bk. [number missing], p. 69). Nevertheless, Pliny asserts that the same temple still remained in his own time (Pliny, bk. V, *Natural History*, chap. 26, p. 712). Whatever may be true about the temple’s destruction, we have shown elsewhere that Theophilus of Antioch, praised by Lactantius, wrote that the Assyrians and Babylonians offered worship and veneration to Bel. Read again Herodotus, bk. III, § 158, p. 223; Jerome on Ezekiel 24:11 and Hosea 2:16; Claudian, *Panegyric I in Praise of Stilicho*; Vossius, bk. I, *On the Origin and Progress of Idolatry*, chap. 24, p. 93; Giraldus, *History of the Gods*, syntagma 2, p. 108 ff. (vol. I, *Apparatus*, bk. II, diss. 4, chap. 2, § 1, p. 502).

Why, moreover, should it be surprising if the Syrians worshiped “Astarte,” whom Caecilius also [Col. 0551D] mentions, since Tertullian is our witness: “Every province and city has its own god, as Syria has Astarte.” Elsewhere, however, as we shall see in its proper place, she is called by him “Atargatis,” and by Cicero the fourth Venus: “The fourth,” he says, “was conceived in Syria and Tyre; she is called Astarte, and tradition says that she married Adonis.” Philo of Byblos likewise says from Sanchuniathon, in Eusebius: “The Phoenicians relate that this same Astarte is Venus.” To Lucian, however, she appears to be the same as the moon, although he had learned from a certain priest and from the Phoenicians that she was Europa. From Sacred Scripture, moreover, some infer that she was Astarte, goddess of the Sidonians, whom King Solomon worshiped [Col. 0552A] and for whom he erected high places, afterward destroyed by King Josiah (Tertullian, *Apology*, chap. 24, p. 26, and bk. II, *To the Nations*, chap. 8, p. 70; *Dissertation on Tertullian’s Apology*, chap. 27, art. 1; Cicero, bk. III, *On the Nature of the Gods*, p. 248, line 30; in Eusebius, bk. I, *Preparation for the Gospel*, chap. 10, p. 38; Lucian, *On the Syrian Goddess*, beginning; 1 Kings 11:5; 2 Kings 23:13). See further, if you wish, Varro and Scaliger’s notes on his words, Eusebius, the *Suda*, Gyraldus, Salmasius, and Vossius (Varro, bk. IV, *On the Latin Language*, p. 14; Eusebius, bk. I, *Preparation for the Gospel*, chap. 10, p. 37; *Suda*, s.v. “Astarte”; Gyraldus, syntagma 13, p. 375; Salmasius, *Exercises on Solinus*, p. 574; Vossius, bk. I, *On the Origin and Progress of Idolatry*, chap. 28, p. 88, and bk. II, p. 206).

Caecilius adds that divine honors were rendered to “Mercury” by the [Col. 0552B] Gauls, as is confirmed by these words of Caesar: “Of the gods they worship Mercury above all. He has the greatest number of images. They regard him as the inventor of all the arts, the guide of roads and journeys, and as possessing the greatest power over the pursuit of gain and commerce.” Tacitus supports Caesar, relating that the Gauls sacrificed human victims to this same Mercury, as we noted above (Caesar, bk. VI, *Gallic War*, well after the beginning; Tacitus, *On the Customs of the Germans*, near the beginning). One may also consult Vossius, although he is criticized by some because he attempted to prove from Livy’s testimony that a mound of Mercury Teutates had been found near New Carthage. For the words of Livy that he cited are not found in the very ancient Puteanus manuscript. To have noted this in passing will perhaps not be unwelcome to anyone [Col. 0552C] who wishes to consult Vossius (Vossius, bk. I, *On the Origin of Idolatry*, chap. 13, p. 134; chap. 37, p. 140; and bk. II, p. 238 ff.).

Finally, no one is unaware that the superstition of the Romans was such that they worshiped all the gods about whom Caecilius boasts. For their city, “although it ruled nearly all nations,” as Leo the Great says, “was enslaved to the errors of all nations; and it seemed to itself to have embraced a great religion because it rejected no falsehood” (Pope Leo, sermon I, *On the Feast of the Apostles Peter and Paul*). Whether, however, they merited dominion over the whole world by this pious worship, as Caecilius calls it and contends, we shall consider shortly.

From all these things Caecilius believes it can be concluded [Col. 0552D] that the gods of the pagans truly exist; that the traditions concerning them which arose from the beginning of the world must by no means be abandoned; and that one must instead persevere steadfastly in this religion of our ancestors. We must examine, according to our customary method, in what manner and by what force of reasoning Minucius attacks and refutes him.

### ARTICLE II

#### How Octavius refutes Caecilius’ argument and shows both that the worship of the gods is not of such great antiquity and that the impious and superstitious traditions of the ancestors—such as those concerning Scylla, the Chimera, the Hydra, and the Centaurs—must not be followed

The argument of Caecilius, which the other [Col. 0553A] pagans likewise employed without exception, has two parts. The first concerns absolutely all pagans; the second, specifically the Romans themselves. Each is utterly overthrown by a corresponding answer from Minucius and by various, extremely weighty considerations. Therefore, so that everything may be treated in proper order, we shall begin from the first points of the discussion and afterward proceed to the others.

First, therefore, it must be clear to anyone who considers without a thoroughly prejudiced mind what has been said thus far that both parts of Caecilius’ argument had already been completely weakened and shattered by those arguments with which Minucius, as we have seen, demonstrated most conclusively that there are not many gods but only one, and that he cares for each and every thing by his divine providence.

[Col. 0553B] Accordingly, after he had fortified both these foundations of true religion with an impregnable bulwark of arguments drawn chiefly from the opinions of the pagan philosophers themselves, he then proceeded to refute the first part of Caecilius’ reasoning. Caecilius had said that one must adhere most steadfastly to the most ancient traditions of our ancestors, traditions coeval with the world, since they had worshiped their gods from the beginning of the world.

But our Minucius shows most clearly that this is absurd and wholly contrary to right reason: “For if,” he says, “the world is ruled by providence and governed by the will of one God, antiquity—delighted or captivated by the fables of the unlearned—ought not to carry us away into the error of mutual agreement, since it is refuted by the opinions of its own [Col. 0553C] philosophers, whose authority rests upon both reason and antiquity.” As you see, he there strikes down and overthrows with a twofold battering ram the antiquity of their religion and worship of the gods vaunted by the pagans. First, through the authority of the philosophers, which no pagan could oppose, he makes the falsity of this supposed antiquity manifest. And the things which we have seen related and proved by Minucius himself and by Clement of Alexandria certainly contributed greatly to the confirmation of this assertion: namely, that these same philosophers drew most of their doctrines from our Sacred Scriptures, though they afterward distorted and corrupted them.

Second, however ancient the pagans’ religion might be, everyone was nevertheless obliged to renounce it because it was composed entirely of fables, utterly absurd lies, monstrous opinions, and the dreams [Col. 0553D] of delirious men. For, as Ambrose admirably teaches when refuting the same argument of Symmachus: “Let an old age that cannot correct itself be ashamed. It is not the gray hair of years that is praised, but that of character; there is no shame in passing over to better things” (Ambrose, epistle 18, § 7, p. 834). You may read more on this subject in Clement of Alexandria, Arnobius—whom we shall discuss in his proper place—and Prudentius (Clement of Alexandria, *Exhortation to the Pagans*, p. 57; Arnobius, bk. II, *Against the Pagans*, p. 90 ff.; Prudentius, bk. II, *Against Symmachus*).

But we cannot pass over Tertullian, who, proceeding still further, skillfully and sharply rebukes the pagans because they ceaselessly cast at Christians—to the point of nausea—the traditions of their ancestors, vaunted with loud [Col. 0554A] and frequently repeated outcries, although they themselves ruined and scorned them: “Where,” he says, “is your religion? Where is the reverence owed by you to your ancestors? In dress, food, furnishings, wealth, and finally in speech itself, you have renounced your forefathers. You are always praising the ancients, yet day by day you live in novel ways. From this it is shown that, while departing from the good institutions of your ancestors, you retain and preserve what you ought not to have preserved, although you failed to preserve what you ought to have preserved.” But we shall say more about these matters in their proper place, when we discuss his books (Tertullian, *Apology*, chap. 6, p. 7; *Dissertation on Tertullian*, chap. 18, p. 15).

Although no one could have been unaware that the ancient beliefs of the pagans were ridiculous and wholly absurd, Minucius nevertheless [Col. 0554B] demonstrates this by several examples, so as to satisfy everyone abundantly. For the pagans believed, he says, that there existed a many-shaped Scylla, a multiform Chimera, a Hydra reborn from its wounds, and Centaurs—horses entwined with human beings. Virgil described Scylla in these verses:

> But Scylla is confined within a cavern’s hidden recesses,  
> Thrusting forth her mouths and dragging ships upon the rocks.  
> Her upper form is human, a maiden with a beautiful breast  
> Down to the groin; below, she is a sea-monster of monstrous body,  
> With dolphins’ tails joined to a womb of wolves.

(Virgil, bk. III, *Aeneid*, v. 424 ff.)

She is represented differently, though no less monstrously, by Homer, whom you may consult, as also Ovid, Ausonius, Natalis Comes, and Vossius (Homer, *Odyssey*, bk. XII, p. 172; Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, bk. IV, fable 1; Ausonius, *Idyll* 4; Natalis Comes, bk. VIII [Col. 0554C], *Mythology*, chap. 12; Vossius, bk. IV, *On the Origin and Progress of Idolatry*, chap. 17, p. 34). The Chimera was depicted by Homer, Hesiod, Lucretius, and Ovid; if these do not suffice for you, you may also consult Virgil and Natalis Comes (Homer, *Iliad* VI, p. 106; Hesiod, *Theogony*, p. 469; Lucretius, bk. V, p. 57; Ovid, bk. IX, *Metamorphoses*, § 11; Virgil, bk. IV, *Aeneid*, 28; Natalis Comes, bk. IX, *Mythology*, chap. 4).

There were various opinions concerning the Centaurs, which Diodorus Siculus reports in these words: “Ixion, inflamed with love for Juno, did not hesitate to solicit the goddess for adultery. Jupiter therefore sent forth a cloud fashioned in the image of Juno and placed it before him in her stead; [Col. 0554D] Ixion coupled with the cloud and begot the so-called Centaurs, human in part. . . . Others relate that the Centaurs were raised by the Nymphs on Pelion and, after reaching adulthood, through passion for mares propagated the two-formed race called Hippocentaurs. Some affirm that the Centaurs born from Nephele and Ixion received the name Hippocentaurs because they were the first to undertake the practice of horsemanship, and that from this the fiction of a double nature passed into myth” (Diodorus Siculus, bk. IV, *Library*, p. 189; idem, p. 153). Earlier he had related how Hercules is said to have defeated these same Centaurs in his fourth contest. Cotta notes the first of these opinions in Cicero, where he says: “Even a single cloud is said to have given birth to the Centaurs” [Col. 0555A] (Cicero, bk. III, *On the Nature of the Gods*, p. 247).

The author of the Eusebian *Chronicle* says: “The war of the Lapiths and Centaurs occurred at this time; Palaephatus writes in his book *On Incredible Tales* that the Centaurs were noble Thessalian horsemen” (Eusebius, *Chronicle*, at the year 772). Scaliger, however, in his observations on these words, freely and boldly rebukes him for citing Palaephatus in confirmation of this opinion, from which Palaephatus differs greatly. Others nevertheless attempt to prove it not only by the authority of Palaephatus but also by that of Tzetzes and Orosius. The latter further added that the Lapiths were called Centaurs by the Thessalians because, fighting from horseback, they appeared to form a single body with their horses (Tzetzes, *Histories*, *Chiliad* VII, chap. 99; Orosius, bk. I, chap. 13). Consult Ovid, Natalis Comes, [Col. 0555B] and Vossius (Ovid, bk. XII, *Metamorphoses*, fable 4; Comes, bk. VII, *Mythology*, chap. 4; Vossius, bk. I, *On the Origin and Progress of Idolatry*, chap. 15, p. 62).

Finally, Minucius adds that the pagans constantly proclaimed that birds, flowers, trees, and other things of this sort had been made from human beings. No one is unaware that such stories occur throughout Ovid’s books of *Metamorphoses*. Jerome, however, when discussing Nebuchadnezzar, encompasses all these things in a few words: “Greek and Roman histories have related that things far more incredible happened to human beings: their myths also tell that Scylla, the Chimera, the Hydra, and the Centaurs, birds and wild beasts, flowers and trees, stars and stones, were made from human beings” (Jerome, on Daniel 4:1).

You see, therefore, how rightly and deservedly Minucius concludes from these [Col. 0555C] and many other examples, to be reviewed below, that Caecilius is altogether mistaken, and that all the other pagans are in error who taught that it is better for everyone to follow the traditions of our ancestors concerning the gods and religion, and that the gods acknowledged by them ought to be feared rather than examined more closely and made the subject of judgment.

# CHAPTER XV

## THE ARGUMENTS BY WHICH MINUCIUS SHOWS THAT THE GODS OF THE PAGANS ARE FALSE ARE CONSIDERED

### ARTICLE I

#### With what folly the pagans proclaimed that human beings had been made gods because of the merit of their virtue or benefits conferred upon other human beings

[Col. 0555D]

A particularly abundant source and origin of the worship of false gods was the insane conviction of the pagans, by which they not only proclaimed but even boasted that their gods had indeed been human beings, but that, because of benefits conferred upon other human beings and outstanding deeds, they had received divinity as a reward—or, as Minucius says, that they were “regarded as gods because of the merits of their virtue or service.” Cicero is for us a witness to this origin of the gods beyond all objection; in words cited by Lactantius, he confirms it in a remarkable manner: “The life of human beings,” he says, “and common custom adopted the practice of raising men distinguished by benefactions to heaven through reputation and popular will. Hence Hercules, hence Castor and Pollux, hence Aesculapius, hence Liber also” (Cicero, bk. II, *On the Nature of the Gods*, p. 223, line 13; Lactantius, bk. I, *Institutes*, chaps. [Col. 0556A] 8 and 15, pp. 43 and 80). Again, in another book, we read these words of his, likewise transcribed by Lactantius: “In most states it can be understood that, for the sake of increasing virtue, so that each of the best men might more willingly face danger for the republic, the memory of brave men was consecrated by the honor paid to the immortal gods” (Cicero, bk. III, *On the Nature of the Gods*, p. 247, line 8; Lactantius, loc. cit.). Lactantius could certainly have produced a third passage from Cicero, where he speaks no less clearly than in those above: “They relate that brave, famous, or powerful men attained to the gods after death, and that these are the very ones whom we are accustomed to worship, pray to, and venerate” (Cicero, bk. I, *On the Nature of the Gods*, p. 212, line 34). Consider, I ask you, whether Minucius was aiming especially at these words of Cicero.

[Col. 0556B] That Latin orator did not say what the beginning of this perverse custom was; but Pliny declares that it was extremely ancient: “This is the most ancient custom of returning thanks to those who have deserved well: that they should enroll such persons among the divinities” (Pliny, bk. II, *Natural History*, chap. 7, p. 144). But however ancient that custom was, it did not arise at the very birth of the world, as Caecilius said. For, as Octavius correctly argues, it began only when “each nation venerated its founder, or a renowned leader, or a chaste queen braver than her sex, or the discoverer of some service or art.”

Grant, if you wish, that it was coeval with the world—something that can by no means be the case. Even then you will never thereby prove [Col. 0556C] that these are true gods, since they are neither eternal nor immortal, and since they received from human beings both life itself and a fictitious divinity; or since, as Octavius says, divinity “was given to the dead as a reward and to those yet to come as an example.” He could have proved this by various arguments, as Athanasius and Theodoret did (Athanasius, *Oration Against the Pagans*, p. 18, vol. I; Theodoret, vol. IV, discourse 3, *On the Angels*, p. 510); but he judged it better to send Caecilius and the other pagans to their own writers: “Read,” he says, “the writings of the Stoics, or the writings of the wise; you will acknowledge together with me” that people were “regarded as gods” because of the merits of virtue and bravery, or of service and benefactions. [Col. 0556D] But some suspect that “historians” should there be read instead of “Stoics,” doubtless because that term is more naturally contrasted with the following “wise men.” Yet this is mere conjecture, and certainly does not suffice by itself to reject the reading of our manuscript, which appears to be confirmed by Cicero’s authority. For where he discusses those who “were duly regarded as gods,” as he himself puts it, and the origin of their great multitude, he adds in the same place: “This topic was treated by Zeno and afterward explained at greater length by Cleanthes and Chrysippus” (Cicero, bk. II, *On the Nature of the Gods*, p. 223, line 20 ff.). It is established, moreover, that Zeno was the founder of the Stoics and that these men were his disciples, as Laertius teaches, who wrote their lives, and as we have observed elsewhere (Laertius, bk. VII, *Lives and Doctrines of the Philosophers*, § 1 ff.; vol. I, *Apparatus*, p. 1123).

[Col. 0557A] Two further witnesses are produced by our Minucius. Concerning the first, he says: “Prodicus speaks of those being assumed among the gods who, by wandering about and discovering new crops, benefited humankind.” Did he not excerpt this from these words of Cicero: “Prodicus of Chios said that things beneficial to human life were regarded as belonging among the gods”? In another book Cicero also reports what Xenophon handed down concerning Prodicus, and we have noted this passage of Xenophon elsewhere (Cicero, bk. I, *On the Nature of the Gods*, p. 212, line 72, and bk. I, *On Duties*, p. 367, line 19; vol. I, *Apparatus*, p. 1245).

The second is called by our author “Perseus,” or Persaeus, “who philosophizes,” as he says, “in the same sense, and links together the crops discovered and the discoverers of the crops themselves under the same names, as the comic [Col. 0557B] saying has it, ‘Venus grows cold without Liber and Ceres.’” The comic poet Terence sang:

> By Hercules, this saying is true:  
> Without Liber and Ceres, Venus grows cold.

(Terence, *Eunuch*, act IV, scene 5.)

But there he indicates that this too had been taken from someone else. From whom, if not Euripides, to whom this Greek verse belongs?

> Venus is dead without Bacchus and Ceres.

The things Minucius related about Persaeus had likewise been drawn, like the preceding material, from the same book of Cicero already cited by us, where we read: “Persaeus, a pupil of Zeno”—as Laertius also says, or his servant, as Athenaeus says—“maintains that those by whom some great benefit for the cultivation of life had been discovered were regarded as gods; [Col. 0557C] and that useful and health-giving things themselves were designated by the names of gods, so that he did not even say that those things had been discovered by gods, but that they were themselves divine” (Cicero, bk. I, *On the Nature of the Gods*, p. 201, line 18; Laertius, bk. VII, *Life of Zeno*, §§ 13 and 54; Athenaeus, bk. IV, *Deipnosophistae*, chap. 17, p. 162). From the cited verse of the Latin and Greek poets, however, it is readily understood that, following Cicero, our Minucius chiefly means Ceres and Bacchus, who were said to have discovered things extremely useful to the life of all human beings. Hence Athenagoras rebukes those same pagans who “make gods of the elements and their parts” (*ta stoicheia kai ta moria autōn theopoiousi*), and call the fruit of the vine Bacchus, the vine itself Semele, [Col. 0557D] and the lightning bolt the heat of the sun (*ton de tēs ampelou karpon Dionyson, kai Semelēn autēn tēn ampelon, kai keraunon tēn tou hēliou phloga*) (Athenagoras, *Embassy for the Christians*, p. 24). How boldly the pagans attributed to Ceres the discovery of grain, to Bacchus that of wine, as Diodorus Siculus relates, and to others the discovery of other things useful to human beings, we shall show in our following dissertations (Diodorus Siculus, bk. III, *Library*, p. 142, and bk. V, p. 232; *Dissertation on Arnobius*, chap. 9, art. 2; *on Lactantius*, chap. 30, art. 5; *on Tertullian*, chap. 25, art. 3). No less clearly shall we demonstrate how rightly our earliest writers, like our Minucius, proved that no person of sound mind could infer from these or any other benefits conferred upon him that those who discovered but did not create them either are [Col. 0558A] gods or merited divinity. For Cicero himself, immediately after the words concerning Prodicus cited by us a little earlier, at once added: “What religion, then, does that Prodicus leave?” (Cicero, bk. II, *On the Nature of the Gods*, p. 212, line 34). Once the true God has been rejected and false gods introduced, there can plainly be no religion, but only empty superstition. But if the discoverers of things useful to human beings cannot be gods, much less can the things discovered by others. “For what,” Cicero further says, “is more absurd than either giving the names of gods to sordid and ugly things, or restoring among the gods human beings already destroyed by death, whose entire worship would consist in mourning?” (Ibid., p. 201, line 21). Nothing, moreover, is truer than this judgment, since before any things were discovered or any discoverers of them existed, those things had undoubtedly [Col. 0558B] been created by him who founded the world and all creatures, and who alone can therefore be God. Who, then, will not marvel that this was one of the chief and most corrupt sources from which idolatry and the impious worship of false gods flowed out and inundated the whole world?

### ARTICLE II

#### Minucius’ argument is examined by which he proves that the gods of the pagans are false from their birth, native country, death, and tombs, especially those of Dictaean Jupiter, Delphic Apollo, Pharian Isis, and Eleusinian Ceres

By yet another argument Minucius utterly overthrows the divinity of all their deities fabricated by the pagans. He again drew it from the things [Col. 0558C] which they themselves handed down and continually vaunted concerning the births, native countries, and tombs of these same gods. There was doubtless no need for him to undertake to prove what they so remarkably boasted of. Nevertheless, as a completely reliable witness and guarantor, he offered Euhemerus in precisely these words: “Euhemerus traces the subject in detail, enumerates their births, native countries, and tombs, and points them out province by province.” Here, as usual, he appears to follow Cicero as his predecessor, who says: “Euhemerus demonstrates both the deaths and the burials of the gods” (Cicero, bk. I, *On the Nature of the Gods*, p. 112, line 37). This Euhemerus, if you wish to know, was a Greek writer whom some believed to have been a native of Agrigentum, others of Messene, some of Cos, and even of Tegea. [Col. 0558D] He composed several volumes of histories in which he committed to writing the things recalled by Cicero and Minucius. Read Plutarch, Athenaeus, Aelian, Augustine, Theodoret, and the others cited by us in the preceding volume of our *Apparatus* (Plutarch, *On Isis and Osiris*, p. 360; Athenaeus, bk. XIV, *Deipnosophistae*, p. 658; Aelian, bk. II, *Various History*, chap. 32; Augustine, bk. I, *On the Agreement of the Evangelists*, chap. 23; Theodoret, discourse 3, *On the Angels*, p. 506). There we observed that this Euhemerus was numbered by many among the atheists, doubtless because of those histories of the gods. But this did not prevent Ennius, as Cicero and afterward Augustine say, from translating his books, or prevent the things he had narrated concerning the births, deeds, [Col. 0559A] deaths, and tombs of those gods from being true (Cicero, loc. cit.; Augustine, bk. VII, *City of God*, chap. 17, § 1, p. 183).

From what that Greek writer said concerning the origin, native country, and tombs of the gods, Minucius touches only upon a few examples, namely, “Dictaean Jupiter, Delphic Apollo, Pharian Isis, and Eleusinian Ceres.” Dicte is a mountain on the island of Crete. In its cave Ops, or Rhea, the wife of Saturn, gave birth to Jupiter and secretly entrusted him to the Curetes, or Corybantes, and the Idaean Dactyls, to be guarded so that, newly born, he would not be devoured by his father like his other sons (Strabo, bk. X, *Geography*, p. 478). Hence Virgil:

> Come now, I shall explain the qualities which Jupiter himself  
> Bestowed upon the bees, as a reward for their having followed  
> The tuneful clashing of the Curetes and their ringing bronze,  
> And fed the king of heaven beneath the Dictaean cave.

[Col. 0559B] (Virgil, *Georgics*, bk. IV, v. 149 ff.)

If you desire another Latin poet, we shall quickly produce Lucretius for you, who sang similarly:

> They tell of the Dictaean Curetes, who are said  
> Once to have concealed in Crete that wailing of Jupiter,  
> When boys around the boy in swift-paced dance,  
> Armed and moving rhythmically, struck bronze against bronze,  
> Lest Saturn should seize him and consign him to his jaws,  
> And deal his mother’s heart an everlasting wound.

(Lucretius, bk. II, v. 637 ff.)

Read further, if you have leisure, Servius on the cited verses of Virgil and on his other verses; Ovid; Diodorus Siculus; Lucan; Strabo; Theophilus of Antioch; Athanasius; and what we have excerpted elsewhere (Servius, on the cited verses and on bk. III of the *Aeneid*, p. 270; Ovid, bk. IV, *Fasti*; Diodorus, bk. V, *Library*, p. 253; [Col. 0559C] Lucian, *On Sacrifices*, p. 183; Strabo, bk. X, *Geography*, p. 468; Theophilus of Antioch, bk. I, *To Autolycus*, p. 75; Athanasius, *Oration Against the Greeks*, § 10, vol. I; vol. I, *Apparatus*, p. 1164). Nor should it trouble you that some assert that Jupiter was raised not on Mount Dicte but on Mount Ida. For the two mountains were near each other, as Aratus attests, although Strabo believed that they were one thousand stades apart (Strabo, bk. X, *Geography*, p. 478).

Moreover, from the already cited Diodorus Siculus we learn how true is what our author later reported: that a she-goat was the nurse of the infant Jupiter, or, as he himself puts it, “Jupiter’s nurse is a she-goat.” For the nymphs, as Diodorus himself says, “fed the infant with a mixture of honey and milk, [Col. 0559D] and offered him the udders of the goat called Amalthea, that he might be more fully nourished. . . . Besides other honors which he bestowed upon the goat that nursed him, he derived from her the surname *Aegiochus*, that is, ‘Goat-Bearer’” (Diod., *Biblioth.*, bk. V, p. 233). Hence Ovid:

> The rainy constellation of the Olenian she-goat rises;
>
> She has heaven as the reward for the milk she gave.
>
> Amalthea, a Naiad famed upon Cretan Ida,
>
> . . . . . . . . . . . .
>
> . . . . . . . . . . . .
>
> . . . . . . . . . . . .
>
> With brazen horns curved backward over her back,
>
> And with an udder such as Jupiter’s nurse might have,
>
> She gave milk to the god.  
> (Ovid, *Fasti*, bk. V, § 2.)

As for his tomb, mentioned by our Minucius and by his intermediary Cyprian, [Col. 0560A] the Cretans, according to Lucian, affirmed that “Jupiter not only lived and was reared among them, but they even show his tomb: τὸν τάφον δεικνύουσι, ‘they show the tomb.’” Cicero, moreover, distinguished three Jupiters, of whom “the third,” he says, was reckoned “the Cretan, son of Saturn, whose tomb is shown on that island.” And Varro, as Solinus notes, “in the work entitled *On Coasts*, affirms that even in his own time Jupiter’s tomb was visited there.” Callimachus, however, sings that the matter is doubtful and accuses the Cretans of lying; but when he says there that Jupiter has always existed, he himself lies absurdly. Read also, if you wish, Theophilus of Antioch, Clement of Alexandria, Origen, Tertullian, Arnobius, Lactantius, Eusebius, and [Col. 0560B] Epiphanius. Vossius, however, thinks there were two Cretan Jupiters: one, the most ancient king of Crete, from whom Crete received its name; the other, a younger one who abducted Europa, and about whom he thinks Cicero and Lactantius speak (Cypr., *De Idol. Vanit.*, p. 11; Lucian, *De Sacrific.*, p. 185, line 39; Cicero, *De Nat. deor.*, bk. III, p. 247, line 34; Solinus, *Polyhist.*, ch. 11, p. 29; Callimachus, *Hymn to Jupiter*, p. 535, vol. I, *Poet. Graec.*; Theophilus, *Ad Autol.*, bk. II, p. 81; Clement of Alexandria, *Admonit.*, p. 24; Origen, *Contra Celsum*, bk. III, p. 137; Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 25, p. 27; Arnobius, *Adv. Gent.*, bk. IV, p. 135; Lactantius, *Instit.*, bk. I, ch. 11, p. 64; Eusebius, *Praepar. Evang.*, bk. III, ch. 10, p. 107; Epiphanius, *Ancoratus*, § 108, p. 108; Vossius, *De Orig.* [Col. 0560C] *et prog. idolol.*, bk. I, ch. 1, p. 61). For us, however, it is sufficient to have proved what our author handed down. Something more must be said about Jupiter later.

How rightly Minucius also placed the Delphic Apollo after Jupiter can again be plainly confirmed from Cicero himself. For he enumerates several Apollos, of whom “the third,” he says, “was born of the third Jupiter and Latona, and is said to have come from the Hyperboreans to Delphi.” Lucian, moreover, says: “They worship those gods as distributed among various regions, and receive them into their own cities. Thus, ὁ μὲν Δελφὸς τὸν Ἀπόλλω, Delphi and Delos claim Apollo, and the Athenians Minerva, displaying and making them their own citizens.” But Diodorus Siculus relates more expressly that most of the gods came forth from Crete: [Col. 0560D] “Ὡσαύτως δὲ μὲν Ἀπόλλωνα πλεῖστον χρόνον φανῆναι περὶ Δῆλον, καὶ Λυκίαν, καὶ Δελφούς. Likewise, Apollo spent a very long time on Delos, in Lycia, and at Delphi.” Delphi was a city of Phocis in Achaia, near Mount Parnassus, exceedingly famous—as everyone knows—for Apollo’s oracle. If you wish to read still other writers on this subject, consult Pausanias, Plutarch, Strabo, and other mythographers. Nevertheless, if you believe Macrobius when he interprets the various names of the Sun, “they call him Ἀπόλλωνα Δελφῶν, ‘Apollo of Delphi,’ because he reveals obscure things by the brightness of light, ἀπὸ τοῦ δηλοῦν ἄφανη, ‘from making invisible things manifest’; or, as Numenius holds, as though he were one and alone. For he says that in the ancient Greek language δελφόν meant ‘one.’ Hence, he says, a brother is called ἀδελφός, as though ‘not one’” (Cicero, *De Natur. deor.*, bk. III, p. 248; Lucian, *De Sacrific.*, [Col. 0561A] p. 185; Diodorus Siculus, *Biblioth.*, bk. V, p. 237; Pausanias, bk. X, p. 320 ff.; Plutarch, *De oracul. Defect.*, p. 433; Strabo, *Geogr.*, bk. IX, p. 417 f.; Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, bk. I, ch. 17).

Minucius next mentions Pharian Isis. But if the writings of Euhemerus, whom he praises, had come into our hands, we would surely know whether he had indicated for us the homeland or the tomb of Pharian Isis, or both. For Herodotus, by whom she is called Ἰοῦν, Io, Diodorus Siculus, and others testify that there were various opinions about these matters (Herodotus, bk. I; Diodorus Siculus, *Biblioth.*, bk. I, pp. 9, 14, and 17, and bk. V, p. 32). Yet by these two words, “Pharian Isis,” our author signifies with sufficient clarity that her tomb was situated on Pharos, the most celebrated [Col. 0561B] island of Egypt, where she was worshiped with the greatest honor. Diodorus Siculus indeed admits (*ibid.*, bk. I, p. 16) that certain writers had asserted that Isis and her husband Osiris were buried at Nysa in Arabia, and that columns had been erected there in honor of each. On one of these the following inscription, engraved in sacred characters, was read:

> I am Isis, queen of this place, instructed by Mercury. No one can abrogate the laws established by me. I am the youngest daughter of Saturn, the latest god. I am the wife and sister of King Osiris. I am she who first discovered grain for mortals. I am the mother of King Horus. I am she who rises in the constellation of the Dog. For me the city of Bubastis was built. Farewell; rejoice, Egypt, my nurse.

But he makes no secret of the fact that he did not place great confidence in these claims.

[Col. 0561C] And certainly, according to Herodotus, the Egyptians assembled in great numbers more than once each year, above all “ἐς Βουβάστιν πόλιν τῇ Ἀρτέμιδι, in the city of Bubastis in honor of Diana. Δεύτερα, ἐς Βούσιριν πόλιν τῇ Ἴσι, in the second place, in the city of Busiris in honor of Isis. In that city is the greatest ἱρόν, temple of Isis; the city itself is situated in the middle of the Egyptian Delta. Isis is she who in the Greek language is called Δημήτηρ, Demeter, that is, Ceres” (Herodotus, bk. II, § 59).

From Strabo, moreover, we learn that Busiris was a city of the Busirite province, which has a harbor at Pharos guarded by herdsmen (Strabo, *Geogr.*, bk. XVII, p. 802). May it not therefore be gathered that this is the Isis whom our author calls Pharian, or [Col. 0561D] Parian—for thus you will see her named on the coins exhibited by Federico Ubaldini? (Ubaldini, *De Symbol. Dian. Ephes. statu.*, p. 365, vol. VII, *Antiq. Graec.*)

Furthermore, since Isis, as the recently cited Herodotus, Diodorus Siculus, and very many others have related, is the same as Ceres, Tertullian doubtless mentioned her in these words: “How is Attic Pallas, or Pharian Ceres, distinguished from the upright beam of a cross?” (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 17).

Pharian Isis was distinguished only by a surname—or rather by the places where she was worshiped—from Eleusinian Ceres, whom our author also mentions after Euhemerus. Strabo left the following in writing: Εἶτ’ Ἐλευσὶν πόλις, ἐν ᾗ τὸ τῆς Δήμητρος ἱερὸν τῆς Ἐλευσινίας, καὶ ὁ μυστικὸς [Col. 0562A] σηκός, ὃν κατεσκεύασεν Ἰκτῖνος, ὄχλον θεάτρου δέξασθαι δυνάμενον. “Next comes the city of Eleusis, in which is the temple of Eleusinian Ceres and the mystic sanctuary, capable of holding a crowd as large as one ordinarily finds in a theater, the work of Ictinus” (Strabo, *Geogr.*, bk. IX, p. 395). Add Cicero as well, whose words are these:

> I pass over that holy and august Eleusis,
>
> Where peoples from the farthest shores are initiated.  
> (Cicero, *De Natur. Deor.*, bk. II, p. 12, line 38.)

Who, then, would not join our Minucius in laughing at and rejecting those fictitious divinities—Ceres, Isis, and the others—whom the pagans admitted to have died and been buried?

## ARTICLE III

**Minucius’s argument is examined, by which he proves that the gods of the pagans were fictitious from Alexander the Great’s letter to his mother, in which he testified that a secret concerning the gods had been disclosed to him, and which made Vulcan their chief; and the sistrum of Isis beside the swallow, and the empty tomb of Serapis, or Osiris, are discussed.**

[Col. 0562B]

Someone will doubtless be surprised that Minucius cites Alexander the Great as a witness to the fictitious divinity of the pagan gods: “In a notable volume,” he says, “which he wrote to his mother, Alexander testified that through fear of his power a priest had disclosed to him the secret that the gods were human beings.” But Cyprian transferred this into his own book *On the Vanity of Idols*, word for word as an unquestionable truth, as we have already seen (Cyprian, *De idolor. Vanit.*, p. 12; above, ch. 2, [Col. 0562C] art. 4, p. 35).

Athenagoras had said earlier: Ἡρόδοτος, καὶ Ἀλέξανδρος Φιλίππου ἐν τῇ πρὸς τὴν μητέρα ἐπιστολῇ (ἑκάτεροι δὲ ἐν τῇ Ἡλιουπόλει, καὶ Μέμφει, καὶ Θήβαις, εἰς λόγους τοῖς ἱερεῦσιν ἀφῖχθαι λέγονται), φασὶ παρ’ ἐκείνων, ἀνθρώπους αὐτοὺς γενέσθαι, μαθεῖν. “Herodotus and Alexander son of Philip, in his letter to his mother—both of whom are said to have entered into conversation with the priests in various Egyptian cities, Heliopolis, Memphis, and Thebes—say that they learned from them that the gods had been human beings” (Athenagoras, *Legat. pro Christian.*, p. 31). Thus, what Minucius and Cyprian after him call a “notable volume,” Athenagoras calls a letter. So too does Augustine, who teaches that this priest, as Minucius likewise says, was Egyptian by birth [Col. 0562D] and surnamed Leo (Augustine, *De Civit.*, bk. VIII, ch. 5, p. 194, and final chapter, p. 218; bk. XII, ch. 10, p. 309; and *De Cons. Evang.*, bk. I, ch. 3).

Rigaltius and Cellarius, however, protest against this. They contend that Minucius and the other writers praised by us erred, and that they substituted Alexander the Great of Macedon for Alexander Polyhistor. They attempt to establish their opinion by two arguments: first, because Polyhistor published *Aegyptiaca* (Egyptian histories); and second, because Tertullian said: “I now offer something from your own literature: what the Egyptians relate, Alexander arranges, and his mother reads” (Tertullian, *De Pallio*, ch. 3, p. 134).

But apart from the improbability that Polyhistor could, through fear of his power, have extorted from an Egyptian priest [Col. 0563A] the secret that the gods were human beings and written a book or letter about it to his mother, Plutarch—whom Rigaltius and Cellarius perhaps trusted more than the Fathers of the Church—certainly relates the same thing in his *Life of Alexander the Great*: Αὐτὸς δὲ Ἀλέξανδρος ἐν ἐπιστολῇ πρὸς τὴν μητέρα, φησὶν γεγονέναι τινὰς αὐτῷ μαντείας ἀπορρήτους, ἃς αὐτὸς ἐπανελθὼν φράσει πρὸς μόνην ἐκείνην . . . . λέγεται δὲ καὶ Ψάμμωνος ἐν Αἰγύπτῳ τοῦ φιλοσόφου διακούσας, ἀποδέξασθαι μάλιστα τῶν λεχθέντων, ὅτι πάντες ἄνθρωποι βασιλεύονται ὑπὸ Θεοῦ· τὸ γὰρ ἄρχον ἐν ἑκάστῳ καὶ κρατοῦν, θεῖόν ἐστιν. “Alexander himself says in a letter to his mother that certain secret oracles had been imparted to him, which on his return he would disclose to her alone. . . . He is also said, after hearing the philosopher Psammon in Egypt, to have approved especially this among his sayings: that all [Col. 0563B] mortals are ruled by God, since whatever commands and exercises dominion in each thing is divine” (Plutarch, *Life of Alexander*, vol. II, p. 680). The man whom Minucius, Cyprian, and Athenagoras call a priest, and Augustine calls Leo, Plutarch there calls the philosopher Psammon. He did not indeed say that Alexander wrote to his mother what he had received from Psammon, but neither does he deny it. What prevents Athenagoras, Minucius, and the others from having obtained more definite information about the matter from another source? Writers of such great authority ought not, therefore, to have been condemned as mistaken on the strength of such slight conjectures.

The words that immediately follow in our author are greatly corrupt and extremely obscure. We read them thus: “There [*Illic*; Royal MS: *Illi*, ‘to him’] he makes Vulcan the chief of all, and afterward the lineage of Jupiter. Look down upon [*Despice*; Royal MS: *et de spicis*, ‘and from the ears of grain’] the sistrum of Isis beside the swallow, and the empty tomb of your Serapis or Osiris, its members scattered [*dispersis*; Royal MS: *adspersis*; Royal MS: *Osiridis*].” From these various readings you doubtless perceive whether some scholars are wrong to consider the passage so corrupt that they have despaired of its being restored without the aid of another, sounder manuscript.

The sense of our author’s first words, insofar as it may be gathered from the reading of the Royal manuscript, which is not unreasonably to be preferred to the others, is this: “To him”—or rather, “that Alexander,” and perhaps better, “there,” that is, in the cited letter—Alexander makes Vulcan the chief of all, namely, [Col. 0563D] of all the gods, and afterward the lineage of Jupiter. This can be excellently confirmed by the following words of Diodorus Siculus transcribed by Eusebius: Ἔνιοι δὲ τῶν ἱερέων φασὶ πρῶτον Ἥφαιστον βασιλεῦσαι πυρὸς εὑρετὴν γενόμενον. “Some of the priests hold that Vulcan, the inventor of fire, should be reckoned the first king, and that Saturn, Jupiter’s father, succeeded him in power” (Diodorus, *Biblioth.*, bk. I, p. 8; Eusebius, *Praepar. Evang.*, bk. II, ch. 1). Whether this is true will be examined in the following article. Yet we think that no one will fail readily to admit that there were considerable disagreements among the pagans concerning the origin of their gods. For most others thought that the whole lineage derived its origin from Saturn, as we shall explain a little later. But whether it began with Saturn or Vulcan, [Col. 0564A] neither these men nor their sons and grandsons could ever have been true immortal gods.

What Minucius afterward said about Isis and her sistrum beside the swallow is certainly very difficult to explain. Some think Minucius’s meaning is this: in his letter Alexander makes the sistrum of Isis from ears of grain, producing a sound like that of a swallow. For ears of grain, when shaken, agitated, and struck together, give forth a sound like that produced by the shaking of a sistrum.

Salmasius, however, suspects that Minucius read in some Greek author’s book that among the emblems of Isis were numbered Χελιδονίαν, σεῖστρον, that is, a chelidonian asp and a sistrum. He translated this “a sistrum beside the swallow,” as though the sistrum made with its rattle a sound like that of a swallow, just as κερκίδες, the rods or battens of a loom, are called [Col. 0564B] χελιδόσιν εἰκελόφωνοι, “similar in voice to swallows,” in a Greek epigram (Salmasius on Solinus, p. 343). From this he judges that our author’s text should be corrected thus: “Aspice sis Isidis ad hirundinem sistrum”—“Consider, if you please, the sistrum of Isis in relation to the swallow.” But if Minucius read some work by a Greek author, it would appear to be none other than the letter of Alexander the Great cited by him, or books by Plutarch or others. Yet who can divine what those works contained on this subject?
