The text, therefore, ought not to be emended by so uncertain a conjecture against the authority of the most ancient manuscript and all the editions.

If, then, you ask what Minucius meant there, we shall frankly confess that we have nothing certain. But if you ask what we conjecture, then, to oblige you, it is useful first to observe what Plutarch related: [Col. 0564C] that Isis was transformed into a swallow (Plutarch, *De Isid. et Osirid.*, p. 356; *ibid.*, p. 376). He next depicts the sistrum as rounded in its upper part, with a cat in human form represented at the top of its curve, and on the lowest part, below the pieces that are shaken, sometimes the face of Isis and sometimes that of Nephthys. But sistra were not of merely one kind; they were of various kinds and diverse forms, as Tollius rightly demonstrates against Bossius (vol. VI, *Antiquit. Graec.*, p. 411 f.), as do others. Moreover, the figure of Isis was represented carrying a sistrum in her right hand. She herself, as we have seen, is the same as Ceres, who was said to have discovered crops. With these points explained, consider, please, whether the following can be said to be our author’s meaning: Alexander wrote in his letter [Col. 0564D] that Isis or Ceres was represented bearing upon her head ears of the grain which, as they said, she had discovered; beneath them a swallow, into which she had been transformed; and in her right hand a sistrum. If, however, something better occurs to you and you suggest it to us, we shall immediately and without the least resistance subscribe to your opinion. Yet it must be admitted that Minucius rightly concludes from this that the divinity of Isis is altogether ridiculous and ought to be rejected.

Finally, in the same letter of Alexander—or “volume,” as our author calls it—it was written that “the tomb of Serapis or Osiris was empty, his limbs having been scattered” or “sprinkled about.” Not without good reason, certainly. For Diodorus Siculus relates that some handed down that Typhon cut the body of his brother Osiris, whom he had cruelly murdered, [Col. 0565A] into twenty-six parts and distributed them among the same number of accomplices in his fratricide (Diodorus Siculus, *Biblioth.*, bk. I, p. 12; and in Eusebius, *Praepar. Evang.*, bk. II, ch. 1, p. 46). Isis later found them and enclosed each part in a fabricated human image. She then summoned the priests of all Egypt and distributed one part to each tribe, for each priest to bury in his own locality. Hence every Egyptian tribe believed that it possessed the tomb of Osiris, although, as our author says, it was empty and vacant. Plutarch says more simply and briefly that Isis, pretending to give the corpse of Osiris, gave each city only an individual image; or, as others think, buried the several parts of his corpse just as they came to hand (Plutarch, *De Isid. et Osirid.*, p. 358).

[Col. 0565B] “Granted,” someone will say; “I concede that the tomb of Osiris was empty. But why did Minucius add, ‘or of your Serapis’?” We shall answer the questioner in Plutarch’s words (*ibid.*, p. 362): “It is better to identify Osiris with Bacchus, and Serapis with Osiris, who was so called after he changed his nature, because Serapis is common to all.” He next observes that most priests taught that Osiris and Apis were the same, and that Apis “should be understood as a beautiful image of the soul of Osiris.” Elsewhere we have shown how the name Serapis was formed from Apis (vol. I, *Apparatus*, bk. III, diss. 2, ch. 4, art. 1, p. 1090). Hence Lactantius doubtless agreed with Plutarch when he said: “There is Osiris, whom the common people call Serapis and Serapides. For the names of the dead are customarily [Col. 0565C] changed when they are consecrated, I suppose lest anyone think that they had been human beings” (Lactantius, bk. I, ch. 21, p. 118). To both let us add Diodorus Siculus, who should have been cited first, in whom we read these words: “They think Osiris to be now Serapis, now Dionysus, sometimes Pluto, sometimes Ammon, at times Jupiter, and not rarely Pan: τὸν Ὄσιριν οἱ μὲν Σάραπιν . . . . νενομίκασι” (Diodorus, *Biblioth.*, bk. I, p. 15).

Why Minucius added “your” you will easily understand if you observe that he is disputing against Caecilius, who was still a pagan and who, as is related at the beginning of this book, had greeted a statue of Serapis that he encountered with impious worship. But whether the tomb was full of the bones of Osiris or Serapis, [Col. 0565D] or empty, it is most certainly established from this that neither they nor others who likewise died could partake of divinity. For God is eternal, having life from himself alone, and therefore can never lose it.

# CHAPTER XVI

## HOW STRONG ARE THE OTHER ARGUMENTS BY WHICH OCTAVIUS PROVES AGAINST CAECILIUS THAT THE GODS OF THE PAGANS ARE FALSE AND NONEXISTENT?

[Col. 0566A]

## ARTICLE I

**How clearly Octavius shows from the first origin of the gods that they were not gods but mere human beings; and, first, concerning their chief Saturn, who fled from Crete and was received by Janus in Italy, where he taught human beings many things—especially how to mint coins and impress letters—and from whose name Saturnia was so called.**

In order that Minucius might forever suppress the utterly intolerable boasting of Caecilius and the other pagans [Col. 0566B] concerning their gods, he demonstrates in the following way that they were by no means gods, but mere human beings from their very first origin: “All the Greek and Roman writers of antiquity handed down that Saturn, the chief of this race”—that is, the race of gods—“was a human being. Nepos and Cassius know this in their histories, and Thallus and Diodorus say it.”

In precisely the same way Tertullian strikes down and vanquishes those same enemies of the Christian religion: “Before Saturn,” he says, “there is no god among you. From him derives the whole lineage of divinity—or at least of the more powerful or better-known divinity. Accordingly, whatever is established concerning the origin will also apply to the posterity. Thus, insofar as literature teaches, neither Diodorus the Greek nor Thallus, [Col. 0566C] neither Cassius Severus nor Cornelius Nepos, nor any commentator on antiquities of this kind, proclaimed Saturn to be anything other than a man” (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 10, p. 12). He repeats the same thing in another book, except that someone or other wrote “Tacitus” in place of “Thallus,” as we shall note in its proper place (*ibid.*, *Ad Nationes*, bk. II, ch. 12, p. 75; *Dissert. in Tertullian.*, ch. 27, art. 1). For Lactantius, who follows him and our Minucius, said this about the same Saturn in almost the same words: “All—not only poets but also writers of histories and antiquities—who committed to memory his deeds in Italy agree that he was a human being: among the Greeks, Diodorus and Thallus; among the Latins, Nepos, Cassius, and Varro” (Lactantius, bk. I, ch. 13, p. 76).

[Col. 0566D] Thus to the four writers praised by Minucius, as also by Tertullian, Lactantius added a fifth, Varro. In this way those vigorous champions turned their enemies’ own forces against them and utterly destroyed and routed them.

But why, you will ask, did those writers dare to affirm so confidently that Saturn was the first and chief of all the gods? Did Alexander, instructed by a priest, not write in the letter cited by us a little earlier that Vulcan was the chief of the gods, and then came the lineage of Jupiter? But what wonder is it if pagans wandering in error held various opinions about the first origin of their false gods? Moreover, this was the judgment of a single priest—or, as Minucius says, a secret. Who, then, would say that he should be believed rather than so many [Col. 0567A] celebrated writers cited by our author? Finally, what is to be said below will sufficiently show that Vulcan could not be called either the first or the chief of all the gods (vol. I, *Apparatus*, p. 755).

Minucius then relates, doubtless from the same writers, that Saturn, as we have noted elsewhere, fled from Crete and took refuge in Italy through fear of his son. There, having been received by Janus, he taught “uncivilized people” many things, as Diodorus Siculus, praised by Minucius, also testifies—especially how to impress letters, mint coins, and make implements. In addition, he wished the place in which he had lain hidden to be called Saturnia, just as Janus called his place the Janiculum. Tertullian had previously committed all these things to writing, as Cyprian and Lactantius did afterward (Diodorus, *Biblioth.*, bk. III, p. 136, [Col. 0567B] and bk. V, pp. 231 and 233; Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 10, p. 12, and *Ad Nationes*, bk. II, ch. 12, p. 75; Cyprian, *De Idol. vanit.*, p. 11; Lactantius, bk. I, ch. 13, p. 76).

Concerning the city of Saturnia and the Janiculum, Virgil sang as follows:

> Moreover, you see these two towns with their shattered walls,
>
> Relics and monuments of men of old:
>
> Father Janus founded this city, Saturn that;
>
> This was named Janiculum, and that Saturnia.  
> (Virgil, *Aeneid*, bk. VIII, line 354 ff.)

But regarding these matters and the minted coin, Ovid—also praised by Lactantius (*Divine Institutes*, bk. I, ch. 13, p. 76)—questioned Saturn thus:

> Much indeed have I learned, but why is one side
>
> Of the bronze stamped with a ship, the other with a double head?  
> [Col. 0567C]

He represented Saturn as answering thus:

> You could have recognized me in the double image, he said,
>
> Had the long passage of time not worn away the work.
>
> The reason for the ship remains: in a ship the sickle-bearing god
>
> Came to the Tuscan river, after wandering through the world.
>
> I remember Saturn being received in this land;
>
> He had been driven by Jupiter from the celestial kingdoms.
>
> Hence the name Saturnia long remained for the people;
>
> The land was also called Latium, because the god lay hidden.
>
> But a dutiful posterity fashioned a ship’s stern upon the bronze,
>
> Attesting the arrival of its guest.
>
> I myself inhabited the ground whose left side is gently washed
>
> By the wave of the sandy Tiber.
>
> Here, where Rome now stands, a lofty forest then flourished,
>
> And that mighty city was pasture for a few cattle.
>
> My citadel was the hill which the common people call by our name,
>
> And which this present age calls the Janiculum.  
> (Ovid, *Fasti*, bk. I, line 231 ff.)

But by what reasoning, someone will object, is Saturn said to have taught the art of minting coins? Does not Servius, on the cited verses of Virgil, ascribe it to Janus alone in this observation: “Janus lived on the Janiculum; because he came as an exile in a single ship, his coinage was stamped on one side with the head of Janus and on the other with a ship” (Servius, p. 509)? But Servius is discussing there both Saturn and Janus, as is his author Virgil. Since, therefore, Saturn, and by no means Janus, “came as an exile in a single ship,” must not Servius be understood to speak of coinage stamped in the name of both?

“Granted,” another will insist; “yet Draco of Corcyra, in Athenaeus, with whom Macrobius agrees, explicitly affirms: νόμισμα χαλκοῦ πρῶτον χαράξαι, ‘a bronze coin was first stamped by Janus’”; and that this is why many cities in Greece, Italy, and Sicily [Col. 0568A] struck money impressed on one side with a two-headed face and on the other with either a raft, a ship, or a crown (Athenaeus, *Deipnosoph.*, bk. XV, ch. 18, p. 692; Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, bk. I, ch. 7). But why, please, was the image of a raft or a ship stamped on this coin? Was it not because, as we have said and as Plutarch states, it was “ἐπὶ τιμῇ Κρόνου πλοίῳ διαπεράσαντος εἰς Ἰταλίαν, in honor of Saturn, who was conveyed to Italy by ship”? (Plutarch, vol. II, *Roman Questions*, p. 274.) What, then, if Janus struck a coin in honor of Saturn, and Saturn another in memory of his host? Whatever the case, Minucius certainly seems to have had as an earlier authority the Ovid cited by us, and more expressly Tertullian, who did not hesitate to commit the following to writing concerning Saturn himself: “By him coinage was first stamped with a tablet and image, [Col. 0568B] and therefore he presides over the treasury” (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 10, p. 12). Cyprian follows his master, as he also follows our Minucius, closely in these words: “He was the first in Italy to institute the impressing of letters and the minting of coins; hence the treasury is called the treasury of Saturn” (Cyprian, *De Idolor. Vanit.*, p. 11). Let us add, if you please, Polydore Vergil, who attempts to confirm this opinion by the authority of Eutropius (Polydore Vergil, *De Invent.*, bk. II, ch. 20).

Minucius therefore rightly concludes from what has been said: “Certainly Saturn was a man, since he fled; certainly a man, since he hid.” Lactantius draws the same conclusion: “Does anyone,” he says, “consider one who fled and hid to be God? No one is so foolish. For one who flees and hides must necessarily fear both violence and death” (Lactantius, [Col. 0568C] *Divine Institutes*, bk. I, ch. 13, p. 76).

## ARTICLE II

**How perversely the pagans said that Saturn was born of heaven and earth; whence this opinion arose; whether the explanation of it given by Minucius is rightly refuted by Lactantius; and whether it may nevertheless be concluded from it that Saturn was not a god but a mere human being.**

It was demonstrated abundantly enough in the preceding article that Saturn was not God, since, as Minucius says, he “was born from a human being.” Indeed, says Tertullian, because he was begotten “from a human being, surely not from heaven and earth,” as the pagans everywhere proclaimed both orally and in writing, at home and abroad—indeed, where did they not? (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 10, p. 12, and [Col. 0568D] *Ad Nationes*, bk. II, ch. 12, p. 75.) If you ask our author why they said with so empty a boast that he had sprung from heaven and earth, he will give you this reason: “Saturn is said to have been the son of earth and heaven because he appeared among the Italians with his parents unknown; just as to this day we call those who unexpectedly appear ‘sent from heaven,’ and persons of obscure and unknown origin ‘sons of earth.’” But this explanation did not please Lactantius, and he refutes it thus:

> Minucius Felix, in the book entitled *Octavius*, argued as follows: that when Saturn had been driven out by his son and had come to Italy, he was called a son of heaven because we customarily say that those whose excellence we admire, or who have arrived suddenly, have fallen from heaven; and a son of earth because we call those born of unknown parents sons of earth. [Col. 0569A] These things indeed resemble the truth, but are not true, because it is established that he was so regarded even then, when he reigned. He could have argued thus instead: since Saturn was a most powerful king, in order to preserve the memory of his parents he gave their names to heaven and earth, which had previously been called by other names; in the same manner we know that names were imposed upon mountains and rivers.  
> (Lactantius, *Institutes*, bk. I, ch. 11, p. 67.)

Then, after enumerating the names of certain rivers, he concludes thus: “It is therefore apparent that he was not born from heaven, which is impossible, but from the man whose name was Uranus; Trismegistus is the authority that this is true.” He adds that these matters were unknown to Minucius, who therefore diverted the history into another interpretation. Finally, he considers it truer that Jupiter, after contemplating earth and heaven from a lofty [Col. 0569B] mountain, gave to the ether above the world the name *Coelum*, or Οὐρανός, Uranus, by which his grandfather was called. But he needed to prove that Saturn’s father, while he was still alive, was actually called “Heaven” by the Italians. This opinion of Lactantius, however, must be discussed in its proper place.

Thus he judges Minucius’s reasoning to be defective. For Minucius ought rather to have said that Saturn was called the son of heaven and earth because, when he was a most powerful king, he imposed the names of heaven and earth upon his parents in order to preserve their memory. He attempts to prove this by the authority of Trismegistus, who had recorded that Saturn’s father was surnamed Uranus, or Heaven. But Trismegistus does not show there whether he said when and from whom Uranus [Col. 0569C] received his name. He could therefore more truly have written that uncivilized people, overwhelmed by Saturn’s supreme royal power, believed that he derived his origin from heaven and earth. For the Sibyl sang this in the following verses, cited by Athenagoras (*Legat. pro Christian.*, p. 14):

> Καὶ βασιλεὺς Κρόνος, καὶ Τιτὰν, Ἰαπετός τε,
>
> Γαίης τέκνα φέριστα, καὶ οὐρανίους ἐκάλεσσαν
>
> Ἄνθρωποι, γαῖάν τε, καὶ οὐρανὸν οὔνομα θέντες,
>
> Οὕνεκα οἱ πρώτιστοι ἔσαν μερόπων ἀνθρώπων.
>
> Then Saturn, Titan, and Iapetus
>
> Reigned; human beings said they had been created
>
> By heaven and earth, calling them by the names
>
> Of earth and heaven, because in excellence
>
> They surpassed all mortal men.  
> (*Sibylline Oracles*, III, line 48 ff.)

But Minucius does not appear to have omitted this explanation altogether. For he distinguished noble men from the ignoble, and said that the latter were surnamed sons of earth and the former sons of heaven [Col. 0569D] by Italians to whom their parents were unknown.

To Lactantius, however, it appears more plausible than true that people born of unknown parents and arriving unexpectedly were named after heaven and earth, from which they were believed to have sprung. Nevertheless, this is proved by other writers, both pagan and Christian. The first pagan writer who may be cited is Titus Livy, who relates that in founding the city of Rome Romulus employed “the ancient policy of founders of cities, who, by gathering around themselves an obscure and lowly multitude, falsely claimed that an offspring had been born to them from the earth” (Livy, bk. I, 58). But how could they have falsely claimed this unless the origins of that obscure multitude had been unknown? Who, moreover, will deny that the same thing must be said of [Col. 0570A] parents and children? Yet if some difficult and captious person wishes this to be proved to him specifically of parents, let him hear Servius’s words concerning Achelous: “He is called a son of earth, as is customarily said of those whose parents are hidden by antiquity” (Servius on Virgil, *Georgics*, bk. I, line 9).

Still more pertinent to our subject concerning Saturn is Aurelius Victor—or whoever was the author of the book *On the Origin of the Roman People*:

> Saturn is believed to have been the first to come into Italy. . . . Such, moreover, is the simplicity handed down concerning the people of old down to that time, that when strangers came to them who, provided only that they were endowed with prudence and wisdom, contributed something toward the ordering of life and the formation of character, because their parents were unknown, they not only themselves believed them to have been produced by heaven and earth, but also affirmed this to posterity—as, for example, this very Saturn, whom they called a son of heaven and earth.  
> (Aurelius Victor, *Orig. gent. Rom.*, beginning.)

Add Tertullian, who left this written about Saturn not merely in one book but in two:

> Because his parents were unknown, it was easy for him to be called the son of those whose children we may all be thought to be. For who does not call heaven and earth mother and father, either for the sake of veneration and honor or from the human custom by which unknown persons, or those appearing unexpectedly, are said to have come down from heaven? Accordingly, because Saturn appeared suddenly everywhere, it fell to him to be called a heavenly being. For the common people also call those whose lineage is uncertain “sons of earth.”  
> (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 10, p. 12, and *Ad Nationes*, bk. II, ch. 12, p. 75.)

Whether these passages suffice to establish our Minucius’s opinion, and whether it was not entirely rightly refuted by Lactantius, we shall await the judgment of more learned men. For we readily admit that it is not ours to settle disputes among men so numerous and of such venerable antiquity. Whatever may be determined, it is certainly established from this, by an altogether unanswerable inference, that this Saturn—whom the pagans babbled was the parent of their other gods—was by no means a god but merely a human being, begotten from a human being just like all other human beings.

## ARTICLE III

**By what force of arguments Caecilius demonstrates that the divinity of Jupiter and of others was false, since they had been begotten from human beings, or, like Romulus and Juba, had been proclaimed gods through the caprice and arbitrary will of others.**
Minucius Felix passes from Saturn to his son Jupiter, and likewise demonstrates that he was a man and by no means God [Col. 0570D]. For Saturn’s “son Jupiter,” he says, “reigned in Crete after driving out his father; there he died, there he had children; the cave of Jupiter is still visited, and his tomb is shown, and in his own sacred rites he is convicted of humanity.” But we discussed these matters a little earlier, and they must be treated again in our subsequent dissertations. Moreover, we shall discuss below the rites of Jupiter which continued to show that he was a man.

Since, therefore, this Jupiter cannot be a god, because he was begotten by another man, it necessarily follows that the others descended from him and from other human beings were by no means gods, but mortal men, infinitely removed from the divine nature. Minucius accordingly declares that he passes over in silence the genealogies of those gods described [Col. 0571A] by the pagans, since it would be as tedious as it would be useless to set them forth. For, he says, “it is pointless to go through them individually and unfold the entire line of that family, since the mortality proved in the case of its first parents has flowed down to the rest in the order of succession.” Did he not take this idea from Tertullian, who had said earlier: “It is also pointless to pursue their titles. . . . What has been established concerning their origin will apply also to their posterity”? (Tertull., *Apologet.*, ch. 10, p. 12.) These, of course, are fictitious gods and mere human beings.

But Minucius presses the pagans more sharply and assails them in these words, nearly all of which Cyprian transcribed: “Why, if they were born, are they not still being born today? Unless perhaps Jupiter has now grown old, Juno’s childbearing has failed, [Col. 0571B] and Minerva has gone gray before giving birth” (Cyprian, *On the Vanity of Idols*, p. 12). Earlier, Theophilus of Antioch had refuted the pagans by the same argument:

> Εἰ γὰρ τότε ἐγέννων, καὶ ἐγεννῶντο, δῆλον, ὅτι ἐχρῆν καὶ ἕως τοῦ δεῦρο γίνεσθαι θεοὺς γεννητούς· ἢ γὰρ ἐγήρασαν διὸ οὐκ ἔτι γεννῶσι· ἢ ἀπέθανον, καὶ οὐκ ἔτι εἰσί.
>
> “For if at that time they begot and were begotten, it is evident that begotten gods ought to have continued coming into being down to the present. If matters are otherwise, the race of gods must surely be considered feeble: either they have been exhausted by old age and have ceased to beget, or they have been utterly removed from the number of the living and reduced to nothing.”

(Theoph., *To Autolycus*, bk. I, p. 81.)

Tatian is briefer, but no less witty: “If,” he says, “you recount a generation of gods, you show that they are mortal: διὰ τί γὰρ οὐ κύει νῦν ἡ Ἥρα; πότερον γεγήρακεν; ἢ τοῦ μηνύσαντος ὑμῖν [Col. 0571C] ἀπορεῖτε; Why does Juno no longer conceive? Has she grown old? Or do you have no one who can disclose the matter to you?” (Tatian, *Oration Against the Greeks*, p. 160.)

Thus Seneca too, as quoted by Lactantius, argues by ridiculing his fellow pagans: “Why is it, then,” he says, “that Jupiter, the most lustful figure in the poets, has ceased to produce children? Has he turned sixty, and has the Papian law fastened a clasp upon him? Or has he obtained the right of three children? Or has it at last occurred to him, ‘Expect from another what you have done to another,’ and does he fear that someone might do to him what he himself did to Saturn?” (Lact., bk. I, ch. 16, p. 88.) That is, he fears that, just as he deprived his father Saturn of his kingdom, so his own sons might deprive him of his. But something must be said below about Lactantius and these words of Seneca. Finally, to omit others, Juvenal too sang:

> [Col. 0571D] Yet who can assert that nothing happens on the mountains  
> Or in the caves? So greatly have Jupiter and Mars grown old.

(Juvenal, *Satires*, VI, v. 62 ff.)

Minucius presses on and utterly destroys false opinions about the gods with yet another argument: “If gods,” he says, “could be created but could not perish, we should have more gods than all the human race; so that by now neither heaven could contain them, nor the air hold them, nor the earth support them.” With this exceedingly sharp weapon, which the Sibyl also employs, Theophilus of Antioch, already cited by us, had thoroughly transfixed the pagans. For from this, he says,

> μᾶλλον καὶ πλείονες θεοὶ ὤφειλον εἶναι τῶν ἀνθρώπων, ὥς φησι Σίβυλλα
>
> “it follows that there ought to be more gods than human beings, as the Sibyl also declares.”

Anyone may readily read the remainder, which is more extensive in Theophilus, as well as similar material in Arnobius, Lactantius—whom we shall discuss in the proper place—and Eusebius (Arnob., bk. III *Against the Pagans*, p. 104 ff.; Lactan., bk. I, ch. 16 ff.; Euseb., *Oration of Constantine to the Assembly of the Saints*, ch. 4, p. 570). [Col. 0572A]

Meanwhile, however, we wish to remind you that this argument possesses such force and weight that Pliny, completely overwhelmed by it, admits that either the number of celestial beings ought to be greater than that of human beings, or the marriages of the gods were not genuine. But it is pleasing to hear the man himself speak:

> “The population of celestial beings,” he says, “may even be understood to be greater than that of human beings, since individuals also make for themselves an equal number of gods out of their own selves by adopting Junos and tutelary spirits; while certain peoples regard animals, and even some obscene things, as gods, [Col. 0572B] and swear by many things still more shameful to mention, including foul foods and other objects. But to believe in marriages among the gods, while throughout so great an age no one is born from them, and that some are always aged and gray-haired, while others are young men and boys, some winged, some lame, some born from an egg, and some living and dying on alternate days, is almost the delirium of children.”

(Plin., *Natural History*, bk. II, ch. 7, p. 142 f.)

What argument, then, I ask you, could have been advanced more effective for abolishing the religions of the pagans than that candid and public confession of Pliny and of other pagans as well?

Nor should you say that Pliny, like those most learned pagan men, rejects these beliefs as fables of an ignorant and uncultivated populace. For this was plainly sufficient for Minucius and the other defenders of the Christian religion utterly to overthrow the impious cults of all pagans, which rested upon these monstrous errors. For who could endure the empty superstitions of those who denied the one eternal God and worshiped and venerated numerous others as gods—mortals, or beings that begot and were begotten? [Col. 0572C] Learned pagans no less than the unlearned rejected the true God and worshiped those ridiculous gods; or, while pretending to worship them, admitted no god at all, or admitted something else still further removed from true divinity because it was created or itself deprived of reason.

Did those men not stray in the same way from the straight path of truth when they foolishly proclaimed that certain mortal human beings had become gods either by virtue of their birth or through the perjury, lust, and arbitrary will of others? Such, however, was “the god Romulus,” as Minucius says, “through the perjury [Col. 0572D] of Proculus,” as we shall explain shortly. “Juba likewise,” he continues, “is a god because the Moors willed it; and the other kings who are deified are called divine, not from belief in their divinity, but to honor their power after its service has ended.” Lactantius subscribed to our author’s statement and committed this to writing:

> “Individual peoples privately worshiped with the highest veneration either the founders of their own nation or city, or men distinguished for courage, or women remarkable for chastity—as the Egyptians worshiped Isis and the Moors Juba.”

(Lactan., *Institutes*, bk. I, ch. 15, p. 81.)

Earlier, however, Tertullian had spoken more generally, suppressing Juba’s name but leaving it understood: “Each province and city has its own god . . . as Mauretania has its own petty kings.” [Col. 0573A] Cyprian follows Tertullian there in his customary fashion and says: “The Moors openly worship kings and do not conceal that name beneath any covering” (Cyprian, *On the Vanity of Idols*, p. 12).

Cellarius, however, suspects that some error lies concealed in the text of our Minucius. For Juba, he says, was king not of the Moors but of the Numidians. We cannot, indeed, deny that Dio Cassius and Plutarch committed this to writing. But did Minucius, or his copyist, or the authors cited by us therefore err (Dio, *Roman History*, p. 193; Plutarch, *Life of Caesar*, p. 732)? Or had Cellarius himself perhaps not examined Strabo’s books carefully enough? For there he could have read these words:

> Νυνὶ εἰς Ἰούβαν περιέστηκεν Μαυρουσία, καὶ πολλὰ μέρη τῆς ἄλλης Λιβύης [Col. 0573B] διὰ τὴν πρὸς Ῥωμαίους εὔνοιάν τε, καὶ φιλίαν.
>
> “Juba now possesses Mauretania and many other parts of Africa, having obtained this because of his goodwill and friendship toward the Romans.”

(Strab., *Geography*, bk. VI, near the end, p. 288.)

Why, then, you will ask, is Juba called king of the Numidians by Dio and Plutarch? Herodian unties the knot of this difficulty. He testifies that Mauretania, where Juba ruled and which was subject to the Romans, was called Numidia by its inhabitants:

> Καπελλιανὸς ἦν τις ὄνομα, ἀπὸ τοῦ συγκλήτου, ἡγεῖτο δὲ Μαυρουσίων τῶν ὑπὸ Ῥωμαίοις, Νομάδων δὲ καλουμένων.
>
> “There was a certain Capellianus by name, a man of senatorial rank, who governed Mauretania, which was subject to the Romans and was called Numidia by its inhabitants.”

(Herodian, *History*, bk. VII, p. 280.)

Cellarius further insists that it is not plausible that Juba, who was defeated by Caesar and laid violent hands upon himself, was placed by the Moors among the gods. [Col. 0573C] But this argument is of the slightest possible weight. For who does not know that a custom became prevalent among the Romans of enrolling their emperors, however wicked and criminal, in the register of the gods by a solemn rite and apotheosis? Nor did they very often await their deaths; rather, while they were still alive, they paid them divine honors, even against their will and resistance. Therefore, immediately after the words cited by us, Minucius added: “Finally, this name is assigned to them against their will: they desire to persevere as human beings, fear being made gods, and, even when already old, do not wish it.” Tertullian, however, presses this point more sharply, as we shall see in our dissertation on his apologetic books. What wonder is it, then, if the Moors, after the example of the Romans, wished their king [Col. 0573D] Juba to be a god?

# CHAPTER XVII  
## HOW WEIGHTY IS ANOTHER ARGUMENT OF MINUCIUS AGAINST THE GODS OF THE PAGANS, DRAWN FROM THEIR RIDICULOUS FORMS AND FIGURES AND FROM THEIR UNWORTHY AND SHAMEFUL DEEDS AND CRIMES

### ARTICLE I  
#### How absurdly Vulcan is imagined by the pagans as lame; Apollo as beardless; Aesculapius as bearded, and sometimes beardless; Neptune as blue-green-eyed, Minerva as gray-blue-eyed, Juno as ox-eyed; Mercury as wing-footed; Pan as hoofed; Saturn as fettered; and Janus as two-faced and four-formed

The ridiculous forms and figures of the gods furnish Minucius [Col. 0574A] with another altogether invincible argument for demolishing their fictitious divinity. “For what,” Minucius asks, “of their very forms and attire? Do they not expose the mockery and disgrace—our manuscripts have *decora*, ‘adornments,’ but wrongly—of your gods?” If you desire to know what those forms were, hear Gregory of Nazianzus describing them in these few verses:

> Ἰθυφάλους, κερόεντας, ἀναύχενας, ἡμιδράκοντας,  
> Θῆρας, θηρομιγεῖς τε γελοῖον εἶδος ἔχοντας.
>
> Ithyphallic and obscene, horned, half-dragons,  
> Beasts without necks and others mingled with beasts,  
> All bearing various laughable faces.

(Greg. Nazianz., *Poem* LXI, p. 142, vol. II.) [Col. 0574B]

Our author, however, pursues this subject far more extensively; and so that the pagans might at last feel shame at worshiping such gods, he enumerates nearly all their monstrous forms and sets them before their very eyes. Although he follows no order based upon their fictitious ages or ranks, yet, because this contributes little or nothing to the force and cogency of the argument, we have thought it better to adhere to his footsteps.

He begins with Vulcan in this way: “Vulcan is a lame and feeble god.” Cotta, in Cicero, uses the same argument to refute the Epicurean Velleius, although he observes more carefully the order of his gods, and objects to him concerning Vulcan in these words:

> “At Athens, indeed, we praise the Vulcan made by Alcamenes, in whom, though he is standing and clothed, a slight lameness is apparent, but without deformity. We shall therefore have a lame god, since this is what we have received concerning Vulcan.”

(Cic., *On the Nature of the Gods*, bk. I, p. 207, line 27.) [Col. 0574C]

Lucian relates that he became lame when Jupiter hurled him headlong from heaven:

> Εἴγε μὴ Λήμνιοι καλῶς ποιοῦντες, ἔτι φερόμενον αὐτὸν ὑπεδέξαντο, ἐτεθνήκει ἂν ἡμῖν Ἥφαιστος, ὥσπερ ὁ Ἀστυάναξ ἀπὸ πύργου καταπεσών.
>
> “Had the Lemnians not kindly caught him while he was still falling through the air, our Vulcan would have perished, just like Astyanax when he fell from the tower.”

(Lucian, *On Sacrifices*, p. 184; Homer, *Iliad* I, v. 590 ff.; idem, *Iliad* XVIII, v. 304 ff.) There he undoubtedly alludes to two passages of Homer’s *Iliad*, also cited by Clement of Alexandria, where Vulcan is said to have been hurled from heaven onto Lemnos and thereby made lame. Athanasius, moreover, when attacking the pagans in the same manner as our author, charges them with representing Ἥφαιστον ῥιπτόμενον, καὶ χωλαίνοντα, “Vulcan as cast down from heaven and made lame by that fall.” Arnobius reports that he was lame in one foot, Gregory in both. Nor are there lacking those who believe that he was cast from heaven twice, first by Juno and then by Jupiter (Clement of Alexandria, *Exhortation to the Pagans*, p. 18; Athanas., *Oration Against the Pagans*, §12, p. 13, vol. I; Arnob., bk. IV *Against the Pagans*, p. 134; Greg. Naz., Orat. 3 *Against Julian*, p. 259, and Orat. 4, p. 308). [Col. 0574D]

The second pair introduced by our author is: “Apollo, smooth-faced through so many ages, and Aesculapius, always bearded.” It was surely for this reason, they say, that Dionysius, tyrant of Sicily, removed Aesculapius’ beard, since he was the son of Apollo, who, as Cicero says, was always beardless. On this subject see further Cicero, Valerius Maximus, Arnobius, Lactantius, and many others. Cicero himself and others assert that the beard was removed not from just any Aesculapius, but from the Epidaurian one [Col. 0575A] (Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, bk. I, p. 107, line 26; idem, ibid., bk. III, p. 252, line 40; Valer. Max., bk. II, ch. 1, *Foreign Examples*, §3; Arnob., bk. VI *Against the Pagans*, p. 206; Lactant., *Institutes*, bk. II, ch. 4, p. 157; Cic., *On the Nature of the Gods*, bk. III, p. 252, line 45). Pausanias, however, when speaking of the Phliasians, records this concerning the image of Aesculapius:

> Κατιόντων δὲ ἐκ τῆς ἀκροπόλεως ἔστιν Ἀσκληπιοῦ ναὸς ἐν δεξιᾷ, καὶ ἄγαλμα οὐκ ἔχον πωγωνεῖα.
>
> “As one descends from the citadel, there is a temple of Aesculapius on the right, containing a beardless image.”

(Pausan., *Corinth*, bk. II, p. 56.) [Col. 0575B]

But if Lucian is to be trusted, Apollo was represented by everyone as beardless, except only by the Assyrians:

> Οἱ μὲν γὰρ ἄλλοι πάντες Ἀπόλλωνα νέον τε ἥγηνται, καὶ πρωθήβην ποιοῦσι· μοῦνοι δὲ οὗτοι Ἀπόλλωνος γενειήτεω ξόανον δεικνύουσι.
>
> “For all others,” he says, “regard Apollo as young and fashion him with the first down of youth; these alone exhibit an image of a bearded Apollo.”

(Lucian, *On the Syrian Goddess*, p. 1071.) Macrobius, however, reports that this was done not by all the Assyrians but by the Hieropolitans: “The Hieropolitans,” he says, “who are peoples of Assyria, reduce all the effects and powers of the Sun to the appearance of a single bearded image, and call that same figure Apollo. His elongated face is shaped by a beard tapering to a point” (Macrob., *Saturnalia*, bk. I, ch. 17). [Col. 0575C]

Third, Minucius says: “Neptune has blue-green eyes, Minerva gray-blue ones” (Minuc., p. 181). Cicero, already cited by us, had said: “It will be permissible to say that Minerva’s eyes are gray-blue and Neptune’s deep blue” (Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, bk. I, p. 207, line 24). Although Diodorus Siculus rejects this as an insipid fiction and believes that Minerva was imagined as *glaukopis* because the air has a blue-gray appearance (Diodor., *Library*, bk. I, p. 88), Lucian nevertheless calls her γλαυκῶπις (*glaukopis*, “gray-blue-eyed”), the epithet by which Homer everywhere commonly designates her; and Homer’s Latin translator renders it now as “gray-blue-eyed,” now as “blue-green-eyed” (Lucian, *Dialogue of Vulcan and Jupiter*, p. 74, and *On Sacrifices*, p. [Col. 0575D] 185). Certainly among Latin writers *caesius*, or blue, is the same color as *glaucus*, blue-green or gray-green, such as, they say, the eyes of cats.

What of the fact that Pausanias testifies that Neptune, of whom Minucius speaks, had blue-green eyes like Minerva? “Concerning the image of Minerva,” these are his words, “which has blue-green eyes, γλαυκοὺς ἔχον τοὺς ὀφθαλμούς, I learn a Libyan story: that Minerva is the daughter of Neptune and Lake Tritonis, and that for this reason she has blue-green eyes like Neptune, καὶ διὰ τοῦτο γλαυκοὺς εἶναι ὥσπερ καὶ τῷ Ποσειδῶνι ὀφθαλμούς.” If anyone should maintain and prove that Pausanias is speaking there of a different Minerva from that of the author cited by us, we shall not oppose him. No one, however, will deny that Cicero and our Minucius posited some distinction [Col. 0576A] between the eyes of Neptune and those of Minerva, perhaps because the eyes of one were greener than those of the other. On these eyes of Minerva, see Arnobius, whom we discuss in the proper place (*Dissertation on Arnobius*, ch. 14, art. 1).

Juno, moreover, as our author next says, was said by the pagans to have “bovine eyes” (Homer, *Iliad* IV, v. 5). He undoubtedly followed Homer, by whom she is called βοῶπις πότνια Ἥρη, “venerable ox-eyed Juno” (*Iliad* XIV, v. 159). The poet’s Latin translator renders this: “Venerable Juno with beautiful eyes.” If you ask the reason, we shall answer that he rendered the Greek name in this way because bovine eyes were regarded as the most beautiful of all. For Lucian (*Images*, p. 590) regards as a most accomplished painter one who made βοῶπίν [Col. 0576B] τινα ποιήσας αὐτῶν, “a certain one among them ox-eyed”—that is, who painted Juno “with bovine eyes.”

Minucius continues (p. 184): “Mercury has winged feet, Pan hoofed feet, Saturn fettered feet.” Surely no one is unaware that Mercury was imagined as the messenger of the gods and therefore as bearing wings upon his head and feet. Accordingly, Homer sang these lines about him when he was sent by Jupiter:

> Ὡς ἔφατ’, οὐδ’ ἀπίθησε διάκτορος Ἀργειφόντης.  
> Αὐτίκ’ ἔπειθ’, ὑπὸ ποσσὶν ἐδήσατο καλὰ πέδιλα,  
> Ἀμβρόσια, χρύσεια· τά μιν φέρον ἠμὲν ἐφ’ ὑγρὴν,  
> Ἠδ’ ἐπ’ ἀπείρονα γαῖαν, ἅμα πνοιῇς ἀνέμοιο.
>
> Thus he spoke, and Mercury the messenger, slayer of Argus, did not disobey.  
> At once he fastened beneath his feet the beautiful sandals,  
> Immortal and golden, which bore him alike over the sea  
> And over the boundless earth together with the breath of the wind.

(Homer, *Odyssey* V, v. 43 ff.) [Col. 0576C]

Pan, however, was said to have hoofed or goat-like feet, as Eusebius relates in these words:

> “Indeed, they themselves describe the appearance and form of their own bodies, as in the case of Pan himself; what he was like we learn from his oracles: ‘Though I am mortal, I now offer prayers, Πανὶ συμφύτῳ θεῷ, θισσοκέρατι, δισσόποδι τραγοσκελεῖ—to Pan, the god born with me, double-horned, two-footed, and goat-legged, distinguished for sensual pleasure.’”

(Euseb., *Preparation for the Gospel*, bk. III, ch. 14, p. 124.) Herodotus indeed acknowledges that painters and sculptors represent him with a goat’s face and goat’s legs; yet he candidly admits that it is not agreeable for him to explain why this was done [Col. 0576D] (Herodot., bk. II, §46). But you may consult Servius’ notes on Virgil and others (Serv. on Virgil).

Concerning Saturn’s “fettered feet,” as our author calls them, we read these words committed to writing by Cicero: “This ancient belief filled Greece: that Heaven was castrated by his son Saturn, while Saturn himself was bound by his son Jupiter.” Our authors Athenagoras and Athanasius support the Latin orator, as does Epiphanius, besides very many others. In accordance with the thought of our Minucius, Epiphanius argues from it as follows: “But one who is held in custody is not only subjected to someone more powerful, but is also ordinarily restrained with bonds because of some wrongdoing” (*Selections* 2, v. 31; Cic., *On the Nature of the Gods*, bk. II, p. 223; Athenag., *Embassy for the Christians*, pp. 19 [Col. 0577A] and 20; Athanas., *Oration Against the Pagans*, §11, p. 12; Epiphan., *Ancoratus*, §106, p. 107).

Moreover, in Lucian, when a priest had asked Saturn himself whether he had truly been hurled by his son Jupiter into Tartarus after being placed in chains, Saturn replies:

> “Since I was already old and gout-ridden with age—from which it also came about that most people imagined that I was fettered, τὸ μὲν ὅλον γέρων ἤδη καὶ ποδαγρὸς ὤν, διὸ καὶ πεπεδῆσθαί με οἱ πολλοὶ εἴκασαν—I lacked the strength to punish so many crimes of this age. . . . And so, taking thought for myself, I yielded my place to Jupiter.”

Cicero and Macrobius finally offer other reasons why he was defeated by Jupiter (Lucian, *Saturnalia*, p. 1022 f.; Cicero, loc. cit.; Macrob., *Saturnalia*, bk. I, ch. 8).

[Col. 0577B] Minucius then continues: “Janus, however, bears two faces, as though so that he may walk backward.” To omit Athenaeus (*Deipnosophists*, bk. XV, p. 592) and very many others, Ovid has these verses about him:

> Janus, two-headed source of the silently gliding year,  
> You alone among the gods above can see your own back.  
> . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .  
> Yet what god shall I call you, Janus of double form?  
> For Greece has no divinity equal to you.

(Ovid, *Fasti*, bk. I, §4, v. 65.) If you ask why they called him two-faced, Plutarch, Macrobius, Cyprian, and Vossius will give you differing explanations (Plutarch, *Roman Questions*, p. 279; Macrob., *Saturnalia*, bk. I, chs. 7 and 9; Cyprian, *On the Vanity of Idols*, p. 12; Vossius, *On the Origin and Progress of Idolatry*, bk. I, ch. 18, p. 71 ff.). Finally, [Col. 0577C] we shall add that this Janus, according to the testimony of the same Macrobius and also of Augustine, was proclaimed by the pagans not only two-faced but also four-faced and four-formed (Macrob., *Saturnalia*, bk. I, ch. 9; Augustine, *City of God*, bk. VII, ch. 4). Who, then, will not lament that dreadful blindness of the pagans, who believed not so much human beings as monstrosities of human beings to be gods, and rendered them divine honors? Yet their insane superstition did not stop there. They worshiped many still more infamous forms belonging to other gods. We must now investigate how our author explains and demolishes these.

### ARTICLE II  
#### With what madness the pagans celebrated Diana as high-girded and a huntress, as the many-breasted Ephesian, and as Trivia with three heads and many hands; Jupiter as sometimes bearded and sometimes beardless; Ammon with horns; Capitolinus bearing thunderbolts; Latiaris drenched in blood; Feretrius not heard—whose monstrosities are as numerous as his names

[Col. 0577D]

Minucius pursues his argument and attacks Diana’s threefold form: “Diana,” he says, “is high-girded and a huntress; as the Ephesian, she is built up with many breasts and udders”—the codex reads *veribus*, “spits”—“and as Trivia she is terrifying with three heads and many hands.” Who does not know that Diana was a huntress? Pausanias [Col. 0578A] (bk. VII, pp. 230 and 234) and others mention this more than once. That in hunting she is rightly said to have been high-girded may be gathered from these verses of Ovid:

> Over ridges, through forests, and across thorny rocks she wanders,  
> Her knee bare and her garment girded up after Diana’s fashion.

(Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, bk. X, fable 12.)

And again elsewhere:

> Such are Diana’s girded-up legs portrayed  
> When, stronger than the strong beasts, she pursues them.

(*Amores*, bk. V, Elegy 22.) There is no need to cite other poems or testimonies of the same Ovid, of Prudentius (epist. IV, hymn on Romanus, v. 257), and of others concerning a matter sufficiently known to all.

Some, however, think that the following words in [Col. 0578B] our manuscript codex are corrupt: “The Ephesian, built up with many breasts and spits.” For certain men could not bring themselves to believe that Diana, being a virgin, had several breasts. They therefore think that the word “Ceres,” who was called many-breasted, must be added. Others judge that instead of *veribus* (“spits”) one should read either *uberibus* (“udders”) or *tuberibus* (“swellings”). But these conjectures are extremely weak, or rather false, and the reading of our ancient codex must not be changed. For Jerome, in his commentary on Paul’s Epistle to the Ephesians, transmitted this concerning both Dianas, the high-girded and the many-breasted:

> “He wrote to the Ephesians, who worshiped Diana—not the huntress who holds a bow and is girded up, but that many-breasted figure whom the Greeks call πολύμαστον (*polymaston*, ‘many-breasted’), so that, by her very image, they might falsely claim that she was the nature of all beasts and living things.”

(Jerome, preface to Paul’s *Epistle to the Ephesians*.) [Col. 0578C]

Nor should you insist that Jerome followed our erring Minucius there and struck against the same rock of error. It is certain that neither erred, since Diana of Ephesus is known to have been mentioned by many, and no one is unaware that she had a most celebrated temple among the Ephesians. But her image was represented there with many breasts, as is evident from the various statues and pictures of her exhibited by Federico Ubaldini in his treatise explaining the symbolic statue of Diana of Ephesus (vol. VII, *Greek Antiquities*, p. 364).

It is no less certain that these statues of Diana, like other statues of the gods, were supported by upright and transverse *verua*, that is, spits or rods, which were supports and stays made of iron. For Lucas Holstenius proves this most explicitly in his letter to Cardinal Francesco Barberini, “On the Supports Affixed to the Image of Diana of Ephesus” (ibid., p. 396). There he exhibits certain images of the same Diana, with her supports and numerous breasts, engraved upon coins. From these facts, therefore, it is clearly established that some critics have unjustly assailed both our author’s text and Jerome’s testimony. [Col. 0578D]

Moreover, Virgil sings in these verses of Diana Trivia as terrifying with three heads, as Minucius says:

> With three hundred mouths she thunders forth the gods, Erebus, and Chaos,  
> And threefold Hecate—the three faces of the virgin Diana.

(Virgil, *Aeneid*, bk. IV, vv. 518 and 511.) [Col. 0579A]

In commenting upon these verses, Servius observes that she is called not only Diana but also Lucina and Hecate; that because of her threefold power she is imagined as triple and three-formed; and that her temples were therefore constructed at crossroads. Varro, however, notes from Ennius that she is called Trivia either because she is commonly stationed at a three-way crossing in Greek towns, or because she is called Luna, the Moon, which moves in heaven in three ways: height, breadth, and length (Varro, *On the Latin Language*, bk. VI, p. 74). Undoubtedly for the first reason Ovid said:

> You see Hecate’s faces turned in three directions,  
> So that she may guard the crossroads divided into three ways.

[Col. 0579B] For this very reason she is called by him “three-headed Hecate,” and by Horace and others “the three-formed goddess.” See Orpheus, Pausanias, and what Eusebius reported from Porphyry, and, if you wish, Prudentius also (Ovid, *Fasti*, bk. I, §3, and *Metamorphoses*, bk. VII, fable 3; Horace, bk. II, Ode 22; Orph., *Argonautica* and *Vow to the Muse*, vol. I, *Greek Poets*, pp. 494 and 501; Pausan., bk. II, p. 72; Euseb., *Preparation for the Gospel*, bk. IV, ch. 23, p. 174; Prudent., *Against Symmachus*, bk. I, §174).

It is therefore no wonder that, since she was three-formed, she was also said to have had several hands. Rigault indeed testifies in his note on this passage of Minucius that he had seen such a figure on a bronze coin belonging to Giovanni Battista Altino. Consult further, if you wish, Caelius Rhodiginus, Vossius, Verderius, Giraldus, and others who discuss the same [Col. 0579C] Diana (Rhodig., *Ancient Readings*, bk. XX, ch. 6; Vossius, *On the Origin and Progress of Idolatry*, bk. II, ch. 25, p. 216 ff.). Who, then, will not join our Minucius in laughing at and detesting such gods?

He strikes the pagans with no lighter a blow when they claimed that Jupiter had various countenances and differing faces. “What,” he asked, “of your Jupiter himself? At one moment he is set up beardless; at another he is placed as bearded.” Earlier, Cotta had pressed Velleius in Cicero as follows: “By that reasoning it will be permissible to say that Jupiter is always bearded” (Cic., *On the Nature of the Gods*, bk. I, p. 207, line 26). But Lucian asks where the pagans had seen this bearded Jupiter (Lucian, *On Sacrifices*, p. 185). If you too should ask this, Prudentius will answer:

> Art, effective in sowing errors,  
> When it wreathes Jupiter with a bristling beard.

[Col. 0579D] (Prudent., *On the Roman Martyr*, v. 243.)

Yet Virgil calls him Anxur:

> And the Circean ridge, over whose fields  
> Jupiter Anxur presides.

(Virgil, *Aeneid*, bk. VII, v. 799.) The name *Anxur* means the same as “beardless,” as Servius reminds us in his note on these verses of Virgil: “In this region of Campania,” he says, “a boy Jupiter was worshiped, who was called Anxur, as though ἄνευ ξυρᾶς (*aneu xyras*), that is, ‘without a razor,’ because he had never shaved a beard,” and so was beardless. He was represented in this youthful form not only in that region of Campania but elsewhere also. Pausanias records [Col. 0580A] that two such images of Jupiter were set up by the Eleans beside the temple of Pelops. Of one he says: “There is a youthful Jupiter, οὐκ ἔχον γένεια, ‘having no beard,’ among the offerings of Smicythus. . . . A little farther on, proceeding straight ahead, there is another image of a youthful Jupiter, dedicated by the Elcitans” (Pausan., *Eliaca*, bk. V, p. 173). To this may be added Naso, by whom the youthful Jupiter is described as follows:

> Jupiter too is young: behold his youthful face;  
> Then look upon his hands—he holds no thunderbolts.

(Ovid, *Fasti*, bk. III, §6, v. 437.)

After this Minucius enumerates other ridiculous forms of the same Jupiter which the pagans were not ashamed to venerate: “When,” he says, “he is called Ammon, he has horns; and when Capitolinus, he then bears thunderbolts.” Cicero had earlier said: “Indeed, the appearance of Jupiter Capitolinus is one thing among us, while that of Jupiter Ammon is another among the Africans” [Col. 0580B] (Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, bk. I, p. 207, line 23). Herodotus explains in these words why Jupiter Ammon was believed to have horns:

> “The Thebans and all who, because of them, spare sheep say that when Hercules wished to see Jupiter and Jupiter was unwilling to be seen by him, he was finally prevailed upon and devised the following expedient: he cut off a ram’s head, clothed himself in the woolly hide he had stripped from it, and thus showed himself to Hercules. For this reason the Egyptians established the practice of making Jupiter’s image with a ram’s face, ἀπὸ τούτου κριοπρόσωπον τὤγαλμα τοῦ Διὸς ποιοῦσι; and the Ammonians received the practice from the Egyptians. They are colonists of the Egyptians and Ethiopians and employ a language intermediate between the two. They also seem to me to have called themselves Ammonians [Col. 0580C] because the Egyptians call Jupiter ‘Ammon.’”

(Herodot., bk. II, §42.)

Hence he is called κερατοφόρος (*keratophoros*, “horn-bearing”) by the Greeks, κριοπρόσωπος (*krioprosōpos*, “ram-faced”) by Lucian, “ram-horned” by Macrobius and Arnobius, and horn-bearing Ammon by the poets Ovid, Claudian, and others (Lucian, *On Sacrifices*, p. 186; Macrob., *Saturnalia*, bk. I, ch. 21; Arnob., bk. VI *Against the Pagans*, p. 197).

Moreover, concerning this same Ammon and also the Capitoline Jupiter, we read these verses of Lucan:

> They had come to the temple which alone the uncultivated Garamantes  
> Possess among the Libyan peoples. There, as tradition tells, stands  
> A horned Jupiter—but not one who brandishes thunderbolts  
> Or resembles ours: it is Ammon with curling horns.

(Lucan, bk. IX, v. 517.)

[Col. 0580D] Jupiter Capitolinus is mentioned very frequently by various writers, especially writers of Roman history. He was called by that name because his temple and image were placed on the Capitol. Titus Livy, Suetonius, Dio Cassius, Plutarch, Pliny, and Valerius Maximus mention him. Finally, his image may be seen upon a very ancient coin of Aurelia Quirina, a Vestal Virgin. On it he sits with the upper half of his body naked and the lower half clothed, bearing a thunderbolt in his right hand and a scepter in his left; around it is inscribed the name: *Jup. Opt. Max. Capitolinus*—“Jupiter Best and Greatest, Capitolinus” (Livy, bk. II, §21; Sueton., bk. II, p. 344; Cassius, *Roman History*, bk. LIV, p. 598 ff.; Plutarch, *Life of Publicola*, p. 104; Pliny, *Natural History*, bk. III, chs. [Col. 0581A] 2 and 8, pp. 91 and 125; Valer., bk. I, ch. 2, §2; Lescalopier on Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, bk. I, §83, p. 118).

Our author mentions two further Jupiters: “Latiaris,” he says, “is drenched in blood,” because human victims, as we have shown, were sacrificed to him; “and Feretrius is not heard.” Plutarch reports various explanations of this surname and sets them forth in these words:

> Φερέτριος Ζεύς, ὡς μὲν ἔνιοι φασίν, ἀπὸ τοῦ φερητρευομένου τροπαίου, κατὰ τὴν ἑλληνίδα γλῶσσαν ἔτι πολλὴν τότε συμμεμιγμένην τῇ Λατίνων. Ὡς δὲ ἕτεροι, Διός ἐστιν ἡ προσωνυμία κεραυνοβολοῦντος, τὸ γὰρ τύπτειν, φερίρε, οἱ Ῥωμαῖοι καλοῦσιν· ἄλλοι δὲ παρὰ τὴν τοῦ πολέμου πληγὴν γεγονέναι τοὔνομα λέγουσι· καὶ γὰρ νῦν ἐν ταῖς μάχαις ὅταν διώκωσι τοὺς πολεμίους, πυκνὸν τὸ [Col. 0581B] φέρι, τουτέστιν παῖε, παρεγγυῶσιν ἀλλήλοις.
>
> “Jupiter is called Feretrius from the trophy that was carried upon a bier (*feretrum*), according to some, the name being derived from the Greek language, which at that time was still extensively intermingled with Latin speech. Others affirm that it is the surname of Jupiter as wielder of the thunderbolt, derived from striking (*ferire*), for the Romans call ‘to strike’ *ferire*. Others say that the name arose from the blows inflicted in war. For even now in battles, when they press upon the enemy to strike them, they repeatedly exhort one another with *feri*, that is, ‘strike!’”

(Plutarch, *Life of Marcellus*, p. 302.) He adds that, in the opinion of certain men, Numa ordered the first spoils and the *spolia opima* (‘spoils of honor’) to be consecrated to Jupiter Feretrius.

Titus Livy, however, attests that this surname was given to him by Romulus. After defeating and killing Acron, king of the Caeninenses, Romulus, “bearing his spoils [Col. 0581C] upon a frame constructed for the purpose”—these are Livy’s own words—“ascended the Capitol; and there, after depositing them beside an oak sacred to the shepherds, he marked out, together with his gift, the boundaries of a temple of Jupiter and added a surname to the god: ‘Jupiter Feretrius,’ he said, ‘I, King Romulus, victorious, bring you these royal arms, and dedicate within the boundaries which I have just mentally marked out a temple as a dwelling place for the *spolia opima* (‘spoils of honor’) which, after kings and commanders of the enemy have been slain, my descendants, following my example, will bring here’” (Livy, bk. I, §10). The same history was committed to memory not only by Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Dio Cassius, Florus, Messalla Corvinus, and others (Dionys. Hal., bk. II, p. 182; Dio Cass., *Roman History*, bk. XLIV, p. 274; Florus, bk. I, ch. 1; Mess. Corv., *On the Progeny of Augustus*, p. 531). [Col. 0581D] But Plutarch himself, already cited by us, also clearly indicates that from this arose the custom of carrying the *spolia opima* of slain commanders to the same Jupiter Feretrius (Plutarch, *Life of Romulus*, p. 27). Hence Propertius too sang:

> . . . . . . . . the derivation of Feretrius:  
> Whenever a commander strikes down a commander with an unerring sword;  
> Or because they bore these conquered arms upon their own shoulders,
Hence rose the proud altar of Jupiter Feretrius.  
(Propertius, Book IV.)

Some, however, think that in this text of Minucius—“Feretrius is not heard”—the final word, *auditur* (“is heard”), is corrupt, and that *aditur* (“is approached”) should be read. For after the death of Romulus, Numa Pompilius ordered the *spolia opima* (spoils of honor) taken from enemies [Col. 0582A] to be carried to Mars or Quirinus, not to Jupiter Feretrius. Moreover, what can the phrase “is not heard” mean? That Jupiter Feretrius is mute? But was not Jupiter Latiaris equally mute?

Others nevertheless judge that the reading in our manuscript codex, *non auditur* (“is not heard”), should be retained, and that the adverb *non* should there be taken for the word *nomen* (“name”), just as if Minucius had said: “The name of Feretrius, of whom there was no image, is no longer heard.” They attempt to prove this by certain examples, but these carry little weight. What, then, if you take the words *non auditur* in their native sense, as meaning “is left unheeded, spurned, disregarded”? Will not Minucius’ meaning be sufficiently open and clear: that Jupiter Latiaris was still being drenched with blood in his own [Col. 0582B] day, but Feretrius was no longer heeded? In any case, whether one reads *auditur* or *aditur*, neither is their meaning very different nor does either appear very foreign to the thought of Minucius.

Finally, Minucius continues: “There are as many monstrosities of Jupiter as there are names.” And therefore Theophilus, in his book *To Autolycus*, said:

> I should like to ask you, O man, just how many Jupiters are to be found. Ζεὺς μὲν γὰρ ἐν πρώτοις προσαγορεύεται Ὀλύμπιος, καὶ Ζεὺς Λατεάριος, καὶ Ζεὺς Κάσσιος, καὶ Ζεὺς Κεραύνιος, καὶ Ζεὺς Προπάτωρ, καὶ Ζεὺς Παννύχιος, καὶ Ζεὺς Πολιοῦχος, καὶ Ζεὺς Καπετώλιος—“First Jupiter is called Olympian; then Jupiter Latiaris, Cassius, Thunderer, Forefather, All-Night Watcher, Defender of Cities, and Capitoline. And indeed Jupiter, the son of Saturn and king of the Cretans, was buried [Col. 0582C] in Crete.”

(Theophilus, *To Autolycus*, Book II, p. 76.) He considers the other Jupiters, however, unworthy of any burial.

Moreover, concerning the virtually infinite crowd and multitude of those Jupiters—whom some imagined to number three hundred—or, as our author rightly called them, monstrosities and portents, see Lilius Giraldus and, if you please and have the leisure, what we have discussed elsewhere (Giraldus, *History of the Gods*, Syntagma 2, p. 72 ff.; Vol. I, *Apparatus*, Book III, Dissertation 1, ch. 9, p. 752).

## ARTICLE III

### Another argument of the same force is explained, which Minucius drew from the shameful and utterly disgraceful deeds of the gods: Erigone said to have hanged herself with a noose; Castor and Pollux alternately living and dying; Aesculapius struck by lightning; and Hercules burned in the fires of Oeta

[Col. 0582D]

From the utterly absurd and plainly ridiculous forms of the gods, Minucius passes to their most shameful and abominable deeds, by which he demonstrates with the greatest clarity that they are wholly unworthy not only of the name of gods but even of human beings endowed with reason. To prove this, he enumerates several of them individually, and we shall follow him in this argument just as we did in the preceding one.

He begins his discussion with Erigone: “She who,” as he says, “was suspended from a noose, so that, as a maiden, she might be made fiery among the stars.” There are two opinions—or rather fables—among pagan writers [Col. 0583A] concerning this Erigone. Some say that she was the daughter of the Athenian Icarius. When drunken peasants killed him, she was alerted to her father’s murder by a dog; and, upon seeing his corpse, she hanged herself with a noose. After her death, the maiden herself and the dog that had alerted her are imagined to have obtained, under their own names, a place among the stars.

Others relate that Erigone was the daughter of Aegisthus and Clytemnestra. She went to Athens with her grandfather Tyndareus to accuse Orestes; but when she there learned that he had been acquitted, she took her own life with a noose.

Minucius, however, seems rather to have had in view the first opinion, according to which they babbled that Erigone and that dog were numbered among the stars, as Statius [Col. 0583B] had sung:

> The stars lend force to my undertaking, and the heat-bearing  
> Dog of my Erigone foams.

(Statius, *Thebaid*, Book IV, v. 538.) If you desire more, you may consult Nonnus, Servius, and others (Nonnus, *Dionysiaca*, Book XLVII, v. 600 ff.; Servius on Virgil, *Georgics*, Book II, v. 388). For this reason Tatian had objected to the pagans: Κύων ὁ τῆς Ἠριγόνης ἐν οὐρανῷ δείκνυται—“Erigone’s dog is shown in heaven” (Tatian, *Oration Against the Greeks*, p. 149).

It is worth observing here that our manuscript codex reads *ut in astra ignata sit* (“that she might be ‘ignated’ among the stars”), undoubtedly through a copyist’s error. The printed editions accordingly have *ignita sit* (“that she might be made fiery”), that is, that Erigone might be placed among the fiery stars. [Col. 0583C] This correction is not altogether to be rejected, since it can be supported not inaptly by the cited words of Statius and Tatian. It did not please Gronovius, however, who preferred to correct the text to *signata sit* (“that she might be marked out”), that is, “placed.” But he ought first to have shown where Minucius uses this manner of expression. In any event, whatever the genuine reading may be, Minucius very plainly means that the pagans’ opinion concerning their gods is altogether absurd, since they solemnly proclaimed that Erigone, after ending her life with a noose, was both a goddess and placed among the stars.

Minucius then says—and Cyprian, his follower, uses the same words: “The Castors,” that is, Castor and Pollux, “die by turns so that they may live” (Cyprian, *On the Vanity of Idols*, p. 11). Lactantius [Col. 0583D] explains the matter somewhat more fully:

> Castor and Pollux, while abducting other men’s betrothed brides, ceased to be twins. For Idas, aroused by grief at the wrong, ran one of them through with his sword; and the poets relate that the same pair live by turns and die by turns.

(Lactantius, Book I, ch. 10, p. 150.) For they imagined that Castor and Pollux fell in love with Phoebe and Talaïta, the daughters of Leucippus, who had been betrothed to Lynceus and Idas. Castor was therefore killed by Lynceus, as some suppose, or by Idas, Meleager, or Policine [name uncertain], as others maintain. Pollux then asked his father Jupiter to bestow immortality upon Castor. When he could not obtain this, he secured instead that half of immortality should be allotted to the one and half to the other. They were therefore said to live on alternate [Col. 0584A] days or, as Pliny says, to be “living and dying on alternate days” (Pliny, *Natural History*, Book II, ch. 7, p. 143). On this matter we have the following verses of Homer, cited by Origen:

> Ἄλλοτε μὲν ζώουσ᾽, ἑτερήμεροι, ἄλλοτε δ᾽ αὖτε  
> Τετνᾶσιν, τιμὴν δὲ λελόγχασιν ἶσα θεοῖσι.
>
> At times they live, on alternate days, and then again  
> At times they are dead; yet they have received honor equal to the gods.

(Origen, *Against Celsus*, Book III, p. 123; Homer, *Odyssey*, Book XI, v. 331 ff.) Hence Tatian, following the same Homer, calls them ἑτερόημεροι Διόσκουροι, “the Dioscuri who live on alternate days” (Tatian, *Oration Against the Greeks*, p. 150). Finally, to omit many others, Virgil sings of them:

[Col. 0584B]

> If Pollux redeemed his brother by taking death in turn,  
> And so many times goes and returns along the path—

(Virgil, *Aeneid*, Book VI, v. 121.) Elsewhere, however, we shall see that this was not accepted by everyone.

Minucius next says—and again Cyprian in precisely the same words: “Aesculapius is struck by lightning so that he may rise to become a god” (Cyprian, *On the Vanity of Idols*, p. 11). If you ask Cicero who this man was, you will receive this answer from him: “The second Aesculapius was the brother of the second Mercury; he was struck by lightning and is said to have been buried at Cynosurae” (Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, Book III, p. 248).

[Col. 0584C]

But if you ask again why he was struck by lightning, Diodorus Siculus replies:

> Pluto lodged a complaint against Aesculapius before Jupiter, on the ground that the number of the dead was continually diminishing through his medical treatment, and accused him of reducing the power of the kingdom below. Angered by this, Jupiter killed Aesculapius with a thunderbolt: Παραξυνθέντα, καὶ κεραυνώσαντα Ἀσκληπιὸν διαφθεῖραι—“Being provoked, he destroyed Aesculapius by striking him with lightning.”

(Diodorus Siculus, *Library*, Book IV, p. 190.) Plato, however, writes that he was struck by lightning because, corrupted by avarice and gold, he “treated a certain wealthy man who was suffering from a fatal illness and at the point of death” (Plato, *Republic*, Book III, Vol. II, p. 408). Or, as Virgil sang, it was because he had restored Hippolytus to life after Hippolytus had been killed through the contrivance of his stepmother (Virgil, *Aeneid*, Book VII, v. 765 ff.). [Col. 0584D] The same was said by Pindar, as cited by Tertullian, Arnobius, and Athenagoras; the last called Hesiod as a second witness, though Hesiod gives the name of the man raised from the dead (Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 14, and *To the Nations*, Book II, ch. 14; Arnobius, Book IV, p. 143; Athenagoras, *Plea for the Christians*, p. 33; Pindar, Ode 3). Read also Lucian, Origen, Arnobius, Lactantius, Theodoret, and—if it is not burdensome—what we noted in the preceding volume (Lucian, *Dialogues of the Gods*, p. 78; Origen, *Against Celsus*, Book III, p. 123; Arnobius, Book IV, p. 143; Lactantius, *Institutes*, Book I, ch. 17, p. 84; Theodoret, Discourse 8, *On the Martyrs*, p. 595; Vol. I, *Apparatus*, Book III, Dissertation I, ch. 9, art. 1, p. 754). Plato, Tertullian, and Lactantius therefore rightly [Col. 0585A] conclude from this, together with our author—as we shall see in the proper place—that Aesculapius cannot be called the son of God.

What more need be said? “Hercules,” to quote the exact words of our author and of Cyprian, “is consumed in the fires of Oeta, so that he may cast off the man” (the Royal manuscript has *Henneis*, but wrongly). The whole matter, or fable, is related by Diodorus Siculus—whom Servius follows—in the following way. After Hercules put on the tunic smeared by Deianira with the Centaur’s potion, which had been prepared for his destruction, he immediately fell into a fatal—or, as Arnobius relates, epileptic—illness. Then, as the illness grew worse and every hope of recovering his health was abandoned, he mounted a funeral pyre in obedience to the Delphic oracle. Philoctetes set fire to it, and soon, after being touched by thunderbolts, it was reduced to ashes together with Hercules’ body. [Col. 0585B] Later, when Iolaus had searched in vain for his bones, the report spread that Hercules had flown away to the gods.

Augustine, moreover, indicates where and when this occurred and who that Hercules was. Then, in close accord with the thought of our author, he argues from it as follows: “As matters now stand, I do not see how that Hercules for whom torches were brought on Mount Oeta, as Accius says, passed from that burning into the eternal home of his father Jupiter.” Consult Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, Book IX, fable 3; Sophocles, *Women of Trachis*, Vol. II of the Greek Poets; Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations*, Book II, p. 138; Seneca, *Hercules on Oeta*; Justin Martyr, *First Apology*, p. 76; Athenagoras, *Plea for the Christians*, p. 53; Theodoret, Discourse 3, *On Angels*, p. 510, and more fully Discourse [Col. 0585C] 8, *On the Martyrs*, p. 594 ff.; Lactantius, *Divine Institutes*, Book I, ch. 9; and Hyginus and Apollodorus, who committed to writing much about these and the other aforementioned opinions of the pagans.

## ARTICLE IV

### Why and how Minucius shows that the gods of the pagans are false from the books of Homer, read by everyone for instruction in life and morals, in which are celebrated Venus wounded; Mars bound and wounded; Jupiter rescued by Briareus, mourning Sarpedon, and enticed by Venus’ girdle; Hercules clearing away dung; Apollo tending Admetus’ cattle; Neptune rebuilding Laomedon’s walls; Jupiter’s thunderbolt fashioned together with the arms of Aeneas; the adultery of Mars and Venus; Ganymede abducted by Jupiter; and how deservedly Homer was expelled by Plato from his city

[Col. 0585D]

Minucius deplores the utterly wretched and unhappy condition of the pagans, who had been taught old wives’ tales about their gods by their parents and had almost imbibed them with their mothers’ milk. Indeed, when they grew older, they learned those tales “through their very studies and disciplines,” in the poems of the poets and especially of Homer. For while drinking poison in what seemed delightful to them, they corrupted their morals by hearing of the disgraceful deeds of their gods. What would they not have done when they heard that Homer—“renowned, praised, and crowned,” as Minucius says, by all peoples—who “in his account of the Trojan War, although he makes sport of the gods, nevertheless mingles them in human affairs and actions? There [Col. 0586A] he matched them in pairs, wounded Venus, bound, wounded, and put Mars to flight. He relates that Jupiter was rescued by Briareus lest he be bound by the other gods; that Jupiter shed bloody showers of tears for his son Sarpedon because he could not save him from death; and that, enticed by Venus’ girdle, he lay with his wife Juno more ardently than he was accustomed to lie with his adulterous partners.”

Tertullian had written precisely the same things, though in different words:

> But when I turn to your literature, by which you are shaped for wisdom and the liberal duties, how much mockery do I find? The gods engaged one another in battle over the Trojans and Achaeans, like matched pairs of gladiators; Venus wounded by a human arrow; Mars nearly wasted away through thirteen months in chains; Jupiter rescued through the agency of a certain monster lest he suffer the same violence from the other heavenly beings; [Col. 0586B] and Jupiter now weeping over Sarpedon’s fate, now foully rutting with his sister while recalling mistresses who had long since ceased to be so beloved.

(Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 14.) We have quoted the complete passages from our Minucius and from Tertullian together, both because they mutually illuminate one another and because they are so similar that Minucius appears to have borrowed his material from Tertullian.

What Tertullian drew only in general terms from pagan literature, our Minucius declares to have been taken from Homer. From this we understand why Minucius and the other defenders of the Christian religion raised these utterly absurd fables—scarcely credible to any person of sound mind—against all the pagans in order to overthrow their false religions. For Homer was held in such honor among them that they taught children the gods’ mockeries celebrated by him [Col. 0586C], while others were shaped by his poems “for wisdom,” as Tertullian says, “and the liberal duties.” Accordingly, imbued with these stories from their earliest years and regarding it as impious to withhold credence from so great a man, as they supposed him to be, they readily believed their gods to be such as he and the other poets had portrayed them, and such as they were later publicly represented in theaters and mysteries, as we shall show below. For this reason Minucius says: “By these and similar inventions and more seductive falsehoods, the minds of children are corrupted; and as those same fables cling to them, they grow old in them even to the full strength of mature age, although truth is readily available—but only to those who seek it.” Moreover, although Homer and the other poets composed such abominable and shameful verses about the gods, they were themselves nevertheless called the theologians of the pagans, as Augustine says [Col. 0586D] (Augustine, *City of God*, Book XVIII, ch. 14, p. 498). It is therefore no wonder that our Minucius and the other most ancient Fathers of the Church repeatedly and seriously assailed this authority of Homer and the other poets, even though it rested upon such ridiculous fables.

Since Minucius and Tertullian cited neither the books nor the passages of Homer in which the things they recount were written, we have therefore considered it our duty to indicate them individually and to cite others by whom the same things are similarly mentioned or confirmed. As for Venus’ being wounded—by Diomedes, of course—which Minucius mentions first, we read of it in Homer’s fifth book of the *Iliad*, v. 335 ff.; it was also cited by Plato, *Symposium Questions*, Book IX, Question 4, p. 739; Virgil, *Aeneid*, Book II, v. 277; Justin Martyr, *Exhortation to the Greeks*, p. 3; Athenagoras, *Plea for the Christians*, p. 21; Clement of Alexandria, *Exhortation to the Greeks*, p. 23; and Athanasius, *Oration Against the Greeks*, § 12, p. 112.

What Minucius also related concerning Mars being bound and wounded you will find celebrated in the same book of Homer’s *Iliad*, v. 385 ff. On this see also Clement of Alexandria and Athanasius in the passages just cited, as well as Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 3, *Against Julian*, p. 258, and Oration 4, p. 308.

Homer also sang—as Minucius next observes—that Jupiter was rescued by Briareus, *Iliad*, Book I, v. 399 ff.; on this see later Justin Martyr, *Exhortation to the Greeks*, p. 3, and Servius on *Aeneid*, Book VI, p. 415.

Next, in the same Homer, *Iliad*, Book XVI, [Col. 0587B] v. 667 ff., you will find what is related concerning the same Jupiter and Sarpedon not only by Minucius but also by Athenagoras, *Plea for the Christians*, p. 21, and Clement of Alexandria, *Exhortation to the Greeks*, both of whom transcribed two verses of Homer.

Finally, concerning the strap or girdle by which Venus, as our author says, enticed Jupiter, you may hear Homer sing in *Iliad*, Book XIV, v. 204 ff. Gregory of Nazianzus, like Minucius, turned this against the pagans in Oration 3, *Against Julian*, p. 258. See there the notes of Billius, who rendered into Latin verse the poet’s lines about that girdle of Venus.

Come now, and let us examine other things no less absurd, likewise doubtless described in other verses of Homer, though Minucius did not identify them: “Hercules,” he says, [Col. 0587C] “carried away dung; Apollo tended cattle for Admetus; and Neptune erected walls for Laomedon.” Diodorus Siculus reports that the fifth labor of Hercules was the one in which he cleared the stable of King Augeas of dung. He explains this at greater length, as do Pausanias, Natalis Comes, and very many others (Diodorus Siculus, *Library*, Book IV, p. 154 ff.; Pausanias, Book V, p. 148). Consider, however, whether our author intended to aim at Homer, *Iliad*, Book II, v. 695 ff.

Homer sang far more clearly of those mentioned by our author: Apollo, who tended Admetus’ cattle, and Neptune, who built walls for the Trojan Laomedon. The first, indeed, occurs in the second book of the *Iliad*, v. 780 ff.; the second in Book XXI, v. 443, passages that Pausanias is recorded as citing (Pausanias, Book VII, p. [Col. 0587D] 226). On both Apollo and Neptune see Lucian, *On Sacrifices*, p. 188; Arnobius, *Against the Pagans*, Book IV, p. 144; Lactantius, Book I, ch. 10; Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 14; Cyprian, *On the Vanity of Idols*, p. 11; Augustine, *City of God*, Book III, ch. 2, and Book XVIII, ch. 13; Servius on Virgil, *Georgics*, Book III, v. 2, and on *Aeneid*, Book I, v. 554; Vossius, *On the Origin and Progress of Idolatry*, Book I, ch. 15, p. 16, and Book II, ch. 12, p. 187. Finally, on Apollo see Callimachus, Ode 2, *To Apollo*; Euripides, the prologue to *Alcestis*; Nonnus, *Dionysiaca*, Book I, v. 323; Ovid, *Art of Love*, Book II, p. 447; Athenagoras, *Plea for the Christians*, p. 22; Tatian, *Oration Against the Greeks*, p. 159; Eusebius, *Chronicle*, Book I, p. 19. And [Col. 0588A] from the passage of Augustine already cited and from another passage of his, some light may be cast upon what we noted elsewhere as having been committed to writing by Clement of Alexandria concerning the same servitude of Apollo (Vol. I, *Apparatus*, Book III, Dissertation 2, ch. 14, art. 1, p. 1090).

Minucius continues and reproaches the pagans with “Jupiter’s thunderbolt fashioned on the anvil together with Aeneas’ arms.” He is undoubtedly speaking of Vulcan’s anvil. Homer, however, relates how on that anvil Vulcan fashioned the arms not of Aeneas but of Achilles (Homer, *Iliad*, Book XVIII, v. 454 ff.). Consider, therefore, whether our author there had in view not only Homer but also Virgil, who sang that Vulcan ordered the Cyclopes, who were fashioning thunderbolts for Jupiter, to leave them aside and make for Aeneas the arms requested by Venus [Col. 0588B] (Virgil, *Aeneid*, Book VIII, v. 422 ff.).
