But the adultery of Mars and Venus, “discovered by Vulcan,” as our Minucius continues, had been sung by Homer and Ovid (Homer, *Odyssey*, Book VIII, v. 267; Ovid, *Art of Love*, Book II, near the end). If we believe Lucian, moreover, a certain dancer represented by himself, without percussion or flutes, but by dance and gesture alone, that abominable adultery of the gods (Lucian, *On Dancing*, p. 515). Hence Clement of Alexandria said: Ἀφροδίτη ἐπ᾽ Ἄρει κατῃσχυμμένη—“Aphrodite was put to shame and disgrace on account of Ares.” Arnobius and Lactantius also discuss it, as we shall note below (Clement of Alexandria, *Exhortation to the Pagans*, p. 21; Dissertation on Arnobius, ch. 10, art. 1; and on Lactantius, ch. 31, art. 1).

[Col. 0588C]

Finally, what Minucius says is found in Homer: “Jupiter’s violation of Ganymede, consecrated in heaven.” Pausanias indeed says:

> Ἔστι δὲ Ὁμήρῳ πεποιημένα, ὡς ἁρπασθείη τε ὑπὸ θεῶν Γανυμήδης οἰνοχοεῖν Διί—“Homer recorded in his verses that Ganymede was abducted by the gods to serve cups to Jupiter, and that in return horses were given to Tros,” that is, to Ganymede’s father.

(Minucius, p. 208; Homer, *Iliad*, Book XX, v. 231 ff., and *Hymn to Venus*; Pausanias, Book V, p. 173.) But if you please, you may consult the Greek itself in the poet at the passage cited by us, as well as Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, Book X, fable 5; Theocritus, Idyll 12, v. 35 ff.; Apollonius, *Argonautica*, Book III, v. 114 ff.; and Nonnus, *Dionysiaca*, Book I, v. 316.

From this entire argument of our author, [Col. 0588D] you can indeed see how deservedly he approves the judgment of Plato, who expelled Homer—“renowned, praised, and crowned,” as we have said, a word also used by Tertullian—from his city on account of those execrable and detestable inventions, as a teacher of licentiousness and impiety, according to Theodoret, or as a plague upon youth, as Origen rightly argues. But Plato himself, and indeed all pagans without exception, ought to have expelled these criminal gods celebrated by Homer, together with the other gods of the pagans, not merely from one city but from every city and every part of the world (Tertullian, *To the Nations*, Book II, ch. 7; Theodoret, Discourse 2, *On the First Principle*, p. 486; Origen, *Against Celsus*, Book IV, p. 186).

# CHAPTER XVIII

## CAECILIUS’ ARGUMENT, BY WHICH HE ATTEMPTS TO PROVE THAT THE GODS OF THE PAGANS EXIST BECAUSE THE ROMANS, THROUGH THEIR DEVOUT WORSHIP OF THEM, MERITED THE EMPIRE OF THE WHOLE WORLD, IS EXAMINED

[Col. 0589A]

## ARTICLE I

### Caecilius’ argument is explained

Caecilius contends that the Roman Empire was extended “beyond the courses of the sun and the very bounds of Ocean” because the Romans had always worshiped, with devout observance and true religion, not merely some gods but all the gods and every divine power. Nor was Caecilius alone in asserting and vaunting this; very many other pagans did the same, and Valerius Maximus above all. For these are his very words:

[Col. 0589B]

> It is no wonder if, for the enlargement and preservation of that empire, the steadfast favor of the gods has always kept watch over a state which appears to scrutinize with such scrupulous care even the smallest details of religion; for our commonwealth must be judged never to have turned its eyes away from the most exact observance of the rites.

(Valerius Maximus, *Memorable Deeds and Sayings*, ch. 1, § 8, p. 8.) Yet the Romans could not have received so great a reward for their piety toward the gods unless those gods truly existed and possessed supreme power.

But what, you will ask, did Caecilius mean when, in so extravagantly proclaiming the various offices of that Roman piety, he confidently asserted that the Romans obtained that greatest of benefits from their gods not by their piety alone but also by military courage? You will undoubtedly understand [Col. 0589C] his thought and meaning without great difficulty if you will first observe that, “during assaults” upon cities, as Pliny writes after Verrius Flaccus, “it was customary for Roman priests to summon away the god under whose protection the town stood, and to promise him the same or a greater worship among the Romans. And,” he continues, “this rite endures in the pontifical discipline; and it is agreed that for this reason the identity of the deity under whose protection Rome stood was concealed, lest any enemy act in the same way” (Pliny, *Natural History*, Book XXVIII, ch. 2, p. 559). Macrobius relates the same thing and supplies the formula by which the Romans, during sieges of cities, were accustomed to summon away their guardian gods and vow temples and games to them (Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, Book III, ch. 9). It is therefore undoubtedly on account of this military custom that Caecilius asserts that the Romans [Col. 0589D] obtained dominion over the whole world from the gods.

Let us consider, if you please, how he attempted to prove it. First, he says, “while they exercise religious valor in arms,” that is, by devoutly summoning the gods away, as we have said, and by making solemn vows, prayers, and sacrifices. Second, “while they fortify the city of Rome with sacred religious observances,” both their own and those of other peoples whom they had conquered. For after vanquishing those peoples, they carried to Rome both their gods and their sacred—or rather profane and abominable—worship. For the same reason Caecilius added: “While they seek gods as guests from every quarter and make them their own.”

He continues and says that the Romans fortified their city not only with these pious and sacred rites, [Col. 0590A] but also “with chaste virgins,” namely, the Vestals, “and with the many honors and titles of priests,” that is, with stipends, revenues, exemptions, and privileges. That this is indeed our author’s meaning, which some have wholly failed to perceive, can be confirmed by the authority of Symmachus, likewise a pagan, and of Ambrose, who answered him. For in his *Memorial* to the emperor Valentinian, Symmachus addresses him in these words: “The law of our ancestors had honored the Vestal Virgins and the ministers of the gods with a modest maintenance and rightful privileges” (Symmachus, *Memorial*, in Ambrose, § 14, p. 831). Ambrose replies:

> They complain that public maintenance is not owed to their priests and ministers. . . . Yet no one has denied votive gifts to the temples or legacies to the haruspices. Only their estates have been taken away, [Col. 0590B] because they did not use religiously the possessions that they defended by the right of religion.

(Ambrose, Epistle 18, §§ 13–16.)

Caecilius further boldly declares that the gods brought the Romans the most certain assistance:

> While under siege and captured except for the Capitol, they worship the gods whom another would already have spurned as angry; and through the battle lines of the Gauls, who marvel at the boldness of their superstition, they advance unarmed with weapons but armed with the observance of religion; while, after the enemy walls have been captured and victory is still raging fiercely, they venerate the divine powers they have vanquished.

He is undoubtedly speaking of the Senones, who, after taking the city of Rome, were besieging the Capitol. Nor did the dull and obtuse Symmachus hesitate to hurl that blunted weapon once more against the Christians, in these fewer words: “These sacred rites repelled Hannibal from the walls and the Senones from the Capitol” (Symmachus, *Memorial*, § 9, p. 830; Ambrose, Epistle [Col. 0590C] 18, § 4, p. 834).

But Gronovius, following some others, conjectures that in our author’s text, and contrary to the evidence of our manuscript codex, *iratus* (“angry,” singular) should be read instead of *iratos* (“angry,” plural). “For the Romans,” he says, “did not despise the angry gods by whom they felt themselves being punished.” He therefore thinks Minucius’ meaning is this: the Romans worship their gods, whom another person, “angry” because they denied him their aid, would already have spurned. Yet the sense will undoubtedly be better if you read: “whom another would already have spurned as angry,” because they therefore brought him no assistance. For what if the term *iratos* (“angry”) is there opposed to “propitious gods,” on whom much may be read in Brissonius? (Brissonius, *On Formulas*, Book I, p. 120 ff.) What Caecilius relates concerning the Capitol besieged by the Senones and the Romans’ religious devotion toward the gods [Col. 0590D] you will find explained by Livy, Valerius Maximus, Florus, and others (Livy, Book V, § 46 ff.; Valerius Maximus, Book I, ch. 1, §§ 10–11; Florus, Book I, ch. 13; ibid., p. 51).

Besides these things, Caecilius regards as another certain proof of Roman religion the fact that “they erect altars to unknown divine powers and to the Manes.” Concerning the former, these are Tertullian’s words:

> I indeed find altars exposed for unknown gods. But that is Attic idolatry. There are likewise altars to uncertain gods, but that is Roman superstition. Now uncertain gods are less known because they are less certain, and consequently unknown because they are less certain.

(Tertullian, *Against Marcion*, Book I, ch. 9.) If you wish to know the words by which those unknown gods were invoked, Gellius, Macrobius, and Brissonius will teach you (Gellius, *Attic Nights*, [Col. 0591A] Book II, ch. 28; Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, Book III, ch. 9; Brissonius, *On Formulas*, Book I, p. 120).

You may perhaps be astonished that it occurred to some to suppose that Caecilius’ word *Manibus* (“to the Manes”) had been corrupted and that *inanibus* (“to empty gods”) should be written in its place. Nothing could have been invented more contrary to the authority of the Royal manuscript codex and to the thought of the author. For who, except in a dream, could have suspected that Caecilius—who there plays the part of a pagan against a Christian—seriously said that the Romans had erected altars to “empty” gods?

But to what purpose, they ask, are the Manes mentioned there, or to whom could they have been unknown? What, then, if the adjective “unknown” refers only to the substantive “divine powers”? Caecilius mentions the Manes there because the pagans frequently invoked them and [Col. 0591B] offered them sacrifices. Nor were they, as these critics maintain, so well known to everyone. For, as Servius observes, some thought them heavenly gods, others gods below, others nocturnal gods wandering between heaven and earth. Servius and Lilius Giraldus say more about them (Servius on Virgil, *Aeneid*, Book III, p. 266; Giraldus, *History of the Gods*, Syntagma 7, p. 205). Nothing, therefore, should be changed in our author’s text, whether you call the Manes known or unknown.

Finally, Caecilius concludes: “Thus, while the Romans embrace the sacred rites of all nations, they have also merited kingdoms.” It is indeed true that the Romans embraced the rites of every nation. For Ovid sang it in this single verse:

> Rome is a place worthy for every god to enter.

[Col. 0591C] (Ovid, *Fasti*, Book I, § 3.) But we shall have another occasion to discuss these matters.

Caecilius and the other pagans thought that from what has thus far been said it could be concluded that their gods truly existed, because the Romans, “while embracing,” as he babbled, “the sacred rites of all nations, also merited kingdoms.” It cannot be denied that this argument would indeed carry no slight weight if it rested upon as much truth as it does falsehood. Tertullian fully perceived its force and set it forth without any concealment whatever in these words:

> I shall not omit the engagement provoked by the presumption of those who say that the Romans, as the reward of their most diligent religious devotion, were raised to so great a height that they took possession of the world; and that they are therefore worthy to flourish beyond all others because they perform their duty toward the gods [Col. 0591D] beyond all others.

(Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 25.) But that most learned African writer demonstrates, as we shall see in the proper place, that this claim is false—indeed, utterly false. We must now examine how this very argument is refuted by our Minucius.

## ARTICLE II

### How Minucius refutes Caecilius’ argument and demonstrates that the Roman Empire was founded not at all upon the Romans’ religion toward the gods, but upon impiety and crimes; that the gods brought the Romans no assistance in extending the boundaries of their realm—not even, first, the foreign and immigrant gods: Thracian Mars, Cretan Jupiter, Argive, Samian, and Punic Juno, Tauric Diana, or the Idaean Mother

[Col. 0592A]

Minucius suppresses the ridiculous boasting about the Romans’ piety toward their gods as easily as they rashly boasted that, through their singular and most chaste worship of those gods, they had merited dominion over the whole world. For whether one considers the beginnings or the advancement of any people, none exhibited greater impiety than the Romans. [Col. 0592B] Everyone certainly knows that their first origin was derived from nothing other than a multitude of depraved men—criminals, incestuous offenders, murderers, and brigands—gathered into an asylum, and that Romulus laid the foundations of his city in fratricide (Augustine, *City of God*, Book III, ch. 6, p. 62; Livy and others). Soon afterward he “carried off other men’s maidens without precedent,” as Minucius says—that is, without any example or good custom. By this form of expression he alludes to Virgil’s line:

> . . . And the Sabine women carried off without precedent.

(Virgil, *Aeneid*, Book VIII, v. 655.)

Romulus then waged war upon “their parents, that is, upon his own fathers-in-law.” These words are indeed read in the Royal codex. We therefore do not see why some perversely conjecture [Col. 0592C] that they were inserted into the text. Add that all these points thus far mentioned are confirmed by the testimony of Cyprian, who excerpted them from this very passage of our author (Cyprian, *On the Vanity of Idols*, p. 16). Since no one disputes that these things are most certain, Minucius rightly concludes against Caecilius that nothing could be “more irreligious,” criminal, and impious than these beginnings of the Romans.

He continues and shows that the Romans extended their empire with the same impiety with which they had begun it: namely, by overthrowing neighboring cities together with their temples and altars; by compelling captured enemies to become partners in their crimes; and by “constructing all their temples from spoils of war—that is, from the ruins of cities, the plunder of gods, and the slaughter of priests,” to use Minucius’ words. Therefore, [Col. 0592D] as he further says, “the Romans committed an act of impiety as often as they celebrated a triumph. They took as many spoils from gods as trophies from nations.” From this he draws the most fully justified conclusion: “The Romans are therefore not so great because they are religious, but because they are sacrilegious with impunity.”

I should like you to consider whether Minucius, when writing this, had not looked to Tertullian’s *Apology*. For in that book, after assailing and crushing the same boast of the pagans, Tertullian completed his argument with this similar conclusion:

> The Romans, therefore, were not religious before they were great; consequently, they were not great because they were religious. Indeed, how could they be great because of religion when their greatness arose from irreligion? For unless I am mistaken, every kingdom or empire [Col. 0593A] is acquired through wars and extended through victories. Wars and victories, moreover, ordinarily depend upon the capture and overthrow of cities. That business cannot be conducted without injury to the gods. The destruction of walls and temples is the same; the slaughter of citizens and priests is equal; nor is the plunder of sacred and profane wealth dissimilar. The Romans therefore have as many acts of sacrilege as trophies, as many triumphs over gods as over nations, and as many spoils of war as there still remain images of captive gods.

(Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 25, p. 28).

What Minucius reports—that temples of the gods were built by victorious Romans out of the spoils taken from enemies and captured cities—is clearly confirmed by Florus’s testimony. For we read that he recorded the following concerning Tarquinius Superbus: “From the spoils of captured [Col. 0593B] cities he erected a temple” (Flor. *Roman History*, bk. I, ch. 7). We have just heard Tertullian say that the Romans’ spoils were the images of captive gods. This is asserted no less explicitly in the following verses of Prudentius:

> Thereafter countless gods did Rome beget  
> For herself from splendid triumphs, when cities had been subdued by valor.  
> Amid the smoking ruins of temples, the armed  
> Right hand of the victor seized the enemy’s images  
> And carried the captive divine powers home, worshiping them.
>
> . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
>
> As often as renowned Rome received with applause  
> The chariot of a triumphant general, so often did she  
> Add altars of gods, and from the spoils make new divine powers for herself.

(Prudent., bk. II, *Against Symmachus*, § 2.)

Lactantius, however, seems to have indicated both temples and images more briefly. For where he recalls that the cities of their enemies were overthrown by Roman arms, [Col. 0593C] he immediately adds: “They consecrate to the gods their spoils of war and their plunder” (Lact. bk. I, *Institutes*, ch. 6, p. 170; *Dissertation on Lactantius*, ch. 33, art. 4). From the spoils, indeed—that is, from the money raised by selling the booty taken from their enemies, as we shall explain elsewhere—they built new temples of the gods; and the images of the gods that they had seized and carried away with them to Rome they consecrated anew and adorned after placing them in their own temples.

Cicero too is our witness that Dionysius the tyrant stripped away the cloak with which the tyrant Gelo had adorned Jupiter from the spoils of the Carthaginians. Moreover, in one of his speeches he says: “Fulvius, who fought against the Aetolians with Ennius as his companion, did not hesitate to consecrate the spoils to the Muses” (Cicer. bk. III, *On the Nature of the Gods*, p. 252, line [Col. 0593D] 87; and *Speech for Archias*, p. 390, line 25).

Octavius proceeds and, in his own name and that of the Christians, asks his adversary and the other pagans which gods came to favor the Romans and assist them in wars undertaken to extend the boundaries of their empire: foreign and immigrant gods, or their own native gods? Yet none of them could have brought assistance to the Romans. Certainly not the former. For how could those gods have favored and assisted the Romans when they had never been able to protect their own dependents and worshipers against the assaults of their enemies? “For,” says Minucius, “neither Thracian Mars, nor Cretan Jupiter, nor Argive Juno—now Punic Juno—nor Tauric Diana, nor the Idaean Mother, nor the Egyptian one, helped the Romans against their own peoples, by whom those gods were worshiped: these were not [Col. 0594A] divine powers, but monstrous prodigies.” Indeed, no one is unaware that those peoples were conquered and routed by Roman arms. Therefore Cyprian, who repeats the same argument from our author, immediately added: “If these had possessed any power at all, they would assuredly have preserved their own kingdoms and those of their worshipers” (Cypr. *On the Vanity of Idols*, p. 13).

If anyone wishes to know who those are whom Minucius called monstrous prodigies rather than divine powers, we shall say that Mars is surnamed “Thracian” because some believed that he originated in Thrace, as we have observed elsewhere (vol. I, *Apparatus*, bk. III, diss. I, ch. 9, art. I, p. 753). Ammianus Marcellinus, moreover (Ammian. bk. XXVII, ch. 4, p. 482), testifies that Mars was held in the highest honor and worship among the Thracians.

As for Cretan Jupiter, who was said to have been born and buried in Crete, [Col. 0594B] and likewise Juno, both Argive and Samian, we have discussed them more than once (vol. I, *Apparatus*, bk. III, ch. 7, art. 4, p. 730; ch. 8, art. I, p. 735; and ch. 14, art. 5, p. 827).

To this may be added Cicero (Cicer. bk. I, *On the Nature of the Gods*, p. 207), who handed down the following concerning the first Juno: “But she is not the same as Sospita or Argive Juno, nor as Roman Juno. Therefore the Argives have one form of Juno, the Latins another.” Concerning this Juno we read the following verse of Virgil:

> To Argive Juno we duly offer rightful honors.

See Pausanias (Pausan. bk. II, p. 59, and bk. III, p. 95), Lucian (Lucian, *On Sacrifices*, p. 185), and Strabo (Strab. bk. V, p. 215, and bk. VI, p. 252), who mention her more than once, as do a great many more recent writers.

[Col. 0594C] Concerning Samian Juno, Aethlius relates the following in Clement of Alexandria (Clement of Alexandria, *Exhortation to the Gentiles*, p. 30): Τῆς Σαμίας Ἥρας, ὥς φησιν Αἴθλιος, πρότερον μὲν ἦν σανίς ὕστερον δὲ ἐπὶ Προκλέους ἄρχοντος, ἀνδριαντοειδὲς ἐγένετο. “The Samian Hera, as Aethlius says, was at first a wooden plank; later, during the archonship of Procles, it was fashioned in the form of a statue.” From this it is evident how ancient her veneration among the pagans was. Read further, if you wish, Pausanias (Pausan. bk. VII, p. 209) and Origen (Orig. bk. IV, *Against Celsus*, p. 196). Virgil mentions both of those Junos, and a third, who was called Punic or Carthaginian, in these verses:

> There was an ancient city—Tyrian colonists held it—  
> Carthage. . . . . . . . .
>
> [Col. 0594D] . . . . . . . . . . . .
>
> Which Juno is said to have cherished alone above all lands,  
> Even preferring it to Samos: here were her arms,  
> Here was her chariot; that this should be the goddess’s kingdom  
> Over the nations, if the fates should somehow permit,  
> Even then she strove for and fostered.
>
> . . . . . . . . . . . .
>
> Chiefly because of what she had done at Troy for her beloved Argos.

(Virg., *Aeneid*, bk. I, v. 16.)

Finally, the Idaean Mother will be discussed below, just as we have already discussed above the monstrous divine powers of the Egyptians. These, then, are the gods and goddesses who, like any others whatever, as Minucius rightly asserted, brought no assistance at all to the Romans. Ambrose later argued against Symmachus in much the same way: “Let them choose which they prefer. If the sacred rites prevailed among the Romans, then they were defeated among the Carthaginians; but if they were triumphed over among the [Col. 0595A] Carthaginians, they certainly did not benefit the Romans either” (Ambrose, Epist. 18, § 6, p. 834).

Minucius therefore rightly concludes from what has been said that nothing could be more absurd than to claim that worshipers abandoned and crushed by gods and goddesses of this kind thereby caused the boundaries of the Roman Empire to be extended. Ambrose argued in precisely the same manner against Symmachus: “Why should I speak of the Senones,” whom Minucius above, as we have seen, indicated without naming them, “who penetrated the hidden places of the Capitol, and whom the Roman remnant could not have endured had not a goose betrayed them by its frightened cackling? Behold what sort of guardians the Roman temples had. Where was Jupiter then? Was he speaking through the goose?” (ibid., § 5; above, art. 1). He similarly pressed the pagans with Hannibal’s victories: “Hannibal long insulted [Col. 0595B] the Roman sacred rites and, though their gods were fighting against him, advanced victorious as far as the city walls. Why did they allow themselves to be besieged, when the arms of their gods were fighting on their behalf?” (Ambrose, ibid., § 4). Consult, if you please and have leisure, what we have annotated there. The Romans, therefore, could neither obtain nor hope for any aid from foreign gods by which their empire might be enlarged. Nor could they obtain it from native gods of their own, as must now be examined.

## ARTICLE III

**The native gods—Romulus, enrolled among the gods through Proculus’s perjury; Picus, Tiberinus, Pilumnus, Picumnus, Consus, Cloacina, Fear, Pallor, Fever, Disease, Acca Laurentia, and Flora—were of no assistance to the Romans in extending the boundaries of their empire; with a discussion of the Larentalian rites and the Consualian and Floralian games.**

[Col. 0595C]

Minucius passes to the Romans’ native gods and plainly declares that they provided the Romans themselves with no greater assistance than did the foreign gods. Indeed, he thought this so certain that it needed no proof, and that nothing more was required than to call those gods by their names. Thus the first listed by him, and afterward by Cyprian—though without observing chronological order—are Romulus, Picus, Tiberinus, Consus, Pilumnus, and Picumnus (Cypr. *On the Vanity of Idols*, p. 11).

Romulus, the founder of the Roman people and City, as no one is unaware, was celebrated by Ennius in Cicero as enrolled in the number of the gods, in this single verse:

> [Col. 0595D] Romulus spends eternity in heaven with the gods.

(Cic., *Tusculan Disputations*, bk. I, p. 119, line 33.)

Yet Romulus became a god only “through the perjury” of Proculus, as our author had said earlier. Titus Livy relates the matter as follows. When various rumors circulated concerning the death of Romulus, and some spread in hushed murmurs that he had been torn apart by the senators:

> Proculus Julius, while the city was troubled by longing for the king and hostile toward the Fathers, came forward before the assembly. A man of weight, as tradition relates, and a witness even to so momentous a matter, he said: “Romans, Romulus, the father of this city, suddenly descended from heaven at the first light of dawn today and presented himself before me. When I stood there filled with awe and reverence, praying that it might be lawful to look upon him face to face, he said: ‘Go and announce [Col. 0596A] to the Romans that the heavenly gods so will it that my Rome should be the capital of the world. Therefore let them cultivate the art of war, and let them know, and hand down this knowledge to posterity, that no human power can withstand Roman arms.’ Having spoken these words,” he said, “Romulus departed on high.” It is astonishing how much credence was given to the man who announced these things, and how greatly the people’s and army’s longing for Romulus was eased once belief in his immortality had been established.

(Livy, Decade I, bk. 1, § 16.)

Ovid (Ovid, bk. II, *Fasti*, p. 492 ff.), Dionysius of Halicarnassus (Dionys., bk. II, *Roman Antiquities*, pp. 118 and 124), and Plutarch (Plutarch, *Life of Romulus*, p. 35) reported this somewhat more fully; Florus (Florus, bk. I, ch. 1), Lactantius (Lactant., bk. I, ch. 15, p. 87), and Augustine (August., bk. III, *City of God*, ch. 15, p. 70) more briefly. Cyprian (Cyprian, *On the [Col. 0596B] Vanity of Idols*, p. 13), as usual, follows in our author’s footsteps. Accordingly, Tertullian (Tertull., *Apology*, ch. 21), speaking of Christ’s ascension into heaven, says: “With far better grounds than your Proculuses are accustomed to make assertions.” For this reason Tatian (Tatian, *Oration against the Greeks*, p. 149), suppressing Romulus’s name, said: Τοὺς βασιλέας, μισθοῦ ἢ δι᾽ ἐπιορκίας τις τοὺς θεοὺς καταγελῶν, εἰς τὸν οὐρανὸν ἀνεληλυθέναι φήσας, πεπίστευται. “Someone, plainly hired for payment or committing perjury and making a mockery of the gods, found people who believed him when he said that certain kings of old had ascended into heaven.”

As for the other Roman gods, we learn from Augustine that Picus and Tiberinus were seriously incorporated into their false and fictitious order (August., bk. IV, *City of God*, ch. 23, p. 104; bk. VI, ch. 10, [Col. 0596C] p. 159; bk. XVIII, ch. 15, p. 499). This is subsequently confirmed by Augustine in these words of Varro: “Romulus consecrated Picus and Tiberinus.” Who Picus was, at what time he reigned, and how he was entered on the roll of the gods Augustine himself relates in another book as follows:

> Picus, son of Saturn, was the first to receive the kingdom of Laurentum, when the woman Deborah was judging among the Hebrews. . . . As for Saturn, the father of this Picus, let the worshipers of gods of this kind consider what they think, for they deny that he was a man; yet others have written that he himself reigned in Italy before his son Picus.

(Ibid.)

He informs us, however, that this second opinion is accepted by its advocates and by Virgil, whom we shall presently cite. Finally, he added: “Picus begot Faunus, the second king of Laurentum; this man too is, or was, a god among them. Before the Trojan War, they bestowed divine honors upon these dead men.” [Col. 0596D]

Virgil, whom Augustine commended, sang the following about Picus:

> . . . Faunus’s father was Picus, and he  
> Traces you, Saturn, as his father.

(Virgil, *Aeneid*, bk. VII, v. 48.)

And again:

> Picus himself sat there with Quirinal augural staff and short  
> Striped robe drawn close, and bore a sacred shield in his left hand—  
> Picus, tamer of horses, whom his wife Circe, seized by desire,  
> Struck with a golden wand, transformed by her drugs  
> Into a bird, and sprinkled his wings with colors.

(Ibid., v. 187 ff.)

[Col. 0597A] Ovid says more concerning Picus’s transformation into a bird; you may read him, as also Servius on those verses of Virgil (Ovid, bk. XIV, *Metamorphoses*, § 7, p. 517 ff.; Serv. on Virgil, p. 457).

The same poet composed these verses concerning Tiberinus:

> Here the god of the place himself, the river Tiberinus,  
> Rose as an aged man amid the pleasant poplar leaves.

(Virgil, *Aeneid*, bk. VIII, v. 31 ff.)

Anyone who desires more concerning him should consult Dionysius of Halicarnassus, bk. I, *Roman Antiquities*, p. 57; Livy, bk. I, p. 2; the author of the book *On the Origin of the Roman People*; and others.

Concerning Pilumnus, let us listen again to Virgil, singing as follows:

> . . . Then Turnus happened to be sitting  
> In the sacred valley within the grove of his father Pilumnus.

(*Aeneid*, bk. IX, vv. 3–4.)

And again in the following book:

> It is shameful that Italians should surround a newborn Troy  
> With flames, while Turnus stands upon his native soil—  
> Turnus, whose grandfather is Pilumnus, whose mother is the goddess Venilia.

(Bk. X, v. 74 ff.)

Servius, moreover, comments on the former verses that Pilumnus—who is doubtless the same as Picumnus and is so named by our author with a slight alteration—was the brother of Pithumnus. The latter, the same Servius says, is reputed to have discovered the practice of manuring fields, and for this reason the name Sterquilinius was given to him. He is also said to have first devised the art of “pounding grain,” and therefore to be worshiped by bakers. Servius nevertheless added that some regarded both Pithumnus and [Col. 0597C] Pilumnus as identical with Castor and Pollux, while others regarded them as *Laudum* gods [reading uncertain], whom Varro likewise conjectures to be gods of marriage. Then, on the poet’s later verses, Servius again observes that Varro calls both of them gods of infants, and that a bed was spread for them on behalf of a woman in childbirth while it was determined whether the newborn child was viable. Finally, he reminds us that some think Pilumnus was given his name because he drives away the evils of infancy; but he rejects this derivation as openly as he more readily accepts the other.

[Col. 0597D] Finally, as regards the god Consus, we read in Plutarch that the solemn games at which the Sabine maidens were abducted were proclaimed by Romulus after he had discovered buried beneath the earth an altar of a certain god whom they called Consus. Plutarch thinks him either the guardian of counsels, surnamed from *consilium* (“counsel”) or from *consules* (“consuls”), or else equestrian Neptune (Plutarch, *Life of Romulus*, p. 25). Livy, for his part, declares that these same games, called the Consualia, were prepared by Romulus in honor of Equestrian Neptune (Livy, bk. I, § 9). Varro, however, says: “The Consualia are so called from Consus, because at that time public holidays are held for this god, and those games at which the Sabine maidens were abducted are celebrated by the priests at his altar in the circus” (Varr., *On the Latin Language*, p. 50). Yet do not too readily suppose that there was a great disagreement among these writers. For Dionysius of Halicarnassus is our witness that the one whom the Romans called Consus was called by the Greeks Ποσειδῶνα σεισίχθονα, “Neptune, Shaker of the Earth,” [Col. 0598A] and that this was the very god in whose honor Romulus instituted the games mentioned above (Dionys. Halic., bk. II, *Roman Antiquities*, p. 100).

Tertullian reconciles these same writers still more fully in the following words:

> From that time the games were called the Consualia, though at first they honored Neptune. . . . They assign the Consualia to Romulus because he dedicated them to the god Consus, whom they regard as the god of counsel—that counsel, namely, by which he then devised the abduction of the Sabine maidens as wives for his soldiers. . . . Even now an altar to that Consus lies buried in the circus, beneath the earth near the first turning-posts, with an inscription of this sort: “Consus mighty in counsel, Mars in war, the Lares in assembly.” At it the public priests sacrifice on the Nones of July; and on the twelfth day before the Kalends of September, the Flamen Quirinalis and the virgins sacrifice.

(Tertull., *On the Shows*, ch. 5, p. 92.)

[Col. 0598B] Read further, if you please, Arnobius, bk. III, *Against the Gentiles*, p. 113; Jerome, *Life of Hilarion*, p. 81; Augustine, bk. IV, *City of God*, ch. 11, p. 97; and Servius on Virgil’s *Aeneid*, bk. VIII, p. 525.

Come now, and let Tertullian appear once more; he joins to Consus the other Roman gods named by Minucius: “Thus,” he says, “a man will invent a god, just as Romulus invented Consus, Tatius Cloacina, and Hostilius Fear” (ibid., bk. I, *Against Marcion*, ch. 18). For Minucius said: “Tatius both discovered and worshiped Cloacina; Hostilius, Fear and Pallor; shortly afterward Fever was dedicated by someone or other.” These words were transcribed word for word by Cyprian (Cypr., *On the Vanity of Idols*, p. 10). Varro (Varr., bk. IV, *On the Latin Language*, p. 18 ff.), as quoted by Augustine (bk. IV, *City of God*, ch. 10, p. 159), mentions these ridiculous divine powers, and also the aforementioned [Col. 0598C] Picus and Tiberinus. Lactantius speaks specifically of Cloacina: “Tatius,” he says, “consecrated an image of Cloacina found in the Great Sewer; and because he did not know whose likeness it was, he gave it a name derived from the place” (Lactant., bk. I, *On False Religion*, ch. 20, p. 104). Consult further, if you wish, Tertullian in the passage just cited (Tertull., loc. cit.; and *On the Pallium*, ch. 4) and in another book, and Augustine (bk. IV, *City of God*, ch. 8, p. 93, and ch. 23, p. 104), who discusses not only Cloacina, but also Fear, Pallor, and Fever, noted by our Minucius.

There are also those who think that this Cloacina [Col. 0598D] is the same as the one Pliny calls Venus Cloacina in these words: “It is handed down that the Romans and Sabines, when they were about to fight over the abducted maidens, laid down their arms and were purified with myrtle sprays in the place where the statues of Venus Cloacina now stand. For the ancients used *cluere* to mean ‘to purify’” (Plin., bk. XV, *Natural History*, ch. 29, p. 212). But since this Venus was a purifier, she seems wrongly to be confused with the Cloacina with whom we are dealing.

We have discussed elsewhere the other monstrous divine powers mentioned there by Minucius and Lactantius—Fear, Pallor, Fever, and Disease (vol. I, *Apparatus*, bk. III, diss. I, ch. 9, art. 4, p. 764 ff.)—and have shown that the pagans, with the utmost foolishness, numbered them among the *Averrunci*, the gods who warded off [Col. 0599A] evil.

The entire troop of such ridiculous gods is brought to a close by “Acca Laurentia and Flora, disgraceful prostitutes,” who, as our author says, “must be counted among the Romans’ diseases and gods.” To understand this, one must observe, or recall from memory, what the ancients handed down: that Romulus and Remus were born to the Vestal Rhea Silvia through an adulterous union with Mars and were reared, as some say, by a she-wolf, or, as others more truthfully [Col. 0599B] relate, by Laurentia. Livy says that, because she prostituted her body openly, they believed she had been called a *lupa* (“she-wolf” or “prostitute”) among the shepherds (Livy, Decade I, bk. 1, § 4). Tertullian therefore calls her a public harlot (Tertull., *Apology*, ch. 13, p. 15). But this did not prevent her from being admitted into the number of the goddesses, or a festival and sacred rites called the Larentalia from being instituted in her honor. Should you ask us to produce witnesses to all these things, in addition to Livy we shall give you Dionysius of Halicarnassus, bk. I, *Roman Antiquities*, pp. 26 and 70; Plutarch, *Life of Romulus*, p. 19, and *Roman Questions*, p. 272; Ovid, bk. III, beginning of the *Fasti*; Servius on Virgil’s *Aeneid*, bk. I, v. 278 ff.; Virgil himself, *Aeneid*, bk. VIII, v. 630 ff.; Pliny, bk. VIII, ch. 17, p. 163, and bk. XV, ch. 18, p. 197; Macrobius, bk. I, *Saturnalia*, ch. 10; Aulus Gellius, bk. VI, *Attic Nights*, ch. 7; Lactantius, bk. II, ch. 20, pp. 101–102, as we shall show in its proper place; Augustine, bk. XVIII, *City of God*, ch. 21, [Col. 0599C] p. 503; and Aurelius Victor, or the author of the book *On the Origin of the Roman People*, near the end, and *On Illustrious Men*, ch. 1.

Flora, says Minucius, was another disgraceful prostitute who, according to Marcus Cato as quoted by Gellius, “openly earned money with her body” (Gell., bk. IX, *Attic Nights*, ch. 20, p. 485). Lactantius says that, after she had amassed great wealth through that most shameful trade, she appointed the Roman people heirs to it on condition that the income from it should fund an annual celebration of her birthday by the staging of games called the Florales or Floralia (Lactant., bk. I, *Institutes*, ch. 10, p. 103). But because, with the passage of time, this most shameful and infamous origin of the games appeared discreditable, they invented the story that she was a goddess who presided over flowers—or, as [Col. 0599D] Augustine says, over grain in bloom—and, changing her former name Chloris, called her Flora (August., bk. IV, *City of God*, ch. 8, p. 94). Since they could not entirely abolish the memory of her trade as a prostitute, they fabricated the story that she was violated not by a man but by the god Zephyr. As though violation by a god could be said to be less disgraceful than violation by a man! Yet Ovid celebrates these matters, no less than the others, as altogether worthy of his gods:

> I was Chloris, who am now called Flora; the Greek letter  
> Of my name was corrupted by its Latin sound.  
> I was Chloris, a nymph of the happy field, where, as you have heard,  
> The abode of fortunate men once was.  
> What beauty I possessed is hard for a modest woman to relate;  
> Yet it obtained a god as son-in-law for my mother.  
> It was spring; I wandered. Zephyr saw me; I turned away.  
> [Col. 0600A] He pursued; I fled; he was the stronger.

(Ovid, *Fasti*, bk. V, v. 195 ff.)

Nor should you doubt that this notorious prostitute was numbered among the goddesses by the pagans, and that her aid was invoked lest the crops ever be spoiled. For Varro recorded the following concerning himself: “Fourth, I invoke Robigus and Flora, by whose favor neither does mildew spoil the grain and trees, nor do they flower out of season. Therefore the public festival of Robigus, the Robigalia, and the games of Flora, the Floralia, were instituted” (Varr., bk. I, *On Agriculture*, beginning). [Col. 0600B] These must be discussed in the following dissertation. Finally, Cornelius Tacitus recorded that Tiberius Caesar dedicated beside the Circus Maximus “the temple of Flora, which had been founded by Lucius and Marcus when they were plebeian aediles” (Tacit., bk. II, after the midpoint).

Who, then, if he possesses any soundness of mind, upon hearing of that utterly ridiculous and infamous rabble of gods and goddesses, would not immediately acknowledge how rightly Minucius concludes his enumeration of them with this not inelegant irony? “It was these, no doubt, who extended the Roman Empire against all the other gods worshiped among the nations?” But come, and let us see by what further weighty arguments he overthrows and disperses this absurd opinion of the same Romans.

## ARTICLE IV

**How false it is that the boundaries of the Roman Empire were enlarged by the gods because honors and privileges had been granted to the Vestals and priests; how great the incontinence and crimes of both were; and concerning adulteries and sacrileges in the temples themselves.**

[Col. 0600C]

With no gentler force Minucius repels the claim we observed Caecilius advancing: that the gods came to the Romans’ aid and gave them dominion over the entire world because of the honors granted and privileges bestowed upon the Vestals and priests. For by what title, Minucius argues, did the Vestals or priests deserve this? Was there greater chastity among the former than among others, or holier religion among the latter? By no means. Indeed, very many Vestals paid the penalty for violated chastity, though others of their company, no less unchaste but more secretive, escaped it.

For the Vestal Rhea Silvia, as we observed shortly above and as Augustine aptly recalls after others, was said to have borne Remus and Romulus through shameful adultery (August., bk. XVIII, *City of God*, ch. 21, p. 503). Why, then, should other Vestals not have believed that they could imitate her wicked example with impunity? Suetonius, moreover, relates that Domitian punished in various and severe ways the unchastity of Vestals that had been neglected by his father and brother: earlier offenses with capital punishment, later ones in the ancient manner. “For,” he adds, “after he had allowed the Ocellata sisters, and likewise Varonilla, freedom to choose the manner of their death, and had banished their seducers, he afterward ordered Cornelia, the chief virgin”—that is, the one placed over the other Vestals—“who had once been acquitted but, after a long interval, was prosecuted again and convicted, to be buried alive, and ordered her violators to be beaten to death with rods in the Comitium” (Sueton., bk. VIII, *Life of Domitian*, § 8). [Col. 0601A] Hence Eusebius notes that, during Domitian’s reign, “three Vestal virgins were condemned for fornication” (Euseb., *Chronicle*, at year 2099). Concerning Cornelia, Pliny writes to Minucianus: “She was led to punishment—I do not know whether innocent, but certainly as though guilty” (Plin., *Letters*, bk. IV, letter 11). Yet Suetonius had no doubt whatever concerning her fornication and just condemnation. Plutarch mentions three other Vestals—Aemilia, Licinia, and Marcia—who, he relates, paid the penalties for unchastity after they had long maintained an unlawful intimacy with men (Plutarch, *Roman Questions*, p. 284). You may also consult Lipsius, if you have leisure (Lips., *Syntagma on Vesta and the Vestals*, ch. III, vol. III, p. 606).

[Col. 0601B] Let us add, if you please, Ambrose, who replies to Symmachus, when the latter argued in the same manner as Caecilius against the Christians and for the pagans, that only seven Vestals survived in his own time, and says of them: “That is not virginity which is purchased for a price and possessed without devotion to virtue” (Ambrose, Epist. 18, *Against Symmachus*, p. 836).

Our author asserts that the shamelessness of pagan priests was no less than that of the Vestals: “For where,” he says, “are acts of fornication more commonly arranged by priests than among altars and shrines? Where are procurers’ negotiations conducted, adulteries planned? Burning lust is more frequently discharged in the chambers of temple attendants than in the brothels themselves.” But consider, I ask, whether in that passage he was not referring to these words of Tertullian: “Adulteries are arranged in temples, procurers’ negotiations conducted among altars; lust is very often discharged in the very [Col. 0601C] lodgings of temple attendants and priests, beneath the same fillets, priestly caps, and purple garments, while incense burns” (Tertull., *Apology*, ch. 15, p. 16). Therefore, in another book, Tertullian represented idolatry itself as speaking thus: “I, idolatry, most frequently provide an opportunity for adultery. My groves know it, and my mountains and living waters, and the temples themselves in the cities: they know how much we contrive for the overthrow of chastity” (Tertull., *On Modesty*, ch. 5, p. 719). What of the fact that Phoenician women, as Athanasius says, believed that by prostituting their bodies before the idols they would make the gods favorable to them (Athanasius, *Oration against the Gentiles*, § 26, p. 24)? But Tertullian must be discussed further in the proper place (*Dissertation on Tertullian’s Apology*, ch. 24, art. 3).

[Col. 0601D] Nor should you say that these things were perhaps either gratuitously fabricated or maliciously exaggerated by Christian writers driven by implacable hatred of the pagans. For they can be proved by almost innumerable testimonies of the pagans themselves, which we omit for brevity’s sake. It will therefore suffice to report some here, beginning with these verses of Ovid:

> Near the temple was a recess of scanty light,  
> Like a cave and roofed with natural pumice,  
> Sacred by ancient religious awe; there the priest  
> Had gathered many wooden images of the ancient gods.  
> She entered it and polluted the sanctuary with forbidden disgrace.

(Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, bk. X, penultimate section.)

Juvenal attacks these most shameful crimes and sacrileges still more vehemently:

> For lately, as I recall, the shrine of Isis, and Ganymede,  
> The secret palaces of Peace and of the Mother brought to Rome,  
> And Ceres—for in what temple does a woman not sell herself?—  
> You, the adulterer better known than Aufidius, used to frequent  
> For what I leave unspoken, and even to make husbands themselves submit.

(Juvenal, *Satire* IX, v. 22 ff.)

You may read still more in his sixth satire, where, among very many other things, he said:

> . . . And now she is awaited in the gardens,  
> Or rather at the sanctuary of the bawd of Isis.

(Ibid., *Satire* VI, v. 485.)

Nor are poets alone, but other pagan writers as well, most certain witnesses to such great crimes. Does Cicero not complain that Clodius was “that man” who “introduced fornication upon the couches of the Good Goddess, and violated by male gaze and by disgraceful fornication those rites which it is unlawful for the eyes of any man, even an unwitting one, to behold”? (Cicer., Oration 30, *On the Response of the Haruspices*, p. 429, line 34.) Did Suetonius not commit the following to writing concerning the emperor Tiberius?

> It is also said that, while sacrificing on one occasion, he was captivated by the appearance of an attendant carrying the incense-box before him and was unable to restrain himself: almost before the sacred rite had been completed, he immediately took the attendant aside on the spot and violated him, along with his brother, a flute-player; and soon afterward, because they reproached one another with the shameful act, he broke the legs of both.

(Sueton., bk. III, *Life of Tiberius*, § 4.)

We certainly should never finish speaking if everything had to be set down that each of these writers and others have repeatedly handed down concerning these detestable crimes.

[Col. 0602C] But even if all those acts were not perpetrated by the priests themselves—as they were by that priest to be discussed below who played the part of Hercules—nearly all of them were certainly privy to such acts. See, therefore, how falsely and shamelessly the pagans claimed that, because honors and privileges had been granted to these priests and Vestals, the Romans had gained dominion over the whole world.

## ARTICLE V

**How Minucius shows that the Roman Empire was neither founded nor enlarged by piety toward the gods, because the Assyrians, Medes, Persians, Greeks, and Egyptians reigned before the Romans and before their pontiffs, Arval Brethren, Salii, Vestals, and augurs.**

Minucius proceeds and refutes, with another argument of no less weight, all the claims that Caecilius and the pagan [Col. 0602D] Romans foolishly boasted concerning dominion over the whole world having been handed to them because of their supreme piety toward their gods. For these gods, whom we have shown to be false, neither gave kingdoms to their worshipers nor extended their boundaries; rather, the one true and omnipotent God alone grants such things to whom and when he wills. Nor is this difficult to prove. For, as Minucius rightly argues and everyone knows: “Before those Romans, by God’s dispensation, the Assyrians, Medes, Persians, and also the Greeks and Egyptians long possessed kingdoms, although they had no pontiffs, Arval Brethren, Salii, Vestals, or augurs.” Tertullian had earlier said that kingdoms are dispensed by that supreme God and that the Romans did not receive theirs from their fictitious gods. For, he says, “the Babylonians reigned [Col. 0603A] before the pontiffs, the Medes before the Fifteen Men, the Egyptians before the Salii, the Assyrians before the Luperci, and the Amazons before the Vestal virgins” (Tertull., *Apology*, ch. 26, p. 28; and bk. II, *To the Nations*, ch. 17, p. 79).

Cyprian, however, puts it somewhat differently: “Kingdoms do not fall to men by merit, but vary by lot. In any case, before the Romans the Assyrians, Medes, and Persians possessed empire; and we know that the Greeks and Egyptians also reigned. Thus, in the alternating succession of powers, the time for ruling came to the Romans also, as it had to others” (Cyprian, *On the Vanity of Idols*, p. 13). That is, kingdoms have shared in the instability and vicissitude of human affairs and, just as they had a beginning, so too they had an end. The Roman Empire began long after many others [Col. 0603B] and, as we have said, was founded and extended by wars, impiety, crimes, and sacrileges. Yet the omnipotent and most equitable God permits these things for perfectly just reasons; and, by his permission, all kingdoms are dispensed to whom and when he wills.

Since there is no room for even the slightest doubt that the Assyrians and the other nations named by our writers possessed their kingdoms before the Romans, it must be certain that neither the Roman Empire nor the kingdoms of other peoples were ever given by their own gods. For why would those gods have given things that were afterward taken away, or upon which the Romans and others encroached with the greatest impiety and the utmost contempt for those gods? If anyone still desires more, he should consult Ambrose and Prudentius, who utterly overthrow this same Roman argument, absurdly repeated by the pagan Symmachus. See also Augustine, who pursues the matter more fully and crushes and routs the same foolish boasting of the pagans (Ambrose, Epist. 18, p. 834 ff.; Prudent., bk. II, *Against Symmachus*, § 4; Augustine, bk. III, *City of God*, chs. 8, 9 ff.; and bk. IV, ch. 3 ff.).

But someone will doubtless ask us who those Arval Brethren and Salii were whom our Minucius mentioned. We shall therefore answer him in these very words of Pliny: “Romulus was the first to institute the priests of the fields, and he called himself the twelfth brother among them, born of Acca Laurentia, his nurse. He gave them, as the most sacred badge of their priesthood, a crown of grain-ears bound together by a white ribbon; [Col. 0603D] this was the first crown among the Romans” (Plin., bk. XVIII, *Natural History*, ch. 2, p. 433). If you ask for another witness, Sabinus Massurius will quickly appear, whose words were transcribed by Aulus Gellius as follows:

> That woman lost one of her twelve sons to death. In his place Romulus gave himself to Acca Laurentia as a son, and called himself and her other sons the Arval Brethren. From that time the college of the Arval Brethren continued at the number of twelve; the badge of this priesthood is a crown of grain-ears and white fillets.

(Gell., bk. I, *Attic Nights*, ch. 7, p. 377.)

Varro, moreover, said that they were called Arval Brethren because they performed public sacred rites so that the fields (*arva*) might bear crops; and for this reason, as Festus says, the sacrificial victims slain by them [Col. 0604A] were called *Ambarvales* (Varro, bk. IV, *On the Latin Language*, p. 21; Festus, ch. 20, *On the Meaning of Words*, and in the fragments).

Who the Salii were Livy will teach you, where he records the following concerning Numa Pompilius: “He chose twelve Salii for Mars Gradivus, gave them the distinctive dress of an embroidered tunic and, over the tunic, a bronze covering for the breast, and ordered them to carry the heavenly shields called *ancilia* and to proceed through the city, singing hymns with ritual stamping and solemn dancing” (Livy, book I, § 20). Servius, however, has far more concerning them, as do, among the Greeks, Plutarch and Dionysius of Halicarnassus, and others whom anyone may readily consult. We ourselves shall later have another occasion to discuss them further (Servius on book VII of the *Aeneid*, p. 503; Plutarch, *Life of Numa*, p. 66; Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book II, p. 29).

[Col. 0604B] The same writers have also committed to writing how that same Numa Pompilius instituted the Pontiffs and Vestal Virgins, and what sort of persons they were, as also the Augurs, who falsely claimed that they could forecast and foretell the future from food either taken into or rejected from the mouths of chickens, or falling to the ground, as Cicero says. But we must explain this more fully in the following chapter (Cicero, book II, *On Divination*, p. 289).

It is sufficiently agreed among all that this was the first institution of those Roman priests and pontiffs, and consequently of their religion and public worship of the gods. Minucius rightly concludes from this that it is false that the Romans merited dominion over the whole world through their devotion to these gods. For before they worshipped them, the Assyrians and the other nations named above [Col. 0604C] held dominion; they likewise venerated their own gods and appointed priests over their worship. Yet those peoples did not receive their kingdoms from these gods of theirs, since their kingdoms were taken away while they were still worshipping them. Therefore the Romans likewise did not acquire their empire through the favor or assistance either of their own gods or of foreign ones—an empire which, as we have shown, was founded and extended by the gravest crimes. But we shall have to treat these matters further in the dissertation.

# CHAPTER XIX

## The Arguments Are Examined by Which Caecilius Thought That the Existence of the Gods Could Be Proved from Miracles, Oracles, Auspices, Auguries, Dreams, and Other Predictions

### ARTICLE I

#### Whether Caecilius Proved the Existence of the Gods from the Miracles of Claudia Quinta, who was said to have drawn along, with her girdle alone, the ship in which the image of the Idaean Mother was being carried; of Castor and Pollux, who announced the Roman victory over King Perseus; from Latinius’s dream, by which the games were renewed; from the self-devotion of the Decii, by which the enemy was routed and defeated; and from the similar self-devotion of Curtius, by which a chasm in the earth is said to have been miraculously filled

[Col. 0604D]

Of all the arguments by which the pagans undertook to prove that their gods truly existed, the principal one certainly appears to be that which they attempted to derive from their gods’ miracles, oracles, auspices, auguries, and other predictions [Col. 0605A] of this kind. For no one could ever rightly deny that this line of argument would carry the greatest weight and importance if it rested on truth, and if all the things that the pagans used to proclaim had surpassed the powers of created nature. Therefore these matters must be carefully examined according to our custom, so that nothing whatever is concealed of what either the pagan Caecilius advances or the Christian Octavius replies, and so that each point, insofar as possible, is both developed and illuminated more fully.

Let us therefore begin with Caecilius’s miracles. By what greater miracle, he said, can the existence of the gods and their assistance to their people be proved than that by which the Idaean Mother “by her arrival both proved a matron’s chastity and freed the City from fear of the enemy”? In these few words, [Col. 0605B] which may be obscure to some, he indicates the celebrated deed of Claudia Quinta found in pagan writers. They relate that a stone image of the Idaean Mother, or Mother of the Gods—that is, Cybele or Ceres—was brought from Pessinus to Rome, on the advice of a certain seer, so that Hannibal might be driven out of Italy during the Punic War. But when the ship carrying the image reached the mouth of the Tiber, it remained so immovable that no human strength could shift it from its place. Then Claudia, whose reputation for chastity had hitherto been doubtful, proved it most clearly when, after pouring out prayers to the goddess, as they said, she alone, using only her own girdle, drew the goddess’s image, together with the ship itself, onto land at the place the Romans desired. Livy, Ovid, and, somewhat less clearly, Cicero handed this account down to posterity, as did the Christian writers Arnobius, Lactantius, Augustine, and others [Col. 0605C] (Livy, third decade, book IX, near the beginning; Ovid, book IV of the *Fasti*, § 3; Cicero, speech 30, *On the Response of the Haruspices*, p. 438; Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 22; Arnobius, book VII, *Against the Pagans*, p. 253 ff.; Lactantius, book II, ch. 7; Augustine, book II of *The City of God*, ch. 7; book III, ch. 12; and book X, ch. 16).

Arnobius, however, replies that, even if this is true, the Romans wrongly believed that through the agency or assistance of this image, or Pessinuntine stone—in which no divinity resided—the victory was won, as the pagans proclaimed, the honor of the City was restored, and the boundaries of the Roman Empire were extended. For afterward, when so many and such great Roman armies were slaughtered and routed, that truly illustrious Mother of the Gods neither checked nor repelled the greatest assaults of war. [Col. 0605D] We have already observed that Minucius similarly said that the tutelary gods of cities and nations brought no assistance to their own peoples, or to the Romans, against their enemies. Here, however, he replies that these miracles are not true but false, since they were accomplished not by any divine power but by the arts, power, and deceptions of demons. This, as we shall show shortly, he demonstrates fully and clearly.

By the same answer he also rejects the objection that Caecilius next makes as follows: “Witnesses are the consecrated statues of the Equestrian Brothers at the lake, just as they had appeared: breathless, with their horses foaming and steaming, they announced the victory over Perseus on the very day it was won.” By the “Equestrian Brothers” he means Castor and [Col. 0606A] Pollux, whom others call the Tyndarids (Cicero, book II, *On the Nature of the Gods*, p. 214; and *Tusculan Disputations* I, p. 119, line 36). He boldly asserts that they performed two miracles: first, that through their protection King Perseus was defeated and captured by the Romans; second, that the victory was announced to the senate in Rome on the very day it was won; and finally, that their statues were erected in memory of so great a miracle. Valerius Maximus (book I, ch. 8, § 1, pp. 62 ff.), Florus (book I, ch. 11), Ammianus Marcellinus (book XXVIII, ch. 4, p. 528), Dionysius of Halicarnassus (book VI of *Roman Antiquities*, p. 350), Plutarch (*Life of Coriolanus*, p. 215), and many others relate the same story. Some of them, however, handed it down to us not as completely certain but as something popularly reported. Indeed, Cicero introduced two representative speakers: Balbus the Stoic, who attempts by this example to prove the presence of his gods, and then Cotta the Academic, who dismisses these things as old women’s tales [Col. 0606B] (Cicero, book II, *On the Nature of the Gods*, p. 214, line 28; and book III, p. 241, line 30).

Caecilius presses another miracle: “A witness,” he says, “is the repetition, following a common man’s dream, of the games at which Jupiter had taken offense.” If anyone finds these words more obscure for their brevity, he will find them explained in the following words of Cicero:

> When the Great Votive Games were first being held during the Latin War, the citizenry was suddenly called to arms. Consequently, the games were interrupted, and renewed games were appointed. Before they were held, however, when the people had already taken their seats, a slave wearing a fork-shaped yoke [Col. 0606C] was led through the circus while being beaten with rods. Afterward, someone appeared to a Roman countryman in his sleep and said that the leading dancer at the games had displeased him, and ordered the man to announce this to the senate. The man did not dare to do so. He was ordered a second time and warned not to presume to test the speaker’s power, but not even then did he dare. After that, his son died. The same warning came a third time in his dreams; then he himself also became disabled. He reported the matter to his friends, on whose advice he was carried into the senate house on a litter. When he had related the dream to the senate, he returned home on his own feet. Thus, the dream having been confirmed by the senate, tradition records that those games were celebrated anew.

(Cicero, book I, *On Divination*, p. 264, line 49.)

Livy [Col. 0606D] describes the matter somewhat more fully (book II, ch. 36). The man whom the Orator and Arnobius (*Against the Pagans*, book VII, pp. 244 ff.) call merely a countryman is called T. Latinius by Livy and Augustine (*The City of God*, book IV, ch. 26, p. 207)—in one edition, Tib. Atinius—a commoner; by Dionysius of Halicarnassus (*Roman Antiquities*, book VII, p. 472) and Plutarch, he is called Τῖτος Λατῖνος (*Titus Latinus*; *Life of Coriolanus*, vol. I, p. 225) and is said to have been fairly wealthy; by Valerius Maximus (book I, ch. 7, § 4), unless there is an error in his printed editions and manuscripts, Ti. Atinius; by Lactantius, Tib. Attinius (book II, ch. 7, p. 176); and by Macrobius (book I of the *Saturnalia*, ch. 11), who writes that this occurred in the year [Col. 0607A] 473 from the founding of the City, Annius.

The Lactantius and Augustine whom we have cited, however, like Minucius, contend that these things should be attributed to the deceits and illusions of demons:

> Most people know all these things; some of you know that the demons themselves confess about themselves the things mentioned a little earlier: that Jupiter caused the games to be repeated by means of a dream; that the Castors appeared with their horses; and that the little ship followed the matron’s girdle. They confess all these things whenever, through the torments of our words and the fires of our prayer, they are driven by us from human bodies.

We shall explain these matters more clearly below and demonstrate how true they are.

What does Caecilius say next? “And the self-devotion of the Decii,” he says, “was duly fulfilled.” By these few words he refers to [Col. 0607B] the Decii, father and son—to whom some add a grandson—who, after devoting themselves for the Roman armies, rushed under arms into the midst of the enemy and by their glorious deaths secured a victory that had seemed hopeless. Various writers, especially Cicero, Valerius Maximus, Florus, Pliny, and Livy, have related these events.

When Balbus the Stoic raises these matters in Cicero, however, Cotta, as though he had wished to anticipate all the other pagans who would later fight against the Christians, replied in these words:

> You, however, think that the gods were appeased by the self-devotion of the Decii. What great injustice was theirs, that they could not be appeased toward the Roman people unless such men perished? That was the generals’ design: they had regard for their country and did not spare their lives. For [Col. 0607C] they thought that the army would follow its general as he spurred his horse and hurled himself against the enemy. And that is what happened.

(Cicero, book II, *On Ends*, p. 61; book I of the *Tusculan Disputations*, p. 130; book III, p. 146; *On Old Age*, p. 416; *Paradox* 2, p. 434; Valerius Maximus, book V, ch. 6, §§ 5–6; Florus, book II, chs. 14 and 17; Pliny, book XXII of the *Natural History*, p. 180; ch. 2, p. 557; Livy, first decade, book XVIII, p. 121; Cicero, book II, *On the Nature of the Gods*, p. 215; and book III, p. 242.)

He was therefore so far from thinking that anything miraculous or any assistance of gods actually present played a part in this victory that, on the contrary, he quite rightly exposes the gods’ extreme injustice, if they had acted in this way. He thus teaches that this self-devotion of the Decii was nothing other than the generals’ στρατήγημα (*stratēgēma*, stratagem), [Col. 0607D] and the customary arts and devices by which they routed their enemies and gained victory over them. Zonaras appears to have subscribed to the opinion of Cotta—or, if one prefers, of Cicero—on this point (Zonaras, book VII of the *Annals*, § 26, p. 363).

Finally, Caecilius adds: “Curtius too is a witness, who by either the bulk or the distinction of his *eques* [here, ‘horse’] leveled the chasm of the deep abyss.” Some think that there is a double scribal error here, and that instead of “*equitis* … *honore*” (“of the *eques* … distinction”) one should read “*equi* … *onere*” (“of the horse … burden”). But this is pointless. For Livy writes that Curtius “mounted a horse adorned as splendidly as possible.” Servius, moreover, observes that in Virgil *eques* (“horseman”) sometimes signifies the same thing as *equus* (“horse”) (Livy, first decade, book VII, p. 106; Virgil, book III of the *Georgics*, v. 116).

[Col. 0608A] In that same Livy, moreover, we read that when a chasm suddenly opened in the middle of the city’s forum and could be filled by no one, M. Curtius, a warlike young man, devoted himself to the gods and, fully armed and mounted on horseback, plunged headlong into the cavern. Immediately, as Valerius Maximus puts it (book V, ch. 6, § 2), once produce had been thrown in as a mark of honor, the earth recovered its former appearance. This seemed no inconsiderable prodigy to Livy as well as to Caecilius. But Varro (book IV, *On the Latin Language*, pp. 36 ff.) reports that three different accounts of the matter were handed down by Procilius, Piso, and Aelius Stilo. What of the fact that Zonaras (book VII of the *Annals*, § 25, p. 360) declares that he will by no means contradict those who judge these things inconsistent with historical truth? [Col. 0608B] Orosius, moreover, rebukes whoever—whether gods or men—thought that the chasm in the earth could not be filled unless it swallowed a living human being (Orosius, book III of the *Histories*, ch. 5). Finally, so as not to pass over Jerome entirely, it is worth observing that he openly taught that even if the deeds of Curtius, the Decii, and others like them were proved true, the Christians’ faith was not only not diminished by them but made more certain:

> If we believe the histories of the pagans, that Codrus, Curtius, and the Decii Mures by their deaths checked the plagues, famines, and wars of cities, how much more must it be believed possible for the Son of God to cleanse by his blood not one city but the whole world?

(Jerome, on Ephesians 1:7.)

Augustine discusses at greater length these extraordinary effects which seemed miracles [Col. 0608C] to the pagans; you will readily be able to consult him (Augustine, book X of *The City of God*, p. 252; and book XXI, ch. 6 ff., pp. 624 ff.).

Besides, Minucius had already utterly overthrown all those examples or arguments raised against Christians by Caecilius or other pagans, by those invincible arguments through which he demonstrated that there is only one God, not many. But not content with this response, he makes it plain to everyone that all these things, as we said shortly before and shall show in the next chapter, were accomplished by the fraudulent arts and deceptions of demons.

### ARTICLE II

#### The Presence of the Gods Is Not Proved by Caecilius from Oracles and the Responses of Seers, Against Which Minucius Sets the Examples of Amphiaraus, Tiresias, and Pythian Apollo, as well as the Ambiguity and Cessation of Oracles

[Col. 0608D]

Although oracles in which future events are foretold in some manner surpassing the power of created things would be of no slight importance for proving the presence of the gods, Caecilius nevertheless says: “I pass over the destinies foretold by oracles.” He immediately gives the reason why he omits an argument of such great weight: “Lest antiquity seem excessively fabulous to you.” And rightly so. For the stronger the argument for asserting the truth of the Christian religion that is drawn, as we shall see elsewhere, from the true and sacred oracles of our Prophets which attained their fulfillment, the more trivial and feeble the argument is if the oracles are fabulous, [Col. 0609A] doubtful, and full of ambiguity. Events proved that the pagan oracles were of this kind so plainly that Caecilius could not deny it.

He therefore retreats to another stronghold, from which he thinks he will more successfully defend his gods and their superstitious worship against the Christians’ assaults. He thus presses the responses which seers were accustomed to give in temples. For he contends that in those very temples, where they believed the gods dwelt, the seers, filled with the gods’ divine inspiration and power, foretold the future, gave safeguards against dangers, remedies for diseases, hope to the afflicted, and consolation or relief to others. But how could those gods have provided these things when Minucius had most clearly demonstrated that they were wholly fictitious and did not exist?

[Col. 0609B] Nevertheless, lest Caecilius complain that the argument drawn from prophecies supposedly uttered under the gods’ inspiration was being evaded, although it had already been overthrown, Minucius therefore refutes several of the more celebrated responses of seers one by one and shows that they are wrongly raised against Christians:

> What, and how much, shall I pursue concerning oracles? After his death Amphiaraus gave responses concerning the future, though he did not know that his wife would betray him for a necklace.

Eriphyle was the name of this wife of Amphiaraus, of whom Cicero says: “We learn in the myths that Eriphyle was possessed by such cupidity that, when she saw a necklace, made, I believe, of gold and jewels,” offered by Polynices, “she was so captivated by its beauty that she betrayed her husband’s life” (Cicero, book IX, *Against Verres*, p. 167, line 3). But we have already discussed Amphiaraus [Col. 0609C] (vol. I, *Apparatus*, book III, dissertation 2, ch. 20, art. 2, p. 1117). To the writers cited there we shall add Jerome, who confirms the opinion of Cicero and our Minucius as follows: “Eriphyle is said to have betrayed Amphiaraus and to have preferred a golden necklace to her husband’s safety” (Jerome, book I, *Against Jovinian*, near the end). See also, if you wish, the scholia on book XI of Homer’s *Odyssey*, v. 325, and Servius’s annotations on book VI of Virgil’s *Aeneid*, v. 44.

Then our author says: “Tiresias, though blind, saw future things, when he did not see present ones.” Earlier, Cicero, from whom Minucius appears to have drawn his material, expressly affirms: “The poets never represent Tiresias the augur, whom they portray as wise, lamenting his blindness” (Cicero, book V of the *Tusculan Disputations*, p. 194, line [Col. 0609D] 17). If by “poets” he includes the Greeks, he undoubtedly means chiefly Homer, their foremost poet, who sang of Tiresias’s blindness in *Odyssey* X, v. 492. In the commentary on this passage, two causes of his blindness are given. Ovid supplies a third: because Tiresias had rendered a judgment concerning the pleasure of women and men contrary to Juno’s opinion, she is said to have blinded him (Ovid, book III of the *Metamorphoses*, § 4, pp. 106 ff.). Others supply a fourth: because he had seen Minerva bathing. We have discussed him elsewhere (vol. I, *Apparatus*, book III, dissertation 2, ch. 20, art. 4, p. 1186). From this you will certainly understand by what right our Minucius ridicules a man who boasted that he foresaw future things, though he did not see present ones.

More serious, and no less true, is what he immediately added concerning Pyrrhus: “Ennius fabricated the responses of [Col. 0610A] Pythian Apollo, when Apollo had already ceased to compose verses.” These words were undoubtedly taken from the following passage of Cicero:

> Am I to consider Herodotus more truthful than Ennius? Was Herodotus any less able to fabricate concerning Croesus than Ennius concerning Pyrrhus? For who believes that this response came from Apollo’s oracle:
>
> **I say that you, descendant of Aeacus, can conquer the Romans [or: that the Romans can conquer you].**
>
> First, Apollo never spoke in Latin. Second, that lot was unknown to the Greeks. Furthermore, by the time of Pyrrhus Apollo had already ceased to compose verses. Finally, although, as Ennius says, “the race of the Aeacids was always foolish,” … Pyrrhus could nevertheless have understood the ambiguity of the verse, which could mean either “you can conquer the Romans” or “the Romans can conquer you,” and thus favored him no more than it favored the Romans…. [Col. 0610B] But the chief point is this: why are oracles no longer uttered in this manner at Delphi—not only in our own age, but already for a long time—so that nothing could now be more despised?

(Cicero, book II, *On Divination*, p. 296, line 21.)

You surely understand how greatly the argument drawn from pagan oracles in favor of their religion is weakened by Cicero himself. And certainly, besides the reasons he adduces, the cessation of oracles before the Orator’s age, and much more after it, as well as their ambiguity, manifestly demonstrates that nothing can be concluded from them in favor of pagan religion. Minucius therefore argued rightly from this against Caecilius and the other pagans, as did other very ancient writers of ours, as we have shown elsewhere. Consult also, if you wish, and read attentively, if you have leisure, what Eusebius reported concerning oracles and their ambiguity from the pagan writers themselves [Col. 0610C] (vol. I, *Apparatus*, p. 770; Eusebius, book V of the *Preparation for the Gospel*, chs. 18–19, pp. 208 ff.; book VI, ch. 1, pp. 256 ff.).

Permit us to add one point to these: what Minucius immediately said was also excerpted from that same Cicero: “Demosthenes, because he knew the responses were contrived, complained that the Pythia was φιλιππίζειν.” For in the Latin Orator we read the following recorded: “Indeed Demosthenes, who lived nearly three hundred years ago, said even then that the Pythia was φιλιππίζειν (*philippizein*, ‘taking Philip’s side’), that is, as though she were acting in concert with Philip. By this he meant that she had been corrupted by Philip” (Cicero, book II, *On Divination*, p. 296, line 38). What could be advanced that is clearer for explaining our author’s meaning or more forceful for refuting the pagans?

[Col. 0610D]

### ARTICLE III

#### Caecilius’s Argument Is Set Forth, by Which He Attempts to Prove That, Because Auspices and Auguries Were Disregarded by Sulpitius, Claudius, Junius, Flaminius, and Crassus, Roman Armies Were Slaughtered and Routed by the Avenging Gods, Who Therefore Existed

Caecilius presses on and, thinking that the argument drawn from auspices and auguries could evidently prove that the gods truly exist, endeavors to reinforce and establish it by various examples: “More frequently,” as he says, “than we wished, the presence of the gods has been attested when auspices were disregarded. Thus [Col. 0611A] the Allia became a name of ill omen.” Here he refers to the famous disaster at the Allia, in which the Roman army, commanded by the military tribune Sulpitius, was slaughtered and routed by the Gauls under their leader Brennus at the river Allia and the eleventh milestone, and the City was captured by them. For this reason they thereafter counted that day—although not all writers agree which day it was—among the unlucky, black, and ill-omened days. Cicero indeed wrote to Atticus: “Our ancestors held the day of the battle at the Allia to be more disastrous than the day on which the City was captured, because this latter evil arose from the former.” Anyone desiring more should consult Livy, first decade, book V, pp. 85 ff., and book VI, beginning, p. 92; Cornelius Tacitus, book XV of the *Annals*, p. 193, and book II of the *Histories*, ch. 230; Gellius, book V, ch. 17; Macrobius, book I of the *Saturnalia*, ch. 17; [Col. 0611B] Plutarch, vol. II, *Life of Camillus*, p. 137, and vol. II, *Roman Questions*, p. 269.

Caecilius next advances and presses other disastrous examples of auspices and auguries being scorned: “The battle of Claudius and Junius against the Carthaginians became instead a death-dealing shipwreck; and, so that Lake Trasimene might become greater and discolored with Roman blood, Flaminius spurned the auguries.” Cicero explains all these things somewhat more fully and clearly when he introduces Balbus the Stoic arguing for his gods in the same manner as Caecilius:

> Shall we be unmoved by the recklessness of P. Claudius in the First Punic War, who even ridiculed the gods in jest? When the chickens, released from their cage, would not feed, he ordered them to be plunged into the water so that, since they would not eat, they might drink. That jest, after his fleet was defeated, brought many tears upon him and a great disaster upon [Col. 0611C] the Roman people. What of his colleague Junius in the same war? Did he not lose his fleet in a storm because he had not obeyed the auspices? Accordingly, P. Claudius was condemned by the people; Junius took his own life. Caecilius writes that Gaius Flaminius, having neglected religion, fell at Trasimene, with a great wound to the commonwealth. From their destruction it can be understood that the commonwealth was enlarged under the commands of those who obeyed religious observances.

(Cicero, book II, *On the Nature of the Gods*, p. 214, line 43.)
