Surely, after hearing these words of Tullius, which encompass at once everything said by Caecilius, you will not wholly disagree with someone who suspects that Caecilius had them in view. Yet if you remain persuaded that he was looking to other passages of the same Cicero [Col. 0611D], where he again refers, though more briefly, to those three commanders, or where he separately and more fully relates the same things concerning Junius and Claudius, and elsewhere concerning Flaminius, we shall not altogether oppose you (same author, book II, *On Divination*, pp. 281 and 289, and book I, p. 268). Valerius Maximus also treats them, as Livy, Plutarch, Florus, and especially Ovid treat Flaminius; Ovid expressly sang on this subject:

> Let Flaminius and the shores of Trasimene be your witnesses  
> That the just gods give many warnings through birds.

(Ovid, book VI of the *Fasti*, p. 685.)

But we shall still have something to say about this history in the following dissertation.

Finally, Caecilius says: “And so that we might recover the standards from the Parthians, Crassus both incurred and [Col. 0612A] mocked the imprecations of the evil omens.” To grasp the meaning of these words, it should be observed that Suetonius handed down the following in his *Life of Octavian Augustus*: “The Parthians readily yielded Armenia when he claimed it, and, when he demanded back the military standards which they had taken from M. Crassus and M. Antonius, they returned them” (Suetonius, *Life of Octavian Augustus*, § 21). From these words it can be gathered that our author’s meaning is this: in order that Augustus might demand the military standards back from the Parthians, Crassus had lost them after disregarding the curses of the evil omens. Cicero had earlier recorded the same thing in fewer words: “We see what happened to M. Crassus when he disregarded the warning of the curses” (Cicero, book II, *On Divination*, p. 260, line 26). But Plutarch, *Life of Crassus*, vol. I, pp. 552 ff.; Dio Cassius, book XXXIX of the *Roman History*, pp. 121 ff.; [Col. 0612B] Florus, book IV, *Roman Deeds*, ch. 11; Eutropius, book VI of the *Roman History*, near the end; Velleius Paterculus, book II of the *History*, before the middle; and others describe this entire history at greater length. To them must be added Valerius Maximus, who concludes it, like Caecilius, with these words: “Thus the gods blaze with anger when scorned; thus human counsels are chastised when they prefer themselves to heavenly ones” (Valerius Maximus, book I, ch. [uncertain], § 11).

### ARTICLE IV

#### How Minucius Utterly Overthrows Caecilius’s Foregoing Argument by Other Examples—Those of Regulus, Mancinus, Paulus, and Julius Caesar—Including a Discussion of the *Tripudium Solistimum*

Before answering Caecilius’s foregoing argument, Minucius restates it as follows: “Claudius, Flaminius, and Junius therefore lost their armies because they did not think they should wait for the chickens’ [Col. 0612C] *tripudium solistimum*.” Anyone may learn what the *tripudium solistimum* was from Cicero, who rejects this kind of divination. The Orator speaks thus:

> The man who, from this very function, is called the *pullarius* brought the chickens in a cage. These, then, are the birds that carry messages between us and Jupiter. What difference does it make whether they feed or not? None at all for the auspices. But because, when they feed, something must fall from their mouths and strike the earth, this was first called *terripavium*, then *terripudium*, and is now called *tripudium*. Therefore, when a morsel falls from a chicken’s mouth, the *pullarius* announces the *tripudium solistimum* to the person taking the auspices.

(Cicero, book II, *On Divination*, p. 289, line 33.)

Some have therefore attempted in vain to correct *solistimum* to *solemnissimum* in our author’s text. [Col. 0612D] For that term properly signified what fell from the chicken’s mouth onto solid ground. Nor was it only there that Cicero said this; he had stated earlier:

> Our magistrates indeed employ compelled auspices, for when a morsel is thrown before a chicken while it feeds, a piece must fall from its mouth. What your books contain, however—that a *tripudium* occurs if something from it falls onto solid ground—this too, which I have called compelled, you call the *tripudium solistimum*.

(Ibid., p. 260, line 13.)

Brissonius has more on these matters, and you will doubtless not regret reading him (Brissonius, book I of the *Formulae*, p. 137).

After this, Minucius weakens and utterly destroys the examples advanced by Caecilius by setting against them examples directly to the contrary, which Cyprian, as was his custom, described in almost the same words (Cyprian, *On the Vanity of Idols*, p. 13). [Col. 0613A] By these he clearly demonstrates that whether auspices and auguries of this kind were observed or scorned and neglected, affairs turned out no less successfully or unsuccessfully for certain commanders. He therefore rightly argues from this that the presence of the gods cannot be demonstrated by them. First he says: “What of Regulus? Did he not observe the auguries and yet was captured?” We have already shown that M. Atilius Regulus was captured by the Carthaginians, whom he had defeated more than once, and put to death with the utmost cruelty. That he observed the auguries before this battle in the customary manner can be gathered from these words of Valerius Maximus, who openly declares that he does not know whether Regulus “surpassed everyone in matters pertaining to the observance of religion” (Valerius Maximus, book I, ch. 1, § 14). For this reason Augustine, together with our author, [Col. 0613B] concludes from it that Regulus taught by his example:

> That the gods are of no benefit to their worshippers for this temporal happiness, since he, though devoted to their worship, was both defeated and led away captive; and because he refused to act otherwise than he had sworn by them, he was tortured and killed by a new, previously unheard-of, and excessively horrible kind of punishment.

(Augustine, book I of *The City of God*, ch. 15, p. 15.)

Minucius sets forth a second example in Mancinus: “He,” as Minucius puts it, “observed religion, and yet was sent under the yoke and surrendered.” Yet the more certain it is that Mancinus, after his disastrous battles against the Numantines, was handed over into their power, the harder it is to say in what sense he is said to have observed religion. [Col. 0613C] For pagan writers testify quite clearly that he was afflicted by such great disasters precisely because he had undertaken the war despite the opposition and resistance of the auspices and of his gods. Listen, I ask you, to Titus Livy:

> While the consul Gaius Hostilius Mancinus was sacrificing, the chickens flew out of their cage; and when he was boarding the ship to depart for Spain, he happened to hear the words: “Stay, stay, Mancinus.” The outcome proved that these auspices had been ominous.

(Livy, epitome of book LV.)

Valerius Maximus relates these things somewhat more fully in the following words:

> The following prodigies happened to the consul Mancinus as he was about to depart for Spain. When he wished to perform a sacrifice at Lavinium, the chickens, released from their cage, fled into the nearest wood and, although sought with the utmost diligence, could not be found. When he boarded a ship at the harbor of Hercules, which he had reached on foot, [Col. 0613D] the following voice, though no speaker could be seen, reached his ears: “Mancinus, remain.” Terrified by it, he changed his route and made for Genoa; and when he had entered a skiff, a serpent of extraordinary size appeared and vanished from sight. Thus he matched the number of prodigies with the number of disasters: an unsuccessful battle, a disgraceful treaty, and a ruinous surrender.

(Valerius Maximus, book I, ch. 6, § 7.)

Thus, Valerius adds, he followed the headlong and mad persistence of Flaminius, whom we discussed shortly before.

How, then, did Mancinus observe religion when, “setting out against the Numantines,” as Aurelius Victor also reports, “though the birds forbade it and some mysterious voice called him back … he struck a treaty on the enemy’s terms, which the senate rejected, whereupon he was surrendered to the Numantines”? [Col. 0614A] (Aurelius Victor, *On Illustrious Men*, ch. 59.) For, as Paulus Orosius also testifies:

> The senate ordered that the treaty be annulled and Mancinus surrendered to the Numantines. His body was stripped, his hands bound behind his back, and he was exposed before the gates of Numantia. Remaining there until night, abandoned by his own people but not received by the enemy, he presented a pitiable spectacle to both.

(Orosius, book V of the *Histories*, ch. 4.)

Does not the example of so wretched a consul therefore favor Caecilius more, since from it he could have concluded that Mancinus was struck with such great calamities because he had scorned the gods’ auspices and religion?

[Col. 0614B] Yet Orosius warns us in the same place that Mancinus was one of those by whom, “so far as lay in them, the prodigies were dealt with according to custom” (ibid.), and yet he was deceived by the haruspices, those contrivers of frauds. Augustine therefore ridicules these very auguries and asks whether different chickens had marched against Numantia (Augustine, book III of *The City of God*, ch. 21, p. 80). Consider, then, whether Mancinus is said in this sense to have observed religion: because he had sacrificed according to custom and, deceived by the augurs, believed the auspices favorable to him.

More certain, therefore, is the example of Paulus next advanced by Minucius. He, as Minucius says, “had voracious chickens,” which therefore portended a successful outcome, “yet he was struck down together with the greater part of the commonwealth.” He is speaking of the battle of Cannae, which all writers of Roman history and others acknowledge was most disastrous both for Paulus and for the Romans, and which Livy declares equal in notoriety to the battle of the Allia [Col. 0614C] (Livy, book XXII, § 50). It is therefore unnecessary to produce several witnesses for a fact both certain and unknown to no one. But we should hear Cotta, who in Cicero argues from this that there is no providence of the gods: “For if,” he says, “they were caring for the human race, why did they destroy Paulus at Cannae? Why was the body of Regulus, of whom I spoke just now, delivered to the cruelty of the Carthaginians?” (Cicero, book III, *On the Nature of the Gods*, p. 252, line 7 ff.) Indeed, Cicero himself concludes from this that there are no divine auspices, since Paulus obeyed them and nevertheless fell together with his army in the battle of Cannae (same author, book II, *On Divination*, p. 289, line 24).

In the same manner he further confirms there what the author mentions last concerning Julius Caesar: that, [Col. 0614D] in defiance and contempt of auguries and auspices, he successfully sailed to Africa before midwinter and was victorious. For on this matter these are the orator’s very words: “What of Caesar himself? When he was warned by the chief haruspex not to cross over to Africa before midwinter, did he not cross? Had he not done so, all the enemy forces would have assembled in a single place” (Cicero, *ibid.*, p. 286, line 15 ff.). He then immediately added the following words, which are especially pertinent to our author’s purpose: “Why should I recount the responses of the haruspices—I could indeed cite countless examples—which either had no outcomes at all or had outcomes contrary to them?” Indeed, this entire book of Cicero, and another as well, would have to be transcribed if we wished to reproduce everything by which he demonstrates the vanity of auspices of this kind and of other forms of divination. [Col. 0615A] But because that would be too lengthy, we have thought it better to refer you to this book and, for the same reason, to Eusebius and Augustine, who similarly argue against them (Eusebius, *Praeparatio Evangelica*, book II, ch. 4 ff., ch. 13 ff.; Augustine, *De civitate Dei*, book IV, ch. 29, p. 109 ff.; and *De divinatione*, vol. VI, p. 505 ff.). From these works, and from what has been argued thus far, you will quickly and easily perceive how weak is the argument that Caecilius and other pagans derived from auguries and auspices in order to prove the presence of their gods.

## CHAPTER XX. AN EXAMINATION OF MINUCIUS’ GENERAL REPLY, IN WHICH HE DEMONSTRATES THAT THE MIRACLES, ORACLES, AUSPICES, AUGURIES, DREAMS, AND OTHER EXTRAORDINARY EVENTS THAT OCCURRED AMONG THE PAGANS PROCEEDED NOT FROM THE POWER OF THEIR GODS, BUT FROM THE DECEITS AND ILLUSIONS OF DEMONS

[Col. 0615B]

### ARTICLE I. What Minucius believed the nature of demons to be, and how correctly he said that they were known to poets, philosophers—especially Plato and Socrates—and also to the Magi, particularly Hostanes

The very arguments of Caecilius and the other pagans which Minucius had refuted individually—whether drawn from auspices and auguries, from oracles and predictions, from dreams, or from any other extraordinary effects, portents, and what they believed to be genuine miracles—he dissolves and utterly destroys by a general reply. Passing over very many events which, though they seemed altogether unusual, had nevertheless occurred by mere chance, he attacks the very source of the error and of the entire corruption or, as he himself says, undertakes to expose the fountain from which all the darkness flowed. [Col. 0615C] He accordingly teaches that the true authors of everything reported to have occurred among the pagans outside the customary order of things were not their gods, but evil demons. Whatever Minucius relates there, Cyprian, as we have often seen, transferred in his customary manner into his own book *On the Vanity of Idols* (Cyprian, *De idolorum vanitate*, p. 13 ff.). Lactantius also pursued the same argument at greater length and borrowed a number of things from our author (Lactantius, book II, ch. 14 ff., p. 216 ff.); just as Minucius himself seems, not without reason, to have taken his material from Tertullian (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 22 ff.). Nor are there lacking other Fathers of the Church, earlier still, who committed similar views to writing; we shall cite them below in the appropriate place.

To make what he had to say more readily intelligible to everyone, Minucius thought it necessary first to explain who the demons were and what their nature was. He determines the matter as follows: “They are,” he says, “impure, wandering spirits, weighed down from their heavenly vigor by earthly stains and desires. These spirits, therefore, burdened and submerged in vice, have lost the simplicity of their substance.” Does he not in these words distinguish the nature of good angels from that of evil angels, or demons? [Col. 0616A] Does he not appear to declare plainly enough that the former, who persevered in the holiness and grace in which they had been created, possessed a wholly simple and spiritual substance, entirely separate from every corporeal thing? For what simplicity other than the simplicity of holiness can the evil ones, who shared the same nature as the good, be said to have lost? He still calls them “spirits” after their sin, but spirits weighed down by earthly stains and desires. He offered no further teaching there about their nature, which we have discussed in the first volume of the *Apparatus* and in the dissertations that follow (vol. I of the *Apparatus*, pp. 491–535 ff. and 988 ff.). Nor did he explain more precisely what those earthly stains were through which they lost the original simplicity of their substance. No one, however, should find this surprising, since, for refuting the vain [Col. 0616B] arguments of the pagans, he thought it sufficient to indicate how subtle, agile, and tenuous the nature of demons is, and to confirm this not only through the testimony of philosophers and poets but also through that of the Magi, whom the pagans could not contradict.

Plato, Minucius says, “endeavors in the *Symposium* to describe the nature of demons. For he holds that it is a substance intermediate between the mortal and the immortal—that is, between body and spirit—compounded from a mixture of earthly weight and heavenly lightness.” And these indeed are Plato’s actual words in the cited *Symposium*: “You see that you have come to the conclusion that you do not consider Love to be a god at all. ‘What, then,’ I said, ‘is Love mortal?’ ‘By no means.’ ‘What, then, is he?’ ‘As we said earlier, something intermediate [Col. 0616C] between mortal and immortal.’ ‘What is he, then, Diotima?’ ‘A great demon, Socrates: Πᾶν γὰρ τὸ δαιμόνιον μεταξύ ἐστι θεοῦ τε καὶ θνητοῦ—for the entire nature of the demonic is intermediate between god and mortal’” (Plato, *Symposium*, vol. I, p. 202). From Augustine, moreover, we learn that demons are defined by Apuleius the Platonist as “living beings subject to passions in soul, rational in mind, aerial in body, and eternal in duration”—eternal, that is, after their creation, if Apuleius is there following the opinion of his teacher Plato (Augustine, *De civitate Dei*, book IX, ch. 8, p. 224).

Demons were no less familiar to Socrates, “who,” Minucius says, “at the nod and discretion of the demon attending him either declined or undertook affairs”; or, as Cyprian later said, “he proclaimed that he was instructed and governed according to the discretion of a demon” (Cyprian, *De idolorum vanitate*, pp. 13–14). Augustine, in turn, relates what Apuleius the Platonist wrote concerning him (Augustine, *De civitate Dei*, book VII, ch. 14, p. 202). But we have discussed elsewhere this companion and guardian—or, as Tertullian says, tutor—of so great a philosopher. Our author does not cite the other philosophers, doubtless because no pagan was ignorant of their opinion concerning demons and there was no substantial controversy requiring a fuller explanation (vol. I of the *Apparatus*, pp. 1113 and 1115).

The same must certainly be said of the poets, whom Minucius calls as witnesses with only these two words, “The poets know,” without identifying any of them by name. But the opinions of the poets, and also of the philosophers, concerning the nature of demons [Col. 0617A] have been treated in the preceding volume of the *Apparatus* and will be treated again in the dissertations that follow (*ibid.*, p. 991 ff.; *Dissertation on Lactantius*, ch. 20, art. 4; and *On Tertullian*, ch. 10, art. 3).

Finally, as our Minucius, Tertullian, and Lactantius say, demons were known to the Magi. Who, indeed, could have known them better than the Magi, who, as the writers we have cited testify, use the impious arts and illusions of those same demons to produce the effects by which they deceive the unwary and persuade them that they perform miracles? Indeed, if we believe Clement of Alexandria, those Magi openly boasted that they had demons as their ministers and servants, whom they had compelled by their incantations. See, if you please, what we have annotated on this passage of Clement [Col. 0617B] of Alexandria, as well as Eusebius, whom we cited there and who collected a great deal about demons from various writers. We shall discuss Lactantius and Tertullian in their proper place (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 22; Lactantius, *Institutiones*, book II, ch. 14, p. 216; Clement of Alexandria, *Admonition to the Pagans*, p. 39; vol. I of the *Apparatus*, p. 1239).

Our Minucius proves that the Magi knew demons by the authority of Ostanes, or Hostanes, their chief. These are his words: “Regarding them—that is, the demons—Hostanes, foremost among the Magi in teaching and practice” (the royal manuscript reads *Sostanes*), “both honors the true God with the majesty that is His due and knows that angels—that is, ministers and messengers of the true God—attend upon His worship, so that at the very nod and countenance [Col. 0617C] of their Lord they tremble in terror. He likewise disclosed that demons are earthly, wandering, and hostile to humanity.” Hostanes is therefore called the foremost of the Magi “in teaching,” that is, in doctrine or skill in teaching magic, “and in practice,” that is, in its exercise and arts. Pliny, however, wrote that this Ostanes, or Hostanes, while accompanying Xerxes in the Persian War, scattered the seeds of the magical art wherever he traveled, though some regarded Zoroaster and others Proconnesius as slightly earlier than he (Pliny, *Natural History*, book XXX, ch. 1, p. 726). Eusebius, moreover, presents verses of Apollo cited by Porphyry, in which Ostanes is called Μάγων ὄχ’ ἄριστος, “the greatest of the Magi.” Earlier, however, Eusebius himself had said that Ostanes wrote an eight-volume work in which he discussed God, as Minucius observes, and doubtless demons themselves, and whose teaching about the nature of things all the others followed (Eusebius, *Praeparatio Evangelica*, book V, ch. 14, p. 202; the same, book I, final chapter, p. 42). [Col. 0617D] And indeed Augustine cites these words of Cyprian concerning the same Hostanes: “The foremost of them”—that is, of the Magi—“Hostanes, both denies that the form of the true God can be seen and says that true angels attend His throne.” Cyprian, however, had undoubtedly borrowed these words from our Minucius, as was his custom. Laertius, Apuleius, and others likewise mention this same Hostanes, and elsewhere we have heard Tatian discussing him (Augustine, *De baptismo*, book VII, ch. 44, p. 185, vol. IX; Cyprian, *De idolorum vanitate*, p. 14; Laertius, Proem, § 1; Apuleius, *Apologia*, p. 100; vol. I of the *Apparatus*, p. 550). [Col. 0618A]

Thus far we have explained what our Minucius taught concerning the nature of demons, not so much from his own opinion, as it seems, as from the opinions of pagan philosophers, poets, and Magi. We must now examine how he shows from these considerations that the events reported to have occurred outside the order of nature were produced not by the works of the gods fabricated by the pagans, but by the illusions of those same demons.

### ARTICLE II. An exposition of Minucius’ arguments demonstrating why and how all things that seemed to have been accomplished beyond the customary powers of nature were produced by the arts and illusions of demons; with an extended discussion of dreams, various kinds of lots, and the frenzy of seers

[Col. 0618B]

We saw in the preceding article in what sense Minucius said that demons had lost “the simplicity of their substance,” or, as his gentler interpreter Lactantius puts it, “the dignity of their heavenly substance”—that is, the preeminence and excellence which they had, of course, defiled by their sins (Lactantius, *Institutiones*, book II, ch. 14, p. 216). Since, therefore, they deservedly suffer the punishments to which they were condemned, “for the consolation of their own calamity,” as our author says and as we shall explain below, “they, themselves ruined, do not cease to ruin” human beings, turning them away from the worship of the true God and hurling them into every kind of error and wickedness (*Dissertation on Lactantius*, ch. 20, art. 6). Cyprian said the same in almost identical words, [Col. 0618C] and both follow Tertullian; Lactantius and Prudentius likewise concur with them. Tatian preceded all of them, and you may read him, but above all Augustine, who treats these matters at greater length (Cyprian, *De idolorum vanitate*, p. 13; Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 22; Lactantius, *Institutiones*, book II, ch. 14, p. 218; Prudentius, hymn on St. Vincent, strophes 20–21; Tatian, *Oration against the Greeks*, p. 155; Augustine, *De civitate Dei*, book II, ch. 23 ff., p. 53 ff.).

Although demons lost the simplicity and dignity of their substance, they nevertheless remained “impure,” as Minucius puts it, “and wandering spirits”—words also used by Cyprian—but “tenuous”; or, as Lactantius says, “tenuous [Col. 0618D] and imperceptible spirits.” By their tenuity, subtlety, and agility “they disturb life,” our Minucius continues, and Cyprian after him; “they trouble sleep, and even secretly creep into bodies; they fabricate diseases, terrify minds, and contort limbs, so as to compel people to worship them,” so that they may be venerated and adored by human beings as true gods and may appear to have healed those whose health they had impaired. Lactantius taught the same in slightly different words. But all of them had Tertullian as their precursor and teacher; he had carried the torch before them with these words: “Their”—that is, the demons’—“own subtlety and tenuity enables them to penetrate both substances of the human being,” namely, body and soul. “Spiritual powers are capable of much, so that, invisible and imperceptible, they appear in their effect rather than in their action.” [Col. 0619A] (Cyprian, *De idolorum vanitate*, pp. 13–14; Lactantius, *Institutiones*, book II, ch. 14, p. 218; Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 22, p. 23.) Thus, by that invisible subtlety of their nature and powers, they appeared to perform miracles which were by no means miracles.

For unwary and credulous pagans “believe,” Lactantius says, “that they benefit them when they cease to harm them, although they can do nothing but harm” (Lactantius, *loc. cit.*, p. 219). For, as we just said, and as Tertullian, Tatian before him, and Eusebius afterward asserted, they injure human beings and afflict them with diseases; and when they cease to injure them, flying away from the sick and withdrawing their harmful operations, they are believed to have cured them. By similar devices and deceits they were also believed to produce other portents and miracles, which we discussed above (Tertullian, *loc. cit.*; Tatian, *Oration against the Greeks*, p. 157; Eusebius, *Praeparatio Evangelica*, book V, ch. 2, p. 181; above, ch. 19, art. 1 ff.).

[Col. 0619B] Moreover, “whatever marvels the Magi perform as tricks,” says Minucius, “they perform through demons; with the demons breathing upon and inspiring them, they produce illusions, making things that do not exist appear to exist, or things that do exist appear not to exist.” Was Lactantius not looking to this passage of Minucius when he wrote: “The whole art and power of the Magi depends upon the inspirations of these demons; when invoked, they deceive human sight by blinding it with illusions, so that people do not see the things that exist and think they see things that do not exist” (Lactantius, book II, ch. 14, p. 218)? Tertullian, however, had anticipated both in these words: [Col. 0619C] “The Magi perform many tricks through conjuring illusions . . . having at their disposal the attendant power of angels and demons once they have been summoned” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 23, p. 24). We have already heard Clement of Alexandria say that the Magi boasted of having demons as ministers of their impiety, whom they summoned with their incantations and compelled to attend upon them; and, as Lactantius further says, they called them forth by their own names—those, evidently, by which they are called in the sacred Scriptures. If you desire witnesses other than Christians, consult Eusebius: he will supply you with several, from whom he demonstrates that none other than demons were, from the beginning, the masters of the maleficent art (Lactantius, book cited, ch. 16, p. 223; Eusebius, *Praeparatio Evangelica*, book V, ch. 8, p. 193 ff.; *ibid.*, [Col. 0619D] ch. 10, p. 199).

From this it is now sufficiently evident with what vain and false display of eloquence Caecilius reproached the Christians: “In sleep we see, hear, and recognize the gods whom during the day we impiously deny, reject, and forswear.” Therefore Octavius, in the name of Minucius and the other Christians, and afterward Cyprian, reply simply that those who “trouble sleep” are not gods but demons; or, as Lactantius puts it, “they terrify souls through dreams”; and Tertullian before him, “they send dreams” (Cyprian, *De idolorum vanitate*, p. 13; Lactantius, *Institutiones*, book II, ch. 14, p. 219; Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 23, p. 24). Indeed, Cicero himself could not tolerate his fellow pagans prattling that dreams [Col. 0620A] were divinely inspired. “Many dreams,” he says, “have been related from histories: those of the mother of Phalaris, of Cyrus the Elder, of Dionysius’ mother, of the Carthaginian Hamilcar, of Hannibal, of Publius Decius. . . . But these are foreign examples and for that reason unknown to us; some of them, perhaps, are also fictitious.” After a lengthy discussion of dreams of every kind, he concludes that no god produces them and declares that divination derived from them should be utterly rejected together with all the rest (Cicero, *De divinatione*, book II, p. 299, line 25; *ibid.*, p. 301, line 10 ff.). Nothing, therefore, is more futile than Caecilius’ argument, by which he and other pagans dreamed that the presence of their gods could be proved from pagan dreams. For if there was anything extraordinary in the dreams they discuss, Minucius [Col. 0620B] and the other most ancient Fathers of the Church confidently assert that it must be attributed to the deceits and falsehoods of demons.

By the same deceits and illusions “they govern lots,” says Minucius, and Cyprian likewise (Cyprian, *De idolorum vanitate*, p. 13). But if someone asks us what these lots are, we shall answer him in Cicero’s own words. He teaches that lots “are almost the same as playing *micatio* [the finger-guessing game], casting knucklebones, or throwing dice. In these, rashness and chance prevail, not reason or judgment. The entire practice was invented through fraud, either for profit, superstition, or error” (Cicero, book cited, p. 291, line 17). What greater madness, then, than to babble that these lots are governed by some god who, if he is the true God, [Col. 0620C] could never either lie or deceive?

Do not, I beg you, set this same Cicero against himself because he had earlier said that a lot should not be despised “if it possesses the authority of antiquity, and if these are the lots which, as we have been told, were brought forth from the earth; when they are drawn, I believe it possible that they should prove appropriately relevant to the matter through divine agency” (*ibid.*, book I, p. 291, line 21). In the first book *On Divination*, he presents his brother as advancing these words. But in the second he refutes him and maintains that no trust should be placed in lots. If he believed that some were drawn by divine agency, he is convicted on this point of sharing the error of his fellow pagans, who ascribed to false gods what, as has been said, was produced by the deceptions of demons. On these and other kinds of lots you may consult Daniel Classen and Caesar Bulenger (Classen, *Theologia gentilis*, book I, ch. 5; Bulenger, *De sortibus*, etc.).

[Col. 0620D] There are, however, other kinds of lots “which,” as the same Cicero observes, “are delivered in prophecy and which we more properly call oracles” (Cicero, *loc. cit.*, p. 291, line 12). These seem above all to be those which demons, as Minucius openly asserts and Cyprian repeats word for word, inspire in seers; while lending their assistance to the taking of auspices, those demons “sometimes animate the fibers of entrails and govern the flights of birds,” and at last, through the ministry of those same seers, “they produce oracles enveloped in many falsehoods” (Cyprian, *De idolorum vanitate*, p. 14). Plato teaches that the entire art of divination proceeds from demons, whose nature is intermediate between God and mortal things. [Col. 0621A] For he says:

> θεὸς ἀνθρώπῳ οὐ μίγνυται, ἀλλὰ διὰ τούτου πᾶσά ἐστιν ἡ ὁμιλία καὶ διάλεκτος θεοῖς πρὸς ἀνθρώπους, καὶ ἐγρηγορόσι καὶ καθεύδουσι· καὶ ὁ μὲν περὶ τὰ τοιαῦτα σοφὸς δαιμόνιος ἀνήρ.

“God does not mingle with man; rather, through this demonic nature all intercourse and communication between gods and human beings is accomplished, both while we are awake and while we sleep. Whoever is skilled in such matters is called a *daimonios anēr*, a daemonic man” (Plato, *Symposium*, vol. III, p. 201 ff.).

Plutarch does not depart from this opinion, nor do other writers cited by Eusebius. Eusebius, however, rightly convicts them of error because they ascribe to good demons what is effected only by wicked and criminal ones (Eusebius, *Praeparatio Evangelica*, book V, ch. [Col. 0621B] 4, p. 184 ff.). Tertullian therefore rightly asserted that these things were done by the subtlety of their substance, through which in an instant they are present everywhere, know and report what is taking place, and “rival divinity by stealing divination” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 23, p. 23 ff.). What trust the pagans themselves placed in auspices you may learn from Cicero, who notes that “the Julian laws were passed contrary to the auspices.” Again, elsewhere he says: “While the consuls sat and looked on, a law was passed declaring the auspices invalid” (Cicero, Oration XXX, *On the Response of the Haruspices*, p. 437, line 27; and Oration XXXII, *For Publius Sestius*, p. 464, line 32).

The vanity of prophecies is also demonstrated most plainly by the seers themselves, “the frenzied seers,” says Minucius, “whom you see running out into public. The seers themselves rave in this fashion even outside [Col. 0621C] a temple; in this fashion they behave like Bacchants; in this fashion they whirl around. The demonic impulse is the same in them, though the manifestation of their frenzy differs.” Yet one critic was displeased by the three words in the royal manuscript, *ipsi absque templo* (“they themselves even outside a temple”), and wished them emended to *ipsi in ipso templo* (“they themselves in the temple itself”). But he needed to prove this by the authority of some manuscript. What, moreover, of the fact that Minucius is speaking about people who ran out into public and foretold destinies? Finally, seers driven by that frenzy—or pretending to be driven by it—prophesied even outside temples. For Apuleius, speaking of those who carried the Syrian goddess through towns and crossroads, says: “One of them behaves still more wildly like a Bacchant and, bringing forth frequent gasps from the depths of his breast, pretends to be afflicted with madness, as though filled by the divine spirit of the deity—quite as if [Col. 0621D] the presence of gods were accustomed not to make people better and more self-possessed, but to render them feeble and sick” (Apuleius, *Metamorphoses*, book VIII, p. 141). Why would he have pretended outside a temple to be driven by the divine spirit of a deity, unless the pagans believed that anyone, in any place, might be filled with that same spirit of frenzy? Virgil describes this prophetic frenzy, madness, and derangement in the following verses concerning the Sibyl:

> But not yet yielding to Phoebus, the monstrous prophetess  
> Rages like a Bacchant in the cave, striving to shake  
> The mighty god from her breast; all the more he exhausts  
> Her frenzied mouth, subduing her wild heart and shaping her by constraint.  
>   
> (Virgil, *Aeneid*, book VI, line 77 ff.)

Lucan writes:

[Col. 0622A]

> . . . Maddened, she rages like a Bacchant through the cavern,  
> Tossing her neck as though it were another’s; the god’s fillets and Phoebean wreaths,  
> Shaken loose from her upraised hair, she whirls through the temple’s empty spaces  
> With wavering head, scattering the tripods that impede  
> Her wandering course, and seething with a mighty fire.  
>   
> (Lucan, book V, line 166.)

It would undoubtedly be useless labor to accumulate further evidence here for a matter sufficiently certain and well known. Yet, if anyone does not find it burdensome, let him also hear a third poet, Statius:

> The holier seer begins; silence must be kept.  
> See, she whirls her neck and, over broad new spaces,  
> Rages like a Bacchant and fills the roadway.  
>   
> (Statius, *Thebaid*, book IV, *On the Life of Domitian*, line 80 ff.)

But if you inquire more closely from Cicero himself what this prophetic frenzy is, he will answer you not so much in his own name as in that of others whom he cites: “There is, therefore, in souls a power of foreknowledge implanted from without and enclosed within [Col. 0622B] by divine agency. If it blazes up more fiercely, it is called frenzy, when the soul, withdrawn from the body, is aroused by divine impulse” (Cicero, *De divinatione*, book I, p. 266, line 44). Nor does he suggest that only certain lowly seers were seized by this frenzy, but the more illustrious figures Bacchis, Boeotius, Epimenides of Crete, and the Erythraean Sibyl (the same, *ibid.*, p. 261, line 20). But there, like Apuleius just quoted and other pagans blinded by false prejudices, he ascribed to the presence and divine impulse of their gods what was effected solely by the illusions and arts of demons (preceding chapter, art. 4). Nevertheless, Cicero undoubtedly appears to have reported the opinion of others rather than his own. For in his two books *On Divination* he amply refutes this error, just as Eusebius and Augustine, whom we cited shortly above, demolish both it and the further error concerning pagan oracles in the same number of books. [Col. 0622C] We shall still have occasion to refute it in our subsequent dissertations (Eusebius, *Praeparatio Evangelica*, books IV and V; and *Demonstratio Evangelica*, § 5, p. 126; *Dissertation on Lactantius*, ch. 20, art. 7; ch. 32, art. 4; *On Tertullian’s Apologeticum*, ch. 8, art. 5 ff.).

### ARTICLE III. How clearly Minucius demonstrated that demons, adjured by Christians and expelled from possessed human bodies, openly declared themselves to have been the authors of the extraordinary effects found among the pagans; and a refutation of those who prattle that these phenomena and the seers’ oracles were produced solely by the devices and frauds of pagan priests

[Col. 0622D]

By another argument, and a wholly unanswerable one, Minucius further demonstrates that all the extraordinary events we have reviewed thus far, and all the predictions of seers, dreamers, and others practicing divination in any fashion whatsoever, proceeded from the deceits and illusions of demons. For he says: “Some of your own people know that the demons themselves confess all these things concerning themselves whenever they are driven from bodies by us, through the torments of our words and the fires of our prayer.” Surely everyone immediately sees the weight of this argument, which is elicited from the public testimony of the adversaries themselves, even against their will. For demons, tormented by the Christians’ words as though by the more grievous instruments of judicial interrogation, and tortured by their prayers as by a still fiercer fire, were compelled to depart from possessed bodies and openly to confess that they had been the authors of those unusual effects.

[Col. 0623A] Our Minucius explains as follows what those words and prayers of the Christians are: “For when adjured by the true and only God, they unwillingly and wretchedly shudder within the bodies, and either leap out at once or gradually disappear, according as the faith of the sufferer assists or the grace of the healer breathes upon him.” Cyprian presents this somewhat more fully, also borrowing some of Minucius’ words: “When adjured by us through the true God,” he says, “they immediately yield and confess and are compelled to depart from possessed bodies. You may see them, at our voice and by the operation of the hidden Majesty, beaten with scourges, scorched with fire, stretched out as their mounting punishment is prolonged, wailing, groaning, and imploring; [Col. 0623B] in the hearing even of those who worship them, they confess whence they came and when they will depart. They either leap out at once or gradually disappear, according as the faith of the sufferer assists or the grace of the healer breathes upon him” (Cyprian, *De idolorum vanitate*, p. 14). He repeats the same in other books and in other words; since these are readily available for everyone to read, we shall not transcribe them here (the same, *Ad Donatum*, p. 4; and *Ad Demetrianum*, p. 191).

Lactantius follows in the footsteps of both authors and says of these same demons: “They fear the righteous—that is, the worshipers of God. Adjured in His name, they depart from bodies; beaten by their words as though by scourges, they not only confess that they are demons but even disclose their names—the names worshiped in the temples. They generally do this in the presence of their own worshipers and certainly not to bring disgrace upon their religion, because they can lie neither to God, through whom they are adjured, nor to the righteous, by whose voice they are tormented” (Lactantius, *Institutiones*, book II, ch. 14, p. 218).

[Col. 0623C] Earlier, however, our Minucius himself had said: “Saturn himself, and Serapis, and Jupiter, and whatever demons you worship, overcome by pain, declare what they are; and they certainly do not lie to their own disgrace when some of you are present.” Tertullian presses the pagans far more vehemently and boldly challenges them to make any test of this matter they please; and unless the demons, when adjured by any Christian whatever, then openly confess who they are, he wishes and demands that the blood of that Christian be shed immediately and on the very spot (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 23, p. 24). [Col. 0623D] Do not imagine, I beg you, that this was an exaggeration by an African writer carried away by the excessively ardent force of his temperament, or that it occurred only by chance on some occasion or solely in his own time. For later Athanasius repeatedly and emphatically affirms that every magical art and all incantations vanish at the sign of Christ’s cross, and that all the deceits of demons are repelled. He attests that this was so firmly proved by experience that, no less boldly than Tertullian, he challenges the pagans to put it to the test. I should like you to hear his words:

> Ἡκέτω δὲ ὁ πεῖραν τῶν προλεχθέντων βουλόμενος λαβεῖν, καὶ ἐπ’ αὐτῆς τῆς φαντασίας τῶν δαιμόνων, καὶ τῆς τῶν μαντείων ἀπάτης, καὶ τῶν τῆς μαγείας θαυμάτων, χρησάσθω τῷ σημείῳ τοῦ γελωμένου παρ’ αὐτοῖς σταυροῦ, τὸν Χριστὸν ὀνομάσας [Col. 0624A] μόνον, καὶ ὄψεται πῶς δι’ αὐτοῦ δαίμονες μὲν φεύγουσι, μαντεῖα δὲ παύεται, μαγεία δὲ πᾶσα καὶ φαρμακεία κατήργηται.

“Let anyone who wishes to test what we have said come forward; in the very midst of the demons’ illusions, the deceit of oracles, and the wonders of magic, let him use the sign of the cross, which they ridicule, and merely name Christ. He will immediately see how swiftly demons flee through Him, oracles cease, and every art of magic and sorcery is brought to nothing” (Athanasius, *On the Incarnation of the Word*, pp. 73 and 88; *ibid.*, p. 89).

Minucius, Tertullian, and the others whom we have already praised consistently affirm that this is accomplished not only by the sign of Christ’s cross but also by the adjurations of Christians. Who, unless he wishes to blind himself, does not plainly see how certain this is, [Col. 0624B] and how often it occurred and was attested? It may be further confirmed by what our author and Cyprian add: “according as the faith of the sufferer assists or the grace of the healer breathes upon him”; that is, according as the faith of the person suffering from the demon is greater or less, or the grace of the Christian adjuring it is greater or less, the demon is expelled more quickly or somewhat later. But whether the demon was expelled immediately or after some brief delay, it was then certainly compelled to confess publicly who it was. Minucius therefore concludes his argument by addressing the pagans themselves as follows: “Believe their own testimony, when they confess concerning themselves that they are demons.” [Col. 0624C] Earlier Tertullian, arguing in like manner against the same pagans, had addressed them with these words: “Believe them”—the demons—“when they speak the truth about themselves, since you believe them when they lie. No one lies to his own disgrace, but rather to his own honor. Credence is more readily given to those who confess against themselves than to those who deny in their own defense” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 23, p. 23; *ibid.*, p. 25). So certain, manifest, and public was this confession of demons that Tertullian firmly affirms in the same place that it regularly made new Christians.

Who, then, will not marvel that certain Christians of our own age—even adherents of the Catholic faith—have gone so far as not to hesitate to assert in books published before the public that not merely some of the things we have reviewed, which we concede to them, but all such oracles, prodigies, portents, alleged miracles, and every mode of prophecy were never produced by any [Col. 0624D] demons, but solely by the deceits, arts, frauds, and illusions of priests and ministers serving idols? Nor are they restrained by the venerable authority of the most ancient and the other Fathers of the Church, by their testimony, which is by no means doubtful, or by the common consensus of them all (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book IX, ch. 11, p. 367). For once it had been posited as certain and established, they say, that numerous demons existed, those credulous and simple men readily persuaded themselves that those demons had been the authors of all these unusual effects.

What then? Were the most ancient Fathers of the Church and the other Christian writers throughout so many centuries so slow, dull, and blind that they could not perceive [Col. 0625A] that the oracles—and also the other things that seemed to occur beyond the ordinary order of nature—were produced not at all by demons but by the contrivances and deceptions of pagan priests? Was it then a greater labor to expose the frauds of pagan priests than to explain, in such elaborate discussions, what the nature of demons was; what philosophers, poets, magicians, and other pagans thought and taught about it; and what contrivances, deceits, arts, and impostures they employed to delude for so long even the more clear-sighted pagans, and indeed Christians who investigated these matters with the greatest diligence? But tell me, I beg you: with what effrontery did Tertullian, Athanasius, and other most learned men of every age dare challenge the pagans to make trial whether demons that uttered oracles, performed certain wonders, and possessed human bodies, [Col. 0625B] when adjured by Christians, would confess openly, either immediately or shortly afterward, who they themselves were or by what name they were called? But if pagan priests rather than demons fraudulently performed these things, why did they allow themselves to be adjured? Why did they not ridicule those who adjured them? Why did they not put them to shame by their silence alone? Why did they falsely claim to be called not by their own names but by those of demons? Why did they permit their emperors—Diocletian, whom we discuss elsewhere, and Julian the Apostate, whom we discuss below—to be terrified and driven away when their mysteries were disrupted? Finally, why did they utterly overthrow the worship of their gods and all their religions by this false declaration? (*Dissertat. in Luc. Caecil.* cap. 5, art. 2; *Dissert. in Lactant.* cap. 9, art. 2). Were not Christians then imitating their divine [Col. 0625C] Teacher, who, in expelling a demon from a man’s body, compelled it to declare its name (Mark 5:9; Luke 8:36)? Who would dare reply that this was a fraud perpetrated by some pagan priest, a fraud unknown even to Christ himself? There is no one who would not shudder to hear a Christian speak in this way. It was well done, therefore, by a most distinguished man of the Society of Jesus, who in a recently published book completely and utterly overthrew that absurd opinion—or rather, paradox. We ourselves have already refuted it in another dissertation, where we discussed the marvelous power of the sign of the Lord’s cross; and it will again be disproved by what must be said in our following dissertations (*Balth. Respons. ad Hist. Orac.*; *Dissert. in Luc. Caecil.* cap. 5, art. 2, p. 180 ff.; *Dissert. in Lactant.* cap. 9, art. 2; and [Col. 0625D] *in Tertullian.* cap. 11, art. 6).

# CHAPTER XXI. ON THE IMAGES AND STATUES OF THE GODS, BENEATH WHICH DEMONS WERE BELIEVED TO LURK AND PERFORM CERTAIN WONDERS, AND WHICH WERE IMPIOUSLY WORSHIPED BY THE PAGANS

## ARTICLE I. With what great impiety the pagans worshiped and adored the statues of their gods, beneath which demons dwelt, and sought and expected divine aid from them, although they had sometimes been fashioned by human hands from the filthiest vessel

The demons abused another device to deceive human beings. For beneath statues and images, Minucius says, they “lie hidden once consecrated”—or, in Cyprian’s wording, “they lie hidden beneath consecrated objects” (Cyprian, *De Idolorum Vanitate*, p. 14). [Col. 0626A] The sense of these two readings is plainly the same. For the pagans consecrated those images of their gods by a solemn dedication. If you wish a particularly authoritative witness to be produced, we shall cite Cicero. After discussing at length the ancient custom and rite of consecrating and dedicating temples, he relates that Quintus Marcius, while censor, had an image of Concord made and set up in public. When Gaius Cassius, also censor, transferred it into the senate house, he consulted the college of pontiffs as to whether there appeared to be any reason why he could not dedicate it. Marcus Aemilius, the chief pontiff, replied on behalf of the college that [Col. 0626B] “unless the Roman people had expressly appointed him to the task and he acted at their command, it did not appear that it could properly be dedicated” (Cicero, Oration XXIX, *Pro Domo Sua ad Pontifices*, p. 424 ff.). Thus the statue of any particular god was consecrated through various ceremonies, and in that way it became a god. For, as our Author argues: “When it is first born—behold, it is cast, fashioned, and carved—it is not yet a god. Behold, it is soldered, assembled, and erected—it is not yet a god. Behold, it is adorned, consecrated, and prayed to; only then, at last, is it a god, once a man has willed it and dedicated it.” Thus he mocks the blindness of the pagans, who foolishly believed that these statues, consecrated according to human discretion, either were their gods or were inhabited by them.

But demons, lurking beneath these images and statues with the exceedingly subtle nature we have described, [Col. 0626C] imparted their own names to them, as Athenagoras says; or, as Tertullian adds, by signs, miracles, and oracles—which we have of course shown to be false or deceitful—they “created belief in their divinity” (Athenagoras, *Legatio pro Christianis*, p. 29; Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, cap. 21, p. 23). Minucius first demonstrates how senseless this pagan error was from the origin of the statues themselves. Our forefathers, he says, being improvident and credulous, worshiped their kings and therefore desired “to see the deceased in images”; or, as Cyprian puts it: “Hence statues were fashioned to preserve through an image the features of the dead” (Cyprian, *De Idolorum Vanitate*, p. 11). Indeed, if we believe Lactantius, the demons themselves taught men to fashion images [Col. 0626D] and statues, and “caused representations of the faces of dead kings to be fashioned, adorned with exquisite beauty, set up, and consecrated” (MS R reads *ornatus*, “adorned”) (Lactantius, *Institutiones*, lib. II, cap. 16, p. 228; vol. I, *Apparatus*, pp. 432 and 736). But we have discussed this origin of statues elsewhere. What greater madness, then, could there be than to worship and adore the images and statues of dead men—very often criminals—or of wholly fictitious gods, as though they were true gods or their seat and dwelling place?

Nor was this unknown, at least to certain better-informed pagans, since Justin Martyr (Justin, *Cohortatio ad Gentes*, p. 18), Clement of Alexandria (Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata*, lib. V, p. 603), and [Col. 0627A] Eusebius (Eusebius, *Praeparatio Evangelica*, lib. XIII, p. 680), against that absurd opinion of almost all the pagans, cite these verses of Sophocles:

> Many of us mortals, wandering in heart,  
> Have established, as comfort amid sufferings,  
> Images of gods made from stones and wood,  
> Or figures wrought in gold or ivory;  
> And by preparing sacrifices and splendid festivals for them,  
> We think that in this way we are acting piously.

> Most of us, our minds deluded, have consecrated  
> Statues of gods, or consolations for misfortune,  
> Fashioned of stone and wood,  
> And then images of gold and ivory.  
> We appease these with victims and observe  
> Festive days for them, thinking ourselves pious in this way.

Thus, even if some more discerning pagans mocked these monstrosities of opinion, no one doubts that “the common people,” Minucius says, [Col. 0627B] “pray to their consecrated images and worship them publicly” as gods, believing that they also perform miracles and come to their aid.

But the pagans ought to have recognized so pernicious an error not only from the aforementioned origin of the statues, but also from the manner in which they were fashioned. For “if the god”—that is, the statue—“is wooden,” Minucius says, “it is perhaps a portion of a funeral pyre or an ill-omened log: it is hung up, cut, hewn, and sawn,” that is, cut with large saws—or rather, as others prefer, planed and polished. “If it is stone, it is cut, carved, and smoothed by an impure man. Finally, if it is bronze or silver, it is melted down and shaped upon anvils with hammers, ‘from a filthy vessel, [Col. 0627C] as was done more than once by an Egyptian king’”—namely, Amasis. Herodotus relates that he made an ἄγαλμα δαίμονος, “an image of a divine being,” or a “statue of a god,” from a golden basin into which he and his fellow banqueters customarily ἐνεμεῖν, καὶ ἐνουρεῖν, καὶ πόδας ἐναπονίζεσθαι, “vomited, urinated, and washed their feet.” Yet the Egyptians worshiped that statue with the highest veneration—or, as Herodotus says, μεγάλως σέβεσθαι, “held it in great reverence” (Herodotus, lib. II, §172). For this reason Justin Martyr sharply rebukes the pagans, who ἐξ ἀτίμων πολλάκις σκευῶν διὰ τέχνης, τὸ σχῆμα μόνον ἀλλάξαντες, καὶ μορφοποιήσαντες, θεοὺς ἐπονομάζουσι, “often take dishonorable vessels, change only their shape by art, give them form, and then call them gods” (Justin, *Apologia*, p. 57).

Nor could the pagans reply that statues of this sort were not gods until after their consecration and dedication, [Col. 0627D] which we discussed a little earlier. For what could be more insulting to divinity than that a god should be made from the most shameful and dishonorable vessel, and that the statue should have been fashioned by impure men—or, as Justin, just cited, says, ὅτι οἱ τούτων τεχνῖται ἀσελγεῖς, καὶ πᾶσαν κακίαν ἔχουσι, “because their craftsmen are licentious and possess every vice” (*Ibid.*)?

Moreover, by what means could these images and statues become gods, or the dwellings of gods, after consecration? What did that consecration contribute to their divinity? Why are they still gnawed and defiled afterward by spiders, swallows, kites, and other animals? Why do almighty Jupiter and the other gods [Col. 0628A] permit these things to be done to them with impunity? Why are human beings compelled to wipe, clean, and scrape them? If the pagans had not been utterly blinded, they ought to have learned from those birds and animals that these statues, as Clement of Alexandria also says, are devoid of every kind of sensation and are worshiped and adored only with the utmost impiety. But we have discussed these matters in our earlier dissertations on the books of the same Clement of Alexandria, and shall do so again in the following dissertations on Arnobius, Lactantius, and Tertullian. You may read still more in Philo the Jew, Athanasius, and Jerome (Clement of Alexandria, *Admonitio ad Gentes*, p. 34; vol. I, *Apparatus*, p. 736 ff.; Philo, *De Decalogo*, p. 753; *De Monarchia*, p. 813; *De Vita Contemplativa*, p. 890; Athanasius, *Contra Gentes*, §13, p. 13; Jerome, lib. XII, on Isaiah cap. 44 [Col. 0628B]). We shall therefore add nothing now, except that from this entire disputation of our Minucius against Caecilius and the pagans it may be gathered quite clearly that either Minucius himself or others, whenever they denied that Christians knew any statues, were speaking—as we observed above—of no statues other than those of false gods worshiped by the pagans.

## ARTICLE II. On the fashioned, anointed, and crowned statue of Serapis which Caecilius adored; on the pagans’ various rites for adoring statues; and whether that statue of Serapis was a boundary-stone image

One of the statues of the gods that we have discussed was undoubtedly that stone statue of Serapis, [Col. 0628C] fashioned, anointed, and crowned. Upon “noticing” it, as our Minucius says, Caecilius “put his hand to his mouth and pressed a kiss with his lips.” What was said in the preceding article about the consecration of statues will readily persuade anyone that the statue representing Serapis was anointed and crowned on the very day of its consecration and dedication. Indeed, ancient writers are reliable witnesses for us that statues of this kind were anointed. For after citing these words from Genesis concerning the patriarch Jacob, “He took the stone and poured oil upon its top,” Augustine wrote: “This pertains to prophecy; Jacob did not pour oil upon the stone according to the practice of idolatry, as though making it a god, for he neither adored that stone [Col. 0628D] nor sacrificed to it” (Genesis 28:18; Augustine, *De Civitate Dei*, lib. XVI, cap. 28, p. 449 ff.).

We likewise read in Clement of Alexandria: Οἱ αὐτοὶ δὲ οὗτοι πᾶν ξύλον, καὶ πάντα λίθον, τὸ δὴ λεγόμενον λιπαρὸν προσκυνοῦντες, “These very people worship every piece of wood and every stone that is, as they say, anointed” (Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata*, lib. VII [printed XVII], p. 713 D). Arnobius later speaks about himself in this manner, while he was still a pagan: “Whenever I caught sight of paintings, ribbons upon ancient trees, an anointed stone befouled with olive ointment, I flattered it, addressed it, and asked favors from it as though a present power dwelt within, although the piece of wood perceived nothing” (Arnobius, *Adversus Gentes*, lib. I, p. 22).

[Col. 0629A] What more is needed? Apuleius rebukes Aemilianus precisely because he possessed no consecrated grove and no anointed stone at all: “There is no shrine,” he says, “situated on his estate, no consecrated grove. And why do I speak of a grove and shrine? Those who have been there deny that they saw within his boundaries even one anointed stone or crowned branch” (Apuleius, *Apologia* I, p. 349). In another book he likewise committed to writing these words, no less relevant to our Author’s purpose: “Nothing could more properly impose a religious delay upon a traveler than an altar wreathed with flowers, a cave shaded with foliage, an oak laden with horns, a beech crowned with hides, or even a little hill consecrated by an enclosure, a trunk fashioned by carving, a turf moistened with a libation, [Col. 0629B] or a stone smeared with ointment” (the same, *Florida*, lib. I, beginning, p. 217).

We have already heard from the writers cited that statues of the gods of this kind were also crowned. Clement of Alexandria further confirms this by the authority of Sophocles and Sappho, adding in the same place: “Those who are instructed by the Word”—that is, Christians—“are kept from crowns . . . because a crown is dedicated to idols. Ἀλλ᾽ οὐδὲ τὴν εἰκόνα τοῦ θεοῦ τὴν ζῶσαν, δίκην εἰδώλων τῶν νεκρῶν, καταστεπτέον. But neither is the living image of God to be crowned after the manner of dead idols” (Clement of Alexandria, *Paedagogus*, lib. II, cap. 8, p. 181). Earlier Justin Martyr had written no less clearly: “Nor do we honor with numerous victims, καὶ πλοκαῖς ἀνθῶν, ‘and garlands of flowers,’ those objects which human beings fashion, place in temples, [Col. 0629C] and call gods, since we know that these are lifeless and dead statues, lacking the form of God” (Justin, *Apologia* II, p. 57 C). Hence Arnobius asks: “Are even the gods presented with wreaths, crowns, and flowers?” Lactantius, in turn: “They eagerly run to the temples of the gods, pour libations to them, sacrifice to them, and crown them” (Arnobius, *Adversus Gentes*, lib. VII, p. 237; Lactantius, *Institutiones*, lib. II, cap. 1, p. 138).

To these may again be added the pagan Apuleius, whom we hear saying: “I looked back at the central pillar supporting the stable’s beams; almost exactly in its middle was a statue of the goddess Epona, seated in a little shrine and carefully crowned with garlands of roses—and fresh ones at that.” Pliny adds: “Even at that time,” he says, “crowns were an honor paid to the gods, to public and private household gods, and to tombs and the spirits of the dead” (Apuleius, *Metamorphoses*, lib. III, shortly before the end; Pliny, *Natural History*, lib. XVI, cap. 4, p. 227). [Col. 0629D] Finally, to pass over Tertullian, who published a book *On the Crown*, and very many others, Ovid sang these verses about the god Terminus:

> Two landowners crown you from opposite sides,  
> And each brings you a wreath and each a gift.

(Ovid, *Fasti*, lib. II, §17.)

Such, therefore, was the statue of Serapis. Upon “noticing” it, as Minucius says, Caecilius “put his hand to his mouth and pressed a kiss with his lips”; that is, he venerated and adored it according to pagan custom. [Col. 0630A] But to make this clearer, it should be observed that this manner of adoring the gods varied. Some, when adoring the statues of their gods, kissed them, as Cicero expressly indicates in these words: “There is a temple of Hercules among the people of Agrigentum. . . . In it is a bronze statue of Hercules himself, and I should be hard pressed to say that I have seen anything more beautiful. . . . Indeed, judges, its mouth and chin are somewhat worn, because in their prayers and thanksgivings people customarily not only venerate it but also kiss it” (Cicero, *In Verrem*, lib. IV, p. 177, line 22 ff.). Others, however, kissed only their own right hand. For when Lucian discusses pagan sacrifices and victims, he records this about poor people: “But if someone is poor, he thus makes satisfaction to the god merely by kissing his own [Col. 0630B] right hand,” φιλήσας μόνον τὴν αὐτοῦ δεξιάν. In another book he says: “Then, after rising from bed in the morning, they worship the sun, οὐχ ὥσπερ ἡμεῖς τὴν χεῖρα κύσαντες, ἡγούμεθα ἐντελῆ ἡμῶν εἶναι τὴν εὐχήν, ‘not as we do, thinking that our prayer is complete once we have kissed our hand’” (Lucian, *De Sacrificiis*, p. 186; the same, *De Saltatione*, p. 505). For this reason Apuleius reproaches Aemilianus because “if he passes any shrine, he considers it wrong to bring his hand to his lips in adoration” (Apuleius, *Apologia* I, p. 349).

Elsewhere he explains in this way how they brought the hand to the mouth: “Many citizens and a great throng of visitors, whom the report of the extraordinary spectacle had assembled in eager crowds, were stupefied with admiration at her inaccessible beauty; [Col. 0630C] bringing their right hands to their mouths, with the forefinger resting upon the upright thumb, they venerated her with religious acts of adoration as though she were the goddess Venus herself” (the same, *Metamorphoses*, lib. IV, p. 67). Pliny says: “In adoration we bring the right hand to the lips and turn the entire body around; the people of Gaul believe it more religious to turn to the left” (Pliny, *Natural History*, lib. XXVIII, cap. 2, p. 564). Jerome too, commenting on these words of Hosea, “Sacrifice men, you who adore calves” (Jerome on Hosea 13:2), wrote: “Where we have translated ‘adoring,’ following Symmachus and Theodotion, Aquila rendered it καταφιλοῦντες, that is, ‘kissing.’ For those who adore customarily kiss their hand, something Job denies having done when he says: ‘If I saw the sun . . . if I kissed my hand, bringing it [Col. 0630D] to my mouth, and if this were reckoned to me as iniquity’” (Job 31:27; Jerome, *Adversus Rufinum*, lib. I, p. 371). You may read other passages entirely similar to these in Jerome and other interpreters of sacred Scripture commenting on the cited words of Job.

With these matters observed, we must investigate our Author’s meaning, concerning which there is no small dispute between two celebrated writers of our age, Lipsius and Salmasius. The former thinks that the words of Minucius cited by us are to be understood as follows: Caecilius first extended his hand toward the statue of Serapis and then kissed it as though it had been purified by contact with the statue. Salmasius, by contrast, contends that the same words of Minucius mean that Caecilius, [Col. 0631A] following pagan custom, first kissed his own hand and afterward extended it toward the statue he was adoring. More scholars incline toward the opinion and explanation of Lipsius. But what if Minucius’s words are said to indicate that Caecilius both brought his hand to his mouth and gave a kiss to the statue of Serapis? For the pagans customarily kissed the statues of their gods, as we saw in Cicero, cited a little above. Nevertheless, weigh each detail and adopt whichever opinion you judge more probable; as far as we are concerned, you will always be free to do so. Brissonius has written much about this custom of adoring statues; we have thought it better to refer you to him than to heap up further material upon a sufficiently familiar subject (Brissonius, *De Formulis*, lib. II, p. 840 ff.).

Finally, some take it as certain that the statue of Serapis mentioned by Minucius [Col. 0631B] was a boundary image—that is, one set up in place of the god Terminus. Could their opinion not be confirmed by these verses of Tibullus?

> For I show reverence, whether it be a solitary post in the fields  
> Or an ancient stone at the crossroads bearing flowery wreaths.

(Tibullus, lib. I, Elegy 1.)

Nevertheless, to confess the truth, they will not easily persuade us that this can be inferred with such certainty from our Author’s words. For he indicates there quite clearly that this statue was placed not in the fields but near the middle of the city of Ostia, in the part facing the seashore. Thus, even if there had been a crossroads there, Minucius nevertheless expressly called it not a statue of Terminus but one of Serapis. Let others judge these matters. We shall have another occasion [Col. 0631C] to discuss the god Terminus (*Dissert. in Lactant.*, cap. 32, art. 2).

# CHAPTER XXII. AN EXAMINATION OF MINUCIUS’S ARGUMENT THAT THE PAGAN GODS DO NOT EXIST, DRAWN FROM THE VERY RITES, MYSTERIES, AND FESTIVALS WHICH THE PAGANS CELEBRATED IN THEIR HONOR

## ARTICLE I. On the rites and mysteries of Isis, in which she was represented as searching with the Dog-Headed One for her lost son or husband and rejoicing when he was found; how ridiculous was the procession of these mysteries, transmitted from the Egyptians to the Romans; and how powerful an argument against the pagan gods may be drawn from it

Although the festivals [Col. 0631D] and mysteries celebrated by the pagans in honor of their gods ought to have made the true divinity of those gods manifest to everyone, Minucius demonstrates from these very observances that their divinity was utterly false and fictitious: “Consider,” he says, “the rites themselves and the mysteries themselves: you will find sorrowful ends, fates, funerals, mourning, and lamentations for wretched gods.” By what blindness, therefore, were the unfortunate pagans struck, that they should regard as gods, worship, and adore those whom every year they represented as more wretched than human beings themselves, depicting them as mourning and lamenting their own ends, fates, and funerals? You will perhaps marvel and will scarcely—indeed, hardly at all—allow yourself to be persuaded that the madness of the pagans, many of whom at least ought to have possessed sound minds, was so great that they seriously believed what [Col. 0632A] they customarily represented concerning their gods in the celebration of these mysteries. Nevertheless, our Minucius demonstrates this most clearly by various examples.

He begins as follows with the rites of Isis: “Isis, together with her Dog-Headed One and bald priests, mourns, laments, and searches for her lost son; and the wretched devotees of Isis beat their breasts and imitate the grief of the most unfortunate mother. Soon, when he is found, Isis rejoices, the priests exult, and the Dog-Headed finder glories. Every year they never cease either to lose what they find or to find what they lose.” Lactantius describes these rites in this way: “The Egyptian rites of Isis concern how she either lost or found her little son. First, the priests, their bodies shaved, beat their breasts and lament, just as she herself did when she lost him. [Col. 0632B] Then the boy is brought forward as though found, and that mourning is changed into joy. Hence Lucan:

> . . . Osiris, never sought enough.

For they always lose him and always find him. Thus the image of an event that truly occurred is reproduced in the rites, and this event—if we have any wisdom—plainly declares that she was a mortal woman and would have been nearly childless had she not recovered her only child” (Lactantius, lib. I, cap. 21, p. 117 ff.). But either Lactantius or a copyist erred there. For the verse cited by him is not Lucan’s but Ovid’s (*Metamorphoses*, lib. IX, fable 8), who sang of many things related by our Minucius and by the same Lactantius. But if Lactantius had wished to cite Lucan, he could certainly have brought forward these verses, which contribute not a little to his argument:

[Col. 0632C]

> Into Roman temples we received your Isis,  
> The demigod dogs, the sistra commanding grief,  
> And Osiris, whom by lamenting you attest to have been a man.

(Lucan, *Pharsalia*, lib. VIII, near the end.)

All these things may be confirmed not only by the testimony of Theophilus of Antioch and of Seneca as cited by Augustine, but also by Julius Firmicus, who briefly explains the same mysteries of Isis as follows: “This is the essence of the Isiac rite. In their inner sanctuaries they keep an idol of the buried Osiris; they mourn for it with annual lamentations and shave their heads. With the shame of a dishonored head they bewail the pitiable fate of their king; they beat their breasts, lacerate their upper arms, and reopen the scars of former wounds, so that through annual mourning the ruin of that deadly and pitiable slaughter may be born anew in their minds. After doing this for a fixed number of days, [Col. 0632D] they then pretend that they have found the remains of the mangled body, and when they have found them, they rejoice as though their mourning had been lulled to rest” (Theophilus, *Ad Autolycum*, lib. I, p. 75; Augustine, *De Civitate Dei*, lib. VI, cap. 10, p. 159; Julius Firmicus, *De Errore Profanarum Religionum*, beginning).

Do not these accounts agree perfectly both with the statements of our Minucius and with what we observed above about the body of Osiris, torn limb from limb and afterward recovered by Isis? But Minucius and Lactantius differ from others in calling Osiris the son of Isis, whereas others call him her brother and husband. Arnobius, however, does not hesitate to call him both husband and son, unless one should say that he distinguishes two persons in these words: “Under the Ethiopian suns, dark Isis mourns her lost son and [Col. 0633A] her husband torn limb from limb” (Arnobius, *Adversus Gentes*, lib. I, p. 20).

Did our Minucius and Lactantius therefore err, as we have already noted Lactantius’s further error in citing Ovid? Yet Diodorus Siculus, who related the killing of Osiris in the manner we reported, afterward wrote the following words concerning Isis and Horus, her son by Osiris—words subsequently copied by Eusebius: “She discovered the drug of immortality, by which she not only restored the soul of her son Horus—who had been overcome by the plots of the Titans, killed, and found in the water—and brought him back to life, but also made him a participant in immortality.” Herodotus and Plutarch likewise testify that Horus was the son of Osiris and Isis; Herodotus reports that he was called Apollo and Horus, while Plutarch says that he was surnamed Harpocrates. [Col. 0633B] Yet in the mysteries of Isis, as Tertullian relates, the pagans venerated Serapis, Isis, and Harpocrates together with their Dog-Headed One—whom Augustine also mentions—with plainly impious worship (Diodorus, *Bibliotheca*, lib. I, p. 15; Eusebius, *Praeparatio Evangelica*, lib. VII, cap. 1, p. 48; Herodotus, lib. II, §144; Plutarch, *De Iside et Osiride*, p. 356 ff.; Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, cap. 6, p. 7; Augustine, *De Civitate Dei*, lib. III, cap. 12, p. 66). These things certainly agree very well, as you see, with the statements of our Minucius and Lactantius. For not only were Horus and Harpocrates the same, but Serapis too—as Lactantius, cited a little above, and others observed—was Osiris himself, as we also noted elsewhere. Nevertheless, if anyone contends and properly proves that the Osiris sought and found by Isis in these rites was her brother [Col. 0633C] and husband, we by no means prevent him from retaining his opinion. But he must always remember not only that this history—or rather, fable—is utterly obscure and confused, but also that Minucius and Lactantius had several supporters and defenders of their opinion.

Far easier to prove are all the things which our Author openly declares to have been performed in the celebration of these impious mysteries: “Isis,” he says, “together with her Dog-Headed One”—that is, Anubis, whose image was carried publicly in procession—“and her bald priests, mourns, laments, and searches for her lost son.” Apuleius vividly described the utterly ridiculous procession of these ceremonies in the following words: “These men, their hair shaved completely away and [Col. 0633D] their crowns gleaming, the earthly stars of a great religion, produced a shrill din with bronze and silver—indeed, even golden—sistra. . . . That messenger between the gods above and below, Anubis, now with a black, now with a golden face, held his lofty dog’s neck erect, bearing a caduceus in his left hand and shaking a green palm branch in his right” (Apuleius, *Metamorphoses*, lib. XI [the printed citation reads II], p. 201). Hence Martial sang:

> The linen-clad and sistrum-bearing throng flees.

(Martial, lib. XII, Epigram 29.)

Juvenal is still more explicit:

> Thus he deserves the foremost and highest honor,  
> Who, surrounded by a linen-clad and a bald-headed troop,  
> Runs along—Anubis, mocking the lamenting populace.

(Juvenal, Satire VI, near the end.)

[Col. 0634A] Finally, Ambrose wrote to Sabinus: “They shave their own heads and eyebrows whenever they undertake the rites of Isis” (Ambrose, Epistle LVIII to Sabinus, p. 1013). See, if you wish, what we have noted on this passage, as well as Jerome, Prudentius, and others (Jerome on Ezekiel cap. 44; Prudentius, *Contra Symmachum*, lib. II).

It is no less certain that the devotees of Isis, as our Author says, beat their breasts during these festivals and imitated the grief of the most unfortunate mother. For in addition to Lactantius and Julius Firmicus, whom we have cited, Herodotus, when discussing those who celebrated the festival of Isis, says: “After the sacrifice, all the men and women—πάντες καὶ πᾶσαι—many thousands of human beings, beat themselves,” τύπτονται. “With what they beat themselves I am not permitted to say; [Col. 0634B] but of them all the Carians who inhabit Egypt do this most conspicuously, to such an extent that they also slash their foreheads with knives,” τὰ μέτωπα κόπτονται μαχαίρῃσι (Herodotus, lib. II, §61). You will find these words of Herodotus reproduced by Athenagoras, who concludes from them that the gods who are represented in their rites as being beaten in so bloody a manner are not immortal (Athenagoras, *Legatio pro Christianis*, p. 32; *ibid.*, p. 14). For what could be more absurd than that the pagans, as he had said a little earlier, should mourn their gods and cruelly beat their breasts on account of them as though they were dead, yet at the same time sacrifice to them as immortal gods? But Dionysius of Halicarnassus and others whom we shall presently cite say more about these ridiculous pagan rites (Dionysius of Halicarnassus, *Roman Antiquities*, lib. II, p. 91).

[Col. 0634C] Minucius continues: “Yet these were once Egyptian rites and mysteries.” Quite correctly, as is evident from Herodotus, Athenagoras, and the others just cited. “Now,” Minucius continues, “they are also Roman rites.” We have already seen this transmitted and asserted in the verses of Lucan cited a little earlier. Suetonius likewise bears witness that Otho, emperor of the Romans, often celebrated the rites of Isis openly in linen religious garb (Suetonius, lib. VII, §12). Commodus, likewise emperor of the Romans, according to Lampridius, “observed the rites of Isis, even to the point of shaving his head and carrying Anubis. . . . He compelled the devotees of Isis to beat their breasts with pine cones almost to the point of death. When he carried Anubis, he struck the devotees of Isis violently on the head with the face of the image.” Lampridius later repeats and confirms this further [Col. 0634D] (Lampridius, pp. 313 and 327).

To this may be added what Valerius Maximus handed down to posterity: that the shrines of Isis were demolished and destroyed by the consul Lucius Aemilius Paulus at the command of the Roman senate. “When the senate had decreed,” he says, “that the shrines of Isis and Serapis were to be demolished, and none of the workmen dared touch them, the consul Lucius Aemilius Paulus laid aside his bordered toga, seized an axe, and struck it against the doors of the temple” (Valerius Maximus, lib. I, cap. 3, final section). Tertullian too, as we shall see in the proper place, recorded that the altars of Isis were destroyed by the Romans and her rites abolished and afterward restored (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, cap. 6, p. 9; and *Ad Nationes*, lib. II, cap. 10, p. 54).

Minucius therefore rightly concludes from these things: “Is it not ridiculous [Col. 0635A] to mourn what you worship, or to worship what you mourn?” In precisely the same way Plutarch, although a pagan, refutes Xenophanes of Colophon and his followers: “The absurdity of the matter,” he says, “was apparent not only to Xenophanes of Colophon and those who followed him, who admonished the Egyptians, Εἰ θεοὺς νομίζουσι μὴ θρηνεῖν, εἰ δὲ θρηνοῦσι, θεοὺς μὴ νομίζειν: either not to mourn those whom they considered gods, or not to regard as gods those whom they believed should be mourned” (Plutarch, *De Iside et Osiride* [printed *Ostride*], p. 379).
