Heraclitus too, according to Clement of Alexandria and afterward Epiphanius, objected to those same Egyptians: “If you regard them as gods, do not mourn or lament them; but if you mourn them, do not suppose that they are gods” (Clement of Alexandria, *Admonitio ad Gentes*, p. 15; Epiphanius, *Ancoratus*, §106, p. 106). [Col. 0635B] Finally, to pass over other pagan and Christian authors, Athanasius and Julius Firmicus reject and hiss down these abominable mysteries by precisely the same reasoning and conclude that in them the pagans worship false gods (Athanasius, *Oratio contra Gentes*, §10, p. 11; Julius Firmicus, *De Errore Profanarum Religionum*, p. 21).

## ARTICLE II. On the Eleusinian mysteries and the festival celebrated in memory of Ceres searching for her daughter Proserpina, who had been abducted by Pluto; on the rites of Jupiter and also those of Cybele Dindymene—or Ceres, or Rhea, or the Mother of the Gods—and of the castrated Attis, which were performed by the Galli, that is, by emasculated men
The Eleusinian rites were similar to the rites of Isis. Each year the pagans customarily celebrated them in honor—or rather to the dishonor—of Ceres [Col. 0635C] as she searched for her daughter Proserpina, or Libera, who had been abducted by Pluto. Minucius, in few words indeed, but words sufficient for the purpose, demonstrates the ridiculous impiety of these mysteries: “Ceres,” he says, “with torches kindled and encircled by a serpent, anxiously and solicitously tracks down Libera, who was treacherously abducted and violated.” Cicero, however, explained this more distinctly in his fourth speech against Verres, in these words:

“This,” he says, “is the belief established by the most ancient writings and monuments of the Greeks: that the whole island of Sicily is consecrated to Ceres and Libera. While other nations hold this opinion, the Sicilians themselves are so thoroughly persuaded of it that the belief appears implanted and innate in their minds. For they believe both that these goddesses were born [Col. 0635D] in these regions, and that grain was first discovered in that land; and that Libera, whom they also call Proserpina, was abducted from the grove of Henna, a place situated in the middle of the island and called the navel of Sicily. When Ceres wished to track her down and search for her, she is said to have kindled torches with the fires that burst from the summit of Etna; bearing these before her, she traversed the whole circuit of the earth. . . . For nearby is a certain cave, facing north and of immeasurable depth, from which they say that Father Dis”—that is, Pluto—“suddenly emerged in his chariot, carried the abducted maiden away with him from that place, and suddenly, not far from Syracuse, plunged beneath the earth; and that a lake suddenly appeared in that [Col. 0636A] place, where down to the present day the Syracusans celebrate annual festivals with a most numerous gathering of men and women” (Cicero, *Fourth Speech against Verres*, p. 179 ff.).

These things are certainly in complete agreement with what Diodorus Siculus relates about the same matter. In confirmation of his account he cites the following Greek verses by the poet Corcinus:

> They say that once Pluto, by secret schemes,  
> Abducted Demeter’s maiden, whose name must not be spoken,  
> And sank into the earth’s dark-shining depths.  
> The mother, yearning for her vanished daughter,  
> Went searching throughout the whole encircling earth.  
> And all Sicily, with its crags of Etna,  
> Filled with streams of fire and hard to approach, groaned aloud;  
> And while the maiden was being mourned,  
> The race nourished by Zeus, bereft of grain, wasted away.  
> Hence even now they continue to honor the goddesses.

[Col. 0636B]

> They say that once the daughter of nurturing Ceres,  
> Abducted by the treacherous devices of Dis,  
> Entered the blackening caverns of the earth;  
> And that her mother, anxiously seeking the lost girl,  
> Wandered around the whole circuit of the world.  
> Then all Trinacria beneath Etna’s hills,  
> Bristling with fire and hurling flaming masses,  
> Groaned; and while the maiden was mourned,  
> The race fostered by Jove, deprived of sustenance, wasted away.  
> Hence it is that they still zealously worship the goddesses.

(Diodorus Siculus, beginning of Book V of the *Library*, p. 201 ff.)

Ovid, however, describes these events more fully, though still in compressed language. For the present we shall transcribe only two of the verses in which he sings that Ceres, when she reached Mount Etna, kindled the aforementioned torches:

> There she kindled twin pine-trees in place of a lamp;  
> Hence even now a torch is used in Ceres’ rites.

(Ovid, Book IV of the *Fasti*, § 6.)

[Col. 0636C] Statius too wrote these two verses to Julius Menecrates in his *Silvae*:

> And you, Actaean Ceres, for whom, in breathless course,  
> We silent initiates shake the votive torch.

(Statius, Book IV of the *Silvae*, penultimate poem.)

In addition, Claudian celebrated the abduction of Proserpina in three books, and at the very beginning of the first book he mentions those torches and serpents as follows:

> . . . Now from the depths  
> Of earth a mighty din is heard; the temple  
> Of the Cecropids bellows, and Eleusis raises her sacred torches.  
> Triptolemus’ serpents hiss; their scaly necks,  
> Bound beneath curved yokes, they lift, and gliding serenely,  
> Rear upright and stretch their rosy crests toward the chants.

(Claudian, Book I, *On the Abduction of Proserpina*.)

Lactantius also spoke of these mysteries of Ceres and their festival days; [Col. 0636D] we too have treated them elsewhere and cited numerous authors whom you may consult and read, and who have expressly discussed them (Lactantius, Book I of the *Divine Institutes*, ch. 21, p. 119; vol. I of the *Apparatus*, Book III, dissertation 1, ch. 9, art. 2, p. 758; and *Notes on Book I of Ambrose, On Virgins*, ch. 4, § 16).

Our author continues: “And what,” he asks, “are the rites of Jove? A she-goat is his nurse, and the infant is snatched away from his ravenous father lest he be devoured; and the clashing of the Corybants’ cymbals drowns out his wailing, so that his father may not hear it.” But the tales told about Jove and the pagans, and about his festival days, have been sufficiently explained by us above (above, ch. 14, art. 3), and also by the Ovid just cited [Col. 0637A] (Ovid, Book V of the *Fasti*, p. 617 ff.). We therefore merely observed that these were the rites not only of Jove, but also of his mother Rhea; they are clearly described by the same Ovid and by Lactantius, as we shall see in the appropriate place (Ovid, Book IV of the *Fasti*, p. 172 f.; Lactantius, Book I, ch. 21, p. 123).

Minucius finally comes to the rites of Dindymenian Cybele:

“But I am ashamed,” he says, “to tell it. Since she herself, an ugly old woman and the mother of many gods, could not entice to debauchery her adulterer, who had unfortunately caught her fancy, she castrated him, evidently so as to make the god a eunuch. Because of this tale, the *Galli* and half-men worship her by inflicting punishment upon their own bodies.”

Although, as our author rightly says, Diodorus Siculus, Pausanias, and Servius relate this tale in one way, while Ovid [Col. 0637B] and Arnobius, as we shall show below, relate it in another—and although it did not appear altogether true to Lucian—Lucian nevertheless presents the account he considers more probable in this manner:

“Attes was Lydian by birth. He was the first to transmit the rites by which Rhea was worshiped; and all the practices used by the Phrygians, Lydians, and Samothracians in their sacred rites they received from Attes. For after Rhea castrated him, he ceased to live as a man, assumed a woman’s form, and put on women’s clothing. . . . He also said concerning the *Galli* in the temple that the *Galli* are not castrated for Juno at all, but for Rhea, and that they imitate Attes.”

He then explains how *Galli* were made and how their male organs were amputated (Diodorus, Book III of the *Library*, p. 134; [Col. 0637C] Pausanias, Book VII, *Arcadica*, p. 223; Servius on Virgil, *Aeneid* IX.135; Ovid, Book IV of the *Fasti*, § 3; Arnobius, *Against the Pagans*, p. 157 f.; *Dissertation on Arnobius*, ch. 26, art. 1; Lucian, *On the Syrian Goddess*, p. 1501 ff.; idem, p. 1075). What you have heard from these passages, and what Lucian relates elsewhere, fully confirms and illustrates the narrative of our Minucius.

Furthermore—to pass over Lactantius, Prudentius, and very many others—Augustine testifies that these mysteries were celebrated at Carthage “down to yesterday,” as he says, that is, down to his own time; and he committed to writing about them precisely the same account as our author:

“They are,” he says, “the rites of the Mother of the Gods, in which the misfortune of the handsome youth Atys, beloved by her and mutilated through female jealousy, is lamented by mutilated men [Col. 0637D] whom they call *Galli*” (Lactantius, Book I, ch. 21; Prudentius, hymn on St. Romanus, near the end; Augustine, Book VI of *The City of God*, ch. 26, p. 154).

He further adds that these horrid rites, fouler than every theatrical obscenity, were observed by the Romans themselves as well (ibid., p. 182). Tatian had therefore earlier reproached the pagans for this:

“They say,” he declared, “that Rhea, whom in the Phrygian mountains they call Cybele, instituted the castration of boys because of Atys, the boy whom she loved” (Tatian, *Oration against the Greeks*, p. 147).

Jerome speaks no less explicitly—indeed, still more clearly—about these same matters and, like Minucius, about the Romans who continued in his own time to celebrate these most shameful mysteries of Cybele:

“These [Col. 0638A] are the men whom today at Rome they call *Galli*, serving the Mother not of gods but of demons, because the Romans had appointed men of that nation, deprived of sexual capacity, as her priests in honor of Atys, whom the prostitute goddess had made a eunuch. Men of the Gallic nation are therefore emasculated so that those who captured the city of Rome may be branded with this disgrace” (Jerome, on Hosea 4:2).

Jerome, however, is criticized by others for having believed that these castrated priests of the Mother of the Gods, or Cybele, were Gauls by nationality. Some consider it more probable that the name *Galli* was given to them after a man named Gallus who, as Stephanus says, was perhaps the first priest of Cybele. Others think that they were so named after the Gallus, a river of Phrygia that flows from the mountains of Celaenae into the Sangarius. [Col. 0638B] This is the opinion not only of Herodian (Herodian, Book I, p. 476), but also of Ovid, who expresses it in these verses:

> Why, then, do we call those who castrate themselves *Galli*,  
> When the land of Gaul lies so far from Phrygia?  
> Between green Cybele and lofty Celaenae, he says,  
> Flows a river named Gallus, whose water drives men mad.  
> Whoever drinks from it goes mad: depart far from here,  
> All who care to preserve a sound mind; whoever drinks from it goes mad.

(Ovid, Book IV of the *Fasti*, § 3.)

Pliny mentions that river; you may consult him, as well as Vossius and Lilius Giraldus, who discuss that tale of Cybele and Atys, their mysteries, and those *Galli*. We too have discussed these matters elsewhere, especially the founder of those mysteries (Pliny, Book XXXI of the *Natural History*, ch. 2, p. 779; Vossius, Book I, *On the Origin and Progress of Idolatry*, [Col. 0638C] ch. 20, p. 78 ff.; Giraldus, *Syntagma IV of the History of the Gods*; vol. I of the *Apparatus*, Book III, dissertation II, ch. 9, art. 2, p. 758 ff.).

Moreover, although Isis, Ceres, Cybele, Rhea, Dindymene, and the Mother of the Gods were said to be the same deity, as we have already noted, and although she was called by still other names, as Plutarch and Strabo observe, nevertheless it is established that the rites and festivals celebrated in memory of Ceres searching for Proserpina were different from those jointly commemorating Cybele and Atys (Plutarch, *Life of Caesar*, p. 111; Strabo, Book X of the *Geography*, p. 169). But whatever their nature, they demonstrate with the utmost clarity both the falsity of these figures’ divinity and the lamentable blindness and madness of the pagans who worshiped them.

## ARTICLE III  
### On Other Superstitious and Absurd Rites of the Pagans, in Which Many Made Libations with Their Own Blood and Punished Themselves with Wounds and the Amputation of Their Genitals; on Their Leading the Gods Begging from Street to Street; on the Luperci Running Naked in the Bitter Winter, Striking Those They Met and Beating Skins; and on the Salii Wearing Caps and Carrying Ancient Shields About

[Col. 0638D]

We think there is no one who, from what has thus far been discussed, cannot readily understand Minucius’ meaning when he attacks the thoroughly absurd and superstitious rites of the Romans who worshiped false gods, and deservedly rebukes every such man:

“He who makes a libation with his own blood [Col. 0639A] and supplicates by means of his own wounds . . . or whose indecent organs have been cut away—how grievously does he dishonor the god whom he propitiates in this manner, since, if God desired eunuchs, he could create them as such rather than make them so?”

For is Minucius not there discussing the mad priests of Cybele, as we were just saying, and also those of Bellona, as we likewise noted earlier (above, ch. 9, art. 2)? Juvenal certainly sang of both:

> . . . See, the chorus enters  
> Of raging Bellona and the Mother of the Gods, and a huge  
> Half-man, a face revered by his obscene inferior;  
> Long ago he cut away his tender genitals  
> With a broken potsherd. For him the hoarse troop and common  
> Drums beat, and his cheek is covered by a Phrygian tiara.

(Juvenal, *Satires* V, around the middle.)

Did not Athenagoras also speak about the same people—though [Col. 0639B] as obscurely about the latter as he did clearly about the former?

> Οἱ μὲν ἀποτέμνουσι τὰ αἰδοῖα, οἱ περὶ τὴν Ῥέαν . . . ἐῶ γὰρ τοὺς ταῖς μαχαίραις, καὶ τοῖς ἀστραγάλοις αἰκιζομένους αὐτοὺς λέγειν.
>
> “Some cut off their private parts—those associated with Rhea. . . . For I leave unmentioned those who torture themselves with knives and knotted scourges.”

(Athenagoras, *Embassy for the Christians*, p. 29.)

But what he said in prose, Martial expressed in verse:

> White arms are less savaged by cruel knives  
> When the inspired troop rages to Phrygian rhythms.

(Martial, Book II, epigram 85.)

Seneca writes of the initiates of the Mother of the Gods:

> Not even if, imitating effeminate men,  
> She should tear her arms with you in sorrow—  
> She whom the troop of the turret-crowned Mother,  
> Roused with hoarse breast, accompanies, beating the boxwood pipe  
> [Col. 0639C] To mourn Phrygian Atys.

(Seneca, *Agamemnon*, act III, scene 2.)

Juvenal harmonizes with both in these two lines:

> Yet what are they waiting for, whose time had already come  
> To sever their superfluous flesh with knives in the Phrygian manner?

(Juvenal, *Satires* II, near the end.)

Lucian too writes:

> Τὴν κεφαλὴν κάτωθεν ἐξ αὐχένος ἐλίσσοντες, τοῖς ξίφεσιν ἔτεμνον τοὺς πήχεις, καὶ τὴν γλῶτταν τῶν ὀδόντων ὑπερβάλλων ἕκαστος, ἔτεμνε καὶ ταύτην· ὥστε ἐν ἀκαρεῖ πάντα πεπλῆσθαι μαλακοῦ αἵματος.
>
> “Twisting their heads from beneath the neck, they slashed their arms with swords; and each man, thrusting his tongue beyond his teeth, cut that as well, so that in an instant everything was drenched with flowing blood.”

(Lucian, *Lucius, or the Ass*, p. 660.)

Apuleius calls the blade with which each cut his own arms [Col. 0639D] double-edged; and, as Tertullian says, these *Galli* and their chief, the *archigallus*, offered impure blood by mutilating their arms. Hence Seneca, as quoted by Augustine, assails the gods of his pagan countrymen on this ground:

“One man amputates his male parts, another cuts his arms. When do they fear the gods as angry, if this is how they earn their favor? The gods ought not to be worshiped in any manner at all, if they desire even this.”

(Apuleius, Book VIII of the *Metamorphoses*, near the end, p. 141; Tertullian, *Apology*, chs. 23 and 25, pp. 24 and 27; Augustine, Book VII of *The City of God*, ch. 10, p. 159.)

Minucius therefore rightly argues in the same manner concerning these men and perhaps also those consecrated to Bellona.

But the blind pagans added another insult to their gods, since, as Minucius [Col. 0640A] continues, “they lead the gods begging from street to street”—that is, the image of Cybele, or the Mother of the Gods. At such times, in utterly shameful mendicancy, they collected every sort of gold and silver coin, says Apuleius (*loc. cit.*), or ὀβολοὺς καὶ δραγμάς, “obols and drachmas,” as Lucian says, together with whatever each person lavishly bestowed upon them (Lucian, *loc. cit.*). In a single word Dionysius of Halicarnassus calls them μητραγυρτοῦντες, “beggars for the Mother” (Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Book II of *Roman Antiquities*, p. 91); others, as we have seen elsewhere, call them μητραγύρται, “collectors of alms for the Mother of the Gods.” Hence Tertullian, as we shall see in the appropriate place, calls it a “begging religion” that went around the taverns (vol. I of the *Apparatus*, p. 784). Who would not marvel that this most sordid custom was confirmed by the pagans’ most sacred laws? [Col. 0640B] Cicero nevertheless presents this law among others pertaining to the worship of the gods: “Except for the attendants of the Idaean Mother, and only on the lawful days, let no one collect alms.” For that very reason they did not dare to abolish this ridiculous custom (Cicero, Book II of *On the Laws*, p. 335, line 14). A little later the same Cicero says: “We have abolished the collection of alms, excepting that which is peculiar to the Idaean Mother for a few days” (ibid., p. 338, line 20). The Idaean Mother, moreover, is the same as the Mother of the Gods and Cybele.

Minucius undoubtedly wrote the following—and no more—about the Luperci: “They run about naked in the bitter winter.” If you ask for this to be proved by reliable witnesses, we certainly have several at hand. Livy is the first to present himself, relating that Evander instituted a solemn rite brought from Arcadia, “so that naked young men, [Col. 0640C] venerating Lycaean Pan, might run about in sport and wantonness” (Livy, Book I, § 5). Next Aelius Tubero, cited by Dionysius of Halicarnassus, related the same origin for this solemn rite, in which young men customarily περιελθεῖν δρόμῳ τὴν κώμην γυμνούς, “ran naked around the village, girded only about their private parts with the hides of animals newly slaughtered” (Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Book I of *Roman Antiquities*, p. 67).

To these may be added Plutarch, who thinks that the beginning of this festival, which they called the Lupercalia, and of the young men’s race may have derived not so much from Evander as from the she-wolf by whom Romulus had been reared. He nevertheless acknowledges that the young men ran about naked, struck everyone they encountered with white thongs, and did not spare women from their blows (Plutarch, *Life of Romulus*, p. 31, and *Roman Questions*, [Col. 0640D] p. 280). Elsewhere he relates that Mark Antony was one of those who ran in this manner in Caesar’s presence (*Life of Antony*, p. 921). Women believed that the blows and lashes of these Luperci could make them fertile. Hear Ovid, if you wish, sing of this:

> Bride, what are you waiting for? Neither by potent herbs,  
> Nor prayer, nor magic spell will you become a mother.  
> Patiently receive the lashes of the fertile hand;  
> Your father-in-law will soon bear the longed-for name of grandfather.

(Ovid, Book II of the *Fasti*, § 9.)

Juvenal, however, mocks this superstition:

> Nor does it help to offer one’s palms to the nimble Lupercus.

(Juvenal, *Satires* II, near the end.)

[Col. 0641A] Prudentius attacks it more sharply:

> What is that shameful procession? Surely it shows  
> That you are base when you run as Luperci.  
> What slave would I not deem utterly base  
> If, running naked through every street,  
> He struck girls with a lewdly wielded lash?

(Prudentius, hymn on St. Romanus.)

Why Minucius says that they ran naked “in the bitter winter” you will learn from Plutarch, who observes in the passages already cited that this festival was held in February, specifically on the third day after the Ides, as Ovid too sang in these verses:

> The third dawn after the Ides beholds the naked Luperci,  
> And the rites of two-horned Faunus will be held.

(Ovid, Book II of the *Fasti*, § 9.)

See further Valerius Maximus and Morestellus [Col. 0641B] (Valerius Maximus, Book II, ch. 1, § 9; Morestellus, dialogue 6, *On Roman Festivals*).

Minucius then continues: “Others,” he says, “walk wearing caps and carry ancient shields about.” There can be no doubt that these are the Salii, whom Livy teaches were instituted by Numa Pompilius:

“He selected twelve Salii for Mars Gradivus, gave them the distinctive dress of an embroidered tunic and, over the tunic, a bronze covering for the breast; and he commanded them to bear the heavenly weapons called *ancilia* and to proceed through the city, singing hymns with ritual stamping and solemn dancing” (Livy, Book I, § 20).

Ovid likewise writes of the same Numa:

> He had already given the Salii—their name derives from leaping—  
> Their weapons and the words to be sung to prescribed rhythms.

(Ovid, Book III of the *Fasti*, § 2.)

[Col. 0641C] There he describes how those weapons—which are called *ancilia*, and which our author calls “ancient shields”—are said to have fallen from heaven. Hence Juvenal sang:

> Who, carrying sacred objects swaying from a hidden strap,  
> Sweated beneath the *ancilia* shields.

(Juvenal, *Satires* II, near the end.)

Virgil, however, writes of these men and of the Luperci just mentioned, confirming in these verses that the Salii went about “wearing caps,” as Minucius says:

> Here he had fashioned the dancing Salii and naked Luperci,  
> Their wool-bearing caps, and the *ancilia* fallen from heaven.

(Virgil, Book VIII of the *Aeneid*, line 663 ff.)

See Servius’ notes on these verses and further material in Plutarch, Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Valerius [Col. 0641D] Maximus, and others (Plutarch, *Life of Numa*, p. 98 ff.; Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Book II of *Roman Antiquities*, p. 129; Valerius Maximus, Book I, ch. 1, § 9).

Finally, Minucius immediately added: “They beat skins; begging, they lead the gods from street to street.” It is certainly established that the latter words refer to the priests of the Mother of the Gods, whom we discussed shortly before. It is disputed, however, to whom the former words, “They beat skins,” should refer. Some suspect that they have been displaced from their proper position and should be placed after the words “they run about in winter.” As though the running Luperci alone beat skins! Why not also the Salii, or the “beggars,” who, according to Apuleius, struck cymbals and drums (Apuleius, Book VIII of the *Metamorphoses*, [Col. 0642A] p. 143)? Nothing, therefore, should be altered in the text of Minucius without the authority of some manuscript. Yet no sane person will deny how rightly our author infers from what has been said that divinity was falsely ascribed to those whom the pagans worshiped with superstitious rites so absurd and so unworthy of the name and dignity of gods.

## ARTICLE IV  
### On Temples Whose Entrances Were Open Either Only Once a Year, or Never to Anyone, or Never to Men; on Certain Sacred Ceremonies from Which Either Women or Slaves Were Barred; and on Other Rites Crowned Either by a Once-Married or by a Many-Times-Married Woman

Let us follow our author as he assails other absurd rites of the same pagans. [Col. 0642B] “They permit certain shrines,” he says, “to be entered once a year.” Such undoubtedly was the shrine of Eurynome, concerning which Pausanias says:

“On the appointed day they open the temple of Eurynome; it is not the ancestral custom to open it at any other time. On that day sacrifices are performed both privately and publicly. I myself did not happen to be present at that time and was therefore unable to see the image of Eurynome” (Pausanias, Book VIII, *Arcadica*, p. 271).

Such also, according to the same witness, was the sanctuary of Dindymenian Mother, whom we discussed above. For we also read these words recorded by him:

“They customarily open the sanctuary of Dindymenian Mother on a single day each year. I happened to be present on that very day.”

Finally, he had earlier said of the shrine of Ceres and Proserpina: “Women have access to it at any time, men [Col. 0642C] once each year” (above, ch. 6, art. 2; Pausanias, Book VII, p. 300; idem, ibid., p. 263).

Our author then says: “Certain shrines it is altogether unlawful to visit.” Pausanias left written the following account of Aepytus, king of the Arcadians, which confirms Minucius’ statement:

“When he dared to enter the temple of Neptune at Mantinea, which even in this present age no human being whatsoever is permitted to approach, he was first deprived of his sight and then, not long afterward, departed this life.”

He later adds that when this same temple was rebuilt by order of the emperor Hadrian, absolutely everyone was forbidden access to it; and that the aforementioned Aepytus, who had violated its sanctity by entering it, was suddenly blinded by the force of seawater and died shortly thereafter. Nor should we [Col. 0642D] omit what the same Pausanias had recorded earlier: “There are altars of the Sun, and a temple of Necessity and Violence, which they say it is unlawful to enter” (Pausanias, Book VIII, *Arcadica*, p. 240; idem, ibid., p. 244; idem, Book II, p. 48).

Minucius continues: “There is a temple which no man is permitted to enter.” One sanctuary of this kind undoubtedly existed, to use Cicero’s words from the speech against Verres:

“At Catana there is a sanctuary of Ceres held in the same religious reverence as at Rome, as in other places, and as throughout nearly the entire world. In its innermost sanctuary there was a very ancient image of Ceres, and men not only did not know what sort of image it was, but did not even know that it existed. Men have no access to that sanctuary; its rites are customarily performed by women [Col. 0643A] and maidens” (Cicero, fourth speech *Against Verres*, p. 178, line 21).

Accordingly, Lactantius cites these words of Cicero to show that there were certain temples which men were not permitted to enter (Lactantius, Book II, ch. 4, p. 159; and Book III, ch. 20, p. 307).

Concerning the sanctuary and festival days of Mysian Ceres, Pausanias records the following details, which may also contribute somewhat to the point made by our Minucius:

“They celebrate festival days for seven days. On the third, all the men leave the temple, while the women remain inside and perform a nocturnal rite according to a custom handed down by their ancestors. They exclude not only men but even drive out male dogs. On the following day the men revisit the women in the temple, and [Col. 0643B] jokes and witty remarks are exchanged in both directions amid much laughter” (Pausanias, Book VII, at the end, p. 236).

What need is there to say more? Dionysius of Halicarnassus informs us that it was unlawful for men to spend the night in the shrine of Vesta. Nor, as Macrobius and Plutarch testify, did men have any access to the temple of the Good Goddess. Plutarch adds that whenever women celebrated her festival in any house, all the men, including even the master of the house himself, had to withdraw from it entirely. Hence Cicero, with the full force of his eloquence, attacks Clodius—whom Plutarch also mentions in the cited passage—because he witnessed and violated rites which no man was permitted to behold, even inadvertently (Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Book II of *Roman Antiquities*, p. 127; Plutarch, *Roman Questions*, p. 268; Macrobius, Book I of the *Saturnalia*, [Col. 0643C] ch. 12; Plutarch, *Life of Caesar*, p. 713; Cicero, speech 30, *On the Response of the Haruspices*, p. 435, line 6 ff., and speech 29, p. 420, line 28).

The poets agree with the Greek and Latin prose writers. Tibullus does so in this verse:

> The rites of the Good Goddess must not be approached by males.

(Tibullus, Book I, elegy 6.)

Propertius likewise writes in these two lines:

> The closed precincts of the women’s goddess and the springs requiring purification—  
> [Entered] with impunity, though her rites were disclosed to no men.

(Propertius, Book IV, elegy 10.)

Seneca informs us that not only men themselves but even their images were excluded from the place (Book XVI, epistle 2, p. 404), as does Juvenal in these verses:

> . . . Where orders are given to veil every painting  
> [Col. 0643D] That represents a figure of the other sex.

(Juvenal, *Satires* VI.339.)

Conversely, it was no less a sacrilege for women to approach certain rites belonging to men. “Some rites,” Minucius says again, “are conducted without women,” because, as Aulus Gellius states, “women abstain from the sacrifice to Hercules” (Gellius, Book XI of the *Attic Nights*, ch. 6, p. 586). Macrobius gives the following reason for this prohibition:

“When Hercules, driving the cattle of Geryon through the fields of Italy, was thirsty, a woman replied that she could not supply him with water because a festival day of the goddess of women was being celebrated, and men were not permitted to taste anything from its provisions. Because of this, when Hercules was about to perform a sacrifice, he cursed the presence of women and ordered Potitius and Pinarius, the custodians of the rites, [Col. 0644A] not to permit any woman to be present” (Macrobius, Book I of the *Saturnalia*, ch. 12).

Hence Propertius sang:

> The Greatest Altar, dedicated after the cattle were recovered—  
> “By these hands,” he says, “this altar was made the Greatest—  
> Let it never stand open to any maiden who would worship there,  
> Lest the thirst of mighty Hercules go unavenged.”

(Propertius, Book IV, elegy 10.)

Juvenal too writes:

> . . . But, driven far off according to an adverse custom,  
> No woman crosses the threshold;  
> The altar of the goddess is open to males alone.

(Juvenal, *Satires* II.87.)

Minucius must undoubtedly still be understood as referring to the ceremonies of this same Hercules when he continues the discourse he has begun: “In certain ceremonies it is [Col. 0644B] a sacrilegious crime for a slave to be present.” So great was that offense, and so hateful to the gods, as the pagans dreamed, that all the Potitii—divided into twelve families—who, at Appius’ instigation, had transferred the rites of Hercules to the lowly service of slaves, died out within a year, while Appius himself was deprived of his sight several years later. Although this divine vengeance rightly appears wholly false and fictitious to people of sound mind, nevertheless Titus Livy, Valerius Maximus, the author of the book *On the Origin of the Roman People*, Aurelius Victor, Lactantius, and others testify that the pagans represented it as wholly true and certain (Livy, Book I, § 8; Valerius Maximus, Book I, ch. 1, § 17; author of the book *On the Origin of the Roman People*, p. 504; Aurelius Victor, *On Illustrious Men*, § 34; Lactantius, Book II of the *Institutes*, ch. 7, [Col. 0644C] p. 175).

Meursius further thinks (Meursius, Book IV of *Greece at Festival*, p. 800, vol. VII of *Greek Antiquities*) that female slaves too were forbidden to approach the Thesmophoria—that is, the rites of Ceres. In confirmation of his opinion he cites the following verses of Aristophanes, though without identifying the passage:

> . . . Σὺ δ’ ἄπιθ’, ὦ Θρᾷττ’, ἐκ ποδῶν,  
> Δούλοις γὰρ οὐκ ἔξεστ’ ἀκούειν τῶν λόγων.
>
> . . . “But you, Thracian maid, go away from here;  
> For slaves are not permitted to hear these words.”

(Aristophanes, *Assemblywomen*, act 3, line 164.)

They are found in his comedy entitled *Assemblywomen*. Who, then, from what has thus far been said, does not clearly perceive the justice of Lactantius’ statement that at Rome [Col. 0644D] and in most other cities there were certain rites which it was unlawful for men to witness, and that those who entered the shrine of Vesta, the Good Goddess, or Ceres were regarded as criminals, even though the shrines themselves had been constructed by men? (Lactantius, Book III of the *Divine Institutes*, ch. 10, p. 307.)

Finally, Minucius says: “A once-married woman crowns one set of rites, a many-times-married woman another.” Quite rightly. For in Tertullian we read: “No one but a once-married woman places the crown upon Womanly Fortune, just as upon Mother Matuta”—that is, Ino, daughter of Cadmus and wife of Athamas, whom the Greeks called Λευκοθέα (*Leucothea*, “White Goddess”) (Tertullian, *On Monogamy*, final chapter, p. 688). We likewise read in Dionysius of Halicarnassus that the image of this same Womanly Fortune was not crowned by women who had married twice [Col. 0645A] or by widows, but that this honor was reserved for women recently married. Servius likewise observes that Womanly Fortune, or her image, was not crowned by women who had married twice (Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Book VIII of *Roman Antiquities*, p. 526; Servius on Virgil, *Aeneid* IV.19).

Moreover, who can be so dull and obtuse that he does not immediately understand, from what we have thus far explained, how impious, cruel, and absurd were the sacred rites, festivals, and mysteries, and how superstitious, ridiculous, and infamous were the ceremonies by which the pagans believed that they worshiped their gods? For what gods, unless wholly fictitious and worse than human beings endowed with right reason, could have allowed themselves to be honored by worship so impious and absurd? We therefore think there is no one who does not see most plainly from these matters, and from everything discussed [Col. 0645B] throughout this dissertation, how surely and evidently Minucius demonstrated that these abominable rites and the whole religion of the pagans must be renounced, and that the Christian religion, which teaches nothing but what is right, pious, and holy, must be received and embraced by all.

# CHAPTER XXIII  
## ON A CERTAIN BOOK THAT MINUCIUS APPEARS TO HAVE PROMISED TO WRITE, AND ON CERTAIN OBSCURE PASSAGES AND SOME WRITERS AND ATHEISTS MENTIONED BY HIM

## ARTICLE I  
### Whether Minucius Wrote a Book on Fate, or Promised That He Would Publish One; and an Explanation of Certain Obscure Passages in Minucius Concerning Sea-Bathing at Ostia on the Tiber, the Court Holidays and “Autumnity”; What the Timbers Placed Beneath Ships Were; What the Children’s Game of Skipping Potsherds Across the Sea, or *Epostracismus*, Was; What Is Meant by Different Suns; and Concerning Mists, Clouds, Lightning, Thunderbolts, and the Moon’s Travails

[Col. 0645C]

Where Minucius rejects the pagan error concerning fate, does he promise that he will someday discuss the subject more fully? “Enough,” he says, “has been said about fate, even if only a little under present circumstances; we shall discuss it elsewhere, more abundantly and fully.” Whether he discharged his pledge is not easy to say. Jerome acknowledges that a book or dialogue entitled *On Fate* was published [Col. 0645D] under Minucius’ own name, but its style seemed to him different from that of the *Octavius*. Who, then, would dare assert that this was the work which our author appeared to promise that he would write? To make the matter clearer, Jerome must be heard:

“Another book—or rather dialogue—is circulated under his name, entitled *On Fate*, or *Against the Astrologers*. Although it too is the work of an eloquent man, its style does not appear to me to agree with that of the preceding book,” that is, the *Octavius*.

Not content to say this only once, he again wrote to Magnus concerning the same book:

“Minucius Felix, an advocate of the Roman forum, in the book entitled *Octavius*, and in the other *Against the Astrologers*—if indeed the title does not falsely identify its author [Col. 0646A]—what part of pagan literature did he leave untouched?”

(Jerome, *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*, § 68; idem, epistle 83 to Magnus, p. 665.)

But if Jerome, so diligent and discerning an investigator of books, judged that this book, which he had read, falsely bore the name of Minucius, on what grounds can we, into whose hands it has not come, form a different judgment about it?

Some will surely be astonished by the man who maintains that Minucius Felix, deterred by the great difficulty of treating this subject, failed to keep his promise lest he be compelled to define something rashly. Our Minucius was utterly averse to such foolish display or dissimulation; his exceptional modesty and candor of mind, as we have seen, shine throughout the entire book of the *Octavius*.

[Col. 0646B] Others think that in the words cited he made no promise, but merely kept his hearers’ minds in suspense. For Minucius had spoken in a not altogether dissimilar manner: “Much could be said in reply to this, if the discourse were not hastening onward.” What more, they ask, did Minucius promise in the one passage than in the other? Yet we cannot conceal that a promise is expressed more in the former words than in the latter. Concerning this work, therefore—whether it was never published or has long since perished—nothing further occurs to us.

Let us therefore come to those words of Minucius which appear to contain some obscurity. At the beginning of his book he calls Octavius his most faithful companion because, whenever Octavius came to Rome, he lodged with Minucius and was his guest. He testifies that, together with Octavius and [Col. 0646C] Caecilius, he made for the sea-baths at Ostia on the Tiber. Augustine later bathed there “because,” he says, “the Greeks called a bath βαλανεῖον (*balaneion*), because it drives away anxiety,” while Minucius relates that these baths were quite useful for drying bodily humors (Augustine, Book IX of the *Confessions*, ch. 12). Can this not be confirmed from what Suetonius recorded concerning the emperor Augustus? “Whenever he had to use sea-water or the warm waters of Albula for the sake of his nerves, he was content with this” (Suetonius, Book II, *Augustus*, § 82). But if loosened nerves, made more relaxed by humors, can be treated with seawater, can it not also be said that Minucius and his companions used the baths at Ostia for the same reason? Moreover, we have books about baths recently published by physicians, which anyone may readily consult.

[Col. 0646D] Minucius went there to bathe “at the time,” he says, “when the vintage holidays had relaxed the business of the courts. For at that time, after the summer’s day, autumnity was bringing itself toward a temperate season.” Statius sings as follows concerning these court holidays:

> Surely now the laws of Latium no longer mingle legal quarrels,  
> And the idle year enjoys peace; the returning harvests  
> Have dismissed the forum, nor now does the crowd of defendants . . .

Source/review notes: The supplied source announces two chronological tables in Section VI but does not contain their data; the edits explicitly mark these inherited source gaps.; The bibliographic abbreviation “Edv.” in the Ausonius citation is materially uncertain in the supplied OCR and should not be silently expanded as “Eclogue.”

At the entrance hall, and the querulous clients ask to be allowed to leave. (Statius, *Silvae*, bk. IV, *To Marcellus*, v. 36 ff.)

Afterward Valentinian the Younger and Theodosius the Great decreed that the duration of these holidays should be limited to two months, by a law issued in the year 389: “Only those days shall lawfully be holidays which the more indulgent year has granted in two months for repose from labor, to temper the summer heat [Col. 0647A] and to gather the produce of autumn.” See, if you wish, Gothofredus’ notes on this law, Tiraquellus’ annotations on Alexander’s books, and the comments of others on law 1 in the Digest, *On Holidays*. Moreover, not only our Minucius but also Cato and Arnobius use the term *autumnitas*, “autumn season” (Theodosian Code, title *On Holidays*, law 2, vol. I, p. 121; Alexander, *Genial Days*, bk. III, ch. 20; Cato, *On Agriculture*, chs. 5 and 158). Scaliger, however, observes somewhere that this term signifies autumnal fruit, and proves it by this distich:

> Take this soft, perishable feast of Liber,  
> Moist with the foliage of Bromius’ autumn fruit.

(Scaliger, notes on Varro, *On the Latin Language*, bk. V, p. 79.)

Minucius next attests that he came to the place “where the little boats, drawn ashore and supported upon timbers, rested suspended above contact with the ground.” If anyone with little knowledge of nautical matters should ask us [Col. 0647B] what those supporting timbers were, we shall answer that they were long, round, and very hard pieces of oak—that is, as some call them, rounded poles or beams—by which ships drawn onto the shore or into port were raised above the ground so that they would not rot, and upon which they were afterward conveyed back into the sea. These timbers were called φάλαγγες and φαλλάγγες by the Greeks, as Pollux and the Suda note, but *pulvini*, “rollers,” by the Latins, as Isidore indicated in these words: “Rollers are devices by which ships are launched and drawn ashore” (Pollux, *Onomasticon*, bk. VII, ch. 33, § 9, p. 371, and bk. X, ch. 31, p. 492; Suda, s.v. φάλαγγες; Isidore, bk. XX, ch. 2). Hence Horace sang:

> [Col. 0647C] Harsh winter is released by the welcome return  
> Of spring and the west wind;  
> And engines haul down the dry hulls.

(Horace, bk. I, Ode 4.)

If, however, anyone wishes to maintain that the supporting timbers upon which the ships rested must be distinguished from the devices by which they were hauled, we shall yield at once if he proves his case.

At that place, moreover, Minucius saw at night, together with his two companions, “boys eagerly competing in the game of throwing potsherds into the sea.” This childish game is described by him in an account as concise as it is elegant. The Greeks call it ἐποστρακισμός, and Publius Julius Pollux explains it thus: ὁ δὲ ἐποστρακισμός· ὄστρακον τῶν βαλαντίων κατὰ τοῦ ὕδατος ἐπιπολῆς ἀφιᾶσιν, ἀριθμοῦντες αὐτοῦ τὰ πρὸ τοῦ καταδῦναι πηδήματα ἐν τῇ ὑπὲρ τὸ ὕδωρ ἐπιδρομῇ· ἐκ γὰρ τοῦ πλήθους τῶν [Col. 0647D] ἁλμάτων ἡ νίκη τῷ βάλλοντι: “*Epostracismus*: They cast a sea-shell upon the surface of the water, counting the skips it makes over the water before it sinks; for victory belongs to the thrower according to the number of skips” (Pollux, bk. IX, ch. 7, p. 444). The Suda is briefer: ἐποστρακίζειν· παιδία τις, ἣν παίζουσιν οἱ παῖδες, ὄστρακα ἀφιέντες εἰς θάλασσαν: “To play with shells or potsherds: a certain game which boys play by throwing a shell or potsherd into the sea” (Suda, s.v. ἐποστρακίζειν). See Eustathius on Homer’s *Iliad*, book Σ, or 18.

Afterward Caecilius, assuming the role of an Academic who doubts the true God and his providence, attempts to establish as certain that everything revolves within itself without any God, [Col. 0648A] and that “when fiery seeds have gathered together, one sun after another continually shines; likewise, when vapors have risen from the earth, mists continually form; when these have thickened and massed together, clouds rise higher; when they descend, rains fall, winds blow, hailstorms crash, or, when storm clouds collide, thunder bellows, lightning flashes red, and thunderbolts blaze forth.” Thus he babbled that all these things occur through their own natural causes, without any movement of divine providence. The sun, indeed, is nourished by gathered seeds of fire and continually shines. He preferred to speak of one sun after another because the sun, continually receiving new fiery seeds, seems to be born anew as another sun each day. It is not unusual, moreover, for poets to use *suns* in the plural for the Sun. Let Virgil stand for them all; he sang:

> [Col. 0648B] Often, I remember, as a boy,  
> I spent the long days in song.

And likewise in another book:

> And let the ripening, dusty summer  
> Bake the scattered clods beneath its suns.

(Virgil, *Eclogues* IX, v. 51; and *Georgics* I, v. 65.)

If you wish the word “sun” in Caecilius, as there in Virgil, to signify a day, we shall not strongly oppose you. For his argument would thereby gain greater force—an argument which, nevertheless, we have shown above to have been utterly overthrown by Octavius.

Concerning mists, clouds, and the other meteorological phenomena mentioned by the same Caecilius, among ancient writers you may read Aristotle, Laertius, Pliny, Lucretius, and Seneca; and among more recent writers, Descartes, [Col. 0648C] Gassendi, Antoine Le Grand, and others who have expressly discussed these matters (Aristotle, *Meteorology*, bk. I, ch. 4 ff.; Laertius, bk. X, § 99; Pliny, *Natural History*, bk. II, ch. 42 ff.; Lucretius, bk. VI; Seneca, *Natural Questions*, bk. II, ch. 12 ff.; Descartes, *Meteorology*; Gassendi, *Syntagma of the Life of Epicurus*, art. 2, § 4, ch. 9 ff.).

Octavius afterward declares that divine providence shines forth in the fact that the moon “completes the month through growth, waning, and travail.” The pagans fabricated various “travails” of the moon, especially the travail which they foolishly believed it suffered when eclipsed through incantations. Therefore, with the clashing of bronze, other noises, and loud shouting, they attempted to assist the suffering moon [Col. 0648D] so that it would not hear the incantations. Hence Juvenal sang of a noisy woman:

> She alone will be able to assist the travailing moon.

(Juvenal, *Satire* VI, after the midpoint.)

Statius describes and mocks those sounds of bronze as follows:

> Whenever the dark sister of the Sun is torn  
> From the astonished stars, nations far away  
> Make their assisting bronze resound, and fear in vain.

(Statius, *Thebaid*, bk. VI, after the midpoint.)

Livy, moreover, relates that the battle begun by Hannibal was accompanied “by a clashing of bronze such as is customarily raised during an eclipse of the moon in the silence of night” (Livy, bk. XXVI, § 5). Finally, lest we dwell too long on a manifest matter, we shall add only these verses of Virgil:

> [Col. 0649A] He reveals the paths of heaven and the stars,  
> The varied eclipses of the sun and the moon’s travails.

(Virgil, *Georgics*, bk. II, v. 478.)

Against this ridiculous superstition, however, the most holy Fathers of the Church frequently inveigh, especially Maximus of Turin in a certain sermon on an eclipse of the moon, which we removed from the works of Ambrose, where it had been published falsely under his name (Appendix to Ambrose, p. 377). Minucius presses these points against the pagans in order to demonstrate both their error and divine Providence from the moon’s waxing and waning.

## ARTICLE II. On Certain Writers Cited by Minucius—Nepos, Cassius, Thallus, and Diodorus—and on the Atheists Theodorus, Diagoras, and Protagoras

[Col. 0649B] Although Minucius’ entire disputation rests chiefly, as we have noted, upon various lines of reasoning, he nevertheless cited many writers of celebrated reputation among the pagans who flatly and completely contradicted their various opinions. Four are named by him in one and the same passage: Nepos, Cassius, Thallus, and Diodorus—undoubtedly Diodorus Siculus, whom Justin Martyr adorned with no slight praise on account of the books of his *Historical Library*, which, published in Greek and Latin, are in everyone’s hands (Justin, *Exhortation to the Greeks*, p. 10).

The first of these writers to be named is Cornelius Nepos, who, as Aulus Gellius reports, wrote a *Life* of his friend Cicero and books *On Illustrious Men*, *Examples*, and *Chronicles* (Gellius, *Attic Nights*, bk. XV, [Col. 0649C] ch. 28; bk. I, ch. 18; bk. VII, ch. 18; and bk. XVII, ch. 21). He is also frequently praised by Pliny, and is said to have died during the reign of Augustus and, in Eusebius’ *Chronicle*, to have flourished at that time. He is called by the same Pliny “a resident of the Po” (Pliny, bk. IX, ch. 39, p. 343; bk. X, ch. 33, p. 411; Eusebius, *Chronicle*, at the fourth year of Augustus; Pliny, bk. VI, ch. 9, p. 373). For this reason Catullus calls him “the one Italian” in these verses, with which he sent and dedicated his book to him:

> To whom shall I give this charming new little book,  
> Just now polished with dry pumice?  
> To you, Cornelius; for you were accustomed  
> To think my trifles worth something,  
> Even when you alone among Italians dared  
> To unfold all history in three papyrus rolls—  
> Learned, by Jupiter, and laboriously wrought.

[Col. 0649D] (Catullus, beginning of bk. I, p. 1.)

Nor should you be troubled by Ausonius, who, while citing these verses of Catullus, there called Nepos a Gaul:

> No less learned and no more kindly  
> Than the man whom Gaul supplied to Catullus.

(Ausonius, *Edv.* [uncertain abbreviation], 7, *To Drepanus*.)

For he did not contradict his own witness, but indicated Gallia Togata, which is the same as Transpadane Italy. Elsewhere he cites the same author’s “*Chronicles of Nepos*” (ibid., Letter III to Probus, Praetorian Prefect). Finally, Lactantius transcribed Nepos’ words, written to Cicero and against Cicero’s opinion concerning philosophy. See Suetonius, Vossius, and the many observations made about him after the publication of his *Lives of Excellent Men* (Lactantius, *Institutes*, bk. III, [Col. 0650A] ch. 15, p. 282; Suetonius, bk. I, § 56, and bk. II, § 77; Vossius, *On the Latin Historians*, bk. I, ch. 14).

Cassius, surnamed Hemina, is said to have lived when Gaius Cornelius Lentulus and Lucius Mummius Achaicus were consuls, in the year 608 from the founding of the City, and is called by Pliny “the most ancient author of Annals.” Some, however, wish “most truthful” to be read there instead of “most ancient,” since he was scarcely seventy years older than Pliny. “Cassius Hemina” is the name used by Macrobius, who cites the second book of his *Histories*, while Solinus calls him simply Hemina (Pliny, *Natural History*, bk. XIII, ch. 18, p. 84; Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, bk. I, ch. 16, p. 247; Solinus, *Polyhistor*, ch. 2, p. 13). It is therefore difficult to say why Tertullian surnames him “Cassius Severus.” For he undoubtedly [Col. 0650B] seems to be speaking of the same man as our Minucius. But this passage of Tertullian must be discussed in our dissertation on his books (Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 10, p. 12).

Thallus, moreover, was a Greek writer whom Africanus, as quoted by Eusebius, attests to have written on Syrian affairs. Justin Martyr, Theophilus of Antioch, Lactantius after him, and Eusebius in his Greek *Chronicle* made mention of him (Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, bk. X, ch. 10, p. 489; Theophilus, *To Autolycus*, bk. III, p. 139; Lactantius, *Institutes*, bk. I, ch. 23, p. 132; Eusebius, *Chronicle*, bk. I, p. 14).

Caecilius also cited three men notorious for their impiety: Theodorus, Diagoras, and Protagoras. “Theodorus,” as he says, “the Cyrenian” or Cyrenaic, “or Diagoras of Melos, who preceded him—each of whom” asserted that there were “no [Col. 0650C] gods.” Did he not here, in his customary manner, follow Cicero, who had said of them both: “Diagoras of Melos and Theodorus of Cyrene believed that there were no gods whatsoever”? And again shortly afterward: “Did not Diagoras, who was called the atheist, and later Theodorus, openly abolish the nature of the gods?” (Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, bk. I, p. 195, line 40; ibid., p. 204, line 32.)

Do you see that these words of the Latin orator allow us to infer why Minucius deliberately added, “or Diagoras, who preceded him”? For Cicero plainly indicates that Diagoras was older than Theodorus. And indeed, in Eusebius’ *Chronicle* at the year 1535 we read: “Diagoras becomes known, as do his followers, the natural philosophers.” At the year 1549: “Diagoras the atheist is widely celebrated in speech.” But afterward, at [Col. 0650D] the year 1697: “Theodorus the atheist becomes known.” Although, therefore, the sequence of years is not recorded with sufficient accuracy in this *Chronicle*, it may nevertheless be inferred from it with no small certainty that Diagoras was older than Theodorus.

Concerning the third man accused of the same impiety, Caecilius speaks as follows: “Protagoras of Abdera, because he discussed the divinity prudently rather than profanely, was both expelled by the Athenians from their territory and had his writings burned in the public assembly.” These words too were undoubtedly drawn from Cicero. After saying that Protagoras openly asserted that he had nothing certain whatsoever concerning the gods—“whether they exist or do not exist, or what sort they are”—Cicero shortly afterward added: “When Protagoras of Abdera had placed this at the beginning of his book, ‘Concerning the gods, I am unable to say either that they exist or that they do not exist,’ he was, by order of the Athenians, banished from the city and its territory, and his books were burned in the assembly” (Cicero, bk. cited, p. 200, line 3; ibid., p. 204, line 33); [Col. 0651A] or, as Laertius says, κατέκαυσαν ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ ὑπὸ κήρυκα, “they were burned in the marketplace at the proclamation of a herald.” The Suda says simply ἐκαύθη, “they were burned” (Laertius, bk. IX, *Life of Protagoras*, § 52; Suda, s.v. Πρωταγόρας).

We read the words of Cicero cited by us transcribed by Minucius, and likewise read that Protagoras’ opinion concerning the gods was said to have been uncertain, equivocal, and doubtful. Nevertheless, Epiphanius expressly asserts that this Protagoras not only doubted whether the gods existed but completely and utterly denied it: ἔφη μὴ θεοὺς εἶναι, μηδὲ ὅλως θεὸν ὑπάρχειν, “He denied that there were gods and utterly abolished all divinity” (Epiphanius, *Exposition of the Faith*, § 9, p. 1088). What then, you will ask? [Col. 0651B] Is denying the gods the same thing as doubting them? If you judge that it is not precisely the same, you must certainly say that it comes very close. For concerning this very Protagoras we read the following in Eusebius: Πρωταγόρας ἄθεον ἐκτήσατο δόξαν· λέγεται γοῦν τοιᾷδε κεχρῆσθαι εἰσβολῇ, ἐν τῷ περὶ θεῶν· οὐκ οἶδα οὔθ᾽ ὡς εἰσίν, οὔθ᾽ ὡς οὐκ εἰσίν, οὔθ᾽ ὁποῖοί τινες ἰδίαν: [Col. 0652A] “Protagoras incurred a reputation for atheism. He is said to have opened his work *On the Gods* with this entrance into the discussion: ‘Whether the gods exist or do not exist,’ he says, ‘or what form they possess, I do not know’” (Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, bk. XIV, ch. 2, p. 720).

Theodoret, moreover, concludes from these very words of Protagoras that his τοὺς ἀμφιβόλους περὶ τοῦ Θεοῦ, καὶ ἀπίστους λόγους were “ambiguous and unbelieving statements concerning God” (Theodoret, Discourse 2, *On the First Principle*, p. 505, and Discourse 6, *On Providence*, p. 561). Yet this utterly intolerable doubt pleased Caecilius, a follower of the Academic sect. Therefore, he was not afraid to assert that Protagoras had discussed divinity “prudently rather”—that is, more judiciously—“than profanely,” or in opposition to religion and truth itself, as they supposed, and that he had consequently been condemned unjustly by the Athenians. [Col. 0652B] But Minucius sharply and deservedly restrained his utterly insane rashness, as we have seen. Finally, we have already discussed something of this Protagoras and the other two atheists in the preceding volume of our *Apparatus*, and, as occasion presented itself, the other writers cited in this book of our Minucius in the present dissertation (vol. I, *Apparatus*, bk. III, diss. I, ch. 11, art. 5, p. 785 ff.).

## ABOUT THE YEAR OF CHRIST 236. AN ANONYMOUS AUTHOR

[Col. 0651]

# CHRONICLE COMPOSED UNDER ALEXANDER SEVERUS (S)

## PROLEGOMENA FROM FR. BLANCHINIUS’ DISSERTATION ON THE PASCHAL CANON OF ST. HIPPOLYTUS

(In Galland, *Library of the Ancient Fathers*, vol. III.)

## SYNOPSIS

[Col. 0651C] I. Various opinions of learned men concerning the author of this *Chronicle*. II. Some have thought that it should be attributed to Hippolytus, bishop and martyr. III. But its author appears to have been either Heron, a philosopher who became a Christian and martyr, or, more probably, an anonymous writer who lived under Alexander Severus. [Col. 0652C] IV. Du Cange’s opinion concerning Hippolytus as the author of the *Chronicle* is presented. V. But the chronicler disagrees with Hippolytus in his calculations. VI. This is demonstrated by examples brought forward. VII. Conclusion of Blanchinius’ demonstration. VIII. Various editions of the aforementioned *Chronicle*.

[Col. 0651C] I. Among the works of St. Hippolytus, bishop and martyr, which we collected and published together in the preceding second volume, some learned men have thought that there should also be included that *Chronicle* which is known to have been written about the year of Christ 236 by an anonymous author, a contemporary of Africanus, who flourished near the end of the reign of Emperor Alexander Severus. [Col. 0651D] The most eminent Charles du Cange embraced this opinion above all others.[^c0071-1] But Pearson [Col. 0652C][^c0071-2] and Dodwell[^c0071-3] adopted another view. The latter maintains that the Anonymous author under discussion wrote a few years after Hippolytus, since the holy martyr and bishop is otherwise known to have begun his Cycle in the first year of the same Alexander Severus. Nevertheless, he says, [Col. 0653A] our Anonymous has many things which seem to agree with Hippolytus’ chronological hypotheses as observed in the latter’s Paschal Canon, so that we may reasonably suspect that the Anonymous was indebted to Hippolytus. Among the opinions of these learned men, we are compelled especially to accept that which the illustrious prelate Francis Blanchinius explained quite admirably on this matter.[^c0071-4] Thus he writes:

[^c0071-1]: [Col. 0651D] Preface to the *Paschal Chronicle*, §§ XVIII and XXV.

[^c0071-2]: [Col. 0652D] Dissertation I, *On the Succession of the First Bishops of Rome*, ch. X, § 1.

[^c0071-3]: [Col. 0652D] Special Dissertation *On the First Succession of the Roman Pontiffs*, ch. 14, § 19.

[^c0071-4]: [Col. 0653D] Ch. 3, § 7 ff.; and in Fabricius, vol. I of the works, p. 14 ff.

II. “We lamented that the book in which Hippolytus had arranged his *Demonstration of the Times of Passover*, as in the Table, had perished. For if that work had come down to us complete, it would have to be regarded as the most precious of all books after Holy Scripture. Before Hippolytus, indeed, no one had arranged the sacred annals in a definite sequence or reduced them to the rule of a Cycle; he was the first Christian writer to accomplish this. [Col. 0653B] The most learned Lord du Cange relieved our grief in the latest edition of the *Paschal Chronicle*. There, after discussing Hippolytus’ Canon and Commentary on Passover at considerable length, with the profound learning that he possesses in every branch of letters, he seemed to offer us some hope that Hippolytus’ book might be found in that ancient codex which Canisius, in volume III of his *Ancient Readings*, and Labbe, in the first volume of his *Library of Manuscripts*, had brought to light for the public benefit. That most eminent man also prepared a third edition of the same little work as number 4 among the *Selections for the Illustration of the Chronicle* which he was preparing. On p. 403, when reproducing its title from ancient parchment in the little index prefixed to the *Selections*, he recommended it as follows:

> IV. *Book of the Generation [Col. 0653C] from Adam down to the order of the things contained in this book.* A work which, in the Preface, we have judged may be ascribed to Hippolytus of Portus; from the edition of Henry Canisius and Philip Labbe, revised against the codex of the Paris College of the Society of Jesus.

“And certainly, in his preface, he is very extensive in seeking conjectures as to why it should be attributed above all others to Hippolytus the Martyr, whom he believes to have been bishop of Portus, one of the seven suburbicarian sees.

III. “But if this marble Canon must be referred to Hippolytus, bishop and martyr—as it is by the judgment of all learned men and indeed of du Cange himself—I am confident that I shall demonstrate that the Canisian and Labbean codex, otherwise noteworthy, does not belong to the same Hippolytus. Rather, it should be referred [Col. 0653D] either to that Heron, a philosopher who became a Christian and martyr, whom du Cange himself conjectures, from a Greek inscription in Spon, section X, no. 22, to have been called to faith in Christ from the office of temple-warden at the temple of Sarapis in the Roman Port. He lived during the reign of Severus Alexander, was thus a contemporary of Hippolytus, and is shown from the testimony of the ancients to have written on chronology and to have fulfilled his martyrdom while still a neophyte. I therefore embrace the opinion which the same praised author appended in the second place in his preface, saying that the book must be assigned either to Hippolytus the bishop ‘or to a contemporary author who lived under Alexander Augustus.’ [Col. 0654A] It is best to transcribe his words from section XVIII of the preface.

IV. “‘Moreover, the *Chronicle* of Hippolytus under discussion is almost the twin of—if it was not identical with—that *Chronicle* published by Henry Canisius in volume III of the *Ancient Readings*, and by Philip Labbe in volume I of the *New Library*, from a manuscript codex of the Paris College of the Society of Jesus, under this title: *On the Divisions and Generations of the Nations*. This *Chronicle* is continued down to the thirteenth and final year of Alexander Severus, during whose reign the author more than once indicates that he lived. In the preface he says that he will describe:

> the division of the nations; the enumerated generations of the ancestors; the periods of habitation; the outbreaks of wars; the periods of the Judges; which kings they were descended from; [Col. 0654B] what captivities befell the people and under which Judges; which priests existed at which times; what division and what destruction occurred; how the generation of Israel’s seed from the Fathers was fulfilled in Christ; and how many and how great are the years, reckoned through their respective periods, from the creation of the world down to the present day.

“‘An index is appended to the preface, one heading of which reads as follows: “An account of Passover, and who observed it and when, from the times of Moses to the present day.” These words refer to what is found in the section where the observance of Passover at intervals by the Jews is discussed. Then it is added:

> But from the generation of Christ, after thirty years, when the Lord suffered, Passover is celebrated. For he himself was the true Passover. From the Passion of the Lord down [Col. 0654C] to the thirteenth year of the reign of Alexander Caesar are 206 years during which Passover has been observed—the Passover that we observe in commemoration of our Lord Jesus Christ. Therefore, all the years from Adam down to the present day amount to 5,738 years.

“‘If anyone wishes to compare these statements which we have presented here with the points we have touched upon concerning Hippolytus’ *Chronicle*, matching them precisely, he will perhaps readily concede that it is the very same *Chronicle*, to which Hippolytus prefixed or appended the tabular list constituting a canon or rule for finding the feast of Passover, which he discussed in the section we have mentioned; and that by this rule he wished the reader to evaluate both past and future years.’

V. “He reasons correctly from these two numbers of years: those from the Passion of the Lord to the thirteenth year of Severus Alexander, and those from the year which, according to the opinion of the ancients, he assigned to the Lord’s Incarnation thirty or thirty-one [Col. 0654D] years before the Passion. Indeed, to add the remaining epochs recorded in the marble Canon, I shall grant that most of them agree with the numbers in the Labbean and Canisian codex. But since the others disagree with them—especially the one defining the interval between the two Passovers, those of the Exodus and of Hezekiah—it is plainly shown that Hippolytus’ marble *Chronicle* differs from a work contemporary with it that disagrees in its calculations. Since it is established that Hippolytus’ numbers come very close to the opinions of the more expert chronologists, as was shown by the comparison on p. 103 ff., whereas the Anonymous’ calculation is manifestly defective, especially in defining the interval from Joshua’s Passover to Hezekiah’s Passover, I think it worthwhile to present the calculations of Hippolytus that survive in this monument. Thus this Paschal Chronology, the most ancient of all and a witness to Hippolytus’ great expertise, may serve to commend the wisdom of the Fathers who, being nearest to the Apostles and apostolic men, illuminated the earliest centuries of the Church both by blood shed for Christ and by their most illustrious writings. I therefore demonstrate the difference between the chronicles as follows.

[Col. 0656A] VI. “In the Canisian, Labbean, and Du Cange editions, the Anonymous’ little work is divided into various sections according to Labbe, or chapters according to Canisius, each of whom copied from different exemplars. Thus, in chapter XVII according to Canisius, or section XII according to Labbe, the following intervals between Passovers are recorded. I shall reproduce the words of the codex from Labbe, adding in the margin the variant readings of Canisius and Du Cange where they differ.

[The interval table announced here is absent from the supplied source.]

[Col. 0655A] “The intervals defined in this way in the Anonymous’ codices do not everywhere correspond to the other sum of years obtained from the individual epochs of the Kings or Judges which we read in the same little work. In order that the whole discrepancy may be visible at a single glance, [Col. 0656A] I shall present in the following table the years of both the Judges and the Kings individually, as they are arranged in the codex.

[The table of the years of the Judges and Kings announced here is absent from the supplied source.]

[Col. 0655] “From the epochs just cited, therefore, there are only one hundred years from the beginning of Hezekiah’s reign to the eighteenth year of Josiah.

“According to the preceding total, the same interval amounts to 114 years. Neither figure, however, agrees with Hippolytus’ marble: there a simple epoch separates the same Passovers by 112 years, while the epoch ‘according to Daniel’ separates them by 113 years.

“The disagreement between the numbers appearing in the written exemplars is far more evident if the interval between Joshua’s Passover and Hezekiah’s Passover is compared. The 592 years [Col. 0657A] from Joshua’s Passover to the beginning of David’s reign, when added to the 342 years from the beginning of David’s reign to the beginning of Hezekiah’s, make a total of 934.

“But in the total of chapter XVII of the Canisian codex and section XII of the Labbean codex, the same interval is reduced by more than four centuries, for the interval from Joshua’s Passover to Hezekiah’s Passover is established as 464 years.

VII. “Hippolytus’ marble does not suffer from these anachronisms and antichronisms—if the expression is permissible. In it we have seen that the intervals derived from the twofold calculation, both the ‘simple’ and that ‘according to Daniel,’ agree very well with the calculations of the more celebrated chronologists. From the arrangement of the cells, the interval from the Exodus to Hezekiah’s Passover is found to be 793 years according to the simple calculation, or 791 ‘according to Daniel.’ [Col. 0657B] Thus the distance of Hezekiah from Joshua’s Passover is 749 years by the simple calculation and 750 by the calculation according to Daniel.

“For the labels EXODUS, JOSHUA, and HEZEKIAH could not otherwise fall into their respective cells unless seven complete lesser periods of 112 years, together with an additional nine years, are assumed to be counted from the Passover of the Exodus to Hezekiah’s Passover; and unless the seven lesser periods, reduced by 32 cells or years according to the simple calculation, or by 33 ‘according to Daniel,’ are said to intervene between Joshua’s Passover and Hezekiah’s Passover. For each lesser period, when complete, returns to the same cell, while every century moves backward twelve cells in the designation of years. It is therefore necessary that the years intervening from the Exodus to Hezekiah, as derived from these cells ‘according to Daniel,’ should be 7, or 119, or 231, or 243, or 345, [Col. 0657C] or 457, or 569, or 681—which no one would assert without being moved by some adequate authority—or finally 793, as we maintain, since the other figures also agree with the calculations of the more expert chronologists, correctly collected from the numbers in Holy Scripture.

“When these matters have been carefully considered, it will be evident, I think, that the corrupt numbers of the Anonymous contemporary with Hippolytus can more easily be restored from the marble *Chronicle* than that Hippolytus’ *Chronicle*, which is fully self-consistent in its marble cells, can be distorted [Col. 0658A] to conform to the corrupt numbers of codices that disagree with one another, were received from anonymous authors, and then were rendered into Latin by anonymous translators. I would prefer the errors of the written codices to be corrected on the authority of this Hippolytan Canon.

“It is easily understood, indeed, that numbers are missing in the written chronicles in Canisius’ chapter XVIII between the epochs of the Exodus and Hezekiah. Perhaps some intermediate epoch stood between them, from the Exodus to the beginning of David’s reign; then followed the one from the beginning of David’s reign to Hezekiah, which is not self-consistent because its numbers have been corrupted. I omit a review of the other antichronisms arising from the variant readings of the Canisian and Labbean codices. Chronographers who compare the totals of years reckoned from the creation of the world according to the Anonymous will collect them; from this it will appear [Col. 0658B] that the distance from Joshua son of Nun to the beginning of David’s reign was 555 years according to the Canisian exemplar, but 495 according to the Labbean, neither of which corresponds to the years enumerated in the list of Judges and Kings.

“Comparison with the codices therefore very strongly commends the trustworthiness of our marble and the excellence of Hippolytus’ work. It also intensifies our longing for the works of so great a Father and Martyr. Those works would have perished entirely had not this splendid vestige of his monument secured a measure of permanence for the surviving remains of his teaching.”

Thus far the most eminent author.

VIII. We have therefore arranged for the publication here of this *Chronicle* by an Anonymous contemporary of Hippolytus, which was first published by Canisius,[^c0071-5] then by Labbe,[^c0071-6] and finally by Du Cange,[^c0071-7] as an appendix to the works of Hippolytus which we collected, arranged, and published together in the preceding second volume. [Col. 0658C] We have based our edition chiefly upon Labbe’s, while occasionally comparing the exemplars of Canisius and Du Cange, from which we have transcribed some variant readings that appeared to be of some value. For who, to speak with Labbe, could cleanse that Augean stable?

[^c0071-5]: [Col. 0658C] Canisius, *Ancient Readings*, vol. II; new edition, vol. I, p. [number omitted in the source].

[^c0071-6]: [Col. 0658C] Labbe, *New Library of Manuscript Books*, vol. I, p. 298.

[^c0071-7]: [Col. 0658C] Du Cange, *Selections for the Paschal Chronicle*, p. 413.

# CHRONICLE OF THE ANONYMOUS AUTHOR WHO IS SAID TO HAVE LIVED UNDER EMPEROR ALEXANDER IN THE YEAR OF CHRIST 236

## BOOK OF THE GENERATION FROM ADAM DOWN TO THE ORDER[^c0071-8] CONTAINED IN THIS BOOK

[Col. 0657]

[^c0071-8]: [Col. 0657D] “Down to the order which is contained.” Thus the manuscript edition of Canisius; “down to . . . [Col. 0658D] the order of the things contained in the volume of this book.”

[Col. 0657D] Enumeration of times and years. The generations of the world down to the present day. The division of the earth among the three sons of Noah. An account of the nations: from whom they arose; which lands and cities fell by lot to each; how many famous islands there are; who migrated and from which nations; how many named rivers; how many named mountains. How many Judges there were, and how many years each judged the people. How many Kings there were in the Tribe of Judah, and how many years each reigned. [Col. 0659A] An account of Passover, and who observed it and when, from the times of Moses to the present day. The Kings of the Persians from Cyrus onward, and how many years each reigned. The Kings of the Macedonians from Alexander onward, and how many years each reigned. The Emperors of the Romans from Augustus onward, and how many years each ruled. The periods of the Olympiads from Iphitus down to the present Olympiad. [Col. 0660A] The names and generations of the Patriarchs. The names of the Prophets. Women who were prophetesses. The names of the Kings of the Hebrews and of the Kings who reigned in Samaria over the ten Tribes, and how many years each reigned. The names of the Priests. The names of the Bishops of Rome, and how many years each presided.

## PREFACE

[Col. 0659]

[Col. 0659A] SINCE it is necessary to be instructed in the truth,[^c0071-9] I thought it necessary, dearly beloved brothers, to compose this brief discourse from Holy Scripture for the strengthening of doctrine, so that through a few explanations [Col. 0659B] we may more quickly recognize the powers of truth, investigated not without reason. By first cutting away the contention engendered by the unlearned, [which] obscures the understanding,[^c0071-10] may it instruct one who is unlearned in such matters. Desiring to exercise the utmost diligence and foresight, we learn in accordance with the truth the division of the Nations and the enumerated generations of the ancestors; the periods of those who inhabited the lands, the outbreaks of wars, the periods and dispensations of the Judges,[^c0071-11] the years of the Kings, and the times of the Prophets—who they were and from [Col. 0660A] which kings they were descended; what captivities befell the people, under which kings and which judges; which priests existed at which times; and what destruction occurred. In what manner[^c0071-12] the generation [Col. 0660B] of the seed of Israel from the Fathers was fulfilled in CHRIST, and how many and how great are the years enumerated through their respective periods from the creation of the world down to the present day.

[^c0071-9]: [Col. 0659D] “To be instructed in the truth.” Labbe’s edition: “for the Deacon to be instructed in the truth.” And shortly afterward: “dearest brother—to strengthen your doctrine.”

[^c0071-10]: [Col. 0659D] “Which obscures the understanding.” Labbe’s edition: “which obscure.” After “understanding,” Canisius’ edition offers “according to” as the preferable reading; the editor conjectures “For Scripture, he says,” which is less satisfactory.

[^c0071-11]: [Col. 0659D] “The periods of those inhabiting—the dispensations.” Labbe: “the periods of habitation and the dispensations,” with the intervening words omitted. “The periods and dispensations of the Judges.” Canisius’ edition: “the dispensations in the time of the Judges.” Correctly, as it seems.

[^c0071-12]: [Col. 0660D] “In what manner.” Thus the editions of Canisius and Labbe. But Du Cange and Fabricius read “which henceforth.”

We thought it appropriate, beginning from Genesis, to set matters forth in accordance with what the words indicate,[^c0071-13] bearing witness not from some position of our own but from Holy Scripture itself. Therefore, taking our point of departure from this, we present our discourse concerning Genesis in due order.

[^c0071-13]: [Col. 0660D] “As it requires, to declare,” Canisius; “as it is appropriate to declare.”

# THE NARRATIVE BEGINS

[Col. 0659]

## SECTION ONE. The Book of the Generation of Human Beings

[Col. 0659B]

[Col. 0659C] On the day when God made Adam, he made them in the image of God.

Adam lived 230 years and begot Seth. Seth lived 205 years and begot Enos. Enos lived 161 years and begot Cainan. Cainan lived 170 years and begot Mahalaleel. [Mahalaleel lived] 165 years and begot Jared. Jared lived 162 years and begot Enoch. Enoch lived 165 years and begot Methuselah. Methuselah lived 167 years and begot Lamech. Lamech lived 188 years and begot Noah. Noah was 500 years old and begot three sons: Shem, Ham, and Japheth. But 100 years after Shem was born, [Col. 0659D] the Flood occurred, when Noah was six hundred years old. Therefore, from Adam to the Flood there are eleven generations and 2,242 years.

These are the generations of Shem. When Shem was 100 years old, he begot Arphaxad in the second year after the Flood. Arphaxad lived 135 years and begot Cainan. Cainan lived 130 years and begot Salah. [Col. 0660B] Salah lived 130 years and begot Eber. Eber lived 134 years [and begot] Peleg.

[Col. 0660C] Up to this man there were five generations, comprising 529 years; from Adam, however, there were fifteen generations, comprising 2,771 years.

## SECTION II. The Division of the Earth and the Three Sons of Noah

After the Flood, the earth was divided among the families of the three brothers Shem, Ham, and Japheth.

To Shem, the firstborn, fell the territory from Persia and Bactria far into India and as far as Rhinocorura.

To Ham, the second, fell the territory from Rhinocorura as far as Gades.

To Japheth, the third, fell the territory from Media as far as Gades toward [Note: [Col. 0660D] “Buroam,” Labbe; “Borram.” Others: “Borream,” the North.] Buroa.

Japheth has the River Tigris, which divides Media from Babylonia; Shem has the Euphrates; and Ham has the Geon, which is called the Nile.

[Col. 0660D] The languages were confused after the Flood. There were seventy-two languages that were confused, and those who were building the Tower comprised seventy-two nations, which were also divided by their languages over the face of the whole earth.

Nebroth the giant, an Ethiopian and the son of Cush, supplied wild animals obtained by hunting as food during the famine [*inediis*]. [Note: [Col. 0660D] *Inediis*. Thus also Cange. Labbe, however, reads *mediis*; Canisius: *Mediis*.]

[Col. 0661A] The seventy-two names are as follows.

## SECTION III

The sons of Japheth were: [Note: [Col. 0661D] Gamer.
