Various readings of the names occur; they may be consulted in Scaliger, *Thesaurus temporum*, p. 45.] Gamer, from whom came the Cappadocians; Magog, from whom came the Celts and Galatians; Madai, from whom came the Medes; Javan, from whom came the Greeks and Ionians; Thobel, from whom came the Thalienses; Mosoch, from whom came the Illyrians; Thiras, from whom came the Thracians; and Cethyn, [Note: [Col. 0661D] “Cethyn, from whom came the Macedonians.” Canisius: “Chetim, from whom came the Trojans, Phrygians, and Macedonians.”] from whom came the Macedonians.

The sons of Gamer were: Ascanaz, from whom came the Sarmatians; Rifan, from whom came the Sauromatians; and Thogorma, from whom came the Armenians.

The sons of Javan were: Elisan, from whom came the Sicilians; [Col. 0661B] Tharsis, from whom came the Iberians, who are also called Tyrrhenians; and Cithu, [Note: [Col. 0661D] *Cithu*. Thus Labbe’s edition. Others: *Cithii*. Canisius, however, has: “Cethim, from whom came the Romans, who are also called Latins; Dodanim, from whom came the Priamians. Fifteen in all.”] from whom came the Romans, who are also called Latins, and the Rhodians: fifteen in all.

From these arose the islands of the nations; the Cypriots, moreover, are descended from the Citienses.

Indeed, among Japheth’s descendants we find also those toward the North, who come from that family of the Citienses.

Among them also are the nations in [Note: [Col. 0661D] *In Ellada*. Canisius: “in the Thebaid.”] Hellas, apart from those who arrived there afterward: the kings who inhabited Athens, the city honored among the Greeks, and the city of the Thebans; for its inhabitants are of the Sidonians. Likewise, all the others subsequently migrated into Hellas. We know these things from the Law and the Prophets.

Thus, at the confusion of the Tower, there were fifteen families descended from Japheth. [Col. 0661C] These nations of Japheth spread from Media as far as the western Ocean, reaching toward the North:

The Medes, Albanians, Garganians, Arrei, Armenians, Amazons, Culi, Corzieni, Benageni, Cappadocians, Paphlagonians, Mariandeni, Tibareni, Chalybes, Mossynoeci, Colchians, Melanceni, Sarmatians, Sauromatians, Maeotians, Scythians, Taurians, Thracians, Bastarnae, Illyrians, Macedonians, Hellenes, Greeks, Libyans, Istri, Vieni, Dauni, [Note: [Col. 0661D] *Dapnes*. Canisius: *Dapneri*; Cange: *Dapies*.] Dapnes, Calabrians, Pici, Latins who are also called Romans, Tyrrhenians, Gauls who are also called Celts, Libyestini, Celtiberians, Iberians, Gauls, Aquitanians, Illyrians, Basanotes, Cyrtani, Lusitanians, Vaccaei, Cunienses, and Britons, who inhabit the islands.

Those among them who know letters are: the Iberians, the Latins who are called Romans, the Spaniards, the Greeks, [Col. 0661D] and the Armenians.

Their boundaries extend northward as far as Gades, from the River Potameda as far as [Note: [Col. 0661D] *Mastusiadilion*. Canisius: *Mastusi ad Ilion*.] Mastusiadilion.

Their lands are these: Media, Albania, Amazonis, Lesser Armenia, Greater Armenia, Cappadocia, [Col. 0662A] Paphlagonia, Galatia, [Note: [Col. 0662D] *Collis*. Labbe: perhaps *Colchis*. Shortly afterward, in place of *Mediacrris*, Canisius has *Media, Derris*.] Collis of India, Bosphorma, Mediacrris, Sarmatia, Tauriana, Scythia, Bastarnia, Thrace, Macedonia, Dalmatia Mollis, Thessaly, Locris, Boeotia, Aetolia, Attica, Achaia, Pellenia, which is called the Peloponnese, [Note: [Col. 0662D] *Arcanea*. Labbe: *Acarnia*. Canisius: *Acarnanna*. Shortly afterward, following Illyria, Canisius gives *Euchnites* in place of *Aodimus*. *Calatia*, Labbe: *Calcetia*, perhaps *Galletia*; Canisius: *Galitia*.] Arcanea, Epirus, Illyria, Aodimus, Hadriace, from which the Adriatic Sea takes its name, Calatia, Lusitania, Italy, Thusgene, Massalia, the country of the Celts, Gaul, [Note: [Col. 0662D] *Hispania. Galli*, Canisius: *Ypanogallia*, perhaps Hispano-Gaul; read *Spanogall*.] Hispania, Galli, Iberia, and Greater Hispania.

Here the land of Japheth comes to an end, extending as far as all the British Isles, which face toward the North.

They also possess these islands: the British Isles, Sicily, Euboea, Rhodes, Chios, Lesbos, Cythera, Zacynthus, Cephallenia, Ithaca, Corcyra, the Cyclades Islands, and a certain part of Asia called Ionia.

[Col. 0662B] Their river is the Tigris, which divides Media from Babylonia. These are the boundaries of Japheth.

## SECTION IV

The sons of Ham were:

Cush, from whom came the Ethiopians.

Mesraim, from whom came the Egyptians.

Phud, from whom came the Troglodytes.

Canaan, from whom came the Africans and Phoenicians.

The sons of Cush were Saba, Evilat, Sabat, Regma, and Sagabacata.

The sons of Regma were Saba and Dadan.

Cush also begot Nebroth.

The ancestral peoples of the Egyptians, together with Mesraim their father, were eight. For Scripture says:

“Mesraim begot Ludim,” from whom came the Lydians; “Enemim,” from [Col. 0662C] whom came the Pamphylians; “Labain,” from whom came Laboez; “Nephtuhim and Pathrusim,” from whom came the Cretans; [Note: [Col. 0662D] *Casluin*. Labbe: *Castoin*; Greek: Χασμωνιεὶμ (*Chasmōnieim*) (Gen. 10:14).] “Casluhim,” from whom came the Lycians and from whom the Philistines went forth; and “Caphtorim,” from whom came the Cilicians.

The ancestral peoples of the Canaanites, together with their father, were twelve. For Scripture says:

“Canaan begot Sidon his firstborn,” from whom came the Sidonians; and the Hittite, the Jebusite, the Amorite, the Girgashite, the Arkite, the Hivite, from whom came the Tripolitans, the Sinite, the Arvadite, from whom came the Aradians, the Zemarite, and the Hamathite, from whom came the people of Amathus.

Their habitation extends from Rhinocorura as far as Gades.

From these arose the following kings or nations: the Ethiopians, Troglodytes, Aggei, Isabini, Ichthyophagi, Velanni, Egyptians, Phoenicians, Libyans, [Note: [Col. 0662D] *Marmaredae*. Labbe: *Marmaridae*.] Marmaredae, Charisilittae, [Col. 0662D] Mysians, Mossynoeci, Phrygians, Magones, Bithynians, Nomads, Lycinii, Mariandeni, Pamphylians, Minisci, Dipisideni, Lygallii, Cilicians, Maurosii, Cretans, Magartae, Numidians, Macrones, and Nasamones.

They possess the territory from Egypt as far as the Ocean.

[Col. 0663A] These islands are shared among them: Corsola, Lupadus, Agaudius, Melita, Cercenna, Menis, Cardinia, Galata, Corsuna, Crete, Gaulus, Rheda, Ethera, Careatus, Astypala, Chios, Lesbos, Tenedos, Imbros, Jassus, Cobus, Cnidos, Nisyros, Megistae, and Cyprus.

Those among them who are literate are the Phoenicians, Egyptians, Pamphylians, and Phrygians.

The boundaries of Ham extend lengthwise from Rhinocorura, which divides Syria from Egypt, as far as Gades.

The names of their countries are these: Egypt; Ethiopia, which stretches toward India; and the other Ethiopia, from which the Ethiopian river proceeds; Erythrea, that is, the Red Sea, facing eastward; Thebaic Libya, which extends as far as the Syrtes and contains these nations—the Nasamones, Macae, and Tautamei; Libya, which [Col. 0663B] extends from Leptis as far as the Lesser Syrtis; Numidia; Masseria; and Mauretania, which extends as far as the Pillars of Hercules, that is, the Heracleotic Pillars opposite Gades.

Toward the northern coast it contains Cilicia, Pamphylia, Pisidia, Mysia, Lycaonia, Phrygia, Camalia, Lycia, Caria, Lydia, the other Mysia, the Troad, Aeolis, Old Bithynia, and Upper Phrygia.

It also contains these islands: Sardinia, Crete, and Cyprus; and the River Geon, which is called the Nile. It forms the division between Ham and Japheth, together with the mouth of the western sea. This is the middle lineage of Ham.

## SECTION V

From Shem, Noah’s elder son, twenty-five families are known; [Col. 0663C] they inhabited the East.

The sons of Shem were: Elam, from whom came the Elymaeans and Assyrians; Arphaxad, from whom came the Chaldaeans; Lud, from whom came the Lazones; and Aram, from whom came the Ethes. Abraham destroyed these earlier peoples.

The sons of Aram were: Oscevi, from whom came the Lydians; Gart, from whom came the Gaspheni; and Mosoch, from whom came the Mossyni.

Arphaxad begot Salah, and Salah begot Heber, from whom came the Hebrews. To Heber were born two sons, Peleg and Deboc, from whom the lineage of Abraham is derived; and Tactem and Joktan.

Joktan begot Elmodal, from whom came the Indians; Saleph, from whom came the Bactrians; Hazarmaveth, from whom came the earlier Arabs; Duran, from whom came the Camebi; Derra, from whom came the Mardi; Ezei, from whom came the Arians; Declam, from whom came the Cedrusi; Gebal, from whom came the earlier Scythians; Abimeel, from whom came the Hyrcanians; Sabat, from whom came the first Arabs; [Col. 0663D] Ophir, from whom came the Armenians; and Evilat, from whom came the Gymnosophists. All these are Bactrians.

There are seventy-two peoples in all from the three sons of Noah.

The habitation of all Shem’s sons extends [Note: [Col. 0663D] “From Bacris.” Labbe: “from Acris.”] from Bacris as far as Rhinocorura, which divides Syria from Egypt, and from the Red Sea at the mouth of Arsinoe, which belongs to India.

These are the nations that arose from them: the Hebrews, who are the Jews; Persians, Medes, Poenes, Arians, Hyrcanians, Assyrians, Indians, Macardi, Parthians, Germani, Elymaeans, Cissians, the first Arabs, Cedrusi, Scythians, [Col. 0664A] the Arabs beyond them, and the Wise Men called Gymnosophists—that is, “naked sages.”

Their habitation extends as far as Rhinocorura and Cilicia.

Those among them who know letters are the Jews, Persians, Medes, Chaldaeans, Indians, and Assyrians.

The habitation of Shem’s sons extends lengthwise from India as far as Rhinocorura, and in breadth from Persia and Bactria as far as India.

The names of their countries are these: Persia, Bactriana, Hyrcania, Babylonia, Corbulia, Assyria, Mesopotamia, Old Arabia, Alimales, India, Arabia Felix, Coele-Syria, Commagene, and Phoenicia, which belongs to the sons of Shem.

## SECTION VI

[Col. 0664B] The nations that possess their own languages are these: the Hebrews, who are also called Jews; Assyrians, Chaldaeans, Persians, Medes, Arabs, Midianites, Adiabenians, Taleni, Alamosenni, Saracens, Magi, Caspians, Albanians, Indians, Ethiopians, Egyptians, Libyans, Hittites, Canaanites, Perizzites, Hivites, Girgashites, Jebusites, Idumaeans, Samaritans, Phoenicians, Syrians, Cilicians, Tarsians, Cappadocians, Armenians, [Note: [Col. 0664D] *Hibeni*. Labbe: *Hiberi*.] Hibeni, Librani, Scythians, Colchians, Sanni, Bosporani, Asians, Isaurians, Lycaonians, Pisidians, Galatians, Paphlagonians, Phrygians, Achaeans, Thessalians, Macedonians, Thracians, Mysians, Bessi, Dardanians, Sarmatians, Germans, Pannonians, Paeonians, Noricans, Dalmatians, Romans who are also called Latins, Ligurians, Gauls who are also called Celts, Aquitanians, Britons, Spaniards who are also called Tyrrhenians, Moors, Baccuates and Massennes, Gaetulians, Africans who are also called Barbarians, Mazicei, [Col. 0664C] and Garamantes who are also called Marmaredae, whose territory extends as far as Ethiopia.

## SECTION VII

I have thought it necessary also to explain the settlements and appellations of the nations.

I shall begin in the East. The inhabitants of the lands of the Persians and Medes are the Parthians and the neighboring nations, extending peacefully as far as Coele-Syria.

The inhabitants of the Arab lands are the Arabs called “Fortunate,” for they are designated by this name.

The inhabitants of the Chaldaean lands are the Mesopotamians.

The inhabitants of the Midianite lands are the Cynedocolpitae, Troglodytes, and Ichthyophagi.

The nations and appellations of the Greeks are five: Ionians, Arcadians, [Col. 0664D] Boeotians, Aeolians, and Laconians.

Their settlements were among the Pontics, Bithynians, Trojans, Asians, Carians, Legii, Pamphylians, Cyrenaeans, and many islands—that is, the ten Cyclades enclosed by the Myrtoan Sea. Their names are:

Andros, Tenoemteo, Naxos, Ceos, Gyaros, Delos, Fynus, Rhenea, Cyrnos, and Marathon. There are also twelve other, larger islands that contain many cities and are called the Sporades, in which Greeks settled. Their names are: Euboea, Crete, Sicily, Cyprus, Cos, Samos, Rhodes, [Col. 0665A] Chios, Thapsus, Lemnos, Lesbos, and Samothrace.

Euboea belongs to Boeotia; likewise, from Ion come these sixteen Ionian cities: Clazomenae, Mytilene, Phocaea, Priene, [Note: [Col. 0665D] *Eryt*. Labbe: *Erythra*.] Erythrae, Samos, Teos, Colophon, Cius, Ephesus, Smyrna, Perinthus, Byzantium, Chalcedon, Pontus, and the free city of Amisus.

The nations and settlements of the Romans, who are also Citienses, are these: the Tuscans, Emilienses, Picentes, Campanians, Apulians, and Lucanians.

The nations and settlements of the Africans are these: the Lebdeni, Cinti, Numidians, Nasamones, and Saci.

The islands containing cities are Sardinia, Corsica, Girda, which is also called Benigga, Cercyna, and Galata.

The nations and settlements of the Moors are the Musulani, Tingitani, and Caesarienses.

[Col. 0665B] The nations and settlements of the Spaniards are these: the Tyranni and Turreni, who are also called Tarraconenses; the Lusitanians, Baetici, Autrigones, Vascones, and Callaeci, who are also called Astures.

Three islands belong to Tarraconensian Spain and are called [Note: [Col. 0665D] *Valliaricae*. Labbe: *Balearicae*.] the Balearic Islands. They contain these five cities: Ebusus, [Note: [Col. 0665D] *Palme*. Labbe: *Palene*.] Palma, Pollentia—which is called Majorca—Tomaene, and Mago—which is called Minorca.

Their inhabitants were Canaanites who fled from the presence of Joshua son of Nun; for those who founded Sidon were themselves Canaanites. The Jebusites founded Gades, and they too were likewise fugitives.

The nations and settlements of the Narbonensian Gauls are the Amaxobii—in Greek, “Sarmatians.”

[Col. 0665C] It was necessary for me to explain these things to you as well, so that you might not be ignorant of the names of unfamiliar nations and peoples, or of well-known rivers.

## SECTION VIII

I shall therefore begin to speak of the nations from the East.

The Adiabenians and Taleni lie opposite Arabia; then the Saracens, and other Saracens, the Ataleni, opposite Arabia. The Albanians lie opposite the Caspian Gates. Greater Midian, whose people Moses defeated, lies between Mesopotamia and the Red Sea. Lesser Midian, however, lies opposite the Red Sea beside Egypt, where Raguel, the father-in-law of Moses, who was also called Jethro, reigned.

To the right of the Cappadocians are the Armenians, Iberians, [Note: [Col. 0666D] *Birrani*. Labbe: *Gircani*.] Birrani, Scythians, Colchians, Bosporani, and Sanni, who are called Sannices, extending as far as Pontus; there are Accessus, Absarus, Sebastopolis, Ussilimen, [Col. 0665D] which is a harbor, and the River Phasis. These nations extend as far as Trapezus.

There are twelve renowned mountains: Caucasus, Taurus, Atlas, [Note: [Col. 0666D] *Parnaysus, Citeron*. Labbe: *Parnassus, Cithaeron*.] Parnassus, Cithaeron, Helicon, Parthenius, Nysa, Lycabettus, Penius, Olympus, and Lebanon.

There are forty-one great and renowned rivers: the Indus, which is also called Phison; the Nile, which is also called Geon; the Tigris; Euphrates; Jordan; Cephisus; Tanais; Menos; Erymanthus; Halys; Asopus; Thermodon; Erasinus; Rius; Borysthenes; Alpheus; Taurus; Eurotas; Maeander; Hermus; [Col. 0666A] Axius; Pyramus; Bajus; Hebron; Sangarius; Achelous; Peneus; Evenus; Spercheus; Cayster; Simois; Scamander; Strymon; Parthenius; Ister; Illarius, which is also called the Danube; Rhine; Rhône; Baetis; Eridanus; and Thember, which is now called the Tiber.

Thus the inhabited world was divided into three portions among Noah’s three sons.

Shem the firstborn received the East; Ham, the Mediterranean region; and Japheth, the West. Having shown which nations were created from which son, we must now proceed through the years.

## SECTION IX

Peleg, at the age of 130, begot Reu.

Reu, at the age of 132, begot Serug.

[Col. 0666B] Serug, at the age of 130, begot Nahor.

Nahor, at the age of seventy-nine, begot Terah.

Terah, at the age of seventy, begot Abraham.

Abraham was seventy-five years old when God commanded him to depart from his own land and his father’s house and to come into the land of Canaan.

Thus, from the division of the earth until Abraham came into the land of Canaan, there were five generations, comprising 616 years; from Adam, however, there were twenty generations, comprising 3,387 years.

He lived in Canaan for twenty-five years and begot Isaac.

Isaac, at the age of sixty, begot Jacob.

Jacob, at the age of seventy-six, begot Levi.

Levi, at the age of forty, begot Kohath.

[Col. 0666C] Kohath, at the age of sixty, begot Amram.

Amram, at the age of seventy, begot Aaron.

In Aaron’s eighty-third year the children of Israel departed from Egypt under the leadership of Moses.

Thus the total is 430 years.

The people spent forty years in the wilderness under Moses.

Joshua son of Nun, after crossing the Jordan, spent twenty-seven years in the land: he waged war for seven years, and after taking possession of the land lived twenty years.

Thus, from the time Abraham came into the land of Canaan until the death of Joshua son of Nun, there were seven generations, comprising 500 years; from Adam, however, there were twenty-seven generations, comprising 3,884 years.

## SECTION X

[Col. 0666D] After Joshua’s death, the people sinned and were handed over to Cushan-Rishathaim, king of Mesopotamia, whom they served for eight years. When they cried out to the Lord, Othniel, the younger brother of Caleb, of the tribe of Judah, arose; he declared war upon Cushan-Rishathaim himself and killed him, and he led the people for thirty-one years.

When the people sinned again, they were handed over to Eglon, king of Moab, and served him for eighteen years. When the people repented, Ehud, a man of the tribe of Ephraim, arose; after killing Eglon, he ruled the people for eighty years.

[Col. 0667A] After Ehud’s death, the people transgressed and were handed over to Jabin, king of the Canaanites, whom they served for twenty years. Under him Deborah, the wife of Lapidoth, of the tribe of Ephraim, prophesied; and through her Barak son of Abinoam, of the tribe of Naphtali, led the people. He declared war upon King Jabin and killed him, and he reigned as judge with Deborah for forty years.

After his death, the people sinned and were handed over to the Midianites for seven years. Gideon, of the tribe of Manasseh, rose against them and, with 300 men, destroyed 120,000 of the enemy. He ruled the people for forty years.

His son was Abimelech.

After him Tola, son of Puah, son of Caram, of the tribe of Ephraim, presided over the people for twenty years.

After him Jair the Gileadite, of the tribe of Manasseh, judged [Col. 0667B] and presided over the people for twenty-two years.

After him, the people sinned and were handed over to the Ammonites for eighteen years. When they cried out to the Lord, Jephthah the Gileadite, of the tribe of Gad and the city of Mizpah, arose as their leader and led them for six years.

After him Elon judged for ten years.

After him Hebron son of Allelon the Pirathonite, of the tribe of Ephraim, judged for eight years.

After him, the people sinned and were handed over to the Philistines for forty years.

Afterward, when the children of Israel repented, Samson, son of Manoah, of the tribe of Dan, arose. He made war upon the Philistines and ruled for twenty years.

After him Eli the priest judged for twenty years.

Afterward Samuel the prophet anointed Saul as king, and [Col. 0667C] he himself judged the people for thirty years.

Later, when David was reigning, he brought the ark out of the house of Aminadab and turned aside the calves; and as he was returning, Aminadab’s son, named Uzzah, put forth his hands and was struck down. David was afraid and brought it into the house of Obed-Edom the Gittite, where it remained for three months.

Saul reigned for thirty years. His commander was Abner son of Ner. Samuel himself anointed David as king.

Thus, from Joshua until David returned and assumed the kingship over the tribe of Judah, there were nine generations, comprising 480 years; from Adam, however, there were thirty-four generations and 4,364 years.

## SECTION XI

[Col. 0667D] Thereafter David reigned for forty years and six months.

He reigned in Hebron for seven years and six months, and in Jerusalem for thirty-three years. Under him Abiathar, son of Abimelech and descended from Eli, was priest, as was Zadok, who came from another lineage.

In David’s time Gad and Nathan prophesied. David’s commander was Joab, son of Zeruiah, [Note: [Col. 0667D] “Sister.” Labbe conjectures that one should read “nephew.”] David’s sister. David counted the people, and the number of the children of Israel whom he counted was 1,100,000; the children of Judah numbered 470,000. He did not count Levi and Benjamin. The number of those of Israel who fell was 70,000.

[Col. 0668A] After David, his son Solomon reigned for forty years. Nathan still prophesied under him, as did Ahijah of Shiloh; and Zadok was priest among them.

After Solomon, his son Rehoboam reigned for fourteen years. Under him the kingdom was divided, and Jeroboam, Solomon’s servant, of the tribe of Ephraim, reigned in Samaria. Ahijah the Shilonite and Shemaiah son of Elam prophesied under Jeroboam.

After Rehoboam, his son Abijah reigned for seventeen years.

After Abijah, his son Asa reigned for forty-one years. In his old age he suffered from pain in his feet. Azariah prophesied under him.

After Asa, his son Jehoshaphat reigned for twenty-five years. Under him Elijah, Micaiah son of Imlah, and Obadiah son of Hananiah prophesied. Under Micaiah there was [Col. 0668B] the false prophet Zedekiah son of Chenaanah.

After Jehoshaphat, his son Jehoram reigned for twenty years, and Elijah prophesied under him. After Elijah, Elisha prophesied under Jehoram’s son Ahaziah, under whom the people in Samaria ate their own children and doves’ dung, while Jehoram was reigning in Samaria.

After Jehoram, his son Ahaziah reigned for one year; and under him Gothol and Labdone prophesied.

After him Athaliah, the mother of Ahaziah, reigned for eight years. Rising up, she killed her son’s children, for she was descended from Ahab, king of Israel. But Ahaziah’s sister, named Jehosheba, who was the wife of Jehoiada the priest, secretly carried away Joash, Ahaziah’s son, and Jehoiada the priest placed the government in his hands. Elisha prophesied under Athaliah.

[Col. 0668C] After her, Joash son of Ahaziah reigned for forty years. He killed Zechariah, son of Jehoiada the priest.

After Joash, his son Amaziah reigned for eight years.

After Amaziah, his son Uzziah reigned for fifty-two years. He was leprous until his death. His son Jotham judged in his place. Under Uzziah prophesied Amos, Isaiah his son, Hosea son of Beeri, and Jonah son of Amittai from Gath-hepher.

After Uzziah, his son Jotham reigned for sixteen years. Under him the prophets were Isaiah, Hosea, Micah the Morasthite, and Joel son of Pethuel.

After Jotham, his son Ahaz reigned for fifteen years. Under him the prophets were Isaiah, Hosea, and Micah; Uriah was priest. Under him Shalmaneser, king of the Assyrians, deported those who were in Samaria to Media [Col. 0668D] and Babylonia.

After Ahaz, his son Hezekiah reigned for twenty-five years. Under him the prophets were Isaiah, Micah, and Hosea.

After Hezekiah, his son Manasseh reigned for fifty-five years.

After Manasseh, his son Amon reigned for two years.

After Amon, his son Josiah reigned for thirty-one years. He destroyed the idols and the altar of Samaria. Under him the Passover was celebrated in the eighteenth year of his reign; for from the time Joshua son of Nun died, the Passover had not been observed as it was then. Under him Hilkiah the priest, father of the prophet Jeremiah, found the book of the Law in the sanctuary in the eighteenth year of Josiah’s reign. Also prophesying under him were Huldah, the wife of [Col. 0669A] Shallum, keeper of the priestly vestments; Zephaniah; and Jeremiah, under whom Hananiah was a false prophet.

After Josiah, Zephaniah reigned for five years and eleven months.

After Zephaniah, his son Jehoahaz reigned for four months. Pharaoh Necho, king of Egypt, bound him and brought him into Egypt, appointing Eliakim in his place. Eliakim, who was surnamed Jehoiakim, reigned for eleven years. Under him Jeremiah, Buzi, and Uriah son of Shemaiah from Kiriath-jearim prophesied. Nebuchadnezzar bound Jehoiakim, king of Judah, with bronze chains and led him into Babylon.

After Jehoiakim, his son Jehoiachin reigned for three years. Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, brought him to himself in fetters, together with others.

[Col. 0669B] Through him, Jehoiachin’s brother was appointed in his place; his name was Zedekiah, also called Jeconiah, and he reigned for eleven years.

In the twelfth year he deported him to Babylon after putting out his eyes, and removed the people with him except for a few who later went down into Egypt. Jeremiah and Habakkuk prophesied under Zedekiah; in the ninth year of his reign Ezekiel prophesied in Babylonia. After him came the prophets Nahum, Malachi, and Daniel, who saw the vision concerning the weeks in the first year of King Darius, son of Ahasuerus, of Median descent, who reigned over the kingdom of the Chaldaeans.

In the first year of his reign Cyrus permitted the people to return to Jerusalem. At the time when the Temple was being built, Haggai and Zechariah prophesied together. [Col. 0669C] After them Nehemiah son of Hachaliah, of Israelite descent, rebuilt the city of Jerusalem in the years of King Artaxerxes; after him came the second Mordecai.

## SECTION XII

Thus, from David to the deportation of Zedekiah, who is also called Jeconiah, there were eighteen generations, comprising 478 years and nine months; from Adam to the Babylonian deportation under Jeconiah, however, there were fifty-one generations, comprising 4,842 years and nine months.

After the Babylonian deportation until the generation of Christ there were fourteen generations and 660 years; from the generation of Christ until the Passion, thirty years; and from the Passion to the present year, which is the thirteenth year of Alexander’s reign, 206 years.

[Col. 0669D] Thus the total from Adam to the thirteenth year of Emperor Alexander is 5,738 years.

But so that we may also demonstrate this in another way—not only through the periods of the kings, but also by counting the years from the time the Passover was observed—we shall set them out together:

From Adam to the Flood: 2,242 years.

From the Flood until Abraham’s departure from his land: 1,145 years.

From then until the Israelites departed from Egypt under the leadership of Moses, when they also celebrated the Passover: 430 years.

[Col. 0670A] From the Exodus from Egypt until the crossing of the Jordan, when Joshua celebrated the Passover: forty-one years.

After 464 years Hezekiah celebrated the Passover.

After Hezekiah, Josiah celebrated the Passover in the 114th year.

After Josiah, Ezra celebrated the Passover after 108 years.

After Ezra, [Note: [Col. 0669D] “Of the Savior.” The italicized words are supplied from Labbe’s edition.] until the generation of Christ the Savior, the Passover was celebrated after 563 years.

Thirty years after the generation of Christ, when the Lord suffered, the Passover was celebrated; for he himself was the rightful Passover.

From the Passion of the Lord until the thirteenth year of the reign of Emperor Alexander Caesar, the Passover was observed for 206 years—the Passover that we observe in commemoration of [Col. 0670B] our Lord Jesus Christ.

Thus the total number of years from Adam to the present day is five thousand seven hundred and thirty-eight.

## SECTION XIII. The Kings of Persia from the Time of Cyrus

Cyrus reigned over the Persians for thirty years. After him, Cambyses reigned for nine years; Smerdis the Magus, eight months; Darius, thirty-six years; Xerxes, twenty-six years; Artaxerxes Longimanus, thirty-six years; Xerxes, sixty days; Sogdianus, seven months; [Col. 0670C] Darius Nothus, eighteen years; Artaxerxes, brother of Cyrus the Younger, sixty-two years; Ochus, who was also called Artaxerxes, thirty-three years and seven months; Arses Nothus, three years; and Darius, twelve years. This is the Darius whom Alexander the Macedonian deposed in a battle that defies description. The total is 245 years.

After these rulers, chronology among the Greeks becomes clear through the reckoning of the Olympiads. Up to Alexander the Macedonian there were 114 Olympiads, amounting to 456 years from Iphitus, who instituted the Olympiads.

From Alexander to Christ there were eighty Olympiads, amounting to 320 years.

[Col. 0670D] From Christ to the thirteenth year of Alexander’s reign there were fifty-eight Olympiads, amounting to 236 years.

Thus, up to the thirteenth year of Alexander Caesar, there were altogether 253 Olympiads, amounting to 1,012 years.

## SECTION XIV. The Names of the Creation

Adam, Seth, Enos, Cainan, Mahalaleel, Jared, Enoch, Methuselah, Lamech, Noah, Shem, Arphaxad, Salah, Heber, Peleg—under whom the earth was divided—Reu, Serug, Nahor, Terah, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Judah, Perez, Hezron, [Col. 0671A] Aram, Aminadab, Nahshon, Salmon, Boaz, Obed, Jesse, David, Solomon, Rehoboam, Abijah, Asa, Jehoshaphat, Jehoram, Ahaziah, Joash, Amaziah, Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, Hezekiah, Manasseh, Amon, Josiah.

Josiah begot Johanan, Jehoiakim, and their brothers; Eliakim, who is also called Jehoiakim; and Zedekiah, who is also called Jeconiah and was named Shallum.

At the time of the Babylonian deportation, Jehoiakim begot Jeconiah and Zedekiah. Jeconiah begot Shealtiel, Fanneas and Sale, Saer and Jeconiah, Ortamno and Deebi and Filifania, Zerubbabel and his brothers Abiud, Meshullam, and Hananiah, and their sister Shelomith, and Sedbel, Thoul, Archia, Asadia, and Sobesec.

The sanctuary was rebuilt in the time of Zerubbabel, whose son was Abiud; then came Eliakim, Azor, [Col. 0671B] Zadok, Achim, Eliud, Eleazar, Matthan, Jacob, and Joseph, to whom the Virgin Mary was betrothed; she bore Jesus Christ by the Holy Spirit.

## SECTION XV. The Names of the Prophets

Adam, Noah, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, Aaron, Joshua son of Nun, Eldad and Medad, Nathan, David, Solomon, Elmodac, Ahijah the Shilonite, Shemaiah son of Elam, Hananiah, Elijah, Micaiah son of Imlah, Obadiah, Elisha, Abladan, Amos, Isaiah, Hosea son of Beeri, Jonah, Micah, Raban, Joel son of Pethuel, Jeremiah son of Hilkiah the priest, Zephaniah, Buzi, Ezekiel, Uriah, Shemaiah, Habakkuk, Nahum, Daniel, Malachi, Haggai, Zechariah, and, under Christ, Simeon [Col. 0671C] and John the Baptist.

Likewise, the women who were prophetesses: Sarah, Rebecca, Miriam the sister of Moses, Deborah, Huldah, and, under Christ, Anna, Elizabeth, and Mary, who bore Christ.

## SECTION XVI. The Names of the Kings

Saul, of the tribe of Benjamin.

After the kingship was transferred to the tribe of Judah: David, Solomon, Rehoboam, Abijah, Asa, Jehoshaphat, Jehoram, Ahaziah, Jotham, Ahaz, Hezekiah, Manasseh, Amon, Josiah, Jehoiakim, Eliakim, Zedekiah, and Jeconiah. Under the last of these, the deportation by Nebuchadnezzar took place.

The names of the kings who reigned in Samaria over the ten tribes from the time the kingdom was divided:

[Col. 0671D] Jeroboam son of Nebat, twenty-two years.

Nabath his son, two years.

Baasha son of Ahijah, twenty-four years. He took vengeance upon the house of Jeroboam.

Elah son of Baasha, two years.

Zimri, twelve years.

Ahab his son, twenty-two years.

Ahaziah son of Ahab, and Jehoram son of Jeconiah, twelve years. Under him those who were in Samaria ate their own children and doves’ dung.

Jehu son of Nimshi, twenty-eight years. At the beginning he was devout; he exacted vengeance upon the house of Ahab by killing Jehoram, Jezebel, and Ahaziah, king of Judah.

Jehoahaz, seventeen years.

[Col. 0672A] Joash his son, sixteen years. He killed King Amaziah and tore down 400 cubits of the wall of Jerusalem.

Jeroboam son of Joash, fifteen years.

Azariah son of Jeroboam, three months.

Shallum son of Abiah, one month.

Unornane son of Gadi, ten years.

Pekahiah son of Menahem, two years.

Pekah son of Remaliah, ten years. He besieged Jerusalem while Ahaz was reigning but did not take it.

Hoshea son of Elah, eight years. Under him the ten tribes were deported into the land of the Medes by Shalmaneser, who also took Hoshea himself away in chains, while Ahaz was reigning over the two tribes in Jerusalem.

## SECTION XVII. The Names of the Priests

[Col. 0672B]

Aaron begot Eleazar, Phinehas, Ahijah, Razaza, Moriat, Arnaria, Ahitub, Settis, and Achivas; the son of the last was Elijah the prophet. Then came Shallum, Joram, Amos son of Jehoiada, Zedekiah, Zedekiah, Jehel, Uriah, Tieem, and Shallum, who begot Hilkiah, whose son was Jeremiah the prophet; and Azariah son of Azazae, Sareu, and Jehozadak, who begot Joshua, who was priest when the Temple was restored after the captivity; then Hilkiah, Joiakim, and Caedue.

Likewise, there was another lineage from which came Ezekiel the prophet: Jode, Fatuea, Amorius, Zadiar, Samuel, Evexia, Melchius, Shallum, Comorius, Barracim, Zephaniah, Maxses, Hilkiah, Buzi, and Ezekiel.

Likewise, there was another lineage from which came Eli the priest, whose sons Phinehas and Hophni seized the sacrificial offerings. The head [Col. 0672C] of the lineage descended from the sons of Gad was Ahimelech, followed by Abiathar, Urin, Nathan, and Eli.

Likewise, there was the Levitical lineage from which came Samuel the prophet: Korah, who opposed Moses; his son Elkanah; then Zuph, Abiar, Zeraam, Chelchanu, and Samuel. Samuel had two sons who accepted bribes, Joel and Abijah.

The beginning of the lineage of the Levites, from whom come the priests, ministers, and Levites, is as follows: Amram son of Kohath, son of Levi, son of Jacob. Levi begot Gershon, Kohath, and Merari. The sons of Gershon were Shimei and Emeher. These were sons of Levi.

The sons of Kohath were Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel. Amram begot Moses, Aaron, and Miriam. By Elisheba, the sister of Nahshon, Aaron begot Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar. [Col. 0672D] Nadab and Abihu died while offering profane fire. After Aaron, Eleazar received the priesthood; after Eleazar, Phinehas. Ithamar also had a son.

Izhar, the brother of Amram, was himself a Levite. His sons were Korah, Nepheg, and Zichri; the sons of Korah were Assir, Elkanah, and Abiasaph. This Korah opposed Moses and Aaron and was swallowed up with Chao at Viriseel.

Hebron, the brother of Amram, [begot] Aercius; his sons were Mishael, Elizaphan, Setis, and Dile. These Levites were assigned for service.

Aaron and all his sons were assigned to the Ark of the Covenant, to minister before it and carry it. The tithe was made their portion, consecrated to the priests, together with the firstborn, [Note: [Col. 0672D] “And the things … firstborn.” These words are absent from Labbe.] the things established for sacrifices, and what belonged to the firstborn and was designated for the Levites. [Col. 0673A] The law prescribed that, from whatever they received from the people in tithes, they should give a tithe to the priests, so that it might be reckoned to them as an offering.

At their institution six cities of refuge were also given to them, together with pasturelands suitable for sowing, extending two thousand cubits around each city, and forty-two other cities: ten to the priests and thirteen to the Levites.

I think we have spoken at greater length than we had expected. These matters are nevertheless necessary for those who wish to inquire more scrupulously and who have read widely; I believe that they will readily understand what has been written. Those who have read little, however, may also arrive more easily at understanding through the matters that we have explained in this abbreviated inquiry.

## SECTION XVIII. The Kings of the Macedonians According to the Alexandrians

[Col. 0673B]

Alexander, son of Philip, after Darius, 7 years. Ptolemy, father-in-law of Lagus, 52 years. Ptolemy his son, Philadelphus, 38 years. Ptolemy his son, Euergetes, 30 years. Ptolemy, son of Euergetes, 25 years. Ptolemy Philopator, 17 years. Ptolemy his brother, 23 years. Ptolemy Physcon, 2 years. Euergetes, 26 years. Ptolemy Alexas, 20 years. Alexander, brother of Ptolemy Alexas, 18 years. Ptolemy Dionysius, 29 years. Cleopatra his daughter, 25 years. Altogether they make 346 years.

The following material is absent from Canisius.

## SECTION XIX. Emperors of the Romans

[Col. 0673C]

Augustus, 57 years. Tiberius, 22 years, 7 months, 23 days. Gaius, 3 years, 9 months. [Col. 0674A] Claudius, 13 years, 1 month, 28 days. Nero, 13 years, 8 months, 28 days. Galba, 5 months, 26 days. Otho, 8 months, 7 days. Vitellius, 9 months, 15 days. Titus, 3 years, 2 months, 2 days. Trajan, 17 years, 8 months, 6 days. Hadrian, 20 years, 10 months, 28 days. [Col. 0673]

### LETTERS OF THE ROMAN AND CARTHAGINIAN CONFESSORS (C, S)

### LETTER OF CELERINUS TO LUCIANUS

(Pamelius, Rigaltius, Baluze, Paris, XX; Oxford, Leipzig, XXI.)

[Col. 0673C]

The **summary** of this and the following letter is given in Cyprian’s Letter XXII:

“I have also sent you,” he says, “copies of the letter that Celerinus, that good and steadfast confessor, wrote to Lucianus, likewise a confessor, and of Lucianus’s reply to him, so that you might know both our labor and diligence in every matter and learn the truth itself: how God-fearing Celerinus the confessor is, how cautious, and how modest through humility and fear of our sect; whereas Lucianus, as I have said, is less skilled in understanding the Lord’s reading and, through his ready compliance, is troublesome in leaving our modesty exposed to ill will. [Col. 0673D] For although the Lord said that the nations were to be baptized in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, and that sins were forgiven in Baptism, this man, ignorant of the commandment and the law, directs that peace be granted and sins forgiven in [Col. 0674C] Paul’s name, and says that Paul commissioned him to do this—as you will observe in the letter written by that same Lucianus to Celerinus,” etc.

To avoid excessively breaking up Baluze’s work, we relegated this and the following letters to the Cyprianic Letters in volume IV; nevertheless, because of the precise chronology, we have recalled them here in their proper place. See below, vol. IV, col. 274.

(Pamelius, XIX; Rigaltius, Baluze, Paris, XVIII; Oxford, Leipzig, XXIV.)

(See below, vol. IV, col. 271.)

### LETTER OF THE PRESBYTERS MOSES AND MAXIMUS, THE DEACONS NICOSTRATUS AND RUFINUS, AND THE OTHER CONFESSORS PERSEVERING IN THE FAITH OF THE TRUTH AND RESIDING AT ROME, TO CYPRIAN

(Pamelius, Rigaltius, Baluze, XXVI; Paris, XXV; Oxford, Leipzig, XXXI.)

[Col. 0675B]

The **summary** of this letter is recited below in Novatian’s letter written in the name of the Roman clergy:

“Although,” they say, “you also have the letter of the confessors whom the dignity of their confession still confines here in prison, and whose faith has already once crowned them for the evangelical contest in a glorious confession—a letter agreeing with our own, in which they upheld the strictness of evangelical discipline and rejected unlawful petitions as incompatible with the Church’s honor.”

The Roman confessors gratefully acknowledge the consolations they received from Cyprian’s letter.—Martyrdom is not punishment but blessedness.—The words of the Gospel are torches for kindling faith. [Col. 0676A] Cyprian’s judgment in the case of the lapsed is accepted.

It is mentioned in Cyprian’s Letter XXXII, and you have it in full below, vol. IV, col. 290.

### LETTER OF THE PRESBYTERS AND DEACONS RESIDING AT ROME TO CYPRIAN

(Pamelius, Rigaltius, Baluze, XXX; Paris, XXIX; Oxford, Leipzig, XXXVI.)

**Summary.—**The Roman Church sets forth its judgment concerning the lapsed, a judgment agreeing with the decrees of the Church of Carthage.—The indulgence extended to the lapsed must be measured according to the standard of the Gospel.—That the peace granted by the confessors rests only upon grace and favor is clear from the fact that the lapsed are referred to the bishops.—The seditious demand for peace is attributed to the faction of Felicissimus.

[Col. 0676B] (See below, vol. IV, col. 303.)

### LETTER II OF CALDONIUS, WITH HERCULANUS AND VICTOR, TO THE CLERGY OF CARTHAGE

(Pamelius, Rigaltius, Baluze, XXXIX; Paris, XXXVIII; Oxford, Leipzig, XLII.)

**Summary.—**Caldonius, Herculanus, and the others carry out what Cyprian had commanded them in his Letter XXXVII, and notify the clergy that Felicissimus has been excluded, adding the names of those who had joined him. It is an ancient form of a letter of excommunication.

# PROLEGOMENA

## ARTICLE I. HISTORY OF THE LIFE OF ST. CORNELIUS

[Col. 0677C]

### I

Decius, especially hostile to the priests of God, as Cyprian puts it, [Note: [Col. 0677D] Cyprian, Letter LII, p. 168, Venice edition, 1758.] took care that no successor should be appointed to Fabian at Rome. Because he prevented it, the Roman see remained vacant for sixteen months and fourteen days, from the beginning of the year 250—when Fabian was crowned with martyrdom on January 20, or the thirteenth day before the Kalends of February—until the year 251. During this interregnum the government of that Church rested with the Roman clergy, who also sent Cyprian an eloquent letter concerning the case of the lapsed. [Note: [Col. 0677D] See Cyprian’s Letter XXXI, cited in that edition.]

Taking advantage of Decius’s absence, Cornelius was elected on Wednesday, June 4, 251, by the common consent of the Roman clergy. [Col. 0677D] Concerning his ordination, Cyprian wrote the following to Antonianus, who had become somewhat anxious and wavering on that same subject because of Novatian’s letters: [Note: [Col. 0677D] Cyprian, Letter LII, pp. 165 ff.]

“I now come, dearest brother, to the person of our colleague Cornelius, so that you may know the true Cornelius with us—not from the falsehoods of malicious detractors, but from the judgment of the Lord God, who made him bishop, and from the testimony of his fellow bishops, whose entire number throughout the whole world has agreed in harmonious unanimity. For what commends our dearest Cornelius to God and Christ and his Church, and likewise to all his fellow priests, with praiseworthy testimony, is that he did not attain the episcopate suddenly, but was promoted through all the ecclesiastical offices, often merited the Lord’s favor in divine ministries, and ascended through every grade of religion to the sublime summit of the priesthood. Then, moreover, he neither sought nor desired the episcopate, nor did he seize it, as others do whom the swelling of arrogance and pride inflates; rather, he was quiet and modest, like those who are customarily chosen by God for this office. Because of the modesty of his virginal conscience and his innate and carefully preserved humility, he did not, as some do, use force in order to become bishop; instead, force was used upon him, so that under compulsion he accepted the episcopate. He was made bishop by very many of our colleagues who were then present in the city of Rome and who sent us honorable and commendatory letters concerning his ordination, distinguished by the testimony of their praise. Cornelius, moreover, was made bishop by the judgment of God and his Christ; by the testimony of almost all the clergy; by the vote of the people then present; and by the assembly of ancient priests and good men—when no one had been appointed before him, when Fabian’s place, that is, Peter’s place and the rank of the priestly chair, was vacant.”

Thus Cyprian speaks of Cornelius’s election, to which sixteen bishops assembled from the nearer provinces agreed together with the Roman clergy, as did two who had come to the city from Africa, namely Pompeius and Stephanus. Hence the same Cyprian says to Antonianus concerning the number of bishops who had approved Cornelius’s ordination: “Unless, perhaps, you regard as a bishop the man who, though a bishop had already been appointed in the Church [Col. 0679A] by sixteen fellow bishops, strives to be made an adulterous and alien bishop by deserters”—that is, by Novatian’s supporters. [Note: [Col. 0679D] Cyprian, passage cited.]

Cyprian argues that Cornelius was adorned with outstanding merits and virtues from the very fact that, while Decius was still alive, he undertook the government of the Roman Church:

“Indeed, after he had accepted an episcopate that was neither canvassed for nor extorted, but assumed by the will of God, who makes priests, what courage there was in the episcopate he had undertaken! What strength of spirit! What firmness of faith! We ought both to perceive this thoroughly with an undivided heart and to praise it: he sat fearlessly at Rome in the priestly chair at a time when a tyrant hostile to God’s priests was threatening things speakable and unspeakable, when that tyrant would have heard far more patiently and tolerantly that a rival prince had arisen against him than that a priest of God had been appointed at Rome.”

Cyprian therefore declares that even before his martyrdom Cornelius was already a martyr in intention.

### II

Anastasius the Librarian—or whoever preceded him—writes that Cornelius was Roman by nationality and born to a father named Castinus. Certain copies of the *Acts* agree with him, as does, regarding his Roman origin, the *Catalogue of the Roman Pontiffs* from the library of the Most Serene Queen of Sweden, published by Henschenius before volume I for April. Perhaps, then, he was descended from the Cornelian gens, that most celebrated of Roman families, as Francis Blanchinus judged—on the basis, I suppose, of Cornelius’s name—in his historical notes on the aforementioned librarian.

St. Cyprian, in the repeatedly cited Letter to Antonianus, is an irrefragable witness that Cornelius ascended to the summit of the supreme pontificate through all the ecclesiastical orders and through distinguished services to the Church. Yet we find his deeds recounted by no one. Nevertheless, since he belonged to the Roman clergy, a share—and perhaps no small share—of the outstanding actions performed by that clergy during that calamitous tempest in the Church, while the Chair of St. Peter stood vacant after Fabian’s martyrdom, must undoubtedly be attributed to him. Various letters among Cyprian’s survive, from which it is evident with how much zeal that clergy cared not only for the Roman diocese but also for that of Carthage and others. [Note: [Col. 0679D] See Cyprian’s Letters XXX, XXXI, and XXXII.]

Novatian, a Roman presbyter, at the instigation of Novatus, a presbyter of Carthage, slandered Cornelius as though he had been irregularly created bishop of Rome. [Col. 0679D] He acted so cunningly and maliciously that he drew certain confessors over to his side and, through three bishops compelled partly by fraud and partly by force, was secretly ordained bishop of Rome, thus initiating the first schism in the Roman Church. For this reason Cornelius summoned a council of sixty bishops to Rome in the year 251, condemned Novatian and his followers with anathema, and decreed that confessors who had lapsed should be admitted to reconciliation and penance. At this council the case of the lapsed was concluded by a definitive judgment, and it was established that the lapsed should not be admitted to communion [Col. 0680A] unless they had completed a prolonged and full penance; yet assistance was to be given them in the supreme crisis of life, and absolution and communion were not to be denied them.

The author of the *Pontifical Book* relates that this same pontiff transferred the bodies of Saints Peter and Paul from the catacombs. [Note: [Col. 0680D] This translation is regarded as uncertain by Baronius at the year 221, §3; Pagius at the same year, §3; and Blanchinus in his notes on Anastasius the Librarian, vol. II, p. 205.] He adds at the end that Cornelius was exiled to Centumcellae and that his face was battered with lead-weighted scourges by order of Decius. [Note: [Col. 0680D] This kind of instrument of torture was like a whip made of cords, at the ends of which leaden balls were fastened. Baronius on the *Roman Martyrology*, June 6; Gallonius, *On the Tortures of the Martyrs*, p. 204.]

During Cornelius’s pontificate, not only did the storm of persecution—which had seemed to be extinguished by the death of Decius—rise anew under Gallus and Volusianus and buffet the Church, but a twofold schism also disturbed it. The first, led by Novatus of Carthage and Novatian, the Roman presbyter, especially troubled the Roman Church. The second, although originally incited by the same Novatus, was led by Felicissimus and, being wholly opposed to the errors of the Novatians, disturbed the Church of God in Africa. For just as the Novatians, with detestable severity, contended that all hope of pardon must be utterly denied to the lapsed, so the others, with equally damnable indulgence, from the very first day of the persecution—while the recent crimes of the offenders were still burning hot, and not only the devil’s altars but even the hands and mouths of the lapsed themselves were still smoking from their abominable sacrifices—did not cease to communicate with the lapsed and to obstruct the performance of penance, as Cyprian testifies in Letter LV to Cornelius.

When Felicissimus saw that he had been condemned by the African bishops assembled in council, he sailed to Rome, hoping to steal back in the Roman Church the right of communion from which he had fallen, and attempted to deceive the holy Cornelius, the Supreme Pontiff. [Col. 0680C] But he obtained nothing except confirmation of his condemnation, as is clear from the above-cited letter of St. Cyprian.

### III

At the very beginning of the persecution in the year 252, Cornelius, the Roman pontiff, was banished by the emperor Gallus to Centumcellae (Civitavecchia). Cyprian commends his constancy in the faith in the highest terms in his letters: [Note: [Col. 0680D] Cyprian, Letter LVI.]

“We have learned, dearest brother,” he says, “of the glorious testimonies to your faith and courage, and have received the honor of your confession with such exultation that we count ourselves also participants and companions in your merits and praises.”

And after much more:

“There the courage of the bishop leading the way was publicly proved, and the unity of the brotherhood following him was displayed. While among you there is one mind and one voice, the whole Roman Church has confessed. The faith that the blessed Apostle proclaimed concerning you has shone brightly, dearest brothers.”

These and many other words Cyprian wrote to Cornelius, who, worn out by the hardships and labors of exile, died there as a martyr shortly afterward, on September 14:

“After this,” says the *Pontifical of Damasus*, “he was expelled to Centumcellae, and there received his repose with glory.”

Jerome teaches the day of his death when he says of Cyprian: [Note: [Col. 0681D] Jerome, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, in the *Catalogue*, chapter 67.]

“He suffered in the eighth persecution, under Valerian and Gallienus, on the same day as Cornelius at Rome, though not in the same year.”

That is, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of October, the day on which Cyprian is known to have been crowned with martyrdom and on which the memory of both men is celebrated.

### IV

By what kind of death or punishment the holy pontiff died is wholly unknown. For the *Acts* that report his martyrdom at Rome under Decius prove nothing at all concerning these matters, since learned men reject them as spurious. The author of the most ancient catalogue of pontiffs says only that at Centumcellae he “received his repose with glory.” Some have therefore believed that he died a natural rather than a violent death, though one hastened by the hardships of exile and perhaps also of imprisonment, and that he is therefore rightly venerated by the Church as a martyr.

Nevertheless, weighty testimonies are not lacking which suggest that the ambiguous phrase, “he received his repose with glory,” should be understood of a martyrdom consummated by capital punishment. First, St. Cyprian in Letter LVIII to St. Lucius, Cornelius’s successor, expressly calls him a blessed martyr. He does the same in Letter LVII to St. Stephen, likewise pope:

“The glorious honor of our predecessors, the blessed martyrs Cornelius and Lucius, must be preserved. . . . For they, filled with the Spirit of God and established in glorious martyrdom, judged that peace ought to be granted to the lapsed.”

Eusebius agrees in the *Chronicle*, saying:

“Cornelius was the twentieth to assume the episcopate of the Roman Church after Fabian’s glorious death, and held it for two years; he too was crowned with martyrdom.”

St. Pacianus, in Letter II to Sympronianus, implies with sufficient clarity that St. Cornelius was put to death. St. Jerome speaks still more clearly in the *Life of St. Paul the Hermit*, vol. IV of the *Works*, Paris edition, part 2, col. 69:

“Cornelius at Rome and Cyprian at Carthage endured martyrdom in blessed blood.”

Prosper likewise speaks clearly in the complete *Chronicle*:

“Cornelius was the twentieth to assume the episcopate of the Roman Church after Fabian’s glorious death, and held it for two years; after two years he was crowned with the same martyrdom.”

### V

“Eusebius says that Cornelius held the episcopate [Note: [Col. 0681D] Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VII, chapter 2.] ‘for about three years,’ but in the *Chronicle*, with which Jerome agrees, [Note: [Col. 0681D] Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 66.] ‘for two years.’ In the *Pontifical Book* it is ‘three years and ten days’; in the Corbie manuscript, as in the Bucherian catalogue, ‘two years, three months, and ten days’; in the Fossés manuscript, now the Colbert manuscript, as also in Bollandus from the manuscript formerly belonging to the queen of Sweden and now in the Vatican, he is said to have held the pontificate for ‘one year, two months, and three days.’

“Antonius Pagius observes, however, that the aforementioned Bucherian catalogue—which says that Cornelius sat ‘two years, three months, and ten days, from the consulates of Decius IV and Decius II until Gallus and Volusianus’—is corrupt both in specifying the years of Cornelius’s pontificate and in designating the consulships of the Decii. For there was neither a fourth consulship of the elder Decius nor a second of the younger Decius. It is certain from the consular lists that Gallus and Volusianus succeeded Decius Augustus in his second or third consulship and Decius Caesar in his first. Therefore the catalogue just mentioned should have ascribed not two years but one year to Cornelius.

“Consequently, the aforementioned Pagius judges that it should be corrected by substituting ‘one year, under the consulship of Decius III and Decius’ for the words ‘two years, under the consulship of Decius IV and Decius II.’ It follows that if Cornelius sat for one year, as that catalogue states, together with ‘three months’ and ‘ten days,’ and if trustworthy monuments attest that he was crowned with martyrdom ‘under the consulship of Gallus and Volusianus’—that is, in the year of Christ 252—on September 14, then he entered the pontificate on June 4 in the year of Christ 251.”

“This opinion also commended itself to the learned Tillemont, [Note: [Col. 0682D] Tillemont, *Memoir on St. Cornelius*, vol. III, article 13, p. 351.] who further concludes from several arguments that Cornelius was certainly not ordained before Easter Day in 251. It is probable that, not long after Decius had departed from the city for the expedition against the Goths—which occurred around springtime in 251—the Roman clergy and people took the opportunity to assemble and agreed upon the election of Cornelius.

“And these words of Cyprian concerning Decius [Note: [Col. 0682D] Cyprian, passage cited, no. 19.]—‘he would hear more tolerably that a rival prince had arisen against him than that a priest of God had been appointed at Rome’—may be interpreted to mean that the tyrant learned in the same report both that Julius Valens had usurped imperial power and that Cornelius had been chosen bishop of the city. Julius, moreover, assumed the purple around May 251 and was killed not long afterward.

“Finally, Eusebius can be reconciled both with this view and with himself as follows: when he writes that Cornelius held the episcopate ‘for about three years,’ he intended to reckon the period between Fabian’s death and that of Cornelius; but when he teaches that Cornelius sat ‘for two years,’ he counted one completed year and part of a second as two.”

Thus far our Coustant. [Note: [Col. 0682D] Coustant, *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, p. 123.] See also the historical commentary of Constantine Suysken, most distinguished among the Bollandists, on St. Cornelius, Pope and Martyr, §§II, III, and IV, and especially §XII, pp. 177 ff., volume IV for September.

## ARTICLE II. WRITINGS OF ST. CORNELIUS, POPE AND MARTYR

[Col. 0682D]

### I

The holy pontiff is said to have committed to writing many monuments of his apostolic solicitude, the greater part of which have nevertheless perished. [Note: [Col. 0682D] This and what follows are taken from Gallandius, *Great Library of the Ancient Fathers*, vol. III, Prologue, p. 35, chapter VII.] Eusebius speaks of them as follows: [Note: [Col. 0682D] Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VI, chapter 48.]

Ἦλθον δ᾽ οὖν εἰς ἡμᾶς ἐπιστόλαι Κορνηλίου Ῥωμαίων [Col. 0683A] ἐπισκόπου πρὸς τὸν τῆς Ἀντιοχέων ἐκκλησίας Φάβιον.—Ταύταις ἄλλη τις ἐπιστολὴ συνήπτο τοῦ Κορνηλίου περὶ τῶν κατὰ τὴν σύνοδον ἀρεσάντων, καὶ πάλιν ἑτέρα περὶ τῶν κατὰ Νοούατον πραχθέντων.

That is, in Valesius’s translation:

“Letters of Cornelius, bishop of the Romans, sent to Fabius, prelate of the Church of Antioch, still survive.”—“Appended to these was another letter by the same Cornelius concerning the decisions made at the synod, and again another concerning the crimes of Novatus.”

On this passage the learned Cotelerius observes [Note: [Col. 0683D] Cotelerius on chapter 3 of St. Polycarp’s Letter.] that by the words ἐπιστόλαι Κορνηλίου (“letters of Cornelius”), Eusebius meant only a single letter of Cornelius. Jerome, too, certainly perceived this. For when, following Eusebius, he includes Cornelius among the ecclesiastical writers, he says: [Note: [Col. 0683D] Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 66.]

“Cornelius, bishop of the city of Rome, [Col. 0683B] wrote to Fabius, bishop of the Church of Antioch.”

The distinguished scholar establishes the point by adducing several examples of expressions of this kind. Learned interpreters of Scripture have observed, he says, with reference to the books of Maccabees, that “letters” may be said even of a single letter. Thus St. Polycarp, addressing the Philippians, says according to the ancient translator: [Note: [Col. 0683D] Polycarp, *Letter to the Philippians*, chapter 3.]

“Neither I nor any other person like me will be able to follow the wisdom of the blessed and glorious Paul . . . who, even when absent, wrote letters to you”:

ὃς καὶ ἀπὼν ὑμῖν ἔγραψεν ἐπιστολάς.

Yet shortly afterward, according to the same translator, that holy bishop of Smyrna is found to mention only one letter of Paul addressed to the Philippians:

“You who are,” he says, [Note: [Col. 0683D] The same work, chapter 11.] “at the beginning of his letter.”

Another example is available from Eusebius himself, whose words are: [Note: [Col. 0683D] Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VI, chapter 11.]

Μνημονεύει γέτοι [Col. 0683C] καὶ αὐτὸς ὁ Ἀλέξανδρος ἐν ἰδίαις ἐπιστολαῖς ταῖς πρὸς Ἀντινοΐτας εἰς ἔτι νῦν παρ᾽ ἡμῖν σωζομέναις τῆς Ναρκίσσου σὺν αὐτῷ προεδρίας, κατὰ ταῦτα λέξιν ἐπὶ τέλει γράφων τῆς αὐτῆς ἐπιστολῆς—

“Alexander himself, moreover, in his own letters to the people of Antinoë, which are still preserved among us, mentions that Narcissus shared the episcopal presidency with him, writing as follows at the end of that same letter.”

St. Jerome, encompassing this briefly, renders it as follows: [Note: [Col. 0683D] Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 62.]

“He”—Alexander—“at the end of a certain letter that he writes to the people of Antinoë concerning the peace of the Church,” etc.

For, to use the words of the learned scholar, [Note: [Col. 0684D] Smith, scholium on St. Polycarp’s Letter, p. 110.] it is common usage among authors of every kind that, when speaking of a single letter, dialogue, or book, they sometimes employ the plural number.

### III

Furthermore, regarding the cited passage of Eusebius, it should be observed with his learned translator that the historian of Caesarea lists only three letters of Cornelius: the first to Fabius, bishop of Antioch, concerning the Roman synod and the agreement of the bishops of Italy and Africa; [Col. 0683D] the second concerning the synod’s decrees; and the third, addressed to the same Fabius, bishop of the city of Antioch, concerning the crimes of Novatian, from which Eusebius has preserved for us a most illuminating excerpt.

Jerome, however, enumerates four: [Note: [Col. 0684D] Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 66.]

“Cornelius,” he says, “bishop of the city of Rome, to whom eight letters of Cyprian survive, wrote a letter to Fabius, bishop of the Church of Antioch, concerning the Roman, Italian, and African synod; another concerning Novatian and those who had lapsed; [Col. 0684A] a third concerning the proceedings of the synod; and a fourth, very lengthy letter to the same Fabius, containing the causes and condemnation of the Novatian heresy.”

But, as Cotelerius observes after Valesius, [Note: [Col. 0684D] Cotelerius, passage cited.] the greatest doctor seems to have been otherwise occupied when he examined the passage of Eusebius. For after mentioning Cornelius’s first letter to Fabius of Antioch, Eusebius immediately adds:

“Other letters besides these survive, composed in the Latin language by Cyprian and by the other bishops who had assembled with him in Africa. From these it is gathered that they too approved the granting of assistance to those who had fallen into temptation, and that the author of the impious opinion, together with those who had defected to his party, should deservedly be excluded from the fellowship of the Catholic Church.”

After reporting these matters, Eusebius mentions Cornelius’s second letter, [Col. 0684B] concerning the decisions made at the synod—namely, the Roman synod. Therefore the letter that St. Jerome cites in second place must be ascribed not to Cornelius but to Cyprian. Nor, moreover, does Rufinus appear to have understood Eusebius’s words correctly, since he himself interprets what the bishop of Caesarea relates about Cornelius’s second letter as referring to the first, addressed to Fabius, bishop of Antioch.

### IV

What concerns us more, however, says the most learned Gallandius, [Note: [Col. 0684D] Gallandius, *Great Library of the Holy Fathers*, vol. III, Prolegomena, chapter 6, no. 4, p. 23.] is to observe with the learned translator of Eusebius that the first and third of Cornelius’s letters were written in Greek by that holy pontiff.

“For,” says Valesius, “although Eusebius adduces many testimonies from the third letter, he nowhere says that they were translated from Latin into Greek—something he is nevertheless always accustomed to note whenever he cites the testimony of a Latin author, for example when he quotes passages from Tertullian’s *Apologeticum* or letters of the Roman emperors.”

Furthermore, Eusebius himself sufficiently indicates here that Cornelius’s first letter to Fabius was written in Greek. For after mentioning it, he adds that another letter, written in Latin by Cyprian, was attached to it. He certainly would not have added this unless the previously mentioned letter of Cornelius had been written in a different language. These considerations are sufficiently pertinent, and this opinion is approved by the most learned men. [Note: [Col. 0684D] Bollandus, *Acts of the Saints*, September, vol. IV, p. 180; Coustant, *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, p. 145, vol. I, note a; and Mansi, *Most Extensive Collection of Councils*, vol. I, col. 817, note 1.]

### V

In addition to these letters composed in Greek, St. Cornelius also wrote several letters to St. Cyprian. Two of them—namely, Letters 46 and 48—are still read among Cyprian’s letters; the others likewise have perished.

In addition, two Decretals circulate under his name, produced by Isidore Mercator and reproduced by Labbe [Note: [Col. 0684D] Labbe, *Councils*, vol. I, col. 668 ff.] and Mansi [Note: [Col. 0684D] Mansi, *Most Extensive Collection of Councils*, vol. I, cols. 811–817.]. The first is addressed to the [Col. 0685A] universal Church and deals with the translation of Saints Peter and Paul, as though performed by him, and with Novatian and other heretics; the second, addressed to Rufus or Rusticus, an Eastern bishop, treats of the sacrament—that is, the oath—of bishops and of their judicial cases. Both are rejected as spurious by scholars, and even by Labbe himself; indeed, each proves its own falsity by the consular dates appended to it. For the former was “issued on the seventh day before the Ides of September” (elsewhere, the eighth), “in the consulship of the most illustrious Decius and Maximus”; the latter was dated “on the eleventh day before the Kalends of June,” under the same consuls. Yet the consular lists establish that the latter of these did not enter the consulship until the year 253—that is, the second year after Decius’ death and several months after the martyrdom of St. Cornelius. If anyone should wish “Maximus” [Col. 0685B] there to designate “Gratus,” who is also said to have borne that name, this will accomplish nothing, since Gratus’ consulship belongs to the year 250, when Cornelius had not yet been ordained pontiff. Noël Alexandre adduces several indications of manifest forgery [Note: [Col. 0685D] Noël Alexandre, *Ecclesiastical History*, third century, ch. 4, art. 3, p. 72.]. Among these are, first, the citation of Holy Scripture according to the Vulgate version; and sayings gathered from the Acts of the Council of Carthage, from the letter *On the Life of Clerics* addressed to Oceanus under the name of St. Jerome, from the Fifth Roman Council under Symmachus, from St. Ambrose’s Letter 20, and from elsewhere.

Our Coustant, in *Letters of the Supreme Pontiffs*, col. 26, further observes that a decree stipulating that an oath must be taken by those who are fasting, and that children must not be compelled to swear before their fourteenth year—extant [Col. 0685C] in Gratian’s compilation, Cause 22, question 5, canon 16—was likewise wrongly ascribed by Ivo and Burchard to our holy pontiff.

Certainly fictitious as well is that sharp and vehement letter which, after Cyprian’s letters in the Venetian edition that we use, col. 303, is reproduced among the doubtful works as though it had been sent by Cornelius to Cyprian on the subject of not rebaptizing heretics. For it is established that this controversy was not debated under Cornelius, but first arose between Cyprian and Stephen, Cornelius’ successor after Lucius; it is likewise established that the greatest harmony always prevailed between Cornelius and Cyprian [Note: [Col. 0685D] See Maran, *Life of St. Cyprian*, §35, p. 115.].

XI. The Most Eminent Robert Bellarmine, in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under St. Cornelius, mentions another very brief [Col. 0685D] letter to Lupicinus, bishop of Vienne. It is extant in volume III of the Paris edition of the *Library of the Fathers* from the year 1589, in Labbe’s *Councils*, vol. I, col. 829, and in Jean du Bois’s *Antiquities of the Library of Fleury*. Baronius, who first brought it to light from that collection, transcribed it under the year 255, no. 47; our Coustant, in the appendix to vol. I of the *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, p. 25, regards it as suspect.

Although Labbe notes nothing about this letter except that Baronius obtained it from the Library of Fleury, [Col. 0686A] he nevertheless makes his own judgment sufficiently clear when he comments as follows on the two certainly genuine letters that he places immediately after it: “This letter and the following one, together with those written by the Roman clergy, show how far bronze coins differ from lupine counters, and plated wares from the golden writings of the ancients.” Tillemont [Note: [Col. 0686D] Tillemont, *Mémoires*, note XV, on Cornelius, vol. III, p. 352], the already cited Noël Alexandre and Coustant, and others likewise place it among the forged works; and it certainly displays substantial indications of forgery. First, the title “archbishop” was not in use in the age of Cornelius; and even if it had been, the holy pontiff, who called himself merely a bishop, would not have addressed Lupicinus of Vienne by that title. Baronius, it is true, omits the title “archbishop” in the *Annals* under the year 255, no. 47, where he presents the letter as genuine; but in the cited *Library* [Col. 0686B] *of the Fathers* and in Labbe’s *Collection of Councils* it is also headed in this form: “Cornelius, bishop of Rome, to his brother Lupicinus, bishop of Vienne, greetings.” Apart from the uncertainty as to which text more closely conforms to the Fleury manuscript, even this salutation does not accord with Cornelius’ method of writing. For in his letters addressed to Cyprian, which are still extant, he omits the episcopal title of each and begins with these words: “Cornelius to his brother Cyprian, greetings”; Cyprian likewise regularly did the same in his letters to Cornelius.

Second, it is doubtful whether St. Lupicinus already presided over the church of Vienne while Cornelius was still alive. This difficulty must certainly be raised against Baronius’ position, for under the year 262, no. 58, he writes that St. Florentius, Lupicinus’ predecessor, suffered martyrdom under Valerian. The Most Eminent Annalist failed to notice this when he admitted the aforementioned letter—or, conversely, when he placed Florentius’ martyrdom so late. The cited Jean du Bois says of the same St. Florentius: “He lived through the times of Gordian, Philip, Decius, Gallus, and Volusian”; but of Lupicinus: “The blessed martyr Lupicinus succeeded him and governed the see while Valerian and Gallienus were among the living.” Jean Chenu has the same account in his work on the bishoprics of Gaul. Indeed, Tillemont [Note: [Col. 0686D] The same author, ibid.] regarded it as highly probable that Lupicinus did not obtain that see until after the year 374. Third, this letter itself was written either after Decius and before the persecution initiated by Gallus, or after that persecution had begun. If the former, with what appearance of truth does it say that “Christians [Col. 0686D] everywhere are being subjected to various tortures, and that many have already been crowned with martyrdom”? If the latter, why does Cornelius not mention his own confession or exile, since it is established from what has been said that he was among the first to confess and to be arrested? Other features of the same letter that also displease certain scholars may be seen in Tillemont and Coustant. Nevertheless, I would not wish to assert with the latter that the word *Missas* (“Masses”), which occurs in it, is certainly later than the age of Cornelius.

VII. Tillemont further notes that Erasmus thought the treatise *On Discipline and the Good of Chastity*, which is included among the doubtful [Col. 0687A] works of St. Cyprian, could be ascribed to St. Cornelius. But since no reason is offered except that it was composed by a bishop absent from his flock, I do not see why it should be attributed to St. Cornelius in exile at Centumcellae rather than to any other bishop absent from his people. Erasmus was no less conjectural when, again according to Tillemont’s testimony [Note: [Col. 0687D] Tillemont, *Mémoire on Cornelius*, vol. III, art. XXII, p. 208.], he believed that the discourse addressed to the heretic Novatian, similarly ascribed by some to Cyprian, was also a work of Cornelius. Indeed, as Tillemont observes, it is not improbable that it was written after the persecution of Gallus, at the beginning of which the holy pontiff was exiled and crowned with martyrdom, and that his confession and martyrdom are recalled in it under the figure of the Good Shepherd.

## ARTICLE III. SYNOPSIS OF CORNELIUS’ LETTER TO FABIUS OF ANTIOCH

[Col. 0687B]

Eusebius provides a substantial fragment [Note: [Col. 0687D] Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VI, ch. 43.] from Cornelius’ third letter to Fabius. In it Cornelius describes the devices Novatian employed to have himself ordained bishop, abusing the simplicity and pliability of three bishops, one of whom acknowledged his fault and repented of it. He then observes that at this time there were already in the Roman Church forty-six presbyters, seven deacons, and the same number of subdeacons; forty-two acolytes; fifty-two doorkeepers and exorcists together with readers; and more than fifteen hundred widows together with the *thlibomenoi* (θλιβόμενοι), that is, the needy, as Rufinus not inappropriately renders the term. The Lord’s grace and kindness supplied food for all of them. From this passage it is possible to infer how many basilicas the Christians then had at Rome. For since individual presbyters governed their own basilicas, if there were forty-six presbyters, it must be said that there were the same number of basilicas. Blondel makes a very serious error regarding this passage when he abridges it in such a way as to make no mention of the subdeacons, and then thinks he can establish from this omission that no subdeacons had yet been instituted at Rome. But both the Greek text of Eusebius and Rufinus’ Latin translation demonstrate the falsity of that reading. Optatus likewise reports [Note: [Col. 0687D] Optatus, book II, *On the Donatist Schism*.] that forty or more basilicas existed at Rome when Victor of Garba was sent there by these schismatics shortly after [Col. 0687D] the outbreak of the Donatist schism. “For they,” says Optatus, “among the forty [Col. 0688A] and more basilicas there, had no place in which they could assemble.” Blondel, *Apology*, p. 223, interprets this passage as referring to the age of Optatus himself, but Valesius rightly notes that Blondel misunderstood it [Note: [Col. 0688C] Valesius on this passage of Eusebius.].

Cornelius adds that Novatian could not have hoped to attain the episcopate, since, having been baptized on his sickbed, he had not received the imposition of the bishop’s hands—that is, the sacrament of Confirmation. Nor, after he recovered from his illness, did he receive the remaining rites which, according to the rule of the Church, “must be received, nor was he sealed by the bishop, τοῦ τε σφραγισθῆναι ὑπὸ τοῦ ἐπισκόπου [‘to be sealed by the bishop’]. Since, then, he had by no means received this seal, how could he have received the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0688C] Behold the sacrament of Confirmation! Rufinus rendered Cornelius’ Greek words in Latin as follows: “Nor were the remaining rites that customarily follow baptism solemnly completed in him, nor was he perfected by the seal of chrism.”]?” Cornelius then writes that Novatian was ordained a presbyter only at the bishop’s request, contrary to the command of the Church, which prohibited the ordination of persons baptized in this manner [Note: [Col. 0688C] See canon XII of the Synod of Neocaesarea and canon XLVII of Laodicea.]. He next reproaches him for having denied his priesthood during the persecution and for compelling his followers, while giving them the body and blood of Christ, to swear that they would never return to Cornelius, at the point when they should have answered “Amen,” as was the custom of the Church [Note: [Col. 0688C] The holy Fathers Ambrose, Jerome, and Augustine mention this custom. Jerome, in fact, *Against the Errors of John of Jerusalem*, addressed to Pammachius, says: “With what conscience shall I approach the Eucharist and answer ‘Amen’ when I doubt the charity of the one who offers it?” Augustine’s statement in *Sermon* 272, new edition, pertains to this: “You hear ‘The body of Christ,’ and you answer ‘Amen.’” And in book XII, *Against Faustus*, ch. 10: “For the blood of Christ has a mighty voice upon earth when, after it has been received, all respond, ‘Amen.’” That rite is explained by Ambrose, book IV, *On the Sacraments*, ch. 5, in these words: “Therefore, when you receive, it is not without purpose that you say ‘Amen,’ already confessing in spirit that what you receive is true.” Cyril of Jerusalem agrees with these statements in his final *Catechesis*.]. Finally, he informs Fabius that the Roman confessors had abandoned Novatian’s party, and that many bishops—whose names he sends to him—had condemned Novatian in council.

In the judgment of the very learned Dupin [Note: [Col. 0688D] Dupin, *Library*, vol. I, Latin ed., Cologne, p. 280.], Cornelius’ style, insofar as one can judge it from the few letters that survive, is not especially elevated; nevertheless, it gives sufficient weight to what he says, adapts its subject matter to itself, and by no means spares his opponent.

[Col. 0689]

## NOTICE OF NON-EXTANT LETTERS RELATING TO CORNELIUS, BY DOM COUSTANT, O.S.B.

### I

[Col. 0689A]

1. Letters from Cornelius to Cyprian or to other bishops of Africa, in which he announced that he had been made bishop of Rome. These breathed a certain modesty and simplicity, qualities wholly absent from the writings of Novatian, full of abuse and slander, which reached Africa not long afterward. Cyprian therefore ordered these letters of Cornelius to be read to the people and rejected Novatian’s writings. According to Cyprian himself, “the sanctity and truth alike of divine tradition and ecclesiastical institution required” that, as soon as the bishop of Rome had notified the bishop of Carthage of his ordination by letter, the latter should in turn address letters to him; and, once knowledge of his ordination had been conveyed to the individual colleagues in his province, Cyprian was to direct them to send brethren with letters to the newly appointed bishop. Cyprian testifies that he did not fail in this duty.

### II

2. A letter from Cyprian to Pope Cornelius, transmitted through the bishops Caldonius and Fortunatus, requesting that Cornelius read to the faithful at Rome the letters that Cyprian himself had written both to the clergy and to his Carthaginian people concerning the faction of Felicissimus and the five presbyters—that is, Letters XXXVIII and XL in Pamelius’ edition. Accordingly, he then sent copies of those same letters through the aforementioned bishops, and afterward sent them again through Mettius and Nicephorus.

### III

[Col. 0689C]

3. A synodical letter from the bishops of Africa to Cornelius, signed in their own hands and conveyed by the subdeacon Mettius and the acolyte Nicephorus.
