In it they informed him what they had determined and pronounced concerning the case of Felicissimus and the five presbyters who adhered to him: namely, as is recalled above in Letter XII, written in the following year, no. 9, that those men had been excluded by their sentence. It was perhaps composed as a result of the “council of very many bishops” recalled by Cyprian in Letter I to Stephen I, no. 2, in which “Novatian was judged an enemy of the Church,” and it was pronounced that no one was permitted to communicate with him.

### IV. Where the Penitence of the Major Clergy Is Also Discussed: Whether During the First Three Centuries They Were Subject to Public Penitence

[Col. 0689D]

4. To the beginning of Cornelius’ pontificate may be assigned both the proceedings of the Roman synod concerning the lapsed and the various letters of Cornelius mentioned by Jerome, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, ch. 76, and Eusebius, *History*, book VI, ch. 43. Jerome speaks of them as follows:

> Cornelius, bishop of the city of Rome, to whom eight letters of Cyprian are extant (we still possess the same number), wrote a letter to Fabius, bishop of the church of Antioch, concerning the Roman, Italian, and African synod; another concerning Novatian and those who had lapsed; a third concerning the proceedings of the synod; and a fourth, very lengthy letter to the same Fabius, containing the causes of the Novatianist heresy and its anathema.

Of those four letters nothing has reached us except certain notable fragments of the last, which we owe to Eusebius. That writer has the following concerning the same proceedings and letters:

> When a synod had assembled at Rome, at which sixty bishops and a much greater number of presbyters and deacons met, and when the prelates in the provinces—probably those of Italy—had deliberated separately, a decree of this kind was promulgated to all, doubtless by Cornelius: Novatus [read: Novatian] and those who had insolently exalted themselves with him, and all who had presumed to assent to his most inhuman opinion, so foreign to brotherly charity, were to be regarded as strangers to the Church; but the brethren who had lapsed through misfortune and temptation were to be treated and sustained with the remedies of penitence. Letters sent by Cornelius, bishop of the Romans, to Fabius, prelate of the church of Antioch, are still extant; in them are set forth both the proceedings of the Roman synod and the judgments of all those throughout Italy, Africa, and the other provinces of those regions. To these was joined another letter of the same Cornelius concerning what had been decreed in the Roman synod.

5. The time at which the council just mentioned concerning the lapsed was held—and consequently the time at which the letters on that subject were written by Cornelius—may be gathered from these words of the Roman clergy to Cyprian in Letter XXXI:

> Before the appointment of a bishop, we thought that nothing should be altered; but we believe that care for the lapsed should be moderated by an intermediate course, so that, while we await a bishop being given to us by God, the case of those who can endure delay may meanwhile be held in suspense.

For everyone sees that, once Cornelius had been given by God as pontiff at Rome, no reason remained why the matter should be held in suspense any longer. Indeed, since Novatian denied pardon to the lapsed, it was particularly necessary that it be settled quickly by holding a council. We therefore number among Cornelius’ earliest affairs both this council and the letters through which he arranged for its decree to be made known to the various provinces and ratified by them.

6. To the same council appears to belong the decree concerning which Cyprian speaks as follows in Letter LXVIII:

> Although there are many other serious offenses in which Basilides and Martialis are implicated, men of that sort attempt in vain to usurp the episcopate for themselves, since it is clear that such men can neither preside over the Church nor offer sacrifices to God. This is especially so since long ago Cornelius, our colleague, a peaceable and righteous priest, who was also honored with martyrdom by the Lord’s gracious favor, decreed together with us and absolutely all the bishops established throughout the entire [Col. 0691A] world that men of this sort might indeed be admitted to penitence, but must be barred from clerical ordination and priestly honor.

Although it is clear that in this decree priests who had lapsed were removed from priestly dignity and function and permitted access to penitence, it is not sufficiently explicit what penitence was to be required of them.

7. The learned Morin’s opinion, in book IV, *On Penitence*, ch. 12—an opinion to which very many subscribe—is that during the Church’s first three centuries the major clerics, no less than laymen, were subject to public penitence. He advances especially in support of his opinion the following passage written by Cyprian to Fidus in Letter LIX of Pamelius’ edition, or LXIV of the Oxford edition:

> We have read your letter, dearest brother, in which you informed us concerning Victor, formerly a presbyter, that, before he had performed full penitence and made satisfaction to the Lord God against whom he had sinned, our colleague Therapius rashly granted him peace at an untimely moment and with precipitate haste. This matter has moved us considerably, since there was a departure from the authority of our decree: before the lawful and full period of satisfaction, without the request and knowledge of the people, and when neither illness pressed nor necessity compelled, peace was granted to him.

In this passage the decree from which Cyprian says there had been a departure may be understood as that very decree which the same prelate, in Letter LXVIII just cited, recalls as having been issued by Cornelius together with himself and absolutely all the bishops established throughout the world. It follows that by the authority of that decree a definite period of satisfaction and penitence was prescribed for presbyters who had lapsed, and that it was by no means to be remitted unless the “request of the people,” or “pressing illness and compelling necessity,” counseled otherwise. Yet here too it is left unstated whether the “full” penitence required of them was public or not. Nor does Cyprian state the matter more clearly in Letter LXIV, or LXV, which he begins as follows:

> I have been gravely and sorrowfully disturbed, dearest brothers, because I have learned that Fortunatianus, formerly a bishop among you, after the grievous fall that brought about his ruin, now wishes to act as though he were unimpaired and has begun to reclaim the episcopate for himself . . . although he ought to make satisfaction and devote himself day and night, with tears, prayers, and entreaties, to imploring the Lord; yet he still dares to claim for himself the priesthood that he betrayed, as though it were lawful, after approaching the altars of the devil, to approach the altar of God.

8. But what the mind of Cornelius and the bishops of the whole world was may be gathered and interpreted more securely from that very letter of Cyprian in which their decree is praised. For in it Basilides is represented as someone who had already begun to obey and comply with that decree, to such a degree that, “laying aside the episcopate on account of the wound to his conscience, he turned to the performance of penitence, beseeching God and being sufficiently grateful if it should fall to him to communicate even as a layman.” For if the words stating that Basilides “turned to the performance of penitence” are by no means to be understood as public penitence, there is no underlying reason why we should interpret as public penitence the decree by which Cornelius, together with the other bishops of the whole world, determined that “men of this sort could be admitted to the performance of penitence.” But Basilides turned to perform that penitence without abandoning hope of recovering the episcopate; indeed, he obtained it from Stephen by deception. Yet the law always prevailed in the Church that those who had performed public penitence were left no hope either of entering the clergy or of returning to it. His penitence, therefore, was not public.

As for the statement that he regarded it as a benefit “if it should fall to him to communicate even as a layman,” Cyprian himself clarifies it in Letter 72, where he writes as follows to Pope Stephen concerning those who had rebelled against the Church:

> We plainly add and append, dearest brother, by common consent and authority, that if there are any presbyters or deacons who were previously ordained in the Church and afterward proved faithless and rebellious . . . they too, when they return, are to be received on this condition: that they communicate as laymen and regard it as sufficient that they are admitted to peace, although they had proved enemies of peace.

Those men, therefore, on returning, ought to have regarded the lay communion granted to them as a benefit because it would have been permissible to prescribe for them beforehand a definite period of penitence and to defer that communion until they had completed it—not because custom required deacons, presbyters, or bishops of this kind to undergo the solemn rites of public penitence. Indeed, if, among those who read in Gregory the Great, book II, indiction X, Letter 6, concerning Demetrius, formerly bishop of Naples and guilty of the gravest crimes, that “he was reserved for penitence and deprived of the honor of the priesthood,” or in book VI, indiction XIV, Letter 41, that “Massa, bishop of Nicotera, was assigned to penitence for certain faults,” and other similar passages, there is no one who understands “penitence” in those passages to mean public and solemn penitence, what prevents the same term in the decree enacted by Cornelius together with the bishops of the entire Christian world from being understood in the same way?

9. Furthermore, I am greatly moved by the fact that Cyprian testifies that this decree belonged not only to Cornelius and the Italians but also to the Africans—indeed, to “absolutely all the bishops established throughout the whole world.” For a decree confirmed by so great and so universal a consensus ought to have been abrogated only by some solemn law. Or, if anyone supposes that it could have become obsolete of itself and fallen into disuse, he must surely admit that it could scarcely have happened that this occurred so quickly and simultaneously in all the Church’s provinces, without at least some memory of the contrary usage surviving among its leading men.

Yet Siricius is witness that in the fourth century it was not permitted in the Roman Church for clerics to perform public penitence. In Letter I, no. 18, he presents this as a practice received from ancient or even perpetual usage:

> Just as no cleric is permitted to perform penitence, so too, after penitence and reconciliation, no layman is ever permitted to obtain the honor of the clerical state.

Leo afterward clearly confirmed this very point when Rusticus, bishop of Narbonne, asked him “concerning a presbyter or deacon who, having acknowledged his offense, requests penitence, whether it should be granted to him through the imposition of hands.” Leo replied in Letter II, ch. 2:

> It is foreign to ecclesiastical custom that those who have been consecrated to the presbyteral honor or to the rank of deacon should, for some offense of their own, receive through the imposition of hands the remedy of performing penitence; this undoubtedly descends from apostolic tradition.

Was so great a pontiff truly so ignorant of the sacred canons that he would present as apostolic tradition a custom contrary to a law enacted in the third century by the bishops of the entire world? But, so that the agreement between the discipline of the fourth or fifth century and that of the third may be seen more clearly, the same custom denies the aforesaid clerics not every form of penitence, but only public penitence. Leo therefore immediately adds:

> Hence those who have lapsed in this way must seek a private withdrawal in order to merit God’s mercy; there their satisfaction, if it is worthy, may also be fruitful.

For it was just that peace and communion should not be restored to those from whom worthy satisfaction was required until they had made full satisfaction. Accordingly, this reply of Leo can easily be reconciled with Cyprian’s earlier words in the letter to Fidus.

10. It would indeed be astonishing if a decree concerning a matter of the greatest importance—a matter that the Roman clergy in the third century had not dared to decide until God should give them a pontiff—was afterward enacted by that same clergy together with the holy pontiff granted to them from heaven and with several other bishops, yet could have fallen so completely into oblivion, despite the fact that frequent application ought continually to have refreshed its memory, that in the following century it was wholly unknown in the same Church. But it would seem no less astonishing how it could at the same time have been equally unknown among the Africans, who had sought, praised, confirmed, and by their practice toward the lapsed approved that same decree—so much so that Optatus could say near the end of book II:

> It is known and established among many that during the persecution certain bishops, falling away through indolence from the confession of God, offered incense; and yet none of those who survived either imposed a hand upon the lapsed or ordered them to bend their knees.

With what ignorance or rashness could Optatus have affirmed this and, in the same place, accused the Donatists—who imposed hands upon deacons, presbyters, and bishops—as guilty of an impious and unheard-of crime, if they had done nothing except what Cyprian and the other African prelates, together with Cornelius and the other bishops of the whole world, had commanded in the preceding century and confirmed by their own example?

But the Council of Carthage teaches us that Optatus was free from every charge of ignorance and that the crime of rashness fell upon the Donatists alone. At that council—doubtless so that no one might imitate the schismatics’ rash ventures and impious machinations—it was confirmed, near the end of the fourth century, in canon 11:

> If presbyters or deacons should at any time be convicted of some graver fault for which they must be removed from ministry, the hand is not to be imposed upon them as upon penitents or as upon lay members of the faithful.

Augustine too, the light of the African Church, observes in book I, ch. 1, *On Baptism against the Donatists*, that upon the aforesaid clerics “the hand is not imposed among the laity.” In this observation of Augustine—and much more plainly in the immediately preceding words of the Council of Carthage—the distinction between the penitence of clerics, at least of the major clerics, and the penitence of laymen is apparent.

11. The same distinction is no less manifest in the petition that Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, presented to the emperor Constantius while residing at Constantinople at the beginning of the year 360. In it, no. 2, he addresses that emperor concerning the unjust cause of his exile:

> Confident in the condition of my conscience, I shall disclose that you, Augustus, have been circumvented and your Caesar mocked, on this condition: if I am shown to have done anything unworthy not only of a bishop’s holiness but even of a layman’s integrity, I shall no longer look through pardon for restoration to the priesthood, but shall grow old within the penitence of a layman.

He would surely have requested this in vain if custom had indiscriminately bound layman and cleric by the same law of penitence. Those therefore are greatly mistaken who think that the major clerics, no less than laymen, were at some time subject to public penitence and suppose themselves supported by this passage because they hear a bishop permit himself to be compelled “to grow old within the penitence of a layman.” They ought to have noticed that Hilary, from his certain consciousness of his own integrity and innocence, grants here not something customarily done, but something wholly unusual and unprecedented, which he is confident will never occur at all.

Nor can it be established from this that bishops were customarily consigned to the penitence of laymen any more than one may establish, from Paul’s statement in Galatians 1:8, “Even if we or an angel from heaven should preach a gospel contrary to what we preached to you, let him be anathema,” that a heavenly angel is still liable to anathema. This passage of Hilary therefore considerably opposes them, since it expressly teaches that there was then one penitence for a bishop and another for a layman. Hilary said this both from the custom that he knew to be practiced in the West, of which he was a bishop, and from the custom he saw received in the East, where he was residing—a custom that accordingly prevailed alike in both West and East. So great a consensus of the whole Church could have arisen from no other source than either apostolic tradition or that common law which Cyprian reports was enacted with the consent of “absolutely all the bishops established throughout the whole world.” What was decreed at that time, therefore, was only that bishops or other major clerics who had lapsed should be deprived of their rank of honor and, after satisfaction and a penitence appropriate to them, restored to peace and communion.

12. Nor does what we have transcribed from Eusebius’ *History* concerning the penitence of Natalius in the time of Pope Zephyrinus conflict with this. There we read what that bishop—if indeed he was a bishop—did spontaneously, from the vehement disposition of a penitent mind, not what any ecclesiastical law imposed upon him. The Church’s constant rule concerning offenders in every age was that pardon should be granted to no guilty person, of whatever condition, who did not repent. Even before pardon was granted, worthy satisfaction for offenses was always customarily exacted, unless it was compensated from some other source. Consequently, in the first three centuries of the Church, just as in the subsequent centuries, major clerics guilty of the gravest crimes were not only deposed from their rank of honor but also punished with appropriate penalties by which they might make satisfaction to the God whom they had offended.

Hence Cyprian was indignant that peace had been given to the presbyter Victor “before the lawful and full period of satisfaction.” Hence Leo too judged that lapsed presbyters and deacons must seek “a private withdrawal, where their satisfaction, if worthy, might also be fruitful.” Hence John II, in his letter to Caesarius, likewise deposed Contumeliosus from the episcopate and ordered that he be sent to a monastery, “where, mindful of his offenses, he is not to cease shedding tears in penitence, so that . . . he may be able to merit mercy from Jesus Christ.” Hence Pope Gregory commands in book III, Letter 50: “We will that Paul, formerly a bishop, remain in penitence in the monastery where he is”; and in book V, Letter 14:

> We determine that the deacon and abbot from Porto Venere, whom you report to have fallen, neither ought nor is able in any way to be recalled to holy orders. Deprived of holy orders, he should indeed be assigned by you to penitence.

If no one interprets these and other passages of this sort as referring to public penitence, why should we understand similar passages concerning the major clerics of the first three centuries differently, contrary to the judgment of the supreme pontiffs and Fathers who lived in the fourth and fifth centuries?

### V

[Col. 0695C]

13. At about the same time, Cyprian, on the advice of all the brethren, sent Cornelius the names of the bishops established in Africa “who, unimpaired and sound, preside over the brethren in the Catholic Church,” so that he himself, and through his efforts the other bishops, might know “to whom they should write and from whom they should in turn receive letters.” Accordingly, if anyone whose name was omitted from this letter dared to write, they would know that he “had been stained either by a certificate or by sacrifice, or was one of the heretics.” Employing a similar precaution when writing to Fabius, bishop of Antioch, Cornelius appended at the end of his letter the names of the bishops who had condemned Novatian, whether in the Roman synod or by letter, as Eusebius reports in book VI of the *History*, ch. 43.

### VI

[Col. 0695D]

14. A letter from Cornelius to Cyprian, conveyed by the presbyter Primitivus, in which Cornelius indicated that he was disturbed because, when letters were being addressed to him from the colony of Hadrumetum in the name of Polycarp, bishop of that colony, Cyprian and Liberalis, on coming there, had caused them to be addressed not to Cornelius but to the Roman presbyters and deacons, as though his ordination were doubtful. Cyprian explains above, in Letter IV, why this had been done by himself and Liberalis.

### VII

15. A letter from Cornelius to Cyprian, sent through the confessor Augendus, in which Cyprian was warned that Nicostratus, Novatus, Evaristus, Primus, and Dionysius, adherents of Novatian, had sailed to Africa.

### VIII

[Col. 0696A]

16. A letter from Cornelius to Dionysius, bishop of Alexandria, against Novatian.

### IX
17. A letter of Dionysius of Alexandria in reply to the aforesaid letter, concerning which Eusebius gives the following brief summary:

> “Dionysius writes to Cornelius, bishop of the city of Rome, whose letter against Novatus [read: Novatian] he had received. In this letter he indicates that Helenus, bishop of Tarsus in Cilicia, and the others who had assembled with him—namely Firmilian, bishop of Cappadocia, and Theoctistus, bishop of the province of Palestine—had invited him to attend the synod of Antioch, at which certain persons were attempting to strengthen the schism of Novatus. He also writes that he had been informed that [Col. 0696B] Fabius had died, and that Demetrianus had been appointed bishop of the church of Antioch in his place. He also mentions the bishop of Jerusalem in these words: ‘As for Alexander, he was cast into prison and died a blessed death.’”

Eusebius then adds the following concerning the same Dionysius:

> “There follows another letter of the same Dionysius to the brethren residing at Rome, concerning the office of a deacon, sent through Hippolytus. He likewise writes another letter to the same persons concerning Peace, and also concerning Repentance. Again, he writes another to the Confessors residing there, who were still at that time favorable to the position of Novatus [read: Novatian]. He also sent two further letters to these same men after they had returned to the Church.”

From these words it follows, first, that Dionysius’s letter to [Col. 0696C] Cornelius, in which he reports to him the death of Fabius, was later than Cornelius’s letter to Fabius himself; and, second, that Eusebius did not observe chronological order at all in cataloguing the letters of Dionysius just mentioned. For it may be conjectured that the first two letters were written by Dionysius while the see at Rome was vacant after the death of Fabian; the third, when he learned that the confessors—the presbyter Macarius, Urbanus, Sidonius, and Celerinus—favored Novatian; and, finally, the fourth and fifth together with the letter which he is said to have sent to Cornelius in the first place, when, that is, he had learned, from letters of Cornelius himself, unless we are mistaken, that these same Confessors had returned to the Church. For just as Cornelius announced the confessors’ return to the Church in his letter to Fabius of Antioch, so it is also permissible to conjecture that at the same time [Col. 0696D] he communicated this very fact by letter to Dionysius, head of the church of Alexandria, and that not long afterward Dionysius wrote back to Cornelius the matters which Eusebius committed to record.

## X

18. A letter of the pseudo-bishop Fortunatus, transmitted to Cornelius through his envoys, who traveled to Rome together with Felicissimus. Cyprian writes the following about those envoys:

> “After all this, furthermore, once they have had a pseudo-bishop appointed for themselves by heretics, they dare to sail and carry letters from schismatics and profane men to the chair of Peter and to the principal Church, from which priestly unity arose; nor do they reflect that those Romans are the men whose faith was praised by the Apostle’s proclamation, [Col. 0697A] and to whom faithlessness can gain no access.”

Again, a little later, he speaks as follows about the same men:

> “But what am I to say about those who have now sailed to you with Felicissimus, a man guilty of every crime, sent as envoys by the pseudo-bishop Fortunatus, and bringing you letters as false as the man whose letters they bear is himself false?”

He observes that the falsity of those letters consisted in this: Fortunatus boasted in them that twenty-five bishops had been present at his ordination, whereas it was established that he had been ordained “by only five shipwrecked and excommunicated men who had assembled”—namely Privatus, an old heretic who had long before been condemned by the judgment of ninety bishops; Felix, whom Privatus had appointed a pseudo-bishop outside the Church; Jovinus and Maximus, who were first condemned by the judgment of nine bishops [Col. 0697B] and afterward excommunicated once again by a larger number at a council; and Repostus of Suturnuca, who during the persecution had not only fallen himself but had also caused the greater part of his people to fall through sacrilegious persuasion.

> “These five,” says Cyprian, “together with a few men who had either sacrificed or had guilty consciences, chose Fortunatus as a pseudo-bishop for themselves.”

Cornelius refused for some time to receive this letter of Fortunatus, and did not accept it until after threats and menaces had been made.

## XI

19. Cyprian’s letter to Cornelius concerning the aforesaid Fortunatus, written at the same time as the preceding one and conveyed through the acolyte Felicianus, whom Cornelius had sent to Africa together with Bishop Perseus. But while Felicianus was delayed by the wind or detained in order to receive other letters, [Col. 0697C] Felicissimus, who was hastening onward, arrived before him; and thus the letters of Fortunatus were delivered to Cornelius before Felicianus reached Rome.

## XII

20. A letter of Cornelius, “sufficiently full of brotherly love, ecclesiastical discipline, and priestly censure,” delivered to Cyprian through the acolyte Satyrus. In it he stated that Felicissimus, an enemy of Christ who was not a new offender but had long before been excommunicated for his many and most serious crimes, and condemned by the judgment not only of Cyprian himself but also of very many bishops, had been rejected by him; and that when Felicissimus arrived accompanied by a crowd and faction of desperate men, he had been driven from the Church with the full vigor proper for bishops to exercise. It is evident that this letter of Cornelius was written [Col. 0697D] after Felicissimus had come to the city with the envoys of the pseudo-bishop Fortunatus following the latter’s ordination, and before Felicianus, returning from Carthage with the letter of Cyprian just mentioned, had yet arrived there.

## XIII

21. Another letter of Cornelius to Cyprian, more apprehensive than the preceding one, was enclosed and sent together with it. In this letter Cornelius indicated that he had been somewhat disturbed by the threats and menaces of those who had come from Fortunatus:

> “For they had assailed him with the utmost desperation, threatening that, if he did not accept the letters they had brought, they would read them publicly and utter many shameful and disgraceful things worthy of their own mouths.”

Cornelius therefore judged that he ought to yield to them [Col. 0698A]—not, as it seems to me, through any fault of cowardice or faintheartedness, but because he feared some greater harm and wished to avert it. Such are the circumstances in which holy and vigilant shepherds, whichever way they turn, fear dangers and sins. Augustine laments over these throughout the letter formerly numbered 250, now 195, to Paulinus, and from this concludes in section 2:

> “See why human life upon earth is wholly a trial: a person is tempted even where, so far as he can, he is conformed to the likeness of the heavenly life.”

Cornelius was certainly striving to conform himself to the ordinances of the heavenly life when, by accepting the disgraceful writings himself, he prevented their being read publicly, since he foresaw that they would cause scandal and offense to the people. Cyprian nevertheless disapproved of this action and rebuked it severely. [Col. 0698B] Cornelius did not take that rebuke resentfully, nor did the Christian friendship existing between those holy prelates suffer any harm because of it.

22. In the same letter Cornelius remonstrated with Cyprian because he had not written to him immediately about Fortunatus’s new ordination. At the same time, he ordered Fortunatus to come to Rome to be judged there. Cyprian, once again disapproving of this, wrote back that he and all his colleagues had established that each person’s case should be heard in the place where the offense had been committed. The dispute over the adjudication of cases which arose between Cornelius and Cyprian on account of Fortunatus and his envoys broke out afresh in the time of Pope Zosimus and Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, over the case [Col. 0698C] of Apiarius. Even then, however, the African prelates, in their reply to Pope Celestine, adhered to the decree of the council just cited.

## XIV

23. Another, very brief letter inscribed in the name of Cornelius to Lupicinus, bishop of Vienne, which came forth from the library of Fleury, we have relegated to the appendix. The other two letters fabricated by Isidore Mercator we do not separate from the rest of his wares.

## XV

24. In the editions of the councils, only the following decree is transcribed from Gratian’s compilation, Causa XXII, question 5, chapter 16:

> “It also seems fitting that anyone who dares to swear upon holy things should do so fasting, with all propriety and fear of God; and that children under fourteen years of age [Col. 0698D] should not be compelled to swear.”

The same decree is attributed to Cornelius by Ivo, part XII, chapter 69, and by Burchard, book XII, chapter 12; but by the same Ivo, part XII, chapter 33, and by Regino, book II, chapter 312, it is cited as if from book I of the Capitularies. In actual fact, it was excerpted from the Capitulary of Aachen of the year 789, chapter 63. Again, the final part of it, concerning children not being compelled to swear, joined to another provision concerning girls who swear, is reported by Gratian in the same place, chapter 15, as coming from the Council of Elvira. Likewise, from the same council Ivo, part XII, chapter 81, produces that other provision concerning girls who swear; Burchard, however, book XII, chapter 26, cites it not from the Council of Elvira, in which it does not in fact occur, but from the Council of Ireland, chapter 3.

[Col. 0699]

# Letters of Saint Cornelius, Pope and Martyr, and the Letters Written to Him

## In the Year of Christ 251

[Note: [Col. 0699A]

**Letter I.—** Sent through the agency of the presbyter Primitivus around the end of July in the year 251. **Coustant.**]

# First Letter  
## Saint Cyprian, Bishop of Carthage, to Saint Cornelius, Pope

(Erasm., II, 11; Pamel., Rigalt., Baluz., XLI; Paris., XL; Oxon., Lips., XLIV; Coustant, I, 125; Galland., III, 333.)

[Col. 0699A]

**Summary.—** The depravity of Novatian’s envoys is exposed, and for that reason they are excluded from communion. When they ask to be heard publicly, this is refused. As they seek everywhere to procure associates in schism and heresy, they are restrained.

[Col. 0700A]

**Cyprian to his brother Cornelius, greetings.**

[Note: [Col. 0699B]

**I. Dearest brother.** In that Christian simplicity which flourished during the earliest centuries of the Church, all Christians, even bishops, called one another brothers, without any distinction between the bishop of Rome and the others, as Erasmus observed on Letter LII and as we too stated in the notes on the letter of [Col. 0699C] Pope Gregory IV in Agobard. In subsequent centuries this changed, and it has long been customary for the bishop of Rome to call the other bishops brothers, while the bishops call him father.

Nevertheless, Jean de Launoy, doctor of theology at Paris, when reproducing on page 539 of his *History of the College of Navarre* a letter of Gérard Machet, bishop of Castres, to Gilles Laqueator, commonly called Le Lasseur, a papal referendary—which he mistakenly believed had been written to the pope—observes that even at that period, that is, in the reign of Charles VII, king of France, bishops were free to call the Roman pontiff “brother,” because Gérard says at the beginning of that letter, “I should deservedly be considered ungrateful, dearest brother,” and that this would remain permissible for as long as the Roman pontiff called other bishops brothers, since the brother of any brother is a brother.

The excellent man’s error arose because the names of those to whom Gérard writes are not placed in the titles of the letters, as is normally done, but after each letter. Mabillon similarly observes [Col. 0699D] on page 45 of his *Italian Journey* that he had seen many manuscripts of letters in which the address was placed not at the head of the letters but at the end. Accordingly, because Launoy saw the words “To our most holy lord the pope” written after Machet’s Letter CX, he believed that the letter after which this address appeared had been written to the pope; but it was written, as I have said above, to Gilles Laqueator, the papal referendary. Letter CXII must likewise be assigned to him; in it the bishop, following the custom of those times, calls the papal referendary his brother.

I thought it proper to point this out when the occasion offered. If anyone wishes to consult the manuscript of Gérard’s letters which Launoy used, it now survives in the Colbert Library, having been brought there through the generosity of the canons of the most illustrious Church of Saint Martin of Tours. Concerning Gilles I shall meanwhile also mention in passing that he was a canon of the church of Narbonne and a councillor of the king of France in his supreme court of the Parlement of Toulouse, as is written in the necrology of the church of Narbonne, where he was buried [Col. 0700C] in March 1484. **Baluze.**

**Sent by Novatian.** This embassy is mentioned in Letter LV, page 83. **Baluze.**

**The presbyter Maximus.** He belonged to the party of Novatus, as is shown by Pope Cornelius’s letter to Fabius of Antioch in Eusebius. He afterward returned to the Church. This is shown by that same letter of Cornelius and by the pontifical records edited by Gilles Bouchier from the Fasti of Cuspinian and from the manuscript of Nicolas-Claude Fabri de Peiresc cited by Rigaltius in his observations on Letter LXVII of Saint Cyprian. For the following is written there under Cornelius:

> “During his episcopate Novatus, outside the Church, ordained Novatian in the city of Rome and Nicostratus in Africa. After this had taken place, the confessors who had separated themselves from Cornelius returned to the Church with the presbyter Maximus, who had been with Moses.”

The same is also found in the pontifical records attributed to Anastasius the Librarian. The two letters of Dionysius, bishop of Alexandria, written to certain confessors of Novatian’s party who had returned to the Church, in Eusebius, book VI, chapter 46, appear to have been addressed to them.

But what is said in the pontifical records about the ordination of Novatian and Nicostratus presents some difficulty. For how could Novatus, who was not a bishop, ordain Novatian and Nicostratus? He “ordained” them, evidently, in the same manner in which Cyprian writes in Letter XLIX, page 63, that Felicissimus was made a deacon by him; that is, he established him as a deacon through his own faction. See the *Cyprianic Annals* for the year 250, §21. **Baluze.**

**Machaeus.** The old copies vary greatly concerning this man’s name. Although the matter is not of great importance, I should note that in some places he is called Matthaeus, elsewhere Macahaeus, Macheus, and Machaeus. [Col. 0701C] I have retained the reading supported by the greater number of old copies. **Baluze.**

**Caldonius and Fortunatus.** Bishops of the African Church, who had been sent to Rome to investigate what had occurred in the Roman Church after Fabian’s death, as is also clear from the following two letters. **Baluze.**

**Lucida.** I found this reading in eleven ancient books. Seven other ancient books prefer *elucida*. I consider the former reading better, both because it is presented by most of the best old books and because the word [Col. 0701D] *elucida* is not particularly Latin. It is nevertheless found in the Speyer edition, the old Venetian edition, and Morel’s edition. The other editions down to that of Rigaltius have *elucidata*. Rigaltius, and the English editors after him, wrote *elucida*. Reinhart preferred *elucidata*. **Baluze.**

**From there (*istinc*).** We have restored this on the authority of six old copies, for the others either omit the word or have *istic*. The reading we introduce, however, seems better, so that the meaning is that Pompeius and Stephanus brought back from there (*istinc*), that is, from the city of Rome, clear testimony concerning the legitimate election of Cornelius and the false ordination of Novatian. Yet the word *istic* in that passage has the same meaning, as below in Letter XLIX. **Baluze.**

**At the assembly (*in statione*).** Most of the old books and the early editions do not recognize the preposition. Manutius was the first to add it. Lombert translated this passage *en pleine assemblée* (“in full assembly”). Others may judge whether rightly. In the Reims manuscript of Saint-Denis one reads *infestatione*, through a copyist’s error, as I believe. See the observations on Letter XLVI. **Baluze.**—Pamelius observed that the term *statio* here means a gathering and assembly. **Coustant.**—What he here calls a *statio*, he calls a gathering or assembly in the following letter, where he repeats the same matter at greater length. As may be gathered from Tertullian, *On the Soldier’s Crown*, the ancients did not call every ecclesiastical gathering a *statio*, but only one held on the Lord’s Day; hence it was called a “day of stations,” the metaphor being taken from soldiers, who are said to “make a station” when they establish a guard at a fixed place.

Thus Christians assembled on Sundays, now in one basilica, now in another, and sometimes at the *martyria*, that is—as Rhenanus rightly observed—the tombs of the martyrs. [Col. 0702D] They prayed to God while standing, took part in the Sacrifice, and, according to Tertullian in his book *On Prayer*, received the Body of the Lord. Finally, if any difficulty had arisen, it was discussed in that assembly; hence, according to the same author in his book *On Fasting*, the stations were sometimes prolonged until evening. **Pamelius.**

**Primitivus.** A Roman presbyter, in my opinion. For it is apparent from Letter XLV, page 59, that Cornelius sent him to Africa. In the Acts of the Passion of Saint Stephen, Pope, Primitivus is named among the twelve clerics of the Roman Church detained by order of the emperor Valerian. Another Primitivus is mentioned in Ado’s martyrology on the fifth day before the Kalends of July. He was a son of Saint Symphorosa. An ancient inscription from Worms, sent by Pithou, survives in Gruter; in it Victorina Primitiva is named. In the collection of inscriptions of the Church of Saint Paul in Rome, page 174, there is mention of Primitivus, prefect of the craftsmen, and of another man of the same name on page 12, and of Primitiva on pages 43 and 55. **Baluze.**]

## I

There came to us, dearest brother, men sent by Novatian: the presbyter Maximus, the deacon Augendus, a certain Machaeus, and Longinus. But when we learned from the letters they carried with them, and from their speech and assertions, that Novatian had been made bishop, we were moved by the depravity of an unlawful ordination made contrary to the Catholic Church, and judged that they must immediately be excluded from communion with us. And [Note: [Col. 0699A] Thus the Colbert manuscript of the highest quality. In the printed editions, however, the particle *and* is missing here, and shortly afterward the text reads: “For I also … awaited.” Our reading is supported by the Corbie manuscript, in which the conjunction *and* likewise occurs here, and by several English manuscripts, which below [Col. 0700A] have “Now I also.”], after the claims which they obstinately and persistently attempted to maintain had meanwhile been refuted and beaten down, I [Note: [Col. 0700A] “For I,” Thu. Corb. Foss.; “Now I also,” Bod. 1, Lin.; “For I also,” Oxon.] and [Col. 0701A] a great many colleagues who had assembled with me awaited the arrival of our colleagues Caldonius [Note: [Col. 0701B] *Calidonius*, Foss. Mich. Vict.] and Fortunatus, whom we had recently sent as envoys to you and to our fellow bishops who had been present at your ordination, so that, when they arrived and brought back the truth of what had taken place, the dishonesty of the opposing party might be broken by greater authority and by the clear proof they supplied. [Note: [Col. 0701B] *Elucidata*, Pamel., with the manuscript edition of Corb.; *Elucida*, Oxon. With two Colbert manuscripts we prefer *lucida*.]

But our colleagues Pompeius and Stephanus arrived in addition; they too, in order to inform us from there, produced clear evidence and testimony in accordance with their dignity and trustworthiness. Thus there was no need to hear any further those who had come as envoys from Novatian. When they broke out at the assembly [Note: [Col. 0701B] “When the assembly,” Corb. ms.; “Into the assembly,” Lam. Ebor. Bod. 2, NC. 1, 2.] in envious abuse and tumultuous shouting, and demanded that the charges which they claimed to bring and prove be examined publicly [Col. 0701B] by us and by the people, we replied that it was inconsistent with our dignity to permit our colleague—already chosen and ordained, and approved by the commendable judgment of many—to be subjected to further controversy beyond what was honorable through the slanderous voice of jealous rivals. [Note: [Col. 0701B] “To be discussed,” manuscript of Saint-Arnulf at Metz, Manut., Rig., Oxon.; then, in Pamel., Morel., Reinhart, as in the Corbie manuscript [Col. 0701C] and the more recent Colbert manuscript: “Beyond reputation by a slanderous and jealous mouth.” We follow the older Colbert manuscript; Baluze, from manuscript 13: “to have his reputation discussed by a slanderous mouth.”]

Because it would take too long to compile in a letter all the arguments by which they were refuted and suppressed and exposed as having created a heresy through their unlawful endeavors, you will hear every detail most fully from our fellow presbyter Primitivus when he comes to you.

## II

And, as though their raging audacity could never cease, [Col. 0702A] here too they endeavor to tear apart Christ’s members into parties of schism [Note: [Col. 0701C] “A party,” the older Colbert manuscript; and shortly afterward, “to divide the body,” [Col. 0702B] with *one* omitted.], and to divide and mangle the one body of the Catholic Church, [Note: [Col. 0702B] “To divide the body of the Church,” Pem., NC. 2.] running from door to door through the homes of many people, or from town to town through certain cities, in order to seek companions for their obstinacy and error from among those who have been torn away. [Note: [Col. 0702B] The word *scissis* (“those who have been torn away”), which we reproduce from the old Colbert manuscript, is absent from the Oxford edition. In its place Pamelius, as in a Colbert manuscript, has *scissi* (“having been torn away”).]

We have given them our answer once, and we do not cease to instruct them [Note: [Col. 0702B] “We shall not cease to instruct,” NC. 2; “now to give,” Bod. 3.] to put aside their destructive dissension [Note: [Col. 0702B] “departure,” Bod. 3.] and contention and to know that it is impiety to abandon their mother. They must recognize and understand that, once a bishop has been appointed and approved by the testimony and judgment of his colleagues and the people [Note: [Col. 0702C] “In the judgment of God,” Ver.], another can in no way be appointed. Accordingly, if they wish to take peaceful and faithful counsel for themselves, and if they profess that they are champions of the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0702C] Thus our manuscript. But the editions have “the Gospel of Christ.”] and of Christ, they must first return to the Church.

I wish you, dearest brother, always good health.

## In the Year of Christ 251

[Note: [Col. 0702D]

**Letter II.—** It was transmitted through the subdeacon Mettius and the acolyte Nicephorus somewhat later than the preceding letter. **Coustant.**—The author of the pontifical records says that this letter was written by Cyprian in prison, as I shall presently state, and sent through the lector Celerinus. Pearson, however, in the *Cyprianic Annals*, believes that these words of the pontifical records refer to Letter LVII—mistakenly, in my opinion. For the letter sent through Celerinus dealt with the ordination of Cornelius, which is not discussed in Letter LVII. [Col. 0703C]

The same most distinguished man rightly observes that there is an error in the pontifical records at the place where it says that this letter was composed by Saint Cyprian in prison. Yet one ought not therefore to suppose that what the author of these records relates there is altogether false and fictitious. It is an error, not a falsehood. The correction is easy. What is said about prison must be referred to Celerinus, who is known to have been detained in prison with Moses, Maximus, Nicostratus, Urbanus, and Sidonius. Celerinus therefore received Cyprian’s letter in prison and sent it from there to Cornelius. This seems to be how the confused wording in the records should be restored.

But what the same most distinguished man adds from Ado, which he numbers among the frivolous and empty fictions of later times—namely, that in that letter Cyprian wrote to Cornelius about how much Celerinus had endured for the faith and confession of Christ—does indeed present great difficulty. For Ado does not write that praises of this Celerinus occurred in the letter that approved the election of Cornelius. These are Ado’s words [Col. 0703D] for the eighteenth day before the Kalends of October:

> “At that time the blessed Cyprian writes to him concerning the lector Celerinus, and how much he endured for the faith and confession of Christ.”

These things, therefore, occurred in some other letter of Cyprian which we do not possess. **Baluze.**]

# Letter II  
## Saint Cyprian, Bishop of Carthage, to Saint Cornelius, Pope

(Erasm., II, 10; Pamel., Rigalt., Baluz., Paris., XLI; Lips., Coustant, 127; Galland., III, 333.)

[Col. 0702B]

**Summary.—** What Cyprian did, in accordance with the usage of divine tradition and ecclesiastical institution, when he was more reliably informed of Cornelius’s legitimate ordination. That the letters of [Col. 0703A] Cornelius, not those of Novatian, were publicly read. Why, in addition to Cornelius’s letters announcing that he was bishop, he desired the testimony of those who had taken part in his ordination. He asks Cornelius to read the letters which he sends him concerning the case of Felicissimus, the presbyters, and their adherents.

**Cyprian to his brother Cornelius, greetings.**

[Note: [Col. 0703D]

**I. We recently sent.** Marca, discussing this embassy of Cyprian to Cornelius in book V of *On Concord*, chapter 2, says that Caldonius and Fortunatus were sent as envoys of Cyprian and the Council of Carthage so that they might strive, so far as possible, to restore by their counsels the unity of the Church, which had been divided by Novatian’s faction, and so that they might report to the Africans what they had learned concerning Cornelius’s ordination. **Baluze.**

**Obstinate persistence.** The constitution of the emperor Honorius against Pelagius and Celestius says: “But because the excessively persistent evil of the obstinate required that the constitution be issued a second time.” *Pertinacia* (“persistence”) is generally used in a bad sense, [Col. 0704B] as we observed in the notes on the *Capitularies*, page 1110. **Baluze.**

**Increasing (*gliscente*).** Shortly afterward, looking back to Paul’s words in Ephesians 5:32, “This mystery is great; but I speak of Christ and the Church,” Cyprian considers the bishop to be the spouse of the church to which he is legitimately ordained; hence he wishes the man who is unlawfully introduced into that same church, contrary to the mystery of the divine ordering, to be regarded as an adulterer. It is thus apparent both that the custom of considering bishops the spouses of the churches to which they are bound is ancient and that it rests upon Paul’s own words. [Col. 0704C] **Coustant.**

**A bishop for themselves.** Novatian. Baronius wrote that this happened in the year 254; Pearson, in 251. **Baluze.**

**Colleagues.** That is, the bishops who had taken part in Cornelius’s ordination. Sixteen were present at it, among whom two Africans, namely Caldonius and Fortunatus, are listed. None of the letters announcing Cornelius’s ordination survives. **Coustant.**

**With joy.** Thus all the old copies, both ours and the English, and all editions before that of Rigaltius. I therefore greatly wonder that this most learned man preferred the authority of the Benevento manuscript, in which he says *with sorrow* is written, to the consensus of the old copies and editions. Although this reading could be good if referred to the schismatics’ persistence, nevertheless, because no other copy supports it and all the rest oppose it, I do not think that it should be preferred to a reading resting upon so many authorities—especially since the reading which I restore with Reinhart makes excellent sense when referred to Maximus, Urbanus, and the other schismatics, who were rumored, though the report was not entirely certain, to have returned to the Church. When this news was received through the letters of Caldonius and Fortunatus and the report of Pompeius and Stephanus, joy had arisen among the clergy of Carthage, although it was incomplete because the report was uncertain, as is also apparent from Letter XLVI, page 60. [Col. 0704D] **Baluze.**

**Our province.** Below, Letter XLV, page 59: “But since our province extends rather widely.” For it has Numidia and Mauretania adjoining it. From this the English editors therefore inferred that “the province” here means Africa, Numidia, and Mauretania, which were subject to the see of Carthage. Certainly Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, says in chapter LV of the code of canons of the African Church that he bears the care of all the Churches. This interpretation of the English editors may furthermore seem to be supported by the reading of the Reims manuscript of Saint-Denis, in which one reads “our provinces.” Salvian, book IV, chapter 4: “The regions of Africa know.” **Baluze.**

**Should be sent.** Supply “to you,” so that they might profess that they approved and maintained communion with him, as is explained below in Letter IV. [Col. 0705C] **Coustant.**]

## I

In accordance with what was fitting for servants of God, and especially for just and peaceable bishops, dearest brother, we recently sent our colleagues Caldonius [Note: [Col. 0703B] *Calidonius*, Foss. Vict. Mich.] and Fortunatus, so that not only through the persuasion of our letters but also through their own presence [Note: [Col. 0703B] “your presence,” in the older Colbert manuscript.] and the counsel of all of you they might strive and labor, so far as they could, to reunite the members of the divided body within the unity of the Catholic Church [Col. 0703B] and join them together by the bond of Christian love.

But since the obstinate and inflexible [Col. 0704A] persistence of the opposing party not only refused the bosom and embrace of the root [Note: [Col. 0703B] “nurse,” old manuscript, Baluze.] and mother, but, as discord increased [Note: [Col. 0703B] “Increasing for the worse, so that it grew savage,” the same manuscript. Another, more recent manuscript, with the Oxford edition: “Increasing and growing savage for the worse.” With Pamelius and the Corbie manuscript, the preferable reading is: “Increasing and growing worse again” [Col. 0704B].] and grew worse again, also appointed a bishop for itself and, contrary to the mystery once handed down of divine ordering and Catholic unity, established outside the Church an adulterous and rival head, we sent our letter to you after receiving both your letters and those of our colleagues, and likewise after the arrival of the good men and our dearest colleagues Pompeius and Stephanus. By them all these matters were firmly affirmed and proved to us with common joy [Note: [Col. 0704B] “All these things with sorrow,” Oxon.] [Note: [Col. 0704B] “Were firmly asserted,” Oxon.] [Note: [Col. 0704B] “Proved; when these matters had become known, in accordance with,” Ver.], just as both the holiness and truth of divine tradition and ecclesiastical institution required.

Moreover, in conveying these same facts throughout our province to the knowledge of each of our colleagues, we instructed them also to send our brethren with letters [Col. 0704B] [Note: [Col. 0704B] “To be brought back,” Bod. 3, Lin. Ebor. NC. 1, Foss. Vict. Mich.].

## II

Although our mind and purpose had already then been made known [Col. 0705A] to the brethren and to the entire people there [Note: [Col. 0705B] “Made manifest,” Corb., Bod. 3], when, after letters had recently been received from both parties, we read your letter and announced the appointment of your episcopate to the ears of each person, nevertheless, mindful also of our common honor and maintaining respect for priestly dignity and holiness, we rejected the bitter, accusatory charges that had been heaped together in the book transmitted to us from the opposing side. We considered and weighed at the same time that, in so great and religious an assembly of brethren, with the priests of God sitting together and the altar set in place, such things ought neither to be read nor heard. For things that may, when heard, stir up scandal by their contentious [*discordiosus*] style and confuse brethren situated far away and across the sea through uncertain opinion must not readily be brought forth or heedlessly and rashly published.

[Note: [Col. 0705B] Thus the old Colbert manuscript. But the recent manuscript and the Fuxensis manuscript: “to the contentious and those who do not hear,” Colb. Corb.: “they are discord and to the disobedient,” perhaps for “to the contentious and disobedient,” that is, “those who do not obey.” In the printed texts, however: “when heard, things written in a contentious style.” “By a contentious style, scandal,” Bod. 1, 2. NC. [Col. 0705C] Lin. Ebor. Thu. Foss. Mich. Vict.]

Let those answer for it who, serving either their own fury or their own lust, and forgetful of divine law and holiness, [Col. 0705B] are eager meanwhile to bandy about things they cannot prove; and who, when they cannot destroy and overthrow innocence, are satisfied to sprinkle stains upon it by lying report and false rumor.

[Note: [Col. 0706B] “Dash against,” Lamon manuscript.]

Certainly, so far as befits superiors and priests, care must be taken that such things, when written by certain persons, are rejected by us. For what then will become of what we learn and teach to have been written: “Restrain your tongue from evil, and your lips from speaking deceitfully” [Note: [Col. 0706B] “Speaking deceit,” Lam., Ebor., NC. 1, Bod. 1] (Ps. XXXIX, 13)? Likewise elsewhere: “Your [Col. 0706A] mouth abounded in malice, and your tongue embraced deceit; sitting, you spoke against your brother, and against your mother’s son you placed a stumbling block” (Ps. XLIX, 20). Likewise, what the Apostle says: “Let no evil speech proceed from your mouth” [Note: [Col. 0706B] “Go forth,” Lin., NC.], “but what is good” [Note: [Col. 0706B] “But if anything is good,” Lam., Ebor., NC. 1, Bod. 1] “for the building up of faith, that it may impart grace to those who hear” (Eph. IV, 29).

Moreover, we show that these things ought to be done if, whenever such writings have been composed through the slanderous rashness of certain persons, we do not allow them to be read among us. And therefore, dearest brother, when writings of this kind against you and against the fellow-presbyter sitting with you had come to me, I ordered those portions to be read to the clergy and people which expressed religious simplicity and did not resound with any barking of curses and abuse.

[Note: [Col. 0706C]

## III. Our colleagues

We learn from what follows that the testimonies not only of Caldonius and [Col. 0706D] Fortunatus, African bishops, but also of others who had been present at Cornelius’s appointment, were awaited. COUSTANT.

### By letters having been written

Thus the old editions together with our manuscripts. And below, indeed, in Epistle 3, we shall hear Cyprian saying that he was writing a short letter; and in Epistle 4, no. 4: “They wrote letters from there.” But the Oxford edition, following Pamelius, has “done”—a reading that we readily acknowledge is not foreign to Cyprian’s style. From this passage one understands how great, from the Church’s very beginnings, was always the concern to foster unity and communion. Since, moreover, by Christ’s institution the center of this unity was the apostolic see, it was of the greatest importance that its prelate should be unknown to no one, and that everyone should testify as soon as possible that he adhered to him. COUST.

### Wandering about

[Col. 0707C] Thus some old books. Others have *balabundas*, *belabundas*, *volabundas*, *vagabundas*, or *errabundas*, according to the pleasure of the ancient copyists. BALUZ.

### Remained fixed

The Manutius edition preferred this reading. Morel and Pamelius rejected it. Yet it is found in twenty-three ancient copies, whereas the reading “persevered” is found in only three. Indeed, two or three of the older editions have “remained fixed” or “persevered.” Here, however, one should remember an observation I have made in more than one place: when ancient copyists saw two variant readings but were uncertain which should be retained, they inserted both, leaving the reader’s judgment unimpaired. It is therefore probable that the word “persevered,” which follows “remained fixed” in these two manuscripts and in the old editions, derives from the gloss of some scholar wishing to explain what “remained fixed” meant in this passage.

Pamelius, who thought that this word could not be equivalent to [Col. 0707D] “persevered,” did not doubt that, of the two readings joined together in the old editions and in some ancient books, one had to be rejected and the one signifying perseverance retained. Yet he could have seen in Nonius Marcellus that *supersedere* means “to remain” or “to persevere,” as though to stay settled in one’s will and purpose. BALUZ.

### Letters

It is regrettable that these letters have perished through the ravages of time. EDD.]

## III

As for our having asked for the writings of our colleagues who [Col. 0706B] had been present there at your appointment, we were not seeking anything new in forgetfulness of ancient custom. For it would have been sufficient for you to announce by a written letter that you were bishop [Note: [Col. 0706B] “For you to announce by letters that you had been made bishop,” Lam., NC. 1, Ebor., Lin.], had there not been on the opposing side a dissenting faction which, by its criminal and slanderous fabrications, was disturbing the minds of many colleagues and brethren alike and confusing their hearts [Note: [Col. 0706B] “Shaking,” NC. 1, Bod. 1, 2, Ebor.].

To settle this matter, we considered it necessary that the firm and solid authority of our colleagues who were writing to us from there should be secured. By proclaiming in their letters testimonies worthy of your character, life [Note: [Col. 0706C] “Your blameless life,” Lin.], and discipline, [Col. 0707A] they removed every scruple concerning doubt and disagreement even from rivals and from those who delight either in novelty or in the perversity of affairs. And in accordance with our judgment, weighed by sound reasoning [Note: [Col. 0707B] “Freed.” Oxford edition following Pamelius. Corb. manuscript: “freed.” Several others: “weighed.” The reading “weighed” is preferable, with Manutius and the older Colbert manuscript. Below, Epistle II, no. 4, we shall read: “after the judgment had been weighed through consultation with everyone”; and no. 3: “after the reasoning had long been weighed and pondered”], they sincerely and firmly approved your priesthood in the minds of the brethren tossed upon this flood.

For this above all, brother, is what we labor and ought to labor to accomplish: that, so far as we can, we take care to maintain the unity handed down by the Lord and through the Apostles to us, their successors; and that, so far as lies within us, we gather back into the Church the wandering and straying sheep whom the obstinate faction and heretical temptation of certain persons separates from their mother. Only those are to remain outside who have refused to desist from their obstinacy or frenzy [Col. 0707B] and to return to us; they themselves will render an account to the Lord for the division and separation they have caused and for the Church they have abandoned.

[Note: [Col. 0707B] “Who persevered, or shall have persevered, in their obstinacy or frenzy,” printed editions; corrected with the aid of the older manuscripts, in which “remained fixed” occurs. This readily crept in for “to remain fixed,” because both are sometimes used indiscriminately. Here, however, “to remain fixed” is governed by the verb “refused.” Pamelius notes that in two printed texts he encountered “remained fixed or persevered.” From this it is gathered that the phrase “or persevered” was first added through the work of scholiasts, and that later, either together with “remained fixed” or after that word had been rejected, “persevered” prevailed.]

[Note: [Col. 0707D]

## IV. The clergy there

For Cyprian this is equivalent to “our clergy.” Accordingly, above, at the beginning of no. 2, “our” is not added to “the people there.” [Col. 0708C] I refrain from citing similar examples, from which it would become evident that “our” is superfluously added in the editions of Pamelius and Oxford. The two letters mentioned here still survive, namely nos. 38 and 40 in Pamelius’s edition. At the end of the one sent to Caldonius and his associates, one reads: “Transmit these letters of mine . . . to the clergy at Carthage, adding the names of all who have joined themselves to Felicissimus.” Epistle 40, moreover, is expressly addressed to the people concerning the five presbyters of Felicissimus’s faction. COUSTANT.

### Mettius

He is also mentioned in the following epistle. Although it is of little importance to know his true name, I nevertheless note that in the old books he is called Mettius, Messius, Messio, Missius, and Mersius. For the old books do not agree concerning his name. BALUZ.]

## IV

As regards the case here of certain presbyters [Note: [Col. 0708B] “The presbyters,” Ver., NC. 2] and Felicissimus, our colleagues sent you a letter signed by their own hands so that you might know what was done here. From their letter you will learn what they thought and what judgment they pronounced after hearing them.

You will do better, [Col. 0708A] however, brother, if you also order to be read there to the brethren copies of the letters which, out of our common affection, I recently sent to you for reading through our colleagues Caldonius and Fortunatus. I had written them concerning the same Felicissimus and the body of presbyters associated with him, to the clergy there and also to the people.

[Note: [Col. 0708B] “To the clergy there,” not “to the people.” In Manutius. In the editions of Pamelius and Oxford: “to our clergy there and to the people.” In the Corb. manuscript: “to our church and to the people.” With Morel and the excellent Colbert manuscript, we prefer: “to the clergy there and also to the people.”]

These letters set out both the ordering and the rationale of what was done [Note: [Col. 0708B] “Concerning the ordering and rationale of what was done,” old Colbert manuscript, Bod. 1; then *loquamur*, “let us speak,” where most manuscripts, like the printed editions, have *loquantur*, “let them speak.” The reading *eloquantur*, “set forth,” from the recent Colbert manuscript is preferable. The first letter of this verb readily fell out, since the preceding [Col. 0708C] word ended with the same letter], so that the brotherhood may be instructed by us concerning everything, both there and here. I have now also transmitted the same copies through Mettius the subdeacon, sent by me, and Nicephorus the acolyte. I pray that you may always fare well, dearest brother.

**In the Year of Christ 251**

[Note: [Col. 0708C]

## Epistle III

Sent together with the preceding letter and delivered expressly to the subdeacon Mettius, who had been dispatched to the City together with the acolyte Nicephorus. [Col. 0708D] COUSTANT.—The English editors noted that this epistle is absent from Erasmus’s edition. That is untrue. They noted further that it appears as Book V, Epistle 9, in the Manutius edition. But I very much believe that error must be imputed to the printer, since it was published as Book II, Epistle 9, in that edition, which followed the Erasmian. BALUZ.

### To you; to us

I restored this reading because it seemed to me to fit Saint Cyprian’s meaning better. Otherwise the other reading, which has “to you,” is good. Both have many sound witnesses. The former rests on the authority [Col. 0709C] of fifteen old copies and occurs in the Speyer edition, the old Venetian, the Erasmian, and the Manutius editions. The latter is found in eight ancient manuscripts and in the editions of Rembolt, Morel, and Pamelius. BAL.

### Confessors

Moses and Maximus. See what was said above on Epistle XLI.

### Mettius

Here too this subdeacon’s name is written in very different ways. We have retained the commonly received reading, since the matter is of little importance. Another reading frequently found in old copies has “Ethippus” or “Ettius.” See what Pamelius notes there. On the Mettian family see Jean Tristan de Saint-Amant in volume II of his *Commentaries*, pp. 465, 501. BALUZ.

### A short letter

That is, Epistle XLIV in Pamelius’s edition and XLVI in the Oxford edition, which is addressed to Maximus, Nicostratus, and the other confessors. COUSTANT.]

# EPISTLE III. FROM THE SAME TO THE SAME

*(Erasm. II, 9; Pamel., Rigalt., Baluz. XLIII; Paris XLII; Lips.; Coustant, p. 130; Galland III, 335.)*

[Col. 0708B]

**ARGUMENT.—Concerning the letter that he wrote to the confessors who had been led astray by Novatian and Novatus.**

**CYPRIAN TO HIS BROTHER CORNELIUS, GREETINGS.**

I considered it both religiously appropriate for you and necessary, [Col. 0709A] dearest brother, to write a short letter to the confessors who are there and who, led astray by the obstinacy and perversity of Novatian and Novatus, have withdrawn from the Church. In it I appealed to them, out of our mutual affection, to return to their mother, that is, the Catholic Church.

I instructed that this letter first be read to you by Mettius the subdeacon [Note: [Col. 0709C] “By Ethippus the deacon,” Mich., Foss., Ar., NC. 1, Lam., Bod. 2, 3; likewise “to the same Ethippus,” Corb.], lest anyone falsely claim that I had written anything other than what is contained in my letter. Nevertheless, I instructed the same Mettius, whom I sent from me to you, to conduct the matter according to your judgment; and if you think that the same letter should be delivered [Note: [Col. 0709C] “Entrusted,” Foss., Mich., Vict.] to the confessors, he is then to hand it over. I pray that you may always fare well, dearest brother.

**In the Year of Christ 251**

[Note: [Col. 0709D]

## Epistle IV

Cornelius delivered to Primitivus, a presbyter of Carthage who had carried Cyprian’s preceding Epistle I, the letter to which Cyprian now replies. Thus one should suppose no much greater interval between the aforesaid epistle and this one than was required for Primitivus to travel to Rome and, after resting his body for a short time, to return to Carthage. COUSTANT.—Old copies of this epistle are extremely rare. Pamelius had none. The English editors were no richer. I had seven: namely, the manuscripts of de Thou, Fossés, Saint-Arnoul of Metz, Bec, Saint-Victor, Saint-Denis of Reims, and Foix. BALUZ.

### In the name of Polycarp

The Oxford editor notes that it was once [Col. 0710C] customary, whenever a letter was sent from a particular church, for it to be sent in the name of that church’s bishop, even if he was absent. The presbyters and deacons of Hadrumetum followed this custom in their bishop’s absence. COUSTANT.—He was bishop of Hadrumetum and is frequently mentioned by Cyprian. He attended the Council of Carthage concerning the baptism of heretics. BALUZ.

### To the presbyters

It was also established custom that letters sent to a particular church were addressed to its bishop [Col. 0710D], unless the see was vacant. The presbyters and deacons of Hadrumetum had at first observed this custom when writing to Cornelius; afterward, on the advice of Cyprian and Liberalis, they addressed their letters to the Roman presbyters and deacons. Cornelius was therefore rightly disturbed that Cyprian and Liberalis seemed to call his episcopate into question. COUSTANT.]

# EPISTLE IV. FROM THE SAME TO THE SAME

*(Erasm. IV, 8; Pam., Rigalt., Baluz., Paris XLIV; Lips.; Coustant, p. 131; Galland III, p. 335.)*

[Col. 0709B]

**ARGUMENT.—While reliable testimony concerning the appointment of Cornelius was awaited, Cyprian and Liberalis had advised the clergy of Hadrumetum to address their letters to the Roman presbyters and deacons rather than to Cornelius. When Cornelius remonstrated about this, Cyprian now answers that complaint. He adds that the validity of Cornelius’s episcopate, established in the clearest light and confirmed by the replies of his colleagues, [Col. 0709C] is acknowledged.**

[Col. 0710A]

**CYPRIAN TO HIS BROTHER CORNELIUS, GREETINGS.**

## I

I have read your letter, dearest brother, which you sent through our fellow-presbyter Primitivus. In it I found that you were disturbed because, although letters from the colony of Hadrumetum had been addressed to you in the name of Polycarp, after we—Liberalis and I—had arrived at that same place, letters began to be addressed from there to the presbyters and deacons.

[Note: [Col. 0710D]

## II. There

That is, in Africa. COUSTANT.]

## II

We wish you to know and believe with certainty that this was done through no fickleness or insult. Several of us colleagues who had assembled together had decided that, after our fellow-bishops Caldonius and Fortunatus had been sent to you as delegates, all matters should meanwhile be kept entirely in suspense until those same colleagues of ours returned to us, either after affairs [Col. 0710B] there had been restored to peace or after the truth had been ascertained. The presbyters and deacons residing at Hadrumetum, however, in the absence of our fellow-bishop Polycarp, did not know what had been decided by us in common.

But when we came there in person [Note: [Col. 0710C] “We came to the present place,” Speyer], and they learned of our decision, they too began to observe the same course as the others, so that the agreement of the churches situated there should differ in no respect.

[Note: [Col. 0710D]

## III. A province spread more widely

Epiphanius, bishop of Salamis in Cyprus, writing to John of Jerusalem and speaking of his own province, says: “Because the province was great and extends widely.” That letter survives among those of Jerome. BALUZ.

### It also has

The recent Colbert manuscript has “for it has.” “For it also has” would not be displeasing. Then the same manuscript, together with several others and the printed edition, has: “Numidia and the two Mauritanias adjoining it.” We restore the reading of the older Colbert manuscript, which is also that of two English manuscripts of good quality. [Col. 0711B] The Oxford editor thinks that the word “two” crept into the text from the margin. Nevertheless, he also observes that Mauritania, according to Pliny, Book V, chapter 1, was divided through the cruelty of Gaius Caesar into two parts, Caesariensis and Tingitana, and that a third part, namely Sitifensis, was finally added to them.

[Col. 0711C] COUST.—“For it has Numidia.” This is the reading of the old books, except that some have “also” in place of “for,” following the common habit of the ancients in interchanging these conjunctions. In his note on Epistle XLII, Rigaltius thought that everything said there about Numidia and Mauritania was interpolated and had crept into the text from the margin. Yet it occurs in all the editions and in seven ancient manuscripts—that is, in all the ancient manuscripts seen by me. I do not see why these words should be considered interpolated.

It is certain that Carthage, which was the rival of the city of Rome, held primacy over all the provinces within Africa, as is written in law XXII, *Concerning Recruits*, in the Theodosian Code; and that the bishop of Carthage had responsibility for all the churches of Africa, as Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, says in the code of canons of the African Church; and that all African bishops, including Numidians and Moors, customarily assembled at the councils of the bishop of Carthage, as is evident also from the council of Saint Cyprian. [Col. 0711D] Saint Cyprian therefore names Numidia and Mauritania here to show that his province was widely extended, since in addition to Africa properly so called it also had adjoining it Numidia and Mauritania, which were themselves broad and extensive provinces. Mela nevertheless writes that Numidia is narrower than Mauritania. BALUZ.

### Mauritania

Thus the old books and old editions. Manutius was the first to print “the two Mauritanias.” [Col. 0712B] From this arose the commonly received text. Yet in the council of Saint Cyprian mention is made of the bishops of Africa, Numidia, and Mauritania, but not of the Mauritanias. The Manutius reading is nevertheless supported by Pliny, who in Book I, chapter 2, and Book XIII, chapter 15, names the two Mauritanias; likewise by Tacitus in Book I of the *Histories*, where the two Mauritanias are mentioned; [Col. 0712C] and by Martianus Capella in Book VI, in his description of Africa. Correctly so: for Dio Cassius, Book VI, relates that the emperor Claudius divided Mauritania, after it had been subjected to the Romans, into two parts, Tingitana and Caesariensis. Herodian, Book XII, names Numidia and Mauritania as subject to the Romans. See Marca, chapter 87 of the book *On Primacies*. BALUZ.]

## III

Certain persons, however, sometimes disturb minds and spirits by their statements, when they report some matters otherwise than the truth stands. For we know that, as we explained the matter to each person who sailed, so that they should not sail with any occasion of scandal, we exhorted them to acknowledge and hold fast to the root and mother-church of the Catholic Church.

[Note: [Col. 0710C] “We know that we explained the matter and exhorted them,” Speyer, anonymous.]

But because our province is more widely spread and also has [Col. 0711A] Numidia and Mauritania adjoining it, we decided—lest the schism created in the City confuse the minds of the absent through uncertain opinion—that, through bishops, with the truth of the matter retained by us and greater authority secured for confirming your appointment [Note: [Col. 0711B] “Your appointment having been made,” Speyer], only then, after every scruple had been removed from the breasts of each individual [Note: [Col. 0711B] “Excluded from their breasts,” Ver.], letters should be written, as they now are, by absolutely everyone situated there, so that all our colleagues might firmly approve and maintain both you and communion with you—that is, the unity and love of the Catholic Church.

We rejoice that this has come about by divine action and that our counsel has proceeded providently [Note: [Col. 0711B] Thus the older manuscripts. Other books have: “has been beneficial”].

[Note: [Col. 0712C]

## IV. The fellow-bishops Caldonius

Amusing are those who relate that he passed from Africa into Lusitania and was bishop of Braga there. BALUZ.]

## IV

For thus both the truth and the dignity of your episcopate have now been established in the clearest light and by the most manifest and firmest confirmation: from the replies of our colleagues who wrote letters to us from there, [Col. 0711B] and from the report and testimonies of our fellow-bishops Pompeius, Stephanus, Caldonius, and Fortunatus, everyone came to know both the necessary origin, the just rationale, and the glorious innocence of your appointment. [Note: [Col. 0711B] Thus the old anonymous manuscript and Speyer. “Will become known,” Rig.]

That we, together with the rest of our colleagues [Note: [Col. 0711B] “With the rest of our colleagues,” Oxford], may administer this steadfastly and firmly, and hold fast [Col. 0712A] in the harmonious unanimity of the Catholic Church, divine favor will bring to completion.

[Note: [Col. 0711B] “That we may maintain the unanimity of the Church in harmony,” the early editions with two manuscripts, Morel, Manutius, Pamelius, and Oxford. The recent Colbert manuscript: “that we may maintain the peace of the Church in harmonious unanimity.” The older manuscript, which omits the word “peace” but otherwise presents the same reading, seemed to the others more authentic. Soon afterward the same manuscript has: “divine protection will bring to completion.”]

Thus the Lord, who deigns to choose and appoint priests for himself in his Church, may also guard by his will and assistance those whom he has chosen and appointed, inspiring them as they govern [Note: [Col. 0712B] The old Colbert manuscript has “governingly”: perhaps more correctly. Otherwise the structure of the sentence appears to require “those governing”], and supplying both vigor to restrain the obstinacy of the wicked and gentleness to foster the repentance of the fallen. I pray that you may always fare well, dearest brother.

**In the Year of Christ 251**

[Note: [Col. 0712C]

## Epistle V.—Cornelius to Cyprian, etc.
