The more recent Colbert manuscript, like the early editions of Cyprian, has “Cyprian to Cornelius”; but the Manutius edition of 1563 correctly presents the title in this and the immediately following epistle. The Corbie manuscript also originally displayed that title, but an ancient hand restored in it: “Cornelius to Cyprian.” That the letter is in fact Cornelius’s is placed beyond doubt by Cyprian below in Epistle 7.

Some prefer to call it a fragment of another epistle, others a memorandum, and others a short letter. Cyprian himself, in the cited Epistle 7, calls it a letter. [Col. 0712D] The opinion of those who regard it as a fragment appears to be supported, first, by the fact that Novatian, although not yet named, is designated by the words “this criminal man”; and second, because Cyprian, in replying to this epistle, records that he then learned certain matters concerning Evaristus and Nicostratus which are not contained in it.

Yet the following letter, whose integrity no one doubts, will establish that Novatian’s name was deliberately suppressed in this epistle and a pronoun substituted for it, since Cornelius conducts himself there in the same [Col. 0713A] way. Other pontiffs later imitated this practice, notably Celestine in dealing with Nestorius; so too did the Fathers, either because they thought that, at the rise of heresies, the names of the heresiarchs should be spared, or because they recoiled from uttering them.

[Col. 0713B] Nor do the particular details that Cyprian recounts—details concerning Nicostratus and Evaristus that are not expressed in this letter—prove any more certainly that the epistle has been mutilated, since he could have learned them from the mouth of Nicephorus. At first this epistle alone was entrusted to Nicephorus as he hurried to Africa. Then, when he was on the point of departure, the following epistle was also added. He carried both together. COUSTANT.

In almost all the ancient manuscripts this epistle is said to be from Cyprian to Cornelius. I found it said to be from Cornelius to Cyprian nowhere except in the Corbie manuscript and in one of my own. Nevertheless, in excerpts sent to me from manuscript 199 of the Vatican Library, I read that it was written by Cornelius to Cyprian in the following form: “Epistle of Cornelius to Cyprian concerning the faction of the schismatics. Cornelius to Cyprian, greetings. Lest anything.” It therefore cannot be doubted that it truly belongs to Cornelius. Pamelius thought that it was incomplete and merely a fragment; Rigaltius thought it was a continuation, or rather an addition, to one of the preceding letters. BALUZIUS.

### This criminal man

Jerome speaks of this man as follows in *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 70: “Novatian, a presbyter of the city of Rome, attempted to seize the priestly chair [Col. 0713C] in opposition to Cornelius and established the doctrine of the Novatians, who are called in Greek Καθάρων, ‘the Pure,’ refusing to receive apostates as penitents.” More may be seen in Cornelius’s letter to Fabius, which follows shortly, and in several letters of Dionysius of Alexandria preserved by Eusebius.

Most noteworthy, however, is that in the surviving letters Cornelius always suppresses the name of his adversary Novatian. Concerning the various spellings of that name, I shall say something here. The celebrated Lardner, in *On the Credibility of the Gospel History*, Part II, vol. V, note at the end of the volume on chapter 47, argued at length that this man’s true name, like that of his contemporary, the African Novatus, was Novatus. He also cited several authors, including Latin ones, who exhibit this spelling, though perhaps in imitation of the Greeks, who almost always wrote Νοούατον or Ναυατόν, “Novatus.”

Yet it is well known that Cyprian always designated the man by the name Novatian, to say nothing of writers of later ages. Indeed, in the Greek historian Eusebius, Book VII, chapter 8, where certain extracts from [Col. 0713D] a letter of Dionysius of Alexandria to Dionysius of Rome are reported, the name is written Νοουατιανῷ, “to Novatian.” Moreover, in the letter of the Alexandrian prelate to Novatian himself, preserved by Eusebius in Book VI, chapter 45, not only Jerome and Rufinus in certain editions, but also Syncellus and Nicephorus, exhibit the same spelling. Perhaps, therefore, one must conclude that Eusebius actually wrote Ναυατιανῷ, “to Novatian,” in this place—not Νουάτῳ, “to Novatus,” as is commonly read—because he had found the former in the manuscripts of Dionysius.

Furthermore, nothing contrary seems capable of being inferred from the derivative *Novatiani*, as if it had been formed from the name Novatus, since otherwise those followers would have had to be called *Novatianani*. For this consideration did not induce Scaliger to believe that the man was called Novatus. See his *Observations on the Chronicle of Eusebius*, [Col. 0714A] p. 236.

It should also be added here that followers of Tatian were called *Tatians* after Tatian by Epiphanius in his work *On Heresies*, and similarly by other authors, just as the Novatians were named after Novatian. Cyprian nevertheless calls them *Novatianenses* in the letter to Jubaianus, or Epistle 73, near the beginning.

Finally, I shall warn the reader that this question derives no illumination from the titles of those two works, [Col. 0714B] *On the Trinity* and *On Jewish Foods*, which are customarily ascribed to Novatian, since they appear to have been given those titles on the authority of Saint Jerome, not on the evidence of the manuscripts themselves. Meanwhile, *Novatianus* was derived from the name *Novatus*, just as *Fabianus* from *Fabius* and *Bassianus* from *Bassus*. Indeed, Fabius, bishop of Antioch, is frequently called Fabianus by authors. ROUTH.

### Prostrated by the powers of God

That is, says Nathaniel Marshall, the English translator of Cyprian, by the ecclesiastical judgments pronounced against him, which were considered ratified in heaven. ROUTH.

### Had been expelled from there

That is, from Carthage. Concerning this Cyprian says by way of introduction in the preceding Epistle 1: “There came to us, dearest brother, sent by Novatian, the presbyter Maximus, the deacon Augendus, a certain Machaeus, and Longinus, etc.” There, however, Cyprian teaches that they were not driven from the city but excluded from communion.

Furthermore, the presbyter Maximus just mentioned was afterward made pseudo-bishop of Carthage by Novatus. [Col. 0714C] He is therefore distinct from the presbyter and confessor Maximus, who was first led astray by Novatian and returned to the Church somewhat later. See the epistle immediately following. Nor should the aforementioned Augendus be confused with the man who carried Cornelius’s letter to Cyprian. COUSTANT. Baluzius makes a similar observation concerning Augendus: that this man is distinct from Augendus, the deacon of Novatian’s party, who is mentioned in Epistle IV.

### In the earlier letter

It does not survive. COUSTANT.

### Dionysius

In one of my old books “Zoticus” is written. The English edition attests that it is read in this way in one Bodleian manuscript. So also Morel’s edition. BALUZIUS.

### That he had already arrived there

That is, at Carthage. Cornelius’s opinion was not false if we interpret it with reference not to the time at which he was writing, but to the time at which he judged that his letter would be delivered to Cyprian. For the second embassy of Novatian had arrived there the day before this letter was delivered. COUSTANT.

### His patroness

From this a learned man suspects that he had been a slave and [Col. 0714D] bondservant. This would be more readily persuasive if Cornelius had used the word “mistress,” not “patroness.” It was all the more important that this deacon’s crimes become known because he boasted more extensively of the title of confessor and thereby deceived the common people. COUSTANT.

Canon 82, called a Canon of the Apostles, permits even bondservants, with their masters’ consent, to be admitted to the higher ecclesiastical orders. As Coustant indicated, Nicostratus appears to have been a freedman, not a slave, and thus all the less liable to exclusion from ecclesiastical rank.

### The Church’s deposits

That is, ecclesiastical funds, which were regarded as the deposits of widows and orphans because they were preserved for the purpose of relieving them, as may be gathered from the following Epistle VII, II. 1, otherwise Epistle 49 or [Col. 0715A] 52 of Cyprian: “Nicostratus, however, after losing the diaconate entrusted with sacred administration, after abstracting ecclesiastical funds by sacrilegious [Col. 0715B] fraud, and afterward refusing to restore the deposits of widows and orphans, went not so much to Africa, etc.” Nor was it difficult for a deacon, to whom the distribution of those funds had been entrusted, to embezzle deposits of this kind. COUSTANT.

### An originator of the schism

The Colbert manuscript has: “with the originator of the schism.” Evaristus is called an originator of the schism insofar as he advised others to follow it. Nor did he desist from this enterprise even after he was deposed from the episcopate. Accordingly, Cyprian writes in reply below, in Epistle VII (49), that he, “having made shipwreck of truth and faith, was INCITING similar shipwrecks among certain persons like himself.”

Moreover, if this Evaristus, as is very probable, was one of Novatian’s consecrators, he is not undeservedly called an originator of the heresy, since by this consecration he provided both an opportunity and authority for the heresy. COUSTANT.

Pacianus, in his letter to Sympronian against the treatises of the Novatians, writes: “I do not know what Novatian did, what Novatus committed, with what Evaristus swelled up, or what Nicostratus announced.” [Col. 0715C] And below he speaks of “those who received Evaristus and Nicostratus, and the others who withdrew from the Church, polluted in tongue, hand, and conduct.”

Henry Valesius concluded from this epistle that this Evaristus was one of Novatian’s consecrators, in his notes on Book VI, chapter 43, of Eusebius’s *Ecclesiastical History*—that is, on Cornelius’s letter to Fabius, which I have placed below. BALUZIUS.

### And a successor to the people

Thus all the old books and editions. The English editors, on I know not what authority, printed *succensorem*, “an inflamer,” with, as I judge, no meaning, while noting that perhaps *succursorem*, “a helper,” should be read. But I do not know where they found the word *succursorem*, which would in any case be quite useless in this passage. For Cyprian says that Zetus was appointed bishop in place of Evaristus and given as successor to the people over whom Evaristus had previously presided. BALUZIUS.

*Succussorem*, which Fell had in fact conjectured should be read, appears to have been understood by him in the sense of “instigator” or “agitator,” for the *Old Glosses* have [Col. 0715D] *succusso*, κατασείω, “I shake violently.” See Valesius’s note on the **COUNCIL OF ANTIOCH** above, vol. II, p. 502. ROUTH.

### To the people over whom he had previously presided

In the Corbie manuscript: “he had previously been”; then, in the first hand, “Zelus,” and on revision, “Zeno,” which Pamelius also attests that he read in the Cambron manuscript. One English manuscript prefers “Zoticus.” Coustant is mistaken here, for Fell had previously noted “Zoticus” for “Dionysius” at line 14. It is clear from this that a successor to Evaristus was appointed by the authority of those who had removed him from the episcopate. COUSTANT.

### Zetus

This name is absent from the old editions and from some old books. It is nevertheless found in one of my manuscripts and in the Manutius edition. In the Foix manuscript it is written “Gestus.” [Col. 0716A] The Corbie manuscript, in which “Zetus” was first written—compare Coustant above—has “Zeno” by correction. [Col. 0716B] Pamelius attests that it was written in this way also in the Cambron manuscript. A certain Zetus, though an earlier one, is mentioned by Propertius, Book III, elegy 8; by Horace, Book I, Epistle 18; and also in a certain tragedy of Seneca. BAL.]

But here he committed greater and more serious offenses. “But Novatus committed these things here,” Bodl. 1. FELL. This seems to refer to Evaristus, Novatian’s associate and helper, who, Cornelius says, conducted himself worse at Rome than in his own see. Coustant takes the same view; his interpretation concerning this Evaristus is given below. ROUTH.

“Should always have attached to his side.” The Colbert manuscript has “should have bound to his side”; and then, “Always fare well, dearest brother”; two others have, “Fare well, dearest brother.” COUSTANT.

“I hope, dearest brother, that you may always fare well,” etc. We have added this on the authority of the Reims manuscript of Saint-Denis. In the Fux manuscript it is written, “Always fare well, dearest brother.” In one of my manuscripts simply: “Fare well, dearest brother.” BALUZIUS. Fell noted that he had likewise read this in the Verona and Bodleian 1 manuscripts. Nevertheless, like the earlier editors of Cyprian and Coustant after him, he does not include the closing formula in the text. The words “Fare well, dearest brother” occur at the end of the immediately following letter; there, however, they had been omitted in the older editions. [Col. 0716C]

## LETTER V

(Erasmus III.12; Pamelius, Rigaltius, Baluzius XLVIII; Oxford and Leipzig L; Paris XVII; Coustant, col. 133; Galland III, p. 336; Routh, *Reliquiae sacrae* III, pp. 5 and 18.)

[Col. 0712B] **SUMMARY.—The character of those whom Novatian again sent as envoys to Carthage.**

**CORNELIUS TO HIS BROTHER CYPRIAN, GREETINGS.**

So that nothing might be lacking to the future punishment of this criminal man, [Col. 0713A] after he had been laid low by the mighty works of God, when Maximus, Longinus, and Machaeus had been expelled from there, he rose up again. And, just as I informed you in my earlier letter, which I sent through Augendus the confessor, I believe that Nicostratus, Novatus, Evaristus, Primus, and Dionysius [Note: [Col. 0713A] “Zoticus,” Bodl. 1.] have now reached your city.

Care must therefore be taken [Col. 0714A] that it become known to all our fellow bishops and brothers [Note: [Col. 0713A] “That they become known,” Corb.] that Nicostratus is guilty of many crimes: not only did he defraud and rob his earthly patroness, whose accounts he managed, but also—and this is reserved for his everlasting punishment—he carried off substantial deposits belonging to the Church. Evaristus, moreover, [Note: [Col. 0714A] “With the instigator,” Corb.] was the instigator [Col. 0715A] of the schism, and Zetum, his successor among the congregation over which he had formerly presided, was appointed bishop in his place. [Note: [Col. 0715A] The Oxford edition has *succensorem*; and in the notes, *successorem*, Manutius; Verona, perhaps *succussorem*. *Successorem* should be retained with the other manuscripts: the word refers not to Evaristus, but to Zetum, who was substituted for him.]

Through his wickedness and insatiable depravity [Note: [Col. 0716A] “Insatiable greed, such things,” Bodl. 1.], he committed greater and more serious offenses here [Note: [Col. 0716A] “But Novatus committed these things here,” Bodl. 1.] than those which he continually practiced there among his own people. Thus you may know what sort of leaders and protectors this schismatic and heretic always has attached to his side. [Note: [Col. 0716A] Thus Bodl. 1: “Always. Fare well, dearest brother.” Verona, Bodl. 1.]

## LETTER VI OF SAINT CORNELIUS, POPE, TO CYPRIAN, BISHOP OF CARTHAGE

(Erasmus III.11; Pamelius, Rigaltius, Baluzius XLVII; Paris XLV; Oxford and Leipzig XLIX; Coustant I, cols. 135–139; Galland, *Bibliotheca veterum Patrum* III, p. 337; Routh, *Reliquiae sacrae* III, pp. 6 and 23.)

[Col. 0716A]

[Note: [Col. 0716C]

**LETTER VI.—Cornelius to Cyprian.** Here too, in the early editions of Cyprian, the title had been “Cyprian to Cornelius,” as it still stands in the Colbert manuscript. The very same title also stood in the Corbie manuscript, but it was corrected by a later hand—and correctly so, as both the context itself and Letter VIII appended below (Letter 47, otherwise 51) prove. This letter was attached to the preceding one, which had been handed to Nicephorus before his departure, and was carried by the same acolyte. Yet if anyone prefers to think that this letter was written first and the preceding one attached to it, he must at least concede that both were composed at the very hour of Nicephorus’s departure. Therefore, it matters little or nothing which is placed first. COUSTANT.

Before the Manutius edition, this letter was said to be from Cyprian to Cornelius. Manutius corrected the heading, and Pamelius followed Manutius. Consequently, what Rigaltius says is false: that Pamelius wrote it thus on the basis of conjecture. Pamelius himself states that he found this reading in the Cambrai manuscript and in the Manutius edition. The same appears in the Corbie manuscript, in which, after the words quoted from it by Rigaltius, there follows: “Cornelius to his brother Cyprian, greetings.” It likewise appears in the Grenoble manuscript and in one of my old manuscripts, in which, as in the Corbie manuscript, it is written: “Here begin the replies of Cornelius to Cyprian concerning the schismatics.” I have had eight old copies of this letter. The English editors had only one, from the Bodleian Library. No other letter of the holy martyr, moreover, suffered more severely from the audacity of ancient copyists [Col. 0716D–0717A] than this one. BALUZIUS.

Rigaltius says: “This letter appears similar to that which Eusebius, *History* VI.43, reports to have been written by Cornelius to Fabius; there Urbanus, Sidonius, and Maximus are also numbered among the most steadfast confessors.” FELL. It is the letter from which excerpts immediately follow.]

**SUMMARY.—How the confessors, the presbyter Maximus, Urbanus, and Sidonius, renounced the schism and were received into the Catholic Church.**

**CORNELIUS TO HIS BROTHER CYPRIAN, GREETINGS.**

[Note: [Col. 0717B]

### I. “We endured”

The Reims manuscript of Saint-Denis adds “or shame.” BALUZIUS.

**Concerning those confessors.** Maximus, Nicostratus, and the others mentioned in Letters 41 and 42. I am strongly inclined, however, to think that this Nicostratus is different from the one named in Letter 48. (This is the letter of Cornelius which I cited immediately above; Baluzius, however, followed Pamelius’s numbering.) BALUZIUS.

There will perhaps be some who interpret these words as referring to Novatus when they read: first, that in Cyprian’s Letter 7.4, printed below, he is called the same “crafty old deceiver”; second, that in Letter 8.2 the confessors are said to have departed from the Church at his instigation; and third, that the following is written in the Bucherian catalogue: “Novatus arrived and separated Novatian and certain confessors from the Church.” Yet although the first stain of evil at Rome also began with Novatus, it is not he who is indicated here, but Novatian, presbyter of the Roman Church, who, incited by envy and ambition, became the leader and principal author of the schism at Rome.

He must certainly be understood as the man on whose account the confessors acknowledge below that they had sinned by allowing hands to be imposed upon him as though upon a bishop, and with whom, for that reason, they seem to have had a certain communion. Accordingly, in Letter 44, or 46, to those same confessors, Cyprian writes that he was deeply grieved “when,” he says, “I learned that you there”—that is, at Rome—“had consented, contrary to ecclesiastical discipline, contrary to the law of the Gospel, and contrary to the unity of the Catholic institution, to the appointment of another bishop.” But Novatus was never chosen as bishop even by the schismatics.

The subject here is the man by whose treachery and seductive eloquence the confessors were ensnared. This applies to Novatian, who, since he possessed eloquence, misused it to seduce those godly men; nor did he refrain from lies and perjury in order to deceive them. For although he burned with an unrestrained desire for the episcopate, he concealed it within himself and did not fear to affirm under certain dreadful oaths that he had no desire whatsoever for the episcopate, as Cornelius recounts in Letter 9.2. Hence he deserved to be called a “crafty old deceiver.” For this reason [Col. 0717C–D] the confessors are also said in the same Letter 9 to have returned to the Church once they had recognized the man and his fraud and cunning, as well as his lies and perjuries.

Therefore, when Cornelius concludes this letter, he judges that Cyprian should send it to the other churches, “so that all may know that the deceit and betrayal of this schismatic and heretic”—of whom he speaks at its beginning—“are being brought to nothing day by day.” Accordingly, Cyprian replies in Letter 8.2: “Nor will anyone now easily be deceived by the loquacious words of the raging schismatic.”

Nevertheless, these statements [Col. 0718A] can readily be reconciled with what we set out above, because, as Cyprian says in the preceding Letter 3, “The confessors, seduced by the obstinacy of Novatian and Novatus, departed from the Church.” COUSTANT.

**“We were filled with such joy.”** “We attained such joy,” Corb. FELL. The Colbert manuscript has “such great joy”; then the same manuscript has “attained,” and Corbie has “attained.” COUSTANT. The Reims and Fux manuscripts likewise read so. In six other manuscripts and in the older editions, it is written: “We attained such great joy.” See the notes on Letter 42, p. 432. BALUZIUS.

**“We gave thanks when they.”** We have retained this reading because it makes good sense. It was introduced in the Manutius edition and is also found in the Fux manuscript. But six old manuscripts and the Morel edition, which followed Manutius, prefer: “when we understand that, having recognized their error and abandoned the poisonous cunning of the evil man, as of a serpent, they have returned to the Church from which they had departed.” The old editions are also substantially the same. BALUZIUS.

**“They now reported that the swelling pride of these men had been softened.”** We have restored the old reading—“they reported the swelling pride of some and the softness of others”—which Manutius eliminated, for what reason I do not know. It is excellent, and is preferred not only by the old editions but also by the eight ancient copies which we use and by the Verona manuscript, from which variant readings were copied into the margin of the Manutius edition in my own copy.

The meaning of these words appears to me to be as follows. When the pardon of the lapsed was being discussed before Cornelius, and he doubted whether they had returned to the Church truly and sincerely, and therefore questioned the testimony of those who had stood firm, they reported that some of the lapsed were swollen with pride, because, of course, they had suffered torments for the name of Christ and therefore took pride in this fact, while others, by contrast, were exceedingly soft—that is, dejected because of their fall. For, as Tacitus writes, “the spirits of mortals are soft in calamity.” Cornelius concluded from this that their testimony was not adequate to prove that those men had been completely changed. Rigaltius therefore rightly judged that the true reading was that of the Verona manuscript, in which it was written, “yet on evidence not adequate.” BALUZIUS.

Coustant, following “the Manutius edition,” reads: “They now reported that the swelling pride of these men had been softened.” I have followed both the Oxford edition, in which many variant readings are appended to this passage, and editions older than that one, and have departed here from Baluzius, whose arguments did not satisfy me. ROUTH, who writes “their swelling pride.”

**“Yet on evidence not adequate,” etc.** “Yet on evidence not adequate, we could not easily be induced to believe that they had suddenly changed,” Verona manuscript; “that they had suddenly,” Bodl. 1. FELL, who, like Coustant and others, nevertheless has *fides* (“the evidence”) rather than *fide* (“on evidence”) in his text.

**Maximus.** He was discussed more fully in connection with Letter XLI. [Col. 0719B] Pamelius wrote that he suffered martyrdom under Maximinus. But the martyrologies state that this occurred under Valerian. See Baronius under November 19. BALUZIUS.

**“But because many offenses committed by them had preceded.”** That is, had been perpetrated and completed. In this sense it was said of Evaristus in the preceding letter: “But here he committed greater and more serious offenses.” Accordingly, the confessors are soon said to have been questioned by the presbyters concerning the things they had done. COUSTANT.

**“Our fellow bishops.”** The Corbie manuscript has “our fellow bishop.” “Our fellow bishops” should be retained: namely, those who had taken part in the assemblies [Col. 0719C] or councils convened for this purpose. For at the beginning of Cornelius’s pontificate, according to Eusebius, VI.43, sixty bishops, together with a much larger number of presbyters and deacons, assembled and condemned Novatian and his adherents. At the least, Pompeius and Stephanus are indicated here, African bishops who had taken part in Cornelius’s ordination. The letters of Cornelius mentioned here do not survive. COUSTANT.

**“Were required to explain.”** “Were pressed upon them,” Bodl. 1. FELL. The Grenoble manuscript has “were questioned.” This reading seems better, but the other manuscripts and editions oppose it. BALUZIUS.

**“Had been the authors of the heresy.”** Here too I judged that I should depart from Baluzius, who, without giving any reason, prints *haereticis* (“heretics”) instead of *haeresis* (“of the heresy”) in his text. The alternative reading is certainly furnished by the editions of Erasmus, Manutius, Rigaltius, and Oxford, as well as by Coustant.

“See,” says the English translator, “how they confess that they deserve condemnation under the law of heresy solely because they had appointed a new bishop while the see was occupied, without having any cause arising from the deprivation of the other.” But one may rightly doubt whether the word “heresy” here also indicates Novatian’s opinion concerning repentance, just as below, where these same confessors call Novatian “a schismatic and heretical man”; and perhaps also in that passage of Cyprian concerning the same confessors: “After you had come out of prison, schismatic and heretical error received you.” Letter LI, otherwise 54. Compare Coustant a little below at p. 28 and at the beginning of Cornelius’s letter to Fabius. ROUTH.

**“That they should allow hands to be imposed upon him as though upon a bishop.”** [Col. 0720B] The conjunction *et* (“and”) was wrongly substituted for the pronoun *ei* (“upon him”). For Cornelius continues, as in the preceding letter, deliberately to suppress Novatian’s name. Above, he considers it sufficient to indicate him by the expressions “a cunning man and crafty old deceiver,” and shortly thereafter “an evil man”; here merely by the pronoun “him”; and at the close by the designation “this schismatic and heretic,” without naming him anywhere.]

### I

We endured great concern and anxiety [Col. 0717A] over those confessors who had been ensnared by the deceit and wickedness of a cunning man and crafty old deceiver, and had been almost deceived and estranged from the Church. Yet we were filled with equally great joy [Note: [Col. 0717A] “Such great joy,” Colbert manuscript. Then the same manuscript has “attained”; Corbie, “attained.”], and gave thanks [Note: [Col. 0717A] The old Corbie manuscript, together with the more recent Colbert manuscript and one English manuscript, has: “We give thanks, when we understand that, having recognized their error and escaped the poisonous cunning of the evil man as of a serpent”—the word “escaping” having been added here by a later hand—“they have come to the Church.…” The reading of the other manuscripts is sounder, [Col. 0718A] and is illustrated and confirmed by Letter IX to Fabius, §1, printed below. From it, it is also evident that Novatian is indicated here by the expression “the evil man.”] to almighty God and Christ our Lord when they, having recognized their error and understood the poisonous cunning of the evil man, like that of a serpent, came with a sincere will to the Church from which they had departed, as they themselves profess from their own hearts.

And at first, indeed, our brothers of proven faith, lovers of peace and seekers of unity, reported that the swelling pride of these men had now been softened. Yet the evidence was not adequate || for us easily to be induced to believe [Note: [Col. 0718A] “Yet on evidence not adequate, we could not easily be induced to believe that they had suddenly changed,” Verona; “that they had suddenly,” Bodl. 1.] that they had been completely changed.

Afterward, however, the confessors Urbanus and Sidonius came to our presbyters, declaring that Maximus, confessor and presbyter, [Note: [Col. 0718A] The Corbie and Colbert manuscripts have “second presbyter,” which is unsatisfactory.] likewise wished to return to the Church with them. But because many offenses committed by them had preceded [Col. 0719A]—which you too learned from our fellow bishops and from my letters—it was decided, so that they should not be believed rashly, that they should be heard declare from their own mouths and by their own confession the things which they had reported through their delegation. [Note: [Col. 0719B] The same manuscript, together with the Colbert manuscript, has “from his own mouth”; and shortly afterward, “I had reported” for “they had reported.”]

When they had arrived and were required by the presbyters to explain what they had done [Note: [Col. 0719B] “Were pressed upon them,” Bodl. 1; Grenoble manuscript, “were questioned.”]—and finally, because numerous letters filled with calumnies and curses had been sent in their name throughout all the churches and had disturbed almost all the churches—they affirmed that they had been deceived and had not known what those letters contained. They said only that they had been led astray [Note: [Col. 0719B] “Only that, having subscribed, led astray by his cunning, they had also wholly committed themselves to the schismatics,” Bodl. 1. Vatican: “Nor did they know whether anything was contained in these, only that they had been led astray so as to allow a hand to be imposed upon him as though for the episcopate; and when they had been among the other heretics, and lest they should be reproached,” Verona. “Nor indeed did they know what was contained in those letters; only that, having been led astray, they had also committed themselves to the schism [Col. 0720B] and had been the authors of the heresy, so as to allow a hand to be imposed upon him as though for the episcopate. When these and other things had been charged against them, they pleaded that they should be abolished and removed from their midst,” Benevento.] into committing themselves to schism as well and into becoming authors of the heresy, by allowing hands to be imposed upon him as though upon a bishop. When these and other things had been charged against them, they pleaded that they should be abolished and removed from memory.

[Col. 0719B]

[Note: [Col. 0720B]

### II. “That the presbyteral council should be convened”

Both Fell and Baluzius say that this was an assembly of the presbyters of the Church of Carthage. Both had forgotten, however, [Col. 0720C] that the letter before them was written by Cornelius of Rome, not by Cyprian of Carthage. Baluzius makes the same error below at pp. 29 and 32. ROUTH.

**“Their case.”** Salmasius defended this form of expression against Milton, who had accused it of being a solecism. ROUTH.

**Sidonius.** Pamelius added “and Macarius,” solely on the basis of conjecture, as he himself admits, because it is evident from the following three letters that Macarius returned to the Church with the others. We have deleted the words, because we have found Macarius’s name in none of the old copies we used, nor in the editions preceding Pamelius. BALUZIUS. Nevertheless, Baluzius’s own text—which was not entirely prepared by Baluzius himself and was published after his death—retained “and Macharius.” I have omitted it with Coustant.

**“Had joined.”** The Corbie manuscript has “joined.” Although most of those who had defected to the schism under the influence of the confessors are said here to have returned to the Church with them, [Col. 0720D] both the words of those returning below and the cries of the people rejoicing over their return concern only the confessors. Likewise, Cyprian, in Letter VIII below, replies concerning the return of the confessors alone.

We further observe here that so distinguished an assembly of the clergy, at which five bishops were also present, was unwilling to decide anything concerning the proposed case except with the knowledge of the people. From this it may be gathered that Cornelius did what we read Cyprian proposing to his own presbyters and deacons in Letter VI, or XIV: “Since,” he says, “from the beginning of my episcopate I resolved to do nothing by my private judgment without your counsel and without the consent of the people.” COUSTANT.

**“A great gathering took place.”** At the church in which the confessors were received, as the distinguished Marshall judges.

**“Today.”** The Corbie manuscript has “on this day.” There is no difficulty in the word “today,” [Col. 0721A–B] because Cornelius, as he testifies below, arranged for this letter to be sent to Cyprian at the same hour and in the same moment in which these things occurred. For another reason, Cyprian congratulates those same confessors in Letter LI, or LIV, as follows:

“After you had come out of prison, schismatic and heretical error received you. The situation was as though your glory had remained in prison; for the dignity of your name appeared to have remained there when the soldiers of Christ did not return from prison to the Church, into which they had previously entered amid the praise and rejoicing of the Church.”

Here Cyprian, in harmony with Cornelius, declares that the confessors had been ensnared not only by schismatic but also by heretical error. From this it may be inferred that Novatian’s heresy concerning repentance did not originate later than his schism. COUSTANT.

From several passages of Cornelius’s letter to Fabius, fragments of which I shall presently present, I have been persuaded that the controversy concerning repentance arose before Novatian’s episcopate was openly discussed, whatever he concealed in his mind concerning that office; for Cornelius himself, who accuses him, says that his desire for it was at that time hidden [Col. 0721C] and unknown.

**“Bishop of the most holy Catholic Church.”** It is beyond doubt that the Church of the city of Rome is indicated here. These are the words of Cornelius himself in the letter just mentioned:

*ὁ ἐκδικητὴς οὖν τοῦ εὐαγγελίου* (Novatian) *οὐκ ἠπίστατο ἕνα ἐπίσκοπον δεῖν εἶναι ἐν καθολικῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ, ἐν ᾗ οὐκ ἠγνόει, πῶς γάρ; πρεσβυτέρους εἶναι μϛʹ, διακόνους ἑπτὰ*, etc. §3.

“Thus the champion of the Gospel” (Novatian) “did not know that there must be one bishop in a Catholic Church, in which he was well aware—for how could he not be?—that there were forty-six presbyters, seven deacons,” etc. §3.

**“Chosen by God,”** that is, by the inspiration of God and of his Christ, and according to the prescription of the divine laws. Thus Pontius, Cyprian’s deacon, writes concerning him:

“While still a neophyte and, as people thought, a newcomer, he was chosen for the office of the priesthood and the rank of bishop by the judgment of God and the favor of the people.”

And a little later:

“I shall not pass over that remarkable event either: how, when the whole people, under the Lord’s inspiration, rushed forward in love and honor for him, he humbly withdrew, yielding to his seniors, and judged himself unworthy of the title belonging to so great an honor, so that he might thereby become still more worthy.” P. 3, *Life of Cyprian*.

Cyprian himself [Col. 0721D] likewise calls his election “the vote of the people and the judgment of God” in Letter XL, otherwise XLIII. Moreover, in Letter LXVII, or LXVIII, he shows that the method of celebrating ordinations received by the Church was established “according to divine teachings”—namely, those contained in the divine Scriptures—“and according to the will of God, not according to human presumption.” For that reference to God and to the brothers in the election of Saint Matthias appears chiefly pertinent here. Acts 1:29ff. [sic]. ROUTH.

**“We suffered an imposture.”** Trebellius Pollio, in his *Gallienus*, writes:

“When a certain man had sold glass gems as genuine to the emperor’s wife, and she, upon discovering the matter, wished him to be punished, Gallienus ordered that the man should be dragged away as though to a lion. Then he released a capon from the cage; and while everyone marveled at the ludicrous affair, he ordered the herald to proclaim: ‘He practiced an imposture and suffered one.’”

Aelius Lampridius relates that Vetronius Turinus, an impostor who had deceitfully promised many things and received enormous rewards for his empty promises, was accused and convicted by order of Alexander Severus. At the emperor’s command he was bound to a stake and killed by smoke, which Alexander had ordered to be made from straw and damp wood, while a herald proclaimed: “He who sold smoke is punished by smoke.” The emperor Nero showed greater clemency toward Caesellius Bassus. See Tacitus, *Annals*, Book XVI. BALUZIUS.

**“By the seductive eloquence of treachery.”** Thus the old editions and five old copies. Manutius printed “by treachery and seductive eloquence,” followed by Rigaltius, Fell, and Coustant. Four old manuscripts have *factiosa* (“factious”) for *captiosa* (“seductive”); others read, “through a sense of the deed, we appeared mad” [reading uncertain]. The Reims manuscript of Saint-Denis has: “captured by his eloquence. For we appeared senseless.” BALUZIUS. Corbie has “factious.” Colbert: “captured by his eloquence, we appeared senseless.” COUSTANT. “Senseless through the factious eloquence of treachery,” Erasmus’s edition of 1520.

**“And heretical.”** These words are absent from the older editions and from four ancient manuscripts. They are found, however, [Col. 0722C] in the Manutius edition and in two manuscripts. That they should be retained is evident from what follows. One of my old manuscripts reads “heresy-founder,” and the Grenoble manuscript has “with the heresiarch.” BALUZIUS.

**“One bishop in the Catholic Church.”** From this, Baronius inferred that the title of the bishop of Rome at that time was “Bishop of the Most Holy Catholic Church,” and consequently that there ought to be one bishop—that is, the Roman bishop—in the Church. But this is not the true sense of Cyprian’s [Cornelius’s] words. He means only that, just as we believe in one Christ and one Holy Spirit, so we must believe that there is only one bishop in each individual church, since the episcopate is one and undivided, extended through the harmonious multitude of many bishops, a share of which is held by each in its entirety, as he says in Letter LII, p. 73, and in the book *On the Unity of the Church*, p. 195. See our notes on Agobard’s book *On the Privilege and Right of the Priesthood*, chapter 2. BALUZIUS.

Furthermore, the most learned John Forbes writes very well and very truly in *Historico-Theological Instruction*, Book XVI, chapter 3, §40: [Col. 0722D]

“The confessors intend to say nothing other than that this is the law of the Catholic Church: that in one city there should be only one bishop. In the phrasing familiar to those centuries, the ancients called every particular orthodox church a Catholic Church, and designated its bishop ‘Bishop of the Catholic Church,’ as the examples cited above and many others demonstrate.”

Thus Forbes. He had taken one of those examples from the synodical letter of the Antiochenes placed above in Eusebius, *History* VII.37:

*ἠναγκάσθημεν οὖν*, they say, … *ἕτερον ἀντ᾽ αὐτοῦ*—that is, in place of Paul, bishop of Antioch—*τῇ καθολικῇ Ἐκκλησίᾳ καταστῆναι ἐπίσκοπον.*

“We were therefore compelled … to appoint another in his place”—that is, in place of Paul, bishop of Antioch—“as bishop for the Catholic Church.”

**“In the Catholic Church.”** That is, the Roman Church. The word “Church” is absent from three old copies. It is well known that the ancients often spoke simply in this way when referring to the Catholic Church, omitting the word “Church,” because “Catholic” implied “Church.” For a sect which is not Catholic is not the Church, since it is outside—that is, outside the Church—as our most holy author Cyprian frequently likes to express it. See Quesnel on Letter 26 of Saint Leo and our notes on Marca’s dissertation concerning the letter of Pope Vigilius. BALUZIUS.

The Colbert copy has “to be in the Catholic,” omitting the word “Church,” which in the Corbie manuscript also was added only by a later hand. Nor was it unusual among the ancients to express “the Catholic Church” solely by the word “Catholic.” Similar to this profession of the confessors is Cyprian’s statement in Letter 40, or 43, to his people: “There is one God, and one Christ, and one Church, and one chair founded upon Peter by the voice of the Lord.” Cyprian writes this in order to prove that those who adhered to the faction of Felicissimus were outside the Church. COUSTANT.

I omit Coustant’s little question, which follows immediately there, so that all controversy and offense arising from an easy answer to it may be avoided. Moreover, an example of this Hellenistic usage occurs in the fragment *On the Canon of the New Testament*, which I shall presently publish; there I have also cited other examples from more than one Latin writer.

**“Who would not be moved?”** This is how the Benedictines edited the words, although Baluzius noted nothing about that reading. The common reading is: “Would we not be moved by this profession of theirs?” But Fell says that Bodl. 1 reads: “Who would not be moved by this profession of theirs?” Coustant noted [Col. 0723C] that the same reading was supplied by a later hand in the Corbie manuscript.

**“To recognize his own place.”** That is, he was received with the honor and rank of presbyter preserved. Following this example, both the Nicene Fathers in Canon 8, in the case of the Novatians, and the African fathers at the Conference of Carthage, in the case of the Donatists, allowed those returning to the Church to retain their honors. COUSTANT.

The manner in which Maximus was restored to his former status will be discussed below in connection with Letter LII. (That is, the following notes are attached to the words, “Evaristus, once a bishop, has not even remained a layman.”) Rigaltius says:

“Once a bishop had been deposed from the episcopate, even if repentant, neither the place nor dignity of bishop was restored to him. When his penance was completed, Christian communion was restored to him, but lay communion, so that he remained in the Church as a layman. But Evaristus, after being deposed from the episcopate, did not remain in the Church.”

It should be noted that the Church sometimes restored schismatic clergy to their full status. Thus the Nicene Fathers restored the Novatians. Moreover, it is well known that the Arians themselves were received by the Alexandrian Fathers with their honors intact. It is therefore no wonder that Maximus, on returning to the Church, was commanded to recognize [Col. 0723D] his own place, especially since it is probable that, in consideration of their honor as confessors, he and his companions had not yet been subjected to the Church’s censures and the thunderbolt of anathema. FELL. More will be noted below, near the beginning of the Third Council of Carthage, concerning penitent clergy.

**“We remitted everything to almighty God.”** If someone were received back into communion, that would be an external privilege. It seems, however, that the ancients believed that they had no further involvement in the internal forum except to ask God for the offender’s absolution. MARSHALL, who refers the reader to his notes on Cyprian’s works.

**“To you, in writing.”** Thus the Benedictine edition. The word “in” is ordinarily absent. Coustant notes:

“The Corbie manuscript has ‘to you in writing’; the Colbert manuscript, ‘letters written out to you.’ Shortly afterward, in both manuscripts, as also in one English manuscript, the word ‘hastening’ is missing; but the following word ‘to go down’ necessarily requires it. Moreover, he was hastening because responsibility for the preceding letter had already been entrusted to him.”

Fell, however, supplied the following variant:

“At the same hour and the same moment we transmitted this writing to you, and immediately sent the acolyte Nicephorus down to you with the intention of sailing,” Verona. “Immediately sent down to you to sail, with the intention,” Corbie. [Col. 0724B] ROUTH.]

### II

When the whole course of events had therefore been reported to me, it was decided that the presbyteral council should be convened [Col. 0720A]—five bishops were also present, and they too were present today—so that, after our deliberation had been firmly established, it might be determined by everyone’s consent what procedure should be followed in their case. And so that you might learn the disposition of all and the judgment of each, it was also decided that our opinions should be brought to your attention; you will read them appended below.

After these proceedings, Maximus, Urbanus, and Sidonius came into the presbyteral council, together with most of the brothers who had joined themselves to them. [Note: [Col. 0720B] “Joined,” Corbie.] With the most earnest entreaties they desired that what had previously been done should pass into oblivion and that no mention of it should be made. Thus, as though nothing had been either committed or said, and with everything mutually forgiven, they might now present to God a clean and pure heart, following the Gospel saying [Note: [Col. 0720B] In the Colbert and Corbie manuscripts: “the saying, ‘Blessed are the pure in heart, because now’ or ‘because they hope for the Lord.’” In Cyprian’s book *To Quirinus*, chapter 79, the same passage of Matthew is read as follows: “Blessed”—in the old Colbert manuscript, “Happy”—“are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.”], “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” [Col. 0721A] (Matthew 5:8).

As a necessary consequence, this whole proceeding had to be made known to the people, so that they might see established in the Church those whom they had long seen, with grief, wandering in error. When their intention became known, a great gathering of the brotherhood took place. All spoke with one voice, giving thanks to God and expressing the joy of their hearts with tears, embracing them as though they had been released from the punishment of prison that very day. [Note: [Col. 0721A] “On this day,” Corbie.]

To reproduce their own words:

“We know,” they say, “that Cornelius was chosen [Col. 0722A] by almighty God and Christ our Lord as bishop of the most holy Catholic Church. We confess our error. We suffered an imposture; we were ensnared by treachery and seductive eloquence. [Note: [Col. 0721A] “Factious,” the same manuscript. Colbert: “Captured by his eloquence, we appeared senseless, as though some sort of…”] For although we appeared to have some sort of communion with a schismatic and heretical man, our sincere mind nevertheless always remained in the Church. For we are not unaware that there is one God, that there is one Christ the Lord [Note: [Col. 0722A] “To have had our contest,” Bodl. 1.], whom we confessed, one Holy Spirit, and that there ought to be one bishop in the Catholic Church.” [Note: [Col. 0722A] “Our Lord,” Bodl. 1.] [Col. 0723A]

Who would not be moved by this profession of theirs [Note: [Col. 0723A] “Who would not be moved?” Corbie manuscript, by a later hand, as in one English manuscript. “Who would not be moved by their profession?” Bodl. 1.], so that, now established in the Church, they might confirm what they had confessed before the secular authority? Accordingly, we commanded the presbyter Maximus to recognize his own place [Note: [Col. 0723A] Thus Corbie; Rigaltius has “to pardon.”], and we received the others with the overwhelming approval of the people. [Col. 0724A] We remitted everything, however, to almighty God, in whose power all things are reserved.

[Note: [Col. 0724B]

### III. “Intending.”

We have restored the reading of the old editions, which alone is sound and is further confirmed by several old manuscripts. Erasmus was the first to alter it slightly, putting *festinantem* (“hastening”) for *destinantem* (“intending”). Erasmus, however, does not appear to have done this without authority. For I myself found it written thus in the Corbie manuscript—not in the form reported in Rigault’s edition and in the English edition (see a little above; these editions present in the text, “hastening from the station to you”; Coustant likewise printed it), but in the form found in that old manuscript, where the very words read: “I immediately sent him on to you as he was hastening to go down to embark.” Rigault, however, says that in that manuscript the reading is: “I immediately sent them on to you, with the intention of embarking.” Later the reading that adds “from the station” was introduced.

Those two words are not Saint Cyprian’s [or Cornelius’s], but those of some ignorant copyist. I think there can be no doubt that this happened in the way I am about to describe. [Col. 0724C] First, it must be observed that those words do not occur in the old manuscripts that have the word *festinantem*, nor in the earlier editions. Morel was the first to introduce them, doubtless from some old manuscript; for I too have seen three in which they occur. That corruption, as I noted before, was introduced through the ignorance and carelessness of an old copyist who did not know his letters. When he encountered a badly written exemplar and could not guess how the word following *navigandum* should be written, he inserted the word that came into his mind, and from *festinantem*, or rather *destinantem*, made *detestationem*, as it is written in one Vatican manuscript and in the Verona manuscript. This is precisely the kind of way in which, in the old Reims manuscript of Saint-Denis, *infestationem* is read for *in statione* in Letter 41. Old books are full of errors of this kind.

Thus, in that Vatican manuscript and in the Verona manuscript, this passage was written as follows: “I immediately sent the acolyte Nicephorus on to you, to go down to embark, the destination.” [Col. 0724D] Then another copyist, no more competent, substituted *destinatione* as a single word for *destinationem*, as it is read in another Vatican manuscript and in one of my own. And this is the reading which, although false, now prevails in the commonly printed editions. Moreover, even the corrupt reading of these manuscripts shows that *destinantem* rather than *festinantem* should be read. **Baluze.**

I agree with Baluze in restoring the old reading. Yet if the wording *de statione* (“from the station”) were genuine, Coustant would then rightly demonstrate from Cyprian’s Letters 4 and 42 (otherwise 44 and 45) that *statio* here means a religious assembly in the churches, to which the faithful customarily came to celebrate the sacred mysteries. Moreover, after the mysteries had been completed in these assemblies, as the distinguished Marshall, the English translator, observes while citing Cyprian’s same Letter 44, they were accustomed to conduct other business. **Routh.**

**“Assembly.”** The Corbie manuscript has “gathering.” In one Vatican manuscript the reading is: “In this assembly of the people, to give thanks together with us to Almighty God and Christ our Lord.” **Baluze.**—That is, concerning the aforesaid assembly of clergy and people. Thus Cyprian also, above in Letters 1 and 2, records the spiteful insults offered by Novatian’s envoys against Cornelius as having been made, in Letter 1, “at the station,” and in Letter 2, no. 2, “in the religious assembly of the brethren,” in which both the priests were seated and an altar had been set up. From this it is evident that *statio* means a religious assembly in the churches, in which the faithful gathered to celebrate the sacred mysteries.

**“When their instigators.”** That is, those by whose authority especially they had been drawn into the schism and kept in it.]

### III

These things, therefore, brother, we wrote and transmitted to you at that very hour [Note: [Col. 0723A] “At that very hour and moment we transmitted them to you in writing, [Col. 0724A] and we immediately sent the acolyte Nicephorus on to you, to go down, with the intention of sailing,” Verona manuscript; “to go down to embark, with the destination, we immediately sent them on to you,” Corbie manuscript.], at that very moment; and I immediately sent the acolyte Nicephorus on to you from the station, as he was hastening to go down to embark, [Col. 0725A] so that, without any delay, you might give thanks to Almighty God and Christ our Lord as though you were present in this clergy and in this assembly of the people.

We believe, moreover—indeed, we now confidently hold it as certain—that the others also who are situated in this error will shortly return to the Church, when they see their instigators acting together with us. I think, brother, that you ought to send this letter to the other churches as well, so that everyone may know that the deceit and treachery of this schismatic and heretic are being brought to nothing day by day. Farewell, dearest brother. [Note: [Col. 0725B] “Always farewell, dearest brother,” Colbert manuscript. This prayer, however, is omitted in the Corbie manuscript.]

[Note: [Col. 0725C]

## LETTER VII—NOTES

### I. “Both diligently”

From the very beginning of this letter, Cyprian teaches that he received the two preceding letters of Cornelius together, through the same acolyte Nicephorus. In the present letter he answers the first, and in the following letter the second.

### “Novatian and Novatus”

The Greeks confuse this Novatus with Novatian, and falsely make him the heresiarch and founder of the Cathari. Yet the two are distinguished in many respects. Novatian was a Roman; Novatus was a presbyter of Carthage. Novatian arrogated the Roman episcopate to himself; Novatus was never appointed bishop by anyone. Novatian, affecting a certain appearance of purity and deriving from it the name and origin of the sect of the Cathari, took away even from the penitent lapsed the hope of pardon. Novatus, however, adhered to the presbyters of Felicissimus’s faction, who wished peace and communion to be granted to the lapsed immediately, even when the canonical rules of penance had been disregarded; and yet he did not cease to ally himself with Novatian. Conscious, of course, of grave crimes, his object was not to preserve ecclesiastical discipline, but to escape the punishment due for his crimes by stirring up disturbances in the Church. Consequently, Novatus must by no means be called the founder and author of the Novatian or Catharist heresy, although he may deservedly be regarded as Novatian’s principal supporter in the schism.

### “There”

This stands for “thither,” just as below *illic* stands for *illuc*. For so it is written in the old books and in the Speyer edition, as well as in the old Venetian edition and the Manutius edition. Likewise, in Saint Gregory, Book VII, Indiction 2, Letter 118, and Book IX, Letter 10, and perhaps elsewhere, *illic* is written for *illuc* in the Fleury manuscript.

### “Faction”

That is, Novatian’s second delegation, undertaken by Nicostratus, Novatus, Evaristus, Primus, and Dionysius, as is explained in the following letter; the first delegation had been undertaken by Maximus, Longinus, and Machaeus.

### “From being a bishop”

That is, cast down from episcopal rank to such an extent that he did not even remain in that same church with lay communion, since he had suffered shipwreck in the faith.

### “There”

That is, in Africa. The reading *illinc* (“from there”) is therefore false, as though that word referred to the city of Rome, from which Evaristus and Nicostratus had fled to Africa. This is sufficiently established when it is written that they fled from the city, so that the word *illinc* is unnecessary. Thus, as I have said, the word *illic* refers to Africa. It must nevertheless be admitted that some old manuscripts present *illinc*. But the greater number have the other reading. See what we said on the word *istinc* at Letter 41, p. 430.

### [Col. 0727B] “And shall cleave to his wife”

We added this clause, not only because it occurs in Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians, from which this passage is taken, but especially because I saw it written thus in four old manuscripts and in the Fleury manuscript. It is nevertheless absent from three old manuscripts.

### “Of Christ likewise”

Some manuscripts present “Christ.”]

## LETTER VII OF SAINT CYPRIAN, BISHOP OF CARTHAGE, TO POPE CORNELIUS

*(Erasmus II.8; Pamelius, Rigault, and Baluze XLIX; Paris XLVIII; Coustant I, col. 139; Galland, Library of the Ancient Fathers III, p. 338.)*

[Col. 0725B]

### Summary

He praises Cornelius for the diligence with which he warned him at the proper time about Novatian’s pernicious schemes and the character of his new envoys. He recounts Novatus’s crimes at greater length and commends his own efforts to bring back those whom Novatus had led astray.

### CYPRIAN TO HIS BROTHER CORNELIUS, GREETINGS

### I

You acted both diligently and lovingly [Note: [Col. 0725B] “And lovingly,” Bodleian 3.], dearest brother, [Col. 0726A] by hastening to send us the acolyte Nicephorus, who both announced to us the glorious joy concerning the confessors who had returned and instructed us most fully concerning the new and pernicious schemes of Novatian and Novatus [Note: [Col. 0725B] Thus Vossianus 2; Nicolas-Camus 1, 2; Lambeth; Lincoln; York; old Erasmus; Manutius. “New pernicious schemes,” Rigault.] for attacking the Church of Christ.

For when the guilty faction of heretical depravity had come thither the day before—a faction already itself lost and destined to destroy others who might agree with it—Nicephorus arrived the next day with your letters. From them we learned, and began to teach and instruct the others, that Evaristus, cast down from being a bishop, had not even remained a layman, but, banished from his chair and people and exiled from the Church of Christ, was wandering through distant provinces and, having himself suffered shipwreck in truth and faith, was stirring up similar shipwrecks among certain persons like himself [Note: [Col. 0725B] “Contemplating,” Bodleian 1.]; [Col. 0726B] and that Nicostratus [Note: [Col. 0726B] “Nicostratus also,” Lambeth.], after losing his diaconate in the sacred ministry [Note: [Col. 0726B] Thus Vossianus 2; Lambeth; York; Nicolas-Camus 1, 2. “As a deacon,” Rigault.], after sacrilegiously and fraudulently embezzling church funds and refusing to return the deposits of widows and orphans [Note: [Col. 0726B] “Admitted,” Bodleian 1, 3.], had not so much wished to come to Africa as fled from there—from the City—because of his consciousness of robberies [Note: [Col. 0726B] “Conscience,” Bodleian 3.] and unspeakable crimes.

And now, a deserter and fugitive from the Church, as though changing one’s region were to change the person, he further [Note: [Col. 0726B] “Of his own accord,” Compiègne.] boasts of himself and proclaims himself a confessor, although one who has denied Christ’s Church can no longer either be called or be a confessor of Christ. For the apostle Paul says: “For this reason a man shall leave his father and mother, [Col. 0727A] and the two shall become one flesh; this mystery is great [Note: [Col. 0727B] “This mystery,” Bodleian 3.], but I speak with reference to Christ and the Church” [Note: [Col. 0727B] “I speak in Christ and with reference to the Church,” Lambeth, Bodleian 1.] (Eph. 5:31). Since, I say, the blessed Apostle says this and with his sacred voice testifies that the unity of Christ and the Church alike [Note: [Col. 0727B] “And Christ alike,” York; Nicolas-Camus 1; Lincoln.] coheres by indivisible bonds, how can one be with Christ who is not with Christ’s bride and in his Church? Or how does one assume responsibility for directing or governing the Church when he has despoiled and defrauded the Church of Christ?

[Note: [Col. 0727C]

## II. “An enemy of quiet”

These words do not occur in four old manuscripts or in the early editions. They do, however, occur in ten old manuscripts.

### “Persecution”

Here Novatus is marked as the leader and standard-bearer of the faction that certain presbyters had stirred up against Cyprian. Of them that same bishop speaks as follows in Letter X, or XVI:

> Since the unrestrained and reckless presumption of certain men is attempting by its rashness to disturb the honor of the martyrs, the modesty of the confessors, and the peace of the whole people, it is no longer proper to remain silent . . . when some of the presbyters, mindful neither of the Gospel nor of their own position . . . claim everything for themselves, with insult to their superior.

For those men, by opposing Cyprian’s ordination, exposed the blessed martyrs to hostility, set the glorious servants of God against their priest—that is, against Cyprian himself—and did not cease to disturb the people. Cyprian appears to identify those presbyters in Letter VI, or XIV, with these words:

> As to what our fellow presbyters Donatus and Fortunatus, Novatus and Gordius, wrote to me, I was unable to write any reply by myself.

[Col. 0727D] For he distinguishes these men, as already separated, from his presbyters and deacons, to whom he is speaking. **Coustant.**

### “To Rome”

Most manuscripts have “at Rome.” I think that reading is sound. I nevertheless did not wish to alter anything. It is enough for me to have given this warning.

### “Carthage by Rome”

Carthage is called Rome’s rival by Pliny, Velleius Paterculus, and Florus, and “rich in resources,” as Virgil says. Herodian, Book VII, says that it was inferior to Rome only in resources, population, or size. It is described as close to overseas regions by Aulus Gellius, Book X, chapter 27, and by Augustine in chapter 3 of the first letter to Eleusius, Glorius, and the Felixes. See Salvian, Book VII, chapter 16.

### “Made a bishop”

Not because Novatus was endowed with the power to ordain, but because through corrupt schemes he brought it about that Novatian was ordained. For Novatian, as we learn from Letter IX, no. 2, was ordained by three ignorant bishops. Those who persuade themselves from this passage that Novatus was a bishop are therefore gravely mistaken. Nor are we without suspicion [Col. 0728C] that these words of the Bucherian catalogue were composed in imitation of Cyprian’s words:

> During his episcopate [Cornelius’s], Novatus ordained Novatian outside the Church in the city of Rome, and Nicostratus in Africa.

Thus Nicostratus may have slipped into this catalogue in place of Felicissimus. If that is so, there is no foundation for those who think that Nicostratus was ordained bishop in Africa. **Coustant.**

### “He had made a deacon”

From this Baronius inferred that Novatus had been a bishop in Africa. Petavius embraced this opinion in his commentary on Epiphanius. Yet it is not true. That he was only a presbyter is clear from Eusebius’s *Chronicle*, Jerome’s *On Illustrious Men*, the *Book of Pontifical Deeds*, and Pacian’s third letter to Sympronianus. Indeed, it is also inferred from this letter of Cyprian that he was only a presbyter. He was a presbyter of the African Church.

When Cyprian says that Novatus, through his own faction and ambition, made Felicissimus a deacon, this must not be understood as meaning that Felicissimus was ordained deacon by Novatus, [Col. 0728D] but that through the faction of that utterly depraved man he was established in the rank of the diaconate, as we have already said at Letter XLI, p. 430.

I find that Hippolytus the martyr attached himself to Novatus, but later passed from him to the Church. Prudentius writes of him as follows:

> I find that Hippolytus, who once,  
> A presbyter, had touched the schism of Novatus,  
> Denying our position by following his,  
> Advanced as far as martyrdom and bore away  
> The shining rewards of bloody suffering.

On Hippolytus, see Baronius under January 30 and in the *Ecclesiastical Annals*.

### “Conscience itself”

Seneca, Letter XCVII: “It is characteristic of the guilty to tremble.” Tacitus, Book V of the *Annals*, writes that Nero, trembling in every limb—whether because the divine power terrified him or because he remembered his crimes—was never free from fear. The author of the *Letter to Demetrias* among Jerome’s works says:

> Hence it is that frequently, while the executioner remains hidden, the torments of conscience rage against the author of the crime, and a secret punishment of the mind pursues the concealed culprit.

Rufinus on Psalm 25: “He who bears guilt fears judgment.” Petronius: “Gods and goddesses, how badly it goes for those who act outside the law! They are always expecting whatever they have deserved.” Hildebert, Letter XVI: “For it is customary for the guilty to dread the punishments they fear.” Cicero, *Speech for Milo*: “Great is the power of conscience in both directions: those who have committed no offense do not fear, while those who have sinned think that punishment is always before their eyes.” Muretus on Book I of Plato’s *Republic*:

> But we must also note carefully what Plato says here with complete truth: people conscious of having committed many unjust deeds never find rest, but are repeatedly shaken by horror at the punishments they know they have deserved, so that they are often even roused from sleep.

See the scholia of Jacques de Billy on Gregory Nazianzen’s *Oration on the Plague of Hail*.

### “His wife’s womb”

In the earlier centuries of the Church, as Jerome notes in Book I *Against Jovinian*, because virgins either were not as numerous as was necessary, or did not possess—or were not thought to possess—conduct appropriate to virginity, married men were often chosen for the priesthood. They were ordained, however, under the condition that from then on they abstain from marital intercourse. Jovinian himself, despite being an opponent of continence, was compelled to admit that one who fathers children while in the episcopate cannot be a bishop; otherwise, if discovered, he will not be regarded as a husband but condemned as an adulterer.

Jerome therefore does not hesitate to affirm against Vigilantius: “The churches of the East, of Egypt, and of the Apostolic See accept as clerics either virgins or continent men.” Supporting him are Siricius, Letter I to Himerius, chapter 7; Innocent, Letter II to Victricius, chapter 10; Ambrose, Book I of *Duties*, chapter 50, [Col. 0729D] no. 257, and Letter LXI to the people of Vercellae, no. 62; Epiphanius, Heresy 59, no. 4; and the very ancient author of the *Questions from Both Testaments*, in the appendix to Augustine, vol. III, p. 142. Augustine also notes, at the end of Book II *On Adulterous Marriages*, that even when clerics were often compelled by an unforeseen force to accept this honor, the obligation of continence was nevertheless customarily imposed upon them.

They were not, however, compelled to put away their wives. Hence Leo says in Letter II to Rusticus, chapter 3:

> In order that a carnal marriage may become spiritual, they must neither put away their wives nor possess them otherwise than as though they did not possess them; thus the love of marriage is preserved, while marital intercourse ceases.

Consequently, it sometimes happened that some returned to their former custom. But this offense was not left unpunished, as is shown by the example of Genebald, bishop of Laon, whom Saint Remigius, archbishop of Reims, kept confined for a long time on this account. Novatus is here accused of falling into the same fault. Nor should Cyprian be thought to approve the matter as lawful merely because, overwhelmed by the horror of the parricide, he is carried away entirely with exposing the enormity of this crime. If Novatus struck his wife in this way so that the offense might remain hidden through a hastened miscarriage, this too will prove that the law of continence was then imposed upon presbyters. **Coustant.**

### “His wife’s womb”

Pacian, in his second letter to Sympronianus:

> Novatus, I say, after betraying his father, abandoning the Church, and causing his wife’s child to be expelled.

The same author, in Letter III, or the treatise *Against the Novatians*:

> Novatus came from Africa after defrauding widows in the church of Carthage, despoiling orphans, withholding the Church’s money, casting his father out of his house, and allowing that same father to die of hunger and remain unburied; after striking the womb of his pregnant wife with his heel and causing her child to be expelled.

Novatus had the distinguished example of the divine Nero, whose wife Poppaea, as Tacitus writes in Book XVI of the *Annals*, met her death through a chance outburst of her husband’s anger, when he inflicted upon her a heavy kick.

### “Now he dares”

This refers to the hands of those who had offered incense to idols, whom Cyprian is also accustomed to call *sacrificati*, “those who had sacrificed.” There would have been no occasion to reproach Novatus with this unless, defending not only Novatian’s schism but also his doctrines, he had denied pardon to those who had sacrificed. At the same time, however, he supported the party of Felicissimus, who, taking the contrary view together with his followers, granted peace to the lapsed without penance. Thus Novatus turned to every position that seemed more conducive to averting punishment for his own crimes. **Coustant.**]

### II

There had been no need for anything about Novatus to be reported from there to us, since Novatus ought rather to be made known to you through us. He was always eager for innovations, frenzied with the rapacity of insatiable greed [Note: [Col. 0727B] “Insatiable,” Lambeth; York; Bodleian 1, 2, 3; Nicolas-Camus 1, 2.], swollen with the arrogance and senselessness [Col. 0727B] of proud conceit [Note: [Col. 0727B] “Proud, swollen with conceit,” Bodleian 3.]; always ill regarded here by the bishops; always condemned as a heretic and a traitor by the voice of all the priests; always prying so that he may betray, flattering for the purpose of deceiving, never faithful so as to love; a torch and fire [Note: [Col. 0728B] “Pitch and fire,” Pamelius; Lambeth; York; Nicolas-Camus 1; Bodleian 2.] for kindling the conflagrations of sedition; a whirlwind and tempest for causing shipwrecks of faith; an enemy of quiet, an opponent of tranquility, a foe of peace.

Finally, when Novatus withdrew thence from you—that is, when the storm and whirlwind departed—some measure of quiet arose there; and the glorious and good confessors who, at his instigation [Note: [Col. 0728B] “Who here,” Bodleian 2, 3; York; Lincoln; Nicolas-Camus 1.], had departed from the Church returned to the Church after he departed from the City.

This is the same Novatus who among us first sowed the conflagration of discord and schism; who separated certain brothers here from their bishop; who, during the persecution itself, became another kind of persecution for our people, bent on overturning [Note: [Col. 0728B] In the same manuscript, “on turning” and, below, “to turn the Church.”] the minds of the brethren. It is he who, without my permission or knowledge, established his henchman Felicissimus as a deacon through his own faction and ambition. And when, together with his own tempest, he sailed to Rome also to overthrow the Church, he attempted similar and equal crimes there, tearing away a portion of the people from the clergy and rending the concord of a brotherhood that cohered well and loved one another.

Certainly, because Rome in its greatness ought to take precedence over Carthage, he committed greater and graver crimes there. The man who had made a deacon here against the Church made a bishop there. Nor should anyone be surprised at such men. **The wicked are always carried along**, demented by their own frenzy [Note: [Col. 0728B] “By fraud and frenzy,” Bodleian 3.]; and after they have committed crimes, they are harried by the very conscience of their criminal mind. Nor can those remain in [Col. 0729A] God’s Church who have maintained neither the deifying and ecclesiastical discipline through the conduct of their actions [Note: [Col. 0729A] “Conduct, nor peace of morals,” Bodleian 1, 3.] nor peace in their morals.

The orphans despoiled by him, the widows defrauded, and the Church’s money withheld exact from him those punishments that we see [Note: [Col. 0730A] “We perceive,” Nicolas-Camus 2; Lincoln.] in his frenzy. His father also died of hunger in the street and was not even buried by him afterward when dead. His wife’s womb was struck by his heel, and, as miscarriage hastened, the child was forced out in an act of parricide. And now he dares to condemn the hands of those who sacrificed, although he himself is guiltier in his feet, by which the son who was being born was killed!

[Note: [Col. 0730C]

## III. “Cast out of the presbyterate”

That is, thrown down and expelled. The same thing is expressed more clearly below: “as one who was to be expelled from and excluded from the Church.” The verb *excito* has the same force in Tertullian, Book IV *Against Marcion*, chapter 16, where it is said that wickedness, if it were not checked through vengeance, would gouge out every eye and knock out every tooth because of its confidence in impunity. **Coustant.**

### “Prohibited from communion”

That is, reduced to lay communion or expelled from the Church. I would rather believe the latter.]

### III

He had long feared this consciousness of his crimes. For this reason, he regarded it as certain that he would not merely be cast out of the presbyterate, but also prohibited from communion. With the brethren pressing the matter, the day of inquiry was imminent, on which his case would be heard among us, had the persecution not intervened first. Welcoming the persecution with a kind of prayer that he might escape and profit from his condemnation, he committed and stirred up all these offenses, so that, as one who was to be expelled from and excluded from the Church, he might anticipate the priests’ judgment by a voluntary departure—as though anticipating the sentence were the same as escaping the punishment.

[Note: [Col. 0730D]

## IV. “Experienced deceiver”

At the beginning of the preceding Letter VI we observed that Cornelius designates Novatian by the term “experienced deceiver.” Here, however, Cyprian means by the same word Novatus, who has been the whole subject of the immediately preceding discussion. Just as Cornelius had written to Cyprian in Letter V concerning Novatian’s adherents, “So that you may know what sort of leaders and protectors this schismatic and heretic always keeps attached to his side,” so Cyprian replies that he is laboring so that those deceived by Novatus may flee the experienced deceiver’s pernicious side. From this it is clear that persons are said to be “attached to someone’s side” not only when they accompany him bodily, but also when they follow him in mind and adhere to his opinions. **Coustant.**]

### IV

As for the other brethren whom we grieve to see deceived by him, we labor so that they may flee the experienced deceiver’s pernicious side, escape the deadly snares of the tempter, and return to the Church from which he deserved to be divinely expelled. With the Lord’s help, we trust that through his mercy they can indeed return. For no one can perish except one who is known to be destined to perish, since the Lord says in his Gospel: “Every planting that my heavenly Father has not planted will be uprooted” (Matt. 15:13).

Only one who has not been planted in the precepts and admonitions of God the Father will be able to depart from that Church; only such a one, after abandoning the bishops, will be able to remain in frenzy with schismatics and heretics. But the mercy of God the Father, the clemency of Christ our Lord, and our patience will unite the others with us. I wish you, dearest brother, always to fare well.

[Note: [Col. 0731C]

## LETTER VIII—NOTES

### I. “Savior”

We restored this reading, following the authority of certain old manuscripts and of the English edition, in which it is noted that four English manuscripts also present this reading. Elsewhere *salutari* (“saving”) is read. **Baluze.**

### “Not continually”

Two English manuscripts have, “is not divided.” Other books more correctly have, “not continually.” For it cannot be denied that the unity had then been divided to some degree. Immediately afterward five other manuscripts have “violated” in place of “corrupted.” **Coustant.**

### “Corrupted”

It must be admitted that almost all the old books have “seems” or “is avoided.” Morel’s edition, the Grenoble manuscript, and one of my manuscripts present “violated.” The English editors also testify that they read it thus in five old manuscripts.

### “With faithful soundness”

The early editions and two old books have “with faith.” But all the others have “faithful.” Although both readings therefore establish the same sense, I prefer the one supported by the authority of the greater number of old books.

### “To glory”

Supply “of confession.” This is explicitly stated in Cyprian’s Letter XLIV, or XLVI, to those same confessors:

> Return to the mother from whom you went forth, from whom you came to the glory of confession amid that same mother’s exultation.

### “Nor should they test”

Eleven of our books and seven English manuscripts present, “Nor should they be tested in the faith of love and unity.” My old manuscript has, “Nor should the faith of love and unity be tested in them.” This reading seems better.

### “Of love”

The Oxford edition has, “and the faith of truth.” At the same time it notes that eight manuscripts, together with Manutius, present, “Nor should they be tested in the faith of love and unity.” The Compiègne manuscript does indeed have “should be tested,” but retains “faith.” Either reading of those manuscripts is barbarous and unworthy of Cyprian’s style. Nor can it be said that those good confessors were merely tested concerning faith and unity, since it is established that they were drawn away from unity and became authors of heresy.

For this reason I do not approve the reading, “Nor should they grow lukewarm in the faith of love and unity,” which Pamelius notes that he found in the Cambron manuscript. For the faith of those confessors seemed extinguished rather than lukewarm.
