The same learned man, together with four manuscripts and the other editions, prefers, “Nor should they test the faith of love and unity,” and thinks that the verb *tentare* is used there in the sense of examining, or even attacking with hostile intent.

While preserving the reading supported by the authority of the greater number of manuscripts, both written and printed, we do not approve his interpretation. Cyprian said “they should test” rather because the confessors were a trial and stumbling block to the faith of unity, insofar as the leaders of the schism abused their example to draw the faithful away from unity and keep those whom they had seduced within the schism. For in the schism, as is explained below, they seemed to see the confessors’ communion following them. Cyprian therefore rejoices in Letter LI, or 54, [Col. 0732D] that the confessors of Christ did not become leaders of error after they had stood forth as praiseworthy models of virtue and honor.

### “The people and the brotherhood”

The confessors themselves, in Letter L, or LIII, among Cyprian’s works, report that they made peace with Cornelius and the entire clergy, to the joy also of the whole Church, through the ready love of all.]

## LETTER VIII

*(Erasmus II.12; Pamelius, Rigault, and Baluze XLVII; Oxford and Leipzig LI; Paris XLVI; Coustant I, 143; Galland III, 340.)*

[Col. 0731B]

## SAINT CYPRIAN, BISHOP OF CARTHAGE, TO POPE CORNELIUS

He rejoices at the confessors’ return to the Church. How greatly that return benefits the Catholic Church.

### CYPRIAN TO HIS BROTHER CORNELIUS, GREETINGS

### I

We profess, dearest brother, both that we have given and that we continue without ceasing to give the greatest thanks to Almighty God the Father and to his Christ, our Lord and God and Savior [Note: [Col. 0731B] Thus Lambeth; Nicolas-Camus 1; York; Bodleian 2. “Saving,” Imperial manuscript.], [Col. 0732A] because the Church is divinely protected in such a way that its unity and holiness are neither continually [Note: [Col. 0731B] “Are not divided,” Bodleian 1; Lincoln.] nor entirely corrupted by the obstinacy of treachery and heretical depravity [Note: [Col. 0732B] “Violated,” Pamelius; Benedictine edition; Lambeth; York; Nicolas-Camus 1.].

For we read your letter and exultantly received the most abundant joy of our common prayer: that Maximus the presbyter and the confessors Urbanus, Sidonius, and Macarius had returned to the Catholic Church—that is, that after laying aside error and abandoning schismatic, or rather heretical, frenzy, they had returned with faithful soundness to the dwelling place of unity and truth. Thus they returned in glory to the place from which they had gone forth to glory, so that those who had confessed Christ might not afterward desert Christ’s camp, nor those who had not been defeated by force and violence become a trial to the faith of love and unity.

Behold the integrity of their praise, safe and unstained; behold the dignity of the confessors, uncorrupted and firm: they have withdrawn from deserters and fugitives and abandoned the betrayers of the faith and assailants of the Catholic Church. Deservedly, as you write, both clergy and people [Note: [Col. 0732B] “People, brotherhood,” Compiègne.] and the whole brotherhood received them on their return with the greatest joy, since, when confessors preserve their glory and return to unity, everyone regards himself as their companion and as sharing in their glory.

[Note: [Col. 0752D]

## II. “Of this event”

Although Manutius and Morel printed “of this day,” and although the same reading is found in most very old manuscripts, I nevertheless prefer the reading presented by the old editions, which I found in three excellent old manuscripts. For a little later the holy Martyr says, “there, where the event itself was taking place before everyone’s eyes.” For “was taking place,” five old books have “is celebrated.”

### [Col. 0733A] “In heaven”

In the same manuscript “one” is absent, and shortly thereafter “how much more” occurs—which may be interpreted “with how much stronger reason”—in place of “how much greater.”

### “I wish you”

This wish is absent from the Compiègne manuscript.]

### II

We can estimate the joy of this day from our own feelings. For when the entire number of the brethren here rejoiced at your letter, which you sent concerning their confession, and received with the greatest eagerness this news of common rejoicing, what must have happened there, where the event itself and the present joy were taking place [Col. 0733A] before everyone’s eyes?

For the Lord says in his Gospel that there is the greatest joy in heaven over [Note: [Col. 0733A] “Over a sinner . . . how much more,” Compiègne.] one sinner who repents (Luke 15:7). How much greater is the joy, alike on earth and in heaven, over confessors returning with their glory and praise to the Church of God and, through the faithfulness and proof of their example, making a path of return for the others?

For error had led certain of our brethren here astray, because they thought that they were following the communion [Col. 0734A] of the confessors. When this error was removed, light was poured into everyone’s heart, and it was shown that the Catholic Church is one and cannot be rent or divided. No one will now easily be deceived by the glib words of a raging schismatic, since it has been proved that the good and glorious soldiers of Christ could not long be kept outside the Church by another’s deceit and treachery. I wish you, dearest brother, always to fare well.

## IX. FRAGMENTS FROM THE LETTER TO FABIUS, BISHOP OF ANTIOCH

[Col. 0733B] The heading prefixed by Pierre Coustant in his edition of the *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*.

I. How the confessors deceived by Novatian exposed his frauds and made them publicly known to the Church.  
II. Contrary to every law, after being ordained he arrogates the episcopate to himself.  
III. He is not deterred from schism by the number of the Roman clergy and people.  
IV. When illness pressed upon him, he was affused, or baptized, in bed, but was never confirmed.  
V. During the persecution he preferred to deny that he was a presbyter rather than assist the brethren.  
VI. Contrary to the laws, despite the opposition of the clergy and many of the people, he was advanced to the presbyterate through the bishop’s favor.  
VII. How, when distributing the body and blood of Christ, he compels each person to swear allegiance to him.  
VIII. That he is deserted by everyone.

[Note: [Col. 0733B] The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Note: [Col. 0733B]

### Αʹ. “But so that you may know,” etc.

Concerning the Novatian heresy and the letters of Cornelius, Eusebius prefaced the following remarks in Book VI, chapter 43 of the *Ecclesiastical History*:

> Since Novatus [Novatian], a presbyter of the Roman Church, was carried away by arrogance against these people—that is, against the lapsed—on the ground that there was no longer any hope of salvation for them, even if they accomplished everything required for genuine conversion and pure confession, he became the founder of a distinct sect of those who, in their puffed-up reasoning, proclaimed themselves “pure.”
>
> On this account a very large synod was convened at Rome, consisting of sixty bishops and a still greater number of presbyters and deacons. The pastors in the other provinces also deliberated separately in their respective regions concerning what was to be done. A decree was presented with the agreement of all: that Novatus [Novatian], together with those who had been carried away along with him and those who chose to approve the man’s brother-hating and utterly inhuman opinion, should be regarded as alien to the Church; but that those of the brethren who had fallen into calamity should be healed and treated with the medicines of repentance.
>
> Accordingly, letters came to us from Cornelius, bishop of the Romans, to Fabius, bishop of the church of Antioch, explaining the matters concerning the Roman synod and the decisions of all those throughout Italy, Africa, and the regions there. Other letters, composed in the Latin language, also came from Cyprian and the bishops with him in Africa. Through them it was made clear that they too agreed both that those who had undergone trial ought to receive assistance and that the founder of the heresy, together with all those similarly carried away with him, should rightly be proclaimed an exile from the Catholic Church.
>
> To these was attached another letter of Cornelius concerning the decisions approved at the synod, and again another concerning the acts undertaken against Novatus [Novatian]. There would be no objection to quoting portions of this letter, so that those who encounter the present work may know the facts concerning him. Accordingly, while instructing Fabius about the sort of character Novatus [Novatian] had possessed, Cornelius writes these very words: “But so that you may know,” etc.

]
] **I.** “And that you may know that this admirable man had long been aspiring to the episcopate [Col. 0735A] and had escaped notice by concealing this rash desire within himself, using as a cloak for his madness the fact that at first he had the confessors with him, I wish to explain. Maximus, one of our presbyters, and Urbanus, who twice obtained the highest glory arising from confession; Sidonius also; and Celerinus, a man who, having most steadfastly endured every torture through God’s mercy, and having strengthened the weakness of the flesh by the vigor of his faith, utterly defeated the adversary—these men, then, after discerning his character and detecting the cunning and duplicity within him, his perjuries and falsehoods, his refusal of communion and his wolfish friendship [λυκοφιλία], [Col. 0737A] returned to the holy Church. In the presence of a considerable number of bishops, presbyters, and a very great many laymen, they disclosed all the devices and wicked schemes that he had long kept hidden within himself, lamenting and repenting that, after being persuaded by that deceitful and malicious beast, they had for a short time withdrawn from the Church.”

Then, after a few words, he says:

> [Note: [Col. 0737D]
>
> **II.** “Beloved brother.” I have changed—if this matters at all—the order of the words on the authority of the Bodleian and Norfolk manuscripts and George Syncellus. Shortly afterward, George omits καιρῷ (“time”). —ROUTH.
>
> “By certain dreadful oaths.” The Norfolk manuscript has: “Through these dreadful men” [Διὰ τούτων ἀνδρῶν φοβερῶ]. But Rufinus, the ancient translator, appears to have found the sound reading that has been adopted. —ROUTH.
>
> The edition of Stephanus omits τό. —STROTH. To the edition of Stephanus add Syncellus. —ROUTH.
>
> “As though from some machine” [ὥσπερ ἐκ μαγγάνου τινός]. Here ἐκ μαγγάνου means the same as ἀπὸ μηχανῆς, a proverbial expression frequent among the Greeks; for μάγγανον means the same as “machine.” I am surprised that neither Musculus nor Christophorson noticed this. —VALESIUS. The Savile, or Bodleian, manuscript gives μαγκάνου with κ. —ROUTH.
>
> “For this doctrinal innovator,” etc. Christophorson rendered this into Latin as follows: “This inventor of a new sect and, if it please God, defender of ecclesiastical doctrine”; [Col. 0738C] Valesius, however: “He who presented himself as a teacher and defender of ecclesiastical discipline.” The word δογματιστής signifies something more than “teacher” and somewhat less than “inventor of a new sect.” It is evident that Novatian is ironically proclaimed here “the defender of ecclesiastical discipline,” and in section 3 “the champion of the Gospel,” because he himself laid claim to this illustrious title. Accordingly, Cyprian writes above, Epistle I, §2, concerning him and his followers: “If they profess themselves defenders of Christ’s Gospel, let them first return to the Church.” Novatian in particular, as Valesius observes, dedicated his book *On Jewish Foods* “to the people who persist in the Gospel.” In this he is imitated by the innovators of our age, who, though they have departed from the ancestral faith, are not ashamed to boast that they are champions of the pure Gospel. —COUSTANT.
>
> But a similar address is prefixed to the book *On Public Shows* among the Pseudo-Cyprianic works: “Greetings to the people standing in the Gospel,” meaning those who had not lapsed. Moreover, if Novatian had written that excellent little book *On the Trinity*, or *On the Rule of Faith* [Col. 0738D], at the time when Cornelius wrote these words, he was assuredly no poor δογματιστής, or theologian. —ROUTH.
>
> “The episcopate not given to him from above.” Compare the note above on Cornelius’s Epistle II to Cyprian. Cornelius was ordained by divine authority—that is, legitimately—when, with the consent of the people, he was made bishop by sixteen bishops, as Cyprian relates in the Epistle to Antonianus. —ROUTH.
>
> “So that” [ὡς ἄν]. Gruter’s readings and those of Bishop Castellan’s codex have οὓς ἄν, though without ἄν. —STROTH. But ὡς ἄν must be retained because of the following ἐξαπατήσῃ (“he might deceive”). Shortly afterward the Norfolk manuscript has εἰς τὴν Ῥώμην (“to Rome”) for εἰς Ῥώμην. —ROUTH.
>
> “Whatever it might be” [ἥ τις δήποτε οὖν]. The edition of Stephanus prints ἡτισδηποτοῦν as a single word. —STROTH. Syncellus has ὡς δή τις πᾶσα instead of ὡς δῆθεν πᾶσα ἥτις δήποτε οὖν. —ROUTH.
>
> “When they had arrived.” Theodoret, in Book III of the *Compendium of Heretical Fables*, chapter 5, writes that Novatian himself went into Italy to bring those bishops to Rome [Col. 0739A]; that afterward, when he had reached a certain village together with those three bishops, he compelled them to lay hands upon him; and that they complained of this when they came to Rome. But Cornelius’s letter refutes this account. —VALESIUS.
>
> “As we have already said” [ὡς ἔφθημεν]. The edition of Stephanus has ὡς ἔφημεν, “as we said.” The adopted reading [Col. 0739B] occurs in Christophorson’s readings and in Valesius’s edition. —STROTH. Add to these the Bodleian manuscript and Syncellus. The Norfolk manuscript has προέφημεν, “as we said before.” Shortly afterward the same manuscripts have τούτων πονηρῶν, “of these wicked men,” for τῶν πονηρῶν. —ROUTH.
>
> “Villainy” [ῥᾳδιουργίαν]. The edition of Stephanus has the genitive ῥᾳδιουργίας. —STROTH. Add Syncellus; in him and in the Norfolk manuscript immediately afterward you also find τεταραγμένων, “disturbed,” for τεταγμένων, “arrayed,” while Syncellus has the dative αὐτοῦ for αὐτῷ.
>
> “Drinking and carousing.” This should be understood virtually as a hendiadys together with the other expression, “at the tenth hour.” For it should not rashly be believed that they were actually drunk. All ecclesiastical acts had to be performed before noon; in the afternoon, however, it may easily happen that someone who has used wine immoderately does not perform his office properly. An adversary permits himself to infer actuality from possibility. Hence Cornelius repeats hyperbolically, in the words “drinking and carousing,” what he had already said by “at the tenth hour.” —STROTH.
>
> This is probably correct; yet [Col. 0739C] I would not suppose that μεθύοντας here means “drunk,” but rather “men who had used wine more freely than usual.” Thus in Genesis 43:34 and John 2:10 the verb μεθύειν signifies somewhat cheerful drinking, an idiom which very learned men show at those passages to arise not only from Hebrew but also from Greek usage. —ROUTH.
>
> “By a certain shadowy and ineffectual laying-on of hands.” Cornelius calls Novatian’s ordination a mere outline and a nullity because it was performed by bishops of another province, not by those who possessed the right of consecrating the Roman pontiff, such as the bishops of Ostia and Tibur and others; because it was performed by men overcome with drink; under compulsion; at the tenth hour of the day; in the presence of neither the people nor the clergy; and, finally, when another bishop had already been legitimately ordained. Moreover, since Cornelius himself, both here and in the Epistle to Cyprian, testifies that Novatian was consecrated by three bishops, I am surprised that Pacian writes in Epistle 2 to Sympronianus: “Or Novatian, whom a letter fabricated as bishop [Col. 0739D] in his absence? Whom the linen-covered seat received although no one consecrated him?” And shortly afterward he speaks of him thus: “He was made bishop without legitimate consecration—and therefore was not made one at all—by the letter of those who pretended to be confessors.”
>
> From Pacian’s words it appears possible to infer that Novatian was ordained bishop in his absence by a letter from certain confessors, in the same manner in which public offices were customarily conferred by a prince through a letter. By the “linen-covered seat” Pacian means the pontifical chair, because it was draped with linen. Augustine also attests this in Epistle 203: “At God’s future judgment, neither raised apses nor veiled chairs will avail.” The same is attested by the synodical letter of the Egyptian bishops reported by Athanasius in the *Apology*: “How, then, do those who lament the throne adorned in episcopal fashion,” etc. Pacian can, however, be reconciled with Cornelius if we say that Novatian was first designated bishop [Col. 0740A] by a letter from the confessors in prison, but was afterward ordained by those three bishops. —VALESIUS.
>
> “A certain shadowy” [εἰκονικῇ τινί] means one which displayed an image of the laying-on of hands rather than its reality. It is therefore less surprising that Pacian regarded such an ordination as void and null, and wrote of it in Epistle 2 as follows [Col. 0740B]: “A letter fabricated”—or made—“Novatian bishop in his absence,” because the confessors’ letter written to Novatian in his absence, by which they agreed that hands should, as it were, be laid upon him as bishop, furnished the occasion and authority for making him bishop. Pacian continues: “The linen-covered”—that is, episcopal—“seat received him although no one consecrated him.” He presently explains “although no one consecrated him” by repeating the same point in these words: “I know that Novatian was made bishop **without legitimate consecration**, through the letter of those who pretended to be confessors.”
>
> He therefore said that Novatian was placed in the episcopal seat although no one consecrated him because he was convinced that Novatian had been “made bishop without legitimate consecration,” and could boast only of an imaginary, vain, and utterly null consecration. The confessors themselves, according to Cornelius’s testimony in Epistle VI, §1, admitted that they had been brought to such a point “that they permitted hands to be laid upon him as though upon a bishop.” Nor does Cyprian, in Epistle 44 or 46, conceal his grief from them upon discovering that they “had consented that another bishop” [Col. 0740C]—other than Cornelius—“should be made.” Pacian, however, teaches us something that Cornelius and Cyprian had left unstated: namely, that they signified this consent by letter.
>
> Indeed, it would be very surprising if such a violent ordination, performed at an improper hour by bishops overcome with wine and carousing, had not horrified the devout confessors who were present. From this it also follows that Novatian misused this letter from illustrious confessors to seduce simple bishops, so that they would not shrink from laying hands upon him. But why did Pacian say of men who, as the testimony of Cornelius, Cyprian, and others establishes, had suffered imprisonment for the faith, that “they pretended to be confessors”? Because by withdrawing from the Church they had obscured and forfeited the glory of their confession, just as a person practiced in many works of righteousness loses the title and praise of being righteous upon committing sin. —COUSTANT.
>
> “Whom we also admitted to communion as a layman.” Rufinus renders this passage very well [Col. 0740D]: “And, upon the people’s interceding for him, he was received into lay communion.” By these words Cornelius indicates that the bishop who, together with his other two colleagues, had ordained Novatian was deposed by Cornelius and reduced to the rank of laymen. For when Cornelius wished to excommunicate him as an author of a wicked schism, the people petitioned him, and Cornelius granted him lay communion—that is, permitted him to communicate among the laity. The other bishops who ordained Novatian were not only deposed but also separated from the communion of the whole Church.
>
> Cyprian speaks similarly in the Epistle to Antonianus about the bishop Trophimus, who, after creating a schism in the Roman Church, subsequently confessed his error and brought back into the Church with him the multitude of brethren whom he had led away; Cornelius then received him. “Trophimus,” he says, “was nevertheless admitted on the condition that he communicate as a layman, not as though he were to usurp the place of a priest.” I believe this Trophimus to be the very man of whom Cornelius speaks in this letter [Col. 0741A], one of those who ordained Novatian. For Cyprian calls him a priest—that is, a bishop—and testifies that he had previously drawn the brotherhood away from the Church, but afterward returned, humbly sought pardon, and was received by Cornelius into lay communion [Col. 0741B].
>
> Furthermore, Evaristus appears to have been another of the bishops who ordained Novatian, as I infer from Pope Cornelius’s letter numbered 48 among Cyprian’s Epistles. In the spurious acts of Novatian’s martyrdom cited by Eulogius in Book VI, Novatian is said to have been made bishop at Rome by two bishops, Marcellus of Aquileia and Agamemnon of Trier. Moreover, the Mazarin, Medicean, Fuk., and Savile codices read ἐκοινωνήσαμεν ὡς λαϊκῷ, “we admitted him to communion as a layman,” a reading adopted by Christophorson. The particle ὡς is absent from the edition of Robert Stephanus. —VALESIUS.
>
> Valesius identifies that bishop as Trophimus, about whom Cyprian writes at greater length in the following Epistle 10 to Antonianus. But what Cyprian says there about this Trophimus can only with the greatest difficulty be reconciled with what Cornelius now relates about Novatian’s ordainer. For when Antonianus, moved by Novatian’s false letters, asked Cyprian to write to him “on what grounds Cornelius communicates with Trophimus and those who had offered incense,” that prelate replies [Col. 0741C] in §9 that Cornelius “was stained by no pollution from a certificate, as some people boast, nor did he enter into sacrilegious communion with bishops who had sacrificed.”
>
> Then in §19 he adds: “For as regards Trophimus, about whom you wished information to be written to you, the matter is not as the rumor and falsehood of malicious persons reported it to you. . . . After a consultation had been held there with very many colleagues, Trophimus was received, in whose favor the return of the brethren and the restored salvation of many provided satisfaction. Trophimus was nevertheless received on the condition that he communicate as a layman, and not, as the letters of malicious persons reported to you, as though he were to usurp the place of the priesthood.”
>
> Those who weigh these and Cyprian’s other words about the reception of Trophimus will discover: first, that Trophimus had been stained by the pollution of those who sacrificed; second, that he returned to the Church with a very large number of brethren, “all of whom would not have returned to the Church except with Trophimus”; and third, that Cornelius received him after consultation not with his own people, as occurred in the reception of Novatian’s ordainer, but with very many colleagues [Col. 0741D]—that is, in a well-attended council of bishops. Hence the false report was spread that Cornelius communicated with those who had sacrificed and had restored Trophimus, though guilty of that crime, to his former priestly rank.
>
> If we also investigate who those malicious men were by whose letters and rumors these falsehoods were sown, perhaps none other than Novatian will be found, since Antonianus, moved by Novatian’s letters, questioned Cyprian about falsehoods of this kind. Certainly either Novatian or his associates sowed them. Yet no one should persuade himself that Novatian or his followers were displeased with, or counted as an accusation against themselves, the fact that his ordainer had been received by Cornelius and granted communion. —COUSTANT.
>
> The Norfolk manuscript and Syncellus, like the edition of Stephanus, omit these words. —ROUTH.
>
> “We admitted him to communion as a layman.” In ancient times it was customary for laypeople, after receiving the Eucharist from the bishop, to give him a kiss. Jerome, in Epistle 62 against John of Jerusalem, writes: “Does anyone communicate with you unwillingly? [Col. 0742A] Does anyone extend his hand, turn away his face, and offer Judas’s kiss amid the sacred feast?”
>
> Paul the Deacon, in *Lives of the Fathers of Mérida*, chapter 7, speaking of Bishop Fidelis, writes: “‘Go,’ he said, ‘receive communion and give us a kiss. Bid everyone farewell, because you are nevertheless about to depart [Col. 0742B], and arrange your household with all haste; and if you desire it, receive the remedy of penance.’ After he had immediately received penance and arranged his household, he bade everyone farewell and departed from the body the following night.” —VALESIUS.
>
> “All the people who were present.” The word παρόντος, “present,” is absent from the edition of Robert Stephanus. The Mazarin, Medicean, Fuk., and Savile codices, as well as Syncellus, read παντὸς τοῦ παρόντος λαοῦ, “all the people who were present.” —VALESIUS. Stroth adds this reading from the margin of the Geneva edition and Gruter’s readings; to these I add the Norfolk manuscript. —ROUTH.
>
> “And for the other bishops,” etc. Valesius plausibly conjectures that Evaristus, in whose place Bishop Zetus is said in the preceding Epistle 5 to have been appointed, was one of these two bishops. From this it is readily understood how Cornelius could write in the cited epistle that “Evaristus was an author of the schism.” The statement here that successors were ordained for those two bishops also in some sense implies that no one was substituted in place of the bishop who was received into lay communion. Yet once a bishop is declared reduced to lay communion [Col. 0742C], it is sufficiently evident that his see is vacant and must be provided for. —COUSTANT. Syncellus has τῶν δὲ λοιπῶν, “and of the others.”

**II.** “Beloved brother, it is impossible to express how great a change and transformation we have seen take place in him within a short time. For that most illustrious man, who had given assurances by certain dreadful oaths that he did not aspire to the episcopate at all, suddenly appears as a bishop, thrown into the midst as though from some machine. For this doctrinal innovator [Col. 0737B], this defender of ecclesiastical knowledge, when he attempted to divert and seize for himself the episcopate that had not been given to him from above, chose two associates who had despaired of their own salvation, so that he might send them to some small and utterly insignificant part of Italy and there deceive three bishops—rustic and exceedingly simple men—by a fabricated undertaking.

“He emphatically assured and insisted to them that they must come to Rome with all haste, on the pretext that whatever dissension had arisen might be resolved through their mediation together with that of other bishops. When they arrived [Col. 0739A], being, as we have already said, men too simple to deal with the schemes and villainy of the wicked, they were shut up by certain men of the same disposition as himself. At the tenth hour, when they had been drinking and carousing, he violently compelled them, by a certain shadowy and ineffectual laying-on of hands, to give him the episcopate—which, although it did not belong to him, he claims through treachery and cunning.

“Of these bishops, one returned to the Church not long afterward, lamenting and confessing his sin. We admitted him to communion as [Col. 0741A] a layman, after all the people who were present had petitioned on his behalf. We also ordained successors to the other bishops for the places where they had been, and sent them out.”

> [Note: [Col. 0742C]
>
> **III.** “The champion, therefore, of the Gospel.” This is said ironically of Novatian, who boasted that he was a defender of Christ’s Gospel, as Cyprian teaches in the first Epistle to Cornelius. A book by Novatian *On Jewish Foods* survives today, which he entitled: “To the people persisting in the Gospel.” —VALESIUS. The word οὖν, “therefore,” is absent from the Norfolk manuscript. Syncellus has ὁ δὲ ἐκδικητὴς οὖν τοῦ, “but the champion, therefore, of the . . .” —ROUTH.
>
> “That there ought to be one bishop in the catholic Church.” The same words are found in Pope Cornelius’s Epistle to Cyprian, where the confessors who abandoned Novatian and returned to the Church are said to have used these words: “For we are not ignorant that there is one God; that there is one Christ the Lord, whom we confessed; one Holy Spirit; and that there ought to be one bishop in the catholic Church.” Here the Roman Church is specifically called the catholic Church because it is the root and mother of the catholic Church [Col. 0742D], as Cyprian says in the Epistle to Cornelius. In the same way, at the beginning of his Epistle to Antonianus, Cyprian calls the Roman Church the catholic Church: “so that he might now know that you communicate with him—that is, with the catholic Church.” —VALESIUS.
>
> This rule was so well established and widely known that the confessors returning to the Church in the preceding Epistle VI, §2, profess it as something known to everyone and which no one is permitted to ignore. Thus Cyprian too, in the following Epistle to Antonianus, §7, after proving on many grounds that Cornelius had been legitimately ordained, finally adds: “Since there cannot be a second after the first, whoever is made after the one who ought to be the sole bishop is no longer a second bishop, but none at all.” —COUSTANT.
>
> “There are forty-six presbyters.” From this passage it can be inferred how many basilicas the Christians then had at Rome. For since the individual presbyters governed their own basilicas, if there were forty-six presbyters, it must be said that there were the same number of basilicas. Certainly Optatus, in Book II, testifies that there were forty and [Col. 0743A] more basilicas at Rome around the time of Diocletian’s persecution: “For the few who, amid forty and more basilicas, had no place in which to assemble ought not to have been called a flock or a people.”
>
> Optatus is speaking there of the basilicas that existed at Rome during Diocletian’s persecution, about fifty years after Pope Cornelius’s letter, not of the basilicas that existed at Rome in his own day, that is, in A.D. 378, as Blondel wrote in his *Apology [Col. 0743B] for Jerome*, p. 223. See Baronius at the year of Christ 57, whom Blondel attempts in vain to refute in the book just mentioned. —VALESIUS.
>
> From the number of presbyters and poor persons mentioned here, Gilbert Burnet, bishop of Salisbury, with Moyle defending the calculation in his *Works*, vol. II, p. 152, inferred that there were no more than fifty thousand Christians at Rome at that time. Coustant, however, notes that “forty-four” crept into Valesius’s Latin translation through mere carelessness; and Stroth points out that the readings of Castellan’s copy have τεσς. μζʹ. Syncellus, however, has δύο, “two.” But Rufinus, the ancient translator, agrees with our manuscripts of Eusebius. —ROUTH.
>
> Long after these times, the number of seven deacons, in imitation of the ancient Jerusalem custom, was retained and observed in many churches, especially the Roman Church, as the celebrated Bingham shows in *Ecclesiastical Antiquities*, Book II, chapter 20, §19. Compare Mosheim, *On Christian Affairs before Constantine the Great*, Century I, §37, p. 121, and Vansleb, *History of the Church of Alexandria*, part I, chapter 15 [Col. 0743C]. Thus, at the very end of the fifth century, I find that Symmachus was appointed bishop at Rome “when he was one of the seven deacons” [ὡς ἕνα τῶν ἑπτὰ διακόνων ὄντα], as Photius relates in his *Questions*, first published by Fr. Fontanius at Florence in 1785, Question VI, p. 44.
>
> That “forty-four” entered Valesius’s Latin translation through mere carelessness is conclusively demonstrated by his own note on these words: “From this passage it can be inferred how many basilicas the Christians then had at Rome. For since the individual presbyters governed their own basilicas, if there were forty-six presbyters, it must be said that there were the same number of basilicas.”
>
> Blondel errs more seriously concerning this passage when he cites it in such a way as to make no mention of subdeacons, and then thinks it established that no subdeacons had yet been appointed at Rome [Col. 0743D]. But both the Greek text of Eusebius and Rufinus’s Latin translation demonstrate the falsity of that reading. Optatus also relates in Book II that forty and more basilicas existed at Rome when Victor of Gabii was sent there by the schismatics shortly after the rise of the Donatist schism. “There,” Optatus says, “amid forty and more basilicas, they had no place in which to assemble.” Valesius rightly notes that Blondel misunderstood this passage when, in the *Apology*, p. 223, he interpreted it as referring to Optatus’s own age. —COUSTANT.
>
> Since all authorities known to me provide the adopted reading, I wonder how Blondel’s error arose; Pearson had censured it before Coustant in the *Cyprianic Annals*, at the year 252, §111. Shortly afterward δέ is absent from the Norfolk manuscript, while Syncellus has δυσί, “two,” instead of δύο after πυλωροῖς, “doorkeepers.”
>
> “Widows together with the afflicted.” This word occurs in the letter of the Roman clergy to the clergy of Carthage concerning Cyprian’s withdrawal: “Whether they are widows, or *thlibomeni* who cannot support themselves, or those who are in prison, or those driven from their homes, they ought certainly to have persons to minister to them.” The common edition wrongly reads *clydomeni*, and others have emended it still worse to *clinomeni*. It should undoubtedly read *thlibomeni*—that is [Col. 0744A], “the needy,” as Rufinus translates it, or “those who cannot support themselves,” as the Roman clergy explain it.
>
> In Epistle IV Cyprian calls them “the poor and needy who are suffering.” Possidius calls them “those placed in affliction,” writing in chapter 27 of the *Life of the Blessed Augustine*: “In visitations he observed the limit defined by the Apostle, so that he visited only orphans, widows, and those placed in afflictions.” That is how the text reads in the manuscript codex of St. Mary of the Royal Mount. John Chrysostom [Col. 0744B], in Homily 67 on Matthew, says that the church of Antioch in his day, although it possessed only moderate revenues, fed daily more than three thousand widows and virgins, apart from guests, lepers, and prisoners, and apart from the clerics to whom it supplied clothing and provisions. —VALESIUS.
>
> In the passage from the Epistle of the Roman Clergy, the identity of the *thlibomeni* is immediately explained by the appended words “who cannot support themselves”—that is, who are unable to maintain themselves and supply themselves with the necessities of life, as is evident from Cyprian’s *Testimonies*, §61: “Therefore, having support and covering, let us be content with these.” Tertullian uses the same word “support” with the same meaning in *On Idolatry*, chapters 5 and 8. There, in rebuking craftsmen who would not cease making idols, he raises against himself their customary plea, “I have no other means by which to live,” and then refutes it as follows: “If the necessity of support is pleaded in this manner, there are other kinds of work that furnish the means of living without transgression of discipline—that is, without making an idol.” Thus “to support” means to furnish the means of living [Col. 0744C]. Rufinus therefore did not badly substitute “the needy” for *thlibomeni*. —COUSTANT.
>
> As for the reading *thlibomeni* placed in the Cyprianic epistle, the Benedictine edition gives *clinomeni*. There Baluze says that θλιβόμενοι is indeed a good emendation, but that it ought not to have been introduced into the text without stronger authority, since the other readings could also be sound. Baluze further informs us that this emendation, which the English editors appear to have taken from Valesius’s note on Eusebius, belongs neither to Valesius nor to the English, but to François Bosquet, who first proposed it in Book I of his *Histories of the Gallican Church*. Stroth, however, notes on Eusebius that Gruter’s readings and those of Castellan’s codex wrongly give θλιβομένοις for θλιβομένοις. George Syncellus has συνθλιβομένας, “widows suffering together,” for σὺν θλιβομένοις, “together with the afflicted.” —ROUTH.
>
> “All of whom.” Christophorson had translated: “No one [Col. 0744D] amid so great a multitude of ministers . . . no one from so great a number of needy persons enriched by God’s providence . . . no one, finally, from that vast and innumerable gathering.” What displeases me in this translation is that, contrary to the Greek text, he distinguished the Church’s ministers from the needy, as though the former, unlike the latter, were not sustained by the riches of divine providence. Rufinus certainly understood this passage otherwise, for he says of the presbyters, deacons, and other clerics no less than of the widows and needy: “All of whom God feeds in his Church.”
>
> Later, church revenues were distributed into four portions: one portion went to the bishop, another to the other clerics, a third to the needy, and a fourth to the buildings. Previously, however, although their division was not the same, they were nevertheless by no means spent on other purposes. —COUSTANT. As for the word χάρις, “grace” or “generosity,” which immediately follows, the author imitates St. Paul, who frequently used it for beneficence and almsgiving, elsewhere as well as in the “First Epistle to the Corinthians.” —ROUTH.
>
> [Col. 0745B] “Turned him back” [ἐνέτρεψε]. George Syncellus reads ἐπέστρεψε, less correctly. The Fuk. codex has ἀνέτρεψε. —VALESIUS.

**III.** “The champion, therefore, of the Gospel did not know that there ought to be one bishop in the catholic Church. Yet he was not ignorant—how could he have been?—that in it there were forty-six presbyters [Col. 0743A], seven deacons, seven subdeacons, forty-two acolytes, and fifty-two exorcists, readers, and doorkeepers together; and more than fifteen hundred widows together with the afflicted, all of whom the grace and loving-kindness of the Master [Col. 0745A] sustains.

“Yet not even so great and so necessary a multitude within the Church—so rich and numerous a body through God’s providence, together with an exceedingly great and innumerable people—turned him back from such despair and renunciation and recalled him to the Church.”

And again, after other matters, he adds the following:

> [Note: [Col. 0745B]
>
> **IV.** “Because from the beginning he had lived in the Church,” etc. “In the Church” here is equivalent to “in the ministry of the Church.” “From the beginning” appears to me to mean nothing other than “from early life” and “from infancy.” Perhaps at that time the prevailing discipline was that those who were to be admitted into the clergy customarily “devoted themselves from infancy to the service of the Church,” as Siricius says in Epistle I, §13, or, as Zosimus expresses the same thing in Epistle IX, §5, “gave their names from infancy to ecclesiastical ministries,” and thus earned the episcopate through all the grades of the clergy.
>
> Accordingly, although Cyprian in the following Epistle, §7 [Col. 0745C], does not explicitly say that Cornelius gave his name to ecclesiastical ministries from the beginning—that is, from infancy—he nevertheless commends him because “he did not reach the episcopate suddenly, but, having been promoted through all ecclesiastical offices and earned God’s favor in divine administrations, ascended through every grade of religious service to the lofty summit of the priesthood.” The question here, therefore, is whether Novatian was adorned with similar merits; and it is demonstrated that he lacked them. —COUSTANT.
>
> If Novatian was born of pagan parents, as indeed appears more readily inferable from Cornelius’s words ἀφορμὴ τοῦ πιστεῦσαι γέγονεν, “became the occasion of his believing,” I would prefer to interpret the phrase “to have lived in the Church from the beginning” as referring to anyone’s upbringing from tender years onward in the Church’s communion. And although, as you will see, Coustant immediately afterward annotates the word πιστεῦσαι, “to believe,” in the contrary sense, its simpler and more usual meaning pleases me better: Novatian took occasion from the help given him by the exorcists to embrace the faith. —ROUTH.
>
> [Col. 0745D] “To contend for her.” The Norfolk manuscript has περὶ αὐτῆς, “concerning her.” The Bodleian manuscript has ἠγωνίσθαι, “to have contended,” and Syncellus erroneously has ἠγωνίσαι. A little earlier Syncellus also has ἀνεστραφῆναι for ἀνεστράφθαι, “to have lived,” where the margin of the Geneva edition has ἀνατετράφθαι, “to have been brought up.” —ROUTH.
>
> “An occasion for receiving the faith” [ἀφορμὴ τοῦ πιστεῦσαι]: namely, for receiving that faith which thereafter gives the recipient the designation “believer” or “one of the faithful.” Apart from the custom of the Jerusalem church, and perhaps of a few others, this designation was anciently given only to those initiated by baptism. Those who were previously called catechumens, elect, or candidates were customarily called “the faithful” only when they had been baptized.
>
> Hence in the Council of Elvira a catechumen, and even a Christian, is distinguished from one of the faithful. For there, as is evident from Canons 45 and 59, the name “Christian” is common to both the catechumen and the baptized, but the designation “faithful” belongs only to the baptized. Cyril of Jerusalem, although he also gives this name “faithful” to the elect—because they were already beginning to be initiated into the solemn rites of baptism—nevertheless carefully distinguishes it from the designation “catechumen” [Col. 0746B]. Thus he says in *Catechesis* I, §4: “Formerly you were a catechumen; now you will be called one of the faithful”; and in *Catechesis* V, §1: “How great a dignity the Lord bestows upon you, transferring you from the order of catechumens to the order of the faithful.”
>
> Accordingly, Valesius’s interpretation is not approved when he renders this passage: “To whom Satan furnished the cause and beginning of believing,” unless after “believing” one mentally supplies “with that faith which gives the believer the designation ‘one of the faithful.’” For perhaps Novatian was already at that time numbered among the catechumens, and therefore was not altogether without a beginning of belief. Cornelius certainly understood baptism by τοῦ πιστεῦσαι, “believing”; but he appears deliberately to have avoided τοῦ βαπτισθῆναι, “being baptized,” because Novatian received this sacrament through περίχυσις—that is, by sprinkling [Col. 0746C] or pouring, both words being synonymous in Cyprian’s Epistle LXXVI to Magnus. —COUSTANT.
>
> Nicephorus, however, paraphrases the words as follows in Book VI, chapter 3: “For him, Satan, who had taken up residence within him, also became the occasion of believing in Christ” [ᾧ καὶ τὸ εἰς Χριστὸν πιστεῦσαι πρόφασις ὁ Σατανᾶς ἦν ἐνσκηνώσας αὐτῷ]. This late and virtually compelled faith appears to be contrasted with “having lived in the Church from the beginning” [τῷ ἐξ ἀρχῆς ἐν τῇ Ἐκκλησίᾳ ἀνεστράφθαι]. —ROUTH.
>
> Christophorson rendered these words into Latin as follows: “When he had been delivered from that evil spirit by the assistance of the exorcists, and afterward had fallen into so serious an illness. . . .” But if Novatian had been delivered from the evil spirit before this illness, Satan could by no means be said to have furnished him the cause for receiving baptism.
>
> Rufinus summarizes the same words of Cornelius thus: “He also adds that this same Novatus”—read “Novatian”—“was afflicted by an unclean spirit in his youth; and after spending some time among the exorcists, he fell into so grave an illness that his recovery was despaired of.” This confirms what we conjectured above [Col. 0746D]: namely, that before receiving baptism Novatian was not without at least some beginning of faith. For what would he have been doing among the exorcists if he were utterly devoid of faith?
>
> Perhaps what befell him was something that Cyprian, in Epistle LXXVI to Magnus, testifies was customarily done to and experienced by similar persons in his own age: “Through the exorcists, by a human voice and divine power, the devil is scourged, burned, and tortured; and though he repeatedly says that he is departing and releasing God’s servants, he deceives in what he has said.” Accordingly, that prelate wishes anyone troubled because certain persons baptized during sickness testify that unclean spirits still remain in them to know “that the devil’s persistent malice retains its power as far as the saving water, but in baptism loses all the poison of its wickedness.”
>
> He presently adds: “We experience this, finally, in the facts themselves: those who under urgent necessity are baptized during illness, and who have obtained grace, are freed from the unclean spirit by which they were previously agitated.” It is therefore evident that baptism was conferred even upon those who were afflicted by unclean spirits, and that they did not need first to be delivered from them [Col. 0747A] before receiving this sacrament. The Synod of Elvira established this very thing in Canon 37: “It is decreed that those afflicted by unclean spirits should be baptized if they have reached the extremity of death.” From this passage of Cornelius it is clear that the council decreed nothing other than what had already been done, at least in Novatian’s case.
>
> I too am more inclined to think—and Valesius below does not disagree—that Novatian’s illness and demonic possession were present at the same time, even though Rufinus’s translation also seems to convey something different. [Col. 0747B] Coustant seeks to confirm from Rufinus’s version that Novatian was not without at least some beginning of faith before receiving baptism. “For what,” he asks, “would he have been doing among the exorcists if he were utterly devoid of faith?” One can answer from Tertullian that there were formerly certain pagans who acknowledged that benefits of this kind had been conferred upon them by Christians. See Tertullian elsewhere and especially his short work *To Scapula*, chapter 4.
>
> I admit, however, that Pearson thought differently on this matter, and perhaps more correctly. He writes in the *Cyprianic Annals*, at the year 231, section V: “For at first he had been a philosopher, and indeed a Stoic; then, while he was among the catechumens, he was exorcised as a demoniac, and was baptized only upon his sickbed.” At column 745 above, line 14, the Norfolk manuscript and the margin of Syncellus had εἰσφοιτήσας, “having entered,” for φοιτήσας, “having attended.” —ROUTH.
>
> “Exorcists” [ἐπορκιστῶν]. Someone might perhaps think that ἐξορκιστῶν should be read, but ἐπορκιστῶν is also found in Syncellus and Nicephorus. —STROTH. Although Syncellus actually reads ἐξορκιστῶν—for Stroth had inferred otherwise merely from Valesius’s silence—[Col. 0747C] no change is therefore necessary. Among others, the author of the *Apostolic Constitutions* has ἐπορκιστής in Book VIII, chapter 26. Moreover, Syncellus and the Norfolk manuscript here give ὡς for ὅς. —ROUTH.
>
> “In which” [ᾗ]. Gruter’s readings and those of Castellan’s codex have οὗ, “where.” —STROTH. Add the Norfolk manuscript and Syncellus. —ROUTH.

*Ἐν αὐτῇ τῇ κλίνῃ* (“In the very bed”). From this, people of this kind were called *Clinics* (*Clinici*), from the Greek word κλίνη, meaning “bed.” Now although Cyprian was not unaware that the term κλινικός was used by physicians and Evangelists of paralytics and sick persons lying in bed, or even of physicians who care for such patients, nevertheless in Epistle 76 to Magnus he indicates in these words that he does not know how this name came to be transferred to a certain class of baptized persons: “As for the fact that they call those who have obtained the grace of Christ through saving water and legitimate faith not Christians but Clinics, I cannot discover whence they derive this name.” Perhaps this usage began with Novatian’s own baptism and, devised out of hatred for him, immediately gained currency. Yet Cyprian speaks in the cited epistle in such a way that he appears not to have known how that schismatic had been baptized—a circumstance that naturally causes surprise. Thus, although the practice of pouring water upon catechumens in bed when death threatened cannot then be called new, Cyprian nevertheless implies that the usage by which they began to be called Clinics was recent. COUSTANT.

*Περιχυθείς* (“having had water poured over him”). Rufinus correctly translates it “having had water poured over him.” For sick persons baptized in bed, since they could not be immersed by the priest, had only water poured over them. Accordingly, baptism of this kind was regarded as less solemn and less perfect, since it appeared to be received not voluntarily but from fear of death by persons suffering delirium and no longer endowed with any awareness. Moreover, since “baptism” properly signifies immersion, such a pouring could scarcely be called baptism. For this reason Clinics—for so those who had received baptism of this kind were called—are forbidden advancement to the rank of presbyter by Canon 12 of the Council of Neocaesarea. [Col. 0748A] John Chrysostom clearly describes such a baptism of a man lying in bed and at the point of death in Homily 60, *To the Catechumens*, volume II. Cyprian, however, in Epistle 76 judges this baptism to be full and legitimate and says that Clinics are in no respect inferior to those who received baptism in the Church while healthy. VALESIUS.

Cyprian indeed spoke thus in accordance with his customary reserve and modesty, “prejudging no one,” as he himself says. But at least in the Roman [Col. 0748B] Church in Novatian’s time, Clinics were barred from every clerical rank, as is evident from what Cornelius writes below. Albaspinaeus, however, gives a different explanation—whether it is truer I doubt—for the exclusion of Clinics from sacred orders: namely, that those whom ill health had prevented from learning the first elements of the faith could not perform sacred duties. See his notes on Canon 12 of Neocaesarea, following his *Observations on the Rites of the Ancient Church*, p. 372, Helmstedt edition. ROUTH.

*Ἔλαβεν* (“he received”). Christophorson has τὸ βάπτισμα ἔλαβεν, “he received baptism.” Certainly either τὸ βάπτισμα must be added or it must be understood, although that would be a harsh ellipsis. Nicephorus also appears to have read this expression, writing as follows: ὥστ’ ἀποθανεῖσθαι προσδόκιμον ὄντα, τὸ ὕδωρ αἰτῆσαι λαβεῖν· ὃ καὶ ἐν αὐτῇ τῇ κλίνῃ ᾗ ἔκειτο, περιχυθὲν δῆθεν ἐβάπτιζεν, “so that, when he was expected to die, he asked to receive the water; and this, poured upon him in the very bed in which he lay, supposedly baptized him.” STROTH.

There is nothing in the Greek corresponding to the word “faith.” In its place Valesius, following Christophorson, supplied the word “baptism.” It seems preferable here to understand the preceding expression τὸ πιστεῦσαι, “to believe.” COUSTANT.

I do not agree; rather, I think “baptism” must be understood after the verb here, as likewise “Spirit” is understood in the words of Dionysius of Alexandria preserved by Eusebius, τοῦ γὰρ ἁγίου παρ’ αὐτοῦ τετυχήκεσαν, “for they had received the Holy [Spirit] from him,” *Epistle to Philemon*, book VI of the *History*, chapter 7, where no manuscript at all except the Medicean recognizes the word πνεύματος after ἁγίου. Yet Coustant rightly says below that Cornelius deliberately abstains from the word “baptism” wherever he speaks of the rite by which Novatian was initiated. The Norfolk manuscript corruptly has ἔλεγεν (“he said”) for ἔλαβεν (“he received”). ROUTH.

*Κατὰ τὸν τῆς Ἐκκλησίας κανόνα* (“according to the rule of the Church”). Those who had received baptism while lying in bed were required, after recovering from their illness, to approach the bishop so that he might supply what had been lacking in their baptism. The ancient author of *On Not Rebaptizing Heretics*, recently edited by Nicolas Rigault together with Cyprian, says: “Or, if baptism has been administered by the lesser clergy under the pressure of necessity, let us await the outcome, so that it may either be completed by us or be left for completion by the Lord.” Cornelius therefore charges Novatian here with having been baptized in bed, under the urgent necessity of illness, by the exorcists who were caring for him—for this is what the words of his letter indicate—and with failing afterward, once he had recovered his health, to approach the bishop so that the remaining solemnities of baptism might be supplied, as ecclesiastical rule prescribed. This is expressly prescribed in Canon 47 of the Council of Laodicea and in chapter 38 of the Council of Elvira. VALESIUS.

Magnus, later uncertain about baptism of this kind, consulted Cyprian as to “what he thought of those who obtain the grace of God in sickness and infirmity: whether they are to be regarded as legitimate Christians, since they have not been washed with saving water but have had it poured over them.” In Epistle 76 Cyprian, replying to him, also notes this further kind of doubt concerning the same people: “Whether they have indeed obtained the Lord’s grace, but in a shorter and lesser measure of the divine gift and of the Holy Spirit, so that they are indeed regarded as Christians but are nevertheless not to be placed on an equal footing with the others.” In the same place Cyprian replies that he judges anyone to be a Christian “whoever has obtained divine grace in the Church according to the law and right of faith”; that “there is no doubt that baptism received by sprinkling [Col. 0749A] or pouring is legitimate”; and, finally, that “the divine benefits cannot be mutilated or weakened in any respect.”

Nor does Cornelius now doubt whether Novatian obtained baptismal grace because he had water poured over him rather than being washed—that is, because he received baptism by sprinkling rather than by immersion—but for the reason for which the Council of Neocaesarea in Canon 12 judges such a man unworthy of the honor of the presbyterate: namely, “because his faith does not arise from free choice but from necessity”—οὐκ ἐκ προαιρέσεως γὰρ ἡ πίστις αὐτοῦ, ἀλλ’ ἐξ ἀνάγκης. [Col. 0749B] Here one may also observe in passing that the word πίστις (“faith”) is used in place of “baptism.” Cornelius’s doubt was all the more reasonable because, on recovering from his illness, Novatian neglected to have what he lacked supplied. COUSTANT.

*Τοῦ τε σφραγισθῆναι ὑπὸ τοῦ ἐπισκόπου* (“and to be sealed by the bishop”). Rufinus interpreted these words as referring to the seal of chrism. I understand the imposition of hands, by which bishops conferred the Holy Spirit upon the baptized; the words that follow plainly declare this. For Cornelius adds: τούτου δὲ μὴ τυχών, πῶς ἂν τοῦ ἁγίου Πνεύματος ἔτυχε; “And since he did not obtain this, how could he have obtained the Holy Spirit?”—although the Mazarine, Medicean, and Fuk manuscripts read τούτων δὲ μὴ τυχών, “since he did not obtain these things.” Our interpretation is confirmed by Cyprian’s words to Jubaianus: “This is also done among us now: those baptized in the Church are presented to the rulers of the Church, and through our prayer and the imposition of hands they obtain the Holy Spirit and are consummated with the Lord’s seal.” Σφραγίζειν properly means “to consign” or “to seal.” But “to consign” and “to impose the hand” are the same thing, as the Letter of Innocent to Decentius, chapters 3 and 6, teaches; [Col. 0749C] Marcus likewise confirms this in the *Life of Porphyry, Bishop of Gaza*, whose passage we shall cite below.

Ambrose—or whoever authored those books—writes on chapter 4 of Paul’s Epistle to the Ephesians: “Finally, in Egypt presbyters consign if the bishop is not present.” The author of the *Questions on the Old and New Testaments*, published among the works of Augustine, has the same in Question 101: “For in Alexandria and throughout Egypt, if the bishop is absent, the presbyter consecrates.” Write “the presbyter consigns,” as in the passage of Ambrose cited above. An ancient inscription reported by Baronius under the year of Christ 367 reads: “Picentia, a legitimate neophyte, consigned by Pope Liberius on the fifth day before the Kalends of September,” etc.

This consigning of the baptized was sometimes performed with chrism—namely, whenever someone had been baptized under the urgent necessity of illness by members of the lesser clergy and had not been chrismated. For then the bishop who afterward supplied the solemnities of baptism had to both chrismate and impose hands. But upon those who had received complete baptism, only the hand was imposed by the bishop, without chrismation, as an Orange canon teaches. To this pertains the ancient epigram about Marea in Gruter, p. 1177:

> And you taught that priests, with God as judge,  
> may touch no one twice with holy chrism.

Moreover, to return to Novatian’s baptism, this seems to me to have been the source of the Novatian custom of not employing sacred chrism in baptism, as Theodoret attests in book III of the *Compendium of Heretical Fables*: evidently because Novatian, their founder, had received baptism without chrismation. VALESIUS.

Rufinus rendered these words in Latin as follows: “Nor were the remaining rites that customarily follow baptism solemnly completed in him, nor was he consummated with the seal of chrism.” Valesius, interpreting Rufinus’s words in his annotations on this passage as referring to the seal of chrism conferred in baptism, does not think that Cornelius himself is speaking of the seal that we receive [Col. 0750A] in the sacrament of confirmation. But what prevents us from interpreting Rufinus’s words as referring to that same sacrament, and understanding them as spoken of the seal about which Cyprian writes in Epistle 73 to Jubaianus: “This is also done among us now: those baptized in the Church are brought to the rulers of the Church, and through our prayer and the imposition of hands they obtain the Holy Spirit and are consummated with the Lord’s seal”? For he too calls that a seal whose proper function is to consummate the recipient.

Someone might fault Rufinus for adding the word “chrism,” which is not expressed in the Greek text. Yet his addition in no way conflicts with the practice of that time; indeed, it explains it aptly. For Cyprian, in Epistle 70, teaches together with the whole African council: “It is also necessary that one who has been baptized be anointed, so that, having received chrism—that is, anointing—he may be God’s anointed and may possess within himself the grace of Christ.” That the anointing there is declared distinct from the sacrament of baptism is proved both by the immediately preceding words and by the particle “also,” as well as by the phrase “one who has been baptized,” not “one who is being baptized” or “one who is to be baptized.”

Valesius further thinks that, because Novatian had received baptism without chrismation, there arose the custom of which Theodoret speaks in book III of the *Compendium of Heretical Fables*, chapter 5: “Novatian’s successors do not provide the most holy chrism to those whom they baptize. For this reason, the most praiseworthy Fathers ordered that those who join the body of the Church from this heresy be anointed.” But in Canon 8 the Nicene Fathers prescribe only that the Novatians be received through the imposition of hands. In agreement with them, [Col. 0750C] Siricius, Epistle 5, chapter 8, and Innocent, Epistle 2, chapter 8, decree “that those coming from the Novatians or Montenses be received through the imposition of hands”—Innocent alone adds the words “of hands”—without any mention of anointing. Although Theodoret in that passage transmits some things about Novatian that are not sufficiently exact for a precise account of events, he undoubtedly has Canon 7 of the First Council of Constantinople in view. COUSTANT.

The distinguished Weismann says well in his *Ecclesiastical History of the New Testament*: “I shall never believe that Cornelius—to whom they attribute the denial that Novatian received the Holy Spirit in his baptism because the bishop’s sealing or confirmation was not conferred upon him at the same time—assigned greater efficacy to episcopal confirmation than to baptism itself. He recoiled from Novatian’s baptism; for this reason, when recounting it, he added: ‘If indeed it should be said that such a man received it.’ He also recoiled from, and undoubtedly ascribed to an evil origin, Novatian’s neglect and contempt of the customary rite of sealing in the Church. In this agitation of mind he poured forth those words, certainly hyperbolical, from which one may by no means extract a formal doctrine and heresy.” Century III, §16.4, p. 254.

Furthermore, two eminent men disputed the question whether consignation or confirmation was anciently regarded as a part of the rites of baptism: Hammond, in his posthumous book *On Confirmation*, maintained the negative position; and Dallaeus, in *On the Religious Practices of the Latins*, had affirmed it. Because Christophorson’s *Readings* have οὐδὲ τοῦ σφραγισθῆναι (“nor to be sealed”) instead of τοῦ τε σφραγισθῆναι (“and to be sealed”), Hammond seeks to establish that οὐδέ, or οὔτε, both from the construction of the words and from this passage in Nicephorus: ὅ γε οὐδὲ τῶν λοιπῶν τῆς Ἐκκλησίας συμβόλων ἠξιοῦτο, ὧν χρεὼν τοὺς τοιούτους μεταλαμβάνειν κατὰ τὸν τῆς Ἐκκλησίας θεσμόν, ἀλλ’ οὐδὲ ὑπὸ ἐπισκόπων, τὴν νόσον διαφυγών, ἐσφραγίσθη ἐς ὕστερον, “He was not deemed worthy even of the remaining symbols of the Church, in which such persons must participate according to the ordinance of the Church; nor, after escaping the illness, was he subsequently sealed by bishops.” See Hammond, *On Confirmation*, chapter IV, section 1.

But, with deference to so great a man, it seems to me wholly unnecessary to alter anything in the received text, for after ὧν χρὴ μεταλαμβάνειν κατὰ τὸν τῆς Ἐκκλησίας κανόνα, “in which one must participate according to the rule of the Church,” there follows τοῦ τε σφραγισθῆναι, [Col. 0751B] “and to be sealed.” That reading is also found in the first, or Stephanus, edition, contrary to Dallaeus’s own belief; for in discussing the reading he approves it as though Valesius had first introduced it. Moreover, most of the readings called Christophorson’s are of too uncertain an origin to carry great weight without additional manuscript testimony.

As for the reading τούτων δὲ μὴ τυχών (“since he did not obtain these things”) instead of τούτου δὲ μὴ τυχών (“since he did not obtain this”), mentioned by Valesius, it is also supplied by the Savile, or Bodleian, manuscript and was perhaps found by Nicephorus, who has: τούτων δὲ τῶν μυστικῶν μὴ τυχών, πῶς ἂν etc., “Since he did not obtain these mystical things, how could he,” etc. ROUTH.]

**4.** Come, then, let us next say in what deeds or in what modes of life he trusted when he laid claim to the episcopate. Was it perhaps because from the beginning he had conducted himself within the Church, had fought many contests on her behalf, and had encountered many great dangers for the sake of religion? Certainly not. For the occasion of his coming to faith was Satan, [Col. 0745B] who entered into him and dwelt within him for a considerable time. [Col. 0747A] While he was receiving assistance from the exorcists, he fell into a severe illness and was thought to be on the very point of death; in the very bed in which he lay, he had water poured over him and received [baptism]—if indeed one ought to say that such a man received it. Yet, after escaping the illness, he did not obtain the remaining things in which one must participate according to the [Col. 0749A] rule of the Church, including being sealed by the bishop. Since he did not obtain this, how could he have obtained the Holy Spirit? [Col. 0751A] And again, a little later, he says:

[Note: [Col. 0751B]

**5.** *Βοηθήσῃ τοῖς ἀδελφοῖς* (“that he should assist the brethren”). After these words, in our Mazarine, Medicean, Fuk, and Savile manuscripts, and in Syncellus, the following are added—the edition of Robert Stephanus had omitted all of them except [Col. 0751C] ἐπικουρίας δεομένοις, “those needing assistance”: ὅσα θέμις, καὶ ὅσα δυνατὸν πρεσβυτέρῳ κινδυνεύουσιν ἀδελφοῖς καὶ ἐπικουρίας δεομένοις βοηθεῖν, “in every way lawful and possible for a presbyter to assist brethren in danger and in need of aid.” Rufinus appears to have read these words in his manuscript, for he translates: “He also writes concerning him that, during the persecution, while he was hiding in a certain little cell and was asked by the deacons, as was customary, to assist catechumens at the point of death,” etc. A little earlier, where ἐξελθὼν τοῦ οἴκου (“coming out of the house”) was read, we restored οἰσκίσκου (“little house” or “cell”) on the authority of the same manuscripts and George Syncellus. Rufinus translates it “cell.” VALESIUS.

In Rufinus’s interpretation—“when he was asked to assist catechumens at the point of death, he was afraid to come out of the cell in which he was hiding and denied that he was a presbyter”—excessive freedom on the interpreter’s part is evident, since he refers Cornelius’s words, which were spoken of all persons needing the assistance of a presbyter, solely to catechumens, whom deacons too could assist. Accordingly, I am likewise dissatisfied with Theodoret’s exposition of the same narrative in book III of the *Compendium of Heretical Fables*: “Those who sought to obtain the remedy [for their lapse] charged him with having often been asked to hasten to them and strengthen by his words those assailed by the tyrant’s devices, but with having hidden himself and attempted to remain concealed, even denying that he was a presbyter.” This passage makes clear how justly Cornelius asked above whether Novatian “had encountered many great dangers for the sake of religion.” COUSTANT.

For the words ὅσα θέμις κτλ., by which Valesius enlarged the discourse, the Norfolk manuscript must be added as a witness, as must the readings enumerated by Stroth from the Venetian manuscript and Christophorson’s *Readings*, together with Nicephorus. The reading οἰκίσκου is likewise confirmed by the Norfolk manuscript. A little above, that manuscript, like Syncellus, gives πρεσβύτερον ἑαυτὸν εἶναι, “that he himself was a presbyter,” with only the word order reversed. ROUTH.

*Βοηθεῖν* (“to assist”). Omitted by the Stephanus edition. It is supplied by the same witnesses mentioned just above. STROTH. Add the Norfolk manuscript. ROUTH.

*Ἑτέρας γὰρ εἶναι φιλοσοφίας ἐραστής* (“For he was a lover of another philosophy”). Cyprian says of the same man: “Although he may boast and proclaim his philosophy or eloquence in proud language, one who has maintained neither brotherly charity nor ecclesiastical unity has lost even what he formerly possessed.” *Epistle to Antonianus*, p. 73, Baluze’s edition. I add that Novatian deserved the penalty of deposition under Canon 62, called Apostolic, which decrees concerning a cleric: Εἰ μὲν τὸ ὄνομα τοῦ Χριστοῦ ἀρνήσηται, ἀποβαλλέσθω, εἰ δὲ τὸ ὄνομα τοῦ κληρικοῦ, καθαιρείσθω, “If he denies the name of Christ, let him be cast out; but if he denies the name of cleric, let him be deposed.” ROUTH.

*Καταλιπών* (“having abandoned”). Christophorson’s *Readings* and translation have κατέλιπε, “he abandoned.” STROTH.]

**5.** He who, through cowardice and love of life, denied during the persecution that he was a presbyter. For when he was urged and entreated by the deacons to come out of the little cell in which he had shut himself up and assist the brethren—in every way lawful and possible for a presbyter to assist brethren in danger and in need of aid—he was so far from obeying the deacons who entreated him that he went away and withdrew in anger. For he said that he no longer wished to be a presbyter, since he was a lover of another philosophy.

Passing over a few things, he again adds the following, saying:

[Note: [Col. 0752B]

**6.** *Ἐν ᾗ πιστεύσας* (“in which, having come to faith”). Elsewhere I would not object to Valesius’s translation, “after receiving baptism,” for this is what the words properly signify: “in which, after receiving baptism, he began to be called and regarded as one of the faithful.” Yet I have thought it best to adhere to the letter, since I have observed that Cornelius consistently abstains from the word “baptism” when speaking of the rite by which Novatian was initiated. Rufinus rendered the single word πιστεύσας by two Latin words, “having obtained grace.” This comes to the same thing. For baptism is frequently designated among the ancients by the expressions “grace,” “the grace of God,” or “the grace of Christ.” What else does Cyprian mean in Epistle 76 to Magnus—“You asked what I think of those who obtain the grace of God in sickness and infirmity”—except, “what I think of those who are baptized in sickness”? So too in Leo’s Epistle 18, §4, where he teaches that baptism must be celebrated on the Sabbath of Easter: “The very nature of the work therefore teaches the legitimate day for the general celebration of grace, on which,” etc. Here “the celebration of grace” plainly means the same as “the celebration of baptism.” COUSTANT.

*Κατηξιώθη τοῦ πρεσβυτερίου* (“he was deemed worthy of the presbyterate”). From this it appears that Novatian was ordained a presbyter directly, the orders of diaconate and subdiaconate being omitted. Such was then the custom in the Church, as is taught by the examples of Origen, Paulinus of Nola, and others. The examples of Ambrose [Col. 0752D] of Milan and Nectarius of Constantinople, who were ordained bishops while still neophytes, are also well known. VALESIUS.

Perhaps we ought merely to laugh at the archdiaconate supposedly bestowed upon Novatian several centuries after his death by Eulogius, bishop of Alexandria and a writer of the sixth century, in Photius, Codex last, col. 1622. According to Eulogius’s tale, Novatian owed that office to the favor of Cornelius.

Furthermore, to note this in passing, in more recent times, at the beginning of the seventeenth century, when several ecclesiastical ministers of the Scottish nation came to England to become bishops, those examples of Ambrose and Nectarius resolved the doubt whether men who had not yet been made presbyters ought to be consecrated to episcopal offices. See Heylin’s *History of the Presbyterians*, book XI, chapter 4, p. 382. Compare Spottiswood’s *Ecclesiastical History of Scotland*, book VII, p. 514, and Skinner’s *History of the Same Church*, vol. II, chapter 43, p. 252. Later, after Charles II had been restored to his ancestral kingdoms and the former government of the Church had returned with him, at least two Scottish ministers who had not yet [Col. 0753A] received episcopal ordination were first made deacons and presbyters and then consecrated bishops. See the *Life of James Sharp, Archbishop of St Andrews*, published in 1723, p. 55, compared with Collier’s *Ecclesiastical History of Great Britain*, vol. II, p. 887. Shortly afterward Syncellus has ὡς instead of ὅς. ROUTH.

[Col. 0753B] *Ὑπὸ παντὸς τοῦ κλήρου καὶ λαϊκῶν* etc. (“by all the clergy and laypeople,” etc.). In former times presbyters could not be ordained by a bishop without the consent of the clergy and people. As for the people’s vote in the election of presbyters, the Fathers of the Council of Nicaea attest it in their synodical letter to the bishops of Egypt. There, concerning the clerics who had preserved themselves pure and untainted by the schism of Meletius, they decree:

> Εἰ δὲ τινά ποτε συμβαίη ἀναπαύσασθαι τῶν ἐν τῇ Ἐκκλησίᾳ, τηνικαῦτα συναναβαίνειν εἰς τὴν τιμὴν τοῦ τετελευτηκότος τοὺς ἄρτι προσληφθέντας, μόνον εἰ ἄξιοι φαίνοιντο, καὶ ὁ λαὸς αἱροῖτο συνεπιψηφίζοντος αὐτοῖς καὶ ἐπισφραγίζοντος τοῦ τῆς Ἀλεξανδρείας ἐπισκόπου.

> But if it should ever happen that one of those in the Church falls asleep, then those who have recently been admitted may advance to the dignity of the deceased, provided only that they appear worthy, that the people choose them, and that the bishop of Alexandria concur in the vote and confirm it.

Sozomen understood these words of clerics, although they seem rather to be taken of bishops. For when the Fathers of the Nicene Synod, for the sake of peace, had decreed that bishops ordained by the schismatic Meletius should remain in their rank, but without exercising any episcopal function, they now prescribe that if a Catholic bishop ordained by the bishop of Alexandria should die, then the Meletian received by the synod under the condition I have mentioned should succeed to the place of the deceased, provided the people elected him and the bishop of Alexandria confirmed his election.

Yet from other passages of the same letter it is sufficiently evident that the people’s vote was necessary in the ordination of clerics. In the same letter the most holy Fathers forbid the bishops who had adhered to Meletius to possess the right or authority to put forward the names of those to be promoted to ecclesiastical orders; they declare that this competence belongs only to bishops of the Catholic Church who had always remained untainted by every schism. For the pontiffs announced to the people the names of those who were to be ordained presbyters or deacons, so that anyone who happened to have an objection against the candidates might testify to it publicly, as is read in the Sacramentary of Gregory the Great.

A remarkable passage on this subject occurs in blessed Chrysostom’s Homily 18 on the Second Epistle to the Corinthians: “Hear,” he says, “how, in the time of the Apostles, they repeatedly made those whom they governed partners in their deliberations. For when they appointed the seven deacons, they first referred the matter to the people; and when they chose Matthias, Peter discussed the matter with everyone then present, both men and women. For this authority does not consist in the pride and arrogance of those who preside, nor in any servile abasement of those subject to them, but is spiritual. Its principal excellence consists in undertaking greater labors for the care of your salvation, not in demanding greater honor. For all ought to dwell in the Church as in one house and to be disposed as one body.”

Indeed, the people’s vote was so necessary in the election of presbyters that the people in church frequently demanded and compelled that someone be made a presbyter with tumultuous cries. Paulinus testifies in his sixth Epistle to Severus that this happened to him at Barcelona. Augustine reports the same concerning Pinianus, the son of Albina, in Epistle 225 to Albina.

That the consent of the clergy was also necessary is taught by the ancient author of the *Questions on the Old and New Testaments*, chapter 101. He writes there that a presbyter who is to be ordained is led in by a deacon, presented to the bishop, and ordained upon the deacon’s testimony. “It is through the deacon’s testimony,” he says, “that he becomes a presbyter.” And shortly afterward: “For those who are to be ordained are led in so that, while surrounded on either side by them, they may appear worthy of the honor. I admit that this is their act, but only in the capacity of an official. For the deacon is sent by the bishop to render service to the one being ordained.” We have this whole rite very well described in the Sacramentary of Gregory the Great, p. 236; on that passage see the annotations of the very learned Hugo Menardus. VALESIUS.

*Ἐπὶ κλίνης* (“upon a bed”). The Stephanus edition has ἐν κλίνῃ, “in a bed.” STROTH. Immediately afterward the Norfolk manuscript has ἐπιχυθέντα (“one upon whom water had been poured”). ROUTH.

*Εἰς κλῆρόν τινα γενέσθαι* (“to enter any clerical rank”). Κλῆρος signifies an order or rank of ecclesiastical ministry. Thus a little earlier Cornelius said κλῆρον πρεσβυτερίου, “the rank of the presbyterate,” and Eusebius and Irenaeus more than once use κλῆρον ἐπισκοπῆς, “the rank of the episcopate.” Therefore εἰς κλῆρόν τινα here means “into any clerical rank.” Epiphanius, in the heresy of the Meletians, says: Οἱ δὲ ἀπὸ κληρικῶν ὑπάρχοντες διαφόρου κλήρου, πρεσβυτερίου τε καὶ διακονίας καὶ ἄλλων, “Those who belong to the clergy are of different ranks: the presbyterate, the diaconate, and others.”

Tertullian calls it a *sors* (“allotted rank”). Thus in *On the Veiling of Virgins*: “A woman is not permitted to speak in church, nor to teach, baptize, offer, or claim for herself the allotted rank of any male function, much less of the priestly office.” The ancient author of *On Not Rebaptizing Heretics* certainly speaks in the same way: “Since it is fitting that no believer of sound mind should maintain this, least of all anyone whatsoever appointed in any clerical rank, and much less any bishop should dare it.” Again in the same book: “Indeed, on this very account an additional burden is imposed upon him, even if he was previously most faithful or appointed in some clerical rank.”

The same writer distinguishes the clergy into greater and lesser. By “lesser clergy” he means deacons and the other lower orders, as when he says on p. 129: “Or if you say that a man of this kind cannot be saved, we deprive all bishops of salvation, since you bind them to dangers most certain, as though they were required personally to assist all people under their care who become ill in regions scattered here and there, because the other members of the lesser clergy cannot render the same service to those in danger.” And much more clearly on p. 134: “And therefore, since our salvation consists in the baptism of the Spirit, which is generally joined with the baptism of water, if baptism is administered by us, let it be assigned completely and solemnly and in accordance with everything written, and let it be administered without the omission of anything; or, if it has been administered by the lesser clergy under the pressure of necessity, let us await the outcome,” etc. Here you see presbyters clearly distinguished from members of the lesser clergy. For he says that members of the lesser clergy confer baptism only when necessity is imminent, which by no means applies to presbyters. Compare the passage of the writer cited by Coustant at the end of his note on the words ποιήσας γάρ. VALESIUS.
