Valesius departs somewhat from the Greek text by translating it thus: “Nor should anyone among those who, under the urgent force of illness, had had water poured over them in bed as he had, be admitted into the clergy.” For the words “anyone among those,” which exclude every exception, say more than the article τόν; likewise “into any clerical rank” conveys something more pointed than simply “into the clergy.”

Some time after Cornelius’s age, the Council of Neocaesarea moderated the severity of this discipline. It excluded a man upon whom water had been poured in bed not from every clerical rank, but only from the presbyterate; indeed, it permitted him to be advanced even to this rank “on account of his subsequent zeal and faith, and the shortage of men.” Fabian—or whoever ordained Novatian—had anticipated that an exception of this kind was permitted by ecclesiastical rule. Nor does one conjecture rashly who supposes that this bishop was particularly pleased by Novatian’s ability and eloquence, which are apparent in his writings and especially in the letter preserved as Cyprian’s Epistle 31, suspected to have been written by Novatian himself.

Those who opposed Novatian’s ordination when he was advanced to the order of the presbyterate, citing ecclesiastical rules that forbade the admission to any clerical rank of anyone upon whom water had been poured in bed, ought on the same reasoning to have opposed him earlier if any rank had already been conferred upon him. Valesius and Tillemont therefore infer that the dignity of the presbyterate was conferred upon him by a direct leap, the other, lower orders being passed over. COUSTANT.]

**6.** For this illustrious man abandoned the Church [Col. 0751B] of God, in which, after coming to faith, he was deemed worthy of the presbyterate [Col. 0753A] through the favor of the bishop who laid hands upon him for the rank of the presbyterate. Although that bishop was opposed by all the clergy and also by many laypeople—since it was not lawful for one upon whom water had been poured in bed because of illness, as it had been upon this man, to enter any clerical rank—he asked that he be permitted to ordain this man alone.

[Col. 0755A] He then adds to these another of the man’s worst offenses, speaking as follows:

[Note: [Col. 0755C]

**7.** *Ποιήσας γὰρ τὰς προσφορὰς καὶ ἐπιδιδοὺς τοῦτο* (“For after making the offerings and handing this over”). It was the proper office of the presbyter to place the Eucharist and the cup into the hands of the faithful, and this was properly called ἐπιδοῦναι, “to hand over.” Chrysostom, Homily 46 on Matthew, says: Οὐχ ὁρᾷς ὅτι τῷ ἱερεῖ μόνῳ θέμις τὸ τοῦ αἵματος ἐπιδιδόναι ποτήριον, that is, “Do you not see that it is lawful for the priest alone to present the cup of the Lord’s blood?” From this Chrysostom argues as follows: “You, therefore, are a priest when you present bread and the cup to a poor person.”

In certain churches, however, deacons distributed the Eucharist to the people. The author of the *Questions on the Old and New Testaments*, chapter 101, appears to indicate this in the following words: “It is therefore the deacon’s office to receive from the priest and then give to the people.” Jerome—or some other author—in the book *On the Seven Ranks of the Church* says: “As consecration belongs to the priest, so the administration of the sacrament belongs to the minister. The former sanctifies what has been offered; the latter distributes what has been sanctified.” Before all of these, Justin Martyr says the same in the *Apology*, in a passage I have already cited above. Cedrenus, under the eighteenth year of Constans, writes: [Col. 0755D] σκανδαλιζόμενος γὰρ εἰς αὐτόν, ἔκειρε πρότερον αὐτὸν διὰ Παύλου πατριάρχου διάκονον, ὃς καὶ μετέδωκε τῷ βασιλεῖ τῶν ἀχράντων μυστηρίων ἐν ἁγίῳ ποτηρίῳ, “For, being offended at him, he had previously had him tonsured as a deacon through the patriarch Paul; and he [the newly ordained deacon] also imparted the immaculate mysteries to the emperor in the holy cup.”

Finally, after deacons ceased to present the Eucharist to laypeople, they were permitted to provide wine to the laity after communion. We gather this from the *Life of Alcuin*, concerning whom an ancient writer relates: “Moreover, when after communion in the body and blood of Christ he gave them the mixed cup with his own hand, that same Louis, distinguished above all for humility, bowed before the holy father and kissed his hand.” The Second Council of Arles, canon 15, provides that a deacon must not presume to hand the body of Christ to the faithful when a presbyter is present. VALESIUS.

Valesius has “after making the oblation.” Adhering here to the Greek, we retain “after making the offerings,” that is, after the bread and wine had been consecrated. From this we plainly learn that Novatian personally presented Christ’s body to his followers rather than doing so through the ministry of deacons. Whether he handed the blood of our Savior to them in a different manner may be doubted because of the words appended below: “Swear to me by the body and blood of our Lord.”

It cannot, however, be denied that it was then accepted practice for the faithful to receive the blood, or even the body, of Christ through the ministry of deacons. For Justin writes in his second *Apology to Antoninus*: “After the presider has completed the thanksgiving and all the people have made their acclamation, the deacons distribute to each person present a portion of the consecrated bread, wine, and water.” At least in Africa the cup containing the blood of Christ was customarily presented by deacons, as Cyprian teaches in *On the Lapsed*: “But when the solemn rites had been completed, the deacon began to offer the cup to those present.”

That the same custom was practiced at Rome is indicated in Ambrose, *On Duties*, book I, chapter 4, by the devout remonstrance of St Lawrence the archdeacon, who addresses St Xystus the pontiff as follows: “To him to whom you entrusted the consecration of the Lord’s blood—that is, the distribution of the Lord’s consecrated blood—to him to whom you entrusted participation in the completion of the sacraments, do you deny participation in your own blood?” To the same ministry may conveniently be referred the general statement about the deacons of the Roman [Col. 0756C] Church by the ancient author of the *Questions on the Old and New Testaments*, in the Appendix to Augustine, vol. III, chapter 101: “It is therefore the deacon’s office to receive from the priest and then give to the people.”

But priests have nowhere been forbidden personally to perform what they customarily entrusted to deacons. . . . Indeed, if we listen to Chrysostom in Homily 46 on Matthew, “it is lawful for the priest alone to present the cup of the Lord’s blood.” Yet since that holy doctor does not add “to the people,” nothing prevents his statement from being explained by the words of the *Questions on the Old and New Testaments* quoted immediately above.

In short, priests were always permitted by virtue of their office to hand the body and blood of Christ to the people, while deacons were permitted to do so as ministers of the priests, by a certain concession and when necessity required. Or, to speak with the author of the *Apostolic Constitutions*, book VIII, chapter 28: “The deacon does not offer; but once the offering has been made by a bishop or presbyter, he gives it to the people, not as a priest but as one who ministers to priests.”

Hence the Fourth Council of Carthage, canon 37, first gives this admonition: “Let the deacon know himself to be the minister of the presbyter as well as of the bishop”; and then in canon 38 adds: “When a presbyter is present, let a deacon distribute the Eucharist of Christ’s body to the people only if necessity compels and he is ordered to do so.” Moreover, as the cited author of the *Questions on the Old and New Testaments* observes in the passage mentioned, “The greater order contains the lesser within itself. For a presbyter also performs the office of a deacon, exorcist, and reader.” COUSTANT.

*Διανέμων . . . ἐπιδιδούς* (“distributing . . . handing over”). Syncellus has διανείμας (“having distributed”); the Bodleian manuscript has ἐπιδούς (“having handed over”). After τὸ μέρος (“the portion”), the Norfolk manuscript adds τῆς αὐτῆς δυνάμεως (“of the same power”); perhaps the reading should be τῆς αὐτῆς διανομῆς (“of the same distribution”). Immediately afterward, instead of τοῦτο ὀμνύειν (“to swear this”), Syncellus has αὐτῷ ὀμνύειν (“to swear to him”). ROUTH.

*Ἀμφοτέραις ταῖς χερσί* (“with both hands”). The Stephanus edition omits ταῖς. STROTH.

*Ἀφείς* (“releasing” or “letting go”). The Stephanus edition has ἀφιείς. STROTH. Immediately afterward Syncellus has ἕως ἄν (“until”) instead of ἔστ’ ἄν. In Nicephorus and the Norfolk manuscript, the order of the words κατὰ τοῦ σώματος καὶ τοῦ αἵματος (“by the body and the blood”) is reversed. ROUTH.

*To him* (αὐτῷ). The translators did not understand this passage. [Col. 0757B] Musculus renders it: “And the wretched man did not taste it unless he had first devoted himself to him.” Christophorson, apparently following in Musculus’ footsteps, renders it thus: “And the unhappy man did not taste it before he had thus devoted himself to him”—as though the word αὐτῷ referred to Novatian. I would prefer to read ἑαυτῷ, “to himself,” with George Syncellus, in whom this entire passage is written as follows: Καὶ ὁ ἄθλιος ἄνθρωπος οὐ πρότερον γεύεται εἰ μὴ πρὸτερον ἑαυτῷ καταράσαιτο. That is: “And the wretched man is not permitted to taste before he has called down curses upon himself.” For every oath has an imprecation attached to it. Although this is not expressly stated in the sacramental rite by which Novatian constrained those wretched people, it is nevertheless tacitly understood, as I noted on Ammianus Marcellinus. Furthermore, our four codices—the Mazarin, Medicean, Fuketian, and Savilian—also read καταράσαιτο, just as Syncellus does (καταράσεται in Stephanus’ edition). **VALESIUS.**

Syncellus has ἑαυτῷ, which Valesius approves and which indeed pleases us better. Nicephorus [Col. 0757C] has ἐκείνῳ, “to that man,” though from this it is apparent that he read αὐτῷ. **STROTH.**

Strothius likewise noted that Gruter’s *Lectiones* has καταράσαιτο; to these add the Norfolk manuscript. Meanwhile, if you prefer αὑτῷ, it should be written with a rough breathing. Constantius believes that the daily desertion of Novatian by his followers appears to have driven him to demand this oath. This oath, meanwhile, impiously exacted and given, made the sorrowful schism permanent by excluding the authority of the Church. **ROUTH.**

*Instead of saying … “Amen”* (Ἀντὶ τοῦ εἰπεῖν . . . τὸ Ἀμήν). This is what Cornelius shortly before called “instead of giving the blessing” (ἀντὶ τοῦ εὐλογεῖν). For when the faithful received the Eucharist from the priest’s hand, after the presbyter had said, while handing it to them, “The body of the Lord,” they customarily answered “Amen,” as blessed Ambrose testifies in Book IV of *On the Sacraments*, chapter 5:

> “Therefore it is not without purpose that, when you receive it, you say ‘Amen,’ already confessing in spirit that you receive the body of Christ. The priest says to you, [Col. 0757D] ‘The body of Christ.’ And you say, ‘Amen,’ that is, ‘It is true.’”

Jerome, to Pammachius, against the errors of John of Jerusalem:

> “With what conscience shall I approach the Eucharist of Christ and answer ‘Amen,’ when I doubt the charity of the one who offers it?”

Cyril of Jerusalem, in his final catechesis:

> Καὶ κοιλάνας τὴν παλάμην, δέχου τὸ σῶμα τοῦ Χριστοῦ, ἐπιλέγων τὸ, Ἀμήν.
>
> “And, making your palm hollow, receive the body of Christ, adding the word ‘Amen.’”

Augustine, Book XII *Against Faustus*, chapter 10:

> “For the blood of Christ has a mighty voice on earth when, after it has been received, everyone answers ‘Amen.’”

The faithful also said “Amen” more frequently during the solemnities of the Mass. For when the priest consecrated the bread and wine, they answered “Amen,” as will be discussed more fully below at chapter 9 of Book VII; and after the reading of the Gospel and the Prophets they customarily said “Amen” and signed themselves, as Augustine testifies in Letter 166. **VALESIUS.**—Immediately afterward, Syncellus and Nicephorus found ἐπανήξω, “I shall return,” in place of ἀνήξω; and the Norfolk manuscript has ἔφη, “he said,” in place of λέγει, “he says.” **ROUTH.**]

### 7

For after making the offerings and distributing to each person his portion, as he hands it over he compels the wretched people to swear instead of giving the blessing. He grasps the hands of the recipient in both his own and does not release them until they have sworn and said the following—for I shall use that man’s own words:

> “Swear to me by the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ that you will never abandon me or return to Cornelius.”

And the wretched man does not taste until he has first called down a curse upon him—or, according to Syncellus, [Col. 0757A] upon himself. And instead of saying “Amen” when receiving that bread, he says:

> “I shall never again return to Cornelius.”

And after other matters he again says the following.

[Note: [Col. 0757D]

### 8. *Whom the blessed Moses also …* (Ὃν καὶ Μωσῆς ὁ μακάριος)

Cyprian speaks frequently in his letters about this Moses, [Col. 0758B] a presbyter of the city of Rome. After the martyrdom of Fabian, bishop of Rome, in the second consulship of Decius, with Gratus as his colleague, in the year of Christ 250, Moses was arrested together with the presbyter Maximus and the deacon Nicostratus. He was cast into prison and died there after remaining imprisoned for eleven months and eleven days, as is stated in the ancient *Book of the Roman Pontiffs*. Cyprian also confirms this in Letter XV, to the presbyters Moses and Maximus and the other confessors, where among other things he says:

> “Let the magistrates now depart, and let consuls or proconsuls glory in the insignia of their annual dignity and in their twelve fasces. Behold, heavenly dignity has been marked in you by the splendor of a year-long honor, and by the duration of its victorious glory it has already passed beyond the revolving circle of the turning year.”

**VALESIUS.**

In Cyprian’s Letters XVI and XXV to this Moses and his fellow confessors, as well as in Letter XXVI from those same confessors to Cyprian, the name of Moses is consistently placed first, ahead of all the others. Valesius believes that he died in prison, [Col. 0758C] basing his view on these words of the Bucherian catalogue under Fabian:

> “After his [Fabian’s] death, the presbyters Moses and Maximus and the deacon Nicostratus were arrested and sent to prison. At that time Novatus arrived from Africa and separated Novatian and certain confessors, after Moses had died in prison, where he had been for eleven months and eleven days.”

Yet it is clear even from this that the catalogue is not accurate there, since it narrates Novatian’s schism as though it occurred after Moses’ death, whereas Cornelius plainly testifies here that it preceded it. If, however, we consult Cyprian, he, in imitation of Cornelius, varies the titles with which he adorns Moses according to the different times. For in Letter X below, no. 5, looking back to the time when Moses subscribed to Novatian’s celebrated letter concerning the lapsed, he calls him a confessor who was then still living; but with reference to the time when Cyprian himself was writing to Antonianus, he calls him “now already a martyr.” Yet even from this no certain argument against Valesius’ opinion can be established, since Cyprian considers even those who, [Col. 0758D] though not tortured, nevertheless end their lives in prison to be martyrs.

Although, therefore, I incline to believe that one who is commended for an outstanding and admirable martyrdom showed himself admirable in steadfastly enduring different kinds of torture, nevertheless his martyrdom could have been called outstanding and admirable because of the long duration of his extremely harsh imprisonment, by which he could not be deterred from confessing Christ even unto death. Although Moses was only a presbyter, he excluded Novatian from communion, not by the power and authority of a judge, but by that caution which every believer may exercise toward those whose perverted faith and pestilential life are plainly detected. **COUSTANT.**

The name is written in the more usual form Μωυσῆς in the Norfolk manuscript. **ROUTH.**

*He excluded him from communion* (Ἀκοινώνητον ἐποίησε). Musculus translates this “he excommunicated him.” Christophorson renders it “he barred him from the fellowship and communion of the faithful,” which amounts to the same thing. I, however, cannot approve this interpretation. For the presbyter Moses had no right to excommunicate his fellow presbyters; [Col. 0759A] the one thing he could do was separate himself from communion with them—namely, when they came to visit him in prison. Moreover, ancient writers customarily speak of priests who abstain from communion with others [Col. 0759B] as though they themselves were excluding those persons from their communion.

The presbyter Paulinus, in the *Life of Blessed Ambrose*, says:

> “But Maximus himself he separated from the fellowship of communion, admonishing him to do penance for the blood of his Lord that had been shed.”

This passage of Paulinus must be understood as I have said. For Ambrose did not sever the emperor Maximus from the communion of the entire Church, since he had no jurisdiction over him; rather, he merely abstained from communion with Maximus and his bishops, as he himself testifies in his report to Valentinian. See what I noted above concerning private communion and excommunication.

Moreover, what Cornelius writes here about Novatian’s having been condemned by Moses’ prior judgment seems to me to have been done by Moses shortly before his death. For at first Moses the confessor was in communion with Novatian. And when the Roman clergy wrote to Cyprian the letter numbered both first and thirty-first among Cyprian’s letters, Moses was still maintaining peace with Novatian. [Col. 0759C] Both of them subscribed to that letter. Indeed, Novatian himself had composed it, as Cyprian testifies in his letter to Antonianus. From it Novatian’s talent and eloquence may incidentally be recognized, for that letter is, as must be admitted, most elegant. It was written when Moses had already spent a year in prison, as is clearly gathered from Cyprian’s letters previously sent to Moses. **VALESIUS.**

*Together with the five presbyters* (Σὺν τοῖς πέντε πρεσβυτέροις). Who those five presbyters were who made the schism with Novatian is unknown to me. For I do not think that one of them was the presbyter and confessor Maximus, who, together with Urbanus, Sidonius, Nicostratus, and the other confessors, was deceived by Novatian and supported his party for a time. For Maximus and the other confessors joined Novatian’s party only after Moses had died, as the ancient author of the *Book of the Roman Pontiffs* testifies:

> “At that time,” he says, “Novatus arrived from Africa and separated Novatian and certain confessors from the Church, [Col. 0759D] after Moses had died in prison.”

Novatian had indeed separated himself from the Church before Moses’ death, which occurred in February during the consulship of Decius for the third time and Etruscus; but the confessors went over to Novatian’s party only after Moses’ death. Such was Moses’ influence and authority. Cyprian certainly implies this in Letter 51, in these words:

> “After you came out of prison, schismatic and heretical error received you, and so it was as though your glory had remained in prison.”

Yet it is established that the confessors were released from prison only after Moses’ death. For why should they have been released rather than Moses? They therefore followed Novatian after Moses’ death.

Consequently, I do not agree with Baronius, who, under the year of Christ 254, no. 66, says that the confessors favored Novatian against Cornelius while they were still in prison. Nor would I readily grant Baronius what he writes in the same place, namely that the presbyter Moses favored Cornelius against Novatian. For Moses appears to me to have died shortly before Cornelius’ ordination. [Col. 0760A] Cornelius became bishop in April of the year of Christ 251, in the consulship of Decius Augustus for the third time and Decius Caesar, according to Baronius’ opinion; but Moses had died in February of the same year, after remaining in prison for the space of a year, [Col. 0760B] as I observed above.

Furthermore, one of those five presbyters who had separated themselves from the Church together with Novatian appears to have been the presbyter Maximus, who had the same name as Maximus the confessor and whom Novatian afterward sent to Africa as his legate. **VALESIUS.**

Valesius admits that he does not know who those five Roman presbyters were who separated themselves from the Church together with Novatian. He nevertheless thinks that one of them was the presbyter Maximus, who had the same name as Maximus the confessor, whom Novatian afterward sent to Africa as his legate, and who was ordained bishop at Carthage. Tillemont, *Histoire ecclésiastique*, vol. III, p. 442, thinks that Hippolytus may be added to him. According to Prudentius, Hippolytus was at first devoted to Novatian, but later repudiated his schism and wiped away that stain by a celebrated martyrdom.

Care must be taken here not to confuse the five presbyters whom the martyr Moses separated from his communion with the five presbyters of Novatus’ faction, about whom Cyprian [Col. 0760C] says much both below, in Letter 12 to Cornelius, and in Letter 40 to his own people. The latter were Africans, the former Romans; the latter were devoted to Felicissimus, the former to Novatian; the latter granted peace to the lapsed without requiring any penance, while the former denied it even to the penitent. **COUSTANT.**

I could scarcely understand how Valesius could say that the presbyter Moses had not favored Cornelius against Novatian when, as Constantius noted above, Cornelius testifies in this passage that Novatian’s schism preceded Moses’ death—unless Valesius, like Pearson in the *Annales Cyprianici* under the year 251, §1, held that Novatian’s schism over the reception of the lapsed occurred before Cornelius became bishop. Tillemont opposes this opinion in Note III on Cornelius, *Mémoires*, vol. III, p. 347, Brussels edition. Yet the controversy, at least concerning the reception of those same persons, appears to have arisen before Cornelius was made bishop; see above, p. 28. Moreover, the word πέντε, “five,” is absent from the Norfolk codex. **ROUTH.**]

### 8

Know, moreover, that he has already been stripped bare and left deserted, as the brethren abandon him every day and return to the Church. Moses also—the blessed martyr who recently among us underwent a noble and admirable martyrdom—while he was still in the world, perceived that man’s audacity and madness and excluded him from his own communion, together with the five presbyters [Col. 0759A] who had separated themselves from the Church along with him.

[Note: [Col. 0760C]

### 9. *At Rome* (Ἐπὶ Ῥώμης)

The Norfolk manuscript has Ἐπὶ τῆς Ῥώμης, “in the city of Rome,” as shortly below, and [Col. 0760D] τὸν κατάλογον, “the catalogue.” **ROUTH.**

*He mentions* (Μνημονεύει). Some, comparing these words of Eusebius with those by which Jerome, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 66, relates that Cornelius wrote to Fabius concerning the Roman, Italian, and African synods, believe that the holy doctor was referring there to this letter of Cornelius. But he appears rather to mention other letters of the same pope to the same Fabius, in which, according to Eusebius, p. 242, “both the proceedings of the Roman synod and the judgments of all those throughout Italy, Africa, and the other provinces of those regions are set forth.”

Why Cornelius, in writing to Fabius, so accurately recorded both the names and churches of the bishops who had attended the Roman council and those who had approved the decrees of that synod by letter may be gathered from Cyprian’s following Letter XII, no. 8. There, after that same prelate had said to Cornelius that he had recently sent “the names of the bishops who, sound and unimpaired, preside over the brethren in the Catholic Church,” he immediately adds:

> “This certainly was resolved by the counsel of all our people, [Col. 0761A] so that a short way might be provided for dispelling error and discerning the truth, and so that both you and our colleagues might know to whom you ought to write and from whom you ought in turn to receive letters.”

He warns that the others whom he omitted from his letter had either been stained by sacrifice or by a certificate, or had been corrupted by heresy. Cornelius therefore did the same thing, so that it would not be unknown which bishops were worthy of communion and which were unworthy. Tillemont conjectures that from that time onward, and for the same reason, the Roman pontiffs took care that, if any bishops had recently been admitted to the episcopal college, [Col. 0761B] the other prelates throughout the world should be informed of the matter. We shall certainly read that Cyprian requested Pope Stephen to inform him as soon as possible whom he would appoint in the place of Marcian, bishop of Arles. **COUSTANT.**

As regards this replacement of Marcian, Cyprian admonished Stephen to send letters against Marcian the Novatianist—communion with whom the Africans had already previously refused—to the people of Arles,

> “by which, Marcian having been excluded, another might be appointed in his place”;

that is, as Fell explains it,

> “and there he should exhort the people of Arles to proceed to the election of a bishop.”

Letter LXVIII, otherwise LXVII. Or, what amounts to the same thing, as Richer formerly taught in the appendix to volume I of his *History of the General Councils*:

> “Marcian having been removed from office, they should by unanimous consent appoint another in his place,”

p. 802.

Something granting greater force to the authority of the letters might, however, be suggested to us not only by the form of the words, but also by the example just related of Cornelius’ replacement of certain bishops. This much, at least, is apparent: some care for the people of Arles belonged to the office of the Roman [Col. 0761C] bishop.

As for that Italian synod which Jerome inferred for himself from Eusebius’ words cited above, Basnage, under the year 252, section VI, p. 366 of his *Annals*, does indeed defend it against Pearson, who doubted it; whether successfully, others may judge. And after I had written these things, I found some learned men who still agreed with Pearson.

Finally, for the sake both of the truth and of St. Cornelius, I shall append here the words of Cyprian, who together with the other [Col. 0762A] African bishops had once decreed that all matters should be left undecided until his legates, as well as other bishops, returned from Rome once peace had been restored or the truth ascertained. For he afterward writes the following to Cornelius:

> “We rejoice that this happened by divine providence and that our plan proceeded prudently. For thus the truth and the dignity of your episcopate have now alike been established in the clearest light and by the most manifest and secure confirmation, so that from the replies of our colleagues who sent us letters from there, and from the report and testimony [Col. 0762B] of our fellow bishops Pompeius, Stephen, Caldonius, and Fortunatus, the necessary origin and just grounds of your ordination, as well as your glorious innocence, might be known to all.”

Letter XLV, or XLVIII. See also the letter to Antonianus, p. 68.

Furthermore, what the great Dionysius of Alexandria thought about Novatian and his cause is shown by a fragment of his letter to the bishop of Rome who bore the same name, in Eusebius, Book VII, chapter 8:

> Νοουατιανῷ μὲν γὰρ εὐλόγως ἀπεχθανόμεθα, διακόψαντι τὴν Ἐκκλησίαν καὶ τινας τῶν ἀδελφῶν εἰς ἀσεβείας καὶ βλασφημίας ἑλκύσαντι, καὶ περὶ τοῦ Θεοῦ διδασκαλίαν ἀνοσιωτάτην ἐπεισκυκλήσαντι· καὶ τὸν χρηστότατον Κύριον ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦν Χριστὸν ὡς ἀνελεῆ συκοφαντοῦντι.
>
> “For we rightly abhor Novatian, because he rent the Church, dragged some of the brethren into impieties and blasphemies, introduced a most profane teaching about God, and slandered our most gracious Lord Jesus Christ as though he were without mercy.”

The same holy man also addressed Novatian himself as follows:

> Διονύσιος Νοουατῶ (Ναυατιανῷ aliter legitur) τῷ ἀδελφῷ χαίρειν. Εἰ ἄκων, ὡς φής, ἤχθης, δείξεις, ἐὰν ἀναχωρήσῃς ἑκών· ἔδει μὲν γὰρ καὶ πᾶν ὁτιοῦν παθεῖν, ὑπὲρ τοῦ μὴ διακόψαι τὴν Ἐκκλησίαν τοῦ Θεοῦ . . . καὶ νῦν δὲ εἰ πείσαιο ἢ βιάσαιο τοὺς ἀδελφοὺς εἰς ὁμόνοιαν ἐλθεῖν, μεῖζον ἔσται σοι τοῦ σφάλματος τὸ κατόρθωμα.
>
> “Dionysius to Novatus [otherwise read ‘Novatian’], his brother: greetings. If, as you say, you were led into this unwillingly, you will prove it by withdrawing willingly. For you ought to have suffered absolutely anything rather than rend the Church of God. . . . And even now, if you could persuade or compel the brethren to come into concord, your achievement would be greater than your fault.”

Eusebius VI.45.

Concerning Novatian’s [Col. 0762C] accusations against Cornelius, Pearson writes the following in the passage mentioned above, but at §VII:

> “Meanwhile Novatian openly argued against the ordination of Cornelius, publicly denounced it as illegitimate, and attempted to annul it. To accomplish this, he brought many abominable charges against Cornelius himself and published a book full of bitter accusations, teaching above all that no one should communicate with him, because he held communion with the lapsed.”

**ROUTH.**]

### 9

At the end of the letter he also drew up a catalogue of the bishops who had assembled at Rome and condemned the folly of Novatus, recording both their names and the community over which each of them presided. He also mentions the names and the cities from which each wrote of those who had not assembled at Rome but had signified by letter their agreement with the judgment of the aforementioned bishops. Cornelius wrote these things to Fabius, [Col. 0761A] bishop of Antioch, to inform him. Eusebius cited these words of Cornelius in Book VI of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 43.

[Col. 0734B] [Note: [Col. 0734B]

### I

> “For Novatus, a presbyter of the Roman Church, being puffed up with arrogance against them, as though no hope of salvation remained for them thereafter even if they fulfilled everything pertaining to sincere conversion and a pure confession, became the founder of a peculiar sect of those who, [Col. 0734C] puffed up with mental pride, called themselves Cathari, ‘the Pure.’
>
> “For this reason a synod assembled at Rome, at which sixty bishops and a much larger number of presbyters and deacons gathered; and after the prelates in the provinces had separately deliberated about what ought to be done, a decree of the following kind was promulgated to all: Novatus and those who had insolently exalted themselves together with him, and all who had presumed to assent to his most inhuman opinion, alien to brotherly charity, were to be regarded as aliens from the Church; but the brethren who had fallen into calamity were to be treated and sustained with the remedies of penance.
>
> “Letters of Cornelius, bishop of the Romans, sent to Fabius, prelate of the Church of Antioch, are still extant. In them both the proceedings of the Roman synod and the judgments of all those throughout Italy, Africa, and the other provinces of those regions are set forth. Other letters are also extant, written in Latin by Cyprian and the other prelates who assembled with him in Africa. [Col. 0734D] From these it is gathered that they too resolved that assistance should be given to those who had fallen into temptation, and that the author of the impious opinion, together with those who had defected to his party, should deservedly be expelled from the fellowship of the Catholic Church.
>
> “To these was attached another letter of the same Cornelius concerning the decrees made at the synod, and again another concerning the crimes of Novatus. There is nothing to prevent us from inserting something from it here, so that the readers of our history may clearly understand matters pertaining to Novatus. Cornelius, therefore, informing Fabius what kind of disposition and character Novatus possessed, writes thus: ‘And so that you may know,’ etc.”

This letter concerning Novatian’s actions, together at least with the one named first, was sent to Fabius [Col. 0735B] of Antioch—who, as Eusebius relates in chapter 44, at one time favored Novatian’s schism—in order to move him and change his mind. Since all the letters treated the same subject, they reached Eusebius’ hands joined together.

Peter Constantius, who published the following fragments in *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, pp. 146 ff., says:

> “Jerome, in his book *On Illustrious Men*, enumerates four letters of Cornelius to Fabius and testifies that this one was very lengthy. It was written after the error of the Novatianists had been condemned in the councils of Italy and Africa, and after the confessors Maximus and his companions had returned to the Church, when Novatian had already been stripped bare and left almost alone, as the brethren deserted him daily and returned to the Church—see the end of these excerpts—and thus some time after the preceding letters.”

So much for Constantius.

Valesius, however, correctly determined that Eusebius mentions only three letters of Cornelius. Unless I am mistaken, he was led by the same arguments [Col. 0735C] as Cotelerius in his note on Polycarp’s Letter, §3, where that learned man, after adducing several examples, shows that Eusebius’ words ἐπιστολαὶ Κορνηλίου, “letters of Cornelius,” should be understood of a single letter, as Jerome himself perceived and translated them: “Cornelius wrote a letter to Fabius.” Jerome nevertheless erred in attributing another letter to Cornelius. Fabricius reached the same conclusion as Valesius in his notes on another chapter of Jerome, namely chapter LXXII. But Tillemont took a different view in *Mémoires ecclésiastiques*, Note XII on Cornelius; and Valesius himself had translated the words into Latin as “Letters of Cornelius.”

A similar conclusion nevertheless appears necessary concerning the letter of Cyprian and the Africans. Rufinus calls this single letter “a book written most magnificently,” and Jerome carelessly attributed it to Cornelius. See the note on Jerome above.

Although Valesius demonstrates that the first and third letters of Cornelius appear to have been written in Greek, I do not understand why he thinks that the second letter, concerning the synod’s decrees, was written in Latin, since [Col. 0735D] all of them appear to have been written to Fabius, a Greek-speaking man, and those synodical decrees were commemorated both in the first letter and in this second one—unless for that reason one were to suppose that this second letter was sent to someone other than Fabius.

I thought that something more should be noted concerning Fabius’ favor toward Novatian’s party. Eusebius says in Book VI of his *History*, chapter 46:

> Κορνηλίῳ τῷ κατὰ Ῥώμην γράφει, δεξάμενος αὐτοῦ τὴν κατὰ τοῦ Νοουάτου ἐπιστολήν· ᾧ καὶ σημαίνει δηλῶν ἑαυτὸν παρακεκλῆσθαι ὑπό τε Ἐλένου τοῦ ἐν Τάρσῳ τῆς Κιλικίας ἐπισκόπου, καὶ τῶν λοιπῶν τῶν σὺν αὐτῷ· Φιρμιλιάνου τε τοῦ ἐν Καππαδοκίᾳ, καὶ τοῦ κατὰ Παλαιστίνην Θεοκτίστου, ὡς ἂν ἐπὶ τὴν σύνοδον ἀπαντήσει τὴν κατὰ Ἀντιόχειαν, ἔνθα τοῦ Νοουάτου κρατύνειν τινες ἐπεχείρουν τὸ σχίσμα· πρὸς τούτοις ἐπιστέλλει μηνυθῆναι αὐτῷ Φάβιον μὲν κεκοιμῆσθαι· Δημητριανὸν δὲ διάδοχον ἐκείνου τῆς κατὰ Ἀντιόχειαν ἐπισκοπῆς καθεστάναι.
>
> “He writes to Cornelius at Rome after receiving from him his letter against Novatus. He also informs him that he himself had been invited by Helenus, bishop of Tarsus in Cilicia, and by the others with him, as well as by Firmilian of Cappadocia and Theoctistus of Palestine, to attend the synod at Antioch, where certain persons were attempting to strengthen the schism of Novatus. In addition to these things, he writes that it had been reported to him that Fabius had fallen asleep and that Demetrian had been appointed his successor in the episcopate of Antioch.”

Commenting on the words ἔνθα [Col. 0736B] τοῦ Νοουάτου κρατύνειν τινες ἐπεχείρουν τὸ σχίσμα, “where certain persons were attempting to strengthen the schism of Novatus,” George Syncellus, on p. 365 of his *Chronography*, associated Fabius, bishop of Antioch, himself with those supporters of Novatian. Eusebius, however, at the beginning of chapter 44 of the same book, had spoken of Fabius as ὑποκατακλινομένῳ πῶς τῷ σχίσματι, “somehow inclining toward the schism”; yet these very words indicate only a very slight inclination toward Novatian, not an eager zeal to establish the schism.

Dionysius certainly informed Cornelius of these movements of the Novatianists only after Fabius had died, and it is not established that the council of Antioch was summoned while Fabius was alive. Valesius, though this is even less probable, asserts in his note on Book VII, chapter 5, of Eusebius’ *History* that Fabius attempted to establish the Novatianist position by convening a council. For this very council, to which Dionysius was invited by the bishops, appears more probably to have been summoned against those who favored Novatian.

Moreover, after the words ἵνα δὲ γνῷς, “and so that you may know,” punctuation would be required if one maintained that ὅτι, “that,” and the words following depended upon εἰπεῖν βούλομαι, “I wish to relate.” [Col. 0736C] **ROUTH.**

*That admirable man* (Θαυμάσιος οὗτος). That is, Novatian, whom Cornelius is quite accustomed to designate by a vague pronoun. **COUSTANT.**

*The presbyter Maximus* (Μαξίμος πρεσβύτερος). Concerning this presbyter Maximus and the confessors Urbanus and Sidonius, and how they abandoned Novatian and returned to the Catholic Church, see the letter of Pope Cornelius to Cyprian, which is placed above.

At the same time there was also another Maximus, a presbyter of the Roman Church, whom Novatian sent as his legate to Cyprian in Africa together with Machaeus and others; but Cyprian excluded them from his communion. The schismatics afterward made this Maximus a bishop in Africa, as Cyprian teaches in his letter to Cornelius. **VALESIUS.**

On these confessors see Cyprian’s Letters 27 and 54 in the Oxford edition, Pamelius 23 and 51, and Cornelius to Cyprian, Letter 49 in the Oxford edition, Pamelius 46. **READING.**

*Celerinus* (Κελερῖνος). Since Cyprian, whenever he mentions these same confessors, [Col. 0736D] everywhere names Macarius in place of this Celerinus, Tillemont thinks that the same confessor bore two names, namely Macarius and Celerinus. At the same time he warns that this man is distinct from Celerinus, the reader of the Church of Carthage, who is frequently commended by Cyprian. **COUSTANT.**

*Having endured* (Διενέγκας). The edition of Robert Stephanus has Διανύσας, “having completed”; but the Medicean codex reads Διενέγκας, and George Syncellus has Διενεγκών. The Mazarin codex, as well as the Fuketian and Savilian, supports the Medicean. **VALESIUS.** Strothius added the reading of Christophorson; I add that of the Norfolk codex. [The wording of this bibliographic notice is uncertain.] 

*And falsehoods* (Καὶ ψευδολογίας). The Savilian, or Bodleian, manuscript and George Syncellus, who included this passage in his *Chronography*, have Καὶ τὰς ψευδολογίας, “and the falsehoods.” **ROUTH.**

*Aversion to communion* (Τὴν ἀκοινωνησίαν). Cornelius appears to speak thus because of Novatian’s peculiar opinion, which Eusebius, Book VI, chapter 43, calls μισάδελφον καὶ ἀνανθρωποτάτην, “abhorrent to brotherly [Col. 0737C] charity and most inhuman,” because this heretic deprived the lapsed of every hope of communion and peace.

The same heresy is called the “Cainite heresy” both in Cyprian’s treatise *To Novatian* and by Jerome at the beginning of his letter to Oceanus, though for somewhat different reasons. The author of the aforementioned treatise so calls it because “it strives only to kill”; Jerome does so because, like Cain despairing and saying, “My iniquity is greater than that I should deserve pardon,” it utterly denies the hope of forgiveness for certain sins, and therefore “says that there are some sins which Christ cannot cleanse by his blood.” **COUSTANT.**

*This in the presence of bishops*, etc. (Τοῦτο μὲν ἐπισκόπων etc.). Five are said in Letter VI, no. 2—the preceding letter—to have been present. It is strange that only presbyters are mentioned here and that deacons and other clerics are passed over in silence, especially since laypeople were also present. Letter VI, no. 2, does indeed say that the presbyterate assembled on this occasion. But that word customarily designated the body of the clergy by its principal part. [Col. 0737D] Perhaps for the same reason here too the entire clergy is signified by the name “presbyters.” **COUSTANT.**]

### I

So that you may know how that admirable man, inflamed with desire for the episcopal dignity, [Col. 0736A] concealed within himself and kept hidden his reckless and unbridled ambition, while presenting as a veil for his madness the fact that he had had the confessors with him from the beginning, I wish to relate the matter.

Maximus, a presbyter of our church, and Urbanus, both of whom gained outstanding glory from a repeated confession, as well as Sidonius and Celerinus—a man who, through God’s mercy, most courageously endured every kind of torture and, strengthening the weakness of his flesh by the courage of his faith, utterly defeated the adversary—these men, then, came to know him. They discerned his fraud and cunning, his perjuries and falsehoods, his disposition averse to fellowship and communion, and [Col. 0738A] his wolflike conduct, and returned to the holy Church.

In the presence of several bishops, presbyters, and a great many laypeople, they disclosed all his deceptions and crimes, which he had long concealed and suppressed within himself. They groaned and grieved because, having been misled by that fraudulent and malicious beast, they had defected from the Church for a short time.

### II

Then, after a few words, he says:

It is scarcely credible, dearest brother, what great instability and change we saw take place in him within a brief space of time. For that admirable man, who had pledged his word with certain fearsome oaths that he had no desire whatsoever for the episcopate, suddenly appears as a bishop, thrust into the midst as though by some stage device. [Col. 0738B]

That founder of doctrines and champion of ecclesiastical discipline, when he attempted unlawfully to seize and steal for himself an episcopate by no means granted to him by God, chose two companions whose salvation was despaired of and appointed them to go to a small and utterly insignificant part of Italy. From there he summoned three bishops, thoroughly ignorant and simple men, and deceived them by a fraudulent scheme. He affirmed and steadfastly asserted that they must travel to Rome as quickly as possible, so that every dispute, from whatever source it had arisen, might be settled through their intervention together with that of [Col. 0740A] the other bishops.

When they arrived—men, as we have already said, of rather simple disposition and insufficiently experienced in the arts and deceptions of the depraved—he had them shut in by certain persons like himself whom he had prepared for this purpose. At the tenth hour, when they were drunk and stupefied by overindulgence, he forcibly compelled them, through a fictitious and empty imposition of hands, to confer the episcopate upon him. He claimed it by treachery and fraud, although it belonged to him by no right.

Not long afterward, [Col. 0742A] one of those bishops returned to the Church, confessing his sin with lamentation and tears. When the entire people who were present had interceded for him, we received him into lay communion. We also ordained successors to the other two bishops and sent them to their places.

### III

Did that defender of the Gospel, then, not know that there ought to be one bishop in the Catholic Church? He was not unaware—for how could he have been?—[Col. 0744A] that in it there were forty-six presbyters, seven deacons, seven subdeacons, forty-two acolytes, and fifty-two exorcists, readers, and doorkeepers, together with more than fifteen hundred widows and afflicted persons (*thlibomenoi*). [Col. 0746A] The Lord’s grace and kindness supply sustenance to them all.

Yet so great and necessary a multitude in the Church, so immense a number enriched and abounding in the resources of divine providence, together with an immeasurable and innumerable people, neither deterred him from such despair and audacity nor recalled him to the Church.

### 4

Again, after other matters have been interposed, he adds the following:

Come, then; let us next explain by what deeds and manner of life he dared to aspire to the episcopate. Was it because from the beginning he had lived his life in the Church, had undergone many struggles on its behalf, and had faced many great dangers for religion’s sake?

Certainly not. For the occasion of his receiving the faith was Satan’s entry into him and prolonged residence within him. [Col. 0746B] When assistance was given to him by the exorcists, he fell into an extremely severe illness, so that he was thought to be on the very point of death. On the very bed where he lay, [Col. 0748A] he received the faith by affusion—if indeed a man of this kind should be said to have received it.

But even after he had been delivered from his illness, he did not receive the remaining rites that must be received according to the rule of the Church, nor was he sealed by the bishop. [Col. 0750A] Since he did not receive this seal, how could he have received the Holy Spirit?

[Col. 0752A]

### 5

Again, somewhat later, he says:

During the persecution, out of fear and excessive love of life, he denied that he was a presbyter. For the deacons admonished and entreated him to leave the chamber in which he had shut himself and assist the brethren to the extent that it was permissible and right for a presbyter to aid brethren who were in danger and in need of assistance. Yet he was so far from complying with the deacons’ request that, on the contrary, he went away and departed in indignation. For he answered that he no longer wished to be a presbyter, but was possessed by love and enthusiasm for another philosophy.

### 6

After briefly passing over a few matters, he again adds the following, [Col. 0752B] saying:

For that illustrious man abandoned the Church of God, [Col. 0754A] in which, after receiving the faith, he was honored with the presbyterate through the grace and indulgence of the bishop, who laid his hand upon him and advanced him to the order of presbyter.

The entire clergy and many of the laity objected, because it was not permissible for a person who, like him, had received baptism by affusion on his sickbed under the pressure of illness to be admitted to any clerical order. The bishop, however, requested that he be permitted to ordain this one man.

[Col. 0756A]

### 7

He then adds another crime, by far the gravest of all those committed by him, speaking as follows:

After making the offerings and distributing a portion to each person, while handing it over he compels the wretched people to swear instead of giving the blessing. He holds the hands of the person who has received the portion clasped within both of his own hands and does not release them until they have sworn and said the following—for I shall use that man’s own words:

> “Swear to me by the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ that you will never [Col. 0758A] abandon my party or return to Cornelius.”

And the wretched man does not taste until he has called down evil upon himself. When receiving that bread, instead of saying “Amen,” as he ought, he says:

> “Henceforth I shall not return to Cornelius.”

### 8

After other matters he again says the following:

Know that he has now been stripped bare and deserted, as the brethren abandon him every day and return to the Church. Even Moses, the blessed martyr who recently among us completed an outstanding and admirable martyrdom, while he was still alive perceived that man’s audacity and madness and separated him from his own communion, together [Col. 0760A] with the five presbyters who had likewise separated themselves from the Church along with him.

9. Of the remainder of the letter Eusebius adds only the following summary: “At the end of the letter he drew up a catalogue of the bishops who had assembled at Rome and condemned the madness of Novatus (read: Novatian), adding their names and the church governed by each. He likewise carefully records the names and cities of those who, although they had not been present at Rome [Col. 0762A], had nevertheless approved the judgment of the former by their own vote, and from which each had sent letters.”

**YEAR OF CHRIST 252.**

[Note: [Col. 0761C]

**LETTER X.—**In the first part of this letter there is so much relating to Cornelius that we have judged that it ought to have a place among the letters either written by him or addressed to him. Thus, while in the preceding letter we heard how irregularly and contrary to all the laws of the Church Novatian’s ordination had been performed, we shall now learn from a competent witness how lawfully Cornelius was established in the chair of Peter. This letter was written after Decius, as is indicated in no. 8, perished amid the war and fighting against the Goths. This occurred at the end of the year 251; accordingly, this letter is not inappropriately assigned to the year 252. COUSTANT.—We append the latter part of this Letter to the former, lest, with one relegated to this volume and the other to the next, the Letter should appear mutilated and, as it were, lame in both feet. EDD.]

# LETTER X, OR THE FIRST PART OF THE LETTER OF ST. CYPRIAN TO ANTONIANUS, IN WHICH CYPRIAN DISCUSSES ST. CORNELIUS

(Erasm. IV, 2; Pamel., Rigalt., Baluz. LII; Paris LI; Oxford, Leipzig LV. Only the first part in Coustant I, col. 159; Galland III, p. 347.)

**SUMMARY OF THE FIRST PART.—**Cyprian dispels the false opinions instilled into Antonianus by Novatian’s letters. He clears himself of the suspicion of fickleness concerning the case of the lapsed. He relates how canonically Cornelius was promoted to the place of Peter, and how courageously he conducted himself in it.

**CYPRIAN TO HIS BROTHER ANTONIANUS, GREETINGS.**

[Note: [Col. 0762]

**I. I received the first.** This is the reading of most manuscripts, both ours and the English manuscripts, as well as two Vatican manuscripts. Others have, “We received the first letters.” So too the old editions. [Col. 0763B] Certain old books and Rembolt’s edition omit the word *first*, which is also omitted in manuscript 199 of the Vatican Library; nevertheless, I think that it suits [Col. 0763C] this passage. BALUZ.

**Maintaining.** This is the true reading, confirmed by eleven old books. *Binding*, however, is written in three ancient manuscripts and in the editions preceding Pamelius’s. The error arose from the ignorance of copyists who, not knowing how to read the text, wrote whatever came into their minds according to their own whim. The scribe of the Tours manuscript was more scrupulous. For he wrote “binding or maintaining,” leaving the judgment entirely to the reader. BALUZ.

**Our colleague Cornelius.** I do not know what great or extraordinary thing some find in this passage, so as to conclude from it that there is equality among bishops and that the Roman bishop is no greater than the others. It is certainly established that all bishops, since they belong to the college, are colleagues, and that throughout all ages they have called one another colleagues and brothers, as they still do. And yet no Catholic doubts that the Roman bishop possesses a great prerogative and authority. BALUZ.

[Col. 0763D] **With himself,** that is, to be in communion with the Catholic Church. Certainly even this passage confirms the authority of the Roman Pontiff; for if it is true that the person who communicates with Cornelius, the Roman Pope, communicates with the Catholic Church, then that Church over which Cornelius presides will be the Catholic Church; and consequently the sign by which the Catholic Church is distinguished from the conventicles of heretics is the succession of the Roman Pontiffs. PAMEL.]

## I

I received your first letter [Note: [Col. 0761C] *I received your letter*, Lam., Bod. 3, Ver., Corb.], dearest brother, [Col. 0763A] firmly maintaining the concord of the episcopal college and adhering to the Catholic Church. In it you indicated that you were not in communion with Novatian, but followed our counsel and maintained one common agreement with our fellow bishop Cornelius. You also wrote that I should forward a copy of that same letter to our colleague Cornelius, so that, laying aside all anxiety, he might now know that you were in communion with him—that is, with the Catholic Church.

[Note: [Col. 0763D]

**Having been disturbed, it had begun to waver.** Something similar had happened even to Cornelius himself. For although he had at first displayed toward the representatives of Felicissimus’s faction a firmness wholly worthy of a bishop, he afterward appeared to yield somewhat to their threats and intimidation. Cyprian remonstrates with him about this in Letter XII, no. 2. So deceptive were Novatian’s letters, and so great the stratagems of his supporters! COUSTANT.

**Trophimus.** He is coupled with those who offered incense in such a way that there can scarcely be any doubt that he too offered incense to the idols. His offense does not appear very dissimilar to the crime of a certain Repostus, who is said in the following Letter XII, no. 9, not only to have fallen himself during the persecution but also to have caused the greater part of his congregation to fall through sacrilegious persuasion. COUSTANT.—He was indeed admitted, but only to lay communion; and this was in accordance with the Church’s most widely accepted custom whenever any of the clergy had lapsed, since for such persons deposition took the place of excommunication.]

## II

But afterward other letters of yours arrived, sent through Quintus, our fellow presbyter [Note: [Col. 0763B] *our fellow presbyter*, Bod. 3.], in which I observed that your mind, disturbed by Novatian’s letters, had begun to waver. For although [Note: [Col. 0763B] *For since both this was by counsel and in your agreement*, Lam., Ebor., NC. 1.] you had previously established your counsel and agreement firmly, you requested in this letter [Note: [Col. 0763B] *requested in the letter that I reply to you*, Bod. 1, Lam., Ebor., NC. 1.] that I should write back to tell you what heresy [Col. 0763B] Novatian had introduced [Note: [Col. 0763B] *Novatian introduces*, Bod. 2, NC. 1.], or on what grounds Cornelius grants communion to Trophimus and to those who offered incense. If, indeed, out of concern for the faith you are anxiously troubled about this and carefully investigate [Note: [Col. 0764B] *out of concern for the faith, the truth of a doubtful matter*, Lam., Ebor.] the truth of a doubtful matter, the anxious uncertainty of a mind agitated by the fear of God is not to be reproved.

[Col. 0764A] [Note: [Col. 0764C]

**Rock.** Eight old books and all editions before the Manutian edition add *strong*. The Fuxensis reads “with strong stability,” as in Manutius’s edition. The word *strong*, however, is absent from twelve ancient copies. BALUZ.

**And indeed, first, since you appear to have been disturbed also by my conduct, etc.** As is sufficiently evident from the book and the preceding letters *On the Lapsed*, Cyprian was at first, while the persecution was still raging, somewhat stricter toward the lapsed, since he judged that they should not be admitted to peace except after completing penance, unless perhaps, at the intercession of the Martyrs, the danger of death was imminent. He wished this rule to be observed not only for those who had sacrificed but also for the *libellatici*. But once peace had been granted to the Church and it first became possible to assemble, that severity was somewhat moderated at a council of the bishops of Africa. They decided—as he says below in this same letter—that, after the individual cases had been examined, the *libellatici* should meanwhile be admitted, but that those who had sacrificed should receive assistance at the point of death. Antonianus therefore blamed Cyprian for having changed his judgment, while Cyprian gives his reasons for the change in policy. He shows that this decision had pleased not himself alone, but first the Roman clergy and then many bishops, and indeed that it had also been confirmed by Cornelius in the Roman synod. Let this suffice for understanding the passage. PAMEL.

**Their conscience.** In the second part of this letter the same bishop demonstrates the widely unequal condition and different sin of those whom Cyprian designates by the single term *libellatici* and those who sacrificed to idols, whom he also calls “those who sacrificed.” They were called *libellatici* because, after giving the magistrates a payment by which they bought themselves free from torture, they received a certificate (*libellus*) from them. Either they personally approached the magistrates and declared, or instructed another person who went in their stead to declare, that they were Christians, that they were not permitted to sacrifice, and that they could not approach the devil’s altars; for that reason they were giving payment, so that they might not do what was unlawful. And indeed, as Cyprian testifies in the same place, they acted in good faith in this way, since they considered it lawful and not forbidden. Nor would they have been guilty if, after offering money, they had received certificates by which they were freed from persecution. Their offense, however, consisted in the fact that the certificates themselves attested that they had approached the altars and had complied with edicts or laws issued against the Gospel; and this was afterward read publicly, as the Roman clergy relates in Cyprian’s Letter XXXI. COUST.]

## III

Nevertheless, since I see that, after the first declaration in your Letter, you were subsequently disturbed by Novatian’s letters, I set down this principle first, dearest brother [Note: [Col. 0764B] *dearest brother*, Bod. 2, Lam., Ebor.]: serious men, once founded with solid stability upon a strong rock [Note: [Col. 0764B] *and always upon the rock*, Lam., Ebor., NC. 1.], are moved, I will not say by a light breeze, but not even by a wind or a whirlwind. Otherwise, a doubtful and uncertain mind is frequently agitated by varying opinions, as though by gusts of assailing winds, and is turned away from its settled purpose, with a certain reproach of fickleness. Lest Novatian’s letters should produce this effect either in you or in anyone else, brother, I shall, as you requested, explain the grounds of the matter briefly to you.

And indeed, first, since you appear to have been disturbed also by my conduct, both my person and my case must be vindicated before you, lest anyone suppose that I have lightly departed from my purpose and that, although at first and from the beginning I defended the vigor of the Gospel, I afterward appear to have turned my mind away from my former discipline and severity, so that I thought peace should be readily granted to those who had stained their conscience by certificates or [Col. 0765A] had committed abominable sacrifices [Note: [Col. 0765B] *should be granted by me*, Bod. 1.]. Neither of these courses was taken by me without long and carefully balanced deliberation.

[Note: [Col. 0765C]

**Concerning the case of the lapsed.** Supply: “to make a decision.” See the aforementioned Letter XIV. COUSTANT.]

## IV

For while the battle line was still engaged at close quarters and the struggle of the glorious contest was raging in the persecution, the strength of the soldiers had to be aroused by every exhortation and with full force. Above all, the minds of the lapsed had to be encouraged, as it were, by the trumpet blast of our voice, so that they might pursue the path of repentance not only with prayers and lamentations, but—since an opportunity was being given to renew the contest and recover salvation—might rather be urged by our rebuking voices [Note: [Col. 0765B] *by our rebukes*, Bod. 3.] toward the ardor of confession [Note: [Col. 0765B] *the ardor of confession*, Lam.] and the glory of martyrdom.

Indeed, when the presbyters and deacons had written to me concerning certain persons, saying that they were immoderate and were insistently pressing to be received hastily into communion, I replied to them in a letter of mine that is still extant, and added this as well:

> “If they are in too great a hurry, they have within their own power what they are asking for [Note: [Col. 0765B] *than what they ask for*, Bod. 1, Neap., MR.], since the very circumstances grant them more than they ask. The battle line is still engaged, and [Note: [Col. 0765C] *and among us daily*, Corb.] the contest is celebrated daily. If they truly and firmly repent of what they have done, and if the ardor of faith prevails, the one who cannot endure delay can be crowned.”

Nevertheless, I deferred deciding what ought to be established concerning the case of the lapsed, so that, when rest and tranquility had been granted and divine indulgence permitted the bishops to assemble together, we might then, after exchanging views and balancing the common counsel of all [Note: [Col. 0766B] *after deliberation*, Lam., Ben., Bod. 2, Ebor.], determine what ought to be done. If anyone, however, wished rashly to grant communion to the lapsed before our council and before a judgment had been established [Note: [Col. 0766B] *constituted*, Lam., Bod. 3.] by the counsel of all, he himself was to be excluded from communion.

[Note: [Col. 0765D]

**From their reply.** I do not dislike the reading *from the replies*, found in the Oxford edition as in the Colb. and Corb. manuscripts. For although Cyprian quotes verbatim only the words of the Roman clergy’s Letter XXXI, he nevertheless appears at the same time to praise the judgment of the Confessors who replied to him on the same matter in Letter XXVI:

> “Since so great an offense, which has spread with almost incredible devastation throughout nearly the whole world, ought not to be handled except, as you yourself write, cautiously and moderately, after consultation with all the bishops, presbyters, deacons, confessors, and even the laypeople who have remained steadfast.”

The aforementioned clergy give the following reason for such circumspection in the cited Letter XXXI:

> “For it seems to us exceedingly invidious and burdensome not to have many persons examine what appears to have been committed by many, and for one person to pronounce judgment when so great a crime is known to have spread among many. For no decree can be firm which does not appear to have had the consent of very many.”

COUSTANT.

**Although it pleases us.** This is taken from Letter XXXI. BALUZ.

**It was added.** Pacian copied this passage in his treatise against the Novatians addressed to Symphronianus. BALUZ.

**That to the lapsed.** Here Cyprian no longer reproduces the Roman clergy’s own words, but briefly summarizes the judgment they had explained at greater length. It is the letters of this clergy—not, as Rigaltius wrote, those of Cyprian himself—that are said here to have been sent throughout the whole world while the see was vacant. They breathe a wisdom worthy of the clergy of the foremost Church. For they, in no way driven by an excessive concern for their own authority, did not disdain to summon to themselves the neighboring bishops and those from distant regions who were present in Rome, and to make use of their counsel. [Col. 0766D] They resolve that before the appointment of a bishop they should introduce no innovation. They think only that assistance should be given to the lapsed if they have shown signs of a truly repentant disposition and danger of death is imminent.

There was therefore no reason for the Oxford editor to attempt to depreciate and diminish the authority of those letters on the ground that they had been written by Novatian. For the authority of letters depends not upon the person who writes them, but upon the person in whose name they are written, as well as upon the agreement of those who subscribe them. Cyprian did not conceal that the letters of the Roman clergy had been written and signed by Novatian, so that it might become clear that the teaching he afterward advanced—that the lapsed should not be admitted to repentance—was accepted by that heretic not because truth persuaded him, but because ambition perverted his judgment. COUSTANT.]

## V

I also wrote very fully about this to the clergy at Rome [Note: [Col. 0766B] *to the Roman clergy*, Corb.], who were then still acting without a bishop, and to the confessors Maximus the presbyter and the others held in custody, who are now joined with Cornelius in the Church. That I wrote this you will be able to learn [Note: [Col. 0766B] *can be learned*, Lam., Bod. 2.] from their reply; for in their letter they expressed themselves as follows:

> “Although, in so important a matter, we approve what you yourself have considered—namely, that the Church’s peace must first be awaited, and that only then, after a common consultation [Col. 0766B] with the bishops, presbyters, deacons [Note: [Col. 0766B] *deacons*, above, Letter of Novatian; *deacons likewise*, Lam. [Col. 0766C] Bod. 2.], confessors likewise, and laypeople who have remained steadfast, should the case of the lapsed be considered.”

It was further added—at that time Novatian was writing, reading aloud in his own voice what he had written, and the presbyter Moses, then still a confessor but now already a martyr, was subscribing—that peace should be given to lapsed persons who were sick and at the point of death. These letters were sent throughout the whole world and brought to the knowledge of all the churches and all the brethren everywhere.

[Col. 0767A] [Note: [Col. 0767C]

**The headings of the decisions.** Optatus calls them “headings of the directives” in the first book *Against Parmenianus*. Whether this is the origin of the penitential canons, as Baronius judged, I leave for others to investigate. BALUZ.

**Appeared.** This is the reading of several excellent manuscripts and the old editions. This reading seems to me better than that of the Manutian edition, which reads *had appeared*. BALUZ.

**After holding a council.** In the year 251, as Pearson says in the *Cyprianic Annals*, where it is reported from Eusebius that sixty bishops assembled for this Roman council. The same author, and Pagi after him, states that it was held in September. BALUZ.—Our manuscripts read *by counsel*. We are expressly taught here that the Carthaginian council concerning the case of the lapsed preceded the Roman council held by Cornelius concerning the same case. Accordingly, when Cornelius is said in Eusebius, book VI, chapter 43, to have sent to Fabius the proceedings of the Roman synod together with the judgments of the Africans and others, Eusebius must there be understood to speak of the judgments by which the Africans preceded the Roman synod, not those by which they subscribed to that synod. COUSTANT.

**Agreed.** Something is missing here, perhaps “that he had duly attained the episcopate,” or something similar. For the sense is incomplete. BALUZ.]

## VI

Nevertheless, in accordance with what had previously been determined, once the persecution had abated and the opportunity to assemble had been granted, a large number of bishops—whom their faith and the Lord’s protection had preserved whole and unharmed [Note: [Col. 0767C] *the Lord’s protection had preserved*, Bod. 3.]—assembled together. After passages from Scripture [Note: [Col. 0767C] *the divine Scriptures*, Lam., Ebor., Ben., Bod. 2, NC. 1.] had been presented at length on both sides, we weighed a balanced settlement with salutary moderation [Note: [Col. 0767C] *with salutary reason*, Bod. 3.].

Thus neither was the hope of communion and peace wholly denied to the lapsed, lest they should fail through despair all the more [Note: [Col. 0767C] *lest rather they should fail through despair because of this*, Bod. 3.] and, because the Church was closed to them [Note: [Col. 0767C] *was closed to them, and the world*, Bod. 3; *was shut*, Colb.; *was brought*, Corb.], follow the world and live as pagans; nor, on the other hand, was the discipline of the Gospel relaxed so that they might rush rashly into communion. Rather, penance was to be prolonged, the Father’s mercy was to be sought with sorrow, and the circumstances, intentions, and necessities of each person were to be examined, in accordance with what is contained [Col. 0767B] in the document which I trust has reached you, where the individual headings of our decisions have been written down.

And if the number of bishops in Africa appeared insufficient, we also wrote to Rome about this matter, to our colleague Cornelius. He too, after holding a council with very many of his fellow bishops, agreed with us in the same judgment, with equal seriousness and salutary moderation.

[Note: [Col. 0767D]

**Examination.** Five ancient books and the older editions read *example*, and at first sight I approved that reading. For I saw that Morel had retained it, disregarding the edition of Manutius. The authority of these five old books confirmed my opinion, for they read, “to consider by the example and reason of our life and discipline.” I thought that the word *examination*, which Manutius produced, had arisen from the correction of some ancient copyist. Supposing that these words did not cohere and that the old reading was therefore corrupt, he had made *examination* from these two words joined together, deleting the first and retaining the other. But now, since I see that in Letter LXVIII the Fuxensis manuscript reads *example and reason*, as will be noted there, in place of the *examination* found in the other books and editions, I have not doubted that this reading is better. For above, in Letter VII, it reads: “This persecution is a testing and examination of the heart.” BALUZ.]

## VII

It was necessary for me to write to you now about this, so that you may know that I did nothing lightly. Rather, as I had previously set forth in my letters, I deferred everything to the common counsel of our council. I granted communion to none of the lapsed beforehand, while there still remained a means by which a lapsed person might receive not only pardon but even a crown.

Afterward, however, as the concord of the college, the need to gather the brotherhood together, and the benefit of healing the wound required, I yielded to the necessity of the times and judged that provision must be made for the salvation of many. And now I do not depart from those decisions which were once approved in our council after common consultation, although many matters are debated by the voices of many people and lies against the priests of God, uttered from the devil’s mouth, are spread everywhere in order to shatter the concord of Catholic unity.

But as a good brother and a fellow priest of one mind with us, you ought not readily to accept what malicious men and apostates say. Rather, you should consider what your colleagues—modest and serious men—do, on the basis of an examination of our life and discipline [Note: [Col. 0768C] *to consider by example and reason*, Corb.; *by exhortation*, Colb.].

[Note: [Col. 0768D]

**Otherwise quiet.** From the eight manuscripts listed in the Oxford edition we restore the word *at other times*, with the support of Colb. and Corb., of which one reads *others* and the other *to others*. Nothing more is needed to persuade us that in every statement in which Cyprian commends Cornelius’s election, he indirectly assails and condemns Novatian’s ordination as lacking the same conditions. Indeed, a certain person is designated not obscurely even by name: Novatian. From this it is also evident to everyone that what was subsequently enacted in written laws concerning the elections of prelates had been accepted in practice during the earlier centuries. COUSTANT.

[Col. 0769A] **Of virginal conscience.** The Colb. manuscript reads *of virginity and continence*. Seven English manuscripts read *of his virginal continence*. Although we retain *of virginal conscience*, we nevertheless judge that these words proclaim Cornelius to have been adorned not only with the virtues befitting virgins but also with virginity itself. COUSTANT.—I have restored the reading which I found in nineteen of our old books and in eight English manuscripts. The word *conscience*, preferred by the editions, I found in only two ancient manuscripts. Below, in this same letter, it reads “the resolve of continence.” In the book *On the Dress of Virgins*, p. 174, we read that continence follows Christ and virginity is destined for the kingdom of God. Lactantius, book VI, chapter 23, says that this kind of continence is the summit and consummation of all virtues. Quintilian, book VIII, chapter 4, praises the unconquered continence of Socrates.

Elsewhere *continence* signifies abstinence in food and drink, as in Aulus Gellius, book IV, chapter 1, and book V, chapter 2. In the petition of Marcellinus and Faustinus, the remarkable continence of Macarius, a Roman presbyter, is praised because he neither relieved his stomach with wine nor tended his body with nourishment from meat, but, softening his harsher foods with oil alone, devoted himself to fasting and prayer. Jerome, in the letter to Laeta concerning the education of her daughter, says: “In Lent the sails of continence must be spread.” See Cassian, *Conference* II, chapters 16 and 26. Julius Capitolinus, in *Aelius Pertinax*, says: “But following the emperor’s example, since he conducted himself more sparingly, cheapness arose from the general continence.” Jerome, on chapter five of the Letter to the Galatians, says:

> “Continence is necessary not only in desires and appetite, but also in the three remaining passions, namely sorrow, joy, and fear.”

Likewise, on chapter two of the Letter to Titus:

> “It should also be known that continence is necessary not only in the activity of the flesh and in every form of desire, but in all things: lest we seek undeserved honors, lest avarice be inflamed, and lest we be overcome by any passion.”

See Cyprian in the book *On the Dress of Virgins*, p. 174: “Continence, however,” etc. Elsewhere *continentia* is used for maintenance, that is, necessary sustenance, as Franciscus Pithoeus observes in his glossary to Julianus Antecessor. BALUZ.

**He himself suffered compulsion.** John of Salisbury, *Policraticus*, book VIII, chapter 23:

> “The ancients were once dragged forward against their will, and though inclined toward martyrdom, they fled the foremost sees as something worse than prison and the cross.”

And the emperor Justinian, law V, *Si quamquam*, Code, *On Bishops and Clerics*, says:

> “For surely a man is unworthy of the priesthood unless he has been ordained against his will.”

Jerome, in the *Epitaph of Nepotian*:

> “He complained that he was unable to bear it and alleged that his youthful age was unsuitable for the priesthood. But the more he resisted, the more he stirred up the enthusiasm of everyone for him; by refusing he deserved what he did not wish to be, and he was all the worthier because he declared himself unworthy.”

The same author, in the *Epitaph of Paula*, addressed to Eustochium:

> “By fleeing glory she deserved glory, which follows virtue like a shadow and, abandoning those who seek it, seeks those who despise it.”

Boethius, in the second book of *The Consolation of Philosophy*:

> “Thus it comes about that honor is added not to virtues through rank, but to ranks through virtue.”

And the saying concerning St. Honoratus, bishop of Arles:

> “The rank itself came to the man who had refused to come to the rank.”

Pope St. Gregory, book IV, Letter 45, says that, among other reasons, he ordained Marinianus bishop because he fled the episcopate, which he accepted against his will. What is written concerning Eusebius, the elected archbishop of Caesarea, in Gregory Nazianzen’s funeral oration for his father, is worth reading. See the *Book of Daily Formulas of the Roman Pontiffs*, in which the man who hides himself lest he be made a bishop is said to be worthier of the episcopate. See also Cressollius, book III, chapter 1 of the *Mystagogus*. Yet this resistance on the part of bishops-elect was afterward rare. For when bishops began to be held in honor and wealth increased, episcopates, as Sulpicius Severus says, began to be sought through corrupt ambitions. On this subject, the elegant and eloquent Letter XXI of book V by Isidore of Pelusium should be consulted. Gregory Nazianzen, in his oration in praise of Basil:

> “For the dignity of the priesthood is secured not so much by virtue as by wickedness and fraud; and it is not the better and worthier, but the more powerful, who sit upon thrones.”

Yet this modesty of great men flourished not only in the Church of Christ but also in the commonwealth and the empire. Julius Capitolinus records a speech by Clodius Albinus to the soldiers, which begins:

> “I have been brought unwillingly to imperial power, fellow soldiers; and even this proves it, that I scorned Commodus when he bestowed upon me the title of Caesar.”

Aelius Lampridius, writing about Alexander Severus, who was made emperor against his will, says:

> “I shall explain the reasons by which both the senate was compelled to do this and he was compelled to endure it.”

In Flavius Vopiscus, the emperor Probus says:

> “I never desired imperial power, and I accepted it unwillingly.”

Claudian, in the panegyric on the fourth consulship of the emperor Honorius:

> Virtue is worthy to be chosen. Of its own accord the suppliant purple  
> Offered itself, and he alone, in asking, deserved to reign.

See what Joannes Tristanus of Saint-Amant notes concerning the election of Pertinax in the second volume of his *Commentaries*. BALUZ.

**He was made bishop by very many colleagues.** Namely, by sixteen bishops, as we are taught in the second part of this letter. Among them were two Africans, whom the author of the *Cyprianic Annals* writes were deliberately sent so that they might take part in the election of the Roman Pontiff, though he proves this by no argument. It is more probable that, having been sent to Rome for other reasons, or having come of their own accord, they were summoned to the aforementioned election. COUSTANT.—Below he says that there were sixteen bishops who had taken part in Cornelius’s ordination.
