Among them, as is evident from Letter XLII above, were the Africans Caldonius, Fortunatus, Pompeius, and Stephanus.

It is apparent from this passage that in that age the Roman bishop or pope was ordinarily appointed by the college of priests—that is, by the bishops—on the testimony of the clergy and by the vote of the people. For the custom of electing the Roman Pontiff has often varied. First, St. Peter designated his successors Linus, Cletus, and Clement. Anacletus and the others, down to the second schism between Damasus and Ursicinus, were chosen by the votes of the clergy and people and ordained by the bishops, if any happened to be present, as may be gathered from this passage.

At the election of Damasus, however, the authority of the emperors began to intervene: at first only in a schism, in order to quell disturbances, as Valentinian settled the matter between Damasus and Ursicinus, Honorius between Boniface and Eulalius, and King Theodoric between Symmachus and Laurentius. [Col. 0771A] Thereafter it intervened even apart from schism, lest a disturbance perhaps arise. Indeed, the matter gradually reached the point that they did not dare receive consecration without the emperors’ consent.

This custom lasted down to Emperor Constantine III. Moved by the holiness of Benedict II, he permitted the clergy and Roman people alone, as before, the free power of electing and designating the Pontiff. Later Pope Adrian, after convening for this purpose a Lateran synod of 153 bishops, granted to Charlemagne—even though it had previously been conceded to no emperor—the right of electing the Pontiff, because he had driven the Lombards from Italy. His son, however, renounced that right shortly afterward, as is evident in Distinction LXIII in Gratian, chapter *Ludovicus* [Col. 0771B]. Thus the Romans once again possessed the free election and consecration of the Pope for a long period, down to Leo VIII. Since Leo had been placed in the Apostolic See by Otto I through force and arms, he again transferred the entire right of electing the Pontiff from the clergy and people to the emperor.

Otto’s successors made use of that privilege—or, rather, abused it—down to Henry IV. For the most just reasons, therefore, that right was again recalled to the Romans by Gregory VII, even shortly before his pontificate, when the opportunity was furnished by the schism among Benedict, Sylvester, and John under Emperor Henry III. For Stephen IX, Nicholas II, and Alexander II were appointed without the emperor’s consent.

When Henry V again obtained this right surreptitiously through stratagems from Paschal II, it was revoked once more by Paschal himself in the Lateran synod. Finally, the right of electing the Pontiff was transferred to the cardinals alone. The precise time when this began is not equally certain; for although a certain decree of this kind was promulgated by Nicholas II, the votes of the Roman people and clergy nevertheless still intervened on several occasions afterward. The constitutions concerning the conduct of the election in conclave were issued by Gregory X at the Council of Lyons. These statements are drawn partly from Onofrio Panvinio and Platina, and partly from the *Hierarchy* of Albertus Pighius. PAMEL.

**By the judgment of Christ.** Baronius concludes from this that Cornelius was designated bishop by some divine sign or portent. But Cyprian appears to have meant nothing other than that all the conditions which, by the judgment and prescription of God and Christ, ought to be observed in the election of bishops were fulfilled in Cornelius’s election. Cyprian himself explains his meaning below, Letter XII, no. 5, when he proves by these words that Fortunatus had been appointed in his place to no purpose:

> “No one, AFTER THE DIVINE JUDGMENT, after the vote of the people, and after the consent of the fellow bishops, would now make himself judge—not of the bishop, but of God.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Unless someone is of such sacrilegious rashness and so depraved a mind that he thinks a priest can be made without God’s judgment.”

[Col. 0771D] COUSTANT.—Jerome, on the first chapter of the Letter to the Galatians:

> “We now see very many persons appointed to the priesthood not by God’s judgment, but by purchasing the favor of the multitude.”

BALUZ.]

### On the Testimony of the Clergy

The compiler of the *Cyprianic Annals* observes that Baronius, by altering Cyprian’s words, assigns the vote in the election of priests to the clergy and the testimony to the people. In the preceding note we heard the same prelate speaking of his own ordination: “After the vote of the people.” Yet Cyprian writes above, Epistle I, no. 2, that once a bishop has been appointed and approved by the **testimony** and judgment of his colleagues and the people, another can by no means be appointed. The part played by the people in the election of bishops is explained at greater length by the same prelate in Epistle 68, Pamelius’s edition. First he states that the people themselves “have the greatest power either to choose worthy priests or to reject the unworthy.” He then immediately adds:

> We see that it derives from divine authority that a priest should be chosen in the presence of the people, [Col. 0772A] before the eyes of all, and should be approved as worthy and suitable by public judgment and **testimony**.

Soon afterward, explaining the manner in which God willed a priest to be appointed under the Law, he says:

> God commands a priest to be appointed before the whole synagogue; that is, he teaches and demonstrates that priestly ordinations ought to take place only with the knowledge of the people standing by, so that, in the people’s presence, either the crimes of the wicked may be disclosed or the merits of the good proclaimed, and that the ordination examined by the vote and judgment of all may be just and legitimate.

Here “the vote and judgment of all” signifies nothing other than what, in the immediately preceding sentence, was called “public judgment and testimony,” [Col. 0772B] and above “the testimony and judgment of his colleagues and the people.” He next adds:

> For this reason it must be diligently observed and maintained, in accordance with divine tradition and apostolic practice—as is maintained among us also and throughout almost all the provinces—that, for the proper celebration of ordinations, the nearest bishops of that province should assemble among the people over whom the candidate is being ordained, and that the bishop should be chosen in the presence of the people, who know most fully the life of each person and have observed the conduct of every individual through his manner of life.

There is indeed nothing there about the people’s vote; but he immediately adds:

> We see that this was also done among you in the ordination of our colleague Sabinus: the episcopate was conferred upon him by the vote of the entire brotherhood and by the judgment of the bishops who had assembled in person and had written letters about him to you.

Celestine, Epistle 4, chapter 5, wishing no bishop to be given to an unwilling people, commands that the consent and desire of the clergy, the people, and the order be required. Leo likewise decrees in Epistle 9, chapter 6:

> Let the subscription of the clergy, the testimony of the honored men, and the consent of the order [Col. 0772C] and people be secured: he who is to preside over all should be chosen by all.

And in Epistle 12, chapter 5:

> Let him be placed over all whom the consent of the clergy and people has demanded. . . . Only let no one be given to those who are unwilling and have not requested him.

See Julius, Epistle 1, no. 14. **COUSTANT.**

### On the Vote of the People

See Petavius’s notes on Synesius, p. 56 of the second edition. See also the book of Florus, deacon of Lyons, *On the Elections of Bishops*, in the appendix to Agobard. **BALUZ.**

### “By the Body of the Priests of Old . . .”

That is, unless I am mistaken, by the number of selected and senior presbyters. For since the bishops by whom Cornelius was ordained have already been mentioned, we cannot agree with the compiler of the *Cyprianic Annals*, who refers this phrase to those same bishops. Admittedly, in Cyprian the word “priests” commonly means bishops; but presbyters are also sometimes understood under that name. For the prelate can mean nothing else in Epistle XXXV, or XL, where, after stating that he had been admonished to enroll the presbyter Numidicus [Col. 0772D] among the presbyters of Carthage, he observes that Numidicus was not without reason preserved alive through the most grievous torments:

> But so that the Lord might join him to our clergy and adorn the number of our presbyterate, depleted through the lapse of certain men, with glorious **priests**.

Julius I writes in Epistle 1, no. 14, that according to the prescription of the ecclesiastical canon a bishop ought to be appointed in the church itself, from the **priestly order** itself (ἀπ᾽ αὐτοῦ τοῦ ἱερατείου, “from the priesthood itself”), from the clergy itself, by the bishops of that province. **COUSTANT.**

In Ivo, part 5, chapter 359, and in Gratian, 7, q. 1, chapter 5, as also in one old manuscript of mine, the reading is “by consent.” Cyprian uses the same word in Epistle LV, p. 82, when writing to Cornelius about his own election. The Roman Correctors emended Gratian from Cyprian’s text—wrongly, in my opinion. For since the gloss required the word “consent” to be retained in Gratian’s text, they ought not to have rejected it. **BALUZ.**

### “Fabian’s Place”

In the Oxford edition the following annotation is appended here: [Col. 0773B]

> Rigault says: “Someone may conjecture that Cyprian’s hand wrote only, ‘When Fabian’s place and the priestly chair were vacant’; and indeed the author’s meaning permits nothing else.”

Nothing is added from which Rigault’s conjecture may either be confirmed or weakened. It is assuredly rejected by the complete agreement of all the manuscripts, by which it is shown that, in Cyprian’s judgment, the man who sits upon the Roman chair holds Peter’s place. The same prelate plainly asserts this very thing in Epistle XII, no. 13, printed below. **COUSTANT.**

Thus all editions and old manuscripts, with the exception of the Chartres manuscript, in which “rank” is written. Rigault nevertheless thought that this was not Cyprian’s and that it therefore came from a gloss. I do not know whether this opinion of his will have many followers. Optatus of Milevis, in book I, spoke of the chair of Peter or of Cyprian, and in book II said that the episcopal chair had been conferred in the city of Rome. **BALUZ.**

[Col. 0773C] **“Ecclesiastical Ordination.”** The Corb. manuscripts read “the ordination of the Church.” Soon afterward Cyprian uses the words “though he boasts greatly of himself,” etc. He is referring to Novatian and implying that he possessed certain gifts which he himself, or his followers, advertised very highly. In the second part of this epistle he speaks more openly of the same man as follows:

> Though he may boast of himself and proclaim his philosophy or eloquence in proud tones, he who preserved neither brotherly charity nor ecclesiastical unity has lost even what he formerly possessed.

**COUSTANT.**

### “He Is an Outsider”

Optatus, book II: “Whatever is outside is alien.” **BALUZ.**

### “He Is Outside”

Jerome, in the *Apology against Rufinus*:

> What shall I say of heretics who, although they are outside, call themselves Christians?

The same writer, in the Epistle to Oceanus:

> Jews, heretics, and pagans are outsiders and outside the Church.

That is the common opinion of Catholics. Nevertheless, Diego de Zúñiga, in book I, chapter 7, disputing *On True Religion* against Melchior Cano, [Col. 0773D] who had said in book IV, chapter 2, that heretics do not belong to the Church and are not to be numbered among the Church’s parts, contends that heretics do belong to the Church. In one old manuscript, instead of what is read here in Cyprian, “he is outside,” the reading is “he is an enemy.” **BALUZ.**

### “He Cannot Be Second”

Gerhoh of Reichersberg employed these words against Guibert of Ravenna in his book *On the State of the Church under Emperor Henry IV*, chapter 14, though without naming Cyprian; for he made Cyprian’s words his own. Cyprian wrote this against Novatian, who arranged to be elected by certain factionalists in opposition to Cornelius, who had been elected first. Since Cornelius therefore sat upon the chair of Peter, Novatian, who had occupied the same chair, could not be bishop of the city of Rome, because one appointed after the one man who ought to stand alone is no longer second, but no one at all, since a single chair cannot hold two. This is the true and genuine meaning of Cyprian’s words.

Consequently [Col. 0774B] the interpretation of Francisco Torres and certain others cannot be endured: they interpret “one and sole bishop” here as referring to the Roman bishop, as though he alone were the one bishop in the Church, while all the others were neither true bishops nor successors of the Apostles, but vicars of that one bishop. This is contrary to all the testimonies of antiquity.

In the *Life of Saint Anselm, Bishop of Lucca*, written by a contemporary author who was also his penitentiary, a passage from Cyprian is cited. Writing against the antipope Wibert, that author says:

> And so, to use the words of the most holy martyr Cyprian, neither this man nor that one is anyone at all, because neither the one nor the other is anyone’s successor or predecessor: both are parricides, both are utterly criminal violators of their mother the Church. [The opening wording is textually uncertain.]

The passage, however, appears to have been composed from two passages: this one, namely, and another in Epistle 76, p. 152: [Col. 0774C] “Succeeding no one, sprung from himself.” **BALUZ.**

### VIII

I come now, dearest brother, to the person [Note: [Col. 0768C] “To the person of our colleague,” Lam. Bod. 2.] of our colleague Cornelius, so that you may know Cornelius together with us [Col. 0768B] more truly—not from the falsehoods of the malicious and detracting, but from the judgment of God [Note: [Col. 0768C] “But from the judgment of the Lord God,” Oxon. Baluz.], who made him bishop, and from the testimony of his fellow bishops, whose entire body throughout the whole world has consented in harmonious unanimity.

For what commends our dearly beloved Cornelius to God and Christ and His Church, and likewise to all his fellow priests, by praiseworthy testimony, is that he did not suddenly attain the episcopate. Rather, he was advanced through every ecclesiastical office, and, having often won God’s favor in divine ministries, he ascended through every rank of religious service to the lofty summit of the priesthood.

Then, moreover, he neither sought [Note: [Col. 0768C] “Nor did he himself seek,” Oxon.; “He neither desired it himself,” Lam. Ebor. NC. 1.] nor desired the episcopate itself, nor did he seize it, as do others whom the swelling of their arrogance and pride inflates. Instead, quiet in other respects and modest, and such as those usually are who are divinely chosen for this place, [Col. 0769A] on account of the modesty of his virginal conscience [Note: [Col. 0769A] Thus Sic. Ver. Benev. Bod. 1, 2. Lam. Ebor. NC. 1. Lin.; “virginal continence,” Lam. Ebor. NC. 1. Bod. 1, 2, 3. Pem. MR.] and because of the humility of the reserve innate in him and faithfully preserved, he did not, like some men, apply force so as to become bishop; rather, force was applied to him [Note: [Col. 0770A] “He applied force,” Lam. Bod. 2.], so that he was compelled to accept the episcopate.

[Col. 0770A] And he was made bishop by very many of our colleagues who were then present in the city of Rome [Note: [Col. 0770A] “In the Roman city,” Bod. 1.] and who sent us concerning his ordination letters that were honorable and commendatory, and distinguished by the testimony of their praise.

Cornelius was made bishop [Col. 0771A] by the judgment of God and His Christ, by the testimony of almost all the clergy, by the vote of the people then present, and by the body of the priests of old and of good men, [Col. 0772A] when no one had been appointed before him, when Fabian’s place—that is, Peter’s place—and the rank of the priestly chair [Col. 0773A] [Note: [Col. 0773A] “And the chair,” Ver.] were vacant.

Once this place had been occupied by the will of God and confirmed by the consent of us all, whoever thereafter wishes to become bishop must necessarily be made one outside, and he who does not maintain the unity of the Church cannot possess ecclesiastical ordination. Whoever he may be, though he boasts greatly of himself and claims very much for himself, he is profane, he is an outsider, he is outside. And since there cannot be a second after the first, whoever is appointed after the one man who ought to stand alone is no longer second, but no one at all.

[Note: [Col. 0774C]

### IX. “A Rival Emperor”

That is, Julius Valens, who usurped imperial power at Rome in the year 251 but did not hold it for long, as Aurelius Victor teaches. Soon afterward Pamelius, in place of the words “a priest of God,” wrongly substituted from the Affligem manuscript “a rival priest.” Nor did he grasp Cyprian’s meaning when he interpreted this passage as follows: Cornelius endured a rival emperor more patiently than he did Novatian, a rival priest. For there the verb “would hear” is predicated of the tyrant Decius, not of Cornelius. **COUSTANT.**

Lucifer of Cagliari, in the book addressed to Constantius, *On Dying for the Son of God*: “Rival emperors rise against him.” Cyprian does not say that a rival emperor had been raised against Decius, but that Decius would have endured much more patiently the raising of a rival emperor against himself than the appointment of a priest of God at Rome. In this one sees Cornelius’s marvelous constancy: he sat fearless, awaiting the executioners of his body and the avengers of the raging tyrant, as Cyprian says in Epistle LII to Antonianus.

Yet some were found who [Col. 0774D] attempted to divine which emperor was then raised against Decius. They wrote that it was Lucius Priscus who was raised against him, because Aurelius Victor writes in his *Book of the Caesars* that dominion was conferred upon him amid an incursion of the Goths, after many had reached that place following the plundering of Thrace; for this reason, he says, Decius departed from Rome as quickly as he could, at the earliest opportunity.

But I cannot leave this passage without noting the rashness of Saumaise, who in chapter six of *On the Primacy of the Pope*, p. 86, against the authority of all the ancient manuscripts and editions, contends that “an evil emperor” should be read here instead of “a rival emperor.” He endeavors to prove this conjecture of his from the testimonies of ancient authors who speak of evil emperors. No one fails to see how useless those observations are in this passage. Moreover, the sense cannot stand with Saumaise’s conjecture. **BALUZ.**

### “A Priest of God”

I found this reading in nineteen of our manuscripts, in six English manuscripts, in Thomas Waldensis, [Col. 0775B] title 14, *On the Sacramentals*, chapter 123, and in all editions preceding Pamelius’s. The other reading, “a rival priest,” which Pamelius asserts to be most certainly true but Rigault to be undoubtedly false, was found, according to Pamelius’s own testimony, in only one Affligem manuscript, just as I too found it in only one manuscript, which had belonged to François Pithou.

And yet the most illustrious Cardinal du Perron, in his reply against the king of Great Britain, p. 99, says that it is found in the older and more accurate copies. To prove this he cites in the margin the Affligem manuscript and Pamelius’s edition, with no other testimony. I am surprised that Rigault retained in his edition a reading that he himself calls undoubtedly false, as it in fact is.

For the meaning of this passage is that Decius, the enemy of our sect, [Col. 0775C] which he desired to eradicate, so dreaded a priest of God in the city of Rome, the capital of the empire, that he would have heard much more patiently and tolerably that a rival emperor had been raised against him than that a priest of God had been appointed at Rome, as Rigault correctly explains these words. This was not because he feared the Roman bishop as a man who, so far as the commonwealth was concerned, was by no means an object of fear or dread to an emperor, as some have believed; rather, because he was an enemy of the cross of Christ, burning with a desire to suppress Christianity, as the most distinguished Henry Dodwell says, he very greatly desired that no successor should be given to the deceased Pope Fabian, believing that our religion would perish if it had no bishop. In addition, I think, he feared that in a city eager for revolution the number of Christians—who were, as Cyprian says, an exceedingly large and numerous people—would increase. **BALUZ.**

### “So Long a Time”

I found this reading in eight ancient manuscripts. The other reading, “in such times,” is presented by the old editions before the Manutius edition and by six old manuscripts. **BALUZ.**

[Col. 0775D] **“Awaiting . . . the Executioners.”** For, according to Pacian in Epistle 3, he endured repeated persecutions from the angry emperor. Hence the slanders of his rivals are refuted—those who kept saying that he had been contaminated by the stain of a certificate. **COUSTANT.**

### “And Fear”

See the appendix of Rigault’s observations on Cyprian, where he correctly interprets this “fear” of Cyprian’s. **BALUZ.**

### “He Suffered”

Above, Epistle XXXVII, p. 50:

> For their valor or honor is not diminished so as to prevent them too from being gathered among the blessed martyrs. As far as depended upon them, they endured whatever they had been prepared and ready to endure. He who offered himself to torments and death beneath the eyes of God suffered whatever he was willing to suffer.

Erasmus was undoubtedly looking back to these passages of Cyprian when interpreting the passage in Josephus’s book *On the Sovereignty of Reason*, where it reads:

> And although fortune denies him the opportunity of experiencing them, he has nevertheless endured all that he was willing to suffer.

For those who had undergone tortures but had not been killed were also counted as martyrs. Commodianus, Instruction 48:

> There are many [Col. 0776B] martyrdoms without the shedding of blood.

Saint Paulinus, Poem 14, on Saint Felix:

> He gained the heavenly honor of a martyr without bloodshed.  
> For he died a confessor, having incurred sufferings not by choice.

And a little later:

> Martyrdom without slaughter is pleasing, if the mind  
> And faith are ready to endure and glow warmly for God.  
> The will to suffer suffices and is the highest verbal attestation of merit.

Sulpicius Severus, in his epistle to Aurelius concerning Saint Martin:

> For although the circumstances of the time could not provide him with martyrdom, he will nevertheless not lack the glory of a martyr, because in desire and virtues he both could and wished to be a martyr.

Jerome, in the epistle to Rufinus beginning “God bestows more,” recalls the Egyptian confessors who were already martyrs in will. Arnulf of Lisieux, in [Col. 0776C] the epistle written to Saint Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, published on p. 487 of volume II of d’Achery’s *Spicilegium* and among Saint Thomas’s epistles, book I, Epistle 85:

> For although the cause has not yet reached the shedding of blood, devotion nevertheless supplies the merit of suffering.

**BALUZ.**

### “The Tyrant Defeated”

Rufinus on Psalm XL:

> How, then, did the holy martyrs prove victorious even in their sufferings? Because although they could be killed bodily, they could never be broken in spirit. Those who killed them, however, were defeated.

**BALUZ.**

### “Later Defeated”

The emperor Decius, who perished with his son in the year 251 in the war he was waging against the Persians, as Pagius writes, correcting Baronius, who wrote that this happened while Decius was fighting against the Goths ravaging Moesia and Thrace. **BALUZ.]**

### IX

Then, after he had accepted an episcopate that had neither been solicited [Col. 0774A] nor extorted [Note: [Col. 0773A] “By canvassing or extortion, but by God’s—,” Lam. Bod. 2; “by lot,” Fab.], but assumed by the will of God, who makes priests—what courage he displayed in the episcopate itself once he had assumed it, what strength of spirit, what firmness [Note: [Col. 0773B] “What firmness of faith,” Bod. 3.] of faith! With a sincere heart we ought both to perceive this thoroughly and to praise it: he sat fearless at Rome upon the priestly chair at a time when the tyrant [Note: [Col. 0774A] “At a time when the tyrant,” Lam. Bod. 2.], hostile to the priests of God, was threatening things speakable and unspeakable, when he would have heard much more patiently and tolerably that a rival emperor had been raised against him than that a priest of God had been appointed at Rome [Note: [Col. 0774A] Thus Lam. Ebor. Bod. 1, 2. Lin. NC. 1. Spir. Vet. Innom. Eras. Manut.; “a rival at Rome,” Pam.]!

Should not this man, dearest brother, be proclaimed with the highest testimony to his courage and faith? [Col. 0775A] Should he not be counted among the glorious confessors and martyrs, since he sat for so long awaiting the executioners of his body and the avengers of the raging tyrant, who might attack Cornelius with the sword, crucify him, roast him with fire, or rend his entrails and limbs [Note: [Col. 0775B] “Lacerate,” Lam. Bod. 2. Ebor. NC. 1.] with some unheard-of kind of punishment, because he resisted the deadly edicts and trampled upon threats, tortures, and torments by the strength of faith?

Although the majesty and goodness of the protecting Lord also protected, once made, the priest whom He had willed to be made [Note: [Col. 0775B] “Whom He had willed to suffer,” Benev.], nevertheless, so far as his devotion [Col. 0776A] and fear were concerned, Cornelius suffered whatever it was possible for him to suffer; and by his priesthood he defeated beforehand the tyrant who was later defeated by arms and war.

[Note: [Col. 0776C]

### X. “Communication”

Three English manuscripts read “communion.” The word “communication” is more characteristic of Cyprian. The disgraceful and malicious allegations that were soon afterward said to be spread about Cornelius appear to have consisted of this twofold accusation: [Col. 0776D] namely, both that he had been stained by the blemish of a certificate and that he had communicated with those who had sacrificed. The latter accusation arose because he communicated with some of those who were said to have sacrificed. But Cyprian clears him of this charge by showing that he communicated only with a man who, after his case had been heard, had been proved innocent, or who had been admitted to communion by the Church’s judgment. Likewise, everything he suffered for confessing the faith plainly demonstrates that he was innocent of the former charge. **COUSTANT.**

Although I know that the currently received reading has “communication,” that this is a good reading, and that I found it in six ancient manuscripts, I nevertheless preferred the reading presented by all editions older than the Manutius edition and by twelve ancient copies. **BALUZIUS.**

] [Note: [Col. 0776D]

### X.—“Certain Disgraceful Things about Him”

This is the usual practice: in every dispute one party always imputes disgraceful things to the opposing party, as is evident also from Epistles XLVIII and XLIX of Saint Cyprian [Col. 0777B] against Novatus and Novatian, and from the end of Firmilian’s epistle, where it is recorded that Cyprian was called by Pope Stephen a “false Christ,” a “false apostle,” and a “deceitful worker.” Innumerable examples of this kind occur in historical writers. So too in the *Petition* of Marcellinus and Faustinus against Pope Damasus and in the epistle of the Council of Aquileia against Ursicinus, Damasus’s rival. In Optatus we read that accusations were fabricated against Caecilian, bishop of Carthage, so that his ordination might be called defective. There is no need to range through the histories of later times. See nevertheless our notes on the *Lives of the [Col. 0777C] Avignon Popes*, pp. 702, 1239. **BALUZ.**

### “Communion”

Although I know that the currently received reading has “communication,” that this is a good reading, and that I found it in six ancient manuscripts, I nevertheless preferred the reading presented by all editions older than the Manutius edition and by twelve ancient copies. **BALUZ.]**

### X

As for the fact that certain disgraceful and malicious things are spread about him, I do not want you to be surprised. You know that this is always the devil’s work: to lacerate the servants of God with lies and to defame a glorious name with false reports, so that those who shine brightly in the light of their own conscience may be befouled by the rumors of others.

You should know, however, that our colleagues have investigated and have ascertained with complete certainty that he was stained by no blemish [Note: [Col. 0776B] “That he was now stained by no,” Lam. Bod. 2.] of a certificate, as some proclaim; nor [Col. 0777A] did he enter into sacrilegious communication [Note: [Col. 0777B] “Sacrilegious communion,” Lam. Ebor. NC. 1.] with bishops who had sacrificed. Rather, he joined with us only those whose cases had been heard and whose innocence had been established.

[Note: [Col. 0777C]

### XI. On Trophimus

Among the examples by which Novatian’s adherents sought to persuade others that Cornelius had entered into sacrilegious communication with those who had sacrificed, they cited the case of Trophimus. Hence it follows that the opinion in Valois’s notes on Eusebius, p. 133, cannot stand: he thinks that this Trophimus was Novatian’s ordainer, who, moved to repentance, returned to Cornelius and was admitted, with the consent of the people, to lay communion. **COUSTANT.**

### “Our Dearest Brother”

The common editions, which took their text from Erasmus’s, add “Cornelius.” But since I did not find the name of Cornelius in the ancient editions, [Col. 0777D] and it is likewise absent from sixteen ancient manuscripts, I judged that the authority of so many ancient copies ought to prevail against the error. Indeed, I found the name of Cornelius in no old manuscript except the Saint-Éloi manuscript. Therefore, since I have no doubt that it came from a gloss, I removed it. That Trophimus belonged to the Roman clergy is evident from the beginning of this epistle. It necessarily follows from this that these statements refer to Cornelius, although his name is not expressed. **BALUZ.**

With due respect to such distinguished men, we would say that Valois and Baluze alike were mistaken: although they set out upon different paths, they agreed in assigning Trophimus to the Roman clergy. For, after carefully considering Saint Cyprian’s epistles both to Antonianus and to Pope Stephen (Epistle LXVII, Baluze’s edition), a certain learned modern scholar, a man by no means of the lowest rank, has asserted and thoroughly demonstrated in a recent dissertation that two men named Trophimus of Arles must be distinguished, one contemporary with the Apostles and the other with Saint Cyprian; and that the latter is the very man discussed both in this [Col. 0778B] Epistle LII of Cyprian and in Epistle LXVII to Pope Stephen. Cf. *Mémoires pour servir à l’histoire de l’introduction du Christianisme dans les Gaules*, by M. le Marquis de Fortia d’Urban; Paris, 1838, pp. 31 and 36; Gregory of Tours, *Works*, new edition, Paris, 1837, vol. IV, p. 337; *Annales du Hainaut*, vol. VII, p. 97; *Annales de philosophie chrétienne*, vol. XVII, pp. 7, 119. **EDITORS.**

### “Yielded to Necessity”

In the Corb. and Colb. manuscripts, as in the early editions, the reading is “to necessity.” Cyprian himself said above, no. 6, that he had yielded to the necessity of the times. In both places “yielded” means “complied with it,” namely, by relaxing somewhat the rigor of discipline, as the advantage of gathering the [Col. 0778C] brotherhood required, as is declared in the cited no. 6. **COUSTANT.**

### “They Would Have Come Accompanied by Him”

The word “would have come” is absent from the Corb. manuscript, together with the entire sentence. On this occasion Cornelius did nothing except what had previously been done, or at least approved, in the Church. For according to Tertullian, *On Prescription*, chapter 30, peace was promised to Marcion, or Cerdo, when he confessed his repentance, on condition that he restore to the Church the others whom he had instructed to their destruction.

For a remission of this kind Augustine, in Epistle formerly numbered 50 and now 185, chapter 10, no. 45, gives the following reason:

> Experience of many diseases compels the discovery of many remedies. But in cases of this kind, where, through grievous ruptures of dissension, it is not this or that individual who is in danger, but where whole peoples lie slaughtered, something must be taken away from severity so that sincere charity may bring aid in healing greater evils.

For the devout mother Church, desiring solely the salvation of her children, therefore uses severity toward certain persons only to prevent the ease of obtaining pardon [Col. 0778D] from destroying many. Consequently, when she sees that indulgence offers her the gain of very many, she does not hesitate at all to attract them to herself by this means.

For this reason the African Church judged that even their offices should be preserved for those who bring a multitude back with them to the Church. For when the *Code of Canons of the African Church*, chapter 68, decrees that those ordained in Donatus’s party, if they wish to pass corrected into the Catholic Church, should not be received in their offices, it immediately adds:

> But excepting those through whom provision is made for Catholic unity—that is, through whom Catholic unity, in the places where they dwell, shall appear either to be fully accomplished or to be assisted by manifest gains of brotherly souls.

This compensation made for unity, as the same Church calls it in that passage, was therefore Cornelius’s sole reason for not delaying to grant Trophimus peace and communion. Thus throughout different ages one and the same Spirit of the Church is discerned, although it uses different remedies according to the diversity of the times. It has always cared for the health of each member in such a way as to provide for the unity of its entire body, upon which that member’s salvation depends. **COUSTANT.**

[Col. 0779A] **“Dearest Brother.”** Cyprian adds more to these words, in which he first commends the Church’s wisdom and charity in granting peace to the lapsed, and then sets forth Novatian’s schism [Col. 0780A] and heresy. But because these matters do not directly concern Cornelius, we have judged that they should be omitted as foreign to our purpose. **COUSTANT.]**

### XI

For concerning Trophimus also, about whom you wished information to be written to you, the matter is not as the rumor and falsehood of malicious men reported it to you. For, as our predecessors often did, our dearest brother Cornelius yielded to necessity in order to gather our brethren together.

And since the greater part of the people had withdrawn with Trophimus, when Trophimus now returned to the Church, made satisfaction, confessed his former error with penitent supplication, and with complete humility and satisfaction called back the brotherhood that he had recently drawn away, [Col. 0777B] his prayers were heard. It was not so much Trophimus as a very great [Col. 0778A] number of brethren who had been with Trophimus who were admitted into the Lord’s Church [Note: [Col. 0777B] “But also how very great,” Bod. 3.]. None of them would have returned to the Church unless they had come with Trophimus accompanying them.

Accordingly, after deliberation had been held there with very many colleagues, Trophimus was received, on whose behalf the return of the brethren and the restored salvation of many made satisfaction. Trophimus was nevertheless admitted on the condition that he communicate as a layman, not—as the letters of malicious men reported to you—as though he were usurping the position of a priest.

### XII

But the report made to you that Cornelius communicates indiscriminately with those who sacrificed [Note: [Col. 0777B] “Cornelius was reported to you,” Lam. Bod. 3. Ebor. NC. 1. [Col. 0778B] Lin.] likewise arises from the fabricated rumors of apostates. For those who withdraw from us cannot praise us [Note: [Col. 0778B] Thus Lam. Ebor. NC. 1. Bod. 2; “from us” is absent from Oxon.]; nor ought we to expect [Col. 0778B] to please those who, being displeased with us, [Col. 0779A] [Note: [Col. 0779A] “Who displease us,” Lam. Ebor. NC. 1. Bod. 3.] are rebels against the Church and violently persist in soliciting brethren away from the Church. Therefore, dearest brother, do not readily listen to or believe whatever is spread either about [Col. 0780A] Cornelius or about us.

## THE SECOND PART OF SAINT CYPRIAN’S EPISTLE TO ANTONIANUS

[Col. 0779B]

### SUMMARY

The lapsed must be assisted when they are at the point of death, though the condition of all is not equal; the case of the *libellatici* is especially deserving of favorable consideration; Novatian introduced the tenets of the Stoics into the Church.—In a doubtful matter the milder course should be adopted.—Christians must by no means be deterred from martyrdom because indulgence is shown to the lapsed; those who deny peace to the lapsed oppose Holy Scripture. On Novatian’s character as a philosopher and Stoic.—It follows from the admission of adulterers to repentance that the lapsed also must be admitted. He who urges repentance after taking away the hope of pardon is mocking the penitent.

[Note: [Col. 0779C]

### XIII.—“Offocari”

Although I do not doubt that very many will disapprove of the change I have made in this passage—caring little, of course, whether it is read in this or some other way, provided that the meaning remains the same, especially if the alternative presents less trouble and difficulty—I have nevertheless made the change and removed from here the word *suffocari* (“to be suffocated”), which ignorant scribes substituted for the true reading. Since the word *offocari* was unknown to them, [Col. 0779D] they boldly substituted for it the reading they believed more suitable.

That this restoration is necessary is proved by the authority of many ancient copies. I found *offocari* written in fourteen old manuscripts, and the edition produced in England attests the same reading in five English manuscripts.

Tertullian, at the end of *On Idolatry*:

> Whatever waves of it choke them (*offocant*).

Jerome, in the epistle of consolation to the Virgin:

> What he restrains he does not choke (*offocat*), but confines.

Augustine, *Confessions*, book V, chapter 11:

> But bodily things held me especially captive and, as it were, choked me (*offocatum*) as I reflected upon them.

Seneca, *On the Shortness of Life*, chapter 2:

> Look at those to whose happiness people flock: they are choked (*offocantur*) by their own possessions.

Festus:

> *Offucare*: to put water into the throat for swallowing.

The ancient glosses found in a manuscript containing certain writings of Cyril:

> ἀποπνίγω: “I choke” (*offoco*), “I suffocate” (*suffoco*).

The Greek–Latin *Onomasticon*, formerly published at Basel but afterward reprinted by Bonaventura Vulcanius:

> *offoco*, ἀποπνίγω: “I choke.”

Florus, book II, chapter 11, speaking of the Gallograecians:

> But some were bound fast by the strangeness of the sight, when they attempted the chains with their bites and mouths, when they offered their throats to be choked by one another.

[Col. 0780C] In the same manner they also said *obrogare*, as in Livy, Cicero, Florus, and perhaps elsewhere. In Saint Augustine, book VI *Against the Donatists*, chapter 17, it is written: “the wrath of condemnation and the choking effect (*offectura*) of error.” There the most distinguished authors of the new edition of Saint Augustine’s works observe that the editions of Amerbach and Erasmus have *offocatum*, but that most manuscripts have *offectura*, while in Cyprian the reading is *offectura*. [Col. 0780D] This is, of course, in the opinion delivered by Munnulus of Girba in the Council of Carthage concerning the baptism of heretics, as we shall state there. **BALUZ.**

### “Are to Be Equated”

Six old manuscripts read: “That man has been equated.” This reading may be good. **BALUZ.**

### “Struggled”

It must be admitted that I found this reading only in the Fossatensis manuscript, which is certainly excellent, and in the oldest editions. Other manuscripts, admittedly greater in number, have “resisted.” I nevertheless prefer the reading I have printed, because “to struggle” properly belongs to combatants, such as the martyrs were; and it is certain that they did not resist, but endured torments and deaths with a willing spirit.

Cyprian himself says in the book *To Demetrianus*, p. 221:

> None of us resists when he is arrested.

And in the book *On the Good of Patience*, p. 250, speaking of Abel, he says:

> He neither opposes nor resists his fratricidal brother, but, humble and gentle, is patiently killed.

**BALUZ.**

### “Completion” (*Perfunctione*)

In five old manuscripts “suffering” (*passione*) is written. Five others, two English manuscripts, and the Morel edition have “agreement” (*pactione*). Two others have *passione* or *patione*.

[Col. 0781C] **“Many While Living.”** Thus ten old manuscripts. Two others and the earlier editions have “saved.” The Corbie manuscript has “paying,” by an obvious error. **BALUZ.]**
XIII. For if any are overtaken by infirmities, assistance is given to them in danger, as was agreed. Yet after assistance has been given and peace granted to those in peril, [Col. 0779C] they cannot be strangled [Note: [Col. 0779C] Thus Bod. 1, 2; Lam.; Ebor.; NC. 1; Lin.] or crushed by us, or driven by our own force and hand [Col. 0780B] to the issue of death, as though, because peace is granted to the dying, those who have received peace must necessarily die. Rather, this very fact reveals a sign [Note: [Col. 0779C] “Judgment,” Oxon.] of divine goodness [Note: [Col. 0779C] “Goodness,” Cod. S. Dyon.; Rem. “Patience.”] and paternal gentleness [Note: [Col. 0779C] “Gentleness,” Fux.]: those who receive a pledge of life in the peace granted to them are also preserved here in life [Note: [Col. 0780C] “These also,” Neap.] after receiving that peace. And therefore, if after peace has been received a reprieve is granted by God, no one ought to make this a charge against the priests, since it was once agreed that assistance should be given to the brethren in danger.

Nor should you suppose, dearest brother, as some appear to do, that those who obtained certificates ought to be placed on the same level as those who sacrificed, since even among those who sacrificed both the circumstances and the grounds are often different. For the man who immediately rushed of his own will to the impious sacrifice is not to be equated with the man who struggled and contended for a long time and arrived at that deadly act under compulsion [Note: [Col. 0780C] “Was driven by necessity; nor he who,” Cod. Gratianop.]; nor the man who betrayed both himself and all his household with the man who himself approached the ordeal on behalf of everyone and, through his own experience of danger [Note: [Col. 0780C] “Agreement,” Lam.; Ebor.; Bod. 1, 2; NC. 1; Ver. “Suffering,” Ben.; Neap.], [Col. 0781A] protected his wife, his children, [Col. 0780C] and his entire household; nor the man who compelled his tenants [Note: [Col. 0781C] “His intimates,” Bod. 1.] or friends to commit the crime with the man who spared his tenants and coloni, and who also received under his own roof and into his hospitality very many brethren [Note: [Col. 0781C] “Brethren, but also more,” Gratianop.] who were departing as exiles and fugitives [Note: [Col. 0781C] “Began to provide hospitality,” Bod. 3.], thereby displaying and presenting to the Lord many living [Note: [Col. 0781C] “Paying much,” Corb.] and unharmed souls to intercede for the one soul that had been wounded.

> **Note [Col. 0781C]**
>
> **XIV.—While the bishop was expounding.** Optatus, book V: “It remains for you to say that he communicated with the people. It is established that he spoke something among the people, but for the purpose of introducing some matter, not, however, of expounding it, which belongs to bishops.” See our notes on Lupus of Ferrières, p. 479. **BALUZE.**
>
> **When we were heard.** A correction above the line in the Monastery manuscript reads: “when our lamentations were heard.” It is plainly from a gloss. **BALUZE.**

XIV. Since, therefore, there is great diversity even among those who sacrificed, what lack of mercy and what bitter harshness it is to join those who obtained certificates with those who sacrificed, when the man for whom a certificate was accepted can say:

“I had previously read and, while the bishop was expounding the matter, had learned that one must not sacrifice to idols and that a servant of God ought not to worship images. Therefore, so that I might not do what was unlawful, when the opportunity of obtaining a certificate was offered—which certificate I would not have accepted unless the opportunity had been pointed out—I either went to the magistrate [Col. 0781B] or commissioned another person to go, and declared that I was a Christian, that it was not lawful for me to sacrifice [Note: [Col. 0781C] “Altogether unlawful for me,” Vat.], that I could not approach the altars of the devil, and that I was giving a payment for this purpose, so that I would not do what is unlawful.”

Yet now even this man, who has been stained by a certificate, after learning from our admonitions that he ought not to have done even this—although his hand is pure and no contamination from the deadly food has polluted his mouth—nevertheless weeps when he hears us and laments that his conscience has been polluted. He is now admonished concerning his offense and declares that, having been deceived more by error than by crime, he is henceforth instructed and prepared.

> **Note [Col. 0781D]**
>
> **XV.—Weary.** The old editions and several ancient books have “fallen.” That reading can be confirmed from the Gospel according to Matthew, to which this passage refers, since it is clear from it that the sheep was not merely weary but fallen. I nevertheless prefer the former reading. For that sheep is rightly called weary because it had labored through much wandering, to use Jerome’s words in the letter *On the Prodigal Son* to Pope Damasus. **BALUZE.**

XV. If we reject the repentance of these people, who possess some confidence arising from a tolerable conscience, they are immediately swept away—with their wives and children, whom they had preserved unharmed—into heresy or schism [Note: [Col. 0781C] “Into heresy as into schism,” MR.], at the devil’s invitation. [Col. 0781C] And on the day of judgment it will be charged against us both that we did not tend the wounded sheep [Col. 0782A] and that, for the sake of one wounded sheep, we destroyed many that were whole. The Lord left the ninety-nine healthy sheep, sought the one that was wandering and weary, and, when he found it, carried it upon his own shoulders (Luke 15; Matt. 18); yet we would not merely fail to seek the fallen [Note: [Col. 0781C] “The weary,” Lam.; Bod. 2; Ebor.; NC. 1; Ver.], but would even drive away those who come to us. And although false prophets do not now cease to ravage and tear apart Christ’s flock, we would give [Note: [Col. 0782C] “We shall give,” Bod. 3.] dogs and wolves an opportunity, so that those whom the hostile persecution did not destroy we ourselves might destroy by our harshness and inhumanity.

And where, dearest brother, will there be room for what the Apostle says: “I please everyone in all things, not seeking what is profitable to me, but what is profitable to the many, so that they may be saved. Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (1 Cor. 10:33; 11:1)? And again: “I became weak to the weak, so that I might win the weak” (1 Cor. 9:22). And again: [Col. 0782B] “If one member suffers, the other members suffer with it; and if one member rejoices, the other members rejoice with it” (ibid. 12:26).

> **Note [Col. 0781D]**
>
> **XVI.—Sins are equal.** Jerome, in his letter to Pammachius *On the Dormition of Paulina*, in the first book *Against Pelagius*, and in book II *Against Jovinian*, says that the Stoics maintained that sins are equal. Lactantius, chapter 38 of the *Epitome*, speaking of Zeno, the master of the Stoics: [Col. 0782C] “For his assertion that sins are equal arises from the same mercilessness with which he assails compassion as though it were a disease.” Plutarch, in his book *On Stoic Self-Contradictions*, writes that neither is one sin greater than another nor does one virtue excel another. Cassian, book V, chapter 11: “For all the virtues have one nature, although it appears [Col. 0782D] to be divided into many kinds and names.” Seneca, Letter 120: “For vices border upon virtues.” And Jerome, *Against the Luciferians*: “Vices lie close to virtues.” So also Quintilian, book III, chapter 7, and book VIII, chapter 3. Cicero, book III of *On Duties*: “I myself have argued that whoever possesses one virtue possesses them all.” See also the *Paradoxes*, where these matters are treated more fully. Yet in the first book *On the Orator*, the same author wrote that the discourse of those who say that whoever possesses one virtue possesses them all is thorny and meager. Seneca appears not to have approved that position. For he says in Letter 66: “How can goods be equal? Therefore, the virtues are equal to one another.” See Muretus there. See also Saint Augustine’s reply to Nectarius’s letter concerning the affair at Calama. **BALUZE.**
>
> **Exceedingly gentle.** In six of our ancient books and four English manuscripts, “the gentlest” is written. This comes closer to the common edition of the book of Numbers, which has “the meekest.” **BALUZE.**
>
> **Has shown mercy.** Erasmus was the first to print it thus. I found this reading in nine ancient manuscripts. Three others and the early editions read “is merciful.” That is the reading of the Vulgate edition of the Gospel according to Luke. **BALUZE.**

XVI. The reasoning of the philosophers and Stoics is one thing, dearest brother; they say that all sins are equal and that a serious man ought not readily to be moved. But there is a very great difference between Christians and philosophers. And since the Apostle says, “Take care that no one plunder you through philosophy and empty deceit” (Col. 2:8), we must avoid what does not [Note: [Col. 0782C] Thus Lam.; Bod. 3; Ebor.; Lin.; NC. 1. “Things which do not must be avoided,” Oxon.] proceed from the clemency of God but descends from the presumption of a harsher philosophy.

Concerning Moses, however, we read it said in Scripture: “And Moses was an exceedingly gentle man” [Note: [Col. 0782C] “The gentlest,” Lam.; Ebor.; Bod. 2; NC. 1.] (Num. 12:3). And the Lord says in his Gospel: “Be merciful [Note: [Col. 0782C] “Therefore be merciful,” Bod. 3; “As also the Father,” Ver.], just as your Father has shown mercy to you” [Note: [Col. 0782C] “Is merciful,” Bod. 3.] [Col. 0782C] (Luke 6:36). And again: “The healthy have no need of a physician, [Col. 0783A] but those who are ill” (Matt. 9:12).

What medicine can the man practice who says, “I tend only the healthy, who have no need of a physician”? We ought to offer our aid and our remedy [Note: [Col. 0783C] “Our aid and remedy to the wounded,” Bod. 1.] to the wounded. Nor should we suppose that those whom we see wounded by deadly persecution are dead, but rather that they lie half-alive [Note: [Col. 0783C] “Wounded,” Lam.; Bod. 2; Ebor.; NC. 1.]; for if they were entirely dead, confessors and martyrs would never afterward be made from those same people [Note: [Col. 0783C] “The same people would never,” Bod. 3.].

> **Note [Col. 0783D]**
>
> **With the consolation.** Thus seven ancient books and the Manutian edition. The early editions, therefore, and seven other ancient books have “consolation.” The negation is absent from four ancient manuscripts. In one of mine it is written: “he departs in the consolation of peace and communion.” **BALUZE.**

XVII. But because there is within them that which, when repentance follows [Note: [Col. 0783C] “Repentance frequently,” Lam.; Ebor.; Lin.; NC. 1; Bod. 2.], may recover strength for faith, and may be armed with strength for courage through repentance [Note: [Col. 0783C] “From the strength of repentance,” Ebor.; NC. 1; Bod. 2; “The strength of repentance is armed,” Vatic.]—something that cannot be armed if a person collapses in despair, if, harshly and cruelly separated from the Church, he turns to pagan ways and worldly works, or, rejected by the Church, passes over to heretics and [Col. 0783B] schismatics, where, even if he should later be killed for the Name [Note: [Col. 0783C] “The name of Christ,” Bod. 2.], he will not be able to receive the crown in death, because he is situated outside the Church and divided from unity and love—for this reason, dearest brother, it was agreed, after the circumstances of each individual had been examined, that those who obtained certificates should meanwhile be admitted and that those who sacrificed should be assisted at the point of death. For there is no *exomologesis* in the underworld, nor can anyone be compelled by us to repent if the fruit of repentance is withheld.

If the battle comes first [Note: [Col. 0783C] “If, therefore, the battle,” Lam.; Ebor.; NC. 1.], he will be found strengthened by us and armed [Note: [Col. 0783C] “Will be found also armed,” Lam.; Ebor.; Lin.; NC. 1.] for battle. But if infirmity presses him before the battle [Note: [Col. 0783C] “If infirmity comes,” Lam.; Ebor.; NC. 1; Bod. 2.], he departs with the consolation of peace and communion.

> **Note [Col. 0783D]**
>
> **Bear.** The Sorbonne manuscript has “bearing”; the Fux manuscript, “carry.” And this is the reading of the Vulgate edition of the Epistle to the Galatians. **BALUZE.**
>
> **Supporter.** The common reading, which most ancient manuscripts prefer, has “righteous.” Yet in five equally ancient manuscripts “supporter” is written. Pamelius testifies that it was also read in this form in the Affligem manuscript. I believe this reading is better, both because the English scholars testify that the Bodleian manuscript reads “He is himself supporter and intercessor,” and because it departs from the Vulgate edition of John’s Epistle. It is established, moreover, that Cyprian did not use the edition we use today. For immediately afterward he writes “offenses,” as he customarily does, in place of what our Vulgate reads as “sins.” Although I have seen “sins” written in two ancient copies, this arose, I think, through the audacity of those who believed that passages of Holy Scripture quoted by Cyprian ought to be corrected according to our Vulgate edition. Furthermore, I think that the scribe of the Bodleian manuscript read “supporter” in his exemplar and, wishing to explain it, [Col. 0785B] added “and intercessor.” It is certain that one of these terms is sufficient. **BALUZE.**

XVIII. For we do not prejudge the Lord who will judge, so as to prevent him, if he finds the sinner’s repentance full and just, [Col. 0783C] from then ratifying what has been established here by us [Note: [Col. 0783C] “Has been established,” Lam.; Ebor.; NC. 1.]. But if anyone deceives us by feigning repentance, let God, who is not mocked (Gal. 6) and who looks upon the human heart (1 Sam. 16), judge those matters that we have perceived less fully, and let the Lord correct the judgment of his [Col. 0784A] servants.

Provided only, dearest brother, that we remember that it is written, “A brother who helps a brother will be exalted” (Prov. 18:19), and that the Apostle also said: “Let each of you take heed, lest you too be tempted; bear one another’s burdens [Note: [Col. 0783C] “Your burdens,” Lam.; Ebor.; NC. 1.], and thus you will fulfill the law of Christ” (Gal. 6:1–2). Likewise, rebuking the proud [Note: [Col. 0783D] “Likewise the proud,” Lam.; “He states,” Lam.] and breaking their arrogance, he states in his epistle: “Let the one who thinks he stands take care lest he fall” (1 Cor. 10:12); and elsewhere he says: “Who are you to judge another’s servant? He stands or falls before his own lord. But he will stand, for God is able to establish [Note: [Col. 0784C] “To strengthen,” Lam.; Lin.; Ebor.; Bod. 1, 2, 3; NC. 1.] him” (Rom. 14:4).

John, too, declares that Jesus Christ our Lord is an advocate and intercessor for our sins, saying: “My little children, I write these things to you so that you may not [Col. 0784B] sin; and if anyone sins, we have as our advocate with the Father Jesus Christ the supporter, and he himself is the propitiation [Note: [Col. 0784C] “He is himself supporter and intercessor,” Bod. 3; “He himself is intercessor,” Lam.] for our offenses” (1 John 2:1–2). And Paul the Apostle also wrote in his epistle: “If, while we were still sinners, Christ died for us, much more, now justified in his blood, shall we be delivered [Note: [Col. 0784C] “Set free,” Ver.; Man.] through him from wrath” (Rom. 5:8–9).

XIX. Reflecting upon his goodness and clemency, we ought not to be so bitter or harsh, or inhuman in cherishing the brethren [Note: [Col. 0784C] Thus Bod. 1, 2. “Priests,” Oxon.; Lam.; Ebor.; Lin.; NC. 1. “And harsh,” Bod. 3.], but should grieve with those who grieve and weep with those who weep, and lift them up as far as we can by the assistance and consolation of our love. We ought neither to be so unyielding and obstinate [Note: [Col. 0784C] “Obstinate and stubborn,” Cod. Gratianop.] as to beat down their repentance [Note: [Col. 0784C] Thus Bod. 1, 2; Lam.; Ebor.; MR. “To pour back,” Imp.], nor, again, so lax and yielding as rashly to relax the terms of communion [Note: [Col. 0784C] “We ought to relax,” Lam.; Ebor.; Bod. 2.].

Look: our wounded brother lies there, injured by the adversary in battle. On that side the devil strives to kill the man he wounded; on this side Christ exhorts us not to let the man he redeemed perish entirely [Note: [Col. 0784C] “That which perish,” Bod. 3.]. Which of the two do we assist? On whose side [Note: [Col. 0784C] “On which side,” Bod. 1; Neap.] do we stand? Do we favor the devil [Note: [Col. 0784C] “Do we serve the devil,” Lam.] so that [Col. 0785A] he may destroy, and pass by our half-alive brother as he lies there, like the priest [Note: [Col. 0785B] Thus Lam.; Ebor.; NC. 1; Bod. 1, 2.] and the Levite in the Gospel (Luke 10)? Or, as priests of God and Christ, imitating what Christ both taught and did, do we snatch the wounded man from the adversary’s jaws, so that, once healed [Note: [Col. 0785B] “Now healed,” Bod. 1, 3.], we may reserve him for God the Judge [Note: [Col. 0785B] “We reserve,” Bod. 1.]?

> **Note [Col. 0785B]**
>
> **XX.—For adulterers also.** Two ancient copies add, “that is, adulterers.” But that is a gloss. The decree of Pope Zephyrinus in Tertullian’s book *On Modesty*: “I remit the offenses of both adultery and fornication for those who have completed their penance.” Here I advise Baronius and Rigault in passing that they wrongly supposed Zephyrinus’s edict to have been framed in this way: “The bishop of bishops decrees: I remit the offenses of adultery,” etc. For the bishops of Rome never used that ambitious and offensive manner of speaking, especially in that ancient period. They placed only their own names at the head, as can also be seen in [Col. 0785C] Pope Cornelius’s letters to Cyprian. **BALUZE.**
>
> **It is one thing, when cast into prison, not to leave it, etc.** For Cyprian these statements are equivalent: to stand awaiting pardon; when cast into prison, not to leave it until one has paid the last farthing; and, tormented by prolonged grief for one’s sins, to be cleansed and purified for a long time by fire. The following, conversely, are also equivalent: to attain glory; immediately to receive the reward of faith and courage; and to have purged all sins by suffering. Through these expressions he undoubtedly distinguishes the state after this life of the fallen who had not yet completed their penance from the state of the martyrs. Accordingly, this passage contributes wonderfully to confirming the Church’s tradition concerning Purgatory, as Martin Pérez de Ayala, the most reverend Bishop of Guadix, also observed before me. Cyprian is alluding to the Scriptures, Matthew 5 and 1 Corinthians 3. The former passage is interpreted in the same way by St. Jerome on Matthew and Ambrose on Luke, chapter 12; the latter by Origen, Homily 6 on Exodus and Homily 8 on Leviticus; Ambrose, Theodoret, and Oecumenius in their commentaries; [Col. 0785D] Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter 69, on Psalm 36, and *City of God* XXI, chapter 26; Paulinus of Nola in his paraphrase of Psalm 1 and his letter to Severus; and Gregory, *Dialogues* IV, chapter 7.
>
> So that we may not quarrel over the name, the suffrages for the dead offered in sacrifices and ecclesiastical prayers, which have existed from the age of the Apostles onward, indicate that there is some place in which they are punished. Otherwise, prayer that they may be released from punishment would be made in vain. Nevertheless, the name “Purgatory,” or “purgatorial punishments,” is not so recent, as is recalled by St. Augustine, *Enchiridion*, at the chapter cited; *City of God* XX, chapter 25, and XXI, chapter 13; Gregory at the place cited, on the third penitential Psalm, and frequently elsewhere; and Bede on Psalm 37 and in a certain manuscript sermon upon John 1, “John bears witness concerning him.” Besides Cyprian in this passage and the others cited above, the purifying fire is also mentioned by St. Jerome at the end of his commentary on Isaiah; Ambrose on Psalm 118, sermon 10; Maximus in the *Diadochus*, *On Spiritual Perfection*, chapter 100; Damascene, *On Those Who Have Fallen Asleep*; Eustratius of Constantinople, in his book *On the Activity* [Col. 0786B] *of the Soul after Death*; and Gennadius Scholarius, in his book *On Purgatory against the Greeks*, where he cites many opinions of the ancient Greeks. **PAMELIUS.**
>
> **Awaiting the day.** I found it written thus in five ancient manuscripts and in the edition of Manutius. The excellent and most learned Dom Pierre Coustant also testifies, in his preface to the works of Saint Hilary, §229, that he saw it written in this way in the highly esteemed Saint-Germain manuscript. In his annotation on this passage, Pamelius considers “the day of judgment” here to mean the day of each individual’s particular judgment.
>
> Nicolas Le Fèvre, by contrast, in his printed copy of Cyprian, now mine, thinks that it ought to be understood as the Last Judgment, in accordance with an opinion held by many great men, both Greek and Latin, in the primitive Church: they maintained that only the martyrs enjoy divine glory before that Last Judgment, while the others are deferred until it, and that this was also Tertullian’s position. Rigault copied this passage of Nicolas Le Fèvre in the additions to his observations on Cyprian. The controversy that occurred in the time of Pope John XXII concerning the beatific vision is well known. On this matter see Erasmus’s annotations on chapter 7 of Paul’s First Epistle to the Corinthians; our notes on the lives of the Avignon popes, pp. 788 and 798; and our preface to the history of Tulle. Others understand this passage of Cyprian as referring to the fire of Purgatory. Jean Daillé attacks them vehemently in book IV, chapter 10, *On Human Punishments and Satisfactions*. **BALUZE.**
>
> Rigault says: Concerning Pamelius’s note, where it is said that the passage must be understood of the day of each person’s particular judgment, Nicolas Le Fèvre remarks: “No; rather, it refers to the Last Judgment, according to an opinion held by many great men, both Greek and Latin, in the primitive Church, who maintained that only the martyrs enjoy divine glory before that Last Judgment, while the others are deferred until the Last Judgment. This was also Tertullian’s position.”
>
> But that was not the position of our Cyprian, who repeatedly teaches in his book *On Mortality* that the person who fears death is the one who is unwilling to go to Christ; and that it is then that peace comes to God’s servants, then that their rest is free and tranquil, because, drawn out from the storms of this world, “we seek the harbor of our dwelling and eternal tranquility, when, after this death has been paid off, we come to immortality.” Then the righteous are called to refreshment and the unrighteous are dragged away to punishment; protection is more swiftly granted to the faithful, punishment to the faithless. Hence, “Let us embrace the day that assigns each person to his own dwelling, that, after snatching us from here and freeing us from worldly snares, restores us to Paradise and the heavenly kingdom.”
>
> Meanwhile, it must be acknowledged that all the ancients believed that the day of judgment would bring terrors that even the saints must fear; hence perhaps prayers were composed even for martyrs. “We always offer sacrifices for them,” Cyprian says in Epistle 39, “whenever we celebrate the sufferings and anniversaries of the martyrs with annual commemoration.” See what was said on Epistles II and XII. **FELL.**

XX. Nor should you suppose, dearest brother, that the courage of the brethren is thereby diminished or martyrdoms cease because penance has been granted to the fallen and the hope of peace offered to the penitent. The strength of those who truly have faith remains immovable, and among those who fear and love God with their whole heart [Note: [Col. 0785B] “With the heart alone toward God,” Bod. 1.] integrity steadfastly and firmly endures.

For adulterers, too, are granted a period of penance by us, and peace [Col. 0785B] is given to them. Yet virginity does not therefore disappear from the Church, [Col. 0786A] nor does the glorious resolve of continence [Note: [Col. 0786B] “Continence and resolve,” MR.] grow feeble because of the sins of others. The Church flourishes, crowned with so many virgins, and chastity and modesty preserve the constancy of their glory; nor is the strength of continence broken because penance and pardon are granted to the adulterer.

It is one thing to stand awaiting pardon, another to attain glory; one thing, when cast into prison, not to leave it until one has paid the last farthing (Matt. 5), another immediately to receive the reward of faith and courage (1 Cor. 3); one thing, tormented by prolonged grief [Note: [Col. 0786B] “By the torment of grief,” Lam.] for one’s sins, to be cleansed and purified for a long time by fire [Note: [Col. 0786B] “To be divinely purified,” Bod. 2, 3; Lam.; Ebor.], another to have purged all sins by suffering; one thing, finally, to await the day of judgment for the Lord’s sentence, another immediately to be crowned by the Lord.

> **[Col. 0787A] Note [Col. 0787C]**
>
> **XXI.—Our predecessors.** That is, the bishops who governed the African Church before Cyprian’s time. Cyprian therefore says that certain African bishops thought peace should not be given to adulterers. That this opinion existed in Africa before Cyprian’s time is also clear from Tertullian’s testimony; in the book just cited he vehemently declaims against Pope Zephyrinus because the latter remitted the offenses of adultery and fornication for those who had completed their penance. Meanwhile, however, the bond of concord remained among the African bishops, although some held different views about reconciling the fallen. **BALUZE.**
>
> Albaspinaeus rather ill-advisedly asserts that pardon was not granted to adulterers before Novatian’s time, when Cyprian openly teaches the contrary here. Far more probable is Morinus’s position: he maintains that penitential punishments were more lenient until the time of Novatus, and he establishes this from the apostolic censure in 1 Corinthians 5, from the practice of John related from Clement of Alexandria by Eusebius, *History* II, chapter 17, and from other writings of the ancients.
>
> Certainly, when Tertullian inveighs against Zephyrinus as a patron of unchastity, he acknowledges that the “Psychics,” that is, the Catholics, had formerly admitted adulterers to penance. “This title, therefore,” he says, “will also be directed against the Psychics, against the former fellowship of my own opinion with theirs as well, so that they may cast this against me all the more as a mark of fickleness.”
>
> Moreover, Dionysius, Bishop of Corinth, who was earlier than Zephyrinus, decreed that persons found guilty of any crime whatsoever should be received through penance. In his letter [Col. 0788C] to the Amastrians, as quoted by Eusebius, book IV, chapter 23: “He commands that those who turn back from any sort of fall or transgression whatsoever, or indeed from heretical error, be welcomed” (*Τοὺς ἐξ οἵας δ’ οὖν ἀποπτώσεως ἢ πλημμελείας, εἴτε μὴν αἱρετικῆς πλάνης ἐπιστρέφοντας δεξιοῦσθαι προστάττει*).
>
> Finally, St. Ignatius, in his Epistle to the Philadelphians, pronounces universally: “All who come repentantly to the unity of the Church are to be received” (*Ὅσοι ἂν μετανοήσαντες ἔλθωσιν ἐπὶ τὴν ἑνότητα τῆς Ἐκκλησίας, προσδέχεσθαι αὐτούς*). **FELL.**
>
> **And indeed.** Saint Augustine quotes this passage in his letter to Vincentius the Rogatist. **BALUZE.**

XXI. And indeed, among our predecessors, certain bishops here in our province did not think that peace should be granted to adulterers, and they entirely closed off any place for penance in cases of adultery. Yet they did not withdraw from the college of their fellow bishops, nor did they rupture the unity of the Catholic Church through obstinate adherence to their own harshness or censure, so that, because peace was given to adulterers by others, the bishop who did not give it would separate from the Church. While the bond of concord remains and the indivisible sacrament of the Catholic Church endures, each bishop arranges and directs his own conduct, being destined to render to the Lord an account of his purpose.

> **Note [Col. 0788C]**
>
> **XXII.—Penance to the fallen.** The Grenoble manuscript reads, “they do not think indulgence should be granted to the fallen.” Below, at the end of this epistle, it reads: “and that pardon and indulgence are not to be denied to the penitent.” **BALUZE.**
>
> **Have performed.** I found this reading in ten ancient manuscripts. The English scholars saw six in which it is also found. In five others that I examined, however, “have done” is written. That is the reading of the Vulgate edition of Revelation. **BALUZE.**
>
> **Joy.** The Fux manuscript reads, “joy before the angels of God in heaven,” from a gloss, as I think. **BALUZE.**
>
> **Over one sinner.** I did not wish to change anything, although I know that many excellent manuscripts prefer “over a single sinner.” For the edition I retain is also supported by the authority of numerous ancient books. **BALUZE.**
>
> **Delights.** I have seen it written thus in many ancient manuscripts and in the oldest editions. Manutius changed it and wrote “rejoices.” I certainly admit that the Manutian reading occurs in many ancient manuscripts and in the Vulgate edition of Holy Scripture. But it is established that Cyprian did not use that edition. I therefore preferred the reading of the early editions. **BALUZE.**
>
> **Malice.** I emended it thus, following the authority of the old editions, eleven of our ancient copies, and three English manuscripts. For the text of Joel’s prophecy also has “ready to relent over malice.” Manutius printed the plural, “acts of malice.” But I found that reading in only five ancient books. The Verona manuscript read [Col. 0789D] “injuries inflicted.” See Fronton du Duc’s notes on the homilies of Saint John Chrysostom, p. 14. **BALUZE.**
>
> **Preserving.** In one ancient book of mine it is written, “when he has corrected, so that he may show mercy, preserving”; in the Dijon manuscript and the more recent Reims manuscript, “showing mercy to those preserved.” **BALUZE.**
>
> **Rod.** The Grenoble and Monastery manuscripts add “iron.” Below, in this very epistle: “earthen vessels will be broken by him to whom the iron rod has been given.” Rufinus on Psalm 2: “By the iron rod is meant inflexible justice.” **BALUZE.**

XXII. I am astonished that some are so obstinate that they do not think penance should be granted to the fallen, or believe that pardon should be denied to the penitent, although it is written: [Col. 0787B] “Remember from where you have fallen, and repent, and do your former works” (Rev. 2:5). This is certainly said to one who is known to have fallen and whom the Lord exhorts to rise again through works, because it is written: “Almsgiving delivers from death” (Tob. 4:10)—certainly not from that death which Christ’s blood extinguished once for all, and from which saving Baptism and the grace of our Redeemer delivered us, but from that death which afterward creeps in through offenses.

In another place likewise, time for repentance is given, and the Lord threatens the person who does not repent [Note: [Col. 0787B] “Those who do not repent,” Lam.; Bod. 2; Ebor.]: [Col. 0788A] “I have many things against you,” he says, “because you permit your wife Jezebel, who calls herself a prophet [Note: [Col. 0787B] “Prophetess,” Bod. 3; “female prophet,” Vulg.; “prophet,” Bod. 1, 2.], to teach and seduce my servants, to commit fornication and eat things sacrificed [Note: [Col. 0787B] “Of the sacrifice,” Lam.; Ebor.; NC. 1; Manut.]; and I gave her time to repent, but she does not wish to repent of her fornication. Behold, I cast her upon a bed, and those who committed fornication with her into the greatest tribulation, unless they repent [Note: [Col. 0787C] “Have performed penance,” Bod. 1, 2, 3; Lam.; Ebor.; Lin.; NC. 1; “Have done penance,” Oxon.] of their works” (Rev. 2:20, 22). The Lord certainly would not exhort them to repentance unless he promises indulgence to the penitent.

And in the Gospel he says: “I tell you, thus there will be joy in heaven over one sinner who repents, more than over ninety-nine righteous persons who have no need of repentance” (Luke 15:7). For since it is written [Note: [Col. 0788B] “It is written, the Lord God,” Lam.], “God did not make death, nor does he delight in the destruction of the living” (Wis. 1:13), he who certainly wishes no one to perish desires sinners to repent and through repentance to return anew to life.

Therefore he also cries out through the prophet Joel and says (Joel 2:12): “And now the Lord your God says this: Return [Note: [Col. 0788B] “The Lord God: come, return,” Lin.] to me with your whole heart, together with fasting and weeping and mourning; tear [Note: [Col. 0788B] “Tear,” Bod. 2.] your hearts and not your garments, and return to the Lord your God, because he is merciful and gracious, patient and abundant in compassion, and one who bends his sentence [Note: [Col. 0788B] “Changes his sentence,” Benev.] against the malice inflicted [Note: [Col. 0788C] Thus Bod. 1; Lam.; Ebor.; NC. 1. “The acts of malice inflicted,” Oxon.]” (Joel 2:12–13).

In the Psalms [Col. 0789A] also we read at once of the severity and the clemency of God, who threatens and at the same time spares, who punishes in order to correct and, when he has corrected, preserves: “I shall visit their crimes with a rod,” he says, “and their offenses with scourges. But I shall not withdraw my mercy from them” (Ps. 88:33–34).

> **Note [Col. 0789D]**
>
> **XXIII.—Goodness.** The English scholars noted that the Bodleian manuscript reads “the source of goodness and mercy and loving-kindness.” So too in the Pithou manuscript, except that the word “source” is absent. **BALUZE.**

XXIII. The Lord also, displaying the loving-kindness of God the Father in his Gospel, says: “What man among you, if his son asks him for bread, will offer him a stone; or if he asks for a fish, will offer him a serpent? Therefore, if you, although you are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your heavenly Father give good things to those who ask [Note: [Col. 0789C] “Those who ask him,” Oxon.] him?” (Matt. 7:9–11).

Here the Lord compares a father according to the flesh with the eternal and abundant loving-kindness of God the Father. If an evil earthly father, grievously offended [Col. 0789B] by a sinful and wicked son, nevertheless afterward sees that same son reformed—having cast off the offenses of his former [Note: [Col. 0789C] “Former things,” Bod. 3.] life and been corrected by the sorrow of repentance [Note: [Col. 0789C] “And repentance, and corrected by sorrow,” Man.] toward sober and good conduct and the discipline of innocence—he both rejoices and congratulates him, and embraces with the delight of paternal exultation the son whom he had previously cast out. How much more does that one true and good Father, merciful and gracious—indeed, goodness [Note: [Col. 0789C] “Goodness itself,” Oxon.; “the source of goodness and mercy and loving-kindness,” Bod. 3.] and mercy and loving-kindness itself—rejoice in the repentance of his children? He no longer threatens punishment against those who repent, weep, and lament, but instead promises pardon and indulgence.

Hence in the Gospel the Lord calls those who mourn blessed (Matt. 5), because the person who mourns calls forth mercy; the person who is obstinate and proud heaps up for himself wrath and the punishment of the coming judgment. And [Col. 0789C] therefore, dearest brother, we have judged that those who do not repent, and who do not bear witness to sorrow for their offenses with their whole heart and by an open profession of their lamentation, must be entirely barred from the hope of communion [Col. 0790A] and peace if they begin to entreat during infirmity and danger. For it is not repentance for their offense but the warning of imminent death that compels them to ask, and the person who gave no thought to the fact that he would die is not worthy to receive consolation in death.

> **Note [Col. 0789D]**
>
> **XXIV.—By sixteen.** Pacian, in his treatise against the Novatians: “Cornelius, now bishop at Rome, had been appointed by sixteen bishops and had received possession of the vacant see.” **BALUZE.**
>
> **There is one episcopate.** “A notable passage,” Pamelius says, “for the Roman episcopate.” But he did not grasp Cyprian’s meaning, which is clear.
