There are various passages in Cyprian far more favorable to the Bishop of Rome, such as this one in Epistle LV, p. 86: “After all this, moreover, once a pseudo-bishop has been established for themselves by heretics, they dare to sail and to carry letters from schismatics and profane persons to the chair of Peter and to the principal Church [Col. 0790D] from which priestly unity arose.” Even in the period when scholastic theologians debated freely, there was one who said that all priests could be called one and the same priest, as may be seen in Giles of Rome, chapter 21 of the book *On the Pope’s Renunciation*. **BALUZE.**
Schismatics are fervent at the beginning. Here, taking the opportunity, I shall correct a passage from the acts of Pope Alexander III that is very corrupt and distorted in Baronius’s *Annals*, namely at the year 1159, § 74. It should therefore be restored as follows from an old manuscript codex of the Royal Library:

> Then indeed the heart of that heresiarch was greatly exalted, raising itself above itself like one mad and blind, unaware that, according to the saying of the blessed martyr Cyprian, schismatics are always fervent at the beginning, but cannot achieve growth, nor can they increase what they began unlawfully; instead, they immediately fail together with their perverse rivalry.

BALUZ.]

## XXIV

As regards the person of Novatian, however, dearest brother, concerning whom you wished me to write what heresy he had introduced, know that, in the first place, we ought not even to be curious about what he teaches, since he teaches outside. Whoever and whatever he may be, he is not a Christian who is not in the Church of Christ. Although he may vaunt himself [Note: [Col. 0789C] “Although he may vaunt himself and conduct himself as he pleases”: Lam., Ebor., NC. [Col. 0790C] 1, Bod. 2.] and proclaim his philosophy or eloquence in proud tones, one who has maintained neither brotherly charity nor ecclesiastical unity [Note: [Col. 0790C] “retained unity”: Oxon.] has lost even what he formerly was.

Unless, perhaps, you regard as a bishop [Col. 0790B] one who, after a bishop had been appointed in the Church by sixteen [Note: [Col. 0790C] “seventeen”: Bod. 3.] fellow bishops, strives through canvassing to be made an adulterous and alien bishop by deserters; and who, although there is one Church established by Christ throughout the whole world and divided into many members, and likewise one episcopate diffused through the harmonious multitude of many bishops, nevertheless attempts, after God’s ordinance and after the interconnected and everywhere-united unity of the catholic Church, to create a human church, and sends his new apostles through numerous cities to establish certain novel foundations of his institution. Though bishops have long since been ordained throughout all the provinces and in the individual cities—men ancient in years, sound in faith, tested under oppression, and proscribed in persecution—he dares to create other pseudo-bishops over them.

As though [Col. 0790C] he could either traverse the whole world by the obstinacy of his novel enterprise, or tear apart the framework of the ecclesiastical body [Note: [Col. 0790C] “ecclesiastical order”: Bod. 3.] by sowing his discord [Note: [Col. 0790C] “tear it apart by contamination”: Lam., Bod. 2.], he does not know that schismatics are always fervent at the beginning, but cannot achieve growth [Col. 0791A] or increase what they have begun unlawfully; instead, they immediately fail together with their perverse rivalry. Nor could he retain the episcopate even if he had previously been made a bishop, should he withdraw from the body of his fellow bishops and from the unity of the Church [Note: [Col. 0791C] “depart from unity”: Lam.], since the Apostle admonishes us to bear with one another, lest we withdraw from the unity established by God, and says: “Bearing with one another in love, diligently striving to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Eph. IV, 2–3). Therefore, one who observes neither the unity of the Spirit nor the bond of peace, and separates himself from the bond of the Church and the college of priests, can possess neither the power nor the honor of a bishop, because he was unwilling to preserve either the unity or the peace of the episcopate.

[Note: [Col. 0791C]

### XXV.—How Great a Swelling of Arrogance

Saint Augustine transcribed this passage in Book IV of *On Baptism against the Donatists*, chap. 12, as did Gratian, though not as completely [Col. 0791D] as Augustine, at 23, q. 4, chap. *Quamvis*, where it is cited from Augustine, not from Cyprian.

Salvian, Book IV, chap. 12: “For the greatest accuser of guilty men is the arrogance that usurps innocence.” The same author, in his letter to Eucherius: “For arrogance is generally the attendant of a new honor.” Honors very often change character. BALUZ.

]

## XXV

Then, moreover, how great a swelling of arrogance there is, [Col. 0791B] how great a forgetfulness of humility and gentleness, how great a display of his own arrogance, that anyone should either dare or believe himself capable of doing what the Lord did not grant even to the Apostles: to suppose that he can distinguish the tares from the wheat (Matt. XIII), or, as though it had been granted to him personally to carry the winnowing-fan openly and cleanse the threshing-floor, to attempt to separate the chaff from the grain. And although the Apostle says, “In a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and earthenware” (2 Tim. II, 20), he appears to choose the vessels of gold and silver while despising, casting away, and condemning those of wood and earthenware—although it is only on the Day of the Lord that the wooden vessels will be consumed by the fire of divine burning, and the earthenware vessels will be shattered by him to whom the iron rod has been given (Ps. II).

[Note: [Col. 0791D]

### XXVI.—Defrauders

That is, idolaters. For he will say shortly afterward, “a defrauder, which is idolatry.” Jerome, in his letter to Heliodorus *On the Praise of the Solitary Life*: “Every fornicator, or unclean person, or covetous person, or defrauder—which is the service of idols—has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God.” This is taken from Paul’s Epistle to the Ephesians. BALUZ.

**He who commits adultery.** Much could be said on this subject, from which I refrain. Nevertheless, I cannot remain silent about something that I know must be corrected in Commodian, *Instructions* 10 and the following instruction, where *moechus* (“adulterer”) and *moechia* (“adultery”) must be restored in place of the *Maius* and *Maia* printed by Rigaltius. The same restoration must also be made in *Instruction* [Col. 0792C] 12, where Rigaltius printed *Maria* in place of *moecha* (“adulteress”). For I am presenting the readings of an old book. BALUZ.

**Lusts.** The Foix codex reads “shameful acts.” In the letter to Donatus, p. 4: “Then it delights in threats, shamefulness in mastery.” Salvian, Book VI, chap. 8: “places and dwellings of shameful acts.” BALUZ.

**Nor should they flatter themselves.** Saint Augustine cites this passage in Book IV of *On Baptism against the Donatists*, chap. 5; so too Hincmar in his work *Fifty-Five Chapters*, chap. 47, p. 563. BALUZ.]

## XXVI

Or, if he has appointed himself the examiner and judge of heart and reins, [Col. 0791C] let him judge all things equally. Since he knows that it is written, “Behold, you have been made well; sin no more, lest something worse happen to you” (John V, 14), let him separate defrauders and adulterers from his side and company, since the case of the adulterer is much [Col. 0792A] graver and worse than that of the certificate-holder (*libellaticus*): the latter sinned under compulsion, the former voluntarily. The latter, believing it sufficient that he had not sacrificed, was deceived by an error [Note: [Col. 0791C] “deceived by an error, the former”: Lam., Ebor., NC. 1.]; the former, after assailing another man’s marriage or entering a brothel—the sewer and muddy abyss of the common people—violated a sanctified body and the temple of God with detestable pollution, as the Apostle [Note: [Col. 0792C] “according to the Apostle”: Lam., Ebor., NC. 1.] says: “Every sin whatsoever that a man commits is outside the body; but he who commits adultery sins against his own body” (1 Cor. VI, 18).

Yet repentance is granted even to such persons, and the hope of lamenting and making satisfaction is left to them, according to the same Apostle, who says: “I fear lest perhaps, when I come to you, I may mourn many of those who sinned before and did not repent of the uncleanness, fornications, and lusts that they committed” (2 Cor. XII, 20–21).

[Col. 0792B] [Note: [Col. 0792D]

### XXVII.—Idolaters

All the old books and the more ancient editions, both here and shortly afterward, have *idolatris* and *idolatriae* written; nevertheless, I was unwilling to alter anything, although I know that these forms are commonly written in ancient codices of the old Latin authors, and although I have an example of this spelling in Antoine d’Albon, archbishop of Lyon, who wrote it thus in his edition of Rufinus’s commentaries on the Psalms. Respect seemed due to antiquity. But the delicate sensibilities of our age also had to be satisfied. BALUZ.

**Another to be defiled.** The Foix codex: “they say that another is defiled.” In the Sorbonne codex and in one of mine: “they say that another is excused.” BALUZ.

[Col. 0793C] **The person himself is held accountable.** I preferred this reading because I found it in fifteen old books. Otherwise I would readily [Col. 0793D] have changed it to restore the reading found in the ancient editions, where it reads, “is held guilty.” For I also found that reading in four ancient copies. BALUZ.]

## XXVII

Nor should the new heretics flatter themselves in this matter by saying that they do not communicate with idolaters, since among them there are both adulterers and defrauders who are held guilty of idolatry, according to the Apostle’s words: “For understand and know this: every fornicator, or unclean person, or defrauder—which is idolatry—has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God” (Eph. V, 5). And again [Note: [Col. 0792C] “And again he says”: Lam., Ebor., NC. 1.]: “Therefore put to death your members that are upon the earth,” setting forth “fornication, uncleanness, evil desire, and covetousness, which are the service of idols; because of these the wrath of God comes” (Col. III, 5–6).

For since our bodies are members of Christ, and each of us is a temple of God, whoever violates God’s temple by adultery violates God; and whoever, in committing sins, carries out the devil’s will serves demons and idols. Evil deeds do not come from [Col. 0792C] the Holy Spirit; rather, desires born from the adversary’s prompting and from an unclean spirit compel men to act against God and serve the devil.

Thus, if they say that one person is defiled by another’s sin, and contend by their own assertion that the idolatry of the offender passes to one who does not offend, then according to their own declaration they cannot be excused from the guilt of idolatry, since it is established by apostolic proof that the adulterers and defrauders with whom they communicate are idolaters.

For us, however, in accordance with our faith and the prescribed rule of divine preaching, the principle of truth applies: each person is himself held accountable for his own sin, and one person cannot become guilty for another, since the Lord forewarns us and says: “The righteousness of the righteous shall be upon him, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be upon him” (Ezek. XVIII, 20). And again: “Fathers shall not die for their children, nor shall children die for their fathers. Each shall die in his own sin” (Deut. XXIV, 16).

Reading and holding this, therefore, we believe that no one should be barred from the fruit of satisfaction [Col. 0793B] and the hope of peace, since we know, in accordance with the faith of the divine Scriptures, that with God himself as author and exhorter sinners are brought to perform repentance, and pardon and forgiveness are not denied to those who repent.

[Note: [Col. 0793D]

### XXVIII.—Those Who Lament

Two old books have merely “the demented.” BALUZ.

**Work frequently.** That is, as I understand it, frequently perform works of mercy toward the poor; frequently give alms. See the book *On Works and Alms*. Commodian, *Instruction* 55: “You do not perform works,” that is, alms. See also *Instruction* 69. BALUZ.

**Ownership and.** I found this reading in fifteen ancient copies and in the editions of Manutius and Morel. Pamelius put “is” in place of “and.” Rigaltius followed him. The English editors restored the old reading, which is certainly better. In the Foix book it reads, “ownership and right belong.” BALUZ.]

## XXVIII

O mockery that frustrates the brotherhood! O perishable deception of wretched people who lament and are demented! O ineffective and empty tradition of heretical institution! To exhort men to the repentance of satisfaction [Note: [Col. 0793C] “to satisfaction”: Bod. 3.] and then withdraw the remedy from their satisfaction; to say to our brothers:

> Mourn and pour forth tears; groan by day and night; and, to wash away and cleanse your offense, perform works generously and frequently. But after all this you will die outside the Church. You will do everything pertaining to peace, but you will receive none of the peace [Col. 0793C] that you seek. [Note: [Col. 0793C] “you will find what you seek”: Lam., Ebor., NC. 1.]

Who would not perish at once? Who would not fail through sheer despair [Note: [Col. 0793C] “at once through sheer despair”: Lam., Ebor., NC. 1.]? Who would not turn his mind away from his resolve to lament?

Do you [Col. 0794A] think a farmer can work if you tell him:

> Cultivate the field with every skill of husbandry; diligently persist in its cultivation. But you will reap no harvest, press no vintage, gather no fruit from your olive grove, and pluck no apples from the trees.

Or if, while advising a man who possesses the ownership and use of ships [Note: [Col. 0793C] Thus Lam., Ebor., Corb., NC. 1, Lin. Imp. has: “Or if to him who possesses the use”; Benev.: “To whom while”; Vatic.: “To whom ownership.”], you say:

> Brother, purchase timber from excellent forests; frame the keel [Note: [Col. 0794C] “a strong keel”: Bod. 1, 2.] with the stoutest and choicest oaks; work so that the ship may be built and equipped with nails, ropes, and sails. But once you have done this, you will see no profit from its operations and voyages.

[Note: [Col. 0793D]

### XXIX.—Within

I prefer this reading, which the old editions, the Morel edition, and three old copies [Col. 0794C] have, also because shortly afterward Cyprian says that when the Lord comes to his Church, he will assuredly judge those whom he finds within it. [Col. 0794D] Below, Epistle 55, p. 88: “the people situated within.” There are also many similar expressions in Cyprian. Optatus, Book III: “We who dwell within and have never withdrawn from the root.” Heretics, who are outside, do not dwell within. See the notes on Epistle 76. BALUZ.

**Not even if they are killed.** The holy martyr repeats this point often, especially in the book *On the Unity of the Church*, p. 198. Hence arose the familiar saying, “It is not the punishment but the cause that makes a martyr,” which appears in Rufinus on Psalms XXXIV and XLIII and is frequently cited by Saint Augustine. Saint Pope Gregory, Book II, Indiction 10, Epistle 37, quotes it from Cyprian.

It appears, however, to have been taken from the book *On the Twofold Martyrdom, to Fortunatus*, where it is written thus: “For one who is killed is not immediately a martyr. Murderers and pirates are also killed. It is not the punishment but the cause that makes a martyr.”

Similarly, Primasius, on the third chapter of Paul’s Epistle to the Galatians, says: “It is not the punishment but the cause that makes a man guilty.”

And Saint Jerome, in Book II *Against Rufinus*, speaking of charity, which he says is [Col. 0795B] greater than faith and hope and which Paul desires rather than presumes, adds that without it “blood poured out even in martyrdom, and a body delivered to the flames, has no crown of rewards.”

The same author, on the fifth chapter of the Epistle to the Galatians:

> See how great a good charity is. If we undergo martyrdom in such a way that we wish our remains [Col. 0795C] to be honored by men; if, pursuing popular reputation, we fearlessly pour out our blood and give away our substance until we ourselves are reduced to beggary, such a work is owed not so much a reward as a punishment, and its torments belong more to unbelief than its crown to victory.

Saint Augustine, in the book *On the Correction of the Donatists*, chap. 2:

> Therefore, those who suffer persecution on account of iniquity and the impious division of Christian unity are not true martyrs; those who suffer for righteousness are.

And shortly afterward:

> The punishment of the impious can be similar, but the cause of the martyrs is dissimilar.

The Donatists who had endured the most grievous torments for Christ’s name in the persecution of Diocletian were therefore to be lamented. See their acts in Book II of our *Miscellanies*.

Guibert of Nogent, Book I, chap. 3, *On the Relics of the Saints*: “The Donatists suffered things no less severe than the martyrs, but because they were exiles from charity, they suffered in vain.”

Stephen of Tournai, in his second letter, speaking of the killing of John, dean of Orléans: “Both cause and punishment together made [Col. 0795D] our John a martyr.”

Caesarius of Heisterbach, Book VIII, chap. 64: “The cause, not the punishment, makes martyrs.” See the notes on the *Lives of the Avignon Popes*, p. 1280. BALUZ.]

## XXIX

It is to close off and cut away [Note: [Col. 0794C] “cut off”: Ver., Benev.] the path of grief and the way of repentance, so that although throughout all the Scriptures the Lord God speaks graciously to those who return to him and repent, repentance itself is abolished by our harshness and cruelty when the fruit [Col. 0794B] of repentance is withheld [Note: [Col. 0794C] “the fruit of repentance is forbidden”: Lam., Ebor., NC. 1, Bod. 2.].

But if we find that no one ought to be prevented from performing repentance, and that peace can be granted through God’s priests to those who entreat and implore the Lord’s mercy, in accordance with his own merciful and compassionate nature, then the groaning of those who mourn must be admitted, and the fruit of repentance must not be denied to those who grieve.

And because there is no confession in the underworld, nor can *exomologesis*—public confession—be performed there, those who have repented and prayed with their whole heart must be received within the Church and reserved there for the Lord, who, when he comes to his Church [Note: [Col. 0794C] Thus Lam., Bod. 3, Ebor., Lin.; “is to come to the Church”: Oxon.], will assuredly judge those whom he finds inside it.

Apostates and deserters, however, or adversaries and enemies who scatter Christ’s Church, cannot, according to the Apostle, [Col. 0794C] be admitted to the Church’s peace even if they are killed outside for the Name, since they maintained neither the unity of the Spirit nor that of the Church.

## XXX

For the present, dearest brother, I have briefly reviewed these few matters [Col. 0795A] out of many, as best I could, both to satisfy your desire and to unite you more and more closely to the fellowship of our college and body. If, however, you have the opportunity and ability to come to us, we shall be able to discuss more matters together and to treat more abundantly and fully those things that make for saving concord. I pray, dearest brother, that you may always fare well.

# EPISTLE XI

(Erasm. I, 2; Pamel., Rigalt., Baluz., LIV; Paris. LIII; Coustant. I, 167; Galland. III, 350; Routh, *Reliq. sacr.* III, 69 and 108.)

(This synodical letter of the second Council of Carthage under Saint Cyprian is given below among the acts of the Councils of Carthage celebrated in the time of Saint Cornelius.)

## IN THE YEAR OF CHRIST 252

[Note: [Col. 0795D]

### EPISTLE XII

Since this letter is of great importance among Cyprian’s epistles, a few words must be said about the time and occasion of its composition.

Persecution was imminent in the year 252 when Cyprian wrote this, and during the very days in which he composed this letter to Cornelius, he had again been demanded for the lion in the circus by the clamor of the populace, on account of the sacrifices that the people were ordered by a published edict to celebrate. The sacrifices of which Cyprian speaks appear to have been decreed because of the plague then raging under Gallus and Volusian.

The occasion for writing this letter was as follows. The party of Felicissimus dared to ordain Fortunatus as bishop at Carthage. He was one of the five presbyters who had long since fled from the Church and had been condemned by a judgment of bishops in the previous year. The schismatics had repeatedly asserted that twenty-five bishops would come to perform this ordination, but only five [Col. 0796B] attended, and they were branded with numerous marks of infamy.

Once ordained in this way, Fortunatus sent Felicissimus to Rome with letters to Cornelius. At first Cornelius rejected Felicissimus, as was proper; but afterward, moved by that man’s lies and threats, and also by the silence of Cyprian himself, whose letters had not yet been delivered, [Col. 0796C] he wrote two letters to the bishop of Carthage. In the first he reported that Felicissimus had been driven away by him; in the second, however, he indicated that he himself had been disturbed and frightened.

These events led Cyprian to write this Epistle LV to Cornelius. In it he shows that a bishop must not be frightened by fear of any danger whatsoever; vigorously defends his innocence against the schismatics’ accusations; excellently describes their conduct and wicked conspiracy; and finally proves that they ought not to have sailed to the principal Church, from which sacerdotal unity arose, since it has been established—and is equally fair and just—that a case be heard in the place where the offense was committed.

There is no doubt that after receiving this letter Cornelius formed a fair judgment of Cyprian and no longer gave ear to the wicked schismatics. BALUZ.]

# EPISTLE XII OF SAINT CYPRIAN, BISHOP OF CARTHAGE, TO SAINT CORNELIUS, POPE

(Erasm. I, 3; Pamel., Rigalt., Baluz., LV; Paris. LIV; Lips., Oxon. LIX; Coustant I, col. 172; Galland. III, p. 362.)

[Col. 0795B]

[Col. 0796A]

## CONCERNING THE FIVE PRESBYTERS AND FORTUNATUS THE PSEUDO-BISHOP

Concerning Cornelius’s two letters: the first, in which he reported that Felicissimus and those who had come with him had been repulsed; the second, in which he indicated that, moved by their threats, he had accepted the letters they had brought.

A bishop ought not to be deterred by fear of evils from defending ecclesiastical discipline.

Cyprian then relates that he himself was the lawful bishop, while Fortunatus had been chosen as bishop by five bishops—three of whom had been condemned, the fourth had been ordained in heresy by a condemned bishop, and the last had fallen in the persecution—and by a few men with guilty consciences. He next vividly explains the teaching of Fortunatus’s followers concerning the lapsed, the manner in which they do not cease to communicate with them, and [Col. 0796B] how they obstruct the performance of repentance.

They strive in vain to go to Rome to seek confirmation for a pseudo-bishop created by themselves. The Africans decree that a case must be heard where the offense was committed.

The great readiness and kindness with which Cyprian receives those returning to the Church.

[Note: [Col. 0796C]

### I.—I Have Read Your Letter, Dearest Brother, Which You Sent Through Our Brother Saturus the Acolyte

The appointment of Saturus as reader is mentioned above in Epistle XXIV; hence the reading of Manutius in this passage does not commend itself: [Col. 0796D] “Saturnus, who was indeed afterward appointed an acolyte.” From this it becomes clear that he had previously also been an exorcist.

For it is evident from the Roman synod under Sylvester, canon 7, that the rank of acolyte was immediately below that of subdeacon. There the presbyter is ordered to obey the bishop, the deacon the presbyter, the subdeacon the deacon, the acolyte the subdeacon, the exorcist the acolyte, and the reader the exorcist.

Nicholas I has something similar in his letter to Emperor Michael. Older than both is Cornelius, in his frequently cited letter to Fabius of Antioch. Speaking of Novatian, he says: “He did not know that there ought to be one bishop in the Church,” where he saw that there were forty-six presbyters, seven deacons, seven subdeacons, forty-two acolytes, and fifty-two exorcists together with readers and doorkeepers.

Pope Caius, the first of that name, also gives similar information where he enumerates the ranks through which one ascends to the episcopate. Ignatius, in his letter to the Antiochenes, and Apostolic Canon 42 mention the psalmist or cantor. The duties of all these are described by the Fourth Synod of Carthage, in which Saint Augustine took part. I have discussed these matters at somewhat greater length because of those who denounce the so-called seven ecclesiastical orders as innovations.

[Col. 0797C] Whether *acolythus* or *acoluthus* is the more correct spelling, I do not know. Certainly all the manuscript codices and the ancient authorities mentioned, as well as the Greek exemplar of the Synod of Carthage, read it in the former way, deriving it from ἀπὸ τοῦ κωλύειν, “from preventing,” so that the man is called not prevented but released and free, and one who, having now been initiated into sacred things, is permitted to take part in them—insofar as he supplies the subdeacon with the empty cruet so that wine may be provided.

Others, who read *acoluthus*, interpret it as deriving ἀπὸ τοῦ ἀκολουθεῖν, “from following,” so that he is, as it were, an attendant and servant of the higher orders. PAMEL.

**Saturus.** Previously appointed a reader by Saint Cyprian. See Epistles XXIV, XXIX, XXXII. BALUZ.

**Acolyte.** I have followed the common spelling, although I know that all the ancient [Col. 0797D] copies and editions write *acolytum*, without aspiration, as do the most learned men Jacques Goar, Dominique Macri, and Du Cange. Interpreters have not yet agreed on the word’s derivation, as Pamelius has also noted here. The very learned Jean Morin says in his work on sacred ordinations that acolytes are nowhere mentioned until after the year 250 after Christ’s birth. BALUZ.

**Felicissimus.** An adversary of Saint Cyprian, as Cyprian shows at length in this very letter. BALUZ.

**Excluded.** This is the true reading, which I found in ancient codices. The more recent Remigian and Bec manuscripts have “displayed.” Eight other old manuscripts and the old editions have “shown.” Although I do not doubt that these readings are utterly false, I have nevertheless recorded them so that one may readily gather from this how false readings were introduced into the books of ancient writers through the ignorance and audacity of copyists.

I shall use this [Col. 0798C] opportunity to quote a verse from Commodian’s *Instruction* 59, not as Rigaltius printed it, for he emended it badly, but as it is read in an old codex of the monastery of Saint-Aubin at Angers, from which Sirmond copied it. For Rigaltius published it from Sirmond’s transcript and did not see the old exemplar. The verse therefore reads:

> Put on the garments required to keep out the cold,

which gives excellent sense. *Ostare frigus* means “to remove or prevent the cold.” From this, says Du Cange, the French formed *oster*. BALUZ.

**Bishop.** So read the old editions and eleven old copies. I do not doubt that this reading is better [Col. 0798D] than “bishops,” although the latter is also found in certain very ancient copies. For shortly afterward he says: “It makes no difference from where terror or danger comes to the bishop.” BALUZ.]

## I

I have read your letter, dearest brother, which you sent through [Col. 0797A] our brother Satyrus the acolyte. It was amply filled with brotherly love, ecclesiastical discipline, and sacerdotal judgment. In it you indicated that Felicissimus, no new enemy of Christ but one long since excluded on account of his many very grave crimes and condemned by the judgment not only of myself but also of many fellow bishops, had been rejected by you [Note: [Col. 0797B] “you” in two Colbert and English manuscripts, Pem., Bod. 3. In some others “by you” is added here, superfluously.] there [Note: [Col. 0797C] “by you, and”: Bod. 1, 2, Lam., Ebor., NC. 1; “rejected and by him there.”].

When he came surrounded by a band and faction of desperate men, with the full vigor with which [Note: [Col. 0797C] “the full vigor which”: Bod. 1.] bishops ought to act, you drove him from the Church [Note: [Col. 0797C] “barred him from the Church”: Ver.]—the Church from which, together with those like him, he had long since been expelled by the majesty of God and the severity of Christ our Lord and Judge—lest the author of schism and division, the defrauder of money entrusted to him, the violator of virgins, and the ravager and corrupter of numerous marriages should any longer violate Christ’s incorrupt, holy, and chaste bride by the disgrace of his presence and by his shameless and incestuous contagion.

[Note: [Col. 0798D]

### II.—When I Had Observed

These words could have been omitted without any loss. They are in fact absent from certain ancient codices. We have nevertheless retained them because they appear in the ancient editions and in certain manuscript codices. BALUZ.

**The letters which.** Namely, letters from schismatics and profane persons, as he will say below. They had indeed been written against Cyprian, and Cornelius therefore refused to receive them. BALUZ.

**Was detained.** Although this is the reading in the old books and editions, I nevertheless think there is an error in this passage and that “was deserted” should be read. For it is certain that Christ was not detained by his brothers or disciples, but by the Jews. Hence it is written below that Christ was abandoned by his disciples. BALUZ.

[Col. 0799C] **A brother killed.** The audacity of ancient copyists should be noted in this passage. It is certain that the passage as it stands is sound and needs no interpretation. Yet those who knew that Abel had been killed by Cain inserted the latter’s name here in certain codices. For the Sorbonne codex reads: “Only his brother Cain killed the righteous Abel.” One old codex of mine reads: “Only Cain, his brother, killed the righteous Abel.” The remaining codices and the old editions do not have this addition. On this fratricide, see the discussion below in the notes to the book *On the Good of Patience*. BALUZ.

**Joseph, a brother.** This passage too was subjected to the copyists’ audacity. The de Thou codex and one Bodleian manuscript read: “Joseph was sold by his brothers.” The Sorbonne codex: “Joseph came into Egypt when his brothers sold him.” The Micheli codex: “Joseph came into Egypt when his brothers persecuted him.” One of my codices: “Joseph arrived in Egypt when his brothers sold him.” BALUZ.

**Permits those whom.** Certain old books vary in this passage. One of mine reads: “permits and has promised to crown.” Another of mine, the Beneventan, the Veronese, one Bodleian and the Vossian cited in the English edition, and seven others read: “permits and to be crowned.” [Col. 0800C] The Burgundy codex: “permits, who knows and crowns.” The codex of Saint-Arnoul at Metz: “since God permits him to be betrayed and crowns him.” BALUZ.

[Col. 0800D] **To threaten one who is absent.** Cyprian, namely. Felicissimus and the others who had gone with him to Rome uttered many shameful and disgraceful things against him before Cornelius, even making threats. Cyprian writes that he is astonished that those who, while at Carthage, had him present there, sailed to Rome against him and carried letters from schismatics and profane persons to Peter’s see and the principal Church, as he will afterward say. Thus Rufinus says in the book of his *Apologies against Jerome*: “He chose to tear apart in his absence one whom he could have refuted more forcefully in his presence.” BAL.]

## II

But after reading another letter of yours, brother, which you appended to the first, I was greatly astonished when I observed that you had been somewhat disturbed by the threats and terrors of those who had come. As you wrote, they had assailed you with the utmost desperation, threatening that if you did not accept the letters they had brought, they would read them publicly [Note: [Col. 0798B] “so that publicly”: Bod. 3.] [Col. 0798A] and utter many shameful and disgraceful things worthy of their own mouths.

If matters stand thus, dearest brother—if the audacity of the most wicked men is to be feared, and if evil men accomplish through recklessness and desperation what they cannot accomplish by law and equity—then the vigor of the episcopate and the sublime and divine authority of governing the Church are finished. Nor can we continue to be Christians at all, if matters have come to such a pass that we dread the threats and snares of ruined men.

For Gentiles and Jews also threaten us, as do heretics and all whose hearts and minds the devil has occupied; every day they attest their poisoned rage with frenzied voices. Yet we must not yield because they threaten; nor [Note: [Col. 0798C] “because they threaten, nor therefore”: Lin., NC. 2; “or therefore”: Lam., NC. 1, Ebor., Colb. 1.] is the hostile adversary on that account greater than Christ because he claims and assumes so much for himself in the world [Note: [Col. 0798C] “in this world”: Bod. 1.].

[Col. 0798B] The strength of faith must remain immovable among us, dearest brother; and steadfast, unshaken virtue must resist every assault and onset of the barking waves, like an opposing rock in its strength and mass. It makes no difference from where terror or danger comes to a bishop: he lives exposed to terrors and dangers, yet is made glorious through those very terrors and dangers.

Nor should we consider and look only to the threats of Gentiles or Jews, since we see that our Lord himself [Note: [Col. 0798C] “our” is absent from Oxon.] was detained by his brothers (Mark III, 21) and betrayed by the one whom he himself had chosen among [Col. 0799A] the Apostles (Matt. XXVI, 14). At the very beginning of the world, moreover, only a brother killed the righteous Abel (Gen. IV, 8); a hostile brother pursued Jacob as he fled (Gen. XXVII, 41); and Joseph [Note: [Col. 0799C] “the boy Joseph was sold when his brothers sold him”: the editions are corrected from the older manuscripts.] was sold by his brothers (Gen. XXXVII, 23).

In the Gospel we also read that it was foretold [Note: [Col. 0799C] “we read, it was foretold”: Lam., Lin., NC. 2.] that a man’s enemies would be chiefly those of his own household (Matt. X, 36), and that those who had formerly been joined by the sacrament of unanimity would themselves betray one another.

It makes no difference who betrays or rages, since God permits one to be betrayed [Note: [Col. 0799C] The common editions read: “permits those whom he has determined to be crowned. For neither.” This “for,” like the earlier “whom he determines,” appears in none of our manuscripts. “Betrays, permits, and to be crowned”: Benev., Ver.; “so as also to be crowned”: Voss. 2, Bod. 1.] and crowning. Nor is it a disgrace to us [Note: [Col. 0799C] “Nor to us”: Lam., Ebor., NC. 1, 2, Lin.] to suffer from brothers what Christ suffered; nor is it glorious for them to do what Judas did [Note: [Col. 0799C] “Judas did”: Ver., Lam., Ebor., NC. 1.].

But what self-exaltation is theirs, what swollen, puffed-up, empty boasting by those who make threats—to threaten me there while absent, when they have me here present in their power! [Col. 0799B] We do not fear their insults, by which they daily tear apart themselves and their own lives; nor do we shudder at the clubs, stones, and swords that they brandish in parricidal words. So far as their own intention is concerned, such men are murderers before God; yet they cannot kill unless the Lord permits them to kill. And although we must die only once, they nevertheless kill us daily through their hatred, words, and crimes.

[Note: [Col. 0800D]

### III.—He Has Returned to Earth

The Grenoble codex reads: “He has returned to affliction and earth.” BALUZ.

**He will become dung and worms.** The Corbie manuscript, in a second hand: “like dung, like worms.” Below we have restored “will perish” from all our manuscripts. The Oxford editors note that this reading is also found in most manuscripts of Book III of the *Testimonies*, chap. 5, where Cyprian cites the same passage, although both there and here they retain “has perished” with the other printed editions. COUST.]

### III

But for that reason, dearest brother, ecclesiastical discipline must not be abandoned, nor priestly censure relaxed, merely because we are assailed with insults or shaken by threats, since divine Scripture [Note: [Col. 0799C] In the old Colbert manuscript, the words “divine Scripture” are absent.] comes to our aid and admonishes us, saying: “But he who is presumptuous and defiant [Note: [Col. 0800C] “Defiant, trusting in his own strength,” Bod. 1. Lin. NC. 1.], a man who boasts of himself, shall accomplish absolutely nothing—he who has enlarged his soul like [Note: [Col. 0800C] “Like the underworld,” Lam. Lin. Ebor. NC. 1.] the underworld [Note: [Col. 0800C] In the same manuscript appears *inferus*; in another, as in Corb. and several English manuscripts, *inferi*.]” (Hab. 2:5).

And again: “Do not fear the words of a sinful man, [Col. 0799C] because his glory shall be amid dung [Col. 0800A] and worms [Note: [Col. 0800C] “As worms today,” Bod. 3.]. Today he shall be exalted, and tomorrow he shall not be found, because he has returned to his own earth, and his thought shall perish [Note: [Col. 0800C] “His thought shall perish,” Oxon.]” (1 Macc. 2:62).

And again: “I saw the wicked man exalted and raised above the cedars of Lebanon; and I passed by, and behold, he was not there; and I sought him, and his place was not found” (Ps. 36:37).

Self-exaltation and inflation, and arrogant and proud boasting, arise not from the teaching of Christ, who teaches humility, but from the spirit of Antichrist. The Lord reproaches him [Note: [Col. 0800C] “Whom he reproaches,” Bod. 3.] through the prophet and says: “But you said in your heart: ‘I shall ascend into heaven; above the stars of God I shall set my throne. I shall sit upon a lofty mountain, above the lofty mountains toward the north [Note: [Col. 0800C] “The mountains of the north,” Lam. Ebor. NC. 1. Bod. 2.]. I shall ascend above the clouds; I shall be like the Most High’” (Isa. 14:13–14). And he added, saying: “But you shall descend into the underworld, into the foundations of the earth; and those who [Col. 0800B] see you shall marvel at you” (ibid., 15).

Hence divine Scripture elsewhere threatens such people with a corresponding punishment and says: “For the day of the Lord Sabaoth shall come upon everyone who is insolent and proud, and upon everyone who is lifted up and exalted” (Isa. 2:29).

Thus each person is immediately revealed by his own mouth and words, and in speaking discloses whether he has Christ in his heart or Antichrist, according to what the Lord says in his Gospel: “Brood of vipers, how can you speak good things when you are evil? For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth brings forth [Note: [Col. 0800C] “The mouth speaks,” Lin.]. A good man brings forth good things from a good treasury [Note: [Col. 0800C] “The treasury of the heart,” Lin.], and an evil man brings forth evil things from an evil treasury” (Matt. 12:34).

Hence also that sinful rich man, who implores assistance from Lazarus, placed in Abraham’s bosom and established in refreshment, [Col. 0800C] while he himself is tormented and burned by the heat of the consuming flame, [Col. 0801A] [Note: [Col. 0801B] “Is burned by its heat,” Lam. Ebor. NC. 1. Bod. 1; “was being burned,” Bod. 1.] (Luke 16:23), suffers punishment especially in his mouth and tongue among all the parts of his body, because, plainly, he had sinned more with his tongue and mouth.

> **[Note: [Col. 0801C]**
>
> **IV.—“Hears me.”** In the Oxford edition, *he who hears me* is added here, and shortly afterward, following the words *rejects me*, there is appended with other witnesses: *he who rejects me, rejects*. The reading that we print from the old Colbert manuscript, which is also supported by Corb., seemed to cohere better. **COUSTANT.**—The English editors presented this passage as follows in their edition: “He who hears you,” he says, “hears me; he who hears me, and him who sent me.” I do not know, however, where they found the words they added, *he who hears me*, since these are read neither in the Gospel nor in the ancient manuscripts and editions of Cyprian. To be sure, in Erasmus’s edition and in the Sorbonne manuscript it is written: “He who hears you,” he says, “hears me; and he who hears you hears also him who sent me.” But this is very different from the English edition. In the Tours manuscript and in one of mine it is written: “He who hears you,” he says, “hears me when heard, and he who hears me hears him [Col. 0801D] who sent me.” See Letter 69 to Florentius, where these words are repeated. **BALUZE.**
>
> **“He who rejects you.”** So also in the same letter to Florentius. In the common edition it reads: “He who despises you despises me.” In his note on chapter 12 of the Gospel according to Luke, Erasmus points out that Jerome somewhere translated it: “He who rejects you rejects me.” He then inveighs intemperately against bishops who exercise tyranny and pursue the business of their bellies. He adds, however: “Yet I know that even wicked men must be obeyed, lest dissension be stirred up, provided that they do not compel us to impiety.” **BALUZE.**
>
> **“You assail” (*insilis*).** It is also written thus in Letter 65, to Rogatianus. But Nicolaus Faber noted in the margin of the Pamelian edition that *incilas* had been written in the old manuscript of the letter that we are now elucidating. Nonius Marcellus says: “*Incilare* means to rebuke or disapprove.” To prove this, Nonius cites authorities from Accius, Pacuvius, and Lucilius. He could also have added evidence from Lucretius and Plautus. The reading noted by Faber appears to be confirmed by Erasmus’s edition, in which *insimulas* (“you accuse”) is written in place of *insilis* (“you assail”). See Erasmus himself on this passage of Acts. **BALUZE.**
>
> **“The ruler of the people.”** Thus the old editions and most of the ancient books. Erasmus wrote *of your people*; Manutius and Morellius retained that reading. Pamelius changed it. See Letter 65 and the Fifth Council of Toledo, canon 5. **BALUZE.]**

### IV

For since it is written, “Nor shall revilers inherit [Note: [Col. 0801B] “Possess the kingdom of God,” NC. 2. Lin.] the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 6:10), and again the Lord says in his Gospel: “Whoever says to his brother, ‘Fool,’ and whoever says, ‘Raca,’ shall be liable to the Gehenna [Note: [Col. 0801B] “Liable to Gehenna,” Voss. 2. Bod. 3.] of fire” (Matt. 3:22), how can those who heap such things not only upon brothers but also upon priests escape the censure of the Lord the avenger [Note: [Col. 0801C] “Of the Lord’s vengeance,” Bod. 3.]? So great an honor is granted to these priests by God’s favor that anyone who refused to obey his priest, judging here for the time being, was immediately put to death.

In Deuteronomy the Lord God speaks, saying: “And whatever man acts in pride so as not to heed the priest or whatever judge shall be [Col. 0801B] in those days, that man shall die; and when all the people hear of it, they shall fear and shall no longer act impiously” (Deut. 17:12).

Likewise, when Samuel was being despised by the Jews, God says to him: “They have not despised you, but they have despised me” (1 Sam. 8:7).

And the Lord also says in the Gospel: “He who hears you,” he says, “hears me [Note: [Col. 0801C] Thus Lam. Lin. Bod. 2. “Hears also him who sent me,” Rig.], and him who sent me; and he who rejects you rejects me, and him who sent me” (Luke 10:16).

And when he had cleansed the leper, he said: “Go and show yourself to the priest” (Matt. 8:4). [Col. 0802A]

And later, at the time of the Passion, [Note: [Col. 0801C] Thus Lam. Bod. 1, 2, 3. Ebor. Voss. 2. Pem. Lin. NC. [Col. 0802B] 1, 2. MR. Spir. Vet. innom. and others. “Him who sent me. And later, at the time of the Passion,” Rigalt.] after he had received a blow from a servant of the priest, and when the servant had said to him, “Is this how you answer the high priest?” (John 18:22), the Lord said nothing insulting against the high priest, nor did he detract in any way from the priest’s honor. Rather, asserting and demonstrating his own innocence, he said: “If I have spoken wrongly, give evidence of the wrong [Note: [Col. 0802B] “Testify concerning the wrong,” Lam. Ebor. NC. 1. Bod. 2.]; but if rightly, why do you strike me?” (ibid., 23).

Likewise, later in the Acts of the Apostles, when the blessed apostle Paul was told, “Is this how you assail the priest of God by reviling him?” (Acts 23:4), although after the Lord had already been crucified those men had begun to be sacrilegious, impious, and bloodstained, and no longer retained anything of priestly honor and authority, Paul nevertheless reflected upon even the empty title itself and a certain shadow of a priest, and said: “I did not know, brothers [Note: [Col. 0802B] Thus Pem. NC. 1, 2. Voss. 2. Lam. Bod. 1, 2. Lin. [Col. 0802C] “Brothers” omitted by Oxon.]” (ibid., 5), [Col. 0802B] “that he is the high priest; for it is written, ‘You shall not revile the ruler of your people [Note: [Col. 0802C] “The ruler of the common people,” Lam. Ebor. Lin. Bod. 1, 2.]’” (Exod. 22:28).

> **[Note: [Col. 0802C]**
>
> **V.—“For heresies have arisen from no other source,” etc.** You have similar passages below in the aforementioned letters to Bishop Rogatianus and to Florentius Pupianus, and likewise in the books *On the Unity of the Church* and *On Jealousy and Envy*. And although in those other passages he may appear to be speaking about himself and all bishops—namely, that all heresies have taken their beginning from contempt for bishops, that is, from schism itself—he is certainly speaking in this passage, and especially at the beginning of the book *On the Unity of the Church*, about the Roman bishop alone. That one passage, as is explained there at greater length, so confirms the primacy of the Roman bishop or pontiff that it could not possibly do so more strongly.
>
> The circumstances of the text here that show that he is speaking of the Roman bishop and supreme pontiff are, first of all, the testimonies previously cited from Deuteronomy, 1 Samuel, the Gospel of John, and the Acts of the Apostles. No one doubts that these apply only to the high priests of the Jews, and consequently they are more aptly referred to the supreme Roman pontiff. Next, he speaks of the judge who acts in Christ’s place. Likewise, he speaks of one priest or one bishop in the Church. It is sufficiently evident, both from Cornelius’s Letter 48 above and from Cyprian’s other letters and his book *On the Unity of the Church*, that Cyprian is not accustomed to use this designation except of the supreme pontiff.
>
> The same point is supported by his statement: “No one would stir up anything against the college of priests”; for if he were speaking about himself alone, one who refused to obey him would not immediately be stirring up something against the other bishops. The same tendency appears on the following page, where, after speaking of the servant set in authority, he immediately introduces mention of St. Peter, upon whom Christ built the Church.
>
> To the same point belongs St. Jerome’s statement against the Luciferians that the Church’s salvation depends upon the dignity of the high priest. “If,” he says, “a certain exceptional authority, preeminent above all others, is not given to him, there will be as many schisms in the churches as there are priests.”
>
> Experience itself certainly teaches us that heresies ordinarily take their beginning from schism—that is, from voluntary separation from the Church, and consequently from the Church’s head, by which I mean the Roman pontiff. In Cyprian you have examples of this in the Novatians; in Augustine, in the Donatists. Hence St. Augustine says to them in Letter 154: “For we charge you with nothing except the crime of schism, which by wickedly persisting you have also made into a heresy.” And in *Against Cresconius the Grammarian*, book 21, chapter 7: “Of the distinction between schism and heresy,” he says, “I more readily approve that according to which schism is said to be a recent dissension within a congregation arising from some diversity of opinions, while heresy is an inveterate schism.”
>
> St. Jerome does not disagree with this when explaining the words in Titus 3, “who is condemned by himself”: “Heretics,” he says, “pass sentence upon themselves by withdrawing from the Church according to their own judgment; this withdrawal appears to be the condemnation of their own conscience.” And shortly afterward: “There is no schism that does not invent some heresy for itself, so that it may appear to have withdrawn from the Church rightly.” Anyone who examines precisely the origins and first seedbeds of individual heresies will find many examples. **PAMELIUS.**
>
> **“One in the Church.”** In the book *On the Unity of the Church*: “The episcopate is one, a share of which is held in its entirety by each bishop.” And in Letter 52 to Antonianus: “Each bishop arranges and directs his own conduct, and will render to the Lord an account of his purpose.” See our notes on Agobard’s book *On the Privilege and Right of the Priesthood*. [Col. 0804C] **BALUZE.**
>
> **“Without your Father.”** I have seen it written thus in the old editions and in nine manuscript codices. Manutius deleted the word *your*, which I did not find in nine other old books. I have nevertheless retained it, because Matthew, from whom these words were taken, reads: “Not one of them falls to the ground without your Father.” This is also found in the Greek. Yet in Letter 69, to Florentius, in which this passage is quoted, the word *your* is absent. **BALUZE.**
>
> **“Does anyone suppose?”** Gerhoh of Reichersberg cites this passage, though incompletely, in his treatise *Against the Simoniacs*, [Col. 0804D] chapter 27. **BALUZE.**
>
> **“You took counsel.”** See the notes of Fronton du Duc on the codex of the homilies of St. John Chrysostom, p. 13. **BALUZE.]**

### V

Since these so great and so numerous examples, as well as many others, have gone before us, examples by which priestly authority and power are confirmed through divine favor, what sort of people do you suppose those to be who are enemies of the priests and rebels against the catholic Church, and who are frightened neither by the threat of the Lord who forewarns them nor by the vengeance of the judgment to come?

For heresies have arisen [Note: [Col. 0802C] “Have sprung up,” Lam. Ebor. Bod. 2. NC. 1.] from no other source, nor have schisms been born, [Col. 0803A] than [Note: [Col. 0803B] Thus our manuscripts; but the editions read, “than from the fact that the priest…”] when obedience is not given to the priest of God, and when no thought is given to the one priest in the Church for the time being and the one judge for the time being in Christ’s place.

If the whole brotherhood obeyed him in accordance with the divine teachings, no one would stir up anything against the college of priests; no one, after God’s judgment, after the people’s vote [Note: [Col. 0803B] “Of his people,” Lam. NC. 1. Ebor.], and after the consent of the fellow bishops, would make himself the judge—not now of the bishop, but of God; no one would rend the Church of Christ by the rupture of unity; no one, self-satisfied and puffed up, would establish a new heresy apart and outside—unless someone is [Note: [Col. 0803B] “Unless there is,” Lam. Ebor. NC. 1. Lin.] of such sacrilegious rashness and ruined mind that he thinks a priest can be appointed without God’s judgment.

Yet the Lord says in his Gospel: “Are not two sparrows sold for a penny? And neither of them [Note: [Col. 0803C] “And not one of them shall fall,” Lin. NC. 2.] falls to the ground without the will of your Father [Note: [Col. 0803C] “Of your Father,” Vir.]” (Matt. 10:29). [Col. 0803B] Since he says that not even the least things happen without God’s will, does anyone suppose that the highest and greatest things happen in God’s Church without God’s knowledge or permission, and that priests—that is, his stewards—are ordained apart from his judgment?

This is to lack the faith by which we live; this is to fail to give honor to God, by whose command and judgment we know and believe that all things are ruled [Note: [Col. 0803C] “Are carried out,” Bod. 1.] and governed. [Col. 0804A]

Certainly, bishops can be appointed apart from God’s will [Note: [Col. 0803C] The editions read: “Those who are appointed outside the Church are appointed, but contrary to…” [Col. 0804B] against the testimony of our manuscripts and most of the English manuscripts.]—but only those who are appointed outside the Church, those who are appointed contrary to [Note: [Col. 0804B] Thus Pem. Bod. 1, 3. Lam. Ebor. NC. 1. Lin.] the ordinance and tradition of the Gospel. As the Lord himself declares among the Twelve Prophets and says: “They appointed a king for themselves [Note: [Col. 0804B] “For themselves,” singular, Lam. Ebor. NC. 1, 2.], and not through me” (Hos. 8:4).

And again: “Their sacrifices are like the bread of mourning; all who eat them shall be defiled” (Hos. 9:4).

And through Isaiah also the Holy Spirit cries out and says: “Woe to you, rebellious children; thus says the Lord: You took counsel not through me [Note: [Col. 0804C] Thus Bod. 1, 2. Lam. Ebor. NC. 1. Oxon.; “counsel, and not through me,” Oxon.], and you made an alliance not through my Spirit, to add sins upon sins” (Isa. 30:1).

> **[Note: [Col. 0804D]**
>
> **VI.—“For I say.”** The old editions and three old copies have: “Moreover I say—I say, for I have been provoked.” But fifteen old copies favor the text as we have printed it. **BALUZE.**
>
> **“Proscribed.”** Pontius the deacon in the *Life of Cyprian*: “Indeed, he immediately obtained the glory of proscription for such merits.” **BALUZE.**
>
> **“To the lion.”** The same Pontius says: “Especially since, in repeatedly renewed acclamations, it was demanded that he be sent to the lion.” Tertullian in the *Apology*: “If the Tiber rises to the walls, if the Nile does not rise over the fields, if the sky stands still, if the earth moves, if there is famine or pestilence, immediately the cry goes up: ‘The Christians to the lion!’” Aelius Spartianus in *Commodus Antoninus*: “Speratus to the lion!” Those condemned to the lion were bound to a stake, as the same Tertullian attests in his book *On Modesty*. Flavius Vopiscus in *The Deified Aurelian*: “Mnesteus, however, was afterward carried off, bound to a stake, and thrown to the beasts.” See Jean Tristan de Saint-Amant, volume 1 of his commentaries, p. 713. **BALUZE.**
>
> [Col. 0805B] **“On account of the sacrifices.”** The author of the *Cyprianic Annals*, under the year 252, no. 10, observes that Gallus and Volusianus, when the plague was growing worse—the plague that had carried off Emperor Hostilian, whom the senate had appointed together with Gallus—caused coins to be struck for Apollo the Healer. For the same reason, as is gathered from these words of Cyprian, they wished sacrifices to be celebrated everywhere by a published edict. When Cyprian refused to obey this edict, the people seized upon this as an occasion to demand in the circus that he be sent to the lion as a rebel against the emperors, although there was no edict of Gallus ordering proconsuls or magistrates to persecute Christians. [Col. 0805C] **BALUZE.**
>
> **“An edict having been published.”** Imperial rescripts were sent to the praetorian prefects, whose responsibility it was to make them known to the people. This was called “publishing” them. The rescript of Honorius and Theodosius against Pelagius—to take this as an example—was sent to Palladius, the praetorian prefect. He, after publishing an edict, ordered the rescript to be executed. At its conclusion it is written: “Edict published.” There are many examples of this practice. **BALUZE.**
>
> **“By the shouting of the people.”** That is, by the acclamations of the common people demanding that he be condemned to the lion. Rufinus, book 5 of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 1, when reporting the letter of the churches of Vienne and Lyons, says that it was written there that the martyrs had bravely endured acclamations against themselves, and that they had been seized and thrust into prison solely because of the people’s acclamations. The same author, book 4, chapter 9, reports a rescript of Emperor Hadrian forbidding provincials to be permitted to accuse Christians merely by petitions and acclamations.
>
> Jerome speaks in the same way in his commentary on chapter 3 of the Letter to Titus, when discussing the martyrs’ steadfastness under torture: “Or when someone, stretched upon the rack and amid the metal plates, scorns pain and fears neither the judge’s threat nor the roar of the surrounding people, but, for the sake of the confession that brings martyrdom, contemns and despises every torture.” [Col. 0805D] **BALUZE.]**

### VI

Moreover—I say this because I have been provoked [Note: [Col. 0804C] “Moreover I say—I say because I have been provoked,” Vir.]; I say it in sorrow; I say it under compulsion—when a bishop is appointed in place of one who has died; when he is chosen in time of peace by the vote of the entire people; [Col. 0804B] when he is protected by God’s help in persecution; when he is faithfully united with all his colleagues; when he has already been approved by his people for four years in the episcopate; when in tranquility he serves discipline, and in the storm is proscribed with the title of his episcopate applied and appended; when he has so often been demanded for the lion in the circus, and honored in the amphitheater by the testimony of the Lord’s favor; when even in these very days, during which [Col. 0805A] I wrote this letter to you, he has again been demanded for the lion in the circus by the shouting of the people because of the sacrifices that the people were ordered by a published edict to celebrate—when such a man, dearest brother, appears to be attacked by certain desperate and ruined persons situated outside the Church, it is evident who is attacking him.

It is certainly not Christ, who either appoints or protects priests, but that adversary of Christ [Note: [Col. 0805A] “Christ’s adversary,” Bod. 1.] and enemy of his Church, who for this purpose persecutes the one set over the Church [Note: [Col. 0805A] “For this reason, the Church,” Lam. NC. 1. Ebor. Bod. 2.] with his assaults: so that, once the helmsman has been removed, he may rage more fiercely and violently amid the Church’s shipwreck.

> **[Note: [Col. 0805D]**
>
> **VII.—“Peter, nevertheless, upon whom the Church was built by the Lord himself.”** He uses almost the same words below in the frequently mentioned letter to Florentius Pupianus; likewise in the letters to Jubaianus and Quintus, and again in the books *On the Dress of Virgins*, *On the Unity of the Church*, and *On the Good of Modesty*. He is undoubtedly explaining that passage of Matthew 17: “And I say to you that you are Peter, and upon this rock I shall build my Church,” etc.
>
> Nor is this interpretation of the passage new. Tertullian, who was older than Cyprian, also has it in his books *On the Prescription of Heretics* and *On Modesty*; so too Origen in his commentary on Romans, chapter 6, and Homily 3 on Exodus; and likewise most of the other ancients: Hilary, namely, on Matthew; Ambrose, sermon 47; Jerome, book 1 *Against Jovinian*, book 1 *Against the Pelagians*, his commentary on Matthew, the Letter to Marcella, and his commentary on Isaiah, [Col. 0806B] chapters 2 and 16; Chrysostom, Homily 55 on Matthew; Cyril, book 2 of his commentary on John, chapter 12; Epiphanius in the *Ancoratus*; and Pope Leo I, Letter 67.
>
> We have cited these passages at greater length because of Erasmus’s little annotation on the letter to Florentius Pupianus, where he says: “More than once Cyprian makes Peter the foundation of the Church—unless perhaps by the name ‘Peter’ he understood the people professing what Peter had professed.” As though it were more absurd for Peter to be the foundation of the Church than for the people themselves, or all Christians, to be so, as Erasmus says in his annotation on Matthew. If we admit this interpretation, then every Christian will also have the power to loose and bind sins; all Catholics know how absurd that is.
>
> This, therefore, is more truly a distortion of Scripture than referring the passage to Peter together with so many ancient Greek and Latin authors, including Origen himself, whom Erasmus nevertheless cites in favor of his own opinion. For there is no obstacle to Peter’s being called the rock or foundation of the Church. “For even if he is a rock,” says Basil in his book *On Repentance*, “he is not a rock in the same way that Christ is the rock, but as Peter is a rock. For Christ is truly the immovable and unshaken rock, whereas Peter is a rock because of this rock. For God bestows his own dignities without emptying himself: possessing, he gives. He is light, and says, ‘You are the light of the world.’ He is priest, and makes a priest. He is rock, and makes a rock.” Ambrose has similar statements in his commentary on Luke 9, as does Paulinus in Letter 4 to Severus.
>
> Nor is there any reason for Erasmus to flatter himself concerning St. Augustine’s opinion. For although Augustine, both in his final tractate on John and in Sermon 13 *On the Words of the Lord*, interprets the rock as Christ, he himself nevertheless acknowledges in *Retractions* 1.21 that he had also explained that passage as referring to Peter in his book *Against the Letter of Donatus*. Finally, he adds: “Of these two interpretations, let the reader choose which is more probable.” It is evident, however, that the interpretation followed by so many ancient writers is the more probable. **PAMELIUS.**
>
> Our adversaries labor greatly to show that Christ granted nothing to Peter except that he should be first in order and precede the other apostles by some prerogative of honor. Yet their concession of this is highly significant for asserting—even by their own confession—the prerogative of the Roman bishop over the other bishops.
>
> It is nevertheless nothing new for our adversaries to think in this way. It is certain that all those who formerly separated themselves from the catholic Church—as Aeneas Sylvius observed before me in his letter to Martin Mayer, chancellor of Mainz—always raised themselves against the Roman bishops, while the latter always opposed new errors. Hence it is noted that the Roman Church has never suffered any stain in the faith and that faithlessness cannot gain access to it, as is read there. **BALUZE.**
>
> **“One speaking for all.”** I am of the opinion that these words cannot be referred to a prescribed form for holding a council, since the matter did not take place in a council but in a familiar conversation. When Christ asked his disciples what people were saying about him, and they answered that some said he was John the Baptist, others Jeremiah, or one of the prophets, Peter—one speaking for all in the voice of the Church, as Cyprian says—answered that he was the Son of the living God. I find nothing there to indicate that a form for holding a council was then established.
>
> Nevertheless, from that answer made by Peter alone, the most illustrious Cardinal Baronius concluded that Christ then expressed a model for holding a council. His reasoning was that, when Christ asked his disciples whom they believed him to be, Peter was the first of all to say that he was the Son of the living God, and thus delivered such a judgment, taught and decreed what was to be believed by all, and established a canon of faith that would endure forever. Accordingly, there was no need to consult the other apostles or ask what their judgments and opinions on the matter were. It had been sufficient for Christ that Peter had spoken and had fixed firmly what was to be held concerning the faith.
>
> “These bypaths and circumlocutions,” as Quintilian says, “are evidence of weakness.” That interpretation is sought from too far away, and Baronius’s paraphrase has little support in the Evangelist’s words. The one thing that can be concluded from this passage is that Peter spoke rightly, that the other apostles therefore said nothing, and that by their silence they approved what Peter had rightly said. But it does not follow from this that the others could not have expressed their own judgment, or that their successors, the bishops, were deprived of the power to set forth their views in a matter of faith.
>
> Thus the authority [Col. 0808C] of the bishops remains intact, since from the fact that Peter alone spoke while the other apostles remained silent it cannot be concluded that the judgment of the other apostles would have been useless, or that the judgment of the pope alone suffices in the Church of God, or that his judgment alone must prevail against the harmonious and concordant judgment of other bishops who think differently. Otherwise the holding of councils would be useless, if the authority of the pope alone sufficed to resolve controversies arising in the Church of God. The ancients did not think so: they considered the holding of councils necessary against emerging heresies. This cannot be denied. **BALUZE.**
>
> **“You are the Christ.”** We added the word *Christ*, which was absent from the other editions, because we found it in several very old codices, and because it occurs in chapter 6 of the Gospel according to John, from which this passage was taken, and in the Gospel according to Matthew. Yet it is also absent from Letter 69 to Florentius.
>
> **“They would have remained with us.”** Flavian, bishop of Constantinople, made these words his own when writing to the holy Pope Leo: “There are some who by their clothing signify that they are sheep, but inwardly are ravenous wolves, whom we ought to recognize by their fruits. At first sight they appear to be among our number, but they are not among our number. For if they had been among our number, they would have remained with us.” **BALUZE.]**

### VII

Nor should any faithful person who remembers the Gospel and retains the commands of the Apostle who forewarns us be disturbed, dearest brother, if in the last times certain proud and defiant enemies of the priests of God [Col. 0806A] either withdraw from the Church or act against the Church, since both the Lord and his apostles foretold beforehand that such people would now exist [Note: [Col. 0805B] “Would exist even now,” Bod. 2.].

Nor should anyone be surprised that the servant set in authority is deserted by some, since the Lord himself, though he performed the greatest mighty and marvelous works and proved the powers of God the Father by the testimony of his deeds, was abandoned [Note: [Col. 0806A] “Was forsaken,” Ver.] by his own disciples. Yet he did not rebuke [Note: [Col. 0806A] “Did not reprimand,” Voss. 2. Lam.] those who withdrew, nor did he threaten them severely. Rather, turning to his apostles, he said: “Do you also wish to go away [Note: [Col. 0806B] “Wish to depart,” Lam. Ebor. Bod. 2. NC. 1.]?” (John 6:68).

He was plainly preserving the law by which a human being, left to his own freedom and placed under his own free choice, seeks for himself either death or salvation.

Peter, nevertheless, upon whom the Church had been built by the same Lord, speaking as one for all and answering in the voice of the Church, [Col. 0807A] said: “Lord, to whom shall we go [Note: [Col. 0807B] “To whom do we go?” Lam. Ebor. Lin. NC. 1.]? You have the words of eternal life; and we believe and have come to know that you are the Son of the living God” (John 6:69).

He was plainly signifying and demonstrating that those who withdraw from Christ perish through their own fault, but that the Church, which believes in Christ and holds fast once and for all to what it has come to know, never withdraws from him at all [Note: [Col. 0807C] “Withdraws from him,” Lam. Ebor. NC. 1.]. Those are the Church who remain in the house of God.

But those whom we see made firm not with the stability of wheat, but winnowed like chaff by the spirit of the enemy who scatters it, are not the planting planted by God the Father (Matt. 15:13). Of these John also says in his letter: “They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would have remained with us” (1 John 2:19).

Likewise, Paul admonishes us not to be disturbed when the wicked perish from the Church [Note: [Col. 0807C] “Depart from the Church,” Lam. Ebor. NC. 1. Bod. 1.], [Col. 0807B] nor to allow the faith to be diminished because the faithless withdraw: “For what,” he says, “if some of them fell away from the faith? Surely their faithlessness has not nullified the faithfulness of God [Note: [Col. 0807C] The Corb. manuscript reads “has nullified”; the old Colb., “will nullify”]? By no means. For God is true, but every man a liar” (Rom. 3:4).

### VIII

As far as we are concerned, it accords with our conscience [Note: [Col. 0808B] “With our conscience,” Lam. NC. 1. Ebor. Bod. 3.], dearest brother, to take care that no one perish from the Church through our fault. But if anyone voluntarily perishes through his own offense and refuses to repent and return to the Church, we who have taken thought for his health shall be without blame on the day of judgment, while those who refused to be healed by the health-giving benefit of our counsel shall remain under punishment.

Nor should the insults of the ruined disturb us [Col. 0808A] or prevent us from continuing without departure from the right path and the fixed rule, since the Apostle also instructs us, saying: “If I were pleasing men [Note: [Col. 0808C] “If I were pleasing men,” he says, Lam. Ebor. NC. 1; “If I wished to please,” Ver.], I would not be Christ’s servant” (Gal. 1:10).

It makes a difference whether someone desires to win the favor of men or of God. If men are pleased, the Lord is offended; but if we strive and labor to be able to please God, we ought to despise human insults and curses.

> **[Note: [Col. 0808D]**
>
> **IX.—“Fortunatus.”** See what we have noted concerning this man at chapter 10 of book 1 of *The Concord of Priesthood and Empire*. **BALUZE.**
>
> **“Fugitives from the Church.”** In the Corb. manuscript, *a fugitive* in the singular; and [Col. 0809C] shortly afterward, *excluded* in the singular by the second hand, although the first hand presents *excluded* in the plural. Four of those five presbyters appear to be named by Cyprian in Letter 6: namely, Donatus and Fortunatus, Novatus and Gordius, who had, of course, opposed his ordination. If Gaius, presbyter of Didda—whom the clergy of Carthage, with Cyprian’s approval in Letter 28, removed from communion—is added to them, the names of these five presbyters will be obtained. **COUSTANT.**
>
> **“Perseus.”** I think he was a bishop somewhere in Italy. **BALUZE.**
>
> **“Crimes hasten.”** Tacitus says in book 1 of the *Histories* that crimes gain strength through impetuosity. Claudian in book 2 of *Against Rufinus*: “Savage crimes do not permit repose.” St. Jerome in the dialogue *Against the Luciferians*, and Florus, book 3, chapter 1: “Crimes do not remain hidden for long.” Seneca, *Medea*: “Great evils do not remain hidden.” **BALUZE.]**
## IX

As for the fact that I did not immediately write to you, dearest brother, about this Fortunatus, a pseudo-bishop appointed by a few inveterate heretics, the matter was not one that needed to be reported to your attention by us at once and in haste, as though it were something great or alarming—especially since you already knew Fortunatus’s name well enough. He is one of the five presbyters who long ago fled from the Church and who [Col. 0808B] were recently excluded by the judgment [Note: [Col. 0808C] “And also by the judgments,” Lam. Ebor. NC. 1.] of our fellow bishops, many of them men of the greatest weight; concerning this matter they wrote to you in the preceding year. You would likewise recognize Felicissimus, the standard-bearer of sedition, who is himself also mentioned in the same letters written to you long ago by our fellow bishops. He was not only excluded by them here, but was also recently expelled from the Church by you there.

Since I trusted that these matters were known to you, and knew for certain that they remained fixed in your memory and ecclesiastical discipline, I did not think it necessary to report the follies of the heretics to you swiftly and urgently. For it should not concern the majesty and dignity of the catholic Church what the audacity of heretics and schismatics [Col. 0809A] may contrive among themselves. Indeed, Novatian’s faction [Note: [Col. 0809B] “Novatian’s equal,” Ver.] is said now to have made Maximus, a presbyter recently sent to us by Novatian as his envoy and rejected from communion with us, its own pseudo-bishop there. Yet I had not written to you even about this, since all these things are despised by us, and since I recently sent you the names of the bishops appointed there who, sound and uncorrupted, preside over the brethren in the catholic Church.

It was, of course, precisely for this reason that, by the counsel of all our colleagues, it was decided to write to you [Note: [Col. 0809B] Thus Bod. 1, 2, 3; Voss. 2. “To you” is absent from Oxon.]: so that there might be a concise means of dispelling error and discerning the truth, and so that you and our colleagues might know to whom you ought to write and from whom you ought in turn to receive letters. But if anyone apart from those whom we included in our letter—which is no longer extant—should dare to write to you, you would know that he had either been defiled by sacrifice or by a certificate, [Col. 0809B] or was one of the heretics, that is, a perverse and profane man.

[Note: [Col. 0809B] Thus the older Colb. codex, supported by others. The printed editions, however, have *Nactus*.] Nevertheless, having found the opportunity offered by a most intimate friend and cleric, I also wrote to you about this Fortunatus through the acolyte Felicianus, whom you had sent with our colleague Perseus, among the other matters from here that had to be brought to your attention. But while our brother Felicianus was delayed there [Note: [Col. 0809B] “But while this Felicianus,” Ver.], either by the wind or because he was being kept back to receive other letters from us [Note: [Col. 0809B] “Was being kept back by you,” Bod. 3.], Felicissimus hastened [Col. 0810A] to you and arrived before him. For crimes always hasten in this way, as though by haste they could prevail against innocence.

> [Note: [Col. 0809D]
>
> **X.—Fabian and Donatus.** Thus at the end of Epistle 67, to Pope Stephen, p. 117, he says: “For the glorious honor of our predecessors, the blessed martyrs Cornelius and Lucius, must be preserved.” Thus in Optatus, book I, it is written that Caecilian did not withdraw from the chair of Peter or of Cyprian. See Rigaltius’s observation on this passage. **BALUZE.**—From this passage Baronius conjectures, not implausibly, that Cyprian succeeded Donatus in the episcopate of Carthage. For when Cyprian, writing to Cornelius, bishop of Rome, mentions the ninety bishops who had condemned the heretic Privatus in the colony of Lambaesis thirteen years earlier, he also indicates that this same Privatus had been censured with the utmost severity in letters from Fabian and Donatus. Thus, just as Cyprian calls Fabian the predecessor of Cornelius, he may likewise have called Donatus his own predecessor. Accordingly, when writing to Cornelius, he may have said, “of our predecessors—Fabian yours, and [Col. 0810C] Donatus mine.” Nevertheless, Epistle LXVII will show that this manner of speaking does not always refer to predecessors in the same episcopal see. Cyprian calls the Roman bishops Cornelius and Lucius his predecessors, although they never presided over the Church of Carthage; he calls them his predecessors simply as his seniors, because they had lived some years before him and had discharged the same episcopal office, though in other provinces. **RIGALTIUS.**
>
> **Privatus, a proven heretic.** The common editions present “Privatus the heretic.” The Speyer edition, however, the old Venetian edition, and Rembolt have *Probatio*. I found it so written in nine ancient codices, and Pamelius attests that he likewise found it in three ancient codices. The Münster manuscript reads *privatio probatio haeretico*; the Fossatensis has only *probatio*, but “or *privato*” is written above the line. So also in the more recent Victorinus manuscript. The Grenoble manuscript has “Privatus, a proven heretic.” I think this is the genuine and true reading, which is also supported by the reading of the more recent manuscripts from Reims and Dijon, where “Privatus, a thoroughly proven heretic” is written. For I think that one of those two readings must be retained. A little earlier this same Privatus is called “an old heretic,” that is, a proven or thoroughly proven heretic. This also removes the difficulty Pamelius created for himself when he thought that the name Probatius, which he had found in three ancient copies, ought to be deleted; for, as he says, if that name were added, there would be six condemned bishops, although it is established that there were only five. **BALUZE.**
>
> **Of Suturnica.** I have retained this reading because it is commonly received and I have not yet found a better one. Yet, apart from the fact that I have not found that name elsewhere, the ancient copies vary greatly in this passage. Eight of those I have seen, as well as the Manutian edition, have *Sutunurcensis*; another manuscript cited in the English edition has *Uturnicensis*; another, *Urgonensis*; two, *Suturgensis*; and two, *Quoturnicensis*. One of the last is the Corbie manuscript, in which the English editors say that *Quaturnicensis* is written. Erasmus notes in the margin that he read *Quaturnicensis* elsewhere, as Pamelius also attests concerning the Cambron manuscript. Crabb and Surius likewise printed it so in their volumes of the councils. I am surprised, however, that Pamelius noted that Manutius preferred *Sutunuzensis*, since it is certain that the Manutian edition reads *Sutunurcensis*.
