Furthermore, since no information about a bishopric of Suturnica is found anywhere else, it might perhaps not be an absurd conjecture to replace *Suturnicensis* with *Septimunicensis*. See our notes and Gratian, p. 468. The author of the *Cyprianic Annals*, under the year 252, calls him bishop of Thuburbo, but without authority. **BALUZE.**
>
> **By sacrilegious persuasion.** Although I do not doubt that this is the best reading, I have nevertheless thought it necessary to note that eleven ancient books present “persecution.” The edition produced in England attests that it was also read in this way in one English manuscript. When an opportunity arises, however, I shall emend Victor of Vita, in whose book IX, in Huneric’s edict, the latest edition reads “under a suitable persecution,” whereas previously “prosecution” was read. For it is certain that this latter reading must be restored. **BALUZE.**
>
> **Chose as a colleague.** The codex of Saint-Michel has “made companions,” and above the line, “that is, they made him a companion.” Certainly a little earlier Jovinus and Maximus are called companions. **BALUZE.**]

## X

Through Felicianus, moreover, I informed you, brother, that Privatus, an old heretic, had come to Carthage. Many years ago, in the colony of Lambaesis, he had been condemned for many serious offenses by the judgment of ninety bishops; and he had also been censured with the utmost severity in letters from our predecessors Fabian and Donatus, as your own conscience is well aware. When he declared that he wished to plead his case before us in the council we held on the most recent Ides of May [Note: [Col. 0809C] “The Ides of March,” Ver.], and was not admitted, he made this Fortunatus a pseudo-bishop worthy of association with him.

There had also come with him a certain Felix, whom Privatus himself had long ago appointed as a pseudo-bishop outside [Col. 0810B] the Church, in heresy. Jovinus and [Note: [Col. 0810B] *Maximosus* in two Colb. manuscripts.] Maximus were also present as companions of the heretic Privatus. They had been condemned by the judgment of nine of our colleagues for abominable sacrifices and crimes proved against them, and were again excluded by several of us in council during the preceding year.

To these four was also joined Repostus [Note: [Col. 0810B] The old Colb. codex has *Sutunurcensis*; the more recent, *Eturgnensis*; Corb., together with Cambron., *Quoturnicensis*; Lambeth, *Uturnicensis*. From this the Oxford editor thinks that *Utinunensis* should be read, especially since the Conference of Carthage has “Octavius, bishop of the people of Utinuna.”] of Suturnica, who not only fell during the persecution himself, but also caused the greater [Col. 0811A] part of his congregation to fall through sacrilegious [Note: [Col. 0811C] “He himself deserted during the persecution,” Lin. Colb. 1, 2; Compend.] persuasion. These five, together with a few who had either sacrificed or had guilty consciences, chose Fortunatus as their pseudo-bishop, so that, since they were united in a single body of crimes, [Note: [Col. 0811C] Thus Lam. Ebor. Pem. Bod. 1, 2, 3, NC. 1, 2, Voss. 2, Foss. Vict.; thus ms. Colb. and most English manuscripts. Other books, however, have “coming together.” Formerly Compend. had “reckoned,” in place of “chose.”] their ruler might naturally be of the same kind as those who were ruled.

> [Note: [Col. 0812D] **XI.—With lies.** Thus Jerome in the *Epitaph of Marcella*: “He brought a ship full of blasphemies into the Roman harbor.” **BALUZE.**]

## XI

From this, dearest brother, you can now recognize the other lies that those desperate and ruined men have circulated there [Note: [Col. 0811C] “Which they circulated there against us,” Bod. 3.]. Although no more than five pseudo-bishops drawn from those who had sacrificed or from the heretics came to Carthage and appointed Fortunatus as the partner of their madness, they nevertheless, like children of the devil and full of falsehood, dared—as you write—to boast [Note: [Col. 0812C] In ms. Corb., “as I said, to boast”; in the older Colb., “dared to boast in writing.”] that twenty-five bishops had been present. They had already been circulating this lie here among our brethren, saying that twenty-five bishops from Numidia were going to come and appoint a bishop for them. [Col. 0811B] But after they had been exposed and confounded in their lie, when only five shipwrecked and excommunicated men assembled, they sailed to Rome with their cargo of lies, as though the truth could not sail after them and convict lying tongues by proof of the established facts.

And this, brother [Note: [Col. 0812C] “Dearest brother,” Bod. 3.], is true madness: not to consider or understand that lies do not deceive for long; that night lasts only until day dawns [Note: [Col. 0812C] “As long as day has not dawned,” Bod. 3.]; that once the day has grown bright and the sun has risen, darkness and gloom yield to the light, and the robberies that raged through the night cease. Indeed, if you were to ask them for the names, they would not have even people whom they could falsely [Note: [Col. 0812C] “False men,” Compend.] name. So great is even their shortage of wicked men [Col. 0811C] that twenty-five cannot be gathered for them from either those who sacrificed or the heretics. Yet, to deceive the ears of the simple and the absent, the number is inflated by a lie—as though, even if that number were genuine, either the Church could be defeated by heretics [Col. 0812A] or justice by the unjust.

> [Note: [Col. 0812D]
>
> **XII.—Adulteries.** In the Fuxensis codex, “and acts of sexual violation” is added. I was unwilling to add it, however, because I found it in no other copy. **BALUZE.**
>
> **I shall deny him.** Thus the common edition, which is confirmed by six ancient copies. Thirteen others have, “I too shall deny him.” In the common edition of the Gospel according to Matthew and in the Grenoble manuscript, “I too shall deny him” is read. So also below in the book *On the Lapsed*, p. 188. **BALUZE.**
>
> **We decreed concerning communion.** The older Colb. manuscript has “communion,” a reading not to be rejected. The letters written by Cyprian on this matter may be read, namely Epistles X–XVI. In Epistles XII and XV he proposes that the matter should be discussed with the bishops. In Epistle X specifically, he explains the cause of his protest as follows: “Although sinners guilty of lesser sins perform penance for the proper period and, in accordance with the order of discipline, come to *exomologesis*—public confession—and receive the right of communion through the imposition of the bishop’s and clergy’s hands, now, at this raw and unsettled time, while the persecution still continues and the peace of the Church herself has not yet been restored, they are being admitted to communion; their names are being presented; and although penance has not yet been performed, *exomologesis* has not yet been made, and the bishop’s and clergy’s hands have not yet been imposed upon them, the Eucharist is being given to them.” Evidently, as the same bishop says in Epistle II, the lapsed obtained certificates from the martyrs, in some of which it was written, “Let that person communicate together with his own.” They then demanded that communion be imparted not only to themselves but also to all who were asserted, on any grounds whatsoever, to belong to them. **COUSTANT.**]

## XII

Nor ought I, dearest brother, now to act in the same manner [Note: [Col. 0812C] “Equally,” Thu.] as they do and recount in my discourse the things they have committed and continue to commit to this very day. We must consider what it is fitting for priests of God to utter and write, and it should be shame, rather than grief, that constrains us to speak, lest I should appear, under provocation, to be heaping up insults rather than crimes and sins.

I therefore remain silent about the frauds committed against the Church; I pass over conspiracies, adulteries, and various kinds of offenses. Yet there is one thing in their wicked conduct about which I do not think silence is permissible, because the cause involved is not mine or any human being’s, but God’s: from the very first day of the persecution, while the recent crimes of those who had sinned were still hot, and not only the devil’s altars but the very hands and mouths of the lapsed were still smoking from their abominable sacrifices, they did not cease to communicate [Col. 0812B] with the lapsed and to intercede against their performing penance.

God cries out: “Whoever sacrifices to gods shall be utterly destroyed, unless it is to the Lord alone” (Exod. 22:20). And the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever denies me, I shall deny him” (Matt. 10:33). Elsewhere, too, divine indignation and wrath do not remain silent, saying: “To them you poured out drink offerings, and to them you presented sacrifices; shall I not be indignant over these things? says the Lord” (Isa. 57:6). Yet they intercede so that the God who himself testifies that he is indignant should not be entreated. They intercede so that Christ, who declares that he will deny the person who denies him, should not be won over by prayers and acts of satisfaction.

> [Note: [Col. 0813C]
>
> **Against the priests.** The Fuxensis codex has “against [Col. 0813C] the Church and the priests.” But I think this reading is not genuine and arose from the rashness of some ancient copyist. **BALUZE.**
>
> **That malice may complete.** The common editions have “may complete, lest.” I prefer, with mss. Colb., Corb., Vat., and several others, “may complete, and that . . . not,” so that an antithesis may be formed here between the work of diabolical malice and that of divine mercy. **COUSTANT.**
>
> **And that the wounded may not.** See Gronovius, chapter 14 of the *Observations on Ecclesiastical Writers*. **BALUZE.**
>
> **Was previously ashamed or afraid.** Thus eight ancient books. But the word “previously” is absent from the early editions and from three ancient books. Pamelius says that the first part of this sentence should be understood of the lapsed, the second of the certificate-holders. Quintilian, book IX, chapter 2: “Shame restrains good people more powerfully than fear.” **BALUZE.**
>
> **And lamentations.** These words appear to come from a gloss. For we properly say “just acts of satisfaction”; I do not think that the same can be said of “lamentations.” Certainly these two words are absent from our fifteen oldest copies and from four English manuscripts. Lamentation, as Cicero says in the fourth book of the *Tusculan Disputations*, is distress accompanied by wailing. Elsewhere the epithets “sorrowful” and “mournful” are joined to “lamentation.” Perhaps, then, there is a transposition in this passage, so that “by lamentations and just acts of satisfaction” should be restored, as “by entreaties and acts of satisfaction” is read a little later. **BALUZE.**
>
> **True peace.** Below, in the book *On the Lapsed*, p. 186: “That is not peace, but war.” Jerome in the *Dialogue Against the Luciferians*: “Let a counterfeit peace not take away what war preserved.” The same author, in the epistle to Theophilus against John of Jerusalem: “We too desire peace, but a peace in which war is not wrapped up.” Likewise in the epistle to Heliodorus *In Praise of the Solitary Life*: “This tranquility is a tempest.” The *Petition* of Marcellinus and Faustinus: “Impiety is concealed beneath the name of peace.” Pope Leo the Great, in the sixth sermon on Epiphany: “Our peace has dangers of its own.” Cassiodorus, book V, chapter 39: “Thus, through a wicked peace, as though in sport, there fall as many as could scarcely have fallen under the compulsion of wars.” [Col. 0814B] Tacitus in the *Life of Agricola*: “He surrounded with renown a peace which, whether through the negligence or the tolerance of his predecessors, was feared no less than war.” The same author, *Histories*, book I: “A war savage even in peace itself”; and book IV: “In a suspect peace, war is safer.” Livy, book IV: “They preferred an unsuccessful war to a disgraceful peace.” In Demosthenes’ speech *On the Crown*, mention is made of a war that offered more advantages than peace. **BALUZE.**
>
> **Intervening, obstructing, opposing itself against.** A legal term. **BALUZE.**
>
> **Is closed off.** Erasmus introduced this reading. I have found it in only three ancient copies. In the others and in the older editions, “is closed” or “shut” is written. **BALUZE.**
>
> **In the Capitol at Carthage,** as Baronius rightly observed, lest anyone think that the Roman Capitol is meant here. Tertullian calls the latter “the senate-house of the gods” in the *Apology* and “the temple of all demons” in the book *On the Shows*; Cicero, however, in the speech *For Milo*, calls it “the temple of holiness, grandeur, judgment, and public counsel; the head of the world, the altar of our allies, the harbor of all nations.” For although the Capitol, properly speaking, is in the city of Rome, it nevertheless concerned the greatness and majesty of the commonwealth that, after foreign nations and peoples had fallen under the empire and dominion of the Roman people, they should adopt its customs; and that colonies planted among them, propagated as it were from the citizen body—of which, as Aulus Gellius says in book XVI, chapter 13, they seemed to be miniature likenesses and representations—should receive all the laws and institutions of the Roman people, together with capitols, amphitheaters, baths, and the other diversions and consolations of servitude.
>
> Accordingly, many cities in the empire had capitols; a list of them is found in Rycquius’s commentary *On the Roman Capitol* and in Du Cange’s Latin glossary. Nevertheless, because certain passages in Jerome and other ancient writers seem to say that the citadel and the Capitol are the same thing, whereas Livy and others distinguish between the citadel and the Capitol—especially Aulus Gellius, who in book V, chapter 12, places the temple of Veiovis between the citadel and the Capitol—I would suppose that this apparent contradiction can conveniently be resolved by saying that the citadel could easily be confused with the Capitol because the citadel and the Capitol stood upon the same ground, on the Tarpeian Rock, and the citadel was adjacent to the Capitol.
>
> Again, because the Gentiles’ sacrifices were performed on the Capitol, which Christians were ordered to ascend as though intending to sacrifice to the Gentiles’ gods, Christians recoiled from the very word “Capitol” as perilous and hostile, regarding it as the dwelling of demons, the citadel and synagogue of Antichrist. Thus in Jerome’s *Dialogue Against the Luciferians*, we see the Luciferians objecting to the orthodox that when the latter received bishops from the Arians—whom they said to be Gentiles—they seemed to be receiving not so much bishops as priests from the Capitol, and that the catholic Church should therefore be called the synagogue of Antichrist rather than the Church of Christ. A little later the orthodox speaker says, “unless perhaps a man instructed on the Capitol.” Hence [Col. 0815C] Cyprian says below in this very letter, p. 88: “What remains but for the Church to yield to the Capitol?” Tertullian in the book *On the Shows*: “Accordingly, if I enter the Capitol or the Serapeum as one who sacrifices and worships, I shall fall away from God.” In an old glossary in the Royal Library one reads: “Citadel: Capitol.” And immediately afterward: “Capitol: the highest head of a district.” **BALUZE.**
>
> **Heap abuse upon.** Two ancient books have “insult and injury”; the Münster manuscript, “the injury of abuses.” **BALUZE.**
>
> **Their own.** All the ancient books confirm this reading. Erasmus substituted “of the lapsed.” **BALUZE.**
>
> **For it is not.** Saint Jerome cites this passage in the epistle to Mark, presbyter of Calcis: “For among Christians it is not the one who suffers an insult, as someone says, but the one who commits it, who is wretched.” This authority proves that we have correctly placed “suffers” here in place of the previously read “hears.” The excellent codex supplied us with this emendation. Again Jerome, in the epistle to Pammachius against Rufinus: “Which is the greater thing: to endure slander or to commit it?” And below: “Either you commit an injury or suffer one.” The same author in his *Apology Against Rufinus*: “I preferred to suffer injury rather than commit it.” Cicero in the book *On Friendship*: “This honor must be paid to an old friendship, that the one who commits the injury, not the one who suffers it, should be held at fault”; and in book V of the *Tusculan Disputations*: “It is better to receive an injury than to commit one.” And in book I of *On Duties*: “Accordingly, those are to be considered brave and magnanimous who repel an injury, not those who inflict one.” Boethius, in book IV of *The Consolation of Philosophy*, writes that those who inflict an injury are inferior to those who suffer one. Aulus Gellius, book IX, chapter 12: “We likewise speak of the injuries both of those who suffer them and of those who commit them.” See also book XII, chapter 9. See also Cassian, *Conference* 12, chapter 13. Publilius Syrus: “Even those who commit injury hate it.” [Col. 0816C] Quintilian, book VIII, chapter 5: “In every contest, the man who is more powerful, even if he receives an injury, seems to inflict it, because he has greater power.” Seneca, *Thebaid*: “Whenever it is necessary either to deceive or to be deceived, you should suffer it yourself rather than commit the crime.” **BALUZE.**
>
> **Love of the truth.** Some English manuscripts have “choice.” “Love” must be retained with the other books, that is, affection—or, as the Vulgate presents it, charity. **COUSTANT.**
>
> **To recognize offenses.** The Fuxensis codex has: “to purge offenses by good deeds and confessions.” An ancient codex cited by Nicolas Le Fèvre and the old anonymous edition add, as a third step, “to wash away the sins committed.” But since I did not find this addition in the ancient codices I used or in the English manuscripts, I did not dare to add it. **BALUZE.**
>
> **Be available.** The printed editions, together with several manuscripts, have “come to one’s aid.” The reading of the Verona manuscript seemed truer; it is supported by “has taken up” in the old Colb. manuscript, from which “may be taken up” was substituted in two others. Nor is “remain” in the more recent Colb. manuscript displeasing, especially since it aptly corresponds to the preceding verb “lost.” **COUSTANT.**
>
> **Is disarmed.** Tertullian in the book *On Modesty*: “Their rights have been disarmed.” **BALUZE.**
>
> **Vindicating and upholding.** I found this reading in three ancient codices; five others have “vindicating and propitiating.” The old editions and three ancient books have “vindicating, propitiating, and upholding.”
>
> **Peace by presbyters.** Pamelius attests that all the manuscripts he saw have this reading. Although I too found it in eleven ancient codices, I do not reject the reading of the old editions, which I have also seen confirmed by the authority of nine ancient books. It reads: “Peace by presbyters who are not true presbyters.” For Cyprian could have judged those whom he shortly afterward reckons among the heretics not to be true presbyters, just as in Epistle LIX, p. 97, he calls Victor “a former presbyter.” **BALUZE.**
>
> **Those situated outside.** Previously it read: “unless they had established for themselves outside the Church and against the Church a conventicle.” We emended it on the evidence of all our ancient books, seven English manuscripts, and the old editions. Pamelius added the word “unless” from the Cambron manuscript and was consequently compelled to write “had established” in place of “to have established,” so that the sense would hold together, since he thought it could not otherwise do so. I, however, used seventeen ancient books in emending this epistle, and nowhere found the word “unless” except in the Corbie manuscript; yet even that manuscript has “to have established,” as do the others, not “had established.” I therefore reasonably prefer [Col. 0817C] the old reading and think that the sense thus holds together correctly. For immediately afterward there is added: “But after these things,” etc. **BALUZE.**
>
> **By those who do not communicate.** Thus the Oxford edition, together with our manuscripts. In the others, however, the preposition “by” is omitted. Cyprian continues speaking by antithesis: just as he has just said that peace is proclaimed by presbyters who are not true presbyters, so now he teaches that communion is offered by those who do not communicate. He speaks in the same way about those same presbyters of Felicissimus’s faction in Epistle XL, to the people: “Those who themselves do not possess peace now offer peace. Those who have withdrawn from the Church promise to bring the lapsed back and recall them into the Church.” **COUSTANT.**]

## XIII

During the persecution itself we sent letters concerning this very matter, but we were not heard. After repeatedly holding council, we decreed—not only by our unanimous judgment, but also under threat of penalty—that the brethren should perform penance and that no one should rashly grant peace to those who had not performed penance. Yet those sacrilegious men, acting against God, and rashly raging with impious fury against [Col. 0813A] the priests of God, withdraw from the Church and take up parricidal arms against the Church. They labor so that the devil’s malice may complete its work and so that divine mercy may not heal the wounded [Note: [Col. 0813A] “And that the wounded may not,” Voss. 2, Bod. 1, 2, Lam. Ebor. NC. 2.] within his Church. Through the deceit of their lies they corrupt [Note: [Col. 0813A] “Corrupt,” Pem. Lam. Voss. 2, Ebor. Lin. NC. 1, 2.] the penance of the wretched: so that satisfaction may not be made to an indignant God; so that the person who was previously ashamed or afraid to be a Christian may not afterward [Col. 0814A] seek Christ his Lord; so that the person who withdrew from the Church may not return to the Church.

Every effort is made to prevent offenses from being redeemed by just acts of satisfaction [Note: [Col. 0813A] “By just acts of satisfaction,” Lam. Bod. 2, Lin. Ebor. [Col. 0814A] NC. 1.] and just lamentations, and to prevent wounds from being washed with tears. True peace is taken away through the lie of a false peace; the mother’s saving bosom is closed off by the intervention [Note: [Col. 0814A] “Is closed by the intervention,” Lam. Ebor. Lin. NC. 1, Colbert. 1.] of a stepmother, so that the weeping and groaning of the lapsed may not be heard from their breasts and mouths.

Worse still, the lapsed are compelled to use the same tongues and mouths with which they had previously sinned on the Capitol [Col. 0815A] to heap abuse upon the priests and to assail confessors, virgins, and even righteous persons—distinguished by the praise of their faith and glorious within the Church—with insults and abusive words [Note: [Col. 0815B] “They persecute,” Corb. Colb. 1, 2.]. By these acts, it is not so much the moderation, humility, and sense of honor of our people that are struck down as it is those men’s own hope and life that are torn apart. For the wretched person is not the one who hears abuse, but the one who commits it; under the law, the sinner is not the one who is beaten by a brother, but the one who beats his brother. And when the guilty inflict injury upon the innocent, those who suffer the injury [Note: [Col. 0815B] “They rather suffer injury,” Lam. Ebor. NC. 1.] are the very ones who believe they are inflicting it.

For this reason, indeed, their mind is stricken [Note: [Col. 0815B] “Their mind is perverted,” Lam. NC. 1, Ebor. Bod. 2.], their understanding dull, and their perception estranged. It is the wrath of God not to understand one’s offenses, so that penance may not follow [Note: [Col. 0815B] “So that they may not pursue penance,” Lin.], as it is written: “And God gave them a spirit of insensibility” (Isa. 29:10)—so that, evidently, they may not return [Col. 0815B] and be healed, and may not, after their sins, be made well through entreaties and just acts of satisfaction.

The apostle Paul states in his epistle: “They did not possess love [Note: [Col. 0815C] “Choice,” Lam. Ebor. Lin. Voss. 2.] of the truth, so that they might be saved; and for this reason God will send them the working of error, so that they may believe a lie, so that all who have not believed the truth but take pleasure in injustice may be judged” (2 Thess. 2:10).

The first degree of blessedness is not to sin; the second, to recognize one’s offenses [Note: [Col. 0816B] “The third, to wash away one’s offenses,” old anonymous edition.]. In the former, complete [Col. 0816A] and undefiled innocence runs its course and preserves a person; in the latter, a remedy follows and heals. These men have lost both by offending God: the grace received from the sanctification of Baptism has been forfeited, and no penance remains available [Note: [Col. 0816B] “And penance does not come to one’s aid,” Oxon.; “may be taken up,” Benev.] through which guilt might be healed.

Do you suppose, brother, that the crimes committed against God are slight, that the offenses are small and insignificant, when through these men the majesty of an indignant God is not entreated; when the wrath, the fire, and the day of the Lord are not feared; when, with Antichrist threatening, the faith of the militant people [Note: [Col. 0816B] “People of God,” Bod. 3.] is disarmed by removing the strength and fear of Christ?

Let the laity see how they are to take care of this. A greater burden lies upon the priests in vindicating [Note: [Col. 0816B] “A greater burden falls upon,” Lin. NC. 2.] and [Note: [Col. 0816C] “And propitiating,” Corb.] upholding the majesty of God, lest we appear negligent in any respect here, since the Lord admonishes us and says: “And now this commandment is for you, O priests: if you will not listen, and if you will not lay it [Col. 0816B] upon your heart to give honor to my name, says the Lord, I shall send a curse upon you and curse your blessing” (Mal. 2:1).

Is honor, then, given to God when God’s majesty and judgment are treated with such contempt that, although he says that he is indignant and angry with those who sacrifice, and although he threatens eternal punishments and perpetual torments, sacrilegious men come forward and declare: Let no thought be given to God’s wrath; let the Lord’s judgment not be feared; let no one knock at the door of Christ’s Church. [Col. 0817A] Instead, once penance has been abolished and no *exomologesis*—public confession—of the crime has been made, with the bishops despised and trampled underfoot, let peace be proclaimed in deceptive words by presbyters who are not true presbyters [Note: [Col. 0817A] The printed editions have “by presbyters”; “who are not true” is restored with the aid of three manuscripts.]; and, so that the lapsed may not rise or those situated outside return to the Church, let communion [Note: [Col. 0817A] Thus Bod. 1, Thu.; Imp. has “communion to those who do not communicate.”] be offered by those who do not communicate.

> [Note: [Col. 0817C]
>
> **XIV.—*Exomologesis*.** In the Laetiense codex, “that is, confession” was written in ancient times above the line. From annotations of this kind arose so many variant readings and so many synonymous words in the works of Saint Cyprian. See Daillé, book VII, chapters 4, 5, and 10, *On Human Penalties and Acts of Satisfaction*. **BALUZE.**
>
> **By all.** It seemed to me that the reading of the old editions should be restored in this passage; it is confirmed by nine of our copies and seven English manuscripts. Manutius deleted the preposition. **BALUZE.**
>
> **Entangled in frauds.** This appears to have been taken from book XVI of Tacitus’s *Annals*: “He provided an example of the precautions to be taken against those entangled in frauds or defiled by shameful deeds,” etc. Pope Innocent I, in the epistle to Agapetus, Macedonius, and Maximus: “A certain Modestus entangled in many crimes.” Emperor Constantine, in the title of the Theodosian Code *On Repudiations*: “It remains that, if she has proved serious grounds and a conscience entangled in great crimes.” Cassiodorus, book IV, epistle 23: “Basilius and Praetextatus, entangled in magical arts.”
>
> **To the pseudo-bishop.** To Fortunatus. **BALUZE.**]

To the Chair of Peter and to the principal Church . . . access cannot be gained. In an extraordinary fashion, all the commentators who are heretics or modern innovators distort these signal words of St. Cyprian, so that each may scatter them into his own insolent interpretation. Let them therefore be heard and confounded by their own testimony before their mouths are stopped by the decisive judgments of Catholics on this passage. At the head of this troop of enemies, whose ignorance it is easy to pierce through, let us not now hesitate to place Nicolas Rigault, a man of decidedly dubious—not to say wholly ruined—good faith, sometimes carried away to such impudence that, though outwardly a Catholic, he must occasionally be rebuked by the heterodox and deservedly suffer their lashes. He therefore tries in vain to gnaw away at Cyprian’s foregoing statement with the following remarks:

“The schismatics, condemned by a council of the African bishops, had appealed. Accordingly, Cyprian praises the Roman Church, to which they had sailed with a written appeal. Immediately afterward, however, he brands the schismatics with the charge of faithlessness, in order to make them more odious to the Romans, who excelled in faith. For he adapts Paul’s words to this meaning as well. He says that faithlessness neither ought nor is able to gain any access to them. He adds that appellants are by no means to be heard once the case has been examined and sentence pronounced. He then also defends the authority of the bishops within their own province. It had been established by all the bishops—and it was equally equitable and just—that a case should be tried nowhere other than where the offense was committed. Each pastoral bishop had been assigned a portion of the flock for him to govern, and would render an account of his conduct or administration, not at Rome but in heaven, not to Cornelius but to Christ. Thus, after gracefully and prudently praising Cornelius, Cyprian, despite the proclaimed authority or prerogative of the principal Church, denies that it has any part in the case of Novatian, who had already been condemned after an inquiry in Africa.

“Jerome, *Against Rufinus*: ‘Know that the Roman faith, praised by the voice of the Apostle, does not receive deceptions of this kind.’ Almost all the Latin Fathers understood Paul’s words to the Romans in this way, as though faith among the Romans had been more correct and sincere, although the Apostle says only that he gives thanks to God because it was everywhere widely reported that even the Romans, the lords of the world, had embraced the Christian faith. This certainly contributed greatly to the propagation of the Christian faith because of the dignity of the City, which was the capital of the whole world and mistress of the nations. That the faith of the Romans, however, was not altogether commendable when Paul wrote is shown by Paul’s own words. Ambrose too observed this in the preface to his *Commentaries on the Epistle to the Romans*, and indeed on those very words of Paul cited by Cyprian. He says that the faith of the Romans was not then in accordance with the rule of truth handed down by its originators. Nevertheless, because they had begun to worship that which came from the one God, with the name of Christ introduced, the Apostle congratulates them, knowing that they were capable of making progress—both because the renown of their faith meant the advancement of many and because those who had not believed could certainly believe through their example. For, as he says, ‘An inferior readily does what he has seen done by a superior.’

“Finally, Jerome himself, in the preface to the second book on Galatians, says that the Romans had no faith other than that possessed by all the Churches of Christ, but that among them there was greater devotion and simplicity in believing. ‘Where else do people flock to the churches and the tombs of the martyrs with such zeal and in such numbers? Where does the “Amen” echo like heavenly thunder, making the empty temples of the idols tremble?’” —RIGAULT.

“This passage, from which the defenders of papal monarchy carve extraordinary conclusions, will be found to have a very different purpose if the logic and aim of the context are duly weighed. For Cyprian says that those factious men, Fortunatus and Felicissimus, although they themselves were schismatics above all, did not approach Novatian and his followers, who were guilty of the same offense, but—with consummate impudence—assailed Cornelius, the legitimate bishop of the Roman Church and successor of St. Peter. Though divided from the Church, they did not similarly approach those excluded from its communion, but instead importuned the principal or mother Church, where the body of the faithful is found and which Cyprian continually opposes to offshoots (*stolonibus*, Greek ἀποφυάσι, ‘shoots’), the Church united with its legitimate pastor and therefore the Church from which priestly unity arose. They gave no thought to the fact that the Romans were in no way degenerate from those whose faith was praised by the Apostle’s proclamation, and to whom—as has been demonstrated by signal proofs, namely the rejection first of Novatian and then of Fortunatus—schismatic faithlessness cannot gain access.” —FELL.

“‘The principal Church . . . from which unity arose’: that is, the Church established in the chief city and the first in the West to share in episcopal government.” —GOLDHORN.

Let this be more than enough concession to those who go astray; we may now confidently set our Catholic expositors of the Fathers against them.

**The Chair of Peter and the principal Church.** In the same way, below in the letter to Antonianus, Cyprian calls it the place of Fabian, the place of Peter, and Peter’s Chair. In Cyprian’s judgment, therefore, the Roman pontiff is Peter’s successor in the priestly chair and hence in ecclesiastical authority. Likewise, the Roman Church is the principal Church and, as he said above in Letter XLV, the mother of all the churches, since, as we said there from Irenaeus, more serious questions of faith are customarily referred to it and decided by it. Both points are also attested by the most holy pontiffs, martyrs, and doctors, almost all of whom confirm their judgment by that saying addressed to Peter: “Upon this rock I shall build my Church.”

The same is affirmed by Irenaeus in the passage cited; Tertullian, in his book *On the Prescription of Heretics*; Ambrose, in *On the Death of His Brother Satyrus*, chapter 7, and Sermon 47; Jerome, in his letter to Damasus and Book I of the *Apology Against Rufinus*; Cyril, in the passage cited by St. Thomas in *Against the Errors of the Greeks*; Augustine, Letters 106 and 162, Tractate 56 on John, Book II *Against Pelagius and Celestius*, and *Against the Donatists*, Book II, chapter 11; likewise the general councils: Nicaea, canons 18 and 19, as cited by Julius in his letter to the Synod of Antioch; the Council of Chalcedon, in the passage cited by St. Thomas, which was erased by the heretics, as Gregory attests in Book VII, Letter 14; likewise Acts 12 and 3 of the Council of Constantinople, in the judgment against the heretic Anthimus; Synod VI, Act 4, in the profession of faith approved by all the Fathers of the council, Acts 8, 13, and 14; Synod VII, Act 2; also Synod VIII, canon 2; finally, the Lateran Council under Innocent III, and the Councils of Florence and Trent. But enough of this. —PAMELIUS.

“**That they are the Romans, etc., to whom faithlessness cannot gain access.**” This is an elegant passage confirming that the Roman Church or Chair cannot err in faith. Cyprian offers as confirmation the praise of their faith by Paul. Jerome likewise says in *Apology Against Rufinus* III: “Know that the Roman faith, praised by the voice of the Apostle, does not receive deceptions of this kind; even if an angel should proclaim something different from what was once preached, that faith, fortified by Paul’s authority, cannot be changed.” You have similar statements in the *Letter to Pammachius and Oceanus*. Irenaeus likewise says of this Church: “In it the tradition delivered by the Apostles has always been preserved.”

So too Pope Lucius I, to whom a letter of Cyprian is extant: “This holy and apostolic Church of Christ, the mother of all the churches, is shown by the grace of almighty God never to have strayed from the path of apostolic tradition, nor to have succumbed through corruption by heretical innovations; rather, just as at the beginning it received the rule of apostolic faith from its founders, the chiefs of Christ’s Apostles, so it remains inviolate to the end, in accordance with the divine promise of our Lord himself, who said in his Gospels to the chief of his disciples: ‘Peter, behold, Satan has demanded you, that he might sift you like wheat; but I have prayed for you, Peter, that your faith may not fail; and when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers.’”

The same is said by Pope Felix to Benignus, and by Mark to Athanasius and the other bishops of Egypt; and similar things are said by Eusebius, who preceded them, in the letter cited above, and by the Church of Tarragona to the blessed pontiff Hilary. To the same point belong the formulas of reconciliation sent after the schism by John, patriarch of Constantinople and successor of Acacius in the reign of Emperor Justin, to Pope Hormisdas, and by Eulalius of Carthage with the other African bishops to the pontiff Boniface.

Indeed, the Roman faith was always regarded so thoroughly as the Catholic faith that Emperor Gratian issued an edict that all his subjects should retain the faith and religion maintained by Peter, the summit of the Apostles, and at that time by Damasus, bishop of Rome. You have this edict both in the ecclesiastical history and in the Code of Justinian, title *On the Supreme Trinity*. You also have the Fathers’ concordant judgment on this matter in the passages cited above. For the answers to arguments brought forward by opponents to the contrary, and for further material relevant here, see Albert Pighius, *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, Book IV; Cardinal Hosius, *Against Brenz*; and Melchior Cano, *Theological Topics*, Book VI. —PAMELIUS.

“Here we are openly taught that the Chair which Peter established at Rome and left to his successors is the center of the unity of the whole Church. Those who attempt to divert these words of Cyprian to another meaning are refuted by a similar passage in his book *On the Unity of the Church*, where one may read: ‘Upon that one man, Peter, Christ builds his Church, and to him he commands that his sheep be fed.’ And shortly afterward: ‘To make unity manifest, he established one Chair, and by his authority arranged that the origin of that same unity should begin from one. The primacy is given to Peter so that the one Church of Christ and the one Chair may be displayed.’ Let those, therefore, who have been torn away from this Chair—that is, separated from the source and root of unity—consider how they can trust that they remain within the Church, which is only one and outside which there is no salvation.” —COUSTANT.

**The principal Church.** I know well enough that our opponents would wish these words not to occur in Cyprian. They therefore set every device in motion to show that nothing extraordinary is attributed here to the Roman Church, saying that it is called “principal” because of its greatness—as Cyprian says in Letter XLIX, p. 64—because it was established in the chief city, and because it is first in order. Yet they knew that Irenaeus, bishop of Lyons and earlier than Cyprian, had written in Book III, chapter 3, that every Church must come together with the Roman Church because of its more powerful—or “superior,” as others write—principality.

This principal power cannot be referred to the Roman pontiff’s power within the empire, which was altogether nonexistent, but to his power in the Church. That power must have been very great, since Irenaeus calls it principal, lest anyone, as Marca says in *On Concord*, Book I, chapter 3, §6, “dream here of the Roman Empire.” Against this passage of Irenaeus, as one of great authority, Nicolas Gallasius, the translator of Irenaeus, David Blondel, and Jean Le Clerc in his *Ecclesiastical History* argue vehemently. There Le Clerc contends that Irenaeus’s translator ought to have written “superior antiquity,” that is, as he explains it, “greater antiquity.”

They might nevertheless have noticed that Tertullian said in his book *On Prescriptions Against Heretics* that authority was available to us from the city of Rome, and that Cyprian said more than once that the Church was built upon Peter and that the beginning of unity proceeded from it. These words carry great weight in this controversy. Finally, it must be observed that, when Cyprian complains of the audacity of the schismatics who, after the judgment of the African bishops, had appealed to the Chair of blessed Peter and the principal Church, he was in no way referring to the greatness of the city of Rome. They were not seeking the city’s protection, but that of Cornelius. For the case was ecclesiastical.

It must therefore be certain that the issue here is the authority of the bishop of Rome, to whom in ancient times bishops who complained that they had been oppressed by their colleagues were accustomed to flee, as these schismatics did. Cyprian identifies the Chair of Peter with the principal Church, because the Chair of Peter is the principal Church, and the principal Church is the Chair of Peter. I believe this cannot be denied. The author of the *Life of St. Anselm, Bishop of Lucca*, writing against Cardinal Hugh Candidus, says that Hugh nullified the privileges of the principal Church, that is, the Roman Church. Augustine, moreover, in *On Baptism Against the Donatists*, Book II, chapter 1, acknowledges in Peter the primacy of the apostolate. —BALUZE.

**Priestly unity.** Cyprian repeatedly inculcates this doctrine, especially in his book *On the Unity of the Church*. Optatus of Milevis does likewise. —BALUZE.

**Whose faith.** That is, the faith of the Romans. Jerome, in the preface to Book II of his *Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians*: “The faith of the city of Rome is praised. This is not because the Romans possess any faith other than that possessed by all the Churches of Christ, but because among them there is greater devotion and simplicity in believing.”

Bachiarius, in his *Apology*, or *Formula of the Catholic Faith*, published in the second volume of Muratori’s *Anecdotes*: “If, because of one man’s fault, the offspring of an entire province must be anathematized, let that most blessed disciple—that is, Rome—also be condemned. From her not one but two or three, or even more, heresies have now sprung, yet none of them has been able either to occupy or to move the Chair of Peter, that is, the See of faith.” —BALUZE.

**Against the bishop.** The commonly printed texts read “against the bishops,” words absent from the Corbie manuscript. The old Colbert manuscript has *contra episcopo*. We believe one should read *contra episcopum*, “against the bishop,” namely Cyprian, who above, at no. 6, proved that he had been legitimately appointed and had always been regarded as the true bishop. In Letter XL—or 43—he similarly represents the same presbyters as “retaining,” as he says, “their old poison against my episcopate.”

Alternatively, he may here have called them “bishops” by oratorical license, as in the letter to the people cited immediately above he wrote of the same men: “They are alone, since they are not with the bishops—those who rebelled against the bishops.” Yet the present passage seems less compatible with a figurative expression of that kind. —COUSTANT.

**By all of us.** The preposition *ab*, “by,” is missing from the commonly printed texts, but our manuscripts and eight English manuscripts contain it. A decree established by the common consent of the Africans is noted here. —COUSTANT.

**For since it has been established.** Baronius, who read a similar statement in the third letter of Pope Fabian to Bishop Hilary, did not doubt that Cyprian had that letter in view when he wrote these words. In this the most learned man was certainly mistaken. It is certain that the letter of Fabian was wholly unknown to the holy martyr. In Gratian, causa 3, question 6, chapter *Peregrina*, it is attributed to Pope Sixtus in the old editions. The Roman Correctors added that it was taken from a letter of Pope Sixtus III to the Eastern bishops. —BALUZE.

**Let the case be heard there.** The Africans indeed held, as they themselves afterward wrote to Pope Celestine, that all matters should be concluded in the places where they had arisen, and that the grace of the Holy Spirit would not be lacking to any province.

Emperors Valentinian and Valens, law X of the Theodosian Code, title *On Accusations and Indictments*: “Permission to prosecute must not extend beyond the boundaries of the province. For criminal trials ought to be conducted where the offense is said to have been committed.” And law XIII: “An accuser shall not be permitted to proceed beyond the boundaries of the province, because criminal trials ought to be conducted where the offense is said to have been committed.” See Julian the Professor, chapter 210. —BALUZE.

**A few desperate and ruined men.** That is, Felicissimus and the others who had flown with him to Rome after appointing Fortunatus pseudo-bishop, and concerning whom the Africans had pronounced judgment. The Oxford editor therefore departs from Cyprian’s meaning when, in the judgment of that blessed martyr, he regards as “desperate and ruined” those to whom the authority of the bishops in Africa appears less than even that of Cornelius himself, seated at Rome in Peter’s Chair.

Indeed, Felicissimus and his companions are called desperate and ruined, not because they had appealed to Rome, but because of their schism and other abominable crimes. Cyprian, therefore, comparing the African bishops not with Cornelius but with Privatus, Felix, Jovinus, and Maximus—against whom he had shortly before rehearsed the judgments of the Africans—says: “Unless perhaps the authority of the bishops established in Africa appears inferior to the authority of those few desperate men.” —COUSTANT.

**Bound.** Erasmus noted in the margin of his edition that elsewhere the reading is *involutam*, “entangled.” I know that the Verona manuscript also had this reading. The same reading is found in the Corbie and Tours manuscripts. Lactantius, Book IV, chapter 17: “an entangled heart.” —BALUZE.

[Col. 0823D] **Cannot.** Six English manuscripts add *nisi*, “unless,” here; it is absent from our manuscripts. Immediately afterward the same number prefer *fragmina*, “fragments,” to *putamina*, “prunings”; in place of the latter, the Verona manuscript, the two Colbert manuscripts, and the original hand of the Corbie manuscript have *putramina*, “rotten pieces.” —COUSTANT.]

### XIV

Even this did not satisfy them: they had withdrawn from the Gospel; they had taken away from the lapsed the hope of satisfaction and repentance; and they had removed from every perception and fruit of repentance those entangled in fraud, defiled by adulteries, or polluted by the deadly contagion of sacrifices, so that they should not pray to God or make an *exomologesis*—a confession—of their crimes in the Church. Outside the Church and against the Church they had established for themselves

[Note: [Col. 0817A] “They had removed them outside the Church and established for themselves against the Church,” Voss. 2, Lam., York, N.C. 1, 2, Bodl. 1, 2, [Col. 0817B] 3, the manuscript of Pamelius, and the Oxford edition with the Corbie manuscript, except that the latter has “unless they had established outside.” [Col. 0818A] “Unless” is absent from the older editions, as also from the two Colbert manuscripts and eight English manuscripts; these also then give “they had established,” not “they had established [subjunctive],” and, in our judgment, more genuinely. —COUSTANT.]

a gathering-place for their ruined faction,

[Note: [Col. 0818A] The commonly printed texts have “with which”; more correctly the Corbie manuscript and one Colbert manuscript have [Col. 0818B] “to which.”]

to which there might flock a horde of those conscious of evil within themselves and unwilling to pray to God or make satisfaction.

After all this, moreover, once they had had a pseudo-bishop appointed for themselves by heretics, they dared to sail and to carry letters from schismatics and profane men to the Chair of Peter and to the principal Church, from which priestly unity arose [Col. 0821A]. Nor did they consider that these are the Romans whose faith was praised by the Apostle’s proclamation, and to whom faithlessness cannot gain access.

What reason, moreover, was there for coming and announcing that a pseudo-bishop

[Note: [Col. 0821B] “Pseudo-bishops,” Lam., Bodl. 2.]

had been appointed against the bishop? Either what they have done pleases them, in which case they persist in their crime; or, if it displeases them and they withdraw, they know where they should return. For since it has been established

[Note: [Col. 0821B] Thus Voss. 2, Lincoln, Lam., York, Bodl. 1, 2, N.C. 1, 2.]

by all of us, and is equally equitable and just, that each person’s case should be heard in the place where the offense was committed, and since to each pastor a portion of the flock has been assigned

[Note: [Col. 0821B] “A portion of the flock has been entrusted,” Lam., York, N.C. 1, Bodl. 2.]

for each to rule and govern, rendering an account of his conduct to the Lord, those over whom we preside ought surely not to run about from place to place [Col. 0822A] or, by their deceitful and treacherous rashness, shatter the bishops’ closely knit concord. Instead, they should plead their case in the place where they can have both accusers

[Note: [Col. 0822B] “Where they may also have accusers,” Lam., York, Lincoln, Bodl. 3, N.C. 1, Michels.]

and witnesses to their crime—unless perhaps the authority of the bishops established in Africa, who have already judged them and recently condemned by the gravity of their judgment a conscience bound in the many snares of offenses, appears inferior to the authority of a few desperate and ruined men.

Their case has already been examined; sentence has already been pronounced upon them. Nor is it fitting for the judgment of priests to be called into question by the fickleness of a wavering and inconstant mind, since the Lord teaches and says: “Let your speech be: yes, yes; no, no” (Matt. 5:37).

[Note: [Col. 0823D]

### XV—Unless with scandal

We have restored the word *nisi*, “unless,” which seemed to be missing from this passage, following the authority of four old copies. —BALUZE.

**Rotten pieces.** Below in the book *On the Lapsed*, p. 186: “after the rotten portions have been cut away.” Whatever others may think, I believe this reading must be retained, since it is found in all the ancient copies and old editions. The Lamonius manuscript reads “either fragments or spittle.” —BALUZE.

**To be gathered.** The most illustrious bishop of Oxford believed that one should write *colligandae*, “to be bound together.” But all the old books and all the editions oppose this. Reinhart printed *collidenda*, “to be struck together,” perhaps through a printer’s error. —BALUZE.

**Do not consider.** We have retained this passage because we found it in the old editions and in ten [Col. 0824D] old books. Rigault, moreover, reports that he found it in one copy of the Manutius edition, where it had been added from some old book. Nevertheless, he did not place it in the text but among his observations. Manutius had rejected it and was praised for doing so by Pamelius, both because—as Pamelius says—it was missing from all the manuscripts and because it seemed irrelevant to the argument at this point. Pamelius might perhaps have changed his opinion if he had known that it exists in ten old codices and in the one cited by Rigault. Morel did not approve what Manutius had done, for he retained this section in his edition. The English editors omitted it. Nevertheless, it must not be left unsaid that it is missing from thirteen old books. —BALUZE.]

### XV

If those who passed judgment upon them in the preceding year are counted together with the presbyters and deacons, more persons were then present at the judicial examination and inquiry than the very men who now appear to be associated with Fortunatus. For you ought to know, dearest brother, that after he was made a pseudo-bishop by the heretics, he has now been deserted by almost everyone.

Those whose eyes were formerly covered by deceptions, and who were beguiled by false promises that they would all return to the Church together, realized, after they saw that a pseudo-bishop had been appointed there, that they had been frustrated and deceived. Every day they return and knock at the Church’s door. Yet we, who must render an account to the Lord, anxiously weigh and carefully examine who ought to be received and admitted into the Church.

Some are so obstructed by their own crimes, or the brothers oppose them so obstinately and firmly,

[Note: [Col. 0823C] “Or the brothers,” Lam., Bodl. 2, York, N.C. 1.]

that they cannot be received at all

[Note: [Col. 0823C] “They cannot be received except with scandal,” Lam., Bodl. 1, 2, 3, York, N.C. 1.]

without scandal and danger to very many. For certain prunings

[Note: [Col. 0823C] “Rotten pieces,” Verona; “fragments,” Lam., Benevento, Bodl. 1, 2, 3, Lincoln, N.C. 2.]

must not be gathered up in such a way that the parts which are whole and sound are wounded. Nor is that pastor useful or prudent who mixes diseased and infected sheep

[Note: [Col. 0823C] “Contracted,” Compendium manuscript. The Corbie manuscript originally had the same reading, but the letter *r* was subsequently erased.]

with the flock in such a way that he contaminates the entire flock through the affliction of the clinging evil.

[Note: [Col. 0823C] “Do not consider their number. For one who fears God is better than a thousand impious sons, just as the Lord spoke through the Prophet, saying: ‘Son, do not rejoice in impious sons if they multiply around you, when the fear of God is not in them’” [Col. 0824C], Fossombrone.]

O dearest brother, if only you could be present with us here when these wicked and perverse men

[Note: [Col. 0824C] “Subversive men,” Benevento.]

return from the schism! You would see how difficult it is for me to persuade our brothers to be patient, so that, after quieting the anguish of their minds, they may consent to the reception and healing of these evil men. For just as they rejoice and are glad when those who can be tolerated and are less culpable return, so, conversely, they roar and resist whenever those who are incorrigible and insolent, polluted either by adulteries or by sacrifices, and after all this still proud besides, return to the Church in such a manner as to corrupt those of good character within it.

I can scarcely persuade the people—indeed, I have to wring it from them—to allow such people to be admitted. The indignation of the brotherhood has been made more justified by the fact that one man and then another, though the people resisted

[Note: [Col. 0824C] “Though the people held out,” Bodl. 3.]

and objected, were nevertheless received through my leniency and proved worse than they had been before.

[Note: [Col. 0824C] “They proved to be those who did not even preserve their pledge,” Lam., York, Bodl. 2, N.C. 1.]

They could not even keep their pledge of repentance, because they had not come with true repentance.

[Note: [Col. 0824D]

### XVI—Gathering the brotherhood

The Grenoble manuscript reads “unity.” But the other reading is better. This one nevertheless ought not to have been neglected. —BALUZE.

**Through the prophet.** One of my old books reads “through Solomon.” Correctly, for these words are taken from the book of Ecclesiasticus. —BALUZE.

**With true repentance.** The Foix manuscript reads: “not yet with true repentance.” —BALUZE.]

### XVI

But what am I to say about those who have now sailed to you with Felicissimus, a man guilty of every crime, sent as envoys by the pseudo-bishop Fortunatus? The letters they bring to you are as false as the man whose letters they carry is himself false. How manifold is his consciousness of his sins,

[Note: [Col. 0824C] “A witness to his sins,” Bodl. 2.]

how execrable his life, and how shameful! Even if such men were within the Church, they ought to have been expelled from it.

Finally, because they know their own conscience, they do not dare

[Note: [Col. 0824C] Thus our manuscripts. The printed editions read: “nor do they dare to approach us.”]

to come or to approach the threshold of the Church. Instead, they wander outside throughout the province, deceiving and despoiling the brothers. Already sufficiently well known to everyone and excluded everywhere because of their crimes, they even sail there to you. For they cannot have the effrontery to approach us or stand before us, since the brothers bring the most bitter and grievous charges against them.

If they wish to undergo our judgment, let them come. Finally, if they can offer any excuse and defense, let us see what sense of satisfaction they possess and what fruit of repentance they bring. The Church here is closed to no one,

[Note: [Col. 0824C] The printed editions read “is closed,” against the manuscripts. Next, the more recent Colbert manuscript has “nor is the episcopate”; some English manuscripts likewise have “nor is the episcopate.”]

nor is the bishop

[Note: [Col. 0824C] “The episcopate,” Benevento, Voss. 2, Bodl. 3.]

denied to anyone. Our patience, leniency, and humanity are available to those who come. I desire everyone to return to the Church; I desire all our fellow soldiers to be enclosed within the camp of Christ and the dwelling places of God the Father.

I forgive everything; I overlook much. In my zeal and desire to gather the brotherhood, I do not examine with the full rigor of religion even offenses committed against God [Col. 0825A]. By forgiving sins more than I ought, I myself almost sin. With ready and complete love I embrace those who return in repentance and confess their sin with humble and sincere satisfaction.

[Note: [Col. 0825C]

### XVII—He can be killed

Below, Letter LVI, p. 91: “Nor should we fear being killed, since it is certain that when we are killed we are crowned”; and Letter LVII, p. 95: “He understood that the soldiers of Christ cannot be conquered, though they can die.”

Jerome, at the end of his book *Life of the Monk Malchus*, says that a man devoted to Christ can die but cannot be defeated. Tertullian, in the *Apologeticum*: “We conquer when we are killed.” Prudentius, in his poem on the martyr Romanus:

> If you permit us, we live without bloodshed.  
> But if we are punished bloodily, we conquer.

Sulpicius Severus, in his letter to Eusebius, writes that the righteous—that is, the martyrs—while enduring every torment always remained unconquered, and that they conquered the more powerfully the more grievously they suffered. The same author, in Book II of his *Sacred History*: “Never did we conquer in a greater triumph than when ten years of slaughter could not conquer us.”

Agobard, in his book *Against the Law of Gundobad*, chapter 9: “When there was public contention concerning the truth of religion, with some thinking that any created thing should be worshiped as God, while others said that the Creator alone must be worshiped, the victors were those who were killed, not those who killed.”

Seneca, chapter 27 of *On the Happy Life*: “Leap upon me; make your assault. By enduring you, I shall conquer you.” The same author, in his *Consolation to Polybius*: “He understands that I can be injured but cannot be conquered.” See below, p. 463. —BALUZE.

**Again and again.** In the manuscript of St. Michael, the explanation “that is, likewise” was written in ancient times above the line. I am occasionally willing to record such trifles, because from these or similar [Col. 0826C] sources arose most of the errors found in manuscripts of the works of St. Cyprian and other ancient writers. —BALUZE.]

### XVII

If there are any who think that they can return to the Church not by entreaties but by threats, or suppose that they can make an entrance for themselves not by lamentations and acts of satisfaction but by intimidation, let them know for certain that the Lord’s Church stands closed against such people, and that the unconquered and mighty camp of Christ, fortified under the Lord’s protection, does not yield to threats.

A priest of God who holds fast to the Gospel and keeps Christ’s commandments can be killed; he cannot be conquered. Zechariah, the priest of God, supplies and furnishes us with an example of courage and faith.

[Note: [Col. 0825B] “Of fierce courage, Zechariah,” Bodl. 3.]

Since he could not be terrified by threats and stoning,

[Note: [Col. 0825B] “Stonings,” Lam., N.C. 1, Bodl. 2, 3, York.]

he was killed in God’s temple, crying out and repeatedly saying what we too cry out and say against the heretics: “Thus says the Lord:

[Note: [Col. 0825C] Thus Bodl. 1, 2, 3, Lam., York, N.C. 1, 2; the printed texts have “said.”]

You have forsaken the ways of the Lord, and the Lord will forsake you”

[Note: [Col. 0825C] Thus Lam., York, Lincoln; “will leave you,” Oxford.]

(2 Chron. 24:21).

For even though a few rash and wicked men forsake the heavenly

[Note: [Col. 0825C] “Heavenly treasures,” Lam., York, Bodl. 2, N.C. 1.]

and saving ways of the Lord,

[Note: [Col. 0825C] “Have forsaken,” Bodl. 3.]

and because they do not act holily are forsaken by the Holy Spirit, we must not therefore forget the divine tradition. We must not judge the crimes of madmen to be greater than the judgments of priests, or suppose that human efforts possess more power to attack than divine protection possesses

[Note: [Col. 0825C] “Than for,” Voss. 2, Lam., York, N.C. 1, 2; “than that which,” printed editions.]

to defend.

[Note: [Col. 0826C]

### XVIII—Authority and power

The final two words are absent from one royal manuscript. Perhaps, therefore, this should be included among the synonyms in which the holy martyr’s works abound. —BALUZE.

**Concerning a Christian.** The Verona manuscript reads “concerning a bishop.” So too the Foix manuscript. The word “Christian” does not occur in the royal or de Thou manuscript. The Grenoble manuscript has “Catholic.” —BALUZE.

**Let the Church yield to the Capitol.** Jerome, in his dialogue *Against the Luciferians*, said: “A man now instructed in the Capitol.” —BALUZE.

**Gathering.** I do not doubt that the common reading, which has *consessum*, “assembly,” appears much better than this one. Yet since the old editions and eighteen ancient copies have our reading, *congestum*, “gathering,” I prefer it not without reason. It could easily have happened that this word, which has another meaning in pure Latin, acquired a divergent sense among the Africans, as did many other terms. Erasmus was the first to print *concessum*, “concession,” perhaps by conjecture. —BALUZE.]

### XVIII

Is it for this, dearest brother, that the dignity of the Catholic Church, the faithful and incorrupt majesty of the people established within it, and also priestly authority and power must be laid aside—so that those established outside the Church may say that they wish to judge the one placed over the Church;

[Note: [Col. 0825C] “Heretics concerning the bishop,” Corbie manuscript together with the more recent Colbert [Col. 0826B] and Verona manuscripts.—“Heretics who have been established,” Voss. 2.]

heretics to judge a Christian; the wounded to judge the sound; the injured to judge the whole; the fallen to judge the standing; defendants to judge the judge; and sacrilegious men to judge the priest?

What remains except that the Church should yield to the Capitol, and that, when the priests withdraw and remove the Lord’s altar,

[Note: [Col. 0826B] “From the altar of the Lord,” Fabian.]

images and idols should pass with their altars into the sacred and venerable assembly of our clergy? What remains except that still more abundant and ample material should be supplied to Novatian for declaiming and inveighing against us, if those who sacrificed and publicly denied Christ are not only begged to return and admitted without having performed repentance, but in addition begin to exercise dominion through their power to inspire terror?

[Note: [Col. 0826D]

### XIX—Antichrist threatens

Many people have said many different things about Antichrist. It has often been believed that he was approaching—indeed, that he had already been born. There were some, as we said in connection with Lactantius’s book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, who believed that Nero had not died but was still alive, that he would come before the end of the age, and that he himself would be Antichrist. See Catechesis 15 of Cyril of Jerusalem. —BALUZE.

**About to destroy.** Two old books read “about to ruin.” —BALUZE.

[Col. 0827C] **Soundness of mind.** Emperor Theodosius, law I, title *On Jews, Samaritans, etc.*: “If by an excellent medicinal law we attempt to recall them to soundness of mind.”

Julius Caesar, Book VII of *The Gallic War*: “He should be ashamed to return to sanity.”

Aulus Hirtius, in *The African War*: “To be brought back to sanity by some means.”

Lactantius, chapter 34 of *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*: “So that even the Christians might return to right minds.”

Juvenal: “One should pray for a sound mind in a sound body.” —BALUZE.]

Breasts covered. Thus Manutius, though I do not know on what authority. Pamelius and the Oxford editor nevertheless followed him. Morel, with one English manuscript, reads: “breasts freed from the darkness of sins.” Three other English manuscripts read: “breasts beset by the darkness of sins” [Col. 0827D]. Pamelius notes that in other printed and manuscript copies the reading current is: “sinners from the darkness of sins.” The Compiègne manuscript, the more recent Colbert manuscript, and the Corbie manuscript agree with these, except that in the last the preposition *a* (“from”) does not occur before the word “sins.” In the older Colbert manuscript we read: “breasts by the darkness of sins.” This reading would be complete if the preposition *pro* were restored in place of the word “breasts.” COUSTANT.—Covered. An old royal codex has “overwhelmed”; one Bodleian manuscript, “beset.” So too Morel’s edition. In the codex of Saint-Arnoul it is written: “breasts, once the darkness of sins has been shaken off”; in the Bec manuscript: “so that, withdrawing from the darkness of sins.” BALUZE.

The Lord’s protection. The Corbie codex reads: “with God protecting.” The English edition attests that it is so written also in one Bodleian and one Vossian manuscript. BALUZE.

Condition. Thus Erasmus, with the Cambron manuscript; this is also confirmed by the two manuscripts, the Colbert and the Corbie. In two English manuscripts there occurs “agreement,” but in the other books “mutilation.” Pamelius notes that he prefers this reading [Col. 0828C] because he thinks Cyprian is alluding to Paul’s words at Philippians 3:2: “Beware of the dogs, beware of the evil workers, beware of the mutilation.” But there “mutilation” means circumcision, or the Jews; hence there immediately follows: “For we are the circumcision, who serve God in spirit and glory in Christ Jesus, and not in the flesh,” etc. Such an interpretation, however, has no place here. COUSTANT.—Mutilation. Thus the old editions and nearly all the old copies read. In one of my books “mutilation” is read, with “or condition” above the line. From this, therefore—that is, from some similar copy—arose the reading preferred by four old books and the editions of Erasmus, Manutius, and Morel, in which “condition” is written. Two old manuscripts cited in the English edition have “agreement.” One of my old manuscripts and the Grenoble manuscript have “conscience.” Thus the old books vary. And just as human dispositions vary and opinions differ, Pamelius thought the reading “mutilation” better, while Rigaltius preferred “condition.” Yet Rigaltius himself retained Pamelius’s reading in his edition. Jerome, in his Letter to Pammachius and Oceanus: “With astonishing hatred I recoil from mutilation.” BALUZE.]

## XIX

If they ask for peace, let them lay down their arms; if they are making satisfaction, why do they threaten? Or if they threaten, let them know that God’s priests do not fear them. For neither will Antichrist, when he begins to come, enter the Church merely because he threatens; nor will submission be made to his arms and violence merely because he declares that he will destroy those who resist. The heretics arm us while they suppose that their threats terrify us; they do not cast us down [Note: [Col. 0826C] “In our face,” Oxford edition from Voss. 2, Lam., York, Bod. 1, 2, Lin., NC. 1, 2, Thu., Mic., Vict. The older Colbert manuscript, with others cited by Pamelius, reads “in the face.” The words appended read: “they ask in peace,” which the rest of our manuscripts also exhibit.] in peace [Col. 0827A], but rather raise and inflame us, while they make peace itself worse than persecution for the brethren.

We do indeed hope that they will not fulfill in crime what they utter in madness, and that those who sin with treacherous [Note: [Col. 0827C] “And those who with treacherous words,” Lam., Bod. 2.] and cruel words will not also offend by their deeds. We pray and implore God, whom they do not cease to provoke and exasperate, that their hearts may grow gentle; that, having laid aside their madness, they may return to soundness of mind [Note: [Col. 0827C] “Their minds to soundness,” Ver.]; that breasts covered [Note: [Col. 0827C] “Breasts beset,” Bod. 3, Lin. “That of sins and offenses,” Fab. “That breasts freed from the darkness of sins,” Bod. 1.] by the darkness of sins may recognize the light of repentance; and that they may ask instead that the supplications and prayers of the bishop be poured out on their behalf, rather than themselves pouring out the blood of the priest.

But if they persist in their madness, and cruelly persevere in these murderous plots and threats of theirs, no priest of God is so weak, so prostrate and abject, so enfeebled by the frailty [Col. 0827B] of human littleness, that he is not divinely raised up against the enemies and assailants of God, or that his humility and weakness are not given courage by the strength and power of the Lord’s protection [Note: [Col. 0827C] “With the Lord protecting,” Bod. 3, Voss. 2.]. It makes no difference to us by whom or when we are destroyed [Note: [Col. 0827C] “When we perish,” Pam., Bod. 1. The older manuscript, with two English manuscripts: “we perish.”], since we shall receive from the Lord the reward of death and blood. Their condition deserves tears and lamentation [Note: [Col. 0827C] Thus Lam., Bod. 1, Voss. 2. “Lamentable agreement,” Lin., NC. 2. “Condition,” Thu., Corb. “Rather deserving tears and lamentation” [Col. 0828C], Benev.], for the devil so blinds them that, without considering the eternal punishments of Gehenna, they strive to imitate the advent of Antichrist, now drawing near.

[Col. 0828A]

[Note: [Col. 0828D]

### XX.—Most flourishing

That epithet is rightly illustrated by the most distinguished Jean Mabillon in the preface to volume II of the *Museum Italicum*, p. 13. BALUZE.

### Slander

Baluze reads: “disparagement.” I have seen it so written in several ancient codices. I therefore consider this reading better than that which has “slander.” Livy, book II: “Envy is blind and knows nothing other than to disparage virtues and to corrupt their honors and rewards.” BALUZE.]

## XX

And although I know, dearest brother, that because of the mutual love which we owe [Note: [Col. 0828C] “Have,” Ver.] and show one another, you always read our letters to the most flourishing clergy presiding there with you [Note: [Col. 0828C] “Present there with you,” Lam., York, NC. 1, Bod. 2.] and to the most holy and very numerous people, nevertheless I now both admonish and ask you to do at my request what at other times you do spontaneously and honorably: namely, that when this letter of mine has been read, if any contagion of poisonous speech and pestilential sowing has crept in there, all of it may be stripped from the ears and breasts of the brethren, and the whole and sincere love [Note: [Col. 0828C] “With sincere love,” Lam., Bod. 2.] of the good may be cleansed again from every defilement of heretical slander.

[Note: [Col. 0828D]

### XXI.—Bears destruction

There are two readings of this passage in the old books. One is: “The perverse man,” he says, “bears destruction in his mouth and stores fire upon his lips” [Col. 0829C]. The other is: “The perverse man,” he says, “bears perverse things in his mouth and stores—or, storing—the fire of his destruction upon his lips.” The Fossés manuscript has both. Florus read in his codex: “bears perverse things, storing the fire of his destruction.” So too the Bec codex. The Grenoble manuscript has: “bears the fire of his destruction and stores it” [Col. 0829D]. In Proverbs 16 it reads: “An impious man digs up evil, and upon his lips a fire blazes.” BALUZE.

### Although that

I do not sufficiently understand what the word “that” is doing in this passage. Manutius added it, Morel expunged it, and Pamelius restored it. I know that it is found in nine old books, but it is absent from all the others. I would gladly delete it. For I do not see with what word in this period it can be joined, or to what it refers. Thus Jerome, in his Letter to Algasia on Eleven Questions from the New Testament, chapter 10, when citing the passage from chapter 3 of Paul’s Letter to the Colossians, “which INDEED have an appearance of wisdom,” says: “In this passage the conjunction ‘indeed’ is superfluous, something we find the Apostle to have done in many passages because of his lack of grammatical training.” BALUZE.

### Fortified

Thus it is written in five of our codices and four English codices, and also in the ancient editions. Manutius printed “warned.” Morel restored the old reading. Pamelius and the others preferred [Col. 0830C] “warned.” That reading—to conceal nothing—is found in seven of our copies. BALUZE.]

## XXI

For the future, however, let our dearly beloved brethren resolutely turn away from and avoid the words and conversations of those whose speech creeps like a cancer, as the Apostle [Col. 0828B] says: “Evil conversations corrupt good characters” (2 Tim. 2:17; 1 Cor. 15:33). And again: “After one admonition avoid a heretical man, knowing that such a person is perverse [Note: [Col. 0828C] “Such a person, since he knowingly sins,” NC. 2.], and sins, and is condemned by himself” [Note: [Col. 0828C] “Through himself,” Benev.] (Tit. 3:10–11).

And through Solomon the Holy Spirit speaks: “The perverse man,” he says, “bears destruction in his mouth [Note: [Col. 0828C] “In his mouth he bears perverse things, storing the fire of his destruction,” Lam., Bod. 2, York, NC. 1, Mic., Vict., Compend. “In his mouth he bears the word of his destruction,” Fab.], and stores fire upon his lips” (Prov. 16:27). Likewise he warns again, saying: “Hedge your ears with thorns, and do not listen to a wicked tongue” [Col. 0829A] (Sir. 28:28). And again: “An evil man obeys the tongue of the wicked, but the righteous man gives no heed to lying lips” (Prov. 17:4).

Although I know that our brotherhood there is fortified, of course, by your foresight [Note: [Col. 0829C] Thus Pem., Bod. 1, Voss. 2, NC. 2, Lin., Thu., Foss.], and is also sufficiently guarded by its own vigilance, so that it can neither be caught by the heretics’ poisons nor deceived, and that the divine teachings and precepts prevail among them to the same degree as their fear of God—nevertheless, out of an abundance of concern or love, I have been persuaded to write these things to you: that no associations be formed with such people, no banquets or conversations be shared with the evil, and that we be as separate from them as they are fugitives from the Church [Note: [Col. 0829C] “Those men are fugitives from the Church,” Ver., Ben.]. For it is written: “But if he also despises the Church, let him be to you as a gentile and a tax collector” (Matt. 18:17). And the blessed Apostle [Col. 0829B] [Note: [Col. 0829C] “The Apostle Paul,” Lam., York, NC. 1.] not only admonishes but commands that people withdraw from such persons: “We command you,” he says, “in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, that you withdraw from all brethren who walk disorderly and not according to the tradition which they received from us.”

There can be no fellowship between faith and faithlessness. He who is not with Christ [Note: [Col. 0829C] “Is not; he is Christ’s adversary,” Lam., York, Bod. 2, Lin., NC. 1.], who is Christ’s adversary, who is the enemy of his unity and peace, cannot remain joined to us. If they come with prayers and acts of satisfaction, let them be heard; if they heap up curses and threats, let them be rejected.

I hope that you, dearest brother, are always in good health.

## IN THE YEAR OF CHRIST 252  
## LETTER XIII: SAINT CYPRIAN TO SAINT CORNELIUS, POPE

(Erasmus I, 1; Pamelius, Rigaltius, Baluze LVII; Paris 56; Coustant I, col. 190; Galland III, p. 360.)

[Col. 0829C]

[Col. 0830A]

### SUBJECT

Cyprian congratulates Cornelius because, by his courageous confession, he presented himself to his people as a leader in confessing the faith; he then launches into praises of the Romans. Next he censures Novatian’s adverse fortune. Finally, he explains how they should mutually prepare themselves for the approaching contest.

### CYPRIAN TO HIS BROTHER CORNELIUS, GREETINGS

[Note: [Col. 0830C]

### LETTER XIII.—I.—Dearest brother

The man who added notes to the Manutian edition torments himself here at great length and to no purpose in an effort to soften the harshness which he thought he detected in these words of Cyprian, as though one could infer from them that Cyprian made no distinction between the bishop [Col. 0830D] of Rome and the others. If that annotator had considered the customs of ancient times, he would easily have extricated himself from this difficulty. See what we have said on this subject in connection with Letter XLI, p. 429. BALUZE.

### Confession; but Baluze, agreement

“Since the Speyer edition and the old Venetian edition,” he says, “have it so written, and since not only the Erasmian and Morel editions agree with it, but also fifteen old copies and Florus’s excerpts, I thought I ought to restore it thus.
