Rembolt was the first of all to print ‘confession.’ Below, in the book *On the Lord’s Prayer*, p. 206, appears ‘conformed by agreement of spirit,’ for which the Moissac codex has ‘confession.’ Likewise below, Letter LXVII, p. 115, reads ‘concordant by agreement of spirit,’ where the Corbie codex has ‘confession.’ From this it is apparent that these two words could sometimes easily be interchanged by ancient copyists.” BALUZE.]

## I

We have learned, dearest brother, of the glorious testimonies to your faith and courage; and we received the honor of your confession with such exultation that we count ourselves also as participants and associates in your merits and praises. For since we have one Church, a united mind, and indivisible concord, what priest [Note: [Col. 0830C] “What priest would not in,” Pem., Voss. 2.] would not congratulate himself upon the praises of his fellow priest as upon his own? Or what brotherhood would not everywhere rejoice in the joy of its brethren [Col. 0830B]?

It cannot adequately be expressed how great the exultation and joy here were when we learned of your successful and courageous deeds: that you had stood forth there as leader of the brethren’s confession; but also that the leader’s confession had increased through the confession of the brethren [Note: [Col. 0830C] “And had increased through the brethren’s confession,” Lam., Bod. 2. “Agreement,” Colb., Comp., Thu., Foss., Vict.]. Thus, by advancing toward glory, you made many companions in glory; and you persuaded the people to become confessors by being the first prepared to confess on behalf of them all. Consequently, we cannot discover what we should proclaim first in you: whether your prompt and steadfast faith, or the inseparable love of the brethren. The courage of the bishop who went before was publicly proved there; the unity of the brotherhood that followed was displayed. While among you there was one mind and one voice, the whole Roman Church confessed the faith.

[Col. 0830C]

[Note: [Col. 0830D]

### II.—Dearest brother

Thus in the cited Colbert codex, as in four English manuscripts. In the others, however: “dearest brothers” [Col. 0831C]. Then in the Corbie manuscript: “the faith which to you,” without the preposition “concerning.” Shortly afterward, the Compiègne manuscript reads “was making provision,” not “was foreseeing.” For the same reason the Romans are commended in Letter XII, no. 13, on the ground that their faith was praised by the Apostle. The Roman clergy themselves, spurred on by these praises of the Apostle, write back to Cyprian in Letter XXXI: “Nor would the Apostle have uttered such great praises of us, saying that ‘your faith is proclaimed throughout the whole world,’ unless this vigor had borrowed the roots of faith from those times; and it is the greatest crime to have proved degenerate from their praise and glory.” COUSTANT.—Dearest brothers. Ten of our old books, three English manuscripts, Florus’s excerpts, and also Manutius’s edition prefer “dearest brother.” We have already frequently noted that this alteration was made by ancient copyists in copies of Saint Cyprian’s works. Either reading is sound. For although the letter was written to Cornelius, Cyprian nevertheless repeatedly turns his address to the entire Roman Church. Thus in Saint Gregory, book I, Letter XXV, written to John of Constantinople, Eulogius of Alexandria, and the others, where the editions have “hence, dearest brothers,” the Moissac codex prefers “dearest brother.” That this is the proper reading is clear from the fact that, since that letter was written by an equal to those bishops, it was necessary for each of them to be addressed in the singular.

In passing, I note here that the letter of Alexander III on behalf of the monastery of Pescara, or Casauria, published in volume V of d’Achery’s *Spicilegium*, p. 525, ought to be emended so that after “to the bishop of Fermo” one should read consecutively: “greeting and apostolic blessing. Inasmuch as”; and the material that intervenes should be restored immediately after the letter, as was also noted by Giovanni Berardi in the chronicle. Hence in the cartulary from which that letter was published, the word “likewise” is always written in red ink. BALUZE.

### Be conquered altogether

This last word, which seems superfluous to me, is absent from the Bec manuscript and the editions of Manutius and Morel. BALUZE.

### Was driven back and defeated

We have added this on the authority of three old copies. One Bodleian manuscript has “thrown into disorder and driven back.” BALUZE.

### Hawk

Two old books have *acceptor*. This means the same thing. See volume II of the *Capitularies*, pp. 684, 750, 830. BALUZE.

### Nor fight back

The phrase “nor fight back” is to be connected not with the nearest verb, “they fear,” but with the preceding “he understood”; that is, he understood that Christ’s soldiers by no means repel force with force. Shortly afterward the common editions have “the guilty” in the singular accusative; the Colbert manuscript, “with the guilty” in the singular ablative. “The guilty” in the plural, as in the Corbie manuscript, accords better with the rest of the sentence. Let those who permit Christians to kill the guilty for a comparatively slight cause attend to these words of Cyprian. COUSTANT.

### In the sight of Christ

From the Colbert and Corbie manuscripts we restore “his,” which was absent from the common editions. In the Corbie manuscript, however, the particle “and” was subsequently added above this word. Hence the Oxford editor notes that five other manuscripts likewise have “and of his Church,” with “his own” omitted. The expression “his Christ” is used here by the same idiom as in the preceding Letter X, no. 7, where it was said: “Cornelius was made bishop by the judgment of God and of his Christ.” COUSTANT.

### Christ’s Church

The old books and old editions vary greatly in this passage. Some ancient editions and some old books have “of Christ and of his Church.” Elsewhere it is written: “of Christ and his Church,” “of Christ or his Church,” and “of Christ, his own Church.” Florus’s excerpts read: “the joy of Christ’s own Church.” I have restored the reading which I judged to yield the better sense and which seems to me to agree better with the holy Martyr’s style. BALUZE.

### Taken by surprise

That is, as Cyprian immediately explains, trembling from fear of a new and unfamiliar event. Thus Saint Jerome, in his Letter to Saint Augustine on the Rebuke of Peter, says: “Sudden wars throw even the bravest soldiers into disorder”; and Tacitus, *Annals* XV, says: “Even brave men are terrified by sudden events”; and in *Histories* I: “Sudden panic terrified them.” Caesar, *Commentaries on the Gallic War* I: “No one is so brave that he is not disturbed by the novelty of the event.” Aulus Hirtius, *Alexandrian War*: “The sudden alarm caused by this event brought great terror upon our men.” Livy, book III: “At the city of Rome too, enormous terror was produced, more because the event was sudden than because there were too few forces to ward off the attack.” Virgil, *Aeneid* VIII:

> When Turnus raised the signal for war from Laurentum’s citadel,  
> And the horns blared with their hoarse song,  
> When he roused the fiery horses and set arms in motion,  
> At once their minds were thrown into disorder.

[Col. 0833C]

Cassius Dio, at the beginning of book XLII, when discussing Pompey’s miserable condition after the battle of Pharsalus, says that things which happen to people contrary to expectation and with the greatest possible unexpectedness both cast down their spirits and confound their reason. Ennodius, in his *Panegyric*: “The steadfastness of the brave totters whenever fearsome objects are thrust before their eyes.” Nonius Marcellus: “*Subiti* is used to mean ‘sudden.’” Again Cyprian, in the book *Against Demetrianus*, p. 224, and in book III of the *Testimonies*, chapter 16, cites this passage from Wisdom 5: “Seeing it, they will be troubled with horrible fear, and will marvel at the suddenness of unexpected salvation.” See the notes there. BALUZE.

### Stand for the offense

Here the position or standing of repentance is indicated. Cyprian speaks of it again in Letter LII, or LV, to Antonianus: “It is one thing to stand awaiting pardon, another to attain glory.” COUSTANT.]

## II

The faith which the blessed Apostle proclaimed concerning you has shone brightly [Note: [Col. 0830C] “Has shone brightly, dearest brother,” Lam., Lin., NC. 1, 2.], dearest brother [Col. 0831A]. Even then he foresaw in the Spirit this praise of courage and steadfast strength, and, bearing witness to your merits by proclaiming things to come, while he praised the parents he spurred on the children [Note: [Col. 0831B] “He spurs on the children,” Vindel., Foss., Corb.].

By being thus of one mind [Note: [Col. 0831B] Thus Foss., Mic., Vict.], thus courageous, you have furnished the other brethren also with great examples of unanimity and fortitude. You have taught them nobly to fear God, to adhere steadfastly to Christ, for the people to join themselves to the priests in danger, for brethren not to be separated from brethren in persecution; that united concord cannot be conquered at all; and that whatever is asked by everyone together, the God of peace grants to the peaceable.

The adversary had leapt forward with violent terror to throw Christ’s camp into disorder; but with the same force with which he came, he was driven back [Note: [Col. 0831B] “With the same force, thrown into disorder and driven back,” Bod. 3. “Driven back by the assault,” Lam., York, Bod. 2.]; and as much fear and terror as he brought, so much courage [Col. 0831B] and strength did he find. He had believed that he could once again trip up God’s servants and, treating them as recruits and novices, as though less prepared [Note: [Col. 0831B] “And as though less prepared,” Lam., York, Bod. 2.] and less wary, shake them in his accustomed manner.

Attacking one man first [Note: [Col. 0831B] “For in the first assault,” Bod. 3.], he had tried, like a wolf, to separate a sheep from the flock, or like a hawk, a dove from the company of those in flight [Col. 0832A] [Note: [Col. 0831B] “Had tried to overcome,” Bod. 3.]. For he who does not have sufficient strength against everyone seeks to ensnare individuals in their isolation. But, blunted by the united army’s equal faith and strength, he understood that Christ’s soldiers were now keeping sober watch and standing armed for battle; that they could not be conquered, though they could die; and that for this very reason they were unconquered, because they did not fear death. He understood also that they did not fight back against their assailants, since the innocent are not permitted to kill even the guilty [Note: [Col. 0832B] “An innocent person,” Lam., Bod. 2.], but readily surrender both life and blood, so that, while such great wickedness and savagery rages in the world, they may depart all the more quickly from the wicked and savage.

What a glorious spectacle that was beneath the eyes of God! What joy, in the sight of his Christ, for his Church: that when the enemy attempted to bring battle upon it, not individual soldiers but the whole camp together came forth! [Note: [Col. 0832B] “And supreme joy for his Church,” Corb., Bod. 3, York, Lin., NC. 1, 2. “Of Christ and of his Church,” Foss., Mic.] For it is certain that everyone would have come if they had been able to hear, since whoever heard hastened [Note: [Col. 0832B] Thus Foss., Corb., Mic., Vict. “Since he ran,” Bod. 3. “Would have come to meet it,” printed text.] and came.

How many of the lapsed were restored there by a glorious confession! [Note: [Col. 0832B] “Who there,” in the Compiègne manuscript—a reading that can be accepted with this punctuation: “were restored; they stood firm.”] They stood firm and courageous, and through the very pain of repentance were made stronger for battle. Thus it became apparent that shortly before they had been taken by surprise [Col. 0833A] and had trembled from fear of a new and unfamiliar event; that true faith afterward returned to itself, gathered its strength from the fear of God, and steadfastly and firmly fortified itself for every endurance; and that they no longer stood awaiting pardon for their offense, but awaiting the crown of suffering.

[Note: [Col. 0833C]

### III.—Poisoned eloquence

It was noted above, p. 416, that Novatian was eloquent. BALUZE.

### The Lord’s *sophia*

That is, Christian wisdom. Formerly the reading was “philosophy.” Rigaltius observes that in the Benevento and Verona codices, and also in the Roman edition, which is the Manutian, *sophia* is written, and that this reading is entirely correct. The old Reims manuscript likewise has it, as does the Morel edition. In its place “physics” is written in the Grenoble codex. To be sure, I have seen “philosophy” written in thirteen ancient codices. Nevertheless, I prefer the reading which Rigaltius says is entirely correct, also because Tertullian frequently uses *sophia*, and because Lactantius, book III, chapter 16, says: “We are immune and free from this calumny, since we abolish philosophy because it is an invention of human thought; we defend *sophia* because it is a divine tradition, and we bear witness that it ought to be received by everyone.” Marius Victorinus, in his hymn on the Trinity, speaking of Christ:

> Irrigating with the teachings of *sophia* the souls sown throughout the ages—  
> And since *Sophia* is Christ, the same Christ the Son teaches.

[Col. 0834B]

Likewise Peter Abelard, *Christian Theology* III, chapter 3: “For it remained for the true *Sophia*, who was to be incarnate, to teach this.” Tertullian, in chapter 4 of book I *To the Nations*, calls the Christian religion “the first wisdom,” as Jacques Godefroy explains, because it turns to the true God after abandoning idols.

John VIII may perhaps have had in view this twofold philosophy mentioned by Lactantius when, in the prologue to the Roman Council, among the other praises with which he adorns Emperor Charles the Bald, he says that Charles honors the Lord’s priests and instructs them in both kinds of philosophy. “Twofold knowledge” means something else in the narrative of the election of Pope Gregory VII, where it is written that he “possessed prudence in twofold knowledge”; and in the chronicle of Saint-Bénigne of Dijon, where Halinard, archbishop of Lyon, is said to have “shone most powerfully with twofold understanding”; likewise in the chronicle of Bèze, where Robert, bishop of Langres, is said to have “flourished in the eloquence of twofold knowledge.”

Finally, in a very ancient manuscript sheet from Rouergue, which appears to be a fragment of the *Life of Saint Gausbert*, abbot of Mont-Salvy on the borders of Rouergue and Auvergne, Hugh, bishop of Die, who was for a long time legate of the Apostolic See in Gaul, is called “a man of twofold knowledge, and by no means moderately learned in sacred literature.” Add the antipope Maginold, whom Sigebert, under the year 1105, says to have been “excellently learned in both kinds of knowledge.”

That by “twofold knowledge” theology and philosophy are to be understood is taught by this passage from the *Memorial of Histories* of John of Paris: “Simon de Beaulieu, archbishop of Bourges, who was made bishop of Palestrina. He was succeeded in the primacy of Bourges by Brother Giles, an outstanding doctor of theology and philosophy, a Roman by birth, of the Order of the Hermits of Saint Augustine; eminently renowned for twofold knowledge, he composed many volumes with subtlety and considerable success.”

“Twofold knowledge” again means something else in the dedicatory letter of Jean Raulin’s *Way of Paradise* and in the dedicatory letter of the same Raulin’s *Doctrinal of Death*, both dedicated “to that most judicious man, Master Jean de Bony, a most excellent doctor in the twofold knowledge of the laws.” There, “twofold knowledge” means that he was a doctor of both branches of law. BALUZE.

### Peaceable

The Corbie manuscript reads “sacrificial.” The other books more correctly have “peaceable.” Here Novatian is reproached with the hardness of the Stoics, who did not know how to be moved by compassion. COUSTANT.

### Bound

Four manuscripts read “defeated.” Rigaltius observes that this shows that Novatian was undeservedly regarded as a martyr by his followers. This at least proves that that schismatic suffered no harassment when Gallus raged against Cornelius and the adherents of sound doctrine. Cyprian explains, with very subtle reasoning, why Novatian was treated in this way. Consequently, the holy man does not allow us to judge that, in a troubled time, truth stands on the side which enjoys peace and is free from persecution. But lest any faithless person flatter himself because he endures persecution, Cyprian immediately teaches that this must sometimes be reckoned a punishment for faithlessness. COUSTANT.—Defeated. I have judged that this should be written in place of “bound,” which later editions have. For although either reading is sound, one seems obliged to stand by the authority of the old editions and ten old copies. The Morel edition also has this. BALUZE.]

## III

What does Novatian say to this, dearest brother? Does he now lay aside his error? Or rather—as is the custom of the deranged—has he been driven into still greater madness by our very blessings and successes [Note: [Col. 0833B] “More widely increased,” NC. 1, Bod. 2, York.]? And the more and more the glory of love and faith grows here, does the madness of dissension and jealousy break out afresh there? Does the wretched man fail to treat his wound, but wound both himself and his followers still more grievously—clamoring with his tongue for the destruction of the brethren and hurling the darts of poisoned eloquence [Col. 0834A]; harsher through the perversity of worldly philosophy than peaceable through the gentleness of the Lord’s philosophy [Note: [Col. 0833B] “The Lord’s *sophia*,” Ver., Benev., Manut.]; deserter of the Church, enemy of mercy, destroyer of repentance [Note: [Col. 0833B] “Obstructor of repentance,” Lin.], teacher of pride, corrupter of truth, destroyer of love [Note: [Col. 0833B] “Betrayer of love,” Lin. “Destroyer of chastity,” NC. 1, Pem. [Col. 0834B] Lam., Bod. 2.]?

Does he now recognize [Note: [Col. 0834B] “Do you recognize?” Bop. 3.] who is the priest of God, what is the Church and house of Christ, who are God’s servants whom the devil harasses, and who are the Christians whom Antichrist attacks? For Antichrist does not seek those whom he has already subdued, nor is he eager to overthrow those whom he has already made his own. The enemy and adversary of the Church disregards those whom he has alienated from the Church [Note: [Col. 0834B] “Whom he alienated,” Lam., Bod. 2.] and led outside, despises them as captives and bound men [Note: [Col. 0834B] “Defeated,” Thu., Foss., Vict.], passes them by, and proceeds to assail those in whom he sees Christ dwelling.

[Note: [Col. 0835B]

### IV.—In confession of the name

Two English manuscripts read “in the name of confession” [Col. 0835C]. “In confession of the name” should be retained, with “of the Lord” understood—a word Cyprian habitually leaves unexpressed. Thus in Letter LII, or LV, to Antonianus, past the middle, he says: “Even if he is afterward killed FOR THE NAME while situated outside the Church and separated from unity and love, he will not be able to be crowned in death.” And near the end of the same letter: “Those who tear apart Christ’s Church, even if they are killed outside FOR THE NAME, cannot, according to the Apostle, be admitted to the Church’s peace, since they have maintained neither the unity of the Spirit nor that of the Church.” Again above, in Letter XI, no. 2, he writes to Cornelius: “How do we teach or encourage them to shed their blood in CONFESSION OF THE NAME?” And at no. 4: “But when he says that the Spirit speaks in those who have been handed over and are placed in CONFESSION OF THE NAME,” etc. COUSTANT.]

## IV

And even if anyone of their kind should be apprehended, he has no reason to flatter himself as though he were in confession of the name [Note: [Col. 0835A] “In the name of confession,” Lin., NC. 2.]. For it is established that if such people are killed outside the Church, it is not a crown of faith but rather a punishment for faithlessness; nor will those whom we see to have withdrawn through the madness of discord from the peaceful and divine house dwell in God’s house among those of one mind.

[Note: [Col. 0835C]

### V.—To draw near

The Michel and Grenoble codices and four English manuscripts have: “now that the day of your contest and struggle is drawing near.” So too the Morel edition and the Bec codex. BALUZE.

[Col. 0835D] **And if either of us should depart from here first, etc.** It is evident from this passage that Cyprian held and believed that even the departed saints pray for the living. He indicates the same thing, though somewhat less clearly, in vol. II, *On Mortality*, when, speaking of the future life, he says: “A great multitude there longs for us, already secure in its own immortality and still concerned for our safety.” Similar statements occur in Origen, Homily 3 on the *Song of Songs* and on *Genesis*; St. Potamiena in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VI, ch. 5; and St. Peter in his Canonical Epistle, ch. I, according to the interpretation of certain Greeks as reported by Oecumenius, when he says: “Moreover, I shall take care that even after my death you may frequently be able to recall these things.”

From this very passage it may also be sufficiently inferred that even at that time the invocation of the saints was in use. Indeed, below, in vol. II, *On the Discipline and Dress of Virgins*, he implores the prayers of holy virgins after this life, saying: “Persevere bravely, advance spiritually, arrive happily; only then remember us, when virginity begins to be honored in you.” That this must be understood of honor after this life is sufficiently indicated by the preceding words: “You go before us with the greater and better portion,” and by the phrase, “arrive happily.”

It is therefore manifestly calumnious for those men to deny that this practice was customary in the Church before the age of St. Gregory, especially since it is also to be found in the Seventh Synod, canon 7, and in the Sixth Synod at its conclusion; in Victor of Africa, book III, *On the Vandal Persecution*; St. Fulgentius, sermon *On the Praises of Mary at the Birth of the Savior*; Peter Chrysologus, Homily VII; Theodoret, *On G… Affections*, book VIII; Leo the Great, sermons 2 and 6, *On the Fast in the Octave of the Apostles*; Caesarius, homily on the litanies; Augustine, book VII of *On Baptism*, ch. 2, the sermon on the death of Cyprian, Sermon 27 *On the Words of the Apostle*, book XII of *The City of God*, ch. 8, and frequently elsewhere; [Col. 0836B] Virgilius Tridentinus, in the *Life of St. Sisinnius* …; Paulinus, *On St. Clarus*, addressed to Severus, in the panegyric for the boy Celsus, [Col. 0836C] and in the poem on St. Felix; Jerome, *On the Praises of Paula* and in the *Life of Hilarion*; Prudentius, very frequently; Ambrose, book I of *On Widows* and the funeral oration for his brother Satyrus; Gregory Nazianzen, homilies on Basil and Cyprian; Basil, sermon on the Forty Martyrs and on Mamas the Martyr; Chrysostom, in the Mass, Homily 49, on *Genesis* V, on *Matthew* I, on the *Epistle to the Philippians*, and Homily 66 to the people of Antioch; Nectarius, on Theodore the Martyr; Ephrem, sermon on the martyrs; Hilary, on Psalm XXIV; Athanasius, oration on the Virgin Mother of God; St. Antony, *Letter to the Arsenoites*; the virgin Justina in Nazianzen’s oration on Cyprian; Origen, on the final chapter of the book of Job and in the lament; and St. Irenaeus, book V *Against Heresies*, where he calls the Virgin Mary the advocate of the virgin Eve.

Likewise the aforementioned Ephrem the Syrian says, addressing Mary in Turenus: “Be our reconciler and advocate at the hour of judgment; deliver us from the fire and darkness to come, for you are the hope of Christians before God.” These words are worthy of notice because of those who malign that canticle of the Church in praise of [Col. 0836D] the Blessed Virgin: “Hail, Queen of mercy,” etc.

The ancients were accustomed to call not only Mary but also other saints sometimes *advocates*, as St. Maximus calls Nazarius and Celsus; sometimes *patrons*, as Ambrose, book X on Luke, ch. 21; St. Augustine, *On Care for the Dead*, ch. 4; Prudentius, Hymns 1 and 2, *On Crowns* (περὶ στεφάνων); Paulinus, Panegyric 3 on Felix and Letter XIII to Severus; and Anton., bishop, in a letter to the emperor Arcadius; sometimes *protectors*, as Chrysostom, Homily 66 to the people of Antioch; and sometimes even *mediators*, as Cyril, book XII of the *Thesaurus*, ch. 10, and Bernard, final sermon on the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin. All these titles wonderfully confirm the aforesaid practice of invocation.

Indeed, anyone who thinks that its origin should be sought still earlier will find these words in St. James’s Liturgy, which the Sixth Synod acknowledges as such in canon 32: “Let us commemorate the most holy, immaculate, most glorious, blessed Mary, our Lady, Mother of God and ever-virgin, and all the saints and righteous, so that through their prayers and intercessions we may all obtain mercy.” For what else, I ask, [Col. 0837A] is it to commemorate the saints so that through their intercessions we may obtain mercy, than to invoke the saints so that they may intercede for us to obtain mercy? **PAMELIUS.**

—**And if either.** In the Oxford edition: “And either,” with *if* deleted, although eight English manuscripts, as well as Corb., Colb., Foss., and the older editions, exhibit it. Shortly afterward the Compendium manuscript has “before God,” not “before the Lord.”

From this passage Pamelius rightly concludes that the saints, after departing from us, care for our affairs and assist us before God by their prayers and patronage. The Oxford editors’ interpretation is certainly forced and foreign to the passage. They comment upon it as follows: “When either of us dies—whether I, who preside at Carthage, or you, who preside at Rome—let whichever survives and is granted to remain longer among the living persevere, and let his prayer for both Churches continue before God.” For the prayer commended there is not that of the survivor, but of the one who departs from here and goes before the other to God.

Moreover, no one would deny that the saints’ fraternal love continues unimpaired in heaven. The Oxford editors themselves say that they have no doubt that souls received into heaven entreat God to have mercy upon those living on earth. Since they hold this conviction, it would seem to follow that they must also be convinced that prayers should be poured forth to those same souls. Yet after stating these premises they add: “But it does not therefore follow that prayers should be offered to the saints.” What, however, forbids this? “Because,” they say, “one makes gods of those whom one petitions.”

Did Paul, I ask, suppose that he was making gods of the faithful whose prayers he urgently requested on his behalf? Did Cyprian make a god of Cornelius when he asked him, if he should depart to God first, that his prayer before the Father’s mercy should not cease on behalf of the brethren? If it is lawful to solicit [Col. 0837C] the prayers of righteous persons dwelling upon earth, why not also those of persons who are now nearer to God in heaven?

Augustine did not believe himself to be departing from Cyprian’s teaching when, in book VII of *On Baptism Against the Donatists*, ch. 1, he invoked him and said: “Therefore let him assist us by his prayers as we labor in the mortality of this flesh as though in a dark cloud, so that, by the Lord’s gift, we may imitate his good qualities as far as we can.”

Those who despair that our prayers can reach the saints do not understand what the Church is, what Christ’s body is, or what that Spirit is by whom all the righteous, whether on earth or in heaven, are bound together into one. For through the benefit of the one Spirit there is mutual communication between the members, however far apart they may be. “For,” Augustine says in book XX of *The City of God*, ch. 9, “the souls of the pious dead are not separated from the Church, which even now is the kingdom of Christ. Otherwise no commemoration of them would be made in the communion of Christ’s body.… For why are these things done, unless because the faithful, even when dead, are his members?”

If, then, they are not separated from the Church; if they are Christ’s members, and indeed living members, who would judge it absurd—or rather, who would not judge it consonant with right reason—that they should, as God wills, perceive the movements and affections of the other members, hear the voices of the Church, and incline with ready affection to assist her? If one prefers to put it this way, our prayer is a kind of letter which, carried into heaven by the help of angels, becomes known to the saints whose patronage we implore. God so ordains and inspires his Church that, when we invoke the saints, the reward owed to those who live piously may be more deeply impressed upon our minds. **BALUZIUS.**

**May it persevere.** I do not know what reasons led Rigaltius to assail this opinion, as though Cyprian could not have held and believed that even the departed saints pray for the living, as Pamelius had said in his annotation on this passage. For when that most learned man says that these words of Cyprian should not be understood of one who has gone before through the martyr’s crown, since one should not pray for a martyr, whose blood, as Tertullian says in the *Apologeticum*, is the complete key to paradise, he is certainly mistaken. Cyprian is not asking that the living man pray for the martyr, but that the martyr pray to the Lord for the living man.

The most illustrious Oxford scholar thought the meaning of this passage to be that whichever Christian survived the other, whether Cyprian or Cornelius, should persevere in prayer for both Churches; nor does he doubt that souls received into heaven entreat God, best and greatest, to have mercy upon those living on earth.

Jerome says in his book *Against Vigilantius*: “If the apostles and martyrs, while still dwelling in the body, can pray for others, at a time when they must still be concerned for themselves, how much more can they do so after their crowns, victories, and triumphs?” Cyprian himself likewise writes at the end of the book *On Mortality*, p. 236, that souls received into heaven, secure concerning their own safety, are still concerned for our salvation. **BALUZIUS.**

**Before the Lord.** Do not alter this reading, because it is sound and is found in twelve ancient copies. I shall say only that the older editions and eight ancient books have “God.” The sense remains the same however one reads it. **BALUZIUS.**

**For the brethren.** From this too, I think, it may be inferred that Cyprian believed that the saints in heaven pray for the living. **BALUZIUS.**

V. We earnestly exhort you, dearest brother, as far as we can, by the mutual love through which we cling to one another, that, since we are instructed by the providence of the Lord who warns us [Col. 0836A] and admonished by the salutary counsels of divine mercy that the day of our contest [Note: [Col. 0835A] “With the day of our contest and struggle now drawing near,” Bod. 2, Ebor., Lin., NC. 1, Mic.] and struggle is now drawing near, we must not cease, together with all the people, to devote ourselves to fasting, vigils, and prayers. Let us apply ourselves to continual groaning and frequent supplications. For these are our heavenly weapons, which enable us to stand and persevere bravely; these are the spiritual fortifications and divine missiles that protect us.

Let us be mindful of one another; in concord and unanimity, let us always pray for one another in both places, and let us relieve afflictions and distress through mutual love. And if either of us from there [Note: [Col. 0836A] “And if either,” Pem., Ebor., Lam., Lin., NC. 1, 2, Bod. 1, 2, 3. “If either from here,” Foss.] should, through the swiftness of divine favor, depart first, [Col. 0837A] let our love persevere before the Lord; let prayer for our brothers and sisters not cease before the mercy [Col. 0838A] of the Father. I wish you always good health, dearest brother.

[Col. 0837]

# FIRST APPENDIX  
## LETTERS ATTRIBUTED TO CORNELIUS  
(C, S)

### NOTICE ON THE FOLLOWING LETTER

[Col. 0837D]

Recovered from the archive of the Church of Vienne and published through the efforts of Jean du Bois in the library of Fleury, it was afterward [Col. 0838D] reprinted by Baronius under the year 355 and among the councils. Yet it presents no greater appearance of authenticity than the preceding letters copied from the same archive.

First, in the salutation itself Lupicinus is called “archbishop,” contrary to the usage of this century. Baronius indeed took care to correct this, substituting “bishop” for “archbishop”; but since he supported his correction by the authority of no ancient manuscript, the mark of forgery remains. Nor was the term *Mass* any more customary in the same age, as has already been observed concerning the spurious letters of Pius. Who would grant, moreover, that before the persecution in which Cornelius perished Christians were permitted to celebrate Mass publicly? Yet this is what the words written under Cornelius’s name in the appended letter imply.

Furthermore, according to Jean du Bois, Florentius, Lupicinus’s predecessor, “lived through the times of Gordian, [Col. 0839B] Philip, Decius, Gallus, and Volusian.” Yet Volusian was created Augustus only in the year 252, before the end of July, while Cornelius died in the middle of September of the same year, having been arrested, confessed God, and been exiled some time earlier—so early that Cyprian had time to learn of his confession and write him a letter of congratulation concerning it. When, then, could this letter have been written? And why does Cornelius say nothing in it about his arrest and confession, or about Lupicinus’s recent ordination?

## LETTER I  
### CORNELIUS THE BISHOP TO HIS BROTHER LUPICINUS, ARCHBISHOP OF VIENNE [Note: [Col. 0839D] “Bishop,” Baronius], GREETINGS

[Col. 0839C]

You should know, most blessed brother [Note: [Col. 0839D] “Dearest,” Baronius], that the Lord’s threshing floor is being most violently shaken by the wind of persecution, and that Christians everywhere are being subjected to various tortures by imperial edicts. For in the city of Rome a prefect [Note: [Col. 0840D] “The emperor,” Baronius] has been appointed for this purpose. Consequently, Christians are permitted to celebrate Mass neither publicly nor in the better-known crypts.

Let Your Charity therefore exhort all who believe in Christ not to fear those who kill the body, but rather him who has power to destroy both body and soul (Matt. 10:28). Many of the brethren have already been crowned by martyrdom. Pray that we may complete the course revealed to us by the Lord. Farewell, brother in the Lord, and greet all who love us in Christ.

## LETTER II  
### OF POPE CORNELIUS TO CYPRIAN

[Col. 0839D]

This letter first appeared from the Bohier and Reims manuscripts in the latest edition of Cyprian prepared through the efforts of Étienne Baluze. It is astonishing that a learned man could have presented it even as doubtful, since it displays no mark of truth. It is unworthy of the friendship that existed between Cornelius and Cyprian until death.

It conflicts no less with historical truth. From history it is clear that the controversy over the baptism of heretics arose between the Roman pontiff and the bishop of Carthage only after Cornelius’s death, and that it was stirred up by the occasion of Cyprian’s second letter to Pope Stephen—as is evident merely from reading that letter of Cyprian. Therefore, when Rufinus writes in book VII, ch. 2, that the controversy over the baptism of heretics began during the pontificate of Cornelius, he must be said to have sinned against accurate chronology, something not unusual for him.

Indeed, that Rufinus there attributes to Cornelius what properly belongs to Stephen will be evident to everyone simply from quoting his words:

> And when Cyprian and nearly all the priests throughout Africa decreed that this ought to be done—that is, that heretics should be rebaptized—Cornelius and all the other priests throughout Italy rejected such a decree while preserving concord, deciding that the rule handed down on this matter by the fathers from antiquity ought to be observed. This rule provided that, after rejection of the false doctrine and confession of the true, they should be purified by the laying on of hands alone.

For if “Stephen” is substituted there for “Cornelius,” Rufinus will agree completely with the statements of Cyprian, Augustine, and other writers.

I received writings from Your Charity that were not pleasing and were contrary to the rule of faith. In them I recognized nauseating matter, and I did not approve the poisons of your discourses against the Catholic Church spread throughout the whole world, with the dreadful weeds you sowed over it. I ask that you swiftly remove and condemn them. You should indeed have done this before the deadly poison scattered through the world killed the minds of the simple and innocent.

It is therefore not right to rebaptize. Root out and disentangle, as we have said, by eloquent and worthy discourse in a later letter, what you wrote in the former—things which the offspring of vipers have deemed must be observed contrary to the Catholic faith. For it does not befit the bishop of so great a city and so excellent a [Col. 0840D] teacher, while you think that the baptism of heresy must be condemned, to dare [printed: “to hear”] to stain true Baptism with words [Note: [Col. 0840D] Perhaps read: “you dare,” as you see], words which, to your grief, conflict with the Apostle when he says: “One God, one faith, one baptism.”

[Col. 0841]

# SECOND APPENDIX  
## DECRETAL LETTERS ATTRIBUTED TO ST. CORNELIUS THE POPE  
(S)

## LETTER I  
### ON THE TRANSLATION OF THE BODIES OF THE APOSTLES PETER AND PAUL, AND ON NOVATUS AND OTHER HERETICS

[Col. 0841A]

[Note: [Col. 0841C]

**Letter I of Pope Cornelius.** Rightly regarded as suspect by Baronius and others, together with the following letter, which enjoys no greater credibility among scholars. **LABBE.**

—Jerome, in the previously quoted words of his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under “Cornelius,” testifies that St. Cornelius wrote several letters. Baronius, under the year 255, no. 3, relates that the first letter he mentions has been lost together with the acts of the councils. I think that the second letter he mentions is this one, and that it is therefore unjustly censured regarding its credibility and authority, since it has secured Jerome as a witness of approved trustworthiness and its contents agree with historical events.

As for its attribution to Cornelius of the translation of the holy bodies of Peter and Paul from the catacombs, it seems probable that this error crept corruptly into the letter from errors in the *Liber Pontificalis*. For the translation more truly belongs to the first century, shortly after their passion, as was demonstrated above from the testimony of the holy pontiff Gregory. **SEVERINUS BINIUS.**

—This is false, for Jerome never saw this rubbish. When did the translation of the holy bodies of Peter and Paul occur? Who was Novatus, and what sort of man was he? **LABBE.**

**Nor from its fruits.** St. Gregory, Letter 114, book VII. See also Letter 49, book VIII. **LABBE.**

**The matron Lucina.** Ado writes similar things in his *Chronicle* and *Martyrology*; they are refuted by St. Gregory, Letter 30, book III, and by Baronius. **LABBE.**

**The bodies were raised.** See Severinus Binius’s annotations in the notes on the *Life of Cornelius*, at the words “In his time,” etc.

**For only so much is required of us.** St. Martin I, in his letter to St. Amandus. **LABBE.**

**Raised up Novatus as an adversary against us.** Novatus was a bishop of the African Church. Against Cyprian’s will, he had ordained Felicissimus, the deacon and schismatic author of the Montenses—so called because the members of that sect assembled on a hill—and, through hatred and envy of Cyprian, had become the ringleader in creating a schism. What sort of man he was Cyprian declares in Letter XLIX in these words: “Nothing needed to be reported to us about Novatus, since Novatus ought rather to be made known to you through us: always greedy for innovations, raging with the insatiable rapacity of avarice,” etc.

But when the Roman see was vacant, he came to Rome to overthrow the Roman Church and more fiercely incited against Cornelius the Roman presbyter Novatian, who was already ill-disposed toward Cornelius through the vice of ambition. This was because Cornelius, with the counsel of his brethren, received repentant lapsed Christians into the Church, although in Africa Novatus himself had replied to Cyprian that the communion of the most holy Church requested by the lapsed should be deferred for a fixed period. More is given in the following notes; Baronius, under the year 254, nos. 32–41, likewise no. 59 and several following. **SEVERINUS BINIUS.**

**Novatus, who ordained Novatian outside the Church.** Novatus had once established in Africa, through his adherents, altar against altar in a dreadful schism. To propagate into the Church overseas as well the unhappy offspring of which he himself, together with Felicissimus, was the single and principal author, he went to Rome. Taking advantage of the vacant see, he fraudulently won the minds of many so that, through their support, either he himself or at least one of his supporters might be placed in the pontifical see, and the schism already created against Cyprian might thereby be more firmly consolidated.

But since, by God’s will, Cornelius was created pontiff sooner than expected, Novatus, by fraud and deceit, after spreading grave accusations against Cornelius, stirred up against him, in addition to many confessors illustrious in glory, three bishops who secretly ordained Novatian as the elected Roman pontiff and created the first schism of the Roman Church. The event is described by Cyprian in Letter XLIX to Cornelius and Letter LII to Antonianus, according to Pamelius’s edition. It is also established by Cornelius’s letter to Fabius of Antioch, which we have arranged to be printed for the first time in this volume of the councils from Eusebius. See Baronius under the aforesaid year, no. 65 and following. **SEVERINUS BINIUS.**

**They caused many to depart from the right faith.** By deceit and fraud they enticed to their position these Roman clerics who were still held in error—Maximus, Nicostratus, Urbanus, Sidonius, Macarius, Celerinus, and others—with the sole exception of the presbyter Moses, as is evident from the aforesaid letter. **SEVERINUS BINIUS.**

**Nicostratus.** Concerning him, see Cyprian, Letters XLVIII and XLIX. **LABBE.**

**Because neither death.** Mercator frequently repeated these and the following words in various letters of the Roman pontiffs. **LABBE.**

**Under Decius.** In the year 250 or the following year. **LABBE.**

**When … were consuls.** These consuls do not occur in the consular lists. **LABBE.**]

Cornelius the bishop, to his dearest and most beloved brethren, sons of God’s holy Church, and to all who serve the Lord in right faith.

Seeing [Note: [Col. 0841B] “Trusting in the benevolence of your charity,” Labbe] the benevolence of your charity, because you are lovers of the Apostles and hold their faith and teaching, I have determined, with the Lord as author, to write you certain things which at the present time it is necessary to know, and which, with the Lord’s assistance and through the merits of the Apostles, have recently been done or are now being done among us in the Roman Church. For, with charity as your patron, I believe that through paternal grace you willingly [Col. 0841B] receive the writings of the Apostolic See, carry out its commands, and rejoice in its progress. Whoever plants himself in the root of charity neither fails in greenness, nor becomes barren of fruit, nor loses the effective work of fruitful love. For charity itself exercises the hearts of the faithful and strengthens their understanding, so that nothing done is burdensome or difficult, but everything becomes sweet, since it is charity’s proper function to nourish concord, keep the commandments, join what has been separated, set crooked things straight, and strengthen the other virtues with the protection of its perfection.

I therefore ask you to rejoice with us, because at the request of a certain devout woman and most noble matron, [Col. 0842A] Lucina, the bodies of the Apostles Peter and Paul have been raised from the Catacombs. First, the body of blessed Paul was raised in silence and placed on the estate of the aforesaid matron, on the Ostian Way beside the place where he was beheaded. Afterward we received the body of the blessed prince of the Apostles, Peter, and fittingly placed it near the place where he was crucified, among the bodies of the holy bishops in the temple of Apollo, on the Golden Hill, in the Vatican of Nero’s palace, on the third day before the Kalends of July. We prayed to God and our Lord Jesus Christ that, through the intercession of his holy Apostles, he might cleanse the stains of your sins, preserve you in his will throughout the days of your life, and render you persevering in the fruit of good works.

Rejoice with these events, for the holy Apostles themselves [Col. 0842B] rejoice over your joy. Always praise God, and may he be glorified in you. For it is written: “What shall I repay the Lord for all that he has repaid to me? I shall take the cup of salvation and invoke the name of the Lord” (Ps. 115). (6)

For only so much is required of us as we can commend [Note: [Col. 0842B] “Contribute,” Labbe] through the dutiful service of our ministry. Hence it is necessary for us to persist all the more in urgent preaching, insofar as a doubled allotment of talents is entrusted to us for a perfect accounting, and the declaration of the Lord’s voice urges us to enter his rest.

The ancient enemy, envying these things, raised up against us Novatus, a rival of the right faith and holy teaching. Outside the Church he ordained Novatian, and in Africa Nicostratus, both heretics, just as he was. By every effort they could make, these men persuaded many to depart from the right and Catholic faith and convinced them to fall after them into a perverse teaching hateful to God.

But just as we have been exceedingly saddened by their evasions and crushed by their destruction, so, with the Lord’s assistance, we have been gladdened by the conversion of others. Almighty God, who mingles joy with sorrow, greatly gladdened us because certain confessors who had formerly been faithful but who, at the devil’s instigation, separated themselves from us and from the right faith, have returned with the presbyter Maximus to the Catholic Church and the right faith, and once again, as before [Note: [Col. 0843C] “as they had been,” Labbe], have become faithful confessors.

[Col. 0843B] Therefore, dearest brethren, we exhort and beseech you through our Lord Jesus Christ: strive by your exhortations and good efforts to convert the aforesaid heretics, and all whom you know to have apostatized from the right faith and teaching, to the Catholic faith and right doctrine, and persuade them to persevere in God’s will. Hasten to lead not only these, but all who have not yet received the right faith, to the Catholic faith.

For, as the Teacher of the Gentiles teaches, neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor things present, nor things to come, nor power, nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature will be able to separate us from the charity of our Lord Jesus Christ (Rom. 8), nor from the right faith that is in him. Therefore do not lose your confidence, which has a great reward. [Col. 0843C] For patience is necessary to us in our struggles against our adversaries, so that, preserving the faith undefiled to the end, we may receive the promise that he promised to those who hasten to contend lawfully.

“For yet a very little while, and he who is to come will come and will not delay” (Hab. 2). “Behold, the judge stands before the door” (James 5), joyfully promising crowns to those who submit to sufferings for his sake. “But if anyone draws back, my soul will not be pleased with him” (Heb. 10); rather, because of his denial he will fall away from the promise. We, however, are not children of withdrawal unto destruction, but of faith unto the gaining of the soul.

Therefore take up [Note: [Col. 0843C] A manuscript of the Paris College of the Society of Jesus, according to Hardouin, reads: “the armor of God”] the armor of God, so that you may be able to resist in the evil day, against [Note: [Col. 0843C] The same manuscript: “against the enemies”] all the enemies of the holy Church and your own enemies. Put on the breastplate of righteousness, and have your feet shod in preparation for the Gospel of peace, in all things taking up the shield of faith, with which you may extinguish all the flaming missiles of the most wicked one [Note: [Col. 0843C] The same manuscript: “fiery”]. Take up [Note: [Col. 0844C] The same manuscript: “Receive”] the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God, through every prayer and supplication (Eph. 6), rooted and grounded in the consolation of the brethren for Christ Jesus [Col. 0844B] our Lord.

And now, brethren, we commend you to the Lord, and [Note: [Col. 0844C] “All” is absent from the same manuscript] all of you to the word of his grace, which is able to perfect us and give us an inheritance with all the saints (Acts 20). May the God of peace and [Note: [Col. 0844C] The same manuscript: “solace”] consolation grant you to be of the same mind toward one another (Rom. 15), so that you may assist one another and not be divided, but with one mind, one mouth, and one heart honor him, for the concord and consolation of the brethren—him who is able to strengthen you according to his Gospel and according to the revelation of the eternal mystery, namely in everlasting times (Rom. 16), in which the gifts of future joys are to be bestowed upon you.

You must also consider most carefully that those who envy the brethren and desire to condemn and destroy them thereby [Note: [Col. 0844C] The same manuscript: “for themselves”] destroy their own doctrines. For the Lord says: “Every kingdom divided against itself will not stand”; and “every body of knowledge and law divided against itself [Col. 0844C] will not stand.”

It is therefore necessary that you receive salutary exhortations in concord, doing nothing through contention, but, unanimous in every endeavor of devotion, obey the divine and apostolic constitutions.

Given on the seventh [Note: [Col. 0844C] “Eighth,” Labbe] day before the Ides of September, in the consulship of the most illustrious Decius and Maximus.

## LETTER II  
### TO RUFUS [Note: [Col. 0845D] Elsewhere, “Rusticus”], FELLOW BISHOP OF THE EAST

[Col. 0845A]

**SUMMARY.—That the Lord’s priests must neither presume to swear, as the common people ordinarily do, nor be compelled to do so. 1. Whether an oath should be taken by bishops. 2. Concerning cases involving bishops, and that whatever is done against persons who are absent is to be regarded as null.**

### CORNELIUS THE BISHOP TO RUFUS [Note: [Col. 0845D] Elsewhere, “Rusticus”], HIS FELLOW BISHOP [Note: [Col. 0845D] Elsewhere, “bishop”], GREETINGS IN THE LORD

[Note: [Col. 0845D]

**By the authority of the See.** Gregory, Letter 32, book XII.]

Your affection requires, dearest brother, that we should answer your inquiries from the authority of the Apostolic See. Although we would hasten to do this not at length but concisely, because of certain vexations that, with our sins obstructing us, have come upon us, we nevertheless permit your diligence to search and investigate the matter more fully through the remaining institutions of the holy Fathers.

For a mind that is worn down and burdened by loads and vexations cannot accomplish as much good as one that is cheerful and free from oppression. We have not set these considerations forth because we wish to deny Your Holiness these and other things that we know will be necessary, but so that what is found here in lesser measure may be investigated more fully elsewhere.

[Note: [Col. 0845D]

**I.—An oath, however, up to this point.** On when an oath may lawfully be taken by, or required from, bishops and the other clergy, see the canonists, Cause 2, question 4, canon *Sacramentum hactenus*, concerning which Covarruvias and many others write at length. **SEVERINUS BINIUS.**

**The institutions of the Fathers.** The letter to Oceanus *On the Life of Clerics*, among the works of Jerome. **LABBE.**

**Rebuke.** Fifth Roman Council under Symmachus. **LABBE.**

[Col. 0847C] **No one.** Ambrose, Letter 29, in the decrees; Ivo, book IV.

**Judges.** Hadrian, collection 17; likewise 5, 8, 30, 32, etc.]

### I

Until now we have by no means known an oath to be required from chief priests or God’s ministers [Note: [Col. 0845D] Gratian likewise reads thus; in the cited manuscript: “or required from the others”], except on behalf of the right faith, nor have we found that they swore voluntarily [Note: [Col. 0845D] In the cited manuscript and in Gratian: “nor that they swore of their own accord”].

Therefore the holy apostle James, strongly prohibiting an oath, speaks as follows: “Above all things, my brethren, do not swear, either by heaven, or by earth, or any other oath whatsoever. But let your speech be ‘Yes, yes; No, no,’ so that you may not fall under judgment” (James 5).

And the Lord says in the Gospel:

> You have heard that it was said to those of old: “You shall not swear falsely, but shall fulfill your oaths to the Lord.” But I say to you: do not swear at all, neither by heaven, because it is God’s throne; nor by earth, because it is his footstool; nor by Jerusalem, because it is the city of the great King; nor shall you swear by your head, because you cannot make one hair white or black. But let your speech be: “Yes, yes; No, no.” Whatever exceeds these comes from evil.  
> (Matt. 5)

That is, from the person requiring the oath [Col. 0845D] and from the person swearing it.

The Lord himself, dearest brother, prohibits these things, [Col. 0846A] namely, that one ought not to swear. All the Apostles especially prohibit them; so do the holy men who preceded us and presided before us over this holy, universal, apostolic Church; so do the Prophets and the other holy teachers dispersed throughout the whole world to preach: they forbid oaths to be taken.

If we were to begin enumerating their examples [Note: [Col. 0846D] Elsewhere: “Following the examples of the saints”], or inserting them in this short document, the hour of the day would fail before their examples prohibiting conduct of this kind were exhausted. Following them, we confirm the laws of the holy Apostles and their successors and prohibit rash oaths from being taken.

Hence the Lord himself also wrote with his own hand upon the stone tablets he gave to Moses, saying: “Take care not to take the name of your Lord in vain” (Exod. 20), and the rest.

As we indicated a little above, [Col. 0846B] we do not know of an oath [Note: [Col. 0846D] Elsewhere: “We do not know of an oath”] being offered to bishops, nor should one ever be taken, because, as was recalled above, the Lord commanded that one must not swear—neither by heaven, because it is God’s throne; nor by earth, because it is his footstool; nor by one’s own head, because no one can create a single hair (Matt. 5; James 5).

For each person, as though standing before the altar, keeps the fear of God before his eyes and preserves his own conscience clean before God. What he retains in his memory he must by no means omit, because “the mouth that lies kills the soul” (Wis. 1). And the Apostle says: “Let each of you speak the truth with his neighbor, because we are members of one another” (Eph. 4). And elsewhere: “Do not lie to one another” (Col. 3).

These are the precepts of the Savior; these are the ordinances of the Prophets, [Col. 0846C] and these the institutions of the holy Fathers. If anyone regards them as vain, he is the enemy of his own soul, because no one acts against the Prophets, against the Apostles, or against the Gospel without danger (Council of Carthage I, chap. 13). And the greatest care must be taken that the sheep entrusted to their shepherd do not presume to rebuke him—unless he has strayed from the faith—or to accuse him, because such accusations have no force and cannot harm him. But let this one thing, dearly beloved, not escape you, as the blessed apostle Peter says: one day with the Lord is as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day. The Lord is not slow concerning his promises [Note: [Col. 0846D] Thus the manuscript; other manuscripts have *concerning the promise*, as do both the Greek and the common Latin text: *the promise*.], but acts patiently for your sake, not wishing any to perish, but all to return to repentance. The day of the Lord, however, will come like a thief; on that day the heavens will pass away with a great rushing sound, and the elements [Col. 0846D] will be dissolved by heat (II Peter 3). Since, therefore, [Col. 0847A] all these things are to be dissolved, you may infer from this what sort of persons you ought to be in holy conduct and godliness, awaiting and hastening the coming of the day of God, through which the burning heavens will be dissolved and the elements will melt in the blaze of fire.

“But you, dearly beloved,” said the apostle Jude (in his canonical Epistle, verse 17), “remember the words foretold by the apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ, who used to tell you that in the last time mockers would come, walking according to their own desires [Note: [Col. 0847B] Thus the manuscript, as in the edition of the Vulgate and also the Greek. Another manuscript has *in ungodliness*. Printed editions have *in ungodly deeds*.] of ungodliness. These are those who separate themselves, natural men, not possessing the Spirit. But you, dearly beloved, building yourselves up upon your most holy faith and praying in the Holy Spirit, keep yourselves in the love of God, awaiting the mercy [Col. 0847B] of our Lord Jesus Christ unto eternal life. And some, once judged, you should rebuke; others you should save, snatching them from the fire. On others, however, have mercy in fear, hating even the garment stained by the flesh.”

For none of the priests should entrust his case to the judgment of outsiders unless an appeal has been made to the Apostolic See. Rather, each should have as his judges men from the same province who are known to him, unless he fears some violence from a reckless multitude there or has judges there who are hostile or suspect. For these reasons, it has been permitted to appeal and resort to judges of greater authority and to other provinces.

[Note: [Col. 0847C]

*Condemns.* Council of Chalcedon, beginning of Session X.

*God.* Sentences of Sixtus 176, and shortly afterward 292 and 203.

*Therefore he is not.* 6, question 1, *He is not wise*. It is nevertheless cited there under the name of Pope Lucius, the successor of Cornelius, where this passage also occurs.

*Fare well.* St. Boniface, Epistle 8.

*Maximus.* In the year 250 or the following year.]

## II

Everything, therefore, that is done or adjudged against [Note: [Col. 0848B] 3, question 6, *Everything that against*.] absent persons, in any proceeding or place whatsoever, is to be made wholly void, because no one condemns a person who is absent, nor [Col. 0848A] does any law condemn him. A human being can therefore easily deceive another human being, but not God, before whose eyes all things are naked and exposed. Hence the prophet says: “The Lord knows the thoughts of men, that they are vain” (Psalm 93). Therefore, one who does harm is not wise. Nor does one who is faithful wish any evil or devise snares against anyone.

We exhort you, brother, and admonish your charity always to assist, strengthen, and console everyone as well as you can. You should forbid the oaths concerning which you wished to consult this holy Roman and universal Church, and you should never harass or harm anyone. Brother, let your Holiness bring these matters to the attention of the rest of our brethren, so that all may avoid these evils. And just as they have been universally forbidden both by the Lord himself and by the holy Apostles and other apostolic men and the rest of the Fathers, so let them be universally observed by all.

We always pray that Your Beatitude may fare well, and we desire that you advance in the sacred virtues, dearest and most beloved brother. Given on the eleventh day before the Kalends of June, in the consulship of the most illustrious Maximus and Decius.

# DECREE

[Note: [Col. 0848C]

From Gratian. Gratian, 16 and 22, question 5. More truly from the *Capitularies*, book I, chap. 63. HARDUIN.]

Taken from the decree of Gratian (1), and not extant in the earlier Decretals.

### That oaths are to be taken by persons who are fasting

It also seems proper that anyone who dares to swear upon sacred things should do so while fasting, with all propriety and fear of God, and that children under fourteen years of age should not be compelled to swear.

[Col. 0847]

# NOTICE

Although the Councils have their own distinct and special collection and do not in themselves belong to our *Library of the Ancient Fathers*—since their already substantial bulk would enlarge it immeasurably—nevertheless it was necessary incidentally to insert some of them among the writings of the Fathers whenever, as is the case with those that follow, they have a necessary and inseparable connection with the works of the Fathers. THE EDITORS.

[Col. 0849]

# THE COUNCILS OF CARTHAGE HELD UNDER ST. CYPRIAN IN THE TIME OF POPE CORNELIUS I, CONCERNING THE CASE OF THE LAPSED

# IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 251: THE FIRST COUNCIL OF CARTHAGE UNDER CYPRIAN

(From the collection of the Councils edited by Giovanni Domenico Mansi, vol. I.)

[Col. 0849B] This Council of Carthage was held at Carthage after Easter in the year of the Lord 254 [Note: [Col. 0849C] The most learned Pagi, who places Cornelius’s accession to the supreme pontificate in the year 251, on the fourth day of June, believes that this first Council of Carthage under Cyprian began in May of that same year, 251, before the ordination of Pope Cornelius, and continued until the month of August. COLETI.], and was convoked on the authority of Bishop Cyprian.

At its opening, the envoys whom Novatian had sent with letters addressed to the African Church were excommunicated by Cyprian. The Fathers assembled in the synod rejected their letters—which the envoys were insistently demanding should be read publicly in the council, although they were utterly full of slanders and falsehoods against St. Cornelius—because they had fully learned the circumstances of the schism from Cornelius’s letters and from the report of certain bishops of that Church returning from Rome. They rejected them as unworthy to be read and heard in so sacred an assembly of priests (Cyprian, Epistles 41, 42, and 55).

Felicissimus, the ill-fated author of the African schism, and those five presbyters of Carthage who were deserters from the faith [Col. 0849C] and schismatic partisans, concerning whom Cyprian writes (Epistle XL), having already been excommunicated twice, appeared at this sacred assembly of bishops to plead their case. They were heard and finally excommunicated a third time. [Col. 0850B] This is clearly established from Cyprian’s Epistles 52 and 55, and likewise from the synodical letter written to Cornelius, which St. Cyprian mentions in Epistle 42 but which, through the ravages of time, has been lost.

It was decreed at this council that the lapsed who were doing penance should indeed be received into the communion of the Church, but that, short of urgent necessity, they should not be admitted before the prescribed period of satisfaction had been completed. Cyprian conveys this in Epistle 52, writing to Antonianus in these words:

“Nevertheless, in accordance with what had previously been determined, when the persecution had subsided and permission had been granted to assemble together, a large number of bishops—whom their faith and the Lord’s protection had preserved sound and unharmed—came together. After passages of Scripture had long been presented on both sides, we weighed out a measured policy with salutary moderation, [Col. 0850C] so that the hope of communion and peace would not be wholly denied to the lapsed, lest they fail still further through despair and, because the Church was closed to them, follow the world and live as pagans; yet, on the other hand, the discipline of the Gospel would not be relaxed so that they might rashly leap into communion. Rather, their penance should be prolonged, the Father’s mercy should be implored sorrowfully, and the circumstances, intentions, and necessities of each person should be examined.”

See Baronius, at the year of Christ 254, nos. 83 through 89. LABBÉ.

[Note: [Col. 0849C]

*In the year of the Lord 255.* Rather, in the year 252, on the Ides of May, according to Pagi’s more exact chronology; consult him at the year 252, no. 8. COLETI.

*The Council of Carthage*, etc. A Council of Carthage that they call the first had in fact already been held at the beginning of this century, when Agrippinus occupied the episcopal see of Carthage, by the bishops of Africa and Numidia concerning the rebaptism of heretics. Some mention of the first Council under Cyprian, however, occurs immediately below, at the beginning of the following epistle—an epistle that in fact pertains to this Council, which is called the Second.

In editing that second Cyprianic Synod, and then the five that follow it, I have always followed the Benedictine, or Baluzian, edition of the works of St. Cyprian, except where I have alerted the reader to a variant reading. For that edition was prepared by Baluze after he had seen J. Harduin’s edition of the Councils, as is evident from his notes. Baluze, however, died—as I demonstrated above at the *Fragments of Cornelius*, p. 18—[Col. 0850C] eight years before the edition of Cyprian was published by the Benedictine monks in 1727. Meanwhile Coustant’s work had appeared: in 1721 he published the *Epistles of the Roman Pontiffs*, in which he included the first and fifth of these synodical epistles.

As regards another council besides these seven Cyprianic councils, Emmanuel Schelstrate, following others, considers two Cyprianic epistles—namely LXV and LXVI, or III and I—to pertain to that eighth council: *Ecclesia Africana*, Dissertation III, chap. 1, p. 121. Pearson, however, in the *Annals of Cyprian*, and Fell in his notes on Cyprian himself, opposed this view. Those most distinguished prelates point out that Cyprian’s words “colleagues who were present” do not always denote a sacred synod. Moreover, it was almost customary for Cyprian to append the bishops’ names to synodical epistles, but no such names appear there.

For that reason, Epistle LXII—or IV in another enumeration—to Pomponius concerning virgins living with male companions would with greater right be reckoned among the synodical epistles, since the names of the bishops who were present are inscribed at its head. Yet I would not readily say that this epistle records a formally convened council.

ROUTH.]

# IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 252: THE SECOND COUNCIL OF CARTHAGE UNDER CYPRIAN, CONCERNING THE SCHISMATICS FELICISSIMUS AND NOVATIAN

(From the collection of the Councils edited by Mansi, vol. I.)

[Col. 0849C] This council was held in the year of the Lord 255, on the Ides of May, [Col. 0850C] at Carthage in Africa, concerning the case of two [Col. 0851A] schismatics, namely Felicissimus and Novatian. The former obstinately maintained that absolutely all the lapsed must be received back immediately without penance. Novatian, by contrast, deviated too far into the opposite extreme and asserted with no less obstinacy that none of those who had lapsed should be received into the Church.

To settle this controversy, therefore, forty-two bishops of the African Church assembled under the authority of Bishop Cyprian. Pursuing a middle course, they determined that peace and reconciliation should be granted to the lapsed who sought to return to the Church, provided that they had fulfilled the penance imposed upon them. They decreed that this was ordinarily to be observed unless either extreme danger to life or an imminent persecution by tyrants—which the Holy Spirit had revealed to Cyprian as impending—required pardon, relaxation, and dispensation from penances already imposed or yet to be imposed.

Privatus, a long-practiced heretic, attempted to enter this synod with [Col. 0852A] his associates in order to plead his case; but because he had already been condemned repeatedly, he was repulsed. For this reason, after gathering certain allies, he appointed a certain Fortunatus—a fugitive and one barred from communion—as a pseudo-bishop against Cyprian. Immediately afterward, Privatus and his associates, through Felicissimus and a great throng of schismatics dispatched to Pope Cornelius, sought the communion of the Apostolic See with extraordinary solicitude in order to avert suspicion of schism and heresy. But after sailing to Rome and repeatedly requesting an audience and reception from the pontiff Cornelius, and attempting to present complaints against Cyprian to him, they were immediately rejected by Cornelius, since from Cyprian’s letters he had already gained sufficient knowledge that they were the authors and defenders of schism and heresy, and were fugitives and absentees. See [Col. 0852B] Baronius at the year 255, no. 5 and following. The synodical epistle sent to Cornelius is extant among Cyprian’s letters as Epistle 54, and we have appropriately reproduced it here.

# OF CARTHAGE, UNDER CYPRIAN

(From the *Synodical Booklet*.)

[Note: [Col. 0852B] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

A divine and sacred local synod, assembled at Carthage, which is called the New City of Africa, by the holy martyr Cyprian, who was its bishop, and by eighty-four other bishops; it repudiated Novatus because he barred repentance to those who had fallen.

[Col. 0852B] A divine and sacred provincial synod, assembled at Carthage, called the new city of Africa, by the holy martyr Cyprian, who was its bishop, and by eighty-four other bishops; it repudiated Novatus because he denied repentance to the lapsed.

[Note: [Col. 0851C]

**SYNODICAL EPISTLE.** It was written by the council held at Carthage in the year 252, on the Ides of May, as we learn from the following epistle. In the manuscripts it is entitled *On the Lapsed*, because it discusses the decree that the aforementioned council enacted in their favor. For in the previous year, at another Council of Carthage, a rather severe measure concerning the lapsed had been established, and Cornelius had confirmed that decree in a Roman synod. The Africans now explain to Cornelius why they had judged that the same persons should be treated more leniently. COUSTANT.

*Cyprian, Liberalis*, etc. Almost all the ancient manuscripts and all the early editions place at the beginning the names of all the bishops. I am therefore greatly surprised that Pamelius omitted them from his edition, and that Rigaltius preferred to report them in his observations as though they were new material, while declaring that he was adding them from the Corbie manuscript. The English editors did better by placing them in the text. The old copies and early editions, however, differ among themselves in the spelling of the names. [Col. 0852C] It would be pointless to record the variant readings. We therefore judged it sufficient to reproduce what is found in the manuscript of de Thou, which Rigaltius also used.

We further advise the reader that one royal manuscript lacks the bishops’ names, and that the title of this epistle there reads simply: “Cyprian to his brother Cornelius, greetings.” In the manuscript of St. Arnulf, however, it reads: “Cyprian, with forty-one brethren, to his brother Cornelius, greetings.” STEPHEN BALUZE.

The learned Cellier believed that the letters of sixty-six bishops to Fidus, which I have appended immediately afterward as though they belonged to Cyprian’s Third Council, were written at this council. For that reason, because in his view those letters ought to be placed in the year 252 rather than 253—that is, before the decree granting indulgence to the suppliant lapsed—he also maintained that the number forty-one here was erroneous, unless one must suppose that fewer or more prelates were present at the council at different times. See him in vol. III, p. 588, and Maran’s *Life of Cyprian*, p. 94.

Certainly, in the passage cited by Cellier at p. 108, St. Augustine confirmed in these words the number of bishops who appear in the letter to Fidus: “But in the epistle that he”—Cyprian—“wrote to Bishop Fidus with [Col. 0853A] sixty-six of his fellow bishops, when he had been consulted concerning the law of circumcision,” etc.; book IV, *To Boniface*, chap. 8, vol. X, p. 481. ROUTH.]

# SYNODICAL EPISTLE OF ST. CYPRIAN, BISHOP OF CARTHAGE, AND HIS COLLEAGUES TO POPE ST. CORNELIUS, CONCERNING THE LAPSED

[Col. 0851B]

**SUBJECT.—**The African bishops explain to Cornelius that an imminent persecution has been repeatedly foreshown by God through visions, and that they have therefore judged that peace should not be deferred for those who have not ceased doing penance. [Col. 0851C]

Cyprian, Liberalis, Caldonius, Nicomedes, Caecilius, Junius [Note: [Col. 0851D] *Junius.* This name and those that follow were added from the manuscripts of Pamelius, Vossius, Corbie, Lamoignon, York, and Lincoln.], Marrutius [Note: [Col. 0851D] *Marruscius* in the Corbie manuscript.], Felix, Successus, Faustinus, [Col. 0852B] Fortunatus, Victor, Saturninus, another Saturninus, Rogatianus, Tertullus, Lucianus, Eutyches, Amplus, Sattius, Secundinus, another Saturninus, Aurelius, Priscus, Herculanus, Victoricus, Quintus, Honoratus, Montanus, Hortensianus, Verianus, Iambus, Donatus, Pompeius [Note: [Col. 0852D] *Pomponius* in the Colbert manuscript.], Polycarpus, [Col. 0852C] Demetrius, another Donatus, Privatianus, another Fortunatus, Rogatus, and Monulus [Note: [Col. 0852D] *Montulus* in the Colbert manuscript.], to their brother Cornelius, greetings.

[Col. 0853A]

[Note: [Col. 0853A]

*Indeed.* The common printed texts have *already long ago*, which is absent from the Corbie manuscripts. In the Colbert manuscript, however, only *long ago* occurs. The reference here is to what had been decreed in the previous year, as soon as the persecution had subsided and peace had been restored to the Church, as explained in Epistle XI, no. 6. COUSTANT.

*We had indeed already long ago decreed*, etc. Harduin says in the index to volume I of the *Councils* that information concerning this first Council under Cyprian—held in the previous year, that is, in 251, against the schismatic Felicissimus and concerning the case of the lapsed—is to be gathered from Cyprian’s Epistle II to the people, XLII to Cornelius, LII to Antonianus, and LIV and LV to Cornelius. The epistle numbers are those of Pamelius.

Moreover, the author of the *Synodical Booklet* records the same synod in these words: “A divine and sacred provincial synod, assembled at Carthage, which is called the New City of Africa, by Cyprian, who was its bishop, and by eighty-four other bishops; it repudiated Novatus because he barred repentance to those who had fallen”; p. 10 of the Strasbourg edition. ROUTH.

In the month of May, when the bishops had gone to Carthage after the Easter solemnities, during which they had remained at home with their brethren, the Second Council of Carthage was held—and specifically on the Ides of May, as is clearly evident from Cyprian’s fifty-ninth Epistle, in which he mentions both this council and the other one celebrated in the preceding year.

In this synod, however, a certain relaxation was made in the decree established at the former council, namely that the lapsed should perform a lengthy and complete penance, but if the danger of illness became urgent they should receive peace at the point of death. In place of that decree, therefore, they established another in the following form: peace was to be given to those who had not withdrawn from the Church of the Lord, but had not ceased from the first day of their lapse to do penance, lament, and entreat the Lord.

The synod reached this judgment not merely to show *epieikeia* (ἐπιείκεια, equitable leniency) to the truly penitent lapsed, but under the compulsion of necessity, since repeated and continual visions warned them that the day of another persecution had begun to draw near. They therefore considered it necessary to arm and equip the truly penitent lapsed for the battle then impending.

After this decree was enacted, a synodical epistle was [Col. 0853D] sent to St. Cornelius, bishop of Rome. It is Epistle LVII, in which the decree itself is both stated and affirmed and defended by many arguments. Cyprian also wrote concerning the council of all his colleagues and sent Cornelius the names of the bishops who were then presiding over the brethren, sound and unharmed, in the Catholic Church, so that he and his colleagues might know to whom they ought to write and from whom, in turn, they ought to receive letters. See *Annals of Cyprian*, at the year 252, section VII. PEARSON.

*They should perform a lengthy and complete penance.* They were not to be received before the prescribed period had been completed, except at the point of death. So Fell indeed explains it. The distinguished Marshall, however, the English translator of St. Cyprian, interprets “complete penance” as passage through every stage of penance. But it seems doubtful whether those stages were at that time well known and clearly distinguished everywhere in the Church.

Moreover, Albaspinaeus, when discussing what “complete penance” means in Cyprian and other authors in *On the Rites of the Ancient Church*, book II, chap. 30, perhaps rightly infers from this very passage [Col. 0854A] that it is not a penance defined by a fixed period, but one that manifests the soul’s grief through signs—that is, tears, weeping, and fasting. And in Epistle XXVIII, otherwise XXXIII, I find Cyprian writing as follows: “that with true repentance, groaning, and complete sorrow they may entreat the Lord.”
