Nevertheless, the words [Col. 0854B] of the epistle that I have placed immediately afterward sufficiently show that some period of penance was formerly prescribed: “that peace might be granted to him before the lawful and complete period of satisfaction,” etc., p. 74.

On another matter, however, the learned Albaspinaeus does not have me equally in agreement. For in book II, chap. 12 and elsewhere, he maintains that this penance was extended even to the end of life, and that the lapsed were not absolved until the very moment when death was to be undergone. Before Cyprian and Cornelius’s decree, he says, the lapsed had been bound permanently by the chain of excommunication, so that they were not released even in death itself or granted absolution.

But one may reasonably doubt whether, whatever harsher determinations some made at that time, so severe a practice or custom belonged to the universal Church before those times. Nor did Albaspinaeus’s arguments appear to me adequate to prove that Cyprian subsequently extended the penance of the lapsed all the way to the last day of life. On the contrary, I considered that position sufficiently refuted by this very epistle and by the distinguished epistle to Antonianus.

Indeed, long before Cyprian, [Col. 0854C] as I demonstrated above from the words of the Christians of Lyons and Vienne, vol. I, p. 330, disputes had arisen concerning the communion of the lapsed, with some proceeding more severely and others more leniently in this matter. Furthermore, Pearson—*Vindication of Ignatius*, part II, chap. 8—points out, while arguing against Albaspinaeus on this very question, that Dionysius, bishop of Corinth, taught that all persons burdened by even the gravest crime were to be received through penance. I read Pearson only after I had written this and everything else pertaining here.

For in his Epistle to the Amastrians, according to the testimony of Eusebius, book IV, chap. 23—or see the corresponding page in my volume I, p. 171—Dionysius “gives them much counsel concerning marriage and chastity, and commands that those returning from any kind of fall whatever, whether misconduct or indeed heretical error, be welcomed.”

Moreover, the Church’s practice and custom in treating the lapsed is set forth in Cyprian’s Epistle XI, otherwise XV, which we know was written before he and his colleagues had established anything concerning this matter. He says:

“I hear that some of the presbyters, neither mindful of the Gospel nor considering what the martyrs have written to us, nor reserving for the bishop the honor of his priesthood and chair, have already begun to communicate with the lapsed, to offer on their behalf, and to give them the Eucharist, although it is proper to arrive at these things in due order. For when, in lesser offenses that are not committed against God, penance is performed for the prescribed time and *exomologesis* (ἐξομολόγησις, public confession) is made after the life of the penitent has been examined, and no one can come to communion unless hands have first been laid upon him by the bishop and clergy, how much more carefully and moderately, in accordance with the discipline of the Lord, must all things be observed in these gravest and most extreme offenses?”

Compare also Epistle X, otherwise XVI, where the following occurs:

“They, contrary to the law of the Gospel, before penance has been performed, before the *exomologesis* of the gravest and most extreme offense has been made”—a solemn and public confession, according to Fell’s explanation—“and before hands have been laid upon them for penance by the bishop and clergy, dare to offer on their behalf and give them the Eucharist, [Col. 0855B] that is, to profane the holy body of the Lord.”

These passages certainly demonstrate not only that it was customary before Cyprian’s time to bring relief to the lapsed at death—which Albaspinaeus denies—but also seem to prove that the custom was to absolve them once their penance had been completed. Yet it is evident, even according to the judgment of that same learned man, that Cyprian later treated the lapsed no more harshly than prior custom had allowed. ROUTH.]

## I

We had indeed decreed long ago [Note: [Col. 0853A] *Already long ago* in the common printed text.], dearest brother, after sharing our counsel with one another, that those who had been overthrown by the adversary and had lapsed amid the assault of persecution, and had stained themselves with unlawful sacrifices, should perform a lengthy and complete penance; and if the danger of illness [Col. 0854A] became urgent, they should receive peace at the point of death [Note: [Col. 0853A] *Toward the point* in the Corbie manuscript.].

For it was not lawful [Note: [Col. 0854A] *It was not the truth* in the Corbie manuscript.], nor did paternal kindness and divine mercy permit, that the Church should be closed [Note: [Col. 0854A] Variant spelling in the printed text.] to those knocking at its door, and that the aid of saving hope should be denied to those grieving and entreating, so that, as they departed from the world, they should be sent to the Lord without communion and peace; [Col. 0855A]

[Note: [Col. 0855C]

*When he himself who gave the law has permitted it.* “When he himself has promised it and has given the law,” in numerous manuscripts mentioned by Fell and Coustant; Coustant also admitted this reading into the text. The distinguished Marshall, the English translator, further notes that, at least according to Cyprian’s understanding, the passage from St. Matthew is to be explained with reference to ecclesiastical censures and their relaxation. ROUTH.

*The day of another assault once more.* In Epistle XIX, Cyprian replied to those who had lapsed in the Decian persecution and were importunately pressing for readmission into the Church that time itself would grant them more than they were asking, and that one who could not endure postponement could be crowned. These words seem to differ considerably from what is said here about the necessity of giving peace to the lapsed: “We teach and incite them in vain to shed their blood in confession of the Name if we deny Christ’s blood to them when they are about to fight.” Yet the statements in the two places are entirely consistent.

First, the condition of the lapsed was different while the Decian persecution continued and after it had ceased. For one who was summoned before the court and defended himself by a lie was perhaps obliged to retract his offense in that very place, before the same judges and the surrounding people, and publicly to profess the truth. He was less strictly bound to do this once the judicial proceedings had ended. The lapsed person was therefore no longer to be forced into those harsh conditions to which he ought to have been compelled while the battle was still being waged.

Second, in the exceedingly difficult case of the lapsed, nothing was to be innovated on private authority. It was therefore not lawful for an individual bishop to admit the lapsed at his own discretion. But after [Col. 0856B] peace had been granted to them by decree of the council, there was nothing to prevent the period of delay from being shortened somewhat by the council’s authority, especially when there was a sufficient reason: namely, the expected persecution.

Third, after the lapsed had spent a suitable period in penance, they had now given evidence of their character, which they had not previously done.

Furthermore, it must be noted that the interests of the lapsed had to yield to the advantage of the Church. However desirable it may have been for them to enjoy the Lord’s full provision and thus be armed for suffering, these considerations had no place until ecclesiastical discipline had been satisfied through the penalties imposed upon offenders. Indeed, it would not have benefited the lapsed, at so raw and untimely a moment, to assail the body of the Lord while they were still almost belching up the death-dealing food of idols, their mouths still exhaling their crime and reeking of deadly contagion. These are Cyprian’s words in the book *On the Lapsed*. Rather, one must wait, and, as the Apostle commands in I Corinthians 11:28, “let a person examine himself, and so eat of the bread and drink of the cup.” FELL.

*Through repeated and continual visions.* Near the end of the Epistle: “This is frequently shown to us by divine revelation.” He mentions the same thing in the Epistle to the Thibaritans, whom he also warns of an extremely severe persecution. RIGALTIUS.

[Col. 0856D] *The sick.* Erasmus added, “if there were any.” I have not found this in any of the ancient copies I use, nor in other editions. BALUZE.

*By the protection of Christ’s blood and body.* In what follows, he teaches that the faithful are raised up and kindled by receiving the Eucharist. Rightly so. For from the Lord’s banquet, mindful of the Lord’s blood and having received the sacrament as the Lord had commanded on that final night, they went forth eagerly as men pledged together and bravely faced the death that the Lord had undergone for their salvation. RIGALTIUS.

If no one denies that true blood is shed for Christ by the martyrs, why should it be denied that Cyprian here proclaims that Christ’s true blood is poured out as drink for those same martyrs? COUSTANT.]

since he himself has permitted it [Note: [Col. 0855B] “He himself has promised it and has given the law,” in Bodleian 1 and 2, NC 1 and 2, York, Lincoln, Victor, Verona, and Benevento.] and has given the law [Note: [Col. 0855B] Thus Bodleian 1 and 2, York, Lincoln, NC 1 and 2, and Verona. “He who gave the law,” Oxford and Leipzig.], so that whatever was bound on earth would also be bound in heaven (Matthew 16:19), while whatever had first been loosed in the Church could be loosed there.

But now [Note: [Col. 0855B] “But since,” Fossombrone and Victor.] we see that the day of another assault has begun once more to draw near; and repeated and continual visions admonish us to be armed and prepared for the contest that the enemy announces [Note: [Col. 0855B] “Introduces,” Bodleian 3.] against us. We must also prepare [Note: [Col. 0855B] “We are preparing,” Bodleian 1, Fossombrone, and Victor.] by our exhortations the people entrusted to us by divine favor, and gather within the Lord’s camp [Note: [Col. 0856B] Thus Pamelius, the Benedictine edition, Vossius 2, Lamoignon, York, Bodleian 3, Lincoln, NC 1 and 2, de Thou, Fossombrone, Victor, and Michel. “Within the camp of the Lord,” printed editions.] absolutely all the soldiers of Christ who desire weapons and demand battle. Compelled by necessity, we have therefore judged that peace must be given to those who have not withdrawn from the Church of the Lord and who have not ceased [Note: [Col. 0856B] “But who have not ceased to do penance,” Oxford.] from the first day of their lapse to do penance, lament, and entreat the Lord; and that they must be armed and equipped for [Col. 0855B] the battle that is imminent.

## II

For we must obey these visions and rightful admonitions, so that the sheep may not be abandoned by their shepherds when they are in danger [Note: [Col. 0856B] “Into danger,” de Thou. “The sheep by their shepherd when they are in danger,” Bodleian 2 and Lamoignon.]; rather, the whole flock must be gathered together into one place, and the Lord’s army must be armed for the contest of heavenly warfare.

The penance of those who grieved was rightly prolonged for a considerable time, so that assistance might be given to the sick at life’s end, as long as there was peace and tranquility, which allowed the tears of those in mourning to be deferred for a long time and relief to be brought belatedly to the dying in their illness. But now peace is necessary not for the weak but for the strong; and communion must be given by us not to the dying but to the living. Thus we will not leave unarmed and naked those whom we rouse and exhort to battle, but will fortify them with the protection of Christ’s blood and body [Note: [Col. 0856B] “Of Christ’s name,” Lamoignon and NC 2.].

And since the Eucharist is celebrated for this purpose, that it may be a safeguard for those who receive it, let us arm with the fortification of the Lord’s full provision those whom we wish [Note: [Col. 0856B] Thus Lamoignon, Pamelius, and Bodleian 1 and 2. “Whom we wished,” Oxford.] to be secure against the adversary. For how can we teach or incite them to shed their own blood in confession of the Name if we deny Christ’s blood to them when they are about to fight? Or how do we make them fit for the cup of martyrdom if we do not [Col. 0856B] first admit them, by right of communion, to drink the Lord’s cup in the Church?

## III

A distinction must be made, dearest brother, between those who have either apostatized and returned to the world that they had renounced, where they live as pagans, or have become deserters to the heretics and daily take up parricidal weapons against the Church—and those who, from the Church’s [Col. 0857A]

[Note: [Col. 0857C]

*And sorrowfully.* These words are absent from four ancient copies. [Col. 0857C] My manuscript reads *sorrowing*. So too does the manuscript of St. Arnulf. BALUZE.

*We both hope and believe.* These words are indeed present in seven ancient manuscripts, but absent from eight others. Erasmus was the first to include them, for they are lacking in the early editions. BALUZE. According to Pamelius, Morel was the first to add these words, since neither Erasmus nor Manutius had printed them. The Roman edition of 1471, a copy of which I possess, reads—not inappropriately—*we have heard* instead of *we hear*. ROUTH.

*Sacrifices of God.* “A sacrifice to God,” in our manuscript. HARDUIN. “Sacrifices of God” is certainly what the Corbie manuscript has, and yet Rigaltius notes that *to God* is written in it. BALUZE. Harduin indicates that his manuscript belonged to the library of the Jesuit College of Louis the Great at Paris. ROUTH.

*We celebrate daily.* In the book *On the Lord’s Prayer*, p. 209: “We receive the Eucharist daily as the food of salvation.” Tertullian, book II *To His Wife*: “Your husband will not know what you taste in secret before all other food; and if he learns that it is bread, he will not believe it to be the bread that it is said to be.” See [Col. 0857D] the chapter *Daily* in Gratian, distinction 2, *On Consecration*. BALUZE.

*Who takes up martyrdom.* Thus Luke 9:23: “Let him take up his cross” (*aratō ton stauron autou*, ἀράτω τὸν σταυρὸν αὐτοῦ). Rigaltius says: “one who obtains martyrdom by divine favor”; “takes up martyrdom,” as below, “taking up arms.” FELL.]

He is baptized in his own blood. Care must be taken lest Cyprian be thought to deny this. For later as well, in Epistle LXXIII to Jubaianus, he wrote that catechumens who undergo death for the sake of the faith are not deprived of the sacrament of Baptism, since they “are baptized with the most glorious and greatest Baptism of blood” . . . and that “those baptized in their own blood and sanctified by suffering are brought to perfection and obtain the grace of the divine promise.” Earlier, “he who takes up martyrdom” means “he who wins the palm of martyrdom.” Moreover, for what follows to be understood as connected with these statements, it must be recalled that in receiving the Eucharist one receives not bare flesh but living flesh animated by the Spirit of Christ, and thus that those who receive the body of Christ [Col. 0858B] receive his Spirit at the same time. Accordingly, although the flesh by itself profits nothing, it nevertheless profits greatly because it has with it the Spirit who gives life. COUSTANT.—“He is baptized in his own blood,” says Rigaltius. “The entire key of paradise is your blood,” says Tertullian; see Epistle LVIII (otherwise LVI). FELL. Epistle LXXIII, p. 136: “Since they are baptized with the most glorious and greatest Baptism of blood.” And shortly afterward he adds that “those baptized in their own blood and sanctified by suffering are brought to perfection and obtain the grace of the divine promise.” See Tertullian in *On Baptism* and in *On Modesty*. The *Passion of Saints Perpetua and Felicity*: “from blood [the supplied text appears incomplete here], from the midwife to the net-fighter, to be washed after childbirth in a second Baptism” [contextually reading *lotura* for the apparent OCR error *latura*]. See Henry Dodwell’s Dissertation 13, which concerns the second Baptism of martyrdom. BALUZIUS.

He cannot be fit. These words appear on the surface to conflict with what the same bishop wrote in reply in Epistle XIV, after learning that some were prematurely and importunately demanding peace and communion from his presbyters and deacons: “If they are in too great a hurry, they have within their own power what they ask, since the present time grants what they ask. The battle line is still engaged, and the contest is held daily: if someone truly and steadfastly repents of what he has committed, and the fervor of faith prevails, he who cannot endure delay can be crowned.” [Col. 0858D] But here it follows that not every capacity for undergoing martyrdom is denied to those who are not granted reception of the Eucharist, but only the ready and unimpeded capacity by which they are made better prepared. Nor should this most vigilant shepherd be judged to contradict himself in these passages; rather, he wisely applied different remedies at different times. When he wished communion to be deferred for penitents, his sole purpose was to prevent the remedy of proven repentance, altogether necessary for the lapsed, from being spurned to the ruin of many. But now, when he grants the Eucharist, his purpose is that, with a most savage persecution threatening, Christ’s soldiers, armed with its most powerful protection, may be able to fight courageously and resist the enemies of the faith with unconquered spirits and in greater safety. Finally, where he says, “They have within their own power what they ask,” it is evident from the following words in his own book *On Mortality* that “with the Lord’s help” must be supplied: “Martyrdom is not in your power, but in God’s gracious favor.” Indeed, even where, concerning one who can scarcely endure having communion deferred, he says, “He who cannot endure delay can be crowned,” he cautiously premises, [Col. 0859C] “if the fervor of faith prevails.” COUSTANT.]

not withdrawing from the threshold, and continually and sorrowfully imploring divine and paternal consolations, now declare themselves ready for battle and profess that they will stand firmly and fight for the name of their Lord and for their own salvation. At this time we grant peace not to those who sleep but to those who keep watch; we grant peace not for pleasures but for arms; we grant peace not for repose but for the battle line. If, as we hear and hope and believe concerning them, they stand firmly and strike down the adversary together with us in the encounter, we shall not regret having granted peace to men so courageous. Indeed, it is a great honor and glory of our episcopate to have given peace to martyrs, so that we, the priests who daily celebrate the sacrifices of God, may prepare offerings and victims for God. But if—which may the Lord avert from our brothers—any one of the lapsed should deceive us by asking for peace dishonestly and, at the time of the impending battle, receive communion without intending to fight, he cheats and deceives himself, concealing one thing in his heart and declaring another with his voice. Insofar as we are permitted to see and judge, we see the face of each person; we cannot search the heart or penetrate the mind. [Col. 0858A] The Searcher and Knower of hidden things judges these matters; he is soon to come and to pass judgment upon the secrets and concealed things of the heart. The wicked, however, ought not to harm the good; rather, the wicked should be helped by the good. Nor should peace be denied to those who are going to suffer martyrdom merely because there are some who will deny the faith, since for this very reason peace must be given to all who are going to serve as soldiers, lest through our ignorance that man who is destined to be crowned in battle begin to be passed over.

[Note: [Col. 0857B] “Sacrifices to God,” Corb.]

[Note: [Col. 0857B] “Peace has been granted,” Bod. 3.]

IV. Nor should anyone say: “He who takes up martyrdom is baptized in his own blood; peace from the bishop is not necessary for one who is going to possess the peace of his own glory and to receive a greater reward through the gracious favor of the Lord.” In the first place, one who is not armed by the Church for battle cannot be fit for martyrdom; and the mind—which the Eucharist raises and kindles—fails when the Eucharist has not been received. [Col. 0858B] For the Lord says in his Gospel: “But when they hand you over, do not consider what you are to say; for in that hour it will be given to you what you are to say. For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matt. X, 19). But since he says that the Spirit of the Father speaks in those who have been handed over [Col. 0859A] and are set in the confession of the name, how can one be found prepared or fit for confession if, after first receiving peace, he has not received the Spirit of the Father, who strengthens his servants and himself speaks and confesses in us?

[Note: [Col. 0857B] “Which the Eucharist, not accepted,” Lam.]

[Note: [Col. 0858B] “Raises up and girds,” Lin. NC. 2.]

[Note: [Col. 0858B] “Do not consider how or what,” Lam. Ebor. Bod. 2.]

In the confession of the name. In one manuscript “his” is added here. This is not foreign to Cyprian’s thought, but it is foreign to his usage. For he characteristically calls the confession of God or of Christ simply “the confession of the name,” as we shall demonstrate in the penultimate note on Epistle XIII. COUSTANT.

Dies. The Corb. manuscript, corrected by a second hand, together with one English manuscript, has “departs.” Cyprian must not be thought to have been doubtful or uncertain about the salvation of these persons. In Epistle LVI, or 58, he discloses his view of the matter in these words: “Even if a robber overcomes him while he is fleeing in the wilderness and mountains, a wild beast attacks him, hunger or thirst or cold afflicts him, or a storm and tempest overwhelms him while he is sailing across the seas, Christ watches his soldier fighting wherever he may be and, to one who dies because of persecution for the honor of his name, renders the reward that he promised he would give in persecution. Nor is the glory of martyrdom less because one has perished not publicly and among many, when the cause of his death is that he dies [Col. 0859D] for Christ.” But just as the faithful would deserve blame if they did not make every effort to depart from this life not without so necessary a viaticum, so too would the shepherds if the faithful had been deprived of so great a gift through their negligence. COUSTANT.

You have comforted. “What was crushed you have not bound up.” Copyists understood this word in the ordinary sense of tribulation or distress and therefore believed that “consolation” corresponded better, contrary to the meaning of the sacred text. The Septuagint reads κατεδήσατε, “you bound up.” Tertullian has *colligastis*, “you bound up.” FELL. I have followed Fell’s edition, in which the reading was thus restored, I believe from manuscript codices, in place of “you have not comforted,” which the printed editions have. Harduin noted that a manuscript of his Society presents “you have not comforted,” but Baluzius recorded that the Sorbonne codex reads “you have not strengthened.” The Vulgate translator [Col. 0860C] has, “What was broken, you did not restore.” ROUTH.

For devouring. The Rheims codex has “for consumption,” the Corbie codex “for plunder,” and the Tours codex “concerning preaching.” BALUZIUS. The Vulgate has “for devouring.” ROUTH.

And they shall no longer feed them. These words are absent from the old editions and from nine ancient books. Pamelius also attests that they were absent from three that he had seen. BALUZIUS. But the Septuagint recognizes the words. Following the Hebrew codex, the Vulgate has: “Nor shall the shepherds feed themselves any longer.” ROUTH.

I shall feed them with judgment. Βοσκήσω αὐτὰ μετὰ κρίματος, “I shall feed them with judgment.” These words are taken from verse 16. God himself will assign his pasture to each of the sheep. FELL.

Rather the harshness of human cruelty. Cyprian himself in Epistle LX: “Made harsh rather by the perversity of secular philosophy than peaceable by the gentleness of the Lord’s philosophy.” Pacian in Epistle II said “an implacable harshness,” against which he sets “the freely given blessings of the Lord and the claims of heavenly clemency.” RIGALTIUS.

Of paternal kindness. Erasmus published, “we set the sweetness of paternal kindness against it.” But I have nowhere found the word “sweetness” in the ancient books. BALUZIUS. Since, however, it is established from the *Variant Readings* included in the Oxford edition that Codex New College 2 has “than against divine sweetness” in place of “than against divine,” I judge that the word “sweetness” should be added before “divine.” ROUTH.

Threatening us. I have restored the pronoun “us” from the editions before the Baluzian, or Benedictine, edition, and likewise the conjunction “and” before “after examining.” ROUTH.

To you also. To Cornelius and his Romans. ROUTH.

Then, further, if he has fled after abandoning all his possessions and, while staying in hiding places and in solitude, happens to encounter robbers, or dies of fevers and weakness, will it not be charged against us that so good a soldier—one who abandoned everything he had and, despising his house and parents or children, preferred to follow his Lord—dies without peace and without communion? Will not either sluggish negligence or cruel harshness be imputed to us on the day of judgment, because we shepherds were unwilling either to care in peace for the sheep entrusted and committed to us or to arm them in battle? Will not the Lord press upon us what he cries out and says through his prophet:

> “Behold, you consume the milk and clothe yourselves with the wool, and you kill what is fat, but you do not feed my sheep. What was weakened you have not strengthened; what was ill you have not fortified; what was crushed you have not bound up; what wandered you have not called back; what perished you have not sought; and what was strong you wore out with toil. And my sheep were scattered [Col. 0860A] because there were no shepherds, and they became food for all the beasts of the field; and there was no one to seek them or call them back. Therefore the Lord says this: Behold, I am against the shepherds, and I shall seek my sheep from their hands, and turn them away so that they do not feed my sheep; and they shall no longer feed them. And I shall draw my sheep from their mouths and feed them with judgment” (Ezek. XXXIV, 3 ff.; ibid. 10 ff.).

V. Therefore, lest the sheep committed to us be demanded back by the Lord from our mouth—the mouth with which we deny peace, with which we set rather the harshness of human cruelty against divine and paternal kindness—it has seemed good to us, at the prompting of the Holy Spirit and with the Lord warning us through many clear visions, since it is foretold and shown that the enemy is threatening us, to gather Christ’s soldiers inside the camp and, after examining each person’s case, to give peace to the lapsed—indeed, to furnish arms to those who are going to fight. We believe that this will also please you in view of the Father’s mercy. But if any one of our colleagues should arise who, with the battle pressing upon us, does not think that peace should be given to the brothers and sisters, he will render an account to the Lord on the day of judgment either for his untimely severity or for his inhuman harshness. We have brought forward what accorded with faith, charity, and pastoral concern, and what was present in our conscience: [Col. 0861A] that the day of battle has drawn near; that a violent enemy will soon rise against us; that the coming fight will not be like the former one but much more severe and more bitter; that this is frequently shown to us by divine revelation; and that by the Lord’s providence and mercy we are repeatedly warned concerning it. We who trust in him can be secure regarding his help and kindness, because he who foretells to his soldiers in time of peace the battle that is to come will grant victory in the encounter to those who fight. We wish you, dearest brother, always good health.

[Note: [Col. 0860B] “Of inhuman cruelty,” Pem.]

[Note: [Col. 0860B] “Than against divine sweetness,” NC. 2.]

[Note: [Col. 0860B] “Since enemies,” Lam. Ebor. Bod. 1, 2. Lin. NC. 1, 2.]

[Note: [Col. 0861A]

Much more severe. It certainly was more severe for Cyprian, who, after the weariness of exile, was finally beheaded in this persecution. But prophets are not [Col. 0861B] always reliable interpreters of their own visions. The gift of interpreting prophecies was altogether distinct from the charism of prophecy. See I Cor. I, 10. FELL. This persecution of Gallus was indeed more severe for Cornelius, as the English translator says in correction of Fell, not for Cyprian, who was to suffer martyrdom several years later under the emperor Valerian. ROUTH.

To be shown . . . to be warned. In several manuscripts “we know” is added after “to us,” through the work of a copyist who failed to notice that the following verb, “to be shown,” had to be referred to the preceding “we have brought forward.” In the common editions, however, “is shown” soon occurs in place of “to be shown,” and then “they warn” in place of “to be warned.” The Colb. codex, of excellent quality, supported by the Corb. and others, has preserved the genuine reading. COUSTANT. [Col. 0862B] I have followed this learned man at this point. The Benedictine edition has “is shown” and “we warn.” The Oxford edition has “is shown” and “they warn.” But long before Coustant, these two infinitives, “to be shown” and “to be warned,” occurred in the Manutius edition. ROUTH.]

[Note: [Col. 0861A] Thus Bod. 1. Voss. 2. Others omit “and.”]

[Note: [Col. 0861A] “We know that this is frequently shown to us by divine revelation,” Pem. [Col. 0862A] Bod. 1, 2. NC. 1.]

[Note: [Col. 0862A] Thus Lin. Ebor. Lam. NC. 1, 2. Other printed editions have “we are warned.”]

### APPROXIMATELY A.D. 250–270  
### NOVATIAN, ROMAN PRESBYTER

[Col. 0861]

# PRELIMINARY DISSERTATION  
## By Dom Gottfried Lumper, O.S.B.

## CHAPTER ONE  
### THE HISTORY OF HIS LIFE  
#### SOLE ARTICLE

[Col. 0861C]

Novatus and Novatian founded the heresy of the Novatians. Eusebius, Saint Epiphanius, Socrates, Sozomen, [Col. 0862C] Theodoret, and Photius confuse these men and merge them into one; Saint Cornelius, Saint Cyprian, Saint Pacian, Saint Jerome, and the anonymous author [Col. 0863A] of the work *Against Novatian*, falsely attributed to Saint Cyprian and printed in the appendix to Baluzius’s edition of Saint Cyprian’s works, pp. 7 ff., clearly distinguish them.

[Note: [Col. 0861C] Euseb., *Ecclesiastical History*, book VI, ch. 35; in book VII, ch. 8, p. 287, Νοουατιανῷ, “to Novatian,” is read.]

[Note: [Col. 0861C] Epiphan., *Heresy* 39.]

[Note: [Col. 0862C] Sozomen, *Ecclesiastical History*, book II, ch. 8, p. 96, also writes Νοουατιανός, “Novatian.”]

[Note: [Col. 0862C] Theodoret, *Compendium of Heretical Fables*, book III, ch. 5, p. 228, vol. IV.]

[Note: [Col. 0862C] Phot., codices 128 and 280.]

[Note: [Col. 0862C] Cornelius in the epistle to Fabius of Antioch and in the epistle to Saint Cyprian.]

[Note: [Col. 0862C] Saint Cyprian, throughout.]

[Note: [Col. 0862C] Saint Pacian, also in the letter to Sympronianus.]

[Note: [Col. 0862C] Saint Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*, ch. 70.]

To remove this apparent contradiction among the writers, scholars have thus far taken two different paths. Some assign greater weight to the Latin writers and infer from this that the Greeks were mistaken. This is the judgment of Henry Valesius, Petavius, Ruinart, Cave, and Fabricius, with whom almost all the remaining writers agree. Others, on the contrary, favor the diametrically opposite opinion and think that the Greeks preserved this man’s true name much better and more accurately. No one, however, has attempted to demonstrate this more learnedly or painstakingly than Lardner, in a special dissertation printed in *Credibility of the Gospel History*, vol. 9, [Col. 0863B] part II, p. 365. Since this opinion of Lardner is not only hitherto unheard of among critics, but also carefully formulated and for the most part well adapted to elucidating the writings of the ancients, we think it will not be unwelcome to our readers if we present here in summary the arguments of the aforementioned dissertation, together with the appended observations of the distinguished Walch.

[Note: [Col. 0863D] Valesius, notes on Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VI, ch. 45.]

[Note: [Col. 0863D] Petavius, notes on Saint Epiphanius, vol. II of the works, p. 226.]

[Note: [Col. 0863D] Ruinart, *Select Acts of the Martyrs*, p. 180.]

[Note: [Col. 0863D] Cave, *Literary History of Ecclesiastical Writers*, vol. I, p. 129.]

[Note: [Col. 0863D] Albert Fabricius, note on Jerome, in the *Ecclesiastical Library*, p. 158.]

[Note: [Col. 0863D] Christian Wilhelm Franz Walch, *History of Heresies*, part II, pp. 188 ff.]

II. The arguments are these:

1. All the Greek writers call him Novatus. They deserve all the more confidence because Eusebius made use of authentic letters of Cornelius and Dionysius of Alexandria and preserved part of them for the memory of posterity, while Socrates and Sozomen unquestionably had dealings with the Novatians.

2. It is manifestly false that all the Latin writers [Col. 0863C] called him Novatian. Rufinus, certainly, consistently called the same man Novatus in his translation of Eusebius’s *Ecclesiastical History*. In the Roman edition of Saint Ambrose’s works, book I of *On Repentance*, ch. 3, the name Novatus appears. The Benedictine editors do indeed criticize this in their notes, vol. II of the works, p. 393; but it is surely not likely that the Roman editor rashly followed that reading without support from any manuscript. In the fragments of Hilary, p. 1320 of the Maurist edition, “Novatus” is read. Jerome too calls him Novatus in his commentary on Joel, vol. III of the works, p. 1358; on Amos, p. 1407; Epistle XXXVIII, vol. IV, p. 307; Epistle LVI, p. 586; and Epistle LXXXIV, p. 659 of Martianay’s edition, in passages where he is manifestly discussing the Roman presbyter. [Col. 0863D] Furthermore, Philastrius, *On Heresies*, ch. 84; Augustine, *On Heresies*, ch. 38, *On the Usefulness of Fasting*, ch. 9, §11, and *Against Cresconius*, book II, ch. 1; Rufinus, *Exposition of the Creed*, in the fifth volume [Col. 0864A] of Jerome’s works, p. 130; and Pelagius, ibid., p. 1015, call the same man Novatus.

3. According to its grammatical derivation, the name of the sect comes not from Novatian but rather from Novatus. Saint Augustine confirms this observation in the last passage cited above, though others contradict him on this point, as we shall say below.

4. The name Novatus is frequently mentioned among the ancients and is very well known, whereas Novatian’s name is not at all—

To the objection that Cyprian nevertheless almost everywhere calls the Roman presbyter Novatian, Lardner replies that, because it was of great importance to this bishop of Carthage to designate Novatus, the Carthaginian presbyter, as the principal author of the schism, he accordingly called the Roman man Novatian, [Col. 0864B] thereby showing that he was a follower of Novatus of Carthage.

III. We have thought that the following observations should be made concerning this opinion of Lardner. First, as regards the chief point in dispute, the distinguished Lardner’s arguments appear to us neither sufficiently decisive nor preponderant. For apart from the fact that the reason offered for Saint Cyprian’s continually calling a man Novatian who was otherwise called Novatus, without ever indicating his intention in altering the name, is not very plausible, not only Cyprian but Cornelius himself—who, of all men, ought to have known the name of his adversary and rival best—likewise always called him Novatian in his Latin letters. It is also worthy of note that this man’s name never occurs in the Greek letter of Cornelius to Fabius of Antioch, of which Eusebius has preserved for us a substantial fragment. Moreover, it could more readily have happened that the Greeks took the word “Novatian” as a designation derived from the sect’s name for someone otherwise known by the proper name Novatus, and were thus led to believe that this man was called Novatus, without therefore deserving to be charged with confusing two such different persons. Hence later Latin writers, who had manifestly used the works of earlier authors, followed their tracks; this is more likely than that Cornelius and Cyprian were mistaken about the name. Finally, from all Lardner’s considerations it does not necessarily follow that the Latin writers were mistaken. [Col. 0864D] For between those two extremes there still lies a third position, which forms the subject of our second observation. If we gather all the observations together, only this twofold conclusion can be inferred from them. The first is: either one side or the other—that is, either the Latins or the Greeks—was mistaken about the name. Now, since the application of the stated conclusion has commonly been made in favor of the Latins and to the prejudice of the Greeks, in our opinion Lardner has certainly demonstrated with sufficient solidity that this application can properly be reversed, but not that it must be reversed. The alternative conclusion is that truth rests with both sides.

It is, moreover, worthy of observation that the distinguished Lardner neglected to note here that it has often happened [Col. 0865A] that the name of some person is found in different forms in the writings of the ancients. To offer some examples of this: Cornelius’s predecessor is called not only Fabianus among Latin writers but also Fabianus among the Greeks—namely Eusebius—and by other Greeks [the supplied text repeats the same form, so its intended contrast is uncertain]. And from ancient times the founder of Manichaeism was called not only Manes but also Manichaeus. It is likewise known to everyone that Lactantius is called at one time Caelius and at another Caecilius, and that the author of the *Life of Saint Augustine* is called now Possidius and now Possidonius, although this latter nomenclature is censured as erroneous by Schoettgen. It could therefore readily have happened, in the case of men otherwise not born to distinguished rank, that both modes of pronouncing and writing their names were in use, and that Cornelius and Cyprian retained the fuller name all the more willingly because it enabled the two persons—Novatus and Novatian—to be distinguished more easily and accurately.

[Note: [Col. 0865D] Euseb., *Ecclesiastical History*, book VI, ch. 29.]

[Note: [Col. 0865D] Bollandists, *Acts of the Saints*, vol. II, January, pp. 252 and 256; Tillemont, *Memoirs concerning Saint Fabian*, vol. III, *Ecclesiastical History*, p. 362; Bower, *History of the Popes*, part I, p. 83.]

[Note: [Col. 0865D] Fabricius, vol. VI, *Library of Latin Writers of the Middle and Later Ages*, p. 24.]

Third and finally, we observe that it is plainly evident from Lardner’s remarks that even the Latins did not always preserve the distinction between Novatus and Novatian, however diligently later Latin writers insist upon that distinction: namely, that of the two presbyters who were leaders of the Novatian schism, the Carthaginian should be called Novatus and the Roman Novatian. This last observation, which first occurred to our mind from Lardner’s dissertation, is of great usefulness and importance in resolving not a few difficulties arising from the fact that passages in the Latin Fathers concerning Novatus [Col. 0865C] of Carthage are interpreted by writers although they actually concern Novatian. Nevertheless, here we follow the common usage, which also rests upon considerations of its own: the name Novatus is applied only to the African and the name Novatian to the Roman presbyter.

IV. Novatian is believed to have sprung from the Phrygian people early in the century, if Philostorgius is to be trusted. Before he professed Christ, he is said to have cultivated philosophy. For Saint Pacian, writing to Sympronianus, says: “Do you press Novatian upon me? I hear that he was a philosopher of the world.” [Col. 0866A] Saint Cyprian had already taught this earlier, and from him we also learn that Novatian was devoted to the doctrines of the Stoics. Leaving his native home, he went to Rome, passing from the Porch—that is, Stoicism—into the Church. While still a catechumen he was seized by a serious illness and received clinical Baptism. “Yet,” as Saint Cornelius writes, “after being restored to health he did not receive the remaining rites that must be received according to the Church’s rule, nor was he sealed by the bishop.” The same holy pontiff then adds: “He was honored with the presbyterate through the bishop’s grace and indulgence. . . . For all the clergy and many of the laity opposed it, because it was not lawful for anyone who, like him, had been baptized by affusion on his sickbed under the pressure of illness to be admitted to any clerical order. But the bishop asked that he be permitted to ordain this one man.”

[Note: [Col. 0865D] Philostorg., *Ecclesiastical History*, book VIII, ch. XV. Valesius considers this opinion of Philostorgius very plausible because Novatian acquired many followers in Phrygia. Compare Valesius’s note f on book IV of Socrates’s *Ecclesiastical History*, ch. 28, p. 212 of the Turin edition. By contrast, the distinguished Jackson, preface to the works of Novatian, p. 8, and Lardner, *Credibility of the Gospel History*, part II, vol. IX, p. 17, consider it implausible.]

[Note: [Col. 0865D] Pacian, Epistle II to Sympronianus, vol. II, *Library of the Fathers*, Paris, p. 56; Jerome, Epistle to Damasus.]

[Note: [Col. 0866C] Saint Cyprian, Epistle LII to Antonianus. Compare Suyskens, *Life of Cornelius*, p. 84, in the *Acts of the Saints*, vol. IV, September, p. 155.]

[Note: [Col. 0866C] Cornelius, Epistle to Fabius of Antioch, §4.]

[Note: [Col. 0866D] The same, ibid., §6.]

[Col. 0866B] I would indeed suppose, with learned men, that the pontiff—whether he was Saint Fabian or, more probably, one of his predecessors—was moved by Novatian’s considerable knowledge of Holy Scripture and the eloquence with which he was endowed to raise him to the rank of presbyter. He evidently judged that he was permitted to depart from customary ecclesiastical discipline only to this extent, because of the service he hoped Novatian would render to the Church. And that Novatian at first sufficiently answered the expectations formed of him is attested by a substantial witness, an anonymous author contemporary with him, who says:

> “Novatian, always within the one house—that is, Christ’s Church—wept over his neighbors’ offenses as if they were his own; he bore the burdens of his brothers, as the Apostle exhorts; [Col. 0866C] and by heavenly exhortation strengthened those who were wavering in the faith.”

[Note: [Col. 0866D] Bollandists, *Acts of the Saints*, September, vol. IV, p. 156.]

[Note: [Col. 0866D] Whether Novatian’s outstanding merits, or hope and fear, induced the bishop to raise him to the order of presbyters immediately after his Baptism—lest the man recoil from the Christian sacred rites and return to his former defilements, an intention that he perhaps did not conceal, as the distinguished Mosheim speaks, p. 516 of his commentary *On Affairs before Constantine the Great*—and whether for this reason the bishop wished in some fashion to bind him to the Church by this honor and call him back from defection, as the distinguished Walch judges in his *History of Heresies*, part II, p. 197, cannot easily be determined. Suyskens, at the place cited, refutes Eulogius’s false narratives concerning the Novatians.]

[Note: [Col. 0866D] Anonymous author, *To Novatus*, §13, among the works of Cyprian.]

But afterward he openly revealed how unworthy he was of the priesthood to which he had been raised contrary to the Church’s customary discipline. For when the Decian persecution arose and the deacons warned him to leave the room in which he had shut himself up and to discharge the office of presbyter among the brothers who were suffering and oppressed, he denied that he would do so. Indeed, he openly indicated that the presbyter’s office was burdensome to him and that he wished to return to his philosophy, as Cornelius [Col. 0867A] attests. At last he was swept away by so intense a fever of ruinous ambition and began to blaze with such dreadful madness that he was not ashamed “to seize the episcopal chair in opposition to Cornelius,” to use Jerome’s words.

[Note: [Col. 0867D] Cornelius, Epistle to Fabius of Antioch, in Eusebius.]

[Note: [Col. 0867D] Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*, ch. 70. Mosheim, in his commentary *On Christian Affairs before Constantine the Great*, p. 513, and Walch, *History of Heresies*, part II, p. 231, attempt to remove from Novatian the charge of ambition and envy, but in my opinion their attempt is fruitless.]

Cyprian, writing to Antonianus, relates in the following words the devices by which Novatian seized the Roman see and the calumnies by which he attempted to drive Cornelius from it:

> “As for the dishonorable and malicious things that are circulated about him”—that is, Pope Cornelius—“I do not wish you to be surprised, since you know that this is always the Devil’s work: to tear God’s servants to pieces with falsehood and to defame a glorious name with false allegations, so that those who shine with the light of their own conscience may be soiled by the rumors of others. You should know, moreover, that our colleagues have investigated and most certainly discovered that he was stained by no blemish arising from a certificate of sacrifice, as some allege; nor did he enter into sacrilegious communion with bishops who had sacrificed. Rather, he joined with us only those whose case had been heard and whose innocence had been established.”

[Note: [Col. 0867D] Cyprian, Epistle LII.]

He then discusses at greater length a certain Trophimus, who had rightly been reconciled with the Church by Cornelius, and continues:

> “As for the report made to you that Cornelius everywhere communicates with those who sacrificed, this too arises from the fabricated rumors of the apostates. For those who withdraw cannot praise us, nor ought we to expect to please those who, displeased with us and rebellious against the Church, persist violently in enticing brothers away from the Church. Therefore, whatever is circulated about Cornelius and about us, neither readily listen to it nor believe it, dearest brother.”

Cyprian said this about the calumnies spread against Pope Cornelius, the principal one being that he admitted the lapsed to communion indiscriminately. Novatian and his adherents, on the contrary, held that the lapsed must nowhere be admitted to peace and the Church’s communion. Yet Novatus at Carthage, in order to court popular favor, had admitted the lapsed to communion without distinction, as Cyprian relates; but after changing his policy at Rome, he and Novatian left the lapsed no hope of reconciliation or communion. The Catholic Church, however, took the middle course—the safest course—and, after examining the case of each person and after the repentance appropriate to the different offenses had been completed, granted peace and communion to the lapsed.

Meanwhile, since conflicting reports about the elections of Cornelius and Novatian [Col. 0867D] were being spread everywhere, and rumor, the messenger of both truth and falsehood, was circulating contradictory accounts, the African bishops, in order to proceed cautiously in this most serious matter, sent delegates to Rome to investigate it at closer quarters. The delegates had scarcely arrived at Rome when Novatian was suddenly ordained bishop. Cornelius, writing to Fabius, bishop of Antioch, relates at greater length how Novatian seized the Roman see and was ordained bishop: namely, that Novatian, inflamed with desire for episcopal rank, for some time concealed his ambition beneath a display of humility in order to attach the confessors of the faith to himself; but that it soon became apparent who he was and by how great a spirit of pride he was driven:

> “For that distinguished man, who had affirmed with certain dreadful oaths that he did not desire the episcopate, suddenly appeared as a bishop, thrust into the midst as if from some theatrical machine. And he who represented himself as a teacher and champion of ecclesiastical discipline, when he attempted to seize and claim for himself an episcopate by no means granted him by God, joined to himself two men whose salvation was beyond hope, so that he might send them into a small and utterly insignificant part of Italy and, by a fraudulent contrivance, deceive three bishops summoned from there—men altogether ignorant and simple. He affirmed with the greatest insistence that they must set out for Rome at once, so that every dissension, from whatever source it had arisen, might be settled through their intervention and judgment together with that of the other bishops. When these men arrived—men, as we have already said, of a rather simple disposition and not sufficiently practiced in the devices and deceits of ruined men—he had them shut in by certain men very like himself whom he had prepared for this purpose. At the tenth hour, while they were drunk and overcome with intoxication, he forcibly compelled them to confer the episcopate upon him by a certain shadowy and empty imposition of hands; and by fraud [Col. 0868C] and treachery he claimed an office to which he had no right. Not long afterward, one of those bishops returned to the Church, confessing his offense with lamentation and tears. When the whole people interceded for him, we received him into lay communion.”

VI. Those whom he had seduced, in order to confirm them in the schism, Novatian bound by sacrilege. For when he offered the Eucharist, he would take and hold in both his own hands the hands of the person receiving it, and say: “Swear to me by the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ that you will never desert my party or return to Cornelius.” And whereas the recipient of that bread ought to have said, “Amen,” he was compelled instead to reply: “I shall never again return to Cornelius.” Having seized the [Col. 0868D] pseudo-episcopate in this manner, he sent his envoys in every direction to announce it; and, if we believe Socrates [Note: [Col. 0868D] Socrates, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book IV, chap. 28, otherwise 23.], at the same time to proclaim “that they should by no means admit to the mysteries those who had sacrificed to idols, but should exhort them to repentance and leave their forgiveness to God.” Yet, lest he appear to have shamefully usurped the Apostolic See, the crafty man pretended that he had been raised to it against his will, as is evident from the letter of Dionysius of Alexandria quoted by Eusebius [Note: [Col. 0868D] Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book IV, chap. 45.]. In it Dionysius, among other things, admonishes and exhorts him voluntarily to relinquish the Roman See, which he had written that he had ascended against his will: “If, as you assert, you were brought to it unwillingly, you will show us this by returning of your own accord”; for it would have been better to suffer anything whatever than to rend the Church of God with so disastrous a schism, as Dionysius argues at greater length in the same passage. [Col. 0869A] Cyprian imitated Dionysius of Alexandria: having convened a council at Carthage, he ordered Novatian’s envoys, together with his letters, to be rejected [Note: [Col. 0869D] Cyprian, Epistle XLIV, to Cornelius.]. Finally, in the year 251, at a Roman council attended by sixty bishops assembled there, Novatian was wholly expelled from the Church. Yet because he continually taught that the Church neither could nor ought to grant peace to apostates, this severity pleased many, and he became the leader of a heresy that long persisted in the Church [Note: [Col. 0869D] Whether the Novatians should be counted only among schismatics or also among heretics is disputed among critics. In my opinion, the entire matter depends upon differing definitions of “heretic.” See the distinguished Walch’s *Heresiology*, Part II, p. 283 ff.].

[Col. 0869B] What befell this man after his expulsion from the Roman Church is entirely unknown. Whether he ended his life in the persecution of Valerian through the distinguished martyrdom of confession, as Socrates reports [Note: [Col. 0869D] Socrates, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book IV, chap. 28.], is fiercely disputed among writers both ancient and modern, some affirming it and others denying it [Note: [Col. 0869D] See Tillemont, *Mémoires*, vol. III, p. 212 ff., art. 3.].

## CHAPTER II. NOVATIAN’S WRITINGS AND DOCTRINE

### ARTICLE I. On Novatian’s Book *On the Trinity*

I. Besides the letter written before his schism in the name [Col. 0869C] of the Roman clergy, Jerome testifies that Novatian composed the following treatises: namely, *On Easter*, *On the Sabbath*, *On Circumcision*, *On the High Priest*, *On Prayer*, *On Jewish Foods*, *On the Steadfastness of Attalus*, and many others, together with a large volume *On the Trinity* [Note: [Col. 0869D] Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*, chap. 70.]. This is, as it were, an epitome of a work of Tertullian which many attribute to Cyprian—not because Tertullian had deliberately written a book on the Trinity, but because Novatian had taken from Tertullian’s books whatever he said about the Trinity. None of these works survives under Novatian’s name; but it is highly probable that the treatise *On the Trinity* and the book *On Jewish Foods* found among Tertullian’s works are the same works that Jerome ascribes to Novatian.

II. The foremost place among Novatian’s writings is therefore held [Col. 0869D] by the book *On the Trinity*, concerning which Saint Jerome says [Note: [Col. 0869D] The same, ibid.]: “Novatian, a presbyter of the Roman Church . . . wrote . . . a large volume *On the Trinity*,” making, as it were, an ἐπιτομήν (*epitomēn*, “epitome”) of Tertullian’s work [Note: [Col. 0869D] ἐπιτομήν. “I am still attracted,” says the distinguished [Col. 0870C] Vallarsi in his note on the cited passage of Saint Jerome, “by the conjecture of Pamelius, who suspected that ἐπίτασιν (*epitasin*, ‘expansion’) should be restored in place of ἐπιτομήν (*epitomēn*, ‘epitome’), since there is no other book of Tertullian expressly treating the Trinity, nor was there formerly any other, than that entitled *Against Praxeas*; but this is much shorter than Novatian’s composition. Accordingly, the latter could in no way be called an ἐπιτομή, or compendium, of Tertullian’s work, but on the contrary an ἐπίτασις, or expansion of the argument. Nor is it uncommon for Jerome to use the word ἐπίτασις in the sense of treating something more fully, [Col. 0870D] or of denoting an enlargement of some subject. Finally, when, writing against Rufinus in Book II, no. 20, he says, ‘He states that a book of Tertullian entitled *On the Trinity* is read at Constantinople under Cyprian’s name by heretics of the Macedonian party. In this accusation he tells two lies: for the book is neither Tertullian’s nor said to be Cyprian’s, but Novatian’s, whose name it bears in its title,’ he gives no indication whatever that the book had been extracted from Tertullian—something he certainly ought to have guarded against, lest his adversary make an objection.”] [Col. 0870A] “Most people, not knowing this, suppose it to be Cyprian’s.” From this perhaps arose the occasion for Rufinus to write [Note: [Col. 0870D] Rufinus, *On the Falsification of Origen’s Books*, p. 53, appended to vol. IV of Origen’s works, Paris ed., 1759.] that the Macedonians had published Tertullian’s book *On the Trinity* at Constantinople under Cyprian’s name, in order to obtain authority for their heresy. Jerome himself, answering this opinion of Rufinus, says [Note: [Col. 0870D] Jerome, Book II, *Against Rufinus*, §19.]: “He passes on to the illustrious martyr Cyprian and says that a book of Tertullian entitled *On the Trinity* is read at Constantinople under Cyprian’s name by heretics of the Macedonian party. In this accusation he tells two lies. For the book is neither Tertullian’s nor said to be Cyprian’s, but Novatian’s, whose name it bears in its title; and the distinctive character of its style discloses its author’s expression.” As to this passage, I would certainly not have wished the recent editor of Jerome’s works, the distinguished and otherwise learned Domenico Vallarsi, [Col. 0870B] to have omitted that annotation in which readers are warned that “there is no book of Novatian that is an ἐπιτομήν (*epitomēn*, ‘epitome’) of a work of Tertullian” [Note: [Col. 0870D] Vallarsi, note a, p. 313; vol. II, part I, Venice quarto ed., 1767.].

III. Moreover, to use the words of a learned man [Note: [Col. 0870D] Maran, *On the Divinity of Christ*, Book IV, chap. 19, §3, p. 519.], it is certainly no wonder that heretics should misuse the testimonies of the ancients in defense of error; scarcely anything pure and undefiled would now remain if whatever they seized upon to support their cause were branded with the mark of error. But Rufinus acted with less consideration in handing over to the “Pneumatomachi” this book, which speaks admirably of the divinity of the Holy Spirit. For its author teaches that “faith in the Holy Spirit,” just as in the Father and the Son, is necessary [Note: [Col. 0870D] Novatian, *On the Trinity*, chap. 29.]; he claims for the Holy Spirit immutability, which he numbers among the surest marks of divinity; he also attributes to him, in express words, [Col. 0870C] “divine eternity”; and he openly professes that the Holy Spirit performs miracles, bestows immortality, is present everywhere, and accomplishes many other things which faith acknowledges to belong to God alone. Who, then, would not approve Novatian’s doctrine concerning the Holy Spirit, to whom he most precisely ascribes all these things? The remaining statements that Pamelius censures as having been expressed less correctly, and that he supposes likewise to have displeased Rufinus, we shall examine a little below. [Col. 0871A]

IV. Let it be permissible to add one further point relating to that passage which seemed to furnish the aforesaid Pamelius with an occasion for error. Near the end of the work, Novatian appends an excellent assertion of the unity of substance in the Father and the Son, and says the following about the Word of God [Note: [Col. 0871D] Novatian, *On the Trinity*, chap. 31.]: “All things are after him, because all things are through him. And rightly is he before all things, but after the Father, since all things were made through him: God indeed proceeding from God, constituting a second person after the Father insofar as he is Son, yet not taking away from the Father the fact that there is one God.” Very similar and thoroughly authentic are the words of Saint Methodius [Col. 0871B] in his book *On Created Things*, where, discussing the principality of the Word in relation to the Father, he says [Note: [Col. 0871D] Methodius, *On Created Things*, §8.]: Οὐκοῦν ἀρχὴ, μετὰ τὴν ἰδίαν ἄναρχον ἀρχὴν, τὸν Πατέρα, αὐτὸς τῶν ἄλλων γίνεται, δι’ ἧς ἅπαντα δημιουργεῖται: “After, therefore, that unique Principle without a principle, who is the Father, he”—the Word—“becomes the principle of other things, through which all things are created.”

Explaining these words of the holy martyr, Combefis says that Methodius intimates that notion and authority of the unbegotten Father whereby he is also called the source of the internal emanation and of the entire Trinity, and is himself the one ἀρχὴ ἄναρχος (*archē anarchos*, “principle without a principle”). This is certainly not said so as to exclude prior existence, for in this sense the Son also is ἄναρχος (*anarchos*, “without a principle”), as Gregory rightly says in his Theological Oration, and other Greek writers everywhere; rather, it is said by removing αἰτία (*aitia*), a cause, and, as it were, a cause or principle of being. For the Latins do not readily admit the term “cause” in divine matters, just as the Greeks do not readily admit ἀρχή (*archē*, “principle”); both, in a sound sense and with different words, explain what is orthodox. [Col. 0871C]

Novatian’s words must be understood in precisely the same sense. He rightly concluded that there would be two Gods if the Son were unbegotten; for there would be two substances, since neither would have received divinity from the other. Since, therefore, Novatian’s only purpose is to avoid that difficulty which would follow from there being two unbegotten beings, he does not injure Catholic doctrine but confirms it: whether when he asserts that the Father is the one God because the Son received divinity from him, or when he makes the Son for this reason inferior to the Father and for this reason obedient to the Father, because the Father is the fountain and origin of divinity. In sum, to conclude at last, Novatian does not attribute to the Son [Col. 0871D] “all things that belong to the Father” [Note: [Col. 0871D] Novatian, loc. cit., chap. 31.], but he does not deny him anything that belongs to God [Note: [Col. 0871D] See Maran, loc. cit., p. 518.].

V. It remains now to inquire at what time Novatian wrote this commentary. Baronius indeed believed [Note: [Col. 0871D] Baronius, at the year 272, §15.] that the commentary *On the Trinity* had been committed to writing by its author around the year of Christ 270, when Paul of Samosata was condemned by the Fathers of the Council of Antioch; his reason, of course, was that this writer seemed to the great man [Col. 0872A] to have vigorously attacked the Samosatene heresy, although suppressing its name. But nothing prevents us from saying instead that Novatian fought against Artemas, whose heresy Paul of Samosata is known subsequently to have followed and propagated. For thus the Fathers of the Synod of Antioch say [Note: [Col. 0872D] In Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book VII, chap. 30.]: τῷ δὲ Ἀρτεμᾷ οὗτος ἐπιστέλλετω καὶ οἱ τὰ Ἀρτέμα φρονοῦντες τούτῳ κοινωνείτωσαν: “But let this man”—Paul of Samosata—“write to Artemas, if he wishes; and let those who hold the opinions of Artemas communicate with him.”

Others, among them Tillemont [Note: [Col. 0872D] Tillemont, *Mémoires*, vol. III, art. 3, on the Novatians.] and Cave [Note: [Col. 0872D] Cave, *Historia Literaria*, at the year 251, vol. I.], conjecture that Novatian composed his work somewhat earlier, yet after the schism. For, they say, the author mentions Sabellius [Note: [Col. 0872D] Novatian, *On the Trinity*, chap. 12.] and refutes his impiety; and from the letters of Dionysius of Alexandria addressed to Sixtus II [Note: [Col. 0872D] Dionysius of Alexandria, in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book VII, chap. 6.], it is learned that Sabellius spread his heresy only after [Col. 0872B] the middle of the third century. But such an opinion is found to be entangled in no slight difficulties. For Sabellius, as is clear from Philastrius [Note: [Col. 0872D] Philastrius, *On Heresies*, chap. 54.] and Augustine [Note: [Col. 0872D] Augustine, *Heresies*, 41.], was a disciple of Noetus and consequently a propagator of his blasphemies. But what has been handed down concerning Noetus? Namely, Saint Hippolytus—who flourished around the year of the Lord 220, as Tillemont himself acknowledges [Note: [Col. 0872D] Tillemont, loc. cit.]—writing against Noetus, testifies [Note: [Col. 0872D] Hippolytus, *Against Noetus*, §1.] that “not long before,” οὐ πρὸ πολλοῦ χρόνου (*ou pro pollou chronou*), he had openly disclosed his impiety. Because he was expelled from the Church’s communion for this reason, “he died shortly afterward,” says Epiphanius [Note: [Col. 0872D] Epiphanius, *Heresies*, 57, §1.], τελευτᾷ δὲ αὐτὸς ἔναρχος (*teleutāi de autos enarchos*, literally, “but he himself dies, having a beginning” [Greek text materially uncertain]). Now if anyone compares Hippolytus with Epiphanius, he must conclude that Noetus—who “not long before” the year [Col. 0872C] 220 had vomited forth his insulting dogma against God the Father, and who in fact met his death shortly afterward—left that satanic doctrine to be disseminated by his disciples at the beginning of the third century at the latest. Given these facts, who could further persuade himself that Sabellius, the disciple of Noetus, began to revive and promulgate the Noetian heresy only about forty years after the death of his teacher?

I certainly would not deny that in the year of Christ 257 Dionysius wrote περὶ τοῦ νῦν κινηθέντος ἐν τῇ Πτολεμαΐδι δόγματος, that is, in Valesius’s translation, “concerning that dogma which, he says, was recently stirred up at Ptolemais.” But Dionysius does not say that this doctrine had “recently” been introduced among the people of Ptolemais by Sabellius. On the contrary, Eusebius, who had the complete letter of Dionysius before his eyes, in reciting that fragment expressly testifies [Col. 0872D] that the bishop of Alexandria spoke about the Sabellian heretics, περὶ τῶν κατὰ Σαβέλλιον αἱρετικῶν (*peri tōn kata Sabellion hairetikōn*, “concerning the heretics associated with Sabellius”). Dionysius’s words should therefore be understood as referring to the followers of Sabellius, who were then increasing in number, rather than to Sabellius himself. For Sabellius, having long before been imbued with the depraved errors of his teacher Noetus, must have spread them abroad long before that time. Novatian must accordingly be thought to have attacked his heresy before the year 250, when, as a presbyter of the Roman Church, [Col. 0873A] he professed and defended her orthodox doctrine. We find that this opinion first commended itself to Pamelius [Note: [Col. 0873D] Pamelius, in his note on the title.] and was afterward supported at greater length by Jackson.

VI. **Analysis of This Book.**—Novatian’s treatise *On the Trinity* is divided into thirty-one chapters. From chapter I through chapter VIII, he comments upon those words of the “rule of truth,” or “of faith” (which we call the Creed), which command us [Col. 0873B] to believe “in God the Father and Lord Almighty, the most perfect creator of all things.” There, among other divine attributes, he establishes immensity, eternity, unity, goodness, immutability, immortality, and spirituality, partly from reason and partly from Holy Scripture. He adds that neither passions nor bodily members can be attributed to God, and that in Scripture these are predicated of God only ἀνθρωποπαθικῶς (*anthrōpopathikōs*, “anthropopathically,” or in human terms).

From chapter XI through chapter XXVIII, he proceeds to a full explanation of those words of our Creed which commend to us faith in “the Son of God, Jesus Christ, our Lord and God.” He proves from the authority of the Scriptures of the Old and New Covenants [Note: [Col. 0873D] The same, chaps. 12–17.] that Christ was promised in the Old Testament [Note: [Col. 0873D] Novatian, chap. 9.], that he is true man [Note: [Col. 0873D] The same, chap. 10.] and true God [Note: [Col. 0873D] The same, chap. 11.]. [Col. 0873C] In chapter XVIII he refutes the error of the Sabellians and confirms from the authority of Holy Scripture the distinction between the Father and the Son; he then answers the objections of this heresiarch and those of others [Note: [Col. 0873D] The same, chaps. 18–29.].

In chapter twenty-nine he treats faith in the Holy Spirit, saying: “Next the authority of faith admonishes us, after the Father and the Son, to believe also in the Holy Spirit”; he enumerates and confirms the Spirit’s operations from the Scriptures. He then endeavors to connect the unity of God with what he has previously discussed [Note: [Col. 0873D] The same, chap. 30.], and finally presents a summary of the matters expounded [Note: [Col. 0873D] The same, chap. 31.].

### ARTICLE II. On Novatian’s Letter *On Jewish Foods*

I. Saint Jerome mentions the letter *On Jewish Foods* both in his book *On Illustrious Men* and when writing to Damasus [Note: [Col. 0873D] Jerome, Epistle 36 to Damasus, otherwise 125, §1.]. In the latter place the holy [Col. 0873D] doctor declares that he is passing over two short questions, one “concerning clean and unclean animals,” the other “concerning circumcision,” because, he says, “they have been published in Latin by most eloquent men, namely our Tertullian and Novatian.” The latter work of Novatian has perished, but the former survives [Col. 0874A] under the title *On Jewish Foods*.

William Cave [Note: [Col. 0874D] Cave, *Historia Literaria*, under the century of Novatian.] is uncertain whether the work *On Jewish Foods* is certainly Novatian’s. “That seems certain to me,” says Oudin [Note: [Col. 0874D] Oudin, *Commentary on Ecclesiastical Writers*, vol. I, sect. III, p. 283.], “since Jerome expressly mentions it in the cited passage, as does the Greek translator, whether Sophronius or some other unquestionably ancient translator: περὶ βρωμάτων Ἰουδαϊκῶν (*peri brōmatōn Ioudaikōn*, ‘On Jewish Foods’).” Moreover, at the beginning of this work its author says that he had written two letters in which he showed that the Jews had failed to understand “true circumcision and the true Sabbath.” Yet the specifically cited Jerome mentions these two short works among Novatian’s writings. No doubt therefore remains that the work *On Jewish Foods* belongs to the same author.

Finally, on the evidence of this short work *On Jewish Foods*, a letter or treatise *On True Circumcision*, printed among the works of the divine Jerome, is also claimed for Novatian; for Jerome mentions it both in his work *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chap. 8 or 7, and Novatian himself at the beginning of the work *On Jewish Foods*, where he says that he composed a letter *On True Circumcision*, a statement especially well suited to this short work. [Col. 0874B] No reasonable doubt can therefore exist about these works of Novatian, especially since, in Dupin’s judgment, the similarity of style supports the same conclusion [Note: [Col. 0874D] Dupin, *Bibliothèque des auteurs*, vol. I, p. 282, Cologne Latin ed.].

“It is evident,” says Pamelius [Note: [Col. 0874D] Pamelius, note 3 on the Epistle *On Jewish Foods*.], “that this letter was composed in retirement [Note: [Col. 0874D] Novatian, Epistle *On Jewish Foods*, chap. I.], perhaps—if conjecture is permissible—when, as Saint Cornelius writes [Note: [Col. 0874D] Cornelius, Epistle to Fabius of Antioch, §5.], he shut himself up in a house and hid for fear of persecution. When at last he was reproached for this by the Roman deacons and asked to come out and, so far as was permissible for a presbyter and within his power, [Col. 0874C] assist the brethren who were in danger, he was so far from complying with them that he even departed in some anger, declaring that he no longer wished to be a presbyter. Let it suffice, therefore, to note that this was the first occasion of his schism and afterward of his heresy; but, so far as appears, this occurred after this and similar letters had been written.”

Thus the learned man. Jackson also agreed with him [Note: [Col. 0874D] Jackson, loc. cit., p. 10.], judging that Novatian wrote this letter toward the end of the year 250, when he had gone into seclusion to avoid the Decian persecution, which began at Rome near the end of the year 249 and finally subsided at the beginning of 251. Tillemont adopted a different opinion [Note: [Col. 0874D] Tillemont, *Mémoires*, vol. III, art. 3, on Novatian.]: he persuaded himself that at the beginning of this letter he perceived the schismatic man acting as bishop. Dupin had already observed this before him, arguing as follows [Col. 0874D] [Note: [Col. 0874D] Dupin, loc. cit., p. 283.]: “His”—Novatian’s—“opening words rather persuade me that it was written after he had become leader of a party, during the persecution of Gallus and Volusian.”

[Col. 0875A] II. **Analysis of This Treatise.** The purpose of this treatise is to show that the animals which the law of Moses forbids people to eat are not absolutely unclean. To prove this, he says that the fruits of trees were the first food of human beings; that afterward they ate the flesh of animals; and that the law then came and distinguished between the animals it was lawful to eat and those they could not eat, calling the latter unclean—not because they were truly such, since they had been created by God, but, first, so that people might learn to flee the vices figured and represented by those animals [Note: [Col. 0875D] For example, he says that the command not to eat pork was given solely so that we might learn not to live a carnal life; when we are forbidden to eat weasels, this signifies that theft is forbidden; ravens designate sensual pleasures, etc.]; and, second, so that they might serve as a remedy for intemperance.

Christ, the end and fulfillment of the law, explained it and gave people the freedom to eat every kind of meat, provided that they remain within the limits of Christian sobriety. [Col. 0875B] From this he takes occasion to rebuke certain Christians who live intemperately. He observes that this is utterly unworthy of people who ought to pray day and night. Finally, among the kinds of meat that it is lawful to eat, he excepts those sacrificed to idols, from which the first Christians scrupulously abstained; and he concludes with these words, which are a summary of his entire discourse: “Therefore, having explained the nature of meats, he presents the purpose of the law of Moses and shows what the freedom of the Gospel is, provided nevertheless that we devote ourselves to temperance and abstain from meats sacrificed to idols. Let us give thanks to our Lord Jesus Christ, his Son, to whom be honor, praise, and glory throughout all ages. Amen.”

### ARTICLE III. On Novatian’s Letter Addressed to Saint Cyprian in the Name of the Roman Clergy

[Col. 0875C]

I. Cyprian himself also assigns to Novatian another letter, which follows the preceding one and was addressed to Saint Cyprian in the name of the Roman clergy. For when writing to Antonianus [Note: [Col. 0875D] Cyprian, Epistle LII, p. 164, Venice ed. of 1758.], he quotes a passage taken from the same letter [Note: [Col. 0875D] Novatian, Epistle to Cyprian, §6, note 1, in Galland, vol. III, p. 323.] and immediately adds: “It was also added—Novatian writing at that time, reading aloud in his own voice what he had written, and the presbyter Moses, then still a confessor but now already a martyr, subscribing—that peace should be granted to the lapsed who were infirm and at the point of death. These letters were sent throughout the entire world.”

Moreover, the same things that Cyprian says here are reportedly confirmed by an anonymous author contemporary with Novatian, who, [Col. 0875D] speaking of him [Note: [Col. 0875D] Anonymous, *Treatise on the Lapsed*, §13, in Galland, vol. III, p. 374.], says: “I cannot discover, therefore, how this Novatian became so maddened by the frenzy of discord—he who, while always in the one house, that is, Christ’s Church, had mourned the faults of his neighbors as his own; had borne the burdens of his brethren, as the Apostle exhorts; and had strengthened those wavering in the faith with heavenly consolation.” [Col. 0876A]

To these must finally be added Saint Pacian, who flourished in the following century. Addressing Sympronianus, he says [Note: [Col. 0876D] Pacian, Epistle III to Sympronianus, *Bibliotheca Patrum*, vol. III, p. 59, Paris ed., 1644.]: “Why, then, did your Novatian, while still a priest and not even yet a bishop by false title, long before Cornelius became bishop, before” he envied Cornelius’s priesthood, “recommend these things”—concerning the reception of the lapsed? “You have Cyprian’s testimony. . . . For in one place he wrote: IT WAS ALSO ADDED, NOVATIAN WRITING AT THAT TIME,” and the rest that we have just quoted from Cyprian.

He then adds: “What do you say, brother Sympronianus? Novatian wrote these things and, to add the service of his own free will, he also read his writing aloud. His right hand is witness; the hand that wrote them is witness; the tongue that read them is witness. Cornelius, on account of whom all this envy of yours erupted, was not yet bishop. . . . If access to repentance is to be denied, Novatian is guilty, for he wrote, recommended, and read these things. Where then was that unyielding rigor? Where was that savage censure? Had no one preferred Cornelius to your party, the authority of Novatian as writer would have remained.” [Col. 0876B] Thus far that holy prelate.

From these testimonies I consider it sufficiently established that this letter must unhesitatingly be attributed to Novatian. It was written during the year 250, or perhaps at the beginning of 251. For thus says the author [Note: [Col. 0876D] Novatian, Epistle to Saint Cyprian, §4, in Galland, p. 322.]: “Although a greater necessity of deferring this matter lies upon us, since, after the death of Fabian, a man of most noble memory, no bishop has yet been appointed among us because of the difficulties of affairs [Col. 0876C] and of the times.” But Fabian was taken away by martyrdom in the year 250, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of February [20 January], and Cornelius succeeded him at the beginning of June in the following year, 251, as we noted in the appropriate place, although Coustant dates it somewhat differently [Note: [Col. 0876D] Galland, *Bibliotheca Patrum*, vol. III, Prolegomena, chap. IV, §1.].

### ARTICLE IV. On Novatian’s Lost Works

Among Novatian’s lost works we count first all those treatises that Saint Jerome listed in this order [Note: [Col. 0876D] Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*, chap. 70.]: namely, *On Easter*, *On the Sabbath*, *On Circumcision*, *On the Priest*—perhaps *On the Priesthood of the Old Testament*—*On Prayer*, *On Persistence*, and *On Attalus*. A certain treatise *On Circumcision* does indeed circulate among the works of the divine Jerome [Note: [Col. 0876D] *Works of Jerome*, vol. V, p. 150, Martianay ed.; and vol. XI, part 2, Venice ed. of 1771, p. 220 ff.], which others have ascribed to Novatian; but because it mentions the Arians and Manichaeans, it can scarcely be assigned to Novatian. We therefore rightly count the letter *On Circumcision* among his lost compositions. [Col. 0876D] Some have held that Saint Augustine’s Epistle *On Easter*, numbered LV according to the Benedictines, [Col. 0877A] should be regarded as Novatian’s treatise *On Easter* [Note: [Col. 0877D] Lardner, *The Credibility of the Gospel History*, part 2, p. 82.].

The title of Novatian’s composition *On Persistence* seems very obscure to us.
