The Greek translator renders it περὶ ἐνεστώτων (*peri enestōtōn*, “On Present Things”), perhaps “on the provisions of the law presently in force.” We interpret it as *On Persistence*, or perseverance in prayer [Note: [Col. 0877D] The same, ibid., p. 21.].

Time, the devourer of things, has also consumed all Novatian’s letters written to various churches after the schism had occurred. Saint Cyprian very often mentions those letters that Novatian wrote to other bishops after he had occupied the Roman See. Saint Jerome also mentions them in these words: “And at the same time the letters of Novatian, so that, as we come to know the poisons of a schismatic man, we may drink more gladly the antidote of the holy martyr Cyprian” [Note: [Col. 0877D] Jerome, Epistle X to Paul of Concordia, vol. IV of the works, Benedictine ed., p. 17; and vol. I, part 1, p. 24, Venice quarto ed., 1766.]. From this we conclude that these letters [Col. 0877B] still survived in Jerome’s time.

The distinguished Dupin makes the following observations concerning Novatian’s style [Note: [Col. 0877D] Dupin, *Bibliothèque*, vol. I, p. 283, Cologne Latin ed., 1703.]: “This author possessed talent, eloquence, and learning. His style is pure, lucid, and polished; his expressions are choice, his thoughts natural, and his reasonings solid. He has many passages of Scripture aptly cited. Indeed, in the treatises that now survive, excellent order and method are observed, and he always speaks calmly and moderately.” The most learned Ceillier endorses this critical judgment without reservation [Note: [Col. 0877D] Ceillier, *Histoire générale des auteurs*, vol. III, p. 296.]. The short work *On the Reception of the Deniers*, attributed to our author by Pacian [Note: [Col. 0877D] Pacian, Epistle III to Sympronianus.], may be Epistle XXXVI among the Cyprianic letters, written in the name of the Roman clergy according to the Oxford edition.

### ARTICLE V. Editions of Novatian’s Works

[Col. 0877C]

Of the works that we have thus far claimed for Novatian, the book *On the Trinity*, together with the letter *On Jewish Foods*, was first brought to light from a very ancient manuscript by Jean Gagney at Paris in 1545. Gelenius then collated it with a British manuscript discovered in the monastery at Masbury and published it at Basel in 1550, and again in 1562. Pamelius further revised it in many places according to the English manuscript copy of Sir John Clement; he also wove into the text certain conjectures of Latino Latini and readings from the works of Tertullian. His edition was first published at Douai in 1579 and was afterward reprinted several times. Finally, in the following year, 1580, René Laurent de la Barre revised and published it at Paris. [Col. 0877D] Up to this point Novatian lay concealed among the works of Tertullian.

It first appeared separately at London in 1709, under the care of William Whiston, appended at p. 327 to a work bearing the English title *Sermons and Essays upon Several Subjects*; then at Oxford in 1724, illustrated with notes by Edward Welchman; and finally once again at London in 1728, through the efforts of John Jackson, a presbyter of the Church of England, in octavo. Whiston presented his readers with the single book *On the Trinity*. Welchman added two further letters, one *On Jewish Foods* and another written in the name of the Roman clergy. Jackson additionally appended a third letter, which the Roman clergy addressed to Cyprian; yet he himself was uncertain whether such a letter acknowledged Novatian as its author.

All three editors illustrated Novatian with most learned notes and observations, with this difference: Welchman’s notes are entirely orthodox, whereas those of the other two, as regards the dogma of the Son’s divinity, smack of pure and rank Arianism. Thus far concerning the older editions. [Col. 0878B]

The most recent edition, prepared by the distinguished Andrea Gallandi, was based principally upon Pamelius’s text, which he compared with the two later editions, the Oxford and the London; nor did he judge the earlier editions wholly negligible. His chief concern, however, was that dislocated passages should be restored to their proper places, principally under the guidance of Cotelier, who, after Henri Valois, acutely noticed and annotated the transpositions of chapters in the book *On the Trinity*. From this it is clear how greatly this most recent edition of Novatian is to be preferred to all its predecessors.

In 1782 Novatian’s works were reprinted at Würzburg by Stahel, in volume IV among the works of the Latin Holy Fathers, pp. 453–544, in octavo. [Col. 0878C] The distinguished Father Dominikus Schram composed an analysis of both short works, *On the Trinity* and *On Jewish Foods*, in volume VI of his patristic work, pp. 269–319, in 1784. Already in 1777 the distinguished Christian Friedrich Rösler, in volume III of his *Library of the Fathers*, printed at Leipzig, communicated to the learned world excerpts from Novatian’s treatise *On the Trinity* in our vernacular language, accompanied by most learned notes.

## CHAPTER III. NOVATIAN’S DOCTRINE

### ARTICLE I. Dogmatic Points Concerning God and His Divine Perfections

Although very few and very brief works of this ancient Roman presbyter have come down to us, nevertheless in his treatise *On the Trinity*, which was written with a fuller pen, there occur what I would call almost innumerable precious fragments concerning the principal truths of Christian doctrine. [Col. 0878D] For there one discovers what is to be held concerning God and his perfections, what the faith of the Church is concerning the mystery of the most holy Trinity and the divinity of Jesus Christ, and concerning his incarnation.

Novatian, at the beginning of his *Treatise on the Trinity*, teaches that we are bound, as prescribed in the Creed—which he calls the rule of faith, or of truth—to believe in God the Father and almighty Lord, the Creator of the universe. This God not only created heaven and earth, but moreover arranged all these things, adorned and filled with their proper and fitting instruments [Col. 0879A]. He created the human being in his own image and implanted in him mind, reason, and prudence, so that he might imitate God. Although the first principles of his body were earthly, its substance was nevertheless inspired by a heavenly and divine breath; and although God subjected all things to him, he willed that he alone should be free. And lest unfettered freedom should again fall into danger, he imposed a commandment upon the human being; by it he taught that evil was not inherent in the fruit of the tree, but warned that it would arise if, by an act of the human will, the law that had been given were treated with contempt [Note: [Col. 0879D] Novatian, *On the Trinity*, chap. 1.]. Thus, according to Novatian, the forbidden tree was not poisonous or harmful in itself. “And he ought to have been free,” Novatian continues, “lest the image of God should incongruously be a slave; and a law had to be added, lest unbridled freedom should break out into contempt for the giver, so that he might consequently receive both fitting rewards [Col. 0879B] and the penalties deserved. From this mortality returned upon him—through envy, certainly [Note: [Col. 0879D] Through the envy of the Devil death entered the world. *Wisdom*.]—although he could have escaped it by obedience; he fell into that same mortality when, following perverse counsel, he hastened to become God. Yet God nevertheless mercifully moderated his punishment, since it was not so much the man himself as his labors upon the earth that were cursed. His being prevented from reaching the wood of the tree of life did not proceed from the malicious spite of envy, but was intended to prevent him, by living forever before Christ had forgiven his sins, from carrying about with him, as his perpetual punishment, an immortal transgression.” Irenaeus likewise cites an ancient writer [Note: [Col. 0879D] Irenaeus, book III, *Against Heresies*, chap. 23.] who also asserted that it was not so much the human being as the earth that was subjected to the curse. “As Scripture relates,” he says, “God did not curse [Col. 0879C] Adam himself, but the earth in his works, just as one of the ancients said: ‘For God transferred the curse to the earth’”—this is the statement of that ancient author—“‘so that it might not remain upon the human being.’”

Novatian teaches that the regions lying beneath the earth are not devoid of powers arranged and ordered there. For there is a place to which the souls of the pious and the impious are conducted, experiencing preliminary anticipations of the future judgment. According to our author’s understanding, this place is perhaps ᾅδης (*Hades*, the underworld), that great receptacle for souls departing from their bodies [Note: [Col. 0879D] Novatian, *Treatise on the Trinity*, chap. 1. Most of the Fathers adopted the same opinion.].

Concerning the simplicity of God, Novatian teaches as follows [Note: [Col. 0879D] The same, ibid., chap. 5.]: “God is simple and without any bodily concretion … since he is called Spirit.” And when Scripture attributes to God eyes, arms, hands, [Col. 0879D] feet, and other members of the human body, it does not intend to express God’s essence or represent his true nature to us, but only to present him in a manner the human mind can comprehend: “Not as God was, but as the people were capable of comprehending him” [Note: [Col. 0879D] The same, ibid., chap. VI.]. Therefore, the fact that these things are said of God in this way should be attributed not to God [Col. 0880A] but rather to the people: “It is not God, therefore, who is limited, but the people’s understanding.” To this most excellent observation Novatian adds that, by means of bodily members, Scripture indicates not corporeal features but God’s various operations: thus it is the manifestations of divine efficacy that are shown there through bodily members. “For when eyes are described,” the same presbyter continues, “it is expressed that he sees all things. And when an ear is mentioned, it is set forth that he hears all things. And when a finger is mentioned, a particular manifestation of his will is disclosed; and so with the rest. For he has neither bodily members, nor are the functions of members necessary to him, at whose mere … decision all things both serve and stand ready.” For why should he require eyes, who is light? Or why should he seek feet, who is everywhere? Or why should he desire hands, whose mind is the craftsman that orders all things [Col. 0880B], and whose silent will accomplishes them? Nor does he need ears, who knows even unspoken intentions. Or for what reason should he seek a tongue, “for whom to think is to have commanded?” Let us acknowledge candidly that all these ideas are most noble and sublime, and that they indicate the author’s altogether exceptional genius. No less learnedly and subtly does he explain how the passions that Scripture appears to attribute to God must be interpreted, arguing as follows [Note: [Col. 0880D] Novatian, ibid., chap. 5.]:

“And if we read of God’s anger and recognize that hatreds are ascribed to him, we nevertheless do not understand these things as corresponding to examples of human vices. These passions may rightly be so called in human beings, but they will not rightly be so judged in God. A human being can be corrupted by them, because he is capable of corruption; God cannot be corrupted by them, because he is not capable of corruption. For the fact that God becomes angry [Col. 0880C] does not arise from a fault in him, but he does it as a remedy for us. Indeed, even when he threatens, he is being merciful, since by these means human beings are summoned to what is right. For those who lack reason for living an honorable life require fear, so that those who have abandoned reason may at least be moved by terror. And therefore all these things—whether God’s anger, God’s hatreds, or anything else of this sort—since they are brought forward as medicine for us, have arisen from deliberate purpose, not from fault.”

“This, then, is the God,” Novatian concludes [Note: [Col. 0880D] The same, ibid., chap. 8.], “whom the Church knows and reveres; to whom all nature, both invisible and visible, always and in its entirety, bears witness; whom the angels adore and the human mind perceives; who established in the East for the first-formed humans a Paradise, a kind of world of eternal life [Note: [Col. 0880D] Beyond dispute, therefore, Novatian accepted as true the account of Eden and the fall of the human being, as did Theophilus of Antioch, with whom he also agrees completely in other opinions.]; who planted the tree of life and likewise placed another tree, the tree of the knowledge [Col. 0880D] of good and evil; who gave a commandment and established a sentence against transgression.… This God instructed the prophets by the Spirit, and through all of them promised his Son Christ; and when he had pledged that he would give him, he sent him. Through him he willed to become known to us, and poured forth upon us the ample abundance of his mercy, bestowing upon the needy a richly abundant Spirit. [Col. 0881A] And because he is freely generous and good, lest this whole world, turned away from him, should wither for want of the rivers of his grace, he willed through his Son that apostles should be sent throughout the whole world as teachers, so that the created condition of the human race might recognize its instruction and, if it preferred to follow it, might have one whom it could now call Father as God in its prayers.”

Such is the conception of God and of his divine perfections presented by Novatian. Let us now see what he teaches concerning the Mystery of the Most Holy Trinity.

## ARTICLE II. Novatian’s Doctrine concerning the Mystery of the Most Holy Trinity

“The rule of truth requires,” says Novatian [Note: [Col. 0881D] Novatian, book *On the Trinity*, chap. 10.], “that first of all we should believe in God the Father.… The same rule of truth,” he continues [Note: [Col. 0881D] The same, ibid., chap. 1.], “teaches us, after the Father, to believe in the Son of God, Christ [Col. 0881B] Jesus, our Lord and God.” Finally, near the end of the same treatise, he expressly teaches that we must believe in the Holy Spirit, formerly promised to the Church but bestowed at the appointed and appropriate times [Note: [Col. 0881D] The same, ibid., chap. 29.]: “But the order of reason and the authority of faith, in accordance with the arranged sayings and writings of the Lord, admonish us after these things to believe also in the Holy Spirit.” You therefore have three divine Persons clearly distinguished by Novatian, who says a little further below [Note: [Col. 0881D] The same, ibid., chap. 30.]: “And this indeed concerning the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.” From the conjunction “and,” as also from the adverb “also” in the texts cited above, it is inferred that this passage speaks of three distinct Persons, of whom one is not another. It therefore remains certain and firmly established that Novatian cannot be accused by [Col. 0881C] anyone of having favored or anticipated the error of Sabellius. But what of Arianism?

### II

Petavius says that Novatian spoke of the mystery of the Trinity “without sufficient precision, and indeed taught many things absurdly” [Note: [Col. 0881D] Petavius, *Theological Dogmas*, On the Trinity, book I, chap. 5, no. 5.]; and Sandius, placing, as usual, excessive confidence in Petavius’s judgment, numbers him among those who taught before Arius the same doctrine as Arius [Note: [Col. 0881D] Sandius, *Nucleus of Ecclesiastical History*, book I, p. 110.]. But in the judgment of the most learned Bull, those insufficiently precise and absurd statements must be referred either to the Son’s οἰκονομία (*oikonomia*, dispensation), or to that inferiority of the Son in comparison with the Father as his author and principle, which all Catholics acknowledged even after the Council of Nicaea [Note: [Col. 0881D] Bull, *Defense of the Nicene Faith*, p. 134.]. Bull demonstrates that Novatian was in no sense of Arius’s opinion by adducing a few, but most explicit, testimonies from Novatian himself. To this demonstration—we use the words [Col. 0881D] of the illustrious Bull—we need preface only this one observation: Petavius himself elsewhere [Note: [Col. 0881D] Petavius, loc. cit., preface to vol. II, chap. 5, no. 3.] expressly acknowledges that those insufficiently precise and absurd statements that Novatian inserted into his work “depart from the Catholic Rule either merely in manner of expression, or at any rate without impairing the substance of the mystery.” Having briefly noted this, let us approach [Col. 0882A] the matter itself. In chapter 23 the author establishes Christ’s divinity as follows:

“If Christ is only a human being,” he says, “how does he say, ‘I proceeded and came forth from God,’ when it is evident that a human being was made by God and did not proceed from God? But a human being did not proceed from God in the manner in which the Word of God proceeded.”

He adds shortly afterward:

“God, therefore, proceeded from God, since the Word who proceeded is God, who proceeded from God.”

### III

What is said more expressly against Arius even in the Nicene Creed itself? For Novatian explicitly contrasts these two expressions, “to have been made by God” and “to proceed from God”; and he no less explicitly affirms that Christ, in his higher nature, was not made—that is, was by no means created—but proceeded from God himself, and consequently is God from God [Col. 0882B]. The same author says a little later in that chapter:

“If Christ is only a human being, what does it mean that he says, ‘I and the Father are one’? For how are ‘I and the Father one’ unless he who is the Son is also God, who can be called one with the Father precisely because he is from him, because he is his Son, because he is born from him, and because he is found to have proceeded from him, by which he is also God?”

This passage clearly refutes Petavius’s slander against the author of this book when he says that Novatian “explained those words of John 10, ‘I and the Father are one,’ in an almost Arian manner.” To confirm this censure Petavius cites Novatian’s words from chapter XXXII:

“But the ‘one’ of which he speaks pertains to harmony, to the same judgment, and to the fellowship of love itself, so that the Father and Son are rightly one [Col. 0882C] through harmony, affection, and love.”

Yet from the passage we have just cited it is evident, I say, that the author understood those words of John not merely in terms of harmony, or agreement of will—as the Arians did—but also and above all in terms of the communion of substance that exists between the Father and the Son, in complete agreement with Catholics. The author expresses this clearly enough in the very passage cited by Petavius, when he immediately (ἀμέσως) adds these words, which Petavius concealed in bad faith:

“And because he is from the Father, whatever the Son is, he is from the Father; the distinction nevertheless remains, so that he who is the Son is not the Father, since neither is he who is the Father the Son.”

Clearly, in that passage he is attacking only the heresy of Sabellius, which declares the Father and the Son to be one in such a way that it entirely abolishes the distinction of Persons [Col. 0882D]. Against this heresy he teaches that the Father and the Son are indeed one both by agreement of will and by unity of substance, since the Son is derived from the very source of the paternal essence; nevertheless, they are altogether two in subsistence, or Person.

Furthermore, the Son’s τὸ ὁμοούσιον—his being *consubstantial*—is most clearly confirmed by a passage from chapter 11, where Novatian speaks as follows concerning both of Christ’s natures, divine and human:

“For Scripture proclaims Christ as God just as it also proclaims God himself as man. It has described Jesus as a human being just as it has also described Christ the Lord as God. For it does not present him merely as the Son of God, but also as the Son of Man; nor does it merely call him the Son of Man, but is also accustomed to declare him the Son of God. Thus, since he is from both, he is both, lest, if he were only one, he could not be the other. For just as nature itself has prescribed that he who is from a human being must be believed to be human, so the same nature prescribes that he who is from God must also be believed to be God; lest, if he were not also God although he is from God, he should no longer be human either, although he is from a human being, and both should be imperiled in the denial of either, when one is shown to have lost credibility because of the other.”

Surely the mind of anyone who does not immediately perceive that these words teach most openly that Christ is ὁμοούσιον (*homoousion*, consubstantial) with God the Father insofar as he is from God, just as he is ὁμοούσιος (*homoousios*, consubstantial) with us human beings insofar as he is from a human being—and that he is no less true God than true man—is wholly darkened. Moreover, it will not be unpleasant to observe that Novatian, in chapter 13 [Col. 0883B], like the other ancient Fathers everywhere, used for demonstrating the divinity of Jesus Christ those texts of the New Covenant—namely John 1:3 and 14; John 3:13 and 17; John 10:30; John 20:28; Romans 9; Galatians 1; Colossians 1; etc.—which our theologians still employ in their manuals.

### IV

In the course of chapter 29, Novatian ascribes to the Holy Spirit those powers and operations that can by no means belong to a creature. Finally, near the end of the chapter he expressly attributes “divine eternity” to the same Holy Spirit. When in chapter XVI, otherwise XXIV, he says that the Holy Spirit is less than the Son [Col. 0883C], this must be understood in precisely the same manner in which theologians interpret the subordination of the Son in relation to the Father: namely, that the Holy Spirit is called less than the Son not with respect to nature, but with respect to origin, because he is derived from the Father through the Son, as Tertullian says in *Against Praxeas*, chap. 4; and consequently receives all that he has from the Father through the Son, as Novatian says [Note: [Col. 0883C] From the principles of Novatian—who denies that the Son, insofar as he is begotten by the Father, is equal to the Father—it was entirely appropriate and consistent for him to maintain that the Holy Spirit, who proceeds from the Father and the Son, is less than both. Nor does he detract from the divinity of the Holy Spirit by denying in this sense that he is equal to the Son, any more than he detracts from the divinity of the Son when he subjects him to the Father as the principle of origin from whom he received the whole authority of divinity. Indeed, the divinity of the Holy Spirit is strongly commended in this passage. For if the Holy Spirit were a creature, this would be no greater an argument for Christ’s divinity than the fact that other created things are said to receive from Christ [Col. 0883D]. Moreover, when Novatian adds that Christ would have received from the Holy Spirit if he were only a human being or an angel—for the heretics acknowledged that he was an angel—does this not constitute an argument that all created rational beings depend upon the Holy Spirit as the author of holiness? Maranus, *The Divinity of Our Lord Jesus Christ*, book IV, chap. 19, § 3, p. 520 ff.].

The points for which Pamelius criticizes Novatian are exceedingly slight [Col. 0884A], because in chapter 7 he writes as follows:

“Finally, if you understand Spirit as God’s substance, you will have made God a creature, for every spirit is a creature.”

For these words, “every spirit is a creature,” by no means concern the Holy Spirit. Novatian demonstrates that God cannot be designated by human beings with any word that does not fall very far short of that infinite Majesty. Consequently, whether he is called light, spirit, or fire, none of these things is said properly and fittingly of God, because both spirit and fire are created things.

“These things,” he says, “are represented figuratively rather than being literally so. For in the Old Testament God is also called fire, so that fear may be instilled in a sinful people when he is shown as Judge; and in the New Testament he is declared to be spirit, so that he may be proved to be the restorer and creator of those dead in their transgressions [Col. 0884B], through this goodness of the forgiveness bestowed upon believers.”

Here you see that Novatian regarded the appellations “fire” and “spirit” as transferred from material things, and that he did not intend his statement that “every spirit” is a creature to be said of the Holy Spirit. Thus Maranus [Note: [Col. 0884D] Maranus, loc. cit.].

Pamelius next complains that, in chapter 30, Novatian does not call the Holy Spirit God or make any mention of him when, in that chapter, the author demonstrates that the Father and the Son are one God. Novatian does not, indeed, explicitly call the Holy Spirit God by name; but in the preceding chapter he does not remain silent concerning the Spirit’s “divine eternity,” and proves by many arguments that he is God. For what is his purpose when he defends the Spirit’s divine attributes, except to prove what he had promised to prove—namely, that one must “believe also in the Holy Spirit,” and consequently that he is one God with the Father and the Son [Col. 0884C]? Hence, after completing what he had determined to say concerning the Holy Spirit, at the beginning of this chapter he joins the three Persons together as follows:

“And let this brief account concerning the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit suffice for us.”

But if Novatian appears to remain silent concerning the Holy Spirit while showing that the Father and the Son are not two Gods but one, the reason for this must be sought nowhere else than in the fact that the whole effort of the heretics was directed toward overthrowing the divinity of the Son. For if they had once proved that the Son was not one God with the Father, by the same operation they would have severed the Holy Spirit from participation in the divine nature. Likewise, once it had been demonstrated that the Father and the Son [Col. 0884D] are one God “through communion of substance,” as Novatian says, no room remained for doubting that the divinity of the Holy Spirit by no means produced three Gods [Note: [Col. 0884D] Maranus, *The Divinity of Our Lord Jesus Christ*, the book cited, p. 521.].

# ALL THE EXTANT WORKS OF NOVATIAN, ROMAN PRESBYTER

[Col. 0885]

# BOOK ON THE TRINITY (C)

## SUMMARY

[Col. 0885A]

Novatian’s treatise *On the Trinity* is divided into thirty-one chapters. The first comments upon those words of the rule of truth, or faith—which we call the Creed—that command us to believe in God the Father and almighty Lord, the supremely perfect Creator of all things. This extends from chapter 1 through chapter 8; there, among other divine attributes, he establishes God’s immensity, eternity, unity, goodness, immutability, immortality, and spirituality, partly from reason and partly from the Holy Scriptures. He adds that neither passions nor bodily members can be attributed to God, and that in Scripture these are predicated of God only ἀνθρωποπαθικῶς (*anthropopathically*, in terms of human passions). From chapter 9 through chapter 28, he proceeds to a lengthy explanation of those words of our Creed that commend to us faith in the Son of God, Jesus Christ, the Lord [Col. 0885B] our God. By the authority of the Scriptures of the Old and New Covenants he proves that Christ, promised in the Old Testament, is true man and true God. In chapter 18 he refutes the error of the Sabellians, confirms by the authority of Holy Scripture the distinction between the Father and the Son, and then replies to the objections of this heresiarch and of others. He treats faith in the Holy Spirit in chapter 29, saying: “Thereafter the authority of faith admonishes us, after the Father and the Son, to believe also in the Holy Spirit” [Col. 0886A]. He enumerates and confirms the Spirit’s operations from the Scriptures. He then endeavors to connect the unity of God with what was previously discussed, and finally presents a summary of the matters explained (7).

# CHAPTER I

## Novatian, about to discuss the Trinity, sets forth from the Rule of Faith that we must first believe in God the Father and almighty Lord, the supremely perfect Creator of all things. The works of creation are beautifully described. Human free choice is affirmed. God’s mercy in imposing punishment upon the human being is shown. A place is assigned to the souls of the pious and impious after death.

The rule of truth requires that first of all we believe [Col. 0886B] in God the Father and almighty Lord—that is, the supremely perfect Creator of all things—who [Note: [Col. 0885B] “Suspended heaven at a lofty height.” Minucius appears to have imitated this passage of Novatian in *Octavius*, chap. 5, where the following is read: “Though he may have suspended heaven by its own material, though weights may have established the earth, and though the sea may have flowed in from liquid.” You may also see parallels in Lactantius, *Divine Institutes*, book II, chap. 9, near the beginning. And I would not wish you to omit Theophilus, *To Autolycus*, book I, chap. 4.] suspended heaven at a lofty height, established the earth with its mass cast down below, spread abroad the seas in their unfettered liquid, and arranged all these things, adorned and filled with their proper and fitting instruments. For in the firmament of heaven he raised the light-bearing rising of the sun; he filled the gleaming globe of the moon, for the comfort of the night, with its monthly [*mensurnis*] phases [Note: [Col. 0885B] *Mensurnis*. We read this from the English manuscript codex instead of *menstruis*, because that word was customary even for the African, St. Cyprian, in Epistle XXVIII, no. 11, and Epistle XXXIV, no. 23 [Col. 0886B]. Gagnaeus certainly also read it thus formerly. PAMELIUS.—Whiston, Welchman, and Jackson read no differently.]; he also kindled the rays of the stars with various splendors of flashing light. And he willed that all these things should travel by their appointed courses [Note: [Col. 0886B] *Legitimis*, “appointed”: that is, established by divine law. Eusebius uses the same phrase in *Preparation for the Gospel*, book VII, chap. 10. JACKSON.] [Col. 0887A] around the entire circuit of the world, to provide the human race with days, months, years, signs, seasons, and benefits (Gen. 1:14).

On the earth also he raised the loftiest mountains to their peaks, cast the valleys down into the depths, and spread out the plains evenly. He usefully appointed herds of animals for their various forms of service to human beings. He strengthened the hardwoods of the forests to be of benefit for human uses, brought forth crops for food, opened the mouths of springs, and poured water into the rivers that would flow from them. After these things, lest he should fail to provide even delights for the eyes [Note: [Col. 0887C] “Lest he should fail to provide even delights for the eyes.” This is indeed a Tertullianic phrase, as are certain others below: for example, *denotatur*, *edici*, and *viritior* in chap. 2; *qua pater* in chap. 12; and *confibularet* in chap. 18. But it does not therefore follow that this book is Tertullian’s, as is evident even from the fact that all the African writers, including those later than Tertullian—such as St. Cyprian, Minucius Felix, St. Pacian, and Arnobius—are accustomed to use similar expressions. PAMELIUS.—Gagnaeus has a different reading: “Afterward, that he might also provide delights for the eyes themselves.” But the Pamelian reading agrees with the editions based upon the English codex. “Provision was made for the belly,” our author says below in *On Jewish Foods*, chap. 6, using the same construction. JACKSON.], he clothed all things with the various colors of flowers, for the pleasure of those who beheld them.

In the sea itself also, although it was already wonderful both in size and usefulness, he fashioned animals of many kinds, some of moderate and others of enormous bodily size, bearing witness through the diversity of their constitution to the skill of their maker. Not content with these, lest perhaps the roar and course of the waters should invade a foreign element to the loss of its human possessor [Col. 0887B], he enclosed their boundaries with shores, so that when the roaring wave and the foaming surge from the deep gulf reached them, they would return again into themselves and not exceed the limits granted to them, observing the laws prescribed for them—so that human beings might keep the divine laws all the more faithfully because even the elements had kept them.

After these things he also placed the human being over the world, and made him in the image of God (Gen. 1:27). He implanted in him mind, reason, and prudence, so that he might imitate God. Although the first principles of his body were earthly, its substance was nevertheless inspired by a heavenly and divine breath [Note: [Col. 0887D] *Cujus*. Welchman conjectures that *cui* should be read.]. After God had subjected all things to him (Gen. 1:28), he willed that he alone should be free [Note: [Col. 0887D] *Quem*. We have restored this reading with Jackson, so that it refers to the human being. Other editions read *quae*.]. And lest unfettered freedom should again fall into danger, he imposed a commandment (Gen. 2:17) [Col. 0887C], by which it was taught that evil was not inherent in the fruit of the tree [Note: [Col. 0887D] “Was taught” (*doceretur*). I have restored this from Latinus Latinius, because it yields a better sense than the *diceretur* (“was said”) of Pamelius’s edition. JACKSON.], but that it would arise if, by an act of the human will, the law that had been given were treated with contempt.

For he also ought to have been free [Col. 0888A], lest the image of God should incongruously be a slave; and a law had to be added, lest unbridled freedom should break out into contempt for the giver, so that he might consequently receive both fitting rewards and the penalties deserved [Note: [Col. 0887D] “So that” (*ut et*). Thus Pamelius with the other editions. Jackson, however, would prefer *et ut*.], since he now possessed as his own whatever he chose, by the movement of his mind, to direct toward either alternative. From this mortality returned upon him—through envy, certainly [Note: [Col. 0887D] “Mortality.” With Jackson we follow Pamelius, who reads it thus. Other editions have “the envy of mortality,” having understood this passage less correctly.]—although he could have escaped it by obedience; he fell into that same mortality when, following perverse counsel, he hastened to become God (Gen. 3:5). Yet God nevertheless mercifully moderated his punishment [Note: [Col. 0887D] “Moderated.” The context appears to require that the word “God” be added; it was perhaps omitted by a copyist because of its similarity to the following word *dum*. This is the conjecture of Welchman and Jackson. But whether one reads *super terram* with Gagnaeus or *super terra* with Gelenius and others makes no difference.], since it was not so much the man himself as his labors upon the earth that were cursed.

For the fact that he is sought does not arise from ignorance, but reveals the hope that the human being would in future be found and saved in Christ [Note: [Col. 0887D] “Finding” (*inventionis*). The word seems out of place to Jackson, who judges that *resurrectionis* (“resurrection”) or *revelationis* (“revelation”) should be restored from Romans [Col. 0888C] 8:20–21, to which he believes Novatian referred. This is rather inapt. Welchman’s *redemptionis* (“redemption”) is better. But nothing appears to require alteration. The author perhaps alluded to Luke 19:10: “For the Son of Man came to seek and to save what was lost.”]. And the fact that he is prevented from reaching the wood of the tree of life (Gen. 3:22–24) does not proceed from the malicious spite of envy [Col. 0888B], but was intended to prevent him, by living forever before Christ had forgiven his sins [Note: [Col. 0888C] “Had forgiven” (*donasset*). I would have preferred *condonasset*, had I not seen that Novatian used the verb *donavi* in the same sense as here in the epistle written to Cyprian in the name of the Roman clergy. For he thus renders Matthew 18:32: “I forgave you the whole debt.” JACKSON.], from carrying about with him, as his perpetual punishment, an immortal transgression.

Although in the regions above as well—that is, above the firmament itself—which are not visible to our eyes today, he first established angels [Note: [Col. 0888C] “He first established angels.” This was the opinion not only of Novatian, but also of St. Jerome in his commentary on chapter 1 of the Epistle [Col. 0888D] to Titus, and of all the Greeks: namely, that the angels were established first—that is, before every other creature. But St. Augustine, in *The City of God*, book XI, chaps. 5, 6, and 7, book XII, chap. 15, and elsewhere, judges that the opinion more worthy of acceptance is that, according to Ecclesiasticus 18:1, God created all things simultaneously. The Master of the Sentences also follows this opinion, and after him the Scholastic Doctors. It was furthermore defined at the Lateran Council under Innocent III and received into the *Decretals*, chap. *Firmly We Believe*, title *On the Supreme Trinity and the Catholic Faith*. PAMELIUS.], arranged the spiritual Virtues, appointed Thrones and Powers, and created many other immense spaces of the heavens and infinite works of the mysteries, so that this immense world might appear to be almost the latest of God’s corporeal works rather than his only one.

For the regions lying beneath the earth are not themselves devoid of powers arranged and ordered there [Note: [Col. 0888D] “For … themselves are.” Thus Pamelius edited the text from Latinius’s conjecture. Other editions read: “For neither are the things lying beneath the earth themselves.” But the two English editors think that, with *nam* (“for”) deleted, the passage should read: “Nor are the things lying beneath the earth themselves,” etc.]. For there is a place to which the souls of the pious and the impious are conducted, experiencing preliminary anticipations of the future judgment [Note: [Col. 0888D] “For there is a place.” Most of the Fathers, whether Greek or Latin, agree with Novatian in this opinion. Above all others, consult Hippolytus, *Against the Greeks*, vol. II of our *Library*, p. 451 ff.]. Thus we might see the overflowing greatness of his works in every [Col. 0888C] region as not confined within even the most capacious bounds of this world, as we have said [Col. 0889A], but might also conceive the depths and heights beneath [Note: [Col. 0889D] “Beneath” (*infra*). Thus, from Wower’s manuscript, I corrected the word *intra* (“within”), which all the editions have. JACKSON.] this world itself; and so, upon considering the magnitude of his works, might worthily marvel at the maker of so great a mass.

# CHAPTER II

## God is above all things, himself containing all things; immeasurable, eternal, greater than the human mind, inexplicable by speech, and loftier than every height.

Over all these things he himself contains all things, leaving nothing outside himself empty, and leaving no room for a God superior to him—as [Note: [Col. 0889D] “As some suppose.” Namely, the Valentinians, who placed above the Demiurge, that is, God the craftsman, a superior God, Bythus, together with the number of thirty Aeons. PAMELIUS.] some suppose. For he has enclosed the universe within the bosom of his perfect greatness and power, always intent upon his work, passing through all things, moving all things, giving life to the universe, surveying [Col. 0889B] the whole, and so joining the discordant materials into a harmony of all the elements that, from disparate elements, one world has been consolidated by this coherent union, so that it cannot be dissolved by any force, except when he alone who made it commands it to be dissolved (2 Pet. 3:13), in order to bestow upon us other and greater things.

For we read that he contains all things; and therefore nothing could exist outside him, since he has no origin at all and consequently experiences no end—unless, which God forbid, he began to exist at some time and is not above all things, but, having begun to exist after something else, is [Note: [Col. 0889D] “Below.” Jackson likewise restored this word from Wower’s manuscript, where the printed editions have “within.” Welchman also conjectured that it should be so read.] below that which existed before him, found inferior in power because he is shown to be later even in time. For this reason, therefore, he is always immeasurable, because nothing is greater than he; always eternal, because nothing is older than he. For that which is without [Col. 0889C] origin cannot be preceded by anything, since it has no time. He is therefore immortal, not failing at the point of consummation. And because whatever is without origin is without law, [Note: [Col. 0889D] “He excludes the limit of time, since,” etc. Thus Pamelius, whom Jackson follows. Welchman, however, preferred to move the word “since” before “limit.”] he excludes the limit of time, since he acknowledges himself debtor to no one.

Concerning him, therefore, and the things that are his and are in him, neither can the human mind worthily conceive what, how great, and of what kind they are, nor can the eloquence of human speech bring forth a power of expression equal to his majesty. For in contemplating and expressing his majesty, all eloquence is deservedly mute, and every mind is meager: for he is greater than the mind itself, nor can the measure of his greatness be conceived, [Note: [Col. 0889D] “Lest, if he could be conceived,” etc. Thus Pamelius and both Froben editions. But Gagneius and Barrensis read: “Because, if he could be conceived, he must be less than the human mind.”] lest, if he could be conceived, he should be less than the human mind by which [Col. 0890A] he could be comprehended. He is also greater than every utterance and cannot [Note: [Col. 0889D] “Be expressed.” A word customary in Novatian, and therefore rightly retained by Pamelius and Jackson. Others read “be spoken.” Gagneius and Barrensis give the entire passage thus: “Nor can he be spoken: because, if he could be expressed, he must be less than human speech, by which, when he is expressed, he could be encompassed and comprehended.”] be expressed, lest, if he could be expressed, he should be less than human speech, by which, when expressed, he could be encompassed and comprehended. For whatever is conceived concerning him will be less than he; and whatever is uttered, when compared with him, will be something less gathered around him. In silence we can in some measure perceive him; but we cannot explain in speech what he is in himself.

[Note: [Col. 0890D] “For whether you call him LIGHT,” etc. Novatian appears here to have copied Theophilus of Antioch, who has the following in *To Autolycus*, book I, chapter 3: Εἰ γὰρ φῶς αὐτὸν εἴπω, ποίημα αὐτοῦ εἴπω, κ. τ. λ. “For if I call him light, I name his work,” etc. I would have you examine and compare the passage.]

For whether you call him Light, you have named his creation rather than himself; you have not expressed him. Whether you call him Power, you have named and declared his might rather than himself. Whether you call him Majesty, you have described his honor rather than himself. And why do I make this lengthy by running through each individual term? I shall explain the whole matter at once. Whatever you may say of him at all, [Col. 0890B] you will have explained some property or power of his rather than himself. For what can you worthily say or think concerning one who is greater than all words and all perceptions? Only in this one way—and even this insofar as we are able, insofar as we grasp it, and insofar as we are permitted to understand—shall we grasp with the mind what God is: if we conceive him to be that whose nature, quality, and magnitude cannot be understood, and cannot even enter into thought itself.

For if, at the sight of the sun, the sharpness of our eyes grows dim, so that our gaze cannot look upon the orb itself, being overcome by the brilliance of the rays that meet it, the mind’s vision undergoes the same thing in every contemplation of God; and the more intensely it strives to contemplate God, the more it is blinded by the light of its own contemplation. For what can you worthily say of him—to repeat myself—[Col. 0890C] who is more sublime than every sublimity, higher than every height, deeper than every depth, brighter than every light, clearer than every radiance, more splendid than every splendor, stronger than every strength, mightier than every power, more beautiful than every beauty, truer than every truth, braver than every courage, greater than every majesty, more powerful than every potency, richer than all riches, wiser than every wisdom, kinder than every kindness, better than every goodness, more just than every justice, and more merciful than every mercy?

For all classes of virtues [Note: [Col. 0890D] “Of all.” Welchman would prefer “all things,” and his conjecture is also approved by Jackson.] must necessarily be less than he who is both God and Father of all virtues, so that it may truly be said [Note: [Col. 0890D] “That God is that.” Thus Pamelius, Gagneius, and Barrensis. Wower’s manuscript reads: “God is that which is of such a kind,” etc. Welchman, [Col. 0891D] however, conjectures that “God” should be accusative. But the received reading can stand if *Deus* is taken technically—that is, as a proper name. JACKSON.] that God is that which is of such a kind that nothing [Col. 0891A] can be compared with it. For he is above everything that can be spoken. He is a kind of Mind that generates and completes all things, and, without any beginning or end of time, governs by supreme and perfect reason the naturally interconnected causes of things for the benefit of all.

## CHAPTER III  
### That God is the Creator, Lord, and Father of all is proved from the Holy Scriptures

We therefore acknowledge and know this God, the Creator of all things: Lord because of his power, [Note: [Col. 0891D] “And Father.” With Pamelius I have retained the word “and,” which most printed editions omit.] and Father because of his establishment of them. This, I say, is he who spoke, and all things were made (Ps. 148:5); he commanded, and the universe came forth. Of him it is written (Ps. 103:24): “You made all things in wisdom.” Of him Moses says (Deut. 4:39): “God in heaven above and on earth beneath.” According to Isaiah (Isa. 40:12), he measured heaven with his span and the earth with his fist. He looks upon the earth and makes it tremble (Ps. 103:32). He encompasses the circle of the earth, and those who dwell upon it are like locusts. He [Note: [Col. 0891D] “Weighs.” Novatian cites this passage below in chapter 30, where he has “suspends”; Jackson transferred that reading from there to this passage.] weighs the mountains in a balance and the forests in scales (Isa. 40:22, 12)—that is, by the exact measure of divine ordering. And lest the massive bulk, lying unevenly, should readily collapse into ruin if it were not balanced with equal weights, he proportionately equalized this burden of the earthly mass.

He says through the Prophet (Isa. 45:22): “I am God, and there is none besides me.” Through the same Prophet he declares (Isa. 42:8): “I will not give my majesty to another,” so as to exclude all pagans and heretics together with their fabrications, proving that what has been made by a craftsman’s hand is not God, nor that [Note: [Col. 0891D] “Which has been fashioned by a heretic’s ingenuity.” The author imitates Tertullian, who, as Pamelius observes, in *On Prescription* includes in his catalogue of heretics those who fashioned another God for themselves by heretical ingenuity.] which has been fashioned by a heretic’s ingenuity. For something for which a craftsman must be sought in order that it may exist is not God.

He further adds through the Prophet (Isa. 66:1): “Heaven is my throne, but the earth is the footstool of my feet. What sort of house will you build for me, or what place will be my rest?”—to show that much more is he not contained by a temple, [Note: [Col. 0891D] “Whom.” I restored this from Junius and Latinius in place of the common reading “since.” JACKSON.] whom the world does not contain. He declares these things not for his own vaunting, but for our instruction. For he does not seek from us the glory of greatness, but, as Father, wishes to confer religious wisdom upon us.

Moreover, wishing to draw our beastlike minds—swollen and rugged with savage brutality—toward gentleness, he says (Isa. 66:2): “And upon whom [Col. 0892A] shall my Spirit rest, if not upon one who is humble and quiet and trembles at my words?” Thus a person may in some measure recognize how great God is, when, through the Spirit bestowed upon him, he learns to fear him.

Likewise, wishing to come still more fully into our knowledge, and stirring our minds to worship him, he said (Isa. 45:7): “I am the Lord, who made light and created darkness,” so that we should not suppose that some entity called [Note: [Col. 0892D] “Not some entity called Nature.” The author of the *Recognitions*, book VIII, chapter 34: “Those who name Nature in place of God and affirm that all things were made through Nature fail to perceive the error in their terminology. For if they suppose Nature irrational, it is utterly foolish that a rational creature should proceed from an irrational maker. But if it is reason—that is, the *Logos*—through whom it is agreed that all things were made, they needlessly alter the name when they profess belief in the Creator’s reason.” The same author also discusses this subject somewhat earlier, in chapter 20.] Nature were the craftsman of those alternations by which nights and days are regulated, [Note: [Col. 0892D] “We should suppose.” I transferred this word into the text from Wower’s manuscripts, in place of the printed “we suppose,” which does not agree so well with the following “we should recognize.” JACKSON.] but should rather recognize God—which was truer—as their Creator.

Since we cannot see him with the gaze of our eyes, we learn of him from the greatness, power, and majesty of his works: “For his invisible things,” says the apostle Paul, “are perceived and seen from the creation of the world through the things that have been made; his eternal power and divinity also” (Rom. 1:20). Thus the human mind, learning hidden things from manifest ones, may contemplate with the eyes of the mind the greatness of the craftsman from the greatness of the works it sees. Of him the same Apostle says (1 Tim. 1:17): “Now to the King of ages, immortal, invisible, the only God, be honor and glory.” For he escaped the contemplation of the eyes because he surpassed the capacity of thought: “Because,” he says, “from him and through him and in him are all things” (Rom. 11:33). For all things exist from him by his command; they are ordered through him by his Word; and the universe returns into his judgment, so that, while all things are in him and await freedom after corruption has been laid aside (Rom. 8:21), they may appear to have been recalled into him.

## CHAPTER IV  
### God is also good, always like himself, immutable, one and alone, infinite; his proper name cannot be expressed; and he is incorruptible and immortal

[Col. 0892C]

The Lord rightly pronounces him alone good (Luke 18:19). The whole world bears witness to his goodness, for he would not have established it unless he had been good. For if all things were very good (Gen. 1:31), consequently and rightly the good things that were established proved their establisher good; and things that proceed from a good establisher cannot be anything but good. Hence let all evil be far removed from God. For one who claims for himself the perfect name [Col. 0892D] of both Father and Judge cannot be the originator or craftsman of any evil work, [Col. 0893A] especially since he is the avenger and judge of every evil work. Indeed, evil comes upon man from no other source than his having withdrawn from the good God. [Note: [Col. 0893D] “Had withdrawn.” Latinius elegantly reads “to have withdrawn.” This seems the true reading, being a Greek idiom. JACKSON.] This very thing is marked in man: not because it was necessary, but because he himself willed it so. Hence both what evil was became manifest, and—lest envy should appear to exist in God—the source from which evil arose came to light.

He, therefore, is always like himself, and never turns or changes himself into any forms (Jas. 1:17), lest through change he should appear to be mortal as well. For the change involved in transformation is understood to be a kind of portion of death. Therefore no addition of any part or honor ever accrues to him, lest anything should ever appear to have been lacking in one who is perfect; nor is any diminution effected in him, lest some degree of mortality should appear to have been admitted. Rather, what he is, he [Col. 0893B] always is; he who is is always the same; and as he is, so he always is. For increases reveal an origin, and diminutions prove death and destruction. Therefore he says: “I am God, and I am not changed” (Mal. 3:6), always maintaining his own condition, since what was not born cannot be transformed.

For whatever it is in him that [Note: [Col. 0893D] “Can.” I would prefer to read “can be”: the author himself has it thus shortly afterward in this chapter. ID.] can be God must always exist, so that he may always be God, preserving himself by his own powers. And therefore he says (Exod. 3:14): “I am who I am.” That which is has this name precisely because it always retains the same quality of itself. Change removes the name “that which is,” for whatever is ever transformed is shown to be mortal by the very fact that it is transformed. It ceases to be what it had been and consequently begins to be what it was not. Therefore [Col. 0893C] God’s own condition rightly remains always in him, since without the loss involved in change he is always both like and equal to himself.

For what was not born cannot be changed. Only those things undergo transformation which are made or begotten: since things that once did not exist learn to exist by being born, and therefore are transformed in being born. But those things that have neither birth nor craftsman have excluded alteration from themselves, since they have no origin, in which lies the cause of transformation.

Therefore he has also been pronounced one, since he has no equal. [Note: [Col. 0893D] “He has.” From Froben, Welchman reads “he may have,” and punctuates the passage thus: “Since he may have no equal: for whatever can be God,” etc. This is more approved by Jackson.] For whatever God can be, God is; and he must necessarily be supreme. But whatever is supreme can be supreme only when it is beyond comparison. Therefore he must necessarily be alone and one, since nothing can be compared [Col. 0893D] with him, as he has no equal. Nor can there be two infinite beings, as the very nature of things dictates. That is infinite which has absolutely neither origin nor end; for whatever occupies the whole excludes the beginning of another. [Col. 0894A]

[Note: [Col. 0893D] “For if it does not contain everything,” etc. Novatian here closely follows Theophilus of Antioch, *To Autolycus*, book II, chapter 3.]

For if anything does not contain the entirety of what exists, since it is found within that which contains it, it is found to be less than that which contains it and [Note: [Col. 0893D] “Will have ceased to be.” Thus most printed editions, a reading that agrees very well with the following “will have been” and “will have begun.” But Gagneius and Barrensis, whom Welchman follows, read “will cease”—less correctly, as it seems.] will have ceased to be God, having been brought under the power of another, within whose greatness it will have been enclosed as the lesser. [Note: [Col. 0894D] “And therefore that which.” Welchman conjectures that one should read “that which.” Jackson does not dissent.] And therefore that which contained it will rather have begun to be God.

From this it follows that even God’s proper name cannot be expressed, because he cannot be conceived. For whatever is contained by a name is also comprehended from the condition of its nature. A name is the signification of a thing that could be comprehended by that name. But when the subject under discussion is such that it cannot worthily be grasped even by the understanding itself, how shall that which, being beyond understanding, must also be above the signification of any designation, be worthily pronounced by a word of appellation? Thus, when for certain reasons and occasions God adds [Note: [Col. 0894D] “And puts forward.” Wower’s manuscript reads “or puts forward.” JACKSON.] and puts forward his name, we rightly understand that it is not so much the legitimate propriety of a designation that has been declared as a certain established signification, to which people may have recourse and through it appear able to obtain God’s mercy.

He is therefore both immortal and incorruptible, experiencing no diminution whatever and no end. For because he is incorruptible, he is also immortal; and because he is immortal, he is assuredly also incorruptible. Each is mutually intertwined with the other and within itself, [Note: [Col. 0894D] “Intertwined … extended.” The printed editions have the feminine forms *perplexa producta*, contrary to the laws of grammar. We have followed the English editions.] and extended toward the state of eternity by a reciprocal chain, with immortality descending from incorruptibility and incorruptibility proceeding from immortality.

## CHAPTER V  
### Although we find certain expressions of God’s anger and indignation, and hatred, described in the sacred pages, these must not be understood according to examples of human vices

[Col. 0894C]

Although we also [Note: [Col. 0894D] “Read.” Thus the editions of Welchman and Jackson, in place of the common reading “legitimate.”] read of his anger, find certain expressions of indignation described, and recognize references to hatred, we nevertheless do not understand these as being related according to examples of human vices. For although all these things can corrupt a human being, they cannot in any way impair the divine power. These passions will rightly be said to exist in human beings; they will not rightly be judged to exist in God. For a human being can be corrupted by them because he is corruptible; God cannot be corrupted by them because he is not corruptible.

These things therefore possess a power that they may exercise—but where susceptible [Col. 0894D] matter is present, not where an impassible substance is present. For even the fact that God is angry does not arise from a vice in him; he does it for our healing. He is merciful even when he threatens, since by these means human beings are recalled to what is right. For those who lack reason for an honorable life require fear, so that those who have forsaken reason may at least be moved by terror.

Therefore all these things—whether God’s anger, hatred, or whatever else is of this kind—since they are brought forth for our healing, as the matter itself shows, arise from deliberation, not from vice; nor do they descend from frailty, and for that reason they cannot have power to corrupt God. For the diversity of the materials within us from which we are constituted is accustomed to stir up the discord of anger that corrupts us. Such diversity cannot exist in God either by nature or by vice, since he is certainly not understood to have been constructed from bodily compounds. For he is simple and without any corporeal concretion—whatever that whole is which he alone knows himself to be, [Col. 0895B] since he has been called Spirit (John 4:24). Therefore those things that are vicious and corrupting in human beings, because they arise from the corruptibility of the body itself and of matter, cannot exercise the power of corruptibility in God, [Note: [Col. 0895D] “Since.” A very ancient English manuscript reads “because indeed.” JACKSON.] since, as we have said, they arise not from vice but from reason.

## CHAPTER VI  
### Although Scripture often converts the divine countenance into human form, the measure of the divine majesty is not thereby enclosed within the outlines of our body

Although heavenly Scripture often converts the divine countenance into human form, when it says (Ps. 33:16), “The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous”; or when (Gen. 8:21), “The Lord God smelled an odor [Col. 0895C] of sweet fragrance”; or when tablets written by the finger of God are delivered to Moses (Exod. 31:18); or when the people of the children of Israel are delivered from the land of Egypt by a mighty hand and an uplifted arm (Ps. 135:12); or when it says (Isa. 1:20), “For the mouth of the Lord has spoken these things”; or when the earth is declared to be the footstool of God’s feet (Isa. 66:1); or when it says (2 Kings 19:16), “Incline your ear and hear”—[Note: [Col. 0895D] “We.” Others read “But we.” We have omitted “but” with the English editors, in accordance with the course of the author’s words.] we who say that the Law is spiritual do not enclose the measure or form of the divine majesty within these outlines of our body, but extend it without any end through its own fields, so to speak, of unbounded greatness.

For it is written (Ps. 138:8–10): “If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into the lower regions, you are present; and if I take up my wings [Col. 0895D] and depart across the sea, there your hand will seize me, and your right hand will hold me.” For we recognize the rationale of divine Scripture in its tempering of its arrangement. At that time the Prophet was still speaking of God in parables according to the stage of faith—not as God was, but as the people were able to comprehend. That these things, therefore, are thus said of God should be attributed not to God, but rather to the people.

Thus (Exod. 26) the people are permitted to erect a tabernacle, yet God is not confined within the tabernacle. [Note: [Col. 0895D] “Confined.” This word is absent from Welchman, but the others exhibit it.] Thus also (1 Kings 4) a Temple is built, yet God is not wholly shut within the Temple’s narrow limits. God, therefore, is not limited; rather, the people’s perception is limited. God is not narrow; rather, the people’s intellectual grasp is narrow. Finally, in the Gospel the Lord said (John 4:21): “The hour will come when you will worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem.” And he gave the reason, saying (v. 24): “God is Spirit; and therefore those who [Note: [Col. 0895D] “Worship.” Welchman reads “worship him,” following also the Greek Vulgate. Others omit “him”; and perhaps Novatian himself omitted it.] worship must worship in spirit and in truth.” [Col. 0896B]

Thus the operations of divine power are shown there through bodily members; neither God’s form nor corporeal outlines are posited. When eyes are described, it is expressed that he sees all things. When an ear is mentioned, it is declared that [Note: [Col. 0896D] “All things.” Thus Pamelius and others. Gelenius, however, followed by Welchman, reads “all persons.”] he hears all things. When a finger is mentioned, a certain indication of his will is disclosed. When nostrils are mentioned, the reception of prayers as though they were fragrances is shown. When a hand is mentioned, he is proved to be the author of every creature. When an arm is mentioned, it is declared that no nature can resist his strength. When feet are mentioned, it is explained that he fills all things and that there is nothing where God is not.

For neither members nor the functions of members are necessary to him, at whose mere and even unspoken decision all things serve and stand ready. Why should he require eyes, who is Light? Why should he seek [Col. 0896C] feet, who is everywhere? Why should he wish to advance, when there is nowhere outside himself into which he can advance? Why should he desire hands, whose silent will is craftsman enough to establish all things?

[Note: [Col. 0896D] “Nor does he need ears … intentions.” This passage has dropped out of Welchman’s edition. There also, a little afterward, it reads “not merely by any effort,” omitting the preposition “without,” which the others exhibit.]

Nor does he need ears, who knows even unspoken intentions. For what reason should he seek a tongue, when for him to think is to command? These members were necessary to human beings, not to God, because human purpose would be ineffective unless the body fulfilled the thought. But they are not necessary to God: not only do works follow his will without any effort, but the works themselves proceed immediately together with his will.

Rather, he is wholly eye, because he sees wholly; wholly ear, because he hears wholly; wholly hand, because he acts wholly; and wholly foot, because he is wholly everywhere. For whatever that identical reality is, it is wholly equal [Col. 0896D] and wholly everywhere. Whatever is simple has no diversity within itself. Only those things fall into the diversity of members which pass from birth toward dissolution.

[Note: [Col. 0896D] “But these things.” Thus the common reading. Welchman would prefer “than these things.” Jackson, however, proposes “but this,” referring it to the diversity of members. Yet the author appears to have referred “these things” both [Col. 0897C] to the diversity of members and to dissolution.]

But things that are not compounded cannot experience these things. For whatever is immortal is, whatever it may be, that one and simple thing always. And because it is one, it cannot be dissolved, since whatever it is, that very thing, placed beyond the jurisdiction of dissolution, is released from the laws of death.

## CHAPTER VII  
### ARGUMENT—When God is also called Spirit, radiance, and light, God is not adequately explained by those designations

But concerning the Lord’s statement (John 4:24), “God is Spirit,” [Note: [Col. 0897C] “I think.” The English manuscript reads “I should think,” which I would prefer. [Col. 0897D] JACKSON.] I think Christ spoke of the Father in such a way that he wished something still greater than “God is Spirit” to be understood. For although in his Gospel he speaks while bringing about growth [Col. 0897B] in understanding among human beings, [Note: [Col. 0897D] “Bringing about.” Thus Welchman, whom Jackson follows, in place of the printed “for those bringing about.” That this is the genuine reading, says the latter English editor, will be readily apparent to anyone who attends to the passage. For it was Christ who brought about growth in understanding among human beings in his Gospel.] nevertheless he still speaks of God to human beings in the manner in which they are as yet able to hear or comprehend, even though, as we have said, he now strives to bring about religious growth in the knowledge of God.

For we find it written that God is called Love (1 John 4:8), yet God’s substance is not thereby expressed as Love; and that he is called Light (1 John 1:5), yet God’s substance does not consist in this. Rather, all this is said of God only insofar as he can be spoken of. Thus, rightly, when he is called Spirit, not the whole of what he is has been stated. Instead, as the human mind advances in understanding as far as Spirit itself and is itself now turned toward spirit, it may conjecture through “Spirit” that God is something further and greater.

For what he is in accordance with what he is can neither be expressed in human speech, perceived by human ears, nor comprehended by human senses. For if the things God has prepared for those who love him are things which “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor the human heart or mind itself perceived” (1 Cor. 2:9), what is the nature and magnitude of him who promises these things, when both the human mind and human nature fail to understand them?

Finally, if you take “Spirit” to be God’s substance, you will make God a creature. [Note: [Col. 0897D] “For every spirit is a creature.” Pamelius’s criticisms here are exceedingly slight, and he thinks the words similarly displeased Rufinus. For these words, “Every spirit is a creature,” do not in the least concern the Holy Spirit. Novatian demonstrates that God cannot be designated by human beings with any word that does not fall very far short of that infinite majesty. Hence, whether he is called light, spirit, or fire, none of these is aptly and properly predicated of God, because both spirit and fire are created things. “These,” he says, “are figurative rather than literal. For in the Old Testament [Col. 0898C] God is called Fire, so that fear may be instilled in a sinful people when he is shown as Judge; and in the New Testament he is declared to be Spirit, so that he may be proved to be the Restorer [Col. 0898D] and Creator of those dead in their sins, through this goodness of the forgiveness bestowed upon believers.” Here you see that Novatian regards the designations “fire” and “spirit” as transferred from material things; nor did he intend what he says—that every spirit is a creature—to refer to the Holy Spirit. MARAN, *On the Divinity of Our Lord Jesus Christ*, book IV, chapter 19, §3, p. 520.—Welchman had previously expressed the same view. Jackson, however, passes over this particularly noteworthy passage, while otherwise discussing at length matters that are extremely commonplace.]

For every spirit is a creature. God, therefore, [Col. 0898A] will already have been made. Likewise, if, following Moses (Deut. 4:24), you take God to be Fire, by calling him a creature you will have described a created thing, not disclosed the Creator. But these things are figurative rather than literal. For in the Old Testament God is called Fire so that fear may be instilled in a sinful people when he is shown as Judge. And in the New Testament he is declared to be Spirit so that he may be proved to be the [Note: [Col. 0898D] “Restorer and Creator.” Thus Pamelius. Gelenius reads *refertor*, undoubtedly corruptly; Welchman nevertheless retained that reading in his text, while supplying the alternative “restorer” in the notes. The same Welchman next thinks “re-creator” should be read, which Jackson also would prefer.] Restorer and Creator of those dead in their sins, through this goodness of the forgiveness bestowed upon believers.

## CHAPTER VIII  
### ARGUMENT—That the Church knows and venerates this God; and that the entire nature of things, both invisible and visible, always bears witness to him—a nature which his providence rules and governs

[Col. 0898B]

Thus, setting aside the tales and fabrications of the heretics, the Church knows and venerates this God, to whom the whole of nature—both invisible and visible, at all times—bears witness: whom the angels adore, the stars admire, the seas bless, the lands revere, and all the infernal regions [Note: [Col. 0898D] **All.** Jackson thinks that *also* should certainly be read, as being more emphatic.] look up to; whom every human mind perceives, even if it does not express him; at whose command all things [Note: [Col. 0898D] **Are set in motion.** Thus the printed editions. Welchman alone has “are contained.”] are set in motion: springs gush forth, rivers flow, waves rise, all things bring forth their offspring, winds are compelled to blow, rains come, seas are stirred, and everything everywhere pours forth its fertility. He established in the East, especially for the first-formed human beings, a certain world of eternal life, Paradise; he planted the tree of life (Gen. II, [Col. 0898C] 9); he likewise placed there another tree, that of the knowledge of good and evil; he gave a commandment; he established a sentence against transgression (II Pet. II, 5); he preserved the most righteous Noah from the dangers of the flood in accordance with the merit of his innocence and faith (Gen. V, 24); he translated Enoch (Jas. II, 23); he admitted Abraham into the fellowship of friendship (Gen. XXII, 12); he protected Isaac (ibid., vv. 30, 43); he increased Jacob (Exod. III, 9, 10); he appointed Moses leader over the people [Col. 0899A]; he delivered the groaning children of Israel from the yoke of slavery; he wrote the Law; he led the offspring of the fathers into the land of promise; he instructed the prophets by the Spirit; and through all of them he promised his Son, Christ, and when he had pledged [Note: [Col. 0899D] **Had pledged.** Thus the English editors; Pamelius has “had promised.”] that he would give him, he sent him.

Through him he wished to become known to us, and he poured out upon us the ample depths of his indulgence, conferring a rich Spirit upon the needy and rejected. And because he is freely generous and good, lest this whole world, turned away from him, should wither for lack of the rivers of his grace, he willed that the apostles, the instructors of our race, should be sent by his Son into the whole world (Mark XVI, 15), so that the created order of the human race might acknowledge its Creator and, if it preferred to follow him, might have one whom it could now call Father as God in its petitions (Matt. VI, 9).

His [Col. 0899B] providence has not merely extended, and does not merely extend, individually through human beings, but also through cities and states themselves, whose ends he foretold through the voices of the prophets; indeed, it extends even through the whole world itself, whose end, plagues, diminutions, and punishments he described because of its unbelief. And lest anyone suppose that this tireless providence of God does not reach even the smallest things, the Lord says: “Of two sparrows, not one will fall without the will of the Father; and even all the hairs of your head have been numbered” (Matt. X, 29–30).

His care and providence also did not permit either the Israelites’ garments to be worn out or the cheapest sandals upon their feet to deteriorate (Deut. VIII, 4), nor, lastly, the captive trousers of those young men to be burned (Dan. III, 27). [Note: [Col. 0899D] **Their . . . captive trousers.** Thus the printed editions, except Welchman’s, in which, without authority from manuscripts or copies, the editor chose to substitute “the captive men’s trousers.”] And rightly so: for if he has embraced all things here, containing all things—[Col. 0899C] and all things and the whole consist of individual things—then his care, whose providence reaches the whole of whatever exists, will consequently extend even to each individual thing.

Hence it is that he also sits above the cherubim (Ezek. I, 10; Ps. XCVIII, 1), that is, he presides over the diversity of his works, while the living creatures subjected to his throne hold primacy above the rest. Crystal covers everything from above [Note: [Col. 0899D] **Covering.** In Pamelius, apparently through an error, “touching.”], that is, heaven covers all things. At God’s command, heaven had been solidified into the firmament from the fluid substance of the waters (Gen. I, 6), like strong ice dividing in half the waters that had formerly covered the earth, so that, as though upon a back, it might sustain the weight of the upper water with strength hardened by frost.

For wheels also lie beneath it (Ezek. X, 12), signifying the times through which all the members of the world are continually [Col. 0899D] revolved, with feet of such a kind attached to them that these things do not remain forever but pass away (Ezek. I, 18). But throughout all their [Note: [Col. 0899D] **Limbs.** In my judgment Welchman correctly emended the earlier editions, which have “risings.” For the restored word refers to the living creatures that immediately [Col. 0900D] precede.] limbs they are studded with eyes, for [Col. 0900A] the works of God must be contemplated with a sleepless gaze. In their midst, among the coals, is fire: either because this world hastens toward the fiery day of judgment (II Pet. III); or because all God’s works are fiery and are not dark but [Note: [Col. 0900D] **Are vigorous.** Latinius has “shine.” Welchman thinks “are vigorous with light” should be read. But in Jackson’s judgment the printed reading “are vigorous” is better. The author perhaps intended to suggest that God’s works possess an inward fiery vigor or spirit.] vigorous; or also because, lest these things, having arisen from earthly principles, should naturally grow numb from the coldness of their origin, there was added to them all the warm nature of an inward spirit, which, joined to cold bodies, would display equal balances [Note: [Col. 0900D] **Would display.** Welchman would prefer “would provide,” which Jackson strongly approves.] for the enjoyment of life among them all.

This, then, is the chariot of God according to David: “For the chariot of God,” he says, “is multiplied ten thousand times” (Ps. LXVII, 18), that is, [Note: [Col. 0900D] **Innumerable . . . immeasurable.** Gagnaeus, less correctly, as it seems, has “a number infinite and immeasurable.”] innumerable, infinite, immeasurable. For under the yoke of the natural law given to all, some things are held back and restrained as though by bridles, while others are roused and driven onward as though with loosened reins. [Col. 0900B] For the angels themselves, together with all things and with the stars, draw this world, the chariot of God. Although we observe their various courses, we nevertheless see them bound by fixed laws and proceeding toward the limits of the time appointed for them. Thus, as we too marvel with the Apostle at both the craftsman and his works, we may rightly exclaim: “O depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and untraceable his ways!” and the rest (Rom. XI, 33).

## CHAPTER IX

### That the same rule of truth teaches us to believe, after the Father, also in the Son of God, Jesus Christ our Lord and God—the same who was promised in the Old Testament and manifested in the New

The same rule of truth teaches us to believe, after [Col. 0900C] the Father, also in the Son of God, Christ Jesus our Lord and God—but as the Son of God, the Son of this God who is the one and only God, namely, the Creator of all things, as has already been set forth above. For we read that this Jesus Christ—I say again, the Son of this God—was promised in the Old Testament, and we perceive that he was manifested in the New Testament, fulfilling by the presence of embodied truth the shadows and figures of all the mysteries.

For both the ancient predictions and the Gospels testify that he is the son of Abraham, the son of David. Genesis itself testifies to him when it says: “To you I will give it, and to your seed” (Gen. XVII, 8); to him when it shows a man wrestling with Jacob (Gen. XXXII, 24); to him when it says (Gen.
