XLIX, 10): “A ruler will not fail from Judah, nor a leader from his thighs, [Col. 0900D] until he comes to whom it was promised, and he will be the expectation of the nations” (Gen. XLIX, 19).

Moses testifies to him when he says, “Provide another whom you may send” (Exod. IV, 13); the same Moses [Col. 0901A] when he bears witness by saying, “God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers: listen to him as to me” (Deut. XVIII, 15); to him when he says, “You will see your life hanging before you night and day, and you will not believe him” (Deut. XXVIII, 66).

Isaiah testifies to him: “A rod will come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower will rise from his root” (Isa. XI, 1); to the same one when he says, “Behold, a virgin will conceive and bear a son” (Isa. VII, 13); to him when he establishes that healings will be performed by him, saying: “Then the eyes of the blind will be opened, and the ears of the deaf will hear; then the lame man will leap like a deer, and the tongue of the mute will become articulate” (ibid. XXXV, 3, 6); to him when he declares the virtues of his patient endurance, saying: “His voice will not be heard in the streets; he will not break a bruised reed, and he will not extinguish smoking flax” (ibid. XLII, 2–3); to him when he described his Gospels: “And I will establish for you an [Col. 0901B] eternal covenant, the faithful holy things of David” (Isa. LV, 3); to him when he prophesies that the nations will believe in him: “Behold, I have appointed him a leader and commander for the nations. Nations that did not know you will call upon you, and peoples who do not know you will flee to you” (ibid. 4–5).

He testifies to this same one when, concerning his Passion, he cries out: “Like a sheep he was led to slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer, without a voice, so in his humiliation he did not open his mouth” (Isa. LIII, 1); to him when he described the blows of his scourging and his wounds: “By his bruise we have been healed” (ibid. 5); or his humiliation: “And we saw him, and he had neither appearance nor honor. A man under affliction and knowing how to bear weakness” (ibid. 2–3); or that the people would not believe: “All day long I stretched out my hands to an unbelieving people” (Isa. LXV, 2); or that he would rise from the dead: “And on that day there will be the root [Col. 0901C] of Jesse, and he who rises to rule the nations; in him the nations will hope, and his rest will be honor” (Isa. XI, 10); or the time of the resurrection: “As at dawn we shall find him ready” (Hos. VI, 3); or that he would sit at the Father’s right hand: “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet” (Ps. CIX, 1–2); or when he is presented as the possessor of all things: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance and the ends of the earth as your possession” (Ps. II, 8); or when he is shown to be judge of all: “O God, give your judgment to the king, and your righteousness to the king’s son” (Ps. LXXI, 1).

I shall not pursue further here the things announced concerning Christ, [Note: [Col. 0901D] **To all heretics, but also to those themselves who hold the truth.** Welchman seems to have conjectured correctly when he thinks that one should read, “to the heretics themselves, but also to all who hold the truth.” Yet perhaps more correctly: “to all who hold the truth, but also to the heretics themselves.” Transpositions of this kind are not unusual among copyists.] which are better known to all heretics, but also to those who themselves hold the truth.

## CHAPTER X

### That Jesus Christ is the Son of God and truly a human being: against the docetic heretics who denied that he assumed real flesh

[Col. 0901D]

[Col. 0902A] But I give this warning: no other Christ was to have been expected in the Gospel than the one previously promised by the Creator in the writings of the Old Testament—especially since both the things predicted concerning him have been fulfilled and the things fulfilled were predicted beforehand.

Thus I can rightly and steadfastly say to the fictitious Christ of these heretics, who reject the authority of the Old Testament—a Christ contrived from I know not what old wives’ tales, counterfeited and painted in false colors: Who are you? Where are you from? By whom were you sent? Why did you wish to come now? Why are you such as you are? Or by what means could you come? Or why did you not go to your own people—unless it is because you proved that you [Note: [Col. 0901D] **Do not have your own.** Perhaps, with Welchman, one should read, “that you do not have your own.”] have none of your own, since you come to those who belong to another?

What have you to do with the Creator’s world? What have you to do with the Founder’s human being? What have you to do with the fashioned body, from which you wrest away the hope of resurrection? Why do you come to another’s [Col. 0902B] servant? Why do you desire to entice another’s son? Why do you try to snatch me away from my Lord? Why do you compel me to blaspheme the Father and become impious? Or what shall I obtain from you in the resurrection, when I do not receive myself back because I lose my body?

If you wish to save, you should have made the human being to whom you would give salvation. If you desire to rescue me from transgression, you should first have granted me the means not to abandon you. What support from the Law do you bring with you? What testimony of a prophetic voice do you possess? Or what certain promise concerning you can I make to myself when I see that you came as a phantom and not in solidity?

What, then, have you to do with the form of a body if you hate the body? Indeed, you are convicted of bearing the substance of the very body you hate, since you wished to assume even its form. For you ought to have hated the imitation of the body if you hated its [Col. 0902C] reality. Since you are another, [Note: [Col. 0901D] **You ought to have come otherwise.** Correctly “otherwise,” not “another,” as Welchman conjectures. Tertullian explains the sense in *Against Marcion*, book III, chapter 10: “For why did he not come in some other, worthier substance—and especially in his own—lest he should appear to have needed both an unworthy substance and one belonging to another?” JACKSON.] you ought to have come otherwise, lest you be called the Creator’s son if you possessed even the likeness of flesh and body.

Certainly, if you hated birth because you hated the Creator’s union of marriage, you ought also to have refused the imitation of a human being, who is born through the Creator’s institution of marriage. We therefore do not acknowledge as Christ the Christ of the heretics, who existed, as they say, in appearance and not in reality; [Note: [Col. 0902D] **For nothing was real.** I restored the conjunction “for” from Wower’s manuscript. ID.] for he would have done nothing real among the things he performed if he himself was a phantom and not reality.

Nor do we acknowledge the one who bore nothing in himself of our body, since he received nothing from Mary, [Note: [Col. 0902D] **Lest he did not come for us.** For “lest not,” Latinius reads “nor”; Jackson, however, would prefer “for neither.”] lest he should not have come for us, since he appeared visibly not in our substance. Nor do we acknowledge the one who, as other heretics maintained, chose ethereal or astral flesh, lest we understand there to be any salvation for us [Note: [Col. 0902D] **Our.** Thus the printed editions. Welchman substituted the feminine form “our”; Jackson proposed the dative “for our,” that is, referring to the flesh of which the author is speaking, but this is less satisfactory.] in him if we do not recognize in him the solidity of our [Col. 0902D] body as well. Nor do we acknowledge any other whatsoever who bore some different body fashioned out of heretical [Note: [Col. 0902D] **Of the heretics . . . a body of tales.** Others, as Francis Junius notes, read “heretical,” referring it to “tales.” But this is wrong. The same Junius rather suspects that “a fabulous body” should be restored, for it is called *σῶμα μυθῶδες* (“a mythical body”); both *fabularis* and *fabularius* are used, just as *ollaris* and *ollarius*. Hence the word “of the heretics” should not be disturbed, and I approve it. JACKSON. Welchman, however, conjectured that “fable-bearing” should be restored.] tales.

For both the Lord’s birth and his very death refute all these. “And the Word,” says John, “became flesh and dwelt in us” (John I, [Col. 0903A] 14). Thus our body was rightly present in him, since the Word assumed our flesh. And blood therefore flowed down from his hands and feet and from his very side, so that he might be proved a participant in our body, since he died under the laws of our mortality. When he was raised in the same bodily substance in which he died and was authenticated by the wounds of that very body, he also demonstrated in his own flesh the laws of our resurrection, [Note: [Col. 0903D] **Who.** Welchman has “because,” not badly. JACKSON.] since in his resurrection he restored the body that he had received from us.

For the law of resurrection is established when Christ is raised in bodily substance as an example for all others. For when it is written that “flesh and blood cannot obtain the kingdom of God” (I Cor. XV, 50), it is not the substance of the flesh that has been condemned—the flesh [Col. 0903B] constructed by divine hands so that it should not perish—but only the fault of the flesh that is deservedly reproved, because through a human being’s voluntary rashness it made an assault against the rights of the divine law. For in Baptism and in the dissolution of death, the flesh, having been raised up, returns to salvation, since, after the mortality of guilt has been laid aside, it is recalled to the state of innocence.

## CHAPTER XI

### And that Christ is not merely a human being, but also God: just as he is the Son of Man, so also the Son of God

But lest, from our assertion here that our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God the Creator, was manifested in the substance of a real body, we should seem to have surrendered to other heretics who defend the position that he was merely and solely a human being, and who therefore desire to prove him a bare and solitary man—or lest we should seem to have furnished them with material for [Note: [Col. 0903D] **Speaking.** Welchman suspects that “speaking against” should be read; but here, I think, “speaking” has the same force as “disputing.” ID.] argument—we do not describe the substance of [Col. 0903C] his body in such a way as to say that he was [Note: [Col. 0903D] **Solely merely.** Perhaps “solely and merely,” as a little [Col. 0904D] above. JACKSON.] solely and merely a human being. Rather, because the divinity of the Word was mingled into that very concrete union, we maintain according to the Scriptures that he is also God.

For it is a grave danger to say that the Savior of the human race—the Lord and ruler of the whole world, to whom all things were delivered and everything granted by his Father (Matt. XX, 21), through whom all things were established, the totality created, and everything ordered; the King of all ages and times, the ruler of all angels, before whom there is nothing except the Father—is merely a human being, and to deny him divine authority in these matters. For this insult of the heretics will rebound upon God the Father himself if God the Father was unable to beget a Son who is God.

But no blindness of the heretics will prescribe against the truth. Nor, because [Col. 0903D] they hold to something in Christ and do not hold to something else, because they see one thing and do not see another, will what they do not see be taken away from us [Col. 0904A] through what they do see. For they consider in him weaknesses as of a human being, but do not take into account powers as of God; they recall the infirmities of the flesh but exclude the powers of divinity.

Yet if this proof from Christ’s infirmities serves to demonstrate from those infirmities that he is human, then the proof of divinity gathered from his mighty works will serve to establish from his works that he is also God. For if his sufferings display human frailty in him, why should his works not establish divine power in him? Otherwise, if his mighty works do not serve to establish that he is God, neither will his sufferings serve to demonstrate from them that he is also human. For whatever rule is laid down in either case will be found to have been [Note: [Col. 0904D] **Accepted.** Welchman thus corrected the printed reading “suspected,” and Jackson follows him.] accepted. For there will be danger that he cannot be shown to be human from his sufferings if he cannot [Col. 0904B] also be proved to be God from his mighty works.

We must not, therefore, incline to one side and flee from the other, since anyone who excludes one portion of the truth will not possess the perfect truth. For Scripture announces Christ as God just as much as it announces God himself as a human being; it has described Jesus Christ as a human being just as it has also described Christ the Lord as God. For it not only sets him forth as the Son of God, but also as the Son of Man; nor does it call him only the Son of Man, but is also accustomed to report him as the Son of God. Thus, because he is from both, he is both, lest, if he were only one, he could not be the other.

For just as nature itself has prescribed that one who is from a human being must be believed to be human, so the same nature prescribes that one who is from God must also be believed to be God. Otherwise, if he was not also God although he is from God, he would no longer be human [Col. 0904C] either, although he was from a human being. [Note: [Col. 0904D] **And thus in either case.** Welchman printed this with Gagnaeus and Barrensis. Others omit “thus.”] And thus in either case both would be endangered, since one would be proved to have lost credibility through the other.

Therefore, those who read of [Note: [Col. 0904D] **The Son of Man, a human being.** Welchman proposes that one should read, “a human being and the Son of Man,” which I approve; and the analogy of what follows—“God and the Son of God”—appears to confirm it. JACKSON.] the Son of Man, the man Christ Jesus (Matt. I, 1), should read that this same one is also called both God and the Son of God. For [Note: [Col. 0904D] **In what manner.** I would prefer that the two Latin words be read separately; and likewise in the following instances. ID.] just as, insofar as he is human, he is descended from Abraham, so also, insofar as he is God, he exists before Abraham himself (John VIII, 58). And just as, insofar as he is human, he is the son of David (Matt. XXII, 42–44), so, insofar as he is God, he is called David’s Lord. And just as, insofar as he is human, he was made under the Law (Gal. IV, 4), so, insofar as he is God, he was declared Lord of the Sabbath (Luke VI, 5). And just as, insofar as he is human, he undergoes sentence (Matt. XXVII, 26), so, insofar as he is God, he is found to possess all judgment over the living and the dead (John V, 21–22).

And just as, insofar as he is human, he is born after the world, so, insofar as he is God, he is declared to have existed before [Col. 0904D] the world (John XVII, 5). And just as, insofar as he is human, he was begotten from the seed of David (Rom. I, 3), [Col. 0905A] so likewise, [Note: [Col. 0905D] **So likewise.** This is Welchman’s reading in place of the printed “so thus.” Jackson, however, following Francis Junius, printed “so also,” because Novatian speaks in the same manner a little above.] insofar as he is God, the world is said to have been established through him (John I, 10). And just as, insofar as he is human, he comes after many others (ibid. 15), so, insofar as he is God, he comes before all. And just as, insofar as he is human, he is inferior to the others (Isa. LV, 3), so, insofar as he is God, he is greater than all (Acts X, 36). And just as, insofar as he is human, he ascended into heaven (John VI, 62), so, insofar as he is God, he first descended from there. And just as, insofar as he is human, he goes to the Father (John XIV, 28), so, obedient to the Father insofar as he is the Son, he will descend again from there (Acts I, 11).

Thus, if the lowly conditions in him establish human frailty, the majestic powers in him affirm divine power. For there is danger, when you read both, in believing not both but only one. Consequently, since both are read of Christ, both should be believed, so that faith may be true only when it is also complete. For if, of the two, one is omitted from faith, and [Col. 0905B] only one—and indeed the lesser—is assumed for belief, then, the rule of truth having been disturbed, this rashness will not confer salvation but, instead of salvation, will produce from the loss of faith a grave danger of death.

## CHAPTER XII

### That he is God is proved by the authority of the Scriptures of the Old Testament

Why, then, should we hesitate to say what Scripture does not hesitate to express? Why should the truth of faith waver concerning that upon which the authority of Scripture has never wavered?

For behold, the prophet Hosea says in the person of the Father: “I will no longer save them by bow, nor by horses, nor by horsemen; but I will save them in the Lord their [Col. 0905C] God” (Hos. I, 7). If God says that he will save in God, while God saves only in Christ, why, then, should a human being hesitate to call Christ God, when through the Scriptures he perceives that Christ has been designated God by the Father?

Indeed, if God the Father saves only in God, no one will be able to be saved by God the Father unless he has confessed that Christ is God, [Note: [Col. 0905D] **In whom he.** Thus the printed editions. But Jackson deleted “he,” as serving no purpose.] in whom and through whom the Father promises that he will give salvation. Thus anyone who acknowledges him to be God may rightly find salvation in Christ who is God; but anyone who does not recognize him to be God will lose the salvation [Note: [Col. 0905D] **Which.** Thus Pamelius and others. Both Froben editions, with Welchman, have “since,” which does not displease Jackson.] which he will not be able to find anywhere except in Christ who is God.

For just as Isaiah says, “Behold, a virgin will conceive and bear a son, and you will call his name Emmanuel” (Isa. VII, 14), which is interpreted “God with us,” so Christ himself says: “Behold, I am with you even to the consummation of the age” (Matt. XXVIII, 20). God, therefore, is with us; indeed, much more, he is even in us. Christ is [Col. 0905D] with us; therefore he whose name is “God with us” is with us, because he is indeed with us.

Or is he perhaps not [Col. 0906A] with us? How, then, does he say that he is with us? Therefore he is with us. But because he is with us, he has been called Emmanuel, that is, “God with us.” [Note: [Col. 0905D] **God therefore.** Thus the printed editions consistently. Welchman was the first to think that “Christ” should be read here, and Jackson finds such a conjecture attractive. I nevertheless think it should not be admitted, for once the punctuation after “therefore” is removed, the force of the argument becomes clear.] Therefore, because God is with us, he has been called “God with us.”

The same prophet says:

> Be strengthened, hands that hang down and feeble knees; take comfort, you who are fainthearted in understanding; be strengthened, do not fear. Behold, our God will repay judgment; he himself will come and save us. Then the eyes of the blind will be opened, and the ears of the deaf will hear; then the lame man will leap like a deer, and the tongue of the mute will become articulate.  
> (Isa. XXXV, 3–6)

If the prophet says that, at the coming of God, these signs would occur—and they did occur—then either they must acknowledge Christ as the Son of God, at whose coming and by whom these signs of healing were performed; or, overcome by the truth of Christ’s divinity and falling into another heresy, while refusing to confess him as the Son of God and as God, they must confess [Col. 0906B] that he is the Father. [Note: [Col. 0906D] **They must confess.** Thus both English editors, in place of the printed “they will confess.” The preceding “they must acknowledge” supports the correctness of this restoration.]

For, hemmed in by the words of the prophets, they can no longer deny that Christ is God. What, then, do they answer when these signs—which were performed at the coming of Christ—are said to be destined to occur at the coming of God? In what capacity do they understand Christ to be God? For they can no longer deny that he is God. As the Father, or as the Son? If as the Son, why do they deny that the Son of God is God? If as the Father, why do they not follow those who are seen to maintain blasphemies of this kind?

Unless, perhaps, in this contest with them [Note: [Col. 0906D] **Concerning the truth.** Gagnaeus and Barrensis have “of truth,” whom Welchman followed inappropriately.] concerning the truth, it is enough for us in the meantime that, however they are convicted, they confess Christ also [Note: [Col. 0906D] **And God.** Thus all the editions. Welchman alone changed “and” to “to be,” without any manuscript authority, and did not alert his reader to this alteration.] as God—the very one whom they wished to deny was God.

Through the prophet Habakkuk he says: “God will come from the South, and the Holy One from the shaded and densely wooded mountain” (Hab. III, 3). Whom do these people wish to understand as coming from the South (*Africus*)? If they say that [Col. 0906C] God the almighty Father came, then God the Father came from a place by which he is also [Note: [Col. 0906D] **Enclosed.** The verb *cludo* was frequently used by African writers, especially Tertullian and Cyprian; Novatian also uses it more than once, above in chapter 6, here, and below in chapter 17, etc.] enclosed, and he is contained within the narrow bounds of some location. Thus, through these people, as we have said, the sacrilegious Sabellian heresy is embodied: Christ is believed to be not the Son but the Father; and, in a novel fashion, while they rigidly assert that he is a bare human being, Christ is again proved by them to be God the almighty Father.

But if Christ was born in Bethlehem, whose allotted territory looks toward the southern region of the sky, and if he is also called God by the Scriptures, then this God is rightly described as coming from the South, because it was foreseen that he would come from Bethlehem. Let them therefore choose which of two alternatives they wish: is the one who came from the South the Son or the Father? For it is said that God would come from the South.

If he is the Son, why do they hesitate to call Christ God [Col. 0906D] as well? For Scripture says that God would come. If he is the Father, why do they hesitate to associate themselves with the rashness of Sabellius, [Col. 0907A] who says that Christ is the Father? Unless it is because, whether they call him Father or Son, they must necessarily depart from their heresy, even against their will—those who are accustomed to call Christ merely a human being—when, compelled by the facts themselves, they begin to declare him God, whether they choose to call him the Father or the Son.

## CHAPTER XIII

### That the same truth is established from the sacred writings of the New Covenant

[Note: [Col. 0907D] **And thus.** Pamelius has “as if.”] And thus John, when describing the birth of Christ, says: “The Word became flesh and dwelt in us, and we saw his glory, glory [Col. 0907B] as of the Only-Begotten from the Father, [Note: [Col. 0907D] **Full.** Thus Welchman after Gagnaeus. This is the Vulgate reading. Others have the masculine form.] full of grace and truth” (John I, 14).

For his name is also called the Word of God (Rev. XIX, 13), and rightly so. “My heart,” he says, “has uttered a good word” (Ps. XLIV, 2), which he then designates by the name “King” when he adds, “I speak my works to the King.” For through him all works were made, and without him nothing was made (John I, 3). “For whether,” says the Apostle, “thrones, or dominions, or powers, or authorities, visible and invisible, all things subsist through him” (Col. I, 16).

Now this Word is the one who came to his own, and his own did not receive him. For the world was made through him, and the world did not know him (John I, 10–11). This Word, moreover, was in the beginning with God, and the Word was God (John I, 1).

Who, then, would hesitate, when at the [Col. 0907C] end it is said, “The Word became flesh and dwelt in us,” to declare without hesitation that Christ, whose birth is being described, is human because he became flesh, and God because he is the Word of God—especially when he perceives that the evangelical Scripture has joined those two substances into one concord in the birth of Christ? [Note: [Col. 0907D] **Because flesh . . . because the Word.** Latinius reads “insofar as” in both places.]

For he is the one who “comes forth like a bridegroom from his chamber; he rejoiced like a giant to run his course; his going forth is from the highest heaven and his return even to its summit” (Ps. XVIII, 6–7). For his return is to the summit, and “no one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John III, 13). Repeating this same point, he says: “Father, glorify me with the honor that I had with you before the world existed” (John XVII, 5).

And if this Word descended from heaven as a [Col. 0907D] bridegroom to the flesh, so that through the assumption of flesh the Son of Man might ascend to the place from which the Son of God, the Word, had descended, then rightly—since through their mutual union the flesh bears the Word of God and the Son of God assumes the frailty of the flesh—ascending with the flesh as his bride to the place from which he had descended without flesh, he now receives that [Col. 0908A] glory which, because he is shown to have possessed it before the establishment of the world, most plainly proves him to be God.

And no less, since the world itself is said to have been established after him, it is found to have been created through him. By this very fact both the glory and the authority of divinity in him, through whom the world was made, are [Note: [Col. 0907D] **May be proved.** Welchman suspects that the indicative “are proved” should be read.] proved.

If, when it belongs to none but God to know the secrets of the heart (III Kings VIII, 39; Matt. IX, 4; Rev. II, 23), Christ perceives the secrets of the heart; if, when it belongs to none but God to forgive sins (Isa. XLIII, 25), the same Christ forgives sins (Mark II, 5); if, when it belongs to no human being to come from heaven, he descended by coming from heaven; if, when no human being could utter the words “I and the Father are one” (John X, 30), Christ alone [Col. 0908B] utters these words from the consciousness of his divinity; if, finally, the apostle Thomas, instructed by all the proofs and deeds of Christ’s divinity, answers Christ, “My Lord and my God” (John XX, 28); if the apostle Paul also writes in his letters, “Whose,” [Note: [Col. 0908D] **He says.** I think this phrase is superfluous and was perhaps inserted through the efforts of a copyist or dictator who did not attend to the verb “writes” that follows. JACKSON.] “are the fathers, and from whom is Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed forever” (Rom. IX, 5); if the same Paul declares that he was appointed an apostle “not by human beings or through a human being, but through Jesus Christ” (Gal. I, 1, 12); if the same Paul maintains that he did not learn the Gospel from human beings or through a human being, but received it through Jesus Christ—then Christ is rightly God.

Accordingly, one of two alternatives must be established here. For since it is manifest [Col. 0908C] that all things were made through Christ, either he exists before all things, because all things were made through him—and consequently he is God—or, because he is human, he exists after all things, and consequently nothing was made through him.

But we cannot say that nothing was made through him, since we perceive that it is written that all things were made through him. He therefore does not exist after all things; that is, he is not merely a human being, who comes after all things, but is also God, since [Note: [Col. 0908D] **God.** Jackson alone, and without justification, thought that this word, which appears in all the printed editions, should be deleted.] God exists before all things.

He exists before all things because all things were made through him: otherwise, if he is merely human, nothing was made through him; or, if all things were made through him, he is not merely human. For if he is merely human, not all things were made through him—indeed, nothing was made through him.

What, then, do they answer? Was nothing made through him, so that he may be merely human? How, then, were all things made through him? Therefore, he is not merely a human being but also God, since all things exist through him. Thus we must rightly understand [Col. 0908D] [Note: [Col. 0908D] **Nor.** “Not” is a more suitable word and, unless I am mistaken, the true reading. JACKSON.] that Christ, who comes after all things, is not merely a human being, but also God, since all things were made through him. For how could you call him merely a human being when you also behold him in the flesh, unless it is because, when both are perceived, both should rightly be believed?

## CHAPTER XIV

### The author continues the same argument

[Col. 0909A]

And yet the heretic still hesitates to say that Christ is God, though he perceives him to be approved as God by so many deeds and utterances.[^c0097-1] If Christ is only a man, how, when he came into this world, did he come to his own, since no man made the world? If Christ is only a man, how is the world said to have been made through him, since the world is not said to have been made through a man, but man to have been fashioned after the world? If Christ is only a man, how is Christ not merely from the seed of David, but “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us”? For although the first-formed man was not from seed, nevertheless the first-formed man was not formed from a union of the Word and flesh; for the Word did not become flesh [Col. 0909B] and dwell among us. If Christ is only a man, how does he who came from heaven testify to what he saw and [^c0097-2] heard (John 3:31–32), when it is certain that a man cannot come from heaven, because he cannot be born there? If Christ is only a man, how are visible and invisible things—Thrones, Powers, and Dominions—said to have been created through him and in him (Col. 1:16), when heavenly Powers could not have been made through a man, since they must have existed before man himself? If Christ is only a man, how is he present wherever he is invoked (Matt. 18:20), when this belongs not to human nature but to God’s, since only God can be present in every place? If Christ is only a man, why is a man invoked in prayers as Mediator, [Col. 0909C] when invocation of a man is judged ineffectual for the granting of salvation? If Christ is only a man, why is hope placed in him (1 Tim. 1:1), when hope in man is said to be accursed (Jer. 17:5)? If Christ is only a man, why is it not permissible to deny Christ without the destruction of the soul (Matt. 10:33),[^c0097-3] when an offense committed against a man [Col. 0910A] is said to be capable of forgiveness? If Christ is only a man, how does John the Baptist testify and say, “He who comes after me was made before me, because he was prior to me” (John 1:15), when, if Christ is only a man, born after John, he cannot have existed before John—unless it is because, insofar as he is God, he preceded him beforehand? If Christ is only a man, how does the Son likewise do what the Father does (John 5:19), when a man cannot perform works like the heavenly works of God? If Christ is only a man, how, “just as the Father has life in himself, so he gave the Son also to have life in himself” (John 5:26), when a man cannot, after the example of God the Father, have life in himself, since he is not glorious in eternity but was made within the substance of mortality? If Christ [Col. 0910B] is only a man, how does he declare, “I am the bread of eternal life who came down from heaven” (John 6:51), when a mortal man cannot himself be the bread of life, nor could he have come down from heaven, since no substance of frailty was established in heaven? If Christ is only a man, how does he say that “no one has ever seen God the Father except the one who is from God; he has seen God” (ibid., v. 46)? For if Christ is only a man, he could not see God, because no human being has seen God; but if, because he is from God, he has seen God, then by saying that he has seen God he wished himself to be understood as more than a man. If Christ is only a man, why does he say, “What if you see the Son of Man ascending to where he was before?” (ibid., v. 62). Now he ascended into heaven; therefore he was there, since he returns to the place where he was before.[^c0097-4] And if [Col. 0910C] he was sent from heaven by the Father, he is certainly not merely a man; for a man, as we have said, could not come from heaven. Therefore he was not previously there as man, but ascended to the place where he had not been. What descended, however, was the Word of God, which had been there: the Word of God, I say, and God, through whom all things were made and without whom nothing was made [Col. 0911A] (John 1:3). Therefore it was not man who came down from heaven in this way,[^c0097-5] but the Word of God—that is, God—who descended from there.

## CHAPTER XV, otherwise XXIII. He Again Proves from the Gospel That Christ Is God

If Christ is only a man, how does he say, “Even if I bear witness concerning myself, my testimony is true, because I know where I came from and where I am going;[^c0097-6] you do not know where I came from or where I am going. You judge according to the flesh” (John 8:14–15)? See, here too he says that he will return to the place from which he testifies that he previously came—namely, sent from heaven. He therefore descended from the place whence he came, just as he goes to the place whence he descended. Consequently, if Christ were only a man, he would not have come from there; [Col. 0911B] and for that reason neither would he go there, since he had not come from there. But by coming from a place from which man cannot come, he shows that he came as God.

Indeed, the Jews, ignorant and unskilled regarding this very descent, have made these heretics their heirs; to them it is said: “You do not know where I come from and where I am going; you judge according to the flesh” (ibid.). Both these people and the Jews, maintaining that Christ’s birth [^c0097-7] was only carnal, believed Christ to be nothing other than a man. They failed to consider that, since a man could not have come from heaven so as rightly to be able to return there, the one who descended from the place whence man could not come is God.

If Christ is only a man, how does he say: “You are from below; I am from above. You [Col. 0911C] are from this world; I am not from this world” (John 8:23)? If, then, every man is from this world, and Christ is therefore in this world, is he only a man? By no means. Consider rather what he says: “I am not from this world.” Does he therefore lie, since he is from this world, if he is only a man? Or, if he does not lie, he is not from this world. Therefore he is not only a man, because he is not from this world. But lest his identity remain hidden, he stated where he was from: “I,” he says, “am from above”—that is, from heaven, whence man cannot come, for man was not made in heaven. Therefore he who is from above is God, and for that reason is not from this world; although in another respect he is also from [Col. 0911D] this world. Hence Christ is not only God, [Col. 0912A] but also man. Accordingly, just as he is not from this world with respect to the divinity of the Word, so he is from this world with respect to the frailty of the body he assumed. For man is joined to God, and God united with man.

But here Christ leaned wholly toward the one side, that of his divinity alone, because Jewish blindness saw in Christ only the aspect of his flesh. Hence in the present passage, passing over in silence the frailty of the body, which is from the world, he spoke only of his divinity, which is not from the world. The more they had inclined toward believing him to be only a man, the more Christ could draw them toward considering his divinity, so that they might believe him to be God. He wished to overcome their unbelief concerning his divinity by confronting them with his divinity alone, omitting for the moment any mention [Col. 0912B] of the human condition.

If Christ is only a man, how does he say, “I proceeded from God and came” (John 8:42; 16:28), when it is certain that man was made by God, not that he proceeded from God? Just as man did not proceed from God, so the Word of God did proceed from God; of him it was said: “My heart has uttered a good Word” (Ps. 44:2). Because it is from God, it is rightly also with God. And because it was not uttered to no purpose,[^c0097-8] it rightly makes all things. For “all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:3). But this Word through whom all things were made is God.[^c0097-9] “And the Word,” he says, “was God.” God, therefore, proceeded from God, since the Word who proceeded is God—the one who proceeded from God.

If Christ is only a man, how [Col. 0912C] does he say, “If anyone keeps my word, he will not see death forever” (John 8:51)? What else is not seeing death forever but immortality? Immortality, however, is associated with divinity, because the Divinity is immortal and immortality is the fruit of divinity. Yet every man is mortal, and immortality cannot come from what is mortal. Therefore immortality cannot arise from Christ if he is a mortal man. But he says, “Whoever keeps my word will not see death forever.” Therefore Christ’s word grants immortality, and through immortality it grants divinity.[^c0097-10] But if he who is himself mortal cannot furnish this so as to make another immortal, while Christ’s word [Col. 0912D] both furnishes and grants immortality, then [Col. 0913A] he who grants immortality is certainly not only a man; for if he were only a man, he could not grant it. By granting divinity through immortality, moreover, he proves himself to be God, since he bestows a divinity that he could not bestow unless he were God.

If Christ is only a man, how does he say, “Before Abraham, I am” (John 8:58)? For no human being can exist before the one from whom he himself derives; nor can it happen that anyone[^c0097-11] existed earlier than the one from whom he himself took his origin. But although Christ is descended from Abraham, he says that he existed before Abraham. Either, then, he lies and deceives, if he did not exist before Abraham though he was descended from Abraham; or he does not deceive, if he is also God, since he existed before Abraham. Had he not been God, then, since he was descended from Abraham, [Col. 0913B] he could not have existed before Abraham.

If Christ is only a man, how does he say: “And I know them, and my own follow me; and I give them eternal life, and they will never perish forever” (John 10:27–28)?[^c0097-12] Since every man is bound by the laws of mortality and for that reason cannot preserve even himself forever, much less will he be able to preserve another forever. Yet Christ promises that he will give salvation forever. If he does not give it, he is a liar; if he gives it, he is God. But he does not deceive, for he gives what he promises. Therefore the one who grants perpetual salvation is God; a man who cannot preserve himself cannot grant it to another.

If Christ is only a man, what does his statement mean: “I and the Father are one” (ibid., v. 30)? For how are “I and the Father one” unless the Son also is God? [Col. 0913C] He can be called one with the Father precisely because he is from him, because he is his Son, because he is born from him,[^c0097-13] and because he is found to have proceeded from him—by which he is also God. When the Jews considered this offensive and believed it blasphemous, because by these words he had shown that Christ is God,[^c0097-14] and therefore ran for stones and desired to strike him with rocks, he forcefully refuted his adversaries by the example and testimony of the Scriptures:

> “If,” he says, “he called those gods to whom the words of God[^c0097-15] came—and Scripture cannot be broken—do you say of him whom the Father sanctified and sent into [Col. 0914A] this world, ‘You blaspheme,’ because I said, ‘I am the Son of God’?” (John 10:35–36).

By these words he did not deny that he was God; on the contrary, he affirmed that he was God. For if those to whom the words of God came are unquestionably called gods, much more is this one God, who is found to be better than them all. Nevertheless, he appropriately refuted their malicious charge of blasphemy according to the legitimate divine economy (*dispositio*, οἰκονομία).[^c0097-16] For he wished himself to be understood as God in such a way as to be the Son of God, and not to be understood as the Father himself.[^c0097-17] He said that he had been sent (ibid., v. 32) and showed that he had manifested many works from the Father. By this he wished it to be understood that he was not the Father but the Son. And in the final part of his defense he mentioned the Son, not the Father, saying: “You say, ‘You blaspheme,’ because I said, ‘I am the Son of God.’” Thus, with respect to the charge of blasphemy, [Col. 0914B] he says that he is the Son, not the Father; but with respect to his divinity,[^c0097-18] by saying, “I and the Father are one,” he proved himself to be both Son and God. He is God, therefore—but God in such a way that he is the Son, not the Father.

## CHAPTER XVI, otherwise XXIV. He Again Proves from the Gospel That Christ Is God

If Christ is only a man, how does he himself say, “And everyone who lives[^c0097-19] and believes in me will never die” (John 11:26)? For one who believes in a solitary and mere man is called accursed (Jer. 17:5); but here one who believes in Christ [Col. 0914C] is said not to be accursed, but never to die. Consequently, if he is only a man, as the heretics wish, how will whoever believes in him never die, since one who trusts in man is held to be accursed? Or, if he is not accursed but rather destined, as it is written, to attain eternal life, Christ is not only man[^c0097-20] but also God. Whoever believes in him both lays aside the peril of the curse and attains the fruit of righteousness.

If Christ is only a man, how does he say that the Paraclete will take from what is his the things he is to announce? (John 16:14). [Col. 0915A] For the Paraclete does not receive anything from a man; rather, the Paraclete gives knowledge to man. Nor does the Paraclete learn future things from man; rather, the Paraclete instructs man concerning the future. Therefore either the Paraclete did not receive from Christ as man what he was to announce—since man will be able to give nothing to the Paraclete, from whom man himself ought to receive—and Christ lies and deceives in the present passage when he says that the Paraclete will receive from him as man the things he is to announce; or else Christ does not deceive us, just as indeed he does not, and the Paraclete received from Christ what he was to announce.[^c0097-21]

But if he received from Christ what he was to announce, Christ is therefore greater than the Paraclete, since the Paraclete would not receive from Christ unless he were less than Christ. The Paraclete’s being less than Christ proves by that very fact that Christ, from whom he received what he announces, is also God. Thus it is a great testimony [Col. 0915B] to Christ’s divinity that the Paraclete, being found less than Christ, takes from him what he hands on to others. For if Christ were only a man, Christ would receive from the Paraclete what he was to say; the Paraclete would not receive from Christ what he was to announce.

If Christ is only a man, why did he establish for us this rule of belief, saying: “And this is eternal life, that they may know you, the one true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John 17:3)? If he had not wished himself also to be understood as God, why did he add, “And Jesus Christ whom you sent,” unless because he wished him to be understood also as God?[^c0097-22] For if he had not wished himself to be understood as God, he would have added, “And the man Jesus Christ whom you sent.” But as it is, he neither added this nor handed himself down to us as merely a man; rather, he joined him to God,[^c0097-23] so that through [Col. 0915C] this conjunction he wished him to be understood, as he is, also as God.

Therefore, according to the prescribed rule, one must believe in the Lord, the one true God, and consequently in him whom he sent, Jesus Christ, who, as we have said, would by no means have joined himself to the Father unless he wished to be understood as God also.[^c0097-24] For he would have separated himself from him[^c0097-25] if he had not wished himself to be understood as God. He would have placed himself merely among men if he knew himself to be merely a man; nor would he have joined himself to God if he did not know himself also to be God. As it is, he remains silent about the man, because [Col. 0916A] no one doubts him to be man;[^c0097-26] and he rightly joins himself to God, so as to establish for those who would believe the formula of his divinity.

If Christ is only a man, how does he say, “And now glorify me with the glory that I had with you before the world existed” (John 17:5)? If before the world existed he had glory with God and possessed splendor with the Father, then he existed before the world. For he would not have had glory unless he himself had first existed, so that he could possess glory. No one can have anything unless he himself first exists who possesses it. But Christ has[^c0097-27] glory before the establishment of the world; therefore he existed before the establishment of the world. For unless he existed before the establishment of the world, he could not have had glory before the world’s establishment, since he himself did not exist. But a man could not [Col. 0916B] have glory before the establishment of the world, since he came after the world; Christ, however, had it. Therefore he existed before the world. Therefore he who existed before the world was not only a man. He is therefore God, since he existed before the world and possessed glory before the world.

Nor should this be called predestination, because predestination was not stated. Let those who think this add it if they will—but woe is pronounced against those who add, just as against those who take away (Rev. 22:18–19). Therefore what cannot be added cannot be asserted. Once predestination, which was not stated, has been removed, Christ existed in substance before the establishment of the world. For he is the Word through whom all things were made and without whom nothing was made.

Even if he is said to have been glorious by predestination, and predestination is said to have existed before the establishment of the world, let the proper order be maintained: before Christ there will be a large [Col. 0916C] number of human beings destined for glory. For by this predestination Christ will be understood as less than the others,[^c0097-28] since he is marked out later than they. For if this glory existed in predestination, Christ received this predestination to glory last of all: Adam will be seen to have been predestined before him, and Abel, Enoch, Noah, Abraham, and all the rest. For since with God the order both of persons and of all things has been arranged, many will be said to have been predestined before this predestination of Christ to glory.[^c0097-29] And in this way [Col. 0917A] Christ is found[^c0097-30] to be less than the other human beings, though he is found to be better, greater, and more ancient even than the angels themselves. Either, therefore, all these things must be removed so that divinity may be taken away from Christ;[^c0097-31] or, if these things cannot be removed,[^c0097-32] Christ’s proper Divinity must be restored to him by the heretics.

## CHAPTER XVII, otherwise XXV. Likewise from Moses, at the Beginning of Holy Scripture

What if Moses follows this same rule of truth and handed this down to us at the beginning of his writings, so that we might learn that all things were created and founded through the Son of God—that is, through the Word of God? For he says the same thing as John and the others; indeed, John [Col. 0917B] and the others are understood to have received from him what they say. For John says, “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:3); the prophet declares, “I speak my works to the King” (Ps. 44:2); and Moses introduces God commanding first that light come to be, that heaven be established, that the waters be gathered, that dry land appear, that fruit be brought forth according to its seeds,[^c0097-33] that animals be produced, and that luminaries and stars be placed in heaven (Gen. 1). He shows that no one else was then present with God, to whom these works were commanded to be done, except him through whom all things were made and without whom nothing was made.

And if this one is the Word of God—for “my heart has uttered a good Word”—Moses shows that in the beginning the Word existed, that this Word was with the Father, that the Word was moreover God, [Col. 0917C] and[^c0097-34] that all things were made through him. But this Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14)—namely, Christ, the Son of God. Since we understand him both subsequently as man according to the flesh, and before the establishment of the world see him as the Word of God and God, we rightly, according to the institution of the Old and New Testaments, both believe and maintain that Christ Jesus is God and man.

What if the same Moses introduces God as saying, “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. 1:26–27), and below, “And God made man; in the image of God he made him; male and female he made them”? If, as we have already taught, the Son of God is he through whom all things were made, then surely the Son of God is he through whom man also was fashioned, for whose sake all things were made. But when God commands [Col. 0917D] that man be made, the one who makes man is said to be God. Yet it is the Son of God who makes man—the Word of God, through whom all things were made and without whom nothing was made. This Word, however, became flesh and dwelt [Col. 0918A] among us. Therefore Christ is God.

Thus man was made through Christ, as through the Son of God. But God made man in the image of God. Therefore the one who made man in the image of God is God; therefore Christ is God. Accordingly, the authority of the Old Testament concerning the person of Christ rightly does not waver, since it is supported by the manifestation of the New Testament; nor is the power of the New Testament impaired, since its truth rests upon the roots of the Old Testament. Consequently, those who rashly suppose that Christ, the Son of God and of man, is merely man and not also God act against both the Old and New Testaments, since they corrupt the authority and truth of both the Old and New Testaments.

What if the same Moses everywhere presents God the Father as immeasurable and without end—not one who is enclosed by place, but one who encloses every place; not one who is in a place, but rather one in whom every place exists; [Col. 0918B] containing all things and encompassing everything—so that he rightly neither descends nor ascends, because he himself both contains and fills all things? And yet Moses nevertheless introduces God as descending to inspect[^c0097-35] the tower that the sons of men were building, seeking to examine it, and saying, “Come,” and immediately afterward, “Let us descend and confuse their languages there, so that each may not hear the voice of his neighbor” (Gen. 11:7).

Whom do they wish to have been the God who descended to that tower and sought to visit those men at that time? God the Father? Then he is already enclosed by place; and how does he himself encompass all things? Or does Moses perhaps say that an angel descended with angels and said, “Come,” and immediately afterward, “Let us descend and confuse their languages there”? [Col. 0918C] But in Deuteronomy we observe that he related these things as done by God and said that God spoke, where it is written: “When he scattered the sons of Adam, he established the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the angels of God” (Deut. 32:8). Therefore neither did the Father descend, as the matter indicates, nor does an angel command these things, as the matter proves.

It remains, therefore, that the one who descended was he of whom the apostle Paul says: “He who descended is the same who ascended above all the heavens, that he might fill all things” (Eph. 4:10)—that is, the Son of God, the Word of God. But the Word of God became flesh and dwelt among us. This will be[^c0097-36] Christ. Therefore Christ will be declared God.

## CHAPTER XVIII, otherwise XXVI. From the Fact That God Is Said to Have Appeared to Abraham—which Cannot Be Understood of the Father, Whom No One Has Ever Seen, but of the Son in the Form of an Angel

[Col. 0918D]

See, the same Moses relates elsewhere that God [Col. 0919A] appeared to Abraham (Gen. 12:7). Yet the same Moses hears from God that no human being may see God and live (Exod. 33:20). If God cannot be seen, how was God seen? Or if he was seen, how can he not be seen? For John also says, “No one has ever seen God” (1 John 4:12). And the apostle Paul says, “Whom no human being has seen or can see” (1 Tim. 6:16). But Scripture certainly does not lie; therefore God was truly seen.

From this it may be understood that it was not the Father who was seen, since he has never been seen, but the Son, who was accustomed both to descend and, because he descended, to be seen. For he is the image of the invisible God, so that the limitedness and frailty of the human condition might even then begin to grow accustomed to seeing God the Father in the image of God—that is, in the Son of God. For gradually [Col. 0919B] and by degrees human frailty had to be nourished through the image toward that glory, so that it may one day be able to see God the Father.[^c0097-37] Great things are dangerous if they come suddenly. For even the sudden light of the sun after darkness will not reveal the day to eyes unaccustomed to it by reason of its excessive brightness, but will instead cause blindness.

[^c0097-1]: **[Col. 0909C] “Observes” (*animadverti*).** Gagnaeus reads *animadverterit*, which, however, amounts to the same thing.

[^c0097-2]: **[Col. 0909C] “Heard” (*audiit*).** Jackson asserts that this reading occurs in one of Pamelius’s manuscripts; accordingly, we have restored it in place of the editions’ *audit* (“hears”).

[^c0097-3]: **[Col. 0909C] “Be denied” (*negari*).** Perhaps *negare* (“to deny”); but nothing should be changed. **Jackson.**

[^c0097-4]: **[Col. 0909C] “But if from heaven,” etc.** In all the editions, immediately after the words [Col. 0909D] “where he was before,” there follow: “From this, the placing of the hands, showing the figure and form of the future Passion. No one, therefore, hesitates to call Christ an Angel,” etc. When I first read this, I was astounded. For what is the purpose of these words, “From this, the placing of the hands,” etc.? And what have we to do here with Christ as Angel, concerning whom there has hitherto been utter silence? What has become of all the examples of which he presently speaks?

But when I had reached chapter 23 in Pamelius’s edition, I found the argument concerning Christ as both God and man broken off here out of place, and resumed there even more out of place. As I proceeded further, various examples concerning Christ as Angel occurred as far as the end of chapter 27, where Jacob’s placing his hands crosswise upon Manasseh and Ephraim is discussed. Only then does the chapter close with the sentence to which these words, “From this, the placing of the hands,” etc., most properly belong—whereas they do not belong at all to the beginning of chapter 28.

When I had observed this and other things that it would be too lengthy to recount, I rejoiced greatly that I had at last found intact that portion of the book which I had lamented as though it were almost entirely lost, and found that it had merely been placed in the wrong location. Then, considering the cause of so great a confusion, none seemed more probable to me than the carelessness of a bookbinder, who threw one or two gatherings of the manuscript from which all the copies we now possess descended out of their proper order. This seemed all the more probable because the number of pages and lines in each of the two sections thus misplaced is approximately equal.

However that may be, it is sufficiently clear that the order of the leaves was disturbed. From this the treatise was rendered difficult and obscure, though otherwise easy and lucid—as it has now been made again, after the leaves were restored to their proper places. **Welchman.** Jackson after Welchman took the same position. Before either of them, however, Cotelerius had correctly recognized this kind of confusion in Novatian, in *Monumenta Ecclesiae Graecae*, vol. III, p. 634, where he also endeavored to restore the author’s disordered work to its proper sequence.

Moreover, so that the reason for the change and the restoration of the new order may be more clearly apparent, we append a table comparing our edition with that of Pamelius.

| XXV | XX |
| XXVI | XXI |
| XXVII | XXII |

[Col. 0911D] The remaining material proceeds in the same order in both editions.

[^c0097-5]: **[Col. 0911D] “Thus” (*sic*).** I do not know what the word *sic* is doing here. I think *scilicet* (“namely”) should be read. **Jackson.**

[^c0097-6]: **[Col. 0911D] “You do not know where I came from or where I am going.”** This clause of the text is absent from some copies, though Pamelius has it. I think it was omitted through a scribe’s carelessness because of *homoeoteleuton* (ὁμοιοτέλευτον, similarity of endings). For the same reason it is absent from Welchman’s edition, unless he judged that it should be omitted. Our author certainly had it in his manuscript, as is clear from what follows. **Jackson.**

[^c0097-7]: **[Col. 0912D] “Only” (*solam*).** Thus Pamelius and others. Welchman has *solum*.

[^c0097-8]: **[Col. 0912D] “Was” (*est*).** Gagnaeus, Frobenius, and De la Barre omit *est*.

[^c0097-9]: **[Col. 0912D] “Is God” (*Deus est*).** The author’s argument requires the addition of these words, *Deus est*; otherwise the sense is incomplete. They appear to have been omitted by a hurried shorthand writer because of the following *Deus*. Yet I have thought they should be enclosed in parentheses, so that I might alter nothing without manuscript authority. **Jackson.**—Wesseling, using the same reasoning, restored this very passage not much later and defended it at length against the pseudonymous Artemonius in *Probabilia*, chapter 26, pp. 318ff.; yet that distinguished scholar does not appear to have consulted Jackson’s edition.

[^c0097-10]: **[Col. 0912D] “Through immortality it grants divinity.”** Welchman, failing to grasp the force of this passage, reversed these words and those that follow, against the testimony of all previous editions and without the authority of any manuscript, as follows: “through divinity it grants immortality—by granting immortality through divinity—by extending immortality,” etc. Who cannot see—to omit everything else—that by this transposition he introduces a tautology (ταυτολογία) into the author’s text? For if one follows this English editor, Novatian is represented as having written: “Therefore Christ’s word grants immortality, and through divinity grants immortality.”

[^c0097-11]: **[Col. 0913D] “Anyone” (*quisquam*).** We have written this with Jackson in place of the editions’ *quidquam* (“anything”), because of the *quod* that follows. Soon afterward we have reproduced the edition of R. L. de la Barre, who reads *ipse* in place of Pamelius’s *ipsam*; others read *ipsum*. The logic of the context certainly appears to recommend both restorations.

[^c0097-12]: **[Col. 0913D] “I know” (*agnosco*).** From Wower’s manuscript I have restored *agnosco* in place of the editions’ *agnoscam* (“I shall know”), which agrees neither with the Greek text nor with the Vulgate, where the reading is *cognosco*. **Jackson.**

[^c0097-13]: **[Col. 0913D] “Because” (*dum*).** The author appears to have written *et dum* (“and because”). **The same.**

[^c0097-14]: **[Col. 0913D] “Christ.”** Perhaps *Christus* should be read. That is: “Christ had shown himself—to be God.” **The same.**

[^c0097-15]: **[Col. 0914C] “Of God” (*Dei*).** Pamelius omits the word *Dei*. Both the text and the author’s meaning, however, require it; we have therefore restored it to Novatian, following both English editors.

[^c0097-16]: **[Col. 0914D] “Divine economy” (*dispositione*).** Welchman, not understanding this word, substituted *depositione*. But Novatian has in view οἰκονομία (*oikonomia*), a notable term among the ancients, which Tertullian and the Latin translator of Irenaeus repeatedly rendered *dispositio*. **Jackson.**

[^c0097-17]: **[Col. 0914D] “Wished” (*vellet*).** Welchman conjectures that *se velit* should be read. Jackson, however, reads *se vellet*.

[^c0097-18]: **[Col. 0914D] “With respect to” (*spectet*).** Thus the editions. Perhaps *spectat* should be read; Welchman printed it on his own initiative, without manuscript testimony. **Jackson.**

[^c0097-19]: **[Col. 0914D] “Lives” (*vivit*).** With Latinius I have restored this word to the text in place of the editions’ *videt* (“sees”), which agrees with neither the Greek nor the Latin copies. The passage, however, is John 6:40, and Novatian could have copied it through a lapse of memory. **Jackson.**

[^c0097-20]: **[Col. 0914D] “Not man” (*non homo*).** On Gagnaeus’s authority Welchman printed *non est homo* (“he is not man”). **The same.**

[^c0097-21]: **[Col. 0915C] “But if he received from Christ,” etc.** Pamelius censures what Novatian says here concerning the Holy Spirit and warns that it should be read cautiously. Yet according to Novatian’s principles—he denies that the Son, insofar as he was begotten by the Father, is equal to the Father—it was altogether appropriate and consistent that he should hold the Holy Spirit, who proceeds from the Father and the Son, to be less than both. Nor does he detract from the divinity of the Holy Spirit any more when he denies in this sense that the Spirit is equal to the Son than he detracts from the divinity of the Son when he subjects the Son to the Father as to the originating principle from whom he received the whole authority of divinity.

Indeed, the divinity of the Holy Spirit is commended in no slight degree in this passage. For if the Holy Spirit were a creature, the statement that he receives from Christ would be no greater an argument for Christ’s divinity than the statement that other created things receive from him. Furthermore, when Novatian adds that Christ would have received from the Holy Spirit if he were only a man or an Angel—for the heretics admitted that he was an Angel—is this not an argument that all created beings, provided they possess reason, depend upon the Holy Spirit as the author of holiness? **Maran,** *Divinitas Domini Nostri Jesu Christi*, book IV, chapter 19, §3, pp. 520–21.

[^c0097-22]: **[Col. 0916C] “Wished” (*voluit*).** Welchman printed *se voluit* (“he wished himself”) on his own authority, perhaps correctly; but I change nothing without the support of manuscripts. **Jackson.**

[^c0097-23]: **[Col. 0916D] “Joined him to God” (*Deo junxit*).** Both English editors. Perhaps *se Deo junxit* (“he joined himself to God”) should be read. Soon afterward Welchman printed *intelligi se vellet* on his own judgment.

[^c0097-24]: **[Col. 0916D] “Wished” (*vellet*).** Here again Welchman printed *se vellet*, and nowhere warned his reader of additions of this kind.

[^c0097-25]: **[Col. 0916D] “From him” (*ab eo*).** Welchman thinks *se ab eo* (“himself from him”) should be read; and a little later, *se junxisset* (“had joined himself”). But with Jackson nothing should be changed.

[^c0097-26]: **[Col. 0916D] “Him” (*illum*).** Jackson would prefer *illum esse* (“that he is”). But there is no need.

[^c0097-27]: **[Col. 0916D] “Has” (*habet*).** Thus the editions. Welchman restored *habuit* (“had”), correctly, as it appears; although *habet* can stand. **Jackson.**

[^c0097-28]: **[Col. 0916D] “Will be understood” (*intelligetur*).** Thus Pamelius from an English manuscript. Other copies have *intelligitur* (“is understood”), which Welchman followed. Incorrectly. A little earlier I would read, “For Christ will even be less” (*Minor etiam*). **The same.**

[^c0097-29]: **[Col. 0916D] “To glory” (*in gloriam*).** Thus Novatian a little above. Jackson followed this reading, which Welchman also approves. The editions read *in gloria* (“in glory”).

[^c0097-30]: **[Col. 0917D] “Is found” (*deprehenditur*).** With Jackson I would read *deprehendetur* (“will be found”).

[^c0097-31]: **[Col. 0917D] “May be taken away” (*auferatur*).** The editions read *non auferatur* (“may not be taken away”), contrary to the sense of the author’s argument. **Jackson and Welchman.**

[^c0097-32]: **[Col. 0917D] “If these things cannot be removed.”** Gagnaeus, as also Frobenius, reads, “If these things cannot be said to exist only in predestination,” and Welchman followed them. But I have retained Pamelius’s printed reading as more suitable to Novatian; for the alternative seems to have been inserted as an interpretation of the words “cannot be removed.” **Jackson.**

[^c0097-33]: **[Col. 0918D] “Be brought forth” (*provocetur*).** Perhaps *provocentur* (“be brought forth,” plural). **Welchman.**

[^c0097-34]: **[Col. 0918D] “All things” (*omnia*).** The conjunction *et* (“and”) appears to be missing before *omnia*. **Jackson.**

[^c0097-35]: **[Col. 0918D] “To inspect” (*considerare*).** Welchman thinks *considerate* should be read; Jackson regards this as certain.

[^c0097-36]: **[Col. 0918D] “Will be” (*erit*).** Perhaps *erat* (“was”), as Welchman noted; *erit*, however, agrees with the following “will be declared.” **Jackson.**

[^c0097-37]: **[Col. 0919D] “May be able” (*possit*).** Thus, with Jackson, we have corrected the editions’ *posset* (“might be able”). For shortly afterward, in the present tense, the author uses the same construction more than once: “may be able to see him as he is—may be overwhelmed—may not be able to see.”

So that this may not harm human eyes, once the darkness has gradually been broken up and dispersed, the rising of this luminary, ascending imperceptibly by moderate degrees, slowly accustoms human eyes to bearing its entire disk through the gradual increase of its rays. Thus Christ also—that is, the image of God and the Son of God—is beheld by human beings in the manner in which he could be seen. And therefore the frailty and limited capacity of the human condition is nourished, advanced, and educated through him, so that, having become accustomed to behold the Son, it may someday be able to see God the [Col. 0919C] Father himself as he is; lest, struck by the sudden and intolerable brilliance of his majesty, it should be cut off and thus be unable to see God the Father, whom it has always desired to see.

From this it follows that the one who is seen is the Son; and the Son of God is the Word of God; and the Word of God became flesh and dwelt among us: this one, moreover, is Christ. What reason, pray, is there for hesitating to call God one who is shown in so many ways to be understood as God?

Again, when the Angel meets Hagar, Sarah’s maidservant, who had been both expelled from the household and driven into flight, beside a spring of water on the road to Shur (Gen. XVI, 7), he asks the reasons for her flight and receives her answer. He then offers her counsel to humble herself; moreover, he gives her the hope of becoming a mother, pledges and promises that a numerous offspring will come from her womb, declares that Ishmael is to be born from her [Col. 0919D], and, among other things, reveals his place of habitation and describes his conduct. Scripture, however, presents this Angel [Col. 0920A] both as Lord and as God—for he would not have promised the blessing of offspring unless he had been both Angel and God—so let the heretics consider what they are to maintain in the present passage.

[Note: [Col. 0919D] **For, nor, etc.** I have placed these words in parentheses with François du Jon, and have ended the sentence at the word *maintain*, differently from the editions, though the sense supports this arrangement, as will be evident to anyone who carefully weighs the entire sentence beginning with the words *Again, when Hagar*.—JACKSON.]

Was this one who was seen by Hagar the Father, or was he not? For he is presented as God. But far be it from us to call God the Father an angel, lest he should be subordinate to another whose angel he was. They will say, however, that he was an angel. How, then, will he be God, if he was an angel, since this name has never been granted to angels? The only explanation is that truth presses us from both sides into this conclusion: that we ought to understand him to have been the Son of God. Because he is from God, he is rightly called God, since he is God’s Son; and because he is subordinate to the Father and the herald of the Father’s will, he has been proclaimed the Angel of Great Counsel.

[Note: [Col. 0919D] **Because.** Welchman suspects that *qua* ought to be read; and this seems more suitable.—ID.]

[Note: [Col. 0919D] **Because he is subordinate to the Father and.** The sense requires either *and because*, *but because*, or something similar to be read [Col. 0920D]. The next three words, *subordinate to the Father and*, are supplied by Pamelius’s edition, and the author’s argument supports them. Because these same words are absent from other copies, however, Welchman took the opportunity to omit them.—ID.]

Therefore, if this passage [Col. 0920B] suits neither the person of the Father, lest he be called an angel, nor the person of an angel, lest he be pronounced God, but does suit the person of Christ, so that he is both God, because he is God’s Son, and Angel, because he is the herald of the Father’s dispensation, the heretics ought to understand that they are acting contrary to the Scriptures. For although they say that they believe Christ to be an angel, they refuse also to pronounce him God, though in the Old Testament they read that he often came to visit the human race.

[Note: [Col. 0920D] **If this passage.** So Pamelius. In other manuscripts it reads *if the passage*, with *this* omitted; Welchman followed these. But wrongly, for that demonstrative word appropriately indicates the aforesaid passage of Scripture that the author is expounding.—ID.]

Moses adds further that God appeared to Abraham by the oak of Mamre while Abraham was sitting at the entrance of his tent at midday (Gen. XVIII, 1). Nevertheless, when he had seen three men, he called one of them Lord. After washing their feet, he offered ash-baked loaves with butter and an abundance of milk, and urged them, as guests whom he had detained [Col. 0920C], to eat. After this he hears that he is to become a father, learns that Sarah his wife is to bear him a son, is informed of the fate that the Sodomites deserved to suffer, and learns that God had descended because of the outcry against Sodom.

[Note: [Col. 0920D] **His.** Jackson conjectures that *theirs* should be read. But the preceding conjunction seems to stand in the way.]

In this passage the heretics, wishing the one then received as a guest together with the two angels to be regarded as the Father, have believed the Father to be visible. But if he was an angel—since one of the three angels is called Lord—why is an angel, contrary to customary usage, called God? The only explanation is that, so that invisibility may be preserved as the distinctive attribute of God the Father and an angel may be left with the limited condition proper to him, it must be believed that the one who was seen by Abraham and received as a guest was none other than the Son of God, who is also God.

[Note: [Col. 0920D] **Will be believed.** So all the editions without exception, apart from Welchman’s, where *may be believed* was deliberately printed.]

For what he was going to become he rehearsed in the mystery: having become Abraham’s guest, he was to become a guest among [Col. 0920D] Abraham’s children (John XIII, 5). He washed the feet of those children as proof that he was the same one, repaying in the children the right of hospitality that their father had once lent him. Hence, so that there might be no doubt that this one had been Abraham’s guest, it is stated in the account of the destruction of the Sodomites [Col. 0921A] (Gen. XIX, 24): “The Lord rained fire and sulfur upon Sodom and Gomorrah from the Lord out of heaven.” Thus the prophet also says in the person of God: “I overthrew you,” he says, “as the Lord overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah” (Amos IV, 11).

[Note: [Col. 0921C] **The Lord.** So Pamelius; Jackson defends this reading as expressing Novatian’s meaning, since he repeats it shortly afterward. Others read *God*.]

Therefore the Lord overthrew Sodom—that is, God overthrew Sodom. But in the overthrow of Sodom the Lord rained down fire from the Lord. Now this Lord who was seen by Abraham is God; and this God is Abraham’s guest, plainly seen because he was touched. But since the Father, because he is invisible, was certainly not seen even then, the one who is accustomed to be touched and [Col. 0921B] seen was seen, received as a guest, and welcomed.

[Note: [Col. 0921C] **Because.** Welchman rightly emended this in place of the editions’ *in which* [Col. 0921D].—JACKSON.]

[Note: [Col. 0921D] **As a guest.** The same Welchman also correctly restored this word in place of the printed editions’ *by guests*. But he wrongly omitted the words *and welcomed*, which all editions retain.—ID.]

[Note: [Col. 0921D] **Who is accustomed.** Before these words *the Son*, or *the Son of God*, appears to be missing.—ID.]

This one, moreover, is the Son of God: the Lord from the Lord rained sulfur and fire upon Sodom and Gomorrah. This one is the Word of God; and the Word of God became flesh and dwelt among us: this one is Christ. It was therefore not the Father who was Abraham’s guest, but Christ; nor was the Father seen then, but the Son; and the one seen was Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0921D] **Seen.** The sense will be more suitable if we read *the Son* in place of *seen*; I scarcely doubt that this is the authentic reading.—ID.]

Christ, therefore, is rightly both Lord and God, for he was seen by Abraham only because, before Abraham himself, God the Word was begotten from God the Father.

[Note: [Col. 0921D] **God the Word.** So the English editors. The word *God* is absent from Pamelius.]

Furthermore, he says, the same Angel and God consoles and visits the same Hagar when she had been driven from Abraham’s household with her child. For when she had laid the infant down in the wilderness because the water in the skin had run out, and when the boy had cried out and raised weeping and lamentation (Gen. XXI, 17–19), Scripture says: “And God heard the voice of the boy from the place where he was.”

[Note: [Col. 0921D] **And he heard.** Perhaps *and he heeded*; Novatian repeats this very word a few lines later. Next, Wower’s manuscripts cited by Jackson read *had heard the voice of the infant*.]

After stating that the one who heard the infant’s voice was God, Scripture added: “And the Angel of the Lord called Hagar herself from heaven,” identifying as an angel the one whom it had called God and pronouncing as Lord the one whom it had designated an angel. This Angel and God further promises Hagar herself greater comfort, saying: “Do not be afraid, for I have heard the voice of the boy from the place where he is. Rise, take up the boy and [Col. 0922A] hold him, for I will make him into a great nation.”

If this angel is only an angel, why does he claim for himself the right to say, “I will make him into a great nation,” when this degree of power plainly belongs to God and cannot belong to an angel? From this he who can do this is also confirmed to be God; and to prove this very point, Scripture immediately adds: “And God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of living water; and she went and filled the skin from the well and gave the boy a drink, and God was with the boy.”

[Note: [Col. 0921D] **Is confirmed to be God.** So Welchman and Jackson. Others read: *God is confirmed to be God*; less correctly, as it seems.]

Therefore, if this God who opened Hagar’s eyes so that she might see the well of living water and draw water because of the pressing necessity of thirst was with the boy, while this God who calls her from heaven is called an Angel, and above had rather been identified as God when he heard the voice of the crying boy, no other is understood than one who is alike both Angel and [Col. 0922B] God.

[Note: [Col. 0921D] **God … calls her from heaven.** Welchman thinks that *God who calls her from heaven* should be read. Jackson would prefer: *God, calling her from heaven, is called an Angel*. But the commonly received reading [Col. 0922C] has no need of these emendations.]

[Note: [Col. 0922C] **Had rather been God.** So all the editions without exception. Jackson, however, thought that the text required emendation and printed *had been presented as God*, because, he says, *rather* has no meaning in this passage [Col. 0922D]. Yet I think that this emendation should scarcely be admitted, for the commonly received reading is found to yield a legitimate sense. The author is clearly expounding Genesis XXI, 17, where it reads: “But GOD heard the voice of the boy, and the ANGEL of God called Hagar from heaven”; he then writes: “This God—called an ANGEL, although above he had rather been GOD—is understood to be no other,” etc. It is just as if he had said: “He who is said to be the Angel of God who called Hagar from heaven is previously declared to be the God who heard the boy’s voice.” There is this further consideration: if Jackson’s emendation is admitted, the force of Novatian’s language is blunted. The expression *had rather been God* carries great force, whereas Jackson’s restoration, *had been presented as God*, is utterly insipid.]
