Since this cannot appropriately or fittingly be understood of the Father, who is God alone, but can appropriately be understood of Christ, who has been proclaimed not only God but also Angel, it is plainly apparent that it was not the Father who then spoke to Hagar, but rather Christ. For although he is God, the name Angel also befits him, since he was made the Angel of Great Counsel (Isa. IX, 6); and he is Angel insofar as he reveals the bosom of the Father, as John declares (John I, 18).

For if John himself says that this same one who reveals the Father’s bosom is the Word who became flesh, so that he might reveal the Father’s bosom, Christ is rightly not only man but also Angel; nor is he merely Angel, but is also shown by the Scriptures to be God, and is believed by us to be such. Otherwise, if we refuse to understand that it was Christ who then spoke to [Col. 0922C] Hagar, we shall either make an angel into God or number God the almighty Father among the angels.

[Note: [Col. 0922D] **For if.** The old editions read *But if*, which Pamelius rightly corrected.—JACKSON.]

[Note: [Col. 0922D] **But also Angel.** Pamelius restored the word *also* before *Angel* from the English manuscript, and the double reading is immediately confirmed by what follows, *but also God*. Welchman wrongly omitted *also* with the old editions.—ID.]

## CHAPTER XIX, otherwise XXVII  
### That God the Angel—namely, the Son of God—also appeared to Jacob

What if in another passage we likewise read that God is presented as an Angel? For when Jacob was complaining to his wives Leah and Rachel about the injustice of their father, and was saying that he now desired to go back and return to his own land, he also introduced the authority of his dream. At that time, he reports, the Angel of God said to him in a dream (Gen. XXXI, 11–13): “Jacob, Jacob.” “And I said,” he continues, “‘What is it?’ ‘Look,’ he said, ‘with your eyes and see the he-goats and rams mounting the sheep and goats, variegated, white, spotted, ash-colored, and speckled. For I have seen everything Laban has done to you. I am the God who appeared to you in the Place of God, where you anointed for me the standing stone and there vowed a vow to me. Now therefore rise and depart from this land, and go to the land of your birth, and I shall be with you.’”

[Note: [Col. 0923D] **Anointed.** Thus Pamelius’s editions rightly read from the English manuscript; both the Greek and Latin agree with them. Welchman printed *erected*, following the corrupt copies of Gagney and Froben, where it was introduced from a different passage, namely verse 45.—ID.]

If the Angel of God says these things to Jacob and this Angel himself proceeds to say, “I am the God who appeared to you in the Place of God,” we perceive without any hesitation that he is presented not only as Angel but also as God. He says that a vow had been made to him by Jacob in the Place of God, and does not say “in my place.” There is therefore the Place of God, and there is also this God.

Yet there the expression used is simply “in the Place of God”; for it does not say “in the Place of the Angel and God,” but only “of God.” This one, however, who makes these promises is declared to be God and Angel, so that there is rightly a distinction between him who is called God alone and him who is pronounced not simply God but also Angel.

Consequently, if this great authority cannot be understood of any other angel—the authority to confess that he is also God and to testify that a vow was made to him—but only of Christ, to whom a vow can be vowed not because he is merely Angel but [Col. 0923C] because he is God, it is evident that he cannot be understood as the Father, but as the Son, God and Angel. And if this one is Christ, as indeed he is, anyone who calls Christ either a man or merely an angel is in grave peril, because he deprives him of the authority of the divine name, which Christ repeatedly receives upon the testimony of the heavenly Scriptures, which frequently call him both Angel and God.

To all these considerations this also is added: just as divine Scripture repeatedly presents him both as Angel and as God, so too it presents him both as man and as God, expressing what he was going to become and portraying even then in an image what he was to be in the reality of his substance.

“For Jacob,” it says, “remained alone, and a man wrestled with him until morning. And he saw that he could not prevail against him, and he touched the breadth of Jacob’s thigh while he himself wrestled with him. And he said to him, ‘Release me, for the morning star has risen.’ But Jacob said, ‘I will not release you unless you bless me.’ And he said, ‘What is your name?’ And [Col. 0924A] he said, ‘Jacob.’ And he said to him, ‘From now on your name shall not be called Jacob, but Israel shall be your name; for you have prevailed with God, and with men you are powerful’” (Gen. XXXII, 24–27).

[Note: [Col. 0923D] **From now on.** So Pamelius and other copies of the Septuagint, οὐ κληθήσεται ἔτι, “it shall no longer be called.” The English editors, however, read *even now*, a reading that Pamelius himself gives shortly afterward.]

And Scripture further adds (Gen. XXXII, 30–31): “And Jacob called the name of that place, Vision of God. For I have seen God face to face, and my soul has been preserved. And the sun rose upon him; presently he passed beyond the Vision of God, but he limped upon his thigh.”

[Note: [Col. 0923D] **Presently he passed.** Perhaps *presently, when he passed* should be read, as Welchman also suspects. The Vulgate appears to agree with this emendation, for it reads: “And the sun rose upon him immediately after he passed beyond Phanuel.”—JACKSON.]

“A man,” Scripture says, “wrestled with Jacob.” If he was an ordinary man, who is he? Where did he come from? Why did he contend and wrestle with Jacob? What had intervened? What had happened? What was the reason for so great a contest and so great a struggle? Moreover, why is Jacob, who is found strong enough to hold the man with whom he wrestled, also found to have asked a blessing from the one whom he held when the morning star was already rising? The only explanation is that this contest prefigured the future contest between Christ and the children of Jacob, which the Gospel says was brought to completion.

[Note: [Col. 0924D] **Because the morning star is already rising, etc.** Welchman, because of faulty punctuation, regards the passage as mutilated, and Jackson approves his conjecture. Hence both remove some words and transpose others. Certainly without justification. We have meanwhile reproduced Pamelius’s edition, which will plainly appear complete and clear to the careful reader.]

For the people of Jacob wrestled against this man, and in that struggle the people of Jacob were found more powerful, since they achieved the victory of their iniquity against Christ. At that time, because of the crime they committed, they began to limp grievously in the course of their own faith and salvation, uncertain and unsteady. Although they were found superior in condemning Christ, they nevertheless need his mercy and nevertheless need his blessing.

But this man who wrestled with Jacob says: “Even now your name shall not be called Jacob, but Israel shall be your name.” And if *Israel* means “a man seeing God,” the Lord elegantly showed [Col. 0924C] that the one who then wrestled with Jacob was not only man but also God. Jacob was plainly seeing God, with whom he wrestled, although in the struggle he held him as a man.

And so that there could be no remaining doubt, the Lord himself supplied the interpretation by saying: “For you have prevailed with God, and with men you are powerful.” For this reason the same Jacob, now understanding the force of the mystery and perceiving the authority of the one with whom he had wrestled, called the name of the place in which he wrestled “Vision of God.” He also added reasons to support the interpretation [Note: *Vision*] of the Vision of God: “For I have seen God,” he says, “face to face, and my soul has been preserved.”

[Note: [Col. 0924D] **Vision.** This word is absent from the editions and is restored by Welchman.—JACKSON.]

He saw as God the one with whom he had wrestled as though with a man. Indeed, he held the man as a victor, but asked a blessing from him as from [Col. 0924D] God, as one inferior. Thus he wrestled both with God and with man. Accordingly, this contest was there prefigured, but in the Gospel it was brought to completion between Christ and the people of Jacob. In that contest, although the people were found superior, they were found lesser when proved guilty.

Who will doubt that Christ, in whom this figure of the contest was fulfilled, must be acknowledged not merely as man but also as God, since the very figure of the contest appears to have established that man also as God?

Yet even after this, divine Scripture likewise does not cease to call the Angel God and [Col. 0925A] to pronounce God an Angel. For when this same Jacob was about to bless Manasseh and Ephraim, the sons of Joseph, he placed his hands crosswise upon the boys’ heads and said: “God, who has fed me from my youth to this day, the Angel who delivered me from all evils, bless these boys” (Gen. XLVIII, 14–15).

[Note: [Col. 0925C] **And God.** So both English editors. Others omit the conjunction *and*.]

He so thoroughly identifies as the same Angel the one whom he had called God that, at the end of his statement, he placed the person of whom he spoke in the singular, saying, “May he bless these boys.” For if he had wished one to be understood as God and another as Angel, he would have embraced the two persons with a plural expression. As it is, he used the singular number of one person in the blessing, from which he wished the same one to be understood as both God and Angel.

[Note: [Col. 0925C] **One as God.** Welchman and Jackson appear rightly to have restored these words, which copyists omitted because of their customary carelessness in passages with similar endings [ὁμοιοτέλευτα, *homoioteleuta*].]

But God the Father cannot be understood here; Christ, however, can be understood as God and Angel. Jacob also indicated that Christ was the author of this blessing by placing his hands crosswise upon the boys, as though Christ were their father, thereby exhibiting beforehand, through the placement of his hands, the figure and form of the future passion.

[Note: [Col. 0925D] **Thereby placing his hands.** Cotelier, *Monumenta Ecclesiae Graecae*, vol. III, p. 634, rewrites this as *would place*, and the English editors adhere to him. “Blind,” Welchman says, “is anyone who does not see that these words pertain to those immediately preceding and therefore must now be restored to their proper place,” although in all the other editions the two passages are separated widely from one another, the former being placed at the beginning of chapter 15 and the latter at the end of chapter 27. See the notes above on chapter 15.]

[Note: [Col. 0925D] **Future.** Welchman would prefer *of the future*, but Jackson thinks nothing should be changed.]

Therefore, just as no one hesitates to call Christ Angel, so no one should hesitate to pronounce him God, since he understands that this same one was invoked both as God and as Angel for the blessing of these boys [Col. 0925C], through the mystery of the Passion represented in the figure of the hands.

[Note: [Col. 0925D] **And … blessing.** We follow Pamelius’s edition, which Jackson thought should be emended by rewriting *from … the blessing*. Welchman, however, conjectured that *in* should be read in place of *and*.]

## CHAPTER XX, otherwise XV  
### It is proved from the Scriptures that Christ was called Angel. Nevertheless, other passages of Holy Scripture show that he is also God

But if some heretic, stubbornly struggling against the truth, should wish in all these examples [Col. 0926A] either to understand an angel in the strict sense or to maintain that such an angel must be understood, he must necessarily be crushed in this matter also by the power of truth.

[Note: [Col. 0925D] **But if.** So the old editions; and no differently Welchman and Jackson. Pamelius likewise has *but if* from the English manuscript. Next, Jackson, following Wower’s manuscript, preferred to restore *maintain* in place of *should maintain*.]

For if, when all things in heaven, on earth, and beneath the earth are subject to Christ, even the angels themselves, together with all other things subject to Christ, are called gods, Christ is rightly God. And if any angel subject to Christ can be called a god, and this can be said and uttered without blasphemy, much more certainly can this designation belong to Christ himself, the Son of God, so that he may be pronounced God.

[Note: [Col. 0926C] **For if, when all things … And if any angel.** Pamelius reads and supplements the passage precisely in this way, partly from Gagney’s earlier edition. The passage nevertheless still appears tangled. A learned man has observed that the words *gods, Christ is rightly God* seem to be Gagney’s addition and were omitted by Gelenius on the authority of a British manuscript. The reading of that manuscript, with the single word *subject* or *subordinate* added after *are called*, produces the following sound sense: “For if, when all things in heaven, on earth, and beneath the earth are subject to Christ, even the angels themselves, together with all other things that are subject, are called subject or subordinate to Christ; and yet any angel,” etc. This, in my judgment, is the authentic reading.—JACKSON.]

[Note: [Col. 0926D] **Is uttered.** All Pamelius’s editions read *will be uttered*. But the old editions read *is uttered*. Correctly.—JACKSON and WELCHMAN.]

For if an angel who is subject to Christ is proclaimed a god, much more and with greater assurance will Christ, to whom all angels are subject, be called God.

[Note: [Col. 0926D] **Who is subject.** Either *anyone subject* should be read, as shortly before, or *who is subject*. So Jackson. Welchman also conjectured the latter.]

It is not consistent with nature that what is granted to inferiors should be denied to superiors. Thus, if an angel is inferior to Christ and yet an angel is called a god, it follows all the more that Christ is called God [Col. 0926B], since he is found to be greater and better not merely than one angel, but than all angels.

[Note: [Col. 0926D] **Is called.** Perhaps *will be called*, as shortly before.—JACKSON.]

And if “God stood in the assembly of the gods; in the midst, moreover, God judges the gods” (Ps. LXXXI, 1–2), while Christ repeatedly stood in the assembly, then Christ stood in the assembly as God, judging the gods to whom he says, “How long do you show partiality toward human persons?” He is plainly and consistently accusing the men of the assembly of failing to exercise just judgments.

[Note: [Col. 0926D] **God … gods.** Jackson deleted the word *God*, adhering to the Hebrew, Septuagint, and Vulgate; nevertheless, all editions contain it.]

Furthermore, if those who are reproved and blamed nevertheless appear, for some reason, to receive this name without blasphemy, so that they are called gods, much more certainly will he be regarded as God who is said not only to have stood as God in the assembly of gods, but is also found, on the authority of the same reading [Col. 0926C], to distinguish and judge the gods.

[Note: [Col. 0926D] **In the assembly.** Welchman rightly restored these words, with the author’s meaning as his warrant. He also thinks that shortly afterward *is found* should be read in place of *is revealed*, as the author himself soon writes.—JACKSON.]

But if those who “fall like one of the princes” (ibid., v. 7) are nevertheless called gods, much more will he be called God who not only does not fall like one of the princes, but also conquers the very author and prince of wickedness.

What reason, pray, is there for denying this name to Christ when they read that it was also given to Moses, for it is said, “I have made you a god to Pharaoh” (Exod. VII, 1), whereas Christ is found to have been constituted Lord and [Col. 0927A] God not over Pharaoh but over the whole creation? In Moses this name was given sparingly; in Christ, abundantly. In Moses, according to measure; in Christ, beyond every measure whatsoever. For the Father, Scripture says, does not give to the Son according to measure: “For the Father,” it says, “loves the Son” (John III, 34–35). In Moses, it was given for a time; in Christ, without limit of time, for he received the authority of the divine name both over all things and for all time.

But if one who received authority over a single man nevertheless obtains without hesitation, within the narrow limits of the authority given him, this name of God, how much more will the one who possesses authority even over Moses himself be believed to have obtained the authority of this name?

## CHAPTER XXI, otherwise XVI  
### The same divine majesty in Christ is again confirmed from other Scriptures

[Col. 0927B]

I could indeed examine the discussions of all the heavenly Scriptures and stir up, so to speak, an immense forest concerning this aspect of Christ’s divinity. My purpose, however, is not so much to argue against this heresy as briefly to set forth the Rule of Truth concerning the person of Christ.

Nevertheless, although I hasten on to other matters, I do not think that the statement by which the Lord expressed the significance of his majesty in the Gospel should be passed over: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John II, 19). Or again, when in another place and context he declares: “I have authority to lay down my life and to receive [Col. 0927C] it again; for I received this command from the Father” (John X, 18).

[Note: [Col. 0927D] **To receive.** The English editors conjecture that *of receiving* should be read. The Vulgate indeed has *of taking*. But the author represented the Greek λαβεῖν (*labein*, “to receive/take”).]

For who is it who says that he can lay down his own life, or that he can recover his own life again, because he has received this command from the Father? Or who says that he can raise up and rebuild the destroyed temple of his own body, unless it is that Word who is from the Father, who is with the Father, through whom all things were made, and without whom nothing was made (John I, 3); the imitator of the Father’s works and powers; the image of the invisible God (Col. I, 15); the one who descended from heaven (John III, 31–32); who testified to what he had seen and heard; who did not come to do his own will (John VI, 38), but rather to do the will of the Father by whom he had been sent for this very purpose; who, having been made the Angel of Great Counsel (Isa. IX, 6), might disclose to us the ordinances of the heavenly mysteries; and who, [Col. 0927D] as the Word made flesh, dwelt among us (John I, 14)?

Is not this Christ from among us thereby proved to be not only man, because he is the Son of Man, but also God, because he is the Son of God?

And if Christ has also been called by the Apostle “the firstborn of every creature” (Col. I, 15), how could he be the firstborn of every creature unless, according to his divinity, the Word proceeded from God the Father [Col. 0928A] before every creature? Unless the heretics accept this, they will be compelled to show that the man Christ is the firstborn of every creature; and this they will be unable to do.

Either, therefore, he exists before every creature, so that he may be the firstborn of every creature—and is not merely man, because man comes after every creature—or else he is merely man and comes after every creature. And how is he the firstborn of every creature unless that Word who exists before every creature, and is therefore the firstborn of every creature, becomes flesh and dwells among us—that is, assumes this man who comes after every creature—and thus dwells among us with him and in him, so that neither the man is taken away from Christ nor the divinity denied?

For if he exists only before [Col. 0928B] every creature, the man in him is taken away; but if he is merely man, the divinity that exists before every creature is cut off.

[Note: [Col. 0927D] **Only before, etc.** Jackson thinks that *only God before*, etc., should be read so as to correspond with the following *merely man*. Yet although *God* is not read [Col. 0928D], the sense remains complete.]

Both, therefore, are allied in Christ, both are joined, and both are connected. And rightly, since there is something in him that surpasses creation, the concord of divinity and humanity appears to be pledged in him.

[Note: [Col. 0928D] **Humanity.** The editions corruptly read *humility*. I read *humanity* with François du Jon; Welchman also printed this word.—JACKSON.]

For this reason, he who is declared to have become the mediator between God and human beings (I Tim. II, 5) is found to have united God and man in himself.

And if the same Apostle says of Christ that, “having stripped off the flesh, he disgraced the powers, openly triumphing over them in himself” (Col. II, 15), he certainly did not mention that he had stripped off the flesh without purpose, unless he wished it to be understood that in the resurrection he was clothed with it again.

[Note: [Col. 0928D] **And in the resurrection.** The editions read *and the resurrection*, which makes no sense. I have rewritten it *and in the resurrection*, following Novatian himself immediately afterward more than once; Latinius also conjectured this.—ID.]

Let the heretics therefore ask who it is that stripped himself and clothed himself again. For we know that the Word of God clothed himself with the substance of flesh, and that the same one stripped himself again of the same material of the body, which he took up again in the resurrection and resumed as though it were a garment.

But if Christ had been merely man, the man Christ would have neither stripped himself nor clothed himself. For no one ever either strips himself of himself or clothes himself with himself. Whatever is stripped of, or clothed with, something else must necessarily be something distinct from it. Hence it was rightly the Word of God who stripped off the flesh and was clothed with it again in the resurrection. He stripped it off because he had also been clothed with it in the nativity.

Accordingly, in Christ it is God who is clothed, and it is also necessary that he should have been stripped. For this reason, the one who is clothed must likewise be stripped. He is clothed with, and stripped of, the man as though the man were a tunic of woven bodily material. Consequently, as we have said, it was the Word of God who is found now clothed and now stripped.

For he also foretold this beforehand in the blessings: “He will wash his robe in wine, and his garment in the blood of the grape” (Gen. XLIX, 11). If the robe in Christ is the flesh [Col. 0929A], and the garment is the body itself, let inquiry be made as to who that person is whose body is the garment and whose flesh is the robe.

[Note: [Col. 0929C] **The garment itself.** Froben, with Gagney, reads *the one clothed himself*, and Welchman printed the same. But since Novatian employs other unusual words, I have retained in his text the uncommon neuter noun *garment*. The author also uses *garment* and *the clothed one* shortly afterward.—JACKSON.]

[Note: [Col. 0929D] **Whoever.** Welchman would prefer *who*; Jackson scarcely doubts that this is the true reading.]

For it is evident to us that the flesh was the robe and the body the garment of the Word, who washed the substance of the body with blood—that is, with wine—and, by the passion of the man assumed, washed the material of the flesh.

[Note: [Col. 0929D] **Who with blood, etc.** This passage appeared to Pamelius obscure, or even mutilated and corrupt. Welchman offers a remedy by reading it thus: “Who washed the substance of the body in the blood of the grape—that is, in wine—washing the material of the flesh,” or “and washed the material of the flesh, by the passion of the man assumed.” Jackson, with François du Jon, reads and punctuates it somewhat differently: “Who washed the substance of the body and the material of the flesh in blood—that is, in wine—washing it by the passion of the man assumed.”]

Thus, insofar as it is washed, he is man, because the garment that is washed is flesh; but the one who washes is the Word of God, who, in order to wash the garment, became the one who assumed what was clothed. Therefore, from the substance that was received so that it might be washed, he is rightly declared to be man; just as, from the authority of the Word who washed it, he is shown to be God.

[Note: [Col. 0929D] **Just as … is shown.** Others read *so that … may be shown*. Less correctly, as it seems.]

## CHAPTER XXII, otherwise XVII  
### He again confirms the same divine majesty in Christ from other Scriptures

[Col. 0929B]

But why, even though we seem eager to hurry on to another part of the argument, should we pass over that passage in the Apostle?

> Who, being in the form of God, did not consider it robbery to be equal with God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings and found in appearance as a man. He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death—even death on a cross. Therefore God also exalted him above all and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, of those in heaven, on earth, and beneath the earth, and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus is in the glory of God the Father. (Phil. 2:6–11)

“He was in the form of God,” he says. If Christ were merely a man, [Col. 0929C] he would have been described as being in the image of God, not in the form of God. For we know that the human being was made according to the image of God (Gen. 1:27), not according to God’s form. Who, then, is this who, being in the form of God, as we have said, was made an angel? But neither do we read that the form of God is in the angels, except insofar as this one—the preeminent and noble one above all, the Son of God, the Word of God, the imitator of all his Father’s works, since he himself also works just as his Father does (John 5:19)—is in the form, as we have explained, of God the Father.

[Note: [Col. 0929D] “In the likeness.” The author adheres to the Greek ἐν ὁμοιώματι, “in the likeness.” So too shortly afterward he rendered ὑπερύψωσε as “exalted above all.”]

[Note: [Col. 0930C] “In the form.” The printed editions omit “in,” which Jackson rightly restored after Welchman.]

And rightly was he declared to be in the form of God, since he himself is above all, possesses divine power over every creature, and is God after the pattern of the Father. Yet he obtained this very thing from his own Father: that he should be both God and Lord of all, and God according to the form of God the Father, begotten and brought forth from him. Thus, although he was in the form of God, he did not consider it robbery to be equal with God. For although he remembered that he was God from God the Father, he never compared or equated himself with God the Father, mindful that he was from his Father and that he possessed what he is because the Father had given it.

Accordingly, both before assuming flesh and after assuming a body—and, moreover, after the resurrection itself—he rendered and continues to render complete obedience to the Father in all things. From this it is proved that he never regarded divinity as a kind of plunder [Col. 0930B] by which he might make himself equal to God the Father. On the contrary, obedient and subject to all the Father’s command and will, he was willing even to assume the form of a servant—that is, to become that human being—and by being born he assumed the substance of flesh and body, which came from the enslavement of the ancestral sins and of sins according to the human condition. At that time he also emptied himself, since he did not refuse to assume the human frailty of that condition.

[Note: [Col. 0930D] “Even.” Pamelius omits this word, which the others retain.]

[Note: [Col. 0930D] “And.” Welchman judges that this seemingly intrusive conjunction should be deleted.]

[Note: [Col. 0930D] “The human frailty of the condition.” Welchman and Jackson needlessly attempt to disturb this reading of the preceding editions, rewriting it as “the frailty of the human condition.” Minucius, in the *Octavius*, chapter 36, is found using the same manner of speech: “the human defects of the body” for “the defects of the human body.” At that passage the learned Davis offers several examples of such expressions, among which occurs this very passage of Novatian with which we are dealing. See volume II of our *Library of the Fathers*, p. 402, note 12.]

For if he had been born merely a man, he would not thereby have been emptied. A human being is increased by being born, not emptied; for when he begins to be what, while he did not exist, he could not possess, as we have said, he is not emptied but rather increased and enriched. But if Christ is emptied in being born, by taking the form [Col. 0930C] of a servant, how is he merely a man? Of him it would more truly have been said that he was enriched when he was born, not emptied—unless it is because the authority of the divine Word, temporarily coming to rest in order to assume the human being and not exercising its own powers, lowers and lays itself aside for a time while bearing the human being whom it assumed.

[Note: [Col. 0930D] “But if.” Thus the English editors, following Gagnaeus, Frobenius, etc. Others read “And if.”]

[Note: [Col. 0930D] “Exercising.” Latinius reads “putting forth.”]

He empties himself when he descends to injuries and insults, when he hears unspeakable things and endures indignities; yet the splendid fruit of this humility is immediately present. For he received the name [Col. 0931A] that is above every name, which we understand to be none other than the name of God. For since it belongs to God alone to be above all, it follows that the name belonging to him who is above all—God—is above every name. Therefore that name is the name above every name; and it is accordingly the name of him who, although he had been in the form of God, did not consider it robbery to be equal with God.

[Note: [Col. 0930D] “He empties.” I read thus with Gagnaeus, Barrensis, and the first Frobenius edition. The preceding words “lowers,” “lays aside,” and “bears,” and the following words “descends,” “hears,” and “endures,” confirm this reading. Pamelius less correctly reads “he emptied.” —JACKSON.]

[Note: [Col. 0931D] “Above every.” Pamelius printed it thus; this reading agrees with the preceding “above every” from the Pauline text (Phil. 2:9) and Novatian’s subsequent “above every.” The English editions read “above all.”]

[Note: [Col. 0931D] “Who is above all—God.” Jackson thinks it should read: “Who is above all. That name, therefore, is God,” etc.]

For if Christ were not God, every knee of those in heaven, on earth, and beneath the earth would not bend at his name; nor would visible or invisible things, or every creature among all things, be subject or subordinate to a man, when it remembered that it existed before the man. Therefore, since Christ is said to be in the form of God, since he is shown to have emptied himself in his birth according to [Col. 0931B] the flesh, since he is said to have received from the Father the name that is above every name, since every knee in heaven, on earth, and beneath the earth is shown to bend and bow at his name, and since this very thing is asserted to contribute to the glory of God the Father, it follows that he is not merely a man because he became obedient to the Father unto death, even death on a cross. From these preceding points as well, which proclaim Christ’s divinity, the Lord Christ Jesus is shown to be God as well—something the heretics refuse to admit.

[Note: [Col. 0931D] “Birth.” Welchman would prefer “in the birth.” Jackson does not dissent. Shortly afterward both read “emptied himself,” with the older printed editions; but the editions of Pamelius present “emptied,” which we have likewise reproduced, while rewriting shortly before “Therefore, since,” where the English editions have “Therefore also, since.”]

[Note: [Col. 0932D] “Contribute.” Latinius reads “run to his aid.”]

## CHAPTER XXIII, alternatively XVIII  
### This is so manifest that some heretics thought him to be God the Father, while others thought him to have been God alone, without flesh

[Col. 0931C]

At this point I may gather arguments even from the position of other heretics. A mode of proof is strong when it is taken even from an adversary, so that the truth is proved even by truth’s own enemies. For it is so manifestly handed down in the Scriptures that he is God that many heretics, moved by the magnitude and truth of his divinity, extended the honors paid to him beyond due measure and dared to declare or suppose that he was not the Son but God the Father himself. Although this is contrary to the truth of the Scriptures, it is nevertheless a great and preeminent argument for Christ’s divinity. He is God to such a degree—but as the Son of God, born from God—that many heretics, as we have said, accepted him as God in such a way that they thought he should be declared not the Son but the Father.

[Note: [Col. 0932D] “Is.” I would prefer “and,” with Gelenius.]

[Note: [Col. 0932D] “Not the Son.” Welchman reads “him not to be the Son.”]

[Note: [Col. 0932D] “God.” The same Welchman thinks it should read “is God.” Jackson agrees.]

Let them judge, then, whether he is God whose authority moved some so greatly that they thought him, as we said above, to be God the Father himself, confessing Christ’s divinity without restraint and beyond measure because Christ’s manifest divinity compelled them to this: although they read that he was the Son, because they perceived that he was God, they thought him to be the Father.

[Note: [Col. 0932D] “Even.” Jackson does not doubt that the reading should be “also.” Moreover, judging the entire passage disordered, he would rewrite it thus: “Whose authority moved some so greatly to confess Christ’s divinity without restraint and beyond measure that they thought,” etc.—unless someone should judge that “confessing” ought to be read instead of “to confess.”]

Other heretics also embraced Christ’s manifest divinity to such a degree that they said he existed without flesh and removed from him the entire human being he had assumed, lest, as they supposed, they should diminish in him the power of the divine name if they associated human birth with him. We do not approve this; rather, we offer it as an argument that Christ is God to such a degree that some thought him to be God alone, after subtracting the human being, while others believed him to be God the Father himself. Yet the rationale and balanced teaching of the heavenly Scriptures show that Christ is God, but as the Son [Col. 0932B] of God, and that, because the Son of Man was also assumed by God, he must be believed to be human as well.

For if he was coming to the human being in order to be the mediator between God and human beings, it was necessary for him to be with the human being, and for the Word to become flesh, so that in himself he might fasten together the harmony of earthly and heavenly things alike, joining in himself the pledges of both parties and uniting God to the human being and the human being to God. Thus the Son of God might rightly become the Son of Man through the assumption of flesh, and the Son of Man might become the Son of God through the reception of the Word of God. This deepest and hidden mystery, appointed before the ages for the salvation of the human race, is found to be fulfilled in the Lord Jesus Christ, God and man, so that the condition of the human race might be brought to the fruit of eternal salvation.

## CHAPTER XXIV, alternatively XIX  
### They erred because, through a misunderstanding of Scripture, they thought there was no difference between the Son of God and the son of man

[Col. 0932C]

But the material for this error of the heretics arose, I think, from the fact that they suppose there is no difference between the Son of God and the Son of Man, lest, once the distinction has been made, Jesus Christ should easily be proved to be both man and God. For they wish the same identical person—that is, the human being, the son of man—to be regarded also as the Son of God, so that the human being and the flesh, that frail substance, may be said to be the very same thing as the Son of God. Therefore, when no distinction is made between the son of man and the Son of God, [Col. 0932D] but the son of man himself is claimed as the Son of God, Christ is asserted to be merely a man who is identical with the Son of God. By this means they endeavor to exclude:

> The Word was made flesh and dwelt among us. (John 1:14)

and:

> You shall call his name Emmanuel,

which is translated:

> God with us. (Matt. 1:23)

For they put forward and hold up what is related in Luke’s Gospel, from which they attempt to assert not what is actually there, but only what they want to be there:

> The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore also the holy thing that will be born from you will be called the Son of God. (Luke 1:35)

If, then, they say, the angel of God says to Mary, “The holy thing that will be born from you,” the substance of flesh and body comes from Mary; and he declared that this substance—that is, this holy thing begotten from her—is the Son of God. Therefore, they say, that human being himself and that bodily flesh, the thing called holy, is itself the Son of God. Thus, [Col. 0933B] when Scripture says “holy,” we are to understand Christ the son of man as a human being; and when it presents the Son of God, we ought to understand not a human being but God.

[Note: [Col. 0933D] “Not a human being but God.” Thus Pamelius and others. Welchman, however, and Jackson following him, printed the words in reverse order: “not God but a human being,” since, the latter says, the logic of the argument requires this transposition.]

But divine Scripture easily convicts and exposes the deceits and thefts of the heretics. For if it had said only, “The Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the holy thing that will be born from you will be called the Son of God,” perhaps we would have had to struggle against them in another way and seek other arguments and take up other weapons with which to overcome their snares and deceptions. But since Scripture itself, abounding in heavenly fullness, frees itself from the calumnies of these heretics, we readily rely upon the very thing that is written and overcome these errors without any hesitation.

For it did not say, as we have already explained, [Col. 0933C] “Therefore the holy thing that will be born from you”; rather, it added a conjunction, for it says, “Therefore **also** the holy thing that will be born from you.” In this way it showed that this holy thing born from her—that is, this substance of flesh and body—is not primarily the Son of God, but only consequently and in the second place. Primarily, however, the Son of God is the Word of God incarnate through that Spirit of whom the angel reports:

> The Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you.

For this is the legitimate Son of God who is from God himself. When he assumes this holy thing, attaches the Son of Man to himself, and takes and transfers him to himself, by his own union and associated intermingling he causes him also to be, and makes him, the Son of God—something he was not by nature. Thus the primary application of this name, “Son of God,” lies in the Spirit of the Lord who descended and came, while the derivative application of the name [Col. 0934A] lies in the Son of God and of Man; and rightly, as a consequence, this latter is made the Son of God, though he is not primarily the Son of God.

[Note: [Col. 0933D] “In the Son of God and of Man.” We have reproduced the edition of Pamelius, which agrees with what precedes. Welchman omitted the words “of God and”; Jackson at first agreed with him, but later changed his mind and thought it should be rewritten: “the Son of God may be in the human being.”]

Therefore the angel, perceiving this arrangement and setting forth this order of the mystery, did not confuse everything in such a way as to leave no trace of distinction. Rather, he established the distinction by saying:

> Therefore also the holy thing that will be born from you will be called the Son of God.

Had he not distributed this arrangement with its proper balances, but left it confusedly mingled with the rest, he would indeed have given the heretics an opportunity to declare that the Son of Man, precisely insofar as he is human, is the very same Son both of God and of Man.

[Note: [Col. 0933D] “The Son of God and of Man.” Here too we follow Pamelius. Welchman deleted “and of Man.”]

But now, by explaining in detail the order and rationale of so great a mystery, he clearly expressed it by saying, “And the holy thing that will be born from you will be called the Son of God,” proving that the Son of God descended. When he took the Son of Man into himself, he consequently made him the Son of God, because the Son of God associated and joined him to himself. Thus, when the Son of Man adheres to the Son of God in the birth, through that very intermingling he receives on loan and holds as a borrowed possession what he could not possess from his own nature.

[Note: [Col. 0933D] “The Son of God to himself.” The word order will be easier if we read “the Son of God associated him with himself,” or “the Son of God associated with himself,” etc. —JACKSON.]

[Note: [Col. 0934D] “In the birth.” Jackson thinks that “at the birth” must certainly be read; Welchman made the same conjecture.]

And so, by the angel’s declaration, the distinction the heretics reject was made between the Son of God and the son of man, though with their proper association. It compels them to understand Christ, the Son of Man, as a human being who is also the Son of God, and to receive the human being who is the Son of God—that is, the Word of God, as Scripture says—as God. Accordingly, they must recognize the Lord Jesus Christ, [Col. 0934C] joined from both, so to speak, woven and compounded from both, and united in the harmony of the two substances by the fastening together of a mutual covenant with one another, as man and God, on the authority of Scripture itself, which says precisely this.

[Note: [Col. 0934D] “And the human being the Son of God … as God.” Thus Pamelius. The Frobenius edition reads: “And the human being the Son of God, that is, the Word, as it is written, as God.” Welchman followed this reading. The passage seems disordered to Jackson and should be read: “And the Son of God, that is, the Word of God … as God.” Wesselingius adopts the same opinion in *Probabilia*, chapter 36, p. 322.]

[Note: [Col. 0934D] “Woven from both.” Jackson omitted these words, which appear in all the printed editions, since they seem to have arisen from a careless repetition of the preceding “joined from both.” Welchman had likewise ordered them deleted.]

## CHAPTER XXV, alternatively XX  
### It does not follow from Christ’s death that God also must be understood to have died; for Scripture presents Christ not merely as God but also as man

Therefore, they say, if Christ is not merely man but also God, while Scripture reports that Christ died for us and was raised, Scripture is now teaching us to believe that God died. Or if God does not [Col. 0935A] die, while Christ is reported to have died, Christ will not be God, since God cannot be understood to have died.

If they ever understood—or had understood—what they read, they would never speak in so utterly dangerous a manner. But error is always precipitous madness; nor is it surprising if those who have abandoned the legitimate faith descend into dangerous assertions. For if Scripture presented Christ as God alone, and no association of human frailty were mingled in him, their twisted argument here would deservedly have had some force: “If Christ is God, and Christ died, then God died.”

But since Scripture establishes him not merely as God, as we have already frequently shown, but also as man, it follows that what is immortal must be held to have remained incorrupt. For who does not understand that divinity is incapable of suffering, while human frailty is capable of suffering?

[Note: [Col. 0935D] “That.” Nothing compels us to read “so that,” with the English editors.]

Since, therefore, Christ is understood to be mingled and associated both from what he is as God and from what he is as man—for “the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14)—who cannot easily recognize by himself, without any teacher or interpreter, that what died in Christ was not that which is God, but that which is human in him?

What of it if the divinity in Christ does not die, but only the substance of the flesh is extinguished, seeing that even in other human beings—who are not flesh alone, but flesh and soul—it is the flesh alone that suffers the onset of destruction and death, whereas the soul is seen to remain incorrupt, outside the laws of destruction and death? For the Lord himself also said this when exhorting [Col. 0935C] us to martyrdom and to contempt for all human power:

> Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul. (Matt. 10:28)

But if the immortal soul cannot be killed or put to death in any other person, although the body and flesh alone can be killed, how much more certainly could the Word of God and God in Christ not possibly be put to death, when only the flesh and body were slain? If the soul in any human being possesses this nobility of immortality, so that it cannot be put to death, much more does the nobility of the Word of God possess this power, so that it cannot be slain.

[Note: [Col. 0935D] “Although.” Welchman regards this word as corrupt and reads “since, namely.” Jackson agrees, although he remains somewhat doubtful about restoring the passage. Yet both do so without compelling reason, as it seems. I am likewise less persuaded by Jackson’s view in the words shortly afterward, where he reads “the immortal soul.” For everyone sees that the term “immortality” refers to “nobility,” and every ambiguity—if indeed there is any—vanishes when Novatian’s wording is arranged in this or a similar manner: “For if the soul in any human being possesses this nobility of immortality, so that it cannot be put to death,” etc.]

For if human power fails when it seeks to put God’s sacred power to death, and if human cruelty fails when it seeks to put the soul to death, much more ought it to fail when it seeks to put the Word of God to death. Since the soul itself, which was made through the Word of God, is not slain by human beings, much more certainly must it be believed that the Word of God cannot be destroyed.

And if the bloody savagery of human beings can do no more against human beings than kill the body alone, how much more certainly will it be unable to do anything more in Christ than kill that same body alone? Thus, since from these facts it is inferred that only the human being in Christ was put to death, it becomes apparent that the Word was not thereby reduced to mortality.

[Note: [Col. 0936D] “The same.” Welchman, following Gagnaeus, printed the feminine form “the same [body].” The others, with Pamelius, have the neuter “the same.”]

[Note: [Col. 0936D] “Thereby.” Latinius wishes “in him” to be read; suitably enough. What if the author himself wrote *inlico* for *illico*? —JACKSON.]

For if Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—who, it is agreed, were merely human beings—manifestly live, for “all of them,” he says, “live to God” (Luke 20:38), and death does not destroy in them the soul whose bodies it dissolves—for it was able to exercise its right over their bodies but could not exercise it over their souls; one thing in them was mortal and therefore died, while another was immortal and is therefore understood not to have been extinguished, for which reason they were declared and said to live to God—then much more certainly [Col. 0936B] could death prevail in Christ only against the material of the body; it could not exercise itself against the divinity of the Word. For the power of death is broken where the authority of immortality intervenes.

[Note: [Col. 0936D] “Exercise itself.” With Latinius it should perhaps be read “put itself forth”; Welchman accepts this conjecture, though Jackson does not.]

## CHAPTER XXVI, alternatively XXI  
### Against the Sabellians, he proves from the Scriptures that the Son is one and the Father another

But because, on this occasion, Christ is proved by the sacred authorities of the Divine Writings to be not merely man but also God, other heretics break forth and attempt to undermine the established rule of religion concerning Christ, wishing by this very fact to show that Christ is God the Father, since he is asserted not merely to be man but is also declared to be God.

They argue as follows: If it is declared that there is one God, while Christ is God, then, they say, if the Father and Christ are one God, Christ will be called the Father. In this they are proved to err because they do not know Christ but approve only the sound of the name; for they refuse to recognize him as a second person after the Father, but make him the Father himself. Since they can be answered easily, only a few things will be said.

Who does not recognize that the person of the Son is second after the Father, when he reads what the Father then said to the Son:

> Let us make the human being according to our image and likeness. (Gen. 1:26–27)

and afterward finds it reported:

> And God made the human being; according to the image of God he made him?

Or when he has before him:

> The Lord rained fire and sulfur upon Sodom and Gomorrah from the Lord out of heaven? (Gen. 19:24)

Or when it is said to Christ:

> You are my Son; today I have begotten you. Ask [Col. 0936D] of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance and the ends of the earth as your possession. (Ps. 2:7–8)

[Note: [Col. 0936D] “To Christ.” If you listen to Jackson, perhaps the word “it is said” should be added here. But that is unnecessary, for shortly above he said “when he reads what was said … to the Son”; those same two words are to be understood here as well.]

Or when that much-desired scribe says:

> The Lord said [Col. 0937A] to my Lord: Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet. (Ps. 109:1)

Or when, unfolding Isaiah’s prophecies, he finds it written thus:

> Thus says the Lord to Christ, my Lord. (Isa. 45:1)

[Note: [Col. 0937C] “To Christ, my Lord.” Since the Septuagint had written Κύρῳ, “to Cyrus,” copyists, thinking that Isaiah was speaking of Christ Jesus and failing to attend to Cyrus, took the nearby word κυρίῳ, “to the Lord,” and corrupted this passage of Scripture long ago. Therefore Tertullian, *Against the Jews*, chapter 7, and *Against Praxeas*, chapters 11 and 28; Cyprian, *Testimonies*, book 1, chapter 21; NOVATIAN here; and very many Greeks and Latins cited by Jerome on this text, Isaiah 45:1, and on Habakkuk 3:13, read κυρίῳ and interpret it of Christ the Lord. Thus COTELERIUS on chapter 12 of the *Epistle of St. Barnabas*. See the annotations on this passage of Isaiah in volume I of this *Library of the Fathers*, p. 132.]

Or when he reads:

> I did not descend from heaven to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me. (John 6:38)

Or when he finds it written:

> For he who sent me is greater than I. (John 14:28)

Or when he considers what is written:

> I go to my Father and your Father, my God and your God. (John 20:17)

Or when he has this placed among the other texts:

> But in your law it is written that the testimony of two is true. I testify concerning myself, and the Father who sent me has testified concerning me. (John 8:17–18)

[Note: [Col. 0937D] “Placed.” Welchman thus corrected the faulty reading “spoken” in the preceding editions, and Jackson adhered to him. This certainly agrees with the preceding “written,” “set down,” and so forth. Shortly afterward, moreover, we read “is established.”]

Or when a voice answers from heaven:

> I have both glorified it and will glorify it. [Col. 0937B] (John 12:28)

Or when Peter answers and says:

> You are the Son of the living God. (Matt. 16:16)

Or when the mystery of this revelation is confirmed by the Lord himself and he says:

> Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jona, because flesh and blood did not reveal this to you, but my Father who is in heaven. (Matt. 16:17)

Or when Christ himself declares:

> Father, glorify me with the honor that I had with you before the world came to be. (John 17:5)

Or when the same one says:

> Father, I knew that you always hear me; but I said this because of those standing around, so that they may believe that you sent me. (John 11:42)

Or when the definition of the rule is established by Christ himself and he says:

> Now this is eternal life: that they may know you, the one and true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent. I have glorified you upon the earth; I have completed the work that you gave [Col. 0937C] me. (John 17:3–4)

Or when the same one again asserts and says:

> All things have been handed over to me by my Father. (Luke 10:22)

Or when his sitting at the Father’s right hand is confirmed both by the Prophets and by the Apostles (Ps. 109:1; Mark 16:9; Heb. 1:3)?

I make this quite lengthy if I strive to gather absolutely all the statements bearing upon this part of the argument, since divine Scripture throughout both the Old and the New Testament shows that he was born from the Father; that through him all things were made, and without him nothing was made; that he always obeyed [Col. 0938A] and obeys the Father; and that he always possesses power over all things, but possesses it as something handed over, something granted, something bestowed upon him by his own Father.

For what can be so evident in showing that he is not the Father but the Son as the fact that he is presented as obedient to God the Father? Otherwise, if he were believed to be the Father, Christ would then be said to be subject to another God the Father.

## CHAPTER XXVII, alternatively XXII  
### He answers elegantly the passage, “I and the Father are one,” which they used to press in support of their position
But because they frequently press upon us that passage in which it was said, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30), we shall defeat them just as easily on this point. For if, as the heretics suppose, Christ were the Father, he ought to have said [Note: [Col. 0938C] CHAPTER XXVII.—“I and the Father.” Thus the editions of Frobenius and Pamelius. Gagnaeus and Barrensis, however, read: “I, the Father, am one.” But the English editors read: “I, the Father, am one [person].” This appears to be the true reading, since it is repeated by Novatian himself [Col. 0938D] a little later.]: [Col. 0938B] “I, the Father, am one [person]” (John 10:30). [Note: [Col. 0938D] “But when.” Welchman, following Gagnaeus, reads: “But indeed, when.” Gelenius, however, on the authority of a British manuscript, and Pamelius after him, substituted: “But when.” JACKSON.] But when he says “I,” and then introduces the Father by saying, “I and the Father,” he separates and distinguishes the individuality of his own person—that is, of the Son—from the Father’s authority, not merely by the sound of the name but also by the ordering of the power that has been arranged. He could have said, “I, the Father,” if he had understood himself to be the Father.

And because he said “one” (*unum*), let the heretics understand that he did not say “one person” (*unus*). For *unum*, placed in the neuter, signifies concord in fellowship, not unity of person. He is said to be *unum*, not *unus*, because the expression does not refer to number but declares fellowship with another [Note: [Col. 0938D] “Declares” (*expromitur*). “Expresses” (*exprimitur*) is the more suitable reading; Welchman suspects that it should be read so. ID.]. Finally, he adds, “we are,” not “I am,” so that by what he said—“we are” [Note: [Col. 0938D] “We are, and the Father.” Thus the printed editions. Welchman thinks it should read, “We are, I and the Father.” Jackson accordingly restored it in his text, “with the author’s meaning as guarantor,” as he himself says.], and the Father—he might show that there are two persons.

The “one” of which he speaks pertains to concord, to the same judgment, and to that very fellowship of love [Col. 0938C] [Note: [Col. 0938D] “Pertains.” Thus Pamelius, following Latinius, in place of *to pertain* in the old editions; the English editors have also followed this correction.]; so that the Father and the Son are rightly one through concord, affection, and love. And because he is from the Father, whatever that is [Note: [Col. 0938D] “Whatever that is.” Here we follow Pamelius and the other editors who preceded him. Welchman, however, finding this reading difficult, printed “whoever he is.” “For there is nothing here,” he says, “to which ‘that’ can refer.” Jackson makes several other conjectures [Col. 0939D], which find less favor with us.], he is the Son—yet with the distinction remaining, so that the one who is the Son is not the Father, because neither is the one who is the Father the Son. For he would not have added “we are” if he had understood himself, being the one and solitary Father, to have become the Son.

Finally, the Apostle Paul also knows this unity of concord while preserving the distinction of persons. For when writing to the Corinthians, he says: “I [Col. 0939A] planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the increase. Therefore neither the one who plants is anything, nor the one who waters, but God who gives the increase. Now the one who plants and the one who waters are one” (1 Cor. 3:6–8). Who does not understand that Apollos is one person and Paul another, and that Apollos and Paul are not one and the same person? Their respective functions are even presented as different: one is the person who plants, and another the person who waters. Yet the Apostle Paul declared of these two, not that they were one person, but that they were one: so that Apollos is one and Paul another as regards the distinction of persons, but [Note: [Col. 0939D] “But as regards concord.” To complete a passage mutilated by the loss of one clause, I have added the words enclosed in parentheses, as being especially suited to the author’s argument and preceding language; and I do not doubt that these or similar words were omitted by a copyist because of the homoeoteleuton (*ὁμοιοτέλευτον*, similarity of endings) in *pertinet*. Latinius supplied more words as follows: “But as regards concord in one faith and judgment.” JACKSON.] (as regards concord), the two are one.

For when two persons have one judgment, one truth, one faith, one and the same religion, and one fear of God, they are one even though they are two; they are the same thing, because [Col. 0939B] they think the same thing. Those whom the principle of personhood divides from one another are in turn brought together by the principle of religion. And although they are not one and the same persons, because they think the same thing they are the same thing [Note: [Col. 0939D] “They are the same thing.” Thus Pamelius corrected from an English manuscript the reading “they are the same persons,” found in the preceding editions.]; and although they are two, they are one, sharing fellowship in faith even though they retain diversity of persons.

Finally, when Jewish ignorance was provoked by these words of the Lord and recklessly inflamed even to the point of taking up stones, so that they rushed about and said, “We do not stone you for a good work, but for blasphemy, and because you, although you are a man, make yourself God” (John 10:33), the Lord drew a distinction in explaining how he had either called himself God or wished himself to be understood as God. “Do you say of him whom the Father sanctified,” he says, “and sent into this world, ‘You blaspheme,’ because I said, ‘I am the Son of God’?” (ibid., v. 36). Here also [Col. 0939C] he said that he has a Father. He is therefore the Son, not the Father; for he would have confessed himself to be the Father if he had understood himself to be the Father. And he declares that he was sanctified by his Father.

Therefore, because he receives sanctification from the Father, he is less than the Father; and the one who is less than the Father is consequently [Note: [Col. 0939D] “Is consequently, but the Son.” I restore the plainly mutilated sentence as follows: “Consequently he is not the Father [Col. 0940D], but the Son.” Perhaps the word *ille*, occurring three times in close succession, confused a hurried copyist. WELCHMAN.—The same restoration also commends itself to Jackson.], not the Father, but the Son. For if he had been the Father, he would have given sanctification, not received it. And now, by declaring that he received sanctification from the Father, by this very fact [Note: [Col. 0940D] “By this very fact, by which—proves.” Pamelius supplied these words from an English manuscript codex, and Jackson reproduced Pamelius’s edition here. Welchman, however, omitted them along with the old editions.]—that by receiving sanctification from him he proves himself less than the Father—he showed himself to be the Son, not the Father.

Moreover, he says that he was sent, so that through this obedience by which the Lord Christ came, having been sent, he might be proved to be not the Father but the Son. He would certainly have sent someone if he had been the Father; but the Father was not sent, lest, by being sent, the Father should be proved subordinate to another God. [Col. 0940A]

And yet after this he adds something that should dissolve absolutely all ambiguity and extinguish the entire controversy arising from error. For in the final part of the discourse he says: “Do you say, ‘You blaspheme,’ because I said, ‘I am the Son of God’?” Therefore, if the Lord clearly testifies that he is the Son and not the Father, it is an example of great rashness and enormous madness to stir up a controversy concerning divinity and religion contrary to the testimony of the Lord Christ himself, and to say that Christ Jesus is the Father, when one observes that he proved himself to be not the Father but the Son.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. He proves that the statement, “He who sees me sees the Father also,” likewise does nothing for the Sabellians

I shall further add that passage too in which the heretic, while rejoicing as though in a certain eye [Note: [Col. 0940D] CHAPTER XXVIII.—“While the heretic,” etc. Welchman would prefer to read and punctuate the passage as follows: “While the heretic rejoices, as though in some eye of his own, etc.” Jackson reads it thus: “While the heretic rejoices as though in some eye, his own eye—‘eye’ being understood—of truth and light having been lost.”], with the eye of his own truth and light [Col. 0940B] having been lost, may recognize the total blindness of his error. For again and again he objects that it was said: “Have I been with you so long, and you do not know me? Philip, he who has seen me has seen the Father also” (John 14:9). But let him learn what he does not understand.

Philip is reproved, and indeed justly and deservedly, because he had said: “Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us” (ibid., v. 8). For when had he either heard or learned from Christ that Christ was the Father, when, on the contrary, he had repeatedly heard and often learned that he was the Son, not the Father? For when the Lord said, “If you have known me, you have known my Father also; and from now on you know him and have seen him” (John 14:7), he had not spoken in such a way as to wish himself to be understood as the Father. Rather, he meant that the person who has approached the Son of God deeply, fully, and with complete [Col. 0940C] faith and devotion will in every way come through the Son in whom he so believes to the Father, and will see him. For, he says, “No one can come to the Father except through me” (ibid., v. 6).

And therefore such a person will not merely come to God the Father and know the Father himself; he must also hold it so firmly, and anticipate it so confidently in heart and mind, as though he already knew and had seen the Father. For divine Scripture often announces as already done things that have not yet occurred, because they will occur; and things that must certainly happen it proclaims not as future events but recounts as though they had happened.

Thus, although Christ had not yet been born in the time of the prophet Isaiah, he said: “A child has been born [Note: [Col. 0940D] “For us.” Thus the English editors, in place of “for you” in the preceding editions.] for us” (Isa. 9:6). And although he had not yet gone in to Mary [Col. 0941A] (Isa. 8:3), he said, “I went in to [Note: [Col. 0941D] “The prophetess.” Thus the old printed editions, in agreement with the Vulgate; Welchman followed this reading. Pamelius reads “the prophet.” Jackson reads “the prophet,” regarding which Junius wishes “the prophetess” to be read.] the prophetess, and she conceived and bore a son.” And although Christ had not yet revealed the bosom of the Father, Scripture related: “And [Note: [Col. 0941D] “He shall be called.” This is the reading of the editions of Novatian. But, Jackson says, since the logic of the author’s argument requires “he is called” to be read, there is no doubt that Novatian himself wrote it so. Welchman had already made the same conjecture.] his name shall be called the Angel of Great Counsel” (ibid., 9:6). And although he had not yet suffered, it declared, as of a sheep: “He was led to slaughter” (ibid., 53:7). And although the cross did not yet exist anywhere, it said: “All day long I stretched out my hands to an unbelieving people” (ibid., 65:2). And although he had not yet been given the insulting drink, it says: “In my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink” (Ps. 68:22). And although he had not yet been stripped, it said: “They cast lots for my garment; they counted my bones; they pierced my hands and feet” (Ps. 21:19, 18, 17).

For divine Scripture, in its foreknowledge, speaks as accomplished of things it knows will come to pass, and speaks as completed [Col. 0941B] of things still future, because they will undoubtedly occur. And therefore the Lord said in the present passage: “From now on you know him and have seen him.” He meant that the Father would be seen by anyone who followed the Son—not that the Son himself was the Father who had been seen, but that whoever wished to follow him and to be his disciple would obtain the reward of being able to see the Father.

For he is also the image of God the Father. To this should also be added the fact that, just as the Father works, so too the Son works (John 5:17). The Son is the imitator of all the Father’s works, so that each person may regard himself as though he had already seen the Father when he sees the one who always imitates the invisible Father in all his works.

But if Christ himself is the Father, how does he immediately add and say: “He who believes in me will himself do the works that I do, and will do greater works than these, because I go to the Father” (John 14:12)? [Col. 0941C] And he further continues: “If you love me, keep my commandments; and I shall ask the Father, and he will give you another Advocate” (ibid., vv. 15–16). After this he also continues: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word; and my Father will love him, and we shall come to him and make our dwelling with him” (ibid., v. 23). He also [Note: [Col. 0941D] “Added.” Here and a little later Jackson contends that “adds” should be read, so that the discourse may cohere with what precedes and follows: “he adds,” “he says,” “he continues,” etc.] added this: “But that Advocate, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send, will teach you and remind you of everything whatsoever I have said” (ibid., v. 26).

He further introduces [Note: [Col. 0942D] “Introduces.” Thus the printed editions; less correctly, as it seems. Welchman restored “brings forth,” and perhaps Novatian wrote it so. Nor is Jackson’s conjecture, “brings forth and,” attractive merely because “further” follows.] this passage, by which he shows himself to be the Son, and rightly adds and says: “If you loved me, you would rejoice because I go to the Father, for the Father is greater than [Note: [Col. 0942D] “Than me.” Pamelius lacks this pronoun, which the others include.] I” (ibid., v. 28).

And what of his further addition: “I am [Col. 0941D] the true vine, and my Father is the cultivator; every branch in me that does not bear fruit he takes away, and every fruitful branch he cleanses, so that it may bear more fruit” (John 15:1–2)? He presses the point still further and adds: “As the Father loved me, [Col. 0942A] so I have loved you; remain in my love. If you keep my commandments, you will remain in my love, just as I have kept my Father’s commandments and remain in his love” (John 15:9–10). He continues to emphasize it, saying: “I have called you friends, because I have made known to you everything that I heard from my Father” (ibid., v. 15). He also adds this: “But they will do all these things to you because of my name, because they do not know him who sent me” (ibid., v. 21).

The Lord would never have added these statements after the earlier ones, which clearly testify that he is not the Father but the Son, if he had either understood himself to be the Father or wished himself to be understood as the Father. Rather, he wished to express that, when one sees the image of God the Father through the Son, one ought already to regard oneself just as if one had seen the Father. For everyone who believes in the Son is trained [Col. 0942B] in contemplation of the image, so that, becoming accustomed to seeing divinity in the image, one may advance and grow toward the perfect contemplation of God the almighty Father.

And the person who has absorbed this in heart and mind, and believes that all these things will indeed come to pass, has already in a certain sense seen the Father whom he is to see, and already regards himself here as possessing what he knows with certainty he will possess.

But if Christ himself had been the Father, why did he promise as a future reward what he had already bestowed and given? For because he says, “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8), he is found to promise the contemplation and sight of the Father. Therefore he had not yet given it; for why would he promise it if he had already given it? He had given it if he were the Father, for he was seen and touched. [Col. 0942C] But when Christ himself, while being touched and seen, nevertheless promises and says that the person who is pure in heart will see God, by this very fact he proves that he is not the Father: while present and visible, he promised that whoever was pure in heart would see the Father.

Therefore the one making these promises was not the Father but the Son, because, as the Son, he promised that which was yet to be seen. His promise would have been superfluous if he had not been the Son. For why did he promise the pure in heart that they would see the Father, if those who were then present were already seeing Christ the Father? But because he was the Son, not the Father, the Son, as the Image of God, was rightly seen at that time; while the Father, as invisible, is promised and appointed to be seen by the pure in heart.

Let it therefore suffice to have dictated these few points out of many against this heretic also. For a broad and expansive field would open if we wished to examine this heretic more fully, since [Note: [Col. 0942D] “His eyes having been gouged out by these two passages.” Namely John 10:30 and 14:9, in which, the author says, the heretic rejoiced as though in two eyes; but one of these was gouged out for him in this chapter, and the other in the immediately preceding chapter. WELCHMAN.—Since this interpretation is sufficiently clear to anyone who considers it carefully, there seems correspondingly no reason to accept Jackson’s opinion that the true reading is “with light poured forth,” which is presented by Wower’s manuscript.] deprived of those two passages as of certain lights that have been gouged out, [Col. 0943A] he is wholly overcome in the blindness of his doctrine.

## CHAPTER XXIX. He next teaches that the authority of faith admonishes us, after the Father and the Son, to believe also IN THE HOLY SPIRIT, whose operations he enumerates from the Scriptures

Moreover, the order of reason and the authority of Faith, as set forth in the words and writings of the Lord, admonish us after these things to believe also in the Holy Spirit, long ago promised to the Church but given at the appointed and fitting times. For he was promised through the prophet Joel but given through Christ. “In the last days,” he says, “I shall pour out of my Spirit upon my male and female servants” (Joel 2:28). But the Lord says: “Receive the Holy [Col. 0943B] Spirit; the sins of those whom you forgive shall be forgiven, and those of whom you retain them shall be retained” (Acts 2:17; John 20:22–23).

The Lord Christ at one time calls this Holy Spirit the Paraclete (John 14:16–17), and at another declares him to be the Spirit of truth. He is not new in the Gospel, nor was he newly given; for this same Spirit both accused the people through the Prophets and provided advocacy for the Gentiles through the Apostles. The former deserved to be accused because they had despised the Law; and those from among the Gentiles who believe deserve to be helped by the Spirit’s protection, because they strive to attain to the law of the Gospel.

There is indeed a difference among his kinds of service, because the circumstances of the causes differ at different times. Yet he himself is not [Note: [Col. 0943D] CHAPTER XXIX.—“Different.” Gagnaeus and Frobenius, whom Welchman followed, read “is divided.” “Different” derives from the English manuscript and should not be changed. JACKSON.] different because he performs these things in this way, nor is he another when he acts in this manner. Rather, he is one and the same, [Col. 0943C] distributing his services according to the times and to the occasions and critical moments of affairs.

Thus the Apostle Paul says: “Having the same Spirit, as it is written, ‘I believed, and therefore I spoke’; we too believe, and therefore we speak” (2 Cor. 4:13). Therefore it is one and the same Spirit who was in the Prophets and in the Apostles, except that there he was present for a time, but here permanently. There, moreover, it was not so that he would remain in them permanently; here, it was so that he would always remain in them. There he was distributed in moderate measure; here he was poured out in full. There he was given sparingly; here he was abundantly supplied.

Yet he was not manifested before the Lord’s resurrection, but was imparted [Note: [Col. 0944D] “After.” The logic of the passage requires this word, which Latinius restored in place of “through” in the printed editions. ID.] after Christ’s resurrection. For he said: “I shall ask the Father, and he will give you another Advocate, so that he may be with you forever, the Spirit of truth” (John 14:16–17). And: “When that Advocate comes, whom I shall send to you [Col. 0943D] from my Father, the Spirit of truth who proceeds from my Father” (John 15:26). And: “If I do not depart, that Advocate will not come to you; but if I depart, I shall send him to you” (John 16:7). And: “When the Spirit [Col. 0944A] of truth comes, he will guide you into all truth” (John 16:13).

And because the Lord was about to depart into heaven, he necessarily gave the Paraclete to his disciples, lest he should leave them in some sense as orphans—which would have been most unfitting—and abandon them without an advocate and a kind of guardian.

For it is he who strengthened their hearts and minds; he who distinguished the mysteries of the Gospel; he who among them was the illuminator of divine things. Strengthened by him for the Lord’s name, they feared neither prisons nor chains; indeed, they trampled upon the powers and tortures of the world itself, being now armed and strengthened by him and possessing within themselves the gifts that this same Spirit distributes and orders for the Church, the bride of Christ, as though they were ornaments.

For it is he who appoints Prophets in the Church, instructs Teachers, directs tongues, produces mighty works and healings, performs marvelous deeds, grants discernments of spirits, supplies forms of governance, suggests counsels, and arranges and orders all the other gifts of the charisms. He thus makes the Lord’s Church perfect and complete on every side and in all things. [Col. 0944B]

It is he who, in the form of a dove, came down upon the Lord after he had been baptized and remained upon him (Matt. 3:16), dwelling fully and wholly in Christ alone—not impaired in any measure or portion, but lavishly bestowed and sent with all his overflowing abundance [Note: [Col. 0944D] “Lavishly bestowed and sent.” Thus Pamelius from an English manuscript codex, a reading that appears genuine. Gagnaeus and Gelenius, whom Welchman followed, read “lavishly admitted.”]—so that others might obtain from him a certain share of the graces, while the fountain of the whole Holy Spirit remained in Christ, so that streams of gifts and works might be drawn from him, the Holy Spirit dwelling abundantly in Christ.

For Isaiah, already prophesying this, said: [Col. 0944C] “And [Note: [Col. 0944D] “Shall rest … shall fill.” The printed editions read “rests … has filled.” Pamelius suspects an error there. The English editors accordingly restored the text.] the Spirit of wisdom and understanding shall rest upon him, the Spirit of counsel and might, the Spirit of knowledge and godliness, and the Spirit of the fear of God shall fill him” (Isa. 11:2–3). The very same thing is also said elsewhere from the person of the Lord himself: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he anointed me; he sent me to preach the Gospel to the poor” (Isa. 61:1). Similarly David says: “Therefore God, your God, anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Ps. 44:8).

Concerning him the Apostle Paul says: “For if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him” (Rom. 8:9). And: “Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty” (2 Cor. 3:17).

It is he who effects the second birth from water—a kind of seed of the divine stock—and consecrates the heavenly birth; he is the pledge of the promised inheritance (Eph. 1:14), and a kind of written bond of eternal salvation.
