[Col. 0944D] It is he who makes us a temple of God (1 Cor. 6:19) and causes us to become his dwelling; who intercedes with the divine ears for us with inexpressible groanings (Rom. 8:26), fulfilling the offices of advocacy and providing the services of defense; [Col. 0945A] who is given to dwell within our bodies and brings about holiness.

By doing this within us, he brings our bodies toward eternity and toward the resurrection of immortality, as he accustoms them within himself to be mingled with heavenly power and associated with the divine eternity of the Holy Spirit. For in him and through him our bodies are trained to advance toward immortality, as they learn to govern themselves with moderation according to his decrees.

For it is he who desires against the flesh, because the flesh struggles against him (Gal. 5:17). It is he who restrains insatiable desires, breaks immoderate lusts, extinguishes illicit passions, conquers blazing impulses, rejects drunkenness, repels greed, drives away [Note: [Col. 0945C] “Drives away.” Thus Welchman correctly emended the editions’ “flees.” JACKSON.] luxurious banquets, binds together acts of love, unites affections, repels schisms, expounds the rule of truth, refutes heretics, [Col. 0945B] casts the wicked outside, and guards the Gospels.

Concerning him the same [Note: [Col. 0945C] “The same.” Thus Pamelius. Others read “likewise.”] Apostle says: “For we have not received the spirit of the world, but the Spirit who is from him” (1 Cor. 2:12). Concerning him he exults and says: “But I think that I too have the Spirit of God” (1 Cor. 7:40). Concerning him he says: “And the [Note: [Col. 0945C] “Spirit of the Prophets.” The author agrees with the common Latin translator, although the Greek today reads *πνεύματα* (“spirits”). PAMELIUS.] Spirit of the Prophets is subject to the prophets” (1 Cor. 14:32). Concerning him he relates: “But the Spirit plainly says that in the last times some will depart from the faith, attending to deceiving spirits and teachings of demons, through the hypocrisy of those who speak lies and have their own conscience seared” (1 Tim. 4:1).

No one situated in this Spirit ever says, “Anathema to Jesus” (1 Cor. 12:3). No one has denied that Christ is the Son of God or rejected God the Creator. No one puts forward any words of his own against the Scriptures. No one establishes different and sacrilegious decrees; [Col. 0945C] no one writes down contrary laws. Whoever blasphemes against this Spirit has no forgiveness, not only in this age but also in the age to come (Matt. 12:32).

It is he who bears witness to Christ in the Apostles, displays the steadfast faith of religion in the Martyrs, enfolds in Virgins the admirable continence of consecrated [Note: [Col. 0945D] “Chastity.” Thus Jackson correctly emended Welchman’s edition, which reads “love.”] chastity, and guards in all others the uncorrupted and undefiled laws of the Lord’s teaching. He destroys heretics, [Col. 0946A] corrects the perverse, convicts unbelievers, exposes pretenders, also corrects the wicked, and preserves the Church incorrupt and inviolate in the holiness of perpetual virginity and truth.

## CHAPTER XXX. Finally, how greatly the aforesaid heretics derived the origin of their error from observing that it is written, “One God”: even if we call Christ God and the Father God, Scripture nevertheless no more presents two Gods than it presents two Lords or two Masters

And [Note: [Col. 0945D] CHAPTER XXX.—“And these things,” etc. Pamelius complains here that Novatian does not call the Holy Spirit God and makes no mention of him when, in this chapter, the author demonstrates that the Father and the Son are one God. Novatian indeed does not expressly call the Holy Spirit God by name; but in the preceding chapter he does not remain silent concerning his divine eternity, and he proves by many arguments that he is God. For what is his purpose when he defends the Spirit’s divine attributes, if not to prove what he had promised to prove—namely, that one must believe also in the Holy Spirit, and consequently that he is one God with the Father and the Son? Hence also, after completing what he had determined to say concerning the Holy Spirit, he joins the three persons together at the beginning of this chapter: “And let these things concerning the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit have been stated briefly by us.” If Novatian seems to remain silent concerning the Spirit while showing that the Father and the Son are not two [Col. 0946C] Gods but one, the explanation must be sought nowhere else than in the fact that the entire effort of the heretics was directed toward overthrowing the Son’s divinity. For if they had once proved that the Son was not one God with the Father, [Col. 0946D] by the same operation they would have excluded the Holy Spirit from participation in the divine nature. Likewise, once it has been demonstrated that the Father and the Son are one God through communion of substance, as Novatian says, there would no longer remain any room to doubt that the divinity of the Holy Spirit by no means produces three Gods. MARAN, *The Divinity of Our Lord Jesus Christ*, book IV, chapter 19, § III, p. 521.] let these things concerning the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit have been stated by us briefly and set forth concisely, rather than extended through a lengthy discussion. For they could have been extended more broadly, and [Note: [Col. 0946D] “More extended” (*propensiore*). Jackson holds it certain that the author wrote *propansiore*. But the learned man is mistaken, since he attends only to the more common meaning of this word. For *propensus* is sometimes used to mean “extended,” the sense in which Novatian uses it here. Persius, *Satires* I, verse 57:

“When for you, bald man”

Let him stand out fat, with his paunch projecting a foot and a half.

That is: “Since you are fat from an abundance of food, and have a belly extended beyond six feet.”] be developed in a more extensive discussion; [Col. 0946B] since the whole of both the Old and the New Testament could be adduced as testimony that the true faith is thus constituted. But because heretics, always struggling against the truth, are accustomed to draw the pure tradition and the catholic faith into controversy, being scandalized at Christ because he is both declared by the Scriptures to be God and is believed by us to be so, we therefore rightly must discuss the fact that Christ is also God in such a way that it neither obstructs the truth of Scripture nor our faith, by which one God is [Note: [Col. 0946D] **Is brought forth.** Thus Welchman correctly reads, followed also by Jackson, in place of the editions’ *is promised*.] brought forth by the Scriptures and is held and believed by us.

For both those who say that Jesus Christ is himself God the Father, and those who have maintained that he is only a man, have seized upon the origins and causes [Col. 0946C] of their error and perversity from this: when they observed that it was written that there is one God, they thought that they could maintain this proposition in no other way than by believing Christ either to be merely a man or, alternatively, to be God the Father. For this is how they are accustomed to assemble their false accusations, so as to attempt to prove their own error.

Those who say that Jesus Christ is the Father put forward the following argument: If [Note: [Col. 0946D] **If there is one God.** This is the reading of Pamelius’s edition, which [Col. 0947C] Jackson reproduces. The older editions read: “If there is one Christ, but Christ,” etc.; and Welchman retained that reading.] there is one God, and Christ is [Col. 0947A] God, then Christ is the Father, because there is one God; for if Christ is not the Father, then, since Christ the Son is also God, two Gods would appear to have been introduced contrary to the Scriptures. Those, however, who contend that Christ is only a man argue contrariwise as follows: If the Father is one and [Note: [Col. 0947D] **The Son is.** I think that *is* must certainly be read as *and*, so that the argument may proceed properly. A little later, in place of *and if* I should prefer *but if*; I change nothing, however. JACKSON.] the Son another, while the Father is God and Christ is God, then not one God but two gods are introduced equally, the Father and the Son; and if there is one God, it follows that Christ is a man, so that the Father may rightly be the one God.

In truth the Lord is crucified, as it were, between two thieves, just as he once was fastened to the cross; and thus from either side he receives the sacrilegious abuse of these heretics. But neither the Holy Scriptures nor we ourselves furnish them with causes for their destruction and blindness, if they either refuse to see, [Col. 0947B] or are unable to see, the things plainly set forth in the midst of the divine writings. For we both know and read and believe and maintain that there is one God, who made heaven and earth alike, because we know no other, nor shall we ever be able to know another, since none exists. “I am,” he says, “God, and besides me there is no one just and saving” (Isa. 43:11). And elsewhere: “I am the first [Note: [Col. 0947D] **And the last.** *I* appears to have fallen out, and with Jackson the text should read, “and I am the last,” as the Hebrew, Septuagint, and Vulgate have it.] and the last, and besides me there is no God. Who is like me?” (ibid. 44:6–7). And: “Who has measured heaven with his palm, and the earth with his fist? Who has suspended the mountains in a balance, and the forests in scales?” (ibid. 40:12). And Hezekiah says: “That all may know that you alone are God” (Isa. 37:20). The Lord himself, moreover, says: “Why do you question me about what is good? One God is good” (Matt. 19:17). The apostle Paul likewise says: “Who alone possesses immortality and dwells in inaccessible light; whom no human being [Col. 0947C] has seen or can see” (1 Tim. 6:16). And elsewhere: “Now a mediator is not of one; but God is one” (Gal. 3:20).

But just as we maintain and read and believe this, [Note: [Col. 0947D] **Thus, of the Scriptures.** So Pamelius and others. Welchman alone reads and punctuates this passage as follows: “If we ought to pass over no part of the heavenly Scriptures?” Less correctly, it would seem.] so we ought to pass over no part of the heavenly Scriptures, since we must in no way reject those marks of Christ’s divinity that are set forth in the Scriptures, lest, by corrupting the authority of Scripture, we be found to have corrupted the integrity of the holy faith. Let us therefore also believe this, [Note: [Col. 0947D] **Since.** Latinius reads *namely*. But without cause. For *since* sometimes has the same meaning as *inasmuch as*, in which sense it fits this passage perfectly. Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* I.1: “The most ancient learned class is that of the poets, since Homer and Hesiod lived before the foundation of Rome.” The same author, *Letters* IX.12: “I congratulate our Baiae, since, as you write, they have suddenly become healthful.”] since it is most faithful: that the Son of God, Jesus Christ, [Col. 0948A] is our Lord and God; because “in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with [Note: [Col. 0947D] **With God.** Thus we have restored the text with Jackson. In place of *with God*, the editions have *God*; and Welchman adopted that reading. [Col. 0948C]] God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God” (John 1:1–2). And: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (ibid. 1:14). And: “My Lord and my God” (John 20:28). And: “Whose are the fathers, and from whom is Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed forever” (Rom. 9:5).

What, then, shall we say? Does Scripture present two Gods? How, then, does it say that God is one? Or is Christ not also God? How, then, was it said to Christ, “My Lord and my God”? Therefore, unless we maintain all this with its proper reverence and legitimate [Note: [Col. 0948C] **Discussion.** Jackson thinks that *arrangement* should be read. [Col. 0948D] For Novatian himself speaks in this way above, at the end of chapter 15, where, in an argument to the same effect, we read “legitimate arrangement.” A little later the same English editor restored *we shall be believed* in place of the preceding editions’ *we shall believe*.] discussion, we shall rightly be believed to have furnished the heretics with an occasion for stumbling—not, certainly, through any fault in the heavenly Scriptures, [Col. 0948B] which never deceive, but through the presumption of human error, by which they chose to become heretics [Note: [Col. 0948D] **By which.** The old codices read *because*, followed by Welchman. But *by which* is the reading of the English manuscript restored by Pamelius, and it agrees properly with *presumption*, as Jackson correctly observes.].

First of all, the following argument must be turned back against those who presume to raise against us the controversy of two Gods. It is written, as they cannot deny, that there is one Lord (Deut. 6:4; Eph. 4:5). What, then, do they think about Christ? That he is Lord, or that he is altogether not [Note: [Col. 0948D] **Lord.** Welchman thinks the text should read: “that he is Lord, or that he is altogether not so”; this also commends itself to Jackson.] Lord? But they do not at all doubt that he is Lord. Therefore, if their reasoning is true, there are now two Lords. How, then, according to the Scriptures, is there one Lord [Note: [Col. 0948D] **Lord? And Christ is called the one Teacher.** Thus the English editors read and punctuate. Others: “The Lord and Teacher, Christ, is called one.”]? And Christ is called the one Teacher (Matt. 23:8, 10); yet we read that the apostle Paul is also a teacher (2 Tim. 1:11). Therefore there is no longer one teacher, for on this basis we infer two teachers. How, then, according to the Scriptures, [Col. 0948C] is Christ the one Teacher?

In the Scriptures God is called the one who is good (Matt. 19:17; Mark 10:18; Luke 18:19); but [Note: [Col. 0948D] **In the same.** Thus Welchman correctly reads with Jackson. Others: *the same*.] in the same Scriptures Christ too is set forth as good. Therefore, if their inference is correct, there is not one who is good, but two who are good. How, then, according to the faith of the Scriptures, is there said to be one who is good? But if they do not think [Note: [Col. 0948D] **But if.** Thus the older editions, with which Welchman and Jackson agree.] that the statement that there is one Lord can in any way be impaired by the fact that Christ also is Lord; nor the statement that there is one Teacher by the fact that Paul too is a teacher; nor [Note: [Col. 0948D] **Nor that.** This is the reading of Gelenius and Pamelius from the [Col. 0949C] British manuscript, followed by Jackson. But Welchman, following Gagnaeus, reads *neither that*. A little later Jackson would prefer to read *is called*, as Novatian has it in the other instances.] the statement that there is one [Col. 0949A] who is good by the fact that Christ too is called good: by the same reasoning let them understand that the statement that there is one God cannot be impaired [Note: [Col. 0949C] **By the statement that there is one God.** Thus all the editions except Welchman’s alone, where the text reads: “the statement that there is one God, by the fact that God.”] by the fact that Christ too has been declared God.

## CHAPTER XXXI

**That the Son of God is God, eternally begotten of God the Father, who has always been in the Father; that he is a second person from the Father, who does nothing without the Father’s decision; that he is also Lord and the Angel of the great counsel of God, to whom the Father’s divinity has been imparted through communion of substance.**

God the Father, therefore, is the founder and creator of all things, alone knowing no origin, invisible, immeasurable, immortal, eternal, the one God; and nothing, I would say, can be placed above, or even compared with, [Col. 0949B] his greatness, majesty, or power [Note: [Col. 0949C] **CHAPTER XXXI.—From whom, when he himself willed.** St. Hippolytus discusses this passage more fully in *Against Noetus*, chapter 11, from which Novatian perhaps borrowed these things. See [Col. 0949D] volume II of our *Library of the Fathers*, p. 460A, and the annotations made there.].

From him, when he himself willed, the Word, his Son, was born. This Word is not to be understood as the sound of air struck or as the tone of a voice forced from the viscera; rather, he is recognized in the substance of a power brought forth from God. The mysteries of his sacred and divine birth neither an apostle learned, nor a prophet discovered, nor an angel knew, nor a creature recognized; they are known to the Son alone, who has known the Father’s secrets.

He, therefore, since he was begotten by the Father, is always in the Father. I say “always,” however, in such a way as to prove that he is not unbegotten but begotten. Yet he who exists before all time must be said always to have been in the Father, for no time can be assigned to him who exists before time. He is always in the Father, lest the Father should not always be Father; [Note: [Col. 0949D] **Indeed.** Thus the old editions read, and both English editors reproduced that reading. Pamelius restored *because* from the British manuscript.] indeed, [Note: [Col. 0949D] **The Father . . . must precede.** Pamelius attests that the words we have enclosed in parentheses were absent from the English manuscript and that Gagnaeus first added them for explanatory purposes, lest the author appear to favor the Arians. They are also found in Froben’s edition, perhaps from Gagnaeus. Welchman accordingly retained them as well. Maran did no differently in *The Divinity of Our Lord Jesus Christ*, book IV, chapter 19, §2, p. 518. Bull, however, in *Defence of the Nicene Faith*, section III, §7, p. 222, and Jackson omitted all these words.] the Father also precedes him (in a certain respect), since it is necessary that he should be (in a certain manner) prior insofar as he is Father. For (in some sense) it is necessary that he who knows no origin should precede him who has an origin. At the same time, [Note: [Col. 0949D] **At the same time . . . who alone has no origin, he is born.** We could not refrain from supplying from the English manuscript this previously missing sentence, which must nevertheless be read cautiously. PAMELIUS.—Welchman omitted the same sentence; Jackson restored it, following Pamelius. [Col. 0950C]] the latter is lesser inasmuch as he knows himself to be in the former, having an origin because he is born; and through the Father, in a certain manner (although [Col. 0950A] he has an origin insofar as he is born), [Note: [Col. 0950D] **Near.** Thus Pamelius, from the corrupt word *neighbors* presented by the English manuscript. The conjecture of the learned man cited by Jackson, who reads *divine*, is less satisfactory.] near in birth, since he is born from that Father who alone has no origin.

He, therefore, when the Father willed, proceeded from the Father; and he who was in the Father proceeded from the Father; and he who was in the Father, because he was from the Father, was thereafter with the Father, because he proceeded from the Father: namely, that divine substance whose name is the Word, through whom all things were made and without whom nothing was made. For all things are after him because all things are through him. And rightly he is himself before all things, [Note: [Col. 0950D] **But after the Father.** Pamelius attests that these words, and those that soon follow after the word *constituting*—“after the Father insofar as he is Son”—occur in the English manuscript. “But,” he says, “we preferred to leave them in the text, so that no one might derive from it an occasion for error. Nevertheless, against the Arians the statement ‘For he is always in the Father, lest the Father should not always be Father’ is meanwhile sufficient, as is what he says not far from the end of this chapter: ‘He received the beginning of his birth before all time.’ From this it is evident that when he says that the Father precedes, is prior, and goes before, he understands this only, as he adds, insofar as he is Father. In the same manner, therefore, must be understood what he again says: ‘He was thereafter with the Father . . . but after the Father . . . after the Father insofar as he is Son.’”] but after the Father, when all things were made through him who proceeded from him by whose will all things were made. God indeed proceeding from God, constituting a second person after the Father insofar as he is Son, yet not taking away from the Father the fact that there is one God.

For if he had not been born—if one unbegotten were compared with another who [Note: [Col. 0950D] **Were.** Here, and a little later where we read *had not been begotten*, Welchman conjectured that *is* should be read. Jackson printed it thus.] was unbegotten—the equality displayed in both would make two unbegotten beings and therefore two Gods. If he had not been begotten, then, when compared with him who had not been begotten, and when the two were found equal, they would rightly have constituted two unbegotten Gods; and thus Christ would have constituted two Gods. If he were found to be without origin like the Father and were himself the beginning of all things like the Father, then, by making two beginnings, he would consequently have shown us two Gods as well. Or if he himself were not the Son but a Father generating another Son from himself, then, when rightly compared with the Father and shown to be as great as he, he would have made two Fathers and thus would also have established two Gods. [Note: [Col. 0950D] **If he had been invisible . . . because he is not unbegotten.** We supplied from the aforesaid English codex these two and a half sentences, which were missing from the preceding editions, omitting the printed words, “But Christ is not unbegotten,” and adding from those same printed editions the words, “but he is from the Father, because he was begotten.” PAMELIUS.—That is, the editions preceding Pamelius’s read after the words “and thus would also have established two Gods” as follows: “But Christ is not unbegotten; rather, he is from the Father, because he was begotten.” Welchman reproduced the old copies; Jackson, Pamelius’s text. [Col. 0951C]] If he had been invisible, then, when compared with the invisible one and represented as his equal, he would have shown two invisible beings, and therefore would also have established two Gods. If he were incomprehensible, [Col. 0950C] or possessed any of the other attributes belonging to the Father, then, we say, he would rightly have raised the controversy about two Gods which these people fabricate.

As it is, however, whatever he is, he is not from himself, because he is not unbegotten; rather, he is from the Father because he was begotten. Whether he is the Word, [Col. 0951A] or Power, or Wisdom, or Light, or Son, and whichever of these he is, since he is from no other source than the Father, as we have already said above, and owes his origin to his Father, he could not create through the number of two Gods a division within the Godhead, since by being born he derived his origin from him who is the one God. By this manner, since he is both the Only-begotten and the Firstborn from him who has no origin, he [Note: [Col. 0951C] **He.** Welchman thinks that *one* should be read.] is the one beginning and head of all things. For this reason [Note: [Col. 0951C] **For this reason.** With Gagnaeus we supply: “For this reason it”—namely, Scripture—“asserted one God,” and, from the English manuscript, “the beginning and source” rather than “a beginning and source.” PAMELIUS.] Scripture asserted one God, whom it established not as being under any beginning or source, but rather as the beginning and source of all things.

[Note: [Col. 0951C] **The Son.** We again read with Gagnaeus, “But the Son does nothing by his own decision,” in place of what Gelenius had substituted: “This, finally, is the same as doing nothing.” PAMELIUS.] But the Son does nothing by his own decision, nor acts by his own counsel, nor comes from himself, but obeys all his Father’s commands and precepts. Thus, although his birth proves him to be the Son [Col. 0951B] (Heb. 5:8), nevertheless his dutiful obedience declares him to be the minister of the Father’s will, from whom he exists. In this way, by showing himself obedient to the Father in all things, although he is also God, he nevertheless shows by his obedience that God the Father, from whom he also drew his origin, is one. And therefore he could not make two [Note: [Col. 0951D] **Gods.** This word, omitted by the editions, was first restored by Welchman, followed by Jackson.] Gods, because he did not make two origins, since from him who has no origin he received the beginning of his birth before all time.

[Note: [Col. 0951D] **For since . . . while he who is born from him.** We again supply these words from the English manuscript, inserting parentheses. PAMELIUS.] For since the unbegotten is the beginning of the rest (and God the Father alone is outside origin; from him comes this one who was born), while he who is born from him rightly comes from him who has no origin, thereby proving that the one from whom he himself exists is the beginning—even though the one who was born is God, he nevertheless shows that there is one God, whom this one who was born established as being without origin.

He is therefore God, but begotten precisely in order [Col. 0951C] to be God. He is also Lord, but [Note: [Col. 0951D] **Born.** This word is absent from Pamelius, perhaps through the printer’s carelessness, for the others have it.] born [Col. 0952A] from the Father precisely in order to be Lord. He is also the Angel (Isa. 9:6), but an Angel appointed by his Father to announce God’s great counsel. [Note: [Col. 0951D] **Whose . . . by inequality of divinity.** Pamelius restored these words from the English manuscript. Gagnaeus and Froben printed: “so that there should be no dissonance of divinity”; Welchman retained that reading.] His divinity is imparted in such a way [Note: [Col. 0951D] **So that neither by dissonance nor by inequality.** I shall candidly confess that in these words I think *equality* should be read. For with equal care the author excludes both things from the most holy Trinity: discrepancy in nature and substance, and equality in the order of origin. He therefore admits a communion of substance between Father and Son, and believes this to consist in the fact that the entire authority of the Godhead, though imparted to the Son, does not cease to remain in the Father. Yet he always maintains most rigorously that the Son, as begotten by the Father, is not equal in origin to the Father. Accordingly, he interprets Paul’s words in Philippians 2:6, “He did not consider it robbery to be equal with God,” as follows: “Although he remembered himself to be God from God the Father, he never compared or equated himself with God the Father, remembering that he was from his Father and that he possessed the very thing which he is because the Father had given it.” MARAN, *The Divinity of Our Lord Jesus Christ*, book IV, chapter 19, §2, p. 519. [Col. 0952C–D]] that he may not appear to have produced two Gods either by dissonance or by inequality of divinity.

For when all things are subjected to him by the Father, as to the Son, and he himself, together with the things subjected to him, is subjected to his Father (1 Cor. 15:28), he is proved to be the Son of his Father, but is found to be both Lord and God of all other things. Hence, when all things are delivered in subjection to him who is God, and the Son refers everything he has received in subjection to himself back to the Father, he in turn [Note: [Col. 0952D] **Refers it back to the Father; one.** Thus Pamelius. The older editions, followed by Welchman, read, “refers it back to him; hence one.”] refers the entire authority of the Godhead back to the Father. Thus the one true and eternal God, the Father, is shown: from him alone this power of divinity was sent forth, imparted and directed even into the Son, and it returns [Col. 0952B] again to the Father through communion of substance.

The Son is indeed shown to be God, since divinity is seen to have been imparted and extended to him; and nevertheless God the Father is proved to be one, since by successive stages and a reciprocal movement that majesty and divinity, sent back from the Son himself, again returns and is directed to the Father who had given it. Thus God the Father is rightly the God of all things [Note: [Col. 0952D] **And the beginning even of his own Son.** Pamelius supplied these words from the English manuscript. Immediately afterward Welchman thinks that *begot as God* should be read, with Jackson agreeing. A little later Latinius reads *is Lord*.], and the beginning even of his own Son, whom he begot as Lord; while the Son is God of all other things, because God the Father placed the one whom he begot over all things (1 Tim. 2:5). Thus Christ Jesus, the Mediator of God and humanity, having from his own Father all creation’s power subjected to himself insofar as he is God, and being found in harmony with his God and Father while the whole creation is subjected to him, briefly established his Father as the one, sole, and true [Col. 0952C] God, [Note: [Col. 0952D] **Remaining in him.** The passage appeared very obscure to Pamelius and, so far as can be seen, mutilated or corrupt. Gagnaeus read, “him remaining in himself because he heard from him.” Welchman thought that, by adding a single letter and reading *the one remaining* in place of *remaining*, the sentence proceeded correctly and that the author alluded to Hebrews 5:7 in the words “he was heard.” In Jackson, however, a learned man conjectured that the text should be restored as, “remaining also in him, to whom he is also subjected”; yet that reading seems to depart too far from the wording of the exemplar.] remaining in him in that he was also heard (Heb. 5:7).

[Col. 0953]

# LETTER ON JEWISH FOODS (C)

## CHAPTER I

**Novatian, a Roman presbyter, while in his place of retirement during the Decian persecution, was prompted by various letters from the brethren to publish against the Jews—after the two preceding Letters, *On Circumcision* and *On the Sabbath*—this Letter as well, *On Jewish Foods*.**

[Col. 0953A]

Even if, most holy brothers, that day on which I receive your letters and writings is for me the most longed-for of days and one to be numbered among the foremost and blessed—what else, indeed, could now make me [Note: [Col. 0953C] **Freer.** Thus Pamelius. Latinius would prefer *more cheerful*.] freer?—nevertheless, I think no less distinguished a day, and one to be reckoned among the exceptional, [Note: [Col. 0953C] **On which.** This is the reading of Gelenius and Pamelius. Welchman reads *because*, less correctly. Immediately afterward Jackson printed *affections*. “For the sense,” he says, “appears to be: ‘returning similar affections to you.’” But the received reading is clearer. For I think that the word *similar* refers to the letters mentioned shortly before. [Col. 0953D]] on which, returning to you similar letters with the affection of the love I owe you, I too write letters to you with a corresponding desire.

For nothing, most holy brothers, holds me bound by such great [Col. 0953B] bonds, nothing rouses and agitates me with such sharp goads of cares and anxieties, as the fear that you may think some loss has been inflicted upon you through my absence. I endeavor to provide a remedy for this by laboring to make myself present to you through frequent letters. Although, therefore, both the duty I owe, the charge I have undertaken, and the very office of ministry laid upon me demand from me this necessity of writing letters, you nevertheless intensify it still more when you urge me to write by your more frequent letters; and although I am already inclined toward these solemn offices of love, you drive me on still further by showing that you persevere without ceasing in the Gospel. From this it follows that in my letters I do not so much instruct you, since you are already taught, as spur you on, since you are ready.

For you who not only hold the pure Gospel, separated [*excretum*] [Col. 0953C] from every stain of perverse doctrine, but also teach it courageously, do not seek a human master, since by your deeds themselves you show yourselves to be teachers. Therefore I exhort you as you run, awaken you as you keep watch, address you as you fight against the spiritual forces of wickedness (Eph. 6:12), and urge you forward as you strive in the race toward the [Note: [Col. 0953D] **Prize.** Pamelius’s edition of 1635 has *bravium*; Froben’s and the other Pamelian editions likewise have *bravium*. So too both English editors. Immediately afterward Jackson printed “upward” in place of “race,” with an eye to the Greek of Philippians 3:14, [Col. 0954C] τῆς ἄνω κλήσεως, “of the upward calling,” where the Vulgate has “of the heavenly calling.” A little later the same Jackson suspects that *and worthily* should be read.] prize of the calling in Christ (Phil. 3:14), so that, trampling upon and rejecting both the sacrilegious false accusations of the heretics and the idle fables of the Jews, [Col. 0954A] you may hold solely to the tradition and teaching of Christ and so be able worthily to claim for yourselves the authority of that name.

How perverse the Jews are, and how estranged from the understanding of their own Law, [Note: [Col. 0954C] **In the two preceding letters.** One, namely, *On the Sabbath*, and the other *On Circumcision*, which Jerome mentions in *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 70. But these have long since [Col. 0954D] perished.] I believe I demonstrated fully in the two preceding letters. In them it was proved that they are altogether ignorant of what true circumcision is and what the true Sabbath is. Their blindness is refuted still more and more in this letter, in which something is briefly discussed concerning their foods; for on this basis they consider themselves alone holy and everyone else defiled.

## CHAPTER II

**He first teaches that the Law is spiritual, and therefore—since the first food of humanity was solely the fruit of trees, and the use of flesh was subsequently added—the Law that followed later, distinguishing foods, permitting certain animals as though clean and prohibiting others as though unclean, must be understood spiritually. This is especially so because all things were pronounced very good, and even the unclean animals were preserved for offspring in Noah’s ark; otherwise they could have been removed, if they ought to have been abolished because of their defilement.**

[Col. 0954B]

Therefore, first of all it must be laid down that the Law is spiritual (Rom. 7:14). If they deny that it is spiritual, they certainly blaspheme; if, [Note: [Col. 0954D] **Avoiding.** Thus Pamelius correctly reads with Gelenius. Welchman, following Gagnaeus, printed the corrupt word *designating*. JACKSON.] avoiding blasphemy, they acknowledge it as spiritual, let them read it spiritually. For divine things must be received divinely, and holy things must certainly be maintained as holy. Otherwise a grave fault is branded upon us if an earthly and human doctrine is attributed to the sacred and spiritual writings; [Col. 0954C] care must be taken that this does not happen.

It can be avoided if the things commanded by God are treated in such a way that the interpretations adopted do not diminish his authority; [Note: [Col. 0954D] **Lest while.** Thus Pamelius and others. Welchman, following Gagnaeus, reads *but while*.] lest, while certain things are called impure and unclean, their creation should render their Creator infamous. For by rejecting what he made, he will appear to have condemned his own works, which he had approved as good; and in either case he will be marked as inconsistent—which, indeed, is how the heretics wish [Note: [Col. 0954D] **Wish, he will be marked as appearing.** We punctuate thus with [Col. 0955C] Jackson; Welchman also conjectured this. Others punctuate: “wish to appear; he will be marked.” [Col. 0955D]] him to appear—because he either blessed things that were not clean, or later rejected as not good what he had blessed as both clean and good, precisely because they were unclean. The consequent enormity and controversy will remain perpetual if this Jewish doctrine persists, and it must be cut away with all our strength, [Note: [Col. 0955D] **So that, while something.** Welchman thinks the text should read “so that what is monstrously”; Jackson, “so that whatever.”] so that whatever is monstrously handed down by them may be removed by us, and a fitting ordering of his works, together with the harmonious and spiritual inference of the divine [Note: [Col. 0955D] **Law.** Thus Pamelius’s edition of 1635. Others prefer *of the Law*. Immediately afterward Latinius restores *are retained* in place of *may be restored*, a reading approved by Jackson.] Law, may be restored.

But to begin from the commencement of things, and from the point where one ought to begin: for the first human beings the sole food was the produce and fruit of trees (Gen. 1:29). [Note: [Col. 0955D] **For the first.** Thus the Pamelian editions of 1617, 1635, and 1662; this seems to be the true reading. Others: *first*.] For afterward guilt transferred their use from fruit to crops, the very posture of the body confirming the condition of their conscience [Note: [Col. 0955D] **Posture of the body.** Because the body bends downward toward the earth in sowing and harvesting crops. JACKSON.]. Innocence raised human beings—who were to pluck their food from trees and were still conscious of their own rectitude—upward toward higher things; but the transgression they had committed cast them down toward the earth and soil to seek grain.

Afterward the use of flesh was also added (ibid. 9:3), divine grace providing kinds of food suited to human needs [Note: [Col. 0955D] **Altogether at appropriate times.** Thus Pamelius and others. Others omit *altogether*.] altogether at appropriate times. For a milder food was bound to nourish tender and uncultivated human beings, [Note: [Col. 0955D] **And prepared not without labor.** This is the Pamelian reading. But something appears to be missing that would complete the sense; perhaps it should be supplied thus: “and those more advanced”—understand: “were bound to be nourished by food”—“prepared not without . . .”] and food prepared not without labor was intended for correction, lest it should again please them to sin if the labor imposed upon them did not remind them of their innocence. And because it was now no longer Paradise that had to be tended, but the entire world that had to be cultivated, the stronger food of flesh was offered, so that something more might be added to the strength of human bodies for the benefits of cultivation.

All these things occurred, as I have said, by divine grace and ordering, lest either food insufficiently strengthening be supplied, so that those filled by it would grow feeble in their labors, [Col. 0955C] or food excessively tender, by which they would be so burdened in proportion to their strength that they could not bear it. But the Law, which came afterward, ordered foods of flesh by making distinctions. It assigned and permitted certain animals for [Note: [Col. 0955D] **Use.** Isidore of Seville, who copied many passages from this work of Novatian in chapter IX of his *Commentary* [Col. 0956C] on Leviticus, reads *eating*. Our Venerable Bede likewise reads it so twice, and this seems the authentic reading. Immediately afterward Isidore of Seville has, “but prohibited certain others.” JACKSON.] use, as though clean; others it prohibited, as though unclean and liable to defile those who ate them. It established this rule for clean animals: those which chew the cud and divide the hoof are clean; those which do neither of these things, or only one, are unclean (Lev. 11:3–4). Likewise, among fish, [Note: [Col. 0956D] **Only those.** We have followed Jackson, who restored the text thus from Wower’s manuscript. Others: *the same*.] only those covered with scales and equipped with fins were to be clean (Lev. 11:10), [Col. 0956A] while those of the contrary kind were unclean. It also introduced a distinction among birds (ibid., v. 13), [Note: [Col. 0956D] **What each.** The English editors think that *so that*, or *by which each*, should be read.] determining what was to be judged rejected and what clean.

Thus the Law instituted the most elaborate care in making distinctions among animals, whereas the ancient creation had brought them all together under one form of blessing. What, then, shall we say? Are they, then, unclean [Note: [Col. 0956D] **Are they then unclean animals?** Thus Pamelius and Jackson after Latinius. But Welchman, adhering to Froben’s edition, reads: “Are they then unclean animals—for what else does ‘unclean’ mean?—which the Law separated from use as food?” A little afterward the same Welchman, copying Gagnaeus, printed *by command*. We have, however, omitted the preposition, following Pamelius and others.] animals? For what else does “unclean” mean than those which the Law separated from use as food?

And what follows from what we have already said? Is God, then, the creator of unclean things, and will the blame for the things made rebound upon the craftsman who produced unclean things? To say this is surely the height and extreme of madness: to accuse God as though he had created unclean things, and to charge the divine majesty with a crime as though it had made things worthy of rejection. This is especially so since they were both pronounced very good (Gen. [Col. 0956B] 1:31), and, because they were good, they received from God himself the blessing that they should increase and multiply.

Moreover, at the Creator’s command they were preserved in Noah’s ark for the propagation of their kind (ibid. 7:2), so that they might be proved necessary because they were preserved, and good because they were necessary, although there too a [Note: [Col. 0956D] **Distinction was added.** We have restored the text thus with the English editors. Others: “an accusation was attached.”] distinction was added. Yet even then the creation of those unclean animals could have been entirely removed, if it [Note: [Col. 0956D] **Ought to have been.** Welchman thinks *they ought to have been* should be read. Jackson agrees.] ought to have been abolished because of its defilement.

## CHAPTER III

**Unclean animals, therefore, are not to be blamed, lest the blame be referred back to their Creator. Rather, whenever an irrational animal is rejected for some characteristic, that very characteristic is condemned still more in a human being, who is rational. Accordingly, human manners, actions, and dispositions are depicted in the animals.**
[Col. 0956C] In what way, then—as we have shown on the Apostle’s authority—is this spiritual Law to be received spiritually, so that the rationale of the Law may be upheld as divine and certain? First, it must be believed that whatever has been instituted by God is clean and purified by the very authority of its institution; nor must it be blamed, lest the blame be referred back to its Author. Next, the Law was given to the children of Israel so that through it they might make progress and return to the good morals which, [Note: [Col. 0956D] *Which they had received from the Fathers*: Isidore has, “which they had previously received from the Fathers.” JACKSON.] though they had received them from the Fathers, they had corrupted in Egypt through familiarity with a barbarous nation. Finally, even those Ten Words on the tablets teach nothing new, [Col. 0957A] but recall what had been forgotten, so that righteousness within them, like fire, might be rekindled after lying dormant, as though by a breath from the Law. They could indeed make progress by understanding that vices were to be shunned more fully in human beings when the Law had condemned them even in cattle. For when an irrational animal is rejected for some reason, that very fault is condemned all the more in a rational being, namely man. [Note: [Col. 0957C] *And if in it … is found.* I restored this entire passage, corrupted in all the printed editions, to soundness from Wower’s manuscript. The editions had: “And if in that which has something by nature it is marked as though with defilement, it is more blameworthy when that is complained of in man contrary to nature.” [Col. 0957D] JACKSON.] And if something that it possesses by nature is marked in it as though it were a defilement, it is more blameworthy when that same thing is found in man contrary to nature. Therefore, so that human beings [Note: [Col. 0957D] *Might be cleansed … might be reckoned.* Isidore has *might be thoroughly cleansed … that is, so that all who possessed the same vices might be regarded as equal to cattle*. ID.] might be cleansed, cattle were censured—that is, so that human beings who possessed the same vices might also be reckoned equal to cattle. In this way it came about that the animals were not condemned by their Institutor through any fault of their own, while human beings, instructed through the cattle, could return to the spotless nature belonging to their own creation. [Col. 0957B]

For we must consider how the Law distinguishes clean from unclean. The clean, it says, both chew the cud and divide the hoof; the unclean do neither, or do only one of the two. One craftsman made all these creatures, and the one who made them also blessed them. I therefore perceive that the original constitution of both kinds is clean, because the one who instituted them is holy, and the things instituted bear no fault so long as they are what they were made to be. For it is never nature, but a perverse will, that is accustomed to incur guilt.

What, then, is the meaning? Human morals, actions, and [Note: [Col. 0957D] *Wills.* Thus Pamelius. This reading is confirmed by Isidore, *Commentary on Leviticus*, chap. IX; Bede, *Works*, vol. IV, *Exposition of Leviticus*, chap. XI, and *Questions on Leviticus*, chap. IX; and Rabanus Maurus, vol. II, *Commentary on Leviticus*, as Jackson observed. Gagnaeus and Frobenius, however, read *pleasures*, and Welchman retained that reading.] wills are depicted in animals. People are clean if they chew the cud, that is, if they always have in their mouth [Note: [Col. 0957D] *The divine commandments as though they were food.* Isidore, Bede, and Rabanus Maurus read thus with Pamelius. Another reading: “as though they were a certain food.” Another: “as though certain divine commandments were food.” JACKSON.] the divine commandments as though they were food. They divide the hoof if, with the firm tread of innocence, righteousness, and every virtue, they complete the paths of life. For creatures whose foot is divided into two hooves always have a sturdy gait, since the slippery part of one hoof is supported by the firmness of the other and held securely in the solidity of its footing. [Col. 0957C] Thus those who do neither are unclean: their [Note: [Col. 0957D] *Entrance.* I would prefer *gait*, as shortly above. ID.] progress in virtue is not firm, nor is the food of the divine commandments ground down [Note: [Col. 0957D] *In the manner of that chewing of the cud.* I have supplied these words from Wower’s manuscript; Welchman had sagaciously conjectured that they should be read in this way. The printed editions have: “It chews the cud in his mouth.” ID.] in the manner of that chewing of the cud. [Col. 0958A] Those who do only one of the two are themselves not clean, since they are deficient in the other and are not perfect in both. These, then, either do both, as do the faithful, who are clean; or one, as do Jews and heretics, who are defiled; or neither, as do the gentiles, who are consequently unclean.

Thus, through the Law, a kind of mirror of human life was established in animals, in which people might contemplate images of its ordinances. In this way, every vicious act committed by human beings contrary to nature would be condemned all the more, since characteristics naturally established in cattle are themselves censured. For because fish [Note: [Col. 0957D] *Rough with scales.* Isidore and Bede have “scaly and rough.” Shortly afterward, for *bristly*, Bede has *shaggy*; and Isidore has “firm in faith.” ID.] rough with scales are regarded as clean, rough, shaggy, bristly, steadfast, and serious human conduct is approved; but creatures without these qualities are unclean, [Note: [Col. 0958C] *Because … For what*, Bede has, “which … But what.” JACKSON.] because frivolous, slippery, faithless, and effeminate conduct [Col. 0958B] is condemned.

For what does the Law mean when it says (Lev. 11:4), “You shall not [Note: [Col. 0958C] *Eat.* Thus Isidore and Bede, and the editions of Gagnaeus and Gelenius. But the Hebrew, the Vulgate, and all the versions have “you shall not eat” in the plural. Pamelius likewise printed it thus. ID.] eat the camel”? Surely it condemns, through the animal’s example, a [Note: [Col. 0958D] *Enervated.* In quoting the passage, Isidore reads *misshapen*. Bede and Rabanus Maurus likewise quote it from the author in this form. I have no doubt that this is the true reading, for the camel is not an enervated animal, but it is misshapen. ID.] feeble life, twisted by crimes. Or when it forbids the [Note: [Col. 0958D] *The pig as food.* Bede and Rabanus have, “the pig for food.” ID.] pig from being taken as food? It certainly rebukes a life that is filthy and muddy, that rejoices in the mire of vice, and locates its good not in nobility of soul but in the flesh alone. Or when it forbids the hare (ibid. 6)? It accuses men [Note: [Col. 0958D] *Deformed.* I restored this word from Latinius, and Isidore has it. The printed editions have *reformed*. Bede’s *Exposition of Leviticus* reads “deformed into women.” ID.] deformed into women. Who would make the body of a weasel into food (ibid. 29–30)? Rather, the Law rebukes thefts. Who would eat a lizard? Rather, it hates the unstable variability of life. [Note: [Col. 0958D] *Who would eat the spotted lizard? … seeking prey from another’s death.* The printed editions present this dislocated and senseless passage as follows: “Who would eat the spotted lizard? Rather, it curses spots seeking prey from another’s death.” But what could those spots be that seek prey from another’s death? Clearly, as the distinguished Wesseling says in *Probabilities*, chap. 36, p. 320, the copyist was misled by the verb *curses*, which appears twice. Following the learned Jackson here and Wesseling at the place cited, we have therefore restored the passage from Isidore, who used Novatian’s words in his *Commentary on Leviticus*, chap. 9. Bede and Rabanus Maurus also quote the words from the author in this form, except that they have “the violent” for “and the violent.” Yet it must not be passed over here that the very learned Menard, in his notes on the *Epistle of St. Barnabas*, chap. 10, had long before perceived that this passage of Novatian—as well as many other passages noted above—should be restored from Isidore. From Barnabas I also scarcely doubt that Novatian drew his own mystical interpretation of Jewish foods.] Who would eat the spotted lizard? Rather, the Law curses the stains of the mind. Who would eat the hawk, kite, or eagle (ibid. 13, 14, 16)? Rather, it hates plunderers and violent men who live by crime. Who would eat the vulture? Rather, it curses [Col. 0958C] those who seek prey from another’s death. Or who would eat the raven (ibid. 15)? Rather, it curses deceitful wills. When it also prohibits the sparrow, it reproves intemperance; when it prohibits the owl (Lev. 11:16), it hates those who flee the light of truth; when it prohibits the swan (ibid. 18), it hates those proud with uplifted neck; when it prohibits the curlew (ibid. 10), [Col. 0959A] it reproves the garrulous intemperance [Note: [Col. 0959D] *Of an excessively active tongue.* Isidore and Bede have “of excessive speech.” Shortly afterward the same authors have “but in man,” which I approve. Shortly before, for “the proud,” Bede and Rabanus Maurus read “pride.” JACKSON.] of an excessively active tongue; when it prohibits the bat, it reproves those who seek the darkness both of night and of error.

These things, therefore, and others like them the Law curses in animals. In the animals themselves they are not criminal, because they were born to be such; in man they are culpable, because they have been sought contrary to nature, not from his original constitution but from error.

## CHAPTER IV

**That another reason was also added why many kinds of food were withheld from the Jews: namely, to restrain the intemperance of a people who were to serve the one God.**

Since matters stand thus, other reasons were also added for withholding many kinds of food from the Jews. To bring this about, many things were called unclean—not so that they might be condemned, but so that those who were to serve the one God might be restrained. For frugality and moderation of appetite befitted those chosen for this purpose; such moderation is always found close to religion—indeed, if I may so express it, as a blood relation and kinswoman. For luxury is hostile to holiness. How, indeed, will religion be spared by luxury when modesty is not spared? Luxury does not admit the fear of God, since, swept headlong by pleasures, it is carried into sheer recklessness of desire. Once the reins have been let loose, it grows beyond the estate, as expenditure is applied to it without [Note: [Col. 0959D] *Without custom.* Welchman thinks it should read *without restraint*. Jackson proposes *without measure*.] restraint as though it were fodder, and consumes modesty along with the estate; or, like some torrent [Col. 0959B] falling from mountain ridges, it not only surmounts the obstacles before it but carries those very obstacles along with it to the ruin of others.

These remedies, therefore, were devised to restrain the intemperance of the people, so that as much as was taken away from luxury might be added to good morals. For what else did they deserve but to be denied the enjoyment of every pleasure of food, when they had dared to prefer the vilest foods of the Egyptians to the divine banquet of manna, setting the meat-filled stews of their enemies and masters [Note: [Col. 0959D] *Before freedom.* Thus all Pamelius’s editions. Wower’s manuscript has the equivalent, “preferring them to freedom.” But Welchman printed, “placing them after freedom,” which is Frobenius’s corrupt reading and contrary to the author’s meaning. Shortly afterward, the same Welchman, following Frobenius, wrongly has *would mark* [*signaret*] [Col. 0960D] for *would fatten* [*saginaret*], which the Pamelian editions present. JACKSON.] before freedom? [Col. 0959C] They were surely worthy of being fattened by the slavery they desired, since both better and freely given food had wickedly displeased them.

## CHAPTER V

**That there was indeed once a time when these shadows or figures were to be observed; but after Christ, the end of the Law, had come, the Apostle now declared all things clean to the clean, and that true and holy food is right faith and an undefiled conscience.**

[Note: [Col. 0960D] *There was.* Isidore and Bede have: “But there once was a time.” Shortly afterward they have: “They had to be observed or practiced by the people, so that they were to abstain.” ID.] There was, then, some ancient time in which [Col. 0960A] these shadows or figures had to be observed, so that people were to abstain from foods which creation itself had indeed commended but the Law had forbidden. But now Christ, the end of the Law (Rom. 10:4), has come, opening all the Law and revealing its obscurities, [Note: [Col. 0960D] *All the things which the mists of mysteries.* Isidore has: “And all the mysteries which for us.” The author’s meaning here seems incomplete, and from Bede’s quotation we may alternatively read it as follows: “But now Christ, the end of the Law, has come, opening all the Law and revealing its obscurities; and whatever antiquity had covered with the mists of mysteries, the distinguished Master, the heavenly Teacher, and the Institutor of perfect truth makes manifest; under whom deservedly.” ID.] all the things that antiquity had covered with the mists of mysteries. For the distinguished Master, the heavenly Teacher, and the Institutor of perfect truth has come, under whom it is now rightly said (Titus 1:15): “All things are clean to the clean; but to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is clean, for both their mind and conscience are polluted.” Likewise elsewhere (1 Tim. 4:4–5): “For every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected that is received with thanksgiving; for it is sanctified through the word of God and prayer.” Again elsewhere (1 Tim. 4:1–3): “The Spirit expressly says that in the last days some will depart from the faith, giving heed to deceiving spirits and teachings of demons, through the hypocrisy of liars whose own conscience is seared, who forbid [Col. 0960B] marriage and command abstinence from foods which God created to be received with thanksgiving by the faithful and by those who have known God.” And again in another passage (1 Cor. 10:25): “Eat everything that [Note: [Col. 0960D] *Comes.* Thus Frobenius, Pamelius’s edition of 1635, and Welchman. Another reading is *is sold*. Less correctly.] comes to the meat market, asking no questions.”

From these passages it is established that, now that the Law has ended, all these things have been restored to their own blessings. Nor must there be any return to the ritual observances concerning foods, which a definite reason had once commanded and which evangelical liberty has now abolished by restoring emancipation. The Apostle cries out (Rom. 14:17): “The kingdom of God is not drink and food, but righteousness and peace and joy.” Likewise elsewhere (1 Cor. 6:13): “Food is for the belly, and the belly for food; but God will bring both this and that to nothing. The body, however, is not for fornication, but for the Lord, and the Lord for the body.”

God is not worshiped by the belly, nor by foods (Matt. 15:17; Mark 7:19), which the Lord says perish and are purged in the privy by a natural law. [Col. 0960C] For one who worships the Lord through foods is near to having his own belly as his lord. True, holy, and clean food, I say, is right faith, an undefiled conscience, and an innocent soul. Whoever feeds in this manner dines with Christ; such a banqueter is God’s guest. These are the feasts that feed angels; these are the tables that make martyrs.

Hence comes that declaration of the Law (Deut. 8:3): “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God.” Hence comes that declaration of Christ (John 4:34): “My food is to do the will of him who sent me and to complete his work.” Hence also this (John 6:26–27): [Col. 0961A] “You seek me not because you saw signs, but because you ate of my loaves and were filled. Do not labor for the food that perishes, but for the food that endures to eternal life, which the Son of Man will give you; for God the Father has set his seal upon him.”

God, I say, is worshiped by righteousness, self-restraint, and the other virtues. [Note: [Col. 0961D] *For also.* Both English editors suspect that it should read *For*.] For Zechariah also relates (Zech. 7:6): “If you eat,” he says, “or drink, do you not eat or drink [Note: [Col. 0961D] *For yourselves.* Thus the Septuagint, Syriac, and Arabic. The Hebrew and Vulgate have *to yourselves*, as is apparent from Jerome’s commentary on the passage. JACKSON.] for yourselves?” He shows that foods and drinks do not reach God, but man. For God is not fleshly, so as to be pleased by flesh; nor is he [Note: [Col. 0961D] *Astonished.* According to the conjecture of both English editors, it should read *attentive* or *intent*.] engrossed in such pleasures, so as to rejoice in our foods. God rejoices solely in our faith, solely in innocence, solely in truth, solely in our virtues, which dwell not in the belly but in the soul, and which divine [Col. 0961B] fear and heavenly awe—not earthly food—procure for us.

Accordingly, the Apostle denounced those who served angelic superstitions (Col. 2:18–19), who were puffed up by their fleshly understanding and did not hold fast to Christ the head, from whom the whole body, joined together by its connecting bonds and fastened and united by the clasp of love through its mutually dependent members, grows into God. Yet they observe those commandments (ibid. 21, 23): “Do not touch, [Note: [Col. 0961D] *Nor taste.* The English editors restored these words to Novatian. They appear to have dropped from his text through a copyist’s carelessness, because *nor* was repeated.] nor taste, nor handle.” Such things may indeed appear to possess an image of religion, since the body is not spared; yet they contribute absolutely nothing to righteousness, since by voluntary servitude we are recalled to the elements to which we died through Baptism.

## CHAPTER VI

**But that the granting of freedom in foods does not mean that luxury has been permitted, or that self-restraint and fasting have been abolished; for these are especially fitting for the faithful, who must pray to God and give him thanks not only by day but also by night.**

[Col. 0961C]

But it does not immediately follow from the granting of freedom in foods that luxury has been permitted; nor, because the Gospel has [Note: [Col. 0961D] *Dealt.* Welchman thinks it should read *acted*.] dealt more generously with us, has it abolished self-restraint. By this provision, I say, the belly has not been catered to; rather, the true character of foods has been disclosed. What was lawful has been shown—not so that one might plunge into the abyss of desire, but so that the rationale of the Law might be rendered clear.

For the rest, nothing has restrained intemperance as the Gospel has; and no one has [Note: [Col. 0961D] *Given.* This word is absent from Pamelius’s editions, but Gagnaeus and Frobenius recognize it, and the sense appears to require it. JACKSON.] given stricter laws to gluttony than Christ, who is said to have pronounced [Note: [Col. 0961D] *But the poor.* Jackson deleted the particle *but*. But what if the author wrote it ἐμφατικῶς, “emphatically”?] the poor blessed (Matt. 5:3, 6), [Col. 0962A] and those who hunger and thirst happy; but the rich miserable (Luke 6:24), since, in serving the command of belly and appetite, the material for their pleasures could never fail, lest their servitude should be able to cease. They regard it as the proof of happiness to desire as much as they can, except that even so their ability falls short of their desire.

For by preferring [Note: [Col. 0962D] *Lazarus … preferring.* I have supplied these words from Wower’s manuscript. The printed editions wrongly have “Lazarus … enduring”; they omit the intervening words “and to the rich man.” Another reading has *meat* for *dogs*. ID.] Lazarus, amid his very hunger, sores, and dogs, to the rich man (ibid. 16:19), Christ restrained the belly and appetite—the executioners of salvation—by examples. The Apostle too, by saying, “Having food and clothing, we are content with these” (1 Tim. 6:8), gave the law of frugality and self-restraint. Thinking it of little benefit merely to have written this, he also presented himself as an example of his own writings, not without reason adding that avarice is the root of all evils (ibid. 10), [Col. 0962B] for it follows luxury as luxury runs ahead. Whatever luxury consumes through vice, avarice restores through crimes; and so, when the circle of crimes has been traversed, luxury may once more take away whatever avarice had amassed. [Note: [Col. 0962D] *The circle … so that once more.* Both English editors would prefer: “so that, when the circle … once more.”]

Yet among such people there are some who, though they have clothed themselves with the name “Christian,” furnish examples and lessons in intemperance. Their vices have reached such a point that, even while [Note: [Col. 0962D] *Fasting.* This is the genuine word, as the subsequent *while fasting* shows. Latinius reads it thus. Pamelius wrongly has *of fasting*, and shortly afterward wrongly reads “through sleep.” JACKSON.] fasting, they drink in the morning, thinking that drinking after food is not Christian unless wines poured into still empty and vacant veins descend into them immediately after sleep. For it appears that what [Note: [Col. 0962D] *What they drink.* I restored this from Wower’s manuscript. Shortly afterward I follow Pamelius in restoring “if foods are mingled among the wines.” Gagnaeus and Frobenius have “if the intestines are mingled with foods,” a corrupt reading reprinted by Welchman. ID.] they drink has less flavor if foods are mingled among the wines. Thus you may see such people, by a new practice, still fasting and already drunk—not running to the tavern, but carrying the tavern about with them. Whoever [Note: [Col. 0962D] *Whoever among them.* This is Frobenius’s reading, reproduced by Welchman, in place of Pamelius’s “each of whom.” Far too harsh appears the reading that Jackson introduced into the text from Wower’s manuscript: “whom whoever among them.”] greets one of them [Col. 0962C] does not give him a kiss but pours him a drink.

What do such people do after food, when food itself finds them drunk? Or what condition are they in when the sun leaves them at its setting, when at its rising it already sees them languishing with wine? But things worthy of detestation must not be taken as our examples. Only those things by which our soul is made better should be adopted. And although throughout the Gospel the use of every kind of food has been restored to us, it is nevertheless understood to have been restored under the law of frugality and self-restraint. For these virtues are especially fitting for the faithful, who must pray to God and give thanks to him not only by day but also during the nights. This will be impossible if the mind, stupefied by food and wine, is unable to shake off heavy sleep and the weight imposed upon the breast.

## CHAPTER VII

**That care must also be taken lest anyone suppose that this permission has been extended so far that he may partake of things sacrificed to idols.**

[Col. 0963A]

But as to what must especially be observed in the use [Note: [Col. 0963A] *Use.* From Wower’s manuscript Jackson thus corrected the printed editions’ reading, *usage*; and Welchman had conjectured that it should be read in this way.] of foods, care must be taken lest anyone suppose that this permission has been extended [Note: [Col. 0964A] *Extended.* Isidore has *permitted*, and shortly afterward reads *pertains*. JACKSON.] so far that he may also partake of things sacrificed to images. Insofar as something belongs to God’s creation, every creature is clean; but once it has been sacrificed to demons (1 Cor. 10:20–21), it is defiled for as long as it is offered to images. As soon as this has been done, it is no longer God’s but the idol’s; and when it is consumed as food, it nourishes the consumer for a demon, not for God, making him the guest of an image, not of Christ. [Col. 0964A] [Note: [Col. 0964A] *As the Jews also rightly do.* If nothing is missing—which I nevertheless suspect—the meaning is that the Jews also abstain from foods sacrificed to idols. WELCHMAN.—Jackson gives no different interpretation.] The Jews also rightly do this.

Having therefore examined the rationale of their foods, considered the purpose of the Law, recognized the benefit of evangelical grace, preserved the rigor of temperance, and rejected the defilement of things sacrificed to images, we must guard the rule of truth in every respect and give thanks to God through Jesus Christ his Son, our Lord, to whom belong praise, honor, and glory forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0963]

# NOVATIAN’S LETTER TO ST. CYPRIAN, WRITTEN IN THE NAME OF THE ROMAN CLERGY

**The presbyters and deacons residing at Rome, to Pope Cyprian, greetings.** (C)

[Note: [Col. 0963C] *Deacons.* The Speyer edition of 1471 and the old anonymous edition have another Latin form, *diacones*. The letter is likewise entitled in this way in Cyprian, Letter XXX in Baluzius’s edition. Ecclesiastical authors used both forms, and the form *diaconibus* occurs frequently in Cyprian’s letters. JACKSON.]

[Col. 0963B]

## ARGUMENT

He first commends himself to God and then also to the brethren. The faith of the Romans was praised by the Apostle. The crime of those who obtained certificates of sacrifice is nearly equal to the crime of those who denied the faith. To receive the fallen with excessive leniency is the utmost cruelty. The confessors’ letters contributed greatly to preserving ecclesiastical discipline. Cyprian’s letters were also useful to the confessors. The Church’s peace and the appointment of a bishop must be awaited before peace is granted to the fallen. Let the fallen knock at the Church’s doors, but let them not break them down.

## I

Although a mind conscious of having acted well, upheld by the strength of evangelical discipline, and made its own true witness in [Note: [Col. 0963C] *Heavenly decrees.* I found this reading in eight ancient manuscripts. The English editors note that the Vatican manuscript reads *heavenly camps*. Rigaltius rightly says that this reading does not please him. BALUZIUS.] heavenly decrees is accustomed to be content with God alone as its judge, seeking neither another’s praises nor fearing another’s accusations, nevertheless those are worthy of twofold [Col. 0963C] praise who, though they know that their conscience must answer [Note: [Col. 0963C] *Must answer to God alone as judge.* The Verona manuscript cited by Fell has, “must answer to the judgment of God alone.” Jackson conjectures that it should read “must be subjected to God alone.” But the common reading appears to be confirmed by the author himself, who shortly before said, “to be content with God alone as judge.” COUSTANT. GALLAND.] to God [Col. 0964B] alone as judge, nevertheless desire their actions to be approved by their own brethren as well.

It is no wonder, brother Cyprian, that you do this. In accordance with your modesty and [Note: [Col. 0964C] *Innate.* This word is absent from the Lincoln manuscript. Shortly afterward, the word *good* is likewise absent from the same manuscript and from the Speyer edition. Both appear to have been rightly omitted. GALLAND.] innate diligence, you wished us to be found not so much judges of your counsels as participants in them, so that, by approving your deeds, we might share their praise with you and, because we were also their endorsers, might become coheirs of your good counsels. For we are all believed to have performed that same act in which we are all found associated through the same agreement in judgment and discipline. [Note: [Col. 0964C] *What.* The Vatican manuscript has *who*. Shortly afterward the Lincoln manuscript has *to accomplish*. But *having accomplished* is correct because of the following *having been associated*, which has the same construction. JACKSON.]

For what is more fitting in peace, or more necessary amid the battles of persecution, than to maintain the due severity of divine strength? Anyone who relaxes it must always wander amid the unstable course of affairs, be scattered this way and that by the varied and uncertain storms of circumstance and, as though the rudder of judgment had been wrenched from his hands, [Col. 0965A] dash the ship of the Church’s salvation against the rocks. [Note: [Col. 0965C] *The ship, etc.* The manuscript of St. Remigius at Rheims—and the Lincoln manuscript—has, “dash the ship of ecclesiastical discipline against the rocks.” The Dijon manuscript and the more recent Victorinus manuscript have, “dash the ship of the Church against treacherous rocks.” BALUZIUS.—The latter reading is preferable because of the following phrase, “the Church’s salvation,” lest the wording appear inelegant. GALLAND.] Thus it is apparent that the Church’s salvation can be provided for in no other way than by repelling, like so many hostile waves, those who act against that very salvation, [Note: [Col. 0965C] *Those who act against it are to be repelled like so many hostile waves.* We punctuate thus with Jackson. Another punctuation gives: “those who act against it, as though hostile waves were to be repelled.” GALLAND.] and by always preserving the rule of discipline itself like a saving rudder in a storm.

## II

Nor is this a policy that we devised [Note: [Col. 0965C] *Just now, recently.* The Lincoln manuscript omits *now*. GALLAND.] only recently, nor are these safeguards against the wicked remedies that have suddenly occurred to us only now. Rather, [Note: [Col. 0965D] *This severity is ancient.* These words, which were added in the Manutius edition, are absent from the ancient editions and from two ancient manuscripts, but are found in others. BALUZIUS.] this severity among us is ancient, the faith is ancient, and the discipline is shown to be ancient. For the Apostle would not have uttered such great praises of us when he said, “Your faith is proclaimed throughout the whole world” (Rom. 1:8), unless from that time onward this strength had drawn from those days the roots [Col. 0965B] of faith. To have [Note: [Col. 0965D] *Degenerate.* The Lincoln manuscript has the plural, *degenerates*. But the words that follow—*honored*, *ignoble*, and *disinherited*—confirm the common singular reading. JACKSON.] degenerated from such praises and glory is the greatest crime.

For it is less disgraceful never to have attained the proclamation of praise than to have fallen from the summit of praise. It is less criminal never to have been honored by favorable testimony than to have lost the honor bestowed by favorable testimonies. It is less shameful to have lain in obscurity without praise, with one’s virtues unproclaimed, than, having been disinherited from the faith, to have lost one’s own praises. For those things that are uttered to someone’s glory, unless they are preserved by anxious and vigilant labor, swell into an accusation of the greatest crime.

## III

Our [Note: [Col. 0965D] *Earlier letter.* This appears to have been lost. GALLAND.] earlier letter proved that we do not say this falsely. In it we presented our judgment to you in a clear exposition against those [Col. 0965C] who had betrayed themselves as unbelievers by the unlawful declaration contained in their impious certificates, as though they believed they would escape [Note: [Col. 0965D] *Entangling.* One old manuscript of mine has *retaining*. The manuscript of St. Dionysius at Rheims has “by retaining those snares of the devil.” BALUZIUS.—The Lincoln manuscript has, “as though they seemed likely to escape this by retaining those snares of the devil, because.” Bodleian I, the Fossat manuscript, and the old anonymous edition have, “as though they would escape this.” FELL.] those entangling snares of the devil, although by the very fact that they had attested to the deed they were held no less guilty than if they had approached the impious altars. [Note: [Col. 0965D] *Whereby.* Another reading has *because*. Latinius has *when*. GALLAND.]

We also declared our judgment against those who had accepted such certificates [Note: [Col. 0965D] *Had made what they had received* (*accepta fecissent*). Thus the Lincoln, Bodleian I, and Benevento manuscripts and the editions of Manutius, Fell, Welchman, and Jackson. But Pamelius, followed by Baluzius, has “had caused the acts to be performed.” Rigaltius confirms the former reading: “Most correctly,” he says, [Col. 0966C] “the Benevento copy and the Roman edition read, ‘those who had made what they had received’; that is, those who had accepted the certificates submitted to them, for in this manner they had accepted and ratified whatever was contained in them. What was contained in them was that the certificate-holder had on that day ascended the Capitol and offered incense to Jupiter. Although he had not done this, he had nevertheless caused it to be publicly read that he had done so: that is, by the reading of the certificate through which he wished to appear to have complied with the edicts issued against the Gospel. This amounted to abandoning the faith pledged to Christ.” GALLAND.], although they had not been present when this was done; for by commissioning the statements to be recorded in this way, they had assuredly made themselves present. [Note: [Col. 0966C] *By commissioning.* Thus Natalis of Oea gave his opinion at the Council of Carthage under Cyprian on his own behalf and on behalf of Pompeius of Sabrata and Dioga of Leptis Magna, “who commissioned me.” BALUZIUS.]

For the person who [Note: [Col. 0966D] *Ordered it.* This reading appears best, although I found it in only one old manuscript. The others, along with the editions earlier than Pamelius, have *obtained it*. Pamelius altered the text by following Costerius’s conjecture, although he admits that everywhere he had read *obtained*. Thus, in Letter XLIV of the encyclical collection, the Beauvais manuscript writes “those whom divine judgment could *obtain*” for “could *command*.” The error is easy and was also admitted into another old manuscript of the same church, namely the manuscript of Liberatus’s *Breviary*, chap. 18, where, instead of “he dismissed them, obtaining nothing,” as the editions and three old manuscripts have it, the Beauvais manuscript reads “commanding.” Likewise, in Fulgentius Placiades, *Mythologies*, book II, where he treats of Vulcan and Minerva, *Jupiter commanded* must be read in place of the text’s *Jupiter obtained*. BALUZIUS.] ordered a crime to be committed is not immune from it; nor is one free of a crime when, by his consent, it is publicly read that the crime occurred, although he did not himself commit it. Since the whole sacrament of faith is understood to be comprised in the confession of Christ’s name, whoever seeks deceptive tricks as an excuse has denied Christ; and whoever wishes to appear to have complied with edicts or laws issued against the Gospel has already obeyed by the very fact that he wished to appear to have obeyed.

We likewise showed our faith and agreement against those who had polluted their hands and mouths with unlawful sacrifices, having first polluted their own minds, from which the hands and mouths themselves also became polluted. [Col. 0966B] Far be it from the Roman Church to relinquish its strength with such profane readiness and, once the majesty of the faith has been overthrown, to loosen the sinews of severity. While the ruins of our overthrown brethren not only still lie prostrate but continue to fall, excessively hasty remedies of communion—remedies that will surely do no good—must not be provided, nor must new wounds, through a false mercy, be inflicted upon the old wounds of transgression, so that even repentance is snatched from the wretched to their greater ruin.
