For how will the medicine of forgiveness be able to [Note: [Col. 0966D] *Be effective.* I judged that the text should be corrected thus, following the authority of the old copies and editions, in place of the *proceed* preferred by the later editions. I nevertheless admit that I found this latter reading in two of my old manuscripts, the Grenoble manuscript and one Victorinus manuscript, and also in the Manutius edition. The manuscript of St. Dionysius at Rheims and the Lamonian manuscript have *be of benefit*, with the same meaning. BALUZIUS.] be effective if the physician himself, by cutting repentance short, gives free rein to dangers; if he merely covers the wound and does not allow the necessary remedies of time to draw a scar over it? [Col. 0966C] This is not healing but—if we wish to tell the truth—killing.

## IV

You also have the letters of the confessors whom the dignity of their confession has kept imprisoned here to this day, and whose faith, now glorious in confession, has already once crowned them for the evangelical contest. [Col. 0967A] Their letters agree with ours: in them they upheld the severity of evangelical discipline and recalled unlawful petitions to a due regard for the Church’s honor. Had they not done so, the ruin of evangelical discipline [Note: [Col. 0967D] *Ruin … would be repaired.* Baluzius alone printed the plurals, “ruins … would be repaired”; on what authority he is silent. Shortly afterward the same editor has “appropriate,” as does the Oxford edition. Another reading has “an appropriate thing.” GALLAND.] would not easily be repaired, especially since it was appropriate for no one more than for those who had handed themselves over to raging persecutors to be tortured and butchered for the Gospel to preserve unimpaired the steadfastness and dignity of evangelical strength. [Note: [Col. 0967D] *To preserve unimpaired the dignity.* The Vatican manuscript has “to preserve with unimpaired dignity.” Welchman retained this reading, although his text wrongly prints “to be preserved.” Immediately afterward the same editor suspects that the text should read, “than for those who.” GALLAND.] Otherwise, they would rightly lose the honor [Note: [Col. 0967D] *Rightly.* This word is absent from the Lincoln manuscript. Shortly afterward the same manuscript has “in the killing of martyrdom,” erroneously, as I think. GALLAND.] of martyrdom if, when the opportunity for martyrdom arose, they chose to become transgressors of the Gospel. For whoever does not preserve what he has within that from which he possesses it, in violating that from which he possesses it, loses what he possessed. [Col. 0967B]

V. In this matter we owe you, and do render you, the greatest and most abundant thanks: because you illuminated the darkness of their prison with your letters; because you came to them by whatever means you were able to gain entrance; because, although their spirits were already strengthened by their faith and confession, you refreshed them with your addresses and letters; because, recounting their blessed achievements with fitting praises, [Note: [Col. 0967D] “Recounting” (*persecutus*). Bodl. Cod. I reads *prosecutus*; and Baluzius introduced this reading into the text. GALL.] you kindled in them a far more ardent desire for heavenly glory; because you urged onward those already eager; and because, as we believe and hope, you inspired [Note: [Col. 0967D] “Inspired” (*animasti*). Bodl. I and Vat. read “armed” (*armasti*). GALL.] with the strength of your discourse those who are destined to be victors. Thus, although all this appears to proceed from the faith of the confessors and from divine favor, nevertheless they may appear to have become indebted to you in some measure for their martyrdom. But, so that the discourse may return once more to the point from which it seemed to have digressed, [Col. 0967C] you will find appended the sort of letters [Note: [Col. 0967D] “Letters … you will find appended.” No such letters of Novatian appear anywhere. GALL.] that we also sent to Sicily.

VI. Yet a greater necessity for deferring this matter rests upon us, since, after the death of Fabian, a man of most noble memory, [Note: [Col. 0967D] Fabian was taken away by martyrdom in the year of Christ 250, on January 20; Cornelius succeeded him at the beginning of June 251, as we learn from Pagi. GALL.] no bishop has yet been appointed for us, because of the difficulties of affairs and the times, who might regulate all these matters and, with authority and counsel, take account of those who have lapsed. [Col. 0968A] [Note: [Col. 0968C] “Yet … take account.” Cyprian quotes this passage in Epistle LII of Baluzius’s edition, to Antonianus. You will find it below among the letters of Cornelius. The holy martyr adds: “It was also added while Novatian was then writing, and reading aloud in his own voice what he had written,” etc. Pacian copied these words of Cyprian in Epistle II to Sympronianus. GALL.] Yet in so momentous a matter we approve what you yourself also proposed: [Note: [Col. 0968D] “First the peace of the Church.” Cyprian, loc. cit., reads “first that the peace of the Church must be awaited”; and shortly afterward, “with the deacons.” GALL.] first the peace of the Church must be awaited; and then, after a joint consultation has been held with bishops, presbyters, deacons, confessors, and likewise those laypersons who have stood firm, the case of the lapsed must be considered.

For it appears to us exceedingly odious and burdensome that a matter seemingly committed by many should not be examined by many, and that one person should pronounce judgment when so grave a crime is observed to have spread abroad among many; for no decree can be secure unless it appears to have had the consent of a great many. Look upon almost the whole world laid waste, and everywhere the remains [Note: [Col. 0968D] “And ruins.” The Speyer edition and three old books do not contain these two words. The old Venetian edition has them. Two other old books offer “snares” in place of “ruins.” BALUZ.] and ruins of the fallen lying prostrate; and therefore let the counsel sought be as comprehensive as the offense appears to have been widely propagated. [Col. 0968B] Let the medicine not be less than the wound, nor the remedies less than the deaths. [Note: [Col. 0968D] “Deaths” (*funera*). The codex of Saint-Arnoul reads “wounds” (*vulnera*). This reading appears better to me, and I would have placed it in the text had I possessed that codex when this passage was being printed. But if anyone thinks that the word *funera* should be retained, it must be understood as deaths, or rather the corpses of the dead. BALUZ.] Just as those who fell did so because, through blind rashness, they were excessively incautious, so those who endeavor to settle this matter should employ every restraint of deliberation, lest something done otherwise than it ought to be should be judged invalid by everyone.

Accordingly, with one and the same counsel, with the same prayers and tears, let both we—who until now appear to have escaped the ruins of this time—and those who appear to have fallen into these disasters of the age beseech the divine majesty and ask for peace for the ecclesiastical name. [Note: [Col. 0968D] “For the ecclesiastical name.” We have restored this reading, following the English edition and the authority of certain old books. If anyone nevertheless prefers to read “in the name,” I do not object. BALUZ.] Let us sustain, guard, and arm one another with reciprocal prayers. Let us pray for the lapsed, that they may be raised up; let us pray for those who stand, that they may not be tempted to the point of ruin; let us pray that those who are reported to have fallen may recognize the magnitude of their offense and understand that they must not desire [Col. 0968C] an instantaneous or overhasty remedy. [Note: [Col. 0968D] “Desire.” Two old books read, “ought to desire a remedy.” BALUZ.] Let us pray that the effect of indulgence and the repentance of the lapsed may follow, [Note: [Col. 0968D] “Repentance” (*poenitentia*). Formerly *poenitentiam* was read, a reading confirmed by the old editions and seven old copies. Our reading, which appears better, is confirmed by three ancient codices. BALUZ.] so that, having understood their crime, they may be willing meanwhile to show us patience and may not disturb the still-unsettled condition of the Church, lest they appear themselves to have kindled an inward persecution against us [Col. 0969A] and thus add to the accumulation of their crimes the fact that they were also unruly. For modesty is especially fitting for those whose shameless disposition is condemned in their offenses.

VII. Let them indeed knock at the doors, but certainly not break them down. Let them approach the threshold of the Church, but certainly not leap over it. Let them keep watch at the gates of the heavenly camp, but armed with the modesty by which they understand that they were deserters. Let them take up again the trumpet of their prayers, but not one with which they sound the call to battle. Let them indeed arm themselves with the weapons of modesty and take up again the shield of faith that, by denying through fear of death, they had cast aside; but let them believe that even now they are armed against the enemy, the devil, not against the Church, which grieves over their fall.

A modest request, a reverent petition, necessary humility, and a patience [Col. 0969B] that is not idle [Note: [Col. 0969C] “Patience.” The Lincoln Codex reads “repentance.”] will greatly benefit them. Let them send their tears as envoys for their grief; let groans brought forth from the depth of the breast serve as their advocates, attesting their sorrow and shame for the crime committed. Indeed, if they shudder at the magnitude of the disgrace they have incurred, if with a truly healing hand they treat the deadly blow to their breast and conscience and the deep recesses of the winding wound, let them be ashamed even to ask—except that it entails still greater danger and shame not to have sought the aid of peace.

But let all this be done within the sacred bond, under the rule governing the petition itself, with due accommodation to the time; with a humble petition and a submissive prayer. For the one who is petitioned ought to be moved, not provoked; and just as divine mercy must be regarded, so too must divine judgment be regarded. Just as it is written (Matt. 18:32), “I forgave you the whole debt because you entreated me,” [Col. 0969C] so it is written (Luke 12:9), “Whoever denies me before men, I also will deny him before [Col. 0970A] my Father and before his angels.” For just as God is indulgent, so he is also an exacting—and indeed diligent—enforcer of his commandments. Just as he calls people to the banquet (Matt. 22:3), so he casts the one who does not possess the wedding garment, bound hand and foot, outside the company of the saints. He has prepared heaven, but he has also prepared Tartarus. He has prepared places of refreshment, but he has also prepared eternal punishments. He has prepared inaccessible light, but he has also prepared the vast and everlasting darkness of perpetual night. [Note: [Col. 0969C] “And everlasting” (*aeternamque*). So nearly all printed editions. The Vatican Codex reads “and hideous” (*et tetram*), a reading that the English editors did not hesitate to introduce into the text. GALL.]

Seeking for a long time to preserve here the moderation of this balance, many of us, together with certain bishops neighboring [Note: [Col. 0969C] “Neighboring us.” Thus Fell and Baluzius. Welchman and Jackson omit “us.”] and close to us, as well as those [Note: [Col. 0969C] “As well as those.” Welchman thinks that the conjunction “and” is redundant. Jackson, however, understands the sense to be “and with certain persons whom …” Shortly afterward, “situated” is absent from the Lincoln Codex. GALL.] whom the heat of this persecution had driven out from other, far-distant provinces, have judged that nothing should be altered before the appointment of a bishop, but that the care of the lapsed must be regulated with moderation. [Col. 0970B] [Note: [Col. 0970C] “We have judged.” Thus Fell, Welchman, and Jackson, from Bodl. Cod. I. Others read, “we judge.” GALL.] Meanwhile, while we await a bishop’s being granted to us by God, let the case of those who can endure the delay of postponement remain in suspense. [Note: [Col. 0970C] “In suspense … delay … endure.” Morel emended “in suspense” (*in suspenso*) from what had formerly been read, *in suspendio*. One of my books reads “with their expectation suspended.” Shortly afterward the Grenoble Codex reads, “those who are outside can endure affection”; the older editions, “those who are outside can be sustained by postponement.” BALUZ.] But in the case of those whose rapidly approaching end of life cannot bear delay, when penance has been performed and they have repeatedly professed their abhorrence of their own deeds, if by tears, groans, and weeping they have manifested signs of a sorrowful and truly repentant spirit, and when no hope of continued life according to human judgment remains, only then should aid be given cautiously and carefully. God himself knows what he will do concerning such persons and how he will weigh the scales of his judgment; yet we must anxiously take care that neither wicked people praise our readiness as excessive leniency nor truly repentant persons accuse us of harsh cruelty.

We wish you, most blessed and most glorious pope, always to fare well in the Lord and to remember us.

## IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 252–253  
## SAINT LUCIUS I, POPE AND MARTYR

[Col. 0969]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE

[Col. 0969D] **Lucius is ordained pontiff in the year 252, in September or October.**—After the martyrdom of Cornelius, Lucius was ordained in his place on September 25, as Pagi and the Maurists judge, [Note: [Col. 0969D] Pagi, at the year 252, § 14; *The Art of Verification* (*L’Art de vérifier*), loc. cit.] or on October 28 according to Bianchini. Scarcely had he obtained the Roman see when he was ordered into exile. Hence, when Cyprian heard at the same time both of his ordination and his exile, he sent him letters of communion and congratulation in his own name and in that of his colleagues. Although these have perished, the whole matter is nevertheless established by another letter, still extant, sent to the same man after his return. Cyprian writes:

> “Only recently, indeed,” [Note: [Col. 0970D] Cyprian, Ep. 61, to Lucius; otherwise 58.] “dearest brother, we congratulated you when divine favor, by a twofold honor, appointed you both confessor and priest in the administration of his Church. But now we no less congratulate you, your companions, and the entire brotherhood because the Lord’s kindly and abundant protection has restored you once more to his own people with the same glory and with praises to your credit, so that the shepherd might be restored to the flock that must be fed, the helmsman to the ship that must be steered, and the ruler to the people that must be governed; [Col. 0971A] and so that it might be apparent that your banishment was thus ordained by God, not so that the bishop, banished and driven out, should be absent from the Church, but so that he should return to the Church greater than before.”

Thus Cyprian speaks of the exile and return of the pontiff Lucius. It is probable that he returned in the following year, in which he also suffered martyrdom, on March 4 or 5. That he died a violent death may be gathered from Saint Cyprian’s fifty-seventh letter to Stephen: “They”—these are the saint’s words—[Note: [Col. 0971C] Cyprian, Ep. 68, to Stephen; otherwise 67.] “were filled with the Spirit of God and established in glorious martyrdom.” “The glorious honor of our predecessors, the blessed martyrs Cornelius and Lucius, etc., must be preserved.”

Scholars disagree concerning the length of time for which Lucius held the pontificate. Some report that he occupied it for two years. The catalogue of Bucherius, however, indicates that he presided over the Roman Church for a much shorter period, when it reports that Stephen was ordained in his place during the third consulship of Volusianus and that of Maximus. Eusebius testifies to this more clearly, [Note: [Col. 0971C] Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book VII, chap. 2.] assigning him eight months. Nicephorus affirms that he held the pontificate for scarcely seven months. [Note: [Col. 0971C] Nicephorus, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book VI, chap. 7.] Henschenius, however, in his *Historical Chronological Essay*, [Note: [Col. 0971C] *Propylaeum* to the *Acta Sanctorum* for May.] reports that Stephen was indeed ordained in the year 253, but administered the Roman Church for two years as Lucius’s vicar; he therefore also postpones Lucius’s martyrdom by two years.

But since, in Pagi’s judgment, [Note: [Col. 0971C] Pagi, note at the year 253, §§ 2–3; Pearson, *Annals of Cyprian*, year 253.] the vicars of the Roman pontiffs were unknown to the ancient writers and render the chronology of those pontiffs—often already enveloped in difficulties and darkness—still more obscure and intricate, they find scarcely any approval among scholars. We have therefore been content to note, with Eusebius, that he governed the Roman Church for seven or eight months. [Col. 0971C] [Note: [Col. 0971C] When Cyprian calls Stephen the vicar and successor of Lucius, he plainly employs the expression “vicar” in a sense other than its customary one, namely, to signify one who performs another’s duties. For “vicar” and “successor” are the same thing in Cyprian; hence he calls Stephen not only Lucius’s vicar but also Cornelius’s, though he certainly cannot be called Cornelius’s vicar.]

Moreover, those martyrologies and authors who hold that Lucius was put to death during Valerian’s reign are in error. Their opinion is refuted by Dionysius of Alexandria, who records the following concerning Valerian: [Note: [Col. 0972C] Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book VII, chap. 10.]

> “None of the preceding emperors—not even those who are openly said to have been Christians—embraced our people with as much humanity and benevolence as he displayed at the beginning of his reign.” [Note: [Col. 0972C] See Pierre Coustant, *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, pp. 206–207, where he shows how grievously the Bucherian Catalogue and the author of the *Liber Pontificalis* erred concerning Lucius.]

**Lucius’s decretal follows.**—One decretal letter is ascribed to Lucius, and it contains many provisions:

1. That a bishop should always have presbyters and deacons with him as witnesses.
2. Concerning accusations against bishops, or elders, and that a hearing should not be denied to those appealing to persons of higher rank.
3. That a metropolitan should do nothing without the counsel of the bishops, nor they without his, except in matters pertaining to their own churches.
4. That a metropolitan should not hear the case of bishops without the bishops.
5. That later bishops should not prefer themselves to earlier ones or act without consulting them.
6. Concerning those who seize the property of the Church or the offerings of the faithful, and those who consent to the seizure.

The letter was sent to the bishops of Gaul and Spain: “Given on the Kalends of April, when Gallus and Volusianus, most illustrious men, were consuls.” This subscription sufficiently exposes the impostor. Cornelius was still alive on the Kalends of April during the consulship of Gallus and Volusianus. Nor was Lucius so dull or ignorant as to have adorned the Roman emperors with the title “most illustrious men.” These words of chapter 6—“I exhort, adjure, and admonish your charity to keep watch, with all the diligence you owe and are able to exercise, in order to discover heretics”—were taken from Leo I’s second letter. It quotes Psalm 82 from Jerome’s version and employs statements drawn from Gregory the Great, Book XII, Epistle 32. [Col. 0972C] During his pontificate a most savage plague began in the autumn and, raging for fifteen years, depopulated a great many provinces of the Roman Empire.

[Col. 0971]

[Note: [Col. 0971D] Pope Lucius succeeded Cornelius in the year of Christ 255 and was soon driven into exile, but returned to the City shortly afterward, namely in the following year. Saint Cyprian then sent him this letter in his own name and in that of his colleagues, mentioning in it another letter that he had written to Lucius at the beginning of the latter’s episcopate. This is plainly beyond dispute. Nevertheless, Jean de Launoy persuaded himself that the words of this letter do not allow one to infer that another letter had previously been sent to Lucius, because, as he says, Cyprian states that he had congratulated him, but does not state that he had congratulated him by letter. This argument is surely extremely weak, as the author of the *Cyprianic Annals* judged before me. Moreover, Lucius, crowned with martyrdom, was buried in the cemetery of Callistus on the Appian Way. BALUZ.]

## THE SOLE EPISTLE OF SAINT CYPRIAN, BISHOP OF CARTHAGE, TO POPE LUCIUS AFTER HIS RETURN FROM EXILE

He congratulates him upon his return from exile. Nothing was taken from his glory even though he did not end his life in martyrdom. It did not occur without God’s counsel that persecution harassed him, his predecessor, and his Church, but did not touch the Novatians. He vividly depicts the joy of the Roman Church at his arrival.

[Col. 0972D]

## CYPRIAN AND HIS COLLEAGUES TO THEIR BROTHER LUCIUS: GREETINGS

[Note: [Col. 0972D] I.—“We congratulated you.” Namely, by letters, which divine tradition and ecclesiastical institution required to be sent to the Roman pontiff as soon as he announced that he had been made bishop, as Cyprian himself teaches in Epistle XLII. Launoy’s opinion is therefore rightly rejected. He thinks this can be understood to mean that Cyprian congratulated himself and his colleagues upon Lucius’s twofold honor, but did not signify this congratulation to Lucius by letter. COUSTANT.

[Col. 0973C] “In the administration … a confessor.” Those who think that Lucius was exiled with Cornelius before he was chosen as Roman pontiff appear to rely upon this passage, which they interpret as though Lucius had long before been made a confessor and was afterward appointed pontiff. Cyprian, however, means rather that as soon as Lucius undertook the government of the Church, he merited the praise of confession through exile. For when Gallus heard that he had gained nothing by the death of Cornelius if he allowed Lucius, his successor, to remain in the City, he immediately punished him with exile. Nor do the words “restored you once more” signify a double exile or double return, but simply the return of a pontiff who had once been taken from his people and was restored to them anew—the return upon which Cyprian now congratulates him. COUSTANT.

“Ordained by God.” With this agrees the statement of the Bucherian Catalogue: “He was an exile, and afterward, by God’s will, returned unharmed to the Church.” COUSTANT.]

I. Only recently, indeed, dearest brother, we congratulated [Col. 0973A] you when divine favor, by a twofold honor, appointed you both confessor and priest in the administration of his Church. But now we no less congratulate you, your companions, and the entire brotherhood, because the Lord’s kindly and abundant protection has restored you once more [Note: [Col. 0973C] Voss. 2 reads, “restored you once more.”] to his own people with the same glory and with praises to your credit, so that the shepherd might be restored to the flock that must be fed, the helmsman to the ship that must be steered, and the ruler to the people that must be governed; and so that it might be apparent that your banishment was thus ordained by God, not so that the bishop, banished and driven out, should be absent from the Church, but so that he should return to the Church greater than before.

[Note: [Col. 0973D] II.—“With Antichrist approaching.” Rigaltius says: “With persecution approaching.” In Tertullian, *Apology*, chap. 32, when this condition of affairs is described, it is called “the greatest violence threatening the whole world,” and “the close of the age, which threatens dreadful cruelties.” FELL.

“Only of discourse.” Eight old books read “by the mere … of discourse”; two others, “by discourse alone”; another, “only discourse.” BALUZ.]

II. Nor was the dignity of martyrdom less in the three young men (Dan. 3) because, after death had been thwarted, they came forth unharmed from the fiery furnace. Nor did Daniel fail to attain the fullness of his praises because, though cast to the lions as prey, he was protected by the Lord and lived to glory [Note: [Col. 0973C] “Glory.” Lam., Ebor., N C. 1 add “for the confessors of Christ.”] (Dan. 6). In Christ’s confessors, martyrdoms that are deferred do not diminish the merit of confession, [Col. 0973B] but display the wonders of divine protection.

We see reproduced in you what the brave and illustrious young men proclaimed before the king: that they themselves were prepared to burn in the flames rather than serve his gods or worship the image he had made; yet the God whom they worshiped, and whom we also worship, was able to deliver them from the furnace and free them from the king’s hands and from their present punishments (Dan. 3:16). We find this now accomplished in the faith of your confession and in the Lord’s protection of you: although you were prepared and ready, every one of you, [Note: [Col. 0973C] Bod. 2 reads, “ready, all of you.”] to undergo every punishment, the Lord nevertheless withdrew you from punishment and preserved you for the Church.

By your return, the dignity of his confession has not been diminished in the bishop, [Col. 0974A] but his priestly authority has instead increased, so that there may stand at God’s altar a prelate who exhorts the people to take up the arms of confession and achieve martyrdoms, not by words but by deeds; and who, with Antichrist approaching, prepares the soldiers for battle [Note: [Col. 0973C] Bod. 2, Ebor., N C. 1 read, “the soldiers of Christ for battle.”] not merely by the incitement of discourse [Note: [Col. 0973C] Bod. 1 reads, “not merely of discourse.”] and voice, but by the example of faith and courage.

[Note: [Col. 0973D] III.—“A sudden persecution.” Under Gallus and Valerian, as the most illustrious bishop of Oxford judges. For in order to appease the anger of their gods and ward off the plague raging in the commonwealth—a plague whose cause, like that of their other troubles, they laid upon the Christians—they suddenly raised a persecution against them. By contrast, Jerome has “sudden peace” in his *Letter to Pammachius and Marcella*: “A sudden peace alters the rationale of the war.” Petronius also has “sudden tranquility.” BALUZ.

“And the bishop.” The particle “and” is absent from the Corb. manuscript, with no change in sense. COUSTANT.

“With the bishop.” The same manuscript and six other English manuscripts read “with the bishops.” The other books more correctly read “with the bishop,” since Cyprian has just taught, and consistently proclaims elsewhere, that there ought to be only one bishop in one Church. COUSTANT.

“The devil might spare them as his own.” Novatian and his followers ought to have been most ready to undergo martyrdom, since they had withdrawn from the Church’s communion on the ground that it communicated with the lapsed. Hence, as Pacian attests, they called the orthodox “apostates,” “Capitol-goers,” and “Sanhedrin-men.” Socrates indeed says that Novatian, “when the emperor Valerian launched a persecution against the Christians, was martyred” (*ἐπὶ Οὐαλεριανοῦ τοῦ βασιλέως διωγμὸν κατὰ Χριστιανῶν κινήσαντος ἐμαρτύρησεν*), *History*, Book IV, chap. 28. A little book also circulated under the title *The Martyrdom of Novatian*, which Eulogius, bishop of Alexandria, refuted in the sixth book of his work *Against the Novatians*; extracts from it are found in Photius’s *Bibliotheca*. That narrative says that Novatian was a martyr or confessor before he was promoted to the episcopate, which is manifestly false. [Col. 0974D] Pacian certainly states in the clearest words that Novatian never endured martyrdom. He further adds that Novatian had withdrawn from the Church precisely so that the labor of confession might not press upon him. Nor, according to Cyprian, was he ashamed to affirm, when persecution threatened, that he wished to return to philosophy rather than encounter danger to his life. FELL.

“Once, and his own.” Rigaltius’s edition reads, “once, and themselves made his own.” I do not know whence he obtained this reading, for I have found it nowhere except in his edition, although I have seen all the old books that he used. I have therefore deleted “and themselves,” judging that I ought not to place in my edition what is written there and in the English edition without authority. For the English themselves cite nine old books in which the words I have omitted are absent. These words of Tertullian from his book *To the Martyrs* confirm my correction: “Therefore let [the devil] not say, ‘They are mine; I shall test them with petty schisms or dissensions among themselves.’” And in his book *On the Shows*, he says that when the devil was challenged during an exorcism for having dared to attack a believing woman who had gone to the theater, he answered: “I acted with perfect justice; I found her in my domain.” BALUZ.

“And themselves his own.” Oxford edition; less elegantly. In their place nine manuscripts contain only “his own,” while Corb. has “and his own.” Cyprian explains more fully above, Epistle 13, no. 3, to Cornelius, that the devil is accustomed to rage against God’s servants but not to trouble those devoted to himself. COUSTANT.]

III. We understand, dearest brother, and with the whole light of our heart [Note: [Col. 0973C] Pem. reads, “and with the sure light of our heart.”] clearly perceive the saving and holy counsels of the divine majesty: why a sudden persecution [Note: [Col. 0973C] N C. 2 reads, “a sudden tempest.”] recently arose there; [Note: [Col. 0973C] Pem. reads, “arose.”] why secular power suddenly burst forth against the Church of Christ, against the bishop Cornelius, the blessed martyr, [Note: [Col. 0973C] N C. 2 reads, “the martyr, against whom every …”; Bod. 1 reads, “and the rest, every …”] and against all of you. It was so that, to confound and crush the heretics, the Lord might show which was the Church; who was its one bishop, chosen by divine ordination; who were the presbyters joined with the bishop [Note: [Col. 0974C] Lam., Bod. 1 and 2, Ebor., Lin., N C. 1 read, “who with the bishops and presbyters.”] in priestly honor; which was the united and true people of Christ, bound together by love for the Lord’s flock; who were those whom the enemy assailed, [Note: [Col. 0974C] Bod. 1 and 2 read, “assailed, who against …”; Pem., Voss. 2, Lam., Ebor., Lin., N C. 1 and 2 read, “against whom …”] and whom, by contrast, [Col. 0974B] the devil spared as his own. For Christ’s adversary persecutes and attacks none but the camp and soldiers of Christ. The heretics, once prostrated [Note: [Col. 0974C] Pem., Ebor., Lam., Voss. 2, Lin., N C. 1 and 2, Bod. 1 and 2 read, “once made his own.”] and made his own, he despises and passes by; he seeks to cast down those whom he sees standing.

[Note: [Col. 0975] IV.—“At the joy of your arrival.” Pamelius pronounced the old reading, which we restore and which nearly all the old books and editions confirm, to be unsound. He asserted that the faulty punctuation introduced by Rembolt—that is, the reading we restore—obscured the sense. But if there was an error there, Rembolt was not to blame. The same punctuation appears in the Speyer edition and in the old Venetian edition, which preceded the one Rembolt issued. Pamelius, moreover, says that he punctuated as he did according to the text of two old books that he cites; we have found the same punctuation in two manuscript codices as well. BALUZ.

“Scarcely with kisses.” The reading “scarcely with eyes” is an absolutely certain error found in nearly all the old books and editions, since *osculis* (“with kisses”) ought to have been written. The English correctly emended it by conjecture, not on authority, for they cite no old codex as the source of this correction. I found it nowhere except in the Metz Codex of Saint-Arnoul, which I received somewhat late. Below, in the book *On the Lapsed*, p. 181: “Clinging with holy kisses.” I am surprised, however, that I did not notice the correct reading in the English edition. BALUZ.

“While they are present.” The Sorbonne Codex reads, “while the people are present.” Three others read, “can be celebrated while the people are present,” or “demands.” BALUZ.

“Be sacrificed.” The Corb. manuscript reads “remain”; erroneously. What Cyprian teaches here he confirmed by his own example. When men were sent to take him to Utica to be brought before the judge, he withdrew, on the advice of his dearest friends, from his gardens into more hidden places. He did so all the more willingly because, as he says in Epistle 81, or 83, it is fitting that a bishop confess the Lord in the city in which he presides over the Lord’s Church, and that the entire people be glorified by the confession of the prelate who is present. Pontius, in his *Life* of Cyprian, bears witness that he fulfilled this magnificently. COUSTANT.]

IV. And would that the opportunity were now granted us, dearest brother, to be present there when you return, [Note: [Col. 0974C] Lin., N C. 2 read, “returning with you.”] since we love you with reciprocal charity, so that we too, present with the others, might personally enjoy the most joyful fruit of your arrival! What exultation there among all the brethren! What a convergence and embrace of every person who comes to meet you! [Note: [Col. 0974C] Lam., Ebor., Lin., Bod. 1 and 2 read, “of every person hastening to meet you.”] Those who cling to you can scarcely be satisfied with kisses; [Note: [Col. 0974C] Thus Bod. 1. Imp., N C. 2 read, “with their eyes.”] the very faces [Col. 0975A] and eyes of the people can scarcely be sated with seeing.

From the joy of your arrival, the brotherhood there has begun to learn what manner and magnitude of joy will follow when Christ comes. Because his advent will quickly draw near, a certain image of it has already preceded in you. Just as John, his forerunner and precursor, came and proclaimed that Christ had come, so now, when a bishop who is a confessor of the Lord and a priest returns, it becomes apparent that the Lord also is already returning.

In our stead, therefore, I, [Note: [Col. 0975A] Bod. 2 reads, “both I and …”] my colleagues, and the whole brotherhood send these letters to you, dearest brother; and, representing our joy to you through the letter, [Note: [Col. 0976A] Lam. reads, “our joy, of our faith.”] we express the faithful services of our charity. [Col. 0976A] Here also, in our sacrifices and prayers, we do not cease to give thanks to God the Father and to Christ his Son, our Lord, and at the same time to pray and petition that he who is perfect and makes perfect may preserve and perfect in you the glorious crown of your confession. Perhaps he restored you for this very purpose, lest your glory should remain hidden if the consummating martyrdoms of your confession took place outside. For the victim that provides the brotherhood with an example of courage and faith ought to be sacrificed while the brethren are present.

We wish you, dearest brother, always to fare well.

[Col. 0975]

## SOLE APPENDIX  
## LETTERS AND DECREES ATTRIBUTED TO SAINT LUCIUS (S)

[Note: [Col. 0975D] **The letter is suspect by the same right as the other wares of Isidore.**—*The Letter.* Cyprian bears witness in Epistle LXVII that Pontiff Lucius wrote not only this one letter but several decretal letters, in these words: “For they”—he is speaking of the pontiffs Cornelius and Lucius—“filled with the Spirit of God and established in glorious martyrdom, judged that peace should be granted to the lapsed and signified by their letters that, once penance had been performed, the fruit of communion and peace should not be denied.” The letters that Lucius wrote concerning this matter are not extant. The one found under Cyprian’s name as Epistle LXX and bearing the name of Lucius was believed by some to belong to this pontiff; but they were deceived because they did not know that there was a bishop bearing the same name, and wrongly attributed to Pontiff Lucius a letter that belongs to another. Baronius, year 257, no. 4.]

## LETTER OF POPE LUCIUS I TO THE BISHOPS OF GAUL AND SPAIN

[Col. 0975C]

### SUMMARY

That two presbyters and three deacons should accompany the bishop in every place for the sake of ecclesiastical testimony; concerning the accusation of bishops; concerning harmonious unanimity between the metropolitan and the other bishops; and that plunderers and those who remove, usurp, or alienate ecclesiastical property be anathematized as thieves and sacrilegious persons.

I. That a bishop should always have presbyters and deacons with him as witnesses.

II. Concerning accusations against bishops, or elders, and that a hearing should not be denied to those appealing to persons of higher rank.

III. That a metropolitan should do nothing without the counsel of the bishops, nor they without his, except in matters pertaining to their own churches.

[Col. 0975D]

IV. That a metropolitan should not hear the case of bishops without the bishops.

[Col. 0976C]

V. That later bishops should not prefer themselves to earlier ones or act without consulting them.

VI. Concerning those who seize the property of the Church or the offerings of the faithful, and those who consent to them.

## LUCIUS, BISHOP, TO ALL HIS MOST BELOVED BROTHERS DWELLING IN THE WESTERN REGIONS, BOTH IN GAUL AND IN SPAIN: GREETINGS IN THE LORD

We gladly received the letters of your charity (Saint Leo, Epistle XXVIII), which you sent to the See of the blessed apostle Peter concerning your legal affair; but we were deeply saddened by your afflictions. For you informed us that you are being persecuted and defamed both by certain persons who do not hold the right faith but are entangled in errors, and by others who imitate them; that your [Col. 0976D] churches are being stripped of their endowments and of the offerings of the faithful; and that your ministers are being excessively harassed. You therefore stated that many are departing from you and from the right faith because you are unable to provide them with protection or minister the necessities to them.

Do not be surprised, brothers, if malicious and impious people persecute you, since they persecuted Christ himself, our head. Hence you possess the Truth herself as your consoler, who says: “If they called the master of the household Beelzebub, how much more will they so call the members of his household?” (Matt. 10). Again she speaks to console us, saying: “If you had been of the world, the world would love what was its own; but because you are not of the world, but I chose you out of the world, therefore the world hates you” (John 16).

[Note: [Col. 0977D] I.—“Let two presbyters or three deacons never leave the bishop in any place.” It is decreed that, to avoid the dangers of disparagement and defamation, bishops should go nowhere unless accompanied by two presbyters and three deacons, for the sake of the Church’s testimony. The calumnies fabricated by Novatian against Cornelius, discussed above, appear to have provided the occasion for enacting this decree. Baronius, year 257, no. 5.]

I. Because of such people, brothers, we exhort you—as we have also established [Col. 0977A] in this holy Church (*On Consecration*, distinction I, “We Command by Apostolic Authority”)—always to have priests and deacons with you as witnesses. Although one’s own conscience may suffice, nevertheless, because of malicious people, you must also, according to the Apostle, “have a good testimony from those who are outside” (1 Tim. 3). For we have also established in this holy See that two presbyters or three deacons should never leave the bishop in any place, for the sake of ecclesiastical testimony.

II. Bishops, therefore, are not to be lightly accused or disparaged, because an injury done to them (Gregory, *Epistle* 32, book XII) pertains to Christ, whose place they hold and whose embassy they discharge in the Church. Hence, for our consolation and that of all who are with us, it has pleased us to decree—as we find was also done of old [Col. 0977B]—that accusations against elders are not to be brought through others (2, q. 7), but only by those who themselves advance the charges (Anianus, chapter 25, letter I, book IX of the *Theodosian Code*), provided, however, that they themselves appear worthy and irreproachable, and demonstrate by public records (Council of Arles, canon 13) that they are free from every suspicion and hostility and lead an irreproachable life of faith and conduct (Hadrian, *Collection*, chapter 9). Hence it has pleased us that, if an appeal is made from any ecclesiastical judges (Third Council of Carthage, chapter 10) to other ecclesiastical judges where there is greater authority, a hearing is not to be denied.

III. We likewise decree (3, q. 3; there, however, no primate is presented under the name of Callistus), as we find was decreed by the holy Apostles and their successors [Col. 0977C], that if any metropolitan bishop should attempt to conduct any matter outside his own diocese—apart from what pertains solely to his own diocese—without the counsel and consent of all the bishops of the province (Hadrian, *Collection*, chapter 46), he shall place his rank in jeopardy, and whatever he has done shall be regarded as null and void. But whatever it may be necessary to do or arrange concerning the cases of his fellow bishops in the province, their churches and clergy and the needs of secular persons, or concerning any common matters whatsoever, is to be conducted with the consent of all the bishops of the province—not with any pride of domination, but through harmonious and most humble administration, as the Lord says: “I came not to be ministered unto, but to minister” (Matt. XX; Mark X). And elsewhere: “He who is greatest among you shall be your minister” [Col. 0977D] (Matt. XXIII), and so forth. Similarly, the bishops of the province themselves are to conduct everything with his counsel—apart from what pertains to their own dioceses—in accordance with the ordinances of the holy Fathers, so that with one mind and one voice the Holy Trinity may harmoniously be glorified in—

[Col. 0978A]

IV. Likewise (Hadrian, *Collection*, chapter 14), supported by apostolic authority, we command that no metropolitan bishop hear the cases of any of the bishops of his province without the urgent participation of all the other bishops of that province; for such proceedings shall be null, and he himself shall have to answer for what he has done.

V. The bishops throughout the several provinces are to take care that those junior in rank do not set themselves above their seniors, nor undertake anything without consulting them (Council of Milevis, chapter 13; *African Code*, chapter 86), apart from what pertains to their own dioceses. Rather, all are to deliver and determine a harmonious judgment concerning their common cases, because proceedings conducted otherwise would possess no force and will not be regarded as ecclesiastical (Hadrian, *Collection*, chapter 3).

It would be good, brothers, and exceedingly necessary for those who fear God and wish to live devoutly, if within [Col. 0978B] the catholic Church no seed of evil or of any persecution against the Lord’s priests, or against those wishing to live justly and devoutly, were to spring up. But because, as envy prevails, what is worse arises and grows and spreads itself altogether too widely in every direction, it is therefore necessary that it be cut away with the ecclesiastical and apostolic sword, lest it have power to harm or destroy the servants of God [Note: [Col. 0977D] Another reading: “slaves”] and the Lord’s priests [Note: [Col. 0977D] Another reading: “priests”].

For, as is written in the book of Ecclesiasticus:

> The Lord dishonored the assemblies of the wicked, and God destroyed them utterly. God destroyed the seats of proud rulers and caused the meek to sit in their place. God withered the roots of proud nations and planted the humble from among those nations. The Lord overthrew the lands of the nations and destroyed them down to their foundations. He withered some of them, destroyed them, and caused the memory of them [Col. 0978C] to cease from the earth. God destroyed the memory of the proud and left behind the memory of the humble in understanding.
>
> Pride was not created for human beings, nor wrathful anger for the race of women. That seed of humanity which fears God shall be honored; but that seed of humanity which transgresses the Lord’s commandments shall be dishonored. In the midst of his brothers their ruler is held in honor, and those who fear the Lord shall be in his sight. The glory of the rich, the honored, and the poor is the fear of God.
>
> Do not despise a just man because he is poor, and do not magnify a sinful man because he is rich. The great man, the judge, and the powerful man are held in honor, but none is greater than the man who fears God. Free men shall serve a sensible slave, and a prudent and disciplined man will not murmur when corrected, while the ignorant man shall not be honored.
>
> Do not exalt yourself in doing [Note: [Col. 0978D] Another reading: “in your work” or “your work”] your works, and do not delay in a time of distress. Better is one who [Col. 0978D] works and abounds in all things than one who boasts and lacks bread. Son, preserve your soul in meekness, and give it honor according to its worth. Who will justify one who sins against his own soul? And who will honor one who dishonors his own soul?
>
> The poor man boasts in his discipline and fear; and there is a man who is honored because of his substance. But if one boasts in poverty, how much more in substance? And one who boasts in substance should fear poverty. Wisdom will raise the head of the humbled man and cause him to sit among the great.
>
> Do not praise a man for his appearance, nor despise a man because of his looks. The bee is small among flying creatures [Col. 0979A], yet its fruit possesses the first sweetness. Never boast in your clothing, nor exalt yourself on the day of your honor, because the works of the Most High alone are wonderful and glorious, hidden and unseen are his works.
>
> Many tyrants have sat upon the throne, and one who was not suspected has worn the diadem. Many powerful men have been greatly oppressed, and glorious men have been delivered into the hands of others.
>
> Before you inquire, do not condemn anyone; and when you have inquired, correct justly. Before you have heard, do not answer a word, and do not interrupt while elders are speaking. Do not contend over a matter that does not trouble you, and do not stand in the judgment of sinners.
>
> My son, do not let your undertakings be many; and if you become rich, you will not be free from fault. For if you pursue, you will not overtake; and if you run ahead, you will not escape. There is a man who labors and hastens and grieves in impiety, and [Col. 0979B] all the more he shall not abound.
>
> There is a withered man in need of recovery, greatly deficient in strength and abounding in poverty; yet the eye of God looked favorably upon him, raised him from his lowliness, and will exalt his head. Many marveled at him and honored God.
>
> Good and evil, life and death, poverty and respectability come from God. God’s gift remains with the just, and its advancement shall enjoy success forever.
>
> There is one who grows rich by acting sparingly, and this is the portion of his reward when he says: “I have found rest for myself, and now I shall eat of my goods alone.” Yet he does not know that time is passing him by, that he will leave everything to others, and that he will die.
>
> Stand firm in your covenant, converse upon it, and grow old in [Note: [Col. 0979D] Another reading: “work”] carrying out your commandments. Do not remain in the works of sinners. Trust in God, however, and remain in your place. For it is easy in God’s sight suddenly [Col. 0979C] to bring poverty to honor [Note: [Col. 0979D] Another reading: “to honor”]. God’s blessing hastens toward the reward of the just, and in swift honor his progress [Note: [Col. 0979D] Another reading: “bears fruit”] brings justification.
>
> Do not say, “What need have I?” and “What good things will come to me from this?” Do not say, “I am sufficient for myself; how shall this make me worse?” On a day of good things, do not be unmindful of evils; and on a day of evils, do not be unmindful of good things, because it is easy before God, on the day of death, to repay each person according to his ways.
>
> The evil of an hour causes great luxury to be forgotten, and at a man’s end his works are laid bare. Before his death, praise no man, because a man is known in his children.
>
> Do not bring every man into your house, for the snares of the deceitful are many. For just as the entrails of the fetid [Note: [Col. 0979D] Another reading: “of those emitting a stench”] belch forth, and as a partridge is brought into a cage and a roe deer into a snare, so also is the heart of the proud man, like a watcher observing [Col. 0979D] his neighbor’s fall. The plotter turns good into [Note: [Col. 0979D] Another reading: “The plotter turns evils into good.” The manuscript of the Jesuit College of Paris, according to Hardouin, reads: “for he turns good into evil”] evil and will place a blemish upon the elect.
>
> From a single spark the fire increases, and through one deceitful man bloodshed increases. A sinful man lies in wait for blood. Guard yourself against a pestilent man, for he fabricates evils, lest perhaps he bring perpetual mockery upon you. Admit a foreigner to yourself, and he will overthrow you in a whirlwind and estrange you from [Note: [Col. 0980D] Another reading: “the ways”] your own people.  
> (Ecclus. X–XI)

Such men, dearly beloved, must be guarded against with the greatest care until they are either converted or [Col. 0980A] cut off by the divine word.

> Blessed, however, is he who has not slipped through a word from his mouth and has not been pierced by sorrow for sin. Happy is he who has no sorrow in his soul and has not [Note: [Col. 0980D] Another reading: “fallen away”] departed from his hope.  
> (Ecclus. XIV)

For it is written: “Better is one who fears God than a thousand impious men” (*ibid.* XVI). Not everyone who does harm, however, is wise (Sentences of Sixtus 292; 6, q. 1, *Sapiens non est*; and above, in the *Decrees of Cornelius*, 6).

VI. As for the property of your churches (Sentences of Sixtus 292) and the offerings of the faithful, which you have reported are being assailed by certain invaders and taken away from you and your churches, this is unquestionably a very great sin. Scripture itself bears witness (St. Boniface, *Epistle* 19), saying: “Whoever takes [12, q. 2, *Qui abstulerit*] anything away from father or mother and says that this is not a sin is an accomplice of a murderer” [Col. 0980B] (Prov. XXVIII).

God, therefore, who created us, is without doubt our Father; and the Church, which spiritually begot us in Baptism, is our mother. Therefore, whoever takes away, defrauds, and plunders (17, q. 4, *Qui rapit*) the money of Christ and the Church shall be accounted a murderer in the sight (St. Gregory, *Epistle* 36, book II) of the just Judge. Hence it is written: “Whoever plunders his neighbor’s money commits iniquity” (John XIII); but whoever takes away the money or property of the Church commits sacrilege (Jerome, *Epistle* 2).

Hence Judas also, who fraudulently took the money which, at the Savior’s command, was distributed for the Church’s uses—that is, to the poor whom the Church is obliged to feed, the bishops holding the Savior’s place—became not only a thief but both a thief and [St. Augustine, *Tractate* L on John] a sacrilegious man.

[Col. 0980C] Concerning such people, namely, those who plunder, defraud, or take away the Church’s resources, the Lord speaks threateningly to everyone through the Prophet, saying:

> O God, do not remain silent; do not be still, and do not rest, O God. For behold, your enemies have raised a tumult, and those who hate you have lifted up their heads. They have plotted wickedly against your people and entered into counsel against your hidden ones. They said: “Come [Note: [Col. 0980D] The same manuscript reads: “let us scatter”] and let us crush them as a nation, and let the name of Israel be remembered no more.” For they conspired in heart; together [Note: [Col. 0980D] The same manuscript reads: “against them”] they made a covenant against you: the tents of Edom and the Ishmaelites, Moab and the Hagarenes, Gebal and Ammon and Amalek, Philistia together with the inhabitants [Note: [Col. 0980D] The same manuscript reads: “those inhabiting”] of Tyre. Assyria also joined them; they became an arm to the sons of Lot.
>
> Do to them as to Midian, as to Sisera, as to Jabin at the torrent Kishon [Note: [Col. 0980D] Another reading: “Cison”]. [Col. 0980D] They were crushed at Endor; they became like the dung of the earth. Make their rulers like Oreb and Zeeb, like Zebah and Zalmunna—all their princes, who said: “Let us possess for ourselves the beauty of God.”
>
> My God, make them like a wheel, like straw before the face of the wind. As fire burns a forest and as flame devours the mountains, so shall you pursue them in your tempest and trouble them in your whirlwind. Fill their faces with shame, and they shall seek your name, O Lord. Let them be confounded [Col. 0981A] and troubled forever; let them blush with shame and perish, and let them know that your name is the Lord: you alone are exalted over all the earth.  
> (Psalm LXXXII, from St. Jerome’s translation, differing from the Vulgate)

The Prophets forbid these things to be done; the Apostles forbid them; the decrees of their successors and of all the catholic Fathers forbid them and judge [Note: [Col. 0981C] Another reading: “judge it to be sacrilege”] such acts of presumption to be sacrilege. Following their examples, together with you and by apostolic authority, we drive away from the thresholds of holy mother Church, condemn, and anathematize all such presumptuous persons and plunderers of the Church (17, q. 4, *Omnes raptores*) and alienators of her resources (Hincmar, *Epistle* VIII, Mainz editions; Council of Quierzy, in the letter to the bishops of Gaul), and we judge them to be sacrilegious [Col. 0981B].

And not only them, but all who consent to them; for not only those who commit such deeds are judged guilty, but also those who consent to those committing them (Rom. I). The same punishment encompasses both those who act and those who consent.

You, therefore, brothers, watch and pray. Act manfully and be strengthened in the Lord, and, according to the Apostle, let all that you do be done in charity (I Cor. XVI). Therefore do not depart from the right faith (14, q. 1, *A recta ergo*; and in the decrees of Pope Felix) and the apostolic path because of any persecution whatsoever, knowing that, according to the Savior’s declaration, blessed are those who suffer persecution [Note: [Col. 0981C] Another reading: “disturbance”] for righteousness’ sake (Matt. V).

This is the living tradition of the Apostles (Agatho to Emperor Constantine, act VI of the Council of Constantinople against the Monothelites); this is the true charity which must be preached and especially [Col. 0981C] loved and fostered, and which all must hold with confidence. This holy and apostolic Church, the mother of all the churches of Christ, which by the grace of almighty God is proved never to have strayed from the path of apostolic tradition, nor to have succumbed to corruption [Note: [Col. 0982C] Another reading: “corrupted”] by heretical novelties, remains undefiled to the very end in accordance with the rule of apostolic faith which she received at the beginning from her founders, the chief Apostles of Christ. This accords with the divine promise of the Lord and Savior himself, who spoke in his Gospels to the chief of his disciples, saying:

> Peter, behold, Satan has demanded to sift you as one who sifts [Col. 0982A] wheat. But I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail; and when you have at length turned again, strengthen your brothers.  
> (Luke XXII)

Let your excellent prudence therefore consider how good it is to persevere in the stewardship entrusted to you and in the right faith, to resist heretics and the rivals of Christ, and never to turn aside from the path of truth. For the Lord and Savior of all—to whom the faith belongs, who did not hesitate to die for us and redeemed us with his own blood—promised that the faith of blessed Peter would not fail and admonished him to strengthen his brothers. It is known to everyone that the apostolic Pontiffs, the predecessors of my lowliness, have always done this with confidence. My own insignificance also, though unequal and the least of them, nevertheless desires, in the ministry received through divine favor, [Col. 0982B] to follow in their footsteps.

For woe shall be to us who have undertaken the burden of this ministry if we neglect to preach the truth of our Savior Jesus Christ, which the Apostles preached (I Cor. IX). Woe shall be to us if by silence we suppress the truth which we are commanded to pay out to the money-changers—that is, to impart to and teach the Christian peoples (Matt. XXV). What shall we say at Christ’s future examination if we are ashamed to preach the truth of his words? What will become of us when Christ our Lord, the just Judge, demands from us a strict account of the souls entrusted to us and of the office we have undertaken (Luke XVI)?

Therefore, brothers, I exhort (St. Leo, *Epistle* I against the Manichaeans), beseech, and admonish your charity to exercise all the vigilance you ought and [Col. 0982C] can in searching out the heretics and enemies of God’s holy Church, and, lest this plague spread more widely, to root it out from sound minds with all the severity in your power. For just as one who has more diligently carried out what advances the salvation of the people entrusted to him will receive from God the reward of fitting recompense, so before the Lord’s tribunal no one who has refused to guard his people against the authors of sacrilegious persuasion will be able to excuse himself from the charge of negligence.

Given on the Kalends of April in the year 252, while Cornelius was still living, in the consulship of the most illustrious men Gallus and Volusianus.

# DECREES OF POPE LUCIUS, TAKEN FROM GRATIAN

[Col. 0981]

## I. A bishop, priest, or deacon who takes a wife or retains one already taken is to be deprived of office and benefice

[Col. 0981D]

Ministers of the altar (Distinction 81), whether priests or deacons, are to be chosen for the Lord’s offices only if they observe continence. But if, after their ordination, ministers happen to enter the bed of their own wife, they are not to enter the thresholds of the sanctuary, nor become doorkeepers of the sanctuary, nor touch the altar, nor receive from those making offerings the oblation of the whole burnt offering, nor approach or draw near to receive a portion of the Lord’s body, nor discharge the greater offices without the authority of an elder. They may not even carry a pitcher or chalice to the altar.

## FROM THE SAME DECREES

### II. A cleric who frequents the homes of matrons is to be deposed

[Col. 0982D]

A cleric (Distinction 81) is not to approach a woman’s dwelling alone, nor go there frequently without the command of a senior priest. Nor is a priest alone to engage in conversation with a woman alone. Nor is an archdeacon, under the pretext of humility or official duty, frequently to enter the homes of matrons or perhaps send some secret message to a matron through clerics or members of her household. If anything of this kind becomes known, let him be deposed and her be barred from the threshold of the church.

## FROM THE SAME DECREES

### III. On the same subject

[Col. 0983A]

But if by chance there has been some request for intervention [Note: [Col. 0984A] This is Clement’s second epistle to James, the brother of the Lord. HARDUIN], it is to be presented to the bishop. And if the woman is one whom they ought to visit, let the bishop himself go through the intervention. Otherwise, let him send someone from his side with two or three witnesses. No one, however, is to live with an unrelated woman unless she is his sister or a close relative, and even this must be done with great vigilance. For we are not ignorant of Satan’s designs (II Cor. II).

## FROM THE SAME DECREES

*(From the old Penitential in Cantius, Vet. lect., vol. II, part II, p. 131, Basnage’s edition; from Mansi’s new supplement, vol. I, p. 14.)*

### IV. Whoever, for a gift, either denies reconciliation to the worthy or con-[source gap] to the unworthy is guilty of simony

Let no priest accept from anyone who is publicly sinful or incestuous a gift or any temporal [Col. 0984A] advantage—indeed, a spiritual loss—in order to conceal that person’s sin from the bishop or the ministers. Nor, out of regard for anyone’s person, blood relationship, or familiarity, is he to make himself a participant in another’s sins by refusing to disclose the matter to the bishop. Nor is he to presume to receive any favor, goodwill, or gift from a penitent; or bring a less-than-worthy penitent to reconciliation and bear witness to his reconciliation; or, out of any malice whatsoever, exclude from reconciliation any other person who has performed worthier penance. For this is simoniacal and contrary to both God and human beings.

# IN THE YEARS OF THE LORD 253–257: ST. STEPHEN I, POPE AND MARTYR—LIFE, LETTERS, AND DECREES

[Col. 0983]

# PREFACE

From the Pontifical Book of Pope Damasus

[Col. 0983B]

[Note: [Col. 0983B]

**Stephen.** Stephen, a Roman by birth, was placed upon the pontifical throne on the ninth of April in the year of Christ 257, the fourth year of Gallus and Volusianus and the third of Valerian and Gallienus, after the pontifical See had been without a shepherd for thirty-five days. At the beginning of this pontificate, after the two aforesaid emperors, Gallus and Volusianus, had been killed as Cyprian had foretold, the Church enjoyed peace and a certain tranquility until the fifth year of the emperor Valerian and the year of Christ 259. At that time Emperor Valerian, who at the beginning of his reign had been most benevolent and exceedingly well disposed toward [Col. 0983C] the Christians, was in turn incited against them by a certain Egyptian magician and induced to take up arms against them once more. Dionysius of Alexandria in Eusebius, book VII, chapter 9; Baronius, year 257, numbers 6 and 7.

Since, therefore, the peace that had been restored was not destined to last long, Cyprian and the other bishops of the African Church, meeting in the many councils held in Africa, labored with the greatest effort to correct whatever alien to catholic faith and good morals had crept into the Church, eradicate heresies, correct vices, and finally confirm the doctrines of the orthodox faith.

In Epistle 63, written to Caelius, Cyprian refutes the heresy of the Aquarians, who offered water alone in the sacrifice. He says that, while persecution was raging, they assembled for the sacred synaxis very early in the morning—or rather, during the night—and offered water in place of wine, evidently so that when they drank Christ’s blood under the species of wine, the odor of wine might not betray them as a kind of evidence of Christianity. Baronius, year 257, numbers 9, 10, and 11.

Because Marcian, bishop of Arles [Col. 0983D] in Gaul, was at this time deeply devoted to Novatian and had also led many into the same error, Faustinus, bishop of Lyons, together with Cyprian and the other fellow bishops of Gaul, earnestly requested by letters written to Stephen—Cyprian’s letters are extant below—that, in fulfillment of his office and duty, he depose Marcian, the adherent of Novatian, from his see and appoint another in his place. Baronius, year 258, numbers 8, 9, and 10.

Under this Pontiff a most serious controversy began to arise and be debated among the bishops and doctors of the catholic Church, namely: Whether Baptism conferred by a heretical minister according to the legitimate form of the catholic Church and with the requisite intention of the minister—that is, in [Col. 0984B] the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit—is invalid, and therefore must be repeated, because it was administered by a heretical minister.

Cyprian, together with Firmilian of Asia and very many other Eastern bishops, not only affirmed that it was invalid, but also confirmed the same position several times in the many councils held on this subject in Africa: namely, that there is one Baptism, which cannot be found outside the one catholic Church.

Stephen, however, the Pontiff of the Roman Church, taught that it was an ancient apostolic tradition that those baptized by heretics were received [Col. 0984C] by the laying on of hands alone. Accordingly, as Vincent of Lérins says in *Against Heresies*, chapter 9, Stephen taught that nothing was to be innovated in this matter, but that what had been handed down by the Apostles was to be preserved in its entirety. He set the apostolic tradition like an impregnable wall against their opinions and, relying almost exclusively upon it, defined that the Baptism which a heretical minister had conferred according to the form prescribed by Christ and employed by the Church was valid and effective and was by no means to be repeated.

Not only almost all the African Fathers, but also Firmilian, Dionysius, and Cyprian, who had been defenders of the opposing doctrine, acceded to this judgment of Pontiff Stephen. Baronius proves this from Augustine, *Epistle* 48 to Vincentius and *On Baptism Against the Donatists*, book VI, chapter 2; likewise from Jerome, *Against the Luciferians*, and from other arguments, under the year of Christ 258, numbers 49, 50, and 51.

On this controversy, one should read Cyprian’s Epistle 70 together with the following seven letters, Augustine’s *On Baptism Against the Donatists*, Jerome’s [Col. 0984D] *Against the Luciferians*, and Baronius under the aforesaid year, number 2 and those following. One should also note how great is the force of the apostolic traditions, and how great the authority vested in Peter’s successor: fortified by virtually no weapons other than the tradition of his predecessors, he withstood the entire assault of the Eastern and Western bishops and, receiving upon the single shield of tradition their densely discharged missiles drawn from the divine Scriptures, hurled them back.  
**SEVERINUS BINIUS**

As Eusebius states in book VII, chapter 2, Lucius at his death left the episcopal office to Stephen; and indeed, as both Eusebius’s *Chronicle* and the Bucherian Catalogue teach, this occurred during the consulship of Volusianus and Maximinus—or rather [Col. 0985A] Maximus—that is, in the year of Christ 253. According to the testimony of Eusebius, book VII, chapter 5, with whom Jerome agrees in his *Chronicle*, Stephen governed the Church for two years.

Although the Bucherian Catalogue attributes to him four years, two months, and twenty-one days in the See, it nevertheless approaches Eusebius’s reckoning insofar as it assigns his death to the consulship of Valerian III and Gallienus II, that is, the year of Christ 255. At the beginning of the calendar published by the aforesaid Bucherius, the burial of St. Stephen is recorded for the fourth day before the Nones of August in the cemetery of Callistus. Ancient monuments attest that his feast was celebrated on the same day formerly, just as it is now.

If, however, the Third Council of Carthage concerning those who come to the Church from heresy [Col. 0985B]—which immediately followed Stephen’s letter to Cyprian—was held in 256, as scholars generally think, Stephen’s death must be assigned not to the consulship of Valerian III and Gallienus II, as the Bucherian Catalogue represents it, but to that of Valerian IV and Gallienus III, as it appears in the Pontifical Book—that is, to the year 257. Both the four years of this Pope’s pontificate attributed to him in the Bucherian Catalogue [Col. 0986A] and the tradition concerning his martyrdom are more readily reconciled with this epoch. For in the year 255 the Church, according to Dionysius of Alexandria, enjoyed complete peace. Antonius Pagius, Tillemont, and others therefore defer Stephen’s death to the year 257.  
**COUSTANT**

He occupied the See for seven years, five months, and two days. The Pontifical Book and the Acts of Stephen attest that Stephen was crowned with martyrdom after three years, three months, and twenty-two days, under Valerian’s fourth consulship, which is assigned in the consular lists to the year of Christ 260. Accordingly, once the beginning of his pontificate is placed earlier by that interval of time, it follows that he occupied the See for the stated period. Baronius, year 260, number 2.  
**SEVERINUS [Col. 0986B] BINIUS**

“Valerian’s fourth consulship,” etc. The more accurate Acts of St. Stephen likewise assign it to Valerian’s fourth consulship. Baronius proves under the year of Christ 260, number 2, that the reading found in some copies—Valerian’s third consulship and Gallienus’s second—is erroneous.  
**SEVERINUS BINIUS**]

Stephen, a Roman by nationality, son of Julius [Note: [Col. 0983B] Uncertain reading: “Jobius, five”], occupied the See [Col. 0984B] for seven years, five months, and two days. He was crowned with martyrdom. He lived in the times of Valerian, Gallicanus, and Maximus, until the fourth consulship of Valerian and the third of Gallicanus [Note: [Col. 0984B] “Gallienus, consuls”]. He decreed that priests and Levites were not to wear consecrated vestments in daily use, but only in the church. He conducted two ordinations in the month of December: six priests, five deacons [Col. 0986A], and three bishops for various places. He was buried in the cemetery of Callistus on the Appian Way, on the fourth day before the Nones of August. The episcopate then ceased for twenty-two days.

[Col. 0985]

# ACCOUNT OF THE NON-EXTANT LETTERS PERTAINING TO STEPHEN

By Dom Coustant, O.S.B.

## I

[Col. 0985B]

### 1

Letters from Faustinus, bishop of Lyons, and the other bishops of the same province to Pope Stephen, in which they reported that Marcian, bishop of Arles, had joined himself to Novatian, embraced the exceedingly harsh perversity of that heresy, and withdrawn from the fellowship of the bishops [Col. 0985C].

Marcian had advanced to such audacity that he did not fear to pass judgment upon and separate from himself the college of priests who held that peace should be given to the lapsed after due penance, even though he himself did not yet appear to have been excluded from communion by them. Faustinus wrote once and again to Cyprian concerning this same matter (*Epistle* I to Stephen, no. 1). Some suspect that this was done so that, when Faustinus and his associates had obtained nothing from Stephen, they might through Cyprian’s efforts or admonitions procure assistance for the catholic bishops.

Those who preside over affairs of the highest importance are often blamed as sluggish when they are compelled to defer certain matters, whether because of excessive occupation or as a matter of prudence; yet when they exercise diligence, they can scarcely avoid the suspicion of having acted precipitately.

As for Cyprian, he was so far from doubting that Stephen would, at his counsel and exhortation, send letters to the province and people of Arles commanding both that Marcian be excluded from communion and that another bishop be appointed in his place, that he asks at the same time to be informed who had been appointed (*ibid.*, nos. 3 and 5) [Col. 0985D]. That letters of this kind were indeed sent by Stephen is indicated by the fact that Marcian’s name does not appear in the diptychs of Arles, as we have already observed.

In this affair Cyprian, demonstrating his own zeal and solicitude for all the churches, acknowledged by testimony admitting of no doubt the authority of the Roman Pontiff both to remove the bishop of Arles from his see and to appoint another in his place. For the recent author of the *Cyprianic Annals* does not appear worthy of a hearing when he maintains that Cyprian “requested nothing from Stephen”—although he was advising him to send letters to the province—“which he himself was not prepared to perform,” unless one silently adds, “if he had occupied the same see and position.”

### 2

Nothing prevents the letters of Faustinus to Stephen from being assigned to the first year of this pontificate. It is at least clear that they were written before the controversy concerning the Baptism of heretics arose. For there is no doubt [Col. 0986B] that this controversy occurred after the letter which Cyprian subsequently wrote to Stephen concerning Marcian’s case. The aforesaid author of the *Cyprianic Annals* proves that this case belongs to a point already well advanced in the second year of Stephen’s pontificate. It follows that, if Stephen sent to the people of Arles the letters Cyprian was advising, they were composed no earlier than the end of the year 254 [Col. 0986C].

## II

### 3

Basilides, bishop of León and Astorga, had been expelled from the episcopate because of the crime of idolatry and other offenses, and Sabinus had been appointed in his place. Basilides then went to Rome to Stephen, from whom he obtained restoration to his see.

Cyprian explained what he thought of this matter as follows (*from Cyprian, Epistle* 68):

> Nor can the lawfully completed ordination be rescinded [*ibid.*] because Basilides, after his crimes had been disclosed and his conscience laid bare even by his own confession, went to Rome and deceived our colleague Stephen, who was situated far away and ignorant of what had occurred and of the truth that had been concealed. Thus he importuned him to have himself unjustly restored to the episcopate from which he had justly been deposed. The effect of this is that Basilides’ offenses have not so much been erased as multiplied, since to his former sins [Col. 0986D] there has also been added the crime of deception and circumvention. For the man who was negligently deceived is not so much to be blamed as the man who fraudulently deceived him is to be execrated.

That is, he sought to obtain letters by which both communion and his see would be restored to him. For without letters bearing witness both to Stephen’s judgment and to the communion granted him by Stephen, he could have hoped for neither. The words of Cyprian just quoted establish that he importuned Stephen not only for Stephen’s communion but also for the episcopate—and specifically the episcopate from which he had been expelled. For why would he have attempted to rescind the ordination of Sabinus, who had been appointed in his place, by concealing the truth of what had occurred, unless it was so that he might return to the see from which he falsely claimed that he had been unjustly expelled?

4. Pamelius observes that “this passage supports the authority of the Roman pontiff, since it establishes that bishops deposed from their sees in Spain were accustomed to appeal to him.” This observation would acquire new weight if it were established that Martial, bishop of Mérida, who had been removed from the episcopate at the same time, and whom Cyprian [Col. 0987A] likewise notes as having employed deceit in order to usurp the dignity taken from him, had wished to reclaim it for himself by the authority of Stephen himself. They had been preceded by the example of Privatus, bishop of Lambaesis, who, “having been condemned by the judgment of ninety bishops because of many grave offenses” (Cyprian, Epistle XII, no. 10), had sent a legate to Rome so that, while the See was vacant, he might endeavor to obtain letters from its clergy by theft and fraud. Hence the authority of this Church is commended more and more. Although Cyprian certainly does not deny it, he nevertheless does not remain silent about the disadvantages of appeals of this kind, when he represents Stephen as being far away and ignorant of what had taken place, and therefore deceived (Cyprian, Epistle XXX). For this reason, above, in Epistle XII, no. 14, he wrote to Cornelius that it had been determined by all who were with him “that each person’s case should be heard there where the offense was committed, where they can also have accusers and witnesses to their offense.” Later the most equitable pontiff Gregory perceived the same disadvantage; and therefore he referred the case of a certain Peter, a Numidian bishop who had fled to him after being condemned, to the prelates of that same province. Thus he speaks on the matter to Columbus, bishop of Numidia:

“We therefore inform Your Holiness that a certain man named Peter has come to us, asserting that he had been a bishop and requesting from us a remedy for his case. At first, indeed, he related matters that might have deserved compassion; but, upon inquiry, we afterward found the situation to be very different from what he had reported, and his conduct deeply saddened us. But because, separated as we were by so great a distance of travel, we could by no means learn the inner details of his case precisely, we were unable, being naturally uncertain, to decide it, etc.” (Book VI, Indiction 14, Epistle 37, no. 2).

I pass over other instances of this kind. As for the affair of Basilides, however, throughout it Cyprian displays such a manner of proceeding that I am quite willing to agree with the opinion of those who judge that it preceded the famous controversy over the baptism of heretics.

### III

[Col. 0987C] 5. Nothing also prevents us from referring to the period preceding the aforesaid controversy those letters which Dionysius of Alexandria, in the preceding fragment, records as having been written by Stephen to Syria and Arabia. Dionysius indeed says nothing about what was discussed in them; but it is highly probable that Stephen, not content merely to relieve the poverty of those provinces by supplying their necessities, also sought to console the minds of the faithful with kindly and wholesome writings and to encourage them to piety. Moreover, the schism of Novatian, which had penetrated those provinces and whose stain Dionysius afterward reported to have been entirely cleansed from them, provided him with abundant material for discussion.

### IV

6. Helenus, bishop of Tarsus, together with all Cilicia, and Firmilian, together with all Cappadocia and the neighboring regions, had scarcely returned to the unity of the Church in detestation of Novatian’s innovation when they passed into a new dissension; for they had not learned to separate themselves from that other opinion which adamantly required heretics returning to the Church to be baptized.
