Therefore Stephen, says Eusebius, “wrote letters concerning Helenus and Firmilian, and, in short, concerning all the priests established throughout Cilicia, Cappadocia, and all the neighboring provinces, in which he announced that for this reason he would withdraw from communion with them: because they rebaptized heretics” (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VII, ch. 5). Firmilian, censuring those letters, speaks of them to Cyprian as follows:

“For what could be more humble or gentle than to have disagreed with so many bishops throughout the whole world, breaking peace with individuals by various kinds of discord—now with the Easterners, a fact which we trust has not escaped your knowledge, and now with you who are in the South?” (In Cyprian, near the end of Epistle LXXV.)

### V

7. At that very time Cyprian had received similar letters from the same pope [Col. 0988A] for the same reason. When Pompeius, bishop of Sabratha, questioned him about them, he transcribed, among other things, the following:

“If, therefore, anyone comes to us from any heresy whatsoever, let nothing be introduced beyond what has been handed down: namely, that a hand be laid upon him for repentance; since the heretics themselves do not baptize those who come to them from another heretical group, but merely admit them to communion” (Cyprian, Epistle LXXIV).

These words, however, have given occasion to more than one question. But so that those controversies may be settled more securely, it will be worthwhile to collect also the other statements which Firmilian and Cyprian record as having been written by Stephen, whether in the same letters or in others addressed to the Easterners.

8. What Firmilian notes in the following words may, without rashness, be referred to the opening of one or the other epistle: “Stephen boasts of the position of his episcopate and contends that he holds the succession of Peter, upon whom the foundations of the Church were laid.” Thus Stephen would have begun his discourse by commending the dignity of his see, as his successors also imitated him in affairs of this kind. Yet although Firmilian appears to criticize these words, he is nevertheless far from denying that the Church was strengthened and founded by Christ upon Peter. He himself also acknowledges that the power of remitting sins was given first to that Apostle and afterward to the others. Having laid this down, he then concludes:

“The power of remitting sins, therefore, was given to the Apostles, to the churches which they, having been sent by Christ, established, and to the bishops who succeeded them through a vicarious ordination.”

Thus he professes that Peter’s privilege passed to his successors.

9. Moreover, according to the testimony of the same Firmilian, Stephen spoke as follows in his letters: “As though the Apostles had forbidden those who come from heresy to be baptized and had handed this down to posterity to be observed.” The same Firmilian is displeased “that Stephen and those who agree with him contend that the forgiveness of sins and the second birth take place in the baptism of heretics, among whom they themselves also confess that the Holy Spirit [Col. 0988C] is not present; and at the same time they wish there to be one baptism common to us and to the heretics”; likewise, that “they do not think it necessary to inquire who the person who baptized was, because the person baptized could have obtained grace by invoking the Trinity of the names of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.”

Then, after many intervening remarks, Firmilian says that Stephen is not ashamed “to assert this: that through those who are themselves established in every kind of sin, he claims that forgiveness of sins can be given.” He also notes that Stephen and his associates defended themselves by Paul’s example, since Paul did not forbid that “whether through pretext or through truth, Christ should be proclaimed” (Phil. 1:18); and that they objected to those who rebaptized: “What, then, will become of those who, coming from the heretics, were admitted without the Church’s baptism?”

Firmilian also condemns the fact “that Stephen wishes the presence and holiness of Christ to be present with those who are baptized among heretics”; or what the same pope had committed to writing: “The name of Christ is exceedingly effective, so that whoever and wherever he has been baptized in the name of Christ immediately obtains the grace of Christ”; [Col. 0988D] and also this pronouncement by the same pontiff: “Heresy indeed gives birth and exposes its offspring, but the Church receives those who have been exposed.”

Finally, if we are to adhere to the words of the aforesaid bishop of Caesarea, “Stephen was not ashamed to rend the brotherhood; and, besides this, to call Cyprian a false Christ, a false apostle, and a deceitful worker.” Hence the same prelate presents him as “breaking peace now with the Easterners,” evidently through the letter he sent to the East, and now with the Africans, namely through the letter he wrote in reply to Cyprian. Concerning this, Cyprian, writing to Pompeius, speaks as follows: “Does he give honor to God who, as a friend of heretics and an enemy of Christians, thinks that the priests of God who defend the truth of Christ and the unity of the Church are TO BE EXCLUDED FROM COMMUNION?” (Epistle LXXIV.) Augustine also, in his book *On the Single Chapter against Petilian*, retains the word “to be excluded from communion” (*abstinendos*) when discussing the same matter.

10. Those very statements which Firmilian touches upon—or at least most of them—were contained in the epistle which Jubaianus had sent to Cyprian and which that prelate undertakes to refute in Epistle LXXIII, written in reply to Jubaianus. In it Cyprian testifies that he took offense at the claim “that it should not be asked who performed the baptism, since the person baptized could have received the forgiveness of sins in accordance with what he believed.” Firmilian too criticized this above. Cyprian adds that in the same epistle “mention is made of Marcion, so that it says that even those coming from him should not be baptized, because they appear already to have been baptized in the name of Jesus.”

Then, suppressing Stephen’s name, he reports several of his propositions in the following manner: “In vain do certain persons, when defeated by reason, set custom against us”; and shortly afterward, “Nor let anyone say: ‘What we have received from the Apostles, this we follow’”; and a little later, “For as to what certain persons say, as though what the Apostle Paul said supports the heretics: ‘Nevertheless, in every way, whether through pretext or through truth, Christ is proclaimed’”; and immediately thereafter, “No one, however, should set the name of Christ against Christian truth in order to circumvent it, saying: ‘Those baptized in the name of Jesus Christ, wherever and in whatever manner, have obtained the grace of baptism’”; and near the end, “But someone says: ‘What, then, will become of those who in the past came from heresy to the Church and were admitted without baptism?’”

11. From what source, then, comes so great an agreement between the statements which Firmilian and Cyprian attribute to Stephen and his associates, unless either Stephen repeated in his epistle to Cyprian what he had written to the Easterners, or both men had the same letter in their possession? Indeed, [Col. 0990A] there are weighty indications from which we may suspect that the epistle sent by Jubaianus to Cyprian was the very one Stephen had directed to the Easterners. If this is so, it follows that Stephen’s letters both to the Easterners and to Cyprian preceded the Third Council of Carthage under Cyprian; for at this council there were read aloud “both the letter written by Jubaianus to Cyprian and Cyprian’s letter to Jubaianus, as well as his reply to Stephen, and what the same Jubaianus afterward wrote back to Cyprian.”

Moreover, an argument that Stephen wrote to the Easterners and to Cyprian at about the same time is this: when Cyprian had arranged for a copy of the epistle he was writing in reply to Stephen to be transmitted to Firmilian, Firmilian indicated that he had received the letter in which Stephen announced that the Easterners were to be excluded from communion with him before receiving Cyprian’s copy. Now the council of Carthage just mentioned is dated to the Kalends of September, and most scholars agree that it was held in the year 256. Hence nothing prevents us from assigning the aforesaid letters of Stephen to the beginning of that same year, 256, or thereabouts. For the ardor with which Cyprian conducted himself in this matter does not permit us to suppose a long interval between the various writings, replies, or events of that period.

However that may be, the propositions of Stephen committed to writing by Firmilian and Cyprian—whether excerpted from his letter to the Easterners, from his letter to Cyprian, or even from both—are certainly sufficient to bring to an end many disputes concerning baptism that have been filled with contention. Let us put this to the test.

[Col. 0989]

# EPISTLES RELATING TO ST. STEPHEN I, POPE

[Note: [Col. 0989C]

**EPISTLE.**—Although the most distinguished Oxford editor says that he examined about twenty ancient manuscripts of Cyprian, he admits that he encountered none containing this epistle. Yet he does not conceal that the same has happened to other epistles whose authenticity no one has called into doubt. In his judgment, it must be said that Augustine, in book V (read VI) of *On Baptism against the Donatists*, ch. 15, where he mentions Cyprian’s epistle to Stephen, had this epistle specifically in view.

Moreover, in the cited passage Augustine reports the judgment of Crescens of Cirta, who says: “In so great an assembly of most holy fellow priests, the letters of our most beloved Cyprian to Jubaianus were read, and likewise the letter to Stephen.” He then immediately adds: “Someone may perhaps ask what he said concerning this epistle of blessed Cyprian to Stephen, which was mentioned in this opinion, although it was not mentioned at the opening of the council. I believe it was because this was not thought necessary.” Why he does not consider it necessary he immediately explains as follows: “For it has absolutely no bearing on the present question; and I wonder more why this man”—Crescens of Cirta—“wished to mention it than why mention of it was omitted at the opening of the council.” Finally, he adds: “For that epistle has absolutely nothing concerning baptism administered among heretics or schismatics, which is the matter we are now discussing.”

This indeed applies perfectly to the present epistle, but not to the following one, concerning which Augustine did not even suspect that Crescens was speaking, because he had neither seen nor heard anything about it before. And since only two epistles of Cyprian to Stephen are known—namely, this one, which in fact has absolutely nothing concerning baptism administered among heretics or schismatics, and the following one, which is entirely about this subject—it seems to follow that only this first epistle was known to Augustine, while the following one was unknown to him. If, moreover, Cyprian’s celebrated epistle [Col. 0990D] on the baptism of heretics was then absent from Augustine’s copy, what wonder is it if, so long afterward, the present epistle is absent from many manuscripts?

Letters, of course, are a kind of writing that, having been dispatched to different places at different times, can scarcely be collected into a single body and, because of their slight extent, may easily escape the diligence of copyists. Hence it is rare to find ancient manuscripts that contain absolutely all the epistles of a single author, and it often happens that some are preserved in very few copies. Yet the manuscripts preserving this one are not few. It is extant in the manuscripts of Saint-Maur-des-Fossés, Corbie, Foix—now Colbertinus—Verona, Tours, namely St. Martin’s and St. Peter’s of the Monastery, and in the Victorinus and Cambronensis manuscripts. Moreover, there is such complete agreement of its style with Cyprian’s other writings—as Nicolas Rigault and the Oxford editor also observed—and such use of words and propositions familiar to Cyprian, that we are not permitted to doubt its true author. No one, therefore, should be influenced by the conjectures through which Jean de Launoy attempts to deny to Cyprian an epistle supported by so many considerations. Rather, the opinion of that most distinguished man—that Trophimus presided over the Church of Arles in Stephen’s time—should be corrected on this basis.

Certainly, in the year 450, and thus long before Gregory of Tours, upon whose authority Launoy especially relies, the bishops of the province, writing to Pope Leo, held it as certain that Trophimus had been sent to Arles by blessed Peter; and Pope Zosimus supports their opinion in Epistles 1 and 5. As for the date, if this epistle is removed far enough from the beginning of Stephen’s pontificate to be placed before the outbreak of the controversy over the baptism of heretics, the remaining objections raised against its authenticity are easily answered.

In the Corbie and Colbert manuscripts it is entitled: *Concerning Marcian of Arles, Who Also Received Heretics*. I would not dislike: *Who Adopted the Heresy of Novatian*. COUSTANT.

**Which also to you.**—The Oxford edition reads, “which by now to you,” against the manuscripts of Corbie, Colbert, Verona, etc., as well as the editions of Pamelius and Manutius. To those who ardently desire some evil to be healed, remedies always seem slow; but the person charged with effecting the cure is often compelled to delay, either because of the multitude of prior engagements or in order to await the opportune time. Stephen, therefore, should not rashly be accused here of inactivity; perhaps unsettled conditions also prevented him from removing Marcian from his see. COUSTANT.

**Which also.**—I would not have mentioned that I placed *also* (*etiam*) here instead of *by now* (*jam*), which is Rigault’s reading, had I not thought it necessary to forestall the accusation of certain persons who might suppose that I had written so from an itch to contradict, to which I am entirely a stranger. I did so because I have established that all the ancient manuscripts and all editions earlier than Rigault’s present this reading. Therefore I cannot understand why the English editors, to whom that agreement of the ancient editions was known and who knew, moreover, that the Verona manuscript had this reading, preferred to follow an error in Rigault’s edition—which could have arisen through a printer’s fault—rather than the sound text of the ancient editions. BALUZE.]

# EPISTLE OF ST. CYPRIAN, BISHOP OF CARTHAGE, TO POPE STEPHEN

(Erasmus, III, 13; Pamelius, Rigault, Baluze, LXVII; Paris, LXVI; Oxford, Leipzig, LXVIII; Coustant, *Epistles of the Roman Pontiffs*, vol. I, col. 211.)

**SUMMARY.**—He asks Stephen to take care, by sending letters to the bishops of Gaul, that Marcian, bishop of Arles and an adherent of Novatian, may no longer boast that he has not yet been excluded from communion; and at the same time, by writing other letters to the province and to the people of Arles, to arrange for another bishop to be substituted in his place.

**CYPRIAN TO HIS BROTHER STEPHEN, GREETINGS.**

[Note: [Col. 0991C]

**I.—In the same province.** That is, in the same province in which Faustinus was bishop, namely the undivided province of Narbonensis, which at that time also embraced Lugdunensis and Viennensis. Ammianus Marcellinus, book XV: “All the Gauls, however, were governed by authority divided into four parts, one of which, Narbonensis, contained within it Viennensis and Lugdunensis.” From this too one may conjecture that Lyon belonged to the province of Narbonensis, because when that city was founded, as the Roman senate had ordered, it was founded for those who had been expelled from Vienne by the Allobroges. Dio Cassius, book XLVI, moreover, writes that Vienne was a town of the province of Narbonensis. Therefore the new city adjacent to Vienne was undoubtedly assigned to the province in which Vienne was situated, especially since it was founded for the expelled inhabitants of Vienne who had settled in the place where Lyon now stands.

It should therefore not seem surprising that Faustinus was concerned about the condition of a church situated in the same province in which he himself was bishop. That this arrangement long persisted, so that Lyon was reckoned as belonging to the undivided province of Narbonensis, may also seem inferable from the fact that Eucherius, bishop of Lyon, attended the council which Hilary of Arles—who was then metropolitan of the two Narbonensian provinces, as the epistles of Pope Zosimus also attest—celebrated at Orange with the bishops of the cities of undivided Narbonensis. At this council Hilary, as metropolitan of the bishops attending that assembly, was entrusted with the responsibility of admonishing the absent bishops not thereafter to refuse to attend synods, as is clear from canon 29 of the same council. I was therefore wrong when I wrote in my notes on Agobard that Marcian was not bishop in the same province in which Faustinus was bishop. BALUZE.

**Marcian.** The ancient author of the *Disputation of the Synagogue and the Church*, ch. 20, records a certain Marcian among the ancient heretics. But I do not think he was referring to Marcian of Arles. That *Marcion* should be read is proved by the ancient editions of the epistle to Jubaianus, in which it is written, “especially since I observed that mention is also made of Marcian in the same work.” It is certain that *Marcion* should be restored there, as the later editions have it. Yet Eusebius, book VI, ch. 12, does mention a certain ancient heretic named Marcian. BALUZE.

**From the unity of the Church.**—The Corbie manuscript reads “from the truth”; and shortly afterward, “by the confession of the priest,” where the common editions have “by the agreement of the priesthood.” I prefer, with Corbie, “by the agreement of the priests,” especially since below we read: “The body of the priests is numerous”; and farther on, “from the college of priests,” not “of the priesthood.” COUSTANT.

**From the unity of the Church.** I found this reading, which is good, only in the editions of Manutius and Morel, in the Foix manuscript, and in the Chartres manuscript. The remaining ancient manuscripts and editions have “from the truth.” BALUZE. The Oxford editor has the same reading without noting any variant.

**Has withdrawn.** The same Foix manuscript and the edition of Manutius read thus. The Corbie manuscript, Rembolt, and Erasmus present “has separated.” Both readings, however, are absent from two ancient copies and from the Speyer edition. The Tours manuscript reads “has divided himself.” From this alone it is evident that a certain reading cannot be established. BALUZE.

**The most unyielding depravity of heretical presumption.** Here he specifically attacks the Novatians, who rejected the repentance of the lapsed. That sect, or discipline, consisted solely in severity. For that reason, in the immediately following epistle, he will call those men “most unyielding.” This form of expression, moreover, very clearly proves that both epistles have the same author. Furthermore, the phrases occurring throughout this passage—“Marcian, obstinate and proud”; “an enemy of his brothers’ salvation”; “our brothers are cruelly despised”; and “Marcian, an adversary of compassion and mercy”—are undoubtedly from Cyprian’s hand and characteristic genius. Near the end of Epistle LVII, he himself says that Novatian’s discipline is “the severity of human cruelty.”

**Repenting.** I did not find this word except in Manutius’s edition and in the Foix manuscript. I think, however, that it does not belong in this passage. The other manuscripts, though corrupt here, read better, in my judgment: “God’s servants grieving over this.” Erasmus also printed it in this form. The Corbie and Tours manuscripts read “doing” instead of “grieving,” through a manifest error, unless we should read “making satisfaction.” Indeed, the small mark placed beneath this word in the Corbie manuscript appears to indicate that it should be deleted. BALUZE. Once again the Oxford edition has ignored the reading that agrees with it. BALUZE, EDITORS.

**To sinners.** The Foix manuscript presents: “we display to sinners who are to be rebuked.” I think the phrase “who are to be rebuked” comes from a gloss. BALUZE.]

### I

Our colleague Faustinus, who resides at Lyon, has written to me once and again, dearest brother, reporting those matters which I know have certainly also [Note: [Col. 0989B] “Which also,” Verona, Manutius.] been reported to you [Col. 0991A], both by him and by the rest of our fellow bishops established in the same province: namely, that Marcian, who resides at Arles, has joined himself to Novatian and has withdrawn from the unity of the catholic Church and from the agreement of our body and of the priests [Note: [Col. 0991A] “Has separated,” Corbie, Rembolt, Erasmus; “has divided himself,” Tours], maintaining the most unyielding depravity of heretical presumption. The result is that the consolations and assistance of divine compassion and fatherly gentleness are closed to the servants of God who repent [Note: [Col. 0992A] “Who grieve and assail the Church with tears,” Verona, Manutius] and grieve, and who assail the Church with tears, groaning, and sorrow; nor are the wounded admitted so that their wounds may be tended, but, left without hope of peace and communion, they are cast out to be plundered by wolves and made the devil’s prey.

It is our responsibility to take counsel for this situation and bring assistance, dearest brother. For we, mindful of divine clemency and holding the balance by which the Church is governed, exercise vigorous discipline toward sinners in such a way that we nevertheless do not deny the medicine of divine goodness and mercy to raise up the lapsed and heal the wounded.

[Note: [Col. 0993B]

**II.—Most comprehensive letters.** Not letters which merely touch summarily upon the chief points of affairs and are therefore called brief, but letters which treat carefully the entire state of the question concerning the lapsed. Thus, in a law of Honorius and Theodosius concerning shipowners throughout Africa, “an approach by petition” and “a comprehensive appeal” are contrasted. COUSTANT.

**Who long ago.** Rigault notes that these words and those which follow, down to “judged an enemy of the Church,” are not extant in the Corbie manuscript. I marvel at his carelessness in this passage, since it is certain that all these words are extant in the Corbie manuscript. BALUZE.

**Had sent legates.** Namely Maximus, Augendus, Longinus, and Machaeus, whom the Africans first judged should be kept from their communion, as Cyprian testifies in Epistle I to Cornelius, no. 1, and who, a little later, were expelled from Carthage, according to Cornelius in Epistle V. From this we infer that the council mentioned here was held before the end of the year 251. That first delegation from Novatian to the Africans was shortly followed by another, concerning which Cornelius informs Cyprian in Epistle V. COUSTANT.

**By a council of very many priests.** Eusebius, book VI, ch. 43, discusses these men, writing that it was a synod of sixty bishops. And from Cornelius’s letter to Fabius of Antioch, after mentioning τῆς Ῥωμαίων συνόδου, “the synod of the Romans,” he adds: τὰ δόξαντα πᾶσι τοῖς κατὰ τὴν Ἰταλίαν καὶ Ἀφρικὴν καὶ τὰς αὐτόθε χώρας, “the decisions approved by all those throughout Italy and Africa and the regions thereabout.” FELL.

**An adulterous chair.** Above, in Epistle II to Cornelius, no. 1, Novatian is called “an adulterous and rival head,” since, as Cyprian says near the end of Epistle LII to Antonianus, when a bishop had been appointed in the Church by sixteen bishops, he strove by canvassing to have himself made an adulterous and alien bishop by deserters. COUSTANT.

**Novatian, recently crushed.** Three years earlier, when, as Epistle XLI says, the presbyter Maximus, the deacon Augendus, and certain men named Machaeus and Longinus were sent into Africa by Novatian. FELL.

**Throughout the whole world.** This could most properly be said after the event concerning which Dionysius of Alexandria writes in the third epistle below: the concordant return of the whole East to unity. FELL.

**Flatterers.** Supporters, followers, and adherents of Novatian, such as Marcian. RIGAULT.]

[Col. 0993A]

### II

Therefore you ought to send most comprehensive letters to our fellow bishops established in the Gauls [Note: [Col. 0993B] “In Gaul,” Verona], so that they may no longer permit Marcian—obstinate, proud, and an enemy of divine compassion and his brothers’ salvation—to insult our college because he appears not yet to have been excluded from communion by us. For he has long boasted and proclaimed [Note: [Col. 0993B] “Boasts and proclaims, an enemy,” Corbie] that, in his zeal for Novatian and in following his obstinacy, he has separated himself from our communion [Note: [Col. 0994B] “From holy communion,” Verona].

Yet Novatian himself, whom he follows, was long ago excluded from communion and judged an enemy of the Church. And when he sent legates to us in Africa, desiring to be admitted to our communion, he received from here the judgment of the council of very many priests who were present with us: that he had begun to be outside and could not be admitted to communion by any of us [Col. 0993B], since he had attempted, in opposition to Cornelius—a bishop ordained in the catholic Church by the judgment of God and by the vote of the clergy and people—to erect a profane altar, establish an adulterous chair, and offer sacrilegious sacrifices in opposition to the true priest. Accordingly, if he wished to come to his senses and return to sound judgment, he should do penance and return as a suppliant to the Church.

How empty it is, dearest brother, that, although Novatian was recently crushed and refuted, and excluded from communion by God’s priests throughout the whole world, we should still now allow his flatterers to mock us and pass judgment upon the majesty and dignity of the Church.

[Note: [Col. 0993D]

**III.—Let letters be directed to the province.** Cicero truly observed that every conjecture is often drawn in contrary directions by the minds of men. For, as the same Cicero says elsewhere, our thoughts are free, and we contemplate what we wish in such a way that we discern what we see. This is what happened here.

For Pamelius inferred from this passage that already in ancient times the Roman bishops were permitted, for just causes, to excommunicate bishops—indeed, to depose them—and substitute new ones in their place. Cardinal du Perron appears to have followed this conclusion on page 99 of his reply against the king of Great Britain. Baronius discussed the matter somewhat more grandly, saying that from these words of Cyprian it is evident that the authority of the Roman pontiff was then acknowledged both by Cyprian himself and by the other bishops. For in this matter each understood his own power, and all the other bishops their own power within the communion, to be confined within limits [reading uncertain], since the Gallican bishops recognized that they did not possess sufficient power or capacity in themselves to depose a heretical man hated by the people, though they so greatly desired it, and to substitute another in his place. Both they and Cyprian therefore appealed, for the accomplishment of this act, to the authority of the Roman bishop, by which Marcian, the Novatian bishop, might be deposed from his see and another catholic prelate substituted in his place.

Our adversaries, by contrast, think they have discovered in these words of Cyprian a certain equality between the bishop of Rome and the bishop of Carthage—though such that Rome, because of its greatness, ought to precede Carthage. They contend that Cyprian does not recognize in Pope Stephen the right and authority to depose Marcian, but only the capacity to declare that he should be deposed. Marca, however, says that this answer is futile, as indeed it is; for Cyprian expressly demands of Stephen that he condemn Marcian by his letters and thereby decree that another should be substituted.

And so that you may see, reader, how diverse human judgments are, and how diverse their thoughts and opinions, Marca inferred from these words of Cyprian that the authority of the Roman pontiff was already great at that time. By contrast, the most illustrious bishop of Oxford, author of the English edition, judged that the Roman party was using them to its own ruin and directing them against its own throat. He wrote that, in the opposite sense, it could be inferred from them that the Roman bishop was subject to the bishop of Carthage, since Cyprian orders Pope Stephen to send letters to the province so that, after Marcian has been excluded from communion, another may be substituted in his place; and therefore Stephen should be judged to have done nothing except what Cyprian ordered him to do.

This is how we interpret what is written here very obscurely and intricately, and not truthfully, by the Protestant bishop. For although the episcopate is one, a part of which is held wholly by each individual; and although the other bishops ought to come to the aid of the Church if anyone from their college should attempt to create a heresy and tear apart and devastate Christ’s flock, as Cyprian says in this epistle; it nevertheless does not follow from this that the Roman bishop, by virtue of his primacy, did not bear the principal role in affairs of this kind. For why does Cyprian ask Stephen to urge the bishops of Gaul, by means of most comprehensive letters, to depose Marcian and substitute another for him, unless he knew that the defense of the canons had been especially entrusted to the Roman bishop? BALUZE.

[Col. 0995C] **In these preceding years.** This mode of expression indicates that Marcian had been devoted to Novatian’s heresy for more than a single year. It does not, however, compel us to suppose that he had begun following that sect two full years earlier. Since Novatian’s schism is held not yet to have arisen in June 251, it follows that Marcian adhered to Novatian’s heresy not long after its beginning. COUSTANT.

**Bond.** Certain ancient manuscripts and old editions have *glutine* rather than *glutino*. Venericus, bishop of Vercelli, also read it thus in his book *On the Unity of the Church*. Both readings are good, and for that reason we did not wish to change it. BALUZE.

**To be besieged and held.** The common editions, except for the Oxford edition, read “to be possessed and held,” which is mere tautology. “To be besieged and held” was restored in the Oxford edition from the Corbie manuscript. In the Colbert manuscript we read “to be possessed and besieged.” COUSTANT.

**Having avoided.** Baluze reads differently: “buffeted.” We have restored this in place of “having avoided,” which Manutius and others after him printed. Our correction is confirmed by the ancient editions and four ancient manuscripts. BALUZE.]

### III

Let letters be directed by you to the province and to the people residing at Arles, so that, once Marcian has been excluded from communion, another may be substituted in his place, and Christ’s flock—which even to the present day has been scattered, wounded, and despised by him—may be gathered together.

Let it suffice that many of our brothers there have died without peace during these preceding years. At least let help be given to the others who survive and who groan day and night [Note: [Col. 0995C] “Who survive and both day and night,” Oxford] and, imploring divine and fatherly mercy, call for the consolation of our assistance.

For this reason, dearest brother, the body of the priests is numerous, joined together by the mutual bond of concord and the tie of unity: so that if anyone from our college should attempt to create a heresy and tear apart and devastate Christ’s flock, the others may come to its assistance and, like useful [Note: [Col. 0995C] “As useful pastors,” Verona] and merciful shepherds, gather the Lord’s sheep into the flock.

For what if some harbor on the sea, its defenses having been breached, should begin to be hostile and dangerous to ships [Note: [Col. 0996C] “To those sailing,” Verona]? Do not sailors direct their ships [Col. 0995B] to other nearby harbors where there is a safe and wholesome entrance and a secure anchorage? Or if some inn along a road should begin to be besieged and held by robbers, so that whoever enters it is seized through the assaults of those lying in ambush there, do not travelers, upon learning of this situation, seek other, safer inns along their journey, where there is trustworthy hospitality and secure shelter for travelers?

This is what ought now to be done among us, dearest brother: we should receive with ready and kindly humanity our brothers who, having avoided Marcian’s reefs, seek the Church’s saving harbors; and we should provide travelers with an inn like that in the Gospel, in which those beaten and wounded by robbers may be received, tended, and protected by the innkeeper (Luke 10).

[Note: [Col. 0995D]

IV.—“Restoring.” Manutius: “replacing.” Pamelius: “recalling”; [Col. 0996C] the latter was then retained. More harmonious is the reading of the Colbertine, Corbie, and other manuscripts: “restoring.” Thus below: “We ought to gather and cherish all the sheep…” [Col. 0996D] COUSTANT.—“Restoring.” So read all editions earlier than that of Pamelius. Pamelius therefore altered it and, following the authority of the Cambrai manuscript, wrote “recalling,” saying that he preferred this reading to all the printed copies, in which, he says, “replacing” was read. Here Pamelius undoubtedly suffered a lapse of memory. For all the early printed editions have “restoring,” and six ancient copies likewise exhibit that reading. Thus there can be no doubt that this is the true reading. The Foix manuscript has “reforming.” Moreover, the reading that we have restored is confirmed by what immediately follows: “to gather and cherish all the sheep whom Christ acquired by his blood and passion.” BALUZE.

“He will accomplish.” The Colbertine manuscript, together with that of Corbie, has “he will profit.” Above, however, in Letter XI to Cornelius, no. 3, “he will accomplish” occurs. COUSTANT.

“An abomination.” The same Foix manuscript has “abominable.” The following words seem to confirm this reading: “He says that they are abominable and detestable.” BALUZE.]

IV. For what greater or better care belongs to those set over others [Col. 0995C] [Note: [Col. 0996C] “greater care of shepherds,” Verona, Foix] than to provide, with diligent solicitude and salutary treatment, for the restoration and preservation of the sheep? For the Lord speaks and says:

> You did not strengthen what was weak, nor support what was ill, nor bind up what was afflicted, nor recall what had strayed, nor seek what was lost. And my sheep were scattered because there were no shepherds, and they became food for all the beasts of the field, and there was no one to seek or recall them. Therefore [Col. 0996A] thus says the Lord: Behold, I am against the shepherds, and I will require my sheep from their hands, and I will turn them aside so that they may not feed my sheep; henceforth they shall not feed them. I will draw them out of their mouths and feed them with judgment.  
> (Ezek. 34:4)

Since, then, the Lord thus threatens those shepherds through whom the Lord’s sheep are neglected and perish, what else ought we to do, dearest brother, but show complete diligence in gathering and restoring Christ’s sheep, and apply the medicine of paternal compassion to the treatment of the wounds of the fallen, since the Lord admonishes us in the Gospel and says: “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are ill” (Matt. 9:12)?

For although we are many shepherds, nevertheless we feed one flock; and we ought to gather [Col. 0996B] and cherish all the sheep whom Christ acquired by his blood and passion. Nor should we allow our suppliant and grieving brothers to be cruelly despised and trampled underfoot by the proud presumption of certain persons, since it is written: “But the insolent man, the boastful man, will accomplish absolutely nothing—he who has enlarged his soul like the underworld” (Hab. 2:5). And the Lord censures and condemns such people in his Gospel, saying: “You are those who justify yourselves in the sight of men; but God knows your hearts, because what is exalted among men is an abomination in the sight of God” (Luke 16:15).

He says that those who are pleased with themselves, who in their swollen arrogance presumptuously claim something for themselves, are abominable and detestable. Since Marcian has become one of these and, by joining himself to Novatian, has shown himself an adversary of mercy and compassion, let him not pronounce judgment but [Col. 0996C] receive it; nor let him act as though he himself had judged concerning the college of bishops, since he himself has been judged by all the bishops.

[Note: [Col. 0996D]

V.—“Vicar.” The Roman pontiff is frequently so called [Col. 0997A] by ancient ecclesiastical writers, and the Roman pontiffs themselves also called themselves vicars of the apostles Peter and Paul and vicars of the Apostolic See. See our notes on Agobard, p. 115; on Lupus of Ferrières, p. 425; and vol. II of the *Capitularies*, p. 1283. BALUZE.

[Col. 0997B] “Nor could there be a different judgment.” Nevertheless, a difference of judgment later arose between Cyprian and Stephen in the matter of the baptism of heretics. Jerome, in his Letter to Ctesiphon against the Pelagians: “Nor can the outcome be different for those whose judgment is one.” Cicero, in the Second *Philippic*: “I marvel, Antony, that you do not dread the outcome of those whose deeds you imitate.” BALUZE.

“Marcian.” That he was both deprived of communion and deposed from his see is inferred from the ancient diptychs of the Church of Arles published by our Mabillon in the *Annals*, vol. III, [Col. 0998B] p. 432. His name certainly does not appear in them, any more than that of Saturninus, the standard-bearer of the Arians, through whose fraud and wickedness Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, was driven into exile. COUSTANT.]

V. For the glorious honor of our predecessors, the blessed martyrs Cornelius and Lucius, must be preserved. Since we honor their memory, still more ought you, dearest brother, to honor and preserve it by your gravity and authority, for you have become their vicar and [Col. 0997A] successor [Note: [Col. 0997A] “successor to them,” Verona].

For they, filled with the Spirit of God and established in glorious martyrdom, judged that peace should be granted to the fallen, and by their letters affirmed that, once penance had been performed, the fruit of communion and peace should not be denied. This is precisely what all of us everywhere have judged. For there could not be a difference of judgment among us, in whom there was one Spirit [Note: [Col. 0998A] “the Spirit is one,” Verona]. And therefore [Col. 0998A] it is evident that the man whom we see holding a different judgment does not hold the truth of the Holy Spirit together with the others.

Inform us plainly who has been installed at Arles in Marcian’s place, so that we may know to whom we ought to direct our brothers and to whom we ought to write.

I wish you, dearest brother, always to fare well.

[Col. 0997]

# APPENDIX  
## DECRETAL LETTERS ATTRIBUTED TO ST. STEPHEN (S)

[Note: [Col. 0997]

LETTER. This and the following letter, like the preceding ones, are judged spurious by learned men.]

# LETTER I OF POPE STEPHEN I TO BISHOP HILARY

[Col. 0997B]

## SUBJECT.—Who are infamous, and who are not to be admitted to ecclesiastical grades or to make accusations; and concerning the vestments of ministers, that they are to be consecrated.

I. Who are infamous, or who are not to be admitted to ecclesiastical grades [Col. 0997C] or to make accusations.  
II. Concerning the reverence to be shown to superiors.  
III. Concerning ecclesiastical vestments.

**STEPHEN, BISHOP, TO HIS MOST BELOVED BROTHER AND CLOSE FRIEND HILARY: GREETINGS OF DEEPEST CHARITY.**

Although I trust (St. Leo, Letter 46) that your affection is devoted to every good work, nevertheless, because of the intimacy by which you are known to be joined to us, and so that your diligence may become more effective, it has seemed fitting to us that these fraternal letters should be directed to your affection.

We admonish you, dearest brother, always to remain in good ways and to beware of the wicked; to associate constantly with good men of right faith and holy conduct; and to separate yourself from the perverse and from those who lie in wait for their brothers, except when seeking to convert them and restore them to concord. For, as [Col. 0997D] the Apostle says, “Evil conversations corrupt good morals” (1 Cor. 15).

Truth itself also says:

> If your eye causes you to stumble, pluck it out and cast it away from you. And if your hand causes you to stumble, cut it off and cast it away from you.

The same must be done with the foot, because it is better for you to enter the kingdom of heaven one-eyed or lame than, having two eyes, two hands, or two feet, to be cast into the Gehenna of fire (Matt. 18; Mark 9).

And in the book of Ecclesiasticus it is found:

> In a man’s prosperity, his enemies [text defective]; but in his sorrow and adversity [Col. 0998B] his friend is recognized. An enemy sweetens his speech with his lips, but in his heart he lies in wait to overthrow you into a pit. He who touches pitch will be defiled by it; and he who associates with the proud [Note: [Col. 0997D] Others: “will put on pride”] will be clothed with pride. He takes up a burden upon himself who associates with one more honorable than himself. Do not become the companion of one richer than yourself. What fellowship will a cooking pot have with an earthen jar? When [Col. 0998C] they strike against one another, the latter will be broken. The rich man will act unjustly and rage, but the poor man, though injured, will remain silent. If you give to him, he will make use of you; but if you have nothing, he will abandon you. If you possess something, he will feast with you, exhaust you, and himself feel no sorrow for you. If he needs you, he will supplant you; and, smiling, he will give you hope, recounting good things to you, and will say: “What do you need?” He will confound you with his foods until he has drained you twice and three times, and in the end he will mock you. Afterward, when he sees you, he will abandon you and shake his head at you.
>
> Humble yourself before God and await his hands. Take care lest, having been deceived [Note: [Col. 0997D] Others: “folly”], you be humbled in folly. Do not be humble in your wisdom, lest, when humbled, you be led astray into folly. When invited by one more powerful, withdraw; for by doing so he will invite you all the more. Do not be importunate, lest you be thrust aside; and do not remain far from him [Note: [Col. 0998D] Others omit “not”], lest you pass into oblivion. [Col. 0998D] Do not presume to speak with him as an equal [Note: [Col. 0998D] Perhaps “on equal terms,” as in the Vulgate version], and do not trust his many words. For through much conversation he will test you, and, smiling, he will question you about your secrets. His pitiless spirit will preserve your words and will not spare you harm or chains. Guard yourself, and attend carefully to what you hear, because you walk in company with your own downfall. But when you hear those things as though in dreams, look—and you will become watchful.
>
> Throughout your whole life love God, and call upon him for your salvation. Every animal loves its own kind, and so also every man loves his neighbor. All flesh is joined [Col. 0999A] to what is like itself [Note: [Col. 0999C] Others: “will be joined”], and every man associates with one like himself [Note: [Col. 0999C] Others: “will be associated”]. [Note: [Col. 1000C] Others: “just as.”] If ever a wolf will associate with a lamb, so will a sinner with a just man. What fellowship has a holy man with the flesh? Or what good peace has a rich man with the poor? As the wild ass in the desert is the lion’s prey, so the poor are the pasture of the rich. And just as humility is an abomination to the proud, so the poor man is an object of abhorrence to the rich.
>
> When the rich man is shaken, he is supported by his friends; but when the humble man falls, he is expelled even by his acquaintances. When a rich man is deceived, many restore him. He has spoken arrogantly, and they have justified him. The humble man has been deceived, and in addition he is rebuked. He has spoken sensibly, and no place was given to him. The rich man has spoken, and all have fallen silent, and they will carry his word up to the clouds. The poor man has spoken, and they say: “Who is this?” And if he gives offense, they will overthrow him.
>
> Wealth is good when there is no sin upon the conscience, and poverty is exceedingly wicked in the mouth of the impious. A man’s heart changes [Col. 0999B] his countenance, whether for good or for evil. You will find the mark of a good heart and a good countenance only with difficulty and labor.  
> (Ecclus. 12–13)

Beware of this, brother, and do not follow your own desires (Ecclus. 23:30).

[Note: [Col. 0999C]

I.—“As to your consultation of the See.” Those whom Stephen here declares irregular because of infamy, bigamy, bodily or mental defect ought to be ineligible and incapable of receiving sacred orders. This had been established by the Constitutions and Canons of the Apostles long before this pontiff, as is clear from Apostolic Canon XVII and certain following canons. [Col. 0999D] See what we have said there. SEVERINUS BINIUS.]

## I

As to your consultation of the Apostolic See concerning who are infamous or who are not to be admitted to ecclesiastical grades, we believe that you already know the answer; yet, by the authority of the Apostolic See, we do not refuse to instruct you.

We declare infamous those persons who are branded with infamy because of some offense (6, q. 1; and in Ivo’s *Decretum*, book IV): that is, all who reject the norm of Christian law and despise ecclesiastical statutes; likewise thieves, the sacrilegious, and all entangled in capital crimes; violators of tombs [Col. 0999C]; those who willingly violate the statutes of the Apostles, their successors, and the other fathers; and all who take arms against the fathers (Anianus, in the *Sentences of Paul*, book I, title II; constitution II, title XXXIX, *Theodosian Code*), who are branded with infamy throughout the whole world.

Likewise included are the incestuous, murderers, perjurers, plunderers [Col. 1000A] (Proclus to Domnus, Hadrianic Collection, ch. XVII), practitioners of evil arts, poisoners, adulterers, deserters from battle, those who seek to occupy positions unworthy of them, those who unjustly alienate the Church’s property, those who (Anianus on constitution VIII, title XXXIX, book IX of the *Theodosian Code*) slander or accuse their brothers and fail to prove their charges, those who provoke the minds of princes to anger against the innocent (*Theodosian Code*, book IX, title I, ch. XI; Hadrianic Collection, XLVIII), and all who have been anathematized or expelled from the Church for their crimes, as well as all whom ecclesiastical (Anianus, constitution III, title XXXIX, book IX of the *Theodosian Code*) or secular laws pronounce infamous.

Such persons may not be promoted to sacred orders (Hadrianic Collection, CXIX), nor may slaves [Note: [Col. 1000C] Another reading: “not orders nor slaves”] before lawful freedom, penitents, bigamists, those who are in service to a municipal council, those who are not bodily whole, those who do not possess a sound mind or understanding, those who are disobedient to the decrees of the saints, or those who are manifestly insane. None of these [Col. 1000B] ought to be advanced to sacred grades; nor can these persons, freedmen, suspected persons, or those who do not possess the right faith or worthy conduct accuse the chief bishops.

## II

But you yourself have no doubt—even in the case of your own subjects—how obedience (St. Gregory, Letter X, book IV) or reverence ought to be shown to superiors. In this matter it is very useful if praiseworthy humility preserves without compulsion what the rigor of discipline imposes (same author, Letter XXXIV of the same book).

May almighty God, in whose hand are all things, concerning whom it is written, “There is no wisdom, there is no counsel against the Lord” (Prov. [Col. 1000C] 28), grant that you and yours preserve inviolate both the divine ordinances and those of the Apostolic See; that we and all the faithful always ascend to better things; that from day to day we avoid what is worse; and that we pursue and accomplish what is better and pleasing to God.

[Note: [Col. 0999D]

III.—“The vestments…must be consecrated.” Several rules are laid down concerning the vestments used by sacred ministers. First, the vestments that priests, deacons, and the other sacred ministers of the Church use in sacred ministries are to be distinct from those that they ordinarily wear. Second, no one is to use or wear those same vestments outside the sacred ministry. Third, they are ordinarily to be consecrated through an episcopal blessing—or at least that of a priest possessing a privilege in this matter—according to the rite prescribed by the Church. Fourth, they are not to be touched by laypersons.

Some of these provisions, established by earlier pontiffs, are merely confirmed by this decree. For Pope Anacletus, Clement’s successor, says in his first decretal letter: “Let the bishop have ministers with him clothed in sacred vestments.” Soter decreed that they should not be touched by laypersons, even if they were consecrated [Col. 1000C] virgins. See what we have said in the notes on the Lives of Sixtus and Soter.

That these provisions were properly and rightly established is proved by the example of the Old Testament, in which God instituted particular holy vestments for the priests and ministers of God to use in the Temple and in the Lord’s sacrifices, as is clear from Exodus 28. Much more, therefore, as Ivo of Chartres rightly concludes [Col. 1000D] in Letter CXXIV, was it proper in the new law that priests should use sacred vestments for the proper performance of divine worship and ministry, and especially for the consecration of the Lord’s body and blood.

Jerome testifies, in chapter LIV of his commentary on Ezekiel, that what was rightly established on the authority of the pontiffs of the first centuries was received not only in these later centuries but also in earlier ones. There he says: “Divine religion has one manner of dress for ministry and another for ordinary use and common life.” Likewise, in Letter III to Heliodorus, he reports that Nepotian, when near death, said to his uncle: “This tunic, which I used in Christ’s ministry, send to the man most beloved by me in age, my father, brother, and colleague,” etc. Marianus Victorius there interprets that garment as having been a chasuble or *planeta*.

Similarly, Chrysostom, Homily LXXXIII on Matthew, mentions sacred vestments; and in the liturgy he includes prayers [Col. 1001D] that the priest says when putting on the sacred vestments. John the Deacon, book II of the *Life of Gregory*, ch. 57, relates that Pope Gregory, among other gifts, sent priestly and clerical vestments to England. Theodoret, book II of the *History*, ch. 27, mentions a certain sacred vestment that Constantine sent to Bishop Macarius.

Add that Jerome, in book I *Against Pelagius*, writes that bishops, priests, and the entire [Col. 1002D] clergy customarily used white garments in the celebration of the sacrifice. Accordingly, this decree of Stephen concerning sacred vestments was not only properly and fittingly promulgated by him and some of his predecessors, but was also received throughout almost the whole world in every age. Consequently, their use is rejected as though it were a matter of indifference—or simply neglected—only by heretics. SEVERINUS BINIUS.]

## III

The ecclesiastical vestments in which service is rendered to the Lord and divine worship is celebrated with every mark of honor [Col. 1001A] and dignity by priests and the other ministers of the Church must be both consecrated and honorable. Since they have been consecrated and dedicated to God and his service, no one ought to use them for purposes other than ecclesiastical duties worthy of God. Nor ought they to be touched or worn by any except consecrated persons, lest the divine vengeance that struck King Belshazzar come upon those who transgress these rules and presume to do such things, and lest the just scourge of divine vengeance cause them to fall into the depths.

Make these things known to everyone in the regions where you dwell and in all places where you can, and by apostolic authority command them to observe them. For all our people, and all those entrusted to us in the holy apostolic and universal Church, have professed that they will observe these things both now [Col. 1001B] and in future times.

With these few words, brother, I have answered your letter fully. Let your affection be so joined to these provisions that nothing pertaining to the condition of the universal Church is done either doubtfully or negligently (St. Leo, Letter XLVI). Let everything be conducted with such moderation that neither benevolence nor justice is neglected, but that divine judgment is considered in all matters without respect of persons.

So that this may be maintained by right observance, let the integrity of the catholic faith be preserved first of all. And because the way that leads to life is narrow and confined in every respect, let no one deviate from its path either to the left or to the right.

Given on the fifth day before the Nones of May, in the consulship of the most illustrious Valerian and Gallicanus (in the years 254, 255, and 257).

# LETTER II OF POPE STEPHEN I

[Col. 1001C]

## SUBJECT.—Concerning the expulsion of bishops; that whatever is done unjustly against things consecrated to God and against bishops is to be regarded as sacrilege; that no one’s accusation is to be received in writing; and concerning several other useful matters.

I. Concerning accusations against priests.  
II. Concerning bishops despoiled of their property or driven from their sees.  
III. If anyone presumes to accuse bishops, agents, or defenders of the Church before approaching them in charity, he is to be punished.  
IV. Who ought not to be admitted as accusers.  
V. That an accusation is not to be received in writing; that an absent person cannot be accused or make an accusation; and that one ought not to do so before receiving leave to bring a charge. [Col. 1001D]  
VI. Concerning primates and metropolitans, and the referral of bishops’ affairs to them.  
VII. That an accused bishop is to be heard by all the bishops of the province.  
VIII. That every accusation is to be settled within the province, [Col. 1002A] unless an appeal has been made to the Apostolic See; and concerning those implicated in criminal accusations, those who have confessed voluntarily, and former enemies.  
IX. If a cleric accuses a bishop or plots against him.  
X. Whether laypersons ought to administer ecclesiastical property.  
XI. Concerning the persons of accusers.  
XII. Concerning charges against teachers; or that those condemned by divine testimony cannot accuse bishops or testify against them.

**STEPHEN, BISHOP OF THE HOLY APOSTOLIC AND UNIVERSAL ROMAN CHURCH, TO ALL BISHOPS ESTABLISHED THROUGHOUT THE VARIOUS PROVINCES: GREETINGS IN THE LORD.**

We rejoice greatly in the Lord (St. Leo, Letter XL) and glory in the gift of his grace because your faith [Col. 1002B] grows magnificently through good works and spreads most widely. Yet we are exceedingly afflicted and troubled by your oppression, concerning which frequent reports from brothers traveling to us have reached us (same author, Letter LXXXVII and following).

You ought not to have been shaken by such great oppressions at the hands of those by whom you should have been supported, sustained, and honored. Therefore it is necessary, once the evasions of such persons—by which poisonous malice is accustomed to be revealed and goodness and truth obscured (same author, Letter XXXV)—have been set aside, that substantial assistance be given to you by the faithful and that you receive support from this Apostolic See. For by divine grace it is fitting that those should be aided with Christ’s help, lest an imprudent undertaking proceed to the disturbance of the whole Church and those things that were long ago forbidden by our holy predecessors [Col. 1002C] and the other holy Fathers revive anew.

For consideration of our office (St. Gregory, Letter XI, book XII) compels us, for the Lord’s sake, not to abandon those matters that have come to our attention as requiring amendment, but to correct them with appropriate reform. And if secular offices must preserve their proper order and the discipline handed down by their predecessors, who can tolerate ecclesiastical orders being thrown into confusion by rash presumption, reports being disregarded, and matters requiring correction being postponed through failure to provide assistance?

## I

For we have heard that you are being accused by certain persons, not so much because of any fault of yours as at their pleasure, so that they may seize your property. Therefore you are greatly afflicted and shaken—to such an extent that you are even driven from your own sees—and on this pretext your churches and possessions [Col. 1002D] are ravaged and plundered.

These things, dearest brothers, ought not to happen or be repeated anew. Nevertheless, because such abuses are so often committed, it is necessary that the prohibitions against them also be repeated frequently. For whatever is done unjustly against things consecrated to God and against bishops will be regarded as sacrilege, [Col. 1003A] because they are consecrated and ought not to be violated by anyone.

## II

No bishop (2, q. 2, *Nullus episcoporum*), while he has been despoiled of his property or driven from his own see on any pretext, ought to be accused, nor can anyone charge him with a crime, before he has first been restored completely (Roman Councils III and V under Symmachus; Hadrianic Collection). Everything taken from him by whatever contrivance must be restored in accordance with the laws, and he himself must be restored canonically to his own see and former condition. Thus, before any accusation is entertained, the primates and synod must restore completely to the bishop in question all possessions and everything unjustly taken from him, together with all revenues; for not only ecclesiastical but also secular laws prohibit conduct of this kind.

[Note: [Col. 1003D]

III.—“Agents or.” Bishops are called agents of the Church because the administration, care, and disposal of ecclesiastical property have been entrusted to them by apostolic law. See what we have said in the notes on Alexander’s first letter at the words “which to the priests.” SEVERINUS BINIUS.]

## III

Nor ought any of them, or any agent [Col. 1003B] or defender of the churches (Hadrianic Collection, ch. 2, from canon 17 of the Fifth Council of Orléans), to be accused before other persons until those who believe themselves injured by them, or who wish to correct them for certain errors, have first approached them twice or three times in charity, so that they may receive from them either an amicable remedy or a just explanation. Whoever presumes to violate this rule is to be barred from the thresholds of the Church until he makes appropriate satisfaction.

[Note: [Col. 1003D]

IV.—“No outsider shall become either their accuser or their judge.” See the notes on Anacletus’s first letter at the words “foreign judgments,” etc., and likewise at the words “because the Apostles,” etc. SEVERINUS BINIUS.]

## IV

We exclude accusers (3, q. 5, *Accusatores*; and above in the Decretals of Telesphorus and Julius) and accusations that secular laws do not receive and that our predecessors prohibited. For no outsider shall become either their accuser or their judge. Hence it is written concerning Lot: “Have you entered as a stranger—surely not to judge?” (Gen. 19).

No accuser of yours shall be a slave (Hadrianic Collection, various chapters), a freedman, [Col. 1003C] or any suspected or infamous person. Those who live in company with enemies, and all laypersons, are likewise to be rejected, because affection born of friendship is accustomed to provoke an assault of slander. Nor are those to be admitted to accuse you who wish to receive you into their own defamation. [Note: [Col. 1003C] Manuscript: “For no one.” Hardouin.] No anathema [Note: [Col. 1003C] Others: “none of the anathematized”] is to be received (2, q. 2, *Nullus anathematizatorum*), nor is credence to be given by anyone to what such persons either say or write.

[Col. 1004A]

## V

I likewise call those persons anathematized whom bishops have anathematized in their writings, or who anathematize the bishops’ statutes.

No accusation is to be received in writing (2, q. 8), but only from the accuser’s own mouth—provided that the accuser is a lawful and suitable person—and in the presence, of course, of the person whom he desires to accuse; for no one who is absent can either be accused or make an accusation.

Nevertheless, no man of the aforementioned order can be accused (Hincmar, ch. 15, book LV), nor ought he to answer his accusers, before he has been canonically summoned by his primate and has received an opportunity to defend himself and [Note: [Col. 1004C] Others: “to clear himself”] to conduct an inquiry for the clearing away of the charges.

[Note: [Col. 1003D]

VI.—“Let primates be appealed to,” etc. This passage confirms what we said concerning the number and origin of patriarchal sees in the notes on Anacletus’s third letter; see, therefore, what we said there. SEVERINUS BINIUS.

“Whose primates even the gentiles.” Like many other things, this very ancient title of primates and patriarchs was also successfully transferred into the Church. For not only the Jews but also the Egyptians used that title and principal dignity. When Herodotus treats of Egyptian rites, [Col. 1004D] he calls those who hold the foremost place in sacred matters “patriarchs.” [[Col. 1004D] Those words are not found in Herodotus; someone deceived Baronius. LABBÉ.]

Moreover, the emperor Hadrian, Trajan’s successor, used that title in a letter to the consul Servius concerning the inconstancy of the Egyptians. There, according to the testimony of Flavius Vopiscus in his *Saturninus*, he says these words: “When that very patriarch comes to Egypt, he is compelled by some to worship Serapis and by others to worship Christ.” Whether the emperor truly said this and of whom it is to be understood, see Baronius at the year of Christ 132, nos. 13 and 14. SEVERINUS BINIUS.]

## VI

No metropolitans or other bishops (same author above, in the Decretal of Pope Anicetus) are to be called primates except those who hold the chief sees (Hadrianic Collection, 25) and [Col. 1004B] whose cities the ancients judged to possess primacy. Those who have obtained the other metropolitan cities are not to be called primates, but archbishops or metropolitans.

For the cities (Distinction 90, *Urbes*, but under the name of Lucius rather than Stephen) and places over which primates ought to preside were established not by moderns [Note: [Col. 1004C] Latinius reads “but already.” Hardouin], but many ages before the advent of Christ. Their primates were appealed to, even among the gentiles, in more important affairs.

After Christ’s advent, the Apostles and their successors appointed patriarchs or primates in those cities. To them, with apostolic authority preserved in all things, episcopal affairs and more important cases are to be referred after the Apostolic See. And although, because of the Apostle’s prohibition (1 Cor. 6), accusations [Col. 1004C] ought not to be pursued among Christians, nevertheless, if they cannot be prevented, accusations against bishops must be brought by their accusers before the aforementioned primates. Bishops must strive, however, to constrain dissenting brothers toward peace rather than judgment [Note: [Col. 1004C] Others: “encourage”] (Fourth Council of Carthage, ch. 26).

## VII

A bishop (Hadrianic Collection, 25, 27) ought not otherwise to be heard or judged except in the presence of all his fellow bishops of the province and by all those bishops [Col. 1005A], because in their absence he neither ought nor can be heard or judged.

The persons who are not to be admitted to accuse them have already been specified in part above; and both these persons and the infamous are enumerated more fully in the letter that we formerly sent to Hilary [Note: [Col. 1005D] Others add “the bishop”].

## VIII

The right to bring accusations is not to extend beyond the boundaries of the province (3, q. 6, *Ultra provinciae*; and in John’s *Decretum*, book IV), but every accusation is to be heard within the province and settled by the bishops of that province, unless appeal has been made solely to the Apostolic See.

Moreover, accused persons must be denied permission to bring charges (3, q. 11, *Neganda est*; and in John’s *Decretum*, book IV) before they have cleared themselves of the crime under which they labor (see *Theodosian Code*, book IX, constitutions 10, 11, 12; Anianus the Interpreter; [Col. 1005B] Hadrianic Collection). For the testimony against others of persons implicated in crimes is not to be believed unless they have first proved themselves innocent, because a guilty person’s declaration against anyone is dangerous and ought not to be admitted.

Close associates, those who have confessed voluntarily, and those entangled in crimes ought not to be admitted; nor should those who yesterday, the day before, or at some earlier time were enemies (St. Ambrose, Letter LXIV).

## IX

A cleric, therefore, who accuses his bishop (3, q. 4, *Clericus qui episcopum*) or lies in wait for him is not to be received, because he has become infamous and must either withdraw from his grade or be handed over to serve the municipal council.

## X

Although laypersons may be religious (same author in the letter of Pope Fabian), we nowhere read that any of them has ever been granted authority to account for [Col. 1005C] any ecclesiastical property [Note: [Col. 1005D] Perhaps “to administer.” Labbé].

We know [Note: [Col. 1005D] So it reads in the manuscript. Justel], dearest brothers, that the carnal are always accustomed to persecute the spiritual, and the malevolent to defame and tear apart the benevolent. Therefore the Apostles and their successors, as well as the other holy Fathers, did not wish accusations against bishops to be easy; for if they were easy, either no bishop at all or scarcely any would now be found.

They are called the thrones of God (Eleventh Council of Toledo, ch. 5); therefore they ought not to be displaced, afflicted, or disturbed. Of them, therefore, the Prophet says: “The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims the works of his hands” (Ps. 18).

## XI

Those who are not of good conduct, whose life is open to accusation, or whose faith, life, and freedom are unknown cannot accuse them. [Col. 1005D] The persons of the accusers—their faith, life, and conduct—must always first be investigated in detail; afterward, the charges they bring must be examined faithfully. For nothing ought to be done before the persons, faith, life, and conduct of those making the attack have been carefully examined, lest anyone be harassed through another’s envy, enmity, or malicious intent (2, q. 7, *Quaerendum est*; 1, q. 8, *Accusatorum personae*; and in the Decretal of Pope Callistus).

Source/review notes: The wording *patrum invasores, qui in mundo patres* is materially uncertain in the supplied source; the correction marks that inherited textual difficulty without silently inventing a reading.

XII. Let no one entertain accusations (Hadrian, collection 67) against a teacher [Col. 1006A], because teachers ought rather to be supported than injured or defamed. Hence the Apostle says: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ” (Gal. VI). Charity, moreover, is not ambitious, is not puffed up, does not seek its own interests, but those of Jesus Christ (I Cor. 13). He who abides in charity abides in God, and God in him (I John IV). And he who abides in God wishes to harm no one, but desires to help and sustain everyone, just as the Lord himself came to save everyone and to give his life as a ransom for us (Matt. XX).

We silence the voice of those who would accuse priests or testify against them (Hadrian, collection 29), when we recognize that they have been condemned or are dead by human and divine declarations. All who persecute the priests [Col. 1006B] of the Lord, whether secretly or openly, ought therefore to take the greatest care lest they be condemned under the Lord’s precepts. Through the prophet Jeremiah the Lord speaks, threatening such people and saying: “Your iniquities have turned aside [Note: [Col. 1006D] Others add *all things*], and your sins have removed good things from you, because the impious have been found among my people, speaking vanities. They have set themselves to destroy men, and have captured them; as a hunter’s snare is full of birds, so their houses are full of deceit” (Jer. V). And through David he says: “They have devised wickedness in their hearts; all day long they have been engaged in battles. They have sharpened their tongues like serpents; the venom of asps is beneath their lips” (Ps. CXXXIX). And shortly afterward: “Burning coals shall fall upon them; you shall cast them into pits, so that they may not rise again. A talkative man shall not prosper upon the earth; evils shall seize an unjust man unto destruction. I know that the Lord will uphold the cause of the needy and the judgments of the poor” (*ibid.*). Likewise, the same author says: “Let deceitful lips be struck dumb” (Ps. XXX). And again, through Micah he says: “All are judged in blood [Note: [Col. 1006D] Others: *lie in wait*]; each one afflicts his neighbor; all prepare their hands for evil” (Mic. VII, from the Septuagint version).

Foreseeing these people, the Lord commanded the Apostles that his servants should not readily be torn apart, lest perhaps they be destroyed or fall into a temptation of such a kind that they would be wholly unable to bear it. For this reason, the holy Apostles and their successors established the norms of the decrees, so that the voice of such people—which strives more to destroy the innocent and simple than to save them—should not readily be received, but that they themselves should be driven far away by these darts and should be entirely unable to destroy the Lord’s disciples according to their own wishes and cunning [Col. 1006D]. Hence the Lord himself also says: “Shake the dust from your feet as a testimony against them” (Mark VI). And elsewhere Truth itself says of such people: “It is better for him that a millstone turned by an ass be hung about his neck and that he be plunged into the depth of the sea, than that he scandalize one of these little ones” (Matt. XVIII). And the apostle James says: “Judgment without mercy shall be given to him who has not shown mercy” (Jas. II).

For with what effrontery does anyone hope that he will obtain pardon for his sins from God when [Col. 1007A] he wishes to forgive an offending brother nothing through the duty of compassion and clemency? He must assuredly expect that, when he has been placed before the tribunal of the just Judge, he will experience God in judgment as he himself behaved toward his brother: “For with the measure with which we have measured, it shall be measured back to us” (Matt. VII). And John the apostle and evangelist says: “He who hates his brother is a murderer. And you know that no murderer has eternal life abiding in him” (I John IV).

Nevertheless, dearest sons, we exhort you patiently to bear, with the Lord’s assistance, the evils inflicted upon you, and by these apostolic precepts to drive such people far away, lest in the manner of dogs they be able to tear or bite you. Remember also that, according to the Psalmist’s words (St. Boniface, Ep. XXVI), “Man—his days are like grass, and like the flower of the field, so shall he flourish” (Ps. CII). And the Apostle says: “The whole world lies in wickedness” (I John V). Hence we pray that you not fear such people greatly, because they are infamous and cannot do you much harm, since their voice has been extinguished; for God so hates those who are armed against the fathers in the world [the transmitted phrase *patrum invasores, qui in mundo patres* is uncertain] that they are branded with infamy (Proclus to Domnus; Hadrian, collection 71). Arm yourselves, therefore, against them with these apostolic supports, and strengthen your hearts with a sovereign spirit, so that God, who willed you to be called shepherds among his people, may always find you neither negligent nor lukewarm nor fleeing when wolves arrive, but, after the example of the good shepherd, courageously defending the lambs together with their mothers, sons, and daughters, and faithfully bearing back holy Mother Church.

And although (St. Boniface [Col. 1007C], Ep. XXV) the days are evil, nevertheless do not be foolish, but understand what the will of God is (Eph. V). Therefore be strengthened and stand firm in faith, acting courageously, and let all that you do be done in charity (I Cor. XVI); and, according to the holy Gospel, “in your patience you shall possess your souls” (Luke XII). Remember also the holy Apostles and Prophets; and because they labored greatly in the Lord, they therefore obtained everlasting rewards. Know also that, according to the Psalmist’s words, “Many are the afflictions of the just, and from all these the Lord shall deliver them” (Ps. XXXIII).

Therefore, dearest sons, we exhort and beseech you to entreat God with the frequent petitions of your prayers, so that (St. Boniface, *ibid.*), according to the Apostle’s words, both we and you may be delivered from troublesome [Col. 1007D] and evil men, “for faith does not belong to everyone” (II Thess. III). Pray also that our God and Lord, who is the refuge of the poor and the hope of the humble, may mercifully rescue his holy Church—redeemed, namely, by his precious blood—and us, who are bound to teach, govern, support, and protect that same holy Church, from the aforesaid oppressions and temptations of this wicked age and from all our necessities, so that the word of God may run its course (I Cor. XV) and the glorious Gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ may be glorified; and so that his grace in us may not prove empty, lest, without the fruit of the Gospel—may that never be!—we appear barren in God’s sight and return empty of any number of sons and daughters, or be judged guilty concerning the hidden talent when the Lord comes.

For Satan always envies these things. Therefore he raises up such people against us to press and suffocate us, so that he may seize the Lord’s sheep in our absence and cause them to rush into the depths when no shepherds are present [Col. 1008B] to guard and defend them. You, therefore, labor according to your strength, and pray and keep watch lest these things happen, knowing that we are always prepared to bring you assistance in every manner in which the Lord grants us the power, although we ourselves have not been spared by those rivals of God’s holy Church and by our own rivals, and although the afflictions of our heart have been greatly enlarged by our own affliction, yours, and that of the sheep committed to us.

We also beseech you not to neglect the service entrusted to you by the Lord, and to strive, insofar as the Lord grants you the power, to help all the oppressed, all God’s servants, and Christians generally (St. Boniface, Ep. XXVI), so that before Christ’s tribunal you may possess an everlasting reward. And know that remembrance [Col. 1008C] of you is continually made before God. For just as we learn with sorrow that you are being harassed by unjust and wicked men, so we continually suffer with you, praying to God for deliverance and relief from your affliction, which—to our profound distress—is inflicted upon you day by day by the unjust. And prayers are offered daily for you before the bodies of the Apostles, so that with the Lord’s assistance you too may be delivered from troublesome and evil men, and the sheep committed to you may reach, together with you, the everlasting pastures of eternal life.

May the Creator of all peoples, the Creator of all, almighty God, eternally preserve the unity and communion (St. Boniface, Ep. VI) of your charity, strong and advancing toward the salvation of all peoples, in remembrance of us. Amen.

[Col. 1008D] Given on the Nones of April, in the consulship of the most illustrious Valerian and Gallienus (A.D. 255).

# ACTS AND RECORDS OF THE CELEBRATED DISPUTE CONCERNING THE BAPTISM OF HERETICS

## PART ONE. THE PRINCIPAL SURVIVING ANCIENT RECORDS CONCERNING THE BAPTISM OF HERETICS

[Col. 1009]

# DECISIVE PRONOUNCEMENTS OF ST. STEPHEN, POPE AND MARTYR

## PREFACE

[Col. 1009A]

It is certainly a matter for regret that none of the letters written amid those troubled circumstances by the most blessed Pope Stephen I—whether to the Africans or to the Eastern bishops—have come down to us. Indeed, it is also astonishing that none at all have survived apart from only a very few pronouncements, although in the meantime neither the injury of oblivion nor the devouring passage of time has destroyed certain much humbler little works by anonymous authors, works of far slighter substance and importance; and although, moreover, the entire Church had been shaken from its deepest foundations by this exceedingly serious dispute and had consequently fixed its attention upon the holy See of Peter, ready to receive with attentive ears whatever pontifical decisions or decrees might issue from it.

All the more diligently, therefore, must however many pronouncements of Pope Stephen emerge from the letters of Cyprian and Firmilian be collected. They are, moreover, preeminent and deservedly called decisive, since, although men of the greatest and most deserved authority resisted them on either side, they ultimately settled this immense controversy and shortly afterward were received, firmly embraced, and perpetually observed by the Church wherever she extends.

Yet, although we draw these declarations of the holy Pontiff chiefly from Firmilian’s letter, we by no means intend to regard Firmilian’s letter itself as authentic or authoritative.
