Let the entire question remain under adjudication; we ask only that we be permitted to draw from this source—whether doubtful or troubled—those pronouncements which savor of venerable antiquity, and which a cunning interpolator might have thrust from ancient documents into a new medley of spurious materials (*notheíōn*, νοθείων) [Col. 1009C].

## I. The One Necessary Termination of Controversies of Faith

Stephen glories in the position of his episcopate and maintains that he holds the succession of Peter, upon whom the foundations of the Church were laid (Firmilian, Epistle).

## II. A Preeminent Principle of Law

[Col. 1010A]

“If, therefore, anyone comes to us from any heresy whatsoever, **LET NOTHING NEW BE INTRODUCED EXCEPT WHAT HAS BEEN HANDED DOWN**: namely, that the hand be laid upon him for repentance, since heretics themselves, properly speaking, do not baptize one another when they come over to them, but merely admit them to communion” (Cyprian, Ep. LXXIV).

## III. Testimony of Apostolic Tradition Concerning the Baptism of Heretics

“. . . As if the Apostles had forbidden those who come from heresy to be baptized and had handed this down to posterity for observance” (Firmilian, Epistle).

## IV. Intrinsic Arguments of the Testimony

[Col. 1010B]

Stephen and those who agree with him maintain that the remission of sins and a second birth take place in the baptism of heretics, among whom they themselves nevertheless admit that the Holy Spirit is not present; and at the same time they maintain that we and the heretics possess one and the same baptism. . . . They do not think it necessary to inquire who the person who baptized may be, on the ground that whoever has baptized could obtain grace when the Trinity of the names of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit had been invoked. . . . Stephen holds that the presence and holiness of Christ are available to those who are baptized among heretics. . . . The name of Christ avails greatly, so that whoever has been baptized, and wherever it was done, in the name of Christ [Col. 1010C], immediately obtains the grace of Christ (Firmilian, Epistle, *passim*).

## V. Concluding Clause

**HERESY INDEED GIVES BIRTH AND EXPOSES THE OFFSPRING; BUT THE CHURCH RECEIVES THOSE WHO HAVE BEEN EXPOSED** (Firmilian, Epistle). EDS.

[Col. 1011]

# THE ROMAN COUNCIL CELEBRATED UNDER ST. STEPHEN

## FROM THE SYNODICAL BOOK

[Note: [Col. 1011A]

“There were,” says Augustine in his book *On the One Baptism*, chap. 14, “two bishops of the most eminent churches—namely, the Roman and the Carthaginian—Stephen and Cyprian, both established in Catholic unity.” At that time there was a great schism in the Church on account of the doctrine of rebaptism, which the Africans had long before received from Agrippinus, bishop of Carthage, and which St. Cyprian defended with considerable obstinacy. Pope Stephen then assembled a provincial synod at Rome, as the author of the *Synodicon* says; there, as Vincent of Lérins puts it, he attacked that doctrine together, indeed, with his other colleagues, but nevertheless more vigorously than the rest. Finally [Col. 1012A], as it appears, he sent from that synod a celebrated letter to Africa. That letter certainly does not now survive in full, but only its definition, which St. Cyprian preserved for us in Epistle LXXIV to Pompeius:

> “If, therefore, anyone comes to us from any heresy whatsoever, let nothing new be introduced except what has been handed down: namely, that the hand be laid upon him for repentance, since heretics themselves, properly speaking, do not baptize one another when they come over to them, but merely admit them to communion.”

Eusebius, book VII, chap. 3, and Vincent of Lérins in his *Commonitorium* mention this letter of Stephen.]

[Note: [Col. 1011A] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

A divine and holy local synod, assembled at Rome by Stephen, the hieromartyr and pope, which repudiated those who, in the African synod, had unreasonably undertaken to rebaptize those approaching the Catholic Church from every heresy.

[Col. 1012A] A divine and holy provincial synod, assembled at Rome by Stephen, holy martyr and pope, which repudiated those who, in the African synod, had unreasonably permitted those approaching the Catholic Church from any heresy whatsoever to be rebaptized.

[Col. 1011]

# THE CARTHAGINIAN COUNCILS

[Note: [Col. 1011C] Although the Carthaginian councils which we collect here did not treat the same question of rebaptism, we nevertheless judged that all of them should be published as if in a single corpus, since they were held at approximately the same times, under the same supreme Pontiff, by the same Cyprian, and with almost the same bishops. EDS.] (C)

# THE THIRD CARTHAGINIAN COUNCIL UNDER CYPRIAN, HELD IN THE YEAR OF OUR LORD 253: ON THE BAPTISM OF INFANTS

## PREFACE

(Erasm., III, 3; Pamel., Rigalt., Baluz., LIX; Paris., LVIII; Oxon., Lips., LXIV; Routh, *Reliquiae Sacrae*, pp. 74 and 116.)

[Col. 1011B]

In A.D. 257 [Note: [Col. 1011C] This is the seventh Carthaginian council under Cyprian, as Hardouin notes, celebrated in A.D. 253. Pagi, however, at A.D. 254, no. 5, considers it fictitious; consult him], when the persecution had ceased, Cyprian and his fellow bishops of the African Church met according to custom in order to restore the battered Church: partly to preserve the true faith and Catholic unity, and partly also to restore fallen ecclesiastical discipline and form the faithful in good morals.

At this synod it was established, first, that the deacon whom Rogatianus had denounced before the Fathers of the council for insolence and insults offered to him should either be suspended from communion or, unless he amended his offense, be deposed altogether. Cyprian wished the same to be established concerning the other insolent and abusive clerics [Col. 1011C], because defiance among subordinate clerics is dangerous, and from it they have very often been accustomed to lapse into heresy. The words of Cyprian’s reply to Rogatianus on this matter are as follows:

> “These are the beginnings and origins of heretics and the endeavors of schismatics who think wrongly: that they should be pleased with themselves and should despise their superior with arrogant pride. Thus does one withdraw from the Church; thus is a profane altar set up outside; thus is rebellion raised against the peace of Christ and the ordination and unity of God. But if he should continue to exasperate and provoke you with his insults, you will exercise against him the power of your office, either by deposing him or suspending him from communion.”

Second, when at this same synod the Fathers of the council learned that Geminius Victor, a Christian, had at his death named a certain priest, Fortunatus, in his will as guardian of his children, and had thus, according to the decree of a certain council formerly celebrated on this matter in Africa under their predecessors [Col. 1012C], incurred the penalty of excommunication, they declared the deceased Geminius excommunicated because he had called a priest away from the worship of God to secular business. They therefore most sternly forbade that the sacrifice be offered for the deceased or that his name be mentioned at the altar; and by this synodal constitution they confirmed the decree of their predecessors itself.

These facts are established from Cyprian’s Epistle 66, in which he says: “We were gravely disturbed—I and my colleagues who were present, and our fellow presbyters who sat with us,” etc. Baronius, at the year 257, nos. 13 and 14.

At this same council [Col. 1013A], it appears that a response was given to the doubt of certain persons that the baptism of infants in a case of necessity should be advanced to a time before the eighth day. This is especially so because it may certainly be inferred that this council was held when the Church was at peace—not under Lucius, as the Venetian edition has it, but rather around the beginning of Valerian’s reign. The nature of that controversy concerning the baptism of infants may be learned from Cyprian’s Epistle LIX to the presbyter Fidus, appended here.

[Note: [Col. 1013B]

This epistle is synodical. This epistle is mentioned by St. Augustine in his book *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, chap. 11; in book IV *Against the Two Letters of the Pelagians*, chap. 8; and in Sermon 294 of the new edition. Jerome also mentions it at the end of the *Dialogues Against the Pelagians*. See George Cassander’s book against the Anabaptists. BALUZE.

Number LXVI. See what was noted above on Council II, p. 109. ROUTH.

*To Fidus.* Pamelius says that he was unable to discover in what place [Col. 1013C] Fidus was bishop, but that it is nevertheless likely that he was a neighbor of Therapius, who in St. Cyprian’s synod is designated as “of Bulla.” (See above, Council VII, p. 103.) Morel thought that he was only a presbyter. BALUZE.—Pearson says in the *Annals*: “While they were at the council, written letters were brought from Fidus, apparently a bishop,” at the year 253, section IX. ROUTH.]

# CYPRIAN AND THE OTHER COLLEAGUES, SIXTY-SIX IN NUMBER, WHO ATTENDED THE COUNCIL, SEND GREETINGS TO THEIR BROTHER FIDUS

**SUMMARY.—The African Fathers determine that the peace rashly granted by Therapius is to remain valid.—The baptism of newborn infants is confirmed by them.—The superstitious custom of not admitting infants to the kiss before the eighth day is censured.—No one is to be prevented from receiving baptism.**

[Col. 1014A]

[Note: [Col. 1013C]

**I.—“Victor, formerly a presbyter.”** Rigaltius says: This Victor, formerly a presbyter in the Church, had lost both the Church and peace through his failure to keep the faith. Therefore, although he had received peace in some manner—namely, through Therapius’s overly precipitate haste—he had nevertheless by no means recovered his place in the Church, that is, the honor of the presbyterate. Cyprian therefore wrote correctly and in accordance with ancient discipline about “Victor, formerly a presbyter,” who now shared in the Church’s communion among the laity. Thus the same Victor became a presbyter from a layman, a lapsed man from a presbyter, a penitent from a lapsed man, and a layman from a penitent.

We observed above that the Church did not always follow the practice of punishing offending clerics only by deposition [Col. 1013D] to lay communion. It is clear that Victor, after being expelled from the Church, was admitted to penance, and a lengthy penance at that. Although, moreover, at the second synod after Cyprian’s return an indulgence was granted to the lapsed because persecution was imminent, the Fathers nevertheless did not intend that, once peace had been restored and no necessity compelled it, a bishop should relax everything at his discretion. The well-attended synod indicates that peace had now been restored to the Church. Fortunatianus is likewise called “formerly a bishop who had lapsed” immediately afterward in Ep. LXV (otherwise LXIV). FELL.—Although Pamelius acknowledges that the editions of Manutius and Morel have *quondam* (“formerly”) here, he nevertheless preferred the reading of the old editions, in which *quodam* (“a certain”) is written, for the reason, as he says, that it is sufficiently clear from what follows that Victor the presbyter was still alive when Cyprian wrote this epistle. That is entirely certain. But the word *quondam* must not be understood here as though it referred to a deceased man, but to one who, after having received penance following [Col. 1014B] his lapse, had been cast down from the rank of presbyter, just as below, Epistle LXIV, p. 110, one reads, “Fortunatianus, formerly bishop among you.” Moreover, the reading which we restore is presented by the old books and by the very ancient Syriac version of this epistle preserved in the library of the Most Serene Duke at Florence, as I learned from Eusebius Renaudot, a man deeply skilled in that language and in humane letters. So too in the epistle of Pope Felix III to Acacius: “formerly bishops, but now deprived of honor and communion.” Many [Col. 1014C] similar examples can be found. BALUZE.—That clerics who had performed penance were not permitted to recover their place in the Church is sufficiently shown by the example of Basilides, recounted in the synodical letter immediately following this one. The same point is impressed upon us both by Rigaltius elsewhere in his *Notes on Cyprian*, and by Albaspinaeus, *Observations on the Rites of the Ancient Church*, book II, chap. 34, and Bingham, *Antiquities of the Christian Church*, book II, chap. 2, §§ 2 and 4. ROUTH.

**“Our colleague Therapius rashly.”** Baluze, relying on the authority of two old books from which the word *rashly* was absent, omitted it as something added from what followed by some pedant. Yet this reading, which, by that most distinguished man’s own admission, was found in several old copies, I did not think should be eliminated, especially since the word suits the passage well. ROUTH.—

**Therapius.** Bishop of Bulla in the Proconsular province. There were, however, as we have said elsewhere [Col. 1014D], two places called Bulla in that province: one called simply Bulla, of which this Therapius was bishop, and the other Bulla Regia. Epigonius, bishop “of the regions of Bulla,” attended the Carthaginian council under Genethlius. At the Carthaginian conference between Catholics and Donatists there were present Dominicus, the Catholic bishop “of the regions of Bulla,” and Felix the Donatist, who in the acts is called simply “bishop of Bulla.” BALUZE.

**“Of our decree.”** Compare the beginning of the preceding Epistle LIV. ROUTH.

**“Without the request and knowledge of the people.”** He says this very frequently, even after consultation had been held with the people. RIGALTIUS.

**“With no illness pressing and no necessity compelling.”** The English translator notes that two relaxations of penance are indicated in this passage. These had been granted at two synods: one permitted the absolution which he calls “clinical” to persons whose lives were in danger; the other granted pardon to penitents when persecution was imminent and wicked times were threatening. ROUTH.

[Col. 1015B] **“Ought not to be baptized.”** On the baptism of infants, see Joseph Vicecomes, book II, chap. 1, *On the Ancient Rites of Baptism*, and Bucer’s English writings, pp. 655, 667, and 781. See also Florentius Conry’s treatise *On the State of Little Children Who Die Without Baptism*. BALUZE.]

## I

We have read your letter, dearest brother, in which you reported concerning Victor [Note: [Col. 1013B] Thus Lam., Bod. 1, 2; Ebor., NC. 1, 2; Ver., Benev. The recent printed editions read “a certain Victor”], formerly a presbyter, that before he had performed full penance and made satisfaction to the Lord God against whom he had sinned, our colleague Therapius rashly granted him peace at an untimely moment and with over-hasty precipitation.

This circumstance disturbed us considerably, because there had been a departure from the authority of our decree, so that before the lawful and complete period of satisfaction, without the request and knowledge of the people, and with no illness pressing and no necessity compelling, peace was granted to him. But after the matter had long been weighed in our deliberations [Note: [Col. 1014B] “In deliberation we decreed that we should rebuke our colleague Therapius,” NC. 2], it was sufficient to rebuke our colleague Therapius for having acted rashly in this matter and to instruct him not to do anything of the kind in the future. Nevertheless, we did not think that peace, once granted in whatever manner by a priest of God, should be taken away [Col. 1014B]; and for that reason we permitted Victor to enjoy the communion granted to him.

[Col. 1015A]

[Note: [Col. 1015B]

**II.—“As regards the case of infants.”** A notable passage on the baptism of little children against the Anabaptists; it is also mentioned in vol. II, the book *On the Lapsed*. The same baptism is acknowledged by St. Cyril of Jerusalem, *Mystagogical Catechesis* I; Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration II, *On Holy Baptism*; Chrysostom, *Homily to the Newly Baptized*, Homily IX *on Genesis*, and *on Psalm XIV*; and Ambrose *on Luke*. St. Augustine frequently testifies that the same practice was observed by the universal Church, especially in the already-mentioned Epistle 28 and in book III, *On the Merits and Remission of Sins*, chaps. 6, 7, 8, and 9, where he cites almost this entire epistle; likewise in book IV, *Against the Two Letters of the Pelagians*, chap. 8, and book II, *Against Julian*, chap. 3. St. Jerome confirms the same baptism by this pronouncement of Cyprian and his colleagues near the end of book III of the *Dialogue Against the Pelagians*. Indeed, the Council of Milevis, canon 2, condemns with anathema anyone who denies that little children newly come from their mothers’ wombs are to be baptized.

Before St. Cyprian, explicit mention of the same practice can be found in Origen, *Homily 8 on Leviticus*, *on Luke*, and *on the Epistle to the Romans*, chap. 6; Tertullian, *On the Soul*; Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, book II, chap. 39; Justin Martyr, question 56; Clement of Rome, *Apostolic Constitutions*, book VI, chap. 11; and Dionysius the Areopagite, the final chapter of the *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*. Dionysius refers it to the tradition of the Apostles, to which Origen also refers it in his work *on the Epistle to the Romans*, as does St. Augustine in book X, *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chap. 23, and book IX, *On Baptism Against the Donatists*, chap. 24. PAMELIUS.

**“To be sanctified.”** Thus all editions before that of Pamelius and most of the old books. Pamelius wrote “to be sacrificed.” So also Rigaltius, although Goulartius, rejecting Pamelius’s reading, wrote “to be sanctified.” The English editors preferred this reading, rightly indeed, for it is excellent. See Epistle 76, to Magnus, pp. 152 and 155. BALUZE.

**“In our council it seemed good to all.”** Augustine, book IV, *On Baptism Against the Donatists*, chaps. 23 and 24, ascribes infant baptism to apostolic tradition, proposing this rule: “That which the universal [Col. 1016B] Church holds, and which was not instituted by councils but has always been retained, is most rightly believed to have been handed down only by apostolic authority.” Although at this Carthaginian council of sixty-six bishops it seemed good to all that the mercy and grace of God should be denied to no human being who had been born, this was not proposed in order to establish infant baptism, which had long been practiced, but was directed toward refuting the error of Africans who Judaized in this matter [Col. 1016C] and thought that the rite should be deferred until the eighth day, the day formerly appointed for circumcision. FELL.—Baluze notes that the word *all*, which he calls entirely superfluous, is absent from seven ancient manuscripts, although he says it is present in Augustine. Its uselessness, however, is not yet apparent to me. ROUTH.

**“No soul is to be lost.”** St. Augustine cites this passage in his epistle to Jerome *On the Origin of Souls*. BALUZE.

**“According to the course of secular days.”** So below: “According to the world, not according to God.” For with God there is no time. He calls the days “secular,” as they are numbered by human beings in the world. RIGALTIUS.]

## II

As regards the case of infants, whom you said ought not to be baptized when they are within the second or third day after their birth [Note: [Col. 1015B] “than they were born,” Bod. 1, 2; NC. 1, 2; Ebor., Lin., Ben., Ver.], and concerning whom you said that the law of ancient circumcision (Gen. XVII, 12) should be considered, so that you did not think that one who had been born should be baptized and sanctified before the eighth day, an entirely different judgment seemed good to all of us in our council. No one agreed with what you thought ought to be done; instead, we all judged that God’s mercy [Note: [Col. 1015B] “the grace of the merciful God,” Augustine] and grace must be denied to no human being who has been born.

For since the Lord says in his Gospel (Luke IX, 56), “The Son of Man did not come to destroy the souls of men, but to save them,” then, so far as it lies within our power, if this is possible, no soul is to be lost. For what is lacking in one who has once been formed in the womb by the hands of God?

[Col. 1015B] To us and to our eyes, those who have been born appear to receive growth according to the course of secular days. Nevertheless, whatever things are made by God are perfect through the majesty and workmanship of God their Maker.

[Note: [Col. 1016C]

**III.—“The widow’s son.”** Thus the old editions and almost all the old books. Pamelius printed “the Shunammite widow’s son” from a single English manuscript, admitting that the word *Shunammite* was absent from the other ancient manuscripts. The English editors wrote “the Shunammite woman’s.” I removed this word [Col. 1016D], which I do not doubt originated as a gloss. I note, however, that I found it in five old books. BALUZE.

**“Inequality.”** All other editions that I have seen, apart from the Benedictine edition, have either *equality* or *quality*, but Baluze may perhaps have found the received reading in his manuscripts. In any case, riddles of this kind are little removed from that madness of Origen and others which dared to undermine belief in the sacred histories in order to construct a mystical sense for the sacred books. ROUTH.

**“Distinction.”** Three old books have *difference* or *distinction*; another has *distinction*. From similar sources, as we have often noted, so many synonymous words arose in Cyprian. BALUZE.

**“Offers himself as Father.”** Thus almost all the old books and all editions. And this reading is excellent. For it is certain that God presents himself equally to all human beings as Father. He is indeed our Father, but above all the Father of those who believe in him—those who, sanctified through him and restored through the birth of spiritual grace, have begun to be his children, as the holy martyr says in his book *On the Lord’s Prayer*, p. 206. Nevertheless [Col. 1017C], Pamelius prefers the conjecture of Coster, who thought that *equal* should be read; and Pamelius, as he himself says, would have placed that conjecture in his edition had all the manuscripts and all editions not contradicted it. I nevertheless found the word *equal* in two ancient manuscripts. BALUZE.]

## III

That among all, whether infants or those more advanced in age, there is one equality of the divine gift [Col. 1016A] is declared to us by the witness of divine Scripture: Elisha [Note: [Col. 1016B] “the witness—that Elisha,” Lam., NC. 1, 2], praying to God in this manner, stretched himself out over the widow’s infant son who lay dead, so that head was applied to head and face to face, and the limbs of Elisha, as he lay upon him, were joined to each of the little child’s limbs, and feet to feet (IV Kings IV, 34).

If this event were considered according to the inequality of our birth and body, the infant could not be made equal to a mature and grown man, nor could the small limbs fit and correspond to the larger ones. But there divine and spiritual equality is expressed: that all human beings, once they have been made by God, are alike and equal, and that our age may possess [Note: [Col. 1016B] “our age in bodily growth,” Lam., Bod. 2] a distinction in bodily growth according to the world, but not according to God—unless perhaps the grace itself which is given to the baptized is bestowed in lesser [Col. 1016B] or greater measure according to the recipients’ age, whereas the Holy Spirit is given equally to all, not by measure, but by divine goodness and fatherly indulgence.

For just as God shows no partiality (Gal. II, 6), neither does he show regard for age, since, in order that all may obtain heavenly grace, he offers himself as Father to everyone with balanced equality.

[Col. 1017A]

[Note: [Col. 1017C]

**IV.—“Still shrinks from kissing.”** Rigaltius says: Fidus, to whom this epistle of Cyprian is addressed, shrank from kissing newborn infants, naturally smeared and covered with the discharges accompanying birth, and for that reason wished baptism to be postponed until the eighth day after birth. Cyprian dispels this revulsion with the same arguments by which Tertullian refuted the heresy of Marcion, who recoiled from the article of the Christian faith by which we affirm that Christ, the Son of God, was truly born as a human being from the womb of the Virgin Mary. Christ loved that human being amid uncleanness, coagulated in the womb, brought forth through the shameful parts, and nourished amid indignities. For his sake he descended; for his sake he preached. Do you make shameful to him those things which he redeemed? Do you recoil from the still-fresh [Col. 1017D] handiwork of God in an infant? Nature must be revered, not regarded with shame. Thus Rigaltius.

This entire apparatus took its origin from pagan superstition. Macrobius, book I, chap. 16, says: “Nundina is a goddess of the Romans, named from the ninth day of infants after birth, which is called the day of purification. The day of purification is that on which infants also receive their names; but for males it is the ninth day, and for females the eighth.” Once it was granted that infants were not to be admitted to the kiss before the eighth day, it naturally followed that they were not to be baptized; for every Christian was admitted by right of brotherhood to the kiss of peace. FELL.

**“It is a sacramental sign.”** St. Augustine likewise mentions this typological figure in *Against Faustus the Manichaean*, book XVI, chap. 29: “By rising on the third day, which we call the Lord’s Day and which, when counted after the Sabbath, is the eighth, he also declares that the circumcision of the eighth day pertained to the prophecy of himself.” And shortly afterward: “Because this resurrection, faith in which justifies us, was prefigured by that circumcision of the eighth day.” FELL.

[Col. 1018B] **“Fulfilled in reality.”** Certain old books and Morel’s edition have “fulfilled *in* reality,” which may be better.—BALUZE. Add the first edition. ROUTH.]

After the Sabbath, the first day and the Lord’s Day. Two hundred years ago a great controversy was waged and fought with the greatest bitterness on both sides between Paul [Col. 1018C] of Middelburg, who later became bishop of Fossombrone, Peter de Rivo, professor of sacred Scripture at the University of Louvain, and Thomas Bazin, bishop of Lisieux and later archbishop of Caesarea, over whether Christ had risen on the eighth day of the Sabbath, that is, on the Lord’s Day. Peter de Rivo’s treatise was published at Louvain in 1492, and Paul’s response to Peter is found in the sixth book of *The Proper Celebration of Easter*. Thomas’s treatise, however, remains unpublished in the Royal Library. BALUZE.]

IV. For as to your statement that the appearance of an infant in the first days after its birth is not clean, so that any one of us still shrinks from kissing it, we do not think that this ought to constitute an obstacle to the bestowal of heavenly grace. For it is written (Titus 1:15): “All things are clean to the clean.” Nor should any of us shrink from what God has deigned to make. For although the infant is still newly born, it is nevertheless not such that, in bestowing grace and making peace, anyone ought to shrink from kissing it. Rather, in kissing the infant, each of us, in accordance with his religious devotion, ought to think of the still-fresh hands of God themselves, which in the human being only just formed [Note: [Col. 1017B] “newly born,” Augustine; “in a certain manner newly born,” Oxford MS.] we kiss while they are still fresh, as it were, when we embrace what God has made. For the fact that the eighth day was observed in Jewish [Col. 1017B] carnal circumcision [Note: [Col. 1017B] “When,” Lam., NC. 1, Bod. 2, Ebor.; “in circumcision, the eighth day,” Lam., Bod. 2, NC. 1.] was a sacramental sign sent beforehand in shadow and image, but it was fulfilled in reality when Christ came. For the eighth day—which is the first day after the Sabbath—was to be the day [Note: [Col. 1018B] “the first was to be,” Lam., Bod. 1.] on which the Lord would rise, give us life, and grant us spiritual circumcision. [Col. 1018A] This eighth day, that is, the first day after the Sabbath and the Lord’s Day, preceded as an image. That image ceased when reality subsequently came upon us and spiritual circumcision was given to us.

[Note: [Col. 1018C]

V.—*For this reason*, etc. Saint Augustine quotes this passage in Sermon 294, p. 1193 of the new edition. BALUZE.—There Saint Augustine, or someone else, introduced the passage with the following preface: “It is Saint Cyprian whom I have taken into my hands, an ancient bishop of this see. Hear briefly what he thought about the baptism of infants—or rather, what he showed that the Church had always believed.” ROUTH.

*From obtaining grace.* Three old books read “for obtaining grace.” BALUZE.

[Col. 1018D] *Furthermore*, etc. Saint Jerome transcribed this entire passage at the end of the third book *Against the Pelagians*. But in Jerome “remission” is read in place of “remitted”; and where Cyprian correctly has “from our assistance and divine mercy,” Jerome has “from our assistance toward divine mercy.” BALUZE.

*The most grievous offenders.* Those who denied the faith, those who sacrificed, and those who obtained certificates. By “offenders” he means those who abandoned and forsook the faith they had pledged to Christ. We observed this above at Epistle LV (otherwise LII). RIGAULT.—Yet the words “if they afterward believe” more strongly suggest that this passage should be understood of persons who embraced the Christian faith and therefore sought Baptism. Antiquity believed that, through this rite of Baptism celebrated in the divine name, all sins were remitted and destroyed. ROUTH.

*Except that according to Adam.* Among ancient writers it would be difficult to find anywhere else a passage more appropriate and explicit for confirming the doctrine of original sin. On the opinions of the ancients in this matter, one should consult the author of the *History of Pelagianism*, Book II. He nevertheless censures Clement of Alexandria undeservedly, as though Clement had not adequately understood the doctrine of original sin, since what Clement argued in *Stromata*, Book III, was directed against the Encratites, who maintained that “generation is simply accursed” (*τὴν γένεσιν ἁπλῶς ἐπικατάρατον*), as Epiphanius says. [Col. 1019D] They further asserted that Adam had been condemned. Irenaeus, Book I, ch. 30. FELL.—Jerome, Book III *Against the Pelagians*, p. 545, and Augustine in many places, as Cellier noted in *Histoire Générale*, etc., vol. III, p. 590, invoked the authority of this letter against the Pelagians. Besides this and other passages of Cyprian, there are also notable statements about original sin in the book *On the Dress of Virgins*, p. 180. To those ancient authors whom the most learned Vossius presented as defenders of this doctrine in *History of Pelagianism*, Book II, p. 1, thesis 5, I add Theophilus of Antioch, Tertullian—although a certain testimony of his is mentioned by the same Vossius in *Theological and Historical Theses*, Disputation II—Firmilian, and Hippolytus, all very ancient writers. Nor do I doubt that the following statement of Clement of Rome in his *Epistle to the Corinthians*, ch. XXXVIII, deserves to be added to their words. Moreover, in Epistle 66, p. 593, vol. II of the Benedictine edition, Augustine writes: “The blessed Cyprian, indeed, was not establishing some new decree, but preserving the Church’s most firmly settled faith. In order to correct those who thought that an infant should not be baptized before the eighth day after birth, he said that it was not the flesh but the soul that must not be lost; and, together with certain of his fellow bishops, he judged that a child could properly be baptized immediately after birth.” ROUTH.]

V. For this reason, we think that no one should be prevented from obtaining grace by the rule that has now been established, nor should spiritual circumcision be obstructed by carnal circumcision. Rather, every human being without exception must be admitted to the grace of Christ, since Peter also speaks in the Acts of the Apostles and says (Acts 10:28): “The Lord told me that no human being [Note: [Col. 1018B] “no one common,” Bod. 2.] should be called common or unclean.” Moreover, if anything in human beings could hinder their attainment of grace, adults, the mature, and the elderly could be hindered all the more by their graver sins. Furthermore, if [Col. 1018B] even the most grievous offenders [Note: [Col. 1018B] “of offenses,” Thu., Corb.], and those who had previously sinned greatly against God, are granted remission of sins when they afterward believe, and no one is barred from Baptism and grace, how much less ought an infant to be barred—an infant who, being newly born, has committed no sin except that, having been born carnally according to Adam, it contracted the contagion of ancient death [Col. 1019A] through its first birth. Such an infant approaches the reception of the remission of sins [Note: [Col. 1019C] “to be received,” Oxford MS.] all the more readily precisely because the sins remitted to it are not its own but another’s.

[Note: [Col. 1020C]

VI.—*Crying at the beginning of their birth.* Pagan writers regarded the weeping of newborn infants as an omen of the miseries of the life to follow. Cyprian attributes it to piety and commends it as a kind of inarticulate formula of prayer. [Col. 1020D] FELL.—One of the ante-Nicene Fathers, whose name has slipped my memory, interprets the crying of newborn infants as lamentation for the sin and punishment of their origin. ROUTH.

]

VI. And therefore, dearest brother, this was our judgment in the council: that no one should be prevented by us from Baptism and from the grace of God, who is merciful, kind, and compassionate toward all. Since this must be observed and maintained with respect to everyone, we think it must be observed all the more with respect to infants themselves and newborn children [Note: [Col. 1019B] “recently born,” Bod. 2, Lam.]. They have a greater claim upon our assistance and divine mercy for this very reason: immediately at the first beginning of their birth, crying and weeping [Note: [Col. 1020C] “at the beginning, weeping,” Lam., Bod. 2, Lin., NC. 1, 2.], they do nothing other than make supplication. We wish you, dearest brother, always good health.

# THE FOURTH COUNCIL OF CARTHAGE UNDER CYPRIAN, HELD IN THE YEAR 254 AFTER THE BIRTH OF CHRIST: CONCERNING BASILIDES AND MARTIAL, SPANISH BISHOPS WHO HAD OBTAINED CERTIFICATES OF SACRIFICE

(Erasmus, I, 4; Pamelius, Rigault, Baluze, LXVIII; Paris, LXVII; Oxford, Leipzig, LXVII; Routh, *Rell. Scr.*, pp. 77 and 122.)

[Col. 1019B] [Note: [Col. 1020D]

*Concerning Basilides and Martial.* This epistle has so many, such extensive, and such mutually divergent variant readings in the ancient copies and editions that collecting and properly arranging them required me to expend great labor and endure much tedium. I judged that they should be recorded so that I might also provide many striking examples of the audacity of ancient copyists, who dared everything, lawful and unlawful alike, in copying the works of the holy martyr.

To begin at the point where the bishops’ names are written: there are some ancient manuscripts, and also several editions, in which those names are absent. In three ancient manuscripts in which they are omitted, the text reads: “Cyprian and the other bishops, to the presbyters, deacons, and congregations established in Spain.” In one Royal manuscript there is only this: [Col. 1021C] “Cyprian to Caecilius and the other brethren, greeting.” The older editions contain the bishops’ names. Pamelius and Rigault chose to omit them, undoubtedly because they thought them superfluous. Reinhart and the English editors included them.

It is certain that this epistle is a response to the letter that the Spanish bishops had written to the Africans in the affair of Basilides and Martial. There is no mention there of any letter written by them to the Romans. Nevertheless, Baronius, who wishes all ecclesiastical affairs in those ancient times to have been referred to the pope, says that he is led by a plausible and compelling conjecture to suppose that Felix and Sabinus, the Spanish bishops who had been sent to Africa, intended first to have their own election approved by Cyprian’s vote as well, and then, fortified alike with letters from Cyprian himself and from his other colleagues, to sail to Rome, refute the falsehoods of Basilides, and by the authority of the Apostolic See restrain those recalcitrants who had treated the Spanish bishops with contempt. But since, as Cicero says, a slight conjecture carries no weight, this one will be counted among the slight conjectures. BALUZE.

*Nicomedes*, etc. In some manuscripts and in the editions of Pamelius and Rigault, the names of the bishops that follow Polycarp here are omitted. In other manuscripts no name besides Cyprian’s is present; in most codices, however, both manuscript and earlier printed copies, all these names are recorded. ROUTH.

*Lucilianus.* So read eleven of our old books and three cited by Pamelius. Elsewhere it is written and printed as “Lucius” or “Lucianus.” BALUZE.

*Legion.* This is a city of Tarraconensis in Spain, within the territory of the Asturians, founded by the emperor Nerva, who also restored Asturica. Consequently, these cities are appropriately joined here, no less by their proximity than by their common grievance, as is also Emerita, a neighboring city founded by Augustus. Caesaraugusta—see p. 81—is added to these, having been built under the same auspices. The attempted action of Martial and Basilides, a most pernicious example, had brought grave danger upon them. FELL.—These cities are today called León, Astorga, Mérida, and Zaragoza. ROUTH.]

# PREFACE

This council was held in Africa in the year of Christ 258 at the request of the bishops of Spain, so that they might learn the judgment of the African Church concerning the case of Basilides and Martial. The case was as follows.

Basilides, bishop of the church of Legion, and Martial, bishop of the church of Asturica, had lapsed during the persecution and were *libellatici*—that is, men who privately denied the faith and bought themselves off from public worship of idols with money. At the denunciation of the Spanish faithful, they were therefore deprived of episcopal office, and Sabinus and Felix were substituted in their places. When the persecution had ceased, they rashly attempted to secure readmission into the Church without any loss of rank or honor, just as Felicissimus, who had lapsed in Africa, had previously done. When they were frustrated in this attempt and saw Felix and Sabinus installed in their places, Basilides, wasting away with envy, went to Rome, to the Apostolic See. There, complaining that he had been unjustly deprived of his see, he presented to Stephen, the Roman pontiff, a petition filled with numerous falsehoods, and through it humbly requested restoration to his former see and honor.

When the bishops of Spain heard this, the two replacement bishops themselves, Sabinus and Felix, were sent as delegates to the African Church. Letters written to Cyprian and the other bishops of his church were entrusted to each of them, so that those bishops might examine and adjudicate the case of the two *libellatici*. [Col. 1020B] Accordingly, when Cyprian had received the delegates together with the aforesaid letters, he summoned his fellow prelates. In their sacred assembly he arranged for the letters written to him and his colleagues to be read and recited, and for the delegates themselves, having been brought before the council, to set out their own case.

When this had been done, the decision made by the bishops of Spain concerning the deposition of Basilides and Martial, the *libellatici* bishops, and the substitution of Sabinus and Felix was confirmed by those bishops of the African Church who attended this council. Their judgment was that all *libellatici* could indeed be admitted to perform penance, but were rightly barred from clerical ordination and priestly dignity; that these two men had likewise rightly been deprived of their episcopal dignity; and that Sabinus and Felix had rightly been substituted in their places. Having obtained this testimony, Sabinus and Felix themselves, fortified with letters from Cyprian and the other bishops to Stephen and to the bishops of Spain, sailed to Rome, both to refute the falsehoods of Basilides and to restrain by the authority of the Apostolic See those recalcitrants who treated the bishops of Spain with contempt. See Baronius, year 258, nos. 1, 2, 3, 4, 3, 6, 7.

CYPRIAN, CAECILIUS, PRIMUS, POLYCARP, NICOMEDES, LUCILIANUS, SUCCESSUS, SEDATUS, FORTUNATUS, JANUARIUS, SECUNDINUS, POMPONIUS, HONORATUS, VICTOR, AURELIUS, SATIUS, PETER, ANOTHER JANUARIUS, SATURNINUS, ANOTHER AURELIUS, VENANTIUS, QUIETUS, ROGATIANUS, TENAX, FELIX, FAUSTUS, QUINTUS, ANOTHER SATURNINUS, LUCIUS, VINCENTIUS, LIBOSUS, GEMINIUS, MARCELLUS, JAMBUS, ADELPHIUS, VICTORICUS, AND PAUL, TO FELIX THE PRESBYTER AND TO THE CONGREGATIONS ESTABLISHED AT LEGION, AND ALSO TO LAELIUS THE DEACON AND THE CONGREGATION ESTABLISHED AT EMERITA, BRETHREN: GREETING IN THE LORD.

[Col. 1021B]

[Note: [Col. 1022C]

I.—*Fellow bishops.* So read the old books and editions. In Rigault’s edition, however, and in the one prepared by Reinhart, “bishops” is written. The English editors corrected it. Likewise, in Victor of Vita, Book I, ch. 13, “to your fellow bishops” should be written in place of “to all your bishops,” which is written there. For in the following chapter and elsewhere “fellow bishops” is also written. BALUZE.

*Stained by certificates of idolatry.* Concerning the *libellatici*, that is, those who procured for themselves a *libellus*, or judicial certificate, stating that they had satisfied the laws—that is, had sacrificed to the gods—even though they had done nothing of the sort, see the distinguished Mosheim’s discussion, in his customary manner, that is, both learnedly and at length, in his work *On the Affairs of Christians before Constantine the Great*, century III, [Col. 1022D] § 9, pp. 482–489. ROUTH.

*Of abominable crimes.* The Saint-Éloi manuscript reads: “bound by consciousness of abominable crimes.” See above, p. 392, and the following page. BALUZE.]

I. When we had assembled together, we read your letters, most beloved brethren [Note: [Col. 1021B] “dearest,” Ver.], which you composed and sent to us through Felix and Sabinus, our fellow bishops, out of the integrity of your faith and your fear of God. You indicated that Basilides and Martial, stained by certificates of idolatry and bound by consciousness of abominable crimes, ought not to exercise the episcopate or administer the priesthood of God. You desired that we write back to you concerning these matters and that your just and equally necessary concern be relieved by either the consolation or the assistance of our judgment.

Yet it is not so much our counsels as the divine commandments that answer this desire of yours. By them it has long been commanded in a heavenly voice and prescribed by the law of God what kind of persons, and of what character, ought to serve the altar and celebrate the divine sacrifices. For in Exodus God speaks to Moses and warns him, saying: “Let the priests who approach the Lord God be sanctified, lest perhaps the Lord forsake them” (Exodus 19:22). And again: “When they approach to minister at the holy altar, they shall not bring guilt upon themselves, lest they die” (Exodus 28:43). Likewise, in Leviticus the Lord commands and says: “A man in whom there is a blemish or defect shall not approach to offer gifts to God” (Leviticus 21:17).

[Note: [Col. 1022D]

II.—*Declared and made manifest.* So read twelve of our old books and five cited by Pamelius. Two others of ours have “since these things were declared and commanded.” Four others and the old editions read “declared, or commanded, and manifest,” except that “and manifest” is absent from one of them. Pamelius adds that “or commanded” was superfluously inserted in the printed copies, since it does not occur in the manuscripts. I agree with Pamelius that it was added superfluously. It is one of the synonymous expressions in which the old copies of the holy martyr’s works abound. BALUZE.—“Declared and manifest” in the editions of Pamelius, Rigault, and Fell. “Or commanded” appears in editions earlier than Pamelius. ROUTH.

*Without cause.* This is how Cyprian rendered what the Septuagint expressed as *μάτην σέβονταί με*—“they worship me in vain.” “Without cause” means vainly, wrongly. RIGAULT.

[Col. 1023B] *In a holy and worthy manner.* The old books and editions vary greatly in this passage. Some have “in a holy and worthy manner,” others “in a worthy and holy manner.” Two old books read “holy and worthy sacrifices.” BALUZE.

*Be heard in their prayers.* Erasmus notes that Cyprian appears to have thought that nothing is effected by the sacrifice of a wicked priest and, indeed, that the people are thereby more greatly defiled. John Gerson, in his sermon *On the Lord’s Supper*: “State next why Cyprian and very many other doctors, whose words are cited in the decrees, held that nothing is accomplished in the sacraments and nothing conferred by schismatics.” See Gratian’s *Decretum*, Causa 1, question 1. In the first book of Etherius and Beatus *Against Elipandus of Toledo*, it is written that the sacrifice of the altar cannot be offered by just any priest, but only by a holy and righteous priest.

Albert of Stade, in recounting the history of certain [Col. 1023C] heretics who began to spring up in the Church of God in 1248, says that they claimed that priests living in mortal sins could not consecrate the Eucharist. Among the articles of Wycliffe condemned at the Council of Constance one reads: “If a bishop or priest is in mortal sin, he does not ordain, effect the sacrament, consecrate, or baptize.” In the same period, it was charged against John of Varennes, pastor of Saint-Lié in the diocese of Reims, that he had publicly preached that priests who kept concubines did not consecrate the body of Christ, as may be seen in the first volume of Gerson’s works, p. 915 of the latest edition.

In Oderic Raynaldus, year 1420, § 17, there is a bull of Pope Martin V against Nicolas Serrurier, who preached that the orations and prayers of the Mass offered by priests publicly keeping concubines were of no value and that priests publicly keeping concubines were worse than Judas. See Gregory VII, Book IV, Epistles 10, 11, and 20, and our notes on Agobard, p. 66. By contrast, in Gratian, Causa 1, question 1, chapter *Intra catholicam*, a passage is quoted from Augustine in which it is written that within [Col. 1023D] the Catholic Church, in the mystery of the body and blood of the Lord, nothing more is accomplished by a good priest and nothing less by a bad one. See Hugh, archbishop of Rouen, *Dialogues*, Book V, ch. II, and his *Apologetic Epistle to Matthew of Albano*. See also M. Antonius Marsilius, *Treatise on Holy Water*, p. 266. BALUZE.—Cyprian and his colleagues appear to speak only of priests who are contaminated by sins of the kind for which, under ecclesiastical law, they would cease to exercise priestly functions. Add that Basilides had already been lawfully deposed from office. ROUTH.

*A sinner.* Fell reviewed several manuscripts in which “sinners” is written, just as it is read in the Gospel; but even there some manuscripts have the singular *ἁμαρτωλόν*, “a sinner.” ROUTH.

*Care and examination.* I judged that this reading should be restored, although the conjunction is absent from eight old books and from the Aldine edition. The old editions and twelve [Col. 1024B] old books support this reading. The Sorbonne manuscript reads: “For this reason, with full indulgence, sincere examination.” There no one can fail to see that the conjunction has been transposed and that one must read “with full indulgence and examination,” in the same way that the conjunction appears in the books that contain it. The Foix manuscript reads: “For this reason, with full indulgence, example, and reason.” From this the word *examination* was formed, as we observed above in a similar passage at Epistle LII, p. 442. BALUZE.]

II. Since these things have been declared and made manifest [Note: [Col. 1021C] “declared and commanded,” Ver.; “or commanded,” Foss.] to us, our obedience must submit to the divine commandments. Human indulgence cannot show partiality in such matters or grant anything to anyone where a divine prescription intervenes and lays down the law.

For we must not forget what the Lord spoke to the Jews through the prophet Isaiah, rebuking them and expressing indignation because they disregarded the divine commandments and followed human teachings. “This people,” he says, “honors me with its lips [Note: [Col. 1022B] ‘sanctifies,’ Ver.], but their heart [Note: [Col. 1022C] ‘is far from me,’ Lam., Ebor., Bod. 2, NC. 1.] is far removed from me. They worship me without cause, teaching the commandments and doctrines of human beings” (Isaiah 29:13). The Lord repeats this in the Gospel as well and says: “You reject the commandment of God in order to establish your own tradition” (Mark 7:13).

Keeping these things before our eyes and considering them carefully and reverently, in ordaining priests we must choose only prelates who are unstained and upright. Offering sacrifices to God in a holy and worthy manner, they must be capable of being heard in the prayers they make for the well-being of the Lord’s people, since it is written: “God does not hear a sinner [Note: [Col. 1023A] ‘sinners,’ Lam., Ebor., NC. 1.]; but if anyone worships God and does his will, him he hears” (John 9:31). Therefore, it is necessary that those chosen for the priesthood of God be selected with full care and sincere examination [Note: [Col. 1023B] “with the full care of God and with examination,” Bod. 1, 2, Lin., Lam., Ebor., NC. 1.], so that it may be established that they are heard by God.

[Note: [Col. 1024B]

III.—*Nor should the people flatter themselves.* Alger of Liège, the scholastic, quoted this passage in an altered and interpolated form in his book *On Mercy and Justice*, ch. 81. After “defiled by the sacrifice,” he added certain words that occur neither in the commonly printed editions nor in the manuscripts. They read as follows: “For was not the ship in danger of being shattered because Jonah was aboard it in disobedience? When Achan was in Israel with the accursed gold plate, was not the army struck down and driven in flight from the city of Ai? If, then, those ignorant of the fault were punished in this way, what will happen to those who know of it and consent to it?” BALUZE.

*Contagion.* This is a good reading. The reader should nevertheless be advised that the alternative reading, “by contamination,” is also excellent, as Pamelius himself recognized. Accordingly, since one of the two readings had to be retained and the other rejected, we retained the one accepted in the text. BALUZE.

*License.* That is, right, authority, or power. Hence one Royal manuscript reads: “they unlawfully claimed for themselves the right to sacrifice.” Thus *license* is used here very properly in the sense of audacity, as in Cicero’s *Speech for Quintus Ligarius*: “See what license Caesar grants us—or rather, what audacity.” Nazarius, in the panegyric he delivered to Constantine Augustus: “Those who cannot protect what is entrusted to them turn power into license.” BALUZE.

*Claimed.* The Foix manuscript reads “usurped or claimed.” No doubt both readings occurred in the older book from which the Foix manuscript was copied, one in the text and the other above the line, as was frequently done in former times. BALUZE.

*Of these very hard men.* “Of these unjust, very hard men.” The authority of sixteen old copies and the oldest editions compelled me to alter the reading accepted since Erasmus. For all the old copies have “of these unjust, very hard men.” The Foix manuscript, to be sure, reads only “of very hard men,” evidently through the copyist’s carelessness in omitting something. In Numbers 16, from which this passage was copied, one reads: “Withdraw from the tents of impious men.” In Epistle 76 (otherwise 77), p. 155, however, where the same passage is quoted, one reads “of those very hard men.” BALUZE.—At this very passage under discussion, the Aldine, Pamelian, Rigaultian, and Fell editions in my possession exhibit precisely the same reading, “of those very hard men”; the Roman edition of 1471, however, does not recognize the word “those.” Jerome too, [Col. 1025B] in *Against the Luciferians*, p. 128 of the Froben edition, quotes from Scripture “of those very hard men.” I have therefore restored the similar reading “of these very hard men,” which Hardouin and others provide in the edition of the Councils. I thought the word “unjust” should be disregarded because it is merely a double reading, the Septuagint’s word *σκληρῶν* (“hard”) being rendered in different ways by different translators. There are, moreover, many readings of this kind in Cyprian. As for the opinion of both Rigault in his notes and the English translator that by the word “very hard” Cyprian signifies the Novatians, who denied penance to the lapsed, this seems to me less certain and evident. ROUTH.

*Touch the things that belong to them.* The old editions and eleven old books read: “Do not touch any of the things that are theirs.” This appears to have been altered by later copyists in an attempt to restore the reading found in the Vulgate edition of Holy Scripture. BALUZE.—Those eleven old books mentioned by Baluze had been cited by Fell. They render the Septuagint literally, for the Greek reads: *Καὶ μὴ ἅπτεσθε ἀπὸ πάντων ὅσα ἐστὶν αὐτοῖς*—“And do not touch any of the things that belong to them.” ROUTH.

*An obedient people.* The *Discourse on the Persecution of the Donatists*, published in the appendix to Optatus by the most learned Louis Ellies Du Pin, p. 299, § 3: “Before a people that was always excessively obedient to him.” BALUZE.

*From a sinful ruler.* Great authority is granted here to the people, so that they may judge the life and conduct of their bishop and, if it is established that he errs in the faith, abstain from communion with him. For since, as Saint Jerome says in the *Dialogue Against the Luciferians*, a bishop is established in the Church in order to restrain the people from error, how great will the error among the people be when the one who teaches is himself in error? Likewise, in the epistle to Pammachius against John of Jerusalem: “For the ears of the people are holier than the mind of the priest.” See our notes on Agobard, p. 61, and the preface of the most learned man and our very dear friend Dom Bernard de Montfaucon to the minor works of Saint Athanasius, § 6. See also the itinerary of Pope Adrian VI, published in the third book of our *Miscellanies*, p. 451.

Saint Augustine gives an example of a congregation wishing to withdraw from its bishop in his epistle to Nancilio, although the issue did not concern the faith but a new translation of a single word in the fourth chapter of Jonah. We who belong to the Roman communion believe that one must withdraw from the pope if he is a heretic. BALUZE.—But I would have you observe that absolutely no one is permitted, on his own private authority, to withdraw from a legitimate episcopal pastor, much less [Col. 1026B] from the supreme pontiff, so long as no canonical sentence has been passed against him. EDITORS.

*It especially has the power*, etc. Not when moved by its own initiative, but when admonished, through the just and necessary concern of other rulers, by the bishops of other churches, whose counsels correspond to the divine commandments. RIGAULT.]

III. Nor should the people flatter themselves that they can be immune from the contagion [Note: [Col. 1024A] “contamination,” Lam., Lin.] of wrongdoing if they communicate with a sinful priest and lend their consent to the unjust and unlawful episcopate of their own ruler. For through the prophet Hosea the divine judgment threatens and says: “Their sacrifices are like the bread of mourning; all who eat them will be defiled” (Hosea 9:4). It thereby teaches and shows that absolutely all who have been defiled by the sacrifice of a profane and unjust priest are bound by sin.

We find the same thing made manifest in Numbers, when Korah, Dathan, and Abiram claimed for themselves the license to sacrifice in opposition to Aaron the priest. There too the Lord commanded through Moses that the people should separate themselves from them, lest, by joining themselves to the criminals, they too should be implicated in the same crime. “Separate yourselves,” he says, “from the tents of these very hard men, and do not touch [Col. 1025A] the things that belong to them [Note: [Col. 1025B] “the things that are theirs,” Lam., Ebor., Bod. 1, 2, Lin., NC. 2, Thu., Foss., Corb., Mich., Vict.], lest you perish together in their sin” (Numbers 16:26).

Therefore, a people that obeys the Lord’s commandments and fears God must separate itself from a sinful ruler and must not involve itself in the sacrifices of a sacrilegious priest, since the people itself especially possesses the power either to choose worthy priests or to reject the unworthy.

[Note: [Col. 1026B]

IV.—*And Aaron, being gathered.* The Septuagint reads: *προστιθεὶς ἀποθανέτω ἐκεῖ*—“being added, let him die there.” The Vulgate has: “He shall be gathered and shall die there,” that is, he shall be gathered to his fathers. Thus the Foix manuscript mentioned by Baluze reads: [Col. 1026C] “And Aaron, being gathered to his fathers, shall die.” The English Bible version has “to his people.” ROUTH.

*Priestly ordinations only*, etc. Following this example of the Christians, Alexander Severus made his appointments public whenever he wished to give governors to provinces, appoint prefects, or install procurators, that is, financial administrators. He posted their names and said that it was a serious matter that, although Christians and Jews did this when ordaining priests, it was not done in the case of provincial governors, etc. These things may be found in Lampridius. RIGAULT.

*Apostle.* Previously “bishop” was read. Three old copies supplied us with the true reading. BALUZE.—But Fell had earlier restored the word “apostle” from four manuscripts. ROUTH.

*In the midst of the learners.* Acts 1 has *ἐν μέσῳ τῶν μαθητῶν*—“in the midst of the disciples.” The Vulgate reads “of the disciples.” RIGAULT, cited by Fell.—Three old books read “of the disciples,” with the same meaning. A little later “of the disciples” is also written. In Tertullian’s book *On Repentance*: “At the sword of even a single learner.” See Pamelius’s notes. BALUZE.

*The company was together in one place*: *ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτό*, “together in the same place.” Cyprian himself says at the beginning of this epistle: “When we had assembled together.” Psalm 121: *ἧς ἡ μετοχὴ αὐτῆς ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτό*—“whose fellowship is together in the same place.” RIGAULT, cited by Fell.—The Vulgate has: “Now the company of persons together was about one hundred and twenty.” Hear also Baluze, who restored: “Now the company of persons was about one hundred and twenty.” Previously the text there read “the company in one place” or “together.” We corrected and supplemented it on the authority of four old copies. Quite rightly, for in the Acts of the Apostles, from which this passage was taken, one reads “about one hundred and twenty.” BALUZE.—So says the distinguished scholar. Since, however, this reading seemed to me to have been introduced later into Cyprian from the Vulgate translation—just as Baluze himself judged concerning another Cyprianic passage altered by copyists at p. 79—I concluded that the old reading should be restored. Compare also the immediately following note. ROUTH.

*The whole people.* Acts 6:2 reads: *Προσκαλεσάμενοι δὲ οἱ* [Col. 1027C] *δώδεκα τὸ πλῆθος τῶν μαθητῶν*—“Then the Twelve summoned the multitude of the disciples”; and verse 6: *ἐνώπιον παντὸς τοῦ πλήθους*—“before the whole multitude.” Pacian, Epistle III: “whose parts are joined into one.” RIGAULT, cited by Fell.—Two old books read “the whole multitude.” BALUZE.—At this point the Vulgate has: “Then the Twelve, summoning the multitude of the disciples.” ROUTH.

*And not through me.* *Καὶ οὐ δι’ ἐμοῦ ἦρξαν*—“And they ruled, but not through me.” Hosea 8. RIGAULT, cited by Fell.—Shortly afterward, in the words “and perceived each person’s action from his manner of life,” the preposition “from” is expressed by *de*. ROUTH.]

## IV

We see that this very practice also derives from divine authority: that a priest is chosen in the presence of the people [Note: [Col. 1025B] “A bishop in the presence of the people,” Benev.], under the eyes of all, and is approved as worthy and suitable by public judgment and testimony. Thus in Numbers the Lord commanded Moses, saying: “Take Aaron your brother and Eleazar his son, and bring them up onto the mountain before the whole congregation; strip Aaron of his robe and clothe Eleazar his son [Col. 1025B] with it, and let Aaron be gathered and die there” (Num. 20:25–26). [Col. 1026A] God commands a priest to be appointed before the whole congregation; that is, he instructs and shows that priestly ordinations ought to take place only with the knowledge of the people standing by, so that, in the people’s presence, either the crimes of the wicked may be disclosed or the merits of the good proclaimed, and so that an ordination examined by the vote and judgment of all may be just and legitimate.

This was afterward observed in accordance with divine instruction in the Acts of the Apostles, when Peter addressed the people concerning the appointment of an apostle in Judas’s place [Note: [Col. 1026B] Thus Bod. 2, Lam., Ebor., NC. 1; “of a bishop,” Rig.]: “Peter arose,” it says, “in the midst of the disciples; now the crowd was gathered together” (Acts 1:15). We observe that the apostles followed this practice not only in the ordinations of bishops and priests but also in [Note: [Col. 1026B] “but in,” Oxon.] those of deacons [Note: [Col. 1026B] “even of deacons,” Lam., Ebor., Bod. 2, NC. 1]. Concerning this too it is written in their Acts: “And those twelve,” it says, “called together [Col. 1026B] the whole multitude of the disciples and [Col. 1027A] said to them” (Acts 6:2).

This was, of course, conducted so diligently and cautiously, with the whole people assembled, precisely to prevent anyone unworthy from insinuating himself into the ministry of the altar or into priestly office. For God himself makes clear that unworthy men are sometimes ordained not according to God’s will but according to human presumption, and that those things which do not proceed from a legitimate and just ordination are displeasing to God, when he says through the prophet Hosea: “They appointed a king for themselves, and not through me” (Hos. 8:4).

> [Note: [Col. 1027C]
>
> **V.—“Nor can it annul . . . that Basilides, going to Rome.”** This passage too supports the authority of the Roman Pontiff, since it establishes that bishops expelled from their sees in Spain were accustomed to have recourse to him—although Cyprian does not approve of Basilides’ doing so, because he deceived Pope Stephen and fraudulently insinuated himself into his favor. The same was done in the East by St. Athanasius of Alexandria, Paul of Constantinople, Marcellus of Ancyra, and Asclepas, bishop of Gaza, who, after being expelled by the Arians, had recourse to Pontiff Julius and were restored by him to their sees, as Sozomen attests. Stephen, bishop of Carthage, likewise acted before Damasus, together with the Council of Mauretania, when he complained about bishops expelled from their sees; he says that it was established by ancient rules that such a matter should be considered there first, before it was brought to the attention of the Holy See, etc. St. John Chrysostom of Constantinople had recourse to Innocent I; Theodoret of Cyrrhus and Flavian of Constantinople to Leo; and finally Ignatius, bishop of Constantinople, to Nicholas I. To the same subject belongs the tragedy of Anthimus, also bishop of Constantinople, who was expelled from his see by Agapetus and replaced by Menas, as well as the petitions and threats made by the empress Theodora to Pontiffs Silverius and Vigilius for Anthimus’s restoration. Finally, there is that canon of the Council of Nicaea concerning which so great a controversy arose between the African and Roman bishops, but whose authenticity is nevertheless established by the letters of the Roman Pontiffs Felix, Julius, and [Col. 1028C] Zosimus; and there are the statements found in virtually all those early Roman pontiffs and martyrs concerning bishops’ appeals to the Roman See. **BALUZ.**
>
> **“Restored to the episcopate.”** Baronius rightly inferred from this passage that it was a very ancient practice in the Church for bishops from the most distant parts of the world, who believed that they had suffered injustice at the hands of their colleagues, to appeal to the bishop of Rome as the primate of the universal Church. See de Marca, *De concordia*, book I, chapter 10, and Pamelius in his annotations on this letter of Cyprian. What Goulart wrote here against Pamelius is futile. **BALUZ.**
>
> **“Rightfully deposed.”** The previous reading was “justly.” That is certainly an excellent reading. But since “rightfully” is written in the Verona codex, in fifteen of our ancient manuscripts, and in seven English ones, and since Morel likewise printed it, I did not think that I ought to reject a reading supported by so many authorities. The author of the panegyric of Constantine delivered by the people of Flavia appears to have distinguished between these two words. For he says: “You brought it about that we appear justly to have obtained what we could rightfully request.” **BALUZ.**
>
> **“Enmeshed in grave offenses.”** At the beginning of the letter he said: “bound by consciousness of abominable crimes.” Shortly he will say: “entangled in grave offenses.” And elsewhere: “a conscience bound by the many snares of offenses.” **RIGALT., cited by Fell.**—Thus fourteen ancient books and the editions of Erasmus and Morel. But the earlier editions and six ancient books have: “enmeshed in a grave crime.” **BALUZ.**]

## V

For this reason, in accordance with divine tradition and apostolic observance, that practice must diligently be observed [Note: [Col. 1027B] Thus Lam., Bod. 1, 2; “must be observed,” Imp.] and maintained which is also maintained among us and throughout almost all the provinces: namely, that for ordinations duly to be celebrated, all the neighboring bishops of the same province should assemble among the people over whom the one being ordained is to be appointed, and that the bishop should be chosen in the presence of the people, who know each individual’s life most fully and have observed each man’s conduct from his manner of life. [Col. 1027B]

We see that this was also done among you in the ordination of our colleague Sabinus: the episcopate was conferred upon him by the vote of the entire brotherhood and by the judgment of the bishops who had assembled in person and had written letters about him to you, [Col. 1028A] and hands were laid upon him in the place of Basilides.

Nor can the fact that Basilides went to Rome annul an ordination rightfully completed. After his crimes had been disclosed and his conscience laid bare even by his own confession [Note: [Col. 1027B] “and after his conscience had also been laid bare by his own confession,” Bod. 1, 2, Lam., Ebor., NC. 1, 2, Lin., Corb.], he deceived our colleague Stephen, who was far away and ignorant of what had been done and of the truth, so as to solicit his unjust restoration to the episcopate from which he had been rightfully [Note: [Col. 1028B] Thus Lam., Bod. 1, 2, Ebor., Lin., NC. 1, 2, Neap.; “justly,” Oxon.] deposed.

The result is that Basilides’ offenses have not so much been erased as multiplied, since the crime of deceit and circumvention has been added to his former sins. For the man who was carelessly imposed upon is not so much to be blamed as the man who fraudulently imposed himself upon him is to be abhorred. But although Basilides was able to impose upon human beings, he cannot impose upon God, since it is written: “God is not mocked” (Gal. 6:7). [Col. 1028B]

Nor can deceit have profited Martialis so as to prevent the conclusion that he too, enmeshed in grave offenses, ought not to retain the episcopate, since the Apostle admonishes and says: “A bishop must be without reproach, as a steward of God” (Titus 1:7).

> [Note: [Col. 1028D]
>
> **VI.—“And as Felix.”** The conjecture of the English translator is certainly not to be rejected: he believes that this Felix was Martialis’s successor and that, having been sent with Sabinus, Basilides’ successor, he is called a bishop here. **ROUTH.**
>
> **“Felix of Caesaraugusta.”** From this Baronius inferred that he [Col. 1029A] was bishop of Caesaraugusta, [Col. 1029B] and the historians of Aragon embraced his opinion. But Francisco Bivar vigorously assails it in his commentaries on the chronicle of Dexter and contends, on the basis of that chronicle, that this Felix was not a bishop but a presbyter of Vallata Urbicua among the Vaccaei. It is certainly true that Cyprian does not call Felix a bishop. Yet from Cyprian’s manner of writing it is easy and natural to suppose that he was adorned with that dignity. For the notary who recorded the proceedings does not list the dignities of the bishops who held the council with Cyprian at Carthage, but only their names and the cities over which they presided, in this fashion (p. 92): “Caecilius of Bilta, Primus of Misgirpa, Polycarp of Hadrumetum,” and so with the rest. Accordingly, although Cyprian wrote only “Felix of Caesaraugusta,” his silence does not prove that Felix was not a bishop.
>
> One matter seems difficult to me: how the bishop of Caesaraugusta could have written to Cyprian [Col. 1029C] about the case of Basilides and Martialis, since he was not their neighbor but was separated from them by a great distance; nor is it probable that Sabinus and Felix, who could have crossed into Africa by a short route, traveled to the remotest bounds of Spain in order to reach Cyprian by way of the Pyrenees. If what St. Vincent Ferrer said in his sermon on St. Lawrence were true—that St. Sixtus the Pope, while traveling to hold the Council of Toledo, passed through Caesaraugusta—this might perhaps confirm that Sabinus and Felix traveled through Caesaraugusta. But that is established from no source other than St. Vincent’s sermon.
>
> As for what Bivar relates there from Dexter concerning Vallata Urbicua, it is empty, as is his assertion that in Cyprian “Vallata Urbicua,” which he locates not far from Asturica, should be read in place of “Caesaraugusta.” It is consummate wretchedness for a man to be excessively audacious. **BALUZ.**
>
> **“Filthy banquets.”** At these one was obliged to eat food offered to idols, and it was not permissible to drink without making a libation to profane deities. [Col. 1029D] **FELL.**—By the seventh canon of the Council of Ancyra, even those Christians who attended public banquets of this kind were punished, although they had brought from home the food which they themselves ate. **ROUTH.**
>
> **“In the guild.”** Thus all the ancient books and all editions earlier than Pamelius’s. Pamelius therefore changed the text on the authority of a single English codex and printed “and guilds.” I am surprised that this was retained in later editions. **BALUZ.**—Besides the colleges of pontiffs, Arval Brethren, Potitii, and augurs, and others of that kind, which directly concerned pagan idolatry, there were very many associations connected with the administration of the commonwealth, commerce, and crafts. All of these were placed under the protection of some profane deity, and therefore no one could participate in them without becoming a participant in that cult. **FELL.**
>
> **“At profane tombs.”** Rigault says: “In those tombs there were many things pertaining to pagan rites; those who laid their dead there seemed to share in them and to be defiled by them, and for this reason alone [Col. 1030A] they were said to have become participants in idolatry. Moreover, it was utterly [Col. 1030B] inconsistent with Christian charity and ecclesiastical unity to place the bodies of deceased brethren in the tombs of enemies of the Christian name—as though the deceased themselves, precisely when they died, had been outside the Church. The Christian brotherhood therefore rightly rejected the guilds of the pagans as pestilential, and their tombs as receptacles for the dead. For the faithful had their own κοιμητήρια (*koimētēria*, ‘sleeping places’), that is, places for those sleeping in hope of resurrection and eternal blessedness. The pledge of this hope was Christ, who, after being laid in the tomb, revived and rose again. And the angel who met the women seeking the Lord in the tomb said, Οὐκ ἔστιν ὧδε, ‘He is not here.’ That inscription is indeed as magnificent and glorious as it differs from those commonplace inscriptions upon tombs: ‘HERE HE IS LAID,’ ‘HERE HE LIES.’” Thus Rigault.
>
> Furthermore, just as many have observed that almost every religion of the nations consisted in the worship of the dead, so pagan superstition exercised itself scarcely more intensely in any area than in the care of the [Col. 1030C] dead. Hence sacrifices, not infrequently human ones, had to be offered to appease the gods below and placate the shades; hence hair was shorn, baldness deliberately produced, and bodies cut on account of the dead—the practices discussed in Deut. 14:1. **FELL.**—The phrases “according to the custom of foreign nations” and “with foreigners” appear to refer to the gentiles, as they are commonly called: those situated outside the Church and strangers to Christian rites. **ROUTH.**
>
> **“Before the ducenarian procurator.”** Apart from military concerns and the business of war, service about the Roman emperor was of two kinds: the literary service, which worked in the bureaus, and the executive service, which was intensely occupied with the conduct of affairs. The latter were called *magistriani*, and from their school came the *ducenarii* and *centenarii*, or *sexagenarii*, who collected fiscal revenues and were named from the amount of money they received as salary. Dio, book LIII, where he discusses Caesar’s procurators: Καὶ τοῖς γε ἐπιτρόποις καὶ αὐτὸ τὸ ὄνομα ἀπὸ τοῦ ἀριθμοῦ τῶν διδομένων αὐτοῖς χρημάτων, “And in the case of the procurators, their very title was derived from the amount of money given to them.” Capitolinus, in his *Pertinax*: “He was transferred to Dacia with a salary of two hundred thousand sesterces.” An ancient inscription reads: [Col. 1030D] “PROCURATOR OF AUGUSTUS FOR THE PROVINCE OF BAETICA, TO RECEIVE TWO HUNDRED THOUSAND.” Apuleius, *Milesian Tales*: “Having discharged the office of a ducenarian procurator of the emperor.”
>
> This class was exceedingly hostile to Christians. For by reason of their office they reported every matter, great or small, that took place in the provinces. Consequently, confessors of the Christian name were often harassed by them unless they redeemed themselves from the harassment by a shameful bargain, as Cyprian implies was done by this Martialis.
>
> There is a title in book X of the *Code*, “On the collection of taxes,” where Emperor Constantine forbids the *ducenarii* to proceed against any debtor before they have received from the city registrar itemized schedules of the debts; and in the following law: “Let no one,” he says, “in the payment of debts fear imprisonment, blows from leaded whips, weights, or other punishments devised by the insolence of judges.”
>
> In Eusebius there is also a letter from the Synod of Antioch to Dionysius, bishop of Rome, and Maximus, bishop of Alexandria, in which the Antiochene fathers observe that Paul of Samosata displayed such arrogance that he deserved to be regarded as a ducenarian rather than a bishop, so wickedly and [Col. 1031B] insolently did he conduct himself toward the entire brotherhood. The words of the synod in *Ecclesiastical History*, book VII, chapter 30, are as follows: Καὶ οὕτως ὑψηλοφρονεῖ καὶ ὑπερῆρται κοσμικὰ ἀξιώματα ὑποδυόμενος, καὶ δουκηνάριος μᾶλλον ἢ ἐπίσκοπος [Col. 1031C] θέλων καλεῖσθαι, καὶ σοβῶν κατὰ τὰς ἀγορὰς, καὶ ἐπιστολὰς ἀναγινώσκων καὶ ὑπαγορεύων, ἅμα βαδίζων δημοσίᾳ, καὶ δορυφορούμενος, etc.: “And thus he is proud and puffed up, assuming worldly dignities and wishing to be called a ducenarian rather than a bishop; he strides haughtily through the marketplaces, reading letters and dictating them while walking in public, and is attended by a bodyguard,” etc.
>
> This class of men was therefore exceedingly troublesome and so odious and generally hateful to most people—as were also the *circitores* and *curiosi*—but especially to Christians, who were very frequently seized through the cruelty of such officials and dragged before the authorities.
>
> Eulogius, archbishop of Alexandria, in his book *On Ecclesiastical Discipline against Novatus*, mentions a certain work of Novatian whose subject, he reports, was this: Ὅτι βασιλεύοντος Ῥωμαίων Δεκίου καὶ Οὐαλεριανοῦ, Περέννιος Δουκηνάριος πρόσταγμα λαβὼν παρ’ αὐτῶν, πάντας τοὺς ἀνὰ τὴν Ῥώμην καὶ τὰς πέριξ ἐπαρχίας χριστιανοὺς βαρυτάταις βασάνοις καὶ πικραῖς τιμωρίαις εἰδωλολατρεῖν ἐβιάζετο, καὶ πολλοὶ μὲν καὶ ἄλλοι ἐνεδίδουν τῇ βίᾳ, etc.: “During the reign of Decius and Valerian over the Romans, Perennius the ducenarian, having received an order from them, attempted by the most grievous tortures and bitter punishments to compel all the Christians throughout Rome and the surrounding provinces to practice idolatry; and many others yielded to the violence,” etc.
>
> See what we have observed concerning the *beneficiarii* and *curiosi* in the notes on Tertullian, and concerning the *frumentarii* in the notes on Cyprian’s final letter, but above all what Salmasius wrote on Capitolinus’s *Pertinax*. **RIGALT., cited by Fell.**—You will find more learned discussion of the *ducenarii* in Rigault’s observations. See also Beatus Rhenanus’s marginal note on the letter of the Synod of Antioch in Rufinus, book VII, chapter 26, and Joseph Scaliger on Manilius.
>
