> In his legal lexicon, under the word *Ducenarii*, John Calvin cites the fourth letter of book I of St. Cyprian—which is this present letter—in which he says that the following words occur: “Nor so that he grew proud and was raised up by worldly dignities, wishing to be called a ducenarian rather than a bishop.” But I have found these words neither in the editions nor in the ancient manuscripts. **BALUZ.**—The words belong to the passage just cited by Rigault from the Antiochenes’ letter, likewise mentioned by Baluze, part of which appears above in volume II at p. 479, where the note may be consulted. **ROUTH.**
>
> **“And honored also with martyrdom by the Lord’s favor.”** Suppose that Cornelius suffered a natural rather than a bloody death after confessing the Lord, as Pearson holds in his *Annales Cyprianici* under the year 252, [Col. 1032B] §13, citing the author of a very ancient catalogue, whose words concerning Cornelius are: “After this he was exiled to Centumcellae, where he received a glorious falling asleep.” Nevertheless, that great man seems incorrect in suggesting [Col. 1032C] that later authors, rather than Jerome, attributed a bloody death to Cornelius; for in the book *On Illustrious Men*, Jerome says that Cornelius was “crowned with martyrdom for Christ,” while in the *Life of Paul the Hermit*, also written by Jerome, these words occur at p. 240 of the Froben edition: “Cornelius at Rome and Cyprian at Carthage were condemned to a blessed shedding of blood.”
>
> Furthermore, to state the truth, in his Letter LXVII or LXVIII Cyprian calls Lucius, Cornelius’s successor—who was similarly driven into exile but is found not in the Catalogue of Martyrs, but in the *Deposition*, or burial-list, of bishops—a blessed martyr, mentioning Cornelius at the same time. Nevertheless, because of Jerome’s testimony, I think the opinion of those who maintain that Cornelius was killed by the imperial sword is more worthy of acceptance. Maximus, the fifth-century bishop of Turin, likewise commemorates the venerable blood of Cornelius in his sermons, first published by Muratori. See Sermon 4, p. 46 of volume IV of the *Anecdota of the Ambrosian Library*. [Col. 1032D] “And Cornelius was beheaded,” says Anastasius the Librarian in the *Lives of the Roman Pontiffs*, p. 10 of the Mainz edition; but, like the ancient martyrologies, he says this on the basis of acts which appear spurious. **ROUTH.**]

## VI

Therefore, since—as you have written, most beloved brothers, and as our colleagues Felix and Sabinus affirm, and as another Felix of Caesaraugusta [Note: [Col. 1028B] “Caesarea Augusta,” Lam., Lin.], a cultivator of the faith [Col. 1029A] and defender of the truth, signifies in his letter [Note: [Col. 1029A] “signify,” Bod. 2; “signified,” Lam., Ebor., Bod. 1, NC. 1]—Basilides and Martialis have been defiled by the abominable certificate of idolatry; and since Basilides, in addition to the stain of the certificate, blasphemed against God while lying ill and confessed that he had blasphemed, and voluntarily laid aside the episcopate because of the wound to his conscience and turned to the performance of penance, [Col. 1030A] entreating God and being well content if only it should befall him to receive communion even as a layman;

and since Martialis, besides having long frequented the shameful and filthy banquets of the gentiles [Note: [Col. 1030A] “drunken banquets,” Lam., Ben., Ebor., Ben., Ebor., Bod. 2, Lin., NC. 1] in a guild, and having laid his sons in the same guild at profane tombs according to the custom of foreign nations and buried them together with strangers, has also testified in publicly recorded proceedings before the ducenarian procurator that he had submitted to idolatry [Col. 1031A] and denied Christ;

and since there are many other grave offenses in which Basilides and Martialis remain entangled [Note: [Col. 1031B] “may remain entangled,” Lam., Ebor., NC. 1], such men strive in vain to usurp the episcopate for themselves. For it is manifest [Note: [Col. 1031B] “may be more manifest,” Bod. 1, 2, Ebor., Lam., Lin., NC. 1, 2] that men of this sort can neither preside over Christ’s Church nor ought they to offer sacrifices to God—especially since long ago, together with us and with absolutely all the bishops established throughout the entire world, Cornelius our colleague, a peaceful and just priest, who was also honored with martyrdom by the Lord’s favor, decreed that men of this sort could indeed be admitted to perform penance, but must be excluded from ordination to the clergy and from priestly honor.

> [Note: [Col. 1032D]
>
> **VII.—“Irreligious fear of God.”** From a single manuscript Fell printed “fear of God among the irreligious,” while saying that the printed editions had the reading which you see received into the text. But I find “among the irreligious” also in the old Roman edition and in Erasmus’s. Baluze is silent, having retained the other reading. Yet since at the end of the letter you have “with religious fear,” a passage which sheds light on this very one, should we not therefore read: “religious fear of God”? **ROUTH.**]

## VII

Do not be disturbed, most beloved brothers, if among certain persons in these last times either an unstable faith [Col. 1031B] wavers, or an irreligious fear of God [Note: [Col. 1031B] Thus Imp.; “among the irreligious,” Foss., Oxon.] falters, or peaceful concord fails to endure. These things were foretold as destined to occur at the end of the age; and by the Lord’s voice and the testimony of the Apostles it was predicted that, as the world now fails [Col. 1032A] and Antichrist approaches, every good thing would decline, while evil and adverse things would advance.

> [Note: [Col. 1032D]
>
> **VIII.—“Neither by years.”** Two ancient books and the early editions prefer “by arms.” But Pamelius rejected this reading because it was clear to him that King Nebuchadnezzar had not attacked the three young men with any arms, and on the authority of five ancient manuscripts he printed “by years,” a reading which I too found in twenty of our manuscripts. One of my ancient manuscripts has “by furnaces.” I readily believe this [Col. 1033C] reading to be better, since it cannot be said of boys or young men that they were broken by old age and years, and because the word “furnaces” agrees better with the history. For it is certain that Nebuchadnezzar, in order to shake and terrify those young men, uttered threats of many kinds of punishment, held dangers before them, and finally commanded that a furnace—or, to use Sulpicius Severus’s word, a kiln—of blazing fire be prepared, into which they were to be cast.
>
> My opinion is confirmed by Cyprian’s words in Letter LVI, p. 91, where the three young men are not said to have been broken by years but, though frightened by their age, to have proved stronger than the king’s threats and the flames. I have therefore retained the reading which I consider better. Whoever examines these variant readings without prejudice will be able to form a more suitable and independent judgment concerning this emendation of mine. He will thus be able either to correct me or approve me [Col. 1033D] with greater sincerity and certainty.
>
> Cyprian rightly said that the young men were broken neither by furnaces nor by threats. For Cicero, in book I of *On Duties*, said “to be broken by fear”; and Statius, in book IX of the *Thebaid*, “to be broken by threats.” There are other examples as well. **BALUZE.**—As Pamelius himself reports, even before Pamelius the reading “neither by years” appeared in Manutius’s edition—indeed, in the true first edition of Cyprian, the Roman edition. Moreover, the Oxford edition records no variant reading here.
>
> I might perhaps have agreed with Baluze when he restored “neither by furnaces” to his edition—especially since the word “furnace” occurs in the young men’s address to the king in Daniel—had not two considerations stood in the way. The first is the inverted order of the words, “broken neither by furnaces nor by threats.” The second consists in the very words of Cyprian which the distinguished man cited: “Let us imitate the young men Ananias, Azarias, and Misael, who, though frightened neither by their age nor broken by captivity, after Judaea had been conquered and Jerusalem captured, overcame the king in his own kingdom by the strength of faith and proved stronger than the king’s threats and the flames.” [Col. 1034C] Elsewhere too, if I remember correctly, Cyprian draws an exhortation to courage from the tender age of these confessors. I have therefore restored the previously received reading, “neither by years,” that is, by their youthful years—the reading which Baluze, relying upon a single codex, had changed to the alternative “neither by furnaces.” **ROUTH.**]

## VIII

Yet even in these last times the evangelical vigor has not so fallen in God’s Church, nor has the strength of Christian virtue [Note: [Col. 1031B] “Christian virtue,” Lin., NC. 2] or of faith so languished [Note: [Col. 1032B] “vigor languishes,” Ver.; “fear,” Corb.], that no body of priests remains which does not succumb to these collapses of affairs and shipwrecks of faith, but instead, strong and steadfast, safeguards the honor of the divine majesty and the priestly dignity with an observance full of fear.

We remember and maintain that, although the rest succumbed and yielded, Mattathias (1 Macc. 2:19–20) courageously vindicated God’s law; that Elijah (3 Kings 19:10), when the Jews were failing [Note: [Col. 1032B] “stood firm when they were failing,” Lam., Lin., Ebor., Bod. 2, NC. 1] and withdrawing from the divine religion, stood firm and contended nobly; that Daniel [Col. 1032B] (Dan. 6:10, 21–22), deterred neither by the isolation [Note: [Col. 1032B] “isolation,” Bod. 1, 2, Lam., NC. 1, Lin., Ebor.] of a foreign land nor by the harassment of continual persecution, frequently and courageously gave glorious testimonies [Note: [Col. 1032B] “gloriously,” Lam., Lin., Ebor., NC. 1, 2, Foss., Vict., Corb.]; and likewise that the three young men, broken neither by their years nor by threats, faithfully resisted [Col. 1033A] the Babylonian fires and, although captives, overcame the victorious [Note: [Col. 1033B] “victors,” Lin., NC. 2] king.

Let the number of prevaricators or traitors look to itself—those who have now begun to rise up within the Church against the Church and equally to undermine faith and truth. Among very many there remains a sincere mind, an unimpaired religion, and a soul devoted to none but its Lord and God. Another’s faithlessness does not crush Christian faith into ruin, but rather rouses and exalts it to glory, in accordance with the exhortation of the blessed apostle Paul, who says (Rom. 3:3–4): “For what if some of them fell away from the faith? Has their unbelief nullified God’s faithfulness? By no means. For God is true, but every human being a liar.”

But if every human being is a liar and God alone is true, what else ought we, God’s servants and especially his priests, [Col. 1033B] to do but abandon human errors and falsehoods and, by keeping the Lord’s commandments, remain in God’s truth?

> [Note: [Col. 1034C]
>
> **IX.—“Your portion with adulterers.”** The Fuxensis codex has “with adulterers” in the sense of illicit lovers. Above, Letter LXIII, p. 110: “And you placed your little portion among adulterers.” **BALUZE.**—In this passage too Manutius’s edition has “little portion.” Eight manuscripts named in the Oxford edition have “part” for “portion.” **ROUTH.**
>
> **“They did not understand.”** Cyprian agrees with the reading of those codices which have οὐκ ἐνόησαν, “they did not understand,” and afterward οἳ αὐτὰ ποιοῦσι, “those who do these things,” and οἳ συνευδοκοῦσι, “those who approve together with them.” **FELL.**—What Pamelius says there is not found in the ancient manuscripts I found in fifteen of them. **BALUZE.**—The common reading is [Col. 1034D] ἐπίγνοντες, “having known,” without the negative particle, where the Apostle repeats the words. **ROUTH.**
>
> **“They are polluted by contact with the guilty.”** Pacian, Letter III: “To reject the guilty, to flee the touch of sinners.” **RIGAULT.**
>
> **“I wish you.”** Two ancient books and Morel’s edition have “We wish.” Both readings are sound, for the reasons given elsewhere on a similar occasion, p. 393. **BALUZE.** That is, in the note on Cyprian’s Letter VI, where Baluze made the following observations concerning the readings “I wish you” and “I wish you” in the singular: “Although the letter was written to several persons, it was nevertheless written principally and by name to Rogatian, a distinguished person. Cyprian could therefore have directed the closing valediction to him when appending the end of the letter, as was his custom.” Before Morel, Erasmus printed “We wish you.” But in the synodical letter immediately following, where “We wish” is read, the old Roman edition has “I wish,” as here. Evidently the closing formula is sometimes given in abbreviation: “I wish you, dearest brothers, always to fare well.”]

## IX

Therefore, even if some of our colleagues have arisen, most beloved brothers, [Note: [Col. 1033B] “In this matter,” Lam., Ebor., NC. 1] who think that the divine discipline should be neglected and rashly communicate with Basilides and Martialis, this circumstance ought not to disturb our faith, since the Holy Spirit in the Psalms threatens such men, saying (Ps. 49:17–18): “But you hated discipline and cast my words [Col. 1034A] behind you. If you saw [Note: [Col. 1033B] “If you should see,” Bod. 1] a thief, you ran together with him, and you placed your portion [Note: [Col. 1033B] “your part with adulterers,” Lam., Ebor., Bod. 1, 2, Lin., NC. 1, [Col. 1034B] 2, Thu.] with adulterers.”

He shows that those who join themselves to offenders become associates and participants in the offenses of others. The apostle Paul also writes and says this same thing: “Whisperers, slanderers, abhorrent to God, insolent, proud, boasters, inventors of evil things, who, although they had known God’s justice, did not understand that those who do such things are worthy of death—not only those who do them [Note: [Col. 1034B] “do evil things, but also those who consent to them,” Lam., Ebor., Lin., Thu., Vict., Corb.], but also those who consent to those who do them”; “for those who do such things,” he says, “are worthy of death” (Rom. 1:30–32).

He makes clear and establishes that not only those who commit evil are worthy of death and come under punishment, but also those who consent to persons who do such things. For when, through an illicit communion, they mingle with evil persons, sinners, and those who do not perform penance, [Col. 1034B] they are polluted by contact with the guilty; and because they are joined together in guilt, so too they are not separated in punishment.

For this reason, most beloved brothers, we equally praise and approve the religious solicitude of your integrity and faith; and, as far as we can, we exhort you by our letters not to mingle through sacrilegious communion with profane and defiled priests, but to preserve the unimpaired and sincere steadfastness of your faith with religious fear.

I wish you, dearest brothers, always to fare well.

> [Note: [Col. 1035C]
>
> **FIFTH COUNCIL OF CARTHAGE.—In the year 255.** Following Pearson in the *Annales Cyprianici*, I have assigned this council to the year 255 after Christ. For the printed collections of councils vary concerning the date of this and Cyprian’s other synods. Cyprian himself writes as follows about this synod at the beginning of his letter to Quintus:
>
> “Lucianus our fellow presbyter has reported to me, dearest brother, that you desired us to inform you what we think about those who appear to have been baptized among heretics and schismatics. So that you might know what many fellow bishops, together with the fellow presbyters who were present, recently judged concerning this matter in council, I have sent you a copy of that same letter.”
>
> Thus Cyprian. Cyprian afterward sent these same synodical letters [Col. 1035D] to Stephen of Rome and to Jubaianus, together with that letter to Quintus itself, as is established by the letters to Stephen and Jubaianus. **ROUTH.**
>
> **“To Januarius.”** The ancient books differ greatly among themselves here. For in some this man is called Jubaianus, Juvaianus, Jubianus, Juvianus, Jovianus—as in Zonaras and Balsamon—Julianus, or Januarius. Since this discrepancy is now of no importance, I have retained the commonly received reading. Meanwhile, it should be noted that the following title appears in the Thuanean codex: “Here begins the second book to Jubaianus.” In one of my ancient manuscripts: “Here begins the third letter to Jubaianus concerning these same persons, that is, concerning the lapsed.” **BALUZ.**]

# IN THE YEAR OF CHRIST 255, THE THIRD YEAR OF ST. STEPHEN: THE FIFTH COUNCIL OF CARTHAGE UNDER CYPRIAN, THE FIRST ON BAPTISM

*(Erasm. I, 12; Pamel., Rigalt., Baluz. LXX; Oxon., Lips. LXX; Paris. LXIX; Routh, Rell. Scr., pp. 84 and 135.)*

[Col. 1035A]

## Preface

After the practice of rebaptizing those who had been baptized by heretics had long before become prevalent in the African Church, with Agrippinus—or perhaps even Tertullian—as its originator, Novatian imitated it in order that, at least in this way, he might receive into the Church through Baptism the lapsed, whom he taught to be unclean, after they had been washed from all their uncleanness. Magnus, a layman, was the first at that time to raise the question, on account of the Novatians—who observed the same form and rite of baptism as the Catholics—whether those returning to the Church whom they knew to have been baptized by the Novatians ought to be rebaptized. [Col. 1035B]

Among the bishops, the Numidians are found to have been the first to write to Cyprian and the other bishops assembled for this synod at Carthage concerning the repetition of the baptism of heretics. This first synodical consultation on the matter was therefore held in the year 258 [Note: [Col. 1035C] Others: 256], the fourth year of the emperors Valerian and Gallienus, as Cyprian’s Letter 73 to Jubaianus shows.

In it, some of the Africans held, in accordance with apostolic tradition, that those who had been legitimately baptized by heretics should not be rebaptized; others, by contrast, believed that there was only one Baptism belonging to the one Church, and that therefore [Col. 1035C] the true and catholic Baptism could not exist among heretics outside the Church. [Col. 1036A] After this preliminary inquiry it was finally defined that, since there is one Baptism in the holy Church, no one can be baptized outside the Church.

Misinterpreting the tradition of the Apostles and also speaking badly by making a universal and constraining rule, they added—as is established by Cyprian’s Letter 71 to Quintus—that those who, after being duly baptized by Catholics, had defected to the heretics were to be received, if they sought to return to the Church, not through Baptism but by the laying on of hands alone. Baronius, under the year of Christ 258, nos. 17–26 inclusive.

When all these matters had thus been determined, they communicated the judgment and definition of this synod to Januarius and the other bishops of Numidia, as those bishops themselves had requested by letters written to the synod, in this synodical letter, which we have appended below [Col. 1036B] from Cyprian.

CYPRIAN, LIBERALIS, CALDONIUS, [Note: [Col. 1035C] Thus Bod. 1, Ebor., Lin., NC. 1, 2, Benev., Vet. Impr., [Col. 1036C] Erasm., Morel.; absent from Rig.] JUNIUS, PRIMUS, CAECILIUS, POLYCARP, NICOMEDES, FELIX, MARRUTIUS, SUCCESSUS, LUCIANUS, HONORATUS, FORTUNATUS, VICTOR, DONATUS, LUCIUS, HERCULANUS, POMPONIUS, DEMETRIUS, QUINTUS, SATURNINUS, MARCUS, ANOTHER SATURNINUS, ANOTHER DONATUS, ROGATIANUS, SEDATUS, TERTULLUS, HORTENSIANUS, LIKEWISE ANOTHER SATURNIUS, SATTIUS, TO [Note: [Col. 1036C] “Jubaianus,” Ebor., Lin., NC. 1, Ben.] JANUARIUS, SATURNINUS, MAXIMUS, VICTOR, ANOTHER VICTOR, CASSIUS, PROCULUS, MODIANUS, CITTINUS, GARGILIUS, EUTYCHIANUS, ANOTHER GARGILIUS, ANOTHER SATURNINUS, NEMESIANUS, NAMPULUS, ANTONIANUS, ROGATIANUS, AND HONORATUS, THEIR BROTHERS: GREETINGS.

[Col. 1036C]

> [Note: [Col. 1035D]

### I.—“When we were together in council.”

The Greek translator renders this, *ἐν κοινοβουλίῳ* (“in a council”). This letter is prefixed in the Synodical Codex of the Greek Church to the Council of Carthage held under Cyprian, and is presented as, so to speak, its canon; it was followed by the votes of the bishops, who variously elucidated it as *ἐνθυμήματα* or *ἐπιχειρήματα*—“reflections” or “arguments”—as Zonaras says. Balsamon and Zonaras assert that this letter was written in reply to Jubaianus, because they had observed that he was mentioned in Cyprian’s introductory address; although very many Latin manuscripts likewise support this view. But Eastern writers were perpetual strangers to Western affairs, and they were no more correct in translating the letter itself into Greek than they were in judging the occasion and origin of the document.

Meanwhile, however, it must be said that, since this letter was synodical and condemned the baptism of heretics, just as did the following synod of eighty-seven bishops, it was deservedly included in the collections of councils. Thus it had been transmitted to the Easterners, who accepted the decrees of different synods held at different times as rulings of the same council—an error not particularly harmful. It should further be noted that all the African synods under Cyprian were confirmed by the Sixth General Council in Trullo, canon 2. **FELL.**

As regards the canon of the Sixth General Council, the words of the Fathers are:

> *ἐπισφραγίζομεν δὲ καὶ τοὺς λοιποὺς πάντας ἱεροὺς κανόνας τοὺς ὑπὸ τῶν ἁγίων καὶ μακαρίων πατέρων ἡμῶν ἐκτεθέντας, τοῦτ’ ἔστιν τῶν τε ἐν Νικαίᾳ* etc.

> “We also ratify all the other sacred canons promulgated by our holy and blessed Fathers, namely those assembled at Nicaea,” etc.

Then, after naming the decrees of the other councils and Fathers, they proceed—but cautiously—to write:

> *ἔτι μὴν καὶ τὸν ὑπὸ Κυπριανοῦ τοῦ γενομένου Ἀρχιεπισκόπου τῆς Ἄφρων χώρας καὶ μάρτυρος, καὶ τῆς κατ’ αὐτὸν Συνόδου ἐκτεθέντα κανόνα, ὃς ἐν τοῖς τῶν προειρημένων προέδρων τόποις, καὶ μόνον, κατὰ τὸ παραδοθὲν αὐτοῖς ἔθος ἐκράτησεν.*

> “And furthermore the canon promulgated by Cyprian, who became archbishop of the territory of the Africans and a martyr, and by the synod held under him—a canon which prevailed in the territories of the aforesaid prelates, and there alone, according to the custom handed down to them.”

Canon II.

The canons called Apostolic, 46 and 47, also commanded that heretics be baptized anew. But the discipline of immersing again those heretics who had been baptized in the name of the Holy Trinity was pleasing to the greater part of the churches neither before nor after the period of these African councils. Witnesses from a time somewhat earlier than these councils are Cyprian himself and his fellow bishops, who acknowledge in so many places that they are opposing custom. Firmilian himself likewise says in his Letter to his Cyprian:

> “You Africans can indeed say against Stephen that, once the truth was known, you abandoned the error of custom,” p. 149.

So says this prelate of Caesarea in Cappadocia, who immediately afterward boasts that he and his Asian colleagues unite custom with truth and oppose to the custom of the Romans another custom—but one founded upon truth—“holding from the beginning what was handed down by Christ and the apostles.”

Nevertheless, it seems that one should not agree with Hardouin, who, relying on the authority of St. Jerome, inserted into his catalogue of councils an African council subsequent to these Cyprianic councils, in which those very bishops—Jerome’s words in *Against the Luciferians*, p. 117, Forben edition—“who had decreed with him [Cyprian] that heretics must be rebaptized, returned to the ancient custom and issued a new decree.” For many others, especially Basnage in his *Annals*, vol. II, p. 386, rightly observed against Jerome that the Africans’ discipline remained in force until the Council of Arles in the reign of Constantine the Great. That very synod is witness, canon VIII:

> “Concerning the Africans, because they employ a law of their own by rebaptizing, it was resolved that, if anyone comes to the Church from a heresy, he should be questioned concerning the Creed; and if they perceive that he was baptized in the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, hands alone should be laid upon him, that he may receive the Holy Spirit.”

Moreover, if such a council had ever existed, Augustine would certainly, in his Reply against the Donatists, books VI and VII, after every one of the opinions he cites from the Fathers who took part in the third African council on baptism, have persisted in inserting at every turn some reference to their retraction of that opinion. **ROUTH.**

**“To us.”** It is remarkable that these words, which have been propagated from Erasmus’s edition—for they are absent from the other editions—are found in only three ancient copies, although I collated this letter with twenty-six. They are therefore absent from the Tours manuscript, one manuscript of Rheims, and the Bec manuscript. **BALUZIUS.**—Baluzius meant to say: “They are therefore present,” not “They are therefore absent.” Fell, moreover, found them in several manuscripts. **ROUTH.**

**“Which is one and true.”** We have restored this passage on the authority of four ancient books. **BALUZIUS.**—The common reading is, “which is one.” **ROUTH.**

**“Our predecessors.”** Namely Agrippinus and others, whom St. Augustine writes to have numbered seventy, as we noted on the ninth letter, p. 396. See also the notes on Letter LXXIII. **BALUZIUS.**—Baluzius says nothing there concerning the period of Agrippinus, which indeed seems to most scholars too uncertain for anyone to establish anything definite about it. For those whom Cyprian in his Letter LXXIII, or *To Jubaianus*, places “many years and a long age” earlier, Augustine in *Against the Donatists*, book IV, chapter 6, describes as “a few years before Cyprian.” Yet Tertullian, while still a Catholic, shows in his book *On Baptism* that the opinion concerning the invalidity of heretical baptism had already prevailed among the Africans for a long time. There, relying upon the same arguments that Cyprian impresses upon us, he rejects heretical baptism and regards it as void. See chapter 15.

Indeed, in the *Sacred Geography of Africa* prefixed by the distinguished Dupin to St. Optatus, after the words of Tertullian cited on p. XXX—

> “As for heretics, who might worthily reconsider what rule should be observed? For a treatise has been published for us”—

that most learned man says that he does not doubt that these words designate Agrippinus’s decree against the baptism of heretics. From this and from Cyprian’s words he concludes that Agrippinus appears to have occupied the see of Carthage not in the third century, as is commonly thought, but near the end of the second century of the Church. Fell had likewise assigned Agrippinus no different period in his note on that passage of the Letter to Jubaianus, p. 199.

Furthermore, in the Letter to Quintus, which concerns the baptism of heretics, Cyprian says the following with reference to the decree of Agrippinus and the others:

> “Agrippinus, a man of blessed memory, together with the rest of his fellow bishops who at that time governed the Church of the Lord in the province of Africa and Numidia, likewise decreed this and confirmed it after the balanced examination of their common deliberation.”

P. 127, Benedictine edition. **ROUTH.**

**“We unite in equal agreement.”** Perhaps either *conjuncti* (“united”) should be read in place of *conjungimus* (“we unite”), for the sentence limps; or, if a full stop is placed after the words “and observed by us,” *conjungimur* (“we are united”) should be restored. **ROUTH.**

**“Outside the Church.”** An old translation in the more recent Victorinus codex reads: “that is, outside the form of the Church.” Nevertheless, a person is baptized when baptized by a Jew, a gentile, or a heretic, provided that the latter baptizes according to the form of the Church. This is taken from the chapter *A Certain Jew* in Gratian, distinction 4, *On Consecration*, where Pope Nicholas I, replying to the questions of the Bulgarians, says that baptism is valid even if conferred by one who was not known to be a Christian, provided it was conferred in the name of the Holy Trinity or merely in the name of Christ.

Gregory III, on the other hand, writing to Archbishop Boniface, commands that those known to have been baptized by pagans should be baptized anew. That constitution is recorded in book VII of the *Capitularies*, chapter 101, and in Gratian, chapter *Those Baptized by Pagans*, under the same distinction. See also the bull of Eugene IV in Odoricus Raynaldus, year 1439, §15. See Gerhoh of Reichersberg, *Treatise against the Simoniacs*, chapter 22, and Alger the Scholastic of Liège, *On Mercy and Justice*, chapter 52. **BAL.**

**“One baptism.”** Not only in the sense that it must not be repeated, but because it proceeds from the Church, which cannot subsist unless it is one. **FELL.**—It is certain that at that time there was a major controversy between the bishops of the Roman and Carthaginian churches over whether heretics coming to the Church ought to be rebaptized. The beginnings of this controversy are commonly assigned to the pontificate of Pope Stephen. But Rufinus, book VII, chapter 2, writes that it began under the pontificate of Cornelius. Baronius contends that this is false, but certain learned men have thought that Baronius’s opinion was not correct. Certainly the authority of Rufinus, an ancient and learned writer, ought not to be rejected without strong evidence.

It may, moreover, be confirmed by the authority of Cornelius’s letter to Cyprian, which I copied from two ancient manuscripts, one in the library of the monastery of St. Remigius at Rheims, the other in the library of the most illustrious and learned Jean Bohier, *président à mortier* in the Parliament of Burgundy. It was printed above, p. 167. I have not yet been able to discover where Raphael of Volterra found that Cornelius yielded to Cyprian.

Furthermore, it may be noted here that the Armenians, as Guy of Perpignan relates, said that true baptism existed only in the church of Greater Armenia and not in other churches; for that reason they rebaptized those who came to them. **BALUZIUS.**—I have shown elsewhere, at the end of the *Fragments of Cornelius*, p. 65, that this letter of Cornelius to Cyprian, first published by Baluzius, is not authentic but must be rejected altogether. **ROUTH.**

**“Broken cisterns.”** Greek: *Λάκκους συντετριμμένους* (“shattered cisterns”). The Vulgate has “ruined cisterns,” that is, cisterns full of cracks and leaking in every direction. Pacianus, Letter III:

> “Not content with an unconsecrated seat, he fell in love with the broken cistern of an adulterous spring.”

Jerome, *Against the Luciferians*:

> “Blessed Cyprian also attempted to flee from broken cisterns and not to drink from alien water; and therefore, rejecting the baptism of heretics, he addressed an African synod on this matter to Stephen, then bishop of the city of Rome, who was the twenty-sixth after blessed Peter. But his attempt was in vain.”

**RIGALT.**

**“To hold water.”** The Septuagint had said, *ὕδωρ συνέχειν* (“to contain water”). In Balsamon and Zonaras the reading is *σύσχειν*. In Tertullian:

> “They dug for themselves broken cisterns that could not contain water.”

**RIGALT.**

**“From alien water.”** These words are sought in vain anywhere except in the Greek copies. **FELL.**—They are an addition of the Septuagint at the end of the ninth chapter of Proverbs. Although in the margin of the Oxford edition another, somewhat similar passage was marked at Proverbs 6:24—more correctly 5:15—the most learned editor appears afterward to have judged the passage differently, since he supplied no scriptural reference for these same words in Vote V of Council VII, which follows shortly.

Meanwhile, Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata*, book I, chapter 19, placed before the preceding words in Proverbs, *Οὔτε γὰρ διαβήσῃ ὕδωρ ἀλλότριον* (“For you shall not cross over alien water”), the explanation:

> *τὸ βάπτισμα τὸ αἱρετικὸν οὐκ οἰκεῖον καὶ γνήσιον λογιζομένη*

> “regarding heretical baptism as neither one’s own nor genuine.”

Here note well Clement’s opinion concerning heretical baptism, since he wrote in Egypt at the end of the second century. **ROUTH.**

**“The water must be cleansed and sanctified.”** These are liturgical formulas by which the elements of the sacraments are set apart for the uses of the divine mysteries. From this and other evidence they appear not to be as recent as the innovators strive to persuade themselves and others. **FELL.**

### I

When we were together in council, most beloved brothers, [Col. 1037A] we read the letter that you sent to us [Note: [Col. 1037A] “Which you sent,” Bod. 1, Lam., Thu., Foss., Corb., Vict.] concerning those who appear to have been baptized among heretics and schismatics, and whether, when they come to the Catholic Church, which is one and true, they ought to be baptized.

Although you yourselves there maintain the truth and firmness of the catholic rule, nevertheless, since in our common love you thought that we ought to be consulted, we set forth an opinion [Col. 1038A] that is not new, but was established long ago by our predecessors and has been observed by us; and we unite it with you in equal agreement [Note: [Col. 1038A] “In equal confession,” Corb.] (see note). We judge, namely, and hold as certain that no one can be baptized outside, beyond the Church, since one baptism has been established in the holy Church, and since it is written, the Lord saying (Jer. 2:13):

> “They have forsaken me, [Col. 1039A] the fountain of living water [Note: [Col. 1039B] “Of living water freely,” Bod. 1, Foss., Vict., Corb.], and have dug for themselves broken cisterns that cannot hold water.”

And again divine Scripture admonishes and says (Prov. 9:18, according to the Septuagint):

> “Keep away from alien water, and do not drink from the fountain of alien water.”  
> [Note: [Col. 1039B] “From an alien fountain,” Lam., Ebor., NC. 1.]

The water, therefore, must first be cleansed and sanctified by the priest, so that by his baptism it may wash away the sins of the person being baptized, because through the prophet Ezekiel the Lord says (Ezek. 36:25–26):

> “And I shall sprinkle clean water upon you, and you shall be cleansed from all your impurities; and I shall cleanse you from all your idols, and I shall give you [Note: [Col. 1040B] “I shall give within you,” Bod. 1, Thu., Foss., Vict., Mich.] a new heart, and I shall give a new spirit within you.”

But how can one cleanse and sanctify the water when he is himself unclean and the Holy Spirit is not with him, since the Lord says in Numbers (Num. 19:22):

> “And [Col. 1039B] whatever the unclean person touches shall be unclean”?

[Col. 1040A] Or how can one who baptizes give another the remission of sins when he himself cannot lay aside his own sins outside the Church?

---

### II.—“But the very question.”

“When we are immersed,” says [Col. 1040B] Tertullian, “we make, under the hand of the presiding minister, a solemn declaration in response to something more extensive than the Lord specified in the Gospel.” **RIGALT.**

**“The remission of sins through the holy Church.”** Although the Apostles’ Creed prevailed in all the churches, in almost every individual church it varied to some extent, as Rufinus observed long ago. From Cyprian’s words it seems sufficiently clear that the African church formulated these articles as follows:

> “The very question asked in baptism,” he says, “is a witness to the truth. For when we say: ‘Do you believe in eternal life and remission?’” etc.

It is clear that this was the question asked in baptism, and that these were the very words in which the priest led the questioning and which the catechumen repeated in his response. The same words occur in the Letter to Magnus, in a somewhat altered order:

> “Do you believe in the remission of sins and eternal life through the holy Church?”

Certainly the article concerning the communion of saints gained acceptance later in the Western Church. It was not found in the creed of Aquileia in Rufinus’s time; St. Augustine does not acknowledge it in his book *On Faith and the Creed*; nor does it appear in the formula of faith handed down by Maximus of Turin or in that expounded by Chrysologus. It likewise does not occur in the old manuscript of King Æthelstan in the Cotton Library, where the Creed appears in Greek at the end of the Psalter; nor in the Bodleian codex of the Acts of the Apostles, where the Creed is written in Greek in Saxon letters and is known to have been copied a thousand years ago. Indeed, it was not acknowledged by the Greeks in the time of Eusebius, Epiphanius, Cyril of Jerusalem, or the Council of Ephesus.

The article concerning eternal life is itself absent from the copies mentioned above, for their conclusion of the Creed reads:

> *ἁγίαν Ἐκκλησίαν, ἄφεσιν ἁμαρτιῶν, σαρκὸς ἀνάστασιν. ἀμήν.*

> “The holy Church, the remission of sins, the resurrection of the flesh. Amen.”

**FELL.**

**“Can baptize.”** We added these two words on the authority of four ancient copies, one of which is the Corbie manuscript, in which this letter occurs twice. **BALUZIUS.**—The Greek translation of the letter does not acknowledge these words; it has *οἱ αἱρετικῶν συνήγοροι* (“the advocates of the heretics”). **ROUTH.**

**“The grace of Christ.”** The sweetness signified by anointing. “*Christianus*,” says Septimius, “so far as its interpretation is concerned, is derived from anointing. But even when it is wrongly pronounced *Chrestianus*, the name signifies sweetness or kindness.” **RIGALT.**

**“Moreover, the Eucharist is that from which the baptized are anointed with oil sanctified upon the altar.”**—The Oxford editor reads, “oil sanctified upon the altar,” and says:

> “We consider the reading published by Manutius to be the true one: ‘Moreover, the Eucharist is that from which the baptized are anointed, oil sanctified upon the altar.’”

The copies support this. For the Corbie manuscript reads:

> “Moreover, the Eucharist is that from which the baptized are anointed with oil sanctified upon the altar.”

The Verona and Du Tillet manuscripts read as in the Manutius edition. The Greeks in Zonaras and Balsamon wrongly have *ἁγιάζεσθαι ἔλαιον εἰς εὐχαριστίαν* (“oil is sanctified for the Eucharist”). But Cyprian had said very clearly that the Eucharist is oil sanctified upon the altar—oil, that is, blessed through *ἔντευξις*, “intercession,” that is, through an appeal or invocation of the divine power by praises and thanksgivings poured forth and addressed to God.

Thus Matthew, Mark, and John called the Eucharist a *eulogia*, “blessing,” not only in the institution of the Lord’s Supper but also in the multiplication of the loaves. This is easily discovered by carefully comparing the words of the Evangelists. **RIGALTIUS.**

It is further worth observing that Erasmus and Pamelius, considering that in the conclusion of this passage Cyprian speaks distinctly of oil and the Eucharist, as does Augustine when answering his arguments in *On Baptism against the Donatists*, book V, chapter 20—and considering that nothing ought to appear in a conclusion which was not in the premises—substituted *et* (“and”) for *est* (“is”) after “are anointed,” and *sanctificatur* (“is sanctified”) for *sanctificatum* (“sanctified”). This was not unreasonable, if editors possessed the right to amend whatever displeased them, or if “oil and Eucharist” in the conclusion of the argument were to be understood as disparate things.

Albaspinaeus, however, in *On the Eucharist*, book I, chapter 14, accuses them of audacity and contends that the old reading must be retained. In it he thought he had discovered a great mystery: namely, that the oil with which the baptized were anointed was customarily consecrated in the presence of the Eucharist.

But there is no need of such mysteries. The true reason why Cyprian denies that the Eucharist can be celebrated and spiritual anointing conferred among heretics is that he judged that among heretics, in the Eucharist just as in the oil and in baptism, one is not spiritually anointed with the blood of Christ, and that the Eucharist brings to perfection and completes what baptism and oil had begun in this respect. Understood in this way, who will be surprised that, in discussing spiritual anointing, he introduces the mystery of the Eucharist? The ancients certainly called participation in Christ’s blood in the Eucharist an anointing.

Clement of Alexandria, *Paedagogus*, book II, chapter 2:

> *Διττὸν τὸ αἷμα τοῦ Κυρίου· τὸ μὲν γάρ ἐστιν αὐτοῦ σαρκικόν, ᾧ τῆς φθορᾶς λελυτρώμεθα· τὸ δὲ πνευματικόν, τουτέστιν ᾧ κεχρίσμεθα.*

> “The blood of the Lord is twofold. One is his fleshly blood, by which we have been redeemed from corruption; the other is spiritual, that is, the blood with which we have been anointed.”

Gregory Nazianzen, Oration 41:

> *μυστήριον ἔχρισέ με*

> “The mystery anointed me.”

Chrysostom, on the Epistle to the Hebrews, Homily XVII:

> *μύρῳ χρίεις, καὶ πάλιν δυσωδίας πληροῖς*

> “You anoint with perfume, and then fill with foul odor again.”

In truth, just as the Lord testifies (Matt. 23:19) that the altar sanctifies the gift placed upon it, so those who possess neither altar nor Eucharist cannot possess spiritual anointing either. The advocates of the opposing side seem indeed to have admitted the force of this argument, since they decreed that those baptized among heretics should be received by the laying on of hands.

St. Augustine, *On the Trinity*, book XV, chapter 26, refers all this to spiritual anointing:

> “It is written more explicitly concerning him, namely Christ, in Acts 10:38: ‘Because God anointed him with the Holy Spirit.’ Certainly not with visible oil, but with the gift of grace signified by the visible ointment with which the Church anoints the baptized.”

**FELL.**

In correcting this passage we followed principally the reading of the Corbie manuscript. Six manuscripts and the old editions have “oil sanctified upon the altar.” Manutius printed:

> “Moreover, the Eucharist is that from which the baptized are anointed, oil sanctified upon the altar.”

Jerome, in the *Dialogue against the Luciferians*, says that baptism must not be administered without the Eucharist. This practice continued for a long time in the Church of God, as we demonstrated in the notes on Regino, pp. 551 and 657, and in the notes on the *Capitularies*, p. 1236.

At the Hussite Council of Prague, recorded by Cochlaeus in book V of the *History of the Hussites*, it was decreed that communion in the Eucharist should be given to infants. That is all. Yet Odoricus Raynaldus, year 1421, §12, writes that they enacted this “concerning infants to be washed in baptism.” This is not true, for Raynaldus’s addition does not appear in the synod’s decree.

Aeneas Sylvius, in his *Dialogue against the Bohemians and Taborites*, published among his letters, says:

> “This was the ancient madness of the Armenians: as soon as children came into the light, they immediately baptized them and immediately refreshed them with the sacrament of the altar. You too are said to do this, calling the senseless and infants to partake of the Eucharist.”

In the Armenians’ answers to the Latins’ objections, sent to Pope Benedict XII in 1342, it is written that, after baptizing a child, they communicate the baptized child in this way:

> “They touch the child’s lips with the dry body of Christ and put it back; and if the priest is celebrating and the child is baptized at that time, the priest properly dips his finger very slightly into the blood and with it touches the child’s lips.”

**BALUZ.**

Although both the ten manuscripts and the old printed editions cited as witnesses in the Oxford edition supported the reading “oil sanctified upon the altar,” I confess that I was wrong to restore this wording. Erasmus’s reading seems preferable to the others:

> “The Eucharist, and the oil with which the baptized are anointed, is sanctified upon the altar.”

This is clear and agrees especially well with the writer’s arguments and purpose: to prove that chrism cannot exist among heretics—neither the sign itself nor the reality signified. Hardouin, in fact, affirms in his notes on the *Councils*, whose editions contain this reading, that it is likewise furnished by the manuscript of his Society and by other manuscripts of the highest quality.

This had perhaps also escaped the distinguished Maran, who, when Baluzius supplied from the Corbie manuscript the words “with oil sanctified upon the altar,” wrote as follows in the Preface to the Benedictine edition of Cyprian, p. XIX:

> “Baluzius most excellently corrected this passage in place of what was read in the old editions, ‘oil sanctified upon the altar,’ or in Erasmus and Pamelius by a rather free conjecture, ‘the Eucharist, and the oil with which the baptized are anointed, is sanctified upon the altar.’ Cyprian is not saying what Rigaltius and Fell think he said metaphorically—that the Eucharist is the oil with which they are anointed—but rather that the Eucharist is that from which the oil with which the baptized are anointed derives its sanctification, because the oil was sanctified upon the altar amid the very prayers of the sacrifice.”

**ROUTH.** The Leipzig editor restored Erasmus’s reading. **EDITORS.**

**“The created substance of oil.”** Irenaeus speaks of “the created substance of the eucharistic bread and cup,” book IV, chapter 32; again in book V, chapter 2. **MARSHALL.**

**“May not anoint.”** Four ancient books read, “may not fatten.” Pamelius says that St. Augustine, who frequently cites this passage, sometimes writes “anoint” and sometimes “fatten.” Thus even in Augustine’s age there were two readings of this passage. **BALUZIUS.** The common reading is “may not fatten.” **ROUTH.**

### II

But the very question asked in baptism is a witness to the truth. For when we say, “Do you believe in eternal life and the remission of sins through the holy Church?” we understand that remission of sins is given only in the Church, while among heretics, where the Church does not exist, sins cannot be forgiven.

Accordingly, those who assert that heretics can baptize must either alter the question or vindicate its truth—unless they also grant the Church to those whom they contend possess baptism. It is also necessary that the person who has been baptized be anointed, so that, having received the chrism—that is, the anointing—he may be one of God’s anointed and may possess within himself the grace of Christ.

Moreover, the Eucharist [Col. 1040B] is that from which the baptized are anointed with oil sanctified upon the altar [Col. 1041A]. [Note: [Col. 1041A] “Oil … sanctified,” Bod. 1, Lam., Ebor., NC. 1, 2, Lin., Thu., Foss., Vict., Mich., Corb., old printed editions, Rem., Manut., Moret., Oxford, Routh. “And that from which,” Erasmus, Pamelius, Rigaltius, Leipzig. [Col. 1042A] “Is sanctified,” Erasmus, Pamelius, Rigaltius.] But one who possessed neither an altar nor the Church could not sanctify the created substance of oil. Hence spiritual anointing cannot exist among heretics either, since it is established that oil cannot be sanctified and the Eucharist cannot be celebrated among them at all.

We ought also to know and remember [Col. 1042A] that it is written (Ps. 140:6):

> “Let not the oil of a sinner anoint my head.”

The Holy Spirit gave this warning beforehand in the Psalms [Note: [Col. 1042A] “Admonished,” Lam., Ebor., NC. 1.], lest anyone who departs from the proper course and strays from the way of truth should be anointed among heretics [Note: [Col. 1042A] “Heretics of Christ,” Lam.] and Christ’s adversaries. [Col. 1043A]

And what prayer can a sacrilegious and sinful priest offer for one who has been baptized [Note: [Col. 1043C] “For one baptized,” Lam., Ebor., NC. 1.], when it is written (John 9:31):

> “God does not hear a sinner; but if anyone worships him [Note: [Col. 1043C] “Worships God,” Bod. 1.] and does his will, him he hears”?

Who can give what he does not himself possess? Or how can one perform spiritual acts [Note: [Col. 1043C] “Conduct spiritual acts,” Lam., Ebor., Lin., NC. 1.] when he has himself lost the Holy Spirit?

Therefore, the person who comes uninitiated to the Church must be baptized and renewed, so that within the Church he may be sanctified through the holy ones, because it is written (Lev. 19:2; 20:26):

> “Be holy, because I too am holy, says the Lord.”

Thus one who was seduced into error [Note: [Col. 1043C] “In error,” Lam., NC. 1, 2, Lin.] and immersed outside may, in the true and ecclesiastical baptism, lay aside even this very fault: that, as a man coming to God and seeking a priest, he fell through the deceit of error upon a sacrilegious man.

---

### III.—“Upon Peter.”

The Greek version has only:

> *ἐπάνω Πέτρου τοῦ Ἀπόστολου ἀρχῆθεν ἑνότητος τεθεμελιωμένης*

> “upon Peter the Apostle, unity having been founded from the beginning.”

Cyprian himself says in his book *On the Unity of the Church*:

> “Upon one man he builds the Church.”

And shortly afterward:

> “To make unity manifest, by his own authority he arranged that the origin of that same unity should begin from one.”

Pacianus, Letter III:

> “The Lord spoke to Peter—to one man for this reason, that he might establish unity from one.”

He presently commands the same thing to all in common. **RIGALTIUS.**—So read fully twenty-one ancient books and the two cited by Pamelius. The old editions have “rock.” So too the Morel edition and three ancient books. See what was noted above in a similar case on Letter XL, p. 428. **BALUZIUS.**

**“Has stated.”** Perhaps *posuit* (“stated”) should be read. Four manuscripts mentioned in the Oxford edition have *ponit* (“states”). [Col. 1044D] **ROUTH.**

**“Infer and consider.”** The Greek version has *συνιέναι καὶ νοεῖν*, “to understand and perceive.” **FELL.**

**“Reject whatever his adversaries and antichrists do.”** He does not mean that the orthodox should do nothing that heretics do. For in the Letter to Jubaianus, when it was objected that the Novatianists customarily baptized those coming to them, he replies that what the enemies of the Church do is no concern of ours. His purpose is to establish that nothing done by those situated outside the Church is valid or has legal force.

Presently he says, “through all the sacraments of divine grace.” He means not only through the rite of confirmation or the administration of the Eucharist, but also through baptism, which grants entrance into the Church itself. **FELL.**

### III

Furthermore, to approve the baptism of heretics and schismatics is to agree that they have performed a baptism. For one part cannot be void there while another part prevails. If he could baptize, he could also give the Holy Spirit. But if he cannot give the Holy Spirit—because, being situated outside, he is not with the Holy Spirit—then neither can he baptize the person who comes to him, since there is one baptism, one Holy Spirit, and one Church founded by Christ the Lord [Note: [Col. 1043C] “Christ our Lord,” Bod. 1, Lin., Ebor., NC. 1, 2, Thu., Foss., Vict., Corb.] upon Peter [Note: [Col. 1043C] “Upon the rock,” Vict.], with the origin and principle [Note: [Col. 1043D] “From the principle,” Bod. 1.] of unity.

Thus it follows that, since everything among them is void and false, none of the things they have performed ought to be approved by us. For what can be valid and firm before God when it is done by those whom the Lord calls his enemies and adversaries, when he states in his Gospel (Luke 11:23):

> “He who is not with me is against me; and he who [Col. 1043C] does not gather with me scatters”?

And the blessed apostle John also, observing the Lord’s commands and precepts, has stated [Note: [Col. 1044C] “States,” Lam., Ebor., Lin., NC. 1.] in his letter (1 John 2:18–19):

> “You have heard that antichrist is coming. But now many antichrists have arisen. From this we know that it is the last hour. They went out from us, but they were not of us. For if they had been of us, they would surely have remained with us.”

From this we too ought to infer [Note: [Col. 1044C] “We ought to infer,” Ver.] and consider [Col. 1044A] whether those who are the Lord’s adversaries and have been called antichrists can give the grace of Christ.

Therefore, we who are with the Lord, maintain the Lord’s unity, and by his gracious favor administer his priesthood in the Church, ought to repudiate and reject whatever his adversaries and antichrists do, and regard it as profane [Note: [Col. 1044C] “And regard as profane,” Lam., NC. 1, Ebor., Verona.]. To those who [Note: [Col. 1044C] “And if any,” Verona. “And if indeed, rejecting error and depravity,” Corb.] come from error and depravity and acknowledge the true faith of the one Church, we ought to give, through all the sacraments of divine grace, the truth of unity and faith [Note: [Col. 1044C] “And of unity and faith,” Verona, Benevento. Greek: *ἑνότητός τε καὶ πίστεως καὶ ἀληθείας*, “of unity, faith, and truth.”].

We wish you, most beloved brothers, always to fare well.

---

[Col. 1045C]

### SIXTH COUNCIL OF CARTHAGE.—Cyprian

Since, in connection with the correction and elucidation of the works of St. Cyprian upon which I am now engaged, I had undertaken to read the excessively long letter of Jean de Launoy to Jacques Bevilacqua concerning the disagreement between Pope Stephen and Cyprian, I marveled that he could say so much without saying anything. For all the arguments and testimonies he adduces against Stephen are of no weight in this case and possess a certain silliness.

For what relevance to the question of baptism is there in the claims that Cyprian’s reputation was more celebrated than Stephen’s; that Cyprian did not yield to Stephen; that Cyprian convened a council on the question of baptism while Stephen did not; that the churches of East and West did not undertake to defend Stephen’s opinion; and many other matters of this kind that are irrelevant to the case, very many of which are also false? But, as Jerome says in the Letter to Pammachius against John of Jerusalem, no one proves the truth by falsehood.

These assertions could therefore easily be refuted, but they are not worth the effort. Most true, then, is what Optatus says in book [Col. 1045D] V: truth is impeded by partisan zeal. See Facundus, *Against Mocianus*, p. 577 of the first edition. **BALUZIUS.**

# IN THE YEAR OF CHRIST 256, THE THIRD YEAR OF THE PONTIFICATE OF ST. STEPHEN: THE SIXTH COUNCIL OF CARTHAGE UNDER CYPRIAN, FROM THE PROVINCE OF AFRICA AND NUMIDIA, THE SECOND COUNCIL CONCERNING BAPTISM

*(Erasmus II, 1; Pamelius, Rigaltius, Baluzius LXXII; Oxford and Leipzig LXXII; Paris LXXI; Coustant, p. 216; Routh, Reliquiae Sacrae III, pp. 88 and 144.)*

[Col. 1044B]

## PREFACE

He states that he decreed in council that those immersed among heretics or schismatics should be baptized when they returned to the Church; and that those ordained presbyters or deacons in the Church who had lapsed into schism, or those promoted by heretics, should communicate as laymen upon their return—while preserving, nevertheless, the bond of concord with bishops who held a different opinion.

In order that the measures established at the preceding council might be confirmed by a fuller judgment, Cyprian, in this same [Col. 1044C] controversy concerning baptism conferred by heretics, convened in this same year 258 [Note: [Col. 1044D] Elsewhere, 256.] a fuller assembly of bishops and brought seventy-one bishops from Africa and Numidia together at this synod. His purpose was that each should state what he thought concerning the holy and inviolable preservation of the traditions of the elders.

After all the aforesaid bishops had assembled, they confirmed by two additional decrees the same decision defined above in the preceding African councils held concerning this question and the case of Basilides.

The first decree was that those who had been ordained in the Church and had abandoned the faith should, upon returning to the Church, be received only into lay communion.

The second was that baptism conferred by heretics should be regarded not merely as invalid but as nonexistent. Consequently, when such persons returned to the Church and were baptized, they were not rebaptized with a second baptism; rather, baptism was then conferred upon them for the first time, because among heretics they had not truly been baptized but had merely been further defiled by the water of heretics. So Cyprian, Letter 73, *To Jubaianus*. Hence those who believe that he supported Anabaptism are gravely mistaken.

When these measures had been established by the judgment of the aforesaid seventy-one bishops, they were communicated to Stephen of Rome in a letter that we have arranged to append here below from Cyprian. But Stephen, after receiving the synodical letter, rejected this council in his written reply. At the same time he commanded most solemnly that they should not depart even a finger’s breadth from the apostolic tradition of not repeating the baptism of those heretics who had baptized with the same form used by the Church, and that persons baptized by them, if they requested to return to the Church, should be received in no other way than by the laying on of hands alone. These facts are proved from Cyprian’s letter to Pompeius, bishop of Sabrata in Africa. See Baronius, year 258, nos. 27–38 inclusive.

## CYPRIAN AND THE OTHERS, TO THEIR BROTHER STEPHEN: GREETINGS

### I.—“To hold a council.”

Pearson, in the *Cyprianic Annals*, rightly proves, in my opinion, that this council was held in the year 255. **BALUZIUS.**—Pearson shows in the work just mentioned, under the following year, 256, §1, that this council was held before Easter of that year. Cyprian speaks of this same council as follows in Letter 73, *To Jubaianus*:

> “And now too, when we had assembled together, the bishops of both the province of Africa and Numidia, seventy-one in number.”

**ROUTH.**
Completed. Thus twelve old manuscripts. Four others have “discussed” (*tractata*). The old editions and three old manuscripts have “transferred” (*translata*). BALUZIUS.

With your seriousness. This same Stephen will be called by the same Cyprian “proud, ignorant and improvident, inept, obstinate,” in the Epistle to Pompeius. RIGALTIUS.

Fully sanctified. The Colbert manuscript has “plainly” (*plane*), which the Oxford editor also encountered in one of his manuscripts [Col. 1046C]. The reading of the other books is more harmonious. For “fully sanctified” here means what is expressed by “completed” in Epistle LXXIII of the same Cyprian: “so that through our prayer and the laying on of hands they may receive the Holy Spirit and be COMPLETED with the seal of the Lord.” Moreover, it will become clear from our dissertation appended below, nos. 17 and 18, that by the words “if they are born by both sacraments,” Cyprian demands that heretics coming to the Church receive the sacrament of Confirmation together with Baptism. COUSTANT.

By both sacraments. By Baptism and the infusion of the Holy Spirit—that is, as he will say shortly afterward, by water and the Spirit. He repeats this frequently elsewhere. Tertullian, in the book *On the Veiling of Virgins*: “We and they have one faith, one God, the same Christ, the same hope, the same sacraments of washing.” Siricius, in the epistle to Himerius: “On these days alone in the year—that is, Easter and Pentecost—it is fitting that the general sacraments of Baptism be delivered to those coming to the faith.” See Sirmond, chapter five of the second [Col. 1046D] *Antirrheticus*, where he explains this passage of Cyprian. See also vol. II of the *Capitularies*, p. 1236. Furthermore, instead of “both” (*utroque*), five old copies have “each of the two” (*utrumque*). BALUZIUS.—That Cyprian must be understood as referring to Baptism and the laying on of hands after Baptism is sufficiently shown by the fifth vote of the council immediately following, when compared with Canon 17 of the Second Council of Arles. These are the words of the vote: “Some therefore interpret it wrongly for themselves”—the bishop is referring to those same words of John—“when they say that through the laying on of hands they receive the Holy Spirit and are thus received, since it is evident that they ought to be reborn in the Catholic Church by both sacraments.” The canon of the Council of Arles, however, reads as follows: “As for the Bonosians coming from the same error, whom it is evident, like the Arians, to have been baptized in the Trinity, once they have been questioned and have confessed our faith with their whole heart, it is sufficient that they be received into the Church BY CHRISM AND THE LAYING ON OF HANDS.” From this, unless I am mistaken, it is established—as also from the words of Cyprian cited above by Coustant, who meanwhile nowhere, so far as I recall [Col. 1047B], adduced that canon of the Second Council of Arles—that by the words “both sacraments” one must understand neither the water of Baptism and the grace of the Holy Spirit conferred in it, nor Baptism and the laying on of hands for penance, much less Baptism and the Eucharist, but the sacraments of Baptism and Confirmation. Nor do I see Maran explaining this and similar passages differently in his Preface to the *Works of St. Cyprian*, pp. XVII–XVIII, even though he thinks that that Father was not unaware that Stephen and those who sided with him were speaking of the laying on of hands for penance—which was altogether necessary for heretics to receive the Holy Spirit—and not of the sacrament of Confirmation. For it is not inconsistent that Cyprian, seizing an opportunity supplied by his opponents, should have determined that the sacrament of Confirmation must be repeated, although he did not in the least suspect that they were repeating it, but knew that they understood only the laying on of hands for penance, which they considered necessary for conferring the Spirit. Nevertheless, see what I shall note below on the vote of Nemesianus just mentioned, in Council VII, p. 93; and compare what is said shortly below on the eighth vote of the same council. I thought these points especially needed to be mentioned here because the English translator had explained the passage, less correctly, as referring to Baptism and the Eucharist. ROUTH.

Reborn. Four ancient codices have “born anew” (*denuo natus*). This reading does not displease me, since the word “anew” occurs in the third chapter of the Gospel according to John, from which this passage was taken. But I think that Cyprian, who used a different version from our Vulgate, wrote “reborn” (*renatus*). BALUZIUS.—Three manuscripts mentioned in the Oxford edition, as well as the Roman first edition of Cyprian, have “born” (*natus*). ROUTH.

[Col. 1047D] And Spirit. In the Colbert manuscript “Holy” is added here; Pamelius correctly proves that it ought to be absent. The Anonymous author published by Rigaltius at the end of Tertullian’s works appropriately uses the very example from the Acts of the Apostles by which Cyprian now attempts to support his position in order to refute it. For from it he shows that the Holy Spirit could be received without Baptism, just as by other examples from the same Acts he demonstrates that Baptism was conferred without the sacrament of Confirmation. COUSTANT.

To Quintus. Epistle LXXI. BALUZIUS.

To the bishops in Numidia. This is the synodical epistle placed immediately before this one. ROUTH.

Epistle LXX, furthermore, was written in the name of Cyprian, Liberalis, Caldonius, and the others who, gathered in council, had read letters sent by eighteen bishops of Numidia, in which Cyprian and his colleagues were consulted about those who appeared to have been baptized among heretics and schismatics: whether, when they came to the Catholic Church, which is one, they ought to be baptized. The council over which Cyprian presided replied that they were to be baptized. Not long [Col. 1048B] afterward, Quintus, a bishop of Mauretania, consulted the same Cyprian about the same matter and observed that those who did not baptize returning heretics supported their custom by this twofold argument: namely, that they said there was one Baptism and that in this matter they followed ancient custom. Cyprian then sent Quintus the epistle written to the Numidians and added a new one for him. The council, which was held when Cyprian had recently written to Quintus, resolved that both epistles should be sent to Stephen. The Africans certainly desired Stephen to confirm that celebrated decree which they had inserted into the epistle to the Numidians: “He who comes untaught to the Church must be baptized and renewed, so that he may be sanctified within by the saints.” [Col. 1048C] But that pontiff could not approve what he knew with certainty to be contrary to apostolic tradition. Therefore, after assembling a council, he both refuted the letters sent to him and opposed to the decree inserted in them this definition: “If, therefore, anyone comes to us from any heresy whatsoever, let nothing be innovated beyond what has been handed down: let a hand be laid upon him for penance.” From this brief exposition one understands what Stephen means by the words “let nothing be innovated.” For the Africans had said: “He must be baptized and renewed.” Therefore, when Stephen, proclaiming a contrary judgment, says, “let nothing be innovated,” one must supply the words “concerning Baptism”; rather, what has been handed down must be held and observed. From this it is also perceived that the controversy about the Baptism of heretics was first stirred up in Numidia by the decree of Cyprian and his colleagues, and that this decree then furnished the cause and origin of the controversy that blazed so fiercely between Stephen and Cyprian. COUSTANT.]

I. For the settling of certain matters and their refinement [Note: [Col. 1045B] “And from the council,” Bod. 1. “To the council,” Bod. Lam. NC. 1. Ebor.] through examination by common counsel, it was necessary for us, dearest brother, with a number of bishops assembling together, to convene and hold a council. In it, indeed, many matters were brought forward and completed [Note: [Col. 1045B] “Brought forward and discussed,” Lam. Bod. 2. Ebor. NC. 1.]; but it was especially necessary to write to you about the matter, and to confer with your seriousness [Note: [Col. 1046B] “Your reverence,” Lam. Ebor.] and wisdom, which pertains particularly both to episcopal authority and to the unity and dignity of the Catholic Church, proceeding together from the ordering of the divine dispensation: namely, that those who have been dipped outside, beyond the Church [Col. 1046B], and stained among heretics and schismatics by the pollution of profane water, ought, when they come to us and to the Church, which is one, to be baptized, because it is not enough for a hand to be laid upon them so that they may receive the Holy Spirit unless they also receive the Baptism of the Church. For only then can they be fully sanctified [Note: [Col. 1046B] “Plainly sanctified,” Lin.] and be sons of God, if they are born by both sacraments [Col. 1047A], since it is written: “Unless one has been reborn [Note: [Col. 1047B] “Has been born,” Lam. Ebor. NC. 1.] of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John 3:5).

For we find in the Acts of the Apostles also (Acts 10:48) that this was observed by the Apostles and maintained in accordance with the truth of saving faith: when, in the house of Cornelius the centurion, the Holy Spirit descended upon the Gentiles who were present there, aflame with the fervor of faith and believing in the Lord with their whole heart, so that, filled with him, they blessed God in various tongues, nevertheless the blessed apostle Peter, mindful of the divine command and of the Gospel, ordered those same persons, who had already been filled with the Holy Spirit, to be baptized, so that nothing might appear to have been omitted [Col. 1047B], but that in all respects the apostolic teachings might observe the divine command and the law [Note: [Col. 1047B] “By the law of the Gospel,” Lam. Ebor. NC. 1.] [Col. 1048A] of the Gospel.

Moreover, that what the heretics use is not Baptism, and that no one among those who oppose Christ can advance through the grace of Christ, was carefully set forth recently in the epistle written on this matter to our colleague Quintus, who is stationed in Mauretania, and likewise in the letter that our colleagues previously sent to the bishops [Note: [Col. 1048B] “Fellow bishops in Numidia,” Lam. Ebor. Bod. 1, 2, NC. 1, 2, Lin.] presiding in Numidia. I have appended copies of both epistles.

[Note: [Col. 1048C]

II.—Or even if any, etc. The sentence would become clearer if the particle “that” (*ut*) were deleted here and the text read, “even if any presbyters [Col. 1048D] or deacons, whether in the Church,” with the final “who” suppressed. One more recent Colbert manuscript has “or deacons or clerics in the Church”; but numerous passages in this codex, elsewhere plainly corrupt, detract from its authority. Nevertheless, its reading is supported by Innocent I, Epistle XVI to the Macedonians, no. 8, where, concerning those who pass to the Church after having been baptized and ordained by heretics, he says: “It is the law of our Church to grant them only lay communion through the laying on of hands, and not to appoint any of them even to the slightest clerical honor.” He further teaches that those who passed from the Catholic Church to heresy ought to be received in no other way than through penance. Then, in no. 9, he places both among the ancient rules that the Roman Church observes as handed down by the Apostles or apostolic men. Since the appended decree of the African council agrees with these rules, it is unsurprising that Stephen did not contradict it at all. Yet this did not prevail in the Church because the ordination of heretics was regarded as null, but because it was fitting for God’s ministers to be free from reproach and unstained. Accordingly, if some were ever excepted from the general law [Col. 1049C]—for example, the Novatians by Nicene Canon 8, as Innocent acknowledges in the cited epistle, no. 10, and subsequently the Donatists or others—nowhere is it commanded that they be ordained after their return. Indeed, in the *Code of Canons of the African Church*, canon 48, reordinations are prohibited no less than rebaptisms. COUSTANT. Even if the construction “that … them also” is faulty, I nevertheless do not think the text itself should be disturbed. Meanwhile, “if any” (*siqui*) is used for “whoever” (*quique*). ROUTH.

Divine. Three old books have “indivisible” (*individuum*). BALUZIUS.

The arms of ordination and honor. Arms are the instruments of any given thing, says Servius on *Aeneid* II. Here, however, they are insignia or ornaments. Thus Homer also said, ὅπλισθεν δὲ γυναῖκες, “and the women armed themselves,” and the faces of illustrious men were represented upon shields with the breastplate shown in relief. “The arms of light,” ὅπλα φωτός, at Romans 13:12. Suidas: “ὅπλα φωτός, ὁ ἀπόστολος· αἱ τῶν ἀρετῶν ἐργασίαι”—“‘Arms of light,’ says the Apostle: the exercise of the virtues.” RIGALTIUS.—But compare what you have at line 6 of the following page: “What greater crime can there be … than to have fought with rage?” ROUTH.

[Col. 1049D] In the household of faith. In the Church of God, which is the mother of the faithful. Hence also “members of the household of faith,” οἰκεῖοι τῆς πίστεως, at Galatians 6, who belong to the family of faith. RIGALTIUS.—Furthermore, the English translator notes that Cyprian customarily calls the crime of heretics and schismatics “breach of faith” (*perfidia*) because those same men, especially bishops, had betrayed the charge entrusted to them by the Church.

And stood against the Church. Anselm, bishop of Havelberg, imitated these words in volume XIII of D’Achéry’s *Spicilegium*, p. 202. BALUZIUS.]

II. We further state and add, dearest brother, by common consent and authority, that even if there are any presbyters or deacons who were formerly ordained in the Catholic Church [Col. 1048B] and afterward, becoming faithless and rebellious [Col. 1049A], stood against the Church; or if they were promoted among the heretics by pseudo-bishops and antichrists through profane ordination contrary to Christ’s ordering, and attempted outside the Church to offer false and sacrilegious sacrifices in opposition to the one and divine altar—these too, when they return, are to be received on this condition [Note: [Col. 1049B] “By confession and on the condition,” Lam. Ebor. Bod. 2. NC. 1.]: that they communicate as laymen and consider it sufficient that they are admitted to peace, since they had proved to be enemies of peace. Nor ought those returning to retain among us those arms of ordination and honor with which they rebelled against us.

For the bishops and ministers who serve the altar and sacrifices ought to be whole and unstained, since the Lord God speaks in Leviticus and says: “A man in whom there is a blemish or defect shall not approach to offer gifts to God” (Leviticus 21:21). Likewise, in Exodus he gives the same command [Col. 1049B] and says: “And let the priests who approach the Lord God be sanctified, lest perhaps the Lord God abandon them” (Exodus 19:22); and again: “And when they approach to minister at the altar of the Holy One, they shall not bring guilt upon themselves, lest they die” (Exodus 28:43).

But what greater crime can there be, or what more disfiguring stain, than to have stood against Christ; than to have scattered his Church, which he prepared and founded by his own blood; than, forgetting the peace and love of the Gospel, to have fought with the rage of hostile discord against the united and harmonious [Col. 1050A] people of God? Even if they themselves afterward return to the Church, they nevertheless cannot restore and recall with them those who were led astray by them and, overtaken by death outside, perished beyond the Church without communion and peace. Their souls will be demanded from the hands of these men on the day of judgment, since they proved to be the authors and leaders of their destruction. And therefore it is enough that pardon be granted to such persons when they return; nevertheless, breach of faith ought not to be promoted in the household of faith. For what do we reserve for the good and innocent, who did not withdraw from the Church, if we honor those who withdrew from us and stood against the Church?

[Note: [Col. 1049D]

III.—These matters to your conscience. From these words Jerome observed in his work against the Luciferians that blessed Cyprian did not issue these pronouncements with an anathema against those who refused to follow him. For, Jerome says, Cyprian remained in communion with those who opposed his position; rather, because of Novatus and the many other heresies then arising, he had urged that no one be received by him without condemning his own error. RIGALTIUS.

[Col. 1050C] What they have once imbibed. Epistle to Quintus: “Each person ought not obstinately to contend for what he had once imbibed and held, but, if anything better and more useful emerged, willingly to embrace it.” RIGALTIUS.—These words concern that opinion of the opposing party about the Baptism of heretics; compare also what is set down in the acts of the council immediately following. Furthermore, from the words that shortly follow, the English translator concludes that all bishops except Stephen considered it permissible for the faithful to disagree with one another on that disputed matter, which appeared to pertain more to discipline than to faith. Perhaps, however, the prelates said this about certain Africans, not about foreigners; for Quintus, bishop in Mauretania, had informed Cyprian that some Africans judged the matter differently from Cyprian and his followers, as is evident from Cyprian’s own epistle to the same Quintus. ROUTH.—What they have once imbibed. Cicero, book IV of the *Academic Questions*, chapter 3: “But somehow or other, most people prefer to err and to defend most combatively the opinion with which they have fallen in love, rather than to inquire without obstinacy what is stated with the greatest consistency.” Lactantius, book III, chapter 24: “I do not know what to say about those who, once they have strayed, persist steadfastly in folly and defend vain things with vain arguments, except that I sometimes think they philosophize either for amusement or that, though prudent and knowledgeable, they undertake to defend falsehoods, as if to exercise or display their talents upon evil subjects.” Caelius Calcagninus, in his book *On Free Will*, p. 396: “unless certain ill-starred minds possessed such shamelessness that they did not blush to revive and assert even opinions that had been hissed off and condemned—not indeed from love of truth, but for the sake of displaying their talent and courting the breath of popular favor.” In agreement with these, Origen, in book I *Against Celsus*, says that contentiousness and an obstinate determination to resist even manifest truths is a troublesome thing, arising from shame at abandoning customary opinions with which the soul has already been imbued; and that a person is torn away from no habits with greater difficulty [Col. 1051B] than from those that concern opinions. Claudianus Mamertus, in the prologue to the books *On the State of the Soul*: “A great failing of many within the human race is arrogant ignorance and stubborn obstinacy in defending opinions rashly adopted.” Angelo Poliziano, chapter 9 of the *Miscellanies*, reports that Domizio Calderini was stubborn and unyielding, even against the truth, in defense of an opinion to which he had once adhered. BALUZIUS.]

III. We have brought these matters to your conscience, dearest brother, both for the sake of our common honor and out of sincere affection, believing that the things which are equally religious and true are also pleasing to you because of the truth of your religion [Note: [Col. 1049B] “Because of your religion,” Lam. Ebor. Bod. 2.] [Col. 1050B] and faith. For the rest, we know that some are unwilling to relinquish what they have once imbibed, and do not readily alter their purpose, but, while preserving among colleagues the bond of peace and concord, retain certain practices of their own that have once been adopted among them. In this matter [Note: [Col. 1049B] “In this matter we do not,” Jerome.] neither do we compel anyone or impose a law, since [Note: [Col. 1050B] “Since indeed,” Jerome.] every prelate has, in the administration of the Church, the free judgment of his own will [Note: [Col. 1050B] “Each prelate has for you,” Jerome.] and will render to the Lord an account of his own conduct.
