[Note: [Col. 1050B] “I wish,” several manuscripts.] We wish you, dearest brother, always to fare well.

IN THE YEAR OF CHRIST 256, THE THIRD YEAR OF THE PONTIFICATE OF ST. STEPHEN: THE SEVENTH COUNCIL OF CARTHAGE UNDER CYPRIAN, FROM THE THREE PROVINCES OF AFRICA, BEING THE THIRD COUNCIL CONCERNING BAPTISM.

(Oxford, 158. Baluzius, p. 329. Routh, *Rell. Scr.*, pp. 101, 107, 148, and 174. Leipzig ed., p. 265.)

[Col. 1051A] [Note: [Col. 1051B]

SEVENTH COUNCIL OF CARTHAGE.—When they had assembled together. Erasmus was the first of all to publish the acts of this [Col. 1051C] council with titles of glory—that is, with the designations “confessors” and “martyrs” prefixed to the names of certain bishops. The Greek version does not have these titles, nor does Morel’s edition; it is sufficiently established that they were not written in the acts but were added later by some enthusiast. It is therefore very surprising that they were retained in the edition of the Reverend Father Hardouin. Saint Augustine, in book VI of *On Baptism against the Donatists*, responded to the arguments that the bishops assembled at this council advanced in support of their opinion concerning the Baptism of heretics. Humbert, bishop of Silva Candida, had seen this council; in book I *Against the Simoniacs*, chapter IX, he says: “What the glorious martyr and pontiff Cyprian decreed concerning the Baptism of heretics can be clearly learned from his council. For together with his fellow bishops he decreed against it the same things as the aforementioned Apostolic Canons.” For the Apostolic Canons cited by Humbert condemn the Baptism of heretics. See Cabassut’s *Ecclesiastical Survey* [Col. 1051D], p. 7, where he discusses the Canons of the Apostles. BALUZIUS.—Pearson says in his *Cyprianic Annals*: “Although the judgment of so great a synod is not true, and was afterward refuted by St. Augustine on account of the Donatists, this is nevertheless a distinguished monument of venerable antiquity.” At the year 256, § IX. Matthias Dannenmayr, in *Institutions of New Testament Ecclesiastical History*, Period I, chapter IV, § 8, p. 113, says that, since these acts had been preserved for us by Augustine in books VI and VII of *On Baptism against the Donatists*, they were inserted from there into the works of St. Cyprian by their editors. He would more plausibly have said “by Cyprian’s copyists”; for in the Erasmian edition printed at Basel in 1520, it is stated that Erasmus added these acts, together with three epistles of Cyprian, from ancient codices. Indeed, they are found in numerous manuscripts of Cyprian. The ancient collections of councils contain them as well; and, translated from Latin into Greek, they are extant in Zonaras’s *Commentaries on the Canons*, etc., at p. 271 of the Paris edition of 1618. Renaudot, moreover, thought that these very acts had caused the Eastern Jacobites [Col. 1052B] to reject the Baptism of heretics; for when they translated the canons of the ancient councils into Greek—which, Renaudot says, was done “a little after Syria had been occupied by the Muslims”—“they joined these decrees to the rest; and the name of so great a martyr proved a snare to them, since men insufficiently acquainted with ancient history regarded what those eighty-seven bishops had determined about rebaptizing heretics [Col. 1052C] as being of the same standing as the other decrees of the councils.” So much for his remarks. Furthermore, concerning the Venetian edition of Cyprian, which Fell and others call the Speyer edition, but which was printed at Venice by Wendelin of Speyer in 1471, I shall note incidentally that it was arranged according to the form of what was in fact, unless I am mistaken, the first edition, printed at Rome in the same year. The order and number of the folios demonstrate this, while the Venetian edition omitted the epistle to Paul II, Roman Pontiff, prefixed by the bishop of Aleria, who had copied Cyprian in his own hand from an ancient Parisian exemplar. Finally, at the end of the Venetian book stands this colophon: “The reader addresses Wendelin of Speyer, the craftsman who restores to the light the epistles of Blessed Cyprian, 1471.” ROUTH.

Province of Africa. In Pliny, book V, chapter 4, it is the region of Zeugitana, also called Africa in the proper sense: namely, the region which, after Carthage was captured, first came under Roman rule and was reduced to the form of a province, and which lay nearest Rome toward the southwest. FELL.—It is surprising [Col. 1052D] that Tripolis, which was one of the African provinces, was not named at this council, since it is established that Munnulus of Girba, Natalis of Oea, Pompeius of Sabratha, and Droga of Leptis Magna were named in it as present, and these were certainly bishops of the province of Tripolitana—especially since Tripolis is known to have been counted among the provinces of Africa at the Council of Cabarsussi. BALUZIUS.—Fell had advised, as you will see shortly below, that there were seven divisions of Africa with respect to civil administration, but that from the opening of this synod it must be concluded that there were only three ecclesiastical divisions. The division of the provinces was indeed sevenfold, having previously been sixfold; but in those same times Tripolis appears sometimes, in civil terms, to have been included under the province of Africa, while Numidia and Mauretania, which had formerly been under kings, were separately mentioned. ROUTH.

Cyprian said. He cast his own vote last. These words, however, were not offered as a vote, but as a preface and to open the way for the consultation that was to follow. Augustine calls it the “opening discourse” in book II of *On Baptism against the Donatists*. In books VI and VII he transcribed this council word for word, appending refutations to the individual opinions of the bishops. FELL.—With regard to the custom of entering the individual opinions into the acts of a council, Cornelius, bishop of Rome, in the Epistle to Cyprian that I cited above at p. 7, after mentioning the assembly of the presbyterate, at which five bishops were also present, writes: “And so that you might know the inclination of all and the counsel of each individual, it was also resolved that our opinions be brought to your notice; you will read them appended below.” Meanwhile, it is noteworthy that at this extremely ancient African council only bishops cast votes, as is evident from the acts. ROUTH.]

PREFACE

When Pope Stephen had rejected by his reply the statutes concerning the Baptism of heretics enacted at the preceding African council, as we said above, Cyprian did not delay in holding another council at Carthage with a larger number of bishops. Accordingly, after eighty-seven bishops had been summoned from Africa, Numidia, and Mauretania, and had assembled at Carthage on the Kalends of September [September 1] [Col. 1051B] in the year 258, he held this third council on the same question of Baptism. At its opening, after letters written by both sides had been read, he rebuked Stephen without mentioning his name. No more of the acts of this council survive than what has been transferred here [Col. 1052A] from Cyprian and from St. Augustine’s *On Baptism against the Donatists*, book III, chapters 4, 5, and 6, and book VII, chapter 1. Apart from the opinions of the eighty-seven bishops concerning the nullity of Baptism conferred by a heretic, these contain nothing else. Whoever seeks a refutation of those opinions should consult Augustine in the passage cited. It will become clear below that Canon XIX of Nicaea and Canon VIII of Laodicea afford no support to these opinions of the African bishops. Pamelius will supply notes concerning the life, native place, and character of each bishop named below; Baronius also provides more at the year 258, no. 42 and following. SEVERINUS BINIUS.

THE OPINIONS OF THE EIGHTY-SEVEN BISHOPS CONCERNING THE BAPTISM OF HERETICS

When a great many bishops from the provinces of Africa, Numidia, and Mauretania had assembled together at Carthage on the Kalends of September [September 1], together with presbyters and deacons [Col. 1052B], with a very large portion of the people also present; and when the letter written by Jubaianus to Cyprian had been read, as well as Cyprian’s reply to Jubaianus concerning the baptizing of heretics and what the same Jubaianus subsequently wrote back to Cyprian, Cyprian said:

“You have heard, most beloved colleagues, what Jubaianus, our fellow bishop, wrote to me [Col. 1053A]—

[Note: [Col. 1053B]

Acknowledged. So far as I know, this word, “acknowledged” (*confessus*), rests solely upon the authority of the Baluzius edition, where it was admitted without notice. The Greek version of the Acts has only: ἀλλὰ καὶ τῇ ἐπιγνώσει τῆς ἀληθείας χάριν ὡμολόγησεν, “but also acknowledged gratitude for the knowledge of the truth.” More significant, however, is the fact that there are approximately nine other passages in this council which Baluzius altered without, contrary to his custom [Col. 1053C], giving any reason. Since that most learned man had the assistance of nearly thirty written codices in editing his Cyprian, I considered it improper to eliminate readings otherwise good when, in the absence of the witnesses, it was impossible to judge their basis prudently. I therefore contented myself merely with reporting them. But there are, besides, a few other readings likewise introduced silently by Baluzius—for the Preface shows that the Cyprianic text had been printed before his death—which, since they appeared not equally good, I thought should be omitted from the text after giving an account of them. Compare above, p. 27; but there I said that the whole text of Cyprian had not been prepared by Baluzius, whereas I would have put it better if I had said that it was sometimes altered by the Benedictine editors after Baluzius’s death. They themselves acknowledge having done this in the celebrated passage of the book *On the Unity of the Church*; but extraneous considerations impelled them to do it there. ROUTH.

Or removing anyone from the right of communion. Stephen, the Roman prelate, had done this, at least temporarily [Col. 1053D]; hence he deservedly heard these words spoken by Firmilian of Cappadocia: “How many quarrels and dissensions you have prepared throughout the Churches of the whole world! And how great a sin you have accumulated for yourself by cutting yourself off from so many flocks! For you have cut off yourself. Do not deceive yourself. For he is truly the schismatic who has made himself an apostate from the communion of ecclesiastical unity. For while you think that all can be excluded from communion by you, you alone have excluded yourself from communion with all.” P. 150 of the Benedictine edition of Cyprian, near the end of the epistle. Pearson shows in his *Annals*, at the year 256, §§ 8–11, that Cyprian received this letter after the council had been held. BALUZIUS.

Constitutes himself bishop of bishops. In an old text: “constitutes of bishops.” (The common text has: “constitutes himself to be bishop of bishops.”) Several bishops who were not Roman popes were also once adorned with that title. Sidonius, book VI, Epistle I, calls Lupus, bishop of Troyes, “father of fathers and bishop of bishops.” Ennodius, book I, poem 15, calls St. Ambrose [Col. 1054B] “bishop of bishops.” Matthew Paris, speaking at the year 1254 about the death of Hugh, bishop of Ely, says: “Just as he shone forth as abbot of abbots in England, so too as bishop of bishops.” Even princes were sometimes granted the honor of being called bishops of bishops. The Arians, as Lucifer of Cagliari testifies in the book *On Dying for the Son of God*, called Emperor Constantius “bishop of bishops.” The Monk of St. Gall, in the book *On Charlemagne’s Care for the Church*, chapter 27, calls him “bishop of bishops.” Edgar, king of England, as may be read in Isaac Casaubon’s letter to King James and in John Selden’s notes on Eadmer, is called “shepherd of shepherds” at the English synod held under Dunstan. It is well known that Constantine the Great is called “the common bishop” in Eusebius. See Cotelerius’s notes on Clement’s epistle to James and Francesco Bernardino Ferrari, book III, chapter 1, *On the Ancient Form of Ecclesiastical Letters*. BALUZIUS.—Fell, whom I have followed here, had deleted the word “to be” (*esse*), which Hardouin, the editor of the Councils, testifies was absent from the manuscript belonging to his Society of Jesus. Nor does this word “to be” appear in Augustine, book II *Against the Donatists*, where Cyprian’s words are first adduced, for all these synodical proceedings are quoted there twice. ROUTH.

The proper judgment of his own freedom and authority. That is, as Marshall says—although he had argued at greater length against the power of any bishop within another’s jurisdiction—in matters pertaining to ecclesiastical discipline concerning which nothing had previously been decreed in any synod. Nevertheless, I suspect that even after a synod had been completed, some freedom in these matters too was left to the judgment of each bishop. Thus, in the Epistle to Antonianus, p. 72, Cyprian wrote: “Indeed, among our predecessors, certain bishops here in our province did not think that peace should be granted to adulterers and entirely closed the opportunity for penance against them. Nevertheless, they did not withdraw from the college of their fellow bishops or rupture the unity of the Catholic Church by the obstinacy of their severity or censure, so that, because peace was granted to adulterers among others, one who did not grant it would be separated from the Church. While the bond of concord remains and the indivisible sacrament of the Catholic Church perseveres, each bishop orders and directs his own conduct and will render to the Lord an account of his purpose.” Compare, moreover, the excellent letter of Peter Gunning, bishop of Ely, to Sheldon, archbishop of Canterbury, concerning these words of Cyprian at this council and other similar passages, which that most learned man maintains pertain only to bishops of another jurisdiction. It was published in the *Literary Library*, no. XI, attributed to the distinguished Jebb and Wasse. Consistent with this is St. Augustine’s interpretation of Cyprian’s words: “Certainly in those questions which have not yet been examined with perfectly lucid insight,” book III of *On Baptism*, chapter 3, until, as Augustine had said elsewhere, “by a plenary council of the whole world, what was most beneficially held might be confirmed after all doubts had been removed.” ROUTH.

Caecilius of Bilta. Ceillier judges this to be the same Caecilius to whom Cyprian sends his treatise *On the Lord’s Supper*, in *General History of Sacred and Ecclesiastical Authors*, vol. III, chapter 31, § 7, p. 570. ROUTH.]

—when he consulted our modest ability concerning the illicit and profane Baptism of heretics; and you have heard what I wrote back to him, namely, expressing the judgment that we have reached once, twice, and often: that heretics coming to the Church ought to be baptized and sanctified with the Church’s Baptism. Another letter of Jubaianus was likewise read to you, in which, replying to our epistle in accordance with his sincere and religious devotion, he not only agreed but also gave thanks, acknowledging that he had been instructed.

“It remains for each of us to state what we think about this very matter, judging no one and removing no one from the right of communion if he holds a different opinion. [Col. 1054A] For none of us constitutes himself bishop of bishops or, by tyrannical terror, drives his colleagues to the necessity of obedience, since every bishop, in accordance with the allowance of his freedom and authority, possesses his own proper judgment, and can no more be judged by another than he himself can judge another. But let us all await the judgment of our Lord Jesus Christ, who alone and by himself has the power both to appoint us to the governance of his Church and to judge our conduct.”

Caecilius of Bilta said: I know of only one Baptism, in the Church, and none outside the Church. Here there will be [Col. 1055A] [Note: [Col. 1055B]

*Exorcizat* [“he exorcizes”]. In the Verona and Fox manuscripts, *exorcidiat*, [Col. 1055C] which arose from faulty pronunciation, *cizat* being pronounced like *cidjat*, whence others have *cidiat*. RIGALTIUS.—Similarly, in Commodian’s *Instructions*, number 37, at p. 230 of Davies’s edition, the title is *Qui judaeidiant fanatici* [“Fanatics who Judaize”], with *judaeidiant* for *judaizant*; there this passage of Cyprian is compared with Commodian. ROUTH.

*Sacramentum interrogat* [“he asks the sacramental questions”]. The word *sacrilegus* [“sacrilegious”] is added in Baluzius’s edition, perhaps from his manuscripts; nevertheless, unless I am mistaken, the word is absent from all published editions, from the Greek translation, and from Augustine. I deleted it, since the repetition of the word immediately afterward, in *ponit altare sacrilegus* [“a sacrilegious man sets up an altar”], certainly did not please me. I did, however, judge that what Baluzius placed in the text shortly before should be retained: *geruntur* [“are carried on”] in place of the old reading *aguntur* [“are done”], and, presently, at the end of this vote, *Domino* [“by the Lord”] in place of *Deo* [“by God”]. ROUTH.

*Primus of Misgirpa.* A city of Zeugitana. Augustine has “Primus Felix of Misgirpa,” and repeatedly designates and repeats that name. But since it is certain that several men named Felix follow here, and since it is customary to distinguish bishops bearing the same name by adding some identifying designation to the others, [Col. 1055D] there is no slight reason to suspect that the man who gave his opinion here was named Felix, and that because he had spoken before the others he was called “the first,” to distinguish him from Felix of Bagai, another Felix of Uthina, and those of Marazana, Buslacenae, and Gurgites. Thus, by a fairly easy slip, the word *primi*, which indicated only a number, passed into a proper name once the true name had been omitted as though superfluous. The Conference of Carthage and Victor of Vita, among others, mention a bishop of this city. Furthermore, it should be noted that in Africa primates were customarily ranked not according to the resources or prerogatives of their cities, but according to the date of their ordination—to use the words of Leo IX—and were therefore called “elders.” Moreover, when votes were cast, it was the established custom for those first promoted to the episcopate to state their opinions before the others. I therefore think that those who lead the order here were the primates of the provinces. There were indeed seven divisions of Africa in respect of civil government; but from the opening of this synod it may be understood that there were only three ecclesiastical divisions. FELL.—See above, p. 151. Pamelius had noted earlier, [Col. 1056B] “With the manuscript and Manutius, I omitted *Felix*, which was inserted both in the printed editions and in St. Augustine, because Bishop Primus wrote Letter LXVIII above in volume one together with the others.” This letter is that of the council numbered IV above. [Col. 1056C] The city is written *Migirpa* in the editions of Erasmus and Manutius, in Augustine, and in the published councils—and more correctly, for Migirpa, which is mentioned both in the *Notitia* and in the Conference of Carthage, was situated in the proconsular province. See Dupin’s *Sacred Geography of Africa*, prefixed to St. Optatus, p. 32, although Hardouin notes that his manuscript reads *Miscirpa*. ROUTH.

*Polycarpus of Hadrumetum.* This is the man mentioned in Letter XLVI according to Pamelius, no. 45, and perhaps in Letter LXXXVI according to Pamelius, no. 68. FELL.

*Testimonium reddere* [“to bear witness”]. The common reading is *sibi testimonium reddere* [“to bear witness to itself”], which I changed on the authority of the Erasmian edition, Augustine, the Greek translator, and the councils. ROUTH.

*Inter laicos recipi* [“to be received among the laity”]. Thus Cyprian in the letter to Antonianus: “Trophimus was nevertheless admitted in such a way that he should communicate as a layman.” RIGALTIUS.—Add what was said above in the letter of the Council of Carthage IV, p. 82, and the note, p. 17. ROUTH.

*Falsi christi* [“false Christs”]. “False Christians.” We restored this from the authority of the ancient books. The words of Secundianus of Carpis, p. 333 of the acts [Col. 1056D] of the council, confirm this restoration: “If they are not Christians, how do they make Christians?” Yet the reading “false Christs” is not displeasing. BALUZIUS.—Pamelius likewise had mentioned four manuscripts in which “false Christians” was read. But I restored the other expression, both because it was taken from Matthew 24:24 and Mark 13:22, and because Firmilian employs it in his celebrated letter: “And yet,” he says, “Stephen is not ashamed to call Cyprian a false Christ, a false apostle, and a deceitful worker.” ROUTH.

*Qui fidens est in falsis*, etc. [“He who trusts in falsehoods,” etc.]. All these words, taken from the ninth chapter of Proverbs according to the Septuagint, are rejected by the Hebrew copies and the Vulgate translation. ROUTH.

*Extraneo* [“foreign”]. Although the alternative reading *alieno* [“another’s”] is good, I was compelled to change it because of the authority of the ancient copies; for I found *extraneo* written in seventeen of our books and in two English ones. Indeed, the Münster manuscript, which reads *externo* [“external”], proves that this change is legitimate. [Col. 1057C] Below, in the statement of Sedatus of Tuburbo, p. 332, the Grenoble manuscript has *extraneus* [“foreign”] in place of *alienus* [“alien”]. BALUZIUS.—Augustine’s refutation, which has already been mentioned frequently, also recognizes the word *extraneo*, although in the vote itself the other word is found in that same Father. Shortly afterward Baluzius printed *aquas* [“waters”] for *aquam* [“water”], which is the reading of the others. ROUTH.]

one where there is true hope and certain faith. For thus it is written: “One faith, one hope, one Baptism” (Eph. 4:5)—not among the heretics, where there is no hope and faith is false; where everything is carried on through falsehood; where a demoniac exorcizes; where one whose mouth and words emit a canker asks the sacramental questions; where an unbeliever gives faith, a criminal grants forgiveness of sins, and an antichrist immerses in the name of Christ; where one cursed by God blesses, a dead man promises life, a man without peace gives peace, a blasphemer invokes God, a profane man administers the priesthood, and a sacrilegious man sets up an altar. To all these things this evil also is added: that the prelates of the devil dare to celebrate the Eucharist—or else that those who support them say that all these allegations about the heretics are false. See what things the Church is compelled to consent to, and how she is forced to enter into communion [Col. 1055B] with people who lack Baptism and the forgiveness of sins. We must flee and avoid this, brothers, separate ourselves from so great a crime, and hold to the one Baptism granted by the Lord to the Church alone.

Primus of Misgirpa said: I judge that every person coming from heresy must be baptized. For there he thinks in vain that he has been baptized, since there is no Baptism except the one true Baptism in the Church; because there is also one God, one faith, and one Church, in which stand one Baptism, holiness, and the other things. For the things performed outside [Col. 1056A] have no saving effect.

Polycarpus of Hadrumetum said: Those who approve the Baptism of heretics nullify our own.

Novatus of Thamugadi said: Although we know that all the Scriptures bear witness concerning saving Baptism, we must nevertheless express our faith: heretics and schismatics who come to the Church and appear to have been falsely baptized ought to be baptized in the perennial font. Therefore, in accordance with the testimony of the Scriptures and the decree of our colleagues, men of most holy memory, all schismatics and heretics who have been converted to the Church must be baptized; and even those who appeared to have been ordained must be received among the laity.

Nemesianus of Thubunae said: That the Baptism given by heretics and schismatics is not true has been declared everywhere in the [Col. 1056B] Holy Scriptures, since their very leaders are false Christs and false prophets, as the Lord says through Solomon: “He who trusts in falsehoods feeds the winds, and that same man follows flying birds. For he abandons the paths of his vineyard and has strayed from the tracks of his little field. He enters through pathless and arid places and a land destined for thirst, and gathers fruitlessness with his hands” (Prov. 9:12, 18, according to the Septuagint). And again: “Keep yourself from foreign water, and do not drink from a foreign spring, [Col. 1057A] [Note: [Col. 1057C]

*Quia Deus Spiritus*, etc. [“Because God is Spirit,” etc.]. See the book of Dom Pierre Coustant in which the defense of the ancient manuscripts is confirmed, p. 57 (52, 53). BALUZIUS.—Mill likewise discusses in the Appendix to the Notes on the New Testament, p. 31 of the Oxford edition, this Latin addition, “because God is Spirit and is born of God.” Indeed, the clause “and is born of God” is added in the very ancient Latin manuscript of the Gospel held by the Bodleian Library. Fell, moreover, explains “and is born of God” as “and what is born of the Spirit is born of God.” Concerning this interpretation, however, [Col. 1057D] Maran remarks as follows in his Preface to Cyprian, p. 36: “The Oxford editor explains ‘is born of God’ less suitably as ‘what is born of the Spirit is born of God.’ But Nemesianus should then have said, ‘is born of God’ in the neuter. Anyone who pays even moderate attention will see that the meaning of this passage is that what is born of the Spirit is spirit, because the Holy Spirit, since he is God and is born or proceeds from God—for these expressions sometimes have the same meaning—by his supreme power makes those whom he regenerates into spirits.” ROUTH.

*Idololatriae* [“idolatries”]. Baluzius added the word *servitus* [“service”], perhaps from his manuscripts; the Vulgate translation acknowledges it by rendering the expression “the service of idols,” which itself appears to be the origin of the Cyprianic reading. I have therefore omitted the word. ROUTH.

*Lambese.* Λαμαῖσα (*Lamaisa*) or Λαμβαῖσα (*Lambaisa*) in Ptolemy, a city of Numidia, discussed above from Antoninus; moreover, in Letter LIX according to Pamelius, no. 55, Cyprian calls it the “colony of Lambaesis.” FELL.

*Ite, et docete* [“Go and teach”]. All others except Baluzius have “Go, [Col. 1058C] therefore, and teach.” This is also the common reading in the New Testament, for the particle οὖν (*oun*, “therefore”) is added in the printed Greek copies, although very many manuscripts oppose it. Shortly afterward, in votes 10, 29, and 35, where the passage is quoted, “therefore” is absent, as it also is in the author of *On Rebaptism*, at p. 338. ROUTH.

*Domus contrariorum legis* [“The house of those opposed to the law”]. The Septuagint has: οἰκίαι παρανόμων ὀφειλήσουσι καθαρισμόν, “The houses of the lawless will owe purification.” The Hebrew seems to differ from this completely. Nor is it easy to conjecture what the Greek translators had before their eyes, unless perhaps they had mistakenly read “the dwellings of the mocker for expiation.” FELL.

*Primo purgari* [“first to be purified”]. The English translator says: “…through the repentance that must be performed before admission to the Church through Baptism.” But perhaps exorcism is meant, which in votes VIII, XXXI, and [Col. 1058D] XXXVII appears to be commended and imposed upon converts. Furthermore, the seventh canon of the Second Ecumenical Council confirms and establishes the practice of exorcizing, before Baptism, both the heretics named there and pagans. ROUTH.

*Itemque ad Stephanum* [“and likewise to Stephen”]. It is so written in the editions and in almost all the ancient books. These words are absent from the Fuxensis manuscript. That they were rightly omitted there and ought to be deleted may be inferred from the fact that it is certain no mention of any earlier letter of Cyprian to Stephen is made in this synod, as St. Augustine correctly observed in book VI of *On Baptism against the Donatists*, chapter 15, where he also writes that he had not seen that letter of Cyprian to Stephen. Yet this proves that the addition is ancient. See above, p. 502. BALUZIUS.—It is evident there that Baluzius formerly held a different opinion on this matter, for he identifies it as this very letter, which Crescens, bishop of Cirta, says was written by Cyprian to Stephen. He thinks it is no longer extant and was different from Cyprian’s letter to Stephen on the Baptism of heretics, which is numbered LXXII. Pearson, in the *Annals of Cyprian* for the year 256, writes: “Cyprian’s letter to Stephen was also read, a fact which he himself omitted at the beginning of the Acts, but Crescens, bishop of Cirta, noted” (§ 9). ROUTH.]

so that you may live a long time and years of life may also be added to you.” And in the Gospel our Lord Jesus Christ spoke in his divine voice, saying: “Unless one is born again of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John 3:5). This is the Spirit who from the beginning moved over the waters. For neither can the Spirit operate without water, nor water without the Spirit. Certain people therefore interpret matters wrongly for themselves when they say that they receive the Holy Spirit through the laying on of hands and are thus received, since it is manifest that they must be born again by both sacraments in the Catholic Church. For then they will be able to be children of God, as the Apostle says: “Take care to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace: one body and one Spirit, just as you were called in the one hope of your calling; one Lord, one faith, one Baptism, [Col. 1057B] one God” (Eph. 4:3–4). The Catholic Church speaks all these things. And again in the Gospel the Lord says: “What is born of the flesh is flesh, and what is born of the Spirit is spirit, because God is Spirit and is born of God” (John 3:6). Therefore, whatever all heretics and schismatics do is carnal, as the Apostle says: “For manifest are the works of the flesh, which are fornications, impurities, incest, idolatries, sorceries, enmities, strifes, jealousy, anger, divisions, heresies, and things like these; concerning which I foretold to you, as I now foretell, that whoever does such things will not inherit the kingdom of God” (Gal. 5:19–21). Thus the Apostle condemns, along with all evildoers, those who create division—that is, schismatics and heretics. Unless, therefore, they receive saving Baptism in the Catholic Church, which is one, they cannot be saved, but will be condemned with the carnal at the judgment of the Lord Christ.

Januarius of Lambaesis said: In accordance with the authority of the Holy Scriptures, I decree that all heretics must be baptized and only then admitted into the holy Church.

Lucius of Castra Galbae said: Since the Lord said in his Gospel, “You are the salt of the earth; but if the salt has become insipid, with what will it be salted? From that point it will be good for nothing except to be cast outside and trampled by men” (Matt. 5:13); and since, after his resurrection, when sending his Apostles, he commanded them, saying: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me. Go and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name [Col. 1058B] of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28:18–19)—since, therefore, it is manifest that heretics, that is, the enemies of Christ, do not possess the complete confession of the sacrament, and likewise that schismatics cannot be seasoned with spiritual wisdom, because by withdrawing from the Church, which is one, they have themselves become insipid and contrary to it, let it be done as it is written: “The house of those opposed to the law owes purification.” It consequently follows that those who were polluted by being baptized by the adversaries must first be purified and only then baptized.

Crescens of Cirta said: In so great an assembly of most holy fellow priests, the letters of our dearest Cyprian to Jubaianus and likewise to Stephen have been read, [Col. 1059A] [Note: [Col. 1059B]

*Sanctorum testimoniorum* [“of holy testimonies”]. Eight ancient books, including the Séguier manuscript, have *sanctimoniorum* [“of holy precepts”]. Six others have *sanctissimorum* [“of the most holy”], omitting the word *testimoniorum*, which is also absent from Augustine; in its place the Laetian manuscript has *decretorum* [“of decrees”]. See the notes of our Benedictines on book VI of Augustine’s *On Baptism against the Donatists*, chapter 15. See above, p. 407. BALUZIUS.

*Per manus impositionem* [“through the laying on of hands”]. Penitents were customarily admitted to their station of penance through the laying on of hands, and this laying on of hands was repeated rather often. This is indicated in Cyprian’s Letter XV, otherwise numbered 11. Canon XV of the Council of Agde likewise decreed that all must approach the bishop [Col. 1059C] for the sake of penance so that hands might be laid upon them in accordance with the custom received everywhere. Thus Marshall, the English translator. I find at least three kinds of laying on of hands in the acts of this council: one for receiving the Holy Spirit, mentioned in votes V and XXIV and in the letter of the preceding synod; another, the present one, for penance over those who had previously been baptized in the Church and were afterward to be restored through the laying on of hands—that is, while they received absolution—of which vote XXII treats; and finally a third, employed in exorcism, which is named in vote XXXVII and likewise seems to be indicated in VII and XXXI. ROUTH.

The words of the bishop of Rome, which Cyprian cites near the beginning of the letter to Pompeius, are as follows: “If, therefore, anyone comes to us from any heresy whatsoever, let nothing new be introduced beyond what has been handed down, namely, that hands be laid upon him for penance.” After I had written the preceding remarks, I saw that Pierre Coustant, in the Dissertation [Col. 1059D] mentioned above at p. 149, which treats Stephen’s opinion concerning the reception of heretics, teaches in section V, pp. 238–246, that there is nothing in Stephen’s words signifying the sacrament of Confirmation and nothing leading us to suppose that he required any laying on of hands other than this one, which was an indication of penance. That distinguished man nevertheless admits that Firmilian and Cyprian, together with some of their associates, in interpreting these words of Stephen, persuaded themselves that he allowed the repetition of the rite of Confirmation celebrated by heretics. Maran, however, as I said above at p. 146, holds that Cyprian was not truly persuaded of this. Moreover, Coustant further concedes that the ancient author of *On the Baptism of Heretics*, a work placed among the writings of Cyprian, regarded the laying on of hands imposed upon those coming from heresy as pertaining to Confirmation. Coustant says, however, that other passages from ancient authors and certain ritual formulas lead him to believe that there was a twofold laying on of hands over those coming from heresy, each distinct [Col. 1060B] from the rite of Confirmation: one that immediately joined them to the assembly of Catholics through the invocation of the Holy Spirit, and another by which restoration to Holy Communion was deferred so that the fruits of penance might be acquired through a long period. Yet, whatever Coustant or Maran may have said, it is perhaps not equally certain that Stephen’s words excluded the rite of Confirmation, or consignation, by which the Holy Spirit is given; whereas it is clear that the ancient Church sometimes held that heretics who had never belonged to the Church ought to be admitted to communion through this rite of Confirmation, by the conferral of the Holy Spirit upon them. See what is said above concerning Council VI, p. 145, and especially compare that canon of the Council of Arles with the fifth vote of these prelates. Compare also Canon VII of the First Council of Constantinople in Zonaras, below at p. 173.

*Munnulus.* In the Verona manuscript, from this bishop onward almost all the bishops prefix to their opinions the formula [Col. 1060C] *in pace* [“in peace”], which is nowhere read in the Fox manuscript. Compare Rigaltius below, p. 163, who says that the same occurs in the Corbie manuscript from Bishop Satius onward in nearly all the votes to the end. RIGALTIUS. Monnulus is mentioned in the letter to Cornelius written in the name of the council concerning the granting of peace to the lapsed (above at p. 69). FELL. *Munnulus* in place of *Monnulus* appears in Baluzius’s edition, and Hardouin in his edition of the Councils says: “Our manuscript correctly has ‘Munnulus’—so spelled—‘of Girba.’” ROUTH.

*Baptismatis trinitate* [“the trinity of Baptism”]. Because it was performed with a threefold immersion, in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Tertullian says in *On the Crown*: “We are immersed three times.” Basil, in *On the Holy Spirit*, chapter 27, calls it τρὶς βαπτίζεσθαι, “to be baptized three times.” On this subject see Cyril of Jerusalem, Athanasius, Ambrose, Jerome, and other ancient writers passim. FELL.

*Vere renasci* [“truly to be born again”]. The reading of certain ancient books in which it is written “to come, to be born, and to be baptized” is not bad. One of my manuscripts strongly confirms this reading, for it has “to come and to be born and to be baptized.” [Col. 1060D] The words of Cassius of Macomades, p. 332, also appear to confirm it: “when they have begun to come to the Church.” See what we have said on the letter to Donatus, p. 373. BALUZIUS.

*Cancer quod habebant* [“the canker they possessed”]. The English translator compares this with the first vote, where these words occur: “He whose mouth and words emit a canker asks the sacramental questions.” ROUTH.

*Offectura.* I found this reading in that same ancient book of mine and in several others, and also in Augustine, book VI of *On Baptism against the Donatists*, chapter 17. The Séguier manuscript and certain others prefer *damnationis iram et erroris effecturam* [“the wrath of condemnation and the effect that error would produce”]. BALUZIUS. The common reading is *effectura*. Pamelius, however, had already accepted the other reading, and Rigaltius had said that the Fox manuscript reads *offectura*, meaning “that which harms,” and that this is the truest reading. ROUTH.

*Of Cedias.* Dupin, in the *Sacred Geography [Col. 1061C] of Africa* which he prefixed to St. Optatus, shows that this city is not the same as the one called Quidias or Quida, as Fell and Hardouin had thought. ROUTH.]

which contain within themselves so many holy testimonies descending from the divinely inspired Scriptures that all of us, united by God’s grace, ought rightly to agree. I judge that all heretics and schismatics who wish to come to the Catholic Church must not enter it before they have first been exorcized and baptized—with the exception, of course, of those who were previously baptized in the Catholic Church, provided that they are reconciled to the Church through the laying on of hands for penance.

Nicomedes of Segermes said: This is my opinion: heretics coming to the Church should be baptized, because outside, among sinners, they obtain no forgiveness of sins.

[Col. 1060A] Munnulus of Girba said: The truth of our mother, the Catholic Church, has always remained and still remains with us, brothers, especially in the trinity of Baptism, as our Lord says: “Go and baptize the nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28:19). Since, therefore, we know manifestly that heretics have neither the Father nor the Son nor the Holy Spirit, those coming to our mother the Church must truly be born again and baptized, so that the canker they possessed, the wrath of condemnation, and the harmfulness of error may be sanctified through the holy and heavenly washing.

Secundinus of Cedias said: Since our Lord Christ says, “He who is not with me is against me” [Col. 1061A] [Note: [Col. 1061C]

*Vivificandus* [“to be given life”]. We restored this on the authority of the ancient manuscripts. See the notes on the book *On the Lord’s Prayer*. BALUZIUS. There, namely, that most learned man similarly restored *vivificato* [“having been given life”] from the manuscripts in place of *justificato* [“having been justified”]. For although in this passage most editions printed before Fell had *justificandus* [“to be justified”], that prelate printed *innovandus* [“to be renewed”] from a single Bodleian manuscript. Yet the editions of the Councils, like Augustine and even the Erasmian edition of Cyprian in which these acts were first printed, [Col. 1061D] furnish *vivificandus*, which Baluzius adds that he restored on the authority of the ancient manuscripts. ROUTH.

*Hippone regio* [“Royal Hippo”]. A city of Numidia, Augustine’s episcopal see. According to Antoninus’s calculation, it is 218 Roman miles from Carthage and 160 Roman miles from Hippo Diarrhytus. It is now called Bona. FELL.

*Quantum in nobis est* [“as far as it lies with us”]. St. Augustine says in reply: “He saw that many agreed with this opinion, yet these people”—that is, those who voted, οἱ ὁμόφρονες (*hoi homophrones*, “those of like mind”)—“could not separate themselves from their fellowship without violating unity.” In vote XVIII, Bishop Sedatus said: “Therefore, we must strive with every peaceful power to ensure that no one infected and immersed in heretical error refuses to receive the unique and true Baptism of the Church.” Compare Cyprian’s own preface as well. ROUTH.

*Super Petram* [“upon the Rock”]. So St. Augustine reads in the passage cited shortly before. Erasmus also printed it thus, and I likewise found it in five ancient manuscripts. The alternative reading “upon Peter” occurs in the [Col. 1062C] Séguier manuscript and in thirteen others; the most learned Benedictine monks who prepared the latest edition of St. Augustine’s works also note that it is so written in the manuscripts of his works. And I, indeed, who know that St. Cyprian frequently writes that the Church was founded upon Peter, would readily have preferred the reading supported by the authority of a greater number of ancient books, had I not observed that a comparison is here being made [Col. 1062D] between the Church and heresy. The word “rock,” upon which the Church is built, as Augustine says, must therefore be retained. Below, in the statement of Januarius of Muzula, p. 334, it is written: “The Church and heresy are two different things.” BALUZIUS.—Although we have repeatedly issued a warning on this subject—that importunate copyists, wherever mention of the rock occurred, immediately turned it into Peter—it will nevertheless be appropriate to observe here with Rigaltius that Augustine, following the authority of his copy, read: “Christ built his Church upon the rock, not upon the sand.” FELL.

*Velut cancere* [“as though with a canker”]. The word is correct, however much certain grammarians may protest. Lucretius says in book V, “as Cancer turns toward the solstitial bounds,” and Priscian expressly affirms that it may be neuter, as it is employed here. FELL.

*Praesumptores* [“the presumptuous”]. Compare the vote of Secundianus of Thambeae, which is the eightieth. ROUTH.

*Flebiles et tabidos* [“lamentable and wasting away”]. The Fox manuscript wrongly has *flebiles et habiles* [“lamentable and capable”]. He calls the heretics *tabidos*, as though they were wasting away [Col. 1063C] through the grief and squalor of penance. RIGALTIUS.—It is doubtful whether Cassius means those who are squalid from penance and dissolved in tears, or those who are corrupt in morals and deplorable. Below it is said: “the heretical mind, which has been polluted by long decay.” This inclines toward the latter sense. FELL.]

(Matt. 12:30), and the Apostle John calls those who depart from the Church antichrists (1 John 2:18–19), there can be no doubt that the enemies of Christ, who have been called antichrists, cannot administer the grace of saving Baptism. I therefore judge that those who flee from the snares of the heretics to the Church must be baptized by us, who by God’s gracious favor have been called his friends (John 15:15).

Felix of Bagai said: Just as a blind man leading another blind man causes both to fall into a pit (Matt. 15:14), so a heretic baptizing another heretic causes both to fall into death. The heretic must therefore be baptized and given life, lest we who are alive communicate with the dead.

Polianus of Mileum said: It is right for a heretic to be baptized in the holy Church.

[Col. 1061B] Theogenes of Royal Hippo said: In accordance with the sacrament of God’s heavenly grace which we have received, we believe in the one Baptism that is in the holy Church.

Dativus of Bades said: As far as it lies with us, we do not communicate with heretics unless they have been baptized in the Church and received the forgiveness of sins.

Successus of Abbir Germaniciana said: Either heretics may do nothing, or they may do everything. If they can baptize, they can also give the Holy Spirit. But if they cannot give the Holy Spirit, because they do not possess the Holy Spirit, neither can they baptize spiritually. We therefore judge that heretics must be baptized.

Fortunatus of Tuchabori said: Jesus Christ, our Lord [Col. 1061C] and God, the Son of God the Father and Creator, built his Church upon the rock, not upon heresy (Matt. 16:18), and gave the power to baptize to bishops, not to heretics. Therefore those who are outside the Church, who stand against Christ and scatter his sheep and [Col. 1062A] flock, cannot baptize outside.

Sedatus of Tuburbo said: To the same degree that water sanctified in the Church by a priest’s prayer washes away offenses, water infected by a heretical utterance, as though by a canker, increases sins. Therefore we must strive with every peaceful power to ensure that no one infected and immersed in heretical error refuses to receive the unique and true Baptism of the Church; for whoever has not been baptized with it will become a stranger to the kingdom of heaven.

Privatianus of Sufetula said: Let the person who says that heretics possess the power to baptize first say who founded heresy. For if heresy is from God, it can also possess divine pardon. But if it is not from God, how can it either possess the grace of God or confer it upon anyone?

[Col. 1062B] Privatus of Sufes said: What else does one who approves the Baptism of heretics do but communicate with heretics?

Hortensianus of Lares said: Let either the presumptuous or the supporters of heretics determine how many Baptisms there are. We claim for the Church the one Baptism that we know exists only in the Church. Or how can those whom Christ himself calls his adversaries baptize anyone in the name of Christ?

Cassius of Macomades said: Since there cannot be two Baptisms, whoever grants Baptism to heretics takes it away from himself. I therefore judge that lamentable heretics wasting away must be baptized when they begin to come to the Church; and that, once washed in the sacred and divine washing and illuminated by the light of life, they should be received into the Church, having been made not enemies but peaceful people, not strangers but members of the household of the Lord’s faith, not adulterers but children of God, [Col. 1062C] not people of error but people of salvation. The exception is those faithful who were tripped up and passed from the Church into the darkness of heresy; they must be restored through the laying on of hands.

Another Januarius, of Vicus Caesaris, said: If error does not obey [Col. 1063A] [Note: [Col. 1063C]

*Ecclesiae assistimus* [“we stand by the Church”]. The Greek translation has συνιστάμεθα τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ, “we stand with the Church.” ROUTH.

*Quomodo Christianos faciunt* [“How do they make Christians?”]. These words are absent from five ancient manuscripts and from Augustine; in their place one reads simply *fiunt* [“let them become”], so that it would appear one should write, “If they are not Christians, let them become Christians,” as we saw written after the publication of these words in the manuscript of St. Arnulf. For Christians are made, [Col. 1063D] not born, as was observed above at p. 373. BALUZIUS.—In Augustine, indeed, and, according to Fell, in the York manuscript and Bodleian 2, and in Zonaras, who has γινέσθωσαν (*ginesthōsan*, “let them become”), one reads *fiant* [“let them be made”], precisely what the learned man commends to us. Yet it seems to me that the text should be expanded. ROUTH.

*Confirmari oportet* [“it must be affirmed”]. Baluzius printed this correctly emended, perhaps from his manuscripts, while others either omit the verb *oportet* [“must”], though reading either *confirmari* [“to be affirmed”] or *confirmare* [“to affirm”], or place the verb *debemus* [“we ought”] after *confirmare*, not after *observare* [“to observe”]. ROUTH.

*Quietus of Baruch.* The Verona manuscript has: “Confessor Quietus of Burug.” RIGALTIUS.—On these titles, see Baluzius above at the beginning of the notes. ROUTH.

*Baptizatur a mortuo* [“is baptized by the dead”]. This is followed by “and again touches the dead” in the editions of Erasmus and Fell. In the latter of these editions Augustine is cited as a witness to the reading, which is nevertheless rightly rejected in the Benedictine editions of both Augustine and Cyprian. Nor does Cyprian add the words [Col. 1064C] in his letter to Quintus. Indeed, were that possible, the passage from Sirach would thereby be quoted even more ineptly than before. The addition nevertheless appears in Hardouin’s edition of the Councils.

*Blasphemia Trinitatis* [“blasphemy against the Trinity”]. The reader should observe that here and elsewhere the word “Trinity” designates the divine Persons. Thus Tertullian, *Against Praxeas*, chapter 3: “They suppose that the number and ordering of the Trinity constitute a division of the Unity, although the Unity, deriving the Trinity from itself, is not destroyed by it but administered. And so they now repeatedly charge us with preaching two and three gods, while presuming that they themselves are worshipers of one God—as though Unity irrationally contracted did not make heresy, [Col. 1064D] and the Trinity rationally considered did not constitute truth.” FELL. Since Theophilus, bishop of Antioch, had already before Tertullian used the word Τριάδος (*Triados*, “of the Trinity”) of the three divine Persons in book II of *Against Autolycus*, chapter 23, Latin speakers afterward said *Trinitas*—Tertullian and Cyprian, who used this word in more than one place, as did this very Euchratius, a man of the same period. ROUTH.

*A blasphemia* [“from the blasphemy”]. The authority of fifteen ancient copies compelled me to write it thus. Previously the reading was *a blasphemiae suae praesumptione* [“from the presumption of his blasphemy”]. That reading is indeed found in certain ancient manuscripts. BALUZIUS.—Augustine likewise has *a blasphemia suae praesumptionis* [“from the blasphemy of his presumption”]. ROUTH.

*Libosus of Vaga.* In the Verona manuscript: “Confessor and martyr Libosus of Vaga, placed in the new quarry.” RIGALTIUS.

*Lucius of Thebeste.* In the Verona manuscript: “Confessor and martyr Leucius of Theveste, placed in Faustus’s quarry.” RIGALTIUS.]

the truth, much less does the truth consent to error. And therefore we stand by the Church over which we preside, so that, claiming her Baptism for her alone, we may baptize those whom the Church has not baptized.

Another Secundinus, of Carpis, said: Are heretics Christians or not? If they are Christians, why are they not in the Church of God? If they are not Christians, how do they make Christians? Or to what will the Lord’s saying pertain: “He who is not with me is against me, and he who does not gather with me scatters” (Matt. 12:30)? Hence it is evident that the Holy Spirit cannot descend merely through the laying on of hands upon alien children and the offspring of antichrist, since it is manifest that heretics do not possess Baptism.

Victoricus of Thabraca said: If heretics are permitted to baptize [Col. 1063B] and grant forgiveness of sins, why do we stigmatize them and call them heretics?

Another Felix, of Uthina, said: It is doubtful to no one, most holy fellow priests, that human presumption cannot accomplish as much as the adorable and venerable majesty of our Lord Jesus Christ. Mindful, therefore, of the danger, we ought not only to observe this but must also all affirm it: that all heretics who hasten to the bosom of mother Church should be baptized, so that the heretical mind, polluted by long decay, may be cleansed by the sanctification of the washing and reformed for the better.

Quietus of Baruch said: We who live by faith must obey with faithful observance the things foretold for our instruction. For it is written in Solomon (Ecclus. 34:25): “He who is baptized by a dead man—what benefit does he obtain from his washing?” This plainly speaks of those who are immersed by heretics and of those who immerse them. For if those baptized among them obtain eternal life through the forgiveness of sins, why do they come to the Church? But if nothing pertaining to salvation is received from a dead man, and if, therefore, after recognizing their former error they return with repentance to the truth, they must be sanctified by the one life-giving Baptism that is in the Catholic Church.

Castus of Sicca said: Whoever, in contempt of the truth, presumes to follow custom is either envious and malicious toward the brothers to whom the truth is revealed, or ungrateful toward God, by whose inspiration his Church is instructed.

Euchratius of Thenae said: Our God and Lord Jesus Christ, teaching the Apostles [Col. 1064B] with his own mouth, fulfilled our faith, the grace of Baptism, and the rule of ecclesiastical law, saying: “Go and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28:19). Therefore the false and unlawful Baptism of the heretics must be driven from among us and rejected with utter abhorrence, since from their mouths there issues venom, not life; not heavenly grace, but blasphemy against the Trinity. It is therefore evident that heretics coming to the Church must be baptized with the complete and catholic Baptism, so that, purified from the blasphemy of their presumption, they may be reformed by the grace of the Holy Spirit.

Libosus of Vaga said: In the Gospel the Lord says, “I am the truth” (John 14:6). He did not say, “I am custom.” Accordingly, once the truth has been made manifest, let custom yield to truth, so that, even if in the past someone in the Church did not baptize heretics, he may now begin to baptize them.

[Col. 1064C] Lucius of Thebeste said: Blasphemous [Col. 1065A] heretics and unrighteous persons, who mutilate in various ways the holy and adorable words of the Scriptures, I judge worthy of execration and therefore to be exorcized and baptized.

> **Note [Col. 1065C]**
>
> **Of Amaccora.** I do not know how it happened that I wrote “of Amaccora,” as is evident from what I annotated in my notes on the Conference of Carthage between the Catholics and the Donatists, p. 236. When, for that reason, I consulted my edition of that Conference, it happened by chance that I came upon page 122, where I pointed out that Jacques Sirmond—a most learned man whom I can never name without praise—[Col. 1065D] had erred when he wrote that it took place in the second year after the consulship of Varanes. His principal argument was that it may be gathered from Augustine that the Pentecost fast had been completed shortly before the Conference. Since this observation of mine is certain, and nothing can be advanced to refute it, I am surprised that the Reverend Father Jean Hardouin, a man of extensive reading and learning, wished to insinuate, in the first volume of his edition of the Councils, p. 1048, that Sirmond’s opinion ought to be followed. I therefore note the matter here, lest anyone hereafter be mistaken about it. Would that Hardouin had chosen to follow my edition of the proceedings, which assuredly—if I may say so without envy—is much better than the one he produced. **BALUZE.**
>
> **And I myself followed.** Baluze added the pronoun *ego* (“I”), perhaps from manuscripts of his own; and shortly below he printed “because he cannot be an outsider,” where Rigault has “because of outsiders” in place of “an outsider.” The others, however, read: “because they are outsiders, they cannot be with us.” **ROUTH.**
>
> **Our spring is private.** The English translator says that the very ancient application of the Song of Songs [Col. 1066C] to Christ and the Church should be noted. **ROUTH.**
>
> **Leptiminus.** Ptolemy’s Λέπτις μικρά (*Leptis mikra*, “Little Leptis”). A city of Byzacena, whereas Leptis Magna belonged to Tripolitana. According to Antoninus it is 106 Roman miles from Carthage. It is mentioned in the Conference of Carthage and the *Notitia Africae*. **FELL.**
>
> **Not one.** Augustine has “not two.” **ROUTH.**
>
> [Col. 1066D] **Worse than pagans.** Compare the vote of Saturninus of Thucca, that is, no. 52, at p. 102. **ROUTH.**
>
> **Sattius.** In the Corbie manuscript, beginning with this bishop, nearly all prefix **IN PEACE** to their names. By this formula they appear to indicate that they do not wish, by their decision, to remove anyone from communion even if he holds a different opinion. This rule had been stated by Cyprian in the preface to the Synod. **RIGAULT.**
>
> **And defiles Christians.** Augustine says in response: “As for what he placed last, saying, ‘He acts against reason in both respects,’ etc., Cyprian himself, together with his colleagues who agreed with him, rejected it first and foremost. For he did not believe himself to be defiled when, for the sake of the bond of peace, he determined that communion should be maintained with such persons, saying: ‘Judging no one, nor removing anyone from the right of communion if he holds a different opinion.’” See above, at the very beginning of the Council. **ROUTH.**
>
> **Utica.** A city of Zeugitana inhabited by Roman citizens, famous for the death of Cato, as Pliny says. Polybius and Ptolemy call it Ἰτύκη (*Itykē*). It is now called Bizerta. **FELL.**

Eugenius of Ammaedara said: I too hold this same opinion: that heretics must be baptized.

Likewise, another Felix of Amaccora said: Following the authority of the divine Scriptures, I myself also judge that heretics must be baptized, as must those who maintain that they were baptized among schismatics. For if, according to Christ’s ordinance, our spring is private, let all the adversaries of our Church understand that he who is the shepherd of one flock cannot belong to another, nor can he supply saving water to two peoples. It is therefore evident that neither heretics nor schismatics can receive anything heavenly, since they presume to receive it from sinful [Col. 1065B] men who are outsiders to the Church. When there is no standing for the giver, what is given certainly does not benefit the recipient either.

Likewise, another Januarius of Muzula said: I am astonished that, although everyone confesses that there is one Baptism, not everyone understands the unity of that same Baptism. For the Church and heresy are two different things. If the heretics possess Baptism, we do not possess it; but if we possess it, the heretics cannot possess it. There is no doubt, however, that the Church alone possesses the Baptism of Christ, since she alone possesses both the grace and the truth of Christ.

Adelphius of Thasvalt said: Certain people assail the truth without cause, using the false and malicious expression that we “rebaptize,” whereas the Church does not [Col. 1065C] rebaptize heretics, but baptizes them.

Demetrius of Leptiminus said: We preserve one Baptism, because we claim what belongs to the Catholic Church for her alone. Those, however, who say that heretics baptize truly and lawfully are themselves the ones who create not one Baptism but many. For since there are many heresies, [Col. 1066A] the baptisms will also be counted according to their number.

Vincentius of Thibaris said: We know that heretics are worse than pagans. If, therefore, they are converted and wish to come to the Lord, we assuredly possess the rule of truth that the Lord entrusted to the Apostles by divine command, saying: “Go; in my name lay on hands and cast out demons” (Matt. 10:8). And elsewhere: “Go and teach the nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28:19). Therefore they may attain Christ’s promise first through the laying on of hands in exorcism, and secondly through the regeneration of Baptism. I judge that it ought not to be done otherwise.

Marcus of Mactaris said: It is not surprising if heretics, the enemies and assailants of the truth, claim for themselves a thing belonging to another’s power and gracious privilege. What is surprising, [Col. 1066B] however, is that certain of our own men, betrayers of the truth, support the heretics and oppose Christians. We therefore decree that heretics must be baptized.

Sattius of Sicilibba said: If heretics are forgiven their sins in Baptism, they come to the Church without cause. For since sins are what receive punishment on the Day of Judgment, heretics can have nothing to fear from Christ’s judgment if they have obtained the forgiveness of sins.

Victor of Gor said: Since sins are forgiven only in the Church’s Baptism, whoever admits a heretic to communion without Baptism acts against reason in both respects: he neither purifies the heretics nor avoids defiling the Christians.

[Col. 1066C] Aurelius of Utica said: Since the Apostle says that one must not participate in the sins of others (1 Tim. 5:22), what else does one participate in but the sins of others when one communicates with heretics without the Church’s Baptism? I therefore judge that heretics must be baptized, so that they may receive the forgiveness of sins and communion may then be given to them.

[Col. 1067A]

> **Note [Col. 1067C]**
>
> **Jambus.** In the Foxian manuscript, neither here nor in the names of the other bishops are the designations “confessors” or “martyrs” found. **RIGAULT.**—Refer to Baluze’s note placed at the beginning of this Council. The Oxford edition, however, preserved the titles, which I shall indicate for the individual names in these notes. **ROUTH.**
>
> **Germaniciana.** Evidently “New Germaniciana,” to distinguish it from Abbiritana. The bishop of this city at the time of the Conference of Carthage was Innocentius. It belonged to Byzacena and was inhabited by veterans of the Germanic cohorts. [Col. 1067D] What Pliny reports in Book IV, chapter 4, applies to this city, as it does to most of the others: they may rightly be called not only cities but also nations. **FELL.**
>
> **That they deny … ought.** A novel mode of expression, although its meaning is clear.
>
> **Either the Lord is God.** The common editions read: “Either the Lord your God is God.” Augustine, however, has: “Either the Lord is God.” Perhaps the word *tuus* (“your”) arose corruptly from the preceding word. And since in Erasmus’s edition I saw the passage reading, “Either *enin* [sic] God is God,” I judged that the word *tuus* should be deleted. **ROUTH.**
>
> **Jader.** The other editions, except Baluze’s, followed the Erasmian edition—in which the Acts of this Synod first appeared—and augmented this bishop with the title “Confessor and Martyr.” But neither Augustine nor the books named by Baluze at the beginning of this Council conferred such titles on him or on any of the following fathers. **ROUTH.**
>
> **Paulus.** In editions before Baluze, the word “Confessor” was prefixed to this name and to the [Col. 1068C] next two. **ROUTH.**
>
> **Of Obba.** Bobba, a city of Mauretania. It is called Obba in the *Notitia Africae* and the Conference of Carthage, but most manuscripts have Bobba. This nomenclature is supported by Pliny, who places the Augustan colony of Bobba inland in Mauretania, forty Roman miles from Lixus. **FELL.**
>
> **And we both retain and administer it.** It was formerly read, “we retain and administer it.” But “we retain and” is absent from the Séguier manuscript and from the other ancient manuscripts. The anonymous author of the book *On Rebaptism*, p. 354, [Col. 1068D] has: “by the Baptism which meanwhile he administered.” **BALUZE.**—Since Baluze eliminated this, in my opinion without adequate reason, I judged that it should be restored, because it had been retained in the printed texts and also in some editions of Augustine. **ROUTH.**
>
> **Saturninus.** In the books I mentioned above, “Another Confessor” is prefixed. **ROUTH.**
>
> **Doing unlawful things.** I find the distinguished Marshall’s conjecture convincing: he restores “doing lawful things.” **ROUTH.**
>
> **The pagans … the supreme God, etc.** Tertullian certainly proves this from the testimony of the soul itself, though it is not Christian, in his book *On the Testimony of the Soul*. **RIGAULT.**—**The supreme God:** namely Jupiter, who is called the father of men and gods. **FELL.**
>
> **Zama.** A city of Numidia; Ptolemy’s Azama. It is mentioned by Strabo, Pliny, and others. Here Hannibal was defeated by Scipio with great slaughter. **FELL.**
>
> **Irenaeus.** In the books I have mentioned, he is called a confessor. **ROUTH.**

Jambus of Germaniciana said: Those who approve the Baptism of the heretics disapprove our own, since they deny that those who outside the Church were—not, I would say, washed, but soiled—ought to be baptized in the Church.

Lucianus of Rucuma said: It is written: “And God saw the light, that it was good, and he divided the light from the darkness” (Gen. 1:4). If light and darkness can agree, then we and the heretics can have something in common. I therefore judge that heretics must be baptized.

Pelagianus of Luperciana said: It is written: “Either the Lord is God, or Baal is God” (3 Kings 18:21). So too now: either the Church is the Church, or heresy is the Church. But if heresy is not the Church, how can the Church’s Baptism exist among the heretics?

[Col. 1067B] Jader of Midila said: We know that there is only one Baptism, in the Catholic Church. We therefore ought not to admit a heretic unless he has been baptized among us, lest he think that he was baptized outside the Catholic Church.

Likewise, another Felix of Marazana said: One faith, one Baptism—but belonging to the Catholic Church, which alone has the right to baptize.

Paulus of Obba said: I am not troubled if someone fails to vindicate the Church’s faith and truth, since the Apostle says: “For what if some of them have fallen away from the faith? Has their unbelief nullified the faithfulness of God? By no means. For God is true, but every man a liar” (Rom. 3:3–4). But if God is true, how can the truth of Baptism exist among the heretics, among whom God is not?

[Col. 1067C] Pomponius of Dionysiana said: It is evident that heretics cannot baptize and grant the forgiveness of sins, since they do not possess the power to loose or bind anything upon earth.

Venantius of Timisa said: If a husband, setting out on a long journey, entrusted his wife to his friend’s protection, that friend would preserve the woman entrusted to him with the greatest possible diligence, lest anyone violate her chastity and holiness. Christ our Lord and God, departing to the Father, entrusted his bride to us. Shall we preserve her incorrupt and inviolate, or shall we betray her integrity and chastity to adulterers and corrupters? For whoever makes the Church’s Baptism common to the heretics betrays Christ’s bride to adulterers.

Ahymnus of Ausvaga said: We have received one Baptism, and we both retain and administer it. But whoever [Col. 1068B] says that heretics too have the right to baptize himself creates two Baptisms.

Saturninus of Victoriana said: If heretics have the right to baptize, then those doing unlawful things [perhaps: “lawful things,” Marshall] are excused and defended. Nor do I see why Christ should have called them his adversaries, or the Apostle antichrists.

Saturninus of Thucca said: Although the pagans worship idols, they nevertheless know and confess the supreme God as Father and Creator. Marcion blasphemes against him, yet certain men are not ashamed to approve Marcion’s Baptism. How do such priests either preserve or vindicate the priesthood of God, when they do not baptize the enemies of God and thus communicate with them?

Marcellus of Zama said: Since sins are forgiven only by the Church’s Baptism, whoever does not baptize a heretic [Col. 1068C] communicates with a sinner.

Irenaeus of Ululi said: If the Church does not baptize a heretic [Col. 1069A] on the ground that he is said already to have been baptized, heresy is greater than the Church.

> **Note [Col. 1069C]**
>
> **Heresy is greater.** That is, greater than the Church. Augustine replies: “One could say in the same way: if the Church does not baptize a greedy man because he is said already to have been baptized, greed is greater. But this is false; therefore so is the other claim.” Book VII *Against the Donatists*, at the place cited above. Whether this response answers the argument brought forward is for that holy man to determine. **ROUTH.**
>
> **Faustus.** He too is called a confessor in the editions before the Benedictine edition that followed Erasmus, who was the first to add these Acts. **ROUTH.**
>
> [Col. 1069D] **Therapius.** Both he and the next father after him are called confessors in the same editions. **ROUTH.**
>
> **Bussacenis.** I believe *Byzacene* should be restored. Ptolemy calls Byzacium βυζακίνην (*Byzakinēn*); Pliny extraordinarily extols the fertility of this region in more than one passage. The bishop of this city is mentioned in the Conference of Carthage. **FELL.**—It is situated in the province called Byzacena. **ROUTH.**
>
> **Of Aggya.** It appears to be Aggiva, which is mentioned in the Conference of Carthage. **FELL.**—Our manuscript has *Abachia*, from which it is uncertain whether one should read “of Bachia” or “of Achia.” **HARDOUIN.**
>
> **Another Victor.** He is adorned with the title “Confessor” in the place cited above. Hardouin, moreover, notes that in his Society’s manuscript this is the opinion of Tenax, who precedes, and that Tenax’s in turn is the opinion of this Victor. **ROUTH.**
>
> **The Church is not.** As in the preceding vote. I have therefore judged that the word *una* (“one”), following “Church” and unknown to Augustine, should be removed from here. **ROUTH.**
>
> [Col. 1070C] **Verulus.** “The martyr Verulus, concerning schismatics” (so the editions of Fell and others). This is apparently phrased in the same manner as Epistle 42, “Repostus, concerning the exiles”; that is, Verulus was distinguished by martyrdom, although formerly a schismatic. It was noted above that all these honorifics are omitted from most copies. **FELL.**—But it is possible that the words “concerning schismatics” were merely a marginal summary of the vote. **ROUTH.**
>
> **Much less can a schismatic, etc.** Augustine replies as follows: [Col. 1070D] “We have already shown that they possess it, because they do not lose it when they depart; for they do not receive it when they return.” The proof comes from the practice of the Africans themselves, since they did not rebaptize those returning from heresy who had previously been baptized in the Church. **ROUTH.**
>
> **That I should wait.** That is, “I should await.” Similarly, Victor of Octavum says below: “I awaited the counsel of my predecessors.” **FELL.**—Whether Pudentianus’s words “the newness of my episcopate” shed light upon St. Ignatius’s words in his *Epistle to the Magnesians*, τὴν φαινομένην νεωτερικὴν τάξιν (*tēn phainomenēn neōterikēn taxin*, “the apparently youthful rank”), I leave to others to investigate. **ROUTH.**
>
> **Petrus.** Adorned with the title “Martyr” in the printed books I mentioned. **ROUTH.**
>
> **Hippo Diarrhytus.** (*Hyppo Diarrhito* in Fell and others.) Pliny and Mela teach that the town which they call Hypomen Dilutum—called Diarrhytus by the Greeks because of the irrigation provided by its waters—was situated on the African coast; Pliny, Book V, chapter 4. See our notes on the Conference of Carthage, p. 222. **BALUZE.**

Donatus of Cibaliana said: I know one Church and her one Baptism. If anyone says that the grace of Baptism exists among the heretics, he must first show and prove that the Church exists there as well.

Zosimus of Tharassa said: Once the truth has been revealed, let error yield to truth; for Peter too, who had formerly circumcised, yielded to Paul when he preached the truth (Gal. 3).

Julianus of Telepte said: It is written: “No one can receive anything unless it has been given to him from heaven” (John 3:27). If heresy is from heaven, it too can confer Baptism.

Faustus of Timida Regia said: Let those who patronize heretics not flatter themselves. Whoever intercedes on behalf of the heretics against [Col. 1069B] ecclesiastical Baptism makes them Christians and us heretics.

Geminius of Furni said: Some of our colleagues may prefer heretics to themselves, but they cannot prefer them to us. We therefore hold to what we once decreed: that we baptize those coming from the heretics.

Rogatianus of Nova said: Christ established the Church; the devil established heresy. How can the synagogue of Satan possess the Baptism of Christ?

Therapius of Bulla said: Whoever concedes and betrays the Church’s Baptism to the heretics—what else is he but a Judas to the bride of Christ?

Likewise, another Lucius of Membresa said: It is written: “God does not hear a sinner” (John 9:31). How can a heretic, who is a sinner, be heard in Baptism? [Col. 1069C]

Likewise, another Felix of Bussacenis said: In admitting heretics without the Church’s Baptism, let no one prefer custom to reason and truth, because reason and truth always exclude custom.

[Col. 1070A] Another Saturninus of Avitina said: If Antichrist can give the grace of Christ to anyone, then the heretics, who have been called antichrists, can also baptize.

Quintus of Aggya said: He who possesses something can give something. What, however, can heretics give, when it is established that they possess nothing?

Another Julianus of Marcelliana said: If a man can serve two masters, God and Mammon, then Baptism too can serve two: the Christian and the heretic (Matt. 6:24).

Tenax of Horrea Caeliae said: Baptism is one, but it belongs to the Church. Where the Church is not, Baptism cannot be there.

Another Victor of Assuras said: It is written that God is one, Christ one, the Church one, and [Col. 1070B] Baptism one (Eph. 4:5–6). How, then, can anyone be baptized where God and Christ and the Church are not?

Donatulus of Capsa said: I too have always held this opinion: that when heretics, who can obtain nothing outside, are converted to the Church, they should be baptized.

Verulus of Rusiccade said: A heretical man cannot give what he does not possess; much less can a schismatic, who has lost what he possessed.

Pudentianus of Cuicul said: The newness of my episcopate, dearly beloved brothers, caused me to wait and see what my elders would decide. For it is evident that heresies possess nothing and can do nothing. It has therefore been most justly determined that any who come from them are to be baptized.

Petrus of Hippo Diarrhytus said: Since there is one Baptism [Col. 1070C] in the Catholic Church, it is evident that no one can be baptized outside the Church. I therefore judge that those immersed in heresy, or coming to the Church from schism, ought to be baptized.

Likewise, another Lucius of Ausafa said: In accordance with the prompting [Col. 1071A] of my mind and of the Holy Spirit, since there is one God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, one Christ, one hope, one Spirit, and one Church, there must also be one Baptism. I therefore say that whatever has been undertaken or done by the heretics must be annulled, and that those who come from them must be baptized in the Church.

> **Note [Col. 1071C]**
>
> **Lamasba.** Fell indeed caused *Lambesa* to be printed, and in vote VI there occurs “Januarius of Lambase,” where that distinguished man noted that Ptolemy has the city Λαμαῖσα (*Lamaisa*) or Λαμβαῖσα (*Lambaisa*). But if *Lambase* were accepted here also, either two bishops of one city would be created, contrary to custom, or one would have to conclude that there was another city of the same name. This is indeed by no means rare. Thus, when in vote 52 a city named Thucca or Tucca had been mentioned, Fell wrote the following at the third vote after the present one: “Tucca, a city of Mauretania Sitifensis, concerning which see Pliny, Book V, chapter 2, and the *Notitia Africae*; it is distinct from Tucca Terebenthina and a third Tucca in Numidia.” Perhaps, however, Pusillus was bishop of Lamasua, since, as Dupin observes in his *Sacred Geography of Africa*, this episcopal see in the province of Numidia is mentioned in entry 112 of the *Notitia* and in the Conference of Carthage. **ROUTH.**
>
> [Col. 1071D] **Salvianus.** He is called a martyr in the place cited above. **ROUTH.**
>
> **Clarus.** In the same editions they are called “Clarus the Confessor” and “Secundianus the Martyr.” Meanwhile, the expression in this vote, “baptizing the faith of believers,” is unusual. **ROUTH.**
>
> **Have not obtained.** This is one of the readings Baluze introduced without comment. Certainly all the editions of Cyprian that I have seen, as well as Augustine, do not know the reading *non sint* (“have not”). **ROUTH.**
>
> **The Apostle John in his Epistle.** Before this African bishop Aurelius of Chullabi, Irenaeus, Book I, chapter 16—or 13 in another numbering—and Origen, though the latter more doubtfully, in his *Commentary on the Gospel of St. John*, p. 83 of Huet’s edition, had cited this Second Epistle of John. Subsequently the same Epistle was accepted by the author of the *Fragment on the Canon of Holy Scripture* and by Clement of Alexandria, as I show in my comments upon that Fragment. But one might perhaps suspect that Cyprian did the contrary—although the distinguished Lardner, in [Col. 1072C] *On the Historical Credibility of the Gospel History*, Part II, vol.
