IV, Book I, chapter 44, §7.5, assigns considerable weight in this matter to the testimony of Cyprian’s colleague Aurelius, and not without reason—from the fact that that holy man did not cite this very verse either in Book III of his *Testimonies to Quirinus*, chapter 78, where he wishes to show from Holy Scripture that one must not speak with heretics, or in the very many other passages where we might reasonably have expected him to do so, had he accepted the Epistle. Moreover, after I had written these observations, I saw that the distinguished English translator Marshall makes the same point: Cyprian everywhere cites John’s First Epistle without any numerical distinction, as though he had been unaware of the Second. Yet that same Cyprian similarly cites St. Paul’s latter Epistle to the Thessalonians in his Epistle 55, otherwise numbered 59; indeed, the Second Epistle of John is cited in just this same fashion by Aurelius in the present vote. The same translator also errs when he says that Tertullian, in [Col. 1072D] his *Prescription Against Heretics*, twice bore witness to Second John, for Tertullian did not do so even once—not in chapters 12 and 33, which Marshall cites, nor, unless I am mistaken, anywhere else. **ROUTH.**
>
> **Gemellae.** A city of Numidia in Antoninus. A Roman colony was established there under the emperor Hadrian, as Ligorio demonstrates from its coin: **AELIA HADRIANA GEMILLINA**. This Litteus appears to be mentioned in Cyprian’s Epistle 76. **FELL.**—The title “Confessor” was added to this bishop in the editions of Cyprian that I mentioned. **ROUTH.**
>
> **Enlighten.** The very learned English translator notes that this is said emphatically, ἐμφατικῶς (*emphatikōs*), because Baptism is often called φωτισμός (*phōtismos*), “illumination.” **ROUTH.**
>
> **Of Oea.** Pliny, Book V, chapter 4, teaches that it was situated in the province of Tripolitana, as we have said, between the two Syrtes. Ptolemy nevertheless places Sabrata, Oea, and Leptis Magna—which certainly are cities of the province of Tripolitana—on the Lesser Syrtis, evidently, in my opinion, because they are nearer to the Lesser than to the Greater. I do not know whether Virgil, who in Book V [Col. 1073A] of the *Aeneid* places after the inhospitable Syrtis a region desolate through thirst, may have meant by that thirst-desolated region the Tripolitans neighboring the inhospitable Syrtis. In Martianus Capella, Book VI, “the city of Oea” should be read, not “Oeensis” [the transmitted distinction is materially unclear]. St. Augustine teaches in his letter to Marcellinus that Apuleius took a wife from Oea; and Apuleius himself writes that he was made a citizen of Oea. See Cujas, *Observations*, Book VIII, chapter 27. **BALUZE.**

Likewise, another Felix of Gurgites said: I judge that, in accordance with the commandments of the Holy Scriptures, one who was unlawfully baptized by heretics outside the Church should, when he wishes to take refuge in the Church, obtain the grace of Baptism where it is lawfully given.

Pusillus of Lamasba said: I believe that saving Baptism exists only in the Catholic Church. Whatever takes place outside the Catholic Church is a counterfeit.

Salvianus of Gazaufala said: It is established that heretics possess nothing; [Col. 1071B] they therefore come to us so that they may receive what they do not possess.

Honoratus of Thucca said: Since Christ is the truth, we ought to follow truth rather than custom, so that through the Church’s Baptism we may sanctify the heretics who come to us precisely because they were able to receive nothing outside.

Victor of Octavum said: As you yourselves know, I was appointed bishop only recently, and therefore I awaited the counsel of my predecessors. I consequently hold that all who come from heresy are without doubt to be baptized.

Clarus of Mascula said: The declaration of our Lord Jesus Christ is evident: when sending his Apostles, he entrusted to them alone the power given to him by the Father. [Col. 1071C] We have succeeded them, governing the Lord’s Church [Col. 1072A] with that same power and baptizing the faith of believers. Therefore heretics, who outside the Church possess neither authority nor the Church of Christ, cannot baptize anyone with Christ’s Baptism.

Secundianus of Thambae said: We must not deceive heretics through our own presumption, so that, when the Day of Judgment comes, it may be charged against us that they were not baptized in the Church of our Lord Jesus Christ and consequently did not obtain the forgiveness of sins, because through us they were not baptized and did not obtain the pardon of divine grace. Therefore, since there is one Church and one Baptism, when they are converted to us, let them obtain both the Church and the Church’s Baptism together.

Likewise, another Aurelianus of Chullabi said: The Apostle John wrote in his Epistle: “If anyone comes to [Col. 1072B] us and does not possess the teaching of Christ, do not admit him into your house, and do not even say ‘Hail’ to him. For whoever says ‘Hail’ to him participates in his evil deeds” (2 John 10–11). How can such people rashly be admitted into the house of God when we are forbidden to admit them into our private houses? Or how can we communicate with them without the Church’s Baptism when, if we merely say “Hail” to them, we participate in their evil deeds?

Litteus of Gemellae said: “If a blind man leads a blind man, both fall into a pit” (Matt. 15:14). Since, therefore, it is established that heretics, being blind, cannot enlighten anyone, their Baptism is invalid.

[Col. 1072C] Natalis of Oea said: Both I, who am present, and—

> **Note [Col. 1073A]**
>
> **Of Sabrata.** A city of Tripolitana; Pliny’s Sabrata. [Col. 1073B] It is mentioned in the Conference of Carthage, Augustine’s *Against Cresconius*, Book III, chapter 53, and Victor of Vita. Pompeius, bishop of this city, appears to be the very man to whom Cyprian wrote his celebrated letter concerning the Baptism of heretics against Stephen. It may be observed that, from the most remote antiquity, absent bishops did not lose the right to vote, provided they authorized one of their colleagues to act on their behalf. Perhaps the statement in 1 Corinthians 5:4 is not wholly unrelated to this practice: namely, that the bishops of Achaia, assembled synodically, should proceed through the censures of the Church against the incestuous Corinthian, with the spirit of the absent Apostle. **FELL.**
>
> **Of Leptis Magna.** A city of Tripolitana, formed from three cities: Taphra, Abrotonum, and Leptis Magna. Pliny, Solinus, Antoninus, and Ptolemy mention it. Leptis Minor was discussed above. **FELL.**
>
> **Cyprian.** “Confessor and Martyr” is prefixed in the editions I have mentioned. The same title is attributed to Stephen, Cyprian’s adversary, in the ancient [Col. 1073C] martyrologies of Bede and others. **ROUTH.**
My opinion. Although the odium attaching to this doctrine is cast chiefly upon our Cyprian, it was nevertheless supported not only by the votes of eighty-seven bishops of Africa, Numidia, and Mauretania, but was also confirmed by the token of fellowship exchanged among widely separated churches scattered throughout Egypt, Asia, and Europe. Apostolic Canon 46 says: “We command that a bishop or presbyter who has accepted the baptism or sacrifice of heretics be deposed. For what accord has Christ with Belial, or what portion has a believer with an unbeliever?”

Thus, long before the controversy with Stephen arose, the fathers of the synods of Iconium and Synnada had also decreed, as we learn from Dionysius of Alexandria in Eusebius, book VII, chapter 7:

> I have also learned that it was not only now that those in Africa introduced this practice, but that long before, under the bishops who preceded us, it was approved in the most populous churches, in synods of the brethren at Iconium and Synnada, and among very many others. I cannot endure to overturn their decisions and plunge them into strife and contentiousness. For, he says, “You shall not move your neighbor’s boundaries, which your fathers established.” [Col. 1073D]

Firmilian bears almost the same witness concerning the synod of Iconium:

> We confirmed all this long ago, when we assembled together at Iconium, a place in Phrygia, with those who had gathered from Galatia and Cilicia and the other neighboring regions.

He further adds:

> We join custom to truth, and against the custom of the Romans we set custom indeed, but the custom of truth. From the beginning we have maintained what was handed down by Christ and the apostles; nor do we remember that this practice ever began among us, since it has always been observed there: that we acknowledge only one God, and account as holy in baptism only that of the Church.

Cyprian says in his Letter to Jubaianus that many years and a long period had already passed since, under Agrippinus, a man of blessed memory, a very large number of bishops assembled together and established this rule. And in his letter to Quintus he affirms that it was established not by his immediate predecessor, but by his predecessors generally.

Moreover, Tertullian, *On Baptism*, chapter 15:

> There is for us absolutely one baptism, both according to the Gospel of the Lord and according to the writings of the Apostle, since there is one Lord, one baptism, and one Church in heaven. [Col. 1074A] But as for what rule should be observed concerning heretics, someone may properly reconsider the matter. For the command was issued to us; heretics, however, have no fellowship in our discipline, since the very withdrawal of communion plainly testifies that they are outsiders. I ought not to recognize among them what was commanded to me, because we and they do not have the same God, nor the one—that is, the same—Christ. And therefore [Col. 1074B] neither is the baptism one, because it is not the same. Since they do not possess it rightly, they undoubtedly do not possess it at all; and what does not exist cannot be counted. Thus they cannot receive it either, because they do not possess it.

Likewise, in *On Prescription*:

> No one can be built up by that whereby he is destroyed; no one is enlightened by that whereby he is plunged into darkness.

If we come down to the time of the Council of Nicaea, it will appear that the fathers of that synod, contrary to what very many contend, by no means settled this controversy. Jerome does indeed say, in his *Dialogue against the Luciferians*, that the Nicene synod received all heretics except the disciples of Paul of Samosata. Augustine, however, proceeds more cautiously. Although he says that his position concerning baptism was confirmed, all doubts removed, by a plenary council of the whole world; that it was the pure and fully clarified decision of a plenary council and the consensus of the entire catholic world; and, furthermore, that it had now been examined, considered, perfected, and confirmed within the very unity of the whole world—nevertheless, as the Louvain scholars observe, Augustine nowhere specified either the name or the location of this council.

Will anyone believe that the Nicene fathers decreed that those coming to the Church [Col. 1074C] from any heresy whatever, with the exception of the adherents of Paul of Samosata, should be admitted without a repetition of baptism? That, namely, Marcionites, Valentinians, Ebionites, Carpocratians, Manichaeans, and all the rest of that Hydra’s brood were accorded a more favorable position than the followers of the Samosatene?

With Balsamon’s leave, I am led to believe that it is not quite the same whether they are called *Paulianists* (Παυλιανισταί), *Paulicians* (Παυλικιανοί), or *those who have Paulianized* (Παυλιανίσαντες); but that the aforesaid fathers chose this last expression in order to include all heretics who, after Paul’s fashion, had departed in any manner whatever from the orthodox faith:

> Concerning those who have Paulianized and subsequently taken refuge in the catholic Church, a decree has been issued that they must without exception be rebaptized.

These words expressly state who must be admitted through a repetition of the Church’s baptism; but as for admitting others without baptism, there is profound silence.

Zonaras notes only this concerning our Council of Carthage: that its decision was partially set aside, since “it did not prevail in the case of all heretics, nor in that of schismatics.” [Col. 1074D] And as proof of this assertion he adduces, not the Council of Nicaea, but the First Council of Constantinople.

Certainly, the fathers who wrote in various places after the Council of Nicaea—and who must be judged neither to have been ignorant of nor to have despised the decrees of that venerable assembly—did not believe that this decision had been fully clarified, examined, considered, perfected, and confirmed. Optatus of Milevis, replying explicitly to Parmenian the Donatist, who mocked the orthodox as though they ratified the sacraments of all heretics, says that among the heretics themselves there are no sacraments and that their water is false; and in books IV and V he teaches generally that there are no sacraments among heretics. Hence Albaspinaeus adds this scholion:

> From this and many other passages I infer that Optatus does not think heretics capable of baptizing.

Basil the Great held this same position. In canon 1 he says of heretics generally: “It is clear that the Church does not receive these persons without baptism”; and in canon 20, after enumerating the Encratites, Saccophori, and Apotactites, he says summarily: “In a word, we rebaptize such persons.” [Col. 1075A] And in canon 47: “We therefore do not receive them into the Church unless they are baptized with our baptism.”

Cyril of Jerusalem supports these authorities, saying in his preface:

> One Lord, one faith, and one baptism; for only heretics are rebaptized, since the former rite was not baptism.

Athanasius, in his third *Oration against the Arians*, says of their baptism:

> How is what is administered among them not entirely empty and unprofitable, possessing an appearance but in truth providing no assistance whatever toward piety?

And if it is alleged that they baptize in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, he replies:

> Just as a creature is something other than the Son, so what is supposedly administered by them would be something other than the truth, even though, because of what is written, they pretend to pronounce the name of the Father and of the Son.

He further says:

> Many [Col. 1075B] other heresies likewise utter the names alone; but because they do not think rightly, as has been said, and do not possess sound faith, the water administered by them is unprofitable and deficient in piety, so that the person sprinkled by them is polluted still more in impiety rather than redeemed.

Among those who preserve the complete formula of baptism, he enumerates the Manichaeans, Phrygians, and Paulianists. Thus the decree of the First Council of Arles, to which Augustine adhered, had not yet gained general force:

> If anyone comes from heresy, let them question him concerning the Creed; and if they find that he was baptized in the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, let only the hand be laid upon him, etc.

The Council of Constantinople, canon 7, did indeed in this respect extend favor to the Arians, as well as to the Macedonians, Sabbatians, Novatians, Quartodecimans, and Apollinarians, permitting them to be admitted into the Church merely by the application of chrism. But on the other hand it was decreed concerning the Eunomians, Montanists, Sabellians,

> and all the other heresies, that all who wish to join orthodoxy from among them are received as Greeks, and on the first [Col. 1075C] day we make them Christians, on the second catechumens, and then on the third we exorcize them, breathing three times into the face and ears. And thus we catechize them, make them spend time in the Church and listen to the Scriptures, and then we baptize them.

Whether, on grounds of parity, those who have not erred more gravely than the Arians, Macedonians, and the other enumerated heretics are by virtue of this canon to be admitted into the Church through chrism, notwithstanding those words generally censuring “all the other heresies,” I would by no means venture to say. Certainly Balsamon, commenting on the passage, believed “that all who are baptized by a single immersion are baptized again.”

Yet not very long afterward Gregory the Great prohibited triple immersion in Spain, saying in book I, Letter 41:

> Lest, while they do what they were accustomed to do, they boast that they have conquered our custom.

His position was confirmed by the Fourth Council of Toledo, where it was decreed:

> Let us retain the single immersion of baptism.

I acknowledge that the grave and protracted controversy concerning the baptism of heretics was at long last happily resolved by the excellent writings of St. Augustine and, to use his word, fully clarified. The whole Christian world, wherever it extends, yielded to his invincible arguments and possessed at least one faith concerning baptism, which it also always acknowledged to be unique, until in our own age the madness of the Anabaptists broke out afresh, to the grave injury not only of the churches but also of commonwealths.

It is easy to cite the decree in canon 8 of the Council of Nicaea:

> Concerning those who formerly called themselves Cathari but who come to the catholic and apostolic Church, it has been determined that, when hands are laid upon them, they may thus remain in the clergy. [Col. 1075D]

That is, the Novatians are to be regarded not only as Christians but also, if they had been admitted to the clergy, as clerics. Pardon was indeed more readily granted to the Novatians because, as Balsamon says, “they erred not concerning the faith, but were condemned as lacking compassion.”

But if what is contained in the following canons, namely the ninth and tenth, is carefully weighed—that persons guilty of graver crimes, or even apostates, if they happen to have been promoted to sacred orders, “are not accepted by the canon” and, “once discovered, are deposed”—one will suspect that these three canons establish nothing about admission into the Church, but prescribe rules concerning an ecclesiastical rank already received: whether it is to be retained or lost. That is, orders conferred, whether surreptitiously or otherwise, upon men formerly belonging to the Novatian party, “formerly Cathari,” are to be held valid; but those granted to persons discovered to have committed graver crimes or apostasy are to be regarded as wholly invalid. But I determine nothing.

Let me note only one thing. St. Augustine, who in the matter of baptism was very heavily pressed by Cyprian’s authority, sought almost his sole defense against so weighty a precedent in the assertion that nothing had yet been defined by the Church on the matter, and that consequently Cyprian’s error—although he clung tenaciously to the decisions and decrees of his predecessors—was free of guilt. [Col. 1076B] This was especially so because Cyprian condemned no one who, living elsewhere in the world, where these canons had not prevailed, followed the customs of his own church. **FELL.**

After reading this excellent discussion, one may usefully add what Pearson wrote concerning the Africans who persisted in the same position, in his *Annals of Cyprian*, under the year 257, sections II and III. Several other points concerning the baptism of heretics have moreover been noted above, both at the beginning of the Fifth Council of Carthage and of this very synod, and elsewhere.

Furthermore, the distinguished Marshall, the translator of Cyprian, who appended to his edition of Cyprian a learned dissertation on this seventh Cyprianic council, undertook, among many other matters, to prove these two points by numerous arguments. First, he observed—and the distinguished Maran also shows this on pages XIII and XVI of the Preface to the *Works of St. Cyprian*—that among all who disputed in any way concerning the validity of heretical baptism, there was agreement that such baptism had no saving effect until it had been confirmed by the authority of the Church and by the bishop’s action over those returning to the Church.

Second, he argued that Cyprian [Col. 1076C] and, ultimately, everyone judged that the disputed matter concerned discipline more than faith, and consequently that by virtue of its right of dispensation the Church was permitted to regard baptisms of this kind either as invalid or as confirmed, although those ancient writers differed greatly among themselves concerning what the Church ought to do.

As regards this latter point—whether that question was formerly considered to pertain more to discipline than to faith—other very learned men have rightly expressed doubt, even though neither party considered the other’s position so injurious to the faith that it judged its opponents to be heretics. See, among others, Jean de La Placette, Doctor of Theology, in his *Historical-Ecclesiastical Observations*, pages 102–114.

Augustine indeed says explicitly in book V of *On Baptism*, chapter 25, that the peace of Christ prevailed in the hearts of Stephen and Cyprian, so that no evil of schism arose between them in so great a dispute. Meanwhile, however, La Placette believed that Stephen had actually excommunicated the dissenters; this is rendered probable by the passage from Firmilian cited above at page 152. [Col. 1076D]

In the time of Xystus, Stephen’s successor—whom Pontius, Cyprian’s deacon, calls a good and peaceable priest in the *Life* of his master, and whose martyrdom Cyprian himself commemorates in Letter LXXXII, otherwise LXXX—these disputes seem to have been laid to rest. But enough of this.

It is at any rate established that the Roman prelate championed at least the ancient custom of the Western churches, not only for the sake of preserving a tradition that he believed to be apostolic, but also from fear of rebaptizing, or needlessly repeating, the baptism which “those of one mind” (οἱ ὁμόφρονες) with Stephen said, in accordance with Holy Scripture, to be one. Cyprian reports this in his letter to Quintus, page 126, and several other passages demonstrate it.

But would that Stephen, in a matter which—to speak with Augustine—had not yet been decided by the whole Church, had likewise resolved, as St. Dionysius of Alexandria resolved concerning the same matter in his letter to Philemon of Rome cited by Fell above at page 173, not to presume to plunge great and very numerous churches “into strife and contentiousness” (εἰς ἔριν καὶ φιλονεικίαν ἐμβαλεῖν). **ROUTH.**

Pompeius of Sabrata, together with Dioga of Leptis Magna, who entrusted me with their votes, being absent indeed in body but present in spirit, said: We judge as our colleagues do: that heretics cannot have communion with us unless they have been baptized with the Church’s baptism. [Col. 1074A]

Julius of Neapolis said: I do not depart from what we once determined: that we should baptize heretics who come to the Church.

Cyprian of Carthage said: My opinion is expressed most fully [Col. 1075A]—

> **[Note: Col. 1076D]**
>
> **The Letter to Jubaianus.** In place of the letter to [Col. 1077A] Jubaianus, the Greeks substituted the letter to Januarius, and inserted it entire into their manuscripts as though it were a canon of this council. Thus they say that this synod was “earlier than all the synods” (πασῶν τῶν συνόδων προγενεστέραν), and that it was held “under the emperor Decius” (ἐπὶ Δεκίου βασιλέως); they further say that Novatus, a Roman presbyter, gave both origin and name to the Novatian heresy. Thus Balsamon and Zonaras, among others, heap error upon error; and it is almost universal among Eastern writers continually to blunder in matters concerning the West. **FELL.**
>
> Concerning the name of the Roman heresiarch—for the Greeks were not thinking of Novatus, the Carthaginian presbyter—whether it was Novatus or rather Novatian has been discussed above in connection with the letters of St. Cornelius, page 19. Furthermore, that letter to Januarius pertains to the Fifth Council of Carthage; since it was written in the name of the council, I reproduced it above. **ROUTH.**

—in the letter written to our colleague Jubaianus: that heretics, in accordance with the evangelical [Col. 1076A; Col. 1077A]—

> **[Note: Col. 1077B]**
>
> **Adversaries of Christ.** Baluzius added the particle *and* and the words *adversaries of Christ*, perhaps taken from his own manuscripts; but here I judged that the other editions, Augustine, and the Greek translation should rather be followed. **ROUTH.**
>
> **Christians.** Zonaras’s scholion on the Greek translation of the Council:
>
> These, then, are the opinions of the fathers who assembled with the great Cyprian in this synod. But they did not prevail in the case of all heretics, nor in that of schismatics. For the Second Ecumenical Council—as it seems, Augustine’s “plen­ary council of the whole world”—as has already been said, excepted certain heretics and decreed that they should be received without baptism, being anointed only with the divine chrism and each anathematizing his own heresy and all heresies without exception. [Col. 1078B] For this reason these opinions were not even expounded as being unnecessary, since they had no operative force, but were recorded in summary form.

—and apostolic testimony have been called adversaries of Christ and antichrists, and that when they come to the Church they must be baptized with the Church’s one baptism, [Col. 1078A] so that from adversaries they may become friends, and from antichrists, Christians.

This council is extant at page 329 of the Benedictine edition of St. Cyprian.

## OBSERVATIONS OF THE BOLLANDISTS ON THESE WORDS OF THE COUNCIL OF CARTHAGE: “For none of us appoints himself bishop of bishops,” etc.

(*Acta Sanctorum*, under September 14, vol. IV, pp. 300, 315.)

[Col. 1077B]

What St. Cyprian states concerning a Bishop of Bishops and the use of tyrannical terror to impose the necessity of obedience … [Col. 1077C] may be understood as spoken without any fault of an agitated mind and without injury to pontifical authority. The holy primate plainly wished to admonish the assembled bishops that each should state his opinion freely. To this end, observing what he judged most conducive to that freedom, he noted that they were all colleagues; and although he himself held the primacy of Africa, neither he nor any of the others present was a bishop of bishops, nor might anyone tyrannically arrogate such power to himself that he should by his terror compel the others to adopt his views.…

What he adds there concerning the discretion and authority of each bishop—namely, that none can be judged by another, nor can he similarly judge another—must be referred, in a sound sense, to those same assembled bishops; otherwise it is plainly at variance with St. Cyprian’s own actions. Certainly St. Augustine, cited by us at no. 695, understood those words thus:

> I suppose, at any rate, that this applies to questions which have not yet been discussed with fully clarified completeness.

It was entirely true that this question concerning the baptism of heretics—which no general council had up to that time … defined, and which rested upon custom alone—could not be decided by any of the bishops assembled with St. Cyprian in such a way that, by his authority, the others would be compelled to withdraw from their own opinion.

On the other hand, if anyone [Col. 1077D] contends that the saint’s words must be understood generally, he must therefore explain by what right, or by what injustice, that same saint declared in Letter 64 that Fortunatus, bishop of Assuras in the Proconsular province, and in Letter 68 that Basilides and Martial, bishops in Spain, had rightly been deprived of authority for the crime of idolatry, and took measures to exclude them from their sees. By what right did he likewise send Letter 67 to Stephen, the Roman pontiff, asking him to order Marcian, bishop of Arles in Gaul, to be deposed from his see and another appointed in his place, if every bishop possesses, in the freedom of his liberty and authority, a judgment of his own; if he can no more be judged by another than he himself can judge another; and if the judgment of our Lord Jesus Christ must therefore be awaited, since he alone has power both to set them over the governance of his Church and to judge their conduct?

It therefore cannot be denied that the cited words of St. Cyprian must be restricted to a sound sense; otherwise one must say that, through the heat of contention, he suffered something here that was merely human.

Likewise, the case of Fortunatus proves nothing against the same primacy of the Roman pontiff. St. Cyprian complains concerning him in Letter 55 that, through Felicissimus and the other associates in the schism [Col. 1078C], he sailed to Rome to St. Cornelius in order to extort communion from him by lies and calumnies, and that he was summoned, if he wished to make any reply to the sentence pronounced against them, to present himself before Cyprian’s tribunal.

It must be observed that this Fortunatus was one of the five schismatic presbyters of Carthage. We showed above that, because of the schism he had stirred up with Felicissimus, he had already become a fugitive from the Church and had been condemned by the African bishops, and that he was subsequently ordained in Africa as a pseudo-bishop by heretics and schismatics. Accordingly, he could not here be regarded as a bishop.

St. Augustine moreover testifies in Letter 43, otherwise 162, that even in his own time presbyters and other clerics of lower rank were not permitted to appeal to the Apostolic See; yet he affirms, both there and elsewhere, that bishops were permitted to do so. The African prelates had therefore agreed that clerics below the rank of bishop should each be judged within his own province; and this was doubtless done with the Roman pontiff’s assent, lest appeals to the Apostolic See become excessively frequent and furnish an occasion for unjust accusations.

Yet just as this prohibition in St. Augustine’s time did not prevent him from acknowledging—both frequently elsewhere and in the cited passage—the authority [Col. 1078D] and primacy over the other bishops of the Roman Church, “in which,” as he says there, “the primacy of the apostolic chair has always flourished,” so neither can anything against that same primacy be inferred from the similar action of St. Cyprian.

Moreover, what Fell, a heterodox bishop in England—and after him the distinguished Boysen—shamelessly attributes to the most holy prelate is false: namely, that in the judgment of that blessed martyr those must be regarded as desperate and lost who consider the authority of the bishops in Africa inferior even to that of Cornelius himself, seated upon Peter’s chair at Rome.

For if anyone carefully considers the entire passage, he will acknowledge that St. Cyprian contrasts the authority of the bishops in Africa, not with that of St. Cornelius, but with the few desperate and lost men who followed Fortunatus and Felicissimus. For he adds:

> Their case has already been heard; sentence has already been pronounced concerning them; nor is it consistent with the gravity of the priestly censure that it should be criticized through the fickleness and inconstancy of a frivolous mind.… If the number of those who judged them in the previous year is reckoned together with the presbyters and deacons, more persons were then present at the judgment and inquiry than are these same people who now appear to be joined with Fortunatus. For you ought to know, dearest brother, that after he was made pseudo-bishop by heretics, he was soon deserted by almost everyone. [Col. 1079A]

St. Cyprian therefore argued there approximately as follows: it has been established that clerics below episcopal rank must plead their case within their own diocese. But the case of Fortunatus, Felicissimus, and the others was examined before us, and sentence has already been pronounced upon it. Accordingly, they should not be heard at Rome—unless perhaps someone supposes that greater credence should be given to those few desperate and lost men than to so great a number of bishops in Africa and other clerics who judged them in the previous year and were far more numerous than those who now adhere to Fortunatus and have appealed to the Apostolic See.

This I believe to be the genuine meaning of the words. But if anyone contends that the expression “to a few desperate [Col. 1080A] and lost men” must be understood in the dative rather than the ablative case, even so he will not wring Fell’s invention from it or prove that the authority of the African prelates is here equated with pontifical authority. For the sense could then be: unless perhaps these few schismatics suppose the authority of the African prelates to be too slight for them to be obliged to submit to their decision in accordance with the decrees concerning appeals.

This much is certain: no comparison between the African sees and the Roman chair is instituted there, and Fortunatus and his followers are called desperate and lost because of their heresy and crimes, not because they had appealed to the pontiff.

## [LETTER(S)]

[Col. 1079A]

## NOTICE

After the Seventh Council of Carthage, which was rejected by the catholic Church, we append here, in Greek and Latin, St. Cyprian’s letter to Jubaianus, from the canonical collection of John Zonaras, a monk who had formerly been Grand Drungary of the Watch and chief of the imperial secretaries. Theodore Balsamon likewise included Cyprian’s letter in his own collection, but omitted the bishops’ opinions and the acts of the council. **LABBÉ.**

> **[Note: Col. 1079]** The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.

A synod held at Carthage, presided over by the great Cyprian, holy martyr, when he was bishop of Carthage.

## PREFACE OF JOHN ZONARAS

> **[Note: Col. 1079D]** From the Greek folio edition published at Paris in 1618 under the supervision of Fronton du Duc, S.J.

[Col. 1079B]

This synod is the most ancient of all. The synod held at Antioch in Syria against Paul of Samosata, under Aurelian, emperor of the Romans, is indeed earlier than the others; but the present synod is older even than that. For the great Cyprian [**Note: Col. 1079D. Zonaras is mistaken here.**] completed the course of martyrdom under the emperor Decius, whereas Aurelian lived a long interval after Decius. Many emperors reigned after Decius’s death before Aurelian at last succeeded [Col. 1079C] to the imperial power. Thus this synod is by far the most ancient of all.

Eighty-four bishops assembled in it, and the question was raised whether those who renounce heresy and return to their senses, and schismatics who return to the Church, ought to be baptized. For a certain bishop named Jovianus, together with other bishops, had consulted Cyprian by letter on this matter: namely, whether persons of this kind ought to be baptized.

At that time Navatus [**Note: Col. 1079D. Novatian.**], a presbyter of the Roman Church and properly a schismatic rather than a heretic, also professed himself leader of the sect called the Cathari, that is, the Pure. For he differed from the catholics in no respect concerning doctrine, but refused admission to penance to those who, during times adverse to the Christian commonwealth, had been overcome by evil, had succumbed, and had sacrificed to the gods.

When [Col. 1079D] Cornelius, who then presided over the Roman Church, and the bishops subject to him had discussed the question and decreed that even those who had sacrificed should be admitted to penance, Navatus nevertheless relaxed none of his obstinacy. They therefore promulgated a decree cutting him off from the body of the Church as a hater of the brethren.

Having obtained other followers, he began to hold separate assemblies and, through the resulting schism, to rend the Church here and there by means of his adherents. When Jovianus therefore inquired concerning schismatics and heretics, the great Cyprian and his synod wrote in reply to him and his fellow bishops, composing the following letter.

## SYNOD HELD UNDER CYPRIAN, THE MOST HOLY BISHOP OF CARTHAGE AND MARTYR  
### JOHN ZONARAS

[Col. 1080B]

This synod is earlier than all the synods. For the synod held at Antioch in Syria against Paul of Samosata—which was convened under the emperor Aurelian—is indeed earlier than the others; but this one is older even than that. For the great Cyprian completed the course of martyrdom under the emperor Decius, whereas Aurelian was many reigns removed from Decius. Many emperors held power after Decius, and after them Aurelian [Col. 1080C] was deemed worthy of the imperial office. Thus, then, this synod is earlier than all the rest.

Eighty-four bishops assembled in it, when the question arose whether those returning from heresy, and schismatics approaching the catholic Church, ought to be baptized. For a certain bishop named Jovianus wrote concerning this to the divine Cyprian, asking whether persons of this kind ought to be baptized.

At that time Navatus also became leader of the sect of those called Cathari, having been a presbyter of the Church of the Romans. He was properly a schismatic, not a heretic, for he did not differ from the orthodox in matters of doctrine, but denied repentance to those who had yielded under persecutions and offered sacrifice.

When Cornelius, who then presided over the Church of the Romans, and the bishops under him had considered the question raised and decreed that even those who had sacrificed should be received into repentance, [Col. 1080D] Navatus would not abandon his opposition. They therefore cut him off from the Church and repudiated him as a hater of the brethren.

Having acquired others who shared his opinions, he held irregular assemblies of his own, and through him and those in communion with him a schism arose in the Church. When Jovianus therefore inquired concerning schismatics and heretics, the great Cyprian and the synod with him sent this letter in reply to him and his fellow bishops.

> **[Note: Col. 1081]** The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.

## LETTER OF THE GREAT CYPRIAN  
### To Jovianus and His Bishops

> **[Note: Col. 1081D]** *Jubaianus.* But in the editions of Pamelius and Rigaltius it is entitled *To Januarius and the Other Numidian Bishops, on the Baptism of Heretics*. **LABBÉ.**

[Col. 1081A]

While we were assembled in a common council, beloved brothers, we read the letter you sent concerning those who appear to have been baptized by heretics or schismatics and who come to the catholic Church, which is one and in which we are baptized and regenerated.

Concerning these matters we trust that you also, who conduct your ministry within that Church, uphold the stability of the catholic Church’s rule. Nevertheless, because you share communion with us and, on account of our common love, wished to inquire about the matter, we offer no new opinion or one now established for the first time. Rather, we have communicated to you, for your observance, the position that was long ago most carefully and diligently examined by our predecessors, and we join ourselves to you in it, [Col. 1081B] now likewise determining what we have always firmly and steadfastly maintained: that no one can be baptized outside the baptism of the catholic Church, which is one and is found in the catholic Church alone.

For it is written:

> They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water, and have dug for themselves broken cisterns that cannot hold water.

And again, Holy Scripture, foreshadowing this, says:

> Abstain from foreign water, and do not drink from a foreign fountain.

The water must first be purified and sanctified by the priest, so that by its own baptism it may wash away the sins of the person being baptized. For through the prophet Ezekiel the Lord also says:

> I will sprinkle you with pure water, and I will cleanse you; I will give you a new heart and a new spirit.

And when the Lord says in Numbers:

> Everything that the unclean person touches shall be unclean,

[Col. 1081C] How can the one baptizing grant another the remission of sins when, outside the Church, he cannot rid himself of his own sins?

The very question asked at baptism is also a witness to the truth. For when we say to the person being examined, “Do you believe that you receive eternal life and the remission of sins?” we say nothing other than that these things can be given in the catholic Church. Among heretics, however, where the Church is not, remission of sins cannot be obtained. Therefore, those who undertake the defense of heretics must either change the baptismal question or acknowledge the truth.

The person who has been baptized must also be anointed, so that, having received the anointing, he may become a participant in Christ. A heretic, however, cannot sanctify the oil, since he has neither an altar nor a Church. Chrism [Col. 1081D] cannot possibly exist among heretics. For it is clear to us that oil cannot in any way be sanctified among them for the giving of thanks.

We ought to know and not be ignorant of what is written:

> Let not the oil of a sinner fatten my head.

The Holy Spirit also signified this long ago in the Psalms, lest anyone, having been led astray and wandered from the right way, should be anointed among heretics, the adversaries of Christ.

Moreover, how shall prayer be made for the person who has been baptized, if the one praying is not a priest but a sacrilegious man and a sinner? Scripture says that God does not hear sinners, but that if anyone is devout and religious and [Col. 1083A] does his will, him he hears.

We understand the remission of sins to be given through the holy Church. But who can give what he himself does not possess? Or how can one perform spiritual acts when he has cast away the Holy Spirit?

Therefore, the person who approaches the Church must also be renewed, so that he may be sanctified within it by holy persons. For it is written:

> You shall be holy, just as I am holy, says the Lord.

Thus the person who was seduced into error may in the true baptism of the Church himself put off that error—the man who approached God and sought a priest, but, finding error instead, fell into sacrilege.

To approve those who have been baptized by heretics and schismatics is to approve the heresy of those persons themselves. For it cannot be valid in one part only. If one who is outside could not possess the Spirit, he cannot baptize one who comes to him, [Col. 1083B] since there is one baptism, one Holy Spirit, and one Church, founded from the beginning by Christ our Lord upon Peter the apostle, with unity as its foundation.

Accordingly, because the things done by them are false and empty, they are all rejected. For nothing can be pleasing and acceptable to God when it is done by those whom the Lord calls enemies and adversaries in the Gospels:

> He who is not with me is against me, and he who does not gather with me scatters.

Moreover, the blessed apostle John, observing the Lord’s commandments, laid down in his Epistle:

> You have heard that antichrist is coming, and even now many antichrists have arisen. From this we know that it is the last hour. They went out from us, but they were not of us.

Hence we too must understand and consider that, if God’s enemies and those who are called antichrists [Col. 1083C] cannot give the Lord’s grace, then we who are with the Lord and maintain the Lord’s unity, and who in accordance with the honor he has bestowed upon us exercise his priesthood in the Church, must reject, remove, cast away, and regard as profane everything done by his adversaries, enemies, and antichrists. To those who come from error and perversity we must grant the complete knowledge of the true faith of the Church, of the mystery of divine power, and of unity, faith, and truth.

### ZONARAS

This letter commands that all who have been baptized by heretics or schismatics be baptized again if they enter the catholic Church, and it confirms that opinion by various arguments, enthymemes, and testimonies from Scripture.

The Second Ecumenical [Col. 1083D] Council, however, in its seventh canon decrees that not all who leave heresy are to be purified again by baptism. Rather, some, provided that they submit written declarations and anathematize both their own particular heresy and every error alien to the catholic and apostolic Church of God, are to be admitted after being marked with the seal—that is, anointed with holy chrism. All the others, among whom it names certain groups expressly, are to be baptized and received as [**Note: Col. 1083D. Pagans.**] Greeks.

That canon has indeed been explained in its proper place. It therefore readily appears that the ruling of the present canon was not accepted by the later holy fathers. Since, then, two synods issued contrary decrees concerning the same matter, the ruling of the Second Council [Col. 1085A] must be preferred, both because it was later and because it was ecumenical; that is, all who occupied patriarchal sees were present in it, either the patriarchs themselves or their representatives.

Moreover, that this canon was by no means accepted by all the holy fathers may be understood from the second canon of the Council held in Trullo, which is called the Sixth. There the holy fathers, after individually enumerating the canons whose authority must remain valid, pronounce concerning this canon in exactly these words:

> Furthermore, the canon issued by Cyprian, who was archbishop and martyr of the African region, and by the synod held under him, was preserved only in the territories of those prelates, in accordance with the custom handed down by them.

From this passage, therefore, it readily appears that even in the earliest times this canon by no means [Col. 1085B] prevailed among everyone.

This, then, is the text of the letter. The statements made by each individual in the common deliberation of those assembled in the synod are as follows:

**Cyprian said:**
You have heard, most beloved colleagues, what Jubaianus, our fellow bishop, wrote to me, consulting my modest judgment concerning the unlawful and profane baptism of heretics, and what I wrote back to him, expressing the judgment—although it is what we have judged once, twice, and often—that heretics coming to the Church ought to be baptized with the baptism of the Church and sanctified. Other letters of Jubaianus were likewise read to you; in them, replying to [Col. 1085C] our letter in accordance with his sincere and religious devotion, he not only agreed but also gave thanks, acknowledging that he had been instructed. It remains for each of us to state what we think about this very matter, judging no one and removing no one from the right of communion if he should think differently. For none of us sets himself up as bishop of bishops or, by tyrannical intimidation, compels his colleagues to the necessity of obedience, since every bishop, by virtue of his freedom and authority, possesses his own independent judgment, just as he cannot be judged by another, nor can he himself judge another. Rather, let us all await the judgment of our Lord Jesus Christ, who alone has the power both to appoint us to the governance of his Church and to judge our conduct.

[Col. 1085D] 1. Caecilius of Bilta said:

I know one baptism in the Church alone, and none outside the Church. That baptism will be one where there is true hope and sure faith. For thus it is written: “One faith, [one hope,] one baptism” (Eph. 4:5).

[Note: [Col. 1085D] These words, and several others, are absent from the Greek text against which Gentian Hervet’s Latin translation was checked. LABBE.]

It is not among heretics, where there is no hope and faith is false; where everything is conducted through falsehood; where one possessed by a demon performs exorcism; where one whose mouth and words emit a cancerous corruption asks the sacramental questions; where an unbeliever bestows faith, a criminal grants pardon for sins, and Antichrist immerses in the name of Christ; where one accursed by God blesses; one dead promises life; one without peace gives peace; a blasphemer invokes God; a profane man administers the priesthood; a sacrilegious man sets up an altar; [Col. 1087A] and one who serves the devil offers sacrifice to God. Let those who support them say that all these things are false concerning heretics. See what things the Church is compelled to approve, so that she is forced to enter into communion without baptism and the pardon of sins. This, brothers, we must flee and avoid; we must separate ourselves from so great a crime and hold fast to the one baptism granted by God to the Church alone.

2. Primus Felix of Migirpa said:

I judge that every person coming from heresy must be baptized. For he vainly supposes that he was baptized there, since there is no baptism except the one true baptism in the Church. For there is one God and one Church, in which the one baptism and sanctification stand, and in which all other things pertaining to salvation and eternal life are accomplished. Things performed outside the Church have no saving effect.

3. Polycarp of Hadrumetum said:

Those who approve the baptism of heretics render ours invalid. [Col. 1087B]

4. Novatus of Thamugadi said:

Although we know that all Scripture bears witness concerning saving baptism, we must nevertheless declare our faith: heretics and schismatics who come to the Church and appear to have been falsely baptized must be baptized with true baptism. I have therefore baptized everyone converted to the Church, and those who appeared to have been ordained among their clergy I received among the laity.

5. Nemesianus of Thubunae said:

That the baptism given by a heretic or schismatic is not true is declared everywhere in the Holy Scriptures, since their leaders are themselves false Christs and false prophets.

6. Januarius of Lambaesis said:

On the authority of the Holy Scriptures, I decree that all heretics must be baptized and thus admitted into the holy Church.

7. Lucius of Castra Galbae said:

[Col. 1087C] Since the Lord said in the Gospel, “You are the salt of the earth; but if the salt has become insipid, with what shall it be salted?” and since it is evident that heretics—that is, God’s enemies—cannot give anyone life through a spiritual confession, because they have become insipid and are outside the Church, we must baptize those who come to us with holy baptism.

8. Crescens of Cirta said:

I too judge that heretics and schismatics who wish to come to the catholic Church must not be received before they have been exorcized and baptized, except those who were formerly baptized in the catholic Church and afterward deserted it; these, however, are to be reconciled to the Church in penitence through the laying on of hands.

[Col. 1087D] 9. Nicomedes of Segermes said:

My judgment is that heretics coming to the Church are to be baptized, because, having been baptized by a heretic, they obtained no remission of sins outside it.

[Col. 1089A] 10. Secundianus of Carindia said:

Since our Lord Jesus Christ says, “Whoever is not with me is against me,” and the apostle John calls those who depart from the Church antichrists, it is impossible for them to minister the grace of God and saving baptism. I therefore judge that those who take refuge in the Church must be baptized by us.

11. Felix of Bagai said:

Just as a blind man leading a blind man falls with him into the pit, so a heretic baptizing a heretic falls with him into death. The heretic must therefore be baptized among [Col. 1089B] us, lest we who are alive enter into communion with the dead.

12. Successus of Abbir Germaniciana said:

Either heretics are permitted nothing or they are permitted everything. If they can baptize, they can also give the Holy Spirit; but if they do not have the Holy Spirit, neither can they baptize spiritually. I therefore judge that heretics must be baptized.

13. Fortunatus of Thucabori said:

Those who are outside the Church and stand against Christ, since they scatter his sheep and flock, cannot baptize outside it.

14. Sedatus of Thuburbo said:

We must strive with all our strength to prevent anyone infected and stained by heretical error from refusing to receive the unique and true baptism of the Church, without which anyone who has not been baptized is excluded from the kingdom of heaven. [Col. 1089C]

15. Privatianus of Sufetula said:

If heresy is from God, the heretic will also possess divine pardon. But if it is not from God, how can he either possess God’s grace or confer it upon anyone?

16. Munnulus of Girba said:

Since the Lord says, “Baptize all nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,” we know plainly that heretics possess neither the Father, nor the Son, nor the Holy Spirit. Those who come to the Church must therefore be baptized, that they may be born again.

17. Politianus of Mileum said:

[Col. 1089D] It is right that one who comes from heresy should be baptized in the Church.

18. Theognis of Hippo Regius said:

In accordance with the sacrament of God and of the heavenly grace we have received, we recognize the baptism that is in the holy Church.

19. Dativus of Badis said:

So far as it lies with us, we do not enter into communion with heretics unless they have been baptized in the Church and received remission of sins.

20. Privatus of Sufes said:

What else does one who approves the baptism of heretics do but enter into communion with heretics?

21. Hortensianus of Lares said:

We vindicate for the Church the one baptism that we know nowhere except in the Church.

[Col. 1091A] 22. Cassius of Macomades said:

Since there cannot be two baptisms, one who concedes baptism to heretics deprives himself of baptism. I therefore judge that heretics must be baptized when they come to the Church, except those who, having separated from the Church’s faithful, passed into the darkness of heresy; when they return, they must be restored through the laying on of hands.

23. Januarius of Vicus Caesaris said:

If error does not submit to truth, much less does truth consent to error. We therefore stand by the Church over which we preside, so that we may baptize those whom the Church has not baptized.

24. Secundinus of Carpi said:

If heretics are Christians, why are they not in the Church of God? [Col. 1091B] But if they are not Christians, let them become Christians. It is consequently evident that the Holy Spirit cannot descend upon alien children and the offspring of Antichrist merely through the laying on of hands.

25. Victoricus of Thabraca said:

If heretics are permitted to baptize and to give the Holy Spirit and remission of sins, why do we speak falsely against them by calling them heretics?

26. Another Felix, of Uthina, said:

We must affirm that all heretics who hasten to the Church are to be baptized, so that every perversion originating outside may be cleansed, sanctified, and reformed for the better.

27. Quietus of Baruch said:

[Col. 1091C] If those baptized among heretics obtain remission of sins and eternal life, why should they come to the Church? But if they come to repentance, they must be baptized and sanctified with the life-giving baptism that is in the catholic Church.

28. Castus of Sicca said:

One who, despising truth, presumes to follow custom is either envious toward the brothers to whom truth has been revealed or ungrateful toward the God who revealed it.

29. Eucratius of Thenae said:

Heretics coming to the Church must be baptized with the complete and catholic baptism, so that, cleansed from their sins, they may be sanctified.

[Col. 1091D] 30. Libosus of Vaga said:

The Lord said, “I am the truth.” Therefore, once truth has been manifested, let custom yield to truth, so that even if someone in the Church did not baptize heretics in the past, he may now begin to baptize them.

31. Lucius of Thebeste said:

Heretics who are blasphemous and lawless, and who corrupt the Holy Scriptures with diverse words, must be struck with anathema; therefore we must exorcize and baptize such persons.

32. Eugenius of Ammaedara said:

I too judge the same: heretics must be baptized.

[Col. 1093A] 33. Another Felix, of Amacura, said:

Following the authority of the divine Scriptures, I too declare that heretics and schismatics must be baptized.

34. Januarius of Muzula said:

If heretics possess baptism, we do not; if we possess it, heretics cannot. There is no doubt, however, that the catholic Church uses Christ’s baptism, since she alone possesses Christ’s grace, love, and truth.

35. Adelphius of Thasualta said:

They attack the truth in vain by saying that we rebaptize. For the Church does not rebaptize heretics but baptizes them.

36. Demetrius of Leptis Minor said:

[Col. 1093B] Those who say that heretics baptize truly and lawfully introduce not merely two baptisms but many. For since there are many heresies, baptisms will be reckoned according to their number.

37. Vincentius of Thibaris said:

We know that heretics are worse than pagans—

[Note: [Col. 1093D] Schismatics.]

—so if they repent and wish to come to the rule of truth, they must first be exorcized and then baptized. Only then can they attain Christ’s promise.

38. Marius of Mactaris said:

I judge that heretics, as persons possessing nothing, must be baptized.

39. Satius of Sicilibba said:

[Col. 1093C] If heretics are forgiven their sins in their own baptism, they come to the Church without cause. For if they have obtained remission of sins, there is nothing they can fear in Christ’s judgment.

40. Aurelius of Utica said:

Since the Apostle says (1 Tim. 6) that one must not participate in the sins of others, I judge that heretics must be baptized so that they may first receive remission of sins, and we may then enter into communion with them.

41. Jamnus of Germaniciana said:

Those who approve the baptism of heretics disapprove ours.

42. Lucianus of Rucuma said:

If light can agree with darkness, then we [Col. 1093D] and heretics can have something in common. I therefore judge that heretics must be baptized.

43. Pelagianus of Luperciana said:

If heresy is not in the Church, how can the Church’s baptism exist among heretics?

44. Jader of Midila said:

One faith, one baptism; but it belongs to the catholic Church to baptize.

45. Another Felix, of Marrazana, said:

The same.

46. Paulus of Bobba said:

If God is true, how can the truth of baptism exist among heretics, among whom God is not?

[Col. 1095A] 47. Pomponius of Dionysiana said:

Heretics cannot baptize or give remission of sins, since they possess no power to loose or bind anything on earth.

48. Venantius of Thumisa said:

One who makes the Church’s baptism common with heretics betrays Christ’s bride to adulterers.

49. Aymnius of Ansvaga said:

We have received one baptism, and this we retain and practice. But one who says that heretics too are permitted to baptize creates two baptisms.

50. Saturninus of Victoriana said:

If heretics are permitted to baptize, they are excused and defended when they do unlawful things; nor will you find why [Col. 1095B] Christ called them his adversaries or the Apostle called them antichrists.

51. Another Saturninus, of Thueca, said:

Although the Gentiles worship idols, they nevertheless recognize God as Father and Creator and confess him as Lord. Marcion blasphemes against this God; how, then, are those who approve Marcion’s baptism not ashamed?

52. Marcellus of Zama said:

Since sins are remitted only in the Church’s baptism, one who does not baptize a heretic enters into communion with a sinner.

53. Irenaeus of Usulae said:

If the Church does not baptize a heretic because he is said already to have been baptized, heresy is preferred and becomes greater. [Col. 1095C]

54. Donatus of Cybalina said:

If anyone says that the grace of baptism exists among heretics, let him first demonstrate and prove that the Church exists there.

55. Zosimus of Tharassa said:

Once truth has been revealed, let error yield to truth.

56. Julianus of Telepte said:

It is written: “No one can receive anything unless it has been given to him from heaven” (John 3:27). If heresy is from heaven, it can also give heavenly baptism.

57. Faustus of Timida said:

Those who plead for heretics against ecclesiastical baptism make them Christians and us heretics.

[Col. 1095D] 58. Geminus of Furni said:

What we once decreed we still maintain: that we baptize those coming from heretics.

59. Rogatianus of Nova said:

Christ established the Church; the devil established heresy. How, then, can the synagogue of the devil possess Christ’s baptism?

60. Therapius of Bulla said:

What else is one who concedes the Church’s baptism to heretics but a betrayer of Christ’s bride?

61. Lucius of Membresa said:

It is written, “God does not hear sinners.” How can a heretic, who is a sinner, be heard in baptism?

[Col. 1097A] 62. Another Felix, of Uslaccae, said:

In receiving heretics without the Church’s baptism, let no one prefer custom to reason and truth.

63. Another Saturninus, of Avitina, said:

If Antichrist can give anyone the grace of Christ, heretics, who have been called antichrists, can also baptize.

64. Quintus of Aggiva said:

There is one God, one Church, and one baptism. How, then, can anyone be baptized where God, Christ, and the Church are not?

65. Julianus of Marciliana said:

If a man can serve two masters, God and [Col. 1097B] Mammon, baptism can also serve two masters.

66. Tenax of Horrea Coelia said:

Baptism is one, but it belongs to the Church, whose baptism is true.

67. Another Victor, of Assuras, said likewise.

68. Donatulus of Capsa said:

I too have always held that heretics, who can obtain nothing outside, are to be baptized when they come to the Church.

69. Verulus of Rusiccade said:

A heretic can [not] give what he does not possess; much less can a schismatic, who has lost what he possessed.

[Note: [Col. 1097D] “Not.”]

70. Pudentianus of Cuicul said:

If anyone comes from heresy, it has been rightly and [Col. 1097C] justly decreed that he be baptized.

71. Petrus of Hippo Diarrhytus said:

Since the one baptism exists in the catholic Church alone, I therefore judge that those coming from heretics and schismatics, having received nothing from them, must be baptized in the Church.

72. Another Lucius, of Ausafa, said:

Since there is one God and Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, one hope, and one Church, I say that what has been done among heretics must be annulled and that those coming from them must be baptized in the Church.

73. Another Felix, of Gurgites, said:

I judge that, according to the precepts of the Holy Scriptures, lawless persons baptized among heretics, if they take refuge in the Church, must be baptized with the Church’s baptism, where all authority has been given by God.

[Col. 1097D] 74. Pusillus of Lamasba said:

I believe that saving baptism exists only in the catholic Church and that, when it is performed outside the Church, it is a counterfeit.

75. Salvianus of Ganzafala said:

It is established that heretics possess nothing, and therefore they come to us so that they may receive what they do not possess.

76. Honoratus of Tucca said:

Since Christ is the truth, we must follow truth rather than custom, so that we may sanctify with the Church’s baptism the heretics who come to us precisely because they could receive nothing outside.

77. Victor of Octavum said:

[Col. 1099A] I too hold that those coming from heresy must without doubt be baptized.

Clarus of Mascula said:

78. The judgment of our Lord Jesus Christ is evident: he sent his apostles and entrusted this authority to them alone. We have succeeded them, governing God’s Church with the same authority and baptizing those who believe. Heretics, therefore, who possess neither that authority nor the Church, cannot baptize with the Church’s baptism.

79. Secundianus of Thambeae said:

We must not deceive heretics by our own presumption, lest, when the day of judgment comes, those who were not [Col. 1099B] baptized in the Church of our Lord Jesus Christ charge us with the fact that through us they were not baptized and did not obtain pardon and remission of sins. Therefore, since there is one Church and one baptism, when they are converted to us they must obtain baptism together with the Church.

80. Aurelius of Chullabi said:

The apostle John said in his letter: “If anyone comes to you and does not possess the teaching of Christ, do not receive him into the house or say ‘Greetings’ to him. For whoever says ‘Greetings’ to him participates in his evil words and deeds.” How, then, can they be admitted into God’s house, or how can we enter into communion with them without the Church’s baptism, without thereby participating in their evil deeds?

81. Licteus of Gemellae said:

If a blind man leads a blind man, both fall into the pit. Since, therefore, it is established that heretics cannot enlighten anyone, because they are themselves blind, the baptism of such persons is invalid.

82. Natalis of Oea said:

Both I, who am present, and Pompeius of Sabrata and Dioga of Leptis Magna, who commissioned me and, though absent in body, are present in spirit, judge—as do many of our fellow bishops—that heretics cannot have communion with us unless they have been baptized by us.

83. Junius of Neapolis said:

I do not depart from what we once judged: that we should baptize heretics [Col. 1099D] who come to the Church.

84. Cyprian of Carthage said:

My judgment is most fully expressed in the letter written to our colleague Jubaianus: heretics, who according to evangelical and apostolic testimony are called adversaries of Christ and antichrists, must, when they come to the Church, be baptized with the Church’s unique baptism, so that from adversaries they may become friends and from antichrists Christians.

**Zonaras.** These, then, are the judgments of the Fathers who assembled with the great Cyprian in this council; but they did not prevail in the case of all heretics or of schismatics. For the Second Ecumenical Council, as has already been said, excepted certain heretics and decreed that they should be received without baptism, merely anointed with holy chrism and each anathematizing his own [Col. 1101A] heresy, as well as all heresies collectively. For this reason these judgments have not been expounded, since they were less necessary and no longer operative, but have only been recorded in summary form.

## LETTER OF THE GREAT CYPRIAN TO JOVIANUS AND HIS FELLOW BISHOPS

[Col. 1082A]

While assembled in council, beloved brothers, we read the letter sent by you concerning those who come to the catholic Church after appearing to have been baptized among heretics or schismatics—the catholic Church being one, and the Church in which we are baptized and born again. We are confident that, by acting as you do in that place, you yourselves uphold the steadfastness of the catholic Church. Nevertheless, since you share communion with us and wished, because of our common love, to inquire about this matter, we do not offer you a novel opinion or one only now established. Rather, we share and join with you the judgment that was long ago tested with all exactness and care by our predecessors and has also been observed by you. We now likewise decree [Col. 1082B] that it must always be held firmly and securely that no one can be baptized outside the catholic Church, since there is one baptism and it exists only in the catholic Church.

For it is written: “They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water, and dug for themselves broken cisterns that cannot hold water.” Again, Holy Scripture gives forewarning: “Keep away from strange water, and do not drink from a strange fountain.” The water must first be cleansed and sanctified by the priest so that by his baptism it may wash away the sins of the person being baptized. Through the prophet Ezekiel the Lord says: “I will sprinkle clean water upon you and cleanse you; I will give you a new heart, and I will give a new spirit within you.”

How can one who is himself unclean [Col. 1082C] and in whom the Holy Spirit does not dwell cleanse and sanctify water? For the Lord says in Numbers: “Everything that the unclean person touches shall be unclean.” How can one who was unable to lay aside his own sins outside the Church give another remission of sins by baptizing him?

The very question asked at baptism is also a witness to the truth. For when we say to the person being examined, “Do you believe that you receive eternal life and remission of sins?” we say nothing other than that these can be given in the catholic Church. Among heretics, however, where the Church does not exist, it is impossible to receive remission of sins. The defenders of heretics must therefore either alter the interrogatory or vindicate the truth—unless, indeed, they also assign the Church to those whom they confidently affirm to possess baptism.

It is also necessary that the baptized person be anointed, [Col. 1082D] so that, having received the chrism (*chrisma*), he may become a participant in Christ. But a heretic, who has neither altar nor Church, cannot sanctify oil. Consequently, chrism cannot exist at all among heretics. It is plain to us that oil cannot possibly be sanctified among them for eucharistic use. We ought to know, and not be ignorant, that it is written: “Let not the oil of a sinner anoint my head.” This the Holy Spirit also proclaimed long ago in the Psalms, lest anyone, having been tracked down and led astray from the straight way, should be anointed among heretics, Christ’s adversaries.

How can one who is not a priest but a sacrilegious sinner pray for the person being baptized, when Scripture says: “God does not hear sinners; but if anyone is devout and does his will, him [Col. 1084A] he hears”? Through the holy Church we understand remission of sins. But who can give what he himself does not possess? Or how can one who has cast away the Holy Spirit perform spiritual acts?

Therefore, one who comes to the Church must also be renewed, so that within it he may be sanctified through the holy ones; for it is written: “You shall be holy, as I am holy, says the Lord.” Thus one who was beguiled in error may, in true and ecclesiastical baptism, put off this very thing also: that, as a man coming to God and seeking a priest, he encountered a sacrilegious man because he had fallen into error.

To approve the baptism of heretics and schismatics is to assent to those baptized by them. It cannot prevail only in part: if a man was able to baptize, he was also able to give the Holy Spirit; but if he could not, because, being outside, he does not possess the Holy Spirit, he cannot baptize the person who comes to him. For there is one [Col. 1084B] baptism, one Holy Spirit, and one Church, founded from the beginning by Christ our Lord upon the apostle Peter with the declaration of unity.

For this reason, everything done by them, being false and empty, is invalid. Nothing done by those whom the Lord calls his enemies and adversaries in the Gospels can be acceptable or pleasing to God: “Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters.”

The blessed apostle John, observing the Lord’s commandments, wrote beforehand in his epistle: “You have heard that Antichrist is coming; and now many antichrists have arisen, from which we know that it is the last hour. They went out from us, but they were not of us.” Hence we too ought to understand and recognize that those called the Lord’s enemies and antichrists [Col. 1084C] cannot give the Lord’s grace.

Therefore we, who belong to the Lord, practice the Lord’s unity, and minister his priesthood in the Church according to the dignity he has conferred, must reject, repudiate, and cast away everything done by those opposed to him—that is, his enemies and antichrists—and regard it as profane. To those who come from error and perversity to recognition of the true and ecclesiastical faith, we must give the mystery of catholic power, unity, faith, and truth.

**ZONARAS.** This letter commands without exception that those who were baptized by heretics or schismatics and afterward approach the catholic Church must be baptized. It supports its argument by various reflections, proofs, and scriptural passages. But the Second Ecumenical [Col. 1084D] Council, in its seventh canon, does not command all who return from heresies to be baptized from the beginning. Rather, it enumerates some who are to be received upon presenting written declarations and anathematizing, each his own heresy and every teaching that does not accord with the doctrine of God’s holy catholic and apostolic Church, and upon being sealed—that is, anointed—with holy chrism. It determines that all the rest, some of whom it also lists by name, are to be baptized and received as Greeks, that is, pagans.

That canon has been explained in its own place. It is therefore evident that this ordinance was not accepted by the later holy Fathers. Since the two councils introduced contrary provisions on this point, the decree of the second council prevails, both because it was later and because it was ecumenical: at it there were certainly assembled representatives of all the patriarchal thrones, whether the patriarchs themselves or their deputies.

That the present canon was not accepted by all the holy Fathers is also shown by the second canon of the council held in Trullo, called the Sixth Council. For when the holy Fathers of that council enumerated the canons that ought to remain in force, they said the following concerning this canon in these very words:

“Moreover, also the canon set forth by Cyprian, who was archbishop of the region of the Africans and a martyr, and by the council held under him, which prevailed only in the territories of those prelates, according to the custom handed down to them.”

From this, therefore, it is shown that even from the beginning the canon was not operative among all. Such, then, is the content of the letter. The judgments delivered in the common deliberation by each of those gathered at the council are as follows in summary.

[Col. 1086B] **Cyprian said:**

You have heard, beloved fellow bishops, what Jovianus, our fellow bishop, wrote to me, wishing to obtain advice from my modest judgment concerning the impious and unlawful baptism of heretics, and what I wrote back to him, decreeing what we have judged once, twice, and often: that heretics approaching the Church must be baptized with baptism and sanctified. Other letters of Jovianus were then read to you; through them, in his devout reply, he not only agreed with us [Col. 1086C] but also expressed gratitude for coming to knowledge of the truth.

It therefore remains for each of you to say what he thinks about the matter, with none of you being judged in this respect or, should he think differently, being excluded from communion. For no one sets himself up as bishop over the others, nor by tyrannical arrogance forces his fellow bishops to follow him, since each individual bishop possesses authority to act freely according to what he thinks. Just as he cannot judge another, neither can he be judged by another. For we all await the judgment of our Lord Jesus Christ, who alone has authority to appoint a bishop in his Church and to examine and test the conduct of each.

[Col. 1086D] **Caecilius Liberalis said:**

I know one baptism in the Church alone, and nowhere outside the Church. For where the one baptism exists, there truly exist the hope of truth and faith. Thus it is written: “One faith, one baptism.”

It does not exist among heretics, among whom there is no faith or hope, where everything is false; where one possessed by a demon performs exorcism; where one whose mouth speaks pestilential and poisonous things asks the sacramental question; where an unbeliever gives faith, a sinner grants remission of sins, and Antichrist baptizes in the name of Christ; where a dead man promises life, one alien to peace gives peace, a blasphemer invokes God, an impious man exercises priestly ministry, a sacrilegious man sets up an altar, and one who serves the devil offers sacrifice to God.

Let those who defend them say that all these things are false concerning heretics. See what things the Church is compelled to approve, so as to enter into communion with such persons without baptism [Col. 1088A] and remission of sins. Hence, brothers, we must flee and turn aside, separate ourselves from such transgressions, and retain the one baptism bestowed by God in the Church alone.

**Priamus of Mastripa said:**

I decree that every person coming from heresy must be baptized. For he has been baptized there in vain, since there is but one baptism in the Church alone. There is one God, one baptism, and one Church, in which baptism, sanctification, and all other things pertaining to salvation and eternal life are accomplished. Things done outside the Church attain none of these.

**Polycarp of Hadrumetum said:**

Those who approve the baptism of heretics render ours invalid.

[Col. 1088B] **Nousatus of Thannus Regis said:**

[Note: [Col. 1088D] Perhaps *Novatus*.]

Since all the Scriptures bear witness concerning the one and only saving baptism in the Church, we must confess our faith by baptizing with the true baptism the heretics and schismatics who approach the Church after their false baptism. Therefore I baptized all who came from there, and I assigned to the laity those who belonged to their clergy.

[Note: [Col. 1088D] Read: “Since all.”]

**Nemesianus of Thubunae said:**

All the Scriptures bear witness that the baptism given by a heretic or schismatic is not true, since their leaders are themselves false Christs and false prophets.

**Januarius of Laba said:**

According to the commands of the Holy Scriptures, I judge that all heretics must be baptized and thus received into the holy Church.

**Lucius of Castra Galbae said:**

[Col. 1088C] The Lord says in the Gospel: “You are the salt of the earth; but if the salt becomes insipid, with what shall it be salted?” Since, therefore, it is plain that heretics—that is, God’s enemies—cannot give anyone life through a spiritual confession, because they have become insipid and are outside the Church, we must baptize them with holy baptism when they come.

**Crescens of Cirta said:**

[Note: [Col. 1088D] Read: “of Cirta.”]

I too judge that heretics and schismatics, whenever they come to the catholic Church, must not be received before they have been exorcized and baptized, except those who were baptized in the Church and afterward deserted it. These, upon repenting, ought to receive only the laying on of hands.

[Note: [Col. 1088D] Read: “those in the Church.”]

[Col. 1088D] **Nicomedes of Segermes said:**

[Note: [Col. 1088D] Perhaps for “of Segermes.”]

My decision is that heretics approaching the Church [Col. 1090A] are to be baptized, since, having been baptized by heretics, they received no remission of sins outside.

**Secundianus of Carindia said:**
