Our Lord Jesus Christ says, “Whoever is not with me is against me,” and the apostle John calls those who depart from the Church antichrists. For it is impossible for them to minister God’s grace and saving baptism. I therefore judge that those who approach the Church must be baptized by us.

**Felix of Gametae said:**

Just as a blind man leading a blind man falls with him into the pit, so a heretic baptizing a heretic dies together with the baptized person. The heretic must therefore be baptized among us, [Col. 1090B] lest we who are alive enter into communion with the dead.

**Successus of Abbir Germaniciana said:**

Either heretics are permitted nothing or they are permitted everything. If they can baptize, they can also give the Holy Spirit; but since they do not possess the Spirit, neither do they baptize spiritually. I therefore judge that heretics must be baptized.

**Fortunatus of Thucabor said:**

Those outside the Church and opposed to Christ, who scatter his sheep and flock, cannot baptize outside it.

**Sedatus of Thuburbo said:**

We must strive with all our strength to ensure that one who has abandoned the error of the heretics does not hesitate [Col. 1090C] to receive the Church’s unique baptism, since whoever has not been baptized with it is excluded from the kingdom of heaven.

**Privatianus of Sufetula said:**

If heresy is from God, the heretic will also possess God’s gift. But if it is not from God, how can he possess God’s grace and give it to another?

**Munnulus of Girba said:**

Since the Lord says, “Baptize all nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,” we know plainly that heretics possess neither the Father, nor the Son, nor the Holy Spirit. Those coming to the Church must therefore be baptized, that they may be born again.

**Politianus of Mileum said:**

It is right for one coming from heresy to be baptized in the Church. [Col. 1090D]

**Theognis of Hippo Regius said:**

In accordance with the sacrament of God and the heavenly grace we have received, we know the baptism that is in the holy Church.

**Dativus of Badis said:**

So far as it lies with us, we do not enter into communion with heretics unless they have been baptized in the Church and received remission of sins.

**Privatus of Sufes said:**

What else does one who approves baptism among heretics do but enter into communion with heretics?

**Hortensianus of Lares said:**

We too vindicate for the Church the one baptism that we know in the Church.

[Col. 1092A] **Cassius of Macomades said:**

[Note: [Col. 1092D] In the Greek read *Macomades*.]

Since there cannot be two baptisms, one who concedes baptism to heretics deprives himself of baptism. I therefore confirm that heretics must be baptized when they come to the Church, except those who separated from the Church’s faithful and surrendered themselves to the darkness of heresy; when they return, they must be received by the laying on of hands alone.

**Januarius of Vicus said:**

If error does not assent to truth, much less does truth assent to error. Therefore we stand by the Church in which we have also been placed in the presiding seat, so that we may baptize those who were not baptized in it.

[Note: [Col. 1092D] Another reading: “over which we were appointed to preside.”]

**Secundinus of Carpi said:**

[Note: [Col. 1092D] Read: *Carpi*.]

If heretics are Christians, why are they not in the Church [Col. 1092B] of God? But if they are not Christians, let them become Christians. It is therefore plain that the Holy Spirit cannot descend upon alien children and the offspring of Antichrist merely through the laying on of hands.

**Victorinus of Thabraca said:**

If heretics are permitted to baptize, give the Holy Spirit, and grant remission of sins, why do we speak falsely against them by calling them heretics?

**Another Felix, of Uthina, said:**

We must affirm that all heretics approaching the Church are to be baptized, so that the perversion that occurred outside may be corrected and sanctified.

**Quietus of Baruch said:**

[Col. 1092C] If those baptized among heretics obtain remission of sins and eternal life, why do they come to the Church? But if they come to repentance, in which they are also given life through the baptism that is in the catholic Church, they must be baptized and sanctified.

**Castus of Sicca said:**

One who disregards truth and follows custom is either envious toward the brothers to whom truth has been revealed or ungrateful toward God who revealed it.

**Eucratius of Thenae said:**

Heretics coming to the Church must be baptized with right and catholic baptism, so that, having washed away their sins, they may be sanctified.

[Col. 1092D] **Libosus of Vaga said:**

The Lord says, “I am the truth.” Thus, when truth has been revealed, let custom yield, so that even if someone formerly did not baptize heretics in the Church, he may baptize them now.

[Note: [Col. 1092D] We supplied this heading, which was absent, from the Royal manuscript and Beveridge’s edition.]

**Lucius of Theveste said:**

Heretics who are blasphemous and impious, and who falsify the divine Scriptures with deceitful words, must be anathematized. We must therefore exorcize and baptize such persons.

**Eugenius of Ammaedara said:**

I too judge that heretics must be baptized.

[Col. 1094A] **Another Felix, of Amacura, said:**

Following the rule of the divine Scriptures, I too declare that heretics and schismatics must be baptized.

**Januarius of Muzula said:**

If heretics possess baptism, we do not; if we possess it, heretics cannot. It is beyond dispute that the catholic Church uses Christ’s baptism, since she alone possesses Christ’s grace, love, and truth.

[Note: [Col. 1094D] Also read: “If heretics.”]

**Adelphius of Thasualta said:**

Some oppose the truth in vain by saying that we rebaptize. For the Church does not rebaptize heretics but baptizes them.

[Col. 1094B] **Demetrius of Leptis Minor said:**

Those who say that heretics baptize truly and lawfully introduce not only two but many baptisms. For since the heresies are diverse and numerous, the baptisms too are counted according to their number.

**Vincentius of Thibaris said:**

We know that heretics are worse than schismatics. But if they repent and wish to come to the rule of truth, they must first be exorcized and then baptized; for only then can they attain Christ’s promise.

**Marius of Mactaris said:**

I judge that heretics must be baptized as persons possessing nothing.

**Satius of Sicilibba said:**

[Col. 1094C] If heretics receive remission of sins in their own baptism, they approach the Church in vain; for nothing can frighten them at Christ’s judgment if they have received remission of sins.

**Aurelius of Utica said:**

[Note: [Col. 1094D] Read: *Utica*.]

Since the Apostle says not to participate in the sins of others, heretics must be baptized so that they may first receive remission of sins, and we may then enter into communion with them.

**Jamnus of Germaniciana said:**

Those who approve the baptism of heretics reject ours.

**Lucianus of Rucuma said:**

If light and darkness can have communion, then we [Col. 1094D] and heretics can have something in common. I therefore judge that heretics must be baptized.

**Pelagius of Luperciana said:**

If heresy is not in the Church, how can the Church’s baptism exist among heretics?

**Jader of Midila said:**

One faith, one baptism; but it belongs to the catholic Church to baptize.

**Another Felix, of Marrazana, said:**

The same.

**Paulus of Bobba said:**

[Note: [Col. 1094D] Read: *Bobba*.]

If God is true, how can true baptism exist among heretics, among whom God is not?

[Col. 1096A] **Pomponius of Dionysiana said:**

Heretics cannot baptize or give remission of sins, since they possess no authority to loose or bind anything on earth.

**Venantius of Thumisa said:**

[Note: [Col. 1096D] Another reading: *Thunes*.]

One who makes the Church’s baptism common with heretics hands Christ’s bride over to adulterers.

**Aymnius of Ansvaga said:**

[Note: [Col. 1096D] Read: *Aymnius*.]

We have received one baptism and continue in it. One who says that heretics too are permitted to baptize introduces two baptisms.

**Saturninus of Victoriana said:**

If heretics are permitted to baptize, they are without blame when they act unlawfully; nor will you find why Christ [Col. 1096B] calls them adversaries or the Apostle calls them antichrists.

**Another Saturninus, of Thueca, said:**

Although pagans worship idols, they nevertheless recognize God as Father and Creator and confess him as Lord. Marcion blasphemes against this God; how, then, are those who approve Marcion’s baptism not ashamed?

**Marcellus of Zama said:**

Since remission of sins is given nowhere except in the Church, one who does not baptize a heretic enters into communion with a sinner.

**Irenaeus of Usulae said:**

If the Church does not baptize a heretic because he is said already to have been baptized, heresy is preferred and [Col. 1096C] becomes greater.

**Donatus of Cybalina said:**

One who says that the grace of baptism exists among heretics must first prove that a church exists there.

**Zosimus of Tharassa said:**

Once truth has been revealed, let error yield to truth.

**Julianus of Telepte said:**

It is written: “A person can receive nothing unless it has been given to him from heaven.” If heresy is from heaven, it can also give heavenly baptism.

**Faustus of Timida said:**

Those who oppose the baptism of heretics to the Church’s baptism make them Christians and us heretics. [Col. 1096D]

**Geminus of Furni said:**

What we once judged we still maintain: that we baptize those coming from heresies.

**Rogatianus of Nova said:**

Christ built the Church; the devil built heresy. How, then, can the synagogue of the devil possess Christ’s baptism?

**Therapius of Bulla said:**

What else does one who betrays the Church’s baptism to heretics become but a betrayer of Christ’s bride?

**Lucius of Membresa said:**

It is written that God does not hear sinners. How, then, can a heretic, being a sinner, be heard when he baptizes?

[Col. 1098A] **Another Felix, of Uslaccae, said:**

In receiving heretics without the Church’s baptism, let no one prefer custom to reason and truth.

**Another Saturninus, of Avitina, said:**

If Antichrist can give Christ’s grace, heretics, who have been called antichrists, can also baptize.

**Quintus of Aggiva said:**

There is one God, one Church, and one baptism. How can anyone be baptized where neither God, nor Christ, nor the Church exists?

**Julianus of Marciliana said:**

If a man can serve two masters, God and [Col. 1098B] Mammon, baptism can also serve two masters.

**Tenax of Horrea Coelia said:**

Baptism is one, but it belongs to the Church, whose baptism is true.

**Another Victor, of Assuras, said likewise.**

**Donatulus of Capsa said:**

I have always held that heretics, who can receive nothing outside, must be baptized when they come to the Church.

**Verulus of Rusiccade said:**

Can a heretic give what he does not possess? Much less can a schismatic, who has lost what he possessed.

[Note: [Col. 1098D] The manuscripts and Beveridge likewise read this way, but a question mark must be added, or else it must be read: “cannot give.”]

**Pudentianus of Cuicul said:**

If anyone comes from heresy, it has been rightly [Col. 1098C] and justly determined that he be baptized.

**Petrus of Hippo Diarrhytus said:**

Since there is one baptism in the Church alone, I therefore judge that those coming from heretics and schismatics, having received nothing from there, must be baptized in the Church.

**Another Lucius, of Ausafa, said:**

Since there is one God—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—and one hope and one Church, I say that what is done among heretics must be annulled and that those coming from them must be baptized in the Church.

**Another Felix, of Gurgites, said:**

I judge that, in accordance with the divine Scriptures, lawless persons baptized among heretics, if they take refuge in the Church, must be baptized with the Church’s baptism, where all authority has been given by God.

[Col. 1098D] **Pusillus of Lamasba said:**

I believe that there is no salvation through baptism except in the catholic Church alone, and that when it is performed outside the Church it is an imitation.

**Salvianus of Ganzafala said:**

It is established that heretics possess nothing, and therefore they come to us so that they may receive what they do not possess.

**Honoratus of Tucca said:**

Since Christ is true, we must follow truth rather than custom, so that we may sanctify with the Church’s baptism the heretics who come to us because they could receive nothing outside.

**Victor of Octavum said:**

[Col. 1100A] I too hold that those coming from heresy must be baptized without hesitation.

**Clarus of Mascula said:**

The judgment of our Lord Jesus Christ is evident: he sent his apostles and entrusted authority to them alone. We follow them, governing God’s Church by their authority and baptizing those who believe. Heretics, therefore, who possess neither authority nor the Church, cannot baptize with the Church’s baptism.

**Secundianus of Thambeae said:**

We must by no means ensnare heretics through our contentiousness, lest those who were not baptized in the Church of our Lord [Col. 1100B] Jesus Christ accuse us when the day of judgment comes, because through us they were not baptized and did not receive remission of sins. Therefore, since there is one Church and one baptism, when they come to us they must obtain baptism together with the Church.

**Aurelius of Chullabi said:**

The apostle John said in his epistle: “If anyone comes to you and does not bring the teaching of God, do not receive him into the house or say ‘Greetings’ to him. Whoever says ‘Greetings’ to him participates in his words and evil deeds.” How, then, can such persons be received into God’s house, or how can we enter into communion with them without the Church’s baptism, without thereby participating in their evil deeds?

**Victor of Gemellae said:**

If a blind man leads a blind man, both will fall into the pit. Since, therefore, it is plain that a heretic cannot enlighten anyone, because heretics are themselves blind, the baptism of such persons is nothing.

**Natalis of Oea said:**

[Note: [Col. 1100D] Read: *Natalis*.]

Both I, who am present, and Pompeius of Sabrata and Dioga of Leptis Magna, who commissioned me and, though absent in body, are present in spirit, judge—as do many of our fellow bishops—that heretics cannot enter into communion with us unless they have been baptized by us.

**Junius of Neapolis said:**

I do not depart from what we once judged: that we should [Col. 1100D] baptize heretics coming to the Church.

**Cyprian of Carthage said:**

My decision is displayed in its entirety by the letter written to Jovianus, our fellow bishop: heretics, who according to evangelical and apostolic testimony are called adversaries of Christ and antichrists, must, when they approach the Church, be baptized with the Church’s one baptism, so that from enemies they may become friends and from antichrists Christians.

**ZONARAS.** These, then, are the judgments of the Fathers who assembled with the great Cyprian at this council. But they did not prevail with respect to all heretics or to schismatics. For the Second Ecumenical Council, as [Col. 1102A] has already been said, excepted certain heretics and decreed that they should be received without baptism, merely anointed with divine chrism and each anathematizing his own heresy, as well as all heresies without exception. For this reason these judgments were not expounded, since they were unnecessary and no longer operative, but were recorded only in summary form.

## EIGHTH COUNCIL, HELD ABOUT THE YEAR 257

Although I am entirely persuaded that St. Jerome was mistaken when he wrote that the same African bishops who, with St. Cyprian, had sanctioned rebaptism later assembled again, issued a new decree, and changed their judgment concerning baptism, [Col. 1101B] I nevertheless thought that a place should be given in this collection of yours to this meeting of bishops. Likewise, certain councils are reported in the commonly available editions of the councils which, it is nevertheless established, were never held. This is done simply so that nothing connected with this subject, whether true or false, may be omitted.

Jerome therefore says in the *Dialogue Against the Luciferians* that the very bishops who, with blessed Cyprian, had determined that heretics must be rebaptized returned to the ancient custom and issued a new decree by which, evidently, the preceding council’s doctrine concerning the baptism of heretics was condemned.

Many considerations appear to conflict with this opinion of Jerome. First, the authority of the Council of Arles establishes [Col. 1101C] that the doctrine of rebaptism remained in force among the Africans for a long time after Cyprian. Second, this very fact is also proved by the council held at Carthage under Bishop Gratus. Although that council consisted of bishops whose disposition was opposed to rebaptism, [Col. 1102A] it nevertheless demonstrates that the doctrine had not yet been abolished among the Africans, even though most held the contrary view.

Furthermore, it is established that Cyprian’s council still possessed authority in the age of Vincent of Lérins. This is proved by the example of the Donatists, who, as Vincent himself says—and as is also established from the proceedings of the Conference of Carthage and numerous passages in Augustine—boasted that they rebaptized on the authority of that council. [Col. 1102B]

Finally, no testimony to this supposed new decree exists anywhere else in the whole of antiquity. Yet had it existed, the opponents of the Donatists would undoubtedly have made frequent use of it. On the contrary, Augustine observes in Letter 48 that Cyprian is not found to have corrected his judgment concerning the rebaptism of heretics. This can also be gathered abundantly from book II, chapter 8, *Against Gaudentius*.

It is therefore possible that Jerome, seeing rebaptism rejected by the African Catholics—perhaps out of hostility toward the Donatists—supposed that the Africans had returned to the ancient custom immediately after the council held under Cyprian, [Col. 1102C] just as Augustine, in book III, chapter 2 of *On Baptism*, says that they returned to the former custom after Agrippinus.

STEPHEN BALUZE  
(*New Collection*)

[Col. 1101]

## LETTERS CONCERNING THE BAPTISM OF HERETICS

## FRAGMENT OF A LETTER FROM DIONYSIUS, BISHOP OF ALEXANDRIA, TO POPE STEPHEN

### Preface

[Note: [Col. 1101D]

**The first.** Eusebius calls it the first because Dionysius afterward wrote four other letters, both to Xystus and to Dionysius, Stephen’s successors, likewise concerning the baptism of heretics. COUSTANT.

**The first author.** Cyprian himself, in Letter 71 to Quintus and elsewhere, professes that he follows his predecessor Agrippinus. Firmilian, moreover, teaches that the judgment defended by Cyprian [Col. 1102D] had previously been confirmed by the Council of Iconium. Cyprian, therefore, must be considered the first author not of the judgment that heretics should be baptized, but of the controversy over that matter that arose between the Africans and the Roman pontiffs. COUSTANT.

**Novatus.** In his customary manner, Eusebius here substitutes the name Novatus for Novatian. In the preceding passage, a learned man [Col. 1103B] does not think that Eusebius grasped Dionysius’s meaning altogether successfully; instead of saying “when the fury of the persecution had now abated,” he would better have said, “when the storm of the schism had now subsided.” From this passage it is clear that the disturbances described as settled in the fragment appended below are not those most recently stirred up in the East over the baptism of heretics, but those introduced somewhat earlier by Novatian’s faction.

Eusebius was nevertheless not wrong in noting that the letter itself was written concerning the baptism of heretics. For in its first and principal part Dionysius had discussed this subject extensively, as he himself recalls in his letter to Xystus, asking and imploring Stephen—doubtless—not to act precipitately in so difficult a matter or rupture peace with so many distinguished bishops. COUSTANT.]

Eusebius prefaces the appended fragment as follows:

Dionysius addressed to Stephen the first of the letters he wrote concerning baptism, when a considerable controversy had arisen over whether those converted from any heresy whatsoever ought to be cleansed by baptism. For the ancient custom had prevailed that, in receiving such persons, only the laying on of hands accompanied by prayers should be employed.

Cyprian, who then governed the Church of Carthage, was the first to judge that they should not be admitted unless they had first been cleansed from error through baptism. Stephen, however, believing that nothing should be changed contrary to the tradition that had prevailed from the beginning, took this very badly.

Dionysius therefore wrote to him at length concerning this subject. Near the end, he informed him that all the churches everywhere, now that the fury of persecution had abated, had made peace with one another after repudiating the turbulent novelty of Novatus. He writes as follows (Eusebius, book VIII, chapters 2, 3, and 4):

Know, brother, that all the churches situated throughout the East and farther beyond, which had formerly been divided, have now—

[Col. 1103A]

[Note: [Col. 1103B]

**Mazabenes of Aelia.** The sequence of the Greek text would require: “Mazabenes of Aelia, Marinus of Tyre.” Valesius observed that this textual error [Col. 1104B] had long ago been corrected by Rufinus. For it is established that Alexander—whose blessed departure Dionysius reports to Pope Cornelius in Eusebius, book VI, chapter 46—was bishop of Aelia, or, as Eusebius says in the passage cited, Jerusalem, and not of Tyre. COUSTANT.

**You supply.** This refers to the pious custom of the Romans, which Eusebius, book IV, chapter 23, as we have already observed, testifies was maintained from the beginning of the religion down to his own time: namely, that they sent the necessary supports of life to a great many churches, even distant ones. For the same reason, above, page 78, Soter is praised by Dionysius, bishop of Corinth. COUSTANT.

**God.** Other fragments survive of letters that St. Dionysius wrote concerning the baptism of heretics and the Sabellian heresy, both to St. Dionysius the pope and to Philemon—after whose name “presbyters” appears in a materially uncertain construction—and also to St. Xystus the pope. See below, volume V of this library. EDITORS.]
at last returned to unity, and that all the prelates of the churches everywhere are of one and the same mind, and rejoice with incredible joy at the peace unexpectedly restored: namely, Demetrianus, bishop of Antioch; Theoctistus of Caesarea; Mazabanes of Aelia, after the death of Alexander; Marinus of Tyre; Heliodorus of Laodicea, after the death of Thelymidres; Helenus of Tarsus and all the churches of Cilicia; Firmilianus with all Cappadocia. For I have named only the more distinguished bishops, lest perhaps our letter become too lengthy and its discourse too burdensome. All Syria and Arabia—to whom you repeatedly furnish what is necessary, and to whom you have now written—as well as Mesopotamia, Pontus, and Bithynia, and, to sum it up in a single phrase, everyone everywhere throughout the world exults in this concord [Col. 1103B] and brotherly charity, praising God.

[Col. 1102C] Know now, brother, that all the churches throughout the East and still [Col. 1104A] farther afield that were formerly divided have been united, and all their leaders everywhere are of one mind, rejoicing beyond measure at the peace that has come about contrary to expectation: Demetrianus at Antioch; Theoctistus at Caesarea; Mazabanes at Aelia, Alexander having fallen asleep; Marinus at Tyre; Heliodorus at Laodicea, Thelymidres having entered into rest; Helenus at Tarsus and all the churches of Cilicia; Firmilianus and all Cappadocia. For I have named only the more prominent of the bishops, so that I might add neither length to the letter nor weight to the discourse. All Syria, moreover, and Arabia—to whom you give assistance on every occasion, and to whom you have now written—as well as Mesopotamia, Pontus, and Bithynia, and, to speak comprehensively, everyone everywhere exults in this concord and brotherly love, glorifying God.

## LETTER OF ST. CYPRIAN TO QUINTUS  
### ON THE BAPTISM OF HERETICS

(Erasm. p. 397. Pamel. Rigalt. Baluz. Oxon. Lips. LXXI.)

[Col. 1103C]

[Note: [Col. 1103D]

**LETTER TO QUINTUS. I.—“To Quintus, his brother.”** He calls him his colleague as well, and the following letter attests that he was stationed in Mauretania; there it also mentions [Col. 1104D] this letter. RIGALT.

**“While they say that baptism exists even among heretics.”** And among the canons called the Canons of the Apostles it is stated most explicitly: “Those baptized or ordained by heretics can be neither members of the faithful nor clerics.” Canon 68. RIGALT.

**“He who is baptized by one dead, what benefit does he derive from his washing?”** Our Cyprian and other Fathers quite often seize upon anything from the Scriptures that appears to support their argument even merely by the sound of the words, although it must be understood in a very different sense; we have noted some such instances above. But what most people suppose to be cited here from the thirtieth chapter of Ecclesiasticus is altogether at variance [Col. 1105C] with the Wisdom of Sirach. Cyprian says quite correctly, however, that heretics and schismatics who are outside the Church are numbered among the dead—that is, the spiritually dead. Yet Sirach meant nothing of the kind. He said only that one who washes himself “from a dead body” (*apo nekrou*), that is, from contact with a corpse, and washes away the uncleanness he had contracted through contamination by the corpse, loses the benefit of that washing if he afterward returns to contact with the corpse, because he has defiled himself by a new contact with the dead. That meaning contributes absolutely nothing to Cyprian’s intention.

Therefore, whoever was the author of the saying, “He who is baptized by one dead, what benefit does he derive from his washing?”—for I could never believe that Cyprian was the first to employ it—understood by the designation “dead” one of the gods of the nations, who had once been human beings and were already dead when they began to be numbered among the gods; or, if not one of such gods, at least one of the priests or worshipers of such gods, who were likewise numbered by Christians among the dead of this world. Accordingly, so that the author of that saying might transfer Sirach’s words to his own meaning concerning those baptized outside the Church, he omitted what follows in Sirach: “and touches it again.” By that omission, Sirach’s entire meaning is certainly destroyed. Thus, from what Sirach had said—“He who is baptized from a dead body and touches it again derives no benefit from his washing”—he produced an entirely different saying: “He who is baptized by one dead derives no benefit from his washing.” Because this wonderfully pleased the uneducated Christians, on account of the designation “the dead,” which was very familiar to them, Sirach’s meaning was thereafter neglected, and the saying passed into a proverb.

I would therefore prefer to suppose that Cyprian took this, not from Sirach, but from a popular proverb, rather than to say that so great a man had not read or had not understood Sirach. Indeed, one may gather that Augustine also held this opinion from the fact that, in his lengthy disputation against Cresconius, in which he refutes Cyprian’s position rather sharply, he does not relate these very words uttered by Cyprian back to Sirach’s meaning. Instead, taking them as they were then commonly spoken by the people, he interprets them in such a way as to determine that baptism given by one dead—that is, by a heretic or schismatic—outside the Church begins to benefit the baptized person when one so baptized passes into the body of Christ, which is the Church of the living God.

It is also cited in this form by Quietus, bishop of Buruch, at the Council of Carthage, and by Augustine, Book I, *Against Petilian*, chapter 9: “Likewise, when he hears, ‘He who is baptized by one dead derives no benefit from his washing,’ he will answer: ‘Christ lives,’” etc. Those are baptized by the dead who are baptized in the temples of idols; for they themselves do not believe that they receive from their priests the sanctification they imagine, but from their gods, who, because they were human beings, are therefore dead. RIG.

This was not at all a common proverb; rather, the words of Cyprian, who says “it is written: ‘Those who are baptized by one dead,’” etc., establish that a scriptural text is cited here. In support of this conjecture one may add the observation of Joseph Scaliger, *Elenchus*, chapter XI, §8, that people customarily cite the best-known sayings in an abbreviated form. As an example he adduces Matthew 15:5: “A gift—whatever benefit you might have received from me.” We see something similar in Suidas in the use of the proverb “from a sinking [ship],” which, if stated in full, is actually: “Whatever you take from a sinking ship is gain.”

Perhaps St. Paul may be thought to have alluded to this established form of speech at 1 Corinthians 15:29: “What will those who are baptized for the dead accomplish?”—what will those baptized or washed for the dead achieve or gain? St. Luke spoke in the same sense: “He made five other talents.” If the dead can pollute, at least they can do something. And the living who arrange to be purified from an unclean contact acknowledge that punishments await the unexpiated, and consequently that the soul survives after death. It is very well known that the same proverbial expressions are applied in widely different senses. FELL.]

### I

Cyprian [Note: [Col. 1103D] “To his brother Quintinus”: Erasm.] to his brother Quintus, greetings.—Our fellow presbyter Lucianus has reported to me, dearest brother, that you wished us to explain to you [Note: “What we think”: Lam. Bod. 2.] what we think about those who appear to have been baptized among heretics and schismatics. To inform you what judgment a great many fellow bishops, together with the fellow presbyters who were present, recently reached on this matter in council, I have sent you a copy of that same letter.

For I do not know by what presumption some of our colleagues are led to think that those who have been immersed among heretics [Note: “and schismatics”: Lam. Ebor. NC. 1. Bod. 2.] ought not to be baptized when they come to us, on the ground that, as they say, there is one baptism [Col. 1103D]—namely, the one baptism that exists in the Catholic Church. Since this Church [Note: “Since this Church is one”: Bod. 1, 2. Lin. NC. 1. Ebor. “If it is one, and baptism can exist”: Corb. “Namely, that one baptism exists in the one Church, and baptism cannot exist outside the Church”: MR. “Outside the Church”: Lam. Ebor. Lin. NC. 1. Bod. 1, 2.], if it is one, baptism cannot exist outside the Church [Col. 1104C]. For since there cannot be two baptisms, if heretics truly baptize, then they possess baptism; and whoever lends them this protection on his own authority yields and consents to them, so that [Note: “the enemy and adversary of Christ appears to possess”: Lam. Ebor. NC. 1. Bod. 1, 2. Lin.] the enemies and adversaries of Christ appear to possess the power to wash, purify, and sanctify a human being.

We, however, say that those who come from there are not rebaptized among us, but baptized. For they receive nothing there, where there is nothing; rather, they come to us so that they may receive here, where all grace and truth exist, because grace and truth are one. Moreover, some of our colleagues prefer to confer honor upon heretics rather than agree with us. While, by affirming one baptism, they refuse to baptize those who come to us, they thereby either create two baptisms themselves, when they say that baptism also exists among heretics, or else—which is more serious—they strive to place and prefer the filthy [Col. 1104D] and profane immersion of heretics above the true, unique, and lawful baptism of the Catholic Church [Col. 1105A]. They fail to consider that it is written: “He who is baptized by one dead, what benefit does he derive from his washing?” (Ecclesiasticus 34:30). [Note: “from the washing”: Bod. 1. Lin.]

It is evident that those who are not in the Church of Christ are numbered among the dead, and that one who does not himself live cannot give life to another, since there is one Church which, having obtained the grace of eternal life, both lives forever and gives life to the people of God.

[Note: [Col. 1106D]

**II.—“A sheep estranged and wandering.”** No longer from Christ’s flock, but from Novatus’s. Yet the reading “driven away” seems truer. The ancient glosses give *abigator, abactor, abigens*: “one who drives away.” And the jurists used the expression “crime of cattle-rustling.” ID.

**“No prescription, however, is to be based upon custom.”** And yet, after many disputes, custom prevailed. Jerome explicitly attests this in *Against the Luciferians*: “Finally,” he says, “those very bishops who, together with Cyprian, had determined that heretics must be rebaptized returned to the ancient custom and issued a new decree. What are we to do? Our ancestors transmitted it thus to us, and their ancestors likewise to them.” Augustine, Book III, *Against Cresconius*, chapter 33: “This was the Church’s custom before Cyprian’s council. It could neither be overcome nor abolished even by Cyprian’s council.”

We noted above Augustine’s sound reason for this custom. And it appears possible to lay down this general principle: in those mysteries of the Christian faith where the substance itself is established and the faith has been placed in safety, there is no reason for the peace of Catholic unity to be disturbed by either side. The Fathers of the Church treat this commonplace concerning the force and effect of custom in varying ways, according as it serves their purpose.

Cyprian himself speaks against custom not only here but also in Letter LXIII: “For one ought not to follow human custom, but God’s truth.” And in Letter LXXIV: “Nor should a custom that has crept in among certain people prevent truth from prevailing and conquering. For custom without truth is merely the antiquity of error.”

Tertullian spoke in favor of custom in his book *On the Crown*, saying that “the perseverance of observance” makes it a suitable witness to an approved tradition. The same author argues against custom in his book *On the Veiling of Virgins*: “No one,” he says, “can prescribe against truth—not the passage of time, not the patronage of persons, not the privilege of regions. For custom commonly takes its beginning from some ignorance or simplicity, is strengthened into usage through succession, and is then asserted against truth. But our Lord Christ called himself TRUTH, not CUSTOM.” Similar statements occur everywhere in Jerome and Augustine. RIG.

**“Peter, whom the Lord chose first.”** Peter was *prōtoklētos*, “called before all the others.” Matthew, chapter 10: “Now the names of the twelve apostles are these: first, Simon, who is called Peter.” Grotius says: “He was undoubtedly appointed by Christ as head of the college, in order to preserve the coherence of the body…. Cyprian demonstrates this admirably in his book *On the Unity of the Church*, on those words of Christ, ‘I will give you the keys.’ ‘Upon one man,’ he says, ‘he builds the Church; and although after his resurrection he grants equal power to all the apostles and says, “As the Father has sent me, so I send you. Receive the Holy Spirit: if you forgive anyone’s sins, they shall be forgiven him; and if you retain anyone’s sins, they shall be retained,” nevertheless, in order to manifest unity, by his own authority he arranged for the origin of that same unity to begin from one man.’”

For so it reads in the ancient copies, as we shall show in the appropriate place. Optatus of Milevis, Book VII: “All the innocent stand there, and the sinner receives the keys, so that the business of unity might be established. Provision was made for a sinner to open to the innocent, lest the innocent shut the sinners out, and the unity that is necessary become impossible.” RIG.

**“Upon whom he built the Church.”** Upon the rock, from which the name Peter was given to him. We have discussed this matter above. Jerome, on the Lord’s words at Matthew 16:18: “In accordance with the metaphor of the rock, it is rightly said to Peter: ‘I will build my Church upon you.’” RIG.

**“So as to say that he held the primacy.”** This passage is far from weakening Peter’s primacy and, consequently, that of the Roman pontiffs; rather, it confirms it. For since in this very statement Cyprian says that Peter was the first chosen by the Lord and repeats what he has often said—that the Church was built upon him—he would contradict himself if he denied Peter’s primacy. Thus he is doing nothing other than commending Peter’s humility and, by Peter’s example, inviting his other colleagues to concord: so that, just as Peter, though he was first, nevertheless did not insolently boast of his primacy, neither should they cling so tenaciously to their own opinion that they despised others in comparison with themselves.

That the discussion is certainly not about Stephen can also be gathered from the fact that Cyprian had not yet written to him about this opinion; for the letter immediately following, addressed to Stephen, establishes that the present letter was written first. And so he seems to me to be speaking of the same people whom he indicates at the Council of Carthage when he says: “Let no one appoint himself bishop of bishops.” St. Augustine, in the aforesaid Book VI, chapter 2, and St. Jerome, *Against the Luciferians*, expressly understand this of Cyprian’s colleagues. Indeed, St. Augustine, in the aforesaid Book I, uses this passage rather to confirm the primacy of Peter and of the Apostolic See. PAMEL.

Matthew, at the cited passage: “First, Simon, who is called Peter.” Paul’s Letter to the Galatians, as it is commonly read, places Peter between James and John: “James and Cephas and John, who were reputed to be pillars.” Mark’s Gospel, chapter 16, after mentioning the apostles collectively, adds Peter separately: “Tell his disciples and Peter.” But neither that middle position nor this final one detracts anything from the primacy.

For highly trustworthy men attest that in a very ancient copy of Paul the name Cephas did not appear between James and John, as though it were enough that the preceding clause contained the name of Cephas, or Peter; and thus the commentaries of the ancient writers on that passage of Galatians list Peter first. The angel’s words in Mark, “Tell his disciples and Peter,” commend the disciples under a collective name, but designate Peter by name particularly and preeminently—if not by reason of honor, then by reason of the singular divine mercy of which he certainly stood in greater need than the other disciples, because he had denied Christ three times.

Otherwise one could say that, after including the disciples under a common designation, the angel named Peter separately, in the same form in which Homer said “the Trojans and Hector”; the jurists wrote the title “On Servitudes and Water”; and Luke said at Acts 1:14: “with the women and Mary his mother.”

Finally, someone might use Jerome’s solution to Hedibia and say that Mark’s testimony should not be admitted in this matter, because the passage appears only in rare copies of the Gospels, almost all the books of Greece lacking this chapter at the end. Gregory of Nyssa also reports that he had observed this “in the more accurate copies,” Oration 11, *On Christ’s Resurrection*. Learned and prudent men have rightly judged that this solution should certainly not be admitted. RIG.

[Col. 1109C] **“Africa and Numidia.”** Cyprian omits mention of Mauretania, although it too was subject to the see of Carthage and he was writing to a bishop of Mauretania. From this one may conjecture that Agrippinus’s synod was composed of bishops from the province of Africa and from Numidia.]

### II

And they say that in this matter they follow ancient custom, from a time when heresy and schisms were still only in their beginnings among the ancients, [Note: “so that there were there”: Lam. Bod. 2.] so that those there were people who had withdrawn from the Church and had previously been baptized here [Note: “where they had been baptized”: Lam. NC. 1. Bod. 2. Ebor.]. When they then returned to the Church and performed penance, it was not necessary to baptize them.

We too observe this today: if it is established that persons were baptized here and passed from us to the heretics, and if they subsequently acknowledge their sin, cast off their error, and return to the truth and to their mother, it is enough to lay a hand upon them for penance. Thus, because one had been [Note: “already a sheep”: Lam. Bod. 1, 2.] a sheep, the shepherd receives this estranged and wandering sheep [Note: “rejected sheep”: Lam. NC. 1. Bod. 1, 2. “driven-away sheep”: Ver. Thu.] into his own fold.

But if one who comes from the heretics was not previously baptized in the Church, but comes as someone wholly alien and profane, he must be baptized so that he may become a sheep, because there is one water in the holy Church that makes sheep. And therefore, because nothing can be common to falsehood and truth, darkness and light, death and immortality, antichrist and Christ, we must in every respect maintain the unity of the Catholic Church and yield in nothing to the enemies of faith and truth.

No prescription [Col. 1106B] is to be based upon custom; rather, one must prevail by reason. For neither did Peter, whom the Lord chose first and upon whom he built his Church, when Paul subsequently disputed with him about circumcision, insolently claim anything for himself or arrogantly assume that he held the primacy and ought instead to be obeyed by newcomers and those who came later. Nor did he despise Paul because Paul had formerly been a persecutor of the Church. Instead, he accepted the counsel of truth and readily assented to the sound reasoning that Paul asserted, thereby giving us a lesson in concord and patience: we are not to cling stubbornly to our own views, but, if the things sometimes usefully and beneficially proposed by our brothers and colleagues are true and lawful, [Col. 1108A] we are instead to regard them as our own. [Note: “we should instead embrace those very things”: Thu. “we should instead embrace those things”: Foss.]

Paul too, looking to this matter and faithfully consulting concord and peace, wrote in his letter: “Let two or three prophets speak, and let the others examine what is said. But if something is revealed to another who is sitting, let the first be silent” (1 Corinthians 14:29). [Note: “if to another”: Lam. Bod. 1.] In this passage he taught and showed that many things are revealed to individuals for improvement, and that everyone ought not to contend stubbornly for what he had once absorbed and maintained, but freely to embrace anything better and more useful that might emerge.

For we are not defeated when better things are offered to us; we are instructed—especially in matters pertaining to the unity of the Church and to the truth of our hope and faith. Thus we, as God’s priests [Note: “so that we, priests”: Bod. 1, 2. Lin. NC. 1, 2.] placed by his favor over his Church, may know that forgiveness of sins can be given only in the Church and that Christ’s adversaries can claim nothing for themselves concerning his grace.

Agrippinus, a man of blessed memory, together with the other fellow bishops who at that time governed the Lord’s Church in the province of Africa and in Numidia, likewise determined this and confirmed it after a carefully balanced consideration of their common deliberation. We too have followed their judgment as religious, lawful, salutary, and consonant with the faith and the Catholic Church. And so that you might know what sort of letter we composed concerning this matter, we have, out of our common affection, transmitted a copy of it for the information both of yourself [Note: “for your information as well as”: Bod. 2.] and of our fellow bishops who are there.

I hope that you, dearest brother, may always fare well.

[Note: [Col. 1109C]

**LETTER LXXIII.**—I think there can be no doubt that this letter is Cyprian’s. Yet St. Augustine, Book II, *Against Cresconius*, chapter 33, appears to have doubted whether it was Cyprian’s. What reason could have moved him to think this is difficult to say, especially since Cyprian acknowledges it as his own in the preface to the Council of Carthage, and Augustine himself elsewhere frequently attributes it without difficulty to the most holy martyr: in *On the Soul*, chapter 9; Book III, *On Baptism, Against the Donatists*, chapter 2; Book IV, chapter 12; Book V, chapter [Col. 1109D] 1; Book VI, chapter 7; and Book VI, *Against Cresconius*, chapter 32. Jerome too, at the end of his dialogue *Against the Luciferians*, cites it as Cyprian’s.

Simon Goulartius contends that it is a pure paralogism, specifically because Cyprian names the Novatianists among the enemies of the Church and confounds them with the Marcionites, Patripassians, and other heretics who overturn the institution and essence of baptism. Yet this is not true. Cyprian certainly condemns Novatian’s opinion that Marcion’s baptism is true baptism because those attached to his sect had been baptized in the name of Jesus Christ; and it is therefore that he argues against the baptism of Marcion and the other heretics. He also numbers Novatian among them because he believed Novatian’s baptism to be invalid, since Novatian was a rebel and enemy of the Church, in which true and unique baptism exists. Consequently, what Goulartius expounds here could itself truly be called a pure paralogism.]

## IN THE YEAR OF CHRIST 256  
## LETTER OF ST. CYPRIAN TO JUBAIANUS  
### ON THE BAPTISM OF HERETICS

(Erasm. p. 322. Pamel. Rigalt. Baluz. Oxon. Lips. LXXIII.)

[Col. 1109B]

### ARGUMENT

In the year of Christ 256, shortly after the Seventh Council of Carthage, Cyprian wrote a long letter to Bishop Jubaianus. Jubaianus had consulted Cyprian concerning baptism and had at the same time sent him a letter written not by himself but by another person, against Cyprian’s position. [Col. 1110A] Cyprian refutes this letter and with the greatest diligence gathers together everything that he considered capable of supporting his case. He also sends Jubaianus a copy of the letter to the Numidians and the letter to Quintus, and perhaps the decrees of the most recent synod.

[Note: [Col. 1110C]

**I.—“You wrote to me.”** If the title of Letter LXX, which I noted as extant in the Thuanean manuscript, is correct, it appears that this was the first of the letters written to Jubaianus. But if it is the third, as one of my old books reads, it is established that one of the three letters written by Cyprian to Jubaianus is missing. Moreover, if these details are correct, it is easy to gather from the beginning of the present letter that the first is missing and that the synodal letter written to the Numidians is the second. Cyprian himself certainly teaches at the beginning of the present letter that the synodal letter was written before it.

**“Placed outside.”** Jerome, in his *Apology Against Rufinus*: “What am I to say of heretics, who, although they are outside, call themselves Christians?”

**“Reckon.”** Previously the text read “judge.” We changed it [Col. 1110D] because we are certain that all our old copies, with only one exception, and five English copies contain the reading we have established. This reading can be confirmed from several other passages in Cyprian, but especially from the final part of this letter, p. 137, where he says: “Let it be reckoned a just and lawful baptism”; and from the Letter of Firmilianus, p. 149: “Since it has always been observed there that we acknowledge only the one Church of God and reckon holy baptism only to the holy Church.” That authority is too great to be resisted.

**“To Quintus.”** See above, Letter LXXI. It appears from Letter LXXII, in which the same Quintus is mentioned, that he was a bishop in Mauretania.

**“Seventy-one bishops.”** Augustine, in his book *On the One Baptism, Against Petilian*, chapter 13, gives only seventy. See also what he says about this council in Book II, *On Baptism, Against the Donatists*, chapters 7, 8, and 9, and Book III, chapters 2 and 12.

**“To be baptized by us, whoever.”** We corrected the text thus on the authority of fourteen of our old books and [Col. 1111C] seven English ones. Previously it read: “to be baptized by us. Therefore, whoever come from the adulterous and profane water must be washed and sanctified.” It reads thus also in the manuscript of St. Arnulf, except that there it has “those coming.”]

### I

Cyprian to his brother Jubaianus, greetings.

You wrote to me, dearest brother, desiring that there be explained to you [Note: “that there be indicated to you”: Bod. 2.] the movement of our mind—that is, what we think concerning the baptism of heretics, who, placed outside and established beyond the Church, claim for themselves something that belongs neither to their right nor to their power. We can reckon [Note: “judge”: Oxon. and others.] this neither valid nor lawful, since it is established that it is illicit among them.

And because we have already expressed in our letters what we think about this matter, I have sent you, for the sake of brevity, a copy [Col. 1110B] of those same letters: what we decreed in council when a considerable number of us were present, and what I later wrote in reply to our colleague Quintus when he inquired about the same matter.

And now too, when the bishops both of the province of Africa and of Numidia, seventy-one in number, had assembled together, we again confirmed this same matter by our judgment. We determined that there is one baptism, the baptism established in the Catholic Church, and that consequently whoever come from adulterous and profane water are not rebaptized but baptized by us [Note: “by us, whoever come from adulterous and profane water”: Lam. Lin. Ebor. Bod. 1, 2. NC. 1, 2.], so that they may be washed and sanctified by the reality of saving water.

[Col. 1111A]

[Note: [Col. 1111D]

**II.—“Human actions.”** Fourteen of our copies and seven English copies have this reading. The word “nevertheless,” which follows, is absent from several of those same copies. In the Corbie manuscript, *humanitatem* (“humanity”) is read instead of *humana* (“human actions”).

**“By an alien baptism.”** The manuscript of St. Arnulf reads *extrario*.

**“Let us abandon the Church’s truth.”** The same manuscript reads: “Let the Church abandon.”]

### II

Nor are we disturbed, dearest brother, by what you included in your letter: that the Novatianists rebaptize those whom they entice away from us. What the enemies of the Church do is of no concern to us at all, provided that we ourselves maintain the honor of our authority and the firmness of reason [Note: “reason”: Lam. Ebor. NC. 1.] and truth.

For Novatian, after the manner of apes, which, although they are not human beings, nevertheless imitate human actions [Note: Thus Lam. Ebor. Bod. 1, 2. Lin. NC. 1, 2.; “human beings”: Oxon.], wishes to claim for himself the authority and truth of the Catholic Church, although he is not in the Church and, indeed, has furthermore emerged as a rebel and enemy against the Church. For, knowing that there is one baptism, he claims this one baptism for himself, so as to say that the Church exists with him and to make us heretics.

We, however, who hold fast to the head and root of the one Church, know and trust as certain that he has no power outside the Church, and that the one baptism [Note: Thus Lam. Ebor. Bod. 1, 2. NC. 1, 2.; “and of baptism, which is one”: Oxon.] is with us, where he himself had previously been baptized, when he maintained the principle and truth of divine unity.

But if Novatian thinks that those baptized in the Church must be rebaptized outside, beyond the Church, he ought to have begun with himself, so that he might first be rebaptized with an alien and heretical baptism—he who, after the Church, or rather against the Church, thinks that people should be baptized outside it.

What sort of reasoning is it that, because Novatian dares to do this, we should think it must not be done? What, then? Because Novatian usurps the honor of the priestly chair, must we therefore renounce the chair? Or because Novatian strives, contrary to divine law, to set up an altar and offer sacrifices, ought we to cease from the altar and sacrifices, lest we appear to celebrate things equal and similar to his?

It is utterly vain [Col. 1111C] and foolish that, because Novatian claims for himself outside the Church an image of the truth, we should abandon the Church’s truth. [Note: “Let the Church abandon the truth”: Lam. Bod. 1, 2. NC. 1, 2. Lin. Ebor.]

[Note: [Col. 1111D]

**III.—“A long age.”** See Rigaltius’s observations on this passage. See also Sirmond’s notes on Book X of Facundus.

**“He comes for this purpose, that he may learn.”** Thus seventeen of our old books and seven English ones. There can be no doubt that this reading is the best.

**“We ought not to increase the stupefaction.”** Two old books read: “We ought, through stupefaction, to patronize the heretics as heretics, and through our agreement,” etc. Six English copies read: “We ought not, through the support of our agreement, to give stupefaction to the heretics, since,” etc. Thus also in one of [Col. 1112D] our copies. Pontius the deacon used the expression “the stupefaction of paganism” in his *Life of Cyprian*.

**“Through the support of our agreement.”** The manuscript of St. Arnulf reads: “of support and agreement.”]

### III

Among us, however, it is not a new or sudden policy to judge that those who come from heretics [Col. 1112A] to the Church must be baptized. For many years and a long age have already passed since a great many bishops, assembling together under Agrippinus, a man of blessed memory, determined this. From that time to the present day, so many thousands of heretics converted to the Church in our provinces [Note: “of converts”: Lam. Bod. 2. Ebor. NC. 1.] have neither rejected nor hesitated, but have reasonably and gladly embraced the prospect of obtaining the grace of the life-giving washing and saving baptism.

For it is not difficult for a teacher to impart true and lawful teachings [Note: Thus Lam. Bod. 1, 2. Ebor. Lin. NC. 1, 2.; “to them”: Oxon. and [Col. 1112C] others.] to one who, having condemned heretical depravity and discovered ecclesiastical truth, comes for this purpose [Note: Thus Lam. Ebor. Bod. 1, 2. Lin. NC. 1, 2.; “they come so that they may learn whether”: Oxon.]—that he may learn—and learns for this purpose—that he may live. We ought not to increase the stupefaction of heretics through the support of our agreement [Note: “Let us not give stupefaction to the heretics through the support of our agreement, since”: Lam. Ebor. Bod. 1, 2. NC. 1, 2.], when they gladly and readily submit to the truth.

[Note: [Col. 1112D]

**IV.—“It should not be asked.”** See the anonymous book *On Rebaptism*, below, p. 353.

**“Anthropians.”** See the notes of the most learned Jean-Baptiste Cotelier on Book VI of the *Apostolic Constitutions*, chapter 10.

**“Swords and poisons.”** We judged that this reading should be restored, because we found it so written in thirteen of our old books and in seven English ones. Those “swords” and “poisons” refer to the heretics as epithets, as often occurs among orators and historians.]

### IV

Assuredly, because I found it written in the letter whose copy [Col. 1112B] you transmitted to me that it should not be asked who performed the baptism, since the person baptized could receive forgiveness of sins according to what he believed, I did not think this passage should be passed over—especially since I observed that the same letter also mentions Marcion and says that those coming even from him ought not to be baptized, because they appear already to have been baptized in the name of Jesus Christ.

We must therefore consider the faith of those outside who believe, and whether they can obtain any grace in accordance with that faith. For if our faith and that of the heretics are one, grace too can be one. If the Patripassians, Anthropians, Valentinians, Apelleians, Ophites, Marcionites, [Col. 1112C] and the other plagues, swords, [Note: Thus Lam. Ebor. Lin. NC. 1, 2. Bod. 1, 2. Fab.; “with swords and poisons”: Oxon.] and poisons of the heretics, which overturn the truth, confess with us the same Father, the same Son, the same Holy Spirit, and the same Church, then one baptism can also exist there—if the faith too is one.

[Note: [Col. 1113D]

**V.—“Might be baptized.”** The manuscript of St. Arnulf reads “might be left.”

**“A contention hostile to holiness and truth.”** The same manuscript reads: “a contention friendly to vanity and hostile to truth.”]

### V

And lest it take too long to run through all the heresies and recount the absurdities or insanities of each [Note: Thus Ebor. Bod. 1, 2. Lin. NC. 1, 2.; “of each individual”: Oxon.]—for it gives no pleasure to speak of what it is either horrifying or shameful to know—let us for the moment examine Marcion alone, who was mentioned in the letter you transmitted to us, and ask whether the rationale of his baptism can stand.

For after his resurrection, when the Lord sent out his disciples, he instructed and taught them how they ought to baptize [Note: “He instructs and teaches, saying”: Lam. Ebor. NC. 1, 2. Bod. 1, 2. Lin.; “He instituted”: Oxon.], saying: “All power has been given to me in heaven and on earth. Go, therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing [Note: “immersing all nations”: Lam. Ebor. Bod. 1, 2. NC. 1, 2.] them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:18–19). He indicates the Trinity, in whose sacrament the nations were to be baptized.

Does Marcion hold this Trinity? Does he affirm [Note: “Does he know the same one whom we know”: Lam. Bod. 1, 2. Ebor. Lin. NC. 1, 2.] the same Father and Creator whom we affirm? Does he know the same Son [Note: “the same God the Son”: Bod. 2. Lin. NC. 1, 2. Ebor.; “does he know the same Son”: Fab.], Christ, born of the Virgin Mary, who was the Word made flesh, who bore our sins, who conquered death by dying, who was himself the first to inaugurate the resurrection of the flesh, and who showed his disciples that he had risen in that same flesh?

The faith held by Marcion, as also by the other heretics, is altogether different. Indeed, there is nothing among them except faithlessness, blasphemy, and a contention hostile to holiness [Note: “a contention of vanity”: Bod. 1.] and truth.

How, then, can one who is baptized among them be regarded as having obtained the forgiveness of sins and the grace of divine indulgence through his faith, when he did not possess the truth of faith itself? For if, as some suppose, a person could receive something outside, beyond the Church, according to his own faith, then he certainly received what he believed. But one who believes what is false cannot receive what is true; rather, in accordance with what he believed, he received something adulterous and profane.

[Col. 1113C]

[Note: [Col. 1113D]

VI.—**By his own faith outside.** We have thus emended and supplemented the text on the authority of fourteen of our old manuscripts and six English ones, as well as from Morel’s edition.

VI. The prophet Jeremiah subtly censures this profane and adulterous baptism when he says: “Why do those who grieve me prevail? My wound is persistent; how shall I be healed? While it was being made, it became to me like deceitful water that has no faith” (Jer. 15:18). Through the prophet the Holy Spirit makes mention of deceitful water that has no faith. What is this deceitful and faithless water? Surely that which falsely assumes the appearance of baptism and, by a shadowy pretense, frustrates the grace of faith. [Note: [Col. 1114C] “By a shadowy pretense” (*adumbrata simulatione*); “a shadowed pretense” (*adumbratam simulationem*), Bod. 2.] But if, according to a corrupt faith, someone could be baptized outside and obtain remission of sins, then according to [Col. 1114A] that same faith he could also obtain the Holy Spirit, and there is no need for the hand to be laid upon him when he comes, so that he may obtain the Holy Spirit and be sealed. For either he could obtain both outside by his own faith, [Note: [Col. 1114D] “Obtain outside,” Bod. 1, 2; Lam.; Ebor.; NC. 1, 2.] or, having been outside, he received neither of them.

[Note: [Col. 1113D]

VII.—**The origin of unity.** Cyprian frequently commends the unity of the Church, especially in the book *On the Unity of the Church*.

]

VII. It is, moreover, manifest where and through whom remission of sins can be given—the remission, namely, that is given in Baptism. For the Lord first gave to Peter, upon whom he built the Church and from whom he established and displayed the origin of unity, this power: that whatever Peter loosed on earth should be loosed in heaven. And after the resurrection he also speaks to the apostles, saying: “As the Father has sent me, so I send you.” When he had said this, he breathed upon them and said: “Receive the Holy Spirit. If you forgive anyone’s sins, they shall be forgiven him; if you retain anyone’s [Col. 1114B] sins, [Note: [Col. 1114D] “Detain,” Bod. 1.] they shall be retained” (John 20:21–23). From this we understand that none may baptize and grant remission of sins except the rulers established within the Church and grounded in the law of the Gospel and the ordinance of the Lord; but outside, nothing can be bound or loosed, where there is no one who can either bind [Note: [Col. 1114D] “Can bind or loose,” Lam.; Bod. 1, 2; Ebor.; Lin.; NC. 1, 2.] or loose anything.

[Note: [Col. 1114D]

VIII.—**Attempted to usurp.** Thus the Manutius edition and twelve old manuscripts. But Erasmus, Morel, and three old manuscripts have “claim for themselves,” with the same meaning. In the manuscript of Saint-Arnulf, where “they usurped” is read, “with sacrilegious audacity” is added.

]

VIII. Nor, dearest brother, do we put this forward without the authority of divine Scripture when we say that all things have been divinely ordered by a fixed law and a particular ordinance, and that no one can usurp for himself against the bishops [Note: [Col. 1114D] “Against the Church, the bishops,” Lin.] and priests anything that does not fall within his own right and power. For Korah, Dathan, and Abiram attempted to usurp for themselves, against Moses and Aaron the priest, the right to offer sacrifice; yet they did not commit with impunity what they unlawfully dared to do. And the sons of Aaron, who placed strange [Col. 1114C] fire upon the altar, were immediately destroyed in the sight of the indignant Lord. [Note: [Col. 1114D] “Struck down by the indignant Lord,” Lin.] This punishment awaits those who introduce strange water under the false name of baptism, [Note: [Col. 1114D] “Offer it in Baptism,” Ebor.; NC. 1.] so that divine judgment may avenge and punish the heretics for doing against the Church what is lawful only for the Church herself.

[Note: [Col. 1114D]

IX.—**This passage.** Jean Daillé discusses the true meaning of this passage at length in book II of *On the Religious Practices of the Latins*, chapter 12, p. 156.

[Col. 1115C] **The rulers.** I prefer this reading, which I found in all the early editions and in four old manuscripts, to that which Pamelius produced from a single English manuscript, in which “through the rulers” was written. Yet, to conceal nothing, nine old copies present that reading.]

IX. As for what some say concerning those who had been baptized in Samaria—that when the apostles Peter and John arrived, the hand was merely laid upon them so that they might receive the Holy Spirit, yet they were not rebaptized—we see, dearest brother, that this passage [Note: [Col. 1114D] “This passage, brother,” Lam.; Bod. 1, 2; Lin.; NC. 1, 2.] has absolutely no bearing upon the present question. [Col. 1115A] For those who had believed in Samaria had believed with true faith and had been baptized by Philip the deacon, whom those same apostles had sent, within the Church, which is one and to which alone permission has been given to confer the grace [Note: [Col. 1115B] “The grace of Baptism has been given,” Lam.; NC. 1; Bod. 2.] of Baptism and to loose sins. And therefore, because they had obtained legitimate and ecclesiastical Baptism, they ought not to be baptized any further; rather, Peter and John merely supplied what was lacking, so that, after prayer had been offered for them [Note: [Col. 1115B] “Prayer over them,” Lin.] and the hand laid upon them, the Holy Spirit might be invoked and poured upon them. This is also done among us now: those baptized in the Church are presented to the rulers of the Church, and through our prayer and the laying on of hands they obtain the Holy Spirit and are perfected with the seal of the Lord.

[Col. 1115B] [Note: [Col. 1115C]

X.—**Why do we credit an adulterous baptism?** Nine of our old manuscripts and four English ones prefer: “Why do we credit an adulterous and alien thing, hostile to divine unity?” Pamelius likewise read this in his English manuscript. But some old manuscripts have “truth.”

[Col. 1115D] **The Church after the likeness of paradise.** Saint Augustine, book IV of *On Baptism, Against the Donatists*, chapter 1, gives a paraphrastic exposition of this passage and says: “The Church, compared to paradise, shows us that people may indeed receive her baptism even outside, but that no one outside her can either receive or retain the blessedness of salvation.” And he adds: “Thus it comes about that, although the water of paradise is outside paradise, blessedness nevertheless exists only within paradise. Thus, therefore, the Baptism of the Church can exist outside the Church, but the gift of the blessed life is found only within the Church.” See below on Letter LXXV, “From strange water.”

**Is cut down.** Thus the editions of Manutius and Morel and fifteen old manuscripts. Three others and Erasmus have “will be cut down and cast into the fire.” The Fuxensis has “is burned and cast into the fire.”

**Saving, heavenly.** The manuscript of Saint-Arnulf has “saving and heavenly.”]

X. There is therefore no reason, dearest brother, for us to think that concessions should be made to heretics, so that we might imagine that Baptism—which has been given only to the one and only Church—ought to be surrendered. It is the duty of a good soldier to defend the camp against the rebels and enemies of his commander. It is the duty of a glorious general to preserve the standards entrusted to him. It is written: “The Lord your God is a jealous God” (Deut. 4:24). We who have received the Spirit of God ought to possess zeal for the divine faith. By this zeal Phinehas found favor and, having won God’s approval, appeased his indignation while the people were perishing. [Note: [Col. 1115C] “And appeased the anger of the Lord, who was justly indignant,” Lin.; NC. 2.] Why do we, who know only one Christ and his one Church, credit an adulterous and alien thing [Note: [Col. 1115C] “Why do we credit an adulterous and alien thing, hostile to divine unity?” Lam.; Ebor.; Bod. 2; NC. 1; Thu.] that is hostile to divine unity? [Col. 1116A] The Church, representing the likeness of paradise, encloses within her walls fruit-bearing trees; from among these, whatever does not produce good fruit is cut down and cast into the fire. She waters these trees with four rivers—that is, the four Gospels—through which she lavishly bestows the grace of Baptism in a saving, heavenly flood. Can one who is wholly outside the Church water anyone from the Church’s fountains? Can one who is perverse and self-condemned, banished from the fountains of paradise, withered, and overcome by the dryness of eternal thirst impart to anyone the wholesome and saving draughts of paradise?

[Note: [Col. 1115D]

XI.—**Upon one.** That is, upon Peter. See the book *On the Unity of the Church*.

[Col. 1116C] **Received the keys.** Saint Columbanus, in his letter to Pope Boniface, admonishes him that, as the successor of Peter, who received the keys, he should use that power well: “For,” he says, “power will remain with you only so long as right reason remains. For he is the true keeper of the keys of the kingdom of heaven who, through true knowledge, opens to the worthy and closes to the unworthy.” These things must be impressed upon the Romans. For many Roman pontiffs have departed from this rule. To this may be referred what Marca discusses concerning Peter’s privilege in book IV of *On Concord*, chapter 6, and what we have annotated there.

[Col. 1116D] **This is the one.** Saint Augustine quotes this passage in book IV of *On Baptism, Against the Donatists*, chapter 1.

**With faithful devotion.** We have placed this in the text instead of what was formerly read, “by the power of faith.” To be sure, the Corbie manuscript reads “by the power of faith,” and three others “with the devotion of faith.” But all the others and seven English manuscripts prefer “with faithful devotion.”

**If of our possession.** The Reims manuscript of Saint-Denis has, “If we hold the land of our pasture.” This is perhaps better because of what precedes.

**We are considered.** Thirteen of our manuscripts and one Bodleian manuscript have “we consider”; five other English manuscripts, “we have proved to be”; one of mine, “we fear”—with a great difference among these variant readings.

**The water of the Church.** The Grenoble manuscript has: “The water of the Church is faithful and true and saving and holy.” Augustine cites it in the passage praised shortly before, but does not have “and true.”

[Col. 1117C] **Cannot be adulterated.** See our notes on Agobard, p. 45, and what we say concerning this subject in the notes on the book *On the Unity of the Church*.

[Col. 1117D] **If devoted to the Church.** The old manuscript of Saint-Remi has: “For if this devotion belongs to the Church and is in the Church,” etc.]

XI. The Lord cries out that whoever thirsts should come and drink from the rivers of living water that flowed from his belly (John 7:37–38). Where is the thirsty person to go: [Col. 1116B] to the heretics, where there is no fountain or river of life-giving water at all, or to the Church, which is one, founded upon one man who also received her keys, as established by the Lord’s own voice? This is the one Church that holds and possesses all the power of her bridegroom and Lord. In her we preside; for her honor [Note: [Col. 1115C] “And for her honor,” Bod. 2.] and unity we contend; her grace and glory alike we defend with faithful devotion. [Note: [Col. 1116B] “By the power of faith,” Oxon.; “devotedly in faith,” Bod. 1; “with faithful devotion,” Bod. 2; Lam.; Ebor.; Bened.; Lin.; NC. 1, 2; “with the devotion of faith,” [Col. 1116C] Thu.; “with faithful power,” Corb.] By divine permission, we water God’s thirsty people; we guard the boundaries of the life-giving fountains. If, therefore, we hold the right of our possession, [Note: [Col. 1116C] “If, therefore, of our possession,” Ebor.; NC. 1.] if we acknowledge the sacrament of unity, why are we considered violators of truth and traitors to unity? [Note: [Col. 1116C] “Have we proved traitors to unity,” Lam.; Lin.; Ebor.; NC. 1; Bod. 2; “do we consider,” Bod. 1; Thu.] The faithful, saving, and holy water of the Church [Col. 1117A] cannot be corrupted or adulterated, just as the Church herself is incorrupt, chaste, and pure. If the heretics are devoted to the Church and established within the Church, they can make use both of her Baptism and of her other saving benefits. But if they are not within the Church—indeed, if they act against the Church—how can they baptize with the Church’s Baptism?

[Note: [Col. 1117D]

XII.—**Either of the Son or of the Father.** In other editions these words had been transposed, doubtless through the emendation of some critic on account of the order of the persons of the most holy Trinity. For it seemed improper to this critic that the Son should be named before the Father. All the old manuscripts have the text as we have restored it.

]

XII. For no small or trivial concession is made to the heretics when we credit their baptism, since from Baptism begins the entire origin of faith, the saving entrance into the hope of eternal life, and the divine condescension by which God’s servants are purified and brought to life. For if someone could be baptized among heretics, he could surely also obtain remission of sins. If he obtained remission of sins, he was also sanctified [Col. 1117B] and made a temple of God. If he was sanctified, [Note: [Col. 1117C] “And was sanctified; if he was sanctified,” Bod. 1, 2; Lin.; Ebor.; NC. 1, 2; “and was sanctified,” Oxon.] if he was made a temple of God, I ask: of which God? If of the Creator, he could not have been, because he did not believe in him. If of Christ, neither could he have become Christ’s temple, since he denies that Christ is God. If of the Holy Spirit, since the three are one, how can the Holy Spirit be reconciled to one who is an enemy either of the Son or of the Father?

[Note: [Col. 1117D]

XIII.—**As though custom.** Much could be said here from Tertullian, Arnobius, and others concerning the authority of custom. I shall cite only the passage of Saint Jerome at the end of the *Dialogue Against the Luciferians*, where the following is read: “Let him read Cyprian’s letters, in which, before Stephen, bishop of the city of Rome, he assails the [Col. 1118C] error of long-established custom.” He is referring to Letter LXXII, written to Stephen. I think, however, that he was also referring to the letter mentioned by Crescens, bishop of Cirta, at the Council of Carthage, p. 331, as having been written to Stephen. It is no longer extant, but contained various testimonies derived from the divine Scriptures against Stephen’s judgment concerning the baptism of heretics.

**I did it ignorantly.** In the Fuxensis manuscript, “not yet believing” is added. But I have not found this elsewhere. This corresponds to what is quoted from the First Letter to Timothy: “I did it ignorantly in unbelief.”]

XIII. Accordingly, those who are overcome by reason vainly set custom against us, as though custom were greater than truth, or as though in spiritual matters we ought not to follow what has been revealed for the better by the Holy Spirit. For pardon can be granted to one who errs in simplicity, just as the blessed apostle Paul says concerning himself: [Note: [Col. 1117C] “The blessed Apostle,” Lam.; Bod. 1, 2; Ebor.; NC. 1, 2.] “I,” he says, “who formerly was a blasphemer, a persecutor, and an abusive man, nevertheless obtained mercy because I acted [Col. 1117C] ignorantly” (1 Tim. 1:13). But after inspiration and revelation have been given, one who knowingly and consciously persists in the error he had committed sins without the pardon [Note: [Col. 1117C] “Now not under the pardon,” Lin.] accorded to ignorance. For when he is overcome by reason, he relies upon a certain presumption and obstinacy. Nor should anyone say, “We follow what we received from the apostles,” since the apostles handed down only one Church and one Baptism, established only within that same Church; nor do we find anyone who, after having been baptized among heretics, was admitted in that same baptism and received into communion by the apostles, so that the apostles might appear to have approved the baptism of heretics. [Col. 1118A]

[Note: [Col. 1118D]

XIV.—**Defend.** In eleven of our manuscripts and six English ones it is written: “Therefore let the person who defends the heretics not bring forward what Paul stated concerning the brethren, but let him show.”

]

XIV. As for what some say, as though [Note: [Col. 1117C] “They say that, as though,” Ebor.; NC. 1.] the words of the apostle Paul lent support to the heretics—“Nevertheless, in every way, whether as a pretext or in truth, Christ is proclaimed” (Phil. 1:18)—we find that this too can do nothing to defend those who support and applaud the heretics. For Paul was not speaking in his letter about heretics or their baptism, so that he could be shown to have stated anything pertaining to this matter. He was speaking about brethren, some of whom were walking disorderly and contrary to ecclesiastical discipline, while others were preserving the truth of the Gospel in the fear of God. [Col. 1118B] He represented some of them as speaking the word of the Lord steadfastly and fearlessly, but others as being involved in envy [Note: [Col. 1117C] “In the dissension of envy,” Lin.] and dissension; some as maintaining benevolent charity toward him, but others as possessing malevolent dissension. Nevertheless, he patiently endured all things, provided that, whether in truth or as a pretext, the name of Christ whom Paul preached might come to the knowledge of many, and that the sowing of the word, still new and immature, might increase through the preaching of those who spoke. But it is one thing for those who are within the Church to speak about the name of Christ, and another for those who are outside and acting against the Church to baptize in the name of Christ. Therefore, let those who defend the heretics [Note: [Col. 1118C] “Let the person who defends them not bring forward,” Lam.; Bod. 1, 2; Ebor.; NC. 1, 2; Thu.] not bring forward what Paul stated concerning the brethren; rather, let them [Col. 1118C] show [Note: [Col. 1118C] “Let him show,” Lam.; Bod. 1, 2; Ebor.; NC. 1, 2; Thu.] whether he thought any concession ought to be made to a heretic, [Note: [Col. 1118C] “Thought, or whether he approved their faith and baptism,” Lam.; Lin.; Bod. 1, 2; Ebor.; NC. 1, 2.] or whether he approved their faith and Baptism, or determined that the faithless and blasphemous could receive remission of sins outside [Note: [Col. 1118C] “Receive it against the Church,” NC. 1; Lin.] the Church.

[Note: [Col. 1119C]

XV.—**And divine things.** The edition of Erasmus, which is the earliest of all, reads: “How do they handle spiritual and divine things?” [Col. 1119D] Later Manutius, whom subsequent editors followed, printed: “How do they perform spiritual things or handle divine things?” It is manifest that either the word “perform” or the word “handle” must be deleted. Accordingly, since fourteen of our manuscripts and six English ones do not recognize the word “handle,” we have removed it.

**Having rejected.** Three of our manuscripts and six English ones have [Col. 1120C] “having left behind.”

**With sincere and religious faith.** Morel’s edition and three [Col. 1120D] old manuscripts have “with sincere, true, and religious faith.”]
