XV. But if we consider what the apostles thought concerning heretics, we shall find that in all their letters they curse and condemn the sacrilegious depravity of heretics. For when they say that their word spreads like [Col. 1119A] a cancer (2 Tim. 2:17), how can a word that spreads like a cancer into the ears of its hearers grant remission of sins? And when they say that righteousness has no partnership with iniquity and light no communion with darkness (2 Cor. 6:14), how can either darkness illuminate or [Note: [Col. 1119C] “Or acts of iniquity,” Bod. 1; Thu.] iniquity justify? And when they say that such persons are not of God but belong to the spirit of antichrist (1 John 4:3), how do those who are God’s enemies, and whose breasts the spirit of antichrist has occupied, perform spiritual [Note: [Col. 1119C] Thus Lam.; NC. 1; Bod. 1, 2; Ebor.; Lin. “Who handle,” Oxon.] and divine things? Therefore, if, having rejected [Note: [Col. 1120C] “Having left behind,” Lam.; Ebor.; Lin.; NC. 1; Bod. 1, 2.] the errors of human contention, we return with sincere and religious faith to the authority of the Gospel and the apostolic tradition, we shall understand that those who scatter and attack the Church [Col. 1119B] of Christ, and who are called adversaries by Christ himself and antichrists by his apostles, possess no authority concerning ecclesiastical and saving grace. [Note: [Col. 1120C] “May be called,” Bod. 1, 2.]

[Note: [Col. 1120D]

XVI.—**Wherever and however.** This is the true reading, which occurs again below in this very letter. The English supposed that these were Stephen’s words because, as they say, Cyprian censures them below. They might have added that they are indeed attributed to Stephen in Firmilian’s Letter, p. 148.

]

XVI. There is, moreover, no reason for anyone to set the name of Christ against Christian truth in order to circumvent it, saying, “Those baptized in the name of Jesus Christ, wherever and however it was done, have obtained the grace of Baptism,” since Christ himself speaks and says, “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ shall enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 7:21). And again he forewarns and instructs us lest anyone be easily deceived by false prophets and false christs coming in his name: “Many,” he says, “will come in my name, saying, ‘I am Christ,’ and will deceive many.” And afterward he added: “But you, take heed. Behold, I have foretold everything to you” (Mark 13:6, 23). From this it is apparent that things proclaimed in the name of Christ are not immediately to be accepted and adopted, but only those done in the truth of Christ. [Col. 1119C]

XVII. For when the name of Jesus Christ is set forth in the Gospels and the apostles’ letters for the remission of sins, this does not mean that the Son alone can benefit anyone without the Father or against the Father. Rather, it was intended to show the Jews, who boasted that they had the Father, that the Father would profit them nothing unless they believed in the Son whom he had sent. For those who knew God the Father as Creator also ought to have known Christ the Son, lest they flatter and applaud themselves for acknowledging the Father alone without acknowledging his Son, who also said: “No one comes to the Father except through me” (John 14:6). He himself makes manifest that the knowledge of both brings salvation, saying: “Now this is eternal life: that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” [Col. 1120A] (John 17:3). Since, therefore, according to Christ’s own proclamation and testimony, the Father who sent must first be known, and then Christ who was sent, and since there can be no hope of salvation unless both are known together, how are those said to have been baptized among heretics in the name of Christ judged to have obtained remission of sins when God the Father is not known—indeed, is blasphemed—among them? For the rationale applicable to the Jews under the apostles was one thing, but the condition of the Gentiles is another. Because the Jews had already received the most ancient baptism of the Law and Moses, they were also to be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ, in accordance with what Peter says to them in the Acts of the Apostles: “Repent, and let each of you be baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ for the remission of sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy [Col. 1120B] Spirit. For this promise is for you and your children and all those hereafter, as many as the Lord our God shall call” (Acts 2:38–39). Peter mentions Jesus Christ not as though the Father were being omitted, but so that the Son might also be joined to the Father.

XVIII. Finally, when the apostles are sent to the Gentiles by the Lord after his resurrection, they are commanded to baptize the Gentiles in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. How, then, do some say that outside the Church—indeed, against the Church—a Gentile baptized merely in the name of Jesus Christ, wherever and however it was done, can obtain remission of sins, when Christ himself commands the Gentiles to be baptized in the full and united Trinity? Unless, perhaps, one who denies Christ is denied by Christ, while one who denies his Father, whom Christ himself [Col. 1120C] confessed, is not denied; and one who blasphemes him whom Christ called his Lord and God is rewarded by Christ and obtains remission of sins and the sanctification of Baptism. By what power can one who denies God the Creator, the Father of Christ, obtain remission of sins in Baptism, when Christ received from that same Father the very power by which we are baptized and sanctified—whom he called greater than himself, from whom he asked to be glorified, and whose will he fulfilled even to the obedience of drinking the cup and undergoing death? What else, then, is it but to become a partner with blaspheming heretics, if one wishes to defend and assert that a person who grievously blasphemes and sins against the Father, Lord, and God of Christ can receive remission of sins in Christ’s name? And what sort of claim is this: that one who denies the Son of God [Col. 1121A] does not have the Father, yet one who denies the Father appears to have the Son, when the Son himself testifies and says, “No one can come to me unless it has been granted to him by the Father” (John 6:65)? Thus it is manifest that no remission of sins can be received from the Son in Baptism when it is evident that the Father has not granted it, especially since he repeats again and says: “Every planting that my heavenly Father has not planted shall be rooted up” (Matt. 15:13).

[Note: [Col. 1121B]

XIX.—**To be admitted to communion without baptism.** In Lamonius’s manuscript it is written “without the baptism of repentance”; in Letter [Col. 1121C] LXXIV to Pompeius, p. 138: “He wished him to be baptized under the hand of repentance in the Church”; and in Letter LXXVI to Magnus, p. 151: “To be sanctified in the Catholic Church by the true and unique Baptism of repentance.” Tertullian, to be sure, in his book *On Baptism* and in his book *On Repentance*, spoke of the “Baptism” and the “immersion of repentance,” but in a different sense, as it seems. Learned men interested in ecclesiastical antiquity will examine this. And so that they may more easily exercise their diligence in this matter, I shall set down here all the passages in which variant readings of this kind—which I have found nowhere else—occur in Lamonius’s book. They all pertain to the Council of Carthage. Thus, in Cyprian’s address, p. 329, it is written: “To be baptized with the Church’s Baptism of repentance.” Caecilius of Bilta says, p. 330: “He is compelled to enter communion without the Baptism of repentance and the pardon of offenses.” Primus of Misgirpa, in the same place: “I judge that every person coming from heresy must be baptized with the Baptism of repentance.” Novatus of Thamugade, in the same place: “That they ought to be baptized with the Baptism of repentance”; [Col. 1121D] and a little later: “That heretics who have turned to the Church are to be baptized unto repentance.” Nemesianus of Thubunae, in the same place: “Some therefore misinterpret matters when they say that through the laying on of the hand alone, and not with repentance, they receive the Holy Spirit.” And below: “Unless, therefore, they receive the Baptism of repentance in the Catholic Church.” Januarius of Lambaesis, p. 331: “I decree that all heretics are to be baptized by the hand of repentance.” Lucius of Castra Galbae, in the same place: “Those who have been defiled by being baptized by opponents must first be purified and at the same time baptized unto repentance.” Crescens of Cirta, in the same place: “I judge that all heretics and schismatics who wish to come to the Catholic Church are not to enter before they have been exorcized by the hand of repentance.” Nicomedes of Segermis, in the same place: “My opinion is that heretics coming to the Church should be baptized in repentance, and that none outside. . . .” Munnulus of Girba, in the same place: “To be reborn and baptized under the hand of repentance, like a cancer. . . .” Secundinus of Cedias, p. 332: “Those who flee for refuge to the Church must be baptized through repentance.” Pollianus of Milevis, in the same place: “It is right that a heretic be baptized through repentance in the holy Church.” Dativus of Badis, [Col. 1122B] in the same place: “As far as it lies with us, we do not admit a heretic to communion unless he has been baptized through repentance in the Church.” [Col. 1122C] Successus of Abbir Germaniciana, in the same place: “We have judged that heretics are to be baptized unto repentance.” Sedatus of Tuburbo, in the same place: “Let him seek again to receive the unique and true Baptism of the Church through the hand of repentance.” Cassius of Macomades, in the same place: “I therefore judge that pitiable and wasting heretics must be baptized in repentance.” Januarius of Vicus Caesaris, p. 333: “Let us baptize through repentance those whom the Church has not baptized.” Felix of Uthina, in the same place: “Purified by the sanctification of the washing of repentance.” Euchratius of Thenae, in the same place: “That they ought to be baptized with the complete and Catholic Baptism of repentance.” Adelphius of Thasvalte, p. 334: “Since the Church does not rebaptize heretics, but baptizes them through the hand.” Marcus of Mactaris, in the same place: “For this reason we have decreed that heretics are to be baptized through the laying on of hands.” Aurelius of Utica, p. 335: “And therefore I judge that they are to be baptized under the hand of repentance, so that they may receive remission of sins.” Lucianus of Rucuma, in the same place: “For this reason I judge that heretics are to be baptized through the laying on of hands.” Jader of Midila, in the same place: “And therefore [Col. 1122D] we ought not to admit a heretic except through the laying on of hands, lest he suppose himself. . . .” Marcellus of Zama, p. 336: “Let him not baptize a heretic unto repentance.” Geminius of Furni, in the same place: “And therefore we hold to what we once decreed: that we baptize heretics who come to us in repentance.” Felix of Buslacenae, in the same place: “Concerning the admission of heretics without the Baptism of repentance.” Donatulus of Capsa, in the same place: “When they turn to the Church, let them be baptized by the hand of repentance.” Peter of Hippo Diarrhytus, p. 337: “And therefore I judge that those immersed in heresy, or who come to the Church from schism, ought to be baptized in repentance.” Lucius of Ausafa, in the same place: “And that those who come into the Church are to be baptized in repentance.” Felix of Gurgites, in the same place: “Where it is permitted, let them obtain the grace of Baptism through the laying on of hands.” Victor of Octavum, in the same place: “So that whoever comes from heresy may without doubt be baptized unto repentance.” Julius of Neapolis, p. 338: “Let us baptize heretics coming to the Church by the hand of repentance.” Cyprian of Carthage, in the same place: “They are to be baptized with the unique Baptism of the Church, administered by the hand of the blessing of repentance.”

]

XIX. But if Christ’s disciples are unwilling to learn from Christ how much reverence and honor are owed to the Father’s name, let them at least learn from earthly and secular examples, and let them know that Christ did not say without the gravest reproach: “The children of this age are more prudent than the children of light” (Luke 16:8). In this world, if anyone abuses another man’s [Col. 1121B] father—if, insulting and insolent, he rends his dignity and honor with a slanderous tongue—the son is indignant and angry, and strives with all the strength he possesses to avenge the injury done to his offended father. Do you think that Christ grants impunity to the impious and sacrilegious who blaspheme his Father, and forgives in Baptism the sins of those who, even after being baptized, plainly continue to heap the same curses upon the person of the Father and to sin through the unceasing wickedness of a blasphemous tongue? Can a Christian, a servant of God, either conceive this in his mind, believe it by faith, or utter it in speech? [Col. 1122A] And where will the commandments of the divine law be, which say, “Honor your father and mother” (Exod. 20:12), if the name “father,” which is commanded to be honored in a human being, is violated with impunity in God? What becomes of what Christ himself sets forth in the Gospel and says: “Whoever curses father or mother shall surely die” (Matt. 15:4), if he who commands those who curse their fleshly parents to be punished and put to death himself gives life to those who curse the heavenly and spiritual Father and are enemies of Mother Church? What some people emphatically assert is accursed and detestable: that he who threatens that a person blaspheming against the Holy Spirit shall be guilty of eternal sin is himself said to sanctify by saving Baptism those who blaspheme God the Father. And now those who think that such persons, when they come to the Church, should be admitted to communion without Baptism do not think themselves partners in the sins of others—indeed, in eternal sins—when they admit without Baptism those who can lay aside the sins of their blasphemies only in Baptism. [Col. 1122B]

[Note: [Col. 1123B]

XX.—**Ordering.** The text formerly read “dispensation.” We have been compelled to change it because of the authority of thirteen [Col. 1123C] of our manuscripts and seven English ones. I found the commonly received reading in only one. The manuscript of Saint-Remi has “discussion,” through an obvious error. Below, in Letter LXXIV, p. 139, one reads: “To place human tradition before the divine ordering.”

]

XX. Furthermore, how vain and perverse it is that, although the heretics themselves repudiate and abandon either the error or the crime in which they formerly lived and acknowledge the truth of the Church, we should mutilate the rights and sacrament of that same truth, and should tell those who come in repentance that they have obtained remission of sins, when they themselves confess both that they have sinned and that for this reason they are coming to the Church’s mercy. Therefore, dearest brother, we must firmly maintain and teach the faith and truth of the Catholic Church, [Col. 1123A] and through all the evangelical and apostolic precepts demonstrate the rationale of the divine ordering and unity.

[Note: [Col. 1123C]

XXI.—**Be baptized in his own blood.** There is a notable passage concerning the baptism of blood in Tertullian’s book *On Baptism*, and likewise in Rufinus’s *Exposition of the Creed*. Many writers have discussed this subject.

**Benefits a heretic.** Once again we have had to change this reading because of the agreement of our old manuscripts and six English ones. Pamelius also approves this reading in his annotations. Moreover, what immediately follows confirms it. This argument, which Cyprian often employs, is not without fault. For here the considerations advanced by Saint Augustine in his books *On Baptism* have particular force, since it is manifest and evident that Cyprian says nothing concerning heretics and schismatics that could not equally be said concerning [Col. 1123D] those who secretly foster heresy within the Church herself. For even the baptism of blood will not benefit them unless they abandon their error.

**Profit toward salvation.** A single manuscript of Saint-Remi reads: “Can profit toward salvation, because salvation cannot exist outside the Church.” The Dijon manuscript has nearly the same reading.]

XXI. Can the power of Baptism be greater or more excellent than confession, than suffering, so that a person confesses Christ before men and is baptized in his own blood? And yet not even this Baptism benefits a heretic, although he has confessed Christ and been killed outside the Church—unless the patrons and advocates of heretics proclaim as martyrs those heretics who have been killed in a false confession of Christ and, contrary to the Apostle’s solemn declaration that, although they are burned and killed, they can gain nothing thereby (1 Cor. 13:3), assign them the glory and crown of suffering. But if even the Baptism [Col. 1123B] of public confession and blood cannot profit a heretic unto salvation, because there is no salvation outside the Church, how much less will it benefit him if, stained in a hiding place and den of robbers by the contagion of adulterous water, he has not only failed to put off his former sins but has instead heaped up new and greater ones besides? Therefore Baptism cannot be common to us and to heretics, since neither God the Father, nor Christ the Son, nor the Holy Spirit, nor the faith, nor the Church herself is common to us and them. And for this reason those who come from heresy [Col. 1124A] to the Church must be baptized, so that those who, through divine regeneration, are prepared for the kingdom of God by the lawful, true, and unique Baptism of the holy Church may be born through both sacraments, because it is written: “Unless one has been born again of water and the Spirit, one cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John 3:5).

[Note: [Col. 1123D]

XXII.—*First of water.* The Eligian manuscript reads: “because he has not first been born again of water and the Spirit.”

*The truth of the Church.* Thus Erasmus printed it. I have also seen it written in thirteen of our manuscripts and in six English ones. Below, in this very letter: “unless they have first come to the truth of the Church.” Other passages in Cyprian also confirm this reading.

*When to the robber.* Saint Augustine cites this passage in Book IV, chapter 22, *On the One Baptism, Against the Donatists*. Some call this robber a martyr because he confessed Christ, who promised him paradise as he was dying. He was indeed a martyr, that is, a witness to Christ’s Passion. Jerome, in his letter to Paulinus *On the Training of a Monk*: “By contrast, the robber exchanges the cross [Col. 1124B] for paradise and turns the punishment for murder into martyrdom.” Avitus, bishop of Vienne, Letter III: “Thus [Col. 1124C] one of these robbers, exchanging a long life of crime for the brief conclusion of an abridged course, became a physician from a killer, a martyr from a thief.” And Letter IV: “That robber is admitted to paradise because of the confession that followed; he was led through an unjust life so that he might seize martyrdom from a just death.” The author of the book *On the Cardinal Works of Christ*, which is commonly published with the works of Cyprian, held the same opinion. Speaking of the robber, he says: “He changed punishment into martyrdom”; and below: “He became a participant in the kingdom; through confession he became a colleague in martyrdom.” Cardinal Humbert, bishop of Silva Candida, Book II, *Against the Simoniacs*, chapter 42, says that the robber who acknowledged Christ earned the triumph of martyrdom out of a robber’s punishment. Caesarius of Heisterbach, Book VIII, chapter 64: “The cause, not the punishment, makes martyrs. For two robbers were fastened to the cross with Christ, one on either side: one was made a martyr by the power of his confession; for the other, his punishment was the beginning of eternal damnation.” See also the gloss on the chapter *Importuno*, distinction I, *On Penance*, and Rutilius Benzonius, Book II, chapter 43, [Col. 1124D] *On the Jubilee Year*. There were nevertheless some who denied that this honor could be bestowed upon him because, as Hugh, archbishop of Rouen, says in Book V, chapter 9 of his *Dialogues*, he had neither been regenerated by Baptism nor fastened to the cross for the cause of Christ. It therefore followed that he was not a martyr. And yet Rupert, in Book III *On the Gospel of John*, seems to have thought that he was baptized in the water that flowed from Christ’s side. The Reverend Father Edmond Martène, in the account of his journey through Gaul, page 24, testifies that every year a Mass of the Holy Robber is celebrated in the church of Bourges on Holy Saturday. An old inventory of the relics preserved there, published by Gérard de Vic in his *Chronicle of the Bishops of Carcassonne*, teaches that relics of the holy robber once existed, and perhaps still exist, in the church of Carcassonne. Pietro della Valle, a Roman patrician, in Letter XIII of his travels, relates that not far from Ramah he was shown a certain village from which the good robber who was crucified with Christ had originated.

[Col. 1125C] *We preside over faith and truth.* The editions of Manutius and Morel, together with nine old manuscripts, prefer this reading. Erasmus and five other old manuscripts read: “we who rely upon faith and truth.” One of mine reads: “we who rely upon the truth of the faith.”]

XXII. At this point certain persons, as though by human argumentation they could nullify the truth of the Gospel proclamation, raise against us the case of catechumens: if any of them, before being baptized in the Church, should be arrested while confessing the Name and be killed, does he lose the hope of salvation and the reward of confession because he has not first been born again of water? Such people, then, who support and favor heretics, should know that those catechumens, first, hold the faith inviolate and the truth of the Church [Col. 1124B] and advance from the divine camp to conquer the devil with a full and sincere knowledge of God the Father, of Christ, and of the Holy Spirit; and, second, that they are not deprived of the sacrament of Baptism, since they are baptized with the most glorious and supreme Baptism of blood, concerning which the Lord also said that he had another baptism with which to be baptized (Luke 12:50). The same Lord declares in the Gospel that those baptized in their own blood and sanctified by suffering are brought to perfection and obtain the grace of the divine promise, when he speaks to the robber who believed and confessed amid the Passion itself [Col. 1125A] and promises that he will be with him in paradise. Therefore, we who preside over faith and truth must not deceive or mislead those who come to faith and truth and, doing penance, ask that their sins be forgiven; rather, once corrected and reformed by us, they must be instructed by heavenly disciplines for the kingdom of heaven.

XXIII. But someone says: “What, then, will become of those who in the past came from heresy to the Church and were admitted without Baptism?” The Lord has power in his mercy to grant pardon and not to exclude from the gifts of his Church those who were admitted to the Church in simplicity and fell asleep in the Church. Nevertheless, because an error was once made, it does not follow that error must always be made, since it is more fitting for the wise and those who fear God gladly and without delay [Col. 1125B] to obey truth once it has been disclosed and clearly perceived than stubbornly and obstinately to struggle on behalf of heretics against their brothers and fellow bishops.

[Note: [Col. 1125C]

XXIV.—*Baptism is set before them.* Thus Erasmus and fourteen old manuscripts. Manutius printed *BAPTISMS* in capital letters. I also saw it written in this way in the Foix manuscript. I know that learned men approved Manutius’s edition. [Col. 1125D] Nevertheless, I consider it false. For it is certain that in Cyprian, who in many places argues against the baptism of heretics, the word “baptisms” is nowhere—I repeat, nowhere—to be found in that sense. In Letter LXXI: “For since there cannot be two baptisms, if heretics truly baptize, they themselves possess Baptism.” And in Letter LXXIV, writing against Pope Stephen, who approved the baptism of heretics, he says: “He judged the baptisms of all heretics to be right and lawful.” Jerome, on the fourth chapter of the Epistle to the Ephesians: “‘One Baptism’ also stands against Valentinus, who maintains that there are two baptisms, and against all heretics, so that they may know that they do not possess baptisms, but that in the one Church of Christ there is the life-giving fountain.”

*More eagerly.* Thus the editions of Manutius and Morel and ten old manuscripts. Erasmus and the Corbie manuscript have “more boldly.” In place of “more readily,” which the editions and those same old manuscripts prefer, one of mine has “more ruinously.”

*Truth.* Thus fourteen old manuscripts, in place of “unity,” which the editions have. See what was said a little above [Col. 1126C] in a similar case. By contrast, in Jonas of Orléans, *On the Worship of Images*, page 24 of the Plantin edition, the most ancient and excellent manuscript proves that “unity” should be read in place of “truth.”]

XXIV. Nor should anyone suppose that heretics are deterred from coming to the Church because Baptism is set before them, as though they were scandalized by the expression “a second baptism.” On the contrary, by this very fact they are driven all the more to the necessity of coming, through the testimony of truth shown and proved to them. For if they see that by our judgment and sentence it is decided and established that the baptism with which they are baptized there is accounted right and lawful, they will suppose that they also rightfully and lawfully possess the Church and the other gifts of the Church; and there will be no reason for them to come to us, since, possessing Baptism, they will seem to possess the other things as well. [Col. 1125C] But when they learn that there is no Baptism outside and that forgiveness of sins cannot be given outside the Church, they hasten to us more eagerly and readily and implore the gifts and favors of Mother Church, certain that they can by no means attain the true promise of divine grace unless they have first come to the truth [Col. 1126A] of the Church. Nor will heretics refuse to be baptized among us with the lawful and true Baptism of the Church when they have learned from us that Paul also baptized those who had already been baptized with John’s baptism, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 19).

[Note: [Col. 1126C]

XXV.—*Among the prophets.* One royal manuscript reads: “among those born of women and the prophets.” But Saint Augustine, who transcribes this passage in Book IV, chapter 12, *On Baptism Against the Donatists*, does not have “those born of women”; these words are also absent from all the other old [Col. 1126D] manuscripts.

*You begin to seem a heretic to him.* Salvian, Book V, chapter 2: “They are therefore heretics, but without knowing it. In short, among us they are heretics; among themselves they are not. For they judge themselves to be Catholics to such an extent that they stigmatize us with the designation ‘heretical.’”]

XXV. And now, among some of our own people, it is asserted that the baptism of heretics has taken prior possession, and, through a certain odium attached to “rebaptizing,” it is considered a crime to baptize after God’s enemies, although we find that those whom John had baptized were baptized again—that John who was held to be the greatest among the prophets; who was filled with divine grace while still in his mother’s womb; who was sustained by the spirit and power of Elijah; who was not the Lord’s adversary but his forerunner and herald; who not only foretold our Lord in words but also pointed him out with his eyes; who baptized Christ himself, through whom all others are baptized. But if [Col. 1126B] a heretic has been able to acquire the right of Baptism merely because he baptized first, Baptism will no longer belong to its possessor but to its first occupier. And since Baptism and the Church cannot be separated and divided from one another at all, he who was able first to occupy Baptism has likewise occupied the Church; and you begin to seem a heretic to him, since, forestalled by him, you have come later and, by yielding and surrendering, have abandoned the right you had received. Holy Scripture declares how dangerous it is in divine matters for anyone to yield his right and authority, since in Genesis Esau thereby lost his rights of primogeniture and could not afterward recover what he had once surrendered (Gen. 25; Heb. 12:16).

[Col. 1126C] [Note: [Col. 1126D]

XXVI.—*These things briefly to you.* Above, at the end of the letter to Donatus, page 7: “These things for the present in brief, dearest Donatus.” Thus Erasmus and Morel and ten old manuscripts. Five others have “more briefly.” In Saint Augustine, who cites this passage quite frequently, “briefly” is always written. The ancients used *brevi* for *breviter* (“briefly”), as Charisius notes. Many examples of this manner of writing survive in Cicero and elsewhere. See Lambinus’s notes on Cicero’s speech *For Plancius*.

*Neither prescribing for nor prejudging anyone.* Jerome, Book I, *Against Rufinus*: “Prejudging no one’s right to follow what he wishes, nor overturning another’s decision by our own judgment.”

[Col. 1127B] *Is thought contentious.* Five old manuscripts read: “should have thought [Col. 1127C] that he was contentious.” Four others, though with some slight variation, read: “should have thought himself contentious.” One of mine reads: “thinks himself contentious.”

*Gently.* Thus Saint Augustine, Book IV, *On Baptism Against the Donatists*, chapter 8, and Book V, chapter 17. So too the Morel edition, ten of our manuscripts, and seven English manuscripts. Erasmus, Manutius, and the Corbie manuscript read “firmly.”

*The treatise On the Good of Patience.* Saint Augustine cites this passage in Book IV, *On Baptism Against the Donatists*, chapter 8, and Book V, chapter 16.

*Now.* This word, which had dropped out of later editions, is present in the editions of Erasmus and Morel; we restored it on the authority of thirteen of our manuscripts and four English ones. The same word, which the Louvain editors had also omitted, was restored to Saint Augustine by the most learned men to whom we owe the new edition of his works.]

XXVI. These things we have written briefly in reply to you, dearest brother, according to our modest ability, neither prescribing for nor prejudging anyone so as to prevent each bishop from doing what he thinks best, since he possesses the free exercise of his own judgment. For our part, as far as lies within us, we do not quarrel on account of heretics with our colleagues and fellow bishops, [Col. 1127A] with whom we maintain divine concord and the Lord’s peace, especially since the Apostle also says: “But if anyone is thought to be contentious, we have no such custom, nor does the Church of God” (1 Cor. 11:16). We preserve patiently and gently charity of spirit, the honor of the episcopal college, the bond of faith, and the concord of the priesthood. For this reason also, with the Lord’s permission and inspiration, we have now composed, to the extent that our modest ability was capable, a short work *On the Good of Patience*, which I have sent to you out of our mutual affection. I pray, dearest brother, that you may always fare well.

[Note: [Col. 1127D]

LETTER LXXIV.—This letter, first published by Erasmus, is cited by Saint Augustine in Book V, chapter 23, and Book VI, chapter 7, of *On Baptism Against the Donatists*, and by Facundus, Book X, chapter 3, in his work *Against Mocianus*.]

## A LETTER OF SAINT CYPRIAN TO POMPEIUS, AGAINST STEPHEN’S LETTER ON THE BAPTISM OF HERETICS

(Erasm. p. 332; Pamel.; Rigalt.; Baluz.; Oxford; Leipzig, LXXIV.)

[Col. 1127B] The ARGUMENT of this Letter is given as follows by the blessed Augustine in Book V, chapter 23, *Against the Donatists*: “Cyprian also writes to Pompeius about this same matter, where he clearly indicates that Stephen—whom we have learned was at that time bishop of the Roman Church—not only did not agree with him on these points, but even wrote against him and issued contrary instructions.” Concerning this, he says again in chapter 25: “I do not wish now to reconsider those things which he poured forth against Stephen in anger, because there is no need. For precisely the same things are said there that have already been discussed sufficiently; and it is better to pass over those things which carried the danger of a destructive dissension. [Col. 1128A] Stephen, moreover, had thought that those who attempted to overthrow the ancient custom concerning the reception of heretics should be excluded from communion. Cyprian, however, moved by the difficulty of the question itself and most abundantly endowed with the holy compassion of charity, held that those who thought differently should remain in unity. Thus, although he expresses his indignation with greater agitation, yet still fraternally, the peace of Christ nevertheless prevailed in their hearts, so that amid so great a disagreement no evil of schism arose between them.” Thus far Augustine. We have cited his words at greater length because they serve as an antidote against those who endeavor on this basis to obtain confirmation of their schism from the Roman Pontiff.

[Note: [Col. 1127D]

I.—*To Pompeius.* Bishop of Sabratha in the province of Tripolitania. He attended the Council of Carthage under Cyprian. Donatus, bishop of Sabratha, attended the Councils of Cabarsussi and Bagai. In the first Conference of Carthage, chapter 133, Nados, bishop of Sabratha, is named. See our edition of that conference, page 215.

*Brother Stephen.* In one royal manuscript “father” is written. And below, in the Compiègne manuscript and in one of mine, “Stephen our father,” through an error like that by which, in Saint Pope Gregory’s Letter 26 to Victor, bishop of Palermo, Book VII, indiction I, the Fleury manuscript reads: “Your Paternity ought,” where the common and correct reading is: “Your Fraternity ought.” The Reverend Father Hardouin, in the second volume of his edition of the Councils, [Col. 1128B] page 1203, relates that the letter of the Council of Milevis [Col. 1128C] to Pope Innocent reads “to the most reverend Father Innocent” in Justellus’s manuscript. If these readings were not false, Pope Gregory IV would have had some just cause to complain of the Gallican bishops who, writing to the Roman Pontiff, had called him “brother,” whereas, he says, it would have been more appropriate to show him paternal reverence alone. Among the letters of Pope Adrian IV one is found in which he rebukes Emperor Frederick because, when writing to him, he placed his own name before the Pope’s name, “in which you incur the mark of insolence, not to say arrogance.” That letter of Gregory IV survives in Agobard and was thought to be Agobard’s until the most illustrious Pierre de Marca showed that it was Gregory’s; it was published by us under Gregory’s name among Agobard’s works. The Reverend Father Labbe then placed it in the appendix to the seventh volume of the *Councils* and noted that it survives in Agobard. Nevertheless, the Reverend Father Hardouin, in the fourth volume of his edition, page 1275, suppressing Agobard’s name, stated that he was [Col. 1128D] publishing it from the Fleury library, where it does not exist. See the notes on Letter XLI, page 429.

*Arrogant.* Erasmus, three of our manuscripts, and four English manuscripts prefer “superfluous.” One royal manuscript reads “tending to arrogance.” The remaining manuscripts have our reading.

*If anyone, therefore.* These words are taken from Pope Stephen’s letter, quoted above in the letter to Pompeius, page 138.

*To you.* Previously “to us” was read. We have retained the reading of seven old manuscripts. It is evident from the beginning of this letter and from the *Commonitorium* of Vincent of Lérins that Stephen’s letter had been sent to Africa. See our notes on Vincent, pages 445 and 447.

*Let nothing new be introduced.* Pope Celestine’s letter to the bishops of Gaul: “Let novelty cease attacking antiquity.” Tertullian, in *On the Veiling of Virgins*: “It is not so much novelty as truth that refutes heresies.” Optatus, Book VII, spoke of “seeking novelty within the inward parts of antiquity.”

[Col. 1129C] *They do not baptize.* The Lamon manuscript adds “in penance,” and soon afterward: “he forbade one who came to be baptized into the hand of penance in the Church.” There are many examples of this kind in the Lamon manuscript, which we discussed above in the notes on Letter LXXIII, page 502.]

### I

Cyprian to his brother Pompeius, greetings.

Although we have fully covered what must be said concerning the baptism of heretics in the letters whose copies we sent [Col. 1128B] to you, dearest brother, nevertheless, because you wished to be informed of what our brother Stephen wrote back to me in reply to our letter, I have sent you a copy of his response. When you have read it, you will observe more and more clearly the error of a man who attempts to champion the cause of heretics against Christians and against the Church of God. For among the other things—whether arrogant, irrelevant, or self-contradictory—which he wrote ignorantly and without foresight, he also added this statement: “If anyone, therefore, comes to you from any heresy whatsoever, let nothing new be introduced beyond what has been handed down: namely, that the hand be laid upon him [Col. 1129A] for penance, since the heretics themselves, properly speaking, do not baptize those who come to them from one another, but merely admit them to communion.”

[Note: [Col. 1129C]

II.—*Of all heretics.* In Nicholas Eymerich’s *Directorium Inquisitorum* there survive the replies of Pope Benedict XII, then a cardinal, against the errors of the Fraticelli. In them he says that Pope Stephen determined that no one baptized by any heretics whatsoever and coming to the Catholic Church should be rebaptized; [Col. 1129D] but that Saint Cyprian, while celebrating a council with many bishops in Africa, determined the opposite—namely, that those baptized by any heretics whatsoever, if they come to the Catholic Church, must be baptized—and on this point condemned Pope Stephen, as is clear in Cyprian’s letters to Jubaianus, Stephen, and Pompeius; but that the Council of Nicaea corrected both the opinion of Saint Cyprian and that of Pope Stephen by determining that those who come to the Church after being baptized by heretics who do not preserve the Church’s form should be baptized, whereas those baptized by other heretics should not be rebaptized. Francisco Peña, in his commentaries on Nicholas, says that this solution of Benedict’s is false and refutes it. I do not know whether he does so correctly. For Cyprian says that Pope Stephen considered the baptisms of heretics right and lawful. Abraham Bzovius also reports Benedict’s replies against the Fraticelli in his *Annals*, but alters the words of the *Directorium*. For where Nicholas [Col. 1130C] has: “To this Lord Benedict replies,” Bzovius writes: “To this Brother Jacques Fournier, cardinal, replies,” because he knew that Benedict had spoken thus before becoming pope.

*Dipping.* The Grenoble manuscript reads: “dipping and anointing.”

*The Pontic.* We added this word on the authority of twelve of our manuscripts and six English ones. Those that lack it appear to have been abridged by unskilled copyists who believed it superfluous because “Marcion [Col. 1130D] emerged from Pontus” immediately follows. Irenaeus, Book I, chapter 21, wrote “Marcion the Pontic.” Rufinus, Book V, chapter 13, following Eusebius, calls him “the Pontic wolf.” Saint Cyprian meant to say that Marcion, who was Pontic by nation and originated in a remote and barbarous region—namely, Pontus Euxinus—at length emerged from Pontus, where he had been concealed, but had not yet come to Rome. Erasmus, however, has the word “Pontic,” but did not add “from Pontus.” Tertullian, Book I, *Against Marcion*: “Pontus, which is called Euxine, is belied by nature and mocked by its name.” Ennodius, Book XII, Letter I: “Even if Pontic inhumanity makes you forgetful of me.” A place famous for Ovid’s exile. Concerning the period in which Marcion lived, see Petavius’s observations on heresy XLVI in Epiphanius.

*Cerdon under Hyginus.* See Massuet’s dissertations on Irenaeus, page 68, §155.

*He was the ninth.* Saint Irenaeus likewise testifies to this in Book I, chapter 28, saying that Cerdon came to Rome under Hyginus.]

### II

He forbade anyone coming from any heresy whatsoever to be baptized in the Church; that is, he judged the baptisms of all heretics to be right and lawful. And although the individual heresies have their individual baptisms and their different sins, this man, by entering into communion with the baptism of them all, has gathered into his own bosom the accumulated transgressions of them all. And he commanded that nothing new be introduced beyond what had been handed down—as though the innovator were the man who maintains unity and vindicates one Baptism for the one Church, and not, rather, the man who, forgetful of unity, usurps the falsehoods and contagions of a profane dipping.

“Let nothing new be introduced,” he says, “beyond what has been handed down.” From where does this tradition come? Does it descend from the authority of the Lord [Col. 1129B] and the Gospel, or does it come from the commands and letters of the Apostles? For God testifies and forewarns that the things written must be done, saying to Joshua the son of Nun: “The book of this law shall not depart from your mouth, but you shall meditate upon it day and night, so that you may take care to do everything written in it” (Josh. 1:8). Likewise, when sending his Apostles, the Lord commands that the nations be baptized and taught to observe everything whatsoever that he commanded (Matt. 28:19–20). If, therefore, either it is commanded in the Gospel or it is contained in the letters or Acts of the Apostles that those coming from any heresy whatsoever should not be baptized but merely have the hand laid upon them for penance, then let this divine and holy tradition be observed. But if heretics everywhere are called nothing other than adversaries and antichrists; if [Col. 1129C] they are pronounced persons to be avoided, perverted, and condemned by themselves, how is it that those whom the apostolic declaration establishes as condemned by themselves should appear not to deserve condemnation by us? Let no one defame the Apostles [Col. 1130A] as though they had approved the baptisms of heretics or admitted them to communion without the Church’s Baptism, when the Apostles wrote such things about heretics—and this when the more violent heretical plagues had not yet broken forth, nor had Marcion the Pontic yet emerged from Pontus. His teacher Cerdon came to Rome under Hyginus, who was then bishop and the ninth to hold that office in the city. Marcion followed him and, adding further increments to his crime, began more shamelessly than the rest and more unrestrainedly to blaspheme God the Father and Creator; and he more criminally and grievously armed with sacrilegious weapons the heretical frenzy that rebels against the Church.

### III

But if it is established that more numerous and worse heresies arose afterward; if nowhere at all in earlier times was it commanded or written that only [Col. 1130B] the hand should be laid upon a heretic for penance and that he should thus be admitted to communion; and if there is only one Baptism, which is among us, is within, and has by divine favor been granted to the Church alone—what obstinacy, what presumption is it to set human tradition before the divine ordinance and not to perceive that God is indignant and angry whenever human tradition dissolves and passes over the divine commandments? Thus he cries out and says through the prophet Isaiah: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far removed from me. In vain, however, do they worship me, teaching the commandments and doctrines of men” (Isa. 29:13). Likewise, in the Gospel the Lord similarly rebukes and reproves them when he states and says: “You reject the commandment of God in order to establish your tradition” (Mark 7:13). Mindful of this precept, [Col. 1130C] the blessed Apostle himself also admonishes and instructs us, saying: “If anyone teaches otherwise and does not assent to the sound words of our Lord Jesus Christ and to his doctrine, [Col. 1131A] he is puffed up with conceit and knows nothing; withdraw from such a person” (1 Tim. 6:3).

[Note: [Col. 1131D]

IV.—*Profane and alien persons.* The Saint-Arnoul manuscript reads *extrarios* (“outsiders”). The Verona manuscript also had this reading.]

### IV

An excellent and lawful tradition is indeed set before us, with our brother Stephen as teacher, providing us with suitable authority! For in the same passage of his letter he added and appended: “Since the heretics themselves, properly speaking, do not baptize those who come to them from one another, but merely admit them to communion.” To this depth of evil, then, has the Church of God and bride of Christ fallen: that she should follow the examples of heretics; that, for the celebration of the heavenly sacraments, light should borrow discipline from darkness; and that Christians should do what antichrists do.

But what blindness of mind, what perversity it is to refuse to acknowledge the unity of faith that comes from the tradition of God the Father and of Jesus Christ our Lord and God! For if the Church is not [Col. 1131B] among the heretics because she is one and cannot be divided, and if the Holy Spirit is not there because he is one and cannot exist among profane and alien persons, then certainly Baptism also, which abides in that same unity, cannot exist among heretics, because it cannot be separated either from the Church or from the Holy Spirit.

[Note: [Col. 1131D]

V.—*Why does the same majesty.* Read: “why does not the same majesty.” The negative dropped out. The error was introduced by Rigaltius and perpetuated in the English edition.

*Has been made.* In the editions of Erasmus and Morel, which Pamelius preferred to the Manutian edition, the reading is “has not been made.” But the old manuscripts do not have the negative, which certainly appears contrary to Saint Cyprian’s meaning.]

### V

Or if they attribute the effect of Baptism to the majesty of the Name, so that those who are baptized in the name of Jesus Christ, wherever and however they are baptized, are judged to have been renewed and sanctified, why is the hand not also laid upon the baptized person there, in the name of the same Christ, for the reception of the Holy Spirit? Why does not the same majesty of the same Name prevail in the laying on of the hand, which they contend has prevailed in the sanctification of Baptism? For if [Col. 1131C] someone born outside the Church can become a temple of God, why can the Holy Spirit not also be poured out upon that temple? For one who, after his sins have been put off in Baptism, has been sanctified and spiritually reformed into a new man has been made fit to receive the Holy Spirit, since the Apostle says: “As many of you as have been baptized in Christ have put on Christ” (Gal. 3:27). He who can put on Christ after being baptized among heretics can much more readily receive the Holy Spirit whom Christ sent. Otherwise, the one sent will be greater than the one who sent him, so that a person baptized outside might have begun indeed to put on Christ but could not receive the Holy Spirit—as though Christ could either be put on without the Spirit or the Spirit be separated from Christ.

How absurd it also is that, although the second birth is spiritual—the birth by which we are born in Christ through the washing of regeneration—they say that someone can be spiritually born among heretics, where they deny that the Spirit exists. For water alone cannot cleanse sins and sanctify a person unless it also has the Holy Spirit. Therefore they must either concede that the Holy Spirit is present where they say Baptism is present, or else there is no Baptism where the Holy Spirit is not, because Baptism cannot exist without the Holy Spirit.

[Note: [Col. 1131D]

VI.—*He preserved.* Erasmus printed “he saved.” That reading appears in two of our manuscripts and in the Cambron manuscript, as Pamelius testifies. But thirteen others of ours have “he preserved.” Nevertheless, the reading introduced by Erasmus has until now prevailed in every edition. Caelius Calcagninus, Book II, Letter 9, judges that *servatorem* (“preserver”) rather than *salvatorem* (“savior”) should be written.]

### VI

But what sort of claim is it to assert and maintain that people who were not born in the Church can be sons of God? For the blessed Apostle reveals and proves that Baptism is that in which the old person dies and [Col. 1132B] the new is born, saying: “He preserved us through the washing of regeneration” (Titus 3:5). If, then, regeneration is in the washing, that is, in Baptism, how can heresy generate children for God through Christ when it is not Christ’s bride? For it is the Church alone that, joined and united to Christ, spiritually generates children, as the same Apostle says again: “Christ loved the Church and gave himself up for her, that he might sanctify her, cleansing her with the washing of water” (Eph. 5:25–26). If, therefore, she is the beloved and the bride who alone is sanctified by Christ and alone cleansed by his washing, it is evident that heresy, which is not Christ’s bride, can neither be cleansed nor sanctified by his washing and cannot generate children for God.

[Note: [Col. 1131D]

VII.—*He breathed.* This passage, taken from the second chapter of Genesis, is quoted according to the Old Latin version used by Saint Cyprian. That Avitus of Vienne also used [Col. 1132D] this version is clear from his second Letter to Gundobad. Avitus, moreover, censures those who used the version that we use today. Tertullian, however, quotes this passage in the form used by those whom Avitus criticizes. In a letter by a certain Otbert concerning the death of Hugh of Saint-Victor, which the Reverend Father Edmond Martène published in the fifth volume of his *Anecdota*, it is written that, when Hugh was at the point of death, he asked Otbert whether anyone besides him was present there and whether he had celebrated Mass that day. When Otbert replied that no one else was there and that he had celebrated that day, Hugh said to him: “Come near and breathe upon my face in the form of a cross, so that I may receive the Holy Spirit.” Great was Hugh’s faith: he desired someone to breathe upon his face so that, if he could not receive the Holy Spirit by imitation, he might at least come very near to doing so and thus go to Christ with greater confidence.

*Breath.* One royal manuscript has “breath” (*spiraculum*), as in the Vulgate edition of Genesis.

*Before the Church as mother.* Eleven old manuscripts read: “may have [Col. 1133C] before the Church as mother.” But the word “have” is absent from three manuscripts that are likewise ancient and from the early editions. Above, Letter X, page 20: “Let the mother first receive before the Lord’s peace.”

*The obstinacy of our brother Stephen.* Vincent of Lérins, chapter 21, said “with so great an adamant of pertinacity”; Cassiodorus, Book IV, Letter 3, “with raw obstinacy”; the constitution of Gratian and Valentinian under the title *On Heretics* in the Theodosian Code, “the persistent custom of obstinacy.” By contrast, Valerius Maximus, Book III, chapter 2, has “pertinacity in virtue.” For we noted to Baronius, in [Col. 1133D] our annotations on the *Capitularies*, page 1111, that “pertinacity” was sometimes used in a favorable sense.]

### VII

Moreover, it is not through the laying on of hands [Col. 1132C] that anyone is born when he receives the Holy Spirit, but in the Church’s baptism, so that, having already been born, he may receive the Holy Spirit, just as was done in the case of the first man, Adam (Gen. 2). For God first fashioned him, and then breathed into his face the breath of life. Nor indeed can the Spirit be received unless there first exists someone to receive him. But since the birth of Christians is in baptism, while birth and sanctification in baptism are found only with the bride of Christ, who can give birth spiritually and beget children for God, where, and from whom, and for whom was one born who is not a son of the Church, so that anyone could have God as Father before having the Church as Mother? Since, moreover, no heresy whatsoever, nor even any schism, can possess outside the Church the sanctification of saving baptism, why has the harsh obstinacy of our brother Stephen [Col. 1133A] burst forth to such an extent that he contends that even from the baptism of Marcion—and likewise that of Valentinus, Apelles, and the others who blaspheme against God the Father—children are born to God, and says that remission of sins is given there in the name of Jesus Christ, where the Father and the Lord God Christ are blasphemed?

> **Note: [Col. 1131D]**
>
> **VIII.—A priest of God.** So read six of our manuscripts and five English ones. Previously it read: “The reasoning of a priest of God may be sustained on the day of judgment when he asserts and presumes and accepts as valid the baptisms of blasphemers.”
>
> **The sacred obligations of divine military service.** Below, in the book *On the Lapsed*, p. 183: “the sacrament of Christ might be dissolved through headlong rashness.” These expressions are taken from military discipline. See Godeschalcus Stewechius on Vegetius, where he correctly explains the form of the soldiers’ military oath (*sacramentum*). See also St. John Chrysostom at the beginning of the second exhortation to Theodore the Lapsed.
>
> **Of the heavenly camp.** Previously *sacrorum* (“of sacred things”) was read here, which makes no sense. We have restored the true reading on the authority of ten old copies.
>
> **More abundantly.** We found this reading in six of our ancient codices and in five English ones. Previously *liberius* (“more freely”) was written. Thus, at the end of this Epistle, p. 141, through a copyist’s error, in one codex *eadem libertate* (“with the same freedom”) was put for *ubertate* (“abundance”). In the Burgundian manuscript I found [Col. 1134C], in the book *On the Dress of Virgins*, p. 175, *Facultatum libertate locupletes* (“rich in freedom of resources”) for *ubertate* (“abundance”). And in the book *On the Lord’s Prayer*, p. 207, in the Pithou and de Thou codices, *bonitatis libertas* (“freedom of goodness”) occurs for *ubertas* (“abundance”). In this same Epistle LXXIV to Pompeius, in Lamonius’s codex, a little later, “the water collected is restored with the same *libertas*.” For this, the other codices and editions correctly have *ubertas*. In the book *In Praise of Martyrdom*, Morel’s edition reads *uberius atque propensius* (“more abundantly and readily”); for this, some old manuscripts have *liberius* (“more freely”).
>
> **With snakes.** Although this reading is found in only five copies, I nevertheless do not doubt that it should be preferred to the one that had long prevailed. For I do not see what these words would mean: “sprouting with serpentine hair.” Rigaltius recognized this as the true reading; for in the errata he advised that *anguibus* (“with snakes”) should be restored. Horace, Book III, Ode 31: “The snakes are refreshed by the twisted locks of the Eumenides.” The same author, *Epodes* 5: “Canidia, her hair entwined with short vipers.” Seneca, *Medea*: “Be present, avenging goddesses of crime, squalid, your hair loosened into serpents.” Lucan, Book VI:
>
> > And her dreadful hair is bound up with garlands of vipers.
>
> Ludovicus Caelius Rhodiginus, Book I, chapter 40, reports from Avicenna that serpents are conceived especially from women’s hair. We noted a similar error in the second volume of the *Capitularies*, p. 987.

### VIII

At this point, dearest brother, it must be considered, in accordance with the faith and religious duty of the priestly office that we discharge, whether a priest of God can sustain his case on the day of judgment if he asserts and approves and accepts as valid the baptisms of blasphemers, when the Lord threatens and says: “And now this commandment is for you, O priests: [Col. 1133B] if you will not listen, and if you will not lay it to heart to give honor to my name, says the Lord Almighty, I will send a curse upon you, and I will curse your blessing” (Mal. 2:1–2).

Does one give honor to God who enters into communion with the baptism of Marcion? Does one give honor to God who judges that remission of sins is given among those who blaspheme against God? Does one give honor to God who asserts that children are born to God outside, from an adulteress and a harlot? Does one give honor to God who, while not holding fast to the unity and truth that come from the divine law, champions heresies against the Church? Does one give honor to God who, as a friend of heretics and an enemy of Christians, thinks that the priests of God who uphold the truth of Christ and the unity of the Church should be excluded from communion?

If this is how honor is given to God, if this is how the fear and [Col. 1133C] discipline of God are preserved by his worshipers and priests, let us cast away our weapons; let us surrender our hands into captivity; let us hand over to the devil the ordering of the Gospel, the dispensation of Christ, and the majesty of God. Let the sacred obligations [Col. 1134A] of divine military service be dissolved; let the standards of the heavenly camp be betrayed; let the Church succumb and yield to heretics, light to darkness, faith to faithlessness, hope to despair, reason to error, immortality to death, charity to hatred, truth to falsehood, Christ to antichrist. Deservedly, then, do schisms and heresies arise day after day, grow more frequently and abundantly, and, sprouting with serpentine snakes, bring forth against the Church of God the venom of their poisons with ever greater force, while the advocacy of certain persons gives them both authority and stability, while their baptism is defended, while faith and truth are betrayed, and while that which is done outside against the Church is championed within the Church herself.

> **Note: [Col. 1134D]**
>
> **Inviolate.** The Fuxensis codex reads “immaculate.”
>
> **Custom without truth.** Angelus Politianus quotes this passage, though without naming Cyprian, in the preface to his *Miscellanies*. For he says: “Someone has put it beautifully thus: ‘Custom without truth is the antiquity of error.’” Gratian also quotes it, Distinction 8, chapter *Consuetudo*. See the notes on Epistle LXXI, p. 498.

### IX

But if the fear of God is among us, dearest brother; if firmness of faith prevails; if we keep Christ’s [Col. 1134B] commandments; if we guard the incorrupt and inviolate holiness of his bride; if the words of the Lord adhere to our minds and hearts when he says, “Do you think that, when the Son of Man comes, he will find faith on earth?” (Luke 18:8), then, as faithful soldiers of God who serve God with sincere faith and religious devotion, let us guard with faithful courage the camp divinely entrusted to us.

Nor should a custom that had crept in among certain persons prevent truth from prevailing and conquering. For custom without truth is the antiquity of error. Therefore, abandoning error, let us follow truth, knowing that in Esdras also truth conquers, as it is written: “Truth remains and grows strong forever, and lives and prevails unto ages of ages. With it there is no partiality or distinction, but it does what is just; nor is there injustice in its judgment, but strength, and sovereignty, and majesty, and the power of all ages. Blessed be the Lord, the God of truth” [Col. 1134C] (3 Esdr. 4:34–40). Christ, revealing this truth to us [Col. 1135A] in his Gospel, says: “I am the truth” (John 14:6). Therefore, if we are in Christ and have Christ in us, if we remain in the truth and the truth remains in us, let us hold fast to what is true and right.

> **Note: [Col. 1135C]**
>
> **Nor contentious.** These words did not appear in Erasmus’s edition. Manutius and Morel introduced them. Pamelius deleted them because he had not found them in the Cambron codex. They are indeed absent from four old manuscripts, but are present in twelve others and in two Bodleian manuscripts.
>
> **To abandon error.** St. Pope Gregory, in his letter [Col. 1135D] to St. Augustine: “It is indeed characteristic of good minds to acknowledge fault where no fault exists.” Innocent III, in Bzovius under the year 1206, §6: “It is characteristic of good minds to fear fault where no fault at all is found.” By contrast, Quintilian, Book VI, chapter 4: “For obstinately defending a fault, especially one that has been exposed, is a second fault.” Jerome, Book I, *Against Rufinus*: “It is better for you to repent of what you have done than for both a martyr to persist in calumny and the deceived to persist in error. Nor should you blush at changing your judgment. You do not possess such great authority and reputation that you should be ashamed to have erred.” Likewise, in the *Letter to Pammachius on the Best Method of Translating*: “To err is human, and to confess error is the mark of a prudent man.” And in the *Letter to Pammachius and Oceanus against the Errors of Origen*: “The second plank after shipwreck is humbly to confess.” And in the *Letter to Marcella on Five Questions of the New Testament*: “I do not remember ever having said this; and if I had said it, I would not persist obstinately in error.” Rufinus, Book II, *Against Jerome*: “It is certain that error preceded wherever correction followed.” Augustine [Col. 1136C], Sermon CLXX, *On the Words of the Apostle*: “To have erred was human. To remain in error through willful pride is diabolical.” St. John Chrysostom also said the same thing in his first exhortation to Theodore the Lapsed: “For to have sinned is human, but to persist in wicked deeds is not human, but rather diabolical.” Likewise Augustine, in the *Letter to Celer*: “It is shameful to change one’s opinion”—if it is true and right. For if it is foolish and harmful, changing it is both praiseworthy and salutary. “For just as constancy does not allow a man to be corrupted, so obstinacy does not allow him to be corrected.” [Col. 1136D]
>
> **If a channel.** Jerome, in the *Letter to Marcus Celedensis*: “If a stream flows thinly, the fault lies not in the channel but in the spring.”

### X

It comes about through zealous presumption and stubbornness that someone prefers to defend his own depraved and false positions rather than assent to the right and true positions of another. With this in view, the blessed apostle Paul writes to Timothy and admonishes that a bishop ought not to be quarrelsome or contentious, but gentle and teachable (2 Tim. 2:24). A teachable man is one who is mild and gentle in his willingness to learn. For a bishop ought not only to teach, but also to learn, since he teaches better when he daily grows and advances by learning better things. [Col. 1135B] This the same apostle Paul also teaches, admonishing that, if something better has been revealed to another who is seated, the first should be silent (1 Cor. 14:30).

For devout and simple minds, both abandoning error and finding and extracting truth is a straightforward matter. If we return to the head and source of the divine tradition, human error ceases; and when the rationale of the heavenly sacraments has been examined, whatever lay obscure beneath the gloom and cloud of darkness is disclosed in the light of truth.

If a channel carrying water, which previously flowed copiously and abundantly, should suddenly fail, do we not go to the spring so that the cause of the failure may be ascertained there—whether the water has dried up at its source because the veins have gone dry, or whether, flowing full and undiminished from there, it has failed midway on its course? Thus, if it has happened through the fault of a broken or leaking channel [Col. 1135C] that the water did not continue to flow uninterruptedly, persistently, and continually, then, once the channel has been repaired and strengthened, the collected water may be restored for the use and drinking of the city with the same abundance and integrity with which it issues from the spring.

And this is what the priests of God, keeping the divine commandments, ought now to do: if truth has faltered and wavered in any respect, let us return to the Lord’s source and to the [Col. 1136A] evangelical and apostolic tradition, and let the rationale of our conduct arise from the place from which both its order and its origin arose.

> **Note: [Col. 1136D]**
>
> **Eight human souls.** We restored this passage thus on the authority of eight of our manuscripts and six English ones. For below also, in Epistle LXXVI, p. 152, it is likewise read as it is here. The word *hominum* (“human”), however, does not occur in the epistle of St. Peter or in Jerome’s dialogue *Against the Luciferians*.
>
> **Be seen to have been saved.** The editions have *salvus* (“safe”). I restored *salvatus* (“saved”), following the authority of thirteen of our copies and four English ones.
>
> **By the Lord’s unity.** The old Rheims codex and three English manuscripts have “by the power of observing the Lord’s ordinance.”

### XI

For it has been handed down to us that there is one God, one Christ, one hope, and one faith (Eph. 4:5), and one Church, and one baptism established nowhere except in the one Church. Whoever departs from this Unity must necessarily be found among the heretics; and while he champions them against the Church, he attacks the sacred bond of the divine tradition.

We see the sacred bond of this Unity expressed also in the Song of Songs, in the person of Christ saying: “An enclosed garden, my sister, my bride; a sealed fountain, a well of living water, a paradise with the fruit of apples” (Song 4:12–13). But if his Church is an enclosed garden and a sealed fountain, how can one who is not in the Church [Col. 1136B] enter that same garden or drink from its fountain?

Peter himself likewise, demonstrating and defending Unity, commanded and admonished that we cannot be saved except through the one sole baptism of the one Church. “In Noah’s ark,” he says, “a few—that is, eight human souls—were saved through water; similarly, baptism will also save you” (1 Pet. 3:20–21). How concisely and spiritually he manifested the sacred bond of unity! For just as, in that baptism of the world by which its ancient iniquity was purged, one who was not in Noah’s ark could not be saved through water, so neither now can one be regarded as saved through baptism if he was not baptized in the Church, which was founded in the Lord’s unity according to the sacred figure of the one ark.

[Col. 1136C]

> **Note: [Col. 1136D]**
>
> **Had passed over to the heretics.** One royal codex reads, “are shown to have departed to the heretics.” The reading retained by us [Col. 1137C] appears to be confirmed by these words of Cyprian from Epistle LXXI, p. 127: “and to have passed from us to the heretics.”

### XII

Accordingly, dearest brother, this rule is observed and maintained by us, after the truth has been investigated and clearly discerned: all who are converted to the Church from any heresy whatsoever are to be baptized with the Church’s one legitimate baptism, except those who had previously been baptized in the Church and afterward passed over to the heretics. For when these return, they ought, after performing penance, to be received by the laying on of hands [Col. 1137A] alone and restored by the shepherd to the fold from which they had strayed.

I wish you, dearest brother, always good health.

# EPISTLE OF ST. CYPRIAN TO MAGNUS, ON BAPTIZING THE NOVATIANS AND ON THOSE WHO RECEIVE GRACE IN SICKBED

## ARGUMENT

Magnus’s inquiry whether those coming from Novatian must be baptized again is answered. First, unity is established from the testimony of Holy Scripture. Legitimate succession in the chair of Peter is a sure mark of unity. The sacred bond of unity was sanctioned not only by admonitions and examples, but also by punishments imposed upon offenders. Schismatics, although they acknowledge the words of the Creed, deny the faith itself. Examples show with how great a danger the peace of the Church is violated, even though the faith remains intact. Cyprian digresses to the baptism of heretics, whom he denies to be able to give the Holy Spirit; then he answers concerning the washing of the sick, concerning sprinkling for removing uncleanness, and concerning the grace conferred in Baptism, which may be either diminished or increased by our conduct. [Col. 1137B]

> **Note: [Col. 1137C]**
>
> **To Magnus, his son.** These words certainly show—as Baronius also thought—that this man was one of the people, that is, a layman. I readily assent to that judgment, which seems to me the best. A recent author of the *Life of St. Cyprian*, however, contends that he was a bishop, and to prove his opinion adduces an example from Epistle LXI to Euchratius the bishop, at the end of which Cyprian says: “I wish you, dearest son, always good health.” It is indeed so written in the editions of Manutius, Pamelius, Rigaltius, and the English editors. But the old editions have “dearest brother.” We have restored it in this form, following the authority of the old editions and manuscripts. Reinhart perceived the defect in Rigaltius’s edition, which he generally followed, and omitted the word “son,” writing simply: “I wish you, dearest one, always good health.” Thus, once the true reading is restored, the argument of the author of the *Life of St. Cyprian* collapses. As for Cyprian’s calling the layman Magnus “son,” this derives from the discipline of the ancient bishops and presbyters, who, as Jerome says in the *Letter to Salvina on Preserving Widowhood*, by virtue of their priestly office loved all Christians as sons. See our notes on Salvian’s ninth Epistle.
>
> **We say that all.** In Gratian, Causa XXIV, question 1, *didicimus* (“we have learned”) is written.
>
> **Absolutely all who with him.** So read all the old editions before the Manutian edition, which adds “heretics,” as it is also added in Gratian. But I found that word in only three old manuscripts. Since I saw that all the old editions, twenty-two of our manuscripts, and six English ones do not have it, I judged that it should not be retained. For the sense is properly coherent even without it.
>
> **[Col. 1138C] He who is not with me.** The judgments of learned men sometimes slip. The English editors noted that almost this entire passage was taken from the book *On the Unity of the Church*, and therefore that Cyprian rightly used these words as his own. This is not true. For they are not in the book *On the Unity of the Church*, but in Epistle LXX, which was sent to the Numidian bishops, p. 126.
>
> **He who does not gather with me.** Jerome, in the *Letter to Damasus on the Three Hypostases*: “He who does not gather with you scatters; that is, he who is not Christ’s is antichrist’s.”
>
> **Separately.** I have put *separes* in place of what was formerly read, *separatos*, not only because I found it written thus in the old editions, but also because this reading is preferred by seventeen of our copies—including the Séguier manuscript, the oldest of all—and by three [Col. 1138D] English ones. Statius, *Thebaid*, Book IV:
>
> > You, Perseus, separate the righteous Elysian company,  
> > And let the Arcadian, with his potent wand, drive them from the clouds.
>
> I think Orderic Vitalis derived from this what he says on p. 907: “But the nobles who were to lead separate companies on the lawful expedition ought to have hesitated.” See Du Cange’s Latin Glossary.
>
> Mabillon, Book IX of the *Benedictine Annals*, §37, reports from an old narrative that the River Laudosa in our Brittany received the changed name *Separ*, because it divided itself (*se separavit*) to make a way for the people of Vertou, who wished to possess the body of St. Martin, their abbot; the river had blocked that way against the people of the Duriensis region, who were striving in opposition. It is certain that the River Separ in that part of Brittany is mentioned in the old *Acts* published in the second volume of the recent *History of Brittany*, pp. 278–279. Hadrianus Valesius, however, rejects this etymology and says that *Separ* is a Gallic word.

### I

Cyprian to Magnus, his son: greetings.

In accordance with your religious diligence, dearest son, you have consulted our humble judgment as to whether, among the other heretics, those also who come from Novatian after his profane washing [Col. 1138A] ought to be baptized and sanctified in the Catholic Church with the Church’s legitimate, true, and sole Baptism.

> **Variant:** “sole Baptism of repentance”—Lamonius codex. [Col. 1137B]

On this matter, insofar as the capacity of our faith and the holiness and truth of the divine Scriptures suggest, we say that absolutely all heretics and schismatics possess no power or right. Consequently, Novatian neither ought nor can be excepted from being numbered among the adversaries and antichrists, since he stands outside the Church and acts against the peace and love of Christ.

For when our Lord Jesus Christ testified in his Gospel that those who were not with him were his adversaries, he did not designate any particular form of heresy, but showed that absolutely all [Col. 1138B] who were not with him, and who did not gather with him but scattered his flock, were his adversaries, saying: “He who is not with me is against me; and he who does not gather with me scatters” (Luke 11:23).

> **Variant:** Oxford adds “heretics.” [Col. 1137B]

Likewise, the blessed apostle John did not distinguish any one heresy or schism, nor did he set down certain persons separately in particular, but called all who had departed from the Church and who acted against the Church antichrists, saying: “You have heard that antichrist is coming; but now many antichrists have arisen. From this we know that it is the last hour. They went out from us, but they were not of us. For if they had been of us, they would surely have remained with us” (1 John 2:18–19).

> **Variant:** *separes* (“separately”), Bodl. 1, Ben., Lincoln, N.C. 2; *separans* (“separating”), Bodl. 2; *separatos* (“separate”), Oxford and printed editions, etc. [Col. 1138B]

From this it is evident that all who are known to have withdrawn from the love and unity of the Catholic Church are adversaries of the Lord [Col. 1139A] and antichrists.

> **Variants:** So Bodl. 1, 2, Lincoln, Lamonius, York, N.C. 1, 2; “the Lord’s antichrists,” Rigaltius. “Withdrawn from the unity of the Church,” Lamonius. [Col. 1139C]

Furthermore, the Lord also sets down and says in his Gospel: “But if he also disregards the Church, let him be to you as a gentile and a tax collector” (Matt. 18:17). If those who disregard the Church are regarded as gentiles and tax collectors, much more assuredly must rebels and enemies who devise false altars, unlawful priesthoods, sacrilegious sacrifices, and adulterated names be numbered among gentiles and tax collectors, since those who commit lesser sins and are merely despisers of the Church are judged gentiles and tax collectors by the Lord’s sentence.

> **Note: [Col. 1139C]**
>
> **II.—He declares in the Song.** These few words do indeed occur in the book *On the Unity of the Church*, p. 195. Nevertheless, it cannot be inferred from this that they were taken from that book.
>
> **An enclosed garden.** Jerome, in the *Letter to Damasus on the Three Hypostases*: “Among broken cisterns that hold no water, it is difficult to understand where the sealed fountain and that enclosed garden may be.” And below: [Col. 1139D] “But I, following no one as first except Christ, am joined in communion to Your Beatitude and to the chair of Peter. I know that the Church was built upon that rock. Whoever eats the lamb outside this house is profane. If anyone is not in Noah’s ark, he will perish when the flood reigns.” He has regard to the dignity and authority of the principal Church.
>
> **A well of living water.** The English editors correctly note that these words are not found in the sacred text. For they do not occur immediately after “a sealed fountain”; rather, a little below there is “a well of living waters.” Cyprian cited this passage in the same way in Epistle LXXIV to Pompeius, p. 142. It is also cited thus by Augustine in Book XI of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapter 21; Book V of *On Baptism, against the Donatists*, chapter 27; Book II of *Against Cresconius*, chapter 15; and Epistle LV. It is otherwise in Ambrose, who, in Book I of *On Virgins*, chapter 8; the book *On Virginity*, chapter 13; and the *Letter to Sabinus*, does not add “a well of living water” after “a sealed fountain” when citing this passage. This may be evidence that he used a different version from the one [Col. 1140C] Cyprian used.
>
> **To give life and sanctify.** St. Augustine cites this passage in Book VII of *On Baptism, against the Donatists*, chapter 50.
>
> **The Church is one and.** Gerhoh of Reichersberg cites this passage, though incompletely, in his treatise *Against the Simoniacs*, chapter 27. John of Capistrano [Col. 1140D] used it against Felix V, who had been elected pope by the Council of Basel. See his treatise *On the Authority of the Pope and Council*, part 3.

### II

That the Church is one the Holy Spirit declares in the Song of Songs, speaking in the person of Christ: “One is my dove, my perfect one; she is the only one of her mother, the chosen one of her who bore her” [Col. 1139B] (Song 6:9). Of her he again says: “An enclosed garden, my sister, my bride; a sealed fountain, a well of living water” (Song 4:12).

But if the bride of Christ, who is the Church, is an enclosed garden, a thing closed cannot lie open to strangers and the profane.

> **Variant:** “shut up,” Lincoln. [Col. 1139C]

And if it is a sealed fountain, one who is situated outside and has no access to the fountain can neither drink from it nor be sealed there. If, moreover, the well of living water is one, and that same well is within, one situated outside cannot be given life and sanctified by that water, the entire use and drinking of which have been granted only to those who are within.
