Peter too, showing that the Church is one and that only those who are in the Church can be baptized, set down and said: “In Noah’s ark a few—that is, eight human souls—were saved [Col. 1139C] through water; similarly, baptism will also save you” [Col. 1140A] (1 Pet. 3:20–21), proving and attesting that the one ark of Noah was a type of the one Church.

> **Variants:** “will also save us,” Bodl. 3; “proving, namely,” Lamonius, Bodl. 2, York, N.C. 1. [Col. 1139C]

If, then, in that baptism of the expiated and purified world, one who was not in Noah’s ark could have been saved through water, then one who is not in the Church, to which alone baptism has been granted, can now also be given life through baptism.

> **Variant:** “in that baptism of the expiated and purified world,” Lamonius, Bodl. 2, York, N.C. 1. [Col. 1140C]

But the apostle Paul, manifesting this same truth still more openly and clearly, writes to the Ephesians and says: “Christ loved the Church and delivered himself up for her, that he might sanctify her, cleansing her with the washing of water” (Eph. 5:25–26).

> **Variants:** “more clearly and manifestly,” Lamonius, Bodl. 2; “cleansing with the washing,” Lamonius, Bodl. 2, York, N.C. 1. [Col. 1140C]

But if the Church is one—the Church that is loved by Christ and alone is cleansed by his washing—how can one who is not in the Church either be loved by Christ or be washed and cleansed by his washing?

> **Note: [Col. 1140D]**
>
> **III.—If the Church is with Novatian, it was not with Cornelius.** In explicit words he teaches that the legitimate succession of the Roman pontiffs is a mark of the Church, since he says that the Church was with Cornelius because Cornelius succeeded Fabian by legitimate ordination, but was not with Novatian because Novatian, succeeding no one, originated from himself. He said similar things above in the epistle to Antonianus. Hence it is that the ancients too judged that to be the Catholic Church in which the Roman pontiff presided. Thus, according to St. Ambrose’s testimony in his funeral oration, his brother Satyrus inquired of a certain bishop whether he agreed with the Catholic bishops—that is, with the Roman Church. Thus St. Jerome, in the *Letter to Damasus*, teaches that the sealed fountain and the Church’s enclosed garden are in the chair of Peter; that whoever eats the lamb outside that Church is profane; and that if anyone is not in it as in Noah’s ark, [Col. 1141C] he will perish in the flood—undoubtedly alluding to this and similar passages of Cyprian. The same author, in the following epistle to the same man: “If anyone,” he says, “is joined to the Chair of Peter, he is mine.” Thus St. Augustine, *Against the Fundamental Epistle*, chapter 4: “The succession of priests,” he says, “from the very see of the apostle Peter down to the present episcopate holds me in the Church.” Thus the same author, in the *Psalm against the Party of Donatus* and Epistle 165, and Optatus of Milevis, *Against Parmenian*, Book II, refute the Donatists by the doctrine continuously handed down in the Roman Church through the legitimate succession of pontiffs. With the same argument Irenaeus attacks the heretics of his age, especially in Book III, chapter 3, as do Tertullian, imitating him, in the book *On Prescription against Heretics*, and Origen in Book I of *On First Principles*. —PAMELIUS. [Col. 1141D]

### III

Therefore, since the Church alone possesses living water and the power to baptize and wash a person [Col. 1140B], anyone who says that someone can be baptized and sanctified with Novatian must first show and prove that Novatian is in the Church or presides over the Church. For the Church is one, and, being one, she cannot be both within and outside.

If the Church is with Novatian, she was not with Cornelius. But if she was with Cornelius, who succeeded Bishop Fabian by legitimate ordination and whom the Lord glorified not only with the honor of the priesthood but also with martyrdom, Novatian is not in the Church and cannot be reckoned a bishop, since, having disregarded the evangelical and apostolic tradition, he succeeded no one and originated from himself.

> **Variant:** “nor can he be reckoned a bishop,” Lincoln, York. [Col. 1140C]

For one who was not ordained in the Church [Col. 1140C] can in no way possess or maintain the Church.

### IV

That the Church does not exist outside, and cannot be split or divided against herself, but maintains the unity of an inseparable and indivisible house, is made manifest by the faith of divine Scripture [Col. 1141A]. For concerning the sacrament of Passover and of the Lamb—the lamb signified Christ—it is written: “It shall be eaten in one house; you shall not cast the flesh outside the house” (Exod. 12:46).

We see this also expressed in the case of Rahab, who herself likewise bore the type of the Church. She is commanded and told: “You shall gather your father and your mother and your brothers and the entire household of your father to yourself in your house; and everyone who goes outside the door of your house shall be responsible for himself” (Josh. 2:18).

> **Variant:** “This is commanded of her,” Lamonius, York, N.C. 1. [Col. 1141C]

By this sacred figure it is declared that all who are to live and escape the destruction of the world must be gathered into the one house alone, that is, into the Church. But whoever among those gathered goes outside [Col. 1141B]—that is, if anyone, although he has obtained grace in the Church, withdraws and departs from the Church—will be responsible for himself; that is, he will impute to himself his own destruction.

This the apostle Paul explains when he teaches and commands that a heretic is to be avoided as a perverse sinner who is condemned by himself (Titus 3:10). For the man responsible for himself is one who was not cast out by the bishop but fled voluntarily from the Church and was condemned by himself through heretical presumption.

> **Variant:** “For it is he who will be responsible for himself, not…,” Bodl. 1, 2, York, Lincoln, Lamonius. [Col. 1141C]
>
> **Note: [Col. 1141D]**
>
> **V.—Successive.** Previously *succidanea* was written here. That reading is excellent. But since the reading we have restored is also excellent and is found in almost all the old manuscripts, we decided to retain it. One of my old manuscripts incorrectly has *succidua*, another *subitanca*.
>
> **Of the Lord’s peace.** The codex of St. Arnulf has “passion.”
>
> **He becomes an outsider.** St. Augustine cites this passage in Book VII of *On Baptism, against the Donatists*, chapter 50.
>
> **The Lord’s sacrifices.** Two old manuscripts prefer “sacraments.”
>
> **Clusters and grapes.** The codex of St. Arnulf has *botrui* [Col. 1142C]; the Fuxensis, “clusters and grapes”; the Corbie codex, “clusters and bunches”; the old Rheims manuscript, *botris unionibus atque acinis*, where perhaps *botrionibus atque acinis* (“small clusters and grapes”) should be read. For Martial, Book XI, Epigram 28, said: “Nor does he think you worth a whole cluster.” Palladius also, Book II of *On Agriculture*, chapter 33; Book X, chapter 17; and Book XII [Col. 1142D], chapter 12, used *botryones* (“clusters”). Prudentius, in the *Hamartigenia*, speaks of “the rich valley of the cluster.” Ludovicus Caelius Rhodiginus, Book VII, chapter 45: “A certain man was called *Philobotryx* [‘lover of clusters’], because he was remarkably fond of grapes.”

### V

And therefore the Lord, conveying to us the unity that comes from divine authority, sets down and says: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). Bringing his Church back to that unity, he says again: “And there shall be one flock and one shepherd” (John 10:16).

> **Variant:** “And they shall be one flock,” Bodl. 2. [Col. 1141C]

But if there is one flock, how can one be numbered with the flock who is not among the number [Col. 1141C] of the flock? Or how can one be regarded as a shepherd who, while the true shepherd remains and presides in the Church of God [Col. 1142A] through successive ordination, succeeds no one and begins from himself, and thereby becomes an outsider and profane, an enemy of the Lord’s peace and divine unity, not dwelling in the house of God—that is, in the Church of God, in which none dwell except those who are concordant and of one mind—as the Holy Spirit speaks in the Psalms and says: “God, who makes those of one mind dwell in a house” (Ps. 67:6)?

> **Variant:** “but beginning from himself,” Lamonius, N.C. 1, York, Bodl. 2. [Col. 1141C]
>
> **Note: [Col. 1142D]**
>
> **VI.—He cast off.** One old manuscript of mine has “he drove away.” So also in the Grenoble manuscript.
>
> **Another king for themselves.** Seven old manuscripts and the early editions have “an adulterous king.” Erasmus corrected it. Nine old manuscripts, and especially the Séguier manuscript, confirm Erasmus’s correction. Cyprian’s words a little earlier also confirm it: “and, abandoning their own king, appointed another for themselves outside.” Nevertheless, Pamelius preferred to follow the text of the old editions. Rigaltius and Reinhart followed Pamelius. The English editors correctly restored “another.” A similar error introduced into canon 9 of the Council of Elvira was corrected by us in the notes on Regino, Book II, chapter 103, *On Ecclesiastical Disciplines*. Conversely, in chapter 17 of Liberatus, where the editions correctly have “whom Emperor Zeno ordered to be expelled as a heretic and adulterer,” the old codices of the church of Beauvais and the monastery of Corbie have “another,” certainly in error. [Col. 1143D]
>
> **Had dined.** Several old copies prefer this reading. Others have *pransisset*, a variant form with the same meaning. See what we observed on the acts of the Council of Chalcedon, p. 1051.
>
> **Fills out.** We necessarily restored this reading because it occurs in all the old editions and in nineteen manuscript codices. Pamelius changed it and printed *sonat* (“declares”) on the authority of the Cambron codex. He says that the word *satiat*, found in the other codices, is corrupt. One of my manuscripts reads *favet* (“favors”). Here *satiat* means to prove abundantly what was said before, just as Pliny, Book V, chapter 9, says that the Nile rises according as the snows or rains “have filled” Mauritania—that is, have abounded there. Tertullian, in the *Scorpiace*, says that if a scorpion “has filled the wound”—that is, has poured all its poison into it—the former sensations immediately retreat. In the same sense Cyprian, in the book *On Works and Almsgiving*, p. 239, says that entreaties alone have little power to obtain anything unless they are “filled out” by the addition of deeds and works. Ovid, *Tristia*, Book III, Elegy 1, said: “When it has now satiated its anger.” [Col. 1144D]
>
> **Greater understanding.** The codex of St. Arnulf has “with a greater light of understanding.”

VI. Finally, the Lord’s sacrifices themselves declare that Christian unanimity is joined to them by firm and inseparable charity. [Note: [Col. 1142C] “Firm Christian [unanimity],” Bod. 2, Lam., Ebor., NC. 1, 2, Lin.] For when the Lord calls his body bread, formed by the union of many grains, he signifies our people, whom he bore, united together; and when he calls his blood wine, pressed from many clusters and grapes and gathered into one, he likewise signifies our flock [Col. 1142B] joined together by the mingling of a united multitude. If Novatian is united with this bread of the Lord, if he too is mingled with the people of Christ, then he may be regarded as capable of possessing the grace of the one baptism of the Church—if it is established that he maintains the unity of the Church.

Finally, how inseparable the sacrament of unity is, and how utterly without hope those are, and how great a ruin they obtain for themselves from God’s indignation, who create a schism and, after abandoning their bishop, appoint another false bishop for themselves outside, is declared by divine Scripture in the books of Kings, where ten tribes were torn away from the tribe of Judah and Benjamin and, after abandoning their king [Note: [Col. 1142C] “After abandoning their king,” Lam., Bod. 3, Lin.], appointed another for themselves outside:

> “And the Lord,” it says, “was indignant against all the seed [Note: [Col. 1142C] “Against all the seed,” Bod. 1, 2, Lin., NC. 1, Ebor.] of Israel, and removed [Note: [Col. 1142C] “Destroyed,” Lin., NC. 2.] them, and gave them over to plunder until he cast them away from his presence, because [Col. 1142C] Israel was torn away from the house of David, and they appointed Jeroboam son of Nebat as king for themselves” (2 Kings 22:20, [Col. 1143A] 21).

Scripture says [Note: [Col. 1143C] “The Lord said,” Lam., Ebor., Lin., NC. 1, 2.] that the Lord was indignant and gave them over to destruction because they had been torn from unity [Note: [Col. 1143C] “All who were torn from unity,” Lam., Bod. 2, Ebor., NC. 1.] and had appointed another [Note: [Col. 1143C] Thus Lam., Bened., Lin., Bod. 1, 2, Ebor., NC. 1, 2; “an adulterous,” Rig.] king for themselves. And so great was the Lord’s indignation against those who had created the schism that, even when a man of God was sent to Jeroboam to reproach him for his sins and foretell the coming vengeance, he was forbidden even to eat bread or drink water among them. When he failed to observe this and took a meal contrary to God’s command, he was immediately struck by the majesty of the divine judgment, so that, while returning from there, he was killed on the road by the attack [Note: [Col. 1143C] “Returning, by the bite,” Bod. 1.] and bite of a lion.

And does anyone dare to say that the saving water of baptism and heavenly grace can be shared with schismatics, with whom neither earthly food nor ordinary drink ought to be shared? The Lord further confirms this [Note: [Col. 1143C] Thus Bod. 1, 2, Lam., Ebor., NC. 1, 2, Lin.; “declares,” Oxon.] [Col. 1143B] in his Gospel and reveals a greater light of understanding: those same people who had then separated themselves from the tribe of Judah and Benjamin, and who had abandoned Jerusalem and withdrawn to Samaria, were counted among the profane and the Gentiles. For when he first sent his disciples into the ministry of salvation, he commanded them, saying:

> “Do not go into the way of the nations [Note: [Col. 1143C] “The way of the Gentiles,” Bod. 2, Lam., Ebor., NC. 1.], and do not enter a city of the Samaritans.”

In sending them first to the Jews [Note: [Col. 1143D] “First to the Jews,” Lam., NC. 1, Ebor.], he commands that the Gentiles still be passed by. But by adding that a city of the Samaritans also ought to be omitted—where the schismatics were—he shows that schismatics are placed on the same level as Gentiles.

[Note: [Col. 1144D]

**VII.—Remission.** Most of the old books read: “Do you believe in the remission?”

]

VII. But if anyone raises the objection that Novatian maintains the same rule as the catholic Church, baptizes with the same Creed as we do, knows the same God the Father, the same Son, Christ, [Col. 1143C] and the same Holy Spirit, and that for this reason he can claim the power to baptize, since he appears not to differ from us in the baptismal interrogation [Note: [Col. 1144C] “He appears not to differ from us in the interrogation,” Lam., Bod. 2, Ebor., NC. 1.], whoever thinks this objection should be made must know, first, that we and the schismatics do not have one and the same rule of the Creed, nor the same interrogation. For when they say, [Col. 1144A] “Do you believe in the remission of sins and eternal life through the holy Church?” they lie in the interrogation, since they do not possess the Church. Then, moreover, by their own words they themselves confess that remission of sins cannot be given except through the holy Church; and since they do not possess it, they show that sins cannot be remitted there.

[Note: [Col. 1144D]

**VIII.—Paid.** Thus twelve old books. Five others and the Morel edition read “repaid.”

**Nor could they be valid.** One royal manuscript reads: “Nor could the sacrifice irreligiously and unlawfully offered contrary to the right of the divine ordering be valid and efficacious.”

**Assume the primacy.** I do not sufficiently grasp what *primatus* signifies here. For I cannot agree with Pamelius, who refers these words [Col. 1145C] to the primacy of the Supreme Pontiff. Yet neither do I pass over to the opinion of Goulartius, who declares [Col. 1145D] that these words—which are certainly extant in the ancient manuscripts and editions—crept into the text from the margin. I would more readily believe that Cyprian meant to say that Novatian, the leader and standard-bearer of the schismatics, had retained the primacy out of love for it—that is, the episcopal chair which he had seized—just as Rufinus, book V, chapter 28, says that Natalis, out of love for the primacy, refused to heed the visions or revelations by which he was warned to leave the church in which he had been ordained bishop contrary to ecclesiastical rules. Thus Pope Gelasius, in his treatise against the Greeks, says of Peter, the usurper of the church of Alexandria: “Therefore, he could never have seized it for thirty years except when he burned with love of the episcopate and the heat of ambition.” Thus, where Rufinus had said “out of love for the primacy,” Gelasius wrote “out of love for the episcopate.”

]

VIII. As for the statement that they know the same God the Father as we do, the same Son, Christ, and the same Holy Spirit, not even this can assist such people. For Korah, Dathan, and Abiram also knew the same God as the priest Aaron and Moses; living under the same law [Note: [Col. 1144C] “Law and condition,” NC. 2.] and religion, they invoked the one true God who was to be worshiped and invoked. Nevertheless, because they overstepped the ministry proper to their station and, in opposition to Aaron the priest—who had received the lawful priesthood by God’s favor [Col. 1144B] and the Lord’s ordination—claimed for themselves the right to sacrifice, they were struck by God and immediately paid the penalty for their unlawful attempts. [Note: [Col. 1144C] Thus Bod. 1, 2, 3, Lam., Ebor., Lin., NC. 1, 2; “paid,” Oxon.] Nor could sacrifices irreligiously and unlawfully offered contrary to the right of the divine ordering be valid or effective.

The censers themselves, moreover, in which incense had been unlawfully offered, were not to be used thereafter by the priests, but were instead to furnish later generations in need of correction with a memorial of divine indignation and vengeance. [Note: [Col. 1144C] “Were to be displayed,” Bod. 3.] At the Lord’s command, therefore, they were melted down, purified by fire, beaten into malleable plates, and fastened to the altar, in accordance with the words of divine Scripture:

> “A memorial,” it says, “for the children of Israel, so that no foreigner who is not of the seed of Aaron may approach to offer incense before the Lord, lest he become like Korah.”

And yet those men had not created a schism, nor had they gone outside; nevertheless, they had rebelled shamelessly [Note: [Col. 1144C] “Shamelessly,” Lam., Ebor., Bod. 1, 2, Lin., NC. 1, 2.] and in hostility against God’s priests. These men now tear the Church apart, rebel against the peace and unity of Christ, set up a chair for themselves, assume the primacy [Note: [Col. 1144D] “Principality,” Corb.], and attempt to claim the right to baptize and offer sacrifice. How can those who strive against God to do what is not lawful for them [Note: [Col. 1145C] “What is not lawful for themselves,” Lin., Bod. 2; “is not lawful,” Bod. 1.] accomplish what [Col. 1145A] they undertake or obtain anything from God by their unlawful attempts? Therefore those who patronize Novatian or other schismatics of that kind [Note: [Col. 1145C] “Or heretics,” Lam., Ebor., NC. 1.] contend in vain that anyone can be baptized and sanctified there by saving baptism, where it is established that the person baptizing [Note: [Col. 1145C] “Those baptizing,” Lam., Ebor., Bod. 2, NC. 1.] does not possess the right [Note: [Col. 1145C] “The right and boldness,” Bod. 3.] to baptize.

[Note: [Col. 1145D]

**IX.—Boldness of this kind.** Four old books and the early editions read: “license and boldness of this kind.” See the notes on Letter LXVIII, p. 490.

]

IX. And so that the divine judgment against boldness of this kind might be understood more clearly, we find that in such a crime not only its leaders and instigators but also its participants are destined for punishment, unless they separate themselves from fellowship with the wicked. For the Lord commands through Moses, saying:

> “Separate yourselves from the tents of these most hard-hearted men, and touch nothing that belongs to them, lest you perish together in their sin” (Num. 16).

And the Lord fulfilled what [Col. 1145B] he had threatened through Moses, so that whoever had not separated himself from Korah [Note: [Col. 1145C] Thus Lam., Lin., Ebor., NC. 1, 2; “whoever from Korah,” Oxon.], Dathan, and Abiram immediately paid the penalty for his impious fellowship. By this example it is shown and proved that all who, with irreligious rashness, associate themselves with schismatics against their prelates and priests will be liable both for the guilt and for the punishment. So too the Holy Spirit bears witness through the prophet Hosea, saying:

> “Their sacrifices are like the bread of mourning; all who eat them will be defiled” (Hos. 9),

plainly teaching and showing that absolutely all who have been defiled by their sin are joined with its authors in punishment.

[Note: [Col. 1145D]

**X.—Within the Church itself.** Thus twenty-two old books. [Col. 1146C] The Speyer edition, the old Venetian edition, and Rembolt’s edition read “within [Col. 1146D] the Church itself.” So too the Bec manuscript, which comes to the same thing. I therefore cannot agree with Pamelius, who writes “within the very roofs of the Church.” For although he adduces the authority of four old copies, and although two which I have seen have the same reading, I nevertheless persist in the reading which I restored—not only because Manutius and Morel likewise printed it, and because the authority of so many old copies compels me, but chiefly because Cyprian is fond of speaking in this manner, as was shown above in the notes on Letter LII, p. 450.

]

X. What merit, then, can they have before God when punishments are inflicted upon them by divine decree? Or how can such men justify and sanctify those whom they baptize [Col. 1145C], when, as enemies of the priests, they attempt to usurp things belonging to others, unlawful things, and things granted to them by no right? Yet we are not surprised that they themselves contend in accordance with their depravity. Each must indeed defend [Note: [Col. 1145C] “Each must necessarily defend,” Lam., Bod. 1, 2, NC. 1, 2, Lin.] what he does [Note: [Col. 1146C] “Must insolently,” Lam., Bod. 2.], and they are unwilling, once defeated, to yield readily, [Col. 1146A] although they know that what they are doing is unlawful.

What is surprising [Note: [Col. 1146C] “But what is surprising,” Bod. 2, Lam., Ebor., NC. 1.]—indeed, what ought rather to provoke indignation and grief—is that Christians assist antichrists, and that violators of the faith and traitors to the Church stand within the Church itself [Note: [Col. 1146C] Thus Lam., Bod. 1, 2, Ebor., NC. 1, Lin.; “within the very enclosures of the Church,” Oxon.; “roofs,” Pamel.] against the Church. Though in other respects obstinate and unteachable, they nevertheless confess at least this: that all heretics and schismatics lack the Holy Spirit and can therefore indeed baptize, but cannot give the Holy Spirit. On this very point they are caught by us, so that we may show that those who do not possess the Holy Spirit cannot baptize at all.

[Note: [Col. 1146D]

**XI.—Whether they have.** Thus all editions before the Manutian edition and fourteen old books. Manutius therefore wrote “whether they are regarded as having.” I found this reading in seven ancient manuscripts.

**Immersed.** This correction is owed to one of my old books. So too in Letter LXXII, p. 128: “Those who have been immersed outside, beyond the Church.” In Gratian, XXIV, q. 1, chapter *Didicimus*, the reading is “all,” as in the common editions of Cyprian. So too the manuscript of Saint-Arnoul.

[Col. 1147C] **So that it may be received here.** The Foix manuscript reads: “So that they may receive here what they did not receive there; and it is necessary that it cannot be given through those who are known not to possess the Holy Spirit.”

]

XI. For since in baptism each person’s sins are remitted, the Lord proves and declares in his Gospel that sins can be forgiven only through those who possess [Col. 1146B] the Holy Spirit. For after his resurrection, when sending his disciples, he addresses them and says:

> “As the Father has sent me, so I send you.”

When he had said this, he breathed upon them and said:

> “Receive the Holy Spirit. If you forgive anyone’s sins, they will be forgiven him; if you retain anyone’s sins, they will be retained” (John 20).

In this passage he shows that only one who possesses the Holy Spirit can baptize and grant forgiveness of sins. Finally, John, when he was to baptize Christ himself, our Lord [Note: [Col. 1146C] “Jesus Christ himself,” Lam., NC. 1, Ebor.], received the Holy Spirit beforehand, while he was still situated in his mother’s womb (Luke 1), so that it might be certain and manifest that none can baptize except those who possess the Holy Spirit.

Therefore, let those who patronize heretics or schismatics answer us whether they possess the Holy Spirit or do not possess him. If they possess him, why is the hand imposed for the reception of the Holy Spirit upon those baptized there [Col. 1146C] when they come to us, since he has surely already been received there, where, if he was present, he could have been given? But if heretics and schismatics immersed outside do not possess the Holy Spirit, and [Col. 1147A] the hand is therefore imposed among us so that what neither exists nor can be given there may be received here, it is manifest that remission of sins cannot be given through those who are known not to possess the Holy Spirit. And therefore, so that in accordance with the divine ordering and the truth of the Gospel they may obtain remission of sins, be sanctified, and become temples of God, absolutely all who come from the adversaries and antichrists to the Church of Christ must be baptized with the Church’s baptism.

[Note: [Col. 1147C]

**XII.—You also asked.** The early editors of the works of the holy martyr separated this final portion of Cyprian’s letter to Magnus from the first. Pamelius was the first to restore it, by a sound decision. For all the old books in which it is contained—except the Chartres and Saint-Éloi manuscripts, in which the entire first part is absent—and all the old books, I say, have both parts consecutively: some without any division, and some with this addition at the beginning of the second part: “Here begins a second letter to the same man,” or, “Here begins the letter concerning those who receive the grace of God, or baptism, in bed.” But these divisions were introduced by copyists. I therefore judge those [Col. 1147D] copies to be better which have no inscription over the second part and which have at the beginning of the letter: “Here begins the letter to Magnus concerning Novatian and those who receive the grace of God in bed,” as does the Speyer edition also; and at the end: “Here ends the letter to Magnus concerning Novatian and those who receive the grace of God in bed.”

I am surprised, however, that Latino Latini—who saw written in his manuscripts as the title of this letter, “To Magnus, concerning Novatian and those who receive grace in bed”—separated the part of the letter which treats those who receive Christ’s grace in sickness from the preceding part and moved it elsewhere in his edition, that is, the Manutian edition. Unless perhaps the man who presided over the Manutian edition with supreme authority, as Latini complains, changed it on his own initiative without consulting Latini.

**Dearest son.** The Chartres manuscript reads “brother.” So too the older editions.

**Aphronitrum.** That is, “foam of natron,” as in Ovid and Martial. See Pamelius on this passage, Casaubon on Suetonius, and Salmasius on the authors [Col. 1148C] of the *Augustan History*, as well as Henri Estienne’s *Thesaurus of the Greek Language*. Octavius Horatianus, book I, chapter 7: “But if wind is trapped, it is expelled by aphronitrum dissolved in vinegar.”

**Aids.** Salmasius, in his notes on the authors of the *Augustan History*, thinks that *lumentis* should be read. For *lumentum* is properly joined with natron where baths are being discussed. Papias too interprets *lumentum* as “natron,” provided that his text is emended: for in his work “glass” is read instead of “natron.” Octavius Horatianus, book IV: “A poultice of beans, properly prepared.” Martial, book V, epigram 89, said:

> “Because you try to conceal the wrinkles of your belly with bean-meal.”

See also book VI, epigram 93. A remarkable error crept into the second letter of Sulpicius Severus to his sister Claudia in the first book of our *Miscellanies*, where on page 349 “with spiritual lamentations” was first printed. The most learned Jean-Baptiste Cotelier correctly emended this in volume II of the *Monuments of the Greek Church*, p. 541, where he admirably illuminates this passage. Accordingly, the passage of Severus was emended in the second edition. I would gladly accept Salmasius’s emendation, which seems excellent to me. Yet the common reading also has an excellent sense. I therefore did not dare to change it, being without the authority of old copies.

**Is cleansed.** Three old books read “is purified.”

**Water of sprinkling.** Thus almost all the old books. Yet in ten of them and in the early editions the reading is “of aspersion.”

**Both of the receiver and of the giver.** Thus the early editions and almost all the old books. Erasmus printed “both of the giver and of the receiver,” solely by conjecture, I think, because giving must precede receiving, as in Valerius Maximus, book V, chapter 3, “the interchange of giving and receiving a benefit,” and because a little above one reads, “where the full and complete faith both of the giver and of the recipient is acknowledged.” I thought the agreement of so many old books ought not to be rejected, although Rigaltius and the English edition retained Erasmus’s emendation.

]

XII. You also asked [Note: [Col. 1147B] “You asked me,” Lam., Bod. 2, NC. 1.], dearest son [Note: [Col. 1147B] “Brother,” Eras., Spir., early unnamed edition.], what I think about those who receive the grace of God in weakness and sickness: whether they should be regarded as legitimate Christians, since they have not been washed with the saving water but have had it poured over them. In this matter our reserve and moderation prejudges no one, so as to prevent each person from thinking what he judges right [Col. 1147B] and doing what he has concluded.

For our part, insofar as our limited understanding can grasp the matter, we judge that the divine benefits cannot be mutilated or weakened in any respect, and that nothing less can occur where what is drawn from the divine gifts is received with the full and complete faith both of the giver and of the recipient. For in the saving sacrament the contagions of sins are not washed away in the same manner as the dirt of the skin and body is washed off in a bodily and secular bath, so that there should be need of aphronitrum [Note: [Col. 1147C] “And aphronitrum,” Bod. 1, 2; “soap and natron,” Erasm.] and other aids, a bathing-tub, and a pool by which the little body may be washed and cleansed. The believer’s breast is washed in one manner; the human mind [Note: [Col. 1148B] “The mind of an unbelieving person is cleansed,” Lin.] is cleansed in another, through the merits of faith. In the saving sacraments, when necessity compels [Col. 1148A] and God bestows his indulgence, the divine abridgments confer the whole gift upon believers.

Nor should anyone be troubled because the sick appear to be sprinkled or to have water poured over them when they receive the Lord’s grace, since Holy Scripture speaks through the prophet Ezekiel and says:

> “And I shall sprinkle clean water upon you, and you shall be cleansed from all your impurities; and I shall cleanse you from all your idols, and I shall give you a new heart, and I shall put a new spirit within you” (Ezek. 36:25–26).

Likewise in Numbers:

> “And the man who has been unclean until evening shall be purified on the third day and the seventh day [Note: [Col. 1148B] “On the seventh day he will be clean,” Lam., Bod. 2, NC. 1, 2, Ebor.], and he shall be clean. But if he has not been purified on the third day and the seventh day, he shall not be clean, and that soul shall be cut off from Israel, because the water of sprinkling has not been sprinkled upon him” (Num. 19:8, 12, 13).

And [Col. 1148B] again:

> “And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Take the Levites from the midst of the children of Israel, and purify them. And thus you shall perform their purification: you shall sprinkle them all around with the water of purification” (Num. 8:5, 7).

And again:

> “The water of sprinkling is a purification” (ibid. 19:9).

From this it is apparent that the sprinkling of water also has the force of the saving bath and that, when these things are done in the Church, where the faith both of the receiver and of the giver is unimpaired, all things can stand firm and be consummated and perfected by the majesty of the Lord and the truth of faith.

[Note: [Col. 1149C]

**XIII.—Bedridden persons.** Thus most of the old books. In some, here and again a little below, the word is written in Greek capital letters: ΚΛΕΝΙΚΩΣ. Jerome, in the epitaph of Fabiola: “Whom, naked and bedridden, did Fabiola’s clothing not cover?” And a little later: “Who among the bedridden was not supported by her resources?” See Herbert Rosweyde’s *Onomasticon* to the *Lives of the Fathers*, Petavius’s observations [Col. 1149D] on Epiphanius, Beveridge on canon XII of the Council of Neocaesarea, and Du Cange’s Latin glossary. See also Martial, book I, epigram 87.

**Soranus.** “An author most thoroughly instructed in methodic medicine,” as Tertullian calls him in his book *On the Soul*; “a most renowned doctor of medicine,” as Augustine calls him in book V *Against Julian the Pelagian* and book II of the *Retractations*, chapter 62. The Suda records two eminent physicians of this name, both of Ephesus. It is difficult to say which of them is meant by what Saint Cyprian says here, or whether he means the Cilician surnamed “of Mallus,” whom the Suda also mentions. That the Cilician is being discussed here could perhaps be inferred from the fact that Asclepiodotus, as the same Suda says, approved none of the ancient physicians after Hippocrates except this Cilician. For Cyprian joins Hippocrates and Soranus as physicians of the greatest expertise.

Caelius Aurelianus of Sicca writes, in book II of *Acute Diseases*, chapters 1 and 28, that he translated the works of the physician Soranus into Latin. Of the same man he writes as follows in the preface to his books *On Chronic Afflictions*: [Col. 1150C] “Soranus most fully transmitted a careful account of all of them and formed a distinct body of writing, beginning with the affliction of the head.” On the several men named Soranus, see Johann Albert Fabricius’s *Latin Library*. Letters of Marcus Antonius and Cleopatra to Soranus, and his replies, circulate under their names. The author of these letters—which are certainly false and spurious—must have been a man excessively prone to lust and a most licentious lover of obscene words and subjects.

**To heavenly strength.** The Foix manuscript reads: “Might attain most fully to strength by heavenly grace.”

[Col. 1150D] **Are scandalized.** Thus the old editions and four old books. Manutius and others after him wrote “were scandalized.” That reading rests upon the authority of ten old copies. I prefer the older reading, as the better one, at least in my judgment. There will perhaps be some who think otherwise.

]

XIII. Furthermore, as for the fact that some call those who have obtained Christ’s grace through saving water and lawful faith not Christians but *clinici*—bedridden persons—I cannot discover where they derive this name, unless perhaps those who have read more extensive and recondite works have found these *clinici* in Hippocrates or Soranus. For I, who know the bedridden man from the Gospel, know that his weakness did not hinder that paralytic and infirm man, who had lain upon his bed through the long courses of his life, from attaining most fully to heavenly strength. Nor was he merely raised from his pallet by the Lord’s indulgence, but, his powers restored and invigorated, he even picked up his own pallet.

And therefore, insofar as it is granted us to grasp and judge by faith, this is my opinion: whoever has obtained divine grace within the Church according to the law and right of faith is to be judged [Note: [Col. 1149C] “Whoever is judged a Christian,” Lam.] a legitimate Christian. Or if anyone thinks that such people have obtained nothing because [Col. 1149B] the saving water was only poured over them [Note: [Col. 1149C] “If they are empty,” Bod. 1, 2, Lam., Lim., Ebor., NC. 1.], but that they are empty and void, let them not be deceived: if they escape the infirmity of their illness and recover, let them be baptized. But if those who have already been sanctified by the Church’s baptism cannot be baptized, why are they scandalized concerning their own faith and the Lord’s indulgence? Or have they indeed obtained the Lord’s grace, but in a shorter and smaller measure of the divine gift and of the Holy Spirit, so that they are indeed regarded as Christians, yet are not to be placed on the same level as the rest?

[Note: [Col. 1150D]

**XIV.—Manna rained down.** The manuscript of Saint-Arnoul reads “rained down upon them.” Correctly, to be sure. Psalm 77: “And he rained manna upon them to eat.” Columella, book X:

> “And into the mother’s lap it rained in a violent shower.”

Tibullus, book X, elegy 5:

> “So that many a stone might rain down upon the earth.”

Tertullian, in his book *On Patience*: “After the edible rain of manna.”

**Showed.** Four old books read “represented.”

]

XIV. Indeed, the Holy Spirit is not given by measure; rather, he is poured in his entirety upon the believer. For if the day dawns equally for all, and if the sun is diffused over all with the same equal light, how much more does Christ, the Sun and true Day, bestow the light of eternal life with equal impartiality in his Church? We see the sacrament of this equality [Col. 1150A] celebrated in Exodus (Exod. 16), when manna rained down from heaven and, by prefiguring things to come, showed the nourishment of heavenly bread and the food of the Christ who was to come. For there, without distinction of sex or age, a gomor was gathered equally by each person. [Note: [Col. 1149C] “A gomor each gathered equally,” Lam., NC. 2, Lin.]

From this it was apparent that the indulgence of Christ and the heavenly grace which would follow later were to be divided equally among all, without difference of sex, without distinction of years, without respect of persons: the gift of spiritual grace was to be poured out upon all the people of God. Certainly, the same spiritual grace that is received equally [Note: [Col. 1150C] “Was gathered equally,” Lam., Ebor., NC. 1.] by believers in baptism is afterward diminished or increased in our conduct and activity. Thus in the Gospel the Lord’s seed is sown equally, but according to the difference in the soil, some is consumed, while some is accumulated into manifold [Col. 1150B] abundance, with the fruit increasing thirtyfold, sixtyfold, or a hundredfold. Again, when each person is called to receive the denarius, why should that which is distributed equally by God be diminished by human interpretation?

[Note: [Col. 1150D]

**XV.—Were assailed.** Twenty-one old books read “were assailed.” Yet the same books, with few exceptions, and five English manuscripts have “are baptized” a little above. But the Bec manuscript and Morel’s edition read “were baptized.”

[Col. 1151D] **In the cloud and in the sea.** These words are absent from the manuscript of Saint-Arnoul.

]

XV. But if anyone is troubled by the fact that some of those who are baptized while sick [Note: [Col. 1150C] “Were baptized,” Lam., NC. 1, Ebor.] are still assailed [Note: [Col. 1150C] “Were assailed,” Lam., Bod. 1, 2, Ebor., NC. 1.] by unclean spirits, he should know that the devil’s persistent wickedness has power up to the saving water, but in baptism loses all the venom of its wickedness.

We perceive an example of this in King Pharaoh, who, after resisting for a long time and persisting in his unbelief, was able to resist and prevail only until he came to the water; but when he came to it, he was both conquered and destroyed. The blessed apostle [Col. 1151A] Paul declares that that sea was a sacrament of baptism, saying:

> “For I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, that all our fathers were under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses [Note: [Col. 1151D] “Into Moses,” Lam., Lin., Ebor., NC. 1, 2.] in the cloud and in the sea” (1 Cor. 10:1–2, 6).

And he added:

> “Now all these things were figures of us.”

This also takes place today: through the exorcists, by a human voice and divine power, the devil is scourged, burned, and tormented. Although he often says that he is departing and releasing the men of God, he nevertheless lies in what he has said, and with the same lying obstinacy and fraud repeats what was previously done through Pharaoh. Yet when one comes to the saving water and the sanctification of baptism, we ought to know and trust that there the devil is crushed and the person dedicated to God is liberated by divine indulgence. For just as [Col. 1151B] scorpions and serpents, which prevail on dry land, cannot prevail [Note: [Col. 1151D] Thus Lips. and the old witnesses; “can prevail,” Oxon., Rigalt., Pamel.] or retain their venom [Note: [Col. 1152D] “Do not know how to retain,” Lam., Ebor., NC. 1, Bod. 2.] when cast into water, so too the evil spirits [Note: [Col. 1152D] “Or do evil spirits,” Lam., Ebor., NC. 1, Bod. 2; “the spirits too can,” Oxon., Pamel., Rigalt.], who are called scorpions and serpents and yet are trampled upon through us by the power given by the Lord, cannot remain any longer in the body of a person in whom, once he has been baptized and sanctified, the Holy Spirit begins to dwell.

[Note: [Col. 1151D]

**XVI.—Bedridden or walking about.** If it were not clear that the subject here is the *clinici*, that is, paralytics, I would readily think that “Cynics” should be read because of these words of Seneca from Letter [Col. 1152D] XXIX: “But all of them were shouting this same thing from every school: Peripatetics, Academics, Stoics, Cynics.”

]

XVI. Finally, we learn this from the facts themselves: those who, under the compulsion of necessity, were baptized in sickness and obtained grace are freed from the unclean spirit by which they were previously agitated; they live praiseworthy and approved lives in the Church; and with each passing day they advance still further in the increase of heavenly grace through growth in faith. Conversely, some of those who are baptized while healthy are often shaken by the return of an unclean spirit if they afterward begin to sin, [Col. 1151C] so that it is manifest that the devil is excluded in baptism by the believer’s faith but returns if faith subsequently fails.

Unless perhaps it seems just to some that those who are polluted with profane water outside the Church, among adversaries and antichrists, should be judged baptized, while those who are baptized in the Church should be regarded as having obtained less of the divine indulgence and grace; and that so great an honor should be accorded to heretics that those who come from them are not asked whether they were washed or had water poured over them, whether they were bedridden or walking about, while among us something is detracted from the complete truth of faith and the Church’s baptism is deprived of its majesty and holiness.

[Note: [Col. 1152D]

**XVII.—Dearest son.** The manuscript of Saint-Arnoul reads “brother.”

]

XVII. I have replied, dearest son, to your letter to the extent that our small and limited ability permitted, and I have shown what we, so far as it lies within us, think. We prescribe to no one [Col. 1151D] so as to prevent each prelate from determining what he thinks right, since he will render an account of his conduct to the Lord, in accordance with what the blessed apostle Paul writes and says in his letter to the Romans:

> “Each of us will give an account for himself. Therefore, let us not judge one another” [Col. 1152A] (Rom. 14:12).

I pray, dearest son, that you may always fare well.

[Note: [Col. 1153C]

**LETTER OF FIRMILIAN.—** This letter, which Morel was the first to publish, was also possessed by those who supervised the Roman edition of the works of Saint Cyprian in Paolo Manuzio’s printing-house. But they, as Latino Latini says, did not approve of bringing it forth from darkness. Latini himself candidly testifies that he was responsible for, and advised, this decision [Col. 1153D], both because he followed the examples of his predecessors and because he detested the insolence of the man—that is, Firmilian—whose letter it is.

Pamelius, who had found it in six ancient manuscripts, later reprinted it. Nevertheless, with the devotion he bore toward the Christian and ecclesiastical commonwealth, he intimated that he would have omitted it—because it had been written somewhat more vehemently and bitterly than befits a bishop—had it not already been published by Morel. Plainly, the Romans and Pamelius were disturbed by Firmilian’s free style, arising from his anger against Pope Stephen, who held a different opinion from his. But if they had carefully considered how powerful and vehement emotions ordinarily become when the cause of religion and faith is at stake, and if they had also considered how vehemently and bitterly Stephen had written against Cyprian, they would surely have pardoned Firmilian this anger. They would not on that account have thought that this illustrious monument of ecclesiastical antiquity should be condemned to darkness, since it contains many matters of great importance of which we would now be deprived, at great loss to us—as Sirmond judged in a similar case [Col. 1154C] when publishing the *Book of Petitions* of Marcellinus and Faustinus against Pope Damasus. Nor would the concern of the Romans or Pamelius have prevented that letter from coming before the public in this age of literary enlightenment.

For since it is certain that Morel published it from an old book, that it was also extant [Col. 1154D] in the six manuscripts seen by Pamelius, in those in which Latini found it, in seven used by the English in their edition, and in ten against which I collated the works of Saint Cyprian, it is manifest that it could not have remained hidden forever even if Morel had not published it. The manuscripts against which I collated it were one from Saint-Remi, two from Compiègne, two from Saint-Victor, one belonging to Pithou, one from the monastery of Bec, the Liessies manuscript, the Bigot manuscript, and one of my own.

I agree with Pamelius and Rigaltius, who judge that Firmilian wrote it in Greek and that Saint Cyprian translated it into Latin. Firmilian’s letter, therefore, has been found in twenty-six manuscripts. **BALUZE.**

]

# THE COUNCIL OF ICONIUM AGAINST THE CATAPHRYGIANS, CELEBRATED IN THE YEAR 258 UNDER POPE STEPHEN I

The Council of Iconium was held in the year 258—or, more correctly, 256—at Iconium in Phrygia, on the occasion of the Cataphrygian heretics, in order to inquire what ruling should be made concerning the validity of their baptism and that of all other heretics. Bishops from Cappadocia, Cilicia, Galatia, and other neighboring regions of the East attended this synod. They unanimously established and decreed that nothing done by heretics [Col. 1152B] was to be accepted by the Catholic Church: ordinations, baptism, impositions of hands, and every other sacred rite administered by heretics were invalid. Stephen, the Roman pontiff, excommunicated the Eastern bishops who made these rulings and deprived them of communion with the Apostolic See; he also rejected the synod itself as aberrant and as confirming an erroneous doctrine contrary to the tradition of the Apostles. The Easterners did indeed send their own delegates to the Pontiff, to give him in person an account of the proceedings of the synod; but when they came to Rome, they were neither received nor heard by the holy pontiff Stephen. For this reason Firmilian, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, wrote to Cyprian the following letter, [Col. 1152C] which recounts the acts of this council and complains bitterly that the delegates had not been heard. BARONIUS, year 258, §§ 14, 15, and 16.

“It is certain,” says Pagius at the year of Christ 255, §§ 15 and 16, “that the Council of Iconium, at which the rebaptism of heretics was decreed, was celebrated before the pontificate of Stephen. Firmilian explicitly attests this in his letter to Cyprian, where he speaks as follows concerning the Synod of Iconium: ‘All of this we confirmed long ago, when we assembled at Iconium, a place in Phrygia, with those from Galatia and Cilicia and the other neighboring regions meeting together as one.’ Here the pronoun *we* must be understood not of Firmilian himself, but rather of his predecessors, since Firmilian affirms that this synod had assembled long before, and at the end of the same letter indicates its antiquity most clearly, as [Col. 1152D] Valesius observed in his Notes on Eusebius, book VII, chapter 7. For when Pope Stephen, writing to Cyprian, set the ancient custom of the Church in receiving heretics against the proponents of the new doctrine, Firmilian says that this argument might perhaps have force against the Africans [Col. 1153A] and there explains how the Africans might refute it. He demonstrates that it had no force against the Easterners, among whom heretics had always been rebaptized, ever since the Synod of Iconium, which had been convened because of the Montanists.

“Valesius adds to this the testimony of Dionysius of Alexandria in his letter to Philemon, a presbyter of the city of Rome, which he wrote at the beginning of the pontificate of Pope Xystus. There he says: ‘I have also learned that this custom was not first introduced now by the Africans alone, but that much earlier, in the time of preceding bishops, the same ruling had been made in the most populous churches, at councils of the brethren in Iconium and Synnada, and among very many others.’ Hence Valesius believes that the Synod of Iconium assembled toward the end of the reign of Alexander Severus, when Firmilian had recently been promoted to the episcopate of the church of Caesarea, as Eusebius teaches [Col. 1153B] in book VI, and therefore before the pontificate of Pope Cornelius.” Thus far Pagius. Hardouin, in the Index of Councils in volume I, states that the councils at Iconium and Synnada were held about the year 255. On these matters see also Augustine, book III *Against Cresconius*, chapters 1 and 3.

# THE LETTER OF FIRMILIAN, BISHOP OF CAESAREA IN CAPPADOCIA, TO CYPRIAN, AGAINST THE LETTER OF STEPHEN

Its subject is entirely the same as that of the preceding letter, but it is written somewhat more vehemently and sharply than is fitting for a bishop. The principal reason, as I suspect, was that Stephen had also written another letter to Firmilian, Helenus, and the other bishops of those regions, declaring that he would not communicate with them so long as they persisted in [Col. 1153C] that opinion concerning the baptism of heretics. Eusebius teaches this from the letter of Dionysius of Alexandria to Xystus, Stephen’s successor, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VII, chapter 4. And perhaps it would therefore have been more prudent if this letter had never been published; [Col. 1154A] indeed, I think Manutius omitted it deliberately. Yet since it was published by Morel, I was unwilling to pass it over, both because it contains certain matters worthy of record and because the words of the aforementioned letter of Dionysius to Stephen may serve as an antidote. Eusebius gives that letter in the aforementioned book, chapter 3, and Nicephorus reproduces it more fully in his *Ecclesiastical History*, book VI, chapter 7. From these words it is evident that Stephen sang a palinode, as they say:

“Know, brother,” he says, “that the Eastern churches, and even those farther afield, which previously were divided, have been restored to unity, and that all their prelates are now of one mind and in agreement, rejoicing beyond measure at the peace and concord that have come about beyond expectation: especially Demetrianus of Antioch, Theoctistus of Caesarea, Mazabenes of Aelia, successor of the deceased Alexander, Marinus of Tyre, Heliodorus of Laodicea, [Col. 1154B] who was appointed in the place of Thelymedres, Helenus of Tarsus, and all the churches of Cilicia, Firmilian, and all Cappadocia. I have named the principal bishops so that my letter may not become too long and I may not burden you with a multitude of words. But all Syria and Arabia as well, Mesopotamia itself, Pontus, and Bithynia—and, to say it once for all, everyone everywhere—are exulting, glorifying God through concord and brotherly love.”

Thus far Dionysius. Similar statements may be seen in St. Jerome’s *Against the Luciferians* and in St. Augustine, book III *Against Cresconius the Grammarian*, chapters 1, 2, and 3. There, from the confession of the Donatists themselves, he reports that the Eastern bishops rescinded—or rather corrected—the judgment by which they had decided that, on this question of baptism, they ought to agree with Cyprian and the African council. PAMELIUS.

[Col. 1154C] [Note: [Col. 1154D]

**I.—Firmilian.** Bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, a hearer and admirer of Origen, as Eusebius teaches in book VI, chapter 2, of the *Ecclesiastical History*. Eusebius also mentions his great reputation in the Church of God in chapter 46 and in book VII, chapters 5 and 30. See also Basil’s first letter to Amphilochius. He presided over the earlier Synod of Antioch, as Henry Valesius shows in his commentary on Eusebius. He died at Tarsus in Cilicia in the year of Christ 272. BALUZE.

[Col. 1155C] Pearson shows in his *Cyprianic Annals*, at the year 256, section X, that Firmilian wrote this letter in 256, as winter was becoming severe. He died in 272. St. Dionysius of Alexandria, in a letter to Xystus of Rome, recalled the dispute that had arisen between Stephen and the Eastern churches concerning the rebaptism of heretics in these words:

*Ἐπέσταλκεν μὲν οὖν (Stephanus) πρότερον καὶ περὶ Ἑλένου καὶ περὶ Φιρμιλιανοῦ, καὶ πάντων τῶν τε ἀπὸ τῆς Κιλικίας καὶ Καππαδοκίας, καὶ Γαλατίας, καὶ πάντων τῶν ἑξῆς ὁμορούντων ἐθνῶν· ὡς οὐδὲ ἐκείνοις κοινωνήσων, διὰ τὴν αὐτὴν ταύτην αἰτίαν, ἐπειδὴ τοὺς αἱρετικούς, φησὶν, ἀναβαπτίζουσι.*

“Accordingly, Stephen had previously written concerning Helenus and Firmilian, and all those from Cilicia, Cappadocia, and Galatia, and all the neighboring peoples beyond them, saying that he would not communicate with them either, for this same reason: because, he says, they rebaptize heretics.”

In Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* VII.5. Moreover, one of Firmilian’s successors in the see of Caesarea, St. Basil the Great, recalled both his opinion and Cyprian’s concerning the rebaptism of heretics in his *Canonical Letter to Amphilochius*, included in Beveridge’s *Synodicon*. What is more, St. Augustine indicates that in his own time there still survived letters of Cyprian and certain Easterners rejecting baptism given among heretics and schismatics. See Augustine’s book III *Against Cresconius*, chapter 1, and his book *Against Petilian*, chapter 14. Below we shall make further annotations against the opponents of this letter, which has now at last been admitted into the Florentine edition of the Councils. ROUTH.

**In one and the same house.** This is the common reading. I changed *ipsa* (“the very”) to *una* (“one”), relying on the authority of the codex of Simon Goulart, who edited Cyprian in 1593 and recommended that the same change be made. The original was Greek. ROUTH.

**A great love of the will, to come together as one.** These words seem not to be free from corruption. What if, in place of *love of the will* (*voluntatis charitatem*), we restore *eagerness of the will* (*voluntatis alacritatem*)? In the Apostle’s Second Letter to the Corinthians there occurs *ἡ προθυμία τοῦ θέλειν*, “the eagerness to will,” VII.11; and in the old glossaries one finds *ἡ προθυμία*, “eagerness.” ROUTH.]

## I

Firmilian to his brother Cyprian [Note: [Col. 1153C] But *to his brother*, MR. Mich. Goul.], greetings in the Lord.

Through our dearest Rogatian, the deacon sent by you, we received the letter you wrote to us, most beloved brother; and on this account we gave the greatest thanks to the Lord [Note: [Col. 1154C] *the greatest thanks to God*, Ar.], because it has come about that, although we are separated from one another in body, [Col. 1155A] we are thus united in spirit, as though we not only occupied one region but dwelt together in the very same [Note: [Col. 1155B] *one and the same*, Goul.] house.

It is also fitting to say this, because the spiritual house of God is one. “For in the last days,” says the Prophet, “the mountain of the Lord and the house of God will be manifest above the summits of the mountains” (Isa. II). Those who come together in it [Note: [Col. 1155B] *Those who come together in which*, Ar. Bod. 2.] are united with joy, just as in the Psalm it is also asked of the Lord that one may dwell in the house of God all the days of one’s life (Ps. XXVI). Hence it is also shown elsewhere that among the saints there is a great love of the will for coming together as one. “Behold,” he says, “how good and delightful it is for brothers to dwell together in unity!”

[Note: [Col. 1155D]

**II.—As though not only one, etc.** The observations written about this passage by the learned Prudentius Maran, in the *Life of St. Cyprian* prefixed to the Baluze, or Benedictine, edition, should be quoted:

“This letter of Firmilian, which survives in Latin [Col. 1156C] as the seventy-fifth among Cyprian’s letters, so strongly recalls Cyprian’s style that it appears to have had no other translator. In several passages the faithful translator retained the idiom of the Greek language. Shortly after the beginning: ‘They [the angels] are saddened when they see the differing minds and divided wills of certain persons, as though they did not merely invoke one and the same God together, but, being separated and divided from one another, could no longer have either conversation or common discourse’; that is, ‘as though they did not invoke only one and the same God together.’ This final negation is sometimes omitted among Latin authors, but more often among Greek authors.” § 31, p. 118.

The distinguished scholar then proceeds to indicate other similar passages, which will be discussed below in their proper order. ROUTH.

**By the Passion of the Lord.** I do not know how it happened that these words dropped out of the editions published after Morel’s, in which they are present. They occur in all the ancient manuscripts except one old Victorine codex, and also in the codex of the bishop of Accona. [Col. 1156D] The author of this omission was Pamelius, who says that the manuscripts do not contain these words and that the text shows them to be superfluous. I am more surprised at the English editors. Although they had the words in five of their old manuscripts, knew that they also occurred in some of ours, and knew that Rigault had warned in his observations that they should not be rejected, they nevertheless refused to receive them into the text, thinking they had sufficiently discharged their duty to the reader by noting that they had found them in ancient manuscripts. BALUZE.]

## II

For unity, peace, and concord give the greatest delight not only [Col. 1155B] to faithful people who know the truth, but even to the heavenly angels themselves. The divine word says that they rejoice over one sinner who repents and returns to the bond of unity (Luke XV). This certainly would not have been said of the angels whose manner of life is in heaven unless they too were united with us and rejoiced in our unity. Conversely, they are certainly saddened when they see the differing minds and divided wills of certain persons, as though they did not merely invoke one and the same God [Col. 1156A] together, but, being separated and divided from one another, could no longer have either conversation or common discourse.

Except that in this matter we can give thanks to Stephen, because through his inhumanity it has now come about that we have gained proof of your faith and wisdom. But even if we [Note: [Col. 1155B] Thus Ar. Lam. Ebor. NC. 1. Bod. 2. Mich. Vict.; *for* omitted by Oxon.] have obtained this gracious benefit because of Stephen, it does not immediately follow that Stephen performed an act worthy of gratitude as a benefactor. For Judas too, by his treachery and betrayal, through which he acted wickedly against the Savior, cannot be regarded as worthy on the ground that he himself furnished the occasion for such great blessings, so that through him the world and the people of the Gentiles might be freed by the Passion of the Lord [Note: [Col. 1155B] Thus Lam. Ebor. NC. 1 Ar. Bod. 3. Mich. Morel. Goul. [Col. 1156B] *by the Passion of the Lord* omitted by Oxon.].

[Note: [Col. 1156D]

**III.—We found such agreement among our brothers situated so far away.** Cyprian’s opinion concerning the baptism of heretics was favored not only by very many churches throughout Africa, Numidia, and Mauretania, but also by nearly all the churches that professed Christian religion in the East in great numbers. Among these, the most celebrated bishops of distinguished cities were indicated without being named individually in the letter to Stephen that is the first of those seven letters of Dionysius of Alexandria *περὶ βαπτίσματος*, “On Baptism,” mentioned by Eusebius.

In that letter the great Dionysius [Col. 1157C] informed Stephen that the disturbances stirred up by the Novatians in the East had been calmed and that all the churches therefore agreed that penance should be granted to the lapsed. But he had added something concerning the baptism of penitents returning from the heretics, which Eusebius omitted. From this Baronius—and here Pamelius, who followed Baronius in his notes on Cyprian, must also be added—took occasion to affirm as certain [Col. 1157D] that all those churches had so acquiesced in Stephen’s decision that, abandoning Cyprian’s opinion, they agreed to his decree that heretics were not to be baptized.

So far was this from being reported by Dionysius that, after Stephen’s death, the same Dionysius carefully and earnestly warned Xystus, Stephen’s successor, in another letter to consider more attentively the weight of the question and the difficulty of the case. Stephen had indeed notified Helenus and Firmilian, and the other bishops throughout Cilicia, Cappadocia, and the neighboring churches, by letter that he would not communicate with them because they rebaptized heretics. Nevertheless, the matter was of great importance:

*ὄντως γὰρ δόγματα γέγονεν ἐν ταῖς μεγίσταις τῶν ἐπισκόπων συνόδοις, ὡς πυνθάνομαι, ὥστε τοὺς προσιόντας ἀπὸ αἱρέσεως προκατηχηθέντας, εἶτα ἀπολούεσθαι καὶ ἀποκαθαίρεσθαι τὸν τῆς παλαιᾶς καὶ ἀκαθάρτου ζύμης ῥύπον.*

“For, as I understand, decisions have actually been made in the greatest synods of bishops that those who come over from heresy should first be instructed and then washed and cleansed of the defilement of the old and impure leaven.”

Dionysius continues and says that he writes this to Xystus at the request of the bishops of Antioch, Caesarea, Aelia, Tyre, Laodicea, and Tarsus. Indeed, he had also written more fully and abundantly on this matter to his fellow-presbyters Dionysius and Philemon, [Col. 1158C] who had held the same opinion as Stephen. RIGAULT.]

## III

But for the present let us pass over what Stephen has done, lest, by recalling his audacity and insolence, we bring upon ourselves a more prolonged sorrow over the things he has wickedly done. Having learned concerning you, however, that in accordance with the rule of truth and the wisdom of Christ you have settled the matter now under inquiry [Note: [Col. 1156B] *the matter which now follows*, Ar. Lam. Ebor. NC. 1. MR. Bod. 2.], we exulted with great joy and gave thanks to God, because we found in brothers situated so far away such unanimity with us in faith and truth [Note: [Col. 1156B] *unity of truth*, Lam. Ebor. Ar. NC. 1. MR.].

For the grace of God is powerful enough to unite and join by the bond of love and unity even those who appear [Col. 1157A] to be divided by a great expanse of territory. So also in former times the divine power joined Ezekiel and Daniel, who lived later, to Job and Noah, who belonged to the earliest age and were separated from them by an interval of time, in the bond of unanimity, so that, although divided by long periods, they might think alike through the same divine inspiration.

We have observed the same thing in you now: although separated from us by the greatest distances, you have shown yourselves to be joined with us in understanding and spirit. All this is brought about by divine unity. For since it is one and the same Lord who dwells in us, he everywhere joins and unites his own by the bond of unity. Hence the sound of those sent by the Lord, who swiftly run in the spirit of unity, has gone out into all the earth. [Col. 1157B] Conversely, it is of no benefit for some to be near and joined to one another in body if they are divided in soul and mind, since souls that have separated themselves from the unity of God cannot be united at all: “For behold,” he says, “those who distance themselves from you will perish” (Ps. LXXII.27). Such people, however, will undergo the judgment of the Lord according to their deserts, since they depart from the words of him who entreats the Father for unity and says: “Father, grant that, just as I and you are one, so these also may be one in us” (John XVII.21).

[Note: [Col. 1158C]

**IV.—We commit.** Thus Routh reads, in the present tense, instead of the past *we committed*, on the authority of five manuscripts, three of which are mentioned in the Oxford edition, the fourth being Bodleian and the fifth belonging to New College. ROUTH.]

## IV

We received what you wrote as though it were our own [Note: [Col. 1157C] Thus Lam. Ebor. Ar. Mich. Vict.; *we receive*, Oxon.], and did not read it only in passing, but committed it to memory by frequent repetition [Note: [Col. 1157C] *we commit*, Mich. Vict. Goul.]. Nor does it impair its saving usefulness either to retrace the same points in order to confirm the truth or to add certain things in order to augment the proof.

If anything is [Col. 1157C] added by us, it is not added as though something had been insufficiently stated by you, but because the divine word surpasses human nature and the soul cannot conceive it in its complete perfection. For this reason the number [Col. 1158A] of Prophets is so great, so that manifold and divine [Note: [Col. 1158C] Thus Mich. Vict. Ar. Lam. Ebor. NC. 1.; *and* omitted by Oxon.] wisdom may be distributed through many. Hence the first person speaking in prophecy is commanded to be silent if a revelation has been made to the second (I Cor. XIV.30).

For this reason it necessarily happens among us that each year the elders and prelates meet together to settle the matters entrusted to our care, so that any more serious matters may be directed by common counsel, and so that a remedy through penance may be sought also for the lapsed brethren who have been wounded by the devil after the saving washing—not as though they obtained forgiveness of sins from us, but so that through us they may be brought to an understanding of their offenses and be compelled to make fuller satisfaction to the Lord.

[Note: [Col. 1158C]

**V.—The winter season.** From this Baronius concluded that this letter was written in the year 257, some time before winter. But Pearson, in his *Cyprianic Annals*, [Col. 1158D] contends that these events occurred in the preceding year. BALUZE.

**Arose afterward.** This is true, provided the discussion concerns those heretics who were at issue at that time and whom Firmilian names here, since they flourished especially in his own day. But it is equally true that no less pestilential heresies existed in the apostolic age. Tertullian deserves to be consulted on this matter above, in his book *On the Prescription of Heretics*, chapters 33 and 34. ROUTH.

**The time of Basilides.** Learned men hold various opinions concerning the period in which Basilides disseminated his doctrine. On this controversy see the learned and erudite observations written on Ignatius’ letter to the Trallians by our former friend J. B. Cotelier, who assigns the time of Basilides to the reign of Hadrian. See also the observations of the most learned René Massuet on Irenaeus, p. 59, § 112. Jerome severely attacks the foolish errors of Basilides, which he calls monstrosities, in the epitaph of Lucinius of Baetica and in his book *Against Vigilantius*. The same Jerome, in book II *Against Jovinian*, calls him a teacher of lust and the vilest embraces; and in his letter to Ctesiphon against the Pelagians he recalls the impiety of Basilides.]

## V

Since the envoy sent by you was hurrying to return to you and the winter season was pressing, [Col. 1158B] we replied to your writings as fully as we could.

As regards Stephen’s assertion that the Apostles supposedly forbade the baptism of those who come from heresy and handed this down for posterity to observe, you answered most fully that no one is so foolish as to believe that the Apostles handed this down. For it is established that those execrable and detestable heresies arose only later. Marcion, a disciple of Cerdo, is found to have introduced his sacrilegious tradition against God at a late date, after the Apostles and after a long interval from their time. Apelles likewise, assenting to Marcion’s blasphemy, added many other novel and more serious doctrines hostile to faith and truth.

The period of Valentinus and Basilides is also manifest, for they too, after the Apostles and after a long age, rebelled against the Church of God [Col. 1158C] with their wicked lies. It is likewise established that the other heretics [Col. 1159A] afterward introduced their depraved sects and perverse inventions, as each was led by error. It is manifest that they all condemned themselves and, even before the day of judgment, pronounced an inexcusable sentence against themselves. Whoever confirms their baptism—what else does he do but sentence himself along with them, and condemn himself by making himself a participant with such people?

[Note: [Col. 1159C]

**VI.—Vainly invoking the Apostles.** By contrast, Vincent of Lérins, treating this very matter, says: “So that everyone may see more clearly than daylight with how much force, how much zeal, and how much exertion the blessed succession of the blessed Apostles always defended the integrity of the religion it had once received.” Shortly afterward he adds that Pope Stephen considered it fitting that, as he surpassed all others in the authority of his position, so he should surpass them in devotion to the faith. By “the Apostles” here and elsewhere are meant Peter and Paul, whom the Church regards as the founders of the Roman Church.

In our own age the question of a twofold head in the Church has been debated with great contention of minds. I do not wish to report what was [Col. 1159D] said and done on either side at that time. I shall say only that one should read the disputation *On the Singular Primacy of Peter*, written on that occasion by the most illustrious Pierre de Marca, archbishop of Paris.

**According to differences of names.** Although this reading is consistent in all the ancient copies, I nevertheless think that *persons* (*hominum*) should be read instead of *names* (*nominum*). BALUZE.

**Yet on this account there was never any departure from the peace and unity of the Catholic Church.** The distinguished Coustant quotes these words of Firmilian in a note on St. Irenaeus’ letter to Victor, bishop of Rome, who had attempted to separate from the Church the Asians who celebrated Easter on the fourteenth day of the month:

“The speed with which, as may be believed, the peace that had been disturbed for a short time was completely restored caused the rupture of unity to be so thoroughly forgotten that, in Cyprian’s age, no one even recalled that there had ever been a departure from it.”

*Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, p. 99.

Moreover, Anatolius of Laodicea, [Col. 1160C] who flourished before the Council of Nicaea, testified that this dispute over Easter was pacified by Irenaeus, “with both parties,” he says, “persevering in their own rule and not departing from the ancient custom they had begun to follow.” See the passage of Anatolius quoted there. ROUTH.]

## VI

That those at Rome do not in every respect observe what was handed down from the beginning, and that they invoke the authority of the Apostles in vain, can be known even from this: one sees that there are certain differences among them concerning the days on which Easter is celebrated and concerning many other sacraments of divine worship, and that not everything observed at Jerusalem is observed there in precisely the same way. Similarly, in very many other provinces numerous practices vary according to differences of place and name, yet on this account [Col. 1159B] there was never any departure from the peace and unity of the Catholic Church.

Stephen has now dared to do this, breaking with you the peace that his predecessors always maintained with you in mutual love and honor. He also continues to defame [Note: [Col. 1159B] *defames*, Ar. Lam. Ebor. NC. 1. Bod. 2.] the blessed Apostles Peter and Paul, as though they themselves had handed down this practice, although in their letters they execrated heretics and warned us to avoid them. Hence it is evident that this tradition which upholds heretics and maintains that they possess baptism—although baptism belongs to the Church alone—is a human tradition. [Col. 1160A]

[Note: [Col. 1160C]

**VII.—Coming from one to the other.** Rigault annotated this passage in Cyprian’s letter to Pompey, where Stephen’s words are quoted still more fully:

“This text is entirely correct. That is, Montanus does not baptize one who comes from Marcion, nor does Marcion baptize one who comes from Montanus. They do not rebaptize those who come from one to the other.” ROUTH.

**The Holy Spirit.** It is certain that these two words do not occur in our manuscripts or in the four English manuscripts. Pamelius likewise testifies to this concerning one of his own, although he nevertheless added them from a printed codex in whose margins Johannes Cauchius of Utrecht had entered corrections from various manuscripts. [Col. 1160D] It nevertheless remains uncertain whether these two words were added from an old manuscript or merely by a conjecture of Cauchius. For because the word *nor* is added in the old manuscripts after the word *Son*, so that something appears to be missing, Pamelius conjectured that these two words ought to be added; and he added them when he saw his conjecture confirmed by the authority of Cauchius’ copy. Pamelius himself, however, notes in his annotations that Cauchius’ codex contained not only variant readings from old manuscripts but also Cauchius’ conjectures. We have therefore enclosed these two words, which were inserted without authority and merely by conjecture, within brackets. BALUZE.

The variant readings collected in the Oxford edition do indeed indicate that the three words *nor the Holy Spirit* are absent from those four English manuscripts. But in reality, in two of them—the Bodleian and the New College codex—the word *nor* after *Son* appears connected with what follows. The other codex of Cyprian’s letters belonging to the same college does not contain Firmilian’s letter. ROUTH.

[Col. 1161C] **Where the elders preside.** In Greek, *ὅπου προκάθηνται οἱ πρεσβύτεροι*, “where the presbyters preside.” Thus Firmilian also said above: “It was customary among us that each year the elders”—*οἱ πρεσβύτεροι*, “the presbyters”—“and prelates should meet together.” In both passages, unless I am mistaken, the presbyters of the higher order—that is, those who preside—are designated.

Tertullian calls the bishop “the one who presides” in his book *On Modesty*, chapter 14; and bishops are sometimes called by that name of “presbyters” by the ancients. Conversely, presbyters are rarely honored with the title of “bishops,” and then only by accommodation to a passage in the Old Testament. Compare the annotations on the *Council against Noetus*, volume II of *Sacred Remains*, p. 377. There, however, I confess that I was less than correct in doubting whether several bishops assembled together—that is, in a provincial council—were called presbyters of the Church in the third century.

Moreover, the ancients believed that the authority to administer all rites—to baptize, offer, impose hands, and ordain—resided in the bishop, but also that presbyters were permitted to baptize and offer when furnished with the bishop’s authority. “The chief priest, who is the bishop, has the right to give [Col. 1161D] baptism. After him, presbyters and deacons have it, though not without the bishop’s authority, on account of the honor of the Church. When this is preserved, peace is preserved. Otherwise, even the laity have the right,” etc. Tertullian taught this in his book *On Baptism*, chapter 17, before the end of the Church’s second century.

All antiquity agrees with Jerome, however, that the right of ordination belongs to bishops alone. Add to this that the same Firmilian who in these passages called the episcopal order by the name of presbyters elsewhere in his letter distinguished individual bishops, presbyters, and deacons by their own titles. Moreover, below in § 12 he says that bishops succeeded the Apostles through a vicarious ordination. ROUTH.

**Authority.** The Laetian codex reads *faculty*. Pamelius also testifies that he read it thus in the Marchian codex. BALUZE.

**Nor perform anything spiritually.** The first edition provides *or* [Col. 1162C] instead of *nor*, and this is supported by the New College and Bodleian manuscripts; perhaps it should indeed be restored. ROUTH.
