**At Iconium.** Dionysius of Alexandria recalls in his third letter to Philemon of Rome that this council at Iconium and the one at Synnada decreed that heretics were to be baptized again. His words in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* VII.7, are:

*Μεμάθηκα καὶ τοῦτο ὅτι μὴ νῦν οἱ ἐν Ἀφρικῇ μόνον τοῦτο παρεισήγαγον, ἀλλὰ καὶ πρὸ πολλοῦ κατὰ τοὺς πρὸ ἡμῶν ἐπισκόπους ἐν ταῖς πολυανθρωποτάταις ἐκκλησίαις καὶ ταῖς συνόδοις τῶν ἀδελφῶν, ἐν Ἰκονίῳ καὶ Συννάδοις καὶ παρὰ πολλοῖς τοῦτο ἔδοξεν, ὧν* etc.

“I have also learned that this practice was not introduced only now by those in Africa, but that long ago, in the time of the bishops before us, in the most populous churches and at councils of the brethren, at Iconium and Synnada and among many others, this was judged proper; concerning whom,” etc.

That this question was raised at Iconium chiefly because of the baptism of the Montanists is evident from Firmilian’s words below, in chapter 13. ROUTH.

Prudentius Maran says in the *Life of St. Cyprian* prefixed to the Baluze edition, § XXXI, p. CXVIII: “*Unless Paul was inferior to those bishops who now …* Pamelius thought that *concerning whom now* ought to be read; but this is a manifest Hellenism: *τούτοις τοῖς ἐπισκόποις τοῖς νῦν*, ‘to these bishops now existing.’” So he writes. These considerations, however, do not prevent me from thinking that *who now are* should be restored in place of *to whom now*, since the preposition *concerning* before *whom* is absent, so far as I know, from all the manuscripts. ROUTH.]

## VII

You also answered well that part in which Stephen said in his letter that “even the heretics themselves agree concerning baptism, and that, when they come from one to the other [Note: [Col. 1159B] *that to one another*, Oxon.], they do not baptize but merely communicate,” as though we too ought to do this.

Although you have already sufficiently demonstrated in this passage how ridiculous [Note: [Col. 1159B] *you have demonstrated it ridiculous*, Bod. 2.] it is for anyone to follow those who are in error, we nevertheless add, by way of superabundance, that it is not surprising if heretics behave in this way. Although they disagree on certain lesser matters, they nevertheless hold one and the same agreement on the greatest matter of all: that they blaspheme the Creator, inventing for themselves dreams and phantoms of an unknown god. It naturally follows that they [Note: [Col. 1159B] *which*, Lam. Ebor. NC. 1.] should agree in the vanity of their baptism just as they agree in repudiating [Col. 1160B] the truth of the divinity.

Since it would take too long to respond to each of their wicked or superfluous doctrines individually, it is enough to state this one thing briefly and summarily: those who do not hold [Note: [Col. 1159C] *because they do not hold*, Lam. Ebor. NC. 1.] the true Lord, the Father, cannot hold the truth either of the Son or of the Holy Spirit.

Thus also those called Cataphrygians, who attempt to appropriate new prophecies, can have neither the Father nor the Son [Note: [Col. 1160B] *nor the Son; to whom*, Ar. NC. 1. Ebor. Bod. 2. Mich. Vict.] nor [the Holy Spirit] [Note: [Col. 1160B] Thus Lam.; *Holy Spirit; to whom*, Rig.]. If we ask them what Christ [Col. 1161A] they proclaim, they will answer that they proclaim him who sent the Spirit that spoke through Montanus and Prisca. Since we observe that the spirit in them was not the Spirit of truth but of error, we recognize that those who defend their false prophecy against the faith of Christ cannot possess Christ.

Likewise, if any of the other heretics have severed themselves from the Church of God, they can possess no authority or grace, since all authority and grace are established in the Church, where the elders preside and possess authority to baptize, impose hands, and ordain. For just as a heretic is not permitted to ordain or impose hands, so he is not permitted to baptize or perform anything in a holy or spiritual manner, since he is alien to spiritual and deifying holiness.

All of this we confirmed long ago at Iconium, [Col. 1161B] a place in Phrygia, when we assembled as one with those from Galatia and Cilicia and the other neighboring regions, deciding that it must be firmly maintained and defended against the heretics, since some had raised doubts concerning this matter.

[Note: [Col. 1162D]

**VIII.—To whom now.** The preposition is absent from all the ancient copies and from the Morel edition. Pamelius added it by conjecture because he thought the sense could not stand without it. BALUZE.]

## VIII

Since Stephen and those who agree with him contend that forgiveness of sins and a second birth can take place in the baptism of heretics, among whom even they themselves confess that the Holy Spirit [Col. 1162A] is not present, let them consider and understand that spiritual birth cannot occur without the Spirit.

Thus the blessed Apostle Paul rebaptized with spiritual baptism those who had been baptized by John before the Holy Spirit was sent by the Lord, and then imposed his hand upon them so that they might receive the Holy Spirit (Acts XIX). What sort of thing is it that, although we see that Paul baptized his disciples again after John’s baptism, we nevertheless hesitate to baptize those who come from heresy to the Church after their illicit and profane immersion?

Unless Paul was inferior to those bishops [Note: [Col. 1161B] Thus Ar. Lam. Ebor. NC. 1.; but Oxon. reads *concerning whom*.] to whom [now] [Note: [Col. 1162B] Routh conjectures *who are now*.], so that they can give the Holy Spirit to heretics who come to them merely through the imposition of hands, while Paul was not competent to give the Holy [Col. 1162B] Spirit by the imposition of hands to those baptized by John unless he first baptized them also with the baptism of the Church.

[Note: [Col. 1162D]

IX.—But who in the Church is perfect? The manuscript of New College reads excellently: “so that whoever is perfect and wise in the Church may either defend or believe this.” In three manuscript codices named in the Oxford edition, *qui* (“whoever”) is read instead of *quis* (“who?”), and *qui* before *hoc* is absent. Therefore, setting aside Pamelius’s reading—which perhaps arose merely from a conjecture of Cauchius—I have restored that of Morel, though, on the authority of the New College manuscript, I have placed *aut* (“or”) instead of *autem* (“but”) before the verb *defendat*. Moreover, shortly before this I restored the earlier reading *potuerit* in place of *poterit*. ROUTH.—“But who is.” Pamelius emended it thus from the book of [Col. 1163C] Cauchius. For in Morel’s edition, which is the first, it reads: “They are perfect, so that whoever is perfect and wise in the Church. But let him defend and believe this,” etc. In three [Col. 1163D] ancient manuscripts it is written: “They are perfect, so that whoever is perfect and wise in the Church may defend this.” Other old books likewise read this, except that instead of *et sapiens* (“and wise”) they have *aut sapiens* (“or wise”). BALUZE.

IX. There is also the absurdity that they do not think it necessary to ask who the person baptizing may be, on the ground that the person baptized will be able to obtain grace when the triad of the names of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit has been invoked. This, then, will be the wisdom which Paul writes is found among those who are perfect. But who in the Church is perfect [Col. 1163A] and wise [Note: [Col. 1163C] “But whoever is perfect and wise in the Church may defend this,” Ar. Lam. Ebor. Mich. Vict.] who would either defend or believe this: that this bare invocation of the names is sufficient for the remission of sins and the sanctification of Baptism, when these things are effective only when the one who baptizes possesses the Holy Spirit and the Baptism itself has not been instituted without the Spirit [Note: [Col. 1163C] “Without the Holy Spirit,” Lam. Ebor. Bod. 2.]? But they say that someone who is baptized outside, in whatever manner, can obtain the grace of Baptism through his own disposition and faith. This too is undoubtedly ridiculous, as though either a perverse disposition could bring down to itself from heaven the sanctification of the righteous, or a false faith the truth of believers. The Lord himself makes clear that not all who invoke the name of Christ are heard, or that their invocation can obtain any measure of grace, when he says: “Many will come in my name, saying, ‘I am Christ,’ and they will deceive many” (Mark 13:6). There is indeed no [Col. 1163B] difference between a false prophet and a heretic. For just as the former deceives in the name of God or of Christ, so the latter deceives in the sacrament [Note: [Col. 1163C] “The latter by the sacrament,” Bod. 2.] of Baptism: each relies upon a lie to deceive the wills of human beings.

[Note: [Col. 1163D]

X.—“Twenty years ago.” See the *Cyprianic Annals* for the year 256. BALUZE.

“Bitter and savage.” Thus Lactantius, chapter 13 of *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, calls Flaccillus “no insignificant murderer.” BALUZE.

“A certain woman.” See Regino, book II, chapter 364, and our notes on page 592. BALUZE.

“To move the earth.” Two old books read: “she would even promise that the earth would move.” Four English manuscripts: “bringing it about that the earth moved itself.” BALUZE.

“By its own power.” Thus one royal manuscript and the Bec manuscript; this is the true reading. Four old books have *visu* (“by sight”). So too the Dijon manuscript, except that above the line it has written “or *nisu*” (“by effort”). Morel printed *nisu*; Pamelius and others, *jussu* (“by command”). BALUZE.

“Rusticus.” Morel printed *rusticum*, as though it were not a man’s name but a term denoting a simple man. Pamelius and, after him, Rigaltius wrote *Rusticum*, thinking it to be the name of the presbyter of whom [Col. 1164D] Firmilian speaks here. The English editors judged differently and restored the reading found in Morel’s edition, drawing an argument from the letter of Cornelius to Fabius of Antioch in Eusebius, in which Cornelius says that Novatus summoned from Italy three exceedingly simple and wholly ignorant bishops, as Rufinus translates it, by whom he might be made bishop. Amid this diversity of opinions, since I saw that the reading of Pamelius and Rigaltius could be sound and that nothing against it was established by comparison with those Italian bishops, I retained what appeared to have found greater favor with Pamelius and Rigaltius. Concerning Ursicinus, who seized the Apostolic See after the election of Damasus, Rufinus, book XI, chapter 10, testifies that he was made bishop by a certain quite unskilled and rustic bishop. BALUZE.

“One of the presbyters, a rustic.” Thus Morel printed it in the first edition of this letter, as though *rusticus* were a common noun; Pamelius and Rigaltius, however, took it as a proper name. Fell judged otherwise. Baluze is doubtful. Perhaps in this passage the word *rusticus* means not “uncultivated,” [Col. 1165C] as Fell supposes, but “rural”: ἐπιχώριον (*local, rural*). The ἐπιχώριοι πρεσβύτεροι (*local or rural presbyters*) are mentioned in the thirteenth canon of the Council of Neocaesarea. But Firmilian seems to have written ἀγροικικόν (*rural* or *rustic*) in Greek, since in the seventeenth canon of Chalcedon one finds ἀγροικικὰς παροικίας ἢ ἐγχωρίους, “rural or local parishes.” ROUTH.

“Who had previously been regarded as holy.” It frequently happened that hypocrites imposed upon the Church—that is, that after their deaths many were believed to be saints although their conduct had not corresponded to so favorable a reputation—as we demonstrated by numerous examples in the address that we delivered in Paris at the Royal College on 15 April 1692, when we were expounding there the title of the Decretals *On Relics and the Veneration of Saints*. BALUZE.

“Bread.” Four of our books and likewise four English books prefer *pacem* (“peace”). In the Dijon manuscript also *pacem* is written, and above the line “or *panem*” (“bread”). It is certain [Col. 1165D] that the Eucharistic bread is under discussion here. In the comedy *Querolus* one reads: “This alone is what they pursue and observe exclusively: the bread of the Lord.” There a certain learned man—whose handwriting I do not know well, though I think it is that of Pierre Daniel or Desiderius Heraldus—wrote in the margin of his printed copy *panem Deum*, “bread as God,” that is, the Eucharist. The theologians will examine whether this interpretation is sound. BALUZE.

“Without the sacrament.” “Not without the sacrament of the customary proclamation.” Fell says that this is the true reading—for the negative particle *non* was omitted in all the manuscripts and editions except that prepared by Fell himself—and that this is sufficiently evident from the context; for what follows is: “She would also baptize many, employing the customary and legitimate words of interrogation, so that she appeared to differ in nothing from the rule of the Church.” Indeed, the force of the argument would be lost if the solemn words prescribed for the administration of the Eucharist had not been retained. The “customary proclamation” appears to be that ἀνάμνησις (*remembrance*) which the Lord commanded to be made, and of which Saint Paul says (1 Cor. 11:26), καταγγέλλετε τὸν θάνατον τοῦ Κυρίου, “you proclaim the death of the Lord.” The Paschal matter was discussed above in the Letter to Caecilius. Justin Martyr appears to set out this rite in *Apology* 2 (1), where he says: Προσφέρεσθαι τῷ προεστῶτι τὸν ἄρτον καὶ ποτήριον ὕδατος καὶ κράματος, καὶ οὗτος λαβὼν αἶνον καὶ δόξαν τῷ Πατρὶ τῶν ὅλων διὰ τοῦ ὀνόματος τοῦ Υἱοῦ καὶ τοῦ Πνεύματος τοῦ ἁγίου ἀναπέμπει, etc.: “The bread and a cup of water and mixed wine are brought to the presiding minister, and he, taking them, sends up praise and glory to the Father of all through the name of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,” etc. Rigaltius says that it appears one should read: “Or she would offer the sacrament of the customary prayer.” He says “the sacrament of prayer” just as Tertullian says “the sacrament of the prayer.” FELL. It was proper to follow this most learned man, whom Tillemont also obeyed in this matter, *Mémoires ecclésiastiques*, in the *Life of Firmilian*, vol. IV, p. 129, Brussels edition. I have therefore placed the negative particle before the words, though it is wrongly omitted in Baluze’s text, since it appeared formerly to have been swallowed up in the preceding word *Domino*. Nevertheless, the distinguished Maran, in his [Col. 1166D] *Life of Cyprian*, regards the expression as arising from imitation of the Greeks. In the same place, opposing Rigaltius—who wished to replace the words “without the sacrament of the customary proclamation” with “or she would offer the sacrament of the customary prayer”—he proceeds to observe from Basil the Great: “The prayers customarily made during the sacrifice are called by Basil, Epistle 210, ἐκκλησιαστικὰ κηρύγματα, ‘ecclesiastical proclamations.’” Page cxviii. ROUTH.

“She would also baptize.” See the Fourth Council of Carthage, canons 99 and 100. BALUZE.]

X. I also wish to relate to you an event [Note: [Col. 1163C] Routh conjectures that “of a matter” should be added.] that took place among us and pertains to this very subject. For approximately twenty-two years ago, in the period after the emperor Alexander, many conflicts and afflictions occurred here, either generally to all people or privately to Christians. There were also very many and frequent earthquakes, so that throughout [Note: [Col. 1163C] “Throughout,” Lam. Ebor. NC. 1.] Cappadocia and Pontus many places were overthrown, while certain cities were even swallowed up into the depths through a gaping rupture of the ground. Consequently, a severe persecution [Col. 1163C] also arose against us who bear the Christian name. After the long peace of the preceding age, it broke out suddenly, and because the evil was unexpected and unfamiliar [Note: [Col. 1163C] “Unexpected evil,” Bod. 2.], it became all the more terrifying in disturbing our people. [Col. 1164A] Serenianus was then governor of our province, a bitter and savage persecutor.

While the faithful were caught in this upheaval, fleeing here and there through fear of persecution, leaving their native lands [Note: [Col. 1164C] “Leaving them; for there was,” Bod. 2.], and passing into other parts of the regions—for it was possible to travel, since that persecution was local rather than extending throughout the whole world—there suddenly emerged here a certain woman who, being thrown into an ecstatic state [Note: [Col. 1164C] Thus Ar. Lam. Ebor. NC. 1. Bod. 2.; “in ecstasy,” Oxford.], presented herself as a prophetess and conducted herself as though filled with the Holy Spirit. She was driven by the impulse of the chief demons [Note: [Col. 1164C] “Demons,” Ar. Lam. Ebor. NC. 1.] to such a degree that for a long time she troubled and deceived the brotherhood, performing certain astonishing and portentous deeds and promising that she would cause the earth to move [Note: [Col. 1164C] “Performing wonders, she would move the earth,” Lam. Ebor. NC. 1. Bod. 2.]. This was not because the demon possessed such power that it could move the earth [Col. 1164B] or shake the element by its own force, but because an evil spirit, foreknowing and understanding that an earthquake was going to occur, would sometimes pretend that it was itself about to do what it foresaw would happen.

By these lies and boasts she had subjugated the minds of individuals so that they obeyed her and followed wherever [Note: [Col. 1164C] “Wherever she said,” Bod. 2.] she commanded and led. The demon also caused that woman to walk barefoot through rough snow in the bitter winter without being troubled or harmed in any way by that wandering. She also said that she was hastening to Judaea and Jerusalem, pretending that she had come from there. Here she deceived both Rusticus, one of the presbyters, and another man, a deacon, so that they had sexual relations with that woman; this was discovered shortly afterward.

For suddenly there appeared before her one of the exorcists, an approved man whose conduct had always been sound in matters of religious discipline. Encouraged also by the exhortation of very many brethren who were present and were themselves strong and praiseworthy in faith, he roused himself to refute that evil spirit [Note: [Col. 1164C] Routh conjectures “to refute”;] [Col. 1165A] which, with subtle deceit, had shortly before predicted even this: that a certain adversary [Note: [Col. 1165B] “Adversary,” Ar. Lam.] and unbelieving tempter would come. Nevertheless, that exorcist, inspired by God’s grace, resisted bravely and showed that it was a thoroughly wicked spirit which had previously been regarded as holy.

Moreover, among the other things by which she deceived very many, that woman—who had previously contrived many things for the deception of the faithful through the demon’s illusions and falsehoods—frequently dared even to pretend that by an invocation not to be despised she sanctified bread [Note: [Col. 1165B] “Sanctified peace,” Lam. Ebor. NC. 1. Bod. 2. Mich. Vict.] and made the Eucharist; she offered sacrifice to the Lord without [Note: [Col. 1165C] “Not without,” Oxford.] the sacrament of the customary proclamation, and she also baptized many, employing the customary and legitimate words of interrogation, so that she appeared to differ in nothing from the rule of the Church [Note: [Col. 1166B] “They appeared,” Ar. Lam. Ebor. NC. 1. Bod. 2.].

[Note: [Col. 1166D]

XI.—“Defend.” The old books vary greatly in this passage. Some have “defend,” others “assert,” and others “abandon” or “report.” We have retained the reading that we judged better, for shortly afterward one reads: “Those who defend heretics must be questioned by us.” BALUZE.]

XI. What, then, shall we say about her Baptism, in which a thoroughly wicked demon baptized through a woman? Do Stephen and those who agree with him approve even this, especially since neither the formula of the Trinity nor the legitimate and ecclesiastical interrogation was lacking in it? Can it be believed either that remission of sins was given or that regeneration by the saving washing was duly accomplished where everything, although done in an image of the truth, was nevertheless performed through a demon? Unless, perhaps, those who defend the Baptism [Note: [Col. 1166B] “Baptisms,” Bod. 2. Vict.] of heretics also contend that the demon gave the grace of Baptism in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Among heretics, without [Col. 1166A] doubt, there is the same error and the same deception of demons, since among them the Holy Spirit is wholly absent.

XII. What, moreover, are we to make of Stephen’s wish that the presence and holiness of Christ should attend those who are baptized among heretics? For if the Apostle does not lie when he says, “As many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ” (Gal. 3:27), then surely one who was baptized into Christ there has put on Christ. But if he has put on Christ, he has also been able to receive the Holy Spirit, who was sent by Christ; and the hand is imposed in vain upon him when he comes to receive the Spirit—unless he puts on the Spirit from Christ [Note: [Col. 1166B] Ar. NC. 1. Lam. Ebor. add “Holy.”] [Note: [Col. 1166C] Routh conjectures *non ducit*, “does not bring.”], so that Christ is indeed present among heretics but the Holy Spirit is not present there.

[Note: [Col. 1166D]

XIII.—“They must be questioned.” In four ancient manuscripts it is written: “What must be questioned?” From this one might or should infer that these words refer to the letter sent by Cyprian to Firmilian. BALUZE.]

XIII. Let us now briefly run through the other matters that were stated abundantly and most fully by you, especially since Rogatianus, our most beloved deacon, is hastening to you. For the next point is that those who defend heretics must be questioned by us as to whether their Baptism is carnal or spiritual. If it is carnal, they differ in no way from the Baptism of the Jews, which the Jews employ in such a way that by it, as by an ordinary and commonplace washing, only bodily filth is washed away. But if it is spiritual, how can there be spiritual Baptism among those with whom the Holy Spirit is not present? Consequently, [Col. 1167A] the water in which they are immersed is for them only a carnal washing, not the sacrament of Baptism.

[Note: [Col. 1167C]

XIV.—“Children of God.” I do not doubt that this reading is sound. Nevertheless, five old books read [Col. 1167D] “of faith”; my manuscript has “but faithful.” BALUZE.

“He puts on the Spirit from Christ.” The distinguished Maran wrote the following in the passage mentioned more than once: “Since Firmilian supposed that his opponents acknowledged the grace of Christ in Baptism received outside the Church by adults, he refutes them as follows: ‘For if he does not lie.’—‘The Holy Spirit.’ The phrase, ‘unless he puts on the Spirit from Christ,’ means the same as ‘after Christ’; nor is the conjecture of Cauchius and Pamelius probable, who thought it should read: ‘Unless he does not put on the Spirit from Christ.’” Maran’s remarks do not satisfy me. What if *non ducit* (“does not bring”) lies concealed in *induit* (“puts on”)? ROUTH.

“A chaste virgin.” Morel printed “a holy, chaste virgin.” Pamelius deleted the word “holy” because he did not find it in the manuscripts and because it is not found in the Apostle. I nevertheless found it in six manuscripts, though it is absent from four others. Three that have the word “holy” do not have “chaste.” One or the other, however, must be removed. We have retained the one found in the Apostle. BALUZE.]

XIV. But if the Baptism of heretics can possess the regeneration of the second birth, then those baptized among them must be reckoned not as heretics but as children of God [Note: [Col. 1167C] “They must be reckoned not among heretics but among the faithful,” Lam. Ebor. NC. 1. Mich.], for the second birth that takes place in Baptism begets children of God. But if the bride of Christ is one, namely the catholic Church, then she alone begets children of God. For Christ does not have many [Note: [Col. 1167C] “There are many brides of Christ,” Mich. Ar. Lam. Ebor. NC. 1. Bod. 2. Routh.] brides, since the Apostle says: “I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (2 Cor. 11:2); and: “Hear, daughter, and see, and incline your ear, and forget your people [Note: [Col. 1167C] “Your people,” accusative form, Ar. Lam. Ebor. NC. Bod. 2.], because the king has desired your beauty” (Ps. 44:21); and: “Come, bride, from Lebanon; you will come and pass over from the beginning of faith” (Song 4:8); and: “I have entered my garden, my sister, my bride” [Col. 1167B] (Song 5:1). We see one person presented everywhere, because the bride also is one.

The synagogue of the heretics, however, is not one with us, because neither is an adulterous and fornicating woman the bride; hence she cannot bear children of God. Unless, according to Stephen’s view, heresy gives birth and exposes its offspring, while the Church receives those who have been exposed and nurses as her own those whom she herself did not bear, since she cannot be the mother of another’s children. Therefore Christ our Lord, making clear that his bride is one and declaring the sacrament of her unity, says: “Whoever is not with me is against me [Note: [Col. 1167C] “Is opposed to me,” Ar.]; and whoever does not gather with me scatters” (Luke 11:23). For if Christ is with us, while heretics are not with us, heretics are certainly against Christ. [Col. 1167C] And if we gather with Christ, while heretics do not gather with us, they undoubtedly scatter.

[Note: [Col. 1168C]

XV.—“A sealed fountain.” These words are also found in Letter LXXIV [Col. 1168D] and Letter LXXVI. BALUZE.

“So likewise we.” Following the sacred text and the five manuscripts of Cyprian mentioned among the variant readings of the Oxford edition, I arranged for *nos* (“we”) to be printed instead of *vos* (“you”). ROUTH.

“Let them turn.” Concerning this celebrated question I shall note only this: there existed arguments advanced by the other side in those times by which the reasoning of Firmilian and his associates is overturned and Baptism celebrated in the name of the Holy Trinity by any minister is confirmed. These are found, among other places, in Saint Augustine’s annotations on the Seventh Council of Carthage. They may be read in that Father’s books *On Baptism*. ROUTH.]

XV. Nor must we pass over what you necessarily stated: that the Church, according to the Song of Songs, is “an enclosed garden and [Col. 1168A] a sealed fountain, a paradise with the fruit of apples” (Song 4:12–13). But how will those who have never entered this garden nor seen the paradise planted by God the Creator be able to provide anyone with the living water of the saving washing from the fountain enclosed within [Note: [Col. 1167C] “Closed within,” Ar. Lam. Ebor. NC. 1.] and sealed with the divine seal?

Since, moreover, Noah’s ark was nothing other than a sacrament of the Church of Christ—which at that time, while all outside perished, saved only those who were within the ark—we are plainly instructed to recognize the unity of the Church. So too the apostle Peter stated: “Thus likewise Baptism will save you [Note: [Col. 1168C] “Thus likewise Baptism will save us,” Ar. Lam. Ebor. NC. 1. Bod. 2.]” (1 Pet. 3:21), showing that, just as [Note: [Col. 1168C] “Showing because,” Lam. Ebor. NC. 1.] those who were not with Noah in the ark not only failed to be cleansed and saved [Note: [Col. 1168C] Thus Ar. Ebor. Lam. NC. 1.; Oxford omits “and saved.”] through the water, but immediately perished in that flood, so also now [Col. 1168B] all who are not with Christ in the Church will perish outside unless through repentance they turn [Note: [Col. 1168C] “Having turned,” Ar.] to the one saving washing of the Church.

[Note: [Col. 1168D]

XVI.—“The Church … upon the rock.” Shortly afterward he will say that the foundations of the Church were placed upon Peter. See the book *On the Unity of the Church*, where these matters are explained. BALUZE.

“By vicarious ordination.” See our notes on Letter LXXXIV of Lupus of Ferrières. BALUZE.

“By a death equal to theirs.” We restored this on the authority of an ancient manuscript of the Royal Library. Moreover, [Col. 1169D] other old copies, which have “they perished equally with them,” also appear to show that this restoration is legitimate. Five manuscripts and the editions prefer “together.” BALUZE.]

XVI. The nature of the error and the greatness of the blindness of one who says that remission of sins can be given within the synagogues of heretics, and who does not remain upon the foundation of the one Church, once established by Christ upon the rock, can be understood from the fact that Christ said to Peter alone: “Whatever you bind upon earth will be bound also in heaven; and whatever you loose upon earth will be loosed also in heaven” (Matt. 16:19). Again, in the Gospel, when Christ breathed upon the Apostles alone [Note: [Col. 1168C] “In the Gospel upon him alone,” Ar. Lam.], he said: “Receive the Holy Spirit. If [Note: [Col. 1168C] “The Holy Spirit, whose,” Ar.] you forgive anyone’s sins, they will be forgiven him; and if [Col. 1168C] you retain anyone’s sins, they will be retained” (John 20:22–23).

The power of forgiving sins was therefore given to the Apostles, to the churches which they established after being sent by Christ, and to the bishops who succeeded them by vicarious ordination. But the enemies of the one catholic Church in which we are, and our adversaries—the adversaries of us who have succeeded the Apostles—who unlawfully claim priestly offices for themselves against us and set up profane altars: what else are they but Korah, Dathan, and Abiram, sacrilegious through an equal crime and destined to suffer the same punishments as they, together with those who agree with them, just as at that time the participants in and supporters of those men also perished by a death equal to theirs?

[Note: [Col. 1167D]

XVII.—“What else does he do?” We have also supplied this passage on the authority of four old copies. BALUZE.]

XVII. And in this matter I am justly indignant at Stephen’s so open and manifest folly. Although he thus boasts of the position of his episcopate and contends that he possesses the succession of Peter, upon whom the foundations of the Church were laid, he introduces many other rocks and establishes new structures belonging to many churches when, by his own authority, he maintains that Baptism exists there. For those who are baptized undoubtedly complete [Col. 1169B] the number of the Church. But one who approves their Baptism thereby confirms that among the baptized a church also exists there. He does not understand that he who thus betrays and abandons unity obscures and, in a certain manner, abolishes the truth of the Christian rock.

The Apostle nevertheless professes that the Jews, although blinded by ignorance and bound by the gravest crime, have zeal for God [Note: [Col. 1169C] “Confesses that they have,” Ar. Lam. Ebor. NC. 1. Routh.]. Stephen, who proclaims that by succession he possesses the chair of Peter, is stirred by no zeal against heretics. He grants them no slight but the greatest power of grace, in that he says [Note: [Col. 1169C] “Says to them,” Ar. Lam. Ebor. NC. 1. Bod. 2.] and asserts that through the sacrament of Baptism they wash away the filth of the old man, forgive the former sins of death, make children of God by heavenly regeneration, and restore them to eternal life through the sanctification of the divine washing. [Col. 1169C] One who grants and attributes such great and heavenly gifts of the Church to heretics—what else [Note: [Col. 1169C] “What else does he do?” Ar. Lam. Ebor. NC. 1. Bod. 2.] does he do but enter into communion with those for whom he claims and maintains so great a measure of grace? Henceforth he also hesitates in vain to agree with them in other matters and to become their associate, so that he may meet together with them, mingle prayers jointly with them, and establish a common altar and sacrifice.

[Note: [Col. 1169D]

XVIII.—“And wherever.” I am surprised that these words dropped out of Rigaltius’s edition, since they occur in those of Morel and Pamelius and in all the ancient manuscripts. I am more surprised that they were omitted by the English editors, who could not have been unaware that they were contained in the two editions mentioned by me and in their five ancient manuscripts. See what I noted above on Letter LXXIII. BALUZE.]

XVIII. “But,” he says, “the name of Christ contributes greatly to faith and the sanctification of Baptism, so that whoever and wherever [Note: [Col. 1169C] “Whoever and wherever,” Ar. Lam. Ebor. NC. 1. Bod. 2.] someone has been baptized in the name of Christ, he immediately obtains the grace of Christ.” This passage can be answered briefly by saying that, if Baptism performed outside in the name of Christ had power to purify a person, the imposition of the hand there in the same Christ’s name could also have had power to confer the Holy Spirit. The other things [Note: [Col. 1170C] “The other things also among heretics, being just,” Ar. Lam. Ebor. NC. 1. Bod. 2.] done among heretics will likewise begin to appear just and legitimate whenever they are performed in the name of Christ. Yet, as you have explained in your letter, the name of Christ can have efficacy only in the Church alone, to which alone Christ has granted the power of heavenly grace.

[Note: [Col. 1169D]

XIX.—“Not as we do.” I found this reading, which I think the best, in one of my old books. Morel printed “not you”; I found that reading in four ancient manuscripts. Pamelius emended it by conjecture and wrote “the new Prophets,” both because he found his conjecture confirmed by the authority of the English manuscript that he used and because Firmilian had previously mentioned the new prophecies. The common reading accordingly arose from Pamelius’s edition. Firmilian appears, however, to have had in view the heresy of the Marcionites, whom Epiphanius says rejected the Law and the Prophets. Pamelius also notes that in his English manuscript “and the Holy Spirit” is read after “the Father and the Son.” I did not find this in any of the old copies that I used in revising this letter. Pamelius rejected the addition because the Cataphrygians did not acknowledge the same Holy Spirit as the catholics, since they said that not he but Montanus was the Paraclete promised by Christ. BALUZE.

Against Baluze’s contention here that Firmilian had the Marcionites in view, one may rightly object that the ancient Fathers were always accustomed to maintain as certain that the Marcionites acknowledged another and different God, since they denied that the Father of Christ [Col. 1171C] had created the world. Hear Tertullian, while still a catholic, making this very point in the controversy over Baptism: “I ought not,” he says, “to acknowledge among them”—the heretics—“what has been commanded to me, because the God of us and of them is not the same, nor is there one Christ—that is, the same Christ”: *On Baptism*, chapter 15. I have therefore restored the ancient reading, which both appears better and occurs in the Bodleian and New College manuscripts, and perhaps in the other manuscripts commonly cited in the Oxford edition, since no variant reading is noted there. Moreover, from that same edition we know that the addition “and the Holy Spirit” was found in five manuscripts. This very passage of Firmilian shows that these Montanists held a correct view of the Father and the Son. ROUTH.]

XIX. As for refuting the custom which they appear to oppose to the truth, who [Col. 1170B] is so foolish as to prefer custom to truth, or who, once the light has been perceived, would not abandon the darkness? Unless, perhaps, the most ancient custom also assists the Jews in some respect when Christ—that is, the Truth—comes, because they abandoned [Note: [Col. 1170C] Perhaps “rejected.” Routh.] the new way of truth and remained in antiquity.

You Africans can indeed say this against Stephen: that, once the truth became known, you abandoned the error of custom. We, however, join custom also to truth, and to the custom of the Romans we oppose custom—but the custom of truth—maintaining from the beginning what was handed down by Christ and by the [Note: [Col. 1170C] “Apostles,” Lam. NC. 1. Ebor.] Apostles. Nor do we remember that this ever had a beginning among us, since it has always been observed here that we recognize only the one Church of God and reckon holy Baptism as belonging only to the holy [Col. 1170C] Church.

To be sure, because certain persons were doubtful about the baptism of those who, although they do not receive the Prophets as we do, nevertheless appear to acknowledge with us the same Father and Son [Note: [Col. 1170C] “The Son and the Holy Spirit,” Ar. Lam. Ebor. NC. 1. Bod. 2.], a very large number of us assembled together at Iconium, examined the matter with the utmost care, and confirmed that absolutely every baptism established outside the Church must be repudiated.

[Note: [Col. 1171C]

XX.—“Disingenuously.” Thus Morel and four old books; four others have “through faith.” BALUZE.]

XX. As to the text which they put forward on behalf of heretics, saying that the Apostle declared, “Whether through pretext or through truth, Christ is proclaimed” (Phil. 1:18), it is foolish for us to offer a reply, since it is evident that in the letter in which he said this the Apostle mentioned neither heretics nor their baptism. Rather, he spoke only of brethren, whether they were dealing disingenuously with him or persevering in sincere faith. There is no need to examine this in a lengthy discussion; it is enough to read the letter itself and to ascertain from the Apostle himself what the Apostle said.

[Note: [Col. 1171D]

XXI.—“They are reckoned among their number.” We restored this passage on the authority of the very old manuscripts of Compiègne and Saint-Mihiel, in which the word “are reckoned” is transposed, though it nevertheless has the old sign indicating [Col. 1171D] where it must be placed, namely after the word “number.” Thus Rigaltius’s conjectural emendation of this passage falls away. BALUZE.—All the editions read “not only do they say.” But the conjecture common to Prudentius Maran (*Life of Cyprian*, §31, at the end) and Routh—namely, “no slight”—appeared worthy of acceptance. GOLDHORN.—Since, before Baluze’s alteration, the word “are reckoned” had been placed after the verb “died,” Rigaltius wished to emend the passage thus: “they possess—not merely learn—an advantage.” Fell offers a long but quite convoluted interpretation of the words “not only do they say, an advantage.” I should therefore venture to restore: “no slight advantage”; in Greek, Οὐ μέτριον κέρδος ἀληθείας καὶ πίστεως, “no slight gain of truth and faith.” The words “no slight” occur above in §12. After I had written this, I was pleased upon seeing Maran’s words that before me he had wished to emend the passage in almost the same way. “I shall attempt,” he says, “to emend another and far more difficult passage. Concerning those who, having been baptized outside, died in the Church without a new Baptism, Firmilian rules thus: ‘If from the world ... they have not been overtaken by death’ [text uncertain or incomplete]. [Col. 1172C] Rigaltius thinks that the verb ‘possess’ must be restored after ‘are reckoned,’ and thus emends: ‘they possess—not merely learn—the advantage of truth and faith.’ But it could be read much more suitably: ‘they possess no slight advantage,’ in place of ‘not only do they say’ or ‘not merely, as they learn.’” Thus Maran in the *Life of Saint Cyprian*, §31, p. 118. But I think it is not necessary to add “they possess.” ROUTH.

“Partake.” In Pamelius’s edition, evidently through a printer’s error, and then in those of Rigaltius and the English editors, *continguant* is written incorrectly, though not in Goulart’s edition. The English editors indeed write that they found this corrupt reading in four ancient manuscripts. But this does not prove that it should be retained, since it is wholly corrupt and by no means Latin. BALUZE.

“Compelled by the necessity of persecution, he succumbed.” As is evident from the preceding material, a cleric is meant here. A cleric who had lapsed was customarily removed from sacred orders, and he was not permitted to administer the rite of Baptism. ROUTH.]

XXI. “What, then,” they say, “will become of those who came from the heretics and were admitted without the Church’s Baptism?” If they have departed from the world, they are reckoned among the number of those who were indeed catechized among us but died before they could be baptized. They have no slight [text uncertain; transmitted reading: “not only do they say”] advantage [Col. 1171B] from the truth and faith to which they came after abandoning error, even though, having been overtaken by death, they did not attain the completion of grace. But those who still remain in the world should be baptized with the Church’s Baptism so that they may obtain remission of sins, lest, through another’s presumption, they remain in their former error and die without the completion of grace.

Moreover, what a sin it is—whether on the part of those who admit them or of those [Col. 1172A] who are admitted—that, with their defilements not washed away [Note: [Col. 1171B] “That, not having been washed, they partake of communion,” Ar. Lam. Ebor. NC. 1.] through the Church’s washing and their sins not put away, they rashly usurp communion and partake of the body and blood of the Lord, when it is written: “Whoever eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord unworthily will be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord” (1 Cor. 11:27).

[Note: [Col. 1172D]

XXII.—“The God of Christ.” These words are set down as though God were the creator of Christ and of the whole world. One must therefore consider whether the reading of the old Reims manuscript and two English manuscripts should be preferred, which have “our Lord” instead of “Christ.” But if that reading is accepted, the conjunction must be removed. One of my manuscripts reads “of the Lord Christ.” BALUZE.—It is evident from the Oxford edition that the words “the Lord Christ,” not, as Baluze says, “our Lord,” occur in the New College manuscripts. In that manuscript, as also in the Bodleian, the conjunction “and” is not unsuitably absent before the words “of the whole world.” As for the expression “the Father and God of Christ,” the Lord himself spoke similarly to Mary Magdalene in Saint John’s Gospel 20:17. His Apostles wrote similarly. Compare Rom. 15:6; 2 Cor. 11:3; Eph. 1:3, 17; Col. 1:3; Heb. 1:9; 1 Pet. 1:3. ROUTH.]

*Who, although they themselves.* That is, *who themselves* are established in every sin. I have restored the old reading. Fell was the first to print *qui cum ipsi* (“who, although they themselves”) from the manuscripts instead of *qui ipsi* (“who themselves”); this seems, indeed, to have arisen from a conflation of two readings. Pamelius, however, printed [Col. 1173C] *sunt* (“are”) instead of *sint* (“may be”), either from Cauchius’s codex or from Cauchius’s own conjecture. ROUTH.]

XXII. We have also judged that those whom men baptized who had previously been bishops in the Catholic Church and afterward assumed for themselves the power of clerical ordination are to be regarded as unbaptized. And this practice is observed among us: whoever comes to us after being immersed by them is baptized among us with the one true Baptism of the Catholic Church, as an outsider who has obtained nothing, and so attains regeneration through the life-giving washing.

Yet there is a great difference between one who yielded unwillingly, compelled by the necessity [Col. 1172B] of persecution, and one who, with sacrilegious and reckless intent, rebels against the Church, or with impious speech blasphemes the Father and God [Note: [Col. 1172B] “the Lord Christ,” Ar. NC. 1.] of Christ and Creator of the whole world. And Stephen is not ashamed to assert that remission of sins can be given through those [Note: [Col. 1172B] Thus Ar. Lam. Ebor. NC. 1. M. R.; *Qui ipsi*, Rig.] who, although they themselves are established in every sin—as though the washing of salvation could exist in the house of death!

[Note: [Col. 1173C]

XXIII.—From strange water. The English edition observes that this text is sought elsewhere in vain except in the Greek version: namely, that it is absent from the Hebrew codices and the Latin Vulgate, but is nevertheless found in the Syriac, Arabic, and Armenian versions. From this it can be concluded that the same Greek version became established throughout the world even in places where it departs from the Hebrew. Tertullian, Book I, *Against Marcion*: “I should consider no one more shameless than the man who is immersed in another’s water for another god.” See the notes [Col. 1173D] on Epistle LXXIII, “The Church, like paradise.” BALUZIUS.]

XXIII. Where, then, will that which is written have its place: “Keep yourself from strange [Col. 1173A] water, and do not drink from a strange fountain” (Prov. IX, 19, according to the Septuagint), if, after abandoning the Church’s sealed fountain, you accept strange water in place of your own and pollute the Church with profane fountains?

For when you share in the baptism of heretics, what else are you doing but drinking from their abyss and mire, and—though yourself purified by the Church’s sanctification—being defiled through contact with strange filth? Nor do you fear God’s judgment when you bear witness for heretics against the Church, although it is written: “A false witness will not go unpunished” (Prov. XIX, 5).

Indeed, you are worse than all the heretics. For although many of them, after recognizing their error, come from there to you in order to receive the Church’s true light, you support the errors of those who come and, after obscuring the light of ecclesiastical truth, deepen the darkness of the heretical night. And although they acknowledge that they are [Col. 1173B] in sin, possess no grace, and therefore come to the Church, you deprive them of the remission of sins that is given in baptism, when you say that they have already been baptized and have obtained the Church’s grace outside the Church.

Nor do you understand that their souls will be required from your hand when the day of judgment comes, since you denied the Church’s drink to the thirsty and became a cause of death to those who wished to live. And, on top of this, you are indignant.

[Note: [Col. 1173D]

XXIV.—More justly. I cannot omit warning the reader that seven old copies read *injustius* (“more unjustly”). Nevertheless, I have chosen to follow Morel’s edition, which is confirmed by three old copies. ID.

Against him who. Thus Morel and three old books. All the others omit *eum qui* (“him who”), including one English manuscript. ID.

Even the ignorant are hot-tempered. Quintilian, Book I, chapter 1: “Nothing is worse than those who, after advancing a little beyond their first lessons, have assumed a false conviction of their own knowledge. For they are indignant at yielding to those skilled in teaching and, as though by some right of authority—with which this class of men generally swells up—they imperiously, and sometimes even savagely, teach their folly to perfection.” See also Book VI, chapter 4, and Book VIII, chapter 2. John of Salisbury, Book VII of *The Frivolities of Courtiers*, chapter 9: “Yet the man who has spent his life learning only a few things contradicts more quickly and obstinately, and he is confined within such narrow limits that, if you take away one or two words, he becomes speechless and more silent than any statue.” [Col. 1174C] Vitruvius, in the preface to Book III: “I observe that the unlearned rather than the learned prevail through favor.” Jerome, in the *Apology against Rufinus*: “A hot-tempered man is dishonorable.” Nonius Marcellus: “The irascible are called *animosi*.” Augustine, Sermon CLXIV on the words of the Apostle: “To err was human; to remain in error through obstinacy is diabolical.” Agobard, in his book *On Hail and Thunder*, observes that the ignorant speak confidently. Among Latin authors, however, *animosus* was also used for a great man endowed with a brave spirit, while *animositas* meant vehemence and impetuosity of spirit. ID.

[Col. 1174D] Of judgment and speech. Firmilian had perhaps written in Greek, συνέσεως καὶ λόγου, “of understanding and speech.” ROUTH.

Prepares quarrels. Thus it is written in six ancient books; three others have *parit*, “produces.” The former reading, however, seems better to me, because in Proverbs chapter XXIX, from which this passage is taken, it reads: “An irascible man provokes quarrels.” In Cassian, Book VIII, chapter 1, it is written: “A hot-tempered man prepares quarrels.”]

XXIV. See with what ignorance you dare to rebuke those who strive for truth against falsehood. For who had the more just cause to be indignant with the other: the one who champions the enemies of God, or the one who, against him who champions the enemies of God, [Note: [Col. 1173C] “Because he champions against the enemies of God,” Lam.] agrees [Note: [Col. 1173C] Perhaps “contends,” Routh.] on behalf of the Church’s truth?

It is simply evident that the ignorant are also hot-tempered and irascible: through poverty of judgment and speech [Col. 1173C] they readily turn to anger, [Col. 1174A] so that divine Scripture may say of no one more fittingly than of you: “A hot-tempered man prepares quarrels, and an irascible man multiplies sins” (Prov. XXIX, 22).

How many quarrels and dissensions have you prepared throughout the churches of the whole world? And how great a sin have you multiplied for yourself by tearing yourself away from so many flocks! For you have cut off your own self. Do not deceive yourself: the true schismatic is the one who has made himself an apostate from the communion of ecclesiastical unity. For while you suppose that everyone can be excluded by you, you alone have excluded yourself from everyone.

Not even the Apostle’s precepts, warning and saying as follows, could shape you according to the rule of truth and peace:

> I therefore, a prisoner in the Lord, beseech you to walk worthily of the calling by which you were called, with all humility of mind and gentleness, patiently bearing with [Col. 1174B] one another in love, taking every care to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace: one body and one Spirit, just as you were called in the one hope of your calling; one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, who is over all, [Note: [Col. 1174C] “who is over all things,” Lam. Ebor.] and through all, and in us all.  
> (Eph. IV, 1–6)

[Note: [Col. 1174D]

XXV.—For what is more humble? Lactantius used a similar irony in chapter 25 of *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, when speaking of Maximian’s cruelty toward beggars, all of whom he ordered to be gathered together, carried out to sea in small boats, and drowned. Lactantius therefore says: “So compassionate was the man that he took care that no one should be miserable during his reign.” BALUZIUS.

From whom episcopal delegates, etc. There seems no doubt that the delegates were sent to Rome by the Africans rather than by the Easterners. Baronius nevertheless affirms the contrary in the *Annals*, as does Noël [Col. 1175B] Alexandre in his *Ecclesiastical History*. But Pagi, Tillemont, and Basnage, following Pearson, related that Stephen acted in this manner toward the Africans. “What could be clearer from the sequence of their words,” says Pearson in the *Cyprianic Annals*, at the year 56, “than that those delegates, distinguished by episcopal rank, had been sent not by the Easterners but by those who were in the South—that is, the Africans? Nor do I think that the following words of Firmilian”—which he had just cited—“can be understood otherwise: ‘Except that we cannot thank Stephen in this matter, since through his inhumanity toward them it has now come about that we have gained proof of your faith and wisdom’” (above, p. 222). “That inhumanity was nothing other than the rejection of the delegates, [Col. 1175C] through which there could no longer be either conversation or ordinary discourse. Those delegates were sent at the second Council of Carthage.” § VII. ROUTH.

Nor admit them to speech. That is, he would not permit them even to come into his sight. The Count of Flanders employed the same humanity and courtesy toward the delegates of Pope Clement VII: he was so far from allowing them to be heard, says Radulphus de Rivo, that they were not even admitted, but were rejected and ordered to depart unless they preferred to await imprisonment.

Given the opportunity, I shall also emend a passage from the panegyric that Nazarius delivered to Constantine after Maxentius had been defeated, in which Caesar’s moderation toward him is praised. There, among other things, all the ancient codices and editions read: “You call him into partnership. He flees your *appetitum*, turns from it, shudders at it.” The word *appetitum* (“desire”), placed here where it does not belong, exercised the ingenuity of the critics. Some thought *affectum* (“affection”) should be restored; others, *amicum* (“friend”). I am surprised that the true reading, which is easy and [Col. 1175D] obvious, occurred to none of them. We should therefore restore *aspectum* (“sight”), so that the meaning is: “You called Maxentius into partnership in the empire. But he, savage and proud as he was by nature, not only refused to embrace what you offered, but even fled from your sight, turned from it, and shuddered at it”; indeed, he even went out of his way to provoke the man whose favor he ought to have sought, as is stated a little later. BALUZIUS.

Perhaps the soul itself. The more recent Remigian manuscript has: “Perhaps one soul is so unstable.” ID.

One baptism. I do not know how it happened that these words, which occur in Paul’s Epistle to the Ephesians, were omitted here in eight ancient copies. ID.

If there is one Lord. This clause was omitted in Rigault’s edition and restored in the English edition. But I do not know how it came about that the English editors, without the authority of any old book and contrary to the evidence of the ancient copies and Morel’s edition, wrote, “it follows that there is unity,” unless they preferred to embrace the conjecture of Pamelius, who had warned in the margin of his [Col. 1176B] edition that *unitas* (“unity”) should be read, or the authority of Goulart, who placed that word in the text without mentioning Pamelius. Reinhart restored *unus* (“one”) in his edition. ID.—The New College codex has, “because he is one,” which Baluzius printed. I would read, “because God is one,” as the words that follow suggest. These writers customarily use *quia* (“because”) in place of *quod* (“that”). ROUTH.

Pseudo-Christ. This was imitated from chapter eleven of Paul’s Second Epistle to the Corinthians. From this it is clear, says Pamelius, that the vehemence of Pope Stephen’s letter was the reason Cyprian and Firmilian also wrote against him so vehemently. Quite right. [Col. 1176C] There was indeed no other reason why Firmilian, who throughout the entire letter declares the highest love of unity, nevertheless inveighs against Stephen in such a way that it is evident he was carried away by the heat of the dispute.

No one was gentler or more peaceable than Cyprian, and his moderation of spirit shone forth both in all other matters and especially in this controversy concerning baptism. Nevertheless, it is clear from his letter to Pompeius that he sometimes passed from that supreme gentleness to a more vehement defense of his cause. It appears that Cyprian and Firmilian were offended above all because Stephen thought that those who rebaptized should be excluded.

On account of these words, which he thinks are not Stephen’s, Christian Lupus says in his scholia on Tertullian’s book *On the Prescription against Heretics* that he doubts whether Firmilian’s letter is genuine. Yet before Lupus no one had ventured to claim that it was false or to doubt its authority. This readiness to accuse the writings of the ancients of falsity is certainly exceedingly rash and dangerous. For if everyone is permitted to follow empty [Col. 1176D] conjectures of this kind, no monument of antiquity will escape unjust suspicions. BALUZIUS.—Thus Baluzius. Meanwhile, Christian Lupus does not seem to me to have intended to write that he doubted whether Firmilian’s letter was genuine, but rather that he hesitated over whether the abusive names attributed to Cyprian by Stephen had actually been uttered by him. See his *Scholia on Tertullian*, chapter 4, p. 121. Yet one must consider the taunts with which a certain ancient defender of Stephen’s position on the baptism of heretics—the author of *On Rebaptism*, at the end of the works of St. Cyprian—apparently assailed Cyprian himself. Compare the annotations above on Firmilian’s letter. ROUTH.

Who all things. I once thought that *quae omnia* (“all of which”) should be read, before I learned that the first edition actually had that reading; for Pamelius subsequently printed *qui* (“who”) instead of *quae* (“which”) from his manuscript, though, I acknowledge, other manuscripts agree with him. [Col. 1177A] But Firmilian had perhaps written in Greek ἃ δὴ πάντα, “all of which indeed,” or τάδε δὲ πάντα, “but all these things.” ID.

Which he himself. The more recent Remigian codex and Pamelius’s English manuscript read, “which ought undeservedly to have been charged against him.” Thus also four ancient manuscripts cited in the English edition.

All of us. These words seem corrupt to me. What if one read *charissime frater* (“dearest brother”), an error having crept in through ignorance of scribal abbreviations? Jerome likewise observed in his letter to Avitus concerning Origen’s errors that it is difficult to preserve abbreviated notations. [Col. 1178A] Simon Goulart noted that the codex of the Bishop of Acre read: “Together with all the bishops who are in Africa, all the clergy, and the whole brotherhood, we wish you good health.” Reinhart placed this reading in his text as the better one. Nevertheless, I prefer my own conjecture. Yet I have not dared to alter anything, lacking the authority of ancient copies.]

XXV. How diligently Stephen fulfilled these commands and salutary [Note: [Col. 1174C] “health-giving,” Ar. Lam. Ebor. NC. 1.] admonitions of the Apostle, preserving humility of mind and gentleness in the first place! For what could be more humble or gentler than to disagree with so many bishops throughout the whole world, breaking peace with each through different kinds of dissension—now with the Easterners, as we trust is not unknown to you, and now with you who are in the South?

From you he received episcopal delegates [Col. 1174C] with such patience and gentleness that he would not admit them even [Col. 1175A] to the speech of ordinary conversation. Moreover, mindful of love and charity, he instructed the entire brotherhood that no one should receive them into his house, so that those who came might be denied not only peace and communion, but even shelter and hospitality.

This is what it means to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace: to cut oneself off from the unity of charity, to make oneself entirely alien to one’s brothers, and to rebel against the sacrament and the faith in the fury of obstinate dissension! Can there be one body and one Spirit in the presence of such a man, in whom perhaps even the soul itself is not one, so unstable, changeable, and uncertain is it?

But let us leave him aside, insofar as he himself is concerned. Let us instead examine that about which the greatest controversy exists. Those who contend that persons baptized by heretics ought to be received as though they had obtained the grace of legitimate [Col. 1175B] baptism say that our baptism and theirs are one and do not differ in any respect. But what does the Apostle Paul say? “One Lord, one faith, [Col. 1176A] one baptism, one God” (Eph. IV, 5).

If the baptism of heretics is one and the same as ours, then without doubt the faith too is one. If the faith is one, then certainly the Lord too is one. If the Lord is one, it follows that we must say that he is one. But if this unity, which is wholly incapable of separation or division, also exists identically among the heretics, why do we contend any further? Why do we call them heretics and not Christians?

But since neither God nor Lord is one for us and the heretics, nor is there one Church or one faith, nor even one Spirit or one body, it is evident that baptism cannot be common to us and the heretics, since we have absolutely nothing in common.

And yet Stephen is not ashamed to afford such people his protection against the Church and, in order to champion heretics, [Col. 1176B] to rend the brotherhood; and, besides this, to call Cyprian a pseudo-Christ, a pseudo-apostle, and a deceitful worker. Conscious that all these things were present in himself, [Col. 1177A] he anticipated the charge by falsely imputing to another what he himself deserved to hear.

Together with all the bishops who are in Africa, [Col. 1178A] all the clergy, and the entire brotherhood, all of us wish you good health, so that, always being of one mind and one judgment, we may have you united with us even from afar.

[ON REBAPTISM]

[Col. 1177]

# PROLEGOMENA ON THE ANONYMOUS AUTHOR OF THE BOOK *ON REBAPTISM*

## ARTICLE I. Who Was the Author of the Work, and in What Century Did He Flourish?

[Col. 1177B]

The book *On Rebaptism*, says a learned man [Note: [Col. 1177D] Prudentius Maran, *Life of Cyprian*, § 35, p. CXXVI, Paris edition; p. 117, Venice edition.], is attributed by some to the monk Ursinus, whom Gennadius testifies to have written in the fourth century against those who rebaptized [Note: [Col. 1177D] Gennadius, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, ch. 27.]. It is not difficult to observe in this treatise *On Rebaptism* the subjects that Gennadius says were contained in the book of the monk Ursinus. For the author, whoever he may ultimately have been, does nothing other than seek to prove that those baptized in heresy are not to be rebaptized, but, once converted to a sounder faith, are to receive the laying on of hands.

But Ursinus cannot be regarded as the author of this little book unless he is said to have been a bishop in the third century. Our Writer explicitly declares himself to be a bishop. [Col. 1177C] “For if baptism is administered by us,” he says, [Note: [Col. 1177D] Anonymous, *On Rebaptism*, § 10.] “let it be administered fully and solemnly, be marked by everything prescribed in Scripture, and be administered without the omission of any element whatsoever; or, if it has been administered out of necessity by a member of the lower clergy, let us await the outcome, so that it may either be completed by us or left to be completed by the Lord.”

Clear marks of the third century occur in this same Writer. For he speaks of that entire controversy in a way that indicates it had recently arisen and was still continuing. He says [Note: [Col. 1177D] Ibid., § 1.] that it is monstrous for bishops to devise such scandals, and that turbulent men have made it their purpose, even now, to begin conducting their business of persuasion.

In the very passage objected to by Baluzius, he declares it useful [Note: [Col. 1177D] Ibid., § 6.] “to acquiesce, with good reason, in the authority of so many years and so many churches, as well as of the Apostles and bishops, since it is the greatest injury and loss to our most holy [Col. 1178B] mother the Church, after so long a succession of so many centuries, now for the first time suddenly and irrationally to rise up against ancient decisions.”

One should not infer from these words that the author lived in the fourth century, but only that he was not particularly restrained when employing exaggeration. For apart from the fact that not even in the fourth century could he have objected, without absurd exaggeration, that there had been “so long a succession of so many centuries,” he certainly declares in express words that the controversy over the baptism of heretics had then flared up for the first time—a description properly fitting the third century.

Indeed, without naming Cyprian, he even attacks him as a man still alive and using his authority to defend the opposing side. For he asserts [Note: [Col. 1178D] Ibid., § 1.] that “controversies of this kind produce no benefit, except that one man—whoever he may be—is acclaimed among certain frivolous men, with empty glory, as a man of great prudence and steadfastness, and is celebrated among men very like and equal to himself, though endowed with the stupefaction characteristic of heretics—whose one consolation is that they should not appear to sin alone—as having corrected the errors and faults of all the churches.” [Col. 1178C]

Who would have abused Cyprian in so unworthy a manner after he had washed away by martyrdom the stain of the error that he had defended with the utmost moderation of spirit in a matter not yet decided, and after his name, once the heat of contention had cooled, had attained the highest renown throughout all the churches?

What the most distinguished Maran has thus far discussed concerning the age of this anonymous writer is known to have been approved long ago by others eminent in learning and erudition. Rigault, who first published this treatise among the notes on the works [Col. 1178D] of St. Cyprian, using a Sirmondian transcript copied from an ancient codex of the monastery of St. Remigius, judged [Note: [Col. 1178D] Rigault, on the *Works of Cyprian*, p. 133, Paris edition, 1666.] that the author lived not long after the age of Cyprian. The [Col. 1179A] Oxford editor of Cyprian’s works [Note: [Col. 1179D] Fell, part III of the *Works of Cyprian*, p. 21.] followed Rigault. Cave likewise, discussing the question once and again, [Note: [Col. 1179D] Cave, *Literary History*, at the years 253 and 440.] could not be brought to cast his vote for the other opinion.

Tillemont, however, seems to have investigated the matter far more keenly than the others [Note: [Col. 1179D] Tillemont, *Mémoires*, vol. IV, p. 629, note XL, “Sur S. Cyprien.”]. He finally went so far as to determine that the work was written not only while Cyprian was still alive, but even against the bishop of Carthage himself. This is also the opinion of the distinguished Gallandi [Note: [Col. 1179D] Gallandi, *Library of the Ancient Fathers*, vol. III, Prolegomena, ch. 7, p. 24.], for whom the two most learned men Tillemont and Ceillier [Note: [Col. 1179D] Ceillier, *Histoire générale*, vol. III, ch. I, § III, art. IV, p. 156.] had already illuminated the way.

## ARTICLE II. Analysis of This Little Work

At the beginning he clearly sets forth the state of the question. He then observes [Note: [Col. 1179D] Anonymous, § 1, p. 362 in Gallandi; in Cyprian, Venice edition, pp. 736–737; Oxford edition, p. 20.]:

> Certain things have been written or written in reply concerning this new question, in which each side strove with the greatest zeal [Col. 1179B] to destroy the positions of the other.

From this the most learned Ceillier rightly concludes that this author wrote at a time when a number of works for and against the baptism of heretics had already been composed.

“In this kind of question,” the Anonymous author continues,

> as it seems to me, no controversy or dispute at all could have arisen if each of us, content with the venerable authority of all the churches and possessing the requisite humility, had not desired to introduce innovations, since he would have perceived that there was no real ground for contradiction. For everything that is both doubtful and ambiguous, and upon which prudent and faithful men hold differing opinions, must certainly be condemned if it is judged contrary to the ancient and memorable, most solemn observance of all the honored saints and faithful. [Col. 1179C]

Afterward, in § 2, while discussing the question, he distinguishes two baptisms: one of water and the other of the Holy Spirit, in accordance with the words of St. John the Baptist (Matt. III, 11; Mark I, 7; Luke III, 16; John I, 27):

> He who comes after me is mightier than I; I am not worthy to loose the strap of his sandal. He will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire.

And Jesus Christ himself said:

> John indeed baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days from now.

Cornelius received the baptism of the Holy Spirit before he received that of water (Acts I, 4–5); conversely, the Apostles had been baptized in water for a long time before they received the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 1179D] Anonymous, among the works of Cyprian, p. 22, Bremen and Venice editions; pp. 738–739; and in Gallandi, §§ 4–5.].

This anonymous author [Col. 1179D] uses these examples to show that although either one of these two baptisms is ordinarily joined with the other, the baptism [Col. 1180A] of water nevertheless does not cease to confer grace even when separated from the laying on of hands, which was instituted specifically for conferring the Holy Spirit.

“For it cannot be doubted,” says the Anonymous author, [Note: [Col. 1180D] Anonymous, p. 24, Bremen edition; Venice edition, p. 740 ff.]

> that even in the present day it happens that many depart this world after baptism without the bishop’s laying on of hands, and yet are regarded as fully perfected believers. . . . Or if you say that such a person cannot be saved, we deprive all bishops of salvation, since you bind them to such absolutely certain dangers that they must personally bring aid to all the people under their care who fall ill while scattered throughout various regions, because other persons, who rank below clerics, cannot provide the same assistance to those in danger—lest it become necessary for the blood of those who appear to have departed [Col. 1180B] the world empty to be required from the bishops’ hands.

From this he concludes that when baptism in the name of Jesus has preceded, the Holy Spirit may be given to such a penitent and believing person through the bishop’s laying on of hands alone, without any need to inquire what sort of baptism it was that he received in the name of Jesus Christ [Note: [Col. 1180D] Ibid., Bremen edition, pp. 23–24; Venice edition, p. 741.].

He attributes the same efficacy to the baptism of the Holy Spirit without that of water, relying upon this foundation: the power of the name of Jesus Christ is so great “that when invoked over any human being in baptism,” it can bestow no slight “privilege toward attaining salvation. . . .”

And the person over whom, when he was baptized, “the name of Jesus was invoked,” even though he was detained “in some error” or sin, “if he corrects his error, acknowledges the truth of the faith, cuts away every stain of his former way of life, comes to the Church and the bishop, receives the laying on of his hands, and receives the Holy Spirit,” does not lose the fruit of the ceremony in which that preceding invocation of the name of Jesus was lawfully performed. That ceremony by itself is nevertheless insufficient for salvation, but begins to possess efficacy and power “when the error has been corrected, the truth acknowledged, every stain of the former way of life cut away, and the supplement formerly lacking supplied” [Col. 1180C] through the laying on of hands.

He proves this assertion by the example of the Apostles [Note: [Col. 1180D] Ibid., § 9, p. 366 in Gallandi; Bremen edition, p. 26; Venice edition, pp. 742–744.], who did not cease to baptize after they had abandoned Christ and denied the faith.

He then says in § 10 that “baptism conferred by bishops of the worst conduct, or holding erroneous opinions, or comparatively ignorant,” [Col. 1180D] is good and complete: so great a power “belongs intrinsically to divine operations” [Note: [Col. 1180D] Ibid., p. 26, Bremen edition; Venice edition, pp. 746–748.].

He then adds in the same section:

> Since our salvation is established in the baptism of the Spirit, which is also very frequently joined to the baptism of water, if baptism is administered by us, let it be administered fully and solemnly, be marked by everything prescribed in Scripture, and be administered without any separation of that reality; or, if it has been administered out of necessity by a member of the lower clergy, [Col. 1181A] let us await the outcome, so that it may either be completed by us or left to be completed by the Lord. But if it has been administered by outsiders, let the matter be corrected insofar as it can and as the case permits, because the Holy Spirit does not exist outside the Church, and faith cannot be sound not only among heretics but even among those established in schism.

> Therefore, those who repent and are corrected through instruction in the truth and through their faith—which was afterward amended, once their heart had been purified—should be assisted only by spiritual baptism, that is, by the bishop’s laying on of hands and the ministration of the Holy Spirit. For good reason, the complete sign of faith has customarily been administered in the Church in this manner and by this procedure, [Col. 1181B] lest the invocation of the name of Jesus, which cannot be abolished, appear to be treated with contempt by us—which certainly ought not to happen. Nevertheless, if none of the things we have mentioned follows, such an invocation ceases to operate for salvation and remains ineffectual.

> For since the Apostle says that there is one baptism (Eph. IV, 5), the invocation of the name of Jesus must remain, because no human being can take away an invocation once it has been made.

Afterward he explains the baptism of blood designated by Jesus Christ [Note: [Col. 1181D] Anonymous, § 11 in Gallandi, from p. 367; Bremen edition, p. 28; Venice edition, p. 752.] in these words:

> I have another baptism with which I must be baptized.  
> (Luke XII, 50)

“In this passage,” says our Anonymous author, [Note: [Col. 1181D] § 14, in Gallandi, p. 368; Bremen edition, p. 28; Venice edition, p. 752.]

> Christ does not signify a second baptism, as though there were two baptisms, but demonstrates that a baptism of another kind, also contributing to the same salvation, has been given to us. Both these kinds first had to be inaugurated and sanctified by our Lord himself, so that either or both kinds might provide for us this one twofold, saving, and honorable baptism, [Col. 1181C] and so that certain paths of the one baptism might be opened to us in such a way that sometimes one of them could be absent without harm.

> Thus the baptism of water is absent without harm in martyrs who are hearers of the word, although we are certain that, if they have any respite, they are also accustomed to be baptized with water. Likewise, the baptism of their own blood is absent without harm in those who have become legitimate believers, because, having been baptized in the name of Christ, they have been redeemed by the Lord’s most precious blood.

> Both these streams of the Lord’s Baptism proceed from one and the same fountain. . . . They first appeared in [Col. 1181D] the Lord’s Passion, when blood and water flowed from his side after it was pierced by the soldier’s lance, so that the single side emitted two streams of different kinds, yet nevertheless of the same [the reading is materially uncertain here], with the result that whoever drinks believingly from either stream is filled with the Holy Spirit.

> For the Lord showed this when speaking about these streams and signifying the Holy Spirit. Hence St. John the Apostle, joining these things together, says:

> “Three bear witness: the Spirit, the water, and the blood. And these [Col. 1182A] three are one” (I John V, 6).

[Note: [Col. 1182B] The Reverend Father de Rubeis, the distinguished scholar, examines on p. 76 of his dissertation *On the Three Witnesses in Heaven* the complete passage of this anonymous author, who appears to have read in his copy the eighth Johannine *Comma* joined to the sixth verse. The most learned Bossuet is found to have treated this argument [Col. 1182C] more diligently than anyone else against Simon, *Remarks on the Critique of the Library of Ecclesiastical Authors*, vol. II, pp. 575–628.]

From these words we are to infer both that water has customarily bestowed the Spirit, that a person’s own blood has customarily bestowed the Spirit, and that the Spirit himself has customarily bestowed the Spirit [Note: [Col. 1182C] Anonymous, § 15, in Gallandi, p. 369; in Cyprian, p. 29, Bremen edition; Venice edition, p. 753.].

## ARTICLE III. Certain Observations on This Treatise and Its Editions
These seemed to us the principal and more noteworthy points in this short work *On Rebaptism*, which appears to have been written expressly to defend the position of Saint Stephen I, pope, concerning the validity of baptism conferred by heretics. First, it holds that martyrdom is of no benefit to heretics [Col. 1182B] or to those who pour out their blood for the name of Jesus Christ without charity—that is, outside the Church.

> [Note: [Col. 1182C] It makes no difference here whether the one who confesses the Lord is a hearer or one of the faithful, provided that he confesses Christ himself, whom one ought to confess. For the Lord, in confessing him in return before the Father, may himself adorn his confessor with the honor of martyrdom, as he promised. This, however, must not be understood too broadly, as though it could be extended without limit; for even some heretic who nevertheless denies Christ himself may confess the name of Christ, because he believes in another Christ. In Cyprian, p. 77, Bremen ed.; Venice ed., p. 749; in Gallandi, vol. III, § 11, p. 367. For the same reason, even the heretic who is slain while confessing Christ’s name cannot afterward correct whatever false opinion he may have held concerning God or Christ, since by believing in another [Col. 1182D] God or another Christ he has deceived himself: he is a confessor not of Christ, but merely of Christ’s name. Accordingly, the Apostle also says: “Even if I deliver my body to be burned with fire, but have not love, I gain nothing.” For by this deed one who does not possess love for God and Christ gains nothing. Ibid., p. 28, Bremen ed.; Venice ed., p. 751; and Gallandi, § 13, p. 368.]

Second, martyrdom endured in the communion of the Church obtains both the merit of faith and that of charity.

> [Note: [Col. 1182D] He knew that human beings could be baptized not only with water but also with their own blood, so that those baptized by this baptism alone could obtain the complete faith and sincere love of the laver, and thus be baptized in both ways. Ibid., p. 28, Bremen ed.; Venice ed., p. 752; Gallandi, § 14, p. 368.]

Third, the book entitled *The Preaching of Saint Paul* was composed by disciples of Simon Magus;

> [Note: [Col. 1182D] Anonymous author, in Gallandi, §§ 17, pp. 369–370; in Cyprian, Bremen ed., p. 30; Venice ed., p. 755.]
