and these heretics, in imitation of their leader, “desire to deceive those who are more simple-minded or more inquisitive by asserting that they alone transmit baptism whole and perfect, and not, as we do, mutilated [Col. 1183A] and curtailed. They are said to describe it in such a way that, as soon as the candidates descend into the water, fire immediately appears above the water”; for they falsely teach that the baptism of Jesus must be accompanied by material fire.

> [Note: [Col. 1183B] The same, in Gallandi, § 16, p. 369; in Cyprian, Bremen ed., at the page cited; Venice ed., p. 755.]

From the same anonymous author we learn that miracles were performed in his own age, even by heretics themselves. For he says:

> [Note: [Col. 1183B] The same, in Gallandi, § 12, p. 367; in Cyprian, Bremen ed., p. 28; Venice ed., p. 750. “In that name all works of power are ordinarily performed, and sometimes even certain works by outsiders.” Gallandi, § 7, p. 365; Cyprian, Venice ed., p. 744; Bremen ed., p. 25.]

“Without doubt they then associate those works of power with the name of Christ; in that name some even now appear to perform certain works of power and to prophesy falsely.”

Furthermore, certain insufficiently precise statements occur in this short work. Thus, for example, he writes in §§ 4 and 14: “The Holy Spirit did not yet exist, because Jesus had not yet been glorified.”

> [Note: [Col. 1183B] Perhaps the word *given* dropped out through a copyist’s error; it appears necessarily to be supplied from the Vulgate translation.]

And a little later [Col. 1184A] he says

> [Note: [Col. 1184A] “On the day of Pentecost the Holy Spirit came upon them, descending from heaven by God’s will, indeed, and not of his own accord.” The same, in Gallandi, § 6, p. 364; Cyprian, Bremen ed., [Col. 1184B] p. 24; Venice ed., p. 742.]

that “the Holy Spirit descended from heaven by God’s will, not by his own”; and finally, that the baptism of the Holy Spirit is greater than the baptism of water.

> [Note: [Col. 1184B] “For it makes a great difference whether someone has not been baptized at all in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, or whether he falters in some respect when he is baptized with the baptism of water, which is lesser, provided that afterward sincere faith in the truth is firmly established in the baptism of the Spirit, which is undoubtedly greater.” The same, in Gallandi, § 6, p. 365; in Cyprian, Bremen ed., p. 24; Venice ed., p. 744.]

The anonymous treatise *On Rebaptism* first saw the light in 1648, among the works of Cyprian printed at Paris by Nicolas Rigault. It was afterward reprinted in all subsequent editions of Cyprian’s works and included in volume III, pp. 362–371, of the *Library of the Ancient Fathers* prepared by Andrea Gallandi, Venice, 1767; Gallandi also appended learned notes to the same treatise. **LUMPER.**

[Col. 1183]

> [Note: [Col. 1183C]
>
> **ON BAPTISM.** We have retained the title borne by the ancient manuscript. At the end the ancient manuscript has: “Caecilius Cyprian’s *On Rebaptism* ends.”]

# AN ANONYMOUS BOOK ON REBAPTISM: THAT THOSE WHO HAVE ONCE BEEN IMMERSED IN THE NAME OF THE LORD JESUS CHRIST OUGHT NOT TO BE BAPTIZED AGAIN  
(C, G, S)

[Col. 1183C]

> [Note: [Col. 1183C]
>
> **I.—In the name of Jesus Christ our Lord.** In the ancient book *Domini non* (“of the Lord not”) is written. Sirmond judged that this should be corrected to *Dominicum* (“the Lord’s”), and [Col. 1183D] Rigault so printed it. We have written *Domini nostri* (“our Lord”), both because shortly before it is written “in the name of our God Jesus Christ,” and because below it is expressly written [Col. 1184C] “in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.” Thus, in the address of Crescens of Cirta at the Council of Carthage, p. 331, the most ancient manuscript of Saint-Remi of Reims has *dilectissimi non* (“dearest not”) in place of *nostri* (“our”); and in the address of Munnulus of Girba in the same place it has “when the Lord says,” although “when our Lord says” should be read. Similarly, where our edition of Marius Mercator, p. 348, reads *nundum Verbum dicit* [a corrupt phrase, literally, “he says ‘the Word not yet’”], we observed on p. 470 that *non Deum* (“not God”) should be read.
>
> [Col. 1185D] **Arrogance.** Haughtiness, pride, as Rigault rightly observed. That word is used in this sense by Cyprian and by Pontius his deacon. In Marius Mercator, p. 75 of our edition, one reads: “Let Paul of Samosata remain in the arrogance of his teeth.”
>
> **In any rank of the clergy.** That is, in any order of those numbered among the clergy.
>
> **By them.** I thought this ought to be written, since previously the reading was “by others.”
>
> [Col. 1186D] **Kindled.** Rigault conjectured that “kept silent” should be read. The English editors substituted “approaching” for “kindled.” I think “attended to” should be adopted.]

## I

I observe that a question has been raised among the brethren as to what ought preferably to be observed in the case of those who, although baptized in heresy, were immersed in the name of our God Jesus Christ; who afterward departed from it, hastened as suppliants to the Church of God, and repented with their whole heart; and who, only now understanding the condemnation of their error, implored the Church for the aid of salvation. The question is whether, according to the most ancient custom and ecclesiastical tradition, after the baptism which they received outside the Church, yet in the name of Jesus Christ our Lord, it would suffice merely for the bishop to lay a hand upon them so that they might receive the Holy Spirit, and whether this laying on of a hand would provide them with the repeated and consummated sign of faith; [Col. 1184C] or whether a repeated baptism was also necessary for them, as though they would possess nothing unless they had obtained this as well from the beginning, just as if they had never been baptized in the name of Jesus Christ.

Accordingly, it was being asserted that certain writings and replies had been produced concerning this new question, in which each side strove with the utmost zeal to destroy the other’s position. In this kind of question, as it seems to me, no controversy or dispute whatever could have arisen if each one of us, content with the venerable authority of all the churches and with necessary humility, had not been eager to innovate, since he would have perceived no room at all for contradiction.

For [Col. 1185A] anything that is uncertain and ambiguous and has been made the subject of differing opinions among prudent and faithful men must certainly be condemned if it is judged contrary to the most solemn observance, ancient and memorable, of all the veteran saints and faithful. For in a matter long since settled and ordered, whatever is brought forward against the tranquility and peace of the churches will bring nothing except dissensions, hostilities, and schisms. No other fruit is found in it than this alone: that a single man, whoever he may be, is proclaimed among certain frivolous persons, with empty boasting, to possess great prudence and constancy; and, endowed with the arrogance of heretics—whose one consolation in perdition is that they may appear not to sin alone—he is celebrated among those most like and equal to himself as having corrected the errors and faults of all the churches. [Col. 1185B]

For the zeal and purpose of all heretics is to weave as many calumnies of this kind as possible against our most holy mother the Church, and to regard as the highest glory the discovery of anything that might be imputed to her as a charge, even lightly. Since no faithful person of sound mind should maintain such a position—least of all anyone at all established in any clerical rank, and much more so any bishop—it is monstrous that bishops themselves should devise such scandals. Contrary to the commandment of the law and of all the Scriptures, and with extreme irreverence, they do not fear to expose what they regard as the disgrace of Mother Church in this matter, thereby exposing themselves to disgrace and danger, although no disgrace attaches to the Church here except in their own error. [Col. 1185C]

Accordingly, persons of this kind offend still more gravely if it is clearly and forcefully shown that what they condemn as improperly done in the most ancient observance was rightly observed both by those who preceded us and by us, and is still rightly observed. Thus, even if we were to contend on both sides with equal arguments, nevertheless, because the innovation could not be maintained without dissension among the brethren and harm to the Church, a stain ought certainly not to be rashly inflicted upon Mother Church—contrary, as they say, to both divine and human law, that is, contrary to the good and equitable—and the disgrace of such audacity and impiety ought deservedly to be ascribed to those who attempted it.

But since it is not within our power that, according to the Apostle’s commandment, we should all say the same thing (1 Cor. 1:10) and that there should be no schisms among us, [Col. 1185D] we nevertheless strive, so far as we can, to demonstrate the position of this treatise and to persuade turbulent persons at least now to begin attending to their own affairs. We too shall gain very greatly if at last they are willing to acquiesce in this sound counsel. [Col. 1186A]

We shall therefore necessarily gather together into one place all the passages of Holy Scripture that pertain to this side of the question; and those which appear divergent or varied we shall, so far as possible, plainly join together. We shall examine, according to our modest ability, the usefulness and value of each, so that we may commend to all the brethren the Church’s most salutary and peaceful rule and custom as something to be attended to.

> [Note: [Col. 1186D]
>
> **II.—The most ancient baptism of Moses.** Previously the text was printed: “Moses, the most ancient.” That our emendation is certain is shown by a passage from Cyprian’s Epistle 73: “because they had already received the most ancient baptism of the Law and of Moses.”]

## II

As we undertake a discussion of the saving and new—that is, spiritual and evangelical—baptism, we encounter first of all the proclamation well known to everyone, publicly made and begun by John the Baptist. Departing to some extent from the Law—that is, from the most ancient baptism of Moses—and preparing the road for the new and true grace, [Col. 1186B] by the baptism of water and repentance which he administered for the time being, he gradually forestalled and engaged the ears of the Jews with the announcement of the spiritual baptism to come. He exhorted them, saying: “He who comes after me is mightier than I, whose sandal strap I am not worthy to untie. He will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire” (Matt. 3:11; Mark 1:7; Luke 3:16; John 1:27).

For this reason, the beginning of our discussion must also commence here. For the Lord, confirming this same declaration of John after his resurrection in the Acts of the Apostles, commanded them not to depart from Jerusalem, but “to await that promise of the Father which you heard from me: for John indeed baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit, not many days from now” [Col. 1186C] (Acts 1:4–5).

Likewise Peter recounted the same words of the Lord when giving an account of himself before the apostles:

“When I began to speak, the Holy Spirit fell upon them, just as upon us at the beginning; and I remembered the word of the Lord, as he said: ‘John indeed baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit.’ Therefore, if the Lord gave them an equal gift as he gave us who believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was I that I could hinder the Lord?” (Acts 11:15–17).

And again:

“Men and brethren, you know that in former days God chose among us that through my mouth the Gentiles should hear the word of the Gospel and believe; and God, who knows hearts, bore them witness, giving them the Holy Spirit just as he did to us” (Acts 15:7–8).

We must therefore consider the force and power of this declaration. For [Col. 1186D] the Lord says that those who would afterward be baptized because they would believe were to be baptized—not as by John in water unto repentance, but in the Holy Spirit.

Since surely none of us can doubt this proclamation, it is evident how human beings were baptized in [Col. 1187A] the Holy Spirit. For those who believed were, properly speaking, baptized in the Holy Spirit alone, because John drew a distinction and said that he himself baptized in water, but that one was coming who would baptize in the Holy Spirit. By the grace and power of God these things exist, with God secretly bestowing and working this as well; nevertheless, baptism also occurs in Spirit and water, and in addition there is the baptism of the Spirit in each person’s own blood, as the Holy Scriptures make clear to us. For every point we shall set forth, we shall adduce their manifest proofs.

> [Note: [Col. 1187D]
>
> **III.—Had descended.** Thus Rigault and Fell. But Baluze reads “had fallen.”
>
> **When it is found thus.** The Oxford editors, following Rigault, punctuate in this way. Baluze, however, reads: “only then bestowed the Holy Spirit upon them, when it is found thus.” But in Baluze’s reading the repetition of “thus” appears feeble.]

## III

Perhaps at this point you who introduce something new will immediately answer impatiently, as is your custom, that the Lord said in the Gospel: “Unless one is born again of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of heaven” [Col. 1187B] (John 3:3, 5).

From this it is plainly apparent that baptism benefits only the person in whom the Holy Spirit can also dwell. For the Holy Spirit descended upon the Lord himself when he was baptized; thus deed and word correspond equally, nor can this mystery be maintained in any other way.

None of us is found so utterly insane or obstinate as to dare contradict this in violation of right or truth—namely, provided that the circumstances are complete, that everything is conducted in precisely this way within the Church, and that it is perpetually observed by us according to the order of discipline. But if, in the same New Testament, those things which we find united in this matter are sometimes found in some fashion divided and separated, and therefore arranged as though they were individual things, let us see whether they may at times exist even [Col. 1187C] singly and in isolation, not as though incomplete, but as whole and perfect.

For the Holy Spirit is given to each believer through the laying on of the bishop’s hand, just as the apostles did among the Samaritans after Philip’s baptism, laying hands upon them and in this way imparting the Holy Spirit to them. To make this possible, they prayed for them, for the Spirit had not yet descended upon any of them; they had only been baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. Our Lord also, after the resurrection, breathed upon his apostles and said, “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John 20:22), and only then bestowed the Holy Spirit upon them.

> [Note: [Col. 1187D]
>
> **IV.—Baptized by the Lord.** Thus the editions of Rigault and Oxford. Baluze reads “had been baptized by the Lord.” I conjecture that *had been* is intrusive there.
>
> **Did not yet exist.** Perhaps the word *given* dropped out through a copyist’s error; [Col. 1188D] it appears necessarily to be supplied from the Vulgate translation. Yet this passage is cited in the same way below, chapter 14. See Baluze’s note there.
>
> **Since.** We follow Rigault and the Oxford editors; Baluze reads “or since.”
>

>
> **Not.** This is the reading both of Rigault and of Oxford. Baluze, however, reads “nor.”]

## IV

Since this is found to be so, what do you think, brother? If someone, not baptized by a bishop, were to die before receiving the Holy Spirit, even if a hand were laid upon him immediately, would you judge that he had received salvation or not? For even the apostles and disciples—who also baptized others and had themselves been baptized by the Lord—did not immediately receive the Holy Spirit, who did not yet exist because Jesus had not yet been glorified (John 7:39); rather, after his resurrection no small interval of time elapsed before this occurred. [Col. 1188A]

Likewise, when the Samaritans were baptized by Philip, an interval elapsed until the apostles, summoned from Jerusalem, came down to them in Samaria to lay hands upon them and impart the Holy Spirit to them through the laying on of hands. During that interval, one of them might have been overtaken by death without having obtained the Holy Spirit, and might have died deprived of the grace of the Holy Spirit.

Nor can it be doubted that this is customary and ordinarily happens even today: many depart from this world after baptism without the laying on of the bishop’s hand, yet are regarded as fully initiated believers. [Col. 1188B]

Thus the Ethiopian eunuch, while returning from Jerusalem and reading the prophet Isaiah in perplexity, believed, at the prompting of the Spirit, when he heard the truth from Philip the deacon, and was baptized (Acts 8). When he came up from the water, the Spirit of the Lord carried Philip away, and the eunuch saw him no more. He went on his way rejoicing, although—as you observe—a bishop’s hand had not been laid upon him so that he might receive the Holy Spirit.

If you admit this and believe it conducive to salvation, and do not oppose the opinion of all the faithful, you must confess that, correspondingly—and as this discussion proceeds more broadly—that other possibility also can be maintained more broadly: namely, that through the laying on of the bishop’s hand alone, because baptism in the name of Jesus Christ our Lord has preceded it, the Holy Spirit can also be given to another person who repents and believes. [Col. 1188C] For Holy Scripture foretold concerning those who would believe in Christ that they must be baptized in the Spirit. Thus these persons too may not appear to possess anything less than those who are fully initiated Christians, and there may be no need to inquire what kind of baptism it was that they received in the name of Jesus Christ.

Unless perhaps, in the preceding discussion concerning those who had been baptized only in the name of Christ Jesus, you maintain either that they can be saved without the Holy Spirit, or that the Holy Spirit has not ordinarily been bestowed through the laying on of the bishop’s hand alone, or even that it is not the bishop who ordinarily bestows [Col. 1188D] the Holy Spirit.

[Col. 1189A]

> [Note: [Col. 1189D]
>
> **In what manner.** I would prefer *quonam modo* (“in what manner”) to *quoniam modo* (“since only”).
>
> **Only half-complete.** The same learned man thinks that the text should read: “not merely half-complete, as you contend, but the mystery of faith is consummated.”
>
> **And thus, their hearts having shortly before been cleansed.** Thus Baluze. Rigault reads “and flooded,” omitting the intervening words; this is more pleasing. Oxford reads “and cleansed.”]

## V

If this is so, and if the occurrence of any of these circumstances cannot snatch salvation away from a believing person, you yourself also concede that, where necessity intervenes, the mystery of faith, even if half-complete and not consummated as you contend, cannot take salvation away from a believing and repentant person.

Or if you say that a person of this kind cannot be saved, we deprive all bishops of salvation. For you bind them to the most certain dangers by requiring them personally to assist all persons under their care who fall ill throughout the regions in which they are scattered here and there, since other persons of lower rank among the clergy cannot provide the same service to those in danger. Otherwise, the blood of those who appear to have departed from this world empty would necessarily be required at the bishops’ hands.

Moreover, as you are aware, the Holy Spirit is found to have been given by the Lord to believing persons [Col. 1189B] without the baptism of water, as is related in the Acts of the Apostles in this manner:

“While Peter was still speaking these words, the Holy Spirit fell upon all who heard the word; and all the faithful of the circumcision who had come with Peter were astonished that the gift of the Holy Spirit had been poured out even upon the Gentiles. For they heard them speaking in their own tongues and magnifying God. Then Peter answered: ‘Can anyone forbid water, so that these who have received the Holy Spirit just as we did should not be baptized?’ And he commanded them to be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ” (Acts 10:44–48).

Likewise the same Peter afterward instructed us most fully concerning those same Gentiles, saying: “And he made no distinction between us and them, their hearts having been cleansed by faith” (Acts 15:9).

Accordingly, [Col. 1189C] there will be no doubt that people can be baptized in the Holy Spirit without water, since—as you observe—these were baptized before they were baptized with water, thus fulfilling the proclamations both of John and of the Lord himself. For without the laying on of the apostles’ hands and without the laver, which they obtained afterward, they received the grace of the promise. And thus, when their hearts had shortly before been cleansed, God through their faith granted them the remission of sins at the same time. The subsequent baptism therefore supplied this alone: that they might also receive the invocation of the name of Jesus Christ, lest anything seem to be lacking from the completeness of the ministry and of faith.

> [Note: [Col. 1190D]
>
> **The gift poured out.** I readily agree with the same most learned man, who thinks that “poured out” should be restored in the masculine form.
>
> **Righteous.** Rigault reads “these.”
>
> **Then him.** The same Rigault emends this to “three times him.” But Baluze’s edition presents “him also.” Whether this is actually the reading of the manuscript codex he leaves entirely unstated.
>
> [Col. 1191D] **Somewhat rough.** Perhaps the author wrote “rough in some respect,” that is, “to some extent”; as in Tertullian, “Numidians in some respect.” But if someone prefers “somewhat rough,” that certainly can be borne, as in Virgil, “in face and shoulders like a god.” **RIGAULT.**]

## VI

The very disciples of our Lord obtained this same thing from the converse side of the present discussion. Although they had long since been baptized, finally, on the day of Pentecost, [Col. 1189D] the Holy Spirit came upon them, descending from heaven by God’s will, indeed, and not of his own accord. Poured out for this very purpose, he sat upon each one of them, although they, already righteous, had long since, as we have said, been baptized with the Lord’s baptism, [Col. 1190A] as had the apostles themselves.

Yet all of them are found to have deserted the Lord on the night when he was arrested. Peter himself, who had boasted that he would persevere in his faith and had most obstinately resisted the Lord’s own prediction, nevertheless finally denied him. In this way it was shown to us that whatever offenses they had contracted in any fashion during the intervening period were afterward undoubtedly forgiven in them through sincere faith by the baptism of the Holy Spirit.

Nor, I think, was it for any other reason that the apostles commanded those whom they addressed in the Holy Spirit to be baptized in the name of Christ Jesus, except that the power of Jesus’ name, invoked in baptism over any human being, could confer upon the one baptized no small privilege for attaining salvation. Thus Peter relates in [Col. 1190B] the Acts of the Apostles, saying: “For there is no other name under heaven given to human beings in which we must be saved” (Acts 4:12).

The apostle Paul likewise makes this clear, showing that God exalted Jesus our Lord and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven, on earth, and beneath the earth, and every tongue should confess that Jesus is Lord in the glory of the Father (Phil. 2:9–11).

And the person over whom the name of Jesus had been invoked when he was baptized, although he received baptism amid some error, would nevertheless not be prevented at some later time from coming to a right understanding, correcting his error, coming to the Church and to the bishop, and sincerely confessing our Jesus before human beings. Then, when the bishop’s hand was laid upon him, [Col. 1190C] he would also receive the Holy Spirit without losing that former invocation of Jesus’ name, which none of us is permitted to condemn.

If that invocation is bare and isolated while established amid error, it cannot suffice to provide salvation; otherwise, on this reasoning, we would believe that even pagans and heretics who misuse the name of Jesus can attain salvation without the true and complete reality. Yet it is extremely useful to believe that, once the error has been corrected, the truth of the faith acknowledged, and every stain of former conduct cut away, this invocation of Jesus’ name—rightly enacted by God’s mystery in persons of this kind—may obtain the place it otherwise would not have had, and ultimately may not obstruct a right faith or the furnishing of the complete sign, once the supplement of what was lacking has been added. It is also extremely useful to acquiesce, with good reason, in the authority of so many years, so many churches, and likewise of the apostles and bishops. [Col. 1190D]

For it is a very great injury and loss to our most holy mother the Church to rise up now for the first time, suddenly and without reason, against ancient decisions [Col. 1191A] after such a long succession of centuries.

Indeed, it was for no other reason that Peter—who had already been baptized, whom the Lord himself had questioned about what he believed concerning him, and who, because the truth was revealed to him by the heavenly Father, had confessed that our Lord was not only the Christ but also the Son of the living God (Matt. 16:16)—was afterward shown to have resisted that same Christ when he foretold his passion, and on that account was shown to be called Satan (ibid., v. 23), except that it was going to happen that certain persons, although wavering in their own opinion and at times faltering in faith and doctrine, would nevertheless be baptized in Jesus’ name. If, after some interval of time, they could correct this, they would not on that account fall away from salvation, but would at some time recover their senses and through repentance obtain an unimpaired hope of salvation. [Col. 1191B]

This would be especially so when they received the Holy Spirit with whom every human being must be baptized, even though they had manifested something of this kind. For we find in the Gospel not only that Peter underwent this, but also that all the disciples did, although they had already been baptized. The Lord afterward said to them: “You will all be scandalized because of me” (Mark 14:27). As we observe, all of them, after correcting their faith following the Lord’s resurrection, were baptized in the Holy Spirit.

Thus it is not unreasonable for us to believe that even today persons corrected from their former error can be baptized in the Holy Spirit, although, when they were baptized with water in the Lord’s name, their faith had been somewhat defective. For it makes a great difference whether someone has not been baptized at all in the name [Col. 1191C] of our Lord Jesus Christ, or whether he falters in some respect when baptized with the baptism of water, which is lesser, provided that afterward sincere faith in the truth is firmly established in the baptism of the Spirit, which is undoubtedly greater.

## VII

Nor should you think that the Lord’s words contradict this discussion: “Go, teach the Gentiles; immerse them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28:19).

For although this is true and right, must be observed in every way within the Church, and has ordinarily been observed, it must nevertheless be considered that the invocation of Jesus’ name ought not to appear ineffectual to us, because of the reverence and power belonging to that name. All works of power are ordinarily performed in that name, and sometimes certain works are performed even by outsiders.

Otherwise, what is the relevance of those words of Christ, [Col. 1191D] who said that he would deny and would not know those who would say to him on the day of judgment, “Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and in your name cast out demons, and in your name perform great works of power?”—to whom he would answer, even with an oath, “I never knew you; depart from me, you who work iniquity” (Mark 14:27)—unless it was being shown to us that even those who work iniquity can sometimes perform such things through the exceedingly great power of Jesus’ name?

Therefore, this invocation [Col. 1192A] of Jesus’ name ought to be understood as a certain beginning of the Lord’s mystery, common to us and to all others, which can afterward be completed by the remaining elements. Otherwise, such an invocation will be of no benefit when it has remained alone, because after the death of a person of this kind nothing at all can be added or supplied to him, nor can it benefit him in any respect on the day of judgment, when our Lord begins to reproach him with those words recalled above.

Nevertheless, no one can so harshly and cruelly prevent all such persons today from seeking help for themselves through the means we have demonstrated above.

## VIII

But in reply, as is your custom, you will object that when the disciples were baptized they were baptized completely and correctly, and not as these heretics are baptized. You must derive this claim from the character both of the disciples themselves and of the one who baptized [Col. 1192B] them.

We therefore answer this proposition of yours not as accusers of the Lord’s disciples, but because we are compelled to do so; for we must investigate rationally where, when, and how salvation was furnished to each one of us.

It appeared, not without reason, that the disciples believed on many grounds that our Lord had been born and that he was the Christ: because he was of the tribe of Judah and the lineage of David, and because he had been born in the city of Bethlehem; because angels announced to shepherds at that very moment that a Savior had been born to them; because his star, seen in the east, had been most diligently sought out by the Magi, and he had been worshiped and honored with illustrious gifts and distinguished offerings; because, while still a very young boy, he sat in the temple [Col. 1192C] among the teachers of the Law and disputed wisely, to the astonishment of everyone; because, when he was baptized, as had happened to no one else, he was glorified when the heavens opened, the Holy Spirit descended and remained upon him, and his Father and John the Baptist also bore witness to him; because he understood the hearts and thoughts of all beyond ordinary human capacity; because he treated and healed infirmities, defects, and illnesses with the greatest power; because he granted the forgiveness of sins with manifest proof; because he expelled demons by command; because he cleansed lepers by a word; because, by turning water into wine, he enlarged a wedding feast with marvelous joy; because he restored or granted sight to the blind; because he asserted the teaching of the Father with complete confidence; because [Col. 1192D] in a deserted place he satisfied five thousand people with five loaves; because the remnants and fragments filled more than twelve baskets; because in his mercy he raised the dead everywhere; because he commanded the winds and the sea to be still; because he walked on the sea with his feet; and because he accomplished absolutely every work of power.

> [Note: [Col. 1193D]
>
> **Should be rebuked.** I think *corrumperetur* (“should be corrupted”) ought to be read in place of *corriperetur* (“should be rebuked”). **GALLANDI.**
>
> **Escape away.** This expression is certainly more fitting for God than “steal away.” **RIGAULT.**
>
> **Cursing.** Tertullian used the noun *devotamenta* (“curses”). **RIGAULT.**]

IX. From these deeds, and from many others of this kind pertaining to his glory, it seemed to follow that, just as the Jews hold concerning the Christ [Col. 1193A]—though they do not believe it concerning our Lord Jesus Christ—they too should suppose that one so great and of such a character would endure forever without undergoing death, and would possess in perpetuity the kingdom of Israel and of the whole world, a kingdom that would not be corrupted. Hence the Jews even dared to seize him and anoint him as king; this, indeed, he was obliged to escape. His disciples therefore thought that he would grant them eternal life in no other way than by first continuing this temporal life in himself together with the eternal life. Finally, while they were staying in Galilee, Jesus said to them: “The Son of Man is beginning to be delivered into the hands of men, and they will kill him, and after three days he will rise again” (Mark 9:30). And they were exceedingly grieved because, as [Col. 1193B] we have said, they had previously conceived something far different in their minds and thoughts.

Finally, this was also the Jews’ word of contradiction against him: while he himself was teaching them and announcing what was to come, they said: “We have heard from the Law that the Christ remains forever; and how do you say that the Son of Man must be lifted up?” (John 12:34). The disciples likewise held this same presumption concerning Christ, with Peter himself, the leader and chief of the Apostles, breaking out into an expression of his unbelief. For when he had been asked by the Lord, together with the others, what he thought about him—that is, whom he believed him to be—and had first confessed the truth, saying that he was the Christ, the Son of the living God (Matt. 16:16 ff.); and when he had therefore been pronounced blessed by him, because he had attained this insight [Col. 1193C] not carnally but through revelation from the heavenly Father—nevertheless, when Jesus began to show his disciples that he had to go to Jerusalem, suffer many things at the hands of the elders, priests, and scribes, be killed, and rise again on the third day, that same true confessor of Christ, only a few days later, took him aside and began to rebuke him, saying: “May God be gracious to you; this shall not happen to you” (ibid. 22–23). Consequently, he deserved to hear from the Lord: “Get behind me, Satan; you are a stumbling block to me,” because he did not understand the things of God, but those of men.

This rebuke of Peter became still more conspicuously justified when the Lord was arrested, for, terrified by a little servant-girl, he said: “I do not know what you are saying, nor do I know you” (Matt. 26:70 ff.). Again he said the same [Col. 1193D] with an oath, and a third time, invoking a curse and swearing, he asserted that he did not know the man; [Col. 1194A] and he denied him not once but repeatedly. Because this intention of his was to persist until the Lord’s Passion, it was openly disclosed by the Lord long beforehand, so that we too might not be unaware of it.

Finally, after the Lord’s resurrection, one of his disciples, Cleopas, grieving in accordance with the error shared by all his fellow disciples, reported what had happened to the Lord himself as though to a stranger. He spoke as follows concerning Jesus of Nazareth, “who was a prophet mighty in deeds and words before God and all the people: how our priests and rulers handed him over to be condemned to death and fastened him to a cross. But we had hoped that he was the one who would redeem Israel” (Luke 24). In keeping with this, all the disciples also judged the assertions of the women [Col. 1194B] who had seen the Lord after his resurrection to be delirious ravings; and some of them, even after seeing him, did not believe but doubted. Those who were not present at that time did not believe at all until they were afterward reproached and rebuked by the Lord himself in every way. For his death had so offended them that they thought he had not risen again—the very one whom they had believed ought not to die—because, contrary to their expectation, he had once died. Accordingly, as far as the disciples themselves are concerned, they are found not to have possessed an entire and perfect faith, in the ways we have related; and, what is far more serious, as is written in the Gospel according to John, they were even baptizing others (John 3:22).

>

X. Furthermore, what will you say about those who are frequently [Col. 1194C] baptized by bishops of the worst conduct, who nevertheless are at last, when God wills, convicted of their crimes and deprived either of the Lord himself or even entirely of communion? Or what will you determine concerning those who have been baptized by bishops holding perverse opinions or possessing too little knowledge? For in transmitting the sacrament they may not have spoken clearly and completely, or may even have spoken otherwise than they ought; certainly either they asked something improperly, or, when questioning, heard from the respondents an answer that should by no means have been either asked or given in that form. Yet this does not seriously injure our orthodox faith; these simpler men too transmit the mystery of faith, though not as elegantly and systematically as you do.

In your extraordinary diligence, you will surely say that these persons too must be baptized again, especially since something is lacking in them, or obstructs them, so that they cannot [Col. 1194D] receive inviolate that incorruptible divine mystery of faith. But, best of men, let us restore [Col. 1195A] and permit the heavenly powers to exercise their own strength, and let us concede to the graciousness of the divine majesty its proper operations; and, understanding how great an advantage lies in this, let us willingly acquiesce in it.

And therefore, since our salvation is established in the baptism of the Spirit, which is generally joined with the baptism of water, if baptism is administered by us, let it be conferred fully and solemnly, in accordance with everything that is written, and let it be transmitted without the separation of any element whatsoever. Or, if it has been administered under necessity by a member of the lower clergy, let us await the outcome, so that it may either be completed by us or left to be completed by the Lord. But if it has been administered by outsiders, let it be corrected insofar as the nature of the matter permits and admits, because the Holy Spirit is not outside the Church, and because a sound faith cannot exist not only among [Col. 1195B] heretics but even among those established in schism.

Therefore, those who repent and are corrected through the teaching of truth and through their own faith—which has subsequently been amended, their hearts having been purified—should be assisted only by spiritual baptism, that is, by the bishop’s imposition of the hand and the imparting of the Holy Spirit. With good reason, the complete sign of faith has customarily been transmitted in the Church in this way and according to this principle, lest the invocation of the name of Jesus, which cannot be abolished, appear to have been treated with contempt by us. That certainly must not happen, although an invocation of this kind, if none of the things we have mentioned follows it, ceases and remains devoid of saving efficacy.

For since the Apostle says that there is one baptism (Eph. 4:5), the invocation of the name of Jesus must necessarily remain, because what has once been invoked cannot be taken away by any human being. If, contrary to the decree of the Apostles, we dare to repeat it out of an excessive zeal to bestow—or rather to superadd—baptism, then, if the person returning to the Church refuses to be baptized again, the result will be that we deprive of spiritual baptism the person whom we think ought not to be deprived of the baptism of water. [Col. 1195C]

> **Note: [Col. 1196D]**
>
> **XI.—“Many or perverse.”** The reading should be restored to “mutilated.” **Galland.**

XI. What, moreover, will you decide in the case of a hearer of the word who happens to be arrested in the name of Christ, immediately confesses, and is punished before he is permitted to be baptized with water? Will you pronounce that he has perished because he was not baptized with water, or will you judge that something external advocates for his salvation, although he was not baptized with water?

If you judge that he has perished, you will be confronted by the Lord’s declaration: “Whoever confesses me before men, I too will confess him before my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 10:32). For it makes no difference whether the one who confesses the Lord is a hearer of the word or one of the faithful, provided that he confesses the very Christ who must be confessed; because the Lord, by confessing in return his own confessor before the Father, adorns him with the honor of martyrdom, as he promised.

This certainly must not be understood too broadly, as though it could be extended without limit. For some heretic who nevertheless denies Christ himself may confess [Col. 1196A] Christ’s name; because he believes in another Christ, his confession of Christ cannot benefit him in the least. Indeed, the Lord said that it was necessary for us to bring him himself into confession before men, which cannot be done without him and without his venerable name.

Therefore, both elements must remain complete, sincere, undefiled, and inviolate in the person confessing, without any distinction being made concerning the confessor himself—whether he is righteous or a sinner, a perfect Christian or one who is still imperfect, but who, at the utmost peril to himself, did not fear to confess the Lord. Nor is this contrary to the preceding discussion: there, sufficient time remains for correcting things that are mutilated or perverse; and certain privileges have been granted solely to the name of our Lord, whereas martyrdom can be consummated only in and through the Lord himself. Accordingly, no one can confess Christ without his name, nor can the name of Christ, without Christ himself, protect anyone in confession. [Col. 1196B]

> **Note: [Col. 1197D]**
>
> **XII.—“Those against whom Christ.”** The English scholars advised that the reading should be: “those who perhaps refused to believe because of false Christs.” **Galland.**

XII. Accordingly, this whole discussion must be carefully distinguished so that it may become clearer. For the invocation of the name of Jesus can protect a person only if it is afterward duly completed, because the Prophets and Apostles preached in this manner. James says in the Acts of the Apostles:

> “Men and brethren, listen: Simon has related how God first visited the Gentiles to take from them a people for his name; and with this the words of the prophets agree, as it is written: ‘After [Col. 1196C] these things I shall return, and I shall rebuild that tabernacle of David which has fallen; and I shall rebuild what has been demolished in it, and shall raise it up again, so that the rest of humankind may seek God, and all the Gentiles upon whom my name has been invoked—says the Lord who does these things’” (Acts 15:13–17).

Accordingly, both the rest of humankind—that is, some of the Jews—and all the Gentiles upon whom the Lord’s name has been invoked can, and must, seek the Lord. For the very invocation of his name gives them an opportunity, or even imposes upon them the necessity, of seeking the Lord. With such persons the holy Scriptures command us to discuss the truth—whether from all the Scriptures or only some of them—with greater confidence than with Gentiles upon whom the name of the Lord Jesus, the Son of the living God, has not been invoked; just as it has not been invoked upon [Col. 1196D] the Jews, who accept only the ancient Scriptures. Therefore, people of both these kinds—that is, Jews and Gentiles—when they believe fully as they ought, are baptized in the same manner.

Heretics, however, who have already been baptized with water in the name of Jesus Christ, must be baptized only in the Holy Spirit. And death is rightly despised in Jesus—the only name given under heaven in which we must be saved. Yet if they persevere in this condition, they cannot be saved, because after the invocation of his name upon [Col. 1197A] them they did not seek the Lord; just like those who—[corrupt text: “against whom Christ”]—perhaps refused to believe. Concerning them the Lord says: “Beware lest anyone lead you into error. For many will come in my name, saying: ‘I am the Christ,’ and they will lead many into error” (Matt. 24:4–5, 11). And again he says: “Then if anyone says to you, ‘Look, here is the Christ,’ or ‘There he is,’ do not believe it. For false Christs and false prophets will arise, and they will give great signs and wonders, so that, if possible, even the elect may be led astray” (ibid. 23–24).

Those persons will undoubtedly perform such mighty works at that time under Christ’s name. In that name some even now appear to perform certain mighty works and to prophesy falsely. But it is certain that, because they themselves do not belong to Christ, they consequently have no part in Christ. Likewise, if anyone falls away from Christ while clinging solely to his name, he receives little assistance—indeed, he is burdened still more by that name—although he may previously have been most faithful or righteous, honored with some clerical office, or endowed with the dignity of confession. [Col. 1197B]

For all such persons, by denying the true Christ and introducing or following another—although there is no other Christ whatsoever—leave themselves no hope or salvation. They are no different from those who have denied Christ before men and who must necessarily be denied by Christ, without any account being taken of their previous manner of life, understanding, or dignity. For they themselves dared to renounce Christ, that is, their own salvation, and are condemned by the following declaration, because the Lord has stated most plainly: “Whoever denies me before men, I too will deny him before my Father who is in heaven” [Col. 1197C] (Matt. 10:33).

Thus the word “whoever,” also in the declaration concerning confession, shows us most fully that no condition belonging to the confessor can stand in his way. This holds whether the one who denies was previously a heretic, or a hearer, or someone beginning to hear who has not yet been baptized; or whether he was converted from heresy to the true faith, or departed from the Church and afterward returned; and, upon returning, before the bishop’s hand could be imposed upon him, was arrested and compelled to confess Christ before men. In the same way, when someone denies Christ, no previous dignity of his own can protect him unto salvation.

> **Note: [Col. 1197D]**
>
> **XIII.—“Whatever.”** Perhaps one should read: “Wherever.” **Galland.**
>
> **“Than that it itself.”** Rigaltius thought this passage should be emended to read: “to accomplish nothing except that it may appear and be established [Col. 1198D] that he is a heretic.” I would conjecture that one should read: “because by the very fact it appears and is established.” **Galland.**

XIII. For whatever is found to be a person’s final state in a case of this kind, each of us must necessarily be judged in that state, all the things he did previously having been abolished and erased. [Col. 1197D] And therefore, since in martyrdom so great a change of circumstances can occur in a moment of time that everything may be altered in a very brief event, no one who has lost the opportunity for glorious salvation should flatter himself if he has excluded himself from it through his own fault. So too did Lot’s wife: similarly caught in a moment of crisis, she merely looked back behind her contrary to the angels’ command, and became a mound of salt. [Col. 1198A]

For the same reason, the heretic who is slain while confessing Christ’s name cannot afterward correct whatever false opinion he held concerning God or Christ, since by believing in another God or another Christ he deceived himself. He was not a confessor of Christ, but of Christ’s isolated name. The Apostle accordingly says: “Even if I hand over my body to be burned by fire, but do not have love, I gain nothing” (1 Cor. 13:3). For by this deed a person gains nothing if he does not have love for that God and Christ who is proclaimed in this manner through the Law and the Prophets and in the Gospel:

> “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind; and you shall love your neighbor as yourself. For on these two commandments hang the whole Law [Col. 1198B] and the Prophets” (Deut. 6:5; Matt. 22:37–40).

So too John the Evangelist says: “Everyone who loves is born of God and knows God, because God is love” (1 John 4:7–8). Likewise God says: “For God so loved the world that he gave his only Son, so that everyone who believed in him should not perish but have eternal life” (John 3:16).

Thus it would be plainly apparent that the person who does not possess in himself this love—by which God loves us and is loved by us—gains nothing through an empty confession and suffering, except that it appears and is established that he is a heretic who believes in another god or accepts a Christ other than the one plainly proclaimed by the Scriptures of the New and Old Testaments, which without obscurity [Col. 1198C] announce the almighty Father, creator of all things, and his Son.

For what happens to them will be like what happens to someone who expects salvation from another God: then at last, contrary to their expectation, they will be condemned to eternal punishment by Christ, the Son of God the almighty Father and creator, whom they blasphemed, when God begins to judge the hidden things of human beings according to the Gospel through Christ Jesus—because they did not believe in him, although they were washed in his name.

> **Note: [Col. 1198D]**
>
> **XIV.—“Our God.”** Previously the reading was “our God” in the accusative. The sense, however, requires the reading in the form in which we have emended it. **Galland.**
>
> **[Col. 1199D] “If they have any reprieve.”** That is, if the necessity of the threatening danger grants some relaxation and allows some time—what Cyprian likes to call permission and delay to remain in the world a little longer. **Rigaltius.**
>
> **“But the Spirit did not yet exist.”** In the Vulgate edition of John’s Gospel the reading is “the Spirit had not yet been given.” But learned men have already observed that this last word does not occur in the Greek and must be understood implicitly, although some consider it unnecessary. **Galland.**

XIV. Indeed, every baptism of the heretics can be corrected after some intervening period of time, if a person survives and corrects his faith. Thus our God spoke to his disciples in the Gospel according to Luke, saying: “I have another baptism with which to be baptized” (Luke 12:50). Likewise, according to Mark, he had said in the same manner to the sons of Zebedee: [Col. 1198D] “Can you drink the cup that I drink, or be baptized with the baptism with which I am baptized?” (Mark 10:38). For he knew that people must be baptized not only with water but also with their own blood, so that those baptized with this baptism alone can attain the complete faith and the sincere grace of the washing, and can be baptized in both [Col. 1199A] ways, yet equally attain one baptism of salvation and honor, alike and on equal terms.

For when the Lord said, “I have another baptism with which to be baptized,” he did not mean “a second baptism” in this passage, as though there were two baptisms; rather, he showed that a baptism of another kind, contributing to the same salvation, has also been given to us. Both kinds had first to be inaugurated and sanctified by our Lord himself, so that either one or both kinds might provide us with this single, twofold, saving, and honorable baptism. In this way certain paths of the one baptism were opened to us, so that at times one of them might be absent without harm. Thus the baptism of water is harmlessly absent in martyrs who are hearers of the word; yet we are certain that, [Col. 1199B] if they receive any reprieve, they too customarily are baptized with water. Likewise, for those who have been made legitimate members of the faithful, the baptism of their own blood is harmlessly absent, because, having been baptized in Christ’s name, they have been redeemed by the Lord’s most precious blood.

For these two streams of the Lord’s baptism proceed from one and the same source, so that everyone who thirsts may come and drink, as Scripture says: “Streams of living water shall flow from his belly” (John 7:38). These streams first appeared in the Lord’s Passion, when blood and water flowed from his side, pierced by a soldier’s lance, so that the one, unique side emitted two streams of different kinds. Thus everyone who believes and drinks from both streams is filled with the Holy Spirit.

For in speaking of these streams, [Col. 1199C] the Lord showed that he was signifying the Holy Spirit, whom those who were going to believe in him would receive. “But the Spirit did not yet exist, because Jesus had not yet been glorified” (ibid. 39). Therefore, in explaining how the baptism which the Apostle proclaims to be one can be generated, it is plainly on this principle: there are different kinds of one and the same baptism, flowing from one wound as water and blood. Since there are in that place the two baptisms of water about which we have spoken—that is, kinds of one and the same baptism—the baptism of each person must be one in kind, as we have explained more fully.

> **Note: [Col. 1199D]**
>
> **XV.—“The Spirit is truth.”** Thus the Greek text: *τὸ πνεῦμά ἐστιν ἡ ἀλήθεια* (“the Spirit is the truth”). St. Ambrose presents the same reading in book III of *On the Holy Spirit*, chapter 10, §67. But almost all the other Latin Fathers agree [Col. 1200D] with the Vulgate, which reads: “Christ is the truth.” R. P. de Rubeis, a most distinguished man, examines the entire passage of this anonymous author—who appears to have read the eighth Johannine clause joined to the sixth in his copy—in his *Dissertation on the Three Witnesses in Heaven*, p. 76. The most learned Souciet is found to have treated this argument more diligently than anyone else against Simon, *Remarks on the Critique of the Library of Ecclesiastical Authors*, vol. II, pp. 575, 828. **Galland.**
>
> **“The Spirit customarily.”** I agree with the learned man whom I praised above, and have followed his advice in emending and supplying this passage. The emendation is certain. **Galland.**

XV. Since we appear to have divided all spiritual baptism into three parts, let us also proceed to prove [Col. 1199D] the proposition set forth, lest we appear to have done this rashly and according to our own [Col. 1200A] judgment. For John, teaching us concerning our Lord, says in his epistle:

> “This is he who came through water and blood, Jesus Christ—not in water only, but in water and blood. And it is the Spirit who bears witness, because the Spirit is truth; because three bear witness: the Spirit, the water, and the blood. And these three are one” (1 John 5:6–8).

From these words we may gather that water is accustomed to provide the Spirit, that a person’s own blood is accustomed to provide the Spirit, and that the Spirit himself is likewise accustomed to provide the Spirit. For just as water and blood are poured out, so too the Spirit was poured out by the Lord upon all who believed. Human beings can therefore be baptized by water and likewise by their own blood, and then by the Holy Spirit. [Col. 1200B]

For Peter says:

> “But this is what was spoken through the Prophet: ‘In the last days, says the Lord, I shall pour out my Spirit upon all flesh, and their sons and their daughters shall prophesy, and the young shall see visions, and the old shall dream dreams. Indeed, upon male and female servants I shall pour out some of my Spirit’” (Acts 2:17–18).

In the Old Testament we find that this Spirit was not given everywhere or poured out generally, but was shared with others; or else that he spontaneously rushed upon certain people, clothed them, or rested upon them. Thus we observe that the Lord said to Moses concerning the seventy elders: “I shall take some of the Spirit who is upon you and place it upon them” (Num. 11:17). Therefore, in accordance with his promise, God took some of the Spirit who had been upon one person, Moses, and placed it upon [Col. 1200C] them, and they prophesied in the camp. Moses, as a spiritual man, rejoiced that this had happened, although Joshua the son of Nun urged the unwilling Moses to intervene in the matter; and for that reason Moses was not disturbed.

Moreover, in the book of Judges and likewise in the books of Kingdoms, we observe that the Spirit of the Lord either rested upon many persons or rushed upon them—for example Othniel, Gideon, Jephthah, Samson, Saul, David, and many others. This is so thoroughly the case that our Lord most plainly taught us that the Holy Spirit possesses liberty and power to approach spontaneously, saying: “The Spirit blows where he wills, and you hear his voice, but do not know where he comes from or where he goes” (John 3:8).

Thus this same Spirit is sometimes found to rest even upon those unworthy of him, [Col. 1200D] certainly not idly or without reason, but for the sake of some necessary [Col. 1201A] operation. So it was with Saul, upon whom the Spirit of God came, and he prophesied. This also occurred at a later time, after the Spirit of the Lord had withdrawn from him and an evil spirit from the Lord was tormenting him, when he himself finally came for the purpose of killing David, after the messengers whom he had repeatedly sent ahead. They consequently entered the company of prophets and prophesied, so that they could not or would not carry out what they had been commanded to do. We believe that, by God’s will, the Spirit who rested upon them all brought this about in a marvelous manner.

This Spirit also filled John the Baptist while he was still in his mother’s womb, and rested upon those who were with the centurion Cornelius before they were baptized with water. Thus, while the Holy [Col. 1201B] Spirit remains joined to human baptism, he either precedes or follows it; or, when the baptism of water is absent, he rests upon those who believe. He gives us the counsel that we should either preserve baptism in its complete and proper form or, if baptism has happened to have been given by anyone in the name of Jesus Christ, complete it—while preserving the most holy invocation of Jesus Christ’s name, as we have explained most fully, and also preserving the custom and authority of so long a period and so many men, which must be venerable to us.

XVI. Since the first part of this disputation appears to have been explained, we must also address its next part on account of the heretics. For it is exceedingly necessary not to pass over a subject that has once come into our hands, lest some heretic dare, by his cunning, [Col. 1201C] to assail the simpler among the brethren.

For because John said that we must be baptized in the Holy Spirit and fire (Matt. 3:11; Luke 3:16), certain desperate persons, on account of his addition “and fire,” have dared to extend their wickedness to every extreme. These exceedingly crafty people consequently seek to corrupt and violate the baptism of holiness in such a way as even to empty it of effect. Their origin extends back to Simon Magus, whose manifold perversity they practice through various errors. To this Simon Peter said in the Acts of the Apostles: “May your money perish with you, because you thought that the grace of God could be possessed through money. You have neither part nor lot in this word, for your heart is not right before God” (Acts 8:20–21).

They do all these things because they desire to deceive those who are simpler or more curious. Some of them attempt [Col. 1201D] to claim that they alone administer an entire and perfect baptism, unlike us, who administer a mutilated and curtailed one. They are said to confer it in such a manner that, as soon as people descend into the water, fire immediately appears above the water. [Col. 1202A]

If this can be accomplished by some trick—as many tricks of this kind are affirmed to belong to Anaxilaus—or if it is some natural phenomenon, however it may occur; or if those persons only think that they see it; or if an evil work and magical poison can produce fire in water—nevertheless, they proclaim such a fraud and stratagem to be perfect baptism. If faithful people have been compelled to receive it, there can certainly be no doubt that they have lost what they formerly possessed. It is just as when a soldier who has sworn the military oath abandons his own camp and wishes to swear a wholly different oath in the utterly opposed camp of the enemy: it is established that in this way he has been discharged from his former oath.

> **Note: [Col. 1201D]**
>
> **XVII.—*THE PREACHING OF PAUL*.** So reads an ancient manuscript of Reims, according to Rigaltius, who nevertheless restored the name of Peter; and Baluzius retained Rigaltius’s reading in the text, although he expresses a different judgment in his notes. The Oxford editors likewise preferred the manuscript reading, and rightly so. For the anonymous author did not err, as Rigaltius and Baluzius thought, in praising the *Preaching of Paul*. From Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata*, book VI, p. 639, and Lactantius, *Divine Institutes*, book IV, [Col. 1202D] chapter 21, we learn that the *Preaching of Peter and Paul* was one and the same work, circulated sometimes under the name of one, sometimes of the other, and sometimes under both names. The words of Lactantius deserve to be quoted: “God the Teacher,” he says, “when departing, disclosed to them everything that was to come, which Peter and Paul preached at Rome; and that *PREACHING* was committed to writing and endured as a memorial.” These words are certainly said to be most consonant with those that our anonymous author immediately adds here. **Galland.**

XVII. Likewise, if a person of this kind returns to you again, you will certainly hesitate as to whether he possesses baptism or not; [Col. 1202B] and yet you will have to assist this penitent too by whatever means you can.

Among the other authors of this adulterous—or rather murderous—baptism is a certain book fabricated by those same heretics because of this very error, entitled *THE PREACHING OF PAUL*. In that book, contrary to all the Scriptures, you will find Christ, who alone committed no sin whatsoever, confessing a sin of his own and being compelled by his mother Mary, almost against his will, to receive John’s baptism. Likewise, when he is baptized, fire is said to have been seen above the water, although this is written in no Gospel. And after so long a time Peter and Paul—following their conference concerning the Gospel in Jerusalem, their mutual deliberation and dispute, and their arrangement of what was to be done—are ultimately represented as though they first became acquainted with one another in Rome. [Col. 1202C] You will also find certain other absurd and shameful fabrications of this kind: all these things are heaped together in that book.

Those who are not ignorant of the nature of the Holy Spirit understand that what was said concerning fire was said concerning the Spirit himself. For in the Acts of the Apostles, in accordance with this same promise of our Lord (Acts 2), when the Holy Spirit descended upon the disciples on the day of Pentecost so that they might be baptized in him, tongues as of fire were seen resting upon each of them. Thus it was established that they had been baptized in the Holy Spirit and fire—that is, in that Spirit who was either fire or like fire. Such was the fire that burned in the bush without consuming it, and such is the fire that constitutes the spirits of the angels, as Scripture says: “He makes his angels spirits and his ministers [Col. 1202D] a burning fire” (Ps. 103:4).

When you have become like, associated with, or a participant in this fire, you will be able to fear no fire—not even that which, going before the Lord on the day of judgment, will set the entire world [Col. 1203A] ablaze (Ps. 96:3), apart from those who have been baptized in the Holy Spirit and fire.

XVIII. For human beings today the Spirit indeed remains invisible, as the Lord says: “The Spirit blows where he wills, and you do not know where he comes from or where he goes” (John 3:8). But at the beginning of the mystery of faith and of spiritual baptism, this same Spirit was visibly seen both resting upon the disciples like fire and, when the heavens were opened, descending upon the Lord in the likeness of a dove.

For many things—indeed, almost all things—that were to be, but that would nevertheless now be invisible, were then shown to human eyes and unbelief, whether in part, occasionally, or in a figure, in order to strengthen and confirm our faith.

Nor shall I omit what the Gospel [Col. 1203B] rightly proclaims. For our Lord says to the paralytic: “Take heart, son; your sins are forgiven you” (Matt. 9:2), in order to show that hearts are purified by faith so that forgiveness of sins may be obtained. That woman who was a sinner in the city also obtained this forgiveness of sins; the Lord said to her: “Your sins are forgiven you” (Luke 7:48, 50). And when those reclining at table with him began to say among themselves, “Who is this who forgives sins?”—something that the scribes and Pharisees had muttered still more bitterly in the case of the paralytic—the Lord [Col. 1204A] said to the woman: “Your faith has saved you; go in peace.”

From all these things it is shown that hearts are cleansed by faith and souls are washed by the Spirit; bodies, moreover, are washed through water, while through blood one reaches the rewards of salvation more swiftly, by a shortened route.

> **Note: [Col. 1203B]**
>
> **XIX.—“To the rewards of salvation, I think.”** We follow the punctuation of Rigaltius and the Oxford editors. Baluzius, however, punctuates: “one reaches more swiftly, by a shortened route, the rewards of salvation, I think,” etc. Less correctly. **Galland.**
] XIX. I think we have fully expounded the preaching of John the Baptist, from which we began our discourse, who said to the Jews: “I indeed baptize you with water unto repentance. But he who comes after me is mightier than I, whose sandal-strap I am not worthy to loose. He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire” (Luke 3:16). I also judge that we have set forth not inappropriately the teaching of the apostle John, who says that three bear witness—the spirit, the water, and the blood—and these [Col. 1204B] three are one (1 John 5:8). Unless I am mistaken, we have also explained what our Lord said: “John indeed baptized with water, but you shall be baptized with the Holy Spirit” (Acts 1:5). Moreover, I believe that we have given no weak account of the reason for this custom. Let us nevertheless defend it, even though we do so in the final place, lest anyone suppose that we are stirring up the present controversy on a single point. Yet this custom, even by itself, ought to hold the foremost place among those who fear God and are humble.

## Concerning the Anonymous Author of the Treatise against Novatian

[Col. 1203]

## Prolegomena

[Col. 1203C] It is established that the author of the book addressed to Novatian was a contemporary of Cyprian, and there can be no doubt that he wrote during the peaceful beginnings of Valerian’s reign, which were favorable to the Church. For he counts only one persecution after the one that raged under Decius, and says that those who fell in the first were victorious in the second [Note: [Col. 1203C] Anonymous, *Treatise to Novatian*, chap. 6, in Galland, vol. III, *Bibliotheca veterum Patrum*, p. 372; and among the works of Cyprian, p. 17 of the Bremen edition and p. 775 of the Venice edition.]. He also seems to have been an African, both because he plays in this way upon the name of Felicissimus [Note: [Col. 1203C] The same, ibid., chap. 2, in Galland, p. 371; and in Cyprian, p. 16 of the Bremen edition and p. 772 of the Venice edition.]: “What answer can those utterly perverse Novatians make to this—or those few who are now most unhappy [*infelicissimi*]?”; and because, in declaring that the Church alone baptizes according to the heavenly order [Note: [Col. 1203C] The same, ibid., chap. 3, p. 372 in Galland; among the works of Cyprian, p. 17 of the Bremen edition and p. 773 of the Venice edition.], he plainly rejects the baptism of heretics. Mere dissimilarity of style [Col. 1204C] deterred Tillemont [Note: [Col. 1204C] Tillemont, *Mémoires*, vol. IV, pp. 133 and 622, note 37, on St. Cyprian; and the Brussels edition, 1732, p. 56 and p. 22 in the notes.] from attributing this little work to Cyprian.

Yet another argument besides this one seems capable of being advanced. For at the very beginning the author of this book declares that, “while he was reflecting and his mind was seething beyond endurance over what he ought to do concerning the pitiable brethren who, wounded not by their own will but by an assault of the raging devil, had continued even until now—that is, through a long succession of time—to suffer punishment, another enemy had arisen against him, the heretic Novatian, an adversary of paternal compassion itself.” By these words he indicates that he is a bishop and, while very humanely taking thought for the lapsed who had long been doing penance, is distressed that the heretic Novatian should oppose his clemency. Hence, also, further below [Note: [Col. 1204C] Anonymous, loc. cit., chap. 6, p. 372 in Galland, [Col. 1205C] and among the works of Cyprian, p. 17 of the Bremen edition and p. 775 of the Venice edition.], after speaking of those who were wounded [Col. 1205A] in the first battle—that is, in the Decian persecution—but afterward were victorious—that is, in the second combat—he adds that their equals, namely those still remaining under the same guilt of their lapse, were judged by the Novatians unworthy even to be admitted to penance. The author of this work had therefore not yet granted peace to those who had lapsed under Decius. For he is not speaking about others: he calls them the equals of those who, defeated in the first combat, had been victorious in the second; he says that, after a long succession of time, they continued to suffer punishment, and that they still remained under the same guilt of the lapse which others had expiated by martyrdom. Cyprian, however, when the persecution of Gallus and Volusian was imminent, had gathered into the Lord’s flock those lapsed Christians who had done penance from the first day of their lapse, and had given them the blood of Christ, so as to arm them to shed their own blood for Christ [Col. 1205B] [Note: [Col. 1205C] Compare what we discuss concerning the author of this treatise in vol. XI of the *Historia Theologica Critica*, pp. 360–363.]. Thus far the most learned Prudentius Maran [Note: [Col. 1205C] Maran, *Life of St. Cyprian*, chap. 35, p. 127, Paris edition, 1726; Venice edition, 1758, p. 118 ff.], of the Congregation of Saint-Maur.

The Most Reverend Remi Ceillier observes [Note: [Col. 1205C] Ceillier, *Histoire générale des auteurs*, vol. III, chap. 1, art. 4, §2, no. 4, p. 155.] that this anonymous author composed this little work against Novatian [Note: [Col. 1205C] “In that house, had you persevered, Novatian, you might perhaps have been a precious vessel; but now you neither understand nor lament that you have been turned into chaff and stubble”: Anonymous, [Col. 1205D] chap. 1, in Galland, p. 371, and among Cyprian’s [Col. 1206B] works, Bremen edition, p. 16; Venice edition, pp. 771–772.] around the year of Jesus Christ 255, while Novatian was still alive, when the schism of Felicissimus had by then been almost suppressed and extinguished.

In this little book the anonymous author attacks the rigor of Novatian and his adherents:

1. By placing before their eyes the fact that, without incurring the charge of injustice, they could not refuse admission to penance to the many lapsed Christians who sought it, since very many of those who had lapsed during the persecution of Decius stood unconquered during the persecution of Gallus and did not fear to shed their blood and lay down their lives for Christ Jesus [Note: [Col. 1206B] Anonymous, in Galland, p. 372, §6; Bremen edition, p. 17; Venice edition, p. 775.].

2. [Col. 1205C] By proving to them from the authority of Holy Scripture that God is infinitely merciful and always ready to grant forgiveness of sins to those who truly repent [Note: [Col. 1206B] The same, in Galland, chaps. 9–16 and 18, pp. 373–376; and among the works of Cyprian, Bremen edition, pp. 18–21; Venice edition, pp. 776–783.].

3. By refuting the arguments drawn from Holy Scripture [Col. 1206A] with which they gave a specious appearance to their rigor [Note: [Col. 1206B] The same, in Galland, chap. 7, p. 372 ff.; [Col. 1206C] among the works of Cyprian, Bremen edition, p. 18 ff.; Venice edition, p. 775.].

This anonymous author cites the Apocalypse under the name of John, but does not expressly say that it belongs to John the Evangelist [Note: [Col. 1206C] “Hear in the Apocalypse the Lord’s voice rebuking you with just reproaches.” Anonymous, chap. 2, p. 371 in Galland; compare Rev. 3:17. “As the Apocalypse teaches, saying,” etc. The same, chap. 5, pp. 322, 371; compare Rev. 17:15. “Scripture cries out and says.” The same, chap. 13; compare Rev. 2:5. “John also plainly declares concerning the day of judgment and the consummation of the age, saying.” The same, chap. 17, p. 375; compare Rev. 6:12–17. “The same John also says that this was revealed to him in the same Apocalypse,” etc. The same, loc. cit.; and among the works of Cyprian, Bremen edition, p. 21; Venice edition, p. 782; compare Rev. 20:11.].

The same anonymous author writes in this treatise [Note: [Col. 1206C] Anonymous, chap. 13, in Galland, p. 374; and among the works of Cyprian, Bremen edition, p. 19; Venice edition, p. 778E.] that “Novatian, while he was in the Church, lamented the sins of others as though they were his own.” But it is remarkable how he acquired this reputation for humanity and diligence in tending the lapsed. The testimony of Cornelius seems contradictory, for in Eusebius he testifies that during the persecution of Decius Novatian refused to assist brethren in need [Note: [Col. 1206C] Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VI, chap. 43.]. But perhaps this estimate of Novatian’s humanity arose from the most distinguished letter of the Roman clergy, numbered XXXI among Cyprian’s letters, which was written by Novatian and sent throughout the whole world, as Cyprian testifies in Letters I and II. On this matter, however, see [Col. 1206B] what we have discussed elsewhere, where we treated Novatian’s letter written in the name of the Roman clergy [Note: [Col. 1206C] See *Histoire théologique critique*, part XI, section II, chap. [Col. 1206D] 2, art. 3, pp. 42–44.].

Erasmus was the first to publish this treatise among the acknowledged works of Cyprian, at Basel in 1520. The Oxford editor illustrated it with learned notes, which the Maurist editor afterward omitted in 1726, but Galland appended them again in his *Bibliotheca veterum Patrum*, vol. III, pp. 371–376.—LUMPER.

[Col. 1205]

# The Anonymous Treatise Addressed to the Heretic Novatian: That Hope of Pardon Must Not Be Denied to the Lapsed (C, G, S)

[Col. 1205D]

[Note: [Col. 1207D]

**I.—*Excusa sunt*.** I think *excussa sunt* should be read. For the author is referring to Exodus 12:35–36: “The children of Israel—asked the Egyptians for vessels of silver and gold—and despoiled the Egyptians.” GALLAND.

]

## I

While I was reflecting, and my mind was seething beyond endurance, over what I ought to do concerning the pitiable brethren who, [Col. 1206D] wounded not by their own will but by an assault of the raging devil, had continued even until now—that is, through a long succession [Col. 1207A] of time—to suffer punishment, behold, another enemy arose against me: the heretic Novatian, an adversary of paternal compassion itself. Not only would he, like the priest or the Levite signified in the Gospel (Luke 10), pass by the wounded man lying there, but with an ingenious and novel cruelty he would instead kill the injured man—taking away the hope of salvation, denying the Father’s mercy, and rejecting his brother’s repentance.

How astonishingly many bitter, harsh, and perverse things there are! Yet one more readily perceives a speck in another’s eye than a beam in his own (Matt. 7:3; Luke 6:41). But, dearly beloved brethren, let us not be moved or troubled by the unbridled madness of this faithless heretic. Although he stands guilty of so grave a crime of dissension and schism and has been separated from the Church, [Col. 1207B] he does not hesitate, with sacrilegious recklessness, to turn his own crimes back upon us. For although he has now made himself unclean, defiled with sacrilegious filth, he insists that this is what we are.

And although it is written that the dogs will remain outside (Rev. 22:15), and the Apostle taught that these same dogs must be avoided, as we read—for he says, “Beware of the dogs; beware of evil workers” (Phil. 3:2)—he does not cease to stir up his madness by barking, seeking, after the manner of wolves, the dark gloom in which he may easily tear apart with his bestial cruelty sheep snatched from their shepherd in a dark cave.

He certainly declares himself and those whom he gathers to be gold. Nor do we doubt that deserters from the Church, having become apostates, could now readily be turned into gold—but into that gold by which the first sins of the people of Israel were marked out (Exod. 32:2 ff.). [Col. 1207C] The vessels of gold and silver, however, which were shaken out of the Egyptians’ possession (Exod. 12:35–36), remain within the Lord’s dominion, that is, in the Church of Christ. Had you persevered in that house, Novatian, you might perhaps have been a precious vessel; but now you neither understand nor lament that you have been turned into chaff and stubble.

[Note: [Col. 1207D]

**II.—*Nisi desertores* (“unless deserters”).** Here too, as elsewhere, an error had crept into Erasmus’s text, so that *non* (“not”) was read because the old printed edition reads *non*, whereas according to the manuscript codex the sense instead requires *nisi* (“unless”). PAMELIUS.

**The ordination of God.** Here too Gravius and [Col. 1208D] the manuscript codex correctly read *ordinationem* rather than *ordinem*; for the author is alluding to the ordination of Cornelius, concerning which he speaks shortly afterward. PAMELIUS.
