**You have made … an agreement.** I have restored this passage in this way, both from Cyprian’s Letter LV and because of the Greek word συνθήκας (*synthēkas*, “agreements” or “covenants”). Until now *cogitationem* (“thought”) was read. PAMELIUS.

**Most unhappy.** Coster and the manuscript codex read the singular *infelicissime*. This is not bad. But I prefer the former reading, so that by antiphrasis (ἀντίφρασιν) it may allude to Felicissimus, who is often mentioned in Cyprian’s works, especially in the already cited Letter LV. PAMELIUS.]

## II

Why, then, are you puffed up by empty things? You gain losses rather than profits. Why, since becoming poorer, do you believe yourself rich? Hear in the Apocalypse the Lord’s voice assailing you with just rebukes: “You say,” he declares, “‘I am rich and have become wealthy and need nothing’; and you do not know that you are wretched and pitiable and blind and poor and naked” (Rev. 3:17).

Whoever, after abandoning the Church of Christ, does not tremble to defect [Col. 1207D] in blind folly to those reckless leaders of schisms and authors of dissension may be assured that he possesses these resources, these riches of poverty. John calls them antichrists (1 John 2:18); the Evangelist likens them to chaff (Matt. 3:12); the Lord Christ designates them thieves and robbers (John 10:1), [Col. 1208A] as he himself declares in the Gospel, saying: “He who did not enter the sheepfold through the door, but came down by another way, is a thief and a robber.” Again, in the same place he also says: “All who have come are thieves and robbers” (John 8 [sic]).

Who are these if not deserters from the faith and transgressors against the Church of God, who struggle against the ordination of God? The Holy Spirit rightly rebukes them through the Prophet, saying: “You have formed a plan, but not through me, and made an agreement, but not through my spirit, adding sins upon sins” (Isa. 30:1).

What answer can these utterly perverse Novatians make to this—or those few who are now most unhappy? They have burst forth into such insane madness that they have shown reverence neither for God nor for man. There, the episcopate is shamelessly sought without any law of ordination; [Col. 1208B] here, however, men renounce their own sees and the chair entrusted to them by God. There Truth says: “They rejected me so that they might sacrifice to me, and they do not offer the holy offerings of the children of Israel, nor do they approach to offer the holy of holies; but they shall receive their shame in the error by which they went astray” (Ezek. 44:10–13).

Let it suffice to have shown briefly what they are. Hear, therefore, O Novatians, among whom the heavenly Scriptures are read rather than understood—and scarcely even read without interpolation. For your ears are stopped and your hearts blinded (Matt. 13:14), since you admit no light from spiritual and saving admonitions. As Isaiah says, “The servants of God have been blinded” (Isa. 42:19). And they have rightly been blinded, because the will of schismatics is not within the law—that law which points out to us one unique Church, [Col. 1208C] namely in the ark built under Noah by God’s providence before the flood. In it we find enclosed not only clean animals but also unclean ones—to give you a prompt answer, Novatian.

That ark alone was delivered together with everything that was within it; all else not found in it perished in the flood. From that ark, therefore, two birds are released: a raven and a dove. The raven truly bore the figure of unclean men who would remain in perpetual darkness, of apostates who would travel the broad way of the world and feed upon unclean things, and who would never again turn back toward the Church. We read that it was released and did not return again. Those, therefore, who are found to resemble this bird—that is, the unclean spirit—will not be able to return to the Church again; [Col. 1208D] and even if they wish to do so, the Lord will forbid it, for he commanded Moses: “Cast every spotted and unclean thing outside, beyond the camp” (Num. 5:2).

The dove, however, is said to have returned immediately after being released, because it found no resting place for its feet. Noah received it into [Col. 1209A] the ark; and, when it was sent out again after the seventh day, he received it carrying an olive leaf in its mouth (Gen. 8:9–11).

[Note: [Col. 1209D]

**III.—The first and principal.** The passage is obscure and corrupt, even in the manuscript codex, except insofar as the author here makes sufficiently clear that the Church alone possesses the sacrament of Baptism—a position belonging to Cyprian’s error. PAMELIUS.

**Trinity.** Some read “triad.” In my judgment “Trinity” is more correct, for so the manuscript codex reads. PAMELIUS.]

## III

And I, dearly beloved brethren, do not consider these things rashly or combine them by human wisdom, but speak as, through the heavenly Lord’s gracious favor, our minds are permitted to conceive them necessarily and appropriately. I say that the dove herself signifies for us a twofold figure.

The first and principal figure—her own, that is, the spiritual one—has stood from ancient times, that is, from the beginning of the divine dispensation; and through her own mouth she foreshadows the sacrament of Baptism, which was provided for the salvation of the human race and which the Church alone celebrates according to the heavenly order. [The wording of this sentence is textually corrupt.] For, sent from the ark three times and flying through the air above the water, she signified even [Col. 1209B] then the sacraments of our Church. Hence the Lord Christ commands Peter and also his other disciples, saying: “Go, evangelize the nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28:19). That is, the Trinity which acted figuratively under Noah through the dove now acts spiritually in the Church through these three.

## IV

Let us now take up the dove’s second role when she was released from the ark: namely, at the time of the flood, when all the abysses burst forth and the floodgates of heaven were opened over the earth because of the crimes that human beings committed daily before the Lord. As Moses said: “And the Lord God saw that the wickedness of human beings abounded upon the earth, and that all their thoughts were directed toward evil from the beginning of their days, [Col. 1209C] and he said: ‘I will destroy from the face of the earth the human being whom I made, from man even to beast, and from creeping thing even to the birds of heaven’” (Gen. 6:5–7). Thus at the time of the cataclysm the dove is sent out from the ark, while the waters violently assail the earth throughout the whole world.

[Note: [Col. 1210D]

**V.—Predictions.** I read *praedictionum* (“predictions”) in place of *praedicationum* (“preachings”), because what follows is: “whose future fall the Lord had signified in the Gospel,” etc. PAMELIUS.]

## V

That ark bore the figure of the Church, as we said above, which was beaten from this side and that by the surging waters. Thus the cataclysm that occurred under Noah displays a figure of the persecution that very recently poured itself over the whole world. The waters that converged from every direction and swelled when the floodgates had burst signified the nations which swelled up to devastate the Church. As the Apocalypse teaches, saying: “The waters that you saw are peoples and nations and kingdoms” (Rev. 17:15).

The dove, [Col. 1209D] however, which could find no resting place for its feet, bore the image of the lapsed. Forgetful of the divine predictions—or simply ignorant of them, or brazenly pretending not to know—they fell. The Lord had signified their future fall in the Gospel in these words: “He who hears my words and does [Col. 1210A] not perform them I shall liken to a foolish man who built his house upon sand. Storms came and struck against that house, and it fell, and great was its ruin” (Matt. 7:26–27).

And lest we appear rashly to have compared that dove to the image of the lapsed, the Prophet rebukes the city as a dove—that is, in the person of the lapsed—saying: “The dove does not heed the voice”; that is, the illustrious and redeemed city does not receive instruction and did not put its trust in the Lord (Zeph. 3:1–2).

[Note: [Col. 1210D]

**VI.—They will not harm you.** Thus Manutius and Morel read, in place of “will not harm *you*” in the accusative, although the manuscript codex also has the latter. PAMELIUS.

**Secular rulers.** Gallus and Volusian, of course. PAMELIUS.]

## VI

The fact that this dove, as we said above, could find no resting place for her feet signified that the footsteps of the deniers—that is, of those who sacrificed—had been wounded by the slippery serpent’s venom and turned toward a fall, so that they could no longer tread upon the asp [Col. 1210B] and basilisk or trample the dragon and lion (Ps. 90:13). The Lord gave this power to his disciples, as he says in the Gospel: “Behold, I give you power to tread upon all the power of the enemy, and upon serpents and scorpions, and they will not harm you” (Luke 10:19).

Therefore, while so many and such great malignant spirits assailed these persons and rose up to destroy the lapsed, a way of salvation was provided for the wounded: with whatever strength they possessed, they might drag themselves forward with their whole bodies and return to their own camp; once received there, they might treat their wounds with spiritual remedies.

The dove, therefore, was received; and after a few days had intervened, she was sent out from the ark again. When she returned, she displayed not only firm footing but also the emblems of her peace and victory, through those olive leaves which she carried in her mouth. [Col. 1210C] That twofold release, therefore, displays for us a twofold trial of persecution: the first, in which those who lapsed were defeated and fell; the second, in which those who had fallen emerged victorious.

For none of us doubts or is uncertain, dearly beloved brethren, that those who were wounded in the first battle—that is, in the Decian persecution—afterward, that is, in the second combat, persevered so courageously that, despising the edicts of secular rulers, they maintained this unconquered resolve: following the example of the good shepherd, they did not fear to lay down their lives and shed their blood, nor did they shrink from any cruelty of the raging tyrant.

[Note: [Col. 1211D]

**VIII.—Understand; interpret.** The manuscript codex reads, “They understand and interpret.” PAMELIUS.

**You changed it through the designation of a name.** This again comes from Gravius, in place of what others read as “through the name you changed the veil,” especially since the manuscript codex also reads *velim* (“I should like”). PAMELIUS.]

## VII

Behold, these schismatics do not hesitate to call men so glorious and so dear to the Lord “wood, hay, and stubble” [Col. 1210D] (1 Cor. 3:12). Yet they presume that their equals—namely, those who still remain under the same guilt of their lapse—must not even be admitted to penance, on the basis of that declaration of the Lord in which he says: “Whoever denies me before men, I shall deny him before my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 10:33).

Alas! Why do they contend [Col. 1211A] against the Lord’s precepts, so that this offspring of Novatian, following the example of its father the devil, now attempts to exercise those things which Christ will do at the time of his judgment? For Scripture says: “Vengeance is mine, and I shall repay, says the Lord” (Heb. 10:30).

## VIII

We shall answer them concerning this declaration of the Lord, which they understand wrongly and misinterpret to their own advantage. For when he says, “Whoever denies me before men, I too shall deny him before my Father who is in heaven,” this is plainly a reference to the future time: the time when the Lord will begin to judge the secrets of human beings; the time when we must all stand before [Col. 1211B] Christ’s tribunal (2 Cor. 5:10); the time when many will begin to say, “Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and cast out demons in your name, and perform many mighty works in your name?” (Matt. 7:22–23). Yet they will hear the Lord’s voice saying: “Depart from me, all you who have worked iniquity; I do not know you” (John 6:68 [sic]). There what he said will be fulfilled: “I shall deny them also.”

But whom will the Lord Christ deny above all, if not all of you heretics and schismatics, who are strangers to his name? Once Christians, you are now Novatians and no longer Christians: by the subsequent faithlessness of a changed designation you have altered your original faith. I should like you to answer your own proposition. Read and show whom the Lord denied among those who had abandoned or denied him while he himself was still present. [Col. 1211C] Indeed, he said even to the other disciples who remained with him, “Do you too wish to depart?” (John 6:68). Even Peter, whom he had foretold would deny him, the Lord himself did not deny after Peter had denied him, but bore with him; and afterward he himself soothed him as he wept bitterly over that denial.

[Note: [Col. 1211D]

**IX.—Repent**, etc. We likewise owe these words—missing elsewhere—to Gravius and the manuscript codices. THE SAME.]

## IX

What madness is yours, Novatian, that you read only those things which pertain to the destruction of salvation, while passing over those which pertain to mercy? Scripture cries out and says: “Repent, you who go astray; turn back in your heart” (Ezek. 18:30). The same Prophet likewise exhorts and says: “Turn back to me with your whole heart, with fasting, weeping, and lamentation. Rend your hearts and not your garments. Turn back to the Lord your God, because [Col. 1211D] he is merciful and compassionate, abounding in pity” (Joel 2:12–13).

[Note: [Col. 1211D]

**X.—Nor shall I always refrain from avenging you.** A remarkable translation, since the literal Greek is οὐδὲ διὰ παντὸς ὀργισθήσομαι ὑμῖν, which in Latin means, “Nor shall I be angry with you forever.” Omitting the second negation, Coster takes *defendam* to mean “I shall avenge,” a meaning in which Cyprian also uses it elsewhere. Certainly, the negative particle was added later in the manuscript [Col. 1212D] codex. THE SAME.—Not only Cyprian but also the Vulgate translator frequently employs *defendere* in the sense of “vindicate” or “avenge.” See Judith 1:12; 2:1; Romans 12:19. Indeed, we find the verb used in the same sense by the most reputable Latin authors. GALLAND.

**To those who repent**, etc. These are the author’s words, not Isaiah’s, as Morel wrongly judged; even so, the passage remains obscure. PAMELIUS.]

## X

We have heard, then, that the Lord abounds in compassion. Let us hear what the Holy Spirit solemnly declares through David: “If his children abandon my law and do not walk [Col. 1212A] in my commandments; if they profane my ordinances and do not keep my precepts, I shall visit their crimes with a rod and their sins with scourges; but I shall not scatter my mercy from them” (Ps. 88:31–34).

We read that the Lord also said similar things through Ezekiel: “Son of man, the house of Israel dwelt upon its own land, and they defiled it by their crimes. Their uncleanness became like that of a menstruating woman before my face. I poured out my wrath upon them and scattered them among the nations, and I judged them according to their sins, because they defiled my holy name. And because it was said of them, ‘This is the Lord’s people,’ I spared them for the sake of my holy name, which the house of Israel brought into contempt among [Col. 1212B] the nations” (Ezek. 36:18–23). Continuing, he says: “Therefore say to the people of Israel: ‘Thus says the Lord: I do not spare you for your sake, house of Israel, but I shall spare you for the sake of my holy name, which you defiled among the nations; and you shall know that I am the Lord when I have been sanctified among you.’”

Again the Lord says to the same prophet: “Son of man, say to the people of Israel: ‘Why have you spoken, saying: “We waste away in our errors, and how shall we be able to be saved?”’ Say to them: ‘As I live, says the Lord, I do not desire the death of a sinner, but desire that the sinner turn away from his most evil way and live. Return, therefore, from your most evil way. Why do you surrender yourselves to death, house of Israel?’” (Ezek. 33:10–11).

So too through the prophet Isaiah: “I shall not be indignant with you forever, nor shall I always refrain from avenging you” [Col. 1212C] (Isa. 57:16). And because the prophet Jeremiah pleads with the Lord in the person of the sinful people, saying, “Correct us, Lord, but with judgment and not in wrath, lest you make us few” (Jer. 10:24), Isaiah added and said: “For his sin I grieved him a little and struck him, and turned my face away from him; and he was grieved and went away sorrowful upon his paths” (Isa. 57:17). And because he acts, he added and said: “I saw his ways and healed him, and gave him true encouragement, peace upon peace”—indicating that those who repent, plead, and act can be restored, although they have perished miserably and turned away from Christ.

## XI

Indeed, this is confirmed in the Gospel, where the sinful woman is described (Luke 7). She came [Col. 1212D] to the house of a certain Pharisee, where the Lord had been invited with his disciples, carrying a vessel of ointment. She stood at the Lord’s feet, washed his feet with her tears, wiped them with her hair, and pressed kisses upon them, so that the Pharisee was provoked to say: “If this man were a Prophet, [Col. 1213A] he would know who and what sort of woman this is who touches him, for she is a sinner” (Luke 7:39–47).

Thereupon the Lord, forgiver of sins and receiver of penitents, immediately said: “Simon, I have something to say to you.” He replied, “Teacher, speak.” And the Lord said: “A certain moneylender had two debtors, one of whom owed five hundred denarii and the other fifty. When they had nothing with which to pay, he forgave them both.” And he asked: “Which of them loves him more?” Simon answered: “Surely the one to whom he forgave more.” And he continued: “Do you see this woman? I entered your house, and you gave me no kiss; but she has not ceased kissing my feet. You did not wash my feet, but she washed them with her tears and wiped them with her hair. You did not anoint my feet with oil, but she anointed them. Therefore I say to you, Simon, that [Col. 1213B] her sins are forgiven.”

Behold, in his abundant loving-kindness the Lord releases both debtors from their debt. Behold him forgiving sins. Behold the sinful woman repenting, weeping, pleading, and receiving remission of sins.

[Note: [Col. 1213D]

**XII.—Do not rejoice over me, my enemy.** This reading too must be adopted in place of the corrupt “friend.” For in the Greek Septuagint it is ἐχθρά μου (*echthra mou*, “my enemy”). PAMELIUS.]

## XII

Now blush, Novatian, if that is possible. Cease deceiving the unwary with your impious arguments; cease terrifying them by the prescriptive force of a single passage. We read and revere, and do not pass over, the Lord’s heavenly sentence in which he says that he will deny the one who denies him—but will he also deny one who repents?

And why should I strive so long to establish every individual instance of compassion, since God’s mercy was not denied to the Ninevites, though they were foreigners and situated far outside the Lord’s law, when they pleaded because the overthrow of their city had been announced (Jonah 3)? Even [Col. 1213C] from Pharaoh himself, who resisted with sacrilegious recklessness, when he was once being struck by heavenly plagues and turned to Moses and his brother and said, “Pray to the Lord for me, because I have sinned” (Exod. 9:28), God’s wrath was immediately suspended.

And now you, Novatian, pass judgment and proclaim that the lapsed have no hope of peace and mercy. Nor do you lend an ear to the Apostle when he rebukes you, saying: “Who are you to judge another’s servant? Before his own master he stands or falls. But he shall stand, for God is able to make him stand” (Rom. 14:4).

Hence, appropriately and necessarily, the Holy Spirit rebukes you in the person of those same lapsed Christians, saying: “Do not rejoice over me, my enemy, because though I have fallen, I shall rise; and though I walk in darkness, the Lord is my light. I shall endure the Lord’s wrath, because I have sinned [Col. 1213D] against him, until he vindicates my cause and executes judgment and justice and brings me forth into the light. I shall see his righteousness; and my enemy shall see me and shall cover herself with confusion” (Mic. 7:8, 10).

[Col. 1214A]

[Note: [Col. 1213D]

**XIII.—He lamented the sins of his neighbors as though they were his own.** The author is referring to Novatian’s letter written in the name of the Roman clergy, which we published above with Novatian’s other works. GALLAND.

**That Cainite heresy.** Erasmus correctly reads *Cainam* rather than *caninam* (“canine”). For Jerome too gives this name to the heresy which takes away hope that sin may be forgiven. The passage of Jerome [Col. 1214D] is in his *Letter to Oceanus*; he also mentions the same heresy as one which abolishes martyrdom in his book *Against Vigilantius*. It is therefore the same as the heresy of the Gnostics, concerning whom Tertullian writes in the *Scorpiace*. I likewise judge that *Caina*, or at least *Caiana*, should be read in place of *Gaiana* in the opening of Tertullian’s book *On Baptism*, since that heresy also took away the remedy of Baptism. On the other errors of this sect, see the same author’s *Prescription against Heretics*; Irenaeus, book I, final chapter; Epiphanius, Heresy XXXVIII; and Augustine, Heresy XVIII. PAMELIUS.]

### XIII

I ask you, have you not read: “Do not boast, and do not speak lofty things, and let grandiloquence not proceed from your mouth; for he raises the poor from the earth, he raises the needy from the dunghill, and makes him sit with the mighty of the people” (I Kings 2:3, 8)? Have you not read: “Because the Lord resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James 4:6; I Peter 5:5)? Have you not read: “He who exalts himself shall be humbled” (Matthew 23:12; Luke 14:11; 18:14)? Have you not read: “Because God destroys the memory of the proud, and does not abandon the memory of the humble” (Psalm 9:7, 11)? Have you not read: “Because by whatever judgment a man has judged, by that judgment he must himself be judged” (Matthew 7:2)? Have you not read: “Because he who hates his brother is in darkness and walks in darkness; and he does not know where he is going, because the darkness has blinded his eyes” (I John 2:11)?

How, then, this Novatian became so wicked, [Col. 1214B] so utterly lost, and so frenzied with the madness of discord, I cannot discover. He had always, within the one house—that is, the Church of Christ—wept over his neighbors’ offenses as though they were his own; he had borne the burdens of his brethren, as the Apostle exhorts (Galatians 6:2); and he had strengthened those who were faltering in the faith with heavenly consolation. But now, since he began to practice that Cainite heresy, which strives only to kill, he no longer spares even himself in the end.

But if he had read that the righteousness of the righteous will not deliver him on the day when he goes astray, and that the wickedness of the wicked will not harm him from the day on which he is converted (Ezekiel 33:12), he would long since have repented in ashes—he who always opposes those who repent; who works more readily toward the ruin of buildings that stand than toward the reconstruction of ruins that lie fallen; who, by terrifying many most wretched members of our brotherhood [Col. 1214C] with his false opposition, has made them pagans once again, declaring that the repentance of the fallen is vain and cannot benefit them unto salvation, while Scripture cries aloud and says: “Remember whence you have fallen, and do penance; otherwise I shall come to you, unless you do penance” (Revelation 2:5). Indeed, when writing to the seven churches and confronting each one with its particular crimes and offenses, it said: “Repent.” To whom did it speak, if not, surely, to those whom he had redeemed at the great price of his own blood?

> **Note: [Col. 1215D]**
>
> **XIV.—The violence of the water, etc.** He means the persecution which the devil unleashed against the Church. **PAMELIUS.**
>
> **In Zechariah.** This reading, instead of *to*, is based on Coster’s conjecture; the manuscript codex also agrees. **PAMELIUS.**
>
> **From their hands.** Gravius rightly added this phrase, for the Septuagint has it, as does Cyprian, Epistle LIV; so too [Col. 1216D] does the manuscript codex. **PAMELIUS.**

### XIV

O impious and criminal heretic Novatian! After so many and such great crimes were voluntarily committed in the Church by certain persons in former times—crimes which you yourself had known to exist in the house of God before becoming an apostate—and after you had certainly taught, in accordance with faith in the Scripture, that these could be erased from memory when good succeeded them, [Col. 1214D] for Scripture says: “If the criminal turns away from all the crimes which he has committed and does righteousness, he shall live with eternal life and shall not die in his crime” (Ezekiel [Col. 1215A] 18:21)—“for the offenses which he committed shall be erased from memory when good deeds succeed them”—you now reconsider whether the wounds of the fallen ought to be treated, although they fell after being stripped by the devil, through the violence of the water which the serpent spewed from its mouth after the woman (Revelation 12:15).

But what shall I say? The Apostle says: “Do I praise you? In this I do not praise you, because you have come together not for the better, but for the worse” (I Corinthians 11:12–17). “For where there are jealousies and dissensions among you, are you not carnal, and do you not walk according to man?” (I Corinthians 3:3).

Nor indeed ought we to marvel that this Novatian now dares to perpetrate such abominable and grievous things against the fallen, since we have preceding examples of this [Col. 1215B] transgression. That good Saul (I Kings 9:2; 18 ff.), after everything else, was afterward overthrown by envy and attempted to do everything adverse and hostile against David. That Judas, chosen among the Apostles (Matthew 10:4; 26:15), who had always been of one mind and faithful in the house of God (Psalm 54:15), afterward betrayed God himself.

The Lord had indeed foretold that many would come in sheep’s clothing, though inwardly they were ravenous wolves (Matthew 7:15). Who are those ravenous wolves, if not those who conspire with deceitful intent to harass Christ’s flock? Thus we read in Zechariah: “Behold, I raise up a shepherd in the land, who will not visit that which has turned away, and will eat the flesh of the elect and twist their ankles” (Zechariah 11:16).

Similarly, through Ezekiel he rebukes shepherds of this kind—that is, robbers and [Col. 1215C] butchers, as I shall call them in accordance with his judgment—saying: “O shepherds, why do you drink the milk and eat the curds, and bring the strong to nothing? You have not visited the weak; you have not treated the lame; you have not recalled the wandering; and you have allowed my people to wander among thorns and thistles. Therefore the Lord says this: Behold, I shall come against the shepherds, and I shall seek my sheep from their hands, and I shall drive them away so that they do not shepherd my sheep; and my sheep shall no longer be food for them. I shall seek them as a shepherd seeks his flock on a day of darkness and mist. Thus shall I seek my sheep, and I shall seek them in every place into which they have been scattered. That which was lost I shall seek; that which had wandered I shall recall; that which was lame I shall treat; that which is weak I shall preserve; and I shall feed my sheep with judgment” (Ezekiel 34: [Col. 1215D] 3, 4, 10, 11, 16).

> **Note: [Col. 1216D]**
>
> **XV.—For all the deeds . . . impiously.** We have inserted these words into the text from the margin of Gravius, because they are found in the Apostle Jude, especially since the manuscript codex agrees. **PAMELIUS.**

### XV

Who says these things? Surely he who, leaving the ninety-nine sheep, sought the one which had wandered from his flock, as David says: “I have gone astray like a sheep that was lost” (Psalm 118:176). When it was found, Christ brought it back, carrying the tender sinner upon his shoulder; and rejoicing and exulting, after calling together his friends and household, he said: “Rejoice with me, because my sheep which was lost has been found. I tell you,” he says, “that there will be such joy [Col. 1216A] in heaven over one sinner who repents” (Luke 15:6–10).

And continuing, he says: “Or what woman who has ten coins, if she loses one of the coins, does not light a lamp and clean her house throughout the whole day, searching until she finds it? And when she has found it, she calls together her friends and neighbors, saying: ‘Rejoice with me, because I have found the coin which I had lost.’ I tell you that there will be such joy in the presence of the angels of God over one sinner who repents.”

Those, on the other hand, who do not repent of their crimes should learn from the Lord’s own answer what awaits them. For we read in the Gospel that certain persons came from Galilee to the Lord, reporting [Col. 1216B] to him concerning those whose blood Pilate had mingled with their sacrifices. The Lord answered them, saying: “Do you think that those Galileans were sinners above all the other Galileans because they suffered such things? No. For I tell you: unless you repent, you shall all perish in the same way. Or those eighteen upon whom the tower in Siloam fell—do you think that they were indebted to death above all the people who dwelt in Jerusalem? No. I tell you,” he says, “that unless you repent, you shall all perish in the same way” (Luke 13:1–5).

### XVI

Let us therefore rouse ourselves as much as we can, dearly beloved brethren, and, breaking off the sleep of sloth and careless security, let us keep watch to observe the Lord’s commandments. Let us seek with our whole mind what we have lost, so that we may be able to find it; for, Scripture says, “To him who seeks it shall be given, and [Col. 1216C] to him who knocks it shall be opened” (Luke 11:10).

Let us cleanse our house with spiritual purity, so that every secret and hidden place of our heart, illuminated by the true light of the Gospel, may say: “Against you alone have I sinned, and I have done what is most wicked in your sight” (Psalm 50:6); “For the death of sinners is evil” (Psalm 33:22), and in the lower regions there is no repentance (Ecclesiasticus 11:17). Above all, let us keep in contemplation the day of judgment and recompense, and what must be believed by us all and firmly maintained: that “there is no acceptance of persons with God” (Romans 2:11), since in Deuteronomy he commanded that no person should be favored in judgment: “You shall not,” he says, “accept any person, nor shall you judge according to the least or according to the greatest” (Deuteronomy 1:17; 16:19).

He said things similar to these through Ezekiel: “All souls,” he says, “are mine; [Col. 1216D] as the soul of the father, so also the soul of the son: the soul that sins shall itself die” (Ezekiel 18:4). This, therefore, is the one whom we must revere, whom we must hold fast, whom we must propitiate through our full and worthy confession: he who has power to cast soul and body into the Gehenna of fire (Matthew 10:28), as it is written: “Behold, he comes with many thousands of his messengers to execute judgment upon all and to destroy all the ungodly, and to convict all flesh concerning all the deeds of the ungodly [Col. 1217A] which they have impiously committed, and concerning all the impious words which sinners have spoken against God” (Jude 14, 15).

> **Note: [Col. 1217C]**
>
> **XVII.—A river of fire.** Gravius and Manutius read *flame*; but the Greek word, ποταμός (*potamos*, “river”), is opposed to this. **PAMELIUS.**

### XVII

Daniel likewise says similar things: “I saw,” he says, “a throne set in place, and the Ancient of Days sat upon it; and his clothing was like snow, and the hair of his head like white wool; his throne was a flame of fire, its wheels burning fire. A river of fire issued forth before him; thousands of thousands served him, and thousands of thousands stood before him. He sat for judgment, and the books were opened” (Daniel 7:9, 10).

John, however, speaks more explicitly concerning the day of judgment and the consummation of the age, saying: “And when he had opened,” he says, “the sixth seal, behold, there was a great earthquake; and the sun became black as a sackcloth of hair, and the whole moon became like blood; and the stars fell to the earth, just as a fig tree shaken by a great wind [Col. 1217B] casts down its unripe figs; and heaven withdrew like a book when it is rolled up; and every mountain and the islands were moved from their places. And the kings of the earth, all the great men and tribunes, the rich and the mighty, and every slave and free man hid themselves in caves and among the caverns of the mountains, saying to the mountains and rocks: ‘Fall upon us, and hide us from the sight of the Father who sits upon the throne and from the wrath of the Lamb, because the day of destruction has come; and who will be able to stand?’” (Revelation 6:12–17).

Likewise, in the same Apocalypse, John also says that this was revealed to him: “I saw,” he says, “a great white throne, and one sitting upon it, from whose face heaven and earth fled, and no place was found for them. And I saw the dead, great and small, standing before the throne of the Lord; and the books were opened. And another book was opened, which is the book of life; and each was judged according to the things written in the book, according to [Col. 1217C] their works” (Revelation 20:11–13).

And the [Col. 1218A] Apostle, counseling what is good, exhorts us as follows: “Let no one deceive you with empty words, for because of these things the wrath of God comes upon the children of disobedience. Do not become their partners” (Ephesians 5:6, 7).

> **Note: [Col. 1217C]**
>
> **XVIII.—Let that prayer be ready to hand for you.** From the manuscript codex we have restored *for you* in place of *for us*. From this it is apparent—were it not for the phrase, “State your crimes,” etc.—that this book is mutilated and incomplete. Nevertheless, the prayer of Cyprian for the martyrs cannot be the one which he mentions, since no mention is made in it of repentance or the remission of sins, [Col. 1218C] as Erasmus also noted before me. In addition, in the ancient codex from which he copied this book, a sermon of St. Augustine concerning Cyprian is inserted between them; and in the manuscripts of Affligem, Marchiennes, Dunes, and England that Prayer is found together with the following one, though without this book; while conversely this book is found in a manuscript codex without any prayer. **PAMELIUS.**

### XVIII

Let us therefore, with all the strength of our faith, give praise to God; let us make a full confession, since the powers of heaven rejoice over our repentance, all the angels rejoice, and Christ too rejoices. When we have again been burdened with sins and overwhelmed by offenses, he exhorts us, with full and merciful moderation, to cease from crime, saying: “Turn and return from your acts of impiety, and your iniquities shall not be for your punishment. Cast away from yourselves all your acts of impiety which you have committed against me, and make for yourselves a new heart and a new spirit. And why do you hand yourselves over to death, house of Israel? For I do not [Col. 1218B] desire the death of the sinner” (Ezekiel 18:30–32).

“I am, I am he who blots out your crimes, and I shall not remember you; but call them to mind yourself, and let us enter into judgment. State your crimes first, so that you may be justified” (Isaiah 43:25, 26).

While the way to forgiveness lies open, brethren, let us entreat God with full acts of satisfaction. Let us humble ourselves, so that we may be exalted. Let us assent to the divine exhortation by which we may be permitted to escape the day and wrath of the Lord. For it says:

“Look, my son, upon the nations of mankind, and know: Who has hoped in the Lord and been put to shame? Who has remained in his commandments and been abandoned? Or who has called upon him, and been despised by him? For the Lord is gracious and merciful, and in time of tribulation he forgives the sins of all who seek him in truth” (Ecclesiasticus 2:11–13).

He therefore says: “State your crimes first, so that you may be justified.” Let that prayer, full of *exomologesis*—confession—be ready to hand for you.

## Part Two  
## Principal Recent Excursuses on the Same Dispute Concerning the Baptism of Heretics

[Col. 1217]

## L. Thomassin’s Dissertation on the Synods Convened under Pope Stephen in the Controversy over the Baptism of Heretics, at Carthage, Rome, and Elsewhere, in the Years of Christ 256, 257, Etc.

## Synopsis

[Col. 1217C]

The utterly noisome calumny of the innovators is refuted: namely, that Stephen erred in admitting the baptism of all heretics just as much as Cyprian [Col. 1218C] and Firmilian erred in rejecting the baptism of all heretics. From the consensus of all the Fathers it is demonstrated that the discipline of the Roman Church concerning [Col. 1219A] the baptism of heretics was then the same as it was afterward and as it still remains today.

This continues through number XXII. Thereafter, down to the end, another question is resolved in several ways: whether Augustine provides Cyprian an excuse and defense on the ground that the matter had not yet been clarified and settled by a plenary council, although Augustine himself silenced the Pelagians when they demanded a plenary council, declaring that the dispute had been concluded by local synods and the rescripts of the Apostolic See.

## I. The Conflict Between Pope Stephen and Cyprian; the Innovators’ Calumny Against Stephen; the Twofold Controversy to Be Settled Here Against Them

This second question, illustrious and abundant in material and a twin of the preceding one, now presents itself: the conflict between Stephen and Cyprian concerning baptism conferred by heretics. [Col. 1219B] For here too pontiffs distinguished for holiness clash with one another: the Roman pontiff, although superior in rank and possessed of the better cause, is scorned by his colleague; those who resisted the decree of the first see and held more tenaciously than was right to their ancestral custom nevertheless continued to enjoy communion with the Church; and finally the Council of Nicaea pronounced in favor of Stephen.

Thus, in both cases, there is a very great and remarkable correspondence of persons and circumstances. Finally, to complete the parallel: just as Victor, so too Stephen had been held in the highest admiration throughout the course of so many preceding centuries; yet the most insolent innovators of all, in this final dregs of the ages, began to blacken his reputation, as though he too had erred just as much as Cyprian, though in precisely the opposite direction. For just as Cyprian wholly excluded all heretics from the power to confer baptism, so Stephen, as they babble, granted it [Col. 1219C] indiscriminately to all, whether they used a legitimate formula of words in baptizing or a spurious and profane one.

This calumny must therefore first be repelled from that most holy pope and martyr. We shall then proceed to another controversy as well: how Cyprian was almost wholly absolved of blame by Augustine, because before a plenary council the truth had not yet been sufficiently clarified; although elsewhere that same Augustine declares that the Pelagian heretics had been more than adequately disposed of by the authority and judgment of the first see alone, and that there was no longer any need of a plenary council.

## II. That Stephen Did Not Err by Accepting the Baptism of All Heretics Is Proved from Firmilian

Those who are themselves deluded dream that Stephen too was deluded in approving the baptism of all heretics, just as Cyprian was in rejecting the baptism of all, [Col. 1219D] and they infer it from this decree of his reported in Cyprian, Epistle LXXIV:

> “If, therefore, anyone comes to us from any heresy whatsoever, let nothing be introduced beyond what has been handed down: namely, that the hand be imposed upon him for repentance; since the heretics themselves, properly speaking, do not baptize those who come to them from one another, but merely communicate with them.”

Stephen therefore made no distinction, they say, and endorsed baptism consecrated with any words whatsoever, even words utterly alien to evangelical truth.

But Stephen may first be defended from Firmilian’s own letter against him, written to Cyprian, so that the testimony which the force of truth wrings from an adversary himself may be invincible. These are the words [Col. 1220A] of Firmilian:

> “It is likewise absurd that they do not think it necessary to ask who the person was who baptized, on the ground that the person baptized could obtain grace through the invocation of the Trinity of the names of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. But who in the Church is perfect and wise who would either defend or believe that this bare invocation of the names suffices for the remission of sins and the sanctification of baptism? For these things surely avail only when the person baptizing also possesses the Holy Spirit, and baptism itself has not been instituted without the Spirit.”

From this it is plain that Stephen approved only that baptism which the invoked Trinity sanctifies, in which the invocation of the names suffices for the remission of sins; whereas Firmilian further required the person baptizing to be animated by the Holy Spirit. [Col. 1220B]

Again, in the same place, Firmilian presses Stephen as forcefully as he can, in his own opinion, with the example of a sorceress and heretical woman who had baptized many persons according to the Church’s solemn form:

> “She also baptized many, using the customary and legitimate words of interrogation, so that she appeared to differ in nothing from the ecclesiastical rule. What, therefore, shall we say of her baptism, in which a most wicked demon baptized through a woman? Do Stephen and those who agree with him approve even this—especially since neither the formula of the Trinity nor the legitimate and ecclesiastical interrogation was lacking in it? Can it be believed either that remission of sins was granted or that the regeneration of the saving laver was duly accomplished where, although everything was performed in the likeness of the truth, it was nevertheless performed through a demon? Unless those who defend the baptism of heretics also contend that a demon granted the grace of baptism in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy [Col. 1220C] Spirit.”

I cannot even imagine anything clearer than these words.

## III. The Same Is Proved Again from the Same Author

In the same place Firmilian again continues to disclose both his own opinion and Stephen’s, assailing the view that baptism was sanctified by the invocation of Christ unless it was administered by a Catholic man:

> “But the name of Christ,” he says, “contributes greatly to faith and the sanctification of baptism, so that whoever has been baptized in the name of Christ immediately obtains the grace of Christ. This passage could be answered briefly by saying that, if baptism outside the Church, performed in the name of Christ, was valid for purifying a man, then the imposition of the hand there, in the name of that same Christ, could also have been valid for receiving the Holy Spirit.”

[Col. 1220D] Stephen therefore admitted baptism consecrated in the name of the Trinity and in the name of Christ.

Again, in the same place:

> “As to the argument which they advance on behalf of heretics, saying that the Apostle declared, ‘Whether through pretext or through truth, Christ is proclaimed.’”

Would Stephen, with his supporters, have boasted that Christ was proclaimed through adulterated formulas of baptism by which the Church’s faith in Christ and the Trinity was torn apart? Certainly that passage of the Apostle teaches that the truth of sound preaching is not stained by the vice of the preacher.

## IV. Other Arguments from the Same Author

If baptism profaned by some impious [Col. 1221A] and heretical formula of words had been admitted by the Romans, Firmilian would above all have exposed that formula of heresy and attacked it in so lengthy a letter, and would thereby either have inclined the victory entirely to his own side or wrested it from Stephen. Yet although this exceedingly learned man attacks the thoroughly faithless belief of the heretics, nowhere does he touch upon the actual words poured forth by them to defile baptism. Why, moreover, would he have disparaged the Trinity or the majesty of Christ invoked by a heretical mouth, yet have remained silent about the ravings belched forth by that same mouth in contempt of the Trinity and of Christ’s name?

## V. Further Arguments

Add that Firmilian is wholly occupied with arraigning the heretical baptizer and invalidating the baptism because of the minister’s fault. Stephen, by contrast, was wholly occupied—as is evident even from [Col. 1221B] Firmilian’s refutation—with magnifying the power inherent in the sacrament itself, in Christ’s word, and in the invocation of the Trinity, which could by no means be exhausted by any wicked or heretical person from whose mouth those words resounded.

The hinge of the controversy at that time therefore turned upon this: whether the majesty and efficacy of the divine words alone could effect the sanctification of baptism, regardless of the minister by whom they were pronounced; or whether the minister’s faithlessness could corrupt and nullify the power of those words. Consequently, those who assail Stephen with curses do not appear even to have attended to the actual state of the question.

## VI. The Same Is Demonstrated from Cyprian

Almost the same arguments may be extracted from the works which Cyprian published in this controversy. For in his *Epistle to Pompeius* [Col. 1221C] he says:

> “Assuredly, baptism, which consists in that same unity, cannot exist among heretics, because it cannot be separated either from the Church or from the Holy Spirit. Or if they attribute the effect of baptism to the majesty of the name, so that those who are baptized in the name of Christ Jesus, wherever and however they may be baptized, are judged to be renewed and sanctified, etc.”

Stephen therefore attributed the effect of baptism to the majesty of the names and to the invocation of Christ’s name.

And in his *Epistle to Jubaianus*:

> “No one should oppose the name of Christ in order to circumvent Christian truth, saying that those baptized in the name of Jesus Christ, wherever and however they may have been baptized, have obtained the grace of baptism, since Christ himself speaks and says: ‘Not everyone who says to me, “Lord, Lord,” shall enter the [Col. 1221D] kingdom of heaven.’”

Cyprian’s contrary effort and insistence that not merely Christ’s name but the entire Trinity must be invoked for baptism to be valid does no harm to Stephen’s cause. For many Fathers and recent masters of the theological schools have held that baptism can be, or at least once could be, accomplished even by the invocation of Christ’s name alone. However the matter may stand, Stephen, like a great many of the ancient theologians, understood the invocation of Christ to comprehend the divine majesty of the entire Trinity; and this is evident from the words of Firmilian quoted above.

## VII. From the Same Author

Even if heretics invoked the Father, the Son, and the Holy [Col. 1222A] Spirit, or Christ’s name, Cyprian interpreted the Father, Christ, and Holy Spirit possessed by them as not being the same as those of Catholics, because the faith was not the same; and therefore he held that the baptism was not the same. In the *Epistle to Jubaianus*:

> “For if we and the heretics have one faith, we can also have one grace. If they confess the same Father, the same Son, the same Holy Spirit, and the same Church, there can also be one baptism there, if there is also one faith, etc. Does Marcion hold this Trinity? Does he maintain the same God the Father and Creator whom we maintain? Does he maintain the same one Son, Christ, born of the Virgin Mary? etc. Marcion’s faith is far different, as is that of the others; indeed, among them there is nothing except faithlessness.”

Cyprian anxiously investigates [Col. 1222B] not what is invoked, but what is believed by the baptizer, whereas Stephen examined not the baptizer’s faith but the power of the words.

And below:

> “Therefore baptism cannot be common to us and the heretics, since neither God the Father, nor Christ the Son, nor the Holy Spirit, nor the faith itself within the Church is common to us.”

Since Cyprian by this decree includes even the Novatians, who are known to have preserved uncorrupted the faith in the Trinity and in Christ’s flesh, it is plain that he says we do not have the same God and the same Christ in common with heretics even if the invocation of the names is the same.

## VIII. From the Council of Carthage

The Council of Carthage likewise discloses the principal point upon which this dispute depended:

> “Either heretics [Col. 1222C] are permitted nothing, or they are permitted everything. If they can baptize, they can also give the Holy Spirit. But if they cannot give the Holy Spirit, because they do not possess the Holy Spirit, neither can they baptize spiritually.”

In the same place, another bishop who adhered to Cyprian says:

> “Are heretics Christians or not? If they are Christians, why are they not within the Church of God? How do they make Christians?”

Cyprian therefore considered only the person of the ministers; Stephen considered only the efficacy of Christ’s words. For if both the minister had been a heretic and the formula impious, why would Stephen have permitted this to be called baptism even in name? Why would he have approved in a heretic what he would have abominated even in a Catholic man?

Finally, the very terms indicate the matter. The inquiry concerns the baptism of heretics—that is, [Col. 1222D] baptism conferred by heretics—where the only evident ground for doubt is that derived from the person of the heretical baptizer. For if a heretic both baptizes and, in baptizing, invokes profane phantoms of the Deity, who would regard these cases indiscriminately? Who would even call this baptism? Who would confuse it with the baptism of the Novatians and approve both equally?

## IX. From Tertullian

The same point is established from Tertullian. For in the book *On Modesty*, in defense of this very opinion of Cyprian, he says:

> “A heretic, equal to a pagan—indeed, worse than a pagan—is admitted even through the baptism of truth.”

And in the book *On Baptism*:

> “Our God and theirs is not the same; [Col. 1223A] nor is there one Christ—that is, the same Christ. Consequently there is not one baptism either, because it is not the same.”

Lest you suspect that these words concern the Marcionites alone, consult Cyprian again, Book I, Epistle 6, where he argues the same point more fully concerning the Novatians.

## X. Likewise from the Council of Arles

I come to canon 8 of the Council of Arles, in the year 314:

> “Concerning the Africans, because they follow their own rule of rebaptizing, it was resolved that, if anyone comes to the Church from a heresy, they should question him concerning the Creed. If they perceive that he was baptized in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, the hand alone should be imposed upon him, so that he may receive the Holy Spirit. But if, when questioned, he does not confess this Trinity, let him be baptized.”

Why does this canon criticize only the Africans and not the Romans as well, if both were involved in error—[Col. 1223B] different indeed, yet equally absurd? Or, if there was an intention to spare the Romans, why was the name of the Africans not also spared, with the rule of baptism alone being prescribed?

Indeed, the Romans should rather have been transfixed with condemnation as erring far more disgracefully, if they had regarded as valid a baptism conferred by a formula alien and hostile to the faith. For that is more atrocious than invalidating the baptism of heretics of every kind. In the latter case the impiety of the baptizer is always detestable, and so the zeal of the one who detests it is at least excused. But in the former case the profanation both of baptism and of the baptizer is manifest, and hence the ignorance of those who approved it would have been wholly inexcusable.

## XI. From Eusebius

Eusebius too defends Stephen and removes from him [Col. 1223C] every suspicion of error, Book VII, chapter 2:

> “To this Stephen Dionysius wrote the first of the letters composed concerning baptism. At that time a considerable controversy had arisen over whether those converted from any heresy whatsoever ought to be purified by baptism, since the ancient custom had prevailed that in the case of such persons only the imposition of hands accompanied by prayers should be employed. Cyprian, the first of all—who at that time governed the Church of Carthage—held that they should be admitted only after first being cleansed from error through baptism. Stephen, however, judging that nothing should be introduced contrary to the tradition which had prevailed from ancient times, took this very badly.”

He casts all the blame for innovation back upon Cyprian—or upon Cyprian’s [Col. 1223D] predecessor Agrippinus—whereas he says of Stephen only that he resolved to preserve the ancient custom, a matter in which he certainly could not have erred.

## XII. From Stephen’s Own Words

The same point becomes perfectly evident from Stephen’s own words, reported by Cyprian and Firmilian: that nothing should be innovated, but what has been handed down should be preserved. Who does not understand this to be the surest remedy against every error, rather than words by which some error might be administered?

For this discipline of the Roman Church had prevailed from the beginning of the preaching of the Gospel, as Eusebius indicates. Or, if something different from what the Apostles and apostolic men had practiced had afterward been introduced by some Roman prelate, [Col. 1224A] Stephen would not have rested so confidently upon tradition and antiquity. Cyprian or Firmilian would at some point have indicated some beginning of the Roman tradition—or corruption—as though pointing out its cradle, since the learning and fervor of both men in this affair are very well known.

Eusebius notes the recent beginnings of the African discipline, but by no means of the Roman. Finally, Cyprian himself professes that he follows Agrippinus as his authority; yet he nowhere identifies any first leader whom Stephen follows, but repeatedly cries that truth must be preferred to custom and tradition, whose authority he could not overthrow.

Thus he writes in Epistle 71:

> “This indeed Agrippinus established together with the other bishops, his colleagues, who at that time governed the Church of the Lord in the province of Africa and Numidia; [Col. 1224B] and, after weighing it in the examination of a common council, he confirmed it. We too have followed their judgment.”

And in the *Epistle to Jubaianus*:

> “Among us it is no new or sudden thing to judge that those who come to the Church from the heretics must be baptized, since many years and a long period have now passed since a great many bishops, assembling together under Agrippinus, a man of blessed memory, established this; and since then down to the present day so many thousands of heretics converted to the Church in our provinces have obtained the grace of saving baptism.”

He betrays the novelty of his own custom while advertising its antiquity. But since he is unable to deny the antiquity of the Roman discipline, he cries shortly afterward that truth alone must be served:

> “Accordingly, certain persons who are overcome by reason vainly oppose custom to us, [Col. 1224C] as though custom were greater than truth, or as though in spiritual matters we ought not to follow whatever better thing may have been revealed by the Holy Spirit.”

The same error that is therefore imputed to Stephen is imputed to the most ancient tradition of the Churches, and likewise to the Apostles themselves, his teachers.

## XIII. Stephen’s Argument Against Cyprian Is Defended

Cyprian assailed with sneers and taunts Stephen’s argument from the example of the heretics. Yet, with the leave of the most holy martyr, I would say that nothing could have been more appropriate than Stephen’s reasoning, and nothing more ill-considered than Cyprian’s derision of it.

For from this it became perfectly evident that the heretics had introduced no innovation into the solemn formula of baptism [Col. 1224D] and had mingled with it no stain arising from their peculiar delusions, since different heretics did not reject one another’s baptism. For they detested one another’s errors and would therefore also have detested one another’s baptism if it had been corrupted by each sect’s distinctive ravings.

Stephen therefore had the same reason as the heretics for not repeating baptism conferred outside the Church.

## XIV. It Is Likewise Shown from Jerome That Stephen Did Not Err in the Question of Baptism
Moreover, Jerome, in his *Dialogue against the Luciferians*, writes things that not even men of the most shameless effrontery would dare deny were written in defense of Stephen:

> “Blessed Cyprian attempted to flee from broken cisterns and not [Col. 1225A] to drink from another’s water; and therefore, rejecting the baptism of heretics, he sent an African synodical letter on this matter to Stephen, then bishop of the city of Rome, who was the twenty-sixth from Blessed Peter. But his attempt was in vain. Finally, those very bishops who had decreed with him that heretics should be rebaptized returned to the ancient custom and issued a new decree. What are we to do? Our forefathers handed it down to us in this way, and their forefathers likewise handed it down to them.”

You see how he assigns innovation to Cyprian and the antiquity of tradition to Stephen; how, finally, he says that Cyprian’s colleagues eventually repented of their attempt and returned to the ancient custom of Stephen and of their own forefathers. And immediately afterward he maintains, with confirming examples, that Stephen’s judgment and tradition were truly apostolic, truly propagated while the Apostles were still alive [Col. 1225B]. He enumerates the bands of apostates and heretics that harassed the Church in her very cradle, yet of none of them do we read that baptism was repeated:

> “But why should I speak of later persons? While the Apostles were still surviving in the world, while Christ’s blood was still fresh in Judaea, it was being asserted that the Lord’s body was an apparition. The Apostle again labors in childbirth over the Galatians, who had been drawn over to observance of the Law; he attempts by many arguments to draw the Corinthians, who did not believe in the resurrection of the body, back to the true path. At that time Simon Magus and his disciple Menander claimed that they were powers of God. Then came Basilides, etc.; likewise Nicolaus, etc.; Saturninus, etc.; Carpocrates, Cerinthus, his successor Ebion, and the other plagues, most of whom [Col. 1225C] broke forth while the Apostle John was still alive. And yet we read that none of them was rebaptized.”

You see that Jerome employs no division by which he might teach that some heretics should be baptized in the Church and others should not. Rather, he denies universally that any should be baptized again, or that any were baptized again by the Apostles or their successors, even though many of them had already belched forth monstrous fabrications about God. Nor could Jerome have been unaware, amid the great illumination of his age—and especially so long after the Synod of Arles—that no baptism was valid unless sanctified in the name of the Trinity. Therefore, if Simon, Menander, Basilides, Carpocrates, Cerinthus, and Ebion had not corrupted the ecclesiastical form of baptism, so that their baptism was not to be rendered void, it is entirely reasonable to infer the same [Col. 1225D] concerning the others down to the time of Stephen.

## XV. AGAIN FROM THE SAME AUTHOR

Jerome proceeds there to argue the same point from the Apocalypse, where many persons infected with heretical madness are mentioned; yet neither they nor their disciples are commanded to receive baptism, but rather penance for the cleansing of their stains:

> “From the Apocalypse also let us prove that penance ought to be granted to heretics without baptism. In the angel of the Church of Pergamum, the teaching concerning things sacrificed to idols and that of the Nicolaitans is rebuked. Likewise, in the angel of Thyatira, the prophetess Jezebel, the eating of things sacrificed to idols, and fornications are denounced. And yet the Lord exhorts all these persons to penance [Col. 1226A], etc. Did he say: ‘Let those who were baptized in the faith of the Nicolaitans be rebaptized’? On the contrary, he says: ‘Do penance,’ etc.”

Thus Jerome demonstrates that the deeply rooted custom which Stephen defended tooth and nail had been derived from the Apostles themselves and recorded on the very pages of divine Scripture. Moreover, like Stephen, Jerome separates heretics by no distinction: he places them all in one vessel and commands that all be cleansed by penance, not by baptism.

## XVI. AGAIN FROM THE SAME AUTHOR

But clearer than all the rest are the arguments which Jerome presents below against Hilary the deacon, the herald of the Luciferian schism, who thereby became a new Deucalion for the world because he madly insisted that those coming from the Arians must be baptized anew:

> “If heretics do not possess baptism [Col. 1226B], and must therefore be rebaptized by the Church because they were not in the Church, then Hilary himself is not a Christian either. For he was baptized in that Church which has always accepted baptism from heretics. Before the Synod of Rimini was held, before Lucifer went into exile, Hilary, as a deacon of the Roman Church, received those coming from heretics in the baptism which they had previously received. Unless, perhaps, only the Arians are heretics, and it is impermissible to receive baptism conferred by them alone, while baptism conferred by others may be received. You were a deacon, Hilary, and you received those baptized by the Manichaeans. You were a deacon, and you approved the baptism of Ebion. Suddenly, after Arius arose, you began to be wholly displeased with yourself.”

And a little later he introduces the Roman Church addressing Hilary:

> “If you were born in my bosom [Col. 1226C], if you were nourished with the milk of my breasts, and yet raise a sword against me, return what I gave you, and, if you can, become a Christian in some other way. I am a harlot, but nevertheless I am your mother. Do I not preserve fidelity to a single marriage bed? I was such when you were conceived. Do I commit adultery with Arius? I did so before with Praxeas, with Ebion, with Cerinthus, and with Novatus.”

You see how here also he maintains that absolutely all heretics were received by the Roman Church through penance alone, without a new baptism; and he defends this practice as grounded in right, apostolic institution, and the unshaken precept of the divine Scriptures. Accordingly, he concludes that even Arians must be admitted without baptism. Moreover, Jerome wrote these things after the Synod of Arles and after the Nicene decree concerning baptism.

## XVII. FROM THE SAME AUTHOR

[Col. 1226D]

Finally, he consistently strengthens the same point still further:

> “But if anyone should think it must be denied that heretics were always received by our forefathers, let him read the letters of Blessed Cyprian, in which he rends Stephen, bishop of the city of Rome, and the error of the long-established custom. Let him also read the treatises which Hilary himself published against us concerning the rebaptism of heretics; there he will find Hilary himself confessing that Julius, Mark, Sylvester, and the other ancient bishops similarly received all heretics into penance, yet insisting that custom ought not to prejudice truth. The Synod of Nicaea also [Col. 1227A] received all heretics, with the exception of the disciples of Paul of Samosata.”

You see here also that all heretics were received without repetition of baptism by the Roman Church, both after the Synods of Arles and Nicaea and before them. Therefore, if any fault is imputed to Stephen, the same stain must be smeared upon all the Roman bishops after the Synods of Arles and Nicaea—synods at which the Roman See had been represented by legates and of which it had always stood forth as the foremost champion—and upon Jerome himself, their herald. Again you see how favorable and consonant with Stephen was the Synod of Nicaea, which “received all heretics except the disciples of Paul of Samosata”—persons who in Stephen’s age had not yet raised their ill-fated head from hell. Nothing, therefore, could be more impudent or more ignorant than the fiction of the innovators of this age, who prattle that the Nicene [Col. 1227B] Synod supported neither Stephen, who received all without baptism, nor Cyprian, who received none without baptism, but employed a distinction by which the error of each was corrected. For the Nicene Fathers entirely supported Stephen: those heretics whom he ordered to be received without baptism, they too ordered to be received; those whom they decreed should be baptized had not yet arisen, and Stephen could not have foreknown that they would. Finally, Jerome nowhere complains, even in the slightest degree, of an error either by Stephen or by those who did not repeat baptism conferred by heterodox words.

## XVIII. THE SAME IS ESTABLISHED FROM BASIL

To these may be added Basil, *Letter to Amphilochius*, chapter 1. For although he disapproves to some degree of the Roman pontiffs’ custom concerning baptism, he attributes it not to error but to *oikonomia* (pastoral accommodation) [Col. 1227C]. And although he himself subscribes to it less fully, he nevertheless assents to it for the sake of *oikonomia*, so that those who wish may adhere to it. He is somewhat angry with Dionysius of Alexandria for approving the baptism of the Pepuzenes, which departed monstrously from the faith; he mentions Cyprian and Firmilian not without praise; but he wholly abstains from censuring Stephen, who nevertheless, if any credit were due to recent calumniators, had stumbled far more disgracefully than Dionysius:

> “The baptism of the Pepuzenes seems to me to have no rational basis, and I have wondered how this escaped the great Dionysius, who was a canonist.”

And below:

> “The Pepuzenes blasphemed against the Holy Spirit, impiously attributing the title of Paraclete to Montanus and Priscilla. What reason, then, is there for judging the baptism of those who baptize into [Col. 1227D] the Father, the Son, Montanus, and Priscilla to be valid? For those who were not baptized into what was handed down to us have not been baptized. Therefore, even if this escaped the great Dionysius, we must not preserve an imitation of his error.”

Here one may easily perceive the error from which Basil, rather than Dionysius, suffers. For the Pepuzenes had corrupted the faith, not the words of baptism. They baptized not into the names of Montanus and Priscilla, but into the name of the Holy Spirit; because they understood Montanus and Priscilla by that name, Basil, as a somewhat unhelpful interpreter, imagines that they baptized people into the names of Montanus and Priscilla, weighing their intention rather than their words. For that reason the Montanists were not rebaptized by the Romans.

## XIX. FROM SIRICIUS, INNOCENT I, AND POPE LEO I

[Col. 1228A]

Innocent I, *Letter* 22, chapter 4, likewise unconcerned with distinctions, says:

> “The law of our Church is that to those coming from heretics, provided that they were baptized there, we grant through the imposition of hands only lay communion, etc.”

When he says, “provided that they were baptized there,” he indicates that both he and his forefathers required true baptism, consecrated with the words of the Gospel; otherwise it should not even be called baptism. Hence, in chapter 5 of the same letter, investigating why the Synod of Nicaea had been so favorable to the Novatians but so opposed to the Paulianists that it did not even remove the former from the clergy, while invalidating even the baptism of the latter, he says:

> “Plain reason declares that this distinction was made between these two heresies because the Paulianists did not baptize in the name [Col. 1228B] of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, whereas the Novatians baptize in those same awesome and venerable names.”

Thus, although the holy Fathers pronounce without distinction that all who were baptized by heretics should be purified by penance alone, they are nevertheless conscious that nothing is to be called baptism unless it is sealed in the name of the Trinity. Again, since the Paulianists, because they did not baptize in the name of the Trinity, are commanded to be washed anew when they come to the Church, it follows that no other heretics in the time of the Synod of Nicaea had contaminated the mystery of baptism with a heretical formula of words.

This argument receives further strength from Siricius, *Letter* 1, chapter 1, who also argues from the decree of his predecessor Liberius:

> “In accordance with what was established in the synod, we unite Arians with the assembly of Catholics in the same way as Novatians and other heretics—solely through the invocation [Col. 1228C] of the sevenfold Spirit and the episcopal imposition of hands. The whole East and West also observe this.”

You see how little effort he makes to indicate a distinction. Likewise Leo I, *Letter* 37, chapter 2:

> “But if it is established that someone was baptized by heretics, the sacrament of regeneration is by no means to be repeated in his case.”

He plainly does not permit the name “baptism” to be applied except to what was conferred with the requisite observance. And *Letter* 79, chapter 7:

> “For those who received baptism from heretics, when they had not previously been baptized, are to be confirmed solely by the invocation of the Holy Spirit through the imposition of hands, because they received only the form of baptism, without the power of sanctification.”

And *Letter* 92, chapter 16:

> “But those who know that they were baptized, yet declare that they do not know [Col. 1228D] of what faith their baptizers were, are not to be rebaptized, in whatever manner they received the form of baptism.”

You see how they agree not merely with Stephen’s judgment, but with his very words: they regard all heretics indiscriminately and do not rebaptize those baptized by them; yet they clearly imply that none are called baptized except those who received the form of baptism, that is, the invocation of the Trinity.

## XX. LIKEWISE FROM AUGUSTINE

After these let Augustine follow, though he might have preceded them and alone stood in place of them all. But from him, what shall we first select, and what next, in defense of Stephen? For everything he wrote about baptism against the Donatists [Col. 1229A]—every chapter and almost every verse—treats this conflict between Stephen and Cyprian in such a way that all the majesty of sounder discipline and truth resides with Stephen. I shall select only a very few passages from the almost immeasurable mass of innumerable testimonies.

Thus, in Book I of *On Baptism, against the Donatists*, chapter 18:

> “For although Cyprian, a bishop of such great merit, held a view concerning baptism other than what truth, when more diligently investigated, would establish, many of his colleagues nevertheless held—although the matter had not yet been clearly manifested—the position embraced both by the Church’s prior custom and afterward by the whole Catholic world. Yet he did not separate himself from the others who thought differently by breaking communion with them.”

Do you hear that Stephen and those other colleagues of his from whom Cyprian dissented held [Col. 1229B] “the position embraced both by the Church’s prior custom and afterward by the whole Catholic world”?

And in Book II, chapter 7:

> “That question concerning baptism had not yet been diligently examined. Nevertheless, the Church maintained a most salutary custom, which I believe came from apostolic tradition, just as many things are not found in the writings of the Apostles or in later councils, and yet, because they are observed throughout the universal Church, are believed to have been handed down and commended only by the Apostles themselves.”

Therefore, Stephen and the universal Church with him—if Cyprian and his supporters are excepted—maintained not a wandering custom that would afterward require correction, but an apostolic custom that would be confirmed afterward by the plenary Councils of Arles and Nicaea.

And in the same book, chapter 9:

> “A universal council had not yet been held, because the world was held by the strength [Col. 1229C] of custom, and this alone was opposed to those wishing to introduce an innovation.”

And in Book IV, chapter 6:

> “Nor do I find why they reject this custom, which after Cyprian was also confirmed by a plenary council of the whole world, etc.; for when Cyprian sought authority for changing that custom, he found only the Council of Agrippinus, held in Africa alone a few years before him. Since he saw that this was not sufficient for him against the custom of the whole world, etc.”

And in Book V, chapter 23:

> “Until it became clear through a plenary council what was more correct, it was not established by some innovation, but strengthened by antiquity.”

You see the purpose and accomplishment of the plenary council, whether assembled at Arles or at Nicaea. It was not to create a new classification of heretics, but to confirm the ancient custom [Col. 1229D] defended by Stephen, illuminating it with the kindled torch of truth.

And in Book VII, chapter 20:

> “For when the truth was afterward more clearly revealed, error yielded to truth, since that most salutary custom was also confirmed by the authority of a plenary council.”

And in *On the One Baptism, against Petilian*, chapter 14:

> “Behold, there were at one time—to say nothing of others—two men who held different views: they were the bishops of the two most eminent churches, namely Rome and Carthage, Stephen and Cyprian, both established in Catholic unity. Many agreed with the former, and some also with the latter, etc.”

Who, moreover, was more practiced than Augustine in this controversy? Who entered more deeply into the investigation of this question, which was still burning in the dispute with the Donatists? To whom were the words and opinions [Col. 1230A] both of Stephen and of Cyprian more thoroughly known? Those words of Stephen—“from whatsoever heresy”—had not escaped him. Yet he did not infer from them that Stephen had erred; on the contrary, he concluded that Stephen had adhered invincibly to apostolic tradition. And who could perceive more clearly than Augustine the meaning and fruit of the canon of Arles and of the plenary council—not in correcting, but in confirming, the former custom?

## XXI. HOW UNSPEAKABLE IT IS TO CLAIM THAT THE WHOLE CHURCH ONCE ERRED EVEN IN THIS MATTER

Heretics, for whom the bride of Christ is a brothel, eagerly embrace the assertion that the universal Church once lay in darkness in this matter and was entangled in the snares of falsehood. Far be it, however, that Catholic men should ever assent to this [Col. 1230B]. To say nothing of the rest, let them subscribe rather to Augustine, a witness close to the event, than to recent heretics who, almost fourteen hundred years later, continually give birth to new monstrosities of lies and slanders.

Let Augustine teach them not to harbor such base suspicions concerning the Church of Christ. In Book II of *Against Cresconius the Grammarian*, chapter 33, he says:

> “Accordingly, although no example of this practice can certainly be produced from the canonical Scriptures, nevertheless the truth of those same Scriptures is maintained by us in this matter also, when we do what has pleased the universal Church, which the authority of those Scriptures themselves commends. Therefore, since Holy Scripture cannot deceive, whoever fears being deceived by the obscurity of this question should consult concerning it that same Church which [Col. 1230C] Holy Scripture demonstrates without any ambiguity.”

Thus, where Scripture is silent, the rule not only of faith but also of sounder discipline is nevertheless the Church herself, concerning whom Scripture is not silent. But if the universal Church had at some time lain in error, although of a different kind, what purpose would there have been in consulting her? If the universal Church had erred outside a council, why could she not also have erred in a plenary council? Is the representation of the Church safer from error than the Church herself? Is she safer when gathered in one place than when spread throughout the world? Or, when she herself is spread throughout all the earth, is the Holy Spirit, the intimate guest of the heart, likewise dispersed and made to vanish? What Catholic would not be moved to indignation by these claims?

## XXII. LIKEWISE FROM VINCENT OF LÉRINS

[Col. 1230D]

Vincent of Lérins likewise cuts off every opportunity for quibbling in *Commonitorium* I, chapter 9:

> “At one time, therefore, Agrippinus of venerable memory, bishop of Carthage, was the first of all mortals to judge that baptism must be repeated, contrary to the divine canon, contrary to the rule of the universal Church, contrary to the judgment of all his fellow bishops, and contrary to the custom and institutions of the forefathers. This presumption introduced so great an evil that it provided not only a pattern of sacrilege for all heretics, but also an occasion of error for certain Catholics. Therefore, when everyone everywhere protested against the novelty of the matter, and all bishops throughout the world resisted, each according to his zeal, then Pope Stephen of blessed memory, the bishop of the Apostolic See, resisted together with [Col. 1231A] his other colleagues, yet more than all the rest; deeming it fitting, as I suppose, that he should surpass all others as much in devotion to the faith as he excelled them in the authority of his position.
