Finally, in the letter then sent to Africa, he decreed in these words: ‘Let nothing be innovated beyond what has been handed down.’”

Here you perceive how everything is arranged in Stephen’s defense. Vincent wrote these things after the Councils of Arles and Nicaea and after the general Council of Constantinople. He therefore did not suppose that Stephen’s judgment had been rejected by these councils equally with Cyprian’s.

Add to these Facundus, bishop of Hermiane, Book X:

> “Although Cyprian had determined, not only privately, as seemed good to him, but also in an assembled council, that every heretic returning to the Church should be baptized, and although [Col. 1231B] for this reason he resisted when censured by Stephen, the Roman pontiff, treating that same Blessed Stephen abusively, by whom he had rightly been censured, etc.”

And in his book *Against Mocianus*:

> “For this reason also, when Blessed Stephen, prelate of the Apostolic See, learned that Saint Cyprian and the other African bishops had decreed that all heretics should be baptized, he immediately declared to him that, if any dared to do this, they would be expelled from the Church. And the Church maintains the judgment of Stephen rather than that of Cyprian, not only concerning the non-rebaptism of heretics, but also concerning the refusal to tolerate those who rebaptize.”

What could one desire more explicit than these statements?

## XXIII. FROM HINCMAR OF RHEIMS, AND AGAIN FROM AUGUSTINE

Finally, lest I proceed too far, Hincmar, in his short work of fifty-five chapters [Col. 1231C], chapter 19, says:

> “And because the Council of Nicaea commanded that Paulianist heretics coming to the Church be baptized, certain persons said that other heretics also ought to be baptized. The Apostolic See and plenary councils—as the decrees of the Roman pontiffs and Saint Augustine abundantly demonstrate in both words and meaning—utterly rejected this.”

For the Paulianists, as Innocent taught above, did not baptize in the name of the Trinity, whereas almost all other heretics did, even though under those names they did not embrace the same faith as the Catholic Church. Hence Augustine, in Book III of *On Baptism, against the Donatists*, chapter 15:

> “Accordingly, if Marcion consecrated baptism with the words of the Gospel, in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, the sacrament was complete, although his faith—which under those same words entertained an opinion different from what Catholic truth teaches [Col. 1231D]—was not complete, but polluted by fabulous falsehoods. For under those same words, that is, under the names of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, not only Marcion, Valentinus, Arius, or Eunomius, but even the carnal little ones of the Church, of whom the Apostle said, ‘I could not speak to you as spiritual persons, but as carnal,’ might perhaps, if each could be diligently questioned, exhibit as many varieties of opinion as there were people.”

Consult Epiphanius and others who wrote about heresies: although nearly all pursued even minute details, you will scarcely find that the form of baptism was overthrown by any except one or two. Hence Augustine aptly says in Book VI of *On Baptism, against the Donatists*:

> “But who does not know [Col. 1232A] that it is not Christ’s baptism if the words of the Gospel in which the formula consists were lacking there? Yet it is easier to find heretics who do not baptize at all than heretics who do not baptize with those words.”

## XXIV. A SECOND CONTROVERSY IS TOUCHED UPON: WHETHER, AFTER STEPHEN’S DECREE, A PLENARY COUNCIL WAS STILL NECESSARY, AS AUGUSTINE SEEMS TO SUGGEST

By now, I think, it has become sufficiently—and more than sufficiently—clear how little credit should be given to the innovators, since they have attempted to deceive in so manifest a matter and to struggle against the wholly unanimous judgment of all the Fathers.

Let us now prepare to resolve the second part of this controversy. From the testimonies of Augustine set out above, it appeared that he regarded both of Stephen’s opponents as excused [Col. 1232B] because the matter had not yet been defined and elucidated by a plenary council of the Church. Therefore, before the definition of a plenary council, are those who despise the decrees of the Apostolic See implicated in no fault? Was there such equality between Cyprian and Stephen that, amid disagreement on so important a matter, each had an equal right to follow his own judgment?

## XXV. ON THE CONTRARY, FROM THE SAME AUGUSTINE: EVEN BEFORE THE COUNCIL, STEPHEN’S AUTHORITY WAS SUPREME, AND CYPRIAN’S ERROR WAS TO BE EXPIATED, NOT EXCUSED

Augustine himself guarantees that this was by no means the case. For in Book V, chapter 23 of *On Baptism, against the Donatists*, he says:

> “Cyprian writes that Stephen, whom we have learned was then bishop of the Roman Church [Col. 1232C], not only did not agree with him in these matters, but even wrote against him and issued a command.”

Thus, elsewhere above Augustine said that there were two prelates of the most eminent churches holding different views, yet here he acknowledges that one commanded the other.

And in Book I of *On Baptism, against the Donatists*, chapter 18:

> “In that Church, if some still held one opinion on this question and others another, while peace was preserved, until some single refined and purified judgment should please a universal council, the charity of unity would cover the error of human weakness; as it is written, ‘Charity covers a multitude of sins.’ For when charity is absent, other things are possessed in vain; when charity is present, certain things may pardonably be lacking.”

He does not conceal the fact that Cyprian sinned; for immediately afterward he says that Cyprian “attained the palm of martyrdom, so that, if any cloud arising from the human condition [Col. 1232D] had crept into his luminous mind, it might be dispersed by the glorious radiance of his shining blood.”

He then adds that, because Cyprian had thought differently concerning baptism from the way the matter actually stood, “this was compensated for by the abundance of his charity and purged by the sickle of suffering.”

And in Book V, chapter 25:

> “I do not wish now to reconsider those things which Cyprian, when irritated, poured out against Stephen, because there is no need. It is better to pass over those things which contained the danger of a destructive dissension. Stephen, however, had judged that those who attempted to uproot the ancient custom concerning the reception of heretics should be excluded from communion. Cyprian, moved by the difficulty of this question and most abundantly endowed with the affections of holy charity, judged that unity should be maintained with those who held a different opinion. Thus, although he expressed his indignation with greater agitation, he nevertheless did so fraternally [Col. 1233A]. Yet the peace of Christ prevailed in their hearts, so that no evil of schism arose between them in such a dispute.”

You see how Augustine censures Cyprian’s vehemence and maintains that Stephen approved those same things which the universal Church afterward approved: that the baptism of heretics should not be repeated, and that those who repeated it should be excluded from communion. Finally, Stephen at length acquiesced in the dispensation by which Cyprian indulged his own error in order to avert schism. For although by no decree, nevertheless through the very patience with which he restrained the threatened thunderbolt, Stephen consented to this *oikonomia*. Therefore, once Stephen consented to that *oikonomia*, those who awaited a plenary council were no longer despising his authority.

## XXVI. FROM THE SAME AUTHOR: CYPRIAN IS COMPARED WITH PETER—ERRING, BUT BOUND TO LISTEN TO A COLLEAGUE WHO CORRECTED HIM

[Col. 1233B]

What of the fact that Augustine compares Cyprian to Peter hundreds of times: bishop to Apostle, erring man to erring man, martyr to martyr? Yet when Peter yielded to Paul’s correction, those who followed Peter’s error were cut off from the Church. Likewise, the imitators of the martyr Cyprian broke themselves away from unity. Book VII, chapter 1:

> “Heretics born from that error into which Peter strayed and from which Paul recalled him persist in it to this day. Therefore, just as they remained in their perversity, cut off from the Church, although Peter was crowned with the glory of martyrdom in the primacy of the Apostles, so these men—although Cyprian, through the abundance of his charity, was received into the lot of the saints by the splendor of his suffering—acknowledge themselves, by their own doing, to be exiles from unity.”

[Col. 1233C]

Thus Cyprian ought at least to have obeyed Stephen as Peter obeyed Paul. He therefore washed that fault away besides with his blood.

And in Book III, chapter 8:

> “It warns us that it was not impossible for Cyprian to think something about baptism otherwise than truth required—that truth which was maintained by the Church both before him and after him—just as Peter also could think something otherwise than truth held, as we learned from the teaching of the Apostle Paul.”

## XXVII. FROM THE SAME AUTHOR: HOW CYPRIAN CANNOT BE EXCUSED, SINCE HE DISOBEYED APOSTOLIC TRADITION AND THE UNIVERSAL CHURCH

That even Augustine could not absolve Cyprian is further evident from Book II of *On Baptism, against the Donatists*, chapter 7, where he says that, although the matter had not yet been more diligently examined:

> “The Church nevertheless maintained a most salutary custom [Col. 1233D], etc., which custom I believe came from apostolic tradition, just as many things are not found in the writings of the Apostles or in later councils, and yet, because they are observed throughout the universal Church, are believed to have been handed down and commended only by the Apostles themselves. Saint Cyprian therefore says that this most salutary custom had, as it were, begun to be corrected through his predecessor Agrippinus. But as truth, more diligently investigated, has taught, it is more truly believed that it began to be corrupted through Agrippinus, not corrected.”

Elsewhere he repeatedly emphasizes that this custom of not repeating baptism had been observed until then by the universal Church. [Col. 1234A] Cyprian therefore could not be freed from blame, since he despised the custom of the universal Church and a tradition derived from the Apostles themselves, preferring to them the recent corruption introduced by Agrippinus. It is thus less surprising that he made light of the decrees of the Apostolic See, since he treated apostolic traditions and the laws of the universal Church as worthless. From this contempt of Cyprian—which he expiated by martyrdom—nothing can properly be objected against the authority either of the First See, of the universal Church, or of apostolic traditions.

## XXVIII. THE SAME POINTS ARE CONFIRMED FROM JEROME, VINCENT OF LÉRINS, AND FACUNDUS OF HERMIANE

Thus Jerome, in his *Dialogue against the Luciferians* [Col. 1234B], joins together the two authorities which Cyprian attacked in vain: that of the Apostolic See and that of the universal Church:

> “Let him read the letters of Blessed Cyprian, in which he rends Stephen, bishop of the city of Rome, and the error of the long-established custom.”

Likewise Vincent of Lérins, in the passage cited above:

> “Stephen, bishop of the Apostolic See, resisted Cyprian together with his other colleagues, yet more than all the rest; deeming it fitting, as I suppose, that he should surpass all the others as much in devotion to the faith as he excelled them in the dignity of his position.”

It was certainly right that Cyprian should comply with one who surpassed his other colleagues both in devotion to the faith and in the dignity of his position. But what wonder if he did not yield to Stephen, since he instead attached himself to Agrippinus, “the first of all mortals to judge that baptism must be repeated, contrary to the divine canon [Col. 1234C], contrary to the rule of the universal Church, contrary to the judgment of all his fellow bishops, and contrary to the custom and institutions of the forefathers”?

Thus Facundus also said above that Cyprian was “rightly censured” by Stephen, and that the Church adhered to Stephen’s judgment—not Cyprian at that time, indeed, but the Church both then and afterward.

## XXIX. AGAIN FROM AUGUSTINE

Again, although Augustine was not unaware that eighty bishops agreed with Cyprian and fifty with Firmilian, he nevertheless confidently affirms that the entire Christian world stood on Stephen’s side [Col. 1234D]. From this it is once more evident that nothing can be objected here against either Stephen’s authority and decrees or those of the universal Church. Rather, Stephen’s power—and the Church’s—is to be understood as invincible, but exceedingly restrained and tempered by many indulgent concessions of *oikonomia* and pardon.

Book III of *Against Cresconius*, chapter 3:

> “Accordingly, if it must now be believed without qualification that fifty Eastern bishops held the same judgment as seventy African bishops, or even somewhat more, against so many thousands of bishops throughout the world to whom this error was displeasing, why should we not rather say that those few Eastern bishops also corrected their judgment?”

And Book II of *On Baptism, against the Donatists*, chapter 9:

> “A universal council had not yet been held, because the world was held by the strength of custom.”

See also Book IV, chapter 6, as we reported above. [Col. 1235A] Eusebius also, cited above, Book VII, chapters 2 and 3, indicates that the ancient custom which Stephen labored to defend had prevailed from the beginning throughout the whole Church. It is therefore necessary to conclude that Firmilian, carried away by zeal for his own party, strayed outside the path of truth when he boasted too freely of the number of his followers.

## XXX. STEPHEN DID NOT PROCEED BEYOND THREATS; AT LENGTH HE ACQUIESCED IN THE DISPENSATION AND THUS HIMSELF SUSPENDED THE EXECUTION OF HIS DECREE
That Stephen did not proceed beyond threats and intimidation, but, restraining the sacred blade, at least tacitly acquiesced in indulgence, lest the unity of the Church be torn apart for this reason, we gather from many [Col. 1235B] indications. Eusebius says that Stephen took Cyprian’s novel and unprecedented decree, and that of the Council of Carthage, extremely ill; but he does not relate that Stephen’s indignation boiled over any further, or that he attempted anything. Jerome, cited above, said that Cyprian had sent the decree of his council to Stephen, but that his attempt had been in vain; and finally that those same bishops had returned to the more ancient custom. Vincent of Lérins described Stephen’s fervor in the most magnificent terms, but is entirely silent about an anathema. Augustine, *On Baptism, Against the Donatists*, V.23: “Cyprian, writing to Pompeius, indicates that Stephen not only did not agree with him in these matters, but even wrote and issued instructions to the contrary.” That was the limit of his severity. And in *On the One Baptism, Against Petilian*, c. 14: “Although Stephen not [Col. 1235C] only did not rebaptize heretics, but also judged that those who did so, or decreed that it should be done, ought to be excommunicated—as the letters of other bishops and of Cyprian himself demonstrate—Cyprian nevertheless remained with him in the peace of unity.” He judged that they ought to be excommunicated; he did not excommunicate them. Stephen threatened; he did not strike. Cyprian therefore remained in the peace of unity, even with Stephen. Hence Augustine shortly afterward says in the same place: “Behold, there were at one and the same time—to say nothing of others—two men who held different opinions. They were the bishops of two most eminent churches, namely Rome and Carthage: Stephen and Cyprian, both established in Catholic unity. Many agreed with the former, and some also with the latter, while both men remained with them in unity.” [Col. 1235D] Nothing could be clearer than this.

Accordingly, Firmilian’s strident words to Cyprian against Stephen must be somewhat softened. They run thus: “Breaking peace with individuals through various kinds of discord: now with the Easterners, as we trust is not unknown to you; now with you who are in the south. He received the bishops sent as your delegates with such patience and gentleness that he would not admit them even to the speech of an ordinary conversation; and, further, he instructed the whole brotherhood that no one should receive them into his house, so that those who came were denied not only peace and communion, but also a bed and lodging.” Firmilian was indulging in rhetoric and, inflamed by the heat of his cause, flared up rather extravagantly. I do not dispute that Stephen may at first [Col. 1236A] have received Cyprian’s delegates rather harshly, in order to recall him to his duty; but the foregoing arguments conclusively prove that Stephen did not break peace with him. Finally, Cyprian himself, in the letter to Pompeius in which he assails Stephen’s rather harsh letter to him in the harshest terms, nevertheless calls Stephen his brother and nowhere mentions that communion had been broken. To crown the argument, Augustine says in *Against the Donatists*, V.25: “Stephen had thought that those who attempted to overthrow the ancient custom concerning the reception of heretics ought to be shunned. Cyprian thought that unity ought to be maintained with those who held a different opinion. Thus, although his indignation was more impassioned, it remained brotherly; nevertheless, the peace of Christ prevailed in their hearts, so that no evil of schism arose between them in such a dispute.” Stephen therefore [Col. 1236B] somehow consented that those who held different opinions should not be cut off from unity, and that a universal council should be awaited.

## XXXI. FROM AUGUSTINE: CYPRIAN OUGHT TO HAVE YIELDED TO WEIGHTIER AUTHORITY

Consequently, the reason his authority was resisted by many was his charity, which at last inclined him toward pardon and accommodation (*oeconomia*). Otherwise, however greatly Cyprian abounded in authority and richness of knowledge, Augustine himself declares that he nevertheless ought to have yielded to weightier authority, in *On Baptism, Against the Donatists*, II.3:

“You are certainly accustomed to set before us Cyprian’s letters, Cyprian’s opinion, Cyprian’s council, and so forth. Who does not know that canonical Holy Scripture is so far superior to all subsequent [Col. 1236C] letters of bishops that no doubt or dispute whatsoever may arise as to whether whatever is established as written in it is true or right? But the letters of bishops written, or still being written, after the canon was confirmed may be criticized—whether by the perhaps wiser discourse of anyone more expert in the matter, by the weightier authority and more learned prudence of other bishops, or by councils—if they should perhaps deviate from the truth in any respect.”

As you see, the letters of any bishops whatsoever, and hence even Cyprian’s, could be criticized not only by the wiser discourse of any private person, and not only by the assembly of a council, but also by the weightier authority and more learned [Col. 1236D] prudence of other bishops, and thus, above all others, of the Roman Pontiff. For Augustine clearly distinguishes these three.

## XXXII. CYPRIAN AND OTHERS WHO AGREED WITH HIM PERHAPS CAME TO THEIR SENSES

What if Cyprian himself came to his senses before his death? I certainly would not wish to bind the reputation for holiness of either him or Firmilian to this uncertainty. Yet neither would I wish confidently to reject a doubtful matter. Augustine, soberly and wisely in his customary manner, says in *On Baptism, Against the Donatists*, II:

“If Cyprian praises and proclaims that Peter was openly and harmoniously corrected by his junior colleague, how much more quickly would he himself, together with the council of his province, have yielded to the authority of the whole world once the truth had been disclosed? For surely [Col. 1237A] so holy and peaceable a soul could most readily have agreed even with a single man who spoke and demonstrated the truth. And perhaps this happened, but we do not know. For not everything transacted among bishops at that time could be committed to memory and writing; nor do we know everything that was committed to writing.”

You see that the holy Father neither lightly asserts these conjectures nor confidently rejects them. And in Letter 48: “Cyprian either did not hold at all the opinion you recite as his, or afterward corrected it according to the rule of truth, or covered this blemish, as it were, with the abundance of charity.”

Jerome teaches in *On Ecclesiastical Writers* that Dionysius of Alexandria “agreed with the doctrine of Cyprian and of the African synod.” Yet—to say nothing of his letters to the Roman Pontiffs preserved by Eusebius—Basil [Col. 1237B], in his letter to Amphilochius, complains more than once about Dionysius for approving the baptism of the Pepuzenes. Hence there is reason to conjecture that he finally adopted the Roman position. Jerome, moreover, says in *Against the Luciferians*: “Those very bishops who, together with Cyprian, had determined that heretics should be rebaptized returned to the ancient custom and issued a new decree,” etc. Augustine, *Against Cresconius*, III.2, intimates that “the Easterners corrected their judgment.” Baronius is therefore reproached in vain for suggesting something of this sort concerning Firmilian.

If confidence in that matter nevertheless remains uncertain, and if we ought not to indulge the suspicions of our own minds beyond measure, it will be wiser to hear Augustine again, in *On the One Baptism, Against Petilian*, c. 13:

“Nor are we, who acknowledge rather than deny the truth of Baptism even amid the iniquity of heretics, [Col. 1237C] therefore better than Cyprian, just as we are not better than Peter because we do not compel Gentiles to Judaize. I would make the same reply concerning Agrippinus and the other bishops who are said to have held those councils: they held a different opinion, yet persisted in unity with those against whom they differed on this question, where charity covers a multitude of sins.”

And let us again hear Bede, cited above, who praised Aidan’s life as conformed to the evangelical rule, but did not praise the fact that he failed to observe the canonical date of Easter, “either through ignorance, or because, although it had been recognized, he was prevailed upon by the authority of his own nation not to follow it” [the supplied Latin is textually uncertain].

## XXXIII. ANOTHER WAY OF RESOLVING THIS CONTROVERSY IS DISCLOSED, FROM THE DISTINCTION BETWEEN QUESTIONS OF FAITH AND QUESTIONS OF CUSTOM

[Col. 1237D] From this, in turn, another means presents itself of settling the conflict among various points of Augustinian doctrine. For Augustine both cut off from the Pelagians any hope of a plenary council, imposing on them the inexorable necessity of subscribing to the definitions of the African councils and especially of the Apostolic See; and yet afforded Cyprian and his colleagues the opportunity—or furnished them with a defense—not to acquiesce before a plenary council. For these questions differ by an immense interval. The former pertains to faith; the latter pertains more to the customs of the Church. All the faithful must agree in the unity of faith; unity of customs is not always necessary. For those who deviate from the faith no pardon remains unless [Col. 1238A] they return to the right path; those who depart from the proper course of customs are very often tolerated by indulgence. Accommodation has a place here, but not there. Once faith has been defined, it can never and nowhere subsequently be derogated from; disciplinary rules concerning customs, however they may have been established, are not infrequently set aside by a later age, at least through desuetude itself. Even when ecumenical councils sanction certain customs, obedience is either not immediately given or, after being given, later ceases—not without fault, but without injury to ecclesiastical unity. Faith, however, once established, must irrevocably be obeyed. Tertullian says in *On the Veiling of Virgins*: “The rule of faith is altogether one, alone immovable and incapable of reform.”

## XXXIV. VARIOUS EVIDENCES OF THIS DISTINCTION

[Col. 1238B] Perhaps this is why those who differed from the Catholic Church concerning the date of Easter were retained within the bosom of unity and peace until the Council of Nicaea, although the other heresies had been cut off from the body of the Church even before the Nicene Synod. This is why the Nicene Fathers labored vigorously to settle the question of Easter, yet took no care to proscribe again and thunder against, by the authority of an ecumenical synod, the innumerable ancient heresies that had previously been proscribed merely by provincial councils. This is why they also sought to quiet the dispute about Baptism, ordering only the Paulianists to be rebaptized. For just as discipline is by its nature freer and more variable, so a more universal consensus is required wherever it is restricted.

[Col. 1238C] This is why Cyprian contended vigorously and Stephen finally granted indulgence, so that those who held opinions different in any respect should nevertheless not depart from the indivisible bond of unity. Likewise, in the matter of Easter, Irenaeus and others judged that those who clung stubbornly to the less satisfactory observance should not be severed from the body of the Church. Finally, Augustine and Gregory will teach us below, in the appropriate place, that diversity of discipline can sometimes even be an adornment. Gregory, moreover, not merely assented to but even urged that rites differing from those of the Roman Church, wherever they appeared more suitable, should be transplanted into the English Church. In matters of faith, however, no one would grant this license.

## XXXV. THAT THIS QUESTION WAS HANDLED WITH FORBEARANCE AS PERTAINING TO CUSTOMS, NOT TO FAITH, IS PROVED FIRST FROM FIRMILIAN

[Col. 1238D] I am not unaware that these questions about the baptism of heretics may in some manner be referred to a matter of faith—far more so, indeed, than the question of the date of Easter, concerning which Victor called the churches that deviated heterodox. Yet I believe that this one fact shines forth from the writings of the ancient Fathers: they regarded this matter only as a part of ecclesiastical custom and discipline, and did not refer it to the substance and necessity of faith.

Firmilian held that dissent on these matters was possible without injury to the bond of unity, in his letter to Cyprian:

“Concerning the celebration of the days of Easter and many other sacraments of divine worship, one may see that certain differences exist among the Romans, and that not everything observed at Jerusalem is equally observed there. [Col. 1239A] Likewise, in very many other provinces, many things vary according to the diversity of places and names; yet the peace and unity of the Catholic Church has never been abandoned on this account. Stephen has now dared to do this, breaking peace with you—a peace which his predecessors always preserved with you in mutual love and honor.”

Throughout the whole tenor of the letter Firmilian rages against Stephen principally on this ground: that, instead of allowing each to enjoy his own customs, he dissolved the covenant of peace.

## XXXVI. LIKEWISE FROM CYPRIAN

Cyprian held the same view in his letter to Jubaianus. After surrounding his opinion with many arguments, he finally says: [Col. 1239B]

“We have written this brief reply to you according to our modest ability, prescribing or prejudging nothing for anyone, so that each bishop may do what he thinks best, since he possesses the free exercise of his own judgment. For our part, we do not contend on account of heretics with our colleagues and fellow bishops, with whom we maintain divine peace and the peace of the Lord. We patiently and firmly preserve charity of spirit, the honor of the college, the bond of love, and the concord of the priesthood.”

And at the opening of the Council of Carthage:

“It remains for each of us to set forth what we think concerning this very matter, judging no one and removing no one from the right of communion if he should hold a different opinion. For none of us appoints himself bishop of bishops, or by tyrannical terror compels his colleagues to the necessity [Col. 1239C] of obedience, since every bishop, in accordance with the liberty and power permitted him, possesses his own judgment,” etc.

These statements may be advanced with some appearance of reason in a matter of discipline, but in a question central to the Catholic faith they would all be utterly inappropriate. Moreover, the words “Let him do what he thinks best, possessing the free exercise of judgment,” “necessity of obedience,” and “Christ alone possesses the power to judge our action,” plainly refer to discipline, not to faith. For no one is permitted to dissent from his colleagues in matters of faith; if anyone stubbornly dissents, he must be cast out from peace and communion. But the ancient customs of his own church may be retained by any bishop, even if they differ from those of others, and are sometimes tolerated until a plenary council—and even beyond it.

## XXXVII. LIKEWISE FROM STEPHEN, THE SYNODS OF ARLES AND NICAEA, AND OPTATUS

[Col. 1239D]

Stephen held the same view when he commanded what ought to be done, not what ought to be believed, and appealed to the tradition of ancient custom. So too did Eusebius, described above, who mentions custom alone. So too did Jerome, whose lengthy disputation commends nothing other than ancient and long-established custom. The Council of Arles likewise held this view in canon 8, where it says: “Concerning the Africans who employ their own rule, so that they rebaptize,” without casting anything more insulting either at them or at their error. For if this had been considered contrary to the faith, why would it have been called neither madness nor [Col. 1240A] heresy, but merely their own rule of rebaptizing? Finally, the canons here contain only a rule of discipline, whereas in ancient councils a definition of faith was generally arranged separately.

The Council of Nicaea held the same view when it attempted to settle that entire controversy over Baptism, not by the Creed or a confession of faith, but by a single canon, and by this one decree: that from then on the Paulianists alone should be baptized again. We shall discuss in the proper place the Apostolic Canons that pertain to this same matter.

I add one further passage from Optatus, I: “Among whom the sacraments do not exist.” On these words Albaspinaeus comments: “Therefore, from this and many other passages, so far as I can judge, Optatus did not believe that heretics could baptize.”

## XXXVIII. LIKEWISE FROM BASIL

[Col. 1240B] Basil undoubtedly held the same view. In his letter to Amphilochius, after distinguishing heretics, who strive to undermine the very sum of the faith, from schismatics, who separated themselves over remediable questions, he says:

“It therefore seemed good from the beginning wholly to reject heretics, but to admit the Baptism of those who had separated themselves, or of schismatics, on the ground that they still belonged to the Church.”

Yet he immediately says that Firmilian and Cyprian thought that the Baptism of schismatics also should be repeated:

“But since it has seemed good to some Asians, entirely for the sake of accommodation and dispensation toward the many, that their Baptism should be accepted, let it be accepted.”

He says this concerning the Cathari; but immediately afterward, concerning the Encratites:

“Since nothing has been plainly stated concerning them, we ought to annul their Baptism. But if this is likely to become an obstacle to universal accommodation [Col. 1240C], custom must again be employed, and we ought to follow the Fathers who made provision concerning the matters that affect us.”

And below, in canon 47, he says that all those schismatics are rebaptized by him, and recommends the same to Amphilochius, although he says that it would be more expedient for all these controversies to be settled by an episcopal synod.

From this many arguments well up in support of our undertaking. First, he recalls the more ancient tradition, which employed a distinction, and then admits that he dissents from it. Basil would not have assumed this prerogative in a matter of faith. He places the Cathari and the Encratites in the same vessel of schismatics; then he permits the Baptism of the former to be accepted but forbids that of the latter. He would not have varied in this way on a question of faith. He judges that the Baptism of the Cathari may be accepted by dispensation. But in a matter of faith no place is granted to dispensation in this manner. [Col. 1240D] He recommends that the Encratites be rebaptized; yet if this conflicts with the peace of the universal Church and with accommodation, he judges that their Baptism should be admitted. Is this not precisely the variability of discipline?

He longs for a new synod to clear away all those doubts; therefore, scarcely every controversy had been stilled by that celebrated plenary council mentioned by Augustine. Thus, after the Council of Arles and after the Council of Nicaea, the dispute over Baptism still seemed to Basil scarcely to have been sufficiently elucidated. He desired a new synod; and once again the second ecumenical council decreed what was to be followed concerning that matter. Thus, after the enactments of Pope Stephen and of the Councils of Arles and Nicaea, Basil desired a new synod, because the matter was then regarded as one of discipline, not of faith. [Col. 1241A] This remains so even though at other times questions of discipline and custom pertaining to the spiritual principles of Baptism or the sacraments may be drawn into the sphere of faith, as we shall note below in the final section of this dissertation.

## XXXIX. FROM AMPHILOCHIUS

Amphilochius likewise held that, as to whether the Baptism of the Novatians should or should not be repeated, the custom of each individual church ought to be observed. Basil bears witness to this in chapter 1 of the letter written to him: “As regards the Cathari, therefore, you rightly reminded us that the custom of each region ought to be followed.” Balsamon interprets this as follows: “Concerning whether the Novatians ought to be baptized, different opinions have arisen, as you noted, and it was resolved to follow the custom of each region.”

## XL. FROM ATHANASIUS

[Col. 1241B]

Athanasius held the same view. These are his words in *Against the Arians*, Oration III:

“If the perfection of Baptism and complete initiation are given in the name of the Father and of the Son, but the Arians do not confess the true Father—because they deny that anything exists from him and is like his substance—and likewise deny the true Son, instead imagining another, created from things that do not exist, whom they name in Baptism: who, I ask, will not regard the Baptism given by them as altogether vain and useless, since it is nothing but an outward form and an empty semblance? For the Arians do not administer Baptism in the Father and the Son, but in the Creator and a creature, in the Maker and [Col. 1241C] a thing made. Therefore, just as a creature is something different from the Son, so what is thought to be given by them is something different from true Baptism, even though—because they see the names of Father and Son in the Scriptures—they pretend to pronounce them.”

And below:

“Certainly other heresies also, and not a few of them, pronounce this rite merely by name; but because they do not believe rightly or retain a sound faith, the water they possess is useless, being plainly destitute of light and true religion. Thus those sprinkled by them are soiled by false religion rather than redeemed.”

These are the words of a man of utterly stainless faith concerning the baptism administered by heretics and the other heresies, even if it were conferred with an invocation of the Trinity. Hear also what he immediately adds:

[Col. 1241D] “Likewise the Manichaeans, Phrygians, and disciples of Samosata are no less heretics merely because they pronounce the names themselves. So too, thereafter, are the rest and those who agree with Arius: even if they recite the writings and pronounce the names themselves, they deceive and mock those who receive Baptism from them.”

Observe here in passing that the very names of the divine persons, because they are set down in the sacred pages in a fixed formula, were pronounced during baptism by almost all heretics. Stephen, therefore, and the Roman Church, in forbidding that their Baptism be repeated, were implicated in no fault. Moreover, Athanasius openly supports Basil, judging that Baptism is void when, although conferred in the words of the Gospel, the understanding and faith of those who confer it are alien to the Gospel.

## XLI. FROM EPIPHANIUS

[Col. 1242A]

Epiphanius held the same view. The following notable passage from his *Exposition of the Catholic Faith*, no. 13, must be included here:

“Others among the Catholics, who seem more daring, have formed a private faction for themselves and, contrary to the custom of the Church and without a decree of a general council, have no hesitation in baptizing again those who pass from the Arians to their own party, although, as I have said, the matter has not yet been decided by the judgment of a universal synod, because down to the present day the people are still mingled indiscriminately. Among them, many are indeed Catholics, but disingenuously and by pretense they follow the authority of the priests until that execrable sect is separated from the communion of the Church, so that some determination concerning it may then be made. Of those who on their own authority baptize again in this manner, [Col. 1242B] I hear that one is a presbyter in Lycia.”

Henceforth, I think, no one will be surprised if Athanasius, Basil, and Amphilochius wavered and wished Baptism conferred by heretics in the name, but not in the faith, of the Trinity to be repeated. For Epiphanius—thoroughly acquainted with the customs of the Roman and Western Church—likewise wavered. He accused those who washed again persons already washed by the Arians, not of heresy, but of audacity, and repeatedly pleaded only that they should not persist in rebaptizing them before a universal council had issued a definition, especially since the Arians had not yet either withdrawn or been expelled from the communion of the Catholic Church.

## XLII. FROM CYRIL OF JERUSALEM

[Col. 1242C] Cyril of Jerusalem held the same view. In the preface to his *Catecheses*, he says indiscriminately of all heretics: “Heretics alone are rebaptized, since their former washing was not Baptism.”

But what report, even the faintest, of that plenary council assembled from the whole Christian world, so celebrated by Augustine, ever reached Basil, Amphilochius, Cyril of Jerusalem, or finally Epiphanius? Where was that agreement of the world, after a plenary council, that the Baptism of heretics should not be repeated? Yet the Council of Arles was surely the synod indicated by Augustine, held shortly before his birth, as we shall show elsewhere. Can any traces of it anywhere among the Greeks be scented out, even by men of the keenest nose? Neither Zonaras, nor Balsamon, nor any other Greek remembered it.

Moreover, where in the Council of Arles [Col. 1242D] is that abundant elucidation of the truth by which Cyprian’s doctrine was refuted and the reason and wisdom of Catholic and most ancient tradition shone forth most splendidly? Did the adversity of the times destroy such outstanding monuments of Catholic doctrine? Or had the matter been discussed and thoroughly examined among orthodox bishops long before the synod, so that it then came before the synod in that condition? Augustine perhaps intimates this in *On Baptism, Against the Donatists*, II.4:

“How could this matter, enveloped in such great clouds of altercation, have been brought to the lucid clarification and confirmation of a plenary council unless it had first, for a considerable time, been thoroughly examined throughout the regions of the world by many arguments and conferences of bishops on both sides?”

At least it is established from the foregoing that the Greeks [Col. 1243A] had scarcely been touched even by a report of the Council of Arles. Perhaps Augustine therefore calls it “plenary,” not as though it were ecumenical, but—according to his customary usage—as though it were universal, that is, assembled from several provinces, in the manner of a regional or national council. Hence the same Augustine, a little below, when seeking to resolve certain other doubts about Baptism, will desire the authority of a council as great as would suffice for so great a matter. He will likewise wish that “what was begun by a regional council should be concluded by a plenary council.”

Moreover, whence would this doctrine concerning ecumenical councils have come to Augustine, who had heard of almost nothing but Nicaea, scarcely knew Constantinople, and was overtaken by death before Ephesus? Yet he frequently invokes plenary councils and thinks that some may be corrected by others. [Col. 1243B] Nor was Basil above seeking an ecumenical council, but merely a council to settle that dispute. Epiphanius desired the work of an ecumenical synod, being perhaps better acquainted with the disagreement by which some Easterners still differed from the Westerners.

## XLIII. FROM THE SECOND ECUMENICAL COUNCIL

The one hundred and fifty Fathers of the second ecumenical council held the same view. For in canon VII they decree:

“Those who are added to the right faith and to the portion of those who are saved from among the heretics we receive according to the following order and custom: the Arians, indeed, etc.; but the Eunomians, etc.”

The former, namely, were received through anointing with Chrism; the latter through Baptism. They state their custom in the simplest terms and declare that this is the customary practice; they express no greater bitterness toward those who think [Col. 1243C] or act otherwise. Furthermore, they order the Montanists, or Cataphrygians, the Eunomians, and certain others to be baptized again, although it may be gathered from the testimonies of Jerome and others cited above that these were not rebaptized in the Roman Church. The Council of Nicaea had ordered only the Paulianists, not the Montanists, to be baptized again. This canon is absent from the Roman Church’s code of canons.

## XLIV. FROM THE COUNCIL IN TRULLO

The Fathers in Trullo held the same view. In canon II, together with other most widely received synods, they accept also “the canon issued by Cyprian, who was Archbishop of the region of the Africans and a Martyr, and by the synod held under him; this was observed in the territories of the aforementioned prelates, and only [Col. 1243D] according to the custom handed down to them.” Although the Greeks then dissented from Cyprian, they nevertheless judged that this custom of his had been valid in its own place and time.

## XLV. FROM THE CONSENSUS OF THE GREEKS, ESPECIALLY THEODORE THE STUDITE

All the Greeks of old held this view. Among them Basil’s Canonical Letter to Amphilochius was always held in the highest honor, shining above the others in the Greek code of canons. In particular, there was Timothy the Presbyter, a fragment of whose work is quoted by Balsamon. There he lists three classes of those who approach the Church: those received through Baptism, those through Chrism, and those through the mere abjuration of error: [Col. 1244A]

“Those who are baptized are the following: Tascodrugites, Marcionites, Artotyrites, Saccophori, Apotactites, Valentinians, who are also called Basilidians and Hermaeans, Nicolaitans, Montanists, Pepuzenes, Manichaeans, Eunomians, Paulianists, Photinians, Sabellians, Cerinthians, Menandrians, Ebionites, Simonians, Carpocratians, Saturninians, those descended from the impious Marcus, those from Apelles, those from Theodotus the Tanner, Elcesaites, those from Nepos, those from Pelagius and Caelestius, and the Melchizedekites. Those who are anointed with holy Chrism are these: Tetradites or Quartodecimans, Novatians or Sabbatians, Arians, Macedonians, and Apollinarians.”

A little afterward, in the same place, the following is added, excerpted from Theodore the Studite’s fourth letter to Naucratius:

“You requested that I reply point by point concerning the sects [Col. 1244B] and Baptisms, etc. Consult the sacred book of Epiphanius, etc. The classification is divided into three. Those baptized are the Marcionites, Tascodrugites, Manichaeans, and those of the same order down to the Melchizedekites—twenty-five heresies. Those anointed with sacred Chrism are the Tetradites, Novatians, Arians, Macedonians, and Apollinarians—five in all. Those who are neither baptized nor anointed, but anathematize only their own and every other heresy, are the Meletians, Nestorians, Eutychians, etc.”

This is virtually a rather extended interpretation of the seventh canon of the Council of Constantinople. You see how enormously these provisions differ from the custom of the Roman Church, which nevertheless never afterward raised a dispute with the Greeks over the matter, being content to exclude that Constantinopolitan canon from its own code. You see how ignorant [Col. 1244C] or heedless the Greeks were of that plenary council and the canon of Arles concerning Baptism celebrated by Augustine. You see how rightly and deservedly the canon of Arles was addressed to the Africans, whose peculiar rule was to rebaptize.

## XLVI. FROM GENNADIUS

To return again to the Latins, Gennadius held the same view in *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, c. 52:

“We declare that those who were not baptized among heretics with an invocation of the Holy Trinity, and who come to us, ought to be baptized, not rebaptized. For those who were not immersed in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, according to the rule laid down by the Lord, must not be believed to have been baptized. Such are the Paulinians, Proclians, Borborites, [Col. 1244D] Siphori, who are now called Bonosians, the Photinians, Montanists, and Manichaeans, and the various offspring of impiety, or the other plagues deriving their origin or class from them. Some introduce two principles unknown to one another, such as Cerdo and Marcion; others two contrary principles, such as Mani; others three barbarous principles, such as Sethianus and Theodosius; others many, such as Valentinus; and others hold that Christ was a man without God, such as Cerinthus, Ebion, Artemon, and Photinus. If any of these, I say, come to us, we must not ask them whether or not they have been baptized, but only whether they believe the faith of the Church; and they must be baptized with ecclesiastical Baptism.”

You will now be less astonished that the Greeks deviated from the canon of Arles and the rite of the Roman Church when you see that churches neighboring both the city of Arles [Col. 1245A] and Rome deviated from them equally. For Jerome expressly informed us above that many of those whom Gennadius orders to be baptized again were received into the Roman Church without a new Baptism.

I pass over in silence that, in our own age, newly arisen heretics were conditionally rebaptized by many Catholics, and that this had to be prohibited by the Council of Rouen in 1581, the Council of Reims in 1583, the Council of Aix in 1585, the Council of Toulouse in 1590, and the Council of Narbonne in 1609. For Pius V had so determined, as is reported in the Synod of Évreux of 1576, in Bochellus, p. 171.

## XLVII. FROM AUGUSTINE

Finally, Augustine himself held the same view, calling this a custom hundreds of times, both in the passages [Col. 1245B] cited above and in innumerable others that I refrain from collecting here. I add this one passage alone, from *On the One Baptism, Against Petilian*, c. 13:

“To state briefly what I think concerning this matter: to rebaptize heretics, as those men are said to have done, was at that time an error of human judgment; but to rebaptize Catholics, as these men still do, is always an act of diabolical presumption.”

It was therefore the peculiar and heretical perversity of the Donatists that they rebaptized those who had already been washed in the sacred font within the Catholic Church.

## XLVIII. AUGUSTINE FREQUENTLY REQUIRES PLENARY COUNCILS FOR THE REGULATION OF CUSTOMS
The authority of a plenary council was sought by Augustine, not to establish unity of faith, but to bring about unity of custom and discipline throughout the universal Church, [Col. 1245C] because a custom, being of itself free and indifferent, is more conveniently confined to one rite everywhere. This is clear from Epistle 118:

> As for those things which we observe not because they are written but because they have been handed down, and which indeed are observed throughout the whole world, we are given to understand that they are retained as having been commended and established either by the Apostles themselves or by plenary councils, whose authority in the Church is most salutary. Such are the annual solemn celebrations of the Lord’s Passion, Resurrection, and Ascension into heaven, and of the coming of the Holy Spirit from heaven, and anything else of this kind that may occur and that is observed by the universal Church wherever she extends. But other things vary among the different localities and regions of the world, as, for example, that some fast on the Sabbath while others do not, etc. This entire class of things admits freedom of observance. [Col. 1245D] In these matters there is no better discipline for a serious and prudent Christian than to act in the manner in which he sees the church acting to which he may happen to have come.

Here it is manifest that discipline and customs, unlike faith, need not necessarily be restricted and reduced to one formula throughout the entire Church; rather, all churches agree in faith, while in discipline some churches differ from others without blame. But wherever a particular custom either prevails or ought to prevail throughout the entire Church, this rule derives either from the Scriptures, from apostolic tradition, or from plenary councils.

And in Book IV of *On Baptism, Against the Donatists*, chapter 24:

> That which the universal Church holds, and which was not instituted by councils but [Col. 1246A] has always been retained, is most rightly believed to have been handed down by apostolic authority alone.

And in Book II, chapter 7:

> This custom of not rebaptizing heretics I believe to come from apostolic tradition, just as many things are not found in their writings or in the councils of later generations, and yet, because they are observed throughout the universal Church, are believed to have been handed down and commended by the Apostles themselves.

And again the same Augustine, in Book II *Against the Letter of Parmenian*, chapter 13:

> This, indeed, is another question: whether Baptism can be conferred even by those who have never been Christians. Nothing concerning it should be rashly affirmed without the authority of a council sufficiently great for so great a matter.

And in Book VII of *On Baptism, Against the Donatists*, chapter 53, when investigating whether Baptism conferred by a pagan, whether in jest or as part of a theatrical performance, should be considered valid, he says:

> [Col. 1246B] For us it is safe not to advance with any rashness of judgment in matters which have not been initiated in any Catholic regional council and have not been settled by any plenary council.

And in Epistle 119, chapter 15:

> For the celebration of Easter, since the Gospel has already made clear the day on which the Lord rose, the observance of the corresponding days was also added through councils of the Fathers; and the whole Christian world has been persuaded that Easter ought to be celebrated in that manner.

In matters of dogmatic faith, however, one will scarcely ever find Augustine’s mind thus remaining in doubt pending a conciliar definition. Add Epiphanius, cited above, who thought that whether those baptized by Arians ought to be purified again in the baptismal font should be determined by an ecumenical council. Add Basil likewise burning with desire for a council amid this uncertainty concerning the Baptism of heretics. [Col. 1246C] Yet neither Epiphanius nor Basil burned with so great a desire for a council against the Origenists and the many other heresies then rampant.

Finally, the Apostles issued synodically that ecumenical constitution of theirs, as Cyril of Jerusalem calls it in Catechesis 18, concerning articles not of faith but of discipline; and provincial synods were formerly to be convened once or twice every year, not so much to decree anything concerning faith as to safeguard the purity of discipline. Even now, certainly, not a few matters concerning Confirmation, Holy Orders, Absolution, and Matrimony are disputed among the leading schoolmen, while some matters differ even among the churches themselves: what some regard as valid, others consider invalid. But this is an orderly dispute, tempered according to the nature of discipline, although definitions concerning these matters, as concerning quite a number [Col. 1246D] of others, could be fashioned and drawn into the necessity of faith.

Yet so long as the contest proceeds on both sides by means of differing opinions and practices, it is not permissible to applaud both equally. For one position is far preferable to the other—for example, that of those who do not repeat the Baptism of heretics, since it accords with the dignity of the sacrament, ecclesiastical tradition, and the definition of the Pontiffs. But because the Church and the Pontiffs, before a universal synod, connived at and dispensed with the contrary view, those who think and act otherwise may meanwhile be regarded as laboring under some error, though merely a “material” error, as they say.

Bellarmine does not condemn the Church and the Pontiff for extending this indulgence at greater length, Book I, *On Councils*, chapter 10:

> It is probable that by the authority of the Apostolic See that question was regarded as settled among all Catholics. [Col. 1247A] But even if the question had not been settled until the determination of a plenary council, as Augustine says, it would still not follow that it could not have been settled. For although the Apostolic See, with the cooperation of provincial councils, did not lack authority to settle that controversy, those holy Pontiffs nevertheless preferred to defer the definitive determination of that question to another, more suitable time rather than separate so many great men from the Church.

Certainly, in Act 1 of the Seventh Synod, Eustochius, Patriarch of Jerusalem, is praised because he granted monks who embraced Origen’s ravings eight months’ respite to come to their senses and subscribe to the Fifth Ecumenical Synod.

## XLIX. BY NO MEANS FOR QUESTIONS OF FAITH

[Col. 1247B]

But see how the same Augustine teaches us that in questions of faith there is by no means any need to assemble, and that it is by no means lawful to appeal to ecumenical or plenary synods. For in Book I *Against Julian*, chapter 4, after citing the authorities of the Latin Fathers, he says:

> Do you therefore think that they are to be despised because they all belong to the Western Church, and because no bishop of the East has been mentioned by us among them? What, then, shall we do, since they are Greeks and we are Latins? I think that part of the world ought to suffice for you in which the Lord willed to crown the foremost of His Apostles with a most glorious martyrdom. If you had been willing to listen to Blessed Innocent, who presided over that Church, you would even then have freed your perilous youth [Col. 1247C] from the snares of the Pelagians. For what could that holy man have answered the African councils except what the Apostolic See has held from antiquity, and what the Roman Church together with the others steadfastly holds?

And below:

> There is therefore no reason for you to appeal to the bishops of the East, since they too are assuredly Christians, and this one faith belongs to both parts of the world, because this faith is Christian; and certainly the Western land gave you birth, and the Western Church gave you rebirth.

Therefore, because faith is not different in one place and another, as is the discipline of customs, but is one everywhere throughout the world—and thus is the same in the East as in the West, namely, the one Christian faith—it is not permissible to appeal to the bishops of the East or to an ecumenical synod. [Col. 1247D] Rather, everyone must listen to the bishops of his own church, and above all to the Roman Pontiff when he declares the ancient faith of his Church.

And in Book IV addressed to Pope Boniface, final chapter:

> Or was an assembly of a synod really necessary in order that an evident plague might be condemned? As though no heresy had ever been condemned except by the assembly of a synod, whereas in fact those heresies for the condemnation of which such a necessity arose are found only very rarely; and far more—indeed, incomparably more—have deserved to be rejected and condemned in the very places where they arose, and from there could become known throughout the other lands as things to be avoided. But it is evident that their pride seeks even this glory: that on their account a synod of East and West should be assembled. For because, with the Lord opposing them, [Col. 1248A] they cannot pervert the Catholic world, they attempt at least to disturb it.

Here it is not customs but heresies that resound; faith is repeatedly emphasized. Therefore, it is denied that an ecumenical synod is urgently necessary, since by far the greater number of heresies have been stifled without synods of this kind.

## L. SUMMARY OF THIS LATTER CONTROVERSY

They therefore yap in vain, arguing from the example of Firmilian, Dionysius, and Cyprian that it is not necessary to abide by the definitions of the Apostolic See. On the contrary, as is clear from the foregoing:

1. Those who did not yield to them have been shown to have erred, and to have had to wash away this error by some martyrdom, whether bloody or bloodless.

2. Augustine regarded it as not unlikely that Cyprian yielded.

3. Those who did not obey Stephen conformed neither to apostolic tradition nor to the authority [Col. 1248B] and custom of the universal Church. Nothing, therefore, can legitimately be claimed on the basis of their position.

4. Nor did those very men, or their successors, listen afterward to the Councils of Arles or Nicaea. Perhaps they knew nothing of Arles; they interpreted Nicaea so as to accommodate it to their former opinion, as we saw above in Basil. Yet this furnishes no ground for rising up against general synods.

5. Stephen went no further than threats, and he himself acquiesced, for the sake of dispensation and the preservation of unity, in remaining in communion with those who both thought and acted differently. In this respect he surpassed Cyprian by no small distance. Cyprian wiped away his error by the abundance of his charity and the expenditure of his blood; Stephen did not deviate even a finger’s breadth from the path of right. At first, as was proper, he insisted on strict right; when he perceived the [Col. 1248C] danger of schism to be imminent, he adopted a moderate course.

6. Although this question could have been drawn into the domain of faith, like many other articles of customary practice, at that time it was nevertheless being debated peaceably as a part of discipline. Neither Cyprian nor Stephen at first, nor afterward the Councils of Nicaea or Constantinople, nor Basil, nor the later Greeks or Romans—although they differed somewhat—hurled an anathema against their opponents. Therefore, in matters of this kind, when the Roman Pontiffs profess that differing customs of the churches are either praised by them, not blamed, or tolerated, what wonder is it if the other bishops use, or abuse, this freedom?

Gregory, in his letter to Augustine, Bishop of the English:

> It pleases me that, whether in the Roman Church, the Gallican Church, or any other [Col. 1248D] church, you have found something that may be more pleasing to Almighty God, you should carefully choose it.

And so that you may not doubt that this also pertains in some measure to the sacraments, Alexander III, in the appendix to the Lateran Council, chapter 2, *On the Impotent*:

> Although the Roman Church has not been accustomed to separate those lawfully joined in marriage because of sorcery, nevertheless, if the general custom of the Gallican Church holds that a marriage of this kind is to be dissolved, we shall patiently tolerate it.

Six hundred other examples will be noted below in their proper places, showing that the Roman Pontiffs exhort everyone toward agreement even in custom, while tolerating disagreement in the meantime. Finally, Augustine himself, who had insisted that a general council was necessary, restricted this necessity of synods to the regulation of customs, not to the condemnation of heresies.

[Col. 1249]

# DISSERTATION EXPLAINING STEPHEN’S TRUE POSITION CONCERNING THE RECEPTION OF HERETICS

## I. THAT HIS POSITION WAS NOT DEVOID OF REASON

[Col. 1249A]

1. Although Cyprian judges what Stephen wrote concerning the controversy over the Baptism of heretics to be either arrogant, irrelevant, self-contradictory, or written ignorantly and heedlessly, nevertheless, among those things which both Cyprian himself and Firmilian identified as especially unreasonable, we find nothing deserving such censure. Indeed, we discover that in them the arguments later used by the Donatists against the Church were wisely anticipated. For the rebaptizers were already foreshadowing those arguments when, relying on human reason, they maintained that no one gives what he does not possess, and consequently that heretics cannot give the grace which they lack. [Col. 1249B]

But Stephen opposed to this reasoning a custom—not just any custom, but one received from apostolic tradition. What could be wiser? For in divine matters all human reasoning must yield to the authority of God. Cyprian therefore attributed more than was proper to his own reasoning when he said, “In vain do certain persons who are defeated by reason oppose custom to us” (*Epistle* LXXI); and he was wrong to treat Stephen’s statement as vain: “What we have received from the Apostles, this we follow” (*Epistle* LXXIII). Reasoning that opposes so great an authority ought to be regarded with suspicion.

2. Although the same bishop may laugh at and regard as utterly absurd the argument by which Stephen confirmed that tradition, saying:

> A splendid and legitimate [Col. 1249C] tradition indeed is presented to us under the instruction of our brother Stephen, one that would provide us with authority. For in the same passage of his letter he added and appended that the heretics themselves, when members of one sect come over to another, do not baptize them but merely admit them to communion;

nevertheless, those who weigh it more attentively will judge it quite differently. Since all heretics have departed from the Church, it is not surprising that they retain something of her teaching. Indeed, there is no heretic in reality who does not retain something from it. Therefore, when they agree with the Church on some point, however much they may disagree among themselves, it is rightly affirmed that they have retained what the Church handed down to them.

Accordingly, heretics who deny the true body of Christ in the Eucharist are proved to have departed from the ancient and constant faith of the Church [Col. 1249D] by the fact that various sects which for many centuries have differed from the Catholic Church in other matters agree with her in this dogma. Thus, as Cyprian wrote, the Church of God and Bride of Christ had not then “fallen into such a state of evils that she followed the examples of heretics.” Rather, [Col. 1250A] the heretics themselves, when they did not baptize those who came to them from other sects, were following the practice which they had seen customarily and commonly received in the Church before they separated from her.

3. Nor did Stephen ignore the argument which Cyprian and his associates opposed to him as invincible, taking it as certain that those destitute of the Holy Spirit could not give Him and therefore could not confer the grace of Baptism. This argument seemed invincible to them because they did not know how to distinguish either the reality of the sacrament from the sacrament itself, or the minister or instrument from the Lord who employs it. But Stephen, distinguishing these very carefully, taught neither ignorantly nor heedlessly, but suitably and wisely, that “the presence and holiness of Christ attend [Col. 1250B] those who are baptized among heretics” (*Cyprian*, *Epistle* LXXV), Christ being the one who accomplishes what He wills through the ministry of heretics.

For Stephen was rightly persuaded that the name—that is, the authority and power—of Christ avails greatly, so that through Christ’s operation whoever and wherever a person may be baptized in Christ’s name, he immediately obtains the grace of Christ. He was therefore defending what Augustine repeatedly insists that John learned from the dove—namely, as that Doctor explains elsewhere:

> There would be such a property in Christ that, although many ministers were to baptize, whether righteous or unrighteous, the holiness of Baptism would be attributed to no one but Him upon whom the dove descended, of whom it was said: “This is He who baptizes in the Holy Spirit.” Let Peter baptize: He is the one who baptizes. Let Paul [Col. 1250C] baptize: He is the one who baptizes. Let Judas baptize: He is the one who baptizes.

From this one rightly perceives how there can be one Baptism of Christ both in the Church and among heretics, a doctrine which Firmilian resented Stephen for proclaiming.

4. Cyprian therefore cited in vain, in defense of his cause, Ecclesiasticus 34:30 in this form: “He who is baptized by a dead man—what does his washing profit him?” (*Epistle* LXXI). First, he falsely thought that one who receives Baptism from a heretic is baptized by a dead man. For Christ lives, who baptizes through the heretic, and therefore one who receives Baptism from a heretic is by no means baptized by a dead man. [Col. 1250D]

Second, just as he did not possess the complete form of the cited testimony, so neither did he grasp its meaning. For in uncorrupted manuscripts of Ecclesiasticus we read it thus:

> He who washes himself after touching a dead man, and touches him again—what does his washing profit him?

By these words we are taught that [Col. 1251A] the washing of one who had touched a dead man is futile if, after being washed, he touches the same dead man again. When Donatus had abused this same passage, similarly truncated and with the same reasoning, in support of his heresy, Augustine vehemently accused him of violating the divine utterance. But when the same Doctor later encountered books older than the party of Donatus in which the same defect was already present, he was not ashamed to retract and correct what he had written in good faith against that heretic (*Retractions*, Book I, chapter 21, no. 3). Cyprian’s books, in which the clause “and touches him again” was already lacking, prove how correctly Augustine judged the antiquity of those manuscripts. Let this observation suffice in passing.

As for Stephen, when he said, “Therefore, if anyone comes to us from any heresy whatsoever, let nothing be innovated beyond what has been handed down,” [Col. 1251B] he merely wished to set forth an opinion contrary to the decree of the African council, which determined concerning one who comes from heresy:

> He who comes to the Church uninitiated must be baptized and renewed, so that within he may be sanctified through the saints (*Cyprian*, *Epistle* LXX).

His meaning, therefore, is: Let nothing be innovated concerning the Baptism of one who comes in this way, but let only what has been handed down be observed; or, let nothing new be given to him except what tradition has prescribed should be done for him—namely, that the hand should be imposed upon him for penance. He did not wish Baptism to be repeated because he was persuaded that this sacrament derives its power not from the one who ministers it, but from Christ, in whose name it is conferred.

Nor did he say, “The name of Christ avails greatly, etc.,” with a faith different from that by which Augustine later said: “For through any minister whatsoever, it is the Baptism of Him of whom it was said, ‘This is He who baptizes’” [Col. 1251C] (Book V of *On Baptism, Against the Donatists*, chapter 12). But these same words of Stephen gave rise to other questions.

## II. WHETHER STEPHEN ACCEPTED BAPTISM CONFERRED BY HERETICS UNDER ANY FORM WHATEVER

5. There are some who suspect that Stephen failed to observe due moderation in refuting the rebaptizers’ position and accepted the Baptism of all heretics whatsoever, conferred under any form whatever. But to remove a suspicion of this kind it will suffice to repeat these words of his, transmitted to us by Firmilian:

> The name of Christ avails greatly toward faith and the sanctification of Baptism, so that whoever and wherever a person may be baptized in the name of Christ, he immediately obtains [Col. 1251D] the grace of Christ.

Certainly, one who attributes the whole efficacy of Baptism to Christ’s power considers it fruitless if Christ’s name is lacking. It follows that Stephen accepted not every Baptism, but only that which was conferred in Christ’s name and by His authority.

When Cyprian undertakes to refute these same words of the Pope, he confirms that they were spoken in this sense:

> If they attribute the effect of Baptism to the majesty of the name, so that those who are baptized in the name of Jesus Christ, wherever and however they may be baptized, are judged renewed and sanctified, why is the hand not also imposed there upon the baptized person in the name of the same Christ for the reception of the Holy Spirit? Why does the same majesty of the same name not prevail in the imposition of the hand [Col. 1252A] as they maintain that it prevailed in the sanctification of Baptism? (*Cyprian*, *Epistle* LXXIV).

Thus Cyprian reasoned against Stephen, thinking that Stephen accepted the Baptism of heretics while rejecting an imposition of hands received from them for the reception of the Holy Spirit—that is, the sacrament of Confirmation conferred by them—and permitted it to be renewed and repeated. Whether or not he was mistaken in this matter we shall examine below. But from this no doubt remains that Cyprian clearly recognizes and takes as certain that Stephen received only the Baptism of those who are baptized in the name of Jesus Christ.

Nor should anyone be disturbed by the word “however” in the quoted words of Cyprian, since it should all the more certainly be judged to have been added by him as a fuller explanation of the word “wherever,” and to have been understood of any minister who baptizes in the name of Jesus [Col. 1252B] Christ, not of any form whatever, because in Firmilian—who appears to report Stephen’s actual words more precisely—the phrase “and however” does not occur at all.

6. Accordingly, those are mistaken and depart far from Stephen’s meaning who adhere too rigidly to his words, in which he directs that anyone who comes from any heresy be received and that Baptism be innovated in no respect, and who therefore suppose that he accepted Baptism conferred under any form whatever. Stephen spoke in this general manner because he either did not know of, or did not attend to, heretics who baptized under a different form.

Certainly, Augustine observes that “it is easier to find heretics who do not baptize than heretics who do not baptize with these words” ordinarily used in the Church (*On Baptism, Against the Donatists*, Book VI, chapter 25, no. 47). [Col. 1252C] Innocent, *Epistle* XVI to the Macedonians, chapter 10, and Jerome toward the end of the *Dialogue Against the Luciferians*, likewise note that the Council of Nicaea, while excepting only the Paulianists, accepted the Baptism of the other heretics. Because of this rarity it came about that the Fathers, when speaking of the Baptism of heretics, gave no thought at all to making any exception.

Just as Stephen is reported in Firmilian’s letter to have said generally, “What, then, shall be done concerning those who come from heresy and have been received without the Church’s Baptism?” so also Jerome, toward the end of the dialogue just mentioned, says that “heretics have always been received by our predecessors, and the Church has always accepted Baptism from heretics.”

No less general is Leo’s decree, whether in *Epistle* CXLIX to Nicetas, chapter 7:

> Those who received Baptism from heretics, [Col. 1252D] not having been baptized before, are to be confirmed solely by the invocation of the Holy Spirit through the imposition of hands;

or in *Epistle* CLV to Neo, chapter 2:

> If it is established that someone was baptized by heretics, the sacrament of regeneration is by no means to be repeated in his case; but only that which was lacking there is to be conferred, so that through the imposition of the episcopal hand he may obtain the power of the Holy Spirit.

Everyone perceives that by these words Leo wished to express Stephen’s position. Therefore, if no one doubts that in these passages of Leo, Jerome, and the other Fathers concerning the acceptance of heretical Baptism a clause is to be understood—“provided that it was conferred with a legitimate form and the customary words”—neither should anyone doubt that the same clause and condition was understood by [Col. 1253A] Stephen.

Indeed, if the observation of Innocent and Jerome given above is true—namely, that at the time of the Council of Nicaea the Paulianists alone violated the form of Baptism, and that therefore the fathers of that council accepted the Baptism of all other heretics except the Paulianists—then, since the Paulianists had not yet arisen in Stephen’s time, there was no need for the Pope, when defending the acceptance of heretical Baptism, to add any exception on their account.

7. From another source, however, it is certain that he knew or approved no Baptism except the Baptism of Christ. Firmilian, as we have seen, agrees with Cyprian on this point. Moreover, in *Epistle* LXXIII Cyprian first explains Stephen’s position specifically concerning the Baptism of Marcion as follows: “He says that those coming [Col. 1253B] from Marcion ought not to be baptized, because they appear already TO HAVE BEEN BAPTIZED IN THE NAME OF JESUS.” He then notes why the same Pope thinks that those coming from other heretics generally should be received in the same manner:

> No one should oppose the name of Christ in order to circumvent Christian truth, saying that those baptized IN THE NAME OF JESUS CHRIST, wherever and however, have obtained the grace of Baptism.

It is therefore certain both that Stephen accepted no Baptism unless it had been conferred in the name of Jesus Christ, and that he attributed the entire power and efficacy of this sacrament to the holiness of that most powerful name.

Indeed, the anonymous author contemporary or nearly contemporary with those times, first published by Nicolas Rigault from a Remigian copy at the end of Tertullian’s works, and afterward [Col. 1253C] reprinted by Philippe Labbe in volume I of the *Councils*, page 770, thus states at the beginning of the *Treatise on the Baptism of Heretics* the question then under dispute:

> I observe that it is asked among the brethren what should preferably be observed with regard to those who, though indeed in heresy, HAD BEEN BAPTIZED IN THE NAME OF OUR GOD JESUS CHRIST, and afterward, departing from it and flying suppliantly to the Church of God, did penance with their whole heart.

The question at that time, therefore, did not concern those who had indiscriminately been baptized in heresy under any form whatever, but only those who, though indeed in heresy, had been baptized in the name of our God Jesus Christ; or, as the same author soon repeats in other words, those who, though outside, received the Lord’s Baptism IN THE NAME OF JESUS CHRIST. Nor, according to Cyprian’s testimony, did Stephen accept [Col. 1253D] the Baptism of the Marcionites for any other reason than that they baptized in the name of Jesus. From this another question arises.

## III. WHETHER, BY THOSE WHOM STEPHEN CALLED “BAPTIZED IN THE NAME OF JESUS,” HE MEANT THOSE BAPTIZED IN THE NAME OF THE TRINITY

8. The same question may be stated differently: namely, whether Stephen accepted a Baptism in which the name of Jesus Christ was substituted for the three Persons, and thought that one baptized in the name of Jesus Christ, rather than in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, could obtain the grace of Baptism.

It must be observed, however, that Stephen’s manner of speaking about Baptism—which everyone knows to be supported by the authority of the Acts of the Apostles [Col. 1254A]—was familiar not to him alone but also to the ancients. Even Stephen’s own opponents employed it. Thus, in the Third Council of Carthage under Cyprian, chapter 1, Caecilius of Bilta denies that there is Baptism among heretics, “where Antichrist baptizes IN THE NAME OF CHRIST,” not because it is in the name of Christ, but because Antichrist baptizes.

In no different sense, in chapter 21, Hortensianus of Lares asks:

> How can they baptize anyone in the name of Christ, when Christ Himself says that they are His adversaries?

Cyprian employs the same manner of speech in *Epistle* LXXIII, and Firmilian does so in *Epistle* LXXV in Cyprian’s collection. Here Hilary’s warning should prevail. He observes that those passages of Acts in which the Apostles are said to have baptized in the name of Jesus require explanation:

> Lest, he says, the Apostles be found guilty of wrongdoing, since, although commanded to baptize in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, [Col. 1254B] they baptized only in the name of Jesus—if we adhere to the letter (*Hilary*, *On the Synods* 85).

For the Fathers of subsequent centuries will be guilty of the same wrongdoing if, when they said that persons were baptized in the name of Jesus, they did not mean that they had been baptized with the words prescribed by Christ.

But the interpretation by which both the Apostles and the imitators of the Apostles are cleared of blame is not difficult. In the time of the Apostles, the Baptism instituted afterward by Christ had to be distinguished from the baptism delivered by John.
