No more suitable distinction could have been devised than that, since one was already called the baptism of John, the other should be called the Baptism of Christ; [Col. 1254C] and those who received the latter should be said to have been baptized in the name of Jesus—that is, initiated by the Baptism instituted by Christ’s authority, and consequently in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.

9. Accordingly, Innocent, in *Epistle* XVI to the Macedonians, no. 10, confidently declares that those who in Acts 19:5 are said to have been baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus were baptized in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Yet although he decrees in *Epistle* II, chapter 8, that “those coming from the Novatians or Montenses are to be received only through the imposition of hands, because, although baptized by heretics, they were nevertheless baptized in the name of Christ,” he nevertheless takes it as certain that the Novatians and Montenses, or Donatists, [Col. 1254D] baptized with the words prescribed by Christ.

Hence he observes that the Council of Nicaea dealt differently with the Paulianists than with the Novatians:

> Because the Paulianists by no means baptize in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, whereas the Novatians baptize in those same dread and venerable names.

The same must be said of the Donatists, who did not cease to baptize with the words customary in the Church.

Cyprian himself also, no less than Innocent, does not doubt that what is called the Baptism of Christ in Acts was conferred in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. For first he premises:

> Those who had already received the most ancient baptism of the Law and of Moses were also to be baptized in the name of Jesus, according to what Peter says to them in the Acts of the Apostles: “Repent, and let every one of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ.”

Then, explaining these words, he adds:

> [Col. 1255A] Peter makes mention of Jesus Christ, not as though the Father were omitted, but so that the Son might also be joined to the Father.

10. A competent interpreter of Stephen is Firmilian himself, who reported Stephen’s words. Firmilian plainly and openly explains what Stephen and his associates had said—“The name of Christ avails greatly . . . so that whoever and wherever a person may be baptized in the name of Christ, he immediately obtains the grace of Christ”—as follows:

> They do not think it necessary to inquire who the person who baptized may be, because the one baptized could obtain grace through the invocation of the TRINITY OF NAMES: the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit.

Hence it is evident that by the words “to be baptized in the name of Christ,” Firmilian, Stephen, and his associates understood Baptism conferred in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.

This already evident matter is further and further confirmed [Col. 1255B] by the story which Firmilian relates against Stephen and his associates concerning a woman “who previously, through the illusions and deceits of a demon, contrived many things for the deception of the faithful,” and who among other things had also dared “to baptize many, employing the customary and legitimate words of interrogation, so that she appeared to differ in nothing from the ecclesiastical rule.” After relating this deed at greater length, Firmilian immediately adds:

> What, then, shall we say concerning her Baptism? Do Stephen and those who agree with him approve even this? Especially since neither the creed of the TRINITY nor the legitimate and ecclesiastical interrogation was lacking from it?

What purpose would “especially, etc.” serve unless Stephen, adhering to the Church’s form of baptizing, wished it also to be adhered to by others—so much so that Firmilian did not doubt that if anyone [Col. 1255C] omitted or altered some principal element of the Church’s received rule, such as above all the verbal form prescribed by Christ, that person’s Baptism would be rejected by this Pope?

On the same occasion, that bishop also illuminates Stephen’s position remarkably when he assails it as follows:

> Can it be believed that forgiveness of sins was granted or the washing of regeneration duly completed where everything was performed through a demon? Unless those who defend the Baptism of heretics also maintain that a demon gave the grace of Baptism in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.

For from this it is manifest that Stephen admitted no Baptism unless it had been conferred in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.

In a word, the sole controversy between Cyprian, Firmilian, and their associates on one side, [Col. 1255D] and Stephen and the other bishops who defended tradition on the other, concerned the minister, not the form, of Baptism: some thought that it must be asked who the person who baptized was; others thought that this need not be asked.

## IV. WHETHER STEPHEN ATTRIBUTED TO THE BAPTISM OF HERETICS GREATER POWER AND EFFICACY THAN WAS PROPER

11. Augustine thus explains the origin and cause of the entire controversy concerning which we have already said much:

> Nor was there any other reason why, in those times, when this question was being investigated contrary to ancient custom in debates conducted with charity and unity preserved, [Col. 1256A] certain distinguished bishops of Christ—among whom Blessed Cyprian was especially eminent—thought that the Baptism of Christ could not exist among heretics or schismatics, except that the sacrament was not distinguished from the effect or use of the sacrament. And because its effect and use, in liberation from sins and uprightness of heart, were not found among heretics, it was thought that the sacrament itself was not present there either.

(*On Baptism, Against the Donatists*, beginning of Book VI.)

Accordingly, when Cyprian objects, “There is no salvation outside the Church,” the same Doctor replies:

> Who denies it? And therefore whatever belongs to the Church is not efficacious for salvation outside the Church. But it is one thing not to possess something, and another not to possess it beneficially (*ibid.*, Book V, chapter 17). [Col. 1256B]

For one who possesses the sacrament without its effect does not possess it beneficially.

> He who does not possess it must be baptized so that he may possess it. He who does not possess it beneficially must be corrected.

And a few words later:

> Baptism can therefore be common to us and to heretics, just as the Gospel can be common to them and to us, although their error differs from our faith.

12. But if Cyprian strayed from the truth when, failing to distinguish the sacrament from the use or effect of the sacrament, he therefore denied that the sacrament was received from heretics because the effect of the sacrament is not conferred in heresy, must not Stephen likewise be said to have erred when, taking the opposite path, he appears to affirm that not merely the sacrament but also the effect of the sacrament is received from heretics? For since it is agreed that salvation does not exist [Col. 1256C] outside the Church, how can the statements which Cyprian and Firmilian testify were made by Stephen and those who agreed with him be absolved from error? For, if these two are not mistaken, the others were saying “that the remission of sins and a second birth take place in the baptism of heretics; or that, through those who are themselves established in every kind of sin, remission of sins can be given; and that therefore one must not inquire who it was that baptized, because the person baptized was able to obtain grace when the Trinity of the names was invoked; and because the name of Christ is so efficacious that whoever has been baptized in the name of Christ immediately obtains the grace of Christ.”

13. Here it should first be observed that no words of Stephen [Col. 1256D] have reached us except through the writings of his adversaries. Nor is there any doubt that they transcribed them—and perhaps even expressed them—in such a way as might arouse greater hostility against him. Secondly, it must be feared that those who did not distinguish the sacrament from the effect of the sacrament attributed the same confusion to Stephen, so that whatever he said about the sacrament alone, they interpreted, with their preconceived understanding, as though it had also been said by him about the effect of the sacrament, as something consequent upon the former. Yet even if it be supposed that they did not alter Stephen’s aforesaid words but reproduced them with the utmost fidelity, there is nothing in them that can either be charged with error or judged inconsistent with Catholic truth. For if infants [Col. 1257A] are under discussion, it is certain that, wherever and by whomever they have been baptized, they immediately obtain the grace of Christ. If adults are in question, then the statement written in the letter sent by Jubaianus to Cyprian was also true: “that one must not inquire who baptized when the person baptized was able to receive the remission of sins”; not absolutely, indeed, and through the mere reception of the sacrament as in the case of infants, but—as is immediately added there—*according to what he believed*, that is, if he received it with right faith and manifested all that the Christian religion requires for obtaining this grace. Firmilian confirms that this was indeed the opinion of Stephen and those who agreed with him when, concerning those “who think that one must not inquire who it was that baptized,” he testifies as follows: “They say that one who [Col. 1257B] is baptized outside, in whatever manner, can obtain grace through his own mind and faith.” Whenever, therefore, Stephen and the other bishops who agreed with him say that one baptized by heretics can obtain grace, we have the unimpeachable testimony of Cyprian and Firmilian that *according to what he believed*, or according to his faith and disposition of mind, must be understood. In this there is certainly nothing absurd, nothing that does not accord perfectly with the truth. For it can happen that someone who holds the right belief receives baptism from a person whom he does not know to be a heretic. In that case, the heresy of the one administering it will in no way harm the man receiving this sacrament with sound and complete faith.

14. Indeed, even a Catholic can receive baptism, together with the effect of this sacrament, from someone whom he knows to be a heretic. “For the person,” Augustine says, “to whom a separated person administers it [Col. 1257C] can receive it to his salvation, provided that he himself receives it without being separated. This has happened to many who, with a Catholic mind and heart not estranged from the unity of peace, were driven by the necessity of imminent death to fall in with some heretic and received Christ’s baptism from him without receiving his perversity.” At such a time they had only to take care that they not perhaps be thought to have gone over to the heresy and perversity of those from whom they received baptism, and that their example not become a stumbling block to others. Moreover, as the same Doctor explains, “when baptism is given with the words of the Gospel, whatever perversity may characterize the understanding of the person through whom it is given or the person to whom it is given, it is holy in itself because of him whose it is; and if anyone, receiving it through a perverse man, nevertheless receives not the minister’s perversity but only [Col. 1257D] the holiness of the mystery, he is joined in good faith, hope, and charity to the unity of the Church and receives remission of sins” (Book IV, chap. 12). Thus there occurs what Stephen taught: “Heresy indeed gives birth and exposes its offspring, but the Church receives those who have been exposed.”

15. It is likewise Augustine’s consistent teaching that what is called the sacrament is equally holy in all who receive it, and that neither the righteousness nor the perversity of the person administering or receiving it contributes to or detracts from its holiness. “It makes no difference,” he says, “to the holiness of baptism how wicked the person possessing it may be or how wicked the person administering it may be.” Stephen, having received this also from tradition, taught that one must not inquire who had baptized (Book VI, chap. 5). In what sense? [Col. 1258A] Because the wickedness of the one administering the body of Christ does no harm to its holiness, we believe that one must not inquire who the priest is who administers it. But although the sacrament remains complete whether it is administered by an evil person or received by an evil person, its effect is nevertheless very different according as it is received with right faith and an excellent heart or with perverse faith and a corrupt heart. Augustine therefore says: “I say that both the good and the evil can possess, can give, and can receive the sacrament of baptism: the good, indeed, usefully and to their salvation, but the evil ruinously and to their punishment, although it remains equally complete in both” (Book IV, chap. 2). For the same reason, Stephen also taught that those receiving the sacrament of baptism are distinguished by their own mind and faith, and that each person receives [Col. 1258B] the effect of baptism according to what he has believed. Thus, instructed by apostolic tradition, because he held it certain that the sacrament of baptism remained complete in those who came from heresy, he refused to have it repeated; and because he nevertheless knew that it inhered in them ruinously and to their punishment, he required that, when they returned to the Church, a hand be laid upon them for penance. Finally, according to Augustine’s testimony, “it became manifest to the shepherds of the Catholic Church, through whom the original custom—defended by Stephen—was afterward confirmed by the authority of a plenary council, that even a sheep which was wandering outside and had received outside the **MARK OF THE LORD** from its deceitful plunderers, upon coming to the salvation of Christian unity, was to be corrected from error, delivered from captivity, and healed of its wound; yet the **MARK** of the Lord in it was to be acknowledged rather than rejected.” [Col. 1258C] I would by no means affirm that Stephen himself used the term *mark* (*character*), but no one could deny that he defended the reality expressed by that term. Thus he, as an assertor and defender of the right faith, is shown to have sown the seeds of those explanations by which Augustine afterward successfully elucidated and defended Catholic truth against the Donatists. Yet there remains a difficulty to be removed concerning his command that a hand be imposed for penance.

## V. WHETHER STEPHEN INTENDED A HAND TO BE LAID UPON THOSE RETURNING FROM HERESY SO THAT THE SACRAMENT OF CONFIRMATION MIGHT BE CONFERRED UPON THEM

16. Stephen’s statement, “If, therefore, anyone comes to us from any heresy whatsoever, let nothing be introduced anew except what [Col. 1258D] has been handed down, namely, that a hand be laid upon him for penance,” permits of a twofold interpretation. First, it may be understood to mean that nothing is to be introduced anew concerning the baptism of the person who comes, but only what has been handed down is to be observed, namely, that a hand be laid upon him for penance. Or it may be understood in this other way: that in the case of one who has come from heresy to the Church nothing is to be introduced anew except what has been handed down as something to be renewed—namely, that the hand which had been laid upon him in heresy is to be laid upon him a second time when he returns. Interpreting Stephen’s words in this latter manner, Cyprian, Firmilian, and some of their associates persuaded themselves that he permitted the repetition of Confirmation. Hence Cyprian argues against this pope in Letter LXXIII as follows: “But if someone was able to be baptized outside according to a false faith [Col. 1259A] and to obtain remission of sins, according to the same faith he was also able to obtain the Holy Spirit; and it is not necessary to lay a hand upon him when he comes, so that he may obtain the Holy Spirit and be sealed. For either faith outside was able to accomplish both, or one who had been outside received neither of them.” He repeats a similar argument in Letter LXXIV, transcribed by us above at no. 5, and in Letter LXXVI. Following in his footsteps, Firmilian says: “Certainly, he who was baptized there in Christ has put on Christ; but if he has put on Christ, he was also able to receive the Holy Spirit who was sent by Christ, and a hand is laid upon him in vain when he comes to receive the Holy Spirit.” And below, after reporting Stephen’s words concerning the power of Christ’s name in baptism, he immediately adds: “If outside, [Col. 1259B] in the name of Christ, baptism had power to cleanse a person, there too, in the name of the same Christ, the laying on of a hand could have power for receiving the Holy Spirit.” Secundianus of Carpis spoke with the same understanding in chapter 24 of the Third Council of Carthage under Cyprian: “It is established that the Holy Spirit cannot descend upon alien children and the offspring of Antichrist merely through the laying on of a hand, since it is manifest that heretics do not possess baptism.” For this is what he means: Those who believe that baptism exists among heretics, but that only the sacrament of Confirmation cannot be conferred by them, are altogether mistaken, since it is established that they do not even possess baptism.

17. At chapter 5 of the same council, Nemesianus of Thubunae states his opinion as follows: “Christ [Col. 1259C] spoke, saying, ‘Unless one has been reborn of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God.’ This is the Spirit who in the beginning was borne over the water. For neither can the Spirit operate without water, nor water without the Spirit. Some therefore interpret matters wrongly for themselves when they say that they”—heretics and schismatics returning—“receive the Holy Spirit through the laying on of a hand and are thus received, since it is manifest that they ought to be reborn by **BOTH SACRAMENTS** in the Catholic Church.” In this matter Nemesianus appears to have imitated what he had heard in Letter LXXIII, which was then read aloud to the entire council as Cyprian’s letter: “Those who come from heresy to the Church must be baptized, so that those who are prepared for the kingdom of God by divine regeneration through the lawful and unique baptism of the holy Church may be born through [Col. 1259D] **BOTH SACRAMENTS**, because it is written: ‘Unless one has been reborn of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God.’” Cyprian speaks in the same way once again in the earlier Letter II to Stephen, no. 1: “For only then can they be fully sanctified and be sons of God, if they are born through both sacraments, since it is written: ‘Unless one has been reborn,’ etc.” Words of this kind could perhaps be interpreted to mean that anyone is washed with water in vain unless he simultaneously obtains the Holy Spirit, or spiritual grace; and thus that, when those who did not obtain that spiritual grace return, a hand is laid upon them in vain for receiving the Holy Spirit unless they are first washed with water also. But the ancient author of the *Treatise on the [Col. 1260A] Baptism of Heretics*, already cited above in the notes to Letter II, first describes that same opinion in these words: “You who introduce something new immediately answer impatiently”—perhaps “you answer”—“as you are accustomed to do, that the Lord said in the Gospel: ‘Unless one has been reborn of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of heaven.’ From this it is manifestly apparent that only that baptism is profitable in which the Holy Spirit can also be present.” He then explains that the defender of this opinion held that there is no baptism unless the Holy Spirit is also received at the same time through the laying on of the bishop’s hand, so that those two sacraments cannot be separated. Refuting this, the author of the aforesaid *Treatise* proves—both by the example of the Apostles, who, having been baptized by Christ before his death, received the Holy Spirit only after his resurrection, [Col. 1260B] and by many other examples—that baptism can be given and received without the conferral of the Holy Spirit. Conversely, by the example of those concerning whom Peter is recorded as saying in the Acts of the Apostles, “Can anyone forbid water, so that these who have received the Holy Spirit just as we have should not be baptized?” he shows that the Holy Spirit can be conferred without water. Hence he also infers: “And there will be no doubt that people can be baptized in the Holy Spirit without water.” Accordingly, whoever compares what that author discusses in the first part of his *Treatise* with the opinion of Secundianus given above may reasonably suspect that the author wished principally to refute the latter.

18. The same author sets out the question then under debate in this manner: “Whether, according to the most ancient custom and ecclesiastical tradition . . . [Col. 1260C] it was sufficient that upon those who, though outside, had received the Lord’s baptism in the name of Jesus Christ, a hand alone should be laid by the bishop for receiving the Holy Spirit, and that this laying on of a hand should furnish them with the repeated and perfected sign of faith; or whether a repeated baptism was also necessary for them, as though they would possess nothing unless they had also obtained this anew in its entirety.” Thus, in this author’s opinion, the question was not whether the laying on of a hand conferred by the bishop upon those returning from heresy for the reception of the Holy Spirit—that is, Confirmation—was to be repeated, since the parties agreed on this point. Rather, the entire controversy concerned whether baptism also had to be repeated: some affirmed this, while [Col. 1260D] the majority, whose side the author himself supports in reliance upon the most ancient custom and ecclesiastical tradition, denied it. That this same author, by the words “the repeated and perfected sign of faith,” understands the sacrament of Confirmation is demonstrated both by the following passage from Cyprian’s Letter LXXIII: “This is also now done among us, so that those who are baptized in the Church are presented to the rulers of the Church, in order that through our prayer and the laying on of a hand they may obtain the Holy Spirit and be perfected by the seal of the Lord”; and by the rite prescribed in the ancient sacramentaries, in which the pontiff is directed to sign the forehead and say, “The sign of Christ unto eternal life,” or “God seals you with the seal of faith” (*Martène, De antiquis Ecclesiae ritibus*, vol. I, [Col. 1261A] p. 251). It is also unambiguous from the sequence of the cited *Treatise* that the laying on of a hand prescribed for those coming from heresy is regarded in it as the sacrament of Confirmation. Let us now consider whether there are other testimonies of the ancients that support the same opinion.

19. On this matter, the Fathers assembled at Arles in the year 314 write in their letter to Pope Sylvester that they had decreed “that if any heretic comes to the Church, they should question him concerning the Creed; and if they determine that he was baptized in the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, a hand only should be laid upon him.” In canon 8, when issuing the same decree, after the words “a hand only should be laid upon him,” they add, “that he may receive the Holy Spirit.” Siricius explains the Church’s custom concerning the reception both of other heretics and, by name, of those who had received baptism from the Arians, [Col. 1261B] as follows: “We join these, along with the Novatians and other heretics, to the assembly of Catholics—as was established in the synod—by the invocation alone of the sevenfold Spirit through the laying on of the bishop’s hand; and this is also observed by the whole East and West.” The practice of this rite, which Siricius reports was observed by the entire East and West, is exhibited by the Gellone codex copied in the time of Charlemagne, in which we read:

**A Blessing over Those Who Come from Various Heresies**

“Holy almighty Father, who have deigned to rescue your servant from the error of heresy and to recall him to the holy Church, we beseech you, Lord, send into him your sevenfold Spirit, the Paraclete: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, [Col. 1261C] the spirit of knowledge and piety; and fill your servant with the spirit of the fear of the Lord.”

Nor can it be denied that this blessing is altogether similar to that which was pronounced over those who approached the sacrament of Confirmation. Nearly all the ancient sacramentaries provide evidence of this. In the codex of the distinguished church of Beauvais we have:

**Prayer over Those to Be Confirmed**

“Almighty and eternal God, who have deigned to regenerate these servants from water and the Holy Spirit and have given them remission of sins, send into them your Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, and give them the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety; and fill them with the spirit of the fear of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ; and graciously command them to be sealed with the sign of the cross [Col. 1261D] unto eternal life. Through—.”

In the Cahors codex:

**Blessing at Confirmation**

“Almighty and eternal God, who have deigned to regenerate these your male and female servants and have given them remission of sins, send into them, male or female, your sevenfold Spirit, the Paraclete, from heaven: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety; and fill them, male or female, with the spirit of your fear; and seal them, male or female, with the sign of the holy cross unto eternal life, in your mercy. Amen.”

Formulas similar to prayers of this kind to be said over those being confirmed, transcribed or cited from several other ancient books, may be seen in our Edmond Martène, *De antiquis Ecclesiae ritibus*, vol. I, p. [Col. 1262A] 249 ff. This agreement between the blessings pronounced over those coming from heresy and those pronounced over persons being confirmed seems indeed to lend considerable support to those who believe that a hand was laid upon persons coming from heresy by the bishop so that the sacrament of Confirmation might be conferred upon them. Whether it actually supports them, however, we shall presently examine. Here we observe only that the blessing prescribed in the Gellone manuscript is extremely ancient. Eusebius (*History*, Book VII, chap. 2) notes it with sufficient clarity in these words: “An ancient custom had become established, that in the case of persons of this kind”—those who came from heresy—“only the laying on of hands with prayer should be employed.” Siricius mentions it more openly in the passage cited above, and Innocent, who will be quoted below, agrees with him. Leo refers to the same practice no less clearly in Letter [Col. 1262B] CXLIX to Nicetas, chap. 7, where he decrees: “Those who received baptism from heretics, not having been baptized previously, are to be confirmed solely by the invocation of the Holy Spirit through the laying on of hands.” Likewise, in Letter II to Rusticus, chap. 18, he determines concerning the same persons: “Through the laying on of a hand, with the power of the Holy Spirit invoked—the power which they could not receive from heretics—they are to be joined to the Catholics.” And in Letter CLV to Neo: “Let only that which was lacking there be conferred, so that through the laying on of the bishop’s hand they may obtain the power of the Holy Spirit.”

20. As far as Stephen is concerned, there is nothing in his words that suggests the sacrament of Confirmation, and nothing from which we might suppose that he required any laying on of a hand other than one that was an indication of penance. [Col. 1262C] For when he opposed his own judgment to this opinion of the Africans concerning one who comes from heresy, “He must be baptized and renewed,” with the words, “Let nothing be introduced anew except what has been handed down”—that is, let his baptism not be renewed, but let only that which has been handed down be observed—and then added, “that a hand be laid upon him for penance,” he could have said nothing more explicit to exclude the interpretation that he meant the sacrament of Confirmation. Even among those who agreed with Cyprian that baptism was to be conferred upon persons coming from heresy, there were some who adhered to Stephen’s words in regard to the laying on of a hand. Crescens of Cirta, in particular, stated in the aforementioned Third Council of Carthage that, in his judgment, all heretics or schismatics who wished to come to the Catholic Church should not enter before [Col. 1262D] they had been exorcized and baptized, “with the exception, certainly, of those who had previously been baptized in the Catholic Church; yet in such a way that through the laying on of a hand for penance they should be reconciled to the Church.” At the same council Vincentius of Thibaris said: “We know that heretics are worse than pagans. . . . Therefore, first through the laying on of a hand in exorcism, and secondly through the regeneration of baptism, they can then come to Christ’s promise.” Here, since the laying on of a hand that is required is the one administered to those coming from heresy before baptism—the one by which Leo (*Epistle* CLVI) notes that those to be baptized are prepared for this sacrament—there is plainly no room for understanding the sacrament of Confirmation, since that sacrament is conferred only upon the baptized.

[Col. 1263A] 21. Cyprian himself, to use Augustine’s words, “determined with the others that if any persons who had been baptized in the Church returned to the Church from heresies, they should now be received not through baptism but through penance” (Augustine, *On Baptism Against the Donatists*, Book V, chap. 11). Indeed, Cyprian should be said not so much to have decreed this as to have confirmed what had been received in practice. On this matter he himself speaks as follows in his letter to Quintus: “This is what we also observe today: in the case of those who are known to have been baptized here and to have passed from us to the heretics, if they afterward acknowledge their sin, cast off their error, and return to the truth and to their mother, it is sufficient to lay a hand upon them for penance.” From this practice, moreover, a firm argument is produced by which anyone may be convinced that, for persons returning from heresy to the Church, [Col. 1263B] the laying on of a hand that conferred the sacrament of Confirmation was neither prescribed nor employed; it was instead one that displayed at least the appearance of public penance. For one kind of laying on of a hand was not prescribed and employed for those baptized in the Church and another for those initiated into this sacrament in heresy; rather, one and the same laying on of a hand was common to both. But upon those baptized in the Church a hand was laid only for penance, not for receiving the sacrament of Confirmation; therefore the same applies to those baptized outside the Church. The Donatists held this as certain. When it had been promised that, if they returned to the Church, they would be received with their ecclesiastical ranks intact, they said in Augustine’s letter formerly numbered L, now CLXXXV, no. 44: “If, therefore, we must repent [Col. 1263C] of having been outside the Church and opposed to the Church in order that we may be saved, how, after that penance, do we remain clerics or even bishops among you?” They would not have said this unless they had been persuaded that the laying on of a hand served in place of public penance, which customarily excluded a person from the clergy. Innocent prefers to call it an image of penance rather than penance itself. While emphatically denying that the clergy of the Arians and similar heretics were to be received with their ecclesiastical ranks intact, he says the following about their laity: “We receive their laypeople under an image of penance and with the sanctification of the Holy Spirit through the laying on of a hand.” And a little later: “How can it happen that we should judge their profane priests worthy of Christ’s honors when we receive their imperfect laity, with an image of penance, so that they may receive [Col. 1263D] the grace of the Holy Spirit?” (Innocent, Epistle 24 to Alexander, no. 4.) Here he sufficiently indicates that a laying on of a hand was applied to them for the sake of a certain satisfaction. He calls it an image of penance because no burdensome works were imposed upon the person returning to the Church from heresy, nor was communion postponed. Instead, as Leo—already cited—expresses it, he was immediately “joined to the Catholics by the invocation alone of the sevenfold Spirit through the laying on of the bishop’s hand.” Accordingly, Pope Vigilius, in Letter II to Profuturus, no. 4, distinguishes those who were simply baptized in heresy from those “who, after receiving the saving grace of baptism, were baptized again among the Arians and were plunged by death into the profound abyss.” Concerning the latter he decrees: “Their reconciliation is accomplished not by that laying on of a hand which operates through the invocation of the Holy Spirit, but by that through which the fruit of penance is acquired and restoration to holy communion is effected.” [Col. 1264A] These words distinguish two kinds of laying on of a hand: one that exhibits the image and likeness of sorrowful penance, and another that contains its reality; one that, through the invocation of the Holy Spirit, immediately joins a person to the assembly of Catholics, and another by which restoration to holy communion is postponed and obtained through many fruits of penance.

22. Now, just as everyone sees that the various ancient testimonies we have produced thus far [Col. 1264B] refer to the blessing transcribed above at no. 18 from the Gellone codex, so from those same testimonies anyone can readily perceive what the laying on of a hand upon persons coming from heresy has in common with that celebrated over persons being confirmed, and in what respect it differs. It is common to both that the Holy Spirit is invoked over them. For the Church, instructed by Christ, does not consider it sufficient to join those coming to her from heresy to herself by outward worship unless she also unites and binds them to herself by an inward and spiritual bond. But only the Holy Spirit can accomplish this, uniting so many members scattered throughout the world and making one body from them. It is therefore not surprising that the Church prays for the Holy Spirit in the same words both for those coming from heresy and for those being confirmed. Yet although the Church’s prayer for both is common in this respect, it nevertheless differs in this: for the former she prays that they may now begin to possess the Holy Spirit, [Col. 1264C] whom they did not possess; for the latter, that they may possess more abundantly the one whom they already possessed—or, so to speak, that they may possess him more strongly impressed upon them. Hence there is also this difference between the two blessings: for those coming from heresy, the Holy Spirit is simply invoked, with no mention of a seal; for those being confirmed, in addition to the invocation of the sevenfold Spirit, the sealing is also requested. Yet no one is unaware that the primary distinctive feature of Confirmation, by which this sacrament is distinguished from the others, consists in such a sealing. On this matter it will suffice for us to recall a single testimony of Cornelius, who remonstrates with Novatian as follows: “Nor, after he had been delivered from his illness” (Epistle 9, no. 4)—“during which he had received baptism merely by being sprinkled with water—did he receive the remaining things that, according to the rule of the Church, [Col. 1264D] must be received, nor was he **SEALED** by the bishop. But since he did not receive this seal, how could he receive the Holy Spirit?” The words of Cyprian reported above confirm the same point. Since, therefore, that prayer by which sealing was requested for those being confirmed is absent from the blessing by which persons abandoning heresy were received into the Church, it is manifest that this blessing must be distinguished from the sacrament of Confirmation.

23. Nevertheless, because it was common to those being confirmed and those coming from heresy that the bishop’s hand was laid upon both and that the sevenfold Spirit was invoked over both in the same words, some were easily induced by this similarity of ritual to believe that the sacrament of Confirmation [Col. 1265A] was conferred upon both alike. Yet it cannot be denied that the First Council of Constantinople, canon 7, intended this sacrament also to be conferred upon certain heretics whom it names, since it commands that, when they return, their forehead, eyes, nostrils, mouth, and ears be signed with holy chrism, and that those signing them say: “The seal of the gift of the Holy Spirit.” Theodoret, cited above at p. 154, note c, explains why it wished this to be done specifically with the Novatians. Gregory, however, in Book XI, Indiction 4, Letter 67 to Quiricus, testifies that in the West the Arians, whom the same council decreed should be similarly signed, were received by the laying on of a hand alone.

Moreover, the laying on of a hand applied to returning heretics had a twofold effect. Insofar as they were penitents, it washed away from them the stain of heretical guilt; insofar as they had been corrected, it joined them to the Church. [Col. 1265B] Augustine expresses both effects as follows: “But if the laying on of a hand were not applied to one coming from heresy, he would be judged to be altogether free of guilt. Yet for the sake of the bond of charity, which is the greatest gift of the Holy Spirit—without which whatever other holy things may be present in a person are of no avail for salvation—a hand is laid upon heretics” (*On Baptism Against the Donatists*, Book V, chap. 23, no. 33). Hence those who say that a hand is laid upon them either for receiving the Holy Spirit or for penance, or for both, say nothing inconsistent with the ancient faith, nor anything from which it may be inferred that by a laying on of a hand of this kind they understood the sacrament of Confirmation. Least of all can that conclusion be drawn from Stephen’s words.

## VI. STEPHEN IS PRAISED BY THE ANCIENTS AS A DEFENDER OF APOSTOLIC TRADITION, AND IS CHARGED WITH ERROR BY NO ONE EXCEPT THOSE WHO REJECTED THE BAPTISM OF HERETICS OF EVERY KIND

[Col. 1265C]

24. Vincent of Lérins finds no one earlier than Agrippinus, bishop of Carthage, to whom the custom of baptizing heretics returning to the Church can be attributed. He speaks as follows:

“Once, therefore, Agrippinus of venerable memory, bishop of Carthage, was the first of all mortals to judge—contrary to the divine canon, contrary to the rule of the universal Church, contrary to the judgment of all his fellow priests, and contrary to the custom and institutions of the ancestors—that baptism must be repeated. This presumption introduced so great an evil that it not only supplied all heretics with a model of sacrilege but also furnished certain [Col. 1265D] Catholics with an occasion for error. When, therefore, everyone everywhere protested against the novelty of the matter and all priests in every quarter resisted, each according to his own zeal, then Stephen of blessed memory, prelate of the Apostolic See, resisted together with his other colleagues, yet nevertheless more than the others—considering it fitting, I suppose, that he should surpass all the rest in devotion to the faith by as much as he surpassed them in the authority of his office.”

Cyprian himself does not deny that the practice he defended was first introduced into Africa by Agrippinus; nor does he deny the antiquity of the custom that Stephen steadfastly maintained. For he argues that it lacks truth in these words: “Nor should the custom which had crept in among certain persons prevent [Col. 1266A] truth from prevailing, for custom without truth is the antiquity of error.” Thus he is compelled at least to acknowledge its antiquity. Persuaded and compelled by the force of truth, the other bishops who sat with Cyprian in the Council of Carthage were likewise obliged to acknowledge its antiquity. Augustine deliberately collected their judgments in *On Baptism Against the Donatists*, Book III, chapters 5, 6, and following, in order to demonstrate that they had been unable to deny it.

25. Firmilian himself also, although he alleges that among his own people the practice of baptizing heretics was ancient, nevertheless freely acknowledges that among the Africans it was new, in these words: “You Africans can say against Stephen that, once the truth became known, you abandoned the error of custom.” He then adds, in favor of his own province: [Col. 1266B] “We, however, join custom to truth, and to the custom of the Romans we oppose custom—but the custom of truth—holding from the beginning what was handed down by Christ and by the Apostle.” In this conflict of assertions, therefore, while Stephen, who accepts the Baptism of heretics, says on the one side, “We follow what we have received from the Apostles,” and Firmilian, who rejects that same Baptism, affirms on the other side that he holds “what was handed down by Christ and by the Apostle,” which of the two is to be believed? If we test such opposed and contradictory assertions by Augustine’s rule—whereby he judges that to have been handed down by the Apostles which, though nowhere written, is nevertheless practiced by the universal Church—we shall concede that Stephen had a stronger right than Firmilian to claim for himself the authority of apostolic tradition.

Perhaps even in the [Col. 1266C] East the custom of baptizing heretics began with the definition of the Council of Iconium, which Firmilian praises. Indeed, according to Firmilian’s testimony, this definition was occasioned by the doubt of certain persons concerning the Baptism of the Montanists—whether it ought to be accepted. For although there was no error in their confession of the Father and the Son, they nevertheless seemed to err concerning faith in the Holy Spirit. “Therefore,” says Firmilian himself, “many of us assembled together at Iconium, examined the matter with the greatest care, and confirmed that Baptism administered outside the Church must be rejected altogether.” (In Cyprian, Epistle LXXV, pp. 198 and 202.)

But if it was held in the East, as something handed down by Christ and by the Apostle, that the Baptism of heretics must be rejected, whence came the doubt of certain persons [Col. 1266D] concerning the Baptism of the Montanists, who long before were already regarded as heretics and had been condemned under that name? Firmilian, certainly, when he says that he does not at all remember when the Baptism of heretics first began to be rejected in the East, could prove by no example and no authority that it had actually been rejected before. Nor have any writings of the ancients come down to us that would attest the truth of the tradition claimed by him.

Dionysius of Alexandria alone, after explaining the tradition of his own Church concerning the acceptance of the Baptism of heretics, adds the following in favor of the Africans: “I have learned that this custom was not now first introduced by the Africans alone, but that much earlier, in the times of preceding bishops, the same thing had been decreed in the [Col. 1267A] most populous churches, and in councils at Iconium and Synnada, and among very many others.” In these words, although this prudent and peace-loving man omits nothing that might magnify the antiquity of the practice introduced by the Africans, he nevertheless adduces nothing older than the Council of Iconium, which was followed by that of Synnada.

Here one cannot but wonder how Eusebius, although he inserted these words of Dionysius into Book VII, chapter 7, of his *History*, could nevertheless say in chapter 3: “Cyprian, who at that time governed the Church of Carthage, was the first of all to judge that heretics should be admitted only after being cleansed from error through Baptism”—unless we understand Eusebius to mean that Cyprian was the first author, not of the custom introduced, but of the controversy that arose from it, insofar as, when he sent the decree of his council to Pope Stephen, [Col. 1267B] he took it ill that Stephen rejected it.

26. Stephen nevertheless resisted him, not from any passion for contradiction, but solely from zeal to preserve tradition. He did not oppose decree to decree, but forbade the innovation and alteration of what he had received as handed down by the Apostles. But when the question concerns ascertaining the truth of traditions, who would deny credence to that Church which had as its first parent the chief of the Apostles, and which has always been more scrupulous than all others in preserving traditions? It is that Church which, as Ambrose and the other bishops assembled with him testify, “always guards and preserves the Apostles’ Creed inviolate.” (In Siricius, Epistle 8, no. 4.) Rufinus likewise asserts the same thing in his *Treatise on the Creed*.

Even Stephen’s adversaries are unable to deny the antiquity of the tradition that he defended. [Col. 1267C] The multitude of bishops who agreed with him supports it. Stephen himself proves it even by the example of heretics, who accept the Baptism of those coming to them from every quarter. The ancient author of the *Treatise on the Baptism of Heretics* also testifies that it was “received by a most ancient custom and ecclesiastical tradition” (Labbe, vol. I, *Councils*, p. 770) that the Baptism of those who had been baptized outside the Church in the name of the Lord Jesus should be admitted. Eusebius too expressly asserts that the tradition claimed by Stephen had prevailed “from the beginning” (*kratēsasan anōthen* [Greek OCR materially uncertain]) of the Church (Eusebius, Book VII, chapter 3).

Hence Augustine rightly says in Book V of *On Baptism, Against the Donatists*, chapter 23: “The Apostles indeed prescribed nothing concerning this matter; but that custom which was opposed to Cyprian must be believed to have taken its beginning [Col. 1267D] from their tradition, just as there are many things which the universal Church observes and which, for that reason, are rightly believed to have been prescribed by the Apostles, although they are not found in writing.”

I do not repeat the words of Vincent of Lérins, in which he observes that Agrippinus introduced this novelty “against the divine canon, against the rule of the universal Church, against the judgment of all his fellow priests, and against the custom and institutions of the forefathers.” I observe only that, apart from those who thought heretics ought to be baptized, no one can be found who censured anything in Stephen’s position, or even suspected error in it. “What, then,” asks Vincent of Lérins, “was the outcome of the whole affair? What indeed, except the customary and usual outcome? Antiquity was retained, and novelty was cast out.” [Col. 1268A]

And, as Facundus says in his book *Against Mocianus*: “The Church holds the position of Stephen rather than that of Cyprian, not only concerning the refusal to rebaptize heretics, but also concerning the refusal to tolerate rebaptizers.” These final words of Facundus now bring us to the new question with which our entire Dissertation must conclude.

## VII. WHETHER STEPHEN STRUCK THE REBAPTIZERS WITH EXCOMMUNICATION. WHETHER HE CONDUCTED HIMSELF TOO SEVERELY TOWARD HOLY MEN

27. Firmilian writes not only that Stephen “disagreed with so many bishops throughout the whole world,” but also represents him as “breaking peace with particular persons by various forms of discord—now with the Easterners, a fact which, as we believe, is not unknown even to you,” [Col. 1268B] he says to Cyprian, “and now with you who are in the South.” (In Cyprian, Epistle 75, near the end.) A little earlier, turning his address to Stephen, he speaks to him thus: “How greatly you have aggravated your sin by cutting yourself off from so many flocks! For you have cut off yourself. . . . For while you think that all can abstain from communion with you, you alone have abstained from communion with all.”

Moved by these words, some believe that all those, whether in the East or in Africa, who thought heretics ought to be rebaptized were excommunicated by Stephen—especially since Stephen, according to the same Firmilian’s testimony, is said to have repulsed the bishops sent as legates by the Africans in such a way “that he would not admit them even to the speech of an ordinary conversation; indeed, he commanded the whole brotherhood that no one should receive them into his house, so that those who came were denied not only peace, but even [Col. 1268C] shelter and hospitality.”

28. Yet before we assent to an opinion of this kind, while preserving the reverence owed to the holy prelate, it must be observed that Firmilian conducted himself in this affair in such a way as to incur the suspicion of a somewhat over-vehement temper, unable either to observe moderation or to confine his language within the fair laws of exact truth. He speaks as though the entire world conspired with him, while only the smallest portion adhered to Stephen. Nor is he ashamed to say to the chief prelate of the Church, who was defending apostolic tradition together with the bishops of the whole world: “You are worse than all heretics.”

But when a man is shown to have exceeded all measure in these statements, one may rightly suspect that he was likewise swept by the same emotional impulse into exaggeration in what he relates concerning the African legates. [Col. 1268D] An embittered man is ready and inclined to accept, even from a single rumor, everything that favors his preoccupied mind, although experience teaches us that rumor often deceives and, as it passes through the mouths of many, reports events otherwise than they occurred.

But let us suppose that Firmilian said nothing contrary to the truth in what he relates concerning the African legates. Could there not have been certain special and concealed reasons known to Stephen that compelled him to conduct himself toward those legates in this manner? At a later time Hormisdas appeared to some to have dealt unjustly with the Scythian monks who wished it to be said that “one of the Trinity was crucified”; they believed that those monks had been expelled from the city because of this formula. Yet they were ordered [Col. 1269A] to depart, not for that reason, but because of the disturbances they were stirring up at Rome.

Similarly, Stephen had reason to fear that the Africans might create some disturbance at Rome and might abuse Cyprian’s authority—whose name carried great weight in the city—as well as the authority of his councils and the use of human reasoning, in order to undermine the truth of apostolic tradition. According to the testimony of Jubaianus in Cyprian, the Novatianists were already rebaptizing Catholics who came over to them. Nor was Cyprian able to deny this in his reply to Jubaianus. Dionysius of Alexandria likewise testifies in Eusebius, Book VII, chapter 8, that such an outrage was being committed by those heretics, and that for this reason he turned from them with just indignation. Since, therefore, Stephen felt a proper horror at this new frenzy of those same heretics, who were especially active in the City, it is no wonder that he was wholly unwilling to communicate with legates who obstinately defended a similar error. [Col. 1269B]

He had reason to fear that, if he treated them more gently, he might appear to connive at their error and to have uttered empty threats against them. He therefore treated them as persons deemed excommunicate are ordinarily treated; but sometimes such a manner of proceeding is only an indication that communion has been suspended, not entirely removed.

The Africans did not yet regard the Novatianist legates as excommunicated when Cyprian, in Epistle I to Cornelius, no. 1, writes that they came to Carthage and that, when they asked to be heard, a hearing was denied them: “We judged,” says Cyprian himself, “that they must immediately be restrained from our communion.” So too, from the fact that Stephen refused to hear the African legates and immediately restrained them from his communion, it does not follow that he must be thought already to have pronounced a sentence of excommunication [Col. 1269C] against the Africans. Nor would I believe that the names of Cyprian and his associates, if they had already had a place in the sacred diptychs of the Roman Church, were at that time erased from them.

Finally, if we adhere to the testimony of the ancients who lived either in Stephen’s age or afterward, Stephen did not actually excommunicate the Africans or Easterners or cast them out of the Church; he merely announced that he would excommunicate them if they persisted in their position.

29. Taken by itself, Cyprian’s statement to Pompeius concerning Stephen means nothing more: “The friend of heretics and enemy of Christians thinks that the priests of God who uphold the truth of Christ and the unity of the Church ought to be **excluded from communion** (*abstinendos*).” (Epistle LXXIV.) I do not deny that the word *abstinendos* can also be said and understood of persons who had already been excluded; [Col. 1269D] but that it must in fact be understood only of threats of excommunication is established by what Dionysius of Alexandria writes to Xystus, Stephen’s successor:

“Previously he [Stephen] had written letters concerning Helenus and Firmilian and all those established throughout Cilicia and Cappadocia and all the neighboring provinces, saying that for the same reason he would withdraw from communion with them (*oude ekeinois koinōnēsōn*, οὐδὲ ἐκείνοις κοινωνήσων), because they rebaptized heretics.”

Stephen, therefore, had merely threatened Firmilian and his associates that they should not rebaptize heretics, since otherwise he would withdraw from communion with them; accordingly, he had not yet withdrawn from it. Dionysius, moreover, wrote this after Stephen’s death. It follows that Stephen by no means carried out [Col. 1270A] what he had threatened, or at least that Dionysius did not know that he had done so.

Augustine, adhering to the same manner of speaking, says: “Therefore, although Stephen not only did not rebaptize heretics, but also judged that those who did so, or decreed that it should be done, **ought to be excommunicated**, as the letters of other bishops and of Cyprian himself show, Cyprian nevertheless remained with him in the peace of unity.” (*On the Unity of Baptism, Against Petilianus*, no. 23.)

Another African, a most celebrated writer of the sixth century, committed to writing what he had received by tradition concerning the matter in these words:

“Blessed Stephen also, prelate of the Apostolic See, when he learned that St. Cyprian and the other African bishops had decreed that all heretics should be baptized—although, as has been said, they had issued such a judgment without inserting any anathema and without acting against any earlier decrees of a general council, [Col. 1270B] or conniving at heretics—immediately announced to him that, if any should dare to do this, they would be expelled from the Church.” (Facundus, *Against Mocianus*.)

By speaking thus, Facundus could, in my opinion, have adduced nothing clearer to teach that Stephen merely threatened excommunication against those who rebaptized heretics.

30. The same writer declared no less openly how just Stephen’s censure of Cyprian appeared to him when he said:

“If no wise man believes the Church heretical because it praises the teaching of Blessed Cyprian, bishop and martyr of Carthage, although he not only privately, as it seemed good to him, but also after assembling a council, defined that every heretic coming to the Church should be baptized, and on this account resisted when censured [Col. 1270C] by Stephen, the Roman prelate, and defended his own position in writing to Pompeius by as much human argumentation as he could muster, treating that same Blessed Stephen abusively, by whom he had been **rightly censured**.” (Book X, chapter 3.)

Yet this same Cyprian, who was rightly censured by Stephen because he would not allow himself to be separated from an opinion opposed to tradition, deserved Augustine’s praise because he remained with Stephen in the peace of unity. “For in that very matter,” says that Doctor, “in which he thought differently, he decreed that colleagues holding a different opinion were neither to be judged nor removed from the right of communion.” (Augustine, Epistle formerly numbered 48, now 93, no. 36.)

He did indeed decree that heretics coming to the Church should be baptized; but, as Facundus observed above, he inserted no anathema against those [Col. 1270D] who thought that they should not be baptized. Therefore Jerome warns the disciples of Hilary the Deacon, who were misusing Cyprian’s writings: “Let them know that he published these things without anathematizing those who were unwilling to follow him, since he remained in communion with those who opposed his position.” (Near the end of the *Dialogue Against the Luciferians*.)

Cyprian himself expresses his unwavering zeal for the peace of unity in Epistle LXXIII to Jubaianus:

“These are the brief answers we have given you according to our limited ability, dearest brother, prescribing or prejudging nothing for anyone, so as to prevent any bishop from doing what he thinks best, possessing the freedom of his own judgment. As far as lies in us, we do not [Col. 1271A] contend, on account of heretics, with our colleagues and fellow bishops, with whom we maintain divine concord and the Lord’s peace.”

He repeats similar words at the end of Epistle LXXVI to Magnus. We have also already heard him testify to this same principle in the earlier Epistle II, which he composed concerning the council, together with his other colleagues, and addressed to Stephen. Finally, in the celebrated Third Council of Carthage, he addresses his colleagues thus:

“It remains for us to set forth what each of us thinks about this very matter, judging no one and removing no one from the right of communion if he should think differently.”

For Cyprian, as Augustine observed, “moved by the difficulty of the question itself and most abundantly endowed with the holy affections of charity, had determined that unity must be maintained with those who thought differently.” Nor is there any doubt that this difficulty was produced and increased by consciousness of the fact that the custom which he knew had prevailed [Col. 1271B] in the Church and still prevailed in most provinces had been altered among his own people only recently. Therefore, lest he appear to condemn his forebears and almost the whole Church, he allowed each bishop to think or act as he judged best; and thus he considered this question to pertain merely to discipline.

31. From this, at least, some will think it follows that, if Cyprian was rightly praised because, by allowing each person free discretion in his own opinion, he judged that no one should be removed from his communion, Stephen should rightly be censured because he determined that all who dissented from him should be expelled from the Church.

Yet this by no means follows, unless Cyprian’s and Stephen’s circumstances in that controversy were equal, [Col. 1271C] and unless each held, or ought to have held, the same judgment concerning it. But the circumstances were otherwise. It appeared harsh to Cyprian to deny communion to those who preserved what he saw preserved in almost all the churches and what he was not unaware had been observed by his own predecessors before Agrippinus. Stephen, however, judged it consistent with equity that those who, by a most pernicious example, refused to obey the commands of the Apostles received by tradition should be expelled from the Church.

In this dispute Cyprian, unlike Polycrates in the earlier controversy concerning the date of Easter, had no tradition of John available to oppose to the tradition of Peter. For all the churches agreed with Stephen except the African churches and a few provinces of the East. Cyprian and his associates admitted that the same custom had prevailed in Africa down to Agrippinus; nor was any [Col. 1271D] trace of the contrary custom found in the churches of the East before doubt concerning the Baptism of the Montanists gave rise to the decree of Iconium. To what, then, must so great an agreement among the churches of the whole world be attributed, unless to apostolic tradition?

The Africans nevertheless refused to believe that this tradition had proceeded from the Apostles because it seemed to them repugnant to human reason. Yet the more plausible the argument they advanced appears, the more strongly it proves that the custom rejected by that argument could not have been received in all the Churches except by divine tradition.

Vincent of Lérins therefore spoke aptly:

“The holy and prudent man [Stephen] understood that the principle of piety permits nothing other than that everything received in faith from the fathers should be committed to the children in that same faith; [Col. 1272A] and that we ought not to lead religion wherever we wished, but rather to follow wherever religion led; and that it is characteristic of Christian modesty and gravity not to hand down one’s own ideas to posterity, but to preserve what has been received from the forefathers.”

32. Nor did Cyprian and Stephen hold the same judgment concerning that controversy. By departing from ancient tradition, Cyprian was compelled to regard it as though it pertained merely to discipline. Stephen, however, judged the same matter very differently. Nor was it like the earlier controversy concerning the date of Easter, in which each of the disputants could defend and retain his own position without injury to the faith. The dispute concerned a principal article of our religion: namely, the power and efficacy of an absolutely necessary Sacrament, without which no one can be called or regarded as a Christian.

Moreover, the matter concerned defending the [Col. 1272B] unity of Baptism. For faith teaches that this Baptism, which Scripture in express words declares to be “one,” must not be repeated. On this point the parties were in agreement—so much so that Cyprian, fearing that prejudice might be aroused against him if he were thought to wish heretics to be rebaptized, wrote both in Epistle LXXI to Quintus, “We, however, say that those who come from there are not **rebaptized** among us, but **baptized**,” and in Epistle LXXIII to Jubaianus, “Through a certain prejudice, it is considered an outrage to baptize after the enemies of God, as though this were to **rebaptize**.”

How greatly Christians, not without God’s prompting, recoiled from the repetition of Baptism is clearly attested by Augustine in the following words:

“Thus people, by some hidden inspiration of God, so detest anyone’s receiving Baptism a second time when he has already received it anywhere, that those very [Col. 1272C] heretics [the Donatists], when they argue, rub their foreheads, and almost all their laity . . . confess that this alone displeases them there”—that is, in their sect—“namely, that Baptism is repeated.” (Book V of *On Baptism, Against the Donatists*, chapter 5.)

See also what follows there.

Would Stephen not have appeared either to overthrow, or to permit the overthrow of, this dogma that Baptism must not be repeated, if he had allowed the recently introduced custom of rebaptizing heretics to become more firmly established? The greater the merit of those who defended it, the graver was the danger threatening the Church unless the man who possessed the chief authority in the Church vigorously defended the faith received through apostolic tradition. The infection of so great an evil had already corrupted all Africa, which was no insignificant portion of the Church, as well as Cilicia and Cappadocia; and since it did not cease to spread into the neighboring [Col. 1272D] provinces, it would soon have ruined the whole East unless it had been restrained and healed by a prompt remedy.

33. Stephen, therefore, had to interpose the whole weight of his authority against the celebrated decree by which Cyprian, together with his council, had sanctioned the proposition: “He who comes to the Church must be baptized and renewed, so that within it he may be sanctified through holy persons”; and he had to resist courageously those who defended it more obstinately.

For if he had conducted himself more remissly in this cause; if, under the appearance of peace, he had permitted this opinion to prevail—that a person could be sanctified only through holy men; that one who did not possess the Holy Spirit could not give the Holy Spirit through the sacraments; that whoever could not give the Holy Spirit could not baptize; and that Baptism conferred by such a person was invalid [Col. 1273A] and entirely null—what would those do, as Augustine observes (Book V of *On Baptism, Against the Donatists*, chapter 21), who, even within the Church, while seeking a man of God, had encountered a concealed murderer, a drunkard, a robber, or an envious man? What disturbance of consciences, what anxiety, would arise from this?

For although the rebaptizers did not go so far as to say that Baptism conferred by wicked Catholics must be renewed, it nevertheless follows from all the arguments they opposed to Stephen that one who appears to have been baptized by Catholics destitute of charity and grace was not actually baptized and therefore must be renewed. Once this is admitted, who could be confident that he had been baptized? How many would rightly doubt it?

Indeed, Firmilian reports that the following practice had been received [Col. 1273B] in his own church concerning persons baptized by bishops who had been deposed from priestly dignity for the crime of idolatry: “Whoever comes to us after being immersed by those bishops is baptized among us with the one true Baptism, as an alien who has obtained nothing.”

34. In this entire dispute, which must be admitted to have been extremely sharp and vigorous, if men endowed with no ordinary holiness, while they seem to themselves to be carried away by zeal for truth alone, allowed certain words to escape them which the common laws of Christian modesty do not approve, what must not be feared from those disputes that are rashly undertaken for trivial reasons and are often fostered and nourished solely by desire for glory?

But if such disputes cannot be avoided, let the parties conduct themselves in such a way that the person defending the truth cannot be reproached for displaying a schismatic spirit, and the person wandering from the [Col. 1273C] truth may still be able to glory in a Catholic disposition. Let them imitate Stephen and Cyprian, whose minds were always so disposed that they sincerely desired the Church’s peace no less than the faith to remain unharmed, and of whom Augustine says: “Peace prevailed in their hearts, so that in so great a dispute no evil of schism arose between them.” (Book V of *On Baptism, Against the Donatists*, chapter 25.) [Col. 1274A]

From this, too, let lovers of novelty and despisers of ecclesiastical traditions learn to what danger they expose themselves when, on the strength of certain plausible human arguments—or even entirely destitute of such arguments—they do not fear to depart from customs always received and carefully observed in the Church. Even if the Church’s faith, received by constant tradition, could at some time be attacked by men of the highest holiness and authority, it could never be overcome by anyone.

If in his own age, when no decrees of a general council were yet read, Cyprian cried out against Stephen, “Let no one [Col. 1274B] say: ‘We follow what we have received from the Apostles,’” how much more forcefully do we now say, in Augustine’s words:

“What the custom of the Church has always maintained, what this dispute was unable to rend asunder, and what a plenary council”—whether the Council of Arles, canon 8, or likewise the Council of Nicaea, canon 8—“confirmed.” To this is added the fact that, after examining the arguments and testimonies of Scripture on both sides of the dispute, it can also be said: “What the truth has declared, this we follow.” (*Ibid.*, Book IV, chapter 6.)

Elsewhere Augustine marvels—and this is truly worthy of wonder—that although the Donatist Petilian praised and followed Cyprian’s position concerning Baptism, he nevertheless commemorated Stephen among those prelates of the Roman Church “whom he confessed to have exercised an unblemished episcopate.” Such, evidently, is the force of truth that it sometimes [Col. 1274C] extorts fair testimony even from its adversaries. After testimony of this kind, who could suspect any blemish in Stephen’s faith?

[Col. 1273]

# PONTIFICAL AUTHORITY, SHARPLY ATTACKED BY CERTAIN MODERNS ON THE BASIS OF CYPRIAN’S WELL-KNOWN CONDUCT, BUT SOLIDLY VINDICATED BY THE WISEST THEOLOGIANS OF FRANCE

## A HISTORICO-DOGMATIC DISSERTATION

Avignon, 1740.

## PREFACE

[Col. 1273C] Among the various arguments which certain moderns, enemies of Roman infallibility, [Col. 1274C] have attempted to wrench even from the more ancient past in support of their new opinion, none, I think, is more celebrated among them or more frequently employed than that which they have thought to extract from the familiar and widely publicized disagreement between St. Cyprian and St. Stephen, the Roman Pontiff, [Col. 1275A] concerning the Baptism of heretics.

Behold their perennial warhorse and chief engine, with which they batter the sacred authority of the Roman Pontiffs. They turn this argument, in which they chiefly glory, this way and that throughout their writings; they parade it and never cease to press it. They expound it in so many ways and thrust it, appropriately or inappropriately, into so many passages that it often occupies the greater part of a volume. One would say that pontifical authority was so closely bound up with this disagreement of Cyprian’s that it could neither be discussed nor written about without it.

But why should those men not think so, who contend that from this single action of Cyprian’s it follows evidently and necessarily that the doctrine of pontifical inerrancy—to which so many recent flatterers [Col. 1275B] of the Roman Curia, as they say, are not ashamed to render service—did not find acceptance with that most splendid light of the African Church?

It is truly remarkable that so powerful and evident an argument, and one drawn from the earliest antiquity, should have escaped the first and more celebrated men who undertook to overthrow the supreme authority of the Roman Pontiff. I mean Gerson, Almain, Richer, Major, and those few other comrades of theirs who, down to the century just past, attacked pontifical inerrancy in their writings. To none of them, so far as I know, did it ever occur to allege or adduce this disagreement of Cyprian’s in order to assail that inerrancy.

Was so celebrated and universally known a controversy unknown to them? Our moderns would certainly not allow their own masters to be charged with such supine ignorance. Those doctors of the Sorbonne knew what scarcely any novice in theology or history [Col. 1275C] failed to know. Yet the argument which more recent writers wrench from that controversy between Cyprian and Stephen against Roman infallibility, far from appearing evident and necessary to them, was judged so futile and feeble that they did not permit it a place even among the lightest arguments they themselves amassed. So true is it that things are often regarded by disciples as most solid and evident which did not appear to their masters even worthy of mention.

Yet although this argument has only recently been debated among Catholics by the moderns, and is for that reason not unwelcome to lovers of novelty, it does not owe its origin to these theologians. It has more ancient parents, from whom today’s haters of Roman inerrancy borrowed it. [Col. 1275D] They were preceded, namely, by Luther, Calvin, the Magdeburg Centuriators, and Marco Antonio de Dominis. To say nothing of other writers of that weight, these were followed by Casaubon, Herbert Thorndike, Joseph Henry Ott, Basnage, Blondel, John Forbes, and Friedrich Spanheim, all of whom, in order to overthrow the supreme authority of the Roman Pontiff, never ceased to press Cyprian’s views and manner of proceeding in the matter of the Baptism of heretics, and to cast them in the teeth of Catholics a hundred times over, even to the point of nausea. Who could begrudge our adversaries predecessors of this sort? . . .

Nothing new, therefore, has been advanced by our moderns in this affair, nothing that had not long before been fashioned by Lutherans and Calvinists and urged a hundred times, [Col. 1276A] as the learned theologians of France have observed more than once. Above the rest, let us hear the man who devoted himself expressly to elucidating this controversy between Cyprian and Stephen, the Roman Pontiff: D. Chiconot, doctor of the Sorbonne, in the French dissertation *Sur la célèbre dispute entre le Pape S. Étienne et S. Cyprien, évêque de Carthage* [*On the Celebrated Dispute Between Pope St. Stephen and St. Cyprian, Bishop of Carthage*], published at Paris with royal approval in 1725:

“Luther,” he says, “Calvin, Antonio de Dominis, and especially the innovators of the later age shamefully abused the manner in which St. Cyprian the martyr conducted himself toward St. Stephen, the Roman Pontiff, in the matter of the Baptism of heretics, in order to undermine the preeminence of the authority belonging to Christ’s vicar.”

The entire mass of this argument constructed by Lutherans and Calvinists had already fallen into utter contempt when [Col. 1276B] recent haters of Roman infallibility decided to dig it out of the tomb in which it lay buried and, restoring it with new equipment and embellishing it with much labor, to oppose it to the doctrine prevailing among all Catholics. They spared neither investigation, nor vigils, nor lamp oil in repairing the ruins of an argument long since routed and gathering the debris from which they might construct a new engine.

Yet, fully aware that it could not stand unless strengthened by firmer supports than before, they devised two claims hitherto unused. It was not enough for them that Cyprian had resisted Stephen and charged him with error—points that had already been appropriated by the heterodox. Going further, they openly asserted that the decree which Cyprian opposed had been a solemn [Col. 1276C] judgment of the Roman Pontiff, endowed with all the authority it could possess; and nevertheless they contended that Cyprian’s resistance to it was free from every fault. From then on, they devoted all their efforts and all the art at their command to confirming these two principal tenets of the recent doctrine.

As to the first point, they began to proclaim loudly and publicly attest that Stephen’s judgment had been issued with the full authority of the Chair;[^c0132-1] that it had been fortified with all the force that could be conferred by a Roman Pontiff;[^c0132-2] and that it lacked nothing required in decrees issued *ex cathedra*.[^c0132-3] So splendid, magnificent, and ostentatious are the things they have poured forth to describe the majesty of this pontifical rescript that those to whom such things appeal could desire nothing further, nor be capable of desiring anything further.

[^c0132-1]: [Col. 1276D] *Defense of the Declaration of the Gallican Clergy of 1682*, published anonymously at Luxembourg in 1730 under the name of Bossuet, Bishop of Meaux, Part II, Book XIV, chapter 5.

[^c0132-2]: [Col. 1276D] Fleury, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book VII, chapter 32: “The decree of Pope Stephen, invested with all the force that he could give it” (*Le décret du pape Étienne revêtu de toute la force qu’il pouvait lui donner*).

[^c0132-3]: [Col. 1276D] *Letter on Ecclesiastical Power to Martin Steyaert*, printed in 1688: “Cyprian erred; but because the Church had not yet spoken, although Stephen had thought, written, and commanded the contrary—who among our more recent scholastics does not acknowledge that he spoke *ex cathedra*?—Cyprian’s error is nevertheless excused. Stephen, therefore, was not regarded as infallible.”

[Col. 1276D] Yet our modern writers knew very well that many others are delighted less by a grand and splendid display of words than by solid proofs of facts; [Col. 1277A] and that the esteem conceived for them had not reached such a point that full credence would be given to every novelty they proclaimed. They understood perfectly well that their own authority with everyone was not so great that the inerrancy which they deny to the Roman Pontiffs should be assigned to themselves. They therefore prudently judged that what they were boasting about Stephen’s solemn rescript had to be demonstrated not merely by figures of rhetoric, but also by arguments as strong as they could devise. Indeed, so great was their shrewdness in selecting them, so great the power and keenness of their intellect, that I do not hesitate to affirm that arguments more suitable for proving the matter could not have been produced. For what could be more fitting than that, just as things indubitable are proved by things certain and ancient things by ancient evidence, so fabrications should be confirmed by fictions and novelties by recent inventions? This, moreover, our modern writers accomplished manfully and abundantly. [Col. 1277B] For that a decree of such solemnity had issued from Stephen, the Roman Pontiff, was something new and hitherto unheard of. What, then, did the modern writers do? They likewise fabricated new and previously unheard-of arguments to prove it.
