For it was from those writers that the Christian world at last learned that Stephen’s decree had been issued in a Roman council, [Note: [Col. 1277C] Felix Deschamps, in his *Letter on the Supreme Pontiff* [Col. 1277D] to Martin Steyaert, p. 25: “Stephen issued a definitive decree in a Roman council and directed it to all the faithful, by which he intended, under penalty of excommunication, to bind absolutely all the faithful to believe that those baptized by heretics were not to be rebaptized.”] and had been directed and sent by Stephen to all the churches; [Note: [Col. 1277D] The same, ibid.; and Jacques Gilbert, in his treatise *On the Primacy of the Apostolic See*, question 5, § 2: “Stephen issues a definitive decree and directs it to all the faithful, so that he may instruct all of them upon a matter and point of the highest importance, because the validity or nullity of Baptism was at issue, without which no one can be saved; and by that decree he intends to bind absolutely all the faithful to believe that those baptized by heretics are not to be rebaptized.” Likewise the defender of the Gallican Declaration of 1682, part II, book XIV, chapter 5: “Stephen framed a decree and sent it to all the churches.”] and that Stephen’s intention in that solemn decree had most certainly been to propose for the belief of faith by absolutely all the faithful that persons baptized by heretics were not to be immersed again when they were received into the communion of the Church. [Note: [Col. 1277D] Felix Deschamps and Jacques Gilbert in the passages just cited.] Since none of these claims had previously entered the mind of any mortal, they certainly had to be introduced in order to prove something [Col. 1277C] of which there was no trace whatsoever in all antiquity. Our modern writers did this suitably, so as on this side to support and reinforce that argument drawn from Cyprian which had long since been routed in the Lutherans.

As regards the second point, good God, what did they not say, what did they not heap together, in order to present and persuade us that Cyprian’s manner of proceeding against Stephen was not only free of every fault, but also full of charity and equity, and truly worthy of an episcopal and apostolic spirit? Unless these things could be read, what Catholic anywhere, what sane person, could have believed them? At once, so that they might win the reader’s sympathies and make him most ready to receive favorably what they were going to bring forward [Col. 1278A] in Cyprian’s defense, they began to commend Cyprian’s very great merits and to celebrate him with boundless praises. With immense labor they sought from every quarter and amassed whatever might contribute in any degree to Cyprian’s commendation. Both ecumenical and particular councils were summoned; so too the Roman Pontiffs themselves, the Fathers and Doctors of the Church, and as many Greek and Latin historians as could be found. New and old martyrologies and calendars were adduced, together with the Ambrosian Missal, ancient and recent Masses of various churches, prefaces, and the Canon itself. New and old Roman, Spanish, and Gallican breviaries were cited; indeed, the very rubrics of the Breviary were reported, as well as the various litanies of the churches. The translations of Cyprian’s relics were also extolled, [Col. 1278B] together with the solemnities of his feast and the dedication of many churches under his name; nor was it omitted that some had observed a fast on the vigil of St. Cyprian. [Note: [Col. 1278D] On this subject consult, above all others, Launoy, Letter 15 to Bevilaqua, in part 8 of the edition of his letters, Cambridge, 1689; likewise Fr. Gervais, in his *Life of St. Cyprian*, printed in French at Paris in 1717; likewise Dom Lombert, in the preface to the French work entitled *The Works of St. Cyprian Translated into French*, Rouen edition, 1716.] And as though so many monuments did not sufficiently depict and disclose the whole greatness and excellence of Cyprian, as great as it was, they heap and load upon him so many titles, encomiums, and praises, without measure or number, that one can scarcely believe he was a man.

Far be it from us to wish to detract in any way from Cyprian’s very great merits or from the singular veneration which he has rightly obtained among all. Yet we know that not a few impartial judges of affairs cannot endure so many indiscriminate praises poured out upon Cyprian, not only because excessive praise vexes the modest, but because all hyperbolic praise first produces aversion and then [Col. 1278C] contempt. For, they say, there is in law a title *On Claiming More Than Is Due*, so that he who demands more receives less; and it is implanted in us by nature that, when someone is exalted beyond what is just, we strive by a certain natural inclination to bring him down. Who does not proclaim Cyprian the greatest glory and ornament of the African Church, the brilliant light of his age, a most weighty Doctor of the whole Church, a most holy bishop, and a most glorious martyr? Who ever thought of not proclaiming him such? Likewise, who does not or has not acknowledged Cyprian as a bulwark of the faith, a repository of traditions, a palladium of ecclesiastical discipline, a support of evangelical morality, and a monument of Christian doctrine? Because these things are certain and do not at all exceed the limits of truth that must be observed, they are willingly heard and universally approved. But the claims so often paraded about Cyprian—as though he held the primacy among the Doctors and teachers of the Church; as though in sublimity of intellect, maturity of judgment, elegance of expression, purity of doctrine, breadth of learning, and, finally, charity, patience, piety, and the other gifts and virtues of the soul, he could scarcely be compared with anyone; as though he did nothing that was not holy [Col. 1279A] and taught nothing that was not right, so that “he was free even from those very slight errors which were common among the earliest Fathers of the Church” [Note: [Col. 1279D] Dupin, *Library of Ecclesiastical Authors*, vol. I, p. 534, Paris edition, 1688: “St. Cyprian is free, I do not say merely from gross errors, but also from those which are slight and common among the Fathers of the first three centuries.”]—and very many other assertions of this kind, which could scarcely be tolerated in a hyperbolic panegyric, are received coldly, seem tasteless, and are despised and ridiculed, because their excess and extravagance provoke disgust. Thus reason very many who, although well aware that pardon is more readily granted to no one than to the person accused of praising us excessively, nevertheless think that no one should exceed due measure in bestowing such praises.

But whatever may be the truth about this fault imputed to our modern writers, we must all acknowledge that they omitted nothing by which they might dispose and incline the minds of their readers to approve whatever could be supplied, even ever so slightly, [Col. 1279B] in Cyprian’s defense. With their readers’ minds thus disposed and affected toward Cyprian, the modern writers whom we are considering come to the matter itself and undertake by every means to vindicate and defend Cyprian’s manner of proceeding against Stephen.

Let us now at last see what our modern writers have produced in Cyprian’s defense. Fleury, just as he so governed his pen in describing Stephen’s martyrdom that he dismissed so great a defender of tradition to his death without the slightest praise, likewise restrained himself so thoroughly in reporting this letter of Cyprian that he considered it more than sufficient merely to assert that in this letter Cyprian undertook to refute the reply. [Note: [Col. 1279D] *Ecclesiastical History*, vol. II, book VII, no. 28.] And indeed, he indicates to us [Col. 1279C] that he found nothing in Cyprian’s letter even remotely foreign to charity, when he relates that Cyprian’s error did not in any way prejudice his holiness, because in this matter he had always preserved not only the unity of the Church, but charity as well. [Note: [Col. 1279D] Ibid., no. 32.]

Launoy agrees with Fleury. He celebrates Cyprian’s letter to Pompeius as vigorous and forceful; for, after reporting its contents, he says: “Cyprian opposes these things to Stephen vigorously and forcefully.” [Note: [Col. 1279D] Letter 15 to Bevilaqua, part 8 of the *Letters*, p. 807.] Indeed, he relates that posterity judged that letter, no less than Firmilian’s letter to Cyprian, to be most worthy of remembrance: “Posterity,” he says, “judged Stephen’s letters less worthy of remembrance, but the letters of Cyprian and Firmilian most worthy of remembrance.” [Note: [Col. 1279D] Ibid., p. 8011.] Tillemont, who did not hesitate to accuse Stephen [Col. 1279D] even of inhumanity, [Note: [Col. 1279D] *Ecclesiastical History*, vol. IV, article 49, p. 155.] nevertheless confidently affirms that meekness and fraternal charity were not at all violated by Cyprian when writing to Pompeius. [Note: [Col. 1279D] Ibid., article 47, p. 150.]

Lombert, in his preface to the French work entitled *The Works of St. Cyprian, Bishop of Carthage [Col. 1280A] and Martyr, Translated into French*, judged this letter of Cyprian so worthy of magnanimity and episcopal freedom that he relates that it earned praise from Augustine. For, after quoting it, he breaks forth into these words: “Thus freely and generously did St. Cyprian defend his opinion concerning Baptism against Pope Stephen, for which he is praised by St. Augustine.” Hence it is no wonder if he repeatedly insists that Cyprian, in this controversy over Baptism, “always gave the greatest proofs of moderation.” Fr. Gervais surpassed the defenders of Cyprian enumerated thus far. For in the *Life of St. Cyprian*, which he published in French, though suppressing his name, he calls the letter which Cyprian wrote to Pompeius excellent, and says that in it “a truly apostolic vigor” shines forth. [Note: [Col. 1280D] Book V, no. 16, p. 414.] He maintains that so great an unction and [Col. 1280B] Christian moderation are found in it, whether Cyprian is defending himself or attacking and refuting his adversary, that all must acknowledge that he was more intent upon the rights of the Church than upon his own. [Note: [Col. 1280D] Ibid.] For, after recounting all the things which, as we saw above, Cyprian poured forth against Stephen, he cries out: “Behold, certainly, a splendid and thoroughly spiritual ardor! In those holy transports of soul one recognizes a heart wholly kindled by the flames of divine love and breathing nothing but the glory and beauty of the house of the Lord.” [Note: [Col. 1280D] Ibid., p. 419.]

Finally, passing over some other writers of this kind, Dupin signifies to us in his *Ecclesiastical Library* that all the things Cyprian heaped upon Stephen were so many truths—indeed, truths which, though unwelcome [Col. 1280C] to Stephen, the Bishop of Carthage was nevertheless bound to set before him, and which he took care to temper, as much as he could, with his customary pleasantness. For when he compares Cyprian with Tertullian, he writes that adversaries are treated abusively by the latter; “but St. Cyprian,” he says, “is far more moderate: if ever he is obliged to tell his adversaries truths which displease them, he tempers them, as far as he can, with his pleasantness.” [Note: [Col. 1280D] Vol. I, p. 533.] Hence, although he charges Stephen with great harshness in his reply, [Note: [Col. 1280D] Ibid., p. 500.] he nevertheless noted nothing in Cyprian’s letter to Pompeius that seemed less than consonant with moderation. [Note: [Col. 1280D] Ibid.] In this he has as his associate Adrien Baillet in the *Lives of the Saints*. [Note: [Col. 1280D] Vol. III, under 16 September, p. 190, Paris edition, 1701.]

[Col. 1280D] These and many other things of this kind were put forward by innovating theologians to vindicate Cyprian’s manner of proceeding against Stephen. If they seem to anyone inflated and exaggerated, they should indeed be censured on the sole ground that they offend against truth; nevertheless, they may somehow be tolerated, because at least they do not openly attack anyone’s reputation, dignity, or holiness. But the unbridled exertion and violence of our adversaries in praising Cyprian’s manner of proceeding could by no means be contained within these limits.

[Col. 1281A] I pass over that tasteless affectation by which they repeatedly insist, and even strive to prove at greater length, that Cyprian is held in far greater esteem in the Church than Stephen. [Note: [Col. 1281C] Launoy, Letter 15 to Bevilaqua; Fr. Gervais [Col. 1281D] throughout the *Life of St. Cyprian*; Lombert in the cited preface to the works of St. Cyprian.] Those comparisons between holy men whom the Church venerates as inscribed in her calendars, and those contests injurious to both parties over the respective merits of each, which aim to increase the holiness of one by diminishing the other, have long been offensive and can scarcely—if even scarcely—be tolerated in the panegyrical declamations of orators.

I likewise disregard all the efforts of the modern writers to magnify the number of those whom Tillemont, [Note: [Col. 1281D] *Ecclesiastical History*, vol. IV, articles 43, 44, and 45.] Dupin, [Note: [Col. 1281D] *Ecclesiastical Library*, vol. I, p. 540.] Launoy, [Note: [Col. 1281D] Letter 15 to Bevilaqua.] and Fr. Gervais [Note: [Col. 1281D] *Life of St. Cyprian*, book V, nos. 1, 2, and elsewhere.] write to have applauded Cyprian rather than Stephen. According to their reckoning, it would follow that Dionysius of Alexandria; Dionysius [Col. 1281B] and Philemon, Roman presbyters; Jerome; Athanasius; Optatus of Milevis; the Council of Nicaea; Basil; Gregory Nazianzen; Cyril of Jerusalem; Gregory of Nyssa; Ambrose; Augustine; Theodoret; the Roman synod under Gelasius; Fulgentius, Bishop of Ruspe; Gregory the Great; and the Quinisext Council adhered to Cyprian rather than to Stephen. Yet what, in truth, is the fruit of so many efforts and labors? I freely state what I think: in amassing so many adversaries against Stephen, the modern writers manifested what disposition they bore toward Stephen, just as toward the memory of so many Fathers, in contempt of the laws of history and equity.

These things, I say, and other similar matters I pass over, since, compared with what follows, they are too slight to detain [Col. 1281C] us. What, then, do those who profess and wish to appear Catholic, humble sons, and moderate writers relate concerning Stephen, Supreme Pontiff, defender of apostolic tradition, and most holy martyr?

Stephen, say our modern writers, conducted himself toward Cyprian in an utterly unworthy fashion. [Note: [Col. 1281D] Fr. Gervais, *Life of St. Cyprian*, p. 455.] He wrote to Cyprian a letter entirely unworthy of being written by a Roman Pontiff to the Bishop of Carthage; [Note: [Col. 1281D] The same, ibid., p. 412; Baillet, *Lives of the Saints*, under 2 August, p. 111; likewise Tillemont, *Ecclesiastical History*, vol. IV, p. 330.] a proud letter full of insults; [Note: [Col. 1281D] Lombert, in the cited preface, p. 73.] and an exceedingly abusive one. [Note: [Col. 1281D] Lombert, ibid.] Stephen pompously displays arrogance and affects dominion; [Note: [Col. 1281D] Fr. Gervais, *Life of St. Cyprian*, pp. 413 and 461.] he plays the commander and tyrant; [Note: [Col. 1281D] Fr. Gervais, ibid., p. 431.] he replies to Cyprian with great inhumanity; [Note: [Col. 1281D] Dupin, *Ecclesiastical Library*, vol. [number omitted], p. 500.] and shows himself very inhuman toward Cyprian. [Note: [Col. 1281D] Tillemont, *Ecclesiastical History*, vol. IV, article 49, p. 155; Baillet, *Lives of the Saints*, vol. III, under 16 September.] Stephen judges and condemns Cyprian [Col. 1282A] without hearing him. [Note: [Col. 1282C] Fr. Gervais, *Life of St. Cyprian*, p. 436.] He calls him a false Christ, a false apostle, deceitful, and perfidious. [Note: [Col. 1282C] Tillemont, *Ecclesiastical History*, vol. IV, p. 150; likewise Fr. Gervais, *Life of St. Cyprian*, p. 413; Lombert, in the cited preface, p. 72; Baillet, under 16 September, in the passage cited.] He treats Cyprian’s legates in the most insulting fashion. [Note: [Col. 1282C] Tillemont, ibid., p. 155.] He not only denied them peace, communion, hospitality, and sustenance, but commanded everyone else to deny these things to them. [Note: [Col. 1282C] Fleury, *Ecclesiastical History*, vol. II, book VII, p. 283. [Col. 1282D] The same is written by Tillemont, *Ecclesiastical History*, vol. IV, article 49; Lombert, in the cited preface, p. 72; Fr. Gervais, *Life of St. Cyprian*, p. 462; and Baillet, *Lives of the Saints*, under 2 August, p. 111.] Stephen indeed displays zeal, but a zeal suited solely to ravaging everything indiscriminately. [Note: [Col. 1282D] Fr. Gervais, *Life of St. Cyprian*, p. 438.] This zeal of Stephen moved the emperor cruelly to persecute the Church. [Note: [Col. 1282D] Fr. Gervais, *Life of St. Cyprian*, p. 452.] Stephen was tyrannically oppressing a great many churches. [Note: [Col. 1282D] The same, p. 459.] He has no regard for the unity of the Church and cares nothing about tearing it apart. [Note: [Col. 1282D] Lombert, in the cited preface, p. 75; Lombert is copied by Fr. Gervais, *Life of St. Cyprian*, p. 436.] In his rescript to Cyprian, Stephen taught not merely one or two errors, but three errors contrary to the Catholic faith. [Note: [Col. 1282D] Fr. Gervais relates this and attempts to prove it in the *Life of St. Cyprian*, pp. 465–466. Stephen is likewise charged with error by Launoy, Letter 15 to Bevilaqua, and Dupin, *Ecclesiastical Library*, vol. I, p. 540, etc.]

The modern writers were not satisfied with tearing apart Stephen’s entirely blameless life with so many reproaches [Col. 1282B] and burdening it with so many crimes; they assail even his holy death and attempt to wrest from Stephen the palm of glorious martyrdom—indeed, holiness itself. At one moment they indicate that the acts of St. Stephen’s martyrdom are not sufficiently authentic to deserve credence in a history; [Note: [Col. 1282D] Tillemont, *Ecclesiastical History*, vol. IV, p. 31.] at another they maintain that there is some room for doubt as to whether Stephen was truly a martyr. [Note: [Col. 1282D] Ibid.] Here they add that St. Augustine and Vincent of Lérins were unaware that Stephen had been a martyr; [Note: [Col. 1282D] Ibid.] there they relate that one may reasonably believe Stephen died in prison or in some other less illustrious manner, but not by a judge’s sentence and at the hands of persecutors, which alone was then regarded as true and perfect martyrdom. [Note: [Col. 1282D] Ibid.] Yet whatever sort of martyrdom Stephen ultimately suffered, did he [Col. 1282C] at least suffer it for confessing Christ’s name? By no means, according to Dupin. He suffered it, Dupin says, because he was found in the cemetery contrary to the order of Emperor Valerian, who had forbidden Christians by edict, under penalty of death, to frequent the cemeteries. [Note: [Col. 1282D] *Ecclesiastical Library*, vol. I, p. 503.] But finally, even if Stephen did not perish for confessing Christ’s name and was not truly a martyr, will his holiness at least be beyond doubt? On the contrary, it is exceedingly doubtful and rests on no foundation, if Lombert’s pronouncements are valid. For, according to Lombert, the things [Col. 1283A] Stephen did against Cyprian could not be expiated even by martyrdom unless, before his death, Stephen had made peace with Cyprian and the other bishops and had joined anew with them the bonds of charity and unity which he himself had broken. [Note: [Col. 1283D] Lombert, in the cited preface, p. 78.] Behold, then, the entire foundation of Stephen’s holiness placed in his reconciliation with Cyprian—in that reconciliation, I say, of which no trace exists among either ancient or recent writers and which is therefore, to say no more, exceedingly doubtful and uncertain. Stephen’s holiness, therefore, will be as suspect and doubtful to us as this reconciliation of Stephen with Cyprian and the others, imagined beforehand by Lombert, upon which, of course, Stephen’s entire holiness depends, and without which even martyrdom itself would not have profited Stephen.

[Col. 1283B] By these monstrous means they undertook to impart new force and new splendor to this argument, which, thus reinforced, they do not hesitate to declare invincible and evident and to proclaim everywhere. Which party found greater glory—whether the Lutherans and Calvinists in devising that argument, or our modern writers in so splendidly restoring it after it had been demolished—let that man judge who envies neither party its glory. Yet it must candidly be admitted that St. Stephen, the Roman Pontiff, was never treated as badly by any Lutheran or Calvinist as he was by some of our modern writers.

But those men went beyond all bounds who undertook, by fair means and foul, to persuade Catholics that the privilege of unfailing faith asserted for Peter’s successors had been utterly unknown to so noble a Doctor of the Church, and one belonging indeed to primeval antiquity, as Cyprian. [Col. 1283C] What further did the modern writers do, then, to deceive some unwary persons in this matter? Well aware how highly Catholics valued the opinions of French theologians and Parisian Doctors, they began to scatter abroad, here and there, the claim that this argument had seemed to those most wise masters of sacred theology to be an exceedingly strong one for assailing the inerrancy of the Roman Pontiff. Thus they judged that whatever the matter itself lacked had to be supplied by so great a name and title. It must be admitted that their device succeeded in no small measure according to the modern writers’ wishes. Very many foreigners, who often lack the leisure and even more frequently the freedom to read through so many volumes by the Doctors of France, measured the candor of others by their own and in good faith [Col. 1283D] believed men who testified to the matter with great confidence. Consequently, regarding the theologians of France as patrons of this argument, they seemed—and still seem—to grieve and lament that, among the more recent writers, there had been obscured and diminished that gravity and maturity of judgment for which the ancient Doctors of France were esteemed. [Col. 1284A] Even in France, not a few who were insufficiently versed in the writings of the Parisian Doctors likewise lent the modern writers a too-ready ear in this matter. Hence, carried away by so great an authority of their teachers, from whom they deem it sinful to depart, they too called this argument exceedingly effective for assailing pontifical inerrancy without further investigation, and are frequently heard to maintain that it is so.

This was the latest and more successful than all the other ventures of the modern writers, undertaken to impart to their favorite argument some of the strength which it did not possess of itself. We could not tolerate so rash an enterprise, by which the genuine doctrine of the most celebrated writers was so corrupted that a position wholly contrary to their own was ascribed to them. I bore with the greatest indignation that the Parisian Doctors should be blackened to such a degree that they were said to welcome, approve, and repeat the old Lutheran ditty ridiculed and held in utter contempt by all Catholics. We grieved that such odium was being stirred up against the theologians of France as would present them to foreigners as sons degenerate from their fathers and destitute of the Fathers’ wisdom and maturity of judgment, and would consequently provoke the complaints and reproaches of foreigners against them. We saw with the greatest distress so many younger bachelors of the Sorbonne, deceived by the falsely alleged authority of their teachers, believe in good faith that Cyprian had opposed pontifical infallibility, which in no small measure diminished and weakened their inherited and innate ardor for defending the rights of the Apostolic See.

Accordingly, so that we might satisfy our zeal for asserting and establishing ever more firmly [Col. 1284C] the sacred rights and divine privileges of the Apostolic See, as well as our desire to deserve well of the theologians of France in the best way we can, we undertook to weigh the genuine opinion of the French theologians on this point and to vindicate it from this most recent imposture. What, then? Do the Doctors of France not judge Cyprian’s action suitable and appropriate for assailing the inerrancy of the Roman Pontiff? On the contrary, they demonstrate that it is utterly inept and futile. The most learned theologians of France produce and supply the very same answers as the other Catholic Doctors in order to blow away and destroy the argument with which first the Lutherans and Calvinists, and then the modern writers, batter the supreme and immovable authority of the Roman Pontiff on the basis of Cyprian. These answers [Col. 1284D] are so solid and decisive that they could not possibly be more so. Such is the position of those most weighty men, whatever the modern writers may allege and invent to the contrary; and this is what we undertake to prove and confidently expect to persuade even the most difficult critic.

## A Concise Life of Stephen, Most Holy Martyr and Roman Pontiff, Extracted from Ancient Monuments

[Col. 1283]

[Col. 1283D] Stephen, a Roman by nationality and the son of Julius, [Note: [Col. 1283D] *Catalogue of Pontiffs*, composed in the sixth century and published by Henschenius in vol. I for April, in the preliminary dissertation. [Col. 1284D] Anastasius the Librarian, *Life of St. Stephen*.] before [Col. 1284D] he was raised to the supreme summit of the Church, [Col. 1285A] was enrolled among the Roman clergy and served as archdeacon first to Cornelius and then to Lucius, Roman Pontiffs. [Note: [Col. 1285D] The same Anastasius, *Lives of Saints Cornelius and Lucius*, Rome edition, 1718.] In that office he so proved himself to Cornelius that the latter judged him worthy above all others to be the man to whom “all the goods of the Church might most safely be entrusted before his passion.” [Note: [Col. 1285D] The same, *Life of St. Cornelius*.] He so commended himself to Lucius that Lucius chose him alone out of all men to sustain the mass of the Church, then tottering amid the most difficult times. “For he,” says Anastasius, “gave authority over the entire Church to Stephen, his archdeacon, as he was going to his passion”; [Note: [Col. 1285D] *Life of St. Lucius*.] or, according to Eusebius, [Note: [Col. 1285D] *Ecclesiastical History*, book VII, chapter 2, Valesius’s edition, Paris, 1678.] when dying he left the episcopal office to Stephen.

Stephen succeeded Lucius after the latter’s glorious death. [Note: [Col. 1285D] All acknowledge this after Cyprian, Eusebius, Optatus of Milevis, Augustine, Prosper, Nicephorus, etc.] While the Church was breathing again after the persecutions and enjoying peace for a time under Valerian, [Col. 1285B] the holy Pastor obtained greater freedom of action and directed his solicitude even toward the most remote churches throughout the world, “supplying what was necessary to all the provinces of Syria together with Arabia, not merely once but repeatedly.” [Note: [Col. 1285D] Dionysius of Alexandria in Eusebius, book VII, chapter 5.] The holy Pontiff, moreover, sought to console by kind and salutary writings, and to arouse to piety, the souls of those whose bodies he assisted with such charity and generosity, as Dionysius bears witness when he adds to the words just cited: “and to whom you have now written letters.”

Faustinus, Bishop of Lyons, together with the other bishops of the province, informed Stephen that Marcian, Bishop of Arles in Gaul, was greatly devoted to Novatian, not without harm to the Church. [Note: [Col. 1285D] St. Cyprian, Letter LXVII to St. Stephen, above, col. 989.] Stephen, however, proceeded deliberately in view of the gravity of the matter [Col. 1285C] and did not hasten to excommunicate and depose bishops. Cyprian, urged by the Gauls, therefore approached him by letter and appealed to him “to direct letters—and indeed the fullest possible letters—to the province and to the people residing at Arles, by which Marcian, having been excluded from communion, another might be substituted in his place.” [Note: [Col. 1285D] Cyprian, ibid.] Why he wished Marcian to be punished with so severe and grave a censure he explains more distinctly toward the end of the letter: namely, because the honor of the Roman Pontiffs had to be vindicated, since Marcian obstinately dissented from their decrees “concerning the reception of the lapsed”:

> “For,” he says, “the glorious honor of our predecessors, the blessed martyrs Cornelius and Lucius, must be preserved. Since we honor their memory, you, dearest brother, who have become their vicar and successor, must much more honor and preserve it by your gravity and [Col. 1285D] authority. For they, filled with the Spirit of God and established in glorious [Col. 1286A] martyrdom, judged that peace should be granted to the lapsed.”

Meanwhile Cyprian was so far from doubting that Stephen—now that the matter had been brought into such clear light—would, on his advice and exhortation, send letters to the province and people of Arles commanding both that Marcian be excluded from communion and that another bishop be substituted in his place, that he also asks to be informed who had been substituted, in these words:

> “Inform us explicitly who has been substituted at Arles in Marcian’s place, so that we may know to whom we should direct our brethren and to whom we should write.” [Note: [Col. 1286D] Ibid.]

All antiquity is silent as to whether Marcian was then cast down from his see by Stephen. Yet it may serve as an indication that his name is not found in the ancient diptychs of the Church of Arles published by Mabillon. [Note: [Col. 1286D] *Annals*, vol. III, p. 432, Paris edition, 1672.]

[Col. 1286B] At approximately the same time, as is believed, the most pious Pontiff gave a splendid proof of his authority and clemency in the case of Basilides, Bishop of León and Astorga in Spain. After Basilides had been driven from his episcopate by his people because of various crimes of which he was accused, and Sabinus had been substituted in his place, he went to Rome to Stephen and obtained from him restoration to his see. [Note: [Col. 1286D] Cyprian, Letter LXVII to Stephen, above.] Since Cyprian believed Basilides guilty of all the crimes of which he was accused, and since Stephen’s equity was otherwise so well known to him that he did not in the least suspect Stephen of having wished to patronize a criminal, he judged that Stephen had been deceived by Basilides in this matter. He maintained that this could have happened to Stephen because the latter was situated far from Spain and was ignorant both of what had been done and of the truth that had been concealed. [Note: [Col. 1286D] Ibid.]

[Col. 1286C] If Stephen truly allowed himself to be circumvented in this matter, as Cyprian thought, he is not thereby immediately to be blamed for grave negligence, or even slight negligence, since experience establishes that even the most diligent and cautious person is sometimes taken unawares—especially if, like Stephen, he is filled with that charity which believes all things, thinks no evil, and strives to show indulgence to the accused rather than to the accusers. But I do not know whether Cyprian, rather than Stephen, was deceived in this affair. For whatever Cyprian determined in this letter concerning the crimes of Basilides, he determined without hearing the other party—that is, solely from the report of the legates who were the bishops substituted for the deposed men, Basilides and Martial, and from the letters of those who had deposed the latter and substituted the former. But these men were certainly not competent witnesses in their own case, and they could have deceived [Col. 1286D] Cyprian just as readily as Basilides could have deceived Stephen.

Stephen was indeed situated far from Spain; but Cyprian was not so much nearer to the Spaniards that a deception capable of making its way from there to Rome could not also have made its way to Carthage. This is especially so because communications between the Carthaginians and the Spaniards—who were bound by no tie of jurisdiction—were as infrequent as those between the Spaniards and the Romans, to whom they were subject in both civil and ecclesiastical authority, were frequent. I would sooner believe that what was taking place in Spain [Col. 1287A] could be known and examined by Stephen at Rome far better than by Cyprian at Carthage.

But let the crimes of Basilides, if you please, have been better proved to Cyprian than to Stephen. Was Stephen therefore deceived or incautious because he restored Basilides to his see? By no means. For since the deposition of Basilides had been carried out by the Spaniards without consulting the Roman See, to which cases of this kind had to be referred, according to Cyprian himself, [Note: [Col. 1287D] Letters LV to Cornelius and LXVIII to Stephen, above.] and since St. Stephen could not have been ignorant of this, he was obliged to annul the Spaniards’ proceedings, at least until they reopened the case according to lawful order—that is, with the Apostolic See aware of and approving it. Whoever desires more concerning this matter should consult the most eminent Aguirre. [Note: [Col. 1287D] *Spanish Councils*, vol. I, dissertations VII and XIV.]

The devout Pontiff had scarcely quelled, or attempted to quell, the disturbances among the Spaniards [Col. 1287B], when he was compelled to restrain the more serious disturbances among the Africans and Easterners and, in accordance with his pastoral solicitude, which recognized no boundaries, endeavored to recall them from error. For Cyprian, setting aside the ancient and universal custom of the Church which he saw observed everywhere [Note: [Col. 1287D] St. Augustine, *On Baptism, Against the Donatists*, book II, chap. 8, Benedictine ed., Paris, 1679.], had preferred to follow and embrace the innovation, introduced by his predecessor Agrippinus, of rebaptizing those baptized by heretics [Note: [Col. 1287D] Augustine, ibid.]. To establish and extend this practice, he convened two synods at Carthage, in which he decreed, together with the other assembled fellow bishops, that Baptism received outside the Church must be repeated within it [Note: [Col. 1287D] Cyprian, *Letter to the Bishops of Numidia* LXX and *To Stephen* LXXII, above.].

This was a matter of great importance and “pertained more closely to priestly authority and to the unity and dignity of the Catholic Church” than to be put into effect without consulting the Roman Pontiff [Col. 1287C]. The bishops of the Council of Carthage therefore rightly judged that concerning this matter “Stephen especially ought to be written to and consulted” [Note: [Col. 1287D] Synodical letter to Stephen, in Cyprian, LXXII.]. Accordingly, they addressed a synodical letter to Stephen, in which they informed him of what had been done and, commending Stephen’s “seriousness, wisdom, and the truth of his religion and faith,” declared to him that they did not doubt at all, but “believed that those things would please him which were alike religious and true” [Note: [Col. 1287D] Ibid.]—such, namely, as they believed the decrees they had made in the matter of heretical Baptism to be.

When the holy Pontiff learned that such great and rapid movements were being stirred up to proscribe the apostolic tradition, not only in the East, as he had already discovered, but also in Africa—and that this was being done by prelates distinguished by an exceptional reputation for sanctity [Col. 1287D] and learning—he immediately perceived that the more illustrious the bishops who were endeavoring to overthrow the tradition of the Church, the more serious was the danger threatening the Church. He saw that the contagion of so great an evil, which had already infected a large part of Africa, as well as Cilicia and Cappadocia [Col. 1288A], and which did not cease to spread into neighboring provinces, would shortly ruin all Africa and the whole East. In his foresight, therefore, he understood that what was needed against so great an evil was not just any remedy, but an effective and immediately available one. Accordingly, he made timely use of the authority which he possessed over Cyprian and the other bishops, not from any desire for contention, but solely from zeal to preserve tradition, “evidently considering it fitting that he should surpass all the rest in devotion to the faith as much as he surpassed them in the authority of his see” [Note: [Col. 1288D] Vincent of Lérins, *Commonitorium*, chap. 9.]. Through a letter [Note: [Col. 1288D] Ibid.] he commanded him [Note: [Col. 1288D] Augustine, *On Baptism, Against the Donatists*, book V, chap. 23.] that nothing was to be altered in this matter. He commanded him, I say, as a good father, who wishes to prescribe nothing to his children, even where prescription is necessary, without also supplying the equitable basis of the command and explaining it modestly.

For he informed Cyprian that the ancient tradition or custom of the Church, which was then in force and which Cyprian himself “saw observed everywhere” [Col. 1288B], was contrary to his opinion [Note: [Col. 1288D] Cyprian, *Letter to Pompeius* LXXIV, and above.]. By this argument he soundly overthrew the “human” reasonings [Note: [Col. 1288D] Facundus of Hermiane, *In Defense of the Three Chapters*, book X, chap. 3, ed. Fr. Sirmond, Paris, 1696.] upon which Cyprian and the others relied. For who does not know that all human reasoning must yield to the tradition of the Church, and that reasoning which opposes so great an authority must be regarded as suspect, to put it mildly?

Moreover, he confirmed this tradition by the example of the heretics themselves, who did not rebaptize those who came to them [Note: [Col. 1288D] Cyprian, *Letter to Pompeius* LXXIV.]. Cyprian indeed considered this argument of Stephen’s absurd. Yet, as a learned man observed not so long ago, those who examine it more attentively will judge it very differently. For since all heretics have departed from the Church, it is not surprising that they retain something of her doctrine; indeed, in reality there is none who does not retain something from her. Therefore, whenever they, despite their disagreements among themselves, agree with the Church on some point, it is rightly affirmed that they have retained what was handed down to them by the Church. Consequently, Stephen not unreasonably confirmed the ancient custom of the Church which he asserted even from the practice of the heretics themselves.

Here are Stephen’s words, the only ones that survive, as Cyprian reports them in his *Letter to Pompeius* LXXIV: “If, therefore, anyone comes to us from any heresy whatsoever, let nothing be innovated beyond what has been handed down: namely, that hands be laid upon him for repentance, since the heretics themselves, properly speaking, do not baptize those who come over from one group to another, but merely admit them to communion.”

Stephen wrote these things to Cyprian in a style [Col. 1288D] that savors of nothing but “seriousness, wisdom, and truth of religion,” qualities which Cyprian had commended in him [Note: [Col. 1288D] *Letter to Stephen*, LXXIV, and above.], together with a modesty all the more praiseworthy because, at that time, the bishops who disagreed on this question were accusing one another of “presumption, obstinacy, and perversity” [Note: [Col. 1288D] See Cyprian’s *Letter to Quintus* LXXI, *To Jubaianus* [Col. 1289A] LXXIII, and the treatise of the anonymous bishop beginning *They Ought Not*, etc., in Labbe, vol. I, *Councils*, p. 770, and above.].

[Col. 1289A] Finally, lest the most vigilant Pontiff omit anything capable of recalling Cyprian and the other rebaptizers from the deadly error that was spreading more widely by the day, he “warned them that he would withdraw from their communion” [Note: [Col. 1289B] Dionysius of Alexandria, in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VII, chap. 5, and above.] if they persisted in their opinion. His purpose was that those who had been insufficiently moved by his paternal command and by the weight of the reasons he had presented might at least be stirred by threats to abandon their error. This, and no more, according to all the approved monuments of the ancients, was what Stephen, the Roman Pontiff, did to vindicate against Cyprian and the other rebaptizers the ancient and universal tradition of the Church.

[Note: [Col. 1289B] Among the approved monuments of the ancients we do not include Firmilian’s letter to Cyprian, which displays to us the monstrosities of an angry mind, not the words of a holy bishop savoring of truth, religion, equity, modesty, and Christian charity. Firmilian indeed writes that Stephen broke peace with Cyprian, called him a pseudo-Christ and pseudo-apostle, and denied communion and hospitality to his legates; but these things are not found in Stephen’s letters. None of the ancients gave even an obscure indication of these things concerning Stephen. Cyprian himself did not complain to Stephen about them, although, indulging his excitable temperament, he uttered loud and bitter complaints about slighter matters. Augustine did not adduce these things to lessen Cyprian’s blame for his irritation against Stephen, although he labored throughout to do so. These things are wholly inconsistent with the gentleness, mildness, and charity that shone everywhere in Stephen’s life.

If these things must be believed because Firmilian poured them forth [Col. 1289C], it will then also have to be believed that Stephen was audacious, insolent, wicked, manifestly foolish, inhuman, schismatic, a false witness, worse than all heretics, and comparable to Judas himself, the betrayer of Christ. It will have to be believed that the blessed apostles Peter and Paul were defamed by Stephen, and that Sacred Scripture says of no one more than of Stephen: “A passionate man begets quarrels, and a wrathful man heaps up sins.” It will have to be believed that zeal for God was found more among the Jews, blinded by ignorance and bound by the most serious crime, than in Stephen, and that Stephen’s soul was perhaps not even one and the same, so slippery, changeable, and uncertain was it. It will have to be believed that Stephen broke peace with the individual bishops throughout the entire world by every kind of discord, and that he deserved to be called a pseudo-Christ, a pseudo-apostle, and a deceitful workman. It will also have to be believed that the Roman Church falsely claims the authority of the apostles and that the apostolic traditions are not preserved within it [Col. 1289D]. It will have to be believed that the heretics lived only after a long interval from the times of the apostles. For Firmilian poured forth all these things in that letter, to omit others.

These statements reveal a man so agitated and disturbed by bile that he was unable to attend to truth, equity, religion, or charity; consequently, they deprive Firmilian of all credibility when writing to Cyprian. And indeed all antiquity regarded the charges Firmilian made against Stephen as sheer and noisome inventions. Antiquity censures none of these things in Stephen’s conduct against Cyprian; indeed, it most consistently commends Stephen and repeatedly and openly denies concerning him precisely what Firmilian openly affirms. We shall demonstrate this below.

Nor is Firmilian’s testimony in this matter valued more highly even by writers of the French nation, the greater and sounder part of whom freely declare that no credit should be given to him. On this subject one may consult Natalis Alexander, *Ecclesiastical History*, III [Col. 1290C], dissertation 12 on the Church of that century, art. I, p. 687; Frassen, *On the Sacraments*, question 3, p. 96; Tournely, *On the Sacraments*, question 7, art. 2, p. 447; Fr. Constant, *On the Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, vol. I, p. 250; de Révéroni, *Dogmatic Dissertation on the Dispute between St. Cyprian and St. Stephen*, p. 71; and very many others. Time does not permit us to pursue their arguments establishing the falsity of the things Firmilian fastened upon Stephen. It will be useful to assert this one point, which every truly impartial judge will freely concede [Col. 1290D]: what Stephen did against the rebaptizers should be learned from Cyprian, Dionysius of Alexandria, Eusebius, Augustine, Jerome, Vincent of Lérins, Facundus of Hermiane, and all the others who wrote about this matter with calm minds, rather than from Firmilian alone, Stephen’s most hostile adversary, who in the cited letter was unable to keep his speech within the bounds of truth and equity.]

[Col. 1290A] Stephen’s so praiseworthy zeal for preserving the ancestral religion displeased those who loved innovation and had fallen into error. The shepherd’s voice was not heard but despised by those who wrongly believed that only a matter of discipline was at issue. The Roman Pontiff himself was reproached and assailed with insults [Note: [Col. 1290D] St. Cyprian, *Letter to Pompeius* LXXIV, and Firmilian, *Letter to Cyprian* LXXV, among the Cyprianic letters.]. Yet Stephen, though scorned, insulted, and provoked, did not know how to become angry, did not know how to grow indignant, did not know how to complain; he could not be provoked. He bore all things, endured all things, suffered all things; “he tolerated all things for the good of peace and unity” [Note: [Col. 1290D] Augustine, book VI, *On Baptism, Against the Donatists*, chap. 22.].

He did not think of himself as judge, Supreme Pontiff, despised, or offended, but devoted himself solely to paternal and Christian charity. He did not rebuke, scold, or punish his erring, disobedient, and insulting sons, but, “a man everywhere great and endowed with great charity” [Note: [Col. 1290D] Augustine, book I, *On Baptism*, chap. 7.], he bore them with solicitous piety [Note: [Col. 1290D] Augustine, book VI, *On Baptism*, chap. 22.]. [Col. 1290B] Gentle and humble, he did not strive to repel insults or vindicate his wounded honor, but “strove to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” [Note: [Col. 1290D] Augustine, ibid.]. He perceived what a “danger of ruinous dissension was contained in the things his enraged” adversaries had poured forth against him [Note: [Col. 1290D] Augustine, book V, *On Baptism*, chap. 25.]; therefore he covered all things beneath the veil of silence and the veil of charity. He did not even open his mouth to defend his innocence, leaving the care of his vindication to God alone. He watched over the good not of himself but of the Church, over peace rather than his own defense; and “peace alone triumphed in his heart” [Note: [Col. 1290D] Augustine, ibid.]. Nor did he despair of finally moving the hearts of his adversaries by his patience and long-suffering and restoring them to better fruitfulness; to obtain this from God, he endeavored to abound more and more in good works.

Meanwhile, while great disturbances were being raised by the rebaptizers [Col. 1290C] in Africa and the East, he himself at home “imbued everyone with holy admonitions and instruction in the Scriptures” [Note: [Col. 1290D] In the Acts of Hippolytus, Eusebius, and their companions, in Baronius [Col. 1291D] at the year 259. Even Tillemont himself admits that these certainly appear genuine, note 2 on St. Stephen, in these words: “Baronius gives us in his *Annals* the acts of Saints Eusebius, Marcellus, Hippolytus, etc., as genuine acts; they certainly have very much the appearance of being so.”]. The greater he was than others, the less he esteemed himself. He was not accustomed to feed the flock entrusted to him with heavenly doctrine without first confessing his own unworthiness. He asked to be heard not as Pontiff, teacher, or shepherd, but as a sinner. “My little children,” he would humbly say, “hear me, a sinner” [Col. 1291A] [Note: [Col. 1291D] Ibid.].

Since he strove to gain everyone for Christ, he labored with his whole being not only to instruct and sanctify the faithful but also to convert the pagans to the faith. The Acts of Hippolytus, Eusebius, and their companions report how many and how great were the apostolic labors of the most holy Pontiff at that time. In them one may also see Stephen himself so occupied with baptizing pagans that it was as though he either had no other business or lacked presbyters to whom he might entrust that care while he devoted himself to more serious matters. God did not permit Stephen’s many labors to be fruitless: the desired reward was granted to him, “as the number of Christians increased from day to day” [Note: [Col. 1291D] Ibid.].

While Stephen was devoted to these duties of pastoral solicitude and apostolic zeal, he received a letter from Dionysius the Great, bishop of the city of Alexandria. For when reports of what had been done here and there in the affair of the rebaptizers reached this illustrious prelate [Col. 1291B], he easily understood how deeply the Roman Pontiff’s mind must have been afflicted. He found just cause to fear that Stephen, despised or insultingly treated by the rebaptizers, might at last be moved to inflict the penalties with which he had threatened them. Therefore, out of his singular affection for Stephen, he hastened by letter to alleviate his sorrow and implored his clemency on behalf of the rebaptizers.

He carefully announced to Stephen what he did not doubt would be especially pleasing to a Pontiff who so greatly loved the peace of the churches: “that all the churches throughout the East and beyond which had previously been divided” because of Novatian’s depravity “had now at last returned to unity, and that all the prelates of the churches everywhere held one and the same opinion and rejoiced with incredible joy at the unexpected restoration of peace” [Col. 1291C] [Note: [Col. 1291D] In Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VII, chap. 5, and above.]. Nor without pleasure did he recall to Stephen’s memory with what great charity and generosity he had often assisted all the most distant provinces of Syria and Arabia, both by letters and by money; and he informed him that because of this concord they were everywhere leaping for joy [Note: [Col. 1291D] Ibid.]. Finally, promising himself everything from the goodness of the peace-loving Pontiff, he trusted that his prayers would avert the execution of the threats Stephen had directed against the rebaptizers, “praying and entreating Stephen on their behalf” [Note: [Col. 1291D] Ibid.]. The outcome did not disappoint Dionysius’s hope, since Stephen, “a man endowed with great charity, bore the rebaptizers with solicitous piety in the patience of charity” [Note: [Col. 1291D] Augustine, in the passages cited above.].

The savage persecution of Emperor Valerian, which raged more fiercely against the Christians day by day [Col. 1291D], did not diminish Stephen’s zeal and pastoral cares, but increased them. He was the stronger the greater the hardships by which he was oppressed, the more vigilant [Col. 1292A] the more serious the dangers that threatened. In those most calamitous times it became manifest how great was the Pontiff’s courage, how great the shepherd’s love for his flocks, how great his solicitude, how great his constancy in bearing labors, and, finally, how ardent his paternal charity toward all.

By whatever efforts the tyrant labored to scatter the beloved flock, Stephen labored to gather it, seeking out “Christians everywhere and assembling them in the crypts of the martyrs and in cemeteries, that he might teach them all about the kingdom of God and eternal life” [Note: [Col. 1292A] This and what follows down to the end of Stephen’s Life, printed in Roman or, as they call them, cursive letters, we excerpt from the authentic Acts of Stephen. These were composed by Roman notaries shortly after his martyrdom and were approved by the universal Church, both Latin and Greek, throughout so many past centuries, as may be seen in Odoacer Ilbach’s [Col. 1292B] *The Vindicated Acts of the Holy Martyrs*, printed at Rome in 1723, and in the continuators of Bollandus under August 2, who discuss their authority more fully. From them we have borrowed these observations for the benefit of those who may not have the cited authors at hand.

First, the Acts of Stephen are very widely disseminated among all peoples. They survive in many Greek, Italian, French, German, Belgian, and other nations’ manuscript codices. In some of the most ancient of these, the Acts are said to have been written faithfully and gravely in Latin by Roman notaries.

Second, they are most ancient and approved by the universal Church. Pope St. Damasus, in poem 35 among his works collected by Sarrazanius, excerpted certain things from these Acts—namely, what he sings concerning St. Tarsicius, for these things are known to have been described nowhere except in the Acts of St. Stephen. Ado, Archbishop of Vienne, found the Acts of Stephen in the codices of passions collected from every quarter, which he mentions in the [Col. 1292C] preface to the ancient Roman martyrology, and copied them into his own martyrology. The ancient Roman martyrology composed in the eighth century follows these Acts of Stephen in describing his martyrdom and that of others said in these Acts to have suffered. These Acts of Stephen are presented in abbreviated form in all the *Menologia* and *Menaea* of the Greeks, in the martyrology of Emperor Basil as well, and in the martyrologies of Usuard and Notker. In sermon 38, on St. Stephen, St. Peter Damian calls them the authentic history of his passion. Metaphrastes rendered them from Latin into Greek, as may be seen in Lippomano and Surius. Finally, to state everything in a word, all martyrologies and all ancient breviaries—not only the Roman but also those of very many churches throughout the West—and all the *Menologia* and *Menaea* of the Greeks derived the martyrdom of our Stephen from no source other than these Acts.

Third, just as none of the ancients ever doubted the authority of these Acts, so also in the more recent centuries they appeared genuine and entirely trustworthy [Col. 1292D] to those who diligently devoted themselves to illuminating antiquity. Consult, if you please, the distinguished antiquarian Schelstrate, *Ecclesiastical Antiquities*, vol. I, dissertation 2, chap. 7. Recently, however, a few modern writers instructed by the heterodox Pearson have chosen to call the authority of these Acts into doubt. Among them Tillemont is prominent, assembling in note 1 on St. Stephen numerous arguments intended utterly to destroy their authority. Some of these prove at most that certain errors have crept into these Acts which do not concern Stephen’s apostolic labors or martyrdom. Others, which are directed even against Stephen’s deeds, rest on no testimony of the ancients but on mere and exceedingly frivolous conjectures. For example, according to Tillemont, Stephen’s Acts must be rejected because certain miracles performed by Stephen are related in them, and because some persons are said there to have prostrated themselves at Stephen’s feet—as though similar things were never related in other genuine Acts of the ancients.

Moreover, these arguments of Tillemont may be read solidly and abundantly refuted in Ilbach and the Bollandists, in the passages cited above. They certainly will never establish that those Acts of Stephen did not possess the venerable approval of the universal Church throughout so many past centuries in the matters pertaining to Stephen.];

and he did not cease there to exhort them [Col. 1293A] to receive joyfully the crown of martyrdom for Christ: “My brothers and fellow soldiers,” he said, “reject earthly possessions, that you may receive the heavenly kingdom. Do not fear the princes of this age, but pray to the Lord God of Heaven and to Jesus Christ his Son, who is able to deliver us all from the hands of our enemies and from the savagery of the devil, and to unite us to his grace.”

Stephen possessed such grace and wisdom in teaching and exhorting that “many even from among the pagans came together to hear his word.” The effectiveness of Stephen’s discourses is demonstrated by that great multitude of pagans who, after hearing him, immediately enrolled themselves in the Christian religion. The tireless Pontiff consecrated them all “by the mysteries of sacred Baptism,” not through another’s hands but through his own. It is also demonstrated by those noble declarations of the Christians with which, when Stephen commended to them the necessity of faith and the other virtues [Col. 1293B], they responded: “We desire both to abandon our earthly possessions and even to shed our blood for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, if only we may deserve to obtain his grace.”

In order that the holy Pontiff might render strong and steadfast those sentiments of piety which by frequent exhortations he aroused and implanted in the hearts of the faithful, he frequently “offered sacrifice to God for them” and took care that “all should partake of the body and blood of Christ.” He furnished them with such great examples of every virtue that to the Romans, who were eyewitnesses, he seemed and was said to be “filled with the grace of the Holy Spirit,” like another Stephen, the protomartyr.

Thus, by word, deed, and example, Stephen the Roman Pontiff strove to convert the pagans [Col. 1293C] to the faith, strengthen the faithful in the faith, and prepare them to undergo martyrdom courageously. God willed that a Pontiff adorned with so many virtues should also become illustrious through miracles. For Lucilla, the daughter of the tribune Nemesius, whom he begot for Christ through Baptism by his exhortations, had been “blind from birth,” and he also “gave her sight through the power of his prayers.” It is therefore no wonder that under so great a Pontiff Rome saw, and the Church celebrates, so many noble athletes of Christ who contended for Christ even unto the final contest; who, despising threats as they did promises and overcoming flatteries, honors, and riches no less than torments, then attained the palm of martyrdom. Just as Stephen took care everywhere that their “bodies should be sought out,” so the humble and devout Pontiff “did not disdain to bury them himself.”

After so many labors had been undergone for preserving and propagating the Christian religion [Col. 1293D], so many hardships endured, and numerous bishops, presbyters, and deacons appointed [Note: [Col. 1293D] *Catalogue of the Roman Pontiffs* of the sixth century, and Anastasius the Librarian, *Life of St. Stephen*.], and after his exile had already been overcome, as Anastasius testifies [Note: [Col. 1293D] Ibid.], nothing now remained for Stephen except at last to lay down for the sheep that life which he had never feared to lose for them [Col. 1294A], and in a bloody sacrifice to offer himself as a victim pleasing to God, he who had so often offered himself in the unbloody sacrifice. This one proof alone remained for Stephen to furnish of his most ardent charity toward God and men; this one most beautiful spectacle remained for the Supreme Pontiff to present to God and men. An opportunity was given to Stephen, and Stephen did not fail the opportunity. He died for Christ and for the flock, having always lived for Christ and for the flock. He did not refuse to make fruitful with his own blood the field entrusted to him which he had watered with so much sweat, and by a glorious martyrdom he brought his most holy and laborious life to its end.

For when Emperor Valerian learned that Stephen was devoting himself “by his persuasions and exhortations” to recalling the people from idolatry, he sent soldiers [Col. 1294B] and arrested him. “A great many Christians followed the arrested shepherd at a distance with tears.” When brought before the tyrant’s tribunal, he openly confessed “that Christ Jesus, the Son of God, is God together with the Father and the Holy Spirit.” He freely declared to Valerian that the idols “worshiped” by the pagans were “demons,” and that he admonished and exhorted the Romans “to abandon them and return to the living and true God, the creator of heaven and earth.”

After hearing Stephen, the emperor ordered him to be taken into the temple of Mars, where, if he refused to sacrifice to Mars, he was to be punished by beheading. There the holy Pontiff, “raising his eyes to heaven,” poured forth a prayer to God before them all; and suddenly the temple and idol were struck from heaven and collapsed in large part. Seeing this, the terrified soldiers fled. Stephen, accompanied by his followers [Col. 1294C], withdrew to the cemetery of St. Lucina, where, “like a good shepherd, with many consolations and exhortations,” he inflamed the faithful for martyrdom and “offered sacrifice to almighty God.”

When Valerian heard this, he again sent soldiers to arrest him. They found Stephen offering sacrifice to God; and he, “fearless and steadfast before the solemn rites of the altar and continually completing what he had begun, was beheaded there in his own chair” [Note: [Col. 1294C] Besides the Acts of Stephen, the following hand down that Stephen’s martyrdom was consummated by beheading: Anastasius the Librarian in the *Life of Stephen*; the Roman martyrology [Col. 1294D]; the martyrologies of Ado, Usuard, and Notker; the Greek *Menologia*; the Greek *Menaea*; the *Menologion* of Emperor Basil; Metaphrastes in Lippomano; St. Peter Damian, sermon 38 on Stephen; Platina in the *Life of Stephen*; and the Gallican martyrology—in a word, all the ancients who devoted themselves to describing Stephen’s death, none of whom assigns him any other kind of death.

This is the most ancient and, until now, the sole tradition of all the churches concerning Stephen’s death. I believe that it should be accepted rather than the reckless outpouring of Tillemont, who, without witness or proof, conjectures in his notes on St. Stephen that Stephen died in prison, in exile, or in some other less glorious manner, but not by a judge’s sentence or by the hand of persecutors—which at that time was regarded as true and perfect martyrdom. Such is Tillemont’s zeal for promoting veneration of Stephen.], on the fourth day before the Nones of August. “Then there arose a very great lamentation among the Christians, who had sent so great a shepherd ahead of them, with the glory of martyrdom, to the heavenly kingdoms.” They buried his [Col. 1295A] body together with the chair itself, “sprinkled with his blood,” in that same crypt which is in the cemetery of Callistus on the Appian Way.

This is the conclusion of the life of St. Stephen, the first Roman Pontiff of that name. These are the principal deeds of that renowned defender of the apostolic faith, whom the universal Church has continually honored and continues to honor as a glorious martyr: the Latin Church on August 2; the Greek Church on the same day, or the following day, or even on August 30 and September 7, as may be seen in the various Greek calendars in the continuators of Bollandus under August 2. Moreover, all antiquity supports this judgment of the Church concerning Stephen’s martyrdom.

For none of the ancients ever denied or doubted that Stephen was crowned with martyrdom and was a martyr. This is attested by the genuine Acts of Stephen, as we have seen [Col. 1295B]; the martyrology of St. Jerome in Florentinius; the Ambrosian Missal; the *Liber Pontificalis* under the name of Pope Damasus in Labbe; St. Gregory’s *Book of Sacraments*; the ancient Roman martyrology composed around the eighth century; St. Paul, the Roman Pontiff, in his diploma concerning the translation of the relics of St. Stephen; Anastasius the Librarian, where he treats of Stephen; the martyrology of the Venerable Bede; the Greek *Menologia* and *Menaea*; the *Menologion* of Emperor Basil as well; the martyrologies of Ado, Usuard, and Notker in Canisius; Rabanus, Archbishop of Mainz, in his martyrology; Wandalbert; Orderic Vitalis in his *Ecclesiastical History*; Metaphrastes in Lippomano; St. Peter Damian, sermon 38 on St. Stephen; the present [Col. 1296A] Roman martyrology; the Gallican martyrology; and so forth.

It is likewise confirmed by the sacred and very ancient records of numerous churches in Italy, Sicily, Spain, Germany, Lorraine, and Belgium, in which mention is made of relics of St. Stephen, “Pope and martyr, which are preserved there with great veneration.” Until now, there was finally one unanimous opinion concerning Stephen’s martyrdom, when certain modern writers of our age were not ashamed to call into doubt Stephen’s martyrdom, although affirmed by so many most ancient testimonies throughout the universal Church. They did so because St. Augustine and Vincent of Lérins wrote nothing about Stephen’s martyrdom; because in one ancient calendar belonging to some private person Stephen is not adorned with the title of martyr; and finally because St. Pontius, in the life of St. Cyprian, called Xystus, Stephen’s successor [Col. 1296B], “a good and peaceable priest and a most blessed martyr.” From this these clever men infer that Pontius intended by these words to censure Stephen and deny that he was a blessed martyr.

To set forth these modern writers’ arguments for stripping Stephen of his martyrdom—or rather these wretched mockeries of a disordered mind—is already to refute them. Anyone who desires fuller, better attested, and more thoroughly elucidated information concerning Stephen’s martyrdom may consult, among others, Odoacer Ilbach, *The Vindicated Acts of the Holy Martyrs*, printed at Rome in 1723, book V, chapters 6 and 7, and especially the learned continuators of Bollandus under August 2. Mindful and grateful, we candidly and willingly acknowledge and declare that we have been assisted here to no small degree by their laborious researches.

## APPENDIX TO THE LIFE OF ST. STEPHEN, ROMAN PONTIFF AND MARTYR, IN WHICH HIS METHOD OF PROCEEDING AGAINST ST. CYPRIAN AND THE OTHER REBAPTIZERS IS VINDICATED, BY THE TESTIMONIES OF THE ANCIENTS, FROM THE CALUMNIES OF CERTAIN MODERN WRITERS

[Col. 1295]

[Col. 1295C] St. Stephen, as we have seen, in the controversy concerning the Baptism of heretics, commanded Cyprian, Firmilian, and the other rebaptizers not to alter the Church’s tradition of receiving heretics without repeated Baptism; and he warned them that he would withdraw from their communion if they persisted in their opinion.

Those who, carried away by a blind hatred of the Roman Pontiffs, seem chiefly intent upon censuring and defaming their deeds—namely, the modern writers whom we oppose—do not cease to assail Stephen’s manner of proceeding against the rebaptizers and to tear at it with every tooth they possess. They cry out that it was harsh, untimely, rash, and unjust. They contend that Stephen, by issuing commands and threatening excommunication, both exceeded the limits [Col. 1295D] of his power and gave examples of immoderate and unjust severity. They condemn Stephen’s zeal as suited solely to laying everything waste. To put it in a word, they are not ashamed to accuse the most holy Pontiff of an unrestrained lust for domination and swollen arrogance—indeed, of tyranny and the oppression of the churches.

But how very different, indeed, was the judgment of the holy Fathers and of all the ancients concerning Stephen; and how powerful it is for vindicating [Col. 1296C] from those calumnies Stephen’s equitable and wise manner of proceeding against the rebaptizers!

I. Let the writings of all the ancients, both Greeks and Latins, who considered the matter with a calm and untroubled mind, be read. Let that vigorous defender of the Church’s traditions, a bishop contemporary with Cyprian, whose modesty and humility have deprived us of his name, be read in his treatise beginning, “That those ought not to be baptized again, etc.” [Note: [Col. 1296C] The treatise beginning with the words, *That those who have once been immersed in the name of Jesus Christ ought not to be baptized again*, first published, with the permission of Jacques Sirmond, by Nicolas Rigault after Cyprian’s letter to Pompeius; then by Philippe Labbe, vol. I of the *Councils*; and afterward by the English editors of Cyprian’s works among the minor works [Col. 1296D] commonly ascribed to Cyprian. Although its author is anonymous, it nevertheless enjoys great authority among scholars. For if one considers the author’s purpose, he vigorously defended the Church’s cause against Cyprian and his followers in the controversy over the baptism of heretics; if one considers his identity and antiquity, he was a bishop contemporary with Cyprian, as is rightly observed by Tillemont, *Hist. eccl.*, vol. IV, pp. 152 and 629; Fleury, *Hist. eccl.*, vol. II, book VII, ch. 31, p. 278; Dupin, *Bibl. eccl.*, vol. I, p. 531; Noël Alexandre, *Hist. eccl.*, vol. III, p. 691, and vol. V, pp. 488 and 495; Tournély, [Col. 1297D] *De Sacramentis*, p. 375; Baillet, *Lives of the Saints*, under August 2, p. 20; the *Defender of the Declaration of the Gallican Clergy of 1682*, vol. II, p. 266; Fr. Gervais, *Life of St. Cyprian*, p. 422 ff.; Dom Maran, preface to Baluze’s edition of Cyprian’s works, p. 126; Dom Cellier, O.S.B., *History of Sacred Authors*, vol. III, p. 134; and very many others.] Consult Dionysius of Alexandria, [Col. 1297A] Eusebius of Caesarea, Jerome, Augustine, Vincent of Lérins, Facundus of Hermiane, the Venerable Bede, Nicephorus Callistus, and George Syncellus. Let even the writings of the Donatists themselves be examined, together with those of any others who discussed the question debated between Stephen and Cyprian concerning the baptism of heretics. These men certainly were not ignorant of what had been done on either side in this dispute. Just as it was known to everyone that Stephen had issued a command in this matter and had threatened the rebaptizers with excommunication, so very many of them bear witness to it repeatedly. Nevertheless, no one charges Stephen—I do not say with inhumanity or tyranny, but even with the slightest severity toward Cyprian and the others. No one was able to detect anything in Stephen’s manner of proceeding that seemed to him worthy of any censure or [Col. 1297B] criticism.

And certainly, if the writers just mentioned had observed anything of that kind, they assuredly would not have suppressed it. Nor would they have spared Stephen any more than Cyprian, whose very great merits they acknowledged and proclaimed, yet in whom they did not fear to disclose that something deserved blame and something required correction. How great was the ancients’ esteem for Cyprian! How many panegyrists of Cyprian! How many defenders of Cyprian! Launoy gathered almost innumerable examples [Note: [Col. 1297D] Letter 15 to Bevilacqua.]; yet not one of them supports Cyprian in declaring Stephen’s manner of proceeding untimely and less than right. None agrees with Cyprian on this point; none follows Cyprian’s judgment; none excuses Cyprian on the ground that Stephen had treated him too severely. How great was Augustine’s zeal [Col. 1297C] to soften and minimize Cyprian’s errors! What ardor! What partiality in his favor! Yet nowhere does he adopt what Cyprian had poured forth against Stephen in his own defense; nowhere does he intimate that Stephen’s zeal was untimely, so as to lessen Cyprian’s guilt for becoming excessively agitated against him.

In a word, none of the ancients called Stephen’s manner of proceeding against the rebaptizers untimely, severe, or less than wise; none found anything reprehensible in Stephen. And how could those men have criticized or disapproved Stephen’s manner of proceeding when, whenever occasion required, they did not fail to celebrate and commend it, as we shall now see?

II. Stephen “was indeed gravely incensed against Cyprian” [Note: [Col. 1297D] Augustine, *On the One Baptism, Against Petilian*, ch. 14.] when he commanded him and notified him that he would withdraw from communion with him if he persisted in his opinion. But what did all those bishops throughout the world who fought together with Stephen against the rebaptizers on behalf of the Church’s sound doctrine think of this grave indignation on Stephen’s part? Did they believe it inappropriate or untimely? Did they agree with Stephen only insofar as he maintained the Church’s ancient tradition, but not insofar as he was more gravely incensed against Cyprian and the other rebaptizers? Some modern writers have indeed devised this distinction. Yet Augustine, contradicted by none of the ancients, testifies that that entire multitude of bishops agreed with Stephen not only in judging that the baptism of Christ must never be repeated, but also “in being gravely incensed against those who did this.” For in his book *On the One Baptism, Against Petilian*, chapter 14, he says: “Stephen judged that the baptism of Christ must never be repeated and was gravely incensed against those who did this; Cyprian, however, believed that those baptized in heresy or schism, as persons not possessing the baptism of Christ, ought to be baptized in the Catholic Church. Many agreed with the former, while some also agreed with the latter.” [Col. 1298B] Augustine himself indicates how many were with Stephen—the men whom he here calls “many”—when he writes against Cresconius, book III, chapter 3: “Consequently, if we are now to believe without qualification that fifty Eastern bishops held the same opinion as seventy African bishops, or even somewhat more, this was against the many thousands of bishops throughout the whole world to whom this error was displeasing.”

Before Augustine, St. Dionysius of Alexandria had related that Stephen’s judgment—that the rebaptizers who persisted in their opinion ought to be excommunicated—was also the judgment and opinion of the other bishops, as Eusebius testifies in book VII of his *History*, chapter 5, in Valesius’s edition: “To him”—that is, to Xystus, bishop of Rome—“Dionysius wrote his second letter on baptism, in which he sets forth the opinion and judgment both of Stephen and of the other bishops.” What Stephen’s judgment was—which was simultaneously that of the other bishops—is made clear by the words immediately following: “Writing thus concerning Stephen: ‘Previously, indeed, he had written letters concerning Helenus and Firmilian, and finally concerning all the priests established throughout Cilicia, Cappadocia, and all the neighboring provinces, saying that for this reason he would withdraw from communion with them: because they baptized heretics.’”

Nicephorus Callistus also bears witness to the same thing in these words: “Dionysius sent a second letter on baptism to Xystus, setting forth in it the judgment of Stephen and of the others; for he had previously written concerning Helenus and Firmilian that he would not communicate with them for the very reason that they rebaptized heretics” [Note: [Col. 1298D] *Ecclesiastical History*, book VI, ch. 7, Paris edition, 1630.].

[Col. 1298D] Vincent of Lérins likewise relates that Stephen resisted Cyprian. He was not ignorant of the manner in which Stephen resisted him—namely, by issuing a command and threatening excommunication—since he cites Stephen’s letter to the Africans [Note: [Col. 1298D] *Commonitory*, ch. 9.]. Nevertheless, he affirms in these words that the other prelates everywhere applauded Stephen’s intervention: “Stephen, the prelate of the Apostolic See, resisted together with his other colleagues, to be sure, yet more than the others” [Note: [Col. 1298D] Ibid.].

III. St. Stephen judged that heretics ought not to be rebaptized. He furthermore considered that Cyprian and the other rebaptizers ought not to be tolerated, and therefore wrote that he would withdraw from communion with them if they persisted. What did the Church do? She approved and maintained Stephen’s opinion on both points. “Blessed Stephen,” says Facundus, bishop of Hermiane, in his book against Mocianus, “immediately notified Cyprian that if they dared to do this”—to rebaptize heretics—“they would be expelled from the Church; and the Church maintains the opinion of Stephen rather than that of Cyprian, not only concerning the non-rebaptism of heretics, but also concerning the non-toleration of those who rebaptize.”

Let Stephen, then, be condemned by the moderns; let them call him a tyrant and a monstrous oppressor of the churches because he judged that the rebaptizers ought not to be tolerated. He will be acquitted by a weightier judgment; he will be vindicated by the Church herself, which maintained and approved his opinion “also concerning the non-toleration of those who rebaptize.” [Col. 1299B]

IV. Nor did the Roman Church, the mother and teacher of all churches, judge Stephen’s rescript to Cyprian—in which he commanded that the ancient custom be preserved—to be arrogant, full of abuse, or insulting to Cyprian. Every year on August 2, in the Roman Breviary, she presents the memory of that rescript as most glorious for St. Stephen, in these words: “He”—St. Stephen—“forbade those baptized by heretics to be baptized again, writing in reply to St. Cyprian in these words: ‘Let nothing be innovated beyond what has been handed down.’”

V. The anonymous bishop who at that time opposed Cyprian’s innovation himself reveals to us what he thought of Stephen’s rescript, in these words: “In this kind of question”—concerning the baptism of heretics—“it seems to me that no controversy or dispute whatsoever could have arisen if each of us, content with the venerable authority of all the churches and possessing the requisite humility, were not eager to introduce any innovation” [Note: [Col. 1299D] In the treatise beginning with the words, *That they ought not again*, etc., cited above.].

Tell me: does he not here praise with sufficient clarity that command of St. Stephen, “Let nothing be innovated”? And does he not confirm that command as just, not merely according to his own judgment, but as so ratified “by the venerable authority of all the churches” that “each person possessing the requisite humility” ought modestly to have been “content” to acquiesce in it? Surely—to use the words of a learned man—he finds no fault in the one issuing the command who desires in his subjects only “humility,” and indeed “requisite humility.” Rather, he extols the former’s equity to the same degree that he censures the latter’s obstinacy, when he accuses them of “vain glory, audacity, rashness,” and so forth, as may be seen at the very beginning of the treatise. [Col. 1299D]

If, therefore, credence is to be given to a bishop reporting what had passed before his own eyes, you see that “the venerable authority of all the churches” was then opposed to Cyprian and the others who were introducing the innovation of rebaptism. The reason, plainly, is that all those churches had made the authority of Stephen’s command their own by assenting to and approving it. From this it is evident that all those churches considered Stephen’s command just and equitable.
