Moreover, why, according to our author, was such great “humility [Col. 1300A] requisite” in Cyprian in the matter of making no innovation concerning the baptism of heretics, unless because Stephen had commanded that no innovation be made in that question? From this, once again, it appears how great the force and equity of Stephen’s command were in the judgment of the cited author.

VI. Nor did the two distinguished presbyters of the Roman Church, Dionysius and Philemon, disapprove of Stephen because he had threatened the rebaptizers with excommunication. According to the testimony of Dionysius of Alexandria, they agreed with Stephen on this very matter. “Previously, indeed,” says Dionysius of Alexandria in Eusebius, *History*, book VII, chapter 5, “Stephen had written letters concerning Helenus and Firmilian” and the other Easterners, “saying that he would withdraw from communion with them because they rebaptized heretics. But consider, I beg you, the gravity of the matter. For in very great councils of bishops, as I hear, it was indeed decreed that those who come from the heretics to the Catholic Church should first be made catechumens and then be cleansed through baptism from the defilements of the old and impure leaven. Concerning all these matters I sent him a letter, asking and entreating him. But,” he says, “I also wrote to our dearest brothers and fellow presbyters Dionysius and Philemon, who previously agreed with Stephen on this point and had written to me concerning these same matters.”

Nicephorus Callistus likewise relates, on the testimony of Dionysius of Alexandria, that Dionysius and Philemon had been “supporters” of Stephen when he threatened the rebaptizers with excommunication [Note: [Col. 1300D] *History*, book VI, ch. 7, in Fronton du Duc, p. 398.]. How great was the weight of the support given to Stephen by Philemon, and especially by Dionysius of Rome, is sufficiently shown by the praises that the holy Fathers, and particularly St. Basil [Note: [Col. 1300D] Letter 220.] and Athanasius [Note: [Col. 1300D] *On the Synods*, p. 918.], lavished in celebration of Dionysius of Rome’s [Col. 1300C] “integrity of faith, doctrine, learning, wisdom, and other virtues.” It is sufficiently shown also by what Eusebius, following Dionysius of Alexandria, related concerning him in book VII of his *History*, chapter 7, in these words: “That this same Dionysius of Rome, while still a presbyter, was a most learned and altogether admirable man may be known from the testimony of Dionysius of Alexandria.” Finally, it may also be inferred from the fact that he deserved to occupy the chair of Peter after Xystus II.

VII. Dionysius of Alexandria did indeed approach Stephen by letter as a mediator, “asking and entreating” him to refrain from pronouncing a sentence of excommunication, and thus not to carry into effect what he had threatened against them—namely, that “he would withdraw from communion with them.” It is clear from Augustine that the prayers poured forth by Dionysius accorded with Stephen’s will, for Augustine frequently testifies that Stephen preserved peace and charity with Cyprian and, consequently, confined himself to threats of excommunication and proceeded no further [Note: [Col. 1300D] Book V, *On Baptism, Against the Donatists*, ch. 25, and other passages cited above.].

Yet Dionysius nowhere asserts that these threats of Stephen were untimely. Certainly, if he had considered them such, then with the same freedom with which he indicated to Stephen that they ought not to be carried into effect, he would likewise have disclosed that they were premature and less than equitable—especially because, if we are to believe our opponents, he himself supported the rebaptizers. Indeed, he sufficiently indicates that he regarded Stephen’s threats as both just and prudent, since he attempted to avert their execution by prayers alone.

VIII. Eusebius of Caesarea, who had learned from Dionysius, and had inserted into his *History*, that Stephen had notified the rebaptizers that “he would withdraw from communion with them,” rightly writes that Stephen “took it most gravely” that Cyprian and the others should introduce an innovation concerning the baptism of heretics. Far from censuring Stephen in any way because he “took it most gravely,” Eusebius supplies a reason for Stephen’s manner of proceeding that demonstrates its equity exceedingly well. According to Eusebius, Stephen took it most gravely because he believed that nothing should be innovated contrary to the Church’s ancient tradition: “Cyprian,” he says in book VII of the *History*, chapter 3, “judged that only those first cleansed from error through baptism ought to be admitted. Stephen, however, believing that nothing should be innovated contrary to the tradition that had prevailed from the earliest times, took this most gravely.” What, moreover, could be more equitable and wiser than to take most gravely an innovation contrary to the Church’s ancient tradition?

IX. What St. Jerome thought of Stephen may likewise be gathered from his *Dialogue Against the Luciferians*, in which he mentions more than once the conflict that arose between St. Stephen and St. Cyprian concerning the baptism of heretics. There, therefore, he writes that “Stephen was savaged by Cyprian”; but he neither judged nor related that Cyprian had been badly treated by Stephen. Indeed, he ascribes to Stephen’s constancy and zeal the fact that Cyprian’s efforts to alter the Church’s ancient tradition proved fruitless: “Blessed Cyprian,” he says, “attempted to flee from broken cisterns and drink from foreign water; and therefore, rejecting the baptism of heretics, he sent the African synod’s decision on this matter to Stephen, then bishop of the city of Rome, but his attempt was fruitless.”

And so, according to the holy Doctor, the rebaptizers petitioned Stephen in vain; instead, they abandoned their error and, setting aside their recent decree, issued a new one. For he continues: “Finally, those African bishops who had decreed with him”—Cyprian—“that heretics should be rebaptized returned to the ancient custom and issued a new decree.” Behold what the Africans gained by having recourse to [Col. 1301D] Stephen. Could Jerome, I ask, have condemned Stephen’s manner of proceeding toward the Africans, when the Africans and the universal Church had received so great a benefit from it?

Finally, after the words just quoted, the holy Doctor concludes: “What are we to do? Thus our forefathers handed it down to us, and their forefathers to them.” From these words of Jerome you understand that he proposes for the Luciferians’ imitation Stephen’s zeal and diligence in preserving and transmitting to posterity what he himself had received from his forefathers. From this, again, it is evident how far removed the holy Doctor was from the opinion of those who misrepresent Stephen’s zeal as rash and uniquely suited to devastate everything.

X. Antiquity presents no one more inclined or more distinguished than Augustine in defending and excusing Cyprian. How many efforts Augustine made on his behalf, how great his zeal, ardor, eloquence, and constancy, is unknown only to someone wholly unfamiliar with his writings. The holy Doctor knew perfectly well, as he himself related, that in the matter of the baptism of heretics Stephen had “issued a command” to Cyprian [Note: [Col. 1302D] Book V, *On Baptism*, ch. 23.] and had “thought that he should be excluded from communion” [Note: [Col. 1302D] Ibid., ch. 25.]. He had also read Cyprian’s letter to Pompeius, in which Cyprian sharply assailed Stephen’s command and threats of excommunication, attacking the former as untimely and ill-considered and the latter still more sharply as less than equitable.

Why, then, does Augustine not agree with Cyprian when he condemns Stephen’s manner of proceeding? Why does he not excuse Cyprian’s disobedience toward Stephen’s command on the ground that Stephen’s manner of proceeding toward him had been untimely and less than equitable? Augustine devoted himself entirely to lessening and softening Cyprian’s errors. He would have said nothing novel by offering this excuse: Cyprian himself had already preceded him in offering it. Why, then, does Augustine not follow Cyprian’s judgment, which he esteemed so highly, on this point? If it pleases us to speak and hear the truth, Augustine did not judge Stephen’s manner of proceeding to be what Cyprian believed it was. Otherwise, having alleged and devised so many other arguments in the defense he undertook for Cyprian, he certainly would not have omitted the very argument that Cyprian himself had more than once advanced in justification of his right to resist.

Augustine was so far from believing that he could agree with Cyprian’s complaints against Stephen’s manner of proceeding as inequitable and immoderate that, although he was Cyprian’s most vigorous defender, he indicated that those complaints could only be disapproved. For Augustine examines Cyprian’s letter to Pompeius—the one letter, indeed, in which the bishop of Carthage criticized the Roman pontiff’s manner of proceeding—and expressly declares that everything Cyprian had written there against Stephen was not the language of a calm and composed man, but words uttered when “provoked”; words that, not fully master of himself, he had not expressed soberly and gravely but had “poured forth.” Indeed, they were so little consonant with moderation, equity, and charity that they were things “which carried the danger not of a slight but of a ruinous dissension.” Therefore, unable in any way to excuse them, much less approve them, Augustine—a man eminently endowed with Christian charity—declares that “it is better to pass them over.”

Here are Augustine’s words: “I do not wish now to reconsider the things that Cyprian, when provoked, poured forth against Stephen, because there is no need. For the very same things are said there that have already been sufficiently discussed, and it is better to pass over those things which carried the danger of ruinous dissension” [Note: [Col. 1302D] *On Baptism, Against the Donatists*, book V, ch. 25.]. Does Augustine show by these words that he supports Cyprian in censuring Stephen’s resolute manner of proceeding? Does the holy Doctor thereby indicate that, like Cyprian, he regarded it as untimely and less than equitable? Moreover, do not suppose that the words of Augustine which we are expounding are such as can be qualified by other statements of the same holy Doctor. For only in this passage, and nowhere else, does he expressly examine what Cyprian poured out against Stephen; consequently, from it you can and should ascertain Augustine’s mind with certainty.

By what effrontery, to remark in passing, some recent writers have alleged that Augustine located Cyprian’s principal holiness in the manner in which he conducted himself against Stephen, let them themselves consider and disclose to us—as though Cyprian’s many other most illustrious deeds were by no means sufficient to establish and confirm the exceptional holiness he possessed before God and men. In assessing the virtues of saints, let the testimony of saints be assessed; it belongs especially to saints to discern the true merits of saints and to celebrate their praises. Let us therefore learn the merits of the most holy Cyprian from the equally holy Augustine: nothing could be more equitable. But as to those things in Cyprian that Augustine did not approve, but rather judged should be covered with the veil of charity and silence, let us say truthfully that Augustine did not praise them so highly as to locate in them the principal foundations of Cyprian’s holiness.

From Augustine, once again, I should like to ascertain the equity of Stephen’s command and whether Cyprian rightly resisted it. Although Augustine, as we have just seen, professes that he does not wish to reconsider, and that it is better to pass over, what Cyprian in his letter to Pompeius had “poured forth,” when “provoked,” against Stephen, he nevertheless wished to select and cite certain things from that letter that were particularly well suited to proving the equity of the command issued by Stephen and censuring Cyprian’s disobedience. In this we cannot sufficiently admire the force of Augustine’s intellect and the perspicacity of his mind, for whom even Cyprian’s own documents sufficed to demonstrate the blemish in Cyprian’s resistance.

For when Cyprian, chafing under Stephen’s command, had said in the cited letter to Pompeius that “a bishop ought to be teachable, and that he ought not only to teach but also to learn,” Augustine cites and approves these words of Cyprian [Note: [Col. 1303D] Book V, *On Baptism*, ch. 26.], though certainly in a different spirit and for a different purpose from Cyprian’s. Cyprian said that a bishop ought to be teachable in order to show that Stephen ought not merely to have commanded and taught, but also to have learned and to have shown himself teachable by the arguments of others. Augustine, on the contrary, uses this statement of Cyprian to show that it was not Stephen who ought to have been teachable by Cyprian’s arguments, but Cyprian who ought to have been teachable by Stephen’s command. “For,” he says after reciting Cyprian’s dictum, “just as there were many things that the learned Cyprian could teach, so there was also something that the teachable Cyprian could learn.”

Thus, in the same affair Cyprian wanted Stephen to be teachable, while Augustine wanted Cyprian to be teachable. What does this signify, except that according to Augustine, Cyprian ought to have been teachable toward Stephen when he taught and commanded? From this it is evident that Augustine considered Stephen’s command entirely equitable.

Since our opponents rely principally upon Augustine, we shall not be blamed if we linger a little in expounding his mind. How many circuitous arguments the holy Doctor employed in excusing Cyprian, and how many difficulties he encountered, are shown by the various and perplexing reasons he advanced in Cyprian’s defense. At one time he contends that it may be doubted whether Cyprian believed that heretics ought to be rebaptized, and he repeatedly attempts, even through the testimony of others, to render Cyprian’s error doubtful [Note: [Col. 1304D] Book II, *On Baptism*, chs. 31, 33, 35, and 38; book IV, *On Baptism*, ch. 17; book I, *Against Cresconius*, ch. 32; Letter 108 to Macrobius; Letter to Vincentius Rogatista, ch. 10.]. At another time he contends that Cyprian, if he did hold this opinion, corrected the error [Note: [Col. 1304D] Book II, *On Baptism*, chs. 4 and 5; book II, *Against Cresconius*, final chapter; Letter to Vincentius Rogatista, ch. 10.]. At another time he relates that, if Cyprian truly refused to acknowledge baptism among heretics, as Stephen taught, he cleansed that error by the abundance of his charity and the pruning-hook of his suffering [Note: [Col. 1304D] Book I, *On Baptism*, ch. 18; *On the One Baptism, Against Petilian*, ch. 13; Letter to Vincentius Rogatista, ch. 10.].

What else do all these things reveal but the equity of the pontifical command? For if Stephen, by commanding, exceeded the limits of equity and of his own authority, Cyprian would not have been obliged to yield to him. Why, then, would Augustine have had to investigate in Cyprian’s defense whether or not Cyprian had retracted his opinion, since he would not have been bound to retract and correct it? Furthermore, according to Augustine, Cyprian sinned in that “he refused to acknowledge baptism among heretics.” No one doubts that it was a sin which had to be cleansed by the abundance of charity and the pruning-hook of suffering. Yet Cyprian certainly would not have sinned in this respect if he had not been bound to obey Stephen’s command that baptism among heretics must be acknowledged.

In this connection, I am not reluctant to expose certain delusions of modern writers, nor does it seem unprofitable. Some contend that in this conflict with Stephen nothing escaped Cyprian that Augustine considered worthy of any censure. Indeed, they affirm that Cyprian is highly commended by Augustine for the manner in which he conducted himself against Stephen; merely to state their opinion is already to refute it. Two others, more circumspect, distinguish two things in Cyprian’s manner of proceeding: namely, that he resisted Stephen, and that he poured forth certain statements against Stephen that savored too little of Christian moderation and gentleness. They assert that Augustine reproves the latter, but not the former. With their leave, I would say that either they were unwilling to read Augustine’s writings sufficiently, or they failed to attend to them sufficiently; certainly, they are ignorantly mistaken.

For St. Augustine censures in Cyprian not only what he poured forth against Stephen with insufficient restraint, but also the fact that Cyprian himself held a different opinion from Stephen in this question and refused, as Stephen had commanded, to acknowledge baptism among heretics. The bishop of Hippo affirms that this too, in addition to what Cyprian “poured forth” against Stephen when “provoked,” was cleansed by Cyprian’s charity and martyrdom. Let attentive ears now be given to Augustine: “Cyprian,” he says in his letter to Vincentius Rogatista, chapter 10, “either did not at all hold the opinion which the passages you recite represent him as holding”—that there is no baptism among heretics—“or afterward corrected it according to the rule of truth, or covered this, as it were, blemish of his most spotless breast with the abundance of charity.”

Here, according to Augustine, what Cyprian “covered with the abundance of charity” was not what he had “poured forth” against Stephen when “provoked,” but the fact that Cyprian held an opinion concerning the baptism of heretics different from Stephen’s. And in book I of *On Baptism*, chapter 18, he says: “The fact, therefore, that this holy man”—Cyprian—“remained in Catholic unity although he held an opinion concerning baptism different from the actual truth of the matter, which was afterward thoroughly examined and established by the most diligent consideration, was compensated for by the abundance of his charity and cleansed by the pruning-hook of his suffering.” According to Augustine, this is what Cyprian compensated for by the abundance of charity; this is what he cleansed by the pruning-hook of suffering: namely, “that he held an opinion concerning the baptism of heretics different from the actual truth of the matter,” as Stephen taught it to be.

Furthermore, when the Donatist Petilian pressed the authority of Cyprian, who had decreed that heretics returning to the Church should not be received without baptism, Augustine answers with an exclamation: “Oh, how detestable is the error of men who believe that they imitate illustrious men laudably when they imitate certain things those men did wrongly, while remaining strangers to their virtues! Thus some also wish to be compared with the apostle Peter if they have denied Christ; or, if they have compelled the Gentiles to Judaize, they aspire to be called his true brothers. These things were reprehensible in so great a man, but so great was the apostolic grace that they were immediately blotted out. . . . So too in the most glorious martyr Cyprian: if he refused to acknowledge the baptism of Christ given among heretics or schismatics, his merits, extending to the triumph of martyrdom, were so great that even that shadow was dispelled by the light of the charity in which he excelled” [Note: [Col. 1305D] *On the One Baptism, Against Petilian*, ch. 13.].

You see from Augustine that this was “reprehensible” in Cyprian: that he “refused to acknowledge,” as Stephen had commanded him, the baptism of Christ given among heretics and schismatics. According to Augustine, this itself was a certain “shadow” in Cyprian that had to be “dispelled” beneath the light of charity.

Finally, lest we become too tedious in reviewing every passage of Augustine corresponding to these [Note: [Col. 1305D] See book III, *On Baptism*, ch. 19; Letter 108 to Macrobius, ch. 3, etc.], we add only one more to those already cited, taken from book II of *Against the Donatist Gaudentius*, chapter 8:

“Far be it from us,” he says, “that because the most blessed Cyprian held an opinion concerning baptism different from what the truth demonstrated—previously through custom, and afterward through more carefully investigated reason—any one of us who does not share his opinion should therefore dare to prefer himself to him. For his many other great merits, his heart most fully possessed by exceptional charity—through which he remained entirely peaceable with colleagues who held different opinions—and his glorious suffering in the unity of the Church sufficiently showed that he was a branch in Christ, the fruitful root, which the Father would cleanse even from this ground of censure . . . thereby showing that even among the fruitful the husbandman who is in heaven finds something to cleanse.”

What could be clearer? What more explicit? According to Augustine, Cyprian held an opinion concerning baptism [Col. 1306A] different from what the truth was then demonstrating through custom—namely, through the mouth of Stephen. Yet on account of Cyprian’s exceptional charity and glorious suffering, the heavenly Father cleansed him even from “this ground of censure.” Cyprian was therefore reprehensible also because he held an opinion concerning baptism different from Stephen’s. According to Augustine, then, Cyprian was not reprehensible merely because he poured forth certain immoderate and immodest statements against Stephen, but also because he differed from Stephen concerning baptism and, although Stephen held and commanded the contrary, judged that no baptism existed among heretics.

If these modern writers had weighed these matters calmly and attentively, they would never have devised the distinction that can deceive only the unwary or ignorant: namely, that Augustine indeed reproves Cyprian for having poured forth against Stephen certain statements insufficiently consonant with charity and Christian moderation, but not for having obstinately defended his own opinion while Stephen opposed it and commanded the contrary. A hundred times they thrust upon us, inculcate, and insist that Cyprian defended his opinion constantly and immovably, although Stephen, the Roman pontiff, had written and commanded the contrary, and that Augustine never blamed him for this, because Stephen had exceeded the limits of moderation and of his authority, and because Cyprian was bound to yield only to the judgment of the Church.

What is my answer to these assertions? Without clamor, without commotion, without ostentation, but truthfully, plainly, and briefly, I say that, according to Augustine’s genuine meaning, Cyprian was “reprehensible” because “he held an opinion different from Stephen’s”; because “he refused to acknowledge” what Stephen wished to be acknowledged—“namely, that the baptism of Christ exists even among heretics and schismatics.” This, I say, is what Augustine censures in Cyprian; this is what he judged Cyprian to have compensated for by “charity,” indeed by “abundant charity”; this is what he declared Cyprian to have “cleansed by the pruning-hook of martyrdom.”

According to Augustine’s mind, therefore, the command of Stephen, the Roman pontiff, was not of such a kind that Cyprian could resist it without fault. Cyprian ought therefore to have abandoned his own opinion and thought otherwise if he was not to be blamed. Consequently, according to St. Augustine, it was not Stephen who was to be condemned as though by commanding he had exceeded the limits of moderation and of his authority; on the contrary, Cyprian was to be reproved because he chose to hold an opinion different from Stephen’s and to resist him.

### XI

How appropriate, how religious, and how equitable the conduct of Stephen toward Cyprian appeared to Vincent of Lérins, that excellent and ancient Gaul, may be abundantly discerned even from the fact that this most weighty authority recounts that conduct of Stephen and adduces it [Note: [Col. 1306D] *Commonitory*, ch. 9] to prove the thesis proposed at the beginning of the chapter: “This custom has always prevailed in the Church: the more religious a man was, the more promptly he opposed novel inventions.” Indeed, he demonstrates this more explicitly and clearly in these words:

> “In the letter then sent to Africa, he [Stephen] laid down this rule in these words: ‘Let nothing be innovated beyond what has been handed down.’ [Col. 1307A] For that holy and prudent man understood that the principle of piety permitted nothing other than that everything received in faith from the Fathers should be transmitted with the same faith to their children; and that we ought not to lead religion wherever we wished, but rather to follow wherever it led. He understood also that it is proper to Christian modesty and gravity not to hand down one’s own ideas to posterity, but to preserve what has been received from one’s forebears. . . . Then Pope Stephen of blessed memory, the prelate of the Apostolic See, resisted [the rebaptizers], indeed together with his other colleagues, but nevertheless before all the rest, deeming it fitting, as I think, that he should surpass all the others as greatly in devotion to the faith as he surpassed them in the authority of his position.” [Note: [Col. 1307D] Ibid.]

These were the things that Vincent, that most devout and learned Gaul, caused to resound throughout all Gaul concerning Stephen. Although highly honorable to Stephen in his dealings with Cyprian, [Col. 1307B] they appeared excessive or superfluous to no Frank of that time. Indeed, because they accorded no less with the truth than with Gaul’s innate piety toward the successors of Peter, all Gaul gladly heard them and transmitted them to posterity. Would that they had also pleased Launoy! He certainly would not then have burdened Vincent with so many errors for writing about Stephen’s actions, nor entirely deprived him of credibility in this matter [Note: [Col. 1307D] In the letter to Jacques Bevilacqua, no. 15, p. 817].

But what Vincent recalled was far too glorious for Stephen, and Vincent’s manner of expounding the conduct of the Roman pontiffs was far too different from Launoy’s, for him to have found the welcome and favor with Launoy that he deserved. Vincent, modest, peaceable, and a contemporary of Augustine, attributed Stephen’s command not to rash, untimely, and unrestrained zeal, but to Stephen’s own [Col. 1307C] “holiness and prudence”; to his “praiseworthy” zeal to hand down to posterity the same things that he had received from his forebears; and, finally, to Stephen’s “faith” and “devotion,” by which he surpassed the others just as he surpassed them in the dignity of his position.

### XII

Let there now come forward the distinguished and celebrated bishop of the sixth century who cannot appear suspect: whether he pronounces against Cyprian, since he was an African and a devoted admirer of Cyprian; or in favor of St. Stephen, the Roman pontiff, since he was a schismatic—namely, Facundus of Hermiane.

Facundus knew and reported that Cyprian had been censured by Stephen, and indeed under threat of excommunication [Note: [Col. 1307D] *In Defense of the Three Chapters*, book X, ch. 3, from the book against Mocianus]. He likewise relates that Cyprian resisted Stephen and sharpened his pen against him in the letter to Pompeius [Note: [Col. 1307D] Ibid.]. Let us therefore learn from Facundus, who was thoroughly acquainted with [Col. 1307D] the whole affair, whether Cyprian was thus censured by Stephen justly or unjustly, and consequently whether he rightly resisted him. Let us also learn from him whether Stephen treated Cyprian injuriously, or Cyprian treated Stephen so:

> “Cyprian,” he says briefly but openly, “treated the blessed Stephen injuriously, although he had been justly censured by him.”

These are the words, near the middle of book X, chapter 3, of the *Defense of the Three Chapters*, by that African prelate who, in his book against Mocianus, [Col. 1308A] as we saw above [Note: [Col. 1308D] Above], affirmed that Stephen’s judgment “that rebaptizers were not to be tolerated” had also been approved by the universal Church. From this judgment of the Church, supported by all antiquity, he certainly refused, as a sensible man, to depart, lest he incur the indignation and offense of all Christians by becoming the one man among the ancients—and the very first—who was not ashamed to condemn Stephen’s manner of acting and to rise up against him.

### XIII

The circumstances that befell Cyprian in the controversy over Baptism provided the Venerable Bede, a man renowned for learning and holiness, an occasion to make several remarks in passing. The few things that this learned author has transmitted to us concerning that dispute do not in any way detract from Stephen’s zeal and prudence; rather, they also indicate, with no little clarity, [Col. 1308B] the equity of his manner of acting.

For Bede writes that Cyprian both “corrected” his error and “was brought back to the universal norm of the holy Church.” The learned man also explains by what aid and assistance Cyprian was brought back to the universal norm of the Church: namely, “by the instruction of spiritual men.” It is evident that under the designation “spiritual men,” by whose “instruction” Cyprian attained this result, Bede means Stephen and Cyprian’s other opponents.

What more is required to demonstrate the prudence and equity of Stephen’s manner of dealing with Cyprian? Who could deny that manner of acting to have been prudent and equitable, when so beneficial and glorious a fruit and outcome must be attributed to it—[Col. 1308C] when it was able to bring Cyprian back to the universal norm of the Church? Here are the words of the pious writer, taken from question 5 of the *Book of Various Questions*:

> “If through charity you perform the good works that you know, divine grace will grant that, if in anything you think otherwise than you ought, you will one day understand that as well. This is clearly what happened to blessed Cyprian. Together with his fellow bishops in Africa, he decreed, contrary to the custom of the Church, that heretics must be rebaptized. But because, while holding the view that appeared right to him, he strove to abound in good works, he soon merited correction and was brought back, by the instruction of spiritual men, to the universal norm of the holy Church.”

### XIV

What shall I say of George Syncellus, who served under Tarasius, Patriarch of Constantinople? What of Nicephorus Callistus? Both relate that Stephen resisted Cyprian. Nor were they unaware of the manner in which he resisted him—namely, by issuing a command [Col. 1308D] and threatening the gravest penalties; Nicephorus expressly reports this as well [Note: [Col. 1308D] Book VI of the *Ecclesiastical History*, ch. 7]. Yet neither criticizes Stephen; neither censures him in any respect. Rather, both, following Eusebius of Caesarea, assign a reason for Stephen’s conduct that can only render and present it as equitable. For according to the authors just commended, the holy pontiff acted as he did toward Cyprian because he wished and endeavored to introduce into the Church nothing “new,” nothing “contrary to the ancient custom of the Church” [Note: [Col. 1308D] Nicephorus, ibid.; George in Anastasius the Librarian, at the year 246].

[Col. 1309A]

### XV

The ancients judged Stephen’s conduct toward the rebaptizers so appropriate, equitable, and timely that they indicate that it was approved even by the rebaptizers themselves—if not immediately, while their minds were swept away by the heat of controversy, then at least not long afterward, when they had grown calm and composed. Indeed, it was approved in such a way that they even retracted their error.

St. Augustine wishes this to be believed concerning St. Cyprian, although he admits that he did not find it committed to writing:

> “That Cyprian,” he says in letter 93 to Vincentius Rogatista, chapter 10, “held a view concerning Baptism different from the form and custom maintained by the Church is found not in the canonical writings, but in his own letters and those of the council. That he corrected this opinion is not found; nevertheless, it is not unfitting to suppose of such a man that he did correct it, and that the fact was perhaps suppressed by those who [Col. 1309B] were excessively delighted by this error and did not wish to be deprived of so great a patronage.”

In this passage Augustine says only that it is “not unfitting” to suppose that Cyprian corrected his opinion. But in book II of *On Baptism, Against the Donatists*, chapter 5, he asserts that Cyprian retracted his opinion with as much certainty as that great man’s merit itself was certain. For when the holy Doctor considered, on the one hand, that Cyprian had resisted Stephen, and contemplated, on the other, Cyprian’s great merits—which would have been considerably impaired by his obstinacy in error—then, although he did not find a correction or amendment of this opinion in Cyprian’s letters, he confidently pronounced that, even if the written records were silent concerning this correction, Cyprian’s merits nevertheless bore witness to it and did not permit it to remain doubtful:

> “How Cyprian,” he says, [Col. 1309C] “was able to accept the truth discovered contrary to what he had believed—even if the written records are silent, his merits cry aloud; if no letter is found, his crown bears witness.”

St. Jerome agrees with Augustine, expressly affirming that the African bishops retracted their opinion concerning the rebaptism of heretics by issuing a new decree:

> “Those very bishops,” he says, “who, together with Cyprian, had decreed that heretics must be rebaptized, returned to the ancient custom and issued a new decree.” [Note: [Col. 1309D] *Dialogue Against the Luciferians*.]

Augustine reports likewise that the Easterners who favored rebaptism rescinded their judgment; even the Donatists themselves acknowledged it:

> “Your forebears,” says the holy Doctor in book III *Against Cresconius*, chapter 2, “to whom you have borne this testimony—that they were separated from communion with the Easterners for the reason that the latter [Col. 1309D] rescinded their own judgment, by which they had determined that they ought to agree with Cyprian and that African council on that question of Baptism.”

And a little afterward, addressing Cresconius the Donatist himself:

> [Col. 1309D] “Your forebears separated themselves from communion with the Easterners because the two parties held different views on this matter—the Baptism of heretics.”

And in chapter 3:

> “Why should we not say instead that those few Easterners also corrected their judgment—not, as you put it, ‘rescinded’ it? For just as it is praiseworthy not to be moved from a true opinion, so it is blameworthy to persist in a false one.”

In the eighth century the Venerable Bede openly reported that Cyprian had abandoned his opinion, in these words:

> “Cyprian, who together with [Col. 1310A] his fellow bishops in Africa decreed, contrary to the custom of the Church, that heretics must be rebaptized, soon merited correction and was brought back, by the instruction of spiritual men, to the universal norm of the holy Church.”

Thus spoke the ancients just cited concerning the repentance of the rebaptizers, and you will find no one in all antiquity contradicting them. But if Stephen, the Roman pontiff, had not interposed his authority in this affair; if he had not openly displayed apostolic vigor; if he had not opposed the rebaptizers like a wall of bronze—would the African and Eastern prelates so easily have retracted the opinion that they defended with such ardor? Who would not recognize here the finger of God, who willed to crown [Col. 1310B] the zeal and constancy of Stephen and the other bishops who adhered to him with so abundant a fruit? Will you believe untimely a zeal that proved so effective? Would those burdened by it have shown themselves so teachable in response to an inequitable and untimely zeal? From this alone, then, discern the equity of Stephen’s actions.

### XVI

But now, finally, let the one consideration be produced that should be sufficient utterly to silence the shameless mouths of those recent writers who do not cease to rend the memory of this most holy pontiff, and to restrain their unjust audacity. Let the most hostile enemies of St. Stephen themselves be heard—I mean the Donatists. Let them be the judges of the equitable or inequitable conduct of Stephen or Cyprian.

Everyone knows that nothing was dearer to the Donatists than Cyprian, and nothing more familiar to them than Cyprian’s works—especially those he had composed to establish his opinion concerning the rebaptism of heretics. They constantly repeated these against the Catholics [Col. 1310C] and pressed them upon the Catholics. Petilianus, their leader, had read and thoroughly studied them. He had read through, I say, those works of Cyprian in which Cyprian reproached Stephen with many faults because he had issued a command and threatened the rebaptizers with excommunication.

Yet even all this could not so influence Petilianus that he did not freely and openly—against his own cause and against the very authority of St. Cyprian, whose statements against Stephen he thereby exposed as mere calumnies—profess without qualification that Stephen “administered his episcopate without blemish.”

This confession of Petilianus, the Donatist bishop of Cirta in Numidia, so glorious for Stephen, is drawn from these words of St. Augustine in *On the One Baptism, Against Petilianus*, chapter 14:

> “But I want this man [Petilianus] to resolve a question for me. For when he recounted in order the bishops of the Roman [Col. 1310D] Church, he included Stephen among those whom he confessed to have administered their episcopate without blemish.”

What could be more excellent for commending Stephen’s glory, both in all the other things he did and especially in this affair, than the testimony of the Donatists themselves concerning his integrity? Indeed, this truth must have been not only manifest but overpowering, since not even his most hostile enemies could conceal it.

And today certain writers who wish to be regarded as Catholics are not ashamed to misuse the letters of Cyprian and Firmilian in order utterly to stain and tear apart the memory of this most holy pontiff—a memory that even the Donatists of old acknowledged to be entirely without blemish.

[Col. 1311A]

### XVII

Antiquity supplies no more defenders of Stephen because it presents no more authors who either expressly discussed or incidentally mentioned that famous controversy that arose between Cyprian and Stephen. But I am mistaken unless the writers hitherto cited are abundantly sufficient not only to vindicate Stephen’s cause from calumnies, but also to adorn it with distinguished encomiums.

For what man of sound mind could doubt that Stephen acted rightly against Cyprian and the other rebaptizers, when no ancient condemned his conduct, while so many holy Fathers and writers distinguished alike for learning and antiquity—indeed, even Stephen’s most hostile enemies—commended it in him? Who would not acquiesce in a judgment so weighty and so powerful, and, as though wearied, [Col. 1311B] recline upon the couch of so great an authority?

After these testimonies of the ancients, must it still be investigated and examined whether Stephen’s manner of acting against the rebaptizers was right or inequitable, timely or untimely, prudent or ill-considered? But if Stephen’s actions appear less than right to us, will this examination and judgment of ours, whatever its worth, be considered more accurate and weightier than the judgment and examination of all the ancients? Will so many holy Fathers and so many venerable writers be thought to have been carried away or deceived by prejudice, or to have been less than truthful, while we are deemed more clearsighted, more equitable, and so free and immune from all those infirmities of mind or heart that it has at last been reserved for us to disclose and demonstrate the truth that they were unable to attain? [Col. 1311C] Will sensible men, I ask, be persuaded of that?

How vain and foolish our confidence would be if we hoped, by perverse investigations, finally to bring it about that an equitable judge of affairs would set aside the judgment of the ancients, agree with us, and embrace our conclusions! I know, indeed, and daily experience teaches, that certain men of yesterday take greater delight in their own offspring and inventions than in the familiar and widely circulated testimonies of the ancients, and indulge their own conclusions rather than those of the ancients.

What then? So far as I am concerned, let them submit Stephen’s conduct to that examination of theirs. Let them establish its equity or injustice not from the judgment of the ancients but from their own observations. Let them grant nothing to the testimonies of all the ancients who wrote about the dissension between Cyprian and Stephen, and everything to their own investigations; I do not object.

But I ask that they not resent my having been granted neither so much mental penetration in devising theories nor so much intellectual maturity in passing judgments, and therefore discerning ancient events from ancient testimonies and conforming my judgments to those of the ancients. Let them allow me, conscious of my own limitations and incapable of reforming the judgments of the ancients or advancing sounder ones, to regard it as a matter of religious duty, when the deeds of the ancients are at issue, to stand by the approved [Col. 1312A] records of the ancients and to adopt their understanding. I shall state plainly what I think: this way of rightly discerning and assessing the deeds of the ancients has always appeared safer and weightier to me.

After the long and laborious examination of Stephen’s conduct undertaken by our modern writers, then, let Stephen come forth and be publicly proclaimed by them proud, insulting, brimming with abuse, arrogantly aspiring to pomp and domination, savage, tyrannical, a disturber of peace, and an oppressor of churches—in a word, burdened with all the vices and crimes that we reported they had fastened upon Stephen [Note: [Col. 1312C] In the preface].

But I, to whom it has not been granted to uncover so many hidden secrets, who do not wish to be wiser than the ancients, and who desire to disclose what they reported, must—if not think differently about Stephen from those critics (for I cannot search their hearts)—certainly speak differently. [Col. 1312B] Let Stephen therefore appear, so far as I am concerned, after these novel garments—which were not supplied by charity—have been stripped from him, clothed in garments ancient but his own, acquired, if in no other way, by the prescription of so many centuries. Let those garments present him as:

- the religious and prudent [Note: [Col. 1312C] Vincent of Lérins, *Commonitory*, ch. 9] defender and champion of the Church’s tradition in the matter of the Baptism of heretics [Note: [Col. 1312C] Augustine, a hundred times in his books against the Donatists, and with him all the ancients whose testimonies Thomassin reports in Dissertation II *On the Councils*];

- one who, because of his singular zeal to transmit to his children what he had received from the Fathers [Note: [Col. 1312C] Jerome, *Dialogue Against the Luciferians*, and Vincent of Lérins, loc. cit.], took it most gravely that anything should be innovated contrary to the ancient tradition of the Church [Note: [Col. 1312C] Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VII, ch. 3];

- one who, with the Christian modesty and gravity in which he excelled, resisted those who pursued novel inventions [Note: [Col. 1312C] Augustine, *On Baptism*, book II, ch. 8; Vincent of Lérins, loc. cit.] and censured them by full right [Note: [Col. 1312C] Facundus of Hermiane, *In Defense of the Three Chapters*, book X, ch. 3];

- one who surpassed all the rest in devotion to the faith as greatly as he surpassed them in the authority of his position [Note: [Col. 1312C] Vincent of Lérins, loc. cit.];

- one who, although injuriously treated by those in error [Note: [Col. 1312C] Facundus of Hermiane, loc. cit.] and reviled [Note: [Col. 1312C] Jerome, *Dialogue Against the Luciferians*], nevertheless, with solicitous piety, endured everything for the sake of peace, which prevailed in his heart [Note: [Col. 1312C] Augustine, *On Baptism*, book V, ch. 25], and everything for the sake of the unity he strove to preserve [Note: [Col. 1312C] Augustine, *On Baptism*, book VI, ch. 22]—a great man and Father endowed with great charity [Note: [Col. 1312C] Augustine, *On Baptism*, book I, ch. 7; book VI, ch. 22].

Let this suffice to vindicate the manner in which St. Stephen, the Roman pontiff, acted against the rebaptizers.

# FIRST PART OF THE DISSERTATION

[Col. 1313]

[Col. 1313A]

## ARGUMENT.—The argument drawn and pressed from St. Cyprian’s conduct against the supreme and irreformable authority of the Roman pontiff in defining controversies of faith is shown by the wisest theologians of Gaul to be empty and groundless, and is utterly overthrown

Whatever may have been, or may be proclaimed to have been, St. Cyprian’s manner of speaking and acting against Stephen in the controversy over the Baptism of heretics, nothing can be inferred from it against the supreme and infallible authority of the Roman pontiff in defining controversies of faith, if the bishop of Carthage regarded the question then being debated concerning the rebaptism of heretics as a matter not of faith but of mere discipline.

This is universally acknowledged and is perfectly evident. For a man who refuses to embrace some disciplinary prescription of the Roman [Col. 1313B] pontiff does not therefore think the Roman pontiff liable to error when defining controversies of faith. Thus Gaul by no means received several disciplinary provisions enacted at the Council of Trent; yet it certainly never thought of denying the Council of Trent infallible authority in matters of faith.

Moreover, the wisest theologians of Gaul, entering upon the path of the other defenders of pontifical inerrancy, openly acknowledge and unanimously report that St. Cyprian regarded that whole controversy over the rebaptism of heretics as a matter not of faith but of mere discipline. Certainly, no doctrine is more powerful for overthrowing the argument that the modern writers draw from Cyprian’s conduct against pontifical inerrancy.

[Col. 1313C] Furthermore, not yet content with so decisive a reply, and wishing to satisfy more and more fully their zeal for defending truth and pontifical authority, the wisest Doctors of Gaul proceed further and demonstrate that this example of Cyprian can no more be pressed into service to deny the inerrancy of the Roman pontiff than to deny the inerrancy of the universal Church.

For they hold and teach as certain that St. Cyprian knew perfectly well that the custom defended by Stephen, the Roman pontiff, was the custom of the universal Church. From this it follows most manifestly that, if Cyprian judged Stephen to be in error in faith, or liable to error, when he upheld the custom of receiving heretics without a new Baptism—as the modern writers maintain—he likewise considered the universal Church to be in error in faith, or liable to error, since he knew that the universal Church [Col. 1313D] supported the same custom as Stephen. Hence you see that this argument of the modern writers attacks equally the infallibility of the Roman pontiff and that of the universal Church.

I am well aware that theologians of other nations who defend pontifical [Col. 1314A] inerrancy have met this wretched argument of the modern writers, which totters and wavers on every side, with numerous and solid replies. But in my judgment no one has met it more powerfully or more effectively than the Doctors of Gaul, when they teach these two points most openly, as we now undertake to prove them in as many chapters:

1. St. Cyprian referred the question then being debated concerning the rebaptism of heretics not to the domain of faith but to that of mere discipline.

2. St. Cyprian knew perfectly well that the custom defended by Stephen, the Roman pontiff, was the custom of the universal Church.

# CHAPTER ONE

## ACCORDING TO THE UNIVERSAL TEACHING OF THE THEOLOGIANS AND WRITERS OF GAUL, ST. CYPRIAN JUDGED THAT THE QUESTION DEBATED IN HIS AGE CONCERNING THE REBAPTISM OF HERETICS PERTAINED NOT TO FAITH BUT TO MERE DISCIPLINE

[Col. 1314B]

His Eminence Cardinal de Bissy, bishop of Meaux, has the following in part II of his pastoral instruction of 1728:

> “According to the opinion of several learned theologians, the question concerning the Baptism of heretics was judged in St. Cyprian’s time to pertain to discipline rather than to faith. Indeed, St. Cyprian repeatedly asserts that every bishop possesses full freedom to follow a different course of action in this matter. Could he have spoken in this manner about a question that he considered to pertain to faith? Moreover, [Col. 1314C] just as it is certain that a particular discipline may be retained by any national church in such a way that it cannot be compelled by the Roman pontiff to change it, so St. Cyprian and the African bishops could, without prejudice to the obedience owed to the Apostolic See, decline to comply with his decree.” [Note: [Col. 1314D] *Pastoral Instruction Against the Appeal from the Bull Unigenitus to a Future General Council*, p. 63.]

And in the pastoral instruction of 1725 he says:

> “It is maintained every day in Catholic schools that the dispute between Cyprian and Stephen concerned discipline alone.” [Note: [Col. 1314D] *Pastoral Instruction Containing a Refutation of an Adopted Writing, etc.*, p. 55.]

The Most Illustrious Languet, formerly bishop of Soissons and now archbishop of Sens, wrote in his third letter to the bishop of Boulogne, dated May 25, 1722:

> “St. Cyprian regarded his dispute with the Roman See concerning the Baptism of heretics as a point of mere discipline, which in no way concerned faith; learned men have agreed on this since St. Jerome.”

He repeats the same point in another letter to the bishop of Auxerre, [Col. 1314D] written December 25, 1722, no. 27; likewise [Col. 1315A] in the pastoral instruction containing various observations concerning the Instruction of His Eminence de Noailles, 1719, pp. 95–96.

The Most Illustrious de Saleon, bishop of Rodez, writes in his pastoral instruction on the authority of the Church’s decisions:

> “St. Cyprian did not consider this controversy concerning the Baptism of heretics to pertain to faith.”

He then confirms this thesis by various arguments:

> “Not only St. Cyprian,” the learned prelate continues, “and Firmilian, but also the Council of Arles regarded that controversy concerning the rebaptism of heretics as a point of discipline.”

Louis Thomassin . . . (his dissertation was given above in the column).

[Col. 1315B] Louis Dupin writes in his *Ecclesiastical Library*:

> “Cyprian, in his letter, urged Stephen to embrace this discipline concerning the rebaptism of heretics.”

And on page 469:

> “Firmilian confirms the discipline defended by St. Cyprian. . . .”

Launoy writes in his letter to Bevilacqua, no. 15:

> “Becanus,” he says on page 827, “following Bellarmine, says in support of his novel opinion, in order to flatter the Curia: ‘Cyprian was not regarded as a heretic’—as though matters concerning different ways of administering Baptism constituted material for heresy.”

And on page 828:

> “Meanwhile I affirm only that this matter—the question of rebaptism—is not a matter of faith but of discipline, which has undergone its own changes in the Church.”

[Col. 1315C] Antoine Pagi, Doctor of the Sorbonne, writes in his *Critique of Baronius*:

> “The doctrine,” he says in volume I, page 200, “concerning the rebaptism of heretics, which the African bishops defended, was regarded by them as pertaining solely to ecclesiastical ordering and discipline, not to faith. This is clear from the letter of Cyprian and the African synod to Stephen, the Roman pontiff. . . . Cyprian and his colleagues therefore considered the controversy over the Baptism of heretics not to concern faith.”

Gaspar Juenin, a priest of the French Oratory, speaks as follows in his historical and dogmatic commentary on the Sacraments:

> “The Africans and Easterners judged the question of Baptism to pertain to mere discipline, and not to faith or morals. . . . That the aforementioned bishops, both in Africa and in the East, referred the question of Baptism to mere discipline is demonstrated [Col. 1315D] from many considerations. Firmilian clearly affirms that disagreement was possible in this matter while preserving the bond of unity. . . . Cyprian held the same view in Africa,” etc. [Note: [Col. 1315D] Question VI, ch. 2, art. 3, §3, p. 90, Lyons ed., 1696.]

Feu, Doctor and pastor of Paris, writes in his treatise *On Laws*:

> “I reply that there should be no dispute concerning different customs, at least not a bitter dispute involving danger to Catholic peace, as Augustine teaches in letter 118 to Januarius: ‘What is commanded neither against faith nor against good morals is to be regarded as a matter of indifference.’ The holy Cyprian [Col. 1316A] and Firmilian had held the same opinion in letters 71 and 72. For St. Cyprian reports that everyone is free to hold whatever view God has suggested to him, and that no one should be cut off from ecclesiastical communion because of a different opinion. He therefore composed the treatise *On the Benefit of Patience* [the OCR reads “Penance”], to demonstrate that one should not withdraw from brethren who disagree. St. Firmilian likewise writes the same thing to St. Cyprian and confirms it from the practice then received: ‘Many things vary according to the diversity of places and persons, and yet on this account there has never been a departure from the peace and unity of the Catholic Church. . . .’”

[Col. 1316B] The *Theological Institutes*, published by order of the Most Illustrious bishop of Poitiers, contain the following in the treatise on the Sacraments:

> “Note that neither St. Cyprian nor the bishops who adhered to him should be numbered among the heretics, because a question of this kind concerning the Baptism of heretics was then considered to pertain to discipline, not to faith.” [Note: [Col. 1316D] Question III, p. 77, Poitiers ed., 1731.]

In his *Ecclesiastical History of the Third Century*, Noël Alexandre expressly proves this proposition:

> “St. Cyprian and the African bishops did not consider the doctrine concerning the rebaptism of heretics, which they defended, to pertain to faith.” [Note: [Col. 1316D] Dissertation XII, art. 4, p. 690, Paris ed., 1714.]

After adducing several considerations in proof of it, he concludes as follows:

> “If St. Cyprian had considered the rebaptism of heretics a matter of faith, he would have pronounced anathema against those who defended the contrary opinion and would not have remained in communion with them, for he considered it wicked to be joined in communion with heretics. He therefore did not consider that question to pertain to faith [the OCR reads *finem*, ‘end’], but solely to ecclesiastical ordering and discipline.”

[Col. 1316C] The author of the French work entitled *Treatise on Schism* (*Traité du Schisme*) speaks as follows on page 45:

> “In the disagreement between St. Cyprian and St. Stephen, the sole issue was a particular point of discipline, not of faith.”

The author of the work entitled *Treatise on the Obedience Owed to Dogmatic Bulls Issued by the Holy See* (*Traité sur l’obéissance due aux bulles dogmatiques émanées du saint-siége*) writes:

> “All authors,” he says on page 91, “admit that the question concerning the rebaptism of heretics was regarded in Cyprian’s time solely as a point of discipline.”

Ignace Hyacinthe Amat de Graveson, Doctor of the Sorbonne, writes in his *Ecclesiastical History*:

> “Cyprian, Firmilian, and the other Easterners who continued the custom of rebaptizing heretics after Stephen’s decree can be excused because they considered that custom not to pertain to faith at all, but solely to ecclesiastical ordering and discipline.” [Note: [Col. 1316D] Vol. I, Colloquy 6, p. 149, Rome ed., 1722.]

The author of the French work entitled *Theory and Practice of the Sacraments* (*Théorie et pratique des Sacrements*), in the treatise on Baptism, chapter 4, §2, writes:

> “You ask whether the ancient Fathers who considered Baptism conferred by heretics to be invalid regarded this as a point concerning faith. We reply that those ancient Fathers referred the matter to mere discipline, which could differ [Col. 1317A] according to the diversity of times and places. Thus Firmilian, who, etc.; thus St. Cyprian.”

The author of the French dissertation against the appeal from the constitution *Unigenitus* to a future council speaks as follows:

> “The holy Stephen and Cyprian referred this question concerning the Baptism of heretics to mere discipline.”

And a little afterward:

> “Cyprian’s resistance to Stephen cannot be excused in any other way than because the question concerning the Baptism of heretics was being treated on both sides as a question of practice and pure discipline.”

Petitdidier, abbot of Saint-Pierre at Senones, writes in chapter 6 of his French treatise on pontifical infallibility:

> “This, therefore, must be held constantly and with the greatest certainty: Cyprian regarded the question concerning the Baptism of heretics as a point of mere discipline.”

[Col. 1317B] Pierre Coustant, a Benedictine monk of the Congregation of St. Maur, has the following in his work on the letters of the Roman pontiffs:

> “Therefore, lest Cyprian appear to condemn his forebears and almost the entire Church, he permitted each bishop to think or act as he judged best; and for that reason he considered this question concerning the Baptism of heretics to pertain to mere discipline.” [Note: [Col. 1317D] Vol. I, p. 253, Paris ed., 1721.]

De Reveroni, a licentiate of the Sorbonne, has the following in chapter 1 of his dogmatic dissertation on the disagreement between the holy Stephen and Cyprian:

> “Cyprian assigned rebaptism to bare discipline. This opinion, for which we stand, is proved by many arguments.”

Tournély, Doctor and professor of the Sorbonne, speaks as follows in his treatise on the Sacraments:

> “Stephen indeed regarded this question concerning the Baptism [Col. 1317C] of heretics as pertaining to a dogma of faith, as we shall soon demonstrate; Cyprian, Firmilian, and the others did not.”

And on page 435:

> “Cyprian therefore resisted Stephen. Why? Because he loved and favored African liberty more than was equitable and, moreover, was somewhat incensed by the penalty of excommunication threatened by Stephen. He denied that the Roman pontiff possessed the right, in disciplinary matters—as he believed the question concerning Baptism conferred by heretics to be—to compel the other Churches to adopt his opinion and practice. The holy Martyr certainly went farther than was proper: he appears to overthrow all the laws of ecclesiastical subordination and jurisdiction, and he cannot be excused unless his words are restricted to a question of discipline alone. . . .”

[Col. 1317D] Antoine Boucat, a Parisian theologian, writes in his treatise on the Sacraments:

> “That this controversy concerning the rebaptism of heretics was, in the third century and even at the beginning of the fourth, a matter of mere discipline is proved by more than one argument: first, because the holy Cyprian and Firmilian always preserved unity with the holy pontiff,” etc.

And he concludes as follows on page 373:

> “It follows from these considerations that neither Cyprian nor Firmilian sinned, since in this matter they merely defended the discipline that they believed genuine. . . .”

[Col. 1318A] The writer commonly called among the French “Petit Tournély,” or in Latin “Tournély Abridged,” writes in his treatise on the Sacraments:

> “Cyprian considered this entire controversy concerning the Baptism of heretics to pertain to discipline, in which everyone was free to think and to do whatever he wished.”

He proves this [Note: [Col. 1318D] Question VII, art. 3, p. 130, Paris ed., 1730] by many arguments on page 137 and the following pages.

Jacob Hyacinth Serry, doctor of the Sorbonne, in his dissertation *On the Roman Pontiff, Who Knows Neither How to Be Mistaken nor to Mislead*, published in 1734, chapter 8, p. 52, says:

> “We reply that St. Cyprian and the other African bishops considered the question of rebaptizing heretics to concern mere discipline, and by no means the faith; and therefore it is no wonder that the Africans opposed the decree of Stephen I, the Roman Pontiff, since they thought that the Churches spread throughout the whole world were not absolutely bound to embrace the discipline of the Roman Church in every respect, [Col. 1318B] even though they were bound universally to embrace its faith.”

Those who clearly attest that Cyprian traced the origin of his opinion not to Christ or the apostles, but to Agrippinus, his predecessor, must rightly be judged to agree with these statements. For from this it necessarily follows that Cyprian referred his opinion not to faith but to mere discipline—unless they wish to maintain (something no one will suspect of the writers about to be cited) that Cyprian suffered from such great ignorance that he believed something which he considered to have originated with Agrippinus to pertain in some measure to the faith. These authors are as follows.

Isambert, doctor and professor of the Sorbonne, on Question 64, where he treats of the sacraments [Note: [Col. 1318D] Disputation IV, article 1, p. 121, Paris edition, 1639]:

> “Agrippinus,” he says, “the predecessor of St. Cyprian in the episcopate, [Col. 1318C] was the first to judge that Baptism conferred by heretics was null. Thus St. Augustine reports in book II, *Against the Donatists*, chapter 7, from St. Cyprian himself, in the letter to Quintus and the letter to Jubaianus. . . . Cyprian, in the cited letter to Jubaianus, says that the practice he follows is indeed not so very recent, but nevertheless was instituted by Agrippinus, one of his predecessors. . . . Then, both in that letter and in the council of eighty-seven bishops, he says that reason and truth must be preferred to custom; therefore he presupposes that tradition was contrary to his opinion.”

Claude Frassen, doctor of the Sorbonne, in his treatise on the Sacraments [Note: [Col. 1318D] Article III, question 3, p. 88, Paris edition, 1677]:

> “Agrippinus,” he says, “was the first of all to judge and define that the Baptism of heretics was null. . . . For if some earlier author had handed down that doctrine, [Col. 1318D] he would undoubtedly have been praised by St. Cyprian.”

Tillemont, *Ecclesiastical History*:

> “St. Cyprian,” he says, “acknowledges plainly enough that he does not follow the ancient custom in receiving those baptized by heretics” [Note: [Col. 1318D] Vol. IV, article 43, p. 139].

And below:

> “St. Cyprian and Augustine attribute the origin of rebaptism to Agrippinus.”

Fleury, in his *Ecclesiastical History*:

> “St. Cyprian,” he says, “shows in his treatise *On the Unity of the Church* that he received his opinion about rebaptizing heretics from Agrippinus, who had been the first to alter the ancient [Col. 1319A] custom.”

Baillet, *Lives of the Saints*, under December 16, p. 188:

> “St. Cyprian,” he says, “was not the inventor of his opinion, but, as he himself acknowledges in his treatise *On the Unity of the Church*, received it from Agrippinus, who had altered the ancient custom in Africa.”

The author of the work entitled *Remarks on M. Dupin’s Library of Ecclesiastical Authors* speaks as follows:

> “It may be observed that, in the question of the Baptism of heretics, Cyprian acknowledged that the tradition not only of the Roman Church but also of the African Church was contrary to his opinion. Cyprian recognized Agrippinus as the first who began to rebaptize heretics in Africa” [Note: [Col. 1319D] Vol. I, p. 275, Paris edition, 1691].

[Col. 1319B] L’Herminier, doctor of the Sorbonne, in his treatise on the Sacraments:

> “Agrippinus, bishop of Carthage, was the first to introduce this custom of baptizing again those baptized by heretics, as St. Cyprian attests.”

And on p. 133:

> “Cyprian tacitly acknowledged that the ancient custom of the Western Church was opposed to him.”

The learned Father Maran, a Benedictine, has the following in the preface that he placed before Baluze’s edition of Cyprian’s works [Note: [Col. 1319D] P. 15, Paris edition, 1726]:

> “Cyprian recognizes Agrippinus as the source and origin of his opinion concerning the baptism of those baptized in heresy.”

Nor could the author of the *Life of Cyprian* himself deny this:

> “St. Augustine,” he says, “and St. Cyprian trace the origin of this practice of rebaptizing to Agrippinus” [Note: [Col. 1319D] Book V, chapter 1].

[Col. 1319C] Finally, that Cyprian assigned the controversy over the rebaptism of heretics not to faith but to mere discipline is taught in our age by the schools of the Sorbonne and of Navarre alike. Danes, doctor and professor of the Sorbonne, in his theological lectures on the Church delivered at the Sorbonne in 1717, says in Disputation II, question I, article 3, conclusion 4, in his reply to the third rejoinder to the first objection:

> “Polycrates and Cyprian thought, although without justification, that the matter at issue between themselves and the Roman Pontiff belonged to that kind of discipline concerning which each Church was permitted to follow whatever seemed most expedient for itself. . . . Hence Cyprian expressly says in his letter to Jubaianus that the matter at issue between himself and the Roman Pontiff was one concerning which every bishop had freedom of judgment, [Col. 1319D] being accountable to God alone. Would the holy martyr have spoken in this way about a question which he believed to pertain to the faith? Or about one concerning which he believed that a decree could be issued by the universal Church, which each and every bishop would be bound to obey?”

Sovestre, doctor and professor of Navarre, in his theological lectures on the Sacraments delivered at Navarre in 1738, says in article IV, § 2:

> “Cyprian and Firmilian complained in somewhat harsher [Col. 1320A] language about Stephen’s manner of acting. Why so? Because Cyprian and Firmilian regarded this question as a matter of mere discipline.”

There he proves by many arguments that Cyprian thought this question concerning the Baptism of heretics “pertained only to discipline.”

Brillon, doctor and professor of the Sorbonne, and Beuret, doctor and professor of Navarre, in their theological lectures on the Sacraments, delivered at the Sorbonne in 1730 and at Navarre in 1742 respectively, teach that St. Cyprian traced the origin of the rebaptism of heretics back to Agrippinus as its first progenitor.

What more is needed? The professors of the Sorbonne themselves attest that the common opinion of theologians in our age is that St. Cyprian judged the case concerning the Baptism of heretics to pertain not to faith but to [Col. 1320B] mere discipline.

From all these testimonies it is most manifestly evident that the universal opinion of the theologians of France is that St. Cyprian assigned this controversy about rebaptizing heretics not to faith but to mere discipline. I am indeed well aware that several Jansenists and Quesnellists, in order to prepare their way for denying the inerrancy of the Church “dispersed,” as it is commonly called, contend and loudly insist that St. Cyprian judged that this question concerned dogma. But since they depart from the common doctrine of the Catholic theologians of France, I think no one will be so hostile and unfair to the French as to insist that their genuine views should be derived from the Jansenists and Quesnellists rather than from Catholics.

## CHAPTER II  
## ACCORDING TO THE UNIVERSAL TEACHING OF THE THEOLOGIANS AND WRITERS OF FRANCE, ST. CYPRIAN KNEW FULL WELL THAT THE CUSTOM ASSERTED BY ST. STEPHEN WAS NOT PECULIAR TO THE ROMAN PONTIFF, BUT WAS AT THAT TIME THE UNIVERSAL CUSTOM OF THE CHURCH AND HAD BEEN OBSERVED BY ALL BISHOPS FROM ANCIENT TIMES

[Col. 1320C]

His Eminence Cardinal du Perron, in his *Reply to the Response of the King of Great Britain*, has the following on p. 839:

> “The heterodox object that, in the case concerning the Baptism of heretics, when custom or tradition—not one peculiar to certain persons, but the universal tradition of the Church—was brought against Cyprian, he replied that Christ the Lord [Col. 1320D] had not said, ‘I am custom,’ but ‘I am truth.’ But they should also have added that Cyprian was at that time disputing against the true doctrine of the Church.”

The Most Illustrious Languet, archbishop of Sens, in the pastoral document *Containing Remarks on the Instruction of M. Cardinal de Noailles*, published in 1719:

> “Did Cyprian,” he says on p. 95, “and the African prelates rightly resist the Supreme Pontiff and the entire world?”

And on p. 96:

> “Cyprian would have been happier and holier if he had preferred docility to resistance, and if he had been willing to acknowledge that the Apostolic See, joined with the greater number of bishops, had always emerged victorious.”

The Most Illustrious de Saleon, bishop of Rodez, [Col. 1321A] in the pastoral document *On the Authority of the Decisions of the Church*, published in 1738, part I, p. 235:

> “The fault of St. Cyprian,” he says, “was all the less excusable because he resisted not only Stephen’s decree but also the custom of the universal Church.”

And a little later:

> “St. Cyprian himself acknowledges that the custom of the Church was contrary to his opinion.”

He then confirms this from St. Augustine and others.

His Eminence Cardinal de Noailles, archbishop of Paris, in the pastoral document issued on January 14, 1719, openly acknowledges that St. Cyprian resisted and refused to yield not only to the authority of Stephen, the Roman Pontiff, but also to that of the plurality of bishops:

> “St. Cyprian,” he says on p. 73, “did indeed resist the authority of Stephen, the Roman Pontiff, and of the plurality of bishops; [Col. 1321B] nevertheless, according to Augustine, he would have yielded to the judgment of a plenary council.”

In complete agreement with the Most Eminent prelate are the bishops of Pamiers, Senez, Montpellier, Boulogne, Auxerre, and Mâcon in their response to the pastoral document of His Eminence de Bissy, published in 1723, p. 87, and in other works which they made public.

Isambert, doctor and professor of the Sorbonne, on Question 64, where he treats of the Sacraments, Disputation IV, article I, p. 121:

> “St. Cyprian,” he says, “both in that letter—to Jubaianus—and in the council of eighty-seven bishops, says that reason and truth must be preferred to custom; therefore he presupposes that tradition was contrary to his opinion.”

And a little below:

> “Cyprian does not deny that this—the practice of not rebaptizing heretics—is the common [Col. 1321C] tradition of the Church, as Augustine rightly notes in book III, *On Baptism*, chapter 12.”

Father Frassen, doctor of the Sorbonne, in his treatise on the Sacraments, article III, question III, p. 95:

> “Both Cyprian himself and his colleagues in the council openly acknowledged that ecclesiastical custom and tradition were opposed to them, since they repeatedly insist that custom must yield to truth.”

The author of the *Defense of the Declaration of the Gallican Clergy of 1682*, published outside France under the name of Bossuet, formerly bishop of Meaux, part III, book IV, chapter 7:

> “Nor indeed did Stephen proclaim and press anything other than the universal custom, handed down to us from the apostles in the most constant course—a custom which an anonymous work preserved by Rigault, written in Stephen’s time [Col. 1321D] against Cyprian and Cyprian’s followers, calls ‘the most ancient custom of the Church.’ . . . Indeed, while the dispute itself was still raging, Cyprian and his African colleagues freely acknowledged that custom was opposed to them. Augustine notes this frequently.”

Fleury, *Ecclesiastical History*, vol. II, book VII, chapter 26:

> “The bishops who did not rebaptize opposed to Cyprian the ancient custom of the Church. St. Cyprian indeed acknowledges it, but contends that it must be subordinated to reason.”

Dom Cellier, a Benedictine, transcribes Fleury in his *History of Sacred Authors*, vol. III, p. 131.

Tillemont, *Ecclesiastical History*, vol. IV, article XLIII, *On Cyprian*, p. 139:

> “St. Cyprian,” he says, “acknowledges plainly enough that he does not follow the ancient custom of the Church.”

[Col. 1322A] And on p. 144:

> “Most of the bishops of the Third Council of Carthage—in the case concerning the Baptism of heretics—assert, according to Augustine, that truth must be preferred to custom, because even at that time their practice was contrary to the custom of the plurality of the Churches.”

The author of the work entitled in French *Remarks on M. Dupin’s Library of Ecclesiastical Authors* speaks as follows, vol. I, p. 275:

> “It may be observed that, in the question of the Baptism of heretics, St. Cyprian acknowledged that the tradition not only of the Roman Church but also of the African churches was contrary to his opinion.”

Natalis Alexander, *Ecclesiastical History of the Third Century*, Dissertation XII, article I, p. 686:

> “The excommunication by Pope Stephen of Cyprian and of the bishops who agreed with him [Col. 1322B] in the doctrine of rebaptizing heretics would have been entirely just. For who would deny that those are justly excommunicated who defend an error condemned by the Apostolic See and by other churches, and who remain obstinate in that error? Since this, therefore, was Cyprian’s condition, an excommunication pronounced against them by Stephen would not have been unjust.”

Dom Chiconot cites and approves these words of Natalis Alexander in the French dissertation *On the Celebrated Dispute Between Pope St. Stephen and St. Cyprian*, published at Paris in 1725, p. 198. He also adds that theologians commonly teach that St. Cyprian obstinately defended his opinion against the judgment of Stephen, the Roman Pontiff, and of the other churches.

Duhamel, doctor of the Sorbonne, in his *Theology*:

> “Cyprian,” he says, “erred [Col. 1322C] in this matter; but he did not abandon the unity of the Church, and therefore did not fall into schism or heresy, although he did not acquiesce in this tradition of the Church.”

Juenin, in his commentary on the Sacraments, question V, article III, § 6, p. 100:

> “Cyprian himself agreed concerning the ancient tradition of the Church not to rebaptize heretics.”

And a little later he proves from St. Augustine that St. Cyprian had before his eyes this universal custom of the Church everywhere, in these words:

> “Augustine speaks thus of Cyprian: ‘Having everywhere before his eyes the universal and firmly established custom. . . .’ The same holy Doctor asserts that Cyprian acted against the custom of the whole world.”

Du Saussoi, in the booklet entitled in French *The Truth Made Perceptible*, [Col. 1322D] vol. II, p. 59:

> “St. Cyprian did not think himself bound to embrace the opinion of Pope Stephen, although a greater number of bishops undoubtedly adhered to that pontiff.”

The author of the booklet entitled *Reply to the First Admonition of His Lordship the Bishop of Soissons*, published in 1722, has the following on p. 212:

> “St. Cyprian, Firmilian, and several other bishops devoted to them were far inferior in number to the remaining bishops who adhered to Stephen; nevertheless, according to St. Augustine, Cyprian rightly refused to yield to these authorities, however great they might be.”

Father Coustant, a Benedictine, in his work on the *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, vol. I, p. 253:

> “Therefore,” he says, “lest Cyprian appear to condemn his ancestors and almost the entire Church, [Col. 1323A] he allowed each bishop to think or act as he judged best.”

And a little below he continues:

> “It seemed harsh to Cyprian to deny communion to those who observed what he saw observed in almost all the Churches, and what he knew had been observed by his own predecessors before Agrippinus. For all the Churches agreed with Stephen except the African provinces and a few provinces of the East; Cyprian and his associates acknowledged that in Africa the same custom had prevailed down to Agrippinus.”

Tournely, doctor and professor of the Sorbonne, in his treatise on the Sacraments, question VII, article II, conclusion I, p. 377:

> “A far stronger argument is derived,” he says, “from the constant tradition of the Church”—namely, for rejecting the rebaptism of heretics—“and Cyprian certainly sensed this. As though distrusting his own case if he appealed to tradition, [Col. 1323B] he contended that the dispute here must be conducted not from custom or tradition, but from reason.”

Dom Maran, already praised above, in the preface he placed before Baluze’s edition of the works of St. Cyprian:

> “Cyprian,” he says on p. 17, “calls ‘human tradition’ that which, although not established by the authority of any council, was observed with the highest degree of agreement in all the principal churches.”

Brillon, doctor and professor of the Sorbonne, in his theological lectures on the Sacraments delivered at the Sorbonne in 1730:

> “Both Cyprian,” he says in question 3, “and the African prelates acknowledged in the African councils that custom and apostolic tradition [Col. 1323C] were opposed to them; repeatedly in these councils they insist that custom must yield to truth.”

Vogan, doctor and professor of the Sorbonne, in his theological lectures on the Sacraments delivered at the Sorbonne in 1737:

> “St. Augustine,” he says in chapter 8, article 1, “in various places calls this custom ‘universal,’ ‘firmly established,’ and ‘most salutary’; St. Cyprian, according to the same witness, had it before his eyes everywhere, and yet acted against the custom of the whole world.”

Delahaye, doctor and professor of the Sorbonne, in his theological lectures on Baptism delivered at the Sorbonne in 1738:

> “The excommunication of St. Stephen,” he says in chapter 5, article 2, “would have been entirely just if it had been pronounced against the rebaptizers. For that excommunication would have been most just if it had fallen upon those who defended an error condemned by the [Col. 1324A] Apostolic See and the other Churches, and in which they were obstinate. Now such was the error of St. Cyprian and St. Firmilian; therefore they would justly have been excommunicated.”

And in article 3:
