> “From the evidence we have thus far reported, it is established that the greater part of the bishops adhered to St. Stephen; hence it follows that his opinion was the opinion of the Church. . . . It must be acknowledged that active infallibility resides in the greater part of the bishops, and therefore that St. Stephen possessed the truth independently of the Church’s subsequent judgment, which declared that the matter must be believed with explicit faith. For the opinion was not Stephen’s alone, but also that of the greater part of the bishops. Hence St. Cyprian attempts to blunt the force of the argument drawn from the custom of the Church and the greater number of bishops by opposing to it [Col. 1324B] the truth which he falsely claimed.”

That Cyprian, according also to the common doctrine of the theologians just praised, knew that Stephen’s custom had been observed by all bishops from ancient times, we demonstrate as follows. Whoever considers Agrippinus the first progenitor of rebaptism necessarily acknowledges that no bishop before Agrippinus rebaptized heretics, and consequently that the custom of Stephen, the Roman Pontiff, had been observed by all bishops before Agrippinus. But according to the common opinion of the writers and theologians of France, St. Cyprian considered Agrippinus the first progenitor of rebaptism. For this is affirmed by Isambert, Frassen, the defender of the *Declaration of the Gallican Clergy*, commonly identified as Bossuet, bishop of Meaux, [Col. 1324C] Tillemont, Fleury, Baillet, the author of the work entitled *Remarks on M. Dupin’s Library of Ecclesiastical Authors*, L’Herminier, Habert, Father Maran the Benedictine, Father Gervais, Dom Brillon, and Dom Beuret, professors of the Sorbonne, whose words we have quoted above.

This is further taught by Juenin, Natalis Alexander, as well as de Reveroni in his dogmatic dissertation on the disagreement between St. Stephen and St. Cyprian, and almost all the others who have treated of the origin of rebaptism. We therefore rightly conclude that, according to the common teaching of the French, Cyprian also knew that Stephen’s custom had been observed by all bishops from ancient times.

## SECOND PART OF THE DISSERTATION

[Col. 1323]

[Col. 1323D] **ARGUMENT.—The considerations advanced by the wisest theologians of France to refute and overthrow the Moderns’ argument against papal inerrancy, drawn from St. Cyprian, are solid and invincible.**

We have seen how the wisest theologians of France [Col. 1324D] render that argument of the Moderns empty and ineffectual and utterly overthrow it: namely, by maintaining, like the other defenders of papal inerrancy, that St. Cyprian referred the controversy that arose over the Baptism of heretics not to faith but to mere discipline, and that he knew full well that the custom asserted by Stephen, the Roman [Col. 1325A] Pontiff, was at that time the custom of the universal Church and had been observed by all bishops from ancient times. It remains for us to show that these two principal points of the French teaching rest upon solid and invincible considerations. We shall accomplish this in an equal number of chapters.

## CHAPTER I  
## THE CONSIDERATIONS ARE SET FORTH BY WHICH IT IS PROVED THAT CYPRIAN REGARDED THE CASE CONCERNING THE BAPTISM OF HERETICS AS A MATTER NOT OF FAITH BUT OF MERE DISCIPLINE

### I

Cyprian in no way judged that opinion or practice to pertain to the faith whose origin he traced not to Christ or the apostles, but to Agrippinus, his predecessor. But Cyprian traced the origin of his opinion [Col. 1325B] to Agrippinus, not to Christ or the apostles:

> “Among us,” says the holy Doctor in Letter 73 to Jubaianus, “it is not a new or sudden thing for us to judge that those who come to the Church from the heretics must be baptized, since many years and a long period have now passed from the time when, under Agrippinus, a man of blessed memory, very many bishops assembled together and established this; and since that time down to the present day, so many thousands of heretics converted to the Church in our provinces have neither disdained nor hesitated—indeed, they have reasonably and willingly embraced—the opportunity to obtain the grace of the life-giving washing and saving Baptism.”

You see here Cyprian vaunting the antiquity of his opinion, yet tracing it no farther back than the times of Agrippinus. Would he have remained silent about someone earlier than Agrippinus [Col. 1325C] if he had known of anyone who favored his position? He enumerates the many heretics who had long been rebaptized in the African provinces, but not before Agrippinus—only after him: “and since that time,” he says, “down to the present day, so many thousands of heretics,” etc. The holy Doctor therefore knew of no author of rebaptism older than Agrippinus.

It is worthwhile to hear Augustine, who repeatedly affirms that Cyprian derived the beginning of rebaptism from Agrippinus:

> “The blessed Cyprian,” he says in book III, *On Baptism Against the Donatists*, chapter 12, “shows that the matter was not new or sudden precisely because it had already begun to be done under Agrippinus. ‘Many years,’ he says, ‘and a long period have passed from the time when, under Agrippinus, a man of blessed memory, very many bishops assembled together and established this.’ Therefore the matter was made new by Agrippinus himself.”

And in book II, chapter 7:

> “This most salutary custom [Col. 1325D] of the Church, therefore, St. Cyprian says began to be corrected through Agrippinus, his predecessor; but, as the truth discovered through more careful inquiry has taught, it is more truly believed that through Agrippinus it began to be corrupted, not corrected.”

According to Augustine’s testimony, therefore, St. Cyprian proved from the fact that the practice had already “begun” under Agrippinus that in rebaptizing heretics he was not doing something new. The bishop of Carthage thus thought that rebaptism had begun under Agrippinus. Moreover, you see Augustine infer from Cyprian’s words that “a new thing was done by Agrippinus.” Finally, according to Augustine’s most explicit statement, St. Cyprian says that the most salutary custom of not rebaptizing heretics began to be corrected through Agrippinus, [Col. 1326A] his predecessor. According to Cyprian, therefore, Agrippinus had initiated rebaptism.

Let us hear Augustine again:

> “Yet unless Agrippinus before him, together with certain of his fellow bishops throughout Africa, had attempted to abandon this custom”—of not rebaptizing—“even by conciliar judgments, Cyprian would not have dared even to argue against it.”

And in book IV, chapter 6:

> “This custom was so firmly established, and Cyprian himself found it already existing, that when a man endowed with such great learning sought an authority he might follow in changing it, he found only the council of Agrippinus, held in Africa alone a few years before his own time.”

You see from Augustine that Cyprian was moved to alter the Church’s custom solely by the authority of Agrippinus and of certain [Col. 1326B] bishops who agreed with him; that in all the preceding ages he found no authority favoring him except that of Agrippinus’s council; and consequently that he neither found nor recognized any authority older than it.

Again Augustine, book II, *On Baptism*, chapter 8:

> “But when the weary Cyprian was received by the authority of the preceding council held through Agrippinus, he preferred to defend what his predecessors had discovered rather than labor through further inquiry. For at the end of his letter to Quintus he shows what it was upon which, as though upon a bed of authority, he rested in weariness: ‘Agrippinus, too, a man of blessed memory, established this,’” etc.

As you learn from Augustine, Cyprian wished to defend his opinion [Col. 1326C] not as something handed down by Christ or the apostles, but “as something discovered by his predecessors”—namely, by Agrippinus and the bishops who subscribed to his council. It was upon the authority of Agrippinus, not that of Christ or the apostles, that “he rested as one weary.”

And indeed, how could Cyprian have traced the origin of rebaptism farther back than Agrippinus—Cyprian, I say, who, as we shall demonstrate below, knew well that the ancient custom of the universal Church was opposed to him?

### II

That which is defended only as “consonant with the faith and more pertinent to priestly authority and the unity of the Catholic Church” is not defended as a dogma of faith. For whatever is asserted to be consonant with the faith is presupposed not to be of faith; whatever is said to approach the faith more closely, or to pertain more closely to it, is not believed to be a truth of faith. [Col. 1326D] Thus, for example, anyone who asserted that the doctrine of the divinity of the Word was consonant with the faith or approached the faith more closely would, in everyone’s judgment, hold a less than Catholic view of the divinity of the Word. Why? Because he would by no means be judged to refer the divinity of the Word to the dogmas of our faith. Mere ecclesiastical statutes of discipline, however, are rightly called consonant with the faith: they strengthen priestly authority and reinforce the unity of the Catholic Church.

Now St. Cyprian called his opinion concerning the rebaptism of heretics “consonant with the faith,” but did not call it a truth of faith. He asserted that it was “more pertinent to priestly authority and the unity of the Catholic Church,” but not that it was necessary. [Col. 1327A] In Letter 71 to Quintus, he says:

> “We too have followed their”—that is, Agrippinus’s and the others’ who had established rebaptism with him—“judgment as religious, legitimate, salutary, and consonant with the faith and the Catholic Church.”

And in Letter 72 to Stephen:

> “It was especially necessary,” he says, “to write to you concerning this matter and to confer upon it with your seriousness and wisdom, since it is more pertinent both to priestly authority and to the unity of the Catholic Church, as well as to the dignity arising from the ordering of the divine dispensation: namely, that those who have been immersed outside the Church and, among heretics and schismatics, stained by the pollution of profane water, must be baptized when they come to us and to the Church, which is one.”

You would hear the holy Doctor speaking differently about those matters which he defended as dogmas of faith. [Col. 1327B] He did not call the doctrine that the unity of the Church must be preserved merely consonant with the faith, but said that it “must be believed by faith”:

> “Whoever does not hold this unity of the Church,” he says in his treatise *On the Unity of the Church*, “does he believe that he holds the faith? . . . Whoever does not hold this unity does not hold the faith of the Father and the Son.”

He did not say that the doctrine that infants too can be baptized was merely consonant with the faith, but that it must be held by faith:

> “The faith of divine Scripture,” he says in Letter 64 to Fidus, “declares to us that among all, whether infants or those more advanced in age, there is one equality of the divine gift”—of Baptism.

But when he presses certain points of mere discipline, he customarily calls them consonant with the faith. Thus he calls “consonant with the faith” the letters of the confessors in which the names of penitent lapsed Christians were designated in accordance with ecclesiastical custom [Col. 1327C]:

> “And therefore,” he says in Letter 15 to the martyrs and confessors, “I ask that you designate by name in a written petition those”—the lapsed—“whom you yourselves see and know, and whose repentance you perceive to be approaching satisfaction, and in this way send us letters consonant with the faith.”

Thus also he calls his manner of dealing with the lapsed consonant with the faith—namely, his having granted peace to the lapsed when persecution was imminent:

> “We,” he says in Letter 57 to Cornelius, the holy Pontiff, “have brought forth what was in our conscience, as was consonant with faith, charity, and solicitude.”

From these passages it is most plainly established that, not only in the obvious and natural sense but also in Cyprian’s own manner of expression, those things which are said only to be consonant with the faith and more pertinent to it are referred to matters of discipline, not to dogmas of faith.

[Col. 1327D] ### III

That which God reveals or inspires in one of the faithful as something better or more useful, or as something more effective for stirring heretics to return to the unity of the Church, signifies mere practical governance and discipline, and by no means a dogma of faith. Now St. Cyprian contended that his opinion and practice concerning the rebaptism of heretics should be preferred to the ancient custom of the Church as something inspired by God in certain persons because it was better and more useful, and because it more strongly attracted heretics to embrace the unity of the Church. Here are Cyprian’s words in Letter 71 to Quintus:

> “Custom must not be pleaded as a prescription; rather, one must prevail by reason. For neither did Peter, whom the Lord chose first and upon whom he built his Church, when [Col. 1328A] Paul later disputed with him concerning circumcision, claim anything insolently for himself or arrogantly assume anything, so as to say that he held the primacy and that novices and those who came later ought rather to obey him. Nor did he despise Paul because he had formerly been a persecutor of the Church; rather, he admitted the counsel of truth and readily agreed with the legitimate reasoning which Paul maintained, thereby giving us an example of concord and patience: that we should not obstinately cherish our own views, but should instead regard as our own those things which are at times usefully and salutarily suggested by our brothers and colleagues, if they are true and legitimate. Paul too, taking account of this matter, wrote in his Epistle: ‘Let two or three prophets speak, and let the others examine; but if something is revealed to another who is sitting by, let the first be silent.’ In this passage [Col. 1328B] he taught and showed that many things are revealed to individuals for the better, and that each person should not contend obstinately for what he had once imbibed and retained, but should willingly embrace whatever better and more useful thing may emerge; for we are not defeated when better things are offered to us.”

And in Letter 73 to Jubaianus:

> “Moreover,” he says, “when heretics learn that there is no Baptism outside and that the remission of sins cannot be granted outside the Church, they hasten to us more eagerly and readily and implore the gifts and graces of Mother Church.”

Why, therefore, does Cyprian contend that in the case concerning the Baptism of heretics custom must not be pleaded as a prescription? Because, he says, “no one ought obstinately to contend for what he had once imbibed when something better and more useful is offered.” He proves that his opinion and [Col. 1328C] practice concerning the rebaptism of heretics should be accepted as something better and more useful from the fact that heretics, understanding that Baptism outside—that is, outside the Church—is null, will return more readily and eagerly to the unity of the Church.

Did the bishop of Carthage, then, judge that what he offered to others as something better and more useful pertained in any measure to the faith? Did he judge that which he insisted others should accept after setting aside the ancient custom, so that heretics might return more readily and eagerly to the unity of the Church, to be a matter of faith? Is this how articles of faith are customarily urged by the holy Fathers? Are they said to be accepted as something better and more useful? In matters of faith, is no account to be taken of what was observed in the Church from ancient times? Just as these expressions are foreign to matters of faith, so easily—without any labor—we recognize how customary, apt, and fitting they are in matters of ecclesiastical discipline, as befits so great [Col. 1328D] an author.

IV. Matters that are peculiar to particular provinces, and that are thought rightly capable of being retained once they have been adopted there, are referred to questions of discipline, not to dogmas of faith. For the faith is not peculiar to one province or another, but must be the same everywhere and common to all Catholic provinces. “The rule of faith,” says Tertullian in his book *On the Veiling of Virgins*, “is altogether one, alone immovable and incapable of reform.” Moreover, what is adopted in certain provinces denotes practice and discipline, not faith, which is not said to be “adopted.” Finally, in matters of faith the principle that something may rightly be retained simply because it was once adopted is false; otherwise [Col. 1329A] it would have to be said that certain German provinces rightly retain Lutheran tenets because they were once adopted among them. Yet this principle may often quite properly be urged in matters of mere discipline.

Now St. Cyprian numbers his practice of rebaptizing heretics among those things that are peculiar to certain provinces and may rightly be retained simply because they have once been adopted there. For this is how he speaks in Letter 72 to Stephen, the Supreme Pontiff:

> We have reported these things to your conscience, dearest brother—namely, the proceedings in the African council concerning the rebaptism of heretics—both for our common honor and out of sincere affection, believing that, in keeping with the truth of your religion and faith, you too approve what is both religious and true. Nevertheless, we know [Col. 1329B] that some are unwilling to lay aside what they have once imbibed, and do not easily change their purpose, but, while preserving among colleagues the bond of peace and concord, retain certain practices peculiar to themselves that have once been adopted among them. In this matter we neither compel anyone nor lay down a law.

Everyone sees that Cyprian is here indicating to Stephen that he would not readily submit to Stephen’s judgment disapproving the African statute concerning the rebaptism of heretics—not because he thought the judgments of the Roman Pontiff in matters of faith were fallible, but because he relied upon the principle that, even when the Roman Pontiff opposed them, practices that were peculiar to certain provinces and had once been adopted by them could rightly be retained. Such was the practice of rebaptizing heretics.

V. Cyprian openly declares that the issue between Stephen [Col. 1329C] and himself concerned discipline alone. For when St. Stephen, in support of his own opinion, had cited the example of the heretics themselves, who did not baptize those coming to them, St. Cyprian replied that “the Church of God has not fallen so far into evil as to borrow from heretics the discipline for celebrating the sacraments.” According to Cyprian, therefore, Stephen’s offense was that he borrowed from heretics the discipline for celebrating the sacraments; thus Cyprian calls what Stephen defended a discipline. In Cyprian’s judgment, then, the dispute between Stephen and himself concerned a matter of discipline. Here are Cyprian’s words in Letter 74 to Pompeius:

> A truly excellent and legitimate tradition is set before us under the instruction of our brother Stephen, one that provides us with suitable authority. For in the same passage of his letter he further added [Col. 1329D] that the heretics themselves, when members of one group come to another, do not baptize them, but merely admit them to communion. To such evils has the Church of God and Bride of Christ fallen: that she should follow the examples of heretics; that light should borrow from darkness the discipline for celebrating the heavenly sacraments; and that Christians should do what antichrists do.

VI. If Cyprian had thought that Stephen’s custom could not be observed without harm to Catholic dogma, it would have to be said that St. Cyprian thought Catholic dogma was at that time being assailed by St. Stephen, the Roman Pontiff, and by far the greater part of the bishops, and had formerly been assailed by all Catholic bishops. For he knew, as we shall prove below, [Col. 1330A] that the custom Stephen defended was at that time received by far the greater part of the bishops, and had formerly been observed by all bishops. Yet who among Catholics would impute such views to so great a Doctor? You must therefore admit that Cyprian regarded this as a controversy of mere discipline.

VII. If Cyprian had believed it revealed by God that baptism conferred by heretics was no baptism, he would surely have despaired of the salvation of those infants who in the past had died with no baptism other than that given by heretics, for he was not unaware of the necessity of valid baptism for attaining salvation. Yet he himself admits that one ought not to despair of the salvation of all those who in former times died with only baptism given by heretics, provided that they had fallen asleep within the bosom [Col. 1330B] of the Church. Listen to him addressing Jubaianus:

> What, then, will become of those who in the past came from heresy to the Church and were admitted without baptism, and then died? The Lord is able in His mercy to grant pardon, and not to separate from the gifts of His Church those who, having been simply admitted into the Church, fell asleep in the Church.

Hear also Augustine repeatedly testifying to this concerning Cyprian. In Book II of *On Baptism*, chapter 13, he says:

> Although Cyprian thought that those who were baptized outside the communion of the Church did not possess baptism, he nevertheless believed that those simply admitted into the Church could, because of the bond of unity itself, be included within pardon.

And in chapter 14:

> If, therefore, Cyprian presumed that those whom he considered to be without baptism might nevertheless, because of the bond of unity, be included within pardon [Col. 1330C]—

And in chapter 15:

> For if those who came from the heretics did not possess baptism, as Cyprian asserts, they were not rightly admitted; and yet he did not despair of pardon for them from the Lord’s mercy, because of the unity of the Church.

He writes the same in Book V, chapter 2; Book II *Against Cresconius*, chapter 33; and elsewhere.

In Cyprian’s judgment, therefore, one must not despair of the salvation of those who died with only baptism conferred by heretics, provided that they fell asleep within the bosom of the Church and did not die outside the Church’s unity. For because of the bond of this unity, as Augustine testifies, Cyprian presumed that they could be included within pardon. Therefore one must not despair of the salvation of infants who died with only baptism conferred by heretics; for, not yet stained by any taint of heresy, [Col. 1330D] they fell asleep within the bosom of the Church and did not die outside the Church’s unity.

But did the holy Doctor ascribe this indulgence of God to infants who died without any baptism at all? Certainly not. Why, then, does he grant it to infants who died without baptism conferred by Catholics? Only because he judged that the necessity of some baptism for attaining salvation had been handed down by God, but not likewise the necessity of baptism conferred by a Catholic. Consequently, if he maintained that the baptism of heretics must be rejected, he did so not because he believed this had been revealed by God, but for other reasons to be stated below. Cyprian therefore did not bind his opinion concerning the rebaptism of heretics to the faith.

VIII. Cyprian’s teaching is constant and clear: [Col. 1331A] every bishop is free to think differently on this question and to incline to different sides. In Letter 69 to Magnus he says:

> I have replied, dearest son, to your letter insofar as our slight ability has permitted, and have shown what we, so far as lies within us, think concerning the baptism of heretics; prescribing to no one that he may not determine what he thinks best, since every prelate must render to the Lord an account of his own conduct.

And in Letter 72 to Stephen, the Roman Pontiff:

> In this matter—the question of the baptism of heretics—we neither compel anyone nor lay down a law, since every prelate possesses free judgment according to his own will in the administration of the Church, and must render to the Lord an account of his conduct.

And in Letter 73 to Jubaianus:

> We have briefly sent you this reply [Col. 1331B] according to our limited ability, dearest brother, neither prescribing to nor prejudging anyone, so as to prevent any bishop from doing what he thinks best, since he possesses the free exercise of his own judgment. So far as lies within us, we do not quarrel over heretics with our colleagues and fellow bishops, with whom we maintain divine concord and the peace of the Lord.

And at the opening of the Third Council of Carthage he speaks as follows:

> It remains for each of us to state what we think about this matter, judging no one and removing no one from the right of communion if he thinks differently. For none of us sets himself up as bishop of bishops or, by tyrannical terror, drives his colleagues to the necessity of obedience, since every bishop, by reason of the liberty and power [Col. 1331C] that are his, possesses his own judgment.

Now this freedom of judgment, which Cyprian granted to every bishop in the matter of the baptism of heretics, proves decisively that he referred this question in no way to faith, but solely to discipline, which may vary. For who could believe that Cyprian thought every bishop free to think whatever he wished in matters of faith? Would the Bishop of Carthage, then, have thought every bishop free to admit or deny the divinity of the Word, the two natures in Christ, and so forth, which he believed to be so many articles of our faith?

It would be utterly foolish to say that Cyprian granted such freedom to bishops concerning matters that had not yet been defined by a plenary council. For who, even among beginners, does not know that in Cyprian’s time [Col. 1331D] nothing had yet been defined by plenary councils? You might perhaps reply that at that time there was one opinion in the Church concerning the divinity of the Word, but not concerning the baptism of heretics. If, then, several persons had assailed the divinity of the Word, would Cyprian have thought that every bishop was free to think whatever he wished about the Word’s divinity? Was it enough for Cyprian that some dogma should be attacked by several bishops for every bishop thereby to become free to believe it or not believe it? Those who dream such things about Cyprian are to be pitied rather than answered.

Did he think every bishop free to grant or deny that the Church possessed the power to remit all sins? Yet no judgment of a plenary [Col. 1332A] council had then been issued on this matter, nor was there even a single opinion among all the bishops. For Novatian denied such power to the Church, and several bishops from Africa, Numidia, and Gaul followed him, as Cyprian testifies in Letters 55 to Antonianus, 59 to Cornelius the Supreme Pontiff, and 68 to Stephen the Supreme Pontiff. Yet read and reread Cyprian’s writings: nowhere will you find him granting the Novatians such freedom of judgment. For because he considered this Novatian opinion contrary to the Word of God—or, as he himself speaks in the cited Letter to Antonianus, to “the faith of the divine Scriptures”—he denounces the Novatians as heretics in the Letter to Antonianus. In that same Letter to Antonianus and in Letter 68 to Stephen, he calls their opinion “heresy” and “the most obdurate perversity of heretical presumption,” [Col. 1332B] to be punished by the Church’s more severe penalties. So far was he from believing that they were free to think whatever they wished in this matter of faith.

Did he think every bishop free to use wine or water in offering the Lord’s chalice? Hear Cyprian in Letter 63 to Caecilius:

> Let someone answer for it, dearest brother, if any of our predecessors, either through ignorance or simplicity, did not observe and maintain what the Lord taught us to do by His example and instruction. Pardon can be granted to his simplicity through indulgence; but we cannot be forgiven, who have now been admonished and instructed by the Lord to offer the Lord’s chalice mixed with wine, in accordance with what the Lord offered, and also to send letters about this to our colleagues, so that the law of the Gospel [Col. 1332C] and the tradition of the Lord may everywhere be observed, and that there be no departure from what Christ both taught and did.

In vain did the Aquarian bishops object to Cyprian that they were following the ancient custom of their churches and adhering to the footsteps of their predecessors, who had judged that the Lord’s chalice could be offered without wine. Having heard and vigorously refuted all these arguments, Cyprian openly declares that wine must be used by all, “everywhere,” in offering the Lord’s chalice. But by what motive, finally, was the holy Doctor led to deny the Aquarian bishops something that had not yet been sanctioned by any decree of the Church? Learn it from him himself. “Christ,” he says in the cited Letter, “taught us to offer the Lord’s chalice mixed with wine. Therefore let the law of the Gospel and the tradition of the Lord be observed everywhere; let there be no departure from what Christ [Col. 1332D] taught.” Cyprian therefore did not think that, in matters he asserted had been handed down or commanded by Christ, every bishop was free to think or do whatever he wished.

This, then, is Cyprian’s true doctrine: in matters of faith unanimity must necessarily be preserved by all in the Church. I add that this teaching is constant and perpetual in him. In his book *On the Unity of the Church* he says: “Christ commanded that those in the Church be concordant and unanimous.... The Lord teaches and warns us to withdraw from such persons,” namely those reprobate concerning the faith.

And in Letter 25 to Caldonius:

> So that one course of action and one consent may be maintained among all according to the Lord’s commands.

And in Letter 32 to the presbyters of Carthage: [Col. 1333A]

> So that, in ordering the condition of the churches, one faithful consent may be preserved by all.

And in Letter 43 to the whole people:

> Let those who reject God’s commandment and endeavor to establish a tradition of their own be vigorously and firmly rejected by you.

And in Letter 46 to the confessors Maximus and Nicostratus:

> For our unanimity and concord must by no means be divided.

And in Letter 59 to Cornelius the Supreme Pontiff:

> There can be no fellowship between faith and faithlessness.

And in Letter 69 to Magnus:

> None but the concordant and unanimous dwell in the Church of God.... The Apostle Paul teaches and commands that a heretic must be avoided as perverse and sinful.

I pass over similar passages. Yet from those quoted it is permissible to reason thus: a man who judged unanimity in faith so necessary [Col. 1333B] that one must withdraw from those reprobate concerning the faith; who believed, on Christ’s command, that one consent must be preserved by all; and who held that there could be no fellowship between faith and faithlessness—such a man certainly did not think every bishop free to hold divergent views in matters of faith. For what is more contrary to unanimity than such freedom of judgment? But Cyprian judged unanimity in faith so necessary that one must withdraw from those reprobate concerning the faith, and so forth, as is clear from the cited texts. Therefore the conclusion follows.

From all this two points are established:

1. In matters that Cyprian referred to faith, he granted no one the freedom to think differently.

2. Cyprian granted every bishop the freedom to think contrary to his own opinion concerning the baptism [Col. 1333C] of heretics.

It is therefore perfectly clear that St. Cyprian regarded this entire question concerning the baptism of heretics not as a matter of faith, but of mere discipline.

But finally, to close off every escape for our opponents, let this very controversy concerning the baptism of heretics serve as an example. Did Cyprian think every bishop free either to baptize again those baptized by heretics or not to do so, on the hypothesis that Scripture or apostolic tradition contained the teaching that they must not be rebaptized? For when Stephen, the Supreme Pontiff, commanded the Africans to observe the tradition of not rebaptizing heretics, Cyprian replied that Stephen’s command was just and legitimate, and that the Africans truly ought to observe Stephen’s tradition, on the hypothesis that this tradition was evangelical or apostolic. Here are Cyprian’s words in his letter to Pompeius:

> “Let nothing new be introduced,” says Stephen, “except what has been handed down.” From where does this tradition come? Does it descend from the Lord’s and evangelical authority, or does it come from the commands and Letters of the Apostles? For God testifies and declares that those things which are written must be done, saying to Joshua: “The book of this Law shall not depart from your mouth, but you shall meditate upon it day and night, so that you may take care to do everything that is written in it.” Likewise the Lord, when sending His Apostles, commands that the nations be baptized and taught to observe everything whatsoever He commanded. If, therefore, either the Gospel commands [Col. 1334A] or the Letters or Acts of the Apostles contain the teaching that those coming from any heresy whatsoever are not to be baptized, but that hands are merely to be laid upon them unto repentance, let this divine and holy tradition be observed.

According to St. Cyprian, therefore, whatever had been determined by Christ or by the Apostles in this controversy concerning the baptism of heretics had to be observed. Since, then, he granted every bishop the freedom either to rebaptize or not to rebaptize heretics, he clearly thought that nothing concerning rebaptism had been determined by Christ or the Apostles. He therefore did not judge this controversy concerning the baptism of heretics to pertain to the faith.

IX. St. Cyprian acknowledged no tribunal on earth to which he was obliged to yield [Col. 1334B] in the matter of the baptism of heretics; he attributed to Christ alone the power to judge his conduct. At the opening of the Third Council of Carthage he says:

> Let us all await the judgment of our Lord Jesus Christ, who alone, and He only, possesses the power to judge our conduct.

The holy Doctor wrote almost the same to Magnus and to Stephen, the Roman Pontiff. But would this declaration of Cyprian’s be true in matters of faith? In matters of faith, must not every bishop—and indeed an entire nation—comply with a general council? Does Christ alone possess the power to judge the conduct of some bishop or particular council when that conduct bears in any way upon the faith?

It remains, then, that St. Cyprian referred this question concerning the baptism of heretics to those matters of mere discipline that may be so tenaciously retained in particular provinces [Col. 1334C] that not even the authority of the Supreme Pontiff or of a general council has the power to alter them. Here, candid reader, consider, I beg you, how much aid is given to the heretics by those Catholics who, in order to ruin the authority of the Roman Pontiff, never cease crying out that Cyprian wished to defend a dogma of faith in this controversy. If this is once granted to them, it must also be granted to the heretics that, in Cyprian’s judgment, not even a general council is the supreme tribunal for settling controversies of faith. For the holy Doctor denies to a general council, no less than to the Supreme Pontiff, the power to judge his conduct, and most clearly and openly attributes it to Christ alone: “who alone,” he says, “and He only, possesses the power to judge our conduct.”

Indeed, His Eminence de Bissy continues in the pastoral document already cited, [Col. 1334D] from the year 1728, page 62: “Is that to declare that one submits the matter to the decision of a plenary council?”

X. St. Cyprian most steadfastly preserved peace, concord, and communion with those who departed from his opinion. Concluding his letter to Jubaianus, he says:

> So far as lies within us, we do not quarrel over heretics with our colleagues and fellow bishops, with whom we maintain divine concord and the peace of the Lord.... We patiently and firmly preserve charity of spirit, the honor of the episcopal college, the bond of faith, and the concord of the priesthood.

And in Letter 72 to Stephen, the Roman Pontiff:

> Nevertheless, we know that some are unwilling to lay aside what they have once imbibed and do not easily change their purpose, but, while preserving among colleagues [Col. 1335A] the bond of peace and concord, retain certain practices peculiar to themselves that have once been adopted among them. In this matter we neither compel anyone nor lay down a law.

And at the opening of the Third Council of Carthage:

> It remains for each of us to state what we think about this very matter, judging no one and removing no one from the right of communion if he thinks differently.

St. Jerome expressly testifies to this concerning Cyprian in chapter 9 of his *Dialogue Against the Luciferians*; St. Augustine affirms it a hundred times in his books *On Baptism Against the Donatists*. And I would have you observe that the Bishop of Carthage professes that he preserved this peace with those who thought otherwise even before he had encountered the contrary judgment of the Roman Pontiff, as is clear from the words cited both from the letter to Jubaianus and from the letter to Stephen. [Col. 1335B]

But would the holy Doctor have acted in this way toward adversaries whom he believed to be attacking the faith? Cyprian, I say, who in his book *On the Unity of the Church* affirms that “one must withdraw from those reprobate concerning the faith, and indeed by divine command”; who in Letter 43 to the whole people teaches that “those who endeavor to establish traditions of their own contrary to God’s commands must be firmly rejected”; who in Letter 59 to Cornelius teaches that “there can be no fellowship between faith and faithlessness”; and who finally in his letter to Pompeius declares that “one must withdraw from those who do not assent to Christ’s teaching.”

“If anyone,” says Thomassin in Dissertation 2, *On the Baptism of Heretics*, page 48, “obstinately dissents from his colleagues concerning the faith, he must be cast out from peace and communion.” Since, therefore, St. Cyprian believed that this controversy concerning baptism could be debated while preserving among colleagues the bond of peace and concord, [Col. 1335C] and since he firmly preserved communion with those who thought differently, it is manifest that he believed the faith remained unharmed and intact throughout this entire dispute, and was in no way assailed or obscured by his adversaries. He therefore judged this to be a controversy not of faith, but of mere discipline.

But, you will say, St. Cyprian preserved peace with those who thought differently not because he believed that faith was not at issue in this controversy, but because he held that peace must not be broken with those who attacked even the faith so long as the matter had not yet been defined by the Church’s final judgment—as was then the case with the question of rebaptizing heretics.

Shameful fabrications, fit to feed only those who swallow every invention! [Col. 1335D] If Cyprian believed that enemies of the faith were not to be condemned by particular councils or deprived of communion before the Church’s final definition, then he spoke wrongly when he said so often and so generally that “one must withdraw from those reprobate concerning the faith”; that “those who endeavored to establish traditions of their own contrary to God’s commands must be firmly rejected”; and that “one must withdraw from those who did not assent to Christ’s teaching.” He ought to have said that one must withdraw from such persons only after the Church’s definition.

And indeed, was this the manner in which the ancient Fathers dealt with those whom they judged to be assailing the faith? Did the Fathers of Antioch act thus toward Paul of Samosata and his adherents? Did the Alexandrian Fathers act thus toward Arius and the bishops who favored him? Did [Col. 1336A] the Fathers of Milan act thus toward Photinus? Did the Alexandrian Fathers act thus toward Origen and his followers? Did the Fathers of Constantinople act thus toward Eutyches? Did the Fathers of Saragossa act thus toward the Priscillianists? Did they wait for the Church’s supreme definition before condemning them and depriving them of communion? Far be it from us, then, to attribute to Cyprian something that has no basis in his writings and is so alien to the understanding and practice of the ancient Fathers.

Moreover, let our opponents tell us whether Cyprian, out of zeal and devotion for preserving the integrity of the faith, ought to have maintained peace and communion with those by whom—if our opponents are to be believed—he thought a principal dogma of our faith was being ruined in contempt of the authority of the African councils.

Finally, if, according to Cyprian’s mind, before [Col. 1336B] the Church’s final definition those who attacked the faith were not to be condemned by particular councils or deprived of communion, then surely they could never have been condemned by the Church or deprived of communion at all. Not by the Church assembled in general council, since such an assembly was morally impossible at that time; nor by the Church dispersed, as it is commonly called, since the judgment of the dispersed Church depends upon the judgments of particular churches, none of which, on this hypothesis, ought, according to Cyprian, to condemn them before the Church’s definition. How, then, could those whom no particular church had condemned ever have been condemned by the dispersed Church? Here our opponents must come to a halt—or devise something else.

Let it therefore remain unshaken that Cyprian did not think the faith was being attacked [Col. 1336C] by those whom he refused to have condemned by the Councils of Carthage and with whom he constantly preserved peace and communion.

These arguments, with certain others omitted for the sake of brevity, clearly prove that Cyprian regarded the matter of the baptism of heretics as a question not of faith but of mere discipline. For whether the matter itself is examined according to Cyprian’s mind, or his manner of acting in this controversy is considered, both demonstrate the truth of our assertion.

Learn from Cyprian the origin, the nature, and the consequences of his opinion and practice, and refer it to the faith if you can. For he locates its origin not in Christ, not in the Apostles, but in Agrippinus. He defends it not as something to be believed by faith, not as pertaining [Col. 1336D] to the faith, but only as consonant with faith and approaching it more closely; as something better, something more useful; as something peculiar to certain provinces and rightly retained once it has been adopted by them. In a word, he openly professes that he is contending about discipline.

If he had held as a matter of faith that baptism conferred by heretics was no baptism, he would consequently have had no hope for the salvation of infants who died with no baptism other than that of heretics; yet he affirms that one must not despair of their salvation. If he had thought that the faith was being ruined by his adversaries in this question, it would have to be said—something no Catholic will say—that, in Cyprian’s judgment, the Supreme Pontiff and, with him, the greater part of the bishops were at that time in error concerning the faith, and indeed [Col. 1337A] that all the churches of the whole world before Agrippinus had been so.

If you consider Cyprian’s manner of acting, he grants every bishop the freedom in this question to think whatever he wishes; he most steadfastly preserves peace, concord, and communion with those who think otherwise; and he attributes to Christ alone, and to Him only, the power to judge his conduct. Now these statements may be advanced with some semblance of reason in a matter of discipline, but in an article of Catholic faith they would all be utterly out of place. Let us now proceed to resolve the objections.

## OBJECTIONS ANSWERED

### Objection I

Cyprian proves his opinion concerning the rebaptism of heretics from many texts of Scripture, as may be seen in Letters 69 to Magnus, 70 to the bishops of Numidia, 72 to Stephen the Roman Pontiff, 73 to Jubaianus, [Col. 1337B] and 74 to Pompeius. Therefore he believed it had been handed down by God and consequently had to be believed by faith.

**Reply.** Granting the antecedent, I deny the consequence. For passages of Holy Scripture are often cited not only in matters of faith but also in matters of mere discipline, namely, to show the consonance of some discipline with those things that have been revealed by God, so that its equity may be vindicated from this consonance.

Thus St. Basil, in Letter 199 according to the new edition, to Amphilochius, chapter 32, proves from Scripture that a bishop, presbyter, or deacon deposed for some offense ought not, on account of that same offense, also to be deprived of ecclesiastical communion. Thus St. Jerome, in his letter to Theophilus against the error of John of Jerusalem, proves by the authority of both the Old [Col. 1337C] and New Testaments that Paulinianus’s ordination by St. Epiphanius was legitimate, although Paulinianus was at that time only thirty years old. Thus St. Augustine, in *On Faith and Works*, chapter 26, proves by the authority of Holy Scripture that some offenses are to be punished by excommunication, while others are to be healed not by public penance but by certain corrective remedies. Thus St. Leo the Great, in Letter 92 to Rusticus, Bishop of Narbonne, chapter 2, proves from Scripture that presbyters and deacons are not to be subjected to public penance. All these matters certainly concern in no way the faith, but solely the discipline of the Church. Even if, therefore, the holy Doctor proved his opinion by many texts of Scripture, he did not for that reason judge it to pertain to the faith.

And indeed, did not Cyprian himself cite many passages of Scripture [Col. 1337D] to establish matters that, in everyone’s judgment, concerned mere discipline? Who denies that granting peace and ecclesiastical communion to the lapsed before or after the completion of canonical penance is a matter of pure discipline? Yet read Cyprian’s treatise *On the Lapsed*, his Letters 16 to the presbyters of Carthage, 30 to the Roman presbyters, 33 to the lapsed, and 34 to the presbyters of Carthage, and you will find many passages of Scripture cited by Cyprian to establish his opinion in this matter.

Who denies that the mixing of water with wine in offering the Lord’s chalice is a matter of pure discipline and merely an ecclesiastical precept? Yet St. Cyprian proves the necessity of water from the divine Scriptures in Letter 63 to Caecilius. This kind of proof, therefore, [Col. 1338A] was employed by Cyprian in matters of mere discipline as well as in matters of faith. It is thus wrongly concluded from this that St. Cyprian assigned his opinion concerning the rebaptism of heretics to the faith.

I said, “granting the antecedent,” for the holy Doctor never directly proved his opinion from Scripture, as will be evident to anyone who attentively examines his writings on this question. He does indeed prove from Scripture that heretics are Christ’s adversaries, in the letters to Jubaianus and Pompeius; that the Church is one, in the letters to Magnus and Pompeius; that there is one baptism and one faith, in the letters to the bishops of Numidia and to Pompeius; that only those who possess the Holy Spirit can give Him, in the letter to Magnus; that only the rulers of the Church are permitted to baptize, in the letter to Jubaianus; that those who blaspheme the Father [Col. 1338B] cannot obtain the remission of sins, in the letter to Jubaianus; that the Church alone begets children for God, in the letter to Pompeius; and finally, the necessity of baptism, in Letter 72 to Stephen. From all these points, which he confirmed from Scripture, he attempted by various arguments to draw some conclusion in favor of his opinion; but he never directly proved from Scripture that baptism conferred by heretics was invalid, or that those baptized by heretics and coming to the Church had to be baptized a second time.

### Objection II

Cyprian asserts that the origin of faith and eternal salvation depends upon this question concerning the baptism of heretics:

> For no slight or insignificant concession is made when their baptism is credited as valid by us, since from it begins [Col. 1338C] the entire origin of faith and the saving entrance to the hope of eternal life.

But the origin of faith and salvation does not depend upon a controversy of mere discipline. Therefore he did not regard it as a question of mere discipline.

**Reply.** I deny the major premise. For in the cited text he declares that the origin of faith and eternal salvation depends not upon the dispute about rebaptism, but upon baptism—two things which, unless I am mistaken, are plainly different. Indeed, if you attend more closely to Cyprian, the contrary is clearly drawn from his own words. For when he asserts in the same letter that one must not despair of the salvation of those who died with no baptism other than that of heretics, he sufficiently shows that the origin of faith and salvation does not depend upon his opinion. Moreover, from Cyprian’s statement that the origin of faith and salvation depends upon baptism, it cannot be gathered that he bound his position concerning [Col. 1338D] the rebaptism of heretics to dogma.

### Objection III

St. Cyprian expressly teaches that what he defended against Stephen, the Roman Pontiff, had been revealed by God:

> Accordingly, some who are defeated by reason object to custom against us in vain, as though custom were greater than truth, or as though in spiritual matters one ought not to follow that which has been revealed for the better by the Holy Spirit. For one who errs in simplicity can be pardoned; but after inspiration and revelation have been given, whoever knowingly and consciously persists in that in which he had erred sins without the excuse of ignorance, for he relies upon a certain presumption and obstinacy when he is defeated by reason.

Therefore he referred it to the faith.

[Col. 1339A] **Reply.** I distinguish the antecedent. Cyprian teaches that what he defended against Stephen was revealed by God to certain persons as something better and more useful: I grant the antecedent. He teaches that it was revealed by God through revelation in the true and proper sense, contained in the written or transmitted Word of God: I deny the antecedent.

Thus the holy Doctor takes “revelation” here in a broader sense, insofar as every truth, of whatever order, is manifested by God, who is the First Truth; insofar as every gift descending from above is from the Father of lights; and insofar, I say, as the Holy Spirit reveals and inspires everything that concerns either faith or the Church’s discipline and governance.

1. For in the text adduced against us, Cyprian does not say simply that what he defended against Stephen was revealed, but that it was revealed *for the better*. He does not say that it was revealed to the Church, [Col. 1339B] but to certain persons among the faithful, whom he maintains are inexcusable after such inspiration and revelation. Now these two points cannot be understood of true revelation presenting a Catholic dogma. For a dogma of faith is not revealed as something better and more useful, nor is something suddenly referred to the faith merely because it is inspired and revealed by God to certain persons among the faithful.

2. Whoever resists the revelation and inspiration of which St. Cyprian speaks here, according to him, resists reason, or “is defeated by reason.” “Revelation,” therefore, is employed here by St. Cyprian in a broader sense, as embracing every natural truth that God reveals and inspires.

3. St. Cyprian, in his letter to Quintus, clearly shows the sense in which he said that what he defended [Col. 1339C] against Stephen had been revealed by God, in these words:

> “Whatever is at times usefully and salutarily suggested by our brethren and colleagues, if it is true and legitimate, we should rather regard as our own. Paul also, looking to this matter, wrote in his epistle: ‘Let two or three prophets speak, and let the others examine what is said; but if something is revealed to another who is seated, let the first be silent.’ In this passage he taught and showed that many things are revealed to individuals for the better, and that no one should stubbornly contend for something merely because he had once imbibed it and held it, but should gladly embrace anything that proves better and more useful; for we are not defeated when better things are offered to us.”

Who does not see that Cyprian assigns the opinion concerning the rebaptism of heretics to those things which God inspires and reveals to certain persons for the greater benefit of the Church? [Col. 1339D] This revelation manifestly concerns only the Church’s governance and discipline; hence, far from favoring our adversaries, it confirms our assertion, as we saw above.

4. Did St. Cyprian believe as dogmas of faith all the things he had written in his treatise *On the Good of Patience*? Yet he declares that these were inspired by God:

> “For this reason,” he says in his letter to Jubaianus, “we also composed the little book *On the Good of Patience*, so far as our limited ability availed, with the Lord permitting and inspiring us.”

Not everything, therefore, which Cyprian calls inspired or revealed by God concerns the faith. Divine revelation or inspiration is consequently sometimes understood by St. Cyprian in a broader sense. Our answer, therefore, is not some subtle invention after all, but one supplied by Cyprian himself.

[Col. 1340A] **Objection IV.** The holy Doctor believed as a matter of faith that those to whom Christ had not granted the power to baptize could not baptize. But Cyprian denied that Christ had given such power to heretics:

> “It is manifest,” he says in his letter to Jubaianus, “where and through whom the remission of sins—which, of course, is given in Baptism—can be granted. For the Lord first gave this power to Peter, upon whom He built the Church and from whom He both established and revealed the origin of unity, so that whatever Peter loosed on earth would be loosed in heaven. After the Resurrection, moreover, He speaks to the Apostles, saying: ‘As the Father has sent Me, so I send you.’ When He had said this, He breathed upon them and said: ‘Receive the Holy Spirit. If you forgive anyone’s sins, they are forgiven him; if you retain anyone’s sins, they are retained.’ From this we understand [Col. 1340B] that only those who preside in the Church and are founded upon the law of the Gospel and the Lord’s ordinance are permitted to baptize and grant remission of sins; but outside the Church nothing can be bound or loosed, where there is no one who can bind or loose anything.”

Therefore—

**Response.** I distinguish the minor premise. According to Cyprian, Christ had not given heretics the power to baptize, and he endeavored, somehow or other, to demonstrate this by various arguments: I concede. But that he taught it as a matter of faith and as something certain: I deny the minor premise.

Thus, to prove his position regarding the rebaptism of heretics, the holy Doctor endeavors, somehow or other, to show through various inferences that Christ had not granted heretics the power to baptize. In the text adduced in the objection, for example, from the fact that Christ gave Peter and the Apostles the power of binding and loosing, [Col. 1340C] he infers that Christ granted the power of remitting sins only to those who preside in the Church. From this he concludes that the faculty of baptizing does not belong to heretics, and from this he finally concludes that baptism administered by heretics is invalid because it is illicit.

But is everything thought capable of being deduced in some fashion from Scripture therefore believed to pertain to the faith? If matters immediately revealed by God are referred to the faith, are those things also so referred which people think can somehow be inferred from revealed truths through various arguments? When Cyprian cited several passages of Scripture to prove matters which, in everyone’s judgment, concerned changeable discipline, as we saw above, he assuredly thought that what he defended could be inferred from those passages of Scripture which he cited. Did he therefore consign it to the faith? Hence, although St. Cyprian [Col. 1340D] believed that it could be inferred from Scripture that Christ had not granted heretics the power to baptize, he did not therefore judge it to be a matter of faith that they possessed no such power.

I add that Cyprian did not even judge that this could be inferred from Scripture with certainty and necessity.

1. If he had thought that Scripture necessarily implied that Christ gave the power to baptize only to those who preside in the Church, he would have denied this power to Catholic laypeople just as he denied it to heretics, for the former, no less than the latter, do not preside in the Church. Yet nowhere in Cyprian will you find this power denied to Catholic laypeople. Consequently, the Catholics would be most perversely attributing this error to Cyprian here.

[Col. 1341A] 2. If he had thought that it could be gathered with certainty from Scripture that baptism conferred by heretics was no baptism at all, he would have held as certain that infants who died with only the baptism of heretics had not attained salvation; for it is believed with the same certainty that those infants attained salvation as it is believed that they were validly baptized. Yet St. Cyprian does not despair of the salvation of those who in the past had died with only the baptism of heretics, among whom no one will deny that there were many infants.

3. If he believed that Scripture certainly implied that those immersed by heretics had in fact not been baptized at all, how could the zeal with which he burned for the salvation of human beings have permitted him to leave every bishop free not to immerse them? Would he have believed [Col. 1341B] that in necessary matters the safer course must be chosen? Therefore, the arguments Cyprian drew from Scripture to establish his position and practice appeared probable, not certain, even to Cyprian himself. Against the proposed objection, therefore, I conclude that St. Cyprian by no means referred to the faith something that he thought could be inferred from Scripture only through various arguments, and not even with certainty and necessity.

**Objection V.** St. Cyprian calls his position concerning the rebaptism of heretics the faith and truth of the Catholic Church:

> “Therefore,” he says in his letter to Jubaianus, “dearest brother, we must both firmly hold and teach the faith [Col. 1341C] and truth of the Catholic Church, and through all the precepts of the Gospel and the Apostles demonstrate the rationale of the divine dispensation and unity.”

Therefore, he did not assign it to mere discipline.

**Response.** I deny the antecedent. Those who refer the cited words of Cyprian to his position concerning the rebaptism of heretics either have never read Cyprian’s writings and are content to have copied them from one author or another, or they intend to deceive the credulous. Here is Cyprian’s entire text—lengthy, certainly, but not burdensome to those seeking the truth:

> “How vain and perverse it is, moreover, that, although the heretics themselves, repudiating and abandoning either the error or the crime in which they previously lived, acknowledge the truth of the Church, we should mutilate the rights and sacrament of that same truth and tell those who come in repentance that they have obtained remission of sins, when they themselves confess that they have sinned and for that reason come to the Church’s indulgence. Therefore, dearest brother, we must both firmly hold [Col. 1341D] and teach the faith and truth of the Catholic Church, and through all the precepts of the Gospel and the Apostles demonstrate the rationale of the divine dispensation and unity. Can the power of Baptism be greater or mightier than confession and suffering, so that someone confesses Christ before human beings and is baptized in his own blood? Yet even this Baptism does not profit heretics, although they may have confessed Christ and been slain outside the Church—unless the patrons and advocates of heretics proclaim as martyrs those heretics who were killed in a false confession of Christ and, contrary to the Apostle’s declaration that they can profit nothing even if burned and slain, assign to them the glory and crown of suffering. But if even [Col. 1342A] the Baptism of public confession and blood cannot profit a heretic unto salvation, because there is no salvation outside the Church, how much less will it profit him if, in some hiding place and den of robbers, he is immersed in water polluted by adultery and, far from putting away his former sins, has instead accumulated still more new and greater ones.”

You see what, according to Cyprian, is that faith and truth of the Catholic Church which must firmly be held and taught: namely, that heretics cannot obtain remission of their sins within heresy and that Baptism cannot profit them unto salvation. No Catholic denies this, and Cyprian’s erroneous position concerning the rebaptism of heretics certainly did not consist in it. Those, therefore, who refer to his error what Cyprian himself rightly called certain in faith do Cyprian the gravest injustice.

[Col. 1342B] **Objection VI.** They cite Cyprian’s letter to Pompeius, from which they extract these testimonies, which, with mouths wide open, they loudly proclaim to cry out that this is a question of faith and dogma:

> “If truth has faltered or wavered in any matter, let us return to the Lord’s origin, to the Gospel, and to the apostolic tradition, and let the rationale of our conduct arise from the same source from which its order and origin arose. For it has been handed down to us that there is one God, one Christ, one hope, one faith, one Church, and one Baptism established only in the one Church. Whoever departs from that unity must be found among the heretics; and while Stephen defends them against the Church, he attacks the sacrament of divine tradition. . . . What obstinacy and presumption it is to prefer human tradition to the divine ordering and not to perceive [Col. 1342C] that God is indignant and angered whenever human tradition dissolves and transgresses the divine precepts.”

**Response.** What is the purpose of this darkness spread by our adversaries? Let them shake the dust from their eyes and at last see in Cyprian’s texts what everyone sees: namely, that Cyprian says it was handed down that there is one Baptism established only in the one Church. This is true, and all Catholics maintain it; from this tradition they prove that heretics are not permitted to baptize. But does the holy Doctor assert here that it was handed down that the baptism of heretics is invalid, or anything similar? No one reads this; no one sees it; nor will our adversaries themselves see it if they inspect the matter more closely.

But, they say, the holy Doctor asserted that one Baptism was established in the one Church in such a way as to argue that heretics could baptize neither licitly nor validly. [Col. 1342D] I admit this, but that is not at all the matter under discussion. For the question here is not whether Cyprian thought that heretics could not validly baptize, nor whether he attempted to derive this from several texts of Scripture. The question is whether he believed it as a matter of faith, and whether he said that it had been handed down by God that Baptism was one in the Church in such a way that heretics could baptize neither licitly nor validly. But this will never be proved; it will nowhere be read in Cyprian. Indeed, the contrary is demonstrated even from this very letter cited in the objection.

For when Stephen said, “We hold what we have received from the Apostles,” what did Cyprian reply to this appeal to the authority of the Apostles?

> “The Apostles,” he answers, “called heretics Antichrists and declared that they must be avoided; [Col. 1343A] nowhere among the Apostles is there found a command that only a hand should be imposed upon heretics for repentance.”

That is, he confines himself within these limits in order to show that Stephen boasted of apostolic tradition without warrant and that what the Apostles thought about baptism of this kind was unknown. But if St. Cyprian had believed that his own position had been handed down by the Apostles, he surely would have invoked that tradition here. He certainly would not have omitted the reply that Stephen appealed to apostolic authority in the very worst faith when that authority wholly favored Cyprian himself. No more suitable occasion could have arisen for him to allege this decisive tradition, by which his adversaries would have been entirely refuted. Yet Cyprian did not do so. Therefore, he did not judge that the invalidity of the baptism of heretics had been handed down by the Apostles.

[Col. 1343B] The holy Doctor indeed opposes to Stephen’s tradition—which he called human—the evangelical and divine ordering, which he says must be preferred. He does so not because his position concerning the rebaptism of heretics was contained or manifested in this ordering—for we have just proved the contrary even from this very letter—but because he strove to derive his position from it by human reasoning or, as Facundus of Hermiane says, “by human argumentation.”

For what, according to Cyprian, does this evangelical and divine ordering, which he here opposes to Stephen, demonstrate? Does it demonstrate that the baptism of heretics is no baptism? That heretics cannot baptize validly? By no means. Cyprian asserts this neither there nor elsewhere. What, then, does it demonstrate? It demonstrates that “heretics are [Col. 1343C] Antichrists and must be avoided”; it demonstrates “the unity of Baptism.” Behold that divine ordering which Cyprian opposes to Stephen: namely, several evangelical truths from which he labored, by various arguments, to derive his position. But from the fact that Cyprian believed his position concerning the rebaptism of heretics could be derived from several texts of Scripture, one must not conclude that he judged this controversy to concern the faith, as we proved above.

I do not dwell on the fact that, in this letter, St. Cyprian accuses St. Stephen of error; for not every error militates against the faith. Stephen is indeed charged with error, but never with error against the faith. In Cyprian’s mind Stephen erred because he did not judge the position concerning the rebaptism of heretics to be “better [Col. 1343D] and more useful,” as Cyprian says in his letter to Quintus, and therefore wished it to be rejected.

Let this suffice concerning Cyprian’s letter to Pompeius. “For,” to use Augustine’s words, “I do not wish to reconsider those things which Cyprian poured out against Stephen in anger, because there is no need, and it is better to pass them over.” With Vincent of Lérins, that excellent Gaul, I detest “the wickedness of those who fan the memory of that holy man Cyprian with profane hands as though stirring ashes already at rest, and who defame anew, by reviving the controversy, matters which ought to have been buried in silence.”

**Final objection.** It is not probable that St. Cyprian assigned to mere discipline a controversy which concerned the validity or invalidity of Baptism; nor can it be conceived how a man endowed with the greatest perspicacity and most renowned for learning could have held such an opinion.

[Col. 1344A] **Response.** Our assertion rests upon so many and such powerful arguments that only one who gropes at midday could maintain that it lacks probability. Indeed, for it to be rightly and deservedly said that Cyprian thought this to be a controversy of mere discipline, is it necessary to investigate, uncover, and vindicate the manner in which he judged it to be such? Let the manner remain unknown, if one wishes; let the principles by which the holy Doctor was moved to judge thus remain hidden from us, provided that in this controversy he advanced things which present nothing but a question of mere discipline, and provided that he conducted himself in this affair as he would never have conducted himself in a matter of faith. The truth of our assertion will then remain certain and immovable.

Who denies that Cyprian was learned—indeed, a most brilliant light of the Church and a distinguished Doctor? But I also consider Basil learned, and Athanasius learned; yet French writers and theologians themselves everywhere teach that those men regarded this as a controversy of mere discipline. [Col. 1344B]

> **Note:** [Col. 1344D] See the illustrious de Saléon, Bishop of Rodez, *Pastoral Instruction on the Authority of the Church’s Decisions*, part 1, p. 222 ff.; Thomassin, dissertation 2, *On the Baptism of Heretics*, p. 48; Feu, *Treatise on Laws*, question 7, article 3, p. 252; Juenin, *On the Sacraments*, question 6, chapter 2, article 3, § 3, pp. 90 and 92; Launoy, letter 15 to Bevilaq., p. 287; and very many others.

Moreover, it is not without reason conjectured that Cyprian’s position was that the validity of the baptism of heretics depended upon the usages, customs, and arrangements of the individual churches, which could render heretics incapable of baptizing.

1. Cyprian, as we saw, permitted his colleagues to hold differing views concerning rebaptism. He seems to rise up against no one except Stephen, because Stephen wished to subject even the African Church to the Roman custom. [Col. 1344C] Yet, given his zeal for the salvation of souls, Cyprian would never have permitted this freedom to rebaptize or not to rebaptize if he had thought baptism conferred by heretics was nowhere valid. It is therefore necessary that he regarded it as valid in certain churches but void in others. The cause of this distinction appears capable of being derived from nothing other than the explanation just offered.

2. When Magnus inquired about the immersion of the *clinici*—those baptized on sickbeds—St. Cyprian replied that Baptism conferred upon them was valid. Nevertheless, in this very letter to Magnus, Letter 69, he wished the *clinici* to be baptized again among those who denied the validity of such Baptism:

> “If anyone,” he says, “thinks that the *clinici* have obtained nothing, let them not be deceived; rather, if they escape the infirmity of their sickness [Col. 1344D] and regain their health, let them be baptized.”

The holy Doctor therefore judged the Baptism given to the *clinici* to be no Baptism among those who denied the validity of such Baptism; otherwise, he would not have permitted them to rebaptize the *clinici*. For he knew, and indeed had very often taught, that a valid Baptism cannot be repeated. Thus, the Baptism which he believed valid in his own church he regarded as invalid among others.

But he could not hold this view of Baptism unless he believed that individual churches possessed the power [Col. 1345A] to establish impediments by which a Baptism would be rendered null, so that it was validly administered where such impediments had not been established, but invalidly where they had.

3. In fact, those who in ancient times favored the rebaptism of heretics derived both the necessity of rebaptizing them—and consequently the invalidity of Baptism—from the differing arrangements or customs of the churches.

> “As for what concerns the Cathari,” St. Basil says in his first canonical letter to Amphilochius, “it has already been discussed, and you rightly admonished that the custom of each region must be followed, since those who at that time made determinations concerning them adopted differing positions regarding their Baptism. . . . Since it seemed altogether right to certain Asians, for the sake of providing for the many, that their Baptism should be accepted, let it be accepted.”

And shortly thereafter:

> “I therefore judge that, since nothing has been explicitly stated about them—the Encratite heretics—their Baptism should be rejected by us, and that if anyone has received it from them, he should be baptized upon approaching the Church. But if this proves an impediment to the general governance of the Church, custom must again be employed, and we must follow the Fathers who administered those matters which concern us.”

There you plainly see St. Basil derive the necessity of rebaptizing or not rebaptizing heretics from the customs of different regions and the differing statutes of bishops.

Amphilochius held the same view. He judged that, in repeating or not repeating the Baptism of the Cathari, the varying customs of the churches must be observed, as Basil testifies [Col. 1345C] in the words just cited:

> “As for what concerns the Cathari, it has already been discussed, and you rightly admonished that the custom of each region must be followed, since those who at that time made determinations concerning them adopted differing positions regarding their Baptism.”

Firmilian held the same view, comparing rebaptism with matters that receive their force from the varying customs of different regions:

> “Regarding the celebration,” he says in his letter to Cyprian, Letter 75 among the Cyprianic letters, “of the days of Easter and many other mysteries of divine worship, anyone may see that there are certain differences among them—the Romans—and that not everything is observed there in precisely the same manner as it is observed at Jerusalem. In very many other provinces likewise, many practices vary according to differences of places and names; yet the Church’s [Col. 1345D] Catholic peace and unity has never been abandoned on that account. Stephen has now dared to do this, breaking the peace with you which his predecessors always preserved with you.”

We offer these observations concerning Cyprian as a supplementary matter for the learned to investigate and confirm—or, if they prefer, even to attack. However the matter may stand, let that which is universally asserted by the French always remain immovable and unshaken: namely, that Cyprian referred this entire controversy concerning the baptism of heretics to mere discipline.

# CHAPTER II

## ARGUMENTS ARE ADDUCED BY WHICH IT IS DEMONSTRATED THAT ST. CYPRIAN KNEW WELL THAT THE CUSTOM DEFENDED BY ST. STEPHEN, THE ROMAN PONTIFF, WAS AT THAT TIME THE UNIVERSAL CUSTOM OF THE CHURCH AND HAD BEEN OBSERVED BY ALL BISHOPS FROM ANTIQUITY

[Col. 1345D]

[Col. 1346A] 1. The custom of the Church was opposed to Cyprian when he practiced rebaptism: according to Cyprian himself, heretics coming to the Church were received by this custom without a new Baptism. The holy Doctor never denies this custom of the Church; he always acknowledges it. He contends only that it must be subjected to reason, that it ought not to possess prescriptive force, and that it must be abandoned as an ancient error. He therefore was not ignorant that it opposed him.

> “In vain,” Cyprian said when writing to Jubaianus, “do certain persons who are defeated by reason oppose custom to us, [Col. 1346B] as though custom were greater than truth. . . . Yet one must not always continue to err merely because an error was once committed.”

And in his letter to Quintus:

> “No prescriptive claim should be based upon custom; rather, the issue must be decided by reason.”

He is speaking of the custom of not rebaptizing heretics.

And in his letter to Pompeius:

> “Custom without truth is merely the antiquity of error; therefore, abandoning error, let us follow truth.”

Nor may you say that St. Cyprian is speaking there about the custom of some particular church—namely, the Roman Church or some other—which he readily admitted opposed him, but not about the custom of the universal Church.

1. Cyprian acknowledges the existence of the very custom which was raised against him. But the custom raised against him was not peculiar to certain churches, [Col. 1346C] but that of the universal Church. Listen to that vigorous defender of the Church’s traditions, the anonymous bishop already cited, who sharply rebuked Cyprian:

> “In this kind of question”—he says in the treatise beginning with the words *That Baptism Ought Not to Be Repeated*, etc.—“concerning the baptism of heretics, no controversy or dispute whatever could have arisen if each of us, content with the venerable authority of all the churches, had not desired to innovate.”

He does not reproach Cyprian for refusing to obey the authority of some particular church—namely, Rome or another—but for refusing “to be content with the venerable authority of all the churches.”

Listen also to St. Stephen, the Roman Pontiff, in his celebrated rescript:

> “If anyone comes to us from any heresy whatsoever, let nothing be innovated beyond what has been handed down.”

He opposed to Cyprian not merely a Roman tradition, nor one peculiar to certain churches, but an unqualified and consequently universal tradition.

“St. Stephen,” says the defender of the *Declaration of the French Clergy* of 1682, commonly identified as Bossuet, Bishop of Meaux, [Col. 1346D] “pressed the universal custom.”

> **Note:** [Col. 1346D] In *Defense of the Declaration of the French Clergy*, part II, book IV, chapter 7.

“St. Stephen,” says Habert, a doctor of the Sorbonne, “opposed to St. Cyprian the Church’s tradition and custom: ‘If anyone,’ he says, etc.”

> **Note:** [Col. 1346D] In the *Treatise on the Sacraments*, chapter 14, p. 89, Paris edition, 1718.

“Pope Stephen,” says Grandin, doctor and professor of the Sorbonne, “opposed the Church’s tradition [Col. 1347A] to the Africans.”

> **Note:** [Col. 1346D] *Treatise on the Sacraments*, question 3, article 1, section 4, point 2, p. 31, Paris edition, 1710.

“Pope St. Stephen,” says Henry of St. Ignatius, “bore witness concerning the tradition of the entire Church when, in this cause, he wrote to St. Cyprian: ‘Let nothing be innovated except what has been handed down.’”

> **Note:** [Col. 1347D] *Treatise on the Sacraments*, vol. III, p. 12, Liège edition, 1709.

I omit the other French theologians who everywhere bear the same witness concerning Stephen.

2. St. Cyprian opposes only truth to the custom raised against him.
