But if the holy Doctor had thought that this custom was not universal but peculiar only to certain churches, he assuredly would have opposed to it not only the truth, which he believed stood on his own side, but also the custom of other churches favorable to him. He would therefore have declared that his adversaries acted both against truth and against custom. This reasoning is not ours, [Col. 1347B] but Augustine’s:

> “Why,” he asks, “did so many of Cyprian’s colleagues say in the council that reason and truth must be preferred to custom, instead of saying that those who wished to act otherwise were acting both against truth and against custom?”

> **Note:** [Col. 1347D] Book III, *On Baptism*, chapter XII.

3. How could Cyprian have thought that only the custom of the Roman Church, or even of some other church, opposed him—Cyprian, I say, who acknowledged that the custom of the African Church itself was contrary to him? For St. Cyprian and the others in Africa who practiced rebaptism gloried in having abandoned the custom of the African Church, as Firmilian testifies in his letter to Cyprian:

> “As for refuting the custom which they seem to oppose to truth, who is so foolish as to prefer custom to truth? Or who, once he has seen the light, does not abandon darkness? Unless, perhaps, even the Jews are helped in some way by their most ancient custom when Christ—that is, Truth—comes, because, abandoning the new way of truth, they have remained in their antiquity. This, indeed, you Africans can say against Stephen: having recognized the truth, you have abandoned the error of custom.”

Thus, says the illustrious de Saléon, Bishop of Rodez, Cyprian and the other Africans who practiced rebaptism plainly acknowledged that they had changed the ancient custom.

> **Note:** [Col. 1347D] *Pastoral Instruction on the Authority of the Church’s Decisions*, already cited, part I, p. 210.

But, you will object, St. Cyprian clearly affirms in his letters to Quintus and Jubaianus that Agrippinus and several other African bishops had long before decreed that those baptized by heretics should be baptized again upon returning to the Church, and that from that time many thousands of heretics had been received in the African provinces according to this decree. [Col. 1347D] What follows from this? That Cyprian therefore did not find the custom of Africa contrary to him? That after Agrippinus the custom of rebaptizing heretics prevailed in Africa? Not at all.

The cited words of Cyprian do indeed prove that Agrippinus and several African bishops introduced rebaptism into their own churches, and that after Agrippinus some bishops followed his position and practice. [Col. 1348A] But they by no means demonstrate that the majority, or all, of the African bishops favored rebaptism after Agrippinus. Augustine himself so interprets the cited text of Cyprian that it by no means prevents the custom of not rebaptizing from having prevailed in Africa from Agrippinus’ time even down to Cyprian:

> “But how Cyprian can say, ‘And from that time down to the present day, so many thousands of heretics converted to the Church in our provinces did not scorn or hesitate—indeed, they reasonably and gladly embraced—the prospect of obtaining the grace of the vital and saving Baptismal washing,’ I do not see, unless perhaps by ‘from that time down to the present day’ he means that no controversy involving the excommunication of any of those who had been [Col. 1348B] baptized in the Church since the Council of Agrippinus arose. But if, from Agrippinus down to Cyprian, the custom persisted of baptizing those who came from the heretics, why were councils on this matter held by Cyprian? Why does he tell Jubaianus that he was not doing something new or sudden, but something established by Agrippinus? Why would Jubaianus be disturbed by its novelty? Why would he have needed to be reassured by the authority of Agrippinus, if the Church had maintained this practice from Agrippinus down to Cyprian?”

And in chapter 2 of the same book, he testifies that several of those bishops who, with Agrippinus, had changed the former custom of not rebaptizing returned to it, so that after Agrippinus the Church’s ancient custom flourished everywhere in Africa.

From this it is evident that the assertion of Firmilian and Augustine [Col. 1348C] that Cyprian abandoned the custom of Africa is not contradicted by Cyprian’s affirmation that, from Agrippinus down to his own time, many thousands of heretics had been received in Africa through repeated Baptism. Both statements are true. Cyprian abandoned the custom of Africa because he abandoned the custom observed by the majority of African prelates; and many thousands of heretics were received in Africa through repeated Baptism from Agrippinus down to Cyprian because, although the majority of African prelates retained the Roman custom, some nevertheless preferred to follow Agrippinus’ decree, and by these bishops many thousands of heretics were received through repeated Baptism.

This reconciliation should be accepted all the more favorably because otherwise it would have to be said both that Cyprian [Col. 1348D] contradicted himself and that Augustine related falsehoods.

1. Cyprian would contradict himself because, on the hypothesis in question, he would maintain in his letter to Jubaianus that the custom of Africa after Agrippinus supported his opinion, while in his letter to Firmilian he would affirm that he was abandoning the custom of Africa.

2. Augustine would have related falsehoods when he testified so often and so confidently that the African custom—even during the period between Agrippinus and Cyprian—was contrary to rebaptism.

Father Gervasius, in the *Life of St. Cyprian* which he published in French, book V, number V, p. 381, was not ashamed to babble this about Augustine. But who can patiently endure so great a Doctor [Col. 1349A]—more thoroughly versed than anyone in this entire controversy over rebaptism—being repeatedly portrayed by this author as deceived, wandering from the truth, foisting falsehoods upon his readers, and badly interpreting Cyprian?

> **Note:** [Col. 1349D] P. 381 through p. 386, and elsewhere.

“To boast of such things,” Augustine still speaks although dead, “what is it but to rave?”

Perhaps, you will say, our critic was pressed by arguments of such force that not even the most willing defender could excuse Augustine from these errors. Learn the rest from what follows.

“It is not surprising,” says Gervasius, “that Augustine was ignorant of the number of Eastern bishops who defended Cyprian’s position, since he did not even know the number of Africans; for he counts seventy bishops, and no more, in Africa, although eighty-seven are enumerated in a single council.”

[Col. 1349B] Here he presents Augustine to us as ignorant of the number of African bishops who practiced rebaptism, and proves that alleged ignorance by this argument: the holy Doctor, he says, counts no more than seventy bishops in Africa who practiced rebaptism. This is a black falsehood, all the more intolerable because it was both knowingly uttered and fabricated to dishonor so great a Doctor of the Church. Here are Augustine’s words in *Against Cresconius*, book III, chapter III:

> “Accordingly, if it is to be believed at all that fifty Eastern bishops held the same view as seventy Africans—or even somewhat more—against so many thousands of bishops, etc.”

Do these words, “seventy Africans, or even somewhat more,” mean “seventy Africans and no more,” as the author so confidently affirms?

Hear Augustine again:

> “It seemed right,” he says in book I of *On Baptism*, chapter 18, “to Cyprian and nearly eighty of his fellow bishops of the African churches [Col. 1349C] that every person who had been baptized outside the communion of the Catholic Church ought to be baptized again when coming to the Church.”

Does he here, too, count only seventy bishops as supporting Cyprian?

“We have seen,” says Augustine’s critic, “that eighty-seven African bishops attended even one council of Cyprian, a fact unknown to Augustine.” Yet, on your own testimony, wretched Aristarchus, the holy Doctor reports and examines the individual judgments of these eighty-seven bishops in books VI and VII of *On Baptism*. How, then, could Augustine have been unaware that eighty-seven African bishops attended this council of Cyprian?

If, therefore, he did not associate all of them with Cyprian in his error, he acted as he did because, in accordance with his singular fairness [Col. 1349D] and justice, he was unwilling to accuse of error the Catholic judgments of some of those bishops. Our author would have done better to imitate this than to breathe forth unworthy abuse against Augustine.

These are the arguments by which Father Gervasius is driven to reveal Augustine’s ignorance—or, more truly, to reveal his own with perfect clarity. But would that Augustine alone had felt this writer’s viperous tooth! Finally, if Gervasius scorned Augustine’s authority when it opposed him, did he at least revere it when it sometimes favored him? Yet, to say nothing of others, how many insulting, false, and impious things did he not spew against Stephen, the Supreme Pontiff [Col. 1350A] and most holy martyr! One could scarcely find even among the Calvinists anyone who attacked the Pontiff more harshly or bitterly.

Stephen, if Gervasius himself is to be believed, “behaved utterly disgracefully toward Cyprian.” Stephen “pompously affects arrogance and dominion.” Stephen acts “the commander and tyrant,” guilty of inhumanity, harassment, and tyranny. Stephen cares nothing for sundering the unity of the Church; he judges and condemns Cyprian without hearing him. Stephen not only denied peace, communion, and hospitality to Cyprian’s episcopal legates—while branding Cyprian himself a false Christ, false apostle, deceitful man, and traitor—but also commanded that these be denied them by everyone and everywhere. Stephen indeed makes a show of zeal, but a zeal capable only of indiscriminately laying everything waste; this zeal of Stephen moved the Emperor cruelly to persecute the Church. [Col. 1350B] Stephen teaches in his rescript not merely one or two, but three errors contrary to the Catholic faith. Finally, as though all this were by no means sufficient for Stephen’s misdeeds, Gervasius declares that he speaks of Stephen with all possible moderation and restraint.

O heavens, what things do I see! A Frenchman says these things? A Catholic? A priest of God? A son? These things about his Father? About the Supreme Pontiff? About the champion of tradition? About the most holy Martyr? O licentious writing—yet, good heavens, unavenged and unpunished! “O monstrosity, not, as someone says, to be carried away to the farthest lands, but rather, if it were possible, to be driven beyond every heaven and all the earth.” [Note: [Col. 1350C] Augustine, *Against Cresconius*, book III, ch. 5.] Will these things be read? Will they be believed? Will they be handed down to posterity? [Col. 1350C] Words fail, the mind falters, the spirit recoils. Let us pass to matters calm, true, humane, devout, and Catholic. Let us return to our subject. “For these evils call more for prolonged groans than for prolonged books.” Augustine, Letter XXII.

## II

An anonymous bishop contemporary with Cyprian, already commended more than once, relates three things about Cyprian [Note: [Col. 1350C] It is readily apparent that Cyprian, although his name is suppressed, is the principal target of this author. First, he represents his adversary to us as one who writes ornamentally and with studied composition: “Although this does not greatly injure that faith of ours, [you write] ornamentally and [Col. 1350D] with studied composition, whereas I do not write as you do.” Yet no African other than Cyprian is found at that time to have written ornamentally and with studied composition in favor of rebaptism. Secondly, he refutes an adversary who had cited several scriptural texts in favor of his opinion: “To these points,” he says, “perhaps you, who are introducing something new, will immediately answer, as is your custom, that the Lord said in the Gospel: ‘Unless someone is born anew.’” And below: “Nor should you think that what the Lord said—‘Go, teach the nations’—is contrary to this treatise.” And shortly afterward: “But to this you will object, as is your custom, by setting against us the fact that, when the disciples were baptized, they were baptized fully and rightly,” etc. Now, since those texts are found to have been advanced at that time by Cyprian alone, Cyprian was the adversary whom the author was censuring. Among the French, Tillemont, *Ecclesiastical History*, vol. IV, p. 152; the *Defender of the Declaration of the French Clergy of 1682*, part II, book XIV, p. 266; and others hold the same opinion.], and about his followers, in the treatise that begins with the words, “That [they] ought not again,” etc. These things show most plainly that the holy Doctor knew perfectly well that the practice of not rebaptizing heretics was at that [Col. 1351A] time the universal practice of the Church. For he relates:

1. Cyprian and his adherents had put forward a novel opinion concerning the rebaptism of heretics, because they were not content with the venerable authority of all the churches, with which, however, they ought to have been content out of the requisite humility:

> “In this kind of question”—namely, concerning the rebaptism of heretics—he says, “no controversy or dispute whatever could have arisen if each one of us, content with the venerable authority of all the churches and with the requisite humility, had not desired to innovate.”

2. He reproves Cyprian for boasting that he had corrected the faults and errors of all the churches:

> “Let him boast,” he says, “among those most like and equal to himself that he has corrected the errors and faults of all the churches.”

3. He presents Cyprian and Cyprian’s followers as [Col. 1351B] bishops who did not shrink from exposing the shame of Mother Church, if they thought there was any such shame in this question of Baptism:

> “It is,” he says, “monstrous in itself for bishops to entertain such scandals and, with excessive irreverence, not to shrink from exposing the shame of Mother Church, if they think there is any in this matter.”

Now, one who “was not content with the venerable authority of all the churches” refused to obey not only Stephen’s authority but also the authority of all the churches. Cyprian therefore knew that not only Stephen but the other churches everywhere were opposed to his opinion and practice. One who “boasted that he had corrected the errors of them all” certainly was not unaware that all the churches disagreed with him. One who “did not shrink from exposing the shame of Mother Church” [Col. 1351C] openly shows that Mother Church opposed the opinion which he regarded as true.

## III

St. Jerome, in the *Dialogue Against the Luciferians*, vol. IV, part 2, p. 305, has the following:

> “The Church has always accepted Baptism from heretics. . . . But if anyone should think it ought to be denied that heretics were always received by our forefathers, let him read the letters of blessed Cyprian, in which he assails Stephen, bishop of the city of Rome, and the error of long-established custom.”

Two things here show that, in St. Jerome’s mind, St. Cyprian was not unaware that the Church’s custom was contrary to his opinion and practice.

1. St. Jerome infers from Cyprian’s letters, and proves, that the practice of not rebaptizing heretics was the perpetual custom of the Church and of our forefathers. In St. Jerome’s understanding, [Col. 1351D] therefore, St. Cyprian disclosed in his letters this perpetual custom of the Church and of our forefathers. He was therefore not unaware of this custom of the Church that stood opposed to him.

2. According to Jerome, Cyprian charged not only Stephen but also the Church’s custom with error. He therefore knew that not only Stephen but the Church’s custom opposed him.

You will perhaps reply that, according to Jerome, Cyprian did indeed assail a custom, but not the universal custom of the Church. Yet if Jerome were not speaking of the universal custom of the Church, he would by no means prove his point. For from the fact that Cyprian assailed the long-established custom [Col. 1352A] of not rebaptizing heretics, Jerome intends to prove that heretics were always received by the Church and by our forefathers without Baptism. Now, from the fact that Cyprian had assailed this custom as peculiar to certain persons, he would indeed prove that heretics had always been received by some persons without repeated Baptism; but he would by no means prove that they had always been received in this manner, by our forefathers without qualification, and by the Church. Therefore, when St. Jerome says that Cyprian assailed the custom, he has in view the universal custom of the Church.

## IV

St. Augustine—to whom credence must be given in this matter, if to anyone—affirms a hundred times that St. Cyprian knew perfectly well that the custom of the universal Church opposed his practice of rebaptism.

> “That most weighty man, Cyprian,” he says in book II of *On Baptism*, [Col. 1352B] ch. 8, “was unwilling to yield to the truthful custom . . . but, troubled in so obscure a question and seeing everywhere the universal and firmly established custom”—

namely, the custom of not rebaptizing heretics. What could be clearer? Cyprian saw everywhere the universal and firmly established custom of not rebaptizing heretics. And in chapter 9:

> “That this”—Stephen, Roman Pontiff’s custom—“was the custom of the Church is sufficiently shown by the words of blessed Cyprian himself.”

After citing those words, he continues:

> “There he certainly shows sufficiently what was customary, even though he wished it not to be done. . . . Cyprian openly indicates that there was another custom of the Church; and in the council itself”—the Third Council of Carthage—“some of the opinions declare unequivocally that they decreed, contrary to the custom of the Church, what they thought ought to be decreed.”

What could be more explicit? [Col. 1352C] “The words of blessed Cyprian himself sufficiently show” that the custom urged by Stephen was the custom of the Church. Cyprian “sufficiently shows” what was customary, even though he wished it not to be done—that is, that the Church’s custom opposed his opinion. Cyprian “openly indicates” that there was another custom of the Church. And some of the Africans at the Third Council of Carthage “declare unequivocally” that, contrary to the custom of the Church, they had decreed that heretics were to be rebaptized. Were Cyprian and the African prelates therefore unaware that the custom of the Church opposed them?

Let St. Augustine be heard again in book IV of *On Baptism*, ch. 6:

> “Cyprian himself found this custom”—of not rebaptizing heretics—“so firmly established already that, when a man endowed with such knowledge sought an authority [Col. 1352D] to follow in changing it, he found only that, in Africa alone, a council of Agrippinus had been held a few years before him. And when he saw that this did not suffice for him against the custom of the whole world, he seized upon these arguments.”

Cyprian saw, according to this witness—to whom Cyprian’s words and thought were better known than to certain recent theologians—that the authority of Agrippinus, which he followed in rebaptizing heretics, did not suffice for him against “the custom of the whole world.” He therefore certainly knew that the custom of the whole world was opposed to the rebaptism of heretics.

Again, Augustine in book VI of *On Baptism*, ch. 35:

> “If it was the custom,” he says, “as this opinion bears witness, that heretics coming to the Church were received with the Baptism [Col. 1353A] they possessed, why do they accuse the whole world because they are received in this way?”

That is, the bishops of the Third Council of Carthage, among whom was Cyprian. Now, those who accuse the whole world because heretics were received without repeated Baptism are certainly not unaware that the whole world receives heretics in this way.

And in book VII, ch. 2:

> “That it was also customary for them to be received in this way”—heretics without repeated Baptism—“Cyprian himself manifests in many places, as do several bishops at this council”—the Third Council of Carthage—“from which it appears that, if heretics do not possess Baptism, the Church of Christ in those times was filled with transgressors who, supporting them, received them in this way.”

From what does the holy Doctor prove that even in Cyprian’s age the custom prevailed in the Church of receiving heretics without a new Baptism? [Col. 1353B] From holy Cyprian himself, as you see, who manifests it in many places. The bishop of Carthage was therefore not unaware that this was the custom of the Church.

Do not, I beg you, tire of hearing Augustine still further:

> “That such was the custom of the Church”—namely, not to rebaptize heretics—“those very men who constitute this Third Council of Carthage frequently recall,”

he says in book VII of *On Baptism*, ch. 25. Cyprian therefore knew, and the African bishops who attended this council knew, that such was the custom not only of Stephen but also of the Church.

And in Letter 93 to Vincentius the Rogatist, ch. 10:

> “That Cyprian thought otherwise than the form and custom of the Church prescribed is found not in the canonical writings but in his own letters and those of the council.” [Col. 1353C]

If it is found in Cyprian’s letters that he thought otherwise concerning Baptism than the custom of the Church prescribed, Cyprian certainly shows in his letters that the custom of the Church differed from his opinion.

What more could be desired from Augustine in support of our assertion? According to Augustine, St. Cyprian “sufficiently shows, openly indicates, unequivocally declares, frequently recalls, and manifests in many places that it was the custom not only of Stephen but also of the Church” that heretics coming to the Church were received with the Baptism they already possessed. Cyprian “accused” not only Stephen but “the whole world” because heretics were received in this way. Cyprian “saw” that he was acting “against the custom of the whole world.” Cyprian [Col. 1353D] “saw everywhere the universal and firmly established custom” of not rebaptizing heretics. These statements—without ambiguity or circumlocution, enveloped in no darkness, clear, explicit, and repeated a hundred times—firmly and evidently show that Cyprian knew beyond doubt that the custom of not rebaptizing heretics was at that time the custom “of the universal Church,” the custom “of the whole world,” “the custom of the entire world,” which “he saw everywhere.”

## V

That the universal custom of the Church concerning the non-rebaptism of heretics was called into question neither by Cyprian nor by his followers is also made clear by the state of the controversy conducted between Cyprian and others. The anonymous bishop contemporary with Cyprian, already commended several times, clearly explains it in these words: [Col. 1354A]

> “I perceive that it has been asked among the brethren what ought preferably to be observed in the case of those who, though baptized in heresy in the name of our Lord God Jesus Christ, subsequently departed from it and, humbly hastening to the Church of God, did penance with their whole hearts and, now at last understanding the condemnation of their error, implored from her the aid of salvation: whether, in accordance with the most ancient custom and ecclesiastical tradition, after that Baptism of the Lord which they had received outside, though in the name of Jesus Christ, it would suffice merely for the bishop to lay a hand upon them so that they might receive the Holy Spirit, and whether this laying on of a hand would furnish them with a renewed and completed sign of faith; or whether a repeated [Col. 1354B] Baptism would also be necessary for them, on the ground that they would possess nothing unless they had also obtained this anew, just as if they had never been baptized in the name of Jesus Christ. And so it was being reported that certain writings or replies had been produced concerning this new question, in which each party strove with the greatest zeal to destroy the position of the other.”

Here is the state of the controversy: the question is whether the most ancient custom and tradition of the Church should preferably be observed, by which heretics coming to the Church were received with the Baptism that they had received outside; or whether Baptism was still necessary for them because they would possess nothing if they did not receive it.

Now, this statement of the question manifestly presupposes that everyone freely admitted the existence of this most ancient custom of the Church regarding the [Col. 1354C] non-rebaptism of heretics, since the sole question concerning it is whether it ought or ought not to be observed. Hence the cited author, who devotes himself entirely to refuting Cyprian’s arguments, never complains that Cyprian called the very existence of this custom of the Church into doubt. Rather, he repeatedly reproaches him, as we saw above, because he refused to be “content with the venerable authority of all the churches,” and because he did not condemn the rebaptism of heretics, though he judged it contrary to the most solemn observance of all venerable saints and faithful persons:

> “In this kind of question”—concerning the rebaptism of heretics—he says, “it seems to me that no controversy or dispute whatever could have arisen if each one of us, content with the venerable [Col. 1354D] authority of all the churches and with the requisite humility, had not desired to innovate. For everything that is doubtful and ambiguous and is established by differing opinions of prudent and faithful men must certainly be condemned if it is judged contrary to the ancient, memorable, and most solemn observance of all venerable saints and faithful persons.”

He reproaches Cyprian for refusing to acquiesce in the authority of so many years and so many churches; for rising up against the ecclesiastical custom of so many centuries:

> “It is useful,” he says, “to believe through this custom and, with good reason, to acquiesce in the authority of so many years and so many churches, since it is the greatest disadvantage and injury to most holy Mother Church to rise up now for the first time, and without reason, against ancient [Col. 1355A] decisions after the course of so many centuries.”

From all this it is evident that at that time none of those who rebaptized doubted this custom of the Church concerning the non-rebaptism of heretics. Hence the Venerable Bede asserted that Cyprian, with his Africans, wished to determine that heretics were to be rebaptized, not against the practice of Stephen or of another individual, but “against the custom of the Church.” [Note: [Col. 1355D] In *Book of Several Questions*, vol. VII, p. 289.]

## VI

Finally, none of the ancients ever indicated, even once and obscurely, that Cyprian was unaware of this custom of the Church. Our adversaries know this well, for in order to establish Cyprian’s alleged ignorance they have thus far been unable to produce any testimony from antiquity. Certainly we should never have heard that Cyprian was ignorant of this custom, had it not pleased certain recent [Col. 1355B] writers of our age to appear the inventors of a new opinion rather than to profess themselves followers of the ancient faith of so many centuries. What, then? Shall we set aside and despise the many and weighty testimonies that we have thus far drawn from earliest antiquity, and especially from Augustine; likewise reject the common judgment of French writers and theologians on this matter; and subscribe to the views of these few, scarcely born opinions, destitute even of all plausibility? Far be it from us, if we are human beings, if we possess any reason at all, if we possess human sense.

Indeed, I cannot sufficiently marvel that these recent writers could have fabricated and marketed such ignorance on Cyprian’s part. For none of them has portrayed Cyprian’s profound learning in ecclesiastical matters in more vivid [Col. 1355C] colors or displayed it with greater noise and effort. To exalt it, you would say that they had exhausted virtually all the monuments of Supreme Pontiffs, councils, the holy Fathers, historians, and poets; sacred and profane materials, sought everywhere, seized upon, and cited. After so many labors undertaken to illustrate and manifest Cyprian’s learning, who would believe it? They declare Cyprian ignorant of that custom of the Church which, by their own admission, embraced a principal dogma of our faith. Here is the unexpected conclusion of so many encomiums of Cyprian’s learning: Cyprian was ignorant of the custom of the Church that concerned a principal article of our faith. Thus, at their pleasure, Cyprian is learned and ignorant, keen-sighted and dull: keen-sighted enough to recognize the few bishops who favored him, [Col. 1355D] but exceedingly dull when it came to recognizing the countless bishops opposed to him. Cyprian was supplied with abundant time to seek out his followers; yet the decade during which he governed the Church of Carthage could not suffice him to discover his adversaries. Thus these men cast empty darkness over transparent matters, surely deserving to experience every absurdity, even the most extreme. Let their nursery tales, therefore, now yield to our arguments, and let all sensible people say with truthful lips that Cyprian knew perfectly well that the custom defended by Stephen, the Roman Pontiff, of not rebaptizing heretics [Col. 1356A] was at that time the universal custom of the Church—or, to use Augustine’s words, “that Cyprian saw this custom everywhere and as universal.”

Finally, Cyprian also knew that this custom had been observed by all bishops in ancient times, that is, before Agrippinus. For one who judged Agrippinus to have been the first father of rebaptism necessarily acknowledged that no bishop before Agrippinus had rebaptized, and consequently that the custom urged by Stephen, the Roman Pontiff, had once been observed by all bishops. Now, as we proved above, St. Cyprian judged Agrippinus to have been the first father of rebaptism.

And indeed, Augustine repeatedly testifies that Cyprian knew this ancient custom of the universal Church: [Col. 1356B]

> “Nevertheless,” he says in book III of *On Baptism*, ch. 5, “Cyprian himself sufficiently shows what the custom of the Church was, when he says that in the past those coming from heresy to the Church were admitted without Baptism.”

And in book V, ch. 17:

> “It seemed to Cyprian that those coming from heretics ought to be received differently from the way in which they had been received in the past, as he himself testifies, or are received now.”

And in chapter 19:

> “And therefore, if this was the ancient custom, that those coming from heretics were received in the same Baptism of Christ which they had received outside—a fact which not even those who argued against it,” Cyprian and others, “could deny.”

And in Letter 93 to Vincentius the Rogatist, ch. 10:

> “For if, as you suppose, the Church perished by sharing the Sacraments with sinners, the entire Church that had already existed throughout the world had perished earlier, when, as Cyprian says, they were admitted into her without Baptism; and thus Cyprian himself would have had no Church in which to be born.” [Col. 1356C]

Moreover, as we saw above, Cyprian acknowledged and confessed the custom of the Church that was set against him. But not only the custom then prevailing, but also the past and ancient custom of the Church was set against Cyprian, as is clear from the texts cited and from these words of Cyprian writing to Jubaianus: [Col. 1356D]

> “But someone says: ‘What, then, will become of those who in the past came from heresy to the Church and were admitted without Baptism?’ The Lord is able in his mercy to grant pardon and not to separate from the gifts of his Church those who were admitted to the Church in simplicity and have fallen asleep in the Church. Nevertheless, because an error was once committed, it does not follow that error must always be committed.”

From all this it is established that St. Cyprian knew perfectly well that the custom of not rebaptizing heretics was the custom of the Church both in his own time and in times past; that the holy Doctor was by no means unaware that it was observed at that time by Stephen, the Roman Pontiff, and by far the greater part of the bishops; and that in ancient times, that is, before Agrippinus, it had been observed by all bishops.

[Col. 1357]

# TWO DISSERTATIONS ON FIRMILIAN

**By Brother Marcellinus Molkenbuhr, O.S.F. of the Stricter Observance, Jubilee Lector of Sacred Theology**

[Note: [Col. 1357B] The most illustrious Brother Marcellinus Molkenbuhr, of the Order of St. Francis of the Stricter Observance, Jubilee Lector of Sacred Theology, and current Minister of the Saxon Province of the Holy Cross, published two dissertations at Münster in Westphalia in 1790, in quarto, with the following title: *Two Dissertations: I. On the Letter of St. Firmilian, Bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, to St. Stephen, and on His Other Works; II. On the Year in Which Firmilian Died, or in Which Paul of Samosata Was Condemned at the Synod of Antioch.* On the following page he appended to the title these words of St. Augustine from Letter 92 to Vincentius the Rogatist: “Although there are some who contend that Cyprian did not hold this opinion at all, but that it was fabricated under his name by presumptuous liars.” [Col. 1357C] The purpose of the distinguished author in the first dissertation is, after the futile efforts of Christian Lupus and Raymond Missorius, once again to render plausible the claim “that St. Firmilian’s Letter to Cyprian”—“Letter to Stephen” is more probably a typographical error, for all antiquity is ignorant of such a letter—“is not genuine, but was falsely attributed to him by an African Donatist in the fifth century, indeed after Augustine’s time.” —LUMPER.]

# PREFACE

[Col. 1357A] After, in the year 1788, I had published two dissertations on the Roman and Antiochene Chairs of Peter and on the first successors of St. Peter, I did not cease, in the broken intervals of leisure permitted by my duties, to examine more diligently the works of the ancient holy Fathers and historians, to weigh them more critically and attentively, and to inquire further whether I myself might perhaps discover something solid contrary to my asserted opinion, “that Peter never sat at Antioch” [Note: [Col. 1357C] Let the opinion that this author professes concerning St. Peter’s Antiochene episcopate remain entirely his own; neither other Catholic writers nor we ourselves have any intention of adhering to it. —EDS.], prepared, if I had erred, to be the first publicly to retract my judgment.

But so far am I from having discovered anything up to this point contrary to my assertions that, rather, I have been daily confirmed more and more [Col. 1357B] in my former opinions, including those concerning Cephas, fasts, and abstinences. Indeed, as I examined more ancient books further, I have now arrived—contrary to my opinion and expectation—at the conclusion that [Col. 1358A] several works ascribed to ancient authors are, respectively, spurious, mutilated, or interpolated. These are works from which exceedingly grave and intricate controversies have arisen, not only in dogmatic theology but also in ecclesiastical history and chronology, as well as in patrology, especially that of the first four centuries. I cannot refrain from making my thoughts on so difficult a matter public.

I begin with the letter ascribed to Firmilian, which, of all those extant among the Cyprianic letters, is the most famous. In the near future I shall also subject to critical examination the canonical letters of St. Basil the Great and his other works, and the Councils of Elvira, Ancyra, Neocaesarea, Gangra, and Laodicea. Finally, I shall also show [Col. 1358B] that the ecclesiastical history of Eusebius of Caesarea has been interpolated on the matter of rebaptism and the most famous controversy between Pope St. Stephen and St. Firmilian, and likewise on the celebration of Easter in the controversy between Pope St. Victor and Polycrates and Irenaeus. Elsewhere I have already indicated that Eusebius’s book entitled *The Life of Constantine the Great* was mutilated. [Note: [Col. 1358C] *Six Assertions on Fasts and Abstinences against the Theologian of Mainz*, Paderborn, 1785, §39; or *Sechs Streitsätze*, expanded edition, Paderborn, 1786, §39.] I shall also mention the orthodoxy of St. Dionysius of Alexandria, and show that he never favored the rebaptizers; moreover, that in this matter St. Jerome’s catalogue *On Illustrious Men* was badly corrupted. Concerning the Councils of Synnada and Iconium, if my duties permit, I shall speak in due course, when I also examine the letters of St. Cyprian; consequently, I shall also treat the African councils said to have been celebrated in the matter of rebaptism against the definition of Pope St. Stephen, [Col. 1358C] and the remaining matters: a very broad field, surrounded and sown everywhere with thorns.

For the present I shall treat only the Letter of St. Firmilian [Note: [Col. 1358C] The title “Saint,” given again and again in these dissertations to the bishop of Caesarea, was indeed conceded to him by the Greek Church, but consistently denied him by the Roman Church. —EDS.], whose encomium as a holy Father I judge must be set forth here first.

## II

[Col. 1359A] Around the middle of the third century, two leading bishops shone forth in the Greek Church: St. Dionysius of Alexandria in Egypt, and St. Firmilian of Caesarea in Cappadocia. With the greatest vigor and in concert they fought against the heresies of Novatus, the Roman presbyter expelled from the Church by Pope St. Cornelius, and of Paul of Samosata, bishop of Antioch. [Note: [Col. 1359D] Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VI from ch. 43, and book VII from ch. 1 to ch. 30.] I shall not recount here the encomiums of the holy and great Dionysius of Alexandria.

Firmilian is venerated as a saint in the Greek Church [Note: [Col. 1359D] See Natalis Alexander on the third century, or the Greek Martyrology for October 27, or Tillemont.], and not undeservedly. For the very great Third Synod of Antioch [Note: [Col. 1359D] Eusebius, who completed his history before the time of the Council of Nicaea, calls it very great and says that countless bishops assembled there. If Basil, deacon of Constantinople, and the others are to be believed, 180 Fathers attended. See Labbe, vol. III, under the Council of Ephesus, Paris edition of 1671, p. 425.], held against Paul of Samosata in the reign of the Emperor Aurelian, calls Firmilian—who had died by that time—“a man blessed in the Lord” in the letters sent to the Roman Pontiff and the bishop of Alexandria. [Col. 1359B] Furthermore—and this is greater—in order that the bishops assembled there in great number might impart greater authority to their decrees against Paul of Samosata, they appealed to the doctrine handed down by the Fathers. They cited only two men, both recently deceased: St. Dionysius of Alexandria and, especially, Firmilian. They add that the entire synod, before it was willing to pronounce judgment, summoned Firmilian from Cappadocia; that Firmilian intended to come to the synod; and that, while he was on the journey, the whole synod awaited his arrival. It was unwilling to render a final decision until it had heard Firmilian in person. But when Firmilian meanwhile died at Tarsus in Cilicia, the aforesaid synod then issued the decree by force of which Paul [Col. 1359C] of Samosata was separated from the entire Catholic Church under heaven. Nevertheless, the aforesaid Antiochene Fathers expressly add in their synodical letter to the Pope that, while Firmilian lived, they had him in agreement with them, reporting:

> “While he lived, Firmilian came twice to Antioch and condemned that man’s”—Paul of Samosata’s—“foreign doctrines, as we who were present know and testify, and as many others know.”

It should be observed that they maintain a profound silence concerning any books or letters written by St. Firmilian. How great was Firmilian’s authority at that time in the Catholic Church! I shall call this Firmilian “Saint,” with the Greeks, both so that by this designation he may be distinguished more clearly from the [Col. 1359D] pseudo-Firmilian who will frequently appear in what follows, and because he is called a saint not only by Greeks but also by Latin writers such as Tillemont, etc. When St. Gregory of Nyssa wished to adorn St. Gregory Thaumaturgus with a surpassing encomium, he equated him in virtue [Col. 1360A] with our St. Firmilian, formerly the ornament of the Church of Caesarea.

## III

Now, the Greek Eusebius carefully records [Note: [Col. 1360D] Books VI and VII. Tillemont, drawing upon Eusebius, teaches in vol. IV, p. 2, that St. Firmilian, a Greek, was bishop from the year 231 at Caesarea, the metropolis of Cappadocia, and died near the end of 269. From Eusebius, book VII, ch. 30, however, it seems to me much more probable that Firmilian survived until the year 272; on this see below, no. 92.] that St. Firmilian flourished in the Greek Church from about the year 230 to the year 270, under Saints Pontian, Anterus, Fabian, Cornelius, Lucius, Stephen, Xystus, and Dionysius, Supreme Pontiffs of the Roman Church; that Firmilian, as a leading bishop of the East, attended three Antiochene councils—the first celebrated against Novatus and the other two against Paul of Samosata; that the subsequent Fourth Synod of Antioch, which was the third against the Samosatene, most urgently desired and eagerly awaited him; and that St. Firmilian was one of the two deceased Fathers to whose teaching, delivered either in writing or orally, respectively, the last and [Col. 1360B] greatest Antiochene synod appealed in the affair of Paul of Samosata. Yet although the same Eusebius carefully catalogued any noteworthy works or letters of all ecclesiastical writers, especially Greeks, he maintains the profoundest silence concerning whether St. Firmilian—whom he commended uniquely—ever left behind any written letter. Hence it should surely be concluded that St. Firmilian fought strenuously by word of mouth and in person, but did not dispute in writing concerning ecclesiastical matters.

This presumption is confirmed by the fact that St. Jerome nowhere numbers St. Firmilian among the ecclesiastical writers. Indeed, Firmilian does not even appear in St. Jerome’s catalogue *On Illustrious Men* as enlarged by subsequent authors.

## IV

[Col. 1360C] Nevertheless, in later centuries a certain famous letter was brought to light, purportedly from Firmilian, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, to St. Cyprian. Besides numerous absurdities to be unfolded in the course of this work, it chiefly defends the error of the rebaptizers. I confess: whoever composed this letter and wished falsely to attribute it to some great man so as to acquire authority could scarcely have selected from the third century a bishop greater than St. Firmilian. For that St. Dionysius of Alexandria, in no respect inferior to St. Firmilian, was most submissive to the Pope could at that time have been shown evidently from his writings and letters preserved in other churches. But no other written work of St. Firmilian was extant. [Note: [Col. 1360D] Some assert that Firmilian wrote books on the Holy Spirit and that these were seen by St. Basil the Great near the end of the fourth century. But on these see below, no. 89.] Therefore, if the famous letter which [Col. 1360D] we shall now examine is spurious, the impostor nevertheless acted prudently or cunningly in publishing it under Firmilian’s name, so that under this name it might obtain the greatest possible authority.

## V

This letter, therefore, must now be subjected above all others to a more exacting [Col. 1361A] critical examination, since it alone is extant under Firmilian’s name.

# OUTLINE OF THE TWO DISSERTATIONS ON FIRMILIAN

**Dissertation I.—Nos. 1, 2, 3.** Two rules of criticism from Dupin are set forth preliminarily.

**Proposition I.—Nos. 4–12.** The letter circulated under Firmilian’s name appears to have been fabricated by a Latin author.

**Proposition II.—Nos. 13–17.** At least St. Firmilian did not compose it.

**Nos. 18–77.** The letter itself is reviewed section by section and critically examined; under no. 41, the question whether Pope St. Stephen declared Baptism conferred under any formula to be valid. [Col. 1361B]

**Proposition III.—Nos. 78–87.** It is more probable that some African Donatist fabricated the said letter after the fourth century, or that some other heretic did so.

**Proposition IV.—Nos. 88–91.** St. Firmilian published no books in written form.

**Dissertation II.—** On the year of St. Firmilian’s death, in which Paul of Samosata was condemned at the celebrated Synod of Antioch, at which the term *homoousion* (of the same substance) is also said to have been rejected.

**No. 92.** Chronologists disagree.

**Proposition.—Nos. 93–100.** Those events did not occur before the year 272.

## FIRST DISSERTATION  
### On Firmilian’s Letter to St. Cyprian and His Other Works

[Col. 1361C] 1. Before proceeding to my own assertions, I set forth from Dupin [Note: [Col. 1361D] In the preface to his *New Library*. I have cited Dupin because that famous critic presents the letter with which we are concerned as genuine under the entry “Cyprian,” adding: “Cyprian could have hoped for no reply more glorious to himself than the one he received from Firmilian; for Firmilian openly condemns Pope Stephen’s action in sufficiently harsh words and praises Cyprian.”] only the following two rules concerning the question “whether any book is to be regarded as spurious”:

2. I. It is certain, and sufficient reason for doubting a work, that it was not cited by the ancients; consequently it must possess very authentic marks of antiquity if it is to be accepted by everyone. Conversely, when even the slightest conjectures establish the contrary in conjunction with the silence of the ancients, it must undoubtedly be regarded as spurious.

3. II. It often happens that, although each individual conjecture, considered separately, may not appear to carry great weight, nevertheless all of them taken together produce a certain moral certainty. The remaining rules of criticism will be applied in the course of the discussion.

## PROPOSITION I  
### It is more probable that the famous letter to St. Cyprian circulated under Firmilian’s name was composed not by a Greek, but by some obscure Latin impostor.

[Col. 1361D]

4. This is proved, first: This letter does not exist in the Greek language; rather, it was first brought to light only in Latin, long after the time of St. Firmilian. Therefore, anyone who asserts or believes that it was originally Greek violates the principle of sufficient reason, unless he supplies positive evidence proving that it once existed in Greek or adduces indications suggestive of a Greek origin. But no positive evidence can be produced pointing to a Greek birth for the letter in question. Therefore, this Latin offspring should not be asserted to have originated in Greece; [Col. 1362A] for it is not enough for a sound critic that the fabricator of the said letter placed Firmilian’s name above it, or represented himself as a bishop in Cappadocia among the Greeks. Otherwise we should be compelled to accept as genuine innumerable works that are certainly spurious. Accordingly, the aforesaid Latin letter must be regarded as Latin in origin until it is proved that it once existed in Greek. Furthermore, even if it were proved that it once existed in Greek, it would nevertheless have to be regarded as falsely attributed to St. Firmilian, as will be stated beginning at number 13. [Col. 1362B]

5. This is proved, second: Not only does it not suggest a Greek origin, but it contains expressions that indicate that its original language was Latin. For example, pseudo-Firmilian says: “Among us it necessarily occurs that the elders and superiors assemble together each year; in the church the elders by age preside.” A Catholic Greek author of the third century would instead have said, more aptly and precisely: “That the presbyters and bishops assemble together,” etc.; and a Latin translator would have had no reason to alter these words, which are Greek in origin. Moreover, no example occurs in Greek books of bishops among the Greeks in the third century being designated antonomastically as “superiors” (*praepositi*).

The distinguished Joseph Bingham, [Note: [Col. 1362C] Bingham, vol. I, bk. II, *Ecclesiastical Antiquities*, ch. 2, §§ 1 and 5.] a most celebrated writer of the Anglican Church, does indeed assert that bishops [Col. 1362C] were honored in the primitive Church with the title “superiors.” [Note: [Col. 1362C] Bingham likewise suggests at the cited place that bishops were called “presidents” (*praesides*) by the Latins; for Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 39, says: “Approved elders preside, having obtained this honor not by payment but by testimony,” etc. Yet by a similar argument I could prove that the bishops of Antioch were formerly called “governors”; for Eusebius, bk. III, [Col. 1362D] ch. 22, says: “Among those who governed the Church at Antioch, Evodius was the first and Ignatius the second.”] But, first, from the first three centuries he adduces no author except Cyprian alone, who was a Latin in Africa. Second, the letters Bingham adduces appear to me to have been falsely attributed to St. Cyprian.

The title “elders” occurs among Latin writers in Africa: in the third century, in Tertullian; [Note: [Col. 1362D] See the preceding note (3).] in the fourth century, in St. Optatus; [Note: [Col. 1362D] Optatus, bk. I, relates that Mensurius, bishop of Carthage, when he was compelled to leave his church during the persecution of Diocletian, entrusted the ornaments and vessels of the church to faithful elders. At the end of the works of St. Optatus there are letters in which we read: “All you bishops, presbyters, deacons, and elders know.” “Employ your fellow clerics and the elders of the people, men of the Church.” “To the clerics and elders of Cirta . . . greetings.” There, therefore, presbyters are distinguished from elders. To be sure, in Letter 13 of St. Jerome to Rusticus of Narbonne it is said: “The sixth rank, that of the elders, is given to the priests who are called presbyters, who govern the Church of God.” But Marianus Victorinus of Rieti already observed in the sixteenth century that this letter had been falsely ascribed to St. Jerome.] and in the fifth century, in St. Augustine. [Col. 1363A] [Note: [Col. 1363D] St. Augustine, Letter 137: “Greetings to the clergy, the elders, and the entire people of the Church of Hippo.” See Bingham, bk. I, ch. 19, § 19, where the leading men among the Donatists in the fifth century are called “superiors.”] Yet it is very obscure what class of ecclesiastical persons was denoted by “elders”; and more obscure still who those “superiors” and “elders” among the Greeks were who, in third-century Cappadocia, were necessarily required to meet every year to deliberate about ecclesiastical affairs.

6. I said at number 4 that it was composed by some obscure Latin impostor. I further judge that it was composed by a Latin African Anabaptist, or rebaptizer; my reasons will become apparent at various points, especially from number 75 onward.

Moreover, if the authors who venerate the letter in question as a Greek offspring were asked who translated it from Greek into Latin, in what century it was translated, in which churches it was formerly received, or by what ancient writers—contemporary or nearly contemporary—it was first mentioned or acknowledged, they would find nothing substantial to answer. [Col. 1363B]

7. Cave says: [Note: [Col. 1363D] Cave, *Literary History*, under “Firmilian.”] “Firmilian’s letter was translated into Latin, apparently by Cyprian, whose style it plainly exhibits.” Among Catholics, Pamelius had already held the same opinion long ago. [Note: [Col. 1363D] Pamelius, *Life of St. Cyprian*.]

8. But, first, if Firmilian’s letter had already become known in Latin in the third century, how could it have happened that it was never cited by authors of the third, fourth, and fifth centuries? More will be said about this as we proceed.

Second, if the letter exhibits Cyprian’s style, it thereby betrays that its original language was Latin, for Cyprian was a Latin.

Third, let us grant that the same author who fabricated the letters commonly attributed to Cyprian also composed the Firmilianic letter; for the style is altogether the same in both, except that in the Firmilianic letter, or the last one, he spewed out, at the top of his lungs, every insult against Pope St. Stephen that even a buffoon could devise. But the author of the letters commonly attributed to Cyprian is not St. Firmilian; therefore, neither is he the author of the letter commonly attributed to Firmilian. [Note: [Col. 1363D] It could nevertheless be said that the followers of those who either forged or corrupted certain Cyprianic letters later composed the Firmilianic letter from the Cyprianic ones, for the same phrases or barbarisms that occur in certain Cyprianic letters recur in this one; see what is to be said at number 78.]

Fourth, its Latin and style sink to such a level—as will become clear to anyone who rereads it—that they are wholly unworthy of St. Cyprian, whether as author or translator. [Col. 1363C]

9. Lactantius, who was already flourishing toward the end of the third century, reports concerning St. Cyprian: [Note: [Col. 1363D] Lactantius, preface to bk. V of *The Divine Institutes*.] “He composed a very great many works, marvelous in their kind. . . . His talent was facile, copious, and pleasing; and—what is the greatest excellence of discourse—clear, so that one cannot discern whether anyone was more ornate in speaking, more fluent in explaining, or more powerful in persuading.”

Similarly, in the fourth century, [Col. 1363D] St. Jerome [Note: [Col. 1363D] Jerome, *Catalogue of Illustrious Men*.] celebrated St. Cyprian as supremely eloquent; and elsewhere [Note: [Col. 1363D] Id., *Letter to Paulinus*.] he says: “Blessed Cyprian flows on, sweet and placid, like the purest spring.”

[Col. 1364A] 10. The distinction made by Pamelius [Note: [Col. 1364D] Pamelius, *Life of St. Cyprian*.] gives no satisfaction at all. He asserts that Cyprian was supremely eloquent before his conversion, but that after his conversion, out of humility, he chose a humble and subdued style in many of his works. This, I say, gives no satisfaction at all.

For, first, the ancients, such as Lactantius and Jerome, did not observe any such humility in Cyprian, although they were certainly judging works of marvelous quality that St. Cyprian wrote after he had already been imbued with the faith.

Second, humility of this kind in an ecclesiastical teacher would have been very singular, and I do not know whether it would have deserved praise. The other holy Fathers—Ambrose, Jerome, Basil the Great, etc.—did not imitate it.

Third, St. Cyprian himself, a most eloquent rhetorician, certainly wrote many things after his conversion that were not only extremely weighty in meaning [Col. 1364B] but also highly ornate in expression. Examples are St. Cyprian’s letter to Donatus, formerly his companion in receiving Baptism, and St. Cyprian’s letter to the martyrs. [Note: [Col. 1364D] See a fragment of this in the Roman Breviary, Common of Martyrs during Eastertide, second lesson in the second nocturn; likewise in the Common of Virgins, second lesson.] Had he perhaps forgotten, while writing these, to practice his humility?

11. The Bollandists [Note: [Col. 1364D] *Acta Sanctorum*, September, vol. IV, under September 14, in the life of St. Cyprian, no. 222.] assume Firmilian’s letter to be authentic. Nevertheless, they deny that St. Cyprian translated it from Greek into Latin, because it is not probable:

First, that St. Cyprian would have wished to expend his labor so that the invectives of an angry Firmilian against Pope St. Stephen might be rendered into Latin and disseminated more widely;

Second, that he would have been the translator of a letter in which, as though this were Cyprian’s own mind and opinion, it is denied that heretics existed in the time of the Apostles—see what is to be said at number 37—although Cyprian himself had asserted the contrary in his letter to Pompeius and had merely said that, later, persons even fiercer than those condemned by the Apostles had broken forth. But they did not venture to guess who had endowed the letter in question with a Latin form. [Col. 1364C]

12. When everything is duly weighed, it would remain to be said that the Firmilianic letter was brought forth in Latin dress not by St. Cyprian but by some unknown man. But at what time? Who first produced it—a letter unknown to the Greeks and ignored by the ancient Latins, such as St. Optatus of Milevis, Jerome, Augustine, and so forth? Indeed, it did not appear among the Cyprianic works in the earlier printed editions. [Note: [Col. 1364D] It is not found in Manutius, nor in the Basel edition of 1558, which Erasmus of Rotterdam prepared in 1519 from three editions—the Roman, the Badius edition, and another whose name has escaped me—as well as from the most ancient manuscripts, including that of Gembloux, etc.]

Morel was the first to publish it, at Paris in 1564. [Note: [Col. 1364D] Dupin, *New Library*, vol. I, under “Cyprian,” where he enumerates seventeen printed editions earlier than Morel’s in which Firmilian’s letter had not yet appeared.] It suggests neither the style nor the idiom of Greek. [Note: [Col. 1364D] The distinguished Dumesnil, of the most celebrated Society of Jesus and, in this eighteenth century, chancellor of the Catholic University of Strasbourg, comes opportunely to our aid. In bk. VII, *On the Doctrine* [Col. 1365C] *and Discipline of the Church*, § 46, he writes as follows: “If, however, the letter that is extant under Firmilian’s name is genuine, Augustine was ignorant of it; Morel, a Calvinist, was the first to publish it; and it suggests neither the style nor Greek diction. More bitter and full of abuse, it appears foreign to Christian gentleness and consequently less fitting for Firmilian, a holy bishop.”]

Pamelius says that it would have been better if it had never been published. [Col. 1365A] Therefore I am somewhat surprised that Firmilian’s reply to St. Cyprian, which was supposedly Greek in its original form, now appears among the Cyprianic writings only in Latin, whereas St. Cyprian’s letter of consultation to St. Firmilian, which was supposedly Latin in its original form, appears nowhere. Perhaps this too will soon have to be composed. Be that as it may.

## PROPOSITION II  
### It is not probable that St. Firmilian composed the famous letter in favor of rebaptizers and against Pope St. Stephen.

13. This is proved, first: The burden of proof lies upon the person asserting that it was written by St. Firmilian. [Note: [Col. 1365C] This rule of criticism and of both branches of law is very frequently violated. For example, recently, in 1788, Antonius Vogt, in his scriptural commentary published at Mainz, again treated that most celebrated question: “Was the Cephas rebuked by Paul at Antioch Peter?” Or: “Did Peter sin concerning the faith?” Vogt asserts affirmatively that it was St. Peter who sinned, without adequately proving it. To the objection, “Some deny that Peter was ever at Antioch,” he replies: “They deny it, but they do not prove it.” What a critic! Does the burden of proving an alleged event therefore lie upon the person who denies it?]

This proof must be established through contemporary or nearly contemporary witnesses. Such witnesses are entirely lacking. Neither Eusebius of Caesarea [Col. 1365B] nor St. Jerome, who expressly treated ecclesiastical writers, nor St. Optatus, nor St. Epiphanius made any mention of this letter, although it would have been exceedingly famous.

Nor do we read that the heretics who rebaptized in the fourth and fifth centuries—such as the Luciferians, attacked by St. Jerome, and the Donatists, opposed by St. Augustine on account of their Anabaptism—ever appealed to the letter in question, although it would have afforded them the greatest support.

This negative argument of mine, drawn from the silence of all the ancient Catholic and non-Catholic writers, appears to me to possess the greatest weight. I nevertheless admit that it would not completely prove my contention if even one solid positive argument drawn from antiquity could be opposed to it. But none has yet been found; for:

[Col. 1365C] 14. The most learned John Laurence Berti, [Note: [Col. 1365D] Berti, bk. 31, *On the Theological Disciplines*, ch. 13, no. 5. He refers his readers to this passage in his *Compendium of Ecclesiastical History*, published in 1761, when treating the history of the third century.] attempting with all his strength to defend the authenticity of the letter in question against Raymond Missorius, [Note: [Col. 1365D] Missorius, a highly polished writer of the Order of Conventuals, denied in 1733 that the letter in question belonged to Firmilian. Going still further, he also asserted that the whole history of the rebaptizers had been fabricated by Eusebius, and that St. Basil the Great and the other Catholics who later favored the rebaptizers had been deceived by Eusebius. Far be it from me to agree with this latter assertion. I judge rather that Eusebius’s text was interpolated, or that interpolated matter was falsely attributed to him, as I shall show more fully [Col. 1366D] in a separate dissertation on Eusebius as interpolated by heretics.] adduced the following argument, substantially, as his strongest:

“That letter is found under Firmilian’s name [Col. 1366A] in various libraries, especially in a manuscript codex of the Biblioteca Angelica, which Jerome of Pistoia copied from an older exemplar in the time of Pope Nicholas V, and thus in the fifteenth century. Therefore it must be regarded as the genuine offspring of St. Firmilian.”

But I reply, first: If this argument were valid, innumerable apocryphal books would have to be accepted as genuine. An example is the letter of Pope St. Clement I to St. James, the brother of the Lord, which Rufinus translated from Greek into Latin in the fourth century, although sound critics do not acknowledge it as authentic. I omit certain decretals of Linus, Cletus, Evaristus, and so forth, together with many other little works readily found in all sorts of libraries.

I reply, second: Therefore the most ancient public witness that can be adduced for the authenticity of the letter in question—namely, for the claim, note well, that it was written in Greek in Cappadocia in the third century—is one Jerome of Pistoia, note well, a Latin of the fifteenth century? [Col. 1366B] Yes indeed, according to Berti, the principal champion of the said letter.

I consider it entirely unnecessary here to inquire further who that Jerome of Pistoia was or how great his authority may have been. Even if Pope Nicholas V himself, most holy and worthy of the highest esteem, had in the fifteenth century adduced the letter as St. Firmilian’s own, nevertheless in this question of historical fact he would not possess such authority that his testimony would suffice even against the single negative argument already presented.

I reply, third: Nothing further follows from Jerome of Pistoia’s testimony than that in the fifteenth century a letter of Firmilian composed in Latin already existed in the Biblioteca Angelica. That does not conflict with what was said in number 4. From number 12 it is clear that in many other libraries it had not formerly been placed among Cyprian’s works. [Col. 1366C]

15. This is proved, second: Eusebius [Note: [Col. 1366D] Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, bk. V, chs. 23 and 27, where there is also a fragment of the letter composed on this matter by the bishops of Palestine.] and St. Jerome [Note: [Col. 1366D] Jerome, *Catalogue of Illustrious Men*.] mention less noteworthy letters, such as that of Polycrates, who is said to have opposed Pope St. Victor in the second century over a lesser matter, namely, the preservation of his own Church’s custom of celebrating the day of Easter on the fourteenth day of the moon.

If St. Firmilian had likewise opposed Pope St. Stephen I in the cause of repeating Baptism with as much clamor as resounds through the letter; if he had invoked against the Roman bishop the most celebrated synods, as the letter says, held long before; [Col. 1366D] if that Greek, by a letter addressed to the Latin St. Cyprian, had stirred up all Africa against the Roman Church in the third century, or confirmed it in dissent—then this letter of Firmilian would have been more memorable than that of Polycrates. [Note: [Col. 1366D] This is an argument *ad hominem*, for my opponents—Berti and others—accept without any hesitation that Polycrates’ letter is authentic, so that they may more easily defend the authenticity of the Firmilianic letter. See what is to be said at number 71. I shall communicate my particular opinion to the learned in a special dissertation on Polycrates.] Therefore, if it had truly existed, St. Jerome could not have omitted it, and still less could Eusebius, who in his *History* repeatedly and carefully renews the memory of St. Firmilian’s principal deeds. But not even a fragment or the slightest indication of the aforesaid letter occurs in Eusebius. [Col. 1367A]

16. This is proved, third: The letter of pseudo-Firmilian contains certain very remarkable historical claims. For example:

1. That in Cappadocia, during Firmilian’s time, a demon baptized in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, confected the Eucharist, and so forth, as we shall see beginning at number 56.

2. That because, around the year 235, entire cities were swallowed by the earth, a severe persecution was stirred up against our Christian religion as though it were the cause of that evil. [Note: [Col. 1367D] This earthquake must be treated more fully at number 54. It is not established that the emperors decreed a persecution against the Christians because of the earthquake. The pagan populace, however, was continually raging against the Christians and attributed the cause of every public calamity to them. “If cities are shaken by an earthquake; if,” etc., they cry: “The Christians to the lions!” says Tertullian in the *Apology* that he wrote in Africa during a persecution, around the year 202. See Fleury.]

If Firmilian had truly written these things, it appears morally impossible to me that Eusebius of Caesarea could have omitted them from his history. But they were omitted by Eusebius, Jerome, Epiphanius, and so forth. Therefore, etc. [Col. 1367B]

For the rest, I temporarily pass over the common conviction of everyone that St. Firmilian at some time adhered to the rebaptizers, until in another special dissertation I demonstrate that Eusebius’s history was interpolated on this point by Anabaptists. But if St. Firmilian was never, as I am persuaded, involved in the error of the rebaptizers, how far from the truth it will be that this holy man wrote the letter in question! For the moment, however, let this be set aside.

[Col. 1367C] 17. This is proved, fourth: For the letter of St. Firmilian to be authentic, one must admit at the same time that around the year 256 Cyprian sent a messenger from Africa to Cappadocia for the purpose of seeking St. Firmilian’s counsel. This instance of a Latin bishop from Africa consulting a Greek in Cappadocia concerning matters of faith is altogether extraordinary. It is related by no historian, and especially not by the Greek Eusebius, who was the foremost in celebrating St. Firmilian.

There can be no doubt that at that time, besides Pope St. Stephen, there were distinguished bishops among the Latins throughout Spain, Gaul, Italy, and Sardinia. If St. Cyprian the African wished to consult the Greeks concerning matters of faith, why did he not send to the European Greeks, who were ten times nearer to him, especially since delay carried the danger of incurring excommunication?

[Col. 1367D] But if counsel had to be brought back from Asia, why did he dispatch a messenger beyond Asia Minor, from Africa all the way to Cappadocia? More on this subject will be said again at numbers 23 and 34. If Cyprian wished to appeal from the decision of Pope St. Stephen to the Asian bishops, it was nevertheless paradoxical that at that time he should have taken refuge at Firmilian’s tribunal.

[Col. 1368A] For although Firmilian eventually became, after St. Dionysius, a man of the greatest renown—as stated in the Preface, number 2—nevertheless, in the time of Pope Stephen he had not yet attained such distinction that he could have been regarded as first among the Asians either in age or in the dignity of his Church. Indeed, around the year 255 Dionysius, patriarch of Alexandria, wrote to Pope Stephen the names of the more celebrated bishops then in Asia. Among them he still lists Firmilian last, placing before him Demetrian of Antioch, [Note: [Col. 1368D] He appears to have been placed first because of the dignity of his Church.] Theoctistus of Caesarea in Palestine, [Note: [Col. 1368D] Theoctistus had already exercised episcopal dignity before Origen was even a presbyter. See Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, bk. VI, ch. 20; bk. VII, ch. 5.] Mazabanes of Jerusalem, Marinus of Tyre, Heliodorus of Laodicea, and Helenus, bishop of Tarsus.

All these bishops, as well as St. Dionysius of Alexandria and others, were superior to Firmilian in dignity and nearer to Cyprian; for Cappadocia lay far beyond Tarsus, indeed beyond the provinces [Col. 1368B] of Cilicia, of which Tarsus is the metropolis.

Who, then, is the witness who relates that Cyprian the Latin, in so difficult a matter, chose to pass over the counsel of the Latin bishops and appeal to some Greek situated in Cappadocia? Pseudo-Firmilian alone asserts that he is that Greek to whom the Latins appealed.—Let Apella the Jew believe it.—We have many examples, related by the more ancient Greeks, of the Greek Churches consulting the Latins. But, if for the moment we set aside St. Cyprian, no instance now occurs to me of a Latin bishop in ancient times consulting the Greeks in matters of faith.

In the first century, the Greek Corinthians, while John the Evangelist was still living among the Greeks, referred their affairs to St. Clement, bishop of Rome.

In the second century, the cause of Polycrates—or rather of the Quartodecimans—was brought from Asia to Rome. [Col. 1368C]

In the third century, Dionysius, patriarch of Alexandria, consulted Pope Xystus, Stephen’s successor, on the question of Baptism.

Polycarp, Origen, and Hegesippus journeyed to Rome on account of religion, as the Greek Eusebius relates.

18. This is proved, fifth, by examining the letter itself, which from its intrinsic marks will be discovered to be either suspect or even openly spurious. For it contains a very great many things that are, in their respective ways, either heretical or close to heresy, historically false, incompatible with geography and chronology, and otherwise unworthy of Firmilian.

19. Pseudo-Firmilian begins as follows:

> “Firmilian to Cyprian, greetings. Through Rogatian the deacon, sent by you, we received the letters that you wrote to us, [Note: [Col. 1368D] This phrase, “to make letters to another,” and similar expressions occur frequently in the letters commonly attributed to Cyprian.] [Col. 1368D] dearest brother. . . .”

He then continues:

> “For our part, we receive what was written by you as though it were our own, nor have we read it in passing; rather, by frequent repetition we have committed it to memory.”

20. From what follows it will become still more apparent that pseudo-Firmilian sometimes addresses Cyprian in the singular and sometimes in the plural: “sent by you”; “you sent him to us.” Yet he consistently [Col. 1369A] speaks of himself in the plural: “‘We,’ Firmilian, ‘received’”—a style unusual among the Greeks in the third century. Dionysius of Alexandria certainly spoke of himself in the singular. [Note: [Col. 1369C] See Eusebius, bk. VII, chs. 5 and 9, where the patriarch of Alexandria writes as follows to Pope Xystus in his fifth letter on Baptism: “I need counsel and ask your judgment from you, since . . . I fear that I may be mistaken.”]

**Objection I.** Upon receiving the letters from Rogatian the deacon, Firmilian immediately convened a synod and replied in the plural in the name of the entire synod: “We received.”

**Reply 1.** Cyprian too is asserted to have consulted Firmilian in the name of an African council. Why, then, does Firmilian reply in his preface to Cyprian alone: “Which you wrote, dearest brother”?

**Reply 2.** Pseudo-Firmilian excuses himself on the ground that he was compelled to complete his reply too hastily [Note: [Col. 1369C] Dupin says that it was written hurriedly—indeed, most hurriedly. Who would not laugh at that “most hurriedly”?] because Rogatian the deacon, unwilling to wait, was immediately hastening to return to Africa, as will be stated at number 34. [Col. 1369B]

If, therefore, pseudo-Firmilian did not have enough time even to answer Cyprian properly, he certainly could not have held a synod as well. Or else the author of the Firmilianic letter lied in accusing Rogatian the deacon of being a surly messenger who, exhausted by his long journey, was unwilling to remain for just a little while at Caesarea in Cappadocia, so that the bishop St. Firmilian might have had sufficient time to compose a proper reply in so difficult a matter.

**Reply 3.** The author of the letter commonly attributed to Firmilian indicates quite plainly that Firmilian did not convoke a synod on account of Cyprian’s letter of consultation, since pseudo-Firmilian wrote in his reply to Cyprian:

[Col. 1369C] First, that the question had long before been decided in councils [Note: [Col. 1369C] These councils of Asia, which long before—according to Sbaralea, Dissertation I, ch. 2, no. 13, in the year 220 or 215, or earlier—had decreed Anabaptism, appear to have been unknown to Cyprian until that time; for the author of the Firmilianic letter is the first to announce them to Cyprian himself. They must have been held in secrecy from all the Latins, since no pontiff is recorded as having opposed them. But it is difficult to understand how nothing about them became known to the Roman bishop, continually keeping watch over the universal flock, since Asia at that time was still subject to Rome in civil matters as well as ecclesiastical ones. [Col. 1369D] Indeed, those councils of Asia escaped the notice both of their contemporary Origen, Firmilian’s most intimate associate, and of Eusebius and the other Greeks. On another occasion I shall show that the letter of Dionysius, as it is now read in Eusebius, bk. VII, ch. 5, was interpolated. Origen was flourishing as a presbyter at that time and died under Pope Stephen. While he lived, bishops both distant and nearby consulted him in every sort of controversy, especially Firmilian. In the many volumes Origen left behind, no indication occurs of those councils of Asia or of the aforesaid controversy of the Anabaptists. Eusebius had read all Origen’s books. He was ignorant of those councils of Asia, which he ought to have mentioned in bk. VI. In the same place he mentions that around the year 238 Beryllus, bishop of Bostra in Arabia, who was a heretic, was restored to the Catholic faith by Origen in a council of many bishops. But it is evident from Eusebius [Col. 1370D] that it occurred to no one at that time that those baptized by Beryllus also had to be rebaptized, for in bk. VII he asserts that rebaptism first began under Stephen. The acts of that synod convened against Beryllus, and the questions raised against him by Origen, were still extant in Eusebius’s time; see Eusebius, bk. VI, chs. 33 and 20. In Eusebius, the bishops of the Churches of Iconium and Synnada are named, praised for their discipline, and called holy men and blessed brethren; but there is absolute silence about councils held there. From these facts I infer that those councils are fictitious.] of Asia.

[Col. 1370A] Second, that the question had been examined and proved so abundantly in the letter sent by Cyprian that pseudo-Firmilian did not wish to add any new proofs; indeed, he had from that time begun to learn Cyprian’s letter by heart. Compare numbers 19 and 30.

Pseudo-Firmilian therefore does not appear to have held a new synod. The burden of proving the alleged event lies upon the person asserting it.

21. **Objection II.** The author of the Firmilianic letter adds in its conclusion:

> “We all wish that you may fare well, together with all the bishops who are in Africa. . . .”

Therefore he held a synod.

**Reply 1.** But who are all these men whom he gathered together so quickly? He did not write to Cyprian the name of even one of his fellow bishops, nor the place of the assembly. Is this the style in which synodal letters are written? [Col. 1370B]—But perhaps someone will say: Winter was approaching; Firmilian did not have enough time to complete a letter adequate to so important a matter; the African messenger was hastening to return.

**Reply.** Then neither did he have time to convene a synod. And why did he not postpone learning Cyprian’s Latin letter by heart until he had finished his own reply?

For the rest, that architect appears to have assumed the role of a man writing rapidly so that, if he were convicted of flaws he had committed, he might more easily be excused. For example, he forgot to add the place of the council and was afraid to name the bishops who allegedly attended the synod.—One cannot demand of a man writing hurriedly that he report such circumstances.

Nevertheless, I will not believe a man who merely asserts that “rebaptism was formerly defined in a council” unless he explicitly states where, when, and by whom the council was held. [Col. 1370C]

22. It is therefore assumed that St. Cyprian, together with all the bishops of Africa, composed a letter proving with the utmost fullness that “Baptism conferred by heretics is invalid”; and that Firmilian and all his associates valued this letter so highly that, although the same pseudo-dogma had long before been defined in his own and the neighboring provinces, he read it attentively and repeatedly, committed it to memory, and wished to learn it by heart.

Pseudo-Firmilian therefore appears to have valued Cyprian’s Latin letter more highly than all the councils of Asia held by the Greeks on this subject; for this is implied by that singular expression, “by frequent repetition we committed it to memory.”
