I do not know whether it should be more lamented or marveled at that [Col. 1370D] that precious letter, as it is alleged to have been—composed in a council of African Latins, read and repeatedly reread in a council of Greeks, and committed by Firmilian to his own memory immediately, even before he wrote a reply—did not reach posterity. Did it not reach Jerome or Eusebius? Did it indeed perish together with the acts of the aforesaid councils?

[Col. 1371A] But let no one be angry with the ancient ecclesiastical writers, whose duty it would have been to preserve at least some argument from the aforesaid documents. Eusebius, Jerome, and the others are innocent in this matter, since even the Anabaptists themselves in the fourth century were ignorant of those acts of their own councils—and indeed even of their names. Everything remained imprinted upon the memory of pseudo-Firmilian alone. He continues:

23.

> “For this reason we rendered the greatest thanks to the Lord, because it came about that we who are separated in body should be united in spirit . . . so that, as it were . . . dwelling together in the same house. And this is fitting to say, because the spiritual house of God is one; for in the last days, he says . . . the house of God shall be upon the summits of the mountains. . . . And in the Psalm the Lord is asked that one may dwell in the house of God [Col. 1371B] all the days of one’s life. And in another place he says: ‘Behold, how good and delightful it is for brethren to dwell together in unity.’ . . . But it also affords the greatest delight to the angels, to whom the divine discourse says there is joy over one sinner who repents and returns to the bond of unity. . . .”

I. It is true that Sts. Firmilian and Cyprian were separated by a very great physical distance, since St. Cyprian was bishop at Carthage in Africa, where Tunis now stands, while St. Firmilian lived in Greater Asia as bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, a region adjoining Armenia, or even regarded by some as part of it. [Note: [Col. 1371D] See Calepinus, and, among the ancients, Pliny the Elder: Caesarea in Cappadocia was formerly called Mazaca. The ordinary route from Carthage to Caesarea would have had to be taken across the Mediterranean Sea toward Ephesus; the distance between Ephesus and Carthage will be approximately the same as that between Rome and Ephesus. According to Strabo, Book XIV, the journey overland from Ephesus toward Mazaca, or Caesarea, is 3,820 stadia; therefore 475 Roman miles, or—if five Roman miles are reckoned as one German mile—95 German miles, fifteen of which make one degree.—Bingham, vol. 3, *Antiquities of the Church*, placed Carthage at 36 degrees longitude and 35 latitude; Caesarea at 68 degrees longitude and 40 latitude. They are therefore separated by 5 degrees of latitude and 32 of longitude.]

But could it have seemed singular or extraordinary to a Catholic writer that two bishops within the same Roman Empire, though separated in body [Col. 1371C], should be united in spirit? In what does that much-vaunted union consist, over which, as we shall see at no. 26, he rejoiced with great gladness? Was it that by common consent they had expelled from the Church the recently arisen heretic Novatus? St. Firmilian, who had labored vigorously to have the heresy of Novatus expelled from the Eastern Churches, [Note: [Col. 1371D] See Eusebius, Book VI, final chapter; Book VII, chapter 5.] ought not and could not have remained silent about that; yet he wrote no thanksgiving to God for the elimination of Novatus’s heresy. For what reason, then, did he offer the greatest thanks? Because they had united against the pope who defended the ancient traditions, and because they had agreed to tolerate disagreements concerning Baptism. They rage against the Father, but remain silent about the heresiarch Novatus.

II. The texts of Holy Scripture appear to have been employed rather inappropriately; [Col. 1371D] nor does it savor of that pleasurable joy [Col. 1372A] which the angels experience over one sinner who repents. After those preliminary excursions through Holy Scripture, he complains against Pope Stephen:

24. “Through his inhumanity it has now come about that neither conversation nor common discourse can any longer take place.”

I. Therefore Pope Stephen’s judgment must have made a very great impression even upon the minds of the Eastern bishops, since its result was that no one wished any longer to converse with Firmilian, nor could he himself engage in ordinary discourse. How does this cohere with the alleged synod celebrated by Firmilian in support of St. Cyprian? See no. 21. For the rest, I readily admit that if Firmilian had truly been excommunicated by the pope, he would not have been admitted to conversation [Col. 1372B] with Catholics.

II. But it is false that communion between the East and Pope Stephen was interrupted, or that mutual communion among the Easterners themselves was interrupted, as is abundantly clear from the letters of Dionysius of Alexandria to Stephen and to his successors. [Note: [Col. 1372D] See Eusebius, Book VII, chapters 7–11; also the Preface, no. 2.] The fabulist continues and

25. “Presumes to compare Pope Stephen to Judas the traitor—and, indirectly, Cyprian to Christ—adding: ‘But meanwhile let these deeds of Stephen be passed over, lest, while we recall his audacity and insolence, we bring upon ourselves more prolonged sorrow over the things wickedly done by him.’”

What are these wicked deeds on account of which the holy pope could have been likened to Judas the traitor? [Note: [Col. 1372D] In the fifth century the Donatists likewise compared St. Augustine to Judas the traitor. See St. Augustine, Book II, *Against the Letter of Petilian*, chapter 8.] What witnesses does pseudo-Firmilian produce? None; he is content with his own bare assertion [Col. 1372C]. Under the rhetorical figure of *praeteritio*, the impostor pretends that he will not recount the impious deeds of the holy Pope Stephen, lest more prolonged sorrow be occasioned; but we shall repeatedly hear this figure of *praeteritio* recur, and nevertheless it will finally be followed by a careful recital of the things wickedly done by St. Stephen, which are supposedly to occasion more prolonged sorrow.

26. Pseudo-Firmilian, after saying for the first time that St. Stephen’s wickedness must be passed over lest it cause sorrow, returns exultantly to where he began, saying:

“We rejoiced with great gladness and gave thanks to God, because we found among brethren situated so far away such unanimity of faith and truth with ourselves . . . so that you, who are separated from us by the most distant regions [Col. 1372D], proved yourselves to be joined with us in mind and spirit.”

I. That much-vaunted unity of faith and truth, by which those Anabaptists had proved themselves joined in mind and spirit, consisted in their spirited defense of manifest heresy against the pope’s definition; hence, exulting, they gave the greatest thanks to God. But why this repetition, when he had already said the same thing above, no. 23, and had complained that he lacked the time properly to treat the principal question [Col. 1373A]? No. 34. [Note: [Col. 1373D] The impostor seems to have taken singular delight in the letter he had fabricated.]

27. Then he once again mixes in scriptural examples that no one would have expected. For example, after uselessly repeating the distance between the places, he passes most ineptly to the distance between times:

“Just as long ago divine power joined by the bond of unity Ezekiel and Daniel, who were later in age, with Job and Noah, who belonged to the earliest times, though separated from them by an interval of time, so that although they were widely separated in time, they nevertheless held the same sentiments by the same divine inspiration.”

He adds a text ill-suited to this passage, namely from Psalm 18: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth . . . who, running swiftly in unity of spirit, etc.”

[Col. 1373B] Pamelius, who labored greatly to elucidate the letters attributed to Sts. Cyprian and Firmilian, finally confessed concerning the foregoing passage: “In what matter Noah and Daniel held the same view I have been unable to discover . . . Job and Ezekiel, however, both prophesied the resurrection of the flesh, the former in chapter 19, the latter in chapter 37.”

But I now say that Stephen too, together with Job and Ezekiel, and indeed together with Firmilian and Cyprian, “ran swiftly in the unity of the Spirit.” For who has doubted that St. Stephen, just as much as Firmilian and the others, believed in “the resurrection of the flesh”?

28. He proceeds to prove from Holy Scripture that, conversely, physical proximity is of no benefit if union of minds is lacking.

For Scripture says: “Behold, those who distance themselves [Col. 1373C] from you shall perish.” Likewise: “Father, grant that, just as I and you are one, so they too may be one in us.”

I. The first text speaks of the union of man with God; the second is nowhere found in Holy Scripture in those exact words. John 17 reads as follows: “I pray for them . . . that they may be one, as you, Father, are in me and I in you, that they also may be one in us.” [Note: [Col. 1373D] It is likewise recited in this form by St. Cyprian in *On the Lord’s Prayer*, a work praised by St. Hilary in his commentary on Matthew.]

II. Then, I ask, to what purpose are those incongruous digressions, which in no way concern the state of the question? From the portion of the letter read thus far, one could not yet even guess the object of the controversy conducted between Sts. Stephen and Cyprian and allegedly solemnly decided by councils. Far from addressing it immediately, he instead digresses yet again.

29. He begins to praise St. Cyprian’s letter, saying [Col. 1373D], “But we, those things, etc.,” as above, no. 19.

He adds that he will repeat something from it, since this repetition does not impair its salutary usefulness, and that he will add something new to accumulate proof. Yet meanwhile he neither states the question nor adduces those new proofs. Rather, through new circumlocutions there follows an excuse for why he intends to reinforce with new proofs a question which he had said had already been most adequately proved by Cyprian, namely: “Because in the Church of Christ there are many prophets, and if [Col. 1374A] something has been revealed to one”—that is, to pseudo-Firmilian—“the other must remain silent.” Here are his words:

30. “Nor does it impair salutary usefulness either to retrace the same things in order to confirm the truth or to add certain things in order to accumulate proof. If, however, anything has been added by us, it is not added as though something had been less fully stated by you, but because the divine discourse surpasses human nature, and the soul cannot comprehend the whole and the perfect.—For that reason, too, the number of Prophets is so great, so that the manifold wisdom of God may be distributed through many; hence the first who is speaking in prophecy is commanded to remain silent if something has been revealed to a second. For this reason it necessarily happens, etc.,” as in the next number.

I pass over, first, that “salutary usefulness” which the repeater pleads that he is not obstructing when he writes back to St. Cyprian the same things he had received from him [Col. 1374B]. Second, I say nothing about the great number of Prophets. Third, I admit that pseudo-Firmilian, although assisted by the councils of Asia, as is asserted in no. 20, could add nothing new or substantial in support of Anabaptism. [Note: [Col. 1374D] All the principal arguments, drawn either from reason or Scripture, which pseudo-Firmilian boasts of having added are found in the letters ascribed to Cyprian.] Fourth, however, I cannot help wondering at the reason he alleged for recounting the same things, namely: “Because the divine discourse surpasses human nature, and the soul cannot comprehend the whole and the perfect.” But fifth, most suspicious to me is that self-praise by which the author insinuates himself as filled with divine wisdom, as a second-speaking Prophet to whom St. Cyprian, with his African bishops, and we along with them, ought to listen.—Let us therefore listen to this pseudo-prophet, who from the aforesaid text of Paul [Col. 1374C] [Note: [Col. 1374D] 1 Corinthians 14.] most ineptly wrests a new falsehood, namely, that councils must necessarily be assembled every year; for he immediately continues:

31. “For this reason it is customary among us that each year we elders and superiors assemble together to arrange the things entrusted to our care, so that, if there are any more serious matters, they may be directed by common counsel, and also for the lapsed, etc.,” as in the next number.

I. What our pseudo-prophet meant by the *superiors* (*praepositi*), whom he placed after the elders, is obscure; see above, no. 5. He himself seems to have been one of the elders or superiors, a lover of annually assembled councils, which he eagerly desired to attend or at which he wished to sit. [Note: [Col. 1374D] That expression *praepositi* also occurs in the Cyprianic writings, in the eighth letter, under the title of the Roman clergy to Cyprian, in which the Roman clergy say: “We who appear to be superiors and to guard the flock in the shepherd’s place.” Likewise in Letters 7, 11, 13, 15, 23, 27, and *To Magnus*, 76: “Prescribing to no one in such a way as to prevent each individual superior from deciding.” Tertullian the Montanist, *On the Soldier’s Crown*, chapter 3: “We receive the Eucharist from the hand of none other than those who preside.” I cannot agree with Selvaggi, who asserts in Book I, chapter 12, §4, that the titles *superiors* and *presidents* were proper to bishops in the primitive Church.] For he even wished to prove this discipline from Holy Scripture, namely from 1 Corinthians 14.

[Col. 1374D] II. The law concerning annual synods is purely human and ecclesiastical [Col. 1375A], having its first origin in the First Council of Nicaea, which in the year 325—and therefore long after the death of St. Firmilian—first decreed in canon 5: “Let a council be held once before the days of Lent.” In Eusebius’s history, written at the beginning of the fourth century, there is not yet the slightest indication that bishops assembled together every year, or were obliged necessarily to do so. Dupin, indeed, [Note: [Col. 1375D] In the *New Library*, under “Cyprian.”] confidently asserts: “In the third century the Africans were accustomed to convene two councils each year, one in spring and the other in autumn.” But he omitted to prove this assertion. The author of the Cyprianic letters might perhaps be adduced, since he speaks of nothing more frequently than of councils celebrated almost daily; but it is not established that those letters are authentic, and indeed I shall show on another occasion [Col. 1375B] that they are for the most part spurious.

III. For the rest, that doctrine concerning frequently celebrated councils, whether we consider its origin or its purpose, was entirely irrelevant here and contributed nothing to the state of the question. What purpose, then, was served by those digressions of a man writing hastily, when he prescribes to Cyprian still another reason why councils should be celebrated every year, at the same time mixing in a new opinion—and a heretical one? He says:

32. “So that healing may also be sought through penance for brethren who have lapsed and who, after the saving washing, have been wounded by the devil—not as though they obtain remission of sins from us, but so that through us they may be brought to an understanding of their offenses and compelled to make fuller satisfaction to God.”

[Col. 1375C] Among the more serious reasons for which pseudo-Firmilian judges that synods must necessarily be celebrated every year, and by Paul’s prescription (no. 31), he names only one: so that the lapsed and penitents may be publicly tormented. This reason, however, appears highly suspicious to me. From this I conjecture that the author was either a Novatian or a Donatist, though later than the times of St. Augustine and even of Socrates and Sozomen, Novatian authors [Note: [Col. 1375D] St. Augustine wrote in the year 420, Socrates and Sozomen in 440; by this latter time the Novatians had already declined from rigorism into laxism, contending that every particular Church should be permitted to follow whatever discipline pleased it in fasts, celibacy, the celebration of feasts—especially Easter—and whether sacramental confession should or should not be made to a priest. See again Socrates, Book V, chapters 19 and 22; Sozomen, Book VII, chapter 16; both were Novatians.], since they make no mention of the ill-fated Firmilianic Letter.

The heresy of Novatus began around the year 250. St. Firmilian fought vigorously against it, yet in the letter we are examining there is a profound silence about Novatus or his heresy; indeed, that heresy is defended. For the principal errors of the Novatians [Col. 1375D] were: first, that they rebaptized those who had been baptized outside their own Church; second, that they taught that the Church could in no way forgive the more serious sins of the lapsed, even if they were contrite and penitent. They therefore did not admit such persons to the Sacraments, though they subjected them to harsher penances [Col. 1376A] and, in addition, wished them to be left to God.

The Donatists, who arose in the fourth century, around the year 314, embraced the foregoing errors of Novatus. [Note: [Col. 1376D] St. Augustine, *On the Words of the Lord in the Gospel of Matthew*, Sermon II, attacks those who at that time taught that at least the following sins were unforgivable: 1. homicide; 2. adultery; 3. apostasy from the faith—or from their own heresy.] In addition, they added that sinners—at least more serious and public sinners—[Note: [Col. 1376D] They were not sufficiently agreed as to which sins rendered a minister incapable of validly conferring the sacraments. If the baptizer were a secret sinner, they then taught that an angel or God supplied what was lacking; see what is to be said at no. 49.] could not validly confer Baptism or the other sacraments. Our pseudo-Firmilian wishes synods to be celebrated annually, in which sinners are not mercifully absolved by the elders, but those wounded by the devil are more severely punished, or, as he himself says, “are brought to an understanding of their offenses and make fuller satisfaction to God.”

This rigor was always foreign to the Roman Catholic Church and peculiar to the Novatians and Donatists.

[Col. 1376B] 33. At long last pseudo-Firmilian, after prefacing from nos. 18 to 32 so many things wholly irrelevant to the state of the question and, moreover, either false or savoring of heresy, now begins to accommodate himself to the matters about which he pretends to have been questioned by St. Cyprian, namely:

“Whether Baptism is invalid precisely because the person baptizing was a heretic?”

The pope, relying upon apostolic tradition, denied it, and the whole Catholic Church denies it. St. Cyprian and the African bishops are said to have doubted the truth of the Catholic dogma and therefore to have sought counsel from Cappadocia. Pseudo-Firmilian affirms it. But since he must have feared that sufficient arguments would be lacking by which he could overthrow apostolic tradition, [Col. 1376C] before daring to address the question he again offers the following excuse: that he lacks sufficient time to respond properly. For he says:

34. “Since, however, this envoy sent by you was hastening to return, and the winter season was pressing upon us, we replied to your writings as best we could, and indeed . . .”

I. Is this credible? That deacon-envoy, in a matter so difficult and concerning the universal Church, had already traveled at the very great expense of his church many hundreds, indeed thousands, of miles from Carthage all the way to Cappadocia; he had come from afar, indeed from the most distant regions; and under the title of hospitality he would gratefully have been maintained for some time in Cappadocia by St. Firmilian, by whom he is supposed to have been received with the greatest joy [Col. 1376D] (nos. 23, 26). Yet this importunate messenger refused to wait a few weeks or days so that pseudo-Firmilian could complete, with due deliberation, his reply on so difficult a matter? Away with such nonsense! Pseudo-Firmilian [Col. 1377A] (see above, no. 19) confessed that he had sufficient time to read St. Cyprian’s letter slowly, attentively, and repeatedly, and to learn it by heart. [Note: [Col. 1377C] Some assert that Firmilian had so much time that he assembled neighboring bishops. See nos. 20 and 21; and that this Letter was composed in the name of the council. See no. 76.] Therefore he would also have had time to compose an appropriate reply, especially since he simultaneously asserted that the question had long before been decided in Asian councils. He could thus have dispatched the matter all the more quickly by transmitting the acts of those councils to St. Cyprian, to whom those synodal decrees would surely have been far more welcome than useless accounts of other matters and superfluous repetitions. But the winter season was pressing.

II. If St. Firmilian had truly written this Letter, would he not more appropriately have said: “The messenger is hastening to return; the winter season is pressing”? Not, however, that the envoy “was hastening; winter was pressing.” The fabricator of the Letter certainly lived later than the times of St. Firmilian. Hence, looking back upon St. Firmilian’s past time—that is, the time at which he wished the Letter to have been written—he carelessly said: “That messenger was hastening; winter was pressing.”

III. The messenger would have been foolish if he had wished to begin the journey from Cappadocia to Africa with winter approaching; for then he would have had to continue it as winter grew harsher, at the very season when navigation on the Mediterranean is most dangerous, as is clear even from Holy Scripture, Acts 27, from verse 9: “When navigation was now unsafe, because even the fast”—the Ember Days in September—[Note: [Col. 1377C] St. Luke, namely, was writing these things not for Jews but for Christians living at Rome. See the dissertation *On the Chairs*, from no. 17. That the Apostles instituted the Ember fasts is expressly handed down by Pope St. Leo [Col. 1377D], etc., and confirmed by the most ancient consensus of all the Churches. Baronius, however, like many others, thinks that it was December, or the fast of the Jews’ tenth month, falling in our January. But then, around the winter solstice—as Calmet rightly observes on the cited passage—Luke would have written not that navigation became dangerous, but that it was impossible, namely, in that age when the mariner’s compass was not yet known. Further, it is evident from the context of Holy Scripture that the fast which had already passed was not a winter fast; for after taking counsel following that fast, they attempted to sail from Crete to Phoenix, so as to winter there. Therefore full winter had not yet arrived. [The text here appears textually displaced:] “January, and not end until about the middle. Afterward they were tossed at sea for more than fourteen days. Finally, after three further months during which they wintered on the island of Malta, they sailed to Italy. If that fast is said to have occurred around the beginning of January, it must consequently be asserted that the winter season hostile to navigation in Malta begins around the middle of January and does not end until about the middle of April, which is utterly false.” [Col. 1378C]] had already passed, since navigation was now unsafe even merely to sail from one port of Crete to [Col. 1377C] another, more convenient port of the same island, where they intended to winter. See verse 12. And because the harbor near the city of Thalassa was unsuitable for wintering, they decided to sail to Phoenix, a harbor situated on the southern side of the same island of Crete, for the winter. After the Adrumetine ship was wrecked, they reached the island of Malta. There they found an Alexandrian ship that had wintered there and had [Col. 1378A] not dared to cross to nearby Italy, its destination, because of the winter season. Behold, all those aboard the Adrumetine and Alexandrian ships bound for Italy remained for several months on islands of the Mediterranean because of the winter; and Cyprian’s messenger would have hurried from Caesarea in Cappadocia to Ephesus—or to some other coast of Asia Minor—with winter approaching? During the winter would he have crossed the archipelago and the rest of the Mediterranean as far as Carthage in Africa? Who would have granted him a ship? [Note: [Col. 1378C] Formerly navigation on the Mediterranean ceased from the fourth day of November until the seventh of March. See Pliny the Elder, *Natural History*, Book II, no. 37.]

If anyone wished to say that the messenger or bearer of the Letter traveled overland from Carthage to Cappadocia and returned from Cappadocia to Carthage, he would reveal complete ignorance of geography. For that overland journey does not lie along a direct route—which would itself be exceedingly long—[Col. 1378B] but would have extended through an immense circuit: from Carthage southward; then eastward as far as Alexandria through Egypt; from there northward to Jerusalem through Palestine; then to Damascus and Antioch through Syria; finally, turning westward through Bithynia into Cappadocia; and conversely from Cappadocia through Bithynia, Syria, etc. What an immense distance! Going and returning, he would have had to cover approximately 1,500 German miles. And would the messenger have consulted no bishop along the route among the intermediate churches which he necessarily passed nearby? The Churches of Alexandria, Jerusalem, and Antioch were certainly much closer to Cyprian, whether we consider the overland or maritime route.

IV. On the hypothesis of the adversaries who admit the letters of Firmilian [Col. 1378C] and Cyprian as genuine, the following propositions must all be asserted together. [Note: [Col. 1378C] The Bollandists, under September 14, in the *Life of St. Cyprian*, §41; Pagi for the years 255 and 256; Dupin, *New Library*, under “Cyprian”; Fleury, Book I, §§20 and 30. Among non-Catholics, Pearson, bishop of Chester, in his extremely accurate—as Cave calls them—*Cyprianic Annals*. Likewise Cave, under “Firmilian.” If the synod of eighty-seven bishops began on September 1, a very great number of them [Col. 1378D] would have had to travel to Carthage from various dioceses of Africa and Numidia during the dog days, when the sun’s heat in Africa most severely afflicts travelers. The emperors were not yet Christians who might have supplied public conveyances—a benefit Constantine the Great later bestowed upon bishops.]

1. If St. Cyprian had celebrated in the year 256, on September 1, the Carthaginian synod of eighty-seven bishops, [Note: [Col. 1378D] I omit the fact that the beginning of this controversy would have to be assigned to the year 255. In that same year 255, a first Carthaginian synod would have decreed against the pope that the Baptism of heretics was invalid; the same would again have been decreed—the Baptism of heretics was invalid—in the year 256, in another, second synod of seventy-one bishops, before that famous third synod of eighty-seven bishops assembled on September 1. I say nothing also of the synods of Iconium and Synnada. Who would not be astonished that so many large synods were celebrated within so short a time in defense of error, while no synod exists in defense of truth? For what synod is there?] in which—

[Col. 1379A] 2. There was as yet not the slightest indication whatever of St. Firmilian or other Easterners patronizing Anabaptism; nevertheless, by the unanimous consent of the Africans a decree was issued against the definition of the Supreme Pontiff.

3. The decrees of this council were carried to Rome by African bishops and presented to Pope Stephen; but the pope did not admit the aforesaid bishops to an audience and indeed forbade anyone to receive them into a house or under a roof.

4. After those bishops had returned from Rome to Carthage, Cyprian immediately sent his deacon to the remotest boundaries of the Roman Empire—namely, all the way to Cappadocia—to Firmilian, and that same deacon reached him in the same autumn of that same year.

5. Firmilian—whether or not he had first celebrated [Col. 1379B] a synod of several bishops, concerning which see above from no. 20—set about replying, but the importunate messenger refused St. Firmilian sufficient time to respond properly.

6. For with winter approaching, the messenger was hastening to return from Cappadocia to Africa; according to Pagi’s calculation, he returned to Carthage in December. Further, by necessary consequence they assert:

7. That Xystus, Stephen’s successor, had already suffered martyrdom in the year 258; and

8. That St. Dionysius became pope in that same year 258. These assertions are likewise false, as is clear from Eusebius alone, who teaches that Pope Xystus occupied the see for two years. But I shall discuss more fully on another occasion this chronological knot, which I have not yet been able to untie in the *Dissertation on the Chairs*, and shall defend the view [Col. 1379C] that Xystus occupied the see for approximately two years.

I require only geographical eyes to see that the exceedingly strained chronological arrangement of the aforesaid system cannot stand, even if we suppose all its errors to be so many foundations; for the very multitude of events abundantly suggests that the history is fabulous.

35. Pseudo-Firmilian, now at last about to resolve the principal question, begins in chapter 2:

“And indeed, as regards what Stephen said—that there exists a tradition received from the Apostles [Note: [Col. 1379D] Rigaltius used this statement of pseudo-Firmilian to attack the traditions of Catholics.], especially Peter and Paul, according to which those who were baptized by heretics ought not to be rebaptized—you answered most fully.”

This argument of Stephen’s, drawn from tradition [Col. 1379D], was certainly exceedingly strong and fully demonstrative; and I do not doubt that Cyprian and Firmilian—if Firmilian ever adhered to the rebaptizers—submitted to it entirely as soon as Stephen advanced it. Here are my reasons:

Around the year 266, Dionysius of Alexandria summoned the Synod of Antioch against Paul of Samosata, bishop of Antioch, to which very many bishops assembled. Among the foremost, our Firmilian is listed first; then Gregory and Athenodorus from Pontus; Helenus of Tarsus from Cilicia; Nicomas of Iconium from Phrygia; Hymenaeus from Jerusalem [Col. 1380A]; Theotecnus of Caesarea from Palestine; and Maximus of Bostra from Arabia. Countless presbyters and deacons also hastened to Antioch. In this numerous council, at which Firmilian either presided or participated as a principal member, no mention is made of rebaptism as a practice among Catholics. Would it have been possible for nothing to be defined concerning Anabaptism in that entire council if St. Firmilian had obstinately defended it from the year 256 onward? Still more, if Firmilian had written the exceedingly bitter letters against the Roman Church with which we are concerned?

Let us now discover what pseudo-Firmilian replies to the aforesaid argument from tradition. He dares to say:

36. “You answered most fully that no one is [Col. 1380B] so foolish as to believe that the Apostles handed this down, since even . . .”

Therefore Cyprian and the other African bishops would have answered the Supreme Pontiff: “No one is so foolish as to believe the Supreme Pontiff”? Would Firmilian, Origen’s disciple, and the other Asians have praised this reply? What impudence! Is no credence to be given to the Roman bishop, the Supreme Pontiff, when he attests to a fact—to the custom of his own Roman Church? Anyone who gives him credence is foolish; indeed, no one is so foolish as to give credence to the Roman bishop. What impudence! And would this have infected so many holy bishops in the third century, when Origen, out of devotion, traveled from the East to Rome to venerate the most ancient Church? When Origen, the oracle of the whole East [Col. 1380C], submitted his profession of faith to St. Fabian, bishop of Rome? Far be it from me to believe a solitary pseudo-Firmilian confessing his own impudence. For the rest, the existence of the aforesaid apostolic tradition could sufficiently have been proved from other considerations: first, because it had been preserved until then throughout all the Churches; second, because it was not established in what council it had been instituted. [Note: [Col. 1380D] Not even the adversaries dared to assert that rebaptism had always prevailed throughout the universal Church. Pseudo-Cyprian traces its beginning to Agrippinus, who at that time had been dead for twenty years; pseudo-Firmilian to the Councils of Iconium and Synnada, which at that time had long since been celebrated. Neither exists. I judge the very first person to have rebaptized to have been Novatus, expelled from the Church by Pope St. Cornelius in the year 251, who began to rebaptize Catholics around the year 253.]

37. To persuade us that the tradition did not descend from the Apostles, the impostor adduces a new and utterly enormous falsehood. For he denies what is exceedingly well known from the holy Fathers and from Holy Scripture itself: namely, he denies that heresies existed at the time of the Apostles. These are his exact words:

“Since it is established that heresies . . . arose later, [Col. 1380D] for Marcion, the disciple of Cerdo, is found long after the Apostles and after their times to have introduced a sacrilegious tradition against God. Apelles also . . . but the period of Valentinus and Basilides is likewise manifest, because they too lived after the Apostles and after a long age . . . it is also established that the other heretics introduced their depraved sects . . . afterward.”

[Col. 1381A] This passage is noteworthy. Baronius admits [Note: [Col. 1381C] At the year 258, §44.] that our Firmilian, through an excessively violent impulse of anger, blurted out many things that were historically false. If many things were false, then neither do I believe him when he asserts that he was bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, that he was consulted by Cyprian, etc.

The Bollandists [Note: [Col. 1381C] See above, no. 11.], since it is utterly certain that heresies existed in the time of the Apostles, rightly infer from this that it is not credible that St. Cyprian translated the ill-fated Letter, containing so many falsehoods, into the Latin language. I infer further that it is not credible that St. Firmilian composed so mendacious and petulant a Letter or sent it to Africa. [Note: [Col. 1381C] Since St. Ignatius the Martyr, a contemporary of the Apostles, mentioned in his letters to the Trallians and Smyrnaeans the heretics Basilides, Theodotus, Cleobulus, etc., the non-Catholics Daillé and Blondel, giving credence to pseudo-Firmilian, consequently contended [Col. 1381D] that those letters had been falsely ascribed to St. Ignatius. But even Eusebius’s authority alone proves them to be authentically Ignatian; therefore the Letter of Firmilian, being contrary to St. Ignatius, must be rejected as spurious, rather than St. Ignatius’s letter.] Now to the matter itself.

I. It made me laugh that pseudo-Firmilian, while wishing to deceive us, [Col. 1381B] traced the beginnings of heresies back to Marcion, Cerdo’s disciple. Why not to Cerdo, Marcion’s teacher? [Note: [Col. 1381D] Likewise pseudo-Cyprian, when enumerating the ancient heretics, omits all who were earlier than Marcion. Letter 73.] A teacher is, after all, prior to his disciple; but it will presently be stated that before Cerdo there were several heretics whom the impostor suppressed.

II. It is false that Cerdo and Valentinus began their heresies long after the Apostles, after a long age had elapsed from the Apostles; for they spread them at Rome under Hyginus, who was the ninth bishop in the Chair of Peter, and therefore around the year 140. [Note: [Col. 1381D] Hyginus began to occupy the see in the first year of Emperor Antoninus; he governed the Church for four years. See Eusebius.] The Apostolic Age is ordinarily extended to the year 120. For St. John the Evangelist survived into the second century; St. Clement I, pope, who is deservedly also called an Apostle; St. Ignatius of Antioch, who had seen Christ risen from the dead [Note: [Col. 1381D] Ignatius’s Letter.]; and Simeon, Christ’s kinsman and the second bishop of Jerusalem, who was 120 years old [Col. 1381C], suffered martyrdom under Emperor Trajan. Where, then, are those long times, that long age between the end of the Apostolic Age and the beginning of the said heresies?

III. But other heretics also preceded Cerdon. Simon Magus perished [Note: [Col. 1381D] Between the year 43 under Claudius and the death of the Apostles, which occurred around the year 68. See my *Dissertations on the Sees*, nos. 37, 59, 67.], before Peter and Paul were crowned with martyrdom at Rome; Menander succeeded Simon [Note: [Col. 1381D] Among other things, Menander added that those whom he himself had baptized would be immortal even in body, provided that they continued perpetually to adhere to him. See Eusebius, book III, chap. 26, citing Sts. Justin and Irenaeus. Yet it does not follow absolutely from this that Menander rebaptized those who had been baptized by others.], while Peter and Paul were still alive.

IV. Besides the heresies of Simon Magus and Menander, in the time of the Apostles there were the heresies of the Ebionites [Col. 1382A] [Note: [Col. 1382C] Eusebius, book III, chap. 27.], against whom St. John composed his Gospel; and of Cerinthus [Note: [Col. 1382D] See St. Epiphanius, *Heresies* 28, where he teaches that Cerinthus was the man who resisted St. Peter in II Peter II; who stirred up the dissension at Antioch against Paul in Acts XV; and that he was the man against whom St. James wrote in Acts XV: “We have heard that certain persons who went out from among us have troubled you.” Natalis, Calmet, and others agree with St. Epiphanius. The same Cerinthus had circulated certain revelations as though written by a great Apostle (see Eusebius, book III, chap. 28); hence I conjecture that Barnabas, Cephas, James, etc., were alarmed and challenged Paul before the authority of St. Peter, to whose judgment Barnabas and Cephas submitted. Gal. I and II. Likewise Acts XV.], who had two disciples, Saturninus and Basilides, each of whom established a distinct heresy. In the same Apostolic age lived Carpocrates, or Carpocras, from whose disciples the abominable brood of the Gnostics was afterward formed, around the year 130 [Note: [Col. 1382D] See our St. Lawrence Cozza, *On Heresies*, chap. 6, no. 3.].

V. The heresy of the Nicolaitans is mentioned in Apoc. 2:6 and 15. I pass over the names of other heretics recorded by Paul in I Tim. 1:20; II Tim. 1:15 and 2:19; likewise 4:14. Paul to Titus 3:10: “Avoid a heretical man.” Heretics are designated in I Peter II. I John 2:18: “Even now there are many Antichrists.” And elsewhere.

VI. These matters have been treated somewhat more fully so that it may appear more plainly how unworthy of St. Firmilian, the bishop, is that proposition of the Anabaptists which asserts: [Col. 1382B] “In the time of the Apostles there were no heresies.” And consequently, that it was not handed down by the Apostles that Baptism conferred by heretics is valid.

Indeed, since heretics certainly existed in the time of the Apostles, the Apostles must have decided whether the Baptism of heretics was valid or not; therefore, there must have existed an Apostolic tradition on this subject.

38. Pseudo-Firmilian, now grown bolder, passes from error to error—errors both practical and dogmatic—while striving to insinuate that Apostolic traditions, if perhaps any existed on this matter, need not necessarily be retained in the matter of Baptism. To persuade his readers of this, he accuses the Roman Church of “not observing all those things which have been handed down from the beginning or by the Apostles [Col. 1382C].” A grave accusation! But how does he prove it? He says:

> “That those at Rome do not in every respect observe the things handed down from the beginning, and that they vainly invoke the authority of the Apostles, anyone may know from the fact that, concerning the observance of the days of Easter and many other sacraments of divine worship, he sees certain differences among them [the Romans], and that everything observed at Jerusalem is not observed in precisely the same way at Rome.”

I. The ignorant impostor supposes that certain Eastern Christians formerly disagreed with the other churches concerning the day on which Easter should be celebrated [Note: [Col. 1382D] On the occasion of this text, it is customary to dispute whether St. Firmilian adhered to the Quartodecimans. Baronius affirms it; others deny it, since none of the ancients numbered St. Firmilian among those heretics. Since the entire Letter is spurious, that controversy comes to an end.], and he adduces this single [Col. 1383A] example to persuade us that rebaptizations also—which the Roman Church, indeed the entire Roman Catholic Church, condemned—should be tolerated. And because he seems to have known no examples of discrepancies besides that single one, he therefore said that there were “many other sacraments of divine worship.” But what are those many others? And, more precisely, sacraments of divine worship? He passes over them all in his customary fashion, perhaps because winter was pressing on. St. Irenaeus, who had been at Rome, testified very differently concerning the Roman Church, saying: “In her the tradition which comes from the Apostles has always been preserved.”

II. But it is also historically false that in the third century the Churches of Rome and Jerusalem disagreed even concerning the celebration of Easter [Note: [Col. 1383D] Toward the end of the fourth century the heresy of the Quartodecimans gained strength at Jerusalem, according to the testimony of Philastrius (39), cited by Cozza.]. Eusebius, Bishop of Caesarea in Palestine, book III, chap. 23, writing against the Quartodecimans who arose in the time of Pope St. Victor, expressly asserts that throughout all Palestine, and consequently also at Jerusalem, Easter was celebrated, as a matter of Apostolic tradition, on the same day as at Rome—namely, Sunday—because, according to Apostolic tradition, the pre-Easter fasts of Lent were to be ended only on the day of the Lord’s Resurrection. Eusebius adds that, in his own time, the acts of the Palestinian synod—over which Theophilus, Bishop of Caesarea, and Narcissus, Bishop of Jerusalem, had presided—were still extant. In them, the doctrine of those who dissented from the Roman rite is called erroneous and seductive of souls [Note: [Col. 1383D] On another occasion I shall show that St. John the Evangelist was not the author of this heresy, as pseudo-Polycrates asserted.].

It is therefore false that the Churches of Jerusalem and Rome differed in their discipline concerning the date of Easter. [Col. 1383C] He continues:

39. “Accordingly, in many provinces also, many things vary because of differences among people; yet for this reason no one has ever withdrawn from the peace and unity of the Catholic Church, as Stephen has now dared to do, breaking with you the peace which his predecessors always . . . preserved with you, and moreover defaming Peter and Paul, the blessed Apostles, as though they themselves had handed this down—although in their Epistles they execrated heretics and admonished us to avoid them. From this it is apparent that this tradition which supports heretics and defends their possession of Baptism is a human tradition.”

I. What are those “many things”? What are those “many provinces”? What are those places, and who are those people, according to whose [Col. 1383D] diversity many things varied at that time [Note: [Col. 1383D] It is beyond doubt that in later times many disciplinary matters were changed according to differences of places and people; but in the third century the preservation of uniformity was insisted upon with the greatest strictness. When the emperor Philip, whether a Christian or a catechumen, wished to attend the final Easter vigils, he was ordered by the presiding bishop to stand among the penitents because he was guilty in many respects; and he promptly obeyed. See Eusebius, book VI, chap. 34.], and which might have any bearing upon the present question? These [Col. 1384A] vague assertions deserve no credit and are unworthy of St. Firmilian.

II. Secondly, it is false that St. Stephen broke peace with St. Cyprian and the Africans, as nearly everyone admits [Note: [Col. 1384D] 1. Because it cannot be proved from any other source that the pope actually excommunicated St. Cyprian and all the bishops of Africa. 2. Because St. Cyprian’s name was inserted into the Canon of the Roman Missal. Is it at all credible that the Roman Church would have admitted into the Canon of her Missal the name of a man excommunicated by the Supreme Pontiff and of the foremost standard-bearer of those excommunicated?], especially since, as I shall show elsewhere, Cyprian either never opposed Stephen or, upon being admonished, submitted immediately.

III. How absurd is the expression: “Pope Stephen defames Peter and Paul [Note: [Col. 1384D] That phrase, “to defame the Apostles,” also occurs in Cyprianic Epistle 74.]; he supports heretics.” Would someone thereby be said to have supported or defended Judas the traitor, Simon Magus, Menander, etc., merely because he held Baptism conferred by them to be valid?

IV. How weak the inference: “The Apostles abhorred heretics; therefore, they judged their Baptism invalid!” Paul certainly abhorred the false apostles most strongly; yet he did not condemn their preaching of the Gospel, provided that they had not mingled error with it. Consequently, he also held Baptism conferred by them to be valid. To show that the effect of the sacrament does not depend upon its ministers, he rebukes those who boasted that they had been baptized by Paul or Cephas.

V. How manifest the contradiction: “The Apostles execrated heretics; they taught that they were to be avoided,” as is here truly asserted; and yet, “the question of the validity of the Baptism of heretics could not have been decided by the Apostles because there were not yet any heretics in the time of the Apostles,” as was asserted above, no. 37.

40. He fabricates a new and absurd assertion for St. Stephen; namely, he supposes that the Pope taught:

> “The heretics themselves are also in agreement concerning Baptism [Col. 1384C], because when they come from one group to another, they do not baptize but only admit one another to communion—as though we too ought to do this. On this point, although you have already proved sufficiently that it would be ridiculous for anyone to follow those who are in error, nevertheless that . . .”

This passage is noteworthy, for on its account theologians also dispute keenly and at great length about Cyprianic Epistle 74 [Note: [Col. 1384D] See Natalis Alexander on the third century, Dissertation 14; Tournély, *On the Sacraments in General*, question VII; Berti, *On Theological Disciplines*, book XXXI, chap. 13, no. 16.].

41. “Did Stephen judge valid a Baptism conferred under any formula whatever, even without invocation of the mystery of the Most Holy Trinity?”

Many deny it, for the reasons to be stated at no. 52. Some affirm it because they wish the pope to have fallen into heresy. Among them are Blondel, Vossius, Basnage, Marcus Antonius de Dominis, John of Chester, and Launoy, vol. [Col. 1384D] II, p. 2. Du Pin, a doctor of the Sorbonne, also inclines toward this view and, to prove his intention more fully, asserts [Note: [Col. 1384D] In his *Library*. See “Cyprian.”]: “There were scarcely any heretics at that time who baptized in the name of the Most Holy [Col. 1385A] Trinity.” But this last assertion lacks sufficient foundation. With greater justification he would have said that there were few [Note: [Col. 1385C] See these in Irenaeus, book I, chap. 8. I shall deal with the Montanists in the dissertation on the canonical Epistles of St. Basil the Great.] heretics at that time who did not employ the legitimate formula. At least the heretics who most disturbed the Church at that time were the Novatians, and they never corrupted the formula of Baptism. The Paulianists and Sabellians broke out after the time of St. Stephen; but that controversy concerning the heresy of Pope Stephen will be able to cease henceforth, for:

I. Who will any longer believe our pseudo-Firmilian [Note: [Col. 1385C] I judge pseudo-Firmilian to have belonged to the same sect as the author of certain Cyprianic Epistles, for Scriptural texts are cited in both sets of letters in the same manner, one unusual among Catholics. For example, in Augustine’s time the Donatists commonly argued from Psalm 140: “Let not the oil of the sinner anoint my head”; therefore, Holy Unction and the other Sacraments conferred by a sinner are invalid. The same reading occurs in Cyprianic Epistle 76. St. Augustine, book II, *Against Cresconius*, chap. 24, and book IV, chap. 15, answered the Donatists: 1. That the text had been ineptly adduced, since it concerns a sinner who flatters. 2. That the text had been corrupted by the Donatists, since it ought to read: “Let it not enrich my head,” or “It shall not enrich my head.” Behold, the author of the Cyprianic Epistles cited Holy Scripture as it had been corrupted by the Donatists.] when he asserts: “Pope St. Stephen defined that Baptism must not be repeated because it is acknowledged as valid by heretics”? In that case Stephen would certainly have stirred up against himself not merely Firmilian, but all the bishops and laity of the entire [Col. 1385B] world, although at least all Europe remained steadfastly attached to the Pope.

II. It appears false that heretics at that time held Baptisms conferred outside their own sects to be valid. Concerning Menander, see St. Irenaeus, to say nothing of the Tertullianists [Note: [Col. 1385D] Tertullian, after becoming a Montanist, taught in his book *On Modesty* that those who came from heresy were to be baptized like pagans.]. Concerning Novatus, the matter seems beyond doubt, for St. Innocent testifies that the Novatians rebaptized Catholics [Note: [Col. 1385D] Epistle II to Victricius, chap. 8.]. St. Jerome handed down that St. Cyprian began to regard the Baptisms of the Novatians as invalid precisely because the Novatians had regarded the Baptism of Catholics as illegitimate. Finally, St. Dionysius of Alexandria, a contemporary of Novatus, reported to the Pope [Note: [Col. 1385D] Eusebius, book VII, chap. 8.] that “he rejected the sacred washing”—that is, our Catholic washing—for the Novatians did not abolish the sacrament of Baptism [Note: [Col. 1385D] This is clear because Novatians coming into our Church were not baptized. See the Council of Nicaea. But they rebaptized Catholics or Donatists, so that pseudo-Cyprian spoke truthfully when he wrote to Jubaianus in Epistle 73: “The Novatians”—followers of Novatus—“rebaptize those whom they entice away from us.”].

[Col. 1385C] 43. He attempts, by the following argument, to refute the aforesaid false assertion—that in the system of heresies of every kind it followed that “every Baptism was valid”:

> “Heretics . . . maintain one and the same agreement in this: that they blaspheme the Creator, fabricating for themselves certain dreams and phantoms of an unknown God; therefore, [Col. 1386A] it follows that they agree concerning the invalidity of their Baptism.”

44. It is false that all heretics agreed in blaspheming the Creator; for the Novatians, who were then especially well known [Note: [Col. 1386D] St. Firmilian had fought especially against Novatus. Paul of Samosata, who began to deny the divinity of Christ in St. Firmilian’s time, gained strength after the deaths of St. Stephen and Cyprian. Which heretics, then, did St. Firmilian intend to rebuke when, around the year 256, he wrote to Cyprian that they had fabricated phantoms of an unknown God for themselves?], retained unchanged the sound doctrine concerning God and the Most Holy Trinity which they had learned in the Catholic Church. Consequently, their Baptism, together with that of many others, was recognized as legitimate at the Council of Nicaea in 325. The Montanists, who were famous in St. Firmilian’s own time, will be discussed in no. 46.

45. I cannot refrain on this occasion from setting forth the thoughts that have occurred to me. After the time of Pope St. Stephen and Cyprian, very celebrated councils were held: two or three at Antioch between 265 and 272; another at Arles in 314; and afterward, in [Col. 1386B] 325, the general Council of Nicaea. At the last two, because the Donatists had already gained strength, the matter of rebaptization was considered. If, in Africa under Agrippinus and afterward in three large councils of Catholics under St. Cyprian, and likewise in Asia at the synods of Iconium and Synnada, it had been defined against the Roman Church “that no heretic whatsoever could baptize validly,” how was it possible that at the Councils of Arles and Nicaea no mention was made of reconsidering the preceding councils, which had defined the Baptism of every heretic without distinction to be invalid? I cannot untie this knot except by saying that those Anabaptist councils of Africa and Asia [Note: [Col. 1386D] The one objection possessing the appearance of a solid argument that can be raised against me is the following: in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VIII, chap. 3, mention is made that St. Dionysius of Alexandria had heard something about the Councils of Iconium and Synnada. But elsewhere I shall show specifically: 1. That this passage of Eusebius is interpolated. 2. That the passage is so obscure that scholars have not yet agreed concerning the true meaning of its words.] are fictitious. At Arles it was defined against the Donatists that none who had been baptized with the Trinitarian formula [Col. 1386C] should be rebaptized. Afterward, at Nicaea, it was specified who should and who should not be rebaptized.

46. Furthermore, since pseudo-Firmilian ought to have proved that all heretics had erred concerning the Father, he now undertakes this under the rhetorical figure of omission, adducing only the Montanists and saying:

> “Since it would take too long to respond to each one of their [the heretics’] claims, it is enough to state this briefly and summarily: those who do not hold to the true Lord and Father cannot possess the truth either of the Son or of the Holy Spirit. Thus those who are called καταφρυγας (*kataphrygas*, ‘Cataphrygians’), that is, Montanists, ‘according to the Phrygians’ [Note: [Col. 1386D] By the beginning of the third century the Montanists had already been divided into three sects: 1. Those “according to the Phrygians.” 2. Those “according to Proclus.” 3. Those “according to Aeschines.” See our Lawrence Cozza, later a cardinal, in his *Historical-Dogmatic Commentary on Heresies*, published at Rome in 1717, heresy 26, on the Cataphrygians.], and who attempt to appropriate new prophecies, can possess neither the Father, nor the Son, nor the Holy Spirit. If we ask them which Christ they preach, they will answer that they preach him who [Col. 1386D] sent the Spirit that spoke through Montanus and Prisca [Col. 1387A] [Note: [Col. 1387C] Mention is made only of Prisca, although Montanus, according to Tertullian of the Montanist sect and other Catholics—Jerome, Eusebius, Epiphanius, etc.—employed two prophetesses, Priscilla and Maximilla. Philastrius, *Book on Heresies*: “The Cataphrygians confess the Father, Son, and Spirit; they proclaim Montanus, Priscilla, and Maximilla.” It would be remarkable if, in St. Firmilian’s time, Maximilla had fallen into oblivion and Priscilla had through error already been changed into Prisca.]. Since we perceive that in these persons there was not the Spirit of truth but of error, we recognize that those who defend their false prophecy against the faith of Christ cannot possess Christ. Nor can any of the other heretics.”

I. The argument is exceedingly weak. For even if some persons—for example, Lutherans—had believed that Luther was filled with the Holy Spirit and sent by God, it would not therefore follow that they erred concerning the Most Holy Trinity.

II. It is evident, first, from Tertullian himself [Note: [Col. 1387D] See the passage cited above, from no. 72.], the foremost of the Montanists, who survived until St. Firmilian’s time, that down to that age the Montanists generally did not err concerning the Most Holy Trinity. Secondly, St. Epiphanius himself acknowledges this in *Heresy* 48. Thirdly, Eusebius, who is somewhat older than Jerome, [Col. 1387B] frequently records the errors of the Cataphrygians in books IV and V; yet he says nothing about their having erred concerning the Most Holy Trinity, although that error would have been especially noteworthy. Fourthly, at the beginning of the fourth century it was not yet known that any among the Montanists had corrupted the formula of Baptism; for at the Council of Nicaea the Paulianists are ordered to be rebaptized, but there is silence concerning the Montanists [Note: [Col. 1387D] I have reviewed seven different editions in Hardouin. In one, that of Isidore Mercator, the Cataphrygians are found added to the Paulianists; but I judge that single edition to be interpolated.]. At the First Council of Constantinople, in 381, canon 7 says: “The Montanists, who here are called Phrygians, are to be rebaptized with the Eunomians and Sabellians, like the other heretics, especially if they come from Galatia” [Note: [Col. 1387D] The Cataphrygians are also listed among those to be rebaptized in the Council of Laodicea; but it is not sufficiently established, first, whether the Laodicean Council is genuine, or, secondly, when it was held.]. If St. Jerome at the close of the fourth century, Theodoret in the fifth, and St. Gregory the Great in the sixth testify that the formula of Baptism had been corrupted by at least some Montanists, they must be understood as referring to the Montanists existing in their own times [Note: [Col. 1387D] Sts. Jerome and Gregory speak without qualification; Theodoret says, “Some of the Montanists.” The Synod of Constantinople adds, “Especially if those heretics come from Galatia,” an addition which implies that the formula had not been changed by all those heretics.]. From [Col. 1387C] these and other considerations I infer that pseudo-Firmilian came long after the rise of the Montanist heresy, after the fourth century.

III. If the Montanists “according to the Phrygians” corrupted the baptismal formula and consequently had to be rebaptized, nothing follows from this in favor of pseudo-Firmilian’s assertion that no heretic can confer valid Baptism. [Col. 1388A] If even an orthodox person, when baptizing, does not use water or alters the formula, then that rite is not the Baptism of Christ and is invalid; but it does not follow: therefore, a Catholic cannot baptize validly.

47. He continues:

> “But none of the other heretics established outside the Church can possess any power or grace. . . . In the Church the elders preside, who possess the power both of baptizing and of imposing hands and of ordaining.”

“For heretics . . .” Who are those elders who preside in the Church? Why are the names “bishops” and “presbyters,” so commonly used by the Greek Orthodox, again omitted here? See above, no. 31. Bishops alone possess the power of ordaining; elders, or presbyters, do not possess it.

48. He proceeds rather ignorantly:

> “Just as a heretic is not permitted to ordain [Col. 1388B] or to impose hands, so neither is he permitted to baptize . . . when . . .”

Therefore, neither a Catholic layman—indeed, neither a deacon nor a presbyter—will be able to baptize, because he cannot ordain. . . . But he continues:

49. “When a heretic is alien to holiness, which entire matter . . .”

Therefore, neither will a Catholic bishop, if he is in a state of sin, be able to baptize validly. This erroneous doctrine—that a sinner cannot effect the Sacraments—was characteristic of several heretics, but especially of the Donatists [Note: [Col. 1388D] Among them, in the case of a secret sinner, God, or at least an angel, secretly supplied what was lacking. St. Augustine, book XXI, *Against Cresconius*, chap. 18, and in his *Exhortation to Concord*, Epistle 66, drew the following inference against the Donatists: It would therefore be more desirable to be baptized by a secret sinner than even by a holy man, because in the first case God or an angel would baptize, while in the second case a man would wash. The same would hold for the other Sacraments.].

He appeals to the acts of a certain council seen by no one, saying:

> “All of this we confirmed long ago at Iconium, a place in Phrygia, when we had assembled together, with persons coming from Galatia, Cilicia, and the other neighboring regions . . . when some persons entertained doubts concerning this matter. [Col. 1388C] Because Stephen . . .”

50. I. Therefore, “all of this” means: first, that elders possess the power of ordaining; secondly, that one who cannot ordain cannot baptize either; and thirdly, that one who is alien to holiness is also alien to the power of baptizing. All these things, I say, had formerly been defined by the orthodox bishops of Cappadocia, Phrygia, Galatia, Cilicia, and the other neighboring regions. Why? In what year? “Long ago, when some persons entertained doubts concerning this matter.” Who were those doubters? No one is known except pseudo-Firmilian himself, inasmuch as he says: “We confirmed it long ago.”

II. But Pagi, at the year 255, no. 15, while admitting the fated Firmilianic letter as genuine, at the same time acknowledges that the author of the letter did not attend that council held “long ago” [Col. 1388D] [Note: [Col. 1388D] Labbe and Petavius assigned the Synod of Iconium to the year 258, in which they also believed that the Third Council of Carthage under St. Cyprian was held. Hardouin, under the year 331, chap. 2 (p. 130 in my edition), transferred it to around the year 175. I repeat that both the Iconian and Carthaginian Synods are fictitious. See above, no. 21.]. Behold, therefore, the alleged Council of Iconium opposed to the Roman Church, [Col. 1389A] of which no acts survive, and concerning which it is not known in what year it was held, who even one of its named participants was, or against what single named person it was convened. From what archive, from what author, did pseudo-Firmilian derive those definitions issued “long ago” at Iconium? Had they been issued, they would redound to the perpetual disgrace of the Catholic bishops of Cappadocia, Galatia, Cilicia, and the other neighboring regions. But I judge that they were never issued.

51. Finally, he attempts to prove his case from Holy Scripture and utterly to overthrow Catholic dogma when, in chap. 4, he argues substantially as follows from Acts XIX:

> “St. Paul washed again with the Baptism of Christ those who had been baptized with the Baptism of John before the Holy Spirit had been sent; therefore, those who were baptized by heretics,”

among whom the Holy [Col. 1389B] Spirit is not present, must likewise be baptized again. Stephen and the other bishops who agree with the Pope are therefore in error when they contend that the remission of sins and second birth can proceed through the Baptism of heretics. In the case just mentioned, Paul could not give the Holy Spirit except through a new Baptism of Christ. Is Paul inferior to those bishops? Thus pseudo-Firmilian.

I. Therefore, neither can the remission of sins and second birth proceed through Baptism administered by Catholics who are in a state devoid of grace, because the Holy Spirit is not present among them.

II. This argument, which pseudo-Cyprian also employs in Epistle 73 to Jubaianus, rests upon several erroneous suppositions:

[Col. 1389C] 1. That the disciples of John the Baptist were not in a state of grace—indeed, that they could not have been righteous. Or, 2. That John’s Baptism could not sanctify its recipients for the reason that the Holy Spirit had not yet been sent; from which it would follow that, if it had been conferred after the first Pentecost of the Christians, at which the Spirit descended, it could have regenerated its recipient because the Spirit had then already been sent. 3. That even the Baptism of Christ itself did not yet possess its power of justification before that Pentecost [Note: [Col. 1389D] Tertullian taught this opinion in his book *On Baptism*.].

III. Pseudo-Firmilian wanders entirely outside the proper course. What had to be proved was that the Baptism of Christ conferred by Simon Magus or another heretic had to be repeated by command of the Apostles. The Baptism of John, even when conferred by St. Andrew the Apostle or St. Peter, was not [Col. 1389D] sufficient under the New Law.

IV. Whatever the case, from what is now to be said it becomes evident that St. Stephen recognized as valid only the true Baptism of Christ—that is, one conferred under the legitimate formula prescribed by Christ. For pseudo-Firmilian proceeds to attack our dogma from Christ’s words, calling it absurd:

> “This too is absurd: they do not think it necessary to inquire who the person who baptized may have been, because the person baptized could have obtained grace through the invocation of the Trinity of the names of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. . . . But who is wise enough to defend or believe that this bare invocation [Col. 1390A] of the names is sufficient for the remission of sins and the sanctification of Baptism? . . . The Lord himself makes clear that not all who invoke the name of Christ are heard, or that their invocation can obtain any measure of grace, saying: ‘Many will come in my name, saying: I am Christ, and they will deceive many’” [Note: [Col. 1390C] In the Vulgate it reads (Mark 13:21): “And then, if anyone says to you: Behold, here is Christ; behold, there: do not believe him.” [Col. 1390D] I do not know which edition the author used. I thought it should be noted that in Cyprianic Epistle 72 to Jubaianus, the text is employed for the same purpose in precisely the same words: “Many,” he says, “will come in my name, saying: I am Christ, and they will deceive many.” Likewise in the book *On Unity*.].

Who could be so foolish as to conclude in this manner: False Christs will deceive many; therefore, the Baptism of Christ conferred by a heretic is invalid?

52. After our theologian had drawn his conclusion, he immediately strays elsewhere and, in chap. 5, in order to astound the curious reader, introduces accounts wholly irrelevant to the present question. Yet in doing so, he carelessly collides most grievously with chronology [Col. 1390B]:

> “I wish, however, to explain to you also an event which occurred among us and pertains to this very subject. For about twenty-two years ago, in the times after the emperor Alexander, many conflicts and afflictions occurred, whether commonly to all people or privately to Christians. There were earthquakes also.”

I. St. Firmilian was already a bishop in Cappadocia under the emperor Alexander, who died in April 235 [Note: [Col. 1390D] Eusebius, see book VI, chaps. 26 and 31, where he reports concerning him that he had known Firmilian’s principal fellow students, Gregory and Athenodorus, bishops of Pontus, who were still surviving in his own time.]. Therefore, he was a bishop at the time when that event is said to have occurred among the Cappadocians. Consequently, if St. Firmilian had been the author of this letter, he would have named the emperor—for example, Maximinus, under whom those conflicts occurred, whether commonly . . . or privately—and would not have said: “In the times after Alexander” [Note: [Col. 1390D] This argument presses especially hard if the letter was sent to St. Cyprian in the name of the whole council, as several affirm. Could none of those bishops determine the time at which those very recent events had occurred?].

[Col. 1390C] II. This vague expression, “in the times after Alexander,” denotes that the event occurred at some time after Alexander’s death. And in fact those afflictions, as we shall hear in the following section, did not occur until several years after Alexander’s death. But that letter of Firmilian is said to have been written in 256. Behold! Therefore, twenty-two years did not intervene between those afflictions and the time at which the letter was written. Yet let us gratuitously concede that those afflictions began in the same year, 235, in which Alexander died, and indeed immediately after his death; let us concede that those twenty-two years were reckoned from the very beginning [Note: [Col. 1390D] They are said to have been many in number, yet what they were or what kind is not added. Furthermore, the earthquakes were very numerous and frequent. Fleury, book VI, §1, and Pagi assigned those earthquakes to the year 235, relying upon [Col. 1391C] pseudo-Firmilian. Selvaggi, book I, chap. 9, §9, adduces the testimony of Origen, Homily 28 on Matthew. But those nineteen homilies are probably spurious, according to Bellarmine. Secondly, pseudo-Origen says only: “We know that an earthquake occurred among us”; but he does not add where or in what year. Furthermore, I admit that earthquakes occurred in Origen’s time—namely, around the year 242; likewise around the year 202, the year in which Origen began to flourish. See Fleury, book V, §20.] of those calamities; nevertheless, there will be only twenty complete years.

[Col. 1391A] What does Pagi say to this? He says that the twenty-two years must be reckoned with both the first and last years incomplete. But, first, by this manner of speaking, an event that occurred fifteen months ago could be said to have happened almost three years ago—namely, if the first and last years are taken incompletely. Secondly, not even twenty years elapsed from the time of the earthquakes to the year 258, as we shall now see.

53. He continues:

> “There were also very many and frequent earthquakes”—namely, twenty-two years earlier, in the times after Alexander—“so that many things throughout Cappadocia and Pontus were overthrown; some cities were even swallowed into the depths and devoured by the chasm of the ruptured ground, with the result that a severe persecution arose against us Christians.”

[Col. 1391B] I. What were those “many things” that were overthrown? What were those cities in Cappadocia and Pontus? I am surprised that the author did not name a single one for St. Cyprian in that letter [Note: [Col. 1391C] It would have been different in the case of a historian reducing numerous events [Col. 1391D] to a summary, or if, amid the first consternation following the earthquake, he had had to report those misfortunes to Africa.].

II. Eusebius assigns an entirely different reason why, in the times after Alexander, Maximinus began to rage against the Christians: namely, Maximinus’s hatred of his predecessor Alexander, for Alexander’s household numbered several Christians. To extirpate this household, he determined to rage against the Christian name [Note: [Col. 1391D] Eusebius, book VI, chap. 28. He is more to be believed than Selvaggi, book I, chap. 9, §9, who thinks that the cause of that persecution was the imprudence of a certain Christian soldier who refused to wear the military crown upon his head. That Alexander favored the Christians is attested by Aelius Lampridius, a pagan writer, in these words: “Alexander tolerated the Christians. . . . He wished to build a temple to Christ and to admit him among the gods. . . . He permitted the Christians publicly to worship their God. He had learned from the Christians or the Jews: ‘What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another.’” Notwithstanding this, jurists such as Ulpian acted violently against the Christians, so that many martyrs were nevertheless killed under the emperor Alexander. I have added these remarks to forestall objections.].

III. It is true that in the period after Alexander there were a dreadful persecution and great earthquakes; but, first, the earthquakes followed the persecution; second, they were better known to Cyprian than to have needed to be reported to him from Cappadocia [Col. 1391C] twenty-two years later. The persecution began under Maximinus in the year 235. The earthquakes did not become severe before the year 241. Let Julius Capitolinus be heard, a pagan writer who lived around the end of the third century and the beginning of the fourth:

> “In the second consulship of Gordian and the consulship of Papinian, the Persian war arose. . . . During Gordian’s reign there was an earthquake so violent that cities [Col. 1392A], together with their inhabitants, perished in chasms in the earth. On account of these events, immense sacrifices were celebrated throughout the whole city and the entire world [Note: [Col. 1392D] It is more probable that the Christians too were granted liberty to implore their own God]. When the earthquake had subsided, in the consulship of Praetextatus and Atticus, Gordian set out against the Persians. . . . He was killed within the borders of Persia by Philip, his successor.”

But Gordian’s second consulship cannot be placed before the year 241; therefore, between the earthquake and the year 256 there did not elapse twenty-two years, even incompletely reckoned.

IV. Since pseudo-Firmilian asserts that his letter was written twenty-two years after the earthquakes, it must have been published in the year 253, at which time Saints Stephen and Cyprian had already died.

54. “This persecution, which suddenly arose after a long preceding period of peace [Col. 1392B], became all the more terrifying in disturbing our people because the evil was unexpected and unfamiliar; nevertheless, it was only local and did not extend beyond the borders of Cappadocia. . . . Serianus was then governor in our province, a harsh and dreadful persecutor.”

I. In the third century there were general persecutions. First, under Severus there was a most severe persecution [Note: [Col. 1392D] Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VI, chapter 6] throughout Europe, Africa, and Asia, down to the year 211 and beyond—to say nothing of the period of Alexander. Second, there was one under Maximinus from the year 235, at which time Origen is believed to have withdrawn from Palestine into Cappadocia. Third, there was that of Decius from the year 250, and so forth. Where, then, was that long period of peace? [Note: [Col. 1392D] The book of pseudo-Lactantius does not deserve credence in this matter. See my dissertations *On the Chairs of Peter*.]

II. It is false that the persecution stirred up by Maximinus around the year 235 was merely local, restricted within the borders [Col. 1392C] of Cappadocia, since it was directed universally against the clergy. It raged more violently in Palestine, according to Eusebius [Note: [Col. 1392D] Eusebius, book VI, chapter 28. Fleury, book VI, § 3, thinks that fear of this persecution caused Origen to flee from Palestine into Cappadocia, to Saint Firmilian, and that he remained there for two years]. In Italy it carried off Saint Pontian, the pope, as Pagi himself, a defender of the Firmilianic letter, admits [Note: [Col. 1392D] Pagi, at the year 253, no. 3]; and he also concedes that it raged in Illyricum and Thrace. Shall we say that Saint Firmilian blurted out these falsehoods in a fit of anger, as above, no. 37?

III. The harsh and fierce persecutor at that time was the emperor Maximinus, under whom the parents of Saint Basil the Great remained hidden for a long time in the forests of Pontus, as is evident from Gregory of Nazianzus; and I do not know whether Cappadocia then had a special governor named Serianus. Meanwhile, this matter—on which I do not wish to linger—would have to be investigated from secular writers.

[Col. 1392D] IV. Since pseudo-Firmilian supposes that this persecution was unknown to Saint Cyprian and therefore reports it to him twenty-two years later, it is astonishing, first, that he did not add the name of any martyr or the manner of anyone’s passion; second, that he did not mention the more recent persecution under [Col. 1393A] Decius, which had raged in Cappadocia from the year 250 [Note: [Col. 1393D] Fleury reports that in this persecution Saint Mercurius, a military man, suffered martyrdom at Caesarea in Cappadocia: book VI, §§ 40–41].

He adds another highly paradoxical story [Note: [Col. 1393D] More recent writers have inserted this singular event into their ecclesiastical histories: Fleury, book VI, § 4; Pagi, at the year 235; Baronius, at the year 237. To me it seems a fable that should henceforth be eliminated from ecclesiastical histories], namely, that a demon in Cappadocia—or a woman possessed by a demon—consecrated and baptized using the legitimate form:

> “So that nothing might appear to differ from the Church’s rule. What, then, shall we say of this baptism, in which a most wicked demon baptized through a woman? Do they also approve this baptism—those who agree with him [Stephen]? . . . Can it be believed that remission of sins was given . . . where everything, although performed in the likeness of truth, was nevertheless done through a demon—unless those who defend the baptism of heretics [Col. 1393B] also contend that the demon gave the grace of Baptism in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit?”

Moreover, he began the narrative with these words:

> “A certain woman [Note: [Col. 1393D] Tillemont wondered that this story was unknown to Saint Augustine; I do not wonder, since it is a fable fabricated after Saint Augustine’s death] suddenly emerged there”—when the faithful were fleeing from Cappadocia into other regions through fear of the local persecution—“who was driven by the impulse of the principal demons, so that for a long time she troubled and deceived the brotherhood, and promised that she would cause the earth to move. By these lies the demon had subdued the minds of individuals, so that they obeyed her and followed wherever she commanded and led. The woman also said that she was hastening to Judaea and Jerusalem, pretending that she had come from there. Here she deceived Rusticus, one of the presbytery, and likewise another deacon, so that they had intercourse with that woman; this was detected shortly afterward, for one of the exorcists suddenly appeared.
