[Col. 1393C] Among the other things by which she had deceived very many, she also frequently dared to do this: she pretended to celebrate the Eucharist and customarily offered sacrifice to the Lord without the sacrament of the customary proclamation; she also baptized many, employing the customary and legitimate words, so that nothing might appear to differ,” etc., as above.

I. Pseudo-Firmilian reports to Cyprian that these things occurred “there,” that is, in Cappadocia, “almost twenty-two years before”; why does he not say, “They happened here, among us, in my time”? For Saint Firmilian had only recently become bishop in Cappadocia in the year 235. The reason is readily apparent: our fabulist did not live in Cappadocia, and it is impossible for a liar always to remember his own story. See no. 34, II.

II. When that woman had troubled [Col. 1393D] the brotherhood “for a long time,” baptized “many,” deceived “very many”—indeed, “individuals”—and subdued the minds of individuals, and so forth, did no one in Cappadocia oppose so great a calamity? Not at all. For that evil spirit was “immediately” [Col. 1394A] bound; and that a presbyter had had intercourse with the woman was not detected until afterward. Let others determine how that “long time” is to be explained.

> “For there suddenly appeared to her one of the exorcists, a man of proven worth. Roused also by the exhortation of very many brethren who were present and were themselves strong and praiseworthy in the faith, he rose up to bind that wicked spirit.”

I. The name of this exorcist—who, while the bishops, presbyters, and deacons slept, “suddenly, after a long time,” appeared to the woman who had suddenly emerged there—would have deserved to be written to Saint Cyprian in place of that of Rusticus, the presbyter (which is a Latin, not a Greek, name), who is deliberately reported to have had intercourse [Col. 1394B] with the demoniac woman. But does not that narrative plainly disgrace Saint Firmilian the bishop and all the rest of the Catholic clergy? We have the presbyter and deacon whose intercourse with the woman was detected shortly afterward; yet no bishop, presbyter, or deacon who opposed the woman appears. A single anonymous exorcist rose up. But:

II. In the third century, among the Greeks there were not yet exorcists [Note: [Col. 1394D] Among the Latin Romans, however, the first mention of exorcists occurs in a letter of Pope Cornelius written around the year 251 and reported in Eusebius, book VII, chapter 43] who possessed a special order among the minor clergy. See Bingham, book III, chapter 4, §§ 1–2. At that time any Christian cast out demons when encountered, not only from human beings but also from beasts and from places dedicated to the devil, as Origen testifies in book VII of *Against Celsus*, published around the year 253. Saint Cyprian agrees in his letter to Donatus, which is genuine, chapter 6.

[Col. 1394C] After arguing against Stephen from Paul’s words, “As many of you as have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ,” he adds:

> “Let us now briefly run through the other matters that were stated by you abundantly and most fully, especially since Rogatianus, our dearest deacon, is hastening to return to you.”

He then wanders through the Psalms and the Song of Songs, in order to gather from them new arguments for his Anabaptism, or to repeat the arguments that he simultaneously asserts had already been stated “abundantly and most fully” by the Africans. I am weary of following him, since above, p. 34, we have sufficiently examined that excuse drawn from the impatience of a messenger in haste.

Chapter 7. In his anger, he dashes himself against the rock. The Catholics—as is evident from Saint Augustine—constantly opposed to the Donatists and other Anabaptists the tradition of the Roman Church. [Col. 1394D] Let us see how pseudo-Firmilian attempted to demolish this argument. He sets himself up and, speaking abusively against the Catholics in the name of the rebaptizing bishops, declares:

> “What error and how great a blindness in him who says that remission of sins can be given among the synagogues of heretics, and who does not remain upon the foundation of the one Church, which was once established by Christ upon the rock! The power of remitting sins was given to the Apostles, to the churches established by those whom Christ sent, and [Col. 1395A] to the bishops who succeeded them by vicarious ordination [Note: [Col. 1395D] The author of the Cyprianic letters speaks in the same manner in letter 116: ‘the rulers who succeed the Apostles by vicarious ordination.’ In the pseudo-synod of Carthage, no. 87, the rebaptizing bishops say: ‘the Apostles whom we have succeeded.’ Those phrases do not occur among the other holy Fathers. See, however, Bingham, *On Origins*, or *Ecclesiastical Antiquities*, book II, chapter 2, § 2; Selvaggi, *On Christian Antiquities*, book I, chapter 12, § 4, no. 2]. What else are our adversaries but the sacrilegious Korah, Dathan, and Abiram, destined to suffer the same punishments as they? And on this point I am rightly indignant at this so open and manifest folly of Stephen: although he thus glories in the position of his episcopate and contends that he holds the succession of Peter, upon whom the foundations of the Church were placed, he introduces many other rocks and establishes new structures of many churches when, on his own authority, he maintains that Baptism exists there.”

I. The author of the letters of Cyprian and Firmilian kept silent about which Apostle he had succeeded [Note: [Col. 1395D] See my work *On the Chairs*, no. 120, where I observed that, of the twelve Apostles, Peter alone chose a fixed chair, namely, the Roman one]. He was so pleased with that comparison in which he calls his adversaries Korah, Dathan, and Abiram that he employed it five times [Col. 1395B] [Note: [Col. 1395D] Letters 55, 58, 73, 75, and 76, still omitting the book *On the Unity of the Church*]. Now, at last, he speaks even in the singular, asserting: “I am rightly indignant at so open and manifest a folly of the Pope.”

II. He wishes us to adhere to one rock, with no new structures being built. What, then, is to be decided concerning the “ancient” discipline of the Roman Church that heretics are not to be rebaptized? It must be abolished, he says, as we shall hear in the following number.

After saying that “the Jews are bound by ignorance and the gravest crime,” he adds that “Stephen, who proclaims that he possesses the succession to the chair of Peter,” is worse than those obstinate Jews [Note: [Col. 1395D] Harsher things will follow from no. 64], chapter 8. He begins as follows:

> “As for refuting custom . . . who is so foolish as to prefer custom to truth? . . . Unless, when Christ—that is, the truth—came, the most ancient custom assisted the Jews [Col. 1395C] in some respect because, after abandoning the new way of truth, they remained in antiquity. You Africans can indeed say this against Stephen: that, after learning the truth, you abandoned the error of custom.”

“But as for us,” etc. . . .

I. Therefore: first, down to the middle of the third century it had been customary throughout Africa not to rebaptize; second, the African churches had until then shared the Roman error concerning the validity of Baptism; third, only then, after learning the truth, did the Africans cast off that error. What an accusation! Moreover:

II. What sort of parallel is this? Christ abolished the Mosaic law; therefore, the Church must abolish the traditions that it received from antiquity!

> “But as for us [Col. 1395D]—Firmilian and the others—we oppose to the custom of the Romans a custom that is of the truth, holding this from the beginning [Col. 1396A], which was handed down by Christ and the Apostles; nor do we remember that this ever began among us, since it has always been observed there [Note: [Col. 1396D] ‘There,’ that is, among us in Cappadocia. See no. 56], that . . .”

The ignorant impostor had most obstinately contended that the question “Is the baptism of heretics valid?” could not have been decided in the time of the Apostles; see nos. 35, 36, and 47. Now he asserts that it was decided by the Apostles—indeed, by Christ himself—in favor of the rebaptizers, and that this decision had always been observed. What a contradiction!

He repeats what he had already said in no. 49 concerning his synod at Iconium; now, incautiously, he adds the reason why it was celebrated:

> “Certainly, because some doubted the baptism of those who receive the new prophets and yet appear to acknowledge with us the same Father and Son, very many of us assembled together at [Col. 1396B] Iconium, investigated the matter most diligently, and confirmed that absolutely every Baptism established outside the Church must be rejected.”

Behold, then, he now recalls: first, that only at Iconium, after a most diligent investigation, was the law first enacted that every Baptism must be rejected—a law which, in the preceding number, he had derived from Christ and declared always to have been observed; second, he now admits that the Cataphrygians acknowledge the Father and the Son with us, which he had denied above, no. 46.

> “We also judged that those baptized by men who had formerly been bishops in the Catholic Church and afterward assumed for themselves the power of clerical ordination [Note: [Col. 1396D] This phrase, ‘clerical ordination,’ also occurs in the Cyprianic letter 66] must be regarded as unbaptized. And this is observed among us: whoever comes to us after having been baptized by them is baptized among us with the one and true Baptism of the Catholic Church, as an alien who has received nothing [Col. 1396C]. . . . And yet there is a great difference between one who yielded unwillingly, compelled by the necessity of persecution, and one who boldly rebels against the Church with sacrilegious intent, or . . . And Stephen is not ashamed.”

The meaning is exceedingly obscure. Did he intend to say: “If those who were baptized by Roman Catholic bishops come to us, they must be washed with the true Baptism of the Catholic Church”? Or: “We do not permit Catholic bishops who have crossed over to our party to baptize”? Or rather: “A bishop who has once fallen, even through fear, cannot baptize validly”? There is so much error everywhere that anyone who hereafter continued to attribute that letter to Saint Firmilian would be excessively unjust to him.

[Col. 1396D] Chapter 9.

> “And Stephen is not ashamed to assert that remission of sins can be given through men who are themselves established in every kind of sin. . . . To you, therefore, will apply what is written: ‘Keep yourself from strange water, and do not drink from a strange fountain’ [Note: [Col. 1396D] This text, ‘from strange water,’ etc., is absent from the Hebrew manuscripts and the Latin Vulgate; nevertheless, it was employed by Tertullian in book I *Against Marcion*, and by Numerianus in the third pseudo-synod of Carthage under pseudo-Cyprian].”

I. Pseudo-Firmilian must have ascribed [Col. 1397A] the power he possessed as a priest to remit sins to his own personal holiness.

II. The cited text appears to have been taken from Proverbs 5, where it is said: “Drink water from your own cistern, and streams from your own well.” How little this favors the rebaptizers will be apparent to anyone who rereads it.

Finally, he appends a very long—naturally, because the messenger was in such a great hurry—and exceedingly harsh invective against Stephen, declaiming as follows:

> “You pollute the Church . . . Pope Stephen! Nor do you fear the judgment of God when you bear testimony for heretics against the Church, although it is written: ‘A false witness will not go unpunished.’ Indeed, you are worse than all heretics. . . . After obscuring the light of ecclesiastical truth, you heap up the darkness of the heretical night. . . . Nor do you understand that the souls [Col. 1397B] of those who come from heresy and are not rebaptized will be required from your hand when the day of judgment arrives. . . . And are you indignant besides? See with what ignorance you dare to rebuke those”—the Anabaptists—“who strive for truth against falsehood. . . . Except that it is manifest that the ignorant are also passionate and wrathful, since, through poverty of judgment and expression, they readily turn to anger, so that divine Scripture speaks of no one more aptly than of you: ‘A passionate man gives rise to quarrels, and a wrathful man multiplies sins’ [Note: [Col. 1397D] In our Vulgate, Proverbs 29: ‘A wrathful man provokes quarrels, and one easily moved to indignation will be prone to sin’]. How many quarrels and dissensions have you prepared throughout the churches of the entire world? And how great a sin have you multiplied against yourself by severing yourself from so many flocks? For you have cut off yourself; do not deceive yourself. Since the true schismatic is the man who makes himself an apostate from the communion of ecclesiastical [Col. 1397C] unity. For while you think that all can abstain from communion with you, you alone have abstained from communion with all.”

Behold: Saint Stephen, who had defended the tradition of his Roman Church, is called a false witness, a schismatic, an apostate, the greatest of sinners, and worse than all heretics. Alas! How great is pseudo-Firmilian’s insolence!

He interweaves the words of Paul:

> “I therefore beseech you, I who am a prisoner in the Lord, to walk worthily of the calling by which you were called, with all humility of mind and gentleness, patiently bearing with one another in love and earnestly endeavoring to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.”

He then continues with ironies as false as they are bitter.

The first irony:

> “How diligently Stephen fulfilled these commands of the Apostle, preserving humility of mind and [Col. 1397D] gentleness in the first place! For what is more humble or gentle than to have disagreed with so many bishops throughout the entire world and to break peace with each individual by various kinds of discord?”

“Now . . .”

If pseudo-Firmilian is to be believed, the bishops of the whole world opposed the Pope. A great triumph indeed, that the Pope alone carried off victory against the bishops of the entire world! But what are those various kinds of discord? Saint Dionysius of Alexandria, in a letter sent to Pope Stephen, expressly testifies [Note: [Col. 1397D] In Eusebius, book VI, chapter 5] [Col. 1398A] that all the churches of the East had come together harmoniously in peace. Wishing to report the principal men among them to Stephen, he expressly names Saint Firmilian.

Berti objects [Note: [Col. 1398D] Book XXXI, chapter 1, no. 24] that they were harmonious only as regards rejecting Novatus, with the question of rebaptism excepted. But this restrictive interpretation is excessively strained. For, first, Novatus was the chief author of the rebaptizers. If, therefore, the bishops of the East rejected the heresy of Novatus, they must also have rejected his new dogma of rebaptism. Second, Eusebius mentions nothing about various disputes between Stephen and Firmilian; nothing about bishops of the entire world who opposed the supreme Pontiff.

> “Now with the Easterners—a fact which, we trust, is not unknown even to you—and now with you who are in the south, from [Col. 1398B] whom . . .”

One might wonder, if Saint Firmilian truly wrote these things and intended to call his Cappadocians “Easterners,” why he did not say, “now with us Easterners, now with you Westerners.” For Carthaginian Africa lies neither absolutely nor relatively in the south: not absolutely, because it does not lie within the tropics; not relatively to Cappadocia, because Carthage is west of the Cappadocians, just as, for example, Philadelphia in North America lies toward the west for us Westphalians. If Philadelphia is not south of us, neither is Carthage situated south of the Cappadocians. Consult geography.

In Saint Augustine’s time, the African Donatists were accustomed to boast that they were situated in the south, as at no. 81.

[Col. 1398C] The second irony follows:

> “He received with sufficient patience and gentleness the bishops sent by them as delegates—so much so that he would not admit them even to the discourse of ordinary conversation. He further commanded the entire brotherhood, in charity and love, that no one should receive them into his house, so that not only peace and communion but even shelter and hospitality would be denied to them on their arrival.”

Everything narrated here seems to me fictitious, devised after the time of Eusebius, Jerome, and even Saint Augustine. It is known that the African Donatists sprinkled a great many lies into ecclesiastical history, especially against the Roman bishops. By Saint Augustine’s time they had already fabricated the story that Saint Marcellinus, the pope, at the beginning of the fourth century, had burned incense to idols during the persecution of Diocletian [Note: [Col. 1398D] Saint Augustine, *On the Unity of Baptism Against Petilianus*, chapter 16: “Why is there any need for us to refute the charges brought against the bishops of the Roman Church, whom Petilianus the Donatist assails with incredible calumnies? Marcellinus and his presbyters at that time—afterward supreme Pontiffs—Miltiades and Sylvester, are accused by him of the crime of surrendering the divine codices and burning incense. But are they therefore also convicted, or shown to have been convicted by the solidity of any evidence? He says that they were wicked and sacrilegious; I answer that they were innocent. Why should I labor to prove my defense when he has not attempted even slightly to prove his accusation? If there is any humanity in human affairs, I think that we may more justly be reproved if we believe unknown men—whom their enemies accuse without demonstrating their crime by any testimony—to be guilty rather [Col. 1399C] than innocent.” Thus Saint Augustine in the cited [Col. 1399D] work. In book III *Against Cresconius*, he recounts many other historical events fabricated by the Donatists against Catholic bishops. That the fall of Pope Liberius was similarly fabricated by heretics was demonstrated by the Bollandists at September 23 so thoroughly that Berti assented to them]. [Col. 1399A]

With regard to the rebaptizers, they had already advanced so far as to say—whether truly or falsely I do not wish to examine here—that Saint Cyprian rebaptized. Nevertheless, they still numbered Pope Saint Stephen among those who had exercised the episcopate without stain; for they regarded Marcellinus as the first Roman bishop in whom, as a sinner, the succession of Peter had failed.

Now I draw the conclusion. If the Firmilianic Letter had become known in Saint Augustine’s time, or if Stephen had treated the African episcopal delegates of the rebaptizers so uncivilly, or if he had merely threatened Saint Cyprian with excommunication, would the Donatists have allowed Pope Saint Stephen [Col. 1399B] so great an honor? Should they not rather have taught that Stephen was the first in whom Peter’s authority came to an end? Surely, therefore, the aforesaid insults uttered against Saint Stephen must meanwhile be regarded as stinking lies, until they are proved from some source other than pseudo-Firmilian. The testimonies of Fleury, Alexander, Dupin, and Cave are of no assistance, for they all believed pseudo-Firmilian. Baronius and others labored in vain to excuse Stephen, for the entire story is fictitious.

The third irony against the supreme Pontiff [Note: [Col. 1399D] In Cyprianic letter 69, Bishop Florentius Pupianus is introduced as having called pseudo-Cyprian proud. Cyprian therefore proves that he is truly humble and retorts against Florentius: “Are you”—the humble man—“who establish yourself as bishop of the bishop and judge of a judge instructed by God, although the Lord says in Deuteronomy: ‘And whatever man shall be so proud as not to obey the priest or judge who shall be in those days, that man shall die’?” Saint Paul is brought forward, who, even in false and despoiled priests, nevertheless venerated the very empty shadow of the priestly name and said: “I did not know, brethren, that he is the high priest; for it is written: ‘You shall not curse the ruler of your people.’” Pseudo-Firmilian establishes himself as judge of the supreme Pontiff]:

> “This is what it means to preserve unity . . . to cut oneself off from charity, to make oneself entirely a stranger to the brethren, and to rebel against the sacrament and the faith in the fury of obstinate discord. Can there be one [Col. 1399C] body and one spirit in a man in whom perhaps even the soul itself is not one, so slippery, changeable, and uncertain is it? But as far as he is concerned, let us leave him.”

I. Behold: he who by divine institution is the center of unity is declared to be cut off from unity, entirely alien to the brethren, obstinate against the sacrament and the faith, furious, discordant, rebellious, slippery, changeable, and uncertain. And after he had diligently accumulated these insults and blurted out everything he could against Stephen, only then did he finally resolve to abstain from further abuse and instead discuss the principal question.

II. Who could believe that this was the voice of some holy bishop complaining about the Pope, his superior? Still more bitter things [Col. 1400A] will follow at no. 74.

Berti [Note: [Col. 1400D] Book XXXI, chapter 13, no. 5], in order to persuade us that this is Firmilian’s own voice, asserts: “Six hundred examples can be given in which the holy Fathers became similarly inflamed against one another.”

But I believe that no example of this kind can be given. Berti adduces two men, Polycrates and Saint Irenaeus, who obstinately resisted Pope Saint Victor.

Yet in truth: first, those two are not six hundred; second, those two belong to one and the same example, the controversy concerning the celebration of Easter; third, neither of them abused the supreme Pontiff. Saint Irenaeus, as bishop, wrote in the name of the brethren throughout Gaul over whom he presided [Col. 1400B] and implored the Pope not to excommunicate the bishops of Asia [Note: [Col. 1400D] Eusebius, book V, chapter 26. Indeed, even those actions of Polycrates and Irenaeus are not entirely certain; I suspect that Eusebius was interpolated both in the affair of the Quartodecimans and in that of the Anabaptists].

Now, as though wearied and exhausted by his abuse, he again attempts to prove his heretical opinion from the sacred writers:

> “But as far as he”—Stephen—“is concerned, let us leave him; let us instead examine the matter concerning which the greatest question arises.”

He then employs the following sorites:

> “We and the heretics do not have one God and Lord and faith; otherwise they would not be heretics but Christians. Therefore, neither do we have the same Baptism. For Paul, exhorting us to concord, says: ‘One Lord, one faith, one Baptism, one God.’”

Everyone sees that this is a sophism. For we and most heretics have one and the same God, just as we and, for example, the Lutherans have one and the same Baptism [Col. 1400C] handed down by Christ.

Finally, with renewed violence, he again rages against Saint Stephen; and although he lacked time to write a suitable letter, he repeats what he had already written above at nos. 64 and 39:

> “And Stephen is not ashamed to offer the heretics patronage against the Church, and to divide the brotherhood for the sake of defending the heretics; moreover,” etc.

Stephen offered the heretics no patronage against the Church. With the Apostles and the universal Church, he revered their Baptism as valid—not on account of the minister or the minister’s heresy, but on account of the matter and form handed down by Christ. I would be wrongly represented as a supporter of Lutherans or Calvinists if I conceded that the four Gospels accepted by us Catholics have remained complete and [Col. 1400D] genuine among them, and that sound doctrine can be drawn from them.

Moreover, when our most holy father Pope Stephen is beaten so unworthily, all of us who profess the same faith are struck in the face; and are we not indignant?

The final statements now follow, and they are exceedingly grave accusations against the most holy Pope—so much so that the vilest buffoon could not have vomited forth harsher and more bitter taunts. He portrays Saint Stephen as a deceitful workman, a pseudo-apostle, and even a pseudo-Christ. This hurried writer employs circumlocutions and heaps up [Col. 1401A] a new lie, namely, that such taunts first issued from the mouth of the supreme Pontiff himself. Here are his words:

> “Stephen is not ashamed . . . moreover, to call Cyprian a pseudo-Christ, a pseudo-apostle, and a pseudo-workman [Note: [Col. 1401D] Because of those three words, ‘pseudo-Christ,’ etc., Christian Lupus, as cited by Missorius, long ago doubted whether Firmilian’s letter was genuine]. Conscious that all these things applied to himself, he anticipated the charge by falsely casting upon another the things that he himself deserved to hear. We wish you good health,” etc.

Who could believe that Saint Stephen called Saint Cyprian—whose name the Roman Church inserted into its Canon of the Mass from antiquity—a pseudo-apostle and a pseudo-Christ? And that the Pope deserved to hear these things?

I recall that Luther too [Note: [Col. 1401D] In the *Table Talk*] called the pope Antichrist; but I do not know who was more insolent against the supreme head of the entire Christian Church [Col. 1401B]—Luther or pseudo-Firmilian. Pamelius, Rigaltius, Fell, Pearson, Baluze, and Tillemont say that Firmilian must be excused because of the heat of the controversy. But then we shall also have to excuse Luther and virtually every slanderer. He concludes:

> “We all, together with all the bishops who are in Africa, all the clergy, and the entire brotherhood, wish you good health, so that, always unanimous and of one mind, we may have you united with us even from afar.”

This is the famous letter numbered 75 among the Cyprianic letters and published under Firmilian’s name, which until now has vexed the minds of all scholars in an astonishing fashion.

[Col. 1401C] Since I seem to myself to have demonstrated abundantly that it is spurious and wholly unworthy of a true Catholic, I believe that we must proceed further and investigate to what sect the author of this famous letter belonged and approximately when and where he lived.

As was detected several times at nos. 23–26 and 76, he rejoiced in an extraordinary and singularly intense fashion because he had found at a distance persons “united with him and of one mind.” A Catholic bishop would not have exulted so greatly on hearing that at Carthage in Africa there was a bishop who agreed with him in matters of doctrine. At that time Carthage could be regarded as situated approximately in the center of the Roman Empire, which abounded in Catholics; Cappadocia was one of the provinces of that same Roman Empire.

At the beginning of the fifth century Saint Augustine had objected to the [Col. 1401D] rebaptizing Donatists, and had very frequently repeated, that their church was neither spread throughout the whole world nor possessed persons united with it at a distance. What wonder, then, if some Donatist finally forged the aforesaid letter, since it also savors of the Donatist heresy?

## PROPOSITION III

It is more probable that some African Donatist composed the aforesaid letter, but after the time of Saint Augustine.

55. I. First part. Indeed, I infer that it first became known after Saint Augustine’s time [Col. 1402A] for the following reasons:

1. Because no writer down to the age of Saint Augustine mentioned it.

2. Because we do not read that even Saint Augustine had it raised against him by the African Donatists [Note: [Col. 1402D] Since in Saint Augustine’s time the Donatists had not yet made any mention of the Council of Sinuessa, at which Pope Saint Marcellinus is said to have confessed his fall before three hundred bishops, Missorius rightly judges that this was afterward fabricated by the Donatists. See again no. 69]. Yet it would have been exceedingly favorable to them, especially since at that time—namely, around the beginning of the fifth century—the controversy over rebaptism was being contested with the greatest intensity throughout Africa.

3. Because in Saint Augustine’s time the Donatists still numbered Pope Saint Stephen among those pontiffs who had exercised the Roman episcopate without stain. But according to the Firmilianic Letter, Stephen would have been sacrilegious, a pseudo-Christ, and so forth—and this precisely because he had sinned against the rebaptizing African bishops, nos. 75 and 65.

Berti objects [Note: [Col. 1402D] Berti, book XXXI, chapter 13, proposition III, no. 6] that Basil the Great, around [Col. 1402B] the year 375 and thus in the fourth century, also taught that “the baptism of heretics is invalid, but meanwhile the custom of each particular region must be observed”; and yet the Donatists of the fifth century did not appeal to the letters of this Saint Basil, composed in the fourth century. Therefore, the argument drawn from the silence of the Donatists is not conclusive.

Response 1. I also deny that those letters—which until now have created insuperable difficulties for dogmatic theologians—are the genuine offspring of Saint Basil [Note: [Col. 1402D] Certain excerpts from them may be seen in Tournély, *On the Sacraments in General*, question 7, article 2; or in Natalis Alexander at the third century; or in Fleury, *Ecclesiastical History*, book XVII, § 14, all of whom believed them to be genuine]. Discussion of them will recur at no. 90. For now, let us concern ourselves with the Firmilianic Letter. Therefore:

R. 2. Let the antecedent pass; I deny the consequence. Those canonical letters, if they are genuine, were private letters that Basil wrote to Saint Amphilochius, a bishop in the East. The letter of Firmilian [Col. 1402C] was public, quasi-synodical, supported, as is said, by two councils, those of Iconium and Synnada, addressed to all the rebaptizing bishops of Africa, and published around the middle of the third century. If, therefore, it ever truly existed, it could not have remained unknown to the Africans around the beginning of the fifth century.

For the force of the negative argument to appear more clearly, the state of the controversy, insofar as it pertains to this matter, must be recalled.

Saint Augustine had objected to the Donatists by asserting that so many thousands of bishops, including the Eastern bishops, agreed concerning the validity of Baptism conferred by heretics; that the true Church is universal, diffused throughout the whole world; and that the Donatists alone, confined within Africa, taught, against the rest of the universal Church, [Col. 1402D] that such Baptism was invalid.

Cresconius, speaking in the name of the Donatists, admits that the Easterners (Catholics) [Note: [Col. 1402D] The discussion concerned Catholics; for the Donatists were ashamed [Col. 1403C] to appeal to the Novatians, Arians, and Eunomians, as to persons openly declared heretics in the East.] did indeed at that time [Col. 1403A] agree with us Latin Catholics; but he adds at the same time: “Some Easterners once rendered a judgment in favor of rebaptism.”

Saint Augustine replies [Note: [Col. 1403C] Book IV, Against Cresconius.]: “If this judgment was rendered by a few Easterners—which, indeed, depends upon whether it can be demonstrated—they certainly corrected their judgment.” [Note: [Col. 1403C] It should be noted, 1. that the holy Doctor wrote against that grammarian in his capacity as bishop; therefore, from the time of Saint Stephen until then, approximately 150 years had already elapsed; meanwhile innumerable synods had assembled, besides the general Council of Nicaea, at which Easterners and Westerners had met. 2. That the works of Saint Basil the Great and Eusebius of Caesarea, both Easterners, were not unknown to Saint Augustine: he cited Basil’s precise words asserting that fasting had its origin in Paradise; and in his book On Heresies he declares that he had examined Eusebius’s Ecclesiastical History with the utmost diligence. And behold, this Saint Augustine [Col. 1403D] did not know that the Easterners had once rendered a judgment in favor of rebaptism!]

In this controversy Cresconius could and should have named some Eastern bishop, or at least appealed to Saint Firmilian’s letter, or rather to the very numerous synods of Iconium and Synnada commended in it. For if these had truly been celebrated in the third century, they could not have been unknown to the Africans at the beginning of the fifth century; or, if they were still unknown in the fifth century, they must [Col. 1403B] have been fabricated afterward. But they were still unknown in the fifth century, as is evident from the silence of the Donatists; for Cresconius mentions nothing about Saint Firmilian’s letter and nothing about the synods of Iconium and Synnada, at which rebaptism had allegedly once been sanctioned by the Easterners.

What, then, did Cresconius do? 1. He appealed to the Synod of Sardica, asserting that the bishops of the Council of Sardica had written in favor of the rebaptizers to Donatus, a rebaptizer and bishop of Carthage. [Note: [Col. 1403D] At Carthage, around the year 256, Saint Cyprian was bishop; later, in the same place, around the year 312, Donatus—a name borne by several men—began his heresy. The Synod of Sardica was celebrated in 347. Gratus, the Catholic bishop of Carthage and utterly opposed to the heresy of the rebaptizers, attended it. That synod was divided into two parties: the larger party—about 300 bishops—consisted of Western Catholics, including several Africans; the smaller party—76—consisted of Eastern Arian bishops who, having assembled at Philippopolis, likewise published a letter in the name of the Council of Sardica. But it is not sufficiently established that even this letter favored the Donatists in any way. See Fleury, Book XVII, §§ 34 and 52; Socrates, Book II, chap. 20; Sozomen, Book III, chap. 11; Theodoret, Book II, chap. 2.] And because it was too well known that the bishops of Sardica abhorred rebaptism, Cresconius 2. added, admitting that those bishops of Sardica subsequently revoked their decree concerning rebaptism.

Saint Augustine [Note: [Col. 1403D] Book II.] refused to place any confidence in this first assertion of Cresconius, suspecting it to be a lie, [Col. 1403C] if only because “the Eastern Catholic Church would never write to the bishop of Carthage while passing over the Roman bishop.” How could Saint Augustine have dared to answer the Donatists in this way [Col. 1404A] if at that time Firmilian’s synodical letter to Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, had been known in the manner now boasted by our opponents?

Nor is Berti’s evasion of any force [Note: [Col. 1404D] Loc. cit., no. 6.], when he says that Cresconius did not appeal to Firmilian’s letter because Firmilian’s successors rescinded the decree on rebaptism. For I reply: Did not the bishops of Sardica also come to their senses, by Cresconius’s own admission in the preceding number? Yet Cresconius appealed to the bishops of Sardica, concerning whom, moreover, it was highly doubtful whether they had ever favored the Donatists. Why, then, in so desperate a cause did he omit Saint Firmilian’s letter, so favorable to him that it alone could have stopped the mouths of Saint Augustine and all Catholics? Why did he omit it? Because it did not yet exist.

## Part II. That the Said Letter Was Composed by the Donatists

That the said letter was composed by the [Col. 1404B] Donatists [Note: [Col. 1404D] The Donatists and Arians were later allied against the Catholics. If someone should prove with certainty that the letter was fabricated by some Arian, I shall not strongly contradict him; for both the Arians and the Tertullianists flourished in Africa. This I assert beyond doubt: that it was not composed by Saint Firmilian.], I think should be inferred from the following considerations taken together:

1. The letter contains numerous errors wholly unworthy of a Catholic.

2. The Donatists, like the Arians [Note: [Col. 1404D] Prominent among these is Philostorgius, a writer of the fifth century and a most mendacious historian. What they attempted in the fourth century against Saint Athanasius can be unknown to no one.], and the other heretics and schismatics, continually imitated the father of lies; therefore we do them no injustice when, with Saint Augustine, we say that they and their bishops often lied. [Note: [Col. 1404D] Book III, Against Cresconius, chaps. 14, 42, 52, 64, 69, 70, 71; Book IV, chap. 28; see above, no. 69.] Nor shall we err if we suspect them of having been the architects of the letter we are examining; for it is as shameless as it is false, so that it could have had no author except a heretic.

3. Moreover, it favors no heresy more than that of the Donatists. They taught that all the sacraments were invalid—not only [Col. 1404C] those conferred by heretics outside the Church, but also those conferred within the true Church by legitimate ministers who were, however, in a state of sin; see no. 49. They maintained that they and the Catholics still belonged to one and the same Roman Church founded upon Peter; and they found it extremely difficult to bear being called heretics by us Catholics because of that difference of opinions. [Note: [Col. 1404D] See Saint Augustine, Book III, Against Cresconius, chap. 3, where the Donatists teach: there is indeed a schism between us and them, but heresy on neither side.]

4. Pseudo-Firmilian employs exceedingly bitter comparisons, the very ones with which the Donatists were accustomed to terrify their opponents: namely, he likens Pope Saint Stephen and the Catholics who agreed with him to the rebels Dathan, Korah, and Abiram, and therefore as deserving to be swallowed alive by the earth. See above, no. 59. And nothing was more frequent on the lips of the Donatists than to call their opponents [Col. 1404D] Dathan, Korah, and Abiram. [Note: [Col. 1404D] See Saint Augustine, Book III, Against Cresconius, chap. 18. [Col. 1405C] The Donatist party assembled at its Council of Bagai and excommunicated Maximian, likewise a Donatist, who had caused a schism among them; they solemnly declared that this falsifier of truth, another Dathan, Korah, and Abiram, had not yet been swallowed by the earth only because he had been reserved by heaven for a greater punishment. They boasted that 310 Donatist bishops had attended that synod. Let the credit for this claim rest with them.]

[Col. 1405A] Furthermore, the Donatists did not agree among themselves; they were subdivided into various sects, such as the Rogatists, Circumcellions, Montenses, Maximianists, and so forth. They endured in Africa until the seventh century. In Europe they revived under the name of Waldensians in the twelfth century.

## Part III. That Some “African” Fabricated It

I suspect that some “African” fabricated it for the following reasons:

1. Because it appears from the points noted in nos. 76, 86, and 60 that the letter was composed chiefly in praise and defense of the rebaptizing Africans.

2. Because it asserts that Carthage in Africa is situated in the south; for this assertion was peculiar to the Donatists confined within Africa [Note: [Col. 1405D] See Augustine, Against Cresconius; On the Unity of the Church, chap. 14; and elsewhere.], since they vainly boasted that they were situated in the south, and from this they further concluded that their Church was the true one, [Col. 1405B] in which the bridegroom fed his flock and lay down, according to that prophetic passage in the Song of Songs: “Where do you feed? Where do you lie down? In the south.” [Note: [Col. 1405D] Thus the Donatists had corrupted the text, whereas, as Saint Augustine has just advised, it should read: “Where do you lie down at midday?” He also rightly observed that Carthage could in no sense be said to be situated in the south. Hence he turns the text corrupted by the Donatists against them in the following manner: Egypt is most truly situated in the south, because it lies beneath the Tropic of Cancer. If the bridegroom lies down in the south, he must therefore feed among the monks in the Egyptian deserts around the Thebaid; but all those monks are Catholics; therefore the true faith is found among the Catholics. Thus Saint Augustine.]

3. Because, according to Augustine, the Donatist heresy was unable to establish roots outside Africa. The Donatists [Note: [Col. 1405D] See Saint Augustine, On Heresies.], like the Luciferianists, did indeed maintain one of their own as bishop at Rome. They sent men from Africa to that bishop to be ordained, so that they could boast that they had union with the chair of Peter. But that Donatist bishop had no church at Rome; moreover, he had been sent to Rome from Africa and was therefore a guest and stranger at Rome, and had to be regarded as an African.

[Col. 1405C]

## Contrary Arguments

### I. Arguments Intended to Prove That Firmilian Truly Composed the Said Letter

Berti, who boasted that he was the first to defend expressly the attribution of the said letter to Saint Firmilian, besides the other objections already introduced here and there, says: [Note: [Col. 1405D] *On the Theological Disciplines*, Book XXXI, chap. 13, proposition 3. Berti was afterward followed by Father John Sbaraglia, who in 1741 published three substantial dissertations at Bologna.] “It is most evident that the said letter is the genuine offspring of Saint Firmilian, for it is preserved in very many libraries, as Pamelius and Rigault testify.” [Note: [Col. 1405D] I revere Pamelius as a candid and industrious [Col. 1406D] writer; I regret that he was deceived by the authority of certain libraries. Against Rigault’s testimony I could object that Berti himself, loc. cit., no. 14, referring to the letter *To Quintus*, says that Rigault is a mendacious writer.] For the rest, see no. 12. Accordingly, [Col. 1406A] it already existed in the fifteenth century; it is therefore false that it was fabricated in the sixteenth century by the Innovators, or disciples of Luther.

R. 1. The Firmilianic letter did not appear in many other editions, as was already stated in no. 12. In Manutius’s edition, Latinius omitted the disputed letter of Firmilian for the following twofold reason, saying: “I, Latinius, omitted it, not Manutius, both because I followed the copies of our predecessors and because I detested the insolence of the man”—pseudo-Firmilian. Therefore, he had not found it in the Latin copies of earlier writers, which were older than the fifteenth century.

R. 2. I grant that it was not fabricated in the sixteenth century by those called Protestants. Indeed, let us concede even more than Berti proved: namely, that the said letter already existed at the end of the fifth century. But it does not [Col. 1406B] follow from this that Firmilian composed it in the third century. I shall reserve Berti’s strongest argument for nos. 90 and 91.

**Scholion.** In the third century rebaptism was introduced by Novatus [Note: [Col. 1406D] See above, no. 42.], and was indeed rejected together with Novatus by the supreme pontiffs and various councils, notably under Saint Stephen. [Note: [Col. 1406D] This is gathered from the letter of Saint Dionysius of Alexandria to Pope Saint Stephen, which was the first concerning Baptism. See Eusebius, loc. cit.] In the fourth and fifth centuries it revived very strongly and everywhere; hence it was prohibited in Europe by the Council of Arles in 314, in Asia by Nicaea I in 325, and in Africa by the First Council of Carthage in 348. In the fourth century Pope Saint Miltiades took the lead, condemning Donatus in 313 “because he confessed that he had rebaptized,” says Saint Optatus, Book I, no. 24. Furthermore:

### Those to Be Counted Among the Rebaptizers

[Col. 1406C] 1. The Novatians, who arose in the third century.  
2. In the fourth and fifth centuries, the Donatists in Africa.  
3. Certain Arians, according to Saint Augustine, who reports: [Note: [Col. 1406D] *On Heresies*, no. 49.] “We know that Catholics also are rebaptized by Arians; whether non-Catholics are as well, I do not know.”  
4. The Eunomians, who were an offshoot of the Arians. Of them Saint Epiphanius says: [Note: [Col. 1406D] Heresy 76.] “Eunomius rebaptizes not only those who come from the Catholics or from other heresies, but also those who defect from the Arians themselves.”  
5. From among the Anomoeans, Constantius the heretic, when about to die, wished to be baptized again—not by a Catholic, but by an Arian minister—not once, but repeatedly. [Note: [Col. 1406D] Saint Athanasius, book *On the Synods*.]  
6. The Luciferianists, according to Saint Jerome. [Note: [Col. 1406D] *Dialogue Against the Luciferianists*.] Indeed, also the Montanists in the East, according to Philastrius.  
7. Donatism revived among the Waldensians in the twelfth century.

All these derived the validity of Baptism from the holiness [Col. 1406D] of the person administering it. [Note: [Col. 1406D] I omit the Anabaptists who arose in sixteenth-century Germany from the school of Luther; for they require the recipient’s actual faith for the validity of Baptism. Since infants are incapable of actual belief, they teach that infants cannot be validly baptized.] There were, therefore, [Col. 1407A] several different heretics upon whom suspicion might fall that they composed the said letter in their own favor. But the suspicion that regards some African Donatist as its author seems better founded to me.

## Arguments II. That the Author of the Firmilianic Letter Was Not a Donatist

If he had been a Donatist, he would not have taught that rebaptizers and non-rebaptizers ought to be tolerated within one and the same Church. Yet the author of the Firmilianic letter wished them to be tolerated together [Note: [Col. 1407D] See above, no. 39.], as appears still more abundantly from a comparison of the Cyprianic letters and the synods allegedly celebrated by the Africans in the controversy over rebaptism. But how could a Donatist, while preserving the principles of his sect, have taught that the controversy over rebaptism [Col. 1407B] was a merely disciplinary question, to be tolerated while peace remained intact?

R. 1. It is far more difficult to understand how Firmilian and the other Catholic bishops said to have attended councils celebrated in Africa and Asia could, in the third century, so very close to apostolic times, have decreed with a safe conscience: “Are Anabaptists to be tolerated in one and the same Church with Catholics?” The Donatists taught such things, as we shall see in Reply 4.

R. 2. The Donatists also disagreed greatly among themselves. Hence there were several Donatist sects—four are known to us from Augustine [Note: [Col. 1407D] See no. 82.]—and indeed Petilian and Cresconius, who appear to have belonged to one and the same sect, did not agree with each other on the question: “Is a sacrament valid if [Col. 1407C] a secret sinner has baptized?”

R. 3. Nothing is more frequent than for a liar to contradict himself. Saint Augustine certainly refutes Cresconius the Donatist continually out of Cresconius himself. One party of the Donatists had condemned the other Donatists, the Maximianists, as heretics; yet it revered their Baptism as valid, and even received Maximianist clerics in the same rank in which they had been established without ordaining them again, while it rebaptized Catholics. What wonder is it, then, if pseudo-Firmilian sometimes indirectly contradicted his own Donatist doctrine? Nevertheless:

R. 4. He did not contradict his general principle. For the Donatists’ principal complaint was that they suffered unjust persecution from [Col. 1407D] the Catholics, and were treated as heretics by both imperial laws [Note: [Col. 1407D] The gravest civil penalties were enacted by the emperors in the fourth and fifth centuries against Anabaptists—namely, if they dared to rebaptize those who had been baptized by Catholics. On these matters see Berti, Book XXXI, chap. 13, near the end; Bingham, Book XII, chap. 5. Saint Augustine, who, according to Possidius, chap. 14, was sent to Mauretania by the Apostolic or Roman See as its legate, clearly demonstrates that those laws of the Catholic emperors were just. But if pseudo-Firmilian is to be believed, they were utterly unjust.] and ecclesiastical laws, although they still belonged with us Catholics to one and the same Church: there was indeed a schism between us and them, but heresy on [Col. 1408A] neither side. Behold, the aforesaid letter appears to have been composed to avert that severity of the laws and to stir up hostility against the Catholic bishops of that time.

That Donatists were not rebaptized among us Catholics certainly had to be very pleasing to them at heart. Moreover, however, they wished to be permitted to rebaptize Catholics themselves. This, in my opinion, was the chief intention of the tolerant pseudo-Firmilian, when he sought to prove that both Catholics and Anabaptists—that is, Donatists—should be left to their own custom. Had such an agreement been concluded, the Donatists could have sung a complete triumph, namely: “Let the Baptism of the Donatists be valid among Catholics; let the Baptism of Catholics not be valid among the Donatists.” Behold how splendidly pseudo-Firmilian [Col. 1408B] pleaded the cause of his Donatists.

For the rest, if anyone insists obstinately that the letter was fabricated by some Arian or Eunomian (1), or by any other heretic, I shall not contradict him further, provided it is conceded to me that it was not composed by Saint Firmilian, which was what had to be demonstrated.

From what has been said it is now abundantly clear that Saint Firmilian did not truly compose the famous and genuinely heretical letter to Saint Cyprian that is now circulated. It remains to ask whether Saint Firmilian published certain other works. Accordingly, let there be:

## PROPOSITION IV. It Is Not Probable That Saint Firmilian Published Any Books in Writing

[Col. 1408C]

### 56

**Proof 1.** Eusebius of Caesarea was most diligent in recording the monuments of ecclesiastical writers. He often praised Saint Firmilian, but did not transmit even the smallest fragment written by him. Nor does Saint Firmilian appear in Saint Jerome’s *Catalogue of Illustrious Men*, subsequently enlarged.

**Proof 2.** The Synod of Antioch, celebrated around the year 270 shortly after the deaths of Saints Firmilian and Dionysius of Alexandria, appealed to the doctrine of both those holy bishops. It appealed to the existing writings of Saint Dionysius; but as regards Saint Firmilian, the assembled Fathers did not adduce his writings, [Col. 1408D] but alleged suitable witnesses who had once heard Saint Firmilian speak. See the Preface, nos. II, III, and IV. This certainly provides no obscure indication that no writings under Saint Firmilian’s name were known at that time.

## Contrary Arguments from Saint Basil the Great

### I

Those who nevertheless labor to place Saint Firmilian among the ecclesiastical writers construct the following argument, which might seem irrefutable. Saint Basil the Great was Saint Firmilian’s successor in the episcopal see of Caesarea; and although he was not his immediate successor, but lived a hundred years later, he could very easily have learned from the archives of his Church of Caesarea whether and what sort of books Saint Firmilian had once [Col. 1409A] composed. Thus Saint Basil the Great should in this matter be regarded as a witness above every objection.

But Saint Basil the Great, in the book divided into thirty chapters that he wrote to Saint Amphilochius *On the Holy Spirit*, openly testified concerning books composed by Saint Firmilian. For in chapter 29 he says: “That our Firmilian also held this faith—which I have expounded concerning the Holy Spirit—is attested by the books that he left behind.” Therefore, it cannot be denied without the greatest shamelessness that Saint Firmilian wrote some books, whatever they were, and that Saint Basil the Great saw and read them. The negative arguments advanced above must therefore yield to this positive testimony of Saint Basil.

But I reply: I most gladly concede the major; [Col. 1409B] but I deny what is assumed in the minor—namely, that Saint Basil the Great truly wrote that book *On the Holy Spirit* to Amphilochius—because, 1. the ancients were ignorant of this book of Saint Basil; 2. its style is not Basil’s; 3. its opinions are unworthy of Saint Basil the Great, as Erasmus of Rotterdam observed long ago. I shall develop these observations of mine more fully in a special dissertation, soon to be printed, on certain works falsely attributed to Saint Basil the Great. For the present it is enough that this book of Basil is of doubtful authenticity; once this alone is posited, the argument advanced loses its force. One final matter remains on this subject, concerning which see no. 79.

### 57. II

Berti [Note: [Col. 1409D] Berti, Book XXXI, chap. 13, proposition III, proofs 4 and 5.], in order to prove that the letter sufficiently discussed above was truly composed by Saint Firmilian and addressed to Saint Cyprian, argues further as follows: [Col. 1409C] “To whom should we more readily give assent concerning Firmilian’s mind than to the great Basil, bishop of the same city and renowned for such literary glory? In his First Canonical Letter to Amphilochius . . . after writing that, by the judgment of all, the Montanists must be rebaptized . . . he says that it seems to him that all heretics indiscriminately must be rebaptized, as Cyprian and Firmilian once thought.” For Basil says: “But indeed it seemed good to the ancients—I mean Cyprian and our Firmilian—to subject them all”—the heretics—“to one and the same judgment: the Cathari, Encratites, and Hydroparastatae.” Since it is established by so illustrious a testimony, with the addition also of Dionysius’s letter, that Firmilian and Cyprian agreed upon the dogma of the rebaptizers . . . no one, on account of frivolous conjectures, however much smeared with verbal pomp and rhetorical coloring, [Col. 1409D] [Note: [Col. 1409D] He is obliquely indicating Missorius’s elegant style.] will despise the credibility and deride the authority of the ancient manuscripts of the Firmilianic letter, which men of the greatest endurance in labor [Note: [Col. 1409D] Morel and Jerome of Pistoia. See above, nos. 12 and 14.] examined after shaking out their moths and cockroaches.” Thus Berti.

**Reply I.** Basil, or pseudo-Basil, in the passage cited does indeed teach that Firmilian and Cyprian agreed on the dogma of the rebaptizers, but he does not say a word about Firmilian having written such a famous letter in this controversy. The principal question at present concerns the authenticity of this letter, [Col. 1410A] not yet the other question: whether Firmilian rebaptized.

**Reply 2.** In the Firmilianic letter under discussion, no mention is found of the Cathari, Encratites, and Hydroparastatae, whom the cited Basil says that Firmilian subjected to one and the same judgment. Again, are these “all the heretics,” as though there were none besides them?

**Reply III.** As stated in the preceding number, each of Basil the Great’s canonical letters to Saint Amphilochius is spurious. I shall present my further critical arguments in a separate dissertation soon to be published.

## SECOND DISSERTATION  
### On the Year of Firmilian’s Death, in Which Paul of Samosata Was Deposed, and the Third—or Most Celebrated—Synod of Antioch Against Paul Was Held

[Col. 1410B]

### 58

Chronologists disagree greatly concerning this date, which I mentioned in the Preface, no. III. Baronius assigned it to the year 272. Pagi [Note: [Col. 1410D] Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book VII, chap. 29.], followed by Fleury and others, pushed it back to the end of 269. This is the famous synod that is said to have rejected the term *homoousion* (“consubstantial”) in the third century; but this is falsely said, as I shall demonstrate elsewhere. Since, therefore, that synod must frequently be discussed in the dissertations that follow, I judge it expedient to examine this date briefly.

## PROPOSITION  
### The Most Celebrated Synod of Antioch, at Which Paul of Samosata Was Deposed, Was Not Celebrated Before the Year 272

[Col. 1410C]

### 59

This is proved by Eusebius, a witness above every objection, who expressly reports that this synod was celebrated under the emperor Aurelian. [Note: [Col. 1410D] Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book VII, chap. 29.] He says:

“Under him”—Aurelian—“at the last [Note: [Col. 1410D] In the preceding meetings Paul had still attempted to veil and conceal his opinion. See Eusebius, chap. 28.] and greatest synod, assembled from very many bishops, that author of the heresy, the Samosatene, and his strange doctrine were detected and were then openly condemned by all; and he was at the same time separated and excommunicated from the entire Catholic Church beneath heaven. Malchion especially refuted him as evasive and obscure in rendering his account. Malchion was the director of the school of Antioch in Greek learning . . . and was honored with the presbyterate of the same diocese. He pressed the Samosatene with his questions, while notaries recorded everything; and we know that these records have survived even to our own times. [Note: [Col. 1410D] I have often observed that Eusebius completed this history before the Council of Nicaea, before the year 325, notably in the dissertation *That Cephas in Galatians 2 Is Not Peter*, no. 26.] . . . Those pastors, therefore, [Col. 1410D] who were then assembled together, wrote by common agreement a letter addressed to Dionysius of Rome and Maximus, bishop of Alexandria, and sent it to all the provinces. In it . . . they set forth Paul’s perverse heterodoxy, the refutations and questions they had raised against him, and also his entire life and character. . . . Firmilian came twice to Antioch and condemned Paul’s strange doctrines. . . . He was now about to come to Antioch for the [Col. 1411A] third time [Note: [Col. 1411D] Therefore, three synods against Paul appear to have been celebrated: at the third Paul was deposed; at the second Paul’s doctrines had already been condemned. Or, if anyone admits only two synods, he will have to concede that Paul’s doctrines were condemned at the first, and that at the second or last Paul was deposed.], and had reached Tarsus. . . . But meanwhile, while we were assembling and awaiting his arrival, he departed this life.”

Then they again describe the life and conduct of the Samosatene in the same letter, saying:

“Puffed up with pride, he usurped worldly dignities and wished to be called a *ducenarius*—an imperial procurator receiving two hundred thousand sesterces—rather than a bishop; and as he walked through the forum . . . he had around him a numerous troop of attendants, some preceding and others following him. . . . He permitted bishops and presbyters from neighboring districts and cities, by whom he was courted, to deliver addresses to the people. . . . For this reason all inwardly groan and lament, but they so fear his power and tyranny that they do not dare accuse him. . . . We have therefore excommunicated this adversary of God [Col. 1411B] and appointed another in his place, namely Domnus . . . as bishop; and we have informed you so that you may write to him and receive letters of communion from him.”

Thus far the Fathers of Antioch. Eusebius continues:

“But when Paul would by no means vacate the church building, the emperor Aurelian was appealed to and rendered a most appropriate judgment, ordering that the building be assigned to those to whom the bishops of Italy and Rome should write as being in agreement in doctrine. In this way Paul was expelled from the Church with the utmost disgrace [Note: [Col. 1411D] This disgrace was greater, or supreme, if Aurelian was appealed to by the Paulianists. Furthermore, it is highly probable that the emperor Aurelian was then present at Antioch.] by the secular authority. Such, indeed, was Aurelian’s disposition toward us at that time; but as his reign progressed he became somewhat estranged from us.”

Thus Eusebius.

But Aurelian did not obtain the Roman scepter [Col. 1411C] before the year 270, as Pagi and everyone else admits. Indeed, he did not obtain the whole Eastern Empire, in which Antioch was situated, before the end of 272. For Queen Zenobia, who had patronized Paul of Samosata, had since 267 forcibly usurped part of the Eastern Empire for approximately five years and held Antioch. In 272, according to Pagi, Aurelian routed Zenobia’s army, recovered Antioch, and finally captured the queen herself in September after she had fled. [Note: [Col. 1411D] See Pagi, *Hypatic Dissertation, or On the Consuls*, final chapter, no. 11.]

From this I infer that the synod which Eusebius describes as having assembled under Aurelian did not meet before 272, when Catholics became free to accuse, condemn, and depose Paul at Antioch. Since [Col. 1411D] Saint Firmilian is reported in the Greek Menologion to have died on 28 October, and the sentence of deposition against Paul was not pronounced until Firmilian’s death had become known, [Col. 1412A] the synod must necessarily have been prolonged at least until the end of that year.

Pagi, loc. cit., and others object that the synod assembled in 269, sat into 270, excommunicated and deposed Paul, but that this sentence of deposition was not executed until Antioch had been recovered by Aurelian; for as long as Queen Zenobia ruled Antioch, she would not have permitted her client, the Samosatene, to be expelled from the episcopal residence.

### 60

I reply:

1. Eusebius says nothing of so great a delay—extending into a third year—between the sentence of deposition and its execution.

2. Firmilian had been invited from Cappadocia to the aforesaid synod and [Col. 1412B] died on the journey. Helenus appeared from Cilicia; Nicomas from Phrygia; Hymenaeus, Theotecnus, and very many other bishops from Palestine. It would not have been advisable for them to travel to Antioch during the war between Zenobia and the Roman emperors, while the rebel Zenobia resided there.

3. Would this most powerful woman have permitted so numerous a synod against Paul to be celebrated at Antioch—in her own city, by foreign bishops? While Zenobia reigned, Paul himself would have employed the attendants mentioned in no. 93. But when Aurelian brought his victorious arms to the city, being at that time most favorably disposed toward the Catholics, it immediately became safe for our bishops to gather at Antioch, accuse Paul, press him with questions, and have notaries record everything. Therefore, the synod at which Paul was deposed [Col. 1412C] was not celebrated before the year 272.

You will ask: How, then, is the following chronological knot untied? The aforesaid synod sent the acts of the council to Pope Dionysius in Rome, as Eusebius—who saw, read, and transcribed the acts—teaches. But Pope Dionysius died before 270, according to pseudo-Damasus, the *Liber Pontificalis*, and various catalogues. [Note: [Col. 1412D] See Hardouin under the year 431.]

I reply: That knot is easily cut. The aforementioned anonymous authors, as no learned person fails to know, teem with chronological errors concerning the first four centuries. One named witness, Eusebius, is to be preferred to them; in both his *Chronicle* and his *History*, Book VII, chap. 30, he testifies that Pope Dionysius survived beyond the time of Aurelian, who was not slain [Col. 1412D] before the year 275. Likewise, regarding the pontificate of Sixtus II, Eusebius is to be preferred to pseudo-Pontius in the *Life of Saint Cyprian*.

You will insist: At the ecumenical Synod of Ephesus, which began on 12 June 431 and ended in October, the following declaration was promulgated against Nestorius, bishop of Constantinople, and his adherents, and—as the ancient annotations state [Note: [Col. 1412D] See Hardouin under the year 431.]—was sent to Constantinople by Saint Cyril, bishop of Alexandria [Note: [Col. 1412D] He had been appointed president of the Council of Ephesus by the pope.]:

“I adjure the recipient of this document by the Holy Trinity to make it public [Col. 1413A] to the bishops, presbyters, deacons, lectors, and laity dwelling in Constantinople; and furthermore to provide them with a copy for the rebuke of the heretic Nestorius, who holds opinions similar to those of Paul of Samosata, struck with anathema 160 years ago. . . . If anyone, therefore, presumes to teach . . . let him be anathema.”

Therefore, if this declaration is to be believed, 160 years elapsed from the time when Paul was excommunicated to the deposition of Nestorius, who in the aforesaid declaration is no longer honored with the title of bishop.

I reply: If we reckon these 160 years as a round number, the date of the final Synod of Antioch against Paul can more fittingly, as calculation will show, be assigned to the year 272 than to the year 269, the latter being the date maintained by Pagi [Note: [Col. 1413D] Under the year 272, no. III.], whom Fleury [Col. 1413B] and others followed.

Pagi answers [Note: [Col. 1413D] At the year 429, no. XVI.]: That declaration was indeed published in 431 at the Council of Ephesus; but it had already been drafted in 429 by Eusebius, at that time still a layman and jurist of Constantinople, later bishop of Dorylaeum, who was the first of all to refute the teaching of Nestorius, his own bishop. Therefore, the final Council of Antioch against Paul was held in 269.

I reply: 1. How does Pagi know that it had already been drafted in 269 [read: 429]?

2. Granted that this Eusebius, while still a layman in 429, was the first to take notice of his bishop’s teaching, it is nevertheless [Col. 1413C] improbable—and cannot be established by any adequate testimony—that he composed such a declaration, and did so in 429, when Nestorius had not yet been condemned.

3. With equal right, those who wished to relegate the final Council of Antioch to the year 270 or 268 could say that the declaration quoted above at no. 97 was drafted in 430 or 428, in which latter year Nestorius, bishop of Constantinople, began to divulge his heresy.

4. In 431 it was publicly presented at Ephesus, as Pagi asserts, and sent to Constantinople. It must therefore also be presumed that it was composed in 431, not in 429, and at Ephesus, not at Constantinople. Why could it not also be said that it was sent to Constantinople after the Council of Ephesus had ended?

[Col. 1413D] 5. If anyone admits that three Councils of Antioch were held against Paul of Samosata, that Paul had already been excommunicated at the second—in the sense that his teaching had been declared heretical—and that the 160 years reported above at no. 97 are to be counted from this second council, Pagi’s position will be entirely deprived of all its force.

## Corollary

Since, therefore, the final Council of Antioch, at which Paul was deposed, was not held before the year 272, it follows that St. Firmilian survived until that year. Let these words be written in his honor.

[Col. 1414A]

## Observations on These Two Dissertations, by the Work and Study of Father Gottfried Lumper

After reading these two dissertations, we encountered not a few things that we judge ought to be restrained by the censor’s pen. First, learned men long ago warned that the two rules of criticism which the distinguished Molkenbuhr sets forth from Dupin in nos. 1, 2, and 3 are not sufficiently accurate [Note: [Col. 1414C] See Honoré de Sainte-Marie, *Observations on the Rules and Use of Criticism*, vol. I, dissertation III, art. II, §§ I [Col. 1414D] ff., pp. 144–171.].

With regard to Proposition I, no. 4, I observe that this letter of Firmilian was originally written in the Greek language. This is certainly inferred from that language’s idioms, which the faithful translator preserved throughout, and which were noted by the most eminent scholars James Pamelius [Note: [Col. 1414D] Concerning the words of Firmilian occurring at the beginning of this letter, “to come together as one,” Pamelius observes: “It is a Graecism,” etc.] and the author of the *Life of Cyprian* [Note: [Col. 1414D] In Baluze, p. 118; see part XII of the *Critical-Theological History*, p. 596, notes a and b.]. There is therefore sufficient reason to assert that it was originally Greek.

[Col. 1414B] At no. 5. Origen, a writer of the third century, will teach our most learned dissertation-writer that bishops were called προστάται (*prostatai*), “superiors” [Note: [Col. 1414D] Origen, book VIII *Against Celsus*, no. 75, p. 798, vol. I, edition of the monks of St. Maur: “But if those who preside in the Church—that fatherland which is according to God, I mean the Church—those who are called προστάται, superiors, and who preside according to the things ordained by God,” etc. Consult Petavius, book III, *On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, chap. VIII, § IV ff., p. 844.]. Moreover, the term “superiors” was used not only by the Fathers when speaking of bishops, but also by those who translated the sacred books of the New Testament into Latin [Note: [Col. 1414D] Epistle to the Hebrews, chap. XIII, 7, 17, 24.].

At nos. 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, and 12. See part XII of the *Critical-Theological History*, §§ 10 ff., from p. 596 through p. 603, and especially pp. 614, 615, and 616.

With regard to Proposition II, nos. 13, 15, and 16, I observe that the silence of Eusebius, Jerome, etc., must not be pressed too far; otherwise it would follow that Athenagoras’s *Apology* to the emperor Marcus Aurelius, the *Hypotyposes* of Theognostus of Alexandria, the works of St. James of Nisibis, Hymenaeus, Narcissus, and many others were spurious [Col. 1414C] because neither Eusebius nor Jerome mentioned them [Note: [Col. 1414D] See Honoré de Sainte-Marie, loc. cit., p. 148.].

At no. 17, I think it should be observed that it is not improbable that St. Cyprian, in the controversy over rebaptism, had recourse to Firmilian, especially since Stephen first disputed about that matter with the Asians and then with the Africans, as the most learned Maran has demonstrated [Note: [Col. 1414D] Prudentius Maran, *Life of St. Cyprian*, § 29. See part XII, *Critical-Theological History*, p. 118.].

From no. 18 through no. 77, the distinguished dissertation-writer attempts to show, from the internal evidence of the aforementioned letter of Firmilian, that it was falsely attributed to St. Firmilian. Yet what he notes at no. 19 from [Col. 1415A] the Firmilianic letter concerning the singular and plural numbers, as well as the question proposed at no. 20—namely, whether Firmilian wrote the praised letter after a council had been held and in its name—proves very little in my opinion. For it can be answered that St. Firmilian composed the reply after consulting the clergy of his own church, and hence sometimes addresses Cyprian in the plural and sometimes in the singular. Moreover, the incongruous citations from Holy Scripture which the distinguished Molkenbuhr notes in this letter under nos. 24, 27, 28, and 31 can in no way prove that it is spurious, since something similar may be observed even in other writers of this age.

At no. 32, the distinguished dissertation-writer states that the reason alleged for holding councils more frequently smacks of the heresy of Novatus and Donatus. What a fortunate [Col. 1415B] author he is in sniffing out heresies, of which I find not even a trace! Furthermore, I pass over no. 23, concerning the distance of Carthage from Caesarea; the singular joy from above, which he reheats at no. 26; and the author’s self-praise at no. 30—all of which are entirely irrelevant.

With regard to no. 38, I observe that the words of St. Firmilian are not to be taken in the strictest sense. Rather, the beginnings of the first more celebrated and widely disseminated heresies burst forth from hell after the age of the Apostles; this is clear from the context itself. Moreover, neither Simon Magus nor Menander is counted among the heretics by more recent heresiologists [Note: [Col. 1415D] Walch, *History of Heresies*, vol. I, pp. 160 ff. and pp. 189–190.]. The Ebionites, Saturninus and Basilides—whom he erroneously calls disciples of Cerinthus—and Carpocrates disseminated their errors not in the apostolic age [Col. 1415C] but only in the second century.

At no. 38, he notes practical-dogmatic errors in Firmilian’s letter, because Firmilian allegedly attempts to insinuate that apostolic traditions, if perhaps any existed concerning this matter, need not necessarily be retained in the matter of Baptism. But let the distinguished dissertation-writer show us where this is found in the praised letter. Furthermore, what theologian has ever dreamed that merely disciplinary apostolic traditions must necessarily be retained, and that the contrary opinion would constitute a practical-dogmatic error?

At no. 39, he accuses Firmilian because he calls human a tradition which the pope had called apostolic. Should it therefore have been called something more than human, or divine? Good God! What theology is this? At no. 2, the distinguished dissertation-writer asserts, without records or witnesses, that St. Cyprian submitted immediately after being admonished by [Col. 1415D] St. Stephen.

At no. 45, he counts the African and Asian councils in which rebaptism was decreed among the spurious councils, on the frivolous ground that no mention was made of reconsidering them at the Councils of Arles and Nicaea, although St. Dionysius of Alexandria [Note: [Col. 1415D] “For in the largest councils of bishops, as I hear, it was in fact decreed that those who came from the heretics to the Catholic Church should first become catechumens and then be cleansed through Baptism from the filth of the old and impure leaven.” Dionysius in [Col. 1416C] Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VII, chap. 5; and in the cited book, chap. 7: “I have learned, moreover, that this practice was not introduced now for the first time by the Africans alone, but that much earlier, in the times of former bishops, the same thing was decreed in the most populous churches, [Col. 1416D] in councils of the brethren at Iconium and Synnada, and among very many others.”] and [Col. 1416A] St. Augustine [Note: [Col. 1416D] “Accordingly, if it must now be believed altogether that fifty Eastern bishops held the same view as seventy African bishops—or even somewhat more—against so many thousands of bishops throughout the whole world who rejected this error, why should we not instead say that those few Eastern bishops themselves corrected their judgment, rather than, as you say, rescinded it?” Augustine, book III, *Against Cresconius*, chap. 3, p. 552, latest Venice quarto edition.] mention them.

Already at no. 20 the dissertation-writer conjectures that the Asian councils are fictitious. There too, as though dreaming, he writes that in Eusebius the bishops of the churches of Iconium and Synnada are listed, praised for their discipline, and called holy and blessed brethren, but that complete silence is maintained concerning councils held there. He does not indicate where he read this in Eusebius; I, however, found rather the contrary—namely, an explicit mention of these councils, but no mention of the other associated details.

At no. 34, he argues on geographical grounds that Firmilian’s letter is spurious, and from no. 53 through no. 56 on chronological grounds; but quite ineptly. For, omitting the rest, I shall note here only two of the author’s errors. The first is his view that the fast [Col. 1416B] of the Four Seasons in September was the fast of which St. Luke spoke in Acts 27:9. This is false; yet he maintains that Leo the Great and the most ancient consensus of all the churches establish that it was instituted by the Apostles. I would certainly wish him to demonstrate to me this most ancient consensus of all the churches concerning the fasts of the Four Seasons, and that Leo the Great must be understood as referring to an apostolic institution in the strict sense. The other error is that, against the unanimous judgment of scholars, who assign only two years to St. Sixtus, or Xystus, in the Roman see, he assigns him eleven years from a corrupt passage of Eusebius, in which XI must be read as II.

At no. 56, he attacks with various petty arguments the story of the woman possessed by a demon who baptized, consecrated, and so forth, and denies that exorcists existed among the Greeks in the third century. [Col. 1416C] Father Goar, on the contrary, teaches in his *Euchologion of the Greeks*, from the testimony of Dionysius and Ignatius the Great, that they already existed. But whatever the case, this much is certain: from the beginning of the fourth century, the power of exorcising was assigned to a particular order in the Church, among both Greeks and Latins, as may be gathered from the Councils of Antioch and Laodicea, from Epiphanius, Paulinus, and Sulpicius Severus, and from certain rescripts of Gratian and Theodosius [Note: [Col. 1416D] Council of Antioch, canon: “Let the country bishops appoint readers, subdeacons, and exorcists.” Council of Laodicea, canon XXIV: “It is not fitting that anyone of the ecclesiastical order, including ministers, readers, cantors, exorcists, or doorkeepers,” etc. The same is established from Epiphanius, *Exposition of the Faith*, no. 21; Paulinus, *Fourth Natal Poem of St. Felix*; Sulpicius Severus, *Life of St. Martin*, chap. 5; *Theodosian Code*, book XII, title I, law 121, and book XVI, title II, law 24.].

The distinguished dissertation-writer notes in this letter the invectives which the author poured forth without restraint against Pope Stephen at no. 25 and nos. 59, 60, 65, 66, 77, 73, 74, [Col. 1417A] and 75; and from this concludes at no. 77 that the letter is spurious and wholly unworthy of a true Catholic. But the distinguished dissertation-writer’s reasoning rests upon a false supposition concerning the inerrancy of the Roman Pontiff and his unlimited, absolute, and monarchical power over the universal Church. Once this supposition falls, it is clear that the rest also falls.

Furthermore, I do not deny that Firmilian wrote somewhat more bitterly than was fitting for a holy bishop, and that he did not follow the standard of piety with complete exactness. But holy men too have indeed more than once suffered something human, as I could demonstrate by many examples. Let the conduct of the greatest doctor, St. Jerome, toward St. Augustine in the controversy concerning the observance of the ceremonial Law stand in place of them all [Note: [Col. 1417C] See Jerome’s Epistles 105, 112, and 115, and Augustine’s Epistle 116, otherwise 97, to Jerome.].
