Here this just judgment of the distinguished Baluze, speaking [Col. 1417B] of Pamelius and the Roman editors of Cyprian’s works, is especially apt [Note: [Col. 1417C] See *Works of Cyprian with the Notes of Étienne Baluze*, [Col. 1417D] p. 509.]: “If they had attentively considered how great and vehement emotions customarily become when the cause of religion and faith is at issue, and had also considered how vehement and bitter Stephen was when writing against Cyprian, they would certainly have pardoned Firmilian this outburst of anger.”

With regard to the first part of Proposition III, see the first two conjectures of the learned dissertation-writer refuted in part XII of the *Critical-Theological History*, §§ 8, 9, 10, and especially § 11, from p. 617 through p. 623. Finally, the third conjecture proves nothing at all to the contrary.

At no. 82, he attempts to prove that the author of the Epistle was a Donatist, or at least a heretic; [Col. 1417C] but the most learned dissertation-writer should remember that he has not yet adequately demonstrated to learned men that the aforementioned Epistle contains many errors wholly unworthy of a Catholic, is as shameless as it is false, and favors no heresy more than that of the Donatists. Indeed, it may even be asserted that the praised Epistle of Firmilian opposes the Donatists, as schismatics, more than it benefits them. For it is evident that it is directed entirely toward preserving unity and restoring the bond of unity broken by St. Stephen.

At no. 83, on the basis of mere conjectures—and exceedingly uncertain ones at that—he asserts that the author of the aforesaid Epistle was an African.

[Col. 1418A] It is false that rebaptism was introduced by Novatus, as the dissertation-writer states at no. 85, since it had already been in use before then.

In Proposition IV, no. 89, he asserts from a merely negative argument that St. Firmilian composed no books; yet he attempts to weaken St. Basil’s positive testimony only with frivolous little arguments. Moreover, he denies that St. Basil was the author of the book *On the Holy Spirit to Amphilochius*, although the ancients St. Jerome [Note: [Col. 1418C] Jerome, *Catalogue of Illustrious Men*, chap. 116.] and Theodoret [Note: [Col. 1418C] Theodoret, *Dialogue* I, vol. IV, p. 40; Hadrian I, Epistle to Charlemagne, and *On Images*, chap. 8; St. John Damascene, Oration I *On Images*, p. 318, [Col. 1418D] vol. I.], and all more recent critics without exception, attribute the praised book to St. Basil the Great. At no. 91, reply III, he finally carries his audacity so far that he does not blush to affirm that every one of St. Basil the Great’s canonical epistles to St. Amphilochius is spurious.

[Col. 1418B] At no. 14, he notes that he considers the entire history of those who rebaptized to have been interpolated, or falsely attributed to Eusebius.

At no. 45, he professes the same opinion concerning book VII, chapter—not 3, as he cites it, but 4—saying thus of Eusebius: “But elsewhere I shall show specifically that this passage of Eusebius is interpolated.” Finally, at no. 71, he judges as follows: “Indeed, those events concerning Polycrates and Irenaeus are not altogether certain; I suspect that Eusebius was interpolated both in the controversy over the Quartodecimans and in that over the Anabaptists.” If these critical judgments of our most distinguished dissertation-writer prevail, it will certainly be all over with the finest monuments of antiquity and with all historical credibility.

We do not consider it worth the trouble to discuss at length here what the most learned Molckenbuhr sets forth in his other dissertation [Col. 1418C] concerning the year of St. Firmilian’s death, in which Paul of Samosata was deposed, and concerning the third Council of Antioch, held only in the year 272. See the final section of the present part XIII of the *Critical-Theological History*, where we have treated expressly of the Councils of Antioch in the case of Paul of Samosata. Here I observe only that the commonly accepted opinion today is that Pope Dionysius died either in 268 or certainly in 269, and that the opinion maintaining that he was still alive in 275 has been rejected by all scholars.

[Col. 1417]

# Annals of the African Church in the Age of Cyprian  
## By Morcelli

# The Christian Year 243  
## Donatus, Bishop of Carthage

### I

On the Kalends of January, Gaius Julius Arrianus and Aemilius Papus assumed the consulship, at a time when Gordian Augustus was defeating the Persians in the East. Yet a more important [Col. 1418D] and glorious victory in the annals of the African Church appears to have been won that year by the presbyter Caecilius over the great Cyprian.

For the deacon Pontius—who writes that Cyprian, in the year 243, was “still a neophyte” (*Life of Cyprian*, no. 5; see the Bollandists, vol. III, September, [Col. 1419A] p. 197) and, “as was thought, a novice,” and was later elected by God’s judgment and the people’s favor to the office of the priesthood and the rank of the episcopate—also indicates that Cyprian accomplished many things before his priesthood which require a longer span of time and show that he had submitted himself to his teacher at an earlier date (*ibid.*, nos. 2 and 3).

This teacher was Caecilius, whom Octavius and Minucius had once led from the haunts of idolatry into the bosom of the Church: “a righteous man of praiseworthy memory,” as Pontius calls him (*ibid.*, no. 4), “and at that time a presbyter both in age and in honor,” whose companionship Cyprian enjoyed.

Cyprian, scarcely able to endure this instruction, had long resisted, believing it impossible to cast off his old habits and enter upon that distinctive mode of life which was being proposed. For he later described his own turmoil in these words [Col. 1419B] in his letter to Donatus:

> When I lay in darkness and blind night, and when, wavering and uncertain, I was tossed upon the sea of this turbulent world and drifted with wandering steps—ignorant of my own life, estranged from truth and light—I thought it entirely difficult and hard, given my conduct at that time, to do what divine mercy promised me for my salvation: that a person could be born anew; and that, being brought to life in a new life through the bath of saving water, he could put off what he had previously been and, although the structure of his body remained, change the person in spirit and mind. “How,” I said, “is so great a conversion possible?”

Nevertheless, with God as its author, Caecilius prevailed and gave the Church such a man as, in the wretched and disastrous times already impending, she could have wished for more readily than hoped for: a man outstanding not only in ability [Col. 1419C] and learning, but especially admirable in counsel, wisdom, and constancy.

Cyprian, however, now considered himself not defeated but vindicated into liberty. Henceforth he wished to be called Caecilius Cyprianus after the name of his patron, whom, as Pontius says, “he loved with every honor and all observance, regarding him with dutiful veneration, no longer merely as a friend and equal of his soul, but as the parent of his new life.”

### II

[Col. 1419D] We know from a letter which Cyprian once wrote in exile to the clergy of Carthage that he was then an inhabitant of Carthage. For, indicating that he longed to return, he says: “Where, indeed, could it be better or more joyful for me than there, where God willed me to believe and to grow?” (Epistle XXXVI).

But these very words suggest that he was born elsewhere. Yet I would not suppose his native land to have been very distant, since he owned gardens near Carthage (Pontius, *Life*, no. 15), which, together with his estates, he sold that year so that with the money obtained he might relieve the poverty of the needy (*ibid.*, no. 2).

# The Christian Year 244  
## Donatus, Bishop of Carthage

### I

This year is marked by the consuls Peregrinus and Fulvius Aemilianus. It was disastrous for the Republic because of the murder of Gordian Augustus. Philip himself, who next assumed the imperial power, was said to have been responsible for it, although he was already believed at that time to be a Christian. Because of so great a crime, when he wished that year to be present at Antioch at the Christians’ sacred assembly, he is said to have been rejected [Col. 1420A] by Bishop Babylas (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VI, chap. 34). John Chrysostom adorned this constancy of Babylas with exceptional praises (*Works*, vol. II, p. 545).

### II

Meanwhile, Cyprian at Carthage was wholly devoted to the study of the divine Scriptures, so that he excelled in Christian doctrine as greatly as he excelled in the liberal arts and secular disciplines. Jerome testifies (*On Illustrious Men*, chap. 53) that, among the other writings of the Fathers, he continually read Tertullian. Jerome says that he learned this from an aged man of Concordia, who in his youth had heard it at Rome from Cyprian’s secretary. The latter was accustomed to report that “Cyprian never allowed a single day to pass without reading Tertullian, and frequently said to him: ‘Give me the master,’ meaning Tertullian.”

From him, nevertheless, Cyprian learned to select whatever good he contained in such a way that he prudently [Col. 1420B] rejected the bad, and later frequently refuted it while suppressing the author’s name.

# The Christian Year 245  
## Donatus, Bishop of Carthage

The emperor Marcus Julius Philippus and Tiberius Fabius Titianus entered upon the consulship.

Tertullian is thought to have died this year. At any rate, according to Jerome’s testimony (*On Illustrious Men*, chap. 53), he is said to have lived into extreme old age. Until the middle of his life he was a Catholic; thereafter a Montanist; and toward the end even a heresiarch. [Col. 1420C]

Would that those who favor the memory of so great a writer, and who believe that he eventually returned to a sound condition, could confirm this by some evidence or by some certain authority of the ancients! On the contrary, there are no traces of a repentant spirit in his writings. His sect continued down to Augustine’s time, and the memory of his fall and defection still persists. Thus he appears plainly to have met the end toward which he had long been led by his obstinacy and contempt for the Catholic Church.

Have we not, even in our own age, seen men with similar beginnings flourish in character and learning, men who had often guided others toward upright living, yet whose final years we lamented as swept away and disfigured by partisan zeal and the breezes of popular favor, despite the fruitless efforts of good men who wished to recall them to the counsels of their former life? This, surely, is the punishment divinely appointed for pride: that it voluntarily brings destruction upon itself.

# The Christian Year 246  
## Donatus, Bishop of Carthage

[Col. 1420D] The consuls Bruttius Praesens and Nummius Albinus opened the year; but we are entirely ignorant of which governors Africa had at that time.

Cyprian, however, having now been engaged with the sacred Scriptures for two years, showed himself equally prepared to defend religion and to bring his conduct into conformity with it. For in this year he began his writing career with that highly ornate and polished *Epistle to Donatus*, his friend. In it he depicts the errors of his former life, extols the power of the Baptism he had received, and, by recalling the grace of the divine benefit, reveals how great human vices are and from what great dangers he had been rescued.

Cyprian, however, being fresh from the school and not yet forgetful of a certain artificial brilliance, treated these matters in a style which, once he had become devoted to gravity, [Col. 1421A] he never used afterward. Augustine calls it “a frothy circuit of words,” criticizing this first work of Cyprian as follows (*On Christian Doctrine*, book IV, chap. 14):

> There is something of this sort in an epistle of the most blessed Cyprian. I think it either happened for this reason or was done deliberately, so that posterity might know what sort of language the soundness of Christian doctrine recalled from such excess and restrained within a graver and more modest eloquence—the kind that is safely loved and devoutly pursued in his subsequent writings, but is very difficult to attain.

# The Christian Year 247  
## Donatus, Bishop of Carthage

### I

[Col. 1421B] The consuls were the emperor Marcus Julius Philippus for the second time and Marcus Julius Philippus Caesar, son of the Augustus, who himself was also named Augustus by the senate near the end of the year.

The book of Cyprian now entitled *On the Vanity of Idols* appears to belong to this year. Formerly, however, it carried as its title a statement of its subject matter—words now regarded as the book’s opening: “That idols are not gods; that there is one God; and that salvation has been given to believers through Christ.”

This book, above all, shows that Cyprian had repeatedly read Tertullian and Minucius, since he imitated much in each and even excerpted certain things from each. Furthermore, his learning is evident throughout, including a more than ordinary acquaintance with Greek writers and with all branches of learning. He thereby clearly confirmed that such knowledge is not useless to a Christian.

[Col. 1421C]

### II

In the same year Bishop Donatus, now an elderly man and, as I suppose, foreseeing the future, regarded Cyprian—whose ability, learning, virtue, and religion he admired—as altogether worthy of being enrolled among the presbyters of his church.

Nor can it be maintained that Cyprian was initiated into sacred office at a later date, since Pontius writes of him (*Life*, no. 3):

> There are many things he did while still a layman, many things he did when already a presbyter, and many things which, following the examples of the righteous of old in similar imitation, he accomplished by winning the Lord’s favor through obedience to the whole of religion.

Nor, indeed, may the beginning of his episcopate be postponed beyond the span of the following year, since this is indicated not obscurely in his epistles.

Many hold the opinion that Cyprian wrote, while he was a presbyter, the three books of *Testimonies Against the Jews*, as well as the book [Col. 1421D] *On the Dress of Virgins*, which Jerome twice calls an excellent volume—in his epistles to Eustochium and to Demetrias. Certain expressions employed by Cyprian in these works also support this opinion.

# The Christian Year 248  
## Cyprian, Bishop of Carthage

### I

Once again the consulship was held by the Augusti: Philip the father for the third time and Philip the son for the second.

There is no doubt that the Augusti were appointed consuls again this year principally because it was the thousandth year from the founding of the City. On that account, extremely elaborate games were held on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May, the day on which the thousand-and-first year began, and likewise on the following nine days. Distributions were also made to the people by [Col. 1422A] the Augusti, and none of the things known to have been done on other occasions during the Secular Games was omitted.

### II

In that same year, however, the Church of Carthage lost Bishop Donatus. Antiquity has concealed almost all his deeds in oblivion and has thereby deprived us of his praises. For nothing concerning him has reached us apart from his condemnation of a particular heretic, which we recalled above.

Nevertheless, it must be judged that it was not without his labors and merits that, not long after his death, the presbyters and deacons of the Roman Church, writing to Cyprian, commended the Church of Carthage—recently governed by Donatus—with this splendid praise: “We know,” they say, “the faith of the Church of Carthage; we know its discipline; we know [Col. 1422B] its humility” (Epistle 30 among Cyprian’s letters).

### III

After the death of Donatus, when a successor was to be chosen, the eyes of the whole Christian people turned toward Cyprian, and he alone seemed especially suitable to be entrusted with that most extensive church. When he perceived this, he began to withdraw from public view in order to avoid the episcopate.

> When the whole people, with the Lord’s inspiration, rushed forward in love and honor for him, he humbly withdrew, yielding to his elders and judging himself unworthy of the title of so great an honor.

So says Pontius (*Life of Cyprian*, no. 5).

But this modesty increased the people’s zeal. The same author continues:

> A numerous brotherhood had surrounded the doors of the house, and anxious love moved about every entrance. Escape was therefore cut off, and the people’s will had to be obeyed. [Col. 1422C] They had anxiously awaited his coming, and at last received him when he came with exultant joy.

Yet amid that supreme harmony of souls, we know that five presbyters opposed Cyprian. They later devised many further things against him (Cyprian, Epistle 40), and were never appeased by his gentleness, his example, or his kindnesses.

> I say it unwillingly, but I must say it. Certain men resisted him—even so that he might prevail. Yet with what gentleness, patience, and benevolence he indulged them; with what clemency he forgave them! He later counted them among his closest friends and intimates, to the astonishment of many. For to whom could such forgetfulness in so retentive a mind fail to be a marvel?

So says Pontius (*ibid.*, no. 5).

# The Christian Year 249  
## Cyprian, Bishop of Carthage

[Col. 1422D]

### I

The consuls who entered office were Fulvius Aemilianus for the second time and Vettius Aquilinus.

This year was altogether sorrowful for the Church. The two Augusti named Philip, under whose favor the Christian cause had been safe, were killed by a military faction, and supreme imperial power was transferred to Decius, whom public authority armed with every resource while he burned with hatred against the Christians.

### II

Nevertheless, the whole year passed peacefully in Africa, and Cyprian was able to devote himself assiduously to instructing the people and to give responses concerning matters of duty to bishops who consulted him.

Eucratius, bishop of Thenae, had written to him about an actor who, after professing himself a Christian at Thenae, continued to practice acting, and had asked whether this ought to be tolerated. [Col. 1423A] Cyprian replied (Epistle 61) that this man, since he was a master and teacher not in the education but in the destruction of boys, ought not to be admitted to communion with the Church. For it seemed consistent neither with the divine majesty nor with evangelical discipline that the modesty and honor of the Church should be defiled by so disgraceful and infamous a contagion.

> Let no one excuse himself on the ground that he has personally withdrawn from the theater, while nevertheless teaching it to others. For he cannot be considered to have withdrawn if he appoints substitutes and provides numerous successors in place of himself alone, contrary to God’s ordinance—training and teaching how a male may be broken down into a female, how sex may be changed by art, and how the devil, who stains God’s creation, may be pleased through the sins of a corrupted and emasculated body.

But because he understood that the man, once admonished, would plead the poverty into which he would necessarily be reduced after abandoning his trade, Cyprian first urged Eucratius to support the man’s need from the goods of his own church. So that nothing might be lacking for the actor’s correction, however, Cyprian himself added words that left him no excuse:

> But if the church there does not have enough to provide food for those in distress, he may transfer himself to us and receive here whatever he needs for food and clothing. Thus he need not teach others deadly things outside the Church, but may himself learn saving things within the Church.

[Col. 1423B]

### III

Cyprian is also believed to have received in the same year a letter from Pomponius, bishop of Dionysiana, in which the latter sought his judgment concerning virgins who lived with men.

[Col. 1423C] For that corrupt custom was already creeping through Africa. It later wandered throughout the East as well, stained the splendor of the most sacred orders, and was frequently assailed and brought into the greatest disrepute by the most severe rebukes of Gregory of Nazianzus, Jerome, and John Chrysostom.

The Greeks called such virgins συνείσακτοι (*syneisaktoi*, “women brought in to live with clerics”). Presbyters and deacons were not ashamed to keep them in their homes or as companions of their beds, though they repeatedly declared that they themselves were preserving chastity inviolate.

Cyprian accordingly replied to Pomponius (Epistle 62):

> Such cases must be dealt with quickly, so that the parties may be separated while they can still be separated as innocent persons.

Then, as far as the clergy were concerned:

> Although absolutely everyone ought to observe discipline, it is much more fitting for superiors and deacons to take care of this, since by their conduct [Col. 1423D] and character they should provide others with an example and instruction. Therefore, dearest brother, you acted wisely and firmly by excluding the deacon who frequently stayed with a virgin.

He also adds a statement concerning the penalty by which those who did not obey the command should be restrained, and finally recalls the chastity prescribed for the Church’s sacred ministers, which Pomponius ought to defend with every effort:

> Therefore, lest the undisciplined be consumed and perish, take care, dearest brother, that, so far as you are able, you govern the brotherhood with saving counsels and look after each individual’s salvation. Narrow and confined is the way by which we enter into life, but the fruit is supreme and great when we attain glory. Let those who have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of Heaven please God in all things, and let them not offend God’s priests [Col. 1424A] or the Lord’s Church through the scandal of their depravity. And if for the present some of our brethren appear to be grieved by us, let us nevertheless remain steadfast in salutary persuasion.

IV. Cyprian, moreover, a most diligent censor of morals, was accustomed first to test those whom he intended to enroll among the clergy, and to conduct an examination of each one before his presbyters; nor did he admit them immediately, but deferred it until the following year. Thus in this year Saturus and Optatus were made by him “next in rank to the clergy”; he finally incorporated them in the following year, when he had already withdrawn from Carthage. For he recalls an examination of this kind in Letter XXIV, which he sent from his hiding place to the clergy, in these words:

“You should know that I have appointed Saturus reader and Optatus the confessor subdeacon, [Col. 1424B] men whom we had long before, by common counsel, placed next in rank to the clergy: on the occasions when we assigned Saturus a reading once and again on Easter Day, and when, together with the presbyters who were teachers, we carefully tested the readers, we appointed Optatus among the readers as teacher of the hearers, examining whether everything required in those who are being prepared for the clergy was found in them.”

If, as I think, bishops employed such diligence and allowed such an interval, they would more rarely enroll among the clergy men of whom they must afterward be ashamed.

## CHRISTIAN YEAR 250. CYPRIAN, BISHOP OF CARTHAGE

### I

The consuls who held office this year were the emperor M. Messius Decius for the second time, and Annius Maximus Gratus. In the very month of January, however, Decius’s fury against the Christians erupted in Rome; and Fabian, the supreme pontiff, was the first to suffer a glorious martyrdom, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of February. As Cyprian writes, “the honorable consummation of his life corresponded to the integrity of his administration” (Letter III, to the Roman Presbyters).

Soon afterward Celerinus, a citizen of Carthage, descendant of martyrs, and a most illustrious confessor, was arrested in Rome; Cyprian repeatedly adorned him with many praises. He was a young man, though of great courage, and “for nineteen days,” as Cyprian himself relates (Cyprian, Letter XXXIV), “confined in the custody of the prison, he was held in the stocks and in chains.” When, as I suppose, he was released out of consideration for his youth and returned to Africa, he brought with him scars as witnesses to his confession. “Bright signs of wounds,” Cyprian said, “shine upon his glorious body; prominent and visible marks are impressed upon the sinews and limbs of the man, wasted by long decay.” [Col. 1424D]

### II

But while Celerinus was in chains at Rome, Decius’s edicts had already reached Carthage, declaring a cruel and impious war upon the Christians. An indication of the impending disaster had been given to Cyprian long beforehand. The divine master of the household had presented himself to his sight,

“with a young man sitting at his right hand. This young man, anxious and somewhat indignantly sorrowful, sat holding his cheek in his hand, with a mournful expression. Another, standing on the left, carried a net that he threatened to cast in order to catch the surrounding people. And when the beholder wondered what this meant, he was told that the young man sitting in this way on the right was grieved and sorrowful because his commands [Col. 1425A] were not being observed; but that the one standing on the left rejoiced because an opportunity was being given him to receive from the master of the household the power to rage.”

So Cyprian relates (Letter VII, to the Clergy), and he is thought to have witnessed the vision himself. He then adds:

“And we saw fulfilled what had been shown: while we despised the Lord’s precepts and failed to keep the saving commandments of the law that had been given, the enemy received the ability to harm us and enveloped in the cast of his net those who were insufficiently armed and insufficiently prepared to resist.”

Once the edicts against the Christians had been promulgated, all the pagans in Africa, as though aroused by the trumpet-call to battle, began to roar against the Church of God and to oppose every person of outstanding goodness. At Carthage especially, when the people were seated in the amphitheater or the circus, they dared with loud cries to demand that Cyprian, before all others, be thrown to the lion, because both his rank and his holiness were more conspicuous. A victim was being sought for slaughter—that victim devoted to God, for whom God had nevertheless appointed another time.

“There was preserved,” says Pontius (*Life*, no. 8), “a man whose character, among his other qualities, was spiritually well balanced, so that amid the rebounding waves of colliding schisms he might steer the Church’s middle course along a carefully measured boundary.”

Cyprian plainly judged that, amid such intense hatred from the wicked, the opportunity to be present to advantage and to offer help to his people in person had been taken from him. He therefore considered that he must then follow the evangelical counsel, especially because, as he himself says, he also feared (Letter XIV, to the Roman Presbyters) “lest the disturbance that had begun should be inflamed by our shameless insistence on remaining present.” He therefore withdrew and, hiding far from the city, evaded [Col. 1425C] the onslaught of the raging populace.

Yet even from his hiding place he seemed, in some manner, to remain present and watch over his Church, and to discharge his episcopal office with the greatest diligence: so little was unknown to him or shut off from him. What his concerns then were, and how he fulfilled every part of his duty, we learn from Cyprian himself. For he was afterward obliged to defend himself before the presbyters and deacons who governed the Roman Church after Fabian’s death against those who had sent letters to Rome condemning his withdrawal:

“Yet although absent in body,” he says in the same place, “I was not wanting either in spirit, action, or counsel, but according to the Lord’s precepts, so far as I could, I aided our brethren with my modest abilities. And what I have done is declared to you by the thirteen letters [Col. 1425D] issued as circumstances required, which I have transmitted to you. In them neither counsel to the clergy, nor exhortation to the confessors, nor reproof of the exiles when it was necessary, nor our address and persuasion to the whole brotherhood to implore God’s mercy was wanting, insofar as, according to the law of faith and the fear of God, our modest ability, with the Lord’s prompting, was able to exert itself.”

### III

Cyprian diligently performed all these duties, by which many took courage and, despising life, fought bravely for the heavenly reward. Yet that first terror of Decius’s fury also struck down many. Cyprian himself does not deny this in the book which, once peace had been established, he wrote *On the Lapsed*. [Col. 1426A]

“At the very first words of the threatening enemy,” he says (*On the Lapsed*, p. 436, ed. Baluze), “a very great number of the brethren betrayed their faith. They were not struck down by the violence of persecution, but struck themselves down by a voluntary fall.”

He then describes the weakness, panic, and faithlessness of a great many in these words:

“They did not wait even to be arrested and brought forward, or to deny when questioned. Many were defeated before the battle-line, struck down without an encounter; nor did they even leave themselves the excuse that they seemed to sacrifice to idols unwillingly. Of their own accord they ran to the forum; voluntarily they hastened to death, as though they had long desired it, as though they embraced an opportunity now given that they had always wished for. How many were deferred by the magistrates because evening was drawing on! How many even begged that their destruction not be postponed! . . . For many, their own [Col. 1426B] destruction was not enough: with mutual exhortations the people were driven to ruin, and death was offered from one to another in a deadly cup. And lest anything should be lacking to complete the accumulation of guilt, infants too, either presented or dragged forward by their parents’ hands, lost as little children what they had received at the very beginning of their birth”—

so far, that is, as this lay within the power of the parents by whose wickedness they were betrayed.

There were also many who, to avoid harassment by the pagans, obtained from the magistrates, in return for money, a certificate declaring that they had sacrificed to the gods, although in reality they had abstained from so great a crime. These were afterward called *libellatici*, “certificate-holders”; their policy and deed the Church always detested.

### IV

Frequent letters from the presbyters whom Cyprian had left as guardians and overseers of the Church reported all these things to him in his retreat, [Col. 1426C] where he was pleading with God day and night and wasting away with grief and sorrow. But from time to time he also received good and welcome news: amid that sacred ordeal [Latin *defectione*; reading uncertain], there had been no lack either of courageous confessors or of unconquered martyrs.

The search for Christians at Carthage had scarcely begun when the presbyter Rogatianus and Felicissimus were arrested and, because of their distinguished confession, led away in chains. Others joined them shortly afterward, including certain women and several children. Cyprian then congratulated them in a letter (Letter LXXXI) and also urged them to follow Rogatianus and Felicissimus in all things.

Meanwhile the proconsul Fortunatianus had returned to Carthage and ordered the Christians to be summoned before his tribunal. They were brought forward in great numbers and, when they stood before him, declared with exalted courage that they were Christians. Some were then taken back to prison to await the judge’s sentence; very many were punished with exile and ordered to leave their native soil. Sixty-five of these reached Rome. Celerinus writes (Letter XX among Cyprian’s letters) that they were received there as guests by the sisters Candida and Numeria, who had also gone out to meet them at the port of Ostia and conduct them into the city.

Among the exiles was the young Aurelius, whom Cyprian afterward made a reader because of his merits (Letter XXXIII); likewise Statius and Severianus, mentioned by Celerinus (ibid., Letter XX). The former is believed to have died as a martyr in Rome after being a confessor (Pamelius on Cyprian, p. 46).

Also numbered among them were the presbyter Felix; Victoria, who had been his wife; and Lucius. These had shamefully succumbed in the first conflict, but soon, detesting the crime they had committed, when they were questioned again, answered that they acknowledged and worshiped Jesus Christ as God. For this they were deprived of their possessions and driven into exile. Caldonius, a bishop who himself was overseeing Christian affairs at Carthage together with Cyprian’s presbyters, therefore received them into communion, and Cyprian pronounced that they had rightly been received (Letters XVIII and XIX).

It also happened that a certain woman named Bona was dragged by her own husband to sacrifice. While her hands were being held by those who were performing the sacrifice, she cried out openly (Caldonius in [Col. 1427B] Letter XVIII among Cyprian’s letters), “I did not do it; you did it!” Accordingly, she too was made an exile.

### V

Up to this point the Christians had been attacked by confiscation of their goods, exile, chains, and imprisonment. In April the tortures, killings, and martyrdoms began. Mappalicus appears to have been the first to gain the laurel, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May; his name is still celebrated in the sacred calendars. Concerning him Cyprian also says in his letter to the martyrs and confessors (Letter 8):

“A voice filled with the Holy Spirit burst forth from the martyr’s mouth when the most blessed Mappalicus, amid his tortures, said to the proconsul, ‘Tomorrow you will see the contest.’ And what he said as a testimony to his courage and faith, the Lord fulfilled. The heavenly contest was displayed, and God’s servant was crowned [Col. 1427C] in the struggle of the promised contest.”

For that most courageous martyr died during the interrogation itself, according to the testimony of the confessor Lucianus, who wrote to Celerinus in Rome concerning the death of Mappalicus and the other martyrs (Letter 21 among Cyprian’s letters).

The companions of Mappalicus were Paul, who died immediately after his tortures; Bassus, who died in the stocks, or wooden foot-shackle; and Fortunio, after he was taken back to prison. There were also Fortunata, Victorinus, Victor, Herennius, Credula, Herena, Donatus, Firmus, Venustus, Fructus, Julia, Martialis, and Aristo, all of whom were killed by starvation in prison.

Cyprian’s letter to the martyrs and confessors (Letter 8) contains their praises and was addressed to those who still survived and awaited the same end:

“The proof has been given in the glorious struggle of our brethren, who became leaders for the rest in overcoming the tortures and provided an example of courage and faith, meeting them in the battle-line until the battle-line itself succumbed in defeat. With what praises shall I proclaim you, most courageous brethren? With what tribute of speech shall I adorn the strength of your hearts and the perseverance of your faith? You endured the harshest interrogation until the consummation of glory; you did not yield to the torments, but rather the torments yielded to you. The crowns brought an end to the sufferings that the instruments of torture did not end.” [Col. 1427D]

At Cyprian’s own admonition (Letter 37), the clergy duly laid in tombs the bodies of the martyrs and confessors who had died in chains. The presbyters of the Roman Church also carefully instructed the Church of Carthage concerning this duty, calling it a matter of the greatest importance [Col. 1428A] (Letter 3 among Cyprian’s letters).

At the same time Cyprian wished the day on which each person had received his crown to be recorded, although he had someone at Carthage who kept him informed of daily events:

“Finally,” he says, “record also the days on which they depart, so that we may celebrate their commemorations among the memorials of the martyrs. Although Tertullus, our most faithful and devoted brother, in keeping with the rest of the solicitude and care he expends upon the brethren in every service of active charity, and who is not wanting there in the care of the bodies, has written, continues to write, and informs me of the days on which our blessed brethren in prison pass to immortality through the departure of a glorious death; and offerings and sacrifices are celebrated here by us in commemoration of them, [Col. 1428B] which, with the Lord’s protection, we shall soon celebrate together with you.”

### VI

Another letter of Cyprian to the clergy of Carthage records other martyrs sent up to heaven in this year. In it he announced that he had incorporated the confessor Numidicus into the college of Carthaginian presbyters:

“For you should know,” he says (Letter 25; see the Bollandists, vol. II, August, p. 411), “that we have been admonished and instructed by divine favor that the presbyter Numidicus should be enrolled among the presbyters of Carthage and sit with us among the clergy: a man radiant with the brightest light of an illustrious confession, and exalted by the honor of his courage and faith. By his exhortation he sent before him a great number of martyrs who were killed by stones and flames. He joyfully beheld his wife, who clung to his side, burned together [Col. 1428C] with the others—though I would rather say preserved. He himself, half-burned, overwhelmed with stones, and abandoned for dead, was afterward found half-alive when his daughter, searching with the anxious devotion of filial duty for her father’s body, drew him out and revived him; separated from the companions whom he himself had sent ahead, he remained unconquered.”

Among these martyrs should apparently also be numbered those whom the Greeks still honor (see the Bollandists, April 10, p. 860): Terentius and Africanus with their companions, who suffered martyrdom in Africa under Decius Augustus. Theodosius the Great afterward arranged for their relics to be brought to Constantinople into the church of Euphemia called “in the Rock” (Theodorus Lector, book II, no. 62; and below, year 384, §1).

Had the other provinces also possessed another Cyprian, something concerning their martyrs too would certainly have been transmitted down to us; and it has been noted that even at that time those provinces contained churches and bishops in great number. [Col. 1428D]

### VII

Meanwhile some of those who had been driven into exile dared to disregard the magistrates’ decrees and return home. When Cyprian learned of this, he sharply rebuked and reproved those who returned, especially because, by going back to the country from which they had been banished, they might be arrested and perish no longer as Christians but as though they were criminals (Letters 6 and 14).

Yet he was troubled more seriously by the confessors themselves, who still survived in prison and were supporting with a certain excessive leniency the Christians who had recently fallen during the danger. For the latter, being deeply ashamed that they had violated their fidelity to God and greatly desiring to be readmitted to the Church from which they had fallen away through betrayal, frequently went to the confessors [Col. 1429A] and asked them to admit them to communion and to commend each one to his bishop.

Some of the confessors, however, were so indulgent that they admitted every disgraceful offender to communion without delay; and after giving him a certificate attesting precisely this, they also pressed the bishop to restore him to the Church once he had cast himself at the bishop’s feet.

The foremost of those confessors was a certain Lucianus, certainly a man of proven courage and unconquered endurance, but one who knew little of the Church’s ordinances and the teachings of the Gospel. He not only gave certificates in his own name and in the names of others to those requesting them (Cyprian, Letter 22), but had also offered forgiveness and peace to lapsed persons who were absent. He had replied to Celerinus, who had commended to him Numeria and Candida, women defiled by sacrifice, in these words:

“According to the command of Paul”—that is, Paul who had died as a martyr and had shown himself merciful toward the lapsed—“and according to our deliberation, once their case has been set forth before the bishop and *exomologesis*, or confession, has been made, let not only these women have peace, but also those whom you know to be close to our heart” (Letter 21 among Cyprian’s letters). [Col. 1429B]

Finally, he dared to send Cyprian himself the following kind of letter in the name of all the confessors (Letter 16 among Cyprian’s letters):

“All the confessors send greetings to Pope Cyprian. Know that we have granted peace to all those concerning whom it has been established to your satisfaction what they have done since their offense, and we wished this rule to be made known through you to the other bishops as well. We wish you to have peace with the holy martyrs. Lucianus wrote this in the presence of a member of the clergy, an exorcist, and a reader.” [Col. 1429C]

Anyone may readily understand how reluctantly Cyprian bore this, since he had to tolerate it in men whom he singularly loved and revered, while recognizing that an attack had been made upon the authority of the Church, which he above all was bound to uphold. He was also grieved and greatly distressed because certain presbyters—those, namely, whom he had faced as competitors when he assumed the episcopate—were encouraging that impunity for the lapsed, communicating with them of their own accord, and administering everything rashly and without order.

### VIII

Since matters stood thus, Cyprian did not think that they should be ignored any longer. He composed very grave letters, full of prudence, to the clergy, the confessors, and the lapsed, so that he might admonish each group concerning its duty. [Col. 1429D] His opening words to the clergy were (Letter 9):

“For a long time, dearest brethren, I restrained my patience, as though our modest silence might promote peace. But since unrestrained and precipitous presumption is attempting by its rashness to disturb both the honor of the martyrs, the modesty of the confessors, and the tranquility of the whole people, we must remain silent no longer, lest excessive silence proceed to the danger both of the people and of ourselves. For what danger from offending the Lord should we not fear, when some of the presbyters, mindful neither of the Gospel nor of their own position, considering neither the Lord’s future judgment nor the bishop now placed over them, claim everything for themselves with insult [Col. 1430A] and contempt for their superior—a thing that was never done at all under our predecessors?”

He especially censures the novelty of the affair and this disorderly method of proceeding:

“For,” he says, “whereas in the case of lesser sins sinners do penance for the proper period, and according to the order of discipline come to *exomologesis*, or confession, and receive the right of communion through the laying on of the hands of the bishop and clergy, now, at an unripe moment, while the persecution is still continuing and the peace of the Church itself has not yet been restored, they are admitted to communion; their names are presented; and although penance has not yet been performed, *exomologesis* has not yet been made, and the hand of the bishop and clergy has not yet been laid upon them, the Eucharist is given to them.”

In a second letter he addresses the martyrs and confessors themselves in these terms (Letter 10):

“The concern belonging to our office and the fear of the Lord compel me, most courageous and blessed brethren, to admonish you by our letter that the same persons by whom the faith of the Lord is preserved with such devotion and courage should also preserve the Lord’s law and discipline.” [Col. 1430B]

He then transfers the blame to the presbyters and deacons who had come to them without prescribing any limit and without explaining the laws of the Church and the precepts of the Gospel:

“For,” he says, “to grant things that result in destruction is to deceive. The lapsed person is not raised up in this way, but is driven all the more toward ruin through offense against God. Let them therefore learn from you what they ought to have taught.”

He next accuses the lapsed themselves of requesting too shamelessly something that ought to be denied to those who were neither modest nor sincerely repentant; and finally he shows what restraint the confessors themselves especially ought to observe:

“All this,” he says, “can be done if you regulate with religious consideration the things requested from you, discerning and restraining those who, in granting your favors, show partiality either from a desire to gratify others or in pursuit of a market for unlawful trafficking. Concerning this matter I have written letters both to the clergy and to the people, and I ordered that both be read to you. But you must also bring this matter under your careful attention and correct it: you should designate by name those to whom you desire peace to be given. For I hear that certificates are being issued to some in such a form that they say, [Col. 1430C] ‘Let such-and-such a person communicate with his people.’ This was never done at all by the martyrs, for an uncertain and blind petition would afterward burden us with ill will. The expression ‘such-and-such a person with his people’ extends widely, and twenty, thirty, or more may be presented to us who claim to be the relatives, connections by marriage, freedmen, or household servants of the person who receives the certificate. I therefore ask that you designate by name in the certificate those whom you yourselves see and know, and whose penitence you perceive to be approaching satisfaction; and thus send us letters consistent with faith and discipline.” [Col. 1430D]

Finally, in a third letter, he undertook to restrain the lapsed, who had dared to write to him as though they were a corporate body and the public Church (Letter 27, which agrees remarkably with the teaching of Ignatius the Martyr). He began with the bishop’s authority, which all were bound to obey:

“I am astonished,” he says, “that some, with audacious rashness, wished to write to me in such a manner that they composed a letter in the name of the Church, when the Church is constituted in the bishop, the clergy, and all who stand firm. Far be it—nor may the Lord’s mercy and unconquered power permit—that the multitude of the lapsed should be called the Church, since it is written (Letter 12), ‘God is not the God of the dead, but of the living.’ We certainly desire that all should be brought to life, and in our prayers and groans we plead that they be restored to their former condition. But if certain lapsed persons wish themselves to be the Church, and if the Church is with them and in them, what remains but [Col. 1431A] that we ourselves should entreat them to deign to admit us into the Church?”

After this he exhorts them, mindful of the crime by which they were bound, to display modesty and shame, and to imitate certain members of their own company who were especially commended by gentleness, modesty, and religious devotion. If they wished to receive an answer from him, they should rewrite the letters they had sent, distinguish what each person requested, and also append the names of the individuals. Nevertheless, he also took thought for those who, while subject to the law of penance, had fallen into danger of death. For he explicitly wrote to his clergy (Letter 12) that,

“without awaiting our presence, they may make *exomologesis*, or confession, of their offense before any presbyter who is present; or, if no presbyter can be found and death begins to press upon them, even before a deacon, so that, when the hand has been laid upon them for penance, they may come to the Lord with the peace that the martyrs, in letters addressed to us, desired should be given them.” [Col. 1431B]

These words seem to prove that those who had then been cast out from the fellowship of the devout and were making satisfaction to the Church for their offenses had long since been absolved by an almost private judgment, and required only admission and a formal sentence. Even a deacon, in the presbyter’s absence, could pronounce this by the bishop’s authority after the guilty persons themselves had disclosed the old stain of their crime. For who could believe that these wretched people were deprived of the opportunity, after obtaining forgiveness of sins, to bear a lengthy punishment with equanimity and, before God—which was what they chiefly sought—while placating the Church, to obtain for themselves an eternal reward by humility, tears, and abstinence? (See Francolini, *On the Roman Clergy*, book I, disputation XI.) [Col. 1431C]

### IX

By these and other letters of this kind, Cyprian accomplished a great deal and plainly strengthened the courage of the presbyters whom he found faithful and obedient. Thus they did not hesitate to bar from their sacred rites even a presbyter and deacon from outside their Church who were receiving the lapsed. We learn this from Cyprian, who praised what they had done:

“You acted uprightly and with discipline, dearest brethren,” he says (Letter 28), “when, in consultation with my fellow bishops who were present, you judged that communion should not be maintained with Gaius, presbyter of Diddensis—or perhaps Idensis—and with his deacon. By communicating with the lapsed and presenting their offerings, they were repeatedly detected in their corrupt errors; and although, as you wrote to me, they were admonished once and again by my colleagues not to do this, they obstinately persisted in their presumption and audacity.” [Col. 1431D]

They were soon afterward strengthened by a letter from the presbyters of the Roman Church, who at that time, as they said, were guarding the flock in the shepherd’s place. Setting forth the procedure that they themselves observed in the city toward the lapsed, they exhorted the Carthaginian clergy to employ the same method. They also prudently admonished them that, if some among that number of people should happen to fall ill, they must certainly be assisted, provided, they said, that “they repent of what they have done and desire communion” (Letter 2 among Cyprian’s letters). [Col. 1432A]

Following their authority, Cyprian himself also wrote to the clergy (Letter 13):

“Those who have received a certificate from the martyrs and can be assisted by their aid before the Lord concerning their offenses, if they begin to be oppressed by some illness and danger, should, after making *exomologesis*, or confession, and after you have laid your hand upon them for penance, be sent to the Lord with the peace promised them by the martyrs.”

But as far as the others were concerned, it remained settled and fixed that no one among the lapsed should be admitted before peace had been restored to the Church and the bishops had returned. Accordingly, Cyprian answered the Roman presbyters as follows (Letter 14):

“As for the cases of the others, even though they have received a certificate from the martyrs, I have plainly ordered that they be deferred and reserved until our presence, so that when peace has been given to us by the Lord and a greater number of superiors have begun to assemble together, we may also consult with you and be able to arrange and reform each matter.”

He also showed his own clergy why this was fitting (Letter 13):

“For,” he says, “it is irreligious, and harmful even to those who are hastening, that, while the confessors who have been made exiles, driven from their native country, and deprived of all their possessions have not yet returned to the Church, certain lapsed persons should hasten to precede the confessors themselves and enter the Church before them!” [Col. 1432B]

### X

While these things were taking place, some hope of peace was already beginning to shine; yet Cyprian’s return was still prevented by the hatred of the pagans, who had marked him especially for slaughter. He therefore did not yet dare to come out of his hiding place, although he was now permitted to manage the Church’s affairs somewhat more freely.

Thus, when he had received another letter from the Roman clergy (Letter 30 among Cyprian’s letters), brought by the reader Saturus and setting forth what had been decreed at Rome concerning the lapsed, he sent it to his presbyters at Carthage. He also added the letters he had preserved from the Roman confessors Moyses and Maximus, so that they might copy and circulate them. Hence it came about that a very great agreement among all the Churches concerning this matter was soon established.

Cyprian likewise judged that it would contribute to the honor of his Church if he enrolled among the clergy every outstanding confessor. When several presbyters happened to meet him, he therefore ordained two readers in their presence (Letter 33). [Col. 1432D] The first was Aurelius, whose praises he recounts as follows:

“Our brother Aurelius, an illustrious young man, already approved by the Lord and dear to God, still young in years but advanced in the praise of courage and faith, lesser in the natural condition of his age but greater in honor, has fought here in a twofold contest: twice a confessor and twice glorious through the victory of his confession—both when, after winning in the race, he was made an exile, and when he afterward fought in a still more courageous struggle, a triumphant conqueror in the battle of suffering.”

The other was Celerinus, who counted both his grandmother, his paternal uncle, and his maternal uncle among the martyrs (Letter 34). As we have said, he had been in chains at Rome; after obtaining his liberty, he had returned to Africa and approached Cyprian himself in his hiding place. He was appointed reader in such a way that a manifestation of the divine will brought him, despite his reluctance, to accept it. Cyprian writes thus concerning him to the clergy and people:

“Exult, therefore, and rejoice with us in our letter, by which my colleagues who were present with me and I report to you that our brother Celerinus, glorious alike in courage and character, has been joined to our clergy—not by human approval, but by divine favor. When he hesitated to give his consent to the Church, he was compelled by its admonition and exhortation in a vision during the night not to refuse us when we urged him.” [Col. 1433A]

Cyprian, moreover, intended greater honors for both men:

“You should know,” he says, “that these men have for the present been appointed readers, because a lamp had to be placed upon a lampstand so that it might shine for all, and their glorious faces had to be placed in a higher position, where, seen by the entire surrounding brotherhood, they might present to those who behold them an incitement to glory. You should know, moreover, that we have already designated them for the honor of the presbyterate, so that they may be honored with the same allowances as the presbyters and share equal portions of the monthly distributions. They will sit with us when their years have advanced and been strengthened, although no one can be regarded as immature in natural age who has completed the measure of his life by the dignity of glory.” [Col. 1433B]

There was, besides, among the most illustrious of the confessors the presbyter Numidicus, whom we mentioned above, a survivor of burning and stoning. Cyprian incorporated him into his college of presbyters and also assigned him the superintendence of his own district as soon as he should reach Carthage.

“And he will be promoted,” he says (Letter 35), “when God permits, to a higher position in his district, when, under the Lord’s protection, we have returned in person.” [Col. 1433C]

After this, in another letter, Cyprian considered that relief must be provided for the need of the destitute. He exhorted his presbyters and deacons to exercise diligent care for widows, the sick, and all the poor; and with no less concern he commended strangers:

“For if there are any needy strangers,” he says (Letter 36), “provide their expenses from my own sum, which I left with our fellow presbyter Rogatianus. And lest that sum should perhaps already have been entirely expended, I have sent him another portion through Naricus and Colytus, so that the work of charity toward those in distress may be carried out more generously and readily.” [Col. 1433D]

### XI

As the year was now drawing to its close, Cyprian’s final letter to the clergy exhorted them to pour out unceasing prayers to God:

“I admonish your religious solicitude,” he said (Letter 7), “that, to appease and entreat the Lord, we should groan not with the voice alone, but also with fasting, tears, and every kind of supplication.”

At the same time he foretold that the end of their troubles was near, having been so instructed by God, whom he had entreated day and night for his people:

“Finally,” he added, “to his least servant—although burdened with very many offenses and unworthy of his favor—he nevertheless deigned, in his goodness toward us, to give this command: ‘Tell him,’ he said, ‘to be confident, because peace is coming; but the reason for the brief delay in the meantime is that there still remain some who are to be tested.’” [Col. 1434A]

By these words, I think, there was signified the internal conspiracy of certain persons that was already impending.

“If the Lord sees us humble and peaceable,” he says, “united with one another, fearful of his wrath, and corrected and reformed by the present tribulation, he will keep us safe from the enemy’s assaults. Discipline has gone before; pardon will follow.”

## CHRISTIAN YEAR 251. CYPRIAN, BISHOP OF CARTHAGE

### I

The consuls who entered office were the emperor C. Messius Decius for the third time [Col. 1434B] and Q. Herennius Etruscus Messius Decius Caesar—

> **Note:** [Col. 1434D] Both are called Decius in the African inscription published by Octavius Falconerius in the *Supplement to the Athletic Inscriptions*, no. 8.

—that is, father and son, who perished toward the end of the year in the Gothic War. As long as they remained at Rome, nothing was safe for the Christians; indeed, the Christians could not even assemble to elect Fabian’s successor. Many confessors were also awaiting martyrdom in prison, prominent among them Moyses and Maximus. The book *On the Praise of Martyrdom* is thought to have been conveyed to them in this year, a work believed to be Cyprian’s, although it differs very greatly from his style.

## II

But the African Church had begun to enjoy somewhat greater security from the pagans, though not with the result Cyprian had desired. For when fear of persecution had been dispelled, the people’s former license revived, and the way was again opened to vice. Not even the confessors were all free from stain and [Col. 1434C] guilt.

“I am grieved,” Cyprian wrote to the clergy (Epistle 5), “when I hear that some are behaving wantonly and insolently, occupying themselves with follies or dissensions; that the members of Christ, who have now confessed Christ, are being defiled by illicit intercourse; and that they cannot be governed by the deacons or presbyters.”

And when writing to Rogatian and the other confessors, he said (Epistle 6):

“I hear that some are corrupting your company and destroying by their depraved conduct the glory of your distinguished name. You yourselves, as lovers and guardians of your glory, ought to rebuke, restrain, and correct them.”

Having learned of these things, Cyprian earnestly entreated the presbyters above all to discharge vigorously, in his place, the duties required by the administration of religion; [Col. 1434D] for although he himself desired it most ardently, the way for his return was not yet open.

“Although,” he says (Epistle 5), “the circumstances compel me to hasten and come to you in person—first because of my longing and desire for you, which is the foremost object of my prayers, and then so that we might together discuss those matters concerning the governance of the Church which the common good requires, and, after examining them by the counsel of many, settle them—nevertheless, it has seemed better for the present that I should remain in concealment and quiet, out of consideration for other advantages that concern the peace and welfare of us all. An account of these will be given to you by Tertullus, our [Col. 1435A] most beloved brother. In addition to all his other care, which he devotes zealously to divine works, he was also the author of this counsel: that I should act cautiously and with restraint, and not recklessly expose myself to public view, especially in the very place where I had so often been demanded and sought.”

There was, indeed, a great number of pagans of every rank at Carthage. By their fury he had even been proscribed (Pontius, *Life*, no. 7) and stripped of all his possessions (Cyprian, Epistle 69). Amid so great a hatred on the part of wicked men, Tertullus rightly judged that the life of the man upon whom the welfare of the Church then chiefly depended ought by no means to be placed in danger.

## III

But while Cyprian was grieving over this conduct of the people, a more serious evil was already threatening from Felicissimus, a wealthy citizen of Carthage and himself a Christian, but a man marked by vice [Col. 1435B] and hostile in spirit toward Cyprian.

Perhaps at the beginning of the year Cyprian had sent to Carthage, with money, two bishops, Caldonius and Herculanus, and with them his most highly esteemed presbyters, Rogatian and Numidicus,

“to meet the needs of the brethren at his own expense, and, if any also wished to practice their trades, to assist their wishes by an additional payment sufficient for the purpose; at the same time, to ascertain their ages, circumstances, and merits, so that he himself might become better informed about them and might select for the service and support of the Church” those who were worthy and especially commended by their virtues (Cyprian, Epistle 38).

But while they were diligently carrying out the instructions they had received, behold, Felicissimus, surrounded by a band of wicked men, attempted to restrain the bishops and presbyters. He dared to intervene so that no one could be paid, [Col. 1435C] and so that no census or register might be drawn up. He even threatened those who had come to receive assistance that “those who wished to obey Cyprian would not communicate with him on the Mount.”

These events seem to have occurred in the territory of Carthage. It is believed that he called his estate and house, situated upon a hill, “the Mount”; it was perhaps then open to Christians, who could assemble there more safely because meetings could not at that time be held in the city without danger. It is also credible that this was why the Donatists, who similarly separated themselves from the Catholic Church, were called *Montenses*, “people of the Mount” (see Baronius, at the year 254, no. 38).

When Cyprian learned of these things, he was not deterred by the audacity of a man who, in reckless fury, set himself up as the leader of a faction and the instigator of sedition. Nor did he permit his authority [Col. 1435D] to be despised with impunity or the peace of the Church to be disturbed by an unpunished crime. Instead, he sent a most severe letter to the same bishops and presbyters whom he had ordered to exercise delegated authority there. In this letter he excluded Felicissimus from the sacred rites and threatened that those who were his followers would be liable to the same penalty unless they abandoned him.

“Meanwhile,” he says (Epistle 38), “since Felicissimus has threatened that those who obey us—that is, those who communicate with us—will not communicate with him on the Mount, let him receive the sentence that he himself first pronounced: let him know that he is excluded from us, since to his frauds and robberies, which we have discovered by the clear light of truth, there is also added the charge of adultery. Our brethren, men of weight, have reported that they detected [Col. 1436A] this and have affirmed that they will prove it. We shall investigate all these matters when, with the Lord’s permission, we have assembled together with a larger number of our colleagues.

“Augendus also, who, with no thought for either the bishop or the Church, has similarly associated himself with Felicissimus in conspiracy and faction, must, if he persists any longer with him, bear the sentence which that factious and reckless man has brought upon himself. And whoever joins himself to his conspiracy and faction should know that he will not communicate with us in the Church, since he has voluntarily preferred to be separated from the Church.”

So that these matters should not remain known only to a few and confined within the bounds of that Mount, Cyprian ordered the same letter to be forwarded to the clergy at Carthage, with the names added of those who had joined themselves to Felicissimus.

## IV

There was no delay. The bishops [Col. 1436B] assembled with the presbyters, summoning also their colleague Victor, who, I think, presided over a neighboring church. They issued an edict of the following kind, a copy of which was to be sent both to Cyprian and to the other bishops (Epistle 39 among the letters of Cyprian):

“Caldonius, with his colleagues Herculanus and Victor, likewise the presbyters Rogatian and Numidicus. We have excluded from communion Felicissimus and Augendus, likewise Repostus, one of the exiles, Irene of the Rutili, and Paula the seamstress, as you should have learned from my written notice. We have likewise excluded Sophronius, himself one of the exiles, and Soliassus Budinarius.”

Thus far the edict, in the form in which it has reached us. I would readily concede that more names had then been subscribed to it.

Once it had been promulgated, what Felicissimus was planning immediately became apparent. [Col. 1436C] For five presbyters of Carthage, who had previously attempted to deprive Cyprian of the episcopate, presented themselves as Felicissimus’s principal supporters in this revolt. They are thought to have been Fortunatus, who was afterward declared bishop of Carthage by the faction; Novatus, who soon afterward was the originator at Rome of Novatian’s schism; Donatus and Gordius, whom Cyprian records as once having written to him together with Fortunatus and Novatus (Epistle 5); and finally that Gaius of Ida, a supporter of the lapsed, whom the college of presbyters at Carthage had removed from sacred ministry in the preceding year.

By their votes, as though they wished to repay his favor, Felicissimus was created a deacon. In order that they might have many followers, these same men began to invite the lapsed and to offer hope of pardon to them all. Nor were there lacking those who placed their trust in the betrayers of the faith [Col. 1436D] and deserted to their camp and their Mount.

Cyprian, however, to whom his presbyters were sending detailed letters about all these affairs, attempted in an excellent letter to keep the people faithful to their duty (Epistle 40):

“They now offer peace,” he said, “who themselves possess no peace. They promise to restore and recall the lapsed to the Church, though they themselves have withdrawn from the Church.”

He added words capable of encouraging some and deterring others:

“This is the final and last trial of the present persecution, and it too, under the Lord’s protection, will soon pass away, so that after Easter Day I may be restored to you together with my colleagues. In their presence, in accordance also with your judgment and the common counsel of us all, as was once agreed, we shall be able together to arrange and settle the matters that must be done. [Col. 1437A]

“But if anyone, refusing to do penance and make satisfaction to God, goes over to the party of Felicissimus and his satellites and joins himself to their heretical faction, let him know that afterward he will not be able to return to the Church or communicate with the bishops and the people of Christ.”

## V

There can be no doubt that many, moved in spirit by this letter from their bishop, came to their senses and, changing their resolution, rejected the schism. For all held his courage in the highest admiration and revered his authority.

Thereafter Cyprian, who had remained in concealment for more than fourteen months, returned to his church when affairs had become largely tranquil, and blessed the whole clergy and people with his presence and address. At the same time, bishops from every quarter assembled at Carthage to debate with him in council the most serious affairs [Col. 1437B] of the Church.

First, it had to be determined by the common judgment of all in what order and by what method the lapsed ought to be received into the Church. This matter had indeed been discussed more than once by letter, but there was still a need for a rule that would establish the practice and bring an end to the complaints of the lapsed.

It was also necessary to investigate the schism of Felicissimus and that entire faction of seditious men, which already seemed likely to become the source and origin of many evils in Africa. Meanwhile, Cyprian was preparing remedies for these diseases that might be particularly appropriate at that time. Nor did he labor only at home but also abroad, for he burned with a remarkable desire to assist everyone.

There were two short works which he appears to have composed during these days: [Col. 1437C] the book *On the Lapsed* and the book *On the Unity of the Church*. By the former he drew those guilty of violating their faith toward God, broken by shame, to undertake penance; by the latter he recalled divided minds desirous of revolution to peace and concord, deterring them by threatening an unhappy end.

## VI

In addition to these things, the long-desired news arrived from Rome. In the seventeenth month after Fabian’s death, it had finally become possible to deal with the matter of a successor, and by the greatest consensus of all the supreme pontificate had been conferred upon Cornelius.

He is thought to have been appointed on July 6, when the emperor Decius, who until then had forbidden the creation of a bishop at Rome, had departed for war and Julius Valens had seized imperial power in his place—power which he soon lost together with his life.

The bishops, therefore, who had long debated the various cases of the lapsed [Col. 1437D] and had drawn up the individual articles of their decisions, judged that Cornelius too should be consulted about them. They had agreed, Cyprian says (Epistle 52, to Antonianus),

“that the hope of communion and peace should not be entirely denied to the lapsed, lest they fail still further through despair and, because the Church was closed to them, follow the world and live as pagans; but, on the other hand, that the discipline of the Gospel should not be relaxed, allowing them recklessly to rush into communion. Rather, their penance should be protracted for a long time, the Father’s mercy should be implored with sorrow, and the circumstances, intentions, and necessities of each person should be examined. Meanwhile, those who had obtained certificates should be admitted, while assistance should be given at the point of death to those who had sacrificed.”

When these decisions were conveyed to Cornelius, [Col. 1438A] “he too,” Cyprian adds, “after taking counsel with a great many fellow bishops, agreed with us in the same judgment, with equal gravity and salutary moderation.” The entire Christian world afterward acquiesced in his decree as well (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VI, chapter 43).

So that the bishops might have a rule by which to judge both the gravity of offenses and the appropriate penalty, they also composed a document “in which,” Cyprian says, “the individual articles of their decisions were written down.” A copy of it was sent to all the bishops. In this one may recognize the beginning of the penitential canons, which posterity celebrated once they had been gathered into a fixed volume (see Morinus, *On Penance*, Appendix, p. 3).

The case of the bishops Jovinus and Maximus was afterward heard. It was established that they had already been condemned by the judgment of nine colleagues, both for other crimes [Col. 1438B] and because they had burned incense to empty gods (Cyprian, Epistle 55).

With them was Privatus of Lambaesis, who had long before been censured by Bishop Donatus. All were once again rejected and treated as outsiders, because they had opened no approach to the Church for themselves by any sign of a penitent spirit or any indication of a reformed life.

The case of Felicissimus and the presbyters who adhered to him was similar. For Cyprian calls him (ibid.) “an enemy of Christ—not a new enemy, but one long since excluded from communion because of his many and most serious crimes, and condemned not only by my judgment but by that of a great many fellow bishops.”

He also testifies that he sent the Roman clergy a detailed written account of the proceedings concerning Felicissimus and his presbyteral body (Epistle 42), and states above all [Col. 1438C] that Novatus had been “condemned by the voice of all the bishops” (Epistle 41). It is certain that they were heard in the council (Epistle 42); but when the Fathers were about to pronounce judgment, Felicissimus went into hiding and finally traveled to Rome with his associates (Pacianus, Epistle III).

## VII

From the moment of their arrival, everything at Rome was thrown into confusion, and a very grave calamity descended upon the Church. According to Cyprian’s testimony (Epistle 49), Novatus above all was then

“a torch and fire for kindling the flames of sedition, a whirlwind and tempest for bringing about shipwrecks of faith, an enemy of quiet, an opponent of tranquility, and a foe of peace.”

A little earlier, Novatian, a presbyter of the Roman Church, had been a rival candidate of Cornelius. More distinguished for learning than for virtue, he had been passed over in the vote and bore his rejection with difficulty. When Novatus attached himself to Novatian’s friendship [Col. 1438D] and saw that he was angry with Cornelius and plotting revolution, he easily drove the man—after many charges against Cornelius had been fabricated through calumny and malice—to usurp the pontificate himself. He even found a considerable number of followers and supporters, among whom were several confessors.

Everything concerning this tumult and the wicked division of the Novatians was conveyed to Cyprian in letters from many people. Nor were letters lacking from the schismatics themselves, who burdened Cornelius with a great many lies, while Cornelius, by contrast, had sent a most restrained letter on his own behalf (Epistle 42).

For this reason, a very large number of bishops from Africa assembled at Carthage and, at Cyprian’s instigation, determined that their colleagues Caldonius and Fortunatus [Col. 1439A] should be sent as envoys to Rome. They were to investigate the facts in person and report what they discovered as quickly as possible.

Finally, from their report and at the same time from the testimony of two bishops, Stephen and Pompeius, who had been present at Rome when the pontificate was conferred upon Cornelius by the consensus of all, the whole of Africa recognized Cornelius alone as the legitimate bishop and rejected Novatian with equal unanimity. The envoys of Novatian and their documents were likewise rejected, and it was forbidden that these should be read anywhere to the people.

Yet this was not enough for Cyprian. He also devoted his efforts to bringing back to the Church and to Cornelius the confessors whom Novatian had deceived at Rome. Thus, writing to Cornelius (Epistle 43), he says:

“We considered it both religiously proper and necessary, dearest brother, [Col. 1439B] to compose a brief letter to the confessors who are there and who, seduced by the obstinacy and depravity of Novatian and Novatus, have withdrawn from the Church. In it I would appeal to them, in accordance with our mutual affection, to return to their mother, that is, to the Catholic Church.”

Nor did Cyprian labor in vain. For by sending at the same time the work he had written *On the Unity of the Church*, he brought it about, through both that work and his letters, that they acknowledged their error, rejected the schism, and implored pardon and peace from Cornelius.

Cornelius himself describes their return at length in a letter to Cyprian (Epistle 46 among the letters of Cyprian), specifically naming Maximus the presbyter, Urbanus, Sidonius, and Macarius, and reporting the declaration they had made. How greatly Cyprian rejoiced at this news is shown by his letter to the confessors [Col. 1439C] (Epistle 51):

“Having read your letter, dearest brethren, which you sent me concerning your return, ecclesiastical peace, and fraternal restoration, I confess that I rejoiced as greatly as I had rejoiced before, when I learned of the glory of your confession and received with exultation the heavenly and spiritual praise of your service.

“For this too is another confession belonging to your faith and glory: to confess that there is one Church; not to become a participant in another’s error—or rather, depravity; and to return to the same camp from which you set forth, and from which you sprang forward with the greatest courage to wage battle and subdue the adversary.”

## VIII

Meanwhile, the envoys whom [Col. 1439D] Novatian had sent out as though he were bishop of the city were traveling throughout Africa: Maximus the presbyter, Augendus the deacon, Machaeus, and Longinus. Writing to Cornelius about them, Cyprian complains most severely (Epistle 41):

“And lest their frenzied audacity should ever cease, here too they attempt to tear the members of Christ into parties of schism and to rend and mutilate the body of the Catholic Church. Running from door to door through the houses of many and from town to town through certain cities, they seek companions for their obstinacy and error.”

Yet they accomplished scarcely anything. Everywhere the bishops gave them this reply:

“They should lay aside their destructive dissension and contention; they should know that it is impious to abandon their mother; and they should acknowledge and understand that, once a bishop has been appointed and approved by the testimony and judgment [Col. 1440A] of his colleagues and of the people, another can in no way be appointed.”
