Accordingly, when they had lost hope of revolution and understood that they had incurred the hatred of all good men, they finally left Africa.

Yet the African churches were not permitted to remain free for long from the plague of such men. Before long, others received a commission from Novatian. Among them was Novatus, notoriously stained by every crime, who had originated the schism both in Africa and at Rome.

Cornelius immediately wrote to Cyprian concerning them (Epistle 48 among the letters of Cyprian), and in addition sent the acolyte Nicephorus to give him reliable information concerning the character of the envoys and the entire faction.

Having learned these things, Cyprian warned all the bishops about the crimes of each individual. Then, upon their advice, he drew up a register for Cornelius [Col. 1440B] in which the names of the Catholic bishops of Africa were written (Epistle 54), so that anyone whom Cornelius did not find in that list should be regarded as an outsider and a schismatic. Such were the persons whom those envoys afterward appointed in various places.

## IX

As the year was now coming to an end, while the cruelty of the Decii toward the Christians had not yet subsided, it was suddenly announced that they themselves had perished and that Gaius Vibius Gallus was ruling in their place together with his son Volusianus. No one should doubt that the Africans rejoiced greatly over their elevation. For they are said to have come from that same region and to have been born on the island of Meninx, which was afterward called Girba (Victor, *ibid.* [citation uncertain]). There is also extant at Tunis an inscription testifying that a public work there was restored by them (Maffei, *M. V.*, p. 459, no. 2).

# THE YEAR 252  
## CYPRIAN BEING BISHOP OF CARTHAGE

[Col. 1440C]

## I

Gaius Vibius Trebonianus Gallus Augustus, for the second time, and Gaius Volusianus Caesar assumed the consulship while they were in Moesia. From there, after concluding a treaty with the Goths, they came to Rome at the beginning of the year.

From Rome, Novatian attempted to corrupt the African churches, as he did churches everywhere else, by embassies and letters. Thus he also wrote to Antonianus, a Numidian bishop, in order to draw him into his sect. Having fabricated many disgraceful accusations against Cornelius, he almost won Antonianus over. But because Antonianus had previously reported those charges to Cyprian and awaited his advice, he was strengthened by an excellent letter from Cyprian (Epistle 52), rejected Novatian, and acknowledged that the Catholic Church was the one over which Cornelius presided. [Col. 1440D]

For Cyprian had clearly shown how legitimate Cornelius’s authority was, and had carefully explained with how much deliberation he received the lapsed into the Church. He had also demonstrated admirably that Novatian had claimed the honor of the pontificate for himself by violence and fraud, and that, contrary to the teachings of the divine Scriptures, he rejected all the lapsed and everyone bound by any crime whatsoever, consigning them to perpetual and unprofitable mourning.

Cyprian also uttered the following lament, which reveals a most compassionate spirit intent upon the common good:

“O mockery devised to deceive the brotherhood! O frail delusion of wretched people who mourn and are out of their minds! O ineffective and empty tradition of a heretical institution! To exhort people to the penance of satisfaction, yet remove from satisfaction its remedy; to say to our brethren: ‘Mourn and shed tears and [Col. 1441A] groan day and night; labor abundantly and frequently to wash away and cleanse your offense. Yet after all this you will die outside the Church. You will do everything that pertains to peace, but you will receive none of the peace you seek.’”

## II

Those who had been unable to ruin Antonianus in Numidia now undertook a more serious crime at Carthage. For they brought Maximus back to Africa—his first embassy having proved fruitless—and appointed him bishop of Carthage for their faction.

Cyprian judged the audacity of his opponents so worthy of contempt that he did not even think it necessary to write anything immediately to Cornelius about the deed. For somewhat later, in a letter sent to Cornelius on another matter, he introduced the following mention of Maximus [Col. 1441B] (Epistle 55):

“The party of Novatian is said now to have made Maximus the presbyter, recently sent to us as an envoy by Novatian and rejected from our communion, their pseudo-bishop in this place. Yet I had not written this to you, since such things are held in contempt by us.”

Besides Maximus, Nicostratus too, one of the same group of envoys, was made a bishop in Africa by the Novatians. Cyprian says of him (Epistle 49):

“How does he assume responsibility for ruling or governing the Church when he has despoiled and defrauded the Church of Christ?”

For this man, while a deacon of the Roman Church, had become infamous for “sacrilegiously embezzling ecclesiastical funds and refusing to surrender the deposits belonging to widows and orphans.” He had fled from the city and brought these splendid merits to Africa as qualifications for the Novatianist episcopate.

All these things [Col. 1441C] were being done at the instigation of Novatus, whom Cyprian compared to a squall and whirlwind (ibid.), because tranquility began wherever he withdrew, while a turbulent tempest was stirred up wherever he arrived. He had lately thrown everything into disorder while at Rome, and now in Africa he was once again assailing the Church.

## III

Amid these events, Cyprian, laboring for the proper instruction of his people, published that most beautiful short work *On the Lord’s Prayer*, which Augustine and Hilary commended so highly. For in it he seemed to anticipate and refute the Pelagians when he explained the words “Your will be done on earth as it is in heaven” [Col. 1441D] as follows (p. 491, Baluze edition):

“Not that God should do what he wills, but that we should be able to do what God wills. For who resists God so as to prevent him from doing what he wills? But since we are hindered by the Devil from obeying God in every respect, both in our mind and in our actions, we pray and ask that God’s will may be done in us. For it to be done in us, there is need of God’s will—that is, of his aid and protection—because no one is strong by his own powers, but is made secure by God’s kindness and mercy.”

Moreover, the very formula of prayer which he explains differs somewhat from the one we now use. Its final clauses are as follows:

“And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors; and do not allow us to be led into temptation, but deliver us from evil. Amen.”

He understood “evil” itself as every kind of evil, and not as the Greeks do, ἀπὸ τοῦ πονηροῦ (*from the evil one*).

“At the end,” he says, [Col. 1442A] “we place the words ‘but deliver us from evil,’ encompassing all the adversities which the enemy contrives against us in this world.”

In warning also how attentively we ought to apply ourselves to prayer when making supplication, he at the same time informs us about the ancient rites of the sacrifice (p. 501, ibid.):

“Let every carnal and worldly thought depart, and at that time let the mind think of nothing except that alone for which it prays. For this reason the priest, before the prayer, prepares the minds of the brethren by first giving the preface, saying, ‘Lift up your hearts’ (*Sursum corda*), so that when the people respond, ‘We have them with the Lord’ (*Habemus ad Dominum*), they may be admonished that they ought to think of nothing but the Lord.”

Finally, he commanded them, whenever they were present at the sacrifices, to conduct themselves modestly and to pray almost silently (p. 495, ibid.):

“And when,” he says, “we assemble together with the brethren and celebrate the divine sacrifices [Col. 1442B] with God’s priest, we must be mindful of modesty and discipline. We must not scatter our prayers indiscriminately in unrestrained voices or cast forth with tumultuous loquacity a petition that should be commended modestly to God, because God is the hearer not of the voice but of the heart.”

## IV

It was already Easter, which that year was celebrated on April 11, when Cyprian received a letter from six bishops who had perhaps assembled at Capsa to consecrate a new bishop. This was certainly Capsa in Byzacena, which was then reckoned as belonging to the Proconsular province, since that province had not yet been detached from the territory of Carthage and given its own governor.

It is clear that Numidian Capsa is not meant, because Cyprian mentions below the proconsul, to whom Numidia certainly was not subject. [Col. 1442C]

The bishops’ reason for writing was that Bishop Superius had referred to them the question whether it was lawful to admit to communion three Christians—Ninus, Clementianus, and Florus—who, after enduring many grievous sufferings for Christ, had indeed been overcome by the violence of tortures and

“had fallen away, through prolonged torments, from the degree of glory toward which they had been advancing with the full strength of faith; yet after this grievous fall, incurred not voluntarily but under necessity, they had not ceased to perform penance throughout these three years” (Cyprian, Epistle 53).

The bishops judged that Cyprian should be consulted and further requested that he seek the judgment of his colleagues upon the entire controversy in council.

But because a synod had been appointed for the following month, [Col. 1442D] Cyprian, lest they remain in uncertainty any longer, disclosed at once what he himself thought about the matter:

“And indeed,” he says, “as far as my own judgment is concerned, I believe that the Lord’s indulgence will not be lacking to those who are known to have stood in the battle line, confessed the Lord’s name, and overcome the violence of the magistrates and the assault of the raging populace by the immovable steadfastness of their faith; who endured imprisonment, long resisted the tortures that tore them amid the threats of the proconsul and the roar of the surrounding populace, and withstood torments repeatedly renewed over a long period.

“Thus, what appears to have been overcome in the final weakness of the flesh may be relieved by the defense of their preceding merits. For such persons, it should be enough to have lost their glory; we ought not, however, to close against them the opportunity for pardon or deprive them of the Father’s loving-kindness and of our [Col. 1443A] communion. We believe that, in order to implore the Lord’s mercy, it may suffice that for three years, as you write, they have mourned continually and sorrowfully, with the greatest lamentation of repentance.”

Thus Cyprian moderated that Novatianist severity which at the time seemed almost pleasing to the Numidian bishops. Nevertheless, he promised to submit the question to the Fathers as soon as they had assembled at Carthage.

“Since, however,” he says, “you have written asking me to discuss this matter most fully with a larger number of colleagues; since so important a matter demands greater and more earnest deliberation through consultation among many; and since almost all are now remaining with the brethren in their own communities during the opening solemnities of Easter, once they have fulfilled their duty of celebrating the solemnity among their own people and have begun to come to me, [Col. 1443B] I shall discuss the matter more fully with each of them. Thus, regarding the question upon which you have consulted us, a settled judgment weighed by the counsel of many bishops may be established among us and communicated to you in writing.”

## V

The Ides of May, May 15, brought the beginning of this council (Cyprian, Epistle 55), at which sixty-six bishops were present.

There was more than one reason for convening it. Besides the preceding controversy, which the synod must be understood to have resolved in accordance with Cyprian’s judgment, a letter full of complaints had come from their brother Fidus against their colleague Therapius. Fidus complained that Therapius had granted peace to a certain Victor, formerly a presbyter,

“before he had completed full penance and made satisfaction to the Lord God against whom he had sinned, at an untimely moment and with overhasty speed” (Cyprian, Epistle 59).

When the letter had been read in the council, [Col. 1443C] the Fathers were displeased

“that there had been a departure from the authority of the decree, so that peace was granted to him before the lawful and complete period of satisfaction, without the request or knowledge of the people, and when no sickness was pressing and no necessity compelled it.”

Therapius could easily have consulted Cyprian on the matter, for he was bishop of Bulla in the Proconsular province. Nevertheless, nothing harsh was decreed against him.

“After carefully weighing the matter in our counsel for a long time,” Cyprian says, “we considered it sufficient to rebuke our colleague Therapius because he had acted rashly, and to instruct him not to do anything of this kind in the future. Yet we did not think that peace, once granted by a priest of God, however it had been given, should be taken away. Consequently, we permitted Victor to enjoy the communion that had been granted to him.”

## VI

The opinion of the same Fidus concerning the baptism of infants [Col. 1443D] was then proposed. He believed that

“infants ought not to be baptized within the second or third day after their birth, and that the law of ancient circumcision should be considered, so that he did not think a newborn ought to be baptized and sanctified before the eighth day.”

But in that assembly of bishops there was no one who believed that the ancient custom of circumcision possessed any force in determining the days for Baptism or could impose any such requirement. A reply was therefore sent to Fidus in the council’s name:

“This was our judgment in the council: that through our agency no one ought to be prevented from Baptism and the grace of God, who is merciful, kind, and loving toward all. Since this must be observed and maintained in regard to everyone, [Col. 1444A] we think it must be observed still more in regard to infants themselves and those newly born. They deserve our assistance and the divine mercy all the more for the very reason that, immediately at the first beginning of their birth, in their crying and weeping they do nothing but make supplication.”

From this same reply we learn that it was then customary for those present at a Baptism to kiss the infant. For Fidus had objected:

“The foot of an infant in the first days after birth is not clean, so that each of us still shrinks from kissing it.”

The Fathers replied:

“Not even this ought to be an impediment to the granting of heavenly grace. For it is written: ‘To the pure all things are pure’ (Titus 1:15). Nor ought any of us to shrink from what God has deigned to make. For although the infant is still newly delivered from birth, [Col. 1444B] that is no reason why anyone, in granting grace and making peace, should shrink from kissing the child. In the kiss of an infant, each of us, in accordance with his religious devotion, ought to contemplate God’s own hands still fresh upon it—hands which, in a certain manner, we kiss in the person who has just been formed and newly made, when we embrace what God has made.”

Augustine frequently mentions this same letter and used its authority to defend the ancient doctrine of the Church concerning original sin (*Sermon* 294, chapter 20).

While these matters were being transacted in the council, Privatus of Lambaesis, whom we have said was condemned several times before, was so audacious that he did not hesitate to attempt once more to gain admission to the council, and not alone, but surrounded by a band of his associates. [Col. 1444C] The bishops resisted, however, and judged that none of them should be admitted.

After the council had finally concluded, [Col. 1444D] Cyprian appears to have written to Bishop Epictetus and the people of Assuras (Epistle 64), urging them steadfastly to reject Fortunatianus, who, though already deposed from the pontificate because of his impious sacrifice, dared to claim that honor for himself.

“This matter,” he says, “has grieved me: first, because of the man himself, who, wretched as he is, has either been wholly blinded by the darkness of the Devil or deceived by the sacrilegious persuasion of certain persons. Although he ought to make satisfaction and devote himself day and night to tears, prayers, and entreaties in order to implore the Lord, he still dares to claim for himself the priesthood which he betrayed—as though, after approaching the Devil’s altars, he could proceed to the altar of God; or as though he did not provoke against himself the Lord’s still greater wrath and indignation on the day of judgment, since, having been unable to serve the brethren as a leader in faith and courage, he now presents himself as a teacher of treachery, audacity, and recklessness.”

Then, explaining what they ought to do, he adds:

“But if Fortunatianus—either forgetful of his crime through the Devil’s blindness, or having become the Devil’s minister and servant for the deception of the brotherhood—persists in this madness, labor as much as you can and, amid this darkness of the raging Devil, recall the minds of the brethren from error. Let them not readily consent to another man’s madness or make themselves participants in the sins of those without hope. Rather, let them maintain unbroken the perpetual course of their salvation and of the integrity they have preserved and guarded.”

Because there was also everywhere a great number of the lapsed, he wished to give them his admonitions as well:

“But let the lapsed,” [Col. 1445A] he says, “recognizing the magnitude of their offense, not cease to implore the Lord, nor abandon the Catholic Church, which is the one and only Church established by the Lord. Rather, persevering in acts of satisfaction and imploring the Lord’s mercy, let them knock at the Church, so that they may be received back there where they had been, and may return to Christ, from whom they withdrew.”

### VII

Meanwhile the bishops had returned to their churches; but Privatus, the heretic, and the whole faction of Felicissimus were bearing down upon Carthage. There, in order to avenge the rejection they had suffered from the council, they set up against Cyprian a bishop from their own sect. This was Fortunatus, one of the five presbyters whom Cyprian had long counted among his adversaries. Cyprian relates the affair to Cornelius as follows (*Epistle* 55):

> “There had come,” he says, “with Privatus a certain Felix, [Col. 1445B] whom Privatus himself had long ago appointed outside the Church as a pseudo-bishop in heresy. Jovinus and Maximus also appeared as companions of Privatus, a convicted heretic; because of abominable sacrifices and crimes proved against them, they had been condemned by the judgment of nine bishops, our colleagues, and had again been excluded from communion by a larger number of us at the council of the preceding year. To these four was also joined Repostus of Tuburnica, who not only fell personally during the persecution but, by sacrilegious persuasion, caused the greater part of his congregation to fall as well. These five, together with a few who had either sacrificed or had guilty consciences, co-opted Fortunatus as their pseudo-bishop, so that, with crimes thus united in one body, the ruler would naturally be of the same kind as those who were ruled.”

The faction, moreover, had previously boasted [Col. 1445C] that twenty-five bishops from Numidia would be present to appoint a bishop for them.

> “But after,” Cyprian adds, “they were exposed and confounded in this lie of theirs, when only five shipwrecked men, excluded from communion by us, had assembled, they sailed to Rome with their cargo of falsehoods—as though the truth could not sail after them and, by proof of the established facts, convict their lying tongues.”

It was, however, a consolation to Cyprian that even among them there was so great a scarcity of wicked men that twenty-five could not be gathered for their side even from among those who had sacrificed and the heretics.

What is remarkable is that this faction was wholly at odds with the Novatians, over whom Maximus presided. The latter barred penitents from access to the Church; the former, on the contrary, boasted that they admitted everyone to their communion and remitted everyone’s punishment. Cyprian wrote [Col. 1445D] to the same Cornelius:

> “Every effort is made to prevent transgressions from being redeemed by acts of satisfaction and righteous lamentation, and to prevent wounds from being washed clean with tears. True peace is abolished by the falsehood of a counterfeit peace; the saving bosom of the mother is closed by the intervention of a stepmother, so that the weeping and groaning of the fallen may not be heard from their hearts and mouths. Furthermore, the fallen are actually compelled, with the very tongues and mouths by which they formerly sinned on the Capitol, to revile the priests and to assail with insults and slanderous words the confessors, the virgins, and all the righteous who are distinguished by the praise of their faith and glorious in the Church.”

But it has always been characteristic of heretics not to know moderation—the moderation by observing which the Catholic Church shows herself to be the teacher of truth and the foster-mother of virtue.

### VIII

[Col. 1446A] When Felicissimus reached Rome with several ringleaders of the faction, although he himself had already been rejected by Cornelius, he nevertheless persisted in advocating for his Fortunatus. He spread many falsehoods against Cyprian among the public and attempted to intimidate Cornelius into having the Roman Church take his sect under its patronage. And so great and violent was Felicissimus’s fury that it almost shook Cornelius’s resolve. Cyprian therefore undertook to strengthen him by a letter:

> “But when,” he says, “I read your other letter, brother, which you appended to your first communication, I was greatly astonished when I perceived that you had been somewhat disturbed by the threats and terrors of those who had come. For, as you wrote, they had approached you, threatening in utter desperation that, if you did not receive the letters they had brought, [Col. 1446B] they would read them publicly and utter many shameful and disgraceful things worthy of their own mouths.”

After this he discusses at considerable length and with great eloquence the duties of bishops, and openly declares his contempt for that faction:

> “What self-exaltation is this,” he says (*ibid.*, *Epistle* 55), “what swollen, inflated, and empty boasting on the part of these threatening men—to threaten me there in my absence, when they have me here present and within their power? We do not fear their insults, by which they daily tear apart themselves and their own lives; nor do we dread the clubs, stones, and swords of which they boast in their murderous words.”

Thereafter, if Cornelius had perhaps been somewhat afraid of Felicissimus and the other emissaries of Fortunatus, it must be supposed that, after reading Cyprian’s letter and having it read aloud in the presence of the clergy as well, he repelled all their attempts.

Fortunatus [Col. 1446C] certainly achieved nothing in Africa according to his wishes. For Cyprian writes of that entire band of impious men:

> “Because they know their own conscience, they do not dare to approach us or come to the threshold of the Church; instead, they wander outside through the province, deceiving and despoiling the brethren. But now that they are sufficiently known to everyone and have everywhere been excluded because of their crimes, they sail even there to you. For they cannot have the effrontery to approach us or stand among us, since the charges brought against them by the brethren are most bitter and most serious.”

Many, by contrast, who had adhered to Maximus or Fortunatus detested the schism and returned to the Church. So that these wretched people might not perish outside, Cyprian admitted them rather readily, even though the people were sometimes indignant.

> “O dearest brother,” he wrote to Cornelius, [Col. 1446D] “if only you could be here with us when these depraved and perverse people return from the schism! You would see what labor it costs me to persuade our brethren to be patient, so that, after calming the anguish of their minds, they may consent to receive and heal these evil people. For just as they rejoice and are glad when those who are tolerable and less culpable return, so, on the contrary, they growl and resist whenever the returning people are incorrigible and insolent, defiled either by adultery or by sacrifice, and, after all this, still arrogant besides—returning to the Church in such a way that they would corrupt the good dispositions within. I can scarcely persuade the congregation—indeed, I have to wrest it from them—that they should permit such people to be admitted.”

### IX

Cyprian and the other bishops throughout Africa were carrying out these duties of peace and charity when the Christian name had already begun once more to be placed in jeopardy. [Col. 1447A] For when the emperor Gallus, after Hostilian, the son of Decius, had been removed and Volusian had been proclaimed Caesar and Augustus, had brought the wars to an end, and everything at Rome and throughout Italy had been pacified, he imitated the cruelty of Decius. By a law enacted against the Christians, he ordered them to be persecuted everywhere and condemned to death.

It is thought that the reason for adopting this policy was that, when a plague was then devastating most of the provinces of the Roman world and sacrifices had been decreed to appease the gods, the Christians rejected that superstition and abstained from the temples. The entire blame for the calamity was accordingly laid upon them, and everyone cried with one voice that the angry gods must be appeased with Christian blood.

And so, in Africa itself, when Cyprian was writing to Cornelius the matters we have just recounted, the law of Gallus [Col. 1447B] had already been promulgated and the edicts of the magistrates posted. Indeed, while the people were seated in the circus, they had again demanded that Cyprian himself be thrown to the lion. He had also already learned by divine revelation (*Epistle* 54) that:

> “The day of contest was drawing near, that a violent enemy would soon arise, and that the coming battle would not be like the former one, but far more serious and fierce.”

Therefore, since he was greatly concerned for everyone’s salvation, he summoned as many bishops as he could amid so great a danger—there were forty-two of them—and referred to the Fathers the question of granting peace to the fallen, something that was then of the greatest importance in the Church. He urged them, with battle impending, to equip the unarmed and, in a common danger, to bring to everyone the assistance for which they asked.

> “We must obey,” he said (*ibid.*), “the righteous revelations and admonitions, [Col. 1447C] so that the sheep may not be abandoned by their shepherds in the hour of danger, but the whole flock may be gathered together into one, and the army of the Lord armed for the struggle of the heavenly campaign. The repentance of those who grieved over their fall was deservedly prolonged for a longer time, so that assistance might be given to the sick at the point of death, so long as rest and tranquility prevailed, which allowed the tears of the mourners to be deferred for a long while and help to be given late to those dying in sickness. But now peace is necessary not for the weak but for the strong; communion must be given by us not to the dying but to the living. Thus we must not leave unarmed and naked those whom we rouse and exhort to battle, but must fortify them with the protection of the Blood and Body of Christ. And since the Eucharist [Col. 1447D] is celebrated precisely so that it may be a safeguard to those who receive it, let us arm with the defense of the Lord’s abundant provision those whom we wish to be safe against the adversary.”

By these and other arguments of this kind, Cyprian readily brought all the bishops to his opinion. And since they all reached the same judgment, it was also decided that they should write on the matter to Cornelius, the Supreme Pontiff, whom they believed to hold the same opinion.

### X

But Cornelius had already entered the contest when the letter of the African Fathers was delivered to him. For, under the pressure of the emperor Gallus’s presence, the magistrates at Rome vied with one another to hasten the destruction of the Christians. The first assault was upon Cornelius, whom they knew to be the leader of them all.

His splendid confession amid that sudden terror appears to have prompted the pagans [Col. 1448A] to remove so unconquered a leader from the sight of the others and to arrange for his deportation to Centumcellae, as the ancient tradition relates. Cyprian certainly extols it with many praises in the letter that he immediately addressed to him in exile (*Epistle* 56):

> “We have learned, dearest brother,” he says, “of the glorious testimonies to your faith and courage, and we have received the honor of your confession with such exultation that we count ourselves also participants and companions in your merits and praises.”

He then congratulates him for having become the leader of the brethren’s confession and for having gained, by going before them, companions in glory and a confessing people.

He also asked what had become of Novatian:

> “Has he now laid aside his error?” he says. “Or rather, as is the custom of madmen, has he been driven into greater fury by our very blessings and prosperity? And the more and more the glory of love and faith increases here, does the madness of dissension and jealousy grow more virulent there? [Col. 1448B] The wretched man does not heal his own wound, but wounds both himself and his followers still more grievously, clamoring with his tongue for the destruction of the brethren and hurling the darts of poisonous eloquence—made hard by the perversity of secular philosophy rather than peaceful through the gentleness of the Lord’s wisdom; a deserter of the Church, an enemy of mercy, a destroyer of repentance, a teacher of pride, a corrupter of truth, a destroyer of charity. Does he now recognize who is the priest of God, what is the Church and the house of Christ, who are the servants of God, whom the devil attacks, who are the Christians, and whom Antichrist assails? For he does not seek those whom he has already subdued, nor does he desire to overthrow those whom he has already made his own.”

And indeed Novatian was not counted by the pagans [Col. 1448C] among the Christians. Whatever his followers later fabricated, he was left untouched and continued to destroy many, a perpetual enemy of the Church. But not long afterward Cornelius’s martyrdom was consummated on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of October; six years later, on that same day, Cyprian’s own palm of victory also made it illustrious. When an assembly could be held, the Roman Church, once again rejecting Novatian, selected from her own bosom Lucius, a presbyter of proven virtue, to succeed Cornelius.

### XI

At about the same time, after the council had been dismissed, the bishops returned to their churches and devoted diligent effort to receiving and strengthening the fallen, [Col. 1448D] so that, summoned once more to the contest, they might courageously set about washing away by steadfast confession and by their very blood the stain they had recently incurred under Decius.

Among them Cyprian was preeminent in zeal and benevolence toward everyone. He not only consoled his own people of Carthage by receiving them kindly and inflamed them with the desire for martyrdom, but also embraced the neighboring cities in his love, never ceasing to assist individuals and rouse them by exhortations to steadfastness. He was ready to hurry anywhere, had it then been permissible for him to leave Carthage.

He had in fact decided to travel to Thibaris, where the townspeople had invited him, had not the good of the Church compelled him to remain at home. Nevertheless, in a splendid letter entitled “On Exhortation to Martyrdom,” he set forth admirably what he would have said to the people of Thibaris had he been present (*Epistle* 56; see Jerome on Cyprian’s eloquence, *Epistle* 68, no. 10).

The letter itself to the people of Thibaris seems to indicate that similar letters on the same subject were sent by him to other [Col. 1449A] cities, especially to those that perhaps had no bishop. It contains teachings particularly suited to those times and appropriate to every Christian. Among them, the statement in which he expressly discusses flight especially deserves mention:

> “Nor let anyone, dearest brethren,” he says, “be troubled when he sees our people driven into flight by fear of persecution and scattered, because he does not see the brotherhood assembled or hear the bishops preaching. At that time all those for whom it is unlawful to kill, but necessary to be killed, cannot remain together. Wherever, in those days, any one of the brethren may be, separated from the flock for a time by the necessity of the circumstances—separated in body but not in spirit—let him not be disturbed by the horror of that flight; nor, when he has withdrawn and is in hiding, let him be terrified by the solitude [Col. 1449B] of the deserted place. He is not alone who has Christ as his companion in flight. He is not alone who, preserving the temple of God, is never without God wherever he may be.
>
> “And if, while he is fleeing in the wilderness and mountains, a robber should overpower him, a wild beast attack him, hunger, thirst, or cold afflict him, or a storm and tempest drown him as he hastens across the seas on a perilous voyage, Christ watches his soldier wherever he fights; and to one who dies under persecution for the honor of His name He gives the reward that He promised to give at the resurrection. Nor is the glory of martyrdom less because a man did not perish publicly and among many, when the cause of his death was that he died for Christ. For the testimony of his martyrdom that Witness suffices who tests [*probat*] [Col. 1449C] and crowns the martyrs.”

It was of the greatest importance that all should know these things. Cyprian hoped that those who had learned them, if perhaps they believed themselves unequal to interrogation and trembled for fear of torture, would take thought for their safety through flight, lest, after being captured, they violate their faith and be polluted by abominable sacrifices.

### XII

The final letter of the closing year was received from Cyprian by Lucius, the Supreme Pontiff. A short while before, almost immediately after assuming the episcopate, Lucius had been driven into exile; but now, having returned, he had come back to his Church amid the great rejoicing of all. As soon as Cyprian learned of this, he considered it his duty to congratulate him upon his return:

> “Recently indeed,” he says (*Epistle* 58), “we congratulated you, dearest brother, when divine favor, bestowing a twofold honor, appointed you both confessor and Priest in the governance of His Church. But now we congratulate you no less, together with your companions [Col. 1449D] and the whole brotherhood, because the Lord’s kindly and abundant protection has, with the same glory and to your praise, restored you once again to His people. Thus the shepherd has been restored to spare the flock, the pilot to govern the ship, and the ruler to guide the people; and it has become apparent that your banishment was divinely ordered in such a way that the bishop, banished and driven out, should not be absent from the Church, but should return to the Church a greater man.”

Near the end he recalls his Church’s devotion to Lucius and expresses his confident hope for his martyrdom:

> “By making our joy present to you through this letter, we express the faithful services of our charity. Here too, in our sacrifices and prayers, we do not cease [Col. 1450A] to give thanks to God the Father and to Christ His Son, our Lord, and at the same time to pray and entreat that He who is perfect and makes perfect may guard and perfect in you the glorious crown of your confession. Perhaps He recalled you for this very purpose: that your glory might not remain hidden if the martyrdoms of your confession were consummated outside. For the victim that provides the brotherhood with an example of courage ought also to be sacrificed in the presence of the brethren.”

## Christian Year 253  
### Cyprian, Bishop of Carthage

### I

Gaius Vibius Volusianus Augustus, for the second time, and Marcus Valerius Maximus entered upon the consulship.

The martyrdom of Lucius shows that the Christians were again persecuted at Rome, and in it Cyprian’s [Col. 1450B] prophecy was fulfilled. For Lucius is said to have attained the laurel on the Nones of March; after him the Roman Church bestowed the pontificate upon Stephen.

That the Church was persecuted no less savagely in Africa at the same time is indicated by Cyprian’s book addressed to Demetrianus. Whether Demetrianus was the proconsul or an assessor to the proconsul, he was certainly a most bitter and cruel enemy of the Christian name, as well as an inept sophist and abusive reviler.

In that book Cyprian enumerates as follows the various forms of punishment that Christians then underwent (*To Demetrianus*, p. 516; see the Bollandists, vol. IV, September, p. 289):

> “You deprive the innocent, the righteous, and those dear to God of their homes; you strip them of their property, burden them with chains, shut them in prison, and punish them by the sword, wild beasts, and fire. Nor are you even [Col. 1450C] content with an abridgment of our sufferings and the simple, swift brevity of punishment. You apply prolonged tortures to bodies that are to be mangled; you multiply numerous torments to lacerate the entrails. Your savagery and brutality cannot remain content with customary tortures: ingenious cruelty devises new punishments.”

Nor can that book of Cyprian be assigned to another year, since Pontius (*Life of Cyprian*, no. 7) shows that it was written after the book *On the Lord’s Prayer*, while Cyprian himself specifies that it was the time of the plague (*To Demetrianus*, pp. 508 and 514), which invaded Africa in this year.

For Demetrianus was above all reviving the old slander that, whatever adversity arose anywhere and whatever calamity the commonwealth suffered, the Christians were rightly accused and were its cause; because they despised the divine powers, the angered gods exacted from all mortals the punishment for violated majesty.

Cyprian undertook to refute [Col. 1450D] this slander in that book during this year, which appeared likely to be especially disastrous for the commonwealth. After recalling the incursions of the barbarians and the barrenness and famine by which the Roman world had long been afflicted—not through the Christians’ fault, but through the crimes of the pagans, which were increasing daily—he also added the following (*ibid.*, p. 514):

> “You make accusations concerning the pestilence and plague, although by that very pestilence and plague the crimes of individuals have either been exposed or increased: mercy is not shown to the sick, while greed and plunder gape after the dead. The same people who are timid in performing the duties of charity are reckless in seeking impious gains; they flee from the funerals of the dying but seize the spoils of the dead. [Col. 1451A] Thus it appears that the wretched sick may perhaps have been abandoned in their illness precisely so that they cannot escape it while being cared for.”

### II

But if the pagans, amid that universal panic, relaxed in any measure their credulous hostility toward the Christians, another field certainly opened to the Christians in which their virtue might display itself and become known.

> “Afterward there broke out,” says Pontius (*Life of Cyprian*, no. 9), “a dreadful plague and an excessively devastating, detestable disease. With abrupt violence it carried off countless people every day, each from his own dwelling; in an unbroken sequence it invaded the homes of the trembling populace. Everyone shuddered, fled, avoided contagion, and impiously exposed their own relatives, as though, by excluding the person who was about to die from the plague, one could exclude death itself. Meanwhile, throughout the whole city there lay no longer bodies but the corpses of very many, [Col. 1451B] and demanded mercy for themselves from passersby through contemplation of their common lot.”

Such was then the appearance of Carthage, a densely populated city. Amid so great a destruction of human beings and so miserable a scene of neglect and mourning, no pagan could be found who would undertake the care even of his own people and bring aid to those who implored it.

But the Christians could not behold these things without pity, nor could they permit so many wretched people—even those most alien to them—to remain without assistance amid such need and abandonment. They had also been inflamed to these supreme duties of charity and mercy by Cyprian’s discourse. For he had previously assembled the people and instructed them through the noble teachings of the Gospel:

> “It was nothing remarkable” (Pontius, *Life of Cyprian*, no. 9) “if we cherished only our own people with the service of charity that was their due; but one could become perfect who did something more than the publican or pagan—who, overcoming evil with good and practicing the likeness of divine mercy, loved even his enemies, and who, as the Lord teaches and exhorts, prayed for the salvation of those who persecuted him.”

He had then added:

> “God continually causes His sun to rise and repeatedly supplies rains to nourish the seeds, bestowing all these things not only upon His own but also upon those who are alien to Him. And why does one who professes that he too is a son of God not imitate the Father’s example? It is fitting that we correspond to our birth, and it is improper that those who, as is established, have been reborn through God should be degenerate. Rather, the descent of a good father should be demonstrated in his offspring by emulation of his goodness.”

What more need be said? Even sluggish spirits were roused by Cyprian’s words to vigorous exertion, with a marvelous zeal for helping everyone.

> “The ministries,” Pontius says (*Life*, no. 10), “were therefore immediately distributed according to the circumstances and ranks of the people. Many who, because of the constraints of poverty, could not provide financial assistance rendered more than money, compensating through their own labor with a reward more precious than all riches.”

### III

But amid these cares Cyprian perceived that there were some who, cast down by the magnitude of the calamity, collapsed in spirit and did not know how patiently to endure and bear with equanimity the things that occurred by the supreme counsel and will of God, the Lord of all.

Not forgetting these people either, he prepared the best remedy for their affliction by writing a book for their instruction, which he entitled *On Mortality*. In it he endeavored to show that very many benefits flowed to Christians from death itself.

> [Col. 1452A] “What else,” he said (*On Mortality*), “takes place in the world but a battle daily waged against the devil, but a struggle against his darts and weapons in continual conflicts? We contend with greed, with lust, with anger, and with ambition; there is a continual and burdensome struggle with fleshly vices and worldly enticements. The human mind, besieged and hemmed in on every side by the devil’s assaults, can scarcely meet each attack, scarcely resist it. If greed is laid low, lust arises; if lust is suppressed, ambition succeeds it; if ambition is despised, anger grows fierce, pride swells, drunkenness entices, envy shatters harmony, and jealousy severs friendship. You are forced to curse, though divine law forbids it; you are compelled to swear, though it is unlawful. The spirit undergoes so many persecutions [Col. 1452B] every day, the heart is pressed by so many dangers—and does it delight us to stand here for a long time among the swords of the devil, when we ought rather to desire and pray to hasten to Christ more speedily through the intervention of death?”

He counted this first among the benefits: to be free of so many evils and to exchange this wretched and transitory life for a blessed and eternal existence. But he also taught that the bodily afflictions then being suffered were not evils for Christians:

> “The fact,” he says (*ibid.*), “that now the bowels, loosened into a flux, drain the body’s strength; that a fire conceived deep in the marrow burns up into wounds of the throat; that the intestines are shaken by continual vomiting; that the eyes blaze from the force of the blood; that the feet or certain parts of the limbs of some are amputated because of the contagion of diseased putrefaction; that, through the losses and injuries suffered by the body as the sickness breaks forth, the gait is either enfeebled, or the hearing stopped, or the sight blinded—[Col. 1452C] all this contributes to the demonstration of faith. What greatness of heart it is to struggle with the virtues of an unshaken spirit against so many assaults of devastation and death! What sublimity it is to stand erect amid the ruins of the human race and not lie prostrate with those who have no hope in God!”

He now even maintained that so many deaths should be regarded as benefits:

> “We are heedless and ungrateful, dearest brethren,” he says (*ibid.*, p. 155), “toward the divine benefits, nor do we recognize what is being bestowed upon us. Behold, virgins depart in secure peace with their glory intact, not fearing the threats, corruptions, and brothels of the coming Antichrist. [Col. 1452D] Children escape the danger of an unstable age and happily attain the reward of continence and innocence. The delicate matron no longer fears torture, having escaped the fear of persecution and the hands and torments of the executioner through the swiftness of death. The lukewarm are set aflame by fear of mortality and of the times; the lax are restrained, the sluggish roused, deserters compelled to return, pagans constrained to believe, and the ancient people of the faithful summoned to rest. A new and numerous army is gathered for the battle with greater strength, ready to fight without fear of death when the battle comes, because it enters military service in the season of mortality.”

Finally, he exhorts them cheerfully to despise death and joyfully to consider where they were going:

> “We count Paradise [Col. 1453A] as our homeland,” he says (*ibid.*), “and have already begun to regard the Patriarchs as our parents. Why do we not hasten and run, so that we may see our homeland and greet our parents? A great number of our dear ones awaits us there—a dense and numerous throng of parents, brothers, and children longs for us, already secure in their own safety yet still anxious for our salvation. What common joy there will be for them and for us when we come into their sight and embrace! What delight there is in the heavenly kingdoms, without fear of dying; and, with the eternity of life, what supreme and perpetual happiness!”

### IV

Thus Cyprian had now learned to philosophize, and this wisdom, which he possessed in conjunction with eloquence, was then a source of assistance and consolation to many mortals. [Col. 1453B] For the plague ranged widely and afflicted provinces everywhere for several years, now more mildly and now more severely.

In this year, however, the Christians—terrified on one side by the plague and on the other overwhelmed by the deadly edicts of the emperors—were relieved in part when the danger being prepared against their religion and faith was driven away. For in the month of May news arrived that Gallus and Volusian had been killed by the soldiers and that Gaius Julius Aemilianus, who was said to be a Moor by birth (*Victor, Epitome*), ruled in their place.

But in the third or fourth month thereafter, when he too had been killed by the army, it was announced that the imperial power was in the hands of Publius Licinius Valerian, who had long flourished in the reputation of virtue and was then said to be especially favorably disposed toward the Christians. Soon afterward, some limit [Col. 1453C] appears also to have been placed upon the plague, for it is evident that Cyprian held assemblies.

### V

But it was an altogether sorrowful cause that impelled Cyprian to summon the clergy and people. He had received a letter from the Numidian bishops reporting that barbarians had invaded that province in great numbers, devastated the countryside, and carried many captives, including virgins, into slavery.

Those bishops, eight in number, therefore asked both Cyprian and the entire Church of Carthage to supply some money for the ransom of the captives. Cyprian’s letter to them still survives. It breathes that ancient charity and greatness of mutual love that once commended all Christians so highly; and from it we learn what Cyprian and the Church supplied.

First, as soon as the bishops’ letter was read, it is evident that everyone wept and lamented.

> “With the greatest groaning of our heart,” he says (*Epistle* 60), “and not without tears, we read your letter, dearest brethren, which in the solicitude of your love you wrote to us concerning the captivity of our brothers and sisters.”

Their compassion was immediately followed by kindness and generosity, for, as Cyprian adds:

> “The entire brotherhood, reflecting upon everything described in your letter and examining it with grief, promptly, willingly, and generously contributed financial assistance for the brethren. They are always, in accordance with the steadfastness of their faith, inclined toward the work of God; but now, in contemplation of such great suffering, they were still more inflamed toward works of salvation.”

The sum of the contribution [Col. 1454A] was two thousand five hundred shield-coins (*scutati nummi*). For Cyprian specifies it thus:

> “We have sent,” he says, “one hundred thousand sesterces, collected here in the Church over which, by the Lord’s favor, we preside, through contributions from the clergy and people residing with us. You will distribute them there in accordance with your diligence.”

Cyprian also wished the bishops to know how much each person had contributed, and he explained why he desired this:

> “So that,” he says, “you may remember in your prayers our brothers and sisters who have contributed so promptly and willingly to this most necessary work, as they always do, and may make a return to them for their good work in your sacrifices and prayers, I have appended the names of each. I have also added the names of our colleagues and fellow priests who, being themselves present, [Col. 1454B] contributed something according to their means, both in their own names and in the names of their congregations. In addition to the amount of our own contribution, I have indicated and sent the smaller sums given by them as well. All of these, as faith and charity require, you ought to remember in our prayers and in your supplications.”

From this passage we understand that it was customary among the African churches that, if any calamity anywhere afflicted a particular church, the others would all, by their common zeal, bring it whatever assistance they could.

Two further things in Cyprian’s letter are admirable: first, that he regarded the bishops’ request as a benefit bestowed upon him; second, that he admonished them never to be reluctant to ask for assistance whenever need should arise. [Col. 1454C]

> “We give you the greatest thanks,” he says, “because you wished us to be participants in your solicitude and in so good and necessary a work, thereby offering us fertile fields in which we might cast the seeds of our hope and await a harvest from the most abundant fruits produced by this heavenly and saving work.”

He then added concerning the danger that might again threaten them:

> “We indeed pray that nothing of this kind may occur in the future and that our brethren, protected by the majesty of the Lord, may be preserved unharmed from dangers of this kind. Yet if, in order that the charity of our spirit may be tested and the faith of our heart examined, anything of this kind should occur, do not hesitate to inform us in your letters. You may hold it as certain that our Church and the entire brotherhood here pray in their supplications that such things may not occur again; [Col. 1454D] but if they do occur, they will willingly and generously furnish assistance.”

### VI

Having discharged these duties, Cyprian judged that it would serve the Christian cause if he further nourished and inflamed, by publishing a book on that subject, the spirits already moved by compassion and still glowing with it. Accordingly, at about the same time he published the golden little work entitled *On Works and Almsgiving*, in which he bestowed the highest praise upon those who generously supplied the Church from their possessions, so that the needs of the poor might be relieved.

From it we also learn that even then hollow collection-boxes or treasuries stood in the sacred buildings, into which each person deposited a contribution; and that it was likewise customary for bread and wine to be offered for the sacrifice. For he reproves as follows certain matrons who neglected these things (*On Works and Almsgiving*, p. 569):

> “You are wealthy [Col. 1455A] and rich, and do you believe that you celebrate the Lord’s Supper—you who pay no attention at all to the *Corban* [the offering], who come to the Lord’s Supper without a sacrifice, and who take a portion of the sacrifice that the poor person offered?”

It is credible that even then deacons were assigned to the individual districts of the revered city of Rome, who knew the names of the poor and relieved their need. Certainly, in the synod that we learn was held many years later under Boniface (in Hardouin, *Councils*, vol. II, p. 1082), one Gaudiosus is cited as “deacon of the fifth district.” Thus it should be thought that Cyprian, following particularly the example of the city of Rome, appointed deacons of this kind and entrusted to them the care of the wretched among the common people, which they carried out under the presbyters.

## Christian Year 254  
### Cyprian, Bishop of Carthage

### I

The Augusti were named consuls: Publius Licinius Valerian [Col. 1455B] for the second time, and Publius Licinius Gallienus.

Under these consuls the affairs of the Christians were peaceful; but the commonwealth began to be disturbed by incursions of the barbarians and endangered by the revolt of the provinces. Africa nevertheless remained loyal, and no trouble was brought upon the Church except by domestic enemies.

Among these was a certain wealthy citizen of Carthage, a follower of Felicissimus, who daily assailed Cyprian with abuse. He fabricated many false and disgraceful accusations against him, called him the author of every evil, and alienated from him the minds of as many good people as he could.

This man’s name was Florentius Pupianus. Cyprian calls him “brother” because he was a Christian; but no evidence demonstrates that he was either a presbyter or a bishop.

Cyprian had indeed patiently endured many things from Pupianus. But when he also received from that man a wholly irreligious and abusive letter, [Col. 1455C] he finally undertook to refute him, writing him a most weighty epistle. In it he vigorously defends his own dignity and authority, which Pupianus was attempting to undermine, and declares that his adversary, as a patron of schism, stands outside the Church.

> “Therefore,” he says (*Epistle* 69), “you ought to know that the bishop is in the Church and the Church in the bishop; and that if anyone is not with the bishop, he is not in the Church. Those people vainly flatter themselves who, although they do not have peace with the priests of God, creep in and believe that they secretly communicate with certain persons, when the Church, which is catholic and one, has not been torn or divided, but is joined together and bound by the adhesive bond [*glutino*] of priests who cleave to one another.”

[Col. 1455D] His final words are:

> “You have my letter, and I have yours; on the Day of Judgment, before the tribunal of Christ, both will be read aloud.”

## II

Cyprian had another adversary hostile to the whole Catholic Church—namely Novatian, who by now numbered far more followers outside Africa than he had had in Africa, and these not only among the laity but also among the clergy. Easily foremost among them was Marcian, bishop of Arles, much to the indignation of the other bishops of Gaul, whom their common profession united in Catholic agreement with Stephen, the Supreme Pontiff. Accordingly, just as many had complained about the matter to Stephen himself [Col. 1456A] (Cyprian, Epist. 67), so Faustinus, bishop of Lyons, who both knew the dignity of the Church of Carthage and was well aware of Cyprian’s learning joined with the highest virtue, also wrote to Cyprian against Marcian. From him he obtained an agreement that Cyprian himself should send Stephen an altogether weighty and forceful letter, showing that Marcian must be removed from office and that provision must be made for the Church by appointing a successor.

After a few preliminary remarks concerning the hardness and implacable severity of the Novatians, Cyprian addresses Stephen as follows:

> Therefore you ought to send the fullest possible letters to our fellow bishops established in Gaul, so that they may no longer permit Marcian—obstinate, arrogant, and an enemy of divine mercy and his brethren’s salvation—to insult our college, on the ground that he does not yet appear to have been excluded by us, although he has long boasted and proclaimed that, in supporting Novatian [Col. 1456B] and following his obstinacy, he has separated himself from communion with us, whereas Novatian himself, whom he follows, was long ago excluded and judged an enemy of the Church.

Then, after recounting Novatian’s condemnation at greater length, he continues insistently:

> Let letters be sent by you into the province and to the congregation established at Arles, so that, Marcian having been excluded, another may be substituted in his place, and the flock of Christ, which down to the present day has been scattered, wounded, and despised by him, may be gathered together.

Finally, he especially asks to be informed about the bishop appointed in Marcian’s place:

> Inform us plainly who has been substituted for Marcian at Arles, so that we may know to whom we ought to direct our brethren and to whom we should write.

Stephen must be supposed to have complied with Cyprian and to have deposed Marcian, for the ancient diptychs of the Church [Col. 1456C] of Arles (in Mabillon, *Annales*, vol. III, p. 432) do not record Marcian. But who succeeded him is less clear. Yet even this did not satisfy Cyprian: he judged that Novatian himself must be opposed, lest the evil spread more widely; and in the short work that he entitled *To Novatian the Heretic*, he assailed Novatian’s perverse doctrine and implacable disposition remarkably well, using testimonies from the divine Scriptures.

## III

Meanwhile, the churches of Spain also sought Cyprian’s authority and counsel. At that time thirty-six bishops from Africa had assembled at Carthage (Cyprian, Epist. 68). No one among the Spaniards was unaware that Basilides, bishop of Legio and Asturica, and likewise Martial, bishop of Mérida, had been defiled by certificates [Col. 1456D] of idolatry and bound by consciousness of unspeakable crimes, and had consequently fallen from office. Successors had therefore already been appointed to each: Sabinus to Basilides and Felix to Martial; and these had also come as delegates to Cyprian.

But the Spaniards were disturbed by the audacity of the deposed bishops, who claimed their former dignity for themselves. For this purpose Basilides had even gone to Rome and, as Cyprian attests, “had deceived Stephen, so as to maneuver himself back, unjustly, into the episcopate from which he had rightly been deposed.” Martial had employed no less deceit in order that he too might retain the office from which he had been expelled. Accordingly, after the churches’ letters had been read and [Col. 1457A] their delegates heard in council, Cyprian replied in accordance with his colleagues’ judgment that everything appeared to have been done in due order and lawfully, and that the offenses of these ambitious men had not been erased by Stephen’s authority, fraudulently interposed, but rather compounded. Then, after reviewing the crimes of each, he addresses the clergy and people of both churches as follows:

> Therefore, since, as you have written, dearly beloved brethren, and as our colleagues Felix and Sabinus affirm, and as another Felix of Caesaraugusta, a cultivator of the faith and defender of the truth, signifies in his letter, Basilides and Martial have been contaminated by an abominable certificate of idolatry; since Basilides, moreover, in addition to the stain of the certificate, blasphemed against God while lying ill, confessed that he had blasphemed, voluntarily laid down his episcopate because of the wound to his conscience, [Col. 1457B] turned to the performance of penance, implored God, and counted it sufficient cause for gratitude if only he might be granted communion even as a layman; and since Martial too, in addition to having long frequented the shameful and filthy banquets of the Gentiles in their association, and having deposited his sons in the same association at profane tombs according to the custom of foreign nations and buried them together with aliens, has also testified, in publicly recorded proceedings before the ducenarian procurator, that he complied with idolatry and denied Christ; and since there are many other grave offenses in which Basilides and Martial are implicated and held fast, such men attempt in vain to usurp the episcopate for themselves. For it is manifest that men of this kind can neither preside over the Church of Christ nor ought they to offer sacrifices [Col. 1457C] to God—especially since, long ago, together with us and with absolutely all the bishops established throughout the world, our colleague Cornelius, a peaceable and righteous priest who was also honored with martyrdom by the Lord’s favor, decreed that men of this kind may indeed be admitted to perform penance, but must be barred from ordination to the clergy and from priestly honor.

By these letters of Cyprian and his council, the scruple that troubled the Spaniards was at last removed; and the bishops were rejected, since it was established that their return to the seat of their dignity had been barred.

## IV

But another matter was now pressing, on account of which Cyprian had summoned the bishops of the Proconsular Province. For he had received letters from the bishops of Numidia [Col. 1457D] asking for his opinion “concerning those who appear to be baptized among heretics and schismatics: whether, when they come to the Catholic Church, which is one and true, they ought to be baptized.” The matter seems to have been called into controversy there at that time by those who knew the custom of the other churches and therefore did not think that adherence should be given to the ancient decrees of Agrippinus, bishop of Carthage.

Cyprian had indeed imbibed and deeply internalized the opinion that sacred Baptism among heretics and schismatics could not be valid, because they were outside the Church. He therefore regarded the force of the custom pleaded in opposition as slight and feeble, and affirmed that it ought to yield to truth. Thus, when the question began to be discussed in council, by reason of the authority he possessed among them all he readily brought each man over to his own opinion; and the following reply was sent to the Numidian bishops [Col. 1458A] (Epist. 70):

> Concerning this matter, although you yourselves there maintain the truth and firmness of the Catholic rule, nevertheless, since on account of our common affection you have thought that we should be consulted, we set forth no new opinion of our own, but join with you in equal agreement an opinion established long ago by our predecessors and observed by us: namely, judging and holding as certain that no one can be baptized outside, beyond the Church, since the one Baptism has been established in the holy Church.

And so forth.

The council had scarcely been dismissed when the same controversy was referred to Cyprian from Mauretania. Quintus, bishop of Burugis, asked what his opinion was “concerning those who appear to be baptized among heretics and schismatics.” Cyprian replied [Col. 1458B] (Epist. 71):

> That you might know what very many fellow bishops, together with the fellow presbyters who were present, recently judged in council, I have sent you a copy of that same letter.

Not content with this, he added many arguments which he considered remarkably effective in defending his position:

> For I do not know by what presumption certain of our colleagues are led to think that those who have been immersed among heretics ought not to be baptized when they come to us, on the ground that they say there is one Baptism—which is one, of course, because the Church is one, and Baptism cannot exist outside the Church.

And other statements of this kind.

At perhaps about the same time, Rogatian, bishop of Nova in the same Mauretania, had complained to Cyprian [Col. 1458C] about his deacon, “because, unmindful of the priest’s station and forgetful of his own office and ministry, he had provoked him with insults and injuries.” Cyprian praised the man’s moderation, because he had preferred to complain about the deacon rather than use his authority to punish him. Nevertheless, he judged that a limit must be placed upon indulgence:

> The deacon about whom you write ought to do penance for his audacity, acknowledge the honor of the priest, and make satisfaction in complete humility to the bishop set over him.

And he adduces a most serious reason for punishing the offense:

> For these are the beginnings of heretics, and the origins and endeavors of ill-minded schismatics: that they become pleased with themselves and, with arrogant swelling, despise the one set over them. [Col. 1458D] Thus men withdraw from the Church; thus a profane altar is established outside; thus they rebel against the peace of Christ and against God’s ordering and unity.

## V

Peaceful times and leisure for debate brought other matters into controversy, quite apart from the fact that the very question concerning Baptism seemed somewhat difficult and obscure to many. It was therefore necessary to convene a council again before the end of the year; seventy-one bishops came to it, some from the Proconsular Province and some from Numidia. Cyprian himself attests (Epist. 72) that many matters were then “brought forward and transacted” there; but there are two in particular which he identifies and explains.

The first, which had also been discussed in the preceding council, was that:

> Those who have been immersed outside, beyond the Church, and stained among heretics and schismatics by the defilement of profane water, ought to be baptized when they come to us and to the Church, which is one. [Col. 1459A]

The second was:

> If any presbyters or deacons were first ordained in the Catholic Church and afterward stood as faithless rebels against the Church, or if among heretics they were advanced by pseudo-bishops and Antichrists through a profane ordination contrary to Christ’s ordering, and attempted outside to offer false and sacrilegious sacrifices in opposition to the one altar and the divine sacrifice, they too, when they return, are to be received on this condition: that they communicate as laymen and regard it as sufficient that they are admitted to peace, since they had stood forth as enemies of peace; nor ought they, on returning, to retain among us those weapons of ordination and honor with which they had rebelled against us.

It is established that both provisions were sanctioned by the common consent of the council. [Col. 1459B] But they judged that concerning both matters a letter should especially be written to Stephen, the Supreme Pontiff, and the matter discussed with his—so they say—gravity and wisdom.

The synod’s letter survives, in which the same decisions are stated; it also mentions the letters that, as we indicated above, had been written to Quintus in Mauretania and to the bishops of Numidia:

> Moreover, that the baptism which heretics employ is no baptism, and that no one among those who oppose Christ can profit through the grace of Christ, was carefully explained recently in the letter written on this matter to our colleague Quintus, established in Mauretania; likewise in the letter which our colleagues had previously written to the fellow bishops presiding in Numidia. [Col. 1459C] We append copies of both letters here.

The final statements of the synodal letter are, however, especially worthy of mention. From them it becomes manifest that this entire controversy over Baptism was by no means considered to pertain to the substance of Catholic profession, and that those who held the contrary position were equally regarded as Catholics:

> We know that some men are unwilling to relinquish what they have once imbibed, or readily to change their settled opinion, but, with the bond of peace and concord among colleagues preserved, retain certain practices of their own which have once been adopted among them. In this matter we neither coerce anyone nor impose a law, since each prelate possesses free judgment of his own will in the administration of the Church and will render to the Lord an account of his conduct.

(See Somier, in Anastasius Bianchi, vol. II, p. 220.)

## VI

[Col. 1459D] After this letter had been sent to Stephen in the name of Cyprian and all the Fathers, the council was dismissed. But when the bishops returned to their churches, they filled all Africa with disputes. Bishops who had found the Roman custom in their own churches dissented, and it is credible that some of their number wrote to Stephen on the matter. There were also some who wished to be instructed by Cyprian’s testimony and for that reason sent him carefully composed letters.

Prominent among these was Jubaianus, bishop of an unknown city, whom one might nevertheless suppose to have been primate of Numidia (see Schelstrate, *Antiquitas Ecclesiae*, vol. II, p. 281; Zonaras calls him Jovinianus), since Cyprian is said subsequently to have replied to him and to his fellow bishops. Jubaianus wrote to Cyprian [Col. 1460A] from his province in such a way as also to append a copy of a treatise—either received from Rome or published in Africa—in which Cyprian’s position was refuted. Cyprian therefore considered it his duty, in replying to Jubaianus at greater length, also to set forth the reasons by which he thought his opponents’ arguments could be refuted. For he understood that his response would come into everyone’s hands.

But on this question, which was then somewhat obscure, Cyprian had settled in his mind that nothing good could proceed from heretics because they were evil, and that they were no less denied the right to baptize than the right to remit sins by granting absolution. He gave insufficient consideration, however, to the efficacy of Baptism itself, which depended in no way upon the minister. This is approximately the substance of the letter to Jubaianus. Yet he concludes the letter in such a manner as to indicate that he wished rather to debate and defend his own position [Col. 1460B] than to prescribe or define anything:

> These things, dearly beloved brother, we have written briefly in reply according to our limited ability, neither prescribing nor prejudging anyone, so as to prevent each bishop from doing what he thinks right, since he possesses the free exercise of his own judgment. For our part, so far as lies within us, we do not quarrel on account of heretics with our colleagues and fellow bishops, with whom we maintain divine concord and the Lord’s peace.

Finally, because he had learned that many bishops did not agree with him and that many could not tolerate an opponent, and that as a result some dissension of minds had arisen, he attests that he had applied a remedy to this evil:

> We patiently and gently preserve affection of spirit, the honor of the college, the bond of faith, and the concord of the priesthood. For this reason also, to the extent that our limited ability availed with the Lord’s permission and inspiration, we have now composed the treatise *On the Benefit of Patience*, which I have transmitted to you out of mutual affection.

That excellent short work of the most holy man still survives and is handled by readers. He composed it in such a way that he did not censure any one of his opponents even by the slightest indication, but explained to all, in the fullest measure, how much good there is in that virtue.

# CHRISTIAN YEAR 255  
## CYPRIAN BEING BISHOP OF CARTHAGE

## I

Once again the consulship was held by the Augusti, and the emperors P. Licinius Valerianus III and P. Licinius Gallienus II entered office as consuls. Stephen, the Supreme Pontiff, had now received the letters of Cyprian and his council, and was deliberating with his presbyters and with the bishops who happened to be present at Rome about the manner in which he should reply and deter the whole African synod from its purpose. For the Roman Church bore witness that it had possessed an ancient and unbroken custom: those returning from heretics whom it received were subjected to the laying on of hands for penance, but it did not undertake to wash anyone with Baptism.

Vincent of Lérins therefore says (*Commonitorium*, ch. 9):

> When everyone everywhere protested against the novelty of the matter, and all the priests in every quarter resisted, each according to his own zeal, [Col. 1461A] then Stephen of blessed memory, prelate of the Apostolic See, resisted together with his other colleagues, yet above the others. He considered it fitting, I think, that he should surpass all the rest in devotion to the faith as much as he exceeded them in the authority of his office. Finally, in the letter then sent to Africa, he laid down this rule in the following words: “Nothing is to be innovated beyond what has been handed down.” For the holy and prudent man understood that the principle of piety admitted nothing else than that everything received in faith from the Fathers should be transmitted to their children in the same faith; and that we ought not to lead religion wherever we wished, but rather to follow wherever it led; and that it is characteristic of Christian modesty and gravity not to hand down one’s own inventions to posterity, but to preserve what was received from one’s forebears.

[Col. 1461B] Stephen’s letter itself, however, whatever its character may have been, has not reached us. Nothing else survives from it except the small passage read in Cyprian’s letter to Pompeius—whatever, in the end, this letter too should be considered to be:

> If, therefore, anyone comes to you from any heresy whatsoever, let nothing be innovated beyond what has been handed down: namely, that the hand be laid upon him for penance; since the heretics themselves, strictly speaking, do not baptize persons coming from one party to another, but merely admit them to communion.

(Cyprian, Epist. 74; on this decree of Stephen, read Missorius, *Disputatio critica*, p. 385.)

## II

I would readily grant that Stephen’s response, if such it was, greatly displeased Cyprian. But I cannot at all be induced to believe that Cyprian, after once receiving from “the Chair of Peter and the principal Church [Col. 1461C] from which priestly unity arose” (the same, Epist. 55) a letter not in accordance with his own opinion, became so enraged that he suddenly forgot everything he had publicly professed: that he coerced none of his colleagues, imposed a law upon none, and preserved affection of spirit, the honor of the college, the bond of faith, and the concord of the priesthood.

For the actions he is accused of taking against Stephen are no light matters, but rather such as would scarcely seem possible in so great a man. If the letter said to have been sent to Pompeius, bishop of Sabratha, must be attributed to Cyprian, he not only refused to acquiesce in Stephen’s judgment but also stirred up others against him. On account of such a reply he accused Stephen [Col. 1461D] of error, as though “he were attempting to defend the cause of heretics against Christians and against the Church of God.” He asserted that many things had been written by Stephen “ignorantly and incautiously,” and that they were either “arrogant, irrelevant to the matter, or self-contradictory.” He called Stephen’s constancy “harsh obstinacy” and urged the bishops to reject Stephen’s doctrine:

> Therefore let us abandon error and follow truth.

Surely no one who weighs these statements will think that they ever proceeded from the mouth of a man who, not only before this time but continually thereafter as well, manifestly distinguished himself by holiness of life, zeal for concord, gravity of character, and the voluntary and prolonged endurance of arduous and difficult circumstances. For this reason Augustine too indicated more than once that he regarded that letter as suspect [Col. 1462A] (*Against Cresconius*, book II, ch. 31, etc.); and others believed it had been fabricated by the Donatists to support their cause (see Missorius, *Disputatio critica in epistolas Cypriani et Firmiliani*, p. 264).

## III

Cyprian, however, regarded Stephen’s reply not as a law imposed upon him but as the judgment of a private individual, and decided to ascertain for a third time what the African Church thought concerning the Baptism of heretics. A third council was therefore announced for the Kalends of September, so that bishops might attend in large numbers even from Mauretania and the other more distant churches.

By now that controversy had crossed the sea and reached the East also; and in many churches the two positions were being debated with no slight dissension. Letters had also been sent to Stephen reporting that it had already become the custom of many bishops to immerse again in Baptism heretics returning to the Church. Stephen found this so grave that he threatened many of them that, unless they came to their senses, he would withdraw from communion with them (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VII, ch. 5).

But it was not granted to Stephen to put an end to the error, which was removed not long afterward by the authority of Xystus, his successor, and through the efforts of Dionysius of Alexandria.
