For if we believe Eusebius (*Ecclesiastical History*, book VII, ch. 5), Stephen died this year after serving two years in the pontificate, on the fourth day before the Nones of August, the day on which his memory is celebrated in the ancient Martyrologies; and Xystus succeeded him.

## IV

[Col. 1462C] Meanwhile, bishops had assembled from every quarter at Carthage for the synod, eighty-five in number. Of these, Natalis of Oea had brought the mandates of the bishops Pompeius of Sabratha and Dioga of Leptis Magna, who had remained at home; on their account eighty-seven bishops were said to hold the same opinion. Those who held the other opinion did not set foot outside their own territories.

The acts of this council survive and present to us the sequence of its proceedings. First, very many bishops are said to have assembled on the Kalends of September from the province of Africa, Numidia, and Mauretania, together with presbyters and deacons, a very large portion of the people also being present. Before them were read Jubaianus’s letter to Cyprian, the letter Cyprian had sent to Jubaianus, and the letter he had in turn received from him; in these, I think, Stephen’s reply [Col. 1462D] was also contained.

After this Cyprian said:

> You have heard, dearly beloved colleagues, what our fellow bishop Jubaianus wrote to me, consulting our limited judgment concerning the illicit and profane baptism of heretics; and what I wrote to him in reply: namely, judging—as we have judged once, twice, and often—that heretics coming to the Church ought to be baptized and sanctified with Baptism. You have likewise heard another letter of Jubaianus read to you, in which, replying to my letter in accordance with his sincere and religious devotion, he not only agreed but also gave thanks and confessed that he had been instructed. It remains for each of us to state what we think concerning this very matter, judging no one and removing no one from the right of communion if he should think differently. For none of us appoints himself bishop of bishops [Col. 1463A] or drives his colleagues by tyrannical terror to the necessity of obedience, since every bishop, by virtue of his freedom and authority, possesses a judgment of his own, and can no more be judged by another than he himself can judge another. But let us all await the judgment of our Lord Jesus Christ, who alone possesses the power both to appoint us to the governance of his Church and to judge our conduct.

They then proceeded to deliver their opinions. Caecilius of Bilta was the first of all to state his own; the others followed according to seniority. Although different men employed different words, not a single one dissented from Cyprian’s opinion. Thus Cyprian spoke last:

> My opinion is most fully expressed [Col. 1463B] in the letter written to our colleague Jubaianus: when heretics—who according to the testimony of the Gospel and the Apostles are called adversaries of Christ and Antichrists—come to the Church, they must be baptized with the one Baptism of the Church, so that from adversaries they may become friends, and from Antichrists, Christians.

One might think these words were written more according to the opinion of the ancients than according to our own.

## V

What the Fathers established or did after this we do not know at all. Those who think that delegates were sent to Rome to the Supreme Pontiff in order to inform him of the synod’s decrees can produce no letters written for that purpose. Those, on the other hand, who say that the deacon Rogatian was sent by Cyprian as a delegate all the way to Cappadocia, to Firmilian, bishop of Caesarea, [Col. 1463C] so that Cyprian might inform a man whom he knew to hold the same opinion of the African synod’s agreement, possess neither Greek letters of Firmilian nor Latin letters of Cyprian to produce.

The Latin letter of Firmilian which they do present (among Cyprian’s letters, Epist. 75) was known neither to Dionysius of Alexandria, nor to Eusebius, nor even to Augustine. It is of such a character that it could have been written not by a holy man commended by many, but only by a wicked and infamous heretic: so abusive and shameless is it toward Stephen, successor of the Apostle Peter (see Missorius, ibid., p. 18, and his *Notes*, p. 112). I would indeed judge it to have been produced by the same person who forged Cyprian’s letter to Pompeius. For it was greatly in the Donatists’ interest that examples of this kind should survive, since they endeavored to diminish the authority of the Supreme Pontiff and evade his judgment.

It is nevertheless credible that Cyprian at this time wrote the extant letter to Magnus, since in it he touches upon and explains, with like reasoning, everything that had anywhere been disputed concerning the Baptism of heretics. Magnus—whoever he may have been, whether one of the people or a man initiated into the sacred ministry, for Cyprian calls him “son”—had asked whether those coming from Novatian ought likewise to be baptized. Cyprian replied [Col. 1464A] (Epist. 81):

> Insofar as the capacity of our faith and the sanctity and truth of the divine Scriptures suggest, we say that absolutely all heretics and schismatics possess no power or right. Therefore Novatian neither ought nor can be excepted from the rule that, because he stands outside the Church and acts against the peace and love of Christ, he is to be numbered among the adversaries and Antichrists.

Magnus had also posed another question concerning those who had been baptized near death, which Cyprian resolves as follows:

> You have also asked, dearly beloved son, what I think about those who obtain the grace of God in sickness and debility: whether they are to be regarded as legitimate Christians, because they have not been washed in saving water but sprinkled. On this point our diffidence and modesty prejudges no one, so as to prevent each person from thinking what he believes and doing what he has decided. For our part, insofar as our limited understanding apprehends, we judge that the divine benefits can in no respect be mutilated or weakened, and that nothing less can be obtained there [Col. 1464B] where what is drawn from the divine gifts is received with the complete and entire faith both of the giver and of the recipient.

The final words of the letter also display Cyprian’s customary modesty and singular zeal for concord:

> I have replied, dearly beloved son, to your letter to the extent that my slight and limited ability availed, and I have shown what we, insofar as lies within us, think; prescribing to no one, so as to prevent each prelate from determining what he thinks right, since he will render to the Lord an account of his conduct.

# CHRISTIAN YEAR 256  
## CYPRIAN BEING BISHOP OF CARTHAGE

## I

The consuls M. Valerius Maximus and Manius Acilius Glabrio mark this year, in which Aspasius Paternus was appointed proconsul of Africa. In the same year Xystus, who had been substituted in Stephen’s place, after himself receiving a letter concerning the controversy over Baptism from Dionysius, bishop of Alexandria (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VII, ch. 5), seems finally to have removed the dissension and restored peace to Africa and the East. For this reason he was called by the deacon Pontius (*Life of Cyprian*, no. 14):

> A good and peaceable priest.

He nevertheless faithfully defended Stephen’s position and, as was proper, made it common to the universal Church.

Jerome seems to indicate that this position was also received and confirmed in Africa by a new decree, when he says (*Dialogue Against the Luciferians*, no. 23):

> Blessed Cyprian attempted to flee broken cisterns and not to drink from alien water; and therefore, rejecting the Baptism of heretics, he sent an African synod concerning this matter to Stephen, then bishop of the city of Rome. But his attempt was fruitless. Finally, those very bishops who had decreed with him that heretics should be rebaptized returned to the ancient custom and issued a new decree.

The words of Vincent of Lérins point in the same direction.

> [Note: [Col. 1464D] *Commonitorium*, no. 10. See Beda, *Book of Various Questions*, question 5, on the Apostle’s words, “Let each abound in his own understanding.”]

> What, finally, was the force of that African council or decree? By God’s gift, none. Rather, all of it, as though dreams, as though fables, as though superfluous matter, was abolished, antiquated, and trampled underfoot.

Except that so important a matter was unknown to Augustine, who wrote thus concerning Cyprian [Col. 1465A]:

> [Note: [Col. 1465D] *On Baptism Against the Donatists*, book II, ch. 4; see Epist. 93, no. 36; see Boschius in the Bollandists, vol. I, August, p. 118, § 4.]

> Certainly so holy and peaceable a soul could most readily have agreed even with one man who spoke and demonstrated the truth; and perhaps this was done, but we do not know.

Against this, however, one may cite Cyprian’s own silence: afterward he said nothing further about that question and made no mention of the letters which he had previously composed and published with the greatest care.

## II

Cyprian had indeed directed his diligence and care to another object: namely, to cultivate and strengthen the minds of his clergy and people, recalling them to their former union in case some taint of animosity had infected them in that dissension. For this reason he composed that most beautiful treatise which he entitled *On Jealousy and Envy*, describing in particular the evils which flowed from envy into human life as from a fountain [Col. 1465B]:

> Far and wide extends the manifold and prolific ruin of jealousy. It is the root of all evils, the source of calamities, the nursery of offenses, the material of transgressions. From it hatred rises; from it animosity proceeds. Jealousy inflames avarice when someone cannot be content with what is his own because he sees another richer. Jealousy arouses ambition when someone sees another higher in honors. When jealousy blinds our perceptions and brings the secrets of the mind under its dominion, the fear of God is despised, Christ’s teaching is neglected, and the day of judgment is not foreseen. Pride puffs up, cruelty embitters, perfidy betrays, impatience shakes, discord rages, and anger burns; nor can one who has been brought under another’s power any longer restrain or govern himself. [Col. 1465C] Hence the bond of the Lord’s peace is broken; hence brotherly love is violated; hence truth is adulterated, unity is rent, and men leap into heresies and schisms, while priests are disparaged, bishops are envied, and a man either complains that he himself was not ordained instead, or disdains to endure another as his prelate.

Thus Cyprian, referring, I think, to the recent bitterness of spirit which he had unwillingly witnessed and whose removal especially gladdened him.

## III

Amid these events, Caecilius, bishop of the people of Bilta, who had attended the council in the preceding year, returned to his church and found that a certain opinion—one that might seem to have originated with the Encratites—had gradually spread among those who abstained from wine: namely, that water, not wine, ought to be offered and consecrated in the Sacrifice. He rejected so great an innovation and wished to remove it altogether, but thought the matter would succeed more happily if he consulted Cyprian and could interpose his authority.

Accordingly, after sending him a carefully composed letter concerning the entire affair, he received a long letter from Cyprian that would put an end to that opinion and recall absolutely everyone to the ancient custom. This letter is entitled (Epist. 63) *On the Sacrament of the Lord’s Chalice*. In it Cyprian shows above all that it was instituted and prescribed by our Lord himself that bread and wine should be offered in the Sacrifice, just as [Col. 1466A] it had also been foretold by many prophecies of the divine Scriptures.

He nevertheless teaches that water must be mixed with the wine, judging that the people are signified by the water:

> For because Christ bore us all, he who also bore our sins, we see that the people are understood in the water, while the blood of Christ is shown in the wine. But when water is mixed with wine in the chalice, the people are united to Christ, and the congregation of believers is coupled and joined to him in whom it has believed.

He rejects the difficulty of those who feared “that through the taste of the wine they might smell of the blood of Christ.” He wishes letters to be written to his colleagues “so that everywhere the law of the Gospel and the tradition of the Lord may be observed, and there may be no departure from what Christ both taught and did.”

Finally, he concludes the letter with these words:

> It therefore accords with our religion and fear, and with the very station and office of our priesthood, dearly beloved brother, that in mixing and offering the Lord’s chalice we preserve the truth of the Lord’s tradition, and, at the Lord’s admonition, correct what previously appears to have been done erroneously among certain persons; so that, when he begins to come in his glory and heavenly majesty, he may find us holding what he admonished, observing what he taught, and doing what he did.

From the same letter it may also be learned that the common practice among the Africans in the Sacrifice was the use of unleavened bread. For, in connection with so great a mystery, Cyprian mentions bread “united and joined together from flour and water,” without any mention of leaven (see Ciampini, *On the Perpetual Use of Unleavened Bread*, ch. 3, p. 45). This practice continued in Augustine’s age as well.

[Col. 1466C] IV. Toward the end of the year, Cyprian was informed that Geminius Victor, bishop of Furni, who had attended the synod the previous year, had died of illness. Cyprian was indeed deeply grieved to have lost a colleague; but far more grievous was the news he learned at the same time: that Victor had died after first appointing the presbyter Geminius Faustinus guardian in his will. For Cyprian knew that it had long before been decreed in a council of bishops (Cyprian, *Epistle* 66; see Bollandus, vol. IV, September, p. 211) “that no one should appoint any cleric or minister of God as guardian or curator in his will.” The following reason had been appended to this decree: “Since those who have individually been honored with the divine priesthood and appointed to clerical ministry ought to serve only the altar and the sacrifices, and to devote themselves to prayers [Col. 1466D] and supplications.” Nor was the penalty unknown which those same bishops had established against those who disregarded the law; for, after deciding that no one should be permitted to do this, they added: “And if anyone should do so, no offering shall be made for him, nor shall the sacrifice for his falling asleep be celebrated. For,” they said, “he who wished to call priests and ministers away from the altar does not deserve to be named at God’s altar in the prayer of the priests.”

Cyprian, therefore, who well remembered that he ought to be the defender and champion of the sacred canons, wrote without hesitation to the clergy and people residing at Furni. After mentioning the earlier law, he gave the following direction:

“And therefore, since Victor, contrary to the rule recently established by the priests in council, dared [Col. 1467A] to appoint the presbyter Geminius Faustinus as guardian, no offering is to be made among us for his falling asleep, nor is any supplication in his name to be offered in the Church, so that the decree of the priests, made devoutly and necessarily, may be observed by us, and at the same time an example may be given to the other brethren, lest anyone summon priests and ministers of God, who are devoted to his altar and Church, away to secular troubles. For it will be possible to ensure hereafter that this is no longer done in the case of clerics, if what has now been done is punished.”

Moreover, since Cyprian relaxed none of the severity of that law, it must not be supposed that he himself undertook the management of the wife and children of the presbyter Caecilius, through whose efforts he had become a Christian and whom he revered as the father of his new life. Pontius does indeed write of him in these words (*Life of Cyprian*, [Col. 1467B] no. 4): “Finally, Caecilius, won over by Cyprian’s devoted services and deservedly moved to a love of extraordinary depth, when he was departing from this world and his summons was already near, entrusted his wife and children to him, so that the man whom he had made a participant in the fellowship of the sect he might afterward make the heir of his dutiful affection.” Nevertheless, I believe that Cyprian discharged his obligation to his Caecilius in such a way that, in love and concern, he acted as a father to his household, but sought out and appointed upright and suitable men from outside the clergy as managers of the property and guardians of the children.

V. A year had not yet elapsed when letters reached Africa reporting that the Church at Rome was in grave danger: that the emperor Valerian, who had previously shown remarkable favor to the Christians (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VII, ch. 10), [Col. 1467C] had been alienated by the guile and fraud of Macrianus, whose counsel he followed, and was threatening destruction; that many had already been cast into chains; and that edicts against the Christian name would shortly be sent into the provinces. Many were indeed dismayed at the announcement of so great a calamity and, terrified by the prospect of death, lost heart. Yet there were not lacking those whose eagerness stood out and stirred the courage of the others toward glorious martyrdoms. There was also someone who desired Cyprian to write something by which the hearts of all might be set aflame with zeal for an unconquerable confession.

Cyprian, who had always done such things of his own accord, instructing the people with exhortation suited to the occasion, did so all the more when asked. He issued to Fortunatus the second work “On Exhortation to Martyrdom,” filled [Col. 1467D] with most sacred testimonies capable of kindling even the most sluggish and remiss person with longing for so blessed an end. He had arranged the little work in twelve chapters, placing beneath each one authorities from Holy Scripture that explained and confirmed the titles of the individual chapters, so that everyone might have ready at hand material, as it were, not only for reading and meditation but also for conversation and writing.

“And lest,” he says (p. 708, ed. Baluze), “I should prolong my discourse, dearest brother, and weary the hearer or reader with a profusion of more expansive writing, I have made an abridgment: after setting out the headings that one ought both to know and to retain, I have attached passages from the Lord, and have strengthened what I proposed with the authority of the divine reading, so that I may seem not so much to have sent you a treatise of my own [Col. 1468A] as to have supplied material for those who compose treatises.”

In this, he says, he also took care that “in so necessary an exhortation, one that makes martyrs, the delays and impediments of our own words must be cut away, the circumlocutions of human discourse removed, and only those things set down which God speaks, by which Christ exhorts his servants to martyrdom.”

I regard it as sufficiently established that this letter was written to Fortunatus, bishop of Thuccabor. For Cyprian calls him “brother,” and only one Fortunatus by name, the bishop of Thuccabor, is cited among the bishops who had recently assembled at Carthage for the council. But one may rightly judge that copies of it were also sent to others, so that it might benefit as many people as possible.

## CHRISTIAN YEAR 257. CYPRIAN, BISHOP OF CARTHAGE

[Col. 1468B]

I. The emperors again became consuls: Valerian for the fourth time, Gallienus for the third. Conspiracies of barbarians and Persian movements were already summoning them to war. Yet there remained in the City men who would take up Valerian’s hatred against the Christians and carry his cruelty to its full extent. Martyrs were already being numbered at Rome who, first to seize the laurel, had marked out for the rest the road to heaven with their own blood. In Africa, however, private letters alone had thus far increased the alarm, and nothing had yet been publicly announced. The bishops therefore appear to have had ample time to spend exhorting the people to constancy and strengthening their spirits by imparting the divine mysteries. [Col. 1468C] For this was their chief concern, and it was principally for this reason that Cyprian had formerly argued that the lapsed should be received back: lest they be exposed unarmed to the enemy’s attack.

“For how,” he said (*Epistle* 54, to Cornelius), “do we teach or encourage them to pour out their blood in confession of the Name if, when they are about to enter battle, we deny them the blood of Christ? Or how do we make them fit for the cup of martyrdom if we do not first admit them within the Church, by right of communion, to drink the cup of the Lord?”

II. At last the emperors’ edicts themselves were brought to Carthage, addressed to the proconsul Aspasius Paternus. They commanded (*Proconsular Acts of the Martyrdom of Cyprian*, concerning Paternus; see Lupus, *Epistolae Severae*, M., § III, p. 8) [Col. 1468D] “that those who did not practice the Roman religion must acknowledge the Roman rites.” There is no doubt that Paternus had been instructed first to proceed against the bishops and presbyters and the entire clergy, and immediately to banish any among them whom he found resistant. For afterward, too, when matters came to slaughter and bloodshed, it is apparent that the bishops and their order were the first destined for death (Cyprian, *Epistle* 82).

Accordingly, at Carthage Cyprian entered the arena before the others, to serve as an example to many of how they were to triumph over the enemy. Nemesianus and his fellow confessors indeed accord him this praise in the letter by which they replied to his most gracious communication (*Epistle* 78, among Cyprian’s letters):

“You yourself know, dearest brother, that our cherished desire is fulfilled in seeing you, our teacher and beloved, [Col. 1469A] attain the crown of a great confession. For, like a good and true teacher, you were the first to declare in the proconsul’s official proceedings what we, your disciples, ought to say when following you before the governor; and, sounding the trumpet, you roused the soldiers of God, equipped with heavenly arms, to the battle of encounter. Fighting in the foremost rank, you slew the devil with the spiritual sword; and with your words you marshaled the ranks of the brethren on every side, so that snares might be laid everywhere for the enemy and the severed sinews of the corpse of that public enemy might be trampled underfoot.”

We have not learned from our predecessors in what month Cyprian was taken into custody. But the proconsular acts testify that he was brought forward on the third day before the Kalends of September and stood before the proconsul in the audience chamber. After the latter had Cyprian brought [Col. 1469B] before him, he said: “I have accordingly made inquiry concerning your identity. What answer do you give me?”

Cyprian, whom continual labors and long discipline had prepared for that contest, answered: “I am a Christian and a bishop. I know no other gods except the one and true God, who made heaven and earth, the sea, and all things that are in them. We Christians serve this God; to him we pray day and night, for ourselves and for all human beings, and for the safety of the emperors themselves.”

When the proconsul asked whether he persisted in the same resolve, Cyprian added: “A good resolve, which knows God, cannot be changed.”

Paternus, therefore, recognizing the man’s constancy and dispensing with circumlocutions, said: “Can you, [Col. 1469C] then, in accordance with the command of Valerian and Gallienus, depart into exile for the city of Curubis?”

“I shall depart,” Cyprian replied.

The proconsul then stated that he had received orders not only concerning the bishops but also the presbyters. “I therefore wish,” he said, “to learn from you who the presbyters are who reside in this city.”

Cyprian replied: “In your laws you have rightly and beneficially decreed that there are to be no informers. Therefore they cannot be disclosed or denounced by me. They will, however, be found in their own cities.”

The proconsul nevertheless pressed him, saying: “I am making inquiry here, in this place, today.”

Cyprian answered: “Since our discipline forbids anyone to offer himself voluntarily, and this is likewise displeasing to your own judgment, they cannot present themselves; but when sought out by you, they will be found.”

[Col. 1469D] Paternus accepted this and said that he would find the presbyters. But he added that the emperors had given him still other commands. “They have also ordered,” he said, “that assemblies are not to be held in any places and that no one is to enter the cemeteries. Therefore, if anyone does not observe this salutary command, he will be punished with death.”

Cyprian’s answer was: “Do what you have been ordered to do.”

And this was the end of his confession; for thereafter the proconsul ordered him to be deported into exile.

III. Cyprian reached Curubis, a town situated on the Promontory of Mercury, after the Ides of September. Among his domestic companions he had a voluntary fellow exile, the deacon Pontius (Pontius, *Life of Cyprian*, no. 12), who later wrote his life, after having vainly desired to share his death.

During Cyprian’s first night at Curubis, [Col. 1470A] a vision was presented to him in his sleep by which he was given sure hope of martyrdom. He did not conceal the matter from his companions; rather, according to Pontius, he related everything precisely in these words (*ibid.*):

“There appeared to me,” he said, “when I had not yet been lulled into the repose of sleep, a young man of extraordinary size. As he led me, as it were, to the governor’s residence, I seemed to be brought before the tribunal of the proconsul then seated there. When he looked at me, he immediately began to write a sentence on a tablet, though I did not know what it was, for he had asked me nothing in the customary interrogation. But the young man who stood behind him read with great attention whatever had been written down; and because he could not express it to me in words, he showed by an explanatory gesture what was contained in the writing on that tablet. For, extending his hand and flattening it like a sword, [Col. 1470B] he imitated the stroke of the customary execution and expressed what he wished me to understand as clearly as articulate speech. I understood that the sentence would be one of martyrdom.

“I immediately began to ask and entreat that a postponement of even one day might be granted me, until I could arrange my affairs in due order. After I had repeated my entreaties many times, the judge again began to write something—I do not know what—on the tablet. From the serenity of his countenance, however, I perceived that his mind had been moved, as though by a just request. Moreover, the young man who had earlier disclosed the indication of my martyrdom by gesture rather than speech repeatedly made secret signs, hastening to indicate by twisting one finger after another that the delay requested until the next day had been granted. Although the sentence had not been read, and although [Col. 1470C] my heart rejoiced greatly with gladness at the postponement I had received, I nevertheless trembled so much from fear that the interpretation might be uncertain that the remnants of dread continued to buffet my exultant heart with utter terror.”

The event showed that the day granted him for arranging his affairs was a year; when that had elapsed, Cyprian completed his martyrdom on the same date, the eighteenth day before the Kalends of October. The affairs that he wished first to arrange concerned the relief of the needy, the care of the confessors, and the general welfare of the Church. These he settled, partly by letters and partly through the efforts of those who frequently traveled to him, to the greatest benefit of all.

IV. While Cyprian was now in exile at Curubis, bishops, presbyters, and deacons—not only at Carthage but also here and there in other cities—were being dragged before tribunals. [Col. 1470D] As soon as they had professed themselves Christians, the judges condemned them to the mines. At that time these were marble quarries, particularly of the kind commonly worked in Numidia, whence come the many Numidian columns still standing in the City, which the visitor admires (see J. Castalio, in Gruter’s *Lampas*, vol. IV, p. 5).

There survive letters of Cyprian that bear witness to this cruelty, written “to Nemesianus, Felix, Lucius, another Felix, Licteus, Pollianus, Victor, Jader, and Dativus, fellow bishops, and likewise to their fellow presbyters and deacons and to the others stationed in the mine.” He describes their sufferings in such a way as to seek to lighten them by comparison with the blessedness close at hand:

“O feet,” he says (*Epistle* 77), “blessedly bound, which are released not by a smith but by the Lord! O feet blessedly bound, which are directed along the saving road to Paradise! O feet [Col. 1471A] bound for the present in this world, that they may be forever free with the Lord! O feet for a time impeded by fetters and crossbars, yet soon to run to Christ on a glorious course! Let jealous cruelty or malignant spite detain you here in its bonds and chains as long as it wishes: you will soon pass from the earth and these punishments to the kingdoms of heaven.

“In the mines the body is not cherished on a bed and mattresses, but it is cherished by the refreshment and consolation of Christ. Limbs exhausted by labor lie upon the ground, but to lie with Christ is no punishment. Members unwashed by baths are squalid and disfigured with neglect and filth, but what is outwardly soiled in the flesh is inwardly washed in the spirit. Bread there is scarce, but man lives not by bread alone, but by the word of God. Your freezing bodies lack clothing, but whoever has put on Christ is both abundantly clothed [Col. 1471B] and adorned. The hair bristles on a head half shorn; but since Christ is the head of man, whatever form that head bears must be fitting when it is distinguished on account of the Lord’s name.”

Suspecting, moreover, that they were grieved and distressed because they could not perform the sacred rites in that prison, he wiped away this sorrow and mourning as well:

“But neither,” he says, “dearest brothers, can any loss of religion or faith be felt there because the priests of God are now not given the opportunity to offer and celebrate the divine sacrifices. Indeed, you both celebrate and offer to God a sacrifice at once precious and glorious, one that will contribute greatly to your recompense of heavenly rewards”—and so forth.

Those unconquered confessors say that they were residing at the “Siguan Mine” [Col. 1471C] (*Epistle* 80, among Cyprian’s letters), that is, near Sigus, a town of Numidia between Macomadia and Cirta. All the bishops themselves were indeed Numidians and had attended the Council of Carthage two years earlier: Nemesianus of Tubunae, Felix of Bagai, Tucius of Theveste, Felix of Bamaccora, Licteus of Gemellae, Pollianus of Milevis, Victor of Octava, Jader of Midila, and Dativus of Badias. You may identify them all in the commentary that we prefixed to the *Annals*.

V. Thus far the fury of the pagans had broken out against the bishops and clergy. But it soon spread readily to the people as well. [Col. 1471D] For because, as the proconsul Aspasius had declared at Carthage, the emperors by their decree forbade assemblies to be held or anyone to enter the cemeteries, it was inevitable that many should be accused on this charge and, after acquitting themselves in an illustrious confession, be taken into custody.

To this belong the words that Cyprian wrote to the confessors at the Siguan Mine:

“Finally,” he says (*Epistle* 77; see Bollandus, vol. III, September, p. 483), “a large portion of the people followed your example, confessed together with you, and was crowned together with you, joined to you by the bond of most steadfast charity and separated from its leaders neither by prison nor by the mines. Nor are virgins absent from their number: to the sixtyfold fruit there was added the hundredfold, and a twofold glory advanced them to the heavenly crown. Among the children also, courage greater than their age surpassed their years through the praise of confession, so that every sex and every age adorned the blessed flock of your martyrdom.”

Cyprian had written these words from Curubis [Col. 1472A] to the confessors, and they brought them the greatest consolation. But he had given them not only letters but also aid by sending supplies, which they warmly attest that they received in a letter sent to Cyprian (*Epistle* 78, among Cyprian’s letters):

“Therefore those condemned with us join us in giving you the greatest thanks before God, dearest Cyprian, because by your letters you revived our laboring hearts, tended our limbs wounded by clubs, released our feet bound in fetters, evened the hair on our half-shorn heads, illuminated the darkness of the prison, leveled the mountains of the mine, placed fragrant perfumes before our nostrils, and shut out the foul odor of smoke. Your ministry, moreover, and that of our dearest Quirinus accomplished this through what you sent by Herennianus the subdeacon and by Lucianus [Col. 1472B], Maximus, and Amantius the acolytes to be distributed, supplying whatever had been lacking for our bodily needs.”

Who that Quirinus was, who joined his efforts with Cyprian’s so that the confessors might be relieved more generously, is not sufficiently established—unless he is to be regarded as the man to whom Cyprian dedicated the books of *Testimonies against the Jews*. I would believe that he was a fairly wealthy citizen of Carthage and an old friend of Cyprian.

It is likewise unclear what end those confessors met. It seems probable to me that the greater part died in the prison. For when Cyprian had again sent money there, only three bishops replied—Felix, Jader, and Pollianus (*Epistle* 80, among Cyprian’s letters)—[Col. 1472C] making no mention of their companions, perhaps because they had previously written to him of their deaths. Yet there also survives a letter from Bishop Lucius to Cyprian, giving thanks in his own name and that of the brethren (*Epistle* 79, among Cyprian’s letters) because he had sent them a gift together with Quirinus. It is therefore also permissible to suppose that the confessors, having increased in number, were subsequently divided among several prisons, and that the names of bishops are consequently absent from their letters because they were no longer together in a single place.

Whatever end was ultimately imposed upon the lives of so many confessors, from the time of Ado the Roman Church has honored their memory on the fourth day before the Ides of September and testifies that they “completed the contest of their glorious confession.” To this same period, I think, should be assigned the deacon Timothy, who was long confined in prison in Mauretania and afterward burned by fire, [Col. 1472D] thus achieving martyrdom. Both Latins and Greeks now celebrate him with many praises in their calendars on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of January.

VI. As for the remainder, amid so great an upheaval in Africa Cyprian conducted his watch at Curubis in such a way that, in spirit, thought, duty, and active assistance, he seemed present wherever calamity oppressed Christians and the hatred of their adversaries brought them into danger. We possess only a few of his letters, but it must be acknowledged that very many were written by him throughout all Africa, since it is established that letters were also sent by him into Italy (*Acts of the Martyrs*, Oxford, p. 53), to Augustinus and Felicitas, who met their deaths at Capua at that time.

He is also thought to have issued to the martyrs a work distinct from the one mentioned above, [Col. 1473A] entitled *On Exhortation to Martyrdom*. For Pontius, who mentions it, shows that he is referring to another work when he adds (*Life of Cyprian*, no. [uncertain or omitted in the source]): “Who, finally, would animate with the trumpet-call of heaven so many confessors, marked upon their foreheads with a second inscription and preserved alive as examples of martyrdom?” Certainly in the surviving letters of Cyprian no persons bearing brands are mentioned; perhaps that mark was burned into the confessors later, after the work had been suspended and they had each been ordered to return home.

## CHRISTIAN YEAR 258. CYPRIAN, BISHOP OF CARTHAGE

I. The consuls were Marcus Aurelius Memmius Tuscus and Pomponius Bassus. At this time Valerian, after traversing Illyricum, had reached Byzantium; [Col. 1473B] at Rome Cornelius Saecularis held the prefecture of the City.

Meanwhile Cyprian, still an exile at Curubis, eagerly awaited the longed-for day of his martyrdom and at the same time, insofar as was permitted, cared for the Church and for all the needy and afflicted. While the affairs of the Christians seemed to be in a milder condition, Galerius Maximus was appointed to succeed the proconsul Aspasius Paternus. On arriving at Carthage, he recalled Cyprian from Curubis and ordered him to retire to gardens near the city. Cyprian had sold these gardens when he became a Christian, in order to distribute the money obtained from them to the poor; but afterward, I suppose, he received them back because the purchaser had bequeathed them to him in his will.

[Col. 1473C] He remained there as though in open custody, in such a way that he was informed daily of the condition of his church and had members of his household ready for service, who would set out wherever he wished at his command. Thus, since he especially desired to know what was happening at Rome and what the fortunes of that Church were, he readily found men who would sail to Rome at once and return shortly with certain information.

He subsequently reported what they had learned to Successus, bishop of Abbir Germaniciana, when the clergy in Africa too, especially, were now, as he himself says, “beneath the stroke of the contest” (*Epistle* 82):

“Know that those whom I had sent to the City for this purpose have returned, so that, whatever rescript might have been issued concerning us, they might bring back to us the truth ascertained by themselves. For many diverse and uncertain reports are being tossed about in rumor; but the true facts stand as follows. [Col. 1473D] Valerian has written back to the senate that bishops, presbyters, and deacons are to be executed immediately. Senators, eminent men, and Roman knights, after losing their rank, are also to be stripped of their goods; and if, after the confiscation of their property, they persist in being Christians, they are also to be punished with death. Matrons are to be stripped of their property and banished. Members of the imperial household, however, whoever either had confessed earlier or should now confess, are to be forfeited to the fisc, put in chains, assigned, and sent to the imperial estates.”

These measures pertained principally to the City, where Xystus had indeed been slain before the others. “Know,” he says, “that Xystus was executed in the cemetery on the eighth day before the Ides of August, and with him four deacons. The prefects in the City also press this persecution daily, so that if any are brought before them, they are executed [Col. 1474A] and their goods claimed for the imperial treasury.”

But Valerian had already given equivalent orders to the governors of the provinces, concerning which he had written to the senate at the same time. Those orders were then either being conveyed to Carthage or had already arrived. “The emperor Valerian also appended,” he says, “to his address a copy of the letters he composed to the governors of the provinces concerning us. We expect these letters to arrive daily, standing in accordance with the firmness of faith in readiness to endure martyrdom, and awaiting from the help and mercy of the Lord the crown of eternal life.”

II. Cyprian had written this from his gardens to Successus, so that the latter might transmit it to the other colleagues and all the churches. Meanwhile the proconsul Galerius went to Utica, intending there [Col. 1474B] to make a beginning of the slaughter and execution of Christians.

When Cyprian learned this—whose desire was to pour out his life first in the midst of his own church and in the presence of those whom he himself had trained for martyrdom—he was extremely distressed that the opportunity to leave this final example to his church should be taken from him. He therefore adopted a plan of withdrawing while the proconsul was absent from Carthage. From the hiding place to which he had gone, he sent his final letter to his church and thus explained the reason for this decision (*Epistle* 83):

“When word had been brought to us, dearest brothers, that official warrants had been sent to convey me to Utica, and when, on the advice of my dearest friends, I had been urged to withdraw temporarily from our gardens, I consented because a just reason intervened: it is fitting that a bishop [Col. 1474C] confess the Lord in that city in which he presides over the Lord’s Church, and that the entire people be glorified by the confession of its present prelate. For whatever a confessor-bishop speaks at that moment of confession, he speaks, through the inspiration of God, with the mouth of all.

“Moreover, the honor of our so glorious church would be impaired if I, the bishop and leader of another church, should receive at Utica the sentence arising from my confession and depart from there as a martyr to the Lord. For I both pray with continual supplications and desire with every longing—and am bound—to confess among you, for myself and for you, to suffer there, and from there to depart to the Lord.

“We therefore wait here, established in a hidden retreat, for the arrival of the proconsul returning to Carthage, that we may hear from him what the emperors have commanded [Col. 1474D] concerning Christian laypeople and bishops, and may say what the Lord wills to be said at that hour.”

Thus far Cyprian, who did not cease even at the last to exhort his people to remember what they had often heard from him, to preserve peace and tranquility, to take care not to create danger for anyone, and not to allow anyone to offer himself voluntarily before the tribunal of the pagans.

III. At Utica, however, the proconsul, when Cyprian was not found, did not allow the axes to remain idle for long. Three hundred Christians were in chains at Utica, many from the city itself or neighboring towns, and many also from Carthage; for Prudentius calls them Cyprian’s disciples (*Peristephanon*, Hymn XIII, v. 88). We read in an ancient sermon, which long bore Augustine’s name, that they included both sexes and every age. [Col. 1475A] The same author also describes the manner of their death:

“No old man, already broken by declining years, withdrew his trembling neck from the executioner as his throat withered; no old woman, enfeebled by her sex and worn out by age, escaped the right hand of the bloodstained slayer; the sweetness of this life did not call the young back from the crown. The bloody executioner did not recoil from the quivering limbs of dying little children; but if perhaps any infants clinging hungrily to their mothers’ breasts were able to escape the persecutor’s sword, they died crushed beneath the fall of corpses amid their mothers’ tender embraces” (*Sermon* 317, in the Appendix to Augustine’s Works).

But Prudentius says that he had learned by report (*ibid.*, v. 76) that those martyrs, when an altar was placed on one side and on the other a pit of smoking lime, and they were commanded either to sacrifice to the gods or to cast themselves alive into the lime, all three hundred together [Col. 1475B] eagerly leapt forward at a rapid run. Consumed by the lime, they were thereafter called the “White Mass” (*Massa candida*). Ado also accepted this account and transferred it to his martyrology (eighth day before the Kalends of September).

Augustine, however, was unaware of this manner of their death and, in the sermon that he delivered “On the Festival of the Martyrs of the White Mass” (*Sermon* 306, ch. 2; likewise Bollandus, vol. IV, August, p. 263), offered this explanation of the designation: “It was called a mass because of the multitude of their number, and white because of the radiance of their cause.”

It appears probable to me that the report which reached Prudentius’ ears arose from the fact that the bodies of the martyrs were cast into that lime-pit so that they might be consumed more quickly. [Col. 1475C] Their memory nevertheless endured for a long time, especially among the people of Carthage, who, as appears from the calendar of that Church, celebrated them after the Ides of August. It endures in the Roman Church, which has long honored them on the ninth day before the Kalends of September, though formerly it commemorated them on the fifteenth day before those Kalends.

IV. At last the proconsul left Utica, made mournful by so many killings, and withdrew for reasons of health to a suburb of Carthage called Sextus. Cyprian likewise lost no time in returning from his hiding place to his gardens.

“Meanwhile,” says Pontius (*Life of Cyprian*, no. 14), “many men of eminent and most distinguished rank and lineage, noble also by the nobility of this world, met with him. Because of their old friendship with him, they repeatedly advised him to withdraw; and lest mere counsel be insufficient, they even offered him places to which he might retire. But he, his mind fixed upon heaven, had already disregarded the world and [Col. 1475D] did not assent to their flattering persuasions.”

Amid these events, when he now thought of nothing except the desired end of his life and rejoiced that the time for his binding had come, so that, free and blessed, he might reach his heavenly homeland, “suddenly,” as we read in his acts, “on the Ides of September, in the consulship of Tuscus and Bassus, two chief officers came to him, one the staff-rider of the office of the proconsul Galerius Maximus, and the other a mounted guard from the same office. They lifted him into a carriage, placed him between them, and conveyed him to Sextus.”

The proconsul nevertheless did not wish Cyprian to be brought before him that day, but postponed the matter until the next day, which was the anniversary of the day on which, at Curubis, Cyprian had learned through a vision the sure indication of his martyrdom. He was conducted to the house of the *strator* in a nearby district called Saturnus, between the “Venerea” [Col. 1476A] and the “Salutaria,” which I would believe to have been well-known roads in that region, and lodged with him.

When the Christians learned what had become known throughout Carthage, nearly all of them, anxious and distressed at the peril of their common father, hurried there. So great was the crowd in that district before the *strator*’s house that Cyprian ordered certain men to guard the girls who had also come and were spending the night outside the doors.

The following day, when Galerius had ordered his record-keepers and the remaining crowd of court attendants and lictors to be present at Sextus, Cyprian was at last brought before him. The proconsul sat in judgment in the Sauciolum atrium, so called from the punishment of the guilty (see Council of Mâcon II, canon 19); Cyprian stood opposite him, and every face was turned toward him.

[Col. 1476B] The proconsul fixed his eyes upon him and said: “Are you Thascius Cyprianus?” (*Proconsular Acts*, nos. 3–4). From this, of course, we know that he belonged to the Thascian family.

When Cyprian replied, “I am,” the proconsul added: “Have you presented yourself as pope to men of a sacrilegious persuasion?”

“I have,” Cyprian said.

The proconsul added: “The most sacred emperors have ordered you to perform the rites.”

Cyprian replied: “I will not.”

“Consider your own welfare,” the proconsul said.

Cyprian answered: “Do what you have been ordered to do. In so just a matter, there is no deliberation.”

The proconsul then, according to custom, summoned his assessors into consultation. When they had agreed among themselves upon Cyprian’s condemnation, before reading the sentence from the tablet he delivered the following preamble, [Col. 1476C] which, insulting as it was, served equally to exalt the most holy bishop’s lifelong labors and steadfast virtue:

“You have long lived with a sacrilegious mind, have gathered to yourself many men of a criminal conspiracy, and have made yourself an enemy of the Roman gods and sacred laws. Nor have the pious and most sacred sovereigns Valerian and Gallienus Augusti, and Valerian, most noble Caesar, been able to recall you to the observance of their rites. And therefore, since you have been apprehended as the author and standard-bearer of most wicked crimes, you yourself shall serve as an example to those whom you have gathered together with yourself in your wickedness. Discipline shall be established by your blood.”

Having spoken this preamble, he pronounced the decree as follows: “It is our judgment that Thascius Cyprianus be executed by the sword.”

Cyprian’s final words were: “Thanks be to God.”

[Col. 1476D] V. At this the whole multitude of Christians groaned deeply, and some were heard saying: “Let us too be beheaded with him.” When Cyprian began to be led outside to the open field, they all followed him with a great commotion so that they might witness his end at close quarters; centurions and tribunes guarded his flanks, and a ring of soldiers surrounded him (Pontius, *Life of Cyprian*, no. 18). They had not yet reached the place of martyrdom, and many had already climbed the trees, while the rest of the crowd stood around the field. Then Cyprian, having advanced into the midst (*Proconsular Acts*, no. 5), took off the red cloak he was wearing and, bending his knees and bowing his head, silently poured out prayers to God. He then removed his dalmatic as well and handed it to the deacons, while he himself, remaining in a linen garment, bared his neck to the executioner. When the man arrived, Cyprian turned to his own people [Col. 1477A] and ordered that twenty-five gold pieces be given to him. He then covered his own eyes with a band; since he could not tie it himself, Julian the presbyter and Julian the subdeacon fastened it for him with their own hands. Meanwhile, others spread linen cloths and handkerchiefs beneath him to catch the martyr’s blood. Thus was severed that sacred head which had been the greatest glory and supreme defense of the Church of Carthage.

His lifeless body lay in public until nightfall, while even the pagans streamed in from every direction to look upon it. During the night the Christians took it up and, with great pomp as though in a triumphal procession, preceded by wax candles and torches, conveyed it to the grounds of the procurator Macrobius Candidianus, which lay on the Mappalian Way beside the reservoirs. A distinguished church was subsequently dedicated in his honor at that place; another no less celebrated was founded at the very field where he had completed his martyrdom, [Col. 1477B] concerning both of which we have spoken elsewhere (*On the Bishops of Carthage*).

“Thus at last it came to pass,” says Pontius (*Life of Cyprian*, no. 19), “that Cyprian, in the very city in which he had lived such a life and in which he had first accomplished many illustrious deeds, was also the first to adorn the insignia of the heavenly priesthood with glorious blood.”

What need is there for me to speak of his glory among later generations, when it has traveled throughout the whole world and no region can be found to which the name of Cyprian has not reached? It is nevertheless pleasing to transcribe the concluding verses [Col. 1478A] from Prudentius’ poem in heptameters, which present to us that ancient and widely diffused glory (*Hymn* XIII, v. 96; also Buonarr., *Osservaz. sui vetri*, p. 142):

> Sorrowful Africa wept when the man died through whose teaching  
> She was made more refined, and in whose eloquence she proudly claims instruction.  
> Then, weeping, she built his tomb and consecrated his ashes.  
> Cease to weep for so great a good man: he possesses the kingdom of heaven,  
> Yet no less does he hover over the earth, nor does he depart from this world.  
> He expounds, speaks, treats, teaches, instructs, and prophesies.  
> Nor does he rule the peoples of Libya alone: he goes as far as the rising  
> And setting of the sun. He cherishes the Gauls and instructs the Britons;  
> He presides over Hesperia and plants Christ among the farthest Iberians.  
> In short, on earth he is a teacher, and in heaven likewise a martyr:  
> Here he instructs humankind; from there, as patron, he bestows holy gifts.

Africa preserved the relics of the most holy martyr until the year 806, when the envoys of Emperor Charles Augustus transported them to Gaul (Ado, in the *Martyrology* for 14 September, etc.).

VI. After Cyprian’s death there was very little peace at Carthage, for not long afterward the proconsul Galerius [Col. 1478B] Maximus died (*Proconsular Acts of Cyprian*, no. 5); and in his place the procurator of Caesar began to discharge the office [text apparently defective]; and (*Passion of Saints Montanus and Lucius*, nos. 2 and 6), being hostile to the Christians, he again filled everything with terror and, as the instigator also of a popular disturbance, sought pretexts for persecuting the Christians. Consequently, no deliberation and no assembly concerning the appointment of Cyprian’s successor could be held within the year. The same thing happened at Rome for a similar reason: Dionysius was proclaimed successor to Xystus, who had died a martyr that year, only after nearly a full year had passed.

## ABOUT THE YEAR OF THE LORD 257  
## SAINT PONTIUS, DEACON OF CARTHAGE

[Col. 1477]

# PROLEGOMENA  
## BY D. GOTHOFRED LUMPER

(*Critical Theological History of the Holy Fathers*, vol. XIII, pp. 45–51.)

## ARTICLE I  
### On Saint Pontius, Author of the *Life of Saint Cyprian*

[Col. 1477C]

I. Saint Jerome numbers among the ecclesiastical authors [Note: [Col. 1477C] “Pontius, Cyprian’s deacon, who shared exile with him until the day of his passion, left an excellent volume on the life and passion of Cyprian.” Jerome, *Catalogue of Illustrious Men*, ch. 68.] Pontius, who committed to writing not only the acts of martyrdom but also the other deeds in the life—at least from the time when he embraced the faith of Christ—of that most holy Carthaginian prelate Cyprian, an admirable man, whose deacon he had been. Honorius of Autun agrees with Jerome [Note: [Col. 1477C] Honorius, *On the Luminaries of the Church*, bk. I, ch. 69.]. Some learned men, Rigaltius among them, appear to have questioned whether this work might be spurious. And it must certainly be admitted, Dupin says [Note: [Col. 1477C] Dupin, *Bibliotheca Auctorum*, p. 278, Cologne Latin edition.], that it was written with so much affectation of eloquence that it might have incurred suspicion of falsity had Jerome not acknowledged it as genuine. [Col. 1478C] But after the testimony of that learned Father, there appears to be no room for doubt about it.

II. Pontius, apparently an African by birth, was Cyprian’s deacon in the African Church and his companion in all the struggles of his life. Nothing further is known with certainty concerning him, although acts of Pontius, said to have been recorded by Valerius—his fellow-member of Cyprian’s household and likewise a deacon—are found in Baluze [Note: [Col. 1478C] Baluze, vol. II, *Miscellanea*, p. 124, year 1679.]. His name was entered in the Roman Martyrology under 8 March [Note: [Col. 1478C] Cf. the Bollandists’ *Acta Sanctorum* for 8 March, vol. I, p. 750 ff.]; and Fabricius, in his notes on Jerome, observed that Trithemius drew upon those acts when recounting the deeds of Pontius [Note: [Col. 1478C] Fabricius, *Bibliotheca Ecclesiastica*, p. 153, says that Trithemius drew upon those *Acts* when he wrote that Pontius, by the rest of his preaching and labor, converted the two emperors named Philip to Christ.].

“We read nowhere,” say the Bollandists [Note: [Col. 1478C] Bollandists, loc. cit., p. 751.], “how long Pontius survived after the martyrdom of Saint Cyprian,” nor [Col. 1479A] by what kind of death he ended his life. No one, so far as we recall, reports that he was perfected by martyrdom. “For it is ridiculous,” they continue, “that Jacobus Philippus of Bergamo, in book VIII of the *Supplement to the Chronicles*, under the year 259, writes as follows:

> Pontius, however, the presbyter of Cyprian himself, a man sufficiently learned and exceptionally well instructed in sacred declamation, came to Gaul during this period after Cyprian’s death and obtained the palm of martyrdom in the city of Cimiez. For by his preaching and labor he had converted the two emperors named Philip to Christ; and among other things, as stated above, he left behind him an excellent volume concerning the life and passion of Cyprian, his teacher and father. And because he was held to be a saint, his feast is celebrated on the second day before the Ides of May [14 May].

[Note: [Col. 1479D] Trithemius speaks in the same way about Saint Pontius in his *Catalogue*, ch. 42.]

In this narrative [Col. 1479B] Pontius the deacon is confused with another Pontius, a martyr whose memory is celebrated on 14 May. After Aubertus Miraeus [Note: [Col. 1479D] “And he is distinct from Saint Pontius, the Gallic martyr entered in the same martyrology under 14 May,” in Fabricius, *Bibliotheca Ecclesiastica*, bk. VI.], Ruinart [Note: [Col. 1479D] “Take care, however, not to confuse him with the martyr Pontius, who is said to have brought the emperors named Philip to faith in Christ; more concerning him may be found in the Bollandists under 14 May.” Ruinart, note 62, in *Acts of the Martyrs, Authentic and Select*, p. 188, Verona edition.] and Ceillier [Note: [Col. 1479D] Ceillier, *Histoire générale des auteurs*, vol. III, ch. 1, art. 7, p. 223.] pointed this out.

## ARTICLE II  
### The Writings of Pontius the Deacon

III. There survives a narrative by this Pontius concerning the *Life and Passion of Saint Cyprian*. To use Ruinart’s words [Note: [Col. 1479D] Ruinart, *Acts of the Martyrs*, p. 171.], it must be regarded as all the more faithful and certain because he had been present for most of the events and reports what he had seen and heard while personally present. For Pontius himself, Cyprian’s inseparable companion, concludes his narrative in these words [Note: [Col. 1479D] Pontius, *Life and Passion of Saint Cyprian*, §19.]:

> Divided between joy at his passion and grief at remaining behind, my mind is pulled in opposite directions, and my heart, far too narrow, is burdened by these two emotions. I rejoice greatly—exceedingly greatly—over his [Col. 1479C] glory; yet I grieve still more because I remained behind.

Accordingly, Pontius’ little book, which Scaliger calls “a most polished volume” [Note: [Col. 1479D] Scaliger, *Annotations on the Chronicle of Eusebius*, p. 236.], appears worthy of the highest esteem at least on the ground that its author was an eyewitness (*autoptēs*, αὐτόπτης), even if in narrating events he perhaps employed a more ornate style than befits a historian.

IV. This was indeed the judgment rightly passed upon the work of this holy deacon by the most learned men, especially Baronius, who says [Note: [Col. 1479D] Baronius, under the year 261, §39.]:

> Those same acts, frequently cited and likewise quoted by us above, are equally supported by the testimony of Augustine, who inserted into his discourse on the feast day of Saint Cyprian the same events that Pontius the deacon also recorded. But even if no testimony from others were available, by their very candor they claim for themselves sure and uncorrupted [Col. 1479D] credibility in every respect.

Thus speaks the greatest father of the annals of the Church. The Bollandists judge no differently [Col. 1480A] [Note: [Col. 1480D] Bollandists, *Acta Sanctorum Martyrum*, vol. I, March, p. 750, no. 4.].

Rigaltius, however, on a very slight foundation, appears not merely to have raised doubts about the reliability of Pontius’ history but even to have disparaged it. For he writes [Note: [Col. 1480D] Rigaltius, on Cyprian, Epistle LXXXIII; LXXXI in the Oxford edition.] that Pontius pursued the charm of rhetorical expression more than the diligence proper to historical narration; that, moreover, he touched upon none of the deeds of the most holy man contained in the latter’s letters; and he complains especially that Pontius omitted what Saint Cyprian writes concerning himself [Note: [Col. 1480D] Cyprian, Epistle LXXXIII; LXXXI in the Oxford edition.], namely, that when the holy martyr learned that he was being sought by the *frumentarii*—the imperial intelligence officers—he remained in hiding for a time.

Indeed, the critic went so far as not to hesitate to pronounce a judgment of this sort [Note: [Col. 1480D] Rigaltius, after the preface, in the note on the *Acts of the Martyrs* beginning: “When Saint Cyprian the Martyr,” etc.]:

> We consider this account of Cyprian’s martyrdom to be the most ancient, just as it is the briefest. Pontius, out of pious affection for his [Col. 1480B] bishop, ingeniously invented many things with rhetorical license. Others too, each according to his own capacity, added many things foreign to the age and foreign to the persons; they also removed certain very good things. Thus only a few elements now remain that we can vouch for as genuine.

[Note: [Col. 1480D] Ernest Salomon Cyprian likewise judged that the same material had been interpolated through the officiousness of copyists of a very recent age, but without producing any solid argument; the final words, *ad Hieronymum docuit*, are uncertain (“he maintained this with reference to Jerome”).]

Such are his words. To use the words of Labbe [Note: [Col. 1480D] Labbe, *Historical Dissertation on Ecclesiastical Writers*, vol. II, p. 232.], they were written with a perverse passion for novelty, to the detriment of Catholic truth. I consider them utterly false and irreconcilably opposed both to the most certain authority of Saint Jerome—who testified that Pontius left an “excellent volume” on the *Life and Passion of Cyprian*, such as all Catholics distinguished for learning now acknowledge it to be—and to the judgment of all upright men concerning Pontius’ holiness and fidelity. For that little work is wholly genuine and deserves the first rank among the ancient acts, lives, and encomia [Col. 1480C] of the martyrs of old. If this life should become suspect to any sensible person, then all other acts whatsoever will likewise be suspect, as will Saint Augustine’s own sermon concerning Cyprian, an exceptional treasure (*keimēlion*, χειμήλιον) of venerable antiquity. Thus far the learned man. These matters may be seen treated more fully by the Bollandists [Note: [Col. 1480D] Bollandists, loc. cit.].

## ARTICLE III  
### On the Acts Appended to Pontius’ History, and on the Editorial Care Bestowed upon Both by Learned Men

Now, concerning those *Acts* that are commonly appended to Pontius’ little work, hear the judgment of the distinguished Ruinart, says Gallandi [Note: [Col. 1480D] Gallandi, *Library of the Ancient Fathers*, vol. III, Prolegomena, ch. 10, p. 30.], whose edition we have arranged to have printed [Note: [Col. 1480D] Ruinart, *Acts of the Martyrs, Authentic*, p. 171 ff., §1.]:

> The *Acts of the Passion of Saint Cyprian*, as we now possess them, contain his two confessions before the proconsul, excerpted from the official records themselves. That Saint Augustine saw and read those records is clear from his Sermon 309 in the latest edition, since almost the whole of that sermon is composed from the words of these *Acts*. How highly records of this kind were esteemed by the faithful is shown by the fact that, even while Cyprian was still alive, the records of his first confession were already in everyone’s hands. Besides Pontius, Nemesianus and the other martyrs confined in the mines affirm this in the letter numbered LXXVII among the Cyprianic letters in the new edition and LXVIII in Pamelius: “Like a good and true teacher,” they say, “you were the first to pronounce in the proconsul’s official proceedings what we disciples, following you, ought to say before the governor; and, sounding God’s trumpet, you stirred the soldiers of God, [Col. 1481B] equipped with heavenly weapons, to the battle of combat.”  
>   
> These records, then, together with accounts of what took place during his final confession and death itself, were collected by the faithful into a single dossier. Together with Pontius’ little book on the *Life of Cyprian*, they have come down to us; and all of them were prefixed to the works of Saint Cyprian himself in the Oxford edition.

[Col. 1482A] [Note: [Col. 1482B] In the Maurists’ Paris edition as well, the *Life* and the consular *Acts* were prefixed to his works, pp. 129–148 in the Venice edition of 1748.]

> We here present both once more, collated afresh against several manuscript codices: the *Life* has been compared with two codices of the highest quality and venerable antiquity. One, belonging to Saint-Pierre of Fossés, is more than eight hundred years old; the other, formerly from the celebrated library of the monastery of Fleury, appears to be more than six hundred years old. The proconsular *Acts*, however, are found in many codices, including some of great antiquity, but are pure and altogether genuine in only a few. If any variants worthy of notice occur, we shall add them in the notes.

Thus far the distinguished Ruinart.

[Col. 1481]

# THE LIFE AND PASSION OF SAINT CAECILIUS CYPRIAN, BISHOP OF CARTHAGE AND MARTYR  
## BY PONTIUS THE DEACON  
(C, S)\*

[Note: [Col. 1481D]

**CHAPTER I.—The little word *vel*.** We have restored it from the Fossés and Fleury codices; it appears necessary for emphasis. **RUINART.**

**Our forebears.** After the Gospel and the Acts of the Apostles came the briefly narrated passions of the Christians who followed thereafter. Of this kind are those ancient *Acts of the Martyr Polycarp*, part of which Eusebius gave in book IV, while our Armagh scholar published the whole; likewise those of Perpetua and Felicity, of [Col. 1482D] which Tertullian makes mention, as well as many others that, through interpolation, lost the credibility they would otherwise have deserved. During the Decian persecution, the task of recording the acts of the Carthaginian martyrs was entrusted to Tertullus. **FELL.**

**Would not remain unknown.** Through Cyprian’s modesty, knowledge of these things was withheld from the public. But these words are missing from Manutius’ edition. **FELL.**

**Recorded all of them.** He appears to refer to the *Acts of Saints Perpetua*, etc., which we published above (vol. III of our *Library*, p. 14). Pontius does indeed say that many—or almost all—things concerning those martyrs had been written down. But this passage must not be interpreted as though the acts of absolutely all the martyrs had been recorded by Pontius’ time. Henry Dodwell nevertheless understood it in this way, [Col. 1484D] *Cyprianic Dissertation* XI, no. 3. **RUINART.**]

## CHAPTER I  
### The Author Explains His Reasons for Writing. He States That the Acts of the Martyrs Were Formerly Carefully Committed to Writing

[Col. 1481C]

CYPRIAN, a devout bishop and glorious witness of God, wrote many works through which the memory of his worthy name survives. And although the abundant fruitfulness of his eloquence and of God’s grace extends itself through such fullness and richness of discourse that perhaps it will not fall silent until the end of the world, nevertheless this further distinction is owed to his works and merits [Note: [Col. 1481C] “And that others may be directed in writing by his example,” Bod. 1, Surius. [Col. 1481D] *Imp.* “May be directed” is absent from the Manutius and Fossés codices.]: that his example should be set down in writing. I have therefore resolved to record a few things in summary form—not because the life of so great a man remains unknown to anyone [Note: [Col. 1481D] The word *vel* (“even”) is from the Fossés and Fleury codices.], even among the pagans, [Col. 1482C] but so that an incomparable and magnificent example may also be handed down to our descendants in immortal remembrance.

It would surely have been harsh if, when our forebears gave so much honor to laymen and catechumens who attained martyrdom, out of reverence for martyrdom itself [Note: [Col. 1482C] “Owed,” Bod. 1, Manutius.], that they recorded many things concerning their passions—or, I might almost say, nearly everything—so that they might come to the knowledge even of us who were not yet born, the passion of Cyprian, so great a priest and so great a martyr, should be passed over: a man who, even apart from martyrdom, had things to teach, and that the deeds he performed while he lived [Note: [Col. 1482D] “And the things he did while he lived.” These words are absent from the Fossés and Manutius texts.] should not be made known.

These deeds are indeed so numerous, so great, and so wonderful that I am daunted by contemplating their magnitude and confess myself unequal to producing language worthy of the honor of his merits, or to following deeds so magnificent in such a way that they appear as great as they truly are—except that the multitude of his glories [Note: [Col. 1483D] “Glorious multitude,” Bod. 1, Fossés, Fleury.] is sufficient in itself and has no need of another’s praise. Adding to the burden is the fact that you desire to hear much about him—or, if it were possible, everything—burning with ardent longing to learn even his deeds, though for the present his living words have fallen silent. In this respect, if I were to say that our resources of eloquence [Note: [Col. 1483D] “Powers of eloquence,” Bod. 1.] fail, I would say too little. Eloquence itself lacks [Note: [Col. 1483D] “Is deficient,” Fleury.] an adequate power capable of satisfying your desire with a full breath. Thus we are severely pressed from both sides: he burdens us with his virtues, while you weary us with your entreaties [Note: [Col. 1483D] “Our ears,” Manutius, Fossés.].

[Note: [Col. 1484D]

**CHAPTER II.—Would be believed.** Pagans and the faithful themselves could scarcely persuade themselves that Cyprian had embraced the Christian religion. **RUINART.**]

## CHAPTER II  
### He Recounts What Cyprian Did After Baptism. The Necessity of Continence. Cyprian’s Other Virtues

[Col. 1483B]

Where, then, shall I begin? From what point shall I undertake the opening account of his good deeds, if not from the beginning of his faith and his heavenly birth? For the deeds of a man of God ought not to be counted from any other point than that at which he was born to God. His studies and the liberal arts may indeed have imbued his devoted heart, but I pass over them. For as yet they pertained only to the advantage of the world [Note: [Col. 1483D] “Of life, but of the world,” Bod. 1.].

After he had learned the sacred Scriptures and, the cloud of the world having been dispersed, emerged into the light of spiritual wisdom, I shall relate whatever deeds of his I witnessed and whatever I learned concerning his earlier works [Note: [Col. 1483D] “Whatever I learned concerning his earlier works,” Fossés, Fleury, Surius—and indeed more correctly.]. I ask only this indulgence: that whatever I say inadequately—and I must necessarily speak inadequately—be charged against my ignorance rather than detracted from his glory.

Among the first rudiments of his faith he believed nothing more worthy of God than that he should preserve continence. For he held that his heart could then become fit and his understanding attain the full capacity for truth [Note: [Col. 1483D] “Capacity, if,” Fossés, Manutius.], if he trampled the lust of the flesh beneath the strong and unimpaired vigor of holiness [Note: [Col. 1484D] “Tenor of holiness,” Bod. 1, Fossés, Fleury.]. Who has ever heard of so great a wonder? His second birth had not yet opened the eyes of the new man with the full splendor of divine light [Note: [Col. 1484D] “Had clothed him in light,” Bod. 1.], and already, by the mere preparation for light, he was overcoming the old and former darkness.

Then, what is greater still, when from divine reading he had already learned certain things—not in proportion to the condition of a beginner but in proportion to the haste of his faith—he immediately seized upon whatever he discovered would profit him in earning God’s favor. By selling [Col. 1483D] his possessions [Col. 1484A] to relieve the need of the poor [Note: [Col. 1484D] “To relieve the need of many poor people,” Bod. 1.], distributing the proceeds from whole estates [Note: [Col. 1484D] “All the proceeds,” Manutius. “From the proceeds” is absent from the Fossés and Fleury codices.], he united two good things at once: he both despised worldly ambition, than which nothing is more destructive, and fulfilled the mercy that God preferred even to his sacrifices—a mercy not practiced even by the man who said that he had kept all the commandments of the Law (Matt. 19:20). With the headlong speed of his devotion, he almost began to be perfect before he had learned how.

Who, I ask, among the men of old did this? Who among the most ancient elders in the faith, whose minds and ears the divine words had struck for very many years, expended anything comparable to what this man—still untrained in the faith and perhaps not yet likely to be believed—accomplished in glorious and admirable works, outstripping the maturity that comes with long standing? No one reaps as soon as he has sown. No one has pressed a vintage from newly dug [Col. 1484B] trenches. No one has ever sought ripe fruit from saplings only recently planted. In him everything ran its course incredibly [Note: [Col. 1484D] “Incredibly swiftly,” Fleury.]. If it can be said—for the fact surpasses belief—the threshing preceded the sowing [Note: [Col. 1484D] “The harvest preceded the sowing,” Roman text.], the vintage the vine shoot, and the fruit the root [Note: [Col. 1484D] “The branch preceded the root,” Bod. 1.].

[Note: [Col. 1485D]

**CHAPTER III.—At his wife’s persuasion.** From this passage the English editor had inferred that Cyprian had a wife; but upon examining the matter more attentively, he observed that Pontius is speaking here of Job, not Cyprian, as he himself informs the reader in the corrections. The Reverend Father Anthony Pagi had struck the same reef under the year 248; being no less candid than learned, however, he likewise corrected that error in the second edition. **RUINART.**]

## CHAPTER III  
### He Is Quickly Advanced to Holy Orders. He Continually Sets the Saints Before Himself for Imitation

The writings of the Apostle say (1 Tim. 3:6) that recent converts ought to be passed over, lest, while the stupor of paganism still adheres to their not yet established understanding, their untaught newness should commit some offense against God. Cyprian was the first and, I think, the only man [Col. 1484C] to show by his example that one may be advanced more by faith than by time.

Even if the eunuch in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 8:37) is described as having been immediately baptized by Philip because he believed with all his heart, the comparison is not equivalent. That man was both a Jew and, as one returning from the Temple of the Lord, was reading the prophet Isaiah; he also hoped in Christ, although he did not yet believe that Christ had come. Cyprian, by contrast, came from the uninstructed nations and began with a faith as mature as that with which perhaps only a few have finished.

There was consequently no pause and no delay in respect of God’s grace. I have said too little: he immediately received the presbyterate and [Note: [Col. 1484D] Or “the priesthood,” Fossés, Fleury.] the priesthood [Note: [Col. 1484D] “Immediately emerged,” Bod. 1.]. For who would not believe a man of such a believing mind worthy of every degree of honor?

There are many things he did [Col. 1484D] while still a layman, many after he had become a presbyter, [Col. 1485A] and many that, following the examples of the righteous of old with like imitation, he accomplished by rendering to the Lord the service of complete devotion and thereby winning his favor. For he frequently spoke on this subject: if he read of anyone celebrated by God’s praise, he advised that inquiry be made into the deeds by which that person had pleased God.

If Job (Job 1) was made glorious by God’s testimony, being called a true worshiper of God to whom no one on earth could be compared, Cyprian taught that whatever Job had previously done must likewise be done, so that, by doing equal things ourselves, we might call forth a similar testimony from God concerning us. Job despised the losses of his property and advanced so far in tested virtue that he did not even feel the temporal losses that tried his piety. Neither poverty nor pain broke him; his wife’s persuasion did not turn him aside, nor did the dreadful punishment of his own body shake him. His virtue remained fixed in its seat, and his devotion, founded upon deep roots, did not yield before any assault of the tempting devil, so as to prevent him [Note: [Col. 1485C] “Because,” editions.] from blessing his God with grateful faith even amid adversities.

Cyprian’s house stood open to whoever came. No widow returned with an empty fold; no one lacking sight failed to be guided with him as companion; no one weak in gait failed to be carried with him as bearer; no one defenseless against the hand of a more powerful man failed to be protected with him as guardian. “Those who desire to please God,” he would say, “ought to do these things.” And thus, passing through the examples of every good person, while always imitating those who were better, he made himself likewise worthy of imitation.

[Note: [Col. 1485D]

**CHAPTER IV.—Caecilius.** The Fossés and Fleury codices read *Caecilianus*. As Jerome testifies in the *Catalogue*, Saint Cyprian received the name Caecilius from him. His feast is commemorated in the Roman Martyrology on 3 June. **RUINART.**

**Entrusted his wife to him.** This was evidently before Cyprian was initiated into the priesthood—unless this guardianship was merely a friendly commendation. For otherwise it was forbidden that guardianship be entrusted to clerics, as is clear from Cyprian himself.
