In Epistle I of the new edition, Epistle 66 in Pamelius, he forbids any offering to be made or any prayer to be regularly offered in the church for Victor, who at his death had appointed the presbyter Geminius Faustinus as guardian. For, he says, it had been established by his episcopal predecessors that if any brother at his death appointed a cleric to a guardianship or trusteeship, no offering was to be made for him, nor was the sacrifice for his falling asleep to be celebrated. It is therefore surprising that Baronius, under the year 250, understood this passage as though Cyprian at his death had entrusted his wife and children to Caecilius, whereas Caecilius, on the contrary, did this. See Pagi at the passage we cited just above. **RUINART.**]

## CHAPTER IV  
### Cyprian Is Brought to the Faith by Caecilius

Cyprian also enjoyed intimate companionship among us with Caecilius, [Col. 1485C] a righteous man of praiseworthy memory [Note: [Col. 1485C] “Caecilianus,” Fossés, Fleury.], who was then his elder in both age and the honor of the presbyterate and had corrected him from worldly error by bringing him to knowledge of the true divinity. Cyprian loved him with the fullest honor and every mark of respect, looking up to him with reverent obedience, no longer as a friend and equal of his soul but as the father of his new life [Note: [Col. 1485C] “He followed,” Bod. 1.].

Caecilius, in turn, won over by Cyprian’s services and deservedly moved [Col. 1486A] to immeasurable affection [Note: [Col. 1485C] “By his merits,” Bod. 1.], when departing from the world with his final summons now close at hand, entrusted his wife and children to him. Thus he made the man whom he had brought into fellowship in the sect subsequently the heir also of his familial devotion.

[Note: [Col. 1486D]

**CHAPTER V.—** Namely Felicissimus, the ringleader of the schism, together with the others whom Caldonius and the other deputies of Cyprian during his absence excommunicated: Epistle 42, 39 in Pamelius. See also Epistle 41, 38 in Pamelius. **RUINART.**]

## CHAPTER V  
### While Still a Neophyte, He Is Compelled to Assume the Episcopate

It would take too long to go through every detail; it is burdensome to enumerate all [Note: [Col. 1485C] “Holy,” Oxford.] his deeds. As proof of his good works, I think this alone sufficient: by the judgment of God and the favor of the people, while still a neophyte and, as it was thought, a newcomer, he was elected to the office of the priesthood and the rank of bishop.

Although he was still in the earliest days of his faith and at an unformed age in the spiritual life, his noble disposition shone forth in such a way that, although he did not yet hold the office, [Col. 1486B] he nevertheless gleamed with the radiance of hope and promised complete confidence in the priesthood that was approaching.

Nor shall I pass over this remarkable fact: when the entire people, with the Lord’s inspiration [Note: [Col. 1485C] “With inspiration,” Bod. 1.], rushed forward in love and honor for him, he humbly withdrew, yielding to his elders and considering himself unworthy of the title of so great an honor, so that he might thereby become still more worthy. For the man who disclaims what he deserves is made more deserving.

With what burning ardor the people then surged! With spiritual longing they desired, as the outcome revealed, not merely a bishop. For in the man whom, by a hidden [Note: [Col. 1486C] “While he was hiding,” Fossés, Fleury.] divine foreknowledge, they demanded in this way [Note: [Col. 1486C] “They demanded as one destined to be,” *Imp.*], they were seeking not only a priest but also a future martyr.

A great company of the brethren had besieged the doors of the house, and anxious love circled every entrance. [Col. 1486C] Perhaps the apostolic experience he desired might then have befallen him (2 Cor. 11), so that he would be lowered through a window, if [Note: [Col. 1486C] “If nevertheless with,” Fleury.] he had also been made like the Apostle in the honor of ordination [Note: [Col. 1486C] “Were made like,” editions, Fleury.].

One could see all the others waiting in suspense and [Note: [Col. 1486C] “In suspense, with anxious,” Oxford.] anxiety for him to come, and receiving him with extraordinary joy when he arrived. I say it unwillingly, but it must be said: some opposed him, only to be overcome by him. Yet with what gentleness [Note: [Col. 1486C] “Held in suspense by gentleness,” Manutius.], patience, and benevolence he treated them! How mercifully he forgave them, subsequently counting them among his closest friends and intimates, to the astonishment of many. For who could fail to marvel at such forgetfulness in so retentive a mind?

[Note: [Col. 1487D]

**CHAPTER VI.—Loved them as a catechumen.** Pontius noted above, no. II, that immediately after embracing the faith Cyprian sold his possessions to relieve the need of the poor. **RUINART.**]

## CHAPTER VI  
### He Shines Forth in Episcopal Virtues

Who could adequately relate how he conducted himself thereafter? What devotion [Note: [Col. 1487D] “What devotion there was,” Bod. 1.] was his! What vigor! How great his mercy, how great his discipline [Note: [Col. 1487D] “How sober his discipline,” Bod. 1.]! So much holiness and grace shone from his countenance that it overwhelmed [Note: [Col. 1487D] “Summoned,” Bod. 1.] the minds of those who beheld him.

His expression was dignified and cheerful: neither was his severity gloomy nor his affability excessive [Note: [Col. 1487D] “Nor his cheerfulness excessive,” Bod. 1.]; rather, a tempering balance blended both, so that one might wonder whether he deserved more to be revered or to be loved—except that he deserved both reverence and love. [Col. 1487B]

Nor was his dress out of keeping with his countenance; it too was moderate, occupying the middle course. Worldly pride had not puffed him up, yet neither had affected poverty rendered him altogether shabby, because this kind of dress is no less a form of ostentation than [Note: [Col. 1487D] “Because an otherwise ostentatious frugality displays this,” Fossés; “frailty,” Fleury.] frugality ambitiously displayed in that fashion.

And what would the bishop do for the poor whom he had loved as a catechumen? Let the ministers of devotion consider it—whether those whom the discipline of their own order has instructed for the duty of good works, or those whom their common reverence for the sacrament has bound to the service of manifesting love. The episcopal chair received Cyprian already such a man in his own right; it did not make him so.

[Note: [Col. 1487D]

**CHAPTER VII.—Was demanded for the lion.** Cyprian himself attests this in Epistle 55 of Pamelius’ edition, 59 in the English edition, addressed to Pope Cornelius. He mentions his proscription in Epistle 66, otherwise 69, addressed to Pupianus. **RUINART.**

**The Lord’s reading.** The Fossés codex reads “the Lord’s love.” Here Pontius refers to books written by Cyprian. Cyprian himself wrote a defense of his withdrawal to the Romans in Epistle 20, otherwise 15. **RUINART.**]

## CHAPTER VII  
### He Is Proscribed and Demanded for the Lion; He Prudently Withdraws

[Col. 1487C]

Immediately, then, in return for such merits he attained even the glory of proscription. For it was fitting that the man who, within the secret recess of conscience, flourished in the full honor of religion and faith should also be publicly distinguished by the celebrated renown accorded him among the pagans. Indeed, with the speed with which he always attained everything, the crown of martyrdom owed to him might even then have hastened upon him—especially since repeated popular demands called for him to be thrown to the lion—had it not been necessary for him to pass through every rank of glory and so reach the highest; and had not the impending ruin [Note: [Col. 1487D] “Impending ruins,” Bod. 1, Foss.] needed the aid of so fruitful a mind [Note: [Col. 1487D] “Needed so fruitful a mind,” Bod. 1.]. Imagine, then, that at that time [Col. 1487D] he had been taken away through the favor of martyrdom. Who would have shown the benefit [Col. 1488A] of grace that advances through faith? Who would have restrained virgins, as though with the reins of the Lord’s teaching [Note: [Col. 1487D] “Of the Lord’s love,” Foss.], within a discipline befitting chastity and a manner of dress worthy of holiness? Who would have taught repentance to the lapsed, truth to heretics, unity to schismatics, peace and the law of evangelical prayer [Note: [Col. 1487D] “Of evangelical peace,” Bod. 1.] to the children of God? Through whom would blasphemous pagans [Note: [Col. 1487D] “Pagans accustomed to blaspheme,” Bod. 1.] have been defeated when the charges they level against us were turned back upon themselves? By whom would Christians of more tender feeling [Note: [Col. 1488D] “Of better feeling,” Bod. 1.] at the loss of their own—or, what is more serious [Note: [Col. 1488D] “What is more serious, those about to suffer death itself for the faith,” Bod. 1.]—of weaker faith, have been consoled by hope of things to come? From whom would we have learned mercy thus, from whom patience? Who would have checked the livid spite arising from the poisonous malignity of envy with the sweetness of a saving remedy [Note: [Col. 1488D] “With the sweetness of the spiritual,” Bod. 1. “Salvation,” Bod. 1.]? Who would have raised up so many martyrs by exhortation from the divine word? Who, finally, [Col. 1488B] would have inspired so many confessors—marked upon their foreheads with a second inscription and preserved alive as examples of martyrdom—with the trumpet blast of heaven? Well, well indeed, and in a truly spiritual manner, did it then come about [Note: [Col. 1488D] “Truly by God’s providence,” Bod. 1.] that a man necessary for so many and such excellent works was granted a delay before the consummation of martyrdom.

Do you wish to know that his withdrawal was not an act of fear? To offer no other defense: afterward he himself suffered martyrdom, though surely, by his accustomed practice, he would have avoided suffering if he had avoided it before as well. That fear was real [Note: [Col. 1488D] “But,” Oxon.], but righteous: a fear that dreaded offending the Lord; a fear that preferred to obey God’s commands rather than to be crowned in such a way. For his mind, dedicated to God in all things and thus [Note: [Col. 1488D] “Faith,” Oxon.] made subject to divine admonitions, believed that unless [Note: [Col. 1488D] “Lest, if,” Bod. 1, Morel.] he obeyed the Lord, who then commanded him to seek concealment [Col. 1488C] [Note: [Col. 1488D] “Who did not suggest this place of concealment,” Bod. 1, Morel.], he would sin even by undergoing martyrdom itself.

## CHAPTER VIII. And this occurred by the design of divine Providence.

I think, finally, that even now something should be discussed [Note: [Col. 1488D] “Said, although,” Bod. 1, Foss., Morel.] concerning the benefit of the delay, although we have already touched briefly upon it. For [Note: [Col. 1488D] “For while we perceive the things that are seen to have followed afterward, it follows that we must prove the withdrawal,” Foss., Flor.] from those things which are seen to have followed afterward, it follows that we must prove that his withdrawal was conceived not from human faintheartedness but, as indeed it was, was truly divine. The unprecedented and bitter fury of a hostile persecution had devastated the people of God; and because the crafty enemy could not deceive everyone by a single stratagem, wherever an unwary soldier [Col. 1488D–1489A] had exposed an undefended flank, he struck down individuals by differing forms of savagery and various kinds of destruction. There had to be someone capable of treating wounded men—pierced by the varied cunning of the attacking enemy—with the remedy of heavenly medicine [Note: [Col. 1489D] “With heavenly skill,” Bod. 1.], either cutting for a time or soothing, according to the nature of the wound. A man of intellect, and, besides his other qualities, of spiritually balanced judgment, was preserved: amid the rebounding waves of colliding schisms, he could steer the Church along the middle course [Note: [Col. 1489D] “Between the middle,” Flor.], keeping an even boundary. Are these not, I ask, divine designs? Could this have happened without God? Let those who think such things can occur by chance consider the matter. The Church answers them [Note: [Col. 1489D] “His Church,” Foss.] in a clear voice, saying: “I do not admit, I do not believe, that those who are necessary are preserved without God’s command.”

## CHAPTER IX. While a dreadful plague rages, by an effective address he induces his congregation to assist those infected by it, including pagans.

[Col. 1489B]

Let us nevertheless run through the remaining events, if you please. Later, a dreadful pestilence broke out, and the excessive devastation of a loathsome disease, carrying off innumerable people each day from their own homes in a violent onrush, invaded one after another the houses of the trembling populace. Everyone shuddered, fled [Note: [Col. 1489D] “Wept,” Flor., Foss.], avoided contagion, and impiously exposed their own relatives—as though, when that person was about to die of the plague [Note: [Col. 1489D] “As though, when they themselves were about to die of that plague,” Foss.], anyone could shut out death itself as well. Meanwhile, throughout the whole city there lay no longer bodies, but the corpses of multitudes, demanding mercy from passersby through the contemplation of their common lot. No one regarded anything [Note: [Col. 1489D] “That,” Flor.] except cruel gains. No one trembled at the thought that the same outcome might befall him; no one did for another what he wished to experience [Note: [Col. 1489D] “What he wished to be done to himself,” Sur., Oxon.] himself.

It would be a crime to pass over what, amid these circumstances, the bishop of Christ and God [Note: [Col. 1489D] “Bishop and man of God,” Bod. 1.] did—the man who surpassed the priests of this world in compassion by as much as he surpassed them in the truth of his religion. First he assembled the congregation in one place and instructed it [Note: [Col. 1489D] “Instructs and teaches,” Flor.] concerning the benefits of mercy, teaching from examples in the divine reading how greatly works of compassion [Note: [Col. 1489D] “Works of charity,” Bod. 1, Morel.] contribute toward winning God’s favor. He then added that it was nothing remarkable if we tended only our own people with the service demanded by charity; rather, that the person capable of becoming perfect [Note: [Col. 1490D] “For the person capable of becoming perfect,” Bod. 1.] was one who did something more [Note: [Col. 1490D] “Something good,” Foss.] than the publican or pagan: one who, overcoming evil with good (Rom. 13:21) and practicing an imitation of divine clemency, loved even his enemies; one who, as the Lord advises and exhorts, prayed for the salvation of those who persecuted him. God continually causes his sun to rise (Matt. [Col. 1489D] 5:45), and repeatedly supplies rain to nourish the seeds, providing [Col. 1490A] all these things not only to his own people but also to strangers. Why, then, does one who professes himself to be a son of God not imitate the example of his Father [Note: [Col. 1490D] “Ought to imitate the example,” Bod. 1, Rom., Morel.] [Note: [Col. 1490D] “Let him imitate,” Bod. 1.]? “It is fitting,” he said, “that we answer to our birth, and it is not proper for those known to have been reborn through God to prove degenerate; rather, the emulation of the good Father’s goodness should be demonstrated in his offspring” [Note: [Col. 1490D] “Rather, it is fitting that the emulation of the good Father’s goodness be transmitted in his offspring.” Other reading.].

[Note: [Col. 1489D]

**CHAP. X.—From the rostra.** The name was given from the Roman rostra to the places from which an address was delivered to the people. RUINART.]

## CHAPTER X. On the same subject.

I pass over many other things [Note: [Col. 1490D] “And many,” Bod. 1.], and great ones indeed, which the need to keep this volume within due measure does not permit to be recounted [Note: [Col. 1490D] “Repeated in discourse,” Bod. 1.] in a more extended discussion. Concerning them, it is enough to have said only this: if the pagans could have heard those things from the rostra, perhaps they would immediately have believed. What, then, would the Christian [Col. 1490B] people do, whose very name comes from faith?

Duties were therefore assigned at once according to each person’s condition and rank. Many who, because of the constraints of poverty, could not furnish the benefits of monetary expenditure furnished more than money, compensating by their personal labor and earning a reward dearer than every form of wealth. And who, under so great a teacher, would not hasten to be found taking some part in such service, through which he might please both God the Father, Christ the Judge, and, meanwhile, so good a priest? Thus, through the abundance of overflowing works, good was done to all (Gal. 6:10), not only to members of the household of faith. Something more was done than is recorded of the incomparable devotion of Tobit. Let him pardon it, pardon it again, and pardon it repeatedly—or, to speak more truly, let him rightly concede that, although very much was possible before Christ [Col. 1490C], something more was possible after Christ, to whose times fullness belongs (Tob. 2). Tobit gathered up only those of his own race who had been slain by the king and cast out.

[Note: [Col. 1489D]

**CHAP. XI.—Exile.** Cyprian says that he was banished for confessing the name of Christ in Epistle 76 of the new edition, 77 in Pamelius. RUINART.

**Proceedings.** We have already said that the *Proceedings of the First Confession* were published even during Cyprian’s lifetime; the martyrs commend them in Epistle 77, otherwise 78. RUINART.]

## CHAPTER XI. He is driven into exile at Curubis.

Upon these excellent and devout deeds came exile. For impiety always makes this kind of return: it gives worse things in exchange for better ones [Note: [Col. 1490D] “The best people with the worst things,” Bod. 1.]. As for what the priest of God replied when questioned by the proconsul, there are the *Proceedings* to report it. Meanwhile, the man who had done something good for the city’s welfare is shut out of the city [Note: [Col. 1490D] “Meanwhile from the city,” Bod. 1.]; the man who had labored to prevent the eyes of the living from suffering the horror of the infernal abode; the man, I say, who, keeping watch in the vigils of compassion—what an outrage!—had, by unrequited goodness [Col. 1490D], taken care that, when everyone abandoned the city’s hideous aspect, the deserted commonwealth and forsaken native land should not find that many of its people had become exiles [Col. 1491A].

But let the world consider [Note: [Col. 1491D] “Let it see this,” Bod. 1.] why exile is counted among punishments. To them their native land [Note: [Col. 1491D] “To us our native land is less dear, and it shares a common name; we who even our parents themselves,” Oxon. and old editions. “And the whole affection is directed toward parents,” Morel.] is exceedingly dear, and its name is shared with that of their parents; we, however, abhor even our parents themselves if they counsel anything contrary to the Lord. For them, to live outside their own city is a grievous punishment; for a Christian this entire world is one house. Accordingly, even if he has been banished to a hidden and remote place, a man engaged in the affairs of his God cannot reckon it exile. Add that one who serves God wholly is a stranger even in his own city. For while, through the self-restraint of the Holy Spirit, he abstains from carnal desires, laying aside the way of life of the former man, he is a stranger to earthly life even among his fellow citizens—or, I might almost say, among his very parents. Furthermore, although under other circumstances these things could appear to be a punishment [Note: [Col. 1491D] “Such a punishment could appear,” Oxon. 1. “If this were elsewhere a punishment,” Morel.], nevertheless, in causes and sentences of this sort, which we undergo as trials for proving virtue [Col. 1491B], it is no punishment, because it is glory [Note: [Col. 1491D] “It is glory. I do not wish,” Bod. 1.].

But grant, indeed, that exile is no punishment for us. Let the testimony of their own conscience assign to them as the ultimate crime and the worst wickedness the fact that they can inflict upon the innocent what they themselves consider a punishment. I do not now wish to describe the pleasantness of the place, and for the moment I pass over its provision of every delight. Let us imagine that the place was filthy in situation, squalid in appearance, possessing no wholesome waters, no charm of vegetation [Note: [Col. 1491D] “No vigor of pleasantness,” Bod. 1.], no proximity to the shore, but was removed into an inaccessible part of the world amid vast woodland crags [Note: [Col. 1491D] “On a vast woodland crag,” Rom.] and inhospitable defiles [Note: [Col. 1491D] “Inhospitable rocks,” Bod. 1, Morel.] of an utterly deserted solitude. Even such a place might bear the name of exile when Cyprian, the priest of God, had come to it; yet, if human services failed him there, either birds would minister to him as to Elijah, or angels as to Daniel. Far be it, far be it [Note: [Col. 1491D] “Far be it” once only, Oxon., Bod. 1.] from anyone to believe that anything would be lacking [Note: [Col. 1492D] “To suppose anything,” Bod. 1. “To suppose that anything would be lacking,” Oxon.] to even the least person, provided that he was engaged in confessing the Name. So far was that bishop of God [Note: [Col. 1492D] “Still less the bishop of God,” Bod. 1.], who had always devoted himself to works of mercy [Note: [Col. 1492D] “Had devoted himself, [would be in need] of any resources of good things,” Bod. 1, Morel.], from needing the resources of all these things.

[Note: [Col. 1491D]

**CHAP. XII.—Curubis.** An episcopal city of the proconsular province. RUINART.

**Appeared.** Cyprian was instructed through visions concerning almost everything that was to befall either himself or the Church, as he frequently relates. See Epistle 11, otherwise 8; Epistle 66, otherwise 69; etc. In Epistle 16, otherwise 10, besides visions, he also reports ecstasies experienced by children during the daytime. Certainly, few of the more ancient and reliable *Acts of the Martyrs* lack visions of this kind. See H. Dodwell’s Fourth Cyprianic Dissertation. [Col. 1492D] RUINART.

**Flattened in the manner of a spatha.** Vegetius, bk. II, ch. 15, numbers among the heavy weapons the larger swords, which they call *spathae*. FELL.

**With his fingers twisted one after another.** This is the sign of an action being restrained or delayed. Thus a thumb turned downward was a sign of condemnation, one raised upward of acquittal. FELL.

**My affairs.** Above, no. 2, Cyprian is said at the beginning of his conversion to have distributed all his estates for the use of the poor. Accordingly, this passage seems to refer to his household goods, or certainly to the gardens that had been restored to him, below, no. 15, or finally to the property of the Church, as may be gathered from the following section. RUINART.]

## CHAPTER XII. He is visited by many. Refreshed by a heavenly vision, he is divinely warned that he must undergo martyrdom and that it will be delayed.

Let us now take up, with thanksgiving, what I had placed second [Col. 1492A]: that through divine provision, in keeping with the spirit of so great a man, an open and suitable place was supplied—a lodging secluded according to his wish, together with whatever was promised beforehand to be added to those who seek God’s kingdom and righteousness. And, to omit the frequent visits of the brethren and the affection shown him even there by the local citizens, which restored everything of which he seemed to have been deprived, I shall not pass over the marvelous visitation of God. By it God willed his bishop, even in exile, to be so assured of his coming suffering that Curubis [Note: [Col. 1492D] Thus Bod. 1. “At Curubis,” Rigalt.] possessed him not merely as an exile but also, with fuller confidence in his imminent martyrdom, as a martyr.

For on the day on which we first stayed in the place of exile—for the favor of his affection had chosen even me from among his household companions to be a voluntary exile; would that this had also been permitted during his martyrdom! [Col. 1492B]—he said:

> “Before the repose of sleep had yet lulled me, there appeared to me a young man of extraordinary stature. As he led me, as it were, to the governor’s residence, I seemed to be brought before the tribunal of the proconsul who was then seated in judgment. As soon as the proconsul looked upon me, he immediately began to write a sentence on a tablet, although I did not know what it was, for he had asked me nothing in the customary examination.
>
> “But the young man standing behind him very attentively [Note: [Col. 1492D] “Very eager to see whatever…,” Morel.] read everything that had been written [Note: [Col. 1492D] “Whatever was being done,” Bod. 1.]. Since he could not communicate it from there in words, he showed me by an explanatory gesture what the writing on that tablet contained. Extending his hand and flattening it in the manner of a *spatha*, he imitated the stroke of the customary execution; by this likeness to plain speech he conveyed what he wished [Note: [Col. 1492D] “What he wished to be done from there,” Bod. 1.] to be understood. I understood that the sentence would be martyrdom.
>
> “I immediately began to ask and plead [Col. 1492C] that I be granted a delay of even a single day, until I could set my affairs in lawful order. When I had repeated my pleas many times, the proconsul again began to write something—I know not what—on the tablet. Yet from the serenity of the judge’s countenance I perceived that his mind had been moved, as it were, by the justice of my request. Moreover, the young man who a little earlier had disclosed the indication of martyrdom by gesture rather than speech hastened, by a secret and repeated sign, to signify that the delay requested until the following day had been granted [Note: [Col. 1492D] “That what was requested had been granted,” Bod. 1.], twisting his fingers one after another.
>
> “Although the sentence had not been read [Note: [Col. 1492D] “Although there was only the sentence,” Bod. 1.], and although I rejoiced with an exceedingly glad heart in the joy of receiving the delay [Col. 1493A], nevertheless I trembled so greatly from fear that my interpretation might be uncertain that the remnants of dread still beat upon my exultant heart with utter terror [Note: [Col. 1493D] “Still with much trembling,” Bod. 1.].”

## CHAPTER XIII. The author interprets this vision and proves that it was truthful.

What could be clearer than this revelation? What could be more blessed than this favor? Everything that later followed was foretold to him beforehand. Nothing was diminished from the words of God [Note: [Col. 1493D] “Nothing from the words of God,” Bod. 1, Morel.]; nothing was mutilated from so holy a promise. Consider each detail [Note: [Col. 1493D] “And each detail,” Morel.] according to the manner in which it was shown. When the sentence of martyrdom was being contemplated, he requested a delay until the following day [Note: [Col. 1493D] “He requests until the following day,” Bod. 1, Morel.], asking that on the day he had obtained he might put his affairs in order. This single day signified the year for which [Col. 1493B] he was to live in the world after the vision. For, to speak more plainly, he was crowned, once the year had elapsed, on the very day on which this had been shown to him a year before.

Although in the divine Scriptures we read of the Lord’s day and not a year [Note: [Col. 1493D] “Although a year,” Bod. 1, Morel.], we nevertheless understand that period as due to the promise of future things. Therefore, it makes no difference if now only a year was shown under the figure of a day [Note: [Col. 1493D] “If now under…,” Bod. 1, Morel.], because that which is greater ought to be fuller [Note: [Col. 1493D] “By which that is fuller,” Bod. 1.].

As for the fact that it was explained by a gesture rather than by speech, the explicit utterance was reserved for the moment of the event’s realization. For something is customarily declared in words when that which is declared is fulfilled. And in truth no one understood why this had been shown to him until he was crowned afterward on the very day on which he had seen it. Nevertheless, during the intervening time, his impending [Col. 1493C] martyrdom was known by everyone as certain; but the definite day of the martyrdom was kept silent from all those same people, as though they did not know it.

Indeed, I find something similar in the Scriptures. For because the priest Zechariah did not believe in the son promised to him through the angel, he became mute (Luke 1:59), so that, when he was about to write rather than report the son’s name [Note: [Col. 1494D] “Concerning the son’s name,” Bod. 1, Morel.] [Note: [Col. 1494D] “Rather than read it aloud,” Bod. 1.], he asked for tablets by a gesture. Rightly, therefore, here too, where God’s messenger expressed by gesture rather than speech the bishop’s imminent martyrdom, he both admonished his faith and fortified the priest.

The reason for requesting the delay arose from putting his affairs in order and disposing of his will. Yet what affairs did he have, or what will was there to arrange, except the condition of the Church? The final delay [Col. 1493D] was therefore granted so that whatever had to be arranged concerning the care of supporting the poor might be settled as a final judgment [Col. 1494A] [Note: [Col. 1494D] “Final indications,” Morel.]. And I think that for no other reason—indeed, for this reason alone—permission was granted even by the very men who had driven him out [Note: [Col. 1494D] “By those who had driven him out, it was granted,” Bod. 1.] and were about to kill him: so that, while present among the poor who were present, he might relieve them with the last—and, to speak more fully, the entire—resources of his final distribution. His affairs having therefore been arranged so devoutly and disposed according to his will [Note: [Col. 1494D] Thus Bod. 1, Morel. “His will having been disposed,” Rigalt.], the following day drew near.

[Note: [Col. 1493D]

**CHAP. XIV.—Withdrawal.** He withdrew for several days so that he would not be taken to Utica to be executed. For the *frumentarii* had been sent for this purpose by the proconsul. Hence below the *princeps* is said to have “rushed upon” him—that is, to have hastened—because he thought Cyprian truly wished to escape. See the final epistle, 81 in the Oxford edition, 83 in Pamelius. RUINART.]

## CHAPTER XIV. When persecution is imminent, Cyprian refuses to flee and exhorts his people to martyrdom.

News had now come from Rome concerning Xystus, the good and peaceable priest and therefore most blessed martyr. Now only the executioner’s arrival stood between him and death—the executioner who was to strike the devoted neck of the most holy victim. And all those days were so filled with the daily expectation of dying that a crown could have been ascribed to each of them.

Meanwhile, many men of distinguished and illustrious rank and lineage, noble also by worldly status, gathered around him. Because of their long-standing friendship with him, they repeatedly advised withdrawal; and, lest mere advice be too little, they even offered him places to which he might retire. But he had already disregarded the world, his mind raised toward heaven, and he did not assent to their flattering counsels. Perhaps even then he would have done what many faithful people requested if he had also been commanded by divine authority.

Nor should that sublime glory of so great a man pass without proclamation: when the world was already swelling with arrogance and, emboldened by the emperors, panting to persecute the Name, he instructed God’s servants, whenever opportunity was given, with exhortations from the Lord, and inspired them to trample upon the sufferings [Col. 1494C] of the present time by contemplating the glory that was to follow. Such, evidently, was his longing for sacred discourse that he wished the fulfillment of his desire for martyrdom to come upon him in such a manner that, while speaking about God, he might be killed in the very act of preaching.

[Note: [Col. 1494D]

**CHAP. XV.—The *princeps*.** An account of these officials is given in the registers of dignities of the Roman Empire. They were the highest-ranking and principal officers serving under the *magister officiorum*, as Gothofredus explains. Moreover, it is well known that soldiers were divided into *Velites*, *Principes*, and *Triarii*. FELL.

[Col. 1495D] **From the commemoration of his illustrious work.** This alludes to the feasts of the martyrs, at which vigils were observed. RUINART.

**Gentle custody.** That is, free and by no means harsh. RUINART.

**Kept vigil at his martyrdom.** Thus vigils precede the festive anniversaries of the martyrs’ heavenly births. FELL.

**A man’s belch.** In French we would call this “belch” a *caprice*.—“Belch” is used proverbially here for choice or whim. St. Cyprian used the same word in Epistle LXII to Pomponius, where, speaking of men who had slept with virgins, he says: “Let us hold fast to the divine commandments, and let us not permit our brethren to go astray and live according to their own choice and belch.” BOLLAND.]

## CHAPTER XV. He is arrested. The congregation keeps watch through the night before the doors.

Such were the daily acts directed toward making the priest a sacrifice pleasing to God, when suddenly, at the proconsul’s order, the *princeps* rushed with his soldiers to Cyprian’s gardens—to the gardens, I say, which he had sold at the beginning of his faith and which had been restored by God’s favor [Note: [Col. 1494D] “And by God’s favor,” Bod. 1, Morel.], and which he certainly would have sold again for the use of the poor had he not wished to avoid provoking hostility during the persecution [Note: [Col. 1494D] “Had he not wished them to be seized during his martyrdom,” Bod. 1, Morel.]—[Col. 1494D–1495A] or rather, to speak more truly, the *princeps* believed that he had rushed upon him suddenly. For how could a mind always prepared be taken by surprise, as though by an unforeseen assault?

Cyprian therefore came forward, now certain that what had long been delayed would be completed. He came forward with a lofty and upright spirit [Note: [Col. 1495C] “And serene, displaying cheerfulness,” Morel.], displaying cheerfulness in his countenance and courage in his heart. But because his hearing was postponed until the following day, he was returning from the governor’s residence to the house of the *princeps*, when suddenly a rumor, spreading throughout Carthage, gained strength: Thascius had now been brought forth. Apart from the celebrated knowledge of him arising from his glorious reputation, there was no one who did not also know him from the commemoration of his most illustrious work. Everyone ran together from every direction to the spectacle—glorious to us because of our devotion to the faith [Note: [Col. 1496C] “Glorious alike,” Bod. 1.], but pitiable to the pagans.

After he had been received and placed in the house of the *princeps*, a gentle custody kept him there for one night, so that, as usual, we, his companions and dear friends, remained in fellowship with him [Col. 1495B]. Meanwhile, the whole congregation, anxious lest anything should be done during the night without its knowledge, kept watch before the doors of the *princeps*. Divine goodness then granted to him, who was truly worthy of it, that God’s people should keep vigil even at their priest’s martyrdom.

Yet perhaps someone may ask why he was sent back from the governor’s residence to the *princeps*. Certain people, of course, invent the explanation that the proconsul was then unwilling to proceed. Far be it from me, in events divinely conducted, to complain of the proconsul’s sluggishness or weariness. Far be it from me to admit this evil into the conscience of a devout mind: that the fate of so blessed a martyr depended on a man’s whim. No: that following day, which divine favor had foretold a year before, truly had to be the following day.

[Note: [Col. 1495D]

**CHAP. XVI.—Covered with linen.** Bishops’ seats were customarily covered with linen, as is clear from Pacian, who in Epistle 2 to Sympronianus reproaches Novatian because, although no one had consecrated him, he took possession of a linen-covered seat. Augustine also appears to imply this in Epistle 23 to Maximinus, a Donatist bishop, where he says that neither stepped apses nor veiled chairs will benefit anyone at Christ’s judgment. RUINART.

**The *tesserarii*.** The *tesserarii* are those who announce the watchword throughout the soldiers’ quarters or demand it from the sentries. Vegetius treats of them in Book II, *On Military Affairs*, ch. 7, where the *tessera* is said to be the commander’s order by which the army is moved either to labor or to battle. RUINART.—**The *tesserarii*.** Vegetius, bk. II, ch. 7, says that they are those who announce the watchword throughout the quarters of the soldiers or praetorians. Tacitus, bk. XVII, calls Barbius Proculus “a *tesserarius* scout.” FELL.

**Might possess.** Thus Christians eagerly competed to seize some of the martyrs’ relics. FELL.]

## CHAPTER XVI. On the following day he is led before the proconsul’s tribunal.

[Col. 1495C]

At last another day dawned—that designated, promised, divine day, which, had the tyrant himself wished to postpone it, he would never have been able to do: a day gladdened by the future martyr’s foreknowledge and, after clouds had been scattered throughout the whole compass of the world, radiant with a brilliant sun.

He left the house of the *princeps*, but as a prince of Christ and God, and was surrounded on every side by columns of a mingled multitude. So vast [Col. 1496A] an army accompanied his procession that it was as though an organized force were coming to conquer death. On his way he passed through the stadium. It was fitting, and done almost deliberately, that the man who, his contest completed, was running toward the crown of righteousness should also pass by a place suited to athletic struggle.

But when they arrived at the governor’s residence, since the proconsul had not yet appeared, a more secluded place was assigned to him. There, after the long journey, he sat drenched in profuse sweat. The seat happened to be covered with linen, so that even under the stroke of martyrdom he might enjoy the honor of the episcopate. One of the *tesserarii*, formerly a Christian, offered him his own belongings, as though Cyprian might wish to exchange his damp clothes for drier ones. Yet the man evidently desired nothing else in offering these things but to possess the sweat—already bloody, as it were—of the martyr who was departing to God.

Cyprian answered him [Col. 1496B], saying: “We are applying remedies to complaints that perhaps will not exist today.” It is no wonder that one who had despised death in his mind despised discomfort in his body.

Why say more? Suddenly his arrival was announced to the proconsul. He was brought forward, led up, and questioned concerning his name. He replied that he was. And there the words ended.

[Note: [Col. 1496D]

**CHAP. XVII.—To prophesy.** This alludes to Caiaphas, who unknowingly prophesied concerning Christ’s death, John 11:59. RUINART.

**He had been a standard-bearer.** He was not only a leader in the Christian army, but was marked in his body with his commander’s emblem and character, according to the custom of the ancient military service [Col. 1497C]. See Gal. 6:17. Moreover, by his martyrdom he raised still higher the Cross, the Lord’s standard, which he had proclaimed in words, and preached it more felicitously. FELL.]

## CHAPTER XVII. Sentence is pronounced.

The judge therefore read from the tablet the sentence that Cyprian had not read shortly before in his vision—a spiritual sentence that must not be spoken of lightly; a sentence worthy of such a bishop and such a witness; a glorious sentence, in which he was called the standard-bearer of a sect, an enemy of the gods, one who would himself serve as an example to his followers, and one through whose [Col. 1496C] blood discipline would begin to be established.

Nothing could be fuller than this sentence, nothing truer. For everything said in it, though spoken by a pagan, was divine. Nor is this surprising, since high priests are accustomed to prophesy concerning suffering. He had been a standard-bearer, for he taught men to carry the standard of Christ; an enemy of the gods, for he commanded that idols be destroyed; and he served as an example to his own people, for, before the many who were to follow in the same manner, he was the first in the province to consecrate the firstfruits of martyrdom. Discipline also began to be established by his blood—the discipline of the martyrs, who, emulating their teacher by imitating a similar glory [Col. 1497A], themselves likewise established the discipline of their example with their own blood.

[Note: [Col. 1497C]

**CHAP. XVIII.—In the likeness of Zacchaeus.** I do not know whether a slight mistake occurred here on the part of Pontius or of the copyists, with “Zacchaeus” written in place of “Christ.” For it is clear that this alludes to Luke 19, where Zacchaeus, as Christ approached, ran ahead and climbed a sycamore tree in order to see him. Evidently St. Cyprian is said here to have been seen by others who had climbed trees. BOLLAND.

**Their common desire.** Compare the *Proceedings*, no. 5, where the crowd of brethren said: “Let us too be beheaded with him.” RUINART.]

## CHAPTER XVIII. He is beheaded.

When he went out through the doors of the governor’s residence, a crowd of soldiers accompanied him; and lest anything be lacking in his martyrdom, centurions and tribunes guarded his flanks. The place itself where he happened to suffer is level [Note: [Col. 1497B] “On level ground,” Gal.], so that, with trees growing densely on every side, it afforded an elevated spectacle. But because the vast extent of the space and the excessively confused crowd denied them a view, his supporters had crept up into the branches of the trees, lest even this be denied him: that, in the likeness of Zacchaeus (Luke 19:4), he should be seen from the trees [Col. 1497B].

After binding his eyes with his own hands, he tried to hasten the executioner’s delay. It was the executioner’s office to wield the sword, yet his right hand faltered, and he could scarcely direct the blade with trembling fingers. At last the hour of glorification ripened for accomplishing the precious man’s death; strength granted from above made the centurion’s hand firm and at length released its powers to act.

O blessed people of the Church, who suffered together with such a bishop—with eyes and feelings alike and, what is more, with a publicly proclaimed voice—and who, just as they had always heard when he preached, were crowned with God as judge! For although what their common desire sought could not come to pass—that the entire congregation should suffer together in fellowship of equal glory—whoever sincerely wished to suffer under the eyes of Christ, who watched, and within the hearing of the priest, sent to God, through a competent witness of his desire, what were in some fashion letters of embassy [Col. 1498A].

## CHAPTER XIX. The first martyr among the bishops of Carthage.

[Note: [Col. 1497C]

**CHAP. XIX.—Priestly crowns.** Crowns acquired not from baldness, but from illustrious virtue. The rabbis add three other crowns to the crown of kingship: namely, the crown of the Law, the crown of the priesthood [Col. 1498C], and the crown of a good name. Cyprian shone forth adorned with this triple diadem, and added another, the crown of martyrdom.

The apostle of the Africans appears to have been Simon the Zealot, concerning whom Nicephorus, bk. II, ch. 40, says: *Αἰγύπτῳ Κυρήνῃ τε καὶ τῇ Ἀφρικῇ προσβαλών, Μαυριτανίαν τε καὶ ὅσον τῆς Λιβύης ἐστὶ, τῷ εὐαγγελίῳ διαδραμών*, etc.—“Having reached Egypt, Cyrene, and Africa, and having traversed with the Gospel Mauretania and as much of Libya as there is,” etc. FELL.

**That I am not his companion.** The ancient martyrologies, as also the present Roman Martyrology, commemorate the feast of Pontius on March 8. Take care, however, not to confuse him with Pontius the martyr, who is said to have brought the emperors named Philip to faith in Christ; concerning him, see more in the Bollandists under May 14. In the seventh century St. Rusticula, abbess of Arles, caused an altar to be dedicated in honor of St. Pontius, as Florentius the priest relates in her *Life*. But he does not explain who that Pontius was. RUINART.]

Thus, when his martyrdom had been consummated, it was brought to perfection that Cyprian, who had been an example of every good thing, should also be the first in Africa to imbue the priestly crowns with blood, because he had also begun to be the foremost man of this kind after the apostles. For from the time when the episcopal succession at Carthage began to be reckoned, no one, however good a priest, is remembered to have attained martyrdom. Although devotion always consecrated to God is, in dedicated men, counted as martyrdom, Cyprian nevertheless advanced even to the perfect [Col. 1498B] crown, the Lord bringing him to consummation. Thus, in the very city in which he had lived in such a manner, and in which he had first done many illustrious deeds, he was also the first to adorn the insignia of the heavenly priesthood with glorious blood.

What shall I do at this point? My mind is divided between joy at his martyrdom and grief that I remain, and my heart, far too narrow, is burdened by these two affections. Shall I grieve because I was not his companion? But his victory must be celebrated in triumph. Shall I triumph over his victory? But I grieve that I am not his companion. Yet I must confess to you truthfully and without concealment what you yourselves also know: such has been my state of mind. I rejoice greatly—exceedingly greatly—in his glory; yet I grieve still more because I remained behind.

[Col. 1497]

# THE PROCONSULAR PROCEEDINGS OF SAINT CYPRIAN, BISHOP AND MARTYR. (C, S)

## I. St. Cyprian’s first confession before the proconsul Paternus. He refuses to betray the presbyters.

[Col. 1497D]

[Note: [Col. 1497D]

I.—Under the Emperor Valerian. The account of Cyprian’s passion according to the editions of Manutius and Morel prefixes, in place of a prologue, a remarkable [Col. 1498D] tale which sufficiently reveals the century in which it arose. It runs as follows:

When [Col. 1499C] the glorious name of Christ, hated by the pagans, was being assailed with the utmost determination so that it might be eradicated, and there was a persecution in the city of Rome, the most blessed Cornelius, endowed with the highest virtues, then governed the pontificate of that city. Arrested by the governor and afflicted with prolonged tortures, he ended his temporal life by the sword, destined to receive from God a life everlasting [Col. 1499D] and without end. But when this hatred had also been inflicted upon the territories of Libya, many Christian peoples, preferring to lose this transitory life and attain the things promised by God, were afflicted with various tortures and brought to their consummation. They relate that the governor then also had a limekiln kindled and, after live coals with incense had been set before its opening, said to the Christians: “Choose one of two things: either offer incense to Jupiter upon these coals, or plunge into the lime.” Then three hundred men, armed with faith and confessing Christ, the Son of God, to be God, hurled themselves with the utmost swiftness into the fire and were submerged amid the vapors of the powdered lime; Christ consecrated them to himself. In those days, while such things were taking place, the blessed prelate Cyprian governed the Church of Carthage. He was arrested by the pagans and, while Paternus the proconsul was sitting in the city, was brought before an unjust tribunal.

In the ancient martyrology it begins: “In the consulship of Tuscus and Bassus, in the council chamber,” as the Salisbury and Gallican codices read. Evidently, when the accounts of the exile and passion were combined into one for the Church’s use in annual commemoration, the chronological designation that belonged only to the passion was prefixed to both. FELL.

“In the council chamber.” Greek glosses: σέκρετον, “court, archive”; σέκρετον, “council.” Hesychius. FELL.

“We are not informers.” Informers had been driven from the city and expelled from the courts by imperial rescripts. Hence the saying: “The informer received what he gave—exile.” Cyprian therefore rightly appeals to the laws; “We are not informers” would otherwise be a feeble thing to say. FELL.

“Voluntarily surrender himself.” In Cyprian’s final letter he says: “The Lord wished us to confess rather than profess.” FELL.

“And this is displeasing also to your judicial judgment.” Thus Arrius Antoninus said to the Christians, who as though in a concerted body were demanding death: ὦ δειλοί, εἰ θέλετε ἀποθνῄσκειν, κρημνοὺς ἢ βρόχους ἔχετε, “O wretches, if you wish to die, you have cliffs or nooses.” Tertullian, *To Scapula*. FELL.]

[Col. 1498D] In the fourth consulship of the Emperor Valerian and the third of Gallienus [Note: [Col. 1497D] “In the consulship of Tuscus and Bassus.” Old Martyrology; Salisbury, Gallican, and Fossatensis manuscripts. “The writings of the noble emperors have reached me, ordering that those who abhor the ceremonies are to be compelled, even against their will, to sacrifice to the gods and perform sacrifices.” *Acts of the Passion*.], on the third day before the Kalends of September, [Col. 1499A] at Carthage in the council chamber, the proconsul Paternus said to Bishop Cyprian:

“The most sacred emperors Valerian and Gallienus have deigned to send me letters in which they have ordered that those who do not observe the Roman religion [Note: [Col. 1499B] “Those who observe the Roman religion ought to acknowledge the ceremonies.”] must acknowledge the Roman ceremonies. I have therefore inquired [Note: [Col. 1499B] “I inquire, therefore.” Gallican, Salisbury. “I ask you concerning your name: [Col. 1499C] what answer do you give me?” Codex Conchensis.] concerning your name. What answer do you give me [Note: [Col. 1499C] “Answering.” Gallican, Salisbury.]?”

Bishop Cyprian said: “I am a Christian and a bishop. I know no other gods [Note: [Col. 1499C] “I worship no other gods.” Salisbury, Gallican.] except the one true God, who made heaven and earth, the sea, and everything in them. We Christians serve this God; we entreat him by day and night for ourselves [Note: [Col. 1499C] “For ourselves and for the safety.” Salisbury, Gallican.], for all human beings, and for the safety of the emperors themselves.”

The proconsul Paternus said: “Do you therefore persist in this resolve [Note: [Col. 1499C] “Do you persist in refusing to sacrifice?” *Acts of the Passion*.]?”

Bishop Cyprian answered: “A good resolve that acknowledges God cannot be changed [Note: [Col. 1499C] “Cannot be changed. Not only concerning the bishops.” Gallican, Salisbury, *Acts of the Passion*.].”

The proconsul Paternus [Col. 1499B] said: “Can you, then, in accordance with the command of Valerian and Gallienus, depart into exile for the city of Curubis?”

Bishop Cyprian said: “I shall depart.”

The proconsul Paternus said: “They have deigned to write to me not only concerning the bishops but also concerning the presbyters. I therefore wish to learn from you who the presbyters residing in this city are.”

Bishop Cyprian answered: “In your laws you have wisely and beneficially determined that there are to be no informers [Note: [Col. 1499C] Thus the Gallican and Salisbury manuscripts. “That we are not informers.” *Acts of the Passion*, printed edition.]. Accordingly, they cannot be disclosed or denounced [Note: [Col. 1499C] “Accordingly, we cannot produce them; nor do they themselves voluntarily surrender, since Holy Scripture forbids this. If sought by you, [Col. 1500B] they will be found.” The proconsul said: “It has been ordered that they hold no assemblies.” *Acts of the Passion*.] by me. They will, however, be found in their own cities [Note: [Col. 1500B] “They will be found in their own cities.” The proconsul Paternus [Col. 1500C] said: “They will be found by me.” Salisbury, Gallican.].”

The proconsul Paternus said: “Today I am making inquiry here [Col. 1500A].”

Cyprian said: “Since discipline forbids anyone to surrender himself voluntarily, and this is displeasing also to your judicial judgment, they cannot present themselves; but if sought by you, they will be found.”

The proconsul Paternus said: “They will be found by me.” And he added: “They have also ordered that no assemblies be held in any places and that no one enter the cemeteries [Note: [Col. 1500C] “Enter the cemeteries; anyone discovered doing so is to suffer capital punishment.” Saint Cyprian answered: “Do what you have been ordered.” After this the blessed martyr was led into exile, by order of the proconsul Aspasius, to the city of Curubis. After many days he departed. *Acts of the Passion*.]. Therefore, if anyone fails to observe this most salutary command, he will suffer capital punishment.”

Bishop Cyprian answered: “Do what you have been ordered [Note: [Col. 1500C] “Do what you have been ordered. And when Cyprian, chosen by God, had left the city of Curubis.” Salisbury, Gallican.].”

## II. He is sent into exile at Curubis. Recalled from there by Galerius, he is arrested.

[Note: [Col. 1500D]

II.—“To be deported.” Saint Augustine, Sermon 309: “For his confession of faith in Christ he was sent into exile at Curubis,” etc. RUINART.

“It had been revealed.” Augustine, ibid., no. 2: “Having returned, he remained in his gardens, and there he daily expected men to come for him, just as it had been revealed to him,” etc. See the *Life* above, no. XII. RUINART.

“Consuls.” Baronius, at the year 261, no. 25, advises that “Fuscus” should be read, on the authority of Trebellius Pollio. RUINART.

“Orderly of the staff.” It makes no difference whether one says *strator* or *stator*, for the manuscripts recognize both; the former word is of Greek origin, the latter Latin. They appear to be much the same as those later called prison registrars (*commentarienses*). Constantine’s excellent law to Florentius the *Rationalis*, worthy of being written in letters of gold, [Col. 1501C] graphically depicts the character of these men. The reader will pardon me for presenting the passage in full, since it ought by no means to be mutilated. Code, book IX, title 4, “On the Custody of Defendants”:

“In every case in which a defendant has been produced, whether an accuser exists or concern for public security has brought him in, an inquiry must be held immediately, so that the guilty may be punished and the innocent acquitted. But if the accuser is absent for a time, or the presence of accomplices appears necessary, this must be secured as swiftly as possible. Meanwhile, the man produced must not have iron manacles placed upon him that cling to his bones, but longer chains, so that torture may be absent while secure custody remains. Nor should one who is confined endure the darkness of an inner cell, but he should be sustained by access to light; and when night has doubled the need for custody, he should be received in the prison vestibules and in healthy places, and when day returns he should immediately be brought out into the public light at the first rising of the sun, lest he be destroyed by the punishments of prison—a thing known to be wretched for the innocent and insufficiently severe for the guilty.

“This also shall be observed: neither those who perform the office of orderlies nor their [Col. 1501D] assistants shall be permitted to sell their cruelty to accusers, deliver innocent persons to death within the prison walls, or, by withholding them from a hearing, consume them through prolonged wasting. For the judge will face fear not only for his reputation but also for his safety if any orderly has exhausted anyone beyond the proper period through starvation or by any other means, and the judge has not immediately subjected both the person responsible for custody and his assistants to capital punishment.” FELL.—On these men, see Du Cange’s *Glossary*, where *statores* are said to be so called because they “stood” ready for commands, while *stratores* were those who cared for the ruler’s horses. *Stratores* may also derive from *sternere*, “to lay down,” because they punished condemned prisoners in jail or saddled horses. RUINART.

“Equerry.” ἀναβολεύς, “marshal,” among medieval Latin writers: the person who mounts an armed emperor or commander upon his horse. Of their occupation Manilius says:

[Col. 1502B] “This man will ride aloft upon the chariot,

Or load horses with weapons, or lead them into battle.”

Ammianus Marcellinus, book XXX, chapter 5, calls such a man a “soldier-equerry.” FELL.

“Lifted him.” Augustine, Sermon cited above, no. 3: “Two men were sent, who even lifted him into the carriage.” RUINART.

“They brought him to Sextus.” This place appears to have been so called because it was six milestones from the city. RUINART.

“Salutaria.” Nearly all the manuscripts have “Veneria.” Colbertinus 1 and Mombritius read “between Venaria and Salutaria”; Germanensis 1, “between the two streets Veneria and Salutaria.” RUINART.

“To be protected.” All the manuscripts except Colbertinus 1 read “to be chastised.” The other reading is nevertheless preferable. For Augustine read it thus, as is evident from the cited Sermon, no. 4: “What of the fact,” he says, “that when his case had been deferred to another day and the multitude of brothers and sisters assembled there and spent the night before the doors, he ordered the girls to be protected?” Likewise Saint Fulgentius, Sermon 6: “Detained by the governor, he protected the chastity of the virgins….” RUINART.]

Then the proconsul Paternus ordered the blessed Bishop Cyprian to be deported into exile. When he had remained there [Col. 1500B] for a long time, Galerius Maximus succeeded Aspasius Paternus as proconsul. He ordered the holy Bishop Cyprian, after he had been recalled from exile, to be brought before him.

When Cyprian, the holy martyr chosen by God, had returned from the city of Curubis, to which he had been sent into exile by order of Aspasius Paternus, then proconsul, he remained in his own gardens in accordance with the sacred command. There he daily expected men to come for him, just as it had been revealed to him. While he was staying there, suddenly, on the Ides of September, in the consulship of Tuscus and Bassus, two chief officers came to him [Note: [Col. 1500C] “Two chief officers from the staff of the proconsul Galerius Maximus; and lifting him.” *Acts of the Passion*.]: [Col. 1501A] one was an orderly on the staff of the proconsul Galerius Maximus, who had succeeded Aspasius Paternus; the other was an equerry [Note: [Col. 1501B] “A proconsular cavalryman.” Gallican. “A sequestrator.” Salisbury. “An equerry.” Ancient manuscript cited by Gothofredus.] from the guards of that same staff [Note: [Col. 1501B] “And also guards of that same staff, and both.” Salisbury.]. They lifted him into a carriage, placed him between them, and brought him to Sextus, where that same proconsul Galerius Maximus had withdrawn in order to recover his health.

The proconsul Galerius Maximus ordered Cyprian to be kept for him until the next day. At that time the blessed Cyprian was taken away and withdrew with the chief officer and orderly of the staff of that same proconsul Galerius Maximus, a man of senatorial rank. He remained with him in his lodging, on the street called Saturnus, between Venerea and Salutaria [Note: [Col. 1501B] “Between Venena and Salutaria.” Colbertinus, Mombritius. “Between the two streets Veneria and Salutaria.” Germanensis 1. “Salaria.” Printed edition. “Saltuaria.” Other manuscripts. “Having returned from exile, he was living in his own gardens. While he remained there, two chief officers from the staff of the proconsul Galerius Maximus came to him and, lifting him into their carriage, brought him to the proconsul at the place where he was staying to restore his health. Taken into custody by an attendant of the staff, he withdrew to the man’s lodging, on the street [Col. 1502B] called Saturnus, and lived there; and the whole people of the brethren gathered to him.” *Acts of the Passion*.]. The whole people of the brethren gathered there. When Saint Cyprian learned of this, [Col. 1501B] he ordered the girls to be protected [Note: [Col. 1502B] “The girls to be chastised.” Gallican, Salisbury. “Praying in the street.” Gallican. “They had come to hear the word of God, since they remained before the chief officer’s door out of love for the glorious martyr.”], because [Col. 1502A] everyone had remained in the street before the door of the chief officer’s lodging.

## III. He is brought before the proconsul. His second confession.

[Note: [Col. 1502C]

III.—“Sauciolus.” An obscure word. It appears to be the name of an atrium in which defendants were put to death. The Oxford editor observes that it was decreed at the Second Council of Mâcon, canon 19, that no cleric should approach the place where defendants were examined, [Col. 1502D] or be present in the Sauciolus atrium, where someone was to be executed in accordance with the character of his guilt. The Colbertinus manuscripts and Germanensis 1 have “the Secutiolus atrium”; Conchensis, “Saloutius.” RUINART.

“Papa.” Perhaps *papatem* should be read, as our Mabillon judges in his notes on the Acts of Saints Mammarius and others, *Analecta*, vol. IV, p. 105. In the Greek Acts of Saints Conon and his son, in the Bollandists for May 29, no. 4, the governor asks the martyr whether he is a priest or a deacon: Παππὰς ἢ διάκων; the martyr answers that he is a layman. And in the published and manuscript Acts of Saints Modestus and Vitus, the boy Vitus repeatedly calls Modestus his *papas*. RUINART.

“Most sacred.” Augustine, no. 5: “For when he saw his unshakable mind, after saying to him, ‘The rulers have ordered you to perform the ceremonies,’ and Cyprian had answered, ‘I will not,’ he added, ‘Consider your own welfare,’” etc. Then, no. 6: “‘Do,’ he said, ‘what you have been ordered. In so just a matter there is no deliberation.’ For the other had said: ‘Consider your own welfare.’ To this the answer was: ‘In so just a matter,’” etc. RUINART.]

And so on the next day, the eighteenth day before the Kalends of October, early in the morning [Note: [Col. 1502B] “When morning had come.” *Acts of the Passion*. “Very early in the morning.” Gallican. “When morning had come, the blessed Cyprian was brought before the proconsul, who looked at him and said: ‘Are you Thascius Cyprian, who have presented yourself as *papa* to people of a sacrilegious mind? The most sacred emperors have ordered you to sacrifice. Consider your own welfare, lest you perish.’ Then the angry proconsul said: ‘For a long time….’” *Acts of the Passion*.], a great crowd assembled at Sextus in accordance with the command of the proconsul Galerius Maximus. That same day the proconsul Galerius Maximus ordered Cyprian to be brought before him as he sat in the Sauciolus atrium. When he had been brought forward, the proconsul Galerius Maximus said to Bishop Cyprian:

“Are you THASCIUS CYPRIAN?”

Bishop Cyprian answered: “I am.”

The proconsul Galerius Maximus said: “Have you presented yourself as *papa* to people of a sacrilegious mind?”

Bishop Cyprian answered: “I have.”

The proconsul Galerius Maximus [Col. 1502B] said: “The most sacred emperors have ordered you [Col. 1503A] to perform the ceremonies.”

Bishop Cyprian said: “I will not.”

Galerius Maximus said: “Consider your own welfare.”

Bishop Cyprian answered: “Do what you have been ordered. In so just a matter there is no deliberation.”

## IV. Sentence is passed upon him, and he is ordered to be beheaded.

[Note: [Col. 1503B]

IV.—“Having conferred with his council.” As was the custom of Roman governors, who consulted the advisers sitting behind a curtain concerning the sentence to be pronounced. See Acts 25:12. FELL.

“Valerian, most noble Caesar.” His father, while hastening to Persia, proclaimed him Caesar. There the most unfortunate old man expiated this persecution of the Christians through the most wretched captivity and through a still more wretched death, if that were possible. FELL.

“It is decreed.” The same Augustine, no. 6: “Into what utterance should our heart burst forth, if not into the venerable martyr’s own final words? For when Galerius Maximus had read the decree from the tablet, ‘It is decreed that Thascius Cyprian be put to death by the sword,’ he answered, ‘Thanks be to God.’ Since we therefore possess concerning the matter…let us also say, ‘Thanks be to God.’” Thus the sermon ends. RUINART.]

Galerius Maximus, having conferred with his council, pronounced the sentence reluctantly and with difficulty, in the following words:

“You have long lived with a sacrilegious mind, and have gathered to yourself very many people in an impious conspiracy. You have made yourself an enemy of the Roman gods and the sacred laws, nor have the pious and most sacred rulers Valerian and Gallienus Augusti, and Valerian, most noble Caesar, been able to recall you to the observance of their ceremonies. Therefore, since you have been discovered to be the instigator and standard-bearer of the vilest crimes, you yourself will serve as an example to those whom you gathered to yourself in your wickedness: discipline shall be sanctioned by your blood.”

Having said this, he read the decree from a tablet: “It is decreed that Thascius Cyprian be put to death by the sword.”

Bishop Cyprian said: “Thanks be to God [Note: [Col. 1503B] “I give thanks to almighty God, who deigns to release me from the bonds of this body.” Gallican, *Acts of the Passion*.].”

## V. He is beheaded before a great crowd of people. His body is taken away by the faithful at night and buried.

[Note: [Col. 1503C]

V.—“Into the field of Sextus.” The *Roman Martyrology* transformed the “field of Sextus” into “the sixth milestone from Carthage beside the sea.” FELL.

“His cloak and *byrrus*.” Either *lacerna* (“cloak”) or *byrrus* must be regarded as an addition. The most eminent Cardinal Baronius argues at length that from this passage we learn what the dress of bishops was. Indeed, that lynx-eyed man shows us that the linen garment in which Cyprian stood was the linen vestment common to all bishops, which some call the ephod and in Italian *rochetto*. The *byrrus*, meanwhile, was a red-colored silken clerical garment. Thus, he claims, the ancient dress of bishops is demonstrably represented: over their ordinary garment they put on a linen vestment; over it, a loose tunic; and finally a *lacerna byrrus* covering only the shoulders—the kind of clothing that we now see worn by the cardinals of the holy Roman Church and by those bishops elevated to that dignity from the religious orders. Thus we may now further learn that Cyprian was either a cardinal of the Roman Church or was elevated from the religious orders to episcopal rank.

There is certainly nothing of which those enslaved to partisan zeal cannot persuade themselves—and even hope to persuade others. Do clerics of the Roman Church go out in public conspicuous in their own proper dress when they are staying in regions where they fear for themselves: wearing swords and, to use the words of our countryman Campion, “clothed in the most absurd attire”? The proconsul would foolishly have concerned himself with discovering bishops and presbyters [Col. 1504B] if their dress made them conspicuous to everyone. Anyone who does not detect in what follows the interpolations of copyists, worthy of their respective centuries and abilities, has an exceedingly dull nose. When those most obliging men believed that a tunic did not sufficiently correspond to episcopal dignity, they supplied a dalmatic. FELL.—The Oxford editor considers one or the other of these words an addition. Certainly Germanensis 1 has only *byrrus*. The learned Du Cange further notes from Festus in his *Glossary* that *byrrus* formerly meant “red.” If the word should be understood in that sense here, the reading of several manuscripts would be preferable: [Col. 1504C] “he stripped off his red cloak.” Sulpicius Severus, *Dialogue* I, chapter 14, speaks of the *byrrus* and *lacerna* as two distinct kinds of garment; see Baronius at the year 261, no. 41, where he says more on this subject. But it is astonishing that Baronius discovered the present-day vestments of bishops in these words. It would first have to be proved that bishops once used such ornaments. When Saint Odo, abbot of Cluny, was covered with a *byrrus* in the manner of a cope, God’s servants took hold of it at the edge of the fringe and kissed it out of reverence. From John, author of his *Life*, book II, no. 5, *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis S. Benedicti*, saec. V, p. 167. RUINART.

“Dalmatic.” The Fossatensis, Colbertinus, Conchensis, Sainte-Geneviève, and other manuscripts have “tunic” in place of “dalmatic,” but far more manuscripts have “dalmatic.” In any event, the name “dalmatic” was not unknown to the ancients. Commodus is said by Lampridius to have appeared in public wearing a dalmatic. Baronius collected more concerning the dalmatic in his notes on the *Roman Martyrology* for May 31, where he discusses Paschasius the deacon. ID.

[Col. 1504D] “They should give the executioner twenty-five gold pieces.” The Oxford editor suggests that this gift is owed to the copyists. Augustine favors this view in the passage cited, where he says that the martyr’s final words were “Thanks be to God,” which he pronounced immediately after the sentence was read. Nevertheless, all the manuscripts that we have been able to examine commemorate this generosity of Cyprian. Maximilian, whose acts we shall present under the year 295, asked that the garment his father had prepared for him be given to the executioner. RUINART.—This largesse appears to have arisen from the copyists’ generosity. But if individual gold pieces are worth five shillings in our currency, the little sum given would amount to six pounds and five shillings in the money called sterling. FELL.

[Col. 1505A] “With wax candles and *scholaces*.” Cardinal Baronius, at the year of Christ 261, no. 36, says: “Here the ancient custom of burying Christians is disclosed: the clergy of various ranks and schools went before them, each carrying lighted torches, in an altogether magnificent procession.” Thus, while Valerian held imperial power, Christians had various ranks and schools; and they celebrated martyrs’ funerals by proceeding in ordered formation, according to the present-day rite of processions. Here, as everywhere else, we miss fidelity and dignity in ecclesiastical history.

Rigaltius says: “The copies read, ‘to the wax candles and *scholaces*.’ Quite correctly. *Scholaces* is a word of Greek origin, signifying twisted withes or ropes from which waxed torches were made for illumination at night. Torches and *scholaces* were the candles that tightly bound the case of Numa’s books on every side. For they possessed a flexible toughness suitable for bindings, and when buried underground did not rot, being packed with cedar oil and wax.”

In the dead of night the brethren had gone to remove the body, lest the Africans attempt against Cyprian what the Asian pagans perpetrated against Polycarp. On this matter see Eusebius, book IV, chapter 15. [Col. 1506B] In John 18 the Jews are said to have come μετὰ φανῶν καὶ λαμπάδων, “with lanterns and torches.” FELL.

“*Scholaces*.” We have restored this passage thus from several manuscripts. In the printed texts and some manuscripts, “Candidus” appears instead of “Candidianus.” Baronius thinks the word *scholacium* designates the schools of clergy with candles, etc. Rigaltius, however, thinks it means torches for dispelling the darkness of night; Du Cange observes in his *Glossary* that most people called such torches *scholaces*. That Christian cemeteries were called “sandpits” or “areas” is clear from the Acts of Saints Montanus and others and from Tertullian, *To Scapula*, chapter 3. See Baronius under January 3 in his notes on the *Roman Martyrology*. RUINART.]

After this sentence, the crowd of the brethren said: “Let us also be beheaded with him [Note: [Col. 1503B] “And while he was being led away, the people, weeping and wailing, said: ‘Let us be beheaded with him.’” *Acts of the Passion*.].” Because of this an uproar arose among the brethren, and a great crowd followed him.

Thus Cyprian was led into the field of Sextus [Note: [Col. 1503B] “When the glorious martyr had been led out, he removed the cloak and *byrrus* that he was wearing, folded it, and placed it beside [Col. 1504B] his knees; then he took off his tunic and handed it to the deacons.” *Acts of the Passion*. “He took off his tunic.” Salisbury.]. There he stripped off his cloak and *byrrus*, bent his knee to the ground, and prostrated himself before the Lord in prayer. When he had removed his dalmatic [Note: [Col. 1504B] “Tunic.” Fossatensis, Colbertinus, Conchensis, Saint-Genor manuscript.] and handed it to the deacons, he stood in his linen garment [Note: [Col. 1504B] “At the line.” Salisbury. “Standing in his linen garment.” *Acts of the Passion*. “In linen garments.” Gallican.] and began to await the executioner.

When the executioner arrived, he ordered his people to give that executioner twenty-five gold pieces [Note: [Col. 1504B] “He ordered them to give.” Salisbury.]. Meanwhile, linen cloths and handkerchiefs [Col. 1505A] were being placed before him by the brethren [Note: [Col. 1505A] “The brethren, weeping, placed linen cloths and scarves before him, lest the holy blood, as it flowed, should be absorbed by the earth.” [Col. 1506A] *Acts of the Passion*.].

Afterward the blessed Cyprian covered his eyes with his own hand. Since he could not tie the ends of the handkerchief for himself, Julian the presbyter and Julian the subdeacon tied them for him.

Thus the blessed Cyprian suffered. Because of the curiosity of the pagans, his body was placed nearby. From there it was taken away during the night with wax candles and *scholaces* and carried, with vows and great triumph, to the burial grounds of the procurator Macrobius Candidianus, which are on the Mappalian Way beside the reservoirs. [Col. 1506A] A few days later, the proconsul Galerius Maximus died.

## VI. He suffered on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of October, under the rulers Valerian and Gallienus.

The most blessed martyr Cyprian suffered on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of October, under the emperors Valerian and Gallienus, but during the reign of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom belong honor and glory for ever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 1505]

# APPENDIX: THE PASSION OF SAINT CYPRIAN FROM THE MANUSCRIPT OF VICTOR AND ALSO BODLEIAN MANUSCRIPT I. (S)

[Note: [Col. 1505D]

“The Passion of Saint Cyprian.” Rigaltius says: “We believe that this account of Cyprian’s martyrdom, just as it is the shortest, is also the most ancient. Pontius, moved by pious affection for his bishop, ingeniously invented a great many things with rhetorical freedom. Others likewise added many things, each according to his own understanding—things foreign to the period and foreign to the persons—and they even removed certain very good things, so that scarcely anything now remains that we can present as genuine. The very things that the poet Prudentius reports as received from common tradition when he sets out to describe Cyprian’s passion have passed into history by being inserted into the Acts.” FELL.

“Proconsul, a most distinguished man.” It is known from the Code of Justinian and other ancient writings that a proconsul was honored with the title “most distinguished man”; but its constant insertion, as occurs here, must be regarded as the elegance of copyists, whose perpetual custom is to corrupt everything they emend. FELL.

“Specifically for this purpose and personally.” Some fool from the herd of petty lawyers inserted these words. RIGALTIUS.

“And for everyone to come on the day.” It appears that one should read, “and that people should come for him every day.” Augustine: “And from there he daily expected men to come for him.” Cyprian himself, Letter 82, where he speaks of Valerian’s letters: “We expect these letters to arrive daily.” RIGALTIUS.

“In his lodging.” Pontius: “a comfortable custody.” RIGALTIUS.

“Between Venerea and Salutaria.” Between the temple of Venus and the temple of Salus. The Acts from the Fossatensis and Pratensis manuscripts read “between Venaria and Salaria.” Other manuscripts read “Salutaria.” What is written in the Victorian manuscript—“between Venaria and Salutaria”—should not be dismissed. For that reading leads me to think that “inter Venaria Salutaria” was written by some petty scholar who had read in Pontius that the place where Cyprian happened to suffer was planted thickly with trees on every side. RIGALTIUS.]

[Col. 1505C] When Cyprian, the holy martyr chosen by the Lord, had returned from the city of Curubis, to which he had been sent into exile by command of Aspasius Paternus, then proconsul and a most distinguished man, pursuant to a sacred rescript issued specifically for this purpose and personally, he remained in his gardens. He expected that on the appointed day people would come by every means [Note: [Col. 1505C] Thus Bodleian 1. “That people should come by every means.” Printed edition.], just as it had been revealed to him.

While he was staying there [Note: [Col. 1505C] “While that same man was staying there.” Bodleian 1.], suddenly, on the Ides of September, in the consulship of Tuscus and Bassus, two chief officers came to him. One was an orderly on the staff of the proconsul Galerius Maximus, a most distinguished man, who had succeeded Aspasius [Col. 1506C] Paternus; the other was an equerry belonging to the guards of the staff of that same most distinguished man. They placed him in a carriage [Note: [Col. 1506C] “They placed him in it and brought him to Sextus.” Bodleian 1.], and both held him and carried him to Sextus.

There that same Galerius Maximus, proconsul and most distinguished man, ordered him to be presented on another day, that is, the next. Thus the same Cyprian withdrew with the chief officer and orderly of the staff of the proconsul Maximus, a most distinguished man, and remained with him in his lodging on Saturnus Street, between Venerea and Salutaria. There the whole people of the brethren remained before the door.

When Cyprian learned of this, [Note: [Col. 1507B]
