“The whole people of the brethren remained.” The nocturnal gatherings of Christians were formerly regarded with suspicion by pagans, and the violation of girls’ chastity was commonly alleged against them. See Tertullian, *To His Wife*, book II; Justin and Athenagoras in their *Apologies*; and Minucius Felix. For that reason Cyprian was so concerned about protecting the virgins. Pontius seems to relate that keeping of the night watch to the especially solemn vigil that preceded Easter, which Eusebius calls ἡ μεγάλης ἑορτῆς παννυχίς, “the all-night vigil of the great feast,” book II, chapter 17, and ἡ μεγάλη τοῦ πάσχα διανυκτέρευσις, “the great all-night observance of Easter,” book VI, chapter 9. From this one may conjecture that in those centuries, according to accepted custom, vigils by no means preceded the anniversaries of martyrs, even when they were bishops. For he observes as something peculiar that God’s people kept vigil even at the passion of a bishop. FELL.

“While he sat in the Sauciolus atrium.” “While he sat wrapped up and wounded.” Until now no one has produced this reading from any copy. The commonest reading is “while he sat in the Sauciolus atrium”; and in the Acts edited by Manutius and Morel, the proconsul’s atrium itself is called “Sauciolus.” But it appears scarcely probable that any atrium had a proper name. Faber attests that “Seleutiolus” is found in an ancient manuscript.

What is written in this Victorian manuscript, therefore—“wrapped up and wounded”—may, if anyone is displeased by “wounded,” be emended by a very slight alteration: [Col. 1508B] “Very early in the morning at Sextus, in accordance with the command of Galerius Maximus, proconsul and most distinguished man, he was brought before him while he sat in the atrium, wrapped up and dizzy.” This writer, who said *venaria* for hunting grounds or hunting preserves, might likewise have said *heluciosus* for *helucosus*, so that *helucosus* or *heluciosus* means ὁ καρηβαρῶν, “one suffering from heaviness or dizziness of the head.”

It should be noted that the same writer also relates that the proconsul had withdrawn for reasons of health to the place called Sextus—evidently a pleasant place amid hunting grounds and woods. It should also be noted that in this narrative [Col. 1508C] the proconsul questioned and addressed him only with difficulty and reluctance. Thus he sat in the atrium wrapped perhaps in cloths and mufflers, as the sick or wounded customarily do; hence someone later said “wrapped up and slightly wounded.” This conjecture is strengthened by the fact that the other Acts read: “A few days later the proconsul died.” RIGALTIUS.—Yet however much Rigaltius may please himself with his conjecture, it is established that *Sauciolum* designates the atrium of the governor’s residence. At the Second Council of Mâcon, canon 19, it is said: “No cleric is to approach the place where defendants are examined, or be present in the Sauciolus atrium, where someone is to be put to death in accordance with the character of his guilt.” If anyone says that this word was drawn from Gothic barbarism and was added by a copyist of a later age as an explanation of “atrium,” I shall by no means oppose him. FELL.

“Of hardened madness.” Something has been disordered here. For these are the proconsul’s words concerning Cyprian’s steadfastness and the strength of the Christian faith, as though Galerius had said in his address to the martyr: “Nor have our pious and most sacred rulers, by the religious system of their most fortunate times, been able to recall you from hardened madness to the full observance of the ceremonies,” etc. RIGALTIUS.]

[Col. 1507A] he ordered the girls to be chastised, because they were all lying in the street before the door of the chief officer’s lodging.

And so on the next day, that is, the seventeenth day before the Kalends of October, very early in the morning, at Sextus, in accordance with the command [Note: [Col. 1507A] “Of Galerius Maximus, while he sat in the atrium, wrapped up and wounded.” [Col. 1507B] Rigaltius. “Voluntarily, Sauciolus.” Bodleian 1.] of Galerius Maximus, proconsul and most distinguished man, he was brought before him as he sat in the Sauciolus atrium.

When he had been brought forward, that same Galerius Maximus, proconsul and most distinguished man, said to Cyprian [Note: [Col. 1508A] “‘Are you Thascius Cyprian?’ He said: ‘I am.’ Galerius Maximus [Col. 1508B] said….” Bodleian 1.]:

“Have you exhibited the office of *papa* to people of a sacrilegious mind?”

Cyprian said: “I have.”

Galerius Maximus, proconsul and most distinguished man, having spoken with his council, pronounced the sentence only with difficulty and reluctance, in the following words:

“You have long lived with a sacrilegious mind and have gathered to yourself very many people in an impious conspiracy. You have made yourself an enemy of the Roman gods [Col. 1508A] and the sacred religions; nor have our pious and most sacred rulers Valerian and Gallienus Augusti, and Valerian, most noble Caesar, been able for so long a time, by the religious system of their most fortunate times, to recall you from hardened madness to the full observance of the ceremonies and to the possession of a sound mind.

“And therefore, because you have been discovered to be the instigator and standard-bearer of a most vile crime, you will perish by the very example of the crime that you taught; so that, since sacrilegious obstinacy has persisted through your exertions, discipline may be sanctioned by your blood.”

And he read the decree from the tablet:

“It is decreed that Thascius Cyprian be put to death by the sword.”

[Col. 1509]

# GENERAL INDEX TO THE WORKS OF TERTULLIAN

[Note: [Col. 1510] In this index, Roman numerals I and II refer to PL I and II. Arabic numerals refer to Migne’s columns.]

## NOTICE
[Col. 1509] Many readers have perhaps been greatly annoyed to find this general index to the works of Septimius not in its proper place, as would have been fitting, but only at the end of the second volume. Yet, since neither time nor space was available, provision was made both to prevent the bulk of the book from increasing beyond measure and to ensure that this index was compiled accurately. For when, after completing our edition of Tertullian’s works, we set about preparing an index of subjects, and had gathered from various quarters and brought together the indexes of Pamelius, Rigaltius, Priorius, and Semler, we were extraordinarily dismayed to discover that virtually the same index—with scarcely an exception for that of Pamelius—had been passed carelessly from hand to hand, teeming with the same errors, gaping with the same omissions, and suffering from the same negligence. Indeed, as usually happens, a bad example led to still worse results. Hence, if there was anything of good quality in Pamelius’s index—and I would not wish to deny that there was—Rigaltius, in his customary manner, removed it as far as he could; and, as far as he was able, whether by surreptitiously omitting the text or by presenting it otherwise, he sprinkled over it the foul-smelling itch of a Calvinist in hiding. Then Priorius, otherwise a worthy man, rashly thrust that work of Rigaltius into his excellent edition. But far worse was the magnificent Semler, as his flattering associates call him: for just as he returned to the unpolished text of the first edition, disregarding three centuries of careful critical revisions, so too he seems merely to have chewed over again Heraldus’s index, crude and undigested though it was.

Among many points, the following may be noted as arranged differently or, unless I am mistaken, more correctly:

1. The editors repeatedly disrupted the alphabetical order of the letters, which is so necessary in a little work of this kind.

2. They neglected what I might call the grammatical order of the subject matter with such blindness that incongruous passages (*περικοπάς*, “extracts” or “entries”) are found everywhere; for example: “The Germans are permitted to cross the frontiers,” whereas it should read: “they are not permitted”; “Marcion teaches that the Christ who had never been foretold did not come,” whereas, on the contrary, it should read: “that Christ came”; “God the Father, invisible, becomes visible in the Son through his works—[Col. 1510] indeed, through the Law.” Elsewhere they have turned the sense completely upside down, not only by changing affirmations into negations or negations into affirmations, but by introducing an entirely new proposition. Tertullian says: “It [patience] advances even the vain disciplines of the world to praise and glory.” Semler, more correctly, in his index: “The vain disciplines of the world advance to the praise and glory of God,” etc.

3. These German editors reached such a degree of carelessness that, if an erroneous page reference had crept into the preceding indexes, they adopted the same error wholesale, although they were using an entirely different pagination. Thus they did not preserve even numerical order;

4. Much less, therefore, did they preserve logical order: for either individual words and related topics are brought forward indiscriminately in groups, or matters differing as widely as heaven and earth are joined together. We have endeavored above all to restore this philosophical connection among the subjects.

5. They very often disregarded the chronological order, obvious to everyone, even in the most familiar matters. Hence the hero of Larissa becomes Hercules; John the Baptist is treated indiscriminately together with John the Evangelist.

6. Nothing, however, is more wantonly ruined—and nothing deserved to be reviewed more accurately—than the dogmatic arrangement of the subjects and the sequence of Catholic teaching. Thus they would by no means permit the words “The keys were given to Peter” to be followed by this excessively Roman statement: “Through him they were given to the Church.” Hence there is not the slightest trace of the sacrament of Confirmation. Hence, too, innumerable propositions of some importance are missing, which we considered it a matter of the highest religious duty to cite carefully.

All points of Tertullian’s teaching, however, whether true or erroneous, are carefully indicated. There are added, moreover, to complete the whole, proverbial maxims and the immense wealth of material found in the excellent work of Dom Nicolas Le Nourry. It is therefore evident that this new recension of our index surpasses the others because it confronts the aforesaid blemishes without sparing any of them, because our arrangement is far richer, and because, above all, we have collected innumerable new matters required by Catholic dogmatic theology.

[Col. 1509] The first numerical reference, written in Roman numerals, indicates the volume; the second, written in Arabic numerals, indicates the column; and the letter indicates the portion of the column falling under that letter.

Nothing will run its course without rivalry, because nothing will be without an adversary, II, 277 A. All rival things enter into competition, II, 143 A. What rivalry with a divine and with a human thing is, I, 536 A. Apart from the devil and his angels, there will be no other rival of God, I, 1312 B.

How undeservedly AENEAS was called pious and a god, I, 599 A. He betrayed or abandoned his fatherland, I, 598 B. A coward, he did not appear after the battle at Laurentum, I, 599 A.

AENESIDEMUS upholds the unity of the soul, II, 669 A. His opinion on the soul’s substance, II, 660 B.

THE AEONS of the Valentinians, II, 47 A, 68 A, etc.; of the Ophites, II, 64.

THE EQUANIMITY of Christians, I, 511 ff. The wondrous faithfulness of equanimity, I, 1254 A. Human affectation is the stupor of a doglike equanimity, I, 1251 B.

THE MORE SACRED TREASURY, I, 446 A.

The necessities of all life depend upon BRONZE and iron, I, 1310 A.

AESCHINES, a heretic, and those who are *kata Aischinēn* (κατὰ Αἰσχίνην), “according to Aeschines,” II, 72 A.

ANSCHARIA, goddess of the people of Asculum, I, 621 A.

AESCULAPIUS, son of Apollo and Coronis, or Phoronis, or Arsinoë, born of an uncertain father, I, 352 A. Revealer of medicines, I, 413 A; II, 88 B. He was the first to investigate remedies, II, 87 B. Because of his medical practice and greed, he was struck by Jupiter with a thunderbolt, I, 352 A. The Athenians worshiped Aesculapius and his mother, I, 605 D. His priests wore the cloak, II, 1031 A, and whitened sandals, ibid. They ministered standing, I, 612 B. Socrates commanded that a cock be offered to him, II, 648 A. If Aesculapius is questioned by Christians, he will confess that he is a demon, I, 413 B. Aesculapius supplies life to Socordius, Denatius, and Asclepiodotus, who were otherwise to die on another day, I, 413 A.

AESOP’S jackdaw, II, 562 B.

AESOP the actor furnished a banquet from costly birds, II, 1049 A.

SUMMER, a season naturally fraught with danger, II, 122 A. It dissolves souls, II, 732 B. Summer crops and winter crops depend upon the rains, I, 487 A.

AGES operate through bodies, II, 746 B. The five ages of a human being: infancy, childhood, adolescence, youth, and old age, II, 746 C. The duties appropriate to each age, ibid. So trustworthy is age that it cannot be concealed even by dress, II, 906 B. The authority of age, II, 905 B. The forwardness of an age that owes modesty is to be chastised, II, 203 A. God requires honor for greater age, and requires it especially from the younger, II, 417 A.

A definition of ETERNITY, II, 201 A. What its credential is, ibid. The condition of eternity is nothing other than always to have existed and always to be going to exist, by the prerogative of having neither beginning nor end, ibid. It cannot admit diminution or subjection, II, 203 B, 207 A, 689 A. Eternity has no time, for it is itself all time, II, 255 A, B. It is without age, ibid. With God, eternity itself governs the uniform condition of times, II, 326 B. God heals eternal things by means of momentary ones, II, 132 B. Nothing is eternal except after the resurrection, II, 880 A. Enoch, a candidate for eternity, II, 601 B.

AETHALIDES and Hermotimus had fallen upon a bean among their common provisions, II, 702 A.

AFFERENDA, a goddess, I, 601 A.

The BREATH is less than the spirit; and although it issues from the spirit, like a little breeze from it, it is nevertheless not the spirit, II, 294 C. The Greek Scripture calls the breath “soul,” not “spirit,” ibid. God’s breath is nothing other than a vapor of the spirit, II, 696 A. The soul is God’s breath, II, 652 A, 696 A, 804 A.

The Phoenicians occupied AFRICA, II, 700 A, 1035 B. The greater part of Africa was wrested from the Atlantic Ocean, I, 481 A, 577.

THE AFRICANS’ goddess Caelestis, I, 419 A.

AGAPE, or love, the Christians’ supper, I, 474 A, 623 A. How they conducted themselves at this banquet, I, 477 A. *Agape* was called the sacred Eucharist, I, 1210 A.

Our MASTER OF THE CONTEST (*agonothetes*) is the living God, I, 624 A, B.

AJAX saw Ulysses among the cattle, II, 675 C.

ALBANA, a goddess, I, 600 C.

ALBARIUS, a reader, I, 670 A.

[Col. 1513] Supporters of ALBINUS and the Albinian faction, I, 457 ff. The pagans alone were guilty in his cause, I, 699 B.

ALBINUS’S opinion concerning souls, II, 697 A, B.

ALBURNUS, a god, I, 290 A. Discovered by Metellus, II, 266 C.

CURIUS’S GAMBLING, II, 1049 A.

ALCINOUS’S orchard, II, 1036 A.

ALEXANDER, a Valentinian heretic, II, 780 B ff.

The loftiness of ALEXANDER THE GREAT, I, 337 A. Inferior only in glory, II, 1045 A. After conquering Asia and the other regions, he never possessed them in their entirety, II, 611 B. He who had conquered the Median nation was conquered by Median clothing, II, 1045 A. The water of Nonacris in Arcadia killed him, II, 714 B. He reigned for twelve years, II, 614 A.

God approved ALLEGORY, II, 487 C. Allegorical form is not present in every prophetic utterance, II, 822 B. See PROPHETS.

The more diligent customarily added ALLELUIA to their prayers, I, 1194 A. Likewise in the Psalms, ibid.

God everywhere forbids MARRIAGES WITH FOREIGNERS, II, 487 A. The foreign peoples were conquered by the Maccabees, II, 606 C.

THE GREEK ALPHABET providing an occasion for a new heresy, II, 70 A.

The coldness of the air in THE ALPS, II, 692 B.

FUNERAL-PYRE ALTARS, II, 1041 B.

SHEEP OF ALTINUM, II, 1039 A.

Who the ALVEI are, I, 322 A.

Those to whom all things are BITTER, II, 675 C.

THE AMAZONS, I, 308 A. Their kingdom is older than the Roman kingdom, I, 432 A.

What AMBITION is, I, 1314 A. What the powers of ambition are, I, 1314 B. There is no renunciation of ambition in poverty, II, 282 A. To what hardships and insults the ambitious subject themselves in order to attain honors, I, 1246 B ff.

MADNESS, a spiritual force, since prophecy consists in it, II, 684 B.

To love FRIENDS belongs to everyone, but to love enemies belongs only to Christians, I, 698 D.

AMMON, rich in sheep, II, 1038 B.

The oracle of AMPHIARAUS at Oropus, II, 730 A.

The oracle of AMPHILOCHUS at Mallus, II, 730 A.

At the entrance to THE AMPHITHEATER many kinds of food were bought, I, 493 A.

ANACHARSIS, a philosopher, did not exchange philosophy for the kingdom of Scythia, II, 1045 B. He mocked those ignorant of music, I, 265 A.

THE ISLAND OF ANAPHE, I, 480 A.

ANATOMY known to the ancients, II, 662 A, 692 A.

ANAXAGORAS, together with Xenophanes, calls exhaustion sleep, II, 721 B. His confused opinion concerning the soul, II, 666 A. He denied a deposit to enemies, I, 512 A.

A saying of ANAXARCHUS when he was being pounded with a pestle for barley broth, I, 532 A.

ANAXIMANDER believes there are many worlds, II, 1032 B. He declared all the heavenly bodies and the air to be god, II, 260.

ANAXIMENES’ opinion concerning the substance of the soul, II, 660 B.

ANCHARIA, goddess of the people of Asculum, I, 421 A.

ANDREAS, a physician, II, 670 A.

ANGELS are spiritual substances, I, 405 A. They are nevertheless bodies, but of their own kind, II, 765 A. Whether they consist of material spirit, II, 294 B. We believe angels to be divine functionaries, II, 713 A. God made the angels in his paradise in the second formation of the form of living beings, II, 297 A. They are endowed with free choice, I, 1306. All the angels look down from heaven and take note of individuals, II, 658 A. They know what is done everywhere as easily as they announce it, I, 407 A. In an instant they are everywhere, ibid. The Holy Spirit calls “angels” those whom God appointed ministers of his power, II, 623 A. How Christ is the Angel of Great Counsel, II, 778 A, B. An angel attending prayer, I, 1174 A. The angel of Baptism, I, 1206 A. An angel intervenes in the waters, I, 1205 ff. The Apelleians taught that some renowned angel created the world, II, 769 A. Angels were at times as though human beings, II, 885 A. Christians prayed with reference to the angels’ rejoicing, I, 1159 ff. Angels transformed into human corporeality, II, 757 C. The reason for angels’ assumption of bodies, II, 764 A. It is a property of angelic power to take a body for itself from no material, II, 765. The angels’ flesh was not imaginary, but of true and solid human substance, II, 333 A, B. They did not bear flesh of their own, since by nature they were spiritual substances, II, 764 C. Abraham washed the angels’ feet, II, 757 B. In what substance they appeared, II, 333 A. The name “angels” acknowledged by poets and philosophers, I, 405 A. Plato did not deny their existence, ibid. Apostate angels, I, 405 A. Their prince is Satan, ibid. Angels who deserted God, lovers of women, betrayers of astrology, II, 671 B. We read that they fell from God and heaven because of their desire for women, II, 899 A. They were ensnared by the daughters of men, II, 319 A. Demons, the more corrupt offspring of the fallen [Col. 1514] angels, I, 405 A. By abusing freedom of choice, angels fell into sins, I, 1306. After the fevered moments of their lusts, the angels sighed for heaven, I, 1306 A. No restoration is promised to the fallen angels, II, 777 C. Christ received no command from the Father concerning the salvation of angels, ibid. Satan, the angel of malice, I, 613 A. Whether the evil angel of perdition was impatient, I, 1257 A. An angel seduced the human being, II, 294 B. An angel of deception in the virgin Philumena, II, 18 B. An angel beat the bare neck of a certain Montanist sister in a dream, II, 912 B. The deserting angels disclosed the operations of metals, revealed the properties of herbs, divulged the powers of incantations, and marked out every form of occult inquiry, even the interpretation of the stars, I, 459 A, 1306 A. How the wicked angels rewarded the beauty of women, the cause of their fall, I, 1306 C. Christians renounce the evil angels when receiving Baptism, I, 1306 ff. They will judge angels, ibid. See DEMONS; DEVIL.

Definition of the SOUL, II, 686 A. It is a simple substance, ibid. Incorporeal, II, 652 A, 654 A, B. It is spirit, just as day itself is light, II, 664 A. It is rational, II, 295 B. The soul is free and possesses its own choice, II, 295 B, 686 A. Rational, capable of knowledge and understanding, II, 295 B. Understanding is always present in it, II, 680 B. If the soul is diminished, it perishes, II, 722 A. Whether soul and spirit are one, II, 664 A. The soul is God’s shadow, the breath of his spirit, the work of his mouth, II, 805 A. It descends from God, I, 377 A. The soul comes from God’s breath, II, 652 A, 686 A, 696 A, 804 A. It is the image of God, II, 295. For the mind has the same movements and sensations as God, though they are not of the same character as God’s, II, 304 A. The soul’s substance, which it drew from God himself, corresponds to the form of God, II, 290 B. According to several philosophers, the soul is divine and eternal, I, 610 A. The soul was born and made by its constitution at the beginning, II, 652 B. “Soul” is the name of its own substance, II, 654 A. The soul’s Greek name, *psychē* (ψυχή), means “cold,” II, 692 B, 696 A. The soul has its own proper designation and does not need the body’s common designation, II, 510 B. The whole account is owed to the soul, in whose name mention of the whole human being is inscribed, II, 667 B. The soul is the whole of what we are, II, 775 A. The soul does not fall even in name, because it does not collapse in condition, II, 819 B. Every soul belongs to one kind, II, 720 B, 690 B, C. In soul we are all equal, though not in training, I, 682 B. On the soul’s resemblance in parents, II, 653 B, 693 A. The transmission of soul and flesh from Adam in the woman, II, 713 A, 804 A. Whether two souls come together into one, II, 693 A. The soul is frequently endowed with foreknowledge, II, 295 B. Many proofs have established the soul’s power of divination, II, 689 C. The soul is invisible, II, 658 B. Why, ibid. The soul’s body is visible only to the spirit, II, 658 B. The immortality of the soul is known by nature among many, II, 798 B, C. “Every soul is immortal,” Plato’s declaration, II, 795 C. But mortal in Epicurus’s opinion, I, 610 A. The soul can be overshadowed, but cannot be extinguished, II, 720 B. The soul’s immortality is asserted by many arguments, II, 613 B, 668 A, B. The soul’s consciousness of God from the beginning is an endowment, II, 257 C. It matters little whether the soul’s consciousness was formed by God or by the writings of God, I, 617 B. How the soul’s quality is to be interpreted, II, 294 C. The Valentinians distinguish souls by a twofold property, II, 583 B. The soul is always in motion and active, II, 722 A. It is always busy and active by the perpetuity of its motion, which is a characteristic of Divinity, II, 725 B. The soul moves the body, and its exertions appear externally, II, 654 B. Whether there is in the soul a supreme vital and cognitive faculty, which they call the *hēgemonikon* (ἡγεμονικόν), “ruling faculty,” II, 670 A. Its qualities are comprehended only by intellectual senses, II, 654 B, C. The soul’s senses, II, 654 C. The soul’s sinful thoughts are customarily imputed even without their execution, II, 719 B. Tertullian assigns a form to the soul, while Plato denies it, II, 659 A. The soul’s sentient nature, II, 775 A. Plato divides the soul in two, into the rational and irrational, II, 668 B, 672 A. Zeno divides it into three parts, or even six; Seranus into seven, Chrysippus into eight, Apollophanes into nine, certain Stoics into ten, and Posidonius into two more than that, ibid. How the soul remembers dreams, II, 726 A. It does not sleep with the body, II, 722 A, 725 A, 819 B. The human soul is naturally Christian, I, 377 A. In what sense, I, 378 B, 610 B. The soul is prior to the written word, II, 616 B. Prior to prophecy, II, 257 C. Whether it was created before the body, II, 712 B, 858 B. The soul is sown in the human being himself, and from the beginning there is one seed, just as there is also one seed of the flesh for the propagation of the entire race, II, 712 A. A human being’s soul is propagated like a shoot from its rootstock in Adam, [Col. 1515] II, 682 A. The soul is sown in the womb together with the flesh, II, 695 A. Together with it, it also receives its sex, II, 712 A. On the soul’s conception, against those who introduce it after the body’s birth, II, 858; as Plato held, II, 691 A, and Hicesius, namely from the impact of cold air, II, 692 B. The soul is uniform in seed, multiform in offspring, II, 683 A. The soul’s form, II, 659 A. Its shape is human in every respect, II, 660 A. The soul, fashioned and conformed to the body from the beginning in Adam, produces the seed both of the whole substance and of this condition, II, 661 B. Where the soul’s seat is, II, 651 B, 671 ff., 814 A. The age of the soul, II, 746 ff. All the soul’s natural properties, as essential properties of it, are present within it and develop together with it, II, 682 A. The soul’s growth is not substantial but developmental, II, 715 A. The soul unfolds with all its equipment, in both understanding and sense, II, 682 A, 715 C. At whatever age the soul departs, it remains at that age until the last day, II, 747 A. God inserted the soul and mingled it with the flesh in so complete a union that it may be uncertain whether the flesh carries the soul about, or the soul the flesh, II, 805 A. Dumb and irrational souls recognize in due time the remedies divinely assigned to them, I, 1248 A. Some philosophers say that the soul, being incorporeal, is nourished by incorporeal things, namely the pursuits of wisdom, II, 656 A. It is also nourished by corporeal things, II, 655 A. And by the arts, II, 956 A. The flesh is the soul’s house, and the soul the flesh’s tenant, II, 717 A. All the soul’s living belongs to the flesh, II, 805 B. The flesh is the organ of all the soul’s thought, II, 814 A. The soul is never without the flesh as long as it is in the flesh, II, 814 A. It does nothing without that without which it does not exist, ibid. Whatever is done in the heart is done by the soul in the flesh, with the flesh, and through the flesh, II, 813 C. The soul acts and impels in all things; the flesh’s part is obedience, II, 814 A. There are certain acts of the soul without participation of the body, II, 750 B ff. For their completion, however, it awaits the agency of the flesh, II, 817 A. See BODY. The soul has a corporeality of its own, II, 182 B, C, 817 A. The soul’s corporeality is evident from the Gospel, II, 656 B. It has a body; it has members, II, 817 A. Whether it is therefore fleshly, II, 773 B, C. The soul’s body is of its own quality, as is the spirit, II, 510 B. The soul is a body, as shown by its participation in corporeal sufferings, II, 653 C. The soul cannot be called an animate or inanimate body, II, 654 A. The soul is nothing if it is not a body, II, 657 A. If it had no body, the soul’s form could not receive the body’s image, II, 657 A. The soul possesses shape, boundary, length, breadth, and height, II, 659 A. The soul is corporeal, possessing its own kind of substantial solidity, II, 816 C. Because of the very subtlety of its fineness, belief in the soul’s corporeality is endangered, II, 661 A. Whether the soul’s storehouse is the coldness of the air, II, 692 B. The soul’s color is airy and luminous, II, 660 A. One writer argues that the soul is an animate body; why, II, 872 C. Sense is the soul of the soul, II, 775 A. The human soul can in no way be transferred into beasts, II, 703 A. The soul should rule the flesh, as being nearer to God, II, 805 B. God always addresses, summons, and calls upon the soul, II, 668 A. The source of the soul’s natural fear of God, I, 612 A. No soul is without guilt, because none is without a seed of good, II, 720 B. Evil in the soul arises from the defect of its origin and from the advent of a wicked spirit, II, 720 A. Whether the soul sinned in the human being, and whether the corruption of a portion can be referred back to the original whole, II, 294 C. The soul sinned through free choice, II, 296 A. It could sin; it ought not to have sinned, ibid. Whether Christ came for the sake of our soul alone, II, 667 B. Every soul is reckoned in Adam until it is reckoned anew in Christ, and remains unclean until it is so reckoned anew, II, 719 A. In this world we carry both the soul and the body itself exposed to every injury, I, 1262 A. The soul’s struggles, fasts, and dry foods, II, 806 A. The soul is sanctified not by washing but by purification, II, 865 A. The soul is capable of suffering, II, 666 B. It can suffer nothing without stable matter, that is, flesh, I, 253 A. Even in this life, while the body remains unharmed, the soul alone is tormented, II, 750 A. Likewise, when the body is afflicted, the soul secretly seeks joy for itself, ibid. In the underworld it knows how to grieve, be tormented, and rejoice without the flesh, II, 656 B, 751 A. The example of Lazarus proves this, II, 817 A. The soul brings ruin upon the body when it is breathed out, II, 819 B. On the state of the soul after this life, II, 738 B, 743 A. The philosophers’ various opinions concerning the soul’s place of reception, II, 739 A, B. Every soul is held in the underworld until the day of the Lord, II, 745 A, B. Only the souls of martyrs dwell immediately after death in paradise with God, II, 856 A. The souls of the righteous are received into Abraham’s bosom until the resurrection, II, 444 ff. Whether wicked souls live as exiles in the underworld, II, 747 A, B. Whether souls suffer anything in the underworld, II, 749 C. The soul first tastes judgment, [Col. 1516] because it first introduced the offense, II, 814 C, 818 A. Without waiting for the flesh, the soul is refreshed just as it is punished, II, 751 A, B. The souls of the dead await the day of judgment and, according to their merits, are destined either for torment or for refreshment, both everlasting, I, 613 B. It was formerly believed that the souls of the dead could be appeased with human blood, I, 644 C. On the souls of infants who die at the fountains of their mothers’ breasts, II, 746 B. Whether certain souls cling to bodies after death, II, 736 ff. Plato teaches that souls return into a body, II, 697 A.

ANIMALS born of earth and born of water, II, 299 B. Not all animals live and breathe, II, 662 A. The supreme Craftsman enhanced the smallest animals with special abilities or powers, II, 261 B. Knowledge of natural things never fails in animals, II, 688 B. The Creator’s greatness in animals, II, 261 A. See BEASTS. Nothing animate is without sense; nothing sentient is without a soul, II, 775 A.

The MIND, or understanding, *nous* (νοῦς) among the Jews, is nothing other than the soul’s innate and implanted impulsion, etc., II, 666 A. The mind is so conjoined with the soul, not as another substance but as a function of the substance, II, 667 A. It is the soul’s instrument, not its protection, II, 668 A. The mind is sentient, not merely intellectual, II, 679 A. The mind hears; the mind sees, II, 677 B. The ruling mind readily shares with the spirit what has been brought into its dwelling, I, 1269 B. The mind carries the whole human being about and transfers him wherever it wishes, I, 623 B. Every good of the mind is either innate, taught, or compelled, II, 980 B. Things that sharpen or dull the mind, II, 683 B, C.

ANNA, Samuel’s mother, gave glory to God through the Spirit, II, 389 A.

THE BETROTHAL RING, I, 302 A. It was gold, ibid. The wedding ring, I, 685 A. Rings were made from iron, I, 1310 A. Summer rings were lighter, winter rings heavier, I, 304 C. After the disaster at Cannae, the Romans’ rings were measured by the bushel, I, 485 A.

YEARS, months, and days are marked by the Creator’s suns, moons, and stars, II, 483 A.

ANTELII, demons presiding over doorways, I, 684 A; II, 97 B.

A ship’s YARDARMS are like the arms of a cross, II, 346 A, 626 C.

Who the CANNIBALS are, I, 321 A, 323 A.

ANTIPODES, I, 370 A.

ANTICHRIST, the man of transgression, the son of perdition, II, 829 A. He was believed already to be near, II, 117 A. The resurrection will take place after Antichrist’s eradication, II, 385 A. Marcion was Antichrist, II, 331 C. All who deny that Christ came in the flesh are antichrists, II, 46 B. Likewise, those who do not believe Jesus to be the Son of God, ibid. All who rebel against Christ are antichrists, II, 16 B.

ANTINOUS, a god, I, 600 B; II, 266 C. Unhappy Antinous, II, 97 A.

ANTIPHON, an authority, II, 720 A.

THE ANTIPODES mentioned, I, 570 A.

ANTIQUITY regarded many authors even as gods, II, 649 A. Those who are always praising antiquity while living each day by novelty are rebuked, I, 305 A, 572 B, C. Christ, the illuminator of antiquity, II, 461 A.

MARCION’S ANTITHESES, II, 361 A, B.

ANTONINUS PIUS enacted no law against the Christians, I, 297 A. See CARACALLA. Marcion and Apelles lived during the reign of Antoninus, II, 42 A.

ANTONY’S drunkenness, II, 1049 A.

ANUBIS, a god, I, 597 A. *Anubis the Adulterer*, a comedy, I, 358 A.

Physicians used the RING-KNIFE, II, 692 A.

The filleted wreaths of ANYTUS, Socrates’ accuser, II, 647 B.

AORI, II, 747 B.

THE APATURIA, rites of Father Liber, I, 474 A.

APELLES, Marcion’s disciple, II, 42 B. From disciple to corrector, II, 400 C. And afterward a deserter from Marcion himself, II, 71 A, 754 C. A prohibitor of marriage, II, 46 A. Deserting Marcionite continence, he fell into relations with a woman, II, 42 B. And he stumbled upon the virgin Philumena, II, 18 B, 43 A, 71 C. He followed her as a prophetess, II, 71 C. He was separated from Marcion because of incontinence, II, 71 A, 763 A. The heresy of Apelles, II, 71, 335 B. Induced by Philumena’s signs and deceptions, he introduced a new heresy, II, 18 C. He affirms that some unspecified angel is the Creator, II, 47 A, B. He makes the God of the Law and of Israel a fiery being, II, 47 A, 686 B, 801 A. His error concerning souls, II, 686 B. And concerning the human body, II, 801 A. He posits male and female souls before bodies, II, 712 B. He undermines the resurrection of the flesh, II, 46 A. Apelles wrote the *Revelations* (*Phaneroseis*), II, 43 A, 71 C. And the books [Col. 1517] that he entitled *Syllogisms*, II, 71 C.

BOAR. See ROUGH.

APICIUS, II, 971 B. A celebrated cook, I, 282 A. He gave his name to cooks, ibid. Apician seasonings, II, 706. Apician gourmands, II, 1049 A.

APION, I, 387 A. Josephus wrote against him, I, 378 A. See APPION.

APIS, the Egyptians’ god, II, 261 B. His edifices, ibid.

John’s APOCALYPSE unfolds the order of times, II, 830 A. Marcion rejects it, II, 366 C.

APOCRYPHAL writings condemned by their own confession, II, 649 B.

APOLLO, smooth-faced and beardless, I, 574 B. He pastured the flocks of King Admetus, I, 352 A. We read that among the Greeks Apollo was called *thyraion* (θυραῖον), “of the doorway” [the source’s πυραῖον is an evident textual corruption], I, 684 A; II, 97 B. Apollo’s ambiguous and deceptive oracles, I, 408 ff. He was worshiped at Delphi because he killed the dragon, II, 85 B. His priests do not marry, I, 1284 A. He did not defend Delphi from the hand of Pyrrhus, I, 607 B. The Apollinarian games, I, 638 A, 1205 A.

APOSTATES did not associate with the other Christians, I, 565 B, C. Their crime, ibid.

The pillars of the APOSTOLATE—what they are, II, 268 B, 364 C.

Who the APOSTOLICS are, II, 363 B. They handed down teachings contrary to the Apostles, II, 45 A. Apostolic churches, II, 33 B.

An APOSTLE must preach publicly, II, 755 B. The Apostles did not preach doctrines differing from one another, II, 37 A. They entrusted some things openly to everyone, others secretly to a few, II, 37 B. They discussed certain things separately among their intimates, II, 38 C. We have the Lord’s Apostles as our authorities; they themselves did not choose to introduce anything according to their own judgment, but faithfully assigned to the nations the teaching received from Christ, II, 18 B. How the Apostles’ tradition is to be discerned, II, 270 B, 366 C. They proclaimed no other Christ than the Christ of the God whom Christ preached, II, 322 C. The Apostle was accustomed to offer counsel when he had no commandment from the Lord, and to say certain things on his own authority; but he too possessed the Spirit of God, II, 81 C. Among the Israelites the Apostles unsealed the Old Testament and authenticated the New, II, 849 B. That which is not condemned by the Apostles, but indeed defended by them, will be an indication of its genuineness, II, 48 B. The Apostles founded churches by preaching, both orally and through letters, II, 33 A. While writing to some, the Apostle writes to all, II, 512 B. The Apostles’ authentic letters were publicly read in the churches, II, 49 A. The Apostles’ chairs, II, 49 A. Apostles, or “those sent,” II, 32 A. Why Christ chose only twelve, II, 387 A. Seventy were enrolled in addition to the twelve, II, 418 C. The Apostles took women with them, not wives, II, 940 A. Of them, Peter alone had married, II, 939 C. Whether they were baptized, I, 1213 A. After receiving the promised power of the Holy Spirit for mighty works and utterance, the Apostles first scattered the seed of Christ’s teaching throughout Judaea and then throughout the world, II, 32 A, B, 920 A. They founded churches in every city, ibid. Some say that the Spirit was in the Apostles, but not the Paraclete, II, 72 A, 920 A. Why they were reproved by Paul, II, 364 C. The Apostles, fountains and rivers destined to irrigate the world of the nations, II, 387 B. Like jewels, destined to illuminate the Church’s sacred garment, which Christ put on, ibid. The stones of the Jordan, solid in faith; the fountains of Elim, ibid.

APOTHEOSIS, a solemn procession, I, 451 B.

APPION, a historian, I, 387 B. See APION.

Praises of WATER, I, 1202 ff. Certain marvelous kinds of water, II, 734 C. Water, more pleasing than the other elements, I, 1202 A. God caused water to obey him in his own sacraments, I, 1203 A. The entire nature of waters was established by God, I, 1205 A. The first waters were commanded to bring forth living beings, I, 1202 B. From the waters came swimming and flying creatures, II, 228 B. The work of fashioning the human being himself was completed with the waters participating, I, 1202 B. They were figures of Baptism, I, 1203 A. That water is made medicinal by religion—
[Beginning of entry missing] … pagans believed, I, 1205 A. Their waters are widowed, I, 1204 B. The devil broods over them in streams, springs, and so forth, imitating the things of God, I, 1205 B. Pagans everywhere purified villas, houses, temples, and entire cities by sprinkling water carried around them, I, 1204 B, sq. In the Apollinarian and Eleusinian games they immersed themselves in water for regeneration and immunity from punishment for their perjuries, I, 1205 A. Murderers did the same, ibid. Water carried in a sieve, I, 409 A. Water is the seat of the divine Spirit, I, 1202 A. The Spirit sanctifying the waters, I, 1204 A. Sanctified by the Holy One, the nature of the waters itself began to sanctify, I, 1204 A. All waters, by virtue of the ancient prerogative of their origin, receive the sacrament of sanctification [Col. 1518] when God is invoked, ibid. Christ sanctified the waters in his baptism, II, 615 B. At Cana of Galilee he inaugurated the first beginnings of his power with water, I, 1210 B. Christ is never without water, I, 1210 A. How this is so, ibid. We little fishes, according to our Fish (ἰχθύν, ichthyn), Jesus Christ, are born in water, I, 1198 A. See BAPTISM. To drink the water of baptism sweetened by the wood of Christ’s Passion, II, 79 A. In foreign kingdoms, to be baptized unto another god, II, 274 A. Water for washing the hands after supper, I, 477 A. To offer water for the feet of the saints, I, 1295 A. Punishment by water is a more cruel kind of death, I, 318 A.

**WATER-BEARERS (AQUARIOLI),** I, 495 A.

**EAGLES’** eyes can endure the sun, II, 658 B. By the boldness of their young birds’ pupils they judge the nobility of their offspring, ibid.

**AQUILICIUM,** sacrificed to Jupiter, I, 487 A.

**ALTARS** of the gods, I, 347 sq. The titles of those to whom they were dedicated were inscribed upon the altars, ibid. Those who breathe upon the altars—who they are, I, 413 A, B. From the sacrificial odor they conceive the divine presence; they strive after it by belching and preface it by panting, ibid. Acts of prostitution were conducted among the very altars of the pagans, I, 363 A. See TEMPLE.

**ARABIAN** frankincense, II, 90 B. Frankincense was brought out of Arabia, I, 493 A. Tears of the Arabian tree, I, 444 A. Who the gods of the Arabs were, I, 418 sq. Arabian women cover not only the head but the entire face so completely that, leaving one eye uncovered, they are content to enjoy half the light rather than expose the whole face, II, 912 B.

**THE WORKSHOP OF ARACHNE,** II, 1039 A.

**SPIDERS’** webs, II, 261 B.

**ARATUS** depicted various monsters among the constellations, II, 142 A.

**THE FREE POWER OF CHOICE,** II, 685 A. It is natural and mutable, ibid. The image and likeness of God had to be constituted with freedom of choice and power of its own, II, 291 B. Freedom and power of choice, exercised voluntarily by a human being, make the good his own, II, 291 C, sq. Freedom of choice was granted to humanity in either direction, II, 292 A, B. Even though we know what God wills and what he does not will, we nevertheless possess the will and choice to select either one, II, 916 A. What lies within our choice ought not to be referred to the will of God, ibid.

**TREES** live but do not understand, according to Aristotle, II, 680 C. How they grow, II, 890 A. Trees, even while still trunks and shoots, possess the power of a soul, II, 681 A. Trees of wisdom and knowledge, II, 681 C. Trees planted around the temples of the gods, I, 315 A.

**THE ARK,** a figure of the Church, I, 696 A, 1209 A.

**ARCESILAUS** divided the gods into three classes, I, 589 B.

**ἈΡΧΗ (ARCHĒ),** a word that denotes primacy not only of order but also of power, II, 215 A.

**POOR ARCHEMORUS,** II, 97 A.

**ARCHIAS,** leader of the Corinthians, fortified Syracuse, II, 1036 A.

**ARCHIMEDES’** hydraulic mechanism, II, 669 A.

**THE ARCHIVES** of the most ancient nations, I, 387 A. The Roman archives, II, 370 A.

**THE ARCHIGALLUS** offered his own blood as a propitiatory sacrifice for the safety of Marcus Aurelius, who had died six days earlier, I, 425 A.

**ἌΡΧΟΝΤΕΣ (ARCHONTES)** are rulers and magistrates, II, 215 A, 339 B, 620 A.

**ARCHUS,** or **ARGUS,** reigned for one year, II, 614 A.

**THE ARGAEAN MOUNTAINS** of rigid air, II, 692 B.

**THE CRUELTY OF THE ARENA,** I, 467 A.

**SILVER.** See GOLD.

**ARGUIS,** a god, I, 606 A.

**ARIADNE’S** garland of gold and Indian gems, II, 85 A. Ariadne depicted among the constellations, II, 142 A.

**LABERIUS’ RAM,** with backward-curving horns, fleece-covered, and testicle-dragging [probably *testitrahus*; source reads *tetistrahus*], II, 1031 B. The ram, a siege engine, II, 1031 B; invented by the Carthaginians, II, 1032 B.

**DIVINERS (ARIOLI),** or **SOOTHSAYERS (HARIOLI),** are mentioned, I, 495 B.

**ARISTARCHUS,** chief of grammarians, I, 282 A.

**ARISTEAS’** testimony concerning the Greek translation of the Old Testament, I, 380 A.

**NO ONE** among the gods of the pagans was more just than Aristides, I, 336 B.

**ARISTIPPUS,** clad in purple, lives dissolutely beneath an appearance of great dignity, I, 513 A.

**ARISTODEMUS,** an authority, II, 727 B.

**ARISTOPHON,** an authority, II, 727 B.

**ARISTOTLE,** Plato’s friend, II, 682 C. He shamefully flatters Alexander, I, 512 A. He shamefully caused his intimate friend Hermias to be displaced from his position, ibid. Aristotle’s line of argument, II, 651 B. Aristotle on dreams, II, 717 A, 730 A. He calls sleep “a torpor of the heat surrounding the heart,” II, 721 C. Miserable Aristotle, who instituted dialectic! II, 20 A. See DIALECTIC. [Col. 1519]

**THE ARMOR OF CHRIST** and spiritual warfare, II, 517 A.

**ARMENIA,** already Christian, II, 610 B.

**ARRIUS ANTONINUS,** a cruel persecutor of Christians in Asia, I, 704 B.

**NO ART** exists that is not either the mother or a relative of another art, I, 670 B. The soul is nourished by the arts, II, 656 A. The seeds of every art and every age are implanted in us, II, 682 C. Demons inspired artistic talents, I, 1328 A, 643 B, C. There are as many veins of art as there are human desires, I, 670 B. All arts formerly related either to the manufacture or to the worship of idols, I, 668 sqq. The liberal arts are enumerated, II, 1050 A.

**ARTAXERXES** reigned for forty years, II, 614 A.

**ARTEMON,** a writer, II, 729 A.

**ARTISANS:** the Romans summoned them from Etruria, II, 1050 A.

**HARUSPICES,** I, 495 B. Haruspices of both gods and the dead, I, 347 A. They were consulted about the death of the Caesars, I, 459 A. They are compared with magicians and soothsayers, I, 495 A, 642 A.

**ASCENT,** a god, I, 606 A.

**ASCLEPIADES,** the physician, on the ruling faculty in the soul, II, 670 A.

**ASCLEPIADES,** the Cynic, traveled throughout the world riding on a cow and begging, I, 605 B.

**ASCLEPIADOTUS,** restored to life, I, 413 A.

**HASDRUBAL’S** wife threw herself with her sons into the burning of Carthage, I, 584 A. For what reason, ibid.

**THE GREATER PART OF ASIA** was wrested from the Atlantic Sea, I, 481 A, 577. In Asia there is a chasm in the ground, II, 1034 B. The Athenians occupied Asia, II, 700 A. Cyrus submerged and crushed Asia, II, 727 A. Exotic luxuries were transferred from Asia into Libya and Europe, II, 1040 A. The churches of Asia Minor were established by John, II, 366 C. Persecution in Asia, I, 704 B.

**ASINIUS CELER** prepared a dish consisting of a single red mullet, II, 1048 B.

**ASINIUS GALLUS:** how much money he paid for a table, II, 1048 A.

**THE ASS** in Aesop’s well, II, 416 D. Pagans worshiped asses together with Epona and Isis, I, 577 C. The Jews were falsely accused of having worshiped the figure of an ass, I, 364 A. How falsely Christians were accused of having worshiped the head and figure of an ass, I, 364 A. Tacitus provided the occasion for this slander, ibid. With what shamelessness a worthless Jew carried around a ridiculous picture bearing this inscription: “THE GOD OF THE CHRISTIANS, ONOCHOETES,” I, 372 sq., 579 A.

**ASPER** refused to condemn Christians, I, 703 A.

**THE ASP** borrows its venom from the viper, II, 331 C.

**NINUS,** the first king of the Assyrians, II, 1034 B. Another Herod was king, II, 339 C. This kingdom was older than the Roman Empire, I, 432 A. Their gods did not protect it, I, 608 B. Secular histories become accessible from the time of the Assyrians, II, 1035 A.

**ASTARTE,** or **ATAGARTIS,** goddess of Syria, I, 418 A.

**NOTHING IS TO BE ATTRIBUTED TO THE STARS,** I, 268 A.

**ASTROLOGY** was permitted until the Gospel, I, 672 A. Why, ibid. The association between astrology and magic, I, 612 A.

**THE ASTROLOGER** makes stellar conjectures, II, 1050 A. The arts of astrologers, like those of haruspices, augurs, and magicians, were disclosed by the deserting angels and forbidden by God, I, 459 A. Astrologers are censured, I, 268 C, D, 701 sq.; II, 671 B. They consulted demons concerning the future death of the Caesars, I, 459 A. Why ancient astrologers calculated a person’s nativity from the beginning of conception, II, 693 B.

**THE ASTRONOMER** observes the flying course of the stars, II, 1050 A.

**ASTYAGES,** ruler of the Medes, saw his daughter Mandane in a dream, II, 727 A.

**ATAGARTIS.** See ASTARTE.

**ATHAMAS** and **HAGAR** saw beasts in their children, II, 675 C.

**ATHENS,** the eloquent city, II, 651 B. Those keenest in wisdom and speech are born at Athens, II, 683 A. Minerva did not defend Athens against Xerxes, I, 607 B. Numentinus, a god of the Athenians, I, 596 A. See ATTICA. The Athenians occupied Asia, II, 700 A. The cicadas of the Athenians, II, 903 A. The Athenians understood Paul when he spoke about the resurrection of the flesh, II, 850 A.

**CHRISTIANS WERE REGARDED AS ATHEISTS,** I, 327 B, C.

**ATHOS,** son of Heaven and Earth and father of Saturn, I, 601 C.

**THE STRICTER DISCIPLINE OF ATHLETES,** I, 624 B. To what end, ibid.

**THE ATLANTES,** a Libyan people: whether they ever dream, II, 733 C.

**THE ATLANTIC SEA** carried away lands, I, 481 A, 577; II, 1034 A.

**THE ATOMS OF EPICURUS,** II, 703 B.

**THE ATELLAN PERFORMER,** I, 649 B.

**ATTIC IDOLATRY:** what it was, II, 255 C. The Attic mysteries: what they were, I, 474 A. See PALLAS. Attic wisdom will be brought low, I, 473 A. The steadfastness of an Attic courtesan under torture, I, 584 A. See GREEKS.

**ATTIS,** castrated, I, 361 A. [Col. 1520]

**ATYS,** a god from Pessinus represented upon the stage, I, 576 C.

**ONCE THE AUTHOR IS KNOWN,** the examination of any subject becomes clearer, II, 103 B. The disagreement among things is the same as that among their authors, I, 1256 B.

**HEARERS** ought to desire baptism, not presume upon it, I, 1240 A. The first baptism of hearers is unbroken fear, I, 1239 B.

**HOW HEARING IS DECEIVED,** II, 674 B.

**AUFIDIUS LURCO** was the first to corrupt bodies by fattening [reading *sagina* for the apparent OCR error *sagitta*], II, 1048 B.

**AUGUSTUS,** formerly called Julius Octavius, II, 728 A. Organizer of the empire, I, 450 A. While still a very young boy, he was foreseen as emperor in dreams, II, 728 A. He was unwilling even to be called “lord,” I, 450 A. Augustus, the most trustworthy witness of the Lord’s nativity, II, 370 C, 405 A. The census of Augustus throughout the whole world, ibid. In Judaea, through Sentius Saturninus, II, 405 A, B. Augustus reigned for another forty-eight years after Cleopatra, II, 614 sq. He reigned for fifteen years after Christ was born, ibid. All the years of his reign totaled fifty-six, ibid.

**MARCUS AURELIUS** wrote a letter concerning the rain obtained through the Christians, I, 295 A, 703 C. He was a protector of the Christians, I, 295 A. He imposed a still harsher punishment upon the accusers of Christians, I, 295 sq.

**THE FACTIONS AND COLORS** of the charioteers in the circus, I, 641 B.

**GOD REQUIRES THE EARS OF THE HEART** from his hearers, II, 404 A. The delicate skin of the ears exhausts a moneylender’s account-book, I, 1314 B. Pearls hung from the ears of the Parthians, I, 1328 A.

**GOLD AND SILVER:** their origin, I, 1309 A; II, 803 B. Earth made more glorious, though no nobler than iron and bronze, I, 1309 B. Whence the value of gold and silver arises, I, 1310 sq. They are goods not by their intrinsic reality but by their rarity, I, 1328 A. Sinning angels disclosed their materials, ibid. Gold and silver are native and abundant among certain barbarians, I, 1309 A, 1311 A. Pagan literature reports that, among one people, gold itself serves for chains, I, 1328 A. They load even criminals with bonds of gold and silver, II, 1309 A, 1311 A. Gold and silver are the chief materials of worldly adornment, I, 1309 A. They belonged only to persons of distinction, I, 1328 B. In women, no limb is considered light enough to go without gold, I, 304 A.

**AUSES,** son of Nun and successor of Moses, II, 343 A, 622 A. When he is surnamed Jesus, ibid. He was a figure of Christ, II, 622 A, B. See JOSHUA.

**THE AUSPICATOR** at weddings, on the husband’s side, II, 928 B.

**AUTEM (“BUT”),** like a clasp, is a connective particle attached to link the narrative together, II, 221 B.

**AUTUMN,** at other times a tempter of bodily health, drenches souls with the most vinous juices of fruits, II, 732 B.

**THE AVARICE OF THE PAGANS,** who place money before the soul, I, 1261 C.

**BIRDS,** when rising, lift themselves toward heaven, extend the cross of their wings in place of hands, and utter something that seems like a prayer, I, 1196 B.

**AXIONICUS,** a Valentinian heretic, II, 547 A.

**THE AXLE,** the rack that twists the heavens, II, 143 B.

**UNLEAVENED BREAD,** more familiar to the Creator, II, 436 C.

# B

**TOWER OF BABYLON**, exceedingly proud, II, 174 C. Babylon bears the figure of the city of Rome, II, 339 C, 620 B. In what manner, ibid.

**KINGDOM OF THE BABYLONIANS**, older than the Roman, I, 432 A.

**ORGIES OF BACCHUS**, formerly suppressed, I, 304 A, 306 A. The frenzies of the Bacchanalia, in which they did not spare Christians even when dead, I, 461 A. See **LIBER**.

**BALAAM**: the Lord suggested to the prophet what he had not contemplated, I, 456 B.

**TIME FOR THE BATHS**, I, 492 A.

**BAPTISM** is altogether one, according both to the Lord’s Gospel and to the writings of the Apostles, I, 1216 A. In what things the rationale of Baptism may be discerned, I, 1203 A. How great the weight of Baptism is, I, 1222 A. Baptism is the sealing of faith, and this faith is begun and commended by the faith of repentance, I, 1239 A. The sealing of Baptism is, in a certain sense, the garment of faith, I, 1215 A. Without Baptism salvation belongs to no one, I, 1213 A. Whether Baptism is necessary for those for whom faith is sufficient, I, 1214 C. Why it was not prescribed before Christ, I, 1215 A. The water of Baptism is a blessed sacrament, I, 1197 A. In what manner, ibid. How the waters are sanctified in Baptism, I, 1204 A. The Holy Spirit remains over the waters, sanctifying them from himself, ibid. The intervention of angels in Baptism, I, 1204 B, 1206 B. The rite and effects of Baptism, II, 806 A, B. In Baptism there is regeneration, II, 280 A, 862 A. And remission of sins, I, [Col. 1521] 1238 A; II, 280 A. By Baptism filth is washed away, but stains are made white by martyrdom, II, 147 C. In the waters we do not receive the Holy Spirit; rather, having been cleansed in the water, we are prepared under the angel’s agency for the Holy Spirit, I, 1206 B. The spirit is bodily washed in the waters, and the flesh is spiritually cleansed in those same waters, I, 1204 B. The carnal act of Baptism is that we are immersed in water; its spiritual effect, that we are freed from sins, I, 1207 A. We are baptized not so that we may cease sinning, but because we have ceased, since we have already been washed in heart, I, 1239 B. Baptism is a symbol of Christ’s death, I, 1238 B. What it means to be baptized for the dead, II, 495 A, 864 C sq. In Baptism we die through a representation, but in reality we rise again in the flesh, II, 862 B. Baptism is not to be conferred rashly, I, 1220. Whether delaying Baptism is more advantageous, I, 1221 sq. To whom the right to baptize belongs, I, 1218 A. Preaching must precede Baptism, I, 1216 A. As must confession of all preceding sins, I, 1222 C. And repentance, I, 1229 A. Those about to enter Baptism prepared themselves with frequent prayers, fasts, kneelings, and vigils, ibid. Baptism was formerly celebrated at Easter and Pentecost, I, 1222 A. Every time is suitable for Baptism, I, 1222 B. We are baptized not once but three times, at each individual name for each individual person, II, 190 A. We are baptized three times, answering something more than the Lord laid down in the Gospel, II, 79 A. In Baptism, beneath the hand of the presiding minister, we renounce with our own mouth the devil, his pomp, and his angels, I, 635 B; II, 79 A. After emerging from Baptism, they were anointed all over, I, 1206 C. Hands were laid upon them, I, 1207 A. They were refreshed with milk and honey, II, 79 A, 262 A. They received the sacred Eucharist, ibid. And from that day they abstained from the daily bath throughout the whole week, II, 79 A. Why, II, 190 A. Baptism is a new birth, I, 1224 A. By faith, through Baptism, one must live in newness of life, II, 862 B. How temptations after Baptism are to be restrained, I, 1223 sq. A second Baptism, or that of blood through martyrdom, I, 1217 A; II, 135 B. After Baptism there still remains a second resource in *exomologesis*—public confession and penance, I, 1247 B. John’s Baptism did not confer the Holy Spirit or remission of sins, I, 1211 A. It was from God, I, 1211 A; II, 453 A. Yet by commission, not also by power, I, 1211 A. For it was also human, I, 1211 A, 1213 B. And not heavenly, I, 1211 B. The devil practices baptism among his own, I, 1205 A. Marcion reserves Baptism for death or repudiation, II, 382 B. By washing, pagans were initiated into certain sacred rites, I, 1204 B.

**BARALIRIS**, or **BARDIRIS**, **BIRADIRIS**, an Illyrian who, following a dream, ruled from the Molossians as far as Macedonia, II, 728 A.

**BEARD**, reddened by touch, I, 410 A.

**BARBARIAN LANDS** had churches of Greeks, II, 890 B.

**CHILDREN OF THE BARBARIANS** rush into battle, first anointed in the sun, armed with rags, and provisioned with butter, II, 338 A, 618 B. Rumor is sometimes slanderous toward barbarians, II, 733 B. A great power of demons rules in the climate of the barbarians, ibid. The barbarians’ *stropuli* [uncertain term], II, 903 A.

**EPISTLE OF BARNABAS**, received among the Churches, II, 1021 A.

**HERESY OF BASILIDES**: wherein it consists, II, 62 A, B, 796 B. He taught many absurdities, II, 62. Basilides denies that the God of the Jews is God and calls him an angel, ibid. B.

**BAXA AND SOCCUS**, types of footwear, are gilded every day, I, 670 B. See **SHOES**.

**BLESSEDNESS** of the slave whose master insists upon his correction and whom they deem worthy of their anger, I, 1266 B. How hope of blessedness makes people better, I, 529.

**Βέκκος (*Bekkos*)**, what it is, 570 B.

**BELENUS**, god of the Noricans, I, 419 A, 596 A.

**PRIESTS OF BELLONA** were consecrated with blood, I, 321 A. The dark garment of those initiated into this goddess’s rites, and the grim fleece upon their heads, II, 1045 A.

**WAR** is the shearing of the growing human race, II, 700 B.

**NINUS**, offspring of Belus, II, 1035 A.

**DIVINE BLESSING**, I, 1299 A. To receive spiritual blessing through faith, II, 475 B. Who are discharged from office by the sacrament of blessing, II, 1007 C. To be blessed by the gods of the nations is to be cursed by God, I, 693 A. Blessing is the supreme sacrament of discipline and conduct, I, 611 B. A blessing exchanged on the roads is nothing other than a mutual greeting upon meeting, II, 419 B.

**BY DOING GOOD**, no one has sinned, I, 1230 B.

**BENEFICIARIES** (*beneficiati*), II, 118 C.

**QUEEN BERENICE**, II, 688 B, 747 B.

**BEROSSUS THE CHALDAEAN**, I, 387 B.

**BERYL** is not therefore a watery substance merely because it shimmers with a filtered brilliance, II, 660 B.

**BEASTS**, provided and delivered by the Lord for our uses, I, 1255 A. They change their appearance in place of clothing, II, 1036 A. Beasts can change their habits [Col. 1522], but never their natural knowledge, II, 688 B. See **ANIMALS**, **WILD BEASTS**.

**BEAST-FIGHTERS**, I, 317 A. They ate their last meal in public, I, 492 A. At public games they were sacrificed to Jupiter, I, 317 A. The school of beast-fighters bears witness to insults against the emperors, I, 455 A. A certain Jewish beast-fighter, a scoundrel, hired himself out daily to cheat the beasts, I, 579 B.

**POOL OF BETHSAIDA**, a figure of Baptism, I, 1205 C. Until Christ’s coming it served to cure Israel’s infirmities, but after Christ it ceased, II, 637 B, 734 B.

**BIAEOTHONATI**—those who died violent deaths, II, 747 sq.

**THE BIBLE**, translated into the Greek language, I, 380 A. See **ARISTEAS** and **SEPTUAGINT**.

**PRACTICE OF LIBRARIES**, I, 610 B. The libraries of Pisistratus and Ptolemy Philadelphus, I, 379 sq. Ptolemy’s libraries at the Serapeum are displayed together with the Hebrew writings themselves, ibid.

**BLASPHEMY**, which must be avoided altogether, II, 681 B. How and when the blasphemies of the impious are to be avoided, ibid.

**BLASTUS**, a heretic who secretly sought to introduce Judaism, II, 72 B.

**BOEOTIA** had the oracle of Trophonius, II, 730 A, 1039 A.

**BOMBYX**, a kind of little worm, II, 1039 A. Threads of the silkworm, ibid.

**GOODNESS** without reason is not goodness, II, 291 A. Unless goodness is governed by justice so that it is just, it will not be goodness if it is unjust, II, 298 B. The demand for goodness that is not owed magnifies the goodness that is owed, II, 273 A. Works of goodness, II, 287 C. The second degree of goodness is toward strangers; toward neighbors it is the first, II, 397 A. God’s goodness is eternal, II, 287 C. And innate and natural, II, 271. The Creator’s first goodness—what it is, II, 287 B, C. If it is not natural, it is neither eternal nor equal to God, II, 271 C. There are definite rules for examining God’s goodness—which they are, II, 271 A. The Creator’s works bear witness to his goodness, II, 290 A.

**GOOD**, what it is, II, 933 A. The fruit of the knowledge of good and evil, II, 398 A. Good and evil are known by nature, though not by the teaching of God, II, 398 A. The magnitude of certain good things, as also of evil ones, is unbearable, I, 1249 A. Something is not good merely because it is not evil, nor is it therefore not evil merely because it does no harm, I, 1279 A. Nothing unjust is good, II, 298 C. Everything just, however, is good, ibid. Nothing is contrary to good except evil, II, 932 B. Good would have flourished more fully without the breath of evil, II, 210 C. Pagans interpret evil and good according to their own choice and caprice, I, 653 A. Every good belongs to God, I, 1256 A. God dispenses good to each person as he deigns, I, 1250 A. Nothing is so good as the knowledge and enjoyment of God, II, 287 B. Good ought not to be avoided, because it is a sin to refuse good, II, 107 C. Whoever does not fulfill the good is bound by guilt, I, 1233 A. Those who belong to God must pursue the good with their whole mind, I, 1256 A. Good things scandalize no one except an evil mind, II, 892 B. No one is good by nature except God alone, II, 291 B.

**OX**, god of the Egyptians, I, 129 A. Its priests observed continence, II, 928 C.

**ARMS OF WOMEN** are confined by rings of gold, I, 1306 A.

**BRACHMANS**, who they were, II, 490 B.

**THE BRITONS** are enclosed within the circuit of the Ocean, II, 611 B. Regions of the Britons inaccessible to the Romans are subject to Christ, II, 610 C. The British sea furnishes a species of shellfish, I, 1311 A.

**TRUMPET-SHELLS AND SEA-SHELLS** travel into the mountains, II, 1033 B.

**BUSIRIS** and his sepulchral altars, II, 1041 B.

**THE DESTRUCTION OF BYZANTIUM**, I, 702 A. See **CAECILIUS**.

**BYTHOS**, an aeon of Valentinus, II, 68 A, 551 A, 666 A.

# C
CACABACEUS, II, 234 B. CACABULUS of Saturn, I, 344 B. CACTUS, II, 1036 A. A CORPSE (*cadaver*) is so called from falling (*cadendo*), II, 819 B. We say that the body FALLS (*cadere*) to the earth through death, as the fact itself attests, II, 492 A. The CADUCEUS of Mercury, I, 576 C. CAECILIUS CAPELLA, during the Byzantine catastrophe, exclaimed, “Christians, rejoice!” I, 702 A. CAECINNA Severus issued a decree of the Senate that matrons should not appear in public without the *stola*, II, 1044 B. Two kinds of BLINDNESS, I, 327 A. CAECULUS, a god, I, 606 A. CAELESTIS, goddess of the Africans, I, 419 A, 596 A. Beasts were yoked to her, I, 341 A. Penalties imposed by Caesar Augustus upon CELIBATES and the unmarried; [Col. 1523] subsequently repealed, I, 286 ff.

CAESAR escaped in the battle at Philippi, II, 728 B. Why many once observed the Caesars, I, 453 A. Newly elected Caesars—or those seeking election—lavished gifts upon the people, I, 455 A. They would have believed in Christ if they had not been necessary to the age, or if Christians too could have been Caesars, I, 403 A. The Romans called the Caesars gods and mocked them, I, 583 C. Temples, altars, priests, and a sacred couch were established for Caesar beside those of the gods, I, 247 A. Why Christians did not celebrate the festivals of the Caesars, I, 452 A.

The CAIAN heresy, I, 1198 A; II, 65 A. The heresy of the Cainites, II, 46 B.

CAIN, the first murderer and the first fratricide, I, 1258 A. Why God rejected his sacrifice, II, 601 A. How impatiently he endured this rejection, I, 1258 A. He represented the people of Israel and its sacrifices, II, 601 A. The seed of Cain—or rather of Ham—was in the ark, lest the seed of wickedness perish, II, 66 A–B.

CAIUS SEIUS, a good man, except that he was a Christian, I, 280 A.

Public CALAMITIES are the pruning of the human race as it grows luxuriant, II, 700 B. Calamities served as admonition for Christians and punishment for pagans, I, 489 A. To moderate or remove calamities, Christians entreated God day and night, I, 486 ff. Christians were not the cause of public calamities, I, 479 ff., 571 A–B; rather, the pagans were, I, 488 ff. Many calamities occurred before the Christian name had been heard: before Tiberius, I, 480 ff.; and under Hilarianus, I, 701 A. After Christ’s birth they were far fewer than before, I, 486 f. Why God permitted Christians to be afflicted by them, I, 489 A.

SHOES, the peculiar torture belonging to the toga, II, 1046 B. The filthiest protection for the feet, ibid. Unless the Tyrian is shod in gold, she is not sufficiently Greek in fashion, II, 1043 A. The shoes, or sandals, of philosophers were gilded, II, 1043 A–B.

CALIGULA (GAIUS) reigned for three years, eight months, and thirteen days, II, 616 A. He enacted no law against Christians, I, 294 A.

The CUPS of the primitive Church displayed an engraved image of the Good Shepherd, II, 1000 C. How anxiously Christians endured the spilling of anything from the sacred cup onto the ground, II, 80 A.

CALIENDRUM, II, 1044 A.

CALLIMACHUS draped Juno with a vine, II, 85 A–B.

CALLINICUS, an author, I, 535 A.

CALLISTHENES, an author, II, 728 A.

They transform the CAMENAE into waters, II, 366 A.

Memorial CANAE, I, 386 A.

CANDELABRA in Christian assemblies, I, 313 A.

CANDELIFERA, a goddess, I, 600 C.

Candidates of the devil, II, 86 B.

The heat of the DOG DAYS, II, 124 B, 267 A.

The disaster at CANNAE occurred before the Christian name had been heard, I, 485 A. See RING.

CANTABRA were erected upon complete crosses, I, 369 A, 579 A.

Pagans worshipped GELDINGS, I, 365 A.

The SONG of the early Christians, I, 273 A, D; 477 A. See PSALMS.

The CAPHAREAN rocks, notorious for shipwrecks, II, 739 B.

HAIR still giving off an odor was found at Carthage after five hundred years, II, 854 C. Women dyed their hair saffron-yellow, I, 1322 A. The force of cosmetics burns damage into the hair and destruction into the brain, ibid. Old age, the more it strives to be concealed—namely by changing the color of the hair—the more it will be exposed, I, 1322 B. The skill of hairdressers, I, 1323 f. The enormities of sewn and woven hairpieces, I, 1323 A. A delicate neck carries whole forests and islands, I, 1314 B. Let a virgin cover the citadel of her head with the encircling veil of her hair, II, 900 A.

The CAPITOL is censured, I, 427 A, 430 A, 487 A, 573 B. The Capitol besieged by the Senones, I, 485 A. The Capitol, the senate-house and temple of all demons or gods, I, 646 A. Which gods were rejected from the Capitol, I, 373 B. Entry into the Capitoline temple was forbidden unless a tax had been paid, I, 345 A, 574 A. In times of calamity the Romans implored heaven at the Capitol, I, 487 A. The Capitoline games, II, 637 B.

What the HEAD (*capitulum*) of an animal is, I, 375 A; II, 1037 B.

GOATS prophesying through the art of demons, I, 411 A.

CAPTIVES were formerly sacrificed at funerals, I, 645 A.

CARACALLA had been reared on Christian milk, I, 703 B–C. He was surnamed Germanicus and Parthicus, I, 583 A.

PRISON, the devil’s house in which he confines his household, I, 620 A. In prison Christians trampled him underfoot, I, 621 A. Prison was their training ground, II, 624 C. How great are the benefits of prison, I, 622 ff. Outside prison the Christian has renounced the world; in prison, prison itself as well, I, 622 B. It provides the Christian with what the wilderness provided the prophets, I, 623 B. Prison has darkness, but the devout are light, II, 622 A. Women crawled into prison [Col. 1524] to kiss the martyrs’ chains, I, 1294 B.

CARDEA, a goddess, I, 683 C; II, 97 B.

The FLESH is the hinge of salvation, II, 806 A. Flesh is nothing other than earth transformed into its own shapes, II, 771 A. It is earthly matter, I, 1280 A. What the name “flesh” means, II, 497 A. “Flesh” is a common designation, II, 510 B. Various epithets of the flesh, II, 807 B. What the sensation and life of the flesh are, II, 1014 B. Flesh fashioned by the hand of God, I, 1231 B. In what sense it is called sinful, II, 719 A, 814 A, 816 A. Flesh exists through God’s word with respect to its form, II, 801 B. Flesh has its own places of withdrawal—in waters, in fires, and so forth, II, 885 C. Flesh exists as body before it exists as animate body, II, 873 B. The twofold corruption of the flesh, II, 851 A–B. It is proper to the flesh to be corrupted by sufferings, II, 852 A. The flesh is the whole apparatus of the soul’s thought, II, 814 A. The flesh is the soul’s minister and handmaid, II, 805 C. Flesh serves; spirit rules, I, 1204 A. The visible form of the flesh is the citadel of the soul, II, 813 C. How great the communion and fellowship between flesh and soul, I, 1231 B. Flesh without a soul is not a human being, II, 850 C. Whatever is done in the heart is performed by the soul in the flesh, with the flesh, and through the flesh, II, 813 C. If all things are subject to the soul through the flesh, that through which you make use of them must necessarily be subject to the flesh also, II, 805 C. The flesh does nothing by itself, II, 816 A. Flesh breathes when it possesses the spirit, but expires when it loses it, II, 465 B. Dying belongs to the very flesh to which living also belongs, II, 805 B. It is sown in corruption when it is dissolved into earth, II, 495 C.

The flesh will be raised so that blood may be vindicated, II, 835 B. The character in which it will rise again, II, 800. All flesh and blood rise again equally in their own proper quality, II, 808 A. The restoration of the flesh is easier than its first formation, II, 810 A. In the kingdom of God the flesh is reformed and made angelic, II, 632 B. After the resurrection the flesh will assume an angelic condition, II, 854 A. Those who deny the resurrection of the flesh live carnally, II, 808 C. Certain heretics deny the salvation of the flesh, II, 66 B, 452 B. The virtues of the flesh must also be judged, II, 813 B, 815 A. Spirit and flesh share guilt with one another, I, 1204 A. The flesh is the soul’s partner and co-heir in temporal and eternal things, II, 805 C. Nothing is properly reproached in the flesh except as an insult to the soul, which subjects the flesh to its own service, II, 808 B. Whatever is proclaimed concerning blood is directed toward the flesh, II, 835 B. Not only must the things that cast the flesh into shadow be taken into account, but those that illuminate it must also be considered, II, 808 A. The Apostle condemns the works of the flesh in such a way that he appears to condemn the flesh itself, II, 859 C. Why the flesh is rebuked in the Scriptures, II, 719 B. Faith needs external counsel against the necessities of the flesh, II, 914 C. The affliction of the flesh is an appeasing victim offered to the Lord through the sacrifice of humiliation, I, 1269 B; II, 806 B. It is of no benefit to fatten the flesh while starving the spirit, I, 620 A. Corpulence impedes wisdom, II, 683 B. The flesh is the bride who, in Christ Jesus, has covenanted with the bridegroom through blood, II, 885 C. Christ, the redeemer of the flesh, II, 797 A. He restores the flesh from every affliction, II, 759 B. Through the sacraments the flesh, together with the soul, is claimed for God, II, 806 A–B.

How monstrous it is to eat human flesh, I, 322 A. Whether the first human beings ate flesh, II, 958 C. Carnal things signify spiritual things in the Law, II, 374 C. Carnal things always precede as figures of spiritual things, I, 1206 A. Christ’s flesh alone was to be taken from human flesh without a man’s seed, II, 783 ff. It was not sinful flesh, II, 781 A. He did not borrow it from the stars or from the substances of the higher world, II, 335 B, 763 A. Why, by assuming flesh and soul, he appears to have possessed a fleshly soul, II, 773 A. Some affirm that Christ’s flesh sits in heaven devoid of sensation, II, 792 A. The flesh in the angels was of true and solid human substance, II, 333 B.

CARPOCRATES, a disciple of Simon, magician, and fornicator, II, 709 C. His heresy concerning Christ and the resurrection of bodies, II, 66 B. His disciples equated their own souls with the Apostles themselves—indeed, even with Christ—and even preferred their souls to them, II, 686 B.

CARTHAGE, a city fiercely devoted to the pursuits of war (Virgil), II, 1032 A. The foundress of Carthage gave herself to the funeral pyre, I, 532 A. Walls were imposed upon it by Statilius Taurus, as Sentius Saturninus relates, II, 1031 A–B. The Punic city, rival of Rome, I, 427 A. The schools of rhetoric at Carthage, II, 553 A. Fires hung over the walls of Carthage in Tertullian’s age, I, 701 B. The Carthaginians, noble in antiquity and fortunate in novelty, II, 1030 C. What the ancient form of their clothing was, ibid. The contests of the Carthaginians, II, 133 B. Carthage to be decimated in its martyrs, I, 532 A.

Who the CASINIENSES were, I, 420 A. Their god Delventius, ibid.

To put a HELMET or MASK upon someone, II, 774 B.

CASSINUM, a town of Campania, I, 420 A.

CASSIUS CLEMENS, I, 457 A. Pagans alone were guilty of the Cassian sedition, I, 699 B.

CASSIUS SEVERUS, I, 330 A, 602 C.

[Col. 1525] It is fitting that we rejoice in the indignation of divine CHASTISEMENT, I, 1266 B.

The CHASTITY of the primitive Christians, I, 326 A. Pagans, haters of chastity, I, 472 f. Every husband an enforcer of chastity, I, 1320 B. See CONTINENCE.

CASTOR, son of Jupiter, II, 378 C. Horses allotted to Castor and Pollux by Mercury, I, 641 A. The Castors as gods, I, 606 A. Apparitions of the gods Castor and Pollux, I, 409 A. Eggs are assigned to the honor of the Castors, II, 639 B.

The Church is the CAMP of light; paganism, the camp of darkness, II, 92 B.

CASTRATION places no restraint upon lust, II, 282 A.

What the CASTRENSES are, II, 95 A. Military duties, II, 92 B.

CATABOLIC spirits, II, 698 B.

CATACLYSM. See FLOOD.

A triumphal CATAPHRACT, II, 1043 A.

CATAPHRYGIANS, II, 72 A.

The ears of CATECHUMENS must be watered with divine discourses, I, 1236 B. See HEARERS. The catechumens of heretics are perfected before they are instructed, II, 56 B.

The CHAIRS of the Apostles still preside in their own places within the apostolic churches, II, 49 A.

CATHOLICS alone possess what was instituted by Christ, II, 23 A. Catholic tradition, II, 931 C. Whatever is done against catholic truth is regarded as novel, II, 931 B–C.

CATILINE sealed his conspiracy with human blood, I, 321 A.

CATO, grave and wise, I, 337 A. Cato the censor is a pimp, I, 473 A. He shared his wife with his friends, I, 472 A. Cato was the first to bring a fresh fig to Rome, I, 606 C. He learned Greek literature when already an old man, II, 1039 B.

The *Laureolus* of CATULLUS, II, 565 A.

The CAUCASUS, a precipitous mountain, II, 247 B.

What the CAVEA is, I, 361 A, 579 B.

CEA—also called Chon, Co, Con, or Coon—an island, collapsed, I, 480 A.

The Tablet of CEBES, II, 53 A.

Provision CELLS, II, 834 B.

The CELTS, spending the night beside the tombs of brave men, seek oracles, II, 740 B.

The CENSUALES of the Greeks, I, 388 A.

The CENSUS of Augustus. See AUGUSTUS.

Banquets costing a HUNDRED THOUSAND sesterces, I, 300 A.

The CENTO custom, II, 53 A.

CEPHEUS depicted among the constellations by Aratus, II, 142 A.

Who first brought CHERRIES to Rome, I, 334 B, 606 B.

Tragedies of CERBERUS, II, 85 B.

CERDO introduced two first principles—that is, two gods, one good and the other savage, and so forth—II, 70 B, 249 A. He held varying opinions about Christ’s nativity and the resurrection of the flesh, II, 70 B–C.

CERES was made a goddess because of the discovery of crops, and how absurdly, I, 334 A. She revealed crops; she did not create them, ibid. Ceres’ chariot was drawn by beasts—serpents, I, 341 A. Ceres takes pleasure in gloomy garments, II, 1045 B. Ceres Pharia, or Farrea, is not distinct from the upright timber of the cross, I, 366 A, 578 A. All the attire of Ceres’ initiates was white: their ribbons, caps, and badge of privilege, II, 1045 A. The priestesses of Ceres, even while their husbands were alive and consenting, were widowed through an amicable separation, II, 953 A. The women of African Ceres, having voluntarily renounced marriage, grow old, II, 928 C. The Cerealian games, I, 638 A.

CERINTHUS put forward the God of the Jews not as Lord but as an angel, II, 67 A. He maintained that Christ was merely a man born from Joseph’s seed, ibid.

Greater CONTESTS are followed by greater rewards, I, 704 A.

The DEER, a slow-footed, wild, lowly, rough quadruped, II, 1037 A. When pierced by an arrow, it knows that it must heal itself with dittany, I, 1248 A. The deer, arbiter of its own age, after feeding on a serpent grows languid from the poison into renewed youth, II, 1037 A.

The CHALDAEAN seed is brought into Egypt, II, 1035 B.

The Sethians said that the seed of HAM was preserved in the ark, II, 66 A–B. For what purpose, ibid.

The nature and behavior of the CHAMELEON are described at length, II, 1037 f.

CHARIS, an aeon of Valentinus, II, 551 A. Praxeas drove out the charisms, II, 155 B.

The MUTUAL LOVE of Christians, greatly admired even by pagans, I, 704 A. Among brothers and fellow-servants, hope, fear, joy, grief, and suffering are shared, because the Spirit is shared, I, 1245 A. See CHRISTIANS; LOVE.

The CHARITES, goddesses, II, 85 A.

CHARON of Lampsacus, historian, II, 727 A.

The swallow’s CHELIDONIA, I, 1248 A.

CHILON the Spartan, while embracing his victorious son at Olympia, breathed his last from joy, II, 739 A.

EARTHY (*choicus*), II, 578 B, 865 B.

“CHRESTIAN” was the pagan mispronunciation of “Christian,” I, 281 A.

[Col. 1526] The Jews were not permitted to prepare the royal CHRISM while in captivity, II, 634 A. After baptism the faithful are anointed with it, I, 1206 C. Christ is so called from chrism, I, 1207 A. Likewise the Christian, I, 281 A.

The foundation of CHRISTIANITY is Christ, II, 484 C. Christianity is built up when it is afflicted, I, 704 f. It will therefore never fail, ibid. It has as many enemies as there are outsiders: Jews, soldiers, and members of one’s own household, I, 307 f. The Christian religion was substituted for the Jewish religion, I, 617 A.
