It is dated from the renewal of the Testament, from the Lord’s Passion, II, 1001 B. How it arose, I, 290 B, 307 A, 567 A–B, 571 B. It began together with hatred of itself, I, 307 A. It pleads for no exemption on its own account, I, 259 A. Why, ibid. It was condemned by the unjust laws of depraved emperors, I, 294 A, 296 A. Yet not all emperors persecuted it, I, 291 ff. Indeed, not a few pagan governors were favorably disposed toward it, I, 703. Some in ancient times falsely pretended to belong to the Christian sect, I, 704 A. The sum of the Christian religion’s doctrine, I, 375 ff. Supported by the ancient records of the Jews, I, 386 A, 392 A. Whoever recognizes the truth of the Christian religion immediately follows it and desires to die in its defense, I, 536 A. No one is ashamed or repentant of having embraced this religion, I, 269 A. All rejoice and glory in it, ibid. Stoic, Platonic, and dialectical Christianity, II, 20 B.

The name of the CHRISTIANS is derived from sweetness or kindness, I, 281 A. It arose under Augustus; under the reign of Tiberius its teaching shone forth, I, 290 B. Every sex, age, condition, and rank passed over to this name, I, 263 A. How hateful the Christian name was to pagans, I, 277 ff.; 281 ff.; 566 A–B. It is hostile to a rival system, I, 278 A. The effects of this hatred among relatives, I, 280 B f. Christians were harassed merely for the name, I, 277 ff., 285. Confession of the name, not investigation of a crime, was the ground of condemnation, I, 271 A, 278 f. The hatred of injustice toward the Christian name, I, 261 A. One who does what Christians do not do is excluded by the Christian name, I, 278 A. Christians are older than the Phrygians and other nations, I, 570. No one was a Christian before Christ, II, 1001 C. Whoever is not a Christian is dead, II, 745 B. No one is greater than the Christian, II, 15 A. No one is a Christian unless he perseveres to the end, ibid. Christians are made, not born, I, 378 B, although the soul is said to be Christian by nature, I, 377 A. It does not belong to everyone to believe what belongs to Christians, II, 655 B. Christians are not made from pagans except by first having been lost, then sought by God, and brought back by Christ, II, 992 B. Christians were astonished that they had not previously rejected pagan errors, I, 269 A. Pagans acknowledged that they were better than they had formerly been, I, 564 A.

How great the multitude of Christians, I, 262 A, 700 B, 704 B. They filled every place, I, 462 A, except the temples alone, I, 463 A. Christians were not Brahmans, gymnosophists, or forest-dwellers, I, 490 B; nor dog-headed people or people with shade-giving feet, I, 570 A. They were free persons, not slaves, I, 451 A. They knew how to die for freedom, I, 565 A. Pagans called them foreigners, I, 446 B. Yet they lived together with them, I, 490 B. They shared trades and services with them, I, 491 A. Both had the same food, dress, and household equipment, I, 490 B. Christians were distinguished from them only by modesty, patience, and the correction of their former vices, I, 700 B f. Driven by no ambition, they had renounced public affairs, I, 465 A. They were cold toward every passion for glory and rank, ibid. They kept apart from public assemblies, I, 465 A. When setting forth their teachings, they considered lying a sin, I, 403 B. True Christians are described, I, 269 A, 511 f., 624 A. Christians can be recognized by nothing other than the correction of their former vices, I, 701 A. Christian instruction comes from the porch—that is, the books—of Solomon, II, 20 B. The corrupt morals of the pagans compared with the pure morals of Christians, I, 472 ff. Their knowledge, discipline, and conscience are widely different, I, 501 f., 516 f. [The source apparently repeats “knowledge” through an OCR error.] Their virtues are likewise profoundly dissimilar, ibid. Pagans praised and admired the virtues of Christians, but could not endure that they had become Christians, I, 280 A, 564 A. Pagans hated those whom they did not know at all, I, 261 A. Why, ibid. Once they came to know them, they immediately loved them, I, 262 A, 559 B.

Who and what Christians were, I, 468 ff. Their blameless life, I, 704. They were gathered into one body by consciousness of their religion, unity of discipline, and a covenant of hope, I, 468 A. Gathered together, they were what they were when dispersed; collectively, what they were individually, I, 478 A. A Christian is nowhere anything different, II, 93 A. No one is greater than the Christian, II, 15 A. No one is a Christian unless he perseveres to the very end, ibid. The Christian is a disciple of heaven, a trader in life, a builder of realities, an enemy of error, and one who completes, expresses, and guards the truth, I, 514 A. He believes what has been handed down, II, 745 B. A Christian is not permitted to seek more than it is permitted to find, II, 651 A. No more may be discovered than what is learned from God, ibid. After Christ we have no need of curiosity, nor of inquiry after the Gospel, II, 21 A.

[Col. 1527] Christians are followers of spiritual things, I, 1320 A. How great Christians’ love for one another, I, 471 A. They called one another brothers, ibid. Through love they held everything in common except their wives, I, 472 A. How great their charity toward the needy, and especially toward martyrs, I, 470 f., 475 A, 619 A. They did not have sufficient means to assist all the needy people and gods of the pagans, I, 494 A. Their compassion spent more street by street than pagan religion did temple by temple, ibid. A Christian does not injure even an enemy, I, 512 A. They loved their enemies and prayed to God for them, I, 446 A. They were enemies of no one, I, 700 A. They kept faith even with the nations, I, 512 A. They could have avenged every injury inflicted upon them by pagans: with a few torches, or by openly declaring war, I, 462 A; or by refusing to cast demons out of possessed human bodies, I, 464 A; or merely by withdrawing from the pagans, I, 463 A–B.

The continence of Christians, I, 326 f., 510 A. How great the chastity of spouses, I, 472 A, 510 A. They abstained from every excess after marriage, I, 326 f. They did not transform the female sex, I, 510 A. In spirit they were blind to lust, I, 511 A. The two guardians of Christian holiness are monogamy and continence, II, 939 A. Many remained in a state of virginity—the old and the young, I, 327 A. They even bound themselves to it by a vow, II, 905 A. See VIRGINITY.

They abstained from spectacles, processions, public games, and theatrical performances, I, 466 f., 493 A. They did not attend the pagan festivals of the Saturnalia, and why, I, 492 A. They likewise rejected the Liberalia, ibid. How they used flowers and garlands, I, 492 f. Nothing was more welcome to them than departure from this world, I, 489 A. The world is a prison to the Christian, I, 622 A. See WORLD. Outside prison he renounced the world; in prison, prison itself as well, I, 622 B.

How Christians prayed to God, I, 442 f. Sometimes with hands outstretched, embodying the Lord’s Passion, I, 1169 f. See PRAYER. They worshipped God through Christ, and for what reason, I, 567 C f. They venerated Christ’s cross, I, 577 C f. On the Lord’s Day they gave themselves to joy, I, 371 A. How holy the Christians’ solemn assemblies were, I, 468 ff. What they were like, ibid. What their fasts were, and how rigorous, I, 487 A; II, 954 C, 971 B. They rejected none of the fruits of God’s works, but certainly used them with moderation, I, 491 A. What Christian pleasures are, II, 659 ff.

Christians could not be compelled to worship the gods, I, 699 B. In refusing to worship them, they were guilty of no impiety, ibid. It was a sin for them to sacrifice to false gods, even if their inward resolve remained opposed to the act, I, 433 A. They did not even know the temples of the pagans, I, 363 A. Christian soldiers were forbidden to keep watch in temples of the gods, II, 92 A.

Christians were undeservedly accused of treason against human majesty, I, 436 ff. They never called the emperor “god,” but addressed him by the ordinary title “lord,” I, 450. They did not worship images of the Caesars or swear by the emperor’s genius, I, 447 B. They knew that the emperor had been appointed by God and honored him sincerely, I, 448 B, 700 A. They prayed to God for his safety, I, 433 A. They offered daily prayers for his life, his household, and his army, and for the Senate and people, ibid.

How great the Christians’ power over demons, I, 413 A, 463 B, 677 B, 700 B, 703 B; II, 112 D. The whole power of demons yields to the breath of Christian wisdom, I, 647 B–C f. See DEMONS; DEVIL.

In times of calamity Christians entreated God’s mercy with fasting and the severest works of repentance, I, 487 A. Rolling themselves in sackcloth and ashes, they assailed heaven with importunity, ibid. How undeservedly pagans called them the authors of public calamities, especially war, famine, and plague, I, 479 ff., 571 A–B.

Pagans proclaimed Christians guilty of every crime and enemies of the gods, emperors, laws, morals, and the whole order of nature, I, 277 A, 306 ff., 580 f. How shamelessly they were called an unlawful and desperate faction, I, 464 B ff., 468 ff., 532 A; hostile to the emperors and the commonwealth, I, 452 ff., 459 B f., 699 f. They were held guilty on the sole and false public testimony of rumor, I, 310 ff., 567 f. They were falsely accused of three horrible crimes: namely, killing an infant in their sacred assemblies, eating its flesh and blood, and committing fornication, adultery, and incest, I, 306 f., 580 ff. They were condemned merely for a name unknown to pagans, I, 281 ff., 563 f. The injustice of pagan judges is proof of the Christians’ innocence, I, 534 A. See CHRISTIANITY.

Christians rejoiced more at being condemned than acquitted, I, 698 D. Nearly every day they were besieged, betrayed, and overwhelmed in their assemblies, I, 308 A. How absurdly pagans invoked the severity of their own laws to persecute them, I, 285 ff. They were condemned by no law except those of the most wicked emperors, I, 294 A. How absurd the cry: “The Christians to the beasts! To the lions!” I, 341 A, 480 A, 571 A; II, 651 A, 825 B. The death of so many Christians caused great loss to the commonwealth, I, 496 A–B. [Col. 1528] Why God permitted them to suffer so greatly, I, 488 f. Whenever they were mown down, they became more numerous, I, 535 A. The blood of Christians is seed, ibid. See PAGANS.

CHRIST: whether this is a name or a title, I, 192 B–C f. Christ is so called from *chrism*, that is, anointing, which furnished the Lord with his name, I, 1207 A. Christ Jesus, in the very mystery of his name, is the true and supreme priest of the Father, II, 330 C. Why he is called the Nazarene, II, 372 A–B. He was Son under the name of God and King and almighty and most high Lord, II, 181 C. The name “Christ,” arising not from nature but from a dispensation, becomes proper to him by whom it is found to have been ordained, II, 341 C. See JESUS.

Christ is God’s λόγος (*logos*), Word, Reason, Wisdom, and Son, I, 399 f. The primordial Word, II, 868 C. By performing miracles he proved himself to be God’s λόγος (*logos*) and true God, I, 1400 B. Christ was made second to the Father and, with the Spirit, third, II, 170 A. By bringing forth the Word from himself, the Father makes the Son, II, 317 A. Christ is from the Father, spirit from Spirit, as a ray from the sun and light from light; the one begotten did not depart from the source, nor is the substance separated, I, 399 A–B. He is other than the Father in measure, not in number; in degree, not in condition, ibid. He is true God, ibid. He possesses true divinity as his own reality, I, 399 A. Christ is the Son and Spirit and substance of the Creator, II, 328 C, 386 C. The representative of the Father, II, 187 B. But he is not the Father, II, 181 A, C. In what sense he is the Father’s vicar, II, 328 C. The primordial, first-begotten Word, stirred by power and reason and sustained by spirit, I, 400 B. What he received from the Father, II, 843 C. All the old and new Scriptures foretell Christ as the Son of God, II, 186 B. Christ, the Spirit of God, always existed, even before the flesh, II, 489 B. Why he is called the Angel of Great Counsel, II, 778 A. Marcion dared to destroy the original documents concerning Christ, II, 755 B. See SON.

From Adam through the patriarchs and prophets, in vision, dream, mirror, and enigma, Christ was always preparing his course from the beginning, II, 174 C. From the beginning he associated and conversed with the patriarchs and prophets, already learning from the beginning to be the human being whom he was to become at the end, II, 317 A. Christ always spoke in the prophets, being the Spirit of the Creator, II, 328 B, 386 C. He is the seal of all the prophets, II, 615, 632 A. In forming the human being, God was thinking of Christ, who was to become human, I, 802 B. The Law signified Christ, II, 447 A. Christ was figured in the person of Moses, II, 316 A; in Joshua, II, 343 A–B; and in Isaac and Joseph, II, 346 A, 626 A–B. Christ is shown under the figure of the flower destined to spring from the rod arising from the root of Jesse, II, 489 B. Christ figured as a bull, II, 346 B–C.

Christ was promised not as a war-maker but as a bringer of peace, II, 351 C, whatever the Jews may say to the contrary, II, 617 f. He is depicted by the prophets under two conditions corresponding to two advents, I, 400 A; II, 329 f., 638 C: one lowly and the other glorious, II, 330 f. Christ was proved to be such as he had been announced, II, 349 B. Christ, illuminator of antiquity, II, 461 A. Christ, ancient amid new things, II, 410 A. The second Adam, II, 789 C; and the last, II, 868 C. The only new king of the new ages, II, 348 A. Christ announces a new kingdom, II, 356 ff. Whether Christ is yet to come or has already come, II, 609 B. Refutation of the Jews’ claim that Christ is yet to come, II, 610 A.

Christ, the true temple of God, II, 635 C. Christ, the authentic high priest of God the Father, II, 447 A. The universal priest of the Father, II, 376 A. God’s proper and legitimate chief priest, the high priest of the uncircumcised priesthood, II, 493 B. The chief priest of eternal sacrifices, II, 609 B. The Father’s arbiter and minister, II, 317 B–C. Christ is not the peddler of any god other than the Creator, II, 270 C, 322 C. Christ, mediator between God and humanity, II, 885 B. Christ the warrior, II, 340 A, 620 B. Christ, mighty in war and bearing arms, will receive the spoils not only of Samaria but of all nations, II, 618, 621 B.

Christ, a human being mingled with God, and in what sense, I, 399 B. Christ, illuminator and guide of the human race, I, 395 A. Arbiter and teacher of Christian grace and discipline, ibid. The sole hope of the whole world, II, 760 C. Healer of ailments, II, 373 A. The true examiner and refiner of human stains, II, 447 A. One who invites to eternal, not merely long, life, II, 424 D. Christ, lord both of the Sabbath and of the Law, and of all the Father’s dispensations, II, 396 A. Christ the bridegroom, II, 382 A.

Christ without glory, ignoble, dishonored, II, 344 B. All the disgrace of Christ as God is the mystery of human salvation, II, 317 C. Christ’s love for humanity, II, 772 f. It was not fitting for Christ to be born from human seed, II, 781 f. The inaugurator of a new birth had to be born in a new way, II, 781 C. Christ’s flesh was holy, II, 933 C; not sinful, II, 781 A. See FLESH. Christ received from the Father the fabric of flesh and soul, II, 843 C. Although Christ had determined to lie hidden under human form, he nevertheless imitated nothing of human impatience, I, 1252 B. Christ was human because he was flesh, not because he was soul, II, 874 A. Christ possessed two [Col. 1529] substances, divine and human, II, 194 A. Christ alone was a human being without sin, because Christ was also God, II, 720 B. That Christ was a true human being is proved, II, 14 B, 378 f. The Marcionites maintained that Christ was a phantom, II, 331 C.

Christ came forth from the Father as a ray from the sun, a stream from a spring, and a shoot from a seed, II, 183 A. He did not depart from the source of God the Father, but came forth from it, I, 399 B. He descended into the Virgin and, formed as flesh in her womb, ibid. He had no mother through an act of unchastity, as Jupiter did, I, 396 f. Even the mother whom he appears to have had was not married, I, 397 A. Christ was born of a Virgin, II, 782 A–B. He is from Mary’s flesh, since he is from David’s seed, II, 350 A. He was revealed in the twelfth year of Tiberius Caesar, II, 264 A; and deigned to descend from heaven, II, 267 A, 614 B. Christ was made little so that the human being might become greatest, II, 317 C. Lowliness was supremely fitting for Christ as God, II, 316 ff. Whether he was the son of a craftsman or of a prostitute, I, 662 A. Whether Christ passed through every stage of infancy, II, 411 B–C f. Flesh endowed with spirit is nourished, grows to maturity, speaks, teaches, acts—and is Christ, I, 399 B. The reasons for the incarnation, II, 773.

Marcion said that one Christ appeared under Tiberius and another was promised by the Creator, II, 264 A, 368 B–C. To the present day the Jews deny that Christ has come, II, 331 B. Why, ibid. Christ, the one who deviated from and destroyed Judaism, II, 329 B. The Jews regarded him as a deceiver in his signs and a rival in his teachings, ibid. Christ was seen, heard, and encountered, mingling in himself humanity and God: God in his powers, humanity in his lowliness, II, 317 B–C. From the beginning he acted in the Father’s name, II, 317 A, 378 A. Through Christ we know God, II, 647 B. Through Christ the Father is more fully revealed, II, 170 A. It was reserved for Christ to unveil everything previously hidden, set doubtful matters straight, complete what had been foretasted, and make present what had been foretold, II, 796 A.

After Christ Jesus we have no need of curiosity, nor of inquiry after the Gospel, II, 21 A. Christ’s teaching must be sought and preserved, II, 23 A. Christ is known above all by the power of his word, II, 375 B. All Christ’s sayings are set forth for everyone, II, 22 B. He conducted himself as God so that humanity might be taught to act divinely, II, 317 C. He disdained no one’s table or roof, I, 1233 A. He rejected no one who wished to adhere to him, ibid.

How many and how great Christ’s miracles were, I, 400 B. By them he proved himself God, ibid. How shamelessly they were said to have been performed by magical powers, I, 400 A. Christ wished to be acknowledged as the Son of God by human beings, not by unclean spirits, II, 373 B. He rejected the proclamation of an unclean spirit, ibid. Christ was never without water, I, 1210 A. How he baptized, I, 1212 A–B.

Both Christ himself and the prophets foretold his Passion, I, 401 A. Christ’s Passion is described, I, 1252 ff. How great Christ’s patience, II, 348. He wished to be fattened upon the pleasure of patience, I, 1254 A. Unless Christ had remained unrecognized, he could not have suffered at all, II, 327 C. As he had foretold, Christ was violently crucified by the votes of the Jews, I, 400 B f. Christ’s abandonment on the cross is explained, II, 195. Christ had to die for the very reason that whatever is born dies, II, 764 B. Christ died voluntarily, I, 401 A, forestalling the executioner’s task, ibid. We say that Christ died not in his divine but in his human substance, II, 194. At Christ’s death the extraordinary darkening of the sun was foretold and recorded in the secret records or archives, I, 401 A. His body was placed in a tomb, ibid. Nothing was found there except the grave-clothes, I, 402 A. In dying, Christ descended to the souls of the prophets and patriarchs, II, 657 A, 742 C. In what year he suffered, II, 612 ff.

Christ rose again on the third day after his death, I, 401 f. He afterward appeared to his disciples, I, 402 A, teaching them what they were to teach, ibid., 492 A. Why he did not display himself to the public, ibid. Whether Christ’s flesh in heaven is devoid of sensation, II, 792 A. Nothing is clearer than the reality of Christ’s body after his resurrection, II, 466 C. Pilate reported Christ’s deeds to Tiberius Caesar, I, 403 A. Tiberius wished Christ to be enrolled among the gods, I, 290 A. From the time of his Passion Christ began to reign, II, 628 B. Christ’s kingdom and name extend everywhere, II, 611 C. They are bestowed equally upon all, II, 612 A. He is believed everywhere and reigns and is worshipped among all nations, II, 611 C.

CHRYSIPPUS resorted to hellebore, II, 656 A. A flatterer of Chrysippus, I, 612 C. His opinion concerning the soul, II, 653 C.

**FOOD.** Diet either destroys or wounds every discipline, II, 960 C. What the delicacies of foods are, II, 1048. In the beginning God assigned to humanity only herbs and the produce of trees for food, II, 958 C. Why the Mosaic Law prohibited the eating of certain animals, II, 306 A. Why Christ desired food, II, 468 A. Prayer preceded and followed the food of Christians, I, 477 A, 1193 B. See **ABSTINENCE; SUPPER; BANQUET**.

**CHICKPEA**, II, 258 C.

[Col. 1530]

**CICERO** learned from a dream that Octavius Augustus, then unknown to him, would put an end to the storms of civil discord, II, 728 A. He purchased a citrus-wood tabletop for five hundred thousand sesterces, II, 1048 A. Ciceronian tables, II, 706 A. Cicero’s *Tusculan Disputations*, I, 525 A. Cicero’s nurse had already perceived his dignity while he was still an infant, II, 729 A.

**TAME**, or **TRACTABLE**, dispositions, II, 591 A.

**CILICIA** possessed the oracle of Mopsus, II, 730 A.

**CINCIUS SEVERUS**, at Thysdrus, gave Christians a means of answering so that they might be released, I, 703 A.

**HAIRDRESSERS**, I, 1301 B.

**POST**, or cross, II, 1047 A.

**ITINERANT PERFORMERS**, II, 58 B. The itinerant sect of magicians, I, 672 B. Their itinerant impostures, I, 411 A.

**GOLDEN BRACELETS** adorned women’s arms, I, 1306 A.

**CIRCUMCISION** was given to the people as a sign by which Israel could be recognized, not as a means of salvation, II, 603 A, B. Abraham had received circumcision, which served as a sign of that time, not as a privilege conferring salvation, II, 602 sq. Circumcision, a mark of servitude, does not cleanse a person, II, 601 A. It was always observed on the eighth day because of the threat of death, ibid. It was destined to cease, II, 604 A. Carnal and temporary circumcision was allotted to a disobedient people; spiritual circumcision was given for the salvation of a faithful people, II, 603 C.

**CIRCUS**, originally consecrated to the Sun, I, 639 B. Named after Circe, ibid. Its ornaments, ibid.; and its frenzies, I, 648. In it the Romans spared neither rulers nor citizens, I, 649 A. In the circus, tiers and *apuliae* [uncertain reading], I, 652 B.

**CITIES** all arose after the Flood, I, 482 A. The human race once existed without cities, I, 432 A. To obliterate the city under the guise of a tavern, I, 452 B.

**CLAUDIUS**, when chosen emperor, was the first to promise each soldier fifteen thousand sesterces, I, 455 A. He enacted no law against Christians, I, 294 A.

**CLAUDIUS HERMINIANUS**, a savage persecutor of Christians in Cappadocia: how he died, I, 702 A.

**CLAUDIUS SATURNINUS**, his book *On Crowns*, II, 86 A, 91 A, 97 A.

**KEYS** were entrusted to wives for safekeeping, II, 927 A. The key of the Law is the interpretation of the Law, II, 429 C. The keys of the kingdom of heaven were given to Peter and, through him, to the Church, II, 142 C. See **PARADISE**. The keys of the devil, II, 142 C.

**THE CLAZOMENIANS** comfort Hermotimus with a temple, II, 724 C.

**CLEANTHES’** opinion concerning the soul, II, 653 B. His testimony on the same subject, II, 693 B.

**CLEMENT**, bishop of the Church of the Romans, ordained by Peter, II, 45 A.

Let not the abundance of **HEAVENLY MERCY** give free rein to the presumption of human rashness, I, 1240 B.

**CLEOMACHUS**, a boxer, deserving to be crowned among the Novian fullers, II, 1042 B.

**CLEONYMUS**, a boxer cured by Achilles in a dream, II, 729 A.

**CLEOPATRA** reigned alone for twenty years, II, 614 B. She then reigned jointly under Augustus for thirteen years, ibid. Cleopatra’s death, I, 584 A, 625 C.

**CLIDEMUS OF ATHENS**, while being crowned with gold by actors for his excellence, died from joy and glory, II, 739 A.

**CLOACINA**, a goddess, II, 266 A.

The **SHIELDS OF THE PERSIANS** were adorned with an image of the sun, I, 370 A.

**COOKS** received their name from Apicius, I, 282 A.

A **RICH MAN** remains unmarried only with difficulty, I, 1301 A.

**CAELESTIS**, goddess of the Africans, I, 419 A. Promiser of rains, I, 413 A.

**HEAVEN**, the dwelling of the living God, I, 377 A; and the Christian’s homeland, II, 260 A. When praying, the Christian soul looks toward heaven, not the Capitol, I, 377 A. At the passing away of the world, the kingdoms of heaven will be opened, II, 744 A. See **PARADISE**. In heaven there is no sex, I, 1307 A. Basilides taught that 365 heavens had been established by angels, II, 62 B.

**CEMETERY**, II, 738 A, 796 B.

The expense of **DINNERS** was fixed by ancient laws, I, 298 A. Dinners costing one hundred sesterces, I, 300 A. How immoderate their expense was, ibid. The free and final meal of those condemned to the beasts, I, 492 A. The character of the Christians’ supper, I, 473 sqq. The preparation of the supper in the parable signifies the fullness of eternal life, II, 437 C.

The Christians’ **ASSEMBLIES BEFORE DAWN**, I, 273 A, 281 B; II, 79 B. They were attacked in their very assemblies, I, 308 A. Who were excluded from them, I, 469 A. See **SYNAXIS**.

A **THOUGHT** without deed and without effect is an act of the flesh, II, 814 A. The flesh is the entire apparatus of the soul’s thought, ibid. Whether thoughts that are recognized externally through the flesh are administered through the flesh, ibid.

**COLABARSUS** constructed a new heresy from the Greek alphabet, II, 70 A.

[Col. 1531]

The **LOVES OF THE COLCHIANS**, II, 247 A.

**COLLEGIATE ATTENDANTS**, I, 644 B.

A **COLLEGE** of musical arts, etc., I, 644 B.

**CONVERSATION**, a sign of familiarity, II, 413 A.

At **COLOPHON**, a demonic spring makes people delirious, II, 734 B.

The property of **COLOR** inheres in every body, II, 660 B. Adulterated colors come not from God but from the devil, the falsifier of nature, I, 1312 B, 1321 A. At first there were only two colors of the circus factions, white and red, I, 641 B. See **WOOL**.

The **DOVE**, a bird not only innocent but also chaste, II, 940 B. It has no gall, I, 1209 A. “Dove,” in Greek περιστερά (*peristerá*), has the numerical value 801, II, 70 A. The dove customarily signifies Christ, II, 544 B. The Holy Spirit descended upon Christ in the form of a dove, and why, I, 1208 A. Where the body of this dove is, II, 758 A.

The **PILLARS** of Sessia, named from sowing; of Messia, from harvesting; and of Tutelina, from the protection of crops, II, 639 C.

The **CHILDREN OF COLYTHUS** speak a month sooner, II, 683 A.

A woman’s **HAIR** serves as a covering for her, II, 899 C. See **HAIR**.

The Roman **ASSEMBLIES FOR ELECTIONS**, I, 464 B.

The **EPILEPTIC DISEASE** was said to be cured by human blood, I, 322 A.

What an **OPPORTUNITY FOR SINNING** is, I, 1237 A.

The **RECORDS OF THE ROMANS**, I, 292 A.

Letters are necessary for matters of **COMMERCE**, II, 87 B. See **BUSINESS**.

**COMMUNION OF PEACE**, II, 32 B.

**ECCLESIASTICAL COMMUNION**, II, 45 B. See **EUCHARIST; EXCOMMUNICATION**.

**SHELLS** carried into the mountains by the Flood, II, 1033 B. Shellfish, the fruits of the sea, I, 1311 A.

The **COUNCILS OF THE PAGANS**, I, 464 B. Councils are a representation of the entire Christian body, II, 972. Stations and fasts preceded them, ibid. Councils drawn from all the churches throughout the Greek regions, ibid.

Roman **PUBLIC ASSEMBLIES**, I, 464 B.

Strictly speaking, the one natural **DESIRE** is the desire for food, which God established in the beginning, II, 716 B. The Apostle grants us a rational desire, II, 673 B. Solitary desire is forbidden, I, 499 A. When desire uses the eyes as its arbiters, II, 716 B. The desire of the flesh defends the functions of age, demands a harvest of beauty, and rejoices in its own disgrace, I, 1280 B. Worldly desire has as its causes glory, avarice, ambition, and discontent, I, 1281 A. See **LUST**.—The Graves of Desire still existed in the author’s time, II, 976 A.

A **CONGIARIUM** (largess) was distributed to the soldiers, I, 455 A.

**CONFESSION** is brought about through persecution, and persecution reaches its end in confession, II, 143 C. Confession is simple and explicit in the name of martyr, II, 455 C. Christians who confessed were condemned by pagans as other accused persons were, I, 702 B. Confessors, II, 77 C. Once a confession of crimes has been made, the judicial examination proceeds no further, I, 276 A. Confession alleviates sin as much as concealment aggravates it, I, 1243 A. From confession repentance arises, and satisfaction is arranged, I, 1243 B. Confession is the counsel of satisfaction; concealment, that of obstinacy, ibid. How great an evil it is to conceal an offense during *exomologesis* (public confession), I, 1245 B. In Cain and Adam examples are set before us of sins that should be confessed rather than denied, II, 314 C. Confession results in the good works of repentance, II, 312 A. Sins and shameful deeds are not to be confessed publicly, I, 1222 C. Confession must precede Baptism, I, 1222 B, C. See **REPENTANCE**.

**CONFIRMATION** clothes a person with the Holy Spirit, II, 50 A. It is a sacrament, II, 54 A. After Baptism, neophytes received it through the laying on of hands, I, 1207 sqq. In that laying on of hands the flesh is overshadowed so that the soul may be illuminated by the Spirit, II, 806 B.

**MARRIAGE; WEDLOCK.** See **MATRIMONY; NUPTIALS**.

**CONSEVIUS**, a god, I, 600 C. His function, ibid.

Every believer may **INSTITUTE AND DEVISE** a practice, provided only that it agrees with God, conduces to discipline, and advances salvation, II, 81 B.

The festival of the **CONSUALIA**, I, 637 A.

**CUSTOM** generally begins from some sordid ignorance or simplicity, II, 889 A. It is strengthened into usage through succession and is thus asserted against truth, ibid. The force of custom, II, 890 sqq. Reason supports custom, II, 80 A. It makes no difference whether a practice rests upon Scripture or upon reason, since reason also commends law, II, 81 A. Custom is to be cultivated, lest it fail to be the interpreter of reason, II, 81 A. Let custom stand for so long as we may oppose custom even with custom, II, 890 B. Where no law exists, tradition gives customary force to a practice, II, 81 B. Even in civil affairs custom is accepted as law when law is lacking, ibid. Custom confirms tradition, of which it is a competent witness, ibid. No one rejects a custom that he cannot condemn, II, 891 A.

[Col. 1532]

Christ called himself the Truth, not Custom, II, 889 A.

**CONSUS**, a god, I, 600 C. He is also Neptune, I, 637 A, 640 A. God of counsel, I, 637 A. Discovered by Romulus, II, 266 C. His stronghold in the circus, I, 637 A. He lies concealed underground near the turning-posts, I, 637 A, 640 A.

No one **DESPISES** what he knows does not exist at all, I, 572 C.

**CONTINENCE** is necessary to human beings at every moment, just as prayer is, II, 926 A. A vow of continence, II, 905 A. The Apostle prefers the good of continence to marriage, II, 486 C. Continence honors the law of marriage and moderates its license, II, 931 A. Continence is an instrument of eternity, I, 1285 A. Through continence you will acquire a great wealth of holiness, II, 925 C. Continence is more arduous for women, II, 903 B. More arduous and more glorious is the continence that is conscious of its own right—namely, that of widows, I, 1287 B. Continence rests upon virtue; virginity upon grace, II, 903 B. Continence is not inferior to virginity, ibid. See **VIRGINITY**. The continence of heretics is not to be praised, II, 931 A.

**OBSTINACY** overthrows fear, I, 1233 A.

Whether all things **CONSIST OF OPPOSITES**, II, 657 C.

How **CHANGES** toward good or evil are recognized, I, 266 A, 559 C, sq.

The **LORD’S BANQUET**, I, 1294 B. The character of the Christians’ banquet, I, 477 A. At the Lord’s Supper the Holy Spirit admonishes the guests, II, 437 D. What the pagans’ public banquets were, and how abominable, I, 452 B. See **FOOD**.

**NIGHTTIME ASSEMBLIES**, I, 1294 B.

**COOKS** take their name from Apicius, I, 282 A.

The **CORINTHIANS**, together with Archias, fortify Syracuse, II, 1036 A. An earthquake swallowed up the Corinthian Sea, I, 481 A.

**CORNELIUS NEPOS**, I, 330 A.

**CORNELIUS RUFUS**, a patrician, was expelled from the Senate because he possessed ten pounds’ weight of silver, I, 299 A.

The origin of **CROWNS** is something to be ashamed of because it arose from falsehood, II, 85 A. The Greeks are acknowledged to have been either the originators or the elaborators of the practice, ibid. A crown upon a woman’s head is a procurer of beauty, the supreme mark of wantonness, the uttermost denial of modesty, and a concentration of allure, II, 98 A. The golden crowns of provincial priests, I, 687 C. The pagans crowned brothels, latrines, mills, prisons, gladiatorial schools, amphitheaters, even the rooms where the slain were stripped, and acts of lust themselves, II, 97 B. Harpocration’s ivy crowns, II, 85 B; the laurel crowns of Bacchus, II, 86 A; and of soldiers, II, 84 B. Christians did not wear crowns, I, 493 A. The crown of Christian soldiers, II, 94. Christ’s crown of thorns, as a figure of the sins that the earth of the flesh brought forth for us, II, 98 B. It was prefigured by the thickets in which the horns of Abraham’s ram were entangled, II, 636 B, C.

Everything that exists is a **BODY** of its own kind, II, 774 B; as is whatever possesses something through which it exists, ibid. Body is the substance of each thing, I, 230 A. Between body and nothingness Tertullian recognized spiritual substance, II, 230 A. The property of color inheres in every body, II, 660 B. The great difference between the divine and human body, II, 303 C. What the human body is, II, 844 C. The body is that which loses the soul and, by dying, becomes dead, II, 491 C. From flesh it is earthly; from blood, watery, II, 771 A. No body can have blood unless it is flesh, II, 461 B. The wondrous arrangement of the body’s members, II, 882 sqq. Corresponding to the arrangement of the members is the order of the vices, II, 955 B. Whether the human body is the work of angels, II, 801 A. It is shaped like a cross, I, 678 B. According to Plato’s view, our body is a prison, II, 741 A. Whether the body, acting as a tomb, confines the soul and detains it in the death of worldly life, II, 820 B. The body is the vessel of carnal works, but the soul is what compounds within it the poison of any evil deed, II, 491 C. The animal spirit is the charioteer of the body, II, 740 B. The corruption of the body is accidental; integrity is proper to it, II, 878 B. We are born in this integrity, ibid. After the soul has departed, the bodies of the dead become heavier, II, 658 A. The bodies of the dead were devoured by certain Scythians, I, 321 A. In a cemetery, one body made room by withdrawing so that another body could be placed beside it, II, 738 A. Why bodies treated with burial spices are set apart in mausoleums and monuments, II, 834 B. Nails and hair grow in the tomb, II, 736 B. Many heretics deny that salvation has been promised to the body, II, 796 B. How the body is said to be sown an animal body, II, 872 C, 875 A. At the resurrection the same bodies in which people died will receive their souls, I, 746 B. The flesh feeds upon Christ’s body and blood so that the soul too may be fattened upon God, II, 806 B. See **EUCHARIST**. According to the Apostle’s teaching, the body is God’s temple when it is in Christ, II, 741 A. Emaciation does not displease Christians, for God did not bestow flesh by weight, II, 978 A. The Apostle connects contempt for bodies with the excellence of martyrdoms, II, 856 A. A body, or association of persons gathered together, I, 468 A.

[Col. 1533]

The **BODY OF TIMES**, an age, I, 432 A.

A **CORRUPTIVE THING** is not the same as corruption, II, 870 B.

God, the **FEEDER OF RAVENS**, II, 951 C.

**CORYBANTIC BRONZES**, I, 426 A.

The Greeks called the world κόσμον (*kósmon*, “cosmos”), I, 375 A. Why, ibid.

The **WEALTH OF CRASSUS**, I, 337 A. He died from laughter, II, 739 A.

**CRATES’** manner of dress, II, 1046 B.

**CRATIPPUS**, writer, II, 729 A.

The greatness of the **CREATOR** in animals, II, 261 A. See **GOD**.

Nothing is to be **BELIEVED RASHLY**, II, 468 D. What it means to believe rashly, ibid. See **FAITH**.

**CREDITORS** cut their debtors into pieces, I, 287 A.

**GREEK-STYLE**, or **CHALK-WHITENED, SANDALS**, II, 1045 A.

A **LITTLE SANDAL**, or **RATTLE**, II, 1044 A.

**CHRIST’S RATTLE**, II, 618 A.

They fabricated the tale that **CRETE** was Jupiter’s birthplace and tomb, I, 426 A. Cretans are liars, II, 683 B.

**JUDGES**, or censors, II, 129 A.

**CRITIAS** said that the soul consisted of blood, II, 653 A.

**CRITOLAUS’** opinion concerning the soul, II, 653 A.

The **CROCODILE**, a god of the Egyptians, II, 302 A.

**CROESUS**, deceived by the ambiguity of oracles, I, 408 A. No god of the pagans was richer than he, I, 337 A. He secretly cooked a tortoise together with lamb’s flesh, I, 409 A.

**CRUSTUMIUM**, or the town of the Casinians, I, 420 A.

The character of the **CROSS** is a sign derived from wood, I, 577 C. A part of the cross is present in a ship’s yardarm, II, 346 B. The nations recognized the cross, I, 366 sq. The origin of the gods was fashioned from a cross by sculptors, I, 340 sqq., 365 sq., 579 A. How the pagans worshiped crosses, I, 366 sqq., 578 A. The human body is shaped like a cross, I, 678 B. The sign of the cross is present in a person who prays with outstretched hands, I, 578 B. The horror of the punishment of the cross, II, 629 B. Regulus was the first to suffer the punishment of the cross, I, 584 A, C. Christians were placed upon crosses, I, 340 A. Christ’s cross was prefigured in the Old Law, II, 636. Christ’s cross was composed of an upright and a transverse beam, or yardarm, and a seat or footrest, I, 366 A, 578 A; II, 626 C. In what sense Christ’s cross is foolishness, II, 481 sqq. By the power of the cross Christ now winnows the world through the cross, and will afterward winnow it through judgment, II, 346 B. Christians are devotees of the cross, I, 365 sq. The posture of the cross is necessary for those who will fight against the devil, II, 347 A. We sign our bed and our little body with the cross, I, 1296 A. At every entrance and departure, when dressing and putting on shoes, at baths, at tables, at lights, in bedrooms, upon seats—whatever activity occupies us—we wear down our forehead with the sign of the cross, II, 80 A.

The **TRUMPET AND LANCE OF THE GNAT**, II, 261 B.

**WORSHIP** must be entirely free and voluntary, I, 435 sq. No one, not even a human being, would wish to be worshiped by someone unwilling, I, 418 A. It belongs to human right and natural liberty for each person to worship what he thinks proper, I, 699 A. Human error worships everything except the Creator of all things himself, I, 666 A. By a woman’s adornment we mean the attire that they call feminine finery, I, 1309 A. No mode of dress is cursed by God except feminine dress upon a man, II, 281 B.

**COVETOUSNESS** does not consist only in desiring what belongs to another, I, 1261 A. With what excuses people disguise the insatiable desire of the flesh, II, 927 A. See **DESIRE**.

The Roman **SENATE-HOUSES**, I, 464 A.

**CURIOSITY** concerning divine matters must be avoided by Christians, II, 20 B. Let curiosity yield to faith, II, 27 B. Many curious speculations are suspect in the exposition of parables, II, 997 B. Through curiosity women introduce rivalry in lust, I, 1288 A. Heretics pour out the lust of curiosity, II, 27 A. The curiosity, or superstition, of the Caesars, I, 296 sq.

**CURIS**, father of the Faliscans, I, 421 A.

**CURIUS’ DICE-PLAY**, II, 1049 A.

The chariot’s inventor, **TROCHILUS OF ARGOS**, I, 641 B. See **FOUR-HORSE CHARIOT**.

**PRISONERS AWAITING JUDGMENT**, I, 496 B.

**CYBELE**, a goddess represented in theaters, I, 570 A. She sighs for the disdainful shepherd Attis, I, 359 A. She migrated to Rome, I, 424 sqq. She did not know of the emperor Aurelius’ death, I, 425 A. Beasts yoked to Cybele, I, 341 A. The chief priest of Cybele poured out his own blood as a libation to her, I, 425 A.

The **BLOODSTAINED MOUTHS OF THE CYCLOPES**, I, 308 A.

The **CYNOCEPHALI**, a people, I, 312 C.

Who the **CYNOPENNAE** are, I, 312 A, 570 A.

The **KINGDOMS OF CYRENAICA**, now Christian, II, 611 A.

**CYRUS** both overwhelmed and oppressed Asia, II, 727 A. Scars left upon him by a she-bear, II, 751 A. He reigned for twenty-four years, II, 614 A.

# D

**DACI.** The nation of the Dacians subjected to the yoke of Christ, II, 611 A.

**DEMONS.** They have no individual name, but find a name where they also find a pledge, [Col. 1534] I, 684 A. Their substance is spiritual, I, 404 B, 438 A; II, 717 B. Impure, subtle, invisible, incomprehensible, polluted, unchaste, and ruined spirits, I, 415 B. Christians believed that demons truly exist, I, 405 ff. Their name known to poets and philosophers, I, 405 A. The common people frequently use the word “demon” as a curse, ibid. The demons called *Antelii*, I, 684 A; II, 97 B. A demon is everywhere, and its curse is everywhere, I, 618 B. Demons are everywhere in a single moment, I, 407 A. They emulate divinity by stealing divination, I, 408 A. They discern things through God’s ordering, ibid. When, from their dwelling in the air, they already perceive rain, they promise it in advance, I, 409 A. Things that appear to have occurred beyond the order of nature are nothing but their illusions, ibid. By their arts and illusions they produced the oracles and miracles that pagans ascribed to the agency of their gods, I, 408 ff. They reside in idols, I, 646 A. They are refreshed by victims and the odor of sacrifices, I, 415 B. They give ambiguous responses, I, 408 A. The demon of the Pythian oracle, I, 1175 A. Food for demons, I, 700 B. They are the magistrates of this age, I, 688 B. *Daemonium* is a diminutive of *daemon*, I, 447 B f. There is a race of demons born from the intercourse of wicked angels with women, I, 405 A. Demons condemned in advance for the day of judgment, I, 415 B, 434 A. Whether they work to destroy human beings as a consolation for their own perdition, I, 434 A. From the beginning of the world they have plotted humanity’s destruction, I, 406 A. Demons possess the subtlety and fineness necessary to attack both components of a human being, ibid. A demon is accustomed to join itself to the soul because of their common substance and their difference in nature, II, 693 A. Almost no human being is without a demon, II, 748 A. The lusts of demons directed toward dreamers, II, 732 B. Among the lustful activities of demons is both the removal and the introduction of dreams, II, 733 B. Demons bring about premature and frequent deaths, II, 748 A. They sometimes hide beneath the identities of the dead, II, 748 B. Demons fear, flee from, and hate Christians, I, 413 A. They serve Christians, I, 413 B, 434 A. They do not dare lie to them, ibid. Every day Christians reject, refute, expose, and expel demons from human beings, I, 700 B. Adjured by Christians of any kind, they are driven from the human bodies they possess, I, 413 A, 463 B, 677 B, 700 B, 703 B. How boldly the pagans were challenged to conduct a similar test, I, 413 A. Deliverance from demons is a cure of illness, II, 373 B. See **ANGELS (evil), CROSS, DEVIL, SATAN, SERPENT**.

**DALMATIANS.** Fierce, II, 683 B.

**DAMASEUS.** Formerly assigned to Arabia, II, 339 A.

**DAMIGERON.** II, 747 B.

**TRANSMISSION OF CONDEMNATION.** Its origin, I, 613 A.

**DANAUS.** Later than Moses, I, 386 A.

**DARDANUS.** II, 747 B.

**DARIUS.** Reigned over the Babylonians and Parthians, II, 611 B. How many years he reigned, II, 614 A.

**DARIUS,** also named Melas, reigned for twenty-two years, II, 614 A.

**DAVID.** Ruled the one Jewish nation, II, 388 C. Became guilty of murder and adultery, II, 14 B. Through bloodshed he forced a marriage upon himself, II, 937 A. Having confessed the offenses committed against the house of Uriah, he obtained pardon, II, 305 A. By confession he expiated the killing of Uriah, whose cause was his adultery, II, 990 B.

**DEBTORS.** How they were punished in former times, I, 287 A.

**DEBT.** In Scripture it is a figure of transgression, I, 1162 A.

**DECIMA, the goddess.** II, 713 A. A tenth part of one’s goods owed to Hercules, I, 349 f. Withheld from him by pagans, ibid.

**THE NUMBER TEN.** Parent of the remaining numbers and perfecter of human birth, II, 714 A.

**BEAUTY.** By nature an incitement to lust, I, 1317 B. The desire to please through beauty does not arise from an entirely sound conscience, ibid. Beauty is not to be condemned as a bodily blessing, an addition made by divine craftsmanship, or a kind of elegant garment for the soul, I, 1319 A. Yet it is to be feared because of the insult and violence of those who behold it, ibid. See **FORM**.

**THE DEAD.** It was formerly believed that the souls of the dead were propitiated with human blood, I, 644 C. Certain barbarians ate the bodies of the dead, I, 321 A. A certain dead woman was raised after a priest offered prayer, II, 737 B, C. Christians made offerings and prayed for the dead on annual commemorative days, II, 79 B, 942 C. See **DEAD PERSONS**.

**DEJERATIO.** What it is, I, 692 A. Forms of oath commonly used among pagans, I, 436 A, 692 A, B.

**INFORMERS AGAINST CHRISTIANS.** Subjected to a more dreadful punishment, I, 291 A, 296 A.

**TRANSGRESSION.** Every transgression is either committed or conceived in thought, I, 1232 A. Some transgressions are carnal, that is, bodily, while others are spiritual, I, 1231 B. Even intentions to transgress, without outward effects, are customarily imputed to the soul, II, 719 B. Transgressions of the will forbidden, I, 1232 C f. Principal transgressions, I, 1258 B. The seven stains of capital transgressions, II, 375 A, B. Why transgressions [Col. 1535] do not appear in the flesh, I, 1204 A. There are certain transgressions of daily occurrence to which we are all subject, II, 1020 A. Transgression has a harder brow, having been taught shamelessness by the transgression itself and within it, II, 891 A. There is no necessity to transgress for those whose sole necessity is not to transgress, II, 93 A. Every transgression is irrational, II, 673 A. The instigation of transgressions comes from the devil, ibid. Transgression flows from its own source into the various channels of crimes, I, 1258 B. The cessation of transgression is the root of pardon, II, 1001 A. Punishment is appointed for transgressions committed in flesh, spirit, deed, and will, while pardon through repentance is promised, I, 1233 A. Every transgression is expunged either by pardon or by punishment, II, 985 A. The primordial transgression is expiated through the practice of greater abstinence, II, 958 B f. See **SIN, REPENTANCE**.

**PLEASURES.** They must be examined, since the strength of faith may be emasculated by their softness and indulgence, I, 1332 A.

**DELOS.** The island was destroyed, I, 480 A; II, 1034 A.

**DOLPHINS.** They were vowed to Neptune, I, 639 C.

**DELPHI.** Apollo did not defend the city from the hand of Pyrrhus, I, 607 B. The Delphic inscription: **KNOW YOURSELF**, II, 676 B.

**DELVENTIUS.** God of the people of Casinum, I, 420 A.

**DEMETRIUS OF PHALERUM.** I, 387 B. Why he is called the most highly approved of grammarians, I, 379 A. Superintendent of Philadelphus’s library, ibid. He obtained the translation of the books of the Old Testament from Hebrew into Greek, ibid.

**DEMIURGE.** II, 572 ff.

**DEMOCRITUS.** Calls the spirit’s want sleep, II, 721 C. His opinion concerning the soul, II, 667 A, B. He blinded himself because he could not look at women without desire, I, 510 f.

**THE ELOQUENCE OF DEMOSTHENES.** I, 337 A.

**TRANSFORMATION.** Must be distinguished from every indication of destruction, II, 876 A. What “to transform” means, ibid.

**TEETH.** Given to moderate the strokes of the tongue and to mark the articulations of the voice by their contact, II, 883 C. They remain incorrupt in the tomb—for what purpose, II, 885 A. The setting of the teeth, II, 882 A; their rows, I, 312 B.

**DEPORTATION.** Christians underwent it, I, 341 A.

**DEPOSITS.** Christians faithfully restored deposits entrusted to them, I, 703 C. The deposits of piety—what they are, I, 470 A.

**DEBRICES.** See **SCYTHIANS**.

**GOD.** “God” is his proper name, I, 451 A. Whence he is called Θεός (*Theos*, “God”), I, 590 D. The name of his very substance, that is, divinity, I, 591 A; II, 199 C. Through the fault of human error, “god” has become a common designation, II, 497 C. The name “god,” as though the natural name of divinity, can be shared with all to whom divinity is claimed to belong, II, 341 C. God is reckoned God from his substance, not from his name, II, 254 A. God cannot exist without a cause—that is, without a reality corresponding to the name, II, 259 C. God alone is without origin, II, 468 C, D. He was neither begotten at all nor made, II, 203 C. God alone existed before all things; he was himself world, place, and everything to himself, II, 160 A. Yet he was not absolutely alone, since he had Reason within himself and, within Reason, the Word, whom he would make second to himself by inwardly setting him in motion, II, 160 D. God is a body, although spirit, II, 102 C. See **BODY**. God is spirit, wholly free of every bodily concretion, I, 399 A. What God’s hands, feet, and eyes signify, II, 303 C. The Platonists called God incorporeal, the Stoics corporeal, I, 517 A. Heaven is God’s seat, I, 377 A. How varied the philosophers’ opinions were concerning God’s nature, I, 507 ff., 516 ff., 588 C f.; and concerning his seat, I, 518 A, 588 C.

That God exists is proved from the creation of the world and its contents, I, 375 f.; from motion, I, 590 C; also from the testimony of our soul, I, 376 f.; from Holy Scripture, I, 375 ff.; and from the power granted to Christians to expel demons, I, 416 ff. God has as his witnesses the entirety of what we are and that in which we exist, II, 258 A. Things worthy of God prove God, II, 266 A; as do his works and benefits, II, 265 A.

That God is one is proved by the authority of the divine Scriptures, I, 375 f.; because he created the entire world from nothing, I, 524 A, as an adornment of his majesty, I, 375 B; by the common agreement of pagan philosophers, I, 515 f.; from his other works, I, 375 f.; from the innermost perception and testimony of the human soul, I, 376 f.; and from his infinite perfections, II, 249 C ff., 376 A. All people naturally recognize and revere the one God, I, 588 A, B. God is either one or no God at all, II, 250 A. God is one, and is not God otherwise, II, 249 C. If he is God, he must necessarily be one, II, 201 B. Whether God has always been Lord, II, 199 B, C. God must be believed to be the supreme greatness, but one and singular, II, 201 B, 251 A. He is called another God with respect to person, not substance, for distinction, not division, II, 166 B, 168 B, C. God is the Word, but with God, because he is God from God, because he is with the Father beside the Father, II, 173 B. God brought forth the Word as a root brings forth a shoot, a spring a river, and the sun a ray, II, 163 C. See **CHRIST, SON, FATHER, WORD, TRINITY**, etc., etc.

God is the supreme greatness, established in eternity, unborn, unmade, without beginning and without end, [Col. 1536] II, 240 B, C. God is the supreme greatness in form, reason, force, and power, II, 249 C ff. Through the singularity of his excellence, he possesses a certain solitude, II, 251 B. God is supremely great, supremely good, and one, II, 286 B. He alone knows how great he is, I, 376 A. Nothing is equal to God, and his nature differs from the created condition of all things, II, 757 B. This is preeminently proper to God: he admits comparison with no example, II, 250 C f. Everything in God is natural and innate, II, 271 A. In God everything must be rational, just as it is natural, II, 272 B. God must be believed immutable and incapable of assuming form, since he is eternal, II, 190 D. He is beyond estimation, even though estimated by human senses, I, 375 B. Incomprehensible, although represented by grace; invisible, although seen, ibid. It is plainly foolish to judge God by our own perception, II, 759 B. God is perfect in all things, II, 274. He is most perfect, I, 334 A, 375 f. He alone is perfect, II, 304 A. Some deny God his own properties—simplicity and power, I, 1201 B.

God is eternal, before all time, I, 375 f., 397 A, 432 A; II, 160 A. A new god is necessarily a false god, II, 255 A, B. From eternity God was rational, though not yet “verbal,” and why, II, 160 A, B. God sees all things, I, 500 A, 1232 A. He is at once invisible and visible, II, 170 C ff. See **FATHER**. God was seen according to human capacity, not according to the fullness of divinity, II, 170 C. Freedom, not necessity, belongs to God, II, 212 A. Neither perversity nor deceit belongs to God, II, 166 D; nor weakness or falsehood, II, 774 B. Nothing is impossible to God except what he does not will, II, 756 B. God must be believed on no other principle than that he is believed able to do all things, II, 809 A. For God, to be able is to will, and not to be able is not to will; but what he willed, he was both able to do and demonstrated, II, 166 A. Examples of divine power, II, 810.

God is immeasurable, I, 376 A. Every place is in God, but he himself is not in a place, because he is the ultimate boundary of the universe, II, 175 C. God is within the abysses and is present everywhere, but through force and power, II, 184 C. God alone is blessed by virtue of his intrinsic incorruptibility, II, 304 A. God is wholly good, since for the sake of good he is all things, II, 300 B. God’s goodness always acts in concert with reason, II, 273. God is supremely good from his own standpoint, just from ours, II, 812 B. Although God is good by nature, he is nevertheless also just, II, 984 A. The true God grants all his gifts equally to the profane and to his own people, II, 699 B. God deals equally with the whole human race, both showing indulgence and rebuking, I, 489 A. Nothing from God is sudden, because nothing from God is unordered, II, 323 B. Plato and the Platonists affirm God’s providence; Epicurus and the Epicureans deny it, I, 517 A. What things are unworthy of God, the supremely good, II, 266 A, 278. In what things God’s patience appears, I, 1252. How great God’s patience is, II, 813 A.

God is a just and severe judge, II, 302 A. His justice is the fullness of his divinity, II, 300 B. He is not contentious, II, 699 A. What God condemns is nowhere and never excused, I, 653 A. He neither condemns his past judgments nor is ignorant of the future, II, 311 A. Insofar as God is God, he neither admits evil nor condemns good, II, 373 D. With him there is no place for repentance concerning either good or evil, ibid. God alone is without sin, II, 720 B. He is not the cause of sin, II, 296 B; nor of evil, II, 209 ff.

God is the creator of the universe, governor of the whole world, fashioner of humanity, and planter of all nations, II, 599 A. By his nature God knows no idleness; if he ceased to act, he would not exist, II, 271 B. God moves in orderly fashion, matter in disorder, II, 235 C. God’s movement is free and eternal, ibid. God is the first author of all motions, I, 590 C. He created the world and all things from nothing, I, 324 A. By his word he commanded them to be made, by reason he ordered them, and by his power he established them, I, 375 A; as an adornment of his majesty, I, 375 B. He completed all his works in order, II, 222 C. God’s breath was capable, so to speak, of firing clay into another quality—just as clay is fired into earthenware, so it was fashioned into flesh, II, 804 A. Whenever the clay was being shaped, Christ, the future man, was in view, II, 802 B. What is born is God’s work; what is artificially fashioned is the devil’s business, I, 1321 B. God is not pleased by what he himself did not produce, I, 1312 B. Everything not from God is perverse, I, 1317 A. Everything belongs to God, and nothing to us, I, 1261 A. Nothing belonging to God has a price, I, 470 A.

What God purposed and revealed, he provided beforehand throughout the intervening span of the ages in figures, riddles, and allegories, II, 483 B. God was found to be little so that humanity might become greatest, II, 317 C. God lived upon earth and assumed the lowliness of human condition, II, 303 A. He allowed himself to be born in his mother’s womb, endured growing to maturity, etc., I, 1252 B. God—and indeed the more exalted God—laid the pinnacle of his majesty beneath such humility that he subjected it even to death, and death on a cross, II, 316 C. Whether God was crucified, II, 760 B, C. God truly crucified, truly dead, and truly raised again, ibid. And this we must believe by faith, II, 317 C. To believe God dead [Col. 1537] and yet living for ever and ever belongs to Christians, II, 303 B. Marcion denied that God was changed into a human being, II, 757 A. God could not enter into human relations unless he had assumed human perceptions and affections, II, 316 B.

God could not and ought not to have remained unknown, II, 256 f., 265 f., 325 A. The force of his greatness presents him to human beings as both known and unknown, I, 376 A. Philosophers declared that God is difficult to discover and describe, I, 509 A. God has always been known and was never hidden, because he has always shone forth, II, 285 A. He is unknown only to heretics, ibid. In Paul’s time no one disputed about God, II, 270 A. God is known to everyone through nature and conscience, II, 798 C. God must first be known through nature and then recognized through doctrine, II, 266 B. Those ignorant of God must necessarily also be ignorant of what belongs to him, I, 1227 A. The greater part of humankind knows the God of Moses, II, 257 C. The Romans worshiped the God of the Jews, I, 432 A. Moses’ pen traces knowledge of God from the beginning of the world, from paradise and Adam, and not merely from Egypt and Moses, II, 257 B. We are instructed concerning God by the Prophets and Christ, not by philosophers, II, 303 B. We know God through Christ, II, 647 B. God is known to no one without Christ, II, 647 B. Christ is fully known to no one without the Holy Spirit; the Spirit is imparted to no one without Baptism, ibid. The acknowledgment of God sufficiently understands what duty rests upon it, I, 1255 B.

God must be feared, II, 278 C, D. God is believed the more when he is feared the more, II, 104 A. God gives authority to discipline; discipline does not give authority to God, II, 383 C. God is a hearer not of the voice but of the heart, just as he is its beholder, I, 1175 A. God suffices for everything, I, 1232 A. Whoever has God has everything, I, 1281 B. Just as God appointed a span of life for humanity, so humanity drew upon itself the condition of death, II, 294 A. We shall be gods if we merit becoming those of whom he foretold, but by his grace, not by any property of our own, II, 202 B. The Christian soul’s natural testimony concerning God, I, 611; II, 798 A. The Christians’ God represented as an ass-headed figure (*onochoites*), I, 372 A, 579 B. Pagans ought not to deny Christians the ability to worship God, I, 699 f. We worship God through Christ, I, 403 B.

The gods of paganism derive their origin from Saturn, I, 329 A, 601 B; or, according to Varro, from Jupiter, Juno, and Minerva, ibid. Gods and demons share the same kind of name, I, 413 A. Whence people fashioned so many gods for themselves, I, 133 A. History and monuments testify that such gods were once human beings, I, 328 ff. It is certain that several of them reigned, I, 428 A. Above their innumerable gods they placed another, more exalted deity, I, 332 B, D. Human mediocrity finds it easier to fabricate gods than to follow the true God, II, 266 C. Antiquity erred in its worship of the gods, I, 306 A. So many and such great gods could not be worshiped by everyone, I, 573 A, 645 f. The existence of the gods cannot be proved even by certain alleged signs, miracles, and oracles, I, 395 ff., 408 ff.

Xenocrates devised a twofold class of gods, and Dionysius, Arcesilaus, and Varro another, threefold class—namely, physical, mythical, and national or popular gods, I, 587 ff. These classifications are refuted, ibid. The natural philosophers brought the gods low, I, 502 A, because they said they were the elements of the world, I, 589 B. The mythical class of gods, invented by poets, is rejected, I, 594 B. They said those gods were dead heroes, ibid. Literature and actors’ performances portray their foulness, I, 358 f. Their crimes and most shameful deeds were represented in the amphitheater, theaters, on the stage, and in comedies and tragedies, I, 353 ff., 358 ff., 573 ff. The national or popular class of gods is rejected, I, 595 ff.

The gods are shown to be false, I, 349 ff.; by the testimony of pagan conscience, I, 328 A; because they could have received divinity neither from themselves nor from others, I, 333 ff.; and by the public confession of demons adjured by Christians, I, 413 ff., 417 A, B. They are again shown to be false from their bodily forms—human, goat-like, bovine, leonine, avian, and those of other animals, I, 374 A, 574 ff., 577 C. Their servitudes, chains, battles, and wounds, I, 351 A, 575 B. They were mere human beings, I, 328 A, B. They were made gods either because of virtue and certain illustrious deeds, I, 334 f.; because of benefits bestowed upon humanity, ibid.; or because of things they invented, I, 606 C. The whole fabrication of the gods is insulting and impious, I, 339 ff. Gods made according to human whim, I, 344 A, 347 A, 596. Not without a decree of the senate, I, 290 A, 304 f., 344 B, 375, 575 A; nor without Caesar’s will, I, 439 A. Gods and domestic vessels were customarily fashioned from the same material, I, 339 A.

The pagans destroyed the gods they feared; those they defended, they mocked, I, 344 A—even in their own temples, I, 363 A. They feared them less than the emperors, I, 437 A. The gods ought to have avenged their injuries rather than rewarded acts of flattery, I, 431 A. They laughed at Roman emperors being made like themselves, I, 347 A. See **DEMONS**.

The number of local gods was infinite, I, 645 f. They were imagined to preside over marriages and the begetting of children, I, 600 C. Each province and city had its own god, I, 418 f., 596 A. How falsely they were called the guardians and tutelary deities of provinces and cities, I, 424 ff., 607 A, B. They gave kingdoms to no one, [Col. 1538] I, 423 ff.; nor could they give them, ibid.; nor could they protect kingdoms, their temples, or themselves, I, 438 ff.; nor confer salvation upon anyone, ibid. They allowed their own homelands to be overthrown, I, 426 ff.

Who the public gods were, I, 598 A. Put up for sale under the spear and by the quaestor’s notice, I, 345 ff. How the majesty of the gods was turned into a source of profit, I, 346 A. Altars exposed for unknown gods among the Athenians, II, 255 C; and for uncertain gods among the Romans, ibid. Private and household gods, I, 344 B. Sold according to each person’s whim, I, 344 B, 347 A; and pawned or exchanged, ibid. The holier and more ancient they were, the more liable they were to taxation, I, 346 A. Gods selected and rejected, I, 344 A, 596; adopted, I, 596 A, B. Begging gods, I, 494 A; for whom the Christians did not suffice, ibid. Different people worshiped different gods, I, 344 A. In what dress and with what insignia the gods were honored, I, 347 A, 360 ff., 547 B; with a dishonorable head, I, 360 A. Whom the pagans called one “possessed by a god,” I, 413 A.

Who the gods of the Roman pagans were, I, 597 B f. They are rejected, ibid. Wrongly divided by Varro into certain, uncertain, and chosen gods, ibid. They might somewhat more appropriately have been divided into common and private gods, but this too is refuted, ibid. Their private gods, I, 419 ff., 606; foreign gods, I, 423 f. It is false that the Roman Empire was founded or extended because of their worship, I, 422 ff. They surrendered their own homelands to devastation by the Romans, I, 424 ff. The Jews despised them, I, 432 A. Marcion introduces two gods, like two clashing rocks of shipwreck, II, 248 B.

**DEVIL.** Whether he was created by God, II, 296 B, C. He was created by God for good, II, 297 B. In what sense the designation “devil,” arising from his accusation, can apply to the Creator, II, 519 A. The devil produces a counterfeit of divinity, II, 86 B. He wishes to make Christ a liar, I, 655 A. The devil is an imitator of divine things, I, 977 A. He imitates the things of God, I, 1205 A; II, 102 B; the truth, II, 154 D; and the sacraments, II, 928 C. He imitates the realities of the divine sacraments, II, 54 A. He imitated the exacting character of Jewish law, II, 55 A. The devil is an adulterator of nature, I, 1312 B. He broods over pagan waters so that people may be deceived, I, 1205 B. What is born is God’s work; what is artificially fashioned is the devil’s business, I, 1321 B. The Valentinians call the devil the Demiurge who rules the world, II, 576 A. The devil’s serpentine force, I, 651 A. Weakness and wickedness belong to him, I, 1164 A. The devil’s devices must be recognized, II, 102 B. His fiery darts, through which the scorching and conflagration of faith are effected, II, 106 C.

He is always at work and daily adds something to his devices of iniquity, II, 889 B. The birth of impatience in the devil, I, 1256 A. He perverts the understanding of heretics, II, 54 A. The devil is the author of transgression, II, 296 B, 301 B. The instigation of transgression comes from the devil, II, 673 A. Creator of the evils of sin and guilt, II, 301 A, B. He struck down the first human beings, I, 651 A. He thinks himself sovereign if he dislodges the saints from the religion of God, II, 620 B. He even teaches one to offer the cheek patiently to be struck, I, 655 A. That most obstinate enemy never gives his wickedness any rest, I, 1241 A. The devil’s sole work is to test what is within you—whether you will consent, II, 916 B. He does not produce the will within you but finds the will already in his possession, ibid. The devil will have no power over the servants of the living God unless the Lord permits it, II, 104 D, 105 C. He receives his power from God’s servants, II, 106 A. Initial faith in the devil is built up from the beginnings of instruction, II, 675 B. The devil’s pomp, which we renounce in the seal of faith, II, 65. If you have renounced the devil’s pomp, know that whatever you touch from it is idolatry, I, 689 B. The devil’s reply when, during an exorcism, he was accused concerning a Christian woman whom he had possessed in the theater, I, 657 B. See **DEMON, SATAN, EVIL SPIRIT**.

**ARISTOTLE’S DIALECTIC.** A chameleon-like craftsman of building up and tearing down, constrained in its propositions, harsh in its conjectures, and a producer of contentious arguments, II, 20 A. Dialectical Christianity is rejected, II, 20 B.

**Διαμαστίγωσις (*diamastigōsis*), that is, scourging.** A most solemn observance among the Lacedaemonians, I, 626 A.

**DIANA.** Goddess of the Scythians, II, 136 B, 953 A. Diana represented as a virgin, I, 574 B; scourged, I, 358 A.

**DIASARES.** See **DUSARES**.

**DIDO.** Burned herself alive so that she would not experience a second marriage, I, 625 B; II, 929 A, 952 B. Dido’s steadfastness, I, 584 A.

**DAY.** It dies into night and is buried everywhere in darkness, II, 810 A. Prayer should be offered at the beginning of the day, I, 1193 B. Three more notable hours divide the day, I, 1192 A, B; II, 966 B, C. They were more solemnly observed in divine prayers, ibid. Every nation observed one day of the week as a festival and holiday, I, 579 A, B. See **LORD’S DAY**.

**DIESPITER.** A god, I, 600 C. His function, ibid.

**TWICE-MARRIED MEN.** Removed from priestly office, II, 922 A. The Apostle does not permit twice-married men to preside, I, 1286 A.

**FINGER OF GOD.** What it signifies, II, 427 A, B. The calculating gestures of the fingers, I, 387 A.

**DIGNITIES OF THE AGE.** Hostile to God, I, 690 A. The insignia of dignities, I, 300 A.

[Col. 1539]

**LOVE.** The supreme sacrament of faith and treasure of the Christian name, I, 1268 B. Perfect love drives demons away and gives life to confession, II, 147 A. Nothing can be loved without that through which it is what it is, II, 759 B. With God as teacher, patience accompanies love, I, 1269 A.

**FLOOD.** It did not cover only the plains, as Plato thought, but destroyed the entire world, I, 481 A; II, 1033 A. This is proved by shells and trumpet shells found on mountains, II, 1033 B. In the flood even the heights floated, ibid. All cities are later than the flood, I, 482 A. Through the waters of the flood ancient iniquity was cleansed, I, 1209 A.

**DIODORUS THE GREEK.** I, 330 A; II, 85 A.

**DIOGENES.** A little dog barking from his tub, II, 1043 B. With muddy feet, and with another kind of pride, he trampled Plato’s proud couches, I, 511 A; II, 1043 B. He lit a lamp at midday while searching for a human being, II, 247 B. He desperately loved the prostitute Phryne, I, 510 A. When asked what was being done in heaven, what answer he gave, I, 588 C.

**DIOGENES** (perhaps Diagoras). Mocked Hercules, I, 355 A.

**DIOMEDES.** He and his bloodstained mangers, II, 1041 B.

**DIOMEDES THE ACHAEAN.** Almost killed Aeneas, I, 351 A.

**DIONYSIUS OF RHODES.** II, 728 A f.

**DIONYSIUS THE STOIC.** How he divided the gods into three classes, I, 589 A. He distinguished them into gods that were born and gods that were fabricated, I, 605 A.

**THE DIONYSIAN MYSTERIES.** I, 474 A. Instituted among the Greeks by Liber, I, 643 A.

**DIS, or Pluto.** Represented in the amphitheater conducting the funeral processions of gladiators, I, 576 C.

**LEARNERS.** Who they are, II, 15 B, 43 A.

**DISCIPLINE.** Nature is the first of all disciplines, II, 82 A. Doctrine is the indicator of discipline, II, 58 B. License is very often a test of discipline, II, 923 C. Those who deny punishment despise discipline, II, 808 C. Evidence from discipline contributes to the proof of truth, from which no one who remembers the future judgment can safely turn aside, II, 50 A. The vices of the flesh and the age draw people far away from divine disciplines, I, 1283 A. The vain disciplines of the age, I, 1251 A. The Holy Spirit determines Christian discipline, II, 1001 C. The adversarial spirit is revealed by the difference in its preaching: first corrupting the rule of faith and thereby corrupting the order of discipline, II, 931 C. Secret discipline, I, 610 A.

**DISCIPLES.** They cannot exist without the teaching of masters, II, 367 B. Passive disciples, II, 548 A. The disciples believed Moses and the Prophets before they heard and believed Christ, II, 445 B. By listening to Christ, the disciples sketched out the Church, II, 768 C.

**DISCORD.** The discord of things is the same as that of their authors, I, 1256 B.

**BANDS OF REVELERS RUNNING ABOUT.** At pagan banquets, I, 477 A.

**THE RICH MAN.** Rarely found in the house of God; and, if one is found, rarely celibate, I, 1301 A. Churches are contemptible to wealthy matrons swollen with pride in their title, ibid. The Gospel’s “woe to the rich” is explained, II, 392 ff.

**RICHES.** Contempt for riches commended, I, 1260 B. The casting away and loss of riches, I, 1260 C. The Lord is found in no riches, I, 1260 B. Through riches many works of justice and love are performed, II, 393 A.

**DIVINATION.** Of the soul, II, 689 C; of demons, I, 408 f.

**DIVINITY.** Living and genuine divinity is assessed neither by novelty nor by antiquity but by its own power, II, 255 A. It has no degrees, since it is one, II, 204 A. It belongs to divinity to reckon as accomplished whatever it has decreed, II, 326 B. That which is subject to humanity must not be regarded as divinity, I, 416 A. The devil produces both a counterfeit of divinity, II, 86 B, and its meretricious enticement, I, 733 A. Those who prejudge divine things from human things are utterly foolish, II, 759 B. No divine utterance is so loosely composed that only the words are to be defended while a rationale for the words is constructed, II, 23 A.

**DIVORCE.** See **REPUDIATION**.

**DOCTRINE.** The indicator of discipline, II, 58 B. Every doctrine that savors of opposition to the truth of the churches, Apostles, Christ, and God must be judged false in advance, II, 33 B. Christ commanded nothing toward all people other than what the Creator commanded toward brothers, II, 937 A. The doctrine of the Apostles is the doctrine of Christ, II, 18 B. The more remote doctrine of the Apostles, II, 37 B. The kinds of adulterated doctrines that existed under the Apostles, II, 47 A. Every doctrine that agrees with the apostolic churches must be reckoned as truth, II, 33 B.

**TEACHING AND LEARNING.** Their principles differ, I, 675 A.

**DOMIDUCA.** A goddess, I, 600 C.

**DOMINION.** Just and orderly dominion alone is both feared and loved, II, 279 A.

**THE LORD’S DAY.** A feast day, I, 579 A; II, 79 B. On it Christians gave themselves to rejoicing, I, 371 A. It was considered unlawful to fast or to worship on one’s knees on the Lord’s Day, II, 79 B. The Lord’s Day observance was called the “day of the sun,” I, 371 A; II, 119 A. Whence that custom arose, I, 579 A, B.

[Col. 1540]

**LORD.** A name not of substance but of power, II, 199 C. “Lord” is the name of a power that is also to be feared, II, 278 C. To whom it was given, I, 450 f. “Lord” is a name of God, I, 450 A. The one God is Lord, I, 451 A. When Scripture adds the name “Lord,” II, 200 A.

**DOMITIAN.** A portion of Nero in cruelty, I, 293 A. More impure than Physcon, more effeminate than Sardanapalus, II, 1042 B. He quickly suppressed his attacks upon the Christians, I, 293 A. He recalled the Christians who had been banished, ibid.

**DONATIVE.** The soldiers’ donative, I, 455 A. What the donative of eternal life is, II, 862 A. The martyrs awaited Christ’s donative in prison, II, 77 A.

**OUR SLEEP AFTER DEATH.** Where it takes place, II, 744 A.

**DOSITHEUS THE SAMARITAN.** The first who dared deny the inspiration of the Prophets, II, 61 A.

**DRAGON.** From a distance it draws in human beings—or, according to another reading, birds—with its breath, II, 90 C. Jewels are extracted from dragons’ foreheads, I, 1311 A.

**DRUSILLANUS.** A slave of the emperor Claudius, II, 1048 A. He constructed a fiftyfold appetizer [the precise measure is uncertain], ibid.

**HARDNESS.** It must be overcome, not encouraged, II, 125 B.

**DUSARES,** or Diasares, Disares. God of the Arabs, I, 419 A, 596 A.

# E
## E

**EBION’S heresy**, II, 46, 67 A. It denies that Christ is the Son of God, II, 46 C. It presents Christ as a mere man, constituted solely from the seed of David, II, 778 B. It does not agree in every respect with Cerinthus, his teacher, II, 67 A.

**DRUNKENNESS AND LUST:** two demons allied and leagued together, I, 643 A.

**CHURCH:** the mother of Christians, I, 1154 B; II, 952 A. The true mother of the living, II, 723 B. It was prefigured by the wounding of Christ’s side, ibid. Christ is the head of the Church, II, 517 B. The Church is a virgin, the one bride of the one Christ, II, 382 A, 943 C. The Church exists where there is one or two; indeed, Christ is the Church, I, 1245 B. The Church is the body of three—namely, of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, I, 1206 C. Properly and principally, the Church is the Spirit himself, in whom is the Trinity of the one Godhead—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, II, 1226 A, B. The Church is the Spirit acting through a spiritual person, not the Church as a number of bishops, ibid. Where there are three, there is the Church, even if they are laypeople, II, 922 B. The Church was instituted by the Apostles, the Apostles by Christ, and Christ by God the Father, II, 33 B, 50 B. Origins of the churches, II, 32 B. Apostolic churches, II, 32 A, B. The apostolic churches are the mother churches and original sources of the Christian faith, II, 33 B. The Apostles founded churches in every city, and from them the other churches thereafter borrowed—and daily continue to borrow—the offshoot of faith and seeds of doctrine, so that they might become churches, II, 32 B. Churches founded by the Apostles or apostolic men are not to be despised, II, 32 sq. How they produce their registers of origin, II, 44 C, sq. Churches daily founded in Christ’s teaching are considered no less apostolic, by reason of the kinship of their doctrine, than those founded by Apostles or apostolic men, II, 45 B. So many and so great churches are that one first Church derived from the Apostles, from which they all come, II, 32 B. Peter’s Church, II, 1025 A. These churches are governed by no other principle than the one tradition of the same mystery, II, 32 B. The Church is a sojourner on earth, living among enemies, I, 260 A; yet it has its lineage, dwelling place, hope, favor, and dignity in heaven, ibid. It pleads for nothing concerning its own case, because it does not marvel at its condition either, I, 259 A. At times it desires only one thing: not to be condemned without being known, I, 260 A. The Church is in a state of alarm during persecution, II, 104 A. It cares for the imprisoned, I, 623 A. The little boat buffeted by the storm in the Gospel bore the figure of the Church, I, 1214 A. The leaders of the Church are not permitted to flee during persecution, II, 114 sqq. The unity of the Church is affirmed, II, 891 A; and its holiness, I, 1286 B. The authority of the Church establishes a distinction between the ordained order and the laity, II, 922 B. Nothing is to be handed down in the Church except what was commissioned by Christ, II, 18 B. Every doctrine agreeing with the apostolic churches must be reckoned as truth, II, 33 B. Ecclesiastical communion, II, 45 B. See **EUCHARIST, EXCOMMUNICATION**. The prescriptions of ecclesiastical discipline concerning a woman extend also to a virgin, II, 901 B.

**ECLIPSE:** an unusual eclipse of the sun in the territory of Utica, I, 701 B. Another famous one at Christ’s death, I, 401 A, recorded in the Roman archives, ibid.

**ECSTASY:** the power of the Holy Spirit that produces prophecy, II, 665 B. Ecstasy comes upon the soul in opposition to repose, II, 725 C. It is a displacement of the senses and something resembling madness, ibid. In ecstasy, understanding may be overshadowed, but it is not extinguished, II, 726 B. Difference between ecstasy and dreams, II, 725 sq.
