When a person is placed in the Spirit [Col. 1541], especially when beholding God’s glory or when God speaks through that person, the person must lose awareness, being, of course, overshadowed by divine power, II, 413 C.

**EDEA**, a goddess, I, 600 C.

**EDULIA**, a goddess. See **ELUDA**.

**Εἴδωλον** (*eidōlon*, “idol”): whence the word is derived, I, 665 A.

**ALMS:** those who refuse to give them, I, 1261 sq.

**ELEMENTS:** among the Romans, the first letters are commonly called “elements,” II, 476 C. Every position, arrangement, and motion of the elements, etc., constitutes judgments of the Creator, II, 299 B. The functions of the elements departing from their proper course, I, 391 A. Physical superstition regards the elements as God, II, 477 A.

**ELEPHANT:** the most witless beast, II, 803 A.

**ELEUSINIAN MYSTERIES**, II, 313 D, 539 A. It is sacrilege to disclose them, I, 309 A.

**ELEUTHERIUS**, bishop of Rome, II, 42 A.

**ELIJAH.** See **HELIAS**.

**ELIM:** the twelve springs, figures of the Apostles, II, 418 C.

**ELOGIA**, that is, censures and accusations, I, 271 A; discharged by judicial sentences, I, 496 A.

**ELUDA**, a goddess, I, 600 C.

**ELYSIAN FIELDS**, I, 520 A; II, 444 B.

**EMBRYOSPHACTES**, or *Embryonectes, Embryorectes, Embryopactes,* and *Embryosectes*: what it is, II, 692 A.

**CORRECTION** does not precede guilt, II, 366 A. Where there is no fear, there is consequently no correction, I, 1228 A. Where there is no correction, repentance is necessarily vain, ibid.

**EMMANUEL** means “God with us,” II, 337 A, 617 B.

**EMPEDOCLES** said that the soul consists of blood, II, 653 A. He located the cause of an acute or dull disposition in the quality of the blood, II, 683 B. Empedocles and Parmenides call sleep a cooling, II, 721 B. Empedocles’ friendship and enmity, II, 657 C. He raved that he was a god, II, 702 B, 1043 B. He believed himself to be a shrub and a fish, II, 702 B. Empedocles’ madness, II, 651 B. He leapt into the fires of Mount Etna, I, 532 A; II, 702 B. Why, ibid.

**ENNIAN UPPER ROOMS**, II, 550 B.

**ENNAEA**, II, 551 A.

**ENOCH:** the most ancient prophet, I, 665 C, 684 A. He possesses testimonial authority in the Apostle Jude, I, 1308 B. Enoch shows us that we can please God without the burden of the Mosaic Law, II, 601 B, sq. He condemns idolatry, I, 665 C, sq. What he instructed his son Methuselah, I, 1307 B. Enoch was translated from this world and has not yet tasted death, as a candidate for eternity, II, 601 B. Enoch and Elijah were translated, and their death was not encountered—that is, it was deferred, II, 733 A, 881 A. They are to extinguish Antichrist with their own blood, II, 733 A. The Book of Enoch defended, I, 665 B, 1308 A. The Jews and certain others reject it, I, 1308 A. Why, ibid. Could this book have been preserved through the Flood? I, 1308 sq.

**ARISTOTLE’S ENTELECHIES**, II, 703 B.

**ENTHYMESIS OF THE VALENTINIANS**, II, 564 A.

**Ἐπερχόμενος** (*Eperchomenos*, “the Coming One”), Marcion’s god, II, 416 C, 422 D.

**EPHALIDES** threw a bean into the common provisions, II, 701 C.

**EPHESIANS (TO THE):** the heretics call Paul’s Epistle to the Ephesians the Epistle to the Laodiceans, II, 500 B.

**EPHORUS**, an author, II, 728 A.

**EPICHARMUS**, comic poet, II, 677 B, 729 A.

**EPICURUS:** what sort of god he imagined, II, 391 C. He releases divinity from affairs, dissolves the order of things, and scatters everything into passivity as the product of chance, II, 726 B. Epicurus’ atoms, II, 703 B. His void and emptiness, II, 564 A. He maintains that the soul is made of atoms, II, 653 A. He locates it throughout the whole breastplate of the chest, II, 672 A. In his view the soul is not divine but mortal, I, 610 A; II, 19 B. Epicurus, according to the common opinion, denied that death concerns us, II, 721 A. He disparages all torment and pain, I, 500 A. Epicurus’ insensibility, II, 651 B. The Epicureans said that God arose from atoms, I, 517 sq., 588 C. Whether he exists outside the world, ibid. How falsely they denied Providence, ibid. They were permitted to determine some truth concerning pleasure, I, 467 A. The Epicureans call sleep a diminution of the animal spirit, II, 721 B. They hold that the senses do not deceive, but opinion does, II, 675 A. The school of Epicurus teaches that nothing remains after death, II, 795 B.

**EPIMENIDES**, asleep for nearly fifty years, II, 724 C.

**EPIPHANES** reigned for twenty-five years, II, 614 B.

**BISHOP:** the high priest, I, 1218 A. Bishops were chosen as men advanced in age and approved, I, 469 A. They received this honor not by payment but by testimony, ibid. The order and successions of bishops, II, 44 C. The Church, not a number of bishops, II, 1026 B. They presided over Christian assemblies, I, 469 A. The conferral of Baptism, I, 1218 A, and administration of the Eucharist, II, 79 B, belonged to them. Virgins were commended to the Church by them, II, 57 A. They were accustomed to enjoin fasts upon the whole people, II, 972 A, B. What form the Apostles gave to the episcopate, II, 119 A. Among heretics, one man is bishop today and another tomorrow, II, 57 A.

**EPIS­TATES:** Christ is our overseer, I, 624 B.

**EPISTLES:** [Col. 1542] Paul’s epistles mutilated by Marcion, II, 470 C. The aim of the Epistle to the Galatians, II, 470 C, sq. The ecclesiastical order is treated in the epistles to Titus and Timothy, II, 524 B.

**EPONA**, a goddess, I, 365 A, 577 D.

**EQUESTRIAN GAMES**, I, 641 A.

**EQUIRIA:** games Romulus named for Mars, I, 636 C.

**ERASISTRATUS** taught that the soul is in the membranes, II, 671 B. He gave his name to a school of physicians, I, 282 A.

**REBELLIOUS SLAVE-PRISONS**, I, 434 B.

**ERICHTHONIUS**, son of Minerva and Vulcan: a demonic portent—indeed, the devil himself, not a serpent, II, 24 B.

**ERIGONE**, a false goddess, I, 606 A. Depicted among the constellations, II, 142 A.

**ERROR:** one errs without punishment unless one commits an offense, II, 24 B. How delightful is the recognition of errors, I, 659 C. What is found as one and the same among everyone is not an error but something handed down, II, 40 B.

**ISAIAH** is sawn apart through the power of patience, I, 1270 B; II, 137 B.

**EZRA** restored the entire corpus of Jewish literature, I, 1308 A.

**ESSENCE** of things is the very “what” through which a thing is what it is, II, 664 A.

**“IS”** is the chief term of definition; “was” makes a statement of relation, II, 221 C sq.

**PAGANS:** understanding God only in part, they did not seek him, I, 485 A. In time of tribulation they invoked the God of the Christians, I, 703 B, C. By not believing, they believe—how, II, 780 A. They invented gods for themselves to worship, I, 486 A. They despised them, I, 699 B. They were impious, sacrilegious, and irreligious toward their own gods—how, I, 344 A. They were permitted to worship whatever god they wished, I, 344 A, 417 sq.—except the true God, I, 416 sqq. Rejecting their household gods, they honored certain gods chosen by themselves, I, 344 A, 596. They worshiped beasts of burden and geldings, I, 365 A. They invoked the divine powers of kings enrolled among the gods, appealed to their guardian spirits, and swore by them, I, 700 A. They had appointed Saturday for leisure and feasting, I, 371 A. They ruined the laws concerning divine matters, I, 298 sqq.; and the more sacred ordinances as well, ibid. Let no one learn the resurrection of the flesh from a pagan, II, 799 A. Departing from the institutions of their ancestors, pagans retained what they ought not to have retained and preserved things that were not good, I, 305 A. In dress, diet, equipment, property, and speech, they had dismissed their ancestors, I, 305 A, 572 B, C. Their immoderate banquets and gluttony, I, 473 sqq., 477 A, and avarice, I, 445 sq. Their more barbarous modesty, II, 912 B. They were guilty of homicide, of eating human flesh and drinking human blood; of fornication, adultery, and incest—the crimes of which they accused Christians, I, 271 sqq., 312 sq., 567 sqq., 571 sq. They also hated chastity, I, 472 sq. How dreadful their adulteries, ibid., and their incest, I, 325 sqq. They exposed or slaughtered their children, I, 315 sqq. How great was the injustice of those who condemned and killed Christians, unknown and undefended, solely because of their name, I, 280 sqq. By killing Christians they inflicted great harm upon the commonwealth, I, 496 sq. When pagans censured Christians, the very terms of their censure compelled them to praise them, I, 280 A. See **CAIUS**. Christians prayed for the confounding of the Gentiles, I, 1259 sq. During public disasters, pagans performed certain acts of public repentance by which they tried to appease the gods; and what these acts were, I, 487 sq.; II, 967 C. Though fed daily and about to dine again immediately, while the baths, taverns, and brothels were operating, they offered the *Aquilinia* rites to Jupiter, I, 487 A. They were fastidious and seditious, I, 456 sqq. Enemies of the emperors and the commonwealth, I, 457 A, 583 A, B. The Roman tongue spared no emperor, especially in the circus, I, 454 A, 583 B. They were always longing for the spectacle of one new emperor after another presiding over the distribution of a largess, I, 455 A. They broke into the palace, I, 458 A. Some were bolder than all the Ligerians and Parthenians, ibid. Associates or applauders of criminal factions, ibid. Astrologers, augurs, haruspices, magicians, I, 459 A. How falsely they made vows and sacrifices for the emperor’s safety, while swearing by their guardian spirits and celebrating their solemnities, I, 458 A, 700. See **GENTILES**.

**ETRURIA.** See **HETRURIA**.

**EUBULUS**, II, 652 C.

**EUCHARIST:** the reality of the sacrament of the Eucharist is established, II, 348 A, 460 C, sq. In the Eucharist the substance of Christ’s body and blood is present, II, 461 A, B. He made bread his body, I, 1260 A; II, 461 A. The bread is Christ’s body, ibid. In what sense bread is called a figure of Christ’s body, II, 460 C. Christ’s body is reckoned as present in the bread, I, 1160 A. Christ consecrated his blood in wine, II, 462 A. We are distressed if any of our cup or bread falls to the ground, II, 80 A. In the Eucharist the flesh feeds upon Christ’s body and blood, so that the soul too may be fattened upon God, II, 806 B. See **BREAD**. Ancient Eucharistic practice among the early Christians, II, 79 A, B. They received it in their hands, I, 669 A, from the priest’s hand, II, 79 A, B. Before any other food they tasted the Eucharistic bread, I, 1296 A. The sacrament of the Eucharist, both at mealtime and as commanded by the Lord to all, was also received at assemblies before dawn, II, 79 A, B. The Ophites bring in a serpent to bless their Eucharistic elements, II, 64 A.

**EUPHORBUS:** [Col. 1543] changed into Pythagoras, II, 698 A, 708 B, 796 A. Euphorbus’ shield, formerly dedicated at Delphi, II, 698 A.

**EUPHORION**, an author, II, 728 A.

**EVE:** a figure of the Church, II, 723 B. A beautiful comparison of Eve and Mary, II, 782 B. Into Eve, while still a virgin, crept the word that built up death, ibid. How she was deceived by Satan, I, 1257 A, B. She believed the serpent as though he were the Son of God, II, 65 A. She would never have sinned at all if she had persevered patiently under the divine prohibition, I, 1257 A. Eve gave birth to the fratricidal devil, II, 782 B. See **ADAM**.

**GOSPEL:** the substance of the New Testament, II, 196 B. Its authority, II, 363 B. The Gospel and Christ belong to him to whom both the Law and nature belong, II, 504 A. The Gospel corpus has as its authors Apostles—John and Matthew—or apostolic men—Luke and Mark, II, 363 B, C. Mark’s Gospel is affirmed as Peter’s, and Luke’s as Paul’s, II, 367 A. The duty of promulgating the Gospel was imposed upon the Apostles by the Lord himself, II, 363 B. The Gospel proclamation is God’s trumpet, II, 828 A. Marcion mangled the Gospels, II, 247 B, 363 B. The Law is the root of the Gospels, II, 125 B. Christ separates the newness of the Gospel from the oldness of the Law, II, 382 B. In the Gospel the same Divinity is proclaimed that had always been known in the Law, but the discipline is not the same, II, 471 B. The evangelists belong to no other than the one to whom the Law belongs, II, 487 C. The difficulties of the Law become facilities in the Gospel, II, 474 C. Gospel grace is nullified if Christ is brought back under the Law, II, 72 B. We have no need of inquiry after the Gospel, II, 21 A.

**EVERGETES** reigned twenty-five years, II, 614 B.

**ANOTHER EVERGETES** reigned twenty-seven years, II, 614 B.

**EXCOMMUNICATION:** separation from participation in prayer, the assembly, and every sacred fellowship, I, 469 A, 677 A; from every communion of the brotherhood, I, 1292 C. It is the highest preliminary judgment of the judgment to come, ibid. It was imposed only for grave offenses, ibid. One handed over to Satan is no longer rebuilt in the Church after his fall, II, 1023 A. Believers who entered marriages with pagans were subject to excommunication, I, 1292 C. See **BELIEVERS**.

**EXOMOLOGESIS** is that by which we confess our offense to the Lord, I, 1243 B. It is a discipline for prostrating and humbling a person, ibid. sq. After Baptism there remains in *exomologesis* a second means of aid, I, 1247 B. How great an evil it is to conceal an offense during *exomologesis*, I, 1245 B. See **REPENTANCE**.

**EXORCISMS** drive demons away, I, 657 B; II, 92 B, 748 B.

**EXORCISTS** cast demons out of the bodies of the possessed, I, 413 A, B.

**FUNERAL RITES** sealed by the sacrifice of captives and slaves, I, 645 A. See **VISCERATIO**. Christian funeral rites were performed with the prayers of priests, II, 737 B, C.

**EXTASIS.** See **ECSTASIS**.

## F

**BEANS:** the Pythagoreans reject them as a burdensome and wind-producing food, II, 732 C.

**FABIUS**, presbyter, to whom the book *On Flight in Persecution* was written, II, 103 A.

**FABLES:** why philosophers and poets invented them, I, 519 sq. Pagans fabricated some resembling things contained in Holy Scripture in order to weaken its authority, I, 395 sq., 399 B sq.

**FACE:** the mirror of all intentions, II, 814 A. Women soften a more austere face by washing it, II, 906 B.

**CRIME** places those whom it troubles on an equal footing, I, 300 A.

**A MADE THING**, as a body, is capable of being seen and touched, II, 814 A. A good deed has God as its debtor, as does an evil deed, I, 1230 B. No one has sinned by doing good, ibid.

**THE JUNO OF THE FALISCANS**, I, 421 A. She received her name from Father Curis, ibid.

**RUMOR:** the name for uncertainty, I, 310 A. It delights in falsehood and lives by it, I, 309 A. Why it is an evil, ibid. Nothing is swifter than rumor, I, 309 A, 566 B. No one believes rumor except the inconsiderate, I, 310 A. How great an evil it is to injure someone’s reputation, ibid. Rumor arises either from arbitrary suspicion or from pleasure in lying, I, 310 B, 567 A. Rumor lives only so long as it proves nothing, ibid.; only so long as it is uncertain and false, ibid. Rumor is sometimes slanderous toward barbarians, II, 733 B. The desire for fame after death is innate in almost everyone, I, 615 B.

**HUNGER:** faith does not fear it, I, 578 B. Faith knows that hunger, no less than every kind of death, must be despised for God’s sake, I, 679 A. During hunger there is no restraint of appetite, II, 282 A.

**FARIA.** See **PHARIA**.

**FARMUS**, a god, I, 600 C.

**FASCINUM:** what it is, II, 910 A.

**MUNICIPAL CALENDARS** cited, I, 638 A.

**FATE:** Zeno calls it god and word, I, 398 sq. Which pagan philosophers said that everything happens by fate, I, 268 A, 398 A, 560 B. By it the gods stand, even Jupiter himself, I, 428 A. [Col. 1544] Pagans attributed to fate an evil mind’s departure from innocence, I, 268 A, 560 B.

**FAUNUS**, son of Picus, I, 599 B.

**FEVER**, among the other fatal modes of departure allotted to humankind, II, 13 A.

**THE KALENDS OF FEBRUARY** celebrated among the pagans for the dead, II, 494 C.

**FELICULA**, an island, II, 550 B.

**EXCESS OF BILE** corrected by bitter drinks of every kind, II, 132 B.

**WOMAN.** See **FEMALE**.

**FENESTELLA**, commentator on the annals, II, 590 A.

**BITES OF WILD BEASTS** are ornaments of youth, as the bear’s scar was in Cyrus, II, 751 A. See **BEASTS, CATTLE**.

**JUPITER FERETRIUS:** Romulus instituted games in his honor, I, 637 B.

**WEDNESDAYS AND FRIDAYS:** station fasts, II, 956 A. School holidays, I, 674 B.

**IRON AND BRONZE** are of greater use to human beings than gold and silver, I, 1310 A. People prefer to die by iron rather than by water, I, 318 A.

**CHRISTIAN FEASTS**, I, 682 A. They celebrated them with an octave, I, 682 C sq. See **PASSOVER, PENTECOST**. How they celebrated the Lord’s solemnities, II, 119 A. At feasts Christians allowed the body some indulgence, I, 682 C. Pagans claimed no Christian solemnity for themselves, ibid. Their own feasts had no octave, ibid.

**GREEN FIG:** first brought to Rome by Cato, I, 606 C.

**BELIEVERS** are God’s temples, altars, lamps, and vessels, II, 89 A. Believers who contract marriages with pagans are guilty of fornication and must be subjected to excommunication, I, 1292 C.

**FAITH** is set within a rule, II, 27 B. What the rule of faith—the creed—is and what its character is, II, 26 B. It was instituted by Christ, II, 27 A. It is altogether one, alone immovable and incapable of reform, II, 889 A. Among Christians it gives rise to no questions except in dealings with heretics, II, 27 A. Both the rule and the reward of faith must be learned, II, 451 B. What must be believed was instituted by Christ, II, 23 A, 24 B. Most wretched are we if we do not believe the Lord even when he swears, I, 1234 B. Reason supports faith, II, 80 A. Let curiosity yield to faith, II, 27 B. The believer has fixed the whole extent of seeking and finding, II, 24 A. To believe is not given to everyone, because not everyone is a Christian, II, 655 B. The unlearned and simple are always the greater part of believers, II, 157 C. When we believe, we desire to believe nothing further; for this is the first thing we believe: that there is nothing further we ought to believe, II, 21 A. Praiseworthy is the faith that believes a command must be observed before it has learned it, II, 78 B. It is a perversion of faith not to believe what has been proved and to presume what has not been proved, II, 146 A. Faith shows the road by which we reach God, II, 421 B. The necessary disgrace of faith, II, 761 A. Discussion of what is necessary to faith is neither idle nor fruitless, I, 1256 A. Perverse people have violated, by heretical adultery, the virgin faith handed down by Christ, II, 59 A. A happy faith indeed, if it is to obtain those things which the enemies of God and Christ not only use but even abuse, II, 832 C. Faith did not exist on earth before Christ, I, 1260 A. Before the Lord’s Passion, salvation came through faith alone, I, 1215 A. Faith has always stood in the Creator and in Christ, but conduct and discipline changed, II, 270 A. Our faith owes obedience to the Apostle, II, 29 A. The quality of faith can be assessed from the character of one’s conduct, II, 56 A. An account of faith itself must above all be rendered before Christ’s tribunal, II, 59 A. Faith undergoes temptation and testing, II, 12 D. It is endangered after Baptism, II, 914 C. During persecution it is more vigilant and disciplined in fasts, II, 104 A. It does not fear hunger, I, 678 B. It owes the debt of martyrdom, II, 138 B. Faith needs external counsel against the necessities of the flesh, II, 914 C. The marvelous bond between faith and patience, I, 1260 A. Patience proved Abraham’s faith, I, 1259 B. Faith is perfected through love, II, 479 A, B. Unimpaired faith is secure concerning salvation, I, 1222 A. Christians are protected by faith, not money, II, 119 A. The condition of faith does not admit a plea of necessity, II, 93 A. Those who assemble fearfully in church reveal a faith plainly frivolous and cold, II, 106 C. Where there is faith, even wild beasts can do no harm, II, 421 B. If it can move mountains, much more can it move a soldier, II, 119 A. How old faith is, II, 906 B.

**ALTAR OF FAITH**, I, 417 A.

**FIGURES** prophesy and pass away when fulfilled, II, 937 A. The Lord and his Apostle spoke figuratively, II, 341 B.

**SON OF GOD:** whether he exists, who he is, and how he exists, II, 159 C. He is called **Λόγος** (*Logos*, “Word”) by the Greeks, I, 398 A, 400 B, 415 A; II, 160 A; and “Word” and “Wisdom” by the Latins, I, 398 sq.; II, 161 sqq. “Son” is a new name of the Father, I, 1155 A. The Son is second from the Father, II, 163 C, D. Whether the Son was seen by the Patriarchs, and also the Father, and how, II, 170 sqq. We derive the Son from no other source but the Father’s substance; he does nothing without the Father’s will and has received all power from the Father, II, 159 A. [Col. 1545] The Son of God is true God, to whom all the names of the true God are attributed, I, 399 A, 404 A, 415 A; II, 161 C sqq., 176 B, 183 sqq., 422 C, 802 B, C. He is on a par and equal with his eternal Father, Most High and almighty, ibid. His divinity is true and the same as the Father’s, I, 399 A. How explicitly Tertullian affirms that his substance and that of the eternal Father are the same, ibid.; even when the author was a Montanist, II, 158 sqq., 169 sqq., 183 sqq., 188 sqq., 422 C. This doctrine was handed down by the Apostles and thereafter, I, 399 A; II, 162 A. He was brought forth from God, Spirit from Spirit, God from God, and both are one God, ibid. Begotten from unity of substance and by procession, I, 399 A. He went forth from the Father as a ray from the sun, a stream from a spring, and a shoot from a seed, II, 163 C. He came forth from the womb but did not withdraw from it and is not separated from it, I, 399 A. He is distinguished from the Father not in status but in degree, not in substance but in person, I, 397 sqq. Second in order, not in nature, II, 157 B, C. Why John says, “I and the Father are one,” rather than “we are one person,” II, 183 C. Tertullian attempts to explain the generation of the Son, I, 399 A, because he is God’s Word, which possesses a substance of its own, ibid.; begotten by a spiritual procession from the Father’s substance and therefore the Son of God, ibid. Why he is properly called the Son of God, but the Holy Spirit is not, I, 163 sqq. How and why he endeavors to explain this generation of the Son through certain examples: the sun and its ray, the root and its shoot, the spring and its river, I, 399 A, B; II, 160 C, 163 B, 169 sqq., 183 A; and the inward human word, II, 160 C. He is distinguished from the Father by the designation of person, not of substance—for distinction, not division, II, 166 sqq. He possesses the same eternity as the Father, II, 162, 176 B, C, 183 C, 422 C, D. Sons of Christ: those reborn into him, II, 493 B. The Romans exposed or slaughtered their own sons, I, 325 A. See **INFANTS**.

**END OF THE WORLD:** imminent, I, 447 A. It is delayed only by the continued existence of the Roman Empire, ibid.

**SCOURGING:** what the greatest solemnity of the Lacedaemonians was, I, 626 A. The backs of slaves were torn open by whips, I, 301 A, C, D.

**FLORAL GAMES**, I, 638 A.

**GOD**, cultivator of flowers, II, 951 C. Christians used flowers, I, 492 A. To pursue a flower with one’s head is as contrary to nature as to take food with one’s ear or sleep with one’s nostril, II, 83 A.

**FLUVIONA**, a goddess, I, 600 C.

**BRAZIER** in pagan rites, I, 324 A.

**HEARTHS AND COUCHES** were brought out into public by pagans, I, 452 B.

**FEMALE** is the natural designation, II, 894 B. The general form of the natural designation is “woman,” ibid. Only one female was fashioned from Adam’s ribs, to demonstrate the unity of marriage, II, 920 B. Continence is more laborious for women, II, 903 B. A Christian looks upon a woman with his eyes unharmed, I, 511 A. Women’s modesty collapsed, I, 301 sqq. Churches are distasteful to wealthy matrons swollen with the prestige of their name, I, 1301 A. There is no distinction between matrons and prostitutes (*lupae*, literally “she-wolves”), II, 1044. See **WINE**. A woman’s attire displays a twofold form, I, 1309 A. An attack upon women’s luxury, I, 1221 sqq.; II, 1309. Women sin against God when they anoint their skin with preparations, stain their cheeks with rouge, and smear their eyes with soot, I, 1325 A. When they correct and add to his work, they find fault with the Creator, ibid. Those additions come from the devil, ibid. See **ADORNMENT, WOMAN**. Many women, and indeed highly distinguished ones, had attached themselves to Christ, II, 703. They were defended by pagan prefects against the raging populace, ibid.

**EXCESSIVE INTEREST** is usury, II, 398 C.

**FETUS:** when it is endowed with a soul in the womb, II, 691 A, B, 693 sqq.

**FORCULUS**, god of doors, I, 680 C; II, 97 B, 142 B.

**APPEARANCE:** a believer does not demand it, I, 1319 B. Whether it is permissible to enjoy praise for one’s appearance and glory in bodily beauty, ibid. Where chastity is present, beauty is vain—and why, ibid. A believing husband does not demand beauty of appearance; a pagan husband does not trust it, I, 1320 C. The deceits of one’s own appearance, I, 1325 A. Even Scripture suggests that embellishments of beauty are invariably associated with, and proper to, a prostituted body, I, 1330 B. See **ADORNMENT, WOMAN**.

**BEAUTY:** women both enhance what has been given and seek what has not been given, I, 1319 B.

**FORNICATION:** how great an offense it is, II, 987.

**ANT-HILLS**, II, 261 B. Whether ants, gnats, and moths lack lungs and arteries, II, 703 A.

**MEN BRAVE UNDER TORTURE** were awarded statues, images, and inscriptions, I, 534 A.

**FORTUNA BARBATA**, I, 601 A.

**THE GODDESS WOMANLY FORTUNE:** no woman placed a crown upon her unless she had been married only once, II, 952 C.

**BROTHERS:** Christians, I, 471 A. The designation “brotherhood,” I, 471 A; II, 32 B, 891 A.

**VEGETABLE MARKET** leased out for taxation, I, 345 A.

**ON THE FOREHEAD** Christians marked themselves with the cross, II, 80 A.

**FRUITS:** [Col. 1546] how they are formed, II, 890 A. See **FLOWER, GRAIN, SEED**.

**FRUGALITY** despises the world, I, 1288 A. See **ABSTINENCE**.

**GRAIN OF WHEAT:** a marvelous description, II, 871 A, B.

**FLIGHT:** permitted to the Apostles, but not to us, II, 109 A. The command to flee was temporary in the case of the Apostles, II, 140 A. This command had its particular rationale, II, 140 B, C.

**ONE STRUCK BY LIGHTNING FROM HEAVEN** is preserved, so that thereafter he may be reduced to ashes by no fire, I, 527 sqq. See **THUNDER**.

**FUSCIANUS**, prefect of the City, I, 582 A. His sentence passed upon a worthless father, ibid.

**FUTURE EVENTS** are sometimes declared in the Prophets as though they had already occurred, II, 326 B.

## G

**GAIAN HERESY:** see **CAIAN HERESY**.

**GABINIUS AND PISO**, consuls, though not Christians, expelled several gods, I, 305 A.

**GALBA** reigned seven months and six days, II, 616 A. He did not manumit other men’s slaves, although he would more readily have set free freeborn persons, II, 478 B.

**GAUL:** diverse peoples of Gaul already subjected to Christ, II, 610 C. The Gauls sacrificed to Mercury, I, 316 A. Gallic faces, or mules [reading uncertain], I, 1281 B. Gallic and German women had saffron-colored hair, I, 1322 A. African women envied their beauty, ibid.

**GALLI**, priests of Cybele, cut off their own genitals and gashed their arms, I, 413 A, 425 sqq.

**HEN** lays from her own substance, II, 557 A.

**GALLOGREEKS**, descended from the Gauls, I, 316 D.

**GANYMEDE**, I, 606 A. See also I, 600 B.

**FEATHERS OF THE GARAMANTES**, II, 903 A.

**GEHENNA** is a subterranean storehouse of hidden fire for punishment, I, 520 A, 1247 B. It is perpetual, ibid. *Exomologesis* extinguishes Gehenna, ibid.

**GEMS:** whence they come, I, 1310 B. Together with gold, they are joined to pride, ibid. Thunderstones do not have a fiery substance merely because they flash with a glowing redness, II, 660 B.

**WHAT IS SAID GENERALLY:** let us understand it generally even when it admits a particular interpretation, I, 635 A. See **GENUS**.

**GENIUS:** a name for demons, I, 447 B; II, 718 A. Guardian spirits were under the power of Christians, I, 447 B. The emperor’s genius, I, 447 B, 583 A, B. Pagans swore by it, but Christians never did, ibid.; I, 700 A.

**GENTILES:** worshipers of a multiplicity of divinities, II, 170 A. The Gentiles’ complaints against Christians, I, 261 sqq. See **CHRISTIANS, PAGANS**. Why God did not give the Gentiles a law as he did the Jews, II, 599.

**NATION:** each nation has its own language, but the substance of language is common, I, 618 B. All nations have one soul but different voices, one spirit but different sounds, ibid. A.

**GENUS:** what is attributed to a genus extends also to the species, I, 1203 B. Cain, Abel, and Seth were in a sense the sources of the human race, II, 583 A. The increase of the human race, II, 699 C. It is diminished by public disasters, II, 700 B. See **HUMAN BEING**.

**KNEELING** forbidden on the Lord’s Day and from Easter to Pentecost, II, 79 sqq. Some did not kneel on Saturdays, I, 1191 A. Whoever extends his knees toward the brethren touches Christ and entreats Christ, I, 1245 B.

**GERMANS** are not permitted to cross their boundaries, II, 611 B. They were already subject to Christ, ibid. The Germans’ ringlets, II, 903 B. German bearers, I, 1281 B. Marcus Aurelius’ German campaign, I, 295 A, 703 C. See **GAULS**.

**GERYON**, II, 579 A. Threefold yet one, II, 1041 B.

**GETULIANS:** the nation does not cross its boundaries, II, 611 B. Various peoples of this nation had undergone Christ’s yoke, II, 610 C.

**GIANTS:** their most ancient corpses were not devoured, and their skeletons still survive, II, 854 B.

**GLADIATORS**, I, 620 A. Their trainers and overseers, ibid. They are cursed by Christ, I, 1254 A. Innocent men enter the arena so as to become sacrificial victims for public pleasure, I, 651 B. Gladiatorial spectacles were praised by pagans, I, 584 B. Unwilling men were driven by whips and rods to commit homicide, I, 653 B. They devoured wild beasts fattened upon human blood and flesh, I, 322 A, 584 B, C. They drank the blood of others whom they themselves had killed, I, 323 A.

**GLORY:** all glory is vain and stupefied, I, 1320 A. How great is the power of vainglory, II, 1042 B, sq. What it means to glory in the flesh, I, 1320 A. Desire for glory induces people to endure hardships, I, 626 A. Nothing is more hateful than glory, II, 911 A. The devout have no pursuit of glory, because glory is the means of self-exaltation, I, 1319 C. Glory is unlawful for those whose approval consists in the humiliation of the cross, II, 908 A.

**GNOSTICS:** derived from the Valentinians, II, 594 A. When [Col. 1547] they burst forth, II, 123 A. They reject martyrdoms, ibid. The heretical seeds of the Gnostics, II, 678 A.

**GOMORRAH AND SODOM:** the earth still smells of their conflagration, I, 482 sq. Its fruits turn to ashes, I, 453 A.

**THE GRACCHI:** thoroughly obscene, II, 1031 A.

**AESOP’S JACKDAW**, II, 562 B.

**GREEKS** seek their own wisdom, not God’s, II, 481 C. The gods of the Greek philosophers, II, 260 B. Greek skill in fashioning images, I, 430 A. Through them, the pursuits of the wrestling school were transferred to the Romans, II, 1040 A. Cato the Elder thought that they should be expelled from the City, II, 1039 B. A Greek woman gave birth to five sons at once, II, 656 A. See **ATTICA**.

**GREECE**, conqueror of Phrygia in the Trojan War, I, 425 A. Conquered by the Romans, ibid. Throughout Greece and certain of its barbarian regions, there are many churches, II, 890 B.

**GRAMMARIANS:** so named from Aristarchus, I, 282 A. Paul imposes silence upon them, II, 786 A.

**SEED** is sown without the clothing of a husk, without the foundation of an ear, without the protection of an awn, and without the pride of a stalk, II, 871 B. Seeds decay in the earth, ibid. A. God gives each seed a body as he wills, ibid. See **FRUITS**.

**DIVINE GRACE**, more powerful than nature, has in us the free power of choice subject to it, II, 685 A.

**THE LORD’S FLOCK:** the people of the Church; and Christ is the good shepherd, II, 992 A.

**GLUTTONY:** a murderer from the beginning in Adam, II, 958 A. Lust passes through voracity, II, 953 B. The companions of gluttony are lust and luxury, II, 953 B, 977 B. In hunger there is no restraint of appetite, II, 282 A. The gluttony of the Caesars, I, 298 sqq.

**GYMNASIA**, I, 661 B.

**GYMNASTIC ARTS** arose as disciplines of the Castors, Herculeses, and Mercuries, I, 664 B.

**GYMNOSOPHISTS OF INDIA**, II, 260 C. What divine powers they worship, ibid.

## H
HADRIAN, emperor, investigator of all curiosities (superstitions), I, 296 A. Entirely devoted to magical arts, ibid. sqq. He enacted no law against Christians, ibid.

HERESY, etymology of, II, 18 A, B. Every heresy comes from professors of wisdom, II, 260 B. Heresies are instigated by philosophy, II, 19 A. They all rest upon the powers of subtle speech and the rules of philosophy, II, 521 B. They do not differ from idolatry, since both their authority and their activity derive from the same source as idolatry, II, 55 B. They tear people away from unity no less than schisms and dissensions do, II, 17 B. Whatever savors of opposition to the truth will be heresy—even an ancient custom, II, 889 A. Heresy is an undertaking of human rashness, II, 366 B. Heresies bring eternal death and the burning of a greater fire, II, 13 B. Paul numbers them among the works of the flesh, II, 18 A. The Apostle named all the heresies known in his time, II, 47 B. Some constructed a new heresy from the Greek alphabet, II, 70 A. Why heresies must exist, II, 17 A. How powerful heresies are, and among whom, II, 13 B. They are very powerful among those who have little or no strength in the faith, II, 14 A. Many are vainly and thoughtlessly scandalized by the very fact that heresies have such power, II, 12 D, sq. Why, ibid. All heresies, when examined in many particulars together with their authors, are found to disagree radically, II, 58 A. They cannot exist without the Scriptures, II, 51 A, 53 A, 886 B. They could not exist unless the Scriptures could also be wrongly understood, II, 850 B. The Scriptures themselves have been so arranged by God’s will that they would furnish materials to heretics, II, 53 A. Heresies are refuted not so much by their novelty as by the truth, II, 889 A.

HERETICS arose from the seed of the philosophers, I, 519 A; II, 19 A, 204 C. The same subject matter is bandied about among heretics and philosophers, II, 19 B. They adulterated Sacred Scripture to conform to the opinions of philosophers, I, 519 A. They corrupt the Scriptures, II, 30 A. They deleted not merely syllables but entire pages, II, 515 D. They frame their questions solely from the Scriptures, II, 799 B. Among them there is a lust for argument, II, 780 B. Their sophistries and subtleties twist plain, ordinary words into questions, II, 222 A. They always seize upon bare or simple expressions and drag them by conjecture wherever they please; or, conversely, they dissolve conditional and rational expressions by imposing upon them the condition of simplicity, II, 404 C. It is customary for heretics to twist everything simple, II, 214 A. They provoke the devout to engage in rhetoric and philosophy, II, 801 A. Conscious of their weakness, they never present their positions in an orderly fashion, II, 797 A. How a disputation with heretics is to be undertaken, I, 797 A, B. One must not fight them from the Scriptures, III, 29 A. Those whom we prove, without recourse to the Scriptures, to have no claim upon the Scriptures must not be admitted to undertake a challenge concerning the Scriptures [Col. 1548], II, 31 A, 51 A. For there the victory is either nonexistent or equally uncertain, II, 31 A. Heretics are enemies of the truth, II, 27 B. They conspire to overthrow the one truth, II, 56 B. Their work proceeds from the destruction of the truth, II, 57 B. Among heretics everything is alien and opposed to our truth, and we are forbidden to approach them, II, 25 B. What is characteristic of all heretics, II, 179 B. Among them there are generally no schisms, and why, II, 57 B. At their own discretion they remake the faith, II, 58 A. In believing, they do not believe, II, 780 A. Their doctrine does not agree with the doctrine of the Apostles, II, 45. They abolish marriage, II, 930 C. They deny that God is to be feared, II, 58. Yet no heretic except Marcion raised a controversy concerning God as Creator of all things, II, 47 A. Most heretics do not even have churches; without mother, without see, orphaned in faith, exiles from themselves, they wander far and wide, II, 58 A. They cannot demonstrate successions of bishops deriving from Christ, II, 45 A. They are not Christians, II, 28 A; nor can they be, II, 51 A. Having lost the name of Christ, they assume the names of their own sects, ibid. The manner of life of heretics is described, II, 56. Their dealings with very many magicians, itinerant charlatans, astrologers, and philosophers—that is, with those devoted to curiosity, II, 58 B. What difference there is between a pagan and a heretic, II, 780 A. They strive not to convert pagans but to overthrow Christians, II, 57 B. All are puffed up; all promise knowledge, II, 56 B. Nowhere is advancement in offices and sacred orders easier than in the camp of rebels, II, 57 A. They show no reverence toward their leaders, II, 57 B. Among heretics everything is unrestricted and unregulated, II, 58 B. Why they are condemned by their own judgment, II, 18 B. It is proper that they be compelled to their duty, not persuaded into it, II, 125 B. Heretics of Judaism, II, 61 A.

HAMAXOBII, unsettled wanderers, II, 247 B.

HAMMON, shepherd of sheep, II, 1038 B.

HANNIBAL. See CANNAE.

HARPOCRATES with his dog-headed companion, I, 305 A. Expelled from the council chamber of the gods; his altars and statues were overthrown and later restored, I, 305 A, 573 B.

HARPOCRATION, writer, crowned with ivy in recognition of his industry, II, 85 B.

HEBION. See EBION.

HEBREWS rightfully take gold and silver vessels from the Egyptians, II, 308 sq. Their Hebrew letters and speech were rendered into Greek style by the Seventy translators, I, 380 A.

IVY strives upward and, with no one leading it, suspends itself, II, 681 B. It prefers to climb walls as a woven woodland rather than be trampled on the ground through self-inflicted injury, ibid. It is the nature of ivy to protect the brain from *helucus* [uncertain reading], II, 85 B.

HEGEMONIKON, what philosophers call by this name, II, 814 A.

HELEN, his Tyrian woman, was rescued from a brothel by Simon the heretic, II, 708 B, sq. He said that she was the same Helen who proved so ruinous to Priam, ibid.

ELIJAH, consummator of the New Testament and eventual restorer of the Jewish people, II, 413 B. Elijah has not yet discharged the debt of resurrection, II, 735 A, 881 A. Elijah is to come not by returning from death but by being translated back, II, 711 B. Nor is he to be restored to the body, from which he was not removed, but returned to the world, from which he was translated, ibid. Not by restoration to the rights of life, but by completion of his prophecy, ibid. He will be the same in person, in name, and in his human identity, ibid. See ENOCH. The spirit of Elijah, represented in Elisha, succeeds Elijah, II, 636 A.

HERACLEON, heretic, held opinions similar to Valentinus, II, 69 C, 546 B.

HERACLIDES, writer, II, 740 B, 788 A.

HERACLIDES OF PONTUS maintained that the substance of the soul is light, II, 660 B.

HERACLITUS, that “obscure” philosopher, II, 318 A, 651 A; teaches that the substance of the soul is air, II, 660 B, and that it consists of fire, II, 653 B, which he regarded as a god, II, 19 B, 260 B, 517 A. He defends the unity of the soul, II, 669 A. He thinks that the soul’s ruling faculty is moved from within, II, 671 B. What he thought about its limits, II, 651 A. The melancholy of Heraclitus, II, 651 A. Having smeared himself with cattle dung, he burned himself to death, I, 625 B.

HERBS: the properties of herbs were disclosed by the apostate angels, I, 1306 A.

HERCULES: *The Three Hungry Herculeses*, I, 358 A. *The Three Mocked Herculeses*, a comedy, ibid. Hercules wears now poplar on his head, now wild olive, now parsley, II, 85 B. Hercules was prostituted as a woman in Omphale, and Omphale as a man in Hercules, I, 605 B; II, 1011 B, sq. He was imagined to have descended to the underworld, I, 605 B. Because a boy was lost, he deserted the expedition of the Argonauts, ibid. Ensnared by the poisons of his wanton wife, he burned himself alive, I, 605 C. He is consumed by the fires of Oeta, I, 355 A. He was represented burning alive on stage [Col. 1549], I, 576 A. He was mocked by Diogenes (perhaps Diagoras), I, 355 A. See TITHE. The descendants of Hercules, II, 1035 B.

HERMAS, whose writing is entitled *The Shepherd*, II, 1000 B, C, 1021 A. That book is apocryphal, ibid.

HERMATELES, author, I, 640 A.

HERMIAS, an intimate of Aristotle, I, 512 A, B. Driven by Aristotle from his position, ibid.

HERMIPPUS, author, II, 729 A.

HERMIPPUS OF BERYTUS, II, 729 sq.

HERMOGENES, character and life of, II, 197 sq. He was accustomed to marry more wives than he painted, II, 951 B. He perverts the ways of the Lord, II, 45 B. Hermogenes introduces two gods, II, 201 B. He makes God a liar, II, 202 A, B. He denies that God could have made anything from himself, II, 198 B, 205 A, B. He teaches that matter was necessary to God for the works of the world, II, 216. God made the world from this preexistent matter, II, 204 B. He introduces matter as unbegotten and compares it with God as begotten, II, 46 B, 198 sqq. He says that matter is evil, II, 208 A, B. He makes it both corporeal and incorporeal, II, 229 C, sq. By the word “earth” (Gen. 1) he understands matter, I, 218. His sound reasoning discovers some third thing between the corporeal and the incorporeal, II, 230 A. He attacks the arguments of certain persons who say that evils were necessary so that good things might be understood through illumination by their opposites, II, 210 C. He presumed that the soul’s origin consisted in a contribution from matter rather than in God’s breath, II, 646 C, 664 B.

The oracle of HERMONIA in Macedonia, II, 730 A.

HERMOTIMUS: the people of Clazomenae granted a temple to Hermotimus after his death, II, 649 B. Pythagoras wrote that he had formerly been Hermotimus, II, 698 A. The soul of Hermotimus departed from his body, II, 649 B, 698 A, 702 A, 705 A.

HEROD was king of the Assyrians, II, 339 C. Why he killed John, II, 443 B, C, sq.

HERODIANS said that Herod had been Christ, II, 61 A.

HERODOTUS, historian, II, 740 B. Later than Charon of Lampsacus, II, 727 A.

HEROPHILUS, physician—or butcher—dissected six hundred people in order to investigate nature, II, 662 A, 692 A. He located the soul’s seat around the base of the brain, II, 670 B, sq.

HESIOD’S Pandora, II, 84 C, 562 B.

ETRURIA occupied by the Lydians, I, 636 A. It first established the names of the rites belonging to superstitious religion, ibid. Etruscan crowns, II, 95 B.

HICESIUS, physician and betrayer both of nature and of his own art, II, 691 A. He superinduced a soul upon children already born through the impact of cold air, II, 692 A.

HIERA, island, sank into the depths, I, 480 A.

JEREMIAH the prophet is stoned, II, 137 B.

JERICHO, although captured on the Sabbath, II, 309 B. How it was captured, II, 606 B.

HIEROGLYPHS. See OBELISK.

HIEROPHANT, I, 313 A; II, 260 C.

HIEROMUS. See IROMUS.

JERUSALEM, mother city of religions and fountain of salvation, II, 447 C.

HILARIANUS, prefect, I, 701 A.

HIMAEREA, a woman, dreamed of the tyranny of Dionysius of Sicily, II, 728 A.

HIPPARCHUS said that the soul consists of fire, II, 663 A.

HIPPIAS is killed while plotting against the state, I, 513 A.

HÍPPIOS (ἽΠΠΙΟΣ, “of horses”), an epithet of Neptune, I, 641 A.

HIPPO, or Hippona and Epona, was worshiped by pagans, I, 365 A, 577 D.

HIPPOCRATES wrote that the soul lies in the brain, II, 671 B.

HIPPON said that the soul consists of water, II, 653 A.

GOATS: what the two goats in the Old Law signified, II, 640 B, C. The sacrifice of a goat, I, 418 A.

SWALLOW: if it has blinded its young, it knows how to restore their sight with its own *caledonia* [celandine], I, 1248 A.

THE SPANISH LANDS: all their furthest regions already believed in Christ, II, 610 C.

SACRED HISTORIES extend back to the very birth of the world; secular histories begin with the Assyrians, II, 1035 A. How extensive the Roman histories are, I, 571 B.

HISTORIANS: the earliest Roman historians were later than the last prophets, I, 387 A.

ACTOR: a disgraceful and dishonorable actor represents the likeness of any god whatever, I, 360 A, 576 B. Writings for actors, I, 358 A. They portray the gods’ foulness, I, 359 A, 576 B. They represented Phaethon being dragged down from heaven, ibid.

HOMER remembered that he had been a peacock, according to Ennius, II, 707 A, 796 A. He assigned two gates to dreams: one of horn for truth, one of ivory for falsehood, II, 726 C. How greatly he made sport of the gods, I, 575 B. He treated divine majesty in terms of the human condition, ibid. The industriousness of Homeric piety, II, 745 B.

HOMEROCENTOS: this is what they customarily call those who fashion their own works out of Homer’s poems in the manner of a cento, stitching many pieces gathered from here and there into a single body [Col. 1550], II, 53 A.

MURDERERS: cruel punishment of, I, 653 B. Pagan murderers washed themselves with water to obtain impunity for their crime, I, 1205 A.

HOMICIDE in every form is forbidden by the single command: “You shall not kill,” I, 632 B. Every killing outside a forest is brigandage, II, 986 C. To prevent birth is an accelerated act of homicide, I, 319 A. How great the vengeance for homicide is among human beings, II, 706 B.

HUMAN BEING, a rational animal, II, 160 B. “Human being” is one name shared by all nations, I, 618 A. A human being is the handiwork of the Creator, I, 514 C. Created by God from nothing, I, 524 A. How fashioned by God, II, 82 A, B. The human being was first a molded figure and then a complete whole, II, 802 A. The work of fashioning the human being was completed from earthly matter with the cooperation of the waters, I, 1202 B. Let the human being recall his origin, I, 523 A. He was composed from a twofold substance, II, 452 B, 850 C. A human being is body as well as soul, II, 841 A. A human being is nothing other than flesh, II, 275 B. Properly called flesh, II, 802 A. See SOUL, FLESH, BODY. The human being was constructed by God himself for this purpose: that he might be able to be a lord, since he was made by the Lord, II, 801 C. All things are servants to the human being, I, 1256 B; II, 707 B. Beautiful description of the creation of the human being, II, 802 B, C. Creation of the human being according to the demiurge, II, 578 A. Whatever the clay was being molded into, Christ was contemplated as the human being who was to come, ibid. Christ, a human being mingled with God, II, 780 A. The human being was created in the image of God’s Son, who was to become a more certain and truer human being, II, 168 A. Fashioned in the likeness of the Son and the Spirit, ibid. Made in the image of God—that is, of Christ—II, 802 B, C. The human being was made in God’s image not in bodily outlines but in freedom and power of choice, II, 290 B. A human being was not established by God for death; God desires him restored to life, II, 294 A. If the human being had not sinned, he would have known God only as supremely good, I, 812 B. See ADAM. He was worthy to know God, II, 291 A, B. A preacher of Christ is worthier than Satan, II, 373 B. Why the human being was assigned to the earth and cast away from God’s sight, I, 1257 C. He is disposed toward good not by nature but by instruction, II, 291 C. Nothing is more necessary to a human being than care for the true God, II, 285 A. Whatever benefits the human being serves God, I, 1230 A. His entire substance is destined for salvation, II, 863 B. Who Paul’s “inner human being” is, II, 661 A, 850 C. The inner and outer human being: one in two respects, II, 661 A. Through the services of the outer human being, which minister to the inner human being, the fruits of divine gifts are conveyed by the senses to the soul, II, 82 B. Diversity gave balance to the human being himself, both in body and in perception, II, 264 C. See RACE. Angelic substance promised to human beings, I, 1307 A. The human being, under the title of the Pythian oracle, is lord of all the living and the resurrected, I, 525 A. Human beings were uncivilized in the time of Saturn, I, 331 A. Which people ate human flesh, I, 313 A. Some consumed human substance in a horrific crime, I, 323 A. Africans, Gauls, and Romans sacrificed human beings to their gods, I, 314 B, 316 sq. Where and for how long, ibid.

HOURS: the three hours, as the most distinguished in human affairs—which divide the day, distinguish occupations, and are publicly announced—were observed more solemnly in prayers to God, I, 1192 A, B; II, 966 C, B. Peter observed the ninth hour in accordance with ancient custom, II, 966 C.

HORON, an aeon of the Valentinians, II, 565 A, 577 A.

HORTENSIUS, the orator, was the first who could bring himself to kill a peacock for food, II, 1048 B.

HOSPITALITY: the exchange of tokens of hospitality among Christians, I, 1295 A; II, 32 B.

HOSTANES, II, 747 B.

SACRIFICE to God: a contrite heart, II, 608 B. Pagans sacrificed victims that were exhausted, diseased, and scabby, I, 349 A. See SACRIFICE.

HOSTIA, goddess of the Sutridans, I, 421 A.

HOSTIUS’ sacrilegious charms, I, 358 A, 576 B. His comedies, ibid.

HOSTILIUS invented Fear as a god, II, 266 C.

CONTEMPLATION OF THE HUMAN CONDITION, I, 626 C, sq. See HUMAN BEING.

HUMBLE: no one is humble unless patient, I, 1267 A. Christ teaches that those who always wish to be greater ought to become like little children, II, 417 A.

HUMILITY is professed by Christians, I, 1326 B. Some, undefeated under chastisement, offer the humility of their soul to God, I, 1327 A. Nothing is dearer to God than humility, II, 911 A.

HYENA changes sex annually, alternating between male and female, II, 1037 A.

HYDRA overcome by Hercules, II, 1042 A. The use of its blood, ibid.

HYDROPHOBICS, who they are, I, 1205 B.

WINTER in some fashion hardens souls, II, 732 B.

HYPOCRISY: God condemns all hypocrisy, I, 655 B.

HYPOCRITES have friendship with the devil, I, 1236 A. Their repentance never occurs, ibid.

HYPSOMA, the exaltation of the sun and its dwelling place, I, 701 B.

[Col. 1551]

## I

IAO, an expression used by the Valentinians, II, 565 A.

IBIS, goddess of the Egyptians, II, 302 A.

ICHTHYS (ΙΧΘΥΣ, “fish”): Christ; we little fishes are born in water, I, 1198 A.

PLATO’S IDEAS. See PLATO.

THE UNEDUCATED always constitute the greater part of believers, II, 157 C.

IDOLATRY, the principal crime of the human race, the supreme guilt of the world, the entire ground of judgment, I, 663 B. Sister of adultery, II, 129 A. Sacred Scripture uses the language of debauchery and fornication in its reproach of idolatry, I, 663 C. It is a form of funeral observance for the dead, I, 645 A. The chief form of injustice, I, 664 A. Affinity between idolatry and heresy, II, 55 B. It is composed of things belonging to God, I, 1313 A. All idolatry consists in the worship of human beings, I, 683 A. Human error worships everything except the Creator of all himself, I, 666 A. None of its solemnities is without ostentatious worship and adornment, I, 663 D. Among pagans no art, profession, or occupation can be free from the designation of idolatry, I, 677 B. A Christian will not practice idolatry with impunity, and why, I, 1313 A. The Jews were continually devoted to the crime of idolatry, II, 598 B. Magic is a second idolatry, II, 748 A.

IDOL: some time ago there was no idol, I, 664 D. Whence the name “idol” comes, I, 665 A. The names of dead idols are nothing, just as their images themselves are nothing, I, 643 B. God forbids both the making and the worshiping of an idol, I, 665 B. Nothing is more unclean than it, II, 90 A. In idols dwell the demons of the dead, I, 645 A. Satan and his angels had filled the whole world with idols, I, 640 B. See SCHOOLMASTER, IMAGES.

FIRE, the soul of the world according to Varro, I, 589 A. Fire is twofold: one kind common to human beings, another from heaven, I, 527 A. Fire appearing in God’s judgment, ibid. Fires hung above the walls of Carthage through the night, I, 701 B. Showers of fire upon Sodom, II, 1034 A. Fire is the supreme punishment, I, 625 A. Testimony concerning eternal fire, I, 528 A. From its very nature fire has the divine provision of incorruptibility, I, 527 A. The likeness of that fire will exist whose reality also exists, II, 435 A. This is confirmed by comparison with the fire by which Etna and Vesuvius burn perpetually, I, 527 A. Wicked and impious human beings will be tormented in eternal fire, I, 520 A, 1284 A.

IGNORANCE does not always excuse; sometimes it places a heavier burden upon the person afflicted by this fault, I, 261 sq. It is better not to know, lest you come to know what you ought not, II, 27 B. It is better not to know through God, because he has not revealed, than to know through a human being, because that person has presumed, II, 648 B. Some prefer not to know because they already hate, I, 265 A. Pagans, exceedingly curious about other matters, deliberately affected ignorance of the religion of Christ alone, I, 261 sqq.

IMAGE: how it differs from reality, II, 295 A. In all things reality precedes the image, II, 41 B. An image is reckoned according to representation, likeness according to eternity, I, 1206 A. Although an image is a fashioned representation of reality, the image itself possesses the reality proper to itself, II, 837 C. The human being—that is, the spirit—is the image of God, for God is spirit, II, 295 A. The image and likeness of God is contained in freedom and power of choice, II, 290 B, sq. God’s image must be recognized in the human being in that the human mind has the same movements and perceptions as God, though they are not of the same kind as God’s, II, 304 A. By a rival operation God recovered his image, which had been taken captive by the devil, II, 782 B. The use of images was not condemned by Tertullian, I, 667 B, C. He approved the bronze serpent, the cherubim, and other images, ibid. An image of the Good Shepherd depicted on a sacred cup, II, 1000 A. Why God formerly prohibited images to the Jews, II, 310 A, B. Images and statues of the gods must be rejected, I, 430 A. No animal was fashioned as an idolater: what was not in the ark must not be in the Church, I, 696 B. Brave men were awarded statues amid their torments, I, 524 A.

RAINS: continual rains destroyed everything at Carthage (around the year 212), I, 701 A. Achamoth purified the rains of heaven, II, 568 A. See RAIN.

THE WORLD’S UNCLEAN THINGS, human lusts, I, 622 A. When Christians encountered something unclean, they spat it out with a breath, I, 1296 A.

IMPATIENCE: how many disasters it is accustomed to incur, I, 1265 B. Its cradle, I, 1257 A. Its birth in the devil himself, I, 1256 B. What the causes of impatience are, I, 1260 sqq. Its greatest goad is lust for vengeance, II, 722 B. Every sin must be ascribed to impatience, I, 1258 B. Impatience and malice conspire with one another, I, 1257 A. Through impatience the first parents perished, I, 1257 B. Before Christ, impatience availed itself of opportunities afforded by the Law, I, 1260 A. The poisons of impatience must be cut away, I, 1267 B. To resort to impatience in every misfortune is characteristic of pagans, I, 1261 C. Pagans live impatient with God alone, I, 1274 A.

EMPEROR, inferior to God alone, I, 448 A. Second after God, I, 700 A. This is a great name, and why, I, 449 A. The emperor’s power comes from the same source as his spirit and life, I, 441 sq. Unless he is a human being [Col. 1552], he is not an emperor, I, 449 A. He is appointed by God, I, 448 B. Emperors desire the true God to be propitious to them above all others, I, 441 A. Provincial governors reported to emperors whatever new event had occurred among them, I, 290 B, 403 A. What dutifulness, religious observance, and loyalty are owed to them, I, 460 A. What Roman loyalty toward emperors consisted in, I, 583 B. Christians believed them to have been chosen by God, I, 448 B, 700 A. How Christians rendered them the loyalty due, I, 460 A, B. They honored them sincerely, and how, I, 448 B, 700 A. They prayed to God for their safety, I, 433, 700 A, B. But they were never willing to sacrifice, I, 436 A. The emperors’ safety, more august than all guardian spirits, I, 447 B, was neither to be sought nor expected from false gods, I, 440 A. Pagans swore by their guardian spirit, I, 583 B. But Christians steadfastly refused to do so, I, 447 B. They considered it sacrilege to call them gods, I, 441 sqq., 585 C. They swore by the emperors’ safety, I, 447 B; pagans did so even against their children and spouses, I, 599 A. Pagans rendered the same honor as to gods to their emperors, both dead and living, I, 347 A. They called them gods, I, 583 B. With what great impiety they affirmed this, I, 489 A. Emperors preferred to live rather than become gods, I, 585 C. Before apotheosis it was a curse to call them gods, I, 451 B. Pagans feared emperors more than gods, I, 437 A. Images of dead and living emperors, treated as gods, were placed and honored in temples, I, 347 A, 576 sq., 665 sqq. Emperors celebrating a triumph were reminded of their frailty, I, 449 A. They were masters of the gods, I, 347 A. Imperial solemnities, vows, and rejoicings were celebrated, I, 452 B; at the beginning of the month and year, I, 1298 A. With what impious worship pagans celebrated them, I, 452 B: by bringing hearths and couches out into public and feasting upon a victim, ibid.; by defiling the city with the guise of a tavern and forcing the wine to become mud, ibid.; by running about in crowds to commit outrages and pursue enticements to lust, ibid.; by covering their doorposts with laurels, I, 453 A; and by interrupting the day with lamps, ibid. Emperors were assailed with insults and defamatory pamphlets, I, 583 B. They were killed in their own palace, ibid.

THE ROMAN EMPIRE will stand as long as the world stands, I, 700 A. See ROMANS.

UNCHASTITY is not excused on account of the weakness of the flesh, II, 951 A. The theater is the council chamber of unchastity, I, 649 A.

INACHUS, contemporary of Moses, I, 386 A.

INCANTATIONS: the evil angels made known the powers of incantations, I, 1306 A.

ADVERSITIES are less than their rewards, II, 852 A.

INCORPOREAL: nothing is incorporeal except what does not exist, II, 774 B. See BODY.

UNBELIEF marvels but does not believe, I, 1201 B. Wretched unbelief, which denies to God his own attributes, ibid. A.

THE INDIAN SEA produces shells, I, 1311 A. The gymnosophists of India, I, 260 C.

INDIGNATION is rational when it arises from zeal for discipline, II, 673 C.

FASTING is always the consequence of grief, II, 962 C. It rekindles the health that overfeeding had extinguished, II, 958 C.

NEWBORN INFANT: the impediments encountered in birth, II, 758 C. Why infants weep upon entering life, II, 682 A. The movements of an infant’s soul immediately upon emerging from the mother’s womb are described, ibid. Whether infants dream, II, 733 B. Infants killed in the womb to preserve the mother’s life, II, 691 C, sq. How they were extracted, ibid. Psammetichus entrusted newborn infants to a tongueless nurse, I, 570 A, B. Why, ibid. At Athens certain children speak a month earlier with a precocious tongue, II, 685 A. Infancy is naturally spirited and emotional, II, 682 B. An infant who will become a human being is already a human being, I, 320 A. Christ, by receiving praise from the mouths of nursing infants and little children, declared neither childhood nor infancy dull-witted, II, 682 A. See INNOCENTS. Infants were destroyed in the womb by their mothers, II, 909 B. They were exposed to cold, hunger, and dogs, I, 318 A, 325 A. Pagans devoured them after cooking them, I, 580. Christians were called killers of infants, I, 306 A. In Africa infants were sacrificed to Saturn down to the proconsulate of Tiberius, I, 314 B. Their parents caressed them so that they would not be slaughtered while weeping, I, 316 A.

THE UNDERWORLD is located within the earth’s depths, II, 742 B, sq. Its fire will be everlasting, I, 520 A, 1284 A. See FIRE. The bronze bars of the underworld, II, 857 B. The pagan account of the underworld is not to be rejected, I, 527 A. Who suffer the punishments of hell, I, 335 B, sq. Whether all souls are driven there, II, 742. The underworld is one thing, Abraham’s bosom another, II, 742.

DISSUASION FROM INFERIOR THINGS is preference for superior ones, I, 1279 A.

WEAKNESS comes from the devil, I, 1164 A.

INTELLECT: from what it is produced, II, 683 A. Intellects are more acute among eastern and southern peoples, II, 692 B. What the devil’s inventions are, II, 102 B.

ENEMIES must be loved, and God must be entreated on their behalf, I, 446 A. Love of enemies belongs to Christians alone, I, 698 D.

[Col. 1553]

INIQUITY is employed in such a way that justice may be proved by putting iniquity to shame, II, 104 C.

INITIATION, I, 312 A. How it took place, I, 313 A. Profane initiations always exclude outsiders and guard against witnesses, I, 309 A.

INJURIES must be borne patiently and not returned, I, 499 A. The remedy for injury is patience, I, 1266 A. Christ prohibits not merely retaliation but also vengeance, and even the recollection and reconsideration of an injury, II, 395 B, C. See PATIENCE.

THE CHIEF FORM OF INJUSTICE is idolatry, I, 664 C.

THE INNOCENT INFANTS consecrated their testimony to Christ with their blood, II, 544 A.

TO LIBERATE THE INNOCENT befits divine benevolence, II, 815 A. The innocence of Christians, I, 496 sqq.

INO, goddess. See MATUTA.

TO SEE DIFFERENT MADMEN IN DIFFERENT PEOPLE, II, 675 C.

INSIGNIA of rank and honorable birth among the Romans, what they were, I, 300 A, D.

INSTITUTION: it is not the original institution of anything that should be condemned, but its deviation from the proper course, II, 281 A.

INSTRUMENT. See SCRIPTURE.

ISLANDS swallowed by the waves of the sea or by earthquakes, I, 480 A, 571 B; II, 1034 A.

TO UNDERSTAND is the same as to perceive, II, 678 C.

THE ENVY OF INIQUITY, I, 260 A.

INVISIBLE THINGS possess before God both their own body and their own form, through which they are visible to God alone, II, 162 C.

IONIANS, companions of Neleus, furnish Asia with new cities, II, 1035 B.

ANGER arises from impatience, I, 1258 A.

IRENAEUS, a most inquisitive investigator of all doctrines, II, 548 A. Tertullian acknowledges that he drew from Irenaeus, ibid.

IROMUS the Phoenician, king of Tyre, I, 387 B.

ISAAC, monogamous, II, 936 D, 952 B. Isaac carrying the wood prefigured Christ’s death, II, 346 A, 626 A, B. Isaac was preserved together with the wood when the ram was offered, II, 636 B.

ISIS first carried on her head the ears of grain she had discovered, II, 86 A. The linen accoutrements of Isis, I, 612 B. Isis was expelled from the council chamber of the gods and restored, I, 305 A, 573 B.

ISRAEL always sinned against God through impatience, I, 1259 A. Through fasting Israel immediately wiped away its sin, II, 962 A. See JEWS.

ISTER, deceitful, II, 247 B.

ISTHMIAN GAMES, rites established for Neptune, I, 644 A.

ITALY was first called Oenotria and afterward Saturnia, I, 330 A, 602 C. It was occupied by the Phrygians, II, 700 A.

## J
## J

**JACOB** was a figure of the later and more highly favored people, II, 356 C. Why the dew of heaven is promised to him first, and then the richness of the earth, II, 357 A. What his ladder signified, ibid. He saw the Lord Christ, ibid. B. He wrestles with the angel with the whole mass of his body, ibid. C. By imposing his hands obliquely in the form of a cross, he prefigured Christ in himself, I, 1208 A.

**JALDABAOTH**, the sum-total Aeon, II, 64.

**JANUARY FESTIVALS**, I, 681 C, sq.

**JANUS**, from *janua* (“door”), I, 683 C; II, 97 B. Two-faced Janus, I, 436 A. Janus, or Janes, as the Salii maintain, king of Italy, receives Saturn, I, 330 A.

**FASTING** is an act of reverence toward God, II, 963 A. What kind of fast the Lord chose, II, 834 A. What the Christians’ fasts were, and how rigorous, I, 487 A; II, 954 C, sq., 971 B. They did not fast on the Lord’s Day, II, 79 B; nor from Easter to Pentecost, II, 80 A. Some did not fast even on the Sabbath, II, 973 B. Fasts interrupted by the necessity of joy and thanksgiving for salvation, I, 1227 A. Fasts prescribed before Baptism, I, 1222 B, and before councils, II, 972 C. Bishops are accustomed to command fasts for the whole people, II, 972. A fast, or station, until the ninth hour, II, 966; and until evening, II, 967 B. Fasts merit from God not only a change in nature, the averting of dangers, or the obliteration of sins, but also the recognition of mysteries, II, 963 A. Droughts driven away by fasts, I, 703 C. Israel immediately erased its sin by fasting, II, 962 A. Christians nourished their prayers with fasts, I, 1244 A. What strength those who fast have with God; heaven fights on behalf of such persons, II, 962 B. So that man might more readily be formed for fasting to God, he was accustomed to few and unpretentious foods, and was to feel no hunger for richer fare, II, 306 B. The rigorous fasting of the Montanists, II, 97 B, 971.

**JERICHO.** See **HIERICHO**.

**JEREMIAH.** See **HIEREMIAS**.

**JERUSALEM.** See **HIERUSALEM**.

**JESUS**: why Christ wished to be so called, II, 342 C. It is the proper name of the Son of God, whereas “Christ” is an additional designation, II, 193 B. Whoever [Col. 1554] wishes to see Jesus should believe him to be the son of David through the Virgin’s lineage, II, 451 B. See **CHRIST**, **SON**.

**JOHN THE BAPTIST**, the conclusion of the Law and the Prophets, was called not a prophet but an angel, II, 137 B, 623 A. Yet he was an ordinary man and, as it were, one of the crowd, II, 402 B. In what sense he was greater among those born of women, II, 403. He was established as a kind of boundary between the old and the new, at which Judaism was to end and from which Christianity was to begin, II, 441 A. He is scandalized upon hearing of Christ’s mighty works, II, 402 A, B. Why he was slaughtered by Herod, II, 137 B, 443, sqq. See **BAPTISM**.

**JOHN**, Christ’s most beloved disciple, a eunuch, II, 952 B. His praise, II, 496 B, sq. Nothing escaped his knowledge, II, 34 B. He is the author of the Apocalypse, II, 46 B, 938 C. He founded the churches of Asia, II, 366 C. He exchanged tokens of fellowship with the African churches, II, 49 B. At Rome he was plunged into burning oil, but suffered no harm, and was banished to an island, II, 49 B. The region of paradise was revealed to him in the Spirit, II, 744 A. John died, though there had vainly been hope that he would remain until the coming of the Lord, II, 735 B.

**JOB**, his patience and praise, I, 1271 A. The devil could not have inflicted any temptation upon him unless he had received power from God, II, 105 A.

**JONAH**, swallowed by a sea-monster, after three days emerges from the fish’s belly unharmed and incorrupt in flesh and soul, II, 840 A. An image of the Lord’s Passion, II, 999 C.

**JONATHAN**, son of Saul, erased through intercession the guilt of having broken the fast, II, 378 A.

**JORDAN**, a river serving as an arbiter of boundaries, II, 1034 A.

**JOSEDECH** was clothed in no filthy garment whatsoever, but was always adorned in priestly vesture and was never deprived of the priestly office, II, 640 A.

**JOSEPH** prefigured Christ because he suffered persecution from his brothers and was sold into Egypt on account of God’s grace, II, 346 A, 626 B. He had only one wife and was better than his father, II, 937 A. He was sold into Pharaoh’s household, desired by the less-than-chaste queen, and cast into prison by the king’s command, I, 596 B. He disclosed means of deliverance from prison and received as his wife the daughter of King Pharaoh, ibid. The Egyptians regarded Joseph as a god under the name Serapis, I, 596 B, C.

**JOSEPH the Jew**, a native-language authority on Jewish antiquities, I, 388 A.

**JOSHUA**, a figure of Christ, II, 343 A, B. He did not marry twice, II, 937 A. See **AUSES**.

**JUBA**, king, I, 387 B.

**JUDAS the traitor** is defended by certain persons, who declare him admirable and great because of the benefit he is vaunted as having conferred upon the human race, II, 65 A. They hope for his restoration, II, 355 B.

**JUDAEA**, a people divided from the beginning into tribes, families, and households, II, 450 B.

**THE JEWS** read the sacred Scriptures publicly, I, 381 A. Through Moses they learned to worship God, I, 403 B. They found a spring of water in the desert when a wild ass pointed it out, I, 364 A. Their kingdom flourished as long as they obeyed the divine commandments, I, 393 A. After forsaking God, they served idols, II, 598 B. Cast out because of their sins, they began to be outside God, II, 21 B, 393 sq. By hoping only for earthly things, they lose heavenly things, II, 833 A. They wash every day because they are defiled every day, I, 1169 A, 1217 A. The Jews’ greeting, II, 480 B. Why the Jews rejected Christ, II, 329 A. They knew that Christ had been promised, I, 399 B, sqq. They deny his first advent and await the second, I, 400 A. They extend their hope toward the coming of Christ, II, 610 A. No Jew remains to the present day from whose lineage Christ could be born, II, 634 A. All power of understanding was taken away from the Jews, II, 328. Their hearts are covered and veiled, II, 499 A. They themselves bring about what was written: that they were punished by the loss of wisdom and understanding, and of the fruit of eyes and ears, I, 400 A. This was the deserved consequence of their offense, ibid. When Christ performed innumerable miracles, they said that he was a magician, I, 400 A, B. By violent voting they extorted the sentence that he be crucified, ibid. From Tiberius until the time of Vespasian they had an opportunity for repentance, II, 354 A. Now they wander as vagrants throughout the world, I, 393 sq. They suffered dispersion because of Christ, the meaning of the Scriptures agreeing with the outcome and sequence of events, II, 638 B. The Jews were forbidden even to greet their homeland by setting foot upon it, and by what law, I, 394 A. The Jews are enemies of Christians through rivalry, I, 308 A. They most cruelly harassed Christ’s disciples, I, 403 A. A certain utterly depraved Jew, at the cost only of his skin, carried around in the games a ridiculous image of the Christians’ God, bearing the still more absurd inscription **ONOCHOETIS**, I, 372 A, 579 B. For forty days, in the reign of the emperor Severus, a city hung from heaven in Judaea during the morning hours, even pagans being witnesses, II, 356 A.

**JUDGE**: every judge is a requiter of the cause, I, 1230 B. He can both discharge the duty of his jurisdiction and remember humanity, or because he himself is under the sword, I, 702 B. If judges condemn persons unheard, [Col. 1555] they will deserve suspicion of some guilty awareness, since they refuse to hear what, once heard, they could not condemn, I, 260 A.

**JUDGMENT**: whence the first origin of judgment—from sin, I, 1257 B. It is unlawful to pass judgment concerning unknown matters, I, 261 A. Its sure and most equitable rule is that no one be condemned undefended and unheard, I, 270, sqq. Pagans followed this rule against pagans, but never against Christians, I, 274 B, D. The injustice of pagan judgments toward Christians, I, 270, sqq. In these proceedings, the charge was not a crime but the name, I, 278 A. Judgment belongs to God alone, II, 103 C. God’s judgment is full and perfect, and consequently everlasting, II, 813 A. He established an eternal judgment concerning the grateful and the ungrateful, I, 699 A. His judgment does not turn upon fetter or cap of freedom, but upon the eternity either of punishment or of salvation, I, 1255 A. The day of the Last Judgment is described, I, 660 B, C. All human beings must present themselves before this judgment, I, 523 A. The merits of every human being will be examined, I, 527 A. Nor can this be denied by the pagans, I, 415 A, 519 B, sq. Fear of judgment conduces to good, not evil, II, 299 C.

**JULIAN LAWS** concerning the marriage of the social orders, and whence they were so called, I, 286. See **LAW**.

**JULIUS.** See **AUGUSTUS**.

**BEASTS OF BURDEN** were worshiped by pagans, I, 365 A.

**JUNO**, born on Samos, raised there, and married to Jupiter, I, 427, sq. She could not endure the destruction by the Romans of Carthage, which she had preferred to Samos, II, 427, 607 B. The judgment involving her and Minerva, I, 359, sq. A table is set before her throughout the entire week, II, 718 A. She was represented in the substance of air, II, 261 A. Why she was called Juno Curis, or Curetis, I, 421 A.

**JUPITER**, son of Saturn, concerning his cruelty, I, 317 A. Born on the island of Crete and on Mount Dicte, I, 426, sq. Where Jupiter’s tomb is, I, 427 A. His nurse, I, 426 A. It is falsely imagined that he allowed Crete, his homeland, to be shaken by the Roman fasces, ibid. What the “Christian Jupiter” is, I, 317 A, D. In his name pagans unwittingly acclaimed the true God, I, 703 C. Jupiter, a scaly, horned, gilded, feathered lover, I, 396 A. Changed into a bull and a swan, II, 760 A. The ancients represent him in the substance of heat, II, 261 A. Jupiter is drenched with human blood at public games, I, 317 A; II, 136 C. He taught incest, I, 325 A. He could give no growth to the Roman Empire, I, 427 sq. He did not prefer the Capitol to Crete, his homeland, and to the most delightful scent of his nurse, I, 426, sq. He feared thunder, I, 334 A. Why he cannot be a god, I, 333 A. His crimes committed under various assumed forms, I, 396 A, 575 C, sq. He laments Sarpedon’s fall, I, 351 A. He is subject to fate, I, 428 A. Assailed by other gods; wanton and adulterous, I, 575 C. His depraved lust and the various transformations it occasioned, II, 760 A. His disgraces were sung in the theaters, I, 576 B. His praises were sung by actors, I, 359 A. *Jupiter’s Will*, a comedy, I, 358 A. Jupiter Pluvius, I, 296 A. Varro introduced three hundred Joves, or Jupiters, I, 355, sq., 576 A.

**GOD SWEARS** by himself, so that, when God swears, you may believe that there is absolutely no other god, II, 315 C. O most wretched are we, if we do not believe even the Lord when he swears, I, 1234 B. Swearing by Hercules, I, 692 A; by the guardian spirits of the Caesars, I, 700 A. Pagans swore by the guardian spirits of the emperors, I, 583 B. To swear by Caesar’s guardian spirit was worse than to swear by the gods, I, 575 A. They swore for the safety of the rulers, to the prejudice of their children and spouses, I, 583 B, 599 A. Christians swore by the emperor’s safety, but not by his guardian spirit, I, 447 B.

**JURIDICINA**, what it is, II, 1047 A, B.

**BY HUMAN RIGHT AND NATURAL AUTHORITY**, it belongs to each person to worship what he thinks proper, I, 699 A. Civil law cited by Tertullian, II, 656 A.

**JUSTIN**, philosopher and martyr, II, 548 A.

**JUSTICE** is the fullness of divinity, displaying God as perfect, both Father and Lord, II, 300 B, C. He does not repent of justice, II, 313 B. God the Judge presides over the justice that he must exact and uphold for himself, I, 1230 B. In it he establishes the whole substance of his discipline, ibid. Justice, the avenger of violence, II, 747 A. Severity is its due, II, 303 A. Every principal aspect of justice is an administration of goodness, II, 299 C. The developments of justice through different periods, II, 890. When it is perfected amid injustice, II, 104 C.

**TO BE JUSTIFIED** now by faith without the order of the Law, II, 447 C. A woman justified through repentance arising from faith, II, 403 C.

**JUVENTAS**, goddess, I, 600 D.

## L

**LABERIUS’S** sayings concerning the doctrine of Pythagoras, I, 521 A.

**LABOR** is necessary, II, 487 B.

[Col. 1556]

**MILK**, how it is formed in the breasts, II, 787 A. God nurtures his own as infants with milk and honey combined, II, 262 A.

**THE LACEDAEMONIANS** first devised the *paenula* for the games, I, 302 A. The flogging of Lacedaemonian boys, I, 626 A. What benefit the Spartans’ scourges produced, I, 533 A.

**LACONIA** possessed an oracle of Pasiphaë, II, 730 A.

**EVERY SHOWER OF TEARS** is dried up by divine indulgence, II, 880 A.

**ALL PUBLIC REJOICING** is a procurer of luxury, II, 96 A.

**LAYPERSONS** are priests, II, 922 B. They must not assume the office of bishops for themselves, I, 1218 A. Among heretics they perform priestly duties, II, 57 A. Where three laypersons are, there is the Church, II, 922 B.

**LAÏS**, a prostitute, I, 347 A.

**LAMECH**, the first to marry two women, made three persons into one flesh, II, 920 C. Through him violence was done to God’s institution, II, 934 C.

**LANA**, goddess, I, 606 A.

God showed how **WOOLS** could be dyed with the juices of herbs and the secretions of shellfish, I, 1327 B.

**SYLLA’S DISHES**, most splendid, II, 706 A.

**CHRIST LABORED TO HEAL** ailments and infirmities, II, 762 C.

**LAODICE**, before she had yet given birth, foresaw that her son Seleucus would possess the kingdom of Asia, II, 728 A.

**TO THE LAODICEANS**: heretics assign this title to Paul’s epistle that is addressed to the Ephesians, II, 500 B, 512 B.

**NEPTUNE** constructed **LAOMEDON’S WALLS**, I, 352 A.

**STONES** upon which the pagans’ sacred rites were described, I, 313 D.

**LARENTIA, LAURENTIA, LUPERCA**, an utterly promiscuous she-wolf or prostitute, I, 423 A, 428 A, 599 sq. Made a goddess, ibid.

**LARES**, private gods of households, I, 573 C, 637 B. Tertullian censures them, I, 344 B.

**LARISSAEAN HERO.** See **ACHILLES**.

**LATERENSES**, who they were, II, 466 A.

**LATIAN GAMES**, I, 638 A.

Prayer stupefies **ROBBERS**, I, 1196 A.

**THE LAUREL** was consecrated to Apollo and Liber, II, 94 A. Pagans shaded their doorposts with laurels, I, 453 A, 683 B.

**WASHING.** See **BAPTISM**.

**THE ROBBER OF THE BATHERS**, I, 496 B.

By **WASHINGS**, the nations exalt their gods, I, 1204 B.

**LAZARUS**, the foremost example of resurrection, II, 873 A. In Lazarus the flesh was not soulish, nor was the soul fleshly, II, 776 A, 873 A.

**LEAENA**, a prostitute, refused to betray those privy to the conspiracy, I, 626 A.

**COUCHES** spread in the middle of the forum, I, 452 B.

**MUTUAL PANDERING**, I, 1311 A. The pandering of the pagans among the altars and in the booths of temple-keepers and priests, I, 363 A. Pandering of divinity, II, 733 A.

**THE AUGUR LENTULUS’S** pronouncements concerning women’s dress, II, 1044 A. His sacrilegious charms, I, 576 B.

**LENTULUS**, writer of mimes, II, 1042 B.

**THE LION** is a father only once, II, 727 B.
