**THE WRITINGS OF LEO THE EGYPTIAN**, II, 86 A.

**LEPIDUS’S** violent mockeries, II, 1031 A.

**LEVICOIA**, or **Levicola**, I, 606 B.

**LEVITES** existed before the priesthood of the Levitical law, II, 600 B.

**LAW** should owe the consciousness of its justice not to itself, but to those from whom it seeks obedience, I, 289 A, 566 A. Equity alone commends a law, I, 288 A. Law distinguishes a human being from a beast, II, 289 A. A law is not imposed upon someone who does not have within his power the obedience due to the law, II, 290 B, C. A law that does not wish to be tested is suspect, I, 566 B; and one that rules without having been tested is wicked, I, 289 B. An unjust law demands no honor or obedience, I, 286 sqq., 566 B. If a law errs, it comes from human beings, not from heaven, II, 885 A. Contempt of the law was assigned to man’s freedom of choice, II, 290 C. Who is to be regarded as a detractor from the Law, or as one who fulfills it, II, 429 D. Laws mitigated by public consent, I, 287 A. How great the authority of divine law is, I, 499 sq. It is far superior to human laws in sanctity and authority, ibid. Divine laws can never be infringed with impunity, I, 500 A.

God’s Law, before Moses, was first given in paradise, II, 600 B. Why a law was given to Adam, II, 289 A, B. The primordial law was given to Adam and Eve as, so to speak, the matrix of all God’s commandments, II, 599 B. Before the Law of Moses, written on tablets of stone, there existed an unwritten law, which was understood naturally and observed by the patriarchs, II, 600 A. God gave the same law to all nations, as accords with his goodness and equity, II, 599 A. The Law was given to Abraham after four hundred and thirty years, II, 600 B. The Law of Moses was given at the time when the Jews had departed from Egypt, after an interval and span of many years, [Col. 1557] II, 600 B. It was promulgated not by God’s harshness but according to the principle of supreme benevolence, II, 306 C. Why it was burdened with so many observances, II, 306 A. It possessed a hidden meaning, II, 306 C. The force of the figurative Law is shown, II, 374 C. The significances of the Law, namely both prophetic and figurative in nearly all respects, II, 306 C. The Apostle abominates accusation of the Law, II, 505 B; the Law did not deceive, but sin did so by taking occasion from the commandment, ibid. Cerdo rejects the Law and the Prophets, II, 78 B, as does Apelles, II, 71 B. Hermogenes defends the Law of God according to his own lust and despises it, II, 198 A. See **MOSES**, **TESTAMENT**, **THEOTIMUS**.

The burdens of the Law, not its remedies, lasted until John, II, 989 C. See **CHRIST**. It was to be abolished from the preaching of John onward, II, 474 B. It is the root of the Gospels, II, 125 B. How greatly it differs from the Gospel, II, 361, 600 B. Holy men joined the Law and the Prophets with the evangelical and apostolic writings, II, 49 B. The yokes of works were rejected, not those of disciplines, II, 989 C.

The laws of Christians, enacted by God and Christ, are superior to all others, I, 498, sqq. They prohibit anger and even solitary lust, I, 499 A; abusive speech and the returning of injury, ibid.; the blood of animals, things strangled, and carrion, I, 324 A.

The authority of human laws, I, 499 B. The best laws of the ancients were drawn from our sacred laws, I, 499 B. Human laws bind human beings in relation to God, II, 289 A. How imperfect they are, I, 289 A, 499 B. They can be weakened and violated with impunity, ibid. They are often harmful or useless, I, 285, sqq. They are commonly violated by the offender’s choice or necessity, I, 499 B. Laws amended and rendered obsolete, I, 566 B. See **CUSTOM**. Laws amended, trampled underfoot, and abrogated by pagans, I, 286, sq. They are brought to ruin once the short duration of the punishment is considered, I, 499 B. No law ought to condemn a person unless convicted of the crime or confessing it, I, 702, sq. The laws command that wicked persons be brought to light, not concealed, I, 276 A. Laws against Christians were enacted by the worst and most unjust emperors, I, 292, sqq. Lycurgus’s laws were amended by the Lacedaemonians, I, 286 A. The laws of the Romans increased beyond measure, I, 286 A, 572 B. Whether they were all observed, I, 298, sq. Sumptuary laws restraining ostentation and expense, I, 298 A. The Aemilian law fixed the expense of dinners, ibid.; as did the Antian law, ibid. How the Papian and Julian laws concerning the marriage of younger persons were abrogated by Severus, I, 286 A. There were laws concerning the institution of new gods, I, 290 A.

**MOUNT LEBANON** bears among the Greeks a name meaning incense, II, 382 B.

**FESTIVE, BITING, AND DEFAMATORY PAMPHLETS**, where they were posted, I, 583 B.

**A BOOK** is later than speech, I, 616 A.

**FATHER LIBER**, or Bacchus, after his mother’s womb had been cut open, drew the air while still alive, II, 692 C. He was made a god because of the invention of wine, I, 334 A. He triumphed over the Indians, II, 86 A. Beasts were attached to his image, I, 341 A. He was encircled with a laurel crown, II, 86 A. He was expelled by the Senate from all Italy, I, 304, sq., 575 B. Pagans reclined publicly at table during Liber’s mysteries, I, 492 A. Christians refused to take part in them, ibid.

**LIBERALIA**, games, I, 636 B, 643 A. What the duties of the Liberalia were, I, 492 A, 636 B.

**FREEDOM** belongs to God, not necessity, II, 212 A. Freedom is bestowed by him under whom there had been slavery to the Law, II, 478 B. Christians knew how to die for freedom, I, 565 A.

**FREE WILL.** See **WILL**.

**FREEDMEN**, still breaking their whips, I, 301 A. Their luxury, I, 300 A, and their ornaments, II, 879 B, C.

**LUST** is a companion everywhere, I, 326 A. It has defiled marriage, II, 695 B. To boil over into every form of lust is the highest fruit of life for all who do not fear God, II, 279 A. Even among the nations lust is not ascribed to marriage, but to acts that are extraordinary, unnatural, and monstrous, II, 509 B. Castration imposes no restraint upon lust, II, 282 A. Through the inquisitiveness of lust, women stir up rivalry, I, 1288 A. What the monstrosities of lust are, II, 987 A. With what pretexts the insatiable appetite of the flesh is given a respectable coloring, II, 927 A. It is not excused by the weakness of the flesh, II, 951 A. Lust and gluttony are allied vices, II, 953 B. A new council-chamber of public lusts, I, 1298 A.

**A LIBYAN PEOPLE**, the Atlantes, are said to pass through death in blind sleep, II, 733 B.

**LICENSE** is commonly a test of discipline, and why, II, 923 C. What is not always and everywhere lawful is nowhere and never lawful, I, 653 A.

**THE WOOD of Christ’s Passion**, II, 635 A, was prefigured in the death-bearing tree of paradise, ibid.; in the wood by which Moses sweetened the bitter water, ibid.; and in the wood that Elisha cast into the water, II, 636 A, B. What had been lost in Adam through wood is restored through the wood of Christ, II, 636 B. See **CROSS**. [Col. 1558] Some pagans worshiped a rough piece of wood, I, 366 A.

**LIMENTINUS**, a god named from *limen* (“threshold”), I, 685 C; II, 97 B.

**CLAY** is nothing other than rich moisture, II, 696 A. From it comes the generative fluid, ibid. Clay assumed the image of Christ who was to come in the flesh, II, 802 C. It was effaced and absorbed into flesh when man was made into a living soul, II, 804 A.

**THE GREEK AND LATIN LANGUAGES** are considered closely related to each other, I, 618 A. Every nation has a different voice and sound, and each its own speech, but the matter of speech is common to all, ibid. See **LETTER**, **LITERATURE**.

**TO THE BLEARY-EYED**, a single lamp seems many, II, 249 A.

**LIQUID alone**, always perfect, fruitful, simple matter, pure of itself, offered itself to God as a vehicle worthy of God, I, 1202 A. See **WATER**.

**MERCURY** first explained **LETTERS**, II, 87 B. The soul is prior to the letter, I, 616 B. The divine Scriptures are far earlier than secular writings, I, 617 A. Whence the order of the letters themselves derives, I, 616 C. Letters are necessary for commerce, affairs, and our devotions toward God, II, 87 B. Things are preserved in letters, just as letters are read in things, II, 822 B. Certain heretics maintained that the entire fullness of truth had been arranged in Greek letters, II, 70 A. Among the Romans the first letters are customarily called “elements,” II, 476 C. Young people were trained through them for practical wisdom and the liberal duties, I, 350 B. Christians do not fail to obtain any right to Christian letters, II, 51 A. It is more permissible for the faithful to study letters than to teach them, I, 675 A. Letters of peace, II, 155 B.

**LITERATURE** is an instrument for every aspect of life, I, 675 A. Its necessity, ibid. Whether human beings lived as mutes before literature and its dissemination, I, 616 B, C. See **LANGUAGE**. The first pledge to the devil begins with the rudiments of education, I, 675 B. Divine literature is more fertile in its capacity for every subject, II, 53 A. The literature of the age, I, 683 C. Those who are called authors constitute the whole literature of the age, II, 729 A.

**EVERY PLACE** is in God, but God himself is not in a place, II, 175 C. Places do not of themselves defile us, but the things done in those places do, I, 640 B, 647.

**ΛΟΓΟΣ (*LOGOS*, “WORD” or “REASON”)**, what it is, I, 398 A, 400 B; II, 160 A. It was unknown neither to Zeno nor to Cleanthes, I, 398, sq. See **CHRIST**, **SON**.

**LOQUACITY** in edification is never shameful, if indeed it is ever shameful, I, 1256 A.

**LOT**, Abraham’s proven brother, because on account of the merits of righteousness, without observing the Law, he was delivered from the burning of Sodom, II, 602 A.

**LUCANIA**, formerly joined to Italy, I, 481 A. The force of the waves cut Lucania off from Italy and relegated it to the name of Sicily, II, 1034 A.

**LUCANUS**, a heretic, follower and disciple of Marcion, II, 71 A. His heresy concerning the soul and the resurrection, II, 798 A.

**LUKE**, a follower of Paul, II, 364 A. He was not an apostle but an apostolic man, not a master but a disciple, ibid. Luke and Mark wrote the history of the Gospel from the Apostles, II, 363 C. The authority of Luke’s Gospel is defended, II, 365 B. Luke’s arrangement is ascribed to Paul, II, 364 B, 367 A. Until Marcion, the text of Luke remained complete, II, 367 C. Marcion “corrected” it, II, 367. Cerdo accepts this Gospel alone, and not even the whole of it, II, 70 C.

**LAMPS** in the Christians’ sacred assemblies, I, 313 A. And in their vestibules, I, 683 A. See **LIGHTS**. Pagans broke up the daylight with lamps, I, 453 A. The Romans clouded their vestibules with lamps of the greatest height and brightness, I, 459 A, 683 A.

**LUCINA**, the goddess who brings childbirth into the light, II, 713 A.

**LUCIUS**, a wise man, immediately came over to Christianity, I, 280 A.

**LUCRETIA**, after suffering the violence of rape, drove a knife into herself in the sight of her relatives, in order to procure glory for her chastity, I, 625 A. With her own blood she washed the flesh that had been defiled, II, 929 A, 952 C.

**LUCULLUS** was the first to introduce cherries from Pontus into Italy, I, 334 B.

**THE ORIGIN AND ETYMOLOGY OF THE GAMES**, I, 636 A, B, 638 B. The Consualia games, I, 636, sq. The Equisia, I, 636 C. The Liberalia, ibid. B. The Lupercal games, ibid. The Apollinarian, Latian, Megalensian, and other games, 638 A, C. Sacred and funerary games, ibid.

**A SCHOOLMASTER** is never without his tablet of the seven idols, I, 674 A.

**LIGHTS** kindled in Christian assemblies, I, 307 A, 313 A. Christians were said to wallow in lusts after the lights had been extinguished, I, 307 A.

**THE MOON**, a male god, a comedy, I, 358 A.

**SHE-WOLVES**, markets for the populace’s lusts, II, 1044 B. [Col. 1559] It is customary every day to make ready the appearance of a female wolf, I, 547 A.

Laurels and lamps were customarily hung on the doors of **BROTHELS**, I, 684 C, 1298 A. At festivals, Roman houses were brothels, I, 453 A.

**THE LUPERCIAN GAMES**, why they were so called, I, 636 B.

**RAVENOUS WOLVES**, who they are, II, 16 B.

**LURCOBNIAN SEASONINGS** [reading uncertain], II, 706 A.

**LUXURY**, the destroyer of chastity, II, 929 A. See **CONTINENCE**, **LUST**.

**THE LUXURY OF THE ROMANS**, I, 298, sqq.; of Roman women, I, 304 A. An attack upon luxury, I, 1314, 1325 sq.

**LYCURGUS’S LAWS** were amended by the Lacedaemonians, I, 286 A. On that account he took his own life, I, 286 A, 512 A.

**THE LYDIANS** entered into a treaty by drinking blood, I, 381 A. Migrants from Asia, they settled in Etruria under the leadership of Tyrrhenus, I, 636 A.

**LYMPHATI**, who they are, I, 1205 B.

**THE WINE-LIKE SPRING OF THE LYNCESTIANS** makes people drunk, II, 734 B. Its outflow likewise produces intoxication, II, 568 A.

## M
**MACEDONIA** has the oracle of Hermonia, II, 730 A. **MACEDONIANS**, on hearing the tragedy of Oedipus—how they behaved, though themselves guilty of incest [syntax uncertain], I, 325 A. **MACCABEES**, by fighting on the Sabbaths, restored the ancestral law to its former condition of life, II, 606 C. **MAGIC** is nothing but deception, II, 747 C. Magic is a second idolatry, a manifold plague of the human mind, the artificer of every error, the destroyer of salvation and of the soul, II, 748 A. Magic is twofold, I, 612 A, B. Astrology is a species of magic, I, 612 ff. See **ASTROLOGY**. Egyptian magic, which rivaled Moses, prolonged God’s patience down to the Gospel, I, 672 B. See **ASTROLOGICAL SCIENCE**. **MAGICIANS** knew that demons existed, I, 405 A. They dash children to death to obtain an oracular utterance, I, 411 A. They produce apparitions, I, 410 A. They send dreams, I, 411 A. They bring the souls of the dead into disrepute, ibid. They appear to do certain things beyond the order of nature, which they accomplish through the illusions of demons, I, 407 f., 412 A. Consultation of them was invented by the apostate angels, I, 459 A. Magicians were consulted concerning the life of the Caesars, ibid. See **ASTROLOGERS**. The Persian Magi, II, 260 A. The East generally had Magi as kings, II, 339 A, 619 B. Magi and astrologers were the first to announce the birth of Christ and to present him with gifts, I, 672 A. Those who seek **MAGISTRACIES**—to what hardships and insults they subject themselves, I, 1246 B f. And all this for the fleeting joy of a single year, I, 1247 A. See **OFFICE**. Speech delights the **MAGNANIMOUS**, I, 1196 A. The **MAGNET** attracts iron, II, 236 B. **GREATNESS** is proved in moderation, II, 261 B. In dress, food, equipment, wealth, worship, display, and speech, the pagans had renounced the customs of their **ANCESTORS**, I, 305 A, 572 B. Having spurned their institutions, they lived in some novel fashion every day, ibid. See **ANTIQUITY**. By uttering **CURSES**, the uneducated populace keeps company with demons, I, 405 A. No **EVILDOING** is without fear, because none is without consciousness of itself, II, 401 A. In evildoing there is no regard for order, I, 1264 B. **EVILDOERS** eagerly seek concealment, tremble when discovered, deny when accused, and attribute their crime to the stars or to fate, I, 267 f. **EVIL SPEECH** is forbidden, I, 499 A. **MALICE** comes from the devil, I, 1164 A. It has always been hateful to the Lord, I, 1264 B. Human beings are inclined toward malice because of the defect in their nature, I, 467 B. Among the Greeks, “evils” are sometimes used to mean vexations and injuries, not malign acts, II, 313 A. Whence comes **EVIL**, II, 210 B. The nature of evil is agreed upon by everyone, so that not even the guilty themselves dare defend evil as good, I, 266 A, 559 D. The pagans attributed it to the stars or to fate, I, 268 A. That which does not possess the natural characteristics of evil is not evil, I, 269 A, 560 A. Its marks, ibid. Something is not therefore not evil merely because it does no harm, I, 1279 A. It is not the thing in which evil is done that is condemned, but the deed that is done, II, 497 A. There is a rank of evil which is placed at the highest point or in the midst of the worst things, II, 988 A. Evils are necessary for illuminating goods, which are understood through their contraries, II, 210 D. The goodness of God, perceived from the beginning of things, will persuade us that no evil could have proceeded from God, II, 292 C. In what sense he is said to create evils, II, 301. The operation of evil is broad and diffuse, I, 1266 A. Through evil one arrives at misery, I, 1245 C. A false evil is more readily believed than a true good, I, 467 B. Nature suffuses every evil either with fear or with shame, I, 266 A. [Col. 1560] Both offenses and punishments are called evils, II, 301 A. Evils of guilt and evils of punishment, ibid. Avenging, not sinful, evils, II, 313 A. The **EVIL**, suffused with fear and shame, seek hiding places, I, 267 f. To be unfruitful for them is a great fruit, I, 495 B. They do not wish what they recognize as evil to be their own, II, 268 A. **MALLUS** had the oracle of Amphilochus, II, 730 A. **MAMMON** is said of money, II, 439 C. **MANDANA**, daughter of Astyages, II, 727 A. **MANETHO** the Egyptian, I, 387 A. The insignia of the **MANUMISSION** of slaves, II, 879 C. Christians performed prayer with their **HANDS** washed, I, 1168 A. They prayed with hands outspread, conforming themselves to the Lord’s Passion, I, 1199 f. They also washed them after eating, I, 417 A. A hand is laid upon the baptized through a blessing that invokes and invites the Holy Spirit, I, 1207 A. Through the laying on of hands the flesh is overshadowed, so that the soul too may be illuminated by the Spirit, II, 806 B.

The history of **MARCION** is narrated, II, 42, 71 A. Marcion was a shipmaster, II, 266 C, 327 B. More savage than the beasts of barbarous lands, etc., II, 247 B. How he was crueler than Pharaoh, II, 282 B. A follower of the Stoics, II, 19 B. A disciple of Cerdo, II, 71 A. The teacher and precursor of Apelles, II, 42 B; and likewise of Lucanus, II, 71 A. He derives the fundamental principle of his faith from the school of Epicurus, II, 521 A. He appropriates part of the doctrine of the Sadducees, II, 46 A. In the first ardor of the catholic faith he contributed money to the Church, II, 365 D. He did not love himself, since he withdrew from the Church and the faith of Christ, II, 759 A. Marcion’s letter, II, 505 C, 755 B. His Gospel, II, 361 A, 368 A. He ascribes no author to his Gospel, II, 363 B. Marcion invents two gods, II, 248 B, 361 B; or even three, II, 264 A. Whence his god came, II, 19 A, B. He denies that this god is moved, II, 438 B. He establishes unequal gods: one a fierce judge, mighty in war; the other gentle, placid, and merely good and supremely good, II, 252 C f. Marcion was the first who dared introduce, besides the Creator, another God of goodness alone, II, 47 A. He asserts that the God of the Law is one, and the God of the Gospel another, II, 363 B. When the light of faith was extinguished, he lost the God whom he had found, II, 247 B. He denies that God was truly transformed into a human being, II, 757 A, B. He denies Christ’s flesh and his birth, II, 46 C, 754 B. He introduces two Christs, II, 264 A. He teaches that the Christ who came was one who had never been foretold, II, 327 B. Marcion, the prohibitor of marriage, II, 46 A, 281 f., 486 C. He baptizes no one unless celibate or a eunuch, II, 280 B, 382 B. He reserves baptism until death or divorce, ibid. He admitted no resurrection of the flesh whatsoever and promised salvation only to the soul, II, 491 B, 495 B. Marcion rejects and mutilates the Holy Scriptures, II, 758 A. He separated the New Testament from the Old, II, 43 B, 268 A. He gnawed away the Gospel, II, 247 B. He chose Luke to cut to pieces, II, 364 A. By interpolating Luke’s Gospel, he made it his own, II, 361 A. The **MARCIONITES** are censured, II, 41 A, B. They reject the Creator, II, 262 B. Their new god, II, 255 ff., 267. They were for the most part astrologers, II, 266 A. The Marcionites permit themselves what Marcion permitted himself, namely, to renovate the faith according to their own judgment, II, 58 A. **MARCUS AURELIUS**. See **AURELIUS**. **MARK**, Peter’s interpreter, wrote the Gospel that is affirmed to be Peter’s, II, 367 A. See **LUKE**. **MARCUS** the Magician, a heretic, II, 546 B. **MARCUS** the heretic fashioned a new heresy from the Greek alphabet, II, 70 A. He denied the resurrection of the flesh, ibid. His heresy concerning the creation of the human body, II, 801 A. Prayer calms the waves of the **SEA**, I, 1196 A. See **ATLANTIC**, **BRITANNIC**, **CORINTH**, **INDIAN**. A **PEARL** is the hard and round excrescence of a shellfish, I, 1311 A. Pearls are the insignia of everyday social life, I, 1296 A.

**MARY** sprang from the line of David, II, 624 A. She was a virgin, though Ebion resists this, II, 897 f. Her virginity is defended, I, 397 A. The beautiful comparison and contrast between Mary and Eve, II, 782 B. Mary, after Christ, the mediatrix of our salvation, II, 782 A. Why Tertullian says that she had not married, I, 397 A; II, 790 B. Mary, Mother of God, II, 190 C. Christ was formed as flesh in her womb while her virginity remained inviolate, I, 399 B. Mary was a virgin with respect to a man, not with respect to childbirth, II, 790 A. Mary a virgin in childbirth, II, 190 C, 760 A, 781 C f. After childbirth she married once, II, 939 B. Whether she adhered to Christ while he preached, I, 762 C. In Christ’s mother is joined a figure of the Synagogue, and in his unbelieving brothers a figure of the Jews, II, 767 B, C. Every **HUSBAND** is an exactor of chastity, I, 1320 B. **MARS** in trine aspect, II, 266 A. Depicted in the form of a soldier, I, 574 B. Mars bound and almost consumed in his chains, I, 351 A, 575 C. [Col. 1561]

A **MARTYR**, though publicly branded, glories; when accused, he offers no defense; when questioned, he confesses voluntarily; when condemned, he gives thanks, I, 269 A. The tortures of the martyrs, I, 626 B. Unknown, unheard, undefended, and condemned and slaughtered by the pagans solely because of their name, I, 260 ff., 559 ff. Cast into prison, I, 497 A. The populace raged against them under no prescription of law but with innate fury, I, 456 A, 461 A. It drove them out with stones rather than boxing gloves, I, 521 A. See **TRAJAN**. None of them was cast into prison and condemned for any crime, I, 497 A. By the harshest tortures the pagans tried to compel them, contrary to every law, to deny their crimes and that they were Christians, I, 284 ff., 560 B, C. Only the name “Christian” was written upon the tablet recording their condemnation, I, 279 A. Under peril of death, I, 531 A, they were not to be punished with swords, clubs, crosses, and beasts because of their teachings, I, 529 A, B. During their trials sausages stuffed with blood were offered to them, I, 324 A, 560 B. They were prepared for every kind of punishment, I, 445 A. How many, how great, and how horrible were the punishments by which they were tortured and slaughtered, I, 340 f., 445 A. Banished to islands, I, 341 A. Condemned to the mines and the beasts, and very often to the lion, I, 341 A, 445 A, 480 A, 658 A; II, 825 B, 927 C. Fastened to crosses and stakes, I, 340 A. Condemned to death, I, 531 A. How often the pagans shouted for them to be thrown to the lion, I, 445 A, 480 A, 658 A; II, 825 B. A woman condemned to the pimp rather than to the lion, I, 535 A. Others burned by fire, I, 461 A, 531 A, 704 A. Their bodies, dug out of their graves, were cut apart, ibid. Designated martyrs, I, 619 A. The slaughter of martyrs inflicted great damage upon the commonwealth, I, 496 A. No city bore with impunity the shedding of Christian blood, I, 701 A. How greatly the constancy of the martyrs is to be praised, I, 584 A. The pagans unjustly censured it, ibid. The martyrs deserved no less praise from them than those whom they extolled for steadfastly enduring death, I, 532 A, 584 A, B. While bound to a stake and burned alive, they triumphed in the attire of victory, with a robe and a gilded chariot, I, 531 A. Immediately after death they are endowed with eternal felicity, I, 1270 A; II, 745 A. One distinguished by the prerogative of martyrdom proceeds immediately to paradise, not to the underworld, II, 856 A. Some voluntarily offered themselves to tyrants, I, 704 B. How they endured tortures inflicted upon them in the manner of soldiers, I, 530 B. With what charity Christians aided martyrs confined in prison and condemned to the mines, I, 470 f., 619 ff. They commemorated yearly the birthdays of the holy martyrs, II, 79 A. The blood of the martyrs is the seed of Christians, I, 535 A. Through their punishments and slaughter the Christian people increased all the more, I, 704 C f. By their death they made more disciples than the most eloquent orators, I, 535 f. Their blood is more eloquent than Cicero, more fluent than Seneca, more articulate than Diogenes, Pyrrho, and Callinicus, ibid. Their unconquered constancy under every kind of punishment—or, as the pagans said, their inflexible obstinacy—persuaded others that their religion was true, I, 535 f. Sinners took refuge with the martyrs to obtain pardon, II, 1027. How John beheld the souls of the martyrs, II, 658 A.

**MARTYRDOM** is the contest in which Christians, under peril of death, struggle before pagan tribunals and conquer when they are killed, I, 531 A. It is a victory that possesses the glory of pleasing God and the prize of living forever, ibid. Martyrdoms rage fiercely, but unto salvation, II, 132 A. Faith is indebted to martyrdom, II, 139 B. Through martyrdom all sins are forgiven, I, 536 A; the whole grace of God is purchased, ibid. The divine authority of martyrdoms, II, 125 ff. Martyrdoms are tests of faith, II, 136 A. The proclamation and reward of martyrdoms, II, 137 A. Instruments of martyrdom, I, 340 f. Contempt for the body contributes excellence to martyrdom, II, 856 A. Praxeas was puffed up by boasting of martyrdom, II, 155 B. Martyrdom is a second baptism, I, 1270 A. The baptism of blood, II, 135 B. There is a perfect martyrdom without suffering, II, 138 A. The **MASSAGETAE** were inhuman, II, 247 B. They ate the flesh of their parents when the latter were worn out by old age, I, 321 B. The **GREAT MOTHER** depicted in the form of the earth, II, 261 A.

**MATTER** is not named in the Scriptures, II, 219 A. No matter is without evidence of its origin, even if it is transformed into a new property, II, 771 A. That which lacks matter does not admit the operation of wisdom, II, 329 A. The Pythagoreans, Stoics, and Plato himself held matter to be unbegotten, II, 567 A. Zeno makes it equal to God, II, 19 B, as does Hermogenes, II, 198. The **MATERIARIAN** heretics, II, 218 C. **ASTROLOGICAL SCIENCE** (*mathesis*) was permitted until the Gospel, and why, I, 672 A. Today it concerns Christ, ibid. See **ASTROLOGY**, **MAGIC**. **ASTROLOGERS** had wicked angels as their teachers, I, 671, [Col. 1562] f. They were expelled from the city and from Italy, II, 671 B. The Marcionites were for the most part astrologers, II, 266 A. See **MAGICIANS**.

**MARRIAGE** exists when God joins two into one flesh, or, finding them already joined, seals their union in the same flesh, II, 941 B. Through the bond of marriage two are made one in flesh, I, 1302 B; II, 896 B. Its numerical multiplication began with a cursed man, II, 920 C. See **LAMECH**. The necessity and causes of marriage, I, 1280 A. It is a great sacrament, II, 518 A. It must be defended when it is accused under the name of filthiness for the destruction of the Creator, who accordingly blessed wedlock because of the honorable nature of the thing, II, 281 A. Excess, not the state itself, is immodest, II, 695 B. Lust, not the condition, has defiled it, ibid. Marriage, a shared indignity, II, 903 B. Its modest concealment in private, II, 806 B. The felicity of a marriage that the Church arranges, the oblation confirms, the angels announce when it has been sealed, and the Father ratifies, I, 1302 A, B. Secret unions—that is, those not first professed before the Church—are evil, II, 987 A. Children who marry without their parents’ consent do so neither rightly nor lawfully, I, 1302 B. Whether a marriage contracted under compulsion is valid, II, 443 A. Those enrolled in the priestly order must have been married no more than once, II, 922 A. Believers who enter marriages with pagans are guilty of fornication, I, 1292 C. See **WEDDINGS**, **MONOGAMY**. The felicity of marriage, fostered among the ancient Romans by good morals, I, 303 A. Roman laws compelled people to marry, II, 927 C. Marriage was forbidden to slaves, I, 1300 B. Among the pagans, betrothed women were led veiled to their husbands, II, 905 B. A second marriage must be called nothing other than a form of fornication, II, 924 A. In a second marriage two wives stand about the same husband, one in spirit, the other in flesh, II, 926 B, C. The shame is twofold, ibid. You will find the dissolution of marriage permitted by God’s command neither in the Gospel nor in Paul’s own epistles, II, 919 A. Christ makes marriage to a divorced woman unlawful, II, 441 C f. Patience heals a marriage that has been divided, I, 1268 A. While the first marriage remains, to marry is adultery, II, 442 B. See **DIVORCE**. Eve, the **WOMB** of the female sex, II, 896 B. Jerusalem, the womb of religion, II, 447 B. The indecent attire of **MATRONS**, II, 1044 A. Their ostentation in temples, I, 1301 A. The **MATRONALIA**, I, 682 B. **MATTHEW**, as the Lord’s companion, was the most faithful expositor of the Gospel, II, 789 A. **MATUTA MATER**, II, 953 A. The petty kings of **MAURETANIA**, I, 419 A. The **MOORS** are vain, II, 683 B. That nation does not cross the boundaries of its own territories, II, 611 B. Subjected to the yoke of Christ, II, 610 C. They formerly worshiped Versutina, I, 596 A. **MAVILUS** of Hadrumetum, martyr, I, 702 B. **MAXIMILLA** adhered to Montanus, II, 954 B.

**MEDICINE**, the sister of philosophy, II, 650 B. It required the resources of its art to expand the discussions concerning the soul, II, 650 B. Treatment with the knife, the cautery, and the burning of mustard is indeed like the savagery of medicine; but the fruit of their operation excuses them, II, 431 C f. See **AESCULAPIUS**. At the appropriate time, irrational creatures recognize the medicines divinely assigned to them: the deer, dittany; the swallow, celandine, I, 1248 A. **PHYSICIANS** received their name from Erasistratus, I, 282 A. They are the proper judges of all lethal things or causes, and of bodily conditions themselves, II, 739 C. What judgment must be passed upon a physician who allows a disease to grow by delaying assistance and prolongs the danger by postponing the remedy, so that his cure may be more costly or more impressive, II, 272 A. The physician is to be admired because he generally applies qualities of remedies matching the qualities of the complaints, II, 132 A. For he checks fevers by burdening them still further with heat, and extinguishes burning by wasting it with thirst instead, ibid. He gathers up an excess of bile with all manner of bitter draughts, and arrests a flow of blood by opening yet another little vein, II, 132 B. Physicians relegate everything contrary to life, health, and assistance beyond the bounds of nature, II, 723 A. The human being always creates work for the physician first and draws the peril of death upon himself, ibid. The kingdom of the **MEDES** is older than the Roman kingdom, I, 432 A. The **MEGALENSIAN** games, I, 638 A. The **MEGARIANS** purchase provisions as though they were going to die the next day, etc., I, 474 A. **MELAMPUS** brought the rites of Bacchus into Greece, I, 404 A. The initiations of **MELAMPUS** at Argos, I, 404 A. **MELCHIZEDEK**, though uncircumcised and not observing the Sabbath, was chosen for the priesthood of God, II, 602 A. Whence was he called priest of the Most High God, unless before the Levitical law there had been Levites who offered sacrifices to God? II, 600 B. **MELETUS**, the accuser of Socrates, I, 647 B. By fellowship in **HONEY and MILK**, God makes his people infants, II, 262 A. See **BAPTISM**.

**MEMORY**, according to Cicero, is the treasury of all learning, II, [Col. 1563] 688 A. It is the preservation of sensations and understandings, ibid. The availability of memory is soundness of mind, II, 726 A. Its glory is as great as the injury caused by forgetfulness, II, 688 A. **MEMORIALS**, or monuments, I, 386 A. **MENANDER** the Samaritan, a disciple of Simon, II, 734 B, 736 A. His teaching concerning baptism, II, 61 B, C. **MENANDER** of Ephesus, I, 387 B. His luxurious clothing, II, 1043 B. His raven bath [reading uncertain], II, 735 A. Menander’s error concerning the creation of bodies, II, 801 A. A **LIE** is not built up without demolishing truth, II, 284 C. It is the servant of desire, II, 676 A. No one lies to his own disgrace, but rather for his honor, I, 415 B. To lie about one’s own religion is the greatest impiety, I, 403 B. Faith is more readily inclined toward those who confess against themselves than toward those who deny in their own favor, I, 455 B. **PTOLEMY OF MENDES**, I, 387 B. The priests of Cybele **BEGGED**, I, 346 A. **MENEDEMUS**, the philosopher, was a champion of Providence, I, 380 A. He approved the Greek translation of the Old Testament, ibid. He admired the seventy-two translators for their agreement in judgment, ibid. **MENELAUS** pursues the Helen whom he has lost, II, 709 B. Those who divine by **TABLES** through the illusions of demons, I, 411 A.

A **REWARD** from God as exactor and remunerator, I, 460 A. Reward depends upon free choice, II, 292 B. In proportion to the difference in rewards, a difference in works must also be believed, II, 424 C. Reward and peril depend upon the outcome of the resurrection, II, 823 A. See **UNDERWORLD**, **MERIT**. To undertake the profitable risks of **COMMERCE**, with desires for gain, I, 1262 A. **MERCURY** first explained letters, II, 87 B. The inventor of letters, I, 616 C. The originator of the first garment, II, 1038 A. Winged upon his bald head, fiery upon his caduceus, I, 576 C. Represented by actors as testing dead gladiators with a cautery, I, 362 A. He skinned a little sheep, II, 1038 B. Mercury Trismegistus, teacher of all natural philosophers, II, 567 A. The opinion of the Egyptian Mercury concerning the soul, II, 705 B. Plato revered him, II, 649 A. The Mercury of the Gauls, II, 136 C. They sacrificed persons of higher rank to him, I, 316 A. **PROSTITUTES** did not wear the same clothing as matrons, I, 302 A. See **ATTICA**. The world was made **MERITORIOUS**, II, 550 B. **MERIT** depends upon free choice, II, 292 B. To be unwilling to earn merit is to transgress, II, 917 B. An equal deed has equal merit, I, 1264 C. A diversity of merits is established, II, 134 C. The order of those who rise again will be arranged according to their merits, II, 356 B. **MEROPES**, II, 1032 B. **DICAEARCHUS OF MESSENE**, II, 670 A. The pillars of **MESSIAH**, II, 639 C. Christians condemned to the **MINES**, I, 341 A, 480 A. Demons disclosed the workings of mines, I, 1306 A. **METELLUS** discovered the god Alburnus, II, 266 C. What **METEMPSYCHOSIS** is, II, 711 B. It is thoroughly refuted, II, 697–711. What **METENSOMATOSIS** is, II, 702 f., 708 B.

Where there is **FEAR OF GOD**, there are honorable seriousness, startled diligence, anxious care, tested selection, deliberate fellowship, etc., II, 58 B. **MIDAS** entrusted his enormous ears to Silenus, II, 649 A. The rose garden of Midas, II, 98 B, 1036 A. Solemn **MIGRATIONS** of peoples, II, 700 A. **MILESIAN** sheep, II, 1039 A. A **SOLDIER** lost in battle is more glorious than one saved in flight, II, 112 B. Soldiers were crowned with olive, II, 94 A. No soldier comes to war amid luxuries, nor proceeds from the bedchamber to the battle line, I, 624 A. Thus Christians are called to God’s military service, ibid. Christians are Christ’s soldiers, II, 927 A. By disarming Peter, the Lord unbuckled every soldier’s sword-belt, I, 691 A. Soldiers’ exercises in peace and war, I, 624 A, B. Their equipment and weapons, II, 76 B, 92. Before God, a believing civilian is as much a soldier as an unbelieving soldier is a civilian, II, 93 A. How the soldiers of Mithras were initiated, II, 102. Whether **MILITARY SERVICE** is altogether appropriate for a Christian, I, 690 A, B; II, 91 B f. It is lawful up to the issue of the crown, II, 94 A. Nor does it permit impunity for offenses or immunity from martyrdoms, II, 93 A. Service in royal households, II, 95 A. The dreams of the **MILLENARIANS** [*milliariorum*], II, 355 C f. Plato’s **THOUSAND-YEAR** age, II, 700 C. **MILTIADES**, the sophist of the Churches, II, 548 A. A particularly impudent **MIME-ACTOR** represents Hercules on the stage, I, 362 A; and a shameless mime-actress represents Minerva, I, 360 A. The mime represents obscenity even through women, destroying the sex of modesty, I, 649 B. The absurdities of mime, ibid.

**MINERVA**, goddess of arts and arms, II, 94 A. She first constructed a ship, II, 87 B. They ascribe to her the ordering of wool-working and the construction of looms, II, 1039 A. How absurdly the pagans made her a goddess for the invention of a trifling coin, I, 334 A. Her judgment and Juno’s, I, 359 f. When she undertook to found the city of Athens, she did nothing but foresee the character of the region and promise excellent talents, II, 683 A, B. She did not defend her city from Xerxes, I, 607 B. Minerva’s basin, I, 314 B. The **MINERVALIA**, I, 644 B. The tribunal and judgment of **MINOS** and Rhadamanthus, celebrated by Plato and the poets, I, 415 A.

By many **MIRACLES**, Christ proved himself to be the **Word** (*Λόγος, Logos*) of God, and to be both God and man, I, 400 A, B. See **NATURE**. Whatever miracles occur among the pagans are done as testimony to them, II, 738 A. They were performed through the evil arts of demons, I, 406 A. Demons, assuming the apparitions of Castor and Pollux, announced the victory over King Perseus, I, 409 A. They caused a beard to become red merely by touch, I, 410 A; caused a ship to be moved by a girdle, ibid.; and water to be carried in a sieve, I, 409 A. Ptolemy’s **MISCELLANIES**, II, 562 B. Patience is the mother of **MERCIES**, I, 1251 A. The Father of mercies is the same who is called merciful, compassionate, and abundant in mercy, II, 498 A. The initiations of **MITHRAS**, II, 54 A, 102 A. His lions philosophically represent mysteries of a dry and burning nature, II, 261 A. **MITHRIDATES**, as a result of a dream, gained possession of Pontus, II, 728 A.

Praise of **MODESTY**, II, 915 A. It provides for shamefastness, I, 1288 A. Nothing is more acceptable to God than modesty, II, 911 A. How greatly the modesty of Christians excels that of pagans, I, 511 A. It is as much the duty of a holy man to endure having seen a virgin as of a holy virgin to endure having been seen by a man, II, 891 B. What the **MONARCHY** of God is, II, 158 A. The **MONARCHIAN** heretics, II, 164 D. Whether **MONOGAMY** is burdensome, II, 932 A, B. Its discipline is neither new nor foreign, but rather both ancient and proper to Christians, II, 933 D. Among pagans it is held in the highest honor, II, 928 B. It is recognized even among animals, lest even beasts be born from adultery, II, 935 A. The monogamy of Adam and Eve endured to the end, II, 934 B. Lamech was the first to break it, ibid., C. **MONOGENES**, father-Aeon, II, 352 A. **MOUNTAINS** burn and endure, I, 528 A. How they dripped sweetness, II, 326 C. Shells found in mountains, II, 1033 B. Christ is the mountain cut away without hands, filling the whole earth, II, 604 A.

**MONTANUS** teaches that one should fast more often than marry, II, 954 C. His fasts, II, 970 B f. In Montanus the Paraclete said more than Christ uttered in the Gospel, II, 72 B. Some said that the Paraclete uttered not only more, but also better and greater things, ibid. The fasts of the **MONTANISTS**, II, 954 C. Whether the Roman Pontiff approved their errors, II, 155 B. The oracle of **MOPSUS** in Cilicia, II, 730 A. Diseases opposed to sleep: frenzy and heart disease, II, 723 A. See **PHYSICIAN**, **MEDICINE**.

**DEATH** is that which not only corrupts flesh and blood but also consumes them, II, 869 B. No death is anything other than the collapse of the members, II, 819 A. Its dominion effects nothing but the dissolution of the flesh, II, 862 C. It is defined as nothing other than the separation of body and soul, II, 695 A. It did not follow humanity by nature, but through guilt, which itself was not natural, II, 738 B. It occurs by God’s law, not through a human offense, II, 942 A. Nothing ordinarily dies except what is born, II, 764 A. The manner of dying is the cause of being born, ibid. One who ceases to function ceases to live, II, 691 C. Although death has various outcomes, none is so gentle that it does not occur by violence, II, 739 A. That very agency which produces death is violence, ibid. Premature and atrocious deaths are the work of demons, whom the ancients assigned to courses [reading uncertain], II, 748 A. If death is not total, it is not death, II, 738 A. Some said that when the body was extinguished, a portion of death remained with a portion of the soul until burial, II, 737 B, C. The pagans believed that those overtaken by premature death wandered here until the remainder of their allotted years was completed, II, 746 A. Death is one thing, and what is mortal another, II, 875 B. What is mortal is one thing, and mortality another, II, 870 B. Death does not receive immortality, but that which is mortal does, II, 875 B. The adamantine gates of death, II, 857 B. Death is everywhere, and consciousness of death and testimony to it are everywhere, I, 618 B. Frequent deaths devastate very many things, I, 390 A. All things die in order to live again, I, 524 f. Epicurus denied that death pertains to us, II, 721 A. Seneca thought that after death all things, including the soul, come to an end, II, 721 A, 795 B. The common people suppose that nothing remains after death, II, 795 B. Some think death must be understood spiritually, II, 820 B. Sleep is the image of death, II, 724 B. Through it you are initiated into faith, meditate upon hope, learn to die and to live, and learn to remain awake while you sleep, 724. Death is useful and sweet to a Christian, by God’s ordering, II, 133 A. What you regard as death is a departure, I, 1264 A. Whether it is to be feared, I, 614 ff. We fear death, though we cannot escape it, I, 615 A. The fear of death is not so great as the fear of tortures, I, 625 A. Philosophy teaches contempt for death, as Zeno of Elea says, I, 533 A. Grief over death ought to be absent when the resurrection of the dead is certain, I, 1263 B. Our death could not be undone except through Christ’s death and resurrection, I, 1212 C. Christ’s death is the weight and fruit of the Christian name, I, 332 B. Christians were prepared to die for one another, I, 471 A. The difference between the death of a believer and that of a pagan, II, 745 A. The pagans consoled death with acts of homicide, I, 645 A. Among the barbarians of Pontus, the death of those who departed in such a way as not to be edible was accursed, II, 247 A. At the point of death many pagan governors confessed that they had sinned against the Christians, II, 702 A, B.

The word **DEAD** properly applies to the body, II, 491 C, 819 B. In former times the dead were crowned, II, 89 C. What kind of incense, and how much, Christians used in burying the dead, I, 493 A, 676 A. Longing for the dead must be moderated by patience, I, 1264 A. The emotion of grief at the loss of loved ones is not exempted from the charge of impatience, I, 1263 B. For a dead person to be raised is nothing other than to be made whole, II, 878 C. One must pray for the deceased and petition for refreshment for them, II, 942 C. Public oblations for the deceased, II, 737 C. Christians made oblations and prayers for them on the anniversary of their death, II, 79 B, 942 C. It was formerly believed that the souls of the deceased were propitiated with human blood, I, 644 C. See **DECEASED**. **MOSCHION** thought that the soul was wafted throughout the whole body, II, 671 B.

**MOTION** is not a substantive thing but an accident, II, 230 B. It pertains not to substance but to the condition of substance, II, 231 A. All things are moved either by themselves or by others, II, 230 B. God is the first author of all motions, I, 590 C. Perpetuity of motion is a mark of divinity, II, 725 B. God moves in an ordered manner, matter in a disorderly one, II, 235 C. God’s motion is free and eternal, ibid.

**MOSES**, the first prophet, I, 382 A. A prophetic, not a poetic, shepherd, II, 85 A. About nine hundred years older than Saturn, II, 697 A. Contemporary with Inachus, I, 386 A. How much older he was than Danaus, ibid.; and older than the Trojan disaster and Homer, I, 387 A. He lived before the Lycurguses and Solons, II, 305 A. Moses, the arbiter nearest to God, II, 937 A. Whether he saw God, II, 622 B. The Son of God spoke to Moses, ibid. When Moses pleaded slowness of speech, the Lord promised to be his mouth, II, 456 B. His hand, made dead and then restored, was a sign of the resurrection, II, 835 A, 876 C. The people were granted to him for the present time, II, 326 B. He taught the Jews to worship God, I, 403 B. One who rejects the God of Moses has nothing to do with Moses, II, 763 B. Praying on the mountain, he prefigured Christ, II, 346 A. Why he circumcised his son, II, 602 B. Moses wrote history prophetically down to his own age, I, 382 A. He does not appear to have been the first, in the temple of his writings, to consecrate the God of the world, II, 257 B. His books are older than all the rest, I, 387 A. The law of Moses must not be regarded as though it were the principal law, but as a subsequent law, which at a definite time God also presented to the nations and, as promised through the Prophets, reformed into something better, II, 600 C.

The **MULES** of matrons, I, 1301 B. **WOMAN** is not by nature a name for “wife”; rather, “wife” is by condition a name for “woman,” II, 896 B. Under the single name “woman,” the Holy Spirit intended even a virgin to be understood, II, 894 A, B. The word “woman” pertains to sex, not to a stage of that sex, II, 895 A. Whether *mulier* and *femina* have the same meaning, I, 1185 f. By naming a woman, you name whatever belongs to womanhood, II, 895 A. Woman is the devil’s gateway, the first deserter of the law, I, 1305 A. A woman is made with difficulty [reading uncertain], II, 909 B. The dress of Christian women, I, 1321 A, 1333 f. A woman’s appearance displays two kinds: attire and ornament, I, 1309 A. The proud adornment of women is described, I, 1306 A, 1310 B, 1325 A. Among the Jews they walked veiled, II, 80 B. What a woman’s finery is, ibid. A man who dresses in women’s clothing is condemned in the law, I, 655 B. See **EYE**, **LUXURY**. No male function in the Church is permitted to a woman, II, 902 A; neither teaching, baptizing, nor offering, ibid. How brazen heretical women are, II, 56 B. They dare to teach, dispute, and perhaps baptize, ibid. Roman women formerly knew nothing of gold, I, 302 A. They abstained from wine, ibid. Drunken women were killed by their husbands, I, 302 f. But afterward, how shamefully their morals changed, I, 304 A. See **WINE**. Betrothed women have Rebecca as their example, II, 904 B. A certain Greek woman gave birth to five sons at once, II, 656 A. The modesty of a woman in labor must be honored because of her danger and treated with reverence because of nature, II, 758 C. A woman who went to the theater returned from it with a demon, I, 657 B. Another, who had heard a tragic actor, did not live beyond the fifth day, ibid. See **ATTICA**. The women of Pontus prefer military service to marriage, II, 247 A.

The devil is called **RULER OF THE WORLD** (*munditenens*), II, 576 A. The **WORLD** was created, furnished, and ordered by God with every instrument of reason’s governance, I, 334 A. He made it from nothing by the Word through which he commanded, by the reason through which he arranged it, and by the power through which he was able, I, 375 A, B. God’s goodness produced the world; his justice gave it measure, II, 299 A. The world is animated by the Spirit who animates all souls, I, 324 A. A great work and worthy of God, II, 260 A. It consists of all good things, I, 288 B. It is composed of diverse substances and functions, II, 1032 B. Every location and disposition of the elements, and the effect, motion, state, rising, and setting of each, are judgments of the Creator, II, 299 B. Among the Greeks, “world” bears the sense of ornament and adornment, II, 233 C. Why they assigned it the name **κόσμος** (*kosmos*, “ordered adornment/world”), I, 375 A. It becomes more cultivated and better furnished from day to day than formerly, II, 700 A. Everything is now accessible, everything known, everything engaged in business, ibid. Everywhere houses, everywhere people, II, 700 B. The world has been made meritorious, II, 550 B. According to Plato, the world is round and headless, I, 591 C. Pythagoras said that the world was uncreated, I, 333 A. Other philosophers maintain that it was unbegotten and unmade, II, 609 A. Plato taught that it was made by God, I, 333 A. According to Simon Magus, it was fashioned by angels, II, 62 B, 708 B f. According to Varro, the soul of the world is fire, I, 589 B. This is refuted, ibid. Heretics interpret “the world” as “the Lord of the world,” II, 481 B. The whole configuration of the world will pass away, II, 801 B, 833 B. It is to be destroyed together with the Roman Empire, I, 447 A. Christians prayed to God in their assemblies that its end might be delayed, I, 447 A, 468 B. The world is God’s rival, II, 898 B. Satan and his angels have filled the whole world, II, 640 B. The devil is called ruler of the world, II, 576 A. In what sense the world is a prison, I, 622 A. Its chains, uncleannesses, and darknesses—of what kind and how great they are, ibid. It is the dwelling place of the dead, that is, of those ignorant of God, II, 821 A. The vice of the world is the desire to acquire, I, 1283 A. No one is taken out of this age without God’s will, I, 1285 A. Christ now winnows the world through faith by the power of the cross; afterward he will winnow it through judgment, II, 346 B. **MUNICIPAL CITIZENS** mentioned, I, 387 A. **MUNICIPAL FESTIVALS**, II, 76 A. **SERVICE** (*munus*) is so called from duty (*officium*), since *officium* is also the name of an inferior station,
II, 644 B ff. Duties (*munia*) that lead to sin must be abandoned altogether, even if one’s livelihood comes solely from them, I, 667. **GIFTS.** Those who prize gifts do not please Christ, II, 457 B; nor do those who pursue recompense, ibid. **MURTIA**, goddess of love, II, 640 A. **MUSAEUS**, venerated at Athens, II, 649 B. He bound the Athenians to initiatory rites, I, 404 A. **MUSIC.** Anacharsis mocked those ignorant of music, I, 865 A. **MUSICAL FESTIVALS**, I, 644 B. **MUTIUS** burned his right hand upon the altar, I, 532 A, 625 B; with joy, II, 751 A. **MUTINUS**, or **Mutunus Tutinus** (Priapus), a most shameful god, I, 423 A, 601 A. **MYSTERIES.** Christians kept their mysteries secret, I, 308 A.

# N

**NEBUCHADNEZZAR**, together with his subordinate rulers, had the boundaries of his kingdom extending from India to Ethiopia, II, 611 B. He dreams by divine agency, II, 731 C. His repentance, I, 1269 B. Confession restored him to his kingdom, I, 1248 A.

**THE TOWN OF THE NARNIANS**, I, 420 A. Their god Visidianus, ibid.

**THE NASAMONES** had their own oracles at the tombs of their parents, II, 749 B.

**NATAL DAYS.** Christians commemorated the natal days (anniversaries) of the martyrs annually, II, 79 A. An idol’s birthday was celebrated with all the pomp of the devil, I, 674 B.

**BIRTH.** A normal birth occurs at approximately the beginning of the tenth month, II, 714 A. See **TENTH**. Birth in the seventh month is also viable, more readily than in the eighth, ibid., sq. The mystical rationale for these facts, ibid. Our birth has been reformed by heavenly regeneration, II, 759 B. The Roman archives bear witness to Christ’s birth, II, 370 C. The inaugurator of a new birth had to be born in a new manner, II, 781 C.

**NATURE** is the first discipline of all, II, 82 A. The teacher of the soul, I, 616 A; II, 811 A. Whatever nature may be, we believe it to be something rational, a work of God, II, 722 B. It is the same outwardly as inwardly, II, 907 A. It is impaired either by deprivation or by excess, but preserved by the proper measure, II, 723 A. It is to be revered, not regarded with shame, II, 695 C. Marcion censures its works, which ought to be revered, [Col. 1567] II, 336 A. Nature cannot will its own nonexistence, for it loves itself in such a way that, if it ceases, it does not exist, II, 271 B. One who has no nature has no natural instruments at his disposal, II, 266 B. Certain things are known by nature, II, 798 B. What these are, ibid. The devil is the corrupter of nature, I, 1312 B. He infected it by introducing the seed of sin, II, 514 C. Nature is one thing, the corruption of nature another, II, 720 A. To consecrate nature, II, 907 B. The entire creation is subject to renewal; how this is so, II, 810 B, C. The order of nature is described, II, 810. It is a greater thing to transform nature than to create matter, II, 765 B. Fasts obtain from God a transformation of nature, II, 963 A. Everything contrary to nature deserves to be branded as monstrous in everyone’s judgment, but among us it also incurs the charge of sacrilege against God, the Lord and Author of nature, II, 83 A. Natural things must be believed capable of transformation, II, 684 B. Knowledge of natural things is not lacking even in beasts, II, 688 B.

**SHIPWRECK.** Many who have been saved from shipwreck thereafter renounce both ship and sea, I, 1241 A.

**SAILORS** always rejoice at a common feast, II, 562 A. The wantonness of sailors’ festivities, ibid.

**A SHIP** was first constructed by Minerva, II, 87 B. A ship drawn by a belt through the operation of the devil, I, 410 A.

**NAZARENE.** Why Christ was so called, II, 372 B. Why the Jews called Christians Nazarenes, ibid.

**NECESSITY** is more sacred, I, 345 A. An opportunity that removes what necessity had imposed should be embraced, I, 1286 A.

**PLEASURES FROM SACRIFICES TO THE DEAD** (*necrothytae*), I, 646 B.

**NECTABIS**, II, 747 B.

**DENIAL** is wholly idolatry, just as idolatry is denial, I, 693 B. It is prompted by shame, II, 141 A. God repays denial with denial, II, 140 C. It is a refusal of martyrdom, II, 115 C. Whether denying Christ is the same as denying something in Christ, or denying oneself to be a Christian, II, 140 B, C.

**A DENIER** is one who abandons his faith, II, 25 A.

**COMMERCE** has invaded the entire world, II, 700 A. It was forbidden to the first Christians because of the danger of idolatry and perjury, I, 676. If covetousness, which is the cause of acquisition, departs, there will be no necessity for commerce, ibid. A.

**THE NEMEAN RITES**, sacred to Hercules, I, 644 A.

**NEOPHYTES** are appointed by heretics, II, 57 A.

**NEOPTOLEMUS**, a tragic actor, was warned in a dream and saved from a collapse, II, 729 A.

**THE NEPTUNALIA**, games, I, 638 A.

**NEPTUNE** is equestrian—the one whom the Greeks called Ἵππον (*Hippon*, “Horse”), I, 641 A; the Romans, Consus, I, 636 C. He built Laomedon’s walls, I, 352 A. Dolphins were vowed to him, I, 639 C.

**NERO** was the first at Rome to stain with blood the rising faith, I, 292 A. He was the first of the Caesars to draw the sword against the Christians, II, 151 B. Hence their honor, I, 293 A. Suetonius denies that he ever dreamed, II, 725 A, 733 B. He reigned twelve years, nine months, and thirteen days, II, 616 A.

**NERSIA**, or Neurtia, Nortia, Nursia, goddess of the people of Volsinii, I, 421 A.

**NESTOR’S MIXED DRINK** (*cocetus*), II, 562 B. The honey of his eloquence, II, 702 B.

**NICANDER**, II, 749 B. A writer and painter, II, 121 A.

**NICOLAS**, one of the first seven deacons, a heretic, II, 63 A.

**THE NICOLAITANS**, condemned in the Apocalypse, II, 63 A. They were advocates of lust and luxury, II, 280 C. Their debaucheries, II, 46 B. They ate food sacrificed to idols, ibid. Their foul and sacrilegious error, II, 63 A.

**NICOLAITANS**, other heretics, namely the Cainites, II, 46 B.

**NIGIDIUS**, a heretic, forestalls the ways of God, II, 43 B.

**NIGER AND THE FOLLOWERS OF NIGER**, named after Niger, and their faction, I, 457, sq.; 699 B. Christians did not belong to his party, ibid.

**NOTHINGNESS** belongs to God, just as the totality does, I, 525 A.

**NINEVEH**, though sinful, is delivered from destruction through repentance, II, 962 A. God turned the appointed destruction away from the Ninevites, II, 313 B.

**NINUS**, offspring of Belus and king of the Assyrians; the period in which he reigned, II, 1035 A.

**NOAH**, Enoch’s great-grandson, I, 1307 B, sq. He was found righteous by natural righteousness, II, 600 B. Though uncircumcised and not observing the Sabbath, he was saved from the Flood, II, 601 B. Why his burnt offerings were pleasing to God, II, 310 A. He succeeded Enoch in the commission to preach, I, 1307 B, sq.

**A NAME** is in itself neither good nor evil, I, 278, sqq. The sharing of names prejudges the conditions of those who share them, II, 253 B. Names have their own boundaries between being spoken and being real, I, 565 B. Fidelity in names safeguards the proper qualities of things, II, 376 B. “The Name,” without qualification, means the Christian profession, I, 1165 A; II, 806 B, 851 B. How hatred of it can exist, I, 278 sq. See **CHRISTIANS**.

**NONA**, a goddess, II, 713 A.

[Col. 1568]

**NONACRIS** in Arcadia poisoned Alexander, II, 568 A, 734 B.

**THE NORICI** had Belenus as their particular god, I, 419 A, 596 A.

**NORTIA.** See **NERSIA**.

**KNOW THYSELF**, the oracle of the Pythian priestess, I, 525 A.

**A CLERK** of a certain pagan judge, when thrown down by a demon, is delivered by a Christian, I, 703 A.

**KNOWLEDGE AND ENJOYMENT OF GOD** are the highest good, II, 287 B.

**EVERYTHING NEW** and unknown appears sudden, II, 420 A.

**NIGHT** establishes the rule for the proper enjoyment of sleep, taking away even the color of things, II, 722 B, C. Christians spent the night in prayers, I, 477 A, 1296 A.

**THE CLOUDS.** Pagans said that Christians counted the clouds while praying, I, 417.

**THE BAREFOOT PROCESSIONS** (*nudipedalia*) of the pagans, I, 487 A; II, 976 C.

**DILIGENCE** does not occupy itself with trifles, I, 1288 A.

**NUMA POMPILIUS**, the introducer of highly elaborate superstitions, or of idolatry, I, 404 A, 429 A, 608 A.

**NUMENTINUS**, a god of the Athenians, I, 596 A.

**NUMBER** begins after one, II, 922 A. See **TENTH**, **FIRST**. The numbers of Pythagoras, II, 703 B. The numbers of the Valentinians, II, 553, sqq.

**THE LONG-HAIRED NUMIDIANS**, II, 1040 A.

**COINAGE** was first stamped by Saturn, I, 330 A.

**MARKET DAYS**, she-wolves of popular lusts, II, 1044 B.

**MARRIAGE.** If marriage did not exist, there would be no holiness, II, 282 A. It consists of that which also constitutes fornication, II, 925 A. Marriage arises from sight and intention, just as fornication does, II, 905 A. At weddings an *auspex* was present on the husband’s side, II, 928 B. A Christian must not contract marriage with pagans, and why, II, 696 A. The Apostle commands marriage “in the Lord,” I, 1290 A. Marry where you can also die, II, 453 C. Christians who have departed this world are promised no restoration of marriage on the day of resurrection, I, 1276 A. Marcion abolished marriage, II, 247 B, as an evil and a business of immodesty, II, 282 A. Tertullian did not cast marriage away, but laid it aside; nor did he prescribe holiness, but commended it, II, 279 C. You no more abolish first marriages by rejecting second ones than you condemn food by fasting more frequently, II, 950 C, D. Second marriages are not to be undertaken, II, 915 B. A limit upon marriage is laid down among the Montanists, on the authority of the Paraclete, II, 281 B. He condemned second marriages, II, 983 B. See **MATRIMONY**, **MONOGAMY**.

**NOUS** (*Nus*, “Mind”), an aeon, II, 551 B.

**NYMPHODORUS**, a writer, II, 749 B.

# O

**OBEDIENCE.** A splendid example in Abraham, I, 1164 A. How unjust and ungrateful it is not to obey God, I, 1255 A, B. See **SUBMISSION**.

**AN OBELISK** of enormous size, prostituted to the Sun, I, 640 A. Its inscription is superstition from Egypt, ibid.

**OFFERINGS.** Why Abel’s offerings were acceptable to the Lord, II, 310 C. Christians made offerings for the anniversaries of the martyrs and for the dead on an annual day, II, 79 B, 926 C.

**FORGETFULNESS.** Whether the soul is capable of it, II, 687 B. Whence comes the power to remember a preceding forgetfulness, II, 689 A, B. Whether it comes from time, ibid. See **MEMORY**.

**OBODAN**, a god of the Arabs, I, 596 A.

**SUBMISSION** is the art of earning favor, I, 1255 A. For the rendering of submission, the authority of the commander takes precedence over the advantage of the servant, I, 1234 A. We ought to obey, not because the command is good, but because God has commanded it, ibid. We owe the rendering of submission to the Lord God, I, 1255. The principle of submission is established by the correspondence of minds, ibid. No one allows himself to submit to an evil person, II, 376 B.

**OBSERVANCE.** A long-established observance must be maintained even if no Scripture has determined it; custom has certainly confirmed it, provided that it was first handed down, II, 967 A. The necessity of an observance is recognized when the authority of its rationale—which must be traced back to the beginning—has become evident, II, 957 B. See **CUSTOM**, **TRADITION**. Nature, which is the first discipline of all, defends the rationale of Christian observances, II, 82 A.

**THE EGYPTIAN MIDWIVES.** Why God treated them well, II, 417 B.

**TO KILL** is to take the soul away from the flesh; to make alive is the opposite, II, 835 C.

**OCHUS**, who is also Cyrus, II, 614 A.

**THE GODDESS VALENTIA** of the people of Ocriculum, I, 421 A.

**OCTAVES** of Christian festivals or solemnities, I, 682 C, sq. Pagan festivals did not have them, ibid.

**WOMEN’S EYES** were in early times adorned with black powder, I, 1306 A. They blackened them with soot, I, 1321 A. How they offended God in doing so, ibid. Adorned women draw after them the eyes and sighs of young men, I, 1320 A. The particular torments of the eyes in the abyss; what they are, II, 845 C.

[Col. 1569]

**THE BLINDNESS OF HATRED**, I, 280 A. The justice of hatred must be judged not by its outcome but by conscience, ibid. To hate someone whom you do not know is the height of perversity, I, 261 A. A thing deserves hatred only when it is known whether it deserves it, ibid. The pagans’ hatred toward the Christian name, I, 261, sqq. See **CHRISTIANS**, **NAME**.

**OEDIPUS**, portrayed by an actor, was mocked by the Macedonians, I, 325, 581. Pagans applauded the representation of his crime, ibid.

**OENOTRIA**, afterward called Italy, I, 330 A, 602 C.

**RESENTMENT** accompanies a frustrated will, II, 277 C.

**OFFICIAL CROWNS**, II, 93 B.

**THE VALENTINIAN OGDOADS**, II, 46 B.

**OIL.** Catechumens were anointed with oil in Baptism, I, 1207 A; II, 262 A. The sick are healed through oil, II, 703 B.

**THE MOTION OF A POT BOILING OVER ON EVERY SIDE**, II, 234 A.

**THE OLYMPIAN GAMES**, sacred rites instituted for Jupiter, I, 644 A.

**OLYMPIAS**, Alexander’s mother, II, 727 B.

**A WHOLE** is complete and entire, lacking no part of itself, II, 900 B.

**OMPHALE**, the harlot of Hercules, I, 605 B; II, 1041 B, sq.

**A WILD ASS** showed the Jews a spring of water in the desert, I, 364 A.

**ONOCHOETES**, a god of the Christians fabricated by a scoundrelly Jew, I, 364 A, 579 B.

**THE TIME FOR ACTION** is in the flesh, II, 496 D. In every action there are three principal elements, II, 215 B, C. See **WORK**.

**THE OPHITES**, heretics who worshiped the serpent, II, 63 B, sq. Their aeons, II, 64 A, B.

**CORPULENCE** impedes wisdom; slenderness assists it, II, 683 B.

**EVERY OPINION** originates in sense-perception, I, 675 A. There is a great distance between opinion and truth, I, 565 B.

**A WORK** must necessarily be inferior to its craftsman, II, 295 C. No one is worthy to inhabit the works of God except God’s own image and likeness, II, 288 B. If works are made from some matter, they are nevertheless, in that very respect, made from nothing, since they were not what they now are, II, 290 A. The yokes of the works of the Law have been cast off, not those of its disciplines, II, 989 C. Works that are truly good and Christian; what they are, I, 1294, sqq. No work is certain when its reward is uncertain, II, 823 A. See **GOOD**, **MERIT**.

**ORACLES.** How they were delivered among the pagans, I, 413 A. They were produced through the deceptions of demons, I, 408 A. Their ambiguities, I, 408, sq.

**PRAYER** leads the spirit to God, II, 926 A. One who prays is near heaven, ibid. Prayer alone is that which has overcome God, I, 1195 B. It washes away sins, repels temptations, extinguishes persecutions, consoles the fainthearted, delights the magnanimous, guides travelers, calms the waves, etc., etc., I, 1196 A. The duties of prayer, I, 1164 A. It is the wall of faith, our arms and weapons against the one who watches us from every side, I, 1196 A. Prayer proceeds from conscience, II, 926 A. If conscience blushes, prayer blushes, II, 926 A. The intention of prayer must be wholly free from every disturbance of mind whatsoever, I, 1167 A. Every creature prays, I, 1196 A, B. How rash it is to pass the day without prayer, ibid. Prayer is necessary for human beings at every moment, II, 926 A. One must pray before eating, I, 1193 B; before bathing, ibid.; and at the coming of daylight and night, ibid. One must rise at night for prayer, I, 1294 B, 1296 A. Prayers are to be nourished by fasting, I, 1244 A. Some washed their entire bodies before every prayer, I, 1168 A. The custom of sitting after prayer, and its origin, I, 1171, sq. Legitimate prayer; what it is, I, 1165 A, 1195 A. God alone could teach how he wished to be prayed to, I, 1265 A. The religious discipline of prayer was ordained by Christ himself, ibid. The Lord’s Prayer is constituted of three things: the words by which it is uttered, the Spirit through whom it has such power, and the meaning through which it is taught, I, 1151 A. Christ’s prayer is placed before one’s own prayers, I, 1165 A. The Jews prayed three times a day, I, 1193 A. Their prayers upon the shore, I, 579 B. The words in which John taught people to pray are not extant, I, 1152 A. Christians prayed with hands outstretched, I, 442 A, 1171 A; turned toward the region of the East, I, 370, sq., 579 A; without a prompter, from the depths of the heart, I, 443 A; with the head uncovered, I, 442 A; out of chaste flesh, an innocent soul, and the Holy Spirit, I, 444 A. How pleasing to God was the power of their prayers, I, 468 A. In public assemblies, they rose at night to pour out prayers, I, 273 A, 381 A, 468 A, 477 A; II, 79 B. They prayed to God for everyone, I, 468 A; and for a delay of the end of the world, ibid., B. They prayed before and after eating, I, 477 A. Pagans prayed to their gods with a prompter going before them, I, 443 A. They prayed with hands outstretched, I, 442 A, turned toward the East—and why, I, 371 A, 579 A—but polluted by idolatry and every kind of crime, I, 465 A.

**ORBANA**, a goddess, I, 606 A.

**ORDINATION**, I, 1256 A. All the ordinations of heretics are rash, frivolous, and inconstant, II, 757 A.

[Col. 1570]

**ORDER** must be derived from first principles, II, 297 A. The authority of the Church established the distinction between the ordained order and the laity, II, 922 B.

**ORESTES**, in his madness, saw his mother in his sister, II, 675 C.

**THE POWER OF THE EAST**; what it is, II, 339 A.

**OROPUS** possessed an oracle of Amphiaraus, II, 730 A.

**ORPHEUS** was venerated in Pieria, I, 403 B; II, 649 B. He introduced the sacred rites and festivals of Liber, I, 403, sq.

**ORPHEUS**, an author, I, 649 B.

**THE MOUTH.** Why it was given to the human being, II, 882 B. The cavern of the mouth, ibid.

**KISSES** inflame lust, II, 909 C. Women were kissed by their husbands and relatives to discover whether they had drunk wine, I, 303 A. The practice was later prohibited because of the women’s intemperance, I, 304 A. Christ had to be betrayed with a kiss, II, 463 A. The kiss of peace is the seal of prayer, I, 1176, sq. It is to be given at sacrifices, I, 1177, sq. It was not given during the days before Passover, I, 1178 A.

**OSIDIUS GETA** rendered the tragedy *Medea* in the fullest possible form from Virgil, II, 53 A.

**OSIRIS** is always buried, sought while still alive, and found with rejoicing; what this signifies, II, 261 A. Osiris is the same as Liber, II, 85 B.

**BONES** almost five hundred years old were seen at Carthage still moist, and hair still fragrant, II, 854 C.

**THE EMPEROR OTHO** reigned for three months and five days, II, 616 A.

**THE GOSPEL SHEEP** is properly the Christian, II, 992 A. God’s sheep are the Christians, II, 105 C.

**EGGS** are assigned to the honor of the Castors; why, I, 639 C.

# P
**PACUVIUS.** The tortoise in Pacuvius, II, 1037 A.

**CLOAKS (*paenulae*).** Why and by whom their use was devised, I, 301 A; their use at theatrical spectacles, and why, ibid.

**PAGANS.** See **GENTILES**.

**ATHLETICS.** The business of the devil is the spectacle of the stadium, I, 651 A.

**PALLAS.** The Attic Pallas is indistinguishable from the upright beam of a cross, I, 366 A. See **MINERVA**.

**PALLIUM.** What kind of attire it was, II, 1031 A. Nothing is more convenient than it, even when doubled, II, 1046 B. Its great benefit: at the thought of it, even wicked conduct blushes, II, 1050 A.

**PALM TREES.** The seventy palm trees in the desert prefigured the seventy disciples, II, 563 A.

**PALM-EMBROIDERED GARMENT.** What it was, I, 531 A.

**BOUNDARY POSTS.** The fixing of boundary posts for God, II, 969 B.

**PANCARPON.** What it was, II, 563 A.

**PANDORA.** Pandora’s head was the first to be crowned by the Graces, when she was receiving gifts from all, II, 84 C. Hesiod’s Pandora, II, 562 B.

**BREAD.** What “daily bread” means, I, 1160 ff. Christ calls bread his body, I, 1160 A; II, 461 A. Having taken and distributed it to the disciples, he made that bread his body, II, 460 C. By bread he represents his body, II, 262 A. By the sacrament of the bread and the cup, the reality of the Lord’s body and blood is established against Marcion’s phantom, II, 489 A. See **EUCHARIST**.

**PANTOMIME.** From childhood the pantomime suffers bodily hardship so that he may become an artist, I, 649 B. Pantomimes, after assuming the masks of gods, danced upon the bodies of the slain or dying, I, 576 B.

**PAPIAN LAWS.** I, 286 A. Why they are called utterly futile, I, 287 A. The emperor Severus repealed them, I, 286 ff.

**PARABLE.** There is no one to whom a parable is not applicable, II, 838 A. How its interpretation is to be undertaken, II, 996 B. Why Christ spoke to the Jews in parables, II, 841 A, B.

**THE MONTANIST PARACLETE.** His power, II, 886 B, C. He taught many things which the Lord deferred until his coming, II, 950 B. He is the guide into all truth, II, 103 A. He alone is to be called and revered as teacher after Christ, II, 890 B. What his administration is, ibid. A. He supplied the Montanists with new teaching, II, 931 B. He is the restorer rather than the institutor of monogamy, ibid.

**PARADISE.** It is a place of divine delight, appointed to receive the spirits of the saints, I, 520 A; II, 297 B. Its gatekeeper, the sword (*rhomphaea*), yields to none except those who have died in Christ, II, 747 A. Your blood is your key to paradise, ibid. Man will be recalled to paradise in the same condition in which he was expelled from it, II, 833 C. See **HEAVEN**, **THE LOWER REGIONS**.

**PARALYSIS.** It reveals the state of the mind, II, 683 B.

**PARASCEVE.** It is devoted to fasts, II, 973 A.

**PARASITES.** For the glory of a freedom enslaved under contract to the belly, they aspire to being fattened amid insults, I, 475 A.

**FAMILIAR SPIRITS (*paredri*).** II, 698 B.

**WALLS.** They make improper use of Tyrian, hyacinth-colored, and royal hangings in place of paintings, I, 1312 A.

[Col. 1571]

**PARIS.** He rendered judgment among the three goddesses, I, 359 ff. This was celebrated in song by actors, ibid.

**PARRICIDE.** It differs greatly from homicide, I, 316 A.

**CHILDREN OF UNMARRIED WOMEN (*Parthenii*).** The Romans were bolder than they, I, 457 A.

**PARTNERS.** The Jews were partners in Marcion’s error, II, 343 A.

**CONNECTIVE PARTICLE.** II, 221 B.

**PARTULA.** The goddess who governs childbirth, II, 713 A.

**PASSOVER.** A figure of Christ, II, 486 A. The Lord’s Passover—that is, Christ’s Passion (or the Parasceve), II, 630 B. Christ chose Passover Day on which to suffer, II, 460 A. On that day, on which the religious observance of fasting is common and, as it were, public, we have rightly laid aside the kiss, I, 1178 A. We celebrate Passover in an annual cycle, in the first month, II, 973 A. Blastus, a Judaizing heretic, says that Passover must be observed in no other way than according to the Law of Moses, on the fourteenth day of the month, II, 72 B. Christians kept vigil throughout Passover night, I, 1294 B. From Passover Day until Pentecost they rejoiced, II, 80 A. That season is to be spent in complete exultation, II, 973 A. See **GENUFLECTIONS**, **FASTS**.

**PASIPHAË.** An oracle in Laconia, II, 730 A.

**PASSIBLE.** Whether every body is passible, or everything passible is a body, II, 657 B.

**CHRIST’S PASSION.** Christ fulfilled everything written concerning his Passion, II, 460 B.

**GOOD SHEPHERD.** Christ, II, 992 A. Depicted on a cup, II, 1000 C.

**THE SHEPHERD.** The book of Hermas, apocryphal, II, 1000 B, C; 1021 A.

**FATHER.** A name of affection and power, I, 1154 A.

**THE ETERNAL FATHER.** Before the world was created he was alone and yet not alone—how this is so, II, 160 A. He is invisible, II, 171 A, 187 A; impassible and incapable of suffering with another, II, 194 C. The Father must have a Son in order to be Father, II, 165 A. The Father testified concerning the Son before the Son testified concerning the Father, II, 323 A. The Father is the whole substance, while the Son is a derivation and portion of him, II, 164 B. The name “Lord” accrues to the Father, and the Son likewise receives it through the Father, II, 480 C. The Praxeans say that the Father descended into the Virgin and was himself born and suffered, II, 154 D. See **SON**.

**FATHER OF THE SACRED RITES.** I, 313 A.

**FATHERLAND.** One must live for one’s fatherland, II, 1047 B. See **THE PUNIC WOMAN**.

**PATRIARCHS.** They were uncircumcised, II, 602 A, B. It was lawful for them to make use of marriage in many forms, I, 1277 A. The New Law removed this license, ibid. They mingled marriages not only with several wives but also with concubines, II, 921 A. God permitted this until the world should be restored, ibid. Christ delivered the Patriarchs and Prophets from the lower regions of the earth, II, 742 C ff.; 657 A.

**A PATIENT PERSON.** Who he is, I, 1272. No one is humble unless patient, I, 1267 A. We cannot suffer for God unless the Spirit of God is in us, II, 195 A. Yet the Spirit himself is not the sufferer, but supplies the ability to suffer, ibid. To suffer the very thing one has done to others is most bitter, II, 306 A. Who was said by the gentiles to suffer because of God, I, 413 A.

**PATIENCE.** Its praise, I, 1271 B ff. Its usefulness and pleasure, I, 1263 A. Where God is, there too is patience, his foster-child, companion, and servant, I, 1272 B ff. It both follows and precedes faith, I, 1259 B. With God as teacher, patience accompanies love, I, 1268 B. The whole discipline of patience is comprised in the command to love one’s enemies, I, 1260 B. Love is trained by the disciplines of patience, I, 1268 B. What the method and discipline of patience are, I, 1273 A. Its distinctive property is not to be envious, I, 1268 B. In losses, it is training in giving and sharing, I, 1261 A. What the exercise of patience in the body is, I, 1269 B. The loss patiently borne prepares in advance a distaste for wealth, I, 1260 B. God is the example of patience, I, 1251 B ff. Forms of divine patience, I, 1252 A, B; 1254 B. God’s patience is the nature, operation, and excellence of a certain innate property, I, 1251 B. Christ’s patience, I, 1252 B ff. It opens God’s ears, I, 1269 A. As he was about to depart, Christ desired to be filled with the pleasure of patience, I, 1254 A. Before Christ, patience did not exist on earth, because neither did faith, I, 1260 A. He taught a new patience, restraining even retaliation and the remembrance of injury, II, 395 B. All philosophers unanimously praise patience, I, 1251 A. The patience of the gentiles is false and disgraceful, I, 1273 A. The devil teaches his own followers a peculiar patience, ibid.

**ACCIUS’S DISH.** II, 562 B.

**PATRICIUS.** A certain Patricius was removed from the Senate because he possessed a god made of [an uncertain number of] pounds of silver, I, 299 A.

**PATROCLUS.** Patroclus demanded funeral rites from Achilles, I, 745 B.

**PAUL.** Apostle of Christ, teacher of the nations in faith and truth, vessel of election, founder of churches, and censor of disciplines, I, 1221 A; II, 327 A, 1009 A. The peaceable apostle, I, 1216 A. An immovable pillar of the disciplines, II, 1011 A.

[Col. 1572]

His praise, II, 789 A. Paul was promised beforehand in Genesis, II, 148 A, B; 469 C. He is foreshadowed in Benjamin, II, 148 A, and in Saul, II, 470 A. He sprang from the tribe of Benjamin, II, 469 C. Whether he alone put on Christ in baptism, I, 1213 A. Whether he preached the same doctrine as the other Apostles, II, 35 ff. He rebuked the Apostles because they were not walking with a straight step, II, 268 B; 364 C; 474 A, B. But the question concerned only the Law, II, 474 A. In Peter he rebuked not any ignorance but his conduct, II, 35. He visited Peter by the duty and right of faith and preaching, II, 33 C. How he warmed the infants in faith like a nurse, II, 949 C. Paul attained birth into Roman citizenship when he was reborn there through the nobility of martyrdom, II, 151 B. As a persecutor, before being made an Apostle, he was the first to shed the Church’s blood, II, 148 A. He left the Gospel sealed with his own blood, II, 366 C. At Rome, II, 49 B, he is torn apart, II, 151 A. At Rome he is crowned with the same end as John the Baptist, II, 49 B. It is fitting that Peter is made equal to Paul in martyrdom, II, 36 C ff. Through Nero’s savagery they sowed Christian blood, I, 403 A. Paul wrote his letters in Greek, I, 1186 A. Works were wrongly attributed to him by a presbyter of Asia, I, 1219 A.
