Cerdo accepts neither all nor the whole of the Apostle’s letters, II, 70 C.

**THE POOR.** The Lord always justifies the poor and condemns the rich beforehand, I, 1260 B. Prayer feeds the poor, I, 1196 A. It is gain to incur expense in the name of piety, if the poor are assisted, I, 474 ff. With how great a charity Christians relieved the poor, I, 470 A. No one is poor in spirit unless humble, I, 1267 A.

**PAVENTINA.** A goddess, I, 600 C.

**FEAR (*Pavor*).** A god, I, 600 C, invented by Hostilius, II, 266 C.

**PEACOCK.** Most beautiful and adorned with whatever color it wishes, II, 1030 B; but its feathers are silent, and its voice displeases, II, 707 A. The orator Hortensius was the first who could bring himself to kill a peacock for food, II, 1048 B. Homer remembers that he was once a peacock, in Ennius’s dream, II, 707 A; 708 B.

**PEACE.** The peace of the pious is war against Satan, I, 621 A. See **KISS**. The right of peace was shared among the churches, II, 891 A. The Roman bishop grants peace and withdraws it, II, 155 B. Peace was granted to penitents, I, 621 A; II, 42 B; by martyrs, I, 621 A. Heretics indiscriminately share peace with everyone, II, 56 B.

**SINNER.** He is handed over to the devil, as though to an executioner, for punishment, II, 106 A. Before receiving pardon he must bewail himself, because the season of repentance is likewise a season of danger and fear, I, 1238 A. The example and dangers of the restored sinner, I, 1241 A, B.

**SIN.** Original sin is affirmed, I, 813 A. Sin deserves to be called nothing other than an evil deed, I, 1230 B. The will is the origin of the deed, for one sins only by the will, I, 1232 B. Not only sins of deed but also those of will must be avoided and purged by repentance, ibid. A. Every sin must be attributed to impatience, I, 1258 B. There are carnal sins and spiritual sins, I, 1232 A. The seven capital sins, II, 375 A, B. Intermediate and slight sins, II, 983 B. The greatest or supreme sins, ibid. Whoever sins undoubtedly commits idolatry, I, 664 A. Offices that lead to sin must be abandoned altogether, I, 667. It is not the thing within which evil is done that is condemned, but what is done, II, 497 A. We are scarcely torn away from evil by the Creator’s dreadful threats, II, 300 A. God alone is without sin, and Christ alone is the human being without sin, II, 720 B. For all sins committed in flesh or spirit, by deed or will, the same one who appointed punishment through judgment also promised pardon through repentance, I, 1233 A. Fasts obtain from God the blotting out of sins, II, 963 A. Whether there are remissible and irremissible sins, II, 985 ff. How joyful the forgiveness of sins is, II, 65 D. Prayer washes away sins, raises the fallen, supports those who are falling, and sustains those who stand, I, 1196 A. See **TRANSGRESSION**.

**MONEY.** Money exists for the soul, not the soul for money, I, 1262 A. Those who increase their wealth put money before the soul, I, 1261 C. How the burning desire for money is extinguished, II, 306 A.

**LIVESTOCK.** Provided and entrusted by the Lord for our uses, I, 1255 A. Worshiped by the gentiles, I, 365 A. Cattle and wild beasts pray and bend their knees; on emerging from their stalls and caves, they look up to heaven with mouths not idle, I, 1196 B.

**PELASGIANS.** Mentioned, II, 1031 B.

**PELOPONNESE.** Occupied by the people of Amyclae, II, 700 A.

**HOUSEHOLD GODS.** Each person worshiped the Penates kept in his own home, I, 344 B.

**PENTECOST.** I, 682 C ff. A most ample period for arranging baptisms, I, 1222 A. See **PASSOVER**.

**PENULA.** What it is, I, 301 A.

**PERAGENOR.** A god, I, 600 C.

**TRAVELERS.** Prayer escorts them, I, 1196 A.

**PEREGRINUS.** He cast himself upon a funeral pyre, I, 625 A.

**DANGERS.** Fasts obtain from God the averting of dangers, II, 963 A. No fear of an uncertain danger is justified, II, 823 A.

**PERIPATETICS.** They say that the soul consists of a fifth substance, II, 653 A.

[Col. 1573]

**PERIPHLEGETHON**, or **PHLEGETHON**. A river among the dead, I, 520 A.

**PERJURERS.** They immersed themselves in water to expiate their crime, I, 1205 A.

**PERMISSION.** It arises from indulgence, II, 917 A. It comes, as it were, from an unwilling will, ibid. Not everything permitted by God proceeds from his sheer and entire will, ibid.

**PERO BOOTS.** Extremely effeminate, II, 1046 B. Men wearing *perones* desire pearls to emerge from mud, I, 1312 A.

**PERPETUA.** A most steadfast martyr, I, 715 A. Her vision near the day of her Passion, ibid.

**PERSIANS.** They believed the sun to be a god and worshiped it, I, 369 A. They had it depicted on their shields, I, 370 A. Persian incest with mothers, I, 325 A.

**PERSECUTION.** Its condition must be considered—whether it comes from God or from the devil—so that how it is to be faced may be more readily settled, I, 107 A. The sources of persecution are the synagogues of the Jews, II, 143 A. To burn in persecution’s heat is to be tested concerning the constancy of one’s faith, II, 106 B. Prayer extinguishes persecutions, I, 1196 A. What takes place in persecution is the glory of God as he approves or rejects, II, 104 A. In a time of persecution God is believed and feared more, ibid.; faith is more vigilant and disciplined, ibid.; attention is given solely to fear and hope, ibid. See **CHRISTIANS**, **GENTILES**.

**PERSEUS.** Born from Jupiter, I, 606 A. A false god, ibid. Depicted among the constellations by Aratus, II, 142 A.

**PERSON.** The term was employed by Tertullian, II, 167 C, D. Christ is the person of God, the Lord, II, 500 B. In one person we see a twofold state, not confused but joined: God and the man Jesus, II, 191 C.

**PERSUNDA.** A goddess, I, 601 A.

**PETROMA.** What it is, I, 313 D.

**PETITION.** Every petition can both deceive and be deceived, I, 1221 B.

**ROCK.** Christ, proclaimed in many ways and figures, II, 622 B.

**ROCKY BATTLE LINE.** What it is, II, 622 B.

**PETER.** The disciple dearest to Christ, II, 387 C. Why his name was changed, ibid. Peter, the rock on which the Church was to be built, II, 34 B. Upon him the Church was constructed, II, 1025 A. To him were given the keys of heaven, and through him to the Church, II, 142 C. Whether the power of loosing and binding was conferred upon Peter with respect to the capital sins of the faithful, II, 1026 A. He recognized Christ as the one promised in the Scriptures, II, 410 B. Only in the spirit did he see Moses and Elijah, II, 413 C. Peter was the first to baptize, II, 1025 B. He baptized in the Tiber, I, 1203 B. Nothing was hidden from him, II, 34 B. He is rebuked for inconstancy, having been overcome by Paul, II, 35 ff.; 364 C; 474 A. He ordains Clement bishop of the Romans, II, 45 A. Peter’s church, II, 1025 A. Peter is struck down, II, 151 A. He left the Gospel sealed with his own blood, II, 366 C. Peter suffered at Rome and is made equal to the Lord’s Passion, II, 49 B, when he is fastened to the cross, II, 151 B. See **PAUL**.

**PHAËTHON.** Represented by actors as cast down from heaven, I, 359 A.

**MANIFESTATIONS (*phanerōseis*) OF THE GIRL PHILUMENE.** II, 43 A; 71 C.

**PHARAOH.** He denied God, II, 301 C. His heart was hardened, ibid.

**PHARIA**, or **FARIA, FARREA** (Ceres). I, 366 A.

**PHARISEES.** By introducing certain additions to the Law, they were separated from the Jews, II, 61 A. Whence they received this name, ibid.

**PHERECYDES.** Pythagoras’s teacher, II, 649 B; 698 B. He reports that Saturn was crowned before all others, II, 85 A.

**PHIDIAS.** His hands fashioned the Olympian Jupiter from ivory, II, 803 A.

**PHILADELPHUS.** Soter’s successor; he reigned thirty years, II, 614 B. See **PTOLEMY**.

**PHILIP OF MACEDON.** While he was not yet a father, he had seen the womb of his wife Olympias sealed with a ring, II, 727 A.

**PHILOCHORUS.** An authority, II, 729 ff.

**PHILOMELA’S REMEDIES.** I, 570 B.

**PHILOPATOR.** He reigned seventeen years, II, 614 B.

**PHILOSOPHY.** Whence it was so called, I, 384 A. It is the battering, exclusion, and insult of truth, II, 65 A; 652 A. Its poisons, II, 650 A. Speechless philosophy is content with life itself; the very garb makes its proclamation, II, 1049 A, B. It is the material of secular wisdom, a rash interpreter of the divine nature and ordering, II, 19 A. It enjoyed freedom of intellect for extending investigations concerning the soul, II, 650 B, C. Uncertainties are investigated at length, while assumptions are debated at still greater length, ibid. Heresies are instigated by philosophy, II, 19 A. Under its name all heresies are condemned by the Apostle, II, 521 A. Those who fast from philosophy nevertheless remain alive, II, 655 B. See **DIALECTIC**.

**PHILOSOPHER.** An animal of glory, II, 647 A. A producer of words, destroyer of realities, friend and adulterator of error, I, 514 A. A disciple of Greece and of men, ibid. Philosophers as corruptors and adulterers, I, 509 ff. Men of glory, lustful for eloquence, I, 516 A. Retailers of wisdom and eloquence, II, 651 B. Patriarchs of heretics, I, 519 A; II, 19 A, 204 C.

[Col. 1574]

Who their god is, II, 317 B. A man exists before a philosopher, I, 616 A. Among the gentiles, every philosophical sect is approved, I, 563 B. Of them, only those who scorned the gentiles’ gods were condemned, ibid. Many were rewarded with statues and salaries, ibid. In virtues they are plainly unlike Christians, I, 502–514, as also in knowledge and discipline, I, 507 A. Their mind is improvident, II, 656 A. By affecting truth they corrupted it, I, 504 A; 506 A. They barked against their rulers, I, 502 A. They could not cast out demons, I, 503 A, which they believed to rank immediately after the gods, ibid. What sort of gods, and which ones, they invented, I, 347 A. They worshiped the gods no more than others did, I, 353 ff. The philosopher directs his whole being toward acquiring fame, I, 507 ff. He is harsh when he knocks at the doors of truth, I, 609 B. Their excessive concentration often fails to see what lies before their feet, II, 656 A. The absurd opinions of certain philosophers, I, 520 ff. They are refuted, ibid. They disagree among themselves through the various caprices of their sects, I, 1251 A. They agree on patience alone, ibid. More diversity than fellowship is found among philosophers, since diversity is detected even within their fellowship itself, II, 649 B. They mingled what they had discovered with uncertainty, I, 516 B. From truth they argued against truth, I, 519 B. They had read the Prophets, II, 649 B. They corrupted many things drawn from the Scriptures, I, 515 ff.; 520 A. Their ingenuity distorted the Old Testament, I, 516 A; 519 A. At times they held opinions close to ours, II, 648 B. Philosophers dared make no certain assertion concerning God, I, 516 ff. They maintain that this world is ungenerated and unmade, II, 809 A. They agree that all things consist of opposites, II, 657 C. Some of them gave the name “pleasure” to rest and tranquility, II, 659 B.

**PHILUMENE.** II, 18 B; 71 C; 763 A; 791 A.

**PHOENIX.** By conducting its own funeral, it renews the most certain proof of resurrection, II, 811 B. See **IROMUS**.

**PHOENICIANS.** They pour forth into Africa, II, 700 A; 1035 B.

**PHOSPHORUS.** An utterly cold Latin rhetorician, II, 553 B.

**PHRYGIAN HERETICS.** II, 72 A.

**PHRYGIANS.** They were the first race, I, 570 B. They give birth to the Romans, II, 1035 B. Comic poets mock the Phrygians as timid, II, 685 B.

**PHRYNE.** Diogenes’s prostitute, I, 510 A.

**CONSUMPTION.** It preserves the mind, II, 683 B.

**PHYGELLUS.** He failed with respect to the truth, II, 828 B.

**PHYSICAL PHILOSOPHERS.** Their master was Mercury Trismegistus, II, 567 A. Physical superstition holds the elements to be gods, II, 477 A. Why there is such great disagreement among them concerning the nature of God, I, 587 ff.

**PHYSCON.** A most lustful king, II, 1042 B.

**PICTURES ON CUPS.** II, 991 C; 1000 C.

**PILATE.** A Christian in conscience, he wrote to Tiberius Caesar about the deeds Christ had performed, II, 403 A.

**PINDAR AND CALLIMACHUS.** They relate that Apollo put on the laurel after killing the dragon Delphine, II, 85 B.

**FISH.** Fish of the sea, a holier food, II, 262 B. A certain stony substance is found in fishes’ brains, I, 1311 A. We Christians are little fishes, according to our Fish (*ἰχθύς*, *ichthys*), Jesus Christ, in whose water we are born, I, 1198 A. Nor are we saved otherwise than by remaining in the water, ibid. ff. See **PYRRHUS**.

**PISISTRATUS.** His zeal for establishing libraries, I, 379 A.

**PISO AND GABINIUS.** Consuls, I, 305 A.

**DESIRE TO PLEASE.** The desire of men to please women, and of women to please men, is innate through a defect of nature, I, 1325 A. Nothing is more hateful to God than the pursuit of pleasing others, II, 911 A.

**PLATO.** A corrupter of young men, I, 510 A. His pride, I, 511 A, trampled upon by Diogenes, ibid. The honey of his eloquence, II, 702 B. His honor, II, 651 B, and his Christianity, II, 20 B. He especially devoted himself to the Egyptian Mercury, II, 649 A. For the sake of his belly he was sold to Dionysius, I, 513 A. He dies in his sleep, II, 639 A. Plato said that God was difficult to discover and impossible to express, I, 509 A. He asserted divine providence, I, 517 A. He did not deny the existence of angels, I, 405 A. He established the tribunal of Minos and Rhadamanthus and the judgment of the dead, I, 415 A. He holds the stars to be gods, calling this class of gods fiery, II, 260 B. His opinion concerning the world, II, 1033 B; concerning ungenerated matter, II, 667 A; and concerning the soul’s immortality, II, 795 C. He locates the soul’s seat in the head, II, 671 B. He divides it in two, into rational and irrational parts, II, 672 A, B. He maintains that there are certain invisible, incorporeal, supermundane, divine, and eternal substances, which he calls Ideas, II, 678 A. His error concerning the Flood, I, 481 A. Plato, the provisioner of all heretics, II, 686 C. How this is so, II, 687 A.

**PLATONISTS.** They said that God is incorporeal, I, 517 A. They acknowledged God’s providence, ibid.

**FULLNESS.** What the Creator’s fullness in Christ is, II, 520 A, B.

**PLEROMA.** Valentinus introduced the Pleroma and thirty Aeons, II, 68 A. At the summit of the highest heights presides the thirtyfold Pleroma, with Horos marking the outermost boundary, II, 577 A.

**PLINY THE YOUNGER.** He asks Trajan what is to be done about Christians, I, 272 ff. See **TRAJAN**.

[Col. 1575]

**PLUTO.** He was said to conduct the corpses of the dead with a hammer, I, 362 A; 576 C.

**RAIN.** Divinely obtained during the reign of Marcus Aurelius, II, 295 A; 703 C. See **RAINSTORM**. The Heavenly Virgin, promiser of rains, I, 413 A.

**REPENTANCE.** Repentance is wholly a confession of sin, II, 769 B. Its name in Greek is formed not from confession of sin but from a change of mind, II, 314 A. See **EXOMOLOGESIS**. The causes of repentance are sins, II, 985 A. Its spur comes from faith, II, 403 B; its instrument is fear, I, 1240 A. Repentance is life when it is set before death, I, 1233 B. God is appeased by repentance, I, 1243 A. Through affliction of flesh and spirit we make satisfaction for former deeds, I, 1223 A. The remedy of repentance is common to soul and body, I, 1232 A. To the extent that you do not spare yourself, God will spare you, I, 1243 B. The season of repentance is a season of danger and fear, I, 1238 A. Repentance does not perish, because it finds patience, I, 1268 B. Works of repentance performed by Christians in a time of public calamity, I, 486 ff.; and by gentiles, I, 487 A. The fruit of repentance is pardon, II, 1001 A. God promised pardon for all sins through repentance, I, 1233 A. As often as one sins, so often is one forgiven, I, 1240 C. Repentance would be practiced in vain if it lacked pardon, II, 785 B. Repentance recalls us into the Lord’s favor, I, 1231 B. Once it has been recognized and undertaken, it must never thereafter be revoked by repetition of the sin, ibid. From repentance the fruit of amendment ripens, II, 1001 A. Where there is no amendment, repentance is necessarily vain, I, 1228 A. By all means let it grieve one to sin again, but let it not grieve one to repent again, I, 1242 A. Let the abundance of heavenly mercy not produce wantonness in human rashness, I, 1240 B. The second repentance is one and only one, I, 1243 B. God placed a second repentance in the vestibule, to open to those who knock—but now only once, because it is now the second time, I, 1241 B. Who is indebted to this repentance, I, 1242 A. The more laborious proof of this repentance, I, 1243 B. What God’s repentance is, II, 311 C; 313 B, C. At the beginning of the world God consecrated repentance in himself, I, 1229 A. A confession of repentance occurs even with respect to good deeds, to the reproach and condemnation of one who has proved ungrateful for a benefit, II, 312 A.

**PENITENTS.** How great and of what kind their rites are, I, 1243 ff. The discipline of voluntary penitents is the same as that of other public penitents, I, 487 A.

**POETS.** How vain they are, I, 609 B. They love nothing other than singing, II, 707 A. They continually mutter such things to us, so that we neither hear anything certain nor see it, II, 677 B. Poets are not to be believed even when awake, II, 707 A. Plato judged that they should be expelled from the city, and why, I, 595 A. A man exists before a poet, I, 616 B. The poets knew that demons existed, I, 405 A. They sampled many things from our Scriptures, or even corrupted them, I, 515 ff.; 520.

**POLLIO.** See **VEDIUS**.

**POLYCARP.** Ordained by John, II, 45 A. He governed the church of Smyrna, ibid.

**POLYCRATES OF SAMOS.** No god of the gentiles was more fortunate than he, I, 337 A. His daughter foresaw the cross from the Sun’s anointing and Jupiter’s washing, II, 728 B.

**FRUITS OF SODOM.** When touched, they turn to ash, I, 483 A.

**POMPEII**, or **TARPEII**. Fire poured over this city of Campania from its own mountain, I, 485 A; 571 B; II, 1034 B.

**POMPEY THE GREAT.** Inferior only to his theater, I, 642 B. He placed a temple of Venus above the theater, and why, ibid. He was the first to bring cherries to Rome, I, 334 B; 606 B. After capturing Jerusalem, he found no image in the Temple, I, 364 ff. No god of the nations was more exalted than he, I, 337 A. Pompey’s three altars, II, 1031 B.

**PONTIFEX MAXIMUS.** The Roman *pontifex maximus* and the wife of the Flamen marry only once, I, 1287 A; II, 928 B; 953 A.

**THE EUXINE PONTUS.** Its description, II, 246 ff. How inhospitable it is, II, 247 A. The fiercest peoples inhabit it—if living in a wagon can indeed be called inhabiting, II, 246 C. They prefer military service to marriage, II, 247 A. They devour the corpses of their parents, ibid. Their lust is promiscuous and naked, II, 246 C. Nothing in Pontus is so grim and barbarous as the fact that Marcion was born there, II, 247 B.

**PEOPLES.** Innumerable peoples inhabit the whole earth, II, 700 A, B.

**TO BEAR.** The Greeks also regularly use it in the sense of “to take away,” II, 373 A.

**TWO GATES.** Homer assigned two gates to dreams, II, 726 C.

**POWERS OF THE AGE.** How they are hostile to God, I, 690 A. See **PURPLE**.

**POTINA.** A goddess, I, 600 C.

**DRINK.** Its restriction is a part of xerophagy, II, 965 B. As the food is, so too is the drink, ibid.

**DIVINE COMMANDMENTS.** We must fulfill them not because the thing commanded is good, but because God commanded it, I, 1234 A. It is presumptuous to debate the goodness of a commandment, ibid. Remembrance of the commandments will pave a way to heaven for our prayers, I, 1166 A.

**PREACHERS.** They are so called from their official duty of speaking beforehand, I, 378 B. No others are to be accepted except Christ’s Apostles, II, 33 A.

[Col. 1576]

To preach comes first; to baptize comes afterward, I, 1216 A.

**PREFERENCE.** Preference for superiors discourages the weak, I, 1279 A.

**WARFARE.** Its occupations are harshness, deceit, and injustice, II, 621 A.

**GOD’S FOREKNOWLEDGE.** Defended, II, 293 B, C. It has as many witnesses as there are prophets, II, 290 A. God foreknew all things by ordering them, and ordered them by foreknowing them, ibid.

**PRESCRIPTION.** In summary proceedings, it is proper for truth to prevail by prescription, II, 323 A. See **QUESTION**.

**DIOMEDES’ BLOODSTAINED MANGERS.** II, 1011 B.

**PRESIDENTS.** The bishops are presidents of Christian assemblies, I, 469 A. Heretics do not show reverence even to their own presidents, II, 57 B.

**PRAESTITIA.** A goddess, I, 600 C.

**PRESUMPTION.** It is an impediment to fear, I, 1318 A. It is a portion of shamelessness; it inflates the petitioner and despises the giver, I, 1240 A. One who presumes is proud, ibid.; he reveres less, takes fewer precautions, and runs greater danger, I, 1318 A.

**PRAXEAS.** A heretic, II, 74 A. He abolished the peace of the churches of Asia and Phrygia with the Roman Church, II, 155 B ff. At Rome he managed two affairs of the devil: he expelled prophecy and introduced heresy, II, 156 A. He teaches that the Father himself is Jesus Christ, II, 154 D.

**PREMA.** A goddess, I, 601 A.

**PRESBYTER.** Among heretics, the one who is a presbyter today is a layman tomorrow, II, 57 A.

**FIRST.** That which comes from the first is in a certain sense first, II, 987 B.

**PRIMACY.** Those who seek positions of primacy are rebuked by Christ, II, 429 A.

**THE PRINCIPAL.** That which is above all things, before all things, and from which all things come, II, 201 B.

**BEGINNING.** “Beginning” or “commencement” is a word denoting inception, not the name of any substance, II, 214 B, C.

**PRISCA.** A prophetess, II, 809 A.

**PRISTINUS.** What kind of martyr he was, II, 970 B.

**PROBOLĒ.** What it is, II, 202 D.

**PROCLUS.** Proclus and those who are “according to Proclus” (*κατὰ Πρόκλον*), II, 72 A.

**PROCULUS.** Also called Torparcion, the steward of Evodia, I, 703 B; the dignity of virginal old age and Christian eloquence, II, 549 A. He miraculously cured the emperor Severus with oil, I, 703 B.

**REFUSAL TO BENEFIT.** Nothing is more malicious than to be unwilling to benefit another when one can do so, II, 272 A.

**STOREROOMS (*promae cellae*).** II, 854 B.

**MERITING.** To be unwilling to earn merit is to sin, II, 917 B. Obedience is the art of earning merit, I, 1255 A. See **MERIT**.

**PROMETHEUS.** Who the true Prometheus is, I, 378 A; II, 247 B.

**PROPHETS.** They are so called from their official duty of speaking beforehand, I, 378 B. God sent them from the beginning of the world, and why, ibid. A. They were flooded with the divine Spirit, ibid. Christ always spoke in the Prophets, II, 328 B. He is the seal of all the Prophets, II, 632 A. They sometimes announce future events as though already past, II, 326 B. They wrote many things figuratively, through allegories, enigmas, and parables, II, 326 C. Their words are to be understood differently from the way they are written, ibid. Whether they delivered all their messages through images, II, 821 A. Their utterances do not always, nor all of them, have an allegorical form, II, 822 B. Faith merits an understanding of prophetic obscurity, II, 422 A. Their speech manifestly announces the resurrection of the dead, II, 822 A, B. The Prophets were men worthy through righteousness and innocence, I, 378 A. They always suffered in the world on account of divine religion, II, 636 B. The latest Prophets are more ancient than the earliest Roman lawgivers and historians, I, 387 A. Whether they were translated into paradise, II, 744 A. The things foretold by the Prophets remain in the treasuries of literature and are not hidden, I, 378 B ff. After Christ’s birth there is no longer vision or prophet, II, 615 B; 632 B. We have succeeded to the place of the Prophets, II, 636 B.

**PROPERTIES.** The preservation of properties is fidelity to names, II, 776 B.

**PRUDENCE.** Prudence alone could shake and reveal God, II, 545 A.

**PSALMS.** Almost all sustain the person of Christ, II, 167 A. They represent the Son addressing the Father, ibid. The singing of psalms, II, 660 A; by alternating choirs, I, 1194 A. Psalms and hymns resound between two spouses, and they challenge one another as to who can sing better to their God, I, 1304 A. Valentinus’s psalms, composed with great shamelessness, II, 781 B; 786 A.

**PSAMMETICHUS.** He entrusted newborn infants to a tongueless nurse, and why, I, 570 A, B.

**FALSE APOSTLES.** They are adulterous evangelists, II, 364 ff. Deceitful workers who transform themselves through hypocrisy of conduct, not through preaching an adulterated subject, II, 502 C. They perform the greatest miracles to fortify the deception of their corrupted preaching, II, 59 B.

**PSYCHICS.** They do not receive the Spirit, nor do the things of the Spirit please them, II, 931 A.

**PTOLEMY PHILADELPHUS.** Most learned and profoundly knowledgeable in every kind of literature, I, 379 A. His exceedingly rich library at Alexandria in the Serapeum, I, 378 ff. There he deposited the Hebrew books of the Old Testament, which he had requested from the Jews and had translated into Greek under his supervision, I, 379 A.

[Col. 1577]

**PTOLEMY** (another). He reigned thirty-eight years, II, 614 B.

**PTOLEMY THE HERETIC.** He agreed with Valentinus in all respects, II, 69 B; 548 B. His *Miscellanies*, II, 562 B.

**PUBERTY.** It begins at approximately the fourteenth year, II, 716 A; and at the twelfth for females, ibid.; 905 A.

**PUBLICANS.** Why their name was so execrable, II, 997 B.

**PUDENS.** A governor who dismissed a certain Christian after he had been denounced, I, 703 A.

**PUDICITIA.** A goddess, daughter of Faunus, I, 599 B.

**CHASTITY.** It is the doorkeeper and priestess of God’s temple, I, 1316 A. It permits nothing unclean or profane to be brought in, ibid. Where God is, there is chastity; there too is dignity, its helper and companion, I, 1325 B. Without dignity it will not be preserved, ibid. How the dignity of chastity is displayed, ibid. God is glorified in the body through chastity and through attire appropriate to chastity, I, 1330 A. Whether chastity consists solely in the integrity of the flesh and avoidance of fornication, I, 1316 B. Whether it requires anything external in the ordering of dress and adornment, ibid. Chastity is the flower of conduct, the honor of bodies, the ornament of the sexes, the integrity of blood, the fidelity of lineage, the foundation of holiness, and the prior judgment of every good mind, II, 980 A. Although rare, not easily perfected, and scarcely ever perpetual, it can nevertheless be possessed to some extent, if nature has laid the foundation, discipline has persuaded, and censure has restrained, ibid. B. For Christian chastity it is not enough to be chaste; one must also appear so, I, 1332 A. Chastity is the principal discipline of the Christian name, II, 982 B. How greatly Christians detested its defilement, I, 535 A. They valued chastity above life, II, 983 A. The gentiles strove through torture to wrest it from them, II, 982 B ff. Chastity is now judged to be not the renunciation but the moderation of lusts, II, 980 B. Because the chastity of the world is vain, it is of no avail before God, ibid. Whatever chastity exists among the gentiles is acknowledged to be so imperfect and unformed, I, 1316 B. Women of the nations lack the consciousness of true chastity, ibid. See **CONTINENCE**, **LUST**, **BEAUTY**.

**MODESTY.** It precedes bodily injury, II, 141 A. Its armor, II, 911 B. Words hostile to modesty creep in through talkativeness, I, 1288 A. To surrender modesty through kisses and clasped right hands, II, 905 B. Some are more mindful of modesty than of health, I, 1244 B.

**CHILDREN.** They know and understand, II, 683 A, B. Childish little sayings, II, 575 A. The exposure of children, I, 325 A. Gentiles sometimes sexually violated exposed children, ibid. ff.; even the parents did so, I, 582 B. See **INFANTS**.

**BEAUTY.** Its use and fruit are luxury, I, 1319 B. Where chastity is, beauty is vain, ibid. See **COMELINESS**.

**THE PUNIC WOMAN.** She cast herself with her children into the flames of her burning fatherland, I, 598 B ff.

**PURPLE.** The garment of kings, I, 687 C. Purple or the other insignia of powers and dignities bear the stain of their profanation, I, 688 A.

**THE FAINTHEARTED.** Prayer consoles them, I, 1196 A.

**BOXER.** His crown presses upon his wounds, I, 134 A.

**PYRIPHLEGETHON.** Why it was invented, I, 520 A.

**PYRRHO.** His doctrine, I, 535 A.

**PYRRHUS.** He practiced the deception of fish, II, 698 A; 701 B. Apollo gave him an ambiguous oracle, I, 409 ff.

**PYTHAGORAS.** He sought tyranny among the Tyrians, I, 511 A. For this reason they wished to burn him alive, ibid. B.

He abstained from animals and fish, II, 701 B. Because he was unwarlike and inactive, avoiding the conflicts of Greece, he preferred the repose of Italy, being devoted to geometry, astrology, and music, ibid. He committed himself not only to a shameful but also to a reckless falsehood, II, 697 B. He is mocked by Laberius, I, 521 A. Pythagoras imagined that God originated from and was composed of numbers, I, 517 A. The opinion of Pythagoras and Empedocles concerning metempsychosis and metensomatosis, I, 521 A, 613 B; II, 702 A. The PYTHAGOREANS rejected beans, II, 732 C. The PYTHIAN demon, I, 1175 A. Its verdict declared Socrates the wisest man, II, 648 A. See NOSCE [KNOW]. PYTHONIC spirits, II, 698 B. Whether the PYTHONESS truly brought Samuel before Saul, II, 749 A.

## Q

**FOUR-HORSE CHARIOT.** Erichthonius was the first to harness a four-horse chariot, I, 641 A. Romulus was the first to display one at Rome, ibid. B. Chariot-racing frenzy, II, 279 A, 993 B. See **COLOR**.

**SEEKING, knocking, and asking:** their forms, II, 21 ff.

**JUDICIAL EXAMINATION BY TORTURE,** I, 276 A. Its use in uncovering crimes, I, 274 A, B; 275 B. It was employed against the guilty to extort the truth; only from Christians did the judges strive to hear a lie, I, 275 A.

**QUESTION.** To delimit the substance of a question within fixed bounds, II, 599 A. It is a just and proper rule that the meaning of an answer must pertain to the point of the question proposed, II, 453 B. Whence fruitless questions arise, [Col. 1578] II, 20 A. Christians must avoid endless questions, II, 651 A. The Apostle hates indeterminate questions, II, 20 A, 651 A. Questions are very often contrived from the accidental features of terms, as also from the shared meanings of words, II, 875 A. Questions are to be resolved from the Scriptures alone, II, 799 B.

**QUAESTOR’S** spear and written notice, I, 345 A.

**QUALITIES,** when they are changed, take possession of names, II, 776 B.

**REST** is the proper relief of bodies, II, 725 B.

**QUINTILLA,** a most monstrous heretic, I, 1199 A. She forbade water to be administered in Baptism, ibid., f.

**QUIRINUS.** Why Romulus received this surname, I, 599 B.

## R

**ASTROLOGER’S STAFF:** the astrologer abuses heaven with it, I, 673 B.

**ABDUCTION OF VIRGINS,** even now regarded as just and lawful among the Romans themselves, I, 637 A.

**REASON,** a thing belonging to God, I, 1227 A. God also is rational, and reason was first within him, II, 160 A. This reason is his own consciousness, ibid. He willed that nothing should be treated or understood without reason, I, 1227 A. Reason without goodness is not reason, II, 291 A. It lends support to tradition, custom, and faith, II, 80 A. The Christian name is regarded as an enemy of reason, I, 278 A.

**GUILT** of the soul precedes the body’s offenses, II, 275 A. Spirit and flesh share guilt with each other: the spirit because it commands, the flesh because it ministers, I, 1204 A. See **ACCUSED**.

**REBECCA** already belonged to the discipline of Christ because of her chastity, II, 904 C. From her womb came two peoples and two nations, II, 598 A, B.

**REBELS.** How easily advancement is gained in their camp, II, 57 A.

**EASTERN AND SOUTHERN REGIONS** are inhabited by more numerous populations, II, 692 B.

**KINGDOM.** Every kingdom and empire is sought through war and extended through victories, I, 431 A. God alone can bestow and establish kingdoms, I, 431 f., 608 B. Whether a kingdom has been promised to us on earth, II, 35 B. We confess that a kingdom has been promised to us upon earth, but before heaven and in another condition, II, 355 A. Those to whom it belongs to enter the kingdom of God must put on the power of incorruptibility and immortality, II, 865 A.

**RULES.** Their outward appearance bears the colors of ignorance, II, 548 A. To know nothing contrary to the rule is to know everything, II, 27 B. The rule of faith, II, 26 B, 889 A.

**REGULUS’** courageous spirit, I, 532 A, 625 C. He willingly consecrated with his whole body the novelty of a manifold and hidden cross, I, 584 A, C.

**NOTHING WHATEVER** that pertains to us is to be rejected by us, I, 1308 A.

**RELIGION** incurred envy as soon as God began to be worshiped, I, 137 A. The religion of Christ began together with hatred of itself, I, 307 A. To counterfeit religion is the greatest impiety, and why, I, 403 B. One person’s religion neither harms nor benefits another, I, 699 A. Nor does it belong to religion to compel religion, which must be embraced freely, not by force, ibid. The Christian religion was substituted in place of the Jewish, I, 392 A. Its truth is clearly demonstrated by a straightforward exposition of its teaching, I, 468 ff., 501 ff.; by the sacred oracles of the Prophets, which attained their fulfillment, I, 377 B, f., 389 ff., 501 A; by the unconquered endurance of the martyrs, I, 536 A, 705 f.; by the Christians’ very great power over demons, I, 413 A, 677 A, B; and by the public confession of demons adjured by Christians, ibid. See **CHRISTIANS**, **CHURCH**. The religions of the gentiles are shown to be altogether false, I, 404 A, 411 ff.

**KIDNEYS,** privy to the seeds, II, 582 B.

**REJECTION OF GOOD THINGS** is not ratified by God, I, 1230 A.

**DIVORCE** arises from discord or produces discord, II, 942 A. How unbridled and intolerable its license is, I, 303 f. It is, as it were, the fruit of marriage, I, 304 A. The justice of divorce has Christ as its defender, II, 442 C, though in such a way that he renders marriage with a divorced woman unlawful, II, 441 C. He made the prohibition of divorce conditional, II, 442 B. Whether divorce existed from the beginning, II, 442. Who first introduced it, I, 303 A. It was unknown at Rome for six hundred years after the city’s foundation, ibid.

**RESURRECTION** belongs to that which has fallen, II, 820 A. Nothing can rise again except that which fell, II, 491 C. For the dead to be raised is nothing other than for them to be made whole, II, 878 C. The resurrection is the gate of the heavenly kingdom and the confidence of Christians, II, 795 B. Hope of the resurrection is disdain for death, I, 585 A. The entire recurring order of things bears witness to it, II, 810 C. Reward and peril depend upon the outcome of the resurrection, II, 823 A. The resurrection of the flesh is harder to believe than the one Godhead, [Col. 1579] II, 797 C. No philosophy agrees concerning it, II, 521 A. The world is not ignorant of it, even when it errs, II, 796 A. It ought not to be rejected by the gentiles, and why, II, 583 f. The resurrection of the flesh was already accepted by the Jews with a simple and familiar faith, without any question concerning its quality, II, 849 C. One edict of God hangs over all: the resurrection of the dead, II, 819 A. It is shown to be possible for God, I, 522 ff.; that God wills it, ibid.; and that it is necessary, ibid.; II, 812 ff. Nor should one inquire too curiously how it can take place, II, 813 A. Whether it is rightly inferred that a dead human body must be raised to life because the soul can suffer nothing without it, I, 523 A, 813 B; II, 750 B, C, 816 ff. Some say that the resurrection is appointed for the soul alone, and why, II, 848 B. After Moses, Paul maintained the resurrection of the flesh, II, 850 A. The apostolic documents and many examples attest the resurrection, II, 849 A. It is proclaimed by deeds as well as words, II, 835 A. By what examples it is confirmed, I, 524 f.; II, 812 A, B: by the rising and setting of light and the stars, by the seasons and their fruits, ibid.; because man is lord of things that die and rise again, ibid.; from Pythagoras’ opinion concerning the transmigration of souls, I, 521 A; from Plato’s and Epicurus’, ibid.; from the phoenix, II, 811 B; and from Mithras, II, 55 A. If it is undermined in the resurrection of Christ, our own resurrection also is overthrown, II, 332 C. Some distort the resurrection into a figurative meaning, II, 820 B. The resurrection will be enacted after the eradication of Antichrist, II, 835 A. It will occur at the last moment of time and on the first threshold of eternity, I, 526 A. In what order the dead will rise, II, 864 C. All who have died from the beginning will be raised, reviewed, and reconstituted according to each one’s merits, I, 378 A. The body rises again, in whatever manner it has been dissolved, I, 525 ff. There will be only one resurrection, because God has so willed, I, 525 ff. After the resurrection the members will be released from their functions; they are not therefore unnecessary, II, 882 C. Then we shall be the same persons we are now, and not others afterward, I, 527 A: the worshipers of God will indeed remain forever with God, clothed over with the proper substance of eternity; but the profane and those who are not wholly devoted to God will remain under the punishment of equally perpetual fire, ibid. We are restored to life as what we are born, not as what we are damaged into, II, 878 B.

**RETRIBUTION** has never been established without prior notification, II, 419 B. See **REWARD**.

**ACCUSED PERSON.** No one is to be condemned merely on account of his name, I, 278 ff. How carefully his crimes are to be investigated, I, 278 A. Greater credence should be given to one who confesses voluntarily than to one who denies under compulsion, I, 274 ff. Under Roman law, accused persons who confessed were condemned, I, 276 A.

**REVELATIONS** must be tested to determine whether they are from God, II, 222 B.

**KING** upon his throne reaches as far as God, yet remains beneath God, II, 251 A. But when compared with God, he ceases to occupy the highest place, since supreme greatness has been transferred to God, ibid. The insignia of a king: robe, diadem, and scepter, I, 629 A. See **ANOINTING**.

**RHADAMANTHUS,** judge of the dead, I, 415 A.

**RHÔNE,** a river of Gaul, I, 583 B.

**RHODIAN AND PONTIC LAW,** II, 327 B.

**RHODES,** an island that emerged from the sea, I, 480 A.

**LAUGHTER.** Worthy laughter is permissible, II, 550 A. It befits truth to laugh, because it rejoices, ibid.

**ROBIGO,** a goddess, II, 637 B.

**RITES.** The various rites of the Church, I, 1294 A, B. The rites of religion among the Romans, who were poor in former times, I, 430 A, 608 A.

**ROME,** a city commemorating the Trojan race, I, 424 A. The city of seven hills, I, 454 A. For some of its gods, rustic Rome is older than they are, I, 432 A. There the assembly of demons established its seat, I, 640 A, B. The city of Rome is represented figuratively by Babylon because it is the vanquisher of God’s saints, II, 339 C, 620 B.

**ROMANS.** They derive their origin from Aeneas, I, 424 A. Phrygians gave birth to them, II, 1035 A. Their empire was begun and enlarged through crimes, I, 430 ff. They thought that its end would be the same as that of the whole world, I, 431 A. Christians also held this view, I, 700 A. What the Roman state is, II, 829 A. The summit attained by the Roman name is not to be attributed to merits of religious devotion, I, 439 A. On the contrary, their greatness arose from irreligion, I, 430 A. How far their kingdom extends, II, 611 B. They occupied the world, I, 439 A. Yet they did not extend their kingdom beyond the Germans, Britons, Moors, and Getulians, II, 610 C, f. They fortified their empire with the protection of their legions, II, 611 C. Roman religious observance is most meticulous, I, 422 B. Their entire religion is military, I, 367 A. At the public games they drenched Jupiter Latiaris with human blood, I, 317 A; II, 136 C. Their empire was founded before any worship of the gods had been instituted at Rome, I, 429 A. They were great before they were religious, I, 430 A, 608 A. They committed as many sacrileges as they raised trophies, I, 431 A; celebrated as many triumphs over gods as over nations, ibid.; and gathered as many spoils as there were images of gods, ibid. They were guilty of injuring the divine majesty, I, 431 A. Roman gravity is mocked, I, 473 A. See **GODS**, **GENTILES**.

[Col. 1580]

**CATHOLIC CHURCH AT ROME,** II, 42 A. Happy Church, upon which the Apostles poured out their whole doctrine together with their blood, II, 49 A, B. Peter and Paul bequeathed to the Roman Church the Gospel sealed with their blood, II, 366 C. From that Church authority is available to us, II, 49 A. The African churches exchanged tokens of fellowship with it, II, 49 B. The authority of the bishop of Rome, II, 155 B.

**ROMULUS.** Whether he is the same as Quirinus, I, 641 B. He invented the god Consus, II, 236 C. He was the first to display a four-horse chariot at Rome, I, 641 B. He had Proculus as guarantor of his ascent into heaven, II, 369 B. Why he did not merit divinity, I, 599 B.

**ROSES** gathered from the garden of Midas, II, 98 B, 1036 A.

**RUCINA,** a goddess, I, 600 C.

**UNFORMED** is that which is imperfect, II, 222 B.

**RUFUS’ BANQUETS,** II, 1049 A.

**RUTILIUS,** a most holy martyr, II, 108 B, C. His history, ibid.

## S
**SABBATH.** It was a temporary commandment, II, 605 B, C, ff. In the past the righteous did not observe the Sabbath, II, 601 A, B. The Maccabees fought courageously on the Sabbath, II, 606 C. Whether its observance is a remedy for salvation, II, 601 A. The Pharisees were wholly mistaken about the Sabbath law, failing to notice that it conditionally prescribed a cessation from works of a specified kind, II, 385 A. The law of the Sabbath prohibited human works, not divine works, II, 309 B, ff. We must always keep the Sabbath by abstaining from every servile work, not merely every seventh day but throughout all time, II, 605 B. The Sabbath that God wishes us to observe, ibid. Christ makes the Sabbath day, holy from the beginning through the Father’s blessing, still holier through his own blessing, II, 386 A. Christ is called Lord of the Sabbath because he defended it as his own possession, II, 385 C. He utterly abolishes the Sabbath of the Jews, II, 384 ff. Christians never fasted on the Sabbath except on the Preparation Day of Passover, II, 973 B. Some did not even kneel, I, 1191 A.

**SABAEAN FRANKINCENSE,** more costly than other kinds, I, 493 A.

**RAPE OF THE SABINE WOMEN,** I, 637 A.

**PRIESTS** were forbidden to marry again, I, 1286 B; II, 922. A twice-married priest is deprived of exercising the priesthood, II, 938 B, C.

**THE EARLIEST RITES OF THE ROMANS** were simple, I, 430 A.

**FATHER OF SACRED RITES.** See **HIEROPHANTS**.

**SACRAMENTS OF THE CHRISTIANS,** I, 1286 A; II, 806 A, B. God causes matter to serve in his own sacraments, I, 1203 A. To make a response using the words of the sacrament, I, 624 A. One tradition of the same sacrament governs the laws of the churches, II, 32 B. The sacrament, or mystery, of allegory, II, 478 A. What the sacraments of the figures are, II, 470 A. The sacrament of the wood, II, 635 A, B ff. See **CROSS, WOOD**. Fasts obtain from God knowledge of the sacraments, II, 963 A. Satan imitates the realities of the divine sacraments in the mysteries of idols, II, 54 A.

**SACRIFICES.** Their rational institution, II, 310 B. A sacrifice acceptable to God, II, 608 B. To offer sacrifice, I, 1329 B. What sacrifices are pleasing to God, II, 806 B. God must be propitiated with spiritual sacrifices, II, 310 B, C, 608 ff. Why God instituted the burdens of sacrifices and the troublesome scrupulosities of works and offerings, II, 306 B, C. The Jews were required to sacrifice in only one place, II, 607 C. Sacrifices consisting of earthly offerings and spiritual sacrifices, II, 608. The difference between the sacrifices of Cain and Abel, II, 607 A, B. In these the twofold sacrifices of the two peoples were prefigured, ibid. C. Spectators at a sacrifice, I, 686 A, and participation in it, I, 1177 ff. See **CHRISTIANS, GENTILES, THE DEAD, SYNAXES, DISTRIBUTION OF SACRIFICIAL MEAT**.

**SACRILEGIOUS PERSONS.** Christians were formerly regarded as such, I, 699 B.

**SADDUCEES,** arising from the root of the Samaritan error, II, 61 A. Their distinctive opinion, II, 46 A. They dared to deny the resurrection of the flesh, II, 46 A, 61 A. They admit the salvation of neither soul nor flesh, II, 846 A. Their cunning question about repeated marriages, II, 937 C. Who the adherents of the Sadducees were, II, 796 B. Their kindred, II, 754 A.

**AGE.** The age belongs to God; worldly things belong to the devil, I, 648 A. In this age everything is imaginary and nothing is true, II, 96 B. See **WORLD**.

**ARROW.** Who first wounded bodies with one, II, 1048 B.

**SALT.** Children were treated medicinally with salt and honey, II, 412 A.

**SALII.** One intending to dine with the Salii needed a creditor, I, 474 A.

**SALMACIS,** a spring, II, 568 A.

**SOLOMON** reigned only within the boundaries of Judaea, from Dan to Beersheba, II, 611 B. As a figure of Christ, he took to himself as bride the Church drawn from idolatry, II, 382 B. Although endowed by the Lord with every grace and all knowledge, he was led into idolatry by women, II, 14 B. He even lost the glory he had possessed before God, being dragged into idolatry by women, II, 494 B. Solomon is rejected, but only after he had been possessed by foreign women and enslaved to the idols of the Moabites and Sodomites, II, 311 B. God’s wrath came upon Solomon after his debauchery and idolatry, II, 350 C.

[Col. 1581]

**SALVATION.** The flesh is the pivot of salvation, II, 806 A. Nothing is so worthy of God as the salvation of the human being, II, 316 C. By hoping, fearing, and taking care, we shall be saved, I, 1318 A. One who is watchful can truly be secure, I, 1318 A. The work of salvation and preservation is not man’s but belongs properly to God, II, 385 B.

**GREETING,** or a mutual blessing when people meet on the road, II, 419 B.

**SAVIOR.** There is one Savior, Christ, II, 778 A.

**SAMARIA** had revolted from Israel, possessing that schism formed from the nine tribes settled by Jeroboam at Samaria, II, 339 B, 620 A. What the spoils of Samaria are, II, 339 A, B, 619 C. Idolatry is denoted by the name Samaria, ibid.

**SAMIAN SOPHIST.** What he thought about souls after death, II, 697 A, B.

**SAMOS,** an island that floated to the surface, II, 1034 A. Samian vessels, I, 430 A, 607 A.

**MYSTERIES OF SAMOTHRACE,** I, 309 A. It was forbidden to disclose them, ibid.

**SOUL OF SAMUEL.** Whether it was summoned by the woman with the familiar spirit, II, 740 A.

**FORMS OF SANCTIFICATION.** How many there are, II, 915.

**DESIGNATED FOR HOLINESS,** and therefore for salvation: the children of believers, II, 718 B.

**HOLY ONE OF GOD,** Christ, II, 371 B. No one was holy before the Holy Spirit was manifested from heaven, II, 1001 C.

**SANCTUS,** made a god because of his hospitality, I, 599 C.

**BLOOD** is nothing other than red fluid, II, 771 A. To arrest a flow of blood by additionally draining a small vein, II, 132 B. Empedocles located the cause of a keen or dull disposition in the quality of the blood, II, 683 B. In ancient times a covenant was struck by drinking blood, I, 321 A. It was formerly believed that the souls of the dead could be propitiated with human blood, I, 644 C. Christ desired to fulfill the figure of his saving blood, II, 460 A. The blood of Christians is seed, I, 583 A.

**WISE PERSON.** No one is wise unless faithful, II, 15 A. The sages of Greece, I, 387 A.

**WISDOM** flows from the order of simplicity, II, 544 B. Corpulence impedes wisdom; leanness promotes it, II, 683 B. See **SOPHIA**. Human wisdom is an imitator and falsifier of truth, II, 20 B. Worldly wisdom is a reckless interpreter of the divine nature and dispensation, II, 19 A. See **PHILOSOPHY**.

**BOOK OF WISDOM,** ascribed to Solomon, II, 544 B.

**SARDANAPALUS,** notorious for his lusts, II, 1042 B.

**SARDINIA.** A certain hero there deprived those who slept in his shrine of visions, II, 733 B.

**SARMATIANS,** sluggish in mind, II, 692 B. Now subjected to Christ, II, 611 A.

**SARMENTICII, “FAGGOT-MEN.”** Christians were so called, I, 531 A.

**ORACLE OF SARPEDON** in the Troad, II, 730 A.

**SATAN,** prince of the demons, I, 405 A. He was formerly the most eminent of the angels and the wisest of all, II, 297 A. He fell from his heavenly eminence, ibid. B. He is the angel of malice, the author of every error, etc., I, 613 A. He is the informer and accuser of the saints, II, 710 C. He imitates God’s sacraments, II, 928 C. He taught Cain to begin with murder, I, 1258 A. Whether he loses his own quality when he transforms himself into an angel of light, II, 877 A. He will be permitted to do nothing against the servants of the living God unless the Lord permits it, II, 104 D. Why God permits this, ibid. See **DEVIL**.

**SATISFACTION** is arranged through confession, I, 1243 B. We make satisfaction for former sins through the struggle between flesh and spirit, I, 1225 A.

**SATURNINUS,** a disciple of Menander the Simonian, II, 686 A.

**SATURNINUS THE HERETIC** called God the “unbegotten Power,” II, 61 A. He taught that God remained in the highest and infinite regions, in the upper realms, ibid. According to him, inferior angels made the world, ibid. See **SENTIUS**.

**SATURN,** the source of all—or at least of the greater or better-known part—of divinity among the gentiles, I, 329 A, 601 B. The first and parent of all the gods, ibid. Why he is called the son of Heaven and Earth, I, 331 A, 601 ff. How falsely, ibid. How Saturn is Time, I, 602 B. Saturn represented as square, II, 266 A. He was not a god but a man, who received his kingdom and life from another man, I, 329 ff., 602 C. He lived a mortal life, I, 330 A, 602 ff. He is said to have castrated his father, I, 601 C. These things are not to be explained allegorically, I, 321 A, 602. He was received by Janus, I, 330 A, 602 ff. The people of that age were uncivilized, I, 331 A. Saturn was the first to fasten tablets together, I, 330 A, 602 ff. He taught men to stamp coins, ibid. Why he presides over the treasury, I, 330 A. He commends the cloak, II, 1045 A. He was crowned before all others, II, 85 A.

[Col. 1582]

In secular society it was permissible to propitiate the Africans’ Saturn with a human victim, II, 136 C. Infants were sacrificed to him in Africa, and for how long, I, 595 B: until the proconsulship of Tiberius, and afterward in secret, I, 314 ff. His priests, who sacrificed human beings to him, were fastened to trees, ibid.

**SATURNALIA,** festivals, I, 492 A, 681 C ff. Saturday was appointed for leisure and eating, I, 371 A.

**SAUL,** better than the rest, was afterward ruined by envy, II, 14 B. When he was chosen, he had not yet become a despiser of the prophet Samuel, II, 311 B.

**THE LADDER** Jacob dreamed of shows some ascending to the upper realms and others descending to the lower, II, 103 C, 357 A.

**SCANDAL** is not the example of a good thing but of an evil one, building a person up toward evil and sin, II, 892 A.

**SCAPULA,** a judge struck by God after condemning a martyr, I, 702 B.

**SCAURUS.** His impurity, II, 1049 A.

**STAGE.** See **THEATER**.

**SCHISM** is unity among heretics, II, 57 C. Rivalry is the mother of schisms, I, 1218 A.

**SCHOOLS** were honored with holidays, I, 674 B. A believing pupil will not attend them because of their defilements, II, 675 B. See **SCHOOLMASTER**.

**SCIAPODS,** II, 312 B.

**KNOWLEDGE** makes the soul more adorned, not richer, II, 656 A. To know nothing is to know everything, II, 27 B. After Christ Jesus we have no need of curiosity, nor of inquiry after the Gospel, II, 20 B ff. The Apostle forbids endless questions, II, 651 A. Knowledge of natural things is not lacking even in beasts, II, 688 B.

**SCIPIO,** cut from his mother’s womb, drew living breath, II, 692 C. He destroyed Carthage, II, 1031 A. More righteous and more martial than every god of the gentiles, I, 337 A.

**SCORPION** harms with its tail, II, 121 ff. Remedies for its sting, II, 122 A. The earth festers forth a great scorpion from a small evil, II, 121 A. Scorpions and serpents signify spiritual forces of wickedness, II, 421 B.

**HOLY SCRIPTURE.** Its majesty and authority, I, 386 ff., 446 A, 468 ff.; II, 167 B. Its fullness is to be revered, II, 218 A. Its antiquity, I, 384 A, 386 A, 515 A. It is older than other literary compositions, I, 520 A. The documentary corpus of the divine Scriptures, I, 377 A. Their reverent reserve, II, 960 C. Scripture belongs to God, II, 510 C. The authority and integrity of the Old Testament cannot be doubted, I, 384 A. The books of the Old Testament were produced by men filled to overflowing with the divine Spirit, I, 378 A, B. Every Scripture is divinely inspired and suitable for edification, I, 1308 A. Those who do not receive it cannot belong to the Holy Spirit either, II, 34 C. The Scriptures foretold what would occur after Christ, II, 319 B. The Old Testament pertains no less to Christians than to Jews, I, 386 A. Why and how, I, 394 A. The books of Scripture were translated from Hebrew into Greek, I, 378 ff., and deposited in the library of Philadelphus at the Serapeum, I, 380 A. See **EZRA**. The Jews read them publicly, their freedom to do so being subject to tax, I, 381 A. They were read in Christian assemblies, I, 477 A. Christians did not conceal them, nor could they, I, 446 A. Philosophers and poets drew much from them, either borrowing or corrupting it, I, 515 ff., 520 A. Scripture divided into chapters, II, 127 B. No one comes to our writings unless already a Christian, I, 610 A. Whoever studies the Holy Scriptures will be compelled to understand and believe in God, I, 381 A. No one knows the marrow of Scripture better than Christ’s own school, II, 146 B. Nourishments of faith derived from understanding the Scriptures, I, 1299 A. Through their proclamation Christians renewed their hope and confidence, I, 489 B. Faith saves, not proficiency in the Scriptures, II, 27 B. Christian instruction comes from Solomon’s porch, II, 20 B. Scripture lays down the law, nature bears corroborating witness, discipline requires it, II, 510 B. The Apostle writes to all when he writes to certain persons, II, 512 B. The harmony of all the Scriptures, II, 632 B. No divine utterance is so disjointed and diffuse that only its words are maintained while the rationale of those words is not established, II, 23 A. Holy Scripture is always broadly divided, I, 634 B. Divine literature is richer in proportion to the capacity of each subject, II, 53 A. The meaning of Scripture requires the guidance of a definite interpretation, II, 22 C. Simplicity itself commends commonly held perceptions, as do the mutual accord of judgments and the familiarity of the opinion, II, 799 B. They are therefore considered all the more trustworthy because they define things plainly, openly, and in a manner known to all, ibid. Scripture denies what it does not record, II, 934 C. Where it makes no mention of temptation, it does not admit an interpretation involving temptation, II, 404 D. It commonly uses a figurative transference of human terms, based upon a comparison of offenses, II, 620 A. Where the truth of the Scriptures, their interpretations, and all Christian traditions is found, II, 31 B. Questions must be resolved from the Scriptures alone, II, 799 B. A falsified meaning clamors against the truth just as much as a corrupt pen corrupts it, II, 30 A.

[Col. 1583]

How great a sacrilege it is to interpolate the Scriptures, II, 51 ff. Their adulteration always accompanies variation in doctrine, II, 51 C. The adulteration of the Scriptures and their interpretations must be assigned to the place where diversity of doctrine is found, II, 51 C, 146. One person overturns Scripture with his hand, another overturns its interpretations through his meaning, II, 52 A. See **MARCION**. The Scriptures have been so disposed by God’s will as to supply heretics with materials, II, 53 A. Heretics frame their questions from the Scriptures alone, II, 512 B. They twist the simplicity of ordinary words into a question, II, 222 A. We accomplish nothing with heretics through encounters over the Scriptures, II, 30 ff.

**WRITING** comes after speech, I, 616 B. A hand is heard upon wax more clearly than every sound; a letter speaks more loudly than every mouth, I, 694 A. The hand can write nothing that the soul has not dictated, whether conceived by itself or handed down by another, ibid. A. See **TRADITION**.

**SCYTHIANS** entered into a covenant by drinking blood, I, 321 A. They ate the flesh of dead human beings, ibid. Subjected to Christ, II, 611 A. The Scythians occupy the Parthian lands, II, 700 A. They overcome the Persians, II, 1035 B. See **ANACHARSIS**.

**SECTS.** The name of no sect is evil unless there is something evil in it, I, 282 ff. None is to be hated merely because of its founder’s name, ibid. Nor is it justly condemned on that account, ibid. Tertullian calls the Christian religion a sect, I, 259 A.

**SECOND.** What is second is not at all distant from what is first, II, 987 B.

**SECUNDUS THE HERETIC** agreed with Valentinus, II, 69 B, 548 B.

**DILIGENCE** does not produce trifles, I, 1288 A.

**SELGIC SHEEP,** II, 1039 A.

**SEMAXII, “HALF-AXLE MEN.”** Christians were so called, I, 531 A. Bound to the stake of half an axle, they were burned within a surrounding mass of brushwood, ibid.

**SEED.** Animal seed comes from a distillation of the soul, II, 696 A. Bodily seed comes from a purification of the flesh, ibid. The generative fluid is animated by God’s breath, ibid. Every fruit is already present in its seed, I, 320 A. The blood of Christians is seed, I, 535 A.

**SENECA,** often one of ours, II, 682 C. His *Fortuitous Events*, I, 535 A. He assailed the gods of the gentiles in the bitterest words, I, 343 A. His statement concerning the arts and ages of all things, II, 682 B. He teaches that everything, even the soul, comes to an end after death, II, 721 A, 795 B.

**SENONES** besieged the Capitol, I, 485 A.

**SENSES** originate from the soul, II, 675 A. The soul is furnished with every instrument of sensation, II, 805 B. Every opinion arises from the senses, II, 675 A. To perceive and to understand are one, II, 678 C. To perceive is to undergo, and to undergo is to perceive, II, 667 A. Nothing animate is without sensation, and nothing sentient without a soul, II, 775 A. In the human being there are bodily senses and intellectual senses—which they are, II, 654 A. Incorporeal things are presented to the senses, ibid. C. Sense precedes the pen, I, 616 B. The senses are the ministries of the outer person, II, 82 B. The question concerning the five senses, II, 674 ff. Whether they are liable to error, II, 674 B, C. Philosophers located the ruling faculty of sensation, some in the brain and others between the eyebrows, II, 814 A. Heretics captivate minds by appealing to a favorable consensus of perceptions, II, 799 B. The Stoics say that the sense undergoes an impression but does not form an opinion, for it is the soul that acts, II, 675 A. God can be apprehended by the senses, I, 375 B. The fruits of divine gifts are conveyed to the soul by the senses, II, 82 B.

**SENSIBILITY.** In the *Timaeus* Plato declares it irrational and entangled with opinion, II, 674 ff.

**SENTINUS,** a god, I, 600 C.

**SENTIUS SATURNINUS,** writer concerning the census of the Jews under the emperor Augustus, II, 405 B, 1031 B.

**SEPTIMONTIUM,** a festival, I, 606 B, 674 B.

**SEVENTY-TWO TRANSLATORS** of the Old Testament, I, 379 ff.

**BURIAL.** The repose of burial, the asylum of death, I, 461 A. Frankincense was used in burying Christians, I, 493 A, as were the prayers of presbyters, II, 737 B, C. Governors prohibited burial chests, I, 701 A. In a cemetery, someone gave the Body [of Christ] in communion to the body of a deceased person, II, 738 A. According to the gentiles, when the unburied are admitted to the underworld, II, 745 B. How Christ’s burial was removed from their midst, II, 629 C.

**SERAPEUM,** or temple of Serapis. With what magnificence it was constructed at Alexandria, I, 380 A. No one was permitted to enter it without paying a tax, I, 574 A. The Greek translation of the Old Testament was deposited there, I, 380 A.

**SERAPIC DINNERS.** What they were, I, 474 A.

**SERAPIS,** a god, I, 305 ff. Rejected from the Capitol by the gentiles and expelled from the senate-house of the gods, but afterward restored, ibid.

**SPEECH** is the voice and sound of the mouth, air set in motion and intelligible to hearing, II, 162 B. Otherwise it is something empty, void, and incorporeal, ibid. It proceeds from an organ of flesh, II, 805 B.

[Col. 1584]

It is formed from spirit, and spirit is the body of speech, II, 163 B. Speech precedes writing, I, 616 B. Whether it was invented by human beings, I, 616 B, C. The birth of Speech was completed when God said, “Let there be light,” II, 161 B. It then assumed its form and adornment—sound and voice, ibid. Diffuse speech is burdensome and vain, II, 894 B.

**SPEECH AS GOD,** constituted in the image of God, II, 802 C. God brought forth Speech as a root brings forth a shoot, a spring a river, and the sun a ray, II, 163 B, C. Some in their simplicity say that Speech was with God in the beginning, whereas it would be more fitting to regard Reason as older, II, 160. God, however, was not “speaking” from the beginning, but he was rational even before the beginning, ibid. Speech is God, and the Speech of the Lord remains forever—that is, by continuing in its own form, II, 191 A. How Speech became flesh, II, 190 D. In the Gospel, more than in the other Scriptures, I find Speech to be both the minister and the arbiter of the Ruler, II, 218 A. See **CHRIST, SON, ΛΟΓΟΣ (*LOGOS*, “WORD”), WORD**.

**SPEECH,** an aeon of the Valentinians, II, 553 ff.

**SERPENTS** seek dry and waterless places, I, 1198 A. The serpent’s cast skin and old age, II, 1036 B. From the beginning the serpent preyed upon the divine image, II, 544 B. It is accustomed to tempt, ibid. The bronze serpent placed upon the wood, and why, II, 682 A. Why Moses raised an image of a serpent, I, 667 B; according to the Ophites, II, 64 A. This representation does not pertain to idolatry but to healing, I, 667 B, C ff. It was a figure of Christ’s cross, I, 667 C; II, 347 B.

**SLAVES** were customarily beaten with whips, I, 301 A. Marriage was forbidden to them, I, 1300 B. Their chains were made of gold, I, 1328 A. Slaves—captives or persons purchased under an evil omen—were sacrificed at funerals, I, 645 A. Others were thrown to moray eels as food, II, 1048 B. See **GALBA**.

**ROMAN DINNERS** cost one hundred sesterces, I, 300 A.

**SETHOITES** taught that two men, Cain and Abel, were created by angels, II, 65 B. Because of these two, great disputes and dissensions arose among the angels, etc., ibid. Their opinion concerning the seed of Ham, II, 66 A, B.

**SEVERITY** is good if it is just and if the judge is good—that is, just, II, 302 C ff. It is something owed to justice, II, 204 A. What severity’s obligations are, II, 303 A.

**THE EMPEROR SEVERUS** was mindful of the Christians, I, 703 B. At the beginning of his reign he favored them, ibid. A. He retained in his palace the Christian Proculus, who had healed him with oil, ibid. He repealed the Papian and Julian laws, I, 286 ff. He intended to build a temple to Christ, I, 290 C.

**SEX.** There is no sex in heaven, I, 1307 A. In the solemn function of the sexes, soul and flesh act together: the soul through desire and impulse, the flesh through deed and action, II, 695 B.

**SIBYNAE,** a kind of hunting spear, II, 361 C.

**DROUGHTS** dispelled by the kneeling and fasting of Christians, I, 703 C, 1195 C. See **RAINSTORM, RAIN**.

**SICILY.** The origin of its name, I, 481 A. How it was formed into an island, II, 1034 A. Dionysius, tyrant of Sicily, II, 728 A.

**HEAVENLY BODIES.** Plato regarded them as gods, II, 260 B. The differentiated confusion of the stars, II, 1033 A.

**SIGE, “SILENCE,”** Mother or Silence, II, 551 A, B, 666 A.

**SIGN.** Every sign belongs to the one to whom the thing signified belongs, II, 458 C. The Romans worshiped their military standards, swore by them, and preferred them to all the gods, I, 367 ff., 579 A.

**TO SIGN** the bed and the little body, I, 1296 A. At every advance and movement, at meals, upon going to bed, and wherever daily life takes us, we wear down our foreheads with the sign of the cross, II, 80 A. The flesh is signed so that the soul also may be fortified, II, 806 B.

**SILENCE,** an aeon of the Valentinians, II, 68 A. See **SIGE**.

**THE OBLIGATION OF SILENCE** was assigned by the ancients to all mysteries, I, 309 A, 567 C.

**SILENUS,** a Phrygian, asserted the existence of another world, II, 220 B. He chatters beside Midas’s ears, II, 1032 B; the ears that he earns, II, 649 A.

**LIKENESS** shares honor with truth, II, 518 A. Through likeness of soul we correspond to our parents in character, II, 693 B.

**SIMON MAGUS,** purchaser of the Holy Spirit, II, 708 B. Cursed by the Apostles, he was cast out of the faith, I, 672 B, C ff. He dared to call himself the supreme Power—that is, the supreme God, II, 62 B, 708 B ff. He taught that the world was established by angels, ibid. A statue was erected to him as to a god, I, 346 ff. See **HELENA**. The followers of Simon the heretic promise that they can set the souls of the prophets in motion, II, 749 A. Simonian magic is a discipline that serves angels, II, 46 C. It was condemned by Peter in the person of Simon, ibid.

**SIMONY.** How severely it was condemned, I, 469 ff.

**SIMPLICITY,** joined with wisdom, II, 544 B. It alone will be able to recognize and reveal God, ibid.

[Col. 1585]

Heretics wish simplicity to mean the overthrow of discipline, while calling our care for discipline pandering, II, 56 B. They twist the simplicity of ordinary words into questions, II, 222 A.

**IMAGES** were invented by the Etruscans, I, 430 A. They were made from earthly and cheap materials, and from little vessels intended for common and extremely humble use, I, 399 ff. They are valued according to their metals, I, 341 A. In ancient times there were no images of the gods among the Romans, I, 430 A, 608 A—that is, before Numa Pompilius, ibid. Before they were fashioned in human likeness, how ridiculous they were, I, 339 ff., 366 ff., 578 A, B. The gentiles believed such things to be gods, I, 488 A, 579 A, and believed gods to be made by a ridiculous consecration, I, 339 ff. Images of the gods suffer from the gentiles the same things as condemned Christians do, ibid. First, they are headless, ibid. They are built upon a cross and a stake, I, 340 ff., 579 A. They are shaped with axes and polished with planes and scrapers, ibid. They are defiled, violated, broken, reduced to fragments, destroyed, and consumed, I, 344 A. They are fouled by kites, mice, and spiders, I, 343 A. Whether they should be made depended upon the emperor’s decision, I, 439 A. Craftsmen altered their fate, I, 339 ff. They converted them into another form, pawned them, and sold them, I, 344 B. The holier the god, the dearer the price for which its image was sold, II, 346 A, 576 A. Anyone could choose or reject them, I, 344 ff. See **IDOL**.

**BOSOM OF ABRAHAM.** What it is, II, 444 B.

**SIRENS,** monstrous and fabulous singers, I, 308 A. Their bloodstained mouths, ibid.

**EMERALDS** lay hidden in women’s rings or girdles, I, 1312 A.

**OFFSPRING.** To provide substitute and posthumous offspring, II, 938 A. It is more probable that offspring is named from its origin than that origin is named from its offspring, II, 219 B.

**SOBRIETY** assists in obtaining dreams, II, 733 A. See **ABSTINENCE, WOMAN, GLUTTONY, DREAMS**.

**RENUNCIATION OF FELLOWSHIP** is never a prejudgment of guilt, II, 981 B.

**SOCRATES** was declared by the oracle to be the wisest of all human beings, I, 503 A—but falsely, ibid. All that wisdom of his arose deliberately from habitual equanimity, not from confidence in ascertained truth, II, 647 B. He was a corrupter of youths, I, 509 A. Socrates was a philosopher who acted as a pimp, I, 373 A. He shared his wife with his friends, I, 372 A. He acknowledged demons, I, 405 A. A demon attended Socrates from childhood—a truly dreadful tutor, I, 405 A; II, 647 B, 718 A. He customarily said, “If the demon permits,” I, 503 A. He consoled his wife when she cried out like a woman, II, 647 A. Socrates did not believe that the gods existed, I, 589 A. He destroyed them, I, 354 A. His madness in swearing by the dog and the goose, I, 353 ff. When about to die, how impiously he ordered that a cock be sacrificed to Aesculapius on his behalf, I, 503 A, 589 A. His disputation concerning the soul after he had drained the hemlock of his sentence, II, 647 A. His condemnation, I, 563 A. Why he suffered capital punishment, ibid.

**SOCRATES OF ARGOS,** I, 605 C.

**SODOM AND GOMORRAH,** cities consumed by fire, I, 382 A. Their impiety earned showers of fire, II, 1033 A ff. The earth still smells of the conflagration, I, 483 A. There is vast desolation there: a bereft region, everything ashes, II, 1034 A, B. See **FRUITS**. Those cities would have escaped if they had fasted, II, 962 C. The people of Sodom and Gomorrah, II, 339 B, 620 A, 1034 A, B.

**SUN,** a body, since it is fire, II, 658 B. Epicurus imagined that the sun was only a foot across, I, 591 C. One sun alone regulates this world, II, 285 B. The Peripatetics said that it was far larger than the earth, I, 591 C. For whom it is not healthful, II, 285 B. The proverb, “Written by the ray of the sun itself: so plainly does it shine,” II, 863 B. The eyes of owls do not know the sun; those of eagles endure it, II, 658 B. Infants of a barbarian people were anointed facing the sun, II, 338 A. The extraordinary failure of the sun when Christ died was recorded in the archives, I, 401 A. At the assembly in Utica, the sun’s light was almost extinguished; this was so great a portent that it could not have suffered this through an ordinary eclipse, I, 701 B. The sun mourned its son, who had been taken down from heaven, I, 359 A. The Persians believed it to be the true God and worshiped it, I, 369 A. Why, I, 370 A, 579 A. Why its worship was imputed to Christians, I, 369 A. It was depicted upon linen and shields, I, 370 A. Its image shone from the summit of the temple, I, 369 A. The circus is principally consecrated to the Sun, ibid. B.

**SOLITUDE,** the Creator’s customary domain, II, 373 D. See **GOD**.

**CONCERN FOR KINSHIP** is inquisitive in a different way from the concern belonging to servitude, I, 459 B.

**DREAMS** come from God, II, 731 B, C. Very many are sent by demons, II, 731 B, and by magicians, I, 411 A. No one can dream at will, II, 732 A. The outcomes and effects of dreams, II, 724 A. The trustworthiness of dreams is reported from their fulfillment, not from their appearance, II, 749 C. Epicurus judged them wholly vain, II, 726 B. Whether any nature is exempt from dreams, II, 734 A. Whether infants dream, II, 733 B.

[Col. 1586]

The difference between dreams and ecstasy, II, 325 ff. Honors and talents are revealed during sleep; cures are bestowed, thefts disclosed, and treasures conferred, II, 728 B. Sobriety assists dreaming, II, 733 A, B. More certain and more elaborately fashioned dreams occur toward the end of the night, II, 732 B. Homer assigned two gates to dreams: the horn gate of truth and the ivory gate of deception, II, 726 C. See **CICERO, NERO, SOPHOCLES, PHILIP, THRASYMEDES**.

**SLEEP** is the restorer of bodies, renewer of strength, test of health, pacifier of labors, and physician of toil, II, 722 B, C. See **NIGHT**. It comes to the body for rest, but not to the soul, II, 722 A, 725 A, C, 819 B. A human being is refreshed by sleep more than wearied by it, II, 322 A. It is the end of work, II, 722 A. It is not contrary to nature, as certain philosophers hold, II, 721 B ff. The various opinions of philosophers concerning sleep, ibid. The natural rationale of sleep and its rational nature, II, 724 B. Reason precedes it, II, 722 B. It is not always induced by weariness, ibid. A. Much preparation for it lies in food and drink, II, 723 A. It is so useful that without it no soul can subsist, II, 722 B. See **SORANUS, STOICS, STRATO**. Sleep is the mirror of death, II, 734 A, 750 B. Sleep, so salutary and so rational, is fashioned as an image even of the death that is now public and common to all, II, 723 B. The body, lying motionless in sleep, is shown as it lay before life and as it will lie after life, II, 723 C. Sleep proves how very much the soul can accomplish even without the body, II, 724 A. In dreams good deeds cost nothing and sins incur no danger, II, 726 A.

**SOPHIA, “WISDOM,”** is God’s Spirit and his Son, II, 212 ff.; and his Speech, II, 213 A. She was begotten from eternity, II, 212 ff. She was not without a beginning, II, 213 A. She occupies the place of understanding and knowledge, II, 212 C.

**SOPHIA,** an aeon of the Valentinians, II, 553 ff. They also call Sophia “Earth” and “Mother,” II, 575 A.

**SOPHOCLES,** the tragedian, recovered through a dream a golden crown that had been lost from Athena’s citadel, II, 729 A.

**SORANUS,** a physician, wrote four books on the soul, II, 655 A, B. His opinion concerning the soul, II, 658 A, 668 B; concerning infanticide, ibid.; and concerning sleep, II, 724 C.

**SOTER** reigned at Alexandria for thirty-five years, II, 692 A.

**ANOTHER SOTER** reigned for thirty-eight years, II, 692 A.

**SPARTEOLI.** Who they were and whence they were so called, I, 474 A, D.

**SPECTACLES.** No spectacle is without a disturbance of the spirit, I, 647 B. The origin of spectacles lies in idolatrous superstition, I, 466 A. Their entire apparatus consists of idolatry, I, 635 B. With how many crimes they are defiled, I, 466 A, 630 ff. Whether Christians may attend a spectacle, I, 493 A, 655 ff., or behold its pleasures, I, 647 A. With regard to the pleasures of spectacles, the condition of those persons is discredited who by nature perceive all the things from which the instruments of spectacles are made, yet lack knowledge of them, II, 84 A.

**MIRROR.** Nothing is the mirror of another—that is, it is not coequal with it, II, 233 B. To consult a mirror on every occasion, I, 1325 A. Sleep, the mirror of death, II, 743 A, 750 B.

**HOPE.** Christ is the one hope of the whole world, II, 760 C. The hope of Christians is in heaven, I, 260 A. In this interval hope consists in contemplation through faith—not manifestation or possession, but expectation, II, 826 B. What the anchors of our hope are, I, 1332 B. By hoping we shall fear; by fearing we shall take care; by taking care we shall be saved, I, 1318 A.

**HOPE,** a goddess, I, 600 C.

**SPEUSIPPUS,** Plato’s nephew and successor, perished in adultery, I, 510 A.

**TO BREATHE** is to emit breath from oneself, II, 663 A.

**HOLY SPIRIT.** He is the third person of the Most Holy Trinity, II, 163 C, D ff. The third name of the Godhead and the third degree of majesty, II, 196 A. He is of the same nature as the Father and the Son, ibid. He proceeds from the Father and the Son, II, 159 B. Why he is not called Son, II, 163 A. Holiness is his distinctive nature, II, 933 C. He was manifested through the animal of simplicity and innocence, I, 1208 A. He is the Lord’s Vicar, II, 809 B. Christ sent his vicarious power to guide believers, II, 26 B. The Holy Spirit is the teacher of truth, II, 34 C, 196 A. The determiner of Christian discipline, II, 1001 B. Believers possess him, II, 920 A. He is recognized spontaneously and does not await an admonition to holiness, II, 933 C. The Holy Spirit is granted to no one without the sacrament of faith, II, 647 B. Christ is known by no one without the Holy Spirit, ibid. The Spirit of God is in us when we suffer, yet he does not himself suffer, but grants us the ability to suffer, II, 195 A. Who the Spirit borne over the waters was, I, 1208 A; II, 227 A. The Spirit of God turned Saul into another man, II, 665 A. The portion of the Holy Spirit that, in the form and measure of prophecy, had acted in John to prepare the Lord’s ways, now necessarily had to depart from John—that is, to be gathered back into the Lord as into the sum and mass from which it came, II, 402 B. See **PARACLETE, XYSTARCH**.

[Col. 1587]

The Spirit is the same as the Speech of God, II, 189 A, B.

**EVIL SPIRIT** attaches itself to every human being from the very gateway of birth, lying in wait to catch souls, II, 717 B. What an unclean spirit, burdened under exorcism, answered, I, 657 B. The adversarial spirit appears through divergence in preaching, first adulterating the rule of faith and thereby adulterating the order of discipline, II, 931 C. See **DEMON, DEVIL, SATAN**.

**SPIRIT** is a body of its own kind, in its own form, II, 162 C. Whether spirit and soul are two distinct things, II, 664 A, B. The animate spirit is the charioteer of the body, II, 740 B. See **SOUL, BODY**. Certain substances are spiritual, I, 404 B. Gentile philosophers were unable to explain the idea of a spiritual and incorporeal reality, I, 516 ff.

**BRIDE OF CHRIST,** pure and holy, lacking even a blemish of the ears, II, 981 A. See **CHURCH**, and **MARRIAGE, WIFE**.

**STATILIUS TAURUS** erected the walls, II, 1031 A.

**STATINA,** a goddess, II, 718 A.

**STATION.** What it is, I, 1181 ff. It is established from the Old Testament, II, 967 ff. Military stations, I, 1183 A; II, 92 A, 967 A. From these stations Christians derived the term for their fasts, I, 1183 A. On station days one should attend the sacred assembly even if one does not receive the body of Christ, I, 1182 ff. Stations before councils, II, 972 C. A station is to be observed until the hour when the world, darkened from the sixth hour at the Lord’s death, performed its mournful office, II, 967 A, B. To prolong a station until evening, II, 967 B ff. Stations on Wednesday and Friday, II, 956 A, 973 A. The half-fasts of stations, II, 961 B. See **FASTING**.

**STATUES** were erected to courageous men amid their torments, I, 534 A. Philosophers were rewarded with statues, I, 502 A. Statues are memorials of resurrection, I, 634 A.

**STATE.** The state of each thing is something definite and gives a law to perception, so that its perceived state is as the thing itself is, II, 107 B.

**STAR** differs from star in glory, not in substance, II, 866 A. See **HEAVENLY BODY**.

**STEPHEN** assumed an angelic eminence, II, 877 A. While he was being stoned, he saw Christ still standing at God’s right hand, as one who would sit there thereafter, II, 195 C.

**STERCULUS,** the god who scatters manure over the fields, I, 423 A, 599 B. How perversely he is made a god, ibid.
