**FOR A BARREN WOMAN TO GIVE BIRTH** contrary to nature was no more difficult for God than for a virgin, II, 165 C.

**STESICHORUS,** an author, I, 641 A. Blinded because of the abuse directed against Helen of Troy in his poem, he afterward recovered his sight, II, 709 A.

**BODILY MARKS.** What they are, II, 480 A.

**CONTRIBUTION.** Each month Christians offered one in the common chest,
I, 470 C. **TEMPLE CONTRIBUTIONS** (*stipites templorum*), I, 494 A. **AN UNWORKED POST** (*stipitem non elaboratam*) was worshiped by certain pagans, I, 366 A. **STOICS**, named after the place where they held their gatherings, I, 282 A. They declared God to be corporeal, I, 517 sq., and situated outside the world, I, 518 A. They maintain that matter flowed through God as honey flows through the honeycomb, II, 236 B. They prefer to believe that God, in his most provident arrangement for humanity, implanted dreams in us as the distinctive consolation of a natural oracle, II, 731 A. They affirm that sleep is the dissolution of sensory vigor, ibid. B. Their opinion concerning the soul, II, 653 A. They do not charge every perception, nor perception at all times, with falsehood, II, 674 C. Stoic Christianity, II, 20 B. **STOLA**, the garment of girls, I, 688 B. **STRABO**, author, II, 728 A. **STRABO THE NATURAL PHILOSOPHER** said that heaven and earth were God, II, 260 B, 729 A. He taught that the soul is in the central region of the eyebrows, II, 671 B, or in the membranes, ibid. He defends the unity of the soul, II, 670 B. He says that sleep is the separation of the conjoined spirit, II, 721 B. **NEW YEAR’S GIFTS** (*strenae*) mentioned, I, 672 B, 682 B. **STYGIAN MARSHES**: the poet related that they wash away death, II, 734 B. **THE PEN** comes after thought, I, 616 B. **SUBIGUS**, a god, I, 601 A. **SUBSTANCE** is one thing, and the nature of a substance another, II, 704 C. The one substance that God bestowed upon Adam and made the matrix of all people, II, 684 A. No substance is worthy for God to assume, II, 335 A. One substance in three who cohere, II, 168 C. See **TRINITY**. **SWEAT** is an indication of heated digestion, II, 622 A. **SUETONIUS**, author, II, 637 B, 725 A. **THE SOUL** is in a certain sense an auxiliary substitute (*suffectura*) for the spirit, II, 280 B. **SUPREME GREATNESS** must necessarily be unique, II, 250 sqq. See **GOD**. **SUMPTUARY LAWS** restrain ostentation and expenditure, I, 302 sqq. They were later disregarded, ibid. **COMMON SUPERSTITION**, which is ordinary idolatry, when ashamed of the names and stories of ancient dead persons represented in images, takes refuge [Col. 1588] in the interpretation of natural phenomena and conceals its disgrace beneath cleverness, II, 260 C. The pagans’ superstitions are shameful and idle, I, 305 A. Luxury and ambition are more prevalent than every superstition, I, 671 A. **PUNISHMENT BY WATER**, a kind of death more cruel than the others, I, 308 A. Those who repent not only thwart eternal punishments but conquer them through temporal affliction, I, 1244 A. **FINGER-COUNTING GESTURE** (*supputaria digitorum gesticula*), I, 387 A. **SUSANNA** was vindicated at her trial, II, 81 A. **UNCHASTE SUSPICIONS** must be avoided in every way, I, 1331 A. **TO ENDURE TO THE END** means nothing other than to suffer the end, II, 139 B. **SUTRIUM’S** city-goddess, Nortia, I, 421 A, 596 A. The Sutrian Veneti, II, 1046 B. **THE SIBYL**, a true prophetess of the truth, existed before all literature, I, 385 A, 603 B. Her verses concerning Saturn, ibid. The pagans attributed her oracles to demons, ibid. Tacitus’s testimony concerning the pagans’ Sibyls, I, 385 A. **SULLA**: no god of the pagans was more fortunate, I, 337 A. His most splendid platters, II, 706 A. **THE SYLLOGISMS OF APELLES**, II, 71 C. **SYMBOL**. See **FAITH**, **SACRAMENT**. Under the pressure of necessity, God permits the symbol of death, I, 1238 B. **THE SYNAGOGUES OF THE JEWS**, sources of persecutions, II, 143 A. **CHRISTIAN ASSEMBLIES** (*synaxes*): how holy they were, I, 468 sqq. On what day they were held, I, 371 A, 579 A; II, 79 B. They assembled into a gathering, so that, as though forming a hand, they might encircle God with prayers, I, 468 sqq. In the assemblies they prayed and read the Holy Scriptures, ibid. Exhortations, corrections, and divine censure took place, I, 469 A. Approved elders presided, ibid. Contributions were offered at them and preserved in a chest, I, 470 A. These were distributed to the needy, ibid. How modest and frugal the meal was in the assemblies, I, 477 A. Water, handwashing, lamps, hymns, prayer, and conversation, ibid. With what great shamelessness the pagans attempted to defame these assemblies, I, 478. **SYRACUSE** is fortified by the Corinthians together with Archias, II, 1036 A. **SIRMIUM**, a city, I, 425 A. **THE GODDESS OF THE SYRIANS**, Atargatis, I, 418 A, 596 A. **THE SYZYGIES OF THE VALENTINIANS**, II, 68 A.

# T

**Greek T (tau),** a form of the cross, II, 353 A.

**TABLETS** recording births, betrothals, and marriages, II, 906 A. Tablet of condemnation, I, 279 A.

**TAVERNS:** how numerous they were at Rome, I, 452 B.

**PLAYING AT THE BOARD,** II, 768 A.

**RECORD-KEEPERS,** I, 474 A.

**TACITUS,** the most loquacious teller of falsehoods, I, 364 A, B. Why, and how falsely, he said that an image of an ass was consecrated by the Jews, I, 364 A.

**RETALIATION** is forbidden, II, 395 sq.

**TALLUS.** See **THALLUS**.

**TARENTUM,** a town, II, 1029 A.

**TARPEII,** or the city of Pompeii, was overwhelmed by fire from its own mountain, I, 485 A, 571 B. The Tarpeian games, I, 637 B.

**TATIAN,** a heretic and disciple of Justin Martyr, II, 72 A, 974 A. His entire doctrine savors of Valentinus, 72 A.

**TATIUS** discovered Cloacina, II, 266 C.

**THE FIGURE OF THE BULL** as referring to Christ, II, 626 B.

**TAURINE FABLES,** I, 317 A.

**THE PEOPLE OF TELMESSUS** invalidate no dreams, but blame weakness of interpretation, II, 727 A.

**THE LIMIT OF RASHNESS** is an attestation of fear, I, 1241 A.

**TEMPLES OF THE GODS:** in ancient times the Romans had none, I, 430 A. Temples founded for emperors, whether living or dead, I, 347 A. Guarded by watches of the imperial soldiers, I, 438 sq.; II, 92 A. The pagans worshiped their paneled ceilings, I, 418 A. Laurels and lamps were hung upon their doors, I, 458 sq., 684 C. They were shaded by trees, I, 315 A. The pagans could not enter their own temples without paying a fee for the temple site, for access to the sacred rites, and for contributions, I, 346 sq., 493 sq., 574 A. Who complained that their contributions had diminished, I, 494 A; and that revenues had declined because Christians did not frequent the temples, I, 493 sq. How greatly they were deserted, I, 306 A, 494 sq. Polluted by prostitution and adultery, I, 373 A. The pagans despoiled their own temples and swore by them, I, 699 B. Christians were not permitted to maintain them, I, 687 B. Nor did Christians know them by daylight, I, 363 A. A servant of God may enter them without endangering discipline when compelled by an ordinary necessity, II, 640 B. Christ is God’s universal temple, in which God is worshiped, II, 351 B.

**TIME,** the arbiter and determiner of beginning and end, II, 255 B. Periods of time are composed of days, months, and years, II, 453 A. Whence the reckoning of time arose, II, 287 B. God ordained the changes of the seasons [Col. 1589], I, 608 B. Time reveals all things, I, 310 A. All things await their time, II, 890 A. Every earlier thing supplied a standard beforehand for what came later, II, 256 B.

**DARKNESS** is visible to man, II, 222 B.

**TEMPTATION** must have some underlying matter upon which to act, II, 766 B. Temptation is preceded by a question arising from doubt, ibid. C. Temptations follow after Baptism, I, 1225 sq. The way must not be opened to them, I, 1318 sq. Through the conflict between flesh and spirit we have constructed defenses in advance against the temptations that are to follow, I, 1223 A. Prayer repels temptations, I, 1196 A.

**THE EARTH** was virgin, not yet subjected to labor, and from it we understand that man was made by God into a living soul, II, 782 A. Whether what was made was earth is a great question, II, 222 A, 1034 B. It is the womb of our flesh, II, 262 A, B. It is a place of deposit, in which seeds are laid down and from which they are reclaimed, II, 872 C. Why it was cursed, II, 832 A. The world changed in form during the flood, II, 1033 B. See **FLOOD**. Even now, however, it changes its appearance locally when its physical situation is disturbed, II, 1033 B. Two earths are set forth in Holy Scripture—which they are, II, 219 B. The land of promise is the possession of eternal life, II, 622 A. The holy land is to be interpreted as the flesh of the Lord, II, 833 A. Land truly holy through the indwelling of the Holy Spirit, ibid. Signs of earthly origin, II, 771 A, B. How the loss of earthly possessions is to be borne, I, 1260 B.

**TERTULLIAN** was born at Carthage in Africa, II, 1032 A. He imbibed the false superstitions of the pagans with his mother’s milk, I, 378 B, 1227 B. He delighted in profane spectacles, I, 652 A. He fell into shameful vices of the flesh, II, 881 B. He called himself a sinner bearing every mark of guilt, I, 1224 B, 1233 B, 1248 B. Having assumed the philosophers’ cloak, he withdrew from the tumult of business, I, 1047 A. He also wrote in Greek, I, 1216 B. He admits that he drew material from Irenaeus, II, 548 A. Speaking in the person of Christ, he addresses the heretics ironically, II, 60 A.

**A POTSHERD** made from clay is no longer clay, II, 776 C.

**THE OLD TESTAMENT** is buried in Christ, II, 973 A. The passing away of the old and succession of the new, II, 415 A. The New Testament had to be ratified upon the same stage on which the Old had been drawn up, II, 414 B. See **LAW, SCRIPTURE**.

**THALES OF MILETUS,** chief of the natural philosophers, I, 383 A, 389 A. While examining the heavens, he fell into a well, II, 656 A. He said that the soul consists of water, II, 653 A. His answer to Croesus when the latter asked about the gods, I, 592 A.

**THALLUS,** I, 330 A, 383 A, 387 B, 402 B.

**TAMAR** adorned herself and played the prostitute, II, 1330 B.

**THE THEATER** is properly a sanctuary of Venus, I, 642 A. A council chamber of unchastity, I, 649 B, C. An art comprising every kind of shamefulness, ibid. B. Theaters arise for the corruption of morals, I, 299 A. How obscene and abominable they are, I, 301 A, 638 sq.; II, 993 B, C. People attended them wearing cloaks, I, 301 A. They could not be seen either alone or naked, ibid. Their prohibition follows from the prohibition of unchastity, I, 650 B. Nothing is approved in the theater except what is disapproved elsewhere, I, 649 B. A woman who had gone to the theater returned with a demon, I, 657 B. Theaters were formerly open and without roofs, I, 301 A, 302 B.

**AT THEBES** it is reported that dull-witted and brutish persons are born, II, 683 A.

**THE EXAMPLE OF THECLA** was wrongly attributed to Paul, I, 1219 A.

**THEMISTOCLES:** no god of the pagans was more renowned for military glory, I, 336 B.

**THEODOTUS,** a Byzantine heretic, said that Christ was not God but a mere man, II, 72 B.

**THEODOTUS,** another heretic, likewise denied Christ’s divinity, II, 72 C.

**THEOPOMPUS,** II, 220 B, 725 A. See **THRASYMEDES**.

**THEOTIMUS,** a heretic, devoted much labor to the figurative representations of the Law, II, 546 B.

**A REPOSITORY OF DIVINE TREASURE,** II, 857 A.

**THRASYMEDES:** Theopompus reports that he never dreamed, II, 725 A, 733 B.

**AN INCENSE-DEALER,** though a Christian, made his house a storeroom for a demon, I, 677 A.

**INCENSE** was burned by Christians, but not in the manner of the pagans, II, 90 B. They also employed incense in burials, I, 493 A. See **SABAEAN INCENSE**.

**IN THE TIME OF TIBERIUS** the Christian name entered the world, I, 290 A. Tiberius wished to enroll Christ among the gods, I, 290 A. He threatened accusers of Christians with punishment, I, 291 A. He prohibited the sacrifice of infants to Saturn, I, 314 A. He reigned twenty-two years, seven months, and twenty days, II, 615 B. From Tiberius to Antoninus there were approximately one hundred and fifteen years, together with half a year and half a month, II, 267 B.

**TIMAEUS,** a writer, I, 636 A, B.

**TIMIDITY** can persuade one of anything, II, 118 B.

**FEAR:** no fear of an uncertain danger is just, II, 823 A. The origin of fear is knowledge, I, 588 A. Its matter, way, cruelty, judgment [Col. 1590], vengeance, and condemnation, II, 373 C. Fear is the foundation of salvation, I, 1318 A. Fear of man is honor toward God, I, 1241 A. It contributes to good, not evil, II, 299 C. Some sin through fear, I, 1236 A. Presumption is an impediment to fear, I, 1318 A. Nothing overthrows fear like obstinacy, I, 1235 A.

**THE PLAIN TOGA,** I, 685 A. The white toga, I, 688 A. It is called the manly toga, I, 685 B. Its description, II, 1046 A. Who wore it, I, 685 A. It passed from the Pelasgians to the Lydians, from the Lydians to the Romans, and from the Romans to the Carthaginians, II, 1031 B. Togas have done more harm to the commonwealth than breastplates, II, 1048 A.

**THUNDERCLAPS** are signs of God’s impending wrath, I, 701 B.

**TRADITION** is put forward in many rules of discipline as their author, custom as their confirmer, and faith as their guardian, II, 80 A. In many disciplines of the Church no authority from Scripture is found, ibid. An unwritten tradition may be defended in observance if it is confirmed by custom, II, 81 B. Where law is lacking, tradition gives custom its established practice, ibid. Reason supports tradition, II, 80 A. What is found uniformly among many is not an error but a tradition, II, 40 B. Where true faith is found, there too is the truth of Christian traditions, II, 31 B. Our doctrine is judged by the tradition of the Apostles, II, 33 B sq. That is apostolic tradition which has been held inviolable among the churches of the Apostles, II, 270 B. Whether they handed down everything, II, 37 sq. In its own time apostolic tradition suffered no corruption concerning the rule of God, II, 270 B. Obedience is owed to tradition, II, 80 A; even to unwritten tradition, II, 81 B. If you are a Christian, hold fast to what has been handed down, II, 755 B. A Christian believes what has been handed down, II, 745 B. See **OBSERVANCES**.

**TRAGEDIES AND COMEDIES** are promoters of lusts and crimes—bloody and lascivious, impious and extravagant, I, 650 B. See **THEATER**.

**THE EMPEROR TRAJAN** both condemns and absolves Christians, I, 373 A, B. His ruling concerning Christians is full of confusion, ibid.

**TRANSFIGURATION** is the destruction of the former state, II, 197 A.

**TRANSGRESSION,** a cause of perdition, II, 842 B.

**SOLEMN MIGRATIONS OF PEOPLES,** II, 700 B.

**THE TRIBUNAL OF GOD** demands the human being safe and whole, I, 883 A. See **JUDGMENT**.

**THE TRINITY OF PERSONS,** Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, is defended most vigorously, II, 156 sq. All the Scriptures display the distinction and manifestation of the Trinity, II, 166 A, B. The Trinity, considered rationally, establishes the truth, II, 158 A. The Trinity, proceeding from the Father through interwoven and connected degrees, neither opposes the monarchy and also preserves the ordered state of the divine economy, II, 164 A. In the Trinity the unity is ordered: the three differ not in condition but in degree, not in substance but in form, not in power but in aspect; yet they are of one substance and one power, II, 157 B. See **SON, FATHER, HOLY SPIRIT, UNITY**.

**THE VALENTINIAN TRINITY,** II, 19 A, 684 A.

**TRIPTOLEMUS** mentioned, II, 238 C.

**THE TROAD:** the oracle of Sarpedon, II, 730 A.

**TROCHILUS OF ARGOS,** inventor of the chariot, I, 641 B.

**THE ORACLE OF TROPHONIUS** in Boeotia, I, 404 A; II, 730 A.

**MINERVA’S LADLE,** I, 344 B.

**THE TUNICS OF THE CARTHAGINIANS,** II, 1031 B.

**THE COLUMNS OF TUTELINA,** named after the guardian deities of crops, I, 639 C.

**TUTUNUS,** a god, I, 601 A.

**TYPHON,** II, 747 B.

**AT TYRE** people wore gold upon their feet, II, 1043 A.

**TYRRHENUS,** leader of the Lydians into Etruria, I, 636 A.

# U

**BREASTS:** how their milk flows, II, 787 A. See **MILK, WOMB**.

**VENGEANCE** appears to be a consolation for pain, I, 1264 B. Lust for vengeance is the supreme incitement to impatience, ibid. It pursues the business either of glory or of malice, ibid. Because of impatience under pain, we cannot regulate the measure of vengeance, I, 1266 A. Vengeance is forbidden, II, 395. When left in God’s hands, it is cleared of malice, I, 1264 B. Through fear of vengeance, all iniquity is restrained, II, 395 C.

**THE BLESSED ANOINTING** after Baptism derives from the ancient discipline, I, 1206 C. The flesh is anointed so that the soul may be consecrated, II, 806 B. The anointing runs over us carnally but produces its effect spiritually, I, 1207 A. The Law commands that the anointing chrism of kingship must not be compounded in captivity, II, 634 A. The anointing of athletes in the sun, II, 618 A, B.

**THAT IS UNIQUE AND SINGULAR** which has no equal, II, 201 B.

**UNITY,** deriving the Trinity from itself, is not destroyed by it but administered through it, II, 138 A. The unity of the Church is established, II, 32. Unity gathered together irrationally produces heresy, II, 158 A.

**EVERYTHING THAT EXISTS ONCE IS ONE,** II, 922 A. Whatever is not one [Col. 1591] is number, ibid.

**CITIES** are now as great as huts once were, II, 700 A. See **CITY**.

**THE STARS OF THE BEAR** in the north, II, 143 B.

**INTEREST** is the surplus of a loan, II, 398 C.

**AT UTICA,** an eclipse of the sun, I, 701 B.

**THE PAGANS SHARED THEIR WIVES,** I, 472 A. This is forbidden to Christians, ibid. How plurality of wives was permitted to the Patriarchs, I, 1277 A. See **MARRIAGE, NUPTIALS**.

# V

**WOE,** an exclamation of imprecation and threat, II, 462 A, B. Christ’s “woe” in the Gospel is explained, II, 392 sq. “Woe to those who are pregnant and nursing” will be far more grievous and bitter during the shaking of the entire world than during the devastation of Judaea, II, 952 A.

**VALENTIA,** goddess of the people of Ocriculum, I, 421 A.

**VALENTINUS:** where, when, and how he lived, II, 42. He had hoped for the episcopate, being qualified for it both by intellect and eloquence, II, 546 A. He was a Platonist, II, 21 B, 42 A, 786 A. A fellow pupil of Apelles, II, 754 C. Valentinus and Marcion compared, II, 52 B. He was more honorable and generous than Marcion, II, 251 C. That heretic introduced many fables, II, 67 B. He is an adulterator of the truth, II, 43 B. His heresy, II, 68, 779 B, C. His monstrous names, II, 141 A. His Aeons, II, 19, 46 B, 68, 251 C, 551 sq., 686 C. Genealogies of the Aeons, II, 551 A. He scatters his Aeons about and traces the defect of one Aeon back to the origin of God the Creator, II, 47 A, 379 A. Valentinus’s swarm infused the soul with the seed of Sophia (“Wisdom”), II, 686 C. He denies the resurrection, II, 46 A. His error concerning Christ, II, 69 B. He devised subject matter to suit Scripture, II, 52 B. He expounds the New Testament differently and, without question, corrects it, II, 43 B.

**THE VALENTINIANS** are censured, II, 41 sq. Their origin, II, 546 A, B. When they creep forth, II, 545 A. The first tetrad of their faction is defended as the womb and origin of all the rest, II, 552 A. Their heretical seeds, II, 678 A, and their initiation, II, 540 A. They permit themselves what Valentinus permitted himself, II, 58 A. They take greater care over nothing than concealing what they preach, II, 538 B. They possess an art by which they persuade before they teach, II, 543 B. They affirm that the resurrection has already taken place, II, 46 A.

**VARRO:** how great his learning was, I, 587 B. He traces the origin of the gods back to Jupiter, Juno, and Minerva, I, 601 B. He devised a threefold class of gods: physical, mystical, and national, I, 387 B. He divided the gods of the Romans into uncertain, certain, and select gods, I, 597 B. He dreamed that they were living beings moved by themselves, I, 590 A. He introduced three hundred Jupiters, I, 355 sq., 576 A. He interprets *ludi* (“games”) from *lusus* (“play”), I, 638 B.

**VARSUTINA,** goddess of the Moors, I, 396 A.

**VESSELS** for food and drink made of bronze, II, 1310 A. The flesh is called a vessel by reason of its capacity, II, 716 A.

**THE VESSELS OF THE JEWS:** why God distinguished meticulous rules of every kind concerning them, II, 306 C.

**DEMONS DELIGHTED IN THE UTTERLY IMPURE TONGUES OF SEERS,** I, 415 B.

**TAXES** were paid by Christians with complete good faith and with greater care than by the pagans, I, 494 A. By how many frauds and falsehoods the pagans evaded them, ibid. sq.

**VEDIUS POLLIO** used to throw slaves to be attacked by moray eels, II, 1048 B.

**THE VEIL,** the dress of a virgin dedicated to God, II, 893 A. Every public exposure of a virtuous virgin is an experience of violation, II, 892 B. So dangerous a face ought to be kept in shadow, II, 899 B. The virgin takes refuge in the veil upon her head as though in a helmet or a shield, II, 910 A. The proper measure of the veil was revealed to a certain Montanist sister, II, 912 B. Carthaginian women were veiled in such a way that they were neither uncovered nor covered, II, 912 A. Pagan Arabian women cover their whole face, leaving only one eye free, ibid. See **VIRGIN**.

**VENETIAN SHOEMAKERS’ WORKSHOPS,** II, 1046 B.

**PARDON IS EASILY GIVEN FOR DIFFICULT THINGS,** I, 1289 B.

**VENILLIA,** a goddess, I, 600 C.

**WHY THE GENITALS ADJOIN THE BELLY,** II, 953 B.

**THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN WINDS AND BREEZES,** II, 295 A.

**VENUS,** wounded, I, 351 A. Judged by a shepherd, I, 359 sq. The myrtle was sacred to her, II, 94 A. Venus, mother of Aeneas, ibid.

**WORD.** See **SPEECH**. Nothing is to be preferred to the Word of God, II, 405 C. Administration of the Word of God in the Church, II, 329 B; among heretics, II, 57 B. The inward human word, I, 160 C. Words possess meaning not by sound alone but also by sense, II, 136 B.

**TRUTH,** an Aeon of Valentinus, II, 552 sqq.

**TRUTH** precedes the image in all things, II, 41 B. The false must necessarily precede, II, 368 A. What the rule of truth is, I, 519 B. The testimony of truth, which everywhere occupies the foremost place, II, 48 B. What its integrity is, I, 653 A. The Christian is the restorer and guardian of truth, I, 514 A. Where God is not, neither is there any truth, II, 58 B. Truth is discovered by no one without God, II, 647 B. Christ called himself Truth, not custom, II, 889 A. Nothing is true among those who do not know God as the presiding authority and teacher of truth, I, 1316 B. Among the pagans truth was condemned throughout all former time, I, 563 C. They possess no fullness of truth because they do not possess God, the teacher of truth, I, 653 A. Truth does not require antiquity, II, 697 C. Where truth is to be sought, II, 31 B, 48 B. How delightful its revelation is, I, 659 C. It befits truth to laugh, because it is joyful, and to mock its rivals, because it is secure, II, 550 A. Every heresy is driven out by the wedge of truth, II, 270 C. The Lord’s enemies are to be overcome by the simplicity of truth, not by curiosity, II, 310 A. Truth is ashamed of nothing except being hidden, II, 545 A. It lies open to falsehood, II, 258 B. It is loved by few, II, 982 A. The unencumbered power of truth loves few, II, 319 A. It befits truth to employ all its strength, not as though it were struggling, II, 322 D. There is a great distance between opinion and truth, I, 565 B. Truth is always hated, I, 354 A. People prefer not to know it because they already hate it, I, 261 A. Everything directed against truth has been constructed from truth itself by spirits of error that put this rivalry into operation, I, 519 B. The devil has sometimes imitated truth, II, 154 D. What is earlier is truer; what is from the beginning is earlier, II, 248 A, 366 C. Whatever is first is true; whatever is later is adulterated, II, 157 B.

**IN SPRINGTIME** the soul is more tranquil, II, 732 B.

**THE EMPEROR VERUS** enacted no law against Christians, I, 297 A.

**THE EMPEROR VESPASIAN,** in the first year of his reign, conquered the Jews, II, 616 A. He enacted no law against Christians, I, 297 A. He reigned eleven years, II, 616 A.

**VESPRONIUS CANDIDUS** dismissed a Christian, as a citizen, to satisfy his own people, I, 703 A.

**VESTA** was interpreted as fire, II, 261 A.

**THE VIRGINITY OF THE VESTALS,** II, 953 A. They maintained a perpetual fire, I, 1284 A.

**THE ENTRANCE HALLS OF THE ROMANS** were illuminated by very splendid and lofty lamps, I, 459 A.

**A CLOTHING WORKSHOP,** II, 1039 A.

**CLOTHING** is proper to each person both for daily use and for honor and dignity, I, 687 B. Consideration of wealth, birth, or rank permits sumptuous clothing, I, 1326 A. Purple and sky-blue garments do not please God, I, 1312 B. Among us no attire is lawful if it is assigned to an unlawful act, I, 691 A. Clothing enters together with speech (language), II, 1039 B. Necessity and ambition introduced various forms of clothing, ibid. To change its garb is the customary function of all nature, II, 1032 B. Purple-bordered garments, palm-embroidered robes, *trabeae*, broad stripes, and fasces, I, 687 C sq. Idols also were clothed in these, ibid. What the garments of the Carthaginians were formerly like, II, 1030 C, 1031 B. What women’s clothing was like in former times, II, 911. The clothing of matrons and prostitutes was different, I, 301 A. Later it became indistinguishable, ibid. The *stola* was for girls and the purple-bordered garment for boys, I, 688 B. See **CLOAK**. Allegory of clothing in Scripture, II, 834. What it means to be clothed with the Holy Spirit, II, 50 A.

**MOUNT VESUVIUS,** always burning, an image of hell, I, 527 A.

**WHAT IT MEANS TO PREPARE THE WAY OF THE LORD,** I, 1213 B.

**HUMAN VICTIMS,** II, 136 C. See **PAGANS, MERCURY, SATURN**.

**VICTORY,** a goddess of the pagans, and the nature of her image, I, 366 sq., 379 A.

**VICTORINUS,** a heretic, II, 74 A.

**TO SEE AND TO BE SEEN** belong to the same lust, II, 891 B.

**WIDOWHOOD** is praised, I, 1286; II, 806 B, C sq., 928 sq., 932 sq. For widowhood formally pledged before God, nothing is necessary except perseverance, ibid. The priesthood of widowhood, ibid. A virgin widow—a monstrosity, II, 902 B. See **VIRGINITY**.

**VIDUUS,** or Vidius, the god who bereaves the body of its soul, I, 606 A.

**VIGELLIUS SATURNINUS,** the first to wield the sword against Christians, lost his eyesight, I, 702 A.

**PATIENCE AS THE EXPECTANT WAITING FOR DIVINE VENGEANCE:** in what sense, II, 395 B. See **VENGEANCE**.

**THE USE OF WINE:** why it was formerly forbidden to women, I, 302 A. Their relatives kissed them on the mouth to discover whether they had drunk wine, I, 303 A. Through drunkenness women admit every kind of evil, I, 1288 A. The Romans secured their wine cellars with wax and a seal, I, 303 A, B.

**THE APOSTLE** scorned a viper’s bite, II, 122 B.

**VIRGINITY,** a sacrifice pleasing to God, II, 806 B. It rests upon grace, whereas continence rests upon virtue, I, 1287 B; II, 903 B, 915 A. True, complete, and pure virginity fears nothing more than itself, II, 910 A. It does not wish to endure even the eyes of women; it has eyes of another kind itself, ibid. Forced and unwilling virginity admits disgraceful acts, II, 909 A. Ostentatious virginity, II, 892 B. Its dangers, II, 909 B, C. Why virginity and continence are to be preferred to marriage, ibid. Very many Christians formerly preserved their virginity, I, 327 A, B. See **CONTINENCE**.

**A VIRGIN** may be regarded as happier, but a widow as more laborious in virtue, I, 1287 B. Praise of virgins, I, 1280 B. The Apostle intended “virgin” to be understood within the term “woman,” II, 900 A. Virgins ought to be veiled, I, 1184 A; II, 888 sqq. The public exposure of a virtuous virgin is an experience of violation, II, 892 B. The Corinthians formerly veiled their virgins, II, 901 B. See **VEIL**. Many churches throughout Greece keep their virgins secluded, II, 890 B. The virgins of men vie against the virgins of God, II, 892 A. A virgin entrusted to Christ was violated by heretics, II, 59 A. Virgins of both sexes among the pagans, II, 928 C sq., 953 A.

**VIRTUE** is built up by hardship and destroyed by softness, I, 624 B.

**DISTRIBUTION OF FLESH (*visceratio*),** which customarily took place either at a solemn sacrifice or at the funeral of some eminent person, II, 331 B, 640 C.

**HOW SIGHT IS DECEIVED,** II, 674 B. See **EYE, SEEING**.

**VISIDIANUS,** god of the people of Narnia, I, 420 A.

**LIFE,** an Aeon of the Valentinian body, II, 553.

**LIFE,** the conjunction of body and soul, II, 695 A. Hence, where the soul is, there too is life, ibid. We recognize life from conception, ibid. What worldly life is, II, 861 A. Christ invites us to eternal life, not merely a long life, II, 424 D.

**THE VITAL ORGANS** were appropriately assigned by God the Craftsman to all animals according to the constitution of each kind, II, 662 A.

**VITELLIUS** reigned eight months and ten days, II, 616 A. His memoirs, II, 728 A.

**THE VINE,** though still tender and immature, nevertheless already understanding its functions and wishing to cling to something by whose support it may grow, will, even without a reed or forked prop (*cervus*), spontaneously twine around anything it touches—and indeed rather eagerly; it hastens to become secure, II, 681 B.

**THE ORDER OF THE VICES** corresponds to the arrangement of the bodily members, II, 953 B.

**VITUMNUS,** a god, I, 600 C.

**VOLETA,** a goddess, I, 600 C.

**VOLUMNUS,** a god, I, 600 C.

**VOLUPIA,** a goddess, I, 600 C.

**VOLSINII,** or Vulsinii; the people of Volsinii, I, 487 A, 571 B. Fire from heaven overwhelmed them, ibid. Their goddess Nortia, I, 421 A.

**THE WILL,** free and compelled, II, 917 A, B. A will that exists without the stimulus of desire, II, 276 C. God’s hidden and manifest will, II, 917 A. How one must speak of it, II, 925 B. God’s will must be considered deeply and emphatically, including what he wills in secret, II, 916 C sq. It is not characteristic of a good and sound faith to refer everything to God’s will in such a way that we fail to understand that something lies within ourselves, II, 915 B sqq. Every offense will be excused if we contend that nothing occurs within us apart from God’s will, II, 915 C. How many evils follow from this, ibid. Not everything that God permits proceeds from his sheer and entire will, II, 917 A. See **PERMISSION**.

**THERE IS NO GREATER PLEASURE** than disgust with pleasure itself, I, 659 C. Pleasure must be shunned by Christians, I, 659 A. What their pleasure is, I, 659 sqq. Where pleasure is, there also is the interest through which pleasure acquires its savor, I, 647 B. Philosophers gave the name “pleasure” to rest and tranquility, I, 659 B.

**A VOW OF CONTINENCE,** II, 905 A.

**VULCAN,** the craftsman, I, 574 B.

**VOLCANIC MOUNTAINS,** figures of eternal fire, I, 1247 B.

**VULTURES,** being only female, become mothers without a male, II, 557 A.

**THE WOMB** transfers its fountain into the breasts, II, 787 A. From the opening of the womb the Apostle recognized that the Virgin Mary had undergone the experience proper to marriage, II, 790.

**XENOCRATES,** II, 652 C. He said that the soul has its seat at the crown of the head, II, 671 B.

# X

**XEROPHAGY,** the eating of angelic bread, II, 960 B. In practices of xerophagy lies the exercise of a religious discipline at once most ancient and most efficacious, II, 964 B. The Montanists observed xerophagies, II, 955 A.

**OUR GYMNASIUM-MASTER (*xystarches*)** is the Holy Spirit, I, 624 B.

# Z

**ZACCHAEUS,** although a foreigner, may nevertheless have acquired some knowledge of the Scriptures through intercourse with the Jews, II, 451 C.

**ZECHARIAH** is slain between the altar and the sanctuary, leaving the enduring stains of his blood upon the stones, II, 137 B.

**ZENO** sought tyranny among the people of Priene, I, 511 A. His vigor, I, 651 B. His constancy under torture, I, 533 A. By whom and why he was killed, ibid. The tortures inflicted by Dionysius failed to reach his soul, II, 751 A. By his death he proved that philosophy teaches contempt for death, I, 533 A. Zeno said that air and ether were God, II, 260 B. His system is found wherever matter is placed on an equality with God, II, 19 B. He acknowledged the *Logos* (λόγος) of God, I, 395 A. He defines the soul as an implanted spirit, II, 653 A. He divides it into three parts, II, 668 B.

**THE ZODIAC** contains the Bull and the Lion, II, 143 B.

**A FIERY ZONE** at the entrance to paradise, I, 520 A. The bonds of the celestial zones, II, 143 B.

**PROLEGOMENA** Ibid.

**PREFACE BY THE AUTHOR OF THESE ACTS** 14  

**The Passion Begins** 16  

**CHAPTER I.** After the saints have been arrested, St. Perpetua overcomes her father’s opposition, is baptized with the others, and is cast into a grim prison. Anxious about her infant, she understands from a vision granted to her—of a ladder erected toward heaven [Col. 1594], the ascent of St. Saturus and herself, and a morsel offered to her—that martyrdom is soon to come. 16  

**CHAPTER II.** Perpetua, assailed by her father, strengthens him. Brought with the others before the tribunal, she confesses that she is a Christian and is condemned with the rest to the beasts. She prays for her dead brother Dinocrates, whom she understands in a vision to be suffering the pains of purgatory and then to be delivered from them. 29  

**CHAPTER III.** Perpetua is again tempted by her father. Her third vision, in which she is brought to wrestle against an Egyptian, with a prize set before her; she fights, conquers, and receives the prize. 38  

**CHAPTER IV.** In a vision granted to St. Saturus, he and St. Perpetua are carried by angels into a great light and see the martyrs. Conducted to the throne of God, they are received with a kiss. They reconcile Bishop Optatus and the presbyter Aspasius. 42  

**CHAPTER V.** St. Secundulus dies in prison. St. Felicity, who is pregnant, after prayers have been poured forth, gives birth in the eighth month without pain. The unconquered spirit of St. Perpetua and St. Saturus. 45  

**CHAPTER VI.** They are led joyfully from prison into the amphitheater, especially Perpetua and Felicity. All refuse to put on profane garments; they are scourged, yearn for the beasts, and are exposed to them. Saturus is twice unharmed. Saints Perpetua and Felicity are thrown down and recalled to the Gate of Life. St. Saturus, wounded by a leopard, exhorts a soldier. They kiss one another and are killed by the sword. 49  

**AN APOLOGETIC DISSERTATION BY CARDINAL JOSEPH AUGUSTINE ORSI, [Col. 1595] IN DEFENSE OF THE ORTHODOXY OF THE HOLY MARTYRS** 61  

**CHAPTER I.** The orthodoxy of Saints Perpetua, Felicity, and their fellow martyrs is vindicated by external arguments drawn from the authority of the Church and the ancient Fathers. 62  

I. Testimony on behalf of Perpetua and her fellow martyrs from Tertullian, a contemporary writer. Ibid.  
II. The deacon Pontius praised the Acts of those same martyrs in no obscure terms. Ibid.  
III. From Bucher’s exceedingly ancient calendar it is demonstrated that the cult of Perpetua and Felicity was of very great antiquity in the Roman Church. 64  
IV. St. Augustine mentions those same martyrs with praise in various passages and celebrated them in three discourses. On a very slight conjecture, Basnage denies that the first of these, found in the printed editions, belongs to the holy Doctor, and strives in vain to disparage and undermine it. 66  
V. The most celebrated of the churches of Carthage, and the mother church of the others, was made illustrious by the relics of Perpetua and Felicity and was named after them. 67  
VI. Their names are numbered among those of the more celebrated martyrs in the daily canon of the Mass. 71  
VII. The argument established from these testimonies, which Basnage vainly [attempts to refute; verb missing in the source]. 72  

**CHAPTER II.** Basnage’s external arguments against the holy Martyrs are answered. 74  

I. That the compiler of the Acts of Perpetua and Felicity was infected with the Montanist heresy. 75  
II. Ruinart’s arguments on behalf of the compiler of the Acts are refuted, and by various arguments his Montanism is asserted. 76  
III. Dodwell’s argument for the orthodoxy of the same writer. 80  
IV. The first foundation of his argument is overthrown. 82  
V. The second foundation of the same argument is overturned. 83  
VI. Catholics were not regarded as heretics by the Montanists. 85  
VII. The Montanists did not consider themselves wholly estranged from the communion of the Catholic churches. 88  
VIII. They also aspired to communion with Catholic martyrs. 93  
IX. Tertullian mentioned with praise not only Perpetua, but other Catholic martyrs as well. 94  
X. Other heretics besides the Montanists published the Acts of Catholic martyrs. 95  
XI. From the Montanist author of the Acts himself, it is shown that our martyrs were alien to this sect. 96  

**CHAPTER III.** A general answer is given to Basnage’s internal arguments against our Martyrs. 97  

I. Basnage’s internal arguments against the holy Martyrs. Ibid.  
II. The credibility of the compiler of the Acts should be impugned rather than the orthodoxy of the holy Martyrs called into doubt. 98  
III. Reasons are adduced by which the *genuineness* (γνησιότης) of the Acts might be called into question. The first reason is drawn from certain foreign words that are in no way suitable to Perpetua, by whom the greater part of them is said to have been written. 99  
IV. The second reason is drawn from the similarity of style, which points to one and the same writer, although the texts are said to have been written by three different persons. 101  
V. Neither the authority of Tertullian nor that of a contemporary writer would prevent us from doubting the trustworthiness of the Acts if they actually contained anything unworthy of Catholic martyrs. 102  

**CHAPTER IV.** The abundance and profusion of visions and other heavenly gifts during the earlier centuries of the Church are discussed. It is demonstrated that the ancient Christians, who in everyone’s judgment were genuine martyrs of Christ, availed themselves of these divine charisms of the Holy Spirit with no less confidence than Perpetua did. 104  

I. Nothing actually occurs in the Acts of our Martyrs that smacks of Montanus’s workshop. 105  
II. St. Justin Martyr compares the prophets of his own time with the prophets of old. From this it is established that they exercised the prophetic spirit with no less confidence than the latter. 106  
III. On the beginnings of the Montanists. None of the most ancient writers regarded the Montanists as false prophets merely because they employed revelations as though at the command of the Holy Spirit. 108  
IV. A notable testimony of St. Irenaeus concerning the variety and abundance of charisms in those times. 109  
V. How readily the power of the Holy Spirit was available to the ancient Christians for restraining and driving out demons. 111  
VI. The memorable example of Potamiana, no less remarkable than that of Perpetua. 113  
VII. From Cyprian’s letters and the deacon Pontius it is shown how greatly Cyprian’s life abounded in visions and revelations. 115  
[Col. 1596] VIII. The Acts of other martyrs are filled with the same gifts of the Holy Spirit. 121  
IX. In the age of Perpetua and her fellow martyrs, the fountain of charisms overflowed more abundantly than in Cyprian’s time. Ibid.  

**CHAPTER V.** Nothing is contained in Perpetua’s revelations that is not entirely appropriate to a Catholic martyr. 122  

I. It is not unworthy of Christ the Lord to be represented in the figure of a shepherd milking sheep. 123  
II. In what way Perpetua understood from her first revelation that death was impending over her. 125  
III. Nothing absurd is contained in the revelation in which Perpetua seemed to herself to be transformed into a male and to wrestle with the devil. 128  
IV. The inept comparison of Perpetua’s revelations with the revelations of the Montanists. 131  
V. Perpetua’s vision of Dinocrates situated in a place of punishment. 132  
VI. Basnage’s difficulties concerning the aforesaid vision. Ibid.  
VII. The place in which Perpetua saw Dinocrates was purgatory. Basnage’s cavils are repelled. 133  
VIII. The Montanists’ opinion concerning the receptacles of souls is not correctly explained by Basnage. Those heretics did not hold a single opinion on this matter. 135  

**CHAPTER VI.** The virtues of our martyrs and the fruits of their visions show that they were inspired by the divine Spirit, and that their revelations are to be attributed to God. 137  

I. In distinguishing true prophets from false, primary consideration must be given to their conduct. Ibid.  
II. Certain passages of the Acts in which the virtues of our martyrs are vividly described. 138  
III. Nothing can be observed in their conduct that smacks of Montanus’s training. 141  
IV. It is demonstrated by the example of St. Ignatius Martyr that Perpetua and her fellow martyrs did not violate the laws of nature at all. 142  
V. The prayers and vows of other martyrs for the crown of martyrdom. 143  
VI. Besides Perpetua, other martyrs either incited beasts against themselves or voluntarily employed instruments of cruelty to hasten martyrdom. 145  
VII. The examples of ancient Christians who either offered themselves voluntarily or deliberately provoked the savagery of governors against themselves excuse Perpetua’s action. 146  
VIII. The memorable deed of Saints Andronicus and Tarachus. 148  
IX. From the different effects of each, it is demonstrated how widely the spirit of Perpetua and her fellow martyrs differed from the spirit of the Montanists. 149  
X. The honorable and excellent fruit of the revelation of Perpetua and Saturus. 151  

**CHAPTER VII.** From the fulfillment of their prophecies and from miracles, it is demonstrated that Perpetua and her fellow martyrs were inspired by the prophetic spirit, and that their doctrine and way of life were exceedingly alien to Montanist doctrines and practices. 152  

I. Events corresponded in every respect and exactly to Perpetua’s revelations. Ibid.  
II. On the miracles related in the Acts of our martyrs. 154  
III. Perpetua and Saturus saw in Paradise not only the souls of martyrs, but those of other faithful persons as well. 156  
IV. They were in communion with Catholic martyrs. 157  
V. The soul of Dinocrates was transferred to eternal glory through Perpetua’s prayers. Ibid.  
VI. Bishop Optatus, mentioned in the Acts, presided over Catholics. At that time there was no Montanist bishop at Carthage. 159  
VII. The diet of our martyrs in prison was ordinary and customary, and utterly opposed to Montanist laws concerning fasting. 161  
VIII. On the Catholic Church’s solicitude in nourishing and supporting her confessors. 162  
IX. Catholic martyrs by no means refused food prepared for them through the devotion of the faithful, or even delicacies. 165  
X. *Recapitulation* (ἀνακεφαλαίωσις) of the argument. 166

**F. B. ALDUINUS’S DISSERTATION ON THE *OCTAVIUS*** 199
