**LOGICAL ANALYSIS OF THE *OCTAVIUS*** 225  

**THE *OCTAVIUS* OF MINUCIUS FELIX** 231  

**PROEM** Ibid.  

**CHAPTER I.** From the very beginning of the dialogue, Minucius relates how greatly he delighted in the recollection of the events that had occurred to him with Octavius while the latter was staying with him at Rome, and especially in the recollection of this disputation. [Col. 1597] 232  

**CHAPTER II.** Octavius’s arrival at Rome during the courts’ vacation is most welcome to Minucius. The two decide to go to the seaside baths at Ostia, taking along Caecilius, Minucius’s companion. As they proceed together toward the sea, Caecilius sees an image of Serapis, brings his hand to his mouth, and reverences it. 235  

**CHAPTER III.** Octavius, indignant at the act of a superstitious man, sharply reproaches Minucius, declaring that the disgrace of this impious deed falls no less upon Minucius himself, as Caecilius’s host, than upon Caecilius. 237  

**CHAPTER IV.** Somewhat saddened by this rebuke, in which Octavius censured Minucius on his account, Caecilius asks to be allowed to dispute with Octavius concerning the truth of his religion. Octavius agrees with his companion, and Minucius sits between Caecilius and Octavius. 240  

**CHAPTER V.** Caecilius begins his argument. First, he asserts that everything in human affairs is doubtful and uncertain, and consequently that it is deplorable that Christians, generally uncultivated and illiterate, should dare to determine anything certain concerning the highest realities and the divine majesty. From this he argues that the world is governed by no providence and concludes that it is better to adhere to the ancient religions handed down by tradition. 242  

**CHAPTER VI.** Every nation, and later the Romans, so worshiped its own divinities that through their cult they attained supreme dominion over the entire world. 250  

**CHAPTER VII.** Roman auspices and auguries were omitted with regrettable results and observed with fortunate results. 253  

**CHAPTER VIII.** The impious audacity of Theodorus, Diagoras, and Protagoras, who sought either to abolish religion toward the gods entirely or at least to weaken it, is utterly intolerable. Still less tolerable, however, is the furtive and light-shunning nation of Christians, who despise the gods; and while they fear dying after death, they meanwhile do not fear to die. 256  

**CHAPTER IX.** The religion of the Christians is foolish, for they venerate a crucified man and the very instrument of this punishment. They are said to worship the head of an ass and to adore the very nature of their parent. They are initiated by the killing of an infant and by blood; and amid shameless darkness they mingle indiscriminately with one another as chance determines. 260  

**CHAPTER X.** Whatever they worship, they strive with all their might to conceal. They have no altars, no temples, and no known images. Their God, like that of the Jews, is said to be one; although they can neither see nor display him, they nevertheless regard him as troublesome, restless, and perversely inquisitive. 263  

**CHAPTER XI.** They also assert that the whole world will one day be consumed by fire; and after the resurrection of our bodies they promise the righteous an eternity of most blessed life and the unrighteous an eternity of the greatest punishments. 266  

**CHAPTER XII.** What will befall the Christians themselves after death may be inferred from the fact that they are now deprived of every resource and oppressed by the greatest calamities and miseries. 271  

**CHAPTER XIII.** Caecilius finally concludes that the new religion must be rejected and that one must not pronounce rashly on doubtful matters. 273  

**CHAPTER XIV.** With the disdain of an arrogant spirit, Caecilius challenges Octavius to answer his arguments. Minucius replies modestly that Caecilius should not exult in his considerable eloquence or in the artful variety of his speech; rather, each of his arguments must be carefully weighed. 275  

**CHAPTER XV.** Caecilius retorts to Minucius, with some indication of wounded feeling, that he is departing from the duty of an impartial judge by weakening the force of Caecilius’s argument. Octavius is entirely free to refute everything that Caecilius has put forward. 278  

**CHAPTER XVI.** Octavius therefore begins his reply and trusts that he will wash away the most bitter stain of abuse with a flood of truthful words. He then turns to weakening each of Caecilius’s arguments. First, therefore, he maintains that no one should resent the fact that Christians, however unlearned, discuss heavenly matters, for it is not the authority of the disputant but the truth of the disputation itself that must be considered. 279  

**CHAPTER XVII.** He indeed admits that a human being ought to know himself, but firmly denies that this knowledge can be acquired unless he first recognizes the totality of things and God himself. From the very constitution and adornment of the world, however, every rational person knows that it was created by God and is ruled and administered by him. 284  

**CHAPTER XVIII.** God provides not only for the entire world, but also for each of its parts. That all things are governed by the command of one God is proved by the example of earthly empires. Although he is infinite and immeasurable, and known in his full magnitude to himself alone, and although he can neither be seen nor named by us, his glory nevertheless becomes evident if supplementary epithets are removed. 287  

[Col. 1598]

**CHAPTER XIX.** Moreover, the poets called him the father of gods and human beings, the creator of all things, mind, and spirit. Indeed, the more eminent philosophers themselves held almost the same view of the one God as the Christians. 292  

**CHAPTER XX.** But if the world is ruled by Providence and governed by the command of one God, ignorant antiquity must not drag us into the error of mutual agreement—an antiquity that delighted in its fables and introduced ridiculous traditions. It is no less clearly shown that the worship of the gods was always foolish and impious, since the earliest mortals venerated their kings, renowned leaders, and inventors of the arts like gods on account of their illustrious deeds. 297  

**CHAPTER XXI.** Octavius confirms this by the testimony of Euhemerus, Prodicus, Persaeus, and Alexander the Great, who enumerate the gods’ native lands, birthdays, and tombs. He also sets forth the gods’ unhappy ends, deaths, and funerals. Furthermore, he mocks the ineptitudes and rank absurdities that the pagans peddle concerning their gods’ form and appearance. 299  

**CHAPTER XXII.** These fables, first handed down by ignorant people, were afterward celebrated by others, especially the poets, who by their authority did no small injury to the truth. The minds of children are corrupted by such inventions and sweeter falsehoods, and consequently the wretched grow old in them, although the truth is readily accessible to those who seek it. 306  

**CHAPTER XXIII.** Although the pagans acknowledge that their kings were mortal, they nevertheless fashion them into gods, even against the kings’ own will—not from belief in their divinity, but as an honor bestowed by grateful posterity. Yet the true God has neither beginning nor end. Octavius next inveighs against the images and statues of the gods. 309  

**CHAPTER XXIV.** By a brief survey, moreover, he demonstrates how ridiculous, obscene, and cruel were the rites observed in the celebration of the mysteries of certain gods. 312  

**CHAPTER XXV.** He next shows that Caecilius was wrong to boast that the Romans, who gained dominion over the entire world, did so by duly observing superstitions of this kind. On the contrary, the Romans were assembled in crime at their beginning and grew through the terror of their savagery. Thus the Romans became so great not because they were religious, but because they committed sacrilege with impunity. 315  

**CHAPTER XXVI.** Octavius turns against Caecilius himself the feebly hurled weapon drawn from the auspices and auguries of birds, by citing the examples of Regulus, Mancinus, Paulus, and Caesar. By other examples he demonstrates that the argument drawn from oracles is no more valid. 320  

**CHAPTER XXVII.** To establish this securely, he treats the matter more profoundly and traces it back to its first origin. This, namely, is the source of error: demons hide beneath statues and images, dwell in shrines, animate the fibers of entrails, direct the flights of birds, govern lots, and pour forth oracles shrouded in false responses. Yet they are compelled to confess that these things were done not by a god but by themselves when, adjured by Christians through the true God, they flee from possessed bodies. For this reason they flee from Christians when they are near and stir up so great a hatred of them among the pagans that people begin to hate them before knowing them, lest, once they know them, they either be able to imitate them or be unable to condemn them. 323  

**CHAPTER XXVIII.** They inflict upon them not only hatred, but also unspeakable accusations, which no one has yet been able to prove. Such is the work of demons, for false rumor is both sown and fostered by them. Octavius demonstrates with unsurpassable force that Christians are as falsely charged with sacrilege, incest, sexual outrage, and parricide as it was certain and true that precisely the same crimes—or crimes wholly similar and still greater—were actually committed by the pagans themselves. 327  

**CHAPTER XXIX.** Nor is it any more true that Christians worship a man affixed to a cross for his crimes, for they rightly believe him not only innocent but also God. The pagans, by contrast, invoke as divinities the kings whom they themselves enrolled among the gods, make supplication before their images, and implore their guardian spirits. 331  

**CHAPTER XXX.** Octavius also proves utterly shameless the slander that Christians drink the blood of an infant killed by themselves. The pagans, he says, both cruelly expose newborn children and kill them before birth by a cruel abortion. Christians are permitted neither to see nor to hear of homicide. 333  

**CHAPTER XXXI.** The charge that Christians hold a banquet polluted by incest is as far removed from all plausibility as it is certain that the pagans are truly guilty of incest. Christian banquets are not only chaste but sober. So far removed from them, finally, is the desire for incest that some are ashamed even of a chaste union. 335  

**CHAPTER XXXII.** Nor can it be said that Christians conceal what they worship because they have no shrines and no altars. They are indeed persuaded that God cannot be confined within any temple, nor can an image of him be fashioned. Present everywhere, he sees all things, even the most secret thoughts of our mind; and we live near him and in his very bosom. 338  

[Col. 1599]

**CHAPTER XXXIII.** But if it is nevertheless said that God did not aid the Jews, the writers of the Jewish annals are certainly most ample witnesses that the Jews abandoned God before they were abandoned by him. 342  

**CHAPTER XXXIV.** It is not surprising that this world will finally be consumed by fire, for all things that have a beginning also have an end. Nor do the ancient philosophers reject the opinion that the world will be burned. It is nevertheless certain that God can raise from death to life the human being whom he fashioned from nothing. All nature, moreover, rehearses the resurrection that is to come. 344  

**CHAPTER XXXV.** Octavius next shows that righteous and pious people are to be endowed with everlasting happiness, but the unrighteous are to be afflicted with eternal punishments. He then clearly demonstrates that the morals of Christians are far holier than those of the pagans. 348  

**CHAPTER XXXVI.** No less clearly he teaches that fate is nothing other than what God has spoken. The mind is free; consequently, a person’s action, not his birth, is judged. He afterward makes it perfectly clear that the poverty reproached in Christians is not a disgrace but a glory, and that their suffering bodily evils is not punishment but military service. 350  

**CHAPTER XXXVII.** Torments most unjustly inflicted for the confession of Christ are spectacles worthy of God. Octavius clearly demonstrates this by comparing certain exceptionally courageous pagans with the holy martyrs. He further explains that Christians do not attend spectacles and processions because they know with absolute certainty that they are no less [text defective] than cruel. 352  

**CHAPTER XXXVIII.** They likewise abstain from food sacrificed to idols, lest anyone think either that they are yielding to demons or that they are ashamed of their religion. They do not, however, despise every color and fragrance of flowers. They are accustomed to use flowers when scattered, loose, and soft, and to encircle their necks with garlands; but they consider it superfluous and useless to crown the head of a corpse. With the same serenity with which they live, they also bury their dead, awaiting with the surest hope the crown of eternal happiness. Their true religion, therefore, once the superstitions of the pagans have been rejected, is to be embraced by all. 355  

**CHAPTER XXXIX.** When Octavius had thus finished his speech, Minucius and Caecilius remained for some time stunned into silence, their faces intent. Minucius, indeed, fell silent in admiration of Octavius, inwardly turning over what he had heard. 357  

**CHAPTER XL.** Caecilius, however, exclaimed that he had been conquered by Octavius, that he was now the conqueror of error, and that he henceforth professed the Christian religion; fuller instruction in the mysteries of the faith was meanwhile postponed until the following day. 358  

**CHAPTER XLI.** Finally, they all depart glad and cheerful: Caecilius because he believed, Octavius because he conquered, and Minucius because the former believed and the latter conquered. 359  

**INDEX OF THE CHAPTERS OF THE *OCTAVIUS*** 359  

**LETTER OF L. HOLSTENIUS ON THE SPITS OF DIANA** 365  

**D. LE NOURRY’S DISSERTATION ON THE *OCTAVIUS*** 371  

**CHAPTER I.** Analysis of the book. Who its author was, and who Caecilius and Octavius were, who are introduced in it as disputants. Ibid.  

**ARTICLE I.** Analysis of this book. Ibid.  
**ARTICLE II.** Whether Minucius Felix was the author of this book, and who he was. 380  
**ARTICLE III.** Who Caecilius and Octavius were, who are introduced as disputants in this book. 383  

**CHAPTER II.** On the age, style, title, subject, divisions, manuscript codices, and editions of this book; on various scholars’ observations upon it; on corrupt passages; and on what Minucius drew from others and others from him. 386  

**ARTICLE I.** At what time this book was published. Ibid.  
**ARTICLE II.** In whose language and in what style this book was composed; what its title is; what purpose Minucius Felix had in it; and whether he pleaded the Christians’ cause fully and perfectly. 389  
**ARTICLE III.** On the manuscript codices and various editions of this book. 391  
**ARTICLE IV.** On various scholars’ notes and observations upon this book. 392  
**ARTICLE V.** On certain passages of this book that are corrupt or suspected of corruption. 398  
**ARTICLE VI.** What Minucius drew from other writers—Cicero, Seneca, and Tertullian—and conversely what Cyprian and others drew from this same book of Minucius. 402  

**CHAPTER III.** New annotations on the book of Minucius Felix; and first, the arguments by which Caecilius denies that God exists and Octavius proves that he does are weighed. 409  

**ARTICLE I.** What will be treated in these notes and how; and first, whether Christians ought to be excluded from this disputation is investigated. Ibid.  
**ARTICLE II.** The arguments by which Caecilius attempts to prove that Christians and others have no right to dispute concerning God are weighed. [Col. 1600] 414  
**ARTICLE III.** Octavius’s replies, by which he dissolves and overthrows Caecilius’s preceding arguments, are set forth. 416  
**ARTICLE IV.** The arguments by which Caecilius denies that God exists and Octavius demonstrates that he does are examined. 420  
**ARTICLE V.** Another argument of Minucius is weighed, by which he demonstrates that God, known through the innermost sense of human beings and through their very conscience, truly exists. 422  

**CHAPTER IV. On the One God** 425  

**ARTICLE I.** The argument is examined by which Octavius shows, on the authority of the pagan poets Homer and Virgil and of the philosophers Thales, Anaximenes, Diogenes of Apollonia, Anaxagoras, Pythagoras, and Xenophanes, that there is only one God. Ibid.  
**ARTICLE II.** On the other pagan philosophers: Antisthenes, Speusippus, Democritus, Strato, Epicurus, Aristotle, Heraclides Ponticus, Theophrastus, Cleanthes, Zeno, Chrysippus, Diogenes of Babylon, Xenophon, Aristo, and Plato. 430  
**ARTICLE III.** Another argument of Octavius concerning the one God, drawn from examples of earthly kingdoms and natural phenomena, is weighed. 437  

**CHAPTER V. On the Name, Nature, and Attributes of God** 440  

**ARTICLE I.** Who and what God is, what his name is, and how he is known by human beings, although he cannot be seen with bodily eyes. Ibid.  
**ARTICLE II.** By what arguments Minucius proved that God is infinite, eternal, immeasurable, and knows all things. 444  

**CHAPTER VI. On Divine Providence** 446  

**ARTICLE I.** The arguments by which Minucius shows that the world and all things, both collectively and individually, are governed by God’s Providence are examined; here also concerning Britain, the Nile, the Euphrates, and the Indus. Ibid.  
**ARTICLE II.** The arguments of the pagan Caecilius against divine Providence, drawn from the prosperity of the wicked and the adversities of the good, are scrutinized; here also concerning the tyrant Dionysius, Phalaris, Rutilius, Socrates, Camillus, and the misery of the Jews and Christians. 449  
**ARTICLE III.** How Octavius weakens and destroys Caecilius’s preceding arguments. 453  
**ARTICLE IV.** How Octavius dissolved Caecilius’s argument drawn from the torments and death of the martyrs; here the proposed examples of Scaevola, Regulus, and Aquilius are explained, together with the great number of martyrs and the necessity of divine grace for undergoing martyrdom. 457  
**ARTICLE V.** How Octavius answers Caecilius’s final argument against divine Providence, drawn from the Christians’ opinion concerning fate. 460  

**CHAPTER XII. On Other Doctrines of the Christian Religion** 462  

**ARTICLE I.** The arguments by which Caecilius attacks the resurrection of our bodies and Octavius defends it are scrutinized; here also concerning metempsychosis and the authors and advocates of that opinion, Pythagoras and Plato. Ibid.  
**ARTICLE II.** Octavius’s other arguments proving the resurrection of our bodies, and Caecilius’s contrary arguments, are examined. 464  
**ARTICLE III.** The arguments are weighed by which it is shown that wicked people are to be tormented with eternal punishments and everlasting fire, but that the pious and righteous are to be endowed with perpetual happiness; here also concerning the fires of Mount Etna and Vesuvius, the Stygian marsh, and the fiery river of hell. 468  
**ARTICLE IV.** The arguments by which Octavius proves against Caecilius that the world will one day perish by fire are examined, together with the opinions of the Stoics, Epicureans, and Plato on this matter. 472  

**CHAPTER VIII. On the Three Accursed Crimes—Infanticide, the Eating of Human Flesh, and Incest—of Which Christians Were Accused by Caecilius and Other Pagans** 478  

**ARTICLE I.** What that accusation was and of what kind, what occasions gave rise to it, and how long it endured. Ibid.  
**ARTICLE II.** The general arguments by which Octavius refutes the crimes alleged against Christians by Caecilius and the pagans are weighed. 481  

**CHAPTER IX.** It is demonstrated how false were the first two crimes alleged against Christians: that they killed an infant amid their sacred mysteries and afterward devoured its flesh; and that the pagans, on the contrary, were truly guilty of them. 484  

**ARTICLE I.** The arguments by which Minucius wholly absolves Christians from both crimes are scrutinized. Ibid.  
**ARTICLE II.** It is shown how certainly Minucius convicts the pagans of homicide, since they exposed newborn children or killed them by cruel abortion before birth, and since the Carthaginians also sacrificed their own children to Saturn, the devourer of his children, and then attempted to suppress their cries with caresses and kisses; and for what reason they did so. 488  
**ARTICLE III.** In what further way Minucius shows that guests were sacrificed by the Taurians, the Pontic peoples, and the Egyptian Busiris; human beings by the Gauls to Mercury; and a Greek man and Greek woman, a Gaulish man and Gaulish woman, and others by the Romans to Jupiter Latiaris. 493  
**ARTICLE IV.** On other crimes arising from that savage custom of slaughtering [Col. 1601] human beings: namely, Catiline’s conspiracy sealed with human blood; the rites of Bellona drenched in human gore; the remedy sought for epilepsy by drinking it; and beasts fattened upon it by devouring human beings in the arena. 497  

**CHAPTER X. On the Third Crime, Namely the Infamous Sexual Outrage, Adultery, and Incest Allegedly Committed after the Banquet, of Which Christians Were Accused** 499  

**ARTICLE I.** How greatly Christians abhorred this crime, how chaste their marriage was, and how many persevered in perpetual virginity. Ibid.  
**ARTICLE II.** How Minucius turns Caecilius’s argument against the pagans and demonstrates from their own records that they contracted marriages with their mothers and sisters, and that their gods were polluted by sexual outrage, adultery, and incest. 502  

**CHAPTER XI. On the Absurd Worship Which Caecilius Most Falsely Charges Christians with Offering to an Ass’s Head and a Priest’s Genitals** 505  

**ARTICLE I.** How false this accusation is; whether the Jews or Gnostics gave occasion for it; and whether they were the first of all actually to worship an ass’s head. Ibid.  
**ARTICLE II.** How Minucius had proved the pagans guilty of this or a similar or worse crime, since they impiously worshiped and venerated asses together with Epona and Isis, as well as the heads of oxen and rams. 508  
**ARTICLE III.** How Minucius further proved that the pagans worshiped and adored gods compounded of goat and man and bearing the faces of lions and dogs, as well as the ox Apis, serpents, crocodiles, other birds and beasts, and often even the breaking of wind. 511  
**ARTICLE IV.** That Christians did not worship a priest’s genitals; that the pagans are convicted of more shameful abominations; and what gave occasion for accusing Christians of that most disgraceful veneration. 515  

**CHAPTER XII.** Other accusations of Caecilius and Octavius’s answers to them are examined. 517  

**ARTICLE I.** How undeservedly Caecilius condemns the Christian assemblies and fasts, and says that they are people of a desperate faction, a light-shunning nation, recognizing one another by secret signs and loving one another before they are acquainted. Ibid.  
**ARTICLE II.** With what justification Caecilius said that temples were despised by Christians as though they were tombs, and that they had no temples, no altars, and no known images; and the inept cavils of more recent iconoclasts are refuted. 521  
**ARTICLE III.** How Octavius refutes Caecilius’s charge that Christians worship a man affixed to a cross for a crime; here also concerning Christ’s supreme divinity; how clearly Octavius shows that the Egyptians honored a criminal man, and the Romans kings and emperors, with divine worship, and swore by their guardian spirits; and whether Christians were permitted to swear by their welfare. 527  
**ARTICLE IV.** In what sense Minucius said that crosses are neither worshiped nor desired by Christians. 531  
**ARTICLE V.** How Minucius turns back upon the pagans their weapon of charging Christians with worship of the cross: they honored crosses in images of the gods, military standards, banners, and trophies, while the sign of the cross is represented in billowing ship-sails, in the yoke, and in a person praying with arms outstretched. 533  

**CHAPTER XIII.** Other heads of Caecilius’s most unjust accusations are weighed. 536  

**ARTICLE I.** With what injustice Caecilius reproaches Christians for abstaining from respectable pleasures, spectacles, processions, circus and gladiatorial games, and the shameful scenes of the theater. Ibid.  
**ARTICLE II.** How Minucius answers Caecilius’s other disparagements—that Christians do not attend public banquets and sacred contests and abstain from food sacrificed to idols; here it is shown what those public banquets of the pagans were and how greatly they differed from those of Christians. 540  
**ARTICLE III.** Other criticisms by Caecilius are examined, in which he censures Christians because they did not adorn their heads with flowers or their bodies with perfumes, reserved ointments for funerals, denied garlands to the dead, and did not cremate their bodies but buried them; here also concerning the custom of burying bodies and its antiquity. 542  
**ARTICLE IV.** That Christian morals were holy, while pagan morals were corrupt; why their discipline is called inferior by Caecilius; how greatly those same Christians excelled pagan philosophers in piety and learning; and that pagans and Christians were nevertheless friends and addressed one another by the name of brothers. 546  

**CHAPTER XIV.** Caecilius’s arguments by which he attempts to prove that his gods truly exist and that the religion of the pagans is consequently true are scrutinized. 550  

**ARTICLE I.** Caecilius’s first argument is explained, by which he attempts to prove that his gods are real from ancestral tradition and the most ancient worship of the gods—namely, Eleusinian Ceres, the Phrygian Mother or Cybele, Aesculapius of Epidaurus, Chaldean Bel, Syrian Astarte, Tauric Diana, and [Col. 1602] Gallic Mercury. 550  
**ARTICLE II.** How Octavius refutes Caecilius’s argument and shows both that the worship of the gods is not of such great antiquity and that the impious and superstitious traditions of the ancestors are not to be followed.
traditions, such as those concerning Scylla, the Chimera, the Hydra, and the Centaurs. 552

**CHAPTER XV.** The arguments by which the gods of the Gentiles are shown to be false are examined. 555

**ARTICLE I.** With what folly the Gentiles proclaimed that men had been made gods because of their virtuous merits or the benefits they had conferred upon other men. Ibid.

**ARTICLE II.** Minucius’ argument proving that the gods of the Gentiles are false from their birth, native country, death, and tombs—especially those of Dictaean Jupiter, Delphic Apollo, Pharian Isis, and Eleusinian Ceres—is examined. 558

**ARTICLE III.** Minucius’ argument proving that the gods of the Gentiles are fictitious from Alexander the Great’s letter to his mother—in which he testified that a secret concerning the gods had been disclosed to him and made Vulcan their chief—is examined; and Isis’ sistrum addressed to the swallow, and the empty tomb of Serapis or Osiris, are discussed. 562

**CHAPTER XVI.** How cogent are the other arguments by which Octavius proves against Caecilius that the gods of the Gentiles are false and nonexistent. 566

**ARTICLE I.** How clearly Octavius shows from the earliest origin of the gods that they were not gods but mere human beings; and first, indeed, their chief Saturn, a fugitive from Crete, who was received by Janus in Italy, where he taught men many things, especially how to mint coins and imprint letters, and after whom the country was named Saturnia. Ibid.

**ARTICLE II.** How perversely the pagans said that Saturn was born of heaven and earth; whence this opinion arose; whether Lactantius rightly refuted Minucius’ explanation of it; and how it may nevertheless be concluded from this that Saturn was not a god but a mere man. 568

**ARTICLE III.** By what weighty arguments Caecilius demonstrates the falsity of the divinity of Jupiter and of others who had been born of human beings, or who, at the lust and arbitrary will of others—as Romulus and Juba were—were proclaimed gods. 570

**CHAPTER XVII.** How weighty is another argument of Minucius against the gods of the Gentiles, drawn from their ridiculous forms and figures and from their unworthy and shameful deeds and crimes. 573

**ARTICLE I.** How absurdly the pagans represent Vulcan as lame, Apollo as beardless, Aesculapius as bearded and sometimes beardless; Neptune as having sea-green eyes, Minerva blue-gray eyes, Juno bovine eyes, Mercury winged feet, Pan hooves, Saturn fetters, and Janus two or four faces. Ibid.

**ARTICLE II.** With what madness the pagans celebrated Diana as high-girt and a huntress; Ephesian Diana as many-breasted, and Trivia as having three heads and many hands; Jupiter as sometimes bearded and sometimes beardless; Ammon with horns, Capitoline Jupiter bearing thunderbolts, Latiarian Jupiter drenched in blood, and Feretrian Jupiter unheard of—whose monstrous forms are as numerous as his names. 577

**ARTICLE III.** Another argument of the same weight is set forth, which Minucius drew from the unworthy and most shameful deeds of the gods: Erigone was said to have hanged herself with a noose; Castor and Pollux to die by turns; Aesculapius to have been struck by lightning; and Hercules to have been burned in the fires of Oeta. 582

**ARTICLE IV.** Why and how Minucius shows that the gods of the Gentiles are false by citing the books of Homer, read by everyone for instruction in life and morals, in which are celebrated Venus wounded, Mars bound and wounded, Jupiter rescued by Briareus and weeping for Sarpedon, and ensnared by the girdle of Venus; Hercules carrying away dung; Apollo pasturing Admetus’ cattle; Neptune rebuilding Laomedon’s walls; Jupiter’s thunderbolt forged together with Aeneas’ arms; the adultery of Mars and Venus; and Ganymede abducted by Jupiter; and how deservedly Homer was expelled by Plato from his commonwealth. 585

**CHAPTER XVIII.** Caecilius’ argument is examined, by which the existence of the gods of the Gentiles is proved on the ground that the Romans, through worshiping them, merited dominion over the entire world. 589

**ARTICLE I.** Caecilius’ argument is set forth. Ibid.

**ARTICLE II.** How Minucius refutes Caecilius’ argument and demonstrates that the Roman Empire was founded in no way upon the Romans’ religious devotion toward the gods, but upon impiety and crimes; and that the gods afforded those Romans no assistance in extending the boundaries of their realm—not even, first, the foreign and immigrant gods: Thracian Mars, Cretan Jupiter, Argive, Samian, and Punic Juno, Tauric Diana, or the Idaean Mother. 592

**ARTICLE III.** The native gods were of no assistance to the Romans in extending the boundaries of the empire: Romulus, enrolled among the gods through the perjury of Proculus; Picus, Tibernus, Pilumnus, Picumnus, Consus, Cloacina, Fear, Pallor, Fever, Disease, Acca Larentia, and Flora; with a discussion of the Larentalia rites and the Consual and Floral games. 595

**ARTICLE IV.** How false it is that the boundaries of the Roman Empire were enlarged by the gods because honors were granted and privileges given to the Vestals and priests; how great was the incontinence and criminality of both groups; and the adulteries and sacrileges committed within the temples themselves. [Col. 1603] 600

**ARTICLE V.** How Minucius shows that the Roman Empire was neither founded nor enlarged through piety toward the gods, since the Assyrians, Medes, Persians, Greeks, and Egyptians ruled before the Romans and before their pontiffs, Arval Brothers, Salii, Vestals, and augurs. 602

**CHAPTER XIX.** The arguments are examined by which Caecilius thought that the existence of the gods could be proved from miracles, oracles, auspices, auguries, dreams, and other predictions. 604

**ARTICLE I.** Whether Caecilius proved the existence of the gods from the miracles of Claudia Quinta, who was said to have drawn, with her girdle alone, the ship carrying the image of the Idaean Mother; of Castor and Pollux, who announced the victory won by the Romans over King Perseus; from Latinius’ dream, through which the games were restored; from the self-devotion of the Decii, through which the enemy was routed and defeated; and from the similar self-devotion of Curtius, through which a chasm in the earth is said to have been miraculously filled. Ibid.

**ARTICLE II.** The presence of the gods is not proved by Caecilius from oracles and the responses of seers, against which Minucius sets the examples of Amphiaraus, Tiresias, and Pythian Apollo, as well as the ambiguity and failure of oracles. 608

**ARTICLE III.** Caecilius’ argument is proposed, by which he attempts to prove that, because Sulpicius, Claudius, Junius, Flaminius, and Crassus scorned auspices and auguries, Roman armies were slaughtered and routed, the gods taking vengeance and thereby proving their existence. 610

**ARTICLE IV.** How Minucius utterly overturns the foregoing argument of Caecilius by other examples, those of Regulus, Mancinus, Paulus, and Julius Caesar; with a discussion of the *solistimum* and the *tripudium*. 612

**CHAPTER XX.** Minucius’ general reply is examined, by which he demonstrates that miracles, oracles, auspices, auguries, dreams, and other extraordinary events among the pagans proceeded not from the power of their gods but from the deceptions and illusions of demons. 615

**ARTICLE I.** What Minucius believed the nature of demons to be, and how rightly he said that they were known to poets and philosophers—above all to Plato and Socrates—and even more to magicians, and especially to Hostanes. Ibid.

**ARTICLE II.** Minucius’ arguments are set forth, by which he demonstrates why and how all those things which appeared to have been effected beyond the customary powers of nature were accomplished through the arts and illusions of demons; with a fuller discussion of dreams, various kinds of lots, and the frenzy of seers. 618

**ARTICLE III.** How manifestly Minucius demonstrated that demons, adjured by Christians and expelled from the bodies of possessed persons, openly declared themselves the authors of extraordinary effects among the pagans; and a refutation of those who babble that these things and the oracles of seers were produced solely by the devices and frauds of pagan priests. 622

**CHAPTER XXI.** On the images and statues of the gods, beneath which demons were believed to lurk and perform certain wonders, and which were impiously worshiped by the pagans. 625

**ARTICLE I.** With what impiety the pagans revered and adored the statues of their gods, beneath which demons dwelt, and sought and expected divine assistance from them, although they had sometimes been fashioned by human hands from the foulest vessel. Ibid.

**ARTICLE II.** On the fashioned, anointed, and crowned statue of Serapis which Caecilius adored; with a discussion of the Gentiles’ various rites for adoring statues and whether that statue of Serapis was a boundary-stone image. 628

**CHAPTER XXII.** Minucius’ argument is examined, by which he infers that the pagan gods do not exist from the very rites, mysteries, and festivals that the pagans celebrated in their honor. 631

**ARTICLE I.** On the rites and mysteries of Isis, in which she was represented as searching with Cynocephalus for her lost son or husband, and rejoicing when he was found; how ridiculous was the procession of these mysteries transmitted from the Egyptians to the Romans; and how cogent an argument against the gods of the Gentiles may be deduced from it. Ibid.

**ARTICLE II.** On the Eleusinian mysteries and the feast day celebrated in memory of Ceres searching for her daughter Proserpina, who had been abducted by Pluto; on the rites of Jupiter, and also those of Dindymenian Cybele—that is, Ceres, Rhea, or the Mother of the Gods—and of the castrated Attis, which were performed by the Galli, or castrated men. 635

**ARTICLE III.** On other superstitious and absurd rites of the Gentiles, in which many made libations of their own blood and offered supplication by wounds and the excision of their male organs, and led their gods begging from street to street; on the Luperci, who ran naked in the bitter winter, scourging those they met and striking them with hides; and on the capped Salii carrying ancient shields about. 638

**NOVATIAN’S BOOK ON THE TRINITY.** 885

**CHAPTER I.** Intending to discuss the Trinity, Novatian proposes from the rule of faith that we must first believe in God the Father and almighty Lord, the supremely perfect creator of all things. The works of creation are beautifully described. Human free will is affirmed. God’s mercy is shown in the punishment imposed upon man. The place of the souls of the pious and impious after death is established. 886

**CHAPTER II.** God is above all things, himself containing all things, immeasurable, eternal, greater than the human mind, inexpressible in speech, and more exalted than every height. 889

**CHAPTER III.** It is proved from the Holy Scriptures that God is the creator, lord, and parent of all things. 891

**CHAPTER IV.** He is also good, always like himself, immutable, one and alone, infinite; no proper name of his can be uttered; and he is incorruptible and immortal. 892

**CHAPTER V.** If we accept the descriptions in the sacred pages of certain instances of his wrath and indignation and hatred, these must nevertheless not be understood after the pattern of human vices. 894

**CHAPTER VI.** Although Scripture often adapts the divine countenance to human form, the measure of the divine majesty must nevertheless not be enclosed within the outlines of our body. 895

**CHAPTER VII.** Likewise, when God is called spirit, brightness, and light, God is not adequately explained by those designations. 897

**CHAPTER VIII.** The Church, therefore, knows and venerates this God; and the whole of nature—both invisible and visible, always and in its entirety—which his Providence rules and governs, bears witness to him. 898

**CHAPTER IX.** Furthermore, the same rule of truth teaches us that, after the Father, we must also believe in the Son of God, Jesus Christ our Lord and God, who was promised in the Old Testament and manifested in the New. 900

**CHAPTER X.** Jesus Christ is the Son of God and truly man, against the Docetic heretics, who denied that he had assumed true flesh. 901

**CHAPTER XI.** Indeed, Christ is not merely man but also God; just as he is the Son of Man, so too he is the Son of God. 903

**CHAPTER XII.** For he is proved to be God by the authority of the Scriptures of the Old Testament. 905

**CHAPTER XIII.** The same truth is established from the sacred writings of the New Covenant. 907

**CHAPTER XIV.** The author pursues the same argument. 909

**CHAPTER XV.** He again proves from the Gospel that Christ is God. 911

**CHAPTER XVI.** Once again he proves from the Gospel that Christ is God. 914

**CHAPTER XVII.** Likewise from Moses, at the beginning of the sacred writings. 917

**CHAPTER XVIII.** It is also proved from the fact that God is said to have been seen by Abraham; this cannot be understood of the Father, whom no one has ever seen, but of the Son in the appearance of an angel. 918

**CHAPTER XIX.** That God the Angel—namely, the Son of God—also appeared to Jacob. 922

**CHAPTER XX.** It is proved from the Scriptures that Christ was called an angel. Nevertheless, other passages of Holy Scripture show that he is also God. 925

**CHAPTER XXI.** The same divine majesty in Christ is again confirmed by other Scriptures. 927

**CHAPTER XXII.** He confirms the same divine majesty in Christ once again by other Scriptures. 929

**CHAPTER XXIII.** This is so manifest that some heretics thought him to be God the Father, while others thought that he was God alone, without [Col. 1607] flesh.

**CHAPTER XXIV.** They erred because, through a misunderstanding of Scripture, they thought that there was no difference between the Son of God and the Son of Man. 932

**CHAPTER XXV.** Nor does it follow that, because Christ died, God too must be understood to have died; for Scripture presents Christ not only as God but also as man. 934

**CHAPTER XXVI.** Against the Sabellians, however, he proves from the Scriptures that the Son is one and the Father another. 936

**CHAPTER XXVII.** He gives an excellent answer to the saying, “I and the Father are one,” which they advanced in their own support. 938

**CHAPTER XXVIII.** He proves that the saying, “He who sees me sees the Father also,” likewise does nothing to support the Sabellians. 940

**CHAPTER XXIX.** He next teaches that the authority of faith admonishes us, after believing in the Father and the Son, also to believe in the Holy Spirit, whose operations he enumerates from the Scriptures. 943

**CHAPTER XXX.** Finally, he explains how greatly the aforementioned heretics derived the origin of their error from observing that it was written, “There is one God”; and that, even if we call Christ God and the Father God, Scripture no more presents two gods than it presents two lords or two masters. 946

**CHAPTER XXXI.** But the Son of God is God, eternally begotten from God the Father and always existing in the Father; he is a second person distinct from the Father and does nothing without the Father’s will; he is also Lord and the Angel of the great counsel of God, to whom the Father’s divinity has been communicated through communion of substance. 949

**NOVATIAN’S LETTER ON JEWISH FOODS.** 953

**CHAPTER I.** Novatian, a Roman presbyter, while in his place of retirement during the Decian persecution and prompted by various letters from the brethren, published this work *On Jewish Foods* against the Jews, after his two preceding letters *On Circumcision* and *On the Sabbath*. Ibid.

**CHAPTER II.** First of all, he teaches that the Law is spiritual. Accordingly, since the first and only food of human beings had been the fruit of trees, and the use of meat was added later, the Law that subsequently followed—distinguishing foods, permitting certain animals as clean and prohibiting others as unclean—must be understood spiritually; especially since all things were pronounced very good, and even unclean animals were preserved for offspring in Noah’s ark. They could otherwise have been removed, if they ought to have been destroyed because of their uncleanness. 954

**CHAPTER III.** Unclean animals must therefore not be blamed, lest the blame be carried back to their Author. Rather, whenever an irrational animal is rejected for some reason, that very thing is all the more to be condemned in rational man. Human habits, acts, and wills are therefore depicted in animals. 956

**CHAPTER IV.** To these was added another reason why many kinds of food were taken away from the Jews: namely, to restrain the intemperance of a people destined to serve the one God. 959

**CHAPTER V.** There was indeed a certain period during which these shadows or figures were to be practiced; but after Christ, the end of the Law, came, the Apostle now says that all things are clean to the clean, and that the true and holy food is right faith and an undefiled conscience. Ibid.

**CHAPTER VI.** But because freedom in foods has been granted, it does not follow that luxury has been permitted or that self-restraint and fasting have been abolished; for these are especially fitting for the faithful, who are to pray to God and give thanks not only by day but also by night. 961

**NOVATIAN’S LETTER TO ST. CYPRIAN, WRITTEN IN THE NAME OF THE ROMAN CLERGY.**—He commends himself first to God and then also to the brethren. The faith of the Romans was praised by the Apostle. The crime of the *libellatici* is nearly equal to the crime of those who denied the faith. To receive the lapsed with excessive leniency is the height of cruelty. The confessors’ letters contributed greatly to preserving ecclesiastical discipline. Cyprian’s letters were also useful to the confessors. The peace of the Church and the appointment of a bishop must be awaited before peace is granted to the lapsed. Let the lapsed knock upon the Church’s doors, but let them not break them down. 963

**LETTER OF ST. CYPRIAN TO JUBAIANUS.**—In the year of Christ 256, shortly after the Seventh Council of Carthage, Cyprian wrote a long letter to Bishop Jubaianus. Jubaianus had consulted Cyprian concerning Baptism and had at the same time sent him a letter written not by himself but by another person against Cyprian’s position. Cyprian refutes this letter and most diligently gathers everything that he believed could support the defense of his case. He also sends Jubaianus a copy of his letter to the Numidians and to Quintus, and perhaps the decrees of the most recent synod. 1109

**LETTER OF ST. CYPRIAN TO POMPEIUS, AGAINST STEPHEN’S LETTER.**—The argument of this letter is stated by St. Augustine in Book V, chapter 23, *Against the Donatists*: “Cyprian,” he says, “also writes to Pompeius concerning this same matter; there he openly indicates that Stephen, whom we have learned was then bishop of the Roman Church, not only did not agree with him on these matters, but even wrote and issued instructions against him.”

Augustine speaks of it again in chapter 25: “I do not wish to reconsider what Cyprian poured forth in anger against Stephen, because there is no need. For precisely the same things are said there as have already been sufficiently discussed; and it is better to pass over matters that carried the danger of pernicious dissension. Stephen, moreover, had thought that those who attempted to overthrow the ancient custom concerning the reception of heretics should be excluded from communion. Cyprian, however, moved by the difficulty of the question itself and most abundantly endowed with the holy affections of charity, held that those who thought differently should remain in unity. Thus, although he expressed his indignation with greater agitation, yet still fraternally, the peace of Christ nevertheless prevailed in their hearts, so that amid such disagreement no evil of schism arose between them.”

Thus far Augustine. We have quoted him at greater length because these words serve as an antidote against those who attempt to use this controversy to obtain confirmation of their own schism from the Roman Pontiff. 1127

**LETTER OF ST. CYPRIAN TO MAGNUS.**—Magnus’ inquiry whether those coming from Novatian must be baptized again is answered. First, unity is established from the testimony of the Holy Scriptures. Legitimate succession in the chair of Peter is a sure mark of unity. The sacrament of unity is sanctioned not only by admonitions and examples but also by punishments imposed upon offenders. Schismatics, although they acknowledge the words of the Creed, deny the faith itself. Examples show how dangerously the Church’s peace is violated, even when the faith remains intact. Cyprian digresses to the Baptism of heretics and to their being able to give the Holy Spirit—[source breaks off].
he denies; he then replies concerning the baptism of the bedridden (*clinici*), concerning sprinkling, concerning the removal of uncleanness, and concerning the grace conferred in Baptism, which may either be diminished or increased by our own conduct.

Ibid. **PART TWO.—THE PRINCIPAL DISCUSSIONS BY RECENT AUTHORS ON THE SAME CONTROVERSY CONCERNING THE BAPTISM OF HERETICS.**

1217 **L. THOMASSIN’S DISSERTATION ON THE SYNODS ASSEMBLED UNDER POPE STEPHEN AT CARTHAGE, ROME, AND ELSEWHERE, IN THE MATTER OF THE BAPTISM OF HERETICS, IN THE YEARS OF CHRIST 256, 257, ETC.**

Ibid. **Synopsis.**

Ibid. **I.** The dispute between Pope Stephen and Cyprian. The calumny of the innovators against Stephen. A twofold controversy against them is to be resolved here.

1219 **II.** That Stephen did not err in accepting the baptism of all heretics is proved from Firmilian.

Ibid. **III.** The same is proved from the same author.

1220 **IV.** Further arguments from the same author.

Ibid. **V.** And still further arguments.

1221 **VI.** The same is demonstrated conclusively from Cyprian.

Ibid. **VII.** From the same author.

Ibid. **VIII.** From the Council of Carthage.

1222 **IX.** From Tertullian.

Ibid. **X.** Likewise from the Council of Arles.

1223 **XI.** From Eusebius.

Ibid. **XII.** From Stephen’s own words.

Ibid. **XIII.** Stephen’s argument against Cyprian is defended.

1224 **XIV.** Likewise, it is shown from Jerome that Stephen did not err.

Ibid. **XV.** Again, from the same author.

1225 **XVI.** Once more, from the same author.

1226 **XVII.** From the same author.

Ibid. **XVIII.** The same conclusion is established from Basil.

1227 **XIX.** From Siricius, Innocent, and Leo, Roman Pontiffs.

1228 **XX.** Likewise, from Augustine.

Ibid. **XXI.** How impious it is even to say that the whole Church ever erred in this matter.

1230 **XXII.** Likewise, from Vincent of Lérins.

Ibid. **XXIII.** From Hincmar of Rheims, and again from Augustine.

1231 **XXIV.** The second controversy is broached: whether, after Stephen’s decree, there was still a need for a plenary council, as Augustine appears to imply.

1232 **XXV.** On the contrary, from the same Augustine it is shown that even before the council Stephen’s authority was supreme, and Cyprian’s error was to be expiated, not excused.

Ibid. **XXVI.** From the same author: Cyprian is compared to Peter, who erred but listened to the colleague who corrected him.

1233 **XXVII.** From the same author: how impossible it is to excuse Cyprian, who was disobedient to apostolic tradition and to the universal Church.

Ibid. **XXVIII.** The same points are confirmed from Jerome, Vincent of Lérins, and Facundus of Hermiane.

1234 **XXIX.** Again, from Augustine.

Ibid. **XXX.** Stephen went no further than threats and finally acquiesced in a dispensation, and thus himself suspended the execution of his decree.

1235 **XXXI.** From Augustine: Cyprian ought to have yielded to the weightier authority.

1236 **XXXII.** Cyprian and the others who agreed with him perhaps came to their senses.

Ibid. **XXXIII.** Another path toward resolving this controversy is opened, based on the distinction between questions of faith and questions of custom.

1237 **XXXIV.** Various proofs of this distinction.

1238 **XXXV.** That this question was treated with moderation as pertaining to customs, not to faith, is proved first from Firmilian.

Ibid. **XXXVI.** Likewise from Cyprian.

1239 **XXXVII.** Likewise from Stephen, from the Synods of Arles and Nicaea, and from Optatus.

Ibid. **XXXVIII.** Likewise from Basil.

1240 **XXXIX.** From Amphilochius.

1241 **XL.** From Athanasius.

Ibid. **XLI.** From Epiphanius.

1242 **XLII.** From Cyril of Jerusalem.

Ibid. **XLIII.** From the Second Ecumenical Synod.

1243 **XLIV.** From the Synod in Trullo.

Ibid. **XLV.** From the consensus of the Greeks, especially Theodore the Studite.

Ibid. **XLVI.** From Gennadius.

1244 **XLVII.** From Augustine.

1245 **XLVIII.** Augustine frequently requires plenary councils for the regulation of customs.

Ibid. **XLIX.** By no means for questions of faith.

1247 **L.** Summary of this latter controversy.

1248 **DISSERTATION EXPLAINING STEPHEN’S TRUE [Col. 1611] POSITION CONCERNING THE RECEPTION OF HERETICS.**

1249 **I.** Stephen’s position was not without rational foundation.

Ibid. **II.** Whether Stephen accepted baptism conferred by heretics under any form whatsoever.

1251 **III.** Whether, when Stephen spoke of those baptized in the name of Jesus, he meant those baptized in the name of the Trinity.

1253 **IV.** Whether Stephen attributes greater power and efficacy than is proper to the baptism of heretics.

1255 **V.** Whether Stephen wished hands to be laid upon those returning from heresy so that the sacrament of confirmation might be conferred upon them.

1258 **VI.** Stephen is praised by the ancients as a defender of apostolic tradition, nor is he accused of error by anyone except those who rejected the baptism of every kind of heretic.

1265 **VII.** Whether Stephen excommunicated those who rebaptized. Whether he conducted himself too severely toward holy men.

1268 **PONTIFICAL AUTHORITY, SHARPLY ATTACKED BY CERTAIN MODERNS ON THE BASIS OF THE WELL-KNOWN ACTION OF CYPRIAN, BUT SOLIDLY VINDICATED BY THE WISEST THEOLOGIANS OF FRANCE: A HISTORICAL-DOGMATIC DISSERTATION.**

1273 **PREFACE.**

Ibid. **APPENDIX TO THE LIFE OF ST. STEPHEN, ROMAN PONTIFF AND MARTYR**, in which his manner of proceeding against St. Cyprian and the other rebaptizers is vindicated, by the testimonies of the ancients, from the calumnies of certain modern authors.

1295 **PART ONE OF THE HISTORICAL-DOGMATIC DISSERTATION.**

1313 **Argument.** The argument extracted from the conduct of St. Cyprian and pressed against the supreme and irreformable authority of the Roman Pontiff in defining controversies of faith is shown by the wisest theologians of France to be empty and groundless, and is utterly overthrown.

Ibid. **CHAPTER I.** According to the universal teaching of the theologians and writers of France, St. Cyprian judged that the question debated in his age concerning the rebaptism of heretics pertained not to faith but merely to discipline.

1314 **CHAPTER II.** According to the universal teaching of the theologians and writers of France, St. Cyprian knew perfectly well that the custom maintained by St. Stephen was not peculiar to the Roman Pontiff, but was at that time the universal custom of the Church and had been observed by all bishops from ancient times.

1320 **PART TWO OF THE DISSERTATION.**

1323 **Argument.**—Solid and unanswerable are the arguments advanced by the wisest theologians of France to defeat and overthrow the modern authors’ argument against pontifical inerrancy drawn from St. Cyprian.

Ibid. **CHAPTER I.** The considerations are set forth by which it is proved that Cyprian regarded the case concerning the baptism of heretics as a matter not of faith but merely of discipline.

1325 **Objections are answered.**

1337 **CHAPTER II.** The considerations are presented by which it is proved that St. Cyprian knew perfectly well that the custom defended by St. Stephen, the Roman Pontiff, was at that time the universal custom of the Church and had been observed by all bishops from ancient times.

1345 **DISSERTATIONS OF FR. M. MOLKENBUHR ON FIRMILIAN, BISHOP OF CAESAREA.**

1357 **PREFACE.**

Ibid. **OVERVIEW OF BOTH DISSERTATIONS ON FIRMILIAN.**

1361 **DISSERTATION I.**—Nos. 1, 2, 3. Two rules of criticism, taken from Dupin, are set forth by way of introduction.

Ibid. **Proposition I.**—Nos. 4–12. The letter circulated under Firmilian’s name appears to have been fabricated by a Latin author.

Ibid. **Proposition II.**—Nos. 13–17. At least St. Firmilian did [Col. 1612A] not compose it.

1365 **Nos. 18–77.** The letter itself is reproduced section by section and critically examined; at no. 41: Whether Pope St. Stephen declared valid baptism conferred under any form whatsoever.

1368 **Proposition III. Nos. 78–87.** It is more probable that a certain African Donatist fabricated the aforesaid letter after the fourth century, or else that some other heretic did so.

1401 **Proposition IV.**—Nos. 88–91. St. Firmilian published no books in writing.

1408 **DISSERTATION II.**—On the year of St. Firmilian’s death, in which Paul of Samosata was condemned at the most celebrated Synod of Antioch, at which the term *homoousion* (“consubstantial”) is also said to have been rejected.

**Proposition. Nos. 93–100.** Those events did not occur before the year 272.

Ibid. **ANNALS OF THE AFRICAN CHURCH IN THE AGE OF CYPRIAN.**

1417 **ST. PONTIUS, DEACON OF CARTHAGE.**

1477 **PROLEGOMENA.**

Ibid. **ARTICLE I. The history of Pontius’s life.**

Ibid. **ARTICLE II. His writings.**

1479 **ARTICLE III. On the Acts appended to Pontius’s history, and on the editorial care bestowed upon both works by learned men.**

1480 **THE LIFE AND PASSION OF ST. CYPRIAN, BY PONTIUS.**

1481 **CHAPTER I.** The author explains his reasons for writing. He states that the Acts of the Martyrs were formerly committed to writing with care.

Ibid. **CHAPTER II.** He recounts what Cyprian did after his baptism. The necessity of continence. Cyprian’s other virtues.

1483 **CHAPTER III.** He is quickly promoted to holy orders. He continually sets the saints before himself for imitation.

1484 **CHAPTER IV.** Cyprian is brought to the faith by Caecilius.

1485 **CHAPTER V.** While still a neophyte, he is compelled to assume the episcopate.

1486 **CHAPTER VI.** He shines forth in episcopal virtues.

1487 **CHAPTER VII.** Proscribed and demanded for the lion, he prudently withdraws.

Ibid. **CHAPTER VIII.** This occurred by the design of divine Providence.

1488 **CHAPTER IX.** While a dreadful plague is raging, by an effective address he induces his congregation to bring aid to those infected by it, even to pagans.

1489 **CHAPTER X.** He is driven into exile at Curubis.

1490 **CHAPTER XI.** He is visited by many. Consoled by a heavenly vision, he is divinely forewarned of the martyrdom he is to undergo and of its postponement.

1491 **CHAPTER XIII.** The author interprets this vision and proves that it was truthful.

1493 **CHAPTER XIV.** With persecution imminent, Cyprian refuses to flee and exhorts his people to martyrdom.

1494 **CHAPTER XV.** He is arrested. The congregation keeps watch through the night before the doors.

Ibid. **CHAPTER XVI.** The next day he is led before the proconsul’s tribunal.

1495 **CHAPTER XVII.** Sentence is pronounced, and he is beheaded.

1496 **THE PROCONSULAR ACTS OF ST. CYPRIAN.**

1497 **I.** St. Cyprian’s first confession before the proconsul Paternus. He refuses to betray the presbyters.

Ibid. **II.** He is sent into exile at Curubis. Recalled from there by Galerius, he is arrested.

1500 **III.** He is brought before the proconsul. His second confession.

1502 **IV.** Sentence is pronounced against him, and he is ordered to be beheaded.

1503 **V.** He is beheaded before a great crowd of people. His body is taken away by the faithful during the night and buried.

1504 **APPENDIX. THE PASSION OF ST. CYPRIAN.**

1505
[Col. 1611] END OF THE THIRD VOLUME.
